text: An article on Wednesday about JPMorgan Chase’s ability to withstand $20 billion in penalties to settle a barrage of government legal actions gave an incorrect comparison of the penalties paid by the bank and the payroll of the New York Yankees. That amount could finance the team’s payroll for 100 years, not for 10.
match_headline: JPMorgan Chase Nears a $2 Billion Deal in a Case Tied to Madoff

text: An article on Wednesday about a Texas woman kept on life support because she was pregnant misspelled the given name of a lawyer and bioethicist at Drexel University who discussed the ethics of the hospital’s decision. She is Katherine A. Taylor, not Katharine.
match_headline: Pregnant, and Forced to Stay on Life Support

text: An article on Dec. 19 about food stamp fraud misstated the percent of total loss because of trafficking, lying on applications and erroneous payments to recipients. It is 4.07 percent, not 4.7.
match_headline: Food Stamp Fraud, Rare but Troubling

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Asian carp invading the Great Lakes described a fluke incorrectly. It is a flatfish, not a flathead fish.
match_headline: Bracing for Carp in Great Lakes, but Debating Their Presence

text: An article on Wednesday about a new biography of Roger Ailes, chairman of Fox News Channel, misidentified the company’s parent company in some editions. It is 21st Century Fox, not News Corporation. The article also misidentified, in some copies, the organization that the television producer Randi Harrison was preparing to join while negotiating her salary with Mr. Ailes. It is NBC, not CNBC.
match_headline: Biography Casts Critical Light on Fox News Chief

text: An article on Wednesday about a lawmaker’s plan to introduce a bill altering the financial regulation known as the Volcker Rule misstated the loss that Zions Bank estimated it would need to post because of the rule. It is $387 million after taxes, not $387 million before taxes.
match_headline: House Financial Services Chairman to Seek Volcker Rule Change

text: An article on Wednesday about the solo show “The Surrender” at the Clurman Theater in Manhattan, starring Laura Campbell, misspelled the surname of the actress who originated the role when the show was presented in Madrid and Edinburgh. She is Isabelle Stoffel, not Stofell.
match_headline: A Rite of Sexual Submission: Bed to Book to Off Broadway

text: A critic’s notebook article on Monday about the Vienna Philharmonic’s New Year’s concerts, which were surrounded by turmoil last year because of new revelations about the orchestra’s ties to Nazi officials, misspelled part of the title of a 1992 book about the orchestra by Clemens Hellsberg that detailed some of the Nazi connections. It is “Demokratie der Könige” (“Democracy of Kings”), not “Democratie der Könige.”
match_headline: Waltzing Right Past History in Austria

text: A report on the Currents page last Thursday about wallpaper by John Derian for Studio Printworks misstated the price of the wallpaper. It is $45 a yard, not $45 a foot.
match_headline: Spiders That Went to Design School

text: An article on Dec. 26 about the romance of Prince Harry and Cressida Bonas and the press speculation about a possible engagement referred incorrectly to Sarah Ferguson. Although she lost the honorific Her Royal Highness after her divorce from Prince Andrew in 1996, she is still known formally as Sarah, Duchess of York; she is not a former duchess.
match_headline: Poised to Marry a Prince? She Will Not Be Spared

text: An article last Thursday about the ways in which several news anchors, most recently, Robin Roberts, have made public their sexual orientation misstated part of the name of the organization to which Thomas Roberts was giving a speech when he announced he was gay. It is the National Lesbian and Gay Journalists Association, not the National Gay and Lesbian Journalists Association.
match_headline: ‘In Other News’: TV Personalities’ Low-Key Coming Out

text: A report in the Browsing column last Thursday misspelled the given name of the owner of Electric Nest, a boutique in Brooklyn. She is Leana Zuniga, not Liana Zuniga.
match_headline: Out of the Shower, Onto the Runway

text: An article on Wednesday about the extreme cold across the nation misspelled the surname of the owner of Bishop’s Store in Maine. He is Ray Levesque, not Lebesque.
match_headline: Arctic Blast Proves Unwelcome Novelty, Especially Across South

text: Because of an editing error, a picture with the You’re the Boss column on Thursday was published in error. The photograph was of Todd Leeloy, general manager of OrangeSoda in American Fork, Utah, with some of his employees; it did not show Carlos and Constance Vega at the Port Jervis, N.Y., plant where their red sauce is made.

An article on Monday about the final Broadway performance of “Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark,” using information from a spokesman for the show, misstated the number of performances during its run. He says it was 1,248, not 1,268. (The error was repeated in headlines.)
match_headline: Low on Funds, ‘Spider-Man’ Dims Its Last Lights

text: Because of an editing error, a television review on Tuesday about the new CBS series “Intelligence” omitted a description of the character Riley, played by Meghan Ory. She is a Secret Service agent assigned to protect Gabriel Vaughn, the commando turned human computer who is the focus of the show.
match_headline: An Army of One, Enhanced by a Chip

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts to map the human brain gave outdated information about one of the consortiums that is part of the Human Connectome Project. While the Laboratory of Neuro Imaging used to be based at U.C.L.A., it moved to the University of Southern California last year.
match_headline: The Brain, in Exquisite Detail

text: An article on Friday about brain death and what the diagnosis means misstated the date on which Jahi McMath was declared brain-dead following complications from surgery at Children’s Hospital Oakland. She underwent surgery on Dec. 9 and was declared brain-dead on Dec. 12, not on Dec. 9.
match_headline: At Issue in 2 Wrenching Cases: What to Do After the Brain Dies

text: An article on Tuesday about a presentation by Israeli officials highlighting negative statements about Israel and Jews in official Palestinian Authority media and textbooks referred imprecisely to the online location of Hitler quotes associated with Palestinian schools. The quotes appeared on the Facebook pages of the schools; the schools do not have their own websites. The article also referred imprecisely to the online location of an allusion to the Balfour Declaration of 1917 and to the declaration itself. The declaration was alluded to disapprovingly on the Facebook page of the presidential guards of Mahmoud Abbas, the Palestinian Authority president, not on the guards’ website. And the declaration said the British government favored the establishment of a Jewish homeland in Palestine, but did not explicitly endorse the idea of a Jewish state.
match_headline: Israeli Official Points to ‘Incitement’ by Palestinians

text: An article on Dec. 30 about the appointment of Zachary W. Carter as Corporation Counsel described incorrectly a prosecution Mr. Carter undertook. The case involved the killing of Yankel Rosenbaum, which took place during the Crown Heights riots; it did not set them off.
match_headline: De Blasio Names City’s Top Lawyer, Appearing to Signal a Further Shift in Policy

text: An article on Thursday about a FIFA official saying that the 2022 World Cup in Qatar would likely be held between mid-November 2022 and mid-January 2023 erroneously included one country among those that competed against Qatar to host the event. England bid for the 2018 World Cup, which was awarded to Russia, not the 2022 tournament. (Qatar beat Australia, Japan, South Korea and the United States for the 2022 event.)
match_headline: Official Suggests 2022 Cup Won’t Be in Summer

text: A picture on Friday with a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column about plans by Nicholas Hytner, director of Britain’s National Theater, to form a theatrical production company when he leaves his current post next year was published in error, and the report misidentified the person shown. The picture showed Nick Starr, Mr. Hytner’s partner in the new enterprise, not Mr. Hytner.
match_headline: Director of Britain’s National Theater to Form New Company

text: A critic’s notebook article on Friday about unfinished paintings in the Metropolitan Museum of Art referred incorrectly to one, “Virgin and Child With Saints” by a Flemish artist known as the Ghent Painter. It has been on loan to the Met since 1999; it did not enter the museum’s collection in 1889.
match_headline: The Fascination of the Unfinished

text: An article on Dec. 29 about C. Ramon Contreras Orozco, a civil servant in a violent area of central Mexico whose effort to help his countrymen gain asylum across the border is testing American asylum policy, referred imprecisely to the outcome of claims by Mexicans seeking asylum in the United States. While most claims are never granted, that happens because they are either withdrawn, abandoned, rejected by a judge or otherwise moved into a different category of the claims process; the reason for the low approval rate is not because most asylum claims ultimately are rejected by a judge.
match_headline: A Civil Servant in Mexico Tests U.S. on Asylum

text: An article last Sunday about changes to Gov. Rick Perry’s staff during his final year in office misidentified the agency for which Phil Wilson, an aide who will head the Lower Colorado River Authority, currently works. It is the Texas Department of Transportation, not the Texas Department of Insurance.
match_headline: As Perry Exits, His Appointees Look for Havens

text: An essay last Sunday about a husband and wife’s trips to college football games this season misstated the day of the Sugar Bowl. It was Thursday, Jan. 2, not Friday, Jan. 3.
match_headline: A College Football Fan Is Born a Weekend at a Time

text: An obituary last Sunday about Dr. W. V. Cordice Jr., a surgeon who helped save the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s life in 1958, misstated his age in some copies. As the obituary correctly noted, Dr. Cordice was born on June 16, 1919; therefore he was 94, not 95. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Dr. W.V. Cordice Jr., 94, a Surgeon Who Helped Save Dr. King, Dies

text: A chart last Sunday in the special Oscars section listing The Times’s film critics choices for Academy Award nominations in several categories duplicated Manohla Dargis’s picks in the best adapted screenplay category under A. O. Scott’s name. Mr. Scott’s picks in the category are: Sofia Coppola for “The Bling Ring”; Abdellatif Kechiche and Ghalia Lacroix for “Blue Is the Warmest Color”; Richard Linklater, Julie Delpy and Ethan Hawke for “Before Midnight”; John Ridley for “12 Years a Slave”; and Joss Whedon for “Much Ado About Nothing.”
match_headline: ‘It’s Just How He Carries Himself’

text: An article last Sunday in the special Oscars section about Alfonso Cuarón, who directed “Gravity,” referred incorrectly to another of his films, “Great Expectations.” It was his third feature film — not his second, which was “A Little Princess.”
match_headline: A Circuitous Route to Outer Space

text: An article last Sunday about the Thomas Adès opera “The Tempest” misidentified the soprano who sang the part of Ariel at the Metropolitan Opera in 2012, in a new production by Robert Lepage. She is Audrey Luna — not Cynthia Sieden, who sang the role in London in 2004.
match_headline: Tomorrow’s Valhalla

text: An article on Dec. 29 about the cost for overseas movies to compete for an Oscar, misstated the cost to mount a high-end Oscar campaign for a foreign film. It is $100,000, not $200,000.
match_headline: Bring Your Film Here, Then Run

text: An article on Dec. 15 about the year in art misidentified the source of a complaint against the Brooklyn artist Lauren Clay, who planned to exhibit miniature versions of David Smith’s stainless-steel “Cubi” sculptures. It was VAGA, the art licensing and rights organization, not the Smith estate, that contacted Ms. Clay. The article also erroneously attributed a statement to VAGA. It did not state that Ms. Clay should have paid for permission to make her miniature Smiths.
match_headline: Rays of Light and Menacing Shadows

text: An article last Sunday about Liz Goldwyn, a Los Angeles filmmaker, artist and writer whose ties to Hollywood go back to her grandfather, the film mogul Samuel Goldwyn, described incorrectly her working relationship with the editor of Vogue magazine. Ms. Goldwyn was an early supporter of fashion designers whose work was later featured in Vogue; she was not a “talent spotter” for Anna Wintour. The article also referred incompletely to Ms. Goldwyn’s involvement in the documentary “Pretty Things.” Besides being one of the producers, she was also the director.
match_headline: Liz Goldwyn: Making a Name for Herself

text: A review last Sunday about three small electric cars misstated the electricity usage of the Fiat 500e. It traveled 3.6 miles per kilowatt-hour, not 3.6 kilowatt-hours per mile.
match_headline: Electric Service From $199 a Month

text: An article last Sunday about the Lizzie Borden Bed & Breakfast Museum in Fall River, Mass., misstated part of the title of a book about Lizzie Borden by two historians at the Fall River Historical Society. It is “Parallel Lives: A Social History of Lizzie A. Borden and Her Fall River” (not “The Social Life of”).
ref_headline: Parallel Lives: A Social History of Lizzie A. Borden and Her Fall River
match_headline: A Fresh Eye on Fall River, Mass.

text: An article on Dec. 29 misidentified the location of Mount Greylock Regional High School, where Cheryl Denelli Righter, an organ donor whose face was transplanted onto a recipient, went to school. It is in Williamstown, Mass., not North Adams.
match_headline: Still a Senior in High School, and a Five-Time Champion

text: An article on Dec. 29 about Abigail Van Buren, the Dear Abby columnist, misspelled the surname of the performing group whose songs Van Buren sang. The group was the Andrews Sisters, not Andrew.

An article last Monday about college sports teams that cleanse their histories after running afoul of the law or N.C.A.A. rules misstated the circumstances under which Reggie Bush lost the Heisman Trophy he had won in 2005. He gave back the award after he was found to have accepted improper benefits while in college; it was not “revoked.”
match_headline: O.J. Who? Rogues Vanish From Annals of Sport

text: An article on Thursday about a settlement between the asset management company BlackRock and the New York attorney general in which BlackRock agreed to stop surveying Wall Street analysts to get advance clues about their views on companies misstated, in some copies, the way in which BlackRock used the information it gathered. The information was fed into trading algorithms, not into logarithms. (An algorithm is a computer science term for a procedure to calculate an answer; a logarithm is a mathematical operation that simplifies certain complicated multiplication and division calculations.)
match_headline: BlackRock Agrees to End Wall Street Analysis Previews

text: An article on Thursday about the Duke University alumni pep band misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a member of the class of 1970 who played at the Dec. 19 game against U.C.L.A. at Madison Square Garden. He is Rick Tigner, not Tijner.
match_headline: Blue and White of Duke’s Pep Band Gets a Touch of Gray

text: A picture in the Observatory column on Tuesday with a report about the rarity of blue petunias was published in error. It showed a morning glory, not a blue petunia.
match_headline: Mutant Petunias Sing the Blues

text: An article on Thursday about documents linking members of Gov. Chris Christie’s staff to a traffic jam in Fort Lee, N.J., misspelled the surname of Mr. Christie’s campaign manager in some editions. He is Bill Stepien, not Stepian.
match_headline: Christie Faces Scandal on Traffic Jam Aides Ordered

text: An article on Saturday about the provisional identification of a guillotine thought to have been used to execute thousands of people during the Nazi era misstated the number of people who were beheaded under the Nazis. It is more than 5,000 — not about 3,000, which is the number executed by Johann Reichhart, public executioner in Munich in the Nazi era. The article also misspelled Mr. Reichhart’s surname as Reichart.
match_headline: A Guillotine in Storage Bears Signs of a Role in Silencing Nazis’ Critics

text: An article on Wednesday about a settlement in the case of Martin H. Tankleff, a Long Island man who served 17 years in prison before a state appeals court vacated his conviction misstated the details of the confession used in the murder case. A confession was partly written by a detective and attributed to Mr. Tankleff; it was not written or signed by Mr. Tankleff.
match_headline: Long Island Man Gets $3.4 Million for 17 Years in Jail

text: An article on Friday about the improving fortunes of Dick Clark Productions as networks increasingly covet event programming gave an outdated reference from Nielsen to the ratings for the most recent broadcast of “New Year’s Rockin’ Eve,” a Dick Clark property. The ratings increased 2.7 percent compared with last year’s show. They did not decline slightly.
match_headline: Awards Shows Help Clark Productions Bounce Back

text: An article on Saturday about the public relations challenge facing Target after a data breach involving tens of millions of customers misstated the charge to which Michael R. Milken, once a client of Marina Ein, who commented on handling such crises, pleaded guilty. It was securities fraud, not insider trading.
match_headline: To Regain Trust, Target Must Do More, Crisis Experts Say

text: An article on Monday about an audio innovation by the band NightBus, using information from the band’s record label, misspelled the surname of one of its members. She is Hannah Melbourn, not Melbourne.
match_headline: Dance Band Experiments With ‘Three-Way Stereo’

text: An article on Saturday about the expulsion from Harvard Law School of Mathew Martoma, a former SAC Capital Advisors’ employee now on trial for insider trading, gave an incorrect spelling from court documents for his original given name. He was Ajai, not Ajay.
match_headline: In Insider Case, Harvard Classmates on Different Sides of the Court

text: An article on Monday about NBCUniversal News Group’s partnership with a video clip start-up rendered part of the name of the start-up incorrectly in some copies. It is NowThis News, not Now This News.
match_headline: NBC’s News Unit Teams With Video Start-Up NowThis News

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Jan. 6 about a $20 million pledge to Jazz at Lincoln Center from Robert J. Appel, using information from a news release, erroneously attributed a distinction to the gift. SFJAZZ Center received a $25 million gift from an individual donor, thus Mr. Appel’s is not the largest single private contribution to date in support of jazz.
match_headline: $20 Million Donation for Jazz at Lincoln Center

text: A report in the Weekend Miser column on Jan. 3 about “fiddle sermons” gave an outdated name for the museum where they are being presented by Peter Schumann. It is now the Queens Museum, no longer the Queens Museum of Art.
match_headline: A Season’s Worth of Cheap Thrills

text: An obituary on Thursday about Anna E. Crouse, who helped establish the TKTS booth to provide affordable tickets to Broadway theaters, referred incorrectly to her mother, Pauline Ives. She was the first wife of the novelist and scholar John Erskine, not the second.
match_headline: Anna E. Crouse, 97, Dies; Championed Discount Tickets for Broadway

text: An article on Tuesday about President Obama’s struggle to prevent Senate Democrats from backing a bill that could thwart his diplomatic efforts with Iran referred incorrectly to Mr. Obama’s threatened veto of the legislation. If he vetoes the bill, it will be the third veto of his presidency, not the first. (He vetoed the Interstate Recognition of Notarizations Act of 2010 and a Continuing Appropriations bill in 2009.)
match_headline: Obama Fights a Push to Add Iran Sanctions

text: An article on Saturday about the release of further documents related to the lane closings in Fort Lee, N.J, misstated the circumstances under which David Wildstein was employed by the Port Authority. Mr. Wildstein, who ordered the closings, was hired by an official at the Port Authority, not appointed by Gov. Chris Christie. The error was repeated in a picture caption with the article. And it was also repeated in an accompanying article about the political nature of the Port Authority and another one about the allies of the governor having referred to the mayor of Fort Lee as a “little Serbian.”
match_headline: Bridge Scandal Papers Point to Cover-Up by Chris Christie Allies

text: An article on Tuesday about philanthropic foundations’ committing $330 million to help Detroit avoid cuts to retirees’ pensions and to save the Detroit Institute of Arts’ collection misstated Darren Walker’s position at the Ford Foundation, one group contributing money. He is president, not director.
match_headline: Foundations Aim to Save Pensions in Detroit Crisis

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Wednesday about the crash of an American military helicopter on the coast of eastern England misstated the name of the village near the site of the crash. It is Salthouse, not Saltmarsh.
match_headline: U.S. Military Helicopter Crashes on Coast of England

text: An article on Tuesday about the United States government’s trillion-dollar spending plan misstated the level of funding in the bill for the National Institutes of Health relative to what the agency received after across-the-board spending cuts known as sequestration. The amount would be $1 billion more, not $1 million more.
match_headline: House and Senate Negotiators Agree on Spending Bill

text: An article on Monday about the chemical spill in West Virginia misstated the year and the circumstances of the Bhopal disaster in India. It was 1984, not 1985, and the deaths were caused by a release of gas, not by a giant explosion.
match_headline: Critics Say Spill Highlights Lax West Virginia Regulations

text: A critic’s notebook article on Tuesday about Globalfest at Webster Hall misidentified the nationality of a brass band that performed, Fanfare Ciocarlia. It is Romanian, not Serbian. The error also appeared in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: The Whole World Gets Into the Groove

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about a concert that will present the latest installment of John Zorn’s Masada project, part of the Newish Jewish Music Festival, misstated part of the title of another concert in the festival. It is “Havana Nagila,” not “Hava Nagila.”
match_headline: The Echoes of War, From One Century to the Next

text: An obituary in some copies on Jan. 5 and in some editions on Jan. 6 about Harvey K. Littleton, who helped found the so-called studio glass movement in the United States, misstated the year he founded the studio glass program at the University of Wisconsin at Madison. It was 1962, not 1963.
match_headline: Harvey K. Littleton, a Pioneer in the Art of Glass, Dies at 91

text: A column by Bill Keller on Monday, about Lisa Bonchek Adams’s fight with cancer, referred incorrectly to the number of children she has. It is three, not two.
match_headline: Heroic Measures

text: An article on Monday about the chain of events surrounding the closing of access lanes to the George Washington Bridge misstated the date of a firefighting drill conducted on the bridge. It began on Oct. 5, not on Oct. 9. And a picture caption with the article misstated, in some editions, the circumstances of David Wildstein’s employment at the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. Mr. Wildstein, who ordered the closings, was hired by the Port Authority, not appointed by Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey.
match_headline: A Bridge to Scandal: Behind the Fort Lee Ruse

text: An article on Jan. 8 about indictments in a large-scale defrauding of the Social Security disability system by retired New York police officers and firefighters misstated the given name of a former police officer accused of helping to run the scheme. He is John Minerva, not Joseph.
match_headline: Charges for 106 in Huge Fraud Over Disability

text: An article on Sunday about a likely presidential run by Egypt’s top military leader, Gen. Abdul-Fattah el-Sisi, misstated, in some editions, the days that voting on a constitutional referendum were to be held. The two-day vote took place on Tuesday and Wednesday; it did not begin on Monday.
match_headline: Presidential Run Likely for Egypt’s Top General

text: An article on Saturday about the rising waters of Lago Enriquillo in the Dominican Republic misidentified a crop grown near the lake. It is yuca, a root crop — not yucca, which is part of the agave family.
match_headline: Rising Tide Is a Mystery That Sinks Island Hopes

text: An article on Tuesday about the end of a decades-long court battle over the desegregation of school districts in Little Rock, Ark., misidentified the military unit that President Dwight D. Eisenhower sent to that city in 1957 to deal with the controversy. He mobilized federal troops, the 101st Airborne — not the National Guard. (He did, however, take control of guard troops on the scene.)
match_headline: With Ruling, Funds to Aid Desegregation in Arkansas Are Ended

text: An article on Wednesday about testimony in the insider trading trial of Mathew Martoma, formerly of SAC Capital Advisors, misstated, in some copies, the date of a bank deposit slip showing payment to the witness, Dr. Joel S. Ross, who admitted passing confidential data to Mr. Martoma. The slip was dated March 2007, not 2008.
match_headline: Traders of Tips Meet at Grand Central, and Eat the Evidence

text: An article on Monday about Darryl Middleton’s long career in European professional basketball leagues misstated the season Dominique Wilkins played for Panathinaikos in Greece. It was 1995-96, not 1996-97.
match_headline: The Basketball Player’s Guide to the (European) Galaxy

text: A report in the Observatory column on Tuesday about the diet of the ancient human ancestor known as Nutcracker Man referred incorrectly to C4 in some editions. It describes a method of photosynthesis; it is not an isotope of carbon.
match_headline: Nutcracker Man’s Secret: He Didn’t Crack Nuts

text: An article on Dec. 26 about the architectural preservationist Virginia Savage McAlester referred incompletely to the important role of Lakewood Bank in the revitalization of Swiss Avenue in Dallas. While the bank did not make mortgages on Swiss Avenue properties from the late 1950s until the early 1970s, it did authorize such lending starting around 1972.
match_headline: Virginia Savage McAlester: Leading the Ultimate House Tour

text: An article last Thursday about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s preference for New York designers referred incorrectly to the blue Corneliani suit that he bought at Rothmans in the spring of 2013 during his mayoral campaign. Mr. de Blasio wore it at his inauguration, but not on primary and election nights.
match_headline: The de Blasios: Dressed for (and by) New York

text: An article on Wednesday about President Obama’s shift from critic to defender of government surveillance misstated the month in 2007 when he gave a speech at the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars. It was in August, not in October.
match_headline: Obama’s Path From Critic to Overseer of Spying

text: An article last Friday about the release of the California budget misstated the length of time before the California State Teachers Retirement System could be depleted. It is 30 years, not 10.
match_headline: With Surplus in Hand, California Eyes Debt

text: An article on Wednesday about competition in the computer security market misstated the job title of Nir Zuk of Palo Alto Networks, a computer security company. He is founder and chief technology officer — not chief executive, a title that is held by Mark D. McLaughlin.
match_headline: Tech Security Upstarts Enter Fray

text: An article on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about renovations at Queens Plaza in Long Island City misstated the rent at a nearby residential high-rise called 27 on 27th. It is about $45 a square foot annually, not monthly.
match_headline: A Major Renovation on the Doorstep of Queens

text: An article on Wednesday about FirstEnergy’s agreement to work toward reduction of carbon emissions in response to pressure from shareholders described imprecisely the shareholder proposals that Allie Rutherford, a corporate governance executive at Ernst & Young, said were meeting with success. They are proposals involving environmental or social issues, not shareholder proposals over all.
match_headline: Under Investor Pressure, Utility to Study Emissions

text: An article on Wednesday about Prader-Willi syndrome, a disease characterized by insatiable appetite, misidentified methionine aminopeptidase 2, the substance inhibited by the drug beloranib. It is an enzyme, not a hormone. The article also misspelled the name of a protein found in low levels in the blood of people with the syndrome. It is brain-derived neurotrophic factor, not neurotropic.
match_headline: Seeking Clues to Obesity in Rare Hunger Disorder

text: An article on Wednesday about the Chicago Bulls’ recent transition from contending in the N.B.A. to rebuilding for future seasons misidentified a player the Bulls lost to free agency after the 2011-12 season. He is Ronnie Brewer, now of the Houston Rockets — not Corey Brewer, of the Minnesota Timberwolves.
match_headline: Bulls, Built to Win Now, Decide to Disassemble

text: An article on Monday about the Nets’ trip to London for an N.B.A. game on Thursday misidentified one of the teams they defeated in a five-game winning streak this month. Besides Oklahoma City, Atlanta, Golden State and Miami, they beat the Cleveland Cavaliers, not the Philadelphia 76ers.
match_headline: It’s Brooklyn, Basketball and Branding as Nets Head to London

text: An article on Friday about the execution of Dennis McGuire in Ohio misstated the year of the rape and murder for which he was convicted. It was 1989 — not 1994, which was the year Mr. McGuire was convicted.
match_headline: Ohio Execution Using Untested Drug Cocktail Renews the Debate Over Lethal Injections

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about Alicia Guillén, a mother who wants to help her teenager pursue educational opportunities despite living under threat of homelessness, misidentified the agency that is helping her look for an apartment. It is the Jewish Board of Family and Children’s Services, a beneficiary agency of UJA-Federation of New York, one of seven organizations supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund. UJA itself does not provide direct services.
match_headline: Dreaming a Dream for a Daughter Talented in Art

text: An article in some editions on Friday about a medical emergency that led to the wrongful arrest of a City University of New York professor on the Upper West Side of Manhattan misstated the location of the 20th Precinct station house. It is on West 82nd Street, not on West 83rd.
match_headline: Professors Detail Brutal Tangle With Police

text: A report in the N.F.L. roundup on Thursday about Ben Kotwica’s move from the Jets to the Washington Redskins misstated, in some copies, the length of time he served as the Jets’ assistant special-teams coach before taking over the unit in 2013. He held that position four years, not six.
match_headline: Giants Fire Two Longtime Assistants

text: Because of an editing error, a film review on Friday about the Japanese melodrama “Like Father, Like Son” referred incorrectly to the director, Hirokazu Kore-eda. He is Mr. Kore-eda, not Mr. Hirokazu.
match_headline: After Old Mistakes, Hard Choices Must Be Made

text: Because of a production error, the crossword puzzle in Friday’s print editions, by Ian Livengood, was published in error. The puzzle that should have been published in print on Friday, by Kevin G. Der, did appear online on Friday, however. The Livengood puzzle will be published online on Friday, Jan. 24, and the Der puzzle will appear in print that day.
match_headline: What This Puzzle Forms

text: An article last Sunday about the Modern Language Association’s considering a censure of Israel omitted part of the name of one pro-Israel group that criticized the academic association. It is the Israel on Campus Coalition, not the Israel Campus Coalition.
match_headline: Another Academic Group Considers Israel Censure

text: An article in some editions on Jan. 5 about Cheryl McCray, a bipolar woman who received money from an agency supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund to replace ruined furniture, misstated the name of her hometown. It is Brooksville, Fla., not Brooksfield.
match_headline: After Decades of Unexplained Mood Swings, a Quiet Place to Call Home

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about Polina Edmunds’s performance at the United States figure skating championships misstated, in some copies, her placement in the women’s short program. She finished second; she did not win.
match_headline: U.S. Figure Skating Team Awaits Difficult Winnowing

text: An article by The Associated Press in some editions last Sunday about Penn State’s hiring of James Franklin to be its football coach misidentified the division in which East Stroudsburg University, his alma mater, plays football. It is Division II, not Division III.
match_headline: Tunisian Constitution, Praised for Balance, Nears Passage

text: An article last Sunday about the glut of independent movies referred incompletely to the history of John Cassavetes’s “Woman Under the Influence” (1974) with the New York Film Festival. While the festival did indeed turn it down initially, it eventually accepted the film.
match_headline: As Indies Explode, an Appeal for Sanity

text: A chart on Jan. 5 in the special Oscars section listing The Times’s film critics choices for Academy Award nominations included “The Counselor” by Cormac McCarthy in the wrong category. It is an original screenplay, not an adapted screenplay.
match_headline: Modesty, With a Little Smoldering

text: An article last Sunday about the scarcity of one-bedroom apartments in new condominium developments omitted the name of one of the developers of Walker Tower. It was developed by the JDS Development Group and Property Markets Group, not just by JDS. The article also misstated the current number of units in the building. It is 47 after combinations, not 53.
match_headline: A Scarcity of New One-Bedrooms

text: An article last Sunday about Brandee Barker, a Silicon Valley image consultant, referred imprecisely to the relationship of Bill Campbell, an executive coach, to Ms. Barker. While she has consulted with him recently, he was not on her team when she was the head of public relations for Facebook.
match_headline: They Want Her on Their Side

text: An article last Sunday about D-Rev, a nonprofit organization that creates medical equipment for developing countries, misspelled the name of a country where the organization sent an associate to assess markets. It is Colombia, not Columbia.
match_headline: Light-Bulb Moments for a Nonprofit

text: Because of an editing error, the cover article last Sunday about 52 places to go in 2014 misstated the name of a festival in Varazdin, Croatia. It is the Spancir Festival, not Spanor.
match_headline: 52 Places to Go in 2014

text: An article on Wednesday about efforts to get Syrian rebels to attend a peace conference misstated the given name of the last Roman Catholic secretary of state to visit the Vatican before John Kerry, who met last week with Vatican officials about a Middle East peace agreement. He was Edmund S. Muskie, not Edward.
match_headline: Kerry Urges Syrian Rebels to Go to Peace Meeting

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the World Briefing column on Thursday about a steady decrease in piracy omitted the source for a statement attributing the decrease to fewer pirate gangs operating off the coast of Somalia. The comments were by Pottengal Mukundan, the director of the International Maritime Bureau, which studied the issue.
match_headline: Global Piracy Hits Lowest Level Since 2007, Report Says

text: An article on Thursday about a cheating scandal involving 34 officers at Malmstrom Air Force Base who oversee the nation’s nuclear warheads misidentified, in some copies, the state in which the base is located. It is in Montana, not in North Dakota.
match_headline: Cheating Accusations Among Officers Overseeing Nuclear Arms

text: A picture caption on Friday for an article in Weekend about Ballet Next, the three-year-old company that recently unveiled a program of three works by the choreographer Brian Reeder, misstated the surname of the company’s director. As the article correctly noted, she is Michele Wiles, not Wines.
match_headline: 1 Choreographer, 3 Works, 2 Premieres, 14 Feet and 2 Pianos (but 1 Pianist)

text: An article on Thursday about the use of cellphones on elevated subway lines misidentified, in some editions, the agency that said it would consider lifting a ban on cellphone use during flights. The article also misstated part of the agency’s name in other editions. It is the Federal Communications Commission — not the Federal Aviation Administration or the Federal Communications Administration.
match_headline: Phones in Subway: On Elevated Lines, Hear the Future

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about a parody by Bruce Springsteen and Jimmy Fallon based on the closing of access lanes to the George Washington Bridge misidentified the venue for a benefit for victims of Hurricane Sandy where Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey and Mr. Springsteen embraced.  It was Rockefeller Center, not Radio City Music Hall.
match_headline: Christie and Springsteen: A Tale of Devotion, and a Very Public Snub

text: A picture credit on Monday with an article about NBC’s plans for a live performance of “Peter Pan” on Dec. 4 misstated the surname of the photographer. The picture, of the cast of the 1960 Broadway version, was taken by Art Selby, not Shelby.
match_headline: NBC Plans Live ‘Peter Pan’ for Next Holiday Season

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a speech by President Obama on the government’s collection of data misattributed a quotation about the issue. It was President Obama, in his speech — not Fred Cate, a professor at Indiana University — who said: “Corporations of all shapes and sizes track what you buy, store and analyze our data, and use it for commercial purposes. That’s how those targeted ads pop up on your computer and your smartphone periodically.”
match_headline: In Keeping Grip on Data Pipeline, Obama Does Little to Reassure Industry

text: An article on Friday about the charter school movement in Phoenix misidentified the program through which Julia Meyerson, the founder and executive director of Vista College Preparatory, visited 40 high-performing charter schools across the country. It is the Building Excellent Schools program; the Arizona Charter Schools Association was not involved.
match_headline: Arizona Hopes New Charter Schools Can Lift Poor Phoenix Area

text: An article on Friday about plans by Time Warner Inc. to move its headquarters to the Far West Side misstated, in some editions, the middle initial of the chairman of the Related Companies, which developed the sites of both the old and new headquarters of Time Warner. He is Stephen M. Ross, not Stephen J. The article also misstated, in some editions, the number of stories of an office tower on the Far West Side where Related signed a deal with Coach to be the anchor tenant. It will have 52 stories, not 47.
match_headline: Time Warner Is Planning a Move to Hudson Yards

text: An article in some editions on Monday about Maria Sharapova’s loss to Dominika Cibulkova at the Australian Open misattributed a quotation about the health of Sharapova. It was Sharapova herself — not Victoria Azarenka, a two-time defending champion — who said: “I think it’s a success in terms of that I’m back and that I’m healthy. That’s quite important. Otherwise I wouldn’t give myself a chance to play. So on that note, yeah, I have to look at the positives and see where I have come from in four or five months. I haven’t played a lot of tennis in those six months. So I certainly would have loved to play a little bit more before playing a Grand Slam.”
match_headline: Sharapova Follows Williams Out the Door

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Monday about the running games of the Seattle Seahawks and the San Francisco 49ers in Sunday’s N.F.C. championship game misidentified the team that was leading at halftime, 10-3. It was San Francisco, not Seattle.
match_headline: Lynch’s Third-Quarter Blast Breaks Pacific Northwest Logjam

text: An article on Saturday about a concert of hockey-related music at the Hockey Day in Canada festival misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a country music artist. He is Merle Haggard, not Marle.
match_headline: In Small Town in Canada, Celebrating Hockey With Songs

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about NASA’s budget and the future of some missions referred incorrectly to a proposed mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa and misstated the cost. The spacecraft would study the moon through repeated flybys, not enter orbit around Europa, and its estimated cost would be $2 billion, not $5 billion.
match_headline: The Final Frontier’s Financial Limits

text: An article on Tuesday about the lack of crowd noise at the Super Bowl described incorrectly the system used to determine the site of the N.F.L. championship game 50 years ago. The site alternated between the Eastern Conference champion and the Western Conference champion; the team with the best record did not always host the championship game.
match_headline: Super Sunday, and the Crowd Goes, Um, Silent

text: An article on Jan. 15 about the likelihood that the Manhattan literary landmark Rizzoli Bookstore may have to move again because there are plans for its building on West 57th Street to be torn down misstated the time period during which René Lalique designed the windows at the base of the Coty building, which was next door to the bookstore’s original location. It is the early 20th century, not the 1860s.
match_headline: Bookstore May Have to Flee the Wrecking Ball, Again

text: An article on Jan. 10 about the New England Patriots’ ability to overcome injuries referred imprecisely to their offensive and defensive rankings. While they were third in total offense, 15th in total defense, and last in rushing yards allowed per game, those rankings were for the American Football Conference, not for the N.F.L.
match_headline: Patriots’ Response as Teammates Fall: Next!

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about plans for new video and CD releases of a 1992 concert at Madison Square Garden celebrating Bob Dylan misstated the name of a performer who took part. She is Nanci Griffith, not Nancy Griffiths.
match_headline: Excerpt: 'Rake'

text: An obituary on Jan. 15 about the longtime federal bankruptcy judge Burton R. Lifland rendered incorrectly the name of one of the companies whose cases he handled. It was Eastern Air Lines, not Eastern Airlines. The error also appeared in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Burton R. Lifland, Bankruptcy Judge in Big Cases, Dies at 84

text: A graphic last Thursday with an article about toilet repair reversed the labels for the GE silicone caulk and Jelmar’s calcium, lime and rust cleaner.
match_headline: Seizing the Throne

text: An article on Jan. 13 about local opposition to a casino in Saratoga Springs, N.Y., misidentified the sponsor of horse races held in the city in 1863. The races were sponsored by John Morrissey — not by John Hunter and William R. Travers. (Mr. Travers and Mr. Hunter were involved in races in 1864.)
match_headline: Upstate, Opposition to a Casino Is a Surprise

text: An article on Thursday about an American manufacturer’s disadvantages in seeking a contract to supply parts for Cape Wind, America’s first major offshore wind farm, described incorrectly the relationship between that manufacturer, Mass Tank, and EEW, a German company. While Mass Tank included EEW as a partner on its bid, it did not bring the company to the Cape Wind project. EEW had already been seeking work on the project on its own.
match_headline: U.S. Offshore Wind Farm, Made in Europe

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about Japanese players who joined the Yankees misstated the year Hideki Irabu, a pitcher for the Yankees from 1997 to 1999, died. It was 2011, not 2001.
match_headline: A Japanese Thread in the Bronx

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Thursday about this week’s Billboard album chart, on which Bruce Springsteen’s “High Hopes” is No. 1, referred incorrectly to Mr. Springsteen’s ranking among the acts with the most No. 1 albums on Billboard’s chart. With 11, he is now alone in third place with one more than Elvis Presley, not tied with Presley for third place.
match_headline: Betting on the Handicappers, Not the Horses

text: An article on Friday about whether the United States is willing to discuss how to handle the criminal case against Edward J. Snowden misstated the position of Senator Charles E. Schumer of New York on the future of Mr. Snowden. Mr. Schumer has said Mr. Snowden should return to stand trial; he has not called on the United States to offer Mr. Snowden a plea bargain or some form of clemency.
match_headline: U.S. Willing to Hold Talks if Snowden Pleads Guilty

text: An article on Friday about a worsening of the decade-old crisis in Darfur, the western region of Sudan, misstated, in some copies, its estimated population and the United Nations’ estimates of the number of people killed or displaced by the conflict. The population is more than nine million, not six million; an estimated 300,000 people were killed, not 400,000; and nearly two million were displaced, not 2.5 million.
match_headline: Number of Darfur’s Displaced Surged in 2013

text: An article on Jan. 16 about the entanglement of the American Embassy School in New Delhi in a diplomatic spat between the United States and India over the arrest of an Indian consular official in New York misstated the reason that the diplomat, Devyani Khobragade, left the United States. She was expelled after India refused a State Department request that it waive immunity for her; she did not leave after refusing to settle the charges against her in exchange for a modest fine. (Although a potential plea was discussed, there was no such offer.)
match_headline: School in India Ensnared in U.S. Diplomatic Spat

text: A critic’s notebook article on Friday about a live re-creation of the 1974 album “No Other” by Gene Clark, a former member of the Byrds who died in 1991, included a reference to “a notorious Hollywood incident” in which Mr. Clark and David Geffen, who was the head of Elektra/Asylum Records “nearly came to blows at a restaurant.” (The album was issued on the Asylum label.) Although a biography of Mr. Clark and a documentary about him recount such an incident, Mr. Geffen says that in fact it never happened.
match_headline: An Ex-Byrd’s Album Is Given New Flight

text: Because of an editing error, an article by The Associated Press in some copies last Sunday about a federal judge in Montana who sent hundreds of offensive emails from his federal account misstated the year that the judge, Richard F. Cebull, was appointed to the bench. It was 2001, not 2011.
An article last Sunday about the funeral for the poet Amiri Baraka misspelled the surname of a poet who spoke at the service. She is Asha Bandele, not Bandale.
match_headline: Remembering Amiri Baraka With Politics and Poetry

text: An article last Sunday about the battle over New York’s carriage horse industry quoted incorrectly from comments by an activist who wants to see the trade banned. The activist, Edita Birnkrant, called the horses’ environment a “chaotic, unnatural environment,” not a “chaotic natural” one. The article also misspelled the surname of a former president of the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. He is Ed Sayres, not Sayers.
match_headline: Who Speaks for the Carriage Horses?

text: An obituary last Sunday about the sculptor Chryssa misstated the year that an article about her appeared in The New York Herald Tribune. It was 1966, not 1968. (The New York Herald Tribune ceased publication in 1966.)
match_headline: Chryssa, Artist Who Saw Neon’s Potential as a Medium, Dies at 79

text: An article last Sunday about the new film “Visitors,” which focuses on a gorilla named Triska, misattributed a quotation about the link between humans and animals. It was the anthropologist Loren Eiseley — not the movie’s director, Godfrey Reggio, who was quoting Mr. Eiseley — who said, “We, as human beings, have not seen ourselves until we have been seen through the eyes of another animal.”
match_headline: You Watch This Film as It Watches You

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about classical concerts this year that will commemorate the start of World War I in 1914, using information from the source of the photograph, misidentified the composer Alban Berg. He is shown third from the right, not third from the left.
match_headline: Great Music for the Great War

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Jan. 12 about the visual artist and composer R. Luke DuBois, who uses up-to-date technologies in his work, misstated his relationship with Cantaloupe Music. He has released work on the label, but he does not own it.
match_headline: Portraits From Clips and Bytes

text: An article last Sunday about automakers’ “design languages” misspelled the surname of BMW’s chief of design in some editions. He is Adrian van Hooydonk, not van Hooyndonk.
match_headline: If Your Car Could Talk, Would It Speak ‘Sensual Clarity’?

text: A review on Jan. 5 about “Furious Cool,” an account of the career of the comedian Richard Pryor by David Henry and Joe Henry, misstated the origin of the material in the book from Jennifer Lee Pryor. It was from pre-existing sources, particularly her memoir, “Tarnished Angel.” She was not interviewed for the book, and was not a “contributor.” The review also misstated her relationship with Richard Pryor at the time of his death in 2005. She was his wife, not a former wife. (Though their first marriage, in the early 1980s, ended in divorce, the couple remarried in 2001.)
match_headline: Man on Fire

text: A picture caption on Jan. 12 with an article about textile mills misstated the name of a mill shown in Fall River, Mass. It is Fall River Knitting Mills, not Northeast Knitting Mills. The article also referred incorrectly to the location of the dye house G.J. Littlewood and Son. It is the Philadelphia neighborhood of Manayunk; there is no Manayunk, Pa.
match_headline: Fruits of the Loom

text: An article on Jan. 12 about the singer Rosanne Cash misstated the name of a film about her father, Johnny Cash. It is “Walk the Line,” not “I Walk the Line.”
match_headline: Rosanne Cash Goes Home

text: An article on Jan. 12 about the snowboarder Shaun White misidentified the town in Colorado where White’s former sponsor, Red Bull, built a halfpipe for him. It is Silverton, not Breckenridge.
match_headline: The Flying Tomato Would Rather You Not Call Him That Anymore

text: An article last Sunday about why renters renovate their apartments described incorrectly the function of a banquette table in the kitchen that Kurt Franz renovated in his East Village walk-up. The table, which has a TV built into its surface, pivots up to provide access to the banquette (which doubles as a cot), not for TV viewing.
match_headline: Why Renters Renovate

text: An article last Sunday about arts spaces, restaurants, bars and shops below street level in London included outdated information about a tavern called Ruski’s in Kensington. After the section had gone to press, Ruski’s announced on its website that it was temporarily closed and moving to another location, scheduled to open in March.
match_headline: Underground London

text: An article last Monday about the construction of a replacement for the Tappan Zee Bridge misidentified a town at one end of the bridge. It is South Nyack, not West Nyack. The article also misstated the date for the opening of the bridge in 1955. It was Dec. 15, not Dec. 16.
match_headline: A Colossal Bridge Will Rise Across the Hudson

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the funeral of Myls Dobson, a 4-year-old who was beaten to death, misstated part of the name of the Harlem church where the service was held. It is First Corinthian Baptist Church, not First Corinthians Baptist Church. The error also appeared in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Letting Go of a 4-Year-Old Who Was Beaten and Burned

text: A picture credit on Wednesday with an obituary about John Dobson, who is credited with developing the first high-powered portable telescope that amateur astronomers could build inexpensively, misidentified the photographer who took the picture of Mr. Dobson delivering a lecture. The picture was taken by Mark Leet, not by Gerard Pardeilhan.
match_headline: John Dobson, an Inventive Itinerant Guide to Stargazing, Dies at 98

text: An article on Thursday about Dawn Zimmer, the mayor of Hoboken, N.J., who has accused the administration of Gov. Chris Christie of trying to link Hurricane Sandy aid to support for a development project, referred incorrectly to recent Hoboken mayors who were imprisoned. Two of Ms. Zimmer’s predecessors — Anthony Russo and Peter Cammarano III — went to prison, but David Roberts, who served between the two men, did not.
match_headline: In New Jersey, Claims Elevate Mayor’s Profile

text: An article on Dec. 15 about mounting calls in Iran to free two opposition leaders, Mir Hussein Moussavi and Mehdi Karroubi, who have been under house arrest since 2011, referred incorrectly to Joseph, the biblical figure to whom one reformist politician compared Mr. Moussavi. According to the Bible, Joseph, a former inmate, became the chief minister of the king of Egypt, not the king himself. A reader pointed out the error in an email shortly after the article was published; this correction was delayed because editors did not follow through on the complaint.
match_headline: Calls Mount to Free 2 Iranian Opposition Leaders

text: An article on Friday about a decision by the attorney general of Virginia not to defend the state’s ban on same-sex marriage misstated the name of the state legislature. It is the House of Delegates, not the House of Representatives.
match_headline: Virginia’s New Attorney General Opposes Ban on Gay Marriage

text: An article on Thursday about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s plans to build or preserve 200,000 affordable housing units over 10 years gave an outdated professional position for Marc Jahr. He left the New York City Housing Development Corporation, which finances affordable housing, this month; he is no longer its president.
match_headline: De Blasio Sets Ambitious Goal for Affordable Apartments

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about twin brothers who built a version of Yale’s online course catalog misstated the surname of one brother in some editions. As the article correctly noted, he is Harry Yu — not Xu, which is the surname of his twin, Peter.
match_headline: Yale Students Tangle With University Over Website

text: A critic’s notebook article on Friday about the Sundance Film Festival referred incorrectly in some instances to the director whose film “Listen Up Philip” was shown at the festival. The director, Alex Ross Perry, is Mr. Perry, not Mr. Ross. The article also misstated the year Aaron Swartz, the subject of a documentary shown at the festival, committed suicide. It was 2013, not 2012.
match_headline: Mirror, Mirror: Sundance Hits 30

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about Martin S. Bergmann, a psychoanalyst who portrayed a philosopher in the Woody Allen film “Crimes and Misdemeanors,” misstated the point at which Mr. Bergmann began reading Freud. It was while he was a student at the University of California, Berkeley — not while he was serving in the United States Army.
match_headline: Martin S. Bergmann, Psychoanalyst and an On-Screen Philosopher, Dies at 100

text: An article on Jan. 14 about the ways in which Pope Francis has reshaped the Vatican in his first year in the papacy referred imprecisely to the pink vestments worn at a Mass on Dec. 15 by Cardinal Raymond L. Burke, a conservative high-ranking American whose influence has been diluted. While pink is the traditional color for the third Sunday in Advent, it is not the main color for the Christmas season over all. (Purple is the main color for Advent, and white is the color for the rest of the Christmas season.)
match_headline: Pope With the Humble Touch Is Firm in Reshaping the Vatican

text: A picture caption on Jan. 15 with the continuation of an article about the early career of Carmen Fariña, the new schools chancellor for New York City, misstated the time frame for a photograph of Ms. Fariña in a classroom with students. It was the 1986-87 school year, not 1981. The caption also misstated the grade level of the students in some editions. They were third-graders, not fourth.
match_headline: New York Schools Chancellor Honed Blunt Style Over 40 Years

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 31 about the refusal of Chinese leaders to meet with Prime Minister Shinzo Abe of Japan to protest his visit to a contentious war shrine in Tokyo misspelled the name of the shrine in some editions. It is the Yasukuni shrine, not Yasakuni. The article also described incorrectly the shrine in some editions. While it pays tribute to some war criminals from the World War II era, it does not house their remains.
match_headline: No Meeting With Leader of Japan, Chinese Say

text: An article on Tuesday about the indictment of a North Carolina police officer in the shooting of a former Florida A & M football player misstated the officer’s given name in some editions. He is Randall Kerrick, not William.
match_headline: Second Grand Jury Indicts Officer in Shooting Death

text: An article on Jan. 20 about a meeting that the mayor of Hoboken, N.J., had with federal prosecutors after accusing Gov. Chris Christie’s administration of trying to link hurricane relief to support for a development project misstated, in some editions, the surname of a contributing reporter. She is Annie Correal, not Corral.
match_headline: U.S. Attorney Said to Meet With Hoboken Mayor

text: An article on Jan. 21 about preparations for the Syrian peace talks in Switzerland misstated, in some editions, the name of a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria that has received limited humanitarian aid during the Syrian crisis. The camp is Yarmouk, not Yamouk.
match_headline: Talks Over Syria Are Set to Begin, but Iran Is Not Invited

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about efforts by historians and others to learn more about executions by the Nazis in Eastern Europe misstated the relationship between the numbers of those killed in executions and those who died in the death camps. More people died in the executions than in Auschwitz-Birkenau, not all of the camps combined.
match_headline: Shedding Light on a Vast Toll of Jews Killed Away From the Death Camps

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the neutral setting of the Geneva peace talks and how it has emboldened opponents of the Syrian government, paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Adnan Hadad, an antigovernment activist. He said he hoped that his opponents — not the rebels — had changed their minds after coming face to face with how they were seen by the rest of the world. The article also misstated Mr. Hadad’s age and misidentified his radio station. He is 29, not 24, and his station is Radio Hara, not Radio al-Kul.
match_headline: At Neutral Site, Syrians Feel Free to Confront the Other Side

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the political team of Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey, which is at the heart of the growing scandal over the closing of lanes at the George Washington Bridge, misidentified the position that Bill Baroni held at the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. Mr. Baroni, who was appointed by Mr. Christie, was deputy executive director, not the executive director. The article also misstated the frequency of meetings by the governor’s political team. Members met regularly, not every morning.
match_headline: For Christie, Politics Team Kept a Focus on Two Races

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about difficulties facing Uber, the software company behind an app used to summon rides, misstated, in some editions, the timing of the activity shown. The picture, of Uber’s founder Travis Kalanick, shows him entering a cab in 2012, not last September.
match_headline: Rough Patch for Uber Service’s Challenge to Taxis

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the basketball star Tom Gola, using information from La Salle University, his alma mater, misstated the surname of one of his sisters, who survives him. She is Catherine Eisele, not Eile. The obituary also referred imprecisely to the 1954 N.C.A.A. championship game, in which La Salle defeated Bradley and Mr. Gola was named the most valuable player. It was the first N.C.A.A. title game to be nationally televised, not the first to be televised. (N.C.A.A. tournament games were first televised regionally in 1952.)
match_headline: Tom Gola, a Philadelphia Basketball Legend, Dies at 81

text: An article last Thursday about a couple’s 704-square-foot home referred incorrectly to the organisms found on the roof. They are plants, which makes them flora, not fauna.
match_headline: Freedom in 704 Square Feet

text: An article last week about an overhaul of the energy market referred incorrectly to the electric generators who are pushing for change. They are energy producers, not electric utilities, which are a separate and distinct type of company.
match_headline: With Strain on Electric Grid, a Push to Prioritize Conservation

text: An article in some editions on Jan. 23 about Russia’s selecting Yevgeny Plushenko for its only spot in men’s figure skating at the Sochi Olympics included a quotation from the NBC commentator Scott Hamilton that misstated Russia’s performance in figure skating at the Vancouver Olympics in 2010. Russia won two medals, a silver by Plushenko and a bronze by the ice dancing team of Oksana Domnina and Maxim Shabalin; Plushenko’s was not “the only figure skating medal they won.”
ref_headline: the only figure skating medal they won.
match_headline: Host’s Pride Rests on an Aging, and Aching, Star Skater

text: A picture caption in some editions last Friday with an article about the Rangers’ 2-1 loss to the St. Louis Blues misidentified, in some copies, the Blues player shown in front of the Rangers’ net on the winning goal. He is David Backes — not Kevin Shattenkirk, who scored the winning goal but was not shown in the picture.
match_headline: Rangers Enter Outdoor Series on Down Note

text: An article on Thursday about a crackdown on prostitution leading up to the Super Bowl misstated part of the name of the court where nearly 20 women were arraigned on Wednesday on prostitution charges. It is Midtown Community Court, not Manhattan Community Court.
match_headline: Jump in Prostitution Arrests in Super Bowl Week

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the naming of a task force to assist the German authorities in establishing the history of hundreds of artworks discovered in the Munich apartment of the son of a well-known Nazi-era art dealer gave an incorrect name from a news release for the museum at which one member of the panel, Shlomit Steinberg, works. It is the Israel Museum, not the European Art Israel Museum.
match_headline: Authorities Name the Rest of Task Force on Seized German Art

text: Because of an editing error, an entry on Thursday in the Scouting Report about the Hall of Innovation, a Nike sponsored Super Bowl event taking place through Sunday, misidentified the venue for the event. It is the Skylight at Moynihan Station, an event space in the James A. Farley Post Office; the event is not at Penn Station, which is across the street. (The entry correctly noted that the Skylight is at 360 West 33rd Street.)
match_headline: Get Game-Ready with Shopping Events Starting the Week of Jan. 30

text: A picture credit on Oct. 3 with an obituary about the actress Ruth Maleczech omitted the name of the photographer. While the picture of Ms. Maleczech and Frederick Neumann in a production of “Through the Leaves” was from the Mabou Mines archive, it was taken by Donna Gray. A reader pointed out the omission of the credit in an email this week.
match_headline: Ruth Maleczech, Beacon of Stage Avant-Garde, Dies at 74

text: An Editorial Observer on Wednesday about Pete Seeger’s appearance at the Farm Aid benefit last September incorrectly described that as his last major public performance. He appeared at Carnegie Hall with Arlo Guthrie on Nov. 30.
match_headline: Pete Seeger, Neil Young and the Importance of Letting Go

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the combative response of Kasim Reed, Atlanta’s mayor, to criticism of his administration’s handling of a winter storm misstated, in some editions, the day of the storm. It was Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: Questions Fly in Storm That Stopped Atlanta

text: An article on Wednesday about same-sex couples’ concerns over a judge’s ruling that a nonbiological parent listed on a birth certificate could not adopt the child misidentified the gender of Luki Anderson and Emily Wilbourne’s child. The couple have a daughter, not a son.
match_headline: N.Y. Judge Alarms Gay Parents by Finding Marriage Law Negates Need for Adoption

text: An article on Friday about Lenovo’s deals to buy both Motorola Mobility and IBM’s low-end server business misstated the role of the law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton. The firm represented Google on its sale of Motorola Mobility to Lenovo. It did not represent Lenovo in that transaction. (Cleary Gottlieb was Lenovo’s legal adviser during its acquisition of IBM’s low-end server business.)
match_headline: After Big Bet, Google Is to Sell Motorola Unit

text: An article on Friday about an exhibition of pop-up books by the Czech graphic artist and illustrator Vojtech Kubasta, at the Grolier Club in Manhattan, misspelled the name of his publishing company in one instance. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is Artia, not Atria.
match_headline: Wizard Who Made Art Jump Off the Page

text: An article last Sunday about the dangers posed by increased shipping of crude oil by rail omitted credit for a data analysis showing the quantity of oil spilled in rail shipments in 2013. It was done by McClatchy Newspapers, using data from the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration. It was not analyzed by the administration itself. In addition, an accompanying chart omitted a label in one section. The bar chart of oil freight rail cars should have indicated the numbers were in thousands. The article also described the Casselton spill incorrectly in relation to last year’s spillage. The 400,000 gallons spilled at Casselton was included in the overall 1.15 million gallons spilled; it was not excluded. And a credit for a picture of a fiery rail accident in Casselton, N.D., in December misidentified the photographer. The picture was taken by Dawn Faught, a local photographer — not by the son of a coffee shop owner on whose phone it appeared.
match_headline: Accidents Surge as Oil Industry Takes the Train

text: A report in the Slap Shot hockey notebook last Sunday about the possible reasons hockey lags behind the other major team sports in popularity in the United States misstated, in some editions, the day of the second outdoor N.H.L. game at Yankee Stadium last week. It was on Wednesday, not on Tuesday.
match_headline: A Blow to the N.H.L.’s Positive Buzz

text: An article last Sunday about Broadway producers weighing the potential of HD broadcasts in movie theaters and other venues misstated the given name of the male partner in BY Experience, which distributes such broadcasts. He is Robert Borchard-Young — not Richard.
match_headline: Off Off Off Broadway (at Your Multiplex)

text: A picture caption with the theater entry on the Week Ahead page last Sunday, using information from the theater company, misidentified the actress sitting with E. Jason Liebrecht. She is Hannah Kenah, not Lana Lesley.
match_headline: Singing, Dancing and Economics

text: An article on Jan. 19 about the composer Jason Robert Brown, who wrote the music and lyrics for a production of “The Bridges of Madison County,” using information from a publicist, misidentified the setting. The musical, scheduled to open on Broadway on Feb. 20, is set in Winterset, Iowa, circa 1965, not Somerset.
match_headline: You’ve Got Another Chance, Broadway

text: A picture caption on Jan. 12 with an article about Alaric Hunt, the winner of a detective-novel writing contest, misstated the relationship between the two adults shown with a young Hunt and his cousins. Janice Hill, his aunt, is pictured with a family friend; he is not her former husband. And the names of the cousins were reversed. Deme Hill is on the left, and Jade Reed is sitting next to her.
match_headline: The Murderer and the Manuscript

text: An article on Jan. 19 about OpAntiBully, a group of online antibullying activists, referred incorrectly to the group’s Twitter account. It was @OpAntiBullyInfo, not @OpAntiBully.
match_headline: The Online Avengers

text: An article on Jan. 19 about the value of meditation misidentified the technique used by scientists to study the effects of meditation on the brain’s white matter. It is diffusion tensor imaging, not functional magnetic resonance imaging.
match_headline: Breathing In vs. Spacing Out

text: A graphic last Sunday about adulterated olive oil sold as “extra virgin” contained several errors. Olives that are used in substandard oil are typically milled days, weeks or even months after being picked — not “within hours.” The graphic conflated two dubious practices that can be found in parts of the olive oil industry. Some unscrupulous producers mix olive oil with soybean or other cheap oils, while others mix vegetable oils with beta carotene and chlorophyll to produce fake olive oil; the two practices are not always combined. Olive oil bottled in Italy and sold in the United States may be labeled “packed in Italy” or “imported from Italy” — not “produced in Italy” — even if the oil does not come from Italy. (However, the source countries are supposed to be listed on the label.) A 2010 study by researchers at the Olive Center at the University of California, Davis, found that 69 percent of imported olive oil labeled “extra virgin” did not meet, in an expert taste and smell test, the standard for that label. The study suggested that the substandard samples had been oxidized; had been adulterated with cheaper refined olive oil; or were of poor quality because they were made from damaged or overripe olives, or olives that had been improperly stored or processed — or some combination of these flaws. It did not conclude that 69 percent of olive oil for sale in the United States was doctored. Finally, the graphic incorrectly cited Tom Mueller, who runs the blog Truth in Olive Oil, as the source of the information. While Mr. Mueller’s blog and other writings were consulted in preparation of the graphic, several of his findings were misinterpreted.
match_headline: Extra Virgin Suicide

text: An article last Sunday about Oaxen Krog & Slip in Stockholm misstated the given name of the chef and owner there. He is Magnus Ek, not Markus Ek.
match_headline: Restaurant Report: Oaxen Krog & Slip in Stockholm

text: An article on Wednesday about a special tribunal to help young women at risk, especially those forced into prostitution, misspelled the name of an Oakland-based nonprofit group that helps girls in crisis. It is Misssey, not Missey.
match_headline: A Court’s All-Hands Approach Aids Girls Most at Risk

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about the theft of a 1715 Stradivarius violin misstated the event after which the violin was stolen. It was a “Frankly Music” concert led by Frank Almond, the concertmaster of the Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra, not a symphony performance.
match_headline: A Violinist’s Triumph Is Ruined by Thieves

text: An article on Tuesday about an American-owned uranium enrichment plant’s struggle to stay in business misstated the extent to which Iran has been able to enrich uranium using centrifuges. It has enriched uranium to one part uranium 235 in five parts, not to one part in 20.
match_headline: Company Struggles to Keep U.S. in the Uranium Enrichment Game

text: An article on Oct. 4 about Bernie Ecclestone, who has wielded control over Formula One racing for decades, misstated the year of the Great Train Robbery, a notorious postwar heist in Britain for which a friend of Ecclestone’s was a getaway driver. It was 1963, not 1962. (A reader sent an email pointing out the error shortly after the article was published, but the email never reached The Times.)
match_headline: In Formula One, a Grip Not Easily Loosened

text: An article on Saturday about the contention of David Wildstein, a former Port Authority official, that “evidence exists” that Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey knew about the closing of lanes on the George Washington Bridge as it was happening misidentified, at one point, the person for whom a lawyer wrote a letter to a panel investigating the closings. The letter was written for Bill Stepien by Kevin H. Marino, his lawyer; it was not written for Mr. Marino.
match_headline: Christie Linked to Knowledge of Shut Lanes

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the latest conviction of Amanda Knox and her former boyfriend in the murder of her roommate in Perugia, Italy, in 2007 referred incorrectly to Ms. Knox’s potential extradition. It would be up to the United States — not Italy — to decide whether to extradite her.
match_headline: Amanda Knox Is Re-Convicted of Murder in Italy

text: An article on Saturday about reaction from environmental activists and oil industry supporters to a finding by the State Department that the Keystone XL pipeline would have little effect on the rate of development of tar sands oil understated the number of barrels of oil that would be sent through the pipeline from Alberta, Canada, to the Gulf Coast. It is 830,000 barrels a day, not just 830,000 barrels.
match_headline: Pipeline Opponents’ Hopes Now Rest Largely on Kerry

text: An article on Thursday about the aftermath of a storm that had hit the Deep South misspelled the given name of a baby who was delivered at home in Birmingham after an ambulance crashed en route to pick up the mother. She is Wynter Mariah Dobbins, not Winter.
match_headline: Atlanta Officials Gamble on Storm and Lose, and Others Pay the Price

text: An article on Friday about the growing demand for dual-language French programs in New York, reinforced by enthusiastic support from the French government, referred incorrectly to Guadeloupe and French Guiana, from which many immigrants in the city hail. They are overseas departments of France; they are not countries.
match_headline: A Big Advocate of French in New York’s Schools: France

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about a master class that Renée Fleming will give at the Juilliard School on Feb. 13 misspelled the given name of another soprano who will take part. She is Hyesang Park, not Hyesung. The report also referred incorrectly to Ms. Fleming’s appearance at the Williamstown Theater Festival this summer. While Chita Rivera will also appear at the festival, Ms. Fleming will not be sharing a stage with her.
match_headline: 50 Years Later, Beatles Steal Another Show

text: An article on Tuesday about the possible removal of the Picasso work “Le Tricorne” from the hallway of the Four Seasons restaurant on Park Avenue misstated the relationship of Samuel Bronfman, father of Phyllis Lambert, who acquired the work in 1957, to the Seagram liquor empire. Mr. Bronfman bought Joseph E. Seagram & Sons distillery in 1928, merged it into his Distillers Corporation and adopted the Seagram name. He did not found Seagram.
match_headline: At Four Seasons, Picasso Tapestry Hangs on the Edge of Eviction

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts by the United States and Europe to assemble an aid package for Ukraine misstated the middle initial of the Russian foreign minister in some editions. He is Sergey V. Lavrov, not Sergey P.
match_headline: U.S. and Europe Work on Aid Package for Ukraine

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about the Senate’s approval of a long-stalled farm bill misstated the vote of Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts. She voted against — not for — the legislation.
match_headline: Senate Passes Long-Stalled Farm Bill, With Clear Winners and Losers

text: An article in some editions last Thursday about new guidelines on handling accusations of sexual assault at Columbia University described incorrectly a committee that issued an open letter deploring the university’s previous approach. The group, the Student Affairs Committee, is the student caucus of the Columbia University Senate, which includes members of the administration and faculty. It is not a committee of the student government.
match_headline: Facing Complaints, Columbia’s President Calls for Transparency in Assault Inquiries

text: An article on Monday about the Seattle Seahawks’ 43-8 victory over the Denver Broncos in the Super Bowl referred incorrectly in some editions to Malcolm Smith’s 69-yard interception return for a touchdown for Seattle in the second quarter. It was the longest interception return for a touchdown in the Super Bowl since the 74-yarder by Tracy Porter of the New Orleans Saints four years ago; it is not the case that it “would be the longest in Super Bowl history if not for the 74-yarder by Tracy Porter.” (The longest is a 100-yard return by James Harrison of the Pittsburgh Steelers five years ago.)
ref_headline: would be the longest in Super Bowl history if not for the 74-yarder by Tracy Porter.
match_headline: Forget Forecast: Seahawks Pour It On in the Super Bowl
