text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the history of N.H.L. teams’ trading their captains misidentified the team Jarome Iginla was traded to last season and the team he signed with as a free agent. He was traded to the Pittsburgh Penguins and was signed by the Boston Bruins — not the other way around.
match_headline: Trading Captain Isn’t a Rarity in the N.H.L., and Usually Isn’t a Productive Move

text: An article on Tuesday about the success of Finnish goaltenders in the National Hockey League misidentified the position played by Esa Tikkanen, a player from Finland who came to the N.H.L. in the 1980s. He was a forward, not a defenseman.
match_headline: Finnish Soul Is Reflected in Goalies

text: An article on Tuesday about the high-speed broadband Internet service available in Chattanooga, Tenn., misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the co-founder of Banyan, a software start-up that moved there to take advantage of the fast connection. He is Toni Gemayel, not Gemeyal.
match_headline: Fast Internet Is Chattanooga’s New Locomotive

text: A picture with an article on Thursday about Google’s appointment of its most senior female executive to oversee YouTube was published in error. The picture showed Anne Wojcicki — not her sister Susan, who is a senior vice president for advertising and commerce at Google and is taking on the new responsibility.
match_headline: Google Appoints Its Most Senior Woman to Run YouTube

text: An article on Wednesday about a debate over the Museum of Modern Art’s proposal to allow free access to its sculpture garden, dropping the requirement of paying the admission fee to the museum, misidentified the original designers of the garden. They were John McAndrew and Alfred Barr Jr. — not Philip Goodwin and Edward Durell Stone, who designed the museum building that opened in 1939.
match_headline: MoMA’s Proposal for Sculpture Garden Pleases and Riles

text: Because of an editing error, the Carpetbagger column on Thursday, about the actor Matthew McConaughey, misstated the nickname of the character he plays in the HBO series “True Detective.” It is the Taxman, not the Accountant.
match_headline: Ex-King of Rom-Coms Finds Serious Success

text: An article on Wednesday about a study by the National Center for Arts Research at Southern Methodist University that found that federally supported arts programs attract people across the income spectrum, not just wealthy ones, referred imprecisely to a National Endowment for the Arts grant related to the work of the photographer Robert Mapplethorpe in citing grants from that agency that drew criticism from some members of Congress. It was made to the University of Pennsylvania’s Institute of Contemporary Arts in Philadelphia to support a touring exhibition of Mapplethorpe’s work, not to Mapplethorpe himself.
match_headline: N.E.A. Funds Benefit Both Rich and Poor, Study Finds

text: An article on Friday about penalties imposed by the United States on companies and individuals accused of evading sanctions against Iran misstated the amount of Iranian money impounded in foreign banks to which Iran will be allowed access under the temporary international agreement on its disputed nuclear program. It is $4.2 billion, not more than $6 billion.
match_headline: U.S. Issues Penalties Over Violations of Iran Sanctions

text: An article on Thursday about a visit to New York by two members of Pussy Riot, the Russian punk group, who were recently released from prison referred incorrectly to the timing of verdicts expected on Feb. 21 in a Moscow political trial in relation to the Olympic Games in Sochi, Russia. The date is a few days before the Olympics are to conclude, not after they are over.
match_headline: Pussy Riot Members Take Tour to New York

text: An article on Friday about a petition started by two Wellesley College students, asking that the college move indoors a sculpture that they described as “a source of apprehension, fear, and triggering thoughts regarding sexual assault for some members of our campus community,” referred incorrectly to the creation of the work, a statue of a nearly naked man. While the sculpture, “Sleepwalker” by Tony Matelli, was made for Mr. Matelli’s solo exhibition at Wellesley, it was not commissioned by the Davis Museum at the college.
ref_headline: a source of apprehension, fear, and triggering thoughts regarding sexual assault for some members of our campus community,
match_headline: At Wellesley, Debate Over a Statue in Briefs

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about the challenges facing Howard University contains several errors.
match_headline: Hard Times at Howard U.

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about the nation’s first Muslim fraternity misspells, in some instances, the surname of the founder of the chapter at the University of California, San Diego. He is Rumzi Khan, not Kahn.
match_headline: Fraternity Life, Islamic Style

text: An article on Jan. 26 about a new book that consists of the single word “Jew” printed six million times to signify the number of Jews killed during the Holocaust erroneously included one month among those whose dates match in the Hebrew and English calendars. While dates in February and April match, that is not the case for March.
match_headline: Holocaust Told in One Word, 6 Million Times

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about a nursing home fire that left a Quebec village stunned and grief-stricken referred incorrectly to the police force that employs Lt. Michel Brunet. It is the Quebec provincial police; there is no Quebec “national” police force.
match_headline: Stunned by Tragedy, a Village in Rural Quebec Turns Inward

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about controversy at the Lafayette Avenue Presbyterian Church over the departure of the interim pastor, the Rev. Carmen Mason-Browne, erroneously cited a survey in saying that 90 percent of the members believed she was a “good fit” for the church. There was confusion at the church over who was being evaluated on that question in the survey, Ms. Mason-Browne or her predecessor, so the survey should not have been used to assess Ms. Mason-Browne’s support.
match_headline: Passions in a Pastor’s Wake

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about a fan’s lawsuit against the National Football League over the apportioning of Super Bowl tickets for sale erroneously attributed a distinction to this year’s Super Bowl. It was the first outdoor Super Bowl to be held at a cold-weather site, not “the first championship game in N.F.L. history” to be held under such circumstances. (Before the Super Bowl began, in 1966, the N.F.L. held many championship games at cold-weather sites.)
ref_headline: the first championship game in N.F.L. history
match_headline: Lone Fan Tackles the N.F.L. Over Super Bowl Ticket Prices

text: An article last Sunday about the Beatles’ first visit to the United States 50 years ago misstated the number of concerts they performed when they arrived. It was three, not two — one at the Washington Coliseum and two at Carnegie Hall. The article also misstated part of the name of the Beatles’ style of haircut. It was known as a pudding basin cut — not pudding “basic.”
match_headline: Beatle Fans Hear Yesterday Again

text: An article last Sunday about the Russian stage director Dmitri Tcherniakov and his new production of Borodin’s “Prince Igor” at the Metropolitan Opera gave an outdated reference to the credentials of Gianandrea Noseda, who is conducting the opera. He is the former — not current — guest conductor of the Mariinsky Theater. (He held the post from 1997 to 2007.)
match_headline: A Perfectionist Does Opera His Way

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Israeli spy movies misstated the opening date in the United States for “Bethlehem,” a well-received thriller in Israel. It will open March 7, not Feb. 21.
match_headline: Navigating an Informant’s Shadow World

text: A picture caption on Jan. 26 with the cover article about Chinatowns in the United States misidentified the crabs shown at the Atlantic Times Square mall at Monterey Park, Calif. They are Canadian Dungeness crabs, not blue crabs.
match_headline: Chinatown Revisited

text: A picture credit on Jan. 26 with a review of “The Visionist,” by Rachel Urquhart, using information from the book’s jacket, misspelled the surname of the photographer who took the picture of the author. She is Sarah Shatz, not Schatz.
match_headline: Possession

text: A review on Jan. 26 about “The Guts,” by Roddy Doyle, misstated the last literary appearance of Jimmy Rabbitte, the novel’s hero, and his father, characters who have recurred in Doyle’s work. The two appeared in the 2007 story collection “The Deportees”; it is not the case that readers “haven’t seen them” since Doyle’s novel “The Van,” which was set in 1990 and published in 1991.
match_headline: Commitment

text: A review on Jan. 19 about “Duty: Memoirs of a Secretary at War,” by Robert M. Gates, misstated at one point the date of the United States military’s troop surge in Iraq. As noted elsewhere in the review, the surge was implemented in 2007; it was not “the 2008 surge.”
ref_headline: Duty: Memoirs of a Secretary at War,
match_headline: In Command

text: An article on Friday about David Wildstein, a former Port Authority official at the center of the scandal surrounding Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey and the closings of lanes leading to the George Washington Bridge, gave an incorrect political affiliation in some editions for Paul Aronsohn, the mayor of Ridgewood, N.J., and a frequent target of Wally Edge, the name Mr. Wildstein used when he had a blog about politics. Mr. Aronsohn is a Democrat, not a Republican.
match_headline: On Blog, an Ex-Christie Ally Showed Approach to Politics

text: An article on Jan. 30 about a government report that detailed auditors’ concerns on American aid to Afghanistan referred incorrectly to the report’s accusation that the State Department and the United States Agency for International Development were not forthright with Congress. While the two agencies did share risk assessments with Congressional staff members, the report said they did not provide related information that detailed the most troubling aspects of the aid program. The article also misidentified the parties who, according to the report, had taken less than 10 percent of the measures they could have to reduce the risk that the money would be lost to mismanagement or corruption. The report blamed Afghan ministries, not American officials.
match_headline: U.S. Aid to Afghans Flows On Despite Warnings of Misuse

text: An article on Friday about the expected ascension of Senator Mary L. Landrieu, Democrat of Louisiana, to chairwoman of the Senate Energy Committee, rendered incompletely the name of a former Louisiana Democratic senator who was the chairman or ranking member of the Senate Energy Committee from 1983 to 1997. He is J. Bennett Johnston Jr., not merely Bennett Johnston Jr.
match_headline: Energy Role Is Lifting Democrat in Louisiana

text: An article in some editions on Jan. 30 about Radio Row, home sports talk radio stations from around the world during Super Bowl week, misidentified the radio network for which Michael Harmon is a host. It is Fox Sports Radio, which is based Los Angeles, not Fox Sports Radio Los Angeles.
match_headline: Before Big Game, Stepping Into Media’s Big Top on Radio Row

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Rangers’ 2-1 loss to the Edmonton Oilers misstated, in some copies, the name of the Edmonton Oilers’ division. They are in the Pacific Division of the Western Conference, not the West Division.
match_headline: Streak Over, Rangers’ Focus Turns to Penguins, Then Sochi

text: An obituary on Friday about Ralph Kiner, the baseball star and longtime Mets broadcaster, misstated the year Hack Wilson, who like Mr. Kiner was known for his home-run power, hit 56 home runs for the Chicago Cubs. It was 1930, not 1932. The obituary, using information from the National Baseball Hall of Fame and the Mets, also misstated the names of two of Mr. Kiner’s daughters, who survive him, and omitted mention of one of his marriages. The daughters are Tracee Kiner Jansen, not Tracey Jansen, and Kimberlee Kiner, not Kimberlee Manzoni; his fourth marriage, to Ann Benisch, ended in divorce.
match_headline: Ralph Kiner, Slugger Who Became a Voice of the Mets, Dies at 91

text: An article on Monday about efforts by interest groups to shape hot-button political debates, like the campaign against increasing the minimum wage, misstated the time frame for a Democratic proposal to increase the minimum wage by nearly 40 percent to $10.10 per hour. It is within two and a half years, not by next year.
match_headline: Fight Over Minimum Wage Illustrates Web of Industry Ties

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Jan. 27 about an attack by Islamist militants in Egypt misidentified the government position held by Adly Mansour. He is the country’s interim president, not its interim vice president.
match_headline: Militants Down Egyptian Helicopter, Killing 5 Soldiers

text: An article on Saturday about the arrest of at least 61 people in Russia for unauthorized protests on the opening day of the Winter Olympics in Sochi misspelled the given name of the head of the Kabardine Congress, a social organization in the republic of Kabardino-Balkaria, where one of the protests took place. He is Aslan Byshto, not Alsan.
match_headline: Scores Detained in Russia Before Olympic Ceremony

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about efforts by Senator Pat Roberts, Republican of Kansas, to re-establish ties to his home state in light of efforts by the Tea Party to threaten establishment Republican candidates misidentified the Virginia community where Mr. Roberts lives with his wife in a home owned by the couple. As the article correctly noted, it is Alexandria, not Arlington.
match_headline: Lacking a House, a Senator Is Renewing His Ties in Kansas

text: An article on Friday about the insider trading conviction of Mathew Martoma misidentified, in some copies, the city in Connecticut that is home to SAC Capital Advisors, the hedge fund for which he worked. It is based in Stamford, not in Greenwich.
match_headline: Closing Arguments in Martoma Trial

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the Russian men’s hockey team’s more open policy with the news media at the Olympics misstated the day of Russia’s opening game against Slovenia. It will be Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: Glasnost at Glacial Pace: Russian Hockey Breaks Silence

text: A picture caption on Monday with a theater review “The Tribute Artist,” at 59E59 Theaters in Manhattan, misidentified an actress. She is Mary Bacon, not Keira Keeley, another member of the cast. The review misstated a name the character Jimmy uses when impersonating a fashion designer. It is Adriana, not Antonia.
match_headline: We Have the Stars; We Want the House

text: An article on Saturday about easing a terminal patient’s path to death misidentified the court in New Mexico that authorized doctors to provide lethal prescriptions for terminally ill patients. It was a district court, not the state’s Supreme Court.
match_headline: ‘Aid in Dying’ Movement Takes Hold in Some States

text: An article on Monday about Swiss voters’ narrow approval of a referendum that would reintroduce restrictions on immigration described incorrectly the newspaper Neue Zürcher Zeitung, which criticized the outcome in an editorial. The paper is considered conservative, not left-leaning.
match_headline: Swiss Voters Narrowly Approve Curbs on Immigration

text: An article on Tuesday about the South’s bracing for more winter weather misidentified the organization that had named the current storm Pax. It is the Weather Channel, not the National Weather Service.
match_headline: New Storm Has South Bracing for the Worst

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the arraignment of a woman charged with second-degree murder and first-degree assault in her 2-year-old daughter’s death misstated the gestational age at which the child was born. It was 26 weeks, not 26 weeks prematurely.
match_headline: Mother Pleads Not Guilty in Death of 2-Year-Old

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the expansion of McDonald’s into Vietnam misstated, in some editions, the location where fast-food companies typically seek to pay about $6 a square foot in rent. It is Ho Chi Minh City, not the United States.
match_headline: McDonald’s Opens in Vietnam, Bringing Big Mac to Fans of Banh Mi

text: Because of an editing error, the Wealth column on Saturday, about protecting bank and brokerage accounts from hackers, misstated, in one instance, the name of the investigations firm run by Ken Springer. As noted in another reference, it is Corporate Resolutions, not Office Resolutions.
match_headline: Keeping Swindlers Out of Your Bank and Brokerage Accounts

text: An article on Monday about MADE Fashion Week, a rival to the official New York Fashion Week, gave an incorrect title for Andrea Lim at Lexus, one of MADE’s sponsors. She is engagement marketing manager, not engagement marketing director.
match_headline: Rival Shows Vie for Relevancy in Fashion Week

text: An article on Thursday about the problems in figure skating judging since the sport overhauled its scoring system after a 2002 vote-trading scandal misstated the way the current system encourages risk taking. Skaters are still rewarded at least 70 percent of the value of a jump when they under-rotate, not when they fall.
match_headline: Despite Revamp, Figure Skating Gets Mixed Marks

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about baby boomers’ inheriting their parents’ estates misstated the name of the university where the photograph of a Japanese garden was taken. It is California State University, Long Beach — not the University of California, Long Beach.
match_headline: When Boomers Inherit, Complications May Follow

text: An obituary on Saturday about the political scientist Robert A. Dahl referred incorrectly to two of his survivors and misspelled the given name of one of them. Sara (not Sarah) Connor and Jane Thery are his stepdaughters, not his daughters. The obituary also mistakenly credited a concept to Professor Dahl. The political scientist David Easton — not Professor Dahl — wrote that politics involves “the authoritative allocation of values.”
match_headline: Robert A. Dahl Dies at 98; Yale Scholar Defined Politics and Power

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with the continuation of an obituary about the actress and diplomat Shirley Temple Black misidentified the actor shown with her in a scene from the movie “Stand Up and Cheer.” The actor was James Dunn, not Warner Baxter.
match_headline: Shirley Temple Black, Hollywood’s Biggest Little Star, Dies at 85

text: An article on Wednesday about the re-election campaigns of eight Republican governors who swept into office four years ago misstated the total number of governor’s races this year. There are 36, not 37.
match_headline: In Governors’ Races This Year, Lessons for 2016

text: An article on Tuesday about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s State of the City address misidentified the subjects of Mr. de Blasio’s praise regarding coming contract negotiations with municipal unions. He praised the city’s labor force, not its labor leaders.
match_headline: De Blasio Plans a Minimum Wage and City ID Cards

text: An article on Friday about a brain-dead Canadian woman who is being kept on life support because of her pregnancy misidentified the profession of Jeffrey P. Spike, who said he had some misgivings about a similar case he was once involved in. He is an ethics professor at a medical school in Houston; he is not a physician.
match_headline: Brain-Dead, a Canadian Woman Remains a Silent Partner Awaiting Birth

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Monday about dozens of arrests made in the investigation of a cockfighting ring misstated the distance of the farm in Plattekill, N.Y., where many of the roosters were being raised from New York City. It is about 70 miles, not 150.
match_headline: Eight Are Charged After a Cockfighting Crackdown That Finds 3,000 Caged Birds

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Saturday with an article about the increase in weather-related injuries misidentified the hospital where Zoila de Aguilar was shown being treated. It is St. Francis Hospital in Roslyn, N.Y., not Maimonides Medical Center in Brooklyn.
match_headline: Oops, There Goes Another Fall on the Ice

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about this summer’s Vail International Dance Festival referred imprecisely to the performance of Wendy Whalen’s “Restless Creature” there. While Ms. Whalen is returning to the festival, the performance of “Restless Creature” will be its first at Vail, not a return of that work.
match_headline: Vail Dance Festival Announces Lineup

text: An article on Thursday about Comcast’s pending acquisition of Time Warner Cable described the competition between the two cable companies incorrectly. They compete in no markets, not very few, and their merger will reduce the choice of cable operators for no consumers, not few.
match_headline: Investors Eye Comcast’s Bid for Time Warner Cable With Caution

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about mounting anxiety in India after a series of fatal tiger attacks misstated the average weight of the Bengal tiger. It is 500 pounds, not half a ton.
match_headline: Tiger Population Grows in India, as Does Fear After Attacks

text: An article on Thursday about the scheduling of a trial in the Boston Marathon bombing misspelled the surname of a lawyer representing Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, who is charged in the deadly attack. She is Judy Clarke, not Clark.
match_headline: Judge Sets Nov. 3 as Start of Trial for Boston Bombing Suspect

text: An article on Thursday about a recommendation by the American Dental Association that fluoride toothpaste be used for children under 2 gave an outdated name for the hospital whose dentist in chief said she endorsed the guidelines.  It is Boston Children’s Hospital, no longer Children’s Hospital Boston.
match_headline: Dental Group Advises Fluoride Toothpaste Before Age 2

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the Ukrainian oligarch Victor Pinchuk, a wealthy backer of Hillary Rodham Clinton, misstated the type of factory that was visited by Geoffrey R. Pyatt, the ambassador to Ukraine. It is a metallurgical mill, not a meteorological mill.
match_headline: Trade Dispute Centers on Ukrainian Executive With Ties to Clintons

text: An article on Feb. 5 about the expiration of a tax break for homeowners who received mortgage debt relief or went through a short sale, in which the house is sold for less than the mortgage balance, omitted an exception for some California homeowners. Because under state law borrowers are not personally liable for the unpaid balance on their loans in the event of a short sale, the Internal Revenue Service determined that homeowners in California would not have to count the difference as taxable income. The I.R.S. guidance applies only to California, and does not apply to principle reduction, which is taxable as income.
match_headline: Welcome Relief for Homeowners, Until the Tax Bill Arrives

text: An article on Thursday about Toyota’s recall of all 1.9 million of its newest-generation Prius vehicles omitted two countries in which the Prius is manufactured. It is made in Japan, China and Thailand, not exclusively in Japan.
match_headline: Toyota Recalls Newest Priuses Over Software

text: An obituary on Thursday about the poet and novelist Maggie Estep referred incompletely to the record companies that released her two spoken-word albums. “No More Mr. Nice Girl” was released by NuYo/Imago, not NuYo; “Love Is a Dog From Hell” was released by Mouth Almighty/Mercury, not Mercury.
match_headline: Maggie Estep, Who Brought Slam Poetry to TV, Dies at 50

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the illustrator Erik Blegvad misidentified the town in Vermont where he had a home for many years. It is Wardsboro, not West Wardsboro.
match_headline: Erik Blegvad, Children’s Book Artist With a Subversive Wit, Dies at 90

text: An article on Thursday about the overturning of part of Kentucky’s constitutional ban on same-sex marriage misidentified the court where same-sex couples filed a lawsuit in Missouri and misstated the lawsuit’s intent in one reference. The suit was filed in state court, not in federal court. And as the article later explained, the suit seeks recognition of marriages performed legally elsewhere; it does not challenge Missouri’s ban on same-sex marriage.
match_headline: Part of Kentucky Marriage Law Overturned

text: An article on Wednesday about food co-ops in low-income neighborhoods rendered incorrectly the brand of a chocolate bar sold at the Bushwick Food Co-op in Brooklyn. It is Equal Exchange, not equal-exchange.
match_headline: Food Co-ops in Gentrifying Areas Find They Aren’t to Every Taste

text: An article on Friday about Indonesia’s efforts to reinvigorate its military industry misstated the combined amount of money the government in 2012 injected into Indonesian Aerospace and the state-owned ship builder PAL Indonesia. It was 3 trillion rupiah (about $250 million), not 3 billion rupiah (about $250,000).
match_headline: Indonesian Arms Industry Seeks to Drum Up Business

text: An obituary on Feb. 11 about Paul Ash, the president of the Sam Ash chain of music stores, misstated the date of his death. He died on Feb. 5, not Feb. 4.
match_headline: Paul Ash, Who Made Music Store a Chain, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Feb. 6 about Arthur Rankin Jr., who produced “Rudolph, the Red-Nosed Reindeer” and other animated television shows, referred incorrectly to Marian Mansfield, who was married to Mr. Rankin’s father. She was his stepmother, not his mother. (Mr. Rankin’s mother was the former Mignon Klemm.) The obituary also referred incompletely to the writing of “Rudolph” and other Rankin/Bass productions. Mr. Rankin worked on the scripts and sketched the characters with Mr. Bass and others, notably the writer Romeo Muller — not on his own.
match_headline: Arthur Rankin, 89, Dies; His Puppet Animation Was a Holiday Hallmark

text: An article last Sunday about the financial struggles of Puerto Rico misidentified the governor under which laws meant to entice wealthy investors to the island were enacted. They were signed in 2012 by Gov. Luis Fortuño — not by the current governor, Alejandro García Padilla, who is aggressively promoting them.
match_headline: Economy and Crime Spur New Puerto Rican Exodus

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the effects of a Nigerian law that criminalizes homosexuality described incorrectly the person shown re-enacting the lashing of a man convicted under the law in northern Nigeria. He is a bailiff, not a judge.
match_headline: Nigeria Tries to ‘Sanitize’ Itself of Gays

text: An article last Sunday about the advance of chikungunya fever, a mosquito-borne virus, in the Caribbean referred incompletely to its possible spread beyond that region. While the virus has not yet reached the United States, both species of mosquitoes that carry it can be found in the country, and experts said it could be contracted in the United States in the warmer months. In addition, a picture caption misspelled, in some copies, part of the name of one of two species of mosquitoes that carry the virus. The species is Aedes aegypti, not Aedes aegpyti. (The other one is Aedes albopictus.)
match_headline: Virus Advances Through East Caribbean

text: An article last Sunday about Ramogi Huma, the president of the newly formed College Athletes Players Association who is seeking to organize football and basketball players, referred incorrectly to the rise of television revenue in college sports. Recent television contracts for the five largest conferences, the college football playoff and the postseason basketball tournaments will bring in $1.2 billion more annually than in previous years; the contracts do not bring in $1.2 billion each year. The article also misstated Huma’s involvement with Allen Sack, the founder of the Drake Group, which seeks educational reform in college athletics. While Huma did work on studies that documented scholarship shortfalls, he did not do so with Sack.
match_headline: As Northwestern Players Pursue Unionization, a Voice in the Wilderness Gains a Chorus

text: A picture last Sunday with an article about Bryan Cranston’s portrayal of Lyndon B. Johnson in the Broadway drama “All the Way” carried an erroneous credit. The photograph of Mr. Cranston in a production of the play at the American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Mass., was taken by Evgenia Eliseeva, not by Ursula Coyote/AMC.
match_headline: Presidential Chemistry

text: A review on Feb. 2 about the 2014 Cadillac CTS misstated the output of the TwinPower 4-cylinder engine in a competing model, the BMW 528i. It is 240 horsepower, not 300.
match_headline: The German Lessons Are Paying Off

text: An article last Sunday about Bernie Tiede, who was convicted in 1999 of killing Marjorie Nugent, referred incorrectly to Dr. Richard Pesikoff of the Baylor College of Medicine, who commented on the case. He is a clinical professor of psychiatry, not a clinical professor of psychology.
match_headline: Over 15 Years, a Town’s Stance on a Convict Shifts

text: An article on Feb. 2 about restaurants in Dublin misstated the name of the main street that runs through the Stoneybatter neighborhood. It is Manor Street, not Stoneybatter. The article also referred incorrectly to two restaurants, Chapter One in Dublin and Chapter One in Kent, England. There is no business connection between the two; the one in Kent is not an outpost of the one in Dublin.
match_headline: Dining in Dublin, From Boxty to Blaa

text: An article on Feb. 1 about criticism of the Argentine president, Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, over her absence from the political scene during Argentina’s currency crisis referred incorrectly to the subsidy she spoke about as the currency began to slide. It is for college-age students, not for schoolchildren.
match_headline: As Argentine Peso Falters, President Keeps a Low Profile

text: An article on Thursday about a genetic project involving the bones of King Richard III of England referred incorrectly to the sequencing procedure that British scientists plan to attempt. They will try to sequence his genome, his complete set of genetic information — not his genetic code, which is the set of rules that cells use to turn a sequence of DNA into specific proteins. (The error was repeated in the headline.) The article also referred incorrectly to the spinal deformity that scientists have confirmed the king suffered from. He had scoliosis, a lateral curvature of the spine; he was not hunchbacked, in which the spine is curved forward, although he has been described that way by Shakespeare and others. And the article also misidentified the religious order associated with the Greyfriars Friary in Leicester, where Richard’s body was originally buried. It was a Franciscan friary, not an Augustinian one.
match_headline: Scientists Hope to Sequence Genome of Richard III

text: An article last Monday about Tehran’s only Jewish hospital, Dr. Sapir Hospital and Charity Center, and its place in the history of Iran’s Jewish community rendered the name of an Iranian currency incorrectly. It is the toman, not the “to man.”
match_headline: Jewish Hospital a Fixture in Tehran

text: An obituary last Monday about Gerd Albrecht, a former principal conductor of the Czech Philharmonic Orchestra, referred imprecisely to a 1994 concert at the Vatican at which the orchestra was invited to perform, an invitation he declined on the orchestra’s behalf. While the concert was held three months after the Vatican formally recognized Israel, its primary purpose was to honor the memory of the victims of the Holocaust — not “to commemorate the Roman Catholic Church’s formal recognition of the State of Israel the year before.”
ref_headline: to commemorate the Roman Catholic Church’s formal recognition of the State of Israel the year before.
match_headline: Gerd Albrecht, German Conductor and Lightning Rod, Is Dead at 78

text: An obituary on Feb. 13 about Gabriel Axel, the director of the 1987 film “Babette’s Feast,” misstated the name of a journal in which an article that discussed that film was published in 2009. It was Gastronomica: The Journal of Food and Culture, the journal’s name at the time — not Gastronomica: The Journal of Critical Food Studies, its current name.
match_headline: Gabriel Axel Dies at 95; Directed ‘Babette’s Feast’

text: A map on Feb. 5 with the continuation of an article about the shadow cast over the Sochi Olympics by the conflicts between Islamic militants and Russian security forces in the Caucasus misspelled the name of the Georgian capital. It is Tbilisi, not Tblisi. And the article misspelled the surname of the chairman of the Human Rights Center in Nalchik, who said that Russia stirred resentment by continuing to treat the region as a colony to be conquered. He is Valery Khatazhukov, not Khatashukov.
match_headline: An Olympics in the Shadow of a War Zone

text: An article on Wednesday about Japan’s indecisiveness toward nuclear power nearly three years after the Fukushima meltdowns included an outdated reference in some editions to Shiro Asano, who said losses by antinuclear candidates in the Feb. 9 election for Tokyo governor did not suggest a consensus in favor of nuclear power. He is a retired professor of politics at Keio University, not a current one.
match_headline: Nuclear Issue in Limbo as Indecision Grips Japan

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the relationship between drought conditions and global warning paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Richard Seager, a climate scientist at Columbia University. He said that much of the Southwestern United States — not the West Coast — had been in drought for the past 15 years.
match_headline: Science Linking Drought to Global Warming Remains Matter of Dispute

text: An article on Saturday about discrepancies in attendance numbers on a snowy school day omitted, in some editions, the given name and title of an Education Department official who said that the attendance tracking system worked well for its size. She is Kathleen Grimm, the deputy schools chancellor for operations.
match_headline: After Storm, 100% Attendance Is Not 100% Accurate

text: An article on Dec. 23 about Infosys outsourcing operations in Poland transposed the name of an Infosys employee. He is Iván Guadalupe Luna Aparicio, not Iván Luna Aparicio Guadalupe. This correction was delayed because editors did not follow through after learning of the error.
match_headline: Midsize Cities in Poland Develop as Service Hubs for Outsourcing Industry

text: An article last Tuesday about Wichita State’s pursuit of an undefeated season in men’s college basketball omitted a team that was unbeaten in the regular season in the last 38 years. Besides Rutgers in 1976, Indiana State and Alcorn State in 1979, the University of Nevada-Las Vegas in 1991 and St. Joseph’s in 2004, Indiana was unbeaten in the regular season in 1976 and went on to win the N.C.A.A. title; it is not the case that none of those unbeaten teams won the national championship. The article also omitted an unbeaten team that reached the national semifinals in that time. Besides Rutgers and U.N.L.V., Indiana State did it, with Indiana State advancing to the final.
match_headline: Shockers Pursue Perfection One Victory at a Time

text: An entry in the What’s on Tuesday television highlights in some editions last Tuesday about “Butch Cassidy & the Sundance Kid,” on channels 13 and 49, misidentified the director. He is John Maggio — not Joe Maggio, who is the brother of John Maggio and also a director.
match_headline: What’s on Tuesday

text: An obituary on Friday about William Zeckendorf Jr., a developer whose projects helped refashion Manhattan neighborhoods from the Upper West Side to Union Square, referred incorrectly to the real estate activities of his sons, Arthur and William. They started their own development business; they did not take over his.
match_headline: William Zeckendorf Jr., 84, Dies; Developer Put Stamp on Skyline

text: An article on Feb. 9 about an exhibition in China that honors a Korean nationalist who murdered a Japanese politician in 1909 — a tribute that reflects an escalating feud between China and Japan — misstated the date that the Korean man, Ahn Jung-geun, was executed by the Japanese for his crime. It was March 26, 1910 — not Feb. 14, 1910, which was the date of his sentencing.
match_headline: China Exhibit, Part of an Anti-Japan Campaign, Reflects an Escalating Feud

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about the effect of a drought on agriculture in California’s Central Valley described incorrectly the condition of a tomato field shown in Helm and some other area farmland. The land is unplanted, not abandoned.
match_headline: California Seeing Brown Where Green Used to Be

text: An article on Thursday about a truck theft that ended in the death of a bus driver misstated his age in some editions. The driver, William Pena, was 49, not 43. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Truck Thief’s Getaway Try Ends in a Bus Driver’s Death

text: An article on Monday about the return of NBC’s “The Tonight Show” to New York from Los Angeles misidentified the late-night show’s original home in 1954. It was broadcast from the Hudson Theater on West 44th Street — not from StudioB at 30 Rockefeller Center, the building known as 30 Rock. (The show moved to StudioB in the late 1950s when the host Jack Paar began pretaping it.)
match_headline: ‘Tonight’ Show Returns to New York After Nearly 42 Years

text: An article on Saturday about the rivalry between the United States and Russia in men’s hockey referred incorrectly to the United States’ 1980 upset victory known as the Miracle on Ice. The Americans defeated the Soviet Union in a medal-round game at the Olympics, not in the semifinals. The article also misstated the number of goals Vladislav Tretiak allowed in the first period of that game. It was two, not one.
match_headline: In U.S.-Russia Hockey Game, Cold War Shifts to the Ice

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the men’s super-G ski race at the Sochi Olympics misstated Kjetil Jansrud’s margin of victory over Andrew Weibrecht. It was three-tenths of a second, not three-hundredths.
match_headline: Always Room at the Inn for Another Medal

text: A picture caption on Feb. 11 with an article about the debut of the Portuguese Podengo Pequeno breed at the Westminster Kennel Club dog show erroneously attributed an award to Annie, a basset hound. While she did win best female in her breed, she did not win best of breed, which went to a male dog.
match_headline: Looking Their Best for Westminster

text: An obituary on Saturday about the veteran major league infielder and manager Jim Fregosi misstated a statistic about the pitcher Nolan Ryan, for whom Mr. Fregosi was famously traded in 1971. He gave up 6.6 hits per nine innings in his career, not per nine hitters.
match_headline: Jim Fregosi, All-Star, Dies at 71; Angel Was Traded for Nolan Ryan

text: An obituary on Monday about the gallery owner Hudson misspelled the surname of one of the artists whose first shows he gave. She is Kathe Burkhart, not Burckhardt.
match_headline: Hudson, Gallerist and Nurturer of Artists, Dies at 63

text: An article on Feb. 11 about a debate over whether Israeli companies operating in West Bank settlements do more to help or hurt the Palestinians they employ referred imprecisely to the East Jerusalem neighborhood of Atarot, where Israel opened an industrial zone after the 1967 war. While the Palestinians and most of the world consider it to be occupied Palestinian territory, Atarot was a Jewish village until 1948, and Israel considers all of Jerusalem to be its capital.
match_headline: In West Bank Settlements, Israeli Jobs Are Double-Edged Sword

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the hiring of a prominent Iranian lawyer to represent Amir Hekmati, a former Marine incarcerated in Iran on spying charges, misidentified, in some editions, the person described by Hadi Ghaemi, a rights activist, as having useful Iranian intelligence and judicial contacts. He was referring to Mahmoud Alizadeh Tabatabaei, the lawyer, not to Mr. Hekmati himself.
match_headline: Former Marine in Tehran Jail Retains a Top Iranian Lawyer

text: An article on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about the expansion of a Mormon complex along two blocks of north-central Philadelphia misspelled the surname of the senior real estate manager for the church’s special projects department. He is Michael Marcheschi, not Marchesci.
match_headline: Mormon Church to Expand Development in Philadelphia

text: An article on Monday about Brian Krebs, a blogger on online security issues, gave an outdated job description for Tom Kellermann, a cybersecurity expert who said that Mr. Krebs needed a bodyguard. He is a managing director at Alvarez and Marsal, a turnaround firm, and is no longer the vice president for cybersecurity at Trend Micro.
match_headline: Reporting From the Web’s Underbelly

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with the Your Money Adviser column, about gender differences in premiums for long-term care insurance, misstated the surname of an official of the National Women’s Law Center who commented on the issue. As the column correctly noted, she is Marcia Greenberger, not Greenberg.
match_headline: Long-Term Care Insurance Priced by Gender

text: A chart in some editions on Sunday with an article about the United States’ 3-2 victory over Russia in men’s hockey at the Sochi Olympics misstated the order of the shooters in the eighth round of the shootout. Russia’s Ilya Kovalchuk went first, not T. J. Oshie of the United States.
match_headline: Drama, if Not Miracle, as U.S. Beats Russia

text: An article on Thursday about Facebook’s $16 billion acquisition of the mobile messaging service WhatsApp misstated the surname of a co-founder of WhatsApp in one reference. He is Brian Acton, not Aston.
match_headline: Facebook Enters $16 Billion Deal for WhatsApp

text: An article on Thursday about an election strategy by the nation’s labor leaders that would focus on higher pay for American workers as a way to revive the union movement referred incorrectly to a study by the Congressional Budget Office on raising the federal minimum wage to $10.10 an hour. The study showed that such an increase would lift 900,000 people — not that many workers — above the poverty line.
match_headline: Labor Leaders See Focus on Wages as Key to Union and Democratic Victories

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about the minutes from the most recent Federal Reserve meeting misstated the role of Narayana Kocherlakota at the Fed. As the article correctly noted, he is president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, not a Fed governor.
match_headline: Undeterred, Fed on Track to Temper Its Stimulus

text: A report in the Slap Shot hockey notebook article on Sunday about the lack of players from Massachusetts on the United States men’s hockey team at the Olympics misstated, in some editions, the given name of the defenseman who was born in Natick, Mass., but lists Colonia, N.J., as his hometown. He is John Carlson, not Jack.
match_headline: Olympians May Go From Sochi to N.H.L. Trading Block

text: An article on Friday about the founders of WhatsApp, the text messaging service acquired by Facebook, misstated, in some copies, the number of employees WhatsApp had last summer. It was 40, not 30. And the article misstated part of the name of the venture capital firm that invested $60 million in the service. It is Sequoia Capital, not Sequoia Ventures.
match_headline: Founders of an Anti-Facebook Are Won Over

text: A news analysis article on Friday about the financial benefits of the text messaging WhatsApp to its users misstated one requirement for using the app. It can be accessed through Wi-Fi; it does not require a mobile data plan. The article also misstated the cost of using WhatsApp. The app is free in its first year of use, and $1 a year thereafter. It does not cost $1 in the first year.
match_headline: Privacy Please: Tools to Shield Your Smartphone

text: A picture on Friday with an article about Comcast’s philanthropy and its clout in Washington was published in error. The photograph, part of a panel of portraits of people serving as lobbyists for Comcast, depicted former Representative Chip Pickering, Republican of Mississippi. Mr. Pickering is no longer registered as a lobbyist for Comcast, having left that role at the end of January.
match_headline: Comcast’s Web of Lobbying and Philanthropy

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the consequences of a global borrowing frenzy misidentified the building that was shown. The photograph was of a steel mill southeast of Moscow, not of a residential compound under construction in Wuhan, China.
match_headline: Global Bond Frenzy Raises Concerns

text: An article in some editions on Feb. 9 about John Youngaitis, a taxidermist in Queens, misstated the name of a monkey on display at the front of his shop. It is a golden lion tamarin, not a golden tamarind.
match_headline: A Taxidermist Is a Keeper of a Quiet Zoo

text: An obituary last Sunday about Marty Plissner, a longtime political director for CBS News, referred incorrectly to the origin of the phrase “too close to call.” It has been in use at least since 1933, when The New York Times used it in a sports column; it was not, as Mr. Plissner claimed, “invented at CBS” in the early 1960s, although that was when CBS News began using the phrase in its coverage of elections. (Mr. Plissner’s erroneous claim, as noted in the obituary, also appeared in one of William Safire’s “On Language” columns in The Times, in 1996.)
match_headline: Marty Plissner, 87, Is Dead; Led Political Coverage at CBS

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Andy Karl, who plays the lead in the new Broadway musical “Rocky,” misidentified the musical in which he met his wife, the actress Orfeh. It was “Saturday Night Fever,” not “Legally Blonde.” The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Take a Punch, Hope for a Hit

text: An article last Sunday about Anthony Elms, one of the curators of this year’s Whitney Biennial, which opens March 7, misspelled the surname of one of the artists Mr. Elms has chosen for the exhibition. He is Marc Fischer, not Fisher. The misspelling was repeated in an accompanying picture caption. The article also described incorrectly the way in which recordings made by the peace activist Malachi Ritscher will be presented in part of Mr. Fischer’s installation. They will be presented digitally; there will not be “piles of tapes.”
match_headline: Choose the Artists, Ignore the Critics

text: A review on Feb. 2 about “The Hybrid Tiger,” by Quanyu Huang, and “The Triple Package,” by Amy Chua and Jed Rubenfeld, two books about the levels of achievement by the country’s various cultural groups, referred incorrectly to the news anchor Diane Sawyer. While her birthplace, Barren County, Ky., is in a rural part of the state, it is not part of Appalachia; therefore she is not “Appalachian-born.”
match_headline: Secrets of Success

text: An article last Sunday about Comcast’s consumer pricing structure referred incorrectly to the amount of data that its Internet subscribers can download.  Comcast has been experimenting in some cities with a plan that includes 300 gigabytes of data a month, as well as the option to buy a higher data allowance for $10 per 50 gigabytes; it no longer has a cap of 250 gigabytes a month. (Comcast ended that cap in May 2012.)
match_headline: Comcast vs. the Cord Cutters

text: An article on Feb. 9 about marriage used an incorrect term for an experiment in which women sniff the unwashed T-shirts of men. Selecting the T-shirts of men with genes markedly different from their own is not a form of assortative mating, which is the choosing of similar genes, not different ones.
match_headline: Does a More Equal Marriage Mean Less Sex?

text: An article last Sunday about the Retromobile exhibition in Paris referred incorrectly to the record-setting African trip of Bernard and Claude Marreau. They drove to Algeria from the Cape of Good Hope, not from Cape Horn, which is in South America.
match_headline: At Retromobile in Paris, Early Record-Setters Roar Again

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the capture of Joaquín Guzmán Loera, the world’s most-wanted drug kingpin, misidentified, in some copies, the location where he appeared to have been hiding in 2012. It was in the Mexican state of Baja California Sur, not Baja, Calif.
match_headline: El Chapo, Most-Wanted Drug Lord, Is Captured in Mexico

text: An article on Thursday about disillusionment among Libyans on the eve of a vote to elect members of a constitutional assembly quoted incorrectly from a law passed by Libya’s General National Congress in December. It declared that Shariah law should be “the source of legislation,” not “above the constitution.”
match_headline: Disillusionment in Libya Over Vote on Charter Assembly

text: An article on Friday about trims to President Obama’s forthcoming budget plan misstated part of the name of a Republican group that last week criticized Democrats for “gutting” Medicare Advantage, a subsidized alternative to traditional Medicare. It is the National Republican Congressional Committee, not the National Republican Campaign Committee.
match_headline: Obama’s Budget Omits Trims to Social Security

text: An article in some editions Friday about Elijah Staley, a musician who performed in subway stations for more than 20 years and who died on Sunday, misstated the given name of a videographer who created a short profile of Mr. Staley. She is Jenny Schweitzer, not Jennifer.
match_headline: He Played Blues Concerts Where the Admission Price Was Subway Fare

text: An obituary on Thursday about Mike Stepovich, the last presidentially appointed governor of the Territory of Alaska, misidentified the country from which Mr. Stepovich’s father, Marko, emigrated to Alaska in the late 1890s. It was Montenegro, not Yugoslavia. (The nation of Yugoslavia did not exist at that time.)
match_headline: Mike Stepovich, Who Led Alaska to Statehood, Dies at 94

text: An article on Thursday about an announcement by the government of the Indian state of Tamil Nadu that seven prisoners who were convicted of plotting the 1991 assassination of Rajiv Gandhi, the former prime minister of India, would be freed referred incorrectly to the prisoners. The group includes six men and one woman, not seven men.
match_headline: Indian State to Free 7 Convicted in Rajiv Gandhi Assassination Plot

text: An article on Feb. 8 about a campaign by the British prime minister, David Cameron, to keep Scotland in the United Kingdom misstated the position of the tennis player Andy Murray on the September referendum in which the Scots will vote on whether to preserve the union. He has said he loves competing for Great Britain, but is not “known to favor remaining in the union.”
ref_headline: known to favor remaining in the union.
match_headline: Without Scotland, Premier Says, Britain Would Be Less ‘Great’

text: An article on Saturday about a decision by the Food and Drug Administration to order four tobacco products removed from the market misstated the number of new tobacco products that the agency has rejected since June 2013. It is 13, not 16.
match_headline: F.D.A. Orders 4 Bidi Cigarette Brands Removed From Shelves

text: An article on Friday about Ahmed Muhammed Haza al-Darbi, a Saudi detainee at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, using information from a military spokesman, misidentified the source of the pistachio-colored tie that Mr. Darbi wore at the court hearing in which he pleaded guilty to terrorism-related offenses involving a 2002 attack by Al Qaeda on a French-flagged oil tanker off the coast of Yemen. It was given to him by his civilian lawyer, Ramzi Kassem; Mr. Darbi did not select it from a bag of ties made available to detainees for such hearings.
match_headline: Guantánamo Detainee Pleads Guilty in 2002 Attack on Tanker Off Yemen

text: An article on Saturday about a federal inspector general’s report of continuing problems with disability claims at the Long Island Rail Road misstated his threat to recommend ending or severely cutting the disability program. The inspector general, Martin J. Dickman, was referring to the entire program run by the federal Railroad Retirement Board, not just to claims from the Long Island Rail Road. The article also rendered incorrectly the rail line’s name as the Long Island Railroad.
match_headline: Flaws Persist in L.I.R.R.’s Disability Claims, a Report Finds

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the ordering of a new trial for Adrian P. Thomas, who was convicted of killing his son after a confession fueled in part by false information from the police, misstated the professional affiliation of Dorothy Heyl, who filed a brief in the case. She is a lawyer with Milbank, Tweed, Hadley and McCloy, which represented the Innocence Network on a pro bono basis. She does not work for the Innocence Network.
match_headline: Police Coercion Cited in Order for Retrial in Upstate New York Killing

text: An obituary on Saturday about Garrick Utley, a former anchor and foreign correspondent for NBC News, referred imprecisely to the Persian Gulf war, which Mr. Utley covered. While the crisis began to unfold in 1990, American military involvement did not begin until 1991.
match_headline: Garrick Utley, a Mainstay at NBC News, Dies at 74

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about research that links Middle East Respiratory Syndrome to camels in Saudi Arabia misstated the date a report was published in the online journal mBio. It was Tuesday, not Tuesday, Feb. 18.
match_headline: Camels Linked to Spread of MERS Virus in People

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with an article about a woman who tends to 11 cemeteries on Staten Island misspelled her given name in some copies. As the articled correctly noted, she is Lynn Rogers, not Lynne.
match_headline: Uncovering Legacies in Staten Island’s Neglected Graveyards

text: An article on Tuesday about Target’s difficulties in expanding its retailing base into Canada misstated the company’s expected loss on its Canadian operations last year. It is $800 million to $900 million, not $8 billion to $9 billion.
match_headline: Target Push Into Canada Stumbles

text: An article in some editions on Monday about Dale Earnhardt Jr.’s victory in the Daytona 500 misidentified the driver who finished third. He is Brad Keselowski — not Jeff Gordon, who finished fourth. It also misidentified the social media platform on which Fox News erroneously reported that Jimmie Johnson had won the race because Fox Sports was replaying the 2013 race during a long rain delay. The report was on Facebook, not on Twitter. And the article misstated the highest position Danica Patrick reached in the race. She led two laps; she did not “run as high as seventh.”
match_headline: After a Long Rain Delay, Earnhardt Takes His Second Daytona Title

text: An article on Monday about the Nets’ signing Jason Collins, the first openly gay player in the N.B.A., misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a founding member of Athlete Ally, a nonprofit organization focused on ending homophobia and transphobia in sports. He is Brian Ellner, not Ellnor.
match_headline: Jason Collins, First Openly Gay N.B.A. Player, Signs With Nets and Appears in Game

text: Because of an editing error, the TV Watch column on Tuesday, about the debut of “Ronan Farrow Daily” on MSNBC, used an outdated title for a diplomat whom Mr. Farrow called an “old colleague of mine.” The diplomat, William J. Burns, is the deputy secretary of state, not an assistant secretary of state.
match_headline: Staying on Script, for Now

text: An article on Tuesday about the documentary “Particle Fever” misidentified the university from which the director, Mark Levinson, received a Ph.D. It is the University of California, Berkeley, not the University of Wisconsin.
match_headline: Coming Soon: Heroes of the Higgs

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Harold Ramis, the director, writer and actor, described incorrectly a scene from the movie “Caddyshack,” which he directed. In it, a clergyman is struck by lightning when he curses after missing a putt during the best golf game of his life, not when he thanks God.
match_headline: Harold Ramis, Director, Actor and Alchemist of Comedy, Dies at 69

text: An article on Sunday about the adoption of a resolution by the United Nations Security Council calling on the warring parties in Syria to allow the delivery of humanitarian aid erroneously attributed a distinction to the resolution in some editions. It is the second legally binding measure approved by the Security Council in the Syrian conflict, not the first. (That distinction belongs to a resolution adopted last fall that requires Syria to give up its chemical weapons.)
match_headline: U.N. Orders Both Sides in Syria to Allow Humanitarian Aid

text: An article on Friday about meat and poultry plants that are said to face a shortage of inspectors misidentified the source of a statistic showing an 11 percent vacancy rate for inspectors in the Raleigh, N.C., area. The information came from the Agriculture Department; it was not from data obtained under a Freedom of Information request by Food and Water Watch, a consumer advocacy group in Washington.
match_headline: American Meat Plants Said to Face Shortages of Inspectors

text: An article on Wednesday about a Food and Drug Administration hearing on a fertility method involving genetic material from three people misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the director of an office at the agency. She is Dr. Celia Witten, not Whitten.
match_headline: F.D.A. Weighs Fertility Method That Raises Ethical Questions

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Saturday about a study that found that books that win prestigious prizes draw not only more attention but also more negative online reader reviews misstated the title of a novel by Julian Barnes that was part of the study. It is “The Sense of an Ending,” not “The Sense of Ending.”
match_headline: Get the Laughs, but Follow the Rules

text: An article on Monday about Seth Meyers’s new role as host of “Late Night” on NBC misstated the address of his new studio. It is at 30 Rockefeller Plaza, not 30 Rockefeller Center.
match_headline: Seth Meyers: Smart Guy in the Wiseguy Seat

text: A report in the Week column on Tuesday, about variations in the composition of breast milk depending on the gender of the infant, paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Katie Hinde, an evolutionary biologist at Harvard University. Dr. Hinde said people should be “skeptical of a one-size-fits-all formula,” but did not specifically encourage formula manufacturers to produce different mixtures for boys and girls.
match_headline: Clues to a Very Old Extinction and Pizza for War Zones

text: An article last Friday about concerns by opponents of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela that they have fewer and fewer locations in which to demonstrate and express their discontent referred incorrectly to Globovision, a Venezuela TV station. Before its sale last year, it broadcast more voices critical of the Venezuelan government than other television stations, but it was not the only one to regularly feature government critics.
match_headline: Protests Swell in Venezuela as Places to Rally Disappear

text: An article on Oct. 9 about an announcement that Britain and Iran would each appoint a chargé d’affaires in an effort to improve long-strained relations referred incorrectly to an official with Iran’s foreign ministry who confirmed the announcement. The official, Marzieh Afkham, is a woman. This error was corrected on The Times website on Oct. 9, but editors did not follow through with a correction for print editions.
match_headline: Britain and Iran Move to Repair Diplomatic Relations

text: An article on Feb. 18 about negotiations over renters’ access to a swimming pool controlled by a co-op in Chelsea misstated the role of Rose Associates, a developer and management company, at London Terrace Gardens, the rental complex. It is the manager, not the owner. (The complex is owned by London Terrace Gardens L.P.)
match_headline: Chelsea Complex Divided Over Rare Indoor Amenity

text: A picture caption with an article on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about redevelopment of the historic Smithfield Market in London described incompletely the building shown. While it is part of the market at Smithfield, it is the meat market, not the old fish market and the general market, which are the buildings involved in the redevelopment.
match_headline: Battle Over London Market Raises Development Issues

text: An article on Thursday about the uneven success thus far of health cooperatives under the Affordable Care Act misspelled the name of the health co-op in Iowa and Nebraska. The organization is CoOportunity, not CoOpportunity.
match_headline: Health Law’s Small Co-ops Have Had a Mixed Success So Far

text: An article on Monday about Apple’s acquisitions of small technology companies in recent years misstated, in some editions, the year its rival Google purchased Motorola Mobility. That deal was in 2012, not in 2013.
match_headline: For Hints at Apple’s Plans, Read Its Shopping List

text: An article on Thursday about the first named soccer player found to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy, the degenerative brain disease linked to repeated blows to the head, misstated the year the player, Patrick Grange, died. It was in April 2012, not last April.
match_headline: Brain Trauma Extends to the Soccer Field

text: A report in the Weekend Miser column last Friday about a workshop held that night at the Bronx Museum of the Arts misidentified the neighborhood in which the museum is situated. It is Concourse Village, not Morrisania.
match_headline: Lessons in Street Art

text: An obituary on Thursday about Peter A. Rona, an oceanographer who discovered hot springs at the bottom of the Atlantic, gave an incorrect date for his death from Rutgers University, where he taught. It was Feb. 20, not Feb. 19.
match_headline: Peter Rona, 79, Dies; Explorer Found Hot Springs on Ocean Floor

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about the increasing popularity of Montessori schools that combine secular studies with the teaching of Jewish traditions referred incorrectly to Sam Boymelgreen’s role in the founding of one such school, Luria Academy of Brooklyn. He is one of four founders, not the only one. (The others are Alisa Boymelgreen, Moshe Banin and Jacob Septimus.)
match_headline: Montessori Schools Surge in Popularity Among New Generation of Jewish Parents

text: An article on Thursday about Tesla Motors’ plans for a large-scale lithium-ion battery factory misstated the expected production capacity of the factory. By 2020, it is expected to produce enough batteries for 500,000 cars annually, not 500,000 batteries. (Each Tesla uses thousands of individual lithium-ion batteries in its battery pack.)
match_headline: Tesla Plans $5 Billion Battery Factory for Mass-Market Electric Car

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a counterattack by SeaWorld against “Blackfish,” a critical documentary about whales in captivity, misspelled the given name of an investigator accused of improper dealing with both animal-rights activists and the makers of the film. She is Lara A. Padgett, not Laura. The article also misspelled the surname of one of the film’s producers. He is Tim Zimmermann, not Zimmerman. And the article rendered incorrectly the name of a concert series at SeaWorld. It is “Bands, Brews & BBQ,” not “Brews, Bands & BBQ.”
match_headline: SeaWorld Questions Ethics of ‘Blackfish’ Investigator

text: A map on Friday with an article about increasing rail shipments of crude oil from the Bakken Formation in North Dakota to the Port of Albany located La Crosse, Wis., incorrectly. La Crosse is on the Wisconsin border north of its border with Iowa, not south of it.
match_headline: Bakken Crude, Rolling Through Albany

text: An article on Friday about the Whitney Biennial, which opens next Friday, misstated the age of Etel Adnan, an artist who will have work displayed in the show. She is 89, not 84. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: State of Our Art, According to Whitney

text: An article on Friday about the Chinese artist Xu Zhen, whose work will be on display at the Armory Show in New York next week, misstated the title of a retrospective of his career that is currently at the Ullens Center for Contemporary Art in Beijing. It is “Xu Zhen: A MadeIn Company Production,” not “Xu Zhen: A Production of MadeIn.”
ref_headline: Xu Zhen: A MadeIn Company Production,
match_headline: Wryly Nibbling at His Bread and Butter

text: Because of an editing error, the Big City column in some editions last Sunday, about the evolution of the Gowanus neighborhood in Brooklyn, misstated the name of a website that reported on the God’s Only Demons Motorcycle Club. It is DNAinfo.com.
match_headline: The Once and Future Gowanus

text: An article last Sunday about a documentary film festival that receives financial support from the Crossing, an Evangelical Presbyterian church in Missouri, omitted part of the festival’s name. It is the True/False Film Fest, not the True/False documentary festival. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption. The article also misstated part of the name for the award the festival gives. It is the True Life Fund, not the “festival’s True/Life fund.” The article also misstated the year in which David Wilson, a festival co-director, brought the film “To Be Heard” to the attention of the church, and the year “The Interrupters” was selected for the True Life Fund. Both were in 2011, not in 2012. The article also misstated the year “Bully” was under consideration. It was 2012, not last year.
match_headline: Crossing a Divide, Seeking Good

text: Because of an editing error, an accompanying picture caption misstated the festival status of “After Tiller.” It was a favorite of the Crossing pastor Dave Cover, but it did not win an award. And, finally, a credit for a picture of David Wilson and Dave Cover misidentified the photographer. He is Scott Patrick Myers, not Gerik Parmele.

An article last Sunday about the playwright Will Eno, who has two plays opening in New York this month, misstated the surname of a friend with whom Mr. Eno invented a swimming pool sport. He is Joe Sola — not Solas.
match_headline: Despair Is Looking Up

text: An article last Sunday about the spring theater season in New York misspelled the surname of the actor who will portray the playwright Moss Hart as a boy in the play “Act One.” He is Matthew Schechter — not Schecter. An accompanying picture caption repeated the error.
match_headline: Self-Examination for All to See and Hear

text: An article last Sunday about the renewed popularity of oysters in restaurants referred incorrectly in one instance to a cooperative co-founded by Karen Rivara, an oyster farmer on Long Island. As noted correctly earlier in the article, it is the Noank Aquaculture Cooperative, not the N.O.A.A. cooperative.
match_headline: Loss Leaders on the Half Shell

text: An article last Sunday about a young inventor’s device for testing the texture of granola bars referred incorrectly to the Patent Office status of one of his earlier creations: a compression container for camping gear. The inventor applied for a patent on the container but, after entering college, did not complete the patent process; he has not received a patent.
match_headline: A Young Inventor, Finding the Crunch Factor

text: An article last Sunday about RuPaul misspelled the given name of a creative producer for the performer. He is Mathu Andersen, not Matthew.
match_headline: In Drag, It Turns Out, There Are Second Acts

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about Americans who run nightclubs in Berlin misstated the business relationship between Dan DeNorch and Micharel Ladner, two Americans, and the Berlin club Chesters. They book D.J.'s for the club and host parties there; they do not own it.
match_headline: Brooklyn on the Spree

text: An article last Sunday about adolescent girls who post deliberately ugly self-portraits (or selfies) on the web misstated the role played by Nancy Etcoff, a cognitive psychologist, in the production of the short film “Selfies,” which received funding from the cosmetics company Dove. She is an adviser for the company; she did not directly advise on the film. And because of an editing error, the article referred incorrectly at one point to Marcelle Karp, the mother of Ruby Karp, a girl who posts ugly selfies. She is unmarried and therefore is Ms. Karp, not Mrs. Karp.
match_headline: With Some Selfies, the Uglier the Better

text: A picture caption on Feb. 2 with a Q&A column about James Vincent McMorrow, a musician based in Dublin, misidentified a beach near the city. It is Portmarnock Beach with Howth Head beyond; it is not Malahide Beach, which is half a mile away, and Howth Head.
match_headline: Dublin, Beyond the Guinness Storehouse

text: An article on Thursday about the presence of warlords in Afghanistan’s elections, who are either running for office or are associated with candidates, misidentified, in some editions, the spokesman for Ashraf Ghani, a presidential candidate. He is Hameedullah Farooqi, not Fraidoon Barekzai.
match_headline: Warlords With Dark Pasts Battle in Afghan Election

text: An article on Feb. 8 about the persistence of extremist violence in Tunisia that for many Tunisians has cast into doubt the government’s pledges to bolster the weak economy and fledgling democracy referred imprecisely to a distinction held by the country. While it is considered the smallest country of North Africa, that distinction is based on its land mass. (Others are smaller in population.)
match_headline: Despite Signs of Progress, Security Issues Rise in Tunisia

text: A reporting credit on Thursday with an article about efforts by the new government of Ukraine to win the support of the people who forced President Viktor F. Yanukovych from office misspelled the surname of a contributor and misidentified the city from which she reported. She is Oksana Lyachynska, not Lyachnyska, and she contributed from Kiev, not New York.
match_headline: In Ukraine, Naming of Interim Government Gets Mixed Response

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Friday about the Rangers’ 2-1 victory over the Blackhawks referred incorrectly to the performance of Rangers goaltender Cam Talbot. It was his third shutout in his 18th game in the N.H.L., not his third in his 18th game since he was acquired from the Islanders. The article also misidentified the player who was recently acquired from the Islanders. He is Blackhawks center Peter Regin, not Talbot. The article also misstated the number of Blackhawks players in uniform Thursday who played in the Sochi Olympics and the total number of players in uniform Thursday who played in Sochi. It was 9, not 10, so the total was 15, not 16.
match_headline: Rangers Still Going Strong (So Are Trade Rumors)

text: An article on Wednesday about the unfinished Crimean palace of Viktor F. Yanukovych, the ousted president of Ukraine, referred imprecisely to his possible fate. While the new government in Kiev wants to put him on trial for mass murder, and many are calling for his execution, Ukraine does not now have the death penalty, so it is premature to say that a trial, if held in Ukraine, would “probably” lead to his execution.
match_headline: An Unfinished Ukraine Palace and a Fugitive Leader’s Folly

text: An article on Feb. 12 about a decision by Cuba to build gated housing developments for members of the armed forces and others most loyal to the Castro government after realizing they were falling behind in the country’s new hybrid economy misstated the given name of a retired colonel who writes a blog often critical of the government. He is Fernando Dámaso, not Jorge.
match_headline: Cuba’s Reward for the Dutiful: Gated Housing

text: An article on Jan. 20, 1853, recounting the story of Solomon Northup, whose memoir “12 Years a Slave” became a movie 160 years later that won the best picture Oscar at the 86th Academy Awards on Sunday night, misspelled his surname as Northrop. And the headline misspelled it as Northrup. The errors came to light on Monday after a Twitter user pointed out the article in The Times archives. (The errors notwithstanding, The Times described the article as “a more complete and authentic record than has yet appeared.”)
An article last Tuesday about the issues facing San Francisco and its mayor, Edwin M. Lee, misstated the year in which Mr. Lee was first elected. It was 2011, not 2012.
match_headline: A Mayor in the Middle of Two San Franciscos

text: An article on Monday about reaction among immigrant communities in New York to the crisis in the Crimean Peninsula misattributed, in some editions, a statement calling for a peaceful resolution and noting that the behavior of Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president, was hard to explain. The statement quoted Gregory Davidzon, the host of a Russian-language radio show — not Yuriy Sergeyev, the Ukrainian ambassador to the United Nations.
match_headline: Action by Russia Divides Immigrants in New York

text: An article on Feb. 20 about Signet Jewelers’ proposed acquisition of a smaller rival, the Zale Corporation, misstated the value of the deal.  Signet is paying $900 million in cash, not $690 million, when Zale warrants held by the private equity firm Golden Gate Capital that can be converted into shares are taken in account. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Signet Jewelers to Buy Zale in $900 Million Deal

text: An article on Wednesday about the future of Bitcoin after the collapse of Mt. Gox, the secretive Bitcoin exchange, misstated the affiliation of John O’Brien, who commented on the collapse. He is a spokesman for Coinbase, another Bitcoin company, not for a coalition of Bitcoin companies.
match_headline: First Companies Give to Fund for Victims of Bangladeshi Factory Collapse

text: An article on Sunday about the seizure of the Crimean Peninsula by Russian armed forces misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the ousted Ukrainian president on first reference. He is Viktor F. Yanukovych, not Yanuovych. The article also misspelled the name of a town in eastern Crimea where Russian ships were reported to have landed. It is Feodosiya, not Fedosiya.
match_headline: Ukraine Mobilizes Reserve Troops, Threatening War

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Saturday about the retirement of Robert S. Ford, the State Department’s top representative to the Syrian opposition, misidentified one of the countries where Mr. Ford served as a diplomat. Besides Syria, Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Turkey and Cameroon, he also served in Iraq — not Iran.
match_headline: American Envoy to Syria Steps Down

text: A chart on Feb. 24 with an article about the final medal count for the Sochi Games misstated the number of medals won by Canada and Sweden. Canada won 10 gold medals, not 9, for a total of 25 medals, not 24. And Sweden won 7 silver medals, not 6, for a total of 15 medals, not 14.
match_headline: Strong Finish Gives Russia Most Medals

text: A picture caption last Wednesday with an obituary about the ballet dancer Ivan Nagy omitted credit for the photograph of him. It was taken by Jack Mitchell.
match_headline: Ivan Nagy, Star of American Ballet Theater, Is Dead at 70

text: An article on Tuesday about an interstate commerce feud over California’s demand that out-of-state farmers seeking to sell eggs in California meet its more stringent standards for hen housing misstated egg production at JS West & Companies, a leading California producer. The company expects production next year to drop to 372 million eggs from this year’s 480 million — not to drop to 12 million from 19 million. The article also misstated the number of laying hens in California. It is 19 million, not 26 million.
match_headline: Wishing They All Could Be California Hens

text: An article on Wednesday about the improving fortunes of the very wealthy in 2013, as illustrated by their purchases, misspelled the given name of the artist who was the subject of a Francis Bacon painting that sold for $142.4 million. He is Lucian Freud, not Lucien. The article also misspelled part of the name of a wine that recently brought $476,405 for 12 bottles. It is Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, not Domain.
match_headline: For Rich, ’13 Was Good for Making, and Spending, Money

text: An article on Saturday about the collapse of the Bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox misstated the surname of Mt. Gox’s founder. He is Jed McCaleb, not McCabe.

An article on Feb. 16 about concerns among Indian intellectuals over a decision by Penguin Books India to withdraw Wendy Doniger’s “The Hindus: An Alternative History” because of a lawsuit by a retired headmaster who found the book offensive misidentified the court that granted a stay of publication of another book, “Sahara: The Untold Story.” It is the Kolkata High Court, not the Indian Supreme Court.
match_headline: Indian Publisher Withdraws Book, Stoking Fears of Nationalist Pressure

text: An article on Feb. 25 about the transformation of Mong La, a city in Myanmar near the Chinese border, into a notorious hub of gambling and prostitution since the country emerged from decades of dictatorship referred incorrectly to the status of a wild animal for sale in a live market. The animal, the bamboo rat, is not endangered.
match_headline: A Border City on the Edge of the Law

text: An article on Tuesday about clashes among Indian tribes over new casinos described incorrectly a group involved in the debate. Stand Up for California is a statewide organization that monitors and often takes a position on casinos and other gambling venues by Indian tribes; it is not an antigambling group.
match_headline: Tribes Clash as Casinos Move Away From Home

text: An article on Wednesday about a vote by the City Council in Washington to decriminalize the possession of small amounts of marijuana misstated the number of days that Congress has to review the law before it is enacted. It is 60 days, not 30. The error also appeared on Jan. 16 in an article about a vote in the public safety committee that sent the measure to the full council.
