match_headline: Effort to Decriminalize Small Amounts of Marijuana Gains in District of Columbia

text: An article on Tuesday about the ties between Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey and David Samson, the chairman of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, gave an incorrect location in some copies for a New York airport that was turned over to the Port Authority. The airport, Stewart International Airport, is in Newburgh, not on Long Island.
match_headline: In Job, Appointee Profits and Christie Gains Power

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Feb. 27 about the announcement that Marvel and Disney would film four live-action television series in New York City misidentified the site of the news conference announcing the filming. It was at ABC’s “Good Morning America” studios, not at NBC Studios.
match_headline: Four Marvel TV Shows to Film in New York

text: A headline on a report in the Business Briefing on Thursday about two pharmaceutical companies’ being fined in Italy for colluding to steer doctors away from a lower-priced drug for a common eye problem misstated the relationship between the companies, Novartis and Roche, and the developer of the cheaper drug, Genentech. Roche acquired Genentech in 2009 and Novartis markets both Genentech’s drug, Avastin, and the more expensive alternative, Lucentis, outside of the United States. Genentech is not a “rival” of Roche and Novartis.
match_headline: Italy Fines Novartis and Roche in Collusion Case

text: An article on Friday about the indictments of former leaders of the defunct law firm Dewey & LeBoeuf misstated the size of the firm’s staff. At its peak, the firm employed 1,300 lawyers; that was not the size of its overall staff. The error also appeared on Thursday in an article about the impending charges.
match_headline: 4 Accused in Law Firm Fraud Ignored a Maxim: Don’t Email

text: An article last Saturday about a book on President Harry S. Truman and the founding of Israel by a longtime senior editor at The New Republic that has created a rift within the magazine’s staff referred incompletely to the sale of The New Republic to Chris Hughes in 2012. Martin Peretz was part of a consortium that sold it; he was not the sole owner at the time.
match_headline: A Bastion for Israel, Seething Inside

text: An article on Friday about the New York International Children’s Film Festival referred incorrectly to an organization associated with the festival and to a member of the jury that decides which animated short film and live-action short from the festival become eligible for an Academy Award nomination. The group GKids is the sister organization of the festival, not its parent organization, and the jury member Christine Vachon is a producer, not a director.
match_headline: Warning: Teenagers May Like These Movies

text: A listing of credits on Friday with a theater review of “All the Way,” at the Neil Simon Theater in Manhattan, misspelled the surname of a producer. She is Cheryl Wiesenfeld, not Weisenfeld.
match_headline: Washington Power Play

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with the continuation of an article about the growing role of women in the Mormon Church carried an erroneous credit in some copies. The picture of Ashley Farr, the first in her Mormon family to become a missionary, was taken by Chang W. Lee of The New York Times — not by Michael Friberg, who took other photographs for the article.
match_headline: Missions Signal a Growing Role for Mormon Women

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Thomas Mickens, who began a fitness franchise for older clients after he was released from prison, misidentified, in some editions, the vehicle that he was driving when he stopped at 232nd Street and Merrick in Queens. It was a Nissan Altima, not a Jaguar.
match_headline: Of Crime and Punishment, Redemption and Aerobics

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about the third round of the Honda Classic golf tournament misstated the year Tiger Woods shot a 62 in the final round of the event. As the article correctly noted, it was in 2012, not last year.
match_headline: McIlroy Displays Composure in Place Where He Once Lost It

text: An article previewing the spring dance season on Feb. 23 misidentified the orchestra Nicholas McGegan will be conducting in Boston during a May performance of the choreographer Mark Morris’s new full-evening “Acis and Galatea.” It is the Handel and Haydn Society orchestra — not the Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra, which he will conduct for the same piece in April in Berkeley, Calif.
match_headline: The Change That Just Might Come

text: An article on Feb. 23 about the composer Georg Friedrich Haas, who joined the composition faculty at Columbia University in September, misidentified the recipient of 122 applications for three places in the program. It was Columbia’s composition program — not Mr. Haas himself.
match_headline: Varied Pitches to Fill Empty Spaces

text: An article last Sunday about the headquarters design of technology companies misstated the name of the dining area at Twitter’s offices. It is the Commons, not the Town Square. The article also referred incorrectly to where Dick Costolo, Twitter’s C.E.O., stands when addressing employees at a weekly gathering in the space. He is on a raised platform, not on a walkway above them.
match_headline: The Monuments of Tech

text: A news analysis article last Sunday about the legacy of the Cold War on foreign policy debates in the United States misstated John W. McCormack’s position at the time he accused the Eisenhower administration of appeasement. He was a member of the House of Representatives; he was not yet the speaker.
match_headline: A History Lesson That Needs Relearning

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about two men who collect memorabilia associated with the 1939 World’s Fair reversed their identities in some editions. Dr. Roy Goldberg was shown at the left and Keith Sherman at the right.
match_headline: For Two Collectors, a Weekend Getaway to the 1939 World’s Fair

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about Sherwin B. Nuland, the author of “How We Die,” in referring to his father, Meyer Nudelman, misidentified the person whose death occurred without Mr. Nudelman’s knowing the cause. It was his own death, not that of his father.
match_headline: Sherwin B. Nuland, Author of ‘How We Die,’ Is Dead at 83

text: An obituary on Feb. 27 about Chokwe Lumumba, a civil rights lawyer who became mayor of Jackson, Miss., misstated the year that he persuaded Gov. Haley Barbour to release two sisters from a Mississippi prison after they had served 16 years for an armed robbery they said they had not committed. It was 2011, not 1996.
match_headline: Chokwe Lumumba, 66, Dies; Activist Who Became Mayor in Mississippi

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the use of public transit in the United States having reached its highest level since 1956 misstated the number of passenger trips taken on transit systems in 2008. It was 10.59 billion, not million.
match_headline: Use of Public Transit in U.S. Reaches Highest Level Since 1956, Advocates Report

text: An article in some editions last Tuesday about the refilling of the Jerome Park Reservoir and the limits of neighborhood access to it misspelled the name of an avenue in the Bronx bordering the reservoir. It is Sedgwick, not Sedgewick.
match_headline: Reservoir’s Neighbors Want More Than Return of Their Water Views

text: An obituary on Saturday about Ned O’Gorman, a poet who started a storefront school in Harlem, misstated the number of black children killed in the bombing of a church in Birmingham, Ala., in 1963. It was four, not three. (Mr. O’Gorman named a children’s library after one of the victims, Addie Mae Collins.)
match_headline: Ned O’Gorman, 84, Dies; Poet Founded Innovative Harlem School

text: An obituary on Sunday about the singer and actress Sheila MacRae misstated the title of her 1992 memoir in some editions. It is “Hollywood Mother of the Year,” not “Mother of the Year.”
match_headline: Sheila MacRae, Wife in ’60s ‘Honeymooners’ Sketches, Dies at 92

text: An earlier version of these corrections misstated the date in which they appeared in print. They appeared on March 11, not March 10.

An article on Monday about an effort by a New York hedge fund executive, William A. Ackman, to push regulators to investigate Herbalife misidentified one of the groups that wrote a letter urging an investigation. It is the National Consumers League — not the Consumer Federation (formally known as the Consumer Federation of America). The article also misstated the position at the Indago Group held by Christine Richard, who did research on Herbalife that helped inspire Mr. Ackman. She worked there, but she did not set up the company. An earlier version of this correction referred incorrectly to the Consumer Federation.  It is formally — not “formerly” — known as the Consumer Federation of America.
match_headline: After Big Bet, Hedge Fund Pulls the Levers of Power

text: An article on Tuesday about false leads in the investigation into the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 misstated the year that an EgyptAir jetliner crashed. It was in 1999, not 2002.
match_headline: False Leads Set Back Search for Malaysian Jet

text: An article on Tuesday about a decision by the fraternity Sigma Alpha Epsilon to no longer allow “pledging” as part of its initiation process referred incorrectly to a student, George Desdunes, who died at Cornell. Mr. Desdunes, a sophomore, was a member of the fraternity, he was not a pledge. (He died during a hazing rite in which pledges bound, blindfolded and forced older students to drink.)
match_headline: After Students’ Hazing-Related Deaths, Fraternity Eliminates Tradition of Pledging

text: An article on Feb. 24 about the new generation of Alpine skiing stars that emerged at the Sochi Olympics misstated the number of Olympic medals Maria Höfl-Riesch has won. It is four, not five, so she is not “one Olympic medal from Janica Kostelic’s record haul of six.”
ref_headline: one Olympic medal from Janica Kostelic’s record haul of six.
match_headline: New Generation of Stars Emerges in Alpine Events

text: A picture credit with the What’s on Tuesday television highlights in some editions on Tuesday misspelled the name of the network showing “From Dusk Till Dawn: The Series.” As the entry about the series correctly noted, it is El Rey Network, not El Ray.
ref_headline: From Dusk Till Dawn: The Series.
match_headline: What’s on Tuesday

text: An obituary on Monday about William Clay Ford, the longtime vice chairman of the Ford Motor Company and owner of the Detroit Lions football team, misstated the year of his graduation from Yale in some editions. He graduated in 1949, not 1948. And an accompanying picture caption misstated the name of the car shown, which Mr. Ford was involved in developing. As the obituary correctly noted, it is the Continental Mark II, not the Lincoln Continental Mark II.
match_headline: William Clay Ford, Auto Family Scion and Detroit Lions Owner, Dies at 88

text: An earlier version of these corrections misstated the date in which they appeared in print. They appeared on March 11, not March 10.
An earlier version of th e Front Page correction about Herbalife referred incorrectly to the Consumer Federation.  It is formally — not “formerly” — known as the Consumer Federation of America .

An article on Tuesday about the ways in which the administration of Gov. Chris Christie used the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey as a political tool erroneously included one of Mr. Christie’s senior aides among the people who attended a meeting on Aug. 3 about proposed toll increases. Though Deborah Gramiccioni’s name was on an unofficial list of those attending, she was not at the meeting.
match_headline: Even Before Fort Lee Lane Closings, Port Authority Was a Christie Tool

text: A report in the World Briefing column on March 5 about a claim by Medea Benjamin, an American co-founder of the protest group Code Pink, that she was detained in the Cairo airport and assaulted by the Egyptian police referred imprecisely to Gaza, Ms. Benjamin’s intended destination. Although the United Nations, many individual countries and Gazans themselves regard it as still occupied by Israel, Israel withdrew all its forces and Jewish settlers from Gaza in 2005, while maintaining strict border control.
match_headline: U.S. Activist Says Egyptian Police Assaulted Her

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 3 about the steps that the interim Ukrainian government was taking after Russia took control of the country’s Crimean region described the population of eastern Ukraine incorrectly. Most of the people are ethnic Ukrainian, not ethnic Russian.
match_headline: Ukrainian Government Rushes to Dampen Secessionist Sentiment

text: An article on Monday about a memorial service in Jackson, Miss., for Mayor Chokwe Lumumba misstated the population of the city. It is about 175,000 — not 500,000, which is about the size of the Jackson metropolitan area.
match_headline: Jackson Mourns Mayor With Militant Past Who Won Over Skeptics

text: An article on Wednesday about a new Senate plan to wind down the mortgage finance agencies Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Julia Gordon of the Center for American Progress. She said the new plan included a commitment to serving all markets, not “people of all income levels.” Because of an editing error, the article also misidentified, in some editions, an agency that Representative Jeb Hensarling said the proposal failed to deal with. It is the Federal Housing Administration, not the Federal Housing Finance Agency. The article also misstated, in some copies, an estimate by the economist Mark Zandi of how much the proposal might increase mortgage rates. He estimated they would rise 0.4 to 0.5 percentage points, not 0.25 of a percentage point.
match_headline: Senators Draft Housing Finance Overhaul

text: An article on Tuesday about the resignation of Cyprus’s central bank governor misstated the details of a separate, earlier resignation involving the Hungarian central bank. A deputy governor of the Hungarian bank resigned in 2013 to protest the appointment of a new central bank governor by Prime Minister Viktor Orban. It was not the central bank governor who resigned, and the episode did not happen in 2012. Nor was Mr. Orban new to his office at the time; he was elected in 2010.
match_headline: Sharply Criticized by Government, Head of the Central Bank of Cyprus Resigns

text: An article on Wednesday about inspection reports that found safety problems continuing in Bangladesh garment factories erroneously included one retailer among customers of Dragon Sweater in Dhaka. Though Dragon Sweater’s website listed the British retailer Sainsbury’s among its clients, Sainsbury’s says it has not been a customer for several years.
match_headline: Bangladesh Inspections Find Gaps in Safety

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the coming show “Forbidden Broadway Comes Out Swinging!” omitted a director. Besides writing the show, Gerard Alessandrini will co-direct with Phillip George; the show will not be directed solely by Mr. George.
match_headline: Gerard Mortier, Opera Visionary and Patron of New Work, Dies at 70

text: An article last Thursday about homeowners who decorate their houses based on the films of the director Wes Anderson misspelled the given name of a woman who organized a birthday party for her husband based on Mr. Anderson’s movies. She is Alix Bannon, not Alex. The article also misstated her age; she is 30, not 31.
match_headline: The Wildebeest in the Room

text: An article last Thursday about the figure skater Johnny Weir erroneously included one film among those nominated for best picture at this year’s Academy Awards. “Blue Jasmine,” starring Cate Blanchett, one of Mr. Weir’s favorite actresses, was not one of the nine movies.   The article also omitted the name of  one of the seven figure skating announcers for NBC in Sochi, Russia.  Terry Gannon was also one of them.
match_headline: His Profile, and His Plumage, Grow Ever More Bold

text: An article on Sunday about the discovery that two passengers aboard a missing Malaysia Airlines plane were carrying stolen passports contained several errors in some editions.
match_headline: Passport Theft Adds to Mystery of Missing Malaysia Airlines Jet

text: Because of an editing error, the article misstated the number of tickets China Southern Airlines said it sold for the flight. In addition to those sold to the holders of the stolen passports, it sold five tickets, not four.
match_headline: Use of Stolen Passports on Missing Jet Highlights Security Flaw

text: An article on March 4 about the Russian “protest tourists” crossing the border to join demonstrations by ethnic Russians in southern and eastern Ukraine referred incorrectly to the building captured by pro-Russia demonstrators in the eastern city of Donetsk, and to the people inside the building, who were eventually allowed to leave. It is the headquarters for the regional legislature, not the Parliament; the people inside were regional legislators and legislative employees, not members and employees of Parliament. The same error appeared in both captions. (Donetsk, unlike the Ukrainian region of Crimea, is not autonomous and does not have its own Parliament.)
match_headline: From Russia, ‘Tourists’ Stir the Protests

text: An article on Thursday about lingering questions over car crashes in light of General Motors’ recall of 1.6 million cars to repair a potentially dangerous flaw in the ignition switch misspelled the surname of the vice principal of the Lexington School in Lexington, Ala., where one such fatal crash occurred last December. He is Marty L. Mosley, not Mosely.
match_headline: Huge Recall by G.M. Sets Off Painful Questions on Crashes

text: An article on Tuesday about a talk by Edward J. Snowden, delivered via videoconferencing on Monday to the South by Southwest Conference in Austin, Tex., included an incomplete quotation taken from a transcript of his comments. Mr. Snowden, the former National Security Agency contractor who leaked classified documents, said, “I took an oath to support and defend the Constitution and I saw that the Constitution was violated on a massive scale.” He did not say, “I took an oath to support and defend the Constitution and it was violated on a massive scale.”
ref_headline: I took an oath to support and defend the Constitution and I saw that the Constitution was violated on a massive scale.
match_headline: Excerpts From Snowden’s SXSW Speech

text: An article on Wednesday about regulatory efforts to create a method to oversee virtual currency exchanges misstated the role of Amy Weiss at the Bitcoin Foundation, an industry advocacy group. She was hired as an outside consultant, not as an employee.
match_headline: Bitcoin Foundation Bolsters Its Ranks

text: An article on Wednesday about Roberto and William Isaias of Florida, fugitive brothers from Ecuador whom the Obama administration declined to extradite and whose relatives gave $90,000 to President Obama’s re-election campaign, misstated the jurisdiction of the court in which the Ecuadorean government sued the brothers to recover funds it says were embezzled from a failed bank. It was a state court in Miami, not a federal court.
match_headline: Wanted by Ecuador, 2 Brothers Make Mark in U.S. Campaigns

text: An article last Saturday about a disagreement between Turkish leaders over proposed restrictions on social media referred incorrectly to President Abdullah Gul’s actions in regard to an Internet bill. Before approving it, he pressured lawmakers to amend it to address criticisms; he did not amend it himself. (He does not have the power to do so.)
match_headline: Turkey’s Leaders Spar Over Plan to Muzzle Social Media

text: A report in the National Briefing column on Thursday about a bill that would overturn Kentucky’s ban on elected officials’ seeking multiple positions misstated the day it cleared a committee in the state’s Republican-controlled Senate. It was passed on Wednesday; it was not expected to pass on Thursday.
match_headline: Spurred by Paul, Kentucky Weighs Change to Ballot Rule

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a meeting of the Queens Library trustees that focused on the scandal surrounding the Queens Library system’s president, Thomas W. Galante, referred incorrectly to the investigation of Mr. Galante for possible misuse of money meant to improve the library’s 62 branches. He is under federal and city investigation, not federal and state.
match_headline: Queens Councilwoman Confronts Library Leader

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the State of the Art column, about making cellphones last longer, gave an incorrect description from Gazell.com , a gadget trade-in service, for the photograph of one of its employees. She is removing batteries from traded-in devices, not SIM cards.
match_headline: A Wild Idea: Making Our Smartphones Last Longer

text: A chart on Wednesday with the Economic Scene column, about an economist’s belief that economic inequality will widen and prevail for a long time, misstated a year on the horizontal axis in showing the value of private capital as a percentage of national income. The year at the far right was 2100, not 3000.
match_headline: A Relentless Widening of Disparity in Wealth

text: An article on March 3 about the latest effort to build a car that can break the land speed record reversed the names of the cars that Richard Noble and Andy Green drove to set land speed records. Noble drove a Thrust II in 1983, raising the record to 633.4 miles per hour, and Green drove a Thrust SSC in 1997 to set the current speed record of 763 m.p.h.
match_headline: Driven to Set a Record: Zero to 60, Plus 940

text: An article on Thursday about an Israeli youth hockey team that visited the Washington, D.C., area this week misstated, in some copies, the time period during which Goals & Dreams, a program of the N.H.L. Players’ Association, donated $22 million worth of new hockey gear to children in 32 countries. The donations have been made since the program’s founding in 1999, not this year alone.
match_headline: Harmony in a Land of Milk, Honey and Pucks

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings on Friday about a discussion scheduled for Tuesday with the author David Huyssen misidentified which of Book Culture’s two stores will host the event. It will be at the store at 536 West 112th Street location, in Morningside Heights — not at Book Culture’s store at 2915 Broadway.
match_headline: Spare Times for March 14-20

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Maj. Kurt Chew-Een Lee, a Chinese-American who led Marines into battle against the Chinese in the Korean War, referred incorrectly to the men who served under him. They were Marines, not soldiers.
match_headline: Kurt Chew-Een Lee, Singular Marine, Dies at 88

text: An article last Sunday about a growing distaste for capital punishment among Iran’s middle class misstated the surname of a leader of the Imam Ali Popular Students Society, a group that tries to prevent the execution of juvenile offenders. He is Sharmin Meymaninejad, not Neymaninejad.
match_headline: Mercy and Social Media Slow the Noose in Iran

text: An article last Sunday about a huge construction project in Rio de Janeiro that has uncovered vestiges of Brazil’s prodigious slave trade misstated the surname of a professor of architecture and urban planning. He is Cláudio Lima Carlos, not Lima Castro.
match_headline: Rio’s Race to Future Intersects Slave Past

text: An article last Sunday about an event dedicated to classical music performances contained several errors in some editions. The event is the Worldwide Play-In Weekend, not the Worldwide Music Play-In. The cellist for the G-String Grannies, a string quartet, is Louise Bozorth, not Bozorthe. While Dr. Anthony J. Vine and Margo Rosen performed with the quartet, another musician, Jean Brenner, also joined them for a piece by Tchaikovsky. And Robin Boomer and Fritz Stewart performed as high school students at an Airstream R.V. convention in Lacey, Wash., not Lacy.
match_headline: Musicians Old and Young, Experienced and Not, Join a Global Play-In

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Kevin McCrary, a hoarder on the Upper East Side who is trying to clear out his belongings, misstated the month by which he originally agreed to move out of his apartment. It was the end of November 2013, not October.
match_headline: Buried by His Past

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the actor Aaron Paul, who is in the new movie “Need for Speed” and who played a drug dealer on the TV show “Breaking Bad,” misstated one of the duties of his character, Jesse Pinkman, on “Breaking Bad.” Pinkman had to help babysit a D.E.A. informant shackled in the basement. He did not babysit for the informant.
match_headline: Hitting High Velocity Without the Meth

text: An article last Sunday about the jazz pianist Vijay Iyer, who has a new album out, “Mutations,” misspelled the surname of a filmmaker who collaborated on a concert CD of “Radhe, Radhe: Rites of Holi” with Mr. Iyer and members of the International Contemporary Ensemble. He is Prashant Bhargava, not Bharghava.
match_headline: DNA of a Polymath, Restlessly Mutating

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the new movie “Veronica Mars,” a sequel to the cult TV show of the same name, gave an incorrect spelling from a publicist for the surname of the man shown in a photo of a fan taking a selfie with Kristen Bell, who stars in the film. He is Jake Kallman — not Kellman.
match_headline: ‘Veronica Mars’ Fans Are Happy to Finance a Reunion

text: A review on March 2 about the memoir “Trespassing on Einstein’s Lawn: A Father, a Daughter, the Meaning of Nothing, and the Beginning of Everything,” by Amanda Gefter, misstated the given name of the author’s father. He is Warren Gefter, not Wayne.
ref_headline: Trespassing on Einstein’s Lawn: A Father, a Daughter, the Meaning of Nothing, and the Beginning of Everything,
match_headline: What’s It All About?

text: An article on March 2 about actors in action movies misidentified the Hollywood studio for the forthcoming movie ‘‘Monster Trucks.’’ It is Paramount, not Universal.
match_headline: The Last, Disposable Action Hero

text: An article last Sunday about Chris Anderson, the head of the TED organization, misstated the amount of a prize awarded by the group. It is $1 million, not $100,000.
match_headline: No, His Name Is Not Ted

text: An article last Sunday about the killings of Jiri and Dagmar Fiedler mischaracterized the frequency of murders in Prague. They are not rare, but double murders are.
match_headline: Eulogy for a Source

text: An article last Sunday about the writer’s return to Nicaragua after 25 years misstated the direction she drove from the Institute for Advanced Studies of Oriental and Natural Medicine in Managua to Granada. It was southeast, not southwest. And the article misstated the direction she drove from the Selva Negra Mountain Resort to the town of Estelí. It was west, not east.
match_headline: Revisiting Nicaragua, This Time as a Tourist

text: An article last Sunday about the music scene in New Orleans described incorrectly the Music Box, a project from the group New Orleans Airlift. It consists of multiple structures, not a single cottage. And the article misidentified one of the musicians who visited the venue. He is Dickie Landry, a founding member of the Philip Glass Ensemble; Mr. Glass himself did not visit.
match_headline: Experiencing New Orleans With Fresh Eyes and Ears

text: An article on Tuesday about the role the French government has played in the increasing popularity of the comedian Dieudonné M’bala M’bala by repeatedly charging him with violating anti-hate laws misstated, in some editions, the year that the death of a French Muslim man, mentioned in one of Mr. M’bala M’bala’s videos, occurred. It was in 2010, not 2006.
match_headline: For Hateful Comic in France, Muzzle Becomes a Megaphone

text: An article on Wednesday about the effect the Libyan government’s failure to seize an oil tanker carrying an illicit cargo of oil had on the ouster of the country’s prime minister misstated the title of Badr H. Jafar of Crescent Petroleum, an oil and gas company in the United Arab Emirates. He is the company’s president, not its chairman.
match_headline: Libya’s Prime Minister Ousted in Chaos Over Tanker

text: An article on Friday about a crash at the South by Southwest festival in Austin that has raised concerns over whether the event has become too big misspelled, in some editions, part of the name of a boutique hotel, whose owner commented on the incident, which killed two people and injured 23. It is the Saint Cecilia, not Saint Cecelia.
match_headline: After Fatal Crash, Soul-Searching for South by Southwest

text: A picture credit in some editions on Friday about the search for survivors in the rubble of two buildings that collapsed in Harlem on Wednesday misidentified the photographer. Victor J. Blue, not Todd Heisler, took the picture of workers clearing debris.
match_headline: In 2 East Harlem Buildings Leveled by Explosion, Lives Entwined as in Bygone Era

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Monday about the work ahead for General Motors after its recall of 1.6 million vehicles referred incorrectly to the connection between the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration and Toyota’s recall of millions of vehicles in 2009 and 2010. While the safety agency had received numerous consumer complaints about unintended acceleration in the vehicles, it did not order the recall.
match_headline: Now Comes Hard Part for G.M.: The Repairs

text: An article on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about the growing popularity of outdoor food courts with meals provided by food trucks misstated part of the address of Dinin’ Hall, one such open-air cafeteria in Columbus, Ohio. It is 400 West Rich, not West Ridge.
match_headline: A Place to Park and Cook Up a Storm

text: An article on Wednesday about Medicare Advantage insurance plans misidentified part of the insured person’s financial responsibility in Medicare Part B coverage. It is a 20 percent coinsurance payment, not a 20 percent co-payment. Co-payments are fixed dollar amounts.
match_headline: Medicare Changes Prompt Enrollees to Reconsider Plans

text: An article on Saturday about the wording of the ballot for a referendum on the status of the Crimea region misidentified the Ukrainian city that, along with Crimea, held the referendum. It was Sevastopol, not Stavropol.
match_headline: 2 Choices in Crimea Referendum, but Neither Is ‘No’

text: An article on Thursday about the threat posed to the Middle East peace talks by rocket attacks on Israel by militants from the Gaza Strip and retaliatory Israeli strikes misspelled the given name and the surname of a teacher who lives on an Israeli kibbutz east of Gaza. She is Adele Raemer, not Adel Ramer.
match_headline: Gaza-Israel Escalation Threatens Cease-Fire

text: An article on Sunday about water that was pumped from coal ash ponds at a power plant owned by Duke Energy at the head of the Cape Fear River in North Carolina described the site’s location incorrectly. Though the plant is indeed near Raleigh, it is not upriver of the city. (Cape Fear River passes to the southwest of the city.)
match_headline: Questions as More Wastewater Flows in North Carolina

text: An article on Thursday about a possible replacement for the Pap cervical cancer screening test erroneously included, in some editions, a company among those that sell a test to detect human papillomavirus, the cause of the disease, in the United States. BD sells such a test in Europe, but its test has not been approved for use in the United States.
match_headline: F.D.A. Panel Recommends Replacement for the Pap Test

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a Canadian inquiry into an ignition-switch defect that was linked to a fatal crash in June involving a General Motors vehicle misstated, in some copies, Canada’s rank among General Motors’ global markets. Canada is the automaker’s seventh-largest market, not its second-largest.
match_headline: Canada Explores G.M. Link to Accidents

text: An article on Monday about “Mondays With Marlo,” a weekly talk show starring Marlo Thomas, referred incorrectly in some copies to the significance of Chelsea Clinton’s coming appearance on the show. She will be the program’s 100th guest; she will not be a guest on the 100th show. An accompanying picture caption repeated the error in all editions.
match_headline: Marlo Thomas Carves a Niche on Internet TV

text: Because of an editing error, the attribution for the Quotation of the Day on Monday, taken from a front-page article about the unskilled contract laborers who have been dispatched to clean up and decommission the meltdown-ravaged Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, misstated, in some editions, the given name of the founder of Tohoku Enterprise, a company that maintains nuclear power plants. As the article correctly noted, he is Yukiteru Naka, not Teruyuki.
match_headline: Unskilled and Destitute Are Hiring Targets for Fukushima Cleanup

text: An obituary in some editions on Sunday about the comedian David Brenner misstated the time period during which he started doing comedy. It was in the late 1960s, not the early 1970s. And a more complete version of the obituary in Monday’s editions omitted a credit. Emma G. Fitzsimmons contributed reporting.
match_headline: David Brenner, Stand-up Comic of the Little Things in Life, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on Sunday about Melba Hernández, a longtime associate of Fidel Castro, misstated the name of a political party to which she belonged. It was the Ortodoxo Party, not the Orthodoxos Party.
match_headline: Melba Hernández, a Confidante of Castro From First Volley, Is Dead at 92

text: Because of an editing error, the Cancale Journal article last Wednesday, about efforts by a French businessman to coax fishermen as well as municipalities in the Brittany region of France to sell an invasive species of sea snail, the Atlantic slipper shell, for consumption misattributed a quotation about the shell. It was Frederic Baslé, the owner of a seafood cart at Port de la Houle — not Pierrick Clément, a local food entrepreneur who has been promoting the shellfish — who said, “The shell is just not that pretty.”
ref_headline: The shell is just not that pretty.
match_headline: In France, a Quest to Convert a Sea Snail Plague Into a Culinary Pleasure

text: An article on Saturday about plans by Modesto, Calif., to bring about 1,800 acres of Wood Colony under its jurisdiction misstated the level of professional baseball played by the city’s minor league team, which is named the Nuts. It is Class A, not AAA. (The Wood Colony Nut Company is part of the 1,800-acre community.)
match_headline: A Timeless California Enclave Fears a City’s Sway

text: An article in some editions on March 11 about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s appearance on MSNBC’s “Morning Joe” described incorrectly Mr. de Blasio’s actions regarding three charter schools. The mayor rescinded an offer by the city to give them space in public school buildings; he did not actually “close” the charter schools, which did not exist. (As the article noted elsewhere, the schools had been approved by the Bloomberg administration, but they never opened.)
match_headline: Tense Moments in de Blasio’s TV Interview

text: An article in some editions on March 6 about the winners of this year’s New York Times College Scholarships misidentified the City Council member for whom Eun Byoul Oh, one of the award recipients, worked. He is Paul Vallone — not Peter F. Vallone Jr. (Paul and Peter are brothers.)
match_headline: 10 Students Who Overcame Odds Are Awarded Times Scholarships

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the Federal Reserve’s $79.6 billion payment to the federal Treasury, representing profits from its investments in Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities, described the Fed’s relationship to the Treasury incorrectly. The Fed invests in Treasuries, but it does not buy them from the Treasury. It is thus not “lending to the Treasury.”
match_headline: Fed Transferred $79.6 Billion in Earnings to the Treasury Last Year

text: An article on the Itineraries page on Tuesday about some airlines’ use of technology to improve personal service erroneously included some social media platforms among those monitored by Qantas Airways in its airport lounges. While those platforms do include Facebook, Foursquare and Instagram, they do not include LinkedIn and Pinterest. The article also referred incorrectly to the way Qantas monitors Twitter posts. It spots posts in which a user mentions the airline by name or in a hashtag, not necessarily those sent from one of its lounges.
match_headline: Airlines Use Digital Technology to Get Even More Personal

text: An article on Tuesday about CNN’s heavy investment in coverage of the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 misidentified, in some copies, the network for which Judy Muller, a journalism professor at the University of Southern California who commented on the coverage, was once a correspondent. She worked for ABC, not for NBC.
match_headline: CNN’s Ratings Surge Covering the Mystery of the Missing Airliner

text: An article on Monday previewing the East Region of the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament misstated the number of years since Virginia earned a No. 1 seed in the tournament. It has been 31 years, not 21.
match_headline: East: Unselfish and Deep

text: An obituary last Wednesday about the journalist Joe McGinniss misidentified a newspaper where he worked early in his career. It was The Worcester Telegram, not The Worcester Telegram & Gazette. (The Telegram and the Evening Gazette later merged, but they were separate newspapers at the time.)
match_headline: Joe McGinniss, 71, Dies; Chronicled Politics and Sensational Crime

text: An article on March 7 about problems that states have encountered in shifting to privately managed long-term care programs misstated one reason Minnesota was criticized for its handling of the transition. The state came under congressional fire for shifting state costs to Medicaid, which has partial federal funding — not for shifting Medicaid costs to federal Medicare.
match_headline: Pitfalls Seen in a Turn to Privately Run Long-Term Care

text: An article on March 5 about Syria’s progress in shipping its most toxic chemical weapons out of the country referred incorrectly to the mustard gas in its arsenal. While it is dangerous because it is the only chemical agent in the arsenal that can be put to use quickly without having to be mixed with other materials, it is usually nonlethal, and therefore not its “most deadly agent.” (Sarin, which can kill within 10 minutes, is the country’s most deadly chemical weapon.)
match_headline: Syria Speeds Its Deliveries of Chemicals for Disposal

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Thursday with an article about the two buildings in East Harlem that were destroyed in an explosion misidentified, in some editions, the street that intersects East 116th Street where residents from buildings near the explosion site waited for word on the situation. It is Madison Avenue, not Park Avenue.
match_headline: Standing for More Than a Century, Only to Vanish in an Instant

text: An article on March 7 about the cancellation of a book deal for a Twitter user who wrote about supposed conversations overheard in the elevators at Goldman Sachs rendered his surname incorrectly. He is John LeFevre, not Lefevre. The error also occurred in articles on Feb. 25 and Feb. 26 , and was repeated in an editorial on Feb. 27.
match_headline: Author’s Unmasking Won’t Stop Book

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the San Diego State basketball player Xavier Thames misstated the date of the photograph and described it incorrectly. Thames was shown cutting down the net after San Diego State won the regular-season Mountain West Conference title on March 8, not “after San Diego State won the conference tournament title Saturday.” (New Mexico, not San Diego State, won the conference tournament.)
ref_headline: after San Diego State won the conference tournament title Saturday.
match_headline: For Aztecs’ Leader, Court Is No Place to Run Scared

text: Because of an editing error, an entry about the 100th episode of “Glee” in the What’s on Tuesday television highlights in some editions on Tuesday misspelled the given name of an actress in the episode. She is Dianna Agron, not Diana. The entry also erroneously included one actor among popular guests reprising their roles. Chace Crawford’s appearance on “Glee” was his first.
match_headline: What’s on Tuesday

text: An article last Thursday about homeowners in California who are switching away from traditional lawns because of a continuing drought described incorrectly Hill and Dale, which installed drought-resistant plants for a homeowner. It is a landscaping company, not a landscape architecture firm.
match_headline: Brown Is the New Green

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Thursday about wider acceptance of transgendered people misstated the surname of a longtime New York Times critic who reviewed a photo exhibition at the Whitney Biennial by a transgender couple. He is Holland Cotter, not Carter.
match_headline: In Their Own Terms

text: An article on Tuesday about college courses intended to help professionals navigate the Affordable Care Act misstated the role of Dylan Roby, an assistant professor, in a new online certificate program for medical professionals offered by UCLA Extension, called Transformational Leadership in Health Care. He created the introductory course for the program, not the whole program.
match_headline: New Health Law Is Sending Many Back to School

text: An article on Tuesday about online courses described the operation of futurelearn.com incorrectly. According to the company, it is a web platform, not an aggregator. The article also described the scope of the company’s operations incorrectly. It has partners in the Britain and other countries; it does not focus on Britain and Commonwealth countries.
match_headline: What Color Is Your Online Adult Course?

text: An article on Thursday about a judge’s decision ordering federal election officials to help Kansas and Arizona require proof of citizenship in voter registration misstated, in some editions, the extent of the ruling. The decision affects voters in elections on three levels — federal, state and local — not just state and local. The article also misstated the Congressional action on the National Voter Registration Act, the interpretation of which was the basis of the ruling. The measure was enacted — not signed — by Congress in 1993. (The signing of legislation remains the job of the president.)
match_headline: Two States Win Court Approval on Voter Rules

text: An article on Wednesday about Secret, a new social media app that carries only anonymous comments, misstated its status on Google Play charts. Because the app is not yet available for Android, it is not ranked at all on Google Play; it is not the case that it is “not highly ranked.”
match_headline: New Social App Has Juicy Posts, All Anonymous

text: An article on March 4 about the concerns of India’s Muslims over the rise of Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist whose relations with Muslims have been charged, overstated what is known about a 2002 train fire in Gujarat State that killed 58 Hindu pilgrims. While the Gujarat government, headed by Mr. Modi, concluded that the fire was a Muslim attack, that finding has been disputed by a central government investigation, which concluded that the fire was an accident.
match_headline: India’s Muslims Wary of Rising Political Star

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 13 about unrest in Turkey following the death of a boy who was injured by a police tear gas canister misstated part of the name of Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s party. It is the Justice and Development Party, not the Justice and Freedom Party.
match_headline: Across Turkey, New Unrest as Teenage Boy Is Buried

text: An article in some editions on March 8 about tensions that typically arise when restaurants are planned on parkland misstated the position of Richard N. Gottfried, a state assemblyman, on how the New York City parks department was proceeding with a planned restaurant in Union Square Park. He said that because the restaurant is not a park use, the land would have to be declassified as such by the State Legislature; he does not want the Legislature to approve the declassification.
match_headline: Debate Over Park Eateries Is Older Than Aged Wine

text: An article on Wednesday about Tiger Woods’s withdrawal this week from the Arnold Palmer Invitational, using information from the PGA Tour, referred incorrectly to Adam Scott’s chances of taking the No. 1 ranking from Woods, who dropped out because of a back injury. If Scott were to win this weekend, he could gain ground on Woods, but he would not become No. 1.
match_headline: Bad Back Forces Woods From Palmer Event

text: A picture on March 13 with an article about research on wisdom and aging carried an erroneous credit. The photograph, of the psychologist Erik Erikson and his wife, Joan, in 1988, was taken by Sarah Putnam for The New York Times; it was not by a Times staff photographer.
match_headline: The Science of Older and Wiser

text: An obituary on Thursday about the former Democratic Party chairman and White House official Robert S. Strauss misidentified the president who awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom. It was Jimmy Carter, not Ronald Reagan.
match_headline: Robert S. Strauss, Presidential Confidant and Deal Maker, Dies at 95

text: An obituary last Saturday about Jack A. Kinzler, the longtime chief of the Technical Services Center at NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, misstated the date that an American flag whose staff Mr. Kinzler designed was planted on the moon. It was July 20, 1969, not July 21.
match_headline: Jack Kinzler, Whose Ingenuity Saved Skylab, Dies at 94

text: An article on Wednesday about the wish of some younger Palestinians, including the son of the Palestinian Authority president, President Mahmoud Abbas, to resolve the Arab-Israeli conflict by creating one state that would include both Jews and Arabs misstated the demographics of the area between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea. There are slightly more Jews than Arabs living there, not the other way around.
match_headline: A Divide Among Palestinians on a Two-State Solution

text: A picture last Saturday with the Saturday Profile article , about Mikhlif Al-Shammari, a Saudi human rights activist who supports equal treatment for the kingdom’s Shiite Muslims, was published in error. The photograph was of Salman al-Awda, a Saudi cleric and Muslim scholar, not of Mr. Shammari.
match_headline: Saudi’s Lonely, Costly Bid for Sunni-Shiite Equality

text: A picture caption on March 11 with an article about a prisoner swap between the Syrian government and insurgents referred imprecisely to the service attended after the exchange by a group of Greek Orthodox nuns who were among those released. The Greek Orthodox Church calls its Eucharistic service a liturgy, not a Mass.
match_headline: Release of Syrian Nuns Was Part of a Hostage Swap

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about a civil rights lawsuit filed against the developer of two Manhattan buildings over access for disabled and visually impaired residents misstated the age of the buildings. One Carnegie Hill was finished in 2006 and TriBeCa Green in 2005; they are not both 23 years old.
match_headline: Suit Alleges Developer Violated Civil Rights

text: An article last Saturday about China’s cracking down on the issuance of virtual credit cards misstated the issuer of Q Coin, a digital currency. It was the chat service Tencent, not the e-commerce company Alibaba.
match_headline: China Puts a Stop to Plans for Virtual Credit Cards

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with a review of the Martha Graham Dance Company, at City Center in Manhattan, misstated the surname of the dancer shown at the left. As the review correctly noted, he is Lloyd Mayor, not Manor.
match_headline: Tales of Legends and Curiosities

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about a new Gagosian gallery on Park Avenue misstated the number of sculptures by the Swiss artist Urs Fischer that will be on display at the first show there, next month. There will be one work by Mr. Fischer, not multiple sculptures.
match_headline: A Collector Changes Course

text: An article last Sunday about the appointment of Kathryn Garcia as sanitation commissioner misstated, in some editions, the distance Ms. Garcia lives from her mother in Park Slope. She is two blocks away, not two doors.
match_headline: De Blasio Picks Sanitation Commissioner

text: Because of an editing error, the Off the Dribble N.B.A. notebook last Sunday about the Chicago Bulls’ center Joakim Noah misidentified the team that received three draft picks in the trade that sent Luol Deng to the Cleveland Cavaliers and Andrew Bynum to the Bulls. The Bulls received the picks, not the Cavaliers.
match_headline: Behind the Bulls’ Surge, a Center Playing Like Chamberlain

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about cruise lines that are taking a fresh approach to onboard entertainment misidentified the ship on which the musical “Rock of Ages” is being shown. As the article correctly noted, Norwegian Cruise Lines’ new Breakaway features the musical; the Celebrity, which is a cruise line, not a ship, does not stage the musical.
match_headline: Cruise Quest: Keeping the Entertainment Fresh

text: An article last Sunday about trends in cruising misstated  part of the name of one of the Pandaw River Expeditions ships in Myanmar expected to be launched by the end of the year. It is the Kha Byoo Pandaw, not the Rha Byoo Pandaw.
match_headline: 6 Trends in Cruising

text: An article on March 2 about bringing extinct animals back to life misidentified the position Jacob Sherkow holds at Stanford. He is a fellow there, not a law professor.
match_headline: The Mammoth Cometh

text: An article on March 2 about the Democratic strategist Chris Lehane misspelled part of the name of the university from which John Pérez, the speaker of the California State Assembly and a target of one of Lehane’s campaigns, dropped out. It is the University of California, Berkeley — not Berkley.
match_headline: Chris Lehane Out-Washingtons Washington

text: A review last Sunday about the Mercedes-Benz CLA250 referred incorrectly to the company’s front-drive models. While the CLA is the first front-drive Mercedes sold in the United States, it is not the first in North America.
match_headline: Benz on a Budget, Angling for Youngsters

text: A picture caption on March 9 with an article about the sculptor Erwin Wurm misidentified the subject of a portrait by Andy Warhol shown hanging in the study of Mr. Wurm’s home in Austria. It depicts Karen Lerner, not Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis.
match_headline: The Shape Shifter

text: An article on March 9 about challenges faced by Ukraine’s interim government in fixing the economy and establishing legitimacy misstated the title of Pavlo Sheremeta at one point. As the article initially noted, he is the new minister of the economy — not the minister of finance, a post held by Oleksandr Shlapak.
match_headline: Ukraine’s Fight to Fix Economy Is Also a Fight for Legitimacy

text: An article on Wednesday about problems Crimea may face, judging from those South Ossetia has encountered since Russia declared it independent of the Republic of Georgia in 2008, misstated the middle initial of an analyst at the Carnegie Moscow Center, who noted Russia may find Crimea hard to manage. He is Aleksei V. Malashenko, not Aleksei A.
match_headline: If History Is a Guide, Crimeans’ Celebration May Be Short-Lived

text: An article on Thursday about a tracking system that has reduced the time between arrest and arraignment in criminal courts misstated the middle initial of the judge who is the administrator for New York City’s criminal courts. He is Barry M. Kamins, not Barry A.
match_headline: New York Courts Cut Time Between Arrest and Arraignment

text: An article on Thursday about museums’ online programming misstated the status of Emily Graslie when she was hired last year to create a video series for the Field Museum in Chicago. She was a recent graduate of the University of Montana, not a student.
match_headline: If You Can’t Make It to the Lecture

text: An article on Thursday about an exhibit at the New-York Historical Society on black professional and amateur basketball teams from the first half of the 20th century misstated part of the name of a Harlem athletic club that had such a team. It was the Alpha Physical Culture Club, not the Alpha Physical Culture Society.
match_headline: Remembering the ‘Black Fives’ of Pro Basketball

text: An article on Thursday about “The International Exhibition of Sherlock Holmes” misstated part of the name of the museum where the exhibition made its debut last year. It is the Oregon Museum of Science and Industry, not the Oregon Museum of Science and Technology.
ref_headline: The International Exhibition of Sherlock Holmes
match_headline: Entering World of Literature’s Great Sleuth

text: An article on Thursday about “American Cool,” an exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, omitted part of name of the institution represented by Frank H. Goodyear III, one of the curators of the exhibition. He is the co-director of the Bowdoin College Museum of Art, not of the Bowdoin College of Art.
match_headline: In Washington, 100 Examples of the Epitome of Cool

text: An article on Thursday about the closing of the Higgins Armory Museum in Worcester, Mass., and the display of much of its collection at the Worcester Art Museum misstated part of the name of a journalism organization involved in the exhibition. It is the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting, not the Pulitzer Center for Crisis Reporting.
match_headline: What Comes Next, After the Troops Are Dismissed

text: An obituary on Friday about the Iran-contra prosecutor Lawrence E. Walsh, using information from a family spokesman, misstated the name of one of Mr. Walsh’s daughters, who survives him. She is Janet Walsh Larson, not Janet Maxine Walsh.
match_headline: Lawrence E. Walsh, Prosecutor in Iran-Contra Scandal, Dies at 102

text: An article on Sunday about Senator Rand Paul’s increased fundraising referred incorrectly to the fundraising activities of Marco Rubio, a Florida Republican who like Mr. Paul was elected in 2010 and is considering a White House bid. Between Mr. Paul’s Senate re-election committee and his political action committee he raised $4.4 million last year, which is $500,000 more than Mr. Rubio raised with his Senate re-election committee and his political action committee. But a third group controlled by Mr. Rubio, a joint fundraising committee called the Rubio Victory Committee, was not included in those calculations; when that amount is included, Mr. Rubio raised about $8.3 million in 2013.
match_headline: Paul Has Ideas, but His Backers Want 2016 Plan

text: An article on Friday about new federal prohibitions on the ivory trade in the United States, to take effect this summer, erroneously included walrus tusks as a form of ivory that would be affected. They are governed by separate restrictions already in place.
match_headline: Limits on Ivory Sales, Meant to Protect Elephants, Set Off Wide Concerns

text: An article on Monday about General Motors’ use of social media to help manage customer complaints after its recall of 1.6 million cars misidentified an Alabama law school student who complained to G.M. about her Saturn Ion. She is Deborah Garrett, not Samantha Garrett.
match_headline: G.M. Uses Social Media to Manage Customers and Its Reputation

text: An article on Monday about lobbyists and lawyers hired by Sotheby’s and Christie’s to fight a bill that would give visual artists or their estates part of the profits when works are resold at public auctions misidentified the president under whom one lawyer, Paul D. Clement, served as solicitor general. He served under George W. Bush, not President Obama. Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the article erroneously included Christie’s as an auction house that has hired the Podesta Group to help defeat the bill. The group was hired by Sotheby’s, not Sotheby’s and Christie’s.
match_headline: Lobbyists Set to Fight Royalty Bill for Artists

text: An article on Thursday about efforts by art museums to attract a new generation of benefactors incorrectly included the Detroit Institute of Arts among financially ailing museums that are under pressure to sell art from their collections to help fund their operations. While the Art Institute faced the threat of having part of its city-owned art collection sold, the money from the sale would have gone to the city in its bankruptcy proceedings, not to the museum itself. The article also referred incompletely to the source of pledges intended to avert such a sale. The pledges came from local and national foundations as well as from the museum itself, not just from local groups.
match_headline: Wooing a New Generation of Museum Patrons

text: An obituary on Sunday about Gene Feist, the founder of the Roundabout Theater Company, misstated the year that his twin brother, Harold, died. It was 1997, not 1977.
match_headline: Gene Feist, Founder of Roundabout Theater Company, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Russia’s ouster from the Group of 8 at a meeting in The Hague misidentified, at one point, the geographical area Russia has annexed. It is the Crimean region, not the nation of Ukraine. A picture caption with the article also referred incorrectly to the leaders that President Obama met in The Hague. Most are heads of government, not heads of state.
match_headline: Russia Is Ousted From Group of 8 by U.S. and Allies

text: An article on Sunday about the National Security Agency’s infiltration of the servers of a Chinese telecommunications company considered by the United States to be a security threat misspelled, in two instances, the name of the company. It is Huawei, not Huawai.
match_headline: N.S.A. Breached Chinese Servers Seen as Security Threat

text: An article on Friday about how the Ukraine crisis has highlighted divisions in Europe misstated the timing of the admission of the Baltic states and Poland relative to their admission to NATO. They joined NATO first, then the European Union, not the other way around.
match_headline: Ukraine Upheaval Highlights E.U.’s Past Miscalculations and Future Dangers

text: An article on Tuesday about passage of legislation in Georgia that would ease restrictions on guns misstated in some editions the name of a federal agency opposed to the measure. It is the Transportation Security Administration, not the Transportation Safety Authority.
match_headline: Amid Wave of Pro-Gun Legislation, Georgia Proposes Sweeping Law

text: An article on March 2 about the Clubhouse, a collective in Ditmas Park, Brooklyn, that is home to artists and musicians who want to help sell their borough’s image, misspelled the name of the state in Mexico where Daniel Garcia, a musician, grew up. It is Coahuila, not Couhila.
match_headline: Brooklyn Communal Cool: The Brand

text: An article on Saturday about efforts by the Detroit Symphony and other orchestras and opera companies to attract audiences by web streaming performances misidentified the organization of which Deborah F. Rutter, who commented on the need for new approaches, is president. It is the Chicago Symphony Orchestra Association, which oversees the orchestra and related entities, not the Chicago Symphony.
match_headline: Detroit Symphony Dives Headlong Into Streaming

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on March 17 with a critic’s notebook article about the South by Southwest festival misidentified a member of the band the Strypes. He is Ross Farrelly, not Josh McClorey, another member of the band.
match_headline: Big Money Upends a Festival

text: An article on Tuesday about workplace age discrimination misidentified the position for which Ingrid Hassani was hired at Scripps Health. She is a department care manager, not a department case manager.
match_headline: Discriminate Against the Old? Even the Old Do It

text: An obituary on Friday about the Indian diplomat, author and journalist Khushwant Singh referred incorrectly to his birthplace, Hadali. It is a village in the Thal Desert, not the Thar Desert, although Mr. Singh himself identified it as the Thar Desert in his autobiography, “Truth, Love & a Little Malice,” and it is in what is now Punjab Province in Pakistan, not Baluchistan Province.
match_headline: Khushwant Singh, Provocative Indian Journalist, Dies at 99

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the growing popularity of aggressive playthings and weaponry for girls paraphrased incorrectly a comment by the child psychologist Sharon Lamb. She said that toys that allow aggression were healthy for children; she did not say toys that “stimulate” aggression were healthy.
match_headline: Today’s Girls Love Pink Bows as Playthings, but These Shoot

text: An article on Monday about the gains made by the far-right National Front party in French municipal elections misstated the size of a half-dozen cities where National Front candidates were leading. They had populations of more than 10,000, not less.
match_headline: Far-Right Party Stirs Municipal Elections in France

text: An article on Tuesday about a federal judge’s rebuking the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Department in Arizona for its response to a court order to stop singling out Latinos misstated the job of a sheriff’s employee whose shooting death was cited during the hearing. The employee was a detention officer, not a deputy sheriff.
match_headline: Angry Judge Says Sheriff Defied Order on Latinos

text: An article on Tuesday about a custody battle for the granddaughter of Jerry Remy, the longtime color announcer for the Boston Red Sox, misstated, in some editions, Mr. Remy’s whereabouts on Sunday. He was in the broadcast booth (though largely silent) for Sunday’s game; it is not the case that he was absent.
match_headline: Case Spurs Fan Debate Over Boston Announcer

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the Crime Scene column on Jan. 18, about a man in a wheelchair who was stranded in a snowstorm after a trip to a police station, misspelled his given name. He is Fredrick Brennan, not Frederick. (This correction was delayed because the error was found during research for a follow-up column.)
match_headline: City Newcomer Is Let Down by a Stranger, Then the Police

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about efforts to sign people up for health insurance this year as the deadline for doing so approaches misidentified one of the people seeking health care enrollees in Denver. She is Jeannie Torres, not Meghan McMahon.
match_headline: Insurers Push to Enroll People as Health Care Deadline Nears

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Thursday about L’Wren Scott misidentified the musicians who had performed with her boyfriend, Mick Jagger, on “Saturday Night Live” in 2012. They were not the rest of the Rolling Stones.
match_headline: For L’Wren Scott, Her Identity Was by Design

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the reluctance of countries involved in the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 to share technology even as they cooperate in the operation referred incorrectly in some editions to a plane pictured, based on information supplied by Getty Images. It was landing at Pearce Air Force Base near Perth, Australia; it was not returning from the search for Flight 370.
match_headline: Search for Lost Jet Is Complicated by Geopolitics and Rivalries

text: An article on Thursday about a proposal for winding down Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and overhauling the nation’s housing finance system misstated how taxpayers would be affected in another crisis if there were higher loss requirements for the mortgage lending system’s private backers. In that case, mortgages would be more expensive and taxpayers would be less vulnerable to bailouts, not “more vulnerable.” The article also misstated the job title of Gary Kalman of the Center for Responsible Lending, who commented on the proposal. He is executive vice president, not executive director.
match_headline: Proposed Housing Bill Would Create a Co-op of Mortgage Lenders

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Rangers’ 4-3 overtime victory over the Phoenix Coyotes the previous day misstated, in some copies, the time left in regulation when Dan Girardi scored the tying goal for the Rangers. It was 3 minutes 28 seconds, not 3:18. The article also misstated, in some copies, the day Henrik Lundqvist broke Ed Giacomin’s club record for shutouts. It was Saturday, not Sunday.
match_headline: After Honoring Lundqvist, Sluggish Rangers Rally for a Stirring Victory

text: An article last Sunday about the resignation of Gordon D. Fox as speaker of the Rhode Island House misidentified his hometown. It is Providence (on the east side), not East Providence.
match_headline: Rhode Island House Speaker Resigns Amid Investigation

text: An article last Sunday about entrepreneurs who have left their native France referred incorrectly to Milestone Capital Partners, the firm that employs Erick Rinner, a French executive who has lived in London for 20 years. Milestone is a British-French private equity firm, not a British-based investment bank.
match_headline: Au Revoir, Entrepreneurs

text: A picture caption on March 16 with the Playlist CD review column confused the three members of the Bad Plus. From left to right in the photograph, they are Dave King, Ethan Iverson and Reid Anderson — not Mr. Iverson, Mr. Anderson and Mr. King.
match_headline: A Beating Heart, a Social Conscience and a Deluge of Ideas

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Rangers’ 2-0 victory over the Devils the day before misstated the number of games the Devils had left in the season after the loss. It was 11, not 10.
match_headline: Lundqvist Breaks Another Record in a Key Win

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about flex, a street dance style that is the subject of a documentary by Deidre Schoo, misspelled the nickname of a veteran dancer. He is Bones, not Bone.
match_headline: They’ve Got Moves

text: Because of an editing error, a headline on an article last Sunday about a long-running effort by the State Assembly speaker, Sheldon Silver, and his ally William E. Rapfogel to prevent the construction of low-income housing on a lot on the Lower East Side misstated, in some editions, the length of time the two men worked together to keep the lot vacant. It was nearly four decades, not 47 years. (The lot has been vacant for 47 years.)
match_headline: They Kept a Lower East Side Lot Vacant for Decades

text: An article last Sunday about long-forgotten places in Southern California misstated the extent of the landmass of California City, whose subdivisions are now mostly empty, in the Mojave Desert. The town covers 130,000 acres — not 80,000 square feet, which is 1.84 acres.
match_headline: Exploring Modern Ruins in Southern California

text: A review on March 9 about “Blood Will Out,” Walter Kirn’s memoir of his relationship with Christian Gerhartsreiter, a man who posed for years as a member of the Rockefeller family, misidentified the establishment in Boston at which Gerhartsreiter secured Kirn a room. It was the Algonquin Club, not the “Athenaeum Club.” (There is no Athenaeum Club in Boston; the Boston Athenaeum is a membership library, not a social club.)
match_headline: The Journalist and the Masquerader

text: An article on March 9 about changes in the SAT referred incorrectly to two universities’ policies on the SAT. The test is not optional at the University of Georgia or at Johns Hopkins. The same article erroneously attributed a distinction to Wake Forest University. It was the first Top 30 national university in the U.S. News & World Report college rankings to announce a test-optional admissions policy; it was not the first educational institution to do so. (Several institutions adopted a test-optional policy before Wake Forest.)
match_headline: The Story Behind the SAT Overhaul

text: An article last Sunday about the Salon Doré from the Hôtel de La Trémoille, which is being restored at the Legion of Honor museum in San Francisco, misstated its square footage. It is 625 square feet, not 25.
match_headline: Its Art Elsewhere, a Museum Tries to Stay Relevant

text: A news analysis last Sunday about computer models that predict conflict within and between countries misidentified the university where Kalev H. Leetaru is based. It is Georgetown University, not George Washington University.
match_headline: Spreadsheets and Global Mayhem

text: An article on Friday about the firing of nine Air Force missile launch officers in a cheating inquiry misidentified the command of Col. Donald Holloway. He was a group commander, not a wing commander.
match_headline: Air Force Fires 9 Officers in Scandal Over Cheating on Proficiency Tests

text: An article on Thursday about an Oklahoma judge ruling that the state could not keep secret the identities of the suppliers of lethal-injection drugs misstated in some editions the age of the girl killed in 1997 by Charles Warner, one of the inmates filing the suit. The girl was 11 months old, not 11 years.
match_headline: Oklahoma Told It Can’t Shield Suppliers of Execution Drugs

text: An article on Wednesday about the death of Jason Echevarria, a mentally ill inmate at Rikers Island whose requests for help were ignored in his final hours, misstated, in some editions, the month he was arrested. It is September 2011, not July.
match_headline: Complaint by Fired Correction Officer Adds Details About a Death at Rikers Island

text: An article on Tuesday about the N.F.L. owners’ meetings this week used an outdated name for the division the Green Bay Packers won on the last day of the season. It is the N.F.C. North, not the N.F.C. Central, the name of the Packers’ division from 1967 to 2001.
match_headline: Goodell Holds Off on Discipline for Irsay and Dolphins Players

text: A chart on Monday with an article about the perilous state of New York City’s underground gas distribution network, using information filed by National Grid with a federal agency, misidentified the company’s gas distributor in Rhode Island. It is National Grid itself, not Niagara Mohawk Power Corp., which is a National Grid subsidiary in New York.
match_headline: Beneath Cities, a Decaying Tangle of Gas Pipes

text: An article on Friday about recovery efforts at the landslide in Oso, Wash., misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a coordinator for International K9 Search and Rescue Services. He is Harry Oakes, not Oaks.
match_headline: Mountain That Roared Down Turns Into a Tomb of Debris

text: An article on Wednesday about the Nets owner Mikhail D. Prokhorov’s tempering talk of the team becoming a Russian company misstated the percentage of N.B.A. owners that would have to approve such an ownership transfer. It is three-fourths, not two-thirds.
match_headline: Prokhorov Tempers Talk of Nets Becoming Russian

text: A listing of credits on Tuesday with a theater review of “Mothers and Sons,” at the John Golden Theater in Manhattan, misspelled the given name of a producer. She is Loraine Alterman Boyle, not Lorrain.
match_headline: Paths That Crossed Cross Again

text: An article on Wednesday about a Taliban assault on regional offices of Afghanistan’s Independent Election Commission a little more than a week before the country’s presidential election described the location of the attack incorrectly. It was in western Kabul, not eastern.
match_headline: Taliban Attack Stirs Security Concerns as Afghan Presidential Vote Nears

text: An article on Thursday about a proposal to install barriers on the Golden Gate Bridge as a way to reduce the number of suicides referred imprecisely to research published in 1978 by Richard H. Seiden, which examined whether people restrained from jumping off the bridge from 1937 to 1971 committed suicide elsewhere. While 90 percent did not subsequently commit suicide, not all of them were alive in 1978; some had died of natural causes.
match_headline: Suicides Mounting, Golden Gate Looks to Add a Safety Net

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the designation of an arts district in Astoria, Queens, described incorrectly the relationship between Kaufman Astoria Studios and the UA Kaufman Astoria movie theater nearby. The studio and the movie theater’s owner have a licensing agreement; Kaufman does not own the theater. (Forest City Ratner is the owner.) Also, a picture credit with the article, using information from a publicist, misstated the photographer’s given name. The picture, of a former Kaufman Astoria Studios building that was taken in 1983, was taken by Francene Keery, not Frances.
match_headline: In Astoria Arts District, a Once-Gritty Pocket Will Embody Culture

text: An article on Saturday about BlackBerry’s plan to supply software and services to manage private and public employees’ use of smartphones and tablets misstated the amount that a potential rival in that field, VMware, paid to acquire AirWatch, a provider of mobile management and security. It was $1.54 billion, not $1.81 billion.
match_headline: BlackBerry Sees Hope for Future in Security

text: An article in some editions on March 23 about Michigan’s 79-65 victory over Texas in the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament misstated, in some copies, the number of points Michigan’s Caris LeVert scored. It was 14, not 15.
match_headline: Michigan’s 3-Point Shooters Strike Early and Often Against Texas

text: An article on Monday about the publication of notebooks of the philosopher Martin Heidegger that shed new light on his Nazi beliefs misstated the title of Emmanuel Faye’s book on Heidegger and Nazism. It is “Heidegger: The Introduction of Nazism Into Philosophy,” not “Heidegger: The Injection of Nazism Into Philosophy.” And because of an editing error, the article referred imprecisely to the dates of a seminar from which student notes showed Heidegger speaking of “Semitic nomads” who will never understand the nature of “our German space.” It ran from 1933 to 1934, not “in 1933 or 1934.”
ref_headline: Heidegger: The Introduction of Nazism Into Philosophy,
match_headline: Heidegger’s Notebooks Renew Focus on Anti-Semitism

text: An obituary on Saturday about Felix Fibich, a modern dancer and choreographer who specialized in dances drawn from the Jewish heritage of Eastern Europe, misstated the year his wife, Judith Berg, died. It was 1992, not 1991. And the obituary also misstated the surname of Mr. Fibich’s companion. He is Jaya Pulami, not Palumi.
match_headline: Felix Fibich, Dancer and Choreographer, Dies at 96

text: An article on Tuesday about the sign-up frenzy leading up to the enrollment deadline for the Affordable Care Act misstated the number of telephone calls the federal insurance exchange call center received in the previous week. It was 2.5 million calls, not 2.5 calls.
match_headline: Health Care Signups Reach Frenzy in Final Day to Enroll

text: An article on Monday about the effect of the Affordable Care Act in Louisville, Ky., misstated the annual income of David Elson, a self-employed businessman who has been treated at Family Health Centers. It was $28,000 last year, not $22,000.
match_headline: In New Health Care Era, Blessings and Hurdles

text: An article on Friday about a dispute over whether to move a work by Picasso in the Seagram Building misidentified a board member of the Museum of Modern Art who objected to the building owner’s plan. The board member is Lewis B. Cullman, not Denise Peppas. The article also misstated part of the name of an organization involved in the dispute. It is the New York Landmarks Conservancy (not “Landmark” Conservancy). The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Fate of a Picasso at the Four Seasons Hangs on a Court Case

text: An article on March 19 about Greece’s deal with its foreign creditors on economic reforms necessary to unlock additional rescue funding described the nation’s primary budget surplus incorrectly. It is the surplus before debt payments, not after.
match_headline: Greece Reaches Deal to Release Foreign Rescue Funds

text: An article on Monday about Apple’s patent infringement case against Samsung, using information from Samsung, misstated the number of jurors hearing the case. It is eight, not four.
match_headline: Apple’s War on Samsung Has Google in Crossfire

text: An article on Saturday about the last N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament game at Madison Square Garden before this year, which was played in 1961, described incorrectly the history between the game’s two coaches, Joe Lapchick of St. John’s and Bones McKinney of Wake Forest. They had competed against each other in the N.B.A. — Lapchick as a coach and McKinney as a player and as a player-coach; they did not play against each other in the N.B.A.
match_headline: Remembering a Tournament ‘Final’ at the Garden

text: An article on Monday about Bo Ryan’s first trip to the Final Four as the men’s basketball coach at the University of Wisconsin misstated the number of times the team made it to the N.C.A.A. tournament’s Round of 8 in his first 12 seasons. It was once, in 2005, not twice.
match_headline: For Wisconsin Coach, the Lessons Sink In

text: An article last Wednesday about the baked goods inspired by the Cronut misidentified the owner of Almondine, a bakery in Dumbo, Brooklyn. He is Hervé Poussot, not Jacques Torres.
match_headline: A Real Treat or Half-Baked?

text: An article last Wednesday about bringing back virginica oysters to the Chesapeake Bay misidentified the organization that set up a demonstration oyster farm. It is the Chesapeake Bay Foundation at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science, not the Virginia Institute of Marine Science.
match_headline: A Chesapeake Homecoming

text: An obituary on Monday about the comedian and actor Eddie Lawrence referred incorrectly to his mother, the former Bess Garbowsky. She was a garment worker, not a full-time homemaker.
match_headline: Eddie Lawrence Dies at 95; Comedy’s ‘Old Philosopher’
