text: An article last Thursday about President Obama’s efforts to bolster the NATO alliance after Russia’s takeover of Crimea misstated the number of American soldiers buried at Flanders Field Cemetery in Belgium, where Mr. Obama, in a speech, evoked the clash of great powers that set off World War I, the conflict in which the Americans died, and defined the Cold War. There are 368 American soldiers buried at Flanders Field, not “thousands.”
match_headline: Obama Renewing U.S. Commitment to NATO Alliance

text: An article on Wednesday about the increased contact between people with mental illness and the criminal justice system misidentified, in some editions, a police department that tracks mentally ill people and helps them receive treatment. It is the police department in Los Angeles, not in New York.
match_headline: Police Confront Rising Number of Mentally Ill Suspects

text: An article on Tuesday about Teva’s efforts to stave off generic competition to its multiple sclerosis drug Copaxone misstated the status of the company’s generic version of the blood-thinning drug Lovenox. The application is still pending at the Food and Drug Administration; the generic version has not been approved.
match_headline: Supreme Court to Hear Appeal of Generic Drug Case

text: An article on Tuesday about the potential ricochet effect on London of sanctions against Russia because of its annexation of Crimea misstated the position of the Channel Islands in regard to the sanctions against Russia for its annexation of Crimea. While the islands are independent from Britain and the European Union, they have chosen to mirror the sanctions. It is not the case that Russian assets there are “beyond the reach of the sanctions.”
ref_headline: beyond the reach of the sanctions.
match_headline: Sanctions or Not, Russian Sway in London May Be Bluster

text: A critic’s notebook article on Saturday about the Chiara String Quartet, which has been memorizing works and performing them without sheet music, referred incompletely to the Brahms quintet it recorded with the violist Roger Tapping for a new album that includes the complete Brahms quartets. Brahms wrote two string quintets and it is the String Quintet No. 2 in G, not “the string quintet,” that the Chiara Quartet recorded with Mr. Tapping.
match_headline: Quartets Are Giving Music Stands a Rest

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with a theater review of “Red Velvet,” at St. Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn, misidentified an actor shown. He is Oliver Ryan — not Nic Jackman, another cast member.
match_headline: Grandeur Under Siege

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an obituary about the movie and television writer Lorenzo Semple Jr., using information from the agency Photofest, reversed the names of the actresses shown with Mr. Semple on the set of the movie “The Sporting Club.” Margaret Blye is at the left and Anne Ramsey at the right. Because of an editing error, the obituary referred incorrectly to the broadcast schedule of the “Batman” television show, which Mr. Semple created. It was shown twice a week from January 1966 to August 1967, but only once a week for the 1967-68 season; it did not run “for two years, twice a week.”
match_headline: Lorenzo Semple Jr., Creator of TV’s ‘Batman,’ Dies at 91

text: A chart on Wednesday with an article about United States auto sales in March misstated the sales report from the automaker Kia. The company’s sales rose 11.5 percent in March; they did not fall by that percentage.
match_headline: After Rough Winter, Auto Sales Jumped in March

text: An article on Thursday about Amazon’s new set-top box to stream video, games and other entertainment to customers’ television sets misstated part of the company’s content offerings. It offers several sports channels, not none.
match_headline: With Fire TV, Amazon Seeks a Beachhead in the Living Room

text: An article on Thursday about criticism of a strike by pilots at Lufthansa airlines referred incorrectly to Germany’s ranking in unemployment. At 5.1 percent, its jobless rate is the second-lowest in the European Union, not in Europe over all.
match_headline: For Many Germans, Pilots’ Walkout Crosses a Line

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with the Advertising column, about an Ikea campaign that involves sending a group of employees around the country to help families with redecorating projects, gave an incorrect surname from Ikea for a woman from Englewood, N.J., whose family is involved. She is Samantha Kirsch, not Kravitz.
match_headline: A Home Fixup Campaign for the Web

text: A headline on a report in the Business Briefing column on Thursday about an acquisition in the fuel-cell industry rendered one company’s name incorrectly in some copies. It is Plug Power, not Power Plug.
match_headline: Former Safety Agency Aides, Some Now Aiding the Car Industry

text: An article on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about the relocation of Cartier’s flagship Fifth Avenue store misstated the title of a company official. Emmanuel Perrin is president and chief executive of Cartier North America, not president and chief executive of Cartier International.
match_headline: Cartier Moves North From Perch on Fifth Avenue

text: An article on Wednesday about Tiger Woods’s withdrawal from this year’s Masters misstated the number of major golf tournaments won by Arnold Palmer. It is seven, not five.
match_headline: Back Surgery Puts Woods Out of the Masters for the First Time Since 1994

text: An obituary on March 7 about the biotechnology entrepreneur Alejandro Zaffaroni referred incorrectly to a scholarship he received in the last days of World War II. It was given through the Institute of International Education; it was not a Fulbright scholarship. (The Fulbright scholarship program is administered by the Institute of International Education but did not begin until 1946, after the war ended.)
match_headline: Alejandro Zaffaroni, Entrepreneur on Biotech Frontier, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Thursday about the sculptor Mon Levinson misspelled the surname of his wife. She is Joan Gruzen, not Gruzon. The obituary also misstated the given name of Mr. Levinson’s daughter. She is Nadia Levinson, not Adelaide.
match_headline: Mon Levinson, 88, Op Art Sculptor, Dies

text: An article on Wednesday about the victims of the mudslide in Washington State who lived on Steelhead Drive misstated, on first reference, the surname of a family that lived on the street. Members of the Satterlees family — not Sattlerlees — are missing and presumed dead.
match_headline: Steelhead Drive Is Gone After Mudslide, Along With Many Lives Lived on It

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about efforts by the New York City comptroller to standardize the handling of information technology contracts misstated, in some copies, the amount of a proposed settlement with Hewlett-Packard, which worked on the city’s 911 system. It is $6 million, not $6 billion.
match_headline: Stringer to Increase Oversight of New York City’s Computerization Contracts

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the state of the technology industry in New York City misstated the number of Citi jobs in New York City. The company has 17,000 jobs, not 11,000.
match_headline: Half of New York’s Tech Workers Lack College Degrees, Report Says

text: An article in some editions on March 6 about a video shown at Grand Central Terminal in honor of Chiune Sugihara, a Japanese official who helped Jews escape Lithuania during World War II, omitted an author of “The Fugu Plan,” a book about Mr. Sugihara’s efforts. Besides Marvin Tokayer, Mary Swartz also wrote the book.
match_headline: An Evacuation of Jews, With Help From Japan

text: An article on Friday about Anadarko Petroleum’s settlement of a toxic waste case brought by the Justice Department misstated at one point, and in some editions, the bankruptcy status of Tronox, a spinoff of Kerr-McGee, the Oklahoma energy and chemical company that is now a subsidiary of Anadarko. Tronox emerged from bankruptcy in 2011 and is publicly traded; it is not now bankrupt.
match_headline: Anadarko Pays Billions in Settling Toxins Case

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the University of Minnesota’s win over Southern Methodist University in the National Invitation Tournament final misidentified the coach who, after the game, called Larry Brown, S.M.U.’s basketball coach, a “phenomenal coach, but a really good person.” The comment was by Richard Pitino, Minnesota’s coach — not by his father, Rick, who coaches Louisville. Because of an editing error, the article misidentified, in some copies, the player who made two free throws with about six seconds left. He is Andre Hollins, not Austin Hollins, a teammate.
ref_headline: phenomenal coach, but a really good person.
match_headline: Gophers Give Their Pitino a Championship of His Own

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column last Saturday about the O, Miami Poetry Festival referred incorrectly to the poet Mary Ruefle and referred incompletely to a project involving cards that look like lottery tickets and have poems on them. Ms. Ruefle lives in Bennington, Vt.; she is not a “local poet.” And while she wrote and selected the poems, the artist Agustina Woodgate designed the cards.
match_headline: Getting Poetry to the People in Miami

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about the Pancreatic Cancer Research Walk in Manhattan on Sunday misstated the endpoint of the one- and three-mile walks. Each walk starts at Clinton Cove Park, at 55th Street and Hudson River Park, and also ends there — not at West 43rd Street or West 26th Street, which are the points where walkers will turn around.
match_headline: Spare Times for April 4-10

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about the writer Peter Matthiessen misstates the nature of the LSD-driven therapy he and his late wife, Deborah Love, took part in. They did it as a couple, not as part of a larger group.
match_headline: Peter Matthiessen’s Homegoing

text: An obituary on Friday about the artist Richard Black, who illustrated the original Mr. Clean, misstated the year of birth in some editions. As the headline and the obituary correctly noted, he was 92; therefore he was born in 1921, on Oct. 10 — not in 1912.
match_headline: Richard Black, 92, Artist Who Conjured ‘Mr. Clean,’ Dies

text: An article last Sunday about Republican efforts to limit voting in swing states referred incorrectly to a recommendation from a bipartisan presidential commission on election administration. A report by the commission recommended an expansion of online voter registration — not online voting, which it said cannot be made secure.
match_headline: New G.O.P. Bid to Limit Voting in Swing States

text: An article last Sunday about parents who have set up informal child care arrangements in their workplaces misstated the name of a Beverly Hills candy boutique that had supplied one such office, Alison Brod Public Relations, with child-friendly treats. It is Sugarfina, not Serafina.
match_headline: Creativity and Parenting Can Mix

text: An article last Sunday about single women who own cats described a scene in the television show “30 Rock” incorrectly. In the scene, the character Liz Lemon, played by Tina Fey, rode the subway dressed as an old woman who terrified fellow passengers by telling them she was “pregnant with kitty.” She did not have a daydream about that subway ride.
match_headline: I’m a Cat Lady? Thank You

text: An article last Sunday about Kevin Tsujihara’s bold moves since becoming the chief executive of Warner Bros. misstated the age of Sue Kroll, its president of worldwide marketing and international distribution. She is 52, not 53.
match_headline: Warner’s C.E.O. Is Bullish on the Big Screen

text: An article last Sunday about the artificial leaf, which uses sunlight and water to generate hydrogen as energy, omitted the context for a comment by Daniel Nocera, a Harvard chemist who has long worked on its development. When Mr. Nocera said, “My system is based on water, so if there was a catastrophe we’d just need a mop,” he was referring to another project on which he has worked, the development of a flow battery that relies on liquids to store energy on a large scale; he was not describing the artificial leaf.
ref_headline: My system is based on water, so if there was a catastrophe we’d just need a mop,
match_headline: The Artificial Leaf Is Here. Again.

text: An article last Sunday about New Yorkers who choose to move to a new apartment every year or so misidentified the brokerage where Takk Yamaguchi previously worked. It is Town Residential, not Douglas Elliman Real Estate.
match_headline: Serial Renters in New York City

text: A picture caption last Sunday with the preview of the American League baseball season misstated the number of times Detroit Tigers pitcher Justin Verlander has been to the World Series. It is twice — in 2006 and 2012 — not once.
match_headline: Orioles May Keep Verlander Waiting

text: A picture caption with a museums and galleries listing in the New Jersey Calendar in some editions last Sunday about an exhibition in Westwood misstated the title of the image. And the image, of a plant, was published with an incorrect orientation. The image is “Ensete Superbum,” not “Queen of the Night (Epiphyllum oxypetalum).” And the stem of the plant should have been at the top, with the plant facing downward, not facing toward the left.
match_headline: Events in New Jersey for March 30-April 5

text: An article in some editions on March 16 about several niche restaurants on Long Island that combine the quality of a fine-dining establishment with the affordability and energy of a casual burger joint misidentified the part of the island where Ralph Perrazzo opened BBD’s. It is the North Shore, not the North Fork.
match_headline: Classy Burgers in Relaxed Settings

text: A map on March 23 with the 36 Hours column, on Mexico City, placed the Jumex Museum incorrectly. It is by the Soumaya Museum, to the west of the city center; it is not northeast. A corrected map can be found at nytimes.com/travel .
match_headline: 36 Hours in Mexico City

text: An article last Sunday about Jaisalmer in Rajasthan, India, located the city incorrectly and misspelled in one instance the name of the fort there. Jaisalmer is in western Rajasthan, not eastern. And it is Jaisalmer Fort, as spelled elsewhere, not Jailsamer.
match_headline: Scenes of India, From a Fort and a Camel

text: An obituary last Sunday about the Holocaust survivor Leo Bretholz misstated the given name of his wife, who died in 2009. She was Florine, not Florence. And because of an editing error, the obituary misspelled the name of a Jewish resistance group Mr. Bretholz joined toward the end of World War II. It was La Sixième, not La Sixièeme.
match_headline: Leo Bretholz, 93, Dies; Escaped Train to Auschwitz

text: A picture caption last Monday with the continuation of an article about the latest report by the International Panel on Climate Change misidentified the New York subway station that was shown with flooded tracks after Hurricane Sandy. It is the South Ferry subway terminal, not Grand Central Terminal.
match_headline: Panel’s Warning on Climate Risk: Worst Is Yet to Come

text: An article on March 28 about President Obama’s visit with Pope Francis at the Vatican misspelled the name of the ancient Roman arena that Mr. Obama toured. It is the Colosseum, not the Coliseum.
match_headline: An Exchange of Views, Some in Accord

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the victims of the shooting at Fort Hood misidentified the county in New York that includes Allegany, the hometown of Maj. Patrick Miller, who was wounded. It is Cattaraugus County, not Allegany County.
match_headline: Among Fort Hood Victims, a Sergeant Is Killed, and a Major Is Wounded

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a conviction in the death of Tayshana Murphy, who was a high school basketball star in Manhattan, misspelled part of the name of her high school. It is Murry Bergtraum, not Murray Bergtraum.
match_headline: Jury Convicts Second Man in 2011 Killing of a High School Basketball Star

text: An article on Friday about art galleries in SoHo and TriBeCa and gallery information with it misidentified the location of the Kate Werble Gallery. It is in SoHo, not TriBeCa.
match_headline: Glimpses of the Past and a High-Tech Future

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about Marxfest, a series of events celebrating the Marx Brothers that will be held in New York City in May, misstated the name of the vaudeville performer and writer who will give the “From Angels to Anarchists” talk. He is Trav S. D., not Tray S. D.
match_headline: Brothers of Invention

text: A listing of health-related devices on March 11 described incorrectly the region of the ear viewable with the Cellscope optical attachment for the iPhone. It is the middle ear, not the inner ear. The listing also gave an incorrect price for the AliveCor heart monitor. It is $199, not $10 with a prescription, $199 without one.
match_headline: Report Cites ‘Devastating Toll’ on Health of Syria’s Children

text: Because of an editing error, a letter in the Reactions column on March 25 about mitochondrial DNA transfer misstated the writer’s surname. She is Adrienne Martin, not Marting.
match_headline: Reactions

text: An obituary on Friday about the chef and restaurant owner Roger Fessaguet misstated, in some editions, the year that his first wife, Anne Marie Corre, died. It was 1985, not 1925. The obituary also misstated the given name of Mr. Fessaguet’s lawyer, who confirmed his death. He is John J. Lynch, not James.
match_headline: Roger Fessaguet, a Wizard of Haute Cuisine in New York, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Friday about Sandy Grossman, the director of numerous N.F.L. games including 10 Super Bowls, misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the Indian league that hired him in 2012 to train its camera crews. It is the Elite Football League of India, not the Elite Football Club of India.
match_headline: Sandy Grossman, Maestro of N.F.L. on TV, Dies at 78

text: An obituary in some editions on Monday about the actor Mickey Rooney misspelled part of the name of a 1956 movie in which he starred. It is “Francis in the Haunted House,” not “Frances in the Haunted House.” The obituary also misstated where Mr. Rooney lived. He lived in Los Angeles, not Westlake Village, Calif.
match_headline: Mickey Rooney, Master of Putting On a Show, Dies at 93

text: An article last Tuesday about protests in Albuquerque over a string of fatal shootings by the police misspelled, in some editions, the given name of the city’s police chief, who said the department would review how officers are recruited and trained. He is Gorden Eden, not Gordon.
match_headline: Officials Urge Calm as Protests Take a Turn in Albuquerque

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about a grand jury appearance by the chief spokesman for Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey in the George Washington Bridge lane closing scandal omitted the news organization that first reported that the grand jury was hearing witnesses. The development was reported by ABC News.
match_headline: Grand Jury Questions Christie Aide in an Inquiry

text: An article on Friday about General Motors’ hiring of the crisis management adviser Jeff Eller to join a team of outside advisers after a broad vehicle recall misstated the year Mr. Eller’s former employer, Public Strategies, combined with Hill & Knowlton, and it also characterized the nature of the deal incorrectly. It was in 2011, not this year, and it was a merger; Public Strategies was not purchased by Hill & Knowlton.
match_headline: G.M. Turns to Experienced Crisis Experts

text: An article on Monday about the ways in which a university can burnish its reputation and bond with key supporters at the Final Four of the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament referred incorrectly to arrangements the University of Connecticut made for a group of donors at this year’s Final Four in Arlington, Tex. The donors had the opportunity to purchase rooms in the team hotel and tickets for some of the best seats at the Final Four; they were not “given” hotel rooms and “provided” tickets by the university.
match_headline: For UConn, as Well as the Huskies, a Golden Opportunity to Impress

text: An article in some editions on Monday about Connecticut’s 75-56 victory over Stanford in the women’s basketball Final Four misspelled the given name of a Connecticut reserve forward. She is Kiah Stokes, not Kia. And an accompanying picture caption, using information from The Associated Press, misidentified the Connecticut player pictured with Stanford’s Chiney Ogwumike. Stokes — not Bria Hartley — was shown after colliding with Ogwumike.
match_headline: Two Rivals. Zero Losses. One Trophy.

text: Because of an editing error, a theater review on Saturday about a benefit performance of “Guys and Dolls” at Carnegie Hall, in which Megan Mullally played Miss Adelaide, referred incorrectly to Ms. Mullally and the Off Broadway play “Annapurna.” She is rehearsing the play, not in previews of it. (Previews are scheduled to begin Sunday.)
match_headline: Stand Up, They’re Rocking the Boat, Like 1950 Again

text: An obituary in some editions on Sunday and in early editions on Monday about the author Peter Matthiessen misstated the setting of Mr. Matthiessen’s novel “At Play in the Fields of the Lord.” It is set in Peru, not Brazil. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Matthiessen’s book “In the Spirit of Crazy Horse.” While Mr. Matthiessen and the book’s publisher, Viking Press, were sued for libel damages, Viking did not “withdraw the book” as a result. And it also misstated the given name of one of his sons. He is Lucas, not Lukas or Luke.
ref_headline: At Play in the Fields of the Lord.
match_headline: Peter Matthiessen, Lyrical Writer and Naturalist, Is Dead at 86

text: An article on March 30 about Muqdad Salah, one of the Palestinians freed from an Israeli prison last year as part of the American-brokered peace talks, misstated the number of arrests that led to Mr. Salah’s being banned from Israel. It was three, not two. The article also misstated the timing of his first arrest and his age at the time of the second. He was first arrested in 1982, not during the first Palestinian intifada, which began in 1987. And while Mr. Salah’s second arrest did come during the intifada, in 1991, he was in his mid-20s at the time, not a teenager.
match_headline: Remaking a Life, After Years in an Israeli Prison

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with the continuation of an article about the number of deportations under President Obama misstated, in some copies, the name of the Ohio city where immigrant families meet regularly to discuss deportation issues. It is Painesville, not Plainsville.
match_headline: More Deportations Follow Minor Crimes, Records Show

text: An article last Wednesday about Representative Paul D. Ryan’s budget plan and the role it might play in the midterm elections erroneously included one state among those where Republicans are seeking to take Senate seats currently held by Democrats. Georgia is not one of them. (The seat is currently held by Saxby Chambliss, a Republican; he is not seeking re-election.)
match_headline: Ryan’s Budget Would Cut $5 Trillion in Spending Over a Decade

text: An article on Monday about a new venture of Jonathan N. Grayer, once chief of the education company Kaplan, misstated part of the name of Kaplan’s parent company. It is Graham Holdings, not Graham Industries.
match_headline: Ex-Chief of Kaplan Aims to Build a Rival Digital Learning Company

text: Because of editing errors, reports by The Associated Press in some editions of the baseball roundups on Sunday and on Monday misidentified the home team for the series between the Dodgers and the Giants. It was Los Angeles, not San Francisco.
match_headline: Jeter, With His Final Home Opener Up Next, Climbs Career Hits List to No. 8

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Saturday with an article about the Knicks’ 90-89 loss to the Washington Wizards misstated, in some copies, the number of points scored by the Knicks’ J. R. Smith. As the article correctly noted, he had 32 points, not 24.
match_headline: Knicks Fall to Washington, and Drop Behind Atlanta

text: A listing of credits and schedule information on Monday with a theater review of “The Realistic Joneses,” at the Lyceum Theater in Manhattan, misstated the theater’s address. It is 149 West 45th Street, not West 49th Street. (The same error appeared in a theater entry in the Listings pages of Weekend on Friday and on March 7, March 14 and March 21.)
match_headline: Plugging Away at Living, Come What May

text: An article on Wednesday about efforts by Democrats to use the equal pay issue to gain more women’s votes misidentified the target of criticism by Senator Mitch McConnell, Republican of Kentucky, as the Senate prepared to vote on legislation meant to close the pay gap between men and women. When he referred to “the left’s latest bizarre obsession,” he was criticizing Democrats’ attacks on David H. and Charles G. Koch, conservative billionaires whose political organizations have spent more than $30 million on ads so far to help Republicans win control of the Senate. He was not referring to the pay-equity issue.
match_headline: Democrats Use Pay Issue in Bid for Women’s Vote

text: An article last Thursday about a ruling by a legislative judicial committee in Connecticut that Charla Nash, the Connecticut woman who was mauled by a chimpanzee, cannot sue the state misstated the date Ms. Nash made her case before the panel. She appeared on March 21, not on March 17.
match_headline: Woman Mauled by Chimp Can’t Sue Connecticut

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about comeback efforts of the private equity executive Guy Hands, who lost two-thirds of his wealth in a disastrous deal for the music company EMI, misstated the amount of money that investors say Mr. Hands hopes to raise for a renewable energy fund. It is $2 billion, not 2 billion euros.
match_headline: Tech-Focused Hedge Fund to Return $2 Billion to Investors

text: An article on Wednesday about the EcoCup, a single-serve beverage pod claimed by its makers to be largely recyclable, misidentified the type of plastic used in its manufacture. It is No. 6 plastic, not No. 5.
match_headline: Coffee and Tea Company to Start Selling Recyclable Single-Serving Pods

text: An article last Thursday about Nets Coach Jason Kidd’s foray into rap music in 1994 misstated part of the title of a song by the former basketball player Cedric Ceballos that was on the same album as one by Kidd. It is “Flow On,” not “Float On.”
match_headline: Jason Kidd’s Bad Rap, Now 20 Years Old

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the awarding of the Edward MacDowell Medal for lifetime achievement in the arts to the artist Betye Saar misstated the date the ceremony honoring Ms. Saar will take place in Peterborough, N.H. It is Aug. 10, not Aug. 11.
match_headline: Arts Prize to Betye Saar

text: Because of an editing error, a film review on March 28 about the documentary “Jews of Egypt” referred incorrectly to the father of a person interviewed in the film who was long unaware that he is the man’s son. The father was not interviewed.
match_headline: When ‘Egyptian’ Just Meant Egyptian

text: An article on March 27 about young jewelry designers misstated the year in which Jennifer Fisher, one of the designers, was a finalist for a CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund award. It was 2012, not 2013. The article also misspelled the given name of a fellow designer who is one of Ms. Fisher’s fans. She is Lynn Ban, not Lyn. And a picture of a cuff with the inscription “09.08.01” was erroneously included in designs by Gaia Repossi. Ms. Fisher designed the cuff.
match_headline: Young Designers Reimagine Jewelry

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Ken Forsse, the creator of the talking toy bear Teddy Ruxpin, misspelled the given name of a television producer for whom he once worked. The producer is Marty Krofft, not Mary.
match_headline: Ken Forsse, Who Brought a Toy Bear to Life, Dies at 77

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the guitarist Arthur Smith, whose song “Feuding Banjos” was used, under the name “Dueling Banjos,” in the movie “Deliverance,” misspelled the given name of one of that movie’s stars. He is Jon Voight, not John.
match_headline: Arthur Smith, Musician Who Wrote ‘Dueling Banjos,’ Dies at 93

text: An article last Friday about Specialist Ivan Antonio Lopez, the Army soldier identified as the gunman in the Fort Hood shooting, misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a spokesman for the Lopez family. He is Glidden Lopez, not Glyden.
match_headline: Gunman Had ‘Clean Record,’ With No Violent Sign, Officials Say

text: An article last Friday about the pending retirement of the late-night television host David Letterman gave an incorrect time slot, in some copies, for “The Colbert Report” on Comedy Central, whose host, Stephen Colbert, was chosen on Thursday to succeed Mr. Letterman at “Late Night” on CBS. It is broadcast at 11:31 p.m. Eastern, not at midnight.
match_headline: After 3 Decades, Letterman Says He Will Sign Off

text: An article on Wednesday about the Rev. Al Sharpton’s role as an F.B.I. informer during his dealings with the music business in the 1980s quoted incorrectly in some editions from comments by Mr. Sharpton about The New York Post’s description of him as “Rev Rat.” He said, “I wasn’t with the rats” — not “I’m not with the rats.” The error was repeated in the Quotation of the Day.
match_headline: Details of Sharpton’s Time as Informer Shed Light on a Life With Many Chapters

text: An article on Thursday about plans by the lender Ally Financial to hold an initial public offering for its shares erroneously included one investment bank among those that are leading that process, and omitted another. Along with Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, Barclays is among the lead underwriters in the I.P.O.; JPMorgan Chase is not.
match_headline: Go Daddy Said to Pick Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan for I.P.O.

text: An article on March 29 about contributions by three United States retailers toward a $40 million fund for victims of the Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh last April misidentified the organization through which the donations were made. The retailers contributed through BRAC USA, an affiliate of the Bangladeshi development organization BRAC, not through BRAC itself.
match_headline: 3 Retailers Give Aid to Bangladesh Workers

text: An article last Friday about changes in Hungary since Viktor Orban became prime minister in 2010 misstated the political affiliation of his predecessor, Gordon Bajnai. Mr. Bajnai is an independent who served as prime minister when the Socialists were in power; he is not himself a Socialist.
match_headline: A Village Stadium Is a Symbol of Power for Hungary’s Premier

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about a new award from the Yaddo artists’ colony in Saratoga Springs, N.Y., that will be given to Philip Roth misstated the number of residencies Mr. Roth has had there. It is seven, not six.
match_headline: Philip Roth to Be Honored With Yaddo Medal

text: A picture caption last Friday with an article about art galleries in Brooklyn referred incompletely to an exhibition at the TSA gallery. While Vincent Como is a curator as well as one of the artists who run the gallery, the exhibition shown was organized by Matt Phillips.
match_headline: Chasing a Dream and an Unalloyed Ethos

text: A picture credit last Friday with a film review of “Watermark” misstated the given name of the photographer, who is also a co-director of the film. As the review correctly noted, he is Edward Burtynsky, not Ed.
match_headline: That Bend in the River Might be Manufactured

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Saturday about plans by the United States to reassess the Middle East peace talks referred incorrectly in some copies to Iran’s nuclear program. The country has acknowledged being involved in some nuclear activities, including enriching uranium; there has been no determination made that the country indeed has a “nuclear arsenal.”
match_headline: U.S. to Reassess Status of Talks on Middle East

text: An article on Feb. 23 about the fall of President Viktor F. Yanukovych of Ukraine and his flight from the capital, Kiev, misstated the day of his departure. He left the evening of Friday, Feb. 21, not Saturday, Feb. 22. The same error appeared in an articles on Feb. 24 and Feb. 26 . (The error was discovered this week by an editor.)
match_headline: Archrival Is Freed as Ukraine Leader Flees

text: An article on March 21 about the expansion of American sanctions against Russia after its annexation of Crimea misstated one of the colors of the czarist-era ribbons worn by Russian lawmakers during their vote to ratify treaties making Crimea and Sevastopol part of the Russian Federation. They were black and orange, not brown and orange.
match_headline: Obama Steps Up Russia Sanctions in Ukraine Crisis

text: An article on Friday about the potential reach of an Internet security flaw called Heartbleed misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a spokesman for Intel, one of the companies that is reviewing its products for vulnerabilities. He is Chuck Mulloy, not Malloy.
match_headline: Heartbleed Flaw Could Reach to Digital Devices, Experts Say

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about the Yankees’ 7-3 victory over the Toronto Blue Jays, during which Mark Teixeira injured his right hamstring, misidentified the Yankees’ opponent in the 2010 American League Championship Series, when Teixeira sustained a similar injury. It was the Texas Rangers, not the Los Angeles Angels. The article also misstated the inning in which Teixeira injured his hamstring in Game 4 of that series. It was the fifth inning, not the ninth.
match_headline: Rocked at Start, Tanaka Finds Rhythm and Lifts Yankees to Win

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the debate over who is inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame referred incorrectly to the rapper Fab 5 Freddy in some editions. He was not a member of the group N.W.A., which was passed over for induction this year.
match_headline: Hall of Fame Decides Who Rocks, Officially

text: An article on Thursday about a public art project in Atlanta by the painter and illustrator Tatyana Fazlalizadeh intended to combat street harassment of women misspelled the surname of an artist who commented on the project. She is Jessica Caldas, not Caldes. The article also rendered incorrectly the name of an anti-harassment group. It is Hollaback! — not Holla Back.
match_headline: An Artist Demands Civility on the Street With Grit and Buckets of Paste

text: An entry in the “This and That” feature on Page 48 this weekend about the artist Julian Schnabel misstates the opening date of his show at Gagosian Gallery in New York. It is Thursday; it did not open on Tuesday.
match_headline: Your Turn: A Weekend Thread, Open for Comments

text: A picture caption on Page 60 this weekend with an entry in the Trend Report about new product includes an outdated price for the Eric Trine Octahedron. After the magazine had gone to press, the price was raised to $32, from $25.
An obituary on Thursday about Zeituni Onyango, President Obama’s aunt, misstated her relation to the president’s father. She was his half-sister, not his stepsister.
match_headline: Zeituni Onyango, Obama’s Aunt From Kenya, Dies at 61

text: An article last Sunday about the rising costs associated with the routine treatment of many chronic illnesses described incorrectly glucagon, a drug that families of diabetic children are advised to keep on hand. It is a hormone injection, not an injection of concentrated sugar water. And a caption with an accompanying chart described incorrectly a picture of medical supplies one patient uses to treat her diabetes. It is an emergency glucagon kit, not an emergency insulin kit.
match_headline: Even Small Medical Advances Can Mean Big Jumps in Bills

text: An article last Sunday about soldiers at Fort Hood who are anxious over their futures as the Army post reduces its numbers with the winding down of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan misstated, in some editions, the number of soldiers from Fort Hood who died in those two wars. In Iraq, 519 died, not 361; and in Afghanistan, there were 56 deaths, not 58.
match_headline: War Pain Yields to New Anxiety Inside Ft. Hood

text: An article last Sunday about the Ukrainians who could become important witnesses to the police violence that broke out in Kiev, the Ukrainian capital, just before the government collapsed in February misstated the surname of a small-business man who is recovering in Germany from gunshot wounds he sustained during the upheaval. He is Yuri Kravchuk, not Marchuk. The error also appeared in a picture caption.
match_headline: Tending Their Wounds, Vowing to Fight On

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Rangers’ 3-2 loss to the Ottawa Senators misidentified, in one instance, the player whose shot the Rangers’ Mats Zuccarello deflected in to make the score 3-2. He is Marc Staal — not Eric Staal, his brother, who plays for the Carolina Hurricanes.
match_headline: Zuccarello Provides Spark, but Clinching Must Wait

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about “James Prosek: Wondrous Strange,” an exhibition at the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut, reversed the years in which two pieces of the show were completed. “Blue Marlin” was completed in 2011 and “Zebra” in 2014.
match_headline: Creatures Great, Small and Imagined

text: A picture caption on Page 60 this weekend with an entry in the Trend Report about new products includes an outdated price for the Eric Trine Octahedron. After the magazine had gone to press, the price was raised to $32, from $25.

An article last Sunday about Darby English, a new consulting curator at the Museum of Modern Art who specializes in African-American art, rendered incorrectly the name of the museum that he works for in Williamstown, Mass. It is the Sterling and Francine Clark Art Institute, not the Francine and Sterling Clark Art Institute.
match_headline: Student of History Is Making Some

text: Because of an editing error, a review on March 23 about “A Place in the Country,” a collection of non-fiction writings by W. G. Sebald , referred incorrectly to Sebald’s burial place. It is in the English county of Norfolk, not “near” it.
match_headline: Points of Departure

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the resurgence of the real estate market along the Jersey Shore misstated the number of years since Hurricane Sandy . It is one and a half years, not two and a half.
match_headline: Back to the Jersey Shore

text: An article on March 16 about the affordability of the Upper East Side for young renters misstated the name of a restaurant, since closed, that was a neighborhood hangout. It was Cronies, not Cromies.
match_headline: For Starters, the Upper East Side

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 27 about one of the candidates for president of Indonesia, Prabowo Subianto, a former special forces commander who is running despite allegations that he took part in human rights abuses, referred incorrectly to the next presidency. The winner will be the second Indonesian president directly elected by the public, not its second democratically elected president. (Others have been elected by legislative assemblies.)
match_headline: Indonesia Candidate Tied to Human Rights Abuses Stirs Unease

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Friday about a statement by federal prosecutors in Chicago that a drug trafficker who was one of the leaders of the Sinaloa drug cartel has been cooperating with them misstated, in some editions, the year that the trafficker, Ismael Zambada García, was arrested. It was in 2009, not 2010.
match_headline: Mexico: Convicted Trafficker Now Aiding U.S. Officials

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Friday about a sentencing hearing for Silvio Berlusconi, the former prime minister of Italy, in a tax fraud case misstated, in some editions, the year that he was convicted. It was 2012, not last year.
match_headline: Italian Court Weighs Community Service for Berlusconi

text: An article on Tuesday about the murder of the Rev. Frans van der Lugt, a Dutch Jesuit in Homs, Syria, who offered shelter and aid to both Christian and Muslim families as war engulfed Homs’s Old City district, misstated his age in some editions. He was 75, not 72.
match_headline: Long a Survivor in Syria, a Dutch Priest Is Slain

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about a former City Council member, Charles Barron, who briefly upstaged Mayor Bill de Blasio at the groundbreaking of a housing development in Brooklyn described incorrectly Mr. Barron’s actions at the start of the news conference. He directed his wife, Councilwoman Inez Barron, to move to the mayor’s side; he did not push her there.
match_headline: An Ex-Councilman Upstages the Mayor at His Own Event

text: An article last Monday about the awarding of the Ridenhour prize for truth-telling to Edward J. Snowden and Laura Poitras, the filmmaker who helped Mr. Snowden disclose a trove of documents on government surveillance, misstated part of the name of the location where the award ceremony will be held. It is the National Press Club, not the Washington Press Club.
match_headline: Snowden to Receive Truth-Telling Prize

text: A picture credit with an article in some editions on April 6 about Connecticut’s 63-53 victory over Florida in the semifinals of the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament misstated the surname of the photographer. The picture of DeAndre Daniels was taken by Chris Steppig, not Steppic.
match_headline: A Long Shot Nears Its Goal: UConn Topples Florida

text: An obituary last Monday about Barbara Gibbons, the author of the “Slim Gourmet” syndicated column and cookbooks, misstated the name of the company that carried her column from the late 1970s until the early 1990s. It is United Feature Syndicate, not United Features Syndicate. (The error also appeared in a picture credit in 2011, in an article in 2010, and in several dozen other articles in past years.)
match_headline: Barbara Gibbons, 79, Writer of ‘Slim Gourmet’ Cookbooks, Dies

text: An editorial on Thursday about India’s nuclear policies incorrectly described India’s first nuclear test. It was in 1974, under the National Congress Party. It was not conducted under the Bharatiya Janata Party, which carried out several tests in 1998.
match_headline: A Risk to India’s Nuclear Doctrine

text: An article on Monday about West Point graduates who are reconsidering their career paths in a military no longer fighting two wars misstated the given name of a cadet who wants to be in an Army Special Operations unit. He is Nils Olsen, not Mills.
match_headline: In New Officers’ Careers, Peace Is No Dividend

text: An article on Saturday about a bus crash that killed 10 people in California misidentified, in some editions, the location of Valhalla High School, where Harley Hoyt, who talked about the crash, is a senior. It is in San Diego County, but not in the City of San Diego.
match_headline: In an Instant, a Bus to College Was a Fiery Trap

text: An article on Saturday about the debate surrounding the idea of a new attention disorder, sluggish cognitive tempo, misidentified the institution with which one researcher of the disorder, Stephen A. Marshall, is affiliated. It is Ohio University, not Miami University in Ohio. The article also misspelled the given name of another researcher. He is Stephen P. Becker, not Steven.
match_headline: Idea of New Attention Disorder Spurs Research, and Debate

text: An article last Tuesday about the rescue of a family from a sailboat 900 miles off the coast of Mexico misidentified the type of aircraft from which the California Air National Guardsmen parachuted during the complicated efforts to save the family. It was a transport plane, not a helicopter.
match_headline: 2 Tots, a Sailboat and a Storm Over Parenting

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the Glaad Media Awards in Los Angeles on Saturday night included an outdated name for Glaad. It no longer calls itself the Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation.
match_headline: Awards for Jennifer Lopez and Norman Lear

text: An article on Tuesday about the courtroom artist Elizabeth Williams misstated the title of Lloyd C. Blankfein, who testified in the insider trading trial of Rajat Gupta, one defendant Ms. Williams sketched. Mr. Blankfein is the current, not former, chief executive of Goldman Sachs.
match_headline: Scenes From ‘The Illustrated Courtroom’

text: An article on Monday about the entrepreneur Richard Barton gave an outdated name for the venture capital firm where he is a venture partner. It is Benchmark, no longer Benchmark Capital.
match_headline: The Art of ‘Something From Nothing’

text: A report in the Inside Art column on April 4 about the coming sale of the Andy Warhol painting “White Marilyn,” which has a message from Warhol to the art dealer Eleanor Ward scrawled on the back, referred imprecisely to the Warhol show she organized at the Stable Gallery in 1962. It was his first one-man show in New York; his first solo show was presented by Irving Blum a few months earlier at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles.
match_headline: Richard Prince’s ‘Canal Zone’ to Be Shown at Gagosian

text: An obituary on Friday about the motorcycle designer Massimo Tamburini misidentified the location of his death. He died in the Republic of San Marino, a sovereign nation within Italy’s borders; there is no “San Marino, Italy.”
match_headline: Massimo Tamburini, Sculptor of Shapely Motorcycles, Dies at 70

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the coming parole hearing for Robert Hill, whose conviction in the killing of Donald Manboardes is one of the cases reopened after allegations of misconduct against the detective Louis Scarcella, misstated the month and the year that Mr. Manboardes was fatally shot. It was January 1987, not December 1986.
match_headline: Prisoner to Face Parole Board as Questions Grow About His Conviction

text: An article on April 5 about Ueli Steck’s climb of Annapurna’s south face, for which he was awarded the Piolet d’Or, mountaineering’s highest accolade, referred imprecisely to the climb. While Steck was the first person to complete the climb of the main south face alone, he was not “the first person to successfully climb Annapurna’s south face.” Several groups completed the climb, beginning in 1970.
ref_headline: the first person to successfully climb Annapurna’s south face.
match_headline: Swiss Climber’s Feat Honored Despite Lack of Proof

text: An article on Monday about the Indiana Pacers’ 102-97 victory over the Oklahoma City Thunder referred incorrectly to Kevin Durant’s streak of games with at least 25 points. It ended on April 8, at 41 games; Durant, who scored 38 points for the Thunder on Sunday, did not extend the streak to 42 games.
match_headline: Pacers Can Still Be No. 1, Even After Floundering

text: An article on Monday about Mo Farah’s debut at the London Marathon misidentified one of the events at which Farah won both the 5,000 and 10,000 meters. Besides the 2012 London Olympics, he swept the races at the 2013 world championships, but not at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: A Letdown in London for a British Olympic Champion

text: Because of an editing error, the On the Olympics column on Saturday, about concerns with the 2016 Summer Games in Rio de Janeiro, omitted the given name and title of the person who had not ruled out moving the event. He is Thomas Bach, who is president of the International Olympic Committee.
match_headline: In Brazil, Usual Olympics Worry With Unusual Validity

text: An article on Wednesday about complaints by Tod Williams and Billie Tsien, architects of the Folk Art Museum building, over the Museum of Modern Art’s decision to demolish it as part of an expansion plan misspelled the surname of the architect who designed the tower in which MoMA will have new exhibition space. He is Jean Nouvel, not Novel.
match_headline: Architects Mourn Former Folk Art Museum Building

text: An article on Tuesday about a scarcity of fresh gefilte fish for Passover this year misspelled the surname of a fisheries specialist in Michigan who explained the logistical difficulties that contributed to this year’s shortage. He is Ronald Kinnunen, not Kinnuen. The article also omitted the surname of an owner of Russ & Daughters. She is Niki Russ Federman, not Niki Russ.
match_headline: Gefilte Fish Is Scarce This Passover. Taste Buds Are Ambivalent.

text: An article on Wednesday about plans to return streetcars to H Street in Washington, D.C., decades after they were last used misidentified the location in Oregon where the new cars were manufactured, at a cost of $4 million each. They were made in Clackamas, which is outside of Portland, not in Portland itself. (Some were also manufactured in the Czech Republic.)
match_headline: Washington Retail District’s Future Rides on Streetcars

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with the On Golf column, about golfers who missed the cut at the Masters, misidentified one such golfer in some copies. The player in the top picture shown standing with his club was Jason Dufner — not Phil Mickelson, who also did not make the cut.
match_headline: Excitement Turns Into Exasperation, Even for Stars

text: An article on Saturday about Dan LaCouture, a former Rangers player who is a plaintiff in a lawsuit against the N.H.L., quoted incorrectly from comments by Mr. LaCouture about how quickly he came back from a concussion in 2004. He said, “I came back six, seven days later” — not “I came back six, seven games later.”
ref_headline: I came back six, seven days later
match_headline: Former Ranger Traces Troubles to 2004 Fight

text: An article on Saturday about the second round of the Masters rendered incorrectly in some copies the name of one of the players 50 years or older who made the cut. He is Miguel Ángel Jiménez, not Angel Miguel Jimenez.
match_headline: Derailed by Masters Win, Bubba Watson Seeks Another

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about the Yankees’ 4-2 loss to the Boston Red Sox misstated, in some copies, the number of hits Red Sox pitcher Jon Lester allowed. It was six, not seven.
match_headline: With Hands Spotless and Pitches Filthy, Red Sox’ Lester Shines

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the first-round matchups in the N.H.L. playoffs misstated the game in which Philadelphia Flyers goalie Steve Mason was injured. It was in the second-to-last game of the regular season, not the regular-season finale.
match_headline: A Spicier N.H.L. Playoff Recipe

text: Because of an editing error, the Books of The Times review on Thursday, about “The Selected Letters of Elia Kazan,” edited by Albert J. Devlin with Marlene J. Devlin, misspelled the surname of Kazan’s wife. She was Molly Day Thacher, not Thatcher.
ref_headline: The Selected Letters of Elia Kazan,
match_headline: Combative Director, Even in Letters

text: An article on Tuesday about the author Lydia Denworth and her son Alex Justh, who is deaf and uses a cochlear implant and a hearing aid, paraphrased incorrectly from a comment by Marc Marschark, a professor at the National Technical Institute for the Deaf in Rochester. Dr. Marschark said deaf children have differences that can affect learning. He did not say that “all deaf children have some cognitive challenges.”
ref_headline: all deaf children have some cognitive challenges.
match_headline: A Son’s Deafness Prompts a Scientific Journey

text: A chart on Tuesday with the continuation of an article about rising rents that are out of the reach of the middle class misstated the time span of the data shown. The chart tracked the rise of median rent in various cities from the first quarter of 2000 through the fourth quarter of 2013, not the third.
match_headline: In Many Cities, Rent Is Rising Out of Reach of Middle Class

text: Because of a translation error, an article on Wednesday about the apparent abduction of seven policemen in Afghanistan misstated the surname of a spokesman for the governor of Wardak Province, where the episode occurred. He is Ataullah Khogyani, not Lodin.
match_headline: Taliban Say They Killed 7 Afghan Police Officers

text: An article on April 8 about the sale of the Manischewitz Company to an arm of the private equity giant Bain Capital described part of the company’s history incorrectly. At the time of its 1990 sale to Kolberg & Company, Manischewitz was publicly listed, not family-owned. Also, the sale was negotiated through the board; the company was not “sold by a grandson of the founder.”
ref_headline: sold by a grandson of the founder.
match_headline: ARTnews Sold to Private Company

text: An article on Monday about Bubba Watson’s victory at the Masters misstated, in some copies, the number of consecutive pars he made to finish his final round. It was five, not six.
match_headline: For Grown-Up Watson, the Jacket Still Fits

text: An article last Sunday about the unexpectedly competitive Formula One racing season misstated the timing of notable results by Mercedes-Benz. While its drivers finished first and second at the Bahrain Grand Prix, it was not their first 1-2 finish since 1955. A week earlier, the team took first and second in Malaysia.
match_headline: Formula One’s New-Age Hybrids Find Their Footing

text: An article last Sunday about automotive exhibitions at the 1964 New York World’s Fair misstated Richard Nixon’s middle initial. It was M., not F.
match_headline: When Cars Ruled the World’s Fair

text: A chart last Sunday with an article about the compensation of top American executives in 2013 misspelled the given name of the chief executive of the Coca-Cola Company, whose $18.2 million salary that year placed him No. 26 among the 50 executives listed on the chart. He is Muhtar Kent, not Muhtor.
match_headline: Co-operative Bank Cancels Bonuses as It Posts Steep Loss

text: A picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about an exhibition on Asian indigo dye, at the Charles B. Wang Center at Stony Brook University, misstated the given name of one of the participating artists. She is  Leonie Castelino, not Leone.
match_headline: Seeing Asian Cultures, Through an Indigo Lens

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about a retrospective in Trenton celebrating the 30th anniversary of Aljira, an exhibition space in Newark, misspelled the surname of an artist who was involved in Aljira’s early days. She is Elizabeth Seaton, not Seton.
match_headline: Utopian Vision Born of a Harsh Truth

text: An article last Sunday about canine intelligence referred incorrectly to bonobos, a species studied by Brian Hare of the Canine Cognition Center at Duke University. They are apes, not monkeys.
match_headline: You’ll Go Far, My Pet

text: A picture caption on April 6 with the cover article about the writer’s search for her family’s roots in Spain misstated her relationship to the man shown with his wife. He was the writer’s paternal — not maternal — great-grandfather. And a caption with a photograph of the writer’s grandmother, father and aunt misidentified the location. It was taken in Costa Rica, not in the Dominican Republic.
match_headline: In Spain, a Family Reunion, Centuries Later

text: A chart last Sunday about need-blind colleges and financial aid, using information from Bowdoin College, misstated the percentage of the college’s freshmen with financial need whose need is fully met. It is 100 percent, not 46 percent.
match_headline: Northwestern Requests Review of Labor Ruling

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the evolution of American studies misidentified the university where Curtis Marez, president of the American Studies Association, taught in the American studies department. It is the University of California, Santa Cruz — not the University of California, San Diego.
match_headline: Looking for America Beyond Its Borders

text: A column appearing last Sunday about Ukrainian gas pipelines had a quote that understated the amount of energy saving in new houses in California. They now use one-fourth of the energy used by houses built before 1978.
match_headline: Go Ahead, Vladimir, Make My Day

text: An article on Saturday about the F.B.I.’s involvement in terrorism-related trials misspelled the surname of a Southern Methodist University law professor and former military prosecutor. He is Christopher Jenks, not Jencks.
match_headline: Covert Inquiry by F.B.I. Rattles 9/11 Tribunals

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the popularity of live interactive web entertainment in China misspelled the home province of Mi Tian, a fan of the shows who has spent thousands on virtual gifts for the performers. It is Shandong province, not Shangdong.
match_headline: Lucrative Stardom in China, Using a Webcam and a Voice

text: An article on Saturday about Hillary Rodham Clinton’s impending role as a grandmother misstated Mrs. Clinton’s age. She is 66, not 67. (She will turn 67 on Oct. 26.)
match_headline: What to Expect When a Clinton Is Expecting

text: An obituary on Saturday about Jacques Servier, who created one of the biggest pharmaceutical companies in France, erroneously credited his company, Laboratories Servier, with having developed one of the two drugs in the so-called fen-phen diet drug scandal. It developed fenfluramine, but not phentermine.
match_headline: Jacques Servier, 92, Dies; Accused of Hiding the Risks of Drugs

text: An article on Friday about a United Nations Security Council hearing on an investigative commission’s findings of crimes against humanity and other abuses in North Korea referred incorrectly to Lee Hyeon-seo, one of the North Korean witnesses who spoke at the session. Ms. Lee is a refugee who escaped from North Korea and is now a rights activist based in South Korea; she was never incarcerated in North Korea’s penal system.
match_headline: U.N. Council Takes Up Question of Rights in North Korea

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about Sant Singh Chatwal, a fund-raiser for Hillary Rodham Clinton and other Democratic candidates, who was shown with former President Bill Clinton, referred incorrectly to him in some editions. As the article correctly noted, he is Mr. Chatwal, not Mr. Singh. And because of an editing error, a credit for a picture of Mr. Chatwal shown alone misspelled the surname of the photographer in some copies. She is Mary Altaffer, not Altafer.
match_headline: Clinton Backer Pleads Guilty in a Straw Donor Scheme

text: Because of an editing error, a subheading on a report in the baseball roundup on Tuesday reversed, in some editions, the score of the game between the Boston Red Sox and the Baltimore Orioles on Monday. As the report correctly noted, the Orioles — not the Red Sox — won, 7-6.

A critic’s notebook article on Saturday about “All God’s Dangers,” an oral history of Ned Cobb, a black Alabama sharecropper, misstated the year the book’s author, Theodore Rosengarten, first met Mr. Cobb. It was 1968, not 1969. And the article described incorrectly Mr. Rosengarten’s academic status at that time. He was a graduate student at Harvard, not a recent Harvard graduate. (He received his Ph.D in 1975.)
match_headline: Lost in Literary History: A Tale of Courage in the South

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Hamish Maxwell, the former chairman and chief executive of Philip Morris, misstated part of his full name. He was Hamish Walter Hyslop Maxwell (not Hysolp).
match_headline: Hamish Maxwell, Philip Morris Empire Builder, Dies at 87

text: An article last Thursday about the Syrian conflict’s threat to the ancient city of Palmyra’s archaeological treasures misidentified the auctioneer that is proposing to sell a cache of medieval Islamic coins. It is VCoin, an online company, not Sotheby’s. (Sotheby’s and other leading auction houses are cooperating with Unesco to increase vigilance to prevent the trafficking of stolen Syrian antiquities, according to Nada al-Hassan, chief of Unesco’s Arab states unit.)
match_headline: Syrian War Takes Heavy Toll at a Crossroad of Cultures

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the likelihood that the nomination of Hillary Rodham Clinton for president would block the paths for other women running for the White House, and for those who would like to be vice president, referred incompletely to the possibility that Senator Kirsten E. Gillibrand might be chosen as a running mate. Aside from the debate over a two-woman ticket, Ms. Gillibrand and Mrs. Clinton are both from New York, and the Constitution effectively prohibits the election of a president and a vice president who are from the same state. In addition, the article misstated the significance of having two women running on a presidential ticket. It would be the first such ticket for a major party, not the first time two women have run together. (Jill Stein and Cheri Honkala were running mates on the Green Party ticket in 2012.)
match_headline: With Eyes on a Possible Clinton Run, Debate on a 2-Woman Ticket

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about an increase in mergers among pharmaceutical companies, using information from an image service, misidentified a product being used for a cosmetic procedure. The photograph shows a physician injecting Juvederm — not Botox — into a patient’s forehead to smooth out wrinkles. (Both products are made by Allergan, the subject of a takeover bid by Valeant Pharmaceuticals. )
match_headline: Allergan Bid Adds to Spate of Pharmaceutical Deals

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about Atlético Madrid’s 0-0 tie with Chelsea in the first leg of their Champions League soccer semifinal, using information from The Associated Press, misidentified the Atlético player shown contesting the ball. He is known simply as Diego — not Diego Costa, who is one of his teammates.
match_headline: In a Tie, Atlético Madrid Can Still Declare Victory

text: An obituary on April 14 about the author Gregory White Smith referred incorrectly to a 1991 article in The New York Times by the Jackson Pollock scholar Francis V. O’Connor about Mr. Smith and Steven Naifeh’s book “Jackson Pollock: An American Saga.” While Mr. O’Connor was highly critical of the book, it is not the case that he said Mr. Smith and Mr. Naifeh “were not traditionally credentialed art historians.”
match_headline: Gregory White Smith, Pollock Biographer, Dies at 62

text: An obituary on Wednesday about L. Jay Oliva, a former president of New York University, misspelled the surname of the man he succeeded in that office. He is John Brademas, not Brademus.
match_headline: L. Jay Oliva, Who Led the Rise of N.Y.U. in the ’90s, Dies at 80

text: An article on Monday about efforts by Art Moore, a moderate Republican, to unseat Representative Tom McClintock, a favorite of the Tea Party who represents California’s Fourth Congressional District, referred incorrectly to Mr. Moore’s military service. He remains a major in the Army National Guard; he has not left the service.
match_headline: A Rare G.O.P. Battle Forces an Incumbent to Look Left

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a decision by two former leaders of the Metropolitan New York Council on Jewish Poverty to plead guilty in connection with a plan to embezzle millions from the charity misstated the amount of cash that was found during the execution of a search warrant for William E. Rapfogel, the one who headed the charity most recently. The authorities found $48,000, not more than $400,000.
match_headline: Rapfogel to Plead Guilty in Scheme to Steal Millions From Charity

text: Because of an editing error, an article on April 16 about Police Commissioner William J. Bratton’s use of the basic policing principles of Sir Robert Peel, considered the father of the London police force, described incorrectly Theodore Roosevelt’s role with the New York City police. He was on the board of commissioners that oversaw the department; he was not the sole police commissioner.
match_headline: A London Guide for 1 Police Plaza

text: An article on Thursday about increasing fraud in the market for rare wines misspelled, in some copies, the given name of a wine dealer found guilty in December of selling millions of dollars’ worth of counterfeit wine. He is Rudy Kurniawan, not Rudi.
match_headline: As Wine Fetches Staggering Sums, Fakery Claims Rise

text: An article on Thursday about the sales-promoting advantages of slightly risqué company names misstated the name of the former employer of Corin Mullins, who with her husband, Brian, founded a company that makes a high-fiber cereal called Holy Crap. She worked for Air Canada, not Canada Air.
match_headline: Risqué Names Reap Rewards for Some Companies

text: An article on Thursday about Boeing’s first-quarter earnings misstated, in some editions, the day they were announced. It was Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Operating Earnings Rise 12% at Boeing

text: A picture caption on April 17 with an article about the sale of the Milwaukee Bucks, using information from The Associated Press, misidentified, in some editions, the member of the new ownership group shown shaking hands with Herb Kohl, the previous owner. He is Marc Lasry — not Wesley Edens, also a new owner.
match_headline: Former Senator Is Selling the Bucks After Three Decades

text: An article last Friday about prominent owners and trainers in horse racing who have pledged to make their horses’ veterinary records public misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a Kentucky Derby-winning trainer who served a drug-related suspension. He is Doug O’Neill, not O’Neil.
match_headline: Horse Owners and Trainers Say They’ll Release Veterinary Records

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the Yankees’ 9-3 victory over the Boston Red Sox misstated the number of walks the Yankees’ starting pitcher, Masahiro Tanaka, has allowed in his first four major league starts. It is two, not five.
match_headline: Yanks’ New Additions Torment the Red Sox

text: An article on Tuesday about optogenetics, a technique that allows researchers to turn brain cells on with genetic manipulation and pulses of light, omitted the name of a co-author of a 2002 paper that established proof that optogenetics could work. Boris Zemelman also wrote the paper.
match_headline: Brain Control in a Flash of Light

text: A picture caption on Friday describing an art review in the Weekend section about the exhibition “Goya and the Altamira Family” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art misspelled, in some editions, the given name of one child of that family whose portrait is included in the exhibition. As the review correctly noted, he was Vicente, not Vincente.
match_headline: That Little Lost Boy in Red, Back With His Family

text: Because of an editing error, two picture captions with the App Smart column on the Personal Tech pages on April 17 misidentified the maker of the apps shown. The screen shot showing a list of hotels in Rome was of Hotel Tonight’s app, and the one showing hotels in Amsterdam was of Expedia’s — not the reverse.
match_headline: Finding, Comparing and Booking Rooms From Your Mobile Device

text: A picture caption on Friday with an art review of two shows of works by Andy Warhol misidentified the venue shown. The photograph, of a visitor viewing a set of four small paintings of Jacqueline Kennedy, depicts the show “13 Most Wanted Men: Andy Warhol and the 1964 World’s Fair,” at the Queens Museum. It does not depict the show “Warhol: Jackie,” at the Blain/Di Donna gallery on Madison Avenue, which features different “Jackie” works.
ref_headline: 13 Most Wanted Men: Andy Warhol and the 1964 World’s Fair,
match_headline: Most Wanted and Most Haunted

text: An article last Sunday about poverty in southern West Virginia misstated the given name of Alma and Randy McNeely’s daughter, who gave birth at age 14. She is Angel, not Angela.
match_headline: 50 Years Into the War on Poverty, Hardship Hits Back

text: An article last Sunday about sea captains who desert their ships, including the captain of the South Korean ferry Sewol that sank on April 16 and the captain of the cruise ship Costa Concordia that capsized in Italy in 2012, misspelled, in some editions, the given name and the surname of the captain of the Andrea Doria, who left the ocean liner that sank off Nantucket in 1956 only after other officers refused to leave without him. He was Piero Calamai, not Peiro Calamari. And a reporting credit omitted part of the given name of a contributor. She is Su-Hyun Lee, not Hyun Lee.
match_headline: Breaking Proud Tradition, Captains Flee and Let Others Go Down With Ship

text: An article in some copies last Sunday about General Mills’s reversal of a policy change that would have curbed its customers’ right to sue quoted incorrectly from an email from Mike Siemienas, a company spokesman. Mr. Siemienas wrote that the company’s “terms and intentions” had been widely misunderstood, leading to confusion among consumers; he did not write that its “concerns and intentions” were misunderstood.
match_headline: General Mills Reverses Itself on Consumers’ Right to Sue

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about places in New Jersey that serve afternoon tea misspelled the name of a tearoom in Convent Station. As the article correctly noted, it is Cosy Cupboard, not Cozy Cupboard.
match_headline: Scones, Finger Sandwiches and Tea

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the 100th anniversary of Wrigley Field described incorrectly part of the history of the stadium’s main tenant, the Chicago Cubs. In 1916, Charles Weeghman bought the Chicago Cubs from Cincinnati ownership; he did not buy the “Cincinnati Cubs.”
match_headline: Oh, the Stories Wrigley Field Could Tell

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Nets’ 94-87 victory over the Toronto Raptors in Game 1 of their N.B.A. playoff series quoted incorrectly from comments by Paul Pierce about a headband he threw into the stands. He said, “It might be worth something one day” — not “It could be worth money someday.”
ref_headline: It might be worth something one day
match_headline: Taunts Fly in Toronto, but Nets Get Last Word

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about the Yankees’ 16-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays misstated the inning in which Yankees pitcher Ivan Nova was removed from the game with elbow discomfort. It was the fifth, not the fourth.
match_headline: In a Thrashing, No Yankee Is Safe on the Mound (Not Even an Infielder)

text: Because of an editing error, the Evening Hours column last Sunday misspelled the surname of a guest at the Opera News awards dinner on April 13. He is Stephen Costello, not Castello.
match_headline: Times Minute | The New Stephen Colbert

text: An article last Sunday about intermissions during operas and concerts of classical music erroneously included one opera among those for which Peter Gelb, the Metropolitan Opera’s general manager, has reduced the number of intermissions. Though he has cut the length of intermissions for about a dozen productions, Berg’s “Wozzeck” is not one of them. (The two intermissions for “Wozzeck” were eliminated in 1980.)
match_headline: Bar and Bathroom Lines, Molto Adagio

text: An article last Sunday about Tatiana Maslany, who stars in the TV series “Orphan Black,” misidentified the source of a 2013 post on Twitter that recommended the series. It was from the show’s own Twitter account, which referred to two separate posts by Emily Nussbaum, the television critic for The New Yorker, of suggestions by her followers for shows she should watch; Ms. Nussbaum did not recommend the show.
match_headline: Shape-Shifting Into Success

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an obituary about Jacob Birnbaum, a leader of the movement to free Soviet Jews, misstated the date of the demonstration shown at the Soviet Mission to the United Nations. It was April 1971, not May 1964. (Mr. Birnbaum led the first such protest in 1964.)
match_headline: Jacob Birnbaum, Civil Rights Champion of Soviet Jews, Dies at 88

text: A picture credit last Sunday with an obituary about the documentary filmmaker Warren Forma misidentified the photographer. The picture of Mr. Forma was taken by Arthur Frank, not by Ben Somoroff.
match_headline: Warren Forma, Documentary Filmmaker, Is Dead at 90

text: A picture credit on April 13 with an article about a luxury cruise on the Amazon in Peru misspelled the surname of the photographer who took the picture of a sunset and the cruise ship. She is Megan Koelemay, not Koolemay.
match_headline: Pink Dolphins and Sunsets Along the Amazon

text: An article last Sunday about the role of climbing Sherpas in expeditions on Mount Everest misspelled the given name of a partner in a Nepalese-owned guide service. He is Sumit Joshi, not Summit.
match_headline: The Risks of Everest Are Deadlier for Some

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a dispute among three community boards about which has jurisdiction over the Atlantic Yards development in Brooklyn misstated the uses of the property before a complex was built there. The area included a working rail yard, residential buildings and businesses. It was not an abandoned rail yard.
match_headline: A Community Tug of War in Brooklyn

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Wednesday about rookie players who are excelling in the N.H.L. playoffs misstated the position of one such player, Nathan MacKinnon of the Colorado Avalanche. While he is listed as a center on the Avalanche roster, he has played right wing for most of the season. The article also misstated an honor given to Ryan Suter, the Minnesota Wild player assigned to defend MacKinnon. He was a finalist for the 2013 Norris Trophy, not the winner. (P. K. Subban of the Montreal Canadiens won the award, which is given to the N.H.L’s top defenseman.)
match_headline: Rookies in Their First Playoffs Are Already Looking Seasoned

text: An obituary on Friday about the filmmaker Michael Glawogger misstated his birth date in 1959. He was born on Dec. 3, not on March 12. (The obituary correctly noted that he was 54.)
match_headline: Michael Glawogger, Who Filmed Lives of Desperation, Dies at 54

text: An article on Saturday about baby food companies’ efforts to compete with homemade purées misspelled the surname of a father who spoke about puréeing vegetables for his daughter. He is Jeff Cretan, not Kretan. The article also misstated the period during which pouch packaging for baby food was introduced. Pouches were introduced in the 2000s; they were not introduced by Gerber in 1997. The article also erroneously included an ingredient among those used by Ella’s Kitchen for its premium baby food. It uses blueberries, but not avocados.
match_headline: As Parents Make Their Own Baby Food, Industry Tries to Adapt

text: An article on Monday about new support for the preservation of several old nuclear reactors misstated, in some copies, the extent of an advertising campaign of Nuclear Matters, an industry-backed group. The group’s new ad campaign is running only in print media in Washington; it is not also appearing in broadcast media.
match_headline: Nuclear Industry Gains Carbon-Focused Allies in Push to Save Reactors

text: An article last Tuesday about reports that Manchester United Manager David Moyes would be fired referred incorrectly to the team’s poor performance this season. Manchester United is headed to its worst finish since the 1989-90 season, not the 1990-91 season, and the team had that finish in the Football League First Division, not the Premier League, which began in 1992.
match_headline: Manchester United’s Moyes Is Out, According to Reports

text: A picture caption on Friday with a film review of “Walking With the Enemy” carried an erroneous credit. The picture is from Liberty Studios, not Liberty Films.
match_headline: In a Scary Uniform, Subverting a March to Death

text: An article on Tuesday about a decision by the White House to issue guidelines intended to pressure universities to combat sexual assaults on campus referred imprecisely to the prevalence of sexual assault on college campuses, according to a White House task force. While the task force noted that one in five college students has been assaulted, it was referring specifically to female students, not to all students.
match_headline: White House to Press Colleges to Do More to Combat Rape

text: Because of an editing error, an article on April 22 about the upheaval on the Crimean Peninsula after it was taken over by Russia misstated, in some editions, the origin of the name of Taurida National University in Simferopol, Crimea. The name derives from Greek history, not from Crimean Tatar history.
match_headline: Under Russia, Life in Crimea Grows Chaotic

text: An article on Saturday about the 40th anniversary of the Rubik’s cube included a quotation that misstated, in some editions, the mathematical formula for the approximate number of ways the toy can be twisted. It is 4.3 times 10 to the 19th — not 43 times 10 to the 19th.
match_headline: A Cube With a Twist: At 40, It Puzzles Anew

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the tensions and challenges posed by Mayor Bill de Blasio’s plan to ban horse carriages from Central Park misidentified the office formerly held by Nicolas Sarkozy, who spoke in favor of keeping the carriages during a recent visit to New York. He was the president of France, not the prime minister.
match_headline: For de Blasio, Carriage Horse Ban Is No Walk in the Park

text: An article on Tuesday about the trend of copycat hotel brand names in China misspelled the city in which a Marvelot hotel (a sound-alike to the Marriott brand) is located. It is Shenyang, not Shengyan.
match_headline: Welcome to the Haiyatt. In China, It’s Not the Hotel It Sounds Like.

text: A recipe last Wednesday for Japanese Milk Bread misstated the equivalent metric weight of 1/3 cup of flour, the proper amount for this recipe. It is 45 grams, not 30 grams.
match_headline: Against the Grain

text: An article on Wednesday about the Supreme Court’s decision to uphold the authority of the Environmental Protection Agency to regulate smog from coal plants that drifts across state lines misstated the number of states affected. It is 28, not 27. The article also misidentified, in some copies, the source of a quotation by Karl Marx that Justice Antonin Scalia paraphrased in his dissent.
