It was in the “Critique of the Gotha Programme” — not “The Communist Manifesto” — that Marx wrote, “From each according to his ability, to each according to his need.”
match_headline: Justices Back Rule Limiting Coal Pollution

text: An article on Saturday about the Walton Family Foundation’s investments in education referred incorrectly to the backgrounds of faculty members of a department at the University of Arkansas, which received money from a Walton foundation for its research on charter schools and other education issues. One faculty member — not several — was recruited directly from a conservative research group.
match_headline: A Walmart Fortune, Spreading Charter Schools

text: An article last Thursday about unease among Eastern European members of NATO over Russian aggression in Ukraine and the alliance’s resolve, or ability, to contain it referred incorrectly to Spain’s participation in NATO. It joined in 1982; it is not a new member.
match_headline: Eastern Europe Frets About NATO’s Ability to Curb Russia

text: A news analysis article on Wednesday about the focus in Washington on the problem of sexual assault on college campuses misstated the surname of one of two women from the University of North Carolina who visited Senator Kirsten E. Gillibrand, a sponsor of earlier legislation to deal with the military’s handling of sexual assault in its ranks. She is Andrea Pino, not Pina.
match_headline: Behind Focus on College Assaults, a Steady Drumbeat by Students

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about plans to give a proper burial to 83 immigrants who died in quarantine on Staten Island in the 19th century while waiting to enter the United States described incorrectly the building that is under construction near the site where the bodies were found. It is a court complex that will serve as Richmond County’s State Supreme Court building and also house the county’s criminal court. It is not a federal courthouse.
match_headline: Refugees of Irish Famine to Get a Proper Burial

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the logistics of the move of the Whitney Museum of American Art from its current home on the Upper East Side to a new building in the meatpacking district misstated the cost of the building. It is $422 million — not $760 million, which is the total cost of the project, including the building, the endowment and other expenses.
match_headline: For the Whitney’s Move, Boxes and Burly Men Just Won’t Do

text: An article last Thursday about the stylist Ilaria Urbinati referred incorrectly to her role in the production of the Showtime series “The L Word.” She was a fashion consultant, not a costume designer.
match_headline: Ilaria Urbinati: The Stylist for the Quieter Half of the Red Carpet

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Tuesday about the book “Missing Microbes” misidentified a condition that the author, Dr. Martin J. Blaser, argues is caused by an imbalance of internal microbes. It is inflammatory bowel disease, not inflammatory bowel syndrome.
match_headline: We Kill Germs at Our Peril

text: An obituary on Monday about David W. Burke, an adviser to politicians and businessmen and a former president of CBS News, using information from his family, misstated his date of birth. He was born on April 3, 1936 — not June 7, 1935. (The obituary correctly noted that he was 78.)
match_headline: David W. Burke, Trusted Aide to Powerful Men, Dies at 78

text: An article on Wednesday about an execution by lethal drugs that was botched by an Oklahoma prison on Tuesday night described incorrectly the administering of the drugs to the inmate. Prison officials said an intravenous line was inserted by a medical technician and the drugs were given by unnamed officials. A medical doctor was present but did not give the drugs, the officials said. And the article, using information from a witness, misidentified the person who said, “Something’s wrong” during the execution of Clayton D. Lockett. It was a prison official, not Mr. Lockett.
match_headline: One Execution Botched, Oklahoma Delays the Next

text: An article on April 21 about a series of errors, mechanical failures and wrong decisions that led to the sinking of the ferry Sewol off the southwest coast of South Korea on April 16 misstated the number of passengers. There were 443 — not 476, which was the total including crew members. The error was repeated in an article on April 25 about reasons the ferry sank.
match_headline: Errors Mounted as Chaos Ruled Capsizing Ferry

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on April 21 about a teacher’s complaint that Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School, an elite arts school in New York City, relied too heavily on grades and test scores over talent evaluations in admitting dance students misstated part of the school’s admissions process. It is the only specialized high school in New York City that does not rely primarily on a single academic exam; it is not the only such school to base admission on the test.
match_headline: Teacher Says LaGuardia High School Picks Tests Over Talent

text: An article in some editions last Friday about the challenge of finding space for each child after an increase in prekindergarten applications in New York City misstated the time period by which city officials hope to accommodate 73,000 children in the program. It is the middle of the 2015-16 school year, not 2015.
match_headline: Pre-K Applicants Up 36% This Year; Mayor’s Challenge Is Finding Seats

text: A picture caption with the Gadgetwise column on the Personal Tech pages on Thursday, about advances in smartphone headphones, misstated the price of the Fix earbuds from Skullcandy. As the column correctly noted, they are $50 — not $30, which is the price of the company’s more moderately priced line of headphones.
match_headline: Headphones That Make Smartphone Calls Easier

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about new privacy policies at Facebook carried an incorrect credit. The photograph, of Facebook’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, was taken by Peter DaSilva for The New York Times, not by Ben Margot of The Associated Press.
match_headline: Facebook to Let Users Limit Data Revealed by Log-Ins

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about the naming of the feature-film jurors for the Cannes Film Festival misstated the number of jury members. There are 9, not 10.
match_headline: Cannes Film Festival Announces Feature Film Jury

text: An article and an accompanying chart on April 22 comparing the projected Keystone XL pipeline with other sources of carbon emissions referred imprecisely to projected emissions from tar-sands oil moving through the pipeline. Producing and burning that oil would emit 18.7 million more metric tons annually than would conventional oil, or far less than 1 percent of United States emissions, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. The tar-sands oil would not emit 18.7 million tons total, but about 150 million tons, or less than 3 percent of United States emissions.
match_headline: Keystone Pipeline May Be Big, but This Is Bigger

text: An obituary on April 14 about the Israeli peace activist Ron Pundak misspelled his parents’ surname. Although he spelled his name Pundak, his parents are Herbert and Sussi Pundik.
match_headline: Ron Pundak, a Key Israeli in Oslo Accords, Dies at 59

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Netflix’s resistance to the proposed merger of Comcast and Time Warner Cable described the sports coverage of the Spanish-language network Telemundo incorrectly. It is broadcast as part of Telemundo; it is not a separate sports network.
match_headline: As Netflix Resists, Most Firms Just Try to Befriend Comcast

text: An article on Thursday about a soccer team that fans in the Finnish city of Tampere assembled after the previous team was expelled from the country’s soccer association gave an incorrect pronunciation for the city’s name. It is TOM-per-ay, not tom-per-AY.
match_headline: Fans Lose Soccer Team, Then Build Their Own

text: An article on Friday about an initial public offering of Ares Management, a private equity and debt investing firm, misstated the amount raised. It was $216 million — not $345.7 million, which would have been the amount had a large shareholder, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, decided to sell shares.
match_headline: Ares Management Set to Go Public, Joining Rivals

text: A picture caption with an article in some editions on Wednesday about the Rangers’ 5-2 loss to the Philadelphia Flyers in Game 6 of their N.H.L. playoff series, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the Flyers player shown celebrating with Scott Hartnell and Wayne Simmonds. He is Jakub Voracek, not Claude Giroux.
match_headline: Yet Again, Rangers Seem Averse to Prosperity

text: An article on Friday about the muralist Hildreth Meière misspelled the surname of the co-author of a monograph about her that was published this week and misstated the name of the university in Chicago where she is an architectural historian. She is Kathleen Murphy Skolnik, not Skolnick, and she is at Roosevelt University, not Rockefeller University.
match_headline: If These Walls Could Speak, They’d Say Her Name

text: An obituary on Thursday about Al Feldstein, the longtime editor of Mad magazine, using information from his family, referred incorrectly to his survivors. He is survived by two daughters, two stepsons, a stepdaughter and five step-grandchildren — not five children, a stepdaughter, three grandchildren and two step-grandsons. The obituary also misstated the middle name of Mr. Feldstein’s second wife. She was Natalie Sonia Sigler, not Natalie Lee Sigler.
match_headline: Al Feldstein, the Soul of Mad Magazine, Dies at 88

text: An article last Sunday about BP’s change in attitude toward the settlement that it signed involving the gulf oil spill referred imprecisely to one allegation of fraud involving victim compensation. The claim center’s fraud prevention director alleged that a lawyer within the center, Lionel Sutton, had received an undisclosed fee from a claim he monitored; he did not say that Mr. Sutton had improperly persuaded officials to pay the claim. The article also misstated the circumstances surrounding Mikal Watts’s departure from the plaintiffs’ lawyers committee. He resigned, he was not kicked off.
match_headline: How a Gulf Settlement That BP Once Hailed Became Its Target

text: An article last Sunday about the new movie “Belle,” which uses some of the themes of Jane Austen’s novel “Sense and Sensibility,” misidentified the character who is the sensible one in that book. The character is Elinor — not Marianne, who is impulsive.
match_headline: A Portrait and the History It Holds

text: An article on April 20 about the new movie “Blue Ruin,” a revenge thriller, misstated the amount it cost to make. It was $425,000, not  “a million and sixty thousand.”
match_headline: Spilling Blood as if They Were Kids

text: A listing of biographical information on April 20 with an article about the playwrights Eric Coble and Catherine Trieschmann, who have new plays opening in New York, misidentified the university from which Mr. Coble earned his M.F.A. in acting. It was at Ohio University in Athens, Ohio — not Ohio State University in Columbus.
match_headline: Two Out-of-Towners, Happily So

text: An article last Sunday about Michael Naess, a man who rents out part of his apartment on Airbnb, gave an outdated name in some editions for one country from which some of Mr. Naess’s guests visited. It is the Czech Republic — and no longer Czechoslovakia, which was split into Slovakia and the Czech Republic more than two decades ago. And a picture caption misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a visitor from Italy. As the article noted correctly, she is Giorgia Mazzi, not Georgia.
match_headline: Airbnb Host Welcomes Travelers From All Over

text: An article on April 20 about the 1964 World’s Fair and how it symbolized the end of a phenomenon rather than the modernity it was intended to represent misstated, in some editions, the year of a similar exhibition in Paris. It was 1889, not 1899.
match_headline: The Fair to End All Fairs

text: A headline on the cover last Sunday highlighting an article inside this section misstated the location featured in the Living In column. As the article correctly noted, it is Pelham Bay, not Pelmam Bay.
match_headline: Pelham Bay, the Bronx: A Blend of Urban and Suburban

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about Yankees fans and Mets fans in the neighborhoods around Citi Field misidentified the woman pictured in Leo’s Latticini, a deli in Corona. She is Irene DeBenedittis, not Marie DeBenedittis, her sister and co-owner of the deli.
match_headline: Clinging to Mets in a Rising Tide of Yankees Fans

text: An article last Sunday about the possible effect on universities of a ruling that Northwestern football players could be considered employees misspelled the surname of a member of Connecticut’s General Assembly who is considering a bill that would give University of Connecticut athletes the right to unionize. He is Matt Lesser, not Lasser.
match_headline: Union Effort at Northwestern May Not Mean Much for Public Colleges

text: An article last Sunday about Kinfolk, a lifestyle magazine in Portland, Ore., misstated the surname of one of its founders. She is Katie Searle-Williams, not Searles-Williams. The article also gave an outdated reference to a retail outlet for the magazine. It is no longer sold at Williams-Sonoma.
match_headline: Better Homes and Hipsters

text: A report March 30 in the Arena column about Cricket Court, the country house of the British fashion designer Alice Temperley, misstated its historical background. While William the Conqueror gave the estate to his brother as a gift, he did not build the house for him. Additionally, there is no evidence the house was ever visited, or lived in, by Leo Tolstoy, who was never in exile. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Broken, Not Bound, by an Intimate Tie (Updated With Podcast)

text: Because of an editing error, a review last Sunday about “Forcing the Spring: Inside the Fight for Marriage Equality,” by Jo Becker, omitted part of the name of an organization that undertakes litigation in support of gay rights. It is Gay and Lesbian Advocates and Defenders, not Gay and Lesbian Defenders.
ref_headline: Forcing the Spring: Inside the Fight for Marriage Equality,
match_headline: Eyes on the Prize

text: An article on April 20 about buying polser (sausages) at stands in Copenhagen misstated the population of that country, and therefore the ratio of pigs to humans. Denmark has 5.6 million inhabitants, not nine million, so pigs outnumber the inhabitants by more than 5 to 1, not 3 to 1.
match_headline: Philanthropist Admits Stealing More Than $1 Million From Charity

text: An article on April 13 about urns from Hilda Hellstrom’s “Sedimentation” series misidentified the materials she uses to make them. They are shaped from ceramic resin and pigments, not from marble.

An article on April 20 about same-sex marriage referred incorrectly to the clergymen Martin Luther King Jr. was responding to when he wrote ‘‘Letter From Birmingham Jail.’’ They were white, not black, clergymen.
match_headline: How the President Got to ‘I Do’ on Same-Sex Marriage

text: An article on April 13 about the singers Elvie Thomas and Geeshie Wiley misidentified the song they recorded with the lyrics ‘‘Squat low, papa, let your mama see.’’ The song is ‘‘Eagles on a Half,’’ not ‘‘Skinny Leg Blues.’’
match_headline: The Ballad of Geeshie and Elvie

text: An obituary on April 20 about Gene Estess, the longtime director of the nonprofit Jericho Project, using information from his wife, omitted some survivors and misstated the number of grandchildren. Three daughters from his first marriage survive him: Alison Estess, Valerie Estess and Meredith Estess Hulbert. And he was the grandfather of nine, not seven.
match_headline: Gene Estess, Who Left Wall Street to Aid the Poor, Dies at 78

text: An article on Wednesday about the grave doubts expressed by an International Olympic Committee official concerning Rio de Janeiro’s preparations for the 2016 Summer Games misidentified the Australian city where the official, John D. Coates, made the remarks. He was speaking in Sydney, not in Melbourne.
match_headline: Preparations for Rio Olympics ‘the Worst,’ Committee Official Says

text: An article on April 27 about a claim by an Afghanistan government commission that it had found two secret prisons that had been run by American and British forces misspelled, in one reference, the given name of one of three Americans killed at a hospital in Kabul on April 24, yet another sign of the decaying relationship between Afghanistan and the United States. He was John Gabel, not Jon.
match_headline: Afghan Panel Claims to Find Secret Prisons

text: An article on April 22 about efforts to offer a direct rail link to the Los Angeles International Airport erroneously included one city on a list of major cities with a rail connection. That city, Boston, offers public transportation to Logan International Airport via a bus line, but it does not have a direct rail line.
match_headline: Linking the Los Angeles Airport

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Yankees’ 4-2 loss to the Seattle Mariners and the team’s hope that pitcher Hiroki Kuroda would rebound from last year’s poor finish misstated his pitching record in the final two months of the 2013 season. It was 1-7, not 2-6.
match_headline: With Yankees Seeking More From Staff, Kuroda Offers More of the Same

text: An article on Monday about the political significance of Senator Rand Paul’s spending the day at the Kentucky Derby with his guest, Rupert Murdoch, described incorrectly the jacket Mr. Paul wore. It was herringbone, not houndstooth.
match_headline: At Derby Day With Murdoch, Rand Paul Goes Through His Paces

text: An article on Saturday about the reaction at Princeton University to a freshman’s essay criticizing the use of the phrase “check your privilege” misidentified the hometown of Zach Horton, a junior who spoke in defense of the writer. He is from Dallas, not Houston.
match_headline: At Princeton, Privilege Is: (a) Commonplace, (b) Misunderstood or (c) Frowned Upon

text: An article on Monday about new podcasts to be introduced by the digital magazine Slate misstated the debut date of one of them, Money, hosted by the financial writer Felix Salmon. It is scheduled to begin on Saturday; it did not start on Monday.
match_headline: Slate Raising Its Investment in Podcasts

text: A picture caption in some editions on Saturday with an article about the Nets’ 97-83 victory over the Toronto Raptors in Game 6 of their N.B.A. playoffs series misidentified the Toronto Raptors player defending Deron Williams. He is Kyle Lowry, not DeMar DeRozan.
match_headline: Hobbled With Ankle Injury, Williams Carries Nets to Game 7

text: An article on Saturday about the ways in which different people, sometimes unwittingly, can help lend fake paintings a veneer of credibility misidentified the art institution where a curator who vouched for the authenticity of a Mark Rothko painting that turned out to be a forgery resigned this month. The curator, Oliver Wick, who was at the Beyeler Foundation in Switzerland at the time he assessed the painting in 2008, resigned from the Kunsthaus Zurich, not the Kunsthalle Zurich.
match_headline: Selling a Fake Painting Takes More Than a Good Artist

text: A critic’s notebook article on Monday about the emergence of three highly regarded bel canto tenors who have all recently performed at the Metropolitan Opera misidentified the site of an amusement park where one, Lawrence Brownlee, had one of his first singing jobs. It is in Sandusky, Ohio, not Cedar Rapids, Iowa.
match_headline: Three Stars Who Navigate on High C’s

text: An article on April 28 about the many complications in the proceedings against Seif al-Islam el-Qaddafi, a son of the late Libyan dictator Col. Muammar el-Qaddafi who is accused of helping his father brutally suppress an uprising against the Qaddafi regime, misstated the amount of time that Mr. Qaddafi has been detained by a militia in the Libyan town of Zintan. He has been held for 29 months, or nearly two and a half years, not 17 months.
match_headline: Qaddafi Son Appears on Screen at His Trial

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about a couple who killed a man in Suffern, N.Y., then drove to the George Washington Bridge and jumped to their deaths reversed the ages of the couple in some editions. As the article correctly noted, Gary Crockett was 41, and Nickie Ann Circelli was 40.
match_headline: Man and Woman Killed Her Uncle Then Jumped From Bridge, Police Say

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about General Motors’ opening talks with families affected by cars with a defective ignition switch reversed the identification of the two men shown. Kenneth Feinberg, a victim-compensation expert hired by G.M., is at the left, and Robert Hilliard, a lawyer for the families, is at the right.
match_headline: G.M. Talks to Families With Claims Over Defects

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about Sotheby’s capitulation to a hedge fund manager and his allies who are seeking seats on Sotheby’s board and a change in its strategic direction misstated the hedge fund manager’s given name in some copies. He is Daniel Loeb, not Donald.
match_headline: Sotheby’s Yields to Hedge Fund Mogul and Allies

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Rangers’ 2-0 loss to the Pittsburgh Penguins in Game 3 of their N.H.L. playoff series misstated the surname of one of the Rangers players. He is Jesper Fast, not Fest.
match_headline: Once Again, Weary Rangers Come Up Empty

text: A picture caption in the Observatory column on Tuesday misidentified an animal whose tears were being drunk by a butterfly and a bee. The animal is a spectacled caiman, not a true crocodile. (Caimans and crocodiles are both members of the order Crocodilia.)
match_headline: Crocodile Tears Hit the Spot for Butterfly and Bee

text: An article on Tuesday about renewed efforts in Germany to prosecute former concentration camp guards accused of taking part in Nazi war crimes gave an outdated name for a Holocaust organization in Washington, using information from its director, who commented on the lack of Holocaust prosecutions. It is the Mandel Center for Advanced Holocaust Studies at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington; it is no longer the Center for Advanced Holocaust Studies.
match_headline: Chasing Death Camp Guards With New Tools

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the Ukrainian businessman Dmitry V. Firtash, and how his connections to Gazprom, the Russian energy company, and to Ukrainian politicians make him a crucial figure in the Ukrainian crisis misidentified a former employer of Gajendra Lal, who figured in a criminal case against Mr. Firtash brought by the United States government. Mr. Lal worked for a company helping to set up a titanium mining deal in India; he did not work for the F.B.I.
match_headline: Brash Ukrainian Mogul Prepares to Fight U.S. Bribery Charges

text: An article on Wednesday about the results of the Republican Senate primary in North Carolina on Tuesday omitted part of the name of a poll on the general election senate race in November. It was a New York Times/Kaiser Family Foundation poll, not just a Times poll. The article also misidentified the segment of people polled. It was North Carolina voters, not all North Carolinians.
match_headline: G.O.P. Establishment Sees Its Candidate Win North Carolina Senate Primary

text: An entry in the Metropolitan Diary on April 28 about a New York City auxiliary police officer who helped reunite a disoriented woman on the Upper West Side with her family misstated the slogan that he saw on the door of a police car. The slogan read, “Courtesy, Professionalism, Respect” — not “To Protect and Serve.”
match_headline: New York City Police Officer Is Arrested in Westchester Shooting

text: An obituary on Monday about the economist Gary S. Becker referred incorrectly to the cause of his death. He died from complications of ulcer surgery, not “after a long illness.” It also misstated the year his first wife, Doria Slote, died. It was 1979, not 1969. And the obituary erroneously attributed a distinction to Professor Becker and his colleague Milton Friedman. They were the first two people to receive both the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Science and the Presidential Medal of Freedom — not the only two. (Daniel Kahneman won the Nobel in 2002 and was given the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.)
match_headline: Gary Becker, 83, Nobel Laureate, Dies; Applied Economics to Everyday Life

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Alan J. Friedman, the former director of the New York Hall of Science, misstated his birth date in 1942. It was Nov. 15, not March 15. (The obituary correctly noted that he was 71.)
match_headline: Alan J. Friedman, Who Revived Hall of Science in Queens, Dies at 71

text: A picture caption in some editions on Tuesday with an obituary about the inventor George H. Heilmeier misstated the year the photograph of Mr. Heilmeier was taken. The date of the photograph, taken when he worked for RCA, is uncertain, but it was not 1972. As the obituary noted, Mr. Heilmeier left RCA in 1970.
match_headline: George H. Heilmeier, an Inventor of LCDs, Dies at 77

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a train wreck in the Western Ghats mountain range in India misspelled, in some editions, the name of a city in western India that is the southern terminus of the route traveled by the train. It is Goa, not Gao.
match_headline: Train Derails in India, Killing at Least 18

text: An article on Wednesday about an administration plan to attract more immigrants with technology skills referred incorrectly to the circumstances under which foreigners working in the United States on temporary H-1B visas can obtain employment-based permanent resident green cards. Employers can apply for the green cards at any time during the six-year term of the H-1B visas; they do not have to wait until the end. (Immigrants cannot apply for themselves.)
match_headline: U.S. Plan Aims to Draw Immigrants With Technology Skills

text: An article on April 21 about the number of policy makers in New York City government held over from the previous mayoral administration gave an outdated position for Jody Adams. She became a special adviser at the Department of Homeless Services on April 15; she is no longer a senior adviser at the Administration for Children’s Services. (She worked there briefly during Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg’s administration.)
match_headline: New Mayor and a New Agenda, but Little Change Within the Ranks

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a film review of the documentary “Llyn Foulkes One Man Band,” using information from Film Forum, where the movie is playing in Manhattan, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of Mr. Foulkes, is by Abigail Gumbiner — not by Chris Quilty, one of the directors.
match_headline: A Portrait of the Outsider Artist, Older and Still Unfiltered

text: An obituary on Thursday about Kenneth Y. Tomlinson, who held leadership positions at the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and other federal communications agencies, misidentified the state in which his birthplace, Mount Airy, is located. It is in North Carolina, not in Virginia.
match_headline: Kenneth Tomlinson, Conservative Voice in Broadcast Oversight, Dies at 69

text: An obituary last Friday about the marksman and former F.B.I. agent Walter R. Walsh misstated his mother’s given name. She was the former Dolinda Invernizzi, not Bolinda. The obituary also misidentified the town where Mr. Walsh found the body of the gangster Baby Face Nelson in 1934. It was Niles Center, Ill., not Skokie. (The town changed its name to Skokie in 1940.)
match_headline: Walter R. Walsh Dies at 106; Terrorized Gangsters and Targets

text: An article on May 2 about the unexpected social media protest that erupted after the Israeli Army punished a soldier over a confrontation, captured on video, with Palestinian teenagers overstated what is known about one of the teenagers. Local media initially reported that he had brass knuckles, but the youth later said he was holding prayer beads instead. (The Israeli military is still investigating the episode, including whether any of the youths had weapons.)
match_headline: Israeli Military Officials Caught Off Guard by a ‘Digital Rebellion’

text: An article in some editions on May 2 about the arrest of Dennis Guglielmo of Greenwich Village in the fatal stabbing of his girlfriend, using information from the Police Department, misstated the age of the victim, who was later identified as Alice Birnbaum. She was 59, not 69.
match_headline: Man Arrested in Fatal Stabbing of Girlfriend

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about lagging federal efforts to toughen safety rules for oil tanker cars gave an incorrect identification from The Associated Press for the owner of some tanker cars that derailed April 30 in Lynchburg, Va. While the train was operated by CSX Transportation, the tanker cars are owned or leased by shippers or oil companies, not by CSX.
match_headline: Despite Orders, Federal Tank-Car Safety Measures Are Slow in Coming

text: Because of an editing error, a film review on Friday about “Palo Alto,” in which James Franco appears and is based on short stories he wrote, referred imprecisely to his growing up in Palo Alto, Calif. He was born in 1978 and grew up there primarily in the 1980s and ’90s, not in the 1970s.
match_headline: A Teenage Tone Poem, Balancing Fear With Rash Impulses

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about a discussion next Thursday night by the playwright David Henry Hwang and the composer Huang Ruo about their new opera, “An American Soldier,” misstated the name of the museum in Manhattan where the event will take place. It is the Museum of Chinese in America, not the New Museum of Chinese in America.
match_headline: Spare Times for May 9-15

text: A picture caption on Page 144 this weekend with an article about the prominent role the women of the Ferragamo family play in the company’s designs includes an incorrect name from a publicist for one of the family’s members. She is Ginevra Bassetti Viscoti, not Consolata Visconti.
match_headline: Women of the House

text: An article last Sunday about T. W. Shannon, a member of the Chickasaw Nation who has emerged as a formidable candidate in the Oklahoma Senate race, misstated Mr. Shannon’s potential place in the history of enrolled tribal members in the Senate. If he wins the Republican nomination and is elected this November, Mr. Shannon, whose father is Chickasaw and whose mother is black, would be only the third — not the second — enrolled tribal member to join the Senate in nearly 100 years. (Charles Curtis of Kansas was first, in 1906, and Ben Nighthorse Campbell of Colorado was second, in 1993.)
match_headline: G.O.P. Hopeful Finds Tribal Tie Cuts Both Ways

text: An article in some editions on April 27 about the Yonkers Arts Weekend omitted a group of artists whose work was displayed at the iPark Hudson office complex. Besides artists from Urban Studio, artists from the Torche’ Galerie also exhibited their work.
match_headline: Yonkers as Gallery

text: A picture credit in some editions on April 27 with an article about an exhibition on typewriters at the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut misstated the surname of the photographer whose took pictures of several of the typewriters. He is Greg Fudacz, not Fudach.
match_headline: The Elegance of Clattering Machines

text: A picture caption with the Connecticut Calendar in some editions last Sunday about a performance by the rock band Alice in Chains misspelled the surname of a band member shown. He is William DuVall, not Duval.
match_headline: Events in Connecticut for May 4-10, 2014

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the Long Island Calendar in some editions on April 13 about an exhibition at the Drawing Room in East Hampton omitted a hyphen in the gallery’s web address. It is drawingroom-gallery.com.
match_headline: Events on Long Island for April 13-19, 2014

text: An article last Sunday about the challenges faced by classical orchestras in smaller cities misidentified Deborah Borda’s position with the Los Angeles Philharmonic. She is its president and chief executive, not its executive director.
match_headline: Tested Out Upstate: Classical’s Future

text: An article on April 27 about the cultural persistence of the 2004 movie “Mean Girls” misidentified the producer of a stage musical version of the film. It is Paramount and Lorne Michaels — not Tina Fey. (As the article correctly noted, Ms. Fey’s husband, the composer Jeff Richmond, is scoring the stage version.)
match_headline: 10 Years Later, the Clique Still Reigns

text: A review on April 20 about “Asia’s Cauldron: The South China Sea and the End of a Stable Pacific,” by Robert D. Kaplan, referred incorrectly to “Finlandization,” a concept the author applies by analogy to China’s relations with its neighbors. The term describes the Soviet Union’s influence on Finland during the Cold War, not Russia’s pressure on the country during the czarist period.
ref_headline: Asia’s Cauldron: The South China Sea and the End of a Stable Pacific,
match_headline: Sea Change

text: An article last Sunday about peer-to-peer lending, which began as a way for individuals to lend money to each other online, misidentified a hedge fund that has entered the sector. It is Arcadia Funds, not Arcadia Capitol Advisors.
match_headline: Loans That Avoid Banks? Maybe Not

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Brigid Ryan and Jyoti Chowdhury referred incorrectly to the State Department office in Istanbul to which the bride has been posted. It is a United States consulate — not the embassy, which is in Ankara, Turkey.
match_headline: Brigid Ryan and Jyoti Chowdhury

text: An obituary in some editions last Sunday about the actor Efrem Zimbalist Jr. contained several errors.
match_headline: Efrem Zimbalist Jr., Star of ‘77 Sunset Strip’ and ‘The F.B.I.’, Dies at 95

text: An obituary last Sunday about Gerald Guralnik, one of six physicists who developed a theory that would lead to the discovery of a subatomic particle that helped explain a perennial mystery about the universe — why it contains life and diversity — referred imprecisely to that theory. It explains why some elementary particles have mass and some do not, not why some elements have matter.
match_headline: Gerald Guralnik, a ‘God Particle’ Pioneer, Dies at 77

text: An article on April 27 about the fetishizing of books referred incorrectly to the sale of e-books. E-books have been outselling the paper kind on Amazon since 2011; it is not the case that all e-books have been outselling the paper kind since last year.
match_headline: On Their Death Bed, Physical Books Have Finally Become Sexy

text: An article on Friday about the debate that continues within the Boy Scouts’ organization a year after its national board struck a compromise to allow gay scouts but exclude gay leaders misidentified, in some editions, the hometown of Cate Readling and Mary Anderson, who commented on the issue. It is Oak Park, Ill., not Oak Brook.
match_headline: Compromise on Gays Pleases No One, Scouts Are Learning

text: An article on Thursday about the Norwegian government’s refusal to meet with the Dalai Lama, Tibet’s spiritual leader in exile, to avoid jeopardizing its relations with China referred incorrectly to NTB, a news organization that quoted the prime minister, Erna Solberg. It is a Norwegian press agency, not a broadcaster.
match_headline: Norway’s Leaders Snub Dalai Lama in Deference to China

text: An article on Tuesday about the failure of the Customs and Border Protection agency to deal with hundreds of reports of abuse by border agents misstated the hiring plans of the agency over the next two years. It is adding 2,000 officers, who oversee the ports of entry into the United States — not Border Patrol agents, who oversee other areas along the border.
match_headline: Complaints of Abuse by Border Agents Often Ignored, Records Show

text: An article on April 19 about the crash landing on the moon of NASA’s Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment Explorer spacecraft, using information from NASA, misstated the density of the moon’s atmosphere as compared with Earth’s. It is one-quadrillionth that of Earth’s atmosphere, not 1/100,000th. The error also appeared in an article on Sept. 1, 2013, about the moon mission.
match_headline: Study of Moon’s Atmosphere Ends With Planned Crash

text: An article on Wednesday about Chiara de Blasio, the daughter of New York City’s mayor, who accepted an award in Maryland for speaking out about her substance abuse and mental illness, referred incorrectly to Kathleen Sebelius, who presented the award. Though she has turned in her resignation, Ms. Sebelius is still the secretary of health and human services. (She is expected to stay on until her replacement takes office.)
match_headline: In Speech and Essay, Chiara de Blasio Details Her Depression and Addiction

text: A picture caption on May 2 with an article about the likelihood that Menachem Stark, a Brooklyn landlord who was found dead in January, was killed in a botched robbery, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of Kendel Felix, the lone suspect charged in the case, is a pool photo by Gregory P. Mango, not by Anthony Lanzilote for The New York Times.
match_headline: Developer’s Killing Said to Be Unplanned

text: An article on Thursday about the federal Transportation Department’s new requirement that railroads notify local emergency personnel when oil shipments are traveling through their states misstated part of the name of a railroad company. It is the Canadian National Railway, not Canada’s National Railway.
match_headline: U.S. Issues Safety Alert for Oil Trains

text: An article on Monday about the Alliance Defending Freedom, which has emerged as a legal force for the religious right, misspelled, in some editions, the surname of San Francisco’s mayor in 2004, who was forced by the group to stop granting same-sex marriage licenses. He is Gavin Newsom, not Newsome. (Mr. Newsom is now California’s lieutenant governor.)
match_headline: Legal Alliance Gains Host of Court Victories for Conservative Christian Movement

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about testimony in a legislative inquiry into the closing of access lanes to the George Washington Bridge misidentified the person who defended the work of the New Jersey Office of Intergovernmental Affairs as “good government” and “amazingly nonpartisan.” The comment was by Christina Renna, a former aide to Gov. Chris Christie — not by Bridget Anne Kelly, Mr. Christie’s former deputy chief of staff who was also Ms. Renna’s boss.
match_headline: Ex-Christie Aide, Testifying in Bridge Inquiry, Portrays a Highly Political Office

text: An article on Thursday about big American companies’ weighing a move overseas to reduce their tax bills misstated the position of Goldman Sachs Investment Partners about a possible deal through which Walgreen would acquire an overseas competitor and reincorporate abroad. The investment firm refrained from voicing an opinion; it did not encourage such a move.
match_headline: Growing Pains for a Goldman Sachs Fund

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about Yonder, a music streaming service that will sell specially licensed smartphones that allow users unlimited free downloads, misstated the day the service would begin operating. It will start today; it did not begin operation on Monday.
match_headline: Digital Music Service to Pose New Challenge to Subscription Model

text: An article on Saturday about the Eurovision Song Contest referred incorrectly to the Austrian contestant, Conchita Wurst, the eventual winner. That is the persona adopted by Thomas Neuwirth, who performs in drag. Conchita Wurst is not a transgender singer.
match_headline: Hamster Wheels, Sequins and, Yes, a Lot of Singing

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the On the Road column, comparing the amenities of modern luxury air travel to those of past decades, misidentified the destination of the Panagra DC-6 airliner shown. It was going to South America, not to South Africa.
match_headline: Forget 1960, the Golden Age Is Now

text: An article on Saturday about President Obama’s frustration with Congress misstated the month that Republicans could win control of the Senate. It is November, not September. (Election Day is Nov. 4.)
match_headline: Obama, Aggravated by Gridlock, Stresses Results in Midterms

text: An article in some editions on Monday about an East Village resident who died over the weekend after being beaten on Sixth Street gave an incorrect name from the Police Department for the victim. He was Wen Hui Ruan, not Ruan Wen Hui. The article also misstated the day Mr. Ruan died. It was Saturday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Two Days After He Was Beaten, East Village Assault Victim Dies

text: An article in some editions last Wednesday about a second-degree murder charge being filed against a Queens driver, who fatally injured a deli worker last June in the East Village, misstated, in some copies, the day the driver was told of the grand jury’s indictment. It was Tuesday, May 6 — not Thursday, May 1.
match_headline: Murder Charge for Driver in Drug-Related Crash at a Manhattan Deli

text: An article on Monday about the health status of the chairman of Samsung Electronics, Lee Kun-hee, after a heart attack misstated the nature of a legal battle between Samsung and Apple. It involves patent infringement claims, not copyright infringement.
match_headline: Samsung Leader Stable After Heart Attack

text: A picture caption on Monday with the Advertising column, about the annual television “upfronts” in which entertainment companies woo advertisers for the coming season, gave an incorrect description from a public relations agency about “The Express,” a show about soccer on the beIN Sports cable channel hosted by Andres Cordero. His show is an English-language version of “The Express,” not a Spanish-language one.
match_headline: Already Crowded, Upfront Week Keeps Snowballing

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about an auction of contemporary art at Christie’s in New York on Monday night misidentified the buyer of a painting of a candle by Dan Colen. She is Meredith Darrow, an art adviser — not Pilar Ordovas, a London art dealer.
match_headline: At Christie’s Auction, an Experiment Proves Fruitful

text: A critic’s notebook article on Monday about the Spring for Music festival at Carnegie Hall misstated the name of the biblical book that was included in readings in “Mozart’s Death in Words and Music” by the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra. It is the Book of Revelation, not the Book of Revelations.
ref_headline: Mozart’s Death in Words and Music
match_headline: A Music Festival Dies, and an Orchestra Mourns

text: A review on Wednesday about the National September 11 Memorial Museum in Manhattan misstated the amount of gallery space. It is 110,000 square feet, not 10,000.
match_headline: The 9/11 Story Told at Bedrock, Powerful as a Punch to the Gut

text: A picture caption on April 19 with an article about the arrests of the captain and two crew members of the South Korean ferry Sewol, which sank on April 16, killing more than 250 people, gave an incorrect identification from the European Pressphoto Agency for the person shown being rescued from the sinking vessel. He was an unidentified crew member, not the ship’s captain, Lee Jun-seok.
match_headline: Captain and Two Crew Members Are Arrested in Korean Ferry Sinking

text: An article on Friday about new executive actions by President Obama on energy, as well as private and nonprofit groups’ investments in energy efficiency and renewable energy, misstated the energy efficiency of Walmart. It gets about 25 percent of its electricity from renewable power sources such as solar and wind; it does not get about 25 percent of its electricity from solar power. (The company receives 6 percent of its electricity from solar power.) The article also misstated the amount of power in the United States that comes from solar sources. It is 1.13 percent, not 2 percent.
match_headline: Obama to Give Push on Climate

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a report on global climate change from a leading government-funded military research organization misstated the military rank of David Titley. He is a rear admiral, not an admiral. Also because of an editing error, the article misstated the name of the research organization that released the report. It is the CNA Corporation Military Advisory Board, not the Center for Naval Analyses Military Advisory Board.
match_headline: Climate Change Deemed Growing Security Threat by Military Researchers

text: An article on Friday about the mayoral race in Newark between Ras Baraka and Shavar Jeffries misstated the percentage of the city’s population that is Hispanic. It is 33 percent, not 23. The article also misstated the gender of one of Mr. Jeffries’s children. He has a daughter and a son, not two daughters.
match_headline: Newark Mayoral Race Seen as Referendum on Booker

text: An article last Thursday about the arrest of a New York City councilman, Ruben W. Wills, on fraud and grand larceny charges misstated the election year in which he won his seat by 626 votes. It was 2010, not 2013.
match_headline: Councilman Is Accused of Stealing Public Funds

text: An article on May 5 about Alexander Imich, a 111-year-old Upper West Side resident who is believed to be the oldest man in the world, misstated the role the Wright brothers played in the invention of manned flight. The Wright brothers, whose breakthrough was 111 years ago this coming December, are credited with inventing the first manned airplane that sustained controlled and machined-powered flights; they did not invent manned flight. (Many other individuals are credited with contributions, like gliders, that led to the breakthrough.)
match_headline: An Ever-Curious Spirit, Unbeaten After 111 Years

text: An article last Thursday about new zoning laws in Portland, Ore., meant to encourage small backyard houses misstated the name of a course on building such houses. It is “Building an Accessory Dwelling Unit on Your Property in Portland, Oregon” — not “This Is the Little Life,” which is a website on small backyard house. The article also misstated the surname of a woman who converted a a garage into a home. She is Jen Wantland, not Wetland.
ref_headline: Building an Accessory Dwelling Unit on Your Property in Portland, Oregon
match_headline: Grandma Never Had It So Good

text: A report last Thursday in the Currents column about the book “Goodnight Nanny-Cam” misspelled the surname of one of the authors. As an accompanying image of the book cover showed, she is Lizzy Ratner, not Rattner.
match_headline: A Classic (Again) Ripe for an Update

text: An article last Thursday about the fashion blogger Garance Doré misstated the job title at GQ.com held by John Jannuzzi, a social media expert who has followed Ms. Doré’s career. He is its senior digital editor, not its senior digital projects editor.
match_headline: Garance Doré: A Half, but Whole

text: An obituary on Saturday about the jazz trumpeter Joe Wilder referred imprecisely to his one-week stint at the Village Vanguard in 2006. It was his first extended engagement in New York as the leader of his own group — not his first engagement.
match_headline: Joe Wilder, Horn Player, Dies at 92; Elegance Was His Theme Song

text: An article on May 8 about an abrupt move by President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to take a less aggressive tone on the Ukraine crisis referred incorrectly to Yugoslavia, which experienced sharp divisions not unlike those of Ukraine. Until its breakup in 1991, Yugoslavia was ruled by a Communist party, which maintained a course independent of the Soviet Union. Yugoslavia was not a “Soviet satellite.”
match_headline: Putin Announces Pullback From Ukraine Border

text: An article on Wednesday about a twist in the inquiry into the 2005 assassination of the former Lebanese prime minister Rafik Hariri that had a Beirut television executive facing charges unrelated to the murder itself misstated the amount that an international tribunal in the Netherlands has spent investigating the Hariri case. It is $325 million, not $325,000.
match_headline: Lebanese TV Executive Is Summoned to Hague Court

text: An article on Monday about an American couple’s appearance in a video that they hope will help in their appeal of a conviction, by a court in Qatar, in the death of their daughter as well as raise money for their defense misstated the date of an appellate court proceeding where defense and prosecution arguments are to be heard together. It is June 16, not June 17.
match_headline: A Push to Aid American Couple Held in Child’s Death in Qatar

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the likely return of the Stuyvesant Town-Peter Cooper Village housing development to the auction block misidentified the location of the complex. It is on the East Side of Manhattan, not the Lower East Side. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Stuyvesant Town, Bastion of Affordable Housing, Is on Way Back to Auction

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about a New York State gambling panel’s decision to set investment minimums for new casinos misidentified the developers behind a planned project at the Grossinger’s resort in Liberty, N.Y. It is a project of Foxwoods Catskill Resort, a partnership of Muss Development in Brooklyn and Foxwoods Resort Casino in Connecticut. It is not a project of the Mohegan Tribal Gaming Authority, which has plans for a casino near Monticello.
match_headline: $350 Million Investment Needed to Open Casino Closest to New York City, Panel Says

text: A picture caption in some editions last Friday with an article about Stanley L. Cohen, a defense lawyer who on May 1 both represented a terrorist in one case and pleaded guilty to failing to file tax returns in another, misspelled the surname of Mr. Cohen’s lawyer. He is Randolph E. Daar, not Darr.
match_headline: Split Day in Court, as Defendant and Counsel

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the rookie goalie John Gibson of the Anaheim Ducks misstated the number of days until his 21st birthday when he shut out the Los Angeles Kings in Game 4 of the N.H.L. playoff series on Saturday. At the time, he was 65 days shy of his birthday, not 35.
match_headline: A Sudden Ducks Savior Is a Rookie (Really)

text: A picture on May 9 with the continuation of an article about changes in New York’s Medicaid policy, which have led managed care companies to enroll more adult home residents and low-maintenance patients at the expense of people with greater medical needs, was published in error. The photograph showed the Kings Hotel on 39th Street in Brooklyn, which did not house residents of adult homes affected by Hurricane Sandy. They were sent to a hotel with the same name at 2416 Atlantic Avenue.
match_headline: Medicaid Shift Fuels Rush for Profitable Clients

text: An article in some editions on Friday about a possible deal that would provide $100 million for repairs to Pier 40 at the foot of West Houston Street in Manhattan reversed the third and fourth columns of type. The correct version can be found at nytimes.com/nyregion .
match_headline: Possible Deal May Bring Money to Repair Pier 40 in Manhattan

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about the “Flow.14” art exhibition at Randalls Island Park in Manhattan misstated the opening date. It is tomorrow; it did not open on Friday.
match_headline: Spare Times for May 16-22

text: Because of an editing error, an art review on Friday about “Rachel, Monique” at the Episcopal Church of the Heavenly Rest in Manhattan, an installation by Sophie Calle about the life and death of her mother, Monique Sindler, who was also known as Rachel, referred incorrectly in some editions to an artwork spelling out her final word, “souci.” It was fashioned with real butterflies, not fake flower blossoms.
match_headline: As Maman Lay Dying, Her Spirit Became Art

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the trade-offs for retirees who relocate to Canada misstated the value of Canadian currency relative to United States currency in January. The value was 89.7 United States cents to the Canadian dollar, not 89.7 Canadian cents to the United States dollar. The article also gave an outdated name for the political party that has changed the way potential immigrants are selected. It is the Conservative Party of Canada, not the Progressive Conservative Party (The Conservative Party of Canada was formed in 2003 in a merger between the Progressive Conservative Party and the Canadian Reform Conservative Alliance.)
match_headline: The Trade-Offs of Relocating North to Canada

text: An article on Thursday about the sport of pickleball rendered incorrectly the name of a company that sells equipment for the sport. The company is Pickle-ball Inc., not Pickleball Inc. The article also erroneously included it among new businesses associated with the sport. Pickle-ball Inc. was founded in 1972.
match_headline: A Funny Name, a Serious Sport. Pickleball, Anyone?

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about a national movement to teach computer programming referred incorrectly in some editions to the founder of Code.org, who favored the instruction. The founder, Hadi Partovi, is a man.
match_headline: Reading, Writing, Arithmetic, and Lately, Coding

text: An article last Sunday about the subjects of documentaries who promote their films misstated the surname of the husband of the “Star Trek” actor George Takei, featured in “To Be Takei.” He is Brad Takei — not Altman, his surname before his marriage.
match_headline: Film Stars, but With an Asterisk

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the visual artist Mark Grotjahn referred incorrectly to the titles of three of his works. The painting in his “Circus” series is “Untitled (Circus No. 1 Face 44.18)”; the painting in his “Butterfly” series is “Untitled (Orange Butterfly Blue MG03) #1”; and the bronze sculpture is called “Untitled (African, Gated Front and Back Mask M34.b).” These works were not untitled.
match_headline: Childlike, but Hardly Child’s Play

text: An article in the special Summer Movies section on May 4 about “Dawn of the Planet of the Apes” misidentified Daniel Barrett’s job on that film. He was an animation supervisor, not a visual effects coordinator.
ref_headline: Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
match_headline: The Posture, the Gestures, the Thoughts

text: An article on May 4 about Norm Lewis, cast as Broadway’s first black Phantom of the Opera, misstated when he took over the role of John in “Miss Saigon.” He was the fifth replacement in the role on Broadway; he did not succeed Hinton Battle, who originated the part.
match_headline: Stalking the Role of an Operatic Stalker

text: An article last Sunday about Irv Levin’s sale in 1981 of the N.B.A.’s San Diego Clippers to Donald Sterling, their current owner, referred incorrectly to Mr. Levin’s military service during World War II. He was a bombardier, not a fighter pilot.
match_headline: Clippers for Sale, and the Owner Who Was Desperate

text: An article last Sunday about the battles in the goal crease during the N.H.L. playoffs misidentified the team of Andrew Cogliano. He plays for the Anaheim Ducks, not the Los Angeles Kings.
match_headline: Battles for the Crease Exact a Toll in the Playoffs

text: Because of an editing error, illustrations with an article last Sunday about a new graphic novel about Andre the Giant carried an erroneous credit in some copies. The illustrations from the comic book were by Box Brown, not by Gina Gagliano.
match_headline: Filling Pages Not Difficult With a Life Lived Large

text: A picture caption in some editions on April 27 with an article about an art exhibition in Katonah, N.Y., featuring works by Jasper Johns and John Lund, misstated the year in which the print “Flag on Orange” was completed. It was 1998, not 1958.
match_headline: A Marriage of Visual Masters

text: An article last Sunday about a women’s fashion trend featuring bare midriffs misspelled the surname of a spokeswoman for Physique 57, a workout studio with three locations in Manhattan that reports increased attendance for classes targeting the abdominal area. She is Jennifer Billet, not Billett.
match_headline: The Time of the Tummy

text: An article last Sunday about Colombia’s uncertain prospects as a tourist attraction misstated the national affiliation of the nonprofit foundation Share the Stoke, which has contributed surfboards to some children in a village in the Chocó region as part of an effort to make it a surfing destination. It is American, not Australian.
Because of an editing error, a contributors’ note on the contents page last Sunday misstated the surname of the writer of the article “Lost in Paradise.” She is Julia Chaplin, not Chapman.
match_headline: Lost in Paradise

text: An article on Tuesday about an increase in the number of Major League Baseball teams that are using radical infield shifts referred incorrectly to double plays turned by the Pittsburgh Pirates in recent years. The numbers — 339 in 2012 without the shift and 419 in 2013 with the shift — represented the sum of players involved in double plays each year (a 6-4-3 double play would involve three players), not the total double plays by the team. (There were 126 of those in 2012 and 154 in 2013.)
match_headline: Who’s on Third? In Baseball’s Shifting Defenses, Maybe Nobody

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about a Democratic primary debate involving Representative Charles B. Rangel, State Senator Adriano D. Espaillat and the Rev. Michael A. Walrond misidentified the type of cellphone Mr. Rangel held up at the start of the event. It was an iPhone, not a BlackBerry.
match_headline: Rangel, at Debate, Wields a Phone to Mock His Opponents

text: An article on Thursday about a L’Oréal app that will let iPhone and iPad users virtually try cosmetic products, using information provided by L’Oréal, erroneously attributed a distinction to its partner in the app, the visual effects company Image Metrics. Image Metrics worked on visual effects for the film “The Curious Case of Benjamin Button,” but it did not win an Oscar for that work. (The Oscar for Best Achievement in Visual Effects in that film went to four individuals — Eric Barba, Steve Preeg, Burt Dalton and Craig Barron. Mr. Barba and Mr. Preeg worked for Digital Domain, a visual effects company that received support services from Image Metrics.)
ref_headline: The Curious Case of Benjamin Button,
match_headline: Mirror, Mirror in the App: What’s the Fairest Shade and Shadow of Them All?

text: An article on Friday about efforts by Pepsi and Coca-Cola to recreate the soda fountain experience with touch-screen machines that let customers custom-blend their beverages misstated the number of Coca-Cola products available in Coke’s Freestyle machine when it was introduced. It was 100, not 80. (Newer machines offer 140 products.)
match_headline: Pepsi Challenges Coke in the Race to Design a More Tappable Soda Fountain

text: An article on Thursday about the American soccer player Chris Wondolowski misstated his number of goals in a game last July in which his surname was misspelled on his jersey, and misidentified, in some copies, the opponent that day. He scored three goals, not two, against Belize, not Guatemala. The article also misstated the circumstances of Wondolowski’s move to the Houston Dynamo from the San Jose Earthquakes in Major League Soccer. The Earthquakes relocated to Houston and changed their nickname to Dynamo; Wondolowski was not “traded to the Houston Dynamo.”
match_headline: Forward Has Goals Aplenty but Ground to Make Up

text: An article last Monday about the arrest of Philip Nelson, a Rutgers quarterback, referred incorrectly to the location of Mankato, Minn., where the arrest took place. It is southwest of Minneapolis, not southeast.
match_headline: Rutgers Player Is Charged With Assault in Minnesota

text: A map in some editions on Monday with an article about increased gun violence in the northern Bronx’s 47th Police Precinct misstated the name of a street within its boundaries. It is East 233rd Street, not East 23rd Road.
match_headline: Killings Surge in North Bronx, Testing New Police Tactics

text: A picture caption on Friday with a film review of “Cold Bloom” reversed the identities of the actors shown. Takahiro Miura is at the left, and Asami Usuda is at the right.
match_headline: After an Accident, a Test of Forgiveness

text: An article on Thursday about the financial effect of drawing Social Security benefits at age 62 misstated the retirement age at which a monthly payment of $1,000, for example, would instead be a monthly payment of $1,320 if the recipient waited until age 70 to collect. It is 66, not 62.
match_headline: Social Security at 62? Let’s Run the Numbers

text: A picture credit on Saturday with an obituary about the forensic anthropologist Clyde Snow, using information from The Associated Press, misstated the surname of the photographer who took the picture of Dr. Snow holding a skull. He is David Longstreath, not Longstreet.
match_headline: Clyde Snow, Sleuth Who Read Bones From King Tut’s to Kennedy’s, Dies at 86

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Wyoming’s being the first state to reject national science standards for schools misidentified, in some editions, the organization led by Ron Micheli, who said the standards were prejudiced against fossil fuel development. It is the State Board of Education, not the State Department of Education. The article also misidentified, in some editions, a main agricultural crop in Goshen County, where schools have adopted the standards on their own. It is sugar beets, not sugar cane.
match_headline: Science Standards Divide a State Built on Coal and Oil

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the Long Island Rail Road’s Lost and Found department misstated the service number that passengers can call to check on items. It is 511, not 411.
match_headline: For Long Island Rail Road, a Track Record to Tout: Matching Riders With Lost Items

text: An article on Tuesday about a federal appeals court’s refusal to reconsider a major decision in the 2010 Gulf of Mexico oil spill misspelled the surname of an executive at BP America who commented on the decision. He is Geoff Morrell, not Morell.
match_headline: Court Declines to Review Deal for Gulf Spill

text: An article in some editions on Friday about Rangers goalie Henrik Lundqvist’s history playing in Montreal misstated the given name of a member of the team’s fourth line. He is Derek Dorsett, not Daniel. The article also misstated the score in the Montreal Canadiens’ Game 7 victory over the Boston Bruins. It was 3-1, not 2-1.
match_headline: Lundqvist Will Revisit a Weak Spot

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the British author Geoff Dyer and his new book, “Another Great Day at Sea: Life Aboard the USS George H. W. Bush,” misstated the title of one of his novels at one point in some editions. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is “The Colour of Memory,” not “The Colour of Money.”
ref_headline: Another Great Day at Sea: Life Aboard the USS George H. W. Bush,
match_headline: Wedged Into Warship With Pen in Hand

text: An obituary in some early editions on Monday and in some late editions on Tuesday about Robert F. Erburu, the former chief executive and chairman of the Times Mirror Company, referred incorrectly to the circumstances under which he left the chief executive position in 1995. He was approaching the mandatory retirement age of 65; he did not lose the job because of declining profits.
match_headline: Robert F. Erburu, Who Led Times Mirror Company, Dies at 83

text: An obituary in some late editions on Monday about the singer Jerry Vale misspelled the surname of an owner of the Sands Hotel in Las Vegas, where Mr. Vale performed early in his career. He was Jack Entratter, not Enratter. The obituary also misstated the maiden name of Mr. Vale’s wife. She was Rita Grapel, not Vale.
match_headline: Jerry Vale, Who Crooned Smoothly of Love, Is Dead at 83

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about Arthur Gelb, a former managing editor of The New York Times, referred incorrectly to Edwin Diamond, the author of “Behind the Times: Inside the New New York Times.” He was a former contributor to The Times, not a staff reporter. The obituary also referred incorrectly to the area where Mr. Gelb’s parents once lived. Their border town, Kimyat, was in what was then Czechoslovakia; the town later became a part of what is now Ukraine. Czechoslovakia itself did not become Ukraine. (It became the Czech Republic and Slovakia.)
ref_headline: Behind the Times: Inside the New New York Times.
match_headline: Arthur Gelb, Critic and Editor Who Shaped The Times, Dies at 90

text: An article on Wednesday about additional vehicle recalls by General Motors misidentified, in some copies, the state represented by Senator Lindsey Graham. He is a Republican from South Carolina, not Florida.
match_headline: A Flurry of Recalls at G.M. as Pressure Mounts

text: An article on Saturday about the breeding of California Chrome, the winner of the Kentucky Derby, misstated part of the name of the California racetrack where his dam, Love the Chase, competed. It is Golden Gate Fields, not Golden Gate Park.
match_headline: Top Horse, From a Place Winners Aren’t Made

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the World Briefing column on Saturday about a cargo of exotic reptiles that was seized at Frankfurt Airport in Germany misstated the number of turtles that died after the seizure. It was three, not five.
match_headline: Germany: The Flight of the Iguana

text: An article on Wednesday about a ruling by a federal judge that Pennsylvania’s ban on same-sex marriage was unconstitutional misstated the year in which the state adopted its restrictive marriage law. It was 1996, not 2006.
match_headline: Judge Strikes Down Pennsylvania’s Gay-Marriage Ban

text: An article in some editions last Thursday about a bookstore in the East Village that raised enough money to survive and relocate elsewhere in the neighborhood rendered the store’s name incorrectly. It is St. Mark’s Bookshop, not St. Marks. (The error was repeated in the headline.) The article also misstated the time frame for the store’s move. It is scheduled for this summer, not this fall.
match_headline: St. Mark’s Bookshop in East Village Signs Lease on New Location

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about Rick Nash, who scored goals in the first two games of the Rangers’ N.H.L. playoff series with the Montreal Canadiens, erroneously attributed a distinction to the Rangers’ recent five-game postseason winning streak. It is their longest such streak since they won seven in a row in the 1994 playoffs; it did not tie the 1994 streak.
match_headline: Nash Gets Hot for the Sizzling Rangers

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the casting of Annette Bening as Goneril in this summer’s Shakespeare in the Park production of “King Lear” misstated the date the play closes. It is to run from July 22 through Aug. 17, not through Aug. 5.
match_headline: Commission for Dead Composer, and Other Pieces

text: A subheading on Wednesday with an article about the archive of the author Tom Wolfe, which has been bought by the New York Public Library, misidentified one of the people who criticized him for his New York magazine article “Radical Chic: That Party at Lenny’s.” The criticism came from the sister of Leonard Bernstein, not from Mr. Wolfe’s sister.
ref_headline: Radical Chic: That Party at Lenny’s.
match_headline: From ‘Acid’ to ‘Bonfire,’ an Archive That Sizzles

text: An article last Thursday about Michael Alig, a former Manhattan night life figure who was recently paroled after 17 years in prison for manslaughter, misspelled the name of a gay hookup app. It is Grindr, not Grndr. In addition, the article, using information from Mr. Alig and his publicist, misidentified the source of  a rumor — later proved false — that Mr. Alig was using drugs in the restroom of a restaurant. James St. James, who was with Mr. Alig at the restaurant, started the rumor — not DJ Scotto, another person with Mr. Alig.
match_headline: After Prison, No After-Hours

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Tadeusz Rozewicz, a globally acclaimed Polish poet, misstated his age in the headline. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 92, not 91. The error also appeared in the headline of a capsule summary of the obituary.
match_headline: Tadeusz Rozewicz, Fierce Poetic Voice of Postwar Poland, Is Dead at 92

text: An article last Friday about the killing of two young Palestinians in clashes with Israeli security forces, using information from a hospital, misstated the name and age one of them. He was Mohammad Mahmoud Odeh Salameh, not Muhammad Odeh Abu al Daher, and he was 16, not 20.
match_headline: Two Palestinians Killed in Clashes With Israeli Forces

text: An article on May 10 about a call by the Dalai Lama for an outside inquiry into the self-immolations of more than 130 Tibetans in anti-China demonstrations over the past five years referred incorrectly to the Tibetans who have carried out the self-immolations. Most are ordinary Tibetans, not Buddhist monks.
match_headline: Dalai Lama Urges Outside Inquiry Into Spate of Self-Immolations Among Tibetans

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about a decision by New York City to halt an overhaul of its 911 system described incorrectly the city’s response to a fire in Coney Island on April 6 that killed a police officer. While there were miscommunication and procedural errors, there was no delay in responding to the fire.
match_headline: New York City Calls Halt to Overhaul of 911 System

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the potential for a bubble in Turkish real estate referred incorrectly to Turkey’s housing inventory. The inventory of unsold housing units, now at about 1.5 million, was close to zero several years ago, not one year ago.
match_headline: Alarm Over Istanbul’s Building Boom

text: Because of an editing error, a music review on Monday about a recital by the pianist Emanuel Ax, at Carnegie Hall, misstated part of the title of a work he played that was composed by Missy Mazzoli. It is “Bolts of Loving Thunder,” not “Bolts of Rolling Thunder.”
match_headline: Short Pieces That, Together, Span Centuries

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about the scrutiny Occupy protesters have faced from enforcement officials misidentified, in some copies, the college where the linguist Noam Chomsky, who appeared at an Occupy Boston event, is a professor. It is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, not Harvard Divinity School.
match_headline: Officials Cast Wide Net in Monitoring Occupy Protests

text: A picture caption last Saturday with an article about New Yorkers who have decided that visiting the National September 11 Memorial Museum would be too painful misidentified, in some editions, the relative of one New Yorker, Kathy Bowden, who died on Sept. 11, 2001. As the article noted correctly, her brother was killed, not her son. And because of an editing error, the article misspelled the given name and the surname of  a contributing reporter. He is Derrick Nunnally, not Derek Nunally.
match_headline: As 9/11 Museum Opens, These New Yorkers Will Stay Away

text: An article last Saturday about the fatal shooting by New York City police officers of a suspect in the robbery of a pharmacy after the police tracked him with a GPS device in a pill bottle misstated, in some editions, the prison record of the man, Scott Kato, using information from the New York State Department of Corrections. He served about 12 years in prison on a sexual abuse and robbery conviction and then an additional 16 months for parole violations; he did not serve about 16 years during two stints for sexual abuse and robbery convictions.
match_headline: Robbery Suspect Tracked by GPS and Killed

text: A news analysis article on Thursday examining the ramifications of the criminal conviction of Credit Suisse described incorrectly another firm. While Arthur Andersen was convicted in 2002 of obstruction of justice over an investigation by securities regulators into the financial debacle at Enron, the Supreme Court in 2005 overturned that verdict over flaws in jury instructions. The government chose not to retry the case; thus, the firm is not a “corporate felon.”
match_headline: Credit Suisse Pleads Guilty in Felony Case

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Mets’ 5-3 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers referred incorrectly, in some copies, to Dodgers pitcher Zack Greinke, who entered Thursday’s game with a streak of 21 consecutive starts in which he allowed two earned runs or fewer. He was tied for the major league record with Roger Clemens; he had not set the record. (He broke the mark Thursday.)
match_headline: Struggling Mets Stand Up to an Ace

text: An article last Sunday about colleges that are considering “trigger warnings” or explicit alerts to let students know that the material they are about to read or see might upset them misstated, in some copies, the surname of a professor at Oberlin who criticized the idea. He is Marc Blecher, not Belcher.
match_headline: Warning: The Literary Canon Could Make Students Squirm

text: An article last Sunday about talks in eastern Ukraine aimed at resolving the country’s political crisis misidentified the source of a quotation that called for the Ukrainian government to end its military campaign against the separatists. It was Valeriy N. Holenko, the chairman of Luhansk Regional Council — not Sergei S. Kravchenko, the mayor of Luhansk — who said, “This is the only option in my opinion that can save Ukraine from division.”
ref_headline: This is the only option in my opinion that can save Ukraine from division.
match_headline: Talks in East Aim to Ease Tensions in Ukraine

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about music therapy programs in Westchester and Dutchess counties misspelled the given name of a student at the Institute for Music and Health in Dutchess County. He is Kahlil Henry, not Khalil.
match_headline: Coaxing Lyrical Voices From the Withdrawn

text: An entry in the pop and jazz listings last Sunday in the special Summer Stages section misidentified the state that is home to the Kansas City Rockfest. It is Missouri, not Kansas.
match_headline: Glowsticks, Banjos, Food Trucks for Miles

text: An entry in the theater listings last Sunday in the special Summer Stages section referred incorrectly to the Santa Cruz Shakespeare festival. It is in Northern California, not in Southern California. And another entry rendered incorrectly the nickname of California Shakespeare Theater. It is Cal Shakes, not CalShakes.
match_headline: Nationwide Theater Listings

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about Karga Seven Pictures, which specializes in TV series that combine science and special effects, misidentified the channel that shows Karga’s “Tornado Alley.” It is the Weather Channel, not the Science Channel.
match_headline: Stealth Lessons Sneak Up on Viewers

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about the Rangers’ 7-2 victory over the Montreal Canadiens in Game 1 of their N.H.L. playoff series misstated, in some copies, the number of saves Henrik Lundqvist made. He stopped 20 shots, not 17.
match_headline: An Impenetrable Fortress Proves Porous as the Rangers Take Game 1

text: An article last Sunday about the Western Conference finals matchup between the Chicago Blackhawks and the Los Angeles Kings in the N.H.L. playoffs referred incorrectly to the number of postseason games played by the two teams over the past three seasons. They have played the most among Western Conference teams, not among N.H.L. teams. (The Kings led the N.H.L. in playoff games during that period, with 52, entering this season’s conference finals, followed by the Rangers, with 46, and the Blackhawks and the Boston Bruins, with 41 each.)
match_headline: A Familiar Duel for the West Title

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about California Chrome’s win in the Preakness Stakes misstated the odds of his victory at race time. He was a 1-to-2 favorite, not 2-to-3.
match_headline: California Chrome Wins Preakness for Second Jewel

text: Because of an editing error, the Evening Hours column last Sunday misstated the name of a guest at the Robin Hood Foundation benefit on May 12. He is Bill Ackman, not Ackerman.
match_headline: Evening Hours | Petals and Medals

text: An article on May 11 about former Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner paraphrased incorrectly from a statement by Neil Barofsky, the former special inspector general of the Troubled Asset Relief Program. In an email, Barofsky criticized Geithner and his team — not Geithner, Ben Bernanke and Henry Paulson — for consistently putting ‘‘the interests of the banks over those who were supposed to be helped, like struggling homeowners.’’ The article also misidentif ed the position Lee Sachs held in the Obama administration. He was an economic adviser, not an assistant Treasury secretary.
match_headline: What Timothy Geithner Really Thinks

text: An obituary last Sunday about the reporter William Worthy misstated the position held by Nikita S. Khrushchev when Mr. Worthy interviewed him in Moscow in 1955. He was the first secretary of the Soviet Communist Party; he had not yet become premier.
match_headline: William Worthy, a Reporter Drawn to Forbidden Datelines, Dies at 92

text: An obituary last Sunday about Nancy Malone, an actress who became a television producer and director, misidentified the position she held on the television series “The Bionic Woman.” She was a producer of the show, not a director.
match_headline: Nancy Malone, Actress and TV Director, Dies at 79

text: An article on Friday  about an Egyptian teenager, Abdullah Assem, who is seeking asylum in the United States, misstated, in some editions, the day he gave an interview at the Council on American-Islamic Relations. It was Thursday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Path to an Asylum Request, From Egypt Jail to California Fair
