text: An article on Tuesday about a drastic increase in the amount of heroin being trafficked through New York City misstated, at one point, the day on which two men were arrested in the Bronx carrying 53 pounds of the drug. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it was Friday, May 16, not last Monday. (The arrests were announced last Monday.) The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: New York Is a Hub in a Surging Heroin Trade

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Chicago Blackhawks, who are trying to win their third Stanley Cup in five years, summarized incorrectly Wayne Gretzky’s success with the Edmonton Oilers in the 1980s. Gretzky won four Stanley Cups in five years with the team, not five Cups in seven years. (Gretzky was traded to the Los Angeles Kings before the Oilers won a fifth Cup, in 1989-90.)
match_headline: The Kings’ Six-Goal Surge Steals a Chicago Night

text: An article on May 6 about a swim team based at BronxWorks’ Carolyn McLaughlin Community Center in the South Bronx, using information from the center, misstated the time period during which a pool was built there. It was built in the 1950s, not in 1961.
match_headline: Against the Odds, a South Bronx Swim Team Finds Success

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the growing number of students who have discovered an alternative route to college through fringe sports like rugby described incorrectly the rugby skills being practiced in a park by high school players. They were practicing passes — not forward passes, which are illegal in the sport.
match_headline: Need Scholarship? Join Scrum

text: An obituary last Tuesday about Jack Brabham, the racecar driver and builder, misstated the number of times he won the constructors’ championship as a Formula One car builder. It was twice, not four times. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Brabham’s ownership of the Brabham racing team. He owned it when it won two world drivers’ titles, not four. (Bernie Ecclestone owned the team when it won its third and fourth titles.)
match_headline: Jack Brabham, 88, Who Raced and Built Formula One Winners, Dies

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the signing of a $400 billion gas deal between China and Russia misidentified, in some editions, the city in which President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and President Xi Jinping of China held their conference. It was Shanghai, not Beijing.
match_headline: China and Russia Reach 30-Year Gas Deal

text: An article on Sunday about a political vacuum in Lebanon, created when President Michel Suleiman left office at the end of his term without the country’s political factions having agreed on a successor, misstated the year that the Lebanese civil war ended. It was 1990, not 2000.
match_headline: Lebanon’s Political Standoff Leaves Leadership Vacancy

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about the deep divisions in Ukraine on the eve of a national election misstated the viewpoint of a teacher, Dmitry Pertsov. He said that he supported a united Ukraine, not the current government in Kiev.
match_headline: Calm Streets Mask Deep Divisions in Donetsk

text: An article last Wednesday about The San Quentin News, the inmate-produced newspaper at San Quentin State Prison, misstated the number of such newspapers in the California prisons. There are two; The San Quentin News is not the only one. (A paper is also produced at the prison in Vacaville.)
match_headline: Inmates’ Newspaper Covers a World Behind San Quentin’s Walls

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about a World Trade Organization ruling that favored the United States in a tariff dispute with China over American vehicles reversed, in some copies, the identifications of the two men shown. Representative Sander Levin was on the right, and Michael B. Froman, the United States trade representative, was on the left.
match_headline: U.S. Gains in a Spat With China Over Tariffs

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about critics’ comments on the body shape of the mezzo-soprano Tara Erraught, who sang the role of Octavian in a production of “Der Rosenkavalier” at the Glyndebourne opera festival in England, misidentified the performer shown with Ms. Erraught. She is Teodora Gheorghiu in the role of Sophie, not Kate Royal as the Marschallin.
match_headline: Too Much Looking, Not Enough Listening?

text: A critic’s notebook article on Friday about the Cannes Film Festival misidentified one of the sources of clips in a “filmed letter” from Jean-Luc Godard to two festival officials. It was his film “Germany Year 90 Nine Zero,” not his “Alphaville.”
match_headline: Sunny Cannes Gets Lightning

text: An obituary in some editions on Sunday about the former Nassau County executive Francis T. Purcell referred incorrectly to one of his survivors. Kim Purcell is his son, not his daughter.
match_headline: Francis T. Purcell, Three-Term Nassau County Executive, Dies at 95

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Sunday about President Obama’s plan to recalibrate his foreign policy agenda in the wake of the Syrian and Ukrainian crises misstated, in some editions, the date on which Mr. Obama appeared with Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany, whose relations with the White House have been tense since the disclosure last fall that the National Security Agency had eavesdropped on her telephone calls. It was May 2, not Friday.
match_headline: Obama to Detail a Broader Foreign Policy Agenda

text: An article on Tuesday about a shooting rampage in Southern California and the legal limits of identifying potentially dangerous individuals referred imprecisely in one instance to the weapons involved. They were semiautomatic — not automatic — handguns.
match_headline: Limits to Law and Information Sharing, Despite Gunman’s Danger Signs

text: An article on Saturday about the return of Fleet Week New York after it was canceled last year misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a singer who performed at the event in 2012. She is Katy Perry, not Katie.
match_headline: On the Town, Sort Of: Fleet Week Shrinks

text: A picture caption on Sunday with an article about the first craft brewery on Staten Island reversed the identities of two of the brewery’s founders in some editions. In a photograph of four men seated on kegs, Jay Sykes is second from the left, and John Gordon is third from left.
match_headline: Staten Island Gets a Craft Brewery of Its Own

text: An article on Monday about the engine maker CFM International, a joint venture of General Electric and a unit of the French aerospace company Safran, misstated the background of one of CFM’s founders, Gerhard Neumann. Although Mr. Neumann served in World War II with the Flying Tigers in China and then with the United States Army Air Corps, he did so as an airplane mechanic and engineer, not as a fighter pilot.
match_headline: Exhibit A in G.E.’s Case for Alstom Deal

text: An article on Monday about Ryan Hunter-Reay’s victory in the Indianapolis 500 on Sunday referred incorrectly to a connection between the drivers Ed Carpenter and James Hinchcliffe, who were involved in a crash in the race. They are not teammates.
match_headline: Daring Pass Produces Narrow Victory at Indy

text: An article on Monday about Derek Jeter’s four-hit game in a victory over the Chicago White Sox on Sunday misstated the year in which a broken ankle limited him to 17 games. It was 2013, not 2014.
match_headline: Bat Meets Crystal Ball as Jeter’s 4 Hits Belatedly Fulfill a Prediction

text: An article on May 19, and a picture caption with it, about a dispute between the Museum of Contemporary Art in North Miami and the city over a possible move by the museum to Miami Beach, misidentified the North Miami official who, according to a city ordinance, is empowered to appoint the museum director with the approval of the museum’s board. It is the city manager, not the mayor. (The museum, whose bylaws say it appoints the director, has not approved the city’s choice.) The article also misidentified the board members who say they told the city manager in August of their interest in moving the museum to Miami Beach and merging with the Bass Museum of Art there. They are Andrew Smulian, Kira Flanzraich and Joan Levien Robertson, not Alex Gartenfeld and Ray Ellen Yarkin.
match_headline: North Miami Fights to Keep Its Art Museum

text: A review in the New Music column on Tuesday about the album “Divide and Exit” by the band Sleaford Mods, from Nottingham, England, misidentified the region of England in which Nottingham is situated. It is the East Midlands, not the West Midlands.
match_headline: Southern Rock, Proudly Revised

text: An article last Thursday about men’s formal wear referred incorrectly to a Calvin Klein evening jacket worn by the actor Bryan Cranston at the Metropolitan Museum Costume Institute gala. It had peak lapels, not a notched collar.
match_headline: For Tuxedos, Blue Is the New Black

text: An article last Thursday about decluttering closets referred incorrectly in several instances to a personal-organizing consultant who co-founded Neat Method, based in San Francisco. She is Ashley Murphy, or Ms. Murphy, not “Ms. Walsh.” (No one named Walsh was interviewed for the article.)
match_headline: Conquering the Closet

text: An article on May 15 about the renovation of a 19th-century house in Lakeville, Conn., referred incorrectly to the home’s turret. It is octagonal, not hexagonal.
match_headline: Holleywood Ending

text: An article on May 2 about the disputes surrounding a Boston College archive of interviews with participants in the secular conflict in Northern Ireland erroneously attributed a distinction to Boston. It has the largest percentage of Irish-Americans in the United States, not the largest number. (That distinction is held by New York.)
match_headline: A Heinous Crime, Secret Histories and a Sinn Fein Leader’s Arrest

text: An article on Wednesday about a plan to rid Detroit of blight misstated, in some editions, the number of buildings that are dilapidated or heading in that direction. It is 78,506, not 84,641. In addition, maps with the continuation of the article misstated, in some editions, the percentage of lots that are vacant or that contain buildings in good condition in two neighborhoods. In Brightmoor, 44 percent of the lots are vacant and 44 percent contain buildings in good condition, not 9 percent and 88 percent. In Redford, 17 percent of lots are vacant and 74 percent contain buildings in good condition, not 4 percent and 95 percent.
match_headline: Detroit Urged to Tear Down 40,000 Buildings

text: An article on Saturday about the rising ratings for “Judge Judy” misstated where the show is taped. Taping takes place at Sunset Bronson Studios, not at the adjacent Sunset Gower Studios.
match_headline: Others Fade, but Judge Judy Is Forever: At 71, She Still Presides

text: An article on Sunday about the first day of Pope Francis’ visit to the Holy Land misidentified, in some editions, the metal his cross is made of. It is silver, not gold.
match_headline: Pope Calls for Solutions to Conflicts in Mideast Visit

text: An article on Wednesday about the reaction of the French political establishment to the victory of the far-right National Front in the European Parliament elections misstated the percentage of voters in France who cited immigration as their chief concern in a Harris Interactive survey. It was 37 percent, not 31 percent.
match_headline: Win by Far-Right Party Rattles the French Establishment

text: An article on Thursday about a regulation President Obama will issue on Monday to cut carbon emissions from the nation’s coal-fired power plants referred imprecisely, in one instance, to what the regulation will do. It will give states a menu of options for complying, including creating or joining state cap-and-trade programs, which will force industry to pay for the carbon pollution it creates. The regulation will not directly force industry to pay for carbon pollution through cap-and-trade programs.
match_headline: President Said to Be Planning to Use Executive Authority on Carbon Rule

text: An article on Thursday about legislation being considered in California to restrict gun ownership for people with a potential propensity for violence misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the executive director of the Coalition to Stop Gun Violence. He is Josh Horwitz, not Horowitz. In addition, the article and a picture caption misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a victim of Friday’s shooting near the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is Christopher Ross Michaels-Martinez, not Michael-Martinez.
match_headline: After Attack Near Campus, California Weighs Gun Bill

text: An article on Saturday about New Jersey’s budget problems and the effect they may have on Gov. Chris Christie’s political prospects misstated projections of New Jersey’s budget surplus relative to surpluses of other states. The projection for New Jersey is 0.9 percent of the budget, compared with a national average of more than 8 percent. It is not 3 percent in New Jersey, compared with a median of 5 percent in other states.
match_headline: Budget Woes May Hurt Christie More Than Bridge Scandal

text: A listing in the Transactions column on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about the recent sale of a warehouse in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, using information provided by the building’s broker, misstated the amount of buildable square feet that comes with the property. It is 38,000 square feet, not 28,000.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on May 21, about the softer tone taken by Narendra Modi after an aggressive campaign that lifted his Bharatiya Janata Party to victory in India’s elections, misidentified the gesture that Mr. Modi made upon entering the Indian Parliament building in New Delhi. He pressed his forehead to the steps leading to the entrance; he did not kiss them.
match_headline: Modi, India’s Next Prime Minister, Adopts a Softer Tone

text: Because of an editing error, a capsule summary on Monday referring to an article about the lack of movie theaters in the Bronx referred incorrectly to the status of the Loew’s Paradise Theater. It houses World Changers Church-New York; it is no longer a theater.
match_headline: Options Dwindle for Bronx Residents Trying to Escape to the Movies

text: An article on Wednesday, about the renovation of a landmark postal tower in Washington, D.C., attributed an erroneous distinction to the Washington Monument. While the monument, at 555 feet, is the tallest building in Washington, it is not the tallest structure. (That distinction belongs to the Hughes Memorial Tower, a radio tower, at 761 feet.)
match_headline: A Trump Makeover for Washington’s Old Post Office

text: An article in some copies last Saturday about the first blown save of the baseball season for Yankees closer David Robertson misspelled the given name of the Chicago White Sox player who singled to lead off the ninth inning. He is Dayan Viciedo, not Dyan.
match_headline: Dunn’s Homer Ends Game and Closer’s Perfect Season

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Wednesday about Taylor Townsend’s rise in tennis despite conditioning disputes with the United States Tennis Association misstated the day of her first-round match against Vania King at the French Open. It was on Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Questioned About Body, Townsend Rises and Inspires

text: An article on Tuesday, about mapping brain cells, misstated when the neuroscientist H. Sebastian Seung started studying theoretical neuroscience. It was in the 1990s, not 2006. The article also referred incorrectly to his child. He has a daughter, not a son. In addition, a picture caption with the article misidentified the elements of a mouse retina that were on display. The picture showed bipolar cells, not a starburst amacrine cell.
match_headline: All Circuits Are Busy

text: An article on April 30 about a social media network in Afghanistan, initially financed by the United States, misspelled, on first reference, the surname of the deputy assistant secretary of state for South and Central Asia. She is Eileen O’Connor, not O’Conner.
match_headline: Social Media in Afghanistan Takes On Life of Its Own

text: An article last Sunday listing summertime events around New York City contained several errors. The tap-dancer who will be performing in Brooklyn on June 20 is Jason Samuels Smith, not Jason Samuel Smith, and he will be performing at Herbert Von King Park, not Prospect Park. In addition, the website listing the Central Park Conservancy’s outdoor movie offerings is centralparknyc.org/filmfestival , not centralpark.com .
match_headline: What to Do in New York City in Summer 2014

text: A chart with the Economic Scene column on Wednesday about concentrated markets misidentified the unit of measurement for the download speeds offered by broadband providers. The speeds are measured in megabits per second, not thousands of megabits per second.
match_headline: Concentrated Markets Take Big Toll on Economy

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the installation of the Jeff Koons work “Split-Rocker” at Rockefeller Plaza, using information from the Koons studio, misstated the height of the work. It is just over 37 feet high, not 35 feet. In addition, a report in the column about art installations organized by Andrea Glimcher for a new building planned for 425 Park Avenue misstated the size of the building. It is to be 47 stories, not 31.
match_headline: A Jeff Koons Sculpture Is Coming to 30 Rock

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the film “We Are the Best!,” based on Coco Moodysson’s graphic novel, misspelled the surname of one of the stars of movie. As the article noted correctly, she is Mira Barkhammar, not Barkhammer.
match_headline: Back to Normal Swedish Teenage Angst

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the influence of hip-hop in modern country music misspelled the surname of the music producer shown with Bubba Sparxxx and Colt Ford. As the article correctly noted, he is Shannon Houchins, not Hutchins.
match_headline: Country Music Opens Its Ears

text: A picture caption in the Evening Hours column last Sunday misspelled the surname of a guest at a gala held by El Museo del Barrio on May 21. She is CuCu Diamantes, not Diamanteo.
match_headline: Evening Hours | Indoors and Out

text: An article last Sunday about John Duka, a fashion reporter for The New York Times who died in 1989, misstated the role that Nian Fish played in the creation of a video to be shown at a tribute to Paul Cavaco, the creative director at Allure magazine, that features scenes with Mr. Duka. Ms. Fish was the producer of the video, not its editor.
match_headline: John Duka, a Fashion Wit, Returns in Larry Kramer’s Film

text: An article last Sunday about the flourishing art scene in Newark misspelled the given name of an artist who rents a studio in Gallery Aferro. She is Dahlia Elsayed, not Dalia.
match_headline: Exploring Cafes and Culture in Downtown Newark

text: A map on May 18 with the cover article about a trip between Chicago and New Orleans on a restored Pullman train misspelled the name of a Tennessee town along the rail line. It is Dyersburg, not Dyersberg.
match_headline: All Aboard, for a Trip to the Past

text: An entry with the “On the Market” feature last Sunday, about a property listed at $1.375 million in Brooklyn , misidentified its location. It is at 334 Grand Avenue, not 334 Grand Street.
match_headline: On the Market in New York City

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the 100th anniversary of Maserati misidentified a racecar from 1960 that was nicknamed Birdcage for its frame structure of steel tubing. The car was a Type 61, not a Type 60.
match_headline: Maserati’s Image Builds on a Racing Reputation

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the history of “Sidewalks of New York,” a song that for many years was played at the Belmont Stakes, misidentified the person for whom the race was named. It was August Belmont, a banker and horseman, not August Belmont Jr. (The younger Mr. Belmont built Belmont Park.)
match_headline: Belmont Park Hopes Old Song Will Break Triple Crown Drought

text: An article on Wednesday about a financing round for Fundrise, a crowdfunding website, omitted some investors in a reference to another real estate crowdfunding website, RealCrowd. RealCrowd took in $1.6 million in seed funding from Andreessen Horowitz, Maverick Capital and other investors, not just Y Combinator.
match_headline: Fundrise, a Crowdfunding Website, Raises $31 Million

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the struggles of the Rakuten Golden Eagles this year without their star pitcher, Masahiro Tanaka, who was acquired by the Yankees over the winter, misstated the number of baseball teams in Japan’s Pacific League. It is six, not five.
match_headline: Tanaka’s Japanese Team Is Struggling Without Him

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about the Audio Publishers Association’s awards for audiobooks, including best solo narration by a male performer for David Pittu’s reading of “The Goldfinch,” misspelled the surname of that novel’s author. She is Donna Tartt, not Tart.
match_headline: Inside In Performance

text: An article on April 27 about early results in the Afghan presidential election, which showed Abdullah Abdullah as the clear front-runner, contained a number of errors in some editions.
match_headline: Afghan Voters Signaling a Turn

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the baseball roundup on Monday about the San Francisco Giants’ 8-0 win over the St. Louis Cardinals misidentified the team with the best record in the major leagues. It was visiting San Francisco, which improved to 37-20, not host St. Louis (which fell to 30-27).
match_headline: Pitching for Fun, and for a Future

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the Drama Desk Awards, using information from a news release, omitted a second winner of the award for outstanding actor in a musical and misstated the number of awards won by “A Gentleman’s Guide to Love & Murder.” Besides Neil Patrick Harris in “Hedwig and the Angry Inch,” Jefferson Mays also won for his performance in “A Gentleman’s Guide to Love & Murder.” That musical thus won seven awards, not six. The report also misspelled the surname of the winner of the award for best featured actress in a play. She is Celia Keenan-Bolger (“The Glass Menagerie”), not Keenan-Golger.
match_headline: Drama Desk Embraces ‘A Gentleman’s Guide’

text: An article on Monday about the New York Public Library’s revised renovation plan for the Mid-Manhattan Library and the flagship Fifth Avenue building misstated the projected cost of updating the stacks at that building. It is $46 million, not $24 million.
match_headline: Library Reveals Details and Costs of Upgrade Plan

text: An article on Saturday about a post-show discussion among high school students and cast members of the Broadway production of “Of Mice and Men” misstated the given names of two students. They are Morgan O’Brien and Morgan Ericson (or “Morgan squared,” as they called themselves), not Megan and “Megan squared.”
match_headline: Lit Class Field Trip, Movie Star Edition

text: A picture caption on May 23 with an entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions about Fleet Week misidentified the site where two sailors were shown. It is the East Coast Memorial in Battery Park, not the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Plaza at 55 Water Street.
match_headline: Memorial Day Weekend Listings for the New York Area

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the actress Lee Chamberlin misstated the date of her death. It was Sunday, May 25 — not Wednesday, May 28.
match_headline: Lee Chamberlin, ‘Electric Company’ Actress, Dies at 76

text: An article on May 27 about victims of fatal crashes tied to an ignition switch flaw in some small General Motors cars referred incompletely to a distinction attributed to the G.M. safety issue. While the 13 deaths linked to the ignition flaw are the most officially recognized since the recall of Ford vehicles with Firestone tires in 2000, it may not retain that distinction. Federal regulators have tentatively linked 51 deaths to a 2013 recall involving some Jeep Grand Cherokee and Liberty models.
match_headline: 13 Deaths, Untold Heartache, From G.M. Defect

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the awarding of federal disaster aid to flood-prevention projects misstated the reason that the event was held in Little Ferry, N.J. The site was agreed to by the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development and the office of Gov. Chris Christie. It was not chosen at the suggestion of the governor’s office.
match_headline: Hoboken Mayor Gets U.S. Flood Money in Awkward Ceremony With Christie

text: An article on May 19 about the effect a Supreme Court case may have on immigrant teachers’ children who turn 21 before their parents’ green cards are approved referred incorrectly to the way the parents’ petitions for their children are meant to be tracked by the government. These young adults maintain their place in the immigration process based on the date the parents filed the petitions, not on the date the parents got their green cards. And because of an editing error, an accompanying picture caption misidentified the man shown. He is Mikhel Crichlow, a founder of the International Youth Association, a group started by the children of two of the teachers. The photograph was not of Alina Das, a co-director of the Immigrant Rights Clinic.
match_headline: Court May Hold Fate of Children Knocked Off Citizenship Path

text: An article on Saturday about the success of athletic teams at the University of Wisconsin-Whitewater, which won national championships in football, men’s basketball and baseball in one school year, misstated the number of teams, like Whitewater, that compete in Division III baseball. It is 378, not 377.
match_headline: In Southern Wisconsin, a Winner Takes All

text: An article on Monday about Hideki Matsuyama’s victory in the Memorial Tournament misstated the number of penalty strokes Bubba Watson was assessed after his first golf shot on the 15th hole landed in the fenced-in backyard of a house. It was one stroke, not two.
match_headline: Experience at Muirfield Helps a 22-Year-Old Win in a Playoff for His First PGA Title

text: An article last Wednesday about a revival in Jewish deli food misstated the surname of one of the owners of the food shop Russ & Daughters. He is Josh Russ Tupper, not Tepper.
match_headline: Everything New Is Old Again

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Edward S. Finkelstein, the former chairman of Macy’s, misstated the name of a store chain Macy’s bought in 1988. It was Bullock’s, not Bullock.
match_headline: Edward Finkelstein, 89, Dies; Took Macy’s to Its Highs and Lows

text: An article on May 22 about Pope Francis’ first visit to the Holy Land and his efforts to avoid offending either the Israelis or the Palestinians referred imprecisely to the location of his meeting with the grand mufti of Jerusalem, which took place in East Jerusalem. Although Israel annexed East Jerusalem after the 1967 war, and considers the territory part of Israel, the annexation was never internationally recognized, and the Palestinians and much of the world consider East Jerusalem to be occupied territory.
match_headline: Seeking Balance on Mideast Visit, Pope Pleases Few

text: An article on May 9 about the spread of a devastating kidney disease among sugar cane workers in Nicaragua referred incorrectly to death rates from the disease, often called chronic kidney disease of unknown causes. Nicaragua has the highest death rate among Latin American countries, according to the Pan American Health Organization, but not necessarily the highest rate worldwide. (Because data on the disease is so limited, it is difficult to definitively say which country has the highest rate worldwide, the World Health Organization says.)
match_headline: Deadly Illness in Nicaragua Baffles Experts

text: A picture caption on Monday with the continuation of an article about the financial risks of independence for Scotland misspelled the surname of Scotland’s finance minister. As the article correctly noted, he is John Swinney, not Sweeney.
match_headline: Scots Are Divided Over Independence, and Its Economic Costs

text: An article last Thursday about political efforts to roll back renewable energy incentives and mandates at the state level referred imprecisely to the percentage of net energy generation from renewable sources in 2013. That figure, 6 percent, came from the emerging renewable sources that state mandates are often meant to encourage, including wind, solar, biomass and geothermal; it does not include conventional hydroelectric generation. (Including hydropower raises the figure to 12.9 percent.)
match_headline: A Pushback on Green Power

text: An article on Tuesday about soaring hospital charges for some common inpatient procedures misstated the number of Medicare patients discharged from hospitals in 2011 for the comparable 98 most common diagnoses seen in The Times’s review of data for 2011 and 2012. There were 7.5 million, not 7.45 million, discharged.
match_headline: Hospital Charges Surge for Common Ailments, Data Shows

text: A critic’s notebook article last Thursday about the Sept. 11 memorial at the World Trade Center site referred incorrectly to the square blocks used for seating. They are granite, not concrete.
match_headline: Finding Space for the Living at a Memorial

text: An obituary on Monday about Lewis Katz, a co-owner of The Philadelphia Inquirer, referred incorrectly to the Dickinson School of Law, from which Mr. Katz graduated. Although it is now part of Pennsylvania State University, it was not affiliated with the university when Mr. Katz was a student there.
match_headline: Lewis Katz, Victor in Fight to Own Philadelphia Inquirer, Dies at 72

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about new evidence of dissent and intrigue inside the Chinese military before the 1989 crackdown in Tiananmen Square in Beijing, using information from Agence France-Presse, misidentified the law enforcement officials shown facing off against a group of student protesters in 1989. They were soldiers, not police officers. The same error appeared in a picture caption on June 4, 2013, with an article about the 24th anniversary of the crackdown.
match_headline: Tales of Army Discord Show Tiananmen Square in a New Light

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Friday about an agreement by the former Microsoft chief executive Steve Ballmer to buy the N.B.A.’s Los Angeles Clippers for $2 billion described incorrectly the nature of a conversation in which Donald Sterling, the team’s current owner, was recorded making racist remarks. It was a private conversation, not a private telephone conversation.
match_headline: Steve Ballmer Said to Sign $2 Billion Deal to Buy Clippers

text: An article on May 28 about the heightened visibility of Russian fighters in the conflict in eastern Ukraine omitted the context in a translation of a comment by one fighter who referred to “Afghans” when he said that he and his compatriots are “volunteers, Chechens, Afghans and Muslims who have come to protect Russia.” The Russian word for the Afghan people can also be used to mean Russian veterans of the war in Afghanistan, which is what the fighter meant.
match_headline: Russians Revealed Among Ukraine Fighters

text: An article on Thursday about the arrest of a suspect, Daniel St. Hubert, in the fatal stabbing of a 6-year-old in Brooklyn misstated, in some editions, the conditions of Mr. Hubert’s release from prison shortly before the attack. He completed his sentence; he was not paroled. The error was repeated in a headline, a subheading and a capsule summary in some copies. The article also misspelled the given name of the great-grandmother of Mikayla Capers, a 7-year-old injured in the attack. She is Regenia Trevathan, not Regeina.
match_headline: Ex-Convict Arrested in Stabbing of Brooklyn Children

text: An article last Friday about the success of Palestine’s soccer team, which recently encountered some problems when it reached the Israel border, omitted a word from a quotation by an Israeli official. The official confirmed that a player, Sameh Mar’aba, had been arrested and that he had admitted to meeting an activist from Hamas’s military wing in Qatar before being given “money, a cellphone and written messages which he was requested to transfer to Hamas activists in the West Bank city of Kalkilya,” not “which he requested to transfer” to the Hamas activists.
ref_headline: money, a cellphone and written messages which he was requested to transfer to Hamas activists in the West Bank city of Kalkilya,
match_headline: For Palestine, a Final May Be Just the Start

text: A report in the Weekend Miser column last Friday about “A Comet Lands in Brooklyn,” a World Science Festival event at Pier 1 in Brooklyn Bridge Park, misidentified the site of the pier. It is at Old Fulton Street and Furman Street, not Atlantic Avenue and Furman Street.
match_headline: 85 Degrees, 100 Percent Free

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the actress Anna Berger misstated the given name of her mother. She was Bella, not Stella.
match_headline: Anna Berger, an Actress With a Gift for Matriarchs, Dies at 91

text: An article on Friday about a crackdown in the Xinjiang region of China after a series of attacks for which the authorities blame Islamic separatists referred incorrectly to some of the sentences imposed by courts. Nine people were sentenced to death and three additional people — not three of the nine — were given a two-year reprieve from the death sentences they received.
match_headline: China Sentences Scores in Xinjiang for Acts of Terror

text: An article on Thursday about continuing frustration among senators even after they were briefed on President Obama’s decision to free five Taliban prisoners in exchange for the release of Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl misstated the requirement that some say Mr. Obama violated by not consulting with Congress at least 30 days before transferring detainees from Guantánamo Bay. It is a statutory restriction, not a constitutional requirement.
match_headline: Senators Show Frustration After Briefing on Ex-P.O.W.

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Thursday about opening statements in the bribery trial of Malcolm A. Smith, a state senator, misstated the legal circumstances of some of the men linked to the case. Two men, Daniel J. Halloran III and Vincent Tabone, are also on trial. A third man, Joseph J. Savino, pleaded guilty to charges relating to bribery, and a fourth, Daniel W. Isaacs, has not been charged. Not all four men are on trial alongside Mr. Smith.
match_headline: In Bribery Trial, Lawyer Says Queens State Senator Was Entrapped

text: Because of an editing error, the Advertising column on Friday, about World Wrestling Entertainment’s participation in an ad campaign to promote active fatherhood, misattributed a quotation about the new W.W.E. ads. It was Kevin Roy, an associate professor of family science at the University of Maryland in College Park — not Rick Burton, professor of sport management at Syracuse University — who called the ads “a feel-good campaign, but there are larger issues at hand.”
ref_headline: a feel-good campaign, but there are larger issues at hand.
match_headline: Pro Wrestlers Add Heft to Campaign for Better Parenting by Fathers

text: A critic’s notebook article on Wednesday about the Spoleto Festival USA, in Charleston, S.C., referred incorrectly to Charles Wadsworth’s tenure with the festival’s chamber music series. While he did found the series in 1977 and hosted it until 2009, there were other directors. He did not direct the series until 2009.
match_headline: Spoleto, Known for Its Operas, Has Drama Left Over for the Concert Stage

text: A critic’s notebook article on Wednesday about escape room games, in which people are locked behind a closed door and try to find their way out, misstated the name of a game in some instances. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is Escape the Room NYC, not Escape Game NYC. And a picture caption with the article misstated the given name of one of the people shown playing the game. He is Keith Nevitt, not Heath.
match_headline: In Escape Rooms, Video Games Meet Real Life

text: An article last Saturday about art gallery owners who travel with mobile galleries misstated the age of Aaron Graham, who runs Rodi Gallery with his mother, Elise. He is 23, not 22.
match_headline: Just Like Taco Trucks, Art Takes to the Road

text: A picture caption on Page 48 this weekend with an article about new jewelry misspells the given name of a jewelry designer. She is Loree Rodkin, not Lorree. The caption also misspells the name in Rodkin’s website address, which is loreerodkin.com.
match_headline: De Blasio Remains Mum on Rabbi’s Remarks

text: An article last Sunday about efforts by Colorado to adapt to the legalization of marijuana for recreational use misstated the percentage of marijuana-impaired traffic citations by the Colorado State Patrol. It is 12.5 percent, not 1.5 percent. The article also referred incorrectly to the use of butane in the making of hashish oil. It is used as a solvent; it is not used to cook the oil.
match_headline: After 5 Months of Sales, Colorado Sees the Downside of a Legal High

text: An article last Sunday about high-tech companies in San Francisco that are finding new purposes for old buildings misstated the kind of structure the architect Jeanne Gang has in the works near the Transbay Transit Center, a vast downtown hub that is scheduled to open in 2017. Ms. Gang’s building is residential, not an office tower.
match_headline: Urban Renewal, No Bulldozer

text: An article last Sunday about the Netflix TV show “Orange Is the New Black,” which is returning for its second season, misidentified the prison the show’s staff visited to do research. It is the California Institution for Women in Chino — not the California Institution for Men, which is also in Chino.
match_headline: Jailhouse Blues

text: An article last Sunday about the film-writing team of Michael H. Weber and Scott Neustadter, who adapted the new movie “The Fault in Our Stars” from the novel by John Green, misspelled the surname of a director who rewrote one of their scripts earlier in their career. She is Nancy Meyers, not Myers. And an accompanying picture caption reversed the names of the two screenwriters. Mr. Weber was at the left and Mr. Neustadter at the right.
match_headline: Reviving the Coming-of-Age Movie

text: A picture credit with the Playlist CD review column on May 25, based on information from a publicist, misidentified who took the photograph of the singer-songwriter John Fullbright. It was Kate Burn, not Vicki Farmer.
match_headline: Songs of Love and Longing, and Retro Sounds From ’60s On

text: A review on May 18 about “Japan 1941: Countdown to Infamy,” by Eri Hotta , misquoted one word of a passage from the book. The passage referred to “the typhoons that had prevented the Mongols from invading Japan in the 13th century,” not “that had prevented the Moguls from invading.”
match_headline: The March to War

text: A picture caption on May 25 with an article about some favorite dishes of five food experts in five areas of the world misidentified one dish. The photograph labeled “Mohinga in Myanmar” showed a bowl of Shan noodles, not mohinga.
match_headline: Must-Eat Dishes, From Myanmar to Mexico City

text: An article last Sunday about Hilaria Baldwin described incorrectly the garment she wore in the bathtub handstand picture she posted on Instagram. It was a bikini, not underwear.
match_headline: Hilaria Baldwin Holds Her Center

text: An article on Thursday about negotiations among American, Qatari and Taliban officials that eventually led to the release of the Army sergeant Bowe Bergdahl in exchange for five Taliban militants referred incorrectly to Sergeant Bergdahl at one point. He was an American prisoner, of course, not an Afghan one.
match_headline: Behind P.O.W.’s Release: Urgency and Opportunity

text: An article on Friday about the hunt for the killer of three members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in Moncton, New Brunswick, misstated the number of homicides in New Brunswick in 2012. There were six, not four. (The Mounted Police reported handling four; two more occurred in communities patrolled by other police forces.)
match_headline: Canadian Police Seek Suspect in Killing of Officers

text: An article on Thursday about the bioluminescent bays in Vieques, P.R., referred imprecisely to the business owners that are at odds with island residents. While all of the business owners and locals are American, most of the business owners are originally from the mainland United States, not from Puerto Rico. In addition, the article misstated the length of time that the marine biologist Michael Latz has studied bioluminescent bays. He has done so since 2010, not for three decades, though he has been studying bioluminescence for 30 years.
match_headline: Puerto Rico Debates Who Put Out the Lights in Mosquito Bay

text: An article on Wednesday about a federal judge’s ruling in a civil rights lawsuit over solitary confinement at Pelican Bay State Prison in California misstated the number of hunger strikes by inmates at the prison. There have been three, not two. The article also misstated the number of security housing units, in addition to Pelican Bay, where prisoners are kept in solitary confinement. There are three, not two.
match_headline: Judge’s Decision to Hear Inmates’ Case Threatens Practice of Solitary Confinement

text: A reporting credit last Monday for an article about the crash of a private plane in Bedford, Mass., on May 31 that killed seven people, including an owner of The Philadelphia Inquirer, misstated, in some editions, the middle initial and the location of a contributor. The reporter, Matthew L. Wald (not Matthew V.), reported from Washington, not from New York.
match_headline: Philadelphia Inquirer Co-Owner Among 7 Killed in Massachusetts Plane Crash

text: An article last Monday about plans to establish a series of markers for a self-guided cultural walk in the South Bronx misstated part of the name of the organization that curates a map of long-gone music and dance clubs in the borough. It is the Bronx Music Heritage Center, not the Bronx Music Heritage Society. The article also misstated the role of Elena Martinez at the center. She is a co-artistic director alongside Bobby Sanabria; she is not the sole artistic director.
match_headline: With South Bronx Trail, a History and a Culture Will Be Clearly Marked

text: A map on May 30 with an article about the diagonal elevator planned for the new 34th Street subway station for the No. 7 train mislabeled the avenue on the far right and omitted another avenue. Seventh Avenue, not Eighth, formed the right boundary of the map and Ninth Avenue should have been shown in the middle of the map. A corrected version can be found at nytimes.com/nyregion .
match_headline: In Expansion of No. 7 Line, One Problem: An Elevator

text: Because of an editing error, an article on May 25 about a decision by Pakistan’s prime minister, Nawaz Sharif, to attend the swearing-in of India’s new prime minister, Narendra Modi, despite the history of tensions between the nations referred incorrectly in some editions to an invitation that upset the leaders of Tamil Nadu State in India. It was the invitation extended to Mahinda Rajapaksa, the president of Sri Lanka — not the one to Mr. Sharif. (Tamils in India have long expressed concerns over the treatment of Tamils in Sri Lanka.)
match_headline: In Possible Thaw, Pakistani Leader Agrees to Attend Swearing-In Ceremony in India

text: An article on Saturday about a high-level group of Catholic and Orthodox officials that called on the Vatican to allow married Eastern Catholic priests in North America referred incorrectly to marriage restrictions for the priests outside North America. A married man may become an Eastern Catholic priest in parts of Europe, Asia and Africa, but once an unmarried man is ordained as a priest, he is not allowed to marry. It is not the case that Eastern Catholic priests are already allowed to marry overseas.
match_headline: Group of Catholic and Orthodox Officials Endorses Marriage for Some Priests

text: An article on Friday about the hedge fund manager Mark Spitznagel’s contribution of 20 goats to graze overgrown grass in a blighted Detroit neighborhood described the animals incorrectly. They are wethers, or castrated male goats, not billy goats, which have not been castrated and tend to be obstreperous, malodorous and not well suited to what Mr. Spitznagel called an “urban farming experiment.”
match_headline: Fund Manager Sets Goats Grazing in Blighted Detroit

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about Game 3 of the 1975 Stanley Cup finals, which has become known as the Fog Game because of the low visibility inside Buffalo Memorial Auditorium that day, misstated the score of the series, between the Buffalo Sabres and the Philadelphia Flyers, entering the game. The Flyers led two games to none, not two games to one. It also misstated the score at the time of a power-related suspension of play in Game 4 of the 1988 Stanley Cup finals, between the Boston Bruins and the Edmonton Oilers. It was 3-3, not 2-2.
match_headline: Neither Player Nor Bat Was Ready for the Fog

text: A critic’s notebook article on Monday about the Seattle Symphony, at Benaroya Hall in Seattle, misstated the name of the orchestra’s series that includes the concert performed Friday evening. It is Sonic Evolution, not Sonic Evolutions. (A picture caption repeated the error.)
match_headline: Dutilleux and Ravel Mingle With Sir Mix-a-Lot

text: An obituary on Saturday about the memoirist Susan Spencer-Wendel contained several errors. Ms. Spencer-Wendel’s survivors include a sister, not a brother. Her mother, Tee Spencer, does not survive her. (She died in March.) And Ms. Spencer-Wendel traveled to the Yukon with a friend, not with her husband.
match_headline: Susan Spencer-Wendel, Memoirist About Living and Losing Life, Dies at 47

text: An article on May 29 about a takeover by antigovernment demonstrators of the presidential headquarters in Abkhazia, a breakaway enclave of Georgia that is heavily dependent on Russia, misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a spokeswoman for Aleksandr Z. Ankvab, Abkhazia’s president. She is Madina Bganba, not Bganma.
match_headline: Presidential Building Is Stormed in Restless Georgian Region

text: An article on Friday about a shooting at Seattle Pacific University that left one person dead and three wounded gave an incorrect age from a hospital spokesman for the male student who died and a female student who was hospitalized in critical condition. Both victims were 19, not 20.
match_headline: Shooting Leaves One Dead at Seattle Pacific University

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the death of Alexander Imich, an 111-year-old New York City resident believed to be the world’s oldest man, misstated the day he spoke agitatedly in Polish and Russian to what he said were spirits around him. It was last Wednesday — not Sunday, which was the day he died.
match_headline: World’s Oldest Man, Though Only Briefly, Dies at 111 in New York

text: An article on Monday about organizational flaws of the sort that led to General Motors’ failure to act on a safety defect in millions of small cars misidentified the book in which Diane Vaughn, a Columbia University sociologist, described similar isolation of managers from safety details in NASA’s decision to treat insulation damage to the space shuttle Columbia as a routine maintenance issue. It was “The Challenger Launch Decision: Risky Technology, Culture, and Deviance at NASA” — not “Normalization of Deviance,” which is the title of a chapter in a sociology book to which Ms. Vaughn contributed. It was not the title of a book.
ref_headline: The Challenger Launch Decision: Risky Technology, Culture, and Deviance at NASA
match_headline: G.M. Report Illustrates Managers’ Disconnect

text: An article on Saturday about the men’s semifinals of the French Open tennis tournament misstated the number of times Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic have met in a Grand Slam final. Sunday’s final, won by Nadal, was their seventh such match, not their sixth.
match_headline: For Missing Major Crown, Djokovic Must Dethrone a Dominant King

text: An article on Monday about the restoration of Pinehurst No. 2, the site of this week’s United States Open golf tournament, to its onetime appearance, with bumpy sand and native vegetation, described the curve of the course’s greens incorrectly in some copies. They are convex, not concave.
match_headline: Ready for Spotlight, a Course Is Restored to Its Shaggy Self

text: An article on Tuesday about the Street Art Project, an online gallery of street art created by the Google Cultural Institute, misidentified the French organization that Google worked with to film art at the Tour Paris 13 tower before it was torn down. It was Project Tour Paris 13, not 9ème Concept. Because of an editing error, an accompanying picture caption misspelled the name of the duo whose street art in Dallas is shown. It is Faile, not Faille.
match_headline: Google Adds Graffiti to Its Art Portfolio

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about the Israel Film Center Festival misidentified the film that will be shown this Friday at 7 p.m. at the JCC in Manhattan. It is “Lia” — not “Wonders,” which will be shown at noon on Friday (as well as at 7 p.m. on Tuesday).
match_headline: Spare Times for June 6-12

text: An entry in the Spare Times for Children listings in some editions on May 23 about “The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe,” at St. Luke’s Theater in Manhattan, misspelled the surname of one of the new cast members. He is Rockford Sansom, not Samson.
ref_headline: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe,
match_headline: Spare Times for Children for May 23-29

text: An article on May 31 about an insider trading investigation, using information from people briefed on the inquiry, overstated the scope of an investigation involving the golfer Phil Mickelson. While investigators are looking at his trading in some stocks, Clorox is not among them. The error was repeated in articles on June 1 and June 2 and in the Common Sense column on Saturday. An article about the latest developments in the investigation appears today on Page B1 .
match_headline: A Risk-Taker’s Game: Insider Trading

text: An article on Monday about the owners of a house on West 11th Street in Manhattan that was rebuilt after being destroyed in a 1970 accidental bombing by members of Weather Underground misspelled the given name of one of the movement’s leaders. She is Bernardine Dohrn, not Bernadine.
match_headline: Reconstruction Planned for Infamous Townhouse in Greenwich Village

text: An article on May 31 about bioengineered products that have found their way into household products like soap and lotion through a new technology known as synthetic biology referred imprecisely to the status of regulation of the technology. While the regulatory oversight of products from older genetic engineering techniques may not apply to the products of some newer techniques used in synthetic biology, it is not the case that the field is “largely unregulated.”
match_headline: Companies Quietly Apply Biofuel Tools to Household Products

text: Because of an editing error, a critic’s notebook article on Wednesday about the pianist Yefim Bronfman’s performances of Beethoven piano concertos with the New York Philharmonic, among them three concerts including the fourth concerto, misstated the night of the first concert in some editions. It was last night, not Tuesday night.
match_headline: Beethoven That’s Not for Bruisers

text: Because of an editing error, the Personal Health column on Tuesday, about treatments for breast cancer, misidentified the medical center where Dr. Deborah M. Axelrod, who commented on treatment options, works. Dr. Axelrod, a surgeon, directs breast cancer programs at New York University Langone Medical Center, not at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center.
match_headline: Killing a Patient to Save His Life

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the pitcher Bob Welch referred incorrectly to the circumstances under which he struck out Reggie Jackson in Game 2 of the 1978 World Series. He was called in from the bullpen with one out in the ninth inning, not two, and he retired Thurman Munson on a fly ball before facing Jackson; Jackson was not the first batter he faced. The obituary also misspelled the surname of the pitcher who won 31 games for the Detroit Tigers in 1968. He is Denny McLain, not McClain.
match_headline: Bob Welch, Pitching Ace and Prototype for Today’s Power Arms, Dies at 57

text: An article on Tuesday about widespread dissatisfaction in Brazil over the costs of holding the World Cup and the Olympics erroneously attributed a distinction to Mexico for having also hosted both events in succession. Mexico was the last country in Latin America to do so, not the last country. (The United States was the last; it held the World Cup in 1994 and the Olympics in 1996.)
match_headline: Brazil on Edge as World Cup Exposes Rifts

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with an article about the desertions and the deteriorating morale of soldiers in the Iraqi Army as they struggle with resurgent militant forces misstated, in some editions, the day the photograph of soldiers leaving the Iraqi city of Najaf was taken. It was Sunday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Exhausted and Bereft, Iraqi Soldiers Quit Fight

text: An article on March 26 about a report by the World Health Organization that said air pollution killed seven million people in 2012, more than one-third of those in Asian nations undergoing rapid urbanization, misstated China’s urban population goals. China has said it wants 60 percent of the population — not one billion people — to be living in cities by 2020. (The one billion figure is an unrelated projection by the World Bank.) This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Pollution Killed 7 Million People Worldwide in 2012, Report Finds

text: An article on Thursday about confusion surrounding a judge’s recent ruling on same-sex marriage in Wisconsin misidentified, in some editions, the government office that issued a marriage license to Shari Roll and Renee Currie, the first couple to marry in Dane County last Friday. It was the county registry of deeds office, not the state registry of deeds office.
match_headline: Legal Confusion Follows Federal Judge’s Ruling on Same-Sex Marriage in Wisconsin

text: An article in some editions on June 4 about legislative primary races in New Jersey misstated the significance of the race between Bonnie Watson Coleman and Alieta Eck in the 12th Congressional District. That race guarantees that a woman will be part of the New Jersey delegation, not that the winner will be the only woman in the delegation. (Another woman, Aimee Belgard, is a Democratic candidate in the race for the Third Congressional District.)
match_headline: In New Jersey, a Republican Nominee Will Try to Hold On to a Congressional Seat

text: A headline on Thursday with the continuation of an article about an insider trading investigation referred incorrectly in some editions to the involvement of the golfer Phil Mickelson. According to people briefed on the matter, Mr. Mickelson did not trade in the shares of Clorox at all; his trades in the stock were not “overstated.”
match_headline: Golfer Mickelson’s Role Said to Be Overstated in Insider Inquiry

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an article about Western oil companies’ efforts to expand in Russia without running afoul of sanctions imposed on that country because of its activities in Ukraine reversed, in some copies, the identifications of two of the people shown. David Campbell, head of BP Russia, is at the left, and Igor Sechin, president of Rosneft, is at the right.
match_headline: For Western Oil Companies, Expanding in Russia Is a Dance Around Sanctions

text: A listing of credits last Friday with a film review of “Obvious Child” omitted the material on which the film is based. It is based on a story by the director, Gillian Robespierre; Karen Maine; and Elisabeth Holm, and a 2009 short film by Anna Bean, Ms. Maine and Ms. Robespierre.
match_headline: Right Guy Is Just One in a World of Choices

text: An obituary on May 31 about the novelist and poet Sam Greenlee referred incorrectly to the history of the United States Information Agency, where he served in the 1950s. At that time, it was an independent government agency, not a branch of the State Department. (Its functions were absorbed by the State Department in 1999.)
match_headline: Sam Greenlee, Writer, Producer, Government Agent, Dies at 83

text: An article on Tuesday about the passage of Russian fighters across an increasingly unguarded border into eastern Ukraine to join the separatists there misspelled the surname of a Russian specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who commented on the shadowy but increasingly palpable Russian influence in Ukraine. She is Carol Saivetz, not Saivets.
match_headline: Russians Find Few Barriers to Joining Ukraine Battle

text: An article on Wednesday about challenges faced by France’s National Front as it tries to use its recent election victories to establish itself as a mainstream party misspelled, in some editions, the given name of the National Front’s representative in Bohain-en-Vermandois. As an accompanying picture caption correctly noted, he is Armand Pollet, not Arman.
match_headline: Turning to National Front, but Keeping a Distance

text: An article on May 28 about an especially severe clampdown by China on efforts to mark the 25th anniversary of the brutal repression of the student-led demonstrations in Tiananmen Square misspelled the given name of a news assistant with a Japanese newspaper who was detained. She is Xin Jian, not Jiang.
match_headline: Tiananmen Square Anniversary Prompts Campaign of Silence

text: An article on Sunday about the United States men’s national soccer team’s 2-1 victory over Nigeria misstated the date of its opening game in the World Cup in Brazil, against Ghana. It is scheduled for Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: U.S. Displays Improvement Across the Field and a Breakthrough at the Front

text: An article on Thursday about investors’ wariness toward cloud computing companies misstated the business of Acquia. It makes software based on the open-source method Drupal; it does not make Drupal itself.
match_headline: Investors Wary of Putting Money Where the Cloud Is

text: An obituary on Sunday about the television critic Steven H. Scheuer misstated the name of a television program on which he worked in the early 1950s. It was “Studio One,” not “Theater One.”
match_headline: Steven H. Scheuer Is Dead at 88; He Put the TV Review Before the Show

text: An article on May 25 about the shooting rampage in Southern California omitted six sentences from the opening quotation taken from a video posted by the gunman, Elliot O. Rodger. The quotation (with the omitted sentences shown in italicized type) should have read: “It all has to come to this. Tomorrow is the day of retribution. The day in which I will have my revenge against humanity. Against all of you. For the last eight years of my life, ever since I’ve hit puberty, I’ve been forced to endure an existence of loneliness, rejection and unfulfilled desires. All because girls have never been attracted to me. Girls gave their affection and sex and love to other men but never to me. I’m 22 years old, and I’m still a virgin. I’ve never even kissed a girl. I have been through college for two and a half years, more than that actually, and I’m still a virgin. It has been very torturous. College is the time when everyone experiences those things such as sex and fun and pleasure. In those years I’ve had to rot in loneliness.”
match_headline: Video Rant, Then Deadly Rampage in California Town

text: Because of an editing error, an article on June 1 about a syndicate that manipulated soccer games ahead of the last World Cup misstated a South African soccer executive’s explanation for changes in referee appointments. Leslie Sedibe, the executive, said that a subordinate in the South African Football Association — not someone from an outside company — had lied to him.
match_headline: Fixed Soccer Matches Cast Shadow Over World Cup

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the continuing struggles of an Afghan couple who eloped in March after her family threatened to kill them described Hindu Kush incorrectly in some editions. It is a mountain range, not a province.
match_headline: For Afghan Lovers, Joy Is Brief, Ending in Arrest

text: Because of an editing error, a reporting credit last Sunday for an article about a car accident in which the actor Tracy Morgan was seriously injured misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a contributor. He is Bryon MacWilliams, not McWilliams.
match_headline: Tracy Morgan Critically Hurt in New Jersey Car Crash

text: A chart in some editions last Sunday with an article about choosing a team to cheer for in the World Cup used an incorrect flag for the English team. England’s flag shows St. George’s Cross, a red cross on a white field; it is not the Union Jack. A corrected chart can be found at nytimes.com/nyregion .
match_headline: Your Slightly-Better-Than-a-Dartboard Guide to Choosing a Team in the World Cup

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about different ballet versions of “Cinderella,” using information from a publicist, misidentified two dancers shown performing with the Royal Ballet in a 2010 production of “Cinderella” in London. They are Marianela Nuñez and Thiago Soares — not Roberta Marquez and Steven McRae, who also are members of the company.
match_headline: Dazzling a Prince, Slowly, Gently, on Point

text: An article on June 1 about the Brooklyn band Parquet Courts, which has just released its second album, omitted part of the title of an EP the group released last year. It is “Tally All the Things That You Broke” — not merely “The Things That You Broke.”
ref_headline: Tally All the Things That You Broke
match_headline: Rock Relics With a Signature Swagger

text: A review on May 18 about “American Innovations,” a collection of 10 stories by Rivka Galchen, misstated several of the characteristics of the central characters in some of the stories. It is not the case that the stories “are narrated with one exception by variations of a particular sort of woman: in her 30s, living in New York, nominally Jewish.” Three stories have main characters who live in New York City, while the remaining stories are specifically set elsewhere or implicitly in cities other than New York; one story has a Jewish narrator, while all but one of the others have no indications that the central characters are Jewish; five of the stories have central characters who are said to be in their 30s or might reasonably be assumed to be, but the others have main characters who are specifically younger or implied to be younger. Two of these errors were repeated in the Editors’ Choice column on May 25. It is not the case that “most” of the women in the stories are clearly in their 30s or “nominally Jewish.”
match_headline: The Unpossessed

text: An article last Sunday about the changing nature of Midtown East misstated the location of Turtle Bay Gardens, an enclave of rowhouses in the neighborhood. The houses run between Second and Third Avenues, along 48th and 49th Streets, not along 47th and 48th Streets. Because of that error, the article also referred incorrectly to the home where Katharine Hepburn lived for decades. While she lived in Turtle Bay Gardens, she lived on 49th Street, not on 47th or 48th Streets. The article also referred imprecisely to the role that William Zeckendorf Sr. played in the construction of the United Nations building. While Mr. Zeckendorf assembled the land where it was built, he sold the land to John D. Rockefeller Jr., who subsequently donated it to the United Nations. The land was not “provided” to the United Nations by Mr. Zeckendorf himself.
match_headline: Not Just an Easy Commute

text: An article last Sunday about inclusionary zoning for housing — which lets developers build more housing units if they charge much lower rents for some of them — misstated the action Jerry Brown, now governor of California, took to block mandatory such zoning while he was mayor of Oakland. He cast a tie-breaking vote after the City Council deadlocked on the plan; he did not veto it.
match_headline: Affordable Housing That’s Very Costly

text: An article on May 25 about the methods that the psychiatrist Bessel van der Kolk uses to treat trauma omitted some context for the criticism made by Patricia Resick, a clinical psychologist. While she maintains that van der Kolk sometimes uses techniques in which outcomes are not measured by independent assessors, she was not referring specifically to the studies of yoga or eye movement desensitization and reprocessing that were mentioned in the article. Each of these had blind raters.
match_headline: A Revolutionary Approach to Treating PTSD

text: An obituary last Sunday about the chemist Alexander Shulgin misstated a word in a quotation from him. Dr. Shulgin said: “I understood that our entire universe is contained in the mind and the spirit. We may choose not to find access to it, we may even deny its existence, but it is indeed there inside us, and there are chemicals that can catalyze its availability” — not “that can analyze its availability.”
match_headline: Alexander Shulgin, Psychedelia Researcher, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Friday about the actress Ruby Dee referred imprecisely to the part Sidney Poitier played in the 1950 film “No Way Out,” in which Ms. Dee also appeared. While he was a doctor in a county hospital that had a prison ward, he was not a prison doctor.
match_headline: Ruby Dee, a Ringing Voice for Civil Rights, Onstage and Off, Dies at 91

text: An article on May 27 about the stunned reaction of the European establishment after angry voters elected insurgent and fringe parties to the European Parliament misstated the year that French and Dutch voters rejected a European Union constitution. It was 2005, not 2004.
match_headline: Populists’ Rise in Europe Vote Shakes Leaders

text: An article on Thursday about the reaction of voters in Representative Eric Cantor’s district in Virginia to his primary election loss misspelled part of the name of the TV show whose cast included Ben L. Jones, who challenged Mr. Cantor in 2002. It was “The Dukes of Hazzard,” not Hazard.
match_headline: Cantor Forgot Virginia Roots, Voters Contend

text: An article on Wednesday about relatives of Cardinal John Joseph O’Connor who discovered their Jewish heritage misstated the year of a prominent wedding at B’nai Israel, a Connecticut synagogue where the cardinal’s maternal grandfather served as a rabbi. It was 1889, not 1899.
match_headline: The Rabbi Cardinal O’Connor Never Knew: His Grandfather

text: An article on Thursday about a renewed campaign by the authorities in China to condemn outlawed religious sects after a woman was beaten to death by members of one such sect, the Church of Almighty God, misstated part of an alternative name for the sect. It is Eastern Lightning, not Eastern Lightening.
match_headline: Campaign to Crack Down on Fringe Sects in China Worries Mainstream Churches

text: An article on Thursday about a school shooting in Troutdale, Ore., misstated the type of vest worn by the gunman, Jared Michael Padgett. It was a vest designed to carry ammunition; it was not a bulletproof vest. And because of an editing error, the article misstated the number of public shootings in Oregon while John Kitzhaber has served as governor. There have been three, not two. (Two have occurred since he became governor in 2011. A third shooting was at Thurston High School in Springfield, Ore., in May 1998, during one of Mr. Kitzhaber’s two earlier terms as governor, from 1995 to 2003.)
match_headline: Weapons Stockpile Seen in Oregon School Attack

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the respect Yankees outfielder Jacoby Ellsbury has earned from his rivals quoted incorrectly in some copies from comments by Lloyd McClendon, the manager of the Seattle Mariners. In praising Ellsbury, he said, “He’s what you would call a dirt rat,” not a “dirtbag.”
ref_headline: He’s what you would call a dirt rat,
match_headline: Yankees’ Ellsbury Has Reputation as ‘Dirt Rat’ (It’s Praise)

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the baseball roundup on Thursday misidentified, in some copies, the host team in one of the games. The Kansas City Royals hosted the Cleveland Indians, not the other way around.
match_headline: U.S.O.C. Narrows Bids to Four Cities

text: An article on Saturday about the threat that military victories by Sunni militants in Iraq present to the nation’s Shiites, who had been ascendant after the fall of Saddam Hussein, misstated the electoral status of Prime Minister Nuri Kamal al-Maliki just before the start of the country’s latest crisis. Given the number of seats his bloc had won, Mr. Maliki was in a strong position to secure a third term; he had not been re-elected to a third term by a surprisingly strong margin.
match_headline: Seeing Their Gains at Risk, Shiites Flock to Join Militias

text: An article on Thursday about Morocco’s harsh treatment of dissidents despite repeated promises by King Mohammed VI to establish democratic institutions and respect for human rights paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Navi Pillay, the United Nations commissioner for human rights. She said Moroccan leaders had the political will to carry out promised reforms; she did not say they lacked such will.
match_headline: Morocco’s King Slow to Deliver on Pro-Democracy Vows

text: An article on Sunday about the complications involving the new alliance between the Palestinian Authority and Hamas as well as Israel’s relations with the authority that have been exposed by the abductions of three Israeli teenagers on the West Bank reversed the ages of two of the missing youngsters. Eyal Yifrach is 19 and Gilad Shaar is 16.
match_headline: Rift Bared as Palestinians Aid Israel in Search for Teenagers Missing in West Bank

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about the shake-up in the House because of the primary election defeat of Representative Eric Cantor of Virginia misidentified the House leadership position being sought by Representatives Raul R. Labrador and Kevin McCarthy. As the article correctly noted, it is majority leader, not minority leader.
match_headline: Idaho Republican, Appealing to Right, Enters Race to Replace Cantor

text: An article on the Square Feet pages on April 30 about the restoration of the Frank Lloyd Wright-designed executive offices of S.C. Johnson in Racine, Wis., misstated a detail of the building. While the installation of sprinklers was debated during construction, sprinklers were eventually installed. It is not the case that Wright refused to install them. (The Times corrected the error online shortly after it was pointed out; this correction is only now being published because it went astray during the editing process.)
match_headline: A Corporate Paean to Frank Lloyd Wright

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with a critic’s notebook article about the Electronic Entertainment Expo in Los Angeles misidentified the developer of the new video game Evolve, due for release in October. It is Turtle Rock Studios, not Nintendo.
match_headline: Some New Games to Sink Your Claws Into

text: An obituary on June 3 about the epidemiologist Ciro de Quadros misstated the position he held at the Sabin Vaccine Institute. He was executive vice president, not vice president emeritus.
match_headline: Ciro de Quadros, 74, Dies; Leader in Ridding Latin America of Polio

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Rev. Michael A. Walrond Jr., a challenger in the Democratic primary for the seat held by Representative Charles B. Rangel, misstated the boundaries of New York’s 13th Congressional District. It stretches from Harlem and Washington Heights into parts of the Bronx, but it does not include the South Bronx. The article also misspelled the name of the college that Mr. Walrond’s wife attended. It is Spelman, not Spellman.
match_headline: Pastor New to Harlem Takes Rangel On

text: An article in some editions on Monday about a house fire in Newark, using information from the Essex County prosecutor’s office, misstated the age of Natasha Kinsale, one of six people who died, and her relationship to another occupant of the house. She is 35, not 47, and she is Salome Stewart’s daughter, not sister. The article also misspelled the given name of a youth who died in the fire. He was Stephen Sydney, not Stephon.
match_headline: Six Are Killed in a House Fire in Newark

text: Because of an editing error, the Shortcuts column on Saturday, about teenagers’ difficulty in finding summer employment, described a feature of the website www.teens4hire.org incorrectly. Both the free site and a $39 premium option offer searchable job listings. The listings are not limited to the premium option.
match_headline: If a Teenager Lands a Summer Job, the Value Is Lasting

text: A map last Wednesday with the Square Feet column, about real estate prices in London, located the Westminster area incorrectly. It is near the Thames, not north of Hyde Park.
match_headline: A Bellwether for London Realty

text: An article on Monday about Brazilian soccer style misspelled the surname of the historian who noted that mass culture was becoming more North American or provincial, with the exception of the Brazilian national soccer team. He was Eric Hobsbawm, not Hobsbawn. A chart with the article also misspelled the given name of the Italian captain during the 1970 World Cup final against Brazil. He was Giacinto Facchetti, not Glacinto.
match_headline: How the United States Scored Against Ghana

text: An article on Monday about the Italian national soccer team’s history of making the best of bad situations misstated the given name of the Juventus defender who was ejected for a nasty foul against Roma recently. He is Giorgio Chiellini, not Marco.
match_headline: Where Dishonesty Is Best Policy, U.S. Soccer Falls Short

text: A picture caption in some editions on Monday with an article about the international makeup of the San Antonio Spurs’ roster, using information from The Associated Press, misidentified one of the two Spurs players shown talking. Tiago Splitter of Brazil — not Marco Belinelli of Italy — is at the left, talking to Manu Ginobili of Argentina. The article also misspelled the Italian word for good day. It is buongiorno, not bonjourno.
match_headline: The United Nations of the Hardwood

text: An article on Monday about the dispute between the City of North Miami and the Museum of Contemporary Art there over control of the museum misstated the status of legal actions in the case. The museum has sued the city, but the city has not sued the museum. (The city has filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit and one for injunctive relief.)
match_headline: Museum Power Squabble Borders on the Surreal

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Saturday about next year’s Encores! series at City Center, using information from a news release, misidentified Rob Berman’s role in the productions of “Paint Your Wagon” and “Zorba!” He will be the music director, not the director. (The directors of the three Encores! shows, including “Lady, Be Good,” have not been named.)
match_headline: Early Gershwin Musical to Open City Center’s Encores Season

text: A listing of credits on June 6 with a theater review of “Macbeth,” at the Park Avenue Armory in Manhattan, omitted information about the commissioning and production. The production was commissioned and produced by the Park Avenue Armory and the Manchester International Festival, and the New York presentation was produced in association with Colin Callender.
match_headline: Rushing Headlong Into the Hurly-Burly

text: An article on Tuesday about Vice President Joseph R. Biden’s visit to Brazil during the World Cup to pursue better relations between Washington and Brasília, which had been strained over revelations of the National Security Agency’s surveillance practices, misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the organization of which Julia E. Sweig, is the director for Latin American studies. It is the Council on Foreign Relations (not “of”).
match_headline: Diplomacy and Soccer for Biden in Brazil

text: A report in the National Briefing column last Thursday about illegal migrants sent by border authorities to Arizona misstated the timing of a decision by Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson to send unaccompanied minors to Nogales for initial immigration processing, rather than women with their children. He made it before June 1, not after speaking with Gov. Jan Brewer of Arizona on June 7.
match_headline: Plan Will Change on Young Migrants

text: An article in some editions on Monday about problems New York State has encountered in its effort to reduce the backlog of family court cases described incorrectly the limitations of New York City’s family court system. No new positions for judges have been created for the court since 1991; it is not the case that no new judges have been appointed.
match_headline: Dispute Over Judges Leaves Family Courts in Limbo

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about New York City’s complicated legal requirements for transferring vending licenses misstated the number of such licenses available to nonveterans. As the article correctly noted, it is 853, not 845.
match_headline: Selling Baubles on the Street: License Required

text: A picture on Tuesday with an article about General Motors’ recall of an additional 3.36 million cars for ignition switch problems was published in error. The photograph was of a newly redesigned 2014 Impala, which was not involved in the recall, not a 2014 Impala Limited, which was part of the recall. (The 2014 Impala Limited was a continuation of the previous generation of Impalas that was sold only to rental fleets.)
match_headline: In Another Blow, G.M. Recalls 3 Million More Defective Cars

text: An article on Monday about Argentina’s 2-1 victory over Bosnia and Herzegovina at the World Cup misstated the background of the Bosnian striker Vedad Ibisevic. He was born in Yugoslavia and moved to the United States as a teenager; he is neither “American-born” nor “American-raised.”
