match_headline: Despite a Shadow, Messi Shimmers in Argentina’s Cup Opener

text: An article on Tuesday about Germany’s 4-0 victory over Portugal at the World Cup misspelled the surname of the Portugal center forward who left the game with a leg injury. He is Hugo Almeida, not Almeido. The article also misstated, in some copies, the year Germany last won the World Cup. It was 1990, not 1090.
match_headline: In Defeat, Portugal Shows Its Ugly Side

text: An article last Thursday about several yoga studios that offer beer tastings referred imprecisely to the origins of the trend. While at least one such program, Happy Hour Yoga with Joe Sixpack, started in 2008 in Philadelphia, the practice seemed to gain in popularity after the Bendy Brewski yoga program started two and a half years ago in Charleston, S.C.
match_headline: Bending the Rules to Offer Yoga With a Beer Chaser

text: An article last Thursday about working offline on documents stored in the cloud misstated a capability of the cloud storage service Dropbox. Dropbox’s desktop software allows users to sync their online storage with their computer desktop and access all their files offline. Files do not have to be individually downloaded from the Web to the computer.
match_headline: Security Needs Evolve as Computing Leaves the Office

text: An obituary on June 5 about Mary Soames, the last surviving child of Winston Churchill and the author of a series of books about her family, misidentified her birthplace. She was born in London — not at Chartwell, the Churchill family estate in Kent.
match_headline: Mary Soames, Daughter of Churchill and Chronicler of History, Dies at 91

text: An article on Tuesday about a crackdown by Spanish police on a network of Islamic militants in the North African enclaves of Melilla and Ceuta, part of increased surveillance across Europe of militant groups that have fueled conflicts from West Africa to Iraq and Syria, misspelled the surname of a man who the authorities said had been in online contact with members of the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. He is Mustafa Maya Amaya, not Amata.
match_headline: Spanish Police Target Cells Recruiting War Volunteers

text: An article in some editions on Monday about efforts by people who were adopted in New York to see their original birth certificates misstated the number of states that allow such access. It is 14, not 12. And because of an editing error, the article misstated the time period during which 10,421 original birth certificates were issued at the request of adoptees or their relatives in Illinois. They were issued from May 2010 to April 2014, not after April.
match_headline: New York Adoptees Fight for Access to Birth Certificates

text: An article last Friday about Justin M. Leverenz, head of the emerging markets fund at Oppenheimer Funds, misspelled the surname of a top portfolio manager at the firm. He is Rajeev Bhaman, not Bahman.
match_headline: In Emerging Markets, What Scares Most Investors Entices Oppenheimer

text: An obituary on Monday about the disc jockey Casey Kasem misstated the name of the organization for which he produced broadcasts when he was in the Army. It was the Armed Forces Radio and Television Service, the forerunner of the American Forces Radio and Television Service — not the Armed Forces Network.
match_headline: Casey Kasem, Wholesome Voice of Pop Radio, Dies at 82

text: A picture credit in some editions on Wednesday with an obituary about the author Daniel Keyes misspelled the photographer’s surname. The picture of Mr. Keyes was taken by Miriam Berkley, not Berkeley.
match_headline: Daniel Keyes, Author of ‘Flowers for Algernon,’ Dies at 86

text: An article on Wednesday about a new technology that could map the damage to parts of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear complex in Japan, where a meltdown occurred in 2011 after an earthquake and tsunami, misstated one of the properties of muons, subatomic particles employed in the technology. They can penetrate hundreds of feet into the earth, not all the way through it.
match_headline: Assessing Fukushima Damage Without Eyes on the Inside

text: A chart last Saturday with the Off the Charts column, about indications of growth in the country’s job market, carried an erroneous label. The lower-center chart showed the “Ratio of unemployed workers to unfilled jobs,” not the “Ratio of unfilled jobs to unemployed workers.”
ref_headline: Ratio of unemployed workers to unfilled jobs,
match_headline: Indications of Growth in U.S. Job Market

text: An article on May 22 about the Yankees’ 4-2, 13-inning victory over the Chicago Cubs misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the Yankees player on the disabled list who felt more lower-back pain after playing catch Monday. He is Shawn Kelley, not Kelly.
match_headline: No Runs Allowed, but Still No Wins for Cubs’ Samardzija

text: A picture caption on Friday with a film review of “Miss Lovely” misidentified the actress shown and her role. She is Zeena Bhatia, who plays Poonam, not Niharika Singh, who plays Pinky.
match_headline: The Ugly Side of Bollywood

text: Because of an editing error, an art review on Friday about the “Truppe Fledermaus & The Carnival at the End of the World” exhibition at the Yancey Richardson Gallery in Manhattan misspelled, at one point, the surname of one of the artists who, with Nicholas Kahn, created the works on display. As the review correctly noted elsewhere, he is Richard Selesnick, not Selesnik.
ref_headline: Truppe Fledermaus & The Carnival at the End of the World
match_headline: Kahn & Selesnick: ‘Truppe Fledermaus & the Carnival at the End of the World’

text: An entry about a documentary on Channel 13 in the What’s on Friday television highlights in some editions on Friday misspelled the surname of the ballerina who is the subject of the movie. She was Tanaquil Le Clercq, not Le Clerq. (The film is “Tanaquil Le Clercq: Afternoon of a Faun.”)
ref_headline: Tanaquil Le Clercq: Afternoon of a Faun.
match_headline: What’s On Friday

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about a memorial concert on Monday for Paul Colby, who owned the Bitter End club in Greenwich Village, misspelled the surname of one of the people scheduled to perform. He is Eric Andersen, not Anderson.
match_headline: Memorial Concert Scheduled for Bitter End Owner

text: An article last Sunday about the effect that Representative Eric Cantor’s loss in the Virginia Republican primary could have on business organizations quoted incorrectly, in some copies, from comments by Dirk Van Dongen about Mr. Cantor’s support for the nation’s highway system. Mr. Van Dongen called the highway system “a priority to anybody involved in the interstate transport of goods” — not “a prior to anybody” involved in such transports. The article also rendered the name of Mr. Van Dongen’s organization incorrectly in some copies. He is president of the National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors, not the National Association of Wholesalers.
ref_headline: a priority to anybody involved in the interstate transport of goods
match_headline: A Cantor Effect for Businesses and the G.O.P.

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about Hour Children, a nonprofit organization dedicated to helping female prisoners and their children, misstated the given name of a woman who was shown feeding her baby. She is Lataya Carter, not Latay.
match_headline: The Sister of Second Chances

text: An essay last Sunday by the Norwegian author Karl Ove Knausgaard, about his uneasy relationship with fame, misstated part of the Norwegian title of a book by Asne Seierstad about the mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik, whose yearning to be recognized by others, Knausgaard contended, partly caused his violent act. The book is “En Av Oss” (“One of Us”), not “Ev An Oss.”

A picture caption with an entry in the “This and That” feature last Sunday about the Interval, a new bar in San Francisco, misidentified the type of container in which the bar serves whiskey to its patrons. It is a flask, not a beaker.
match_headline: Now Booking | A Techno-Utopian Bar in San Francisco for Those Who Like to Think While They Drink

text: A picture with the Playlist CD review column last Sunday was published in error, based on information from a publicist. The photograph showed the singer Y’anna Crawley — not Anita Wilson, who has a new album out.
match_headline: Senegal to the Caribbean, With a Stop at the Church of Funk and Soul

text: An article last Sunday about the new science fiction thriller “Snowpiercer,” the English-language debut of the South Korean director Bong Joon-ho, misspelled the given name of the movie’s Czech production designer. He is Ondrej Nekvasil, not Ondoej. An accompanying picture credit also misspelled his name — as Ondej.
match_headline: A Train to Nowhere in a New Ice Age

text: An article on June 8 about the obscure Abstract Expressionist painter Raymond Spillenger referred incorrectly to exhibitions of his work at the Contemporary Arts Museum in Houston. His paintings last hung there in 1959, as part of a “10th Street” group show; none are currently being shown at the museum, which is a noncollecting institution.
match_headline: Abstract Painter’s Afterlife, Reborn

text: A review on June 1 about “How Paris Became Paris: The Invention of the Modern City,” by Joan DeJean, referred incorrectly to the history of Peter the Great’s building of St. Petersburg. The year 1717 was when Peter visited Paris in search of ideas for his new city, which had been founded in 1703; he did not decide in 1717 to build the city.
ref_headline: How Paris Became Paris: The Invention of the Modern City,
match_headline: They Love Paris

text: An article last Sunday about ayahuasca tea, a hallucinogen, quoted incorrectly from comments by Dr. Charles Grob, a psychiatrist who helped administer a study of the tea’s potential benefits. He did not call it a stimulant, which it is not.
match_headline: Ayahuasca: A Strong Cup of Tea

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Clarissa Polk and Tushin Shah referred incorrectly to the groom’s academic honors at the Washington University law school. He graduated magna cum laude, not cum laude.
match_headline: Clarissa Polk, Tushin Shah

text: An article last Sunday about a repair bill and an assessment at 2 Fifth Avenue in Greenwich Village that exceeded $30 million misstated the profession of William Greenberg,  a member of the new board that unseated the incumbents and is now its president. He is a mortgage trader, not a mortgage broker.
match_headline: The Killer Assessment

text: An article last Sunday about how developers are using artwork to attract buyers to luxury condos omitted part of the name of the museum where Julian Schnabel’s new exhibit is opening in October. It is the NSU Museum of Art Fort Lauderdale , not the Museum of Art Fort Lauderdale.
match_headline: Using Artists to Sell Condos in Miami and New York

text: An article on June 8 about Lionel Messi, the soccer player, misstated part of the name of a team that he played against. It is Athletic Bilbao, not Atlético Bilbao.
match_headline: The Burden of Being Messi

text: An article on Wednesday about a mistrial being granted in a bribery case against former State Senator Malcolm A. Smith misidentified, in some editions, the borough in which Vincent Tabone, another defendant in the case, was a former Republican committee vice chairman. It is Queens, not the Bronx.
match_headline: Mistrial Is Declared in Malcolm Smith Corruption Trial

text: An article on Thursday about the recovery and identification of 17 military members killed when their plane crashed in Alaska in 1952, using information from the Department of Defense, misstated the rank of five of the men. Marion E. Hooton was an airman first class, not a senior airman; Carroll R. Dyer, Thomas S. Lyons and Thomas C. Thigpen were airmen second class, not first class; and Howard E. Martin was an airman third class, not airman.
match_headline: Decades Later, 17 Service Members Who Perished in Crash Will Be Laid to Rest

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the sentencing of Liliana Trafficante, who raised money for a nonexistent water park in upstate New York, reversed the positions of two participants in the case. Eugene E. Ingoglia is a federal prosecutor, and John C. Meringolo is Ms. Trafficante’s lawyer. Also, because of an editing error, the article misstated Ms. Trafficante’s legal circumstances at the time of her arrest on state charges in 2012. She was awaiting sentencing in the federal wire fraud case; she was not out on bail pending trial.
match_headline: Woman Sentenced to 41 Months for Fake Water Park Plan

text: An article on Friday about efforts by private investors to make money from the for-profit education sector in Brazil misstated the surname of an education sector analyst with BTG Pactual. He is João Carlos Santos, not Santana. A picture caption with the article also rendered the name of a Brazilian city incorrectly. As the dateline correctly noted, it is São Paulo, not São Paolo.
match_headline: As Demand for Education Rises in Brazil, For-Profit Colleges Fill the Gap

text: An article on Friday about a decrease in robberies and thefts of Apple products equipped with a so-called kill switch to render the device unusable referred incorrectly to the vice president of external and state affairs at CTIA, a trade organization for the wireless industry. The executive, Jamie Hastings, is a woman.
match_headline: Smartphones Embracing ‘Kill Switches’ as Theft Defense

text: An obituary on Thursday about the writer and editor Thomas B. Morgan, who served as press secretary to Mayor John V. Lindsay of New York, referred imprecisely to Mr. Lindsay’s election as mayor in 1969. He was re-elected to a second term that year; he was not the city’s “newly elected” mayor in 1969. (He was first elected in 1965.)
match_headline: Thomas B. Morgan, Writer, Editor and Lindsay Press Aide, Dies at 87

text: A picture caption on Friday with an obituary about Stuart Vaughan, who directed the first productions of the New York Shakespeare Festival, misstated the date of a production of “Macbeth” in Central Park with Colleen Dewhurst and Roy Poole. It was 1957, not 1975. In addition, a subheading in some copies misstated whose wife was passed over for a role that went to Ms. Dewhurst. As the obituary correctly noted, it was Joseph Papp’s wife, not Mr. Vaughan’s.
match_headline: Stuart Vaughan, Director and Shakespeare Expert, Dies at 88

text: An article on Saturday about a vote by the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) to divest from three companies linked to Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory misstated the title of Rabbi Alissa Wise, a staff member of the Jewish Voice for Peace who attended the general convention where the decision was made. She is a co-director of organizing, not the group’s director.
match_headline: Presbyterians Vote to Divest Holdings to Pressure Israel

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an article about more opportunities for Asian-American theater actors in New York misstated, in some editions, the surname of the star of “Here Lies Love,” a show about Imelda Marcos at the Public Theater. She is Ruthie Ann Miles, not Miller.
match_headline: Here Lies Progress: Asian Actors Fill the Playbill

text: An article on Thursday about Dan Brown, a Maine farmer who is battling the state over the unlicensed sale of unpasteurized milk, misidentified the farm operated by Joan Gibson, who supported state licensing and testing of small dairies. It is Milky Way Organic Farm in Levant, Me., not Tide Mill Organic Farm in Edmunds, Me.
match_headline: Maine Court Fight Pits Farmers Against State and One Another

text: An article on Monday about discussions between Vice Media and big media companies like Time Warner and 21st Century Fox misstated the number of hours of television content Vice had produced. Vice has produced about 76 hours of domestic and international programming, not 11 hours, which was the amount Vice had produced for its HBO show.
match_headline: Vice Has Many Media Giants Salivating, but Its Terms Will Be Rich

text: An article on Monday about the 2-2 tie between the United States and Portugal at the World Cup misidentified, in some copies, the American player credited with the assist on Clint Dempsey’s goal. He is Graham Zusi, not DeAndre Yedlin.
match_headline: Late Shock Interrupts U.S. Party

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Saturday about Nina Arianda and Sam Rockwell’s replacing Lauren Ambrose and Chris Pine in a production of the Sam Shepard play “Fool for Love” at the Williamstown Theater Festival this summer misstated the dates of the play’s run. It is scheduled for July 24 through Aug. 2, not June 24 through July 2.
match_headline: The Location May Stay the Same, but Everything Else Will Change

text: An article on Thursday about the pending designation of the Qhapac Ñan, or Andean Road System, as a protected South American site on Unesco’s World Heritage List misstated the number of people served by the road network. Estimates of the population under control of the Inca empire in the 15th and 16th centuries vary widely but the Peru culture ministry puts it at about 10 million — not 40,000, which is the figure reported by the International Council on Monuments and Sites as the number of people estimated to have used the road network at any point in time. (The Qhapac Ñan was added to the World Heritage List on Saturday.)
match_headline: Protection Sought for Vast and Ancient Incan Road

text: An obituary on Friday about the lyricist Gerry Goffin referred incorrectly to Diana Ross’s recording of the song “Theme From Mahogany (Do You Know Where You’re Going To?),” which Mr. Goffin wrote with Michael Masser. It reached No. 1 in 1976, not 1975.
ref_headline: Theme From Mahogany (Do You Know Where You’re Going To?),
match_headline: Gerry Goffin, Hitmaking Songwriter With Carole King, Dies at 75

text: An article on Monday about an Israeli assault on Syrian Army positions that Israel said was in response to an attack in the Golan Heights that killed an Arab-Israeli teenager and wounded two others misstated the year that Israel captured the Golan from Syria. It was 1967, not 1973.
match_headline: Israel Strikes Syria After Youth Is Killed

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a court decision in Turkey ordering the release and retrial of 230 military officers convicted in 2012 of trying to overthrow the government of Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan misidentified the court that ordered the release. It is the Istanbul 4th High Criminal Court — not the country’s constitutional court, which had already delivered a landmark ruling saying that the defendants’ rights had been violated.
match_headline: Turkish Officers Convicted in 2012 Coup Case Are Released

text: An article on Saturday about Pakistanis who were fleeing a government offensive against militants in North Waziristan misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a man whose wife went into labor during the conflict. He is Jalil Khan, not Jail.
match_headline: Aid Scarce as Pakistanis Flee Conflict

text: An article on Monday about a discussion of issues facing the nation’s cities misspelled the surname of the Chicago mayor who was cited as one of those trying to fight poverty with higher wages. He is Rahm Emanuel, not Emmanuel.
match_headline: Mayors Put Focus on How to Raise Wages for Lowest-Paid Workers in Cities

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with an article about new efforts by the White House to curb illegal immigration rendered incompletely, in some editions, the name of a 7-year-old Honduran boy at a shelter in Texas. He is Yorfrin Daniel Cruz, not Daniel Cruz.
match_headline: U.S. Moves to Stop Surge in Illegal Immigration

text: An article on Tuesday about New York restaurants that are forced to relocate after their rents go up, often as a result of the gentrification the restaurants bring about, misstated, in some editions, the year that Union Square Cafe will forfeit its lease. It will occur at the end of 2015, not at the end of this year.
match_headline: Union Square Cafe Joins Other Victims of New York City’s Rising Rents

text: An article on Monday about company-owned insurance on the lives of employees referred incorrectly to the ways in which companies benefit from such policies. Money spent on premiums is taxable — not tax-free. (As the article correctly noted, investment returns on the policies and eventual death benefits are tax-free.)
match_headline: Obama Extends Marriage Benefits to Gay Couples

text: An article on the Itineraries page on Tuesday about JetBlue’s addition of first-class seats that convert to flat beds gave an outdated title for Dave Barger. He is the company’s chief executive, no longer its president.
match_headline: JetBlue Adds Flat-Bed Seats

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about the discovery of 20 previously unknown poems by Pablo Neruda misspelled a word in the title of a coming annotated edition of the poems. It is “Poemas Inéditos: Pablo Neruda,” not “Poemas Inéditas: Pablo Neruda.”
match_headline: Neruda Poems Found

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the magazine publisher Felix Dennis referred imprecisely to his sale of magazines to Quadrangle Capital Partners II in 2007. While he sold Maxim, Blender and Stuff, he retained The Week; he did not sell all of his American magazines.
match_headline: Felix Dennis, 67, Flamboyant Builder of Magazine Empire, Dies

text: An obituary on Monday about Fouad Ajami, a commentator on Middle East affairs, misstated, in some editions, the year Mr. Ajami said Prime Minister Nuri Kamal al-Maliki of Iraq had squandered an opportunity to unify the country and become a dictator. He said it this year, not in 2004.
match_headline: Fouad Ajami, Commentator and Expert in Arab History, Dies at 68

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the singer and comedian Steve Rossi misspelled the surname of the actor whose first name became part of Mr. Rossi’s stage name. He was Steve Cochran, not Cochrane.
match_headline: Steve Rossi, Singer Who Found Fame in Comedy Duo, Dies at 82

text: A picture caption on Sunday with the continuation of an article about Jordan Sullivan, a probationary firefighter with the New York Fire Department, and his first fire, misspelled the surname of one of two other firefighters with whom Mr. Sullivan was shown. He is Dan Natalicchio, not Natalicchi.
match_headline: Baptism by Fire: A New York Firefighter Confronts His First Test

text: An article on May 17 about anxieties among India’s Muslims after the electoral triumph of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party and its leader, Narendra Modi, misstated the number of seats the Bharatiya Janata Party was likely to win in constituencies where Muslims make up at least one in five voters, according to a Reuters analysis of Election Commission data. The party had won or was leading the contest for 47 seats, not 102. (The error was pointed out shortly after the article was published; this correction was delayed because there was no follow-through on additional reporting.)
match_headline: For India’s Persecuted Muslim Minority, Caution Follows Hindu Party’s Victory

text: An article on Monday about homelessness in Hawaii misspelled the surname, at one point, of a man living on the street who criticized the mayor’s treatment of the homeless. He is John McCormick, not McCormack.
match_headline: Honolulu Shores Up Tourism With Crackdown on Homeless

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the action by the Rent Guidelines Board for New York City setting the lowest percentage rent increase of its 45-year-existence misstated the year the lowest increase on two-year leases occurred. That rate, 2.75 percent, was decided on Monday night; it was not 1978. (That year there was a 2 percent surcharge on top of a 6.5 percent increase.)
match_headline: Panel Backs Rent Increase of One Percent

text: An article in some editions last Thursday about the Yankees’ 7-3 victory over the Toronto Blue Jays misstated, in some copies, the position Toronto’s starting pitcher Mark Buehrle held for earned run average in the American League entering the game. He was third, not second.
match_headline: A Struggling McCann Shows Some of the Pop He Was Signed to Provide

text: An article on Monday about the move of the longtime Marvel Comics illustrator John Romita Jr. to DC Comics misidentified the comic on which Mr. Romita was first offered work by the Marvel editor Scott Edelman. It was Spider-Man, not Iron Man.
match_headline: Leaping From Marvel to DC in a Single Bound

text: An obituary on May 25 about the former federal judge Cornelia G. Kennedy erroneously attributed a distinction to her. She was one of the first women to serve as a clerk at the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit — not the first. (At least one other woman, Margaret Lybolt Rosenzweig, preceded her.)
match_headline: Cornelia G. Kennedy, a Pioneering Federal Judge, Dies at 90

text: An obituary in some editions on Wednesday about the actor Eli Wallach misstated the year of a television production of Clifford Odets’s “Paradise Lost” in which he appeared. It was 1971, not 1974.
match_headline: Eli Wallach, Multifaceted Actor on Stage and Screen, Dies at 98

text: A picture on Thursday with the Books of The Times Review about “Diary of the Dark Years, 1940-1944,” written by Jean Guénhenno during the German occupation of France, was published in error. The picture, provided by Oxford University Press, showed the historian and author Christopher M. Bell, not the translator of the book, David Ball.
match_headline: Shedding Light on Nazi-Occupied Paris

text: An obituary on Sunday about Dr. Arnold S. Relman, the longtime editor of The New England Journal of Medicine, misidentified the medical school where he met his wife, Dr. Marcia Angell. It was Boston University School of Medicine, when she was a student and he was a professor there; they did not meet at Harvard Medical School. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated the dates of Dr. Relman’s tenure as editor of the journal. He held the post from 1977 to 1991, not from 1977 to 2000. (Dr. Angell was editor in 1999 and 2000.)
match_headline: Dr. Arnold Relman, 91, Journal Editor and Health System Critic, Dies

text: An obituary on Saturday about Stephanie L. Kwolek, a chemist who invented the technology behind Kevlar, included an outdated reference to a plaque honoring Ms. Kwolek, who was inducted into the Plastics Hall of Fame in 2004. While it once hung at the National Plastics Center and Museum in Leominster, Mass., that is no longer the case; the museum closed in 2008.
match_headline: Stephanie L. Kwolek, Inventor of Kevlar, Is Dead at 90

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about the lack of rigorous research for many legal uses of medical marijuana misspelled, in some editions, the surname of an 11-year-old girl who had persistent seizures and who was part of the campaign to legalize medical marijuana in New York State. She is Kaylie Annable, not Annabel.
match_headline: Politicians’ Prescriptions for Marijuana Defy Doctors and Data

text: An article on June 20 about the roots of France’s disenchantment with its men’s national soccer team misstated the history of minorities who played for England’s national soccer team. Frank Soo, who was half Chinese, played for England in the 1940s; it is not the case that England “did not field a player of color until Viv Anderson in 1978.”
ref_headline: did not field a player of color until Viv Anderson in 1978.
match_headline: Disenchantment in France With Fickle National Team

text: An article last Saturday about Costa Rica’s 1-0 victory over Italy at the World Cup misstated Costa Rica’s world ranking. It is 28th, not 34th. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: A Central American Mouse Roars

text: An article on Thursday about Argentina’s 3-2 victory over Nigeria at the World Cup misspelled the name of a waterway in Pôrto Alegre that provided fans with a hazy view. It is Guaíba Lake, not Guaiaba.
match_headline: Messi Lifts Spirits of Argentines, Even Those Without Tickets

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about charitable organizations that help homeowners recover from Hurricane Sandy referred incorrectly to the pastoral duties of the Rev. Brian Steadman, who heads a rebuilding effort. He is a pastor with Resurrection Brooklyn, a network of churches based in Park Slope; he is not a Coney Island pastor.
match_headline: After the Storm, 20 Months in Limbo

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about an arts exhibition at Wave Hill in the Bronx misstated part of the name of a new project by Gregory Crewdson. It is “Cathedral of the Pines,” not “Cathedral in the Pines.”
match_headline: Chasing Fires in the Dark

text: An article on June 15 about a 50-course meal served by the modernist cuisine cookbook writer Nathan Myhrvold to the Catalan chef Ferran Adrià and to Dwight Garner, who wrote the article, misstated the day the meal took place. It was on a Friday, not a Saturday.
match_headline: An Intense Chef, and His Commandments

text: An obituary last Sunday about Dr. Lorna Wing, a British psychiatrist who was instrumental in identifying autism as a mental disorder of many gradations, quoted incorrectly from an article about her in The Guardian in 2009. The British newspaper paraphrased a comment by her in which it said she pointed out that despite years of medical training, she and her husband knew nothing about autism when their daughter was born in 1956. The Guardian article did not include a direct quotation by her in which she said, “We learned nothing about autism during our medical training.” (In an article on an autism website, Dr. Wing wrote, “We learned nothing about autism during this training.”)
ref_headline: We learned nothing about autism during our medical training.
match_headline: Dr. Lorna Wing, Who Broadened Views of Autism, Dies at 85

text: An article last Sunday about an exhibition at the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin, “The World at War, 1914-1918,” misspelled the first word in the title of a poem by Wilfred Owen, who was killed in the war. It is “Dulce et Decorum Est” (not “Dolce”).
match_headline: Visceral Reality vs. the Big Picture

text: An article last Sunday about the effect World War I had on America’s cultural consciousness misidentified the era in which John Bunyan’s “The Pilgrim’s Progress” — an allegory of hardship and redemption that many British soldiers and officers were familiar with — came out. It was published in the 17th century, not during the medieval years.
match_headline: A War to End All Innocence

text: An article last Sunday about the former actor Richard Beymer and a documentary that he filmed in Mississippi in 1964 misidentified the gang that Russ Tamblyn’s Riff belonged to in “West Side Story” — the movie in which Mr. Beymer starred as Tony in 1961. Riff and Tony were both Jets; neither one was a rival Shark.
match_headline: Right Out of Hollywood, a Witness to History

text: An article last Sunday about the opera composer Michael Hersch misidentified the artist of several paintings that hang in his home studio. They are by Nicholas Cairns — not by his father, Christopher Cairns, who is also a visual artist and Mr. Hersch’s friend.
match_headline: A Survivor, Inspired by Love and Loss

text: A picture caption on June 15 with an article about the director Jan Troell misstated part of the name of his new film. It is “The Last Sentence,” not “The Final Sentence.”
match_headline: Swedish Auteur Takes On a Brave Loner

text: Because of an editing error, an article on June 15 about U.S. Special Operations forces in Africa paraphrased incorrectly comments by Edward Price, the assistant press secretary of the National Security Council. Responding to criticism about the lack of oversight of counterterrorism efforts in Africa, Price said the White House — not the State Department — planned to put such checks in place.
match_headline: Can General Linder’s Special Operations Forces Stop the Next Terrorist Threat?

text: An article last Sunday about Tama Robertson, a broker who works with gay, lesbian and transgender clients, referred imprecisely to New York State’s anti-discrimination laws. While the New York State attorney general argues that existing anti-discrimination laws offer protections for transgender people, New York has not enacted laws specifically intended to protect transgender renters and homeowners.
match_headline: A Guide Who Knows the Turf

text: A headline and a listing of information with the Check In column last Sunday, about a lodge in the Mashpi Rainforest Biodiversity Reserve in Ecuador, misstated part of its name. As the article correctly noted, it is Mashpi Lodge, not Hotel Mashpi.
match_headline: Hotel Review: Mashpi Lodge in Ecuador

text: A reporting credit on Friday with an article about the escalation of the campaign by the Pakistani military against Islamist militants in North Waziristan omitted a contributor. Mark Mazzetti reported from Washington.
match_headline: As Pakistan Advances Against Taliban, Fleeing Civilians Pour Into Northern Towns

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the Mets’ 8-5 loss to the Oakland Athletics misidentified, in some copies, the team that Mets starter Zack Wheeler threw a shutout against in his previous appearance. It was the Miami Marlins, not the St. Louis Cardinals.
match_headline: After Raising Bar, Wheeler Crashes Out in 2 Innings

text: An obituary on Friday about the former United States Senator Howard H. Baker Jr. erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He was the first Republican from Tennessee to be elected to the Senate since the end of Reconstruction; he was not the first Republican ever elected senator in Tennessee. The obituary also misstated the middle initial of the father of Mr. Baker’s second wife, former Senator Nancy L. Kassebaum of Kansas. He was Alfred M. Landon, not Alfred E.
match_headline: Howard H. Baker Jr., ‘Great Conciliator’ of the Senate, Dies at 88

text: An article on Saturday about legal problems facing judges in Broward County, Fla., misstated the status of one judge who was accused of cheating clients and a co-counsel in the settlement of a civil suit she handled as a private lawyer a decade ago. The Judicial Qualifications Commission recommended in April that the judge be removed, but that has not yet happened. (The Florida Supreme Court must act on the recommendation.)
match_headline: Here Comes the Judge, in Cuffs

text: An article on Monday about the struggle to teach math under the Common Core academic standards referred incorrectly to Linda M. Gojak’s association with the National Council of Teachers of Math. She is a former president, not the organization’s current one.
match_headline: Math Under Common Core Has Even Parents Stumbling

text: An article on Monday about the annual Gay Pride March down Fifth Avenue in Manhattan overstated the significance of an uprising in 1969 at the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in Greenwich Village. The incident, in which lesbians and gays fought back against a police raid, is widely seen as a major turning point in the fight for gay rights. But the Stonewall Inn is not the site where the gay-rights movement was born. (National gay-rights organizations had existed for decades before Stonewall.)
match_headline: With Rainbow Neckerchiefs, Celebrating Pride and Progress at Parade

text: An article in some editions on June 13 about a preservation deal in which “Le Tricorne,” a tapestry painted by Picasso, will be sent to the New-York Historical Society, erroneously attributed a distinction to the piece. While it is one of Picasso’s bigger works, it is not his largest in the United States. (That is “Tête,” an iron sculpture on display in Chicago.)
match_headline: After Much Debate, Picasso Curtain Will Be Moved From the Four Seasons

text: An article on Monday about web-based start-ups that equip small local businesses with tools to help keep them abreast of technological change misstated the headquarters of one such start-up, Edelweiss, which is helping independent booksellers and publishers. It is based in Ann Arbor, Mich., not Seattle. The article also misstated the position of John Rubin, who commented on the company’s efforts. He is chief executive of Above the Treeline, which operates Edelweiss — not of Edelweiss itself.
match_headline: Modern Tools for Mom-and-Pops

text: An article on Friday about Teabox, a start-up aiming to bring India’s tea industry into the modern era with the backing of venture capital, misspelled part of the name of one firm that has provided funding to the company. It is Horizen Ventures, not Horizon Ventures.
match_headline: Teabox Seeks to Bring India’s Teas Into Modern Era

text: An article on Monday about a concert by the Vienna Philharmonic to mark the centennial of the assassinations of the Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife, Sophie, in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, misstated the number of countries in the European Union. There are 28, not 27.
match_headline: Remembering World War I in the Conflict’s Flash Point

text: An obituary on Saturday about the singer, guitarist and songwriter Bobby Womack referred incorrectly to his sons Truth and Vincent. Truth Womack died in 1978, and Vincent Womack died in 1986; they do not survive him. The obituary also rendered incorrectly one word in the title of a Sly Stone album that Mr. Womack helped produce. The title is “There’s a Riot Goin’ On,” not “There’s a Riot Going On.”
match_headline: Bobby Womack, Royalty of the Soul Era, Dies at 70

text: A picture caption on Friday with the continuation of an article about foreclosures in Detroit misidentified, in some editions, the person shown sitting on a bed. He is Robert Brown; the picture was not of Renata Lewis, Robert’s mother, who is struggling to pay past-due bills.
match_headline: Detroit Needs Residents, but Sends Some Packing

text: An article on Saturday about conflicting interpretations of the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo as the city marked the 100th anniversary of that event described incorrectly the location of the prison in which Gavrilo Princip, who killed the archduke and his consort, Sophie, died. It was in Terezin, in what is now the Czech Republic, not in a “Hungarian prison.”
match_headline: In Sarajevo, Divisions That Drove an Assassin Have Only Begun to Heal

text: An article on Friday about President Obama’s trip to Minneapolis to talk about challenges facing the middle class misidentified the city in Minnesota that is home to Matt’s Bar, where President Obama ate lunch. The bar is in Minneapolis, not in Corcoran.
match_headline: In a Diner With Obama, a Serving of Ordinary Life

text: An article on Tuesday about Hobby Lobby, the company that took its fight against the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptives mandate to the Supreme Court and won on Monday, misstated the minimum hourly wage earned by full-time Hobby Lobby employees. It is $15 an hour, not $14 an hour.
match_headline: Hobby Lobby Made Fight a Matter of Christian Principle

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the Tea Party’s efforts in Tennessee to defeat Senator Lamar Alexander in the Republican primary referred incorrectly to Lascassas, the home of Joe Carr, one of Mr. Alexander’s opponents. Lascassas is an unincorporated community in Rutherford County; it is not a county itself.
match_headline: Narrow Tea Party Loss in Mississippi Emboldens Its Senate Bid in Tennessee

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the approval of a $511 million loan to build a replacement for the Tappan Zee Bridge misstated the portion of the loan that could be spent on oyster bed restoration. It is $1.2 million, not $2.1 million.
match_headline: Environmental Agency Approves $511 Million Loan for Tappan Zee Replacement

text: An article in some editions on June 20 about the filing of federal charges against two heroin dealers in upstate New York described incorrectly a main property of fentanyl, which was mixed with heroin. It is primarily an analgesic, not an anesthetic.
match_headline: U.S. Authorities Step In to Charge 2 After Deaths From Extra-Lethal Heroin

text: An obituary last Wednesday about the classical-music producer and engineer John McClure referred incorrectly to a job he held before going to work for the Carnegie Hall Recording Company in 1950. He installed high fidelity systems, not stereo systems. (Home stereo systems were not widely available until almost a decade later.)
match_headline: John McClure Dies at 84; Produced Classic Records

text: A picture caption in some editions last Wednesday with an obituary about Stanley Marsh, the Texas millionaire best known for commissioning the public art project known as the Cadillac Ranch, misstated the year the photograph showing Mr. Marsh leaning against a Cadillac was taken. It was 1984, not 1974.
match_headline: Stanley Marsh, Cadillac Rancher, Dies at 76, Shadowed by Charges

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on June 20 with an article about the circumstances behind a fatal stabbing outside a middle school in the Bronx misstated, in some editions, the day two girls visited a memorial to the youth who died. The photograph, of the girls crouched at the site, was taken on Thursday, June 19 — not the day before.
match_headline: Signs of Trouble Preceded Fatal Stabbing at Bronx School

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Madison Keys’s victory over Klara Koukalova at Wimbledon misidentified, in some editions, the player who is seeded 31st at the tournament. The player is Koukalova — not Juan Todero, who is Keys’s coach.
match_headline: With Aplomb, Young Star Passes Test

text: An article on Saturday about Uruguay’s support of the soccer star Luis Suárez after he was barred from the World Cup for biting an opponent misidentified the location of Suárez’s residence near Montevideo in some editions. It is in Lagomar, not in El Pinar.
match_headline: Upon Return to Uruguay, Luis Suárez Is Met With Support

text: An article on June 23 about the contrasts between Brasília and other World Cup host cities misspelled the name of another city in Brazil in one instance. It is São Paulo, not São Paolo.
match_headline: Brasília, a Capital City That’s a Place Apart

text: An article on Monday about Belgium’s soccer captain, Vincent Kompany, whose father is from the Democratic Republic of Congo, misspelled the given name of a former Congolese dictator. He is Mobutu Sese Seko, not Mobuto.
match_headline: Bruised Captain Inspires Belgians

text: An article on Tuesday about the destruction of ash forests by emerald ash borers misstated the number of ash trees in wild forests in North America. It is eight billion, not million.
match_headline: After the Trees Disappear

text: An article last Thursday about several new endeavors that Candy Spelling is undertaking misstated the price she paid for her condominium in Century City, Calif. It was about $35 million — not $47 million, the price she originally agreed to.
match_headline: Another Spelling Production

text: A picture caption with a report on the Browsing page last Thursday about necklaces misstated the maiden name of the designer. As the report correctly noted, she is Nicole Mann Novick, not Nicole Page Novick.
match_headline: Summer With a Fringe Built In

text: An article on Wednesday about a renewed campaign by Ukrainian government forces against separatists misspelled, in some editions, the name of a checkpoint on the border of Russia. It is Dolzhansky, not Dolzhanksy. And because of an editing error, the article misstated the month in 2013 when President Viktor F. Yanukovych of Ukraine balked at signing a trade agreement with the European Union. It was November, not December.
match_headline: Putin Warns Again of Force as Ukraine Fighting Spreads

text: An article on Tuesday about the halting of work in Bulgaria on the South Stream pipeline, the biggest energy project caught in political crossfire over the crisis in Ukraine, misspelled the surname of the American ambassador to Bulgaria. She is Marcie B. Ries, not Reis.
match_headline: A Conduit for Russian Gas, Tangled in Europe’s Conflicts

text: An article on Tuesday about off-the-field problems of African teams during the World Cup misstated the given name of the professor who teaches a course called Global Soccer, Global Politics at the New School. He is Sean Jacobs, not Steve.
match_headline: African Teams Head Home, Cash in Hand

text: A headline in some editions on Wednesday with an article about Rafael Nadal’s fourth-round loss to Nick Kyrgios at Wimbledon misstated Nadal’s seeding at the tournament. While he is No. 1 in the world rankings, he was seeded No. 2 at Wimbledon, not No. 1. In addition, the article referred incorrectly to Novak Djokovic’s seeding. While he is No. 2 in the rankings, he is the No. 1 seed at the tournament, not the No. 2 seed.
match_headline: Teenager Topples Top-Ranked Nadal in Round of 16

text: An article last Sunday about treatment problems at military hospitals misstated part of the name of a hospital with a high rate of surgical complications. It is the San Antonio Military Medical Center in Texas, not the San Antonio Army Medical Center. The error was repeated in an accompanying chart.
match_headline: In Military Care, a Pattern of Errors but Not Scrutiny

text: An article last Sunday about the familiar role Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. finds himself in as he tries to help solve the crisis in Iraq, drawing on his original proposal that the nation be divided along sectarian lines, misstated, in some editions, the name of the Sunni militant group that threatens the survival of the present government. It is the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, or ISIS, not the Islamic State of Syria and Iraq.
match_headline: With Surge of Chaos in Iraq, a Familiar Problem Knocks on Biden’s Door

text: An article last Sunday about a reporter’s discovery that his great-great-grandfather, a police patrolman, had been charged in the 1889 death of a man in Manhattan misstated, in some editions, the page number in The New York Times on which an article about the case appeared. The article, which ran on March 13 that year with the headline “A One-Sided Inquest,” was published on Page 9, not on the front page.
match_headline: A Copper, a Dust-Up and Death

text: A picture caption last Sunday with the continuation of the cover article about the development of noir in San Francisco carried an erroneous credit. The top row of cityscape photographs were by Jason Henry for The New York Times, not by Matthew Ryan Williams. (Mr. Williams took the other photos.) In addition, the article referred imprecisely to the direction taken by the writer from Union Square to the Tenderloin. It was south and west, not “up,” as in north.
match_headline: San Francisco Noir

text: An article last Sunday about two New York galleries that are showcasing Detroit’s art scene misstated the name of the Detroit hospital where the curator Todd Levin was born. Mr. Levin, who organized “Another Look at Detroit: Parts 1 and 2,” which runs through Aug. 8 at the Marianne Boesky and Marlborough galleries, was born in Sinai Hospital, which no longer exists, not Mount Sinai.
ref_headline: Another Look at Detroit: Parts 1 and 2,
match_headline: The Lively Soul of a Decaying City

text: An article last Sunday about the history of “The Star-Spangled Banner” misstated the opening tempo for a version of the song planned by the baritone Thomas Hampson. A jaunty one-beat pickup will substitute for the stately descent of “O say” — not a two-beat pickup.
match_headline: How the National Anthem Has Unfurled

text: Because of an editing error, a review on June 15 about “The Foundling Boy,” by the French author Michel Déon, misstated the name of an organization that supported Julian Evans’s translation of the novel into English. It is Arts Council England, not Arts England Council.
match_headline: European Pastoral

text: A review on June 15 about “The Impossible Exile: Stefan Zweig at the End of the World,” a biographical study by George Prochnik, referred incorrectly to Zweig’s memoir, “The World of Yesterday.” While the memoir was the last full length work he completed before his death, it was not the last book he wrote. (“Schach-novelle,” a novella translated into English as “The Royal Game” or “Chess Story,” was finished somewhat later.)
ref_headline: The Impossible Exile: Stefan Zweig at the End of the World,
match_headline: Man Without a Country

text: An article on June 1 about the high percentage of their incomes that middle-class New Yorkers often pay for housing in Manhattan misstated the incomes of Michael and Melanie Belanger Boyer. Mr. Boyer makes $86,000 a year, not $90,000; Ms. Belanger Boyer makes $19,000, not $21,000.
match_headline: Middle-Class Lament: Rent

text: A picture caption on June 22 with an article about young adults who live with their parents described incorrectly the firm for which Alexandria Romo works. It is a corporate-security firm, not a security-guard firm.
match_headline: It’s Official: The Boomerang Kids Won’t Leave

text: An essay last Sunday on the civil rights movement misstated the name of the political entity organized by Fannie Lou Hamer. It was the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, not the Mississippi Democratic Freedom Party.
match_headline: When Civil-Rights Unity Fractured

text: An article on Thursday about the high costs of vaccines for children contained several errors. The federal Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommends vaccines; it does not mandate them. (It is up to states to mandate vaccines for school entry.) Most states require vaccination with Prevnar, which protects against pneumonia and other diseases, before children can enter preschool or daycare; not all states do. Additionally, the entity that produced an economic review that estimated the benefits of Prevnar was misidentified. It was the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, not Pfizer, which manufactures the vaccine. The article also referred imprecisely to requirements by drug companies that physicians not disclose prices of medicines and vaccines. While many companies require doctors to sign such agreements, Pfizer does not require it for Prevnar.
match_headline: The Price of Prevention: Vaccine Costs Are Soaring

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about a deadly hit-and-run accident in Brooklyn, using incorrect information from the police, misspelled the given name of the victim. She was Joie Sellers, not Joey. The error was repeated in an article and picture caption in some editions on Friday in which the given name of Joie’s sister was also misspelled. She is Charli Sellers, not Charlie.
match_headline: Girl, 12, Fatally Struck by Stolen Van in Brooklyn; 2 Are Critically Injured

text: An article on Wednesday about Graco Children’s Products’ agreement to recall 1.9 million rear-facing infant seats because of a faulty buckle, after refusing the recall for months, misstated the number of similar car seats that another company, the Evenflo Company, balked at recalling. Evenflo is resisting the recall of 200,000 infant seats, not 1.4 million.
match_headline: Graco Recalls 1.9 Million Rear-Facing Infant Seats

text: A review on Thursday of a performance by Adam Schatz’s rock band Landlady at Rough Trade NYC misstated how many albums the group has released. It is two, not one; its latest is “Upright Behavior.” The band’s first album, “Keeping to Yourself,” came out in 2011.
match_headline: Playing in a Part of Something Bigger

text: A picture on Wednesday with a dance review about Tanztheater Wuppertal performing at the Théâtre de la Ville in Paris was published in error. The picture, provided by a publicist, showed a performance from September 2013, not the one under review.
match_headline: Limping in Solidarity and Leaping for Joy

text: An obituary on Monday about Louis H. Brown Jr., the father of O. J. Simpson’s former wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, misstated where he married his wife, Juditha. It was Switzerland, not Germany.
match_headline: Louis Brown Jr., Nicole Simpson’s Father, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Thursday about Stephen Gaskin, the founder of the commune known as the Farm, misstated the year he was asked to step down as its titular leader. It was 1983, not 1973.
match_headline: Stephen Gaskin, Hippie Who Founded an Enduring Commune, Dies at 79

text: An article on Monday about the arrest of six Israelis in the killing of a Palestinian teenager referred incorrectly to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s response to the killing of Muhammad Abu Khdeir. On the day of the killing, Mr. Netanyahu’s office issued a statement saying he had told his minister for internal security to quickly investigate the crime; it is not the case that “days of near silence” passed before he spoke about it. The error was repeated in an editorial on Tuesday.
match_headline: 6 Israelis Held Over the Killing of Palestinian

text: An article on Saturday about the shift wrought by government censorship on social media in China referred incorrectly to the resignation of a railway minister. The minister had been removed from his post before a high-speed rail crash in 2011 that was the topic of intense discussion on Weibo, a social media site; he did not resign because of criticism over the crash.
match_headline: An Online Shift in China Muffles an Open Forum

text: Because of an editing error, an article on June 27 about a report by Australian officials on the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 over the Indian Ocean in March misstated the conclusions of the report. It said the most likely scenario was that the plane’s crew had become incapacitated and listed as a possible cause hypoxia; it did not conclude that hypoxia was the cause.
match_headline: Pressure Loss Is Explored in Vanishing of Jetliner

text: An article on July 1 about the changing nature of Harlem misstated the way the Abyssinian Baptist Church, a leading institution in the neighborhood, obtained financing to develop real estate. It used local and federal funding, not money from the Empowerment Zone program.
match_headline: Beyond Rangel, Harlem Wrestles With Its Identity

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Friday about Brazilian fans being nervous about the national soccer team’s quarterfinal match against Colombia at the World Cup misstated the day that police in riot gear restrained a crowd of fans in Fortaleza, Brazil. It was Thursday, not Friday.
match_headline: Doubts Set In as Pressure Builds

text: A picture with the On Tennis column on Friday, about the recent success of Canadians in the sport, was published in error in some editions, based on information from Getty Images. The photograph showed Jack Graham, the director emeritus of Tennis Canada, with his wife, Michelle Awad, not with Kelly D. Murumets, chief executive of Tennis Canada.
match_headline: For Inspiration, the United States Should Probably Look North

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about performances at the Lincoln Center Festival by the dance company Rosas, using information from Lincoln Center, reversed the identities of the two dancers shown in some editions. Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker, the company’s leader, was on the left and Michèle Anne De Mey was on the right.
match_headline: Back to the Beginning of Elemental Emotions

text: An article on Monday about the shoes some dancers wear at the Midsummer Night Swing series at Lincoln Center misstated the series’ duration. It takes place over three weeks, not two.
match_headline: Thinking on Their Feet

text: An obituary on Monday about David Truong, whose conviction on espionage charges spurred passage of a 1978 law limiting the government’s use of wiretaps, misstated the name of the law. It is the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, not the Federal Intelligence Surveillance Act.
match_headline: David Truong, Figure in U.S. Wiretap Case, Dies at 68

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Spanish novelist Ana María Matute misstated her birth date. She was born on July 26, 1925 — not July 25.
match_headline: Ana María Matute, Spanish Novelist Marked by Civil War, Dies at 88

text: An article on Wednesday about President Obama’s asking Congress to provide $3.7 billion to confront a surge of young immigrants from Central America referred incorrectly to Heritage Action for America. It is a nonprofit group organized under Section 501(c)(4) of the tax code; it is not a political action committee.
match_headline: Obama Asks for $3.7 Billion to Aid Border

text: An article on Tuesday about a federal appeals court’s blocking of Arizona’s policy of denying driver’s licenses to young immigrants misstated the legal status of Dulce Matuz, president and co-founder of the Arizona Dream Act Coalition. Ms. Matuz has a green card and is being sponsored for citizenship by her husband; she is no longer seeking to stay in the United States through the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program.
match_headline: Court Blocks Arizona Policy of Denying Driver’s Licenses to Some Immigrants

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about a Brooklyn Cyclones game dedicated to “Seinfeld” misstated in some editions the night it was played. It was Saturday, as the article stated, not Sunday.
match_headline: Festivus Poles. Close-Talker Mascot. Yada, Yada, Yada.

text: An article in some copies on Tuesday about the Mets’ 4-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves referred incorrectly to a play that led to the Mets’ winning run in the 11th inning. Before Ruben Tejada’s run-scoring single, Juan Lagares advanced from second to third on a flyout, not a sacrifice fly. Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the article misstated the score after David Wright’s home run in the third inning. The Mets led by 2-0, not 2-1.
match_headline: This Time, Mets Tilt a One-Run Game in Their Favor

text: An article on Tuesday about the restoration of the Caryatid statues that have recently gone back on display at the Acropolis Museum misidentified the conflict in which the city of Caryae, from which the statues’ name is derived, sided with the Persians against the Greeks. It was during the Greco-Persian Wars, not the Peloponnesian War, in which Greeks fought one another. The article also misstated the time period since the British Museum acquired one of the Caryatids. It was nearly two centuries ago, not one.
match_headline: Acropolis Maidens Glow Anew

text: Because of an editing error, an art review on Friday about “Amy Sillman: one lump or two,” at Bard College in Annandale-on-Hudson, N.Y., misidentified the site where the show is completing its tour. It is at Bard, not the Institute of Contemporary Art in Boston, where it appeared earlier.
ref_headline: Amy Sillman: one lump or two,
match_headline: Shifting Contexts, Psychodrama and Meta-Works

text: A listing of credits and other information on Friday with a film review of “Life Itself,” a documentary about the movie critic Roger Ebert, referred incorrectly to the film’s rating. It is rated R, not unrated.
match_headline: And Fade Out ... but Not Fade Away

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Rabbi Zalman Schachter-Shalomi, considered the spiritual father of the Jewish Renewal movement, misspelled the surname of an author who wrote about a meeting Rabbi Schachter-Shalomi and other rabbis had with the Dalai Lama in 1990. He is Rodger Kamenetz, not Kamanetz. The obituary also incorrectly paraphrased a comment by Mr. Kamenetz. He said Rabbi Schachter-Shalomi was pained by his estrangement from the Chabad-Lubavitch branch of Hasidism — not from all Hasidism.
match_headline: Zalman Schachter-Shalomi, Jewish Pioneer, Dies at 89

text: An obituary on Monday about Lloyd Garrison, a former New York Times foreign correspondent, misstated the year the Nigerian government ejected him from Lagos. It was 1967, not 1968.
match_headline: Lloyd Garrison, 83, Journalist; Covered Africa for The Times

text: An editorial on Tuesday about the death of a Palestinian teenager in Jerusalem referred incorrectly to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s response to the killing of Muhammad Abu Khdeir. On the day of the killing, Mr. Netanyahu’s office issued a statement saying he had told his minister for internal security to quickly investigate the crime; it is not the case that “days of near silence” passed before he spoke about it.
match_headline: Four Horrific Killings

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the murderous gang violence in Honduras that is a factor in the recent wave of migration of Central American children to the United States misstated the amount of money that President Obama has requested from Congress to address the problem. It is $3.7 billion, not more than $4 billion.
match_headline: Fleeing Gangs, Children Head to U.S. Border

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article in some editions on Tuesday about the gathering of graffiti painters at a funeral home for the viewing for Jason Wulf, an early leader in New York City’s graffiti movement, misidentified the location in Brooklyn of a mural being created in tribute by an artist named RIME. It is in Bushwick, not at the 25th Street subway station in Sunset Park, where Mr. Wulf died.
match_headline: A Graffiti Titan With New York City Cred Is Remembered

text: An article on Monday about the death of a firefighter, Lt. Gordon Matthew Ambelas, in a burning Brooklyn high-rise apartment misspelled the surname of a boy the firefighter rescued in May. He is Mendy Gottlieb, not Gotlieb.
match_headline: Known for Rescues, a Firefighter Dies in a Brooklyn Blaze

text: An article on Wednesday about the effects of currency devaluation in Venezuela misstated an equity position held by Newfoundland Capital Management, a Brazilian hedge fund. While the hedge fund holds a short position in Brink’s stock, it does not hold a short position in Femsa stock. The article also misspelled the city in which Newfoundland Capital is based. It is São Paulo, Brazil, not São Paolo.
match_headline: Profits Vanish in Venezuela After Currency Devaluation

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Participant Media’s effort to measure the social impact of its films referred incorrectly to the availability of methodologies used to create an index for gauging that impact. The general methodologies being developed by the Media Impact Project, which is consulting on the index, will be available to the public; the specific methodologies used for the index will not be.
match_headline: Participant Index Seeks to Determine Why One Film Spurs Activism, While Others Falter

text: An article on Wednesday about the Wessen Lawn Tennis Club in Pontiac, Mich., misstated part of the name of the school at which Bill Massie, the club’s owner, is the architect-in-residence. It is the Cranbrook Academy of Art, not the Cranbrook School.
match_headline: At a New Michigan Club, a Touch of Wimbledon at Members’ Feet

text: An article on Monday about the trial to determine whether Rochelle Sterling acted legally in seizing control of the Los Angeles Clippers from her husband, Donald, and then selling the team to Steve Ballmer misstated his former title at Microsoft. He was chief executive, not chairman.
match_headline: Sterling Case Will Examine Role of a Doctor Who Evaluated Him

text: An article on Thursday about the five goals in 29 minutes that Germany scored in its 7-1 victory over Brazil in the World Cup semifinals on Tuesday misstated, in some editions, the year that Moacir Barbosa, the goalkeeper for Brazil in its loss to Uruguay in the 1950 World Cup final, died. It was 2000, not 2002. The article also misspelled, in some copies, the given name of the player who set up Germany’s third goal. He is Mesut Özil, not Meszut.
match_headline: 29 Minutes That Shook Brazil

text: An article on July 3 about a report from the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board on the National Security Agency’s use of Internet connections in the United States to monitor foreigners communicating with one another abroad misstated the name of the law that provides judicial and congressional oversight of foreign intelligence surveillance activities. It is the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, not the Federal Intelligence Surveillance Act.
match_headline: U.S. Privacy Panel Backs N.S.A.’s Internet Tapping

text: An article on Monday about Domenic M. Recchia Jr., who is challenging Representative Michael G. Grimm for his Congressional seat, misspelled the surname of a man who said he was a longtime supporter of Mr. Grimm. He is Robert Koeth, not Kowth.
match_headline: Staten Island’s Tough-Guy Congressman Faces Somebody His Own Size

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about AbbVie’s increased bid for Shire misidentified the pills shown. The pills were amphetamine salts, a generic form of Adderall XR; they were not Adderall XR.
match_headline: U.S. Drug Maker AbbVie Increases Bid for Shire, as Cost of Moving Abroad Rises

text: An article on Friday about the Emmy nominations omitted a nominee for best actress in a comedy series. In addition to Amy Poehler (“Parks and Recreation”), Melissa McCarthy (“Mike and Molly”), Edie Falco (“Nurse Jackie”), Lena Dunham (“Girls”) and Taylor Schilling (“Orange Is the New Black”), Julia Louis-Dreyfus was nominated for her role in “Veep.”
match_headline: Emmy Nominations Cross a Few Lines

text: An article in some editions on July 4 about a deadly explosion on the Upper East Side in 1914 misstated the name of the organization to which the police linked the bombers. It was the Industrial Workers of the World, not the International Workers of the World.
match_headline: 100 Years Later, Scar Remains From a Strike’s Fatal Legacy in Manhattan

text: An article on Wednesday about waterfront development in East Providence, R.I., misstated the location of the Washington Bridge and the location of the Kettle Point project. The bridge straddles the Seekonk River, not the Providence River. The Kettle Point project is near the East Bay Bike Path, not the East Providence bike path.
match_headline: East Providence Works to Develop Its Waterfront

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Thursday of an exhibition about the choreographer Trisha Brown’s dances, on Governors Island, misstated part of the name of the organization whose arts center houses the exhibition. It is the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council, not Center.
match_headline: Beacons of Creativity, Flung From Rooftops

text: An obituary on Friday about Eileen Ford, who created the Ford Models agency with her husband, Jerry, misstated in some copies the name of the hospital where she died. It is Morristown Memorial Hospital, not Morristown Hospital.
match_headline: Eileen Ford, Grande Dame of the Modeling Industry, Dies at 92

text: An article on Saturday about the re-election bid by the Arizona attorney general, Tom Horne, quoted incorrectly from his comments about voter reaction to his successful legal defense of an Arizona law that made proof of United States citizenship a requirement for voter registration. He said, “They know I’m the only official to have had success fighting against federal government overreach,” not, “They know I’m the only federal official” to have done so.
ref_headline: They know I’m the only official to have had success fighting against federal government overreach,
match_headline: Legal Woes Pose Hurdles for Attorney General Tom Horne of Arizona in Campaign

text: An article on Friday about the 40th anniversary of the opening of an F.B.I. field office in Jackson, Miss., misstated the day of an event commemorating its opening. It was on Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: F.B.I. Honors Office Opened Amid Struggle for Civil Rights

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about how the Justice Department reached a settlement with Citigroup over troubled mortgage securities misidentified, in some copies, who had refused to grant an extension to the bank in negotiation talks. The refusal came from Tony West and Geoffrey Graber, both of the Justice Department, not from Theodore Wells Jr., a lawyer who represents Citigroup, and Mr. Graber.
match_headline: From Benghazi to the Boardroom: The Road to the $7 Billion Citigroup Settlement

text: An article on Saturday about a federal district court ruling that rejected arguments from a bond insurer that it was entitled to casino revenue in Detroit described incorrectly a request from the judge overseeing the city’s bankruptcy for a legal brief from the United States attorney general. He is asking whether Chapter 9 bankruptcy is unconstitutional if it impairs the claims of property owners whose land has been seized under eminent domain or the demands for compensation from people injured in confrontations with the police, not whether it is unconstitutional if it allows cuts to public workers’ pensions.
match_headline: Federal Judge Rules That Detroit Is Entitled to Revenue From Casinos

text: An article on April 28 about New York’s tech scene referred incorrectly to MongoDB, a company in the city. MongoDB is a database company, not a cloud services firm. This correction was delayed because an initial message pointing out the error was overlooked until a message was sent to an editor.
match_headline: Despite Big Ambitions, New York’s Tech Scene Is Still Starting Up

text: An article on Sunday about a Ukrainian government attack on rebel positions that left five civilians dead in Marinka, a farm town in eastern Ukraine, misstated the direction of Marinka in relation to Donetsk. It is southwest of Donetsk, not southeast.
match_headline: Civilians Pay a Price for Gains of Ukraine Forces

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Saturday about a United Nations Refugee Agency appeal for more funding to address the refugee crisis in South Sudan referred incorrectly to the 715,000 refugees cited by the agency in its statement. That is the number expected by year’s end, more than double the previous estimate. It is not the number of South Sudanese who have already fled.
match_headline: South Sudan: Refugee Crisis Worsens

text: An article on July 8 about the problems that Ukrainian farmers and businessmen have experienced since Russia seized the Black Sea peninsula of Crimea from Ukraine in March misspelled the surname of a publicist for Skvortsovo, a Crimean food company. He is Gennadi V. Potapenko, not Potabenko.
match_headline: Aid Elusive, Crimea Farms Face Hurdles

text: An article on Monday about efforts to establish a nonprofit funeral service on Nantucket, Mass., misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a state senator who co-sponsored a measure exempting the service from two regulations governing funeral homes. He is Daniel Wolf, not Wolfe.
match_headline: Even on Nantucket, a Funeral Home Is a Luxury

text: An article on Monday on debt-settlement companies pursuing student-loan borrowers referred imprecisely to the employment status of recent college graduates. More than half are unemployed or have low-paying jobs that do not require a college degree. It is not the case that more than half of college graduates are unemployed.
match_headline: Companies That Offer Help With Student Loans Are Often Predatory, Officials Say

text: An obituary in some copies on Sunday about Arthur J. Walker, a retired Navy officer who was convicted on espionage charges in 1985, misstated the name of a newspaper that interviewed him last year. It is The Virginian-Pilot, not The Virginia-Pilot.
match_headline: Arthur J. Walker, Part of Family Espionage Ring, Dies at 79

text: An obituary on Saturday about the newspaper editor and political aide John Seigenthaler misstated the location of the district represented by Representative Joe L. Evins, whose retirement led Mr. Seigenthaler to urge Al Gore to run for Congress. It was near Nashville; it did not include Nashville.
match_headline: John Seigenthaler, Editor and Aide to Politicians, Dies at 86

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about two recent spy cases in Germany that have strained relations with the United States and revived memories of Cold War espionage misidentified, in some editions, the place that John le Carré described in the title of his novel “A Small Town in Germany.” It was Bonn, the West German capital, not Berlin. Because of another editing error, the article also misstated, in some editions, the value, in dollars, of what one of the men suspected of spying for the Americans received, according to German news accounts, for handing over documents. It was about $34,000, not $18,400.
match_headline: Behind German Spy Cases, Twists Worthy of Films

text: An article on Saturday about Adm. Michelle J. Howard, the first female four-star admiral in the history of the Navy, misstated the year women were first admitted to a United States service academy. It was 1974, not 1976. (Women were admitted to the Merchant Marine Academy in 1974. Women were admitted to the Military Academy, the Naval Academy, the Air Force Academy and the Coast Guard Academy in 1976.)
match_headline: A Four-Star Female Admiral Makes History for the Navy

text: An article on April 3 about the trial of a Queens doctor who was accused of knowingly prescribing painkillers to people who were abusing them misstated the given name of a patient who died. He was Joseph Haeg, not John. This correction was delayed because the error was not discovered until July 9, when the patient’s name was repeated during closing arguments.
match_headline: At Trial, Queens Doctor Is Accused of Recklessly Prescribing Drugs

text: An article on Tuesday about comments by Mario Draghi, president of the European Central Bank, regarding the likelihood of asset bubbles in the eurozone, misstated, in some editions, where he spoke. He addressed members of the European Parliament at a meeting in Strasbourg, France, not in Brussels.
match_headline: Draghi Sees No Risk of Eurozone Bubbles

text: An article on Tuesday about Volkswagen’s decision to build sport utility vehicles at its plant in Chattanooga, Tenn., erroneously attributed a distinction to the plant. Volkswagen opened its first American plant in Westmoreland County, Pa., in 1978; the Chattanooga plant was not its first in this country. (The Pennsylvania plant closed in 1988.)
match_headline: Volkswagen to Add S.U.V. Line to Chattanooga Plant

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the 10th stage of the Tour de France misstated the nationality of Thibaut Pinot, who finished second in the stage. He is from France, not Spain.
match_headline: Another Favorite Crashes Out of Tour

text: An obituary on Monday about the conductor Lorin Maazel misstated the reason the conductor Serge Koussevitzky invited Mr. Maazel to Tanglewood in the summer of 1951. It was to conduct the student orchestra there, not the Boston Symphony Orchestra.
match_headline: Lorin Maazel, an Intense and Enigmatic Conductor, Dies at 84

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the revamping of Time Warner that made it an attractive takeover target misspelled, in some copies, the given name of the company’s chief executive. He is Jeffrey L. Bewkes, not Jeffery.
match_headline: Time Warner Chief’s Turnaround Effort Opened the Door to Fox’s Bid

text: An article on Wednesday about Yahoo’s quarterly earnings misstated the multiple by which the expected valuation of Alibaba, in which Yahoo holds a substantial stake, is expected to exceed Yahoo’s own valuation. It is more than four times Yahoo’s valuation, not more than five times.
match_headline: Slump in Advertising Sales Dragged Quarterly Revenue Down at Yahoo

text: An article on Wednesday about the growing number and popularity of flavored electronic cigarettes rendered incorrectly the name of a website that sells e-cigarettes. It is Viking Vapor, not Viking Vapors.
match_headline: E-Cigarette Makers Are in an Arms Race for Exotic Vapor Flavors

text: An article on Wednesday about Italy’s growing reliance on aid from corporations and international sources to preserve national treasures referred imprecisely to the 25 million euro (about $34 million) refurbishment of the Colosseum in Rome. Part of that money has been spent on the facade, not all of it.
match_headline: Corporate Medicis to the Rescue

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the Praemium Imperiale International Arts Awards from the Japan Art Association erroneously included the Zinsou Foundation, which supports contemporary African art, among the winners. It won the Grant for Young Artists, another award from the association.
match_headline: Steven Holl and Athol Fugard among Winners of Praemium Imperiale Awards

text: Because of an editing error, an art review last Friday about the expansion and renovation of the Sterling and Francine Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Mass., misstated part of the title of an exhibition on display. It is “Cast for Eternity: Ancient Ritual Bronzes From the Shanghai Museum,” not “Annual Ritual Bronzes.”
ref_headline: Cast for Eternity: Ancient Ritual Bronzes From the Shanghai Museum,
match_headline: A Place of Serene Excitement, Inside and Out

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the Conceptual artist On Kawara misstated part of the name of the Paris gallery where he had his first solo show of time-related works. It is Galerie Yvon Lambert, not Galerie Yves Lambert.
match_headline: On Kawara, Artist Who Found Elegance in Every Day, Dies at 81

text: An article on June 30 about an Israeli mother and a Palestinian mother whose sons had both been killed referred imprecisely to the location of Nof Ayalon, which straddles a 1949 armistice line. Although that line generally divides Israel from the West Bank, in the area that includes Nof Ayalon there is a sliver of no man’s land that has a separate status. The same imprecise reference appeared in an article on June 17 about a debate, in the days after three Israeli teenagers had been kidnapped and killed, over activities by settlers that could put them in danger.
match_headline: After West Bank Kidnapping, 2 Mothers Embody a Divide

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Friday about two deaths at Graceland Too, a museum of Elvis Presley memorabilia in Holly Springs, Miss., misstated, in some editions, the year that the photo of the museum’s proprietor, Paul McLeod, was taken. It was 2012, not 2007.
match_headline: Two Lives Collide, and End, at an Elvis Shrine

text: An article on Thursday about Collector’s Night, an annual display of personal collections in Brooklyn, misstated the first presidential election year from which one collector, Jon Cruz, has a pin. It was 1896, not 1894. (There was no presidential election in 1894.)
match_headline: Where Cockroach Legs and Snow White Have Something in Common
