text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the sale of a New Jersey apartment complex amid a dispute involving the Wilf family and its partners, Ada Reichmann of Toronto and her brother Josef Halpern, contained several errors. Another former partner, Ms. Reichmann’s brother Abraham Halpern, is alive, not dead. A lower court ruled in favor of the Wilfs, not the partners, before having its decision overturned by an appellate court in 2006. And Judge Deanne M. Wilson of New Jersey Superior Court ultimately awarded Ms. Reichmann and Josef Halpern $103 million, not $110 million.
match_headline: New Jersey Apartment Complex Is Sold, but a Dispute Continues

text: An article on Friday about efforts by India’s new prime minister, Narendra Modi, to modernize the poor city of Varanasi as a case study for his policies misspelled the surname of an aide to Varanasi’s mayor. He is Raj Kumar Agrawal, not Agarwal.
match_headline: India Aims to Make Forlorn City a Model for Revival

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about families from Asia who travel to New York City for summer camp referred incorrectly, in some editions, to Bali. It is a province of Indonesia, not a country.
match_headline: Asian Families Travel a Long Way for Summer Camp

text: A chart accompanying an article on Friday about Microsoft’s plans to lay off 18,000 employees used an outdated figure for the company’s total workforce. As the article correctly stated, Microsoft now employs 127,000 people, not 100,000. An updated chart is online at nytimes.com/technology .
match_headline: Microsoft to Lay Off Thousands, Most From Nokia Unit

text: An article on Thursday about the 11th stage of the Tour de France misstated the number of stages Tony Gallopin has won in this year’s Tour. His victory on Wednesday was his first, not his second.
match_headline: Refusing to Quit, American Is Surrounded by Cheers After a Lonely Finish

text: An article on Thursday about the new Cleveland Cavaliers basketball coach, David Blatt, misstated the given name of the Philadelphia 76ers coach. He is Brett Brown, not Brent.
match_headline: International Coach Prepares for N.B.A. Debut

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article last Sunday about Lionel Messi’s complicated relationship with Argentina misstated the statistics of Diego Maradona, another Argentine soccer star, at the 1986 World Cup. As the article correctly noted, he scored or assisted on 10 of Argentina’s 14 goals in that tournament; he did not score 10 goals.
match_headline: Adept? Yes. Adored? Not Yet.

text: A listing in the New Jersey  Calendar in some editions last Sunday about performances at the Bananas Comedy Club in Hasbrouck Heights misspelled the surname of a comedian who is to perform on July 25 and 26. He is Dan Naturman, not Nauterman.
match_headline: Events in New Jersey for July 13-19, 2014

text: An article on July 6 about Lanai, Hawaii, misstated the century in which James Dole bought the island and began planting pineapples. It was the early part of the 20th century, not the 18th. And the article misstated the time period that the entrepreneur David Murdock controlled the island. It was 27 years, not 22.
match_headline: Exploring Lanai, Hawaii, Rough Roads to Resorts

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the 36 Hours column on July 6, about the Berkshires, misidentified the location from which one of three photographs was taken. The center photograph, of Lake Pontoosac, was taken from near the lake’s southern shore; it was not taken from Herman Melville’s home, which is several miles away.
match_headline: 36 Hours in the Berkshires

text: An article last Sunday about the revival of downtown Las Vegas misstated the year that Zappos, the dot-com shoe dealer, moved there and revitalized the neighborhood. It was in 2013, not 2012. In addition, the article misspelled the name of a street in the city. It is Fremont Street, not Freemont.
match_headline: Downtown Las Vegas Jumps Again

text: A picture in an entry with the “On the Market” feature last Sunday, about a property listed at $729,000 in Brooklyn, was published in error. It showed the outdoor space for a property listed in West Chelsea for $1.155 million. A slide show online used the photo properly.
match_headline: On the Market in the Region

text: An article in the Mutual Funds & E.T.F.s Report, Part 2 of this section last Sunday, about mutual funds that registered strong performance in the second quarter, misstated a strategy of Daniel Peris, co-manager of the Federated Strategic Value Dividend fund. He aims to buy stocks that his fund can own for as long as they make sense for the portfolio, basing his selections on his three- to five-year projections for dividend growth; he does not aim “to buy stocks that his fund can hold for three to five years.”
ref_headline: to buy stocks that his fund can hold for three to five years.
match_headline: Sticking to Their Guns, Fund Managers Reaped Big Returns

text: An article last Sunday about sobriety coaches for affluent women misstated part of the name of an organization to help addicts started by Deborah Magaldi, who hired a live-in sober companion. It is Hired Power, not Powers.
match_headline: Mothers Find a Helping Hand in Sobriety Coaches

text: An article last Sunday about the Egyptian street artist Ganzeer misidentified the nationality of a curator who recently worked with him on a mural in Bahrain. Alexandra Stock is Swiss-American, not Egyptian, though she worked in Cairo from 2007 to 2012. Because of an editing error, the article misspelled part of the name of an alternative space in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, through which Ganzeer sells his work. It is the Booklyn Artists Alliance, not Brooklyn.
match_headline: Hieroglyphics That Won’t Be Silenced

text: An article last Sunday about Morrissey and his new album, “World Peace,” misstated when his last album was released. “Years of Refusal” came out in 2009, not 2007.
match_headline: Revisiting His Arsenal of Misanthropy

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Stephen McKinley Henderson, who is starring in Stephen Adly Guirgis’s new play, “Between Riverside and Crazy,” misstated part of the name of the college where Mr. Henderson teaches. It is the University at Buffalo, which is part of the State University of New York system; it is not the University of Buffalo.
match_headline: This Time, the Main Attraction

text: A chart in The One-Page Magazine on July 13 about camping in national parks misidentified the location of Yellowstone. It is primarily in Wyoming, not in California.

An article on Thursday about four Palestinian boys, cousins with the surname Bakr, who were killed by an Israeli strike on a beach in the Gaza Strip, misidentified, in some editions, the boy who was an only son with seven sisters. He was Ahed Bakr, not Mohammad.
match_headline: Boys Drawn to Gaza Beach, and Into Center of Mideast Strife

text: An article on Thursday about opposition around the country to housing young migrants from Central America misidentified the California county that includes Murrieta, where protests have occurred. It is Riverside County, not San Diego County.
match_headline: Towns Fight to Avoid Taking In Migrant Minors

text: An article on Sunday about the tunnel network that has become a key element of Israel’s campaign in the Gaza Strip because the tunnels have long been used by Hamas militants to attack Israelis misstated the rank of Gilad Shalit, an Israeli soldier who was captured by Hamas in Gaza in 2006, and the number of years he was a prisoner. He was a staff sergeant, not a lieutenant; and he was held for a little more than five years, not six.
match_headline: Despite Israeli Push in Gaza, Hamas Fighters Slip Through Tunnels

text: An article on Thursday about the arrests of two track workers in a subway crash last week in Moscow in which 22 people died overstated the extent of free entry to the subway system on the day after the accident, a gesture to anxious riders. Entry was free only at stations near the site of the accident, not throughout the system.
match_headline: A Tiny Wire, and a Big Train Wreck

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the expressions of sorrow, anger and disbelief in Malaysia over the loss of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 over Ukraine carried an erroneous dateline in some editions. The article was reported and written in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia — not in Hong Kong.
match_headline: With Grief on Top of Grief, Malaysians Are Tested on Flight 370’s Lessons

text: An article on Thursday about the political relationship between Gov. Jerry Brown of California and Representative Kevin McCarthy, the House majority leader, misstated, in some editions, the year Mr. McCarthy was elected to Congress from California. It was 2006, not 2007.
match_headline: Political Duel for California Governor Spans Nation

text: An article on Monday about the strategies of smaller cable companies to survive as bigger ones consolidate misstated the current valuation of one smaller cable group, Discovery Communications, in some copies. It is nearly $30 billion, not $19.5 billion.
match_headline: Smaller Cable Networks Plan Their Survival Under the Feet of Giants

text: A picture caption on May 23 with an art review of an exhibition of sculptures by Anicka Yi, using information from a publicist, misstated the title of the work shown. It is “Fever and Spear,” not “Fear and Spear.” This correction was delayed because the error was called to the attention of editors only last week.
match_headline: Anicka Yi: ‘Divorce’

text: An obituary on Monday about the author Curt Gentry misstated the year a plane flown by the American spy Francis Gary Powers, with whom Mr. Gentry collaborated on a book, was shot down in Russia. It was 1960, not 1962.
match_headline: Curt Gentry, 83, Co-Author of ‘Helter Skelter,’ Dies

text: An article on Saturday about the flight by Christians and others from the Iraqi city of Mosul after an ultimatum by the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, the militant group that overran Mosul in June, referred incorrectly to the Mandeans. They are a Gnostic community that reveres John the Baptist; they are not Christians.
match_headline: ISIS Forces Last Iraqi Christians to Flee Mosul

text: An article on Friday about the new FIFA rankings of national men’s soccer teams misstated, in some copies, the circumstances of Colombia’s loss to Brazil in the quarterfinals at the World Cup. It was in regulation time, not in a penalty-kick shootout.
match_headline: U.S. Slips in FIFA Rankings Despite Its World Cup Effort

text: An article last Wednesday about the dietary habits of Chrissy Teigen, a fashion model, misstated part of the title of a book by Leela Punyaratabandhu, a Thai chef whose recipe for rice soup with meatballs is a favorite of Ms. Teigen’s. As noted in the accompanying recipe, it is “Simple Thai Food,” not “Simple Thai Cooking.”
match_headline: Hearty Cravings, Sometimes Unfulfilled

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor James Garner referred incorrectly to a production of “The Caine Mutiny Court-Martial” in which he appeared early in his career. Charles Laughton directed that production; he did not star in it. The obituary also omitted a word from an excerpt of a speech Mr. Garner delivered in the movie “The Americanization of Emily.” He said, “And it’s always the war widows who lead the Memorial Day parades” — not “always the widows.”
match_headline: James Garner, Witty, Handsome Leading Man, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Monday about Dr. Albert J. Stunkard, a pioneer of eating-disorder research, misidentified the man who inspired his interest in Buddhism. He was the author D. T. Suzuki, not the Buddhist monk Shunryu Suzuki.
match_headline: Dr. Albert J. Stunkard, Destigmatizer of Fat, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on July 14 about the Indian actress Zohra Sehgal misidentified the director of the movie “The Courtesans of Bombay,” in which she appeared. It was directed by Ismail Merchant, not by James Ivory. The obituary also misstated the kind of dance Ms. Sehgal studied and performed early in her career. It was modern dance, not ballet.
match_headline: Zohra Sehgal, Beloved and Prolific Indian Actress, Dies at 102

text: An obituary on Monday about the swimmer Bill Mulliken misstated the given name of his son, who survives him. He is David, not John.
match_headline: Bill Mulliken, Who Swam to Olympic Gold in 1960, Dies at 74

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the television producer Madeline Amgott misstated, in some editions, the current name of the newspaper that was known as The San Diego Union when she worked there. It is now U-T San Diego, not The San Diego U-T. And because of an editing error, the obituary misstated, in some editions, the year of a debate between New York Democratic senatorial candidates that Ms. Amgott moderated. It was 1980, not 1966.
match_headline: Madeline Amgott, Television Producer, Dies at 92

text: An obituary last Wednesday about the biographer and political scientist James MacGregor Burns misstated, in some copies, part of the title of one of his books. It is “The Power to Lead: The Crisis of the American Presidency” (not “The Crisis of the Presidency”).
ref_headline: The Power to Lead: The Crisis of the American Presidency
match_headline: James MacGregor Burns, Scholar of Presidents and Leadership, Dies at 95

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the effect an influx of South Americans is having on the reinvention of Miami misstated the relationship of the wealthy real estate developer Jorge Pérez to the new Pérez Art Museum Miami. The museum was named for Mr. Pérez; he is not its founder. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Influx of South Americans Drives Miami’s Reinvention

text: An article on Wednesday about David Perdue’s victory in the runoff in the Republican Senate race in Georgia misstated the name of a volunteer organization that was run by Michelle Nunn, the Democratic Senate candidate. It is Points of Light, not Points of Lights.
match_headline: Georgia Republicans Choose David Perdue as Their Senate Candidate

text: Because of an editing error, the Fort Worth Journal article on Monday about efforts by Mayor Betsy Price to encourage residents to ride bikes for exercise misidentified the country in which this year’s Tour de France began. The first three stages were in England, not in France.
match_headline: Want a Word With the Mayor? You’ll Find Her in the Bike Convoy

text: An article on Friday about newly released federal forecast maps for New York City that raise the likelihood of earthquakes but also lower the risk they pose to tall buildings misstated part of the name of the agency that produced the report. It is the United States Geological Survey, not the United States Geodetic Survey.
match_headline: U.S. Raises Threat of Quake but Lowers Risk for Towers

text: An article last Thursday about David Rose, a researcher at the M.I.T. Media Lab who applies technology to simple household objects, misidentified the publisher of his new book “Enchanted Objects: Design, Human Desire and the Internet of Things.” It is Scribner, not Simon & Schuster. The article also omitted part of the name of the school in which Mr. Rose led an enchanted-objects workshop. It is the Copenhagen Institute of Interaction Design, not the Copenhagen Institute of Design.
ref_headline: Enchanted Objects: Design, Human Desire and the Internet of Things.
match_headline: Putting Magic in the Mundane

text: An article on July 3 about the way that tenants in a Brooklyn apartment building decorate the niches in their homes misspelled the surname of one of the couples. They are Terry and John Janetatos, not Janatos.
match_headline: Our Niches, Our Shelves

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the former New York Times reporter Kenneth B. Noble referred incorrectly to the Liberian leader Samuel K. Doe, whom Mr. Noble wrote about during his posting in Africa. He was the first of the country’s leaders who was not descended from freed American slaves; he was not a descendant of freed American slaves.
match_headline: Kenneth Noble, Ex-Times Reporter, Is Dead at 60

text: An article on Tuesday about Ryan M. Pitts, a former Army staff sergeant who was awarded the Medal of Honor for defending a small outpost in the 2008 battle of Wanat in Afghanistan, described incorrectly how eight of nine soldiers died in the conflict. Five of the soldiers died during the initial assault on the outpost, and another three were killed when they came to the outpost as reinforcements; it was not eight of the original nine soldiers who were defending the outpost who were killed. (A ninth soldier at the main base died at the start of the battle.) The article also misstated the number of wounded in the battle. It was 27, including Sergeant Pitts — not 28.
match_headline: Soldier Who Held His Post Is Awarded Medal of Honor

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about Dr. Demetre Daskalakis’s appointment as an assistant health commissioner in New York City omitted part of the name of the bureau that he heads. It is the Bureau of H.I.V./AIDS Prevention and Control, not the Bureau of H.I.V./AIDS Prevention. The article also misstated the bureau’s budget. It is $200 million, not $20 million.
match_headline: Credibility Among Gay Men Gives Leverage to New York City’s New Chief of H.I.V. Prevention

text: An article on Thursday about new recalls by General Motors misstated the reason for an earlier recall of the 2014 Chevrolet Impala. That model was recalled in June because some vehicles might have a “superhold” joint fastener that was not torqued to specification, not because the ignition could shut off while the car was in motion. (The ignition recall involved the 2014 Chevrolet Impala Limited, a version of an earlier production model manufactured only for rental fleets.)
match_headline: New General Motors Recall Covers 800,000 More Vehicles

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the Sports of The Times column, about a group of men in their 90s who set world records at the USA Track & Field Masters Outdoor Championships, misstated the age of one of the men, Roy Englert, in some copies. He is 91, not 92.
match_headline: Track Team Is Peerless and, Seemingly, Ageless

text: Because of an editing error, on article on Thursday about African migrants who try to enter Europe by climbing over the tall fences in the Spanish enclaves of Melilla and Ceuta in North Africa misstated the number of Cameroonians who tried to storm a border fence on May 28. It was 2,000, not 200.
match_headline: At a Spanish Border, a Coordinated Scramble

text: A map on Friday with an article about the crash of an Air Algérie jetliner in Mali mislabeled the body of water off the coast of Nigeria in some editions. It is the Gulf of Guinea, not the Pacific Ocean. And the article misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the airline that lost a plane over eastern Ukraine on July 17. It is Malaysia Airlines, not Malaysia Airways.
match_headline: Weather Suspected in Air Algérie Plane Wreck; 116 Are Feared Dead

text: An article on Friday about a decision by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to allow a tuberculosis laboratory to reopen quoted incorrectly from comments by Thomas Skinner, a C.D.C. spokesman. He said, “any group member wanting to visit a lab (even unannounced) and speak to any staff member working in the lab will be permitted to do so.” He did not say, “speaking in the lab.”
ref_headline: any group member wanting to visit a lab (even unannounced) and speak to any staff member working in the lab will be permitted to do so.
match_headline: C.D.C. Says Tuberculosis Lab, Shut Amid Exposure Scare, Can Continue Its Work

text: An article on Friday about the last mountain stage of the Tour de France erroneously attributed a distinction to the former Belgian cycling star Eddy Merckx from the 1974 race. Merckx was the last overall winner to win four non-time-trial stages in a single Tour, not the last rider to do so. (Marcel Kittel won four last year.) The article also misstated the given name of the owner of the Tinkoff-Saxo team. He is Oleg Tinkov, not Igor.
match_headline: With Lead Extended, It’s All Downhill to Paris

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the Texas Rangers’ struggles this season misstated one of the years the team played in the World Series. Besides 2011, the Rangers were in the World Series in 2010, but not in 2012.
match_headline: Rangers’ Numerous Injuries Shelve a Promising Season

text: An article last Sunday about Daktronics, one of the largest makers of sports video displays, contained an outdated reference to Fulham, the English soccer team that shares an owner with the N.F.L.’s Jacksonville Jaguars, who have two new scoreboards from Daktronics. Fulham was relegated to the Football League Championship after last season; it is no longer in the Premier League.
match_headline: New Dimension in Scoreboard Watching

text: An entry in the Newly Released box with the Video column last Sunday about “The Twilight Zone: Essential Episodes” misstated part of the name of a “Twilight Zone” episode. It is “The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street,” not Main Street.
match_headline: A Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Burst

text: Because of an editing error, the Exclusive column last Sunday, about the listing for sale of an Amagansett home in the Devon Colony, omitted the affiliation of the brokers for the property, Cornelia Dodge and John Scott Thomas. They are agents with Halstead Property.
match_headline: A Classic Hamptons Cottage for $13 Million

text: An article and a map on July 6 about wineries in southern Oregon misspelled part of the name of a mountain seen from Dancin Vineyards in the Rogue Valley. It is Mount McLoughlin, not McCloughlin.
match_headline: Only Hours From Napa, but a World Away

text: An article on July 6 about a veterinarian who treats zoo animals misidentified an elephant as Asian. The elephant was African.
match_headline: Zoo Animals and Their Discontents

text: A chart in The One-Page Magazine on July 13 about NPR personalities misspelled the given name of the host of “Fresh Air.” She is Terry Gross, not Terri.

An article on July 13 about a dispute over building a modern home in a historic district in Raleigh, N.C., misstated when the building permit for the house was issued. It was last October, not September.
match_headline: Don’t Like Your Neighbors’ House? Sue Them.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on July 17 about new sanctions imposed by the United States on Russia to retaliate for its intervention in Ukraine misstated, in some editions, the day that a Ukrainian military transport plane was downed in Luhansk, Ukraine, an act for which Ukraine blamed Russia. It occurred on July 14, not on June 14.
match_headline: Raising Stakes on Russia, U.S. Adds Sanctions

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the effectiveness of acetaminophen in treating back pain misstated the source of a quotation by Dr. Bart W. Koes, a professor of general practice in the Netherlands. It was in an interview — not in an editorial in The Lancet, a medical journal — that he said, “The fact that it’s no more effective than placebo does not mean that it doesn’t work for a given patient.”
ref_headline: The fact that it’s no more effective than placebo does not mean that it doesn’t work for a given patient.
match_headline: Acetaminophen No Better Than Placebo for Back Pain

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the bribery trial of Daniel J. Halloran, a former New York City councilman, misstated the title of Douglas Bloom, a prosecutor who cross-examined him. He is an assistant United States attorney, not an assistant district attorney.
match_headline: Former New York City Councilman in Bribe Case Cites Politics of Daily Life

text: An article on Friday about Jeremy Lin’s joining the Los Angeles Lakers misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the player who replaced Lin as the Houston Rockets’ point guard last season. He is Patrick Beverley, not Beverly.
match_headline: In Joining Lakers, Lin Narrows Focus and Sheds Status as a Sensation

text: Because of an editing error, a subheading on Tuesday with an article about home sleep studies misstated the surname of the chief medical officer for NovaSom, a company that produces a home sleep-test kit. As the article correctly noted, he is Dr. Michael Coppola, not Cooper.
match_headline: A Sleep Apnea Test Without a Night in the Hospital

text: An article on July 19 about the challenge facing the Netherlands as it tries to maintain close ties to Russia at a time of widespread grief and anger over the loss of 189 Dutch nationals on Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, which was shot down over Russian separatist territory in eastern Ukraine, referred incorrectly to a visit by Peter the Great to the Netherlands. It took place more than 300 years ago, not 400, and historians say that while he studied Dutch shipbuilding, there is no evidence that he bought ships there.
match_headline: The Netherlands, a Nation in Mourning but Mindful of Ties to Russia

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Iraqi leaders’ choosing a new president as part of an effort to bolster the government in its confrontation with a Sunni insurgency misstated the circumstances of remarks made by Brett McGurk, the deputy assistant secretary of state for Iran and Iraq. His remarks came in testimony to the House on Wednesday, not in an appearance before the Senate on Thursday.
match_headline: Iraq Picks New President to Confront Militant Threat

text: A picture caption on Monday with a review of Pam Tanowitz Dance, at Lincoln Center Out of Doors, misidentified the dance shown. It is “The Spectators” — not “Passagen,” the other work on the program.
match_headline: An Intricate Combination of Music and Movement

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a film review of “A Master Builder,” referred incorrectly to Wallace Shawn, the star and writer of the film, an adaptation of Ibsen’s “The Master Builder.” He is, of course, Mr. Shawn, not Mr. Wallace.
match_headline: A Power Broker’s World Comes Tumbling Down

text: An obituary on Saturday about Gene I. Maeroff, an author and former education reporter for The New York Times, misstated his wife’s given name. She is Joyce, not Nancy.
match_headline: Gene I. Maeroff, Education Reporter and Author, Dies at 75

text: An editorial on Sunday about letting the states decide whether to legalize marijuana misstated the number of states that permit some form of medical marijuana. It is 35, not 34. The number that have decriminalized marijuana was also incorrect. It is 18, not 17.
match_headline: Let States Decide on Marijuana

text: An article on July 22 about the strong possibility that Tampa, Fla., may lose its cigar industry misstated the number of years cigar factories have been in the city. It is 128 years, not 150. The error was repeated in the front-page headline and in the headline with the continuation of the article.
match_headline: After 128 Years of Rolling Them, Tampa Is Close to No Cigars

text: An article on Saturday about increased Russian involvement in the rebellion of separatist rebels in eastern Ukraine, even after the shooting down of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, referred incorrectly to Ukrainian accounts of Russian interventions. Ukrainian officials said Russian fighter jets and drones had flown into Ukrainian — not Russian — air space.
match_headline: Russia Steps Up Help for Rebels in Ukraine War

text: An article on Tuesday about the publication of an internal campaign document for the Senate race of Michelle Nunn, the Democratic nominee in Georgia, misidentified, in some copies, the organization that Internal Revenue Service filings show had indirectly assisted Islamic Relief USA, the American branch of an international charity. The filings concerned Points of Light, of which Ms. Nunn was chief executive; they were not about Hamas. (Islamic Relief USA has been accused of links to Hamas.)
match_headline: Georgia Democrat’s Senate Campaign Plan, Not Meant for Public Eyes, Is Published

text: An article on Thursday about the sentencing of William E. Rapfogel for stealing from the Metropolitan Council on Jewish Poverty, an organization he once oversaw, misstated, in one instance, the surname of the State Supreme Court justice who oversaw the case. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Justice Larry Stephen, not Stephens.
match_headline: Rapfogel Is Sentenced for Stealing From His Charity

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an article about the demolition of Friendship Baptist Church to make room for a new stadium for the Atlanta Falcons misstated the name of a school founded in the church’s basement in 1881. It was Atlanta Baptist Female Seminary — not Spelman College, which became the name of the school in 1924. And also because of an editing error, the picture credit misstated part of the name of the organization that provided the photograph showing the seminary in 1883. It was from the American Baptist Historical Society, not the Atlanta Baptist Historical Society.
match_headline: Saying Goodbye to Friendship

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Mets’ 3-2 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers referred incorrectly in some copies to the significance of Lucas Duda’s at-bat in the ninth inning. He represented the go-ahead run, not the tying run. (He went on to hit a two-run homer that won the game.)
match_headline: Mets Stun the Brewers With a Burst in the Ninth

text: A news analysis article on Saturday about off-season moves in the N.B.A. misidentified, in some copies, the hometown of forward Chris Bosh, who chose to remain with the Miami Heat rather than sign with a new team. It is Dallas, not Houston.
match_headline: Before Signing, Big Stars Seek a Prize Beyond Fortune and Glory

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Yankees’ 6-4 victory over the Toronto Blue Jays on Friday misstated, in some copies, the date of the Blue Jays’ last victory at Yankee Stadium coming into that game. It was Aug. 29, 2012 — not April 21, 2013. (The Blue Jays won at Yankee Stadium on Saturday.)
match_headline: The Faces Keep Changing, but the Yankees Just Keep Winning

text: Because of an editing error, schedule information on Friday with an art review of shows at three Manhattan galleries misstated the closing date of “From Pre-History to Post-Everything” at the Sean Kelly Gallery. It is Friday, Aug. 8, not this Friday, Aug. 1. The review misidentified the artist in the “More Material” show at Salon 94 Bowery who makes small malformed masks in glazed ceramic. She is Sylvie Auvray — not Sylvie Franquet, another artist whose work is in the show. And a picture caption with the review carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of work in the “More Material” show, which was curated by Duro Olowu, is by Jeff Elstone/Salon 94, New York — not by Duro Olowu, London.
match_headline: Clash of the Items, at a Gallery Near You

text: An article last Wednesday about bars that offer extensive selections of whiskey misidentified one such bar in Manhattan. It is the Flatiron Room, at 37 West 26th Street — not the Flatiron Lounge, at 37 West 19th Street.
match_headline: The Whiskey Bar Is Taking a Step Up

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about efforts by a former director of the Central Intelligence Agency, George J. Tenet, to orchestrate a rebuttal to a Senate Intelligence report that sharply criticizes the agency’s detention and interrogation program misidentified President Obama’s counterterrorism adviser during his first term. He is John O. Brennan — not Denis McDonough, who is Mr. Obama’s current chief of staff, and who earlier advised him on foreign policy and national security issues.
match_headline: Ex-Chief of C.I.A. Shapes Response to Detention Report

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with an article about small, growing restaurant chains that offer organic or locally sourced food misidentified the location of Tender Greens, a restaurant in California. The photograph showed the Tender Greens in West Hollywood, on Santa Monica Boulevard — not in Santa Monica, another of the chain’s locations.
match_headline: Hold the Regret? Fast Food Seeks Virtuous Side

text: An article on Wednesday about an announcement by Emily K. Rafferty, president of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, that she will retire next spring misstated the day of the announcement and of the ensuing speculation in the art world about her working relationship with Thomas P. Campbell, the Met’s director and chief executive. They occurred Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: President of the Metropolitan Museum of Art to Step Down

text: An obituary on Saturday about Alan C. Greenberg, who built Bear Stearns into a global investment banking powerhouse, described the firm’s collapse incorrectly. On the brink of failure, it was taken over by JP Morgan Chase in 2008. It did not go bankrupt.
match_headline: Alan C. Greenberg, 86, Dies; Led Bear Stearns in Good Times and Bad

text: An obituary on Saturday about the novelist Bel Kaufman referred incorrectly to her mother, Lala Rabinowitz Kaufman. She was the second oldest daughter of the writer Sholem Aleichem, not the eldest.
match_headline: Bel Kaufman, Who Told What School Was Really Like, Dies at 103

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the actor James Shigeta misstated, in some editions, the ethnic background of the characters in the movie “Flower Drum Song,” in which Mr. Shigeta starred. They are Chinese-Americans, not Japanese immigrants.
match_headline: James Shigeta, 85, Leading Man in ‘Flower Drum Song,’ Dies

text: An article on July 18 about the beginning of Israel’s ground invasion of the Gaza Strip after 10 days of an aerial bombardment campaign quoted incorrectly from a Twitter message by Peter Bouckaert of Human Rights Watch. He called for an end to illegal targeting, not “an end to the killing.”
match_headline: Israeli Military Invades Gaza, With Sights Set on Hamas Operations

text: An article on Wednesday about growing concern in Russia over President Vladimir V. Putin’s aggressive stance on Ukraine, which has led to more sanctions and strained relations with the West, misstated part of the name of the government newspaper that published a front-page article about the downing of a Malaysia Airlines flight over Ukraine on July 17. The paper is Rossiyskaya Gazeta, not Gazeta Russkaya.
match_headline: As Sanctions Pile Up, Russians’ Alarm Grows Over Putin’s Tactics

text: An article on Wednesday about demands among both parties in Congress that the Obama administration allow a vote on any agreement with Iran on its nuclear weapons program misstated, in some editions, the value of assets that Iran will have access to under an agreement. It is more than $2 billion, not more than $2 million.
match_headline: Lawmakers Voice Skepticism on Iran Nuclear Deal

text: An article on Thursday about the large number of candidates running for mayor of Oakland, Calif., misstated, in come copies, part of the name of an all-black motorcycle club whose members attended a campaign event for the current mayor, Jean Quan. It is the East Bay Dragons, not the Eastside Dragons.
match_headline: A Long Slate of Mayoral Candidates Hints at a Rapidly Changing Oakland

text: An article on Thursday about the corruption trial of former Gov. Bob McDonnell of Virginia and his wife misidentified, in some editions, the state that is home to Homestead Resort, where one of the McDonnell sons, Robert Ryan, played golf with Jonnie R. Williams Sr., the wealthy businessman who is the prosecution’s star witness. The resort is in Virginia, not in West Virginia.
match_headline: Businessman Says Former Virginia Governor’s Wife Sought Money

text: An article on July 24 about New York City officials’ inviting local cultural institutions to offer benefits like memberships or discounts to municipal ID cardholders misstated, in some copies, the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s annual membership income. It is just over $26 million, not about $16 million.
match_headline: New York City Asks Cultural Groups to Help Enhance Municipal IDs

text: An article on July 23 about young Americans stranded by a temporary halt on flights to and from Ben-Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv described incorrectly, in some editions, the location of the West Bank, where some Jewish Americans study at yeshivas during the summer. It is an occupied territory adjacent to Israel; it is not in Israel.
match_headline: Youth Group Stuck in Israel After Flights Are Halted

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a judge’s ruling that Rochelle Sterling had the authority to sell the Los Angeles Clippers after her husband, Donald, had been barred from the N.B.A. misstated part of the name of the court where the trial was held. It is Los Angeles County Superior Court, not California Superior Court. The article also misidentified, in some copies, the government agency with which Donald Sterling settled a housing discrimination suit. It is the United States Justice Department, not the Department of Housing.
match_headline: Donald Sterling Loses Bid to Block Sale of Clippers

text: An article on Thursday about Liverpool’s plans to replace the star forward Luis Suárez misstated, in some copies, the name of a statistical analysis website that gave Suárez an 8.43 rating for last season. It is WhoScored.com.
match_headline: Despite the Loss of a Star, Liverpool Is Hoping to Build on Its Success

text: An article on Friday about concerns over misuse of the prepaid cash card MoneyPak described one attribute of the card incorrectly. It can be used once to transfer cash; it cannot be reused.
match_headline: MoneyPak, a Popular Prepaid Money Card, Opens Path to Fraud Schemes

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about local Muslims who use the sighting of the moon to determine the beginning of the Eid al-Fitr holiday misspelled, in several instances, the surname of a Houston cleric who helped establish guidelines for the process in North America. As the article noted correctly elsewhere, he is Mufti Qamar ul Hasan, not Hassan. The article also misidentified the location of a mosque where a cleric said several members had reported seeing the moon. It is in Jersey City, not New York City.
match_headline: Moon Is Elusive Guide in Calculating Start of Islamic Holiday

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about osteopathic medicine misstates the number of applicants to D.O. schools last fall. There were about 16,500 — not over 144,000, which was the number of applications submitted. The article also misstates the time frame during which no new medical schools opened in the United States. It was 1983 to 2000, not 1980 to 2002. And because of an editing error, the article and an accompanying chart misstate the percentage of medical school graduates attending D.O. schools. It is 22 percent, not 28 percent.
match_headline: The D.O. Is in Now

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about law apprenticeships misspells the given name of a founder of the United Farm Workers union, which has trained lawyers through apprenticeships. She is Dolores Huerta, not Delores.
match_headline: The Lawyer’s Apprentice

text: An editorial on Thursday about the science on marijuana incorrectly stated that marijuana was the principal cause of more than 455,000 emergency room visits in 2011. It was found in combination with other drugs in roughly 327,000 cases and alone in 129,000 cases. It did not necessarily cause the emergency room visit.
match_headline: What Science Says About Marijuana

text: An article last Sunday about Israel’s agreeing to extend a temporary cease-fire in the Gaza Strip, even as Hamas rejected it, misstated the Palestinian death toll in Gaza from July 8 until Saturday, July 26. At that point, the total had topped 1,000, not 1,100, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. And the article, using information from the ministry, also misstated the number of bodies recovered from the rubble during a lull in fighting on July 26. There were 117 bodies recovered, not 147.
match_headline: Israel Extends Cease-Fire in Gaza, a U.N. Request Rejected by Hamas

text: An article last Sunday about Chris Pratt, who stars in the new movie “Guardians of the Galaxy,” misstated part of the name of the disease his late father had for 20 years. It was multiple sclerosis, not muscular sclerosis.
match_headline: Goofy Guy Takes a Galactic Leap

text: An article on July 6 about the composer and record producer Craig Leon, who has recently rerecorded some of his early works, misstated the licensing status of his album “Nommos,” which was rereleased last year by Superior Viaduct. Superior licensed the 1981 “Nommos” from Concord Music Group, which is the legal rights holder. It was not “unauthorized,” even though Mr. Leon said he did not give the project his blessing.
match_headline: 30 Years Later, a Cosmos Reanimated

text: An article last Sunday about the British architect Norman Foster and the four big projects his firm is working on in Manhattan misstated the size of one of them, 425 Park Avenue, an office building that is currently under construction. It is to be 47 stories, not 25. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The article also misstated the significance of his project at 50 United Nations Plaza. It is Mr. Foster’s first residential high-rise in the United States, not his first-ever residential building in the United States.
match_headline: An Architect Gets Busy

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the Hunt column last Sunday, about Julius Towers’s search for an apartment in Manhattan, misstated the size of the Bradhurst Court on West 145th Street, one building he considered. It is seven stories, not nine.
match_headline: Lively Surroundings for Man and Beasts

text: An article last Sunday about emoji, icons used for shorthand communication, misspelled the name of a blog on the subject. It is Emojinalysis, not Emojanalysis.
match_headline: The Emoji Have Won the Battle of Words

text: An article last Sunday about the Bonavista Peninsula, part of the island of Newfoundland, misstated the surname of a guide with Sea of Whales Adventures at one point. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Kris Prince, not Price. In addition, the article misstated the name of a village there, and an accompanying map labeled incorrectly the province that includes the island of Newfoundland. The village is British Harbour, not English Harbour, and it is Newfoundland and Labrador, not just Newfoundland.
match_headline: Ghost Towns, Puffins and Unspoiled Views

text: A map on July 20 with the cover article about retracing a road in Maryland and Pennsylvania cleared by an English general who fought to secure North America for the British misstated the name of a West Virginia town southwest of the trail. It is Morgantown, not Morganstown.
match_headline: On a General’s Trail, Summoning America’s History

text: An article last Sunday about the first American automaker to announce a front-drive passenger car, Ruxton, referred incorrectly to the publication of an advertisement for the car. The ad did not appear in Fortune in 1929. (The magazine’s first issue was published in 1930.)
match_headline: Remembering the Ruxton

text: A news analysis article last Sunday about voting by members of the Security Council over high-stakes conflicts referred imprecisely to the vetoes of draft resolutions by the United States and Russia. The figures cited — 14 vetoes by the United States and 11 by Russia — were for the time period since the end of the Cold War, not the entire period since 1946, when the Security Council was created.
match_headline: Why the U.N. Can’t Solve the World’s Problems

text: An article on Thursday about a possible shift in position by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, that could allow for economic and other aid to the Gaza Strip in exchange for demilitarization by Islamist militants in the Strip gave an outdated title for Sari Bashi of Gisha, an Israeli human rights group. Though she is a co-founder, she is no longer the director.
match_headline: Quest for Demilitarization of Gaza Is Seen Getting Netanyahu Only So Far

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the World Briefing column on Thursday about formal charges being brought against the Uighur scholar Ilham Tohti, who has criticized the treatment by the Chinese authorities of the Uighur, a Turkic-speaking people who practice Sunni Islam, referred incorrectly to Xinjiang, where many of the Uighur live. It is a western region of China, not a province.
match_headline: China Charges Leading Uighur Scholar With Separatism

text: An article last Monday about New York City’s handling of private school tuition requests for special-needs students misstated the middle initial of one of the lawyers representing a family whose petition was initially denied. She is Marion M. Walsh, not Marion K.
match_headline: Balancing Special-Education Needs With Rising Costs

text: A picture caption in some editions on July 24 with an article about the ways in which Muslims in New York mark Ramadan misidentified the type of food that Detective Ahmed Nasser was shown sharing at a meal. He was offering another diner a plate of dates, not figs.
match_headline: For Muslims in New York, Observing Ramadan Is a Blend of Rituals Far and Near

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the decision by Bayern Munich to build a year-round presence in the United States misstated the time period during which the team won five soccer titles. It was 2013, not the 2013-14 season.
match_headline: Deep-Pocketed Bayern Munich Is Open for Business in U.S.

text: An article on Monday about continued wrangling over the results of the Afghanistan presidential election misstated the date of the runoff vote, which is being audited by Afghan authorities with international oversight. It was June 14, not July 7.
match_headline: Disputes Threaten to Derail Audit of Afghanistan Vote

text: A subheading in some editions last Tuesday with an article about the death of José Fermín Sánchez, a laborer on Long Island, in 2010 misstated the status of the case. As the article correctly noted, the police refuse to comment on the case, as the investigation into Mr. Sánchez’s death remains open; it has not been classified as a hate crime.
match_headline: 4 Years Later, Still No Answers in Killing of a Long Island Laborer

text: An article on July 24 about the financial bailout of Cyprus misstated the International Monetary Fund’s estimate of the value of nonperforming loans in the country. It is 22 billion euros, not €11 billion.
match_headline: White House to Begin $10 Billion Rural Investment Fund

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the hedge fund manager Florian Homm, who is wanted in the United States on various fraud charges, misspelled the surname of an F.B.I. spokeswoman who commented on his legal status. She is Laura Eimiller, not Eilmiller.
match_headline: Florian Homm, Toppled Financier, Finds Safe Harbor in Germany

text: An article on Saturday about a lawsuit filed by Kimberly Behzadi against ICM Partners, the talent and literary agency, contending that it violated minimum wage laws by not paying her for an internship, misstated the name of the institution where Ms. Behzadi intends to pursue an M.B.A. It is the University at Buffalo, which is part of the State University of New York system; it is not the University of Buffalo.
match_headline: A Coveted Internship, but Its Holder Sues Anyway

text: An article on Saturday about the black filmmaker Lacey Schwartz, whose movie “Little White Lie” is about her experience growing up believing she was white, referred imprecisely to its premiere. While its official world premiere was at the San Francisco Jewish Film Festival on Sunday, it was screened earlier at the Woods Hole Film Festival in Cape Cod and the BlackStar Film Festival in Philadelphia.
match_headline: After the ‘White Lie’ Implodes, a Rich Narrative Unfurls

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with a review of the Vail International Dance Festival misidentified, in some editions, the choreographer of “Le Parc,” part of which was performed on Friday night. As the review correctly noted, he is Angelin Preljocaj — not Matthew Neenan, who choreographed another work on the program.
match_headline: Where the Stars Come to Shine in New and Unexpected Ways

text: An article on Monday about efforts by Gov. Jay Inslee of Washington, a Democrat, to pass the most far-reaching climate change policies in the nation referred incorrectly to one of his ideas. He is considering a proposal to block construction of ports that would ship American coal to China; he has not made a final decision to do so. The article also referred incorrectly to a state senator whom Mr. Inslee and his supporters tried to defeat last year because she opposed his climate plans. The senator, Jan Angel, was a Republican House member at the time she ran for the state Senate; she was not an incumbent senator.
match_headline: As Oysters Die, Climate Policy Goes on the Stump

text: An article on Saturday about the possibility that California could become the first state to require random drug and alcohol tests for doctors quoted incorrectly from comments by Dr. Richard Thorp, the president of the California Medical Association, who was asked whether doctors could support testing in some form. Dr. Thorp said, “We’re not dealing with a theoretical initiative.” He did not say “theatrical initiative.”
ref_headline: We’re not dealing with a theoretical initiative.
match_headline: California Asks: Should Doctors Face Drug Tests?

text: Because of an editing error, a reporting credit on Monday with an article about the evacuation of British citizens from Tripoli, Libya, amid intense battles between rival militias misidentified the location of one of the reporters. Suliman Ali Zway reported from Tunis — not from Benghazi, Libya.
match_headline: British Citizens Flee Tripoli on Ship as 25 Libyans Are Reportedly Killed in Fighting

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the corruption trial of former Gov. Bob McDonnell of Virginia and his wife misstated, in some copies, the day on which Jonnie R. Williams Sr., the prosecution’s star witness, testified about loans and gifts he offered the couple. It was Thursday — not Monday, July 28.
match_headline: Jury in Ex-Virginia Governor’s Trial Hears of Money Transfer

text: An article on Saturday about biotechnology companies that are developing new drugs for pets erroneously included one such drug among those that are available. Although Elanco, a unit of Eli Lilly, once sold Reconcile, a version of the antidepressant Prozac that treats canine separation anxiety, a spokeswoman said the company has stopped making and selling the drug because of manufacturing problems.
match_headline: Start-Ups Work on Biotech Drugs for Pets

text: Because of an editing error, contact information on Saturday with a review of the National Cryptologic Museum, in Annapolis Junction, Md., misstated the museum’s telephone number. It is 301-688-5849.
match_headline: Security Secrets, Dated but Real

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about plans for the American debut of the Modern Sky Festival, a music showcase established in Beijing, misstated part of a name used by a Taiwanese singer-songwriter who is scheduled to appear at the debut in Central Park in October. The performer, Zhang Xuan, also goes by the name Deserts Chang, not Change.
match_headline: Music Festival From Beijing to Make American Debut in New York

text: An article on July 27 about the fall of a South Korean mogul and religious leader, Yoo Byung-eun, over allegations that he and his family bore at least some responsibility for the sinking of the ferry Sewol, which they controlled through one of their many companies, referred incorrectly to the birthplace of the Rev. Sun Myung Moon, another South Korean religious leader. Mr. Moon was born in 1920 in what is now North Korea; he was not born in South Korea, though his Unification Church was founded there.
match_headline: In Ferry Deaths, a South Korean Tycoon’s Downfall

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on July 21 with an article about increased investment in manufacturing and retail operations across sub-Saharan Africa, fueled by consumer demand among a rising black middle class, misstated the name of a mall near Johannesburg where a saleswoman was shown talking to shoppers. It is the Daveyton mall, not Daveytown.
match_headline: Africans Open Fuller Wallets to the Future

text: Because of editing errors, an article on Tuesday about Germany’s decision to block the delivery of military parts to Russia to increase pressure on Moscow over its involvement in Ukraine referred incorrectly to France’s actions regarding military equipment for Russia and to the equipment itself. France plans to deliver the equipment; it has not done so yet. And it is a Mistral-class helicopter carrier, not a Mistral-class helicopter.
match_headline: Germany Blocks the Delivery of Military Parts to Russia

text: An article on Monday about an earthquake in southwestern China that killed hundreds and injured nearly 2,000 misstated the given name of a woman who said she had been on the way home from a friend’s wedding when the quake hit her village. She is Li Fei, not Feng.
match_headline: Earthquake Kills Hundreds in Southwest China

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Tuesday about the lowering of the speed limit on Broadway to 25 miles per hour misidentified the governor of New York, who is expected to sign legislation reducing the speed limit throughout the rest of New York City. The governor is Andrew M. Cuomo, of course — not Mario M. Cuomo, who is Andrew’s father and was the 52nd governor of New York, from 1983 to 1994.
match_headline: Broadway Is Reined In by a Lower Speed Limit

text: A picture caption on Friday with an art review of two shows — “The Intuitionists” and “Small” — at the Drawing Center in Manhattan misstated the title of a work by Margaret Withers that was shown. It is “between light and obscurity the lush paradise breathed a silent koan” — not “Warm: Silence,” a phrase she was invited to respond to in preparing artwork for “The Intuitionists” show.
match_headline: ‘The Intuitionists’ and ‘Small’

text: An article on Tuesday about a report that was critical of the United States’ physician training system, Graduate Medical Education, misstated part of the name of one of the organizations supporting the report’s recommendations. It is the American Academy of Family Physicians, not the American Association of Family Physicians.
match_headline: Air Force Academy to Examine Conduct of Cadet Athletes

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the New York radio personality Steve Post misstated the duration of his marriage to Laura Rosenberg. They were married for 38 years, not 47. The obituary also referred imprecisely to C. W. Post College, where Mr. Post was briefly the director of radio. It has always been a campus of Long Island University; it is not just “now” a campus of the university.
match_headline: Steve Post, Sardonic Wit on WNYC, Is Dead at 70

text: An article last Thursday about an effort to establish the Mayapple Center for the Arts and Humanities, an artists’ retreat, in Stamford, Conn., misstated part of the title of one of its workshops. It was “Confusing the Controller,” not “Controlling the Controller.”
match_headline: Drawing Ire, Not Artists

text: An article on Wednesday about conflicting assessments of civilian casualties in the Gaza Strip from the monthlong war between Hamas and Israel referred imprecisely to the activity on Tuesday evening at the office of Al Mezan Center for Human Rights, one of the Gaza-based groups conducting a count. While Samir Zaqout, an official of the center, and his aides were updating handwritten logs, they were not “issuing small corrections to earlier news releases.” (Earlier, Mr. Zaqout said, he had made a small correction to one news release.)
ref_headline: issuing small corrections to earlier news releases.
match_headline: Civilian or Not? New Fight in Tallying the Dead From the Gaza Conflict

text: An article in some editions on June 29 about ceremonies in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, marking the centenary of the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife — an event that led to the outbreak of World War I — referred imprecisely to the number of allies the Austro-Hungarian Empire had during the war. While the breakup of the Russian Empire during the war produced about a dozen territories that declared short-lived independence and allied themselves with Austria-Hungary, by most historical accounts, it had three allies — the German Empire, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria — not 15. A reader pointed out the error in an email the day the article was published; this correction was delayed because editors did not follow through on the complaint.
match_headline: Revelry in Sarajevo, Where Shots Started a World War

text: Because of an editing error, an article on July 22 about Israelis’ support for the war in the Gaza Strip and their intimate connection to the military misidentified the soldier whose funeral was attended by 20,000 people, according to the police. He was Sgt. Nissim Sean Carmeli, not Maj. Tzafrir Baror.
match_headline: Strength Is Sought at Rites in Israel

text: An article on July 15 about the pressures on Palestinian civilians trying to go about their lives during the conflict between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip referred incorrectly to Gaza’s borders. Israel controls Gaza’s border with Israel, but not all its borders; Egypt, which has security agreements with Israel, controls Gaza’s border with Egypt.
match_headline: Gaza Families Near Israeli Border Struggle to Build a Life in the Heart of a Conflict

text: An article on July 21 about signs of a decline in the number of unaccompanied children heading from Central America to the United States misspelled, at one point, the surname of a woman who was detained near the Honduran border with Guatemala. She is María Enríquez, not Enriques.
match_headline: Trying to Slow the Illegal Flow of Young Migrants

text: An article on Thursday about the costly new hepatitis C drug Sovaldi and its effect on prison medical budgets contained an outdated reference to the relationship between of the University of Massachusetts Medical School and the state’s prison system. While the medical school used to work with the prison system, it no longer does.
match_headline: Why the Hepatitis Cure Sovaldi Is a Budgetary Disaster for Prisons

text: An article on Wednesday about the business and diplomatic activities of Tony Blair since stepping down as British prime minister used an outdated name for a JPMorgan Chase client that operated an oil field and was involved in a deal pushed by Mr. Blair. It was the BG Group, not British Gas. (The BG Group was formed when British Gas split up in the 1990s.)
match_headline: Tony Blair Has Used His Connections to Change the World, and to Get Rich

text: A report in the Inside Art column last Friday about plans by Christie’s to auction Manet’s “Le Printemps” in November referred incorrectly to the painting’s history. It was not included in the exhibition “Impressionism, Fashion and Modernity,” which opened at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris in 2012 and traveled to the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Art Institute of Chicago.
match_headline: Summer Treats in the Met’s European Galleries

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the State of the Art column, about efforts by the ride-sharing company Lyft to encourage commuters to use the service, misidentified Logan Green’s role at the company. He is a founder and chief executive, not chief operating officer.
match_headline: Lyft Hopes to Coax Commuters to Leave Their Cars

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about the Mets’ 5-1 loss to the San Francisco Giants misstated the given name of a Giants player who tripled in the seventh inning. He is Brandon Crawford, not Brendan.
match_headline: Mets Sleepwalk Through a Loss to the Giants as Harvey Begins Easy Throwing

text: An article on Thursday about American Ballet Theater’s donation of 50,000 documents to the Library of Congress misidentified the company’s founding director. He was Richard Pleasant — not Lucia Chase, who was a founding patron and later co-director.
match_headline: Ballet Theater Donating Trove of Materials to Library of Congress

text: Because of editing errors, a pop music entry in the Listings pages on Friday about Americanafest NYC misstated the starting time of two concerts at Damrosch Park at Lincoln Center. One tonight featuring Rosanne Cash is at 6 p.m., not 6:30, and one tomorrow with Charles Bradley & His Extraordinaires starts at 5 p.m., not 5:30.
match_headline: Pop, Rock & Cabaret Listings for Aug. 8-14

text: A picture caption in the Listings pages on Friday about the puppet play “The Pigeoning” carried an erroneous credit. The photograph is by Rob Long, not Richard Termine. (A caption with a review of the play, on July 15, included the same error.)
match_headline: Theater Listings for Aug. 8-14

text: A picture caption on Friday with a report in the Antiques column about dollhouses and dollhouse furniture misidentified the collection that includes the mid-19th-century English dollhouse whose dining room setting was shown. While the three-tiered stand and the chandelier are from the Flora Gill Jacobs collection, the dollhouse itself belongs to Allerton Cushman III; it is not from the Jacobs collection.
match_headline: Tiny Furniture: A Diaspora of Dollhouses

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 32 this weekend about Garry Kasparov, the former world chess champion, refers incompletely to his ethnicity. He was born in Azerbaijan and is half-Armenian and half-Jewish.
match_headline: Vladimir Putin’s Chess-Master Nemesis

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the mystery writer Dorothy Salisbury Davis misstated, in some copies, her birth date, which she did not learn until later in life. It was April 25, 1916 — not April 26.
match_headline: Dorothy Salisbury Davis, Suspense Novelist, Dies at 98

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the former CBS News president Edward M. Joyce referred imprecisely to a plan by Don Hewitt, the producer of “60 Minutes,” and others to buy CBS News in 1985. While Mr. Hewitt acknowledged the plan, he did so only after it was reported by the trade publication Variety; it was not “announced.”
match_headline: Edward M. Joyce, CBS News Leader During Era of Cost-Cutting, Dies at 81

text: An article last Sunday about efforts by President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to harness the fervor of the Russian Orthodox faithful to his own political goals misidentified the occasion that was, for many Orthodox, the last time a man anointed by God governed Russia. It was the overthrow of Czar Nicholas II in 1917, not his death. (He was assassinated the following year.)
match_headline: Putin Strives to Harness Energy of Russian Pilgrims for Political Profit

text: An article on July 27 about “bonkers TV” — storytelling designed to shock viewers — described WGN America incorrectly. It is a national television network based in Los Angeles, not the local television station WGN in Chicago. The article also misidentified a character who was killed in the episode “The Red Wedding” of the HBO series “Game of Thrones.” The pregnant woman who was stabbed to death was a guest at the wedding, not the bride.
match_headline: Why Jack Bauer Is to Blame for ‘Bonkers TV’

text: An article on July 27 about the increased use of refrigeration in China misspelled the name of a restaurant on the outskirts of Hangzhou that serves locally sourced food. It is Longjing Caotang, not Longjin Caotan.
match_headline: What Do Chinese Dumplings Have to Do With Global Warming?

text: An article last Sunday about shortening the path to a medical degree erroneously included one university among those that have medical schools. Northeastern University has no such school.
match_headline: The Drawn-Out Medical Degree

text: An article last Sunday about Jean Genet’s play “The Maids,” which is being revived in New York as part of the Lincoln Center Festival, misstated the site of the drama’s American premiere in 1955. It was at the Tempo Playhouse in New York, not the Temple Theater.
match_headline: Interpreting ‘The Maids’ Through a Shifting Societal Lens

text: An entry in the Newly Released listings with the Video column last Sunday misidentified the format of Twilight Time’s release of the Woody Allen movie “Radio Days.” It is on Blu-ray, not standard DVD.
match_headline: Get Your Tootsy Frootsy TV Clips!

text: A picture caption on July 27 with the Video column, about the 1943 Lewis Milestone movie “The North Star,” using information from a publicist, misidentified the actor to the right of Dana Andrews. He was Robert Lowery, not Dean Jagger.
match_headline: Soviet Valor, Revised for the ’50s

text: An article last Sunday about building an advertising campaign on Facebook misspelled the given name of Facebook’s vice president for global marketing solutions. She is Carolyn Everson, not Caroline.
match_headline: How Facebook Sold You Krill Oil

text: An article last Sunday about Bitty Foods, which uses crickets to make flour, misstated a former job title of Megan Miller, a co-founder of the company. She headed research and development for the United States branch of Bonnier AB, the global media company; she did not hold that position for the entire company.
match_headline: Jiminy Cricket! Bugs Could Be Next Food Craze

text: An article on July 27 about household wealth in the United States referred incorrectly to households that rank in the 95th percentile in net worth. Their net worth is greater than or equal to that of 95 percent of all households, not greater than 94 percent.
match_headline: The Typical Household, Now Worth a Third Less

text: An article last Sunday about automakers’ efforts to use engine heat more efficiently misstated the surname of a General Motors engineer. He is Joseph Dulzo, not Dutzo.
match_headline: New Frontier in the Efficiency Quest: Cutting Heat Losses

text: Because of a production error, an article on June 19 about the lack of consensus among news outlets and the United States government over what to call the Sunni extremist group besieging Iraq — the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, or the Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant — rendered its Arabic name backward. This correction was delayed by an editing lapse.
match_headline: What to Call Iraq Fighters? Experts Vary on S’s and L’s

text: Because of an editing error, a reporting credit on Aug. 1 with an article about international monitors’ arrival at the site of the crash of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 in eastern Ukraine misidentified the location of one reporter. Andrew Roth reported from Kiev, the Ukrainian capital — not from Shakhtyorsk, 10 miles south of the crash site.
match_headline: Break in Fighting Lets International Team Reach Site of Ukraine Crash

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about an arrest in the deaths of two prostitutes whose bodies were found on Long Island in the 1990s misstated the age of a friend of one of the victims who attended a vigil for the two women. The friend, Stacey Ann, initially said she is 36, but later confirmed that she is in fact 40.
match_headline: Two Decades After Pair of Killings on Long Island, Authorities Make an Arrest

text: An article on Friday about a new IBM computer chip that is said to mimic the way a human brain works omitted the last word in the name of a program known by the acronym SyNapse, which funded IBM’s research. It is Systems of Neuromorphic Adaptive Plastic Scalable Electronics.
match_headline: IBM Develops a New Chip That Functions Like a Brain

text: An article in some editions on July 31 about Liberty guard Anna Cruz, a rookie from Spain, misstated, in some copies, her scoring average at the time. She was averaging 8 points a game, not 7.8.
match_headline: A Rookie as Feisty as She Is Steady

text: An obituary on July 24 about Frederick I. Ordway III, a NASA official who was also an adviser for the movie “2001: A Space Odyssey,” misstated part of the name of the event at which Mr. Ordway met Arthur C. Clarke, who wrote that movie’s screenplay with the director Stanley Kubrick. It was the International Astronautical Congress, not the International Aeronautical Congress.
match_headline: Frederick I. Ordway III Dies at 87; NASA Official Helped Shape ‘Space Odyssey’

text: An article on Monday about Apple University, which teaches employees the company’s style and culture, misstated the title of Joel Podolny, who serves as dean of the in-house university. He is a vice president at Apple, but he is no longer vice president for human resources, nor is he in “in charge” of human resources. (A video frame shot that accompanied the article, with a text overlay that identified Mr. Podolny as vice president for human resources, was from 2012.)
match_headline: Simplifying the Bull: How Picasso Helps to Teach Apple’s Style

text: An article on Friday about the confusion surrounding a planned march across the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge to protest the role the police played in the death of a Staten Island man misstated, in some editions, the surname of a spokeswoman for the National Action Network, which is helping to organize the march. She is Jacky Johnson, not Jones. (Subsequently organizers said the march would be held on Staten Island, not on the bridge.)
match_headline: With March in Chokehold Case, Questions Over Who’s in Charge

text: An article on Friday about Walmart’s move into primary health care clinics misattributed a comment about chronic illnesses. It was Skip Snow, an analyst at Forrester Research — not Matt Nemer of Wells Fargo — who noted that most of the $1.7 billion Americans spend annually goes to handling such illnesses. The article also misstated Mr. Nemer’s area of expertise. He is a retail analyst, not a health care analyst.
match_headline: In Ambitious Bid, Walmart Seeks Foothold in Primary Care Services

text: An article on Aug. 4 about head injuries in Nascar erroneously attributed a quotation to Chris Nowinski of the Boston University Sports Legacy Institute. Speaking about drivers’ risk for chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a degenerative disease found in the brains of athletes who have sustained blows to the head, he said, “One significant impact may be enough to start the degenerative process.” He did not say, “The one big hit — which is something Nascar drivers can experience more than the repetitive — the one big hit is another possible risk.” That quotation was part of a question Mr. Nowinski was asked.
ref_headline: One significant impact may be enough to start the degenerative process.
match_headline: Crashing Without a Cushion

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Friday about the Yankees’ 1-0 victory over the Detroit Tigers misstated the number of wins Yankees starters were credited with in the series against the Tigers. It was two, not three.
match_headline: Yankees Take Series vs. Tigers Behind Starter and a Stopper

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the Yankees’ 5-1 victory over the Detroit Tigers misstated the day of the game in some editions. It was Wednesday, not Friday.
match_headline: Yanks’ Late Rally Gives Them Breathing Room, at a Cost

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the coming season of the Abrons Arts Center in Manhattan misstated the centenary the season will celebrate. It is the centenary of the Henry Street Settlement Playhouse at the center — not of the Henry Street Settlement, the center’s parent organization.
match_headline: Sacred Music and Movement, With an Infectious Beat

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about counterattacks by Kurdish forces on Sunni militants in Iraq following American airstrikes gave an incorrect identification from The Associated Press in some editions for the American military plane shown about to land on a carrier in the Persian Gulf. It is an EA-6B Prowler, not an F/A-18C Hornet.
match_headline: Capitalizing on U.S. Bombing, Kurds Retake Iraqi Towns

text: An article last Wednesday about Israel’s withdrawal of troops from the Gaza Strip on the first day of a 72-hour cease-fire between Israel and Hamas overstated the effect of Hamas rockets on commercial flights in Israel during the monthlong war. While many international flights to and from the airport near Tel Aviv were temporarily suspended after a rocket landed nearby, the airport itself remained open; it did not shut down. The same error appeared in an article on Monday about Gazans’ assessment of the losses and victories of the war.
match_headline: Israel Exits Gaza as Truce Begins

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the actor and comedian Robin Williams misstated the name and title of Prince Charles’s wife, with whom the prince once attended a London performance by Mr. Williams. She is Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall — not Lady Camilla Bowles.
match_headline: Robin Williams, Oscar-Winning Comedian, Dies at 63

text: An article on May 21 about Hezbollah’s new sense of purpose, created by the victories it has achieved by intervening in the Syrian civil war, referred incorrectly to that intervention. It is the first time in decades — not the first time ever — that Hezbollah has dedicated so many resources to fighting other Arabs and Muslims instead of Israel. (Hezbollah engaged in fierce battles with other militants in Lebanon in the late 1980s.) The article was corrected online in May; this correction was delayed by an editing lapse.
match_headline: Syrian Fighting Gives Hezbollah New but Diffuse Purpose

text: An article on Tuesday about the causes for a decline in auto theft misstated the given name of the official in charge of the New York Police Department’s auto crime division. He is Don Boller, not John.
match_headline: Here’s Why Stealing Cars Went Out of Fashion

text: An article in some editions on Friday about a federal fine issued to Corizon, the health contractor at Rikers Island, for failing to protect employees from violence referred incorrectly to the “willful violation” citation issued by the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration. It was the second such citation issued in three years specifically for workplace violence, not for all causes. (OSHA has issued these citations more frequently for other reasons.)
match_headline: Rikers Health Contractor Fined for Worker Assaults

text: An article in some editions on Aug. 3 about Ray Guy’s becoming the first punter inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame misstated the number of seasons he spent with the Oakland Raiders. While Guy played his entire 14-season career with the Raiders franchise, the team was based in Oakland for only his first nine seasons. Guy played his final five seasons, from 1982 to 1986, after the Raiders had moved to Los Angeles.
match_headline: A Group Revels as Its Godfather Is Inducted

text: A critic’s notebook article on Monday about the street dance form known as Detroit Jit referred incorrectly to the word “LeJit.” It is the name of a Detroit Jit group, not a nickname for the dance form.
match_headline: Fast-Stepped Fury, Rooted in Detroit

text: An article on Tuesday about Pittsburgh International Airport’s plans to extract natural gas from deposits under its runways misstated the annual revenue of Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, which also has oil and gas wells on its property. It is $650 million, not $6 billion.
match_headline: Now Arriving at Pittsburgh International: Fracking

text: An article on July 16 about the election of Salim al-Jubouri as speaker of Iraq’s Parliament misstated the amount of time that the nominee for president has to nominate a prime minister, under the Iraqi Constitution. The president must do so in two weeks, not four.
match_headline: Iraqi Parliament Elects Speaker in Effort to Form New Government

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Tuesday about the United Nations Human Rights Council’s appointment of three legal experts to a commission to look into whether violations of international human rights law were committed by Israel and the Palestinian group Hamas during the conflict in Gaza misidentified the nationality of one of the experts, Doudou Diène. Mr. Diène, a lawyer, is from Senegal, not from Ivory Coast.
match_headline: Human Rights Council Plans to Investigate Gaza Conflict

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Sunday with an article about plans for an upscale epicurean village in a Paris neighborhood that have upset some Parisians, who worry that low-income residents will be pushed aside, misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the entrepreneur behind the plans. As the article correctly noted, he is Cédric Naudon, not Naudot.
match_headline: An Epicurean Village Is Too Rich for Some Paris Appetites

text: An article on Tuesday about the use of a robot to deliver items to guest rooms at the Aloft hotel in Cupertino, Calif., misspelled the surname of the president of the Robotic Industries Association in some editions. He is Jeff Burnstein, not Bernstein.
match_headline: ‘Beep,’ Says the Bellhop

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the coming season of the Abrons Arts Center in Manhattan, using information from a publicist, misstated the closing date of the choreographer Mark Dendy’s “Labyrinth,” a retelling of the Theseus myth. It runs from Oct. 9 to Oct. 26 — not to Oct. 12.
match_headline: Geoffrey Holder, Dancer, Actor, Painter and More, Dies at 84

text: An obituary last Thursday about the Zen master Joshu Sasaki referred incorrectly to the poets Gary Snyder and Allen Ginsberg. While they both studied Zen Buddhism, they did not study with Mr. Sasaki.
match_headline: Joshu Sasaki, 107, Tainted Zen Master

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the actress Lauren Bacall misidentified the borough in New York in which she was born. It is the Bronx, not Brooklyn.
match_headline: Lauren Bacall Dies at 89; in a Bygone Hollywood, She Purred Every Word

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the elimination of reduced-fat French fries in some Burger King outlets misstated the number of stores that decided to eliminate the item, called Satisfries. It is slightly fewer than 5,000, not about 7,500. The article also misstated the amount of sodium in Satisfries and regular fries. Satisfries have 300 milligrams of sodium, not 300 grams; regular fries have 480 milligrams, not 480 grams.
match_headline: Burger King to Phase Out Lower-Fat French Fries

text: An article on Thursday about Amazon’s introduction of a credit card reader referred incorrectly to an Internet analyst who commented on the company’s pricing strategy.
