It was Colin Sebastian, an analyst with Baird Equity Research — not “Mr. Baird” — who said: “In typical Amazon fashion, they’re using price as a motivator. It’s pretty obvious in this case that they’re losing money on the swipes at least.”
match_headline: Next Target for Amazon Is Credit Card Readers at Stores

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an article about Jo-Wilfried Tsonga’s win over Roger Federer in the final of the Rogers Cup tennis tournament referred incorrectly to the victory in some copies. As the article correctly noted, it was Tsonga’s fourth win — not his first — against a top-10 player this season. (All four wins against the top-10 players came in this tournament.)
match_headline: On Day of Several Firsts, Tsonga Captures Rogers Cup in Straight Sets Over Federer

text: An article in some copies on Saturday about the Yankees’ 10-6 victory over the Cleveland Indians misstated the number of games the Yankees trailed the Kansas City Royals for the American League’s second wild card at the time of the game. The Yankees were a half-game behind the Royals, not a game.
match_headline: Yankees Continue to Use Stadium to Their Advantage

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the appointment of the architect Amale Andraos as dean of the Graduate School of Architecture, Preservation and Planning at Columbia University misidentified the area of Queens that is the site of a library she and her husband, Dan Wood, designed. It is Kew Gardens Hills, not Kew Gardens.
match_headline: New York Architect Picked to Lead Columbia University Architecture School

text: An article on Thursday about frustration over a decision by the authorities not to release the name of a police officer involved in the fatal shooting of an African-American teenager in Ferguson, Mo., misidentified, in some editions, the university at which Erwin Chemerinsky, who discussed the issue, is a law professor. It is the University of California, Irvine — not the University of California, Los Angeles. (The authorities on Friday identified the officer as Darren Wilson.)
match_headline: Anonymity in Police Shooting Fuels Anger in Missouri

text: An article on Friday about the first civil trial brought against a bank under the Antiterrorism Act misidentified the Arab Bank account from which $60,000 was transferred to a Hamas leader in 2001. The account belonged to Yousef el Hayek, not Osama Hamdan.
match_headline: Hamas Transactions Got Through in Error, Bank Says

text: An article on Friday about restaurant bars misspelled the surname of the owner of the restaurant Riverpark. He is Tom Colicchio, not Collichio.
match_headline: A Heady Mix of Food, Cocktails and Showmanship

text: A critic’s notebook article on Friday about the musical “Finding Neverland” at the American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Mass., misspelled the given name of the writer responsible for an earlier stage version of the show, which ran in Leicester, England, in 2012. As correctly noted in an accompanying listing of credits, the writer of the book for that version is Allan Knee, not Alan. (James Graham wrote the book for the current production.)
match_headline: Fantasies Taxiing for Takeoff

text: An article last Sunday about efforts to send home the body of Nat Nakasa, a South African opponent of apartheid who died in New York nearly 50 years ago, misstated the circumstances of Nelson Mandela’s arrest, an event that influenced Mr. Nakasa’s decision to live in exile. Mr. Mandela was arrested at a roadblock in 1962, not in a raid on a farm in 1963.
match_headline: After Decades in Exile, a South African Writer’s Remains Will Head Home

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about Jason Day’s adventurous par on the second hole during the third round of the P.G.A. Championship misstated, in some copies, the location of the ball for Day’s second shot. It was in a tall grass area near the creek called Floyds Fork, not in the creek itself.
match_headline: P.G.A. Championship 2014: Thinking on His Bare Feet, Jason Day Salvages a Peculiar Par

text: An article on July 20 about “Aisthesis: The Origin of Sensations,” an art show at the Villa Menafoglio Litta Panza in Varese, Italy, referred incorrectly to an installation by James Turrell there, “Sight Unseen.” It is not designed to produce confusion.
match_headline: A Palace of Wonders

text: A picture caption on July 20 with a review of “Price of Fame: The Honorable Clare Boothe Luce,” by Sylvia Jukes Morris, referred incorrectly to the soldiers shown with Luce in 1945. They were not “Fifth Army Group troops.” (There was no Fifth Army Group in World War II.)
ref_headline: Price of Fame: The Honorable Clare Boothe Luce,
match_headline: The Woman

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the comeback of Kevin Sessums, a journalist who writes about celebrities, misstated the decade that he achieved prominence among Hollywood writers who chronicled celebrity culture while also being a part of it. It was the 1990s, not the 1980s. The article also contained a passage in which Mr. Sessums quoted a friend who comforted him when he was upset over having to put his dogs in foster care because he had relapsed into drug use and was told to leave his home. He quoted the friend as saying, “This is what sobriety feels like.” After the article was published, Mr. Sessums said that his friend’s comment had been, “This is what surrender feels like.”
ref_headline: This is what sobriety feels like.
match_headline: His Own Redemption Story

text: A report on Aug. 3 about the marriage of Cheryl Hines and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., included a quotation from Mr. Kennedy that referred imprecisely to Ms. Hines’s marital status when they began dating. While she was in fact still married, as he noted, she had filed for divorce several months earlier.
match_headline: No Curbs on Their Enthusiasm

text: An article last Sunday about tourism in Mansfield, Ashland and Upper Sandusky, Ohio, where much of “The Shawshank Redemption” was filmed, described incorrectly at one point the location of an old oak tree that was featured in the film. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is across the road from Malabar Farm State Park, not in the park. And the article misstated the direction of Upper Sandusky from Mansfield; it is west, not east.
match_headline: Visiting ‘Shawshank’ Sites, 20 Years Later

text: Because of an editing error, the cover story last Sunday about the effort to restore the trails of Acadia National Park on Mount Desert Island in Maine misstated the year that George Bucknam Dorr, a founder of the park, arrived on Mount Desert. It was 1868, not 1968. In addition, the article misspelled the surname of the father of American landscape design, who was involved in formalizing a network of island walks. He is Frederick Law Olmsted, not Olmstead. The misspelling was repeated in a reference to the Olmsted Center for Landscape Preservation.
match_headline: Restoring Acadia’s Trails

text: An article last Sunday about Anat R. Admati, a Stanford finance professor who is seeking stronger regulation of banks, misstated the month in 2014 in which she debated banking issues at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. It was January, not February.
match_headline: When She Talks, Banks Shudder

text: An article on Aug. 3 about the rock band Spoon misstated part of the title of a song by PJ Harvey to which a band member refers. It is ‘‘The Glorious Land,’’ not ‘‘This Glorious Land.’’
match_headline: Spoon, the Molecular Gastronomists of Rock

text: An article on Tuesday about growing concern among Western governments that a Russian mission to aid Ukraine could serve as a pretext for a military incursion misidentified the organization headed by José Manuel Barroso, who warned the Russian president, Vladimir V. Putin, against “any unilateral military actions in Ukraine.” Mr. Barroso is president of the European Commission, not the European Union.
ref_headline: any unilateral military actions in Ukraine.
match_headline: Russian Intervention in Ukraine Is Likely, NATO Says

text: A picture credit on Thursday with an article about an increase in violence at New York City’s prison complex on Rikers Island during the administration of Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg misidentified the photographer in some editions. The photograph, of a bus driving along the coast of the island, was taken by Richard Perry/The New York Times — not by Julie Jacobson/Associated Press.
match_headline: Violence by Rikers Guards Grew Under Bloomberg

text: An article on Saturday about Michael Brown, the unarmed African-American teenager in Ferguson, Mo., who was killed by a police officer misstated, in some editions, the number of years that the officer, Darren Wilson, worked for the police department in Jennings, Mo., before joining the Ferguson force. It was two years, not four.
match_headline: A Youth, an Officer and 2 Paths to a Fatal Encounter

text: An article on Saturday about a security breach at the grocery chain Supervalu that may also affect some food stores it sold to a private equity firm last year misspelled the name of the firm. It is Cerberus Capital Management, not Cerebus.
match_headline: Supervalu Discloses a Data Breach

text: An article on Monday about the development of software to automate the gathering, cleaning and organizing of disparate data misstated the year when “Doing Data Science” was published. It first came out in 2013, not 2014.
match_headline: For Big-Data Scientists, ‘Janitor Work’ Is Key Hurdle to Insights

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the China scholar Pierre Ryckmans misspelled part of the name of his wife. She is Han-fang Chang, not Han-fang Chan.
match_headline: Pierre Ryckmans, 78, Dies; Exposed Mao’s Hard Line

text: An article on Aug. 11 about Democrats and Republicans who are vying for control of statehouses in the fall elections misstated the number of partisan legislative chambers in the United States. It is 98, not 99. (Nebraska’s Legislature, which is unicameral, is nonpartisan.)
match_headline: Midterms Give Parties Chance for Sweeping Control of States

text: An article on Aug. 7 about challenges Mayor Bill de Blasio faces in placating both the police and his political base while handling the case of a man who died during an arrest on Staten Island misspelled the surname of an advocate for immigrants who said city officials had sought to keep lines of communication open. He is Javier Valdes, not Valdez.
match_headline: A Healing That Wasn’t: Liberal Activists and the Police Assail City Hall

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about birds’ feasting on salmon at the mouth of the Columbia River in Oregon misstated which of the two flocked to the area to have their young. It was the birds, not the salmon.
match_headline: Taking Up Arms Where Birds Feast on Buffet of Salmon

text: An article on Monday about Jess Cagle, the new editor of People magazine, overstated People’s drop in total circulation in the first half of 2014. It was slightly less than 1 percent, not 20 percent.
match_headline: Childhood Passion for Celebrity Still Drives the Editor of People Magazine, Jess Cagle

text: An article on Thursday about the dismissal of an adviser to a Chinese government antitrust committee who was accused of accepting payments from Qualcomm, which is under investigation for suspected antitrust violations, paraphrased incorrectly a comment by Christine Trimble, the company’s vice president for government affairs. She said an economic analysis of Qualcomm’s license pricing, done by a consulting firm that used the services of the adviser, Zhang Xinzhu, was a normal part of government inquiries, not of government “negotiations.”
match_headline: Adviser to Government in Chinese Investigation of Qualcomm Is Ousted

text: An article on Tuesday about business owners who network at professional conferences without paying the registration fee described incorrectly an estimate by Meeting Professionals International, a trade group, of spending by business travelers in 2013. The group estimated that business travelers spent $600 billion to $700 billion on meetings and events, which included travel — not on travel alone.
match_headline: Professional Networking, Minus the Fees

text: An article on Tuesday about a new album from the singer Taylor Swift referred incorrectly to her at one point in some copies. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she is Ms. Swift, not Ms. Taylor.
match_headline: Taylor Swift Maximizes Use of Social Media in Release of New Album

text: A subheading in some editions on Tuesday with an obituary about the former United States senator Jim Jeffords misidentified the state he represented. As the obituary correctly noted, he was from Vermont, not Rhode Island.
match_headline: Jim Jeffords, Who Altered Power in Senate, Dies at 80

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Missouri’s efforts to quell the violence in Ferguson by calling in the National Guard misattributed a statement about Michael Brown, the black teenager who was fatally shot by a white police officer. It was the Brown family’s lawyer, Benjamin L. Crump — not family members and the forensic pathologist Dr. Michael Baden — who said that Mr. Brown was trying to surrender at the time he was killed.
match_headline: Missouri Tries Another Idea: Call In National Guard

text: An article on Aug. 6 about the killing of a United States Army general, Maj. Gen. Harold J. Greene, by an Afghan soldier — the first time an American general had been killed in an overseas conflict since Vietnam — referred imprecisely to the rank of rear admiral in the Navy, held by Rembrandt Cecil Robinson, who was killed in 1972 during the Vietnam War. While the lower grade of rear admiral is equivalent to brigadier general, a one-star officer, in the other uniformed services, Admiral Robinson was a two-star officer, with a rank equivalent to major general.
match_headline: U.S. General Is Killed in Attack at Afghan Base; Others Injured

text: An article on July 22 about an analysis of photographs of wreckage from the Malaysia Airlines Boeing 777-200 that crashed that month in eastern Ukraine referred incorrectly, using information from a defense consultant, to the warhead on an SA-11 missile, the type that American officials have said was the probable culprit in the downing of the plane. It is made of steel, not double sleeves of molded, preformed aluminum, and its fragmentation is not necessarily in a diamond-patterned shape.
match_headline: Jet Wreckage Bears Signs of Impact by Supersonic Missile, Analysis Shows

text: An article last Thursday about the first public statement in an Egyptian court by Hosni Mubarak, the former Egyptian president who is being retried on charges of overseeing the killing of hundreds of Egyptians by security forces during the Arab Spring protests, misstated the date that the court said it plans to deliver a verdict. It is Sept. 27, not Aug. 27.
match_headline: Mubarak Tells Court He Gave All For Egypt

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about defense lawyers’ beginning their case in the corruption trial of former Gov. Bob McDonnell of Virginia, and his wife, Maureen, referred incorrectly to testimony by Janet Vestal Kelly, Virginia’s former secretary of the commonwealth. She was called as a witness by the defense, not by the prosecution.
match_headline: Aide Describes Staff Revolt Against Former Virginia Governor’s Wife

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision by the Toronto International Film Festival to place restrictions on which movies can be shown at the festival misstated the new screening guidelines for its first four days. The 11-day festival has closed its first four days to any film that previously played in North America — not anywhere in the world.
match_headline: In the Race for Oscars, Toronto Puts Up a Hurdle

text: An article last Friday about Olivia Prokopova, the world champion in miniature golf, misspelled the given name of her father. He is Jan Prokop, not Yan.
match_headline: Mini Golf as Career? She Gets Past the Obstacles

text: An article on Thursday about the harsh environment for reporters both abroad and in the United States overstated what is known about the location of the execution of James Foley, a journalist who was beheaded by militants with the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. While he may have been killed in Iraq, where ISIS militants move freely in parts of the country, there is no evidence that he was in fact beheaded there.
match_headline: From Missouri to Syria, Journalists Are Becoming Targets

text: An article on Wednesday about the expanded role of Angela Merkel, the German chancellor, in the Ukraine crisis and the diplomatic delicacy that role entails referred incorrectly to the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact of 1939. That secret agreement led to the invasion of Poland by the Nazis and Soviets, not the Nazis alone. It also led to Soviet domination of the Baltic states. It did not lead directly to the Nazi occupation of the Baltics, though the Nazis seized those states from the Soviets in 1941.
match_headline: German Leader Emerges as Key Figure in Ukraine Talks

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Aug. 14 about Navi Pillay, who is winding down a six-year term as United Nations high commissioner for human rights, misidentified the country whose state-run media denounced Ms. Pillay, a South African of Tamil descent, as a “Tamil tigress.” It is Sri Lanka, not Syria.
match_headline: For U.N. Leader on Human Rights, Finish Line Looks Blurry

text: An article on Tuesday about a Chinese crackdown on antitrust pricing violations by multinational companies erroneously included a company among those that have come under investigation in the last year. Accenture, which provides business services to Microsoft, was visited by antitrust investigators to secure documents related to that service; the company itself is not under investigation.
match_headline: China Says Mercedes-Benz Violated Antitrust Rules in Pricing

text: An article on Aug. 14 about girls who have played in the Little League World Series misstated the given name of the husband of Krissy Wendell-Pohl, who played in the 1994 Little League World Series. He is John Pohl, not Jim.
match_headline: A Novelty No Longer

text: An article on Aug. 14 about the election campaign for commissioner of Major League Baseball misstated the nickname of the Oakland team in some copies. It is the Athletics, not the Athletes. The article also misspelled the name of a co-owner of the Athletics in some copies. He is Lew Wolff, not Lou Wolfe.
match_headline: Back-Room Bickering Before the Final Say

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the museum curator Edward G. Leffingwell misstated the surname of a fashion designer who was among the people he befriended in New York in the mid-1960s. She was Tiger Morse, not Morris.
match_headline: Edward G. Leffingwell, Curator, Dies at 72

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Don Pardo, the longtime announcer for “Saturday Night Live,” misstated, at one point, the year that show began. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, it was 1975, not 1976.
match_headline: Don Pardo, the Voice of ‘SNL,’ Is Dead at 96

text: An editorial on the Ebola outbreak on Saturday misstated the amount the Agency for International Development is contributing to help countries curb the spread of the virus. It is about $14.6 million, not more than $27 million.
match_headline: A Painfully Slow Ebola Response

text: An article last Sunday about efforts by organizers of the Electric Zoo, New York’s largest dance music festival, to respond to a recent spate of drug-related deaths at similar events misspelled the name of a music festival where concertgoers have died. It is Bonnaroo, not Bonaroo. The article also misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the director of DanceSafe, a public health group that works with electronic dance music fans. She is Missi Wooldridge, not Woolridge.
match_headline: A Year After Drug Deaths, the Electric Zoo Music Festival Tries Again

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Giants’ 27-26 preseason victory against the Indianapolis Colts misstated the teams’ preseason records after the game. The Giants were 3-0, not 2-1, and the Colts were 0-2, not 1-1. Because of an editing error, the article also misstated the result of Giants quarterback Ryan Nassib’s pass to Adrien Robinson with 55 seconds left. It was incomplete; it was not a 2-point conversion.
match_headline: Giants Get Last Laugh, but First Unit’s Struggles Cause No Smiles

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary last Sunday about the opera singer Licia Albanese referred incorrectly to her career at the Metropolitan Opera. She sang there more than 400 times — not in more than 400 productions. The obituary also referred incorrectly in some editions to Ezio Pinza, a singer with whom she performed. He was a bass, not a tenor. And the obituary misstated, in some copies, the number of grandchildren that survive Miss Albanese. There are two, not three. (Besides her son, Joseph Gimma, survivors also include three great-grandchildren.)
match_headline: Licia Albanese, Exalted Soprano, Is Dead at 105

text: An obituary last Sunday about the writer Leonard Fein referred incorrectly to Haaretz, which published an article about Mr. Fein by Rabbi David Saperstein. It is an Israeli newspaper published in both Hebrew and English, and Rabbi Saperstein’s article appeared in its English-language edition; Haaretz is not an “English-language Israeli daily.”
match_headline: Leonard Fein, Provocative Writer on Jewish Affairs, Dies at 80

text: An article on Aug. 10 about the Delaware Art Museum’s decision to sell a painting by William Holman Hunt and the museum’s subsequent sanctioning by the Association of Art Museum Directors, referred incorrectly to the timing of the resignation of Michael Miller, the museum’s chief executive, from the association. It was in March, not in June on the day before the Holman Hunt was sold.
match_headline: Museum Under Fire for Selling Its Art

text: A picture credit on Aug. 10 with the Playlist CD review column, using information from a record label publicist, misspelled the surname of the photographer who took the picture of Alison May. She is Taschka Turnquist, not Turnquis.
match_headline: If Friends Play Your Songs, They Just May Change Your Tune

text: A review on Aug. 10 about “The Nixon Tapes 1971-1972,” edited by Douglas Brinkley and Luke A. Nichter, and “The Nixon Defense,” by John W. Dean, rendered incorrectly the two given names of Richard Nixon’s personal secretary. She was Rose Mary Woods, not Rosemary.
match_headline: On the Record: ‘The Nixon Tapes 1971-1972’ and ‘The Nixon Defense’

text: An article last Sunday about Muslim women who share pictures of head-scarf styles on social media misspelled the surname of one such woman. She is Ascia Farraj, not Sarrha.
match_headline: A Makeover for the Hijab, via Instagram

text: An article last Sunday about the millennial generation’s civic-mindedness included several errors. Applications to the Peace Corps recently have been in decline, with a 34 percent decrease from the peak in 2009, and applications to Teach for America decreased slightly last year; neither organization has seen “record numbers of new college graduates” applying for jobs.
ref_headline: record numbers of new college graduates
match_headline: Generation Nice

text: A report on the Arena page last Sunday about the book “Worn Stories,” an anthology by Emily Spivack in which famous people talk about a favorite item of clothing, misstated the number of stories in the book. There are 67, not 27. And it referred incorrectly to their authorship. Ms. Spivack compiled 42 through interviews and edited all 67; the subjects did not write them.
match_headline: Why SketchFactor Feels, Well…

text: An article on Aug. 10 about an architectural tour of Mexico City described incorrectly the location of the Condesa District in relation to the Polanco District. Condesa is southeast of Polanco, not southwest. The article also included an outdated name for a collaborative of architects there. It is now ELHC, no longer Tienda de Comercios.
match_headline: Seeing Mexico City, Guided by Architects

text: An article on Aug. 10 about Zero Freitas, a record collector in Brazil, misspelled the name of the city where he lives. It is São Paulo, not São Paolo.
match_headline: The Brazilian Bus Magnate Who’s Buying Up All the World’s Vinyl Records

text: An article on Aug. 17 about efforts by Vietnam and the United States to enhance relations, something that would probably include a lifting of Washington’s ban on the sale of lethal weapons to Hanoi, misstated, in some editions, the position of the labor and religious groups that presented a letter to Senator John McCain, who recently visited the country with other American officials. The letter indicated that the groups could support the gradual lifting of the arms embargo if the government released prisoners of conscience and repealed vague security laws; it did not say that they supported lifting the ban.
match_headline: In China’s Shadow, U.S. Courts Old Foe Vietnam

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Jonas Bronck and the connection between Savsjo, his hometown in Sweden, and what is now the Bronx — where he arrived 375 years ago as the first European settler — misidentified the source of the quotation “the Bronx is burning.” The comment was made by Howard Cosell during a 1977 World Series game, not by Tom Wolfe in “The Bonfire of the Vanities.”
match_headline: A Bronck in the Bronx Gives a Swedish Town a Reason to Cheer

text: An article in some editions on Aug. 4 about efforts in New Jersey to expand paid sick leave misstated part of the name of the group leading the coalition that seeks to put the issue on the ballot. It is the Working Families Alliance, not the Working Families Party.
match_headline: In New Jersey, Workers’ Advocates Aim to Put Paid Sick Time on Ballot

text: An article on Thursday about the digital music service SoundCloud misspelled the surname of the D.J. known as Kaskade, who criticized how it handles copyright violation notices from labels. He is Ryan Raddon, not Reddon.
match_headline: Popular and Free, SoundCloud Is Now Ready for Ads

text: An article on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about the revival of downtown Kansas City, Mo., as a residential area erroneously attributed a distinction to Commerce Tower. The six-story Boley Building, which opened in 1909 to house the Boley Clothing Company store, featured glass walls with terra cotta corners; Commerce Tower was not the city’s first structure with a glass curtain wall.
match_headline: Millennials Going to Kansas City, to Live and Work

text: An article last Monday about Rich Paul, LeBron James’s agent, misstated the location of Glenville, the neighborhood where Paul grew up. It is on the east side of Cleveland; it is not in East Cleveland, a suburb. The article also misstated, in some copies, the date that Paul called Dan Gilbert, the owner of the Cleveland Cavaliers, to inform him that James was returning to the team. It was July 11, not June 11.
match_headline: An Agent of Change

text: An obituary on Aug. 13 about Fabian G. Palomino, an adviser to several Democratic governors of New York State, referred imprecisely to his efforts, as chairman of the Battery Park City Authority, to arrange financing for the Museum of Jewish Heritage. Although he was involved in discussions with a developer, the deal that was being discussed fell through, and the museum eventually opened as a result of a different deal made after Mr. Palomino had left the authority; he did not help arrange financing for the museum.
match_headline: Fabian G. Palomino, 90, Legal Counsel to Democratic New York Governors, Dies

text: An article on Aug. 16 about a decision by the police department in Ferguson, Mo., to identify the officer involved in the fatal shooting of Michael Brown, using information from the department, misstated the number of years that the officer, Darren Wilson, has been a police officer. According to subsequent information from a public records request, Mr. Wilson has served with the Ferguson department for almost three years, not four, giving him five years of experience as a police officer, not six. The error was repeated in an accompanying article about the lives of Mr. Brown and Mr. Wilson.
match_headline: Emotions Flare in Missouri Amid Police Statements

text: An article last Tuesday about threats by prominent Afghans to install an interim government as Afghanistan’s election impasse drags on misspelled the middle name of President Hamid Karzai’s national security adviser. He is Rangin Dadfar Spanta, not Dafdar.
match_headline: Amid Election Impasse, Calls in Afghanistan for an Interim Government

text: An article on Saturday about the construction of the American Veterans Disabled for Life Memorial in Washington misspelled the surname of a senior associate for the architecture firm that designed the memorial. He is Doug Hays, not Hayes.
match_headline: A Prominent Location to Remember Veterans Who Were Wounded

text: An article on Monday about lawsuits filed by the City of Chicago and two California counties that accuse drug companies of marketing tactics that have fueled an epidemic of addiction and cost taxpayers millions of dollars misspelled the surname of the district attorney for Orange County in California who is involved in one of the suits. He is Tony Rackauckas, not Rakaukas.
match_headline: Chicago and 2 California Counties Sue Over Marketing of Painkillers

text: An article on Friday about a national poll that showed a sharp racial divide in the United States amid the unrest in Ferguson, Mo., misspelled the name of the hometown of Simone Grant, a saleswoman who discussed her perceptions of her local police department. It is Coram, N.Y., not Corum.
match_headline: Poll Shows Broad Divisions Amid Missouri Turmoil

text: An article in some editions on Aug. 14 about record rainfall on Long Island misidentified the road on which a maroon car was abandoned. It is the Southern State Parkway, not the Northern State Parkway.
match_headline: Rain on Long Island Breaks a Record, Floods Highways and Sets Cars Afloat

text: An article on Monday about the Yankees’ 7-4 victory over the Chicago White Sox in 10 innings referred incorrectly to closer David Robertson’s blown save. It was his only blown save in the six-game homestand, not his second. (He also lost one of the games, but it was in a nonsave situation.)
match_headline: McCann’s Dramatic Homer Is Welcome Sight for Yankees

text: An article last Tuesday about the Adaptive Climbing Group for amputee and disabled climbers gave an outdated name for the medical practice of Dr. Jeffrey M. Cohen. It is now Rusk Rehabilitation, no longer Rusk Institute of Rehabilitation Medicine. The article also erroneously included a paraclimber among those who participated in a contest last summer. Jon Sedor was not among them.
match_headline: A Group Lifts Paraclimbers to Higher Goals

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor and director Richard Attenborough misstated part of the name of a school where he was a student and later president. It is the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (not Arts).
match_headline: Richard Attenborough, Actor, Director and Giant of British Film, Dies at 90

text: An article on Monday about the life of Michael Brown, the unarmed teenager killed by a police officer in Ferguson, Mo., misstated the surname of Mr. Brown’s uncle, who recalled talking to his nephew about how to interact with police officers. He is Bernard Ewing, not Ewings.
match_headline: Michael Brown Spent Last Weeks Grappling With Problems and Promise

text: An article on Saturday about the Republican primary election for governor in Arizona referred incorrectly to two endorsements received by one candidate, Doug Ducey. The endorsements came from Glenn Hamer, president of the Arizona Chamber of Commerce, and Cathi Herrod, president of the Center for Arizona Policy; the organizations themselves did not endorse the candidates. The article also described incorrectly the 47,000 independent voters who had requested Republican ballots in Maricopa County. The number is more than all of the independent voters who cast ballots in the county — not the country — in the 2012 primary election.
match_headline: As Arizona Primary Nears, Governor Candidates Turn Eyes to Border

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the possibility that the Plaza Hotel could change ownership misidentified a hotel chain in which Prince Al-Waleed bin Talal of Saudi Arabia, a Plaza stakeholder, has holdings. It is the Four Seasons, not the Ritz-Carlton.
match_headline: Legal Woes of Owners Help Put the Plaza Back in Play

text: An article on Saturday about opposition to efforts to revive mines in California’s Gold Country referred incorrectly to one mine that may be reopened near Nevada City, Calif. It has the potential to produce 240,000 ounces of gold, which would need to be extracted from several million tons of gravel; it would not produce 240,000 ounces of ore. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Efforts to Revive Rich California Mine Hit Strong Resistance

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Friday with an article about the Yankees’ 3-0 victory over the Houston Astros misidentified, in some copies, a player who scored one of the Yankees’ second-inning runs. He is Chase Headley, not Carlos Corporan. (Headley was shown sliding past Corporan, the Houston catcher.)
match_headline: With Extra Pep, McCarthy Prevents Sweep With a Shutout

text: An article on Tuesday about Miley Cyrus’s appearance at the MTV Video Music Awards, where she sent a homeless man named Jesse Helt to the stage to accept her award for video of the year, described incorrectly a similar incident at the Academy Awards in 1973. At that show, Marlon Brando sent a woman named Sacheen Littlefeather to decline — not accept — his award for best actor (for “The Godfather”) as a protest against the movie industry’s treatment of Native Americans.
match_headline: VMAs 2014: Miley Cyrus Causes a Stir Again, This Time by Staying in Her Seat

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Emmy Awards described incorrectly the role played by Ty Burrell on the show “Modern Family.” Mr. Burrell, who won an Emmy for best supporting actor in a comedy, plays the son-in-law of the show’s grumpy patriarch — not the patriarch, who is played by Ed O’Neill.
match_headline: Emmys 2014: ‘Breaking Bad’ and ‘Modern Family’ Take Top Honors

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with a critic’s notebook article about the MTV Video Music Awards reversed the given and middle names of Beyoncé and Jay Z’s daughter. She is Blue Ivy Carter. (Her father’s real name is Shawn Carter.)
match_headline: Pop’s Newborns Dominate Video Music Awards Ceremony

text: A report in the Front Burner column last Wednesday about Chili Lab Chili Butters misstated the telephone number for Greene Grape Provisions, a retail source for the butters. It is 718-233-2700.
match_headline: Montauk Pearl Oysters for Your Kitchen and More

text: An editorial on Tuesday about a detention center in New Mexico referred incorrectly to immigrants’ legal rights. They have a right to have a lawyer, but they do not have a right to free legal counsel paid by the government.
match_headline: Deported From the Middle of Nowhere

text: An article on Sunday about events immediately after the shooting of Michael Brown, the unarmed teenager killed by a police officer in Ferguson, Mo., misstated the given name and the surname of Mr. Brown’s uncle, who was shown in a video walking up to the police tape and staring at Mr. Brown’s body. He is Bernard Ewing, not Brendan Ewings.
match_headline: Timeline for a Body: 4 Hours in the Middle of a Ferguson Street

text: An article on Friday about the closing of McDonald’s restaurants in Moscow by the Russian government as tensions with the West over the crisis in Ukraine escalate misstated the number of McDonald’s in Russia. There are 435, not 437.
match_headline: A Fast-Food Symbol of America Falls in Moscow

text: An article on Tuesday about the popularity of an instant-messaging app called Hike, which allows young Indians to conceal aspects of their social lives from their families, misidentified the Indian state in which Rohtak, a city where a graduate student who uses Hike lives, is situated. It is in Haryana, not Punjab.
match_headline: In India, an App for Chats and for Keeping Secrets

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about the Rev. Al Sharpton’s expanded profile, especially in race relations, misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a former governor of New York who attended a march led by Mr. Sharpton last week protesting the death of Eric Garner in police custody. The former governor is David A. Paterson, not Patterson.
match_headline: A Slimmed-Down Al Sharpton Savors an Expanded Profile

text: A picture caption on Aug. 19 with an article about heightened fear among livery cabdrivers after two were killed in recent weeks carried an incorrect date. The picture, of livery cabs waiting for fares under the No. 1 train line, was taken on June 10, 2013 — not the day before the article was published.
match_headline: Livery Drivers Are on Edge After Two Killings This Month in the Bronx

text: An article on Tuesday about Burger King’s merger ambitions and its growth strategy, using information from a company representative, misstated the age of the chain’s chief executive, Daniel Schwartz He is 34, not 33.
match_headline: TV Chief Takes 2-by-4 to a Proposed Cable Merger

text: A news analysis article last Thursday about the effect of the female pitcher Mo’ne Davis’s success in the Little League World Series quoted incorrectly, in some editions, from comments that James B. Peterson, director of the department of Africana studies at Lehigh University, made about Davis to The Philadelphia Inquirer. He said, “The emergence of Mo’ne is a great relief,” not “The emergence of Mo’ne has been a relief.”
ref_headline: The emergence of Mo’ne is a great relief,
match_headline: A Young Player’s Achievements Resonate Beyond a Sport

text: An article last Thursday about Rory McIlroy’s recent string of successes on the PGA Tour referred incorrectly to Adam Scott’s world ranking since last year’s Barclays tournament. This year, Scott rose to No. 1 from No. 2 in mid-May and spent 11 weeks as the top-ranked player before returning to No. 2, his current ranking. After winning the Barclays last year, he did not move to “No. 2 in the rankings, where he has stayed.”
ref_headline: No. 2 in the rankings, where he has stayed.
match_headline: A Major Champion Adjusts to Life as a Major Celebrity

text: An article on Tuesday about a Liberian doctor with Ebola who died after being given ZMapp, an experimental drug, misstated the efficacy against Ebola of the drug called favipiravir or Avigan. It has been shown to be effective against mice; it is not the case that it has not worked against Ebola at all.
match_headline: Liberian Doctor Treated With an Experimental Drug Dies From Ebola

text: An article on Thursday about a 9-year-old girl at a shooting range who accidentally killed her instructor with an Uzi submachine gun misstated the direction the girl had turned before firing the weapon. She turned her torso to the right, not to the left. The article also misidentified, in some editions, the location of a 2008 gun show and the home state of an 8-year-old who was killed at that event. The show was in Massachusetts, not Connecticut, and the 8-year-old was from Connecticut, not from Massachusetts.
match_headline: A 9-Year-Old at a Shooting Range, a Spraying Uzi and Outrage

text: A picture caption last Friday with an article about a reporter’s exploration of her grandfather’s role in a bloody clash between German and French troops at the French village of Mercy-le-Haut in August 1914 misidentified the field in which Hubert Lebrun, who was also researching the battle, was shown standing. It is the field from which German soldiers attacked French soldiers on Aug. 22, 1914 — not the field where German soldiers slept on the night of Aug. 21, 1914.
match_headline: In Steps of Grandfather, a German Soldier in France

text: An article on Monday about the final round of the Barclays golf tournament described incorrectly the position of one of the eventual winner’s shots on the final hole. Hunter Mahan’s approach shot from 140 yards landed near a bunker, not in one — the shot found rough, not sand — before he finished with a bogey. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption. The article also misstated the timing of Mahan’s withdrawal from the 2013 Canadian Open to be at his daughter’s birth. It was before the third round, not after it.
match_headline: At Barclays, Two Surprise Guests, One of Them Tiny, Greet Hunter Mahan

text: An article on Monday about the Mets’ 11-3 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers misstated the given name of a Mets player. He is Daniel Murphy, not David.
match_headline: With a Future in Question, a Showing Beyond Doubt

text: An article on Wednesday about competition among broadcasters, cable networks and digital media companies at the Emmy Awards misstated the number of awards won by HBO at the ceremony on Monday night. It was four, not three. (The network also won 15 Emmys at a ceremony earlier in August.)
match_headline: Explaining Status Quo at Emmy Awards

text: An article on Tuesday about South Africa’s progress against AIDS misspelled the name of the town in the dateline. The misspelling was repeated in a later reference in the article. The town northeast of Pretoria that was cited as an example of such progress is Verena, not Vervena.
match_headline: AIDS Progress in South Africa Is in Peril

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the museum curator Sam Hunter erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He was one of the first recipients of a Hubbard Hutchinson Fellowship from Williams College, not the first. The obituary also misstated the purpose of the fellowship. It is intended to support further work in the fields of writing, art, dance, theater and music; it is not limited to postgraduate work. And the obituary misspelled the surname of an artist who ran a school Mr. Hunter attended. He was Hans Hofmann, not Hoffmann.
match_headline: Sam Hunter, Curator and Museum Founder, Dies at 91

text: An article on Thursday about a report on the deaths and injuries caused by cluster bombs in the Syrian civil war overstated the number of cluster bombs Israel dropped on Lebanon during the conflict with Hezbollah in 2006. It was about 1,800 bombs, containing more than 1.2 million bomblets; it was not “hundreds of thousands” of cluster bombs.
match_headline: Heavy Use of Banned Cluster Bombs Reported in Syria

text: An article on Aug. 22 about the federal government’s tightening restrictions on hydrocodone, the nation’s most widely prescribed painkiller, referred imprecisely to the new rule. While it moves more than 60 products containing hydrocodone into a more restrictive category under the Controlled Substances Act, the new rule does not place hydrocodone itself in that category. (Until now, only one hydrocodone-based drug, Zohydro, which received regulatory approval last fall, had been in the restrictive category.)
match_headline: In Move to Curb Drug Abuse, D.E.A. Tightens Rule on Widely Prescribed Painkiller

text: An article on Thursday about an admission by the University of Southern California football player Josh Shaw that he fabricated a story about the circumstances in which he recently injured his ankles misspelled, in some editions, the name of a celebrity his lawyer has represented. She is Rihanna, not Rhianna.
match_headline: Josh Shaw of U.S.C. Says He Lied About Saving Drowning Nephew

text: A report in the Weekend Miser column on Friday about historic sites in Manhattan associated with the Roosevelt family described incorrectly the schedule for tours of Roosevelt House, at 47-49 East 65th Street, where Franklin D. Roosevelt lived with his wife, Eleanor, and mother, Sara Delano Roosevelt. Free guided tours are available on Saturdays — not Fridays — with a suggested donation of $10. (Group tours are available on Fridays by reservation.)
match_headline: Two Roosevelts and Their Legacies

text: An article last Sunday about dissension among unions over participation in a march on Staten Island to protest the death of a man in police custody misstated, in some editions, part of the name of a major police union. It is the Patrolmen’s Benevolent Association, not the Police Benevolent Association. The article also misspelled the surname of the president of the Retail Wholesale and Department Store Union, which participated in the march. He is Stuart Appelbaum, not Applebaum.
match_headline: Unions Face Backlash for Joining March on Staten Island

text: An article on Page 20 today reports on the possibility of abortions at home as fewer women have access to abortion clinics, including in Texas. After the magazine had gone to press, a federal judge blocked a Texas law that was expected to result in closing all but six clinics (with two more under construction). Texas officials said they would appeal the ruling.
match_headline: The Dawn of the Post-Clinic Abortion

text: A picture caption on Aug. 17 with an article about Aaron Siegel, who invests in distressed consumer debt, misidentified the location of a Buffalo house that is now home to Siegel’s private equity firm. The house is on Delaware Avenue, not Franklin Street. The article also misstated the value of a package of debt that McKellar and Associates Group purchased for 12 basis points. That comes out to about one-eighth of a penny on the dollar, not one-twelfth of a penny on the dollar.
match_headline: Former Goldman Executive to Head Southeast Asia Private Equity Firm

text: An article last Sunday about Lauren Gunderson’s new play, “Bauer,” which focuses on the artist Rudolf Bauer, referred incorrectly to Hilla Rebay, who was once his lover and who helped shape the creation of the Guggenheim Museum. She was from an “aristocratic family,” but it was not Jewish.
match_headline: A Failed Love and a Museum’s Birth

text: An article last Sunday about the people who vote for the Emmys misidentified the network that airs the television drama “The Divide.” It is WE tv, not Lifetime.
match_headline: Emmys 2014: Tunnel Vision vs. Industry Buzz

text: A review on Aug. 10 about “Strange Glory,” Charles Marsh’s biography of the German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, misstated the surname of one of Bonhoeffer’s professors at Friedrich Wilhelms University in Berlin. He was Reinhold Seeberg, not Seeburg.
match_headline: Between God and the Führer

text: A review on Aug. 17 about “Churchill and Empire: A Portrait of an Imperialist,” by Lawrence James, referred imprecisely to A. J. Balfour’s signing of the declaration that bears his name. While he was indeed a British prime minister (from 1902 to 1905), he was foreign secretary when he signed the document in 1917.
ref_headline: Churchill and Empire: A Portrait of an Imperialist,
match_headline: Imperial Son

text: A report last Sunday in the Arena column about “Play With Fire,” a fund-raising event for family-run farms organized by the Northern Chefs Alliance, transposed the identities of two chefs shown. Zakary Pelaccio was at the far right and Matty Matheson was next to him, not the reverse.
match_headline: Emails Show Bigger Fund-Raising Role for Wisconsin Leader

text: A picture last Sunday with an article about a section of  the Marylebone neighborhood in London that is popular with celebrities was published in error. The photograph showed Trunk Clothiers, a men’s wear shop not mentioned in the article; the picture was not of Trunk Labs, a sister shop of Trunk Clothiers. In addition, the article referred incorrectly to the location of Trunk Labs. It is down the street from the Monocle Cafe, not next door to it.
match_headline: Adding Celebrity Sizzle to a London Neighborhood

text: An article on Friday about Sam Kass, the Obamas’ personal chef, referred incorrectly to the area in which he grew up. Mr. Kass is from Hyde Park, a neighborhood in Chicago; it is not a separate town in Illinois.
match_headline: Sam Kass, the Obamas’ Foodmaster General

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Aug. 22 about a teenage boy who died from injuries suffered in a clash in an Ebola-stricken neighborhood in Monrovia, Liberia, gave an incorrect cause of death from a doctor. The boy died of hypovolemic shock, or severe blood and fluid loss — not from hypothermic shock.
match_headline: Liberian Boy Dies After Being Shot During Clash Over Ebola Quarantine

text: An article on Wednesday about a celebration in Queens honoring the Hindu deity Ganesha, using information from festival organizers, misidentified the oboelike instrument that was played at some of the proceedings. It is a nadaswaram, which is more popularly used in southern India; it is not a shehnai, which is more popular in the country’s north.
match_headline: With Bells and Bananas, a Time to Worship Ganesh

text: An obituary on Friday about David Rosand, an art historian and author who specialized in 16th-century Venetian painting, referred incorrectly to his son Eric. Though he went to law school, he is not a lawyer. The obituary also misspelled the name of a home in Italy bequeathed to Columbia University, in part through the efforts of Professor Rosand. It is Casa Muraro, not Casa Murano.
match_headline: David Rosand, an Art History Scholar Whose Heart Was in Venice, Dies at 75

text: An obituary on July 19 about the German artist Otto Piene misstated the number of grandchildren who survive him. There are five, not four. (Mr. Piene’s daughter pointed out the error in an email on Aug. 24.)
match_headline: Otto Piene, German Artist of New Modes, Dies at 85

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the unlikely alliance of American warplanes and Iranian-backed militias that broke a siege by Sunni extremists of the Iraqi town of Amerli referred incorrectly, in some editions, to the Badr Corps militia. The Badr Corps is linked to Iran and is headed by Iraq’s transportation minister, Hadi al-Ameri. It is not linked to the Shiite cleric Moktada al-Sadr.
match_headline: U.S. and Iran Unlikely Allies in Iraq Battle

text: An article on Monday about the Yankees’ 4-3 loss to the Toronto Blue Jays misstated the surname of the Yankees bench coach who was ejected in the seventh inning for arguing balls and strikes. He is Tony Pena, not Perez.
match_headline: Jays Honor Jeter in Final Visit but Treat His Team Rudely

text: An article on Tuesday about a trip to Mexico by Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey that offers him a chance to demonstrate a grasp of international affairs as he considers a run for the presidency misstated the background of Robert B. Zoellick, an informal adviser to Mr. Christie. While Mr. Zoellick did serve in the State Department, he was not a career diplomat.
match_headline: Christie Studies Foreign Affairs for a 2016 Test

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about interviews with three Americans who have been detained in North Korea referred incorrectly, in some editions, to Miamisburg, Ohio, the hometown of one of the prisoners, Jeffrey Edward Fowle. It is a suburb of Dayton, not Akron.
match_headline: In Interviews, 3 Americans Held in North Korea Plead for U.S. Help

text: An article on Monday about a chess tournament in Las Vegas that will offer $1 million in prizes misstated the meaning of the name of a store founded by Amy Lee, who is financing the event. The store, Amy’s Loonie-Toonie, was named for two Canadian coins, the one dollar “loonie,” which has a loon on one side, and, in a portmanteau of the words two and loonie, the nickname for the two-dollar coin, the “toonie.” It was not named for the two sides of the one-dollar coin.
match_headline: Millionaire Chess to Hit Las Vegas, in Gambit to Raise Game’s Profile With Big Prizes

text: An article on Tuesday in some editions about Hanniel Levenson, an associate rabbi with the unaffiliated Jewish Center of the Hamptons, who includes surfing and other outdoor activities as part of a “spiritual playground,” erroneously attributed a distinction to the Hampton Synagogue in Westhampton Beach on Long Island. It is not the only Orthodox congregation in the area. There are a number of Chabad Lubavitch congregations in the Hamptons, which are also Orthodox.
match_headline: A Rabbi’s ‘Spiritual Playground’ Extends to the Surf

text: A critic’s notebook article on Aug. 13 about two productions of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” at the Stratford Shakespeare Festival in Stratford, Ontario, referred incorrectly to the actor Michael Spencer-Davis, who plays Egeus in the production directed by Chris Abraham. While the character is portrayed as deaf, Mr. Spencer-Davis is not deaf himself.
match_headline: Beyond Shakespeare’s Wildest Dreams

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about Glenn Cornick, the original bassist in the band Jethro Tull, misstated the year the photo was taken. The picture, of Mr. Cornick and the other members of Jethro Tull, is from 1968, not 1969.
match_headline: Glenn Cornick, Original Bassist in Jethro Tull, Dies at 67

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a study on the effects of taxi-ride sharing in New York City referred incorrectly at one point to an expert who commented on the findings. As the article noted elsewhere, the expert, Luis M. A. Bettencourt of the Santa Fe Institute in New Mexico, is a man — not “she.” And the caption for a map with the article, showing taxi pickups and drop-offs in the city, misstated the year the data was collected. It was 2011, not 2001.
match_headline: If 2 New Yorkers Shared a Cab ...

text: An article on Wednesday about the tactical discussions doubles partners in professional tennis have between points misspelled the surname of a player. As a picture caption with the article correctly noted, he is Bradley Klahn, not Kahn.
match_headline: All That Back and Forth at the U.S. Open, Between Doubles Partners

text: An article on Tuesday about the crumbling infrastructure of Los Angeles misstated the size of the city’s annual budget. It is $8.1 billion, not $26 billion, which is the budget of Los Angeles County.
match_headline: Infrastructure Cracks as Los Angeles Defers Repairs

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an article about the challenges facing the Hong Kong democracy movement after the imposition of a restrictive voting plan by the Chinese authorities gave an incorrect description, in some editions, of what was occurring in a Reuters photograph and also misidentified the photographer. The photograph was of a clash involving demonstrators and the police outside a hotel. It was not an interruption of a speech by demonstrators. The photograph was taken by Tyrone Siu, not Bobby Yip.
match_headline: Democracy Backers in Hong Kong Face Tough Choices

text: A map that accompanied an article on Monday about the effects that plans for a new capital for the recently divided Indian state of Andhra Pradesh are having on a remote part of the state reversed the positions of the towns of Vijayawada and Agiripalli. Vijayawada is just north of the Krishna River and Agiripalli is northeast of Vijayawada, not the other way around.
match_headline: Redrawing a State in India Drives Land Prices to the Sky

text: An article on Sunday about a pending guilty plea from Charles Shrem, a prominent supporter of the digital currency Bitcoin, misstated in one instance which office was handling the prosecution of Mr. Shrem on charges of aiding and abetting the operation of an unlicensed money transfer business. As noted at one point in the article, it is the United States attorney’s office, led by Preet Bharara, not the Manhattan district attorney’s office.
match_headline: Top Bitcoin Proponent to Plead Guilty to Federal Charge

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts to improve robots’ touch and motion control misspelled the surname of a Stanford education professor who helped develop kits that can be programmed to create virtual devices like springs and dampers. He is Paulo Blikstein, not Blickstein. The article also referred incompletely to the design of the kits; they were designed by a team, not by Dr. Blikstein alone. And a picture credit with the article misidentified the photographer who took a picture of Stanford graduate students testing bands that vibrate in response to arm motions. He is John Todd, not Kristina Copplin.
match_headline: Brainy, Yes, but Far From Handy

text: An article on Wednesday about the risks involved when Chinese fighter jets confront American surveillance planes misspelled the given name of a political science professor at Lingnan University in Hong Kong. He is Zhang Baohui, not Baohai.
match_headline: Air Encounter More Likely to Cause Alarm Than Change

text: An article on Monday about NATO’s lack of preparedness for cyberattacks misidentified the organization for which Julianne Smith, a former Pentagon official who was quoted in the article, works. She is at the Center for a New American Security, not the New America Foundation.
match_headline: NATO Set to Ratify Pledge on Joint Defense in Case of Major Cyberattack

text: An article on Aug. 9 about a joint statement issued by Afghanistan’s rival presidential candidates reaffirming their commitment to accept the results of an internationally monitored recount referred incompletely to the person who would assume the new post of Afghan chief executive under a power-sharing arrangement brokered by Secretary of State John Kerry. The post would go to either the losing candidate or someone he nominated; it would not necessarily go to the losing candidate.
match_headline: Afghan Rivals Back a Deal, Once More, for President

text: Because of an editing error, the Deal Professor column on Wednesday, about the definition of “closely held corporation” for purposes of determining religious protection from federal law, misstated when the Religious Freedom Restoration Act was enacted. It was 1993, not 1933.
match_headline: The Medicare Miracle

text: An obituary on Aug. 27 about the documentary filmmaker William Greaves referred incompletely to the name of a documentary he directed for public television in 1968, and contained an incomplete credit for it. The film was originally broadcast as “Still a Brother: Inside the Negro Middle Class”; it was later retitled “Still a Brother: Inside the Black Middle Class.” And it was made by Mr. Greaves in collaboration with William B. Branch, who wrote and produced it — not solely by Mr. Greaves.
ref_headline: Still a Brother: Inside the Negro Middle Class
match_headline: William Greaves, a Documentarian and Pioneering Journalist, Dies at 87

text: An article on Thursday about how the World Health Organization’s response to the Ebola crisis has been hampered by budget cutbacks referred imprecisely to the W.H.O. donors whose desire to advance specific causes influenced the organization’s agenda. They include governments and foundations, as well as private individuals.
match_headline: Cuts at W.H.O. Hurt Response to Ebola Crisis

text: An article on Thursday about concerns by the World Health Organization over a second Ebola cluster in Nigeria referred incorrectly to Lagos. It is Nigeria’s largest city, not its capital.
match_headline: W.H.O. Concerned About Another Ebola Cluster in Nigeria

text: An article on Aug. 25 about the unexpected release of an American writer, Peter Theo Curtis, who had been held captive in Syria by the Nusra Front, an affiliate of Al Qaeda, misstated the location of the home of Amy Rosen, a cousin of Mr. Curtis who spoke for his family, and misidentified the state to which Mr. Curtis moved after receiving his doctorate. Ms. Rosen lives in New Jersey, not New York, and Mr. Curtis moved to Vermont, not New Hampshire. The article also misquoted Ms. Rosen’s statement thanking Qatar for its role. She said,  “Our family wants to thank the country of Qatar in a big way,” not “My family.”
ref_headline: Our family wants to thank the country of Qatar in a big way,
match_headline: U.S. Writer Held by Qaeda Affiliate in Syria Is Freed After Nearly 2 Years

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about two booksellers opening stores on the Upper West Side misstated the number of bookstores that the Borders chain had in Manhattan. It had five, not three.
match_headline: Signs of Literary Life for Two Booksellers on the Upper West Side

text: A report in the Observatory column on Tuesday about researchers’ detecting subatomic particles called neutrinos produced at the core of the sun misstated their speed. They travel to Earth at almost the speed of light, not the speed of light. (Neutrinos have mass, so they cannot be as fast as light.)
match_headline: Research Aimed at the Heart of the Sun

text: A picture caption with an article on Aug. 19 about China’s efforts to promote social harmony with folk tales portraying ethnic minorities as contented members of an extended family referred incorrectly to the ethnically divided Xinjiang, in China’s far west. It is a region, not a province.
match_headline: In China, Myths of Social Cohesion

text: An article on Aug. 29 about the sharp increase in evictions around the country misstated the length of time that a tenant in Milwaukee, Celeste Wilson, had rented her home before she was evicted. It was seven months, not five years.
match_headline: Evictions Soar in Hot Market; Renters Suffer

text: A picture caption on Friday with an art review of “Willem van Genk: Mind Traffic” and “Ralph Fasanella: Lest We Forget” at the American Folk Art Museum in Manhattan, using information from the exhibition, misstated the year Mr. Fasanella finished the painting “Farewell Comrade/End of the Cold War.” It was 1996, not 1999. (Mr. Fasanella died in 1997.)
match_headline: Visionaries Inhabiting the Margins

text: An essay accompanying the Album column’s picture display in some editions today misstates the birthplace of Arlene Gottfried, the featured photographer. She was born in Brownsville, Brooklyn, not Crown Heights.
match_headline: Her Villages

text: An article last Sunday about artists’ images of war and the exhibition “The Disasters of War, 1800-2014,” at the Louvre-Lens museum in France, referred incompletely to the printmaking methods Francisco de Goya used in his “Disasters of War” series. Many of the works, some featured in the Louvre-Lens show, were done as etchings, though some were executed as engravings.
match_headline: Horror Is a Constant, as Artists Depict War

text: An article last Sunday about Surfer magazine’s founder, John Severson, referred incorrectly to the publication’s evolution. It was published quarterly following its introduction as an annual; it was never published semiannually.
match_headline: The Memories Come Back in Waves

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Pedro Porro and David Loud referred incorrectly to Mr. Loud’s work in the theater. He is a vocal arranger and a music director, not a director of Broadway shows.
match_headline: Pedro Porro, David Loud

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Dr. Florencia Segura and Dr. Ali Damavandy referred incorrectly to the role that the bride’s mother, Alejandra M. Segura, played in the Spanish Catholic Center, a charity in Washington. She has helped with fund-raising; she has not been on its board.
match_headline: Florencia Segura, Ali Damavandy

text: Because of an editing error, a report last Sunday about the marriage of Sandy Jabado and Brett Benowitz misstated a sequence of events during the couple’s time in college. The bride was not a Columbia student when the groom transferred there; as correctly stated elsewhere in the report, the bride was at Fordham University at the time.
match_headline: Two Worlds That Came Together Online

text: A review last Sunday about the 2015 Subaru Outback reversed, in some copies, the second and third columns of type. The correct version can be found at nytimes.com/autos .
match_headline: Few Thrills, but More Frills

text: An article on Aug. 24 about the tennis player Eugenie Bouchard misspelled the surname of a player against whom Bouchard played. She is Ana Ivanovic, not Ivanovich.
match_headline: Eugenie Bouchard Could Be Tennis’s Next Big Shot

text: An article on Wednesday about the wariness of European leaders to confront Russia over the Ukraine crisis as President Vladimir V. Putin has moved aggressively to aid separatists misstated the location of the Royal United Services Institute, where Shashank Joshi, who was quoted in the article, is a senior researcher. It is  in London, not Washington.
match_headline: U.S. and Europe Are Struggling With Response to a Bold Russia

text: An article on Aug. 28 about clashes between Syrian government forces and Islamist militants near the Golan Heights referred imprecisely to the Golan at one point. Although Israel seized the territory from Syria in the 1967 Six Day War and effectively annexed it in 1981, much of the world considers it illegally occupied.
match_headline: Syrian Rebels Take Control of Crossing in the Golan

text: An article on Thursday about plans to reopen an abortion clinic in McAllen, Tex., after a federal court ruling misstated the number of bus passes or sums for gas money the clinic had distributed to women seeking treatment since its closing last fall. The clinic has given out 15 to 20 in total, not 15 to 20 a week.
match_headline: Texas Abortion Clinic to Reopen After Ruling

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Aug. 30 about an IBM project to turn each match of the United States Open tennis tournament into a live-streamed electronic score misidentified the company for which the developer Patrick Gunderson, a collaborator on the project, works. It is the digital production company Tool, not IBM.
match_headline: Even Amid Swirling Winds, Serena Williams Coasts Into Third Round

text: An article on Sunday about President Obama’s decision to delay immigration action until after the midterm elections erroneously included one Democratic senator among several who told White House officials that any action by Mr. Obama before the elections could cost them victory in the Senate. Senator Mark Pryor of Arkansas was not one of them.
match_headline: Obama Delays Immigration Action, Yielding to Democratic Concerns

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Aug. 19 about a sharp increase in the numbers of killings, injuries and abductions of international aid workers misstated the preliminary figure for the number of aid workers killed in 2014 as of mid-August. At the time, it was at least 79, not 83.
match_headline: Attacks on Aid Workers Jump Worldwide, Group Says

text: An article on Saturday about the pending initial offering of the Chinese Internet company Alibaba misstated the amount of money its underwriting banks are expected to share if the stock sale prices at the high end. It is just over $200 million, not just over $2 billion.
match_headline: Lower-Frequency Platform IEX Raises Funding to Become Full Stock Market

text: An article on Saturday about the August jobs report misstated, in some copies, the most recent month in which job creation fell below 200,000. It was January, not February. (The data for January was released in February.).
match_headline: Job Growth Is Sluggish, Raising Fear of Malaise

text: Because of an editing error, the TV Watch column on Monday, about Chuck Todd’s debut as host of “Meet the Press,” referred incorrectly in some editions to the actions of David Gregory, Mr. Todd’s predecessor, in making a point about gun control in 2012. He displayed a gun magazine on the air, not a loaded gun.
match_headline: Meet the Host: Defying the Rules

text: An article on Wednesday about plans for the restoration of the installation “Meeting” by the artist James Turrell at MoMA PS1 in Queens misstated the price being asked for Mr. Turrell’s apartment on Gramercy Park West, which was renovated by Janet Cross of Cross Architecture, a firm seen as a candidate to carry out the “Meeting” restoration. It is $2.85 million — not $2.2 million, which is the price for his apartment on Gramercy Park South that is for sale.
match_headline: A View of the Heavens Needs Some Retouching

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the New Yorker Festival next month referred incorrectly to the scheduled showing of the film “Listen Up Philip,” directed by Alex Ross Perry. It was shown at the Sundance Film Festival in January; its screening at the New Yorker Festival will not be its United States premiere.
match_headline: New Yorker Festival to Feature Larry David

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about an event remembering Robin Williams scheduled for Wednesday at Florence Gould Hall of the French Institute Alliance Français in Manhattan misstated the order of events. A panel discussion will occur before, not after, a screening of “Dead Poets Society.”
match_headline: Spare Times for Sept. 5-11

text: An obituary on Monday about Penelope Niven, the author of an acclaimed biography of the poet Carl Sandburg, misstated the name of the town in North Carolina where she was born. It is Waxhaw, not Waxhew.
match_headline: Penelope Niven, Carl Sandburg Biographer, Dies at 75

text: An article on Aug. 19 about a campaign by Iraqi and Kurdish forces, with the support of American airstrikes, to seize the Mosul Dam in Iraq from Sunni militants misidentified the forces that control Iraq’s Haditha Dam. It is under the control of Iraqi security forces and allied tribes, not Sunni militants.
match_headline: Troops in Iraq Rout Sunni Militants From a Key Dam

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Aug. 5 about concerns in India over recruitment efforts by Islamist extremists after four young Muslim men from the city of Kalyan joined the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria referred incorrectly in some editions to Kashmir and Tamil Nadu. Kashmir is a region that straddles the border of India and Pakistan and Tamil Nadu is an Indian state; they are not a single region. The article was corrected online in August; this correction was delayed by an editing lapse.
match_headline: 4 Young Men Head for Iraq, Citing Fight for Islam, and India Wonders if More Will Follow

text: An article on Aug. 23 about the repercussions of an anti-Chinese tirade by the Australian mining magnate and politician Clive Palmer in a televised interview contained several errors.
match_headline: Case Against Australian Businessman Could Put a Hitch in His Swagger

text: An article on Aug. 29 about the popularity of a cellphone app called Red Alert, which sounds an alarm when rockets are fired into Israel from the Gaza Strip, referred incorrectly to the origins of the English-language version. Ron Dermer, Israel’s ambassador to the United States, contacted Kobi Snir, who developed the app with Ari Sprung, after a congressman heard the app go off on Mr. Dermer’s cellphone during a congressional subcommittee hearing and expressed interest in such a version. Mr. Dermer did not contact Mr. Sprung himself.
match_headline: An Israeli App Tracking the Gaza Conflict Has Followers Near and Far

text: An article in some editions on Aug. 29 about efforts by former students’ lawyers to reinstate a lawsuit claiming that Yeshiva University High School for Boys in Manhattan had covered up reports of sexual abuse misidentified the federal appeals judge who chided Karen Y. Bitar, a lawyer for the school. The comment — “Judge Koeltl knew what he was doing. I’m asking if you know what you are doing” — was made by Judge Guido Calabresi, not by Judge Reena Raggi.
ref_headline: Judge Koeltl knew what he was doing. I’m asking if you know what you are doing
match_headline: Lawyer Seeks to Reinstate Suit Over Alleged Abuse Cover-Up at Yeshiva High

text: An article on Monday about a plan by Jimmy Dean to introduce products for lunch and dinner misstated the surname of the actor who portrays the sun-costume-wearing character in the brand’s commercials. He is Haynes Brooke, not Brooks.
match_headline: Jimmy Dean Goes From Breakfast Nook to Dinner Table

text: An article on Tuesday about the winners of the Albert and Mary Lasker Foundation medical science awards misstated, at one point, the surname of a winner of the award for basic medical research. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Peter Walter, not Walker.
match_headline: Lasker Winner Calls for More Genetic Testing for Cancer

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about a rebound in manufacturing in the Rust Belt as a result of a resurgence in energy production misstated the year when the straight-side press shown with Greg Hess, plant manager at Youngstown Bending and Rolling in Youngstown, Ohio, was built. It was in 1897, not 1819.
match_headline: Boom in Energy Spurs Industry in the Rust Belt

text: An article on Tuesday about a World Health Organization report that warned of an exponential rise in Ebola cases in Liberia reversed the maiden name and the surname of the Liberian president. She is Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.
match_headline: Ebola Cases Reported Up Sharply in Liberia

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a decision by prosecutors in Fall River, Mass., to drop charges against two environmental activists who blocked a coal delivery to a power plant referred incorrectly to legal action taken against the men. While the men were charged, they were not arrested. (The men quit the blockade after being ordered to do so by the Coast Guard and were charged later.)
match_headline: Charges Dropped Against Climate Activists

text: An article on Tuesday about a decision by the Virginia governor to reduce his plans to expand Medicaid misstated the number of states that have taken such action under the Affordable Care Act. It is 27, not 28.
match_headline: After First Plan Is Blocked, Virginia Governor Reduces Medicaid Expansion Goals

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Saturday with an article about a decision by New York City to require affordable housing for any development project that needs a zoning change omitted a credit. The photograph of Mayor Bill de Blasio, at a news conference in Brooklyn, was taken by Michael Nagle for The New York Times. And also because of an editing error, a picture of Carl Weisbrod, the chairman of the City Planning Commission, carried an erroneous credit. The photograph was taken for The New York Times by Michael Appleton, not by Mr. Nagle.
match_headline: New York Will Require More Builders to Add Affordable Units

text: An article on Aug. 27 about 15-year-old Catherine Bellis’s victory in the first round of the United States Open misstated the age of the Croatian player Donna Vekic, another teenager who played that day. She is 18, not 17.
match_headline: Youngest Player in Tournament Makes Biggest Splash

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a film review of the documentary “Born to Fly: Elizabeth Streb vs. Gravity,” carried an erroneous credit. The picture, showing members of Ms. Streb’s dance troupe, is by Aubin Pictures, not by Tom Caravaglia/Aubin Pictures.
ref_headline: Born to Fly: Elizabeth Streb vs. Gravity,
match_headline: A Pursuit That Leaps, Crashes and Swings

text: An obituary on Tuesday about S. Truett Cathy, the founder of the fast-food chain Chick-fil-A, misattributed, in some editions, a quotation about same-sex marriage, which was strongly opposed by a charitable arm of Mr. Cathy’s empire. It was Dan Cathy, Mr. Cathy’s son and the president of Chick-fil-A — not Mr. Cathy — who said, “As it relates to society in general, I think we are inviting God’s judgment on our nation when we shake our fist at Him and say, ‘We know better than you as to what constitutes a marriage.’ ” The obituary also misstated the decade during which Robert Woodruff, Mr. Cathy’s predecessor as a successful Southern entrepreneur, took over the Coca-Cola Company. It was in the 1920s, not the 1930s.
ref_headline: As it relates to society in general, I think we are inviting God’s judgment on our nation when we shake our fist at Him and say, ‘We know better than you as to what constitutes a marriage.’
match_headline: S. Truett Cathy, Chick-fil-A Founder, Dies at 93

text: An obituary on Saturday about Andrew Kay, the designer of the Kaypro II portable computer, referred incorrectly to the author Arthur C. Clarke. While he did acquire a Kaypro II, he did not use one to write his novel “2010: Odyssey Two.”
match_headline: Andrew Kay, Pioneer in Computing, Dies at 95

text: An article on Aug. 21 about a return to makeup looks from the 1990s misspelled the given name of a celebrity stylist who popularized Benefit Benetint, a cherry-colored lip and cheek stain. He was Kevyn Aucoin, not Kevin.
match_headline: The Face Is Familiar? It’s From the ’90s

text: An editorial on Monday about Texas’s voter ID law incorrectly stated that the Supreme Court struck down Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act. It struck down Section 4, which rendered Section 5 inoperable.
match_headline: Voter ID on Trial in Texas

text: An article on Wednesday about the struggles of small police departments to hire minority officers misstated part of the name of the parent organization where Nelson Lim, who discussed the issue, is a senior sociologist. It is the RAND Corporation, not the RAND Institute.
match_headline: Mostly White Forces in Mostly Black Towns: Police Struggle for Racial Diversity

text: An article on Wednesday about the release of an official 12,000-page history of the reign of Emperor Hirohito of Japan described incorrectly the document’s characterization of the emperor’s reaction to Japanese military successes in China during World War II. The document presented him as exulting over the victories, not “exalting.”
match_headline: Before Pearl Harbor, Emperor Warned Against War

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a protest on Interstate 70 near St. Louis over the shooting death of Michael Brown misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the road where a second, smaller demonstration occurred. It is South Florissant Road, not West Florissant Avenue.
match_headline: 35 Arrested as Missouri Police Block Protest on Highway Over Teenager’s Shooting

text: An article on Aug. 3 about concerns over the fate of the East Deck Motel in Montauk, N.Y., misstated the role of one of the hotel’s new investors, Scott Bradley, at Paddle Diva, a stand up paddle-boarding school. He teaches there, but he does not run it. This correction was delayed because the error was called to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Montauk for Members Only
