text: An article in some editions on Monday about the Electric Run, a race in Brooklyn with an electronic dance music theme, misstated part of the name of the nonprofit group that will receive proceeds from the event. It is Building Beats, not Breaking Beats.
match_headline: It’s Electric! Thousands Show Up for Zany Vibe and a Charity Run

text: An article on Monday about the movie “Love & Mercy,” a biography of the Beach Boys’ Brian Wilson, omitted the name of one of the film’s writers. Besides Oren Moverman, it was written by Michael Alan Lerner.
match_headline: Filmmaker Pins Hopes on a Beach Boy

text: An article on Monday about a documentary, “Electric Boogaloo: The Wild, Untold Story of Cannon Films,” misidentified the founders of the Cannon Group, which made the films. The group was founded in 1966 by Dennis Friedland and Christopher C. Dewey, not by Menahem Golan and Yoram Globus. (Mr. Golan and Mr. Globus took control of the company in 1979.)
ref_headline: Electric Boogaloo: The Wild, Untold Story of Cannon Films,
match_headline: Documentary Explores B-Film Kingdom of Golan and Globus

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the shortlist of writers for the 2014 Man Booker Prize for Fiction, widely considered the most prestigious literary award in Britain, misstated the change in the eligibility requirement. This is the first year the prize is open to writers from outside Ireland, the Commonwealth and former Commonwealth countries, provided they write in English and have been published in Britain. It is not the first year it is open to writers from outside the Commonwealth.
match_headline: Man Booker Prize Shortlist Announced

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary by The Associated Press on Sept. 4 about the singer Jimi Jamison misidentified the city where he died. It is Memphis, not Nashville.
match_headline: A Singer of Soul Goes in Search of His Own

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the jazz composer, arranger, bandleader and trumpeter Gerald Wilson referred incorrectly to part of Loren Schoenberg’s work in music. Besides being the artistic director of the National Jazz Museum in Harlem, Mr. Schoenberg, who was quoted praising Mr. Wilson, is a saxophonist and conductor, not a saxophonist and composer.
match_headline: Gerald Wilson, Versatile Jazz Arranger, Is Dead at 96

text: An editorial on Sept. 4 about Scotland’s independence vote in-correctly stated that Scotland and England have lived together in peace since 1707. In 1745, several Scottish clans joined Charles Edward Stuart in an uprising to reclaim the British throne, which was ultimately defeated.
match_headline: Scotland’s Identity, Put to a Vote

text: A picture credit in some editions on Thursday with the continuation of an article about President Obama’s authorization of a major expansion of the military campaign against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria misidentified the photographer. The picture of Mr. Obama shown on the telephone was taken by Stephen Crowley of The New York Times, not by Jim Watson of Agence France-Presse.
match_headline: Obama, in Speech on ISIS, Promises Sustained Effort to Rout Militants

text: An article on Thursday about the announcement that Mayor Rob Ford of Toronto had been hospitalized after learning that he had an abdominal tumor quoted incorrectly from comments by Dr. Rueben Devlin about a CT scan for Mr. Ford. Dr. Devlin said the scan revealed that “it wasn’t a small tumor, but the size isn’t as relevant as what it is” — not “as relative.”
ref_headline: it wasn’t a small tumor, but the size isn’t as relevant as what it is
match_headline: Rob Ford, Toronto Mayor, in Hospital With an Abdominal Tumor

text: An article on Thursday about Apple’s privacy challenges, using information from a company representative, described incorrectly restrictions on where app developers can store health information collected by the company’s forthcoming Apple Watch. While the information cannot be stored on Apple’s iCloud service, there are no restrictions on other cloud storage. It is not the case that developers cannot store the data “on cloud computing services.”
match_headline: With Apple Pay and Smartwatch, a Privacy Challenge

text: An article on Friday about a sports apparel company that used runners instead of professional models this week at its fashion show in New York misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the founder of the company, Oiselle. She is Sally Bergesen, not Bergeson.
match_headline: Runners Take the Place of Models During Fashion Week

text: An article on Friday about the first round of the Tour Championship in Atlanta misspelled the surname of one of the professional golfers in the event. He is Geoff Ogilvy, not Ogilvie.
match_headline: FedEx Cup Leaders Share First Place in Tour Championship

text: Because of an editing error, a letter to the sports editor in some editions on Aug. 31 about the Yankees’ retiring Joe Torre’s number misidentified the hometown of the letter writer, Hank Monaco. He is from Delray Beach, Fla., not Edmonton, Alberta.
match_headline: Letters to the Editor

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Marin Cilic’s victory over Roger Federer in the semifinals of the United States Open misstated the month in which Cilic returned from a four-month doping suspension. It was last October, not in February.
match_headline: Roger Federer Is Ousted by Marin Cilic in Semifinal

text: An article in the New Season issue last Sunday about seven people who are making their Broadway debuts misidentified the movie for which the director Bill Condon won an Oscar for screenwriting. Mr. Condon, who will make his Broadway directing debut with the coming play “Side Show,” won for “Gods and Monsters” — not for “Chicago.”
match_headline: My First Time (It’s a Little Scary)

text: An entry on Teyonah Parris and Tessa Thompson in an article in the New Season issue last Sunday about breakthrough performances in coming films reversed the attributions for quotations by the two actresses. It was Ms. Thompson who commented on race issues in their film “Dear White People” and Ms. Parris who noted that hers is the type of role she has been eager to take on. The entry also misidentified Ms. Parris’s hometown. She is from Hopkins, S.C., not from Atlanta.
match_headline: Breaths of Fresh Acting Talent

text: Because of an editing error, an article in the New Season issue last Sunday about new video games misstated the relationship between Warner Bros. and Monolith, maker of Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor. Warner Bros. owns Monolith; it is not one of Monolith’s affiliated studios. (Those studios include Rocksteady and Warner Bros. Games Montreal, the two studios that have made Batman Arkham games.)
match_headline: Incoming! Video Games Zero In

text: An article on Aug. 31 about the playwright Israel Horovitz and his new movie, “My Old Lady,” whose stars include Maggie Smith and Kristin Scott Thomas, misstated the relationship between Ms. Smith’s character and Ms. Scott Thomas’s in the movie “Gosford Park.”  Ms. Smith played her aunt, not her mother.
match_headline: Glad to Try ‘Something Terrifying’

text: A picture credit last Sunday with a report in the Arena column about Tutto Il Giorno, a restaurant in TriBeCa, misidentified the photographer. The picture of the restaurant’s dining area was taken by Luca Pioltelli — not by Luca Babini, another photographer.
match_headline: Restaurant Story

text: A caption with a photo of people snorkeling in the cover article on Aug. 31 about the Maldives, where luxury resorts coexist with a sometimes strict Islamic culture, misspelled in one instance the name of the island where a Holiday Inn is situated. It is Kandooma Fushi island, as mentioned elsewhere, not Kanduma Fushi.
match_headline: 1,000 Islands, 2 Worlds

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about Jack Ma, the founder of Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce company, misidentified two people standing with him during a visit to Seattle in the 1990s. They are Dave and Dolores Selig, not Bill and Merrilie Aho.
match_headline: The Jack Ma Way

text: An article last Sunday about Christian Rudder, the president of OkCupid, a dating website, rendered incorrectly part of a quotation from his book “Dataclysm,” in which he argues for wider study of people’s online behavior. He wrote that OkCupid’s data presented “an irresistible sociological opportunity,” not “an irresistible social opportunity.”
match_headline: OkCupid’s Unblushing Analyst of Attraction

text: An article on Aug. 31 about Senator Mitch McConnell’s campaign for a sixth term misstated the significance of his win in his first Senate race in 1984. McConnell was the only Republican challenger that year to defeat a Democratic incumbent in the Senate, not the only one to do so in the Senate or the House.
match_headline: Mitch McConnell Is Headed Down the Stretch

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts by the Genting Group, a Malaysian conglomerate that is bidding for the right to build a casino in Tuxedo, N.Y., misstated part of the name of an environmental organization that opposes the project. It is the Natural Resources Defense Council, not the National Resources Defense Council.
match_headline: A Rich Plan in New York’s Casino Race Is No Sure Thing for Cuomo

text: An article on Aug. 31 about United Nations peacekeepers who came under fire in southern Syria during clashes between Syrian troops and rebels misstated the year that United Nations troops began monitoring a cease-fire between Israel and Syria. It was 1974, not 1973.
match_headline: Syrian Rebels Trade Fire With Troops From U.N.

text: A picture caption in some editions on Sept. 4 with an article about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s endorsement of Kathy Hochul in the Democratic primary for lieutenant governor of New York misstated the date they were shown campaigning together. It was the day before the article was published, not on Aug. 30. (Ms. Hochul went on to win the nomination.)
match_headline: De Blasio Endorses Hochul, Cuomo’s Pick for Lieutenant Governor

text: An article in some editions on Sept. 1 about a shooting in Brooklyn in which a gunman and a police officer were wounded misstated the number of shootings in New York City this year as of Aug. 31. It was 792, not more than 800.
match_headline: Officer and Gunman Are Wounded in Brooklyn, Police Say

text: A picture caption on Sept. 1 with an article about the closing of the Showboat, a casino in Atlantic City, misstated, in some editions, the given name of a man shown performing card tricks for visitors during his last shift there. As the article correctly noted, he is Arnaldo Leggi, not Arnold.
match_headline: Showboat Casino Closes Amid Tears and Questions About Atlantic City’s Direction

text: An article on Wednesday about the Yankees’ 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays misstated, in some copies, the length of their losing streak. It was their second straight loss, not third. The error was repeated in the headline. And because of an editing error, a picture caption in some copies misstated the inning in which Rays catcher Ryan Hanigan blocked the plate while tagging out Stephen Drew. It was the fifth inning, not the fourth.
match_headline: Missing Key Players, Yankees Drop Second Straight

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Yankees’ 5-4 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays misidentified, in some copies, one of the two teams that shut out the Yankees in games in which pitcher Michael Pineda made his previous two starts. Besides the Kansas City Royals, it was the Toronto Blue Jays — not the Boston Red Sox.
match_headline: Yankees’ Hits Are Few, but Ex-Met Has a Big One

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article last Monday about the Jets’ 19-14 victory over the Oakland Raiders misstated, in some copies, the score after Chris Ivory rushed for a 71-yard touchdown in the fourth quarter. It was 19-7, not 13-7.
match_headline: 71-Yard Run Helps Jets Overcome Mistakes

text: An article on Wednesday about Penn State’s reaction to the lifting of N.C.A.A. sanctions on its football team misstated the number of seasons the Penn State coach, James Franklin, was at Vanderbilt University. It was three, not two.
match_headline: Penn State Faithful Rejoice After Penalties Are Lifted

text: An article on June 6 about the reason the Obama administration kept the operation to free Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl such a closely held secret described incorrectly the “Gang of Eight,” a group of lawmakers that often receives briefings on covert or highly sensitive programs. While the group is made up of national security leaders, they are from the House and the Senate, not just the Senate. A reader pointed out the error in an email shortly after the article was published; this correction was delayed because editors did not follow through on the complaint.
match_headline: Fears for Sergeant’s Life Led to Secrecy About Swap, Obama Official Says

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Tuesday with an article about efforts by the United States to salvage a nuclear accord with Moscow misstated, in some editions, the date that President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia said, “I want to remind you that Russia is one of the most powerful nuclear nations.” He made the comment in late August when he was photographed visiting a youth camp outside Moscow; he did not make the comment the day before the article was published.
ref_headline: I want to remind you that Russia is one of the most powerful nuclear nations.
match_headline: U.S. Delegation Is to Visit Moscow to Review Claims of a Missile Violation

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about increased competition in the online dating business misstated the position of Barry Diller at IAC/InterActiveCorp, which owns a number of dating sites. He is its chairman, not its owner.
match_headline: IAC, Owner of Match and Tinder, Makes Moves in Online Dating

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the effect of sanctions against Russia on Exxon Mobil’s Arctic oil production plans misstated, in some copies, part of the name of an oil service company that may also feel the pressure. It is Baker Hughes, not Baker Hughers.
match_headline: New Sanctions to Stall Exxon’s Arctic Oil Plans

text: An article on Saturday about how a push for user data from Yahoo set the stage for broad government Internet surveillance misstated the year that Yahoo turned over information on Chinese users to the Chinese government. It was 2004, not 2007.
match_headline: Government Push for Yahoo’s User Data Set Stage for Broad Surveillance

text: An article on Monday about efforts by an alliance of writers to end a dispute between Amazon.com and the publisher Hachette that has cut into their book sales, rendered incorrectly the name of another publisher for which Mishka Shubaly, who writes for Amazon’s Kindle Singles line, is writing a memoir. It is PublicAffairs, not Public Affairs.
match_headline: In Latest Volley Against Amazon, Hachette’s Writers Target Its Board

text: A critic’s notebook article on Saturday about the Toronto International Film Festival, where “The Imitation Game,” about Alan Turing, was one of the films shown, referred incorrectly to the Turing machine. It is a hypothetical machine devised by Turing that was not built; thus it was not used to help break German codes in World War II.
match_headline: Prizes Without Passion

text: An entry in the What’s on TV Friday highlights in some editions on Friday about “Arts in the City,” on CUNY TV, misstated the surname of a reporter on the program. He is Tony Guida, not Guide.
match_headline: What’s on TV Friday

text: An editorial on Sept. 2 about the kidney shortage misstated the number of kidney transplants in the United States last year. It was about 16,900, not 14,000.
match_headline: Ways to Reduce the Kidney Shortage

text: An article on Saturday about a letter to President Obama from the president of Liberia, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, in which she pleaded for American help in her country’s Ebola crisis misidentified the doctor who described in an email what it is like to work with Ebola patients. It was Dr. Kanagasabi Udhayashankara, a pediatric resident at JFK Hospital in Monrovia — not Dr. David Knight, an American physician — who wrote, “It has been three months since I felt the warmth of bare skin that was not mine.”
ref_headline: It has been three months since I felt the warmth of bare skin that was not mine.
match_headline: Liberian President Pleads With Obama for Assistance in Combating Ebola

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about District of Columbia officials’ lobbying a Senate panel to approve a bill granting statehood to the district misattributed a quotation about the bill’s fate. It was Senator Tom Coburn of Oklahoma, the ranking Republican on the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs — not Senator Thomas R. Carper, Democrat of Delaware and chairman of the committee — who said the bill would be debated “even though it has no chance of success in this chamber and is dead on arrival in the House.”
ref_headline: even though it has no chance of success in this chamber and is dead on arrival in the House.
match_headline: District of Columbia Officials Push for Statehood at a Senate Committee Hearing

text: An article on Tuesday about President Obama’s awarding the Medal of Honor to two Vietnam-era soldiers misstated, in some editions, the day the president bestowed the awards. It was Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Medal of Honor Awarded to 2 Vietnam-Era Soldiers

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about llama races in Hammond, Wis., misidentified the animals shown running down the street. They are alpacas, not llamas. (While the llamas were the stars of the day, one race was designated just for alpacas, perhaps to make the llamas’ kissing cousins feel included.)
match_headline: This Isn’t Churchill Downs, and Those Aren’t Horses

text: An article on Monday about the Giants’ 25-14 loss to the Arizona Cardinals misstated, in some copies, the number of times the Giants turned over the ball and the number of times quarterback Eli Manning threw an interception. They had four turnovers, not three, and Manning was intercepted twice, not once.
match_headline: Offense Makes Strides, but Giants Pay for Turnovers and Special-Teams Play

text: An article on Monday about the Jets’ 31-24 loss to the Green Bay Packers misstated, in some copies, the Jets’ lead at halftime. It was 5 points, not 18. The headline repeated the error. (The Jets had an 18-point lead during the first half, but led, 21-16, at halftime.)
match_headline: Jets Build an 18-Point First-Half Lead, Which Aaron Rodgers Duly Vaporizes

text: An article on Saturday about the domestic assault case involving N.F.L. running back Ray Rice misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the Atlantic County, N.J., prosecutor, who has been criticized for allowing Rice to enter a pretrial intervention program intended to spare nonviolent offenders from a criminal conviction. He is Jim McClain, not McLain.
match_headline: Ray Rice Case Draws Attention to a Crime Often Obscured

text: An article on Tuesday about the reinstatement of running back Adrian Peterson to the Minnesota Vikings despite pending child abuse charges in Texas misstated, in some editions, the call letters of a television station in Houston that first reported a new allegation about Peterson on Monday involving a different son. The station is KHOU-TV, not WKOU-TV.
match_headline: Vikings’ Adrian Peterson Cleared to Play as His Lawyer Denies a New Abuse Allegation

text: An obituary on Saturday about the songwriter and record producer Bob Crewe referred incorrectly to two songs he was involved in. He produced the record “Devil With a Blue Dress On & Good Golly Miss Molly,” by Mitch Ryder and the Detroit Wheels, in 1966, not in 1965. And Labelle’s recording of the song “Lady Marmalade,” which Mr. Crewe co-wrote, reached No. 1 in 1975, not in 1974.
ref_headline: Devil With a Blue Dress On & Good Golly Miss Molly,
match_headline: Bob Crewe, Songwriter for Frankie Valli and Four Seasons, Dies at 83

text: An article on Friday about Notre Dame’s lucrative sports apparel deal with Under Armour referred incorrectly to a $400 million renovation of Notre Dame Stadium. The project is set to break ground in November; it has not been completed.
match_headline: Notre Dame and Under Armour Seek Win-Win With Apparel Deal

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about the effect an upheaval in top management at Ferrari might have on the automobile manufacturer’s racing operations misspelled the surname of the last Ferrari team driver to win a Formula One world drivers’ championship, in 2007. He is Kimi Raikkonen, not Raikonnen.
match_headline: At Sputtering Ferrari, Shake-Up at the Top Could Change Tradition

text: An article on Friday about the United States’ 96-68 victory over Lithuania in the semifinals of the men’s basketball World Cup in Barcelona, Spain, referred incorrectly to its victory in Barcelona at the 1992 Olympics. Although the squad, nicknamed the Dream Team, did defeat Croatia for the championship, the game against Croatia in which Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen overtly tried to shut down Toni Kukoc’s offense was in a preliminary round, not in the gold medal contest.
match_headline: Without Glamour of Dream Team, U.S. Is Again Dominating in Barcelona

text: An article on Aug. 29 about the Yankees’ 3-2 loss to the Detroit Tigers referred incorrectly in some editions to the pitch from the Yankees’ Shawn Kelley that the Tigers’ Alex Avila hit to end the game in the ninth inning. It was Kelley’s 27th pitch of the game, not his 17th.
match_headline: In Season of 63 Losses So Far, Yankees Find Few as Agonizing as This One

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the impresario Tibor Rudas, and an accompanying picture caption, referred incorrectly to the credit “Tibor Rudas Presents the Three Tenors.” It was part of the title of almost every one of the Three Tenors’ CDs and concerts — not every one.
ref_headline: Tibor Rudas Presents the Three Tenors.
match_headline: Tibor Rudas Dies at 94; Brought the World the Three Tenors

text: An obituary on Monday about the pianist Joe Sample misstated the year his album “Soul Shadows” was released. It was 2004, not 2008.
match_headline: Joe Sample, Crusaders Pianist Who Went Electric, Dies at 75

text: A report on Aug. 28 in the Currents column about new furniture by British designers sold at Crate & Barrel misstated the width of the Freemont table designed by Russell Pinch. It is 38 inches wide, not 30.
match_headline: Just Out of the Box From Britain

text: Because of an editing error, the Shopping With column last Thursday, about outdoor tables selected by Jonathan Olivares, misidentified Mr. Olivares’s profession. He is an industrial designer, not a furniture designer.
match_headline: Outdoor Heirlooms: Dining Tables

text: A picture last Thursday with an article about Josh Bennett, who hand-knits sweaters for prominent designers, was published in error. The sweater depicting a sunrise over a blue horizon was not knit by Mr. Bennett for the designer Michael Bastian; Mr. Bastian’s company produced it.
match_headline: Grandma Never Knit Like This

text: An article last Thursday about watching fashion shows from the last rows of seats misidentified the show at which Ellen Thomas was interviewed. It was Alexander Wang’s show, not Prabal Gurung’s. The article also misstated the date of that interview; it was Sept. 6 (the date of the Prabal Gurung show), not Sept. 7. The article also misstated the name of Ms. Thomas’s employer. It is StyleList.com , not Style Lyst. And, finally, the article described StyleList.com incorrectly. It is a fashion and beauty website, not an AOL fashion blog.
match_headline: A Chance at Anonymity, if Not a View

text: An article last Thursday about parties held in conjunction with New York Fashion Week misspelled the surname of a performer at a party held by Calvin Klein. She is Rita Ora, not Oro.
match_headline: After the Fashion, the Festivities

text: An article on Wednesday about the complicated role that Asaib Ahl al-Haq and other Shiite militias in Iraq play in the battle against the Islamic State misidentified the city where Sheikh Qais al-Khazali, the militia’s leader, led a deadly attack on United States military forces in 2007. And the article described incorrectly the casualties in that attack. It was in Karbala, not Falluja, and it killed five soldiers, not Marines.
match_headline: Shiite Militias Pose Challenge for U.S. in Iraq

text: An article on Thursday about the rising appeal of the Scottish independence movement despite warnings about the risks of dissolution referred imprecisely to the author Niall Ferguson, who was among those predicting a negative outcome for an independent Scotland. Though Mr. Ferguson often writes about economics, he was trained as a historian; he is not an economist.
match_headline: Scottish Vote Weighs Pride Against Risk

text: An article on Tuesday about remarks by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey that suggested his country would provide refuge to several Muslim Brotherhood leaders who had been forced to leave Egypt misstated the surname of the foreign relations officer of the Muslim Brotherhood and the given name of Turkey’s energy minister. The foreign relations officer is Amr Darrag, not Derrac, and the energy minister is Taner Yildiz, not Kaner.
match_headline: Turkey Open to Bids for Refuge by Muslim Brotherhood Exiles

text: An article in some editions on Sept. 8 about the Brooklyn Public Library’s adding hours and staffing misstated the type of budget for which the library system had $72.1 million before the 2008 recession. It was a discretionary operating budget, not an operating budget. (The system also receives a separate nondiscretionary operating budget from New York City.)
match_headline: Libraries in Brooklyn Add Hours and Staff

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about sports at the Asian Games that might be unfamiliar to people from the West misidentified, in some editions, the two teams shown playing sepaktakraw, or kick volleyball. The caption also carried an incorrect credit. The teams were from Indonesia and Myanmar — not from the Philippines and Singapore — and the photograph was taken by Ye Aung Thu of Agence France-Presse — Getty Images; it was not by Suhaimi Abdullah of Getty Images.
match_headline: At the Asian Games, Topsy-Turvy Sports Are Traditional, Too

text: An article on Tuesday about Tiger Woods’s physical condition and his timetable for returning to competitive golf described his performance in this year’s British Open incorrectly. He played all four rounds, finishing 69th; he did not miss the cut.
match_headline: Tiger Woods Striving to Return at His Tournament in December

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a television review of “Tim & Eric’s Bedtime Stories” and “Mr. Pickles” on Adult Swim, using information from a publicist, reversed the names, in some editions, of the two comedians shown. Eric Wareheim is at the left and Tim Heidecker on the right.
match_headline: A Devil Dog Tears Into People, and Other Tales

text: An article Thursday about the effect of artificial sweeteners on metabolism misstated the title of a researcher who commented on the study. Dr. Frank Hu is a professor of nutrition and epidemiology, not immunology, at the Harvard School of Public Health.
match_headline: Artificial Sweeteners May Disrupt Body’s Blood Sugar Controls

text: An article in some editions on Sept. 10 about primary election results for legislative offices in New York State described the location of the Hudson Valley incorrectly. It is in upstate New York, not in western New York.
match_headline: Democrats Reject Indicted State Senator in Queens but Renominate One in Brooklyn

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about a decision by the principal of Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music and Art and the Performing Arts to decline a request by the performer Nicki Minaj to speak at the school, her alma mater, misspelled the title of her recent hit in some copies. It is “Anaconda,” not “Anacdona.”
match_headline: Twitter Erupts as Nicki Minaj’s Offer to School Is Declined

text: An article on Wednesday about the 2014 fellowships awarded by the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation misstated part of the title of a memoir by one of the winners, the cartoonist and graphic memoirist Alison Bechdel. It is “Fun Home: A Family Tragicomic” (not “Tragicomedy”).
match_headline: MacArthur Awards Go to 21 Diverse Fellows

text: An article on Tuesday about stem cell therapies misstated federal policy concerning research on embryonic stem cell lines. In 2001, President George W. Bush prohibited the use of federal funds for research on new embryonic stem cell lines. He did not prohibit all creation of new embryonic stem cell lines. (Privately funded research at the time was unaffected and President Obama eased the restrictions in 2009.) The article also referred imprecisely to the approach of the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research toward stem cell research. While the majority of the foundation’s current funding is for research in areas besides stem cells, it has not stopped funding stem cell research entirely.
match_headline: The Trials of Stem Cell Therapy

text: A picture on Tuesday with an article about workers at industrial hog farms who carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria over several days was published in error. The photograph showed workers at a pork processing plant, not at a hog farm.
match_headline: Taking a Health Hazard Home

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about a dispute over the remains of Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen that halted his canonization process carried an incorrect credit in some editions. The picture of Archbishop Sheen, in 1979, was taken by Neal Boenzi, a New York Times photographer; it was not by Eddie Hausner, another Times photographer.
match_headline: Tug of War for Bishop’s Body, or Its Parts, Delays Sainthood

text: An article in some editions on Sept. 7 about Toshiyuki Shimada, the music director and conductor of both the Eastern Connecticut Symphony Orchestra and the Yale Symphony Orchestra, misstated the relationship between two composers whose work Mr. Shimada has featured in performances. The composers, William Brittelle and Sarah Kirkland Snider, are co-directors of New Amsterdam Records, a record label in Brooklyn; they are not married. (Judd Greenstein is also a co-director.) The article also misidentified the university from which Mr. Brittelle graduated. It is Vanderbilt, not Yale.
match_headline: A Conductor Promotes Risk-Taking in Music Programs

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about German saboteurs on Long Island during World War II misidentified the woman who contacted the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum in Hyde Park for more information on the crew. She is Elizabeth Neill, the curator of an exhibition on the episode at the East Hampton Historical Society’s Clinton Academy Museum — not Phyllis Barnes. (Ms. Barnes’s father-in-law, Cmdr. Warren Barnes, headed the Coast Guard station that reported the saboteurs’ arrival.)
match_headline: Nazi Saboteurs in the Amagansett Sands

text: A picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about the Prudence Crandall Museum in Canterbury, Conn., using information from the institution, misspelled the given name of one of Ms. Crandall’s students. Sarah Harris Fayerweather, not Sarrah, was shown in the sepia-toned photograph. Because of an editing error, the caption also erroneously attributed a distinction to Ms. Fayerweather. As the article noted correctly, she was the first black student at Crandall’s academy, not the first student.
match_headline: Honoring a Teacher Who Fought for Equality

text: An article last Sunday about the Los Angeles art dealer David Kordansky, which recounted the key role he played in bringing the paintings of the 80-year-old African-American artist Sam Gilliam back into the spotlight, erroneously included a product among the types of things Gilliam bartered his work for at a lower point in his career. While he exchanged art for services such as dental work, he never traded art for laundry detergent.
match_headline: 10 of the Gallerist David Kordansky’s Top Cultural Influences

text: An article last Sunday about the art historian Sir John Richardson misstated the family relationship between King Edward VII and Queen Elizabeth II, who knighted Richardson in 2012. Elizabeth is Edward’s great-granddaughter, not his granddaughter.
match_headline: The Personal Arcadia of John Richardson

text: An article last Sunday about the N.B.A’s Rookie Transition Program, a training camp that teaches draftees to handle the challenges that come with their new professional role, referred incompletely to Latrell Sprewell’s career in the N.B.A. While he was indeed kicked out of the league for going at the throat of P.J. Carlesimo, coach of the Golden State Warriors, and threatening to kill him, he later returned to the N.B.A. to play for the New York Knicks and the Minnesota Timberwolves.
match_headline: Meet Our Guest Pinner: Soo Joo Park, Today’s Model

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an obituary about the New Orleans recording engineer and studio owner Cosimo Matassa misstated the name of the studio in which Mr. Matassa was shown with Jimmy Clanton. It is Cosimo Recording Studios — not the J & M Studio, the name of his original studio.
match_headline: Cosimo Matassa, Whose Studio Created a Rock ’n’ Roll Sound, Dies at 88

text: An article last Sunday about Tony Bennett, Lady Gaga and their new duet album, “Cheek to Cheek,” misstated the date on which their “Great Performances” concert will be broadcast on PBS. It is Oct. 24, not Oct. 28.
match_headline: Chameleon and Lion Sample Songbook

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Dan Stevens, who stars in the new film “The Guest,” misspelled the surname of his wife. She is Susie Harriet, not Hariet.
match_headline: A ‘Downton’ Darling Turned Mr. Hyde

text: An article in the New Season issue on Sept. 7 about new buildings omitted one of the architectural firms involved in the design of the Ryerson University Student Learning Center in Toronto. The center was designed by Snohetta, in collaboration with Zeidler Partnership Architects — not just by Snohetta.
match_headline: Transforming, but Not Disrupting

text: A picture credit in the New Season issue on Sept. 7 with an article about the fall art season misstated the surname of the photographer who took the picture of two 15th-century demons. He is Sean Dungan, not Dunga.
match_headline: In Museums, Masters Old and New

text: A picture on Aug. 31 with a reviewof “The Animals: Love Letters Between Christopher Isherwood and Don Bachardy,” edited by Katherine Bucknell , carried an erroneous credit. The photograph of Isherwood and Bachardy is by Michael Childers , not from Zeitgeist Films.
ref_headline: The Animals: Love Letters Between Christopher Isherwood and Don Bachardy,
match_headline: Stories We Tell Each Other

text: An entry on the combined print and e-book fiction best-seller list on Jan. 19 misstated the year in which the novel “Outlander,” by Diana Gabaldon , was first published. It was 1991, not 2004. The error was repeated on the same list on Aug. 24 and Aug. 31 .
match_headline: What Were the Best Movies You Saw in the Past Year?

text: An article last Sunday about four D.J.s who provided music at New York Fashion Week runway shows conflated the name of a mashup duo with part of the title of its song on the playlist of Sebastien Perrin, one of the D.J.s. It is “The Complete Latch (Sam Smith x Disclosure x Blood Orange),” by the Hood Internet — not “The Hood Internet (Sam Smith x Disclosure x Blood Orange),” by the Complete Latch. The article also misspelled part of the name of an Elton John song. It is “Bennie and the Jets,” not “Benny and the Jets.”
ref_headline: The Complete Latch (Sam Smith x Disclosure x Blood Orange),
match_headline: They Move Like Jagger, if the Music’s Right

text: An article last Sunday about Barbra Streisand’s musings on her life and career as she prepared to release her new album, “Partners,” referred incorrectly to the origins of her hit song “People.” It was written for the 1964 Broadway musical “Funny Girl,” not for the 1968 film version.
match_headline: Barbra Streisand, a Voice to Be Reckoned With

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Moira Weigel and Benjamin Tarnoff misidentified the organization for which the groom’s father, Peter Tarnoff, had been the president. It is the Council on Foreign Relations, not the Council on Foreign Affairs.
match_headline: Moira Weigel, Benjamin Tarnoff

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Piper Goodeve and Gabriel Vaughan misspelled the groom’s surname as Vaughn in several places.
match_headline: The Language of Love Prevails

text: An article on Sept. 7 about spending summers on Lake George in the Adirondacks misstated the web address for the Uptown Cafe in Hague. It is uptownlakegeorge.com, not uptowncafe.org.
match_headline: Refuge and Renewal on Lake George

text: A news analysis article last Sunday about the changing makeup of Jewish voters in New York misspelled the surname of Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s liaison to the Jewish community. He is David Lobl, not Lobel.
match_headline: Are Liberal Jewish Voters a Thing of the Past?

text: A news analysis article last Sunday about the politics around banning assault weapons gave an imprecise and outdated statistic on the use of handguns in killings in the United States. They were used in more than 80 percent of gun murders, not all murders, each year — and in the early 1990s, not in the present.
match_headline: The Assault Weapon Myth

text: A headline last Monday for an article about the estimated number of swings Derek Jeter has taken in his long Yankees career misstated, in some copies, the number of his career hits at the time. The error was repeated in the headline with the continuation of the article. As correctly noted in the article, Jeter had 3,450 hits at the time, not 3,540.
match_headline: Derek Jeter Has 2,734 Games Played and 3,450 Hits. Swings? Here’s a Ballpark Guess.

text: A picture caption on Sept. 11 with an article about an exhibition in Albany of items from the Family Room, a space in Manhattan near ground zero where people mourned relatives who were killed in the 2001 attacks, carried an incomplete credit from the Lower Manhattan Development Corporation. While the corporation provided the photograph showing the Family Room covered in cards, notes and other expressions of love and loss, it was taken by Michael Franz, who once worked for the corporation.
match_headline: A 9/11 Shrine Where Families Mourned for Years, Now Open to Others

text: An article last Monday about the dismissal of the chairman of Libya’s central bank by that country’s newly elected Parliament misstated the given name of the central bank’s chairman. He is Sadik Omar el-Kaber, not Sadel.
match_headline: Libyan Parliament Fires Central Bank Chairman

text: An article on Sept. 5 about a new book that accuses a Central Intelligence Agency official of stopping five commandos from interceding to save the life of Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and an American technician during an attack by militants in Benghazi, Libya, in 2012, misstated the official’s title. The official was the agency’s base chief in Benghazi, not the station chief.
match_headline: New Book Says C.I.A. Official in Benghazi Held Up Rescue

text: A headline on Sept. 6 with an article about an appearance by Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India that was seen by millions of the country’s schoolchildren to mark the annual Teachers’ Day misidentified the venue in New Delhi where Mr. Modi spoke and answered questions. It was at a convention center, not at a school.
match_headline: Indian Leader’s Talk to Schoolchildren Draws Fire

text: An article in some editions on Monday about a NASA mission to analyze the atmosphere of Mars, using information from the agency, misstated the duration of an engine firing that pushed the Maven spacecraft into orbit around the planet. The maneuver lasted 34 minutes 26 seconds, not 33 minutes.
match_headline: NASA Craft Is Orbiting Mars, to Study Its Air

text: An article on Tuesday about new Treasury rules intended to make it more difficult for companies to lower their tax bills by relocating overseas misstated a tax advantage of “earnings stripping,” in which a company loads up a United States subsidiary with debt to avoid paying taxes on income. The interest on the debt is deductible, not the debt itself.
match_headline: U.S. Acts to Curb Firms’ Moves Overseas to Avoid Taxes

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about MGM’s acquisition of a majority stake in Mark Burnett’s production company, One Three Media, referred incorrectly to “Teen Wolf,” an MGM television show. While it is a solid performer for MTV, as the article correctly noted, it is not a “History Channel hit.”
match_headline: MGM Buys Big Stake in Mark Burnett’s Reality TV Production Company

text: An article on Tuesday about the next publisher of The Washington Post, using information from a company spokeswoman, misstated the number of daughters of Frederick J. Ryan Jr., who will assume the post next Wednesday. Mr. Ryan has three daughters, not two.
match_headline: A Tailor-Made Publisher Taking Over Jeff Bezos’ Washington Post

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the composer Unsuk Chin misspelled the surname of the clarinetist for whom she wrote her Clarinet Concerto. He is Kari Kriikku, not Kriiku.
match_headline: Composing Outside the Lines

text: A picture caption on Monday with a theater review of “Mighty Real: A Fabulous Sylvester Musical,” at the Theater at St. Clement’s in Manhattan, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of the star of the show, Anthony Wayne, and other cast members, was taken by Joan Marcus, not by Billy Coyle.
ref_headline: Mighty Real: A Fabulous Sylvester Musical,
match_headline: Exulting in His Fabulous Moment, a Spangled Disco Diva at Fever Pitch

text: An obituary on Monday about the actress and singer Polly Bergen referred incorrectly to a revival of “Cabaret” in which she appeared in 2002. It was on Broadway, not Off Broadway. The obituary, using information from a spokeswoman, also referred incorrectly to Kathy Lander, who survives Ms. Bergen. She is Ms. Bergen’s stepdaughter, not her daughter. And a version of the obituary in some editions on Sunday misstated the year Ms. Bergen won an Emmy Award for her portrayal of the singer Helen Morgan. It was 1958, not 1957.
match_headline: Polly Bergen Dies at 84; Emmy-Winning Actress

text: An obituary on Aug. 27 about Philippine de Rothschild, who helped modernize and expand her family’s wine-producing enterprise, misidentified the member of her family who had used the surname Pascal professionally, as she later did when she acted with the Comédie-Française and elsewhere. Her paternal grandfather, Henri de Rothschild, used the name as a playwright; her father, Baron Philippe de Rothschild, did not use it as an actor.
match_headline: Philippine de Rothschild, Wine Nobility, Dies at 80

text: An obituary on Monday about the jazz trumpeter, flugelhornist and composer Kenny Wheeler misstated his involvement with the Junior Jazz program at the Royal Academy of Music in London. He was the founding patron, not the founder.
match_headline: Kenny Wheeler, Influential Sound in Jazz, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the singer and actress Yoshiko Yamaguchi misstated the location of Manchuria, where she was born. It is in northeast China, not northwest.
match_headline: Yoshiko Yamaguchi, 94, Actress in Propaganda Films, Dies

text: An article on Tuesday about Omar Jose Gonzalez, who made his way past security and through the front door of the White House, prompting criticism of the Secret Service’s handling of the incident, referred incorrectly to Secret Service agents who were fired for having prostitutes in their hotel rooms in Cartagena, Colombia. The incident occurred while they were there in 2012 preparing for a presidential trip, not during the presidential trip.
match_headline: White House Intruder’s Past Raises Concern

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the strong possibility that the number of Ebola victims has been undercounted in Sierra Leone referred incorrectly, in some editions, to a possible victim of Ebola whose body is shown being removed from a house in Freetown, Sierra Leone. The body is that of a man, not a woman.
match_headline: Fresh Graves Point to Undercount of Ebola Toll

text: An article on Monday about the ways that the United States and Hezbollah are trying to defeat the Islamic State, despite being long-time enemies, referred incorrectly to the work of Ali Rizk, an expert on Hezbollah, for the Lebanese news channel al-Mayadeen. He has acted as a translator for the network, not as an analyst. The article also described the Shiite share of Lebanon’s population incorrectly. Shiites are a plurality in the country, not a majority.
match_headline: Though Adversaries on the Surface, U.S. and Hezbollah Share a Goal

text: An article last Thursday about a City Council committee hearing over whether jazz club owners in New York City should contribute to pensions for their performers misidentified, in some editions, an instrument played by the musician Jimmy Owens during his testimony. It is a flugelhorn, not a trumpet.
match_headline: New York City Council Hears Push for Benefits by Jazz Veterans

text: An article on Aug. 30 about the increasing number of matchups between Top 25 teams in the first two weeks of the college football season misidentified the city in which Boise State and Virginia Tech played each other in a 2010 regular-season game. They met in Landover, Md., not in Atlanta.
match_headline: Feast of Season Openers in College Football Worthy of Top Billing

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Aug. 28 about the new SEC Network reversed the rankings at the time of the teams playing in the first game broadcast by the network. South Carolina was ranked ninth, and Texas A&M was No. 21.
match_headline: Powerhouse on the Field Looks to Have a Similar Presence on TV

text: An article on Tuesday about researchers’ studying of polar bears in Hudson Bay misspelled the surname of a scientist who was a longtime collaborator. He is Robert Jefferies, not Jeffries.
match_headline: For Polar Bears, a Climate Change Twist

text: A picture on Tuesday with a report in a roundup of news about the potential threat to animals and plant species around the world because of warmer global temperatures was published in error. It was a photograph of a carpenter bee, not a bumblebee.
match_headline: Secretary General Ban Ki-moon to Open United Nations Meetings

text: An article on Wednesday about a report that linked income levels to academic skills on the web misidentified the exams used to evaluate the Connecticut students who were the focus of the study. They were state standardized tests, not federal exams often known as the Nation’s Report Card.
match_headline: Academic Skills on Web Are Tied to Income Level

text: A Reporter’s Notebook article in some editions on Monday about the corruption trial of former Gov. John G. Rowland of Connecticut described incorrectly Lisa Wilson-Foley’s connection to a plan to have Mr. Rowland disclose the telephone number of her opponent in a congressional race. It was Ms. Wilson-Foley’s campaign — not the candidate herself — who gave the number to Mr. Rowland, who in turn released it on his radio show.
match_headline: Damning Testimony and Telling Emails in Rowland Trial

text: An article in some editions on Sept. 17 about a decision by the trustees of Brooklyn Public Library to approve plans for the Brooklyn Heights branch, using information from a spokeswoman, misstated the height of the mixed-use building that would house the library. It would be 30 stories, not 20. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Trustees Endorse Plan to Sell Land Beneath Branch of Brooklyn Library

text: An article on Monday about the area in Scotland that is hosting this week’s Ryder Cup golf tournament misstated the number of districts in Scotland that voted for independence from Britain in a referendum last week. It was four, not three.
match_headline: With One Battle Over in Scotland, Another Begins

text: A picture caption in some editions on Sept. 5 with an article about the Seattle Seahawks’ 36-16 victory over the Green Bay Packers, using information from Getty Images, misstated, in some copies, the quarter in which Marshawn Lynch was shown scoring a touchdown. It was the fourth quarter, not the third.
match_headline: Seahawks Trounce the Packers to Begin Their Title Defense

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the Antiques column last Friday misspelled the surname of the artist whose print was the basis of the 19th-century Japanese firefighter’s coat that was shown. He was Utagawa Kuniyoshi, not Kuniyoshim.
match_headline: At the Met, Honoring Kimonos and a Scholar of the Same

text: An article on Tuesday about genetic testing for cancer risk referred incorrectly at one point to the role that the genes BRCA1 and BRCA2 play in breast cancer. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, mutations in these genes, not the genes themselves, increase the risk of breast cancer.
match_headline: Finding Risks, Not Answers, in Gene Tests

text: Because of an editing error, a report in some copies of the World Briefing column on Wednesday about a meeting between President Xi Jinping of China and some Hong Kong business leaders in which Mr. Xi reiterated his government’s opposition to political change in Hong Kong referred incorrectly to comments by Peter Lee Ka-kit, a developer who took notes at the meeting. When Mr. Lee said, “If Hong Kong people don’t break from the political tussle to focus on development, Hong Kong will fall behind,” he was offering his interpretation of Mr. Xi’s position; he was not quoting Mr. Xi directly.
ref_headline: If Hong Kong people don’t break from the political tussle to focus on development, Hong Kong will fall behind,
match_headline: Chinese President Sends Signal Against Political Change in Hong Kong

text: An article on Wednesday about the increasing hostility between pedestrians and cyclists competing for space on a six-mile loop road in Central Park where a woman was fatally struck by a bicycle referred incorrectly to the posting of the park’s cycling rules at Bike and Roll’s rental station. The rules are posted on the back of a map at the stand; it is not the case that there is no information about them there. The article also misstated the day the woman, Jill Tarlov, died from her injuries. It was Sunday, not Monday.
match_headline: In Central Park, Cyclists Still Compete With Pedestrians

text: A report in the Weekend Miser column on Friday about the participatory theater work “Everything by my side,” in Hudson River Park in Manhattan, misstated the given name of the creator of the piece. He is Fernando Rubio, not Francisco.
match_headline: Every Word Borges Wrote, Writ Large in Brooklyn

text: An article on Page 108 this weekend about the Italian socialite Marella Agnelli describes incorrectly her residence in Villar Perosa, southwest of Turin, Italy. It was a house, not a townhouse.
match_headline: Marella & Me

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the artist and author Pati Hill quoted incorrectly from comments she made to The New Yorker in 1980 about creating art with copy machines. She said, “Making copies is very near to speaking” — not “Making copies is nearly speaking.” The obituary also referred incorrectly to Ms. Hill’s education. While she did attend George Washington University, she did not graduate from there. And the obituary referred imprecisely to “Electroworks,” an exhibition that included Ms. Hill’s work “A Swan: An Opera in Nine Chapters.” While it was indeed at the Cooper Union museum in 1980, it originated at the George Eastman House in Rochester in 1979.
ref_headline: Making copies is very near to speaking
match_headline: Pati Hill, Author Turned Artist of the Photocopier, Dies at 93

text: An article in some editions on Sept. 14 about the release of a video showing the execution of David Cawthorne Haines, a British aid worker, by the Islamic State terrorist group misspelled, in some copies, the given name of an Italian co-worker of Mr. Haines who was also taken hostage by ISIS but later released after a ransom payment. He is Federico Motka, not Frederico.
match_headline: ISIS Video Shows Execution of David Cawthorne Haines, British Aid Worker

text: An article on Sept. 20 about the N.F.L.’s handling of domestic abuse cases misspelled the surname of the person who contributed research. She is Elisa Cho, not Choi.
match_headline: In Domestic Violence Cases, N.F.L. Has a History of Lenience

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 20 about the approach that Poland’s incoming prime minister, Ewa Kopacz, might take with her country’s neighbors gave an incorrect pronunciation for Ms. Kopacz’s name. She is Eva CO-potch, not co-POTCH.
match_headline: New Leader Likens Poland to ‘Reasonable Polish Woman’

text: An article on Sept. 18 about the murder of Palwasha Tokhi, the seventh journalist killed in Afghanistan this year, misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the head of Bayan Radio, for which Ms. Tokhi worked. He is Hafizullah Majidi, not Majidid.
match_headline: In Brutal Year, 7th Journalist Is Killed in Afghanistan

text: An article on Thursday about two Swiss pilots’ plans to fly a solar-powered plane around the world gave an outdated title for Sultan Ahmed al-Jaber, an executive of Masdar, Abu Dhabi’s renewable energy company, which is backing the flight. He is now chairman, no longer chief executive.
match_headline: Swiss Pilots to Fly Solar Plane Around World

text: An article on Wednesday about environmental pledges from some of the world’s largest companies misidentified the venue where Timothy D. Cook, Apple’s chief executive, made supportive remarks last Monday. He spoke at the Morgan Library and Museum in New York at a climate event, not at the United Nations.
match_headline: Companies Take the Baton in Climate Change Efforts

text: An article on Thursday about China’s plans to connect the Shanghai stock exchange to its counterpart in Hong Kong as a way to open China’s markets to foreign investors omitted part of the name of the program that will connect the two exchanges. It is the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, not Shanghai-Hong Kong Connect.
match_headline: With China Set to Open Stock Trading, Investors Lay Groundwork

text: An article on Friday about the risks of flaws in open-source software misstated the middle initial of one of the elders of the open-source movement. He is Eric S. Raymond, not Eric J.
match_headline: Security Experts Expect ‘Shellshock’ Software Bug in Bash to Be Significant

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about an installation by the French artist JR in the former Ellis Island Immigrant Hospital in New York harbor misstated the percentage of Ellis Island arrivals who passed through the hospital doors. It was around 10 percent, not around 1 percent.
match_headline: Shadows Return to Ellis Island

text: An obituary on Friday about Christopher Hogwood, whose Academy of Ancient Music was a key ensemble in the period-instrument movement, erroneously included one singer among the soloists on the academy’s 1980 recording of Handel’s “Messiah.” The English countertenor James Bowman was not one of them, though he did work with Mr. Hogwood on other projects. The obituary also misspelled the given name of one of Mr. Hogwood’s surviving sisters. She is Frances, not Francis. And the obituary misstated part of the name of a dance troupe that collaborated with the Boston-based Handel and Haydn Society, which Mr. Hogwood led. It is the Mark Morris Dance Group (not Company).
match_headline: Christopher Hogwood, Early-Music Devotee, Dies at 73

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about Julia Pierson, the director of the Secret Service who is being criticized for security lapses within the agency, misstated the year in which she was appointed to the position. It was 2013, not 2012.
match_headline: Appointed to Redeem Secret Service, Director Will Discuss Another Misstep

text: An article on Monday about concerns by the Secret Service over security lapses by the agency, including its handling of a 2011 shooting at the White House and a recent incident in which an armed man entered the White House, misstated the given name of the deputy national security adviser. He is Antony J. Blinken, not Anthony.
match_headline: Secret Service Chief Reviews White House Breaches

text: An article on Monday about a shift in the tone of The New Yorker’s cover art from polite to topical referred incorrectly to one of the more provocative illustrations the magazine has published recently. The image of a football player being chased down the field by police officers appeared in the issue dated Sept. 29, which was on newsstands and online last week; it did not appear “a few weeks ago.”
match_headline: New Yorker’s Magazine Covers Shift From Polite to Provocative

text: An article on Sept. 13 about James Franklin, Penn State’s football coach, referred incorrectly to an example used by the university president, Eric Barron, to illustrate incidents of incivility on campus among faculty, alumni and trustees in the aftermath of the Jerry Sandusky child sexual abuse scandal. Speaking in front of the faculty senate, Mr. Barron said, as an example of an inappropriate comment, “Someone stands up there and says, ‘What do you mean we have a dairy farmer in charge of this committee?’”; he did not refer to vitriol among trustees toward M. Abraham Harpster, a dairy farmer who leads the academic affairs and student life committee. The article also misidentified, in some copies, the county in which a judge ruled that a lawsuit by the family of the former football coach Joe Paterno against the N.C.A.A. and Penn State could move forward. It is Centre County, not Cook County.
ref_headline: Someone stands up there and says, ‘What do you mean we have a dairy farmer in charge of this committee?’
match_headline: The Man in the Middle for the Nittany Lions

text: An article last Tuesday about a new report claiming that dust had interfered with observations of microwave radiation left over from the Big Bang misstated the affiliation of two of the authors. Jean-Loup Puget and Jonathan Aumont work at the Orsay Institute for Spatial Astrophysics — not at the Astrophysical Institute in Paris.
match_headline: Criticism of Study Detecting Ripples From Big Bang Continues to Expand

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actor Don Keefer misstated the year an episode of “The Twilight Zone” featuring Mr. Keefer first aired. The episode, “It’s a Good Life,” was in 1961, not in 1959.
match_headline: Don Keefer, Actor, Dies at 98; Had Bad Thoughts on ‘Twilight Zone’

text: An article last Wednesday about a speech by President Obama at the United Nations in which he challenged China to reduce its greenhouse-gas emissions and join a worldwide campaign to curb global warming misidentified the government position held by Narendra Modi of India, which is the world’s third-largest carbon polluter and has so far resisted outside pressure to cut its coal use. He is India’s prime minister, not its president.
match_headline: Obama Presses Chinese on Global Warming

text: An article on last Wednesday about the farewell speech of the president of Afghanistan, Hamid Karzai, in which he sharply criticized the United States, misidentified the position Ryan C. Crocker held on behalf of the United States during the post-Taliban government in Afghanistan. He was the American chargé d’affaires, not the ambassador. (Mr. Crocker did, however, become ambassador to Afghanistan in 2011.)
match_headline: In Farewell Speech, Karzai Calls American Mission in Afghanistan a Betrayal

text: An article on Sept. 19 about the executive branch’s war-making powers misidentified the home state of Representative Frank Wolf, one of several Republicans who introduced bills that would provide sweeping authority for air and ground warfare. He is from Virginia, not Pennsylvania.
match_headline: Congress’s Inaction Could Be Legal Basis for Stronger Executive War Powers

text: An article on Tuesday about plans by Netflix and the Weinstein Company to release a sequel to the movie “Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon” used an outdated working title for the new film. It is “Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon: The Green Legend,” not “Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon: The Green Destiny.” The error was repeated in an accompanying caption with a picture of the actor Donnie Yen.
match_headline: With ‘Crouching Tiger’ Sequel, Netflix Takes Aim at Hollywood

text: A picture caption on Monday with the continuation of a theater review of “You Can’t Take It With You,” at the Longacre Theater in Manhattan, misidentified one of the actors shown. He is Will Brill — not Fran Kranz, another cast member. And the listing of credits with the review misspelled the surname of a producer. She is Jessica Genick, not Genic.
ref_headline: You Can’t Take It With You,
match_headline: Screwball Magic Does the Trick

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with the continuation of a theater review of “Bright Star,” at the Old Globe in San Diego, misspelled the surname of a cast member. As the review, another caption and the listing of credits correctly noted, she is Carmen Cusack, not Cusak.
match_headline: Love, Loss and Local Color Make a Bluegrass Musical

text: A picture caption on Friday with an art review of “What Nerve! Alternative Figures in American Art, 1960 to the Present,” at the Rhode Island School of Design Museum in Providence, referred incorrectly to a work in the show. The work, titled “Austin Corbin,” was painted by Gary Panter, not “by Mr. Panter and Austin Corbin.”
ref_headline: What Nerve! Alternative Figures in American Art, 1960 to the Present,
match_headline: Recognizing a Vibrant Underground

text: An obituary on Friday about the television newsman John Slattery misidentified his home state. He was born in Springfield, Missouri — not Springfield, Michigan.
match_headline: John Slattery, a Longtime TV Newsman, Dies at 63

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about a strike by Air France pilots misstated, in some copies, the day the French government rejected the French National Union of Airline Pilots’ request for mediation. It was Friday night, not Saturday.
match_headline: Air France Pilots Extend Strike After Request for Mediation Is Denied

text: An article on Friday about a decision by an appeals court allowing a lawsuit filed by Facebook against the Manhattan district attorney’s office to proceed referred incorrectly to the ruling. It was signed by a clerk of the court — not by Justice John W. Sweeny Jr., who presided over a five-judge panel that made the decision.
match_headline: Facebook Lawsuit Over Search Warrants Can Proceed, a Court in Manhattan Rules

text: A picture on Tuesday with an article about a Federal Communications Commission proposal to allow cable and satellite providers to show National Football League games locally even if the game is not sold out was published in error. While Houston was among television markets where “blackouts” sometimes kept the game off television, those occurred when the former Houston Oilers played; games played by the Houston Texans, whose fans were shown in the photograph, have never been blacked out.
match_headline: F.C.C. Appears Poised to Loosen Sports Blackout Rule, Despite Protests by the N.F.L.

text: A report in the baseball roundup on Saturday about the Kansas City Royals’ 3-1 victory over the Chicago White Sox, which gave them their first playoff berth since 1985, misstated the given name of the Royals’ general manager in some copies. He is Dayton Moore, not Drayton.
match_headline: Royals Clinch First Postseason Berth Since 1985

text: An article on Tuesday about what life was like the last time the Kansas City Royals reached the Major League Baseball playoffs, in October 1985, misstated part of the name of the record label that was the subject of the movie “Krush Groove,” which came out that month. It is Def Jam Recordings, not Def Jam Records. And because of an editing error, the article referred imprecisely to the history of Internet domain names. In October 1985, symbolics.com, bbn.com, think.com, mcc.com and dec.com were the only registered domain names that ended in .com; they were not the only registered domain names.
match_headline: Going Back, Back, Back, Back

text: An article in some editions on Sept. 15 about Derek Jeter’s last visit to Baltimore before his retirement misidentified the position the Orioles’ star shortstop Cal Ripken Jr. moved to late in his career. It was third base, not first base.
match_headline: In His Last Visit to Baltimore, Derek Jeter Expresses Pride in His Durability

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a theater review of “The Old Man and the Old Moon,” at the New Victory Theater in Manhattan, reversed the identities of two actors in some editions. Ryan Melia is at the top and Ben Ferguson is at the left. And the review, citing influences on the show, misidentified the book of the Bible in which a man winds up in the belly of a giant fish. It is Jonah, not Genesis.
ref_headline: The Old Man and the Old Moon,
match_headline: Forsaking an Orb to Pursue the Light of His Life

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Thursday about reaction by colleagues of the designer Jean Paul Gaultier to his announcement that he would retire from ready-to-wear collections misspelled the given name of a model who has worked with him. She is Coco Rocha, not Coca. Also because of an editing error, the article misstated Mr. Gaultier’s given name as John.
match_headline: Jean Paul Gaultier: Words to Remember Him By

text: An article on Sept. 23 about pressure on Afghan election officials by senior Western officials to announce a new president of Afghanistan without disclosing the final vote count paraphrased incorrectly in some editions from comments by Thijs Berman, the chief of the European Union observer mission to Afghanistan. Mr. Berman said he believed that two million to three million votes in the runoff election were suspicious and should be examined for possible fraud; he did not say that number of votes were indeed fraudulent.
match_headline: Monitors of Afghan Vote Are Said to Back Secrecy

text: An article last Saturday about the State Department’s new effort to combat the Islamic State’s social media skills with an aggressive online campaign misidentified the university that is home to the Public Diplomacy Institute, where Bruce Gregory, who remarked about diplomats’ use of social media, was once a director. It is George Washington University, not Georgetown University. (Mr. Gregory teaches at both institutions.)
match_headline: Digital War Takes Shape on Websites Over ISIS

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the National Briefing column on Thursday about a Texas court’s refusal to reinstate two money-laundering convictions against Tom DeLay, the former House majority leader, misidentified the court that ruled last year that there was insufficient evidence in the case. It is the Texas Third Court of Appeals, not the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.
match_headline: Coalition Leader Warns of Long Fight Against ISIS in Iraq

text: An article last Saturday about developers who usually focus on commercial projects, but who are now entering the New York City residential market in search of profits, misstated, in some editions, the number of apartments expected at Hallets Point, a development in Queens. It is 2,404, not 1,921.
match_headline: Builders Turn Focus to Housing Market

text: A picture on Thursday with an article about Microsoft’s new Windows 10 operating system was published in error in some editions. The photograph, of warehoused cellphones, was a duplicate of a picture on the same page for an article about people who sell or trade in their cellphones. The photograph was not of Joe Belfiore, a Microsoft executive, showing the new operating system. (His picture accompanied the Microsoft article in other editions.)
match_headline: Microsoft Windows 10 Displays a Familiar Look

text: An article on Friday previewing the National League division series between the Washington Nationals and the San Francisco Giants misstated, in some editions, the number of career home runs by Matt Williams, who is now the Nationals’ manager. It is 378, not 372.
match_headline: Washington Nationals Are a Little Older and Playoff Wiser

text: A picture caption on Friday with an art review of “Thomas Hart Benton’s ‘America Today’ Mural Rediscovered” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, using information from the museum, misidentified a panel from the mural. It is “Coal,” not “City Building.”
ref_headline: Thomas Hart Benton’s ‘America Today’ Mural Rediscovered
match_headline: Brother, Can You Spare a Wall?

text: An article last Sunday about football tailgate parties in luxurious cabooses on a rail spur near the University of South Carolina’s stadium included several errors.
match_headline: As Tailgate Hits Rails, What Else to Do but Chug?

text: A report in the “This and That” feature last Sunday about colorful rings, using information from a publicist, misstated the price of a Holly Dyment ring. It is $8,360, not $15,800.

An obituary last Sunday about Gerald A. Larue, an ordained minister, scholar and the first president of the Hemlock Society, misstated the name of one of his sons and the year the son died. He was Gerald Jr., not Gerald III, and he died in 2001, not in 2000.
match_headline: Gerald Larue Dies at 98; Early Advocate of Right to Die

text: An article last Sunday about the filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson and the making of “Inherent Vice,” based on the novel by Thomas Pynchon, referred incorrectly to Maya Rudolph, a member of the cast. She is Mr. Anderson’s partner, not his wife.
match_headline: Pynchon’s Cameo, and Other Surrealities

text: A picture caption last Sunday with the Playlist CD review column, using information from a publicist, carried a credit that rendered the photographer’s name incorrectly. She is Amy-Beth McNeely, not AB McNeely.
match_headline: Founts of Classic and Progressive in a Straight Ahead Way

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the animated television series “Star War Rebels” referred incorrectly at one point to the role of Dave Filoni in the creation of the show. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is a co-creator, not the creator. The article also misspelled the name of a creature in the “Star Wars” universe. It is a Wookiee, not a Wookie.
match_headline: Empire Renewed

text: An article on Sept. 21 about the new show “Jane the Virgin,” which stars Gina Rodriguez, and the depiction of Latina characters on television referred incorrectly to Ms. Rodriguez’s parents, who were born in Puerto Rico then moved to Chicago. As American citizens, they were migrants, not immigrants.
match_headline: ‘Jane the Virgin’ Aims Beyond Its Latin Ethnicity

text: An entry on the children’s middle-grade best-seller list on Sept. 21 omitted part of the title of a book by James Patterson and Chris Grabenstein . It is “Treasure Hunters: Danger Down the Nile,” not just “Treasure Hunters.” (That was the title of the first book in the series of which “Treasure Hunters: Danger Down the Nile” is the second.) The error was repeated on the same list last Sunday.
ref_headline: Treasure Hunters: Danger Down the Nile,
match_headline: Spare Times for Children, for Sept. 19-25

text: An entry on the children’s picture book best-seller list last Sunday for “Horton and the Kwuggerbug and More Lost Stories” misidentified the illustrator. The illustrations are by the book’s writer, Dr. Seuss , not Charles D. Cohen. (Cohen wrote the introduction.)
ref_headline: Horton and the Kwuggerbug and More Lost Stories
match_headline: Charles M. Blow: By the Book

text: A review on Sept. 21 about “Harlem Hellfighters,” a children’s picture book about the African-American 369th Infantry Regiment written by J. Patrick Lewis and illustrated by Gary Kelley, misstated the year the unit was shipped to France in World War I. It was 1917, not 1918.
match_headline: Waging Two Wars

text: An article on Sept. 21 about Amy Cuddy, a social psychologist who says that certain body postures project and instill confidence, referred incorrectly to the academic affiliation of David Gergen, who said Ms. Cuddy’s technique “gives people a taste of what it feels like to be the president striding into the cabinet room.” He is the director of the Harvard Kennedy School’s Center for Public Leadership — not the Kennedy School for Public Leadership. (No such institution exists.)
ref_headline: gives people a taste of what it feels like to be the president striding into the cabinet room.
match_headline: Amy Cuddy Takes a Stand

text: An article on Sept. 21 about the Paleo lifestyle, whose practitioners emulate prehistoric living, misstated the surname of a blogger on this subject at one point. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she is Michelle Tam, not Nam.
match_headline: The Paleo Lifestyle: The Way, Way, Way Back

text: An article last Sunday about the ubiquity of digital video recording on iPhones misstated, at one point, the surname of a rock musician who had complained about the glowing digital devices of his audience members. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Jack White, not “Mr. Black.”
match_headline: A Defining Question in an iPhone Age: Live for the Moment or Record It?

text: An article on Sept. 21 about American World War I monuments and memorials in France misidentified the river in Fismes where the 28th Division built a bridge. It is the Vesle River, not the Marne.
match_headline: In France, Artifacts of America’s Role in World War I

text: A headline last Sunday about a former New Yorker who collected ballads and poems reflecting the cowboy culture of New Mexico misspelled his surname. As the article correctly noted, he is N. Howard (Jack) Thorp, not Thorpe.
match_headline: In New Mexico, on the Cowboy Trail of Jack Thorp

text: An article on Sept. 21 about theAudience, a social-media marketing company, misspelled the surname of a William Morris Endeavor founder. He is Ari Emanuel, not Emmanuel.
match_headline: Turning Microcelebrity Into a Big Business

text: An article on Sept. 21 about Gary Hart misidentified the location of the Capitol Hill townhouse where he lived in 1987. It is on Sixth Street SE, not Fifth Street. The article also misquoted Bill Clinton’s response after he was accused of having an extramarital affair with Monica Lewinsky. He said, “I did not have sexual relations with that woman,” not “I did not have sex with that woman.”
ref_headline: I did not have sexual relations with that woman,
match_headline: How Gary Hart’s Downfall Forever Changed American Politics

text: An article last Monday about disparities between the percentages of black residents and black elected officials in some cities misstated part of the name of an organization that supplied statistics on black representation on city councils. And an accompanying chart also gave an incorrect name for the group. It is the International City/County Management Association; it is neither the International City/County Council Management Association nor the International City/Council Management Association.
match_headline: Mostly Black Cities, Mostly White City Halls

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Sept. 26 about a violent clash in the Xinjiang region of western China paraphrased incorrectly from a report on the government-run Tianshan website. The report said 40 people described as rioters had been killed in the recent violence, including people shot by security forces and others who had blown themselves up; it did not say that security forces had fatally shot 40 people.
match_headline: At Least 50 Killed in Xinjiang Violence, Officials Say

text: A picture on Tuesday with an article about unsuccessful efforts to rescue missing climbers on Mount Ontake, a volcano in Japan, was published in error. The photograph, supplied by Getty Images with incorrect information, showed Mount Sakurajima, another volcano in Japan — not Mount Ontake.
match_headline: Toxic Gases Delay Rescue on Volcano in Japan

text: An article on Sept. 19 about a video released by the Islamic State extremist group that featured a British hostage, John Cantlie, sitting at a table and talking to the camera, misstated the year that Shajul Islam, a doctor, was acquitted on charges of playing a role in an earlier kidnapping of Mr. Cantlie. It was 2013, not 2012.
match_headline: New Islamic State Video Features British Hostage as Group Spokesman

text: A reporting credit on Sept. 11 with an article about the mistrust and grievances that have led many of Iraq’s Sunnis to regard the country’s Shiite-dominated government in Baghdad as a greater threat than the Islamic State misstated the surname of one contributor. He is Ali Hamza, not Hazem.
match_headline: Sunnis in Iraq Often See Their Government as the Bigger Threat

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about General Theological Seminary and its dispute with eight faculty members omitted the surname of one of those professors. She is the Rev. Mitties McDonald DeChamplain.
match_headline: Seeking Dean’s Firing, Seminary Professors End Up Jobless

text: A picture caption on Friday with the About New York column, about a school therapist who was suspended for helping Aaron Philip, 13, who has cerebral palsy, raise money on Kickstarter misstated, in some copies, the grade Aaron is in at Public School 333. He is an eighth grader, not a seventh grader.
match_headline: Bureaucracy Turns a Hero Into a Rogue

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the Sports Briefing column last Monday about Jeff Gordon’s Nascar victory at Dover International Speedway misidentified the state in which the speedway is located. It is in Delaware, not Maryland.
match_headline: Jameis Winston, Standing Out for Positive Reasons, Leads Florida State Rally

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a decision by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Harrisburg, Pa., to ban wrestling between boys and girls misstated the year and location of the Olympics at which women’s wrestling was introduced as a medal sport. It was the Athens Games in 2004, not the London Games in 2012.
match_headline: With Ban on Wrestling Between Boys and Girls, Diocese Faces a Crossroads
