text: A picture caption in some editions on Friday with an article about plans by the YIVO Institute for Jewish Research to digitally copy and make its collection of Yiddish books and cultural artifacts available online carried an erroneous credit. The photograph, of the crated collection being inspected in 1947, was provided by the YIVO Institute for Jewish Research, not the Center for Jewish History.
match_headline: Split Up by Holocaust, Top Collection of Yiddish Works Will Reunite Digitally

text: A picture caption on Monday with the Media Equation column, about renewed energy and quality at The Washington Post after its purchase by Jeff Bezos of Amazon, carried an erroneous credit. The photograph, of Martin Baron, executive editor, and other Post editors reading a list of last year’s Pulitzer Prize winners, was taken by Marlon Correa of The Washington Post and was distributed by Reuters; it was not taken by Reuters.
match_headline: The Washington Post Regains Its Place at the Table

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about a concert by Robert Plant scheduled for Thursday night at Brooklyn Bowl in Williamsburg, using information from the club, referred incorrectly in some editions to ticket sales. While tickets will be available on Brooklyn Bowl’s website, they will not be available at the club’s box office.
match_headline: Robert Plant Announces Brooklyn Show

text: Because of an editing error, a Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about the New York Film Festival misstated the closing date. It will end on Sunday, not on Oct. 16.
match_headline: Auteurs From Near and Far

text: Because of an editing error, a dance review on Saturday about New York City Ballet, at the David H. Koch Theater at Lincoln Center, misstated, at one point, part of the title of the work by Troy Schumacher that was performed. As the review correctly noted elsewhere, it is “Clearing Dawn,” not Changing Dawn.”
match_headline: The Art Gallery as Spinning Montage

text: An article on Aug. 31 about savings accounts that encourage deposits by giving account owners a chance to win prizes erroneously included a state among those that had modified their banking laws to allow credit unions to offer such accounts. While Indiana and Connecticut had so altered their laws, New York State’s law had not been modified at the time the article was published. (The bill had passed the State Legislature, but the governor did not sign it into law until September.) The error was only recently called to The Times’s attention.
match_headline: Using Gambling to Entice Low-Income Families to Save

text: An article on Monday about the ordeal of a girl who was abducted by smugglers and brought to the United States from Guatemala misstated the field of expertise of David Stoll, who has studied migration in Guatemala. He is an anthropologist at Middlebury College, not a sociologist.
match_headline: A Smuggled Girl’s Odyssey of False Promises and Fear

text: A picture caption last Wednesday with an article about newly released government documents that show that Henry A. Kissinger made contingency plans for an air assault on Cuba in 1976 after Fidel Castro’s military incursion in Angola misstated the year that Mr. Castro sent troops to Angola. It was 1975, not 1976.
match_headline: Kissinger Drew Up Plans to Attack Cuba, Records Show

text: An article on Sunday about chaos in schools in Washington State as a result of disagreements over education policy misstated the status of Lakeridge Elementary School under the No Child Left Behind law. While the school is in need of “corrective action” and must set aside a portion of federal funding for tutoring and student transfers, it is not failing. (Lakeridge is operating under a “safe harbor” provision of the law that allows underperforming schools to avoid the failing label if they have shown significant improvement.)
match_headline: In Washington State, Political Stand Puts Schools in a Bind

text: An article on Sept. 23 about a black bear that killed a Rutgers student referred incorrectly to the deadly encounter, using information from New Jersey officials. It is the state’s first recorded death linked to a black bear; it is not the state’s first such death since 1852. (An incident in 1852 cited by New Jersey officials as having occurred in the state actually happened in Arkansas.) The article also misstated the year New Jersey reinstated its bear hunt. It was 2010, not 2009. And because of an editing error, the article referred incorrectly to an incident in 2011 when a bear entered the camp site of a group on a trip in Sussex County. Two boys in the group were not in fact injured.
match_headline: Black Bear Kills Rutgers Student During a Hike in New Jersey

text: An article on Thursday about a smartphone application purporting to be from a pro-democracy group in Hong Kong that was being used to monitor demonstrators referred incompletely to the potential threat of the application. While it can infect devices running Apple’s iOS mobile operating system, it can do so only on devices that have been “jailbroken” to bypass some restrictions on downloads; it cannot infect unaltered iOS devices.
match_headline: Protesters in Hong Kong Are Targets of Scrutiny Through Their Phones

text: A picture credit on Tuesday with an article about new investors in Bitcoin misspelled the surname of the photographer. He is Matt Tuzzolo, not Tozzolo.

An article in some copies on Tuesday about the St. Louis Cardinals’ 3-1 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 3 of their National League division series misstated the game of last year’s World Series in which the Cardinals’ Kolten Wong was picked off first base to end the game. It was Game 4, not Game 6.
match_headline: Cardinals Ride John Lackey and Two Home Runs to Win Over Dodgers

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some copies on Sunday about the Giants’ 2-1 victory in 18 innings over the Washington Nationals in Game 2 of their National League division series misstated the base Asdrubal Cabrera was on when Anthony Rendon drove him in with a single in the third inning. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, Cabrera was on third, not on second.
match_headline: 18 Innings, Six Hours, One Huge Win for the Giants

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an article about the hopes and fears among Tibetans and Uighurs, ethnic minorities in China’s far west, over Beijing’s response to pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong described incorrectly Xinjiang, the traditional Uighur homeland. It is a region, not a province.
match_headline: From Tibet to Taiwan, China’s Periphery Watches Hong Kong Protests Intently

text: An article on Tuesday about Emmanuel Macron, the new economy minister of France, referred incorrectly to the period during which his wife had been his teacher. It was in high school, not first grade. (In French, “Premiere,” or first grade, refers to high school.)
match_headline: Emmanuel Macron, Face of France’s New Socialism

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a free viewing area at the San Francisco Giants’ AT&T Park misstated one of the years the Giants won the World Series. Besides 2012, they also won in 2010 — but not in 2014 (not yet anyway).
match_headline: One-Third of the View, but for None of the Price

text: Because of an editing error, a Sports of The Times column in some editions on Tuesday about the Washington Nationals’ victory over the San Francisco Giants in Game 3 of their National League division series misidentified the team for which catcher Wilson Ramos plays. It is the Nationals, not the Giants. And also because of an editing error, a picture caption misidentified, in some copies, the Giants player shown. The photograph was of third baseman Pablo Sandoval trying to catch pitcher Madison Bumgarner’s errant throw — not of Bumgarner making the throw.
match_headline: Funny Thing Happened on the Way to a Quick Demise

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Wednesday about the San Francisco Giants’ 3-2 victory over the Washington Nationals in Game 4 of their National League division series misidentified the Washington pitcher whose wild pitch in the seventh inning led to the Giants’ 3-2 lead. As the article initially noted, he is Aaron Barrett — not Matt Thornton, who was replaced by Barrett.
match_headline: The Ball May Not Travel Far, but the Giants Earn a Trip to the N.L.C.S.

text: A headline for a report in the Sports Briefing column in some editions on Saturday about a preseason game between the Rangers and the Chicago Blackhawks misidentified the winner. As The Associated Press report correctly noted, the Rangers won — not the Blackhawks.
match_headline: Wally Hergesheimer, a Small Big Scorer for the Rangers, Dies at 87

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the Sports Briefing column on Friday about soccer matches in the Europa League tournament misspelled the name of the team that held Tottenham to a 1-1 draw. It is Besiktas, not Beisktas. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: A Glamorous Event Injects Cash and Concerns

text: Because of an editing error, a dance review on Wednesday about Pacific Northwest Ballet, at the Marion Oliver McCaw Hall in Seattle, misstated the timing of the company’s farewell performances of Kent Stowell’s “Nutcracker.” They will be this season; they were not last season. The review also misstated the year the company will start performing George Balanchine’s “Nutcracker.” It is next year, not this Christmas.
match_headline: Original Balanchine Stars Help Turn Much-Loved ‘Jewels’ Into Heirlooms

text: An article on Wednesday about a rare attack on Israeli-controlled territory by the Lebanese Shiite group Hezbollah referred imprecisely at one point to Shebaa Farms, where explosives were set off. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, Shebaa Farms is in Israeli-occupied territory. (Although the area has been annexed by Israel, that move has not been recognized by the United Nations.)
match_headline: Hezbollah Attack Along Border With Lebanon Wounds Two Israeli Soldiers

text: An article on Oct. 2 about a new examination ordered by Afghanistan’s new president, Ashraf Ghani, of a fraud case involving the Kabul Bank referred incorrectly to pressure that was said to have been applied to a tribunal created to investigate the fraud. Drago Kos, a member of a committee that conducted an inquiry into the banking scandal, initially blamed “the presidency” for the interference; he later said that he had been referring to the Afghan vice president’s office, not that of President Hamid Karzai.
match_headline: New Afghan Leader, Putting Focus on Graft, Revives Bank Fraud Inquiry

text: An article on Thursday about patients who respond particularly well to some medications misidentified, at one point in some copies, a type of cancer the drug everolimus is commonly used to treat. As correctly noted elsewhere in the article, it is used to treat kidney and breast cancer, not bladder and breast cancer.
match_headline: Finding Clues in Genes of ‘Exceptional Responders’

text: An article on Thursday about 4K and ultrahigh-definition televisions misidentified, in some editions, the organization that predicted 800,000 UHD TVs would be sold in the United States in 2014. It is the Consumer Electronics Association, not the NPD Group.
match_headline: Sharper Image From 4K TVs Is a Gimmick Worth Having

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a possible deal to combine the assets of the Brooklyn Nets and the Los Angeles Dodgers referred incorrectly to the investor group that bought the Dodgers two years ago. The group included Mark Walter and Todd Boehly, top executives at Guggenheim Partners; the group did not include Guggenheim Partners itself.
match_headline: Nets and Dodgers Ponder a Complex Deal to Merge Assets

text: An article on June 14 about the derailed friendship of the Italian-American trailblazers Joe DiMaggio and Frank Sinatra misidentified the California city where DiMaggio was born. It is Martinez, not San Francisco. The article was corrected on The Times website in June, but editors did not follow through with this correction for print editions.
match_headline: DiMaggio and Sinatra: The Feud Between Two Italian-American Pathbreakers

text: An article on Saturday previewing that day’s top games in college football misidentified, in one reference and in some editions, the location of the game between Nebraska and Michigan State. As the article initially noted, the game was at Michigan State, in East Lansing — not in Lincoln, Neb.
match_headline: Saturday’s College Football Games to Watch

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with a dance review of a tribute to the jazz singer Betty Carter, at Dizzy’s Club Coca-Cola at Jazz at Lincoln Center, reversed the identities of two dancers. Frances Bradley is at the left and Alexandria Bradley is in the center. (As the caption correctly noted, Michela Marino Lerman is at the right.)
match_headline: Tapping Feet, Uninhibited, Step Up and Pay Tribute to a Voice of Jazz

text: An article on June 8 about concerns among Iran’s leaders over a steep decline in fertility rates misidentified the measure of population growth that hit a peak after the 1979 revolution. It was the fertility rate, or the average number of children born to a woman during her childbearing years — not the birthrate, which is the number of births per 1,000 people. The article also misstated the fertility rate at that time. It was seven children per woman, not 3.6 children per couple. This article was corrected on The Times website in September after further reporting, but editors did not follow through with this correction for print editions.
match_headline: Urged to Multiply, Iranian Couples Are Dubious

text: An article on Thursday about a decision to destroy the pet dog of an Ebola patient in Spain referred incorrectly to the results of a study that tested whether dogs can be infected with the virus. The researchers found Ebola antibodies, not antigens, in the animals’ blood. (An antigen is a substance to which the body reacts by producing antibodies.)
match_headline: Spain, Amid Protests, Destroys Dog of Ebola-Infected Nurse

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about ripples in the stock market misstated the price decline of crude oil on Thursday. It was 1.8 percent, not 1.5 percent.
match_headline: The Importance of Ignoring the Noise of the Market

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about New York City’s lowering its speed limit to 25 miles per hour, using information from an advocacy group, misstated the number of pedestrian fatalities so far in 2014, and also those at the same time last year. As of Monday, 97 pedestrians had died in 2014 compared with 122 at that time in 2013 — not 164 compared with 189.
match_headline: New York City Council Passes Bill Lowering the Speed Limit on Most Streets

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the final day of a court hearing on whether the confessions of Pedro Hernandez, the defendant in the 1979 death of Etan Patz, should be allowed at his murder trial, misspelled the surnames of two prosecutors involved with the case. The lead prosecutor is Joan Illuzzi-Orbon, not Illuzi-Orbon. And a senior prosecutor to whom Mr. Hernandez gave a second taped confession is Armand Durastanti, not Durasanti.
match_headline: Judge in Etan Patz Case to Decide if Defendant Understood Rights

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about efforts to restore the health of lakes and ponds across New York City parks misstated the given name of the Queens borough president, who has allocated money to improve Meadow Lake in Flushing Meadows-Corona Park. She is Melinda Katz, not Melissa.
match_headline: Long Neglected, Lakes and Ponds in City Parks Will Get Some Attention

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with a television review of “The Affair” misidentified the network on which the show will appear. As the review correctly noted, it is Showtime, not HBO.
match_headline: He Says, She Says. Who Knows?

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about a Revolutionary War commemoration scheduled for Sunday in Lower Manhattan misstated the telephone number for more information. It is 914-772-8213.
match_headline: Spare Times Listings for Oct. 10-16

text: A picture credit on Friday with an article about immersive theater pieces for children at the Park Avenue Armory in Manhattan misspelled the surname of the photographer. Kyle Cassidy, not Cassiday, took the pictures of two performers.
match_headline: A Test in Following Directions

text: An obituary on Thursday about Robert J. Mangum, a former deputy New York City police commissioner and chairman of the New York State Commission on Human Rights, misspelled the surname of his partner of 30 years in some editions. She is Barbara Baxter Cuyjet, not Cuylet.
match_headline: Robert Mangum, a City and Civil Rights Leader, Dies at 93

text: An article last Sunday about the anxiety among the Jewish population of the Golan Heights as violence from the civil war in neighboring Syria threatens to spill over the border referred incorrectly to the 22,000 members of the Druze sect in the Golan Heights, which Israel seized in 1967. Although most do shun Israeli citizenship, it is not the case that they generally volunteer for the Israeli military. (The Druze who live in Israel’s pre-1967 territory are Israeli citizens, and the men are subject to the draft.)
match_headline: In Golan, Imagined Risks Become All Too Real

text: An article last Sunday about the frustrations of Hong Kong police officers after they came under criticism during recent pro-democracy protests referred incorrectly to the force. The police are usually armed, except in some crowd control situations; it is not the case that they are usually unarmed.
match_headline: Scrutinized for Handling of Protests, Police Have Own Troubles

text: An article last Sunday about a Canadian school district that is teaching a detailed course on concussions and other traumatic brain injuries to ninth graders misspelled the given name of the director of research for the youth sports safety organization MomsTeam. She is Lindsey Barton Straus, not Lindsay.
match_headline: Canadian District Goes to School on Concussions

text: An article last Sunday about the Showtime spy thriller “Homeland” misstated the given name of the actress who plays Dana Brody on the show. She is Morgan Saylor, not Megan.
match_headline: Creating Drama ‘by the Seat of Our Pants’

text: A headline last Sunday about the stage adaptation of the James Dickey novel “Deliverance” by the Godlight Theater Company referred incorrectly to the size of the stage the play is being performed on. As the article correctly noted, it is a 12-by-12-foot stage, not “12 square feet.”
match_headline: Journey of the Soul, in a Small Space

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Miles Teller, who stars in Damien Chazelle’s new movie, “Whiplash,” misstated part of the name of the jam-band festival that Mr. Teller was traveling to in 2007 when the car he was in flipped over. He was going to the Gathering of the Vibes, not Gathering of the Tribes.
match_headline: Young Man in a Great Hurry

text: An entry on the combined print and e-book best-seller list on March 30 misstated the year that the English version of Paulo Coelho’s “The Alchemist” was published. It was 1993, not 2003. The error was repeated on the same list on Sept. 28 and last Sunday.
An article last Sunday about Alan Cumming omitted a director for the revival of “Cabaret” in which he now appears. Besides Sam Mendes, Rob Marshall is also directing.
match_headline: For Alan Cumming, Life Isn’t Always a Cabaret

text: An entry with the “On the Market” feature last Sunday about a three-bedroom property in Stamford misstated its price. It was listed at $1,195,000, not $1,347,750.
match_headline: On the Market in the New York Region

text: An article last Sunday about new development in Gowanus, using information provided by Halstead Property, misstated the prices at which new townhouses at 330 and 332 Bond Street are under contract. The houses are under contract at or slightly below their $2.89 million asking prices, not above the asking prices.
match_headline: Gowanus Is Counting on a Cleanup

text: An article last Sunday about LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton, the luxury goods conglomerate, misidentified the men’s wear brand where Antoine Arnault, son of LVMH’s chairman, became chief executive in 2010. It is Berluti, not Brioni.
match_headline: For the Wolf of Luxury, a Chance to Be a Lamb

text: Because of an editing error, the Eat column on Sept. 17, about a beef stew popular in Cuba, misstated the date of the Cuban revolution. It was 1959, not 1953.
match_headline: The Ultimate Cuban Comfort Food: Picadillo

text: An article on Sept. 28 about Lanai, an island owned by Larry Ellison, misidentified the source of a complaint by a senior vice president of Pulama Lanai, the management company set up to oversee the island’s transformation. She was complaining about a former planning commissioner, not a current one. The article also misspelled part of the name of a tennis tournament that is owned by Ellison. It is the BNP Paribas Open, not BPN Paribas.
match_headline: Larry Ellison Bought an Island in Hawaii. Now What?

text: An article on Friday about the biocontainment unit at the Nebraska Medical Center, which is treating Ashoka Mukpo, a freelance journalist who contracted the Ebola virus in Liberia, misstated the dosage of the experimental drug brincidofovir that he is receiving. It is twice weekly, not weekly.
match_headline: With Ebola’s Arrival at Nebraska Center, It’s No Longer a Drill

text: An article on Wednesday about the arrest of Thomas Woodrow Price, the headmaster of Branson School, a prep school in Marin County, Calif., misspelled part of the name of a New Orleans school where Mr. Price had once been headmaster. It is Isidore Newman School (not Isadore).
match_headline: California Prep School Shaken by Arrests of Headmaster and Woman, 21, on Drug Charges

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the fatal beating of a man on Staten Island, using information from police officials, misstated the age of the victim, Frank Baldassarre, in some copies. He was 80, not 82.
match_headline: Staten Island Woman Kills Husband, Police Say

text: An article on Friday about Amazon’s purchase of a building on 34th Street in Manhattan rendered incorrectly in some editions part of the name of the company at which Colin Gillis, an analyst, works. It is BGC Partners, not BCG Partners.
match_headline: Amazon Shops for Real Estate in New York City

text: An article on Wednesday about a new retail hub below Columbus Circle called TurnStyle misstated part of the name of an architecture firm working on the project. It is Architecture Outfit, not Architecture Office.
match_headline: In Depths of Columbus Circle, a Retail Hub Blooms

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the Shaq Summit, a daylong seminar about Shaquille O’Neal’s business ventures, misidentified the woman shown watching a presentation with O’Neal. She is Laticia Rolle, his current girlfriend — not Nicole Alexander, a former girlfriend. And the article described incorrectly one of the products he endorses. It is a medicated powder, not a medicated power.
match_headline: Looming Even Larger Off the Court

text: An article on Wednesday about reactions from fans of the Royals and Cardinals during a drive from Kansas City to St. Louis misstated the surname of a University of Missouri senior who is a Cardinals fan. She is Anna Hormberg, not Hornberg.
match_headline: Same State, but Divergent Paths

text: An article on Tuesday about the Florida Gators’ suspending quarterback Treon Harris after a female student accused him of sexual assault misstated, in some editions, the score by which Florida trailed late in the third quarter against Tennessee on Oct. 4, when Harris entered the game. It was 9-0, not 10-0.
match_headline: Florida Suspends a Player Accused of Sexual Assault

text: An article on Monday about the distrust that Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey faces from social and religious conservatives as he lays the groundwork for a Republican presidential run misstated the basis for a Supreme Court decision exempting family-owned corporations with religious objections from having to pay for insurance coverage for contraception under the Affordable Care Act. The Court ruled that the coverage requirement violated a federal law protecting religious freedom, not that it was unconstitutional.
match_headline: G.O.P. Right Still Has Doubt About Christie

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Kailash Satyarthi, an Indian child rights advocate who shared the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday with Malala Yousafzai, a young Pakistani activist, misstated, in some editions, the number of years after India’s independence that Mr. Satyarthi was born. It was about six and a half years, not five and a half. (India won independence from Britain in 1947; Mr. Satyarthi was born in 1954.)
match_headline: Kailash Satyarthi’s Nobel Peace Prize Caps Decades of Fighting Child Slavery in India

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about strategy changes at UBS referred incorrectly at one point to Knight Vinke. It is an investment firm, not a person.

An article on Sunday about the Kansas City Royals’ 6-4 victory over the Baltimore Orioles in Game 2 of the American League Championship Series misidentified the Orioles pitcher who gave up the hit to Omar Infante as he led off the ninth inning in a 4-4 game. The pitcher was Darren O’Day, who was charged with the loss — not Zach Britton, who replaced O’Day after the hit.
match_headline: In 9th Inning, the Royals Still Have Something Extra

text: An article on Saturday about Game 1 of the American League Championship Series referred incorrectly to the history of the Baltimore Orioles. While the Kansas City Royals were one of the “cornerstones of early American League expansion,” the Orioles were not. (The franchise was the St. Louis Browns before moving to Baltimore for the 1954 season.)
ref_headline: cornerstones of early American League expansion,
match_headline: Royals Keep Magic Alive, Beating Orioles With Homers in the 10th

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the St. Louis Cardinals’ 5-4 victory over the San Francisco Giants in Game 2 of the National League Championship Series misidentified the player who scored the tying run for the Giants in the top of the ninth inning. Matt Duffy, who entered the game as a pinch-runner for Andrew Susac scored the run — not Susac.
match_headline: Cardinals’ 4th Home Run Is Also Last Word in Game 2

text: An article on Saturday about the uncertain future of the Warburg Institute in London, which has trained generations of scholars and has a world-renowned library, misspelled the given name of an art historian who used the collection in Hamburg, where it originated. He was Erwin Panofsky, not Irwin. And because of an editing error, the article misstated part of the title of a book by Noga Arikha, who has a Ph.D. in history from the institute. It is “Passions and Tempers: A History of the Humours,” not “Passions and Tempers: The Story of the Humours.”
ref_headline: Passions and Tempers: A History of the Humours,
match_headline: Scholars Fear Loss of Eden in London

text: An editorial on Monday about voter ID laws misidentified one of the states reviewed by the Government Accountability Office for a report on the effect of the laws. It was Kansas, not Kentucky.
match_headline: The Big Lie Behind Voter ID Laws

text: An article on Saturday about Malala Yousafzai, the young Pakistani activist who shared the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday with Kailash Satyarthi, misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a professor of international relations at Columbia who commented on whether Ms. Yousafzai could transfer her international renown into a force for change. The professor is Vishakha Desai, not Vishaka.
match_headline: Malala Yousafzai, Youngest Nobel Peace Prize Winner, Adds to Her Achievements and Expectations

text: An article in some editions on Sept. 10 about the case of Gigi Jordan, a pharmaceutical executive who gave a fatal dose of drugs to her autistic son in 2010, misstated Ms. Jordan’s age. She is 53, not 54. The error was brought to the attention of editors only last week.
match_headline: Trial to Begin for a Millionaire Who Calls Her Son’s Death ‘Altruistic Filicide’

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about plans for a new musical by Stephen Sondheim and the playwright David Ives, based on two films by Luis Buñuel, erroneously attributed a comment about the timing of the production. Mr. Sondheim did not say at the New Yorker festival that a production was a few years away; he merely confirmed the project. (Oskar Eustis, the artistic director of the Public Theater, which plans to mount the show, said that a production would not come before the 2016-17 season.)
match_headline: Stephen Sondheim Plans a New Musical, Based on Buñuel Films

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Inside Art column on Friday about auctions of artworks and other objects owned by Lauren Bacall, including sculptures by Henry Moore, misidentified the English county in which Moore’s studio, which Bacall visited, is situated. It is in Hertfordshire, not Essex.
match_headline: For Sale: The First Artwork de Kooning Saw Every Workday

text: A review last Wednesday of Huertas, a restaurant in the East Village, referred incorrectly to its Sunday schedule. It is open for brunch, not for dinner.
match_headline: A Serendipitous Trip to Spain

text: An obituary on Thursday about the actress Iva Withers referred incorrectly to her portrayal of Julie Jordan in the musical “Carousel.” She played the role in the original London production of the show, not during a British tour. (As the obituary noted, she also played the role on a tour of the United States and in a Broadway revival.)
match_headline: Iva Withers, a Standby to the Rescue on Broadway, Dies at 97

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the opera singer Rita Shane misstated the name of a magazine that published an interview with her. It is Post, not The Rochester Post.
match_headline: Rita Shane, a Met Soprano Known for Range and Intensity, Dies at 78

text: An article on Oct. 6 about the results of the Brazilian presidential election that forced the incumbent, Dilma Rousseff, into a runoff gave an outdated title for Eduardo Campos, a rival candidate who was killed in a plane crash in August. At the time of his death, he was a former governor of Pernambuco, not still holding office.
match_headline: Dilma Rousseff Emerges as Front-Runner in Brazil’s Election but Faces Runoff

text: An article on Monday about the congressional campaign of Gwen Graham in Florida referred incorrectly to one of her children. She has two sons and a daughter, not three sons.
match_headline: In Florida, a Chance for Democrats to Win One Back

text: An article on Wednesday about a ruling in favor of New York University’s expansion plan misidentified the court that made the decision. It is the Appellate Division of the New York State Supreme Court, not the New York State Court of Appeals.
match_headline: Court Gives Go-Ahead to Expansion by N.Y.U.

text: A headline on Wednesday about the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s so-called Doomsday Book and how it has come into public view in a trial involving the 2008 rescue of the American International Group referred incorrectly to the document’s connection to the A.I.G. bailout. While the Doomsday Book is a collection of memos and legal opinions that can serve as a blueprint for fighting financial crises, Fed officials have said that it did not guide their actions on A.I.G.
match_headline: Fed Is Silent on Doomsday Book, a Blueprint for Fighting Crises

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Friday about New York Comic Con, which celebrates the crossroads of comic books and pop culture, misstated part of the title of a mixed martial arts organization associated with a fan event in Las Vegas. It is the Ultimate Fighting Championship, not the United Fighting Championship.
match_headline: At New York Comic Con, Growing Pains Come With the Crowds

text: A listing of credits on Wednesday with a theater review of “Found,” at the Atlantic Theater Company in Manhattan, misspelled the surname of the production stage manager. He is Mark Dobrow, not Dubrow.
match_headline: Discovering Stories in the Words Left Behind

text: A picture credit on Tuesday with an article about a new book that traces the universe in graphic form through the ages, using information from the publisher, misspelled the name of an institution where a set of pictures depicting space-time’s origins was found. It is the Biblioteca Nacional de España, not Biblioteca Nationale Spain.
match_headline: Cosmos as Masterpiece

text: An obituary on Thursday about Norward Roussell, the first black superintendent of schools in Selma, Ala., misstated the number of years he was superintendent of the Macon County schools in Alabama. It was four years, not eight. The obituary also misspelled part of the name of the bridge where state troopers attacked civil rights demonstrators in 1965. It is the Edmund Pettus Bridge, not the Edmund Pettis Bridge.
match_headline: Norward Roussell, Leader of Selma Schools in Turbulent Time, Dies at 80

text: An article on Thursday about threats against critics of the video game industry misstated, at one point, part of the name of a lobbying group for video game companies. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is the Entertainment Software Association, not the Electronic Software Association.
match_headline: Feminist Critics of Video Games Facing Threats in ‘GamerGate’ Campaign

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Bermuda’s preparations for Hurricane Gonzalo as it approached the island misstated, in some copies, the location of Bermuda relative to North Carolina. It is 670 miles east of North Carolina, not west.
match_headline: Bermuda Prepares for Hurricane Gonzalo

text: An article on Friday about calls to use Yucca Mountain in Nevada as a nuclear waste site misidentified, in some copies, the home state of Representative John M. Shimkus, a Republican, who said the latest report confirmed that the facility was safe and secure. He is from Illinois, not Michigan.
match_headline: Calls to Use Yucca Mountain as a Nuclear Waste Site, Now Deemed Safe

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a man who slashed other passengers on a bus headed to a Connecticut casino before he was killed by a state trooper referred incorrectly to Simon Lee, who works for the bus operator, Dahlia Travel and Tours. While he has driven Dahlia buses to casinos in Connecticut, he was not the driver of the bus where the attack took place. (Mr. Lee later commented on the episode, noting that disruptions on the buses are common.)
match_headline: Connecticut Trooper Kills Man Accused of Slashing 2 Aboard Bus Headed to Casino

text: An article on Oct. 7 about the sale of the Waldorf-Astoria hotel to a Chinese insurance company misstated the relationship between Taj Hotel Resorts, a foreign company, and the Pierre Hotel in New York City. Taj operates the Pierre; it does not own the hotel.
match_headline: Waldorf-Astoria to Be Sold in a $1.95 Billion Deal

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article in some editions on Friday about the Jets’ 27-25 loss to the New England Patriots misidentified the player shown near the goal line in some copies. The photograph was of the Patriots’ Danny Amendola scoring a touchdown, not of the Jets’ Chris Ivory being knocked out of bounds just short of the goal line. (The picture of Ivory ran in an earlier edition.)
match_headline: Against Patriots, Jets Do Everything but Win the Game

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about St. Louis Cardinals reliever Randy Choate, whose error led to the winning run in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series against the San Francisco Giants, misstated, in some copies, the year he had a difficult outing at Fenway Park that shaped how he handled adversity. It was in 2001, not 2000.
match_headline: After Gaffe, Cardinals’ Randy Choate Recalls Lesson Learned Early

text: An article on Page 102 this weekend about the shoemaker Jean-Michel Casalonga, Berluti’s youngest master craftsman, erroneously includes a passage about a point in the company’s history when an African dictator reportedly spent about $85,000 on a pair of shoes. At the time the dictator supposedly bought the shoes, in 1977, the company was under a different ownership; he is not a current client of Berluti’s. (That reference has been removed from the version of the article found at nytimes.com/tmagazine, on the men’s fashion page.)
match_headline: Sweden’s Latest and Greatest Fashion Chain Makes Its Stateside Debut

text: An article last Sunday about the benefits and drawbacks of reading to toddlers from digital devices quoted incorrectly from comments by Claudia Raleigh, whose son, Teddy, was first allowed to use an iPad during his sister’s swim class. Ms. Raleigh said, “You know how hard it is to wait somewhere with a 2-year-old” — not “to sit somewhere.”
ref_headline: You know how hard it is to wait somewhere with a 2-year-old
match_headline: Is E-Reading to Your Toddler Story Time, or Simply Screen Time?

text: An article on Oct. 5 about an apology that Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. made to the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, after Mr. Biden had suggested in remarks that Turkey helped facilitate the rise of the Islamic State terrorist group misidentified, in some editions, the Turkish city in which Mr. Erdogan spoke to reporters on Saturday. He was in Istanbul, not Ankara.
match_headline: Biden Apologizes to Turkish President

text: An article last Sunday about the life of a first-year medical resident at Woodhull Medical and Mental Health Center in Brooklyn misidentified, in some editions, the hospital position held by Dr. Edward Fishkin, who described some of the ailments that the health center’s doctors frequently treat. He is a medical director, not the chief of medicine.
match_headline: To Become a Doctor

text: Because of an editing error, the byline for an article in some editions last Sunday about Baylor University’s 61-58 college football victory over Texas Christian University misspelled the writer’s given name. He is Marc Tracy, not Mark.
match_headline: Baylor Tops T.C.U., Overcoming 21-Point Deficit in 11-Minute Whirl

text: An obituary last Sunday about the German author Siegfried Lenz referred incorrectly to the Waffen-SS, of which Mr. Lenz’s fellow author Günter Grass admitted in 2006 he had been a member. It was the military arm of the SS, the Nazi special police; it was not a “Nazi division.”
match_headline: Siegfried Lenz, Novelist of Germany’s Past, Dies at 88

text: An article on Oct. 5 about Terrence McNally’s 1986 Off Broadway showbiz satire, “It’s Only a Play,” updated for a Broadway run this fall, misstated the year the comedian Joan Rivers was the punch line of a joke in an earlier production of the play. It was in the 1992 version that Rivers was said to have been mauled by a theater producer’s dog — not the 1986 production. (Arlene Francis was the punch line in the 1986 version.)
match_headline: Keep the Jokes, Change the Names

text: An entry on the hardcover fiction bestseller list last Sunday misstated the surname of a character in “To Dwell in Darkness,” by Deborah Crombie. She is Gemma James, not Jones.

A review on Oct. 5 about “The Zone of Interest,” a novel by Martin Amis set in Auschwitz, misidentified the historical figure on whom one of the book’s characters, Paul Doll, the camp commandant, seems loosely based. He was the Auschwitz commandant Rudolf Höss, not Rudolf Hess , who was deputy leader of the Nazi Party.
match_headline: Viper’s Nest

text: A report on Oct. 12 about the wedding of Anna Esther Jacob Fogel and Robert Edward Nelson misidentified the position the bride held when she worked for the Social Innovation Fund, part of the federal Corporation for National and Community Service. She was the program manager, not the manager, of an initiative for the fund.
match_headline: Anna Fogel, Robert Nelson

text: A picture credit last Sunday with the Streetscapes column, about the work of the artist Robert Winthrop Chanler, misidentified the source of the portrait of the artist. It was from the Juley Collection, Smithsonian Museum of American Art — not from the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens.
match_headline: An Aristocratic Painter’s Astonishing Aesthetic

text: An article last Sunday about Nicola Bulgari’s automobile collection referred incorrectly to a 1949 movie in which one of his cars appeared. Although a 1940 Buick woody associated with Bette Davis was used in “White Heat,” she was not in the movie.
match_headline: Rough Gems, Brought to a Fine Polish

text: An article on Friday about a disagreement over a fan at the Florida governor’s debate misspelled the given name of the debate moderator. He is Eliott Rodriguez, not Elliot.
match_headline: Fan Delays Florida Debate, and Mocking Circulates Online

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about possible reasons for a smoke bomb attack on Bar Pitti, a restaurant in the West Village, misstated the given name of a man who dined there several days later. He is Robert Snyder, not Richard.
match_headline: Smoke Bomb Raises Security Concerns for M.T.A.

text: An article on Wednesday about scandals involving Citigroup’s Mexican unit, Banamex, misspelled the given name of the former head of Banamex’s security unit. He is Federico Ponce Rojas, not Frederico.
match_headline: Another Scandal Hits Citigroup’s Moneymaking Mexican Division

text: An article on Friday about a debate over pay for workers in the retailing industry misstated, in some copies, part of the name of an industry trade organization that has warned against raising the minimum wage. The group is the National Retail Federation, not National Retail Foundation.
match_headline: Walmart Workers Demand $15 Wage in Several Protests

text: A news analysis article on Wednesday about the Detroit Lions’ defense misstated, in some copies, the given name of a defensive end on the team. He is Jason Jones, not James.
match_headline: In Detroit, the Lions’ Defense Now Does the Heavy Lifting

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Thursday with the On Pro Basketball column, about the Knicks assistant coach Jim Cleamons’s awkward history with Walt Frazier, a TV analyst for the team, misstated, in some copies, the year the photograph showing Cleamons guarding Frazier was taken. It was 1978, not 1977.
match_headline: Reminder of Knicks’ Dysfunction Is Again Hoping to Solve It

text: An article on July 5 about the pathbreaking career of the tennis star Arthur Ashe misstated the height of his monument in Richmond, Va., relative to Robert E. Lee’s. Mr. Ashe’s monument is about half the height of General Lee’s, not one-fifth the size. The error was corrected on The Times website on July 7, but editors did not follow through with this correction for print editions.
match_headline: Arthur Ashe, Pathbreaker: From Richmond to Wimbledon, and Back

text: An article last Monday about the Taxis Ditch, an often deadly jump in the Velka Pardubicka steeplechase race in the Czech Republic, omitted a credit. Jan Richter contributed reporting.
match_headline: This Leap Is for Horses’ Lives

text: A listing of credits and a picture credit on Wednesday with a film review of “The Vanquishing of the Witch Baba Yaga” at the Museum of Modern Art, using information from the museum, misidentified the distributor. It is Myriapod Productions, not Argot Pictures.
ref_headline: The Vanquishing of the Witch Baba Yaga
match_headline: A Slavic Tone Poem, via Hansel and Gretel

text: An obituary on Saturday about Robert W. Fri, a former director of the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of Natural History, misstated the given name of one of his sons, who survives him. He is Perry Fri, not Harry.
match_headline: Robert W. Fri, Energy Adviser and Director at Smithsonian, Dies at 78

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the opera singer Anita Cerquetti misstated her age at the time she substituted for Maria Callas in the Bellini opera “Norma” in January 1958. She was 26, not 25. (As the obituary correctly noted, she was born on April 12, 1931.)
match_headline: Anita Cerquetti, Opera Fill-In Who Soared, Dies at 83

text: An obituary on Sunday about the former New York State comptroller Edward V. Regan, using information from his family, misstated his mother’s given name. She was Allison Van Buren Regan, not Caroline.
match_headline: Edward V. Regan, Longtime New York State Comptroller, Dies at 84

text: An article on Friday about the possibility that President Obama would appoint an Ebola czar to manage the government’s response to the virus misstated the number of people who have contracted the disease in the United States. It is two, not three. (Two Dallas nurses, Nina Pham and Amber Joy Vinson, contracted the disease in the United States; Thomas Eric Duncan was diagnosed with the disease while in this country but was infected in Liberia.)
match_headline: Obama May Name ‘Czar’ to Oversee Ebola Response

text: An article on Sept. 25 about a visit by President Hassan Rouhani of Iran to New York for the United Nations General Assembly misspelled the surname of a British-Iranian woman imprisoned in Iran since June, a case that drew protests when Mr. Rouhani spoke at the New York Hilton. She is Ghoncheh Ghavami, not Ghavani. And an article on Sept. 26 about a speech by Mr. Rouhani at the United Nations repeated the misspelled surname for her brother, Iman, a British national, who went to the Iranian mission to the United Nations shortly after Mr. Rouhani’s speech and protested her incarceration.
match_headline: Iranian President Praises Cooperation in New York

text: A headline on Saturday about Ron Klain, the administration’s Ebola response coordinator, misstated his relationship to Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. in some copies. Mr. Klain is a former aide to Mr. Biden, not a current aide.
match_headline: Before Ebola, New Czar Handled Political Crises

text: An article on Saturday about calls for and resistance to a ban on travel from West African nations to contain the Ebola outbreak misstated the given name of the Liberian man who died of Ebola in Dallas. He was Thomas Eric Duncan, not Michael.
match_headline: Experts Oppose Ebola Travel Ban, Saying It Would Cut Off Worst-Hit Countries

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the Wall Street Rocks fund-raising concert for veterans at the Highline Ballroom in Manhattan on Nov. 10 misidentified the band in which one of the participants, Aaron Hersey, plays bass. It is Pork Tornado, not Phish. (Phish’s drummer, Jon Fishman, also plays in Pork Tornado.)
match_headline: Semper Fi Fund’s Horsemanship Program Offers Peace to Veterans

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the sale of 21 of Cindy Sherman’s “Untitled Film Stills” at Christie’s next month misidentified the purchaser of those works from Ydessa Hendeles, a curator, artist and former dealer who initially gathered them. They were bought by Mitchell P. and Emily Rales, not by Christie’s.
match_headline: Cindy Sherman’s ‘Untitled Film Stills’ Go to Auction

text: An obituary on Saturday about the defense lawyer James M. LaRossa omitted one of his survivors. Besides two daughters, a sister, four grandchildren and his son Thomas, he is survived by another son, James Jr.
match_headline: James M. LaRossa, Defender of Mob Bosses in Court, Dies at 82

text: An article on Saturday about efforts by relatives of Ludwig and Margret Kainer, German Jews whose art collection was seized by the Nazis, to collect proceeds from the sale of some of the art misidentified the connection of James Palmer, who commented on the issue, to the Mondex Corporation, which helps recover looted property and is aiding the relatives. He is the former president, not the president. (Kamila Gourdie now holds that position.)
match_headline: Heirs Sue Bank Over Sale of Nazi-Looted Art

text: An article on Sept. 30 about missteps by the German military as it tries to assume a role in international crises misstated Germany’s place among the world’s exporters. It ranks third, according to the World Trade Organization; it is not the “leading exporter.”
match_headline: Seeking Global Role, German Military Stumbles

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with the Paris Journal article, about the growing popularity of the vast Paris catacombs among street artists, history buffs and others, misidentified the man shown in the center of a group of people in a gallery in the catacombs. He is an unidentified friend of an artist known as Nobad; he is not Nobad.
match_headline: The Secret Is Out on a Cherished Underground Haven

text: An article on Tuesday about the Republican Party’s ability to maintain its majority in the House of Representatives without the support of Hispanic voters misstated the number of Republican-held congressional districts that the Cook Political Report considers potentially competitive. There are 23 such districts, not 24.
match_headline: Why House Republicans Alienate Hispanics: They Don’t Need Them

text: An article in some editions on Friday about efforts to add a pedestrian lane to the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge used an outdated proposal in describing a roughly 50-mile route that would include the Verrazano as it circumnavigates the waterfronts of three boroughs and New Jersey. As an accompanying map correctly showed, the route would cross the East River by way of the Manhattan Bridge, not by using both the Manhattan Bridge and the Brooklyn Bridge, which had been part of the original plan.
match_headline: Pedestrian Lane Sought for Verrazano-Narrows Bridge

text: An article on Monday about competitive video gaming in South Korea misstated the name of a top Korean college that recently admitted two students based on their successes in e-sports. It is Chung-Ang University, not Chungnam National University.
match_headline: For South Korea, E-Sports Is National Pastime

text: An article on Saturday about the San Francisco Giants’ recent postseason success in even-numbered years contained several errors.
match_headline: If the Leaves Are Falling, the San Francisco Giants Are Rising

text: An article on Tuesday about the new Louis Vuitton Foundation cultural center and contemporary-art museum in Paris, designed by Frank Gehry and clad in glass, and about a retrospective of Mr. Gehry’s career, at the Pompidou Center, misidentified the island in the Seine on which the 13th-century Sainte-Chapelle is situated in citing the long Parisian tradition of major structures featuring glass. It is the Île de la Cité, not the Île St.-Louis.
match_headline: An Architect’s Big Parisian Moment

text: An Editorial Observer on Oct. 7 about the gloomy mood in France misstated the spending cuts announced by the Hollande government. It was 50 billion euros over the next three years, not in 2015
match_headline: After a Dreary Summer, Autumn Chill in France

text: An earlier version of the correction about the island in the Seine on which a 13th-century chapel is situated misspelled the chapel’s name. It is Sainte-Chapelle, not Sainte-Chappelle.

An article on Friday about the experiences of an American physician, Steven Hatch, at an Ebola treatment center in Liberia misstated the circumstances surrounding a blood test for an elderly man who was examined by Dr. Hatch. The test was delayed and the sample carried an incorrect number, but there was no test mix-up that initially suggested that the man was infected with Ebola.
match_headline: In Layers of Gear, Offering Healing Hand to Ebola Patients in Liberia

text: An article on Tuesday about remarks by Hong Kong’s leader, Leung Chun-ying, that disparaged open elections, one of the goals of the pro-democracy protesters in the territory, referred incorrectly to the creation of Hong Kong’s Basic Law, a mini-constitution. It was written before — not after — Britain handed sovereignty of the city back to China.
match_headline: Hong Kong Leader Reaffirms Unbending Stance on Elections

text: An article on Saturday about Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s plan to replace Judge Victoria A. Graffeo on the New York State Court of Appeals with Justice Leslie E. Stein, 57, an appellate division jurist in Albany, misstated, in some editions, the former title of Christine C. Quinn, who publicly urged the governor to replace Judge Graffeo. She was City Council speaker, not president. The article also misspelled, in some copies, the surname of an Albany Law School professor who commented on Mr. Cuomo’s choice. He is Vincent Bonventre, not Bonaventre.
match_headline: Cuomo Picks Democrat for Top State Court, Creating Liberal Majority

text: An article on Oct. 10 about Lincoln Center’s adding solar panels to the roof of the Rose Building referred incorrectly to the building’s connection to the Juilliard School. Part of the Rose Building is used for housing for Juilliard students; the building does not house the school itself. (The school and its classrooms are adjacent to the Rose Building.)
match_headline: Lincoln Center Turns to Solar Power to Provide Some of Its Bright Light

text: An article on Tuesday about Apple’s earnings misstated Apple’s revenue for its 2014 fiscal year in some copies. It was $182.8 billion, not $182.8 million.
match_headline: IPhone Demand Provides Apple With Record-Breaking Quarter

text: An article on Monday about Aaron Kushner, the C.E.O. and chairman of Freedom Communications, misspelled the given name of a former executive of The Orange County Register who settled a lawsuit over his severance from the newspaper. He is Mark McEachen, not Mack McEachen.
match_headline: For Aaron Kushner, a Difficult Foray Into Newspapers

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the San Francisco Giants’ 7-1 victory over the Kansas City Royals in Game 1 of the World Series misidentified the Giants player who went to third base on a wild pitch in the top of the fourth inning. He is Hunter Pence, not Brandon Belt.
match_headline: Giants and Madison Bumgarner Upstage Royals

text: A picture on Wednesday with a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column about the casting of Tatiana Maslany and Thomas Sadoski in a new Neil LaBute play, “The Way We Get By,” was published in error. It showed Steve Pasquale, another actor, not Mr. Sadoski.
match_headline: Tatiana Maslany to Star in New LaBute Play

text: An article last Thursday about men’s wear companies started by several sets of brothers misspelled the name of a British boarding school in an allegorical reference to the sort of Brooklynites who would buy clothes from Bespoken, one of the companies. They would fancy themselves as alumni of Eton, not Eaton.
match_headline: A New Band of Fashion Brothers

text: An article on Oct. 9 about the renovation of a home in Red Hook, Brooklyn, misidentified the material used for the garage door at the back of the house. It is glass, not plastic.
match_headline: In Red Hook, Brooklyn, a House for a Rainy Day

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Currents section on Oct. 9, about a wallpaper by Sheila Bridges called Hudson Toile, misstated the number of years Ms. Bridges has owned a home in the Hudson Valley. It is 15, not 20.
match_headline: Hudson Gothic

text: An article on Thursday about the fear that gripped Ottawa when a gunman fatally shot a soldier before entering the Parliament building and opening fire misidentified, in some editions, the city where Quebec separatists kidnapped two officials, later killing one of them. The abductions occurred in Montreal and one of its suburbs, not in Ottawa.
match_headline: After Shooting, Fear and Anxiety Take Over Ottawa

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Wednesday about an inquiry into how the authorities in Northern Ireland handled a woman’s account of being raped referred incorrectly to Martin Morris, the man who the woman said had attacked her. Mr. Morris is accused of being a member of the Irish Republican Army; he has not been convicted of such a crime, and he denies it.
match_headline: Northern Ireland Orders Inquiry Into Handling of Rape Allegations

text: An article on Wednesday about the opening, in Warsaw, of the Museum of the History of Polish Jews misspelled the surname of a former Warsaw mayor and later president of Poland who agreed to pay for the museum’s construction. He was Lech Kaczynski, not Kazcynski.
match_headline: To Celebrate Its Jewish History, Poland Presents ‘a Museum of Life’

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Wednesday about a letter detailing the sexual assault allegations against the lawyer Sanford A. Rubenstein described incorrectly Mr. Rubenstein’s practice of law. He focuses on civil law, representing plaintiffs; he is not a defense lawyer. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Letter to Manhattan Prosecutor Details Rape Allegation Against Prominent Lawyer

text: An article on Wednesday about accelerating federal and state efforts to require financial institutions to strengthen their defenses against online attacks misstated the disclosure of a detail about an attack on JPMorgan Chase’s systems. Bloomberg News reported in August how long the attack went undetected; it is not the case that it had not previously been reported.
match_headline: After JPMorgan Chase Breach, Push to Close Wall St. Security Gaps

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the N.B.A. Board of Governors’ decision not to change the format of the league’s draft lottery misstated, in some copies, the day the vote was taken. It was Wednesday, not Monday.
match_headline: Rejection of Draft Changes Gives Top Losers in N.B.A. a Victory

text: An article on Oct. 14 about an exhibit at New York University that recreates the Eugenics Record Office referred incompletely to legislation supported by the eugenics movement. While forced sterilization laws were passed, that was done on a state-by-state basis — not at the federal level.
match_headline: When Racism Was a Science

text: An article on Friday about the first Ebola patient in New York City, using information from city officials, misstated the body temperature of the patient, Dr. Craig Spencer, when he notified the authorities of his ill health on Thursday. It was 100.3, not 103.
match_headline: Doctor in New York City Is Sick With Ebola

text: An article last Saturday about the anxiety across Europe over the Ebola virus even though there have been just a handful of cases outside Africa referred incorrectly to Britain’s response to the Ebola crisis. It suspended all flights from the three West African countries most affected by the disease, not from all of West Africa.
match_headline: In Europe, Fear of Ebola Exceeds the Actual Risks

text: An article on Thursday about home movies made mainly by American Jews returning to their Polish hometowns in the 1920s and 1930s that have been used by the documentary filmmaker Peter Forgacs to make an installation at the Museum of the City of New York referred incorrectly to the Polish film “Warsaw Uprising.” It is about the Warsaw Uprising of 1944, not about the people who staged the Warsaw Ghetto revolt in 1943.
match_headline: Precious Windows on a Vanished World

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about the Halloween Harvest at Luna Park in Coney Island misstated the date of one event. Marc Maniac and the Maniac Pumpkin Carvers will create a piece of art today at 2 p.m., not Sunday.
match_headline: Spare Times Listings for Oct. 24-30

text: An article on Page F1 this weekend misidentifies the owner of a collection of landscape photographs of California and the Northwest by the 19th-century photographer Carleton Watkins. The collection belongs to the Stanford University Libraries — not to the Cantor Arts Center at Stanford University, which exhibited the pictures.
match_headline: Museums Morph Digitally

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary in some editions on Friday about Frank Mankiewicz, a Democratic political strategist and a former president of National Public Radio, omitted some survivors. They include an older brother, Donald Mankiewicz; four stepdaughters, Marianna, Margaret and Maureen Koval and Monica Krider; and eight step-grandchildren.
match_headline: Frank Mankiewicz, 90, Press Aide to Robert Kennedy and NPR Chief, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some copies last Sunday about Florida State’s 31-27 victory over Notre Dame in college football misstated Notre Dame’s field position after a last-minute touchdown was called back because of a penalty. Notre Dame was at Florida State’s 18-yard line, not its own.
match_headline: A Flag Appears, Notre Dame’s Momentary Lead Vanishes, and F.S.U. Survives

text: An article last Sunday about the modest rivalry between Kansas City and San Francisco misidentified the performer who sang of Kansas City “they got a crazy way of loving.” It was Little Willie Littlefield — not Fats Domino, who recorded a different version of the song.
ref_headline: they got a crazy way of loving.
match_headline: A Modest Rivalry Gains Some Heft

text: An article on Oct. 5 about bourbon-barrel-aged craft beers in Chicago misspelled the surname of an enthusiast attending an event at a bar there. He is Scott O’Dea, not O’Dey.
match_headline: In Chicago, a Tasting Tour of Barrel-Aged Beer

text: A review last Sunday about the BMW i8 misstated the car’s weight as well as comparisons with two other cars. The i8 weighs 3,455 pounds, not 3,273; it is 480 pounds lighter than the Aston Martin DB9, not 750, and about 1,200 pounds lighter than the Tesla Model S, not 1,400.
match_headline: Yes, Gawkers: Attention Must Be Paid

text: A review last Sunday about the BMW i3 misstated the car’s availability. It is being offered by 285 of BMW’s 339 dealers across the United States; it is not the case that it is offered only in major California cities, the New York City area and Austin, Tex.
match_headline: A New Species of Battery-Driven BMW

text: An article last Sunday about the new Broadway musical “The Last Ship,” which was conceived of by Sting, who also wrote the songs, referred incorrectly to the city where Sting grew up. Though it is known as Newcastle, England, its full name is Newcastle-upon-Tyne, not Newcastle-on-Tyne. An accompanying picture caption repeated the error.
match_headline: From Newcastle to Broadway

text: A news analysis article last Sunday on the conspiracy theories about Ebola referred incorrectly to the spread of a different disease. The Black, or bubonic, plague was not caused by a viral agent but by bacteria.
match_headline: The Ebola Conspiracy Theories

text: A caption for the cover photograph on Oct. 5 for an article about a lawsuit filed in Louisiana against oil companies misidentified the canal shown. It is an unnamed canal near Delacroix, La.; it is not the Barataria- Terrebone Estuary.
match_headline: Under Cover: Louisiana’s Disappearing Coast

text: An article on Sept. 7 about pretesting as a learning technique misstated the given name of the author of a 1939 psychological paper on the retention of knowledge. He was Herbert F. Spitzer, not Herman.
match_headline: Why Flunking Exams Is Actually a Good Thing

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the fashion designer Oscar de la Renta misstated the name of his fragrance for men. It is Pour Lui, not Pour Homme.
match_headline: Oscar de la Renta, Who Clothed Stars and Became One, Dies at 82

text: An article on Friday about donations to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee miscalculated the percentage of all donations that were refunded. It was 0.41 percent, not 0.44 percent.

An article on Thursday about some companies’ offers of discounted solar systems for their employees misspelled the surname of the vice president for global sustainability at 3M, one company involved in the program. She is Gayle Schueller, not Schuler.
match_headline: Home Solar Power Discounts Are Worker Perk in New Program

text: An article on Tuesday about Rear Adm. R. Timothy Ziemer and the global fight against malaria misstated his age when he boarded the plane that had evacuated his wounded mother from Vietnam. He was 21 at the time, not 17. The article also referred incorrectly to his parents’ missionary work. They were missionaries with the Christian and Missionary Alliance; they were not Presbyterian missionaries.
match_headline: The Malaria Fighter

text: An article on Sunday about the shooting at Marysville-Pilchuck High School in Washington state misspelled the surname of one of two 14-year-old girls being treated for gunshot wounds. She is Shaylee Chuckulnaskit, not Chucklenaskit.
match_headline: Tangled Portrait of a Student Emerges in Washington Shooting

text: An article on Thursday about Oscar de la Renta’s life and friendships in the New York region misstated, in some editions, the year his first wife, Françoise de la Renta, died. It was 1983, not 1989.
match_headline: Oscar de la Renta Was Household Name for New York’s Elite

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the death of 4-year-old girl in a homeless shelter, using information from the police, misstated the girl’s given name. She was Linayjah Meraldo, not Lanaysah.
match_headline: 4-Year-Old Girl Is Found Dead in a Shelter in Queens

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s change in tone on handling potential Ebola cases referred incorrectly in some editions to an appearance by Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey and Mr. Cuomo at a news conference in Lower Manhattan on Friday night. Mr. Christie met Mr. Cuomo in Lower Manhattan; they did not ride the subway together to the event.
match_headline: Cuomo, Shifting His Policy on Outbreak, Opens Up Public Rift With de Blasio

text: An article on Monday about Facebook’s increasing effect on journalism misstated the month the company altered its algorithm, causing a decline in traffic at some websites. It was December 2013, not February of this year.
match_headline: How Facebook Is Changing the Way Its Users Consume Journalism

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the United States women’s soccer team’s 3-0 victory over Mexico, which earned the team a spot in the Women’s World Cup, misidentified the Mexican goalkeeper who played in the match. She is Pamela Tajonar, not Cecilia Santiago.
match_headline: U.S. Women Secure Berth in 2015 World Cup

text: An article on Monday about Steve Perry, the former lead singer for Journey who is a die-hard fan of the San Francisco Giants, misstated the section of the AT&T Park where he usually sits. It is 219, not 119.
match_headline: With Giants in Series, One Rock Song Goes On and On and On and On

text: An article on Friday about the artist Hans Haacke, the subject of a solo exhibition at the Paula Cooper Gallery in Manhattan, referred incompletely to the sales contract drafted by activists in the 1970s, which he still uses. The 15 percent royalty an artist gets when a work is resold is 15 percent of the work’s appreciated value, as opposed to 15 percent of the resale price.
match_headline: Contrarian Stays True to His Cred

text: An article on Tuesday about a mass surveillance program by the United States Postal Service omitted credit for a media organization that earlier reported the existence of an audit of the Postal Inspection Service. Although the article said that the audit, which found that the Postal Service approved nearly 50,000 requests last year to monitor the mail of Americans, was “little-noticed,” Politico reported about the audit in June.
match_headline: Report Reveals Wider Tracking of Mail in U.S.

text: An article on Sept. 24 about the rising alarm over a resurgence of anti-Semitism in Europe erroneously included an attack in Sweden among examples of anti-Semitic violence. Although the police suspected that an attack in July in which a man with an Israeli flag in his window was beaten with iron pipes was a hate crime, they concluded that was not the case. (An investigation showed that the victim was not Jewish and that the flag might have been unrelated to the attack.) This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Europe’s Anti-Semitism Comes Out of the Shadows

text: An article on Saturday about the discontent, alienation and radicalism that marked the life of a young man who killed a soldier before storming Canada’s Parliament misspelled the surname of the gunman, who was shot dead, at several points. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he was Michael Zehaf-Bibeau, not Zehar-Bibeau.
match_headline: Ottawa Gunman’s Radicalism Deepened as Life Crumbled

text: An article on Oct. 17 about possible firings at the Department of Veterans Affairs referred incompletely to a claim that 40 veterans died awaiting medical treatment. The claim was made at the time the scandal broke, but a report later by the department’s office of inspector general was unable to substantiate allegations that the veterans may have died because of treatment delays in Phoenix.
match_headline: After Hospital Scandal, V.A. Officials Jump Ship

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the exhibition “Picasso & the Camera,” at the Gagosian Gallery on West 21st Street in Manhattan, misspelled the surname of the photographer with whom Picasso made the work “Diurnes.” He is André Villers, not Villiers.
match_headline: Wielding a Lens as Skillfully as a Brush

text: A report in the In Brief column on Tuesday about a study that has found that the phenomenon of “decision fatigue” exists in doctors, causing them to prescribe more antibiotics at the end of their shifts than at the beginning, referred incorrectly to the phenomenon in judges. Studies have shown that judges are more likely to deny parole — not bail — at the end of the day than at the beginning.
match_headline: Doctors and Decision Fatigue

text: An article on Tuesday about the building of latrines in India and the possibility they will not improve public health referred incorrectly to Odisha, the location of villages that were studied. Odisha is a state in India, formerly known as Orissa; it is not a district.
match_headline: Latrines May Not Improve Health of Poor Children

text: An article on Wednesday about aid workers and health officials in Liberia who have found that far fewer people are being treated for Ebola than anticipated misstated, in some editions, the given name of a clergyman and member of an Ebola task force. He is the Rev. G. Victor Padmore, not John. And the article and a picture caption misspelled the name of a town in Liberia in some editions. It is Gbarnga, not Gbanga.
match_headline: In Liberia, a Good or Very Bad Sign: Empty Hospital Beds

text: An article on Wednesday about plans to screen and release the unfinished last film of Orson Welles, “The Other Side of the Wind,” misspelled the given name of an actress in the cast in some editions. She was Lilli Palmer, not Lili. And because of an editing error, the article misstated the age of Filip Jan Rymsza of Royal Road Entertainment, a production company that said it had reached an agreement to buy the rights to the film. He is 36, not 38.
ref_headline: The Other Side of the Wind,
match_headline: Orson Welles’s Last Film May Finally Be Released

text: An article last Thursday about a second relocation by the New York City Police Museum, which is still waiting for repairs to its First Precinct building damaged by Hurricane Sandy, referred incorrectly to annual visitors at that site. About 100,000 people visited each year, not merely “more than 10,000.”
match_headline: Its Home Still Awaiting Repairs, New York City Police Museum Is Packing Up Once Again

text: Because of an editing error, the On Pro Football column on Tuesday, about plans by General Manager John Idzik to make a winner out of the woeful Jets, overstated the support he expressed for Coach Rex Ryan at a news conference on Monday. While Idzik supported the embattled coach, he did not guarantee Ryan would last the next two months in his job.
match_headline: Jets and John Idzik Have Plan to Succeed, Just Not a Roster to Do So

text: An article on Saturday about Yale running back Tyler Varga referred incorrectly to a picture of him that ran in the Yale student newspaper last week. The caption with the photograph did not describe the play shown, but the picture was not “caption-less.”
match_headline: Yale Running Back Confounds Opponents (and His Teammates, Too)

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with a Critic’s Notebook article about the annual gala concert for the Jazz Foundation of America, at the Apollo Theater, misidentified the drummer shown. He is Billy Hart — not Albert Heath, who also performed.
match_headline: A Jazz Gala at the Apollo for a Noble Cause

text: An article on Tuesday about the use of beavers and their dams as a defense against the effects of a changing climate referred incorrectly to the dams. They create separate ponds in which the animals build their lodges. The dams themselves are not the beavers’ lodges.
match_headline: Reversing Course on Beavers

text: An article on Tuesday about viruses misidentified the position held by a scientist, Luis P. Villarreal, at the Center for Virus Research at the University of California, Irvine. He is a professor at the center and its founding director, but not its current director. And a picture credit with the article, using information from a publicist, misstated part of the name of the organization that publishes The Journal of Virology. It is the American Society for Microbiology — not “of” Microbiology.
match_headline: Ebola and the Vast Viral Universe

text: An article on Wednesday about the different daylight saving time calendars used by Israel and the Palestinian Authority, and how those calendars have been influenced by religious and political considerations, misstated the surname of a woman who has homes in Jerusalem and the West Bank. She is Joharah Baker, not Barker.
match_headline: For Israelis and Palestinians, Another Divide to Contend With: Time

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the cultural preferences of Republicans and Democrats misidentified the city in California where Facebook is headquartered. It is Menlo Park, not Palo Alto. Also because of an editing error, the article referred incorrectly to the origins of Senator Rand Paul’s given name. He was not named after the writer Ayn Rand. (His given name is Randall.)
match_headline: L. M. Kit Carson, Actor and Writer in Independent Film, Dies at 73

text: An article on Thursday about safety lapses in the storage of plutonium waste misidentified the location of a laboratory under scrutiny for its packaging of such waste. It is in Idaho Falls, Idaho — not in Idaho Springs, Colo.
match_headline: In U.S. Cleanup Efforts, Accident at Nuclear Site Points to Cost of Lapses

text: An obituary on Oct. 23 about the developmental psychologist Carolyn Rovee-Collier contained several errors. Dr. Rovee-Collier’s son Benjamin was her first son, not her second. She began teaching at Rutgers University in 1970, not 1972. She was born Susan Carolyn Kent, not Carolyn Kent. In addition, an accompanying picture caption misstated the year the photograph of Dr. Rovee-Collier was taken. It was 1996, not 1986.
match_headline: Carolyn Rovee-Collier, Who Said Babies Have Clear Memories, Is Dead at 72

text: An obituary on Oct. 22 about the French oil executive Christophe de Margerie misidentified his father. Mr. de Margerie was born to Pierre Rodocanachi and Colette Taittinger, not to Pierre de Margerie and Colette Taittinger. (His mother later divorced Mr. Rodocanachi and married Pierre de Margerie, who adopted him.)
match_headline: Christophe de Margerie, Swashbuckling Chief of Total Oil, Is Dead at 63

text: An article on Thursday about Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s first use of the Moreland Act, establishing a commission to investigate electric companies’ shortcomings after Hurricane Sandy, misidentified the person who wrote an email regarding changes to a report on whether to privatize the Long Island Power Authority. Peter Bradford wrote to Mark Green, a fellow commissioner: “Outrageous. We were never polled as to that language.” Mr. Green did not write to Mr. Bradford.
ref_headline: Outrageous. We were never polled as to that language.
match_headline: Cuomo’s Role in Hurricane Sandy Inquiry Foretold Fate of His Ethics Panel

text: An article on Friday about governors who are struggling to define public health policies on Ebola misstated the title of Dr. Alan J. Magill, who criticized Louisiana’s move to block doctors who had treated Ebola patients from attending a New Orleans conference. He is director for malaria at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation’s Global Health Program, not director of the Global Health Program.
match_headline: From Governors, a Mix of Hard-Line Acts and Conciliation Over Ebola

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about the time and cost commitment at some sororities misstates part of the name of the university where a former Chi Omega member, Laura Wright, teaches. It is Western Carolina University, not West Carolina University. The article also refers incorrectly to Nicole Davies. She pledged Alpha Chi Omega but was not initiated; it is not the case that she “de-sistered.” And she is a former, not current, peer adviser at American University. In addition, the article refers incorrectly to fund-raising events attended by Leah Jordan as a member of Alpha Omicron Pi. Her sorority raised money for arthritis; she did not participate in fund-raising events for autism. (Those were held by Alpha Xi Delta.)
match_headline: Greek Letters at a Price

text: An article on Page 92 this weekend, written by two mystery novelists about a journey they took on the Orient Express, carries an erroneous byline for one of the writers. The writer publishes under the pen name Rebecca Chance, and that was the name that was intended to be used in the byline and for her first-person references in the article — not Lauren Henderson. (That is her legal name.)
match_headline: Murder, They Wrote

text: A caption on Page 102 this weekend with the feature “A Picture and a Poem,” which pairs works from one artist and one poet, misstates the title of an artwork by Alex Israel. It is “Study for Self-Portrait (Psychic Neon)” — not “Study for a Self-Portrait (Psychic Neon).”
match_headline: With Self-Portrait of a Lifetime, Picasso Returns to Paris Pedestal
