text: An article last Sunday about New York’s plans for coastal defenses because of Hurricane Sandy described incorrectly the funding for six proposals chosen through Rebuild by Design, an international contest soliciting ways to protect the city. The money for the proposals, including one called the Big U, came from the Department of Housing and Urban Development and was given to government officials. It did not come from Rebuild by Design, and it was not given to the teams behind the winning plans.
match_headline: Building for the Next Big Storm

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Washington Irving’s Hudson Valley haunts referred imprecisely to the location of Irving’s home, Sunnyside. It is on the border of Tarrytown and Irvington; it is not solely in what is now known as Irvington.
match_headline: Where the Headless Horseman Lost His Head

text: An article last Sunday about the legal troubles of Hope Solo, the goalkeeper for the United States women’s national soccer team, misstated the year of the London Olympics, before which Solo tested positive for a banned diuretic. They were in 2012, not 2008.
match_headline: Biggest Test for U.S. Goalkeeper May Come Off the Field

text: An essay last Sunday about the Loma Prieta earthquake that struck minutes before Game 3 of the 1989 World Series in San Francisco misstated the name of the place where the upper level of the Nimitz Freeway collapsed. It was the Cypress Street viaduct, not Cyprus Street. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: When the Earth Shook and the Series Stood Still

text: A picture credit last Sunday with an article about the singer Taylor Swift, who has a new album out, “1989,” misspelled the photographer’s given name. The picture of Ms. Swift wearing a black outfit was taken by Sarah Barlow, not Sara.
match_headline: A Farewell to Twang

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the choreographer Gina Gibney and her passion for finding space for dancers reversed the identities of the two dancers shown. Fiona Lundie is in the air and Jennifer Meckley on the stage.
match_headline: Making Space for Creativity

text: An article on Oct. 19 about the filmmaker Manfred Kirchheimer and his documentary “Stations of the Elevated” misidentified the school attended by the students who helped him make the film. It is the New York Institute of Technology — not the School of Visual Arts.
match_headline: Want to Make a Film? Stand on a Corner

text: An article on Oct. 19 about the HBO mini-series “Olive Kitteridge,” which stars Frances McDormand, referred incorrectly to Ms. McDormand’s character in the 1996 movie “Fargo.” Her character, Marge Gunderson was police chief, and as such oversaw all divisions of the department, including investigations, but she was not herself a detective.
match_headline: A Star Who Has No Time for Vanity

text: An article on Oct. 19 about private wealth in politics referred incorrectly to the Senate seat sought last year by Representative Stephen F. Lynch, a Massachusetts Democrat. It was the seat vacated by John Kerry when he became secretary of state — not the seat that had been held by Scott Brown. (Elizabeth Warren defeated Brown in 2012, so that seat was not in contention last year.)
match_headline: How Billionaire Oligarchs Are Becoming Their Own Political Parties

text: An article on Oct. 12, about a boy’s fascination with battlefields, referred incorrectly to the residents of Hawaii who made up a third of the population at the time of Pearl Harbor. While some were Japanese citizens, most were people of Japanese ancestry; therefore, they were not all Japanese citizens.
match_headline: Won Over by the Battlefield

text: An article on Thursday about the funeral of Benjamin C. Bradlee, a former editor of The Washington Post who led the coverage of the Watergate scandal, referred incorrectly to the presentation of a folded American flag to his widow, Sally Quinn. The flag was placed on the coffin before it arrived at the Washington National Cathedral and then was removed before the coffin was brought into the nave. That flag was folded and later presented to Ms. Quinn. The flag was not placed on the coffin after the coffin was wheeled outside, then folded and brought back into the cathedral to be presented to Ms. Quinn. (A separate flag was placed on the coffin after it was removed from the cathedral.) The article also misstated the name of the hotel in Paris that Mr. Bradlee considered too expensive. It is the Ritz Paris, not the Ritz-Carlton.
match_headline: Capital Mourns Bradlee, and the Passing of an Era

text: An article on Thursday about a legal showdown over whether Maine could impose a quarantine on Kaci Hickox, a nurse who cared for Ebola patients in Sierra Leone, misstated part of the name of the federal organization that established monitoring guidelines for the disease. It is the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, not the Centers for Disease Control and Protection.
match_headline: Threat of Lawsuit Could Test Maine’s Quarantine Policy

text: Because of an editing error, a reporting credit was omitted on Wednesday for an article about the resignation in August of the official who investigated the Secret Service’s 2012 prostitution scandal and then was implicated in his own incident involving a prostitute. Frances Robles contributed reporting.
match_headline: Investigator in Secret Service Prostitution Scandal Resigns

text: An article on Tuesday about Sweetwater, a bar in Brooklyn that some contend is haunted, misstated the number of years it has been open. It is 10, not 9.
match_headline: Flickering Lights, Strange Music and a Ghost at a Brooklyn Bar. Maybe.

text: Because of an editing error, a capsule summary on Friday about the potential acquisition of Spirit Pub Company of Britain by another British brewer and pub operator, Greene King, misstated the deadline for a final takeover offer. Offers must be submitted by Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: British Pub Operator Extends Deadline for Takeover Bid

text: A chart on Tuesday with an article about the Knicks’ triangle offense misspelled the surname of a Knicks player. He is Travis Wear, not Ware.
match_headline: Three Sides to This Story

text: An article on Tuesday previewing the 2014-15 N.B.A. season misidentified the tournament at which Denver Nuggets forward Kenneth Faried started his potential breakout season this summer. It is the FIBA World Cup, not the Pan-American Games.
match_headline: Major Changes, but Not for the Spurs

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the final hours of campaigning for the midterm elections referred incorrectly to the 1.5 million television advertisements aired during the midterm election cycle. The number includes all broadcast television advertisements, including those by candidates — not just advertisements by outside groups.
match_headline: On Election’s Eve, G.O.P. Is Confident, but Voters Are Sour

text: An article on Oct. 22 about the five-year sentence handed down to the South African track star Oscar Pistorius in the death of his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp, erroneously attributed a distinction to Mr. Pistorius. He was the first double-amputee runner to compete against able-bodied athletes at the Olympics; he was not the first disabled athlete to do so. (Single-amputee athletes competed in the Olympics in the early 1900s, and since then blind, deaf and other amputee athletes, including the South African swimmer Natalie du Toit in 2008, have also done so.)
match_headline: Oscar Pistorius’s 5-Year Sentence May Mean Move to House Arrest

text: An article on Oct. 25 about the challenges faced by Bellevue Hospital Center in handling New York City’s first Ebola case misstated, in some editions, the title of Dr. Eric Manheimer, a former Bellevue official who wrote a book about the hospital. He was the medical director, not the chief medical officer.
match_headline: Bellevue Back on Front Line in Another Crisis

text: An article on Tuesday about a federal investigation of Honda Motor’s reporting of deaths and injuries from defective airbags misidentified, in some copies, the company that said it would start an audit of its reporting procedures. It is Honda — not Takata, the airbag supplier. The article also misstated, in some copies, the name of the Florida law enforcement unit that investigated an accident involving a 2001 Accord last month. It is the Orange County Sheriff’s Office, not the Orlando Sheriff’s Office.
match_headline: Investigation of Honda Centers on Failure to Report Deaths From Takata Airbags

text: An article on Saturday about the Discovery Channel’s broadcast of Nik Wallenda’s high-wire walk between two Chicago skyscrapers described the reach of the televised event incorrectly. It was beamed to more than 220 countries and territories, not to that many countries alone. (There are 195 countries in the world, or 196 if Taiwan is included as an independent country).
match_headline: Risking a Life for TV Ratings

text: A listing of credits on Oct. 24 with a review of “Life of Riley,” the final film by Alain Resnais, who died in March, omitted a writer. Besides Laurent Herbiet and Alex Reval (a pseudonym for Mr. Resnais), who wrote the screenplay based on the play by Alan Ayckbourn, Jean-Marie Besset also wrote the dialogue.
match_headline: A Bon Vivant’s Illness Flusters and Fixates Women From His Past

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Tom Magliozzi, one of the two brothers who hosted the NPR show “Car Talk,” contained several errors.
match_headline: Tom Magliozzi, One Half of the Jovial Brothers on ‘Car Talk,’ Dies at 77

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Brittany Maynard, who became a public face for the “death with dignity” movement in the United States after she was found to have terminal brain cancer, referred incorrectly to a woman who asked Ms. Maynard to reconsider her decision to end her own life. That woman is dying from breast cancer that has metastasized — not from “the same cancer” as Ms. Maynard.
match_headline: Brittany Maynard, ‘Death With Dignity’ Ally, Dies at 29

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the challenge facing David Cameron, the British prime minister, now that Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany has signaled her disapproval of his plans to placate anti-European sentiment at home misstated Mr. Cameron’s timetable for a referendum on the European Union. He has pledged to bring it before the voters by 2017, not by 2015.
match_headline: Merkel Toughens Position on Britain’s E.U. Demands

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with the Crime Scene column, about three people involved in a 2012 stabbing in the Bronx, misstated the charge on which one of them was found guilty. As the article correctly noted, Octavio Rivera was convicted of assault, not of attempted murder.
match_headline: 3 People in the Bronx, Drugs and Recollections of a Day’s Bloody Turn

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about a New York City employee who was suspended for answering customer-service calls like a robot misspelled the surname of the employee’s supervisor at one point. As the article noted correctly elsewhere, the supervisor is Barry Novack, not Novak.
match_headline: Health Dept. Worker Suspended. One Complaint: He Talked Like a Robot.

text: An article on Oct. 14 about the case described in the new book “The Great New Orleans Kidnapping Case: Race, Law and Justice in the Reconstruction Era,” by Michael A. Ross, referred incorrectly to coverage of the death of a detective assigned to the case, John Baptiste Jourdain, in 1888. An article in The Daily Picayune of New Orleans mentioned his career on the police force and in the Louisiana State Legislature; it is not the case that there was no such reference in local newspapers.
ref_headline: The Great New Orleans Kidnapping Case: Race, Law and Justice in the Reconstruction Era,
match_headline: A Black Detective, an 1870 Trial and a What If

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Donald Saddler, a dancer and choreographer, misstated his date of birth, in 1918. It was Jan. 24, not July 24.
match_headline: Donald Saddler, Dancer, and a Choreographer on Broadway, Dies at 96

text: A map last Saturday with an article about the fall of Burkina Faso’s longtime president, Blaise Compaoré, mislabeled Liberia as Ivory Coast. The map, which highlighted Burkina Faso’s capital, Ouagadougou, correctly labeled Ivory Coast, which is west of Ghana and southwest of Burkina Faso; Liberia is west of Ivory Coast.
match_headline: Burkina Faso’s President Resigns, and General Takes Reins

text: An article last Saturday about the revival of painful memories of Romania’s Communist past after allegations that a presidential candidate, Victor Ponta, was once an undercover agent, though after the Communist era, misspelled the surname of a former head of Romania’s foreign intelligence service. He is Teodor Melescanu, not Melenescu.
match_headline: Spy Allegations in a Presidential Race Conjure Romania’s Authoritarian Past

text: An article on Thursday about some of the Republicans’ rising stars of the 114th Congress quoted incorrectly from comments by Senator-elect Joni Ernst, who on Tuesday night became the first woman elected to Congress from Iowa. She said: “We are heading to Washington. And we are going to make ‘em squeal!” — not “We are heading to Washington. And we are going to make a squeal!”
ref_headline: We are heading to Washington. And we are going to make ‘em squeal!
match_headline: Rising Stars in the Republican Party

text: An article on Friday about the closing of Cafe Edison, a theater district mainstay, misstated part of the title of a soon-to-be published book by Mimi Sheraton, a former restaurant critic of The New York Times. It is “1,000 Foods to Eat Before You Die,” not “1,000 Places to Eat Before You Die.”
ref_headline: 1,000 Foods to Eat Before You Die,
match_headline: Cafe Edison, a Broadway Haunt, Is Closing

text: An article on Thursday about local initiatives around the country to ban hydraulic fracturing misstated an action by the City of Los Angeles. The City Council voted to order the drafting of an ordinance to ban fracking until it is determined to be safe; it did not ban fracking. (A second vote, on the ordinance itself, would be required to do that.)
match_headline: Split Decision by Voters on Local Fracking Bans

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about the injury status of Nets center Brook Lopez referred incorrectly in some copies to part of the Nets’ policy on interviews. The team trainer and doctor are not allowed to participate in interviews with reporters; it is not the case that such interviews are now allowed.
match_headline: Brook Lopez Stays on Sideline as the Nets Say Little

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about cooperation between the Nets and the Knicks for the 2015 N.B.A. All-Star Game festivities despite their rivalry misstated, in some copies, the day the Nets played the Minnesota Timberwolves this week. It was Wednesday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Nets and Knicks Resuming Rivalry Amid Cooperation

text: An article last Sunday about top free agents available in the baseball off-season misstated the number of months until the 2015 season begins. It is five, not six.
match_headline: Pitchers, Hitters and a Panda

text: A picture in some editions last Sunday with the Nature column , about the yellow-rumped warbler, was published in error. It showed the Audubon’s warbler, not the myrtle warbler. (Both are yellow-rumped warblers, but the range of the Audubon’s warbler is limited to the western part of North America, while the myrtle warbler dwells in the eastern part.)

A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the growing skirmishes between the old guard in Gstaad, Switzerland, and the village’s newer inhabitants, using information from a photo agency, misidentified the building shown. It was the Grand Hotel Alpina, demolished in 1995 — not the Palace Hotel.
match_headline: Gstaad: The Last Resort

text: An article last Sunday about students who sell their class notes, using information from Laura Gayle, a Florida State University student, referred incorrectly to the notes she sold for the course “Introduction to Classical Mythology.” While she said she gets advance permission from some teachers to sell her notes, she did not get permission to sell the mythology class notes. After the article was published, Ms. Gayle’s professor, Ann Glennie (who was not named in the article), emailed The Times to say that she objects to the selling of notes and did not give Ms. Gayle permission.
match_headline: How to Take Better Lecture Notes

text: An obituary last Sunday about Bernard Mayes, a former Anglican priest who started the first suicide hotline in the United States and was later the founding chairman of National Public Radio, paraphrased incorrectly a passage in his autobiography, “Escaping God’s Closet: The Revelations of a Queer Priest.” Mr. Mayes, who was gay, wrote that he was drawn to the priesthood through his attraction to another churchgoer, who was not gay and who at one time intended to become a priest. He did not say he entered the priesthood “after being seduced by a member of the clergy.” The obituary also gave an outdated telephone number for the federally financed national suicide hotline. It is 1-800-273-8255, no longer 1-800-SUICIDE. (Calls to that number, which did receive federal financing for several years, have been rerouted to the current number since 2007.)
ref_headline: Escaping God’s Closet: The Revelations of a Queer Priest.
match_headline: Bernard Mayes, 85, Dies; Started First U.S. Suicide Hotline

text: An article last Sunday about Bradley Cooper, who is starring in a Broadway revival of “The Elephant Man,” referred incorrectly to the London address where Joseph Carey Merrick — the real Elephant Man — exhibited himself. The address is now a sari store — it is not, our sincerest apologies, “a sorry store.”
match_headline: Serious Business

text: An article in the special Holiday Movies section last Sunday about the actress Brandy Burre, who is the focus of the Robert Greene documentary “Actress,” misstated the number of children she has. She is the mother of two children, not three.
match_headline: A Blizzard of Star Turns

text: An article in the special Holiday Movies section last Sunday about the latest animated film from Walt Disney Pictures, “Big Hero 6,” using information from a publicist, misidentified the artist who created the concept art for the campus in the movie. He is Tadahiro Uesugi, not Scott Watanabe. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture credit.
match_headline: Higher Learning in a Hybrid City

text: An article last Sunday about the expansion of colleges’ family weekends referred incorrectly to an activity offered by Wesleyan University at such a weekend last month. It was a stargazing event sponsored by the Astronomy Department, not an astrology walk.
match_headline: This Weekend, College Is for Everyone

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Lucinda Watson and Ted Bell misspelled part of the name of the college in England where Mr. Bell served as a writer in residence from 2011 to 2012. It is Sidney Sussex College, not Sydney Sussex College. (A 2006 college newsletter noted that it was referred to as Sidney or Sydney College during its early years, and that the king had on occasion referred to it as Sydney-Sussex College.)
match_headline: Lucinda Watson and Ted Bell

text: An article last Sunday about the growing number of Peruvian restaurants in London misidentified the city where Sanjay Dwivedi, the chef at Coya, was born. It is London; he is not a “New Delhi-born chef.”
match_headline: London Develops a Peruvian Palate

text: An article on Oct. 26 about Franklin, Tenn., a small town near Nashville, misidentified the instrument that John Hermann plays for the local band Widespread Panic. It is keyboards, not the drums.
match_headline: A Small-Town Gem Near Nashville

text: An article on Oct. 26 about aging and the brain referred imprecisely to the organization for which Jeffrey Rediger is the medical and clinical director. It is McLean SouthEast, a program of McLean Hospital in Middleborough, Mass., not the hospital itself, which is in Belmont, Mass.
match_headline: What if Age Is Nothing but a Mind-Set?

text: An article on Thursday about a report that implicated Chinese officials in the lucrative, and illegal, trade in ivory, which has sharply reduced Tanzania’s elephant population, misstated the prices for ivory at the time of the Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Tanzania. It had doubled to $700 per kilogram, or about $318 a pound — not to $70,000 per kilogram, or $31,800 a pound. And the article referred incorrectly to Dar es Salaam in some editions. It is Tanzania’s largest city, not the capital. (Dodoma is the seat of government.)
match_headline: Chinese President’s  Delegation Tied to Illegal Ivory Purchases  During Africa Visit

text: An article on Thursday about election results in New Hampshire misstated the vote total for Jeanne Shaheen in the Senate race, in which she beat Scott Brown. She had 250,722 votes, not 234,846 votes. (As the article correctly noted, that was Mr. Brown’s total.)
match_headline: In New Hampshire, Jeanne Shaheen Beats Scott Brown to Keep Senate Seat

text: An article on Thursday about the resignation of Christopher Epps as Mississippi corrections commissioner misspelled the name of the newspaper in Jackson, Miss., that published a series of articles about conditions in state prisons. It is The Clarion-Ledger, not The Clarion Leger.
match_headline: Chief Quits as Mississippi Prisons Face Inquiry

text: An article on Oct. 17 about a study that found that the quality of the communication between children and their parents and caregivers was more valuable than the number of words heard in the development of a child’s language skills misspelled the given name and misstated the surname of a developmental psychologist at Stanford. She is Anne Fernald, not Ann Ferald.
match_headline: Quality of Words, Not Quantity, Is Crucial to Language Skills, Study Finds

text: An article on Thursday about the latest Internet sensation of “Alex from Target,” a picture of a teenager bagging merchandise at the retailer that went viral online, described incorrectly a subsequent Internet posting of “Kel from Good Burger.” It was a frame from the 1997 film “Good Burger” starring the actor Kel Mitchell; it was not a photograph of a teenager in a job.
match_headline: Known as ‘Alex From Target,’ Teenage Clerk Rises to Star on Twitter and Talk Shows

text: An article last Monday about an expansion of hours for PBS’s Sunday night “Masterpiece” franchise misstated the title of a six-part mystery to be shown this season. It is “Grantchester,” not “Granchester.” The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: ‘Masterpiece’ Franchise on PBS Is Adding Broadcasts

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Monday about the Red Bulls’ victory over D.C. United in the first leg of an M.L.S. playoff series misstated the score in some copies. It was 2-0, not 2-1. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Rubber-Legged Red Bulls Make a Charge

text: An article on Friday about volunteers who risk their health or lives to help people misidentified a country in which Kim Federici, a retired nurse from Texas, recently worked with Doctors Without Borders. It is Liberia, not Sierra Leone. The article also erroneously included one country among those in which Ms. Federici has worked with the aid group. She has not worked in Mexico.
match_headline: Doing Good in Harm’s Way

text: A reporting credit on Friday for an obituary about the flamenco guitarist Manitas de Plata misspelled the surname of a contributor. Aurelien Breeden (not Bredeen) reported from Paris.
match_headline: Manitas de Plata, Superstar of the Flamenco Guitar, Is Dead at 93

text: An article on Sunday about the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s restoration of a shattered marble sculpture of Adam by the Venetian Renaissance master Tullio Lombardo misidentified which knee of the sculpture required a fiberglass pin. It was the left, not the right.
match_headline: Recreating Adam, From Hundreds of Fragments, After the Fall

text: Because of an editing error, a capsule summary on Saturday for an article about the departure of the editor of Amazon’s only literary imprint misstated the editor’s given name. As the article and a picture caption correctly noted, he is Ed Park, not John.
match_headline: Prominent Editor’s Exit Is Setback for Amazon Publishing Unit

text: Because of editing errors, an article in some editions on Oct. 21 about accusations that Gerry Adams, the leader of Sinn Fein, the former political wing of the Irish Republican Army, took part in a cover-up of rape allegations brought by a Belfast woman referred incorrectly to Martin Morris, who the woman said was her attacker, and referred incompletely to the case against him. Mr. Morris was accused of being a member of the I.R.A.; he has not been convicted of such a crime and, in fact, the charges of I.R.A. membership and rape filed against him were dismissed. The error about the I.R.A. membership allegations also appeared in the headline and in a subheading.
match_headline: Sinn Fein Leader Is Accused of Covering Up Rape

text: An article on Oct. 30 about the confirmation in Tunisia of an election victory by the secular Nidaa Tounes party over the Islamist Ennahda party misstated the number of seats won by a new liberal democratic party called Afek Tounes. It won eight, not 15.
match_headline: Secularist Win Is Confirmed in Tunisia

text: An article in some editions on Friday about President Obama’s formally presenting the Medal of Honor to First Lt. Alonzo H. Cushing, a Union soldier who died at the Battle of Gettysburg after standing up to a fusillade of Confederate fire, misidentified the state in which Lieutenant Cushing was born and the state in which he was later raised. He was born in Wisconsin and raised in New York, not the other way around.
match_headline: Civil War Hero Awarded the Medal of Honor at Last

text: An article on Monday about the video-hosting site Vimeo’s push into original content with a series called “High Maintenance” misspelled the surname of one of the series’ creators in some editions. She is Katja Blichfeld, not Blichfield.
match_headline: With ‘High Maintenance,’ Vimeo Invests in Original Content

text: An article last Tuesday about a settlement by Stryker involving lawsuits from hip replacement patients described incorrectly the mechanism that failed in the devices. The cup used in the devices was ceramic, not metal, and the metallic debris that is said to have caused problems came from other components. The devices were not “all metal.”
match_headline: Stryker Settles Suits by Hip Implant Patients for $1 Billion

text: An article on Saturday about a judge’s approval of a bankruptcy plan for Detroit on Friday and how that ended a threat to the Detroit Institute of Arts, whose artworks could have been sold to help pay off city debt, misstated the institute’s long-range goal for its endowment. The goal is to raise it to $400 million, not to $600 million.
match_headline: ‘Grand Bargain’ Saves the Detroit Institute of Arts

text: A report in the Observatory column last Tuesday about plant reproduction referred incorrectly to the sexuality of most plants. Plants that have both male and female organs are hermaphroditic, not self-pollinating.
match_headline: What Determines the Sex of a Persimmon

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about efforts by Japan and China to step back from a longstanding dispute over islands in the East China Sea referred incorrectly to Japan’s control of the islands. Japan has held them for most years since the 1880s, not since World War II. (From 1945 to 1971, they were controlled by the United States.) The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: China and Japan, in Sign of a Thaw, Agree to Disagree on a Disputed Island Group

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 28 about an announcement by the Israeli government that it would speed up plans for more than 1,000 new apartments in East Jerusalem misstated part of the name of the world body that the Palestinian leadership has asked for a resolution calling for an end to the Israeli occupation. It is the United Nations Security Council, not the United States Security Council.
match_headline: Netanyahu Expedites Plan for More Than 1,000 New Apartments in East Jerusalem

text: An article in some editions last Wednesday about voters’ returning control of the New York State Senate to Republicans referred incorrectly to Simcha Felder, a Democratic state senator from Brooklyn who will be supporting the Republican majority. He is Mr. Felder — not, of course, “Mr. Simcha.”
match_headline: In Rebuke to Democrats, Voters Return Control of New York Senate to G.O.P.

text: An article on Nov. 3 about generating electricity from tides misstated the type of generating capacity exhibited by tidal plants generally. It is power-generating capacity, not energy-generating capacity.
match_headline: Generating Power From Tidal Lagoons

text: An article on Saturday about an F.B.I. agent who impersonated an Associated Press reporter referred incorrectly to a professor at Washington and Lee University who criticized the agent’s actions. The professor, Aly Colón, is a man. The article also misstated the title of his professorship. Mr. Colón is the Knight Professor in Journalism Ethics, not the Knight Visiting Professor in Journalism Ethics.
match_headline: F.B.I. Chief Backs Agent Who Posed as Reporter

text: An article on Monday about a dispute over the Frick Collection’s plans for an expansion that would destroy a garden designed by Russell Page misstated the surname of a longtime neighbor of the museum and an admirer of the garden. She is Charlotte Schwarz, not Schwartz.
match_headline: Frick’s Plan for Expansion Faces Fight Over Loss of Garden

text: A picture caption in the Listings pages on Friday with a film entry about a showing of the 1979 movie “Chilly Scenes of Winter” at the IFC Center in Manhattan tonight, using information from a photo archive agency, misidentified the actress shown with John Heard. She was Gloria Grahame, not Mary Beth Hurt, another actress in the film.
match_headline: Movie Listings for Nov. 7-13

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about the Mennonite Disaster Service misstated the location of Karen Dougherty’s home in Queens, where the group was putting in a new ground floor. It is in Broad Channel, not “the Broad Channel neighborhood of Far Rockaway.”
ref_headline: the Broad Channel neighborhood of Far Rockaway.
match_headline: Church Group Has a Hammer

text: An article on Friday about an increase in charitable giving omitted a source for a report that found that just 64 percent of companies had increased their total philanthropic contributions from 2010 to 2013. The report was done by CECP, in association with the Conference Board — not by the Conference Board alone.
match_headline: New Donor Generation Stimulates U.S. Giving

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with an article about Hungary’s gradual shift away from democratic capitalism and western values under Viktor Orban misstated the timing of Mr. Orban’s most recent election as prime minister. As the article correctly noted, he was last elected in April — not in 2010, which was when he was first elected.
match_headline: Defying Soviets, Then Pulling Hungary to Putin

text: An article on Saturday about the comet Siding Spring and its flyby of Mars referred incompletely to the source of pictures that were taken of the comet on Oct. 19. Both Martian rovers — Opportunity and Curiosity — photographed the comet; the pictures were not solely from Opportunity.
match_headline: Bright Specks of Dust From Comet Siding Spring Light Up Martian Sky

text: An article in some editions last Thursday about Nancy Writebol, an Ebola survivor who donated plasma to help treat Dr. Craig Spencer in New York, misstated the affiliation of Dr. Rick Sacra, another Ebola survivor. Dr. Sacra is a missionary with a group now known as SIM (formerly the Society for International Missionaries); he is not with Samaritan’s Purse.
match_headline: In Exclusive Club of U.S. Ebola Survivors, Kinship Is Sealed in Blood

text: Because of an editing error, an entry in the Metropolitan Diary on Nov. 3 about a trick-or-treater who played his bugle, poorly, for a party at Beekman Place in Manhattan in the early 1960s omitted the name of the host of the party and the gift the child was given. The host was Irving Berlin, and the boy’s reward for playing was a stack of 3.5-ounce chocolate bars.

A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about Detroit’s vulnerability to future fiscal crises despite a deal that allows it to emerge from bankruptcy left the incorrect impression that the old train station shown is connected to the city’s financial woes. While the station is emblematic of the urban decay of the city, it is privately owned and will not benefit from the bankruptcy deal.
match_headline: Palestinians Are Suspected as 2 Israelis Die in Knife Attacks

text: An article in some copies last Thursday about the Rangers’ 4-3 overtime victory over the Detroit Red Wings misstated the duration of the Red Wings’ scoreless streak against Rangers goalie Henrik Lundqvist before Jakub Kindl’s goal in the second period. It was 211:08, not 2:11:08.
match_headline: Seconds From Victory in Regulation, Rangers Overtake Red Wings in Overtime

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with a dance review of “Syncopated Ladies: Live in NYC,” at the Gerald W. Lynch Theater, misidentified the dancer shown in the foreground. She is Maud Arnold — not Chloé Arnold, her sister and the leader of Syncopated Ladies.
match_headline: Hear Those Tapping Shoes? That’s the Sound of Empowerment

text: An article on Tuesday about the Rosetta orbiter’s mission to put a lander on a comet referred incorrectly to the timing of one part of the mission. Rosetta was set to take a sharp turn toward the comet in the early hours of Wednesday, Eastern time, not on Tuesday. (Rosetta successfully made the turn.)
match_headline: Philae Lander Nears a Cosmic Touchdown

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the Olympic swimmer and swimming coach Jack Nelson misstated the surname of one of his daughters, who survives him. She is Jamie Nelson, not Going.
match_headline: Jack Nelson, Olympic Swimmer and Gold Medal Coach, Dies at 82

text: An article on Oct. 28 about renewed scrutiny of immigration laws after an undocumented worker was accused of killing two sheriff’s officers in California referred imprecisely to the Trust Act, which California lawmakers passed to restrict the situations in which local police may detain immigrants for federal authorities. The law allows for some felony traffic convictions to result in an immigration hold. It does not specifically mention traffic violations that do not result in an arrest.
match_headline: U.S. Immigration Laws Face New Scrutiny After Killings

text: An article in some editions on Nov. 4 about efforts to relocate remains belonging to the Van Alsts, an old Queens family, misstated the name of the hamlet in which Joris Stevenson Van Alst, their first ancestor to move to New York, settled. It was Dutch Kills, not Dutch Hills.
match_headline: Long in Repose, Last Remnants of a Founding Family Will Leave Long Island City

text: A report in the Business Briefing column in some editions on Tuesday about earnings at American Apparel misstated the company’s leadership. Scott Brubaker has been the company’s interim chief executive since the departure of its founder and C.E.O., Dov Charney, in June; the company has not been without a chief executive.
match_headline: Investigation of Charney Adds to Loss at American Apparel

text: An article on Oct. 15 about the awarding of the Man Booker Prize to the Australian novelist Richard Flanagan for his novel “The Narrow Road to the Deep North” misstated the origin of the novel’s title. It is taken from the title of a travel diary written in prose and in haiku by the 17th-century Japanese writer Matsuo Basho; it does not come from a line of Basho’s haiku. The error was repeated on Nov. 2 in the Inside the List column in the Book Review.
ref_headline: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
match_headline: Australian’s P.O.W. Novel Wins Man Booker Prize

text: An article on Tuesday about a push by a coalition of community groups and labor unions to get the Federal Reserve to change the way some Fed officials are appointed misstated the timing of the retirement of Charles I. Plosser, the president of the Philadelphia Fed. He has announced that he will leave on March 1, not at the end of March.
match_headline: As Federal Reserve Selects New Top Officials, Coalition Calls for Public Input

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about the Giants’ 38-17 loss to the Seattle Seahawks, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the Seattle player shown on the pass rush against Giants quarterback Eli Manning in the first quarter. He is defensive end Michael Bennett, not free safety Earl Thomas.
match_headline: Surprising for Three Quarters, the Giants Wither in the Fourth

text: An article on Tuesday about Mary Berg, a Polish Jewish teenager who wrote one of the earliest firsthand accounts of the Nazi genocide to be published in English, misspelled the surname of the journalist who helped her turn her diaries into a series of articles and then a book after she came to the United States in 1944. He was S. L. Shneiderman, not Schneiderman.
match_headline: Survivor Who Hated the Spotlight

text: A listing of credits on Oct. 31 with a film review of “Nightcrawler” misidentified the distributor. It is Open Road Films, not Roadside Attractions.
match_headline: The First Responder Is a Cameraman

text: An obituary on Monday about the former Illinois congressman Philip M. Crane misstated the name of the university from which he received a Ph.D. It is Indiana University — not the University of Indiana, which does not exist.
match_headline: Philip M. Crane, Former Illinois Congressman and Conservative Leader, Dies at 84

text: An article on Nov. 4 about a religious defense of Egypt’s forcible removal of families from the Sinai Peninsula from a Muslim cleric, Mufti Shawqi Allam, referred incompletely to his association with the Egyptian government. Although he was appointed by presidential decree after selection by the senior scholars of a government-owned religious institute, the mufti and his rulings are said to be independent of the president under current Egyptian law.
match_headline: Egyptian Cleric Defends Forced Evacuation of Families From Sinai

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Saturday about efforts by Chinese leaders to improve the air quality in Beijing in time for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum referred incorrectly to northwest winds from Mongolia that meteorologists expected would cause air quality in Beijing to deteriorate. To cause such air quality deterioration, winds would have to drop off, not move in.
match_headline: In Beijing, Clearer Views Hide Real Life

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about a vote by Senate Democrats to retain Harry Reid of Nevada as their leader misidentified the senator shown, at the left, with Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Charles E. Schumer of New York. She is Debbie Stabenow of Michigan, not Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire.
match_headline: Frustrated Democratic Senators Vent, but Re-Elect Reid to Be Their Leader

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Saturday about Irina Finkel, a Brooklyn woman with a brain tumor who received money from an agency supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund to pay a utility bill, misstated, in some copies, the age at which she came to the United States from Ukraine. She was 38, not 34.
match_headline: A Resolve to Stay Young, Undimmed by Illness

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about opposition in Rockland County to the construction of a desalination plant misstated the given name of a consultant who said the plant is not needed. He is Albert F. Appleton, not Alfred. And because of an editing error, the article described incorrectly Nyack and Suffern, N.Y., which have water systems separate from the county’s. They are villages, not counties.
match_headline: Desalination Plan Draws Ire in Rockland County

text: An article on Tuesday about a judge’s ruling that will require Harold Hamm, the chief executive of Continental Resources, to pay nearly $1 billion to a former wife, Sue Ann, in a divorce settlement misstated the status of another large divorce judgment involving the Russian oligarch Dmitry Rybolovlev. While Mr. Rybolovlev’s ex-wife, Elena, was awarded $4.8 billion in the divorce, that amount has not yet been paid to her.
match_headline: An Oklahoma Oilman’s Billion-Dollar Divorce

text: An article last Saturday about Bruce Arians’s journey to become coach of the Arizona Cardinals misspelled the surname of the Cardinals executive who hired him, and it misstated his title. The executive is Michael Bidwill, not Bidwell, and he is the team’s president, not its owner. (Bidwill’s father, Bill, is the owner.)
match_headline: Cardinals’ Bruce Arians Took Long Route to Top N.F.L. Job

text: A listing of credits on Friday with a film review of “The Homesman” omitted a distributor. Besides Roadside Attractions, the movie was also released by Saban Films.
match_headline: Plain on the Plains

text: A picture caption in some copies on Friday with an obituary about Gisèle Masson, a founder of the New York restaurant La Grenouille, misidentified the man shown with her and the chef Andre Joanlanne. He is Charles Masson Jr., her son — not Charles Masson Sr., her husband.
match_headline: Gisèle Masson Dies at 89; Fed the Famous at La Grenouille

text: An article on Nov. 2 about a proposal by Ed Miliband, the leader of Britain’s Labour Party, to replace the House of Lords with an American-style Senate referred imprecisely to the way legislation to replace the Lords would take shape. While it is most likely to be proposed by the prime minister’s office, the legislation does not have to originate there; it can be proposed by an individual member of Parliament.
match_headline: Labour Party Leader Backs Replacing House of Lords

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about Adam Tang, who fled to Canada in response to a trial over his high-speed trip around Manhattan, misidentified the person who assistants of the district attorney said should spend some time in jail. He is Mr. Tang — not their boss, Cyrus R. Vance Jr., the district attorney.
match_headline: Manhattan Speeder Says He Has Fled to Canada

text: A picture caption on Nov. 2 with an article about the increased enforcement of embellishment penalties in the N.H.L., using information from Getty Images, misidentified, in some editions, the Winnipeg Jets player penalized for holding the Islanders’ Matt Martin. He is Jim Slater, not Bryan Little.
match_headline: Change of Scenery in N.H.L.: Crackdown on Theatrical Falls

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary last Sunday about Clement Alexander Price, a historian who wrote extensively about Newark, misidentified the Rutgers campus where he received his Ph.D. It is the campus in New Brunswick, not in Newark.
match_headline: Clement A. Price, a Cheerleader for Newark, Dies at 69

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Oct. 26 with an article about the curator and collector Sam Wagstaff and the photographer Robert Mapplethorpe misstated a connection between them. As the article correctly noted, Wagstaff was Mapplethorpe’s patron, not the other way around.
match_headline: The Man Who Loved Photographs

text: An article last Sunday about the Mikhailovsky Ballet, which is performing at Lincoln Center, misidentified the choreographer of the “The Bright Stream” in citing the ballet background of relatives of the Mikhailovsky’s ballet master in chief, Mikhail Messerer. (His mother and uncle starred in a revival by the Bolshoi Ballet.) He was Fyodor Lopukhov — not Leonid Lavrovsky, who also choreographed for the Bolshoi.
match_headline: Russian Troupe Poised for a Global Stage

text: An article last Sunday about Dave Grohl, the leader of the Foo Fighters and the director of an eight-part HBO documentary series, “Sonic Highways,” misstated at one point the title of a song on the band’s new album of the same name. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is “Something From Nothing,” not “Something for Nothing.”
match_headline: Rock Star on a Quest for Heroes

text: A review on Nov. 2 about “Worthy Fights,” a memoir by Leon Panetta, referred incorrectly to legislation that Panetta favored in the late 1980s and to his role in its passage. Panetta, a United States representative at the time, persuaded backers of a bill containing subsidies for dairy farms to support the Hunger Prevention Act of 1988 , which included some provisions related to food stamps. He did not “combine” two bills, “the food stamps bill” and “the . . . farm bill.” (Food stamps had been included in the omnibus farm bill since 1973.)
match_headline: Leon Panetta’s ‘Worthy Fights’

text: Because of an editing error, the Hunt column last Sunday, about three roommates’ search for a Manhattan apartment, misstated the portion of the $2,800 rent that the roommates pay on a rotating basis. It is $934 a month, not $994. (The others pay $933.)
match_headline: The Après-Graduation Apartment

text: A picture caption last Sunday with a cover article about different ways a prospective renter or buyer can learn who lives in a building misidentified the neighborhood where Steven D. Sladkus purchased an apartment. As the article correctly noted, it is on the Upper East Side, not the Upper West Side.
match_headline: The Who of the Matter

text: An article last Sunday about entrepreneurs’ increased willingness to discuss their failures misstated the location of Chris Poole, founder of the successful messaging forum 4chan, who wrote a blog post describing the demise of his company DrawQuest. He is based in New York, not Silicon Valley.
match_headline: Wearing Your Failures on Your Sleeve

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Ying Wang and Patrick Joseph Dooley misstated the name of the bride’s father. He is Dunrui Wang, not Xiaojun Wu Dunrui Wang. As the report correctly noted in another reference, Xiaojun Wu is the name of the bride’s mother.
match_headline: Ying Wang and Patrick Dooley

text: An article on Thursday about a United Nations report that found a sharp rise in opium cultivation in Afghanistan misstated the increase in cultivation in 2013 over the year before. It was 36 percent, not 49 percent.
match_headline: Afghan Opium Cultivation Rises to Record Levels

text: An article on Thursday about the likelihood that the emissions targets of the climate pact between the United States and China will be met misstated, in some editions, the title of India’s leader, Narendra Modi. He is prime minister, not president. And a chart with the article referred incorrectly in some editions to the United States’ carbon emissions. It has much higher emissions per capita than China — not the highest emissions per capita worldwide, a distinction held by Qatar.
match_headline: Climate Accord Relies on Environmental Policies Now in Place

text: A chart on Nov. 6 with a brief article about election results in Massachusetts misstated the vote total for Martha Coakley in the governor’s race, in which she lost to Charles Baker. She had 1,001,279 votes — not 1,041,640 votes, which was Mr. Baker’s total.
match_headline: Blacks, Obama and the Election

text: An article last Monday about New York City’s efforts to identify bodies buried on Hart Island, known as potter’s field, misstated, in some editions, the surname of a Bronx woman whose brother is missing. She is Himirce Melendez, not Ramos. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: New York City Seeks to Put Names to Unidentified Bodies

text: An article on Thursday about a program by the Manhattan district attorney’s office that would help other cities clear their backlog of untested rape kits misspelled, in some editions, the name of a national DNA database. It is Codis, not Cordis.
match_headline: New York Initiative to Help Other Cities Clear Rape-Kit Backlogs

text: An article on Thursday about efforts by the toymaker Hasbro to buy DreamWorks Animation misspelled, in some copies, the name of one of the characters in My Little Pony, a Hasbro brand. She is Fluttershy, not Flutteryshy.
match_headline: Hasbro Is Said to Be in Talks to Buy DreamWorks Animation

text: A picture in some copies on Wednesday with an obituary about the rapper Big Bank Hank, an original member of the Sugarhill Gang, was published in error. Big Bank Hank was not in the photograph, taken in 2005 and supplied by Getty Images; he had left the group by that time and had been replaced by Hen Dogg. In addition, the members of the Sugarhill Gang who were shown in the photograph were misidentified. They were, from left, Hen Dogg, Wonder Mike and Master Gee — not Master Gee, Big Bank Hank and Wonder Mike. And, finally, because of an editing error, a caption with a photograph in other editions that did in fact show Big Bank Hank misstated, in some copies, the year the picture was taken. It showed the original Sugarhill Gang in the late 1970s, not in 2005.
match_headline: Big Bank Hank, an Early Star of Rap, Dies at 58

text: An obituary on Thursday about Harry Pearson, who founded The Absolute Sound, a magazine for connoisseurs of high-fidelity audio, misstated his given name as Harold. The obituary also misidentified the city in North Carolina where he was born and the newspaper where he worked after graduating from Duke University. He was born in North Wilkesboro, not in Charlotte, and he worked for The Commercial in Pine Bluff, Ark., not for The Commercial Appeal in Memphis.
match_headline: Harry Pearson, Founder of Absolute Sound, Dies at 77

text: An article on Saturday about President Obama’s plan to change the nation’s immigration enforcement system misstated the year young immigrants started protests that eventually prodded the administration to act. They began in 2009, not in 2012.
match_headline: The Big Money Behind the Push for an Immigration Overhaul

text: An article on Saturday about an announcement by the jihadist group Islamic State that it planned to begin issuing its own currency overstated what is known about the steps taken by the Islamic State as part of its plan to restore the caliphate that dominated the Middle East more than 1,300 years ago. While some news reports and diplomats from the region said the group had started issuing passports, and images described as those passports were posted by the group’s sympathizers on social media, the Islamic State never announced the issuance of passports, according to the SITE Intelligence Group, which monitors jihadist communications.
match_headline: Islamic State Says It Plans to Issue Its Own Currency

text: An article in some editions last Tuesday about a landlord who pleaded guilty to negligent homicide over a deadly fire misidentified the employer of Edward Josephson, a lawyer who commented on the rarity of jail time in such cases. He is the litigation director for Legal Services NYC, not for Legal Aid NYC.
match_headline: Brooklyn Landlord Pleads Guilty to Negligent Homicide in 2010 Fire

text: An article on Monday about a group of Chinese movie investors who are backing a film called “Abattoir” misidentified one of the actors. The movie features Joe Anderson, not Taye Diggs.
match_headline: Chinese Investors Back Horror Film That May Never Debut in China

text: An article on Friday about Goldman Sachs’s efforts to recruit computer engineers misstated the job title of Afsheen Afshar. He is a managing director and works on developing programs to price derivatives, but he is not chief data scientist.
match_headline: Goldman Sachs Recasts Its Reputation to Woo Tech Talent

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Friday with an article about the struggles of the Colorado Avalanche misspelled, in some copies, the surname of Colorado player who scored the tying goal against the Rangers on Thursday. As the article correctly noted, he is Nathan MacKinnon, not McKinnon.
match_headline: Struggling Avalanche Find an Answer Against the Rangers

text: A listing of credits on Monday with a theater review of “Our Lady of Kibeho,” at the Pershing Square Signature Center in Manhattan, misspelled the given name of a cast member. He is Irungu Mutu, not Iringu.
match_headline: Mysteries of Heaven and Earth

text: A listing of credits on Friday with a theater review of “Lypsinka! The Trilogy,” three shows in repertory at the Connelly Theater in Manhattan, misidentified the show in which Steve Cuiffo and Scott Wittman alternate as Interviewer. It is “Lypsinka: The Passion of the Crawford,” not “Lypsinka: The Boxed Set.”
match_headline: The Wasp Goddess, Imperious, Vulnerable and (Gasp) Unmasked

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about plans by Peter Norton, the Silicon Valley software entrepreneur and collector of contemporary art, to give college and university museums across the United States art from his collection misstated the name of one. It is the Williams College Museum of Art, in Williamstown, Mass. — not the Williams College of Art.
match_headline: Met’s First Plans for the Whitney’s Old Home

text: An obituary on Saturday about Jane M. Byrne, a former mayor of Chicago, referred incompletely to her education. While she did attend the University of Illinois at Chicago, where she took classes toward a teaching certificate, she also attended, and graduated from, Barat College of the Sacred Heart in Lake Forest, Ill.
match_headline: Jane Byrne, Only Woman to Lead Chicago, Dies at 81

text: An article on Oct. 22 about a watch assembly workshop sponsored by the Swiss company Audemars Piguet, using information from a spokesman, misstated the thickness of a wheel crucial to the watchmaking process. It is six hundredths of a millimeter, not “one-600th.”
match_headline: At Workshop on Watches, Making Time Piece by Microscopic Piece

text: An article on Monday about Times Square’s biggest and most expensive digital billboard misstated the surname of the president of the Times Square Alliance. He is Tim Tompkins, not Topkins.
match_headline: Times Square’s Biggest and Most Expensive Digital Billboard Is Set to Shine

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the N.B.A. roundup in some editions on Thursday about an altercation at a Las Vegas nightclub involving Los Angeles Clippers forward Blake Griffin referred incorrectly to legal action taken against Griffin. While he is facing a misdemeanor battery charge, he was not arrested.
match_headline: China Action Against Multinational Firms

text: Because of an editing error, a Sports of The Times column on Friday, about the FIFA investigation into the bidding process for the 2018 and 2022 World Cups, included extraneous words atop the opening paragraph in some editions. The words “Maybe I’m being unfair. May” should have been in the fourth paragraph. The corrected version can be found at nytimes.com/sports .
match_headline: FIFA Looks at Itself and Nods in Approval

text: A listing of credits on Thursday with a theater review of “Basetrack Live,” which played at the Harvey Theater of the Brooklyn Academy of Music, omitted the video designers and editors. They are Sarah Outhwaite, Paul Howells and Estaban Uribe. The credits also omitted the photographer, Balazs Gardi.
match_headline: Tours of Duty and the Price Paid at Home

text: An entry in the New Music column on Tuesday about Azealia Banks’s new album, “Broke With Expensive Taste,” misidentified the label that released it. The label is Prospect Park, not Caroline. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: An Icy Hot Spot Where the Chill Scintillates

text: An entry in the Spare Times for Children listings in some editions on Friday about a New York Philharmonic Young People’s Concert included an outdated name for a preconcert program. It is YPC Overtures, no longer Kidzone Live!
match_headline: Spare Times for Children for Nov. 14-20

text: A recipe last Wednesday with the Good Appetite column, about making brown-butter skillet cornbread, misstated the metric measure of whole wheat flour required. It is 65 grams, not 165 grams.
match_headline: Cornbread That Gets the Most Out of Butter

text: An article on Wednesday about a terrorist attack on a Jerusalem synagogue that killed four worshipers and a police officer included erroneous information from the Israeli police about the child of the officer, Zidan Saif. The child is a girl, not a boy. The error was repeated in an article about the victims.
match_headline: Israel Shaken by 5 Deaths in Synagogue Assault

text: An article on Tuesday about a United Nations report on the global youth population that showed the number of adolescents is higher now than at any time in history misstated the day of the report’s release. It was Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: Global Number of Youths Is Highest Ever, U.N. Reports

text: An article on Wednesday about a speech to the United Nations Security Council by Zeid Ra’ad Al Hussein, the United Nations’ new top human rights official, who called on the Muslim world to denounce the extremist group that calls itself the Islamic State, referred incorrectly to the oil refinery at Baiji in Iraq. It was, until recently, under siege by Islamic State forces; they did not seize control of it.
match_headline: U.N. Urges Arab World to Denounce Islamic State

text: An article on Tuesday about a letter written by an Egyptian-American dissident, Mohamed Soltan, and smuggled out of a Cairo prison where he has been on a hunger strike overstated, in some editions, what is known about the care he is receiving. While he has been hospitalized, it has not been determined whether he is receiving nutrients intravenously.
match_headline: From an Egyptian-American Prisoner on Hunger Strike in Cairo, a Letter Home

text: An article on Nov. 10 about the anticipation in South Korea of a verdict in the trial of crew members of the ferry Sewol, which sank last April, killing 304 people, described the defendants incorrectly. Thirteen of them are men and two are women; they are not all men. (They have all since been convicted and sentenced.)
match_headline: Judgment Awaits for Crew of South Korea Ferry

text: An article on Tuesday about the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s call for a nationwide recall of automobiles equipped with airbags made by the Japanese company Takata misstated the name of a Senate committee planning hearings on the agency’s handling of the issue. It is the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation — not the Senate Energy and Commerce Committee. (The Committee on Energy and Commerce is in the House.)
match_headline: U.S. Regulators Call for Takata Airbag Recall to Be Extended Nationwide

text: An article on Wednesday about the broadening problem of defective airbags from the manufacturer Takata misspelled the given name of a spokesman for Honda Malaysia, who confirmed that a death in that nation was linked to an airbag rupture. He is Jordhatt Johan, not Jordhat.
match_headline: Defective Takata Airbag Grows Into Global Problem for Manufacturer

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with a roundup of the week’s best N.F.L. games referred incorrectly to the touchdown catch defensive end J. J. Watt of the Houston Texans was shown making. As an accompanying report correctly noted, it was his fourth touchdown over all this season, not his fourth touchdown catch. (He has two touchdown catches and two defensive touchdowns.)
match_headline: Goodell Bars Peterson for Rest of Season and Says He Could Miss Games in 2015

text: Because of editing errors, picture captions on Tuesday with a theater review of “Side Show,” at the St. James Theater in Manhattan, misstated the surname of one of the stars. As the review and a listing of credits correctly noted, she is Erin Davie, not Davies.
match_headline: United by Life, Divided by Dreams

text: An article on Nov. 7 about the philanthropist Agnes Gund gave an outdated name for Ms. Gund’s foundation. It is the A G Foundation, no longer the Agnes Gund Foundation.
match_headline: A Patron Gives, of Herself and Her Art

text: An article on Thursday about the effect of accusations of past sexual misbehavior on the current career of the comedian Bill Cosby described incorrectly in some editions the accusations brought in 2005 by Andrea Constand, then an employee at Temple University, Mr. Cosby’s alma mater. She said she had been drugged and molested by Mr. Cosby, not drugged and raped. The article also gave an outdated title for Bruce L. Castor Jr., who commented on the case. He was district attorney in Montgomery County when Ms. Constand made her accusations; he is not the current district attorney. And because of an editing error, the article misstated the time elapsed since Ms. Constand’s suit was settled in 2006. It is eight years, not nine.
match_headline: Comeback by Bill Cosby Unravels as Rape Claims Re-emerge

text: An article on Nov. 10 about ancient manuscripts associated with the life and works of St. Francis of Assisi that were being prepared for exhibition in the United States misspelled the name of the abbey near Padua, Italy, where some of the documents were being restored. It is Praglia Abbey, not Praia. And the article omitted context for a quotation that referred to a poem that is among the manuscripts, “Canticle of the Sun,” as perhaps the foundation of the Italian language and “the first text ever known in vernacular.” The distinction applies to literary texts, not to texts of any kind. (Other texts, including legal documents and brief poems, preceded it.)
match_headline: St. Francis Manuscripts Headed to U.S., in First Trip Out of Italy in 700 Years

text: An article on Wednesday about the end of a tax dispute between the town of Gardiner, N.Y., and a trust that owns property there on behalf of the actor Robert De Niro misidentified the party that would be paying the town’s legal fees. It is Berdon L.L.P., the accounting firm for the trust — not the trust itself.
match_headline: De Niro and New York Town End Fight Over Property Taxes

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a lawsuit filed by the state of Arizona against General Motors, claiming fraud in the handling of recalls of cars with potentially defective ignition switches, misstated the length of time a recall was delayed after the potential defect was identified. It was a decade, not “decades.”
match_headline: General Motors Is Sued by Arizona for $3 Billion Over Recalls

text: An article on Wednesday analyzing the success of the Green Bay Packers misstated in some copies their place in the standings. They are tied for first in the N.F.C. North, their division; they are not tied for first in the N.F.C., their conference.
match_headline: After a Slow Start, the Rodgers Show Hits Its Stride

text: An article in some editions last Friday about an auction of contemporary art at Phillips in New York misstated the age of the artist Lucien Smith, whose painting “When a Man Loves a Woman” was for sale. He is 25, not 35.
ref_headline: When a Man Loves a Woman
match_headline: An Anemic Auction Yields Just $52 Million at Phillips

text: Because of an editing error, an art entry in the Listings pages last Friday about an exhibition of paintings by E. M. Saniga misstated part of the name of the Manhattan gallery where the works were displayed. It is Steven Harvey Fine Art Projects, not Steven Henry Fine Arts Projects.
match_headline: Museum & Gallery Listings for Nov. 14-20

text: An article on Wednesday about finding a place to retire misstated the number of criteria used by the Milken Institute in ranking the “Best Cities for Successful Aging.” It is 84 — not 78, the original number of criteria used in 2012.
match_headline: Finding a Retirement Haven to Suit You

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the Knicks’ new Development League affiliate in Westchester County described the team’s origins incorrectly. The Westchester Knicks are an expansion team; they did not relocate from Erie, Pa. (The Erie BayHawks, the Knicks’ former affiliate in the Development League, are now affiliated with the Orlando Magic.)
match_headline: Knicks’ New D-League Team Mirrors the Parent Club, Right Down to the Losses

text: An article on Wednesday about the rebuilding of the Milwaukee Bucks with new owners, a new coach and the rookie Jabari Parker misstated the timing of the opening of the baseball stadium for the Brewers, another Milwaukee team that had a resurgence under new owners. Miller Park opened before — not after — the team’s sale to Mark Attanasio in 2004.
match_headline: Bucks, Young and Rebuilding, Look to Jabari Parker to Lead the Way Back

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the possibility of North Korea’s hosting a weight lifting world championship misstated, in some editions, the day that this year’s weight lifting world championships ended. It was Sunday, not last Saturday.
match_headline: Weight Lifting Pries Open Doors to a Hermit Kingdom

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about the casting of Diane Lane in the Lincoln Center Theater production of “The Mystery of Love and Sex,” using information from Lincoln Center, misidentified the last New York stage production in which Ms. Lane appeared. It was “Runaways” at the Public Theater in 1978, when she was 13, not “Agamemnon” in 1977, when she was 12.
match_headline: Diane Lane Will Return To New York Stage

text: An obituary on Thursday about Willy Burgdorfer, a medical entomologist who discovered the cause of Lyme disease, referred incorrectly to how the disease responds to treatment. There is controversy over the effectiveness of current treatments, but most patients fully recover after receiving antibiotics; it is not the case that “there is still no cure.”
match_headline: Willy Burgdorfer, Who Found Bacteria That Cause Lyme Disease, Is Dead at 89

text: Because of an editing error, a Woman in the News article on Nov. 9 about Loretta E. Lynch, President Obama’s nominee for attorney general, referred incompletely to the outcome of her prosecution of Officer Charles Schwarz in the Abner Louima police brutality case. While Officer Schwarz was convicted of assault and civil rights violations, his convictions were later overturned. Also because of an editing error, a reporting credit misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a contributor. He is Matt Apuzzo, not Appuzzo.
match_headline: Loretta Lynch, a Nominee for Attorney General, Is Praised for Substance, Not Flash

text: A picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about the fund-raising challenges faced by LaGuardia Community College reversed the identities of two of the three women shown on campus who are major supporters of the school. Karen Dubinsky was in the center and Marilyn Skony Stamm was at the right. (Lisa Selz, at the left, was correctly identified.)
match_headline: How Can Community Colleges Get a Piece of the Billions That Donors Give to Higher Education?

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the deaths of two toddlers in New York City misstated, in some copies, Diane Howard’s relationship with Teoka Spruill, whose 2-year-old daughter, Thaiya Spruill-Smith, was declared dead Friday evening. Ms. Howard is Ms. Spruill’s grandmother, not her mother.
match_headline: Police Examine Death of a Boy and an Attack on a Girl

text: An article last Sunday about the perfect season that Giants kicker Josh Brown has been having misstated the given name of a Giants player who made a bad snap in September. He is Zak DeOssie, not Steve. (Steve DeOssie is Zak’s father, who also played for the Giants.)
match_headline: In Flawed Giants’ Season, a Bit of Perfection

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Yale’s 44-30 victory over Princeton misstated, in some copies, the number of touchdowns scored by Yale running back Tyler Varga. It was three, not two. (He scored twice on rushing plays and once on a passing play.)
match_headline: After Beating Princeton, Yale Could Share Ivy Title

text: An article on Oct. 5 about postseason bonuses received by baseball players misstated the surname of the manager of the 1903 Pittsburgh Pirates, who lost the first World Series. He was Fred Clarke, not Locke. This correction was delayed because editors did not follow through after a reader pointed out the error on Oct. 6.
match_headline: Postseason Paychecks Are All About Sharing

text: An obituary last Sunday about the mathematician Alexander Grothendieck referred incorrectly to one aspect of the influence of his work. While it was a steppingstone to solving several arcane problems well known in mathematics, it was not a steppingstone to proof of the Poincaré conjecture. The obituary also overstated Mr. Grothendieck’s involvement in proving a set of hypotheses posed by André Weil. Mr. Grothendieck proved two of the four hypotheses and developed a new proof of a third; his former student Pierre Deligne proved the fourth. Mr. Grothendieck and Mr. Deligne were not “working together.”
match_headline: Alexander Grothendieck, Math Enigma, Dies at 86

text: An article last Sunday about James Middleton, the younger brother of the Duchess of Cambridge, referred incorrectly to his educational background. He attended Marlborough College, and thus could not have been a classmate of his friend Alexander Gilkes, who attended Eton.
match_headline: James Middleton Will Put a Happy Face on Your S’mores

text: An article last Sunday about Jeffrey Deitch referred incorrectly to the ownership of the auction house Christie’s. The majority shareholder is François Pinault, the founder of Kering, the French luxury-goods conglomerate; Christie’s is not owned by Kering.
match_headline: Jeffrey Deitch Is Back on the Art Auction Scene

text: A headline last Sunday for a report about the wedding of Lily Hayes Kaufman and Matthew Blake Salzberg omitted part of the bride’s name. She goes by Lily Hayes, not merely Lily.
match_headline: Lily Hayes Kaufman, Matthew Salzberg

text: A chart on Nov. 9 with an article about incidences of the Chikungunya virus in the Caribbean may have given the incorrect impression that it was listing the number of cases on each island. The figures in the chart indicate a rate — the total number of cases over a span of roughly 10 months for every 100,000 residents; they do not indicate the actual number of cases on each island, many of which have fewer than 100,000 residents.
match_headline: A Mosquito-Borne Virus Sweeps the Caribbean

text: An article on Nov. 2 about the country music scene in southern Appalachia misspelled the surname of the mandolin player from the Boxcars. He is Adam Steffey, not Steffy.
match_headline: Where the Hills and Hollows Are Alive With Music

text: A map on Nov. 9 with an article about the island of Antigua located the Galley Bay Resort incorrectly. The resort is west of the town of St. John’s, not north. A corrected map can be found at nytimes.com/travel.
match_headline: Seeing the Whole of Antigua

text: Because of an editing error, the Trending column on Nov. 9, about Montserrat and its recovery from a volcanic eruption that buried its capital, Plymouth, misidentified the type of volcano it was. As it was pyroclastic, there were flows of rock, not lava. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Montserrat Seeks a Comeback After a Volcano

text: An article on Saturday about free legal assistance in noncriminal cases for low-income residents misspelled the surname of the coordinator for the National Coalition for a Civil Right to Counsel, who commented on the practice. He is John Pollock, not Pollack.
match_headline: A Push for Legal Aid in Civil Cases Finds Its Advocates

text: An article on Oct. 30 about the racial tone of some midterm election ads that Democrats aired in the South referred incorrectly to the creation of the “super PAC” Senate Majority PAC, which ran an ad on black radio stations in North Carolina saying the Republican candidate, Thom Tillis, supported gun legislation that “caused the shooting death of Trayvon Martin.” The political action committee was created by former aides to Senator Harry Reid of Nevada, the majority leader — not by Mr. Reid himself.
match_headline: In Democratic Election Ads in South, a Focus on Racial Scars

text: An article on Nov. 5 about the large number of hikers climbing Mission Peak in Fremont, Calif., misstated the job title of one hiker, Shevon O. Korth. She is a contract adviser at Chevron’s Environmental Management Company, not a supply chain manager.
match_headline: Challenge at Mission Peak: Finding a Place to Park

text: An article on Monday about the rerelease of the documentary “The Business of Being Born” misstated, at one point, part of the name of a nonprofit organization showing the film. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is Choices in Childbirth, not Choices and Childbirth. And an accompanying picture caption referred incorrectly to the film’s availability on Netflix. While the current version is available, the rereleased version will not be on Netflix. (It will be on thebusinessofbeingborn.com.)
match_headline: Home-Birth Film by Ricki Lake Prepares for Redelivery, Worldwide

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the resignation of Kevin Ramach as president and executive director of the Minnesota Opera misstated the name of the newspaper that reported that Mr. Ramach’s predecessor, Allan Naplan, had resigned after only a year on the job. It is The Star Tribune, not The Minneapolis Star Tribune.
match_headline: Minnesota Opera President Resigns

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with a music review of “Black Mountain Songs,” at the Harvey Theater of the Brooklyn Academy of Music, misstated part of the name of the group that performed the work. As the review and another picture caption correctly noted, it is the Brooklyn Youth Chorus, not the Brooklyn Youth Orchestra.
match_headline: A Youthful Tribute to a Fallen Friend of Art

text: An article in some editions on Monday about plans by New York City and the New York Public Library to take over the Huntington Free Library and Reading Room in the Bronx gave an incorrect figure from the library for the cost of the project. It is $18 million, not $13 million. Because of that error, the article explained the details of the funding incorrectly. The budget includes $12.3 million from City Council capital funds, not $10 million; $3.9 million from the mayor’s office, not $2 million; and $1.8 million from the Bronx borough president, not $1 million.
match_headline: Bronx Library May Get a New Neighbor: Another Library

text: Because of an editing error, a reporting credit on Thursday with an article about heavy snow in Buffalo misidentified the city from which Matt Higgins reported. He was in Amherst, N.Y., not in Buffalo.
match_headline: Snow Piles Up in Buffalo Area, With More Expected; at Least 7 Die

text: An article on Monday about reaction in Silicon Valley to President Obama’s immigration policy misstated the legal authority Mr. Obama used to propose changes on immigration. They are executive actions, not an executive order. The error was repeated in the headline. The article also referred incorrectly to the status of a Swiss student, Johannes Koeppel, after he graduates from the University of California, Berkeley. Without a change in his visa status, Mr. Koeppel will have to leave 18 months after graduation; he does not have to leave immediately.
match_headline: Workers in Silicon Valley Weigh In on Obama’s Immigration Action

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article in some editions on Monday about the Giants’ 31-28 loss to the Dallas Cowboys misidentified the Dallas player heading for a 31-yard touchdown in the third quarter. Dez Bryant was shown — not Cole Beasley, who had a 45-yard touchdown run. The picture credit also misidentified the photographer. Barton Silverman photographed Bryant, not Chang W. Lee.
match_headline: A Great Catch, but a Victory Is Just Out of Reach

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Jets’ 38-3 loss to the Buffalo Bills misstated the given name of the Jets’ punter in some copies. He is Ryan Quigley, not Ray.
match_headline: Bills Thrash the Jets in a Road Show of Resilience

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Tuesday with an article about players on the ballot for the Baseball Hall of Fame misstated, in some copies, the year the picture of the former Houston Astro Craig Biggio was taken. It was 1990 — not 2007, which was the year Biggio retired.

An obituary on Tuesday about the hockey coach Pat Quinn referred incorrectly to the Flames, the N.H.L. team to which he was sent in 1972. At the time, the Flames played in Atlanta — not in Calgary, where they later moved.
match_headline: Pat Quinn, Coach Who Led Canada to Olympic Gold, Is Dead at 71

text: An article last Wednesday recommending a Thanksgiving dish from each state, with a recipe, contained numerous errors.
match_headline: Turkey Hash Is a Great Thanksgiving Leftovers Dish

text: An article on Monday about the politics surrounding an unusual land deal in the North Dakota oil country described incorrectly, in some editions, a redistricting plan that eliminated the State Senate seat of Ryan Taylor, a Democrat who ran against Gov. Jack Dalrymple in 2012. Mr. Taylor’s seat was eliminated in late 2011, as he was preparing to announce his candidacy, not after he lost the election the following November.
match_headline: Senate Democrats Clash With White House on C.I.A. Torture Report

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about California’s experience with the turmoil of immigration described incorrectly a group of immigrants living in the state. It is one-third of the undocumented workers in the country who live in California, not one-third of all illegal immigrants.
match_headline: Turmoil Over Immigration Status? California Has Lived It for Decades

text: Because of an editing error, the Memo From Melilla article on Tuesday, about a legal challenge involving the precise location of the border between Morocco and the Spanish enclaves of Melilla and Ceuta, gave an incorrect conversion, in some editions, for the distance between the current series of fences built to keep Moroccan migrants from Spanish territory and an extra fence that Morocco is building. The distance — about 500 meters — is about 1,640 feet, not 5,000 feet.
