match_headline: At Spanish Enclave, a Debate Over What Makes a Border

text: An article on Tuesday about accusations of misconduct against Paolo Macchiarini, a surgeon who is a pioneer in the field of regenerative medicine, misstated the timing of the complaints against him by doctors in Sweden. The complaints were filed in August and September, not last month.
match_headline: Leading Surgeon Is Accused of Misconduct in Experimental Transplant Operations

text: An article on Friday about a Senate hearing on potentially defective airbags made by the Takata Corporation misstated the circumstances under which Honda agreed to lend cars to owners of vehicles recalled for airbag replacement. Honda’s representative at the hearing, Rick Schostek, said in his written testimony that Honda would make such cars available. He did not agree to that action in the face of questioning by Senator Bill Nelson, the Florida Democrat who led the hearing. The article also misstated the timing of the offer. Honda informed the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in early November that it would make loaner cars available; this was not its first such offer.
match_headline: At Senate Airbag Hearing, Evasion and Uncertainty

text: An article on Saturday about the Buffalo Bills’ preparation for their game against the Jets when they could not practice because of a snowstorm referred incorrectly to the way the players and staff members shared game plans and video. While they used iPads, the tablets were not furnished by the N.F.L.
match_headline: Amid Snowstorm, Bills Shrug, Bundle Up and Make Their Way to Detroit

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article in some editions on Saturday about Islanders forward Frans Nielsen misstated, in some copies, the day he was shown fighting for the puck against the Toronto Maple Leafs. It was Oct. 21, not Friday night, Nov. 21.
match_headline: A Longtime Islander Is Taking Winning in Stride

text: An entry on Tuesday in a listing of coming events about the intersection of science and culture misstated the date for a program at the Cornelia Street Cafe. It is on Dec. 7, not Dec. 5.
match_headline: Science Events: Minimalist Music and a Spotlight on Sex

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision to release the grand jury documents in the Michael Brown shooting misspelled the surname, after the first reference, of the St. Louis County prosecutor who made that decision. He is Robert P. McCulloch, not McCullough.
match_headline: Mixed Motives Seen in Prosecutor’s Decision to Release Ferguson Grand Jury Materials

text: An article on Tuesday about a Confederate plot in 1864 to try to burn down multiple New York City buildings, including a hotel next to a theater where John Wilkes Booth and his brothers happened to be performing “Julius Caesar,” misidentified the role played by Edwin Thomas Booth. He was Brutus, not Caesar.
match_headline: As Booth Brothers Held Forth, 1864 Confederate Plot Against New York Fizzled

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with the continuation of an article misidentified, in some editions, the Missouri official shown speaking at a news conference. He is Robert P. McCulloch, the St. Louis County prosecutor, not Gov. Jay Nixon.
match_headline: Protests Flare After Ferguson Police Officer Is Not Indicted

text: An article on Wednesday about a governing board meeting at the University of Virginia to discuss the university’s reputation in light of sexual assault allegations involving a fraternity misstated the academic year of Hannah Graham, a Virginia student who was murdered in September. She was a sophomore, not a freshman. The error was repeated in a subheading.
match_headline: University of Virginia’s Image Suffers After Campus Rape Report

text: An obituary on Thursday about Francis Fraser, a British underworld enforcer who later chronicled his deeds in books, in films and elsewhere, misstated his date of birth and his age when he died. As the obituary correctly noted, he was born in 1923. But he was born on Dec. 13, not on Nov. 13; therefore he was 90 when he died, not 91.
match_headline: Francis Fraser, Who Cashed In on His Cruelty, Dies at 90

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press obituary on Thursday about Murray Oliver, a five-time All-Star forward in the National Hockey League in the 1960s, misstated the surname of the player to whom he lost the N.H.L.'s rookie of the year award in 1960. He is Bill Hay, not Hays.
match_headline: Player’s Death From Cricket Injury Stuns Sport

text: An article last Sunday about the environmental record and state regulation of the North Dakota oil industry erroneously attributed a distinction to an oil spill last fall on the farm of Steven and Patricia Jensen near Tioga. It is considered the largest on-land oil spill in recent American history, not the largest ever.
match_headline: Reported Environmental Incidents in North Dakota’s Oil Industry

text: A news analysis article last Sunday about the rising tensions between Israelis and Palestinians that center on disputes over the plateau in the Old City of Jerusalem that is known as the Temple Mount by Jews and the Noble Sanctuary by Muslims referred incorrectly to the Islamic Waqf, the council that oversees the site. It is administered by Jordan, not by Palestinians, although most of the people who run the site day to day are Palestinian. The article also referred imprecisely to the tunnels at the Western Wall, which is below the plateau. While they run alongside the wall, and below the level of the exposed portion where Jews gather to pray, the tunnels do not run directly under the wall.
match_headline: Mistrust Threatens Delicate Balance at a Sacred Site in Jerusalem

text: An article last Sunday about Basuki Tjahaja Purnama, who recently became only the second Chinese Christian governor of Jakarta, Indonesia, the capital of an overwhelmingly Muslim nation, misstated the role of Bambang Harymurti, who commented on prejudices against Chinese Indonesians. He is a former editor in chief of Tempo magazine, a leading Indonesian weekly, not a founder.
match_headline: An Ethnic Chinese Christian, Breaking Barriers in Indonesia

text: An article in some copies last Sunday about Harvard’s 31-24 victory over Yale in football misstated the number of times Harvard’s team has finished a football season undefeated. It is 17, not 18.
match_headline: Far From Perfect, Harvard Ends Impeccably Against Yale

text: An article on Nov. 16 about elite universities’ investing in museums and performance spaces misstated the number of years the Harvard Art Museums were closed for renovations. It was six years, not more than eight years. The article also erroneously included an architect as a designer of the Lewis Center for the Arts at Princeton. Steven Holl was the sole designer; Chris McVoy, a partner with Steven Holl Architects, did not work on it. (Mr. McVoy was co-designer of a museum at Virginia Commonwealth University.)
match_headline: On Elite Campuses, an Arts Race

text: An article on Nov. 16 about the choreographer Jonah Bokaer referred incorrectly to a Chaconne that George Balanchine choreographed. It is by Christoph Willibald Gluck, not by Bach. (One of Mr. Bokaer’s projects was a Bach Chaconne.)
match_headline: The Quiet Bravery of a Doomed Revolt

text: A subheading last Sunday with a review of “All My Puny Sorrows,” a novel by Miriam Toews, misidentified the Canadian city to which the heroine travels to spend time with her sister. It is Winnipeg — not Toronto, which is where the heroine herself lives.
match_headline: ‘All My Puny Sorrows,’ by Miriam Toews

text: An article last Sunday about the designation of “vape” as the 2014 Word of the Year by Oxford Dictionaries, which chose it because of its relevance to the expanding legalization of marijuana, referred imprecisely to a Colorado law that took effect on Jan. 1 of this year. It legalized retail sales of marijuana, not its recreational use, which became legal in the state a year earlier.
match_headline: Pop-Ups and Sales to Start 2014

text: An article on Wednesday about the discovery of a Shakespeare first folio at a small library in northern France misidentified the auction house that sold another copy in 2006 and misstated the price. It was Sotheby’s, not Christie’s, and the price was $5.2 million, not $6.8 million. The article also misspelled and omitted part of the name of a university in France where Jean-Christophe Mayer, who commented on the discovery, works. It is the University of Montpellier III, not the University of Montpelier.
match_headline: Shakespeare Folio Discovered in France

text: A news analysis article on Nov. 23 about efforts by China’s leader, Xi Jinping, to showcase his country as the dominant economic power in Asia referred incorrectly to the front page of a local newspaper in the Australian state of Tasmania where he visited after a series of Asian summit meetings. The articles were written in Chinese — not in Mandarin, a form of spoken Chinese. (Standard written Chinese is based on Mandarin.)
match_headline: Asia’s ‘Big Guy’ Spreads Cash and Seeks Influence in Pacific Region

text: An article on Tuesday about a new marquee for the “Tonight Show” host Jimmy Fallon on one of New York’s landmark buildings misstated part of the address of the building. The marquee is at 30 Rockefeller Plaza, not 30 Rockefeller Center. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Jimmy Fallon’s Name Goes on 30 Rock Marquee

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the Frick Collection’s acquisition of a self-portrait by the 17th-century Baroque artist Bartolomé Esteban Murillo misstated the relationship of Henry Clay Frick and Dr. Henry Clay Frick II, who inherited the painting and whose widow recently decided to give it to the Frick Collection. Dr. Frick was Frick’s grandson, not his son.
match_headline: A New Home at the Frick for a Rare Murillo Work

text: An obituary on Saturday about the research biochemist Denham Harman misstated, in some editions, the year he was born. It was 1916, not 1926. (The obituary correctly noted that he was 98.)
match_headline: Denham Harman, 98, Dies; Sought Leverage on Aging

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Nancy H. Teeters, the first woman appointed to the Federal Reserve Board, misspelled the name of the city in Indiana where she was born. It is Marion, not Marian.
match_headline: Nancy H. Teeters, First Woman on Federal Reserve Board, Dies at 84

text: An article on Thursday about President Obama’s new environmental regulations misstated how ozone gets into the air. Ozone is a smog-causing pollutant created by emissions from factories and coal plants; it is not itself emitted into the air. The error also occurred in an article and headline on Wednesday about the announcement of the regulations.
match_headline: Obama Builds Environmental Legacy With 1970 Law

text: An article on Monday about the film “Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb” and Robin Williams’s role in the franchise, misstated the amount of time Mr. Williams worked on the first two “Night at the Museum” films. It was three weeks on the first and one week on the second, not “less than a week” on both.
ref_headline: Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb
match_headline: A Last Hurrah for ‘Night at the Museum’ Franchise, and for Robin Williams

text: An article on Monday about the use of emails from Steve Jobs in lawsuits involving Apple misstated the month that a trial is set to begin in a case in which Apple and five other Silicon Valley companies are accused of conspiring to keep wages down. It is April, not January.
match_headline: Star Witness in Apple Lawsuit Is Still Steve Jobs

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Nov. 19 about the arrest of Kevin Darden in the fatal shoving of a Bronx man at a subway station misstated, in some editions, the day police officers were handing out fliers seeking information on the killing. It was Monday, Nov. 17, not Tuesday, Nov. 18.
match_headline: Man Charged With Fatal Shoving of New York Subway Rider

text: An article by The Associated Press on Nov. 25 about players on the ballot for the Baseball Hall of Fame misstated the number of times pitcher Pedro Martinez won the Cy Young Award during his career. It was three times, not two.

An article on Nov. 22 about the Florida State football coach Jimbo Fisher’s call-in show misstated, in some copies, the number of Seminoles starters this season who have been accused of varying degrees of domestic abuse. It is two, not three.
match_headline: F.S.U. Coach’s Call-In Show Is a No-Sin Zone

text: An article on Sunday about young Japanese who have gone to Guadalcanal to help find the remains of Japanese soldiers killed in the battle for the island during World War II referred imprecisely to the 22,000 Japanese and 7,000 American deaths. They occurred in land, air and sea combat, not just on the island itself.
match_headline: Japanese Unearth Remains, and Their Nation’s Past, on Guadalcanal

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an article about a six-part HBO documentary about Robert A. Durst misidentified the site of an office tower built by the Durst Organization in 1970. It is on the Avenue of the Americas between 43rd and 44th Streets, not at 42nd Street.
match_headline: Stranger Than Fiction? Try Fact

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Gabriel Medina’s pursuit of the Association of Surfing Professionals World Championship Tour title erroneously attributed a distinction to him in some editions. He would be the first Brazilian and the first South American man — but not the first South American — to win an A.S.P. World Championship Tour title. (Sofia Mulanovich of Peru won the women’s title in 2004.)
match_headline: A Young Brazilian Surfer Is Riding a Groundswell

text: A report in the N.H.L. roundup in some editions on Sunday about the Islanders’ strong start to the season misstated, in some copies, goalie Jaroslav Halak’s record after the Islanders’ 3-1 victory over the Devils the night before. He improved to 12-4-0, not 11-4-0.
match_headline: Surging Sabres Edge Canadiens in Shootout

text: Because of an editing error, a theater entry in the Listings pages on Friday about “Soul Doctor,” which is in previews at the Actors Temple Theater in Manhattan, misidentified the director. She is Mindy Cooper, not Daniel S. Wise. (Mr. Wise, who wrote the book, directed the Broadway version of the musical last year.)
match_headline: Theater Listings for Nov. 28-Dec.4

text: An article on Sunday about the dropping of all remaining charges, including murder, against former President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt stemming from his attempt to stay in power during the Arab Spring revolt misidentified the source of a comment that the judges who made the ruling were collaborating with Mr. Mubarak. That comment was by Khaled Ali, a human rights lawyer; it was not by another Egyptian named Khaled Ali, who is a former presidential candidate as well as a human rights advocate.
match_headline: Egyptian Judges Drop All Charges Against Mubarak

text: An article on Nov. 11 about voters’ lack of enthusiasm for an attempted political comeback by Nicolas Sarkozy, the former French president, misstated the timing of a vote for president of the Union for a Popular Movement, Mr. Sarkozy’s center-right party. It was scheduled for late November, not “next month.” The article also misspelled the surname of a high school student who asked Mr. Sarkozy what he intended to do for young people if he won the presidency in 2017. He is Amin Brimou, not Baimou.
match_headline: Sarkozy Tries Quick Comeback, but France May Not Go Along

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the remaining holdouts at the Prospect Park Residence, an assisted-living home in Brooklyn that has announced it is closing, misstated the building’s sale price. It is $76.5 million, not $7.65 million.
match_headline: At Assisted-Living Home Set to Close, Holdouts Dig In as Services Dry Up

text: An article on Wednesday about tonight’s broadcast of “Peter Pan Live!” on NBC referred imprecisely to NBC’s broadcast of “The Sound of Music” last year. It was the first time in decades that a network had staged a musical for live broadcast, not the first live broadcast of a musical in decades.
match_headline: Flying by the Seat of Their Pants

text: A listing in some copies last Sunday misidentified the location of a lecture today. “Economic Implications of Global Rebalancing,” which is to be given at 5:30 p.m. by Robert T. McGee, will be at the MasterCard Worldwide Headquarters in Purchase, N.Y., not at the Stamford Yacht Club in Connecticut. As such, the listing should have been published in the Westchester Calendar, not the Connecticut Calendar.
match_headline: Events in Connecticut for Nov. 30-Dec. 6, 2014

text: An article on Nov. 13 about the use of glass in the bathrooms of luxury Manhattan high-rises misspelled the surname of the man who designed the restrooms in the Felix nightclub at the Peninsula Hotel in Hong Kong. He is Philippe Starck, not Stark.
match_headline: Leaving Shame on a Lower Floor

text: An article on Thursday about the changes in Tiger Woods’s golf game in the five years since a car accident in his driveway set off revelations about his extramarital affairs misstated Sam Snead’s age when he last won on the PGA Tour. He was 52, not 54.
match_headline: 5 Years After Crash, Tiger Woods Is Still Recovering

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about “I Only Read It for the Cartoons: An Evening With (a Few of) The New Yorker’s Most Brilliant Artists,” a panel discussion scheduled for Thursday, misstated the address where the event will take place and the telephone number for information. It will be at 209 East 23rd Street in Manhattan, not 133/141 West 21st Street, and the phone number is 212-592-2010.
ref_headline: I Only Read It for the Cartoons: An Evening With (a Few of) The New Yorker’s Most Brilliant Artists,
match_headline: Spare Times for Dec. 5-Dec. 11

text: A picture caption on Friday with a review of the opening-night gala of Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, at City Center in Manhattan, misidentified two of the dancers shown. They are Jeroboam Bozeman and Yannick Lebrun — not Kirven Douthit-Boyd and Antonio Douthit-Boyd.
match_headline: Talking About Love, Demonstrating Violence

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about Cyrus Vance Jr., the district attorney of New York County, describes incompletely a shooting incident at the Bryant Park ice rink in November 2013 and misspells the given name of a man charged with shooting skaters. He is Corey Dunton, not Cory, and he has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial; it has not been established that he “fired a gun at skaters.” In addition, the article misstates the length of time that Robert M. Morgenthau served as district attorney of New York County. It was 35 years, not 34.
match_headline: Cyrus Vance Jr.’s ‘Moneyball’ Approach to Crime

text: An article on Wednesday about the introduction of new credit card technology in the United States, known as E.M.V., misstated the way in which purchases will be verified with the new cards. Some banks will require a signature and others a four-digit code; not all banks will require a code.
match_headline: Preparing for Chip-and-PIN Cards in the United States

text: An article on Wednesday about online security start-ups misstated the business of one such company, Bromium. It creates secure spaces on computers, not in the cloud, making it less likely that hackers can expand their reach within a laptop or PC, not on a network.
match_headline: Computing Goes to the Cloud. So Does Crime.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the philosopher Patrick Suppes erroneously attributed a quotation to him in some copies. As the obituary noted, he said in 1966 that “in a few more years” schoolchildren would have access to “the personal services of a tutor as well-informed and as responsive as Aristotle.” But he did not go on to say, “It’s fun to imagine that such access might be as close as your local toy store.” Those were the words of the writer of a 2003 New York Times article that quoted Dr. Suppes.
match_headline: Patrick Suppes, Pioneer in Computerized Learning, Dies at 92

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 23 about a growing movement among European governments to recognize Palestinian sovereignty erroneously attributed a distinction to Sweden in some editions. Several European countries, including Malta, Albania and Cyprus, recognized Palestine as a state in 1988, immediately after the Palestine National Council declared independence; Sweden was not the first to do so.
match_headline: Europe Takes Stronger Measures, Albeit Symbolic, to Condemn Israeli Policies

text: An article last Sunday about Pope Francis’ visit to Turkey quoted incorrectly from comments by Tony Quta, an Iraqi Christian who has applied for refugee status in Turkey. He said, “Muslims, Christians are dying in Iraq,” not “Muslim Christians are dying in Iraq.” And because of an editing error, the byline misspelled the reporter’s given name in some editions. She is Sebnem Arsu, not Sebnum.
ref_headline: Muslims, Christians are dying in Iraq,
match_headline: Pope Brings Message of Interreligious Peace to Istanbul

text: An article last Sunday about the continuing significance of camels for Jordan’s Royal Desert Forces misidentified one of the items that officers of the desert forces, a branch of the national police force, used to carry during multiday camel patrols. They carried ghee, or clarified butter, not lard.
match_headline: Tradition Saves Camels’ Spot in Jordan’s Desert Forces

text: A review on Nov. 23 about “Embattled Rebel: Jefferson Davis as Commander in Chief,” by James M. McPherson , misidentified the cabinet post that Davis held before the Civil War, during the administration of Franklin Pierce. He was secretary of war, not state.
ref_headline: Embattled Rebel: Jefferson Davis as Commander in Chief,
match_headline: ‘Embattled Rebel,’ by James M. McPherson

text: A picture caption in the Innovations Issue on Nov. 16 about the longbow, an archery weapon popular in the Middle Ages, misidentifed the group of young women shown at an archery range. They were members of the girls’ archery team at Bloomfeld High School in New Jersey, circa 1950, not a group of Girl Scouts.
match_headline: The Civil Rights of Pregnant Women

text: An article on Nov. 23 about Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey misidentifed the location and the time frame of a presentation he made at a confidential meeting of Republican donors and activists. He spoke in Georgia last March, not in New York City last summer. The article also described incorrectly the governor’s actions regarding a bill to legalize same-sex marriage in his state. The governor vetoed the bill in 2012; he did not fail to halt its passage last year. (In 2013 Christie dropped his legal challenge to a court ruling that allowed same sex marriage in New Jersey.)
match_headline: Chris Christie Is Back

text: An obituary last Sunday about the poet Mark Strand referred incorrectly in some copies to his survivors. He did not have any brothers; he is not survived by a brother, Thomas. The obituary also omitted the name of a survivor. Among the survivors is a daughter, Fritha Strand. In addition, the obituary misstated part of the name of the province in Canada where Mr. Strand was born and misspelled the name of a company that published a number of his books. He was born on Prince Edward Island, not on Prince Edward’s Island, and the books were published by Atheneum, not by Athenaeum.
match_headline: Mark Strand, 80, Dies; Pulitzer-Winning Poet Laureate

text: An obituary Nov. 23 about the builder and entrepreneur Victor Elmaleh erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He and his partners were among the first to import Volkswagens to the United States; they were not the first. (Ben Pon and Max Hoffman began importing Volkswagens at about the same time as they did.)
match_headline: Victor Elmaleh, 95, Builder and Entrepreneur, Is Dead

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary last Sunday about the architect Paul Katz misstated the date of his death. It was Thursday, Nov. 20 — not Thursday, Nov. 27.
match_headline: Paul Katz, Big-Picture Architect, Dies at 57

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the makers of the movie “Still Alice” carried an erroneous credit. The picture, a scene from the film showing Julianne Moore and Kristen Stewart, is by JoJo Whilden/Sony Pictures Classic, not Linda Kallerus/Sony Pictures Classic.
match_headline: Yearning to Make the Connection

text: An article on Nov. 23 about the Irish singer-songwriter Hozier misidentified the label that released his debut album in the United States. It is Columbia, not Island/Rubyworks, which released it internationally.
match_headline: Protesting Injustice, Accepting Fame

text: An article last Sunday about events related to Art Basel Miami Beach omitted part of the name for a performance last Tuesday. It was the “ME3M 4 Miami: Story Ballet About the Internet,” not just “Story Ballet About the Internet.” The article also misidentified the venue for that performance. It is the Castle Beach Resort, not the Thompson hotel. In addition, the article misstated the purpose of a dinner for Peter Marino on Wednesday. It was to honor him personally, not his current exhibition at the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach. And, finally, the article misstated part of the address of the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami. It is 4040 NE Second Avenue, not 3841.
ref_headline: ME3M 4 Miami: Story Ballet About the Internet,
match_headline: Art Basel Miami Beach’s Not-to-Be-Missed Parties and Events

text: An article last Sunday about snus, a type of smokeless tobacco, misstated the comparative risk of contracting lung cancer for smokers and nonsmokers who use the product. The risk is 15 to 30 times greater, not 15 to 30 percent greater.
match_headline: A Lesser Warning? Maybe

text: An article on Wednesday about the election of a Polish gay rights activist, Robert Biedron, as the mayor of a conservative city near the Pomeranian coast misstated the city’s name. It is Slupsk, not Slusk. The article also misstated the year that civil partnerships were first openly discussed in the Polish Parliament. It was 2003, not last year.
match_headline: A Gay Mayor in Poland? No Big Deal

text: An article on Wednesday about a death sentence imposed on nearly 200 defendants by a judge in Egypt over the killing of 11 police officers during a riot last year misstated part of the given name of the Middle East and North Africa director of Human Rights Watch, who commented on the mass sentencing and others like it in the country. She is Sarah Leah Whitson, not Sarah Lee.
match_headline: Egypt Sentences Nearly 200 to Die in Mass Trial Over Killings of Police

text: A caption on Wednesday with an article about a drenching rain in drought-plagued California described the picture incorrectly in some copies. The photograph showed a man walking his dog in Hermosa Beach, Calif., not a cyclist navigating a flooded intersection in San Francisco. And the credit misidentified the photographer. The picture was taken by Monica Almeida, not by Jim Wilson. (A picture of a cyclist taken by Mr. Wilson appeared in other editions.)
match_headline: In Midst of California’s Drought, a Rainy Day Is a Welcome Sight

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about young bankers’ growing preference for private equity jobs misidentified Philip Piro, a former banker. He is in the center of the photograph, not at the right. (The person at right is a friend, Pat Cascarano.)
match_headline: Private Equity Is Top Choice of Young Wall St. Bankers

text: A picture caption in the Listings pages on Friday about “Tamburlaine, Parts I and II,” at the Polonsky Shakespeare Center in Fort Greene, Brooklyn, misspelled the director’s given name. He is Michael Boyd, not Michel.
match_headline: Theater Listings for Dec. 5-11

text: An obituary on Saturday about Arthur Leipzig, the documentary photographer who captured everyday life in New York, misstated the year of his birth. As the obituary, the headline and a front-page capsule summary correctly noted, he was 96; therefore he was born in 1918, not in 1928.
match_headline: Arthur Leipzig, Photographer of Everyday Life in New York, Dies at 96

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the publisher Allan Kornblum misstated, at one point, the name that he gave his company after moving to Minneapolis from Iowa City. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, it was Coffee House Press — not Toothpaste Press, the company’s original name.
match_headline: Allan Kornblum, Independent Publisher, Dies at 65; Sought the Undiscovered

text: An article on Nov. 26 examining the grand jury evidence in the shooting death of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Mo., referred incorrectly to an exchange during the testimony of Officer Darren Wilson, who killed the unarmed teenager. It was a grand juror — not the prosecutor — who asked Officer Wilson, “You felt like your life was in jeopardy?” and then followed up with another question, “And use of deadly force was justified at that point in your opinion?”
ref_headline: You felt like your life was in jeopardy?
match_headline: Amid Conflicting Accounts, Trusting Darren Wilson

text: A picture caption on Saturday with the continuation of an article about the sharp differences in race relations exposed by the deaths of unarmed black men in Ferguson, Mo., and New York City misstated the sentiment that one person interviewed, Ashley Bernaugh, saw in the comments by her family. She considered the comments misinformed, not racist.
match_headline: Police Killings Reveal Chasms Between Races

text: An article last Tuesday about a news media campaign to resuscitate the career of Ray Rice after his suspension from the N.F.L. was lifted misidentified, in some editions, the social media site where his wife, Janay Rice, commented on a violent encounter with him. She posted on Instagram, not on Facebook.
match_headline: To Rescue Image, Ray Rice Turns to Best Ally, the Woman He Hit

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 27 about a polio crisis in Pakistan, made worse because of attacks on health workers by militants and political chaos, misidentified one of the people who accused Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif of corruption and ineptitude. He is Imran Khan, a political opponent, not Mr. Sharif himself.
match_headline: Polio Crisis Deepens in Pakistan, With New Cases and Killings

text: A picture caption last Tuesday with an article describing new data about the early universe referred incorrectly to microwave radiation recorded by the Planck satellite in one patch of sky. The microwaves shown were emitted by dust in the Milky Way, not by the Big Bang.
match_headline: New Images Refine View of Infant Universe

text: An article on Wednesday about a report on teachers’ pay, using information from the study by the National Council on Teacher Quality, omitted a school district among those with the highest purchasing power for educators, when adjusted for the cost of living, and misidentified a city among the three lowest. The District of Columbia was among those with the highest earning power, and Newark, not New York City, was among the lowest. Because of those errors in the report, the article also gave incorrect comparisons for the purchasing power of teachers in two cities. The highest teacher salary in San Francisco would have the purchasing power of $51,022, not $31,692, in Las Vegas. And a Pittsburgh teacher with an exemplary rating can earn a salary with the equivalent purchasing power in Las Vegas of $106,440, not $106,050.
match_headline: Middle-Class Pay Elusive for Teachers, Report Says

text: An article on Monday about the Yoox Group, an Italian company that has emerged as a global leader in online sales of luxury goods, misstated the company’s net earnings in 2013. It was 12.6 million euros, not EUR12.6 billion.
match_headline: Success Draws Competition for Luxury E-Retailer Yoox

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Thursday about the hockey coach Lou Vairo’s career path, which took him from Brooklyn to the United States Hockey Hall of Fame, misspelled, in some copies, the name of the Brooklyn neighborhood where he grew up. It is Canarsie, not Carnarsie. Also because of an editing error, a picture caption with the article misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a member of the 1984 United States Olympic men’s hockey team shown with Vairo and rendered incorrectly the surname of another. They are Ed Olczyk, not Oczyk, and Pat LaFontaine, not La Fontaine. The caption also misstated, in some copies, the 1984 team’s finish at the Winter Olympics. The team came in seventh; it did not win a silver medal. (The 2002 Olympic team, for which Vairo was also a coach, won a silver medal).
match_headline: Coach Helped Hockey Flourish Beyond Asphalt

text: An editorial on Monday about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s promise to end New York City’s horse-carriage industry misstated the amount NYClass, a group opposed to the carriages, contributed to an ad campaign to defeat Christine Quinn, Mr. de Blasio’s primary rival. NYClass says it donated $200,000, not $1 million.
match_headline: Horse Nonsense From City Hall

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about President Obama’s addressing the country’s racial conflicts omitted part of a quotation, and in so doing altered the context. In quoting the president, Valerie Jarrett, one of his senior advisers, said that he told young activists in a meeting last week to “shoot for the sky,” adding, “but ‘better’ is good.” He did not say only “Shoot for the sky.” The article also paraphrased incorrectly from Ms. Jarrett’s comment about the protests surrounding the death of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Mo. She said his death has unleashed a new energy among Americans, not among African-Americans.
match_headline: Unrest Over Race Is Testing Obama’s Legacy

text: An article last Wednesday about a decision by the University of Alabama-Birmingham to terminate its football program misstated, in some copies, the year that colleges vetoed a proposal by the N.C.A.A.'s executive committee to allow an annual $2,000 stipend for players. It was 2011, not 2012.
match_headline: It’s a Game of Spiraling Costs, So a College Tosses Out Football

text: An article last Wednesday about the death of a Turkish-German student who was killed when she tried to stop a man from harassing two girls, a case that has provoked debate over Germany’s efforts to form a multicultural society, referred incorrectly to the student, Tugce Albayrak. Although of Turkish descent, Ms. Albayrak was born in Germany; she was not an immigrant. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: A Student’s Death Exposes German Struggle for a Multicultural Ideal

text: An article on Monday about the Texas physician who misdiagnosed the first case of Ebola in the United States paraphrased incorrectly from written responses the doctor, Joseph Howard Meier, gave to questions. While Dr. Meier acknowledged that his initial diagnosis of Thomas Eric Duncan was inaccurate, he said his care was appropriate based on the information he had at the time; he did not say that he erred in his treatment. The error was repeated in a headline. The article also misstated the travel information that Texas Health Presbyterian Hospital in Dallas received from Mr. Duncan during his initial visit to the emergency room. He told health care workers that he had been in Africa; he did not specify Liberia. That error also appeared in a front-page article on Oct. 4 about the hospital’s having changed its account of how it handled the case.
match_headline: Dallas Doctor in Ebola Case Say Treatment Based on What He Knew at Time

text: An article on Tuesday about Merck & Company’s $8.4 billion deal for Cubist Pharmaceuticals misstated the actions required by Cubist shareholders in the acquisition. The deal is subject to the tendering of a majority of Cubist’s shares, not to a vote by Cubist shareholders.
match_headline: Merck Said to Weigh Acquisition of Rival Drug Maker Cubist

text: An article on Saturday about a class-action case against Apple, using information from an Apple representative, misstated Jeffrey Kowalski’s involvement in the matter. Mr. Kowalski, who bought an iPod Touch in 2008, contacted the judge overseeing the case to offer himself as a plaintiff; the plaintiffs’ lawyers did not fax the judge requesting that Mr. Kowalski be added as a plaintiff.
match_headline: Apple iPod Suit May Lack One Thing: A Plaintiff

text: An article on Dec. 2 about speculation that Giants Coach Tom Coughlin’s job is in jeopardy referred incorrectly in some copies to the performance of the Jacksonville Jaguars in the first half of their victory over the Giants on Nov. 30. They scored 3 points; they were not “blanked in the opening half.”
match_headline: Giants Try to Ignore Speculation on Tom Coughlin

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the closing of the Off Broadway comedy “Tail! Spin!” on Jan. 4 misspelled the playwright’s surname. He is Mario Correa, not Correo.
match_headline: ‘Tail! Spin!’ to Close

text: An obituary on Nov. 22 about the arts critic and foreign correspondent Richard Eder, using information from his family, misspelled the surname of one of his sisters, who survives him. She is Liz McCulloch, not McCullough.
match_headline: Richard Eder, Arts Critic and Foreign Correspondent, Dies at 82

text: An article on Wednesday comparing the protest marches in Berkeley, Calif., to those of the 1960s misstated the title of Nicholas Dirks, who discussed the history of unrest at the University of California, Berkeley. He is chancellor at Berkeley, not president.
match_headline: It’s Not the Old Days, but Berkeley Sees a New Spark of Protest

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the rarity of indictments of police officers through the grand jury system referred incorrectly to a shooting in North Carolina last year when the police killed Jonathan Ferrell, an unarmed black man. Police officers initially fired a Taser at Mr. Ferrell, but missed; the Taser did not strike him. (Later an officer fired 12 bullets at Mr. Ferrell, striking him 10 times.)
match_headline: Grand Jury System, With Exceptions, Favors the Police in Fatalities

text: An article on Monday about reaction in Philadelphia to assault allegations against Bill Cosby misidentified one of the individuals next to Mr. Cosby on a mural in North Philadelphia. He is the Rev. Paul Washington, an Episcopal priest and community activist, not Desmond Tutu. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Philadelphia Laments Bill Cosby’s Now-Tarnished Image

text: An article on Monday about Dr. Ian Crozier, the third American with Ebola to be airlifted to Emory University Hospital in Atlanta from West Africa, misidentified his birthplace in Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe). He was born in Masvingo — not in Bulawayo, which is where he grew up.
match_headline: An Ebola Doctor’s Return From the Edge of Death

text: An article last Thursday about testimony by Officer Daniel Pantaleo before a grand jury in the death of Eric Garner misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a lawyer who said that police officers are an exception to the general practice of not having defendants testify at grand jury proceedings. He is James J. Culleton, not Colleton.
match_headline: Officer Daniel Pantaleo Told Grand Jury He Meant No Harm to Eric Garner

text: An article on Tuesday about several technology executives’ financing of the petition site Change.org misstated the background of one of them, Pierre M. Omidyar. He was the founder of eBay, not its co-founder. The article, using information from people with knowledge of the fund-raising, also erroneously attributed a distinction to Mr. Omidyar. Other executives — not just Mr. Omidyar — are repeat investors in the latest round of financing.
match_headline: Tech Figures Join to Fund Change.org Petition Site

text: An article on Page F16 today, about pension fund investing in Canada, misstates the amount of assets under management for the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board. It is 234 billion Canadian dollars, not 273 billion. The article also misstates the plan’s cost of outsourcing a $10 billion infrastructure investment. It is $51 million, not $15 million. And the article misstates the title of Ashby Monk, who commented on differences between American and Canadian pension fund rules. He is the executive director of the global projects center (not products center) at Stanford University.
match_headline: Canada Finds Key to Pension Fund Investing

text: An obituary last Thursday about the former New York congressman Herman Badillo misspelled the surname of his second wife. She was Irma Deutsch Liebling, not Leibling.
match_headline: Herman Badillo, Congressman and Fixture of New York Politics, Dies at 85

text: A caption on Nov. 20 with the Scene City column misspelled the given name of a guest. He is Allen Leech, not Allan.
match_headline: Keira Knightley and Benedict Cumberbatch Celebrate ‘The Imitation Game’

text: A report on the Browsing page last Thursday about a Shinola cotton sweatshirt misstated the price. It is $120, not $170.
match_headline: All I Want for Christmas Is an Elf-Free Sweater

text: An article last Thursday about entrepreneurs who use the name Brooklyn to sell products and services overseas misspelled the given name of a Manila restaurateur who modeled his business after restaurants in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. He is Ynigo Santos, not Yniga.
match_headline: The Brooklyn Brand Goes Global

text: An article last Thursday about the challenges of operating a sustainable house in Vermont misstated part of the title of a 1992 book by Al Gore. It is “Earth in the Balance: Ecology and the Human Spirit,” not “The Earth in Balance: Ecology and the Human Spirit.”
ref_headline: Earth in the Balance: Ecology and the Human Spirit,
match_headline: Exhausted by a House That Saves Energy

text: A report in the Currents column on Nov. 27 misidentified a principal material used in the construction of the Vipp prefab house. It is galvanized steel, not stainless steel.
match_headline: A Prefab, Fully Stocked

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the Obama administration’s legal efforts to block a request by The New York Times to release thousands of documents from a Justice Department investigation into the torture of detainees by the Central Intelligence Agency referred incorrectly to a decision Attorney General Eric H. Holder made in 2009. He decided to open a criminal inquiry into the treatment of detainees; it is not the case that he decided not to do so.
match_headline: U.S. Tells Court That Documents From Torture Investigation Should Remain Secret

text: An article on Nov. 19 about four Jewish men who were murdered in a Jerusalem synagogue misstated the position of one victim, Rabbi Moshe Twersky, at the Toras Moshe yeshiva in Jerusalem. He was a teacher at the yeshiva, not head of it.
match_headline: Jewish Victims, All From One Jerusalem Street, Were a Congregation’s ‘Wise Scholars’

text: A reporting credit last Friday with an article about a disagreement between officials in Iraq and Lebanon over the identity of a woman who Lebanese officials said was a wife of Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, the leader of the Islamic State jihadist organization, misidentified the location of a contributor. Eric Schmitt reported from Bahrain, not from Washington.
match_headline: Discord Persists About Woman Said to Be a Wife of ISIS Chief

text: An article last Friday about federal health officials’ predictions for this year’s flu outbreak referred incorrectly to the two processes for growing flu vaccine in the United States. While the vaccine is grown in both chicken eggs and in cell broths, most of it continues to be grown in eggs; the use of cell broths is not currently the primary process.
match_headline: Deadlier Flu Season Is Possible, C.D.C. Says

text: An article on Monday about the Jets’ 30-24 loss to the Minnesota Vikings misstated, in some editions, the length of the field goal by the Jets’ Nick Folk that tied the score at 21-21 with 23 seconds left. It was 44 yards, not 33. (He made a 33-yarder in the second quarter.)
match_headline: A Wrong Call on Defense, but the Jets’ Offense Is Also to Blame

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about the history of the Major League Baseball winter meetings, using information from The Associated Press, misstated the surname of the Los Angeles Dodgers scout shown with the Hall of Famer Stan Musial in 1981. He was Ed Liberatore, not Liberton.
match_headline: Baseball’s Annual Winter Meetings Have It All, Except Quietude

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about a new Bob Dylan album to be released in February, “Shadows in the Night,” misstated the surname of one of the writers of a song on the album and misstated the year it was written. The song, “Stay With Me,” is by Carolyn Leigh and Jerome Moross, not Moss, and was written in 1963, not in 1964.
match_headline: Bob Dylan and the 50-Year Itch

text: An article on Wednesday about the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum’s purchase of albums of mementos that belonged to the Holocaust survivor Mary Berg misspelled, in some editions, the given name of another Holocaust survivor who was interned in the Vittel camp in France with Ms. Berg’s family. She is Anne Wolfe, not Ann.
match_headline: Museum Acquires Holocaust Albums

text: An obituary last Friday about the British politician Jeremy Thorpe misspelled the title of the former husband of his second wife, Marion. He was the Earl of Harewood, not Harwood.
match_headline: Jeremy Thorpe, M.P. Accused in Scandal, Dies at 85

text: An article last Saturday about the first test flight of the Orion spacecraft misstated the given name of a NASA spokesman. He is Rob Navias, not Mike.
match_headline: First Flight Test Is Successful for NASA’s Orion Spacecraft

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about the process that led Senator Dianne Feinstein, the chairwoman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, to make public a report on the torture of terrorism suspects omitted credit for the photographer in some copies. The picture, of Ms. Feinstein discussing the report, was taken by Jim Lo Scalzo of the European Pressphoto Agency.
match_headline: For Dianne Feinstein, Torture Report’s Release Is a Signal Moment

text: An article last Saturday about David Lonergan, who rebuilt his home in the Rockaways after it was destroyed by Hurricane Sandy, misidentified the group supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund that helped cover an insurance payment for his fledgling home improvement business. It is Catholic Charities Brooklyn and Queens — not Catholic Charities Archdiocese of New York.
match_headline: After a Storm, Celebrating a Hard-Earned Homecoming

text: A picture caption last Saturday with an article about protests over a Staten Island grand jury’s decision not to indict a police officer in the death of Eric Garner reversed the order of the photographs in some editions. The pictures — of a demonstration leader, of police officers on Fifth Avenue, and of protesters lying down at Macy’s — were displayed counterclockwise from the top, not clockwise.
match_headline: In Unpredictable New York Protests, Organized Criticism of Police

text: An article last Saturday about the results of a student election at Princeton University misstated the name of its electoral body in some editions. It is the Undergraduate Student Government, not the University Student Government.
match_headline: Princeton Students Pick Experience Over Spoof in Presidential Runoff Vote

text: An article on Dec. 3 about efforts to fix Europe’s banking structure misstated the timetable of a referendum on Britain’s membership in the European Union, promised by Prime Minister David Cameron. He has pledged to bring it before the voters by 2017, not by 2015.
match_headline: A Fragmented, Confused Scramble to Fix Europe’s Banking Structure

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about Jessica Bibliowicz’s succession of her father, Sanford I. Weill, as chairman of the board of one of his biggest charitable endeavors rendered the name of the organization incorrectly. As the article correctly noted, it is the Weill Cornell Medical College, not the Cornell Weill Medical College.
match_headline: Leadership of Cornell’s Medical College to Stay in Sanford Weill’s Family

text: An article in some editions on Nov. 29 about changes made in cricket in the wake of players’ deaths erroneously included a reference to a rule change made by Major League Baseball. Though the league banned the spitball, with some exemptions, it was before the 1920 season, not after Ray Chapman was killed by a pitch during that season.
match_headline: Cricket Player’s Death Highlights Sport’s Dangers

text: An article on Tuesday about the growth of rugby sevens, a streamlined and faster-paced version of the sport, referred incorrectly to rugby’s history as an Olympic sport. Rugby was a medal sport at the Olympics in 1900, 1908, 1920 and 1924; it will not be making its Olympic debut in 2016. The article also misstated the duration of standard rugby union games. They are 80 minutes, not 90.
match_headline: Speeding Up and Shrinking, Rugby Extends Global Reach

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about a proposal to turn a government building in Orange County, N.Y., into an arts center referred incorrectly to the architect, Gene Kaufman, who presented details of his plan. He is the sole owner and principal of Gwathmey Siegel Kaufman Architects, not a partner.
match_headline: Architect Submits A Plan to Save Brutalist Building in Orange County

text: An entry in the Spare Times for Children listings on Friday misstated part of the name of the website for the Best Friends Animal Society Super Adoption Event. It is ny.bestfriends.org/super .
match_headline: Spare Times for Children for Dec. 12-18

text: A picture credit last Sunday with the continuation of an article about Republican attorneys general in several states who have formed a secretive alliance with some of the nation’s top energy producers to oppose President Obama’s regulatory agenda misidentified the photographer in some editions. The picture, of Scott Pruitt, the Oklahoma attorney general, was taken by Dylan Hollingsworth, not by Nick Oxford.
match_headline: Energy Firms in Secretive Alliance With Attorneys General

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about Florida State’s 37-35 victory over Georgia Tech in the Atlantic Coast Conference championship game misstated, in some copies, the number of rushing yards for Florida State running back Dalvin Cook, who was shown evading a Georgia Tech tackler. It was 177, not 151.
match_headline: Suspense Never Ends for Seminoles

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Ohio State’s 59-0 victory over Wisconsin in the Big Ten championship game misspelled the surname of the Big Ten’s commissioner in some copies. He is Jim Delany, not Delaney.
match_headline: Buckeyes Capture Big Ten, Bolstering Playoff Hopes

text: An article in some editions on Nov. 30 about the Rangers’ 5-2 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers misspelled, at one point, the surname of the Flyers player who tied the score, 1-1. As the article initially noted, he is Nicklas Grossmann, not Grosmann.
match_headline: Shaking Off Injuries, Rangers Subdue Flyers

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Nov. 30 with an article about the soccer rebirth of Belo Horizonte, Brazil, the city associated with Brazil’s embarrassing 7-1 loss to Germany in the 2014 World Cup semifinals, referred incorrectly to the Brazil Cup. It is a domestic tournament — not “the national championship,” a term reserved for the winner of Série A, the top Brazilian professional league.
match_headline: City Tarnished by Defeat Gets to Bask in Victory

text: An article last Sunday about the maturation of New England Revolution midfielder Jermaine Jones misstated his age in some copies. He is 33, not 32.
match_headline: A Maestro in the Midfield Focuses on the Family Room

text: Because of an editing error, the App City column in some editions last Sunday about Parcel, a delivery service, misstated the date of the app’s release. It was offered in September, not on Nov. 20.
match_headline: By Text, a Package Deal

text: An entry in the “By the Numbers” feature last Sunday about the history of department store holiday windows misidentified the person in charge of the windows at Barneys New York. He is Dennis Freedman, the creative director for Barneys — not Simon Doonan, the chain’s creative ambassador.
match_headline: Behind the Business of Department Store Holiday Windows

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the recovery of an early snowmobile in Labrador misspelled the surname of a member of a snowmobile club and misspelled the given name of a man who helped with the vehicle’s retrieval. The member of the Model T Ford Snowmobile Club is Bob McDonald, not MacDonald, and the man who helped is Antone Harris, not Antoine.
match_headline: Labrador’s ‘First Snowmobile’ Heads Down the Comeback Trail

text: An article last Sunday about the planned Guggenheim art museum in Abu Dhabi, where fair labor practices have been a concern, misidentified a group that has led worker-abuse protests at the Guggenheim Museum in New York. It is the group Gulf Ultra Luxury Faction, not Human Rights Watch.
match_headline: A New Art Capital, Finding Its Own Voice

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about a remake of the 1974 movie “The Gambler” misidentified the director of the original. It was Karel Reisz, not James Toback, who, as noted in the article, wrote the film’s screenplay.
match_headline: Rolling the Dice on a Movie Remake

text: An article on Nov. 30 about how mainstream comic books were once in genuine conversation with the broader culture referred incorrectly to the special effects animator Ray Harryhausen. Though Mr. Harryhausen worked with the director Eugène Lourié on the 1953 monster movie “The Beast From 20,000 Fathoms,” he did not work with Lourié on his 1961 “Gorgo,” which was licensed to Charlton Comics. Tom Howard provided the special effects for “Gorgo.”
match_headline: Modern Mythology, Yours for a Dime

text: Because of an editing error, the Living In column last Sunday, about Hartsdale, N.Y., omitted one school district serving the hamlet. Part of Hartsdale is assigned to the Edgemont Union Free School District; not all Hartsdale students attend schools in the Greenburgh or Ardsley districts.
match_headline: A Mix of Residents and Housing

text: A picture last Sunday with the Surfacing column about Greenville, S.C., and the role of Falls Park, which opened in 2004, and the Reedy River’s 40-foot waterfall, was published in error. The photograph showed an adjacent park and mixed-use development, Riverplace, built two years later.
match_headline: Opening the Gate to a Vibrant Main Street in Greenville, S.C.

text: A review on Nov. 30 about “Stalin. Volume I: Paradoxes of Power, 1878-1928,” by Stephen Kotkin, misspelled the surname of one of Stalin’s bitter opponents in the Bolshevik hierarchy. He was Lev Kamenev, not Kamanev.
ref_headline: Stalin. Volume I: Paradoxes of Power, 1878-1928,
match_headline: ‘Stalin,’ by Stephen Kotkin

text: A picture caption in the special Innovations issue on Nov. 16 about the success of alternating current over direct current described incorrectly how alternating current originates for a home or a business. The alternating of electrical power begins at the power plant, not upon reaching a home or a business.
match_headline: A Video Network Devoted to ‘All Things Home’

text: An article on Nov. 23 about the way zoos have changed misstated the official name that the Bronx Zoo was given in the early 1990s. It was the International Wildlife Conservation Park, not the Wildlife Conservation Society. (The Wildlife Conservation Society is the organization whose work includes running New York City’s four zoos and the New York Aquarium.)
match_headline: The Dark Side of Zootopia

text: An article on Nov. 30 about the worst industrial disaster in Turkey’s history misstated how long it took for Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan to visit the accident site in the town of Soma. He arrived at the scene the day after the mining disaster, not days later. The article also included an erroneous translation of a quotation from Erdogan regarding the year a mine collapsed in Britain, killing more than 200 people. He said the collapse occurred in 1862, not 1838.
match_headline: The Mine Disaster That Shook Turkey

text: An article and an accompanying picture caption last Sunday about a proliferation of very large homes in Southern California described incorrectly Fred Rosen’s reaction to the construction of a 90,000-square-foot dwelling next to his home in Bel-Air. In response to its approval, he helped form the Bel-Air Homeowners Alliance, which is litigating against another construction effort in the neighborhood; he is not trying to stop the construction next to him.
match_headline: In Los Angeles, a Nimby Battle Pits Millionaires vs. Billionaires

text: An article on Friday about the death in Liberia of Michel du Cille, a Washington Post photographer and Pulitzer Prize winner who had been covering the Ebola crisis, misspelled the surname of his wife. She is Nikki Kahn, not Khan.
match_headline: Michel du Cille, 58, Photographer Who Won 3 Pulitzer Prizes, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 6 about the lifting of a British government ban on sending books to prisoners misstated the given name of the High Court judge who made the ruling. He is Andrew Collins, not Lawrence. (Lawrence Collins is a former justice on Britain’s Supreme Court.)
match_headline: British Judge Lifts Restriction on Sending Books to Prisoners

text: An article on Thursday about psychology experiments that architects of the Central Intelligence Agency’s interrogation program drew on as the basis for brutal techniques misstated the name of an association of psychologists. It is The American Psychological Association (not Psychology). And the article misstated the middle initial of a psychologist who conducted early studies on “learned helplessness” in dogs. He is Martin E. P. Seligman, not Martin J.
match_headline: Architects of C.I.A. Interrogation Drew on Psychology to Induce ‘Helplessness’

text: An article on Dec. 5 about a Princeton student, Will Gansa, whose joke campaign for president of Princeton’s Undergraduate Student Government put him into a runoff misstated the details of a similar campaign last year in Harvard’s student government election. The candidate who became president, Gus Mayopoulos, ran for vice president, then assumed the presidency after his running mate stepped down; he did not run for president. (Mr. Gansa overwhelmingly lost the runoff election at Princeton.)
match_headline: Politics Meeting Parody at Princeton in Student Election

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Dec. 4 with the Building Blocks column, about the author Nathan Silver and his dedication to the architecture of New York City, omitted part of the title of his book. As the column correctly noted, it is “Lost New York,” not “Lost in New York.”
match_headline: From Afar, Still Defending New York’s Landmarks, and the Stories They Hold

text: An article on Dec. 2 about Lu Wei, China’s new Internet czar, misidentified, in some copies, the position he once held at the Xinhua News Agency headquarters. He was vice president, not vice bureau chief.
match_headline: Gregarious and Direct: China’s Web Doorkeeper

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about start-ups turning to crowdsourcing for financing described incorrectly how the woman pictured, Leslie Lienau, used Kickstarter. She financed her company through a Kickstarter campaign; she did not finance an iOS app using the service.
match_headline: After Ethics Panel’s Shutdown, Loopholes Live On in Albany

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the Jimmy V Classic college basketball games at Madison Square Garden misstated, in some copies, the day of the games. They were Tuesday night, not last Monday.
match_headline: Louisville and Villanova Pull Away and Stay Unbeaten

text: A picture caption on Dec. 2 with an article about the Turner Prize, awarded annually to a British artist under 50, using information from Agence France-Presse — Getty Images, misidentified the work a person is shown viewing. It is “It for Others” by the winner of this year’s prize, Duncan Campbell — not “Sigmar,” another work by him. And the article referred incorrectly to the work for which the artist Ciara Phillips was nominated. It is titled “Workshop”; it is not unnamed.
match_headline: Innovative Filmmaker Wins Turner Prize for Art

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the ballerina Alla Sizova misspelled the surname of a ballerina who recalled Rudolf Nureyev’s reaction to being given an apartment to share with Ms. Sizova. She was Ninel Kurgapkina, not Kurgapina.
match_headline: Alla Sizova, a Star Ballerina With the Kirov, Dies at 75

text: Because of an editing error, the Nurmahal Journal article on Friday, about a dispute over whether the body of an Indian spiritual leader should remain frozen or be cremated, misidentified, at one point, the source of an order that the leader, Ashutosh Maharaj, be cremated. It was issued by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, not by the Punjab State government. The error was repeated in a subheading.
match_headline: Where a Holy Man Lies Frozen, Threat of a Standoff Looms

text: An article on Friday about a federal lawsuit filed against Immigration and Customs Enforcement over deportation policies misstated the rank of the agency on a list published by the Partnership for Public Service of the best places to work in the federal government. The agency, which is known as ICE, was tied for last among 314 federal agencies; it was not second to last.
match_headline: Lawsuit Against ICE Previews Turmoil That Immigration Overhaul May Cause Its Enforcers

text: A report in the N.H.L. roundup on Dec. 3 about goalie Martin Brodeur’s signing with the St. Louis Blues misstated, in some editions, the number of seasons he played for the Devils. It was 21 seasons, not 22.
match_headline: Martin Brodeur Resumes N.H.L. Career With Blues

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Dec. 9 about the selection of the James Corner Field Operations landscape architecture firm to design 13 acres of new parkland at the Golden Gate Bridge National Recreation Area misidentified a previous project by the firm. It designed South Park at Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in London, not Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park itself.
match_headline: How Franklin Thwarted Counterfeiters

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the political consultant David Garth misstated his birth date. He was born in 1930 on March 5, not on May 26. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated, in some editions, the party affiliation of one of his clients, former Senator John V. Tunney of California. He is a Democrat, not a Republican. And the obituary misstated, in some copies, the surname of Mr. Garth’s sister and misspelled the given name of his niece. His sister was Zelda Rosenbloom, not Rosenfeld, and his niece is Lauren Halky, not Lawren.
match_headline: David Garth, 84, Dies; Consultant Was an Innovator of Political TV Ads

text: An obituary on Dec. 8 about Ralph H. Baer, who invented and patented the first home video game system, misstated the amount the video game company Atari paid in settling a patent-infringement suit filed by Magnavox and Mr. Baer’s employer, Sanders Associates. It was $1.5 million, not $700,000.
match_headline: Ralph H. Baer, Inventor of First System for Home Video Games, Is Dead at 92

text: An obituary on Monday about Neil Reshen, a manager whose clients included Waylon Jennings and Willie Nelson, misstated, at one point, the surname of his daughter Dawn, who confirmed his death. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, her surname is Reshen-Doty, not Reshen-Coty.
match_headline: Neil Reshen, 75, Dies; Manager Won ‘Outlaw’ Singers’ Freedom

text: An obituary on Monday about Sy Berger, who as an executive of the Topps Chewing Gum Company introduced the modern-day baseball trading card, misstated when Topps began marketing Davy Crockett cards. It was after the company began marketing baseball cards in 1951, not before.
match_headline: Sy Berger, Who Turned Baseball Heroes Into Brilliant Rectangles, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Friday about William P. Wilson, a television consultant for Democratic presidential candidates, misstated the party affiliation of Mr. Wilson’s paternal grandfather, William Wilson, a congressman from Illinois. He was a Republican, not a Democrat.
match_headline: William P. Wilson, Kennedy’s TV Aide for Historic 1960 Debate, Is Dead at 86

text: A review last Wednesday about the Dirty French restaurant on the Lower East Side misspelled the name of a bread often served in French restaurants. It is baguette à l’ancienne, not baguette à la ancienne.
match_headline: Restaurant Review: Dirty French on the Lower East Side

text: Because of an editing error, the Borja Journal article on Monday, about the odd celebrity enjoyed by an amateur painter in Spain after she botched the restoration of a church fresco showing Jesus with a crown of thorns, gave an incorrect translation for the fresco’s title, “Ecce Homo,” which refers to the words spoken by Pontius Pilate when he presented Jesus to his accusers. It means “behold the man” — not “behold man.” Because of another editing error, a picture caption with the article misspelled part of the title of the fresco as “Ecco Homo.”
match_headline: A Town, if Not a Painting, Is Restored

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 11 about Birmingham’s bid for the Democratic National Convention misattributed a quotation about giving Republicans the opportunity to also hold their convention in the city. It was Mayor William A. Bell Sr. — not Bill Armistead, chairman of the Alabama Republican Party — who said: “It’s my intent to go and tell the Republicans, after we have the Democratic convention, ‘You all need to come and protect your state.’ ” This correction was delayed because the error came to light only this week.
ref_headline: It’s my intent to go and tell the Republicans, after we have the Democratic convention, ‘You all need to come and protect your state.’
match_headline: Birmingham Courts Democrats and Waves Off Skeptics

text: An article in some editions on Dec. 7 about New York City’s tentative contract with the principals’ union misstated the potential cost of the principals’ pay increases. It is just over $743 million, not $775 million.
match_headline: New York’s Deal With Principals’ Union Includes Back Pay

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the legacy of John B. King Jr., the departing education commissioner for New York State, misquoted, in some copies, a prediction by Andy Smarick, a senior fellow at the Thomas B. Fordham Institute. He said the next education commissioner was likely to be “a known commodity,” not a “noncommodity.”
match_headline: John King Jr., New York State’s Education Chief, to Leave Many Policy Wars Behind

text: An article on Dec. 7 about Giants tight end Larry Donnell misstated, in some editions, the year in which he was limited to four games as a senior at Grambling. It was 2010, not 2011. The article and a picture caption also misstated, in some editions, the year in which he was available in the N.F.L. draft but was not selected. It was 2011, not 2012.
match_headline: For Giants Tight End Larry Donnell, Plan Had No Backup

text: A picture caption with an article on Dec. 8 about the Giants’ 36-7 victory over the Tennessee Titans misstated the outcome of the play shown involving Giants receiver Odell Beckham Jr., Tennessee safety Michael Griffin and cornerback Jason McCourty. It was an incomplete pass; Beckham did not catch it.
match_headline: Giants Put End to Seven-Game Skid With a Rare All-Around Effort

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some copies on Wednesday about the Nets’ 95-91 loss to the Miami Heat the previous day misspelled the surname of the reporter. He is Zach Schonbrun, not Shonbrun.
match_headline: Nets Struggle to Contain Wade and Mother Nature

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about the “Live From Lincoln Center” broadcast of “Curtain Up: The School of American Ballet Workshop Performance,” directed by Matthew Diamond, omitted the director of the documentary sections. He is Elliot Caplan.
match_headline: A Performance Onstage Returns Anew on the Screen

text: An article last Thursday about the fashion designer Wes Gordon’s trunk shows misstated the surname of the owner of Neapolitan, a boutique in Winnetka, Ill., where he staged such a show. She is Kelly Golden, not Gordon.
match_headline: Wes Gordon Revives a Fashion Tradition

text: An article on Thursday about the secret negotiations for a prisoner swap that led to the reconciliation agreement between the United States and Cuba misspelled, in some editions, the surname of one of the men freed, a former Cuban intelligence agent imprisoned in Cuba on espionage charges since 1995, and referred incorrectly to him. He is Rolando Sarraff Trujillo, not Sarraf, and he is Mr. Sarraff, not Mr. Trujillo. The same errors appeared in some editions in related articles, one about the announcement of the agreement — which also misspelled his surname as Sarras — and another about the last members of a Cuban spy ring who were released.
match_headline: Journey to Reconciliation Visited Worlds of Presidents, Popes and Spies

text: A news analysis article on Nov. 19 about tensions between Israelis and Palestinians centered on a holy site in Jerusalem known to Muslims as Al Aqsa, or the Noble Sanctuary, and to Jews as the Temple Mount referred incorrectly to a fire at a West Bank mosque that the Palestinian president, Mahmoud Abbas, mentioned in his demand that Jews “stop incitement against Aqsa.” The cause had yet to be determined; it was not a “recent arson.” (The Israeli police have since determined that the fire was most likely caused by an electrical fault, not arson.)
match_headline: In Jerusalem’s ‘War of Neighbors,’ the Differences Are Not Negotiable

text: An article on Dec. 11 about the death of a prominent Palestinian official, Ziad Abu Ein, in a confrontation with Israeli security forces misstated the number of Israeli teenagers killed in a bombing in the northern Israeli city of Tiberias in 1979 that Mr. Abu Ein was implicated in. Two teenagers were killed, not one.
match_headline: Calls for Calm After Palestinian Official Dies During Protest in the West Bank

text: An article on Dec. 2 about a strong showing by pro-Western parties in an election in Moldova that became another contest between the West and Russia for influence in a former Soviet republic reversed the rankings and percentages of the vote received by the Liberal Democratic Party and the Democratic Party, according to preliminary results. The Liberal Democrats came in second, with 20 percent, and the Democratic Party was fourth, with 16 percent.
match_headline: Moldova Vote Gives Edge to Parties Looking West

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the trial of 35 members of a soccer fan club in Istanbul on charges of trying to overthrow the government during last year’s protests against the administration of Recep Tayyip Erdogan, then the prime minister, misspelled the name of the fan club. It is Besiktas, not Besikta.
match_headline: Soccer Fans in Turkish Protests Stand Trial

text: An article on Dec. 10 about the economic anxieties of many Israelis and the role those concerns could play in elections in March misstated the year that Yair Lapid, the leader of the centrist Yesh Atid party and until recently the country’s finance minister, was elected to Parliament. It was 2013, not 2012.
match_headline: Cost of Living Takes Center Stage in Israeli Elections

text: An article on Monday about Xiaomi, China’s top smartphone maker, misspelled the surname of its chief executive on first reference. He is Lei Jun, not Li, as the article correctly noted in subsequent references. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: The Rise of a New Smartphone Giant: China’s Xiaomi

text: An article on Oct. 24 about low television ratings for the early games of the World Series described incorrectly a catch made by Willie Mays in Game 1 of the 1954 Series. Though he caught the ball as it came over his shoulder from behind, it was not an over-the-shoulder “basket catch.” (In Mays’s signature basket catch, the glove was held palm up and at belt level; Mays had his arms outstretched for that 1954 catch .) This correction was delayed because a reader’s emails did not reach the editors.
match_headline: Series Is On, and Everybody’s Watching ... Football

text: An article on Friday about the potential effects of the détente with Cuba on relations between the United States and Latin America, which has long objected to Washington’s isolation of Cuba, misspelled the surname of a retired toy store owner in Buenos Aires who expressed skepticism about the deal, saying American leaders “must have a knife somewhere under their poncho.” He is Rubén Grimaldi, not Grimaldo.
ref_headline: must have a knife somewhere under their poncho.
match_headline: Cuba Thaw Lets Rest of Latin America Warm to Washington

text: An article on Thursday about indictments in a West Virginia chemical spill misidentified the lawyer for William E. Tis and Charles E. Herzing, two of the men charged. He is Steve Jory — not Matthew Benyon, who was the public relations consultant who released a statement by Mr. Jory.
match_headline: Owners of Chemical Firm Charged in Elk River Spill in West Virginia

text: An article on Tuesday about a New York City high school student’s false claim to have earned millions of dollars trading stocks misstated, in some editions, the day that The New York Post featured the youth on its cover. It was Sunday, not Monday.
match_headline: Riches to Rags for New York Teenager Who Now Says His Story Is Hoax

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Dec. 12 about the acquittal of Robert A. Durst, a troubled member of a prominent New York City real estate family who was accused of trespassing, misstated the year of an earlier case in which he was found not guilty of murder in Texas. It was 2003, not 2001.
match_headline: Robert Durst, Troubled Scion of Real Estate Family, Is Acquitted of Trespassing

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the State of the Art column, about Amazon.com’s vulnerability to technological advances, misidentified the manager of a courier fleet in San Francisco in some copies. She is Ashlie Gudmundsen, not April Conyers.
match_headline: Amazon Not as Unstoppable as It Might Appear

text: An article on Wednesday about the appointment of a new chief executive for the retailer American Apparel after the earlier ousting of its founder and chief misstated part of the name of the firm that Craig Johnson, who commented on American Apparel’s comeback chances, serves as president. It is Customer Growth Partners, not Consumer Growth Partners.
match_headline: American Apparel Ends Role of Dov Charney and Hires a New Chief

text: A picture caption in the Listings pages on Friday about American Ballet Theater’s production of “The Nutcracker,” at the Brooklyn Academy of Music, misstated the starting time of one of the performances today. There are performances at 2 and 7 p.m., not at 2 and 4:30 p.m.
match_headline: Dance Listings for Dec. 19-25

text: An article last Sunday about the fallout faced by the lawyer Sanford Rubenstein after he was accused of rape erroneously included a woman on his list of clients, using information from his spokeswoman. The woman, Alberta Spruill, and her family were represented by Derek Sells, not by Mr. Rubenstein.
match_headline: A Rape Claim Has Put Sandy Rubenstein on the Edge of Disgrace

text: An article last Sunday about coaching changes among the top female tennis players misspelled the surname of Simona Halep’s former coach. He is Wim Fissette, not Fisette.
match_headline: Former Champions, Both Men and Women, Fill the Coaching Ranks

text: An article last Sunday about Joel Simkhai, the founder of the app Grindr, misstated the name of an Apple device that helped popularize the app. It is the iPod Touch, not the iTouch.
match_headline: The Sex Education of Grindr’s Joel Simkhai

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the decline in memorable dialogue from contemporary movies misidentified the movie whose line “Go ahead, make my day” Ronald Reagan used in a speech. As the article correctly noted, it is “Sudden Impact,” not “Dirty Harry.”
match_headline: The Rapid Decline of the Movie Quotation

text: A review on Nov. 23 about “Penelope Fitzgerald: A Life,” by Hermione Lee, misstated the publishing history of Lee’s earlier biographies of Virginia Woolf, Willa Cather and Edith Wharton. When Lee wrote those biographies, she was younger than Penelope Fitzgerald was when Fitzgerald began publishing her own books; they were not written before Fitzgerald began to publish.
match_headline: ‘Penelope Fitzgerald: A Life,’ by Hermione Lee

text: A report in the Open Book feature on Dec. 7 erroneously included Bret Anthony Johnston on a list of authors whose “debut books” were recognized among the Book Review’s 100 Notable Books of 2014. While Johnston’s Notable Book, “Remember Me Like This,” is indeed his debut novel, it is not his first book; he had previously published a collection of stories.
match_headline: Bumper Crop

text: An article on Nov. 30 about the military’s prosecution of sexual-assault cases referred incompletely to the civilian authorities’ handling of a case against Lt. Col. Jefrey Krusinski. While they did not go forward with a charge of sexual battery against Krusinski, they did charge him with assault and battery, for which a jury found him not guilty; it is not the case that they pursued no charges.
match_headline: The Military’s Rough Justice on Sexual Assault

text: An article on Dec. 7 about the discovery of the element francium described incorrectly an incident involving Marie Curie and her assistant Elizabeth Rona. Curie was burning a gaseous byproduct of radium, not radon, which is a noble gas and therefore chemically stable. And the article misstated the beta-minus decay process. In beta-minus decay, a neutron is transformed into a proton, not the opposite.
match_headline: My Great-Great-Aunt Discovered Francium. And It Killed Her.
