text: An article last Sunday about the engineer credited with developing the modern V6 engine, Francesco De Virgilio, misstated the order in which the engine’s cylinders fire. It is 1-4-3-6-5-2 — not 1-2-3-4-5-6.
match_headline: Working in Postwar Italy, He Was the da Vinci of the V6

text: An article on Tuesday about a study analyzing Ebola case counts in West Africa misstated the rate of underreporting of cases of the disease. It was 17 percent, up to a maximum of 70 percent, not 70 percent. And the article, using information from the study’s lead author, misstated the practical implications of the previous estimate to which the new rate was compared. It meant that for every 100 known cases, there would have been 250 real cases, not 350 real cases.
match_headline: Fewer Ebola Cases Go Unreported Than Thought, Study Finds

text: A chart last Monday with an article about the possible merging of more parishes within the Archdiocese of New York misspelled the name of a church in the Bronx. It is St. Frances of Rome, not St. Francis. The chart also omitted the full name of a Westchester County town where the church of St. Matthew is located. It is Hastings-on-Hudson, not Hasting. And the article misspelled the name of a town in Ulster County where the church of St. Francis de Sales is located. It is Phoenicia, not Phonicia.
match_headline: New York Archdiocese Appears Likely to Shutter More Churches

text: An article on Tuesday about the future of a marina lease in Battery Park City misidentified the location of a luxury boat basin operated by Island Global Yachting, a company affiliated with one of the bidders. The Newport Yacht Club & Marina is in Jersey City — not in Newport, R.I.
match_headline: Battery Park City’s Populist Sailing School May Lose Lease

text: An article last Monday about an arrest in the attack on two police lieutenants by protesters over the weekend gave an outdated name for the hospital where the officers were treated. It is NewYork-Presbyterian/Lower Manhattan Hospital, no longer New York Downtown Hospital. (The name was changed in 2013.)
match_headline: Amid Assaults on Officers, New York Police Rethink Their Response to Protests

text: Because of an editing error, the TV Sports column on Tuesday, about the bidding for the Premier League television contract, referred incorrectly to the Premier League team of which ESPN President John Skipper is a fan. It is Tottenham Hotspur, not Hotspurs. (Spurs is the team’s nickname.)
match_headline: In Seeking TV Bids, Premier League Controls the Ball

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about next year’s Jacob’s Pillow Festival in Becket, Mass., misspelled the surname of a choreographer whose company will perform there. She is Liz Gerring, not Gering.
match_headline: Premieres, a New Ensemble and More at Jacob’s Pillow

text: An obituary on March 13 about the model, modeling agent and charm-school director Ophelia DeVore-Mitchell misstated the year she was born, and her age. She was born on Aug. 12 in 1921, not in 1922; therefore she was 92 when she died, not 91. Her family notified The Times of the error this month.
match_headline: Ophelia DeVore-Mitchell, 92, Dies; Redefined Beauty

text: An article on Monday about the failure of Indian, British and American intelligence agencies to prevent an attack by the Pakistani terrorist group Lashkar-e-Taiba in Mumbai in 2008 misidentified a position once held by Shivshankar Menon, a retired Indian official who commented on the intelligence blunder. He was India’s foreign secretary at the time, not its foreign minister.
match_headline: In 2008 Mumbai Attacks, Piles of Spy Data, but an Uncompleted Puzzle

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 4 about a more robust military presence by Iran on foreign battlefields misidentified, in some editions, the country that is not directly coordinating with the United States in its military operations against extremist fighters in Iraq. It is Iran, not Iraq.
match_headline: U.S. and Iran Both Attack ISIS, but Try Not to Look Like Allies

text: An article on Saturday about the punitive approach to juvenile crime taken by Herman C. Dawson, the main juvenile court judge in Prince George’s County, Md., misstated the name of the court that reviewed Judge Dawson’s commitment orders. It was the Court of Special Appeals, not the Special Court Appeals.
match_headline: Judge in Maryland Locks Up Youths and Rules Their Lives

text: An article on Nov. 30 about the angry reaction to a memoir by Suki Kim, a Korean-American who taught English in North Korea, misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the university where she taught. It is the Pyongyang University of Science and Technology, not the Pyongyang Institute of Science and Technology.
match_headline: Tales Told Out of School in Pyongyang Cause Stir

text: An article on Friday about regulators’ deeming MetLife a “systemically important financial institution,” a designation that subjects it to stricter oversight, used an outdated name for the operations of another insurer, American International Group. Although A.I.G. had used the name Chartis for its property and casualty insurance business at one point, it has reverted to using the A.I.G. name.
match_headline: Regulators Deem MetLife a ‘Too Big to Fail’ Institution

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Weekend Miser column on Friday about a holiday carol event in Washington Square Park scheduled for Wednesday omitted the starting time. It is 5 p.m.
match_headline: Singing, Dancing and Other Seasonal Merriment

text: A map on Saturday with the continuation of an article about Cárdenas, Cuba, long a center of revolutionary fervor, located the city incorrectly. It is about 75 miles east of Havana, not part of it.
match_headline: Crucible of Cuban Zeal Redefines Revolutionary

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a recommendation by a New York State board that three resort casinos be approved misstated, in some editions, the relationship between the Genting Group, a Malaysian conglomerate, and Empire Resorts, which has proposed to build a resort near Monticello, N.Y. The family of Genting’s chairman holds a controlling stake in Empire Resorts; Genting itself does not own Empire Resorts.
match_headline: Board Backs Casinos in the Catskills, Near Albany and in Central New York

text: An article on Saturday about a five-player trade made by the Yankees and the Miami Marlins misidentified the team that acquired pitcher Shane Greene from the Yankees in an earlier trade. As part of a three-team deal that allowed the Yankees to acquire shortstop Didi Gregorius from the Arizona Diamondbacks, Greene went to the Detroit Tigers — not to the Diamondbacks.
match_headline: Yankees Acquire Marlins’ Nathan Eovaldi for Martin Prado in 5-Player Deal

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Sunday about the Knicks’ 99-90 loss to the Phoenix Suns misstated the Knicks’ record after the game. They were 5-24, not 5-25. (They are now 5-25.)
match_headline: Knicks’ Latest Major Loss: Faith in Themselves

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about Gabriel Medina’s becoming the first Brazilian to win the Association of Surfing Professionals World Championship Tour title misstated, in some copies, the round where he learned of his title. It was when he entered the water for his quarterfinal run, not for his Round 5 heat. In addition, a reporting credit misidentified, in some copies, a contributor. He is Nick Corasaniti, not Nicholas Confessore.
match_headline: At 20, Gabriel Medina Becomes First Brazilian to Win Surfing Title

text: A listing of credits on Dec. 13 with a theater review of “Howie the Rookie,” which was presented at the Brooklyn Academy of Music, misspelled the producer’s surname. She is Anne Clarke, not Clark.
match_headline: Harsh Tongues, Marinated in Whiskey

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Wednesday about “One-Way Ticket: Jacob Lawrence’s Migration Series and Other Visions of the Great Movement North,” an exhibition planned for next year at the Museum of Modern Art, misstated the year when the Migration Series was last shown at the museum. It was 1995, not 1994.
ref_headline: One-Way Ticket: Jacob Lawrence’s Migration Series and Other Visions of the Great Movement North,
match_headline: Reassembling a History Told in Paint

text: An article on Tuesday about the role of nuclear power in fighting climate change described the status of Japan’s nuclear reactors incompletely. While two of the country’s 50 reactors were recently restarted, they were shut again soon after. (No reactors are currently online.)
match_headline: Nuclear: Carbon Free, but Not Free of Unease

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an obituary about the singer Joe Cocker overstated what was known about the performance shown. The photograph was of Mr. Cocker singing at an unspecified location around 1970, not at the Woodstock music festival in 1969.
match_headline: Joe Cocker Is Dead at 70; Raspy-Voiced Rock Star With Distinctive Moves

text: An article on Dec. 10 about the new popularity of schmaltz among restaurant chefs and home cooks omitted part of the title of a 2013 cookbook by Michael Ruhlman. It is “The Book of Schmaltz,” not merely “Schmaltz.”
match_headline: Schmaltz Finds a New, Younger Audience

text: An article on Wednesday about conserving and restoring forests as a strategy to fight climate change referred incorrectly in some editions to the relative size of the Amazon forest. The Amazon is about two-thirds the size of the lower 48 American states; it does not cover more land than the lower 48 states.
match_headline: Restored Forests Breathe Life Into Efforts Against Climate Change

text: An article on Monday about a Swedish-American automobile executive, Bo Inge Andersson, who was recruited by the Russian government to revive its Lada car brand, misidentified another Russian auto manufacturer that Mr. Andersson was recruited to run in 2009. It is the GAZ Group — not Avtogaz, which is a subsidiary.
match_headline: Trying to Save Russia’s Punch Line of a Car

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an article about the rift between Mayor Bill de Blasio and the New York Police Department’s rank and file officers gave an outdated title for James O’Neill. He is the chief of department, no longer the chief of patrol. (He was promoted in November.)
match_headline: For Mayor de Blasio and New York Police, a Rift Is Ripped Open

text: An article on Saturday about Voice Charter School in Queens, which focuses on music, misstated part of the title of a Gershwin song that students recently performed. It is “I Got Rhythm,” not “I’ve Got Rhythm.”
match_headline: School Finds Music Is the Food of Learning

text: An article on Saturday about videos taken by members of the public that helped the police find suspects in a confrontation on the Brooklyn Bridge misstated, in some editions, the day a man tried to throw garbage cans at police officers, setting off a melee. It was Saturday, Dec. 13 — not Sunday, Dec. 14.
match_headline: In New York, Public’s Video Helps Police, for a Change

text: An article on Tuesday about the possibility that a computer breach at JPMorgan Chase this summer could have been thwarted if the bank had made a simple security fix to an overlooked server misidentified one type of information that hackers gained access to in the attack. Besides home addresses and telephone numbers, customers’ email addresses — not passwords — were exposed, the bank said.
match_headline: Daily Report: Simple Flaw Allowed JPMorgan Computer Breach

text: Because of editing error, an article on Monday about efforts by shipping companies to meet demand of last-minute holiday shopping referred incorrectly to plans by the online retailer Amazon to use Kiva robots in its warehouses to prepare goods for delivery. The company began a big push this summer to use the robots; it will not unveil the effort next summer.
match_headline: Crunch Time for FedEx and UPS as Last-Minute Holiday Shipping Ramps Up

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the actress Billie Whitelaw omitted a word from a quotation that Ms. Whitelaw attributed to Samuel Beckett. She said that Beckett, in expressing his need to remove the acting from a performance, told her, “Flat, no emotion, no color” — not “Flat, emotion, no color.”
match_headline: Billie Whitelaw, Longtime Beckett Muse, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the Austrian singer and songwriter Udo Jürgens misstated the name of the Nazi organization for boys too young for the Hitler Youth, which Mr. Jürgens quit after being hit by a leader. It was the Jungvolk, not the Jugendvolk.
match_headline: Udo Jürgens, Austrian Singer and Songwriter, Dies at 80

text: An article on Dec. 11 about the North Mississippi Avenue neighborhood in Portland, Ore., omitted one of the founders of Land Gallery and misidentified another. Pat Castaldo co-founded the gallery with Aaron Tuller — not with Amber Castaldo, who is the gallery’s manager. The article also misstated the year in which Land was founded. It was 2009, not 2008.
match_headline: Four Square Blocks: Portland

text: A report in the Currents column last Thursday about an auction of items at the Caribou Ranch recording studio misidentified an instrument that was for sale. It is a Gibson Thunderbird bass, not a Gibson Firebird guitar.
match_headline: Where Elton Sang and Rode

text: A picture caption with the Q&A column last Thursday, about Marcia Hinds, the production designer for the film “Annie,” referred incorrectly to a set in the movie. It is the office of the character Will Stacks, not his penthouse apartment.
match_headline: She Really Likes It Here

text: An article on Wednesday about Henning Wehn, a German comedian who lives in Britain and is an avid soccer fan, misidentified the match in which a German team beat England in the 1990 World Cup, and referred imprecisely to that team. It was a semifinal, not the final, and the team was West Germany, not Germany.
match_headline: A German Comedian in London: Working Out the War in Punch Lines

text: A picture caption in the Listings pages on Friday about Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater misstated the time of the company’s evening performance scheduled for Wednesday at City Center in Manhattan. It is 7 p.m., not 7:30.
match_headline: Dance Listings for Dec. 26-Jan. 1

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about concerts and other performances on New Year’s Eve, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the member of Holy Ghost! shown. He is Alex Frankel — not Nick Millhiser, the other member of the duo, which will perform at Irving Plaza in Manhattan. And because of an editing error, the caption referred incorrectly to the duo. They are from New York, not from Britain.
match_headline: For the Biggest Night Out, a Lineup to Match

text: An article on Friday about what to watch on television on New Year’s Eve misstated the year the sitcom “Mister Ed” — a DVD set of the complete series was released this year — first aired. It was 1961, not 1958.
match_headline: Ringing Out the Old With a TV Binge

text: Because of a transcription error, an interview with the comedian Jim Norton on Page 36 of the special “Lives They Lived” issue this weekend quotes incorrectly from his comments about Joan Rivers. In discussing a Rivers comedy routine, he said in part, “It was AIDS jokes” — not “age” jokes.
match_headline: The Lives They Lived

text: An earlier version of an Arts correction rendered part of the name of a sitcom incorrectly. It is “Mister Ed” — not “Mr.” Ed.

An article last Sunday about a Metropolitan Transportation Authority campaign that encourages male subway passengers to sit with their legs closer together to increase seating space referred incorrectly in some editions to an employee of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, which is also asking passengers to conserve space on public transportation. Kristin Geiger is the agency’s spokeswoman, not spokesman.
match_headline: A Scourge Is Spreading. M.T.A.’s Cure? Dude, Close Your Legs.

text: An article last Sunday about President Obama’s family vacation to the oceanfront enclave of Kailua, Hawaii, referred incorrectly to a terrorist threat he had to deal with on Christmas Day in 2009 while in Hawaii. It was the case of the so-called underwear bomber, Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, who tried to blow up a Detroit-bound airliner; it was not the shoe bomber, Richard C. Reid, who tried to blow up a trans-Atlantic airliner with explosives hidden in his shoes, in December 2001, during the presidency of George W. Bush.
match_headline: Obama Sounds Triumphal Note at Start of Hawaii Vacation

text: An article last Sunday about final passage of a proposal to overhaul redistricting for Ohio’s General Assembly misidentified the source of applause after the measure passed in the State House on Dec. 17. Supporters of redistricting seated in the gallery applauded, not House members.
match_headline: In a Break From Partisan Rancor, Ohio Moves to Make Elections More Competitive

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the winter sports roundup last Sunday misidentified, in some editions, the location of the men’s World Cup Super-G race that was won by Kjetil Jansrud of Norway. It is Val Gardena, Italy, not Val d’Isère, France.
match_headline: FIFA Agrees to Release Redacted Ethics Report

text: An article in some editions on Dec. 14 about cultural celebrations in the Hudson Valley omitted a sponsor of three celebrations there for Three Kings Day. Besides Arts Mid-Hudson, the Hudson River HealthCare organization helped produce the events.
match_headline: Uncovering Hudson Valley Artists

text: A review last Sunday about the 2015 Ford Mustang GT misstated the speed rating of the Pirelli tires that come with the optional Performance Package. They are rated Y, not H.
match_headline: The Pony Express Blazes Another Trail

text: An article last Sunday about the actor David Oyelowo, who stars as the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. in the new film “Selma,” misidentified the profession of the character Mr. Oyelowo played in the recent movie “Interstellar.” He played a school principal, not an astronaut.
match_headline: The Man Who Would Be King

text: An article Dec. 14 about a 10-day road trip on what’s called the “Powder Highway” in an area of southeast British Columbia with fine backcountry skiing misidentified the ski-touring lodge in the Valhalla Range outside the town of New Denver where the writer stayed. It is Valhalla Mountain Touring — not Valhalla Mountain Lodge, which is to the south of it.
match_headline: British Columbia’s Powder Highway

text: An article last Sunday about a 21-mile stretch of road in Thailand where gongs are made and sold misstated the surname of the founder of the tour company Isan Explorer. He is Tim Bewer, not Brewer.
match_headline: Thailand’s ‘Gong Highway’

text: An article on Dec. 7 about Taiwan’s environmental movement referred incorrectly to the status of shark fin soup there. While the government has banned shark finning, along with whale shark fin soup, it has not banned shark fin soup.
match_headline: Taiwan, an Island of Green in Asia

text: A review on Dec. 7 about “Even This I Get to Experience,” a memoir by the television writer and producer Norman Lear, reversed two words in the title of the British comedy from which one of Lear’s shows, “All in the Family,” was adapted. It is “Till Death Us Do Part” (not “Do Us”).
ref_headline: Even This I Get to Experience,
match_headline: Norman Lear’s ‘Even This I Get to Experience’

text: A review on Dec. 7 about “Time Out of Mind: The Lives of Bob Dylan,” by Ian Bell, misstated the age of the reviewer, Geoff Dyer. He is 56, not 57.
ref_headline: Time Out of Mind: The Lives of Bob Dylan,
match_headline: ‘Time Out of Mind: The Lives of Bob Dylan,’ by Ian Bell

text: An article on Tuesday about Southwestern Energy’s decision to continue to invest in natural gas despite the recent plunge in prices misstated the day the company closed its purchase of shale gas fields from Chesapeake Energy and saw its stock price drop more than 5 percent. Both occurred on Monday, not on Tuesday. (The stock was down another 1.3 percent on Tuesday.)
match_headline: Natural Gas Glut Isn’t Deterring Southwestern Energy

text: An article on Thursday about Sony Pictures’ release of “The Interview” online following terror threats misstated the nature of efforts by the Motion Picture Association of America to push for new antipiracy measures. The industry group is currently seeking to enforce existing laws to thwart piracy, rather than pushing for passage of a bill on the issue.
match_headline: Sony Streams ‘The Interview’ on YouTube, Google Play and Xbox

text: An article on Dec. 9 about divisions in Israel and among Jews abroad over proposed legislation that would formally identify the country as the nation-state of the Jewish people misspelled the surname of an Arab Israeli fiction writer who said he was detained for two hours at an airport this year while traveling with Israeli authors to Germany. He is Ayman Sikseck, not Siseck. The article also misstated the size of the Arab city of Nazareth relative to a neighboring town, predominantly Jewish Upper Nazareth. Nazareth has nearly twice the population but less than half the land of Upper Nazareth, not twice the population and 5 percent of the land.
match_headline: Israel Struggles With Its Identity

text: An article in some editions on Dec. 22 about Nicole Paige, a woman who received assistance for child care from the Community Service Society, one of the agencies supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, misstated part of the name of a city agency from which she had been receiving assistance in the form of vouchers. It is the Human Resources Administration, not the Housing Resources Administration.
match_headline: Inspired by Her Twins, a Mother Moves From a Shuffle to a Stride

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the soccer roundup on Dec. 22 misstated the reason Liverpool rose one place in the standings. As correctly noted in the headline and elsewhere in the report, Liverpool earned 1 point in a draw against Arsenal; it did not win.

Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Saturday with an article about victories by Chelsea and Manchester City in the Premier League misidentified the team that played in the snow at West Bromwich. It was Manchester City, not Chelsea.

An article on Dec. 14 about Fencing in the Schools, the Olympian Tim Morehouse’s educational nonprofit group, referred incorrectly to the Newark school where he conducted an assembly for third and fourth graders. It is North Star Academy’s elementary school on its Vailsburg campus; it is not Vailsburg Elementary School. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Education With a Dose of Zorro

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about the design of two new open-air clinics in Haiti, including one for cholera patients, referred imprecisely to the Nepalis with whom the outbreak of a cholera epidemic in 2010 was associated. While they were associated with the United Nations, it was as peacekeeping troops, not as aid workers.
match_headline: In Haiti, Battling Disease With Open-Air Clinics

text: An article on Saturday about the wake for Police Officer Rafael Ramos referred incorrectly in some copies to Mayor Bill de Blasio. He arrived at the wake toward the end; it is not the case that he did not attend.
match_headline: Mourners From All Corners of New York City Pay Tribute to a Slain Officer

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about Representative Michael G. Grimm’s decision to resign from Congress misspelled the name of a restaurant that Mr. Grimm owned. It was Healthalicious, not Healthilicious.
match_headline: Michael Grimm, in a Reversal, Will Resign From Congress

text: An article on Dec. 20 about efforts to screen thousands of shipments of toys and other imports rendered part of the name of a federal agency incorrectly. It is the Drug Enforcement Administration, not the Drug Enforcement Agency.
match_headline: At U.S. Ports, Even Santa’s Bag Might Be Peeked Into

text: An article on Dec. 19 about the Boston Celtics’ trading guard Rajon Rondo to the Dallas Mavericks misspelled, in some copies, the given name of a Dallas player who was sent to Boston in the deal. He is Brandan Wright, not Brandon.
match_headline: Celtics Trade Rajon Rondo to Mavericks for Three Players and Two Draft Picks

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an article about sporting events in 2015 misidentified the track shown at Keeneland Race Course in Lexington, Ky. It is Keeneland’s turf track, not the synthetic track that has been replaced with dirt to attract the Breeders’ Cup World Championships.
match_headline: Traffickers Set Freighter on a Course for Italy and Flee, Leaving Migrants Aboard

text: An article on Monday about the Carolina Panthers’ playoff-clinching 34-3 victory over the Atlanta Falcons misstated, in some editions, the number of points that the Panthers’ defense yielded in their last four games. It is 43, not 20.
match_headline: Under .500 and Overjoyed, Panthers Head to Playoffs

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about attendance and box-office grosses for Broadway shows last week misidentified the category in which the musical “The Last Ship” experienced a decrease from the previous week. It was in attendance — not box-office revenue, where it saw an increase of 10.8 percent. The report also misstated the size of the drop in the box-office take for the play “A Delicate Balance.” It was 9.3 percent — not 1.3 percent, which was its decline in attendance.
match_headline: A Feast and a Lions’ Den, Conveyed in Multiple Ways

text: An article on Friday about Dan Hill, a facial coding expert who reads the faces of athletes to determine if they have the right emotional attributes, referred incorrectly to his work at the N.F.L.'s scouting combine. While Hill did evaluate top prospects at the combine, Jeff Foster, who runs the event, did not hire him to do so.
match_headline: Teams Turn to a Face Reader, Looking for That Winning Smile

text: An article on Wednesday about the jailing of the brother of the prominent Russian dissident Aleksei A. Navalny, in what was seen as an effort by the Kremlin to silence Mr. Navalny, gave an outdated affiliation for Lilia Shevtsova, an expert on Russian politics. She is now with the Brookings Institution, no longer the Carnegie Moscow Center.
match_headline: Aleksei Navalny, Putin Critic, Is Spared Prison in a Fraud Case, but His Brother Is Jailed

text: An article on Saturday about Chinese companies that adopt variations of international brand names described incorrectly the font of the logo of Chrisdien Deny, a Chinese apparel chain. It is similar to that of Christian Dior, but it is not the same.
match_headline: Adidos and Hotwind? In China, Brands Adopt Names to Project Foreign Flair

text: An article on Dec. 19 about the effect a hacking of Sony Pictures Entertainment had on internal relationships at the company misstated part of the title of a forthcoming animated film from Seth Rogen, whose “The Interview” film was central to the hacking. It is “Sausage Party,” not “Sausage Factory.”
match_headline: Sony Hacking Fallout Includes Unraveling of Relationships in Hollywood

text: An article on Wednesday about so-called food hubs that seek to connect local farmers with customers misstated the year that an online marketplace called FarmersWeb was founded. It started in 2012, not in 2013.
match_headline: Start-Ups Rise to Close a Gap for Farmers

text: An article on Wednesday about the refurbishing of the Loews Kings Theater on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn, using information from the developers, misstated the theater’s expected ranking among New York’s theaters in size. It will be the fourth-largest, behind Radio City Music Hall, the Theater at Madison Square Garden and the Metropolitan Opera House. It will not be the third-largest.
match_headline: Kings Theater in Flatbush Set to Reopen, and Lift a Neighborhood

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about the year in jazz referred imprecisely to a work by Jorge Luis Borges reprinted in the liner notes for the album “Blue,” by the group Mostly Other People Do the Killing. While written in the form of an essay, it is a work of fiction, not an essay.
match_headline: An All-Year Season of Discontent in Jazz

text: An obituary on Friday about former Gov. Mario M. Cuomo of New York erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He was the second — not first — Italian-American to be elected governor of New York. (Al Smith, who was part Italian-American, was the first.) The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Cuomo’s tenure. His years in office were exceeded in length by George Clinton’s as well as by Nelson A. Rockefeller’s, not just by Mr. Rockefeller’s. And the obituary misstated the year in which two airplanes waited to fly Mr. Cuomo to New Hampshire so that he might place his name on the state’s Democratic primary ballot for president, though he never did. It was December 1991, not 1992.
match_headline: Mario Cuomo, Ex-New York Governor and Liberal Beacon, Dies at 82

text: An article on Dec. 26 about Gov. Jerry Brown’s efforts to reshape the California Supreme Court misattributed quotations about his three judicial nominations. It was Gerald F. Uelmen, a professor at the Santa Clara University School of Law — not David S. Ettinger, a lawyer who writes about the California Supreme Court — who said Mr. Brown’s nomination of Leondra R. Kruger “was kind of a mindblower.” And it was also Mr. Uelmen, not Mr. Ettinger, who said the appointments left the court “well poised to really make a mark. And I think that is what Governor Brown is looking for: leaving a legacy that will restore the luster of the Supreme Court he knew when he clerked for the court.”
match_headline: Jerry Brown, Governor of California, Takes Second Chance to Shape Court

text: Because of an editing error, a chart on Thursday about the television series “Downton Abbey” and The New York Times’s coverage of historical events mentioned on the show misstated the date the Titanic sank. It was April 15, 1912 — not April 16.

A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about criticism of the film “Selma” by Joseph A. Califano Jr. misidentified Mr. Califano’s role in the administration of President Lyndon B. Johnson. After serving in the Defense Department he was appointed special assistant to Johnson; he was not a member of Johnson’s cabinet. (He did serve in President Jimmy Carter’s cabinet as Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare.) The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Depiction of Lyndon B. Johnson in ‘Selma’ Raises Hackles

text: An article on Thursday about a new Los Angeles rock club, the Teragram Ballroom, that is to open in March and is the first West Coast venture by Michael Swier, one of the New York’s most influential club proprietors, misstated the surname of one of his partners in the new venue. He is Joe Baxley, not Baxby.
match_headline: A Bowery Titan Puts Down L.A. Roots

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about efforts by the Marshall Islands to get the International Court of Justice to order the world’s nuclear powers to begin talks on banning nuclear arsenals misidentified, in some editions, the nuclear test shown in the photograph. It was one of the Marshall Islands tests that were part of Operations Crossroads in 1946, not the one known as “Castle Bravo” in 1954.
match_headline: A Former Ground Zero Goes to Court Against the World’s Nuclear Arsenals

text: An article last Sunday about the funeral of Police Officer Rafael Ramos misstated, in some copies, the number of years that the New York Police Department commissioner, William J. Bratton, said he had been attending police funerals. It is 44 years, not 54.
match_headline: A Sea of Blue, Mourning the First of Two Slain Comrades

text: An article last Sunday about a drop in Gov. Chris Christie’s popularity in New Jersey as he considers a run for president misidentified, in some copies, the type of fuel that the proposed Keystone XL pipeline, which Mr. Christie endorsed, is intended to carry. It is oil, not natural gas.
match_headline: Christie Roams, and Popularity Suffers at Home

text: An article last Sunday previewing the Week 17 N.F.L. games misidentified the team the Pittsburgh Steelers defeated, 20-12, in Week 16. It was Kansas City, not San Diego.
match_headline: Week 17 N.F.L. Matchups

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Hannah Kroll and Hal Belok misidentified the degree that the groom is pursuing. It is a doctorate of dental surgery, not a doctorate of dental science.
match_headline: Hannah Kroll and Hal Belok

text: An article on Dec. 21 about the dish called haggis in Scotland misidentified one of the vegetables that is served with haggis in its traditional form. Haggis is usually served with neeps and tatties, which are turnips and potatoes — not parsnips and potatoes.
match_headline: In Scotland, Guts, Glory and Haggis

text: An article on Dec. 21 about toy guns and police shootings referred incorrectly to Tamir Rice’s location when he was shot by an officer in Cleveland. He was outside Cuddell Recreation Center; he did not walk into the center.
match_headline: Off Target on Toy-Gun Regulation

text: An essay on Dec. 14 about kissing in the movies misidentified an actor in a scene from the 1927 film “Wings” that showed two men kissing. The actors were Buddy Rogers and Richard Arlen; Gary Cooper was in the film, but he was not part of that scene.
match_headline: A Brief History of Kissing in Movies

text: An article last Sunday about the director Susan Stroman’s new version of the Lehar operetta “The Merry Widow,” in a fresh English translation by Jeremy Sams, misidentified the composer of the operetta “Die Fledermaus,” which Mr. Sams translated and directed in 2013. He was Johann Strauss II, not Offenbach.
match_headline: Susan Stroman Brings a Broadway Heart to the Met for ‘The Merry Widow’

text: A caption last Sunday with a photo of the sky as seen from the Southern Hemisphere incorrectly referred to a galaxy. While the photo showed the Southern Cross, Milky Way and Carina Nebula, it did not show the Large Magellanic Cloud. (Part of the cloud was in the original image, but it was cropped out of the photo in The Times.)
match_headline: The Dazzle of the Southern Sky

text: An article on Wednesday about tactics used by President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to win Bulgarian approval for a natural gas pipeline under the Black Sea misidentified the professional Bulgarian soccer team that Gazprom, Russia’s state-owned energy giant, agreed to sponsor to sweeten the deal. The team is Levski Sofia, not CSKA Sofia. (While the Bulgarian prime minister originally said Gazprom would sponsor CSKA Sofia, the company later changed its mind.)
match_headline: How Putin Forged a Pipeline Deal That Derailed

text: An article on Thursday about the defeat of Russia’s “white ribbon” opposition, which had tried since 2011 to oust President Vladimir V. Putin from office, misstated the day Aleksei A. Navalny, a prominent critic of Mr. Putin, was convicted of fraud as well as when demonstrators gathered to protest the verdict. The verdict was on Tuesday and the demonstration was that night; those events did not occur last Monday.
match_headline: Anti-Putin Protest Fizzles as Police Sweep Square

text: An article on Dec. 20 about California’s move to allow undocumented immigrants to apply for a driver’s license misstated one application requirement. While automobile insurance is required to register a vehicle in California, insurance is not needed for a driver’s license.
match_headline: Talk of ‘El D.M.V.’ as Licensing Expands to Cover Undocumented Immigrants in California

text: A report in the National Briefing column on Thursday about a search to hire a chief of laboratory safety at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention described the agency’s previous assignment of safety responsibilities incorrectly. While each of the agency’s divisions handled safety separately in the past, there was no single lab safety specialist at each division.
match_headline: New C.D.C. Job Overseeing Laboratory Safety

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the Washington Capitals’ 3-2 victory over the Chicago Blackhawks in the N.H.L.'s Winter Classic misstated, in some copies, the given name of the Capitals player who scored the winning goal. He is Troy Brouwer, not Roy.
match_headline: Battling Sun’s Glare at Ballpark, the Capitals Deliver a Final Bit of Brilliance

text: An obituary on Thursday about the actor Edward Herrmann misspelled his surname, in several instances, as Hermann. The obituary also misspelled, in some editions, part of the name of a television show on which he had a recurring role. It is “Grey’s Anatomy,” not “Gray’s Anatomy.”
match_headline: Edward Herrmann, Actor With a Noble Air, Dies at 71

text: An article on Monday about Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the No. 3 Republican in the House who has been facing criticism for addressing a group of white supremacists a dozen years ago, misidentified a leadership position Tom DeLay held in Congress. He was the House majority leader, not the House speaker.
match_headline: Allies Say Willingness to Talk to Anyone, Nearly His Undoing, Defines Scalise

text: A listing in the Transactions column on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about a recent lease for a ground floor retail space in NoLIta, using information from the building’s broker, misstated the price per square foot for the space. It is $108 per square feet, not $14.40.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Transactions

text: An article on Saturday about the new Murty Classical Library of India, published by Harvard University Press, misspelled the name of an anthology included in the initial texts being issued in some editions. The anthology, of verses by and about the earliest ordained Buddhist women, is the Therigatha, not Therighata.
match_headline: Literature of India, Enshrined in a Series

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about Annie Proulx’s regrets about writing the story “Brokeback Mountain,” which cited an interview in the Paris Review, failed to note that the interview was published in 2009. The report also misstated the year the story was published. It was 1997, not 1999.
match_headline: Proulx Says She Regrets ‘Brokeback Mountain’

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with a dance review of “George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker,” by New York City Ballet at the David H. Koch Theater, referred incorrectly to Andrew Scordato’s performance as Mother Ginger. He has played the role before; it was not his role debut.
match_headline: In the Sweet Shop, Happily Sampling New Concoctions

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about the second season of the Scandinavian police drama “The Bridge,” online at Hulu, misstated the number of people found chained in the hold of a ship in the first episode of the season. It is five, not four.
match_headline: After a Remake for American Viewers, Back to Understatement

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about Ben Ammi Ben-Israel, who led a migration of fellow black Americans to what they consider their ancestral homeland, Israel, misstated the date of his death. It was Saturday, Dec. 27, — not Saturday, Jan. 3.
match_headline: Ben Ammi Ben-Israel Dies at 75: Led Black Americans in Migration to Israel

text: An obituary on Saturday about the country singer Little Jimmy Dickens quoted incorrectly from his song “Country Boy.” The lyrics are: “I’m a plain ol’ country boy/A cornbread-lovin’ country boy/I’ll be lookin’ over that ol’ gray mule/When the sun comes up on Monday” — not “I’m a country boy/A good old-fashioned country boy/I’ll be behind the ol’ gray mule/When the sun comes up on Monday.”
match_headline: Jimmy Dickens, an Outsize Country Singer, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Saturday about the poet Miller Williams misidentified the singer who once told him over drinks that he had a “beer-drinking soul.” He was Hank Williams Sr., not Hank Williams Jr.
match_headline: Miller Williams, Plain-Spoken Arkansas Poet, Dies at 84

text: An article on Dec. 28 about the conflict in Syria evolving into a bloody standoff dominated by the government of President Bashar al-Assad and extremist groups, something that has left many opponents of Mr. Assad feeling disillusioned, misstated the length of the civil war. It will have its fourth anniversary this year and begin its fifth year; it is not headed toward its fourth year.
match_headline: As Syria’s Revolution Sputters, a Chaotic Stalemate

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Dec. 21 with an article about the oil, gas and coal boom in the Xinjiang region of China, where ethnic Uighurs have long been at odds with the nation’s Han majority, referred incorrectly to the Uighurs who live in Karamay, a city at the center of the region’s oil exploration and production. They are a minority there, not a plurality. (Uighurs do constitute a plurality of residents in the Xinjiang region, which includes Karamay.)
match_headline: China Invests in Region Rich in Oil, Coal and Also Strife

text: A headline in some editions on Dec. 21 with an article about the removal of nuclear fuel from the most vulnerable part of the ruined Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant in Japan, where a triple meltdown occurred in 2011, referred imprecisely to the location of the fuel rods that were removed. As the article correctly noted, they were removed from a reactor building, not from a reactor.
match_headline: Fuel Rods Are Removed From Damaged Fukushima Reactor Building

text: Because of an editing error, the Paris Journal article on Dec. 23, about subtle and not-so-subtle shifts in the Christmas displays in Parisian department store windows, referred incorrectly to the holiday window display tradition said to have been pioneered by Macy’s in New York. When Macy’s began its Christmas displays in the 1870s, the department store was located at 14th Street and Sixth Avenue in Manhattan — not in Herald Square, where it moved in 1902.
match_headline: A Window Onto Evolving Traditions in Paris

text: Because of an editing error, a caption for a courtroom sketch on Tuesday with an article about jury selection in the trial of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev for the 2013 bombing at the Boston Marathon misidentified the defendant. He was shown second from the right, not second from the left. (The people at the left were part of his legal team.)
match_headline: Judge Gives Rules at Start of Boston Marathon Bombing Trial

text: An article on Sunday about Megan J. Smith, President Obama’s top technology adviser, misstated Clay Johnson’s part in Mr. Obama’s 2008 campaign. Mr. Johnson co-founded the company that ran the online campaign; he did not run Mr. Obama’s online campaign himself.
match_headline: Adviser Guides Obama Into the Google Age

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the shooting of two police officers in the Bronx misstated the rank of Kim Y. Royster, a Police Department spokeswoman. She is a deputy chief, not a chief.
match_headline: Two Plainclothes Officers Are Shot in the Bronx

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about two grants awarded by the Merce Cunningham Trust misstated the year the trust was founded. It was 2000, not 1990.
match_headline: Money From Merce Cunningham Trust Goes to Two Arts Groups

text: An obituary on Friday about the basketball player Bob Hall, a longtime star of the Harlem Globetrotters, described the term “reams” incompletely. It refers to all of the Globetrotters’ comedy routines, not just their “ball-handling legerdemain.”
match_headline: Bob Hall, Harlem Globetrotter Who Relished the Showman Role, Dies at 87

text: Because of an editing error, the Restaurants column last Wednesday, about Pete Wells’s 10 favorite new restaurants of 2014, misstated the street address for the Simone, which ranked third. It is 151 East 82nd Street, not 51.
match_headline: The 10 Best New Restaurants of 2014

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Bess Myerson, a former Miss America, television personality and New York City official, misstated the number of years she served as the city’s consumer affairs commissioner. It was four years, not five.
match_headline: Bess Myerson, New Yorker of Beauty, Wit, Service and Scandal, Dies at 90

text: An article on Tuesday about Republican efforts in Congress to pass legislation that would redefine a full-time worker under the Affordable Care Act misstated the timing of an article in National Review that addressed the issue of setting the cutoff at 40 hours versus 30 hours. It was published in early November, not this past weekend.
match_headline: Resistance From Right Slows G.O.P. Press to Redefine Full-Time Worker

text: An article on Tuesday about “The Wizard of Watts,” a forthcoming animated television show, misidentified the series on which the director, Carl Jones, got his start in the entertainment industry. It was “The Boondocks” — not “Hogan Knows Best,” which he did not work on.
match_headline: Racially Ignited, a Magical World Is Uncanny

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Yeovil Town’s soccer match against Manchester United in the third round of the F.A. Cup, referred incorrectly to the teams that are eligible for the tournament. The F.A. Cup is open to all clubs in the English league system, not all British clubs.
match_headline: When Goliath Came to Yeovil

text: An article on Wednesday about a new online campaign sponsored by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation that has enlisted artists to help promote vaccination misspelled the surname of the consultant to the foundation who came up with the idea for the project. She is Christine McNab, not McNabb.
match_headline: Gates Foundation Uses Art to Encourage Vaccination

text: An article on Nov. 7 about problematic donations referred incorrectly to the effect the recession in 2008 had on the real estate business of Earle I. Mack, a donor who agreed to have his name removed from the law school at Drexel University in Philadelphia. Though the real estate industry as a whole was heavily affected, Mr. Mack says it is not the case that the recession “hit his real estate business hard.” This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to the attention of editors.
ref_headline: hit his real estate business hard.
match_headline: When a Donation Steers Off Course

text: An article on Thursday about the assault on the French satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo reversed, in some editions, the ages for Said and Chérif Kouachi, brothers whom the authorities named as suspects in the attack. Said Kouachi is 34, and Chérif is 32. And because of an editing error, the article misidentified the area covered by the terror alert that President François Hollande of France raised to its highest level. It is the Île-de-France region, which includes Paris, not all of France. (On Thursday, Mr. Hollande extended the top-level terror alert to a second region, Picardy, as the manhunt for the Kouachis continued.)
match_headline: Terrorists Strike Charlie Hebdo Newspaper in Paris, Leaving 12 Dead

text: An article on Wednesday about the start of same-sex marriages in Florida referred incorrectly to the filing of a federal lawsuit that led to the end of the state’s ban on such marriages. The initial suit was filed by two lawyers, William Sheppard and Samuel Jacobson, both of Jacksonville, on behalf of same-sex couples; it was not filed by the American Civil Liberties Union of Florida. (The ACLU’s lawsuit was consolidated with the other suit.)
match_headline: Same-Sex Pairs in Florida Say Jubilant ‘I Dos’

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Wednesday with the continuation of an article about the funeral of former Gov. Mario M. Cuomo misidentified the son of Mr. Cuomo who was shown blowing a kiss toward the coffin. He is Christopher Cuomo, not Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo.
match_headline: At Funeral for Mario Cuomo, Praise for a Leader’s Role as a Humanist

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about an inmate who was found dead at the Rikers Island prison complex referred incorrectly to a corrections officer who failed to transfer the prisoner to a suicide watch unit. The officer, whose name was not published, is a woman.
match_headline: Rikers Inmate Found Dead Despite Suicide-Watch Alert

text: An article on Thursday about China’s moves to enforce a widely ignored law requiring its expatriate citizens to pay income tax misstated the threshold for the top tax bracket in China. The top bracket, 45 percent, begins at $12,900 a month — not $12,900 a year — after deductions. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: China Wants Taxes Paid by Citizens Living Afar

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about security threats posed by Internet-connected appliances and other home equipment misidentified the senior threat analyst at Bitdefender, which makes antivirus and anti-malware software. He is Bogdan Botezatu — not Bogdan Dumitru, another Bitdefender employee.
match_headline: CES: Security Risks From the Smart Home

text: An article on Thursday about the up-and-down week of news in Major League Soccer misstated the number of teams that made the playoffs last year. It was 10, not eight.
match_headline: Red Bulls Fire Mike Petke Amid a Whirl of Activity in M.L.S.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Hank Peters, a longtime baseball executive with the Baltimore Orioles and the Cleveland Indians, misstated, in some copies, the number of years between the Indians’ appearance in the 1995 World Series and their last previous appearance. It was 41 years, not “more than half a century.”
match_headline: Hank Peters, 90, Dies; Built Baseball Winners in Baltimore and Cleveland

text: An obituary on Thursday about the author Lee Israel misspelled the given name of the writer who reviewed Ms. Israel’s book “Estée Lauder: Beyond the Magic” for The New York Times Book Review. She is Marylin Bender, not Marilyn. (The Times has misspelled Ms. Bender’s given name numerous times over the years, including in her byline.)
match_headline: Lee Israel, a Writer Proudest of Her Literary Forgeries, Dies at 75

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Saturday about the relationship between Mario M. Cuomo and his son Andrew M. Cuomo described incorrectly a telephone conversation the two once had about the governorship. Andrew told his father that he was unimpressed by his own accomplishments as governor — not unimpressed by his father’s accomplishments.
match_headline: One Last Confluence for Mario and Andrew Cuomo, Proud Rivals

text: An article on Friday about the two brothers sought in the murders of 12 people at a newspaper in Paris misspelled the name of a park in northeastern Paris where a group of young jihadists trained. It is Buttes-Chaumont, not Buttes-Chaumon.
match_headline: Al Qaeda Trained Suspect in Paris Terror Attack, Official Says

text: An article on Wednesday about the sentencing of a Palestinian man, Hussam Qawasmeh, for his involvement in the abduction and murder of three Israeli teenagers in the West Bank last June referred incorrectly in some editions to Mr. Qawasmeh’s prison sentence. He was sentenced to three life terms, not 75 years. The error was repeated in the headline in all editions.
match_headline: Palestinian Gets 3 Life Sentences in Killing of Israeli Teenagers

text: An article on Thursday about arguments before the federal appeals court in New Orleans over Texas abortion laws described incorrectly one issue raised by judges. They questioned whether a legally significant “large fraction” of Texas women would live too far from abortion clinics, not whether a large fraction of clinics would close.
match_headline: Texas Abortion Clinic Rules Tested in Appeals Court

text: An article on Thursday about Miss America winners from New York described incompletely, in some editions, the political career of Bess Myerson, who won the title in 1945. She ran for the United States Senate in 1980, losing to Elizabeth Holtzman in the primary; Ms. Myerson did not merely consider running for the seat.
match_headline: Crowns Amid Controversies

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some copies on Tuesday about Canada’s 5-4 victory over Russia in the final of the world junior hockey championship misstated the day of the game. It was Monday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Holding Off Russia, Canada Wins First Title in 6 Years

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about “Toxic Psalms,” the latest production by the Slovenian vocal ensemble Carmina Slovenica, which is being performed at St. Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn as part of the “Prototype: Opera/Theater/Now” festival, misstated the year the composer Caroline Shaw won a Pulitzer Prize for her work “Partita for Eight Voices,” to which “Toxic Psalms” was compared. It was 2013, not 2012.
match_headline: A Visceral Slide Into Darkness

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the Brooklyn Museum’s acquisition of its first painting by the African-American artist Beauford Delaney misstated part of a comment by Teresa A. Carbone, curator of American Art at the museum. She said she believed the museum was the first to display African traditional art as art, in the 1920s, not that it was the first museum to show African-American art as early as the 1920s.
match_headline: Trove of Still Lifes on the Auction Block

text: A report in the Antiques column on Friday about “Becoming Disfarmer,” an exhibition about the commercial photographer Mike Disfarmer at the Neuberger Museum of Art at Purchase College, misstated its closing date. The exhibition runs through March 22, not March 8.
match_headline: Raising the Profile of Columbia’s Art

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about “Reimagining Modernism: 1900-1950,” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, misstated the name of the area of the museum where the installation is on display. It is the Wallace Wing, not the Wallach Wing. It also misstated the number of Marsden Hartley paintings on view. There are five, not nine.
match_headline: A Trans-Atlantic View of Modernism

text: An article last Sunday about a newfound willingness by Republicans to seek an active role for the courts to try to benefit conservative policy goals described incorrectly a challenge to the Affordable Care Act that is before the Supreme Court. The case revolves around an Internal Revenue Service rule, and argues that it is contrary to the text of the act; the case does not challenge the constitutionality of the Affordable Care Act.
match_headline: G.O.P. Turns to the Courts to Aid Agenda

text: An article last Sunday about fast-paced events last February that led to the abrupt downfall of Ukraine’s president, Viktor F. Yanukovych, misspelled the surname of an ally of the president who broke with him over his refusal to sign a trade deal with the European Union. She is Inna Bogoslovskaya, not Bogolovskaya.
match_headline: Ukraine Leader Was Defeated Even Before He Was Ousted

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about fears of gentrification among some residents of Sunset Park, Brooklyn, where the Li-lac Chocolate factory recently opened, referred incorrectly in some editions to two of the borders for Community District 7. Eighth Avenue and Fort Hamilton Parkway are to the east and the waterfront is to the west.
match_headline: Chocolate Factory in Brooklyn Asks: What, Us? Gentrifiers?

text: An article last Sunday about a woman who discovered that her husband’s death was filmed for the television program “NY Med” without the family’s knowledge misidentified, in some editions, the newspaper that quoted the show’s executive producer, Terence Wrong, as saying one of the New York hospitals “was just not delivering enough traumas.” It is The Philadelphia Daily News, not The Philadelphia Inquirer. (The article was posted on the website that both papers share.)
match_headline: Dying in the E.R., and on TV Without His Family’s Consent

text: An article last Sunday about Knicks attendance, ticket sales and ratings during their poor season misstated, in some editions, the number of successive Knicks sellouts at Madison Square Garden at the time. It was 177, not 157. It also misstated, in some editions, the percentage of decline in the Knicks’ television ratings on MSG this season. It is 17 percent, not nearly 30 percent.
match_headline: Filling Garden With Misery and, at Least for Now, Fans

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about the Carolina Panthers’ 27-16 playoff victory over the Arizona Cardinals referred incorrectly in some copies to the significance of the game. It was the Panthers’ first home playoff victory since 2003 — not merely its first home playoff game since then. (Carolina hosted a playoff game last season.)
match_headline: For Panthers, Only Record That Matters Now Is 1-0

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary in some editions last Sunday about Edward Brooke, the former senator from Massachusetts, erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He was the first black senator to be re-elected to office, not the only one. (Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey was returned to office last year after having first won a special election.)
match_headline: Edward W. Brooke III, 95, Senate Pioneer, Is Dead

text: An article in the special Oscars preview section last Sunday about the actor Benedict Cumberbatch, who stars in “The Imitation Game,” referred incorrectly to the character he played in the movie “Star Trek Into Darkness.” The character Khan was a genetically engineered human — not an alien.
match_headline: Showing the Smarts to Play the Genius

text: An article last Sunday about the indie-rock band Sleater-Kinney, which has a new album out, misspelled the surname of the editor in chief of CMJ, which covers the music industry. She is Lisa Hresko — not Hrekso.
match_headline: Sleater-Kinney’s Secret Basement Sessions

text: An article last Sunday about classical musicians’ pondering when they are ready to play certain great works referred incorrectly to the artistic direction of the Marlboro chamber music festival in Vermont. Mitsuko Uchida is the festival’s sole artistic director, not Ms. Uchida and Richard Goode, who had been a festival artistic director until 2013.
match_headline: Wait, You Need to Suffer Some More

text: An article on Dec. 28 about the new movie “The Wedding Ringer” and a trove of unproduced movie scripts referred incorrectly to the status of one of the scripts. “The Alibi” has not been picked up by HBO’s “Project Greenlight,” the old reality competition that is being revived for 2015. (“The Alibi” was considered for the show, but then “Greenlight” executives decided to move forward with a different script.)
match_headline: Life and Near Death of a Miramax Script

text: A review on Dec. 28 about “A Royal Experiment: The Private Life of King George III,” by Janice Hadlow, referred incorrectly to Princess Charlotte, George’s granddaughter. She was one of several legitimate grandchildren of the king’s, not the only one. (The best known was Queen Victoria.)
ref_headline: A Royal Experiment: The Private Life of King George III,
match_headline: ‘A Royal Experiment,’ by Janice Hadlow

text: A review on Dec. 21 about “The Norton Anthology of World Religions. Volume 1: Hinduism, Buddhism, Daoism” misstated the era in which Rabbi Akiba lived. It was the second century A.D., not B.C.
ref_headline: The Norton Anthology of World Religions. Volume 1: Hinduism, Buddhism, Daoism
match_headline: ‘The Norton Anthology of World Religions: Volume II’

text: An article last Sunday about self-improvement through smartphone apps misstated the century in which inventions like radar came along. It was the 20th century, not the 19th. The article also misstated the length of time for each exercise in the Johnson & Johnson 7 Minute Workout. It is 30 seconds, not 60.
match_headline: What Isn’t There an App For?

text: An article last Sunday about the actress Katherine Waterston, who is featured in the new movie “Inherent Vice,” misspelled the given name of a world-renowned singer Ms. Waterston mentioned when discussing the music of the 1970s. She was Janis Joplin, not Janice.
match_headline: Katherine Waterston of ‘Inherent Vice’ Shyly Captivates the Fashion World

text: An article last Sunday about public service announcements on domestic abuse shown during N.F.L. game telecasts misidentified the channels on which the commercials with Amy Poehler, Courteney Cox and Tim Gunn first appeared. The commercials were shown on Fox News and USA Network, among others — not on Comedy Central and MTV.
match_headline: The Team Behind the N.F.L.’s ‘No More’ Campaign

text: An article on Dec. 28 about visiting immigrant communities in Paris outside the usual tourist areas misidentified the arrondissement in which Chez Hanna, a restaurant where you can buy falafel to go, is located. It is in the Fourth Arrondissement, not in the Third. And the article described incorrectly the areas around Paris in which rural migrants from Brittany and Basque Country settled in the 1800s. It was in the outer neighborhoods of Paris, not the northern reaches of the city.
match_headline: Dipping Into a French Melting Pot

text: An article on Dec. 21 about Marissa Mayer, the C.E.O. of Yahoo, misstated the terms of a 2012 agreement between Alibaba, the Chinese Internet conglomerate, and Yahoo. There were economic incentives for Alibaba to hold an initial public offering before the end of 2015; the deal did not include a requirement for Alibaba to hold one by 2014.
match_headline: What Happened When Marissa Mayer Tried to Be Steve Jobs

text: An article on Thursday about a slower pace in New York City’s courts following a drastic drop in arrests misstated the year of the Sept. 11 terror attacks, which also precipitated a drop in cases. It was 2001, of course, not 2011.
match_headline: As Police Go Idle, So Do New York City Courts

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with the continuation of an article about New York City residents’ response to a drastic reduction in arrests and tickets misidentified the people shown writing a parking ticket for a UPS truck in Brooklyn. They are traffic enforcement agents, not police officers.
match_headline: Life in New York City, Where Arrests Are Down and Tickets Are Rarities

text: An article last Monday about the selection by Pope Francis of 15 new cardinals referred incorrectly to cardinals who were chosen last year. They came predominantly from developing countries and from the Southern Hemisphere, not predominantly just from the Southern Hemisphere.
match_headline: Pope Names 15 New Cardinals Reflective of Diversity of the Faithful

text: An article in some editions on Dec. 12 about a police raid on the office of a doctor accused of overprescribing painkillers, using information from court documents, misspelled his surname. He is Moshe Mirilashvili, not Mirilishvili. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: U.S. Arrests Manhattan Doctor in Oxycodone Ring

text: An article on Dec. 23 about Janet L. Yellen’s first year as chairwoman of the Federal Reserve misstated the number of times since 1992 that three Fed officials have dissented at a policy-making meeting. It is three times, not two.
match_headline: Yellen’s First Year at Fed: A Remarkably Steady Course

text: An article last Monday about the success of the Atlanta Hawks this season referred incorrectly to an honor received by center Al Horford. He is the only player on the Hawks’ roster to make an All-N.B.A. team, not the only All-Star. (Horford, Paul Millsap and Elton Brand have made an All-Star team.) The article also referred imprecisely to the Hawks’ playoff history. The Hawks, who currently play in the Eastern Conference, reached the equivalent of the conference finals in 1969 and 1970 when they played in the Western Division finals; it is not the case that “since arriving from St. Louis in 1968, the Hawks have yet to reach the conference finals.”
ref_headline: since arriving from St. Louis in 1968, the Hawks have yet to reach the conference finals.
match_headline: Despite Tumult Around Them, the Atlanta Hawks Have Risen to the Top

text: A report in the baseball roundup on Dec. 12 about a trade between the Cincinnati Reds and the Miami Marlins misidentified the job Mike Hill holds with the Marlins. He is the president of baseball operations — not the general manager, a position held by Dan Jennings.
match_headline: Three Deals Help Red Sox Round Out Their Rotation

text: An article last Monday about criticism of the Olympic stadium designed by Zaha Hadid that is to be built for the 2020 Summer Olympics in Tokyo, and problems with other Olympic stadiums, misstated the amount of debt Montreal was left with after its Olympic stadium was built for the 1976 Summer Games. It was $1.5 billion, not more than $2 billion.
match_headline: National Pride at a Steep Price

text: An obituary on Friday about former Gov. Arch A. Moore Jr. of West Virginia erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He was the first sitting governor of his state to be formally charged with a crime, but not the first governor. (William Wallace Barron, governor of West Virginia from 1961 to 1965, was indicted in 1968 for taking bribes and acquitted, but indicted again in 1971 for jury tampering and pleaded guilty.)
match_headline: Arch Moore, Trailblazing West Virginia Governor, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 7 about an announcement by the Pakistani military that it had killed an Al Qaeda operative wanted in the United States on charges of plotting to bomb several targets, including the New York City subway system, misidentified, in some editions, the source of an official statement on the death of the operative, Adnan G. el-Shukrijumah. It was from the Pakistani Army, not from Inter-Services Intelligence, Pakistan’s spy agency. And also because of an editing error, the article misstated the number of aides to Mr. Shukrijumah who were killed. One was killed, not five. The article also referred incorrectly to five Saudis at the compound at the time of the raid. They were captured, not killed, and the army described them only as of Saudi origin; it did not say they were men, and it is not known if they were. These errors were corrected online on Dec. 7, but editors failed to follow through with this correction.
match_headline: Pakistani Military Kills a Qaeda Leader

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about testimony that a federal grand jury is scheduled to hear concerning loans made to the re-election campaign of Gov. Sam Brownback of Kansas misidentified, in some editions, the political party of Paul T. Davis, who lost to Mr. Brownback in November. He is a Democrat, not an independent.
match_headline: Federal Grand Jury to Look at Brownback Loans

text: An article on the Personal Business pages on Saturday about factors other than money that determine when to retire described the personal history of Mike C. Miller, a lawyer who has decided to retire at 55, incorrectly. He does not smoke and has not had prostate cancer. Those descriptions apply to his late father.
match_headline: When Outside Factors Dictate Retirement Age

text: Because of an editing error, the On Baseball column on Thursday, about the 2015 inductees into the Hall of Fame, referred imprecisely in some editions to a career statistic of one of them, Craig Biggio. He was hit by a pitch 285 times; he was not “beaned,” or hit in the head, that many times.
match_headline: Two Paths to Cooperstown Are Tinged With Black and Blue

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some copies on Friday with an article about N.F.L. dynasties that are in decline described incorrectly the scene shown. The photograph was of Ted Washington of the New England Patriots celebrating New England’s victory in the A.F.C. championship game in 2004 to advance to the Super Bowl; it did not show the Patriots’ Mike Vrabel catching a touchdown pass in the team’s victory over the Philadelphia Eagles in the Super Bowl in 2005. The picture also carried an incorrect credit. It was taken by Charles Krupa of The Associated Press, not by Vincent Laforet of The New York Times. (A picture of Vrabel by Laforet was published in other editions.)
match_headline: N.F.L. Dynasties, on the Decline

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Dec. 19 about Bible exhibitions in Manhattan at the Morgan Library & Museum, the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Biblical Art referred incorrectly to the American Bible Society, which provided books for the exhibition at the Museum of Biblical Art. That museum is an independent institution; the society is not its parent organization.
match_headline: Oldest Testaments: A Close-Up View

text: An obituary on Saturday about the movie executive Samuel Goldwyn Jr., using information from his family, referred incorrectly to his marital history. He was married three times, not twice, and is survived by his third wife, Patricia Strawn.
match_headline: Samuel Goldwyn Jr., 88, Dies; Hollywood Scion and Film Influence

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a Twitter post by Rupert Murdoch on the Paris terrorist attacks paraphrased incorrectly in some editions from his comments. He said that Muslims must be held responsible for the attacks, not that they should apologize for them. Also because of an editing error, the article misidentified, in some editions, the parent of the Fox News Channel, on which a self-described expert on Islamic terrorism charged that the entire city of Birmingham, England, was off limits to non-Muslims. The parent company is 21st Century Fox, not the News Corporation. And because of an editing error, the article misstated, in some editions, Mr. Murdoch’s title at News Corporation. He is the executive chairman, not the chief executive. (Mr. Murdoch is the chief executive of 21st Century Fox. News Corporation was spun off from 21st Century Fox in 2013.)
match_headline: Fox News Beats a Retreat After Gaffes About Islam

text: An article on Friday about the Egyptian government’s destruction of a town on the border of the Gaza Strip as the government expanded a security zone there misidentified the source of the attacks that led to the decision to begin bulldozing the town. The attacks were by militants, not by the military.
match_headline: Egypt Moves to Eradicate Town Near Gaza Strip

text: An article on Tuesday about a proposal by President François Hollande of France to ease the sanctions against Russia in exchange for progress in the negotiations over the future of Ukraine referred incorrectly to Sigmar Gabriel, who raised concerns about the sanctions. He is Germany’s vice chancellor, not “a” vice chancellor of the country. (It has only one.)
match_headline: French Leader Urges End to Sanctions Against Russia Over Ukraine

text: An article last Wednesday about Gov. Jerry Brown’s efforts to build a high-speed train in California misspelled the given name of his wife in some editions. She is Anne Gust Brown, not Ann.
match_headline: To Gov. Jerry Brown, a Legacy Project; to Critics, a Runaway Train

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with an article about a 7-year-old New Jersey boy who died when a falling bench struck him at a school gym misstated the day of the accident in some editions. He was struck last Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Struck by Bench in School Gym, New Jersey Boy, 7, Dies

text: An article on Monday about an effort by Newcastle Brown Ale to recruit additional brands to help it break into the Super Bowl advertising event described the ale incorrectly. It is a beer brand, not a beer maker. (It is brewed by Heineken.)
match_headline: Newcastle Brown Ale Calls for Other Brands to Join a Sly Super Bowl Ad Campaign

text: An article in some copies last Wednesday about a possible deal between the Yankees and infielder Stephen Drew misspelled the surname of the team’s recently acquired shortstop. He is Didi Gregorius, not Gregorious.
match_headline: Yankees Are Said to Be Close to a Deal With Stephen Drew

text: An article on Dec. 30 about the top concerts of the year chosen by New York Times pop music and jazz critics, including a concert by the Replacements, the Hold Steady and Deer Tick at Forest Hills Stadium on Sept. 19, misstated the year the singer and guitarist Paul Westerberg began touring with the reconstituted Replacements. It was 2013; the band did not tour in 2012.
match_headline: Sounds That Lingered: Critics’ Top 10 Concerts

text: An obituary on Monday about the actress Anita Ekberg misspelled part of the name of an Italian newspaper to which she gave an interview on the occasion of her 80th birthday. It is Corriere della Sera, not Corriere delle Sera.
match_headline: Anita Ekberg, International Screen Beauty, Dies at 83

text: A report last Wednesday in the Off the Menu column about the opening of Darrow’s Farm Fresh Takeout, in Manhattan, referred incorrectly to Jean-Georges Vongerichten. While he is the chef of several New York restaurants, he is not a consultant for Darrow’s. The report also omitted a chef at Darrow’s. Besides David Kupperberg, Taylor Thorne is a chef there. (Mr. Thorne once worked at Mr. Vongerichten’s restaurant Jean-Georges.)
match_headline: Dominique Ansel Sets Up a New Bakery

text: An article on Monday about the ideological priorities faced by Republican governors in the new legislative term described incorrectly the rail development for which Gov. Rick Scott of Florida turned away billions in federal aid. It was high-speed rail, not light rail.
match_headline: G.O.P. Governors Face Test in Shift on Ideological Agendas

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the Egyptian government’s release from prison of Khaled al-Qazzaz, a top adviser to the ousted president, Mohamed Morsi, misidentified which of the two men once was a leader of the Muslim Brotherhood, the party that won Egypt’s first free elections in 2012. Mr. Morsi led the group, not Mr. Qazzaz.
match_headline: Egyptian Authorities Release a Morsi Adviser

text: An article on Dec. 23 about a Christmas address by Pope Francis in which he sharply criticized the Vatican bureaucracy referred incorrectly to the proceedings of a consistory. The pope announces the names of new cardinals he has chosen; the cardinals are not elected.
match_headline: Francis Uses Christmas Speech to Criticize Vatican Bureaucracy

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Dec. 31 with an article about the return of American forces to Iraq, this time to train recruits to that country’s military, described the scene incorrectly. The photograph showed American troops traveling between bases in Iraq, not en route to Iraq.
match_headline: U.S. Troops, Back in Iraq, Train a Force to Fight ISIS

text: An article on Saturday about Derrick Hamilton, a self-taught jailhouse lawyer who had his case vacated last week, misstated the year of a double murder for which one of his fellow prisoners, Shabaka Shakur, was convicted. It was 1988, not 1998.
match_headline: Wrongly Convicted Man Was His Own Best Advocate

text: A picture caption on the Automobiles page on Friday with an article about the increasing popularity of auto leasing among American consumers misspelled the make of a sedan leased by Jimmy Zaid. As the article correctly noted, it is an Infiniti, not an Infinity.
match_headline: Auto Leasing Gains Popularity Among American Consumers

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actor Rod Taylor misstated the year that the movie “Do Not Disturb,” in which he appeared, was released. It was 1965, not 1966. The obituary also misstated part of the plot of the movie “The Birds,” in which he also appeared. While his character does meet the character played by Tippi Hedren early in the movie, he does not offer her a ride.
match_headline: Rod Taylor, Star of ‘The Birds’ and ‘The Time Machine,’ Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the filmmaker Francesco Rosi misspelled the surname of a director whom the critic Michel Ciment called one of “the last three giants of Italian cinema,” along with Mr. Rosi and Federico Fellini. He was Michelangelo Antonioni, not Antonio.
ref_headline: the last three giants of Italian cinema,
match_headline: Francesco Rosi, Italian Filmmaker With Political Bent, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Dec. 28 about Dr. Per-Ingvar Branemark, considered the father of the modern dental implant, described his medical background incorrectly. While he was a licensed physician, he was not an orthopedic surgeon.
match_headline: Per-Ingvar Branemark, Dental Innovator, Dies at 85

text: An obituary in some editions on Sunday about the novelist Robert Stone misstated the given name of his daughter. She is Deidre, not Deirdre.
match_headline: Robert Stone, Novelist of the Vietnam Era and Beyond, Dies at 77

text: An article last Thursday about Adam Reed Tucker, a professional Lego modeler, referred incorrectly to the novels of Ayn Rand in describing Mr. Tucker. As a former architect, Mr. Tucker is more like the character Howard Roark, an architect, in “The Fountainhead” — not John Galt, a character in “Atlas Shrugged” who was not an architect.
match_headline: Brick by Tiny Brick

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Thursday about male actors who are increasingly focused on fashion on the red carpet misspelled the maiden name of the costume curator and historian who commented on an awards show in the mid-'80s. She is Deborah Nadoolman Landis, not Nadeoolman.
match_headline: How Stylish Male Actors Have Upped the Red Carpet Game

text: An article last Friday about the sequence of events in the terrorist attack on Charlie Hebdo, the French satirical newspaper, referred incorrectly to L’Humanité, which quoted one of the survivors of the attack. It is a French newspaper, not a magazine.
match_headline: Recounting a Bustling Office at Charlie Hebdo, Then a ‘Vision of Horror’

text: An article on Tuesday about the West Virginia Board of Education and climate science referred incorrectly to a meeting of the board. Science standards were added to the agenda of a regularly scheduled meeting on Wednesday; controversy over the board’s recent changes to the standards did not prompt the meeting.
match_headline: West Virginia Revisits Science Standards

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about Sholem Aleichem, the housing co-op in the Bronx where the former beauty queen and city official Bess Myerson grew up, misstated the roles held by the father and grandfather of Daniel Padernacht, a lifelong resident there. Mr. Padernacht’s grandfather was a superintendent of the property, but not the first one.
