Mr. Padernacht’s father managed the property and was president of the tenants association; he was not a superintendent.
match_headline: At Bess Myerson’s Former Home, Shades of a Bronx Utopia

text: An article on Tuesday about electronic vapor marijuana cigarettes referred imprecisely to the legality of recreational use of marijuana in Oregon. While the state passed a ballot measure in November to allow the personal use and possession of recreational marijuana, it does not go into effect until July 1, 2015.
match_headline: No Smoke, but Haze Around E-Joint

text: An article on Tuesday about Rolf-Dieter Heuer, the director-general of the European Organization of Nuclear Research, or CERN, misstated the anniversary the organization celebrated last year with events at the United Nations General Assembly. It was CERN’s 60th anniversary, not its 50th.
match_headline: An Ambassador for Physics Is Shifting His Mission

text: An article on Tuesday about bats misspelled the given name of a bat ecologist. She is DeeAnn Reeder, not DeAnn.
match_headline: No Time for Bats to Rest Easy

text: An obituary on Jan. 4 about the Polish poet and essayist Stanislaw Baranczak misstated the reason he was unable to accept a job at Harvard for almost three years. The Polish government denied him a passport, not a visa.
match_headline: Stanislaw Baranczak, 68, Polish Underground Poet, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary by The Associated Press on Jan. 6 about the former major league pitcher Stu Miller referred incorrectly to the All-Star Game in which he famously committed a balk. It was the first of two All-Star Games played in 1961, not “the 1961 All-Star Game.” (Major League Baseball had two All-Star Games a year from 1959 to 1962.)
match_headline: Win for ESPN, but Title Game Is the Real Test

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Saturday about questions concerning how the jihadists responsible for the murders of 17 people in Paris were able to execute brazen attacks despite being known to the authorities referred incorrectly to the director of the Foundation for Strategic Research, who was quoted in the article. The director, Camille Grand, is a man.
match_headline: Why Reams of Intelligence Did Not Thwart the Paris Attacks

text: An article on Friday about tensions between the White House and Congress over sanctions on Iran misstated the timing of sanctions that would be imposed under one proposal in the Senate. The legislation includes a trigger that would impose sanctions only after the June 30 deadline for nuclear negotiations with Iran. The sanctions would not be imposed before talks are completed.
match_headline: Obama and Senator Robert Menendez Spar on How to Handle Iran

text: A news analysis article on Tuesday about the quarterbacks involved in the N.F.L. conference championship games referred incorrectly to the success of the New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks against the Indianapolis Colts and the Green Bay Packers. The Patriots are 3-0 against the Colts and the Seahawks are 2-0 against the Packers since quarterbacks Andrew Luck and Russell Wilson entered the N.F.L. in 2012; the Patriots and Seahawks are not “a combined 5-0 against the Colts and the Packers” since then. (New England has lost to Green Bay, and Seattle has lost to Indianapolis.)
ref_headline: a combined 5-0 against the Colts and the Packers
match_headline: Stellar Passers, Sure, but That May Not Be Enough

text: An article last Saturday about the involvement of Boston’s colleges and universities in the city’s bid for the 2024 Summer Olympics misstated the job title of Tom Rutledge, who, with Andrew W. Lo, wrote about the ways universities can help solve the challenges in housing, transportation and financing for the Games. Rutledge is the head of fixed income origination at Magnetar Capital — not chief investment strategist at the AlphaSimplex Group, which is Mr. Lo’s position.
match_headline: Boston, in Old College Try, Uses Campuses in 2024 Olympic Bid

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about the Islanders’ 3-2 victory over the Devils misidentified, in some copies, the Islanders player who scored a goal early in the third period. Josh Bailey made the goal — not Calvin de Haan, who was initially credited with the goal.
match_headline: With Fans in Tow, Islanders Edge Devils to Land in First

text: An article last Monday about a huge rally in Paris to take a stand against Islamic extremism and to commemorate the 17 people killed in the terrorist attacks the previous week misstated the surname of an illustrator who attended the rally. He is Pablo de Gastines, not Gaskins.
match_headline: Huge Show of Solidarity in Paris Against Terrorism

text: A news analysis article on Wednesday about American officials’ rethinking crime control and incarceration in light of a declining crime rate misidentified, in some editions, the university where Daniel S. Nagin, who discussed law enforcement issues, is a criminologist. It is Carnegie Mellon University, not Case Western Reserve University.
match_headline: In a Safer Age, U.S. Rethinks Its ‘Tough on Crime’ System

text: An article on Tuesday about the release by the Cuban government of 53 imprisoned dissidents as part of an agreement with the United States to restore diplomatic relations and bolster economic exchanges misstated the day an American delegation is to go to Cuba for talks. The talks are scheduled for Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Cuba Frees 53 Prisoners, U.S. Says

text: An article on Friday about threats by the Mormon church to excommunicate John P. Dehlin, the host of an online forum for skeptical Mormons, misstated part of the name of the website he founded. It is staylds.com , not staylds.org .
match_headline: Mormon Church Threatens Critic With Excommunication

text: An article on Friday about a turbine in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, the first large-scale wind turbine to be installed in New York City, described incorrectly in some editions the amount of energy that it can generate. It is up to 100 kilowatts of electricity, not 100 kilowatts per hour. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: In Brooklyn, Fertile Ground for a Wind Turbine

text: An article on Friday about quarterly earnings for the money manager BlackRock described the company’s recent growth incorrectly in some copies. An increase of 26 percent year over year referred to growth in the third quarter, not assets under management in the fourth quarter.
match_headline: JPMorgan Chase Chief Says ‘Banks Are Under Assault’

text: An article on Thursday about a new book by the historian Eric Foner, “Gateway to Freedom: The Hidden History of the Underground Railroad,” misspelled the given name of the student who discovered the Record of Fugitives in the holdings of Columbia University in 2007 and called it to the attention of Mr. Foner. She is Madeline Lewis, not Madeleine.
ref_headline: Gateway to Freedom: The Hidden History of the Underground Railroad,
match_headline: Words From the Past Illuminate a Station on the Way to Freedom

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the estimated loss in revenues to New York City during a slowdown by the police erroneously included several factors affecting the total amount cited by city officials. The estimate of less than $5 million in losses did not include the potential loss of revenue from speeding tickets, other moving violations and petty crimes that were not cited.
match_headline: Police Slowdown Cost New York City an Estimated $5 Million in Lost Fines

text: An article in some editions last Tuesday about a City Council transportation committee hearing regarding Uber Technology and other car-service apps misstated the committee’s plans for a hearing on a car-service bill. As of now, one has not been scheduled; a hearing has not been planned for later in January.
match_headline: New York City Council Discusses Cap on Prices Charged by Car-Service Apps During Peak Times

text: An article on Wednesday about the return of high-performance sedans and sports cars at the Detroit auto show misspelled the surname of a Toyota executive and misstated his role at the company. He is Mike Michels, not Michaels, and he is a communications executive, not a top sales executive.
match_headline: Glory Days of High-Powered Muscle Cars Are Back at Detroit Auto Show

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the Nets’ 103-92 loss to the Memphis Grizzlies misstated the given name of a player recently acquired by the Grizzlies. He is Jeff Green, not Gerald. (Gerald Green plays for the Phoenix Suns.) And because of an editing error, the article misstated, in some copies, the surname of the Nets player who made 3 of 12 field-goal attempts. As an accompanying picture caption correctly noted, he is Joe Johnson, not Jackson.
match_headline: Nets Put On Sleepy Show After Morning Workout

text: An article on Wednesday about Kevin Jorgeson, one of the climbers who tried to free-climb El Capitan’s Dawn Wall, misidentified the city in which Marmot, the outdoor apparel and equipment maker that first sponsored him, was founded. It is Grand Junction, Colo., not Santa Rosa, Calif.
match_headline: Climber Yearns for the Summit, and a Shower

text: An article on Tuesday about the harsh treatment of animals at the U.S. Meat Animal Research Center in Nebraska described incorrectly an experiment with cows intended to produce more twins. Eggs — not embryos — were fertilized with semen.
match_headline: U.S. Research Lab Lets Livestock Suffer in Quest for Profit

text: An article on Tuesday about the shifting politics around the issue of net neutrality misidentified one of the behemoth companies against which Netflix says it needs protection to keep its customers from experiencing slow Internet access. It is Time Warner Cable, not Time Warner.
match_headline: Shifting Politics of Net Neutrality Debate Ahead of F.C.C. Vote

text: An article on Tuesday about the Securities and Exchange Commission’s reversal of its rule allowing Whole Foods Market to exclude a shareholder proposal to let large investors nominate directors misstated the status of a proxy filing by Whole Foods. It has been submitted to the S.E.C.; it has not been sent to shareholders as well.
match_headline: S.E.C. Reversal May Clear Way for Shareholders to Challenge Companies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about online insurance sales misstated the role of companies like CoverHound and PolicyGenius in offering insurance. They are online insurance agencies, not insurers.
match_headline: Insurance via Internet Is Squeezing Agents

text: An article on Saturday about a decision by the car-hailing service Uber to require more extensive background checks of its drivers in India referred incorrectly at several points to the head of Uber’s safety division in India. The executive, Deval Delivala, is a woman.
match_headline: Uber to Introduce Driver Background Checks in India

text: An article on Saturday about the Syrian documentary film “Our Terrible Country” misstated the date it will be shown at the Artists Space site at 55 Walker Street in Manhattan. It is Feb. 13, not Feb. 18.
match_headline: When a Revolt Goes Wrong

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about a British judge’s ruling in a lawsuit that Sotheby’s was not negligent in concluding that a painting it sold in 2006 was not by Caravaggio misstated the dollar equivalent of the £11 million for which Sotheby’s was sued. It is about $16.7 million, not about $166.6 million.
match_headline: A Win for Sotheby’s in Dispute Over Painting

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the songwriter Ervin Drake misstated the name of the high school he attended and misidentified the borough in which it was located. It is Townsend Harris High School, not Townsend Harris Hall, and it was in Manhattan at the time, not in Queens, its current location.
match_headline: Ervin Drake, Composer of Pop Songs, Dies at 95

text: A picture credit on Friday with an obituary about the sculptor Milton Hebald misstated the surname of the photographer who took the picture of Mr. Hebald with a model of a life-size tribute to James Joyce. She is Linda Carfagno, not Caragno.
match_headline: Milton Hebald, Whose Sculptures Are in Plain View, Dies at 97

text: An obituary on Sunday about Dr. Vernon Mountcastle, whose studies of how brain cells process perceptions and movement laid the foundations of modern neuroscience, misspelled part of his mother’s given name. She was Anna-Frances, not Anna-Francis.
match_headline: Vernon B. Mountcastle, Brain Explorer, Dies at 96

text: An article on Tuesday about the use of alcohol at sororities included a comment about drinking and college culture from a Cornell student who identified himself as a member of the Delta Chi fraternity. The student, Fielding Williams, does not belong to the fraternity.
match_headline: Sorority Anti-Rape Idea: Drinking on Own Turf

text: An article on Wednesday about an agreement to resolve pollution issues that occurred because of Los Angeles’s use of water from Owens Valley misidentified the method by which water was moved south to the city, beginning in 1913. An aqueduct was used, not an aquifer.
match_headline: Century Later, the ‘Chinatown’ Water Feud Ebbs

text: An article on Friday about prosecutions and convictions by the French authorities of people who voiced support for terrorism in the wake of the Paris attacks, a response that raised questions about a double standard for free speech, misspelled part of the name of the town in eastern France where a man shouted support for the attackers. It is Bourgoin-Jallieu, not Bourgoin-Jalieu.
match_headline: French Rein In Speech Backing Acts of Terror

text: An article on Monday about the recent use of aerial banners to broadcast criticism over the New York region referred incorrectly to the sponsorship of a message demanding that Mayor Bill de Blasio apologize to the New York police. He is Michael Sheehan, a retired Westchester County corrections officer; it is not the case that the sponsor’s identity remained undisclosed. Because of an editing error, a picture caption also misidentified that banner’s sponsor as Retired N.Y.P.D. for a Safe New York. And because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions described incorrectly Ashley Chalmers, the owner of an aerial advertising business. The photograph, of Mr. Chalmers standing by his plane, showed him displaying a banner with a message for the mayor, not preparing to fly it.
match_headline: With Aerial Banners, Taking Grievances to the Skies

text: An article on Friday about a poll on New York City police officers’ relations with Mayor Bill de Blasio misstated, in some editions, the increase in the approval rating for the police commissioner, William J. Bratton. His rating of 56 percent marked an increase of 12 percentage points, not 8.
match_headline: Voters Disapprove of Police Officers’ Protests and Work Slowdown, Poll Finds

text: An article on Monday about the weekend box-office revenue for movies, including the estimated $105.2 million for “American Sniper,” a record for a January weekend opening, erroneously attributed a distinction to “Avatar.” It held the record for the biggest box-office take for a January weekend — $74.4 million in 2010, after adjusting for inflation — not for an opening on a January weekend.
match_headline: ‘Sniper’ Rules Weekend Box Office

text: A listing of credits and other information on Tuesday with a film review of “Mille Soleils” by Mati Diop at the Museum of Modern Art, using information from the museum, misidentified the language spoken in “Atlantiques,” another short film by Ms. Diop that is being shown with “Mille Soleils.” It is Wolof, not Swahili.
match_headline: Stuck, but Trying to Leave

text: An article on Jan. 1 about Evgeny Lebedev, who owns several British news media outlets, including The Evening Standard and The Independent, misidentified Charles Wintour’s former position at The Evening Standard. He was the editor, not the deputy editor. The article also misstated the size of The Independent’s online audience, and its growth rate over the last year. It has 53.3 million unique monthly users, not 35 million; its increase in unique monthly browsers was 85.7 percent, not 87 percent. And the article misstated the proportion of The Independent’s unique monthly users in the United States. It is 30.8 percent, not 35 percent.
match_headline: The Rise of Evgeny Lebedev

text: An editorial on Monday about a case involving judicial campaigns misspelled the plaintiff’s first name. It is Lanell Williams-Yulee, not Yanell. It misstated the number of Florida Supreme Court justices who resigned following corruption scandals. It was three, not four. It also incorrectly identified Justice Paul E. Pfeifer as a former justice of the Ohio Supreme Court. He is a current member of that court.
match_headline: Judges, With Hat in Hand

text: An article on Wednesday about President Obama’s State of the Union address, in which he said better politics would allow Republicans and Democrats to come together on reforming the criminal justice system, referred incorrectly to the death of Eric Garner on Staten Island. He died after being placed in a chokehold by a police officer; he was not shot to death.
match_headline: In State of the Union, Obama Sets an Ambitious Agenda

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the investigation of a deadly 1978 fire in Greece, N.Y., referred imprecisely to the shopping hub there that attracted visitors around the region. Shoppers in 1978 went to Greece Towne and Long Ridge malls — not to the Mall at Greece Ridge, which was created in 1994 by combining the two older malls.
match_headline: After 36 Years, a New York Town Sifts Through Suspicions on a Fatal Fire

text: An article on Wednesday about freshman lawmakers for whom the State of the Union address on Tuesday night was a rite of passage misidentified the theme park to which one of the freshmen took his family over the weekend. Carlos Curbelo, a Republican representative, and his family went to Disney World, in their home state of Florida — not to Disneyland. (Mr. Curbelo delivered the Republicans’ Spanish-language response to President Obama’s speech.)
match_headline: For Freshman Members of Congress, State of the Union Address Is a Rite of Passage

text: An article on Wednesday about an Alabama man who received a traffic citation in Georgia for driving while eating a cheeseburger misstated the surname of the driver in some editions. He is H. Madison Turner, not Harris.
match_headline: A Cheeseburger, a Suburban Traffic Stop and a Ticket for Eating While Driving

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the N.H.L. roundup on Tuesday about the Vancouver Canucks’ 2-1 victory misstated part of the name of their opponent in some editions. They are the Florida Panthers, not Carolina.

A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Dec. 24 about the awarding of the Simone de Beauvoir Prize for Women’s Freedom to the National Museum of Women in the Arts in Washington this month referred incorrectly to this year’s prize. It is honorary; it does not carry a cash award of 20,000 euros this year.
match_headline: Museum of Women Gets Freedom Award

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about Faith Seidenberg, a lawyer who sued the Manhattan bar McSorley’s Old Ale House to admit women, misidentified the area of New York in which McSorley’s is located. It is in the East Village, not in Greenwich Village. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption, which also, using information from The Associated Press, misstated the date the photograph of McSorley’s was taken. The picture, undated, is believed to be from the 1950s or earlier; it was not taken in 1970.
match_headline: Faith Seidenberg, 91, Dies; Took On McSorley’s, an All-Male Haven

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with the continuation of an obituary about King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia misstated, in some editions, the day that his brother Salman bin Abdul-Aziz Al Saud announced that he had assumed the throne. As the obituary correctly noted, it was Friday, not Thursday.
match_headline: King Abdullah, a Shrewd Force Who Reshaped Saudi Arabia, Dies at 90

text: An article on Friday about a planned visit to the United States by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel referred incorrectly to plans for him to speak to the Congress and described such an appearance incorrectly. While he had been invited to address Congress in February, he had not committed to do so. And such an appearance would be during a joint meeting of Congress — not during a joint session, which is held to conduct official business. (Mr. Netanyahu’s plans now call for him to visit in March.)
match_headline: Obama Not Planning to Meet With Israeli Premier

text: An article on Friday about accusations of political meddling by Gov. Rick Scott of Florida in the ouster of Gerald Bailey, the commissioner of the Department of Law Enforcement, misstated the governor’s position on Mr. Bailey’s successor, Rick Swearingen. While Mr. Scott says he will support Mr. Swearingen, he is not opposed to reopening the search for a commissioner; he did not reject a request to do so.
match_headline: Inquiry Sought After Former Commissioner Accuses Gov. Rick Scott of Meddling

text: An article on Jan. 15 about Joseph Morrissey, the Virginia House delegate who was re-elected after he pleaded guilty to charges involving sex with a minor, misstated the circumstances involving James M. Curley, a former Boston mayor who also had legal troubles. Mr. Curley was re-elected mayor of Boston in 1945 while under indictment for mail fraud; he was not re-elected in 1946 while in prison.
match_headline: Virginia Politician Serves 2 Terms: In Jail and in the State Legislature

text: An article on Wednesday about a trend toward more wholesome low-alcohol beverages for health-conscious social drinkers, including a beer made with kombucha, misstated, in some copies, the allowable level of alcohol in kombucha sold as a soft drink. It is 0.5 percent, not 0.05 percent.
match_headline: From Gluten-Free Beer to Kombucha, Alcohol Options for Health-Conscious Drinkers

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the first-round match between Sloane Stephens and Victoria Azarenka at the Australian Open misstated, in some copies, Stephens’s position in the field. She was unseeded, not seeded 32nd. (She is 32nd in the world rankings.)
match_headline: Victoria Azarenka, Unseeded but Still Hungry, Ushers Sloane Stephens to an Early Exit

text: An article on Friday about two art fairs in Manhattan — Metro Curates and the New York Ceramics and Glass Fair — misstated the given name of a dealer who is showing work by the artist José Arias at the ceramics and glass fair. He is Martin Cohen, not Morton.
match_headline: Emporiums of the Waggish and Weird

text: An obituary on Friday about the scientist Jean Lindenmann misspelled the given name of one of his sons, who survives him. He is Jean-Michel, not Jen-Michel.
match_headline: Jean Lindenmann, Who Made Interferon His Life’s Work, Is Dead at 90

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about plans by Architecture for Humanity, a nonprofit design group based in San Francisco, to file for bankruptcy protection, paraphrased incorrectly in some copies a comment by Kate Stohr, a founder of Architecture for Humanity, about the group’s finances. She acknowledged a shortfall in the organization’s unrestricted funds, not that the company had spent money intended for certain purposes on other expenses.
match_headline: A Leader in Socially Conscious Architecture Is Closing Amid Financial Woes

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the jazz scene in New Brunswick, N.J., misidentified the website for the New Brunswick Jazz Project, a nonprofit organization that has helped promote and organize performances. It is nbjp.org — not nbjp.com , a Taiwanese electronics resale website.
match_headline: Already a Hub for the Arts, New Brunswick Enters Its Jazz Age

text: An article last Sunday about top free-agent pitchers who had not yet signed with teams erroneously included a player among the top position players available in free agency. Asdrubal Cabrera was not one of them because he had signed with the Tampa Bay Rays.
match_headline: Two Unsigned Aces Play a Waiting Game

text: An article last Sunday about the new AMC series “Better Call Saul,” which is to have its premiere on Feb. 8, misidentified the entity of which Charlie Collier is president. It is AMC, not AMC Networks. (Josh Sapan is president and chief executive of AMC Networks, which owns and operates AMC.)
match_headline: Before They Went Bad

text: A map with an article on Jan. 4 about the grounding in Alaska of Royal Dutch Shell’s drill rig, the Kulluk, included two imprecise locations. The locations of the rig’s first drill site in the Beaufort Sea and the Sivulliq prospect drill site are approximately 45 and 15 miles from shore.
match_headline: The Wreck of the Kulluk

text: A picture caption on Jan. 11 with a review of “China 1945: Mao’s Revolution and America’s Fateful Choice,” by Richard Bernstein, misspelled the surname of the Chinese Communist Party leader shown with Mao Zedong. He was Zhou Enlai, not Zhu.
ref_headline: China 1945: Mao’s Revolution and America’s Fateful Choice,
match_headline: ‘China 1945,’ by Richard Bernstein

text: An article last Sunday about a proposal to link seven ski resorts above Salt Lake City misidentified the country in which Arlberg, which has a similar linked valley-to-valley ski system, is located. It is in Austria, not Switzerland.
match_headline: In Salt Lake City, a Proposal to Link Ski Trails

text: An article last Sunday about the murder of the hedge fund manager Thomas Strong Gilbert Sr., for which his son, Thomas Jr., has been charged, quoted incorrectly from comments by Michael M. Thomas, a former investment banker, about the effects that wealth can have on families. He said if he were to write a book about his own privileged upbringing, he would title it “Orphans With Parents” — not “Orphans With Families.”
match_headline: The Price of Privilege

text: An article last Sunday about the selection of the 2014 Word of the Year by the American Dialect Society described incorrectly the location of shootings in California last May in a reference to the judges’ consideration of #yesallwomen, a phrase used on the Internet after the shootings. They occurred near the University of California, Santa Barbara — not on the campus.
match_headline: At the Super Bowl of Linguistics, May the Best Word Win

text: An article in the Mutual Fund Quarterly on Jan. 11 about the best-performing mutual funds misattributed two quotations. It was Maneesh J. Modi — not his co-manager Jonathan D. Coleman — who explained Janus Venture’s investment strategies using Boeing and SS&C Technologies as examples.
match_headline: Two Schools of Thought, Adding Up to Success

text: An article last Sunday about how the Danish island Samso achieved renewable energy independence misstated the amount of electricity produced and exported by Samso’s wind farms. They produce 105,000 megawatt-hours, not 105, and export 80,000 megawatt-hours, not 80.
match_headline: Green-Energy Inspiration Off the Coast of Denmark

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about criticism by top Argentine government officials of Alberto Nisman, a prosecutor who was fatally shot a day before he was to testify on his inquiry into the 1994 bombing of a Jewish community center in Buenos Aires, misspelled, in some editions, the brand name of the 22-caliber pistol that was found beside his body. It was a Bersa, not a Bursa.
match_headline: Argentine Leader Criticizes Dead Official

text: An article on Friday about the high rates of opioid prescriptions for women of reproductive age misstated the upper limit of the age range. The study looked at health insurance claims data for women ages 15 to 44 — not to 55.
match_headline: High Rates of Opioid Prescriptions Among Women Raise Birth Defect Fears

text: An article on Nov. 20 about Harvard students’ hoping to force the school to divest its fossil fuel stocks referred incorrectly to the seven students who filed a lawsuit. They are undergraduates and graduate students at the law school and the school of engineering and applied sciences, not just law students and undergraduates. (This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.)
match_headline: Harvard Students Move Fossil Fuel Stock Fight to Court

text: An article last Monday about a Supreme Court case on judicial elections, using information from a supporting brief , misstated the number of Florida Supreme Court justices who resigned following corruption scandals. It was three, not four.
match_headline: Supreme Court to Review Bans on Solicitations in Judge Races

text: An article on Thursday about Boston’s public release of its proposal to host the 2024 Summer Olympics omitted, in some editions, part of a quotation by Dan O’Connell, president of Boston 2024, about the transparency of the bid process. He said, “My apologies for a process that until now, a proof-of-concept process where there wasn’t as much outreach as there should have been, as there might have been.” He did not say “a concept process.”
ref_headline: My apologies for a process that until now, a proof-of-concept process where there wasn’t as much outreach as there should have been, as there might have been.
match_headline: Decree Reflects Rift in Boston Over 2024 Olympics

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Monday with an article about Thierry Omeyer, France’s goalkeeper in handball, misidentified the tournament at which he was competing. The photograph showed a semifinal match against Spain at the Euro 2014 handball championship, not at a semifinal match versus Spain in the recent Tournoi International in Nantes, France.
match_headline: So He Let 20 Goals Past Him? In His Sport, That’s a Great Game

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a new line of Ben Hogan golf clubs misidentified, in some copies, the company that previously produced his clubs. It was the Ben Hogan Company — not the Ben Hogan Golf Equipment Company, which is producing the new line of clubs.
match_headline: Reviving the Hogan Club Line and Returning It to Its Roots

text: An article on Friday about the collapse of Yemen’s government referred incorrectly to an attack Thursday on the Central Bank in Libya, another country whose accomplishments during 2011, the first year of the Arab Spring revolution, have been undercut by recent events. Marauding militiamen took over the Benghazi branch of the Libyan bank, not the entire institution nationwide.
match_headline: U.S. Fears Chaos as Government of Yemen Falls

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about what is likely to be the last large gathering of survivors of the Nazi concentration camps at Auschwitz this week at the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum near Oswiecim, Poland, to commemorate the 70th anniversary of the camps’ liberation at the end of World War II, referred incorrectly to a theater at the museum site that will become an educational center. It was used by Polish troops before the war, not during it. The article also misidentified the hometown of Michal Salomonovic, a survivor who plans to attend the ceremony. It is Ostrava, in the Czech Republic, not Prague.
match_headline: For Auschwitz Museum, a Time of Great Change

text: Because of an editing error, the Saturday Profile article , about Nitsana Darshan-Leitner, an Israeli lawyer who sues groups that finance terrorism operations, misidentified the location of Road 443, whose roadblocks she sued to retain, preventing Palestinians from driving there, years after a series of deadly shootings. The road is in the West Bank, not in Israel.
match_headline: Crusading for Israel in a Way Some Say Is Misguided

text: An article on Friday about the seizure of the Benghazi branch of the Central Bank of Libya, the repository for Libya’s oil revenue, by one of the country’s two warring factions misstated Libya’s daily oil output. It is less than 250,000 barrels a day, not less than 250 a day.
match_headline: Wider Chaos Threatens as Fighters Seize Branch of Libya’s Central Bank

text: An article on Friday about a partnership between Vice News and the director Chris Milk to offer virtual-reality journalism projects misstated the name of Mr. Milk’s virtual reality company. It is Vrse, not Vrse.farm.
match_headline: Vice Uses Virtual Reality to Immerse Viewers in News

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Knicks’ 113-106 victory over the Orlando Magic misidentified, in some copies, the Orlando player who banged knees with Knicks point guard Jose Calderon in the third quarter. He is Elfrid Payton — not Channing Frye, who was setting a screen on the play.
match_headline: In Unraveling Season, the Knicks String Together Reasons for Hope

text: An article last Wednesday about the difficulties faced by Afghanistan’s new president, Ashraf Ghani, in getting his cabinet nominees approved paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Ahmad Nader Nadery, the head of the Afghan Research and Evaluation Unit, a research institute in Kabul. He said that the proposed new cabinet was in some ways better than what the country had seen before — not that it was one of the best the country had ever seen.
match_headline: Charges and Clashing Interests Mar Selection of a Cabinet for Afghanistan

text: An article on Jan. 19 about the recantation by a North Korean defector, Shin Dong-hyuk, of part of his account of years of barbaric treatment in North Korea’s prison camps, misidentified the camp that Chung Kwang-il, a former inmate of North Korean prison camps, was referring to when he said he could not understand why Mr. Shin lied. It was the more brutal Camp 14, not Camp 18.
match_headline: Prominent North Korean Defector Recants Parts of His Story of Captivity

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the royal line of succession dictated by King Salman of Saudi Arabia misstated his rank among the sons of the country’s founder, King Abdulaziz, to reign as king. He is the sixth son to hold the throne, not the fifth.
match_headline: Saudi Arabia’s Succession Line Is Set, but the Nation’s Path Remains Uncertain

text: An article last Wednesday about using X-rays to read ancient scrolls recovered from a villa in Herculaneum referred incorrectly to the effects of the eruption of Mount Vesuvius on Pompeii. Pompeii was engulfed by pyroclastic flows and surges, which are mixes of hot ash and gas; it was not engulfed in lava.
match_headline: Unlocking Scrolls Preserved in Eruption of Vesuvius, Using X-Ray Beams

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the auction of the waterfront commercial district in Fire Island Pines, N.Y., misstated the status of offers made for the property. There were no offers at the asking price; it is not the case that there were no offers at all. The article, using information from an auction house representative, also misstated the price the sellers paid for the property. It was $17 million, not $20 million. In addition, the article misspelled the name of a rebuilt hotel on the property. It is Botel, not Boatel. The article also misstated the year that a previous owner, John B. Whyte, took over the Pavilion nightclub on the strip. It was 1989, not 1980. And, finally, the article misstated plans for the property. While the sellers had planned to add stories to some buildings, they never had plans to build condos.
match_headline: Renowned Gay Mecca on Fire Island Goes to Auction

text: An article in some editions on Friday about Barbara Shaum, who in 1970 became the first woman admitted to McSorley’s Old Ale House during business hours, misspelled in one instance the given name of a neighboring shopkeeper who was the second woman allowed in. She is Sara Penn, not Sarah.
match_headline: The First Woman Let Into McSorley’s Reminisces (Over an Ale, of Course)

text: An article on Monday about a slowdown in the development of solar thermal plants because of uncertainty over continuation of a federal tax credit described incorrectly the design of the Spanish company Abengoa’s Mojave Desert plant in California. Its parabolic solar panels concentrate heat to produce steam, but, unlike Abengoa’s Solana plant in Arizona, it does not have salt tanks to store the heat.
match_headline: Worry for Solar Projects After End of Tax Credits

text: An article last Wednesday about George Washington University forward Yuta Watanabe attributed an erroneous distinction to him. He is believed to be the third Japanese-born player to earn a Division I men’s basketball scholarship; he is not the first.
match_headline: Coming Off the Bench, a Basketball Ambassador

text: An article last Wednesday about cooking with kimchi, the Korean dish made of pickled vegetables, misidentified a traditional soup containing pork belly and kimchi. It is kimchi jigae (or chigae), not simply jigae (or chigae).
match_headline: Cooking With Kimchi

text: An article on Tuesday about suggestions of a shift in Saudi Arabian foreign policy with the elevation of Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, who takes a hard line on security matters, to second in line to the Saudi throne misstated the given name and omitted the middle initial of a former United States ambassador to Saudi Arabia who said the move was an effort to underscore the dynasty’s stability. He is James B. Smith, not Jeffrey. In addition, a contributors’ note was omitted. David D. Kirkpatrick reported from Cairo — not from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, the dateline for the article. (Ben Hubbard reported from Riyadh.)
match_headline: Saudi Succession Hints at Shift in Foreign Role

text: An article on Friday about new comments by President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner of Argentina regarding the death of Alberto Nisman, the lead prosecutor investigating the 1994 bombing of a Jewish center in Buenos Aires, referred imprecisely to the change in her public position. She said she was now convinced that Mr. Nisman had not committed suicide, while earlier she had raised the possibility that he had; it is not the case that she “abruptly reversed herself.” The same imprecision appeared in the headline.
match_headline: In a Shift, Argentine President Says Prosecutor’s Death Was Not a Suicide

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a ceremony in Poland marking the 70th anniversary of the liberation of the Auschwitz-Birkenau death camps at the end of World War II referred incorrectly to one survivor at the ceremony. The survivor, Halina Birenbaum, is a woman. Because of other editing errors, two accompanying picture captions misstated the day of the anniversary events. As the article correctly noted, they took place on Tuesday, not on Wednesday.
match_headline: Outliving Horror for 70 Years and Never Forgetting

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about the deaths of at least 18 people in political violence in Egypt on Sunday misstated the circumstances under which Shaimaa al-Sabbagh, a woman who was killed a day earlier, was shot by the police in Cairo. The shooting took place as the police broke up a peaceful protest, not during a clash with officers.
match_headline: At Least 18 Die in Egyptian Violence

text: A reporting credit on Tuesday for an article about a C.I.A. drone strike in Yemen that killed three suspected Qaeda fighters misstated the given name and the surname of one contributor. He is Shuaib Almosawa, not Shuaibal Mosawi.
match_headline: U.S. Drone Kills 3 Qaeda Operatives in Yemen, Continuing Policy on Strikes

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with an article about the uncertainty among New York State Assembly Democrats over a possible successor to the speaker, Sheldon Silver, misspelled, in some editions, the surname of an assemblyman from the Rochester area who was later selected as interim speaker. As the article noted correctly, he is Joseph D. Morelle, not Morrelle.
match_headline: Long Led by Silver, Assembly Democrats Face Uncertainty on a Successor

text: An article on Wednesday about efforts by a coalition of health care systems and insurers to change the way hospitals and doctors are paid misidentified a health system whose new payment structure sharply lowered hospital stays and readmissions, according to the insurer Aetna. It is NovaHealth in Maine, not Inova Health in Northern Virginia.
match_headline: Industry Group to Back Results-Focused Care

text: An article on Monday about the documentary “The Hunting Ground,” about sexual assaults on campuses, referred incorrectly to the participation of college administrators in the film. Patricia A. McGuire, the president of Trinity Washington University in Washington, D.C., appeared briefly on camera. It is not the case that no senior university officials appeared. In addition, the article, using information from the filmmakers, referred imprecisely to the willingness of other schools to be interviewed. Though the filmmakers said that the six schools at the center of the film and more than 35 others had declined to participate, they did not mention that the president of at least one, Amherst College, agreed to be interviewed. That footage was not included in the documentary.
match_headline: An Unblinking Look at Sexual Assaults on Campus

text: An article last Thursday about an artist who is popular among celebrities misstated his surname at several points. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Daniel Arsham, not Ashram.
match_headline: Why Celebrities Are So Into the Artist Daniel Arsham

text: An article on Monday about Jose A. Ramos, a possible witness in the trial over the 1979 disappearance of 6-year-old Etan Patz in New York City, misstated, in some editions, the year that Mr. Ramos pleaded guilty to sodomizing a boy in Pennsylvania. It was 1990, not 1991.
match_headline: Defense in Long-Awaited Trial Will Argue Another Man Killed Etan Patz

text: An article on Tuesday about an announcement by Kurdish activists that their militias had retaken full control of Kobani, Syria, three months after Islamic State militants seized it referred incorrectly to a Kurdish official who said the victory was the result of improved coordination between Kurdish fighters on the ground and the American-led coalition that has been pounding ISIS positions in Kobani from the air. The official, Asia Abdullah, is a woman.
match_headline: Kurd Militia Says ISIS Is Expelled From Kobani

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Wednesday about the World Food Program’s cutback of refugee aid in Uganda misidentified the nationality of the refugees who are affected. A majority are from the Democratic Republic of Congo, not from South Sudan.
match_headline: Uganda: Agency Cuts Refugees’ Rations

text: An article on Jan. 22 about efforts by two research groups to create genetically engineered bacteria that cannot survive outside a laboratory misstated the ability of the organisms to survive when denied the nutrient they required. One group could not detect any survivors among about a trillion organisms. The other could not detect any survivors out of 400 billion organisms. It is not the case that the researchers determined that only about one in a trillion were able to survive.
match_headline: Scientists Work to Contain Modified Organisms to Labs

text: An article on Wednesday about Loretta E. Lynch’s preparations for a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on her nomination to be United States attorney general misstated the number of Republicans on the committee who would have to vote for Ms. Lynch to send her nomination to the full Senate. If all Democrats voted for her, she would need two — not three — Republican supporters. The error was repeated in an article on Thursday about her appearance at the hearing.
match_headline: Lynch to Cast Herself as Departure From Holder in Bid to Be Attorney General

text: A report in the National Briefing column on Thursday about a study of university endowments referred incorrectly to the 2013 market-value rankings. Yale had the second-largest endowment that year — not Stanford, which was fourth. (Harvard was first.)
match_headline: Harvard’s Endowment Remains Biggest of All

text: An article in some editions Jan. 20 about 69 Vanderbilt Avenue, a 165-year-old home in Brooklyn that was torn down this month, misidentified the city department that ordered the house’s demolition. It is the Department of Buildings, not the Landmarks Preservation Commission. The article also misstated the involvement of John Weiss in the demolition. Though he is the commission’s deputy counsel, Mr. Weiss plays no role in ordering the destruction of a building; therefore, this was not the third building “he was forced to destroy.”
match_headline: An Eyesore, Also a Piece of History, Is Demolished in Brooklyn

text: An article last Sunday about optimism among American policy makers about the Houthis, former rebels who are now the dominant force in Yemen, described incorrectly Charlie Hebdo, which was attacked this month in Paris by two men claiming to be working on behalf of Al Qaeda in Yemen, the focus of counterterrorism operations there that the United States insists will continue. Charlie Hebdo is a satirical newspaper, not a magazine.
match_headline: Experts See Signs of Moderation Despite Houthis’ Harsh Slogans

text: An article last Sunday about the release of a video appearing to show the decapitated body of a Japanese man held hostage by the Islamic State terrorist group referred incorrectly in some editions to Al Furqan, which has posted videos of the group’s beheadings in the past but did not confirm the latest apparent killing. It is a media arm of ISIS, not a website. The article also misstated, in some editions, the number of Americans whom ISIS has beheaded in recent months. It has killed three, not two.
match_headline: Video Appears to Show Decapitated Body of a Japanese Hostage of ISIS

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the well-developed underground jihadist pipeline in Belgium, which was highlighted by the recent thwarting of a terrorist operation, misidentified the area of Brussels where two men were standing. It is central Brussels — not the adjacent Molenbeek district, where nine homes were raided by the authorities.
match_headline: Belgium Confronts the Jihadist Danger Within

text: An article last Sunday about an apartment building in Brooklyn that still lacked regular heat a year after residents sued the landlord misstated, in some editions, the surname of a lawyer with Make the Road New York, an advocacy group whose causes include housing. He is Luis Henriquez, not Hernandez.
match_headline: A Year After Suing Their Landlord, Brooklyn Tenants Still Lack Heat

text: An article last Sunday about the places where European soccer teams train during their winter break misspelled the given name of a German author who has written extensively on soccer. He is Uli Hesse, not Ulli. And because of an editing error, the article misidentified the winner of an exhibition match between A.C. Milan and Real Madrid in December in Dubai. A.C. Milan won.
match_headline: In Winter, It’s Time for a Stoppage

text: An article last Sunday about the first Super Bowl, in 1967, misidentified, in some editions, the broadcast network that featured the Harlem Globetrotters as part of its pregame programming. It was CBS, not NBC.
match_headline: Before the Bowl Was Super

text: An article last Sunday about the FX crime drama “Justified,” which just started its sixth season, misstated part of the title of a series in which Jere Burns appeared. Mr. Burns, who plays the villain Wynn Duffy on “Justified,” was in “Burn Notice,” not “Burn Unit.”
match_headline: R.V.s and Stolen Kidneys: Life on the Fringes in ‘Justified’

text: An article last Sunday about Dr. Patricia Wexler and the Upper East Side condominium that she shares with her husband, Eugene, misstated the age of their daughter, Perri. She is 32, not 34.
match_headline: Her Prescription for Home: Color

text: An article on Dec. 28 about two villages in Hampshire, England, where Jane Austen spent most of her life misstated the side of Winchester Cathedral where her gravestone is located. It is in the north nave aisle, not the south nave.
match_headline: Wandering Jane Austen’s World

text: An article last Sunday about the Academy Award nominees Eddie Redmayne and Emma Stone misstated the actress’s age. She is 26, not 27.
match_headline: Eddie Redmayne and Emma Stone on Acting, Fame and Protecting Their Privacy

text: An article last Sunday about a dating app called the League referred incorrectly to the use of the dating app Tinder. Users swipe the app 1.2 billion times a day, according to the company; that many users do not swipe the app each day.
match_headline: The League, a Dating App for Would-Be Power Couples

text: An article last Sunday about the drawbacks of a strong dollar misstated the size of the European Central Bank’s quantitative easing campaign in United States dollars. It is $1.16 trillion, not billion.
match_headline: The Strong Dollar Is Always Good, Except When It Isn’t

text: An article on Jan. 18 about children adopted from South Korea misspelled the name for Korean karaoke. It is noraebang, not nori bong. The article also described incorrectly an art piece created in conjunction with a lobbying ef ort to change Korean government regulations on adoption. The installation featured paper tags stamped with a number representing each adoptee, not with their names. And the article referred incorrectly to one adoptee’s upbringing in the United States. Kim Stoker was raised in Colorado and Virginia, not in Utah.
match_headline: Why a Generation of Adoptees Is Returning to South Korea

text: An article on Dec. 28 about the consequences of the United States’ refusal to pay kidnappers to free American hostages referred imprecisely to a Syrian journalist who had been held by the Islamic State terrorist group and said American officials did not pursue information he gave them about Americans being held by the group. The surname of the journalist, Louai Abo Aljoud, is an assumed one that he has been using for several years to protect family members still in Syria; Aljoud is not his real family name. This correction was delayed to verify Mr. Abo Aljoud’s information.
match_headline: The Cost of the U.S. Ban on Paying for Hostages

text: An article on Thursday about the death of two Israeli soldiers in a missile attack by Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shiite movement, as they drove in a disputed area near the Lebanese border misstated the surname of one of the soldiers in some editions. He was Sgt. Dor Chaim Nini, not Nimi.
match_headline: Hezbollah Kills 2 Israeli Soldiers Near Lebanon

text: An article on Wednesday about a speech by President Obama on the last day of his state visit to India in which he urged the nation to do more to protect human rights and fight climate change misspelled the surname of an Indian author who criticized the speech. He is Chetan Bhagat, not Bhagwat. And because of an editing error, a picture caption with the article misstated the day of the speech in some editions. It was Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: As Visit Ends, Obama Presses India on Human Rights and Climate Change

text: An article last Monday about the role of Glenwood Management and its founder, Leonard Litwin, in the corruption case against Sheldon Silver, the New York State Assembly speaker, misstated the middle name of Mr. Litwin’s daughter. She is Carole Litwin Pittelman, not Littman. The article also referred incorrectly at one point to Mr. Litwin as Mr. Littman.
match_headline: Developer Who Keeps Low Profile Is Embroiled in Silver Scandal

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a man in Manhattan who was shot by the police misspelled his surname, using information from the Police Department. He is Brian Quattrocchi, not Quattrochi.
match_headline: Detective Shoots Man During Stabbing in Manhattan

text: A picture in some editions on Friday with an article about earnings at ConocoPhillips and Occidental Petroleum was published in error. The photograph showed pumps near Long Beach, Calif., that are owned by the California Resources Corporation, not by Occidental Petroleum.
match_headline: ConocoPhillips and Occidental Post Losses, Reflecting Oil Price Plunge

text: An article in the Personal Business pages on Nov. 22, about donating senior discounts to charities, erroneously included an organization among watchdog websites that evaluate charities on their program, administrative and fund-raising costs. While Charity Navigator and the Better Business Bureau’s National Charity Report Index provide such services, GuideStar does not. A GuideStar representative’s message pointing out this error was misdirected at The Times.
match_headline: Getting a Senior Discount? Here’s How to Give It Away

text: A picture caption in some editions on Thursday with an article about Maria Sharapova’s victory in the semifinals of the Australian Open misspelled the given name of her opponent. As the article correctly noted, she is Ekaterina Makarova, not Ekatarina.
match_headline: Maria Sharapova and Serena Williams Win in Australian Open Semifinals

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Zacarias Moussaoui, a former operative for Al Qaeda who testified that members of the Saudi royal family were donors to the terrorist organization in the 1990s, misstated the title of King Salman of Saudi Arabia when Mr. Moussaoui alleges he met with Salman in Saudi Arabia before the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Salman was a prince, he was not the crown prince. (He became the crown prince in 2012.)
match_headline: Moussaoui Calls Saudi Princes Patrons of Al Qaeda

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the outbreak of measles related to low vaccination rates in some communities referred incorrectly to the position of the Amish on preventive vaccines. While some Amish communities object to vaccinations, “the Amish” as a whole do not.
match_headline: Vaccine Critics Turn Defensive Over Measles

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with the continuation of an article about luxury trips taken by Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey misstated, in some editions, the date of a party he attended for Howard Stern. It was on Jan. 31, 2014 — not last Friday.
match_headline: Chris Christie Shows Fondness for Luxury Benefits When Others Pay the Bill

text: An article on Monday about what analysts see as the failure of the Islamic State’s strategy in apparently killing two Japanese hostages and threatening to kill a Jordanian one without achieving its professed goals misspelled the surname of a British journalist who is one of only two Western hostages known to be still held by the militants. He is John Cantlie, not Cantile. The article also misstated the surname of a member of Jordan’s Parliament who said Jordanians were rallying behind the government. He is Naif Laymoun, not al-Amoun. (ISIS has since released a video showing the killing of the Jordanian pilot as well.)
match_headline: ISIS Tactics Questioned as Hostages Dwindle

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with the Superior Journal article, about an ice wall collapsing in Superior, Wis., misidentified, in some editions, the location of the sculptor when the accident occurred. He was outside near the wall; he was not in his trailer.
match_headline: A Crashing End to a Work of Ice a City Had Warmed Up To

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the rediscovery of a Civil War painting depicting the Battle of Resaca misstated the military rank of Daniel Butterfield, the man who commissioned it. He was a major general, not a commander.
match_headline: Civil War Mural, Obscured for Decades, Resurfaces on a Shelf

text: An article in the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about dating apps misstated, in some copies, the surname of an online dating guru in two instances. She is Julie Spira, not Stira.
match_headline: Led by Tinder, a Surge in Mobile Dating Apps

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a music review of a percussion-focused concert presented by the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, at Alice Tully Hall, reversed the identities of two performers shown. Christopher Froh is at the left and Ian David Rosenbaum is at the right.
match_headline: Wood Taps Give Works a Slick Beat

text: An editorial on Thursday about a legal case against private contractors at Abu Ghraib prison incorrectly identified one defendant. L-3 Services Inc. has settled claims against it and is no longer a defendant in the current lawsuit.
match_headline: Will Anyone Pay for Abu Ghraib?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a decline in the number of college graduates who are joining Teach for America, which serves some of the nation’s most troubled schools, referred incorrectly in some editions to the president of the Education Trust, which has been working to improve education for low-income and minority students. The president, Kati Haycock, is a woman.
match_headline: Fewer Top Graduates Want to Join Teach for America

text: An article on Wednesday about a tour of European capitals by the new Greek prime minister, Alexis Tsipras, and his finance minister, Yanis Varoufakis, to seek political support for renegotiating the terms of Greece’s bailout misidentified, in some editions, the organization led by Jean-Claude Juncker, whom Mr. Tsipras met in Brussels. Mr. Juncker is president of the European Commission, not the European Union. (The commission is the executive body of the E.U.)
match_headline: On Tour, Greek Leaders Wear No Ties and Aim for Looser Belts

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the repairs needed to locks along major American waterways misidentified the lock. It was the Barkley Lock, near Grand Rivers, Ky., not the Kentucky Lock near Paducah.
match_headline: Barges Sit for Hours Behind Locks That May Take Decades to Replace

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Wednesday about a lawsuit that seeks to legalize doctor-assisted suicide for terminally ill patients in New York State misstated, in some copies, Kathleen M. Gallagher’s job title with the New York State Catholic Conference, an organization that generally opposes such measures. She is the director of pro-life activities, not the director of anti-abortion activities.
match_headline: Lawsuit Seeks to Legalize Doctor-Assisted Suicide for Terminally Ill Patients in New York

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Thursday with an article about a City Planning Commission hearing on a proposed tower at 1 Vanderbilt Avenue in Manhattan described the photograph of the building site incorrectly. It was taken looking west, not east.
match_headline: Law Professor Opposes Grand Central Tower Plan

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about “Here’s to the Girls!: Hollywood’s Leading Ladies,” at the 92nd Street Y in Manhattan, included outdated casting information. Mitzi Gaynor, who had originally been announced as a special guest, is no longer taking part. She has been replaced by Robert Osborne, host for the Turner Classic Movies channel, who will make an appearance today and tomorrow.
ref_headline: Here’s to the Girls!: Hollywood’s Leading Ladies,
match_headline: Spare Times Listings for Feb. 6-12

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the best time to take a college admissions test misstates a reason Megan Dorsey, a test-preparation expert in Texas, and her young daughter chose the ACT over the SAT. It is because the ACT is shorter, with fewer sections, not because sections are shorter. (The sections are longer than those of the SAT.)
match_headline: When to Take the SAT

text: A chart on Page 20 this weekend with an article about gender identity at the University of Vermont renders four gender-neutral pronouns incorrectly. The pronouns are zirs and zirself, not zis and zieself (for his/hers and himself/herself); sir, not sie (for him/her); and eirself, not emself (for himself/herself).
match_headline: A University Recognizes a Third Gender: Neutral

text: A column by Gail Collins on Thursday wrongly referred to a book title. It is “God, Guns, Grits and Gravy,” not “God, Guts, Grits and Gravy.”
match_headline: ‘American Sniper’ Moral

text: An article on Friday about efforts by European and American leaders to forge a diplomatic solution to the escalating conflict in eastern Ukraine misstated, in some editions, the day that the office of the Ukrainian president, Petro O. Poroshenko, issued a statement on a meeting he had with Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany and the French president, François Hollande. It was Friday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: U.S. and Europe Working to End Ukraine Fighting

text: An article on Tuesday about France’s challenge in maintaining its revolutionary ideals with an increasingly multicultural society in which Islam is taking a more prominent place referred incorrectly to the demographics of Clichy-sous-Bois, a heavily immigrant Paris suburb where many young people have little sense of national solidarity. According to the town’s website, half of its population is under age 25, not 20.
match_headline: France’s Ideals, Forged in Revolution, Face a Modern Test

text: An article on Friday about a study that mapped DNA found in New York’s subway system misstated the system’s ridership. It carries 5.5 million riders on an average weekday, not during an average week.
match_headline: Among New York Subway’s Millions of Riders, a Study Finds Many Mystery Microbes

text: An article last Monday about a fire at the CitiStorage warehouse in Brooklyn that left decades of personal records accessible to the public included incorrect information from the company’s website about the capacity of the warehouse. It held 1.1 million cubic feet of storage space, not six million cubic feet.
match_headline: Fire at a Brooklyn Warehouse Puts Private Lives on Display

text: An article on Friday about Bode Miller’s crash in the super-G race at the Alpine world ski championships misstated the number of skiers who failed to finish the race. It was 16, not 15.
match_headline: Bode Miller Crashes in Return, Putting His Career in Doubt

text: An entry in the What’s on TV Friday highlights in some editions on Friday about “Theater Talk” on Channel 13 misstated the surname of the actor who performs “I Am Not a Hero” from the show “Brooklynite.” He is Matt Doyle, not Milne.
match_headline: What’s On TV Friday

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Jan. 21 about the American government’s main outpost in Cuba, now set to become a full-fledged embassy for the first time in five decades, misstated the year that the building began to be used as an “interests section.” It was 1977, not 1997.
match_headline: U.S. Outpost in Cuba to Step Out of the Shadows

text: An article last Thursday about a perception by Aleksei A. Navalny, the Russian opposition activist, that Russia’s recent economic troubles may have made President Vladimir V. Putin’s administration vulnerable misidentified the field of law that Mr. Navalny practiced before becoming an anticorruption campaigner. He was in corporate law, not real estate law. The same error appeared in an article on April 17, 2013, about his defiance ahead of a trial on charges of embezzlement.
match_headline: Amid Economic Woes and Public Discontent, Putin Critic Sees Opening

text: An article on Tuesday about the suspension of the $1 million Broad Prize to urban school districts gave an outdated academic position for Julian Vasquez Heilig, who discussed the effectiveness of such incentives programs. He is a professor and director of the doctorate of educational leadership at California State University, Sacramento; he is no longer an associate professor at the University of Texas, Austin.
match_headline: Billionaire Suspends Prize Given to Schools

text: An article on Tuesday about the demotion of A.T. Smith, a deputy director of the Secret Service, referred incorrectly to a hearing of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee at which Mr. Smith was scheduled to testify alongside the agency’s interim director, Joseph P. Clancy. The committee delayed Mr. Clancy’s appearance; the hearing was not postponed.
match_headline: Secret Service Deputy Demoted as Panel Chairman Presses for Firing

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Tina Maze’s victory in the combined event at the Alpine skiing world championships misstated the given name of the top-placing American in the event. She is Laurenne Ross, not Laurence.
match_headline: Tina Maze Wins the Alpine Combined and Basks Atop the Skiing World

text: An article on Monday about the Edward M. Kennedy Institute for the United States Senate, which is to open next month in Boston, described incompletely the role of Edwin Schlossberg, the husband of Mr. Kennedy’s niece Caroline, in the creation of the institute. He designed the exhibits and programs, not just the software.
match_headline: In the Mold of a Senator Who Bartered

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a television review of “Building Wonders,” a three-part “Nova” series on PBS, misidentified the structure shown in some editions. It is a modern carving using ancient techniques — not an ancient stone building in Petra, Jordan.
match_headline: Review: ‘Building Wonders’ Examines Ancient Structures on ‘Nova’

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the new Eaux Claires Music & Arts Festival this summer in Eau Claire, Wis., misstated the day tickets go on sale. It is today; they did not go on sale Wednesday.
match_headline: Review: John Zorn and Talea Ensemble Play at Ecstatic Music Festival

text: An article on Tuesday about Cyclotron Road, a technology incubator program at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, misidentified the department at Stanford from which Craig Peters and Brian Hardin received Ph.D.s. It is the materials science and engineering department, not the physics department.
match_headline: An Incubator for Innovation

text: An article on Jan. 29 about upgraded amenities offered by developers of luxury apartments in New York misspelled part of the name of a performance space designed by the architect Jonathan Marvel, who also designed the Pierhouse apartment development in Brooklyn Bridge Park. It is St. Ann’s Warehouse, not St. Anne’s Warehouse. The article also referred imprecisely to Thomas O’Brien’s role in the Greenwich Lane project. He designed its interiors; he was not the overall designer of the project.
match_headline: Over-the-Top Amenities: Sweating the Details

text: An article last Thursday about a party at MoMA PS1 in Queens on Jan. 31 included a quotation that misidentified the awards show at which Lady Gaga was to appear later that week. It was the Grammys, not the Oscars. The article also quoted incorrectly from comments by Sheikha Hoor Al-Qasimi, a MoMA PS1 board member. She said that she is traveling to Sharjah, in the United Arab Emirates; she did not say she is curating a biennial there.
match_headline: A Selfie With Lady Gaga at MoMA PS1

text: An article on Thursday about NBC’s efforts to contain the damage from admissions by its news anchor, Brian Williams, that he had exaggerated an account of a helicopter journey in Iraq misstated, in some copies, the middle initial of NBCUniversal’s chief executive. He is Stephen B. Burke, not Stephen P.
match_headline: Brian Williams Scandal Prompts Frantic Efforts at NBC to Curb Rising Damage

text: An article on Thursday about the trial of Eddie Ray Routh in the deaths of Chris Kyle, whose life is the basis of the movie “American Sniper,” and his friend Chad Littlefield misstated part of a text message Mr. Littlefield sent to Mr. Kyle. Referring to Mr. Routh, Mr. Littlefield wrote, “He’s right behind me, watch my six” — not “I’m right behind you, watch my six.”
match_headline: ‘American’ Sniper’ Jury Is Told of Troubled Ex-Marine Who Killed Chris Kyle

text: An article on Thursday about the repercussions to the Brazilian economy of a corruption scandal involving the state-owned petroleum giant Petrobras misidentified a target of the continuing investigation. Former executives of the drilling company Sete Brasil are under scrutiny, not the company itself.
match_headline: Corruption Scandal at Petrobras Threatens Brazil’s Economy

text: An article on Wednesday about activist investors’ pushing General Motors to buy back at least $8 billion worth of shares misidentified a Barclays analyst who wrote about the possibility of a stock buyback. He is Brian Johnson, not Andrew Smith.
match_headline: Do Activist Investors Target Female C.E.O.s?

text: An obituary on Friday about David Carr, a media columnist for The New York Times, included an outdated description of his wife’s profession. Jill Rooney Carr is now the international operations manager for Shake Shack; she is no longer an event planner.
match_headline: David Carr, Times Critic and Champion of Media, Dies at 58

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Lindsey Vonn’s performance in the giant slalom at the Alpine skiing world championships referred incorrectly in some copies to her boyfriend Tiger Woods’s availability to the news media at the event. Reporters were not given access to speak to him; it is not the case that he was available.
match_headline: As Tiger Woods Motivates Lindsey Vonn, Her Finale Is Positive if Not Medal Worthy

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the singer Anita Darian misstated the surname of the composer of “Concerto for Kazoo and Orchestra,” for which Ms. Darian played the kazoo in her debut at Carnegie Hall. He is Mark Bucci, not Buzzi.
match_headline: Anita Darian, a Singer With an Eclectic Range, Dies at 87

text: An obituary in some editions on Thursday about Christophe Gbenye, a radical nationalist whose rebel warriors seized control of eastern Congo in 1964, misspelled the given name of a former prime minister of the Democratic Republic of Congo. He is Antoine Gizenga, not Antione.
match_headline: Christophe Gbenye, Radical Nationalist in Congo, Dies at 88

text: Because of an editing error, a picture credit last Sunday with an article about the higher profile that Anne Hidalgo, the mayor of Paris, has enjoyed since the terrorist attacks in her city last month misidentified the organization for which the photographer, Ed Alcock, was on assignment. It is The New York Times, not M.Y.O.P., a French photo agency.
match_headline: Mayor of Paris Grows Into Her New Role as Comforter in Chief

text: An article last Sunday about efforts by Republican lawmakers in Congress to nullify the District of Columbia’s marijuana law misidentified the position held by David Zvenyach, who questioned the timing of such efforts. He is counsel to the Council of the District of Columbia; he is not the city’s general counsel.
match_headline: District of Columbia Sees Loophole in Congress’s Move to Halt Marijuana Law

text: An article in some editions on Feb. 1 about the Canadian track star Cam Levins’s victories in the mile and two-mile races at the Armory Track Invitational referred incompletely to Ray Flynn’s role at the meet. He was the director of the professional portion of the meet, which also included high school and college races; he was not the director of the overall meet.
match_headline: Canadian Upsets Olympic Medalist in Winning 2 Races

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about Shared Belief’s victory over California Chrome at the San Antonio Stakes referred incorrectly to Shared Belief’s future. He has a higher upside than California Chrome as a racehorse, but not “at stud.” (As a gelding, Shared Belief is castrated and therefore cannot be used in breeding.)
match_headline: Shared Belief Edges California Chrome in Showdown at Santa Anita Park

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the third round of the Farmers Insurance Open at Torrey Pines misstated Jimmy Walker’s score on the last hole. He made birdie, not eagle. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Jimmy Walker Chases Victory at Event That Has Mowed Down Top Talent

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the restoration of a mosaic in Upper Manhattan depicting the life of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini misspelled the name of a type of marble used in some of the restoration. It is Carrara, not Carrera.
match_headline: In Upper Manhattan, Restoring the Golden Halo of Mother Cabrini

text: An article last Sunday about the New York City schools chancellor, Carmen Fariña, and the changes she has made misstated the racial makeup of the schools’ gifted and talented programs. They are largely white and Asian, not largely white. Because of an editing error, the article also misstated, in some editions, the middle initial of a former schools chancellor. He is Joel I. Klein, not Joel V. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Chancellor Carmen Fariña Changes New York City Schools’ Course

text: A picture caption in some editions on Feb. 1 with an article about a revival of wheat farming on the East End of Long Island misidentified the location of Mecox Farms. As the article correctly noted, it is in Bridgehampton, not in Water Mill.
match_headline: On the East End of Long Island, Embracing Local Wheat

text: An article last Sunday about the ultraviolent spy movie “Kingsman: The Secret Service” misstated the age of Matthew Vaughn, the film’s director. He is 43, not 53.
match_headline: Enrolled at Her Majesty’s Spy School

text: An article last Sunday about Sheila Heti and her play “All Our Happy Days Are Stupid” described incorrectly a distinction held by Jordan Tannahill, the play’s director. Last year, he became the youngest person to win a Governor General’s award for English-language drama — one of Canada’s highest literary honors for playwrights — not the second-youngest.
ref_headline: All Our Happy Days Are Stupid
match_headline: Revenge of the ‘Impossible’ Play

text: A review on Jan. 11 about “All Eyes Are Upon Us: Race and Politics From Boston to Brooklyn,” by Jason Sokol, misidentified the ballpark where the Brooklyn Dodgers won the final game of the 1955 World Series. It was Yankee Stadium, not Ebbets Field.
ref_headline: All Eyes Are Upon Us: Race and Politics From Boston to Brooklyn,
match_headline: ‘All Eyes Are Upon Us,’ by Jason Sokol

text: An article last Sunday about Spank, an offbeat gay party that has been held in various locations around New York for seven years, misstated the surname of a performance artist who has worked with the owners of Spank. He is Nicholas Gorham, not Gorm.
match_headline: Spank Mixes Artsy Gay Party With Zine

text: An article last Sunday about the publishing industry executive Judith Regan misidentified the newspaper for which the novelist Jess Walter was working in the 1990s when Ms. Regan approached him about publishing his first novel. It is The Spokesman-Review in Spokane, Wash., not The Statesman, which is in Boise, Idaho. The article also misidentified the media position held by Roger Ailes, an executive of the cable news network for which Ms. Regan hosted a talk show. He is the chairman and chief executive of Fox News, not the president of the Fox News Channel. And the article described incorrectly Ms. Regan’s living arrangements while a student at Vassar College. While she lived with other students receiving financial aid, her housing was not designated by the school solely for financial aid students.
match_headline: Judith Regan Is Back. Watch Out.

text: An article last Sunday about the rescue and renovation of Thomas Jefferson’s home, Monticello, misstated the year that a ceremony was held to honor the Levy family’s stewardship of the house. It was 1985, not 1987.
match_headline: The Near Death, and Revival, of Monticello

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about efforts to establish a financial institution specifically to serve the pot industry in Colorado misstated when recreational use of marijuana became legal in the state. It was in December 2012, when the governor signed an executive order declaring a voter-approved amendment legalizing marijuana part of the state constitution, not “a year ago.”
match_headline: The First Bank of Bud

text: A chart on Jan. 25 analyzing the comments of more than 80 readers who responded to an article about a marijuana advocate reversed the labels for the 12 percent who said marijuana is a dangerous substance and the 26 percent who said it should not be promoted as a party drug.
match_headline: In Myanmar’s ‘Black Zones,’ Illicit Chinese Commerce Is Said to Thrive

text: A picture last Tuesday with an article about the killing of an Afghan militant accused of recruiting for the Islamic State was published in error, using information from the National Directorate of Security, Afghanistan’s spy agency. It was not in fact a picture of Mullah Abdul Rauf Khadim, the militant who was killed. Instead, it erroneously showed Shawali Khan, an Afghan man who was not connected to the recruiting. A corrective article is on Page A10.
match_headline: Afghan Strike Is Said to Kill Commander Linked to ISIS

text: An article on Thursday about fears that Indonesia’s popular anticorruption campaign has ensnared the innocent with questionable prosecutions misstated the number of American companies that took a $1 million security deposit to lease two planes to an Indonesian state airline but never delivered them, which led to the prosecution of the head of the airline. Only one American company was involved, not more than one. The article also referred imprecisely to the prison sentences imposed in the United States on two executives from the American company. They followed guilty pleas to criminal charges of tax evasion; a ruling that the executives had failed to honor their commitments was a separate civil case and did not result in prison time.
match_headline: Indonesia’s Graft Fight Strikes Fear Even Among the Honest

text: An article on Monday about congressional efforts to tie approval of any trade accords to a strong attack on international currency manipulations misattributed an estimate that such currency interventions had cost the United States as many as five million jobs over the last decade. That figure came from a study conducted by Joseph E. Gagnon, a scholar at the Peterson Institute, and C. Fred Bergsten, now its director emeritus, not from the institute itself, which does not endorse studies conducted under its aegis.
match_headline: Currency Battle Is Tethered to Obama Trade Agenda
