text: An article on Saturday about a novel by the writer Ernst Haffner that was burned by Nazi students, “Jugend auf der Landstrasse Berlin” (“Youth on the Road to Berlin”), misstated its publication date in the United States, where it will be released under the title “Blood Brothers.” It is March 3; it has not “just been published.”
match_headline: A Gritty Weimar Portrait of Youth Gangs, Restored to Renewed Acclaim

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the staging of an edition of the British music festival Bestival in Toronto in June referred incorrectly to the festival’s founder, Rob da Bank, whose real name is Robert Gorham. He is currently a D. J. for BBC Radio, not a former BBC Radio D. J.
match_headline: Bestival Will Enter North American Music Festival Market in Toronto

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about a discussion of the book “New York’s Underground Art Museum” by William Ayres and Sandra Bloodworth, at the Museum of the City of New York scheduled for Thursday, misstated the given name of an artist who will take part. She is Andrea Dezso, not Andrew.
match_headline: Spare Times Listings for Feb. 13-19

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about a gift of the Norman Rockwell painting “Boy and Girl Gazing at the Moon (Puppy Love)” to the Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge, Mass., misstated the anniversary of Rockwell’s birth that was honored by a Google Doodle in 2010 that used the painting. It was the 116th, not the 106th.
match_headline: A Charming Valentine’s Gift for the Norman Rockwell Museum

text: An obituary in some editions on Friday about Harvey J. Goldschmid, an expert on corporate law and a former member of the Securities and Exchange Commission, misstated the day he died. It was Thursday, not last Wednesday.
match_headline: Harvey Goldschmid, Ally of Ordinary Shareholders, Is Dead at 74

text: An article last Wednesday about home cooks who make their own chocolate misstated the surname of a co-owner of French Bread Chocolates in Asheville, N.C. He is Dan Rattigan, not Brown.
match_headline: The Kitchen-Counter Chocolatiers

text: An article on Nov. 12 about automated weapons paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Paul Scharre, a weapons specialist now at the Center for a New American Security. His position is that smarter weapons, which are more accurate, should be embraced because they may result in fewer mass killings and civilian casualties. He does not think that autonomous weapons, which make targeting and killing decisions without human guidance, should be embraced for that reason. This correction was delayed because editors did not follow through on the complaint.
match_headline: Fearing Bombs That Can Pick Whom to Kill

text: An article on Monday about John Kitzhaber, who resigned as governor of Oregon after questions about whether his fiancée, Cylvia Hayes, benefited financially from their relationship, misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the president of a solar-energy company who served with Ms. Hayes on the state’s Renewable Energy Working Group. He is Alan Hickenbottom, not Hickenbottem.
match_headline: Gov. John Kitzhaber of Oregon and His Fiancée Walked Tangled Path to Exit

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an article about the failure of a Grand Prix racing project in Yeongam, South Korea, misstated the year of the Yeongam track’s last Formula One race. It was 2013, not last year.
match_headline: A Korean Auto-Racing Debacle, but Hope Around the Bend

text: An article on Feb. 2 about the elimination of mandatory dues by some synagogues misstated the number of years Congregation Emanu-El in San Francisco used a voluntary-dues system and referred incorrectly to how it fared with that system. The voluntary dues experiment there lasted 13 years, it was not “short-lived.” And although dues rose after the mandatory system was restored, it is not clear whether dues had fallen when the voluntary system was first put into place.
match_headline: The ‘Pay What You Want’ Experiment at Synagogues

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about setbacks for a redevelopment proposal involving South Street Seaport in Manhattan misstated, in one instance, the role of the Howard Hughes Corporation at South Street Seaport. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, the company controls Pier 17 and major portions of the district under a long-term city lease; it is not the owner. The article also erroneously included an organization among the members of Friends of the Seaport, a group sympathetic to the Howard Hughes Corporation. The Henry Street Settlement House is not part of the coalition. And the article misspelled the surname of an author who wrote about the South Street Seaport district. He is James Lindgren, not Lingren.
match_headline: Despite Amenities, South Street Seaport Redevelopment Plans Stall Over a High-Rise

text: An article on Monday about alternative wireless networks that primarily use Wi-Fi technology described the technology’s regulatory status incorrectly. While Wi-Fi transmissions are unlicensed, they are not unregulated. Federal rules do set some parameters.
match_headline: Cellphone Start-Ups Use Wi-Fi First to Handle Calls and Take On Rivals

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the Knicks’ buying out the remainder of Amar’e Stoudemire’s contract misidentified the team the Knicks were swept by in the first round of the 2011 playoffs, at the end of Stoudemire’s first season in New York. It was the Boston Celtics, not the Nets. (The Knicks were swept by the Nets in the first round of the 2004 playoffs.)
match_headline: Amar’e Stoudemire’s Time With Knicks Done After Buyout

text: A report in the Observatory column on Tuesday about the acoustics of Cremona-era violins referred incorrectly to Nicholas Makris, an author of a recent paper in the Proceedings of the Royal Society: A. He is the paper’s senior author, not the lead author.
match_headline: Sweetest Violins Explained: Holes Fill In Blanks

text: An article last Friday about the International Monetary Fund’s approval of a new $17.5 billion bailout package for Ukraine, which is teetering on the edge of default, referred imprecisely to the circumstances under which Russia can demand to renegotiate the terms of a $3 billion loan provided to Ukraine in 2013. It can do so if Ukraine’s overall debt — not just its external debt, which is the amount owed to foreign creditors — exceeds 60 percent of its gross domestic product.
match_headline: I.M.F. Announces $17.5 Billion Package to Help Kiev Stabilize Economy

text: An article on Tuesday about the violent background of Omar Abdel Hamid el-Hussein, the suspect in the recent terrorist shootings in Copenhagen, misspelled, in some editions, the name of the Danish town where he attended a vocational school. It is Hvidovre, not Hvidore. And because of an editing error, the article quoted incorrectly from a sign that friends of Mr. Hussein placed near the spot where he was killed by the police. It said: “May Allah show mercy. Rest in peace, Captian” — not “Captain.” (Captian is a gangland title of respect.)
ref_headline: May Allah show mercy. Rest in peace, Captian
match_headline: Anger of Suspect in Danish Killings Is Seen as Only Loosely Tied to Islam

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Monday about a reunion of activists who had tried to prevent the razing of the Esperanza Community Garden on the Lower East Side in 2000 misstated, in some copies, when a former protester, Aresh Javadi, helped found the advocacy group More Gardens. It was before Esperanza’s destruction, not after.
match_headline: Wary of a New Threat, Community Garden Activists in New York Look Back

text: An article on Jan. 24 about a settlement in which the company Let’s Buy British Imports agreed to stop importing Cadbury’s chocolate omitted one use of PGPR, an emulsifier. Besides being used in American Cadbury chocolate bars, it is also present in British Cadbury chocolates under the name E476.
match_headline: After a Deal, British Chocolates Won’t Cross the Pond

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about chartering yachts misidentified the location where the Impulsive, a yacht pictured with its captain, Sean Ives, was docked. It is at the Yacht & Brokerage Show in Miami Beach, not at the Miami International Boat Show.
match_headline: The Beginner’s Guide to Chartering a Yacht With a Crew

text: Because of a production error, two articles and the continuation of a third article were omitted from some copies on Thursday. Page B13 should have included an article about Alex Rodriguez’s apology as well as other athletes’ apologies through the years, and an article about the marvelously weird lexicon of cricket. The page also should have included the continuation of the Sports of The Times column on Page B11, about reasons the Yankees should get rid of Rodriguez. The articles can be found at nytimes.com/sports.
match_headline: Memorable Sports Apologies Through the Years

text: An article in some editions last Friday about black viewership of the Academy Awards misstated the years that Ellen DeGeneres hosted the Oscar ceremony. She was the host last year and in 2007, not the last two years.
match_headline: For Oscars Telecast, Few Black Nominees Mean Fewer Black Viewers

text: An article last Saturday about expressions of concern by Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India about crimes against Catholic churches in New Delhi misstated the number of recent cases that the police commissioner said had been resolved. Three out of five have been resolved, not four out of five.
match_headline: Modi Voices Concern at Crimes Seen to Target India’s Christians

text: An article on Wednesday about a White House summit meeting on violent extremism paraphrased incorrectly from comments by the mayor the Belgium town of Vilvoorde, where the Islamic State has been heavily recruiting. He said Vilvoorde has 42,000 people, not 4,200.
match_headline: Obama Urges Global United Front Against Extremist Groups Like ISIS

text: An article last Saturday about some states’ proposals to raise taxes for the poor and cut them for the affluent, using information from a report by Keystone Research Center and Good Jobs First, misstated several estimates of revenue that could be generated by taxing the wealthy at middle-class rates.
match_headline: States Consider Increasing Taxes for the Poor and Cutting Them for the Affluent

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about the Islanders’ line of Casey Cizikas, Matt Martin and Colin McDonald misstated the day on which McDonald scored against the Buffalo Sabres. It was Sunday, Feb. 8, not Saturday, Feb. 7.
match_headline: When the Islanders Call, a Gritty Fourth-Line Wing Delivers

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the former Islanders player Bob Nystrom and his son, Eric, who plays for the Nashville Predators, misstated Eric Nystrom’s age in some copies. He is 32, not 34. The article also misstated, in some copies, the number of saves Islanders goalie Jaroslav Halak had in the game between the Islanders and the Predators on Thursday. It was 30, not 27. And also because of an editing error, a picture caption misidentified the winner of Thursday’s game in some copies. As the article correctly noted, it was the Islanders, not the Predators.
match_headline: Never an Islander, Eric Nystrom Returns Home to Nassau Coliseum

text: An article last Saturday about an effort by USA Swimming and college and club swimming coaches to help university athletic directors reinforce swimming programs facing financial problems misstated the timing of the Olympian Ariana Kukors’s departure from the University of Washington swim team. She left the program several months before — not after — it was disbanded.
match_headline: Sport Works to Stay Relevant in Changing N.C.A.A.

text: An obituary on Jan. 30 about the Greek singer Demis Roussos referred incorrectly to his mother, Olga. She was of Greek origin, not Italian, and she was not the same person as the actress and dancer Nelly Mazloum, and she never performed under that name.
match_headline: Demis Roussos Dies at 68; Greek Singer Was Internationally Known

text: An article last Monday about the 2014 George Polk Awards in Journalism misspelled the given name of the writer who received the award for commentary for an essay in The Atlantic. He is Ta-Nehisi Coates, not Ta-Nehesi.
match_headline: Polk Awards in Journalism Are Announced, Including Three for The Times

text: A picture caption in some editions on Wednesday with an article about preparations of the USA Network television crew for the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show misspelled, in some copies, the given name of the woman shown with a Great Dane named Niko and misstated her role in the competition. She is Mari Lynn Davisson, not MaryLynn, and she is the dog’s handler, not its owner.
match_headline: Meticulous Preparation Is for Broadcasters, Too

text: A report in the N.B.A. roundup last Monday about Russell Westbrook’s 41-point performance in the All-Star Game misstated, in some editions, the year Glen Rice scored 24 points in the first half of an All-Star Game, a record broken by Westbrook, who had 27 points in the first half Sunday. It was 1997, not 1987.
match_headline: Russell Westbrook, Tight-Lipped Before Game, Makes a Statement as the M.V.P.

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Thursday about the Billboard charts misidentified the chart on which Ed Sheeran’s single “Thinking Out Loud” dethroned Mark Ronson’s “Uptown Funk” from No. 1. It is the digital songs chart, not the overall singles chart.
match_headline: Reuben Cox: ‘Topical Songs’

text: An article on Tuesday about 3-D printer prosthetic hands referred incorrectly to the number of children who receive amputations as a result of lawn mower accidents each year in the United States. While approximately 9,000 children suffer injuries from lawn mowers annually, only a fraction of those — not all — result in amputations.
match_headline: Hand of a Superhero

text: Because of an editing error, a letter on Tuesday in response to an article about H.I.V.-prevention methods in Africa referred incorrectly to Bethany Young Holt, executive director of CAMI Health. She is an epidemiologist who has a master’s degree in public health and a Ph.D. She is not an M.D.
match_headline: Your Letters: Carbon Dioxide Storage, H.I.V. Drugs and Ebola Management

text: An obituary last Monday about the confectionary entrepreneur Michele Ferrero omitted part of the given name of his wife, who survives him. She is Maria Franca, not just Maria.
match_headline: Michele Ferrero, Tycoon Who Gave the World Nutella, Dies at 89

text: An editorial on Feb. 12 about patients’ use of experimental drugs incorrectly stated that a Food and Drug Administration form could take a doctor 100 hours to complete. That estimate applies to the time it would take manufacturers to apply for clinical drug trials using that form.
match_headline: Quicker Access to Experimental Drugs

text: An article on Tuesday about laws passed by states to limit the regulatory authority of cities misstated the year in which Democrats in California blocked cities from requiring restaurants to label menus with nutritional information. It was 2008, not 2010. (The law was subsequently amended in 2010.)
match_headline: States Are Blocking Local Regulations, Often at Industry’s Behest

text: An article on Wednesday about the auction of Nobel medals and other awards referred incorrectly to an Oscar that David O. Selznick received for “Gone With the Wind,” which was named best picture. Mr. Selznick won in his capacity as a producer, not as the director. (The film’s director, Victor Fleming, was also honored with an Oscar.)
match_headline: Putting a Price on Simon Kuznets’s Nobel in Economics

text: A listing in the Transactions column on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about a recent lease at 115 Broadway, using information from a publicist, misstated the given name of one of the landlord’s brokers. He is Michael Rizzo, not Richard.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Transactions

text: An article on Monday about James Hahn’s victory at the Northern Trust Open golf tournament misstated his age. He is 33, not 37.
match_headline: Birdie on Third Playoff Hole Gives Father-to-Be His First Victory

text: An article on Friday about trades made at the deadline in the N.B.A. misstated, in some copies, the surname of a player who was recently acquired by the Oklahoma City Thunder. He is Dion Waiters, not Waters.
match_headline: Heat Acquire Goran Dragic Amid Shock and Satisfaction at N.B.A. Trade Deadline

text: An article on Monday about Bol Bol, the son of the former N.B.A. player Manute Bol and a high school basketball player in the Kansas City area, misidentified the high school Bol Bol attended before he transferred to Bishop Miege. He went to Blue Valley Northwest, not Olathe Northwest.
match_headline: Emerging From a Father’s 7-Foot-6 Shadow

text: An article on Tuesday about the identity and homeland of people who spoke proto-Indo-European, a precursor to many languages, including English, misstated the surname of a linguist in two references. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Will Chang, not Chance.
match_headline: The Tangled Roots of English

text: An obituary on Feb. 14 about the Algerian-born writer and filmmaker Assia Djebar referred imprecisely to the authorities who forbade teaching in Arabic in Algerian schools when her father was a teacher. Because Algeria was legally part of France and not technically a colony, they were not “colonial authorities.”
match_headline: Assia Djebar, Novelist Who Wrote About Oppression of Arab Women, Dies at 78

text: An article on Feb. 5 about executive desktop toys misspelled the German expression for “executive toy.” It is “managerspielzeug,” not “managerspielzung.”
match_headline: Designing Distraction: Executive Toys

text: An article on Feb. 12 about efforts by Rosanne Somerson, the president of the Rhode Island School of Design, to furnish the historic house provided to her as the school’s president, misstated the surname of a faculty member. She is Jan Fairbairn, not Fairbanks. The article also misspelled the surname of the design director of the textile company Pollack, who is an alumna of the school. She is Rachel Doriss, not Dorris.
match_headline: It’s Empty at the Top

text: Because of an editing error, Oliver Sacks’s Op-Ed essay last Thursday misstated the proportion of cases in which the rare eye cancer he has — ocular melanoma — metastasizes. It is around 50 percent, not 2 percent, or “only in very rare cases.” When Dr. Sacks wrote, “I am among the unlucky 2 percent,” he was referring to the particulars of his case. (The likelihood of the cancer’s metastasizing is based on factors like the size and molecular features of the tumor, the patient’s age and the amount of time since the original diagnosis.)
match_headline: My Own Life

text: An article on Friday about the Senate Judiciary Committee’s vote to send the nomination of Loretta Lynch as the next attorney general to the full Senate misstated the actions that Senator Roy Blunt, Republican of Missouri, said he would take because of President Obama’s executive actions on immigration. Mr. Blunt said that he would reject Mr. Obama’s nominees for defense secretary and attorney general, not that he would reject all of Mr. Obama’s nominees.
match_headline: Senate Panel Approves Loretta Lynch to Be Attorney General

text: An article on Friday about questions surrounding the death of an owner of a cherry factory around the time the police discovered a marijuana-growing complex on the premises misstated, in some editions, the area of an illicit underground nursery. It is about 2,500 square feet, not 250.
match_headline: Secret Marijuana Farm Beneath Brooklyn Cherry Factory Leaves Many Mysteries

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Saturday about an agreement by the boxers Floyd Mayweather and Manny Pacquiao to fight on May 2 omitted, in some editions, passages about the role of Leslie Moonves, chief executive of CBS Corporation, in the negotiations. And because of that error, the article misidentified the person who said that Moonves and Richard Plepler of HBO were “the adults in the room” when the details of the bout were worked out. The comment was by Bob Arum, the president of Top Rank Promotions — not by Stephen Espinoza, the executive vice president and general manager at Showtime Sports. The complete article can be found at nytimes.com/sports .
match_headline: Floyd Mayweather Jr. and Manny Pacquiao Showdown Is Finally Set

text: Because of an editing error, a dance entry in the Listings pages on Friday about an Eye on Dance event at the Agnes Varis Performing Arts Center in Manhattan misstated the date. It is on Monday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Dance Listings for Feb. 27-March 5

text: An article on Page 48 this weekend about the first slavery museum in the United States misidentifies the source of the phrase “all men are created equal.” It is from the Declaration of Independence, not from the Constitution.
match_headline: Building the First Slavery Museum in America

text: An article on Tuesday about an increase in the number of Afghan refugees being forced out of or pressured to leave Pakistan misstated part of the name of an intergovernmental group that works with migrants and refugees. It is the International Organization for Migration, not the International Organization of Migration.
match_headline: Refugees Are Pushed to Exits in Pakistan

text: A picture caption last Monday with an article about mixed reactions among Chinese-Americans to the indictment of Officer Peter Liang in the death of a man in a Brooklyn housing project stairwell misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a bakery customer in Bensonhurst, Brooklyn, who said she felt the indictment was unfair. As the article noted correctly, she is Vivian Tan, not Vivan.
match_headline: Indictment of New York Officer Divides Chinese-Americans

text: An article on Friday about the effect of net neutrality rules in the Netherlands misstated the position of Martijn van Dam, who commented on the matter. He is the deputy leader in Parliament of the Dutch Labor Party, not the deputy leader of the party as a whole.
match_headline: Dutch Offer Preview of Net Neutrality

text: An article on Wednesday about the selection of Davis Love III as captain of the United States Ryder Cup team misstated, in some copies, the year that Tom Watson was the captain. It was 2014, not 2015. The article also misstated, in some copies, the year the golfer Phil Mickelson criticized the team’s system and the lack of players’ influence. It was also 2014, not 2012.
match_headline: Davis Love III Is Again Chosen to Lead U.S. at Ryder Cup

text: An article on Tuesday about Columbia’s hiring former Penn Coach Al Bagnoli as its new football coach misstated the time and location of next season’s Penn-Columbia game. It is on Oct. 17 in New York — not on Oct. 18 in Philadelphia, which was the date and location of last season’s game.
match_headline: Columbia Hires Ex-Penn Coach Al Bagnoli, Surprising Its Ivy Peers

text: An obituary on Thursday about the marine biologist Eugenie Clark misstated, in some copies, part of the name of an institution where she did research early in her career. It is the Scripps Institution of Oceanography (not Institute). And because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated the institution’s affiliation at the time Dr. Clark was there, in the 1940s. While it was part of the University of California, it was not part of the University of California, San Diego, which was established in 1960.
match_headline: Eugenie Clark, Scholar of the Life Aquatic, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Friday about Irving Kahn, Wall Street’s oldest living active professional investor, referred incorrectly to the location of DeWitt Clinton High School, which Mr. Kahn attended. At the time, it was in Manhattan — not the Bronx, where it relocated in 1929.
match_headline: Irving Kahn, Oldest Active Wall Street Investor, Dies at 109

text: An article on Saturday about Shahid King Bolsen, an American convert to Islam whose online calls for protests against corporate interests in Egypt have fueled a new wave of violence directed at businesses across the country, misspelled the surname of another American who emerged as a propagandist for Islamist violence, through his affiliation with Al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. He was Samir Khan, not Kahn.
match_headline: Online, American Helps Fuel Attacks in Egypt

text: An article on Feb. 17 about engineering reports that were altered to minimize insurance payments on homes damaged by Hurricane Sandy included an incorrect spelling from court documents for the surname of a Long Island woman who discovered that the report on her home had been doctored. She is Deborah Ramey, not Raimey. The article also misstated the name of the firm that was sent to provide a second assessment on Ms. Ramey’s property. It is U.S. Forensic, not U.S. Forensics.
match_headline: Hurricane Sandy Victims Say Damage Reports Were Altered

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actor Leonard Nimoy misstated the year his first autobiography, “I Am Not Spock,” was published. It was 1975, not 1977.
match_headline: Leonard Nimoy, Spock of ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 83

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Feb. 23 about Turkey’s military operations in Syria to recover the remains of a major historical figure and to evacuate the guards at his tomb, which was threatened by the Islamic State, misidentified the Kurdish fighters who have helped battle the militants but who Turkey argues are an extension of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, an outlawed separatist group. They are Syrian Kurds — not the pesh merga, who are the military forces of Iraqi Kurdistan.
match_headline: Turkish Military Evacuates Soldiers Guarding Tomb in Syria

text: A headline on a report in the National Briefing column on Friday about Gov. Gary Herbert’s criticism of the Utah House for not considering his plan to expand health services misidentified the program in question. It is Medicaid, not Medicare.
match_headline: Undermining Children’s Insurance

text: An article on Thursday about walking tours in the Vista Las Palmas neighborhood of Palm Springs, Calif., described the geographic location of the city incorrectly. Palm Springs is in the desert, at the base of the San Jacinto Mountains — not in the mountains themselves.
match_headline: In Mecca of Modernism, a New Pack of Devotees

text: A picture of a stolen Picasso painting, “La Coiffeuse,” in some editions on Friday with an article about its discovery in Newark was printed upside down, erroneously showing the lighter colors at the top. The correctly displayed image can be found at nytimes.com/nyregion . The article also misstated, in some copies, the day on which Loretta E. Lynch, the United States attorney for the Eastern District of New York, filed a civil complaint to forfeit the painting and return it to France. It was Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: Stolen Picasso Work Is Seized in Newark

text: An article on Friday about the early starters in the first round of the Honda Classic golf tournament, who had to practice before sunrise, misstated the date when clocks spring forward for daylight saving time. The change will be Sunday, not Monday.
match_headline: Practicing in the Dark, Some Early Starters Grumble at the Honda Classic

text: An obituary on Saturday about the Rev. Theodore M. Hesburgh, a former president of the University of Notre Dame, referred imprecisely to President Ronald Reagan’s commencement address at Notre Dame in 1981. It was his first major appearance outside Washington after the assassination attempt against him, not his first major appearance anywhere since the attempt. (He had addressed Congress the previous month.)
match_headline: Rev. Theodore Hesburgh, 97, Dies; Lifted Notre Dame and Advised Presidents

text: An article on Tuesday about the divergent approaches of President Obama and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel to the perils of a nuclear-armed Iran quoted incorrectly from a speech by Mr. Netanyahu at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee conference. He said: “Today, we are no longer silent. Today, we have a voice. And tomorrow, as prime minister of the one and only Jewish state, I plan to use that voice” — not “I plan to use that state.” The article also referred incorrectly to the guests the White House invited to a trade meeting on Tuesday at a time that would make it hard for them to attend Mr. Netanyahu’s speech. It was just House Democratic aides, not House Democrats or their aides.
ref_headline: Today, we are no longer silent. Today, we have a voice. And tomorrow, as prime minister of the one and only Jewish state, I plan to use that voice
match_headline: Obama and Netanyahu Play Down Rancor on Iran, but Views Still Differ Sharply

text: A reporting credit with an article on Friday about a debate over whether British intelligence services were at fault for the radicalization of Mohammed Emwazi, the Islamic State militant raised in West London who is known as Jihadi John, misstated the location of one contributor, Eric Schmitt. He contributed from Ndjamena, Chad — not from Washington.
match_headline: ‘Jihadi John’ From ISIS Execution Videos Was Under Watch by British Intelligence

text: An article on Saturday about negative interest rates in Europe misstated the effect on European bond prices as a result of the European Central Bank’s decision to purchase hundreds of billions of euros’ worth of bonds. Prices rose sharply; they did not plunge. (Yields, which move inversely to bond prices, did plunge.)
match_headline: In Europe, Bond Yields and Interest Rates Go Through the Looking Glass

text: An article on Tuesday about a report’s finding that the European Union will fail to meet its goal of significantly reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 unless it takes more aggressive measures erroneously attributed a distinction to Germany. Germany and Belgium — not just Germany — are the only countries in the European Union not on track to meet their 2020 targets in emissions.
match_headline: Europe Unlikely to Meet Climate Goal, Study Finds

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the death of a boy at his family’s home in Brooklyn, using information from the New York Police Department, misstated his age in some copies. He was 3, not 4. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Boy, 3, Is Found Dead in Family’s Brooklyn Home

text: An article on Tuesday about the rapid global expansion of the Abu Dhabi airline Etihad erroneously included a city among those without direct flights from the United States by an American airline. United Airlines recently started thrice-weekly service to Chengdu, China, from San Francisco; it is not the case that no American airline serves Chengdu directly from the United States.
match_headline: Etihad Airways’ Rapid Growth Frustrates Rivals

text: An article last Wednesday about home builders’ targeting of affluent buyers misstated the inspiration for the former estate upon which the luxury-home builder Toll Brothers is building its Liseter development in Newtown Square, Pa. It was Montpelier, James Madison’s home — not Monticello, Thomas Jefferson’s home.
match_headline: In Tepid Housing Market, Builders Cater to Desires of Well-Off

text: An article on Tuesday about consumer spending behavior at a time of lower gas prices misstated the point at which light trucks and S.U.V.s came to account for 56 percent of total auto sales. The figure was for January 2015, not for last year.
match_headline: Saving Big on Energy Bills, People Take It to the Bank

text: Because of an editing error, an Op-Ed article on Tuesday misstated the change the writer experienced while imprisoned in Egypt. He abandoned the ideology of Islamism — not of Islam.
match_headline: The Education of ‘Jihadi John’

text: An article on Wednesday about the passage of legislation banning the sale and possession of beef in the Indian state of Maharashtra erroneously attributed a distinction to Maharashtra. At least one other Indian state, Gujarat, has already banned the sale of beef; Maharashtra is not the first state to do so. The error was repeated in the headline. Because of an editing error, the article also referred incorrectly to the victory by the Bharatiya Janata Party, which had promoted the ban, in Maharashtra state elections in October. It won the most votes, but not a majority.
match_headline: Indian State Bans Possession and Sale of Beef

text: An article on Friday about the cost effectiveness of the United States’ $1.3 billion program to stop H.I.V. infection in Africa misidentified the organization that gave the Young Investigators award to Nathan Lo, a student at Stanford Medical School. It was awarded by the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections, which is affiliated with the International Antiviral Society-USA — not by the International AIDS Society, which is based in Geneva.
match_headline: U.S. Push for Abstinence in Africa Is Seen as Failure Against H.I.V.

text: An article on Tuesday about preparations by the Fire Department of New York to swear in its first lesbian chaplain described incorrectly the class-action lawsuit that led to the hiring of female firefighters. It was filed by just one applicant, Brenda Berkman, not by several women. The article also misspelled the surname of the president of the United Women Firefighters. She is Sarinya Srisakul, not Sriaskul.
match_headline: New York Fire Dept., Diversifying Ranks, Is Set to Swear In First Lesbian Chaplain

text: An article on Wednesday about Nextdoor, a social network aimed at neighborhood-size communities, using information from the company, misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the leader of a neighborhood association in Sacramento. He is Isaac Gonzalez, not Gonzales.
match_headline: Nextdoor Social Network Digs Deep Into Neighborhoods

text: An article on Wednesday about Andrew Lack’s expected return to NBC misstated, in some editions, the occasion for a party at which Brian Williams called Mr. Lack the best boss for whom he had ever worked. The party was for Mr. Williams’s 10th anniversary as anchor of “NBC Nightly News,” not his 10th anniversary at NBC. (He joined the network in 1993.)
match_headline: NBC News Is Said to Woo Former Chief to Return

text: A report on Feb. 5 on the Currents page about Biblioteca wallpaper listed an incorrect telephone number for more information. It is 347-809-3494.
match_headline: Like a Kindle, Just Spread Out

text: An editorial Sunday about governors running for president misstated a proposed cut to the Louisiana State University System budget. It’s 6 percent, not 40 percent, which was widely expected before Gov. Bobby Jindal proposed on Friday to reduce the cut by adjusting tax breaks to raise revenues.
match_headline: Governors Can Run, but They Can’t Hide

text: An article on Wednesday about the eruption of tensions between Iraq and the United States over how to battle the Islamic State misspelled the surname of an aide to Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi and mistranslated comments he made about American forces’ readiness to move against the militants in Mosul. The aide is Ali al-Alaaq, not Alaa, and he said, “If the Americans continue procrastinating about the time it will take to liberate the country, Iraq will liberate Mosul and Anbar without them.” He did not say that the Americans, in fact, continue to procrastinate.
ref_headline: If the Americans continue procrastinating about the time it will take to liberate the country, Iraq will liberate Mosul and Anbar without them.
match_headline: Iraqi Campaign to Drive ISIS From Tikrit Reveals Tensions With U.S.

text: An article on Tuesday about the Chinese military authority’s release of a list of 14 generals who are under investigation or have been convicted of graft misstated the rank of Guo Zhenggang, one of those under investigation. He is a major general, not a rear admiral.
match_headline: China Names 14 Generals Suspected of Corruption

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about work on the replacement for the Tappan Zee Bridge through cold weather misidentified, in some editions, plastic items that workers use to keep the concrete warm. They are blankets, not buckets.
match_headline: Doubling Up on Long Johns and Gloves to Keep Tappan Zee Bridge Project Going

text: An article on Thursday about virtual-reality companies’ efforts to resolve motion sickness problems before putting products on the shelf misstated Google’s role in a funding round for Magic Leap, a company developing an augmented reality headset. It was the lead investor, not the only one.
match_headline: To Bring Virtual Reality to Market, Furious Efforts to Solve Nausea

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about runners in Central Park who brave the cold weather misstated the surname of a 46-year-old runner who came out after the sun came up. He is Mark Kozma, not Koans.
match_headline: Photos: Springy Steps in Icy Gloom

text: An article on Saturday about the Los Angeles Kings’ season since defenseman Slava Voynov was suspended after his arrest on suspicion of domestic violence referred incorrectly in some editions to a detective from Redondo Beach, Calif., who testified during a pretrial hearing in Voynov’s case. The detective, who was not named in the article, is a man.
match_headline: Kings Are Surging Without Slava Voynov as He Awaits Trial

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Rev. Malcolm Boyd, an Episcopal priest and an author who challenged racism, war and religious complacency in the 1960s and ‘70s, referred incorrectly to the Rev. Philip Berrigan, a Roman Catholic priest and peace activist. He was a Josephite, not a Jesuit like his brother Daniel.
match_headline: Rev. Malcolm Boyd, an Author, Activist and Counterculture Rebel, Dies at 91

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about an announcement of retaliatory steps against the United States by President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela, who said Washington was meddling in Venezuelan affairs, rendered incorrectly part of the name of the North Dakota city that is home to four American missionaries who were held and questioned in Venezuela over four days before being released. The city is Devils Lake, not Devil’s Lake.
match_headline: Detained American Missionaries Leave Venezuela

text: An article on Wednesday about the Food and Drug Administration’s announcement that labels for testosterone products must start acknowledging heart risks, using information from the agency, misstated the date by which sponsors of the products have to respond to the agency’s requirement. The deadline is Wednesday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Drugs Using Testosterone Will Label Heart Risks

text: An article on Feb. 20 about an alert from the Food and Drug Administration that a superbug might be spreading because of diagnostic scopes that are difficult to sterilize misstated the number of patients at the Ronald Reagan U.C.L.A. Medical Center who hospital officials said had been sickened by bacteria on scopes. There were seven patients, not nine.
match_headline: Deadly CRE Germs Linked to Hard-to-Clean Medical Scopes

text: An article on Friday about an Alabama coal producer’s libel suit against Terrence Collingsworth, a plaintiffs’ lawyer known for suing multinational corporations on charges of violating human rights overseas, paraphrased incorrectly a comment by Sandra Baron, an expert in libel law. She said it was highly unusual for a lawyer to be sued for slander, not “highly usual.”
match_headline: Companies Turn Tables on Human Rights Lawyers

text: An article on Sunday about the efforts to quicken the pace of sporting events misstated the surname of a former president of IMG Sports and Entertainment who said: “The N.F.L. is three hours long, but when there is a play, it’s a quick pace. But I think with the younger demographic in social media, the pace of play is probably weighted more than the length of game.” He is George Pyne, not Pye.
match_headline: Every Second Counts in Bid to Keep Sports Fans

text: A picture on Friday with the Weekend Miser column , about a series of free Saturday events at the Brooklyn Museum, was published in error. The photograph, provided by the museum, showed members of the group Soul Science Lab, not the band Water Seed.
match_headline: Events at the Brooklyn Museum and the United Palace Theater

text: An article last Sunday about India’s budget misstated, in some copies, the cost of the country’s subsidy programs for food, fuel and fertilizer. It is around $40 billion, not $14 billion. The article also misstated, in some copies, the given name and the surname of the chief economist at Anand Rathi Financial Services in Mumbai, who said the budget reduced stumbling blocks for investors. He is Sujan Hajra, not Sujat Hakra.
match_headline: India’s New Budget Aims to Boost Growth

text: An article last Sunday about the establishment of a food co-op in Windsor Terrace, Brooklyn, misstated Jeremiah Fox’s affiliation with the Windsor Terrace Food Co-op board. Mr. Fox, who is helping oversee the store’s design, will join the board this year; he is not a current member.
match_headline: In Brooklyn, First Comes Gentrification, Then Comes a Food Co-op

text: A listing of information in some copies last Sunday with a dining review of Ani Ramen House in Montclair, N.J., misstated the price range of appetizers and entrees. Appetizers cost between $2 and $6, not between $10 and $14, and entrees cost $12 to $16, not $16 to $34.
match_headline: Pillowy Pork Buns and Noodles to Slurp

text: A picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about an exhibit at the Samuel Dorsky Museum of Art in New Paltz, N.Y., about Videofreex, a creative collective from the late 1960s and 1970s, misidentified the creator of the work “Videophones and Videomirrors.” The project, which included an open mouth superimposed over a person’s face, is by David Cort — not by Ann Woodward, who took a photograph of the piece.
match_headline: Before YouTube, Experimenting With Video

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about PeckaKucha Night Hamptons, a program that invites people to share ideas or projects through brief presentations, described incorrectly the kind of sauerkraut sold by one speaker, Nadia Ernestus. It is handmade, not homemade.
match_headline: The Creativity of Almost Anything

text: An article last Sunday about a long-running barn dance outside Arthur, N.D., referred incorrectly to the 1960s Midwestern rock band Dee Jay and the Runaways, which used to play Johnson’s Barn. The band was from Spirit Lake, Iowa — not Spirit Lake, Minn.
match_headline: Johnson’s Barn, a North Dakota Institution, Plans Its Last Dance

text: An article on Feb. 8 about the classical composer Thomas Adès, who has influenced many younger musicians in pop and classical music, included a misattributed quote referring to Mr. Adès’s “Arcadiana.” It was the Calder Quartet violinist Andrew Bulbrook who said, “Oh, wow, I’m on a concert with the greatest string quartet composed in the last 50 years!” It was not the composer Andrew Norman, though he is an Adès fan. (The error also appeared in a music review about the JACK Quartet and the Calder Quartet on Feb. 26.)
match_headline: They’re Always Borrowing His Stuff

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about a case before the Supreme Court regarding federal subsidies under the Affordable Care Act misstated the day the court was to hear the case, King v. Burwell. Justices heard arguments Wednesday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: How an Adverse Supreme Court Ruling Would Send Obamacare Into a Tailspin

text: An article on Feb. 15 about people who have been publicly shamed as a result of messages they posted on social media misstated the time frame in which Adria Richards, an employee at SendGrid, a Colorado-based email delivery service, was let go from the company. She was terminated the same day a distributed denial of service attack (DDoS) was launched against SendGrid’s website, not the day after.
match_headline: How One Stupid Tweet Blew Up Justine Sacco’s Life

text: A picture caption on Feb. 22 with an article about amateur journalism in the favelas of Rio de Janeiro misstated the name of the area where the police were shown on patrol. The photograph was taken in Vila Cruzeiro, not Vila Aliança.
match_headline: ‘The Media Doesn’t Care What Happens Here’

text: An article on Feb. 15 about the cabaret performer Bridget Everett misspelled the given name of a world-renowned singer mentioned by Ms. Everett. She is Barbra Streisand, not Barbara.
match_headline: Bridget Everett, Curves and All

text: An article on Feb. 22 about the effect of frequent photo-taking on memory misidentified the British broadcaster that airs the program “Black Mirror,” an episode of which features human beings who have developed memory “grains” that record sound and images. It plays on Channel 4, not on the BBC.
match_headline: Shutterbug Parents and Overexposed Lives

text: An article last Sunday about the sartorial choices made by dog handlers on the dog-show circuit misstated the type of tie worn by Jessy Sutton, a dog presenter. It was a regular tie, not a bow tie.
match_headline: Westminster’s Rule No. 1: Don’t Outshine the Dog

text: An article on Feb. 26 about basket studies, which group cancer patients in a new way, referred incorrectly to the treatment Erika Hurwitz underwent for a rare cancer of white blood cells. Before trying a melanoma drug that made her cancer undetectable, she had been treated unsuccessfully with chemotherapy, not with radiation.
match_headline: A Faster Way to Try Many Drugs on Many Cancers

text: An article on Monday about the lack of uniform numbers available to Yankees players because the team has retired so many misstated the number of uniform numbers the St. Louis Cardinals have retired. It is 12, not 13.
match_headline: 2=Jeter, 3=Ruth, 4=Gehrig. ... In the Bronx, Numbers Are Finite.

text: An article on Friday about Jeb Bush’s struggle to win over Republicans in Iowa misspelled the name of a county in the state. It is Greene County, not Green.
match_headline: Jeb Bush May Be One Bush Too Many for Rank-and-File Iowa G.O.P.

text: An article on Friday about a jet that skidded off a runway at La Guardia Airport on Thursday morning and crashed through a fence, stopping just moments before it would have plunged into Flushing Bay, misstated the number of people killed in a jetliner crash at the airport in 1992. It was 27, not 19.
match_headline: Plane Avoids Disaster as It Skids Off a Runway at La Guardia Airport

text: An article on Feb. 23 about an animal-rights activist accused of stealing two ducks from a foie gras supplier in Ferndale, N.Y., misstated, in some editions, the name of the organization that posted video clips from her foray. It is the Animal Protection and Rescue League, not the Animal Rights and Protection League.
match_headline: Two Missing Ducks, a Video and a Felony Charge in an Episode at a Foie Gras Farm

text: A picture on Friday with a report in the DealTalks Online listing about the sale of the Long Island estate of Peter B. Madoff, which was confiscated by the federal government after Mr. Madoff pleaded guilty to crimes related to the Ponzi scheme of his brother, Bernard L. Madoff, was published in error. The photograph showed Shawn Elliott, a real estate broker, not Peter Madoff.
match_headline: Peter Madoff’s Former Home Sells for $3.5 Million

text: An article last Monday about Chinese technology companies’ efforts to monitor food safety misspelled the given name of a shopper who was testing a smartphone tracking feature. She is Xu Guilin, not Guillin.
match_headline: China’s Long Food Chain Plugs In

text: An article on Wednesday about the growth of solar energy production in Japan misspelled the name of an island near Nagasaki on which a real estate developer hopes to build a solar power plant. It is Ukujima, not Ukushima.
match_headline: Japan’s Growth in Solar Power Falters as Utilities Balk

text: A headline on Jan. 31 with an article about Chris Lewis, a top high school basketball player, overstated his connection to Harvard. While Lewis, a junior, has verbally committed to play for Harvard beginning in 2016, he has not applied or been accepted to the university and, thus, is not yet “Harvard-bound.”
match_headline: With Eye on Harvard, Basketball Player Has 2 Careers on His Mind

text: A picture caption in some editions on Friday with an article about the women’s basketball team at Florida Gulf Coast University misspelled the given name of guard Kaneisha Atwater’s son. He is Andarious Fulton, not Aendrious.
match_headline: Success Runs Deeper Than All the 3-Pointers

text: An article on Thursday about the World Press Photo contest misstated the number of times the photographer Gary Knight has been chairman of the contest jury. He has headed it two times, not four. The article also misidentified the subject of a photograph taken by Giovanni Troilo at the studio of the artist Vadim Vosters outside Brussels. The photograph depicts a naked male model stretched out on a table; it does not depict Mr. Vosters.
match_headline: World Press Photo Revokes Prize

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about diplomatic disputes over Indonesia’s campaign to execute drug offenders, mostly foreigners convicted of smuggling, misstated, in some editions, the day that the Reuters news service reported that two Australians had been flown to an Indonesian island where executions are carried out. It was Wednesday morning, not Tuesday evening. Also because of an editing error, the article overstated what was known about the transfer of eight remaining prisoners to the island last week. Some had already been transferred as of last Tuesday, but it was not clear how many; it is not the case that all eight remained to be transferred.
match_headline: Countries Questioning Indonesia’s Push to Execute Drug Offenders

text: An article on Friday about a study of Twitter use by the Islamic State militant group referred imprecisely to the role of Google Ideas in the study. It financed the study, which was published by the Brookings Institution, but did not contribute research or other work; the study was not a “collaboration” of the Brookings Institution and Google Ideas.
match_headline: ISIS Is Adept on Twitter, Study Finds

text: An article on Friday about a leadership void among Russia’s opposition left by the murder of Boris Y. Nemtsov, an outspoken Kremlin critic, misspelled the surname of an opposition politician who said it was not clear that his colleagues could increase their presence in Parliament in 2016 elections. He is Vladimir A. Ryzhkov, not Ryzkhov. The article also misstated part of the address of a website established in Latvia last year by a journalist, Galina Timchenko, after she was fired from a respected Russian news organization. It is Meduza.io, not Meduza.com.
match_headline: With Nemtsov’s Killing, a Leadership Void Widens for Russia’s Opposition

text: An article on Thursday about the role of the chief counsel for Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey in brokering a settlement with ExxonMobil over an environmental contamination lawsuit misstated the middle initial of the judge who was to decide on the case. He is Michael J. Hogan, not Michael S.
match_headline: Christie’s Office Drove Exxon Settlement, Ex-Official Says

text: An article last Tuesday about Padraig Harrington’s victory at the Honda Classic golf tournament misstated, in some editions, his score on the second hole of the playoff, No. 17. He made par, not birdie.
match_headline: Harrington, 43, Beats the Yips and, in a Playoff, a Rival Half His Age

text: An article on Monday about a federal effort aimed at improving children’s health by educating mothers misidentified the profession of S. Josephine Baker, whose work around the turn of the 20th century with poor mothers and children in the immigrant communities of New York City inspired later programs. She was a medical doctor, not a nurse.
match_headline: Visiting Nurses, Helping Mothers on the Margins

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a debate over the confirmation of a Jewish student to U.C.L.A.’s Judicial Board misstated the number of members on the Undergraduate Students Association Council, which ultimately approved the nomination. It has 14 members, not seven.
match_headline: In U.C.L.A. Debate Over Jewish Student, Echoes on Campus of Old Biases

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with an article about tensions at the Brooklyn Children’s Museum over the direction of its expansion misstated the cost of an annex to the museum in the Dumbo neighborhood. As the article correctly noted, the annex is being donated; it did not cost the museum $80 million.
match_headline: With Expansion, Brooklyn Children’s Museum Is Accused of Forsaking Its Community

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about “The Events,” at New York Theater Workshop in Manhattan, misstated the number of choruses involved in the production. It is five, not seven. Another caption with the article misstated the position of Rosemary McKenna with Actors Touring Company, which is producing the work. She is trainee associate director, not assistant music director.
match_headline: ‘The Events’ Uses Local Choirs for Vocals, Minus a Script

text: An article on Tuesday about South Koreans’ divided reactions to a knife attack on the United States ambassador, Mark W. Lippert, in Seoul referred incorrectly in some editions to Mr. Lippert’s facial injuries. He was slashed on his right cheek, not his left.
match_headline: South Koreans Divided on Reactions to Knife Attack on U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert

text: An article on Wednesday about the Senate race in Maryland with the retirement of Barbara Mikulski misstated the position of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, which is rallying behind one candidate, regarding Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat. While the organization has urged presidential candidates to adopt Ms. Warren’s populist positions, it has not endorsed her for president.
match_headline: Top Maryland Democrats Ponder Post-Mikulski Options

text: An article on Wednesday about gamma rays observed in a distant dwarf galaxy that could be evidence of dark matter misidentified one of two groups that found the galaxy, known as Reticulum-2, in data from the Dark Energy Survey. It was a group from Cambridge University, not a group led by Alex Geringer-Sameth of Carnegie Mellon University. (Dr. Geringer-Sameth’s group used the information to scour telescope data and produce the gamma ray observation.)
match_headline: Gamma Rays May Be Clue on Dark Matter

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the shooting of an unarmed black man by police in DeKalb County in Georgia misstated the surname of the victim in some editions. He is Anthony Hill, not Hall. (The error was repeated in a picture caption.)
match_headline: Police Killing of Unarmed Georgia Man Leaves Another Town in Disbelief

text: An article on March 4 about efforts by Columbia University graduate students to unionize misstated the range of the stipends that the university’s teaching and research assistants receive. They are paid $20,000 to $44,000, not $22,000 to $44,000.
match_headline: Columbia Graduate Students Push for a Labor Union

text: An article on Tuesday about the viewing for Cardinal Edward M. Egan’s body misstated, in some editions, his placement as archbishop of New York. He was the ninth archbishop, not the eighth.
match_headline: With Simple Bow, Public Mourning for Cardinal Egan Begins

text: An article on Tuesday about the Princeton women’s basketball team referred incorrectly to the milestone the team would reach by defeating Penn on Tuesday night. Princeton, which won 55-42 and finished the regular season with a 30-0 record, now has the first perfect regular season by an Ivy League basketball team since the Penn men’s team in 1970-71 — not “the first perfect regular season accomplished by a men’s or women’s basketball team in Ivy League history.”
ref_headline: the first perfect regular season accomplished by a men’s or women’s basketball team in Ivy League history.
match_headline: Like Kentucky Men, Princeton Women Close In on Perfection

text: An article on Wednesday about the awarding of the Pritzker Prize to the German architect Frei Otto, who died on Monday, misstated the given name and the surname of an architect who collaborated with Mr. Otto on the West German pavilion for the Montreal Expo in 1967. He was Rolf Gutbrod, not Ralph Gurbrod.
match_headline: Pritzker Prize for Frei Otto, German Architect, Is Announced After His Death

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the architect Frei Otto misstated his wife’s given name. She is Ingrid, not Amanda. The obituary also misstated the year he founded the Institute for Lightweight Structures at the College of Technology in Stuttgart, Germany. It was 1964, not 1954.
match_headline: Frei Otto, Architect, Dies at 89; the Soap Bubble Was an Inspiration

text: An article on Feb. 26 about upcoming sales omitted one of the brands that created a capsule collection with Nordstrom. The collection was created by Topshop, Topman and Nordstrom, not just by Topshop and Nordstrom.
match_headline: Shopping Sales and Events in New York City

text: An article last Thursday about Evening Bar, in the Smyth hotel in TriBeCa, misidentified one of the bars where Anne Robinson, who helped develop the drinks menu, previously worked. It is Booker and Dax, not the Library.
match_headline: At Evening Bar in TriBeCa, a Homey Feeling

text: An editorial on Wednesday about a medical marijuana bill misstated the day that it was introduced in the Senate. It was on Tuesday, not Monday.
match_headline: A Sensible Bill on Medical Marijuana

text: Because of editing errors, an article on Monday about the code of silence in the New Delhi neighborhood that is home to Mukesh Singh, a man convicted of the gang rape of a woman on a bus in 2012 who is featured in a British-made documentary about the crime, misidentified, in some editions, the person who said he was driving the bus on the night of the attack but did not take part, and the person who described intestines being pulled from the victim’s body. In both cases, it was Mukesh Singh, not his older brother, Ram, another of the accused men, who was found hanged in his jail cell before his trial.
match_headline: In Indian Rapists’ Neighborhood, Smoldering Anger and Code of Silence

text: A news analysis article on Wednesday about a debate over protocol touched off by an open letter to Iran sent by Republican senators who object to the nuclear deal President Obama is negotiating with Iran misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a veteran of the Ronald Reagan and George W. Bush administrations who said the letter was “not an interference in negotiations.” He is Elliott Abrams, not Elliot. The article also referred incorrectly to the director of the Foundation for Strategic Research in Paris, who said that if the deal were taken to the United Nations Security Council for approval, it would enshrine legal obligations on Iran. The director, Camille Grand, is a man.
match_headline: Politics and Tradition Collide Over Iran Nuclear Talks

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about concern among Afghans over President Ashraf Ghani’s enlistment of Pakistan’s help to pressure Taliban leaders to join peace talks misstated the timing of a warning by Abdul Rab Rassoul Sayyaf, an Afghan mujahedeen commander, about the perils of getting closer to Pakistan. It took place on Feb. 15, not “in the last week.”
match_headline: Afghan Peace Efforts Reopen Wounds Over Pakistan

text: An article on Wednesday about the BBC’s suspension of Jeremy Clarkson, the host of the British car program “Top Gear,” after a mysterious “fracas” with a producer referred imprecisely to the history of the show. It initially aired in 1977 and was relaunched in 2002; it did not begin in 2002.
match_headline: BBC Suspends Jeremy Clarkson, Host of ‘Top Gear,’ After String of Warnings

text: An article on Wednesday about the copyright infringement trial involving the song “Blurred Lines” referred imprecisely to the damages awarded to the family of Marvin Gaye. The family had the option of choosing $7.3 million in actual damages or $9,000 in statutory damages; they could not collect both.
match_headline: ‘Blurred Lines’ Infringed on Marvin Gaye Copyright, Jury Rules

text: An article on Thursday about families in which members from two generations are retired at the same time misstated the given name of a retiree. He is Erwin Marke, not Earle.
match_headline: Two Generations, Retired and Together

text: An obituary on Thursday about the jazz trumpeter Lew Soloff misstated the year that Blood, Swear & Tears’ second album, his first with the group, was released. It was 1968, not 1969.
match_headline: Lew Soloff, Trumpeter for Blood, Sweat and Tears, Dies at 71

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday about gains made by Iraqi government forces and allied Shiite militias in their nine-day offensive to retake Tikrit from Islamic State militants misidentified the source of the image showing an armed soldier. The photograph was supplied by The Associated Press, which took the image from an A.P. video; the image was not from “a government video.” (Only in unusual circumstances does The Times use pictures or videos from governments.)
match_headline: Iraqi Army Cements Hold on Tikrit, but Islamic State Sends a Message

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Patrick Maxwell, a war veteran who returned to Iraq to fight alongside the Kurds, misstated a crime for which John Walker Lindh, who had enlisted with the Taliban in Afghanistan, received a 20-year prison term. He was sentenced for providing services to the Taliban and for carrying explosives during a felony, but not for conspiracy to murder American citizens.
match_headline: Unsettled at Home, Veterans Volunteer to Fight ISIS

text: An article on Friday about the police shooting in Ferguson, Mo., and how it might slow changes being made in the city misstated the number of years that Kim Tihen, who commented on the incident, has been a councilwoman. It is three, not 17.
match_headline: Just as Ferguson Was Making Progress, Shooting Deals a Setback

text: A subheading in some editions on Wednesday with an article about conflicting trends on complaints about the New York Police Department referred imprecisely to a decline in complaints made directly to the department. While that drop conflicts with other statistics showing that complaints directly to the Civilian Complaint Review Board were up, the decline is not necessarily “deceptive.” As the article noted, the conflicting statistics are a phenomenon that has puzzled officials.
match_headline: Conflicting Trends in Complaints on Police Puzzle New York City Officials

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about The New York Times Scholarship winners for 2015 misidentified the city in Pakistan where one recipient, Mah Noor, was born. It is Faisalabad, not Lahore.
match_headline: 13 Who Defeated Adversity Earn New York Times College Scholarships

text: A picture caption in some editions on Wednesday with an article about Princeton’s 55-42 victory over Penn in women’s basketball, which clinched an undefeated regular season for the Tigers, misspelled, in some copies, the surname of one of the Princeton players shown holding the Ivy League trophy. She is Blake Dietrick, not Dietrich.
match_headline: Unbeaten Princeton Women Take Seat Next to Kentucky

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with a dance review of “Event,” performed by Compagnie CNDC-Angers at the Joyce Theater in Manhattan, misstated the surname of the company’s artistic director, who arranged the Merce Cunningham dances used in the work. As the review correctly noted, he is Robert Swinston, not Swinton. And the review referred incorrectly to the program. It does list the dances; it is not the case that the audience is “not told which dances are being performed.”
match_headline: Review: Compagnie CNDC-Angers Dances Cunningham

text: An article on Thursday about bereavement travel misstated the surname of the author of “My Deepest Sympathies,” a book on condolences. She is Florence Isaacs, not Isaac.
match_headline: Dealing With the Dreaded Bereavement Trip

text: An obituary on March 7 about the movie and television producer Harve Bennett, using information from a friend of his, referred incorrectly to his marital history. He was divorced three times, not twice; his wife, Jani, who survives him, was his fourth wife, not his third.
match_headline: Harve Bennett, Quiz Kid and ‘Star Trek’ Producer, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the journalist Claude Sitton misidentified his birthplace in Georgia. He was born in Atlanta, not Emory.
match_headline: Claude Sitton, 89, Acclaimed Civil Rights Reporter, Dies

text: Because of a translation error, an article last Sunday about an investigation by Iraqi officials into reports that Islamic State militants had destroyed the Hatra archaeological site misstated, in some editions, the age of the site. It dates to the first century B.C., not the 12th. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The article also misidentified, in some editions, the online location of a statement by the Iraqi Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities in which it blamed the international coalition fighting the militants for failing to protect Hatra. The statement appeared on the ministry’s website, not on its Facebook page.
match_headline: Jihadists May Have Wrecked an Ancient Iraqi Site

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the arrests of four executives of one of Chile’s largest financial companies, a tax auditor and a former government official on charges of tax fraud, bribery and money laundering misstated the given name of one of the executives, an accounting manager at the Penta Group. He is Marcos Castro, not Marcus.
match_headline: Executives Are Jailed in Chile Finance Scandal

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about an expansion of the Bridgehampton Chamber Music Festival on Long Island gave an incorrect phone number for information about performances this spring. It is 212-741-9403.
match_headline: Bridgehampton Chamber Music Festival Adds a Spring Series

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the reunion of the Devils team that won the Stanley Cup in 1995 misstated the number of days the 1994-95 lockout cost the N.H.L. It was 111 days — not 114 — from the date of the first scheduled game to the date the first game was played.
match_headline: Twenty Years Later, Devils Toast the Men Who Hoisted the Team’s First Stanley Cup

text: An article last Sunday previewing the first game between the Major League Soccer expansion teams New York City F.C. and Orlando City misidentified the job held by the New York City F.C. official Tim Pernetti, who resigned six weeks before the game. He was chief business officer, not the marketing director.
match_headline: M.L.S.’s Expansion Siblings Are Set to Begin Rivalry, and Central Florida Is Abuzz

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the life of Shayne Oliver, the designer of the fashion label Hood by Air, misidentified the woman Oliver was shown with when he was a child. She is his mother, not his grandmother. And another picture caption referred incorrectly to the performance artist Boychild, a Hood by Air runway model. She identifies as a woman, not as a man.
match_headline: Seattle’s First Downtown, Reimagined

text: An obituary last Sunday about Brian Carman, who helped write the instrumental surf-rock hit “Pipeline,” misidentified the band that had a hit with another surf-rock instrumental, “Wipe Out.” It was the Surfaris, not the Ventures.
match_headline: Brian Carman, Surf Rocker, Dies at 69

text: An article on Friday, March 13 about the record of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem misstated the month that he told Bloomberg View that the settlements were not the core of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. It was May, not October.
match_headline: As Election Day Nears, Benjamin Netanyahu Talks of a ‘Worldwide’ Effort to Defeat Him

text: An article last Sunday about Radio City Music Hall’s “New York Spring Spectacular” referred incorrectly to its authorship. Joshua Harmon, who wrote the Off Broadway hit “Bad Jews,” wrote the show’s book; he did not collaborate on it with Randy Weiner, one of the spectacular’s creative directors.
match_headline: ‘New York Spring Spectacular’ Brings High Kicks to Radio City Music Hall

text: A review on Feb. 1 about “The Man Who Couldn’t Stop: OCD and the True Story of a Life Lost in Thought,” by David Adam, referred incorrectly to the American Psychiatric Association’s 2013 recategorization of obsessive compulsive disorder, which it had previously listed as a type of anxiety disorder. O.C.D. was placed in its own separate category along with some related disorders, not among “impulse disorders” (which are properly called impulsecontrol disorders).
ref_headline: The Man Who Couldn’t Stop: OCD and the True Story of a Life Lost in Thought,
match_headline: David Adam’s ‘The Man Who Couldn’t Stop’

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on March 1 with an article about the Italian city of Ravenna misidentified the location of a set of mosaics. They are at the Basilica di Sant’Apollinare in Classe — not at the Basilica di Sant’Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna. The error was repeated in a listing of travel tips.
match_headline: Ravenna, Italy, Glittering Still

text: An article last Sunday about the Esmeraldas region of Ecuador misspelled the surname of one of the cooks at the hotel Cabañas Iruñas. He is Daniel Facchin, not Fachin.
match_headline: Hidden Gems on Ecuador’s Emerald Coast

text: An article last Sunday about exploring the Ionian coast of Italy described incorrectly a wine, an Aglianico del Vulture, sampled by the writer. It is an Aglianico, not a Primitivo.
match_headline: Discovering the Ruins of Italy’s Ionian Coast

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about competition among luxury brands to be sponsors of the art fair Art Basel Miami Beach misidentified the company that commissioned the artist Georgia Russell to design packaging for a limited edition of Champagne bottles for the fair. It was Ruinart, not BMW.
match_headline: The Brands in Art Basel’s Orbit

text: A picture caption with an article on Feb. 22 about Airbnb in Tokyo misstated the given name of a child whose parents listed their home with Airbnb. She is Eri, not Eni.
match_headline: Meet the Unlikely Airbnb Hosts of Japan

text: An article on Feb. 22 about the photographer Roy DeCarava described one of his pictures incorrectly. It features a young woman in a white graduation dress, not a woman in a bridal gown.
match_headline: A True Picture of Black Skin

text: A map on March 9 with the continuation of an article about efforts to guard the antiquities of Iraq and Syria mislabeled one of the countries where the Islamic State has been looting and destroying ancient artifacts. It is Iraq, not Iran.
match_headline: Race in Iraq and Syria to Record and Shield Art Falling to ISIS

text: An article on Thursday about a petition drive seeking a reinstatement of Jeremy Clarkson, the host of a British car program who was suspended by the BBC because of a “fracas” with a producer, referred incorrectly to Paul Staines, a political conservative who began the petition. He runs a blog called Guido Fawkes; he does not call himself Guido Fawkes.
match_headline: Fans Petition BBC to Reinstate ‘Top Gear’ Host Jeremy Clarkson

text: An article last Tuesday about a United Nations analysis that showed an “alarmingly high” level of violence against women and girls worldwide understated the cost of domestic violence against women and children as calculated by a separate study. It is $8 trillion, not $4 trillion. (Violence against women alone costs $4 trillion, the study said).
match_headline: U.N. Reveals ‘Alarmingly High’ Levels of Violence Against Women

text: A critic’s notebook article on Monday about the E! show “Fashion Police” described incorrectly a hairstyle worn by the actress Zendaya, which was the subject of remarks by Giuliana Rancic on the show. She wore elaborate dreadlocked extensions, not braids.
match_headline: Without Joan Rivers, ‘Fashion Police’ Is Falling Apart

text: A critic’s notebook article on Saturday about John Cameron Mitchell in “Hedwig and the Angry Inch” and Sienna Miller in “Cabaret” misstated the period of time Mr. Mitchell missed after he injured his knee last month. One performance was canceled, then he was out of the show for a week. He was not out for “a few weeks.”
match_headline: ‘Cabaret’ and ‘Hedwig’ Get Tougher Onstage

text: An article on Monday about a political awakening of Arabs in Israel this election year referred incorrectly to voting rights for Arabs in East Jerusalem. A small number — those who hold Israeli citizenship — are entitled to vote in Israeli elections; it is not the case that no Arabs in East Jerusalem can vote.
match_headline: Arab Alliance Rises as Force in Israeli Elections

text: An article on March 8 about the Liberty City Charter School in Miami, of which Jeb Bush was a co-founder, misstated the given name of a student who stood behind Mr. Bush as he gave a speech. He is Ajani Booth, not Ajami.
match_headline: Charter School in Miami Fails, but Proves Useful on Jeb Bush’s Résumé

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Friday about the discovery of radioactive cesium 137 in a sample of powdered tea from Japan tested by the Hong Kong government misstated the results of the testing and the resolution of the matter. The sample had 0.93 percent — not 9.3 times — the legal limit, and the importer withdrew the tea from the market; the Hong Kong government did not ban its sale.
match_headline: Hong Kong Finds Small Amount of Radioactivity in Sample of Japanese Tea

text: An article on Monday about the Azraq refugee camp in Jordan, which currently houses only 14,500 of the 60,000 Syrian refugees expected by the end of last year, misidentified the United Nations agency that warned in December, after a drop in donor funding, that it would have to cut off food aid for Syrian refugees living outside refugee camps. It is the World Food Program, not the World Health Organization.
match_headline: Despite Good Intentions, Vacancies in Refugee Camp in Jordan for Syrians

text: An article on Saturday about Carly Fiorina, an outspoken critic of Hillary Rodham Clinton, quoted incorrectly from a comment she made about Mrs. Clinton. Ms. Fiorina said, “I think if Hillary Clinton faces a woman opponent, she will get a hitch in her swing,” not in her “sway.”
ref_headline: I think if Hillary Clinton faces a woman opponent, she will get a hitch in her swing,
match_headline: Carly Fiorina Shapes Herself as the Republican Foil to Hillary Clinton

text: An article on Thursday about changes at The Orange County Register described incorrectly the employees hired when Aaron Kushner took over leadership of the newspaper in 2012. Of the 440 people hired, about 200 were newsroom positions; not all were journalists. Because of an editing error, the article also misstated the timing of a lawsuit against The Register by The Los Angeles Times. The suit was filed after — not before — The Register’s Los Angeles edition, called The Los Angeles Register, was shuttered. The article also referred imprecisely to The Orange County Register’s circulation figures, using a measure that included branded editions of The Register. Excluding those editions, the Register’s audited circulation for the year that ended last March 31 was 302,802 on Sunday and 182,669 Monday through Saturday, an increase from 290,631 on Sundays and 178,247 on weekdays for the year that ended March 31, 2012, according to the Alliance for Audited Media.
match_headline: Aaron Kushner, Entrepreneur With Plans to Lead a California Newspaper Renaissance, Steps Aside

text: An article last Wednesday about Tidjane Thiam, the choice for chief executive at Credit Suisse, misstated the period in which Mr. Thiam worked at McKinsey, the World Bank and two insurance companies. It was before 2009, not “since 2009.”
match_headline: In Tidjane Thiam, Credit Suisse Gets Risk Expertise

text: An article last Wednesday about visiting South American soccer teams that play Copa Libertadores matches at high altitudes in Bolivia referred incorrectly to the city of Santa Cruz de la Sierra and the reasons teams stay at least a day there before playing at high altitude stadiums. Santa Cruz de la Sierra is a low-lying city; it is not halfway up in terms of altitude. Teams stay there to minimize the time spent at the high-altitude destination; they do not start acclimatizing there.
match_headline: Bolivian Clubs Are at Home in Thin Air

text: A report in the Off the Menu column last Wednesday about the opening of Ganso Yaki, in Boerum Hill, Brooklyn, misstated the restaurant’s phone number. It is 646-927-0303.
match_headline: L’Antagoniste to Open in Bedford-Stuyvesant

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the reopening of Hyper Cacher, a kosher market in Paris, for the first time since a gunman who claimed allegiance to the Islamic State took hostages there on Jan. 9 misstated the total number of people killed during the January terror attacks in and around Paris. Twenty were killed, including the three gunmen, not 17.
match_headline: 2 Months After Attack, Paris Kosher Market Reopens

text: An article on Thursday about Chinese Communist Party leaders’ anger over speculation by the Dalai Lama, the most prominent leader in Tibetan Buddhism, that he might not reincarnate gave an outdated title for Padma Choling, who told reporters that the Dalai Lama had profaned his faith by making the suggestion. Padma Choling is a former governor of the Tibetan autonomous region of China, not the current one.
match_headline: China’s Tensions With Dalai Lama Spill Into the Afterlife

text: An article on Saturday about the dangerous appeal of New York City’s rooftops and moving subway cars to young daredevils misstated the given name of the founder of American Parkour, an academy based in Washington, D.C., that teaches a form of urban adventuring. He is Mark Toorock, not Mike. The article also misspelled part of the title of a James Bond film. It is “Casino Royale,” not “Casino Royal.”
match_headline: On Rooftops and Trains, Daredevil Stunts in New York Can Turn Deadly
