text: An essay in some editions on March 10 about the rivalry between the Rangers and the Islanders referred incorrectly to the Islanders’ 12-60-6 record in their first season in 1972-73. While it was the worst season in N.H.L. history at the time, it is not still the record. The 1974-75 Washington Capitals were 8-67-5.
match_headline: Tracing a Seasoned Rivalry to Its Birth at Nassau Coliseum

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column last Thursday about the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s choice of the architect David Chipperfield to design its new wing for modern and contemporary art referred incorrectly to two of his previous projects. He designed the restoration of the Neues Museum in Berlin, and an addition to the Saint Louis Art Museum. He did not design those museums.
match_headline: Metropolitan Museum of Art Names New President: Daniel Weiss

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about Kendrick Lamar’s new album, “To Pimp a Butterfly,” using information from the liner notes, misspelled the surname of a saxophonist who performs on it. He is Adam Turchin, not Turchan.
match_headline: Kendrick Lamar, Emboldened, but Burdened, by Success

text: A picture caption on Tuesday about a performance at the Village Vanguard in Manhattan misstated the given name of the saxophonist who led the quartet that played. As the review of the performance and another picture caption correctly noted, he is Charles Lloyd, not Charlie.
match_headline: Review: Charles Lloyd Returns to the Village Vanguard

text: An article on Page F6 today about museum programs for teenagers misidentifies a museum. It is the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston — not the School of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
match_headline: Museums Seek to Lure, Then Lock In, Teenage Connoisseurs

text: An article on Page F2 today about the Black Mountain College Museums & Arts Center in North Carolina misidentifies a lake that is the site of the (Re)Happening, an annual tribute to what some regard as the first happening, mounted in 1952 by the composer John Cage. It is Lake Eden, not Eden Lake.
match_headline: In the Spirit of Black Mountain College, an Avant-Garde Incubator

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary last Friday about the architect Michael Graves referred incorrectly to a building in Oregon he designed. It includes only one hammered-copper statue, not statues. The obituary also misstated the name of the building. It is the Portland Building, not the Portland Municipal Building.
match_headline: Michael Graves, 80, Dies; Postmodernist Designed Towers and Teakettles

text: An article on Wednesday about a vote by the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) to change its definition of marriage to include same-sex marriage misstated the membership of the United Methodist Church. It is 12.8 million worldwide — not 5.5 million, which is the number outside the United States.
match_headline: Largest Presbyterian Denomination Gives Final Approval for Same-Sex Marriage

text: An article on Tuesday about the introduction of ShotSpotter, a detection system that pinpoints the location of gunfire in some New York City neighborhoods, misstated, in some editions, the status of a bill that would require quarterly reports on gunshots recorded by ShotSpotter. Letitia James, the public advocate, has already introduced the bill to the City Council; she is not planning to do so.
match_headline: New York Police Begin Using ShotSpotter System to Detect Gunshots

text: An article in some copies on Thursday about the Rangers’ 1-0 loss to the Chicago Blackhawks referred incorrectly to Rangers goalie Cam Talbot’s losses since Henrik Lundqvist last played on Feb. 2. He has lost three times in regulation, not three times over all. The article also misstated Talbot’s record during that span. He is 13-3-3 — not 15-3-3, which is the Rangers’ record during Lundqvist’s absence.
match_headline: Back at Garden, Brad Richards Makes Himself at Home

text: An article on Wednesday about Diana Taurasi’s experiences playing professional basketball in Yekaterinburg, Russia, misidentified the church there that is built over the cellar where the Romanovs were assassinated. It is the Church on Blood in Honor of All Saints Resplendent in the Russian Land — not the Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood, which is in St. Petersburg.
match_headline: Diana Taurasi Focusing on Playing in Russia, Where the Money Is

text: A listing of credits on Wednesday with a theater review of “The Evening,” at the Kitchen in Manhattan, omitted two organizations that are presenting the play in addition to New York City Players. They are the Kitchen and Performance Space 122.
match_headline: Review: In Richard Maxwell’s ‘The Evening,’ Going Gentle Into the Night, or Not

text: An entry in the What’s on TV Thursday highlights in some editions on Thursday about “Masters of Their Craft” from SundanceNow Doc Club, using information from a publicist, misstated the first part of the title of one of the documentaries being shown. It is “Far Out Isn’t Far Enough: The Tomi Ungerer Story,” not “Far Out Isn’t Enough.”
match_headline: What’s on TV Thursday

text: A Critic’s Notebook article last Friday about Asia Week New York misstated the address of the Nayef Homsi gallery, which has a display of religious sculpture. It is at 7 East 75th Street, not 75 East 75th Street. The article also misidentified the gallery showing work by Liang Quan. It is M. Sutherland, not the Kang Collection. The article also misstated the process used by Minjung Kim, whose work is on display at the Kang Collection. She colors rice paper then applies a flame; she does not apply the flame first.
match_headline: Asia Week Celebrates an Array of Art as Vast as a Continent

text: An article last Sunday about Tomi Reichental, a 79-year-old Holocaust survivor now living in Ireland who speaks to schoolchildren about his boyhood in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, referred imprecisely to the wartime location of another camp, Gross-Rosen, the site of a forced march in 1945 during which an estimated 1,400 women died. At the time, it was in German territory, not Polish, although it was soon reclaimed by Poland.
match_headline: Breaking Silence, Survivor Sets Out to Meet Holocaust Past

text: An article on Sunday about the arrests of 10 students at a Los Angeles high school in a series of sexual assaults gave an outdated title for Ramon C. Cortines, who leads the Los Angeles Unified School District. He is the superintendent; he is no longer interim.
match_headline: 14 Students Are Accused in Los Angeles Sexual Assaults

text: Because of an editing error, the On Soccer column last Sunday about the ramifications of holding the 2022 World Cup in the winter misstated the dollar equivalent of 50 million British pounds, one marketing agency’s estimate for the additional revenue British television could generate in a winter World Cup. It is $73.7 million, not $33.9 million.
match_headline: A World Cup Late in the Year Promises Smiles and Headaches

text: Because of an editing error, a theater review in some editions last Sunday about “The Effect of Gamma Rays on Man-in-the-Moon Marigolds,” at the Schoolhouse Theater in Croton Falls, N.Y., misstated the year the play made its debut. It had its world premiere in 1964 in Houston, not in 1970. (It opened off Broadway in 1970.)
ref_headline: The Effect of Gamma Rays on Man-in-the-Moon Marigolds,
match_headline: Keep Mom Away From the Pet Rabbit: A Review of ‘The Effect of Gamma Rays on Man-in-the-Moon Marigolds,’ in Croton Falls

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 8 about McDonald’s efforts to turn around its flagging performance erroneously attributed a distinction to the company. While it is among the world’s largest restaurant chains, with 36,000 outlets globally, it is not the largest. Subway, with more than 43,000 outlets worldwide, is larger.
match_headline: McDonald’s Seeks Its Fast-Food Soul

text: An article last Sunday about the new addition to the Corning Museum of Glass in Corning, N.Y., misstated the name of the new wing. It is the Contemporary Art + Design Wing — not the North Wing. The article also misstated how many glass objects the museum, founded in 1951, has. It is 50,000, not 40,000.
match_headline: New Wing at Corning Museum of Glass Invites the Light

text: An article on March 8 about the middle-distance runner Mary Cain misstated the name of an indoor race held annually in New York City. It is the Wanamaker Mile, not the Winamaker Mile.
match_headline: Mary Cain Is Growing Up Fast

text: An article last Sunday about a cruise from Baltimore to Charleston, S.C., described incorrectly the U.S.S. Wisconsin, docked permanently off Norfolk, Va. It is a battleship, not a destroyer.
match_headline: Cruising the Past, from Baltimore to Charleston

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Sophia Lee and Christopher Suarez misspelled the bride’s middle name. It is Mengfei, not Mengsei.
match_headline: Running and Traveling the World Over

text: An article on Friday about efforts by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel to backtrack from his pre-election declaration that no Palestinian state would be established on his watch erroneously translated his response to a question asked by a right-leaning Israeli news site on Monday, the day before the election. Asked, “If you are prime minister, a Palestinian state will not be established?” he responded, “Indeed,” not “Correct.” (The Hebrew words for these are very similar.)
ref_headline: If you are prime minister, a Palestinian state will not be established?
match_headline: Israel’s Netanyahu Reopens Door to Palestinian State, but White House Is Unimpressed

text: An article on Thursday about a massacre at a museum in downtown Tunis misspelled the given name of one of those injured, a Japanese tourist. She is Nobuko Yuki, not Nobuku.
match_headline: Tunisia Museum Attack Is Blow to Nation’s Democratic Shift

text: An article in some editions on March 15 about the evacuation of American aid workers who may have come into contact with the Ebola virus in Sierra Leone misidentified, in some copies, the country where another American aid worker, Dr. Craig Spencer, had been working before he returned to New York and developed Ebola. Dr. Spencer returned from Guinea, not from Liberia.
match_headline: Americans Evacuated From Sierra Leone After Possible Ebola Contact

text: An article on Jan. 13 about the first day back at school for survivors of a massacre at a school in Pakistan misstated the date of the massacre. It was Dec. 16, not Dec. 15. The error also appeared in a picture caption. The error was discovered recently during the editing of a related article.
match_headline: Grief and Defiance in Pakistan as Survivors of Taliban Massacre Return to School

text: An article on Sunday about the death of the man accused in an attack at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport, using information from the Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office, misspelled the given name of the Transportation Security Administration officer who was wounded. She is Carol Richel, not Carroll.
match_headline: Assailant Shot at New Orleans Airport Is Dead

text: An article on Feb. 7 about luxury retailers’ renewed interest in the United States market misstated the fourth-quarter 2014 results of LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton. Annual sales in Asia dropped 6 percent from the same quarter a year earlier, not over the full fiscal year. Fourth-quarter sales in Europe grew 5 percent, not 3 percent, over the same period a year earlier. And revenue in the United States grew 13 percent, not 8 percent, over the same period. The error was only recently called to the attention of The Times.
match_headline: Rushing to Cater to America’s Rich

text: An article on Saturday about Vladimir Tolstoy, a great-great-grandson of Leo Tolstoy and an adviser on cultural affairs to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, misstated the given name of a Russian writer who died this month and who was praised by Mr. Tolstoy as the best writer of the past half-century. He was Valentin Rasputin, not Vladimir.
match_headline: In Putin’s Nationalist Russia, a Tolstoy as Cultural Diplomat

text: An obituary on Feb. 1 about Richard von Weizsäcker, the first president of the reunited Germany, misstated the timing of his decision to join the German Protestant Church. He joined the church’s lay assembly while he was working in private industry, not after he left it. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Theodor Heuss’s victory in the 1954 election for president of the Federal Republic of Germany. Mr. Heuss was elected the republic’s first president in 1949 and re-elected five years later; he was not “elected the first federal president in 1954.” An email from a reader pointing out these errors went astray at The Times.
ref_headline: elected the first federal president in 1954.
match_headline: Richard von Weizsäcker, 94, Dies: First President of Reunited Germany

text: An article on Tuesday about a Justice Department report on the use of lethal force by Philadelphia police officers misidentified the news organization in Philadelphia that published an exclusive report in 2013 revealing that while crime was down there the number of officers firing at suspects was on the rise. The article was by philly.com, not by The Philadelphia Inquirer. (Philly.com is the website for both The Inquirer and The Philadelphia Daily News, but it also has its own editorial staff.)
match_headline: Justice Dept., Criticizing Philadelphia Police, Finds Shootings by Officers Are Common

text: An article on Friday about the challenges awaiting Israel’s newly united Arab political faction in Parliament misstated the number of Arab citizens of Israel. There are about 1.4 million, not 1.7 million. (The larger number includes 300,000 East Jerusalem Palestinians, the vast majority of whom are legal residents but do not hold citizenship.)
match_headline: Arab Alliance in Israeli Legislature Sees Unity as Vehicle for Progress

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Senator Ted Cruz’s plan to announce his candidacy for the Republican presidential nomination during an appearance at Liberty University misidentified, in some editions, the university’s president. He is Jerry Falwell Jr., not Jerry Falwell Sr. (His father, who died in 2007, founded the university.)
match_headline: Ted Cruz Hopes Early Campaign Entry Will Focus Voters’ Attention

text: A headline on Friday with a review of the Mandarin-language film “Lost and Love,” using information from the film’s distributor, misstated the Mandarin title. It is “Shi Gu,” not “Shu Gi.”
match_headline: Review: ‘Lost and Love’ (‘Shi Gu’) Stars Andy Lau as a Man Searching for His Lost Son

text: An article on March 10 about limiting access to the means by which people die by suicide misstated the results of one study. It found that 60 percent of patients who died by suicide after discharge from an acute care psychiatric unit had been judged to be at low risk for suicide, not that 60 percent of patients who had been judged to be at low risk died of suicide after discharge.
match_headline: Blocking the Paths to Suicide

text: An article on Tuesday about metamaterials, which bend light, sound and seismic waves in ways that do not naturally occur, misstated the date the French construction firm Menard published a paper describing a test of a novel way of counteracting the effects of an earthquake. It was in 2013, not earlier this month.
match_headline: The Waves of the Future May Bend Around Metamaterials

text: Because of editing errors, an entry on Thursday in a listing of spring museum exhibitions omitted part of the museum’s name and misstated the number of works in the exhibition “America Is Hard to See.” It is at the Whitney Museum of American Art, not at the Museum of American Art, and the number of works is 650, not 750.
match_headline: Spring Museum Exhibitions, From Masks to Renoirs

text: A picture on Thursday with an obituary about Patrick McDarby, a designer of sports logos, was published in error. The photograph showed the Jacksonville Jaguars’ current logo, not an alternate logo Mr. McDarby designed.
match_headline: Patrick McDarby, Sport Logo Designer, Is Dead at 57

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with the continuation of an article about the fatal shooting of Anthony Hill by a police officer near Atlanta misidentified the state where Mr. Hill was buried. As the article correctly noted, the burial was in South Carolina, not in Georgia. In addition, the article misstated part of the name of the church that Mr. Hill had attended. The church is in Moncks Corner, the city where he was buried, and therefore it is Moncks Corner African Methodist Episcopal Church (not Moncks “Hill”).
match_headline: Police Shooting Victim in Georgia Tried to Follow ‘Sensible’ Path

text: An article on Saturday about “swatting,” in which pranksters make bogus 911 calls to send police officers to the homes of video gamers live-streaming their gameplay, misidentified the live video site that one such gamer, James Clayton Eubanks, uses to stream his video gaming. While he was streaming on Twitch when the swatting incident reported in the article occurred, he now uses MLG.tv, not Twitch.
match_headline: Online ‘Swatting’ Becomes a Hazard for Popular Video Gamers and Police Responders

text: An article on Wednesday about a marketing campaign by Peet’s Coffee & Tea to highlight its use of fresh, brewed coffee for its crushed-ice coffee drink misidentified the country of origin of Joh. A. Benckiser, which bought Peet’s in 2012. Benckiser, now called JAB Holdings Company, is a German company, not a British one.
match_headline: Peet’s Introduces a Fresh Take on Cold Coffee

text: An article on Saturday about artistic achievements by older adults misstated the name of the musical institution whose concertmaster played a duet with Ari L. Goldman, who took up the cello later in life. It is the Philadelphia Orchestra, not the Philadelphia Symphony.
match_headline: Finding Success, Well Past the Age of Wunderkind

text: Because of an editing error, the continuation of an article on Wednesday about plans for a voter referendum in Boston on whether to bid on the 2024 Olympic Games was omitted from some editions. The complete article can be found at nytimes.com/sports .
match_headline: In Reversal, Boston 2024 Wants Vote on Olympic Bid

text: A report in the Observatory column on Tuesday about mushrooms referred incorrectly to their classification at one point. As the report correctly noted elsewhere, mushrooms are fungi, not plants. The error was repeated in an overline, though the headline itself was correct.
match_headline: Mushrooms That Glow to Continue the Species

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the former Wisconsin congressman Robert W. Kastenmeier referred incorrectly to his position in the House when he and other members pressed the Foreign Affairs Committee to hold hearings on the Vietnam War in 1965. He was not a member of that committee.
match_headline: Robert Kastenmeier, Liberal Voice in House for 32 Years, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the media critic and human rights activist Danny Schechter misstated his mother’s maiden name. She was the former Ruth Lisa Lubin, not Lubing.
match_headline: Danny Schechter, ‘News Dissector’ and Human Rights Activist, Dies at 72

text: An article on Thursday about the beginning of American airstrikes against the Islamic State in Tikrit, Iraq, misstated, in some editions, the location from which a speech by Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi praising the strikes was broadcast. He was in Baghdad, not in Salahuddin Province.
match_headline: Opening New Iraq Front, U.S. Strikes ISIS in Tikrit

text: A picture caption on March 16 with the continuation of an article about the arrest of Robert Durst in the killing of a friend in 2000 carried an erroneous credit in some editions. The picture, of Mr. Durst and his first wife, Kathleen, shown in the 1970s, was taken by James McCormack (not Jim); it was not by Mr. McCormack and HBO.
match_headline: Robert Durst of HBO’s ‘The Jinx’ Says He ‘Killed Them All’

text: A map on Wednesday with an article about the crash of a German jetliner in the French Alps carried an imprecise label marking the plane’s altitude at one location along its flight path. It was about 6,880 feet above the ground — not simply “10,000 feet.” (That is how many feet it was above sea level.)
match_headline: Germanwings Crash in French Alps Kills 150; Cockpit Voice Recorder Is Found

text: An article on March 16 about a dispute over how goods are produced and sold on Etsy, an online market for handmade products, paraphrased incorrectly some comments on the matter by Nicole Burisch, a fellow with the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. She said it was increasingly difficult to distinguish handmade items from mass-produced ones. She did not raise a question about whether a hand-knit sweater or clay pot was handmade.
match_headline: Etsy’s Success Gives Rise to Problems of Credibility and Scale

text: An article on Thursday about provisions in the Trans-Pacific Partnership, as outlined in a classified document, that would allow foreign corporations to sue the United States over actions that hurt their business or investment expectations misstated when the document was made available to members of Congress. Drafts were available for review soon after being written; it is not the case that the latest document was not made available until last week.
match_headline: Trans-Pacific Partnership Seen as Door for Foreign Suits Against U.S.

text: A listing in the Transactions column in the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about a recent sale at 1345-1349 Amsterdam Avenue described the buyer incorrectly. The buyer is a Manhattan investor, not a Brooklyn investor.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Transactions

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary in some editions on Saturday about Malcolm Fraser, a former prime minister of Australia, referred incorrectly to a ranch owned by his parents. It was in western Victoria, near Hamilton, not in Toorak, and the family did not move there until after Mr. Fraser was born in Toorak; he was not born near Hamilton.
match_headline: Malcolm Fraser, a Leader Given Power During Crisis in Australia, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Thursday about the tea company founder Steven Smith misstated his mother’s given name. She was the former Verla Slick, not Berla.
match_headline: Steven Smith, a ‘Marco Polo’ of American Tea, Dies at 65

text: An article in some editions on Friday about Wisconsin’s 79-72 victory over North Carolina in the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament misidentified, in some copies, the winner of a game between Wisconsin and Rutgers on Jan. 11. Rutgers won.
match_headline: A Giant, Upset, Lifts No. 1 Wisconsin Over North Carolina

text: A picture on Thursday with an article about the Kentucky assistant basketball coach John Robic was published in error. The photograph, provided by Denison University, showed Billy Hoyer playing for the school, not Robic.
match_headline: John Robic Is an Assistant Happy to Sweat the Small Stuff for Kentucky

text: An article on Wednesday about Yankees General Manager Brian Cashman’s love of Kentucky basketball misstated, in some copies, the year John Calipari became Kentucky’s coach. It was 2009, not 2011.
match_headline: Yankees’ Brian Cashman Relishes Kentucky Connection

text: Because of an editing error, a theater review on Friday about “New York Spring Spectacular” at Radio City Music Hall, which includes video displays of New York sports stars and other luminaries, misidentified a sports team owned by Madison Square Garden Entertainment, which also owns Radio City Music Hall. It owns the Rangers and the Knicks, not the Rangers and the Giants.
match_headline: Review: ‘New York Spring Spectacular’ Barrels Into Radio City

text: A picture credit on Friday with the Books of The Times review about the novel “The American People, Volume 1: Search for My Heart” by Larry Kramer, using information from the publisher, misspelled the photographer’s surname. The picture, of Mr. Kramer, is by Jean Carlomusto, not Carlamusto.
ref_headline: The American People, Volume 1: Search for My Heart
match_headline: Review: ‘The American People, Volume 1’ by Larry Kramer Retells History With Passion

text: An article on March 20 about signs of spring and things to look forward to as the season arrives referred incorrectly to the migratory habits of some birds. Bufflehead ducks and saw-whet owls live in New York City in the winter and go north in early spring. They do not arrive in New York in the spring. Great horned owls live in the city year-round. They do not leave and return in the spring.
match_headline: Spring Is So Close You Can Almost Taste It

text: A picture credit and a listing of film credits on March 20 with a review of “She’s Lost Control,” using information from a publicist, misidentified the distributor of the movie. It is Monument Releasing, not Visit Films.
match_headline: Review: In ‘She’s Lost Control,’ Crossing Boundaries in Pursuit of Intimacy

text: An article in some editions last Monday about Gabriel and Gayle Sassoon, who lost seven children in a deadly fire in Brooklyn, referred incorrectly to an unrelated family with the same surname. That Sassoon family, based in India and China, traces its roots to Baghdad, not to Syria.
match_headline: From Different Worlds, Sharing a Spiritual Journey, and Now Family Loss

text: An article on Sunday about screening programs for mental health and shifting ideas of pilot fitness described incorrectly a person who was evaluated by Dr. Ryan Shugarman, a psychiatrist in Alexandria, Va., and was found to have suicidal thoughts. The person was a pilot applicant, not a pilot.
match_headline: Germanwings Crash Raises Questions About Shifting Ideas of Pilot Fitness

text: An article on Sunday about former President Bill Clinton’s role in his wife’s likely presidential campaign referred imprecisely to the driver of Mr. Clinton’s S.U.V. The vehicle is driven by a United States Secret Service agent; Mr. Clinton is not “chauffeured.”
match_headline: To Avert Repeat of 2008, Clinton Team Hopes to Keep Bill at His Best

text: An article on Thursday about Apple’s plans for a subscription music streaming service misstated what percentage of Apple’s annual revenue is represented by a theoretical $1 billion in revenue from such a service. It is slightly more than half a percent, not less than half a percent.
match_headline: Apple and Beats Developing Streaming Music Service to Rival Spotify

text: An article on Monday about a move by several media organizations into feature-length films gave an incorrect title, in some copies, for Eddy Moretti at Vice. He is the chief creative officer, not chief content officer. The error was repeated in a picture caption in some copies.
match_headline: News Companies See Movies as Opportunity for Growth

text: An article on March 19 about teenage guides at the National September 11 Memorial Museum misidentified the World Trade Center tower that fell on Sept. 11 while Bill Spade, a retired firefighter, was in the stairwell of the North Tower. It was the South Tower, not the North.
match_headline: Coming of Age as a Guide at Ground Zero

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a discovery by French investigators that one of the two pilots on the Germanwings jet that crashed in the French Alps had left the cockpit before the plane’s descent and was unable to get back in misstated the location of the plane crash relative to Nice. The crash was northwest of Nice, not northeast. Because of other editing errors, a picture caption with the article overstated, in some editions, what was known about the members of a search team looking for clues on a mountainside and referred imprecisely, in some editions, to their formation. Although the searchers were military personnel, it is not known whether any of them are officers, and they were shown climbing a winding path on the mountain; they had not formed a search line.
match_headline: Germanwings Pilot Was Locked Out of Cockpit Before Crash in France

text: An article on Friday about a raid on the offices of a leading human rights organization by Chinese security agents misquoted Maya Wang, a researcher for Human Rights Watch in Hong Kong who said Chinese authorities viewed such groups as potential conduits for subversion. She said the Chinese government saw some nongovernmental organizations as “fomenting color revolution” — one of the Communist Party’s preferred terms for foreign-backed insurrection — not “fomenting counterrevolution.”
match_headline: China Raids Offices of Rights Group as Crackdown on Activism Continues

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Monday about Operation Dragoon Ride, a 1,100-mile United States Army convoy through Eastern Europe meant to reassure allies nervous about Russian intentions, referred incorrectly to the military vehicles making the trip along with the troops. As the article correctly noted, they are Stryker armored vehicles, not tanks.
match_headline: An American Military Convoy in Europe Aims to Reassure Allies

text: An article on Saturday about the Notre Dame basketball player Steve Vasturia misstated his academic year. He is a sophomore, not a freshman.
match_headline: Steve Vasturia Is Modest, Like His Mother, and Tough, Like His Team

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the winners of the Bancroft Prize for history — “Empire of Cotton: A Global History” by Sven Beckert and “Empire of Necessity: Slavery, Freedom, and Deception in the New World” by Greg Grandin — misidentified the publisher of “Empire of Cotton.” It is Alfred A. Knopf, not Harvard University Press.
match_headline: Globally Minded Books Win Bancroft Prize

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with the continuation of a Critic’s Notebook article about a television film of Mark Morris’s dance staging of a Handel oratorio misstated part of the work’s title. As the review and another picture caption correctly noted, it is “L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato,” not “Il Allegro.”
ref_headline: L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato,
match_headline: Mark Morris’s Transcendent ‘L’Allegro,’ Captured on Film for PBS

text: An article on Tuesday about the Gustav Klimt painting “Adele Bloch-Bauer I,” which was looted by the Nazis and is a subject of the new film “Woman in Gold,” about the efforts of Ms. Bloch-Bauer’s niece Maria Altmann to regain it, referred incorrectly to its sale in 2006. While Christie’s helped negotiate the sale, the painting was not auctioned. Because of an editing error, the article also misstated the opening date of an exhibition at the Neue Galerie in Manhattan that includes the painting. It is Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: The Story Behind ‘Woman in Gold’: Nazi Art Thieves and One Painting’s Return

text: A picture on Friday with the Weekend Miser column, using information from a publicist, was published in error and carried an erroneous credit. It showed DJ Sad.Sad.Calzone, not DJ Rokin, who took part in events Saturday at the new headquarters of the Goethe-Institut New York in Manhattan. And the photograph is by stummfilm:dj, not DJ Rokin.
match_headline: At Goethe-Institut New York, a Free Taste of Germany (Beer, Too)

text: An obituary on March 23 about the longtime United States ambassador to the Soviet Union Arthur A. Hartman, using information from his family, misidentified the high school in Queens from which he graduated. It was Bayside High School, not Flushing High School.
match_headline: Arthur A. Hartman, U.S. Ambassador to Soviet Union, Dies at 89

text: Because of an editing error, the Hungry City column last Wednesday, a review of Haldi, an Indian restaurant in Midtown South, misspelled the name of a popular confectionary in Kolkata, India. It is Flurys , not Flsurys.
match_headline: In Curry Hill, a New Kid on the Block

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the deadly explosion and building collapse in the East Village misstated, in some editions, the day officials said a neighboring building, 119 Second Avenue, was in danger of collapse. They said it on Thursday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: East Village Explosion Ignites Fire, Fells Buildings and Injures at Least 19

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about a recommendation from the Liberian government that survivors of Ebola practice safe sex indefinitely misstated the diameter of bacteriophages, a type of virus whose transmission is blocked by condoms, and the diameter of the Ebola virus. Bacteriophages are 27 nanometers, not 27 nanomillimeters, and the Ebola virus is 80 nanometers, not 80 nanomillimeters.
match_headline: Liberia Recommends Ebola Survivors Practice Safe Sex Indefinitely

text: An article on Tuesday about a study that linked negative health effects to living in communities with greater income inequality misstated how the researchers measured inequality. They compared the incomes of people at the 80th and 20th percentiles of income in a given location; they did not compare the number of people with incomes above the 80th percentile and below the 20th percentile.
match_headline: Income Inequality: It’s Also Bad for Your Health

text: An article on Sunday about security enhancements to the fence around the White House referred incorrectly to the barriers that are used to help keep people away from the fence. They are movable crowd-control barricades usually referred to as bike rack barricades by the Secret Service; they are not actual bicycle racks.
match_headline: Wanted at the White House: A Fence That Says Halt! (With Curb Appeal)

text: An article on Tuesday about the shooting of two men by National Security Agency police officers misidentified the section of the Baltimore-Washington Parkway adjoining the N.S.A.’s Maryland campus. It is Maryland Route 295, not Interstate 295. (Interstate 295 is the name of an eight-mile section of the same highway that is farther south and mostly within the borders of the District of Columbia.)
match_headline: Driver Killed as Stolen Car Enters N.S.A. Campus

text: An entry on Friday in a listing of presentations of choral works for the Easter season, about a service at St. Paul’s Chapel in Lower Manhattan, was erroneously included among events on Good Friday. The service will be at 8 p.m. on Holy Saturday, not Good Friday.
match_headline: Choral Voices, Raised in Awe

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about plans for Jason Alexander to succeed Larry David in “Fish in the Dark,” at the Cort Theater in Manhattan, referred incorrectly to attendance at the show. The theater has been sold out, not “mostly” sold out.
match_headline: Jason Alexander Will Succeed Larry David in ‘Fish in the Dark’

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about Miriam Bienstock, one of the founders of Atlantic Records, misstated the amount that Ms. Bienstock and her first husband, Herb Abramson, initially invested in the company. It was $2,500, not $23,500.
match_headline: Miriam Bienstock, Co-Founder of Atlantic Records, Dies at 92

text: An article on March 26 about the challenges of recovering bodies from the crash site of a Germanwings jet that went down in the French Alps misspelled the name of a village that became a gathering place for victims’ relatives and others connected to the crash. It is Seyne-les-Alpes, not Seynes-les-Alpes. The error was repeated in the dateline and in a picture caption.
match_headline: Challenges Weigh Heavily on Recovery Efforts in Germanwings Crash

text: A news analysis article on Sunday about divisions among Western nations over how to respond to Russia’s aggression in Ukraine referred incorrectly to large Russian loan payments due by year’s end, which some analysts say could make Russia more willing to cooperate to get European sanctions lifted. The payments amount to a third of Russia’s foreign-currency reserves; they do not exceed the reserves.
match_headline: Fragile Cease-Fire in Ukraine Inspires Little Confidence in West

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the indictment of nine doctors accused of defrauding Medicaid by running unnecessary medical tests on homeless people, using information from a medical practice’s website, misstated the relationship of one defendant with New York Medical College. The defendant, Joseph Grossman, is a former clinical assistant professor at the college whose contract ended in 2002; he is not currently affiliated with the school.
match_headline: 9 New York Doctors Are Accused of Defrauding Medicaid Using Homeless People

text: An article on Page D4 today about the producer Lee Daniels misspells the given name of his assistant. She is Kacee Devoe, not Kaycee. The article also refers incorrectly to the actor and writer Danny Strong. He was the sole screenwriter for the film “Lee Daniels’ The Butler.” He did not share a screenwriting credit.
match_headline: Lee Daniels Watches ‘Empire’ – and Talks Back to the Screen

text: An obituary on Thursday about Cynthia Lennon, the former wife of the Beatles’ John Lennon, miscalculated in some editions the currency conversion for her settlement when they divorced in 1968. Her £100,000 settlement was the equivalent of about $240,000 at the time, not $150,000.
match_headline: Cynthia Lennon, the First Beatles Wife, Dies at 75

text: An article on March 27 about questions surrounding the motives of Andreas Lubitz, the co-pilot who is said to have deliberately crashed a Germanwings Airbus A320 into the French Alps, misidentified the river that is associated with Düsseldorf, where Mr. Lubitz lived. It is the Rhine, not the Ruhr.
match_headline: Andreas Lubitz, Who Loved to Fly, Ended Up on a Mysterious and Deadly Course

text: A picture caption with an article on July 4, 2014, about the turtles that sometimes reach the runway at Kennedy International Airport misspelled the given name of a volunteer who was helping study the animals. She is Marian Vargas, not Mariam. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Studying What Lures Turtles to a Tarmac at Kennedy Airport

text: An article on Thursday about the long-running case against Sergey Aleynikov, a former Goldman Sachs programmer accused of stealing secret source code from Goldman’s computers, misstated, in some copies, the given name of a prosecutor from the Manhattan district attorney’s office who sought to delay a new trial in the case. He is Daniel Holmes, not David.
match_headline: New Stumble in Trial of Former Goldman Programmer

text: An article on Thursday about a boom in business for tanker ships because of a glut of crude oil misstated the equivalent length in miles of a typical Very Large Crude Carrier, a supertanker made for shipping oil. The ships are about 1,100 feet long, or more than a fifth of a mile, not “almost one-fifth of a mile.”
match_headline: Oil Glut Is a Boon to Shippers, as Buyers Stock Up at Low Prices

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Europe’s intensifying scrutiny of big technology companies misstated the date of the first hearing in a class action against Facebook in Austria. It will be April 9; the case was not heard “less than a week ago.”
match_headline: Antitrust and Other Inquiries in Europe Target U.S. Tech Giants

text: An article on Tuesday about Georgia State guard R. J. Hunter’s decision to enter the N.B.A. draft misstated, in some copies, the injury sustained by his father, Georgia State Coach Ron Hunter, in the postgame celebration of the team’s Sun Belt Conference championship. He tore an Achilles’ tendon, not an anterior cruciate ligament.
match_headline: Father Stays on Sideline as Georgia State’s R.J. Hunter Enters the N.B.A. Draft

text: An article on Tuesday about how the destruction of antiquities by Islamic militants has prompted a debate about the return of such objects to countries where they originated but may be endangered misstated the middle initial of an archaeologist from Boston University who commented on the issue. He is Ricardo J. Elia, not L.
match_headline: Islamic State Destruction Renews Debate Over Repatriation of Antiquities

text: An entry on March 27 in a listing in some editions of musical offerings in New York related to Easter misidentified the denomination of St. Peter’s Church on Lexington Avenue at 54th Street. It is Lutheran, not Roman Catholic.
match_headline: Music for the Easter Holiday Spirit

text: Because of an editing error, the Personal Health column on Tuesday, about the nutritional benefits of nuts and peanuts, used an incorrect unit of measurement to describe the caloric value of some substances. Protein and sugar have four calories (not grams) per gram, and alcohol has seven calories (not grams) per gram.
match_headline: Nuts Are a Nutritional Powerhouse

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about an agreement between the Museum of Jewish Heritage — A Living Memorial to the Holocaust and the National Yiddish Theater-Folksbiene misspelled the given name of the Folksbiene’s artistic director. He is Zalmen Mlotek, not Zalman. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The article also misspelled part of the name of a theater at the museum. It is the Edmond J. Safra Hall, not Edmund.
match_headline: A Trial Partnership for 2 Jewish Cultural Institutions in New York

text: An article on Friday about the appointment of Marc Metrick as president of Saks Fifth Avenue misstated Mr. Metrick’s position at Saks’s parent company, Hudson’s Bay. He is chief administrative officer, not chief marketing officer.
match_headline: President of Saks Steps Down

text: An article last Sunday about The Players’ Tribune, Derek Jeter’s website featuring essays by athletes, misidentified, in some copies, the Mets’ opponent in a recent spring training game lost by pitcher Matt Harvey, a contributor to the website. It was the St. Louis Cardinals, not the Philadelphia Phillies.
match_headline: Athletes Finding Their Voice in Derek Jeter’s Digital Venture

text: An article on Monday about the shooting difficulties experienced by college basketball teams in games held at NRG Stadium in Houston misstated, in some editions, the number of N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament games played there. It is 12, not 13.
match_headline: Shooters Can’t See? Fans, Cover Your Eyes

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the expansion plans of the Pace Gallery in the Chelsea neighborhood of Manhattan, where it has three locations, misstated in some editions the size of a planned new building and its address. It is to be eight stories tall, not six, and the address will be 540 West 25th Street, not 540 West 22nd Street. The report also misidentified the site of another Pace Gallery and offices in some editions. It is on East 57th Street, not West 57th Street.
match_headline: Young and Zazeela’s ‘Dream House’ Is Getting a New Lease at Dia

text: A listing of credits on Friday with a film review of “Cut Bank,” using information from publicity materials, misstated the given name of the screenwriter. As the review correctly noted, he is Roberto Patino, not Robert.
match_headline: Review: ‘Cut Bank,’ Looking to Escape a Small Town and Its Eccentrics

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about gold watches misidentified the band on the Apple watch that was shown. It is the black sport band, not the black classic buckle.
match_headline: Not Your Uncle’s Gold Watch

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about Mark and Jonnie Houston, twin brothers who have opened 10 bars in the Hollywood area, misidentified which of their bars they were in. It is Dirty Laundry, not No Vacancy.
match_headline: Mark and Jonnie Houston Shake Up Hollywood Night Life

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the choreographer Merce Cunningham’s work “RainForest” misstated the year the photo was taken of him and Meg Harper dancing in the piece. It was 1969, not 1968.
match_headline: ‘RainForest,’ Cunningham’s Primeval Rarity, Returns to the Joyce

text: An article on March 15 about the climber Alex Honnold misstated part of the name of the Sacramento institution where his mother teaches. It is American River College, not University.
match_headline: The Heart-Stopping Climbs of Alex Honnold

text: An article on March 22 about optimization erroneously cited an award for George Dantzig, who founded the Systems Optimization Laboratory at Stanford. He did not win a Nobel Prize.
match_headline: A Sucker Is Optimized Every Minute

text: An article last Sunday about the Upper East Side penthouse of the Broadway producers Stewart F. Lane and Bonnie Comley misspelled the given name of Mr. Lane’s 29-year-old daughter. She is Eliana, not Ilian.
match_headline: Broadway Producers and Their Upper East Side Penthouse

text: A caption in the Evening Hours column last Sunday misstated the given name of the president of Fordham University. He is the Rev. Joseph M. McShane, not Michael.

Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Nick Swaggert, the veterans program director for Genesis10, a technology staffing and services firm, misstated the given name of the company’s chief executive. He is Harley Lippman, not Harry.
match_headline: Helping Veterans Get Hired

text: A picture caption in last Sunday’s Q&A column misspelled the name of the city in Taiwan where Lanshu Chen’s restaurant is located. As the article correctly noted, it is Taichung City, not Taiachung City.
match_headline: Lanshu Chen on Dining Well on the Road

text: An article on Wednesday about a law in Arizona that requires doctors who perform drug-induced abortions to tell women that the procedure may be reversible misspelled the given name of the public policy director of Planned Parenthood Arizona, who criticized the measure. She is Jodi Liggett, not Jody.
match_headline: Arizona Orders Doctors to Say Abortions With Drugs May Be Reversible

text: An article on Thursday about the indictment of Senator Robert Menendez misstated the year he was first elected to the House of Representatives. It was 1992, not 2002.
match_headline: Senator Robert Menendez Indicted on Corruption Charges

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the naming of the comedian Trevor Noah as the new host of “The Daily Show” on Comedy Central, using information from Comedy Central, carried an incomplete credit and omitted the photographer’s middle initial. The picture, of Mr. Noah, is credited to Byron L. Keulemans/GQ South Africa, not just to Mr. Keulemans.
match_headline: Trevor Noah to Succeed Jon Stewart on ‘The Daily Show’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the new home of the Whitney Museum of American Art, which is to open May 1 at the southern end of the High Line, from which the museum expects to attract visitors, included an outdated number of visitors to the park. The High Line drew about six million visitors last year; it is no longer the case that is has “nearly five million” a year.
match_headline: Whitney Museum Contemplates a Bigger Future, With Bigger Expenses

text: Because of an editing error, picture credits on Friday with an article about body scrubs misspelled the photographer’s surname. He is Eric Helgas, not Hilgas.
match_headline: How to Scrub Your Body Like a Man

text: An article on Wednesday about an appeal for emergency humanitarian assistance at an international fund-raising conference for victims of the Syrian war referred incorrectly in some editions to the number of Syrians displaced by the war. Twelve million are inside the country and four million have sought refuge in neighboring countries; the exiles are not included among the 12 million.
match_headline: Conference to Aid Syrians Falls Short of Expectations

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about the Islamic State’s seizure of new territory in Syria in recent days referred imprecisely to the militants who seized the northern city of Idlib. As the article correctly noted, Idlib was taken by a coalition of insurgent groups that included the Nusra Front, a rival of the Islamic State, not by the Nusra Front alone.
match_headline: ISIS Seizes New Territory in Deadly Attacks in Syria

text: An article on Sunday about Kenyans who waited outside a funeral home and morgue in Nairobi to identify relatives killed in a massacre at Garissa University College misspelled part of the name of the funeral home in some editions. It is the Chiromo Funeral Parlor, not the Chiroma Funeral Parlor.
match_headline: Kenyans Identify and Mourn Relatives Killed in Attack on University

text: An article on Monday about efforts to get a statue of Sally Ride, the astronaut, physicist and educator, enshrined in the nation’s Capitol misstated the number of women already honored in the National Statuary Hall Collection. It is nine, not eight. (The 10th will be a likeness of Amelia Earhart when it arrives.)
match_headline: California Seeks to Make Way for Statue of Sally Ride in U.S. Capitol

text: An article on March 19 about the selection of Andrew Hamilton, the head of Oxford University, to be the 16th president of New York University misspelled the given name of a professor of international relations and member of Oxford’s Council who said that Mr. Hamilton had been “the right person for the right moment” at Oxford. He is Neil MacFarlane, not Neal.
ref_headline: the right person for the right moment
match_headline: Named Next President of N.Y.U., Oxford’s Leader Inherits Challenges From John Sexton

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about Erik Helland, the strength and conditioning coach for the Wisconsin men’s basketball team, misstated the number of points Kentucky, Wisconsin’s Final Four opponent, was allowing per 100 possessions this season. It was 83.6 — not 53.9, which was the average number of points Kentucky allowed per game.
match_headline: A Strength Coach for Wisconsin Uses an App That Works More Than Thumb Muscles

text: An article on Friday about Lydia Ko’s tying Annika Sorenstam’s L.P.G.A. record for consecutive rounds under par during the first round of the ANA Inspiration tournament misstated Ko’s score on Thursday in one instance. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she shot a 71, not a 72.
match_headline: Turning a Vexing Stroke Into a Weapon, Lydia Ko Matches a Record

text: An obituary in some copies on Monday about Dr. John D. States, who helped persuade New York to enact the nation’s first state seatbelt law, misstated his age and the year of his birth. He was 89, not 88, and he was born on June 16, 1925, not 1926. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: John D. States Dies at 89; Doctor Helped Create New York’s Seatbelt Law

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Serafim Todorov, the last boxer to defeat Floyd Mayweather Jr., misstated, at one point, the score of Todorov’s loss to Somluck Kamsing of Thailand in the featherweight gold-medal match at the 1996 Olympics. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it was by 8-5 — not by 10-9, which was the score of the semifinal between Todorov and Mayweather.
match_headline: He’s the Last Boxer to Beat Floyd Mayweather Jr., and He So Regrets It

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the World Briefing column on Saturday about Bulgaria’s plans to form a special unit to investigate high-level corruption referred incorrectly to the Bulgarian deputy prime minister. The deputy prime minister, Meglena Kuneva, is a woman.
match_headline: Provisional Government in Libyan Capital Forces Out Its Own Prime Minister

text: An article in some editions on Monday about Notre Dame’s 66-65 victory over South Carolina in the women’s Final Four described incorrectly Madison Cable’s winning basket for Notre Dame. She swished her jumper; she did not “bank it in.”
match_headline: Notre Dame Stifles South Carolina’s Gritty Rally to Reach Second Straight Final

text: A headline with a report in the Sports Briefing column on Friday about John Isner’s victory over Kei Nishikori at the Miami Open misstated, in some copies, the round he advanced to in the tournament. As the report correctly noted, it was the semifinals, not the final.
match_headline: Serena Williams Outlasts Simona Halep to Advance to Miami Open Final

text: A picture caption on Friday with a film review of “Manos Sucias” (“Dirty Hands”), using information from a publicist, reversed the identities of the two actors shown. Cristian Advincula is in the foreground, not Jarlin Martínez.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Manos Sucias,’ Brothers Reconnect on a Drug Run

text: A news analysis article on Tuesday about research into the characteristics of mass killers who also take their own lives misstated the source of a statement about the mental health of Andreas Lubitz, the pilot of a Germanwings jet who killed himself and 149 others in the French Alps last month. Prosecutors — not Lufthansa, Germanwings’s parent airline — said he had talked to a counselor about suicide.
match_headline: The Mind of Those Who Kill, and Kill Themselves

text: An article on Tuesday about the discovery of the remains of a top commander in the Lord’s Resistance Army, a guerrilla group that once terrorized central Africa, referred incorrectly to the removal of the body of the commander, Okot Odhiambo, from a grave site in the Central African Republic. The remains were exhumed last month, not three months ago.
match_headline: Body of a Rebel Leader Is Identified in Uganda

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about Indianapolis’s history of hosting major sporting events referred incorrectly to the relationship between Eli Lilly and Company and the Lilly Endowment, which helped revitalize the downtown area. The endowment was created by the members of the Lilly family; it is not the charitable arm of the company.
match_headline: Sports Groups in Indianapolis Fight to Keep Their City Welcoming

text: Because of an editing error, the Sports of The Times column on Saturday about Michigan State Coach Tom Izzo’s struggles against Duke misstated, at one point, the year of Michigan State’s only win against Duke in the N.C.A.A. tournament. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it was in the 2005 round of 16, not the 1999 Final Four.
match_headline: Michigan State’s Tom Izzo Looks to Knock Out a Friend, and a Blot on His Résumé

text: An article on Wednesday about American museums that have begun returning objects to India in response to an investigation of the dealer Subhash Kapoor, who is awaiting trial in India on charges of trafficking in stolen artifacts, misstated, in some editions, the number of objects obtained from Mr. Kapoor by the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco, which is among those that say they do not believe their items were stolen. It is four, not five.
match_headline: Museums Begin Returning Artifacts to India in Response to Investigation

text: An article on Wednesday about a new law in Kansas that makes the state the first to sharply restrict the most common technique used for second-trimester abortions misspelled the surname of a lawyer with the Center for Reproductive Rights, who discussed the legality of the law. She is Janet Crepps, not Creps. The article also misspelled the surname of a fellow with Physicians for Reproductive Health, which defends abortion rights. She is Dr. Kathleen Morrell, not Morell.
match_headline: Kansas Limits Abortion Method, Opening a New Line of Attack

text: An article on Thursday about the effect citizens’ videos have had in raising questions about police officers’ explanations over their use of deadly force misstated, in some editions, the surname of a college student at a demonstration over police tactics. He is Matthew R. Rabon, not Rabo.
match_headline: Video of Walter Scott Shooting Reignites Debate on Police Tactics

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about Wall Street fees that have wiped out $2.5 billion in New York City pension fund gains misidentified the types of investments in the city’s pension funds for which management fees are not traditionally reported. They are investments in publicly traded assets, like stocks and bonds — not privately traded assets, like real estate.
match_headline: Wall Street Fees Wipe Out $2.5 Billion in New York City Pension Gains

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the new podcast “Undisclosed: The State v. Adnan Syed,” which examines the case that was the subject of the hit podcast “Serial,” referred incorrectly to the suggestion to Sarah Koenig, the host of “Serial,” that she look into the Syed case. It was made by Rabia Chaudry, a lawyer who is presenting the new podcast — not by Ms. Chaudry and two other lawyers, Susan Simpson and Colin Miller.
match_headline: Another ‘Serial’ Chapter, From Group of Lawyers

text: A listing of credits on Thursday with a theater review of “Gigi,” at the Neil Simon Theater in Manhattan, misstated, in some editions, the surname of the actor who plays Gaston Lachaille. As the review and a picture caption with it correctly noted, he is Corey Cott, not Scott.
match_headline: Review: Vanessa Hudgens in a Squeaky Clean ‘Gigi’ on Broadway

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the dermatologist Dr. Fredric Brandt misspelled his given name as Frederic. The error was repeated in the headline. The obituary also misidentified the school from which Dr. Brandt received his medical degree. It was Hahnemann Medical College, not the Drexel University medical school. (Hahnemann is now part of Drexel, but was a separate institution at the time.)
match_headline: Dr. Fredric Brandt, 65, Celebrity ‘Baron of Botox,’ Is Dead

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the satirist Stan Freberg misstated the year he last did voice work for cartoons. It was 2014, not 2011.
match_headline: Stan Freberg, Madcap Adman and Satirist, Dies at 88

text: An article on Thursday about President Obama’s call for an end to therapies aimed at “repairing” gay, lesbian and transgender youth referred incompletely to the evolution of Mr. Obama’s position on same-sex marriage. While Mr. Obama began his national political career publicly opposed to same-sex marriage, he did not begin his overall political career opposed to it. (In 1996 he filled out a questionnaire during his first campaign for public office, an Illinois state senate race, saying he supported same-sex marriage. By 2004, when he was a candidate for the United States Senate, Mr. Obama said he did not support same-sex marriage.) The article also described incorrectly an executive order to ban discrimination by federal contractors. The action would cover sexual orientation and gender identity, not gender.
match_headline: Obama Calls for End to ‘Conversion’ Therapies for Gay and Transgender Youth

text: An article on Friday about the 150th anniversary of the end of the Civil War misstated the name of a song played by a brass band during a program at Arlington National Cemetery marking the date. It is “Yankee Doodle” — not “Yankee Doodle Dandy,” the name of a 1942 musical film about the composer George M. Cohan.
match_headline: Civil War’s Lessons Resound 150 Years Later

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the final day of testimony in the trial of Pedro Hernandez, who is charged with murder in the 1979 disappearance of Etan Patz, 6, erroneously included one of Etan’s relatives among those who were in the courtroom. Julie Patz, his mother, was not in attendance.
match_headline: Suspect’s Mental Ability Is at Fore as Jurors in Patz Trial Prepare to Get Case

text: A picture caption in some editions on Wednesday with an article about Connecticut’s victory over Notre Dame in the final of the N.C.A.A. women’s basketball tournament, using information from The Associated Press, misidentified the UConn player shown fighting for a rebound with Taya Reimer and Breanna Stewart. She is Kia Nurse, not Kiah Stokes.
match_headline: UConn’s Win Isn’t Pretty, but Title Is a Perfect 10th for Geno Auriemma

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the Rangers’ 4-2 victory over the Devils on Tuesday referred incorrectly to the Islanders’ qualification for the postseason. The Islanders clinched a postseason berth on Thursday; they had not yet qualified for their second postseason trip in three seasons on Tuesday.
match_headline: As Rangers Return to Playoffs, Devils Again Exit Early

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about a discussion at 2 p.m. tomorrow by Grace Hightower De Niro about her book, “The Women of Rwanda,” misidentified the Book Culture store at which the event will be held. It is the one at 450 Columbus Avenue, not 536 West 112th Street, and the telephone number is 212-595-1962.
match_headline: Spare Times for April 10-16

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about first-generation students in the Ivy League refers imprecisely to whether the government defines first-generation students. While there is no official definition, federal Trio programs for disadvantaged students do define them: students whose parents have no bachelor’s degree. The article also misstates the pledge made by Washington University in St. Louis regarding enrolling freshmen eligible for low-income Pell grants, and when it made that pledge. It announced in January, not last year, that it hoped to increase their rate from 8 percent to 13 percent by 2020, not that it hoped to double the rate by that time.
match_headline: First-Generation Students Unite

text: A picture caption on Page 36 this weekend with a report in the “This and That” feature about a limited-edition bag designed by Max Mara and the architect Renzo Piano to mark the reopening of the Whitney Museum of American Art in Manhattan refers incorrectly to a sketch of the bag. The sketch was made by Max Mara’s design team — not by Mr. Piano, who designed the museum.
match_headline: In ‘Life at the Limits,’ Extreme Creatures at American Museum of Natural History

text: An editorial on Friday about the National Rifle Association’s convention incorrectly described the rules for carrying concealed firearms at the event. Carrying is prohibited at one of the main convention venues, not all of them.
match_headline: No Firing Pins, Please, as the N.R.A. Gathers

text: An article last Sunday about a town in Norway from which eight men have traveled to Syria to fight alongside the Islamic State and other militant groups misspelled the name of the town. It is Fredrikstad, not Frederikstad. The error was repeated in the dateline, in a picture caption and on a map. The article also misidentified the capital of Turkey. It is Ankara, not Istanbul. And because of an editing error, a reporting credit was omitted. Henrik Pryser Libell contributed from Oslo.
match_headline: A Norway Town and Its Pipeline to Jihad in Syria

text: An article last Sunday about findings that could bolster claims that two ancient funerary artifacts represent an authentic link to Jesus misstated the name of a trace element for which the geologist Aryeh Shimron tested Rendzina soil. Dr. Shimron was searching for chromium — not chrome, which is not an element, of course.
match_headline: Findings Reignite Debate on Claim of Jesus’ Bones

text: A listing of information on March 29 about the Big City Book Club misstated the day of the online discussion for “The Island at the Center of the World.” It is Tuesday, April 28, not Thursday.
ref_headline: The Island at the Center of the World.
match_headline: Next for the Big City Book Club: Russell Shorto’s ‘The Island at the Center of the World’

text: An article last Sunday about new characters who will be appearing on HBO’s “Game of Thrones” this season referred incorrectly to the relationship between Prince Doran Martell and Myrcella Baratheon. She is a ward of the prince, not his wife.
match_headline: New Faces on HBO’s ‘Game of Thrones’

text: An article last Sunday about the new Broadway musical “Finding Neverland” misspelled the given name of the man who wrote “The Man Who Was Peter Pan,” the play on which the musical is based. He is Allan Knee, not Alan.
match_headline: After Turbulent Flight, ‘Finding Neverland’ Alights on Broadway

text: A review on March 22 about “The Opposite of Spoiled” rendered incorrectly the name of a retailer whose prices the book’s author, Ron Lieber, describes considering as a guideline to determine his daughter’s clothing budget. It is Lands’ End, not Land’s End.
match_headline: ‘The Opposite of Spoiled,’ by Ron Lieber

text: An article on March 29 about a federal prison in Florence, Colo., misspelled the surname of a well-known inmate. As the article correctly noted in other references, he is Ted Kaczynski, not Kacynski.
match_headline: Inside America’s Toughest Federal Prison

text: An entry with the “On the Market” feature last Sunday misstated the county in which Cold Spring Harbor, N.Y., is situated. It is in Suffolk County, not Nassau.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in New York and New Jersey

text: An article last Sunday about private testing of grocery items for food safety misstated the type of E. coli that is a lethal threat in ground beef. It is E. coli O157, not 1057.
match_headline: Private Eyes in the Grocery Aisles

text: An article on March 29 about the novelist Evan S. Connell and his relationship to Sausalito, Calif., misstated the location of the high school attended by Mr. Connell. It was in Kansas City, Mo., not Kansas City, Kan.
match_headline: Searching for Evan S. Connell’s Bohemian Sausalito

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about a Swedish company’s efforts to convince the Food and Drug Administration that traditional smoking warnings are too harsh to describe its tobacco product, snus, misstated the views of Christofer Fjellner, who represents the Moderate Party of Sweden in the European Parliament. He wants to lift the European Union ban on snus, which is moist, loose tobacco packaged in a pouch like a tea bag and tucked between the lip and the gums; he does not hope for a ban on snus.
match_headline: Swedish Company Asks F.D.A. to Remove Warnings From Smokeless Tobacco Product

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the Mets’ 2-1 loss to the Washington Nationals misstated, in some copies, the way in which Curtis Granderson struck out in the second inning. It was looking, not swinging.
match_headline: Before Loss, Mets Scoff at Talk of Tension

text: An article last Monday about an exhibition in Paris celebrating the film pioneers Louis and Auguste Lumière referred incorrectly to the attempt of another early filmmaker, Georges Méliès, to buy one of the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph machines. The Lumières in fact refused his offer and he eventually purchased filmmaking equipment elsewhere; he did not buy one of their first cinematographs. The article also referred incorrectly to films that Louis Lumière captured on 35-millimeter strips to later project with a cinematograph. They were 17-meter films, lasting about 50 seconds, not 17-minute films.
match_headline: ‘Lumière! Inventing Cinema’ in Paris Celebrates the Birth of Movies

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a dance review of the Stephen Petronio Company, at the Joyce Theater in Manhattan, misspelled the surname of a dancer. She is Davalois Fearon, not Freadon. And another picture caption with the review misidentified the dancer shown with Melissa Toogood. He is Nicholas Sciscione — not Gino Grenek, another member of the company.
match_headline: Review: Stephen Petronio’s ‘Bloodlines’

text: An article on April 3 about Billie Holiday and some of the commemorations of the 100th anniversary of her birth misstated the month she died. It was July 1959, not June.
match_headline: For Billie Holiday’s 100th Birthday, Tributes and New Releases

text: An article on April 3 about the surfing champion Kelly Slater and his new fashion line, Outerknown, misidentified the brand for which Mr. Slater’s collaborator John Moore previously designed. He was in charge of men’s wear design for Hollister by Abercrombie & Fitch, not J. Crew.
match_headline: Surfer Kelly Slater Wades Into Fashion

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the singer and actress Julie Wilson, using information from her son, omitted a survivor. Besides her son Holt McCallany, Ms. Wilson is survived by a granddaughter.
match_headline: Julie Wilson, Sultry Cabaret Legend and Actress, Dies at 90

text: An article on April 2 about a decision in California to impose mandatory water restrictions for the first time misstated the amount of ornamental turf expected to be replaced with plantings that consume less water. It is 50 million square feet, not acres.
match_headline: California Imposes First Mandatory Water Restrictions to Deal With Drought

text: An article on Friday about an increase in black immigrants to the United States erroneously included one country among the Central and South American countries that have emigrants in the United States. Mexico, which has 70,000 black emigrants in the United States, is part of North America, not Central or South America.
match_headline: Black Immigrants Have Quadrupled Since 1980, Study Says

text: An article on Saturday about a vote by the Texas Medical Board to limit the use of telemedicine referred incorrectly to Jason Gorevic’s role with Teladoc, a national company that provides telephone or video consultations with doctors. While Mr. Gorevic is Teladoc’s chief executive, he is not a founder of the company.
match_headline: Texas Medical Panel Votes to Limit Telemedicine Practices in State

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about Internet companies that seek to match consumers with service providers misstated the background of Matt Feldman, the founder of Homlux, a home services company. As the article correctly noted, he is an entrepreneur whose earlier venture was a video company; he is not a handyman. The article also misstated the price Homlux charged to install a kitchen faucet purchased through Amazon. It was $145, not $180.
match_headline: Amazon, Google and More Are Drawn to Home Services Market

text: An article on Thursday about testing the Apple Watch misstated the price of the watch tested, a 42-millimeter stainless steel watch with a Milanese loop band. It is $699, not $649.
match_headline: Dear Diary: My Week Wearing an Apple Watch

text: An article on Saturday about the ebbing fortunes of nonbank financial institutions misidentified the government entity that has the authority to designate a large nonbank financial company “systemically important” to the financial system. That power is held by the Financial Stability Oversight Council, which includes the Federal Reserve and other agencies; it is not held by the Fed alone.
match_headline: The Lessons for Finance in the GE Capital Retreat

text: An article on Monday about the hidden costs of low wages misstated the name of the Chicago suburb where Wanda Brewer, a part-time college teacher who receives Medicaid and food stamps, lives. It is Maywood — not Mayfield, which is a township.
match_headline: Working, but Needing Public Assistance Anyway

text: An article on Saturday about Odin Biron, an American actor who stars in a popular Russian sitcom and announced in February that he is gay, erroneously attributed a distinction to him. Several Americans have graduated from the Moscow Art Theater School’s intensive degree program; Mr. Biron is not one of only two Americans ever to do so.
match_headline: After ‘Interns’ Star Came Out in Russia, a Mix of Fury and Shrugs

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the author Ivan Doig misstated part of the name of a novel he wrote that was reviewed in The New York Times Book Review in 2006. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, the novel is “The Whistling Season,” not “The Whispering Season.”
match_headline: Ivan Doig, Author Who Lived the Western Life, Dies at 75

text: Because of an editing error, the Memo From Panama article on Monday, about a possible new chapter in relations between the United States and Latin America after President Obama met the Cuban president, Raúl Castro, at the Summit of the Americas, referred incorrectly to the United States government’s list of nations that sponsor terrorism, which includes Cuba. Although Cuba has been reluctant to agree to the reopening of embassies in Washington and Havana as long as it remains on the list, being on the list does not prevent Cuba or any nation from reopening embassies. (The White House announced on Tuesday that President Obama intends to remove Cuba from the terrorism list.)
match_headline: Talks With Cuba Earn U.S. Raves in Latin America

text: An article on Tuesday about the fatal shooting of a black suspect by a reserve deputy in Tulsa, Okla., misstated, in some editions, the day the episode took place. It was Thursday, April 2 — not “last Thursday,” April 9.
match_headline: Volunteer for Sheriff Is Charged in Killing After Mistaking Handgun for Taser

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival, in Indio, Calif., misidentified the person that Tyler the Creator, a rapper, insulted during a performance. She is Kendall Jenner, not her sister Kylie.
match_headline: Talent vs. Buzz: the Push-Pull of Coachella

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the author Eduardo Galeano misstated his birth date. He was born on Sept. 3, 1940, not April 13 of that year.
match_headline: Eduardo Galeano, Uruguayan Voice of Anti-Capitalism, Is Dead at 74

text: An obituary in some editions on Thursday and Friday about the newspaper publisher David Laventhol referred incorrectly to his tenure as chairman of the Pulitzer Prize board. He held that position for one term, 1988-89 — not in 1988 and in 1999.
match_headline: David Laventhol, Publisher on Both Coasts, Dies at 81

text: An article on Wednesday about the denial of a request by Yale University School of Medicine, working with the education technology company 2U, to expand a medical program online, described incorrectly in some editions one of 2U’s other partnerships. It involves the University of Southern California’s teaching and social work degrees, not its teaching and nursing degrees.
match_headline: Yale Medical School’s Request to Expand Campus Program Online Is Denied

text: An article on Wednesday about allegations of anti-Semitism involving the Students of Color Coalition at Stanford University misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the campaign manager for Molly Horwitz, who is Jewish and had sought the endorsement of the coalition in her run for the student senate. She is Miriam Pollock, not Pollack.
match_headline: Student Coalition at Stanford Confronts Allegations of Anti-Semitism

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about the sentencing of educators in Atlanta involved in a scandal over inflated test scores misstated, in some editions, the sentence given to one defendant, Angela Williamson. It is two years, not seven.
match_headline: Atlanta School Workers Sentenced in Test Score Cheating Case

text: An article on Wednesday about the 150th anniversary of the death of Abraham Lincoln referred incorrectly to the house from which Theodore Roosevelt as a young boy was said to have watched Lincoln’s funeral procession pass. It was his grandparents’ house, not his house.
match_headline: Abraham Lincoln, the One President All of Them Want to Be More Like

text: An article on Saturday about four people who were found dead at a house in Floral Park, Queens, misstated the location of the neighborhood in some editions. It is in eastern Queens, not southeastern Queens.
match_headline: 4 Are Found Dead at a House in Queens; Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Is Suspected

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Yankees’ 6-5 victory over the Baltimore Orioles referred incorrectly in some copies to Stephen Drew’s .162 batting average last season. It was the third-worst mark over the last century for players with at least 300 plate appearances, not at-bats. The article also misstated, in some copies, the given name of the Orioles player who homered in the sixth. He is Adam Jones, not Chris.
match_headline: Rare Jolt by Stephen Drew Lifts Yanks Over Orioles

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Houston Rockets guard James Harden’s production at the free-throw line this season misidentified, in some copies, the team that beat the Charlotte Hornets on Monday. It was the Houston Rockets, Harden’s current team — not the Oklahoma City Thunder, his former team.
match_headline: Rockets’ James Harden Chases M.V.P. With a Blizzard of Free Throws

text: A picture on Monday with the What’s on TV highlights in some editions, using information from Reuters, was published in error. The picture, with an entry about “Lincoln’s Last Day” on the Smithsonian Channel, shows a fictitious newspaper account of the shooting of Abraham Lincoln that was created for the book “Lincoln Shot: A President’s Life Remembered” by Barry Denenberg. It is not an image of an actual newspaper.
match_headline: What’s On TV Monday

text: An editorial on Tuesday about New York City’s pension funds incorrectly stated that fees for asset managers over the last 10 years reduced the funds’ gains basically to zero. The funds showed positive returns, but their performance fell well short of benchmarks after fees were accounted for
match_headline: New York’s Leaky Public Pension Funds

text: An article in some editions on Monday about group discounts on commuter train lines, using information from New Jersey Transit, gave an outdated cost for chartering a full train. It is $12,000, not $6,000.
match_headline: Group Discounts Benefit Commuter Train Lines and Passengers

text: A caption in some editions on Monday for a picture of three boys in a tree at Carl Schurz Park in Manhattan misspelled the surname of one of them. The boy at the right, hanging from a limb, is Aaron Kuper, not Cuper.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in Brooklyn and Manhattan

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the baseball roundup on Monday about the Padres’ 6-4 victory over the Giants misidentified the location of the game. It was in San Diego, not in San Francisco.
match_headline: Your Monday Briefing

text: An article on Wednesday about the annual production of the play “To Kill a Mockingbird” in Monroeville, Ala., the hometown of Harper Lee, the author of the novel on which the play is based, referred incorrectly to a lawsuit filed by Ms. Lee in 2013 against the Monroe County Heritage Museum, which produces the show. The suit, over items the museum was selling, focused on trademark issues, not on copyright issues.
match_headline: ‘To Kill a Mockingbird’ Is a Stage Hit at Home in Monroeville, Ala.
