text: An article on Tuesday about the release of five women’s rights activists who had been detained in China for weeks after trying to start a campaign against sexual harassment on public transportation misattributed, in some editions, a comment posted on a website, ChinaChange.org , that was part of an interview with Wang Zheng, an associate professor of history and women’s studies at the University of Michigan. It was Yaxue Cao, an editor at the website who conducted the interview — not Professor Wang herself — who said, “The Chinese feminists might have felt that they enjoyed a special freedom, but now they see the barbaric and brutal reality where every Chinese citizen, man or woman, is denied basic political rights.”
ref_headline: The Chinese feminists might have felt that they enjoyed a special freedom, but now they see the barbaric and brutal reality where every Chinese citizen, man or woman, is denied basic political rights.
match_headline: China Releases 5 Women’s Rights Activists Detained for Weeks

text: An article on Friday about approval of a generic version of a drug to treat multiple sclerosis misstated the availability of generic versions of drugs to treat that disease. Generic versions are available for mitoxantrone, which is approved for treatment of multiple sclerosis but is not widely used; it is not the case that there are no generic versions of multiple sclerosis drugs.
match_headline: Generic Version of Copaxone, Multiple Sclerosis Drug, Is Approved

text: An article on Friday about a lawsuit filed against the former Florida State quarterback Jameis Winston by the woman who accused him of sexually assaulting her referred incorrectly to the Tallahassee Police Department’s investigation. Winston was never questioned; it is not the case that he “was not questioned by the Tallahassee Police Department until nearly two weeks after it learned of the allegation.”
ref_headline: was not questioned by the Tallahassee Police Department until nearly two weeks after it learned of the allegation.
match_headline: Jameis Winston Being Sued by Woman Who Accused Him of Rape in 2012

text: A picture caption on Page 44 this weekend with the continuation of an article about British jihadists omits the credit for the photograph of Shiraz Maher, a former Islamic militant. It was taken by George Georgiou for The New York Times.
match_headline: Her Majesty’s Jihadists

text: An editorial on Wednesday about the Senate bill on congressional review of any final nuclear deal with Iran misstated a provision in the bill. After review, Congress may choose to vote on the agreement, but it is not required to do so.
match_headline: A Reckless Act in the Senate on Iran

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the risk Hillary Rodham Clinton would be taking if she aligns her campaign for president too closely with President Obama’s policies misstated the number of years she was in the Senate. It was eight, not six.
match_headline: Hillary Clinton Weighs How to Recast Ties to Obama

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the benefits and drawbacks of Britain’s 10-year-old Freedom of Information law omitted, in some editions, the given name and the position of an official who said local governments were wary about ignoring frivolous requests for information. He is Gareth Cosslett, a communications adviser at the Cumbria County Council.
match_headline: From A to Z (Asteroids to Zombies), the British Just Want the Facts

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Yankees’ 8-4 loss to the Boston Red Sox misstated the given name of one of the Yankees outfielders who had an extra-base hit tick off his glove. He is Garrett Jones, not Brett.
match_headline: Errant Fielding Undermines Yankees in Loss to Red Sox

text: Because of an editing error, the byline for the Neighborhood Joint column in some editions last Sunday, about Silver Moon Bakery in Manhattan, misspelled the given name of the reporter. She is Sylvie Bigar, not Silvie.
match_headline: At Silver Moon Bakery, the Baking Never Stops

text: An article on April 5 about Kamel Daoud, an Algerian writer, misidentified the role of the journalist Léa Salamé on the French television program “On n’est pas Couché.” She is a panelist, not a guest.
match_headline: Stranger Still

text: A chart on April 5 with an article about maps carried an erroneous headline for a list of congested metropolitan areas. The list covered North America and Europe, not the United States and Europe.
match_headline: Letter of Recommendation: The Thomas Guide to Los Angeles

text: An article last Sunday about the Mark Morris Dance Group, which opens a five-night run at the Brooklyn Academy of Music on Wednesday, misstated the surname of a company dancer. He is Aaron Loux, not Roux.
match_headline: Mark Morris’s ‘Spring, Spring, Spring’ Heads to Brooklyn Academy of Music

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the verismo style of opera misidentified the role being performed by Jonas Kaufmann. He was playing Canio in “Pagliacci,” not Turiddu in “Cavalleria Rusticana.”
match_headline: A New ‘Cav/Pag’ at the Met Is Opera Heavy on the Red Sauce

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about Chita Rivera, who is starring in the Kander and Ebb musical “The Visit,” misstated the day the show opens at the Lyceum Theater. It is Thursday, not next Sunday.
match_headline: The Indomitable Chita Rivera, Back on Broadway in ‘The Visit’

text: An article last Sunday about an invitation-only summit meeting that brought together people of varying professions for a salon-like experience in the mountains of Utah misstated the given name of a D.J. in attendance at Powder Mountain. He is Ryan Garza, not Adam.
match_headline: The Ski Resort That Crowdsourcing Built

text: Because of an editing error, a report on March 29 about the marriage of Ariella Morrow and Ryan Tolkin misstated the employment status of the bride’s mother, Livia F. Morrow . She is a second-grade teacher at Public School 63 in Ozone Park, Queens; she is not retired.
match_headline: Ariella Morrow and Ryan Tolkin

text: An article on Friday about a former manager of a dental office in the Bronx who was charged with practicing dentistry without a license misstated the surname of the spokeswoman for the Bronx district attorney’s office. She is Terry Raskyn, not Rafkyn.
match_headline: Unlicensed Dental Work in the Bronx Leads to Arrest

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the discovery of two bodies on railroad tracks in Brooklyn, using information from the police, misstated the location where they were found. The bodies of the unidentified men were found in the area of 15th Avenue and 61st Street, not 67th Street.
match_headline: Two Found Dead on Brooklyn Railroad Tracks

text: An article on Friday about Sony Pictures Entertainment’s displeasure at the posting of its internal documents on WikiLeaks misstated, in some copies, when Sony Pictures issued its statement. It was Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: WikiLeaks Posts Sony Pictures Documents, Angering the Studio

text: An article in some editions on Friday about teams with losing records that make the N.B.A. playoffs misstated the number of teams who have done so in this century. It is 12, not 11.
match_headline: It’s N.B.A. Playoff Time. Pay No Attention to Those Losing Records.

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the differences between the Rangers and the Islanders misstated the number of N.H.L. teams for which Islanders goalie Jaroslav Halak has played. The Islanders are his fifth team, not his third.
match_headline: Rangers or Islanders? Take Your Pick

text: An article last Monday about the 60th anniversary of the decisive seventh game of the 1955 N.B.A. championship series between the Fort Wayne Pistons and the Syracuse Nationals misidentified the Indiana city where Syracuse lost three games of the finals after winning the first two at home. The games were played in Indianapolis, not in Fort Wayne.
match_headline: Tribute on Ice to Gritty Competitors Who Made Syracuse the King of the N.B.A.

text: An obituary on Friday about Thelma Coyne Long, an Australian tennis star, misstated the name of the suburb of Sydney where she lived. It is Maroubra, not Marouba.
match_headline: Thelma Coyne Long, Australian Tennis Champion, Dies at 96

text: An article on Tuesday about the filing of espionage charges by Iran against Jason Rezaian, The Washington Post’s Tehran correspondent, referred imprecisely to the views of the National Iranian American Council, an advocacy group in the United States that has criticized his prosecution. While the group supports nuclear negotiations and improved relations with Iran, it has also been critical of Iran’s government. The group is not viewed as “supportive of Iran” on all issues.
match_headline: Charges Against Jason Rezaian, Washington Post Reporter Held in Iran, Include Espionage

text: Because of an editing error, the Tehran Journal article on Monday, about a visit to Iran by American executives who hope the lifting of economic sanctions will open up business opportunities there, misstated the role of one of the visitors, Dick Simon, in the Young Presidents’ Organization, a business network whose members organized the trip. Mr. Simon is a member of the group, not a co-founder.
match_headline: Billboards in Iran Say ‘Death to America,’ but Officials Say ‘Let’s Make a Deal’

text: An article on Wednesday about India’s plans to use privately owned gold for trade and investment misspelled the given name of India’s minister of state for finance. He is Jayant Sinha, not Jayanth.
match_headline: India, Seeking a Boost, Plans to Put Its ‘Idle Gold’ to Work

text: An article on Monday about challenges facing Box, the cloud computing company, misstated, in some editions, the amount Box raised with its initial public offering. The company raised $175 million at its I.P.O., not “more than $500 million.”
match_headline: Box, Provider of Cloud-Computing Services, Faces Make-or-Break Moment

text: An article on Wednesday about quarterly results of the Chipotle restaurant chain misstated the first time the company exceeded $1 billion in sales in a quarter. It first reached that threshold in the second quarter of 2014, not in the first quarter of this year. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Chipotle Posts Another Quarter of Billion-Dollar Sales

text: An article on Monday about Apple’s strategy for selling the company’s new Apple Watch referred incorrectly to outlets where the Apple Watch will be sold. The device will be sold at some third-party retailers; it will not be sold exclusively through Apple’s own stores and website.
match_headline: Changing Tactics, Apple Promotes Watch as a Luxury Item

text: A report in the Business Briefing column on Wednesday about Credit Suisse’s quarterly results misstated the year the company made a profit of 859 million francs. It was in the first three months of 2014, not 2013.
match_headline: Credit Suisse Profit Rises 23 Percent in First Quarter

text: An article on Tuesday about private equity investors’ agreeing to buy Cirque du Soleil misspelled the surname of a lawyer involved in movie deals in China who noted the potential for Cirque to expand there. He is Joshua B. Grode, not Grod.
match_headline: Sale of Cirque du Soleil Aims to Open Doors in China

text: A headline on Wednesday with a report in the N.H.L. roundup about Game 3 of the playoffs series between the Detroit Red Wings and the Tampa Bay Lightning misidentified the winner of the game in some copies. As the article correctly noted, the Red Wings won.

A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about the National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Masters awards ceremony, at Jazz at Lincoln Center, misstated the surname of an honoree at one point in some editions. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Joe Segal, not Glaser.
match_headline: N.E.A. Jazz Masters Hail From Inside and Outside the Club

text: An article on Tuesday about the physics, biology, psychology and history of the color green misidentified the chemical used in the green ink on dollar bills. It is dichromium trioxide, not chromium trioxide.
match_headline: Our Ever Green World

text: An article on April 9 about the writer Brad Gooch referred incorrectly to the release of the film “Uncle Howard,” a documentary about the late filmmaker Howard Brookner, a former boyfriend of Mr. Gooch. It will be released as a stand-alone feature documentary; it will not be included on Criterion’s DVD release of “Burroughs: The Movie.”
match_headline: In the Gritty New York of the ’70s and ’80s, Not Exactly a Model Life

text: An article on Monday about the military health care system misstated the findings of research on sickle-cell trait, a genetic condition, in African-American military recruits. The studies found that African-American recruits with the trait were 30 times as likely — not 30 percent more likely — to suffer an exercise-related death than those without it.
match_headline: Service Members Are Left in Dark on Health Errors

text: An article on Monday about a debate in Los Angeles over whether members of the Actors’ Equity union should be paid a mandatory minimum wage for their work in small theaters, using information from the Circle X Theater Co., misstated the budget for its production of “Trevor.” It was $34,000, not $40,000. The article also misstated the amount the actors were paid. It was $800 each for the entire run, not about $144.
match_headline: Actors’ Equity Pushes for Minimum Wage, but Not All Members Want It

text: An article on Wednesday about reducing emissions of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, misstated the amount of the gas that escaped worldwide in 2012. It was 3.6 trillion cubic feet, not 3.6 billion.
match_headline: Study Finds Low Cost in Reducing Methane Emissions

text: A picture caption in some editions on Wednesday with an article about the Mets’ 7-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves misidentified, in some copies, the Mets player shown with Kevin Plawecki and Michael Cuddyer after the game. He is Sean Gilmartin, not David Wright.
match_headline: Encouraged by d’Arnaud, a Mets Rookie Has a Strong Debut

text: An article on Thursday about Gregory Pardlo, who won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry on Monday, misstated part of a comment about his verses by Stephen Burt, a poetry critic and English professor at Harvard. Mr. Burt said, “They’re very information-dense and very conscious of playing with genre and trope in kinds of written language,” not “and tropic kinds of written language.”
ref_headline: They’re very information-dense and very conscious of playing with genre and trope in kinds of written language,
match_headline: Gregory Pardlo, Pulitzer Winner for Poetry, on His Sudden Fame

text: An article last Friday about art galleries in Brooklyn and Queens erroneously included one gallery among those recommended in Williamsburg. Smack Mellon is in Dumbo, at 92 Plymouth Street — not in Williamsburg.
match_headline: 10 Galleries to Visit in Brooklyn and Queens

text: An obituary on Thursday about Betty Willis, the designer of the “Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas, Nevada” neon sign, misspelled the name of a hotel in Las Vegas whose marquee was designed by Brian K. Leming Sr., who died on the same day as Mrs. Willis. It is the Fremont, not the Freemont.
ref_headline: Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas, Nevada
match_headline: Betty Willis, Whose ‘Fabulous’ Sign Defined Las Vegas, Dies at 91

text: A picture caption on Friday with the continuation of an article about Comcast’s decision to abandon its effort to take over Time Warner misidentified the building shown. It is Time Warner Cable’s flagship store, not the company’s headquarters.
match_headline: Comcast Is Said to End $45 Billion Bid for Time Warner Cable

text: An article on April 10 about Russians’ reining in their spending misstated the size of the Avia Park mall in Moscow. It is 377,000 square meters, not square feet. (It is 4.1 million square feet.) The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption. The article, using information posted at the shopping center, also misstated the status of H&M and American Eagle Outfitters stores at the mall. The H&M store will open at a later date, but American Eagle Outfitters does not plan to open at the mall; the stores are not open now. The article also referred imprecisely to the Adidas store at the mall. While the Adidas Kids store is open, the main Adidas store is not yet open. And the article, using information from the mall management, referred incorrectly to the ownership of a company that invests in the mall. The company is owned by Igor Rotenberg — not by his father, Arkady Rotenberg.
match_headline: Russian Consumers Reflect the Pinch of Economic Sanctions

text: A headline with the N.B.A. roundup on Friday about the results of Thursday night’s playoff games misidentified, in some copies, one of the teams that moved within a game of sweeping their first-round N.B.A. series. Besides the Bulls, the Cavaliers — not the Celtics — did so, as the article correctly noted.
match_headline: Cavaliers Finish Sweep of Celtics but Lose Kevin Love to Injury

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the baseball roundup on Friday about the San Francisco Giants’ 3-2 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers misidentified pitcher Juan Nicasio’s team in some copies. He plays for Los Angeles, not San Francisco.
match_headline: Two Resurgent Yankees Fuel Road Victory Over Tigers

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about plans by Printed Matter Inc., a nonprofit organization devoted to the distribution and appreciation of books by artists, to move to 11th Avenue in Manhattan from its site on 10th Avenue, using information from its website, misstated the number of titles in its inventory and the number of artists represented by those titles. There are about 15,000 titles by more than 6,000 artists, not more than 40,000 titles by some 28,000 artists.
match_headline: Los Angeles Temple Chooses Koolhaas for a Grand Expansion

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with a film review of “The Great Museum,” a documentary about the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, misidentified the painter of a work shown being installed at the museum. He was Pieter Bruegel the Elder, not Hieronymus Bosch.
match_headline: Review: ‘The Great Museum,’ a Stroll Through the Kunsthistorisches in Vienna

text: An article on Thursday about the number of employees who have been fired at the Department of Veterans Affairs for manipulating wait times of patients misstated the pay eligibility of workers facing termination. Employees are eligible for pay if their terminations are overturned, but not during the appeals process.
match_headline: Few People Lost Jobs With V.A. in Scandal

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the Mets’ 3-2 victory over the Atlanta Braves misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the Mets player who caught Jace Peterson’s deep drive to center field in the seventh inning. He is Juan Lagares, not Legares.
match_headline: Mets Rally Past Braves to Extend Their Streak to 10 Games

text: An article on Thursday about the development of flow batteries for use with the electrical grid described incorrectly the capacity of a large rechargeable battery, in Pullman, Wash. The battery can store about 3.2 megawatt-hours of energy, and can release about a megawatt of power over three to four hours. It does not store a megawatt of electricity; storage is measured in megawatt-hours.
match_headline: Liquid Batteries for Solar and Wind Power

text: An article on Friday about the United States Geological Survey’s first comprehensive assessment of the link between earthquakes and oil and gas operations omitted a response from the American Petroleum Institute because an email to The Times went astray. The industry group did not decline to comment. In the email, Zachary Cikanek, a spokesman for the group, said that from an environmental standpoint, injection wells remained one of the best disposal options available. He noted that the Environmental Protection Agency has released new guidelines to help regulators make decisions regarding issues like well placement and appropriate injections rates for fluids.
match_headline: U.S. Maps Pinpoint Earthquakes Linked to Quest for Oil and Gas

text: An article on Monday about Chipotle Mexican Grill’s decision to stop using genetically engineered ingredients misstated the breadth of the action. While the company will use only products from non-genetically modified organisms in its food preparation, it will continue to serve some soft drinks with sweeteners derived from genetically engineered corn. It will not be “serving” only food free of G.M.O. ingredients.
match_headline: Chipotle to Stop Using Genetically Altered Ingredients

text: An article on Friday about Kleiner Perkins, the venture capital firm, which filed for reimbursement in a gender discrimination suit, misstated the fees paid to Paul Gompers, a professor at Harvard Business School who was a witness in the case. It was $131,400, not $92,700.
match_headline: Kleiner Perkins Seeks Nearly $1 Million From Ellen Pao

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about Mary Keefe, the model for the 1943 Norman Rockwell painting “Rosie the Riveter,” misstated the current dollar equivalent of the amount she was paid for posing. Her total pay, $10 for two sessions — not $5, her pay for each session — would be roughly $144 in today’s dollars.
match_headline: Mary Keefe, Model for Rockwell’s ‘Rosie the Riveter,’ Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the author Frederic Morton misstated the year he wrote a piece for The New York Times about Kristallnacht. It was 1978, not 1990. (The piece was republished in 1990 in a special section commemorating the 20th anniversary of The Times’s Op-Ed page.)
match_headline: Frederic Morton, Author Who Chronicled the Rothschilds, Dies at 90

text: An article on Saturday about a fatal New York City police shooting in 1858 misstated the given name of the man who was killed. He was John Hollis, not Robert. The error was repeated in a caption for an accompanying illustration. The article also referred imprecisely to the makeup of New York City in 1898. While the Bronx was part of the city at that time, the city had not consisted of Manhattan and the Bronx from its beginning “until 1898.” (New York City was limited to the island of Manhattan until 1874, when the Bronx was incorporated, and the other three boroughs were incorporated in 1898.)
match_headline: Police Killing of Unarmed Man Agitated New York ... in the 1850s

text: An article on Tuesday about grants given by the New England Aquarium for marine conservation work described incorrectly a project to recycle torn fishing nets in Chile. The grant for that project was out of the ordinary for the aquarium because it focused on an engineering solution to marine debris rather than on a particular species or habitat — not because it went to a nonprofit rather than directly to researchers.
match_headline: Trying to Save the Oceans, One Small Grant at a Time

text: A review in the New Music column on Tuesday about the album “Orphic Machine” by the clarinetist Ben Goldberg, which was inspired by an essay by Allen Grossman titled “Summa Lyrica: A Primer of the Commonplaces in Speculative Poetics,” omitted a word from a quotation from the preface to the essay. It says, “Above all, this is a text for use, intended like a poem to give rise to thoughts about something else,” not “to rise to thoughts about something else.”
match_headline: Review: Ben Goldberg’s ‘Orphic Machine’ Influenced by Poetry

text: An article on Tuesday about the USA Pavilion at the Expo Milano 2015 world’s fair, which opens Friday, misstated part of the name of one of the organizations funding the pavilion. It is the American Chamber of Commerce in Italy (not Chamber of “Congress”).
match_headline: A Feast of Architectural Styles for Expo Milano 2015

text: An article on Friday about contributions to the Clinton Foundation from people associated with a Canadian uranium-mining company described incorrectly the foundation’s agreement with the Obama administration regarding foreign-government donations while Hillary Clinton was secretary of state. Under the agreement, the foundation would not accept new donations from foreign governments, though it could seek State Department waivers in specific cases. The foundation was not barred from accepting all foreign-government donations.
match_headline: Cash Flowed to Clinton Foundation Amid Russian Uranium Deal

text: An article on Saturday about a ceremony in Yerevan, Armenia, marking the 100th anniversary of the Armenian genocide misspelled the surname of a dentist from Wisconsin who said he came to remember relatives killed then. He is Charles A. Hajinian, not Hijinian.
match_headline: Armenia, on Day of Rain and Sorrow, Observes 100th Anniversary of Genocide

text: A report in the World Briefing column on April 4 about China’s deportation of Xue Feng, an American geologist who had been imprisoned for more than seven years on a vague charge of “illegally procuring state secrets,” referred incorrectly to his employment status at the time of his detention in 2007. Mr. Xue had resigned from IHS, an American consulting company, several months before he was detained; he was not working for IHS at the time.
match_headline: China Deports American Jailed on Spy Charges

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on April 16 about devices and apps useful for the outdoor-living season described incorrectly a feature of the Netgear Nighthawk Wi-Fi Range Extender that is used to connect wired devices to a wireless network. The five ports on the Nighthawk are called Gigabit Ethernet ports, not gigabyte Ethernet ports.
match_headline: Devices and Apps for Heading Outdoors After the Thaw

text: An article on Wednesday about the federal Agriculture Department’s support for two private investment funds that are planning to buy stakes in businesses across rural America, using information from a department spokesman, misstated the surname of the manager of one of the funds, the Innova Ag Innovation Fund. He is Jan Bouten, not Jan Forward.
match_headline: U.S. Backs Private Bid for $125 Million for Rural Investment

text: An article on Tuesday about the Yankees’ approach to marketing Alex Rodriguez’s 660th career home run misstated the actual cost to the team if they paid him a disputed $6 million bonus for the feat (tying Willie Mays for fourth on the home run list). It would be $9 million — not $12 million — because the team would also pay a luxury tax at a rate of 50 percent, not 100 percent. The error was also reflected in the headline.
match_headline: Marketing No. 660 Could Cost Yankees Even More

text: An article on Wednesday about the Minnesota Vikings’ stated plan not to trade running back Adrian Peterson, despite his off-field problems and his displeasure with team management, misspelled the given name of a player who played a significant role for the team last season. He is Jerick McKinnon, not Jerik.
match_headline: Vikings Plan on Keeping Adrian Peterson, G.M. Insists

text: An article on Wednesday about Mubtaahij’s quest to become the first horse to journey from Dubai to win the Kentucky Derby referred incorrectly to his trainer. Mike de Kock works out of South Africa, not South America.
match_headline: A Globe-Trotter in the Kentucky Derby Gate

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with a theater review of “Carousel,” at the Civic Opera House in Chicago, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of the cast members Steven Pasquale, Abigail Simon and Tony Roberts, was taken by Robert Kusel, not by Todd Rosenberg. (Mr. Rosenberg, as the credit noted, did take the other picture that appeared with the review, showing Laura Osnes and Mr. Pasquale.)
match_headline: Review: ‘Carousel,’ a Broadway Turn at Lyric Opera of Chicago

text: An article last Thursday about Sweet Briar and some of the women who graduated from the college misidentified its location. It is outside of Lynchburg, Va., not in Lynchburg.
match_headline: The Independent Women of Sweet Briar

text: An article last Thursday about retail outlets for the Apple Watch, using information from Apple and the owner of the store 10 Corso Como, misstated the month when the watch will be available at the store’s Milan location. It will be for sale in May; it was not available on April 24.
match_headline: The Apple Watch Arrives in Stores (Just Not Its Own)

text: An article last Thursday about the Lilly Pulitzer for Target collection misstated the opening day of Target’s pop-up store in Manhattan. It was last Thursday, not last Friday.
match_headline: Lilly Pulitzer for Target: They Came, They Waited, They Went Home Mad

text: An article last Thursday about the fashion industry’s embrace of sustainability described incorrectly Pitti Filati, which takes place in Florence, Italy. It is a yarn fair, not a fabric fair.
match_headline: This Earth Day, Green Is the New Denim

text: An article on Wednesday about the first night of a curfew imposed to ease unrest in Baltimore referred incorrectly to the suspension of six officers involved in the arrest of Freddie Gray, whose death led to the unrest. The officers were suspended with pay, not without.
match_headline: Crowds Scatter as Baltimore Curfew Takes Hold

text: An article on Tuesday about the removal of “Maus,” a graphic novel about the Holocaust that bears a swastika on its cover, from Moscow bookstores by owners before government raids to rid the city of Nazi symbols ahead of Victory Day, which celebrates the Soviet Union’s defeat of Germany in World War II, misattributed a quotation cited by Boris Kupriyanov, the co-owner of an independent bookstore. The quotation, “An obliging fool is more dangerous than a foe,” is from a fable by Ivan Krylov, a 19th-century Russian fabulist — not from a Russian classic, “Woe From Wit.”
match_headline: ‘Maus’ Book About Holocaust Is Removed in Russia

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the murder conviction and sentencing of the captain of the Sewol, the South Korean ferry that sank a year ago, killing more than 300 people, misspelled his given name. He is Lee Jun-seok, not June-seok.
match_headline: Life Term for Captain in South Korea Ferry Disaster

text: An article on Thursday about efforts by Baltimore civic leaders to temper expectations of the possible public release of a police investigation into the death of Freddie Gray misstated, in some editions, the hours of the curfew in Baltimore. The curfew is from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m., not 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.
match_headline: Baltimore Leaders Try to Curb Expectations Over a Pending Police Report

text: An article last Friday about lawsuits filed by the New York State attorney general against two indoor tanning salon chains, accusing them of playing down the hazards associated with indoor tanning, misstated the relationship between the law firm Harris Beach and Total Tan, one of the chains. The law firm represents Total Tan, it does not own it.
match_headline: Tanning Salons Play Down Hazards, Lawsuits Claim

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the closing of the Carnegie Deli after the discovery of a tapped gas line misstated the reason anonymity was granted to a law enforcement official who said the follow-up investigation was an example of a more cooperative approach between Con Edison and city officials. It was because the investigation is continuing, not because the official wanted to avoid angering City Hall.
match_headline: Closing of Carnegie Deli Amid Con Ed Investigation Disappoints Diners

text: An article on Tuesday about moths that use their legs to help them take flight used an incorrect unit of measurement to describe froghoppers’ movement when they take off. They accelerate during takeoff at 9,000 to 13,000 feet per second squared, not 9,000 to 13,000 feet a second.
match_headline: Legs Give Moths a Flying Start

text: An obituary in some copies on Wednesday about the Hall of Fame hockey player Marcel Pronovost misstated the number of games in the 1967 Stanley Cup finals in which the Toronto Maple Leafs, who had acquired him in a trade in 1965, defeated the Montreal Canadiens. The series lasted six games, not seven.
match_headline: Marcel Pronovost, 84, Dies; Hall of Famer Shared in Five N.H.L. Titles

text: An article on Thursday about efforts by civic leaders to keep Baltimore’s streets calm in the aftermath of Freddie Gray’s death reversed the colors associated with two gangs, the Crips and the Bloods, that were part of a discussion about the city’s problems. Crips wear blue and Bloods wear red.
match_headline: Taking to the Baltimore Streets, but for Peace and Progress

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the erosion of the Syrian Army as it suffers a string of defeats and struggles to replenish its ranks misstated the reason that a Syrian with close ties to the security establishment spoke on the condition of anonymity. The Syrian, who said the Lebanese Shiite group Hezbollah was leading the fight in many places, angering Syrian officers, asked that his name not be used out of concern for his safety, not so he could discuss confidential intelligence assessments.
match_headline: An Eroding Syrian Army Points to Strain

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a shake-up in the line of succession for the Saudi royal family misidentified the Saudi prince who had been banished from the kingdom in his youth for leftist tendencies. He is Prince Talal bin Abdulaziz, not Prince Alwaleed bin Talal. (Prince Alwaleed is Prince Talal’s son.)
match_headline: A Saudi Royal Shake-Up With a Goal of Stability

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the arrest of a nurse accused of scalding to death a toddler she took care of, using information from the Queens district attorney’s office, misidentified her profession. The woman, Oluyemisi Adebayo, is a licensed practical nurse, not a licensed nurse practitioner.
match_headline: Caretaker Is Accused of Killing Queens Toddler in a Scalding Bath

text: An article on Wednesday about China’s evolving attitude toward the Trans-Pacific Partnership erroneously included one country among those in the proposed pact. While South Korea has asked to be part of the partnership, it has not yet joined the negotiations.
match_headline: Once Concerned, China Is Quiet About Trans-Pacific Trade Deal

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Saturday with an article about the Yankees’ 6-1 victory over the Mets misstated the number of innings Michael Pineda pitched for the Yankees. It was seven and two-thirds, not five and two-thirds.
match_headline: Mets’ Ride Ends at Yankees’ House

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Thursday about the lineup for the Celebrate Brooklyn Festival, starting in June in Prospect Park, referred incorrectly to one of the scheduled performers, Taylor Mac. He has not appeared on Broadway, and thus he is not a “Broadway star.”
match_headline: Esperanza Spalding and Taylor Mac in Lineup for Celebrate Brooklyn

text: An article on Friday about wallets misspelled part of the name of the brand of one wallet featured. It is Ernest Alexander, not Earnest Alexander.

An article last Sunday about a 7.8 magnitude earthquake that struck Nepal near its capital, Katmandu, referred imprecisely to the seismic pressure building up in western Nepal. The Indian tectonic plate is being forced underneath the Eurasian plate to the north; although it is pushing back up against the Eurasian plate, it is not itself being forced upward. In addition, a map with the continuation of the article mislabeled, in some editions, the location of Mount Everest. It straddles the Nepal-China border; it is not entirely in China.
match_headline: Earthquake Devastates Nepal, Killing More Than 1,900

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Indonesia’s preparations to execute nine people convicted of drug crimes despite an international outcry misstated the number of drug convicts executed in January. It was five, not six. (A sixth prisoner who was also executed had been convicted of murder.) Because of another editing error, the article referred incorrectly to the execution procedure. The prisoners were given the option of being blindfolded; they were not automatically blindfolded. (One of the nine got a last-minute reprieve, but eight died by firing squad on Wednesday.)
match_headline: Despite Protests, Indonesia Moves Forward to Execute Drug Convicts

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Sunday with the Helsinki Journal article, about an income-based system for assessing fines on speeding drivers in Finland, misstated the amount that Reima Kuisla, a Finnish businessman, was recently fined for speeding. It was 54,024 euros — about $58,000, not $54,000.
match_headline: Speeding in Finland Can Cost a Fortune, if You Already Have One

text: An article last Sunday about the author Jonathan Franzen and his disagreement with the Audubon Society over the extent of climate change’s threat to birds misidentified a species seen during one of his walks in Central Park. It is the white-throated sparrow, not the yellow-throated sparrow.
match_headline: Jonathan Franzen Ruffles Feathers Again

text: An article last Sunday about the Prada Foundation’s new arts complex in Milan referred incorrectly to its financing. The corporation Prada S.p.A., which acts as a sponsor toward the Prada Foundation, has financed the entire complex itself. It was not financed personally by Miuccia Prada and her husband, Patrizio Bertelli, chief executive of the fashion brand.
match_headline: The Prada Foundation’s New Arts Complex in Milan

text: Because of an editing error, a review last Sunday about “The Mad Boy, Lord Berners, My Grandmother and Me: An Aristocratic Family, a High-Society Scandal and an Extraordinary Legacy,” a memoir by Sofka Zinovieff, misstated the author’s relationship to one of her family members, Jennifer Fry. Fry was Zinovieff’s grandmother, not her mother.
ref_headline: The Mad Boy, Lord Berners, My Grandmother and Me: An Aristocratic Family, a High-Society Scandal and an Extraordinary Legacy,
match_headline: ‘The Mad Boy, Lord Berners, My Grandmother and Me,’ by Sofka Zinovieff

text: A review on April 19 about “Michelle Obama: A Life,” by Peter Slevin, referred incorrectly to the site in Chicago where Michelle and Barack Obama held their wedding reception in 1992. By that time, it was the South Shore Cultural Center, not the South Shore Country Club. (The club, which did not allow African-Americans to join, closed in the mid-1970s; the property was acquired by the Chicago Park District, which turned it into the cultural center.)
match_headline: ‘Michelle Obama: A Life,’ by Peter Slevin

text: An article on April 19 about Kneipp Herbal Bath Oil referred incorrectly to the locations of two 19th-century Kneipp-style associations. They were in Denville, N.J., and Dansville, N.Y. — not the Danvilles of those states.
match_headline: Letter of Recommendation: Kneipp Herbal Bath Oils

text: An article on April 19 about the film editor Brent White misspelled the name of the Utah city where he grew up. It is Orem, not Oram.
match_headline: The Man Who Makes the World’s Funniest People Even Funnier

text: An article last Sunday about new developments that are being built in Fairfield County misspelled the surname of an agent with Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices New England Properties. She is Nicole Steel, not Steele.
match_headline: In Fairfield, the Builders Are Back

text: An article last Sunday about the sisters Carly and Lucy Simon misstated part of the lyrics of the Carly Simon song “Older Sister.” The lyric is, “She rides in the front seat; she’s my older sister.” It is not, “She sits in the front seat; she’s my older sister.” The article also misspelled the surname of a member of a world-renowned musical writing team, a friend of the Simon sisters’ parents. He was Richard Rodgers — not Rogers — of Rodgers and Hammerstein.
match_headline: Carly and Lucy Simon on Music, Fame, Sibling Rivalry and, Yes, James Taylor

text: An article on April 5 about hefty markups in the private art market misidentified the dealer in a transaction involving a Modigliani painting. The dealer was Lionel Pissarro, not his brother Joachim.
match_headline: A Multimillion-Dollar Markup on a Modigliani

text: An article last Sunday about Thomas O. Staggs, the heir apparent to Robert A. Iger as chief executive of the Walt Disney Company, misstated the timing of Mr. Staggs’s work at the investment bank Dain Bosworth. It was before earning his M.B.A., not after.
match_headline: Thomas Staggs: Disney’s Heir, Apparently

text: A picture caption last Sunday with the cover article about a proposed canal across Nicaragua misidentified the bird shown. It is an Eastern great egret, not a snowy egret.
match_headline: In Paradisiacal Nicaragua, Contemplating a Canal

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Catherine Ongiri and Jeffery Fikes misidentified the branch of the University of California that awarded the bride a law degree. It is the Hastings College of the Law, not the University of California, San Francisco.
match_headline: Catherine Ongiri, Jeffery Fikes

text: An article last Monday about the opening of two new galleries at the Ellis Island Immigration Museum misstated the role of the Statue of Liberty-Ellis Island Foundation Inc. at the museum. The foundation finances projects within the Statue of Liberty National Monument, including the immigration museum; it does not operate the museum. The error was repeated in a picture caption in some editions.
match_headline: Ellis Island Museum to Update the Story of Immigration in America

text: An article in some editions last Monday about opposition to a group home for juvenile offenders in South Ozone Park misstated part of the name of the road that roughly defines the neighborhood’s northern boundary. It is 107th Avenue, not Street.
match_headline: Opposition Grows as Home for Troubled Youths Comes to Quiet Queens Block

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about health concerns involving a class of chemicals known as poly- and perfluoroalkyl substances, or PFASs, reversed the identifications of the two men shown. Dr. Paul Brooks is on the left and Joe Kiger on the right. Both were involved in a lawsuit against DuPont over a spill of a form of the chemicals more than a decade ago.
match_headline: Commonly Used Chemicals Come Under New Scrutiny

text: An article on Tuesday about the injury status of Rangers players Kevin Klein and Mats Zuccarello misstated, in some editions, the number of times the Rangers have won a playoff series in fewer than six games over the last 10 seasons. Their five-game victory over the Penguins last week was the third time, not the second.
match_headline: Rangers Get Lift on Defense but Incur Loss on Offense

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Islanders’ 2-1 loss to the Washington Capitals in Game 7 of their N.H.L. playoff series misstated the number of saves by Islanders goalie Jaroslav Halak. It was 24, not 25.
match_headline: Capitals Eliminate Islanders, Extending Two Decades of Playoff Futility

text: A picture credit in some editions on Saturday for a photograph of Alex Rodriguez hitting his 660th home run misidentified the photographer. The picture was taken by Elise Amendola of The Associated Press, not by Bob DeChiara of USA Today Sports.
match_headline: Alex Rodriguez of Yankees Ties Willie Mays With 660th Home Run

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the World Briefing column on Thursday about a Twitter post by the mayor of Ankara, Turkey, that promoted a photograph referring to Marie Harf, a State Department spokeswoman, as a “stupid blonde” misstated the context of the mayor’s remarks. The mayor, Melih Gokcek, criticized Ms. Harf for her “silence” on the Baltimore riots, and included a picture of the Baltimore police forcibly subduing a looter; Mr. Gokcek was not criticizing her for her silence about the death of a man who was fatally injured while in police custody, the catalyst for the riots.
match_headline: Turkish Mayor Berates State Department’s Marie Harf for Silence on Baltimore Unrest

text: An article on Wednesday about the acceptance of Rachelle David to the United States Military Academy at West Point, using information from military officials, erroneously attributed a distinction to her. She is expected to become the first female graduate of a yeshiva to attend the academy, not the academy’s first yeshiva graduate ever. (While records are incomplete, Charles Bayar, a graduate of The Ramaz School, in Manhattan, was part of the class of 1971 at West Point.) The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: 17-Year-Old to Become First Female Yeshiva Graduate Entering West Point

text: An article on Saturday about proposed federal regulations for transporting crude oil by rail misstated the given name of a senator from Washington State who questioned the adequacy of the new regulations. She is Maria Cantwell, not Marie.
match_headline: New Oil Train Rules Are Hit From All Sides

text: An article on April 30 about Mayor Stephanie Rawlings-Blake of Baltimore misstated the name of one house in the Maryland Legislature, where her father was once chairman of the appropriations committee. It is the House of Delegates, not the House of Representatives.
match_headline: Baltimore Mayor Treads Fine Line in Divided City

text: An article on Friday about allegations that the German intelligence agency known as B.N.D. helped the United States National Security Agency spy on European partners and companies referred incorrectly to the B.N.D. It is Germany’s foreign intelligence agency, not its domestic one.
match_headline: Germany Is Accused of Helping N.S.A. Spy on European Allies

text: An article on Friday about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s defense of police tactics after scores of protesters were arrested last week misidentified, in some editions, the location where Chief James P. O’Neill told reporters that the police had been “extremely flexible” regarding the demonstrators. He spoke at the Police Academy in Queens, not at Police Headquarters in Lower Manhattan.
match_headline: Mayor de Blasio Defends Police Response to Freddie Gray Protests in New York

text: An article on Tuesday about top earners in the hedge fund industry misstated the amount of new money that has flowed into hedge funds so far this year. It is $18.2 billion — not $95 billion, which is how much hedge fund assets have grown so far this year.
match_headline: For Top 25 Hedge Fund Managers, a Difficult 2014 Still Paid Well

text: An article on Tuesday about Panera Bread’s decision to remove many artificial colors, flavors and preservatives from its ingredients erroneously included one cereal among those from which General Mills has eliminated genetically modified ingredients. Grape-Nuts is made by Post, not General Mills, and therefore is not one of the cereals affected.
match_headline: Panera Bread Plans to Drop a Long List of Ingredients

text: An article on Tuesday about the death of Dave Goldberg, chief executive of SurveyMonkey and husband of the Facebook executive Sheryl Sandberg, misstated his location at the time of his death. He was at a private villa near the Four Seasons Resort in Punta Minta, near Puerto Vallarta in southwest Mexico, not at the Four Seasons itself.
match_headline: Dave Goldberg, Silicon Valley Executive, Died of Head Trauma, Mexican Official Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the falling value of the euro and internal tensions within the European Union misstated a Moody’s projection of the euro’s value. It predicted that the euro would not fall below the dollar this year, not in 2014.
match_headline: As the Euro Slides, a Coin Meets Its Waterloo

text: An article on Monday rounding up the most important business events of the coming week misidentified the German city in which Volkswagen held its annual shareholders’ meeting on Tuesday. It is Hanover, not Berlin.
match_headline: Earnings From Tesla; Volkswagen’s Annual Meeting

text: An article last Wednesday about the chef April Bloomfield and her new cookbook, “A Girl and Her Greens,” misstated the location of Birmingham, England, where Ms. Bloomfield grew up. It is in the West Midlands, not northern England.
match_headline: April Bloomfield’s ‘A Girl and Her Greens’ Delights in the Details

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on April 29 with the continuation of an article about same-sex marriage arguments before the Supreme Court misidentified, in some copies, Mary L. Bonauto, one of the lawyers for the plaintiffs. She was shown second from the right, not second from the left. (April DeBoer, who sued to challenge Michigan’s ban on same-sex marriage, is second from the left.)
match_headline: Gay Marriage Arguments Divide Supreme Court Justices

text: A news analysis article on Wednesday about police unions that are confronting a loss of political power referred incompletely to the enactment of a measure in St. Louis for a civilian oversight board that would look into accusations of police misconduct. While the measure was signed this week, it will not become law until June. And because of an editing error, an accompanying picture caption misidentified the officers shown on duty in Baltimore. They are Pennsylvania state police officers assigned to help maintain order in the city, not members of the Baltimore Police Department.
match_headline: Police Struggle With Loss of Privileged Position

text: An article on Tuesday about an announcement by Avigdor Lieberman, Israel’s foreign minister, that he was resigning and would not join the next government referred imprecisely to his position on Israeli-Palestinian boundaries. He has called for Arab areas of Israel to be transferred to Palestinian control; he has not called for the “transferring” of individual Arab citizens to Palestinian territory.
match_headline: Israeli Foreign Minister Says He Won’t Join Netanyahu’s New Government

text: An article on Tuesday about a global turnaround strategy at McDonald’s misstated the estimated savings from a major reorganization. McDonald’s expects $300 million in savings by the end of 2018, not “some $300 million in net savings a year.”
ref_headline: some $300 million in net savings a year.
match_headline: McDonald’s Chief Promises Turnaround in a Restructuring

text: An article on Thursday about Arthur Caplan, a bioethicist commissioned by Johnson & Johnson to help it develop a program to determine which patients should be given access to experimental drugs, referred incorrectly to the Tuskegee experiments on black patients. Patients with syphilis were left untreated to test the progress of the disease; they were not infected with syphilis as part of the experiments.
match_headline: Eager to Opine on the Toughest Calls in Medical Ethics

text: An article on Thursday about airport hotels with views of runways misstated part of the name of a hotel within Haneda International Airport. It is the Royal Park Hotel The Haneda, Tokyo (not the “Park Royal”). The article also misstated the number of rooms with a runway view on the hotel’s seventh floor. There are two, not four.
match_headline: A Room With a View of the Runway

text: An obituary on April 17 about Dr. Levi Watkins Jr., the first surgeon to successfully implant an automatic heart defibrillator in a human patient, overstated what is known about his background. Though he might have been the first black intern at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, there is no conclusive evidence that is the case.
match_headline: Levi Watkins, 70, Dies; Pioneering Heart Surgeon Pushed Civil Rights

text: An editorial on Wednesday about talks between the Taliban and the Afghan government misidentified the group that claimed responsibility for the shooting of Malala Yousafzai. It was the Pakistani Taliban, not the Afghan Taliban.
match_headline: An Opening for Afghan Peace Talks

text: An article on Friday about the Senate’s passage of a bill that would give Congress a voice in any nuclear agreement between world powers and Iran misstated the status of Senator Robert Menendez, Democrat of New Jersey, on the Foreign Relations Committee following his indictment on corruption charges. He stepped down as ranking member; he did not step down from the committee.
match_headline: Senate Easily Passes Bill for a Voice on Iran Nuclear Accord

text: An obituary on Friday about the folk singer and folklorist Guy Carawan misstated the year of an interview he gave to the NPR program “All Things Considered.” It was 1999, not 2013.
match_headline: Guy Carawan Dies at 87; Taught a Generation to Overcome, in Song

text: An article on Tuesday about a campaign to promote LSD and manufacture other psychedelics in Norway, a country with strict drug controls, misstated the affiliation of the campaign’s co-founder, Pal-Orjan Johansen, with the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. He is a former — not current — researcher there.
match_headline: Odd Push in Drug-Averse Norway: LSD Is O.K.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Alabama lawmakers’ weighing the possibility of allowing slots and casino table games at racing tracks misstated the type of tracks involved. They are for dogs, not horses.
match_headline: Alabama May Turn to the Gambling It Has Long Fought

text: A picture on Thursday with a DealTalks Online report about Point72 Asset Management’s hiring of a former federal prosecutor as general counsel was published in error. The photograph showed Kevin O’Connor, a judge in Sedgwick County, Kan. — not Kevin J. O’Connor, the former United States attorney for Connecticut.
match_headline: Point72 Hires Ex-Prosecutor as General Counsel

text: An article on Thursday about Europe’s broadening of its antitrust investigation of large technology companies to include the e-commerce sector referred incorrectly to Internet Retailer, whose sales figures for Amazon and the German Otto Group were cited. It is a trade magazine that covers e-commerce trends, not a market research group.
match_headline: E.U. Commission Opens Antitrust Inquiry Into E-Commerce Sector

text: An article on Tuesday about the analysis of exit velocity in baseball — the speed of the ball as it leaves the bat — quoted incorrectly from comments by Timothy Chupp, a nuclear physicist at the University of Michigan. He said, “You have to move the bat at 80 miles per hour when it hits the ball” — not at 100 miles per hour. And because of an editing error, another comment was rendered incorrectly. Chupp said batters make adjustments “almost faster than the speed of thought,” not “speed of light.”
ref_headline: You have to move the bat at 80 miles per hour when it hits the ball
match_headline: New Way to Judge Hitters? It’s Rocket Science, Sort Of

text: An obituary on Thursday about the longtime Democratic congressman Jim Wright referred incorrectly to the 1976 election for House majority leader. It was a four-way contest in which Mr. Wright defeated Phillip Burton, Richard Bolling and John McFall — not a three-way contest in which he defeated Mr. Burton and Mr. Bolling.
match_headline: Jim Wright Dies at 92; House Speaker Resigned Amid Ethics Charges

text: An article last Sunday about Sandtown-Winchester, the West Baltimore neighborhood where Freddie Gray grew up and was arrested before he died of injuries sustained while in police custody, referred incorrectly to a distinction held by the neighborhood and the nearby area of Harlem Park. A recent study found the two areas had more residents in jails and prisons than any other neighborhood in the city, not in the state of Maryland.
match_headline: Hard but Hopeful Home to ‘Lot of Freddies’

text: An article last Sunday about Arthur Mondella, the head of Dell’s Maraschino Cherries who killed himself in February as investigators were about to unearth a large marijuana farm at the cherry factory, misspelled, in some editions, the surname of his second wife’s lawyer, who discussed their divorce last year. As the article noted correctly in one other reference, he is Eliot Tannenbaum, not Tanenbaum.
match_headline: The Fall of the Cherry King

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on April 26 about the strong play of Rangers forward Carl Hagelin during the team’s playoff series against the Pittsburgh Penguins misstated, in some copies, the number of power play chances the Penguins had in the series. It was 13, not 16.
match_headline: A Role Player for the Rangers Discovers a Scoring Touch in the Playoffs

text: An entry in the film listings in last Sunday’s Summer Movies special section referred incorrectly to the subject of the documentary “Sunshine Superman.” It’s about BASE jumping (parachuting from fixed structures or cliffs), not sky diving. The entry also misstated the year that the cinematographer Carl Boenish, father of the BASE movement, died. It was in 1984, not 1978.
match_headline: Summer 2015 Movie Releases: A Look at What’s Coming

text: An article last Sunday about the New York City Ballet’s coming production of “La Sylphide” misstated the name of the company for whom Peter Martins staged “La Sylphide” in 1985. It is the Pennsylvania Ballet, not the Philadelphia Ballet.
match_headline: ‘La Sylphide’ Is Taking Flight at New York City Ballet

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the naming of apartment buildings by their developers misspelled the name of the man who commissioned the Stuyvesant on East 18th Street in Manhattan. He was Rutherfurd Stuyvesant, not Rutherford. (Though his name was similarly misspelled in articles as recently as 2013 and 2011, it seems to have always been a challenge. Before 1980, the correct and incorrect spellings appeared in nearly equal numbers in almost 400 Times articles.)
match_headline: Naming a New York Building

text: An article last Sunday about women who try to shame people who harass them online misstated the job title of one such woman. Ashley Brincefield is a management specialist for customs; she is not a customs inspector.
match_headline: Women Turn Tables on Online Harassers

text: An article last Sunday about New Yorkers who move to Los Angeles described incompletely the Los Angeles living arrangement of a former New Yorker. Christina Turner shares her bungalow with a roommate; she does not live alone.
match_headline: Los Angeles and Its Booming Creative Class Lures New Yorkers

text: An article last Sunday about libraries and “Bookface,” the name given to social media images that depict book covers blending into three-dimensional scenery, misstated the name of the city that is home to the Beaverton City Library and misidentified its state. It is simply Beaverton, not Beaverton City, and it is in Oregon, not in Washington. (The city is in Washington County.)
match_headline: Oh, Those Clever Librarians and Their #Bookface

text: An article last Sunday about a family road trip up the California Coast misstated the age of Morro Rock. It is estimated to be 21 million years old, not 200 million years old.
match_headline: Unplugged Along the California Coast

text: An article last Sunday about things to do with children in Atlanta misstated the population of Decatur, Ga. It is about 20,000, not 75,000.
match_headline: Atlanta for Kids

text: A review on April 26 about two books on the internment camps that held Japanese-Americans and others during World War II referred incorrectly to a bill signed into law by President Ronald Reagan. The law, the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, called for the payment of $20,000 specifically to Japanese American citizens and permanent residents of Japanese ancestry who had been interned; since this provision did not apply to members of other ethnic groups, including people of German and Italian nationality or ancestry, a number of whom were also interned, the law did not “pay each survivor of the camps $20,000.”
ref_headline: pay each survivor of the camps $20,000.
match_headline: ‘Infamy’ and ‘The Train to Crystal City’

text: An article on Friday about Dr. Ian Crozier, an Ebola survivor who discovered the virus in his left eye after his medical team thought he had been cured, described incorrectly the protective gear that Dr. Steven Yeh wore when he drew fluid from Dr. Crozier’s eye. Dr. Yeh wore not only a gown and a pair of gloves, he also wore a mask; he did not perform the procedure without a mask.
match_headline: After Nearly Claiming His Life, Ebola Lurked in a Doctor’s Eye

text: An article in some editions last Monday about a special election in Brooklyn to fill a State Assembly seat vacated by Karim Camara misstated the name of the political party backing the candidate Shirley Patterson. It is the Independence Party, not the Independent Party. (Ms. Patterson lost to Diana Richardson, who was backed by the Working Families Party.)
match_headline: Democratic Party Is Without a Nominee in a Brooklyn Assembly Race

text: Because of an editing error, an article on the Itineraries page on April 14 about aircraft seat-swapping misstated the given name of a passenger who was elbowed repeatedly by a fellow passenger who wanted his window seat. He is Tim Nickerson, not Tom.
match_headline: Airplane Seat Swapping Turns Rough-and-Tumble

text: Because of an editing error, a timeline on April 13 about significant events in the Rangers’ season misstated the number of days into training camp that Rangers center Derek Stepan fractured his left leg. It was seven days, not five. The timeline also misstated goalie Henrik Lundqvist’s statistics after he returned from a two-month absence. He had a 2.29 goals-against average and a .924 save percentage — not a 2.00 goals-against average and a .925 save percentage.
match_headline: An Extension Sends Tax Season Into Overtime

text: An article on Friday about St. Louis Cardinals third baseman Matt Carpenter misidentified the position played in college by Albert Pujols, who, like Carpenter, was drafted in the 13th round by the Cardinals. Pujols was a shortstop, not a catcher.
match_headline: For Cardinals’ Matt Carpenter, a Bad Elbow in College Led to Good Things

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the 1990 Syracuse men’s lacrosse team that won the national title misstated the relationship of three lacrosse players who were influenced by Syracuse’s style. Ty Thompson is a cousin to Lyle and Miles Thompson, not a brother.
match_headline: A Syracuse Lacrosse Team Transformed a Sport, Clung to a Disputed Title and Lost a Trophy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about executive changes at Shakespeare & Company, a theater troupe in Lenox, Mass., misidentified the kind of cancer that affected Tony Simotes, the group’s former artistic director. It was throat cancer, not lung cancer.
match_headline: Shakespeare & Company Caught in Its Own Drama

text: An article on May 6 about the mounting unpaid power bills of Palestinians in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip, an issue that is increasing tensions with Israel, referred imprecisely to the status of the 300,000 Palestinians living in Jerusalem. Israel did not automatically grant them citizenship after capturing their neighborhoods during the 1967 war, but they were allowed to apply; most have not because they consider themselves part of a future Palestinian state.
match_headline: Palestinians’ Unpaid Electric Bills in the West Bank Thicken Tension With Israel

text: A reporting credit on Saturday for a report in the World Briefing column about the shooting of a former police chief of Tijuana and Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, misspelled the reporter’s given name in some editions. He is Randal C. Archibold, not Randell.
match_headline: Ex-Police Chief in Mexico Known for Crackdowns Is Shot

text: An article on Saturday about the big victory for Scottish Nationalists in Britain’s recent parliamentary elections referred incorrectly to a former deputy leader of the Scottish Labour Party who lost his seat. The lawmaker, Anas Sarwar, is a man. Because of an editing error, a reporting credit was omitted. Steven Erlanger contributed from London.
match_headline: Scottish Nationalists Rejoice in Big British Election Win

text: An article on May 1 about an announcement that the Chinese Navy would be holding joint exercises with Russia in the Mediterranean this month referred incorrectly to the Chinese vessels off the Horn of Africa that will participate in the drills. They are part of independent Chinese antipiracy patrols, not patrols affiliated with the United Nations.
match_headline: Chinese and Russian Navies to Hold Joint Drills in Mediterranean

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an article about Michael Pineda’s 16 strikeouts in the Yankees’ 6-2 victory over the Baltimore Orioles misstated, in some copies, the number of strikeouts Ron Guidry had in a game in June 1978 to set the Yankees’ record. As the article correctly noted, it was 18, not 17.
match_headline: Michael Pineda Pitches Like an Ace in Dominating the Orioles

text: A chart on Tuesday about the Rangers’ recent success in games when facing elimination and the Washington Capitals’ lack of success in games in which they could win a playoff series misstated Rangers goalie Henrik Lundqvist’s goals-against average in his last 16 elimination games entering Game 7 Wednesday night. It was 1.42, not 1.50.
match_headline: Rangers Let Henrik Lundqvist Stay on the Ice to Add to His Uncanny Record

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the display of Jackson Pollock’s “Mural” at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice misstated the year that the work was given to the University of Iowa Museum of Art. It was 1948, not 1959.
match_headline: Jackson Pollock’s ‘Mural’ Makes a Rare Trip to the Venice Biennale

text: An article last Friday about Russia’s plans for its annual Victory Day military parade, which celebrates the Soviet Union’s triumph over Nazi Germany, referred imprecisely to an estimate of World War II casualties. The figure of 26 million people killed was for all of the Soviet Union, not for Russia alone.
match_headline: A Parade Hailing Russia’s World War II Dead and Marching Further From the West

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Friday about a riot by ethnic Kurds in Mahabad, Iran, who suspected foul play in the death of a Kurdish chambermaid who fell from a fourth-floor window of a hotel referred incorrectly to Mahabad. It is a traditional capital of the Iranian Kurdistan region; it is not the capital of West Azerbaijan Province. (Urmia is.)
match_headline: Riot Erupts in Iran’s Kurdish Capital Over Woman’s Death

text: An article on May 4 about the warehousing of relief supplies for victims of the April 25 earthquake in Nepal misidentified one of the aircraft unloaded from a C-17 transport plane sent by the United States to help carry supplies into devastated areas. It was a UH-1Y helicopter — not a UH-17, which is an earlier vertical takeoff and landing aircraft.
match_headline: Nepal’s Bureaucracy Is Blamed as Earthquake Relief Supplies Pile Up

text: Because of an editing error, a reporting credit on Wednesday with an article about a Chinese multibillionaire who took 6,400 workers on a trip to France and Monaco misidentified the city from which one of the reporters, Dan Bilefsky, contributed. He was in London, not Paris.
match_headline: Chinese Billionaire Takes Over 6,000 Employees on a Trip to France

text: An article on Thursday about the victims of the Amtrak crash, using information from The Associated Press, referred incorrectly to a survivor of Jim Gaines, an A.P. employee who died in the crash. His survivors include a son and a daughter, not two daughters.
match_headline: Three Amtrak Victims With a Common Thread: All Were Heading Home to Family

text: An article on Thursday about the approval of legislation by the Missouri General Assembly that would enact a so-called right-to-work policy misstated, in some editions, the number of Senate Republicans who voted against the bill. It was four, not three.
match_headline: Missouri Passes Anti-Union Bill, but It Isn’t Veto-Proof

text: An article on Wednesday about the American Petroleum Institute’s challenge to new federal rules intended to improve the safety of oil-by-train transportation described its petition incorrectly in regard to upgrading or retrofitting rail tank cars. It is challenging the government’s timeline on that requirement, not the requirement itself.
match_headline: Oil Industry Asks Court to Block Rail Transport Safety Rules

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the historian Peter Gay referred imprecisely to the ship on which he and his family left Germany in 1939. It was the last ship to be admitted to Cuba from Nazi Germany, not the last ship ever admitted. The obituary also referred incompletely to the publication of the five volumes of Mr. Gay’s “The Bourgeois Experience: Victoria to Freud.” They came out in the 1980s and the 1990s, not just the 1980s.
ref_headline: The Bourgeois Experience: Victoria to Freud.
match_headline: Peter Gay, Historian Who Explored Social History of Ideas, Dies at 91

text: An article on Thursday about factors that make lawyers happy described a recent mental health study of Yale Law School students incorrectly. The study said that 70 percent of students who responded to a survey — not 70 percent of all Yale law students — reported being affected by mental health issues.
match_headline: Mentally Ill Inmates Are Routinely Physically Abused, Study Says

text: A picture caption in some editions on Thursday with an article about Senate leaders’ reaching an agreement on a plan to grant President Obama accelerated power to complete a sweeping trade accord misstated the day that Senator Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, was shown speaking with reporters. It was Wednesday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: After Lobbying by Obama, Senate Agrees to Vote on Trade Bill After All

text: A picture caption in some editions on Wednesday with an article about plans to build a Wegmans grocery store at the Brooklyn Navy Yard carried an incorrect credit for a rendering of the store. It is by GreenbergFarrow, not Beyer Blinder Belle.
match_headline: Wegmans to Open at Brooklyn Navy Yard

text: An article in some copies on Tuesday about the Mets’ 4-3 loss to the Chicago Cubs misidentified the player who walked to open the ninth inning for the Mets. Curtis Granderson, a pinch hitter, walked — not catcher Kevin Plawecki.
match_headline: Jacob deGrom Falters on Road, and Mets’ Rally Isn’t Enough

text: An article in some copies on Wednesday about the way in which the Dongfeng Race Team managed inexperienced Chinese sailors in the Volvo Ocean Race misstated the day the seventh leg of the race will start. It is Sunday, not today. (An in-port race is scheduled for today in Newport, R.I.)
match_headline: Chinese Sailors Come a Long Way in the Volvo Ocean Race

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the fiddle player Johnny Gimble misstated the period during which he served in Austria with the Army. It was in the early years of the Allied occupation, not during World War II.
match_headline: Johnny Gimble, Who Fiddled His Way to Fame, Dies at 88

text: An article on Thursday about a 1-1 draw between Juventus and Real Madrid, allowing Juventus to advance to the Champions League final, misidentified the position played by Álvaro Morata, who scored for Juventus in the 57th minute. He is a striker, not a midfielder.
match_headline: With Tie at Real Madrid, Juventus Bars Door to All-Spanish Champions League Final

text: An article on Thursday about the Vatican’s announcement that it would sign a treaty that includes recognition of the “state of Palestine” erroneously attributed a distinction to two nuns who were canonized just days after the announcement. Other speakers of Arabic have been canonized before; the nuns are not the first Arabic-speaking saints. The article also misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the body that gave the Palestinians nonmember observer status in 2012. It is the United Nations General Assembly, not the United States General Assembly.
match_headline: Vatican to Recognize Palestinian State in New Treaty

text: An article on Friday about a political scandal in Macedonia that has led to government resignations and mass protests referred imprecisely to Macedonia. Although it was formed in 1991 as the Soviet Union disintegrated, it had previously been part of Yugoslavia, not the Soviet Union.
match_headline: Tiny Macedonia Confronts a Supersize Scandal

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about an advance by Islamic State militants to the outskirts of Palmyra, Syria, putting them within striking distance of some of the world’s greatest antiquities, misspelled another name used for the city of Palmyra. It is Tadmur, not Tadur.
match_headline: ISIS Advance in Syria Endangers Ancient Ruins at Palmyra

text: An article on Wednesday about the prevalence of forced confessions in China’s criminal justice system understated the national acquittal rate in China in 2013, according to government figures. It was 0.07 percent, not 0.007 percent.
match_headline: Conviction Rates Count More in Chinese Justice Than Innocence

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the reported execution of Gen. Hyon Yong-chol, the second-highest officer in North Korea’s military, on charges of treason misstated, in some copies, the year that he became vice marshal and chief of the general staff of the North Korean People’s Army. It was 2012, not 2013.
match_headline: North Korea Said to Execute a Top Official, With an Antiaircraft Gun

text: An article on Wednesday about Facebook’s direct hosting of news articles, initially from nine media companies, referred imprecisely to the view of James Bennet, editor in chief of The Atlantic. Mr. Bennet said that the fear of publishers was that they might lose control over distribution of their content through Instant Articles, not that they would definitely lose control.
match_headline: Facebook Begins Testing Instant Articles From News Publishers

text: An article on Saturday about the pending closing of the F.A.O. Schwarz store at 767 Fifth Avenue attributed an erroneous distinction to that development. The store was closed at least one other time, for most of 2004. It will not be the first time that New Yorkers have not been able to shop at F.A.O. Schwarz. The article, in some copies, also misstated, in some copies, when F.A.O. Schwarz moved to Fifth Avenue. While it has been at its current location since 1986, it previously operated at two other locations on Fifth Avenue, the first beginning in 1910.
match_headline: F. A. O. Schwarz to Close Its Doors on Fifth Avenue

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with the continuation of an article about the Minnesota Orchestra’s visit to Cuba misstated where the orchestra’s music director, Osmo Vanska, appears in the picture playing the clarinet. He is on the right, not the left.
match_headline: Fire and Ice: Minnesotans Join Orquesta Aragón in Havana

text: An article on Sunday about the reaction in Boston to the death sentence for Dzhokhar Tsarnaev in the 2013 marathon bombing misstated, in some editions, the length of time that the race has finished on Boylston Street. It has been since 1965, not for more than a century. (The earlier finish was on Exeter Street, just off Boylston.)
match_headline: Death Sentence for Boston Bomber, Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, Unsettles City He Tore Apart

text: An article on Thursday about a prolonged and mysterious die-off of honeybees reversed the years that the Bee Informed Partnership began collecting data on bee deaths. It was in 2006 that collection began for winter deaths and 2010 for summer deaths.
match_headline: A Sharp Spike in Honeybee Deaths Deepens a Worrisome Trend

text: An article on April 27 about a man who was fatally shot by police detectives in Manhattan during a struggle at a building that housed mentally ill people, using information from the police, reversed the man’s names. He was David Felix.
match_headline: Suspect Fatally Shot by Detective in East Village Had Mental Illness and a Troubled Past

text: An article in some editions on May 6 about the death of a worker at a hotel construction site in Midtown Manhattan referred incompletely to the recent history of the site. After work was stopped there in July 2013 because of unsafe conditions, the demolition contractor, Titan Industrial Services, was cited. The hotel builder, the Rinaldi Group, was not performing work on the site at that time. In addition, the article, using information from the police, misstated the worker’s surname. He was Christian Ginesi, not Gisci.
match_headline: Worker at Manhattan Construction Site Falls Down Elevator Shaft and Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the shooting by New York police officers of a man suspected in several hammer attacks referred incorrectly in some editions to one of the suspect’s former lawyers. The lawyer, Colby Dillon, is a woman.
match_headline: Police Shoot Hammer-Wielding Man Sought in 4 Manhattan Attacks

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the unfurling of Picasso’s painted stage curtain “Le Tricorne” at the New-York Historical Society, using information from a publicist, misidentified where a conservator cleaned the artwork. It was in Williamstown, Mass., not Williamstown, Pa.
match_headline: Picasso’s Stage Curtain Is Unfurled at Its New Home

text: An article on Tuesday about the Cannes Film Festival misstated the age of the director Xavier Dolan, who is on this year’s jury. He is 26, not 25. The article also omitted part of the title of a film by Gus Van Sant that is in the main competition. It is “The Sea of Trees,” not “Sea of Trees.”
match_headline: Thierry Frémaux Shapes the Cannes Film Festival Schedule

text: An article on March 31 about aggressive moves by Saudi Arabia that coincided with talks between the United States and Iran, Saudi Arabia’s chief regional rival, over the Iranian nuclear program misstated the age of Prince Mohammed Bin Salman, the Saudi defense minister and son of the new king. Saudi Arabia has not officially disclosed his age, and some of his supporters have sought to overstate his age. But Saudi officials and members of the royal family, speaking on the condition of anonymity, say the prince was born in 1985, making him 29 or 30 years old, not 34. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: As U.S. and Iran Seek Nuclear Deal, Saudi Arabia Makes Its Own Moves

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about an agreement by the European Union to use naval forces to intercept ships used by migrant smugglers from North Africa referred incompletely to the possible fate of the migrants on the boats. Besides being returned to nearby African ports, they could also be taken to Europe for asylum review.
