match_headline: E.U. Agrees to Naval Intervention on Migrant Smugglers

text: An article on Monday about Jerusalem Day, a Jewish celebration of Israel’s unification of the city in the 1967 war that Palestinians say reminds them of their second-tier status, misstated the findings of a report by the Association for Civil Rights in Israel on the education of Palestinian children in East Jerusalem. It said that only 41 percent of Palestinian children attended municipal schools there because of a shortage of classrooms; it did not say, “Only around half of all Palestinian children attend school” because of the shortage. The article also omitted the educational status of the remaining 59 percent of Palestinian children. Most of them go to private or semiprivate schools.
ref_headline: Only around half of all Palestinian children attend school
match_headline: A Celebration of Jerusalem’s Unification Helps Point Up Its Divisions

text: A chart last Friday with an article about the acceleration of the Amtrak train that crashed north of Philadelphia last week misstated the dates for the data used to show the speed of trains on the rail line near the derailment. The data was from May 10, 11 and 12 — not March 10, 11 and 12.
match_headline: Latest Updates: Amtrak Derailment in Philadelphia

text: An article last Friday about Russia’s changing policy on support of the ruble referred incorrectly to the chief economist for Russia at Deutsche Bank, who commented on the policy. The economist, Yaroslav Lissovolik, is a man.
match_headline: Changing Course, Russia Will Sell Rubles Instead of Buying

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on May 14 about the documentary “American Ballet Theater: A History,” shown on PBS, misstated the year Oliver Smith became a co-director of American Ballet Theater with Lucia Chase. It was 1945, not 1940.
match_headline: ‘American Ballet Theater: A History,’ a PBS Documentary, Is a Love Letter to a Dance Form

text: A map on Friday with the Lajes Journal article, about Portuguese fears of devastating economic consequences after the United States Air Force completes a major downsizing of its base on Terceira Island, in Portugal’s Azores archipelago in the Atlantic, located Terceira incorrectly. It is west of Lisbon, on the Portuguese mainland; it is not off the coast of Morocco.
match_headline: Americans Start to Leave Air Base in Azores, and Locals Fear Economic Impact

text: An article in some editions on Friday about former Knicks who are playing in the N.B.A. conference finals misidentified the team to which the Knicks traded Trevor Ariza, who now plays for Houston. He went to the Orlando Magic, not to the Los Angeles Lakers. (He was later traded from the Magic to the Lakers.) The article also misstated the draft position of Golden State forward David Lee. He was drafted by the Knicks late in the first round, not in the second.
match_headline: Conference Finalists Are Dotted With Knicks’ Castoffs

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the exhibition “Dance: Movement, Rhythm, Spectacle,” at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, referred incorrectly to the film of Loie Fuller’s “Serpentine Dance” in the exhibition and misstated the date of the dance. The film shows a performance by an unidentified dancer, not by Fuller. And while the film is from the late 1890s, the dance itself was created in the early 1890s, not the late 1890s.
match_headline: ‘Dance: Movement, Rhythm, Spectacle,’ an Exhibition at the Philadelphia Museum of Art

text: A report in the Antiques column on Friday about the Toledo Museum of Art’s sale of some of its holdings in storage and replacements for some of those objects referred incorrectly to the sale of a chandelier made for Jérôme Bonaparte around 1810 that is at the museum. It was purchased privately by the museum for an undisclosed price, not for about $140,000 at an auction last year. (A copy of the chandelier made at the same time was sold at auction last year for that price.)
match_headline: Tattoo History, Antique Typewriters and Letting Go at the Toledo Museum

text: An article last Sunday about the death sentence imposed on ousted President Mohamed Morsi of Egypt for fleeing prison during the 2011 uprising against President Hosni Mubarak misidentified an educator who commented on the case. It was Sahar Aziz, an associate professor at Texas A & M School of Law — not Mona el-Ghobashy, a visiting scholar at Columbia University — who said, “In light of the politically charged environment within which the Morsi prosecutions are taking place, the perception by some may be that these trials are more about political retaliation than bona fide criminal activity.”
match_headline: Egyptian Court Sentences Ousted President Morsi to Death

text: An article in some editions on May 10 about Jewish veterans from the former Soviet Union who held a commemorative march in Brooklyn to honor the Allied victory over Germany misstated part of the name of the building where one veteran, Leonid Rozenberg, spoke before the event began. It is the Shorefront Y.M.-Y.W.H.A. — not the Y.M.-Y.W.C.A.
match_headline: Medals and Memories for Jewish Veterans From Russia

text: A listing of information in some copies last Sunday with a dining review of Tarry Lodge, in New Haven, misstated the restaurant’s address. It is 278 Park Street, not 78 Park Street.
match_headline: A Review of Tarry Lodge, in New Haven

text: An article in some editions on April 26 about Judge Robert W. Sweet’s taking ice skating lessons misstated the name of the court on which he serves. It is the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York, not the United States District Court’s Southern District.
match_headline: Judge Robert Sweet, 92, Finds Balance on the Ice and the Bench

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Rangers’ 2-1 victory over the Tampa Bay Lightning in Game 1 of the Eastern Conference finals misidentified, in some copies, one of the Lightning players who changed allegiances from the Rangers as a free agent. He is Brian Boyle — not Dan Boyle, who plays for the Rangers, but who also played for the Lightning several years ago.
match_headline: Rangers Stay True to Form, Winning by One, Again

text: An article on May 10 about the 1950s radio series “X Minus One” misstated the number of years ago that the series began. It was 60, not 70.
match_headline: Letter of Recommendation: ‘X Minus One’

text: An article last Sunday about “Mad Men” and its creator, Matthew Weiner, referred incorrectly to the episode “Flight One.” It was the second episode of Season 2, not of Season 1.
match_headline: Matthew Weiner, the Creator of ‘Mad Men,’ Prepares for Another Fade to Black

text: An article on May 10 about the Metropolitan Opera’s 2014-15 season misstated how many performances the conductor James Levine was scheduled for during the season. It was 36, not 28.
match_headline: Monitoring the Metropolitan Opera’s Vital Signs

text: An article last Sunday about the pressure people feel to stay in constant digital contact with others misspelled the given name of a businessman who refuses to use email. He is John Paul DeJoria, not Jean.
match_headline: The Tyranny of Constant Contact

text: An article on April 12 about complex and risky maneuvers on the part of insurance companies to increase profits referred incompletely to statistics on the rapid growth of one such maneuver, known as captive reinsurance. While the data appeared in a Treasury Department report issued in 2014, the calculations were originally done by Ralph S. J. Koijen of the London Business School and Motohiro Yogo of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, not by the Treasury Department. The omission was only recently called to the attention of The Times.
match_headline: Risky Moves in the Game of Life Insurance

text: Because of an editing error, a chart with an article last Sunday about chief executives’ pay misstated the percentage by which average compensation for top-paid female chief executives trailed that of top-paid chief executives over all. It is 11.5 percent, not 9.4 percent.
match_headline: For the Highest-Paid C.E.O.s, the Party Goes On

text: A news analysis article on May 10 about the possible health benefits of certain bacteria in foods referred incorrectly to an autoimmune disorder of the digestive system. It is inflammatory bowel disease, not inflammatory bowel syndrome.
match_headline: Invite Some Germs to Dinner

text: An article on Wednesday about a Palestinian proposal before FIFA, the governing body of world soccer, to suspend Israel from the organization misstated part of the name of a competition for professional clubs in Europe from which Israel would be banned if the proposal is approved. It is the Champions League, not the Championship League. The article also referred incorrectly to UEFA. It is the governing body for soccer in Europe, not the European Union’s soccer organization.
match_headline: Palestinians Plan New Tack Against Israel: Soccer Sanctions

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about some of the victims of government torture who are seeking justice from Tunisia’s new Truth and Dignity Commission misstated the start of the time frame for human rights violations that the commission is to review and the year of Tunisia’s independence from France. The time frame begins in 1955, not 1954, and Tunisia became independent in 1956, not 1955.
match_headline: Torture Claims in Tunisia Await Truth Commission

text: An article on Thursday about an executive order on same-sex marriage by Gov. Bobby Jindal of Louisiana misstated the title of a Democratic lawmaker who said the order was “more than likely unenforceable.” He is the Democratic House speaker pro tem, not the Democratic House speaker. (The lawmaker, who was not named in the article, is Walt Leger.)
match_headline: Critics Say Jindal Order on Same-Sex Marriage Is Motivated by 2016 Campaign Bid

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision by the Landmarks Preservation Commission in New York City to reject proposed renovations to the Four Seasons restaurant interior referred incorrectly to its lease, using information from the landlord. It will expire in the summer of 2016, not this summer.
match_headline: Landmarks Commission Rejects Plan to Change Interior of Four Seasons

text: An article on May 15 about Matías Campiani, a private equity executive who was jailed in Uruguay after the collapse of Pluna, that country’s national airline, in which his firm had invested, misstated the title of Gustavo Herrero, who commented on the case. He is the former, not current, executive director of the Harvard Business School Latin America Research Center.
match_headline: An Airline Investment in Uruguay Becomes a Catch-22

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about a new opera, “Cubanacán: A Revolution of Forms,” that had its premiere in Havana this week and includes a scene, based on an actual event, of Fidel Castro and Che Guevara playing golf misidentified the site where they are shown playing, and misstated Guevara’s position in the picture. They played at the Colinas de Villareal golf course, not at a country club that became the site of the arts university Instituto Superior de Arte. And Guevara is at the far left of the picture, not the left foreground.
match_headline: ‘Cubanacán’ Imagines When Che and Fidel Compared Golf Swings

text: An article last Tuesday about challenges facing Beji Caid Essebsi, the Tunisian president, in sustaining the lone success story of the Arab Spring uprisings misstated the age of Rached Ghannouchi, the leader of Ennahda, the Islamist political party that won power after the country’s dictator was driven from office in 2011. Mr. Ghannouchi is 73, not 77.
match_headline: Tunisian President Looks for Help in Sustaining Arab Spring Progress

text: An article on Thursday about the poor record on commuter rail safety in the United States compared with Europe and East Asia, which invest heavily in their railway networks, misstated the length of time that the high-speed TGV trains of France have been operating. They have been in service since 1981, which is more than — not “close to” — three decades.
match_headline: Low U.S. Rail Spending Leads to Poor Safety, Experts Say

text: An article on May 13 about the filing of a lawsuit against Rolling Stone magazine by an associate dean at the University of Virginia in connection with a discredited article on campus rape misstated the timeline of the lawsuit. Though the associate dean, Nicole P. Eramo, had been working with legal counsel since last November, the decision to sue was not made then, according to Libby Locke, one of Ms. Eramo’s lawyers. (Ms. Locke declined to say exactly when the decision was made.)
match_headline: Rolling Stone Rape Article Results in Defamation Suit

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Tuesday with an article about the Rangers’ 6-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Lightning in Game 2 of the Eastern Conference finals misstated the number of shots faced by Rangers goaltender Henrik Lundqvist. It was 26, not 32.
match_headline: Weight of a Hat Trick Buckles the Rangers

text: An article on Thursday about Yankees outfielder Jacoby Ellsbury’s recent injury misidentified, in some editions, the manager of the Class AAA Scranton/Wilkes-Barre Yankees, who informed Ellsbury’s replacement, Slade Heathcott, of his call-up. He is Dave Miley — not Wade Miley, who is a pitcher for the Boston Red Sox.
match_headline: Yankees Face Jacoby Ellsbury’s Downside: His Injuries

text: An article on Wednesday about the selection of Anne Pasternak as the next director of the Brooklyn Museum erroneously included one show of works among those organized by the museum in recent years. A show of works by Wangechi Mutu was organized by the Nasher Museum of Art at Duke University and then traveled to the Brooklyn Museum; it was not organized there.
match_headline: Brooklyn Museum Picks Anne Pasternak as New Director

text: An article on Feb. 15 about an attack on a polio vaccination team in northwestern Pakistan misidentified the disease that was the target of a vaccination campaign used by the C.I.A. as a cover for an espionage operation that led to Osama bin Laden’s hideout in Abbottabad, Pakistan. The disease was hepatitis B, not polio. A reader pointed out the error in an email on May 12.
match_headline: Polio Team Attacked in Pakistan

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a political scientist who is seeking a retraction of a study published in the journal Science, which suggested that gay political canvassers could change conservative voters’ views on same-sex marriage, erroneously included one news organization among those that had issued editors’ notes regarding their initial coverage of the study. NPR did not report on the study and has not posted such a note; the radio program “This American Life,” which is produced by Chicago Public Media and delivered to stations by PRX The Public Radio Exchange, did post a note.
match_headline: Retraction Sought in Study on Views of Gay Marriage

text: An article on Tuesday about Harris Rosen’s largess for the troubled community of Tangelo Park, Fla., misstated Mr. Rosen’s marital status. He is divorced.
match_headline: One Man’s Millions Turn a Community in Florida Around

text: An article on Monday about proposed legislation in Albany that would loosen restrictions on dogs at restaurants referred incorrectly to the position taken by Assemblyman Richard N. Gottfried. He has not made a decision on the bill; he does not oppose it.
match_headline: Hold the Mimosa. I’ll Have a Biscuit.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Amazon’s decision to report revenue and pay taxes in several European countries, rather than funnel the earnings through Luxembourg, described incorrectly, in some copies, a battle over tech companies’ taxes in Europe. The battle is between European countries and American tech companies, not between European tech companies and their American counterparts.
match_headline: Amazon to Stop Funneling European Sales Through Low-Tax Haven

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about New York City Ballet, at the David H. Koch Theater, misspelled the given name of a soloist in “Raymonda Variations.” She is Kristen Segin, not Kristin.
match_headline: City Ballet’s Spring Season Includes ‘N.Y. Export: Opus Jazz’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a paper published in the journal Science that has been called into question amid accusations that an author of the report, Michael LaCour, had misrepresented his study methods and lacked the evidence to back up his findings misstated the title of Lynn Vavreck, Mr. LaCour’s academic adviser. She is a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, not an associate professor.
match_headline: Doubts About Study of Gay Canvassers Rattle the Field

text: An article on Tuesday about the increase of cultural tourism over more earthy pursuits by sailors during Fleet Week misstated, in some editions, the name of a strip club in Manhattan. It is the Diamond Club, not Diamond’s Gentleman’s Club. The article also referred incorrectly to Colt Lauer and the woman he was waiting for as she received a makeover at MAC Cosmetics. They are enlisted sailors, not officers. And the article misstated, in some editions, the rank and age of Joseph McGurr, who said dates were plentiful in New York City without help from the Internet. He is a petty officer, not a chief petty officer, and he is 32, not 22.
match_headline: A Cleaner Fleet Week: What Do You Do With a Cultured Sailor?

text: An article on Monday about Jaime Rodríguez Calderón, the first serious independent candidate for governor in Mexico since a constitutional change in 2012, misstated the given name of an opponent. He is Jesús María Elizondo, not José.
match_headline: El Bronco: Blunt, Frequently Vulgar, and Aiming to Run Nuevo León

text: An article on Saturday about the environmental threat posed by plastic microbeads used as exfoliating agents in personal care products, using outdated information from the National Conference of State Legislatures, omitted two states from the list of those that have enacted laws restricting the use of microbeads. In addition to Illinois, Maine, New Jersey and Colorado, Maryland and Indiana have enacted such laws.
match_headline: Fighting Pollution From Microbeads Used in Soaps and Creams

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about the second annual festival held by the arts group Elastic City misstated the name of an event starting on East Ninth Street in Manhattan that will be led by the writer Wayne Koestenbaum. It is “Making Marks,” not “Marking Marks.” The report also misstated the date for “The Man I Love,” an event in which the classical pianist Leon Fleisher will appear with his son. It is Aug. 17, not Aug. 19.
match_headline: Review: Lars Vogt Presents Late-Career Beethoven and Schubert at Mostly Mozart

text: An article on April 23 about the interdependency of water and power described incorrectly an estimate of how much energy California devoted to water. Before the state’s current drought, according to the estimate, nearly 20 percent of electricity, not of total energy use, went to moving and treating water and to other purposes like heating water for homes or businesses; the estimate covered more than just moving and treating water. The article also misidentified the source of the calculation. The estimate was by the California Energy Commission, not experts at the University of California, Davis.
match_headline: Troubling Interdependency of Water and Power

text: An article on Thursday about the limited options available to Sunni Iraqi civilians fleeing Islamic State violence in Anbar Province misquoted, in some editions, a statement by Valerie Amos, the under secretary general for humanitarian affairs at the United Nations, to the Security Council about the Sunnis’ plight. Referring to the number of people in Iraq needing assistance, she said, “This number is likely to increase further before the end of the year, as conflict continues” — not “as conflict areas” — “and as fear of sectarian-motivated retaliation spreads through newly accessible areas.”
ref_headline: This number is likely to increase further before the end of the year, as conflict continues
match_headline: Sunnis Fleeing ISIS Find Few Doors Open Elsewhere in Iraq

text: An article on Monday about the identification of Vincent Viafore’s body after he disappeared on a kayaking trip misidentified, in some editions, where along the Hudson River he was found. As the article noted correctly elsewhere, it was near the United States Military Academy at West Point — not near Poughkeepsie, N.Y., which is about 20 miles upriver.
match_headline: Body Recovered in Hudson Is Identified as Missing Kayaker’s

text: Because of an editing error, the N.B.A. roundup on Saturday misstated, in some editions, the score of the Western Conference finals at the time. As the headline correctly noted, the Golden State Warriors had a two-games-to-none lead over the Houston Rockets, not a two-games-to-one lead. (The Warriors won the series, four games to one.)
match_headline: Rockets Surge and Resurge, but Warriors Hold On

text: An article on Monday about the Rangers’ 2-0 loss to the Tampa Bay Lightning in Game 5 of the Eastern Conference finals misstated, in some editions, the given name of the Rangers player who tried to block a pass by Anton Stralman that led to the Lightning’s first goal. He is Tanner Glass, not Tyler.
match_headline: A Lightning Blockade Gives the Rangers No Shot

text: An article on Thursday about the Rangers’ success in Game 7s in the N.H.L. playoffs referred incorrectly to a six-game winning streak by goalie Henrik Lundqvist entering Friday’s Game 7 against the Tampa Bay Lightning. He has a six-game winning streak in Game 7s, not in games when facing elimination.
match_headline: Rangers’ Thoughts Drift to a Friendly Place: A Game 7 at Home

text: An article on Thursday about federal health officials’ announcement of new guidelines for treating H.I.V. after a clinical trial showed pronounced benefits for people put on antiretroviral drugs as soon as they learned they were infected misidentified the organization that issued treatment guidelines for American doctors at the time the trial began. It was the Department of Health and Human Services, not the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. (The C.D.C. issues guidelines for preventing disease.)
match_headline: H.I.V. Treatment Should Start at Diagnosis, U.S. Health Officials Say

text: A picture caption with the Appraisal column in some editions on Tuesday about safe rooms in New York City apartments referred incorrectly to the view shown. The picture, which offers two views of the same exterior, shows at right a reflection of the exterior in a window with transparent bulletproof polymer, not a view through such a window.
match_headline: Still Secret and Secure, Safe Rooms Now Hide in Plain Sight

text: An article on Thursday about Yemeni-Americans whose United States passports have been confiscated by American officials in Sana, Yemen, misstated when the United States closed its embassy there. It was before Saudi Arabia launched attacks against rebels in Yemen, not after.
match_headline: Yemeni-Americans, Thrust Into Limbo, Say U.S. Embassy Unfairly Revokes Passports

text: An article on May 22 about an investment in a Brazilian impact investing fund by the Oblate International Pastoral Investment Trust, established by an international order of the Roman Catholic Church, misstated the affiliation of the Rev. Seamus Finn, the priest who is the chief of faith-consistent investment for the trust. Father Finn is a member of the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate; he is not a friar. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Catholic Trust Looks to Brazilian Fund for Social Returns

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the Cleveland Cavaliers’ victory over the Atlanta Hawks in Game 3 of the N.B.A. Eastern Conference finals misidentified the Hawks player who missed the final shot. It was Shelvin Mack, not Jeff Teague.
match_headline: LeBron James Lifts Cleveland to Win With Triple-Double

text: An article on Tuesday about Denver’s 10-5 victory over Maryland in the final of the N.C.A.A. men’s lacrosse tournament misstated the outcome of Trevor Baptiste’s face-off for Denver with 32 seconds remaining. Baptiste lost it.
match_headline: A Coach Reaffirms His Standing as Denver Claims Lacrosse Title

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Wednesday about the Rangers’ 7-3 victory over the Tampa Bay Lightning in Game 6 of the Eastern Conference finals misspelled the surname of the Rangers player who made the score 4-1. He is James Sheppard, not Shepard.
match_headline: Henrik Lundqvist Keeps Rangers Alive Against Lightning

text: An obituary on Friday about the Poconos hotel owner Morris Wilkins misstated the given name of one of his daughters, who survives him. She is Lori Immerman, not Lois. It also misstated part of the name of one of Mr. Wilkins’s hotels. It is Paradise Stream, not Paradise Dreams.
match_headline: Morris Wilkins, Who Lured Honeymooners to Poconos, Dies at 90

text: An article last Sunday about the strategies behind the Islamic State’s recent victories in Ramadi, the capital of Anbar Province in Iraq, and the historic city of Palmyra in Syria referred incompletely to a Syrian journalist, Jalal Zein al-Din, who said the group would remain in territory it had captured in a region from northwestern Iraq to eastern Syria. Jalal Zein al-Din is a pen name he uses to avoid reprisals from the Syrian government and the Islamic State militants; it is not his real name.
match_headline: With Victories, ISIS Dispels Hope of a Swift Decline

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article last Sunday about efforts to determine responsibility for the flooding in Louisiana after Hurricane Katrina misidentified a levee that was among those that failed. The levee shown was along the Inner Harbor Navigational Canal; it was not the 17th Street levee.
match_headline: Decade After Katrina, Pointing Finger More Firmly at Army Corps

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about victories by Denver and Maryland in the semifinals of the N.C.A.A. men’s lacrosse tournament referred incorrectly to Denver Coach Bill Tierney’s appearance in the national title game in 2001. It was the last time he won a championship, not the last time he reached the title game. (He reached the national championship game in 2002 with Princeton, which lost to Syracuse.)
match_headline: Denver Brings the West to the Title Game

text: An article last Sunday about the struggles of South Asian-American men in finding a bride incorrectly characterized Umair Khan’s use of “Rishta aunties,” or matchmakers. He used two Rishta aunties, one suggested by a friend and another by a friend of his mother. His mother did not hire a Rishta auntie.
match_headline: South Asian-American Men Balance Tradition and Modernity to Find a Bride

text: An article last Sunday previewing new offerings on television this summer misstated the given name of one of the Wachowskis, whose mystical thriller “Sense8” will be appearing on Netflix. He is Andy Wachowski, not Larry.
match_headline: Summer TV: New Series, Mini-Series and Movies for Those Bored With the Beach

text: An article on Friday about the Google virtual reality device Cardboard misstated the company’s role in a $542 million investment in Magic Leap, a Florida company that is developing augmented reality technology. Google led several companies that made the investment; it did not make the investment alone.
match_headline: Google Intensifies Focus on Its Cardboard Virtual Reality Device

text: A picture caption on May 12 with the continuation of a theater review of “The Painted Rocks at Revolver Creek,” at the Pershing Square Signature Center in Manhattan, misidentified the actor on the right. He is Leon Addison Brown — not Sahr Ngaujah, another cast member.
ref_headline: The Painted Rocks at Revolver Creek,
match_headline: Review: ‘The Painted Rocks at Revolver Creek,’ an Athol Fugard Play

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the sentencing of Gigi Jordan, who was convicted of manslaughter in the 2010 death of her autistic 8-year-old son, misstated the charge sought against her that jurors were allowed to downgrade because she had acted in the grip of an “extreme emotional disturbance.” It is second-degree murder, not homicide.
match_headline: Gigi Jordan Receives 18-Year Sentence for Killing Her Son

text: An article on Monday about an antitrust suit brought by Motorola Mobility against makers of liquid-crystal display screens erroneously included one company among those that cooperated with a Justice Department inquiry into allegations of price-fixing, pleaded guilty and paid fines, and the article gave an incomplete name for another. Sharp and LG Display — not its parent company, LG — were among those companies; Toshiba was not.
match_headline: Motorola’s Antitrust Lawsuit May Head to Top Court

text: An article in some editions on May 25 about the Yankees’ 5-2 loss to the Texas Rangers misstated the type of hit by Brian McCann that scored Chase Headley and Alex Rodriguez in the bottom of the first inning. It was a single, not a double. And because of an editing error, the article described incorrectly a group of people standing next to the dugout railing listening to Bernie Williams speak before the game. They were Yankees players, not fans.
match_headline: On Night to Remember, Game to Forget as Rangers Sweep Yanks

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on May 19 about the Obie Awards, using information from the organizers, erroneously included a producer of the play “You Got Older,” whose writer, Clare Barron, was honored. While the play was performed at the Here Arts Center, it was a production of Page 73, not Page 73 and the arts center.
match_headline: ‘Hamilton,’ ‘You Got Older’ and ‘Invisible Hand’ Among Obie Award Winners

text: Because of an editing error, the attribution for the Quotation of the Day on Saturday, taken from an article about the sentencing of Ross W. Ulbricht, the founder of an online marketplace for illicit drugs, to life imprisonment, referred incorrectly to the man who accused Mr. Ulbricht of being driven by greed. The man — identified only as Richard — was delivering a victim-impact statement; he was not a witness.
match_headline: Ross Ulbricht, Creator of Silk Road Website, Is Sentenced to Life in Prison

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday and in some editions on Sunday about Joseph R. Biden III, the former attorney general of Delaware and the elder son of Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr., misidentified the location of the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, where he died. It is in Bethesda, Md., near Washington — not in Washington.
match_headline: Beau Biden, Vice President Joe Biden’s Son, Dies at 46

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an obituary about the graphic designer Jerry Dior misstated, in some editions, the year that Major League Baseball recognized Mr. Dior as the creator of its logo. It was 2009, not 2008.
match_headline: Jerry Dior, Designer of Major League Baseball’s Logo, Dies at 82

text: An article on Monday about a growing emphasis on generating media attention to academic research misstated the number of people on the American Association for the Advancement of Science’s digital media team who work to drive traffic to its publications through social media. While the team has 40 members, only three or four of them are involved in social media.
match_headline: Academics Seek a Big Splash

text: An article on May 11 about the temporary grounding of the Airbus A400M fleets of four nations after one of the military transport planes crashed in Spain, killing four Airbus employees, misstated the plane’s weight. It weighs about 76.5 metric tons empty, not 37. (It can carry 37 metric tons of cargo.)
match_headline: 4 Countries Ground Military Transport Planes After Crash

text: An article on Friday about the adoption of a United Nations resolution to combat the plundering of antiquities by the Islamic State, which has ravaged important archaeological sites around Mosul, Iraq, referred imprecisely to an announcement on Monday at the Louvre about an updated blacklist of Iraqi objects. While Irina Bokova, the director general of Unesco, was a guest speaker at the event, the announcement was made solely by the International Council of Museums, not jointly announced with Unesco.
match_headline: U.N. Resolves to Combat Plundering of Antiquities by ISIS

text: An article on May 26 about a swearing-in ceremony for Rachel Notley, the new premier of the Canadian province of Alberta, misstated the number of lawmakers from her New Democratic Party who sat behind her at the ceremony and referred incorrectly to three of them. There were 52, not 51. And while most of them are political novices, three are incumbents; not all 52 were “newly elected.” (Ms. Notley is also an incumbent.)
match_headline: After a Political Reversal in Alberta, ‘Anything Seems Possible’

text: Because of an editing error, a caption for a picture with the National Briefing column on May 22 misidentified the military group shown placing flags at Arlington National Cemetery in preparation for Memorial Day. They are members of the Third Infantry Regiment, not the Third Infantry Division.
match_headline: Before a Soldier’s Rest, a Panoply of Details

text: A headline in some editions on Monday with an article about a crane accident in Midtown Manhattan referred incorrectly to the crane. It dropped an air-conditioning unit; the crane itself did not collapse.
match_headline: Crane Accident in Midtown Manhattan Injures 7 and Damages Buildings

text: An article on the Automobiles page on Friday about limited-production versions of luxury cars misstated the price of the Porsche Panamera Exclusive Series at its Los Angeles debut. The car is priced at about $264,000 in the United States — not $315,000, which is the dollar equivalent of its European price in euros.
match_headline: When an Off-the-Rack Rolls-Royce Just Won’t Do

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Friday’s matches at the French Open erroneously included one player among the French players who advanced to the fourth round that day. Richard Gasquet was not one of them. (He advanced to the third round with his victory on Friday and then to the fourth round with a victory on Saturday.)
match_headline: Forget the Calls. Players Challenge the People Who Make Them.

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the expansion of wine production in the Yakima Valley of Washington misidentified the scene shown. The photograph was of a field of fruit trees in the valley, not of a vineyard.
match_headline: Drought Is Bearing Fruit for Washington Wineries

text: An article on Saturday about the publication of leaked documents that raise questions about the handling of a United Nations investigation into the suspected sexual abuse of African children by French troops misstated the response by United Nations officials to the abuse allegations. They investigated but did not follow up with the French government to ensure that the suspected perpetrators were held to account, the documents suggest, and instead began disciplinary proceedings against the human rights officer who leaked a report on the abuse to the French. It is not the case that United Nations officials failed to act immediately to investigate the allegations.
match_headline: U.N. Role Is Questioned in Sexual Abuse Inquiry

text: An article last Thursday about the defusing of a World War II bomb discovered along the Rhine River in Cologne, Germany, which forced the evacuation of about 20,000 residents, misstated the weight of the bomb. It was 2,200 pounds, not 440. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: A Wartime Bomb, Unearthed in Germany, Recalls Darker Days

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about developers who are increasingly turning rooftops into lounges and observatories referred incorrectly to the development of 70 Pine Street. As the article correctly noted, the building is being converted to rental apartments, not condominiums.
match_headline: Up on the Roof: Top-Floor Attractions Help Maximize Revenues

text: An article on Friday about the fate of chimpanzees in Liberia that were used by the New York Blood Center for medical research referred incorrectly in some editions to Kathleen Conlee, vice president for animal research at the Humane Society of the United States. She does not have a Ph.D. and therefore is not “Dr. Conlee.”
match_headline: Chimpanzees in Liberia, Used in New York Blood Center Research, Face Uncertain Future

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Rangers’ 2-0 loss in Game 7 of the N.H.L.’s Eastern Conference finals against the Tampa Bay Lightning misidentified, in some copies, the team against which Rangers forward Mats Zuccarello is suspected to have sustained a head injury. It was the Pittsburgh Penguins, not the Washington Capitals.
match_headline: Rangers Are Shut Out in Game 7 as Lightning Reach Finals

text: An article on Saturday about the induction of the Haitian novelist Dany Laferrière into the Académie Française, using information from the academy, erroneously attributed a distinction to him. Mr. Laferrière is one of the first non-French citizens — not the first — to be inducted into the academy. (At least two or three other people were not French citizens when elected, the academy now says.)
match_headline: Dany Laferrière, a Guardian of French, Joins the Académie Française

text: An obituary in some editions on Wednesday about the chemist Irwin A. Rose misspelled the given name of one of his sons, with whom he had been living. He is Frederic Rose, not Frederick.
match_headline: Irwin A. Rose, Nobel-Winning Biochemist, Dies at 88

text: An article last Thursday about the popularity of full-bottomed underwear misspelled the surname of the fashion director for accessories, cosmetics and intimate apparel at Bloomingdale’s. She is Erica Russo, not Rousseau.
match_headline: Young Women Say No to Thongs

text: An article on Saturday about Israel’s success in ensuring a sufficient supply of water even during droughts by desalinating Mediterranean seawater and recycling of wastewater referred imprecisely to Sidney Loeb, an American who moved to Israel in 1967 and taught water professionals how to desalinate seawater. He was one of the scientists who invented the reverse osmosis method, not its lone inventor. (The others were Srinivasa Sourirajan, a fellow student at the University of California, Los Angeles, in 1959, and their teacher Samuel Yuster.)
match_headline: Aided by the Sea, Israel Overcomes an Old Foe: Drought

text: A news analysis article on May 26 about the scaled-back agenda of Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, on the anniversary of his swearing-in rendered incorrectly the name of the bank led by Deepak Parekh, who complained that the procedures for obtaining funds had become more onerous under the Modi government. His bank is HDFC Bank, not HFDC.
match_headline: After a Year of Outsize Expectations, Narendra Modi Adjusts His Plan for India

text: Because of an editing error, an article on May 14 about the House’s recent approval of a ban on most abortions 20 weeks after fertilization misstated the Supreme Court’s position on a general standard of fetal viability. Although the court has said that women have a right to an abortion until the fetus is viable outside the womb, it has not said that viability occurs “22 to 24 weeks after fertilization.”
match_headline: House Approves Revised Measure Banning Most Abortions After 20 Weeks

text: An article on Wednesday about research suggesting that chimpanzees have the cognitive ability to cook misstated, at one point, the surname of the Harvard anthropologist who hypothesized that cooking has driven changes in human evolution. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Richard Wrangham, not Wrangell.
match_headline: Chimpanzees Would Cook if Given the Chance, Research Says

text: An article on Tuesday about a decision by the airbag manufacturer Takata to continue using a chemical compound deemed dangerous by experts misstated the point at which the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration began receiving complaints about rupturing Takata airbags. It was in 2001, not “almost 15 years ago.” The error was repeated in articles on Sept. 15, 2014 , and on May 20 , which referred to the complaints as having started in 2000, rather than 2001.
match_headline: Takata Says It Will No Longer Make Side Inflater Linked to Airbag Defect

text: A reporting credit last Friday for an article about the reaction of soccer officials to the arrest of members of FIFA on the eve of its vote for president was omitted. Dan Bilefsky contributed from London, Simon Romero from Rio de Janeiro, and Merna Thomas from Cairo.
match_headline: Sepp Blatter Is Unfazed Entering FIFA Election

text: An obituary on Thursday about Jacques Parizeau, a former premier of Quebec, described incorrectly in some editions his role in the province’s hydroelectric system. He was deeply involved in its nationalization, not in its privatization.
match_headline: Jacques Parizeau, Who Led Second Quebec Separatist Movement, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Thursday about the longtime Alvin Ailey dancer Dudley Williams, using information from Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, misstated the given name of his father and his brother. They are both Ivan, not Iban.
match_headline: Dudley Williams, Eloquent Dancer Who Defied Age, Dies at 76

text: An article on Thursday about a judge’s ordering the Dalton School in Manhattan to rehire David Brune, a drama teacher, misidentified the target of a passage in a letter written by Mr. Brune that led to his firing. The line, “Apologize for not being honest, forthright, upstanding, moral, considerate, much less intelligent or wise,” referred to school administrators, not just to Ellen Stein, the head of the school. The article also misstated the judge’s surname. He is Arthur J. Amchan, not Achman.
ref_headline: Apologize for not being honest, forthright, upstanding, moral, considerate, much less intelligent or wise,
match_headline: Dalton School Ordered to Rehire Teacher Who Criticized Bosses in Email

text: An article on Thursday about the Frick Collection’s decision to abandon a proposed renovation plan that would have eliminated a gated garden referred incompletely to the production of evidence that under the plan the Frick was going back on a promise to make the garden permanent. While the coalition United to Save the Frick produced such evidence last fall, Charles A. Birnbaum, president of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, earlier called attention to that commitment.
match_headline: Frick Museum Abandons Contested Renovation Plan

text: An article on Friday about Greece’s deferral of several payments to the International Monetary Fund until the end of June misstated the decade during which Zambia took advantage of the practice of bundling I.M.F. loan payments into a single sum during a calendar month. It was in the 1980s, not the 1970s.
match_headline: Tsipras and Greece Buy Time From I.M.F.

text: A report in the Sports Briefing column on Wednesday about Commissioner Gary Bettman’s comments on the state of the N.H.L. used an outdated name, in some editions, for the team Bettman said was in no danger of moving. It is the Arizona Coyotes, not the Phoenix Coyotes. (The team changed its name in June 2014.)
match_headline: Gary Bettman Denies Brain Disease Link

text: Because of an editing error, an art review on Friday about “The Cybernetic Fold,” an exhibition by Harry Dodge at the Wallspace gallery, in Chelsea, misidentified the profession of Adam Frank, one of the authors of a 1995 essay that introduced the eponymous term. He is a literary critic, not an astrophysicist.
match_headline: Review: Harry Dodge Meditates on Identity With ‘The Cybernetic Fold’

text: An article on May 24 about an effort in Oakland, Calif., to plant more oak trees erroneously attributed a distinction to the city. Oakland is one of the largest American cities named after a tree — not the largest. (For example, a larger California city, Fresno, derives its name from the Spanish word for “ash” or “ash tree.”)
match_headline: Tree Project Aims to Put the Oak Back in Oakland

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about Nashville’s efforts to control flooding described incorrectly the General Jackson, which cruises the Cumberland River. It is a showboat, not a ferry.
match_headline: Nashville Debates How to Prevent Another Devastating Flood

text: An article last Sunday about concerns raised over Rabbi Jonathan Rosenblatt’s practice of inviting boys and men to have serious conversations with him in the sauna after a racquetball or squash game misstated, in some editions, the given name of a former squash partner who said he felt the rabbi’s name was being smeared. He is Yaacob Dweck, not Yaakov.
match_headline: Debate Over the Rabbi and the Sauna

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about a growing number of establishments in Westchester County dedicated to “paint-and-sip” parties misidentified one of the locations for Muse Paintbar. Its Connecticut studio is in West Hartford, not in Hartford.
match_headline: Painting Parties Mix Creativity and Cocktails

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about sausage makers in New Jersey misidentified the previous owner of Union Pork Store, currently owned by Bozena and Leszek Jablonski. She was Bozena’s mother, not Leszek’s.
match_headline: A New Jersey Sausage-Eater’s Tour of Europe

text: An article last Sunday about the opening minutes of Golden State Warriors practices, when players launch a series of court-length shots, erroneously attributed a distinction to their coach, Steve Kerr, in some copies. The N.B.A.’s coach of the year award was given to the Atlanta Hawks’ Mike Budenholzer this season, not to Kerr.
match_headline: For the Golden State Warriors, Practice Makes Perfect Silliness

text: An article last Sunday about the Keishicho Eagles, a football team made up of members of the Tokyo Police Department in Japan’s X League, misstated the length of quarters under N.C.A.A. rules, from which X League rules are drawn. N.C.A.A. quarters are 15 minutes, not 12. (X League quarters are 12 minutes.)
match_headline: Tokyo Police Respond to the Call of Football

text: An article on May 24 about how drought is affecting tourist spots in California and neighboring states, using information provided by the president and chief executive of the Reno Sparks Convention and Visitors Authority, described incorrectly to what depth the water in Lake Tahoe would cover California. It would be 15 inches, not 15 feet, of water. And because of an editing error, the article described Disney California Adventure incorrectly. It is a theme park, not a water park.
match_headline: Drought Tests California Tourism

text: An article on May 17 about the Senate race in Maryland and the Democratic Party omitted one state among those that were the first to ratify same-sex marriage by popular vote in 2012. Besides Maine and Maryland, Washington voted to do so.
match_headline: The Great Democratic Crack-Up of 2016

text: An article on May 24 about pens misspelled the name of a Japanese bookstore. It is Kinokuniya, not Kinokinuya.
match_headline: Letter of Recommendation: Uni-ball Signo UM-151

text: An article last Sunday about the musician Jamie xx, who has released his first solo album, “In Colour,” misidentified the music label. It is Young Turks, not XL Recordings.
match_headline: Jamie xx Looks Inward and Back on ‘In Colour’

text: A picture caption last Sunday about backpacks for adults misidentified the designers and misstated the prices of the bags shown. The bags shown on the top row, from left, are: Bally, $1,395; Tod’s, $2,165; Salvatore Ferragamo, $2,400; and Dior Homme, $3,500. On the bottom row, from left, are bags by Mark Cross, $1,995; Calvin Klein Collection, $2,695; Coach, $595; and Boss, $595.
match_headline: Fear of Almonds

text: An article last Sunday about Chita Rivera misstated part of the title of the Broadway musical for which she won her second Tony award. It is “Kiss of the Spider Woman,” not “Kiss of the Spiderwoman.”
match_headline: In Sequins or Mufti, Chita Rivera Makes a Big Entrance

text: An article last Sunday about 50 Clinton, a new condominium on the Lower East Side, misstated the given name of a principal of DHA Capital, the developer. He is Josh Schuster, not John.
match_headline: The Lower East Side Goes From Gritty to Glossy

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some copies on Friday about challenges faced by Joseph Ponte, New York City’s correction commissioner, misidentified the state where he was correction commissioner before moving to his job in New York City. He worked in Maine, not in Massachusetts.
match_headline: Correction Commissioner Calls Overhauling Rikers a ‘Long, Heavy Lift’

text: An article on Thursday about a lawsuit accusing CVS of asking its staff to racially profile its customers misidentified the state where the company is based. It is Rhode Island, not Maryland.
match_headline: Ex-Workers Accuse CVS of Racial Discrimination Against Shoppers

text: An article last Monday about the Opera House Hotel and its fortunes in an improving South Bronx misstated part of the name of the company that owns it. It is the Empire Hotel Group, not the Empire Hotels Group.
match_headline: Opera House Hotel in the Bronx Gets High Marks From Guests, if They Can Get There

text: An article on Monday about HackerOne, a tech start-up that aims to mediate between companies with security issues and hackers who are looking to help solve problems, misstated the amount that Google started paying hackers five years ago for identifying bugs. It was $3,133.70, a reference to 31337, the hacker code for “elite” — not $3,177.30.
match_headline: HackerOne Connects Hackers With Companies, and Hopes for a Win-Win

text: An article on Saturday about Walmart’s experimentation with markets allowing online orders to be picked up at regular Walmart stores misstated, in some editions, the number of pilot markets. Walmart is testing the concept in four markets, not five.
match_headline: Walmart, Lagging in Online Sales, Is Strengthening E-Commerce

text: Because of an editing error, a music review on Saturday about two concerts featuring the music of John Zorn misstated the surname of one of the singers who performed his “The Holy Visions” at the Cloisters. She is Sarah Brailey, not Bailey.
match_headline: Review: John Zorn’s Spirit of Restless Invention Flows Forth

text: A listing of credits and schedule information on Friday with a theater review of “Notes of a Native Song,” at the Harlem Stage Gatehouse, misstated the theater’s telephone number. It is 212-281-9240.
match_headline: Review: ‘Notes of a Native Song’ Is Stew’s Homage to James Baldwin

text: A picture caption in some editions on Sunday with an obituary about the singer Ronnie Gilbert, an original member of the Weavers, misspelled the given name of another member of the group. He was Erik Darling, not Eric.
match_headline: Ronnie Gilbert, Bold-Voiced Singer With the Weavers, Is Dead at 88

text: An article on Tuesday about Senator John McCain’s efforts to reshape the Pentagon’s agenda erroneously attributed a distinction to a possible veto of the Defense Department policy bill by President Obama. The bill has been vetoed four times (in 1978, 1988, 1995 and 2007); a veto by Mr. Obama would not be the first time in five decades that a president has rejected the defense policy bill.
match_headline: With Chairmanship, McCain Seizes Chance to Reshape Pentagon Agenda

text: Because of an editing error, the Boston Journal article on Monday about the resignation of Amy Ryan, the president of the Boston Public Library, misstated the year the mayor, Martin J. Walsh, took office. It was January 2014, not this January. The article also misstated the sequence of events on Wednesday when Ms. Ryan announced her resignation. She told reporters that she had no plans to resign after — not before — the mayor’s chief of staff, Dan Koh, had made critical comments.
match_headline: Discovery of Missing Prints Fails to Save Boston Library Leader’s Job

text: A headline on Tuesday about a decision by the California Public Employees’ Retirement System to sever ties with many external investment managers to save on fees misstated the breadth of the retirement system’s action. It applies to a variety of investment management funds, not just to hedge funds.
match_headline: Calpers to Cut Ties With Many Fund Managers to Save on Fees

text: An article on Tuesday about the avoidance of a proxy fight at the retailer American Apparel misstated, in some copies, the timing of one concession the company made to a shareholder who, in return, agreed to withdraw the nominations of two new directors. American Apparel agreed to name a new independent director before its 2016 shareholders meeting, not before the meeting next month.
match_headline: American Apparel Avoids Fight Over Board

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the Cleveland Cavaliers’ 95-93 overtime victory over the Golden State Warriors in Game 2 of the N.B.A. Finals misstated the score after three quarters. Cleveland led by 62-59, not 62-49.
match_headline: N.B.A. Finals: Matthew Dellavedova Shines in Cavaliers’ Taut Win

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with a dance review of the choreographic installation “Settlement House,” at the Henry Street Settlement playhouse and the Abrons Arts Center in Manhattan, reversed the identities of two of the three dancers shown. Jarrod Beck was at the left and Davide Savorani at the right. (Ayesha Fuentes, center, was correctly identified.)
match_headline: Review: ‘Settlement House,’ a Tribute to Henry Street’s 100-Year History

text: An article on Saturday about questions raised about the book “On the Run: Fugitive Life in an American City,” by Alice Goffman, misstated the background of the Northwestern University law professor Steven Lubet, who has asked if Ms. Goffman not only described street crime but also admitted to having committed a felony. He is a former legal services lawyer and a juvenile and criminal defense lawyer, not a former public defender.
ref_headline: On the Run: Fugitive Life in an American City,
match_headline: Alice Goffman’s Heralded Book on Crime Is Disputed

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the chef Roger Vergé misstated the date of his birth in 1930. It was April 7, not April 30.
match_headline: Roger Vergé, a Founder of Nouvelle Cuisine, Dies at 85

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision by a Mississippi school district not to pursue charges against people who disrupted a graduation misspelled the surname of a lawyer for one of those who faced charges. He is Joseph D. Neyman Jr., not Neymann.
match_headline: Mississippi District Won’t Pursue Charges Over Cheers at a High School Graduation

text: A map on June 3 with an article about tensions between a casino developer and the Oneida Indian Nation misidentified the lake near the proposed Lago casino development. It is Cayuga Lake, not Seneca Lake.
match_headline: Tribe Opening New Casino Says a Competitor’s Site Is Too Close for Comfort

text: An article on Wednesday about the appointment of Robert Gibbs, a former White House press secretary, as chief communications officer for McDonald’s misstated the month of the State of the Union address in which President Obama challenged members of Congress to try living on the typical income of fast-food workers. It was January, not February.
match_headline: McDonald’s Hires Robert Gibbs, Ex-Press Secretary for Obama

text: An article on Friday about the Governors Ball Music Festival referred incorrectly to Lana Del Rey’s appearance there. She performed earlier this year at the Sasquatch festival in Washington State. Thus, Governors Ball was not the only American festival to book her this year.
match_headline: Governors Ball, Now in Its Fifth Season, Hits Its Stride

text: An article on May 26 about the unintended consequences of policies created to help working parents omitted an author of a study about a Spanish law’s effect on working parents. Daniel Fernández-Kranz and Núria Rodríguez-Planas were co-authors. Mr. Fernández-Kranz was not the sole author and did not lead the study.
match_headline: When Family-Friendly Policies Backfire

text: An article on Tuesday about an examination of the cellphone used by the engineer on the Amtrak train that derailed in Philadelphia last month, killing eight people, that turned up no evidence that he was on the phone at the time of the accident misstated the time zone in which the accident happened. It was Eastern Daylight Time, not Eastern Standard Time.
match_headline: No Evidence That Amtrak Engineer Used Phone During Crash, Safety Board Says

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about a visit by the rapper Kendrick Lamar to a New Jersey school where his work was used as a teaching tool misidentified the student who paid homage to Mr. Lamar’s album in a poem. He is Alejandro Leon, not Hamza Qureshi.
match_headline: Kendrick Lamar, Rapper Who Inspired a Teacher, Visits a High School That Embraces His Work

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article in some editions on Saturday about the interest shown by several major hospitals in New York’s new medical marijuana program described incorrectly the type of facility that was shown. The white building in Greenwich Village affiliated with the North Shore-L.I.J. system is an emergency center, not a hospital.
match_headline: Hospitals Back Providers Applying for New York State Marijuana Licenses

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the history of escapes from the prison in Dannemora, N.Y., misstated the year Luis Garrastegue, a former inmate there who contemplated fleeing, was released. It was 2003, not 2014.
match_headline: Tunnels, Disguises and Sewers: Clinton Prison’s Inmates Have Found Many Ways to Flee

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a judge’s ruling on the ownership of the 1897 painting “Rue Saint-Honoré, Après-midi, Effet de Pluie” by Pissarro misstated the dollar equivalent for the insurance on the work. It is insured for about nine million euros, which is about $10.1 million, not $7.98 million.
ref_headline: Rue Saint-Honoré, Après-midi, Effet de Pluie
match_headline: Judge Rejects Claim for a Pissarro by Heirs in Nazi Art Case

text: An article on Thursday about boat-booking services, similar to car-hailing services like Uber and Lyft, described incorrectly the original business model of one such service, Boatbound. It started as a tool for wedding planning, not as a wedding-dress rental service.
match_headline: A Rapper’s Ode to Uber, Chengdu Gangster Style

text: An obituary on May 25 about the mathematician John Nash referred incorrectly to treatment he received during one of his hospitalizations. He received insulin shock therapy, not electroshock therapy. The obituary also described imprecisely the book “Theory of Games and Economic Behavior,” by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern, which included a problem that Dr. Nash solved. That book primarily addressed so-called zero-sum games; it did not solely address such games. And because of an editing error, the obituary misidentified the prize Dr. Nash shared in 1994. It was the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, not the Nobel Prize.
ref_headline: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior,
match_headline: John F. Nash Jr., Math Genius Defined by a ‘Beautiful Mind,’ Dies at 86

text: An article on Friday about pending changes in the leadership of 21st Century Fox misstated the job title of one executive, Roger Ailes. He is the chairman and chief executive of Fox News, not the president.
match_headline: Rupert Murdoch to Put Media Empire in Sons’ Hands

text: An article on Thursday about a decision by New York City to end its contract with Corizon for health care at the Rikers Island prison complex misstated the job title of Anthony E. Shorris in some editions. He is the first deputy mayor, not Mayor Bill de Blasio’s chief of staff.
match_headline: New York City to End Contract With Rikers Health Care Provider

text: An article on Friday about the relationship between Lululemon and its founder, Dennis J. Wilson, referred incorrectly to the filing of a prospectus involving Mr. Wilson’s stake in the company. The company made the filing, not Mr. Wilson. The article also misstated the effect of the filing on Mr. Wilson’s association with the company. While the filing allows him to sell his entire 14 percent stake, it does not require him to do so. Thus his association with the company may end; it did not end with the filing.
match_headline: Lululemon’s Founder May Sell His Stake in Company

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the lack of scoring from Chicago Blackhawks stars Jonathan Toews and Patrick Kane in the first three games of the Stanley Cup finals referred incorrectly to Toews’s season in 2009, when Chicago lost the opening game of the Western Conference semifinals against the Vancouver Canucks. It was his first N.H.L. postseason, not his rookie season in the league. (He was a rookie the previous season.)
match_headline: Scorers Have Been Silent, but Blackhawks Remain Confident

text: An article last Sunday about the fight between Gov. Sam Brownback of Kansas and the state’s judicial branch misstated one aspect of a 2014 law that took some powers away from the State Supreme Court. The bill removed the court’s authority to appoint chief judges for the district courts, not its ability to appoint district judges themselves, who are either elected or selected through a merit process.
match_headline: Courts Budget Intensifies Kansas Dispute Over Powers

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the search for two men who escaped from Clinton Correctional Facility in Dannemora, N.Y., overstated, in some copies, what is known about the location where one escapee’s murder victim, William Rickerson, was killed. Mr. Rickerson died on a drive between Allegany State Park and Tonawanda Island, an area that could include Tonawanda, N.Y.; it has not been confirmed that he was killed in Tonawanda proper. In addition, the article, using information from state officials, misstated, in some copies, the year the prison was built. It was 1845, not 1865. And the article misstated, in some editions, the location of Plattsburgh, N.Y., relative to Dannemora. It is east, not west, of the town.
match_headline: With Power Tools and a Ruse, 2 Killers Flee New York Prison

text: An article last Sunday about the lives of older New Yorkers misstated the cost of Access-A-Ride, which transports New Yorkers with disabilities. It is $2.75; it is not a free service.
match_headline: A Group Portrait of New York’s ‘Oldest Old’

text: An article last Sunday about the Canadian soccer star Christine Sinclair misstated the surname of her uncles who played for the Portland Timbers of the North American Soccer League. They are Bruce and Brian Gant, not Grant.
match_headline: Face of Soccer in Canada, on Field and on Stamps

text: An article on May 24 about the author Judy Blume included an incorrect title for her new novel. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is ‘‘In the Unlikely Event,’’ not ‘‘An Unlikely Event.’’
match_headline: Judy Blume Knows All Your Secrets

text: An article on May 31 about depression in pregnant women misidentified the city where one of the subjects, Mary Guest, grew up. It is Seattle, not Portland, Ore.
match_headline: The Secret Sadness of Pregnancy With Depression

text: An article on May 24 about Caleb Orozco’s challenge to a statute criminalizing sodomy in Belize referred incorrectly to a comment about his court case in the newspaper Amandala. It was in a column, not in an editorial, that the newspaper’s editor in chief wrote, ‘‘Homosexuals are predators of young and teenaged boys.’’
match_headline: The Lonely Fight Against Belize’s Antigay Laws

text: An entry in a roundup review of cookbooks on May 31 about “Food52 Genius Recipes: 100 Recipes That Will Change the Way You Cook” misstated the given name of the author. She is Kristen Miglore, not Kirsten.
ref_headline: Food52 Genius Recipes: 100 Recipes That Will Change the Way You Cook
match_headline: Cooking

text: A review on May 17 about “Goebbels: A Biography,” by Peter Longerich, attributed an erroneous distinction to the book’s subject, Joseph Goebbels, the Nazi minister of propaganda. He indeed “remained” with Hitler “until the end,” but he was not the only one of Hitler’s closest associates to do so. Martin Bormann, the head of the Nazi Party chancellery, also remained with Hitler in his Berlin bunker, leaving only after Hitler committed suicide there.
match_headline: ‘Goebbels: A Biography,’ by Peter Longerich

text: An article last Sunday about the new biography “Irrepressible: The Jazz Age Life of Henrietta Bingham” misspelled the middle name of Ms. Bingham’s first love. She is Mina Kirstein Curtiss, not Mina Kerstein Curtiss.
ref_headline: Irrepressible: The Jazz Age Life of Henrietta Bingham
match_headline: Henrietta Bingham’s Jazz Age Life

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Andrea Cohan and Tanya Liszniansky misstated the given name of Ms. Liszniansky’s mother. She is Suzanne Liszniansky, not Susan.
match_headline: Andrea Cohan, Tanya Liszniansky

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Kristen Titus and Michael Noland-Conlow misidentified the institution where Mr. Conlow studied economics. It is the University of Massachusetts at Amherst, not Amherst College in Massachusetts.
match_headline: Digital Experts Head Offline for Love

text: An article on Friday about the pending exit of Twitter’s chief executive, Dick Costolo, misstated the sequence of events involving the role of a potential successor, Anthony Noto, Twitter’s chief financial officer, who recently assumed oversight of marketing at Twitter. While the marketing job had been held at one time by Gabriel Stricker, Twitter’s chief communications officer, Mr. Noto did not directly succeed Mr. Stricker.
match_headline: Twitter’s C.E.O., Dick Costolo, Is Set to Exit, Feeling Heat of Criticism

text: An article on Friday about the status of negotiations between Greece and its international creditors misidentified the organization headed by Donald Tusk, who commented on the issue. He is president of the European Council, not of the European Union.
match_headline: I.M.F. Recalls Negotiators as Deadline Looms for Greek Deal

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about San Francisco Giants pitcher Chris Heston’s no-hitter against the Mets misstated the number of no-hitters Giants catcher Buster Posey has caught in his career. It is three, not four.
match_headline: Giants’ Chris Heston Pitches No-Hitter Against Mets

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Tuesday about an agreement on a new constitution reached by Nepal’s major political parties after nearly a decade of friction referred incorrectly to the affiliation of a Nepalese politician, K. P. Sharma Oli, who said a vote on the document would come as soon as mid-July. He is the chairman of Nepal’s largest communist party, not its largest Maoist party.
match_headline: Earthquake Prods Nepal Parties to Make Constitution Deal

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Tuesday with an article about the prospect of instability in Turkey after an election in which President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s party failed to gain a majority misstated the affiliation of Abdullah Ocalan, whose picture was waved by Turks shown celebrating the election results. He is the jailed leader of the Kurdistan Workers Party, not the People’s Democratic Party.
match_headline: Prospect of Instability Looms as Turkish Voters Deny Erdogan a Majority

text: An article on Friday about the sound-and-light installation “Dream House” by La Monte Young, which will be on display starting today at 545 West 22nd Street in Manhattan, misstated the closing date. The installation is open through Oct. 24, and musical performances there continue through Oct. 23. The installation and performances do not end on Oct. 21. The error was repeated in schedule information with the article.
match_headline: A ‘House’ Finds a New Home

text: An article last Tuesday about efforts by scientists to take the first-ever picture of the black hole at the center of our galaxy by using a worldwide network of telescopes misstated, in some copies, a task that Sheperd Doeleman, the head of the project, once completed at the ALMA telescope array in Chile. He was testing atomic clocks, not installing receivers. And a chart with the article misidentified one of the telescopes in Hawaii that is part of the network. It is the Submillimeter Array, not the Small Millimeter Array.
match_headline: Black Hole Hunters

text: An obituary on May 17 about the architect Francis Fleetwood, who designed more than 200 homes in the Hamptons on Long Island, erroneously included one house among those homes. An 11,000-square-foot mansion on Sagg Pond in Sagaponack was designed by the firm Shope Reno Wharton, not by Mr. Fleetwood.
match_headline: Francis Fleetwood, Architect Who Transformed the Hamptons, Dies at 68

text: Because of an editing error, a letter from Palo Alto, Calif., on Sunday about transgender issues misspelled the writer’s surname. He is Ben Barres, not Barre.
match_headline: Caitlyn Jenner and Gender Stereotypes

text: An article on June 8 about ties between Gov. Scott Walker of Wisconsin and conservative groups misidentified the recipient of two grants from the Bradley Foundation, whose president is close to Mr. Walker. The Bradley Foundation gave a total of $520,000 during the 2010 governor’s race to Americans for Prosperity Foundation, not to Americans for Prosperity.
match_headline: Behind Scott Walker, a Longstanding Conservative Alliance Against Unions

text: An article on March 19 about the hanging of nine prisoners in Pakistan misstated the year that one prisoner, Shafqat Hussain, who was given a reprieve, was sentenced to death. It was 2004, not 2001. (The error was discovered only recently, when an editor was working on a follow-up article.)
match_headline: Pakistan Steps Up Executions of Convicts, but One Gets Reprieve

text: An article on May 23 about Chinese objections to American surveillance flights over contested territory in areas of the South China Sea where China is creating artificial islands referred incorrectly to the concrete manufacturing plants that China is building there. They produce concrete foundations used for runways; they do not provide asphalt.
match_headline: U.S. Flies Over a Chinese Project at Sea, and Beijing Objects

text: An article on Tuesday about Rachel A. Dolezal’s resignation as president of the N.A.A.C.P. chapter in Spokane, Wash., over questions about her race misspelled, in some editions, the given name of her mother, who described the family ancestry as overwhelmingly white. She is Ruthanne, not Rutheanne. The article also misstated the given name of a spokesman at Eastern Washington University, where Ms. Dolezal was an instructor. He is Dave Meany, not Brian.
match_headline: Rachel Dolezal Leaves N.A.A.C.P. Post as Past Discrimination Suit Is Revealed

text: An article on Tuesday about a study of marijuana use by teenagers misspelled the surname of a former Obama administration adviser and president of the group Smart Approaches to Marijuana. He is Kevin Sabet, not Sabett.
match_headline: Medical Use of Marijuana Doesn’t Increase Youths’ Use, Study Finds

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about a shooting in the Bronx that involved the police gave outdated information about another such shooting in East Harlem on Tuesday night, June 9. News reports last Wednesday identified the detective who opened fire as Josh Ulan. It is not the case that his identity had not been released by Wednesday night.
match_headline: Officers Responding to Bronx Dispute Fatally Shoot Armed Man

text: An article on Tuesday about a rebound in charitable giving after the financial crisis omitted credit for some data on gifts from donors in the technology industry. The data on gifts from Bill and Melinda Gates, Sean Parker, Jill and Nicolas Woodman and Jan Koum came from a special report in The Chronicle of Philanthropy.
match_headline: Charitable Giving Rises Past Prerecession Mark

text: Because of an editing error, a jazz entry in the Listings pages on Friday about Eric Revis, at the Jazz Gallery in Manhattan, referred incorrectly to the pianist in Mr. Revis’s trio. The pianist, Kris Davis, is a woman.
match_headline: Jazz Listings for June 12-18

text: An obituary on Friday about the jazz saxophonist and composer Ornette Coleman referred incorrectly to the blues singer Clarence Samuels, with whom Mr. Coleman worked early in his career. He was not blind.
match_headline: Ornette Coleman, Saxophonist Who Rewrote the Language of Jazz, Dies at 85

text: An article on June 8 about the hunt for two escaped prisoners in upstate New York, using information from state officials, misstated the men’s ages. Richard W. Matt is 48, not 49, and David Sweat was 34, not 35, when the article was published. (He has since had a birthday.) The error was repeated in another article on June 8 about the history of the Clinton Correctional Facility, from which the men escaped.
match_headline: Wide Net Cast for Escaped Killers; They Could Be ‘Anywhere’

text: An article on Wednesday about Davide Serra, an Italian hedge fund manager known for acerbic opinions and high investment returns, misspelled the given name of an Italian politician Mr. Serra supports and misidentified the office that politician holds. He is Matteo Renzi, not Mateo, and he is the prime minister of Italy, not the president.
match_headline: Bravado and High Returns From Italian Fund Manager

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on June 4 about the Chicago Blackhawks’ 2-1 victory over the Tampa Bay Lightning in Game 1 of the Stanley Cup finals misstated, in some copies, the number of saves made by Lightning goalie Ben Bishop. He had 19, not 20. The article also misidentified, in some copies, the Chicago goal that Tampa Bay Coach Jon Cooper described as a “seeing-eye single,” comparing it to a baseball play. It was the Blackhawks’ first goal, by Teuvo Teravainen, not their second goal, by Antoine Vermette.
match_headline: Lightning’s Attackers Are Quick, but Blackhawks’ Comeback Is Quicker

text: A picture caption in some editions on Saturday with an article about the 0-0 draw between the United States and Sweden soccer teams at the Women’s World Cup misstated the given name of one of the American players shown defending Sweden’s Amanda Ilestedt and Linda Sembrant. She is Ali Krieger, not Alex.
match_headline: Women’s World Cup: U.S. Earns a Draw the Hard Way

text: An article on Saturday about the golfer Brooke Henderson, a Canadian teenager competing in the Women’s P.G.A. Championship, misstated the number of strokes separating her from the leader, Sei Young Kim, after the second round of the tournament. It was two, not one. The error was repeated in a capsule summary.
match_headline: Teenager Hopes to Skip School, of the Golf Variety

text: An obituary on June 10 about the prosecutor and author Vincent T. Bugliosi misstated the ages of two of the people who were killed along with the actress Sharon Tate in 1969, murders for which Mr. Bugliosi later prosecuted Charles Manson. Abigail Folger was 25, not 26, and Voytek Frykowski was 32, not 37.
match_headline: Vincent T. Bugliosi, Manson Prosecutor and True-Crime Author, Dies at 80

text: An article on June 9 about the political ambitions of Nicola Sturgeon, Scotland’s first minister, whose Scottish National Party won nearly all of Scotland’s parliamentary seats in the British election in May, referred incorrectly to Ms. Sturgeon’s inauguration after winning her first seat in the Scottish Parliament. While she refused to take the traditional oath of allegiance to the queen, she still had to make a solemn affirmation — an alternative to taking the oath — to “bear true allegiance” to the queen; she did not refuse to swear allegiance. The error also appeared in an article on May 6 about Ms. Sturgeon’s popularity with Scottish voters before the May election.
match_headline: Nicola Sturgeon, Star of Scottish Politics, Vows to Secure More Power

text: An article on Saturday about reports from Asian migrants that smugglers on their boat were paid by Australian officials to take the migrants back to Indonesia reversed the given name and surname of a spokesman for the United Nations refugee agency who provided the migrants’ account. He is Babar Baloch. The reversed names appeared in a follow-up article on Sunday. Also, a reporting credit for the article was omitted. Michelle Innis contributed from Sydney, Australia, and Joe Cochrane reported from Jakarta, Indonesia — not from Geneva, the dateline of the article. (The other reporter, Nick Cumming-Bruce, was in Geneva.)
match_headline: Asian Migrants Say Australia Paid Smugglers to Turn Back

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about a public hearing before a New York State wage board misstated the surname of a professor at the City University of New York who testified on the benefits of a higher minimum wage. She is Stephanie Luce, not Lure.
match_headline: Board Hears Support for Raising Food Workers’ Minimum Wage

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about players on losing teams in league championship games who have won the most valuable player award misstated the year the photograph of two such players, the Celtics’ John Havlicek and the Lakers’ Jerry West, was taken. It was in the 1960s, not in 1970. Because of an editing error, another picture caption referred incorrectly to an award given to Anaheim goalie Jean-Sebastien Giguere, whose team lost the Stanley Cup finals to the Devils in 2003. He was the most valuable player of the playoffs, not the finals. (There is no such award given for the finals.)
match_headline: Is LeBron James the N.B.A. Finals M.V.P., Win or Lose?

text: Because of an editing error, a report in some copies of the Sports Briefing column on Monday about results at the Copa América in Chile misidentified the winner of the soccer game between Venezuela and Colombia. Venezuela won, 1-0 — not Colombia.
match_headline: Chile’s Copa América Star in Court After Crashing Ferrari
