text: An article on Thursday about how some authors resist being categorized by language or nationality misspelled the surname of an Argentine-born writer honored by Dany Laferrière, a Haitian-Québécois novelist, in his speech last month at his induction into the Académie Française. He was Hector Bianciotti, not Bionciotti. The article also misstated the year he died. It was 2012, not 2011.
match_headline: Académie Française Honor Highlights Fluid National Allegiances Among Writers

text: A report in the Antiques column on Friday about collecting scrimshaw, using information from Bonhams auction house, misidentified the site of an auction in 2005 where a whale tooth engraved with scenes of whale hunts was sold. It is Brookline, Mass., not San Francisco.
match_headline: A Scrimshaw Collector’s Treasured Carvings

text: An obituary on Thursday about Nelson Doubleday Jr., the publisher who for many years was an owner of the Mets, misstated the date of his death in some editions. He died on Wednesday, not on Tuesday. The obituary also misstated the given name of the man he named chief executive of Doubleday & Company in 1985. He is James R. McLaughlin, not John. The obituary also referred incorrectly to the Mets’ finances in the 1986 season, when the team won the World Series. The Mets’ total earnings — not gate receipts — were $6 million. And the obituary misstated Doubleday & Company’s earnings in 1985 in some editions. In the fiscal year that ended April 30, the company earned $300,000 on sales of more than $400 million, not $7 million on sales of $472 million.
match_headline: Nelson Doubleday Jr., Publisher Who Owned the Mets, Dies at 81

text: An article on Friday about the years Nelson Doubleday Jr. spent as an owner of the Mets misstated his position and the position of his fellow Mets owner Fred Wilpon on the ouster of Fay Vincent as commissioner of baseball in 1992. Both men were against a resolution to ask Vincent to resign; they were not “on opposite sides” of his ouster.
match_headline: Mets Under Nelson Doubleday Were a Lesson in Turning Around a Team

text: Because of an editing error, an article on June 7 about a shift in commercial tuna fishing methods off Spain’s southern coast to respond to the demands of consumers in Japan, the world’s largest tuna market, misstated the 2015 tuna quota for Spanish companies that run an ancient trap-fishing method known as almadraba. It is 756 metric tons, or about 1.6 million pounds, not 2,200 pounds.
match_headline: Spanish Tuna Fishing Melds to Japan’s Taste, Reshaping a 3,000-Year-Old Technique

text: Because of a transcription error, an article last Sunday about the attack on the Dallas Police Headquarters misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a witness to the shooting. She is Anita Grendahl, not Grendhal.
match_headline: Dallas Gunman Killed After Attack on Police Headquarters

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about the audiobook company Audible misstated the surname of the company’s founder, who spoke about studying under Ralph Ellison. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Donald Katz, not Kaplan.
match_headline: At Audible, Work Speaks Volumes

text: Because of an editing error, the On Pro Basketball column in some editions on June 7, about an injury to the Cleveland Cavaliers’ Kyrie Irving during the N.B.A. finals, omitted a word, in some copies, from a quotation by Commissioner Adam Silver referring to high-profile injuries in the league this season. He said: “Our data doesn’t go back that far at least to a point that it’s really reliable in terms of games missed. But at least over a short period of time we don’t see, even versus last year — games missed is not greater” — not “games missed is greater.”
match_headline: Kyrie Irving Is the Latest Casualty in a High-Stakes Game

text: A picture caption in some copies last Sunday with an article about the top American javelin throwers’ competing at the Adidas Grand Prix on Randalls Island reversed the identities of the two American javelin throwers shown. Riley Dolezal is at the left, and Tim Glover at the right.
match_headline: On Randalls Island, the Rhythm and Physics of Throwing a Javelin

text: An article last Sunday about the yearslong process that Pamela Ruiz and Damian Aquiles, a married couple, endured to renovate a home in Havana gave outdated information about the buying and selling of property in Cuba. While such transactions were illegal at the time Ruiz and Aquiles bought their house, that is no longer the case. (The law was changed in 2011.)
match_headline: A Grand Havana Home

text: An article last Sunday about learning local dances in various places around the world misidentified a dance company in Ethiopia that offers classes for expats and locals. It is Destino Dance Company, not Adugna Dance Company.
match_headline: Using Dance to Connect With Locals

text: An article and a picture caption last Sunday about the artist Ayano Sudo misspelled the surname of her best friend in New York. He is Aaron Kolfage, not Kelfage. The article also misstated Mr. Kolfage’s age. He is 27, not 28.
match_headline: Ayano Sudo’s Photographs Blur the Gender Line

text: An article last Sunday about “Deutschland 83,” a German television series set toward the end of the Cold War, misspelled part of the title of a movie in which Sylvester Groth, who plays a Stasi official in the show, appeared. It is “Inglourious Basterds,” not “Inglorious Basterds.”
match_headline: ‘Deutschland 83,’ a SundanceTV Series About an Earnest Stasi Spy

text: A review on June 7 about “Spec-tacle: The Astonishing Life of Ota Benga,” by Pamela Newkirk, referred incompletely to the authorship of an earlier book on the same subject, “Ota Benga: The Pygmy in the Zoo.” That book was co-written by Phillips Verner Bradford, not written by him alone. (Bradford’s co-author is Harvey Blume.)
ref_headline: Spec-tacle: The Astonishing Life of Ota Benga,
match_headline: ‘Spectacle: The Astonishing Life of Ota Benga,’ by Pamela Newkirk

text: An article on June 7 about South Korea’s smartphone industry misstated how fast American broadband Internet speeds will be in the future. The Federal Communications Commission hopes to wire most American homes with broadband Internet with speeds of at least 100 megabits per second, or roughly one-sixtieth of South Korea’s goal, not 100 megabytes per second, or roughly six-hundredths of South Korea’s goal.
match_headline: What Silicon Valley Can Learn From Seoul

text: An article on June 7 about Russian Internet ‘‘trolls’’ referred incorrectly to the Internet platform Yandex. It was subjected to political pressure, but it was not brought under the control of Kremlin allies.
match_headline: The Agency

text: An article on June 14 about the labor movement in Wisconsin misstated the month of a ‘‘right to work’’ hearing in the State Assembly at which Terry McGowan, the president of Local 139, spoke. The hearing was in March, not February.
match_headline: Scott Walker and the Fate of the Union

text: An article on Tuesday about Hamid Karzai, the former Afghan president, whose public profile is increasing at the same time that the government of his successor, Ashraf Ghani, is struggling, misidentified the president who employed Sadiq Mudaber as his top administrative aide. Mr. Mudaber worked for Mr. Karzai, not for Mr. Ghani.
match_headline: Karzai, Vowing That He’s Done, Discusses His Afghanistan Legacy

text: An article on Wednesday about a joint appearance by Mayor Bill de Blasio and his predecessor, Michael R. Bloomberg, at a groundbreaking ceremony on Roosevelt Island misstated the year of Mr. de Blasio’s inauguration. It was 2014, not 2013.
match_headline: De Blasio and Bloomberg Trade Rare Praise. No Hug, Though.

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a series of attacks on Asian women in Manhattan misidentified one of the streets near the location where the second reported attack occurred on June 10. The attacker passed his target near East 30th Street and Park Avenue South, not Park Avenue.
match_headline: Police Search for Assailant in 4 Attacks on Asian Women

text: Because of an editing error, the Quotation of the Day on Friday, taken from a front-page article about Pope Francis’ release of a document about the environment and climate change, following in the tradition of previous popes who have issued encyclicals about timely social questions, misidentified the person who said: “The church must introduce in its teaching the sin against the environment. The ecological sin.” As the article correctly noted, the comment was by Metropolitan John Zizioulas, an Eastern Orthodox theologian who was among those presenting the encyclical at a Vatican news conference — not from Francis, in his encyclical.
ref_headline: The church must introduce in its teaching the sin against the environment. The ecological sin.
match_headline: Leak of Pope’s Encyclical on Climate Change Hints at Tensions in Vatican

text: An article on Sunday about a website that included pictures and a manifesto tied to Dylann Roof, who is accused of killing nine people at a church in Charleston, S.C., included an outdated reference to David Lane, whose slogan on white supremacy was known to Mr. Roof. Mr. Lane died in prison in 2007; he is not currently serving a 190-year sentence.
match_headline: Dylann Roof Photos and a Manifesto Are Posted on Website

text: An article in some editions on June 15 about a judge’s ruling in favor of a development that would block views of the Brooklyn Bridge misstated part of the name of a skyscraper on West 57th Street in Manhattan that drew similar dismay at the time of its construction. It is Metropolitan Tower, not Metropolitan Towers. And the article described incorrectly the location of Metropolitan Tower in proximity to Carnegie Hall. It is down the block, not on an adjacent lot.
match_headline: Judge Clears Way for Pierhouse Complex to Cast Shadow on Brooklyn Bridge

text: An article on Saturday about an internal audit by the Transportation Department that was sharply critical of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration misspelled the surname of the department’s inspector general, whose office conducted the audit. He is Calvin L. Scovel III, not Scovell.
match_headline: Federal Auditor Finds Broad Failures at N.H.T.S.A.

text: An article last Sunday about the Yankees’ 14-3 rout of the Detroit Tigers on Old-Timers’ Day erroneously included a player on a list of former Yankees who are in the Baseball Hall of Fame but who do not have a plaque or monument in Monument Park at Yankee Stadium. That player, Lefty Gomez, was given a plaque in August 1987. The article also erroneously attributed a distinction to the team’s won-lost record. The Yankees’ high for games over .500 this season is nine (they were 21-12 on May 11); the team’s 38-30 record after last Sunday’s game was not “a season-high-tying eight games over .500.”
match_headline: Day Honoring Yankees Stars of Past Ends With an Old-Fashioned Rout

text: An article on Monday about the final round of the United States Open golf tournament misstated, in some editions, the score of the event’s champion, Jordan Spieth, on the 17th hole, which he double-bogeyed. It was 5, not 6.
match_headline: U.S. Open 2015: Jordan Spieth, Not Yet 22, Is 2 for 2 in This Year’s Majors

text: An obituary on Sunday about the historian Allen Weinstein misidentified the university where he became a professor in 1981. It is Georgetown, not George Washington.
match_headline: Allen Weinstein, Historian of Alger Hiss Case, Dies at 77

text: A picture credit on Tuesday with the continuation of an article about the deterioration of South Sudan into chaos after two years of civil war misstated the photographer’s given name. The two pictures of refugees were taken by Tyler Hicks, not Taylor.
match_headline: As South Sudan Crisis Worsens, ‘There Is No More Country’

text: An article in some editions last Wednesday about a parachutist’s testimony in State Supreme Court recounting the night in 2013 that he leapt from One World Trade Center misspelled the prosecutor’s surname. He is Joseph Giovannetti, not Giovanetti. The error was repeated in an article in some editions on Thursday about closing arguments in the trial. (The parachutist, Marko Markovich, and two other men who jumped with him were found guilty on Monday on three misdemeanor counts.)
match_headline: On Stand, World Trade Center Parachutist Stresses His Skill

text: An article last Wednesday about teenagers’ joining New York City’s community boards misspelled the surname of a 16-year-old on Manhattan Community Board 11. He is Mahfuzur Rahman, not Raman.
match_headline: Age 16, and Not Too Young to Join the Community Board

text: An article on Thursday about the arrests of three Postal Service employees in a scheme to defraud an annual holiday gift drive, using information from prosecutors, misspelled the given name of one of the suspects. He is Nickyves Saint-Albord, not Nickyeves.
match_headline: 3 Postal Workers Accused of Posing as Children to Steal From Operation Santa

text: An article on Tuesday about the Sequential Brands Group’s acquisition of Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia, using information from several data sources, misstated the price of the deal. Sequential Brands is paying $353 million for 57.46 million shares outstanding; it is not paying about $200 million for 32.4 million shares outstanding. The $200 million error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Martha Stewart’s Media Empire Sold for Fraction of Its Former Value

text: An article on Tuesday about the Malaysian airline AirAsia’s difficulties in expanding operations to India rendered incorrectly the name of the former employer of AirAsia India’s chief executive, Mittu Chandilya. It is Ingersoll-Rand, not Ingersoll & Rand.
match_headline: AirAsia Faces Red Tape and Tough Competition in India

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with the On Golf column, about Jordan Spieth’s United States Open victory, misstated, in some copies, the day he was shown playing in the Open’s third round. It was Saturday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Jordan Spieth Avoids Sting and Creates Buzz

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the composer and conductor Gunther Schuller omitted a survivor. Besides his sons, Edwin and George, Mr. Schuller is survived by a brother, Edgar.
match_headline: Gunther Schuller Dies at 89; Composer Synthesized Classical and Jazz

text: An article last Wednesday about dishes for Ramadan featuring dates misstated the Indonesian name for the fruit. It is buah kurma, not buah tanggal, which is the term for chronological dates.
match_headline: During Ramadan, Dates Are a Unifying Staple

text: An article on Tuesday about Lester Holt, newly named the permanent anchor of the NBC “Nightly News” broadcast, erroneously attributed a distinction to him. Bernard Shaw of CNN — not Mr. Holt — is the first person of African-American descent to serve as the solo anchor of a weekday evening newscast.
match_headline: Lester Holt Reflects on Rise to NBC’s Anchor Chair

text: An article on Wednesday about the decision by several major retailers to stop selling merchandise containing the Confederate battle flag misidentified the city that is home to the South Carolina State House. It is Columbia, not Charleston.
match_headline: Confederate Flag Sales Soar as Retailers Pull Stock

text: A picture caption on Tuesday for a music review about an 11-hour marathon in Lower Manhattan on Sunday celebrating eclectic forms of music misstated the name of a piano sextet that performed. It is Grand Band, not the Third Angle New Music Grand Band.
match_headline: Review: Bang on a Can Marathon Stays as Eclectic and Playful as Ever

text: An obituary in some editions on Wednesday about the composer James Horner misstated the number of Grammy Awards he won. It was six, not five.
match_headline: James Horner, Film Composer, Dies at 61; His Score for ‘Titanic’ Was a Hit, Too

text: An obituary on Sunday about the sculptor Carl Nesjar misstated the year the sculpture “Bust of Sylvette,” one of many collaborations between Mr. Nesjar and Picasso, was installed in Manhattan. It was 1968, not 1967.
match_headline: Carl Nesjar, Sculptor Who Added Dimension to Picasso, Dies at 94

text: An article last Thursday about women who dress modestly in the heat of spring and summer misspelled, in one instance, the middle name of a jewelry wholesaler who commented on her personal style, and erroneously included her middle name as part of her surname. She is Charlotte Chanler Russell, not Charlotte Chandler Russell, and should have been referred to as Ms. Russell.
match_headline: Women Who Cover Up (Even as the Temperatures Climb)

text: An article last Thursday about Fantastic Man magazine misstated the year the print version of Butt magazine, which was created by the same team as Fantastic Man, was discontinued. It was 2011, not 2005.
match_headline: Fantastic Man Magazine and Its Influence on Men’s Fashion

text: An article on Tuesday about the Council of Conservative Citizens, whose views on race relations resonated in a manifesto apparently written by Dylann Roof, who was charged in the murders of nine people in South Carolina, misstated the year the group joined a fierce debate over displaying the Confederate battle flag on the grounds of the South Carolina State House. It was 2000, not 2010. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Council of Conservative Citizens Promotes White Primacy, and G.O.P. Ties

text: An article on Monday about a report prepared for the European Commission that blamed Macedonia’s authoritarian government for a wiretapping scandal that has rocked the nation described incorrectly the popular protests that have taken place in the capital, Skopje, since May. While the initial protest included clashes with the police, the demonstrations that followed were peaceful; the protests did not turn “increasingly violent.”
match_headline: Macedonia Government Is Blamed for Wiretapping Scandal

text: An article on Wednesday about the future of Sweet Briar College in light of a settlement that will keep the college from closing misattributed a quotation about staffing. It was Cathy Gutierrez, a religion professor — not Tony Lilly, an associate professor of English — who worried that staffing is “going to be extremely patchwork.”
match_headline: Sweet Briar College Is Saved but Is Not in the Clear

text: An article in some editions last Friday about continuing problems at Carnegie Deli, which has been closed since April, misstated the role of the owner’s father in the business. Milton Parker, the father of the current owner, Marian Levine, bought the Carnegie with two partners in 1976; he did not open it.
match_headline: Carnegie Deli to Remain Closed at Least 2 More Weeks

text: An article on Saturday about the death of a shop worker during a robbery in Harlem misstated the surname of a customer who had visited the store the day of the attack. He is Samuel Cisneros, not Lisneros.
match_headline: A Son, Known for His Kindness, Is Mourned After He Is Bludgeoned to Death

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about peppers that are being grown for Bronx Greenmarket Hot Sauce misidentified, in some editions, the high school attended by John A. Crotty, a backer of the sauce. He graduated from Xavier High School, not from the Bronx High School of Science.
match_headline: Hot Peppers Becoming a Cash Crop for Bronx Community Gardens

text: An article on Tuesday about a Senate hearing on recalls and repairs involving potentially defective airbags manufactured by the Japanese company Takata misstated a manufacturing detail about the company’s replacement airbags. Some of the inflaters for the replacement bags use a chemical propellant other than ammonium nitrate, a compound that the company used in the recalled airbags; all five million replacement bags do not contain ammonium nitrate.
match_headline: Lawmakers Spread Anger in Recalls Over Airbags

text: A news analysis article on Thursday about President Obama’s political status after winning a bruising fight with his own party over his authority to negotiate a trade deal with Pacific nations misstated, in some editions, the year in which the Democrats lost the House of Representatives. It was 2010, not 2012.
match_headline: Obama Bolsters His Leverage With Trade Victory, but at a Cost

text: An article on Thursday about criticism the United States soccer team has received for its disjointed style of play so far in the Women’s World Cup misstated, in some editions, the number of international goals scored by Abby Wambach. It is 183 — not 245, which is the number of international games she has played.
match_headline: Women’s World Cup 2015: U.S. Keeps Winning as Critics of Its Style Keep Grumbling

text: An obituary on Saturday about the author James Salter erroneously attributed a distinction to the astronaut Ed White, a former Air Force colleague of his, whom Mr. Salter wrote about in his book “Burning the Days.” Mr. White was the first American to walk in space, not the first person to do so. (The Russian cosmonaut Aleksei Leonov was the first.)
match_headline: James Salter, a ‘Writer’s Writer’ Short on Sales but Long on Acclaim, Dies at 90

text: An article on Friday about the future of state-based health exchanges misstated part of the name of an organization that studied New Mexico’s health care model. It is the National Academy for State Health Policy, not the National Association of State Health Policy.
match_headline: Obamacare Ruling May Have Just Killed State-Based Exchanges

text: An article on Tuesday about a decision by New York City to make the Lunar New Year a school holiday misidentified, in some editions, the form of Chinese that city officials used to announce the news on Twitter. It is traditional Chinese — not Mandarin, a form of spoken Chinese.
match_headline: Mayor de Blasio to Make Lunar New Year a School Holiday

text: An article on Tuesday about the Los Amigos Fishing and Hunting Club, a social organization on the Lower East Side, misspelled the given name of the club’s owner. As an accompanying picture caption correctly noted, he is Felipe Cortes, not Filipe.
match_headline: Holdouts From Rougher Era Endure at Lower East Side Club

text: A subheading in some editions on June 18 with an article about the Cosmos’ victory over New York City F.C. in a United States Open Cup soccer match misstated the score of the match, which was decided in a penalty shootout. It was 2-2 at the end of regulation, not 3-3.
match_headline: Cosmos Knock Off New York City F.C., Another Local Rival, in Open Cup

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 13 this weekend about surveillance by the National Security Agency refers incorrectly to action Congress took on a surveillance program for the agency. It tried to provide oversight; it did not create the program.
match_headline: The Rabbit-Hole of ‘Relevant’

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with an obituary about Mario Biaggi, who served as a Bronx congressman, misstated the year he retired from the New York City Police Department. As the obituary correctly noted, it was 1965, not 1995.
match_headline: Mario Biaggi, 97, Popular Bronx Congressman Who Went to Prison, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with the On Baseball column, about Alex Rodriguez’s baseball legacy, misidentified, in some editions, one of three former Yankees shown watching the Old-Timers’ Day festivities with Rodriguez and omitted the name of another one pictured. The three men are, from left, Charlie Hays, who was not identified; Cecil Fielder, who was misidentified as Darryl Strawberry; and Rickey Henderson, who was correctly identified.
match_headline: Yankees Legends, in Various Shades of Gray

text: An article last Sunday about the obstacles that the Pittsburgh Pirates’ Roberto Clemente faced and surmounted misstated the middle initial of an author of the book “Reconstructing Fame.” He is David C. Ogden, not David G.
match_headline: Clemente, the Double Outsider

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Ana Martinez de Luco, a Catholic nun who runs a can and bottle redemption center in Brooklyn, paraphrased incorrectly from a passage in Leviticus that she likes to cite. It is God, not Jesus, who tells farmers to leave some fallen grain behind for the needy.
match_headline: A ‘Street Nun’ Who Specializes in Redemption

text: An article on June 14 about the writer Jenny Diski rendered incorrectly the name of the institution where her husband, Ian Patterson, teaches. It is Queens’ College, not Queen’s.
match_headline: Jenny Diski’s End Notes

text: An article last Sunday about following in the footsteps of Pete Seeger misidentified the relative of Woody Guthrie who produced an audio tour of his homes in New York. The audio guide was made by his daughter, not by his granddaughter.
match_headline: Pete Seeger’s New York Roots

text: An article last Sunday about the criminal case against Donald L. Blankenship, former chief executive of Massey Energy, described his indictment incorrectly. He was indicted by a federal grand jury, not by federal prosecutors, who presented the case to the grand jury.
match_headline: The People v. the Coal Baron

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of the astrophysicists Kate Grier and Thomas Beatty paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Mr. Beatty about exoplanets. While he noted that he is part of a group that has discovered 10 exoplanets, he did not say that only about two dozen exoplanets have been confirmed. (In all, more than 1,500 exoplanets have been confirmed, according to the exoplanets.org website.)
match_headline: A Marriage Made in the Heavens

text: An article last Sunday about the ways that curatorial lines are blurring between commercial art galleries and art museums misidentified an entity represented by the David Zwirner gallery. It is the Ad Reinhardt estate, not the Ad Reinhardt Foundation.
match_headline: Blurring the Museum-Gallery Divide

text: An article last Sunday about the influence of the late singer Nina Simone on modern musicians misspelled the name of her hometown. It is Tryon, N.C., not Tyron.
match_headline: Nina Simone’s Time Is Now, Again

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Wednesday about Cami Anderson, the departing superintendent of Newark’s public schools, misstated one of the types of schools for which a single lottery had been set up. It is for traditional and charter schools, not traditional and public schools.
match_headline: Schools Chief in Newark Says Debate Lost Its Focus

text: An article on June 10 about Joe Quinn, an Australian player-manager of the Cleveland Spiders of the National League in 1899, rendered incorrectly the title of a book about him. It is “Joe Quinn Among the Rowdies,” not “Joe Quinn: Among the Rowdies.”
match_headline: Matthew Dellavedova Isn’t First Aussie to Charm Cleveland

text: An obituary on Friday about the actor Patrick Macnee referred incorrectly to the timing of his appearance in the 1951 film “A Christmas Carol,” starring Alastair Sim. It was after he left the Royal Navy, not before he joined, in 1941.
match_headline: Patrick Macnee, 93, Dapper and Unflappable in ‘The Avengers,’ Dies

text: An article on Thursday about the families of nine people shot at a church in Charleston, S.C., misstated the circumstances that spurred unrest in Baltimore this spring. The violence occurred after the death of a black man injured while in police custody; it did not involve a shooting.
match_headline: Charleston Families Hope Words Endure Past Shooting

text: An article in some editions on June 21 about the release of diplomatic cables by WikiLeaks that revealed requests for money and favors from Saudi Arabia misstated, in some copies, the amount of money that one cable, quoting a leader in the Muslim Brotherhood, said would be needed to keep former President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt out of prison, suggesting negotiations between Saudi leaders and the Brotherhood after the revolution that toppled Mr. Mubarak. The amount was $10 billion, not $10 million.
match_headline: Cables Released by WikiLeaks Reveal Saudis’ Checkbook Diplomacy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on June 17 about China’s land reclamation work in the South China Sea misstated, at one point and in some editions, China’s plans. A spokesman for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said China had decided to go forward with plans to complete land reclamation work, not continue it. The article also misstated part of the name of the Washington organization where Bonnie S. Glaser, who commented on the land reclamation work, is a senior adviser. It is the Center for Strategic and International Studies, not the Center for Security and International Studies.
match_headline: As Tensions With U.S. Grow, Beijing Says It Will Stop Building Artificial Islands in South China Sea

text: An article on Monday about the conflict between the governor of Maine and the State Legislature misstated, in some editions, the amount of a budget shortfall that Democratic lawmakers say would be created by a plan to eliminate the state income tax. It is $1.7 billion, not $1.7 million.
match_headline: Combative Maine Governor Becomes a Party of One

text: An obituary on Saturday about Yevgeny Primakov, a former prime minister of Russia, misstated, in some copies, the middle initial of the former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. He is Mikhail S., not Mikhail B.
match_headline: Yevgeny Primakov, Former Russian Premier and Spymaster, Dies at 85

text: An article on June 19 about Dylann Roof, who has been accused of killing nine people at a church in Charleston, S.C., included incorrect information from law enforcement documents about an earlier charge against Mr. Roof. The charge, for drug possession, is a misdemeanor, not a felony.
match_headline: Dylann Roof, Suspect in Charleston Shooting, Flew the Flags of White Power

text: An article on June 17 about the use of antibiotics to treat appendicitis misidentified the specialty of Dr. Reginald H. Fitz, who in 1886 investigated why people die from pelvic infections. He was a pathologist, not a surgeon.
match_headline: Antibiotics Are Effective in Appendicitis, Study Says

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about efforts by the bus drivers’ union, Transport Workers Union Local 100, to amend a New York City traffic law described one aspect of the law incorrectly. Drivers who fail to yield can face misdemeanor charges if a cyclist or pedestrian with the right of way is injured; the victim does not have to be seriously injured for the law to apply.
match_headline: Union Pushing to Amend Traffic Law for Bus Drivers

text: Because of an editing error, a picture credit in some editions on Thursday with an article about the arrest of a corrections officer over his role in two inmates’ escape from the Clinton Correctional Facility misidentified the photographer. The picture, of a line of law enforcement officials marching through a field, was taken by Scott Olson/Getty Images, not by Nancie Battaglia for The New York Times.
match_headline: 2nd Prison Worker Is Charged as Search for Escaped Killers in New York Continues

text: An article on Tuesday about a proposed overtime rule change announced by President Obama misidentified which workers would be covered. The change would affect salaried workers earning below $50,440 a year, not hourly workers. The article also overstated plans to adjust the wage threshold over time. Adjustments to the $50,440 figure have yet to be determined; it is not necessarily the case that the wage threshold would be indexed to some measure of inflation.
match_headline: Obama Making Millions More Americans Eligible for Overtime

text: An article on Monday about the Asian markets’ reaction to the Greek debt crisis misstated, in some editions, the day China’s stock markets rose after an interest-rate cut. The markets in China rose 2.4 percent in early trading on Monday morning there, not on Saturday morning. (The two markets in mainland China are closed on Saturdays. By midday Monday, shares were down sharply.)
match_headline: Asia Markets Slide on Fears About Greece; China Extends Tumble

text: An article on June 15 about Brazil’s 2-1 victory over Peru in its opening match in the Copa América soccer tournament misstated, in some copies, the surname of the player who scored Peru’s goal in the second minute. He is Christian Cueva, not Cueza.
match_headline: Brazil Absorbs an Early and Familiar Shock, Then Rewrites the Script

text: A report in the Observatory column on June 16 about the way in which a banded mongoose manages to avoid mating with its nearest relatives misstated part of the name of the journal that published the research. It is Molecular Ecology, not Molecular Biology.
match_headline: Banded Mongooses and Careful Sex

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the author and television commentator Ben Wattenberg omitted several survivors. Besides his wife and four children, Mr. Wattenberg is survived by a sister, the actress Rebecca Schull, and four grandchildren.
match_headline: Ben Wattenberg, Neoconservative Author and PBS Host, Is Dead at 81

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about the chess grandmaster Walter Shawn Browne referred incorrectly to his siblings. He had two brothers and a sister and was thus the oldest of four children, not the oldest of four boys.
match_headline: Walter Shawn Browne, Fast-Moving Chess Grandmaster, Dies at 66

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Thursday with an article about the effect that faltering relations between Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo and Mayor Bill de Blasio had on a relatively weak legislative session described the photograph incorrectly and misstated the month it was taken. Mr. Cuomo was shown in December, not in March, standing alone in front of a set of microphones, not alongside his spokeswoman Melissa DeRosa. And the credit misidentified the photographer. The picture was taken for The New York Times by Kirsten Luce, not by Nathaniel Brooks.
match_headline: Cuomo and de Blasio’s Feud Is a Factor in an Anemic Legislative Session

text: A chart on Wednesday with the Economic Scene column, about carbon emissions, was published in error in some editions. The chart was about Puerto Rico’s debt, the subject of another article in Business Day. A chart about carbon emissions that should have appeared with the Economic Scene column was omitted; it can be found at nytimes.com/business.
match_headline: The Bonds That Broke Puerto Rico

text: An article on Friday about a proposal by a group of researchers that could double the capacity of fiber-optic circuits misstated how often the data carried on laser beams needs to be amplified and regenerated. Modern long-haul fiber networks can go thousands of kilometers without regeneration, not about every 60 miles.
match_headline: An Advance May Double the Capabilities of Fiber Optics

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the Supreme Court’s refusal to hear an appeal of a copyright decision against Google misstated part of the name of the federal appeals court that had reversed a lower court’s decision in a lawsuit originally filed by Oracle. It is the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, not for the Ninth District (The federal appellate system consists of circuits, not districts; the lower federal courts are the district courts).
match_headline: Supreme Court Declines to Hear Appeal in Google-Oracle Copyright Fight

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the United States’ 1-0 victory over China at the Women’s World Cup misspelled the given name of one of the American soccer players who started in place of a suspended teammate. She is Kelley O’Hara, not Kelly.
match_headline: Women’s World Cup: United States Defeats China With a Flick of the Head and a Flip of the Mood

text: An article on Saturday about the National Hockey League draft misstated the position played by Milan Lucic, who was traded to the Los Angeles Kings from the Boston Bruins. He is a forward, not a defenseman.
match_headline: No Shock: Connor McDavid and Jack Eichel Lead N.H.L. Draft

text: An article last Thursday about the Fragrance Foundation Awards misidentified the people who presented an award to J’Adore. It was given by Kellan Lutz and Emma Heming Willis, not by Kendall Jenner. And the article misstated the timing of a performance by Bryan Adams. He performed near the end of the ceremony, not at the end.
match_headline: The Oscars of Fragrance: The Perfumed Envelope, Please

text: An article on June 16 about the seizure of most of the Syrian town of Tal Abyad from Islamic State fighters by a coalition of Kurdish militias and Arab rebels misstated the name of the main Kurdish militias fighting in the area. They are called the People’s Protection Units — not the Democratic Union Party, known as the P.Y.D. (The units are the armed wing of the P.Y.D.)
match_headline: Kurds and Syrian Rebels Storm ISIS-Held Border Town

text: An article on Wednesday about the efforts of the College of the Atlantic in Maine to examine solutions to climate change misstated, in some copies, the month that students reported that two fuses may have been blown when they analyzed energy use of refrigerators at a local store. The students had reported the possible problem in May, not in June.
match_headline: A College in Maine That Tackles Climate Change, One Class at a Time

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with the Books of The Times review, about “Being Nixon: A Man Divided” by Evan Thomas, misidentified the city where Richard M. Nixon is shown in a ticker-tape parade in 1968. He was in Chicago, not in New York.
match_headline: Review: Evan Thomas’s ‘Being Nixon: A Man Divided,’ a Glossy Biography

text: An obituary on Thursday about Nicholas Winton, a Briton who rescued hundreds of children from Nazi-occupied Czechoslovakia, referred incorrectly to the honor bestowed on him in 1983. He was made a member of the Order of the British Empire; he did not “receive” the Order of the British Empire. The error also appeared in an obituary on May 14, 2014, about the British planetary scientist Colin Pillinger and in an article on May 19, 2014, about the death of Louise Wilson, one of the world’s pre-eminent instructors of fashion design.
match_headline: Nicholas Winton, Rescuer of 669 Children From Holocaust, Dies at 106

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a hearing before the New York City Council on legislation that would temporarily freeze the issuing of for-hire vehicle licenses during a traffic congestion study misidentified the borough represented by Councilman Stephen Levin, one of the legislation’s sponsors. His district is in Brooklyn, not Manhattan.
match_headline: Uber Says Proposed Freeze on Licenses in New York City Would Limit Competition

text: An article last Saturday about the history of Great Neck South High School’s mascot, the Rebels, misidentified the flag originally used as part of the Long Island school’s logo, as well as on the General Lee in “The Dukes of Hazzard.” It was the Confederate battle flag, not the original stars-and-bars flag of the Confederacy.
match_headline: Long Island High School Alumni Recall Connection to the Confederate Flag

text: Because of an editing error, the On College Basketball column last Saturday, about the declining influence of college basketball on the N.B.A., misstated the number of Kentucky players selected in the N.B.A. draft. It was six — not four, which was the number of Kentucky players taken in the first round.
match_headline: Road to N.B.A. Is Taking Detour Around College

text: An article on Tuesday about Mets pitcher Steven Matz’s success as a batter in his major league debut misstated the playing status of Jason Marquis, who is the career leader in runs batted in among pitchers who have batted this year. He was released by the Cincinnati Reds in June; he is not “hanging on” with them.
match_headline: Beyond the Mets’ Steven Matz: Other Pitchers With Big R.B.I. Games

text: An obituary on June 25 about the artist Miriam Schapiro misstated the year that she and Judy Chicago established the Feminist Art Program at the California Institute of the Arts. It was 1971, not 1970.
match_headline: Miriam Schapiro, 91, a Feminist Artist Who Harnessed Craft and Pattern, Dies

text: An article last Sunday about a young American woman whose online conversations with members of the Islamic State and others believed to be linked to the group illustrate the intense recruitment tactics that ISIS uses on Westerners mistranslated, in some copies, the Arabic word kufr. It means disbelief, not infidel. (Kaffir means disbeliever, or infidel.) Because of an editing error, a reporting credit misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a contributor who reported from London. She is Kimiko de Freytas-Tamura, not Feytas-Tamura.
match_headline: ISIS and the Lonely Young American

text: An article last Sunday about a biography by Arthur Browne of New York City’s first black police officer, Samuel J. Battle, erroneously attributed a distinction to the blackout that Mr. Browne covered in 1977, early in his reporting career. Though it was a major blackout, it was not New York’s first such blackout. (The first major one was in 1965.)
match_headline: The Story of New York’s First Black Police Officer, Told With the Help of Langston Hughes

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about the funeral service for the jazz musician Ornette Coleman misspelled part of the name of a group that Mr. Coleman played with several times in his career. It is the Master Musicians of Jajouka (not Joujouka).
match_headline: Remembering What Made Ornette Coleman a Jazz Visionary

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary last Sunday about the musician, arranger and educator Harold Battiste misstated his contribution to Ike and Tina Turner’s record “River Deep, Mountain High.” He was among the musicians on the record; he did not write the arrangement, which was by Jack Nitzsche.
match_headline: Harold Battiste, Musician, Mentor and Arranger, Dies at 83

text: An article last Sunday about stargazing in the Elqui Valley in Chile described one part of a telescope at the Pangue Observatory incorrectly. It is the mirror of the telescope that is 25 inches, not the lens. (Modern reflecting telescopes do not have lenses.)
match_headline: In Chile’s Elqui Valley, Intergalactic Sightseeing Is the Star

text: An article last Sunday about visiting food spots in Manhattan featured on “Seinfeld” misstated the cost of two hot dogs and a drink at Gray’s Papaya. It is now $5.95, not “less than $5.”
match_headline: A Food Tour of Seinfeld’s New York

text: A picture last Sunday with an article about the history of the Empty Quarter in California was published in error. The buildings shown near Tule Lake are farmworker housing, not historic World War II-era barracks from the time of Japanese-American incarceration.
match_headline: Exploring Tule Lake, an Austere Land With a Complex History

text: An article on June 14 about Sky, a new rental building at 605 West 42nd Street, using information from the developer, misstated the number of floors. The building has 62 floors, according to city records, not 71 as the developer initially said. (The company now says the building has 69 stories; it arrives at that figure by counting extra height on some floors.)
match_headline: A New Manhattan Rental Designed to Feel Like a Resort

text: An article last Sunday about the photographer Sarah Charlesworth and her friendship with the artists Cindy Sherman and Laurie Simmons misstated the name of the Connecticut town where Ms. Charlesworth lived. It was Falls Village, not Falls River.
match_headline: Recalling Sarah Charlesworth’s Photographs

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the ways that YouTube stars are making the jump to Hollywood reversed the identifications of the two men who make up the comic duo Smosh, who have a movie coming out. Anthony Padilla is on the left outside YouTube’s studios in Los Angeles, and Ian Hecox is on the right. And another picture caption with the article reversed the identifications of the two actresses appearing in the movie “Bad Night.” Lauren Elizabeth Luthringshausen is on the right, and Jenn McAllister on the left.
match_headline: Can 20 Million YouTube Fans Make ‘Smosh: The Movie’ a Hit?

text: An article last Sunday about Yoko Ono’s early recordings misidentified the instrument that Ornette Coleman played on the Plastic Ono Band tune “AOS.” He played trumpet, not saxophone.
match_headline: Hearing Yoko Ono All Over Again

text: A review on June 21 about “The Prime of Life: A History of Modern Adulthood,” by Steven Mintz, in summarizing some of the book’s contents, included its incomplete account of the name of the Log Cabin Republicans, a political group that works in support of gay rights. While various reports since the group’s founding in 1970 have suggested the name involves a reference to Abraham Lincoln’s relationship with his friend and roommate Joshua Speed, long rumored to be sexual, current officers of the group say the name was chosen merely to reflect Lincoln’s ideals of liberty, equality and inclusion and has nothing to do with his and Speed’s friendship.
ref_headline: The Prime of Life: A History of Modern Adulthood,
match_headline: ‘The Prime of Life,’ by Steven Mintz

text: A picture credit on June 21 with a review of “The Diver’s Clothes Lie Empty,” by Vendela Vida, misidentified the photographer who took the author’s picture. She is Chloe Aftel, not Annabel Mehran.
match_headline: ‘The Diver’s Clothes Lie Empty,’ by Vendela Vida

text: A map on June 7 showing electronic waste sites around the world erroneously included one location in Vietnam. A rural village there, Dong Mai, specializes in recycling used lead-acid batteries from cars, motorbikes and other vehicles, but it is not an e-waste site for consumer electronic devices.
match_headline: Gas Station Explosion in Ghana’s Capital Kills Around 100

text: A picture caption last Monday with the continuation of an article about the gay pride parades in New York and San Francisco omitted part of the surname of a man shown kissing his partner behind strings of lights at the Stonewall Inn. The man at the right is Jordan Siegel-Traxler, not just Siegel.
match_headline: Jubilant Marchers at Gay Pride Parades Celebrate Supreme Court Ruling

text: An article last Monday about the Yard Goats, Hartford’s new minor league baseball team, erroneously attributed a distinction to the organization. The Wolf Pack, a farm team for the New York Rangers — not the Yard Goats — is the city’s first professional team since the Hartford Whalers departed after the 1996-97 season. (The Wolf Pack has been in Hartford since the 1997-98 season.)
match_headline: Hartford Yard Goats? The Name Isn’t a Hit Yet

text: An article last Monday about the Comic-Con International convention misstated the number of times it has been held. This year’s will be the 46th installment of the event, not the 45th. The error was repeated in a subheading.
match_headline: Comic-Con, Defending Fantasy Culture and, Now, Its Brand

text: An article on Tuesday about a scientific ethical divide between China and the West misspelled, in one instance, the surname of a member of the National Medical Ethical Committee. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she is Zhai Xiaomei, not Zhao.
match_headline: A Scientific Ethical Divide Between China and West

text: An article on June 2 about the declining standard of living in the Gaza Strip, where residents are losing hope that global powers will intervene to rebuild the enclave after last summer’s 50-day war with Israel, omitted the attribution for a statement that Gaza’s unemployment rate, at 44 percent, is the highest in the world. The source for that statement is the World Bank. (Other sources, like the C.I.A. World Factbook, list higher rates in other countries, particularly in Africa. Macroeconomic statistics like these are frequently revised, so agencies that track them can have varying numbers.) This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Gazans’ Hopes for Rebuilding After War Give Way to Deeper Despair

text: An article on Friday about Nevada ranchers whose cattle graze illegally on federal lands misidentified the city where The Elko Daily Free Press, which printed an obituary of a leader of a march to protest federal land management policy, originates. It is Elko, Nev. — not Battle Mountain View, Nev.
match_headline: Drought Pushes Nevada Ranchers to Take On Washington

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about plans by ComiXology to expand its digital library misidentified the war that is the backdrop of the new series “The Curse of the Wendigo,” in which opposing soldiers must temporarily unite against an evil creature. It is World War I, not World War II.
match_headline: ComiXology Expands Digital Library With French Titles

text: An article on Monday about the film “Tangerine,” which was shot on an iPhone, omitted a writer of the film. Besides Sean Baker, the director, Chris Bergoch also wrote it. The article also misspelled the name of the Steadicam hand-held support used to stabilize shots. It is the Smoothee, not Smoothie.
match_headline: Sean Baker Talks ‘Tangerine,’ and Making a Movie With an iPhone

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about two writers who collaborated on a novel inspired by the experience of their friend Katherine Russell Rich referred incorrectly to the role they played in writing the book, “The Hand That Feeds You.” The two writers, Amy Hempel and Jill Ciment, wrote the entire novel, not most of it.
match_headline: ‘The Hand That Feeds You,’ a Thriller Written as an Act of Love for Its Originator

text: An article on Friday about the composer Danny Elfman and a series of concerts featuring the music he wrote for films by Tim Burton misidentified the site of one concert. It was at the Nokia Theater in Los Angeles, not at the Hollywood Bowl.
match_headline: Danny Elfman Brings Music From Tim Burton’s Films to Lincoln Center

text: An obituary in some copies on Sunday about Boyd K. Packer, a Mormon Church leader, referred incorrectly to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, of which Mr. Packer was the president. It is the second-highest government body of the Mormon Church, not the highest. (The church’s pre-eminent governing body is the First Presidency, which consists of the church’s president and his two counselors.)
match_headline: Boyd K. Packer, Advocate of Conservative Mormonism, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Friday about the architect Donald Wexler misidentified the company that built the steel houses he designed in Palm Springs. They were built by the Alexander Construction Company, not by Anderson Homes.
match_headline: Donald Wexler, Architect Who Gave Shape to Palm Springs, Dies at 89

text: An article on Saturday about Gill Hicks, a survivor of the 2005 London subway and bus bombings who runs an organization dedicated to countering extremism and building peace, misspelled the given name of one of the four suicide bombers and referred incorrectly to the group. Germaine Lindsay, not Jermaine, was the bomber at the King’s Cross subway station. And although all four bombers were raised in Britain, only three were born there; Mr. Lindsay was born in Jamaica and moved to Britain as a child.
match_headline: Survivor of ’05 London Subway Attack Is on Antiterror Mission

text: An article on June 25 about preparations by the Palestinians to submit what they called evidence of Israeli war crimes to the International Criminal Court misidentified the position that Mark Ellis holds with the International Bar Association. He is the group’s executive director, not its president. (David W. Rivkin is the president.)
match_headline: Palestinians to Seek War Crimes Charges Against Israel at Hague Court

text: A picture on Tuesday with an article about the mystery behind the theft of a historical marker in Johnsburg, N.Y., honoring the Civil War photographer Mathew B. Brady was published in error. The photograph, “A Burial Party, Cold Spring, Virginia,” was taken by John Reekie and published by Alexander Gardner. It was not from the Brady studio.
ref_headline: A Burial Party, Cold Spring, Virginia,
match_headline: Adirondack Town Mystery: Who Stole Marker for a Civil War Photographer?

text: An article in the Personal Finance pages on Saturday about insurance coverage for rental cars misstated the limitations of coverage for a rental car from a renter’s own auto insurance policy. While dropping certain insurance categories, such as collision coverage, on a personal policy may leave a rental car uninsured for those categories in some states, that is not the case for all states. (In New York, for example, coverage for short-term rentals is included in compulsory auto liability policies, even if the renter does not carry optional collision coverage on a personal policy.)
match_headline: Check Insurance Coverage When Renting a Car

text: An article on Saturday about results at Wimbledon misstated, in some copies, the score of the final set in two tennis matches on Friday. Nick Kyrgios defeated Milos Raonic, 5-7, 7-5, 7-6 (3), 6-3 — not 3-6. And CoCo Vandeweghe defeated Samantha Stosur, 6-2, 6-0 — not 6-2, 6-2.
match_headline: More Gains at Wimbledon for Americans on a Day With Some Upsets

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about festivals where some orchestra musicians play in the summer misidentified the state in which the Lake Tahoe SummerFest is held. It is Nevada, not California.
match_headline: Orchestra Musicians Head Off to Summer Camp

text: A picture in the Listings pages on Friday with an entry about musical events at the Stone, in Manhattan, was published in error. It showed the guitarist Mark Stewart — not the guitarist Gyan Riley, who is performing at the Stone this week.
match_headline: Classical & Opera Listings for July 3-9

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the movie producer and former concert promoter Jerry Weintraub misstated the year he began working with Frank Sinatra. It was 1972, not 1968.
match_headline: Jerry Weintraub, a Force in Film and Music, Dies at 77

text: Because of an editing error, a picture credit in some copies on Wednesday with an article about congressional efforts to dismantle President Obama’s policies through spending bills misidentified the photographer. The picture, of the president in the Oval Office, was taken by Evan Vucci for The Associated Press, not by Stephen Crowley of The New York Times.
match_headline: Republicans Aim to Hamper Obama’s Policies With Spending Bills

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the sentencing of Bernhard Laufer, a Queens resident who threatened a Muslim man, omitted part of the sentence he was given. Besides being sentenced to six months of home confinement and three years of supervised release, he was also sentenced to time already served, 13 months.
match_headline: Man Who Threatened Muslim Is Sentenced to 13 Months

text: A listing in the Transactions column in the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about a recent sale at 385 Bayview Avenue, using information from the broker’s publicist, described the location incorrectly in some editions. It is in Long Island, not Manhattan.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Transactions

text: An article on Tuesday about the lack of black elected prosecutors across the nation, using information from a study by the Women Donors Network, misstated the number of states that the study said did not have elected prosecutors. It is four, not three. The article, using additional information from the study, misstated the number of states that have exclusively white elected prosecutors. It is 13 — not 15, as the article initially said, or 14, as the study’s authors contend. (The study counts Connecticut as the 14th state, but the state’s attorney general exercises only civil jurisdiction and therefore is not considered to be a prosecutor.)
match_headline: A Study Documents the Paucity of Black Elected Prosecutors: Zero in Most States

text: An article on Thursday about criticism of San Francisco’s immigration policies after a Mexican felon who had been deported five times was charged with a murder on the city’s waterfront misstated the given name of the San Francisco mayor. He is Edwin M. Lee, not Edward.
match_headline: After Killing Tied to Deported Felon, San Francisco Mayor Mulls Policy Shift

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the opening of a trial in which two men are accused in the fatal shooting of a gang member’s 1-year-old son in Brooklyn in 2013 misstated, in some editions, the given name of a member of a separate gang who was shot to death on Tuesday in the Bronx as he held his 1-year-old daughter. He was Allen McQueen, not Alexander.
match_headline: Mother Recalls Last Breath of Slain Boy, 1, as Trial Begins

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the baseball roundup on Monday about the Kansas City Royals’ 3-2 victory over the Minnesota Twins misidentified, in some editions, the player who ripped a pitch down the right-field line to score Lorenzo Cain for the Royals. The hit was by Eric Hosmer — not Aaron Thompson, who was the Twins’ pitcher on the play.
match_headline: Near Citi Field, Plans for Willets West Are Ruled Illegal

text: An article on Monday about Gisela Mandl, who has gone biking, running and swimming every day at 6:30 a.m. for the past 30 years, referred incorrectly to part of her job. She coordinates schedules with businesses that deal with the Del Vecchio family — not with Brooks Brothers, which is owned by the family.
match_headline: On the Trail, Every Day for 30 Years

text: An article on Monday about CoCo Vandeweghe and Denis Kudla, American tennis players who made the second week at Wimbledon for the first time, misstated the way Kudla benefited from the withdrawal of fifth-seeded Kei Nishikori. Nishikori might have been Kudla’s third-round opponent if he had not pulled out of the tournament with a calf injury during the second round; he was not Kudla’s scheduled first-round opponent.
match_headline: A $530 Motivational Tool That Helped Turn CoCo Vandeweghe Around

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Garbiñe Muguruza’s becoming the first Spanish woman to reach the Wimbledon semifinals since 1997 misstated the day Conchita Martinez, a former Spanish player who also had success at Wimbledon, was named the country’s Davis Cup captain. It was Sunday, not Monday.
match_headline: Garbiñe Muguruza Is Excelling on, of All Things, Grass

text: An article on Tuesday about the discovery of Pluto by Clyde W. Tombaugh misidentified the name of one of the schools at which Tombaugh later taught physics. It is New Mexico State University, not the University of New Mexico.
match_headline: March 30, 1930: Pluto Is Discovered

text: An article on July 2 about Europe’s paralysis and mixed messages in handling the Greek debt crisis referred incorrectly to the members of the Eurogroup, which would have to resume negotiations on a new bailout deal. The Eurogroup consists of the finance ministers — not the foreign ministers — of countries that use the euro.
match_headline: In Greek Debt Crisis, Mixed Messages and No Progress

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the approval of a $4.48 million settlement from the Pine Bush Central School District over the anti-Semitic bullying of five students misstated the way in which the settlement money will be distributed to the students. It will be paid directly to three of the students who are over 18 and will be held in trust for the remaining two until their 20s. The money will not be held in trust for all of the students.
match_headline: Settlement Over Anti-Semitic Bullying at Pine Bush Central Schools Is Approved

text: An article on Friday about accusations that Todd West, 22, of Elizabeth, N.J., killed seven people in seven weeks misstated, in one instance and in some copies, the day that the authorities believe he killed three people in Pennsylvania. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it was Sunday, not last Saturday. The article also misspelled the middle name of one of those three victims. He was Trevor Davante Gray, not Davanta.
match_headline: New Jersey Man Charged With Killing 7 People Over 2 Months

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in the baseball roundup in some copies on Thursday about the Yankees’ 5-4 victory over the Oakland Athletics misstated the significance of C.C. Sabathia’s win. It was his first victory in a month, not his first victory of the season.
match_headline: Alex Rodriguez Is Passed Over for American League All-Star Bench

text: An article on Wednesday about the struggles of steel-pan bands in Brooklyn to find rehearsal space in empty lots as the borough has gentrified, using information from the leader of the Metro Steel Orchestra Youth & Culture band, misstated the title of a song the band plays. It is “Cloud Nine,” not “Cloud Nine Lyrikal.” (Lyrikal is a songwriter and performer who wrote the song with Nkosi Blackburne and has performed it.)
match_headline: Steel-Pan Bands in Brooklyn Struggle to Find Rehearsal Space

text: An article on Friday about the reopening of Sagamore Hill, Theodore Roosevelt’s home on Long Island, referred incorrectly to Roosevelt’s son Archie, whose grandson, Tweed Roosevelt, is to speak at a ceremony on Sunday. Archie was Theodore Roosevelt’s second-youngest child, not his youngest.
match_headline: Theodore Roosevelt’s Sagamore Hill Home Cries ‘Bully!’

text: An entry in the Spare Times for Children listings in some editions on Friday about the “Soar With Reading” event held at the New York Aquarium on Friday rendered incorrectly the name of a sponsor. It is JetBlue Airways, not Jet Blue.
match_headline: Spare Times for Children for July 10-16

text: A picture caption on July 3 with a film review of the documentary “Stray Dog,” using information from a publicist, misidentified the people shown with Ron Hall, the subject of the film. Mr. Hall is shown with his great-grandson and his granddaughter, Robin — not with his grandson and his daughter, Cristy.
match_headline: Review: ‘Stray Dog’ Documents a Complex Veteran

text: An article last Sunday about a 19-year-old who could be on a sex offender registry for life after having sex with an under-age girl misstated the name of the Michigan city where they had sex and referred incorrectly to the court where the girl and others appealed for leniency on his behalf. The city is Niles, not Niles City, and the court is Berrien County District Court in Michigan, not a “Federal District Court.”
match_headline: Teenager’s Jailing Brings a Call to Fix Sex Offender Registries

text: An article last Sunday about financial struggles at the National Cathedral in Washington misstated some of the actions of the Very Rev. Samuel T. Lloyd III when he took over the deanship of the cathedral in 2005. While he did invest millions in new programs and staff in an effort to build the cathedral’s first permanent congregation, he did not spend millions on new furniture for the cathedral congregation and a renovation of the dean’s residence nearby. The article also referred incorrectly to the location of the cathedral. It is built on one of Washington’s highest hills, but not on the highest. (The highest hill in the city is in Fort Reno Park.)
match_headline: National Cathedral’s Repair Work: Finials, Finance and Faith

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Mary McBride Band, which has made a specialty of playing in places of conflict and calamity, misidentified the guitarist who played with the band at a concert at Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan. He is Paul Carbonara, not John Kengla. The article also misstated the year of that concert. It was in 2012, not 2013.
match_headline: ‘Home Tours’ Take Mary McBride Band to Zones of Conflict and Calamity

text: Because of an editing error, the Neighborhood Joint column in some editions last Sunday, about Chinatown Ice Cream Factory, misidentified the animal associated with the Chinese Zodiac in 1977, the year the store opened. It was the Year of the Snake, not the Year of the Rat.
match_headline: Chinatown Ice Cream Factory, Where a Scoop of Durian Is Plain Vanilla

text: An article last Sunday about Jill Ellis, the coach of the United States women’s soccer team, misstated, in some editions, the position where Julie Johnston replaced Christie Rampone. She played central defense, not central midfield.
match_headline: Women’s World Cup Final: Jill Ellis, a Serene and Innovative Tactician, Leads the U.S.

text: A review on June 21 about “The Festival of Insignificance,” by Milan Kundera, referred incorrectly to the man whom Kundera was accused, in 2008, of denouncing to the Communist authorities in Czechoslovakia in 1950 (an accusation Kundera has vehemently denied). The man was not “one of his friends.”
match_headline: ‘The Festival of Insignificance,’ by Milan Kundera

text: Because of an editing error, a review on June 28 about “Max Beckmann: The Still Lifes,” edited by Karin Schick and Hubertus Gassner, misstated the era in which a number of “quiet, conventional canvases” included in the book were painted. It was before World War I, not before World War II.
match_headline: ‘New Objectivity’ and ‘Max Beckmann: The Still Lifes’

text: An article on June 28 about microbiota and the brain described incorrectly the affiliation of Elaine Hsiao, an author of a study published in the journal Cell that linked bacteria to behavioral changes. At the time, she was a graduate student in the lab of Paul Patterson, another author of the study, not in the lab of Sarkis Mazmanian.
match_headline: Can the Bacteria in Your Gut Explain Your Mood?

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the Havana Biennial translated incorrectly the phrase Yo También Exijo, which is the name of a Facebook page maintained by a sister of the artist Tania Bruguera. It means “I also demand,” not “I still exist.”
match_headline: Havana’s Vital Biennial Was Trumped by a Stifled Voice

text: An article last Sunday about pipe organs in New York misstated the name of one of the churches mentioned. It is St. Peter’s Lutheran Church, not St. Michael’s Lutheran Church. The article also referred incorrectly to a reference book about music that was cited. It is The Grove Dictionary of Musical Instruments, not The New Grove Encyclopedia Musical Instruments.
match_headline: On the Organ Trail in Manhattan

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the connection between Greeks’ rejection of the latest European loan deal in a national referendum and their historical and cultural strain of defiance referred incorrectly to the occupation of Greece by Axis powers during World War II, which was resisted fiercely by the Greeks. The occupation of Greece was complete in June 1941, when the island of Crete was captured — not April.
match_headline: Greek ‘No’ May Have Its Roots in Heroic Myths and Real Resistance

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about congregants who are trying to prevent the closure of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini Church in Scituate, Mass., misidentified the event at which Pamela Nichols, a flutist, was the musical accompanist. It was a Sunday service conducted by parishioners, not a Mass.
match_headline: Catholics Defy Boston Archdiocese With 11-Year Vigil to Keep Church

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the development of computer chips with much higher capacity misspelled the surname of an IBM scientist shown in a clean room in Albany, N.Y. He is Bala Haran, not Haranand.
match_headline: IBM Discloses Working Version of a Much Higher-Capacity Chip

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the men’s quarterfinals at Wimbledon misidentified the court Richard Gasquet and Stan Wawrinka played on. It was No. 1 Court, not Centre Court.
match_headline: Wimbledon 2015: Richard Gasquet Crashes a Party of Three Stars

text: A picture caption on Sunday with the continuation of an article about reaction to Harper Lee’s newly published novel, “Go Set a Watchman,” misstated, in some copies, the name of the actor who played Tom Robinson in “To Kill a Mockingbird.” He was Brock Peters, not Peterson.
match_headline: While Some Are Shocked by ‘Go Set a Watchman,’ Others Find Nuance in a Bigoted Atticus Finch

text: An article on Wednesday about a warning from leading security technologists that granting American and British governments special access to encrypted communications would put the world’s most confidential data and critical infrastructure in danger described incorrectly a technical flaw in an effort by the Clinton administration to read encrypted communications. The flaw would have allowed anyone with technical expertise to encode the encrypted communications so that even the government could not read it, not allow anyone with technical expertise access to the encrypted communications.
match_headline: Security Experts Oppose Government Access to Encrypted Communication

text: An article on Sunday about a new federal program designed to ferret out terrorists working for government-backed nonprofit organizations referred incorrectly to the status of the program. It will begin on July 27; it did not start on June 27.
match_headline: U.S. Screening on Foreign Projects Roils Aid Groups

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the Republican presidential candidate Donald J. Trump, whose comments on immigration prompted a huge backlash, referred incorrectly to a 2013 ruling by a federal judge against Sheriff Joe Arpaio of Maricopa County, Ariz. The judge issued a civil ruling that Sheriff Arpaio violated the constitutional rights of Latinos by targeting them during raids and traffic stops; Sheriff Arpaio’s tactics did not draw a “federal conviction.”
match_headline: Donald Trump Defiantly Rallies a New ‘Silent Majority’ in a Visit to Arizona

text: An article on Monday about an exhibition in Paris on the architect known as Le Corbusier, which has been criticized for glossing over his involvement with far-right elements in France, referred incorrectly to Zaha Hadid, another architect, in noting that many architects work with “unpleasant regimes.” It cited Ms. Hadid’s having come under fire “after many migrant workers died” building a stadium she designed for the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, but the criticism of Ms. Hadid came before construction of the stadium began, and thus no workers had died building it.
match_headline: Le Corbusier’s Architecture and His Politics Are Revisited

text: A picture caption on Monday with a television review of the animated film “My Depression (The Up and Down and Up of It),” on HBO, omitted two directors. Besides Elizabeth Swados, David Wachtenheim and Robert Marianetti also directed the film.
ref_headline: My Depression (The Up and Down and Up of It),
match_headline: Review: ‘My Depression (The Up and Down and Up of It)’ Offers Hope to Others

text: An article on Friday about Honda’s expansion of a recall of vehicles containing potentially defective airbags made by the Takata Corporation described the propellant in Takata’s inflaters incorrectly. The compound, ammonium nitrate, is a solid, not a gas.
match_headline: Honda Recalls 4.5 Million More Vehicles Over Takata Airbags

text: An obituary on Monday about the opera singer Jon Vickers misstated, at one point, part of the name of a school in Toronto at which he delivered a graduation address in 1969. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, the school, which Mr. Vickers also attended, is the Royal Conservatory of Music, not the Royal Academy of Music. The obituary also misstated, in some copies, part of the name of the television network that broadcast a documentary about Mr. Vickers in 1974. It is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, not the Canadian Broadcast Company.
match_headline: Jon Vickers, Opera Star Known for His Raw Power and Intensity, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Saturday about the Pulitzer Prize-winning poet James Tate misstated the surname of his editor at Ecco Press. He is Daniel Halpern, not Halperin.
match_headline: James Tate, Prolific Pulitzer-Winning Poet, Dies at 71

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about an order from the Supreme Court of India directing the federal government to take over a state police investigation into a sprawling testing scandal omitted, in some editions, part of the given name of the governor of Madhya Pradesh State, who was accused of involvement in the scandal. He is Ram Naresh Yadav, not Naresh Yadav.
match_headline: India Inquiry Into Scandal Over Testing Set to Expand

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about tensions at a United Nations base in South Sudan that is sheltering 30,000 civilians from the country’s civil war and has been targeted by militia fighters misidentified the source of a statement saying that attacks on sites protecting civilians may constitute war crimes. The statement was by the United Nations, not by the United States.
match_headline: South Sudan Enemies Find Uneasy Refuge Together at a U.N. Base

text: An article on July 1 about a vow by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi of Egypt to enact new laws to speed up terrorism trials and more quickly carry out sentences, including executions, a day after a bombing killed Egypt’s top prosecutor omitted, in some copies, part of the name of a nongovernmental organization whose director called the proposed measures alarming. The organization is the Cairo Institute for Human Rights Studies, not the Cairo Institute for Human Rights.
match_headline: Egyptian President Vows Swifter Justice for Terrorists After Assassination

text: An article on Saturday about an appeals court hearing on President Obama’s plan to protect immigrants misstated an order by the federal district judge in the case, Andrew S. Hanen. He ordered the government to cancel and collect about 2,000 work cards with three-year terms that were granted after he halted the programs and to replace them with work cards with the original term of two years; he did not order the cancellation of more than 100,000 deportation deferrals with three-year terms that were granted before his injunction took effect.
match_headline: Obama Plan for Immigration Action Gets a Cold Reception at Appeals Court

text: A picture caption on May 7 with an article about public transportation in Los Angeles misidentified the train shown. The photograph, shot from a platform at Union Station, showed a Metrolink train, not the Metro Gold Line. The error was only recently called to The Times’s attention.
match_headline: In a Car-Obsessed City, Learning to Love Mass Transit

text: A report in the Inside Art column on June 19 about the reconstruction of some early Merce Cunningham dances by the Institute of Contemporary Art in Boston with the Merce Cunningham Trust referred incorrectly to Cunningham’s work at Black Mountain College in North Carolina. He taught there intermittently between 1948 and 1953, not throughout that period. And while he experimented with chance procedures in those years, he did not begin to do so while teaching there. The report also referred incorrectly to Cunningham’s solo work “Changeling.” It was at least his fifth solo involving chance, not his third.
match_headline: Long-Lost Merce Cunningham Work Is Reconstructed in Boston

text: An article on Tuesday about the damage to the credibility of Mexico’s president, Enrique Peña Nieto, caused by the prison break of the notorious drug kingpin Joaquín Guzmán Loera misstated, in some copies, the given name of Mexico’s minister of the interior, who said every element of the government was engaged in the hunt for Mr. Guzmán. He is Miguel Ángel Osorio Chong, not José Osorio Chong. And because of an editing error, a list of contributors to the article misstated, in some editions, the given name of one reporter. She is Paulina Villegas, not Patricia.
match_headline: Mexico Prison Break by ‘El Chapo’ Is a Blow to President Peña Nieto

text: Because of an editing error, an article on July 6 about Pope Francis’ arrival in Quito, Ecuador, to begin his Latin America trip misstated, in some copies, Latin America’s share of the world’s Roman Catholics. It is four out of 10, or 40 percent, not one-fourth.
match_headline: Pope Francis Lands in Ecuador to Begin South America Trip

text: An article on Wednesday about NASA’s New Horizons mission to explore Pluto and the icy region of space beyond it misspelled the name of the H.P. Lovecraft deity for which a splotchy feature on Pluto that resembles a whale was named. It is Cthulhu, not Cthulu.
match_headline: NASA’s New Horizons Spacecraft Sends Signal From Pluto to Earth

text: An article on Monday about an offer by Brooklyn Law School to repay 15 percent of tuition costs to those who have not found full-time jobs nine months after graduating gave outdated information about David P. Miranda’s position at the New York State Bar Association. He is its president, not president-elect. (He took office on June 1.) The article also misidentified the location of the Pace University School of Law. It is in White Plains, not in Manhattan.
match_headline: Brooklyn Law School Offers a Safety Net for New Students

text: An article on Tuesday about the sentencing of Joe Gibbons, who pleaded guilty to a robbery charge after stealing money from a bank and filming it as performance art, misspelled part of the bank’s name in some editions. It is Capital One Bank (not Capitol.)
match_headline: Filmmaker Joe Gibbons Gets a Year in Prison for a Robbery He Called Performance Art

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Renee Powell, one of the first female members of the Royal and Ancient Golf Club, misspelled, in some copies, the name of the city in Illinois that hosted the John Deere Classic, where Powell played a pro-am last week. It is Silvis, not Silvas.
match_headline: At St. Andrews, Renee Powell Rises Above Prejudices to Become a Pioneer

text: An article on Thursday about the reactions from relatives of American prisoners in Iran to news of this week’s nuclear agreement paraphrased incompletely from comments by Naghmeh Abedini, the wife of Saeed Abedini, one of the prisoners. While Ms. Abedini said she had never expected the release of her husband to be part of the agreement, she also expressed disappointment that the United States had not used the leverage of the negotiations to secure the release of all the prisoners before the accord was announced.
match_headline: Nuclear Pact Raises Kin’s Hopes of Freedom for 3 Held in Iran

text: An article on Wednesday about the euro’s loss of appeal, in the wake of Greece’s latest financial crisis, among those countries that are not yet partners in the common currency referred incorrectly to Sweden’s currency, the krona.
