Sweden does not use the euro, therefore the krona is not pegged to it.
match_headline: Greek Crisis Dulls Appetite for Euro in Countries Waiting to Adopt It

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Federal Reserve Chairwoman Janet L. Yellen’s testimony to the House Financial Services Committee paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Representative Scott Tipton, a Colorado Republican. He posited that the Fed was keeping rates low because of continued problems in the economy; he did not suggest that rates “should remain low.”
match_headline: Janet Yellen Warns Congress Against Adding to Fed’s Oversight

text: An article on Thursday about a Senate inquiry into labor practices in Qatar, host of the 2022 World Cup, as part of its investigation into corruption at FIFA, soccer’s international governing body, referred incorrectly in some editions to Sepp Blatter, the head of FIFA. He has announced his pending resignation, but for now remains president of the organization. He is not yet a former president of FIFA.
match_headline: Labor Scrutiny for FIFA as a World Cup Rises in the Qatar Desert

text: An article on Thursday about the purchase of the Wall Group, an agency for Hollywood stylists, by the talent agency WME-IMG misstated the timing of William Morris Endeavor’s purchase of the IMG agency, resulting in the combined agency known as WME-IMG. It was one and a half years ago, not two and a half years ago.
match_headline: WME-IMG to Acquire Wall Group, an Agency for Stylists

text: An article in the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about stand-alone GPS devices misidentified the wiring location for optional backup cameras offered by some device makers. They are wired into the backup light circuit, not the brake light circuit.
match_headline: What Stand-Alone GPS Devices Do That Smartphones Can’t

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about overachievers and underachievers during the first half of the baseball season omitted, in some copies, the name of the 22-year-old Philadelphia Phillies player who offers a sliver of hope for the struggling team. He is Maikel Franco.
match_headline: Baseball’s Over- and Underachievers at the All-Star Break

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about James S. Marcus, a former chairman of the Metropolitan Opera, misstated the date of his death. It was Sunday, July 5 — not Sunday, July 12.
match_headline: James Marcus, Opera Benefactor and Ex-Goldman Partner, Dies at 85

text: An article on Thursday about an attack on a New York City police officer in which her gun was stolen referred incorrectly to the theft of a gun that was used to kill a woman in California. It was reported stolen from a federal agent; the laborer accused of shooting the woman in California has not been charged with stealing it.
match_headline: Off-Duty New York Police Officer Robbed of Gun After Attack

text: An article on the Automobiles page on Friday about teaching drivers to let autonomous cars take over misspelled the surname of a scientist at the University of Michigan’s Transportation Research Institute and omitted his middle initial. He is Anuj K. Pradhan, not Prahan.
match_headline: Trying to Win the Public’s Trust With Autonomous Cars, at 120 M.P.H.

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with a report in the Inside Art column about plans for a Moscow branch of the State Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, Russia, described the image incorrectly. It shows a model of the planned branch, not a rendering.
match_headline: Hermitage Museum to Open a Contemporary Outpost in Moscow

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 54 this weekend about the historical facets of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s musical “Hamilton” omits one president among several who were enemies of Alexander Hamilton. Besides Thomas Jefferson, James Madison and James Monroe, John Adams was also one.
match_headline: Jackson, Hamilton and the Plan to Add a Woman on Our Currency

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about China’s nomad resettlement program, which critics say has led to alcoholism, chronic unemployment and the loss of millenniums-old herding traditions, referred incorrectly to Xinjiang, historically home to many nomads. It is a region of China, not a province. And a map with the continuation of the article mislabeled Myanmar as Thailand in some editions.
match_headline: China Fences In Its Nomads, and an Ancient Life Withers

text: An article last Sunday about challenges for Germany as it transforms to a nuclear-free energy system, starting with the decommissioning of a nuclear plant in Bavaria, misstated the price that Germans now pay for electricity, and referred imprecisely to prices a decade ago. A household of three now pays 29.13 euro cents per kilowatt-hour — not 6.17 euro cents, which is the amount of a surcharge for renewable energy. And it is that surcharge — not the total energy cost — that is about 10 times what it was a decade ago. The article also misstated the position of Hans-Josef Fell, a former lawmaker for the Green Party, toward wind farms in Bavaria. He is fighting efforts to restrict their expansion, not trying to restrict them.
match_headline: Nuclear Plant Closing Reflects Overhaul of German Energy Production

text: An article last Sunday about Margaret Erle Katz’s brief reunion with the son she gave up for adoption more than 50 years ago misidentified the street on which Louise Wise Services, the agency that handled the original case, was located. It was on East 94th Street, not East 92nd. Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the article also misidentified, in some editions, the location of a photograph of Ms. Katz and her son’s family. It was taken on the Oregon coast, not in Portland, Ore.
match_headline: A Son Given Up for Adoption Is Found After Half a Century, and Then Lost Again

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about Martina Hingis and Sania Mirza’s winning the women’s doubles title at Wimbledon referred incorrectly to the significance of Hingis’s title. It was her first Grand Slam women’s doubles title since 2002, not her first Grand Slam title since then. (She won the mixed doubles event at the Australian Open in 2006 and in 2015.)
match_headline: Martina Hingis Returns to Top of Wimbledon, With Help From a Breakthrough

text: An article on July 5 about the time the writer Robert Graves spent on the island of Majorca misstated the number of children he had with his second wife, Beryl Pritchard. They had four children, not three.
match_headline: Robert Graves Found ‘Perfect Tranquillity’ in Majorca

text: An article last Sunday about shopping in Zagreb, Croatia, described incorrectly a cocktail ring sold at the shop Sovilj. It is real gold, not faux gold.
An article last Sunday about staying at a castle in France misspelled part of the title of a movie evoked by a room in the castle. It is “The Royal Tenenbaums,” not “The Royal Tannenbaums.”
match_headline: A French Castle, Now Open to All

text: Because of an editing error, an article on July 5 about the return of fur to fashion runways rendered incorrectly the name of a coat with a coyote-trimmed hood. It is made by the company Canada Goose; it is not a Canada goose coat.
match_headline: Fur Is Back in Fashion and Debate

text: An article last Sunday about artists and entrepreneurs who are moving from Brooklyn to Detroit misstated the length of time that Dream Hampton lived in New York before moving back to her hometown, Detroit. It was 19 years, not 11.
match_headline: Last Stop on the L Train: Detroit

text: An article on June 28 about psychoanalysis and brain scanning misstated Sigmund Freud’s age in 1895. He was 39, not 41.
match_headline: Tell It About Your Mother

text: An article on July 5 about the Tamil Nadu politician Jayalalithaa referred imprecisely to her popularity as a Tamil movie star. She was the most popular Tamil movie actress of her time, not the most popular Tamil movie star of her time.
match_headline: What Happens When a State Is Run by Movie Stars?

text: An article last Sunday about the artist Todd Eberle misidentified the location of James Barron Art. The gallery, where Mr. Eberle’s art is being shown through Aug. 3, is in Kent, Conn., not in Cornwall.
match_headline: A Photographer Finds Symmetry in Gardens and Galaxies

text: An article on July 5 about the Lifetime drama “UnREAL,” which goes behind the scenes of a “Bachelor”-like show, referred incorrectly to Sarah Gertrude Shapiro’s contractual situation concerning the actual “The Bachelor.” The contract of Ms. Shapiro, a co-creator of “UnREAL,” was with Telepictures and bound her to work on any reality shows created by that company. It was not with ABC, which airs “The Bachelor,” which is a Telepictures production.
match_headline: Lifetime’s ‘UnReal’ Recycles a Producer’s Dark Experiences

text: A review last Sunday about “Ally: My Journey Across the American-Israeli Divide,” by Michael B. Oren, misstated part of the name of a political advocacy group whose representatives met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during his visit to Washington in July 2010. It is the National Jewish Democratic Council, not the National Jewish Democratic Coalition.
ref_headline: Ally: My Journey Across the American-Israeli Divide,
match_headline: Michael B. Oren’s ‘Ally: My Journey Across the American-Israeli Divide’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a congressional investigation of Planned Parenthood over the issue of fetal tissue donations misidentified, in some editions, the state represented by Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican contender for president who condemned the organization. It is Texas, not Florida.
match_headline: House Republicans to Investigate Planned Parenthood Over Fetal Tissue

text: A picture caption on July 8 with an article about a murder case in San Francisco involving a Mexican laborer, Juan Francisco Lopez-Sanchez, misidentified the woman shown. She was serving as an interpreter for Mr. Lopez-Sanchez; she is not a prosecutor.
match_headline: San Francisco Murder Case Exposes Lapses in Immigration Enforcement

text: An article in some editions last Monday about a woman’s effort to have statues of Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony erected in Central Park misidentified the nationality of the sculptor Albert Bertel Thorvaldsen, whose likeness stands there. He was Danish, not Dutch. The article also referred incorrectly to Theodore Roosevelt at the time he received a letter from Stanton shortly before her death in 1902. Though he was president, he had assumed the office after the assassination of William McKinley, in September 1901; Roosevelt was not “newly elected.” (He was elected in November 1904.)
match_headline: Fighting to Bring Women in History to Central Park

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the hip-hop mogul Russell Simmons’s criticism of Mayor Bill de Blasio of New York City described incorrectly in some copies a meeting in December at which Jay Z pressed Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo about criminal justice reform. Mr. Simmons was not at the meeting. The article also misidentified the city where the meeting was held. It was in New York, not in Albany.
match_headline: The Rising Activist Voice of Hip-Hop Mogul Russell Simmons Takes Aim at Mayor de Blasio

text: An article on Saturday about a lawsuit challenging Seattle’s new trash policy misstated the mathematical formula in the plaintiff’s lawsuit to determine whether more than 10 percent of a garbage can’s contents should have been placed in another bin. The formula is: The height of the bin and the square of the radius multiplied by Pi, and then divided by 10; it is not the radius and twice the height of the can multiplied by Pi and then divided by 10.
match_headline: Residents Sue Seattle, Saying New Trash Rules Violate Privacy

text: An article on Saturday about a ruling by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission that anti-gay bias in the workplace is illegal referred incorrectly in some editions to the partisan makeup of the commission. While the two members who dissented to the ruling are Republicans, one was nominated by a Democratic president, and the other nominated by a Republican and renominated by a Democrat; they are not both Republican appointees. The article also misidentified the office that dismissed an air traffic controller’s complaint in 2013. It is the Equal Employment Opportunity Office of the Federal Aviation Administration, not an office of the commission.
match_headline: U.S. Agency Rules for Gays in Workplace Discrimination

text: An article on Friday about the bankruptcy filing of Signal International, a maritime construction company found liable for labor abuses involving foreign workers in the United States, misstated the surname of a lawyer at the Southern Poverty Law Center, which initiated the case. He is Daniel Werner, not Warner.
match_headline: In Bankruptcy Filings, Maritime Company Says It Settled Labor Case

text: An article on Monday about the challenges of developing apps for the small screen on the Apple Watch misstated Google’s offerings for the device. Google has a news and weather app for the watch; it is not the case that it has no apps for it.
match_headline: Apple Waits as App Developers Study Who’s Buying Its Watch

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about new express bus service on 86th Street in Manhattan misstated part of the name of a street in the Bronx that also has express service. It is Fordham Road, not Fordham Avenue.
match_headline: Express Bus Service Shows Promise in New York

text: An obituary on Monday about the record producer and conductor Ettore Stratta misstated the year of Barbra Streisand’s album “Je M’Appelle Barbra,” which he produced. It was 1966, not 1970.
match_headline: Ettore Stratta, Music Producer and Conductor, Dies at 82

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about Chattanooga’s response to last week’s shooting rampage at a military facility misspelled, in some editions, the surname of one man shown leading prayers at a memorial. He is George Coffey, not Coffeey.
match_headline: Chattanooga Wears Pride Beside Its Pain After Killings

text: An article on Friday about Dylann Storm Roof, who has been charged with killing nine black parishioners in a Charleston, S.C., church, misstated the type of rifle parts found in his car trunk during an earlier encounter with the police. They were from a semiautomatic — not an automatic — rifle.
match_headline: Dylann Roof’s Past Reveals Trouble at Home and School

text: A report in the National Briefing column last Wednesday about an apology by a Republican official in Oklahoma for comments about people on food stamps reversed two words in the name of the food program. It is the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, not the Supplemental Assistance Nutrition Program.
match_headline: Your Thursday Briefing

text: A picture caption with an article on the Personal Finance pages on Saturday about business owners who give back to the communities in which their companies operate reversed the identities of the two men shown who are members of the family that founded the glass and ceramic material manufacturer Corning in Corning, N.Y. Rob Houghton is at the left and James Houghton at the right.
match_headline: When Impact Investing Stays Local

text: An article on the Personal Finance pages on July 11 about housing for older people, using information from the Aging Life Care Association, misstated the average range of fees for ALCA counseling. The national average range is $100 to $200 an hour — not $75 to $120 an hour, which is the typical range in New Mexico. (In urban areas, the fees may be significantly higher than either of those ranges.)
match_headline: Making Decisions on Elder Housing May Take a Team Effort

text: An article on Friday previewing the quarterfinals of the Gold Cup soccer tournament misstated, in some editions, the number of quarterfinalists that had secured berths for the Copa América next year. It is four, not eight.
match_headline: Surprises Abound in the Usually Predictable Gold Cup

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the Pitchfork Music Festival in Chicago, using information from a publicist, misidentified the festival at which the rapper Chief Keef last performed in Chicago in citing his influence. It was at Lollapalooza in 2012, not at the Pitchfork festival that year.
match_headline: Pitchfork Music Festival in Chicago Welcomes a Polyglot of Styles

text: An obituary last Wednesday about the artist David Aronson erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He joined the School of Fine and Applied Arts (now the College of Fine Arts) at Boston University in 1955 as the first chairman of its Division of Art (now the School of Visual Arts); it is not the case that he “founded what became the College of Fine Arts at Boston University.”
ref_headline: founded what became the College of Fine Arts at Boston University.
match_headline: David Aronson, Expressionist Artist, Dies at 91

text: An obituary last Wednesday about the songwriter Michael Masser referred imprecisely to Diana Ross’s 1973 recording of “Touch Me in the Morning,” which he wrote with Ron Miller. While it was Ms. Ross’s first Top 10 single in three years, it did not “revitalize” her career; she was nominated for an Oscar for her performance in the 1972 movie “Lady Sings the Blues.”
match_headline: Michael Masser, Composer Who Wrote Whitney Houston Hits, Dies at 74

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with the continuation of an obituary about the author E. L. Doctorow misstated, in some copies, the year of the photograph. The picture, of Mr. Doctorow at the Knickerbocker restaurant in Greenwich Village, was taken in 2000, not in 1977.
match_headline: E. L. Doctorow Dies at 84; Literary Time Traveler Stirred Past Into Fiction

text: A news analysis article on July 6 about the possibility that Greece would pay a high price after its resounding “no” vote to European austerity policies in a national referendum misstated the title of Emmanuel Macron of France, who called for creditors to resume political discussions with Greece immediately. Mr. Macron is the French economy minister, who handles economic and industrial policy — not the country’s finance minister, who oversees finance issues. (Michel Sapin is the finance minister.)
match_headline: With Greek ‘No’ Vote, Tsipras Wins a Victory That Could Carry a Steep Price

text: An article on Tuesday about plans to close the Community Bookstore in Brooklyn misidentified, in some editions, the location of a nearby Lululemon store. It is on Smith Street, not Court Street. And the article erroneously included one company on a list of new stores on Court Street. J. Crew has signed a lease for a store there, but it has not opened it yet.
match_headline: Taking Stock (for Once), Self-Styled Hoarder Makes Lucrative Deal to Close Bookstore

text: An article on Tuesday about new bank capitalization imposed by the Federal Reserve described incorrectly the institutions to which the new rules will apply. They apply to eight of the nation’s largest banks, not “solely to the nation’s largest eight banks.” (While seven are the biggest in the nation by assets, one, State Street, is not among the eight largest.)
ref_headline: solely to the nation’s largest eight banks.
match_headline: Federal Reserve Approves Capital Restraints for Big Banks

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about a plan to have murals painted on a large wall at the Pacific Park Brooklyn construction site misstated the names of two streets in Prospect Heights that form the boundary of the block on Dean Street where artists will create the murals. They will be painted on a wall between Vanderbilt Avenue and Carlton Avenue, not Vanderbilt Street and Carlton Street.
match_headline: 10 Murals in Brooklyn to Spruce Up Construction Site

text: An article on July 14 about the history of bicycling, using information from the District Department of Transportation in Washington, D.C., misstated the number of Americans who commute to work by bicycle nationwide and erroneously attributed a distinction to the bike-share program in Washington. The number of bike commuters was 0.62 percent in 2013, up from 0.38 percent in 2000, not “almost 5 percent” compared with 1 percent in 2000. And Washington’s bike-share program was one of the first in the nation, not the first.
match_headline: The Bicycle and the Ride to Modern America

text: An article on Wednesday about the arrest of Sandra Bland after a traffic stop in Texas referred incorrectly in some editions to the reason Ms. Bland got out of her car. She left the car after a trooper pointed a stun gun at her; the trooper did not drag her from the car. The error was repeated in a front-page capsule summary. The article also misstated the reason Ms. Bland was initially stopped. It was for failing to signal a lane change, not a turn.
match_headline: Sandra Bland Was Threatened With Taser, Police Video Shows

text: An article on Tuesday about Yahoo’s quarterly earnings, using information from the company, overstated what is known about the number of people who have tried Yahoo’s daily sports betting games. In the first two weeks that the daily games were offered, 1.3 million users visited all of Yahoo Sports Fantasy sites, including the daily game sites; 1.3 million is not necessarily the number who tried the daily games. (Yahoo would not release that number.)
match_headline: Yahoo Posts Loss, Despite Rise in Its Display Ad Business

text: An article on Thursday about Asian mobile game makers’ interest in expanding into the United States misstated the Japanese company Sega’s interest in Demiurge Studios of Cambridge, Mass. Sega acquired the whole studio; it did not just take a stake in Demiurge.
match_headline: Netmarble Takes Stake in SGN, Extending Asia’s Reach Into U.S. Mobile Games

text: An article and a headline in some editions on Friday about a request to the Justice Department for an investigation regarding Hillary Clinton’s personal email account while she was secretary of state misstated the nature of the request, using information from senior government officials. It addressed the potential compromise of classified information in connection with that email account. It did not specifically request an investigation into Mrs. Clinton. An article about the latest developments is on Page A1.
match_headline: Inquiry Sought in Hillary Clinton’s Use of Email

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about technology to help commuters misstated the timing of the introduction of the Bosch eBike System, which adds power to pedals, on Cannondale bicycles. Cannondale plans to introduce bikes with the system next month, not next year.
match_headline: A Panoply of Products to Improve the Daily Commute

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Yankees’ 9-3 victory over the Baltimore Orioles misstated, in some copies, the type of hit by the Yankees’ Chase Headley that drove in three runs in the first inning. As an accompanying picture caption correctly noted, it was a double, not a triple. (Headley advanced to third base on a throw home.)
match_headline: Alex Rodriguez Tumbles Into the Plate, and the Yankees Keep Rolling

text: Because of an editing error, a subheading in the baseball roundup on Friday about a game between the St. Louis Cardinals and the Kansas City Royals misidentified the winning team in some editions. As the report correctly noted, the Cardinals won, 4-3, not the Royals.
match_headline: A City for the Poor, Rich and In Between

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Antiques column on Friday about an exhibition at the University of Pennsylvania titled “Courtly Treasures: The Collection of Thomas W. Evans, Surgeon Dentist to Napoleon III” misidentified the academic position that Denis F. Kinane holds at the university. He is the dean of the school of dental medicine, not the school of medicine. The article also erroneously included one item among those on exhibit. A still-life painting by Édouard Manet that belonged to Evans can be seen only in the exhibition catalog; it is not in the show.
ref_headline: Courtly Treasures: The Collection of Thomas W. Evans, Surgeon Dentist to Napoleon III
match_headline: A Collection From Napoleon III’s Dentist, Now on View at Penn

text: An article last Sunday about the early travails of the New Horizons mission to Pluto referred incorrectly to the volcanic eruption on Jupiter’s moon Io that the spacecraft observed in 2007. Erupting volcanoes on Io were seen during earlier NASA missions; the New Horizons images were not the first. And because of an editing error, an accompanying picture caption misstated the date and location of a spin test of the spacecraft before its launching. The test shown took place in 2005 at the NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, not in 2006 at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
match_headline: The Long, Strange Trip to Pluto, and How NASA Nearly Missed It

text: An article last Sunday about a new National Security Agency cybersecurity program that reaches down into the ranks of American high school and middle school students misstated the given name of a Marymount University professor who teaches students to defend against hackers. She is Diane Murphy, not Diana.
match_headline: N.S.A. Summer Camp: More Hacking Than Hiking

text: An article last Sunday about plans to build a dune on Fire Island that would require the destruction of several oceanfront homes misstated the location of two communities affected by the proposal. Davis Park and Ocean Bay Park are in the center of Fire Island, not on the western end of it.
match_headline: Fire Island Residents to Lose Their Homes to Make Way for a Dune

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about a rally in Brooklyn at which demonstrators called for federal charges in the death of Eric Garner, who was killed by the police last year on Staten Island, misstated, in some copies, the middle initial of the New York City comptroller, who spoke to the crowd. He is Scott M. Stringer, not Scott A.
match_headline: Family Renews Calls for Civil Rights Charges a Year After Garner’s Death

text: An article last Sunday about the planned community of Sea Ranch, two and a half hours north of San Francisco, and its utopian architectural aspirations referred incompletely to the team that planned the buildings. Lawrence Halprin designed the buildings with the architecture firm MLTW; he did not design them alone.
match_headline: Utopia Rules at Sea Ranch, a Community Born of ’60s Idealism

text: An obituary last Sunday about Helen F. Holt, who led the federal government’s effort to establish and standardize modern long-term care facilities for older adults, misstated the date of her death. It was Sunday, July 12 — not July 11.
match_headline: Helen F. Holt, Who Elevated Elder Care Across the U.S., Dies at 101

text: An article last Sunday about how boxing scenes were filmed in the new movie “Southpaw” referred incorrectly to the boxer Victor Ortiz. He is still a professional fighter; he has not retired.
match_headline: Feeling the Pain and Sweat of the Ring in ‘Southpaw’

text: An article last Sunday about the thriving art scene in Brussels referred incorrectly to the artist whose photographs of chocolate making are on display in “Un-Scene III.” She is Stephanie Kiwitt, not Erika Hock.
match_headline: Brussels Making a Strong Bid for Art

text: An article last week about the North Loop neighborhood of Minneapolis gave outdated information about the Spoon and Stable restaurant. It was named a James Beard finalist for Best New Restaurant 2015; it was not simply a semifinalist.
match_headline: The Week on Instagram

text: A report on July 12 about the marriage of Nicky Hilton and James Rothschild included outdated information about Mr. Rothschild’s career. He is no longer a partner and a vice president of the Monument Capital Group, a position he left in 2012. Since then he has become the founder and chief executive of JR Cap Limited, an investment and advisory company.
match_headline: Nicky Hilton and James Rothschild: Designing a Lasting Partnership

text: An article on July 12 about religion and American law misidentified the academic affiliation of Douglas NeJaime, who was an author of a paper on religion and law. He is a professor at the School of Law at the University of California, Los Angeles, not the University of California, Irvine, where he taught at the time the paper was written.
match_headline: What Are the Limits of ‘Religious Liberty’?

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the arrest of Tareek Arnold, who had escaped after his earlier arrest on attempted murder charges, misstated the location where he fled from the police while being taken to Central Booking on June 23. It was outside the 32nd Precinct station house, not outside the 32nd Precinct.
match_headline: Shooting Suspect Who Escaped From Police Custody in Harlem Is Captured

text: An article on Thursday about the disappearance of 43 engravings by 16th-century artists from the National Library of France misstated the estimated value of the engravings. The collection is worth up to $190,000, not $4.4 million.
match_headline: Employee Held in Paris National Library Theft

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the actor, singer and political activist Theodore Bikel referred incorrectly in part to Bukovina, where Mr. Bikel’s family once lived. One of the countries of which it has historically been a part is Ukraine, not Russia.
match_headline: Theodore Bikel, Master of Versatility in Songs, Roles and Activism, Dies at 91

text: An article on Friday about the increasing importance nationwide of a campaign for raising the minimum wage erroneously attributed a distinction to Wisconsin. While it was among the states where a wage board could set a higher wage for a particular set of workers, that changed on July 12, when a state budget signed into law repealed that power. Now, only the legislature can change the state’s minimum wage.
match_headline: Push to Lift Minimum Wage Is Now Serious Business

text: An article on Saturday about the victims of the shooting at a Lafayette, La., movie theater misstated a biographical fact about one victim, Jillian Johnson. Ms. Johnson was a Louisiana native; she did not move to the state.
match_headline: Lost in Lafayette Gunfire, Two With Bright Futures

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the withdrawal of Boston as the American bid city for the 2024 Summer Olympics misstated the year of the Winter Games that has only two cities bidding to host it. It is 2022, not 2020.
match_headline: Boston’s Bid for Summer Olympics Is Terminated

text: An article on Tuesday about challenges facing Bank of America and its chief executive, Brian T. Moynihan, misstated how the $70 billion in charges for fines, settlements and penalties the bank has taken compares to the market value of U.S. Bancorp. It is nearly as much as U.S. Bancorp’s value, which is about $80 billion; it is not more than that value.
match_headline: Bank of America’s Chief is the Captain of a Ship Becalmed

text: An article on Monday about a record $105 million fine imposed on Fiat Chrysler by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration misstated when the safety agency imposed a $70 million fine on Honda. It was in January, not last year.
match_headline: Fiat Chrysler Gets Record $105 Million Fine for Safety Issues

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the W.N.B.A. star Elena Delle Donne misstated, in some copies, the given name of the league’s president. She is Laurel J. Richie, not Laure.
match_headline: Elena Delle Donne Emerges as Face of the W.N.B.A.

text: An article on Monday about the Baseball Hall of Fame induction ceremony erroneously attributed a distinction to John Smoltz, who was inducted after having Tommy John elbow surgery during his career. He is the only Hall of Fame pitcher to have the operation, not the only Hall of Famer to have it. (Paul Molitor, an infielder inducted into the Hall of Fame in 2004, also had Tommy John surgery.)
match_headline: Pedro Martinez’s Hall of Fame Delivery: Moving, With Light Touch

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the Newport Folk Festival, which paid tribute to Bob Dylan’s famous performance with an electric guitar there 50 years ago, misstated part of the title of a Dylan song that was played. It is “Rainy Day Women #12 & 35,” not “#12 and 25.” The article also misstated part of a lyric from the Dylan song “It’s All Over Now, Baby Blue,” which was also performed. It is, “Forget the dead you’ve left, they will not follow you,” not “Forget the debt you left, they will not follow you.” The article also misstated the title of a song James Taylor sang. It is “Carolina in My Mind,” not “Carolina on My Mind.”
match_headline: Newport Folk Festival Pays Tribute, With a Jolt, to Dylan and Seeger

text: A review last Wednesday about Lupulo, in Chelsea, misstated the restaurant’s practices for taking reservations. It takes some through third-party apps, and some directly, but there is no charge for reservations. They are free.
match_headline: Restaurant Review: Lupulo in Chelsea

text: Because of incorrect information provided by an interpreter, an obituary on Tuesday about Shigeko Kubota, a creator of video sculptures, misidentified one of her sisters, who survives her. She is Keiko Hossho, not Genji Kubota.
match_headline: Shigeko Kubota, a Creator of Video Sculptures, Dies at 77

text: An obituary on Tuesday about A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, India’s 11th president, referred incorrectly to the Supermarine Spitfire, a British fighter plane that he read about as a child. It was a propeller aircraft, not a jet.
match_headline: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, Ex-President Who Pushed a Nuclear India, Dies at 83

text: An article on Tuesday about changing attitudes toward obesity referred incorrectly to the percentage of Americans considered obese. It is 35 percent, not 39 percent, and the figure refers only to adults, not everyone.
match_headline: How Changing Attitudes Went Along With a Drop in Calories

text: An article last Thursday about a scholar who grew up in the United States as an undocumented immigrant misspelled the name of an online classics journal that published one of his articles. It is Eidolon, not Eidelon.
match_headline: From an ‘Undocumented’ Boyhood to a Doctorate

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the use of wearable performance and tracking systems in soccer matches, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the West Bromwich Albion player wearing a Catapult tracking device. He is Craig Gardner, not Craig Dawson.
match_headline: Today’s Soccer Gear: Shorts, Cleats, Shinguards and a GPS Unit

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a series of photographs from the archives of the Sundance Institute’s workshops (known as “labs”) reversed the identities of two people shown in a picture from 1993 with the actor John C. Reilly. The director Paul Thomas Anderson is in the center, and the actor Philip Baker Hall is on the right.
match_headline: Moments From the Sundance Institute Lab Archives

text: A listing of credits with a theater review on Wednesday about “Miss Julie,” at New York City Center, using information from the program, misstated the surname of the writer of the supertitles. (The play is performed in Russian.) She is Fay Greenbaum, not Greenberg.
match_headline: Review: ‘Miss Julie’ Resets a Celebrated Drama in Putin’s Russia

text: An article on Tuesday about Praluent, the newly approved cholesterol-lowering drug , referred incorrectly to the drug Zetia. It is a cholesterol-lowering drug, but it is not a statin. The article also misstated the amount by which statins typically lower cholesterol. It is 25 to 55 percent, not 15 to 20 percent, which is the amount for nonstatin cholesterol drugs.
match_headline: Praluent Looks Cheap to Those With Extreme Cholesterol

text: A subheading with an article on Thursday about the indictment in Cincinnati of Officer Ray Tensing in the death of a motorist referred incorrectly to the shooting. While Officer Tensing has been charged with murder, there has not yet been a legal determination that the case was murder.
match_headline: University of Cincinnati Officer Indicted in Shooting Death of Samuel Dubose

text: An article on Wednesday about a meeting planned for August by Mormon Church leaders to discuss severing ties with the Boy Scouts after a ban on gay adult leaders was lifted omitted, in some editions, the given name and affiliation of the person who described the planned meeting. He is Eric Hawkins, a church spokesman.
match_headline: Top Mormons Could Meet Soon About Leaving Scouts

text: An article on Thursday about the arrest of Adrian Jerry Gonzalez in the death of Madyson Middleton misstated the day on which a friend said he saw Mr. Gonzalez led away in handcuffs. It was Monday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Hunt for California Girl Leads to a Body, and a Neighbor, 15

text: An article on July 13 about Time Inc.’s plan to move its recipe test kitchens to Birmingham, Ala., referred incorrectly to the status of the The San Francisco Chronicle’s elaborate test kitchen, wine cellar and rooftop garden. While the kitchen is used less often, it and the wine cellar remain open. It is not the case that they have been shut down.
match_headline: Time Inc. to Move Test Kitchens to Alabama

text: An article on Thursday about the Federal Reserve’s most recent assessment of the nation’s economic prospects misstated the location of the headquarters of the investment firm Franklin Templeton, an executive of which speculated on when the Fed might begin raising interest rates. It is based in San Mateo, Calif., not New York.
match_headline: September Is Looking Likelier for Fed’s First Rate Increase

text: An article on Thursday about the Yankees staying quiet as the Major League Baseball trading deadline approaches misstated, in some copies, the time of the deadline. It is Friday at 4 p.m. Eastern, not Friday at midnight.
match_headline: Yankees and Cashman Remain Quiet as Trade Deadline Nears

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Sports Briefing column on Thursday about tennis news misstated the age of Roger Federer, who withdrew from the Rogers Cup. He is 33, not 34. (He turns 34 on Aug. 8.) Also because of an editing error, a headline with the report misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the player who defeated Yen-Hsun Lu in the Atlanta Open. As the article correctly noted, he is Vasek Pospisil, not Popisil.
match_headline: Marin Cilic Struggles to Get Back Into Zone After U.S. Open Success

text: A map on Monday with the continuation of an article about infrastructure problems along the Northeast Corridor rail lines reversed the positions of two locations in New Jersey. Iselin is north of Trenton, not south.
match_headline: Aging Infrastructure Plagues Nation’s Busiest Rail Corridor

text: An article on Wednesday about Joyce E. Mitchell’s account of how she came to help two prisoners escape an upstate prison in June misstated, in some editions, when Ms. Mitchell began carrying out errands for one of the men, Richard W. Matt. It was late 2013, not last fall.
match_headline: Prison Worker Who Aided Escape Tells of Sex, Saw Blades and Deception

text: An article on Tuesday about the shooting death of a Palestinian man, Mohammad Atta Lafi Abu Latifa, in the West Bank by Israeli security forces referred incorrectly to the shooting. It was the fourth fatal shooting by Israeli forces in the West Bank this month, not the fourth shooting over all; Palestinians have been injured in other shootings.
match_headline: Palestinian, 18, Dies While Trying to Evade Israeli Security

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about the fourth and final season of “Strike Back,” on Cinemax, misstated the date of the season’s first episode. It was Friday night, not Sunday night.
match_headline: ‘Strike Back,’ on Cinemax, Returns to Overwhelm Bad Guys Everywhere

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about “Allied in the Fight: Jews, Blacks and the Struggle for Civil Rights,” an exhibition at the Center for Jewish History in Manhattan, misstated the telephone number for more information. It is 212-294-8301.
ref_headline: Allied in the Fight: Jews, Blacks and the Struggle for Civil Rights,
match_headline: Spare Times for July 31-Aug. 6

text: An obituary on Monday about Bobbi Kristina Brown, the only child of the pop stars Whitney Houston and Bobby Brown, referred incorrectly to her education. She did not attend Edison High School in Edison Township, N.J. (Attempts to identify what schools she did attend were unsuccessful.)
match_headline: Bobbi Kristina Brown, Daughter of Whitney Houston, Dies at 22

text: A map last Sunday with an article about the growing popularity of a land-based route to Europe followed by migrants from Africa, Asia and the Middle East trying to avoid the hazards of sea crossings transposed, in some editions, the labels for two towns along the route, Subotica and Asotthalom. Subotica is in Serbia, not Hungary, and Asotthalom is in Hungary, not Serbia.
match_headline: Seeking Sanctuary, More Migrants Confront Land Route’s Perils

text: Because of an editing error, a subheading with a review in some editions last Sunday about “By the Water,” at Premiere Stages at Kean University in Union, N.J., misspelled the playwright’s given name. As the review correctly noted, she is Sharyn Rothstein, not Sharon.
match_headline: Review: In ‘By the Water,’ a Search for Calm After the Storm

text: A listing of information in some copies last Sunday with a dining review of Olio in Stamford misstated the restaurant’s address. As the review noted correctly, it is 934 Hope Street, not Spring Street.
match_headline: Restaurant Review: Olio in Stamford Offers a Stew of Global Ingredients

text: An article last Sunday about the final mountain stage of the Tour de France misspelled, in some editions, the given name of the Colombian rider who was in second place overall. He is Nairo Quintana, not Nario.
match_headline: Chris Froome Set to Win Tour de France After Penultimate Stage

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Yankees’ 8-5 victory over the Minnesota Twins misstated the combined distance of Alex Rodriguez’s three home runs, using information from the Twins that was later changed. The distance was more than 1,300 feet, not 1,298 feet.
match_headline: Alex Rodriguez’s Three Home Runs Help Yankees Rally to Stun the Twins

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about student mental health on campus misstated the suicide rate among 15- to 24-year-olds. It was 11.1 deaths per 100,000 in 2013 and 9.6 in 2007, not 11.1 percent and 9.6 percent.
match_headline: Suicide on Campus and the Pressure of Perfection

text: An obituary last Sunday about the actor George Coe misstated the name of the college he attended. It was Hofstra College, not Hofstra University, a name it adopted in 1963.
match_headline: George Coe, Actor and Director of a Bergman Parody, Dies at 86

text: An article last Sunday about Essex Crossing, a development on the Lower East Side, misidentified the agency where Faith Hope Consolo is chairwoman of the retail leasing and sales division. It is Douglas Elliman, not Prudential Douglas Elliman.
match_headline: New Mixed-Income Housing on the Lower East Side

text: An article last Sunday about Subhash Kapoor, who is awaiting trial in India on charges of theft and smuggling antiquities, referred incorrectly to the ownership of the Pierre Hotel in New York, where Mr. Kapoor put two statues on display. While it is operated by an Indian company, it is owned by an American company, not an Indian one. A chart with the article misspelled the name of the area in New Jersey where artwork being shipped to a company owned by Mr. Kapoor was taken to a warehouse in 2006 before being delivered to his Art of the Past Gallery. It is South Kearny, not South Kearney.
match_headline: The Ultimate Temple Raider?: Inside an Antiquities-Smuggling Operation

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about “The End of the Tour,” a movie about the novelist David Foster Wallace, misidentified his hometown. He was born in Ithaca, N.Y., and moved with his family six months later to Champaign, Ill. His hometown was not Bloomington, Ill. The article misstated the number of pages in his novel “Infinite Jest.” It is 1,079, not 1,029.
match_headline: Jason Segel Makes a Career U-Turn as David Foster Wallace in ‘The End of the Tour’

text: An article last Sunday about the songwriters Robert Lopez and Kristen Anderson-Lopez, whose new musical, “Up Here,” will be at the La Jolla Playhouse, referred incorrectly to La Jolla. It is a neighborhood in San Diego. It doesn’t sit outside San Diego’s city limits.
match_headline: Fresh Off ‘Frozen,’ Bobby Lopez and Kristen Anderson-Lopez Prepare a New Musical

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Erin McNamara and Henry Blechman misstated the place of residence of the groom’s parents, Rebecca P. Blechman and Dr. Peter J. Blechman. They live in Fishkill, N.Y., not Chevy Chase, Md., which is where Dr. Blechman grew up, and not Brussels, where Mrs. Blechman was born.
match_headline: Erin McNamara,  Henry Blechman

text: An article on Thursday about a new United Nations report on population trends referred incorrectly to the part of the world with the highest level of life expectancy in 2010-15. It is Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China, not all of China.
match_headline: India Will Be Most Populous Country Sooner Than Thought, U.N. Says

text: A map with an article last Monday about the planned opening of two new sections of Brooklyn Bridge Park in August misidentified the location of Pier 6, one of the new sections. It is the southernmost pier in the park, not the second-southernmost.
match_headline: Brooklyn Bridge Park Opening New Vistas

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Thursday about the Fall for Dance festival at New York City Center starting Sept. 30 misspelled the surname of the choreographer whose work “Solo” will be performed. He is Hans van Manen, not van Mansen.
match_headline: Dance This Week: Balanchine Classics, Percussive Feet and Tango

text: An article last Monday about Donald Trump’s contentious history in Scotland as a developer of golf courses misstated the previous name of Trump Turnberry, the golf resort that hosted the Women’s British Open. It was Turnberry, not Royal Turnberry.
match_headline: Donald Trump, a Figure of Contention, Hosting a Golf Major

text: An article on Sunday about the ferocious start to the fire season in the West misstated, in some editions, the amount of land in the United States that was destroyed by wildfires last year. It is 3.6 million — not billion — acres.
match_headline: Dry Days Bring Ferocious Start to Fire Season

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Donald Trump’s use of racially charged language in the years before his presidential bid described incorrectly the racial backgrounds of the defendants who became known as the Central Park Five. Four — not five — are black and one is Latino.
match_headline: Donald Trump’s Instinct for Racially Charged Rhetoric, Before His Presidential Bid

text: An article on Saturday about the release of a batch of emails from Hillary Rodham Clinton’s tenure as secretary of state referred incorrectly to the professional relationship between Mark Penn, an associate of hers, and Thaksin Shinawatra, a former prime minister of Thailand. Mr. Penn conducted polling for him; he was not a lobbyist for Mr. Shinawatra or others in Thailand.
match_headline: Emails Expand on Mosaic of Hillary Clinton’s Days as Secretary of State

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the shooting death of a Memphis police officer misspelled the surname of an officer involved in an earlier shooting. He is Connor Schilling, not Shilling.
match_headline: Memphis Police Seek Man in Death of Officer

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions on Friday with an article about the reaction of residents of East Elmhurst, Queens, to the planned makeover of La Guardia Airport misidentified, in some editions, the part of the airport that is projected to be about 400 feet from some of the homes. It is the reconfigured terminals, not the control tower.
match_headline: Construction Plans for La Guardia Airport Don’t Faze Its Neighbors

text: Because of an editing error, a credit on Monday for a picture with a music review of “The Melodic Version (1984) of the Second Dream of the High Tension Line Stepdown Transformer,” at Dia:Chelsea on West 22nd Street in Manhattan, misstated the photographer’s surname. The picture, of three musicians performing, was taken by Jung Hee Choi, not Cho.
ref_headline: The Melodic Version (1984) of the Second Dream of the High Tension Line Stepdown Transformer,
match_headline: Review: License and Restriction in a Work by La Monte Young at Dia Chelsea

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Vic Firth, a maker of drumsticks and the former principal tympanist of the Boston Symphony Orchestra, referred incorrectly to the period during which he played under the conductor Serge Koussevitzky. It was when Mr. Firth was a student at Tanglewood, not when he was with the Boston Symphony Orchestra.
match_headline: Vic Firth, Who Gave Drummers Their Sticks, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Samuel Pisar, who survived Auschwitz to become a lawyer, an adviser to presidents and the creator of a text for Leonard Bernstein’s symphony “Kaddish,” misidentified the orchestra that first performed Mr. Pisar’s version. It was the Chicago Symphony, not the New York Philharmonic.
match_headline: Samuel Pisar Dies at 86; Lawyer and Adviser Survived Nazi Camps

text: An obituary on Saturday about Dr. Howard W. Jones Jr., who helped achieve the first birth through in vitro fertilization in the United States, misstated a circumstance in the case of his patient Henrietta Lacks, on whom he performed a biopsy in 1951 that led to a cancer diagnosis, and from whom other doctors removed cells that were then used in medical research. Ms. Lacks, who died later that year, did not “contend” that the cells had been taken and used without her permission. The obituary also referred incorrectly to an account of the matter by Rebecca Skloot in her book “The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks.” She also did not “contend” that the cells had been removed without Ms. Lacks’s knowledge; she said it was accepted fact that the cells had been removed without Ms. Lacks’s knowledge.
match_headline: Howard W. Jones Jr., a Pioneer of Reproductive Medicine, Dies at 104

text: Because of an editing error, an article on July 25 about airstrikes by Turkish forces against three Islamic State targets in Syria misstated part of the name of a militant Kurdish group whose camps in northern Iraq were reportedly bombed by Turkish jets in a separate operation the same day. It is the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, not the Kurdish Workers’ Party.
match_headline: Turkey, Anticipating Attack, Strikes 3 ISIS Targets in Syria With Jets

text: An article on Monday about the New York Department of Environmental Conservation’s role in a proposal to allow a mining company, NYCO Minerals, to operate on state-owned land in the Adirondacks misidentified the entity to which a NYCO spokesman was referring when he said that the department was acting as someone’s “negotiating agent.” He was referring to the state’s negotiating agent, not to NYCO’s.
match_headline: Documents Reveal New York State Agency’s Role in Adirondacks Mining Proposal

text: An article on Saturday about the failure of trade negotiators to complete work on the Trans-Pacific Partnership misstated, in some editions, the position of Ildefonso Guajardo, Mexico’s secretary of economy, on car exports. He was taking a hard line against the export of Japanese cars with any less than 65 percent of their parts from T.P.P. countries, not on Mexican car and truck exports.
match_headline: Talks for Pacific Trade Deal Stumble

text: An article on Monday about an agreement several retailers reached with the New York attorney general to stop selling realistic-looking toy guns, in accordance with New York State law, misstated the number of states that have laws restricting the sale of toy guns. It is a dozen, plus Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia, not half a dozen.
match_headline: New York Reaches Accords With Sellers of Toy Guns

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Yankees’ limited activity at the trading deadline misstated the given name of the outfielder the team acquired from the Seattle Mariners. He is Dustin Ackley, not Justin.
match_headline: Yankees Bypass A-List Trades, Content With Pitchers for Now and Later

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with a theater review of “Freight: The Five Incarnations of Abel Green,” at the Here Arts Center in Manhattan, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of J. Alphonse Nicholson, was taken by Nick Graetz, not by Dennis Cahlo.
ref_headline: Freight: The Five Incarnations of Abel Green,
match_headline: Review: In ‘Freight,’ a Black Man Follows the Script for Five Incarnations

text: An article on Monday about a Chinese yarn manufacturer’s opening of a cotton yarn mill in South Carolina misstated the month the mill opened. Operations began in March, not April. The article also misstated the age of Robbie Sowers, a mill worker. He is 44, not 32.
match_headline: Chinese Textile Mills Are Now Hiring in Places Where Cotton Was King

text: An article on Tuesday about groups who are challenging President Obama’s climate change regulations misspelled the surname of a prominent Washington lobbyist who has worked to devise one of the legal strategies. He is Peter Glaser, not Glazer.
match_headline: Move to Fight Obama’s Climate Plan Started Early

text: An article on July 26 about the Obama administration’s announcement, during President Obama’s visit to Kenya, of legal changes that would further restrict the commercial trade of African elephant ivory in the United States referred incorrectly, in some editions, to the market that is estimated at $20 billion a year. That figure applies to all wildlife trafficking, not just trade in illegal ivory.
match_headline: Obama Administration Targets Trade in African Elephant Ivory

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with a news analysis article about the words of reassurance that Defense Secretary Ashton B. Carter has been giving American allies worried about turmoil around the world misidentified the country where he was shown last month. It is Israel, not Jordan.
match_headline: Pentagon Chief Ashton Carter Adds ‘Secretary of Reassurance’ to His Portfolio

text: An article on July 21 about a video made by abortion opponents, which they said proved that Planned Parenthood sells tissue from aborted fetuses for profit, referred incorrectly to the timing of the release of what was described as the full-length, unedited version of the video showing a Planned Parenthood employee talking about how much clinics charge for specimens. The full video was posted at the same time as the edited version. It is not the case that the full video was not released until “after Planned Parenthood complained of selective, misleading editing.”
ref_headline: after Planned Parenthood complained of selective, misleading editing.
match_headline: Planned Parenthood Tells Congress More Videos of Clinics Might Surface

text: An article on Wednesday about the potential sale of The Economist misstated Eric Schmidt’s affiliation with The Economist. Mr. Schmidt, the executive chairman of Google, is on the publication’s board; he is not a trustee.
match_headline: Up for Sale, The Economist Is Unlikely to Alter Its Voice

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the clothing designer Arnold Scaasi misstated part of the name of a fund-raising event over which he and others presided. It is the Literacy Partners Gala, not the Literary Partners Gala. The obituary also omitted part of the name of an organization that honored Mr. Scaasi in 1996. It is the Council of Fashion Designers of America, not the Council of Fashion Designers.
match_headline: Arnold Scaasi Dies at 85; Dressed Stars and Socialites, His ‘Scaasi Girls’

text: An article and a headline on Thursday about a speech by President Obama on Wednesday about the nuclear deal between Iran and six world powers quoted incorrectly from a comment he made about the choice facing the United States. He said, “Let’s not mince words: The choice we face is ultimately between diplomacy and some form of war — maybe not tomorrow, maybe not three months from now, but soon.” He did not say some “sort” of war.
ref_headline: Let’s not mince words: The choice we face is ultimately between diplomacy and some form of war — maybe not tomorrow, maybe not three months from now, but soon.
match_headline: It’s Either Iran Nuclear Deal or ‘Some Form of War,’ Obama Warns

text: A headline on July 26 about airstrikes by Turkey targeting the camps of Kurdish militants misidentified, in some copies, the country in which the attacks occurred. They were in northern Iraq, not in Syria.
match_headline: Turkey Attacks Kurdish Militant Camps in Northern Iraq

text: An article on Tuesday addressing five questions about President Obama’s climate change plan misstated the year by which an E.P.A. regulation would require a 32 percent overall reduction in greenhouse gas emitted by existing power plants from 2005 levels. it is 2030, not 2025.
match_headline: 5 Questions About Obama’s Climate Change Plan

text: An article in some editions last Friday about a decision by a jury in Manhattan to award $48.3 million to the families of two men killed in a construction accident misstated the surname of the lawyer for one victim’s family. She is Bernadette Panzella, not Panzanella.
match_headline: Families of 2008 Crane Collapse Victims Are Awarded $48 Million

text: An article on Tuesday about economic struggles faced by bodega owners in Manhattan misidentified the avenue at which KSY Mini Mart Deli is located. It is at 109th Street and Amsterdam Avenue, not Columbus.
match_headline: Bodegas Declining in Manhattan as Rents Rise and Chains Grow

text: An article on Thursday about Tesla’s earnings report misstated, in some copies, the percentage by which Tesla stock fell during after-hours trading. It fell by as much as 8 percent, not 17 percent.
match_headline: Tesla Motors Trims Delivery Outlook, Sending Stock Down

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about quarterly earnings at 21st Century Fox misstated the relationship of one of the people shown, Sarah Murdoch, to Rupert Murdoch, Fox’s executive co-chairman. She is his daughter-in-law, not his daughter.
match_headline: Fox, Topping Projections, Reports a Tough Quarter

text: A headline on Thursday about an automaker’s earnings misstated the entity to which the earnings apply. It is Chrysler, Fiat Chrysler’s American subsidiary — not Fiat Chrysler over all.
match_headline: Chrysler Posts a 3% Drop in Profit After $90 Million Fine

text: An article on Thursday about Bank of America’s decision to withdraw clients’ money from a Paulson & Company investment fund misidentified the company that provided investment alternatives to Bank of America clients uncomfortable with the risk profile of Paulson & Company’s funds. It is Bank of America, not Paulson & Company.
match_headline: Bank of America Starts to Pull Clients’ Money Out of a Paulson Fund

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a Securities and Exchange Commission’s rule requiring companies to regularly reveal the ratio of the chief executive’s pay to that of the average employee misidentified Thomas Piketty’s best-selling book that set off a global debate about inequality. It is “Capital in the Twenty-First Century,” not “The Economics of Inequality.”
match_headline: S.E.C. Approves Rule on C.E.O. Pay Ratio

text: An article on Thursday about Qatar’s emergence as a global energy player in liquefied natural gas rendered the name of a Qatari company incorrectly. It is Qatargas, not Qatar Gas.
match_headline: Liquefied Natural Gas Makes Qatar an Energy Giant

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a dispute between the Spanish art collector Jaime Botín and Spanish officials over a Picasso painting he wants to export paraphrased incorrectly from a statement by Rafael Mateu de Ros, Mr. Botín’s lawyer in Madrid, about his client’s appeal to Spain’s Supreme Court. The appeal has been filed and he said Mr. Botín is pressing it; he did not say that Mr. Botín would file an appeal.
match_headline: Spain Says Banker’s Seized Picasso Will Head Back Home

text: An editorial on Thursday about a federal rule requiring public companies to report the ratio of chief executive pay to median employee pay misstated the timing of such disclosures. The ratio must be reported yearly, not every three years.
match_headline: A Long Time Coming, Sunlight on the Executive Pay Gap

text: A map on Thursday with an article about an announcement by officials in Paris that an airplane part that washed ashore on the French island of Réunion almost surely came from the Malaysia Airlines Boeing 777 that disappeared in March 2014 gave an erroneous location for Kuala Lumpur, the capital of Malaysia. It is on Peninsular Malaysia, not on the Indonesian island of Sumatra to the southwest.
match_headline: Réunion Debris Is Almost Surely From Flight 370, Officials Say

text: An article on Thursday about the sentencing of Wojciech Braszczok, a former undercover New York police detective, in the 2013 attack on a motorist by a gang of motorcyclists misstated the age of his co-defendant, Robert Sims. He is 37, not 35. The article also misidentified the borough where Mr. Sims lives. It is Brooklyn, not Queens.
match_headline: Ex-Detective Going to Jail for Role in Manhattan Biker Assault

text: Because of an editing error, a Sports of The Times column on Friday, about a new initiative by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers to cater to female fans, misstated, in some copies, the day of the first game of the N.F.L. preseason. It is Sunday night, not tonight.
match_headline: Buccaneers Offer Women a Modern N.F.L. Lesson Out of the ’50s

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the Yankees’ 13-3 victory over the Boston Red Sox misstated the given name of the Red Sox pitcher whom Mark Teixeira greeted with a run-scoring single in the sixth inning. He is Robbie Ross Jr., not Ricky.
match_headline: Yankees’ Surging Offense Makes Up for Imperfections in Rout of Red Sox

text: An article on Friday about the exhibition “How Cats Took Over the Internet,” at the Museum of the Moving Image in Astoria, Queens, misstated the percentage of traffic about cats and dogs on some websites consulted by the curator, Jason Eppink. It seldom exceeds .3 percent, not 3 percent.
ref_headline: How Cats Took Over the Internet,
match_headline: ‘How Cats Took Over the Internet’ at the Museum of the Moving Image

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about an investigation into a major art theft at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston in 1990 misstated the timing of 1:24 a.m. on March 18, 1990, in relation to the theft. That was when the thieves arrived at the museum; it was not 24 hours before the crime.
match_headline: 25 Years After Gardner Museum Heist, Video Raises Questions

text: An article last Sunday about the 50-year fight over the Voting Rights Act referred incompletely to the significance of Georgia’s revised voter-ID Law. While it did include a provision allowing those without ID to file provisional ballots, the more relevant feature involved offering free voter-identification cards to those who needed them. The article also misidentified the court that upheld the revised voter-ID law. It is the Georgia Supreme Court, not the Supreme Court of the United States. The article also misidentified the location of the residence of a member of the New Black Panther Party who was accused of intimidating voters at a Philadelphia polling station in 2008. He lived in a house a few blocks away from the polling place, not in the building that housed the polling station. In addition, the article misspelled the surname of a state senator who helped pass North Carolina’s sweeping new voting law. He is Tom Apodaca, not Apadoca. And a picture with an accompanying timeline was published in error. It showed President Johnson signing the Civil Rights Act of 1964, on July 2 of that year — not the Voting Rights Act. A picture of Johnson signing the Voting Rights Act, on Aug. 6, 1965, can be found at nytimes.com/magazine .
match_headline: A Dream Undone

text: An article on July 26 about Christianity in the Middle East misstated a statistic regarding the Christian population in the region. It was the percentage of the overall population that is Christian that declined between 1910 and 2010, not the total number of Christians.
match_headline: Is This the End of Christianity in the Middle East?

text: A listing of information in some editions last Sunday with a dining review of Shad Row in Rocky Hill, Conn., misstated the restaurant’s address. It is 277 Meadow Road, not 27 Meadow Road.
match_headline: Review: Burgers (and Seafood) at Shad Row in Rocky Hill

text: An article last Sunday about the British designer Thomas Heatherwick referred incorrectly to the friendship between the activist and actress Joanna Lumley and Boris Johnson, the mayor of London; Ms. Lumley has lobbied Mr. Johnson to build a London Garden Bridge based on Mr. Heatherwick’s design. Ms. Lumley, born in 1946, has known Mr. Johnson, born in 1964, since he was 4 years old. They were not childhood friends.
match_headline: The Price of Thomas Heatherwick’s Imagination

text: An entry last Sunday in the Newly Released video roundup misspelled the surname of one of the stars of “Satan Met a Lady.” He was Warren William — not Williams.
match_headline: Facing Death With a Shrug in Two Versions of ‘The Killers’

text: An article on July 26 about beer and ale in Yorkshire, England, misstated part of the name of a Yorkshire pub. It is the Black Bull in Paradise, not the Black Bull in Heaven.
match_headline: A Tasting Tour of Yorkshire’s Beers and Ales

text: Because of an editing error, an article on July 29 about the inherent complications in an agreement by the United States and Turkey to cooperate in driving Islamic State forces out of a 60-mile strip of northern Syria along the Turkish border misidentified, in some editions, the government position held by Recep Tayyip Erdogan. He is the president of Turkey, no longer the prime minister. (Ahmet Davutoglu holds that post now.)
match_headline: Goals Diverge and Perils Remain as U.S. and Turkey Take on ISIS

text: Because of an editing error, the Lodenice Journal article on Friday, about a village of 1,800 in the Czech Republic that is home to GZ Media, a world leader in the production of vinyl record albums, gave an incorrect guide for the pronunciation of Lodenice. It is LO-dyen-ee-tsay, not lo-DYEN-ee-sah.
match_headline: Czech Company, Pressing Hits for Years on Vinyl, Finds It Has Become One

text: An article last Monday about American Pharoah’s victory in the Haskell Invitational misspelled, in some editions, the surname of an NBC horse racing announcer who called the race. He is Larry Collmus, not Colmus. The article also misidentified the New Jersey city that is home to Max’s Hot Dogs, the lunch spot of the horse’s trainer, Bob Baffert. It is in Long Branch, not West Long Branch.
match_headline: American Pharoah Wins Haskell Invitational

text: An article on April 23 about the discovery of a small drone possibly tainted by radioactive cesium on the roof of the Japanese prime minister’s office in Tokyo referred imprecisely to cesium. While the stable version of the element ranks in the middle of the naturally occurring chemical elements in terms of its abundance in the earth by weight, the radioactive isotopes, like the one possibly found on the drone, are not usually found in nature. The error was called to the attention of editors only late last month.
match_headline: Drone, Possibly Radioactive, Is Found at Office of Japan’s Prime Minister

text: An article on July 16 about comments President Obama made about accusations of sexual misconduct against the comedian Bill Cosby quoted incorrectly from a statement Mr. Obama made in July 2009 about the arrest of the Harvard scholar Henry Louis Gates Jr. Mr. Obama accused the police of acting “stupidly” during that arrest; he did not say a white Cambridge police officer was “stupid.”
match_headline: Asked About Cosby Scandal, Obama Weighs In on a Sexual Violence Discussion

text: An article on Thursday about Yahoo’s efforts to make email more easily searchable described a similar effort by Google incorrectly. Google’s Inbox email service is accessible on desktop web browsers as well as smartphones, although a user must sign up for the service through an app. It is not mobile-only.
match_headline: Yahoo Tweaks Email to Make Search More Personal

text: An article on Saturday about a judge’s ruling regarding the promotion of drugs for uses not approved by the Food and Drug Administration misstated the role of Stephen Paul Mahinka, a lawyer who commented on the ruling. Other lawyers in his firm, Morgan, Lewis & Bockius, advised Amarin, the plaintiff in the case; Mr. Mahinka did not.
match_headline: Court Forbids F.D.A. From Blocking Truthful Promotion of Drug

text: An article on Wednesday about George Wang, owner of the Asia Pacific Stock Exchange in Sydney, Australia, misidentified the university where he studied engineering. It was East China Textile Institute of Science and Technology in Shanghai, now known as Donghua University; it was not Chinese Eastern University.
match_headline: An Exchange in Australia Woos Listings From China

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Liberty’s success during the W.N.B.A. season misstated part of the surname of the star player for the Chicago Sky, whom the Liberty played Friday. She is Elena Delle Donne, not Della Donne.
match_headline: Rebuilding Around Tina Charles Puts Liberty in Playoff Hunt

text: An article on Friday about Jon Stewart’s last appearance as host of “The Daily Show” misstated the day that Denis Leary was a guest during the show’s final week. It was last Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: Jon Stewart Signs Off From ‘Daily Show’ With Wit and Sincerity

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about the Salzburg Festival in Austria, using information from the festival, misidentified the Mozart work that includes the “Laudate Dominum” sung by the soprano Miah Persson as an encore. It is “Vesperae solennes de confessore,” not the “Coronation” Mass.
match_headline: At Salzburg Festival, Musicians Tap Their Inner Mozarts and Schuberts

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about New York Review Books, the publishing offshoot of The New York Review of Books, misstated the name of the Chinese dynasty that produced a work of literary criticism that is part of New York Review Books’ new series, Calligrams. It was the Tang dynasty, not the Tan dynasty.
match_headline: New York Review of Books Fills a Niche by Reviving Forgotten Works

text: A picture caption on Monday with an obituary of the breast cancer surgeon Dr. Carolyn M. Kaelin referred incompletely to the source of the photograph of Dr. Kaelin. While it was supplied by the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, it was taken by Steve Marsel. The caption also referred incorrectly to the date of the picture. It was taken in 2007; it was not undated.
match_headline: Carolyn Kaelin, Breast Cancer Surgeon, Patient Advocate and Patient, Dies at 54

text: An article on Sunday about a letter of support for President Obama’s proposed Iran nuclear deal written by experts in nuclear weapons and arms control omitted a Nobel laureate from a listing of those who signed the letter. He is Philip W. Anderson of Princeton University.
match_headline: 29 U.S. Scientists Praise Iran Nuclear Deal in Letter to Obama

text: An article on July 23 about the resignation of Flavia Pansieri, the deputy United Nations high commissioner for human rights, erroneously attributed a distinction to her. While she was the first high-ranking United Nations official to have been informed of accusations of child sexual abuse by French soldiers in the Central African Republic last year, she was not the highest-ranking one. (Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein, who became high commissioner for human rights in September 2014, was informed of the accusations later that year.) The article also referred incompletely to Ms. Pansieri’s response to an internal United Nations inquiry. While she did not explain why she apparently took no action regarding the allegations until March 2015, she did suggest that she was distracted by budget problems, according to statements given to investigators.
match_headline: U.N. Official Quits Amid Scrutiny of Response to Sex Abuse Accusations

text: Because of an editing error, a reporting credit on July 30 with an article about American investigators’ conclusions that an object that washed up on the shore of the French island of Réunion came from a Boeing 777, making it likely that it was debris from the Malaysia Airlines jetliner that disappeared in March 2014, misspelled the given name of one contributor in some editions. He is Chris Buckley, not Chis.
match_headline: Debris Is Thought to Come From Malaysia Airlines Flight 370

text: An article on Sunday about a surge of undocumented immigrants applying for driver’s licenses in California misstated the percentage of all illegal immigrants living in the state. It is about 25 percent, not 40 percent.
match_headline: California Effort to Issue Driver’s Licenses to Immigrants Receives Surge of Applicants

text: An article on Tuesday about Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals’ acquisition of Therakos, a maker of immunotherapy treatment devices, misidentified the ailment that Therakos’s flagship device treats. It is a blood cancer that affects the skin, not skin cancer.
match_headline: Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals to Acquire Therakos for $1.33 Billion

text: An article on Saturday about victories by the swimmer Katie Ledecky in the 200-meter, 400-meter and 1,500-meter freestyle events at the world championships misstated the number of medals won at the 1976 Olympics by Tim Shaw, who won those three events at the 1975 world championships. He won a silver and a gold, not two silvers and a gold.
match_headline: In Katie Ledecky’s Amazing Feats, Echoes of a Swimmer From the 1970s

text: An article last Wednesday about a woman’s plans to move her backyard garden from Harlem to Brooklyn misstated how the woman, Marie Viljoen, and her husband, Vincent Mounier, moved to New York. Ms. Viljoen came to study opera, and Mr. Mounier joined her later; he did not move with her.
match_headline: A City Garden in Harlem Is on the Move to Brooklyn

text: An obituary on Sunday about Benton L. Becker, who as President Gerald R. Ford’s personal emissary negotiated the pardon of Richard M. Nixon in 1974, misstated the nature of a case Mr. Becker handled as a federal prosecutor against the activist Abbie Hoffman. Mr. Hoffman was charged with desecrating the American flag by wearing a shirt with an image of the flag on it; he was not charged with burning the American flag.
match_headline: Benton Becker, Ford Aide, Dies at 77; Negotiated Nixon Pardon

text: An article on Friday about soul-searching taking place in Israel following bias attacks on gays and Arabs misspelled the surname of a man accused of stabbing six people, one fatally, at the Jerusalem Gay Pride Parade. He is Yishai Schlissel, not Schissel. The article also misstated the day that the Jerusalem Open House, which runs an H.I.V. clinic and support groups for gay Israelis, met with Education Minister Naftali Bennett to press for tolerance education in public religious schools. It was Sunday, not Monday.
match_headline: Soul-Searching in Israel After Bias Attacks on Gays and Arabs

text: A chart on Wednesday with an article about a decline in the number of Americans without health insurance transposed, in some editions, labels showing the uninsured rates for adults considered near-poor or poor. The rate for poor adults is higher, at 28 percent, and the rate for near-poor adults is lower, at 23.8 percent. In addition, the share of adults considered not poor who were uninsured was 7.5 percent, not 4.6 percent. A corrected chart can be found at nytimes.com/us.
match_headline: Number of Uninsured Has Declined by 15 Million Since 2013, Administration Says

text: An article on Saturday about the different shapes of pupils in animals misstated the name of the university where Ronald H.H. Kröger is a biologist and misidentified the country in which it is located. It is Lund University, not Lunds University, and it is in Sweden, not Germany.
match_headline: Eye Shape May Help Distinguish Predator From Prey

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Monday about a decision by the Albany city court to drop a case stemming from a raid on a spa misstated the timing of a judge’s ruling dismissing a prostitution charge against a spa employee. It was July 28, not last week.
match_headline: Prostitution Charge Dropped in Case an Albany Journalist Called Retaliation

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with an article in some editions about Kerry Ryan and John Juback, a couple who met through Mr. Juback’s classified ad seeking a roommate, misstated the period of time they lived together before starting to date. It was one year, not “years.”
match_headline: She Answered His Ad for a Roommate, Moved In and Never Left

text: An article on Monday about Shane Lowry’s victory at the Bridgestone Invitational golf tournament misstated the most recent year Tiger Woods won the event. It was 2013, not 2014. The article also misspelled the given name of one of the golfers who finished four-under 276. He is Rickie Fowler, not Ricky.
match_headline: Frantic Struggle Leaves Unfamiliar Name, Shane Lowry, Atop Leaderboard

text: An article on Monday about the tennis player Victoria Duval’s comeback from Hodgkin’s lymphoma misstated, in some copies, the year of the Haiti earthquake, in which her father almost died. It was 2010, not 2011.
match_headline: Winning Mantra of ‘I’m Not Sick’ Propels Victoria Duval

text: An article on Tuesday about schools that monitor the weight of students and send letters to their homes, using information from Dominique G. Ruggieri, who studied the letters, erroneously included one state among those that require schools to send the letters. Illinois does not do so.
match_headline: Hillary Clinton Emails Take Long Path to Controversy
