text: An obituary last Thursday about Louis Sokoloff, who pioneered the PET scan technique for measuring human brain function, misstated the term from which the acronym PET is derived. It is positron emission tomography — not positive emission transverse tomography.
match_headline: Louis Sokoloff, Pioneer of PET Scan, Dies at 93

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with an obituary of the convicted labor racketeer John Riggi misstated, in some copies, the year the photograph of Mr. Riggi was taken. It was 1969, not 2008.
match_headline: John Riggi, Who Led New Jersey Crime Family, Dies at 90

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the World Briefing column on Friday about Iran’s decision to grant The Jewish Daily Forward a visa misstated the age of the newspaper. The Forward began publishing more than a century ago, in 1897, not nearly a century ago. The article also misstated the length of the visa and the date it was issued. It was good for seven days, not 30, and it was issued July 20, not Aug. 4.
match_headline: Iran: Jewish Newspaper Was Granted Visa in Rare Move

text: An article on Wednesday about a mine spill in southwest Colorado that has flowed into the Animas River misstated the waterway’s relationship to the San Juan River. The Animas is a tributary of the San Juan River, not the other way around.
match_headline: E.P.A. Treating Toxic Water From Abandoned Colorado Mine After Accident

text: An article on Aug. 6 about hiking in the heat in Arizona misstated part of the name of the preserve where hikers use Summit Trail to climb Piestewa Peak. It is the Phoenix Mountains Preserve, not Phoenix Mountain Preserve. The article also misstated the surname of a hiker. He is Dennis Kurth, not Kurtz.
match_headline: As Temperatures Rise in Phoenix, Hikers Embrace Heat on a Grueling Ascent

text: An article on Thursday about the end of the walleye fishing season in Minnesota referred incorrectly to larger walleye that appeared to be eating the smaller fish for food. They are predators, not prey.
match_headline: How Are Those Walleye Biting? On Minnesota Lake, They’re Not

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about prosecutors’ request to deny bail to five men arrested in connection with a trading operation that used corporate information illegally obtained by hackers ahead of its public release misstated the occupation of Steven Brill, who is representing one of the men, Vitaly Korchevsky. Mr. Brill is a lawyer; he is not also a publisher. (Another Steven Brill founded The American Lawyer.)
match_headline: Prosecutors Ask to Deny Bail to 5 Accused in Insider Trading Ring

text: A listing in the Transactions column in the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about a recent lease at 57 Caton Place, using information from the landlord’s broker, described incorrectly the new tenant, Move Loot. It is a full-service online marketplace for selling, buying and moving lightly-used apartment furniture and home décor; Move Loot is not an office furniture sales company.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the effects on children of their parents’ unpredictable work schedules misstated part of the name of a group in which Kris Buchmann, who left a retail job because of the difficulties in arranging child care, is active. It is Organizers in the Land of Enchantment, not Organizers in the Land of Enrichment.
match_headline: The Perils of Ever-Changing Work Schedules Extend to Children’s Well-Being

text: An article in some copies on Wednesday about the Yankees’ 5-4 loss to the Cleveland Indians misstated the given name of the Indians’ starting pitcher. He is Carlos Carrasco, not Hector. The article also misidentified the player who lined out to left field to end the top of the 16th inning. He is Alex Rodriguez, not Mark Teixeira.
match_headline: Yankees’ Loss in 16th Shrinks Their Lead to Half a Game

text: An article on Wednesday about archaeological discoveries on the Palatine Hill in Rome misstated the given name of the professor who led the excavation. She is Clementina Panella, not Camilla.
match_headline: Curiae Veteres Sanctuary in Rome Attracts the Curious

text: An article on Friday about a deal between HBO and Sesame Workshop that will bring first-run episodes of “Sesame Street” exclusively to the premium cable network and its streaming outlets misidentified the organization being criticized on social media for favoring privileged children through the deal. It is Sesame Workshop, not PBS.
match_headline: ‘Sesame Street’ to Air First on HBO for Next 5 Seasons

text: A picture caption on Friday with a film review of “The Great Man,” using information from press materials, misidentified the actor at the top. He is Surho Sugaipov — not Jérémie Renier, another cast member.
match_headline: Review: In ‘The Great Man,’ Friendship and Politics in a War Zone

text: A review on Page 9 in some editions this weekend about “La Cage aux Folles” misspells the given name of a transgender celebrity in referring to current sexual mores. She is Caitlyn Jenner, not Caitlin.
match_headline: Review of ‘La Cage aux Folles’ at Goodspeed Opera House in East Haddam

text: An obituary on Thursday about J. Wallace LaPrade, who was in charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s New York operations in the 1970s, misspelled the given name of a radical fugitive whose sister was the subject of an F.B.I. search. She is Bernardine Dohrn, not Bernadine.
match_headline: J. Wallace LaPrade, New York F.B.I. Chief in ’70s, Dies at 89

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the thoroughbred trainer John A. Nerud misidentified the location of Belmont Park, where he was injured in 1965. It is in Elmont, N.Y., on Long Island; it is not in Queens.
match_headline: John A. Nerud, Hall of Fame Thoroughbred Trainer, Dies at 102

text: An article on Sunday about the workplace culture at Amazon.com erroneously included a company among those that have opened offices in Seattle and that benefit from the outflow of workers from Amazon. Facebook has done so, but LinkedIn has not.
match_headline: Inside Amazon: Wrestling Big Ideas in a Bruising Workplace

text: An article on Monday about President Obama’s future after he leaves office described incorrectly the business founded by Fred Eychaner, who donated $1 million to Mr. Obama’s library. Mr. Eychaner founded Newsweb Corp., which owns community newspapers and radio stations; he did not found a Chicago “television empire.”
match_headline: With High-Profile Help, Obama Plots Life After Presidency

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about efforts to identify the remains of sailors who died aboard the battleship Oklahoma during the attack on Pearl Harbor misidentified the warship on which Ray Emory, who has led efforts to identify victims, served. It was the Honolulu, not the Oklahoma.
match_headline: Decades After Pearl Harbor, a Mission to Honor ‘the Unknowns’ Gains Urgency

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about a Brooklyn man who pleaded guilty to conspiring to provide material support to the Islamic State terrorist organization misspelled his given name. He is Abdurasul Hasanovich Juraboev, not Adburasul.
match_headline: Brooklyn Man Accused of Supporting ISIS Pleads Guilty

text: An article on Friday about the Mets’ 12-3 victory over the Colorado Rockies misspelled, in some copies, the surname of one of the Rockies players who hit a first-inning home run. He is D.J. LeMahieu, not LaMahieu.
match_headline: Mets Overcome Shaky Start and Complete Sweep of Rockies

text: Because of an editing error, the On Comedy column on Monday, about stand-up comedians regarded as very funny but who never became well known, referred incorrectly to such comedians. That type is comedy’s answer “to the storied playground basketball players who would have surely been better than Michael Jordan if not for injury, drugs or some bad break.” It is not the case that that type is not comedy’s answer to such players.
ref_headline: to the storied playground basketball players who would have surely been better than Michael Jordan if not for injury, drugs or some bad break.
match_headline: Catch Charlie Barnett and Other Rising Stand-Up Stars Who Never Hit the Top

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Aug. 7 about the Pollock-Krasner House and Study Center in East Hampton, N.Y., where the show “Elaine de Kooning Portrayed” is on view and about the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, N.Y., misstated the year Ms. de Kooning was born. It was 1918, not 1920.
match_headline: Elaine de Kooning and Andreas Gursky in Close-Up in the Hamptons

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a restaurant in New Jersey that is letting diners decide what to pay for their meals referred incorrectly at one point to a professor of marketing at the University of Minnesota who writes about the psychology of money. The professor, Kathleen D. Vohs, is a woman.
match_headline: What Your Vacation Says About You

text: An article on Tuesday about residents’ responses to an earthquake in the San Francisco area on Monday misidentified the city in which the television station KTVU is located. It is in Oakland, not in San Francisco.
match_headline: Jolt in California Adds to Trove of Quake Commentary

text: An article on Monday about new research showing that blacks and Hispanics with college degrees suffer disproportionately more in economic downturns than white and Asian college graduates gave an outdated position for Prof. William A. Darity Jr. at Duke University, who commented on the findings. He is with the Samuel DuBois Cook Center on Social Equity — not with the Consortium on Social Equity, which no longer exists.
match_headline: Racial Wealth Gap Persists Despite Degree, Study Says

text: An article on Tuesday about the choice of Robert Steven Kaplan, a former Goldman Sachs executive, as president of the Dallas Federal Reserve Bank misstated, in some copies, the name of a public interest group whose director, Ady Barkan, was critical of the Fed’s selection process. It is the Center for Popular Democracy, not the Center for Public Democracy.
match_headline: Former Goldman Executive Is Chosen to Lead Dallas Fed

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Mets’ 3-2 loss to the Pittsburgh Pirates misstated, in some copies, the type of hit Juan Lagares had for the Mets in the bottom of 10th inning. It was a double, not a triple.
match_headline: Mets Face a Truer Measuring Stick in the Pirates, and Fall Short

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about Broadway box-office grosses last week misstated the amounts taken in by “Hamilton” and “Penn & Teller on Broadway.” “Hamilton” grossed $1,459,314, not $1,555,706. That is the amount taken in by “Penn & Teller on Broadway,” not $1,153,386. The report also referred incorrectly to “An American in Paris.” It is a new musical, not a revival.
match_headline: Victoria Clark and Thomas Reidy: An eHarmony, and Musical, Match

text: An article on Friday about a new SeaGlass carousel in Lower Manhattan misidentified the part of the Battery where the carousel is located. It is in the Battery Woodland, not the Battery Bosque. The article also referred incorrectly to Piet Oudolf. He is the horticultural master planner and designer of gardens at the Battery, not the landscape architect. (The Starr Whitehouse firm is the landscape architect.)
match_headline: New York’s New Carousel Puts You in a Whirling School of Mechanized Fish

text: An article on Saturday about SFX Entertainment’s effort to sell itself misstated an earlier bid from its founder, Robert F. X. Sillerman. He offered $5.25 a share, not $5.75.
match_headline: SFX Entertainment Is Back on the Block

text: A listing of credits on Monday with a theater review of “Sweat,” at the Angus Bowmer Theater in Ashland, Ore., misspelled the surname of the associate director. She is Rebecca Wear, not Ware.
match_headline: Review: Lynn Nottage’s ‘Sweat’ Examines Lives Unraveling by Industry’s Demise

text: An article last Thursday about the summer ritual of checking for ticks referred incorrectly to their seasonal biting behavior. Though ticks are dormant when the temperature drops below 40 degrees, they can become active again if winter temperatures rise. Ticks do not always stop biting after a fall freeze.
match_headline: Ticks: Summer’s Unwanted Guests

text: An article on Aug. 13 about the use of facial recognition software by law enforcement agencies misstated the time frame in which San Diego agencies used the software to try to identify people on more than 20,600 occasions. It was since 2011, not over 33 days in January and February.
match_headline: Facial Recognition Software Moves From Overseas Wars to Local Police

text: An article on Thursday about the rape trial involving students at St. Paul’s school in New Hampshire misidentified the lawyer who accompanied the 16-year-old witness out of the courtroom. The lawyer, Catherine J. Ruffle, is the prosecutor, not the victim’s lawyer.
match_headline: In Girl’s Account, Rite at St. Paul’s Boarding School Turned Into Rape

text: An article on Aug. 7 about the damage to Malaysia’s credibility caused by Prime Minister Najib Razak’s declaration that a wing part found on an Indian Ocean island definitely came from the missing Malaysia Airlines Boeing 777 referred incorrectly to reports in The Wall Street Journal and the Sarawak Report, a news website based in Britain, about 1Malaysia Development Berhad, a troubled state investment fund founded by Mr. Najib. Citing investigators’ documents, The Journal and the Sarawak Report said nearly $700 million deposited into accounts believed to be controlled by Mr. Najib came from a company registered in the British Virgin Islands and from SRC International, a Malaysian energy company. Although both news organizations suggest links between the two companies and 1MDB, neither said the money originally came from the fund.
match_headline: Malaysia’s Declarations on Flight 370 and Plane Debris Further Dent Its Credibility

text: An article on Thursday about different positions that Republican presidential candidates have taken on education misstated part of the name of the organization that sponsored a panel discussion on the issue in New Hampshire. It is American Federation for Children (not “of” Children).
match_headline: G.O.P. Hopefuls Display Differences on Education

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a decision by the Riverdale Jewish Center to keep Rabbi Jonathan Rosenblatt, who had been under scrutiny over taking boys into the sauna with him decades ago, misidentified the news outlet that reported the synagogue leaders’ announcement. It was The Jewish Telegraphic Agency, not The Times of Israel.
match_headline: Bronx Rabbi Who Took Boys Naked to Sauna Will Keep His Job

text: An article on Wednesday about the rupture of a Takata airbag in a 2015 Volkswagen erroneously included one automaker among those affected by recalls of Takata airbags and omitted another. The recalls include vehicles from Mitsubishi, but not from Mercedes-Benz.
match_headline: U.S. Investigates Airbag Rupture in a Volkswagen

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about regional airports that are changing their names for marketing purposes misstated the position of The Burbank Leader on a proposed name change for Burbank Bob Hope Airport in California. In an editorial, the newspaper argued against putting “Los Angeles” in the airport’s name; it did not object to dropping “Bob Hope.” (That argument was made in an op-ed article by a local resident.)
match_headline: The Local Airport, by Any Other Name

text: An article last Friday about the first round of the P.G.A. Championship misidentified the body of water Rory McIlroy waded into to hit a shot. It was a small lake near the fifth green — not Lake Michigan, which borders several other holes on the course.
match_headline: P.G.A. Championship 2015: Dustin Johnson Is Calm Before Storming to the Top

text: A picture credit on Tuesday with an obituary of the record producer Bob Johnston, using information from the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum, misstated the source of the photograph of Mr. Johnston with Bob Dylan and Johnny Cash. It is from the Dolph Briscoe Center for American History, not from the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum.
match_headline: Bob Johnston, 83, Dies; Produced Bob Dylan and Johnny Cash Albums

text: An article on Thursday about Russia’s appeal to patriotism to lure vacationers to Crimea this summer, which met with limited success, misspelled the surname of the chairwoman of the City Council tourism committee in the Crimean city of Yalta, who said it earned an unexpected windfall this season because many Russians prefer to stay in hotels, which are plentiful in Yalta. The chairwoman is Lubov V. Gribkova, not Gribokova. The article also misspelled part of the name of a rehabilitation hospital in Saki that is popular with tourists. It is the N. N. Burdenko Sanitarium, not N. N. Budenko.
match_headline: Russia’s Pitch to Vacationers: Crimea Is for Patriots

text: A picture caption on Thursday about church bombings in Las Cruces, N.M., misidentified the object that an F.B.I. agent was shown examining. It is a cross, not a crucifix. (A crucifix is a cross with the figure of Jesus Christ on it.)
match_headline: Bombs at 3 Churches in Las Cruces, New Mexico, Confound the Authorities

text: An article on Thursday about Emilio Cordova, the Dominican Republic’s most celebrated baseball historian, misstated the date in 1963 of a famous pitchers’ duel between Juan Marichal and Warren Spahn. The game was played on July 2, not on June 2.
match_headline: Oh, the Stories He Could Tell

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with the Books of The Times Review about “The Last Love Song: A Biography of Joan Didion” by Tracy Daugherty, using information from The Associated Press, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of Ms. Didion in 1977, was taken by Mary Lloyd Estrin, not by The Associated Press.
ref_headline: The Last Love Song: A Biography of Joan Didion
match_headline: Review: ‘The Last Love Song,’ a Biography of Joan Didion

text: An obituary on June 13 about Jane Briggs Hart, a would-be astronaut, an outspoken critic of the Vietnam War and the widow of Senator Philip A. Hart of Michigan, referred incorrectly to Mr. Hart’s status when he died in 1976. He had chosen not to seek re-election because of ill health, but was still in office at the time of his death; he had not retired. This correction was delayed because an email sent by a reader on June 21 went astray at The Times.
match_headline: Jane Hart, Activist and Nearly an Astronaut, Dies at 93

text: A picture last Sunday with an article about Pete Dye, the architect of Whistling Straits golf course, the site of the P.G.A. Championship, was published in error. It showed his son, P.B. Dye — not Pete Dye — at Montour Heights Country Club in Coraopolis, Pa., in 1986.
match_headline: P.G.A. Championship Course a Site of Intense Rounds, for Gunners and Golfers

text: An obituary last Sunday about Susan Newhouse, the longtime chairwoman of the Fresh Air Fund, using information from a biography of her brother-in-law, Samuel I. Newhouse Jr., referred incorrectly to her father and, in some copies, to her husband. Her father, Harry Marley, was a lawyer, not a junk dealer. And Mrs. Newhouse met her husband, Donald, after he had left Syracuse University, not while he was a student there.
match_headline: Susan Newhouse, Who Guided Fresh Air Fund, Dies at 80

text: A review on Aug. 9 about “World Without End: Spain, Philip II, and the First Global Empire,” by Hugh Thomas, misstated the royal dynasty to which Henry II of France belonged. He was a Valois, not a Bourbon.
ref_headline: World Without End: Spain, Philip II, and the First Global Empire,
match_headline: Hugh Thomas’s ‘World Without End: Spain, Philip II, and the First Global Empire’

text: A review on Aug. 2 about “The Dying Grass,” William T. Vollmann’s novel of the Nez Percé war of 1877, misstated the district in which the war came to an end. It was the Montana Territory, not the Idaho Territory.
match_headline: ‘The Dying Grass,’ by William T. Vollmann

text: A listing on the “ On the Market ” page last Sunday misidentified the location of the house for sale in New Jersey. It is in Middletown Township — not Red Bank, which is the mailing address.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in the New York Region

text: An article last Sunday about Kari Duncan-Cunningham and her husband, Ron Cunningham, owners of the Brooklyn Bell ice cream company, misidentified the neighborhood in Brooklyn where Ms. Duncan-Cunningham’s daughter Jade lives. It is Kensington, not Park Slope.
match_headline: In Brooklyn: Ice Cream With a Family on Top

text: An article last Sunday about Allison McKay, a contestant on “The Price Is Right” who had not received her prizes, misstated how she won. Most of the merchandise was won in the Showcase section of the program, not the Showcase Showdown. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: A ‘Price Is Right’ Winner’s Showcase Letdown

text: An article last Sunday about the actress Rose McGowan referred incompletely to Ms. McGowan’s age. While she initially said she was 35, as the article reported, she later said in an email: “My age, truthfully, is something nebulous. I was born in a commune with no record of my birth. I approximate.” (Several sources give her age as 41.) And because the article did not explain the discrepancy over her age, it should not have stated as fact that she was 15 years old in 1995.
ref_headline: My age, truthfully, is something nebulous. I was born in a commune with no record of my birth. I approximate.
match_headline: A Night Out With Rose McGowan, Now Behind the Camera

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the wedding of Anne Levine and Michael Hill carried an erroneous credit. The picture is by Orchard Cove Photography, not Orchard Grove Photography.
match_headline: Anne Levine and Michael Hill: Riding the (Radio) Waves

text: A picture caption on Aug. 9 with an article about a family trip to Amsterdam misspelled the name of a tower on Muntplein square. It is Muntorren, not Munttorren.
match_headline: 20 Years After Honeymoon, a Return Trip to Amsterdam

text: An article on Aug. 9 about the comedian Issa Rae misstated the date HBO approved her script for “Insecure.” It was December 2014, not the fall of 2013. And Rae hired directors and producers, not writers and producers.
match_headline: The Misadventures of Issa Rae

text: An article on Aug. 16 about the effort to create a new country between Serbia and Croatia called Liberland misidentified the producer of an annual conference known as FreedomFest. The producer is Mark Skousen, not the political commentator Glenn Beck, who has been a speaker at the conference.
match_headline: Welcome to Liberland, the World’s Newest Country (Maybe)

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Aug. 14 about the Islamic State’s codification of sexual slavery in the regions of Iraq and Syria that it has conquered referred incorrectly to the author of an editorial in Dabiq, the group’s online magazine, that lamented the fact that some ISIS sympathizers were questioning the institution of slavery. The author, who was not named, is a woman.
match_headline: ISIS Enshrines a Theology of Rape

text: An article on Monday about the New York Police Department’s early efforts to reintroduce a model of so-called community policing misidentified the Queens neighborhood where the rapper Chinx was killed in May. It was in Briarwood, not in Woodhaven.
match_headline: In New York, Testing Grounds for Community Policing

text: A picture caption on Aug. 14 with an article about the removal of Thura Shwe Mann as chairman of Myanmar’s governing party misidentified Mr. Shwe Mann in some editions. He is shown at right, not at left. (Vice President Sai Mauk Kham is at left.)
match_headline: Conservatives in Myanmar Force Out Leader of Ruling Party

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about clashes between the Macedonian police and a large group of migrants at the Greek-Macedonian border misstated the percentage of the Macedonian population represented by the 42,000 migrants who have traveled through the country in the past two months. They make up 2 percent of the population of 2.1 million, not 5 percent.
match_headline: Macedonian Police Clash With Migrants on Border With Greece

text: An article on Saturday about three firefighters killed in Washington misstated the focus of the master’s degree that one of the three, Andrew Zajac, was pursuing. He was researching the effects of herbicides on an endangered species of dragonflies, not fireflies.
match_headline: Three Killed in Washington Wildfire Are Mourned

text: An article on Monday about cases involving young immigrants and how they have overwhelmed the court system misstated, in some copies, the current status of two brothers who traveled from El Salvador to the United States in 2014. A Nassau County family court judge found that the facts were in order for the brothers, Brayan and José, to receive special immigrant juvenile status, but their application must be approved by the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services. The judge did not grant them special immigrant status.
match_headline: Immigration Crisis Shifts From Border to Courts

text: An article on Saturday about a man who fatally shot a guard and then himself in a federal building at 201 Varick Street in Manhattan included an outdated reference to the building. While it once housed an immigration detention center, the building now has only a service processing center, from which detainees are sent to other facilities.
match_headline: Gunman Kills Guard Then Himself at a Federal Building in Manhattan

text: A headline on Saturday about the Manhattan Theater Club’s 2015-16 season may have left the incorrect impression that the company had announced a new play for its 2015-16 season in response to criticism that the first seven plays were all by white men. As the article correctly noted, the eighth play, which is by a woman, had been in the planning stage before the criticism began.
match_headline: Internet Outcry Over Diversity Leads Manhattan Theater Club to Announce Season Details Early

text: An obituary on Saturday about the physicist Jacob Bekenstein misstated part of the name of the school that Dr. Bekenstein, who was born in Mexico, was attending when he became an American citizen in 1968. It was the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn, not the Polytechnic University of Brooklyn. (It became Polytechnic University in 1985 and is now New York University Polytechnic School of Engineering.)
match_headline: Jacob Bekenstein, Physicist Who Revolutionized Theory of Black Holes, Dies at 68

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a global stock market slide misstated, in one reference, Monday’s change in the Shanghai composite index. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it declined 8.5 percent, not 8.7 percent.
match_headline: A Plunge in China Rattles Markets Across the Globe

text: An article on Saturday about President Obama’s nuclear deal with Iran and the collection of environmental samples at Parchin, a military base outside Tehran, misstated the number of times that the International Atomic Energy Agency was permitted inside the base. Inspectors from the agency entered the base twice — in January and November 2005 — not once.
match_headline: Prospect of Self-Inspections by Iran Feeds Opposition to Nuclear Deal

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Wednesday about State Department positions around the world that do not allow Foreign Service officers to take their same-sex spouses with them referred incorrectly to Michael E. Guest, a former United States envoy to Romania. He was the State Department’s second-ever openly gay ambassador; he was not the second openly gay officer to become an ambassador.
match_headline: State Department Fights for Rights of Gay Envoys

text: An article on Saturday about satellite measurements of air pollution around Middle Eastern cities that have been mired in war and civil unrest misidentified the journal in which a paper on the topic was published. It is Science Advances, not Science.
match_headline: Study Finds Surprising Byproduct of Middle Eastern Conflicts: Cleaner Air

text: An article on Tuesday about a decision by the United States military to reopen a criminal inquiry into a series of at least 17 murders of Afghan civilians in 2012 and 2013 that officials there blamed on Army Special Forces team misstated the surname of the senior Afghan researcher for Human Rights Watch. She is Patricia Gossman, not Grossman.
match_headline: U.S. Army Reopens Criminal Inquiry Into Afghan Civilians’ Deaths

text: An article on Tuesday about the stark racial divide in how New Orleans residents view the city’s recovery since Hurricane Katrina hit in 2005 misstated the day of President Obama’s planned visit to New Orleans. It is Thursday, not today.
match_headline: Racially Disparate Views of New Orleans’s Recovery After Hurricane Katrina

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the ease with which Letitia James uses the courts to further her role as New York City’s public advocate misstated the number of lawsuits that Mayor Bill de Blasio filed when he held that position. It was three, not two.
match_headline: Letitia James’s Ease in the Courtroom Informs Her Role as Public Advocate

text: An entry in the pop music listings on Friday about a performance by the singer-poet Lydia Lunch referred incorrectly to the way in which she earned her nickname. It was by stealing food for — not from — local punk musicians.
match_headline: Pop & Rock Listings for Aug. 21-27

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the effects of the Mount Tambora eruption in 1815 misidentified the painter of a harbor scene depicting a vivid sky shadowed by ash clouds. He was Caspar David Friedrich, not David Caspar Friedrich.
match_headline: A Volcanic Eruption That Reverberates 200 Years Later

text: An obituary on Friday about the Rev. George M. Houser, a founder of the Congress of Racial Equality who was believed to be the last living member of the inaugural Freedom Ride, referred incorrectly to the civil rights leader Bayard Rustin, who also took part in that ride. While Mr. Rustin was a field director for CORE, he was not one of the organization’s founders.
match_headline: George Houser, Freedom Rides Pioneer and a Founder of CORE, Dies at 99

text: An article last Wednesday about the Chinese technique of smashing cucumbers, and its growing popularity among non-Chinese chefs, misspelled part of the name of a menu item at the Ippudo ramen restaurants in New York. It is yamitsuki goma kyuri, not yamitsuki goma yuri.
match_headline: Smashed Cucumber Salad Takes Manhattan

text: An article last Wednesday about Unesco’s designation of more than 1,200 Burgundy vineyards, or climats, as World Heritage sites misstated the era in which the climats’ borders began to be mapped out by Cistercian monks. It was the 12th century, not the fourth century.
match_headline: International Designation Is Sweet Victory for Burgundy

text: An article on July 8 about Islamic fighters from Chechnya who have joined the war in eastern Ukraine on the government side misspelled the surname of a co-founder of the Chechen battalions in Ukraine. The fighter, who was killed in February, was Isa Munayev, not Musayev. The error also appeared in a picture caption with the continuation of the article. A reader pointed out the error in an email only last week.
match_headline: Islamic Battalions, Stocked With Chechens, Aid Ukraine in War With Rebels

text: An article on Aug. 5 about Russia’s submission of a claim to a vast area of the Arctic Ocean misidentified the part of the ocean that would be subject to Moscow’s oversight if the United Nations committee that arbitrates sea boundaries accepts the claim. Russia would control the seabed of the area, not the waters above it.
match_headline: Russia Stakes New Claim to Expanse in the Arctic

text: An article on Saturday about the uncertainty surrounding The Daily News in the wake of Mortimer B. Zuckerman’s decision not to sell it misstated the circumstances surrounding Robert Maxwell’s purchase of the newspaper in 1991. It ended the strike against The Tribune Co., which had owned the publication. Mr. Maxwell’s tenure did not begin with a bitter labor battle.
match_headline: Daily News Struggles to Find Its Identity After Sale Is Called Off

text: An article on Wednesday about the USA television show “Mr. Robot” referred incompletely to a drop in its ratings. While next day ratings showed a decline to 1.3 million viewers from 1.7 million, live-plus-three-days data, which accounts for delayed viewing, also showed the viewership at 2.3 million, down from 2.8 million.
match_headline: Looking Back on ‘Mr. Robot’ and a Season of Hacker Drama

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the resignation of New York City’s film czar, Cynthia Lopez, misidentified the position Luis Castro currently holds and the one he will hold after Ms. Lopez leaves as the commissioner of the Office of Media and Entertainment. Mr. Castro is the first deputy commissioner of the office, not of Mayor Bill de Blasio’s administration, and he will fill Ms. Lopez’s post as the acting commissioner, not as the commissioner.
match_headline: New York City Film’s Czar Resigns

text: An article on Tuesday about the Charlie Parker Jazz Festival misidentified the drummer who played with the band led by the tenor saxophonist Joe Lovano. He is Lewis Nash, not Otis Brown III. And a cover picture with a capsule summary of the article misidentified a musician who performed at the festival. He is Vuyo Sotashe, not Michael Mwenso.
match_headline: Review: Charlie Parker Jazz Festival Subtly Recalls Its Inspiration

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the crossword puzzle creator Merl Reagle misidentified the puzzle of his that was published the day he and Will Shortz, the crossword puzzle editor of The New York Times, appeared in cartoon form in an episode of “The Simpsons,” and that included a 21-letter diagonal corresponding to the final notes of the show’s theme. It was Mr. Reagle’s syndicated puzzle; it was not that day’s Sunday Times puzzle, although that was featured in the episode and also contained references to “The Simpsons.”
match_headline: Merl Reagle, Whose Crossword Puzzles Delighted Clued-In Solvers, Dies at 65

text: A picture on Thursday with an article about changes in New Orleans 10 years after Hurricane Katrina was published in error, based on information from The Times’ photographic archives. The picture showed the St. Bernard Public Housing Development, not the B.W. Cooper housing project. (An accompanying front-page picture did show the rebuilt B.W. Cooper project.) The error first appeared in a picture caption on Nov. 22, 2005, with an article about damage to New Orleans’ public housing projects caused by Katrina.
match_headline: Seeing Life Outside New Orleans Alters Life Inside It

text: An article on Thursday about slowing sales of luxury goods to Chinese customers referred incorrectly to the head of investor relations and corporate communications at Coach, who commented on the situation. That executive, Andrea Shaw Resnick, is a woman.
match_headline: China’s Big Spenders Pull Back, as Stock Market Shudders

text: An article on Thursday about an agreement by five Gap apparel store brands to stop requiring employees to make themselves available for last-minute shifts misstated when the policy change will become effective. It is the end of next month, not the beginning of next year.
match_headline: Gap Says It Will Phase Out On-Call Scheduling of Employees

text: An article on Tuesday about the oceanographer Walter Munk referred incorrectly to La Jolla, the California community where the Scripps Institution of Oceanography is situated. It is a neighborhood within San Diego, not a town outside San Diego.
match_headline: Walter Munk, the ‘Einstein of the Oceans’

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about the findings of the Reproducibility Project, an assessment study of 100 published psychology papers, misspelled the surname of one of the researchers involved. She is Courtney Soderberg, not Soderbergh.
match_headline: Many Psychology Findings Not as Strong as Claimed, Study Says

text: A map on Friday with an article about a crackdown on immigrants from Colombia by the government of Venezuela misspelled the name of another South American country in some editions. It is Ecuador, not Equador.
match_headline: Colombians Flee Venezuela’s Crackdown on Immigrants

text: A headline on Friday with the About New York column, about the continuing ordeal of a Virginia woman 30 years after she was arrested on a gun charge at La Guardia Airport, misstated the location of the gun she was carrying. As the column correctly noted, it was in her luggage, not in a purse.
match_headline: How a Gun in a Suitcase Became a Permanent Ball and Chain

text: An article on the Square Feet page on Aug. 19 about redevelopment of land in Providence, R.I., that was formerly occupied by an interstate highway paraphrased incorrectly a comment by Joseph Azrack, chairman of the I-95 Redevelopment District Commission. He said he would be surprised if the commission did not have commitments for all of its land within five years — not that he “wouldn’t” be surprised if that were the case.
match_headline: Providence, R.I., Is Building on a Highway’s Footprint

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about back-to-school apps misstated a math equation. It is e to the power of i times pi is negative 1 — not e to the power of i times pi is 1.
match_headline: Video Feature: Back-to-School Apps for the Organized Student

text: Because of an editing error, an entry in the theater listings on Friday about the play “Mercury Fur” misidentified the website for New Group, which is producing it. It is thenewgroup.org, not signaturetheatre.org. (The play is at Pershing Square Signature Center.)
match_headline: Theater Listings for Aug. 28-Sept. 3

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Season 2 of the workplace reality television show “Human Resources,” which focuses on TerraCycle, a Trenton company, misspelled the given name of an executive producer. She is Anneka Jones, not Anneke.
match_headline: ‘Human Resources’: Reality TV About a Recycling Company

text: An article last Sunday about Film Fatales, a collective of female directors that addresses gender inequality in the movie industry, misidentified the location of Rhode Island Film Forum festival. It is held in Providence, not Newport. The article also incompletely rendered the title of the film Li Lu directed and was taking to the Las Vegas Film Festival and the Boonies International Film Festival in Pennsylvania. It is “There Is a New World Somewhere” not “A New World Somewhere.”
ref_headline: There Is a New World Somewhere
match_headline: The Film Fatales Collective Trains a Lens on Gender Inequality

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about art inspired by Hurricane Katrina rendered incorrectly the name of an artwork by Carlie Trosclair. It is “Fissure,” not “Fissure?”
match_headline: Ten Years After Katrina, New Orleans Museums Reckon With Recovery

text: An article last Sunday about the legacy of Helen Gurley Brown misstated the name of a television program that drew inspiration from Ms. Brown’s books. It is “Mad Men,” not “Mad Man.” The article also misstated part of the title of Eve Burton, the Hearst Corporation executive who is the co-executor of Ms. Brown’s will. She is a senior vice president, not a vice president.
match_headline: Who Owns Helen Gurley Brown’s Legacy?

text: An article on Monday about pressure on the Federal Reserve from groups with differing ideas on when the Fed should raise interest rates misidentified, in some editions, the group that organized the “Fed Up” campaign, which wants the Fed to keep rates low, to lower unemployment rates and to raise living standards. It is the Center for Popular Democracy, not the Center for Public Democracy.
match_headline: Challenged on Left and Right, the Fed Faces a Decision on Rates

text: An article on Aug. 21 about the rising number of recalls of organic products, using information from Stericycle, a company that handles recalls for businesses, misstated the proportion of recalls of organic products since 2012 that were related to bacterial contamination. It is 87 percent of such recalls, not “all” of them.
match_headline: Recalls of Organic Food on the Rise, Report Says

text: An obituary on Monday about the electrical engineer James L. Flanagan referred incorrectly to Richard M. Nixon, in whose last days as president Dr. Flanagan played a small role. Nixon resigned under threat of impeachment; he was not impeached.
match_headline: James L. Flanagan, Who Helped Make Computers Talk, Dies at 89

text: An obituary in some editions on Monday about the filmmaker Wes Craven misidentified the film of his that featured a dream sequence that inspired his “A Nightmare on Elm Street.” It is “Last House on the Left,” not “The Hills Have Eyes.” The obituary also misstated part of the name of the university from which Mr. Craven received a master’s degree in philosophy. It is Johns Hopkins, not John Hopkins.
match_headline: Wes Craven, Whose Slasher Films Terrified Millions, Dies at 76

text: An article on Saturday about the Republican presidential candidates’ response to China’s currency devaluation misspelled the given name of the president of China. He is Xi Jinping, not Jingping.
match_headline: China’s Vulnerability Is a Test for U.S. Presidential Candidates

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about a fishing boat that sank in the Sandy Hook Channel, using information from the Belford Seafood Co-Op, misstated the surname of the boat’s captain. He is Tom Andresen, not Anderson.
match_headline: New Jersey Police Find Sunken Fishing Boat, but Captain Remains Missing

text: An article on Tuesday about the lagging returns of the hedge fund Greenlight Capital misstated what the fund told its investors on Monday about its positions. The firm said it had pared back its positions, not that it was planning to do so.
match_headline: Greenlight Capital Down 14% for Year; David Einhorn Surveys Investors

text: An article on Monday about renovations at the Wadsworth Atheneum misstated the age of a female Roman torso in the museum’s collection. The object dates from the first to the second century A.D., not to 1000 A.D.
match_headline: The Wadsworth Atheneum in Hartford Puts Final Touches on a Comeback

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision by officials in San Antonio to expand the use of body cameras by sheriff’s deputies, using information from the county sheriff’s office, misstated, in some editions, the number of deputies who currently use such cameras. It is eight, not about 30.
match_headline: After a Killing, Body Cameras Are Expanded in San Antonio

text: An article in some copies on Saturday about the Yankees’ 15-4 victory over the Atlanta Braves misstated the number of games Yankees first baseman Mark Teixeira had missed since fouling a ball off his shin. It was eight, not seven. (Teixeira has now missed 13 of the Yankees’ 15 games since his injury.)
match_headline: With Two Big Bats Out of Lineup, Yanks Still Feast on Subpar Pitching

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Mets’ 9-5 victory over the Philadelphia Phillies misstated the number of home runs the Mets had hit in August at the time. It was 43, not 42. (The Mets finished with 45 in August.)
match_headline: With Nine Unanswered Runs, Mets Finish Sweep

text: An article on Aug. 23 about the wild cards awarded for entry into the United States Open misstated, in some editions, the academic classification of Jamie Loeb, one of the wild cards, at the University of North Carolina. She is a junior there, not a sophomore.
match_headline: Surprise Star of 2013 U.S. Open Receives No Break in Comeback

text: A picture on Tuesday with an article about genetically modifying diamondback moths, a farm pest, with DNA designed to kill female larvae carried an incorrect credit. The photograph, of two mating moths, was taken by Dan Olmstead of Cornell University; it was not provided by the Cornell Alliance for Science.
match_headline: Replacing Pesticides With Genetics

text: An obituary last Thursday about the civil rights activist Amelia Boynton Robinson referred imprecisely to her connection to the origins of the Voting Rights Act. While ideas for what became the act were discussed at her house in Selma, Ala., an early draft of the act was not written there.
match_headline: Amelia Boynton Robinson, a Pivotal Figure at the Selma March, Dies at 104

text: An obituary on Monday about the filmmaker Gary Keys misstated the name of the third of his three documentaries about Duke Ellington, released in 2006. It is “Reminiscing in Tempo,” not “Duke Ellington: Reminiscing in Tempo.” (“Duke Ellington: Reminiscing in Tempo” is an unrelated 1991 documentary directed by Robert Levi.)
match_headline: Gary Keys, Filmmaker Who Documented Duke Ellington, Dies at 81

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the artist Noah Davis referred incorrectly to exhibitions including works from the Museum of Contemporary Art that will be presented at the Underground Museum in Los Angeles, which he founded, under a three-year partnership. All of the shows had been planned by Mr. Davis, not just some of them.
match_headline: Noah Davis, 32, Artist and Founder of Underground Museum in Los Angeles, Dies

text: A map on Tuesday with the continuation of an article about the tens of thousands of migrants and asylum seekers flooding into Europe mislabeled, in some copies, the country on the northern border of Hungary. It is Slovakia, not the Czech Republic.
match_headline: Migrant Crisis Tests Core European Value: Open Borders

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about rising gun violence in Hartford, using information from the police, misspelled the given name of a man who was killed there this year. He was Everett Scott, not Everet.
match_headline: Police and Pastors Seek to Curb Violence as Hartford’s Homicide Rate Soars

text: An article on Thursday about the recent performance of some hedge fund firms gave an outdated figure for assets under management at one such firm, Millennium Management. Millennium says it has $31.5 billion of assets under management — not $27 billion, which was the figure the firm gave in a filing in March.
match_headline: Some Hedge Funds Prosper in Market Tumult

text: An obituary on Thursday about Barbara Brecht-Schall, a daughter of the playwright Bertolt Brecht and the guardian of his literary legacy, misstated part of the name of one of Brecht’s plays. It is “The Resistible Rise of Arturo Ui,” not “The Irresistible Rise of Arturo Ui.”
ref_headline: The Resistible Rise of Arturo Ui,
match_headline: Barbara Brecht-Schall, Guardian of Father’s Plays, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Thursday about the former United States ambassador William McCormick Blair Jr. referred incorrectly to Cyrus Hall McCormick, the inventor of the mechanical reaper. He was the brother of Mr. Blair’s great-grandfather; Mr. Blair was not a direct descendant.
match_headline: William McCormick Blair Jr., Envoy and Confidant of Adlai Stevenson, Dies at 98

text: Because of an editing error, the byline for an obituary on Thursday about the actor Dean Jones misstated the writer’s surname in some copies. He is Mike Flaherty, not Gallagher.
match_headline: Dean Jones, Affable Star in ‘Love Bug’ and a Disney Fixture, Dies at 84

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Wednesday about an Azerbaijani journalist known for her reports questioning the wealth of Azerbaijan’s president, who was sentenced to prison on tax evasion and other charges, misspelled her surname at several points. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she is Khadija Ismayilova, not Izmayilova.
match_headline: Azerbaijan: Journalist Critical of Leader Is Sentenced to 7 1/2 Years in Prison

text: An article on Thursday about a new ad-free subscription option from the streaming service Hulu erroneously included a cable company among those with which Hulu has struck deals to resell its service to their customers. Hulu has such a deal with Cablevision, but not with Charter Communications.
match_headline: Hulu Starts a Commercial-Free Option to Rival Netflix and Amazon

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the late-season rally that carried Jason Gore into golf’s FedEx Cup Playoffs misstated the number of golfers who will move on from the Deutsche Bank Championship at T.P.C. Boston, which concludes on Monday, to the BMW Championship in Lake Forest, Ill., the third of four playoff events. The top 70 players — not 75 — will advance. (Gore was 79th in the standings entering this weekend’s event.)
match_headline: At 41, Jason Gore Brings a Different Look, and Sensibility, to the FedEx Cup Playoffs

text: An article on Friday about art that focuses on manual labor misstated part of the address of the building where the Josep Maria Sert murals are. They are displayed on the lobby ceiling of 30 Rockefeller Plaza, not 30 Rockefeller Center. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Take a Labor Day Tour of Blue-Collar Art

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about DVDs devoted to dance misidentified the ballet that members of the Royal Ballet were shown performing. It is Frederick Ashton’s “Marguerite and Armand,” not his “La Valse.”
match_headline: Bounding Across Space and Time, via DVD

text: An obituary on Aug. 24 about John Correnti, a leader in the American steel industry, misstated the name of the college he attended in the 1960s. At that time, it was the Thomas S. Clarkson Memorial College of Technology — not Clarkson University, a name it adopted in 1984.
match_headline: John Correnti, Steel Industry Executive, Dies at 68

text: An article on Friday about the discordant response among European governments to the migration crisis misstated the Polish government’s position on Muslim migrants from Syria. Although the government has said that it preferred Christians, it did not say that it would accept only Christians.
match_headline: Migrant Chaos Mounts While Divided Europe Stumbles for Response

text: An article on Tuesday about determining the cost of health care at a Utah hospital misstated the given name of a researcher from Harvard Business School who praised the hospital’s efforts. He is Robert Kaplan, not Michael.
match_headline: What Are a Hospital’s Costs? Utah System Is Trying to Learn

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about testimony by a former adviser to Hillary Rodham Clinton before a House committee investigating Benghazi misidentified, in some editions, the man shown. Representative Trey Gowdy, the chairman of a House panel, was pictured climbing a set of stairs — not Jake Sullivan, who testified before the committee.
match_headline: Hillary Clinton Adviser Spends 7 Hours Before Benghazi Panel

text: An article on Aug. 28 about the Carlyle Group’s investments in hedge funds misstated the performance of one fund among commodity-focused hedge funds that have recently sustained losses. The fund, Black River Asset Management, which is owned by Cargill, was down 0.7 percent for the first half of the year; its losses were not “huge.”
match_headline: Carlyle Finds Hedge Funds Hazardous as Its Private Equity Business Dominates

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Eugenie Bouchard’s withdrawal from the United States Open tennis tournament because of a concussion misidentified the source who explained the details of her slip and fall in the locker room on Friday night. The information was from Canadian news reports — not from David Brewer, the U.S. Open tournament director.
match_headline: Eugenie Bouchard Withdraws From U.S. Open

text: An article on Tuesday about Simona Halep and Petra Kvitova’s advancing to the United States Open quarterfinals for the first time misstated, in some copies, the number of U.S. Open quarterfinals appearances that Flavia Pennetta, Roberta Vinci, Serena Williams and Venus Williams have made. It is 33, not 32. The article also described Pennetta’s U.S. Open history incorrectly. She advanced to the round of 8 for the sixth time in her last seven appearances, not in the last seven years. (She did not play in 2012.)
match_headline: Expecting Little, Simona Halep Finally Reaches Round of 8

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about Donald Young’s comeback to beat Viktor Troicki in the third round of the United States Open misstated, in some copies, the two instances in this tournament in which he overcame a two-set deficit to win. He did it in his first and third matches, not the second and third.
match_headline: U.S. Open 2015: Once Again, a Late Burst Propels a Spotlight Grabber

text: An article on Saturday about movies in competition at the Venice Film Festival misidentified Laurie Anderson’s first feature film. It is “Home of the Brave,” in 1986 — not “Heart of a Dog,” which will be screened at the festival.
match_headline: Venice Film Festival Offers a Chance to Watch Suffering, Then to Quaff Champagne

text: A report in the Off the Menu column last Wednesday about Rooftop at Bourbon, a new bar in Queens, misstated the year that the restaurant downstairs, Bourbon Street, opened. It was 1999, not 1998.
match_headline: Saucy in Brooklyn Isn’t Just for Catering

text: An obituary on Monday about Jean Darling, who appeared in the “Our Gang” comedy films as a child and in a 1934 film adaptation of the novel “Jane Eyre,” misidentified the author of the novel. It was Charlotte Brontë, not Emily Brontë. The obituary also misidentified the town in Germany where Ms. Darling died. It is Rödermark — not Rodgau, a neighboring town.
match_headline: Jean Darling, Child Actress in ‘Our Gang’ Series, Dies at 93

text: An obituary in some editions on Sunday and on Monday about Ben Kuroki, a decorated Japanese-American gunner in the Army Air Forces during World War II, referred incorrectly to medals he received. He received three Distinguished Flying Crosses, not three Distinguished Service Crosses. (He was awarded a single Distinguished Service Medal in 2005.) The obituary also described incorrectly the process under which Mr. Kuroki joined the Army Air Forces. He was accepted by a recruiter, not by a draft board official.
match_headline: Ben Kuroki Dies at 98; Japanese-American Overcame Bias to Fight for U.S.

text: An article on Saturday about a visit to Washington by King Salman of Saudi Arabia after months of tensions between Washington and Riyadh over the Iran nuclear agreement misstated Senator Benjamin L. Cardin’s position on the Foreign Relations Committee. He is the ranking Democrat, not the chairman.
match_headline: Obama and Saudi King Sidestep Dispute Over Iran Nuclear Deal

text: An article on Wednesday about Intel’s withdrawal as a sponsor of the Science Talent Search, a prestigious competition for American high school students, misstated the surname of the Harvard freshman who shared this year’s prize for his work in mathematics. He is Noah Golowich, not Gulwich. The article also misstated the surname of a spokeswoman for Intel. She is Gail Dundas, not Dudas.
match_headline: Intel to End Sponsorship of Science Talent Search

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Thursday about rising skepticism among venture capital firms about investing in online security start-ups misidentified a fund that invested in one such start-up, Tanium. It is TPG Growth, not TPG Capital.
match_headline: Scrutiny of Security Start-Ups May Signal Shift in Venture Funding

text: An article on Saturday about the reaction of baseball fans in Boston to the Red Sox’ decision to replace Don Orsillo, a popular broadcaster, misstated the given name of an off-season acquisition by the team who has not worked out well. He is Pablo Sandoval, not Pedro.
match_headline: Ouster of Don Orsillo, Beloved TV Announcer, Fuels a Red Sox Firestorm

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about a collaboration between Sotheby’s and the search engine and database Artsy on an online-only sale of contemporary art referred incorrectly to the involvement of the artists Richard Prince, Cory Arcangel and Jeff Elrod. Sotheby’s and Artsy are seeking works from them; they are not representing them. The report also misstated the year Artsy was founded. While it was made available to the public in 2012, it was founded in 2009, not in 2012.
match_headline: Sotheby’s Auction Coming to an Art App Near You

text: An article on Wednesday about Andrew Bolton’s succeeding Harold Koda as curator in charge of the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute quoted incorrectly from a comment by Mr. Bolton about a lesson he learned from Mr. Koda about the value of juxtaposing the old and the new. He said, “There’s almost a tonic effect,” not “an atomic effect.”
match_headline: Andrew Bolton Chosen to Lead the Met’s Costume Institute

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Aug. 26 with a theater review of a production of “Hamlet” in London, starring Benedict Cumberbatch, misspelled the director’s given name. As the review correctly noted, she is Lyndsey Turner, not Lindsey.
match_headline: Review: Benedict Cumberbatch in ‘Hamlet’

text: An essay on Sept. 1 about Dr. Oliver Sacks referred incorrectly to the way Dr. Sacks once lifted 600 pounds. He squatted 600 pounds; he did not dead lift 600 pounds. (He once dead lifted 525 pounds.)
match_headline: Oliver Sacks: Diverse Elements in Harmony

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts to stop the spread of invasive mussels referred incorrectly to Wicket, a dog that is trained to detect the scent of mussels. As an accompanying picture caption correctly noted, Wicket is female, not male.
match_headline: A Western Showdown With Mussels

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the actor Martin Milner, who starred in the television series “Route 66” and “Adam-12,” misidentified the network on which “Adam-12” was seen. It is NBC, not ABC. The obituary also referred incorrectly to the 1975 movie “Swiss Family Robinson,” in which Mr. Milner starred. It was made for television; it was not theatrically released.
match_headline: Martin Milner, Clean-Cut Star of ‘Route 66’ and ‘Adam-12,’ Dies at 83

text: An article on Thursday about the Mexican government’s conciliatory response to a report harshly criticizing its investigation into the disappearance of 43 college students last year misspelled the surname of the mother of one of the missing college students who said she had doubted the government’s account. She is Cristina Bustamante, not Bustamente.
match_headline: Report Renews Hope and Doubt on Missing Students in Mexico

text: A reporting credit on Wednesday with an article about China’s organization of a meeting of technology leaders in Seattle ahead of a state visit to the United States by President Xi Jinping misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a contributing researcher. He is Yufan Huang, not Hang.
match_headline: China Flexes Tech Muscles Before a State Visit

text: An article on Wednesday about the release from jail of the Kentucky county clerk, Kim Davis, misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the hometown of Linda Clark, a demonstrator outside the county jail where Ms. Davis was housed. It is Olive Hill, Ky., not Olive Hall.
match_headline: Kim Davis, Released From Kentucky Jail, Won’t Say if She Will Keep Defying Court

text: An article on Monday about a graphic novel series that represents the return of the television writer Judd Winick to his comic book roots misstated part of the name of the syndicate with which Mr. Winick once had a development deal. It is Universal Press Syndicate, not United Press Syndicate.
match_headline: Judd Winick’s Age-Appropriate Return to Comic-Strip Roots

text: An article on Thursday about start-ups that are challenging Bloomberg as a data and communications service for Wall Street misstated the age of Morgan Downey, the former Bloomberg executive who is building one such rival, Money.Net. He is 42, not 43.
match_headline: The Bloomberg Terminal, a Wall Street Fixture, Faces Upstarts

text: An article on Thursday about the men’s quarterfinals of the United States Open tennis tournament misstated the length of Kevin Anderson’s fourth-round match on Monday against Andy Murray. Anderson won in four sets, not five.
match_headline: Roger Federer and Stan Wawrinka Prey on Fatigue at U.S. Open

text: A picture caption on Aug. 31 in the preview section on the United States Open with an essay by a writer who is left-handed but learned to play tennis right-handed because of injuries misstated part of the name of the facility where he took lessons. As the article correctly noted, it is the Knickerbocker Field Club, not the Knickerbocker Tennis Club.
match_headline: Battling Arm Injuries, a Tennis Player Changes ... Hands

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the educator Thomas Sobol referred incorrectly to his appointment as New York State education commissioner in 1987. He was appointed by the State Board of Regents, not by Gov. Mario M. Cuomo.
match_headline: Thomas Sobol, 83, Dies; Education Advocate as New York State Commissioner

text: An article on Aug. 23 about a thwarted attack on a passenger train traveling from Amsterdam to Paris, as recounted by French officials, witnesses and the passengers who helped subdue the gunman, misstated the amount of ammunition he carried, using information from French officials. It was at least nine clips of cartridges, not nine cartridges. The same error appeared in an article on Aug. 26 about an announcement by Paris authorities that they were investigating the case as attempted murder in connection with a terrorist attack.
match_headline: A Shot, a Glimpse of an AK-47, and U.S. Servicemen Pounced on Gunman on Train to France

text: An article last Sunday about the future of the protest movement in Guatemala after it helped bring about the resignation of President Otto Pérez Molina misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a music producer and D.J. who took part in the movement. He is Sergio Bacini, not Bacino. The article also misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the editor of Nómada, an online magazine. He is Martín Rodriguéz Pellecer, not Pellicer.
match_headline: Guatemalans Ousted President Otto Pérez Molina. Now What?

text: A picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about Live Action Role Play, or LARPs, misidentified the man playing the role of the Duke in a LARP called “The Dance and the Dawn.” The actor, who is shown being slapped, is David Kotsonis, not John Isabella III. The article also misstated the number of LARPs available through Paracelsus Games that were written or co-written by Warren Tusk. It is four, not six.
match_headline: Becoming a Vampire, or Almost Anything Else, in Live Action Role Playing

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about two new movies that focus on the homeless misstated the title of the film that stars Richard Gere. The movie is “Time Out of Mind,” not “Time Out of My Mind.”
match_headline: ‘Time Out of Mind’ and ‘Shelter’: Next in Line at Cinema’s Soup Kitchen

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the drug-crime movie “Sicario” misidentified the film in which Benicio Del Toro is shown pointing a gun at a man. It is from “Traffic,” not “Sicario.”
match_headline: Emily Blunt Plunges Into the Drug War’s Morass in ‘Sicario’

text: An article last Sunday about a dispute over building a giant sports and entertainment complex in San Francisco misidentified the venue where the Golden State Warriors currently play their home games. It is the Oracle Arena, not the Oakland-Alameda County Coliseum.
match_headline: A Basketball Arena Battles for San Francisco’s Heart

text: An article last Sunday about a woman who wondered if she had not received a new job because she disclosed a pregnancy misstated the relevance of the Family and Medical Leave Act in the case. The act covers employees who have worked 1,250 hours in the 12 months before the start of a leave; it is not applicable to a potential new hire.
match_headline: When to Tell a Prospective Employer That You’re Pregnant

text: An article on Aug. 30 about restaurants in Siem Reap, Cambodia, attributed an erroneous distinction to the city. It is at least the fifth-largest Cambodian city by population, and ranked as high as third by some sources; it is not the second-largest.
match_headline: In Siem Reap, Cambodia, Local Fare Gets a Chance to Shine

text: A review on Aug. 30 about “The End of Tsarist Russia: The March to World War I and Revolution,” by Dominic Lieven, misstated the year of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, in which Germany forced concessions on the Bolsheviks. It was 1918, not 1917.
ref_headline: The End of Tsarist Russia: The March to World War I and Revolution,
match_headline: ‘The End of Tsarist Russia,’ by Dominic Lieven

text: An entry in the “This and That” feature on Page 98 this weekend about two new shows by the land artist Richard Long, using information from a publicist, misidentifies the material Long used for a drawing on display in his New York exhibition. It is red clay mud, not the River Avon mud he used as a child.
match_headline: Two Exciting New Fall Shows for Richard Long

text: An entry in the “This and That” feature on Page 96 this weekend about the favorite publications of the magazine-makers Jop van Bennekom and Gert Jonkers gives an outdated title for the book the two are writing. After the article had gone to press, the book’s publisher changed its title to “Fantastic Man: Men of Great Style and Substance” from “Fantastic Man: 72 Men of Great Style and Substance.”
match_headline: How To | Style Plants

text: An article on Page 164 this weekend about the actor Michael Fassbender, who will play Steve Jobs in the upcoming biopic about the Apple co-founder, misstates the reason for Fassbender’s reluctance to meet Rivka Galchen, the writer of the article, at the Apple store. It was because he did not want fans at the store to distract him from the interview, not because of his discomfort at the “Steve Jobs” promotional movie posters hung in the store. (At the time of his interview with Galchen, the posters did not exist.)
match_headline: Michael Fassbender, Nobody’s Fool

text: An article on Page 182 this weekend about the enduring cultural fascination with New York in the late 1970s and early 1980s, partly stoked by an interest in that era’s bleak realities, misstates part of the name of the institute that named AIDS in 1982. It is the Centers for Disease Control (not Center).
match_headline: Why Can’t We Stop Talking About New York in the Late 1970s?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 30 this weekend about Xavier University erroneously attributes a distinction to South Carolina State University. It is the only public historically black college in the state, not the only historically black college.
match_headline: A Prescription for More Black Doctors

text: An article on Aug. 30 about Serena Williams misidentified the tennis official she confronted at the U.S. Open in 2009 after she was called for a foot fault. The official was a lineswoman, not a chair umpire.
match_headline: The Meaning of Serena Williams

text: An article on Sept. 6 about Republican presidential candidates referred incorrectly to comments about foreign policy and neoconservatives made by Michael Gallagher, the coordinator of Scott Walker’s foreign policy team. He was giving his own views, not those of Walker.
match_headline: Between Iraq and a Hawk Base

text: Because of an editing error, the byline for a review on Sunday of a new contemporary art museum in Los Angeles, The Broad, misidentified the author in some editions. It was written by Holland Cotter, not Bernard Holland.
match_headline: Review: The Broad Is an Old-Fashioned Museum for a New Gilded Age

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about how the upheaval from the closing of lanes leading to the George Washington Bridge in New Jersey has extended to United Airlines misstated, in some editions, the day of the week a money-losing United flight left Newark for Columbia, S.C., an airport near the vacation home of David Samson, a former Port Authority chairman. It was Thursday, not Friday. The article also referred incorrectly to how long New Jersey’s current transportation commissioner, Jamie Fox, had been working for United when he attended a dinner with Mr. Samson and several United officials in 2011. He had been hired several years before, not “recently.” Because of an editing error, the article also misstated, in one instance, the year in which Mark Sokolich, the mayor of Fort Lee, N.J., made his first complaints about being punished for not supporting Gov. Chris Christie’s re-election. As noted elsewhere in the article, it was 2013, not 2014.
match_headline: Inquiry’s Trail: From George Washington Bridge to United’s Executive Offices

text: An article on Friday about the possible consequences for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee after it failed to block the Iran nuclear accord in Congress misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the organization where Dennis B. Ross, who said the group would be able to recoup after taking stock, is a distinguished fellow. It is the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, not the Washington Institute for Near East Studies.
match_headline: Influential Pro-Israel Group Suffers Stinging Political Defeat

text: An article on Friday about head-up displays in automobiles, which project data about the car’s performance into the driver’s view, misstated what the head-up display in an Audi showed in a demonstration at the dealership. It was the car’s speed in miles per hour (mph), not its gas consumption in miles per gallon (mpg).
match_headline: As Head-Up Displays Become Common, Distraction Becomes an Issue

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the former child actor Dickie Moore misstated the given name of the spokeswoman who confirmed his death. She is Helaine Feldman, not Helene. The obituary also referred imprecisely to the scene in the movie “Miss Annie Rooney” in which Mr. Moore kisses Shirley Temple, who was 14 at the time. Although it was widely publicized as Temple’s first on-screen kiss, she had actually been kissed in at least one earlier film, when she was a child actress.
match_headline: Dickie Moore, Child Actor Known for a Screen Kiss, Dies at 89

text: An obituary on Friday about the television producer Merv Adelson, and an accompanying picture caption, misstated his marital history. He was married and divorced four times, not three, and the television journalist Barbara Walters was his third wife, not his second. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated the year Vanity Fair magazine reported that Mr. Adelson was worth nearly $300 million. The magazine reported in 2013 that this had been the case in the early 1990s; it did not report his worth in the early 1990s.
match_headline: Merv Adelson, Las Vegas Developer-Turned-Daring TV Producer, Dies at 85

text: An article on Sunday about Kim Suozzi, a cancer victim who had chosen to have her brain preserved through cryonics, misstated the age of Michael Andregg when he donated to Ms. Suozzi’s fund-raising campaign. He was 31 at the time, not 36.
match_headline: A Dying Young Woman’s Hope in Cryonics and a Future

text: An article on Sunday about the football team at John Jay High School in San Antonio in the wake of a violent hit by two players on a referee misstated the winner of Friday night’s game between John Jay and Del Rio. It was Del Rio, not John Jay.
match_headline: Body Blow on Texas Referee Shakes School and Sport

text: An article on Saturday about a labor dispute between New Orleans and its firefighters misstated, in some editions, the number of firefighters who have died since the litigation over back pay began. It is 115, not 150.
match_headline: New Orleans Mayor Avoids House Arrest in Labor Dispute

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about Megan Barry’s winning the race for mayor in Nashville misstated, in some editions, the surname of Ms. Barry’s opponent. He is David Fox, not Cox.
match_headline: Megan Barry Becomes First Female Mayor of Nashville in Runoff

text: An article on Friday about new federal rules aimed at reducing food-borne illness in the United States misstated, using information from a lawyer for the Center for Science in the Public Interest, the dates that an inspection took place at a Peter Pan peanut butter factory and when a subsequent outbreak of Salmonella happened. The Food and Drug Administration inspected the plant in 2005, not 2007, and people were sickened with Salmonella the following year, in 2006, not “some months later.”
match_headline: U.S. Makes Final an Array of Rules on Food Safety

text: An article on Friday about the trial of three former leaders of the law firm Dewey & LeBoeuf misstated the source of an assertion that Steven Davis, the firm’s former chairman, told another Dewey employee to prevent the firm from breaching its loan terms with several big banks. That claim came in testimony from a prosecution witness, not from an email from Mr. Davis.
match_headline: Prosecutor in Dewey Case Appeals to Common Sense

text: A listing in the Transactions column in the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about a property for lease at 430 Broome Street misstated the approximate annual rent. It is $857,500, not $84,000.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Sunday by The Associated Press about the coming world cycling championships in Richmond, Va., misstated the timing of the event in 1986, when it was last held in the United States. It was held in August and September, after Greg LeMond won his first Tour de France in July — not when LeMond was “still a year away from winning the first of his three Tours.”
ref_headline: still a year away from winning the first of his three Tours.
match_headline: Afghans See American General as Crucial to Country’s Defense

text: A picture credit on Thursday with a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column about plans to present a Billie Holiday hologram at the Apollo Theater misstated the given name of the photographer. It was William Gottlieb, not Steve.
match_headline: Billie Holiday, via Hologram, Returning to the Apollo

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about the finale of “Key & Peele,” on Comedy Central, reversed the identities of the performers when quoting dialogue from the end show. It was Keegan-Michael Key, not Jordan Peele, who asked, “Want to go back?” and Mr. Peele, not Mr. Key, who replied, “Yeah, my girl’s expecting me.” The article also referred incorrectly to the character Meegan, portrayed by Mr. Peele. Though her age is not specified, she is older than a teenager.
match_headline: In ‘Key & Peele’ Finale, Two Performers Flaunt Their Range

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with an art review of “Picasso Sculpture,” at the Museum of Modern Art, misidentified the museum gallery in which “Bust of a Woman” is displayed. It is in the section labeled the Boisgeloup Sculpture Studio, 1930-32, not Monument to Apollinaire, 1927-1931.
match_headline: Review: Picasso, Completely Himself in 3 Dimensions

text: An article on Sept. 9 about a report warning that vast gaps in data on older people threaten to undercut the United Nations’ new goals for raising living standards omitted, in some editions, Sweden from a list of the countries found to be the top 10 places for the elderly to live, and erroneously included Denmark. Sweden is No. 3 on the list, and Denmark, at No. 11, did not make the top 10. A headline in some editions misstated the source of the report. It was by HelpAge International, not the United Nations.
match_headline: Older People Are Invisible in Key Data, Study Warns

text: An article on Sept. 8 on rail bikes, metal vehicles that run on railroad tracks and are powered like bicycles, referred incorrectly to the stretch of track in the Adirondacks used by the bikes. It is used a few times a year by maintenance vehicles and other non-passenger-bearing railroad cars. It is not formally abandoned.
match_headline: Rail Biking Arrives in Adirondacks, but Future of Track Is in Doubt

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about how a subway derailment led to further calls by the chairman of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority for increased funding misstated the year that the chairman, Thomas F. Prendergast, was reappointed by Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo. It was this year, not 2014.
match_headline: M.T.A. Chief Presses New York City for Funding After G Train Derails

text: An article on the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about cities adding convention hotels misstated, in some copies, the job title of Lauro Ferroni of the real estate services firm JLL, who commented on the trend. Mr. Ferroni is the senior vice president and global head of research for the hotel and hospitality group, not the senior vice president and global head of the group over all.
match_headline: Looking for Conventions, Cities Add Hotel Rooms

text: An article on Monday about Novak Djokovic winning men’s singles at the United States Open misstated, in some editions, his record against Andy Murray at Wimbledon. While he has faced Murray there, he has not beaten him.
match_headline: Novak Djokovic Defeats Roger Federer to Win U.S. Open

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Yankees’ 4-1 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays misspelled the given name of a Rays player whose slow roller went for a hit in the second inning. He is Asdrubal Cabrera, not Asdrubel.
match_headline: Dormant for Eight Innings, Yankees Erupt in the Ninth

text: An article in some editions on Aug. 30 about the Jets’ 28-18 victory over the Giants in a preseason N.F.L. game misidentified the Jets receiver who slipped behind coverage to snare an 18-yard touchdown pass in the first quarter. He is Eric Decker, not Brandon Marshall.
match_headline: Ryan Fitzpatrick Finds Rhythm as Jets’ Offense Shows a Pulse

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Fred DeLuca, a founder of the Subway sandwich chain, using information from a spokeswoman, misstated the given name of Mr. DeLuca’s son, who survives him. He is Jonathan DeLuca, not John.
match_headline: Fred DeLuca, Hands-on Co-Founder of Subway Sandwich Chain, Dies at 67
