text: A report in the In Brief column on Tuesday about vaccinations in the United States misstated the number of hospitalizations that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated were prevented by vaccines over the past two decades. It is 21 million, not 21,000.
match_headline: 732,000: American Lives Saved by Vaccination

text: An article and accompanying picture caption last Thursday about WME/IMG, the entertainment and sports management company that now owns, operates or represents 13 fashion weeks around the world, misidentified the location of Skylight Clarkson Sq, where many fashion shows take place. It is in SoHo, not TriBeCa.
match_headline: Fashion Week, Reinvented

text: An article last Thursday about Brandon Maxwell, Lady Gaga’s stylist, referred incompletely to the origin of the “meat dress” worn by the pop singer at the 2010 MTV Video Music Awards. While Nicola Formichetti styled the ensemble and Mr. Maxwell assisted in the fitting, the dress was designed by Franc Fernandez.
match_headline: A Fashion Week Debut, With a Little Help From Lady Gaga

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Syria’s role as an arena for diplomacy for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia misspelled, in some editions, the name of the Ukrainian city from which the lead correspondent, Neil MacFarquhar, reported. It is Lviv, not Liviv.
match_headline: Putin Sees Path to Diplomacy Through Syria

text: An article on Saturday about the Spee Club at Harvard moving to admit women misstated the number of elite all-male clubs at the university. There are eight, including the Spee, not nine.
match_headline: With an Invitation, a Gender Barrier at Harvard Falls

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the death of Adam Purple, a Lower East Side gardener and activist, misspelled the surname of an artist whose work Mr. Purple’s so-called Garden of Eden was compared to. She is Agnes Denes, not Dennis. The article also misstated the timing of a protest in which Mr. Purple’s supporters began creating trails of purple footprints leading to the site of the garden. While one trail may have been created before the garden’s destruction, the campaign took place afterward to call attention to its loss.
match_headline: Adam Purple, Eccentric Environmentalist and Gardener in New York, Dies at 84

text: An article on Tuesday about a concert being held at Madison Square Garden in the hours before a papal Mass there misstated how New York City distributed tickets for Pope Francis’ visit. There were 80,000 tickets available through one lottery, not 40,000 tickets through two lotteries.
match_headline: Celebrity-Filled Show to Precede Pope Francis’ Mass at Madison Square Garden

text: An article on Thursday about the brewer Anheuser-Busch InBev’s bid to take over a rival, SABMiller, misstated, in some copies, the time period over which SABMiller’s shares have fallen more than 11 percent. It is 12 months, not 12 years.
match_headline: Anheuser-Busch InBev Approaches SABMiller on Possible Takeover

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Sept. 8 about the Yankees’ 8-6 victory over the Baltimore Orioles misstated, in some copies, the elbow in which Yankees pitcher Nathan Eovaldi has inflammation. It is his right elbow, not his left.
match_headline: Greg Bird’s Walk Aids Yankees, and His Homer Wins Game

text: An article on Sept. 7 about the ways Yoenis Cespedes electrified the Mets and their fans since arriving in a trade misstated the number of seasons that Mets reliever Jerry Blevins played with Cespedes on the Oakland Athletics. It was two, not three.
match_headline: Yoenis Cespedes Wows the Mets Underhand, Overhand and Many Other Ways

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the baseball roundup on Sept. 3, about the Toronto Blue Jays’ 5-1 victory over the Cleveland Indians, misidentified the location of the game in some copies. It was Toronto, not Cleveland.
match_headline: Yankees Bombard Braves With 21 Hits and Finish Three-Game Sweep

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Taiwan’s pre-eminent performance group, Cloud Gate Dance Theater, referred imprecisely to Taiwan at two points and in a subheading. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, the status of Taiwan, an island off mainland China, is in dispute; it is a separately governed territory that is recognized as part of China. Neither China nor Taiwan claims that it is a separate country.
match_headline: Cloud Gate Dance Theater: A Roving, Bounding Symbol of Taiwan

text: An article on Monday about the imposition of temporary border restrictions by Germany as record numbers of migrants arrive misspelled the surname of the German interior minister, who said it was “desperately necessary” for Germany to limit the number of people coming into the country. He is Thomas de Maizière, not de Mazière. The error was repeated in a picture caption with the continuation of the article. Because of editing errors, that caption and a second one, on the front page, misstated, in some editions, the day on which the events described took place. It was Sunday, not Saturday, that a vessel carrying Syrian and Afghan refugees deflated and a German police officer inspected a Syrian man at a border.
match_headline: Germany Orders Curbs at Border in Migrant Crisis

text: An article on Friday about a White House visit by three Americans who foiled a terrorist attack in France misstated the name of the university attended by Anthony Sadler, one of the heroes. It is California State University, Sacramento, not California State University.
match_headline: A Hero’s Welcome at the White House

text: An article on Thursday about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s plans to help poor schools included an outdated figure for the amount of money in existing education funding that New York City is redirecting toward an effort to add social services and improve results at the city’s 94 lowest-performing schools. It is $85 million a year, not $113.5 million.
match_headline: De Blasio’s Plan to Lift Poor Schools Comes With High Costs and Big Political Risks

text: An article on Monday about Taylor Harry Fritz and Brandon Holt, competitors in junior events at the United States Open whose mothers were professional tennis players, misstated the year Holt and his doubles partner, Riley Smith, will be freshmen at the University of Southern California. It is next year, not this fall.
match_headline: Top Juniors Share Court Pedigrees

text: An article on July 12 about Eritrean riders competing in the Tour de France misstated the relationship between Eritrea and Ethiopia when Eritrea was an Italian colony. Eritrea and Ethiopia were separate entities; Eritrea was not part of Ethiopia at the time. (Eritrea was part of Ethiopia from 1952 to 1993.) This correction was delayed by research.
match_headline: At Tour de France, Riders From Eritrea Hope to Blaze a Grueling Trail for a Continent

text: Because of an editing error, a dance review on Friday about a performance in Brooklyn Borough Hall that was part of the BEAT Festival omitted a word from the title. It is “Dancehall in Borough Hall,” not “Dancehall in Hall.”
match_headline: Review: Blacka Di Danca Shakes His Way Through Borough Hall

text: A reporting credit was omitted from an article on Wednesday about Egypt’s rejection of criticism from Mexico over an accidental airstrike by an Egyptian military helicopter that killed eight Mexican tourists. Merna Thomas contributed reporting from Cairo, and Elisabeth Malkin from Mexico City.
match_headline: Egypt Rejects Criticism Over Airstrike That Killed Mexican Tourists

text: An article on Friday about conservative lawmakers on the far right questioning John Boehner’s resolve to stand up to President Obama over federal funding for Planned Parenthood misstated the state that was represented by Nathaniel Banks, who was elected speaker in 1856 after a lengthy voting process. It was Massachusetts, not Maine.
match_headline: John Boehner, Strong Abortion Foe, Is Imperiled by the Like-Minded

text: An article last Sunday about the Michigan State Dairy Store, an ice cream shop in East Lansing, Mich., that has a flavor named after every Big Ten football team, misstated the surname of Michigan State’s quarterback. He is Connor Cook, not Clark.
match_headline: At Michigan State, Thriving on Saturdays With Help of Sundaes

text: An article this weekend about the Mass that Pope Francis is to celebrate on Friday at Madison Square Garden describes incorrectly his plans after the event, using information from the Archdiocese of New York. While he had intended to greet viewers in an overflow theater, after a change in schedule, he will no longer do so.
match_headline: For Pope Francis’ Mass at Madison Square Garden, God Is in the Details

text: An article last Sunday about the movie “Black Mass,” which focuses on the story of the Boston crime boss Whitey Bulger, referred incorrectly, based on an interview with a source, to the former Bulger hit man, Kevin Weeks. Mr. Weeks did not show up on the set of “Black Mass” and was not there trying to sell one of Mr. Bulger’s old belt buckles.
match_headline: ‘Black Mass’ Resurrects Boston’s Long Memories of Whitey Bulger

text: An article last Sunday about “Allegiance,” a musical about the internment of Japanese-Americans during World War II, misidentified the location of the Heart Mountain camp where the grandparents of the actor Greg Watanabe, who is in the show, were held in World War II. It was in Wyoming, not Colorado.
match_headline: This Broadway Season, Diversity Is Front and Center

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the coming dance season misidentified the festival that will feature Miguel Gutierrez’s “Age & Beauty” trilogy. It is Crossing the Line, not Performa.
match_headline: At Performa and Crossing the Line, Barreling Through the Fourth Wall

text: An article last Sunday about this season’s acting breakthroughs in film referred incorrectly to Geza Rohrig’s professional history. Mr. Rohrig, who stars in “Son of Saul,” graduated from the Jewish Theological Seminary of America, but he did not teach there.
match_headline: Breakthrough Performances of the Fall Season

text: A picture caption last Sunday with the New Season listings for classical music misstated part of the name of the company that will present “Charlie Parker’s Yardbird” at the Apollo Theater.” It is Gotham Chamber Opera, as the listings note, not Gotham Chamber Choir.
match_headline: Classical Music Listings for the Fall Season and Beyond

text: A picture caption on Sept. 6 with the cover article about Havasu Falls misstated the location of the falls. It is near Grand Canyon National Park, not “in a remote portion” of the park.
match_headline: Within the Grand Canyon, the Lure of Havasu Falls

text: A news analysis last Sunday misstated the name of a cartoon character displayed at a Moscow diner. He is Porky Pig, not Porky the Pig.
match_headline: Why Russians Hate America. Again.

text: An article in some editions on Friday about a hearing at which the federal trial of United States Senator Robert Menendez of New Jersey was delayed misstated the way the senator described a woman he was helping to secure a visa to enter the United States. According to email records cited in the indictment of Mr. Menendez and a longtime friend, Dr. Salomon Melgen, Mr. Menendez told his staff he was helping a woman in Spain related to Dr. Melgen obtain her visa; he did not describe her as Dr. Melgen’s niece. (Prosecutors were posing a hypothetical statement when they referred to her as a niece in court on Thursday.)
match_headline: Trial for Robert Menendez, New Jersey Senator, Is Delayed

text: An article on Thursday about a partnership between the American ride-hailing service Lyft and Didi Kuaidi, a Chinese counterpart, misstated, using information from Lyft, the region that 5.6 million Americans visited in 2014. It was all of Asia, not just China.
match_headline: Lyft Announces Deal With Didi Kuaidi, the Chinese Ride-Hailing Company

text: An article on Wednesday about the golf announcer David Feherty’s moving from CBS Sports to NBC and Golf Channel misspelled, in some editions, part of the name of an island off the coast of Scotland from which curling stones are cut, which Feherty said he could see from his bedroom in Northern Ireland. It is Ailsa Craig, not Alisa.
match_headline: David Feherty Moves From CBS to NBC and Golf Channel

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Tuesday about the Mets’ 4-3 victory over the Miami Marlins misstated, in some copies, the result of a 2007 series between the Mets and the Atlanta Braves, which preceded the Mets’ September collapse that season. While the Mets won the series, it was not a sweep.
match_headline: Yoenis Cespedes Uses Bat, and Tape, to Aid Another Win

text: An article on Tuesday about deep-sea exploration misstated the type of weapon used to damage a submarine sunk near the entrance to Pearl Harbor by the American destroyer Ward. It was a four-inch, 50-caliber naval gun, not a mortar.
match_headline: Do Humans Have a Future in Deep Sea Exploration?

text: An entry in the Spare Times for Children listings in some editions on Friday about the Shinnyo Lantern Floating for Peace event on Sunday, at Hearst Plaza at Lincoln Center, misidentified the Buddhist organization that is sponsoring it. It is Shinnyo-en, not the Shinnyo Center for Meditation and Well-Being.
match_headline: Spare Times for Children for Sept. 18-24

text: An article last Tuesday about the accidental killing of Mexican tourists by an Egyptian military helicopter referred imprecisely to the location of the tourists just before the attack. While they were near Bahariya, a common staging ground for tours of the White Desert, a landscape of monumental chalk rock formations, they had not yet reached the White Desert itself. And an accompanying picture caption misidentified the location of the attack. It was near Bahariya, not in the White Desert.
match_headline: Egyptian Military Fires on Mexican Tourists During Picnic

text: An article on Friday about a lawsuit filed in New Orleans that accused judges and court officials of preying on poor people misstated the number of plaintiffs in the case. There are six, not five.
match_headline: Suit Alleges ‘Scheme’ in Criminal Costs Borne by New Orleans’s Poor

text: An article on Friday about automakers’ concerns that software giants like Google and Apple may challenge the industry as software becomes more critical in vehicles misattributed a quotation about Google’s plans. It was Philipp Justus, a Google vice president — not John Krafcik, who runs the company’s self-driving car program — who said, “Google is not a car manufacturer and does not intend to become one.” The article also described the company Foxconn incorrectly. It is a Taiwanese-owned company that manufactures iPhones in China; it is not a Chinese company.
ref_headline: Google is not a car manufacturer and does not intend to become one.
match_headline: Apple and Google Create a Buzz at Frankfurt Motor Show

text: An article on Saturday about a campaign to retain the carried-interest tax break, which benefits mostly hedge fund and private equity executives, misstated the number of lobbyists at the Private Equity Growth Capital Council, which has been lobbying Congress on behalf of the tax break. The council has two lobbyists, not 12.
match_headline: Carried-Interest Tax Break Divides Again, After Trump Revives the Issue

text: An article on Saturday about Niegel Smith, the new artistic director of the Flea Theater in Manhattan, misstated part of the name of the theater where Mr. Smith is directing Taylor Mac’s “Hir” this fall. It is Playwrights Horizons (not Horizon). The article also referred incorrectly to the play “Student Body,” which will be presented by the Flea. It is about college students, not high school students.
match_headline: The Flea’s New Artistic Director Is Dreaming Big

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about the saxophonist Jon Irabagon misstated the size of the group he recently appeared with at the Jazz Standard in Manhattan. It was a quartet, not a quintet.
match_headline: Jon Irabagon Paints Tradition in New Hues

text: An obituary in some copies on Sunday about the author Jackie Collins referred incorrectly to Oscar Lerman, to whom she was married for 27 years, until he died in 1992. He was her second husband, not her first. (Her first marriage, which ended in divorce after four years, was to Wallace Austin.) The obituary also misstated the sequence in which some of Ms. Collins’s books were published. “Hollywood Wives: The New Generation” was published before — not after — “Hollywood Divorces.”
match_headline: Jackie Collins, Best-Selling Novelist of Hollywood, Dies at 77

text: An editorial on Sunday about the prison at Guantánamo Bay incorrectly described the status of a prisoner, Mohamedou Ould Slahi. He has not been cleared for release.
match_headline: How to Close Guantánamo

text: An article on Sunday about the high number of suicides among a Marine battalion that served in Afghanistan misidentified the association that sponsored a 2014 study of 204,000 veterans on post-traumatic stress disorder. It is the American Psychiatric Association, not the American Psychological Association.
match_headline: In Unit Stalked by Suicide, Veterans Try to Save One Another

text: A reporting credit was omitted for the Saturday Profile article, about Erison Turay, who leads a soccer team of Ebola survivors from Sierra Leone. Tommy Trenchard contributed from Kenema, Sierra Leone.
match_headline: In Sierra Leone, Giving the Stigma of Ebola a Good, Swift Kick

text: An article on Friday about a White House campaign to encourage legal immigrants to become citizens gave an outdated name for the association led by Alfonso Aguilar, who commented on the campaign as a former official of the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services. He leads the American Principles Project’s Latino Partnership; it is no longer the Latino Partnership for Conservative Principles.
match_headline: White House Campaign Urges Legal Immigrants to Become (Voting) Citizens

text: An article on Tuesday about the findings of a survey measuring sexual assault at 27 universities misstated the name of the organization that commissioned the survey. It is the Association of American Universities, not the American Association of Universities.
match_headline: 1 in 4 Women Experience Sex Assault on Campus

text: An article on Monday about Volkswagen’s decision to stop selling models of diesel vehicles equipped with software to disable their emissions control systems misstated the name of an emission that, while an air pollutant, also acts to enhance performance and fuel economy. It is nitrogen oxide, not nitrous oxide.
match_headline: Volkswagen to Stop Sales of Diesel Cars Involved in Recall

text: An article on Monday about the discovery of apps with malicious code in the Apple App Store misspelled the name of a Chinese online security company that said it had found 300 infected apps. It is Qihoo, not Qohoo.
match_headline: Apple Confirms Discovery of Malicious Code in Some App Store Products

text: Because of an editing error, the N.F.L. roundup on Monday misstated, in some copies, the number of points the Baltimore Ravens scored in a loss to the Oakland Raiders. The Ravens scored 33 points — not 3 — to the Raiders’ 37.
match_headline: Baltimore Ravens at Oakland Raiders Preview

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Mets’ 5-1 victory over the Yankees misidentified, in some copies, the Mets player who scored on James Pazos’s wild pitch in the eighth inning. The score was by Eric Young Jr. — who entered the game as a pinch-runner for Daniel Murphy, who had tripled — not Murphy.
match_headline: Mets Get a Taste of the Postseason, and Savor It, Against the Yankees

text: An article on Monday about Jason Day’s victory in the BMW Championship golf tournament in Lake Forest, Ill., described Day’s final hole incorrectly. He hit a shot to the left fringe — not to the edge of the green — then left a chip — not a putt — for eagle just short of the cup.
match_headline: Jason Day Holds On to Win, and Grabs Top Ranking

text: An obituary on Thursday about the director Melvin Bernhardt referred incorrectly to a 1984 television version of “Mister Roberts,” which he directed. It was a live broadcast, not a television movie.
match_headline: Melvin Bernhardt, Tony-Winning Director Who Helped Stars Shine, Dies at 84

text: An article on Monday about Pope Francis’ circumspection in avoiding pointed references to politics during his visit to Cuba referred incorrectly to José Daniel Ferrer, the head of the Patriotic Union of Cuba, the nation’s largest dissident organization, who said dissidents had hoped for a public meeting with the pope. He is Mr. Ferrer, not Mr. Daniel.
match_headline: Pope Francis Careful in Navigating Cuban Politics

text: An article on Wednesday about a plea by two Hong Kong democracy activists for President Obama to take up their cause in his meetings with President Xi Jinping of China misidentified, in some editions, the charges filed against one of the activists, Joshua Wong, that arose from widespread protests in the territory last year. Mr. Wong was charged only with inciting and participating in an unlawful assembly — not contempt of court and obstruction of the police. (He was charged with contempt in April and with obstruction in July, in an unrelated incident.) The article also misstated, in some editions, the month that Mr. Wong was charged with incitement. It was last month, not September.
match_headline: Two Activists Visiting U.S. Call for Rights in Hong Kong

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a decision by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court to temporarily suspend the law license of the state’s attorney general, Kathleen G. Kane, misstated, in some copies, the number of Democratic state senators who would have to agree for her to be ousted under state law. It is several, not “more than a dozen.”
match_headline: Kathleen Kane, Pennsylvania Attorney General, Is Suspended From Practicing Law

text: A picture caption in some editions on Sunday with the Sports of The Times column, about the Yankees and Mets playing each other with one eye on the baseball playoffs, misstated, in some copies, the inning in Saturday’s game in which Michael Pineda, the Yankees’ starting pitcher, was relieved. It was the sixth, not the seventh.
match_headline: Mets and Yankees Clash With One Eye on October

text: A report in some editions on Monday in the Sports Briefing column about the Devils’ 2-0 loss to the Boston Bruins in the N.H.L. preseason opener for both teams misstated the surname of the player who scored the Bruins’ two goals. He is Matt Irwin, not Irvin.
match_headline: Devils Lose Preseason Opener

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a pledge of about $90 million by the Dutch government toward the purchase of two Rembrandt portraits it wants to secure for the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam referred incorrectly to the museum. While the collection there is mostly state-owned, the museum is managed independently; it is not state-run.
match_headline: Rembrandt Portraits May Come Home, for Record Price, With Government Help

text: An editorial on Sept. 23 about Republicans and Muslims incorrectly described an encounter between Senator John McCain and a woman at a town-hall meeting in 2008. When she said Barack Obama was an Arab, Mr. McCain shook his head and said, “No, Ma’am.” He did not let the claim go uncorrected.
match_headline: The Republican Attack on Muslims

text: A picture on Thursday with the continuation of an obituary about Yogi Berra, the Hall of Fame Yankees catcher, was published in error. It showed Jackie Robinson of the Brooklyn Dodgers being called out at home after a tag by New York Giants catcher Ray Katt on a failed squeeze bunt attempt by Clem Labine on May 13, 1956. It did not show Robinson’s famous steal of home against Berra and the Yankees in Game 1 of the 1955 World Series.
match_headline: Yogi Berra, Yankee Who Built His Stardom 90 Percent on Skill and Half on Wit, Dies at 90

text: An article on Sept. 13 about the divide between Eastern and Western Europe over how to react to the migrant crisis misstated the extent of damage caused by a fire at the only refugee relocation center in Estonia, where an agreement to accept fewer than 200 refugees over the next two years set off protests. The refugee center was severely damaged, but did not burn to the ground.
match_headline: Eastern Bloc’s Resistance to Refugees Highlights Europe’s Cultural and Political Divisions

text: An article on Tuesday about a return visit to Cuba for the first time in years by some of the island’s exiles, lured by the presence of the pope, misstated part of the former name of the yacht club that the exiles visited. It was the Havana Biltmore Yacht and Country Club (not County).
match_headline: Pope Lures Exiles Back to Cuba, Where a Lifetime Ago Is Yesterday

text: An article on Sept. 11 about Brazil’s national reckoning with the missteps that turned an economic boom into a crisis misstated the age of President Dilma Rousseff. She is 67, not 66.
match_headline: As a Boom Fades, Brazilians Wonder How It All Went Wrong

text: An article on Sept. 10 about a ban imposed by Israel on two Palestinian groups that protested at a contested holy site in Jerusalem misstated the day Israel outlawed the groups. It was Wednesday, Sept. 9, not Monday, Sept. 7.
match_headline: Israel Bans 2 Muslim Groups That Protest at Jerusalem Holy Site

text: A reporting credit on Sept. 16 with an article about Hungary’s blocking of a key crossing point on the first day of an intensified crackdown on refugees and migrants misidentified the town from which two correspondents, Emmarie Huetteman and Katarina Johannsen, contributed. They reported from the Frauenstein that is in Austria, not the one in Germany.
match_headline: Hungary Blocks Migrants in Border Crackdown

text: An article on Thursday about crowd reactions to Pope Francis’ visit to Washington referred incorrectly to a visit by Pope John Paul II, in 1979. He was the first pope to visit Washington, not the first to visit the United States. (That was Pope Paul VI, who visited in 1965.)
match_headline: Pope Francis Gets Ecstatic Reception in Washington

text: A news analysis article on Monday about the effect Pope Francis’ visit to Washington could have on politicians on the left and right misstated, in some copies, the number of Republican presidential candidates who are Catholics. There are seven, not six. (Martin O’Malley, a Democratic candidate, is also Catholic.)
match_headline: Pope Francis’ U.S. Visit Could Benefit Both Left and Right

text: An article on Sept. 17 about a proposal to establish areas in Times Square exclusively for topless painted women, costumed characters and other cash solicitors misspelled the surname of the president of the Times Square Alliance. He is Tim Tompkins, not Tomkins.
match_headline: Special Zones Proposed to Limit Toplessness in Times Square

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an obituary about the filmmaker Marcin Wrona, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the woman shown with him. She is Olga Szymanska, his wife and a producer of his film “Demon” — not Agnieszka Zulewska, an actress in that film.

Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Pope Francis’ lunch with the homeless in Washington rendered incorrectly in some editions a comment Francis made to the diners. He said “Buen apetito” in Spanish — not “Buon appetito” in Italian. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: In Lunch for the Homeless, a Sacred Mission for Pope Francis

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about investors who are pursuing projects aimed at expanding water supplies misspelled, in some editions, the surname of an executive at Water Asset Management, which backs such projects. He is Disque D. Deane Jr., not Dean. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Investors Are Mining for Water, the Next Hot Commodity

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings in some editions on Friday about two street fairs in the Chelsea neighborhood of Manhattan misstated the date of the London Terrace fair. It is today, not Sunday.
match_headline: Spare Times for Sept. 25-Oct. 1

text: A picture caption on Page 96 this weekend with an article about four antiquities dealers who are installing a show of their wares in New York in October in an effort to win over more American collectors misidentifies the owner of a wooden virgin sculpture shown, and refers incorrectly to the sculpture and to other objects in the photograph. The virgin is the property of the gallery Antichita’ Alessandra Di Castro, not that of Galerie J. Kugel. And a decision on which of the objects will be exhibited in New York has not been made; therefore it is not necessarily the case that all of them will be shown.
match_headline: The World’s Most Expensive Pop-Up Shop

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about Roy Sommer, who is 20 coaching victories from becoming the American Hockey League’s career leader, misidentified, in some editions, the player he was shown instructing at a San Jose Barracuda training session. He is Raffi Torres, not Chris Tierney.
match_headline: A Hockey Life Full of Turns in the Minors

text: A picture caption on Sept. 13 with an article about women artists and the male subjects they depict misstated the name of a town in Georgia where a picture of black male rodeo riders entitled “Cowboys” was taken by Deana Lawson. It is Newnan, not Newman.
match_headline: Giants at Cowboys Matchup

text: An article on Sept. 13 about college tuition referred incorrectly to CUNY when describing a program that helped improve the graduation rates of its community colleges. It is the City University of New York (not Universities). The article also referred incorrectly to a measure of income in a comparison of 1974 income and current income when adjusted for inflation. It is median family income, which has risen to about $64,000 a year from $62,000 in 1974, not median household income. And the article also described incorrectly the change in median family income over the past 40 years. It has risen slightly, not fallen.
match_headline: Is College Tuition Really Too High?

text: A picture caption with an article on Sept. 13 about architecture on the University of Cincinnati campus misspelled the name of the architectural firm that worked on the University of Cincinnati’s Richard E. Lindner Center. It is Glaserworks, not Glazier Works.
match_headline: If You Build It, They Will Come ... Won’t They?

text: An article last Sunday about living in Midwood, Brooklyn, referred incorrectly to the residence of Linda S. Goodman, the executive director of the Midwood Development Corporation. She lives in Jamaica Estates, Queens; she is not a longtime resident of Midwood.
match_headline: Midwood, Brooklyn, Where Urban and Suburban Meet

text: An article on Sept. 14 about efforts by the United States to extradite Inocente Orlando Montano Morales, a former Salvadoran vice minister of defense accused of participating in the 1989 massacre of six Jesuit priests, their housekeeper and her daughter at a Jesuit university in San Salvador, misspelled the surname of one of the priests killed, who was the rector of the José Simeón Cañas University of Central America. He was the Rev. Ignacio Ellacuría, not Ellacurría.
match_headline: U.S. Wants Former Salvadoran Ally to Face Justice in 1989 Massacre

text: A map on Sept. 10 with an article about Russia’s confirmation that its military advisers were in Syria omitted the boundary lines for Armenia, which is east of Turkey and northwest of Iran. A corrected map can be found at nytimes.com/world .
match_headline: Russia Defends the Presence of Its Military Advisers in Syria

text: An article last Monday about the closing of the New York Military Academy, using information from alumni, erroneously attributed a distinction to the school’s organ, which the composer Stephen Sondheim, a student there in sixth and seventh grades, fondly remembered playing. It is the second largest theater organ in New York State, not the second largest pipe organ in the state.
match_headline: New York Military Academy’s Sudden Closing, After 126 Years

text: An article on Monday about Pope Francis’ visit to America misstated part of the name of the order of nuns that received an unscheduled visit from the pope. It is the Little Sisters of the Poor, not Little Sisters of Charity.
match_headline: Pope Departs, After Showing a Deft Touch

text: An article last Tuesday about the possibility that a decline in China’s coal industry could benefit worldwide efforts to slow global warming misstated the job title of Chris P. Nielsen, who said he believed that a recent drop in demand would be reversed in coming years. He is a researcher at Harvard University, not a professor.
match_headline: Fading Coal Industry in China May Offer Chance to Aid Climate

text: Because of an editing error, an article on June 28 about Yassine Salhi, accused of beheading his boss before setting off an explosion at an American-owned chemical plant near Lyon, France, misidentified, in some editions, the man described in news articles as cutting an impressive figure, tall, blond and domineering. He is Frédéric Jean Salvi, a radical Islamist who had ties to Mr. Salhi — not Mr. Salhi himself. This correction was delayed because editors did not follow through when the error was pointed out.
match_headline: Suspect in Attack in France Had Ties to Radical Islamist

text: Because of an editing error, a report by The Associated Press in the National Briefing on Saturday about the Dalai Lama’s receiving treatment at the Mayo Clinic misidentified the city in Minnesota where the clinic is located. It is Rochester, not Minneapolis.

A report by The Associated Press in the National Briefing column on Sept. 15 about a hiker who was gored by a goat misstated part of the name of the Washington park where the incident occurred. It is Olympic National Park, not Olympia National Park.
match_headline: Deadly Flood in Utah Blurs Town’s Religious Divisions, Even as Grief Highlights Them

text: An article on Thursday about a proposal by Mayor Bill de Blasio and Cardinal Timothy Dolan to provide more beds for the homeless in New York City this winter misstated, in some editions, the day Pope Francis had lunch with a group of homeless people in Washington. It was Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: Mayor de Blasio and Cardinal Dolan Highlight Plan to Add Beds for Homeless

text: An article on Saturday about New Yorkers who waited hours to see Pope Francis misstated the time period during which a line at one Central Park gate stretched for two and a half blocks. It was eight hours before his arrival, not six.
match_headline: New Yorkers Fast, Jostle, Wait and Cook as Pope Visits

text: An article on Saturday about backlogged cases in the Bronx district attorney’s office that involve violence on Rikers Island misstated, in some editions, the year legislators approved a bill that would have changed the jurisdiction of Rikers Island cases to Queens. It was last year, not this year. (The governor did not sign the bill.)
match_headline: Prosecutors Struggling to Keep Up With Cases of Violence From Rikers

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a dispute in Red Hook, Brooklyn, over a mural that is part of a campaign to protest the imprisonment of an illustrator in Iran for depicting politicians there as animals, referred incorrectly to the garment on the head of the woman depicted in the mural. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is a head scarf — not a niqab, which covers the face.
match_headline: In Brooklyn, a Protest Mural Draws Its Own Protest

text: An article on Tuesday about Royal Dutch Shell’s decision to end its oil exploration efforts in the Alaskan Arctic misspelled the name of an Oregon river over which protesters suspended themselves from a bridge in an effort to block the passage of an icebreaker hired by Shell. It is the Willamette River, not the Williamette.
match_headline: Shell Exits Arctic as Slump in Oil Prices Forces Industry to Retrench

text: An article on Friday about the sensitivities and risks of a meeting on Monday between President Obama and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia misidentified the location of the last formal, scheduled meeting between them, in June 2013. It was in Northern Ireland, the British province — not in Ireland.
match_headline: White House Says President Obama and Vladimir Putin Will Meet Next Week

text: An article on Sept. 19 about the conviction of Karma al-Khayat, a Lebanese television executive, on charges of contempt of court for ignoring an international court’s order to remove broadcasts about confidential witnesses from her station’s website gave an incorrect conversion in dollars for 100,000 euros, the fine the prosecutor is seeking. It is about $113,000, not $130,000.
match_headline: Lebanon Tribunal Gives Mixed Verdict in Confidential Witnesses Case

text: An article on Sunday about a women’s summit meeting at the United Nations that is highlighting friction between the United States and China misstated, in some editions, the title of Kelly Ayotte, Republican of New Hampshire, who is sponsoring a resolution in Congress supporting an American campaign to shame China and several other countries for jailing female leaders. Ms. Ayotte is a senator, not a representative.
match_headline: U.N. Summit Meeting on Women’s Rights Highlights More Tension Between U.S. and China

text: An article on Sunday about Richard A. Diment, a municipal judge in Georgia who threatened to jail traffic offenders who failed to pay their fines, included outdated information about the qualifications for such judgeships. Georgia now requires all newly appointed municipal court judges to be lawyers, a change from the past when no law degree was necessary.
match_headline: Court Conundrum: Offenders Who Can’t Pay, or Won’t

text: An article on Friday about a Food and Drug Administration hearing on the contraceptive device Essure misstated the affiliation of Dr. Charles C. Coddington. He is an obstetrician-gynecologist at the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota, not at the University of Wisconsin at Madison.
match_headline: F.D.A. Panel Weighs Complaints on Essure Contraceptive Implant

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about a lawsuit filed by the owner of Grand Central Terminal against New York City and a developer, SL Green, over air rights misstated the surname of a spokesman for SL Green. He is Jonathan Rosen, not Rose.
match_headline: Owner of Grand Central Sues Developer and City for $1.1 Billion Over Air Rights

text: An article by The Associated Press in some editions on Saturday about state officials ordering a nonprofit insurance cooperative to wind down business omitted part of the name of the organization. It is Health Republic Insurance of New York, not merely Health Republic.
match_headline: Hillary Clinton Proposes Cap on Patients’ Drug Costs as Bernie Sanders Pushes His Plan

text: An article on Tuesday about the evolution of molds used for cheese making referred imprecisely to the isolation of the antibiotic penicillin. While Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, he did not isolate the active substance.
match_headline: That Stinky Cheese Is a Result of Evolutionary Overdrive

text: An article on Tuesday about Dr. Laura J. Esserman, a breast cancer surgeon, misstated the National Cancer Institute’s policy on breast cancer screening. The National Cancer Institute no longer issues recommendations or guidelines for cancer screening; instead, the N.C.I. generates scientific information that other groups use to formulate guidelines and recommendations.
match_headline: A Breast Cancer Surgeon Who Keeps Challenging the Status Quo

text: An article last Thursday about papal-themed parties misidentified the location of Maggiano, a restaurant in Philadelphia. It is in Philadelphia’s Center City; it is not in the city’s “Little Italy” because there is no such neighborhood.
match_headline: Pope Francis’ Visit Offers a Reason to Party

text: An article on Monday about a report by the Pew Research Center on immigration to the United States erroneously included one person among the authors of the study. While Mark Hugo Lopez and Jeffrey Passel wrote the report, Molly Rohal was not a co-author. (She is Pew’s communications manager.)
match_headline: Share of Immigrants in U.S. Nears Highs of Early 20th Century, Report Finds

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with the continuation of an article about New York’s Southern Tier region and efforts there to find the area’s economic footing described incorrectly the barbershop shown in Elmira, N.Y. The photograph was taken on a day in September when the shop had no customers; it is not the case that the barbershop had no customers all month.
match_headline: New York’s Southern Tier, Once a Home for Big Business, Is Struggling

text: An article on Monday about changes at The Daily News in New York misstated the newspaper’s peak daily circulation. It was 2.4 million in 1947, not nearly one million.
match_headline: The Daily News Layoffs and Digital Shift May Signal the Tabloid Era’s End

text: An article on Wednesday about an International Monetary Fund report on risks in mutual fund holdings of high-yielding bonds described incorrectly the outflow from mutual funds this year. Investors in the United States and worldwide have pulled close to $75 billion, not $100 billion, from global bond and equity funds that invest in emerging markets, not funds more broadly.
match_headline: I.M.F. Cautions on Concentrated Positions in U.S. Mutual Funds

text: An article on Thursday about Mexico’s most recent auction of offshore oil leases misstated the surname of a lawyer with Holland & Knight who commented on the results. He is José Antonio Prado, not Pardo.
match_headline: Successful Auction for Oil Drilling Rights in Mexico Follows Weak Debut

text: An article on Thursday about the effect of ad blockers on loading times for web pages and battery life in mobile devices misstated the title of Scott Cunningham, who pointed out the downside of blockers on independent publishers who rely on advertising revenue. He is a general manager of the Interactive Advertising Bureau Tech Lab, not the bureau itself.
match_headline: Putting Mobile Ad Blockers to the Test

text: An article on Page D12 today about what comprises a cappuccino misidentifies the institution with which Andy Smith, a culinary historian, is affiliated. He works at the New School, not at New York University.
match_headline: Is That Cappuccino You’re Drinking Really a Cappuccino?

text: A picture caption on Page D21 today with an article about the artist Robert Loughlin misidentifies, at one point, the painter of the “Brute” series of images. As the first part of the caption correctly notes, the images are by Mr. Loughlin — not by Paul Johnson, the owner of the Johnson Trading Gallery, where they are displayed.
match_headline: Now Trending: The Artist Robert Loughlin

text: An obituary on Thursday about the lawyer Doug Kendall, using information from a spokeswoman, misstated part of the name of his sister, who survives him. She is Carolyn Kendall Stoller, not Carolyn Townsend Stoller.
match_headline: Doug Kendall, Liberal Who Challenged Supreme Court’s Conservatives, Dies at 51

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the actress Catherine E. Coulson misidentified her birthplace. She was born in Elmhurst, Ill., not in Ashland, Ore.
match_headline: Catherine Coulson, the Enigmatic Log Lady of ‘Twin Peaks,’ Dies at 71

text: An article on Thursday about challenges facing the United States as it tries to help Afghan forces regain lost territory and contain a crisis for the American-backed government in Kabul misstated the circumstances of the return of Gen. John F. Campbell, the commander of coalition forces, to Afghanistan from a defense conference in Germany. He returned as planned; he did not cut his trip short.
match_headline: U.S. Struggles for Way to Help Afghans Regain Territory It Thought Was Secure

text: A headline on Friday with an article about Hillary Rodham Clinton’s email server overstated what is known about an investigation into the server’s security. As the article correctly noted, Mrs. Clinton received spam email that was intended to place malware on her computer network; the investigation has not yet determined that the malware effort was successful.
match_headline: Spam Sent to Hillary Clinton Server Prompts Look at Suspected Russian Hacking

text: A headline on Friday with a film review gave an outdated title for the movie. It is “Sherpa” — not “Sherpa: Trouble on Everest.”
match_headline: Review: ‘Sherpa’ Delves Into a Risky Profession

text: An obituary on Sept. 22 about the real estate developer Robert E. Simon Jr. referred incorrectly to his second marriage, to Anne Wertheim Langman. She filed for divorce in 1971; the marriage did not end in 1967. The obituary also misstated the name of one of Mr. Simon’s stepdaughters, who survives him. She is Cristina Zilkha, not Lucinda Zilka.
match_headline: Robert E. Simon Jr., Who Created a Town, Reston, Va., Dies at 101

text: An entry in the “By the Numbers” feature last Sunday about the continuing legacy of Penguin Books gave outdated information about Bodley Head, another British publishing house. While Bodley Head went through a period of dormancy in the 1990s, it was revived by Random House in 2008; it is not defunct.
match_headline: Eighty Years of Penguin Books

text: An article last Sunday about three women involved with the play “Eclipsed,” which focuses on Liberia’s civil war, using information from a publicist, referred incorrectly to a big-budget project that one of the women, the director Liesl Tommy, is working on. It is a stage adaptation of a movie, not a movie.
match_headline: Lupita Nyong’o Shines a Light on Africa

text: An article last Sunday about an exhibition that Steve Martin is curating at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles misstated part of the name of a musical that he is working on with Edie Brickell. It is “Bright Star,” not “Bright Eyes.” The article also referred incorrectly to Mr. Martin’s working relationship with the museum. In 2003, Mr. Martin wrote wall text for artworks in the exhibition “Writings on the Wall”; his tribute to the photographer Cindy Sherman in 2012 wasn’t “his only prior connection to the museum.” And a picture credit with the article misidentified the source of the image “Mountains in Snow: Rocky Mountain Paintings VII.” It was the Thomson Collection/Art Gallery of Ontario, not Michael Cullen.
match_headline: Steve Martin Adds ‘Curator’ to His Wild and Crazy Résumé

text: A review on Sept. 20 about “Undermajordomo Minor,” a novel by Patrick deWitt, misidentified a character who asks the hero what he wants from life. He is a strange visitor dressed in burlap, not the village priest.
match_headline: Patrick deWitt’s ‘Undermajordomo Minor’

text: An article on Sept. 20 about the affection felt for Pope Francis by a self-described “once-erstwhile Presbyterian” misspelled part of the birth name of Pope Francis. He was born Jorge Mario Bergoglio, not Borgoglia.
match_headline: My Crush on Pope Francis

text: A picture caption last Sunday with the Q&A column , about the founder of Bill Chill Adventures, misidentified the woman shown. The photograph was of a member of an expedition — not of the founder, Sarah Aciego.
match_headline: From Alaska to Iceland, Breaking Barriers to Arctic Travel

text: An article on Sept. 20 about Catholic sights in New York misidentified the pope who sent St. Frances Xavier Cabrini from Italy to tend to Italian immigrants in New York. It was Pope Leo XIII, who reigned from 1878 to 1903 — not Leo XII, who reigned from 1823 to 1829.
match_headline: A Tourist’s Guide to Catholic New York

text: Because of an editing error, the Frugal Traveler column last Sunday, about a budget-friendly day in London, misstated, in one instance, the name of a theater in the West End. As the column correctly noted elsewhere, it is the St. James, not the St. James’s. The column also referred imprecisely to a route to the Stepney Green Underground station in East London. While it is possible to get to Stepney Green from Victoria station on the Circle line in 23 minutes, it requires a transfer; it is not direct. (The District line takes about the same time and is direct.)
match_headline: A $1,000 Day in London for $100

text: An article on Sept. 20 about Hello Barbie, a talking toy by Mattel, misstated the role of Michelle Chidoni at the company. She is a spokeswoman, not a marketing chief.
match_headline: Barbie Wants to Get to Know Your Child

text: An article on Feb. 22 about the fund-raising results of the 103rd year of The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, a project that assists struggling New Yorkers, misstated the total amount of money raised during the campaign. The donations, which were collected from New York Times readers from November 2014 through January of this year, totaled $5,793,762 — not $6,130,404. (The previous campaign collected $5,950,183.) The error was recently discovered during a final accounting of the donations.
match_headline: Neighbors Step Up to Help New Yorkers Through Tough Times

text: An article on Tuesday about plans to sell Avatar Studios on West 53rd Street in New York misspelled the surname of a jazz guitarist who had recorded music there. He is Pat Metheny, not Methany. The article also misstated, in some editions, Kirk Imamura’s relationship with the studio’s owner, Chieko Imamura. He is her husband, not her ex-husband.
match_headline: The Music May Stop at a Storied Manhattan Studio

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Yankees’ 4-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox that clinched a wild card in the playoffs misstated, in some copies, the time frame in which Carlos Beltran hit his last four home runs. They came in 13 days, not in the past week.
match_headline: Yankees Hold On to Clinch Wild Card

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the arrest of four Northern California high school students in connection with what law enforcement officials called a highly detailed plan to shoot and kill fellow students misattributed, in some editions, a quotation about a search of the students’ lockers. It was Robert Griffith, the superintendent of the Summerville Union High School District — not Sheriff James W. Mele of Tuolumne County — who said that the “immediate” search had turned up no weapons, “so within a very, very short period of time we knew that we did not have an immediate threat to safety.”
match_headline: 4 Students Arrested in Northern California, Suspected of Plotting Killings in High School

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the longtime Democratic congressman Don Edwards referred imprecisely to a 1969 newspaper article that Mr. Edwards found in his F.B.I. file. Although the article reported that he had decided not to run for re-election, he did end up running — and winning.
match_headline: Don Edwards, Congressman Who Championed Civil Rights, Dies at 100

text: An obituary in some editions on Sunday about the British politician Denis Healey misstated one of his accomplishments as secretary of state for defense. He closed most of Britain’s military bases east of the Suez Canal, not all of them.
match_headline: Denis Healey, 98, Dies; Feisty Labour Leader in a Downsized Britain

text: An article on Monday about the Yankees’ 9-4 loss to the Baltimore Orioles described incorrectly Chris Davis’s two home runs in the game. They were his league-leading 46th and 47th home runs of the season, not his 47th and 48th. And an accompanying chart for the Final American League Leaders included outdated statistics for Davis. He finished the season with 47 home runs — not 45 — and 117 runs batted in — not 113.
match_headline: Sputtering Yankees Are Rewarded After a Victory (by Arizona)

text: An article on Saturday about Christopher Harper-Mercer, the gunman in the massacre at an Oregon community college, misstated, in some copies, the professional background of Laurel Harper, his mother. She had been licensed as a vocational nurse but not as a psychological assistant in California, and she is a licensed practical nurse in Oregon, not in California.
match_headline: Oregon Killer Described as Man of Few Words, Except on Topic of Guns

text: An article on Thursday about an outbreak of toxic algae in the Ohio River, using information from the Ohio River Valley Water Sanitation Commission, erroneously cited two states in the river basin as having banned phosphates in lawn fertilizers. Ohio and Indiana do not have such bans.
match_headline: Toxic Algae Outbreak Overwhelms a Polluted Ohio River

text: An article last Wednesday about a settlement reached by New York City and a police officer, Adrian Schoolcraft, over his 2009 arrest and forced hospitalization misidentified the newspaper that first reported Officer Schoolcraft’s accusations. It is The Daily News — not The Village Voice, which reported on the audio recordings Officer Schoolcraft made.
match_headline: Officer Who Disclosed Police Misconduct Settles Suit

text: An article on Monday about the Jets’ 27-14 victory over the Miami Dolphins in London misidentified the location of the Jets’ loss to the Eagles the previous week. The game was played in East Rutherford, N.J., not in Philadelphia.
match_headline: Jets Cross Atlantic and Cruise Past the Dolphins

text: An article on Monday about St. Ann’s Warehouse, the performing arts organization that is moving into its first permanent home, in Brooklyn, and its artistic director, Susan Feldman, misidentified, at one point, the organization that hired Ms. Feldman in 1979 to help find another use for St. Ann and Holy Trinity Church in Brooklyn Heights. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is the New York Landmarks Conservancy, not the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission. The article also misidentified the first production of the season. It is an all-female “Henry IV” — a hybrid of Shakespeare’s “Henry IV, Part 1” and “Henry IV, Part 2” — not “Henry V.”
match_headline: Susan Feldman and St. Ann’s Warehouse Unveil a Permanent Home

text: An article on Sept. 22 about the Lusi mud volcano in Indonesia misstated, at one point, the surname of a University of Texas geoscientist who sees poor well design as the most plausible explanation for the phenomenon. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Peter Flemings, not Fleming.
match_headline: Indonesia’s ‘Mud Volcano’ and Nine Years of Debate About Its Muck

text: An article on Monday about alternatives to the traditional cable television bundle referred incorrectly to PlayStation Vue’s channel lineup. It includes, not excludes, the Discovery Channel.
match_headline: Unwrapping the Cable TV Bundle

text: A picture caption on Sept. 30 with the continuation of an article about boxing classes for cadets at the United States Military Academy referred incorrectly to the prevalence of concussions there. A higher number of concussions were suffered during boxing than any other sport at West Point, but boxing did now show a higher rate of concussions than any other sport.
match_headline: Concussions in a Required Class: Boxing at Military Academies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the bid for House Speaker by Representative Jason Chaffetz of Utah misstated, in some copies, the type of House panel investigating the 2012 terrorist attack in Benghazi, Libya. It is a select committee, not a subcommittee.
match_headline: For Jason Chaffetz, Quixotic House Speaker Bid Is in Character

text: An article on Tuesday about Laurel Harper, the mother of Christopher Harper-Mercer, the gunman in the Oregon college massacre, misstated her professional background. She is a licensed practical nurse, not a registered nurse.
match_headline: Oregon Killer’s Mother Wrote of Troubled Son and Gun Rights

text: An article on Sept. 15 about the second day of clashes between the Israeli police and Palestinian youths at a contested holy site in Jerusalem that includes Al Aqsa Mosque misstated the officers’ actions during the clashes. They fought with protesters on the perimeter of the mosque, but did not enter it. The article also referred incompletely to the area that a group of Muslim women had been barred from entering because they chased and shouted at Jewish visitors. The entire site, known to Muslims as the Noble Sanctuary and to Jews as the Temple Mount, was off limits to the women; they were not barred just from Al Aqsa Mosque. And the headline with the article misidentified the location of an attack in which a Jewish man was killed after the road he was driving on was pelted with rocks. As the article correctly noted, the attack was in East Jerusalem, not in the West Bank.
match_headline: Jewish Man Dies as Rocks Pelt His Car in East Jerusalem

text: An article on Saturday about American Dream Meadowlands, a shopping mall being built in New Jersey at the site of a project once known as Xanadu, rendered incorrectly the name of Robert K. Futterman’s real estate firm, which specializes in retail. It is RKF Associates, not RFK Associates.
match_headline: Huge Mall Rising at Troubled Site in North Jersey

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the awarding of honorary degrees to Bill Cosby by colleges and universities, some of which have now rescinded them, misstated the year the University of Notre Dame gave him one. It was 1990, not 1980. (The university has a policy of not rescinding such awards.)
match_headline: To Revoke or Not: Colleges That Gave Cosby Honors Face a Tough Question

text: A report in the In Brief column on Sept. 29 about a combination drug that could ease the agitation of Alzheimer’s disease described incorrectly a disorder treated with the combination drug, dextromethorphan and quinidine. The drug is approved for treating pseudobulbar affect, a neurological disorder that involves involuntary crying, laughing and other emotional displays as its main symptom — not involuntary movement of the facial muscles.
match_headline: Is It Old Age, or A.D.H.D.?

text: An article last Thursday about Melania Trump and the passive role she has been playing in the presidential campaign of her husband, Donald Trump, misstated her age at the time she was Melania Knauss and posed for a picture in Talk magazine. She was 29, not 26, making her almost a quarter-century younger than her future husband, not more than a quarter-century younger. The article also misidentified a presidential debate she attended. She was in the audience at the Fox News debate in Cleveland in August; she was not present for the CNN debate at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, Calif. In addition, the article misidentified the position in Congress held by Marco Rubio, one of Mr. Trump’s opponents for the Republican presidential nomination. He is a United States senator from Florida, not a representative. The article also misspelled the given name of Rupert Murdoch’s former wife, who described Mrs. Trump as “a supportive wife, great mother and a lovely person.” She is Wendi Deng Murdoch, not Wendy. The article also misspelled the surname of an editor at The Palm Beach Daily News, who noted that Mrs. Trump is “not gossipy at all, not bitchy and just really nice.” He is Robert Janjigian, not Jangigian. And, finally, the article referred imprecisely to Mr. Janjigian’s role at the newspaper. While he has reported on society, he is in charge of fashion coverage, not society coverage. (Shannon Donnelly is the society editor.)
ref_headline: a supportive wife, great mother and a lovely person.
match_headline: Melania Trump, the Silent Partner

text: Because of an editing error, a report on Sept. 30 in some editions of the World Briefing column about the detention of three Japanese citizens in China on charges of spying referred incorrectly to diplomats from Japan, China and South Korea who were working to arrange a summit meeting for their leaders. The diplomats were working at the same time the detentions were reported; they were not involved in the detentions.
match_headline: Japan: China Detains 2 Japanese on Suspicion of Espionage

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about the search for survivors of the container ship El Faro misstated the location of the effort. The Coast Guard was searching in the Atlantic Ocean, not in the Caribbean Sea.
match_headline: Questions Are Raised About Safety on Ship Missing After Storm

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about fears about lead in the water in Flint, Mich., misidentified the child pictured with LeeAnne Walters, who was shown using bottled water to make pasta. He is her son Garrett, not his twin, Gavin.
match_headline: Flint Officials Are No Longer Saying the Water Is Fine

text: An article in some editions on Monday about a visit by Mayor Bill de Blasio to a church in East New York, Brooklyn, to discuss his plans to rezone the area misstated, in some copies, the number of affordable housing units he has said he would like to preserve. It is 120,000, not 80,000.
match_headline: De Blasio Aims to Sell Wary Churchgoers on Rezoning Plan for East New York

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the growing attraction of the United Nations General Assembly session omitted two major producers of the Social Good Summit, an annual conference on the state of technology, new media and world issues that is held during United Nations week. Besides the United Nations Foundation and the website Mashable, the 92nd Street Y and the United Nations Development Programme were also producers.
match_headline: Forget Coachella and Bonnaroo: The U.N. Is the Place to Be

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision by a prominent Teamsters pension fund, the Central States Pension Fund, to file for reorganization misstated the number of retirees who are currently getting their multiemployer pensions paid by a federal insurance program known as the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation. The multiemployer wing of the federal program currently serves about 50,000 retirees, not one million.
match_headline: Teamsters’ Pension Fund Warns 400,000 of Cuts

text: Because of an editing error, a chart on Monday about contenders for the Heisman Trophy in college football misidentified, in some copies, the university for which quarterback Cody Kessler plays. It is the University of Southern California, not U.C.L.A.
match_headline: Case That Could Erode Amateur Model Takes a Small Step

text: An article on Monday about the Houston Astros’ clinching a wild-card playoff berth to face the Yankees misstated the average age of the Yankees’ starting lineup in their game on Sunday against the Baltimore Orioles. It was 30.8, not 34.8.
match_headline: Innocence Is a Virtue for Young Astros

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the Sports of The Times column on Monday, about Derek Bouchard-Hall, the new president and chief executive of U.S.A. Cycling, described incorrectly the action of the cyclists in the men’s elite race at the World Road Cycling Championships. They were shown during the race, not lining up for it.
match_headline: Cycling Leader Vows to Press the Fight Against Doping

text: An article in some editions on Friday about a federal judge’s criticism of the United States attorney’s office in Brooklyn for putting misleading language in a subpoena issued in the case of a Queens couple charged with drug trafficking misspelled the given name of one of the defendants. She is Eleonora Gigliotti, not Eleonara.
match_headline: Judge Finds Fault With Gag Order in U.S. Attorney’s Subpoena

text: An article on Thursday about the Rangers’ 3-2 victory over the Chicago Blackhawks in their N.H.L. season opener misstated, in some editions, the period in which Kevin Klein scored for the Rangers. It was the first, not the second. The article also misstated, in some editions, the number of saves Rangers goalie Henrik Lundqvist had. It was 32, not 34. (He faced 34 shots.)
match_headline: Before Game, the Blackhawks Rejoice; at the End, the Rangers Do

text: An article on Friday about the film “Stretch and Bobbito: Radio That Changed Lives,” which looks at “The Stretch Armstrong and Bobbito Show” that ran on the Columbia University radio station in the 1990s, misstated the given name of a producer of the film. He is Omar Acosta, not Oscar.
ref_headline: Stretch and Bobbito: Radio That Changed Lives,
match_headline: Stretch Armstrong and Bobbito, Hip-Hop Heralds, Are Saluted in a Film

text: Because of a transcription error, an interview on Sept. 22 with Cornelia Bargmann, a neurobiologist at Rockefeller University in New York, omitted a word in a description of how the drug Herceptin works. Dr. Bargmann said, “It is an antibody against the gene product that sits on the surface of a cancer cell” — not “against the gene that sits on the surface of a cancer cell.”
ref_headline: It is an antibody against the gene product that sits on the surface of a cancer cell
match_headline: Cori Bargmann Puts Her Mind to How the Brain Works

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about a disposal system for unwanted prescriptions misstated, in some editions, part of the name of a group that has a St. Louis affiliate led by Howard Weissman, who commented on the practice. It is the National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence (not Drug Abuse).
match_headline: D.E.A. Effort to Curb Painkiller Abuse Falls Short at Pharmacies

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about a plan to clean up a canal in Berlin to create wetlands and a swimming area misspelled, in some copies, the name of a nightclub mentioned by an official in discussing urban development in the city. It is Berghain, not Bergheim.
match_headline: The Flussbad Plan in Berlin Reimagines a Canal for the People

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with an appraisal of the career of the filmmaker Chantal Akerman, who died Oct. 5, misidentified the person shown standing in a scene from her documentary “No Home Movie.” She is Ms. Akerman’s sister, not Ms. Akerman.
match_headline: Chantal Akerman, Resolutely Upending the Ordinary

text: An article on Oct. 3 about Israel’s efforts to seize on the chaos in Syria to expand settlements in the Golan Heights referred incorrectly to the territory. While most of the world officially considers it to be occupied, and the settlements there illegal, there is no consensus that the occupation itself is illegal.
match_headline: As Syria Reels, Israel Looks to Expand Settlements in Golan Heights

text: An article on Sunday about Geoffrey Marcy, an astronomer who was found guilty of violating sexual harassment policies of the University of California, Berkeley, misstated part of the name of the organization for which Joan Schmelz was the leader of a committee on the status of women astronomers. It is the American Astronomical Society, not the American Astronomical Association. The article also referred incorrectly to a sexual harassment case at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, which cut ties with Walter Lewin, a popular lecturer, and deleted his physics course materials from its website after finding he had harassed at least one student. It took that action in December 2014, not two years ago.
match_headline: Geoffrey Marcy, Astronomer at Berkeley, Apologizes for Behavior

text: A report in the college football roundup on Monday about Southern California Coach Steve Sarkisian’s taking a leave of absence misstated, in some editions, the day of U.S.C.’s game against Washington. It was last Thursday, not Saturday.
match_headline: U.S.C. Coach Steve Sarkisian Taking Leave of Absence

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 1 about the relocation of Condé Nast to 1 World Trade Center misstated the year that 4 Times Square, the company’s previous headquarters, opened. It was 1999, not 1991.
match_headline: Condé Nast Colonizes Lower Manhattan

text: An article on Oct. 3 about Russia and Iran’s expansion of their military efforts to defend the Syrian government, in defiance of President Obama, erroneously included in some copies one foreign leader among those whom Secretary of State John Kerry met with in New York after the day’s developments. Mr. Kerry met with the foreign ministers of Iran and Oman, but not with their Russian counterpart, Sergey V. Lavrov.
match_headline: Obama Sees Russia Failing in Syria Effort

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 6 about Iranians’ success in reclaiming public spaces following the election of a moderate president, Hassan Rouhani, and the signing of a nuclear agreement with world powers referred incorrectly to the end of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s tenure as president. His second and final term in office ended in 2013; he was not unseated by Mr. Rouhani.
match_headline: Cautiously, Iranians Reclaim Public Spaces and Liberties Long Suppressed

text: An article on Sept. 8 about a possible boost to right-wing, anti-immigration European political parties from the continuing influx of migrants overstated what was known about a fire in the town of Rottenburg am Neckar, Germany, a country where there have been more than 200 attacks on asylum seekers or their shelters this year. The fire was being investigated as possible arson; it had not been determined to be arson. (As of this week, the cause of the blaze remains unclear, the German police said.) The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption. This correction was delayed because editors did not follow through when the error was pointed out.
match_headline: Migrant Influx May Give Europe’s Far Right a Lift

text: A caption on Wednesday with a picture essay about an international ultimate Frisbee exhibition game between the Madison Radicals and the Buzz Bullets of Japan misidentified a member of the Radicals who scored. He is Colin Camp, not Seth Meyer.
match_headline: Where Disc Meets Globe: An International Exhibition of Ultimate Frisbee

text: An article on Oct. 3 about the 1949 American League pennant race between the Yankees and the Boston Red Sox referred incorrectly to a game on Sept. 26 that season. It was a day game, not a night game.
match_headline: A Yankees Victory in a Do-or-Die Game, Before Bucky Dent Was Alive

text: An article on Thursday about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s trip to Israel misattributed two quotations about his plans. It was Rabbi Joseph Potasnik, executive vice president of the New York Board of Rabbis — not Michael S. Miller, chief executive of the Jewish Community Relations Council of New York — who said that the mayor’s plan to visit a school in Jerusalem was “acceptable.” And it was Rabbi Potasnik — not Mr. Miller — who said, “I think right now we need a positive step coming from Ramallah.” The article also described incorrectly President Obama’s visits to Israel. While he visited the West Bank, he did not do so “during formal visits to Israel.” The West Bank is not part of Israel.
match_headline: Mayor de Blasio, on Israel Trip, Plans Visit With Palestinians

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Mets’ division series victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers described incorrectly a part of Dodgers pitcher Zack Greinke’s performance. Five of the first six outs he recorded were by strikeout; he did not strike out five of the first six batters he faced. The article also misstated the way the Mets’ previous winner-take-all game, Game 7 of the 2006 National League Championship Series, ended. Carlos Beltran struck out looking — not swinging — against St. Louis Cardinals pitcher Adam Wainwright.
match_headline: Next Stop for Mets: The N.L.C.S.

text: An article on Friday about catcher Russell Martin’s bizarre throwing error in the decisive game of the Toronto Blue Jays’ playoff series with the Texas Rangers described incorrectly another infamous baseball mistake: the baserunning blunder in 1908 by Fred Merkle that helped cost the New York Giants a pennant. That play occurred in a regular-season game; it was not “one of the most infamous gaffes in postseason history.”
ref_headline: one of the most infamous gaffes in postseason history.
match_headline: Amid a Chaotic Scene, Redemption Arrives for Russell Martin

text: A picture caption on Friday with a theater review of “Travels With My Aunt,” at the Clurman Theater in Manhattan, misidentified the actor shown with Thomas Jay Ryan. He is Jay Russell — not Daniel Jenkins, another cast member.
match_headline: Review: ‘Travels With My Aunt’ Taps Into a Hidden Sense of Adventure

text: Because of an editing error, an art review on Friday about “Jim Shaw: The End Is Here,” at the New Museum in Manhattan, misidentified the nationality of the collector who lent the “Thrift Store Paintings” to the exhibition. The collector is Belgian, not German.
ref_headline: Jim Shaw: The End Is Here,
match_headline: Jim Shaw at the New Museum: A Kaleidoscope of Giddy Delirium

text: An article on Page 36 this weekend about Raymond Chow, a defendant in a San Francisco racketeering trial, states that prosecutors were considering additional charges against him for the murders of two reputed gang members. After the article had gone to press, prosecutors charged Chow on Friday with murder and conspiracy to commit murder. Chow has been rearraigned, and has pleaded not guilty to both new charges.
match_headline: Shrimp Boy’s Day in Court

text: An article on Oct. 3 about the surprising pre-election polling strength of Pedro Passos Coelho, the Portuguese prime minister, who was for years the unpopular flag-bearer of austerity, misstated the size of Portugal’s 2014 budget deficit. It was 7.2 percent of gross domestic product, not 7.5 percent.
match_headline: Pedro Passos Coelho, Who Led Austerity Plan in Portugal, Nears Re-Election

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about the El Yunque, the sister ship of the El Faro, which was lost during Hurricane Joaquin, misidentified the body of water where the El Faro sank. It went down in the Atlantic Ocean, near the Bahamas — not in the Caribbean Sea.
match_headline: Sister to Ship That Sank Had History of Problems, Inspection Records Show

text: An article on Tuesday about the ways in which different organizations marked Columbus Day in New York City misspelled the given name of a podiatrist who had come to the city with an Italian folk band to march in the Columbus Day parade. He is Domenico Spinelli, not Dominico.
match_headline: On Columbus Day in New York City, the Party Is No Longer Just for Him

text: An article last Monday about an online series based on the original “Star Trek” television show and produced in Ticonderoga, N.Y., misstated the number of times Sean Kenney portrayed the character Capt. Christopher Pike. It was twice, not four times. (Mr. Kenney appeared on the series two other times as a different character.)
match_headline: A ‘Star Trek’ Dream, Spread From Upstate New York

text: An article on Thursday about India’s efforts to attract manufacturing investment misidentified the animal that is in the “Make India” logo. The promotional campaign banner depicts a lion, not a tiger.
match_headline: India’s Manufacturing Sector Courts the World, but Pitfalls Remain

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Monday about the success of DraftKings and FanDuel employees in playing daily fantasy sports games misspelled the surname of a DraftKings founder in some copies. He is Paul Liberman, not Lieberman. The article also misspelled, in some copies, the given name of a successful player in daily fantasy sports who said he pushed the companies to regulate themselves. He is Cory Albertson, not Corey.
match_headline: In Fantasy Sports, Signs of Insiders’ Edge

text: A picture on Tuesday with an obituary about the pitcher Dean Chance was published in error. The photograph, provided by The Associated Press, was of the pitcher Bob Lee, not Chance. The obituary also misspelled part of the name of the town in Ohio where Chance lived. It is New Pittsburg, not New Pittsburgh.
match_headline: Dean Chance, Cy Young Award Winner and Yankees Nemesis, Dies at 74

text: An article on Saturday about the unpredictability of federal elections in Canada, where voters headed to the polls on Monday, misspelled a middle name of a former Canadian prime minister. He was Pierre Elliott Trudeau, not Elliot. And because of an editing error, an accompanying picture caption misspelled, in some copies, the given name of the current prime minister. As the article correctly noted, he is Stephen Harper, not Steven.
match_headline: In Unpredictable Canadian Elections, Plurality Is More Important Than Popularity

text: An article on Oct. 8 about a video that showed Pope Francis calling the residents of Osorno, Chile, “dumb” for demonstrating against a bishop accused of being complicit in clerical sexual abuse mistranslated part of an email by the archbishop of Santiago, Cardinal Ricardo Ezzati, suggesting that he had intervened in appointments to a Vatican commission set up to advise Francis on child sexual abuse. Saying he hoped that Juan Carlos Cruz, an abuse victim, would not be appointed to the Pontifical Commission for the Protection of Minors, Cardinal Ezzati wrote, “It would mean, among other things, giving credit to and endorsing what Mr. Cruz has astutely constructed” — not “construed.”
match_headline: Calling Protesters in Chile ‘Dumb,’ Pope Francis Sets Off Uproar

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Oct. 3 about a rebuke issued to the Tajikistan government over its crackdown on an opposition party misidentified the source of the rebuke. It was from the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, not the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Tajikistan: U.N. Agency Rebukes Government Over Crackdown on Opposition Party

text: Because of an editing error, the Saturday Profile article , about Neil MacGregor, director of the British Museum, who is moving to Germany to work on the Humboldt Forum cultural project, misidentified the BBC radio series that accompanied the “Germany: Memories of a Nation” exhibition that he curated. The radio series had the same title; it was not “A History of the World in 100 Objects.” (That is the name of an earlier BBC radio series that Mr. MacGregor also worked on.)
match_headline: British Museum’s Director Follows a Fascination to Germany

text: An article on Saturday about mudslides in California misidentified the agency for which Patrick Chandler, as its spokesman, urged residents to heed warnings about the dangerous conditions. It is the California Department of Transportation, not the California Highway Patrol.
match_headline: ‘A Wall of Mud’ in California, and Warnings to Heed El Niño
