text: An article on Sunday about efforts by the Veterans of Foreign Wars post in Denver to attract younger members misstated the war experience of Raymond Starkey, a longtime member who commented on the changes. While Mr. Starkey served in the Pacific during World War II, he was not at Pearl Harbor.
match_headline: A Veterans of Foreign Wars Post in Denver Trades Beer for a Sun Salute

text: An article in some editions last Wednesday about a decision by employees of B & H Photo Video to file a petition to vote on joining the United Steelworkers union misstated the history of B & H. While it has been in Manhattan for decades, it is not a “Midtown institution.” (It did not move to Midtown until 1997.)
match_headline: Workers at B&H Photo Video, Citing Hazards, Move to Unionize

text: An article on Monday about the difficulties of small media companies that straddle the world of apps and web misstated, in some copies, the type of revenue 29th Street Publishing takes a portion of in exchange for creating an app and mobile website for one such company, the poetry and prose journal Little Star. The revenue comes from subscriptions, not ads.
match_headline: Publishers Straddle the Apple-Google, App-Web Divide

text: An article on Saturday about a disappointing end to the baseball season for the Los Angeles Dodgers misidentified the entity that bought the team in 2012. It is Guggenheim Baseball Management, not Guggenheim Partners. (Top executives at Guggenheim Partners are investors in Guggenheim Baseball Management.) The article also misstated the season after which Don Mattingly replaced Joe Torre as manager of the Dodgers. It was the 2010 season, not 2009.
match_headline: Daniel Murphy’s Steal Caps Another Lost Dodgers Season

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about Michigan State’s 27-23 victory over Michigan in college football misstated the number of times Michigan State Coach Mark Dantonio has lost to Michigan since taking over for the 2007 season. It is twice, not once.
match_headline: Botched Punt in Final Seconds Leaves Wolverines Stunned

text: A picture caption on Saturday with a dance review of H. T. Chen & Dancers at New York Live Arts in Manhattan, using information from a publicist, misidentified the dancer shown second from the left. She is Maki Shinagawa, not Ari Someya.
match_headline: Review: ‘South of Gold Mountain’ Explores Chinese Roots

text: A report in the Off the Menu column last Wednesday about Fort Gansevoort Bar-B-Cue, a takeout window in the meatpacking district, misstated the days it is open. They are Wednesdays through Saturdays, not Fridays through Sundays.
match_headline: Maison Hugo Ready to Open in Lenox Hill

text: An article on Wednesday about Baltimore’s struggles after the death of Freddie Gray, who died of injuries suffered in police custody, misstated the ownership of an apartment and a community center, which were set afire during riots in April. The complex is sponsored by, but not owned by, the Southern Baptist Church in East Baltimore. (An investment partnership owns the complex.)
match_headline: Fragile Baltimore Struggles to Heal After Deadly Police Encounter

text: An article on Oct. 4 about the fatal stabbing of two ultra-Orthodox Jewish men in Jerusalem by a Palestinian teenager, using information from the Israeli police, misstated the sex of the 2-year-old child of one of the men, who was shot and injured when the teenager grabbed a gun from the victim. The child is a boy. The article also referred incorrectly to the two men who were fatally stabbed. They were not on their way to pray at the Western Wall. And the article also misstated the given name of another recent victim of Palestinian violence, an Israeli woman who was killed along with her husband Oct. 1 in a drive-by shooting in the West Bank. She was Naama Henkin, not Naomi.
match_headline: Palestinian Kills 2 Israelis in Jerusalem

text: An article on Wednesday about objections to a proposal by some Arab states to classify the Western Wall as part of Al Aqsa Mosque compound in Jerusalem’s Old City erroneously attributed a distinction to the wall. It is one of the holiest sites in Judaism, not the holiest. (The Temple Mount holds that distinction). The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Arab Proposal to U.N. Over Western Wall Stirs New Concern

text: An article on Wednesday about an announcement by the genetic testing company 23andMe that it will return to offering health information, after a two-year hiatus ordered by the Food and Drug Administration, misstated the service the company did provide during that period. It offered ancestry information based on genetic data, but did not offer information on nonmedical traits like eye color, ear wax composition and lactose intolerance. (Those are being offered in the new version of its service.)
match_headline: 23andMe Will Resume Giving Users Health Data

text: Because of an editing error, a subheading in the N.H.L. roundup in some editions on Wednesday misidentified, in some copies, the winner of the game between the St. Louis Blues and the Montreal Canadiens. As the report correctly noted, the Canadiens won by 3-0.

A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about Wrigleyville, the neighborhood surrounding the Chicago Cubs’ Wrigley Field, misstated the surname of a Wrigleyville resident and longtime Cubs fan in some editions. He is Bruce Mullens, not Bruce Mullens-Wricket.
match_headline: Best of Times in Wrigleyville, for a Moment

text: An article on Wednesday about an art exhibition at the French mint in Paris misstated the mint’s age. It is 1,150 years old, not 1,500 years old.
match_headline: At ‘Take Me (I’m Yours),’ Stop, Look and Walk Off With the Art

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the Big Ears music festival next spring in Knoxville, Tenn., included an incomplete and outdated name for a musician scheduled to perform. He is Wadada Leo Smith, not Leo Smith.
match_headline: Review: White Light Festival Opens With a Wrenching Schubert Marathon

text: An article on Tuesday about museums that are digitizing their collections misstated the number of insect specimens at the Museum of Natural History in Berlin. It is 15 million, not 50 million.
match_headline: Museum Specimens Find New Life Online

text: An article on Tuesday about a study of the treatment of first-episode schizophrenia referred incorrectly to the conclusions of the study. Though it studied a program intended to reduce medication dosages, the researchers do not yet know for sure if dosages were lowered or by how much. Therefore, the study did not conclude “that schizophrenia patients who received smaller doses of antipsychotic medication and a bigger emphasis on one-on-one talk therapy and family support made greater strides in recovery.” (The study did conclude that the alternative treatment program as a whole led to better outcomes.) The article also erroneously attributed a statement to Dr. Robert K. Heinssen, who oversaw the research. It was scientists familiar with the project — not Dr. Heinssen — who said that the study’s original proposal, calling for two nearly identical trials, was changed in part because of recruiting problems. (Dr. Heinssen said that one trial was redirected, but did not say why.) And because of an editing error, the article misidentified the institution where Dr. Heinssen is director of services and intervention research. It the National Institute of Mental Health, not the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid.
ref_headline: that schizophrenia patients who received smaller doses of antipsychotic medication and a bigger emphasis on one-on-one talk therapy and family support made greater strides in recovery.
match_headline: New Approach Advised to Treat Schizophrenia

text: An article on Oct. 10 about the Obama administration’s four military approaches to combat the Islamic State and help shape the outcome of the Syrian civil war referred imprecisely to the relationship between the Nusra Front, Al Qaeda’s affiliate in Syria, and rebel militia groups vetted by the C.I.A. While some of the groups have fought alongside Nusra in tactical alliances, none are known to have affiliations with Nusra.
match_headline: 4 U.S. Military Efforts on ISIS and Syria Yield Mixed Results

text: An article on Saturday about Hungary’s closing of its border with Croatia to stem the tide of thousands of migrants quoted incorrectly from comments by Babar Baloch, a spokesman for the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in Hungary. Referring to Hungary’s plan to open transit zones along the Croatian border — as it has already done on the Serbian border — where migrants would begin the long process of applying for asylum, Mr. Baloch said, “If they are going to do it the way they have been doing it with the Serbian border, it will mean that no more people” — not “migrants” — “will be allowed through.”
ref_headline: If they are going to do it the way they have been doing it with the Serbian border, it will mean that no more people
match_headline: Hungary Seals Border With Croatia in Migrant Crackdown

text: An article on Wednesday about the Kansas City Royals’ 14-2 victory over the Toronto Blue Jays in Game 4 of the American League Championship Series misidentified which team led by 2-0 four pitches into the game. It was the Royals. Because of an editing error, the article also referred imprecisely in some editions to the pitching performance of Blue Jays infielder Cliff Pennington. While he was not charged with any runs, he allowed two inherited runners to score; it is not the case that he “did not allow a run.” And also because of an editing error, the article misidentified, in some editions, the team the Blue Jays beat in their division series. They beat the Texas Rangers — not the Houston Astros, who were beaten by the Royals.
match_headline: Royals Accuse Blue Jays, Then Win With an Outburst

text: An article on Oct. 14 about President Obama’s increasing willingness to halt the withdrawal of American troops from Afghanistan misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a senator from Rhode Island who is a sponsor of a paper by the Atlantic Council, a think tank, that argues that troop levels need to be maintained at or close to current levels. He is Senator Jack Reed, not Reid.
match_headline: Obama Is Rethinking Pullout in Afghanistan, Officials Say

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about apps for geographic information and games gave outdated price information for the National Geographic World Atlas app for iOS devices. While it was free at one point, it now costs $2.
match_headline: Video Feature: Using Apps to Let Your Fingers Do the Globe-Trotting

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday previewing the N.F.L. game between the Seattle Seahawks and the San Francisco 49ers misstated, in some copies, the recent season when the San Francisco 49ers advanced to the Super Bowl. It was the 2012 season, not the 2013 season. (The game was played on Feb. 3, 2013.)
match_headline: Thursday’s Matchup: Seahawks (2-4) at 49ers (2-4)

text: An article on Wednesday about plans by Opera Philadelphia to hold annual festivals at sites across the city starting in 2017 referred incorrectly to the costs that will be covered by $10 million the company has raised. It is for the incremental costs of switching to a festival format for four seasons, not for mounting the first four years of festivals.
match_headline: Opera Philadelphia’s New Seasonal Structure Caters to Bingeing

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the installation of Deborah Kass’s first public sculpture in Brooklyn Bridge Park next month, using information from the Paul Kasmin Gallery, misstated the opening date of a show of Ms. Kass’s paintings at the gallery. It is Dec. 9, not Dec. 8.
match_headline: Watteau in Wartime, and a Miami Showcase for Anselm Kiefer

text: A map on Page 6 in some editions this weekend with the continuation of an article about the disparity of wealth in Chelsea misidentifies a street in the neighborhood that marks a divide between the poor and the wealthy. It is 25th Street, not 26th. The error is repeated in text accompanying the map. A corrected version of the map can be found at nytimes.com/nyregion .
match_headline: In Chelsea, a Great Wealth Divide

text: An article on Page 2 this weekend about Abigail Disney and her documentary on gun culture misstates the position on abortion held by Lucy McBath, whose son was shot to death in Florida in 2012. She supports abortion rights; she is not anti-abortion.
match_headline: Abigail Disney Builds a Dialogue on Gun Control

text: A map on Page 2 this weekend that serves as a table of contents for the special Africa issue gives incorrect page numbers for many of the articles. A corrected version of the map at nytimes.com/travel provides links to the articles.

An article on Page 114 this weekend about five technology entrepreneurs includes a profile of Elizabeth Holmes, founder of the blood-testing company Theranos. After the article had gone to press, there were new developments regarding Theranos. Articles in The Wall Street Journal raised questions about some of the company’s technology, and Theranos said it had largely stopped using its finger-prick blood collection tube pending regulatory approvals. Coverage of the developments can be found at nytimes.com/business . The article also profiles Brian Chesky, a founder of Airbnb. That profile should have noted that the writer, Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen, is married to Marc Andreessen, whose venture capital firm is an investor in Airbnb.
match_headline: Theranos, a Blood Testing Start-Up, Defends Its Accuracy

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about a citywide arts festival in Peekskill, N.Y., misidentified the artist whose works are painted on the walls of several homes there. The paintings are by George Korsmit — not by his wife, Saskia Janssen. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption. The article also misidentified the residence of the artist Megan Snowe. She lives in Philadelphia, not Finland.
match_headline: Peekskill as Canvas for Artists Near and Far

text: A picture in some editions last Sunday with the Big City column, about the recent purchase of The Village Voice, was published in error. The photograph, of 36 Cooper Square, showed the former — not current — offices of The Village Voice. (The newspaper’s headquarters are now at 80 Maiden Lane.)
match_headline: Sale Raises Hopes for Reviving The Village Voice

text: A map on Page 2 this weekend that serves as a table of contents for the special Africa issue gives incorrect page numbers for many of the articles. A corrected version of the map at nytimes.com/travel provides links to the articles.
A report in the In Transit column last Sunday about a cycling trip to the South Pole misstated the type of coordinate that a traveler would cross to fly to Antarctica. It is longitude, not latitude.
match_headline: Cycling Tours in Antarctica, for a Price

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 11 about Anheuser-Busch InBev’s ambitions to acquire a rival, SABMiller, described incorrectly Anheuser-Busch’s performance in North America and Europe last year. The company’s volume sales — not its growth — declined in both those areas.
match_headline: Anheuser-Busch InBev’s Growth Playbook Starts With Its Checkbook

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Elyse Feuer and Capt. Douglas Martin misidentified the office in Henderson Hall, a Marine Corps installation in Arlington, Va., in which the groom works. Captain Martin, a judge advocate in the corps, is the officer in charge of the Legal Assistance Office, not the Marine Corps Community Services office.
match_headline: Elyse Feuer, Douglas Martin

text: A review on Oct. 4 about “Changing the Subject,” by Sven Birkerts, misstated part of the title of a book by the reviewer, Tim Parks. It is “Where I’m Reading From,” not “Where I’m Writing From.”
match_headline: ‘Changing the Subject,’ by Sven Birkerts

text: A review on Oct. 11 about “Rosemary: The Hidden Kennedy Daughter,” by Kate Clifford Larson, misspelled the given name of a writer who published books about the Kennedys. He is Laurence Leamer, not Lawrence.
match_headline: ‘Rosemary: The Hidden Kennedy Daughter,’ by Kate Clifford Larson

text: An article on Wednesday about testimony in Federal District Court about the 1978 heist at the Lufthansa terminal at Kennedy International Airport misspelled the name of the crime family to which Vincent Asaro, the defendant, belongs. It is the Bonanno family, not Bonnano.
match_headline: Riveting Retelling of ’78 Lufthansa Heist, but in Court, Not on Film

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Monday with the continuation of an article about the Clinton Foundation’s partnership with Rwanda, which has resulted in both pathbreaking work and the potential for conflicts of interest, misstated the year of a meeting of the Clinton Global Initiative, the annual four-day gathering of world leaders, in some editions. It was 2011, not 2001.
match_headline: Rwanda Aid Shows Reach and Limits of Clinton Foundation

text: An article on Oct. 9 about the history of the holy site in Jerusalem known as the Temple Mount to Jews and the Noble Sanctuary to Muslims misstated the time period in which a special Islamic religious authority has been managing the site. The authority, called the Waqf, was created by the legendary Muslim warrior Saladin after he conquered Jerusalem in 1187, and the Waqf has continued to manage the site since then. The Waqf has not been managing the site only in the decades following the 1967 Arab-Israeli war and Israeli occupation of East Jerusalem.
match_headline: Historical Certainty Proves Elusive at Jerusalem’s Holiest Place

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 15 about assertions by Gallianne Palayret, a United Nations human rights investigator looking into reports that French soldiers had sexually abused children in the Central African Republic, that she had informed French authorities two months earlier than they have acknowledged misstated the timing of her public revelations. Her assertions were first reported Oct. 1 by France 2, a TV station, not the week of Oct. 4.
match_headline: U.N. Official Says French Learned Early of Abuse

text: An article on Thursday about the discovery of a new species of Galápagos tortoise misspelled the given name of the senior author of a paper describing the tortoise, Chelonoidis donfaustoi. She is Adalgisa Caccone, not Adelgisa.
match_headline: New Species of Galápagos Tortoise Is Identified

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Rangers’ 4-1 victory over the Arizona Coyotes described incorrectly Keith Yandle’s goal to make the score 3-1 in the third period. His shot deflected off a Coyotes player into the net; he did not tip in a shot by Derek Stepan.
match_headline: Rangers Extend Mastery of Coyotes at the Garden

text: An article on Thursday about Temple’s success during this college football season misstated Coach Matt Rhule’s position with the New York Giants in 2012. He was an assistant offensive line coach, not assistant defensive line coach.
match_headline: A Hot Start for Temple, Where the Team Motto Is ‘What’s Next?’

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about Canada’s relationship with the Toronto Blue Jays misspelled, in one instance in some copies, the surname of the president of St. John’s Amateur Baseball in Newfoundland. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Mark Healy, not Healey.
match_headline: With Glowing Hearts, a Nation Unites Behind the Blue Jays

text: An obituary on Friday about the actor and comic Marty Ingels misidentified the high school from which he graduated. It is Forest Hills High School in Queens — not Erasmus Hall in Brooklyn, which he attended before transferring to Forest Hills.
match_headline: Marty Ingels, Actor Funny Onscreen and Outrageous Off, Dies at 79

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s decision not to enter the 2016 presidential race misstated, in some editions, how he described a comment he made last week, in which he said Republicans were not “my chief enemy.” Mr. Biden said the comment was not intended as a criticism of Hillary Rodham Clinton; he did not say he intended to criticize her.
match_headline: Joe Biden Says Family Held Sway in Decision Not to Run

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Saturday about the trial of Donald L. Blankenship, the former chief executive of Massey Energy Company who has been accused of violating mine safety rules, misstated, in some editions, the death toll from the 2010 explosion at the company’s Upper Big Branch coal mine. The explosion killed 29 workers, not 20.
match_headline: Ex-Executive Denies Flouting Rules in Deadly West Virginia Coal Mine Blast

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Oct. 14 about the race for Staten Island district attorney misidentified the man speaking at a fund-raising event for the candidate Joan Illuzzi. The man standing at the lectern is Michael R. Long, the chairman of the Conservative Party of New York State, not Rudolph W. Giuliani, the former New York City mayor.
match_headline: Race for Staten Island District Attorney Goes From Quiet to Contentious

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about testimony regarding allegations of misconduct by Louis Scarcella, a former detective, misspelled the surname of one of the lawyers of a man seeking to overturn his murder conviction. She is Rebecca Freedman, not Freeman.
match_headline: Scarcella Coached Robbery Victim Before Lineup, Lawyer Says at a Hearing

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about McDonald’s quarterly earnings described incorrectly the increase in third-quarter sales reported by McDonald’s. The 4 percent sales increase was in stores open more than a year, not all sales.
match_headline: After a 2-Year Funk, McDonald’s Posts a Sales Gain, and Investors Applaud

text: An article on Friday about an additional Volkswagen diesel engine that may be equipped with software to disable its emission control system misstated the year when the engine, the EA 288, was introduced in the United States. It was the 2015 model year, not in 2012.
match_headline: Volkswagen Investigating if Diesel Emissions Deception Was More Extensive

text: An article on Monday about scripted series at the cable channel AMC misstated part of the name of a new series. It is “Fear the Walking Dead,” not “Fear of the Walking Dead.”
match_headline: AMC Doubles Down on Scripted Series

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about Facebook’s difficulties in extending its service to India misspelled, in some copies, the given name of a cellphone salesman in a Mumbai slum. He is Shoaib Khan, not Shohaib.
match_headline: Facebook’s Internet for All Is a Tough Sell in India

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about the Mets’ preparations for the World Series misidentified the playoff series in which the Mets used a starting pitching rotation of Jacob deGrom in Game 1 followed by Noah Syndergaard, Matt Harvey and Steven Matz. It was against the Los Angeles Dodgers in the division series, not against the Chicago Cubs in the league championship series.
match_headline: Despite Thirst for World Series, Mets and Collins Savor Some Time Off

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Kansas City Royals’ 4-3 victory over the Toronto Blue Jays in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series misspelled the given name of the Royals’ starting pitcher. He is Yordano Ventura, not Yordani.
match_headline: Royals Hustle Back to the World Series, Where the Mets Await

text: An article on Monday about the resurgence of art institutions in Beirut, Lebanon, misspelled the given name of the director of the recently reopened Sursock Museum in some editions. She is Zeina Arida, not Zaina.
match_headline: Beirut’s Art Scene Stirs Amid Tumult

text: An obituary on Saturday about Thomas G. Stemberg, a founder of the office-supply retailer Staples, misstated the number of sons who survive him. The six named in the obituary are the only ones; there are not seven.
match_headline: Thomas G. Stemberg, Who Joined a Rival to Found Staples, Dies at 66

text: An obituary on Monday and in some copies on Sunday about the writer Jerome Kass misstated the surname of the husband and wife who wrote the lyrics to the songs in Mr. Kass’s television play “Queen of the Stardust Ballroom.” They are Marilyn and Alan Bergman, not Berman.
match_headline: Jerome Kass, Writer for Broadway, Film and TV, Dies at 78

text: An article last Wednesday about an investigation into an airstrike against a Doctors Without Borders hospital in Kunduz, Afghanistan, that killed at least 22 staff members and patients misidentified the unit whose troops approved the strike against the hospital. The troops were from Third Special Forces Group, based at Fort Bragg, N.C., not First Special Forces Group, from Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington State.
match_headline: Hospital Attack Fueled by Units New to Kunduz

text: An article on Oct. 20 about the low voter turnout in the first two days of parliamentary elections in Egypt transposed the names used by the prime minister, who gave government employees a half-day holiday to encourage more voting, and referred to him incorrectly at another point. He is Sherif Ismail, not Ismail Sherif, and so Mr. Ismail, not Mr. Sherif.
match_headline: Low Voter Turnout Reflects System by Design in Egypt

text: An article on Tuesday about a tentative budget deal between Republican congressional leaders and President Obama misstated the name of the committee that is chaired by Representative Jeb Hensarling of Texas. It is the House Financial Services Committee, not the Banking Committee.
match_headline: Congress Strikes a Budget Deal With President

text: An article on Tuesday about an encounter between a white school police officer and a black female student at Spring Valley High School in Columbia, S.C., misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the superintendent of the district where the episode took place. She is Debbie Hamm, not Ham.
match_headline: Video Shows Officer Flipping Student in South Carolina, Prompting Inquiry

text: An article on Monday about a yearslong effort by President Obama and Michelle Obama to put their more modern aesthetic imprint on the art displayed in the White House misspelled the surname of the artist who painted “Bear Lake, New Mexico.” It was Georgia O’Keeffe, not O’Keefe. Because of an editing error, the article also misspelled the name of a 1955 painting by Mark Rothko. It is “Red Band,” not “Red Ban.”
match_headline: For Obamas, a More Abstract Choice of Art

text: An article on Saturday about how Tyrone Howard, the suspect in the killing of a New York City police officer, was initially rejected from a drug diversion program before another court admitted him misstated what is known about an off-the-record bench conference in a hearing in December. An official said that a 2009 gunfight in which Mr. Howard was suspected of having participated appears, based on indications in the record, to have been cited during the conference, but the official could not confirm that the shooting had been discussed.
match_headline: Suspect in Officer’s Killing Was Deemed Too Violent for Drug Treatment in 2011

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with a theater review of “Before Your Very Eyes,” at the Public Theater in Manhattan, misidentified the performer on the left. She is Rose Bell-McKinley, not Charlotte Beede, another cast member.
match_headline: Review: Children Growing Very Old in ‘Before Your Very Eyes’

text: An article on Monday about a shift in tactics by Palestinian security officers in response to the recent violent uprising in Israel misidentified the university where Andy Clarno, who said the officers were in an “impossible situation,” teaches sociology. It is the University of Illinois at Chicago, not the University of Chicago.
match_headline: Caught Between Protesters and Israel, Palestinian Security Forces Shift Tactics

text: An article on Tuesday about Ruth Ellen Brosseau, who won re-election to the Canadian Parliament last week, four years after entering office as an obscure candidate for the New Democratic Party with no political experience, misidentified the political party whose loss of support among voters is believed to have contributed to her surprise victory in 2011. It is the Bloc Québécois, the federal separatist party — not the Parti Québécois, the provincial party.
match_headline: Accidental Lawmaker in Canada Defies Critics, and Liberal Party Resurgence

text: An article on Friday about a vote by the New Jersey State Senate to override Gov. Chris Christie’s veto of a gun control bill misstated the title of Thomas Kean Jr. in some editions. He is a senator, not an assemblyman.
match_headline: New Jersey Senate Overrides Christie’s Veto of Gun Control Bill

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the N.H.L. roundup in some editions on Monday about the Rangers’ 4-1 victory over the Calgary Flames misstated, in one instance, the number of goals Rangers defenseman Dan Girardi has scored this season. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, Girardi’s goal in the second period was his first of the season, not his fifth. (His teammate Oscar Lindberg, not Girardi, scored his fifth goal Sunday.)
match_headline: ‘Jane the Virgin’ Season 2, Episode 3: Don’t Let Motherhood Hijack Your Goals

text: An article on Sunday about Alex Ovechkin’s pursuit of Sergei Fedorov’s N.H.L. record for most goals by a Russian player erroneously included, in some editions, a trophy among those won by Fedorov in the 1990s. He did not win the 1994 Art Ross Trophy, which is given to the league’s leader in points during the regular season. (Wayne Gretzky won it that year.)
match_headline: Alex Ovechkin Closes In on Mentor’s Record

text: An article on Aug. 2 about Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s deliberations on whether to run for president referred incorrectly to Maureen Dowd’s account of a conversation between Mr. Biden and his son, Beau, who soon before he died from brain cancer in May encouraged his father to run. Ms. Dowd reported in an Op-Ed column on Aug. 2 that Mr. Biden and Beau sat at a table while Beau was sick and discussed the matter, not that they spoke as he “lay dying.”
match_headline: Joe Biden Said to Be Taking New Look at Presidential Run

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Iran’s acceptance of an invitation to join international talks aimed at resolving the Syrian civil war misstated the surname of Saudi Arabia’s foreign minister, who was suspicious of Iran’s intentions. He is Adel al-Jubeir, not Jubeiri. In addition, a reporting credit for the article was omitted in some editions. Thomas Erdbrink reported from Tehran, Sewell Chan from London, and David E. Sanger from Washington. Somini Sengupta contributed reporting from the United Nations, and Rick Gladstone from New York.
match_headline: After a U.S. Shift, Iran Has a Seat at Talks on War in Syria

text: An article on Sunday about the naming of a two-star general, Maj. Gen. William B. Hickman, to lead the United States Army’s investigation into the bombing of a Doctors Without Borders hospital in Kunduz, Afghanistan, erroneously attributed a comment about the Army’s initial review of the bombing. It was Brig. Gen. Wilson Shoffner, a spokesman for Gen. John F. Campbell, the American commander in Afghanistan — not General Campbell himself — who said an assessment team had “determined that the reports of civilian casualties were credible.”
ref_headline: determined that the reports of civilian casualties were credible.
match_headline: General to Investigate U.S. Airstrike on Doctors Without Borders Hospital

text: An article on Wednesday about an invitation to Iran to join talks in Vienna with Russia, the United States and European nations on the Syrian civil war misspelled the surname of Iran’s supreme leader in some editions. He is Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, not Khomeni.
match_headline: Iran Is Invited to Join U.S., Russia and Europe for Talks on Syria’s Future

text: An article on Wednesday about the Republican debate on the cable channel CNBC described the channel’s average audience last year incorrectly in some editions. It was 131,000 viewers at any given moment during the day, not 131,000 per day.
match_headline: CNBC May Be the Big Winner of the Next Republican Debate

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about the Fox shows “Bones” and “Sleepy Hollow” referred incorrectly to the literary character Ichabod Crane. He is a character in a story, not a poem. (Crane is also in “Sleepy Hollow.”)
match_headline: Critic’s Notebook: ‘Bones’ and ‘Sleepy Hollow’ Cross-Pollinate

text: An article last Saturday about challenges facing the Democratic Party in a special election for a State Senate seat in New York’s Southern Tier referred incorrectly to six state senators who were elected as Democrats. One of the Democrats caucuses with the Republicans; five others form their own breakaway caucus and often vote with Republicans. All six do not caucus with the Republicans.
match_headline: Special New York Senate Race Shows Voters’ Anger at Albany

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about a new admissions process from a coalition of elite colleges refers incorrectly to James G. Nondorf of the University of Chicago. He is the dean of admissions and financial aid, but he does not have a Ph.D.; therefore he is not “Dr. Nondorf.”
match_headline: A New Coalition of Elite Colleges Tries to Reshape Admissions

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about international students in Flint, Mich., misstates part of the name of the street connecting the University of Michigan and Kettering University. It is University Avenue, not University Drive.
match_headline: International Students Find the American Dream ... in Flint

text: An article on Page F14 this weekend about a movement to put museum holdings online without copyright restrictions misidentifies the builder of Cooper Hewitt. He was Andrew Carnegie, not Andrew Mellon.
match_headline: New Online Openness Lets Museums Share Works With the World

text: An article on Page F4 this weekend about the ways in which art auctions orchestrate sales for maximum drama refers incorrectly to an arrangement between Sotheby’s and the Los Angeles collector Audrey Irmas. Sotheby’s convinced her, with a sale estimate of about $60 million, that it was time to sell her “Untitled, 1968 (New York City)” by Cy Twombly. There was no minimum price guarantee, Sotheby’s says.
match_headline: How Auction Houses Orchestrate Sales for Maximum Drama

text: An article on Page F2 this weekend about major gallery exhibitions in Manhattan refers incorrectly to films by Ana Mendieta that will be at the Galerie Lelong. None of the films — not some of them — were shot in Cuba. The article also misspells the surname of a director of the Gagosian Gallery. He is Stefan Ratibor, not Rotibor. And the article misspells part of the name of a gallery in one instance. As the article correctly notes elsewhere, it is Mitchell-Innes & Nash, not Mitchell-Inness & Nash.
match_headline: Eager for a Fresh Take, Galleries Mine an Unfamiliar Side to Famous Artists

text: An article on Page F6 this weekend about art sales online includes an outdated number of galleries from which Artsy’s website draws its sales offerings. After the article had gone to press, Artsy said it works with 4,000 galleries, not 3,500.
match_headline: Purchasing Fine Art Is Increasingly Just a Click Away

text: An article on Page F34 this weekend about educational degrees offered by museums misstates the title for Ellen V. Futter of the American Museum of Natural History. She is president of the museum, not its director. The error is repeated in an accompanying caption with a picture of Ms. Futter.
match_headline: Museums, Always Educational, Now Confer Degrees

text: An article on Page F24 this weekend about the popularity of sculpture misstates part of the name of an open-air sculpture park. It is the Storm King Art Center (not Arts).
match_headline: Sculpture Gets Its Day in the Sun as Prices Rise

text: An article last Sunday about hopes by some Roman Catholics that the bishops who met for three weeks at the Vatican to prepare a report on family issues would endorse more accommodations for divorced and remarried Catholics misspelled, in some editions, the given name of an Austrian cardinal who described the report as a “document of consensus.” He is Christoph Schönborn, not Chrisoph.
match_headline: Voice Is Sought at the Vatican on Remarriage

text: An article last Sunday about the actress Saoirse Ronan, whose latest film is “Brooklyn,” misstated when she will appear on Broadway in a production of “The Crucible.” It will be in the spring of 2016, not 2017.
match_headline: With ‘Brooklyn,’ Saoirse Ronan Embraces Her Journey

text: A picture caption with an article on Oct. 4 about Brahms’s 1887 Double Concerto for violin, cello and orchestra misidentified, using information from a publicist, Joseph Joachim in a 19th-century photograph of his quartet. Joachim, for whom Brahms wrote the concerto, is on the left, not the right.
match_headline: Classical Duets of a Singular Nature

text: An article on Oct. 25 about Terry Gross, host of the program ‘‘Fresh Air’’ on National Public Radio, included two incorrect quotations from an interview Gross conducted with the writer Mary Karr. Discussing how Karr started writing memoirs before our culture became so confessional, Gross asked Karr, ‘‘So has that affected your standards of what is meant to be written about and what is meant to maintain silence about?’’ — not ‘‘how does that affect your understanding.’’ And Karr said, ‘‘That’s such a smart question’’ — not ‘‘good’’ question.
match_headline: Terry Gross and the Art of Opening Up

text: An article last Sunday about new lodging options in Africa misstated the Canadian region where the winemaker Norman Hardie is based. It is Prince Edward County, Ontario, not the Niagara region. And the price for the trip offered with Mr. Hardie was given in the incorrect currency. The price is 6,975 Canadian, not U.S., dollars.
match_headline: 10 African Adventures Answer Call of the Wild and Comfort

text: An article last Sunday about a new building at 100 East 53rd Street, using information provided by the developer Aby J. Rosen, misstated the development’s anticipated completion date. It will be in the spring of 2017, not 2016.
match_headline: In Midtown East, the Seagram Building’s New Neighbor

text: An article last Sunday about a type of public speaking that some people call the “NPR voice” misidentified the Manhattan neighborhood where the “Sex and the City” character Carrie Bradshaw lived. It is the Upper East Side, not downtown on the West Side.
match_headline: ‘NPR Voice’ Has Taken Over the Airwaves

text: A report on Oct. 11, about a Sept. 26 wedding ceremony, in which the father of Brittany Peck reached for the hand of her stepfather to include him in the bride’s walk down the aisle, referred imprecisely to “I Loved Her First,” the song another bride had chosen to dance with her biological father. The version played by the D.J. was performed by but not written by Brad Paisley.
match_headline: The Stepfather and the Wedding: A Family’s Viral Story Still Hits Home

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with the continuation of an article about the Republican presidential debate misidentified, in some editions, the candidates shown. The photograph included, from left, Donald Trump, Ben Carson, Carly Fiorina, Ted Cruz, Chris Christie and Rand Paul; the picture did not show John Kasich, Mike Huckabee, Jeb Bush or Marco Rubio.
match_headline: Republican Candidates Take Sharp Tone in Third Debate

text: A picture credit on Oct. 22 with an article about testimony from the survivor of a beating inside a church that left the witness’s brother dead misspelled the surname of the photographer. A picture of the survivor, Christopher Leonard, and his half sister, Sarah Ferguson, in court and a picture of a candlelight vigil were both taken by Tina Russell, not Russel.
match_headline: Survivor of Word of Life Church Beatings Testifies in Court

text: An article last Monday about the entry of private start-ups in the effort to develop energy from nuclear fusion referred incompletely to fusion research carried out with giant lasers at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California. While the lab did in fact miss a 2012 deadline for producing more energy than the lasers put in, it eventually achieved that goal in September 2013.
match_headline: Start-Ups Take On Challenge of Nuclear Fusion

text: An article on Tuesday about plaintiffs’ lawyers who are jockeying for position in lawsuits stemming from Volkswagen’s emissions scandal misstated the number of judges on the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation, which will hear arguments about where to consolidate the federal lawsuits. There are seven judges, counting the chairwoman, not six.
match_headline: Lawyers Jostle for Lead Position in Volkswagen Diesel Suits

text: An article on Friday about Ivy League colleges that are shifting to Friday night football games from the traditional Saturday ones referred incorrectly to last week’s Yale-Penn game in Philadelphia. It was Penn’s first nationally televised night game at 120-year-old Franklin Field, not the first nationally televised night game at the stadium. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Ivy League Embraces Friday Night Football, in Small Doses

text: An article on Friday about bands formed by surviving members of the Grateful Dead misstated the name of the music hall and restaurant that Phil Lesh, the Grateful Dead bass player, and his wife own in California. It is Terrapin Crossroads, not Terrapin Station. (That is the title of a Grateful Dead song.)
match_headline: Grateful Dead Alums Keep On Touring, but Not All Together

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a shift in the Palestinian uprising from Jerusalem to Hebron, the West Bank’s largest city, referred incorrectly to Hebron’s connection to Abraham, the biblical patriarch. Hebron is believed to be the burial place of Abraham, not his birthplace. (Ur, in what is now Iraq, is considered to be his birthplace.)
match_headline: Palestinian Uprising Shifts to West Bank City of Hebron

text: An article last Tuesday about the arrests of four men linked to the fatal shooting of an Italian aid worker in Dhaka, Bangladesh, misspelled the given name of the commissioner of the Dhaka metropolitan police in some editions. He is Asaduzzaman Mia, not Asaduzzmana. Because of an editing error, the article also misspelled the given name of the aid worker in some editions. He was Cesare Tavella, not Cesere.
match_headline: Bangladeshi Officials Say 4 Arrested in Killing of Italian Aid Worker Were Not With ISIS

text: An article on Sunday about an election battle over Houston’s equal rights ordinance misstated the number of jurisdictions across the country that have passed measures to fight discrimination. It is 200 other cities and 17 states, not 200 other cities in 17 states.
match_headline: Tactics and Antagonists Draw Attention to Houston Rights Vote

text: An article last Tuesday about the death of a Nevada woman at a cryotherapy center misstated the substance used to cool the tanks during the procedure. It is liquid nitrogen, not nitrous gas. (Liquid nitrogen turns into nitrogen gas.)
match_headline: Death of Woman in Tank at a Nevada Cryotherapy Center Raises Questions About Safety

text: An article on Oct. 20 about criminal offenders in Marion, Ala., who are given the choice of donating blood to avoid jail time, gave an outdated academic affiliation for Susan Lederer, the author of “Flesh and Blood,” a history of blood transfusions and organ transplantation. She is at the University of Wisconsin-Madison; she is no longer a professor of medical history at Yale, where she wrote the book.
match_headline: For Offenders Who Can’t Pay, It’s a Pint of Blood or Jail Time

text: A caption for a map last Sunday with an article about which Americans still lack health insurance misstated the start of Alaska’s Medicaid expansion. It began in September; it is not scheduled to begin next year.
match_headline: Morning Agenda: Valeant Drops Philidor

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a theater review of “Songbird,” at the 59E59 Theaters in Manhattan, misidentified the actor shown playing the fiddle. He is Drew McVety — not Andy Taylor, another cast member.
match_headline: Review: ‘Songbird,’ a Honky-Tonk Take on Chekhov

text: An article on Saturday about “Hopscotch,” described as a “mobile opera in 24 cars” in which audience members are driven around Los Angeles, misstated part of the name of a neighborhood in the city. It is Boyle Heights, not Boylan Heights.
match_headline: ‘Hopscotch’ Takes Opera Into the Streets

text: An article on Monday about the French author Patrick Modiano, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature last year and whose books are increasingly being translated into English, misstated the United States publishing date for his book “Pedigree.” It was published by Yale University Press in August, not last year.
match_headline: Patrick Modiano, an Author of Paris Mysteries, Keeps His Own

text: An obituary on Sunday about George Germon, a chef who teamed with his future wife, Johanne Killeen, to found the internationally known restaurant Al Forno in Providence, R.I., omitted the names of two of his survivors. Besides Ms. Killeen, he is survived by two sisters, Anita Alfano and Janet Prink.
match_headline: George Germon, Founder of Rhode Island Dining Gem, Dies at 70

text: An obituary on Sunday about Mel Daniels, a Hall of Fame center for the Indiana Pacers, referred incorrectly to Larry Bird, also a member of the Hall of Fame. While Bird coached the Pacers for three years and is currently the team’s president of basketball operations, he played his entire career for the Boston Celtics; he did not play for the Pacers.
match_headline: Mel Daniels, Prolific Rebounder on the Indiana Pacers in the 1970s, Dies at 71

text: Because of an editing error, an earlier version of the National correction about the cryotherapy center erroneously stated that liquid nitrogen turns into nitrous gas. (It turns into nitrogen gas.)
An article on Oct. 26 about the construction of a factory in Buffalo for SolarCity misidentified the company’s chief executive. He is Lyndon Rive, not Peter Rive. (The two are brothers.)
match_headline: Despite Risks, Cuomo Bets on Solar Power to Lift Buffalo

text: An article on Monday about the New York Times food writer Mark Bittman’s move to the start-up Purple Carrot misstated, in some copies, how its founder, Andrew Levitt, originally financed Purple Carrot. It was with $125,000 of his own money, not from a friend. The article also misstated, in some editions, where Mr. Levitt first met Mr. Bittman. It was in Washington, not Boston.
match_headline: Mark Bittman to Join the Meal Kit Firm Purple Carrot

text: An article on Monday about The Brooklyn Rail, an art newspaper, referred imprecisely to Phong Bui’s relationship to The Rail in one instance. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, Mr. Bui is one of several founders of the newspaper, not the person who “conceived” it.
match_headline: The Hustle of Publishing Art News in the Postprint Era

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with a theater review of a Yiddish production of “Death of a Salesman,” at the Castillo Theater in Manhattan, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of Avi Hoffman as Willy Loman, was taken by Ronald L. Glassman, not by Arielle Hoffman.
match_headline: Review: ‘Death of a Salesman’ in Yiddish

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with a Critic’s Notebook article about a film series at the Museum of Modern Art misstated the series’ name. As the article correctly noted, it is To Save and Project, not To Serve and Project.
match_headline: Serial Gems Are Painstakingly Restored for the Screen

text: An article on Tuesday about challenges facing a new alliance of ground forces in Syria, backed by the United States, to combat the Islamic State misstated, in some editions, part of a slogan on the sweatshirt of an alliance fighter in broken boots and tattered fatigues who was held out by an Arab commander as an example of the sorry state of his men. The slogan was “Skateboarding ruined my life,” not “Skateboarding ruined by life.”
match_headline: New U.S.-Backed Alliance to Counter ISIS in Syria Falters

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 27 about a challenge by Britain’s House of Lords to a government proposal to reduce a cash benefit for people in low-paying jobs misstated the dollar equivalent of 4 billion pounds, the original cost of the benefit. It is about $6.1 billion, not $6.1 million.
match_headline: Unelected Chamber in Britain Delays Cameron’s Spending Cuts

text: A reporting credit on Sunday for an article about the stabbing of two businessmen in Dhaka, Bangladesh, who had published the works of a Bangladeshi-American known for his critical writings on religious extremism misspelled part of the name of the town in Bangladesh where Julfikar Ali Manik, one of the reporters, was located. It is Cox’s Bazar, not Cox’s Bazaar.
match_headline: 2 Men Who Published Writings Critical of Extremism Are Stabbed in Bangladesh

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the awarding of the Goncourt Prize to the novelist Mathias Énard referred incorrectly to another finalist, Hédi Kaddour. He is Franco-Tunisian, not Franco-Turkish.
match_headline: Prix Goncourt Goes to Mathias Énard

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the release of new data showing that China burns up to 17 percent more coal per year than the government had previously disclosed misidentified, in some editions, the measurement that the figure of 4.2 billion metric tons applies to. It represents the amount of coal consumed in China in 2013, not the amount of carbon dioxide emitted.
match_headline: China Burns Much More Coal Than Reported, Complicating Climate Talks

text: An article on Monday about the increased demand for toddler story time at public libraries across New York City misstated the designation of 20 New York Public Library branches that will hold extra story time sessions and distribute literacy kits. They are enhanced literacy — not literary — sites.
match_headline: Long Line at the Library? It’s Story Time Again

text: An article in some editions on Monday about Sebastian Almonte, who was able to attend summer camp through assistance from an agency supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, misidentified the organization that provided the money for his camp tuition. It is YM & YWHA of Washington Heights & Inwood — not UJA-Federation of New York.
match_headline: Summer Camp Allows Manhattan Boy to Be a Child Again

text: An article on Wednesday about a content and marketing partnership between Verizon Communications and the National Basketball Association, using information from Verizon, misstated the nature of the partnership. While some marketing elements are exclusive, the deal is not an exclusive content agreement. The N.B.A. retains the right to strike other deals for content.
match_headline: Verizon and N.B.A. Form Partnership for Go90 Content

text: An article on Thursday about quarterly earnings for various media companies misstated the percentage decline in 21st Century Fox’s net income last quarter, compared to the year-ago quarter. Net income declined 35 percent, not 53 percent.
match_headline: Time Warner Cuts Profit Expectations, and Media Stocks Dip

text: An article on Thursday about Puerto Rico’s debt problem misstated the constitutional principle at issue in the prospect of federal regulation of securities sold by state and local governments. It is states’ rights, not the separation of powers.
match_headline: Puerto Rico’s Debt Crisis and the 1975 Law Complicating Matters

text: An article on Thursday about the challenges of achieving diversity in the work forces of various industries misstated the programming language that was in demand before Y2K. It is Cobol, not Cobalt.
match_headline: Defining Diversity in Silicon Valley and on Wall Street

text: An article on Thursday about a planned addition to the American Museum of Natural History in Manhattan misstated the title of the head of the museum, Ellen V. Futter, in some editions. She is the president, not the director.
match_headline: Museum of Natural History Reveals Design for Expansion

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Oct. 29 about the awarding of the Wein Prize from the Studio Museum in Harlem to the artist Njideka Akunyili Crosby referred incorrectly to her at one point. She is Ms. Akunyili Crosby, not Ms. Crosby.
match_headline: Wein Prize Is Awarded to a Nigerian-born Artist

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the arrest of two students in Litchfield, Conn., over Halloween costumes that resembled the Columbine High School shooters misidentified, in some copies, one of the items in the youths’ costumes. The boys were said to have worn baseball hats; they did not carry baseball bats.
match_headline: Charges for 2 Connecticut Students Said to Have Dressed Like Columbine Killers

text: An article on Wednesday about the first College Football Playoff rankings of the season included a quotation that misstated the order of games that affected Memphis’s standing. Mississippi beat Alabama before losing to Memphis; Mississippi’s victory over Alabama was not “subsequent” to its loss to Memphis, as noted by Jeff Long, the chairman of the selection committee. The article also referred incorrectly in some copies to Memphis’s victory over Mississippi. Memphis won at home, not on the road. In addition, the article misstated, in some copies, Texas Christian’s overall and conference records. It is 8-0 and 5-0, not 7-0 and 4-0. The article also misstated, in some copies and in one reference, Baylor’s overall record. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is 7-0, not 8-0. And, finally, the article misidentified, in some copies, the location of Florida’s victory over Mississippi. It was at home, in Gainesville — not on the road.
match_headline: Clemson Tops First Set of College Football Playoff Rankings

text: An article on Page F4 this weekend about some of the country’s biggest foundations that are increasing their support for progressive issues as opposed to institutions misstates the purpose of a gift by Mark Zuckerberg, chief of Facebook. He recently committed hundreds of millions of dollars to a foundation that works to fight homelessness and address other social concerns. He did not commit the money to fight only homelessness.
match_headline: Major Foundations, Eager for Big Change, Aim High

text: An article on Page F8 this weekend about Paul Allen’s philanthropy misidentifies the research institute at whose anniversary celebration Mr. Allen performed with his band, the Underthinkers. It is the Allen Institute for Brain Science, not the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence.
match_headline: Paul Allen’s Philanthropy Mirrors His Passions and Business Approach

text: An article on Page F6 this weekend about work by land trusts to increase the availability of affordable housing renders the name of a nonprofit organization in Marin County, Calif., incorrectly. It is Marin Agricultural Land Trust, not the Marin Agricultural Land Trust Association.
match_headline: Communities Come Together to Make Homes More Affordable

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about an apology that Gerald Harris, a former Manhattan assistant district attorney, extended to Jonas Mekas, whom he prosecuted in 1964 for screening the film “Flaming Creatures,” misspelled the surname of a former New York City mayor who heard the case. He was Vincent R. Impellitteri, not Impelliteri.
match_headline: The Prosecution Resets in a 1964 Obscenity Case

text: An article on Sept. 27 about travel photography misstated the surname of the Swiss physician who first treated homesickness and the year he started doing so. He was Johannes Hofer, not Hoferus, and he first treated it in 1688, not 1678.
match_headline: Far Away From Here

text: An article on Oct. 25 about Anna Stubblefield, who was on trial for sexual assault, referred incorrectly to Sue Rubin. She was not among those present at the trial.
match_headline: The Strange Case of Anna Stubblefield

text: An article on Oct. 18 about horse farms in Northern Virginia and Maryland misidentified the city in California that is home to the Santa Anita horse racing track. It is Arcadia, not Pasadena.
match_headline: Jane Smiley’s Horse Country

text: An article last Sunday about developments in and around the Brooklyn Navy Yard misidentified one of the avenues bordering Navy Green, a housing complex under construction across from the yard. It is Clermont Avenue, not Clinton Avenue.
match_headline: Reinventing the Brooklyn Navy Yard

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about Lou Reed and the reaction of his friends and associates to a recently published biography of the singer misidentified the month in 1980 in which Reed and his first wife, Sylvia Morales, were married. It was in February of that year, not January.
match_headline: Who Was the Real Lou Reed?

text: A news analysis article about Silicon Valley’s philanthropy last Sunday misspelled the surname of the wife of Mark Zuckerberg, the chief executive of Facebook. She is Priscilla Chan, not Chin. It also misspelled the surname of one of the founders of Facebook. He is Dustin Moskovitz, not Moskowitz.
match_headline: Silicon Valley’s New Philanthropy

text: An article on Tuesday about a rift among gun owners in Michigan over concealed weapons in schools erroneously included one place among venues where guns have been banned. Concealed weapons are allowed — not banned — in public libraries in the state. (As the article correctly noted, they are banned in Michigan’s schools and sports arenas.)
match_headline: Rift Emerges Among Gun Owners Over Concealing Weapons in Schools

text: A headline in some editions on Friday with an article about the Thursday night art auction at Sotheby’s misstated, in some copies, the nature of the sale. It was of Impressionist and modern works, as the article noted, but not from the collection of A. Alfred Taubman, the auction house’s former chairman.
match_headline: Warmer Response at Sotheby’s 2nd Night of Auctions

text: An article on Friday about the conviction of two former London traders on charges of rigging an interest rate benchmark known as Libor misstated, in some copies, the number of people the Justice Department has charged in the matter. It is 13 people total, not 15. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption in some copies.
match_headline: Two Former Traders Found Guilty in Libor Manipulation Case

text: An obituary on Monday about the former United States senator, actor and Republican presidential candidate Fred Thompson referred imprecisely to his questioning of the former Nixon White House aide Alexander Butterfield when Mr. Thompson was Republican counsel on the Senate Watergate Committee. While Mr. Butterfield did acknowledge the existence of recording devices in the Oval Office in response to Mr. Thompson’s questioning at a hearing, it was not the case that the questioning “led to the revelation” of the recording system; Mr. Butterfield had already made that revelation at a private meeting with members of the committee staff three days earlier.
match_headline: Fred Thompson, Former Senator, Actor and Presidential Candidate, Dies at 73

text: An article on Saturday about high school students in Cañon City, Colo., who traded naked pictures of themselves misstated the distinction claimed by the Royal Gorge Bridge and Park, a nearby tourist attraction that employs many people from the tightly knit community. Park officials say the suspension bridge is America’s highest, not the world’s highest.
match_headline: Hundreds of Nude Photos Jolt Colorado School

text: An article on Monday about Peabody Energy’s agreement to disclose more to its investors about the financial risks it faces related to climate change described the company incorrectly. It is a private sector company as opposed to a government-owned one, but it is not privately owned. (It is publicly listed on the New York Stock Exchange.)
match_headline: Peabody Energy Agrees to Greater Disclosures of Financial Risks

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about underreported carbon dioxide emissions in 800,000 diesel- and gasoline-powered Volkswagen vehicles in Europe referred incompletely to the approach the United States and European countries take in regulating carbon dioxide emissions from passenger cars. Both the United States and European countries have specific regulations on such emissions; it is not the case that the Europeans are more focused on reducing carbon dioxide emissions than the United States. (European countries have, however, added further incentives, like giving tax credits to owners of gasoline or diesel cars based on their low emissions of carbon dioxide.)
match_headline: Volkswagen Says Whistle-Blower Pushed It to Admit Broader Cheating

text: Because of an editing error, the Sports of The Times column on Monday, about the involvement of black football players at the University of Missouri in protests about race relations on campus, described The Columbia Missourian incorrectly. It is a daily newspaper managed by professional editors and staffed by Missouri School of Journalism students; it is not “the campus newspaper.” (The Maneater is the official student newspaper.)
match_headline: University of Missouri Football Players Exercise Power in Racism Protest

text: An article in some editions on Nov. 2 about the Kansas City Royals’ 7-2 victory over the Mets in Game 5 of the World Series rendered incorrectly a quotation from Royals first baseman Eric Hosmer about the disappointment the team felt after losing last year’s World Series. He said: “We think about it quite often. I’ve said before, and I’ll say it again: I think that’s kind of something that we all turn to mentally, to kind of — when there’s points in time during the season where your team is not going too well. You look in September there, and we started to slide a little bit. But I just think everyone kind of relates back to that and relates to how much that hurt.”
match_headline: Royals Rally Past Mets for First World Series Title Since 1985

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the “Munch and Expressionism” exhibition opening in February at the Neue Galerie New York, using information from the museum, misidentified an artist whose work will be included. He was Richard Gerstl; Karl Gerstner is not in the show.
match_headline: ‘Four Marilyns’ Is Back on the Auction Block

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the car customizer George Barris referred incorrectly to Drag-u-La, a car he created for the television show “The Munsters” in which he incorporated a coffin. It was not the family car. (The family car, known as the Munster Koach, was also designed by Mr. Barris but did not include a coffin.)
match_headline: George Barris, California King of Customized Cars, Dies at 89

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the British government’s suspension of flights in response to concerns that a bomb might have brought down a Russian jetliner over the Sinai Peninsula referred incompletely to the government’s action. Britain suspended flights to and from — not just to — the Egyptian resort city of Sharm el Sheikh.
match_headline: Britain, Concerned About Russian Crash, Halts Sinai Flights

text: An article on Nov. 2 about a bankruptcy filing by Freedom Communications, the media company that owns The Orange County Register, misstated a former position of Rich Mirman, Freedom’s chief executive. He was a casino executive, not a casino owner.
match_headline: Owner of The Orange County Register Files for Bankruptcy Protection

text: An article on the Square Feet pages on Tuesday about the Wilshire Grand Center in Los Angeles misstated the place of the Wilshire Grand Center in the history of tower-based office space in Los Angeles. It will be the first new such space in about 20 years, not 25. (The 26-story MTA Building was completed in 1995.)
match_headline: In Downtown Los Angeles, a Potential Anchor for Offices

text: An article on Saturday about the hospitalization of Sepp Blatter, the suspended president of FIFA, soccer’s world governing body, misspelled the surname of one of his advisers. He is Klaus Stöhlker, not Stöhkler.
match_headline: FIFA’s Sepp Blatter Being Treated for ‘Stress-Related’ Medical Issue

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about Clemson’s 23-13 football victory over Florida State misstated the number of yards Florida State running back Dalvin Cook gained in the game. It was 194, not 198.
match_headline: Passer Recovers and Puts Clemson in One Championship Game

text: An article last Wednesday about a gathering in Buffalo of descendants of authors of slave narratives and other African-American antislavery activists referred imprecisely to William Grimes’s narrative. It was the first by a fugitive slave — not any slave — to include “written by himself” on its title page.
match_headline: Familial Ties to Slavery, Bound by Vintage First-Person Accounts

text: An article on Monday about the Breakthrough Prize misidentified the gene that John Hardy discovered a mutation of in patients who had Alzheimer’s disease. He discovered a mutation in the amyloid precursor protein gene, not presenilin.
match_headline: Breakthrough Prizes Give Top Scientists the Rock Star Treatment

text: An article on Tuesday about medical training dummies that are very realistic referred incorrectly to one of the new simulators unveiled this week by Boston Children’s Hospital. One of the two new simulators is of an adolescent patient, not of a newborn.
match_headline: Artificial Patients, Real Learning

text: An obituary on Oct. 18 about the diplomat Alvin P. Adams Jr., using information from a family member, omitted the name of a survivor. Besides his son, two grandchildren, a brother and his sister Edith Kiggen, Mr. Adams was survived by another sister, Helen Vollmer. (Ms. Kiggen died on Oct. 28.)
match_headline: Alvin P. Adams Jr., Ambassador Who Helped Haiti Pursue Democracy, Dies at 73

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about racial tensions at the University of Missouri that led to the resignations of two top officials, including the president Timothy M. Wolfe, erroneously attributed a comment about Mr. Wolfe in some editions. It was people on campus — not Michael A. Middleton, a deputy chancellor emeritus — who described Mr. Wolfe as stiff and aloof.
match_headline: University of Missouri Protests Spur a Day of Change

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 4 about a planned meeting between President Xi Jinping of China and Taiwan’s president, Ma Ying-jeou — the first such meeting since the Chinese Communist Revolution of 1949 — misstated, in some editions, the timing of a White House statement on the meeting. It was issued on Nov. 3, not on Nov. 4. The article also misspelled the given name of a Chinese professor of political science who said the meeting could set the groundwork for changes that suited China in the long run. He is Wang Yingjin, not Yangjin.
match_headline: China, Taiwan and a Meeting After 66 Years

text: An article last Thursday about an extraordinary rise in public corruption in Kenya, no stranger to graft, erroneously included remarks attributed to Robert Mugabe, the Zimbabwean president, saying that Kenyans were thieves and telling his countrymen to be on alert when visiting Kenya so as not to catch “that disease.” The Spectator, a Kenyan newsmagazine that published the remarks, said last week that they had been fabricated, and were intended as satire.
match_headline: An Anticorruption Plea in Kenya: ‘Please, Just Steal a Little’

text: An article on Nov. 3 about a suggestion by Iran that it might withdraw from new peace talks on Syria because of what Iranian officials described as the unconstructive role of Saudi Arabia, Iran’s rival for dominance in the Middle East, referred incorrectly to a diplomatic meeting in Vienna at the end of October. It included nearly all of Syria’s neighbors, not all of them. (Israel did not participate.)
match_headline: Iran Says It May Quit Talks on Syria Over Saudis’ Role

text: An article on Wednesday about the lack of funding from United States entities for the Korean War Veterans Memorial on the National Mall misspelled the name of the executive vice president at Samsung Electronics. He is Won-Kyong Kim, not Won Kyong-kim. The article also referred incorrectly to the design of the memorial. Frank Gaylord designed the statues and Louis Nelson designed the mural wall; Mr. Gaylord did not design the whole memorial.
match_headline: Korean War Memorial Group Finds More Aid in Korea Than in U.S.

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about an event in the Bronx that drew controversy for its theme of urban ruin referred incorrectly to a piano at the event. It was a party decoration, not part of the “Macabre Suite” show. In addition, a subheading misidentified the event in some editions. It was a pop-up art show, not a pop-art show.
match_headline: Bronx Pop-Up Art Show Prompts Criticism That It Invoked Borough’s Painful Past

text: An article on Wednesday about how designers are representing Arthur Miller’s works on the centennial of his birth, using information from a designer, misidentified the plane shown on promotional artwork for the Grand Canyon University production of “All My Sons.” It is a B-17 bomber — not a P-38, which was primarily a fighter plane.
match_headline: Designing Arthur Miller: Simple Gestures, Big Ideas

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Wednesday about an auction at Christie’s in New York misidentified the subject of a Lucian Freud painting that was sold, “Brigadier.” He is the former husband of Camilla Parker Bowles, Andrew Parker Bowles, not her father.
match_headline: Mixed Night in ‘Strange’ Christie’s Contemporary and Postwar Sale

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the apparent landslide victory in national elections by the Burmese opposition party led by Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate, misstated the total number of seats in Myanmar’s Parliament. It is 664, not 644.
match_headline: Myanmar Election Has Aung San Suu Kyi’s Party Confident of Landslide

text: An article on Wednesday about the lack of public outrage in Russia over accusations that a Kremlin-backed program facilitated doping by Russian track-and-field athletes in the Olympics and other top sports events referred incorrectly to Andrey Babitsky, who said the doping would probably “be stretched to be understood as something done for the public good.” He is a former editor of Russian Esquire and new editor in chief of InLiberty.ru, a libertarian website, not its founder.
ref_headline: be stretched to be understood as something done for the public good.
match_headline: In Russia, Doping Accusations Are Taken in Stride

text: An article on the DealBook page on Wednesday about rising compensation for corporate directors misstated the average pay last year for chief executives of companies in the Standard & Poor’s 500-stock index, according to Equilar. It was $12.2 million — not $22.6 million, which is the average pay for the top 200 highest-paid C.E.O.s.
match_headline: How Much to Pay a Director? There’s No Clear Answer

text: An article on Wednesday about Express Scripts’ decision to stop doing business with Linden Care, a specialty pharmacy used by the drug maker Horizon Pharma, described Linden Care’s business incorrectly, using information from a lawyer representing that company. Dispensing drugs made by Horizon Pharma accounts for about 59 percent of Linden Care’s business, not less than 17 percent. (The 17 percent figure is the portion of Linden Care’s business that comes from dispensing Horizon’s drugs to patients covered by Express Scripts.)
match_headline: Express Scripts Cuts Ties to New York Specialty Pharmacy

text: An article on Wednesday about Major League Baseball’s domestic violence policy in light of the arrest of Colorado Rockies shortstop Jose Reyes on charges of assaulting his wife, misstated, in some copies, the surname of an N.H.L. player who was suspended much of last season over a domestic assault case. He is Slava Voynov, not Yoynov.
match_headline: Arrest of Jose Reyes May Test Baseball’s New Domestic Violence Policy

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the songwriter and producer Allen Toussaint referred incorrectly to his parents, Clarence Toussaint and the former Naomi Neville. They were not songwriters. (Mr. Toussaint occasionally used their names as pseudonyms for his own compositions.) The obituary also misstated Mr. Toussaint’s birth date. It was Jan. 14, 1938, not Jan. 18.
match_headline: Allen Toussaint, New Orleans R&B Mainstay, Dies at 77

text: An obituary on Thursday about the actress Betsy Drake misspelled her father’s given name. He was Carlos Corey Drake, not Carlose.
match_headline: Betsy Drake, 92, Actress Who Starred With (and Wed) Cary Grant, Dies

text: An obituary on Thursday about the civil rights lawyer Jacqueline Berrien misstated the second job title she held at the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. She was associate director-counsel, not director and counsel.
match_headline: Jacqueline Berrien, Head of E.E.O.C., Is Dead at 53

text: An article on Thursday about the ways that people living in northeastern Syria are scrambling to fill the void left by the collapse of their government misspelled the assumed surname of the self-proclaimed caliph of the Islamic State, which controlled much of the area until this year. He is Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, not Baghadi.
match_headline: On the Road in Syria, Struggle All Around

text: An article on Wednesday about the devaluing of some hot start-ups by some mutual fund investors misstated how often mutual funds must report the value of their portfolio holdings. It is quarterly, not “at least every half year.”
match_headline: Dizzying Ride May Be Ending for Tech Start-Ups

text: An article on Thursday about an investigation into the murder of Lois Colley, an 83-year-old socialite in Westchester County, misidentified, in some copies, the location of the hamlet Croton Falls, where her husband’s firm has its offices. Croton Falls is in the town of North Salem, N.Y. — not in North Castle, N.Y.
match_headline: Shock and Few Leads After Murder of Lois Colley, Society Matriarch

text: An article on Thursday about differences in top N.F.L. receivers’ performances based on their quarterbacks misstated, in some copies, the circumstances of Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger’s start in Week 9, when Antonio Brown set a franchise record with 284 receiving yards. It was Roethlisberger’s second game back from an injury, not his first.
match_headline: Steelers’ Antonio Brown Has Been Only as Good as His Quarterback

text: Because of a production error, the continuation of an art review on Friday about “Celebrating the Arts of Japan: The Mary Griggs Burke Collection,” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, appeared with the second and third columns of text reversed. The correct version of the review can be found at nytimes.com/art .
ref_headline: Celebrating the Arts of Japan: The Mary Griggs Burke Collection,
match_headline: Masterpieces of Japanese Art at the Met

text: An obituary on Thursday about the French philosopher André Glucksmann misstated the word for the teaching degree he received in 1961. It is agrégation, not agrégat.
match_headline: André Glucksmann, French Philosopher Who Renounced Marxism, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the former New York State Assemblyman Vito J. Lopez misstated, at one point, when the Ridgewood Bushwick Senior Citizens Council in Brooklyn was established, and what Mr. Lopez’s initial role there was. As correctly noted elsewhere, he founded it in 1973; he was not hired to work there in 1970.
match_headline: Vito J. Lopez, Ex-New York Assemblyman Tainted by Scandal, Dies at 74

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about Sonya Ortiz, a dancer and college student who grew up homeless and whose dorm room was furnished through money from the Federation of Protestant Welfare Agencies, an organization supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, misstated the age of her sister in some editions. Her sister, Suddenley, is 11, not 9.
match_headline: A Dancer Is Driven to Succeed After a Homeless Childhood

text: An article last Sunday about a mechanized book-sorting competition between two library systems misstated, in some editions, the name of a library system serving the Seattle region. It is the King County Library System, not the King County Public Library. The article also described incorrectly in some editions the area served by the system. It serves the area surrounding Seattle; it does not have branches in the city itself. (The city is served by the Seattle Public Library, which is not involved in the sorting contest.) The error about serving Seattle was repeated in the headline in some editions.
match_headline: Libraries in New York and Seattle Area Staging a Battle of the Sorters

text: An article on Nov. 1 about the Giants’ connections to New Orleans misstated the name of the school that quarterback Eli Manning and receiver Odell Beckham Jr. attended there. It is Isidore Newman School, not Isidore Newman High School.
match_headline: Giants Try to Stay Focused as a Noisy Superdome Awaits

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with a review of a play at New World Stages in Manhattan misspelled part of the title. As the review correctly noted, the play is “Shear Madness,” not “Sheer Madness.”
match_headline: Review: ‘Shear Madness,’ Where Getting a Haircut Is Murder

text: An article last Sunday about tax pitfalls of charitable giving misstated the value threshold for donations of property requiring the completion of Section B of I.R.S. Form 8283. It is more than $5,000, not $5,000 or more. The article also misstated the possible tax consequences of donating stock in a closely held business that is about to be sold. Waiting until the sale is a certainty could result in a reduced tax benefit, not strictly a deduction limited to the cost, or basis, of the shares.
match_headline: Navigating the Tax Rules on Charitable Gifts
