text: A picture caption on Sept. 13 with an article about the film director James Ivory and his home in the Hudson Valley referred incorrectly to the fabric in a 1700s Indian coverlet shown in his guest bedroom. The fabric was made in the town of Palampur, not Palamur.
match_headline: James Ivory’s Home Befits His Extraordinary Life

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about winemaking in China misidentified a winery in Ningxia, China. It is Château Changyu Moser XV, not Château Moser.
match_headline: China’s Winemakers Seek Their Own Napa Valley

text: An article on Oct. 18 about lullabies used an incorrect music term to describe Western lullabies. These songs often have a 6/8 meter, not 6/8 tempo.
match_headline: The Melancholy Mystery of Lullabies

text: An article on Oct. 25 about litigation finance misstated the amount of money managed by the firm Gerchen Keller. It has more than $840 million under management, not $475 million in private capital.
match_headline: Should You Be Allowed to Invest in a Lawsuit?

text: An article last Sunday about the new Beatles video collection “1” misstated the name of the label that released it. It is Apple Corps Ltd./UMG, not Apple/UMG Records. The article also misstated the year of the Beatles’ “rooftop concert.” It was 1969, not 1970.
match_headline: The Beatles’ Video Collection ‘1’: Baby, You Can Film My Song

text: An article last Sunday about the movie “Jim Henson’s Turkey Hollow,” using information from Lifetime, which will air the film on Nov. 21, misstated the name of one of the puppets in the movie. It is Thrinng, not Thwring. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: A Jim Henson Thanksgiving, 47 Years in the Making

text: An article last Sunday about the new movie “Trumbo,” which focuses on the Hollywood blacklist, misspelled the given name of Louis B. Mayer’s right-hand man at MGM. He was Dore Schary, not Dory.
match_headline: ‘Trumbo’ Recalls the Hunters and the Hunted of Hollywood

text: An article on Nov. 1 about the new Broadway musical “Allegiance,” inspired by the actor George Takei’s memories of life in an internment camp in World War II, referred incorrectly to people of Japanese descent who were sent to internment camps during World War II. While about 120,000 people were interned, only about two-thirds of them were American citizens; they were not all American citizens.
match_headline: George Takei Guides ‘Allegiance,’ a Musical, Not a Starship

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about a food tour of Chicago misidentified a dish at Isla Pilipina, a Filipino restaurant. It is kare-kare, not paksiwna lechon.
match_headline: Restaurant Review: Abril Cocina in Maplewood

text: An article last Sunday about the artist Zhang Hongtu described incorrectly an artwork on display in a survey of Mr. Zhang’s work at the Queens Museum. It is a print of “Last Banquet,” not the original work.
match_headline: Zhang Hongtu’s Art Studio in Woodside, Queens

text: An article last Sunday about Twitter’s decision to change its star function to a heart described incompletely the origin of the method to change Twitter’s heart icon to a beer one. Although it was posted on Gizmodo.com, the technique was originally written and posted to Twitter by Robert A. McNees, a physics professor from Loyola University Chicago.
match_headline: Twitter Fans Speak Out Against the Heart

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about a new cafe in Manhattan where patrons pay $15 an hour to mingle with cats, misstated the age of the cafe’s owner, Benjamin Kalb. He is 26, not 25. The article also misspelled, in one reference, the name of the cafe. As noted elsewhere, it is Koneko, not Konoko.
match_headline: At a Cat Cafe, Sipping and Purring

text: A caption last Sunday on the Evening Hours page misidentified a guest shown receiving a Literary Lion award from the New York Public Library on Nov. 2. He is Alan Bennett, not Charles Gross.
match_headline: Evening Hours | Dances and Prizes

text: Because of an editing error, an essay last Sunday in The End misstated how long the health of the writer’s mother had been failing before she and her husband decided to commit suicide. It was several months, not five years.
match_headline: Deaths From Suicide

text: An article on Friday about a federal appeals court decision overturning a ruling that California’s death penalty was unconstitutional misstated the city where Federal District Judge Cormac J. Carney, who made the ruling, holds court. It is Santa Ana, not Fresno.
match_headline: Federal Appeals Panel Overturns Anti-Death Penalty Ruling in California

text: Because of an editing error, a pop music entry in the Listings pages on Friday about a concert at Zankel Hall in Manhattan featuring Ry Cooder, Sharon White and Ricky Skaggs misspelled the given name of the host. She is Rosanne Cash, not Roseanne.
match_headline: Pop & Rock Listings for Nov. 13-19

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about René Girard, a theorist of the social sciences, referred incorrectly to his book “Deceit, Desire, and the Novel.” The book introduced his idea that people seek things in life based on what other people want; it did not introduce “the idea of mimesis.” The error was repeated in a picture caption with the obituary, which also referred incorrectly to the book as a novel. It is a work of nonfiction. And the obituary misstated, in some copies, the surname of the author of a coming biography of Mr. Girard. She is Cynthia Haven, not Haden.
match_headline: René Girard, French Theorist of the Social Sciences, Dies at 91

text: An article on Friday about the resignation of Mary Spellman as dean of Claremont McKenna College misidentified the recipient of an email she sent in response to a newspaper article about the marginalizing of students of color. It was sent to a student, not to students.
match_headline: Dean at Claremont McKenna College Resigns Amid Protests

text: An article on Nov. 9 about the role of Assemblyman Ron Kim in legislation affecting the nail-salon industry included incorrect information about some political donations to Mr. Kim from the industry. While Sangho Lee, president of the Korean American Nail Salon Association, said the industry had raised a total of $60,000 for Mr. Kim, Mr. Lee now says that figure was the amount raised by the association from its members, not the amount donated to Mr. Kim. (As the article noted, salon owners donated nearly $25,000 at a fund-raiser for Mr. Kim in July; he later returned $5,000 that came directly from the association.)
match_headline: Backed by Nail Salon Owners, a New York Legislator Now Fights Reforms

text: An article on Saturday about a worldwide glut of oil misstated, in some copies, the growth of inventories of American crude last week. American crude inventories grew last week to a total of 487 million barrels; inventories did not grow by that much during the week.
match_headline: An Oil-Soaked Globe as Production Keeps Climbing and Demand Falls

text: An article in some editions on Friday about a guilty plea in the drug overdoses that sickened nearly a dozen students at Wesleyan University in February misstated the age of Zachary Kramer, the defendant. He is 21, not 22.
match_headline: Guilty Plea in Drug Overdoses at Wesleyan

text: An article on Tuesday about money-losing bets placed by some investment firms in the last fiscal quarter described incorrectly the business of Grantham Mayo Van Otterloo, the Boston-based financial firm co-founded by Jeremy Grantham. It is an asset management firm that runs hedge fund portfolios, mutual funds and other investment products; it is not a hedge fund.
match_headline: Filings Show Rocky Quarter for Many Hedge Funds

text: An article on Tuesday about the Investors Exchange and its application to create a stock exchange misstated the length of the “speed bump” that it would use to slow down high-speed trading. It is 350 microseconds, not 350 milliseconds.
match_headline: Plan for New Stock Exchange Stirs Furious Debate

text: An article on Nov. 10 about changes in the recipes for some classic Campbell’s soups included a quotation about the success of smaller brands in the soup and canned soup categories that misstated the name of one such brand. It is Amy’s Kitchen, not Amy’s Naturals.
match_headline: Campbell Rethinks Its Soup Recipe as Consumer Tastes Change

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Knicks’ 90-84 loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers misspelled the surname of the Cavaliers player whose layup attempt was blocked by Carmelo Anthony in the second quarter. He is Anderson Varejao, not Varejo.
match_headline: LeBron James Springs to Life and Forces Knicks to Relive a Collapse

text: An article on Thursday about trades made by the Yankees during the general manager meetings misidentified, in some copies, the award recently won by the Yankees catching prospect Gary Sanchez in the Arizona Fall League. He was the most valuable player of the league’s Fall Stars Game, not the league’s most valuable player. (The league’s season ends this week.)
match_headline: Yankees Acquire Twins’ Aaron Hicks in Quest for Younger Lineup

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the portrait artist Aaron Shikler misstated his birth date. He was born on March 18, 1922, not on Nov. 12. The obituary also misspelled the surname of Mr. Shikler’s daughter, who survives him. She is Cathy Shikler van Ingen, not van Inen. And the obituary referred incorrectly at one point to Ronald Reagan, whose portrait Mr. Shikler painted for the cover of Time magazine in 1980. He was the president-elect at the time, not the president.
match_headline: Aaron Shikler, Portrait Artist Known for Images of America’s Elite, Dies at 93

text: An article on Tuesday about the uproar in Florence, Colo., over the possibility that Guantánamo Bay detainees could be moved to a nearby prison referred incorrectly, using information from a local official, to an encounter between local officials and visiting federal officials who were surveying prison facilities. Members of the survey team were not pulled over for a traffic stop.
match_headline: Prison Town in Colorado Doesn’t Want Guantánamo Detainees

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about reaction among lawyers to the acquittal of the mobster Vincent Asaro on charges related to the 1978 Lufthansa heist misidentified the author of the book from which “Goodfellas” — a movie that features the airport robbery in a scene — is adapted. The author of the book, “Wiseguy,” is Nicholas Pileggi, not Henry Hill. (Mr. Hill was the subject.)
match_headline: Acquittal of Vincent Asaro Is Latest Setback in Mafia Prosecutions

text: An article on Nov. 7 about the unearthing of 19th-century burial vaults on Washington Square East referred incorrectly to the state of records at the Second Presbyterian Church, successor to a congregation that is recorded as having used the vaults. Church leaders said that Second Presbyterian has records going back to 1756 that are being examined to see if they contain valuable information. It is not the case that the church has no records.
match_headline: Beneath Washington Square, Forgotten Tombs Begin to Yield Their Secrets

text: An article last Thursday about the gossip columnist Hedda Hopper, portrayed in the new movie “Trumbo” by Helen Mirren, referred incorrectly to her support of a Congressional investigation into a suspected Communist presence in Hollywood. Those hearings were conducted by the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1947, not by a committee led by Sen. Joseph R. McCarthy several years later.
match_headline: For Gossip Columnist Hedda Hopper, Flamboyance Was Her Brand

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the continuation of an article about the political aspirations of the Black Lives Matter group misidentified the location of a protest in September before an N.F.L. game between Minnesota and Detroit. It was near a light rail station, in St. Paul — not outside TCF Bank Stadium, in Minneapolis.
match_headline: One Slogan, Many Methods: Black Lives Matter Enters Politics

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision by Washington College in Maryland to shut down the campus as the police searched for a student, Jacob Marberger, transposed part of the name of the fraternity where Mr. Marberger was a member. It is Phi Delta Theta, not Phi Theta Delta.
match_headline: Maryland Campus Closed as Police Continue Search

text: An article on Wednesday about the trial of the former State Senate majority leader Dean G. Skelos and his son Adam on corruption charges misstated, in some editions, part of the name of a company where Adam Skelos worked. It is Physicians’ Reciprocal Insurers, not Principal Reciprocal Insurers.
match_headline: Prosecutors Outline Corruption Trial for Senator Skelos and His Son

text: An article on Saturday about objections by a group of Harvard Law School professors to the documentary “The Hunting Ground” misstated the action taken by the school against Brandon Winston, a student who was accused of sexually assaulting a fellow student and a friend and was ultimately convicted of a misdemeanor nonsexual assault. He was suspended and then reinstated; he was not expelled.
match_headline: Professors Dispute Depiction of Harvard Case in Rape Documentary

text: An article on Monday about the New York Public Library’s storage space for books underneath Bryant Park misstated the extent of the storage area and related spaces that serve it. While they occupy a large part of the area beneath the park, they do not extend west to Sixth Avenue. The article also misstated the circumstances under which the scholar David Nasaw, a critic of a plan now scrapped to store books in New Jersey, met with library officials. He met with them at the library to discuss the subterranean storage area; he did not tour the site with library officials.
match_headline: Beneath New York Public Library, Shelving Its Past for High-Tech Research Stacks

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about Robert Craft, the conductor, scholar and writer known for his long professional association with Igor Stravinsky, misstated the name of the publication for which Mr. Craft wrote an essay asserting that Stravinsky had been bisexual. It is The Times Literary Supplement, not The Times of London Literary Supplement.
match_headline: Robert Craft, Stravinsky Adviser and Steward, Dies at 92

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 29 about growing tensions in Germany, Austria and the western Balkans over the surge of migrants misspelled the surname of the Austrian chancellor in some editions. He is Werner Faymann, not Feymann.
match_headline: Austria and Slovenia Trade Threats as Tensions Over Migrants Grow

text: An article on Friday about efforts by three small groups of people from Syria, Pakistan and Afghanistan to enter the United States through Mexico misstated, in some editions, the surname of an Arizona sheriff who commented on the border crossings. He is Paul Babeu, not Pabeu.
match_headline: Migrants’ Attempts to Enter U.S. via Mexico Stoke Fears About Jihadists

text: An article on Thursday about scaled-back ambitions for an initial public offering by the payments service Square misstated the “ratchet,” or protection for Square’s later investors. At an offering price of $9 a share, the ratchet prompts an additional 10.3 million shares for later investors, not 9.7 million shares.
match_headline: For Its I.P.O., Square Scales Back Valuation by $3 Billion

text: An article on the Automobiles page on Friday about plans for a comeback at Lotus Cars misstated the age of its chief executive, Jean-Marc Gales. He is 53, not 49.
match_headline: For Lotus Cars, a New Chief and a Return to Its Vaunted Lightness

text: An article on Thursday about the winners of Major League Baseball’s Cy Young Awards — the Chicago Cubs’ Jake Arrieta and the Houston Astros’ Dallas Keuchel — erroneously attributed a distinction to the 2015 Cubs. They are the first National League team — not the first team — since the 1991 Atlanta Braves to win three Baseball Writers’ Association of America awards in the same season. (The Seattle Mariners won three awards in 2001.)
match_headline: Jake Arrieta and Dallas Keuchel, Newly Anointed Aces, Win Cy Young Awards

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about an announcement by French officials that the recent terrorist attacks had been carried out by three teams of Islamic State jihadists operating in unison erroneously attributed a distinction to the attacks. They were the deadliest in Western Europe since the 2004 train bombings in Madrid, not the deadliest in all of Europe. (The 2004 school massacre in Beslan, Russia, in which more than 300 died, took place six months after the Madrid attacks, which killed 191. While Russia straddles two continents, Beslan is considered to be on the European side.)
match_headline: Three Teams of Coordinated Attackers Carried Out Assault on Paris, Officials Say; Hollande Blames ISIS

text: An article last Sunday about the “Hunger Games” movies misspelled the surname of a producer on those films. He is Jon Kilik, not Kilic.
match_headline: What It Takes to Save a Mockingjay

text: A picture last Sunday with an article about the Detroit Symphony Orchestra was published in error. It showed the Detroit Opera House —not Orchestra Hall, which is the Detroit Symphony Orchestra’s home.
match_headline: Detroit Symphony Tackles an Adventurous Premiere

text: An article last Sunday about sculptures by Picasso that are being shown at the Museum of Modern Art misidentified the collector who has promised to give a cache of Cubist works to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. He is Leonard A. Lauder — not his brother, Ronald S. Lauder. The article also erroneously stated that Ronald’s middle initial is M. In addition, the article also misstated the year that “The Bathers,” an ensemble of six wood figures, was given to the Staatsgalerie in Stuttgart. It was 1981, not 1980. The article also described incorrectly the spoons included in Picasso’s six “Glass of Absinthe” sculptures. They are made of a white metal alloy; they are not silver-plated. And, finally, the article misidentified the technique that researchers used to examine four of the “Glass of Absinthe” works. It is X-radiography, not X-ray fluorescence spectrometry.
match_headline: Drinking In the Beauty of Picasso’s Sculptures at MoMA

text: An article last Sunday about Princess Anne’s attendance at a luncheon aboard the Queen Mary II, docked for a few hours at the Brooklyn Cruise Terminal in Red Hook, referred imprecisely to the title of the chairman of H.M.S. Victory Preservation Company, for which the event was a fund-raiser. He is Lord Boyce, not Lord Michael Boyce.
match_headline: A Princess Aboard the Queen Mary 2

text: An article last Sunday about the actress Mary-Louise Parker and her recently published memoir described Ms. Parker’s marital history incorrectly. While she has had several long-term relationships, she has never been married.
match_headline: Mary-Louise Parker on Life With and Without Men

text: An article on Nov. 8 about Steve Deace, the radio host, referred incorrectly to professional sports in Iowa. The state has several minor league baseball teams; it is not the case that it has no professional sports teams.
match_headline: Steve Deace and the Power of Conservative Media

text: A review last Sunday about “Destiny and Power,” Jon Meacham’s biography of George H. W. Bush, misstated the year that Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait. It was 1990, not 1991.
match_headline: Jon Meacham’s ‘Destiny and Power: The American Odyssey of George Herbert Walker Bush’

text: A review on Nov. 8 about “Jack Kemp: The Bleeding-Heart Conservative Who Changed America,” by Morton Kondracke and Fred Barnes, misidentified the cabinet post Kemp held under President George H.W. Bush. He was secretary of housing and urban development, not secretary of health and human services. The review also referred imprecisely to the role played by Kemp, along with Senator William V. Roth Jr., in a modest tax cut in 1978. Ideas strongly advocated by the two helped bring about passage of the law, that year’s Revenue Act; they didn’t “pass” the tax cut. (The legislation they themselves sponsored, known as Kemp-Roth, was not part of the Revenue Act.)
ref_headline: Jack Kemp: The Bleeding-Heart Conservative Who Changed America,
match_headline: ‘Jack Kemp: The Bleeding-Heart Conservative Who Changed America’

text: An article on Sunday about Jacob Marberger, a Washington College student found dead of an apparent suicide weeks after being caught brandishing a handgun, misstated Maryland law regarding age restrictions on firearms. While it is generally illegal for people under 21 to possess a handgun or an assault rifle in Maryland, the restrictions do not include all firearms.
match_headline: Missing Maryland College Student Is Found Dead in Apparent Suicide

text: An article on Nov. 13 about an appearance by the secretary of education, Arne Duncan, at Jeremiah E. Burke High School in Boston, which he cited as an example of progress at public schools across the county, misstated the year that the school was recognized as most improved in the city. It was 2015, not 2014.
match_headline: In Swan Song, Arne Duncan Extols School Progress Under His Tenure

text: An article on Saturday about the rapidly increasing deer population on Staten Island described a scientific classification for deer incorrectly. Cervidae refers to its family, not its genus.
match_headline: A Plague of Bucks and Does on Staten Island

text: An article on Friday about Wall Street banks that are facing multimillion-dollar losses on company debt they are unable to sell misstated the position of Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase in regard to debt used by Apax Partners, a private equity firm, to take a controlling stake in Fullbeauty, an apparel company. While both banks were underwriters on the deal and once held some of the debt, neither held the debt at the time the article was published. The article also referred imprecisely to the discount on the Fullbeauty debt. The debt was being offered at as much as a 15 percent discount to its full value in mid-October, when the deal was completed, not at the time of publication. The article also misstated the circumstances of the acquisition of parts of eBay Enterprise by Permira Funds, an investment firm, and Sterling Partners, a private equity firm. While Sterling used debt to finance its purchase of parts of eBay Enterprise, Permira did not.
match_headline: As Investors Shun Debt, Banks Are Left Holding the Bag

text: An article on Monday about lobbying by technology companies misstated part of the name of the organization that employs Sheila Krumholz, who commented on the issue, and also misstated her title. It is the Center for Responsive Politics, not the Center for Responsible Politics, and she is its executive director, not its executive editor.
match_headline: Start-Up Leaders Embrace Lobbying as Part of the Job

text: An article on Saturday about the discovery of an ancient Greek papyrus fragment of the Gospel of John misidentified the university where Larry Hurtado, an expert in early Christian manuscripts who commented on the discovery, teaches. It is the University of Edinburgh, not St. Andrews University.
match_headline: Greek New Testament Papyrus Is Discovered on eBay

text: An article on Nov. 2 about a stunning comeback by the Islamist party of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey in parliamentary elections misstated part of the name of a Kurdish-dominated party that surpassed a legal threshold of 10 percent of the vote to enter Parliament. It is the Peoples’ Democratic Party, not the Peoples’ Republic Party.
match_headline: Erdogan’s Party in Turkey Regains Parliamentary Majority

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 5 about the collapse of the Romanian government after a nightclub fire that killed 32 and set off a wave of protests over corruption misidentified the event that a Romanian political scientist said in an op-ed article was an opportunity to end the “administrative incompetence and the state of perpetual illegality in which we live.” The comments, by Alina Mungiu-Pippidi, referred to the protests, not to the resignation of Prime Minister Victor Ponta.
ref_headline: administrative incompetence and the state of perpetual illegality in which we live.
match_headline: Victor Ponta, Romania’s Premier, Steps Down After Outcry Over Corruption

text: A review on Tuesday about a chamber-music program presented by the New York Philharmonic at the 92nd Street Y in Manhattan referred incorrectly to the cellist at two points. As the review correctly noted elsewhere, he is Carter Brey, and thus Mr. Brey, not Mr. Carter.
match_headline: Review: Rachmaninoff Chemistry at the 92nd Street Y

text: An article on Tuesday about Albert Einstein’s theory of relativity misstated the given name of a classmate of Einstein with whom he published an outline of a gravity theory in 1913. He was Marcel Grossmann, not Jerome.
match_headline: A Century Ago, Einstein’s Theory of Relativity Changed Everything

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Ken Johnson, the only player in major league history to pitch a nine-inning no-hitter and lose, erroneously attributed a distinction in some editions to Pete Rose, who scored the winning run for the Cincinnati Reds in the game against Johnson. He is not in the Hall of Fame.
match_headline: Ken Johnson, Only Loser of 9-Inning No-Hitter, Dies at 82

text: A headline on Tuesday with an obituary of Austin Kiplinger, a publishing executive, misstated his role in the company founded by his father, W.M. Kiplinger. He was co-founder of Kiplinger’s Personal Finance magazine, not co-founder of the magazine’s parent company, Kiplinger Washington Editors.
match_headline: Austin Kiplinger, Co-Founder of a Personal Finance Magazine, Dies at 97

text: A recipe on Nov. 11 for wild mushrooms and brussels sprouts omitted part of the preparation for the chestnuts in the dish. They should be roasted and peeled, not just peeled.
match_headline: A Beloved L.A. Surf Hangout Gets a Second Act

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Mali’s continuing struggle against extremism referred incorrectly, in some editions, to the black flags that flew in Mali before the Islamic State swept across Syria and Iraq. They were the flags of other Islamist militant groups, not the Islamic State.
match_headline: Hotel Attack in Mali Reverses Gains in Fight Against Extremism

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the continuation of an article on Wednesday about a coalition supporting a liberalization of America’s criminal justice laws misstated the given name of the chairman of Koch Industries, who has been involved in the issue. He is Charles Koch, not David.
match_headline: Rare White House Accord With Koch Brothers on Sentencing Frays

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the financial struggles of American golf courses misidentified the war cited in a commemorative plaque at a Donald J. Trump golf course in Virginia. It was the Civil War, not the Revolutionary War.
match_headline: Fewer Golfers, but Some Lush Courses Are Coming Back

text: An article last Thursday about Printed Matter, the nonprofit art bookstore started by Sol LeWitt and the art critic Lucy R. Lippard, described incorrectly a recent fund-raising effort to benefit the store. The auctioned art works were donated by their owners, not by the artists themselves. Because of an editing error, the article also misstated the name of the project for which Handel Architects is best known. It is the National September 11 Memorial, not the National September 11 Memorial and Museum. And because of another editing error, the article also misspelled the surname of an art fair curator in one reference. He is Shannon Michael Cane, not Came.
match_headline: Art Bookstore Printed Matter Has New Home

text: An article on Tuesday about the status of Volkswagen’s investigation into the installation of emissions cheating software on some of its diesel models misstated the number of vehicles in the United States in which Audi said it would install updated software. It is 85,000, not 10,000.
match_headline: Investigation Into Emissions to Take Months, VW Chief Says

text: An obituary on Nov. 10 about the painter Wojciech Fangor omitted a credit line for the examples of Mr. Fangor’s work. It is Wojciech Fangor Estate/Jankilevitsch Collection.
match_headline: Wojciech Fangor, Painter Who Emerged From Postwar Poland, Dies at 92

text: A picture on Sunday with an article about the collision of China’s nuclear goals with the fears of residents in places with plans for atomic energy plants was published in error, using information from Getty Images. It showed a coal-fired power plant near Ninghai, China, not a nuclear plant.
match_headline: China’s Nuclear Vision Collides With Villagers’ Fears

text: An article on Tuesday about a failed effort in the New York State Legislature to halt the state’s plan to cull mute swans misstated, in some editions, the name of a different species of swan in New York. It is the trumpeter swan, not the trumpet swan.
match_headline: Bill Blocking Plan to Reduce Mute Swans Is Vetoed

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about trade negotiations between the United States and China, using information from Agence France-Presse, misspelled the surname of a Chinese Communist Party official who was shown with Penny Pritzker, the American commerce secretary. He is Wang Huning, not Hunig.
match_headline: China and U.S. Say They’ve Made Strides in Trade Talks

text: An article last Sunday about Massachusetts’ decision to drop an educational standards test, known as Parcc, in favor of one designed for the state alone misstated the number of states that will continue to use the Parcc. It is six (and the District of Columbia), not five.
match_headline: Massachusetts’s Rejection of Common Core Test Signals Shift in U.S.

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about the Rangers’ 5-4 victory over the Florida Panthers misstated the given name of the Rangers player who scored the winning goal. As the article correctly noted, he is Rick Nash, not Nick.
match_headline: Duke Gets 32 Points From a Guard, and a Narrow Victory Over Georgetown

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Jiehae Park, an emerging playwright, misstated her role in an adaptation of Haruki Murakami’s story “Sleep.” She will be acting in the play; she will not be writing the adaptation.
match_headline: Jiehae Park’s ‘Peerless’ to World Premiere at the Yale Repertory Theater

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Page 30 today with an article about gentrification in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, reverses the identities of the two women shown. Donna Mossman is at left and Shirley De Matas is at right.
match_headline: Gentrification in a Brooklyn Neighborhood Forces Residents to Move On

text: An article last Sunday about Michael Skolnik, the political director for Russell Simmons, misspelled the given name of a journalist for The Guardian who has covered recent racial unrest in the United States. He is Jon Swaine, not John.
match_headline: Michael Skolnik Taps His Social Network to Fight for Civil Rights

text: A picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about Neversink Spirits, a distillery in Port Chester, misspelled the given name of one of the distillery’s owners. As the article correctly noted, he is Yoni Rabino, not Yani.
match_headline: From Neversink Spirits in Port Chester, N.Y., Local Fruit Brandy

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the advancing age of America’s wealthiest residents misidentified the city shown. It is Palm Beach, Fla., not West Palm Beach.
match_headline: Not So Fast, 1 Percent Whippersnappers

text: An article last Sunday about Cate Blanchett, considered a leading contender for a Best Actress Oscar nomination for her performance in “Carol,” misidentified the venue in Los Angeles where the 1999 Oscars ceremony was held. It was the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion, not the Kodak Theater.
match_headline: Cate Blanchett and Her Red Carpet Journey

text: A picture credit on Nov. 15 with a review of “We That Are Left,” by Clare Clark, misspelled the given name of the photographer. The picture of the Sway tower in England, a structure featured in Clark’s novel, was taken by Tom Jamieson, not Thom.
match_headline: ‘We That Are Left,’ by Clare Clark

text: An article last Sunday about the lyricist Sheldon Harnick misstated the number of shows on which he collaborated with the composer Jerry Bock that were nominated for the Tony Award for best musical. It is five, not four. “The Rothschilds” was nominated in addition to “Fiorello,” “She Loves Me,” “Fiddler on the Roof” and “The Apple Tree.”
match_headline: Sheldon Harnick, ‘Fiddler on the Roof’ Lyricist, Busier Than Ever at 91

text: An article last Sunday about a literary tour of Iceland misspelled the surname of an Icelandic novelist. She is Yrsa Sigurdardottir, not Siggurdardottir. And the article misidentified the literary event the writer Barbara Kingsolver attended. She was on the faculty of the Iceland Writers Retreat; she did not attend the country’s international literary festival.
match_headline: In Iceland, a Literary Tour Explores Rich History

text: An article in some editions on Monday about Susan Bentley, an ironworker who experienced health problems after working at the World Trade Center site, was laid off and subsequently received help from an agency supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, misstated the details of Ms. Bentley’s inclusion in the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund. Eligibility for the fund is determined by its special master; it is not the case that a judge approved her request.
match_headline: Sickened in Rubble After 9/11, a ‘Lost Soul’ Longs for Her Old Life

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about Douglass C. North, a Nobel laureate in economics, misstated the location of the University of Washington, where he taught for 33 years. It is in Seattle, not St. Louis. (He later taught for 28 years at Washington University in St. Louis.)
match_headline: Douglass C. North, Maverick Economist and Nobel Laureate, Dies at 95

text: A picture caption on Nov. 11 referring to an article about the beginning of a combined diplomatic and military approach by President Obama to force President Bashar al-Assad of Syria to leave office misstated, in some copies, the location of a scene showing the aftermath of airstrikes. The strikes were in Douma, a suburb of Damascus, the Syrian capital, not in Damascus itself.
match_headline: Obama Turns to Diplomacy and Military in Syria, and Is Met With Doubts

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 11 about the arrest of a former British soldier in connection with Bloody Sunday, the massacre of unarmed civilian marchers by British soldiers in Northern Ireland in 1972, misidentified the government unit whose investigation led to the arrest of another former British soldier in the attempted murder of a mentally disabled man in 1974. That unit, which was also responsible for the Bloody Sunday arrest, is the Legacy Investigation Branch of the Police Service of Northern Ireland, which examines old cases; it is not the Parachute Regiment of the British Army, the unit involved in the Bloody Sunday massacre.
match_headline: Ex-British Soldier, 66, Is Arrested in Bloody Sunday Massacre

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about victims of the shooting at a Planned Parenthood clinic in Colorado Springs misstated, in some editions, the age of one of the victims, Jennifer Markovsky. She was 35, not 36.
match_headline: Colorado Victims Identified as Iraq Veteran and Woman From Hawaii

text: An article on Friday about Louis Cayer, a Canadian coach who has been a key figure in Britain’s run at a Davis Cup tennis title, misspelled the given name of the Canadian who teamed with Daniel Nestor to win men’s doubles at the 2000 Olympics. He is Sébastien Lareau, not Sebastian.
match_headline: Canadian Coach Gives Boost to Britain’s Davis Cup Chances

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Woodrow Wilson and demands by protesters at Princeton that his name be removed from the Woodrow Wilson School of Public and International Affairs because of his record on racial issues misspelled the surname of a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton who commented on Wilson. He is Julian E. Zelizer, not Zlizer.
match_headline: Woodrow Wilson’s Legacy Gets Complicated

text: A picture caption in the Listings pages on Friday about “Lulu,” at the Metropolitan Opera House, misstated the given name of the conductor who is leading the final performances in the run. He is Derrick Inouye, not Daniel.
match_headline: Classical Music Listings for Nov. 27-Dec. 3

text: An article on Thursday about a standoff between Russia and Ukraine over an electricity cutoff in much of Crimea and the Kherson region of southern Ukraine misidentified the territory that Russian special forces soldiers seized in March 2014. It is the Crimean Peninsula, not mainland Ukraine.
match_headline: Russia and Ukraine in a Standoff Over Crimea Power Outage

text: An article in some editions last Wednesday about a water main break in Hoboken, N.J., misstated, in some copies, the age of Jessica Morrison, who said the inconvenience caused by the break did not compare with the damage caused by Hurricane Sandy. She is 31, not 32.
match_headline: Snapped Water Pipe in Hoboken Upsets City’s Daily Routine

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about the Microsoft Windows 10 update misstated the version number that signals that the November update is running. It is Version 1511, not 15111.
match_headline: Updating Windows 10

text: An article in some copies on Nov. 22 about Saúl Álvarez’s victory over Miguel Cotto in a middleweight boxing match misstated the way in which Julio César Chávez defeated Hector Camacho in 1992, another fight between top boxers from Mexico and Puerto Rico. Chávez won in a unanimous decision, not a knockout.
match_headline: Saúl Álvarez Wins W.B.C. Middleweight Title, Beating Miguel Cotto

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the Knicks’ 100-91 loss to the Orlando Magic misstated, in some copies, the number of points Jose Calderon scored for the Knicks. It was 23, not 25. A subheading with the article also misstated, in some copies, the combined point total of Calderon and Carmelo Anthony. They combined for 51 points, not 53. The article also misstated, in some copies, the number of points Kristaps Porzingis scored for the Knicks. It was 10, not 8. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Tall Lineup Frustrates Porzingis and Knicks

text: An article on Monday about John Mulaney and Nick Kroll, whose “Oh, Hello” comedy routine has been turned into an Off Broadway show, misstated the role of Julie Klausner, a friend and collaborator who commented on the two, in Hulu’s “Difficult People.” She is the sole creator and a star of the series, not a co-creator.
match_headline: In ‘Oh, Hello,’ Nick Kroll and John Mulaney Have a Stage Senior Moment

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about various “Nutcracker” productions and how to choose the right one for children, using information from a publicist, misidentified a dancer in “The Yorkville Nutcracker” at Hunter College from Dec. 10-13. He is Justin Peck from the cast of “The Phantom of the Opera,” not Justin Peck from New York City Ballet.
match_headline: Finding the Right ‘Nutcracker’ for You and Yours

text: A picture caption on Monday about “George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker,” which was reviewed in The Arts section, misstated the surname of a dancer. She is Kristen Segin, not Begin.
match_headline: Review: ‘George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker’ at Lincoln Center

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Russian film director Eldar Ryazanov misspelled the surname of the author of a book about him. He is David MacFadyen, not MacFayden.
match_headline: Eldar Ryazanov, Russian Film Director Known for His Satire, Dies at 88

text: Because of a transcription error, an article on Tuesday about the intelligence and security lapses that allowed the Paris attackers to practice their assault misstated the size of the cartridges recovered by investigators in front of the bars and cafes targeted. They are 7.62 millimeters, not 0.762.
match_headline: How the Paris Attackers Honed Their Assault Through Trial and Error

text: Because of a production error, a reporting credit with an article on Tuesday about people recovering from wounds sustained in the Paris attacks last month omitted, in some editions, the names of four contributors. Milan Schreuer, Lilia Blaise and Caroline Chauvet contributed reporting from Paris, and Sheri Fink from New York.
match_headline: For Survivors of Paris Attacks, Mental Scars May Outlast Wounds

text: An article on Tuesday about Hillary Clinton’s emails from her time as secretary of state that were released by the State Department on Monday misstated the subject of one of those emails. The subject line “Koch” was a reference to Edward I. Koch, the former mayor of New York City, according to the Clinton campaign; it was not an apparent reference to either David H. or Charles G. Koch, the billionaire brothers who have helped finance conservative causes.
match_headline: Clinton Email Is Released After Security Concern Is Dismissed

text: An article on Wednesday about Representative Tim Murphy’s bill to overhaul the mental health system, because of incorrect information in the Federal News transcript, misattributed a quotation calling the bill “partisan.” The quote was from Representative Xavier Becerra, Democrat of California, not Representative Eric Swalwell, who is also a Democrat from California.
match_headline: Paul Ryan Pushes Changes in Mental Health Care After Colorado Shooting

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Thursday about sexual battery cases reported by Florida State University students in 2014 misstated the number of those cases the university reported to the federal government. It was 14, not nine.
match_headline: F.S.U. Reported Few Rape Cases to the U.S.

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the statistical warning signs amid the Rangers’ successful start to the N.H.L. season misstated their team save percentage at the time. It was .942, not .956.
match_headline: With Luck on Their Side Thus Far, Rangers Look to Get Better

text: An article on Tuesday about the film “Youth” and the composer David Lang, who wrote the music for it, referred incorrectly to Mr. Lang’s “Just (After Song of Songs).” While also used in the film, it was written and recorded before it; the piece was not composed for the film.
match_headline: For Paolo Sorrentino’s ‘Youth,’ David Lang Strives for an Unusually Emotional Melody

text: A report in the Observatory column on Tuesday about trap-jaw ants that can jump forward referred incorrectly to the genus of the ants that were studied. Ponerinae is the subfamily they belong to, not their genus, which is Odontomachus.
match_headline: Ants With Leaping Ability

text: A picture caption on Monday with an obituary about Joseph Silverstein, a violinist and conductor, referred incorrectly to his role with the Boston Symphony Orchestra. As the obituary correctly stated, he was the orchestra’s concertmaster for 22 years, not its leader.
match_headline: Joseph Silverstein, Violinist and Boston Symphony Concertmaster, Dies at 83

text: An obituary on Monday about the theater designer Yolanda Sonnabend referred imprecisely to her work on Natalia Makarova’s production of “La Bayadère” for Britain’s Royal Ballet. She designed the costumes, she did not design the entire production. (The sets were designed by Pier Luigi Samaritani.)
match_headline: Yolanda Sonnabend, Designer Who Influenced Choreographer, Dies at 80

text: An article on Wednesday about a new study by researchers at George Washington University that reviewed social media accounts and legal documents of nearly 400 American sympathizers of the Islamic State misstated the Air Force rank of Tairod Pugh, one of the people the researchers investigated, because of incorrect information in the study. He was enlisted personnel, not an officer.
match_headline: ISIS Followers in U.S. Are Diverse and Young

text: An article last Friday about a growing need for interpreters as the number of African immigrants in the Bronx increases misspelled, in one instance, the surname of the city’s commissioner for immigrant affairs. As the article noted correctly elsewhere, she is Nisha Agarwal, not Agrawal.
match_headline: Influx of West Africans in the Bronx Spurs Demand for Interpreters

text: An article on Thursday about the withdrawal of one of two rival groups seeking to revive the bankrupt New York City Opera misspelled the surname of a lawyer for the remaining group, NYCO Renaissance, who said he expects its reorganization plan for the company to be approved. He is Gerard S. Catalanello, not Catalenello.
match_headline: A Group Cedes Its Bid to Revive City Opera to a Rival

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the New Music column, which included a review of the album “Kannon” by Sunn O))), misidentified the singer shown in a performance by the band. He is Attila Csihar, not Greg Anderson.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Kannon,’ From Sunn O))), Brevity and Austerity

text: An obituary on Thursday about Samuel R. Berger, who served as national security adviser in the Clinton administration, misstated the name of the consulting firm that former Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright ran with Mr. Berger. It is Albright Stonebridge Group, not Stonebridge Albright Group.
match_headline: Samuel Berger, Adviser to Clinton Who Shaped Foreign Ties, Dies at 70

text: An article on Thursday about quarantines for people entering the United States from Ebola-affected countries misstated where Dr. Craig Spencer had treated Ebola patients. It was Guinea, not Sierra Leone.
match_headline: Ebola Crisis Passes, but Questions on Quarantines Persist

text: A headline with an article on Friday about the trial of Donald L. Blankenship, the former chief executive of Massey Energy Company, characterized incorrectly, in some editions, the jury verdict in the case. Mr. Blankenship was convicted of a single count of conspiring to violate federal safety standards; he was not convicted of any count holding him responsible for the 2010 accident at the Upper Big Branch mine.
match_headline: Mixed Verdict for Donald Blankenship, Ex-Chief of Massey Energy, After Coal Mine Blast

text: An article on Nov. 25 about the discovery of a newborn baby at a church in Richmond Hill, Queens, misstated the name of the church. It is Holy Child Jesus Church, not Holy Jesus Child Church.
match_headline: Healthy Newborn Found Abandoned in Nativity Scene at a Queens Church

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about efforts by state education officials to determine whether the bar for passing the Algebra I Regents exam was set too high misstated the planned increase in the passing grade for the test. It is scheduled to go up by 9 points, not 14 points.
match_headline: Algebra Scores Prompt Second Look at Revamped Regents Exams

text: Because of an editing error, the Wealth Matters column last Saturday about financial considerations for collectors of rare or unusual objects described one such item, the Enigma machine, incompletely. It was used by the Germans to encode military messages in World War II, not just by the British to decode the messages.
match_headline: Financial Considerations for Collectors of Art, Antiques and the Esoteric

text: Because of production errors, three film reviews on Friday appeared without the names of the reviewers. “Everything Will Be Fine” was reviewed by Nicolas Rapold, and “The Wannabe” and “Bikes vs Cars” by Andy Webster.
match_headline: Review: In Wim Wenders’s ‘Every Thing Will Be Fine,’ Nothing Is

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article last Sunday about Darlington Nagbe of Major League Soccer’s Portland Timbers misidentified, in some copies, the team he was shown facing. It was the Vancouver Whitecaps, not F.C. Dallas. The credit for the picture also misidentified the photographer in some copies. He is Don Ryan of The Associated Press, not Steve Dykes of Getty Images.
match_headline: Versatile Standout Finds a Position, and a Home with Portland Timbers

text: An article last Sunday about the Ten Thousand Things theater troupe in Minneapolis, which takes productions to prisons and homeless shelters, misstated the name of a company that recently performed at a Salvation Army rehabilitation center and an apartment complex for senior citizens. It is the California Shakespeare Theater, not the California Shakespeare Festival.
match_headline: Theater Troupe Gives Those on the Margins a Front-Row Seat

text: A review on Nov. 22 about “Battling the Gods: Atheism in the Ancient World,” by Tim Whitmarsh, misspelled the given name of a 20th-century philosopher who was an influential professor at Columbia University. He was Sidney Morgenbesser, not Sydney.
ref_headline: Battling the Gods: Atheism in the Ancient World,
match_headline: ‘Battling the Gods: Atheism in the Ancient World,’ by Tim Whitmarsh

text: An article on Nov. 22 about Christopher Logue’s version of the “Iliad” misspelled the given name of a translator of the “Iliad.” He was Richmond Lattimore, not Richard.
match_headline: Letter of Recommendation: Christopher Logue, ‘War Music’

text: An article on Nov. 29 about the Kurdish-held Rojava region of Syria misstated the surname of a chairman of the Syrian Democratic Union Party (P.Y.D.) at two points. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Salih Muslim, not Muhammad.
match_headline: A Dream of Secular Utopia in ISIS’ Backyard

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Allison Ferrari and Stephan Panagiotakis misidentified part of the name of the school in Queens at which the groom teaches. It is George J. Ryan Middle School, not George M. Ryan Middle School.
match_headline: Allison Ferrari and Stephan Panagiotakis

text: An article on Nov. 22 about poor areas electing politicians who want to slash the safety net referred incorrectly to the timing of comments attributed to the Republican strategist Scott Jennings on the effect of the Affordable Care Act in Kentucky. It was in December 2014, not this fall.
match_headline: Who Turned My Blue State Red?

text: Because of an editing error, a reporting credit for an article last Monday about a crash involving a cattle trailer in New Jersey that left three people dead and 12 injured was omitted in some editions. Tatiana Schlossberg and Yuhan Liu contributed reporting.
match_headline: 3 Killed and 12 Injured in Crash Involving Cattle Trailer in New Jersey

text: An article on Thursday about the advantages of structuring a charitable organization as a limited liability company misstated which entities are required by the federal tax code to spend a minimum of 5 percent of the value of their endowment each year for charitable purposes. That requirement applies to private foundations, but not to charities.
match_headline: Mark Zuckerberg’s Philanthropy Uses L.L.C. for More Control

text: An article on Nov. 17 about devices that try to track stress erroneously included several variables in the list of things the Embrace watch measures. It tracks skin temperature, movement and skin conductance, but not sleep, respiration, heart rate and heart rate variability.
match_headline: Sleeping In Feels So Good, but May Be Unhealthy

text: Because of an editing error, two picture captions in the Dress Codes column on Friday reversed the descriptions for photos No. 5 and 6. Caption No. 5 should have listed the J. Crew sweater and the Lanvin turtleneck. Caption No. 6 should have listed the Berluti sweater, the Prada T-shirt, the Ami shorts and the Canali scarf.
match_headline: Should I Marry the Son of a Crook?

text: An obituary on Friday about Marcus Klingberg, the highest-ranking Soviet spy ever caught by the Israeli security services, misstated when he was exposed by a double agent. It was the early 1980s, not the early 1960s.
match_headline: Marcus Klingberg, Highest-Ranking Soviet Spy Caught in Israel, Dies at 97

text: An article on Thursday about the shooting rampage in San Bernardino, Calif., using information from the police, misstated the age of Tashfeen Malik, the woman involved in the attack. She was 29, not 27. The error was repeated on Friday in an article about clues left by the suspects and in an article about the secrecy surrounding their plans.
match_headline: San Bernardino Shooting Kills at Least 14; Two Suspects Are Dead

text: An article on Nov. 18 about Abdelhamid Abaaoud, believed to have been the chief architect of the terrorist attacks in Paris, gave an incomplete translation, in some editions, for Katibat al-Battar al Libi, a Libyan branch of the Islamic State in Syria that Mr. Abaaoud was believed to have led. It means Brigade of the Sword of the Prophets, not just Sword of the Prophets.
match_headline: An ISIS Militant From Belgium Whose Own Family Wanted Him Dead

text: An article on Dec. 2 about the growing participation of young Palestinian women in recent violence in the Middle East referred incompletely to the location of the women’s attacks and to their actions. The attacks have been in Jerusalem as well as the West Bank, not just the West Bank, and the women have stabbed, tried to stab or, as Israeli authorities contend, intended to stab soldiers and civilians; they have not just tried to attack or been accused of trying to attack.
match_headline: Young Palestinian Women Join the West Bank Turmoil

text: An article on Nov. 28 about the new Women’s Equality Party in Britain gave an outdated job description for Catherine Mayer, one of the party’s founders. She is a former — not current — writer for Time magazine.
match_headline: New Women’s Political Party in Britain Demands Faster Equality

text: An article on Friday about victims of the San Bernardino massacre misidentified, in some editions, the college attended by one of those killed, Bennetta Bet-Badal. It is California State Polytechnic University, Pomona — not California Polytechnic State University, which is in San Luis Obispo.
match_headline: Where They Shared Their Working Hours, and Their Dying Moments

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about journalists who went through the contents of the home of Syed Rizwan Farook and Tashfeen Malik, who died in a shootout after a shooting rampage that killed 14, misspelled the surname of a lawyer for the Farook family. He is David S. Chesley, not Chelsey.
match_headline: Landlord Lets Reporters Into San Bernardino Suspects’ Home

text: An article on Wednesday about the closing of BlueCrest Capital Management, once one of the biggest hedge funds in Europe, misstated the current size of the firm’s flagship fund. The fund has shrunk to just over $2 billion, not $1 billion.
match_headline: BlueCrest to Close Hedge Fund and Refund Outside Investors

text: An article on Wednesday about the Los Angeles Lakers’ loss to the Philadelphia 76ers in Kobe Bryant’s first game after announcing his impending retirement misspelled, in some copies, part of the name of the high school he attended in the Philadelphia suburbs. It is Lower Merion High School (not Marion). The article also misstated, in some copies, the day on which the Los Angeles Dodgers introduced their new manager. It was last Tuesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: In Philadelphia, a Feel-Good Moment for Kobe Bryant, if a Brief One

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Ellen Robbins, who teaches dance and choreography to children in New York City, included an outdated address, website and telephone number for Loco-Motion Dance Theater for Children, which also offers programs for young choreographers. It is at St. Mark’s Church-in-the-Bowery at 131 East 10th Street in Manhattan, not 155 Christopher Street. The website is lmdt.org , not loco-motiondancetheatre.org . And the telephone number is 917-363-5413.
match_headline: In Each Child, an Inner Choreographer

text: An editorial on the Volkswagen scandal in some editions on Monday misstated the number of vehicles the automaker said it equipped with illegal software to improve emissions results. It was 11 million, not 111 million.
match_headline: Cleaning Up After Volkswagen

text: An article on Monday about Tashfeen Malik, the Pakistani-born woman who took part in the San Bernardino attack, misspelled the surname of a journalist based in Islamabad who commented on friction within her family. He is Zahid Gishkori, not Ghishkori.
match_headline: Tashfeen Malik Was a ‘Saudi Girl’ Who Stood Out at a Pakistani University

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 17 about the political and musical history of the Bataclan, the Parisian music hall that was the scene of the most carnage in last month’s terror attacks, referred incorrectly, in some editions, to Eagles of Death Metal, the band that was playing that night. It is an American rock band, not a heavy metal band.
match_headline: Before Paris Attack, the Bataclan Had Long History in Music and Politics

text: An article on Nov. 21 about Hasna Aitboulahcen, who was killed in a police raid on a militant hide-out outside Paris a few days after the terrorist attacks, making her a likely martyr to the Islamic State, misidentified the nationality of another woman, Sajida al-Rishawi, whom ISIS claimed as a “sister” to its cause. Ms. Rishawi, whose suicide bomb failed to go off during an attack in Amman, Jordan, in 2005, was Iraqi, not Palestinian.
match_headline: For Woman Dead in French Police Raid, Unlikely Path to Terror

text: An article on Monday about the mayoral race in Lewiston, Me., referred incorrectly to a fund-raising record by Ben Chin, one of the candidates. The $87,800 he raised is a record for a mayoral race in Lewiston, not in all of Maine.
match_headline: Mayoral Race in Maine Could Help Define City’s Future Amid Demographic Shift

text: An article on Saturday about the immigration record of Tashfeen Malik, the Pakistani woman who participated in the attack in San Bernardino, Calif., referred incorrectly to her request for a permanent resident green card. The application in September 2014 for Ms. Malik to receive a green card, after she had arrived in the United States on a 90-day K-1 “fiancé” visa, was filed by Ms. Malik, following a standard procedure — not by Syed Rizwan Farook, the American citizen she married who was the other assailant in the attack.
match_headline: Smooth Visa Process for Woman in Attack Is Focus of Inquiry

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the people involved in a deadly three-vehicle accident in New Jersey misstated the name of the town in Maine where the driver of a pickup with a cattle trailer, Troy L. Chase, lives. It is Pittston, not Pittstown. And because of an editing error, an accompanying picture caption misidentified one of the men who died. As the article noted correctly, he was Ravi Naik, not Neel Naik. (The men were cousins.)
match_headline: Worlds Converge in Deadly Crash on New Jersey Highway

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an opera review of “Die Fledermaus,” at the Metropolitan Opera, referred incorrectly to the cast member Susanna Phillips. As the review correctly noted, she is a soprano, not a mezzo-soprano.
match_headline: Review: ‘Die Fledermaus’ in Full, a First Under the Baton of James Levine

text: An article on Dec. 2 about challah breads from various traditions referred incorrectly to the Jewish community in Djerba, a Tunisian island. It is one of the few remaining in North Africa, not Africa’s last thriving one. The article also misstated Djerba’s location; it is off the east coast of Tunisia, not the north coast.
match_headline: A Twist on the Traditional Challah

text: An article on Wednesday about TSG Consumer Partners, a private equity firm that has made strides in gender equality, misstated the number of female investors it had 2004. In that year, when Hadley Mullin, who is now a senior managing director, was hired, there was one other full-time investor and one contractor who were women; Ms. Mullin was not the only female investor there at the time.
match_headline: Pursuing Gender Equality as a Competitive Advantage

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about powerful figures in Latin American soccer who were charged in the latest chapter of the United States’ broad investigation of corruption in international soccer misstated the given name of the president of the Guatemalan soccer federation in some copies. He is Brayan Jiménez, not Bryan. The article also rendered incorrectly in some copies the surname of a former representative to Conmebol, soccer’s governing body for South America. He is Eduardo Deluca, not de Luca.
match_headline: FIFA Case Upends Soccer Politics in Latin America

text: An article last Thursday about a new generation of strongly scented perfumes referred incorrectly to the term “me decade.” The term, as coined by Tom Wolfe in an article published by New York magazine in 1976, was used to describe the 1970s — not the 1980s.
match_headline: Power Perfumes Return to the Scene

text: An article last Thursday about the disappointing box office performance of the movie “Steve Jobs” misidentified the publication for which Larry Magid wrote an essay about Mr. Jobs. It is Forbes, not Fortune.
match_headline: ‘Steve Jobs’ Flops at Box Office, and Silicon Valley Cheers

text: An article on Wednesday about the restaurant chain Chipotle’s difficulties in dealing with food contamination issues misstated, in some copies, a violation found by Boston health department officials who inspected a Chipotle restaurant at Cleveland Circle. They found that meat was being held at an improper temperature, not that the meat was undercooked.
match_headline: Chipotle’s Safety Woes Worsen as Scores of Students Fall Ill in Boston

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the Native American activist John Trudell referred incorrectly to the trials of his fellow activists Bob Robideau, Darelle Butler and Leonard Peltier. They were tried in the killing of two F.B.I. agents during a confrontation in Oglala, S.D., in 1975 — not during the occupation of Wounded Knee, S.D., in 1973.
match_headline: John Trudell, Outspoken Advocate for American Indians, Is Dead at 69

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actor Robert Loggia misstated the number of children who survive him. There are four, not three. (The name of a daughter, Cynthia Loggia Armstrong, was omitted.)
match_headline: Robert Loggia, Rugged but Versatile Character Actor, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Thursday about the former New York Times reporter C. Gerald Fraser misidentified the birthplaces of his parents. His father was from Guyana and his mother was from Jamaica, not the other way around. The obituary also misstated the year Mr. Fraser’s wife, Geraldine, died. It was 1981, not 1951.
match_headline: C. Gerald Fraser, Longtime Reporter for The Times, Dies at 90

text: An editorial on Tuesday about the trial of Donald Blankenship incorrectly implied that he was convicted of having a role in the Upper Big Branch mine explosion. He was convicted of conspiring to violate federal safety standards; he was not found responsible for the explosion.
match_headline: The Dirty Work of a Coal Baron Exposed

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the conviction of a former Oklahoma City police officer on charges of raping women while on duty misstated his age in some copies. The officer, Daniel Holtzclaw, is 29, not 28. (He turned 29 on Thursday, the day of the verdict.)
match_headline: Former Oklahoma City Police Officer Found Guilty of Rapes

text: An article last Sunday about global fossil fuel subsidies misstated the amount of gasoline that sells for 2 cents in Venezuela. That is the cost per liter, not per gallon. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: On Tether to Fossil Fuels, Nations Speak With Money

text: An article last Sunday about the Air Force’s continued use of the B-52 bomber erroneously attributed a distinction to the aircraft. It dropped one of the first — not the first — hydrogen bombs made. (Earlier hydrogen bombs existed, but they were used only for testing, never dropped.)
match_headline: After 60 Years, B-52s Still Dominate U.S. Fleet

text: An article on Nov. 22 about a dispute over a townhouse renovation on the Upper West Side of Manhattan that involved a subterranean river misstated the direction that water once flowed in the river, and in another nearby. It was southeasterly, not north and west.
match_headline: An Ancient Stream Under a Manhattan Building Leads to a Dispute

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about a couple with cancer who received money from the Shorefront YM-YWHA, a beneficiary agency of UJA-Federation of New York, which is supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, to buy a motorized scooter to help the husband travel to doctor’s appointments misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the wife. As the article noted correctly, she is Tatiana Decrescenzo, not Descrescenzo.
match_headline: Her Dream Fading, a Russian Immigrant Finds Solace in Singing

text: An article in some copies last Sunday about Michigan State’s victory over Iowa in the Big Ten championship game in college football misidentified the Michigan State player off whom the football bounced, leading to an interception by the Spartans’ Demetrious Cox. He is Riley Bullough — not Byron Bullough, who is Riley’s brother and also a member of the Spartans.
match_headline: Michigan State Takes Big Ten Championship From Iowa by an Arm’s Length

text: An article last Sunday about the actor, writer and director Nick Sandow misstated his partner’s surname in one reference. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she is Tamara Malkin-Stuart, not Stuart-Malkin.
match_headline: Nick Sandow, of ‘Orange Is the New Black,’ at Home

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about living in Clinton Hill, Brooklyn, misidentified the intersection shown. It is Waverly and Greene Avenues, not Washington and Gates Avenues.
match_headline: Clinton Hill, Brooklyn, a Neighborhood in Transition

text: An article on Nov. 29 about soy-sauce-pickled eggs misstated in Step 2 of the accompanying recipe for short-grained rice the amount of water that should be added to the rice. It is two cups, not one.
match_headline: Drinking Food

text: An article on Dec. 6 about Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama of Tibet, misstated the date on which a meeting occurred between him and Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India. It was August 2014, not October.
match_headline: The Last Dalai Lama?

text: An article on Dec. 6 about race and the moral issues that come with being white in America misidentified the source of a quote from the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates. His comments about slaves being “the down payment” on America’s independence, and freed slaves becoming “this country’s second mortgage” following the Civil War, came from his book “Between the World and Me,” not from an article he wrote for The Atlantic.
match_headline: White Debt

text: A picture with a review on Nov. 22 about “Magna Carta: The Birth of Liberty,” by Dan Jones, was published in error. It showed part of a legal document from a medieval register of writs — not a page from a copy of Magna Carta.
ref_headline: Magna Carta: The Birth of Liberty,
match_headline: ‘Magna Carta: The Birth of Liberty,’ by Dan Jones

text: A map last Sunday with an article about Reims, France, located the city incorrectly. It is about 75 miles west of where it was shown on the map. A corrected map is at nytimes.com/travel .
match_headline: The Legend and Lore of Notre-Dame de Reims

text: An article on Wednesday about the issuance of a “red alert” in Beijing over air pollution quoted incorrectly from comments by one city resident, Kan Tingting, about the closing of schools. Ms. Kan, who stayed indoors with her 3-year-old, said, “I have to watch my child” — not “my son” — “because there is no kindergarten today.” She subsequently used female pronouns, not male ones, to refer to her child, who is a girl. (The pronouns are homophones in Chinese.)
match_headline: Smog So Thick, Beijing Comes to a Standstill

text: An article on Dec. 2 about underwater archaeological sites that have become visible and susceptible to looting during California’s drought misspelled the name of the peoples who lived in the Lake Oroville area in the Sierra Nevada foothills. They were the Konkow Maidu, not Konku Maidu.
match_headline: Receding Waters in California Expose Artifacts to Plundering

text: An article on Nov. 30 about Andy Murray’s leading Britain to the Davis Cup championship erroneously attributed a distinction to his victory at Wimbledon in 2013 in some editions. He was the first British man — not British player — to win the tournament since 1936. (Several British women have won Wimbledon singles titles since 1936, most recently Virginia Wade, in 1977.) The article also misstated the surname of the British player defeated by David Goffin in the opening singles match. He is Kyle Edmund, not Edmunds.
match_headline: Andy Murray Propels Britain to Victory in the Davis Cup

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some copies on Saturday with a report in the N.B.A. roundup about the Philadelphia 76ers’ extending the contract of Coach Brett Brown misstated Brown’s record with the team. He was 38-149 entering Friday, not 28-149.

An article on Sunday previewing the Week 14 N.F.L. games misidentified, in some copies, the location of a game on Dec. 7 between the Washington Redskins and the Dallas Cowboys. They played in Washington, not Dallas.
match_headline: N.F.L. Week 14 Previews and Picks

text: An obituary on Saturday about the museum curator Charles S. Moffett, using information from his wife, referred incorrectly to his two children, who survive him. They are from the second of his three marriages, not the first.
match_headline: Charles S. Moffett, Curator Who Focused on Impressionists, Dies at 70

text: An obituary on Friday about the singer Bonnie Lou misidentified the city where she began singing on the radio as a teenager. It is Bloomington, Ill., not Bloomington, Ind.
match_headline: Bonnie Lou, Country and Rockabilly Star of the 1950s, Dies at 91

text: A column by Gail Collins on Thursday about abortion and guns misstated part of a quote from Donald J. Trump. It was “Is there anybody that doesn’t renegotiate deals in this room?” not “Is there anyone in this room who doesn’t negotiate deals?”
ref_headline: Is there anybody that doesn’t renegotiate deals in this room?
match_headline: Republicans, Guns and Abortion

text: An article on Saturday about the rape conviction of an Oklahoma City police officer misspelled, in some editions, the given name and the surname of a sexual assault victim who spoke after the trial and misstated the given name of another victim who spoke. They are Jannie Ligons, not Janie Liggins, and Sharday Hill, not Shaudae. A picture caption with the continuation of the article also misspelled Ms. Ligons’s given name and surname in some editions.
match_headline: In Rape Case of Oklahoma Officer, Victims Hope Conviction Will Aid Cause

text: An article on Monday about a resident of Baghdad, Iraq, who won the Oregon Lottery misstated the number of annual payments received for the payout. It is 25, not 20.
match_headline: Iraqi’s Oregon Jackpot Raises Questions on Lottery Sales

text: Because of an editing error, an article about Islanders goalies Jaroslav Halak and Thomas Greiss misstated, in some editions, the recent record of the Rangers, whom the Islanders had passed in the standings. They had won two of their last 10 games, not lost two of 10.
match_headline: Jaroslav Halak and Thomas Greiss, a Dependable Goalie Tandem, Lift the Islanders

text: An article on Friday about George Gwozdecky, a former N.H.L. and college coach who is now leading Valor Christian High School in Colorado, misstated, in some copies, the season after which the Valor Christian hockey program was nearly suspended because of a lack of players. It was 2012-13, not 2011-12.
match_headline: From Stanley Cup Finals to a High School Coach

text: An article on Tuesday about Franklin Sirmans, director of the Pérez Art Museum Miami, misstated the amount of money the museum has pledged to raise to add to its endowment. It is $50 million, not $70 million.
match_headline: First-Time Director Settles In at Pérez Art Museum Miami

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Phil Pepe, a New York sportswriter who covered the Yankees for many years, misstated, in some editions, the year of the Yankee catcher Thurman Munson’s death. It was 1979, not 1978.
match_headline: Phil Pepe, Longtime New York Sportswriter, Dies at 80

text: An article on Friday about whether the new climate agreement reached in France will send a clear signal to global financial investors that they should move money away from fossil fuels and toward clean-energy sources transposed the names of the countries that are the world’s largest and third-largest carbon polluters. China is the world’s largest, and India is the third largest.
match_headline: Key to Success of Climate Pact Will Be Its Signals to Global Markets

text: Because of an editing error, the Diplomatic Memo article on Monday, about claims and counterclaims as the United States and Cuba discuss American properties confiscated by Cuba decades ago, misidentified the newspaper that interviewed a grandson of Meyer Lansky, who said Cuba owed his family compensation for a confiscated hotel. The newspaper is The Tampa Tribune, not The South Florida Sun-Sentinel.
match_headline: In Talks Over Seized U.S. Property, Havana Counters With Own Claim

text: An article on Tuesday about a court proceeding in Beijing in the case of Gu Kailai, convicted of murdering a British business associate, referred incorrectly to a recommendation to commute her sentence. It was made by the prison where she is being held, not by the Beijing High People’s Court. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Life Term Is Recommended for Gu Kailai, Wife of Fallen Official

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 17 about Guillaume Le Dramp, a waiter who was among the 19 people killed at La Belle Équipe bistro on the night of the terrorist attacks in Paris, misstated, in some editions, the day the French president, François Hollande, remarked that people from 19 countries had been in the bars, restaurants and concert hall that came under attack. He made the comment on Monday, Nov. 16, not Tuesday, Nov. 17.
match_headline: Waiter Killed in Paris Attacks Is Remembered as a Bon Vivant

text: An article on Wednesday about fund-raising efforts by some hedge fund managers despite recent poor performance referred incorrectly to a fund that is run by John A. Paulson. It is a merger arbitrage fund, not a merger arbitration fund. The article also misstated the amount of money raised in a fund run by Larry Robbins. It is $1.5 billion, not $1.5 million.
match_headline: Battered, Apologetic and Still Pitching Their Hedge Funds

text: An article on Tuesday about the decision by the Major League Baseball commissioner, Rob Manfred, not to lift the permanent ban imposed on Pete Rose referred incorrectly to his history of appeals. This attempt was Rose’s second, not his third. And he first applied for reinstatement to Commissioner Bud Selig in 1997, not to Selig’s predecessor, Fay Vincent, in 1992.
match_headline: Dear Pete Rose: It’s Still a No. Sincerely, Baseball

text: Because of an editing error, a film review on Wednesday about “Dreams Rewired” referred incorrectly to one of the directors and writers, Manu Luksch. She is a woman, and thus is Ms. Luksch, not Mr. Luksch. The review also misquoted two sentences of the narration. They are: “Today in our pockets. Tomorrow woven into our bodies,” not: “Today is in our pockets. Tomorrow is woven into our bodies.”
match_headline: Review: ‘Dreams Rewired,’ a Futuristic Look at the Past

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the hockey coach Glen Sonmor misstated, in some editions, the year of his birth. It was 1929, not 1949. (As the obituary correctly noted, he was 86.) The obituary also misstated the name of the city in Ontario where he died. It is Brantford, not Branford.
match_headline: Glen Sonmor, 86, a Brawling N.H.L. Coach

text: An article last Thursday about Solange Knowles’s visit to Art Basel Miami Beach and the outfit she chose to wear at an event there described incorrectly Ms. Knowles’s fashion style during her teenage years. Although she favored colorful clothing, she did not wear Dutch-African prints.
match_headline: A Night Out With Solange Knowles at Art Basel

text: An article last Thursday about notable architects who are designing tiny houses and pavilions to be sold on the Internet described incompletely the event earlier this month where prototypes of some of those designs were on display. It was the Art Basel Miami Beach art and design fairs, not just the art fair.
match_headline: Tiny Homes You Can Collect

text: An article on Nov. 19 about the many missed clues to the rise of the Islamic State misstated, in some editions, the year that the United States withdrew from Iraq. It was 2011, not 2010.
match_headline: In Rise of ISIS, No Single Missed Key but Many Strands of Blame

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a revelation that one of the Paris attackers, believed to have been hiding in a Brussels house two nights after the attacks, might have escaped because a Belgian law bans police raids on private homes from 9 p.m. to 5 a.m. misattributed a comment about the police stakeout of the home. It was Eric Van der Sijpt, the spokesman for the federal prosecutor in Brussels — not Justice Minister Koen Geens — who said the suspect, Salah Abdeslam, would have been caught if he were in the house. (He remains at large.)
match_headline: Belgium Says Law Limiting Raids May Have Allowed Suspect in Paris Attacks to Escape

text: An article on Friday about a tax cut measure passed by the House of Representatives misstated the total amount of the cuts. It is $650 billion, not $650 million.
match_headline: Under Wire, House Passes Big Package of Tax Cuts

text: An article on Wednesday about slow sales of cold-weather merchandise in an unusually warm holiday season in some parts of the nation misattributed a comment about how the weather had contributed to a weak fall performance at Nordstrom. Retailing analysts made that assessment, not Nordstrom itself.
match_headline: Retailers Feel the Heat of Lost Winter Clothing Sales
