text: An article last Sunday about the gender change of Kricket Nimmons misstated the university affiliation for the Center of Excellence for Transgender Health, which is led by JoAnne Keatley, who commented on the struggles of transgender individuals. The center is at the University of California, San Francisco — not at the University of San Francisco.
match_headline: ‘A Whole New Being’: How Kricket Nimmons Seized the Transgender Moment

text: An article last Sunday about the approval of a landmark climate accord by 193 nations misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the agency that employs Michael Levi, an energy expert, who said, “The world finally has a framework for cooperating on climate change that’s suited to the task.” The agency is the Council on Foreign Relations, not the Center on Foreign Relations.
ref_headline: The world finally has a framework for cooperating on climate change that’s suited to the task.
match_headline: Nations Approve Landmark Climate Accord in Paris

text: An article last Sunday about the Durst Organization, the New York real estate company, misstated the age of Jonathan Durst, one of the company’s leaders, in some editions. He is 59, not 62.
match_headline: The Durst Dynasty’s Rise, a Scion’s Descent

text: A headline on Dec. 6 with an article about Giovanni and Lucia Guarini, an Italian aristocratic couple who renovated their family’s estate in Puglia, misidentified the historical period during which their palace was built. It was constructed in the 17th century, not during the medieval period.
match_headline: The Vibrant Makeover of a 17th-Century Palace

text: An article on Dec. 6 about a variety of tourist attractions in Brussels misstated the city’s location in relation to the Belgium city of Antwerp. Brussels is to the south of Antwerp, not to its north.
match_headline: Why Brussels Is the New Berlin

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary last Sunday about the literary agent Timothy Seldes misstated the date of his death. It was Dec. 5, not Nov. 5.
match_headline: Timothy Seldes, Agent Who Championed Literary Stars, Dies at 88

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary last Sunday about the actress Marjorie Lord misstated, in one reference, the point at which the name of the sitcom “Make Room for Daddy,” on which she co-starred with Danny Thomas, was changed to “The Danny Thomas Show.” It was in the show’s fourth and last season on ABC — not its fifth season, when it moved to CBS.
match_headline: Marjorie Lord, Actress on ‘The Danny Thomas Show,’ Dies at 97

text: An article last Sunday about the year in art misstated the name of the gallery where Clement Siatous showed paintings of an island in the Indian Ocean. It is the Simon Preston Gallery, not Simon Present.
An article last Sunday about the year in classical music partly misstated the name of an opera by the composer Matthew Aucoin. It is “Crossing,” not “The Crossing.”
match_headline: The Best Classical Music of 2015

text: Because of an editing error, a cover article last Sunday about condominium developments on the Upper East Side misstated the name of the founder and chief executive of Simon Baron Development. He is Jonathan Simon, not Simon Baron. The article also referred incorrectly to Vicente Wolf, the interior designer of a project at 12 East 88th Street. He is Mr. Wolf, of course, not Mr. Vicente.
match_headline: An Upper East Side Condo Wave

text: A review on Dec. 6 about “The Catskills: Its History and How It Changed America,” by Stephen M. Silverman and Raphael D. Silver, misstated the surname of the author of an earlier history, “Making Mountains: New York City and the Catskills.” He is David Stradling, not Spradling.
ref_headline: The Catskills: Its History and How It Changed America,
match_headline: ‘The Catskills: Its History and How It Changed America’

text: A picture credit on Dec. 6 with a review about “The Uncollected David Rakoff,” edited by Timothy G. Young, misspelled the surname of the photographer. The picture of David Rakoff was taken by Paul Roossin, not Roosin.
match_headline: ‘The Uncollected David Rakoff’

text: An article on Dec. 9 about a return performance at the Bataclan music hall in Paris by the American band Eagles of Death Metal, which was playing there the night of the terror attacks, misstated the number of people killed at the venue. Ninety died there, not 89.
match_headline: Eagles of Death Metal Return to Bataclan for First Time Since Paris Attacks

text: An article on Thursday about a ruling by the Supreme Court of Japan that upheld a law requiring married couples to share the same surname misstated, at one point and in some editions, the given name of one of the plaintiffs. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she is Kyoko Tsukamoto, not Kyoto.
match_headline: Japan’s Top Court Upholds Law Requiring Spouses to Share Surname

text: Because of an editing error, an Upshot article on Thursday about a politically conservative and disproportionately influential corner of Iowa described Common Core incorrectly. It is a proposed set of national educational standards advanced by governors and local educators that have been adopted by most states. Common Core is not a set of education standards set by the federal government.
match_headline: How a Quiet Corner of Iowa Packs Such a Fierce Conservative Punch

text: An article on Tuesday about the dismissal of Charif Souki, the chief executive of Cheniere Energy, at a time of upheaval in the energy industry erroneously included one energy source among renewable sources that are squeezing gas demand in Europe. They are solar and wind — not coal, which is not a renewable energy source.
match_headline: Low Natural Gas Prices Squeeze Industry and Fell a C.E.O.

text: An article on Thursday about Israel’s adoption of stricter security measures, which Palestinians denounce as collective punishment, referred imprecisely to access to the Aqsa Mosque compound in Jerusalem, the site of many clashes between the Israeli police and Palestinians in recent months. The Israeli authorities have recently allowed nearly all Palestinian residents of Jerusalem to visit, not most Palestinians in general. (Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip generally cannot visit the compound without a permit to enter Jerusalem.) The article also omitted attribution for a statistic about the 115 Palestinians killed since the uprising began. According to estimates from the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights, from Oct. 1 through early December, 60 Palestinians have been shot dead while attacking Israelis or being suspected of doing so.
match_headline: Jerusalem Attacks Subside, but Not Palestinian Ire, as Israel Clamps Down

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about accusations of inauthenticity against Mast Brothers chocolatier in Brooklyn misstated the name of the series written by the blogger Scott Craig about the company. It was called “What Lies Behind the Beards,” not “What Lies Beyond the Beards.” The article also misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a former pharmaceuticals company executive who is charged with securities fraud and to whom some have drawn comparisons on social media. He is Martin Shkreli, not Shrekli. The article also misstated the number of chocolate bars made at Mast Brothers’ North Third Street Shop in Williamsburg. It is 1,500 bars a day, not a year. And the article referred imprecisely to the location of the main Mast Brothers factory. It is adjacent to the Brooklyn Navy Yard, not in it.
match_headline: Unwrapping the Mythos of Mast Brothers Chocolate in Brooklyn

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Friday about the play “Plaid Tidings” referred incorrectly to the fictional band Forever Plaid. The band members died in 1964 after crashing into a bus full of teenagers heading to a Beatles concert; they did not survive.
match_headline: Review: ‘Plaid Tidings’ Brings Back the Forever Plaid Crew

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about the Public Theater’s casting of two transgender actors for its production of the musical “Southern Comfort,” using information from the theater, misidentified the hometown of one, Aneesh Sheth. While she has lived in Seattle, she is from New York, not Seattle.
match_headline: Public Theater Casts Two Transgender Actors in ‘Southern Comfort’

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about some favorite lines a book critic encountered in his reading this year misidentified the novel by Nell Zink that was quoted. It is “The Wallcreeper,” not “Mislaid.”
match_headline: Reading Is About the Lines That Leap Off the Pages

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Friday about the gift of a sculpture by David Smith to the Smithsonian American Art Museum, using information from the Smithsonian, misstated part of the name of the community where Smith had his studio. It is Bolton Landing, N.Y., not Bolton’s Landing.
match_headline: Smithsonian Announces Gift of David Smith Sculpture

text: An article on Thursday about a move by Argentina’s new president, Mauricio Macri, to devalue the nation’s currency misstated, in some editions, the International Monetary Fund’s forecast for Argentina’s economy and the name of the Buenos Aires consultancy where Gastón Rossi, a former deputy economy minister who said the devaluation was inevitable, is a director. The economy is predicted to grow — not shrink — by 0.4 percent this year, and Mr. Rossi works at LCG, not LSG.
match_headline: Argentina Set to Devalue Its Currency

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the death of a Hezbollah commander, Samir Kuntar, in an airstrike in Damascus, Syria, referred incorrectly to the television channel Al Manar, which reported that the building struck was home to families. It is the Hezbollah television channel, not the official Syrian government channel.
match_headline: Commander of Hezbollah Freed by Israel Is Killed in Syria

text: A headline on Nov. 23 for an article about a death sentence handed down by a Saudi court for an artist and poet, Ashraf Fayadh, on charges of apostasy referred incorrectly to his background. Although he was born in Saudi Arabia, he is of Palestinian descent but stateless; he is not Saudi.
match_headline: Artist’s Death Sentence Follows a String of Harsh Punishments in Saudi Arabia

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about a $5.45 billion deal to sell Stuyvesant Town-Peter Cooper Village, Manhattan’s largest apartment complex, to the Blackstone Group misidentified one of developers that bought Stuyvesant Town-Peter Cooper Village in 2006. It is Tishman Speyer Properties and BlackRock Realty Advisors, not Blackstone Group.
match_headline: $5.45 Billion Deal for Stuyvesant Town Completed After Threatened Lawsuit

text: An article on Monday about a partial settlement in a bias lawsuit brought by minority members of a sheet metal workers union misspelled, in some copies, part of the name of a law firm that represented the workers. It is Debevoise & Plimpton (not Plympton).
match_headline: New York Sheet Metal Workers Case Highlights Persistence of Workplace Discrimination

text: An article last Wednesday about new food terms that became popular in 2015 misidentified the online lexicon that had added the terms cakehole, cat cafe, cheffy, hangry, wine o’clock and beer o’clock. It is OxfordDictionaries.com , not the online Oxford English Dictionary.
match_headline: ‘Hangry’? Want a Slice of ‘Piecaken’? The Top New Food Words for 2015

text: An article on Wednesday about the unseasonably warm weather in New York misstated the current record-holder for the most abnormally warm month recorded in New York City. It is January 1932, not March 1945.
match_headline: Unseasonable Greetings in a New York Searching for Jack Frost

text: An article on Nov. 24 about a report from the United Nations saying that weather-related disasters have killed more than 600,000 people over the past two decades referred incorrectly to the 4.1 billion others affected by such disasters. Those people were wounded, displaced or left in need of emergency assistance; not all of them were wounded.
match_headline: Extreme Weather Tied to Over 600,000 Deaths Over 2 Decades

text: An article on Nov. 24 about Israel’s plans to establish bypass roads for Israeli drivers in certain areas of the West Bank, in response to demands by settlers for better security, referred incorrectly to the six Jews killed by Palestinians in the previous five days. One was an American; they were not all Israelis.
match_headline: Benjamin Netanyahu Plans Separate Bypass Roads for Israelis in Parts of West Bank

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Nov. 24 with an article about Secretary of State John Kerry’s push for a more aggressive approach to combating the Islamic State misidentified, in some editions, the Emirati foreign minister, Abdullah bin Zayed, who visited a mosque in Abu Dhabi with Mr. Kerry the previous day. Sheikh Zayed is the man standing in the foreground waiting for Mr. Kerry, not the man lacing up his shoes along with Mr. Kerry.
match_headline: John Kerry Adds Voice to Those Urging Bigger Push Against Islamic State in Syria

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the declining number of hotel telephone operators and the push among them for higher severance pay referred incorrectly to the prevalence of cellphone use globally. Although it is estimated that there are 6.8 billion cellphone subscriptions in the world, it is not the case that “an estimated 6.8 billion of the world’s 7 billion inhabitants have cellphones.”
ref_headline: an estimated 6.8 billion of the world’s 7 billion inhabitants have cellphones.
match_headline: Automation Claims Jobs of Phone Operators at New York Hotels

text: An article on Saturday about the multimillionaire pharmaceuticals executive Martin Shkreli’s relationship with Hunter College High School, which he failed out of but to which he later donated $1 million, misstated how much he marked up the prices of drugs produced by companies he snapped up. While he increased the price of Daraprim by more than 5,000 percent, he did not increase the price of any drugs by a factor of thousands.
match_headline: Martin Shkreli’s Arrest Fuels Debate Over $1 Million Donation

text: An article on Monday about the inflation-adjusted price of the gifts in “The 12 Days of Christmas” misstated the increase in the government’s Consumer Price Index for the previous 12 months. It was 0.5 percent, not 0.2 percent.
match_headline: Have Your Goose and Afford to Roast It, Too

text: An article on Monday about Just Capital, a nonprofit organization created by the hedge fund manager Paul Tudor Jones II and the self-help author Deepak Chopra to address income inequality, described Mr. Chopra’s eyeglass frames incorrectly. They are embedded with crystals, not diamonds.
match_headline: A Plan to Rank ‘Just’ Companies Aims to Close the Wealth Gap

text: Because of an editing error, a picture credit on Monday with an article about Jakob Poeltl, a top Austrian player at the University of Utah, misidentified the photographer. The picture of Hubert Schmidt, Poeltl’s former coach at D.C. Timberwolves in Vienna, was taken by Gyula Sopronyi, not by Sam Hodgson.
match_headline: Jakob Poeltl’s N.B.A. Dreams Began in an Unlikely Place: Austria

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about Mariah Carey misstated how long ago her song “All I Want for Christmas Is You” was released. It was 21 years ago, not 19. The article also misstated the name of Ms. Carey’s spoiled-brat alter ego. She is Bianca — not Mimi, who is her good alter ego.
ref_headline: All I Want for Christmas Is You
match_headline: Mariah Carey’s List Is Short: All She Wants Is Immortality

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about three new classical music Christmas albums misidentified a language the vocalists use on one, “Christmas in Medieval England.” It is Middle English, not Old English.
match_headline: A Classical Christmas, Across the Centuries

text: An article on Nov. 25 about Belgium’s reputation as the world’s most prosperous failed state misspelled the surname of a risk analysis executive in Brussels who said, “Everything in Belgium is politicized.” He is Claude Moniquet, not Moniqué.
match_headline: Terrorism Response Puts Belgium in a Harsh Light

text: An article on Dec. 1 about Qin Yi, 93, the only survivor of a group of Chinese women once known as the “four great actresses,” whose glamour on stage and screen stirred audiences during the turmoil at the birth of modern China, misidentified the position the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, held in Shanghai in 2007, when he visited Zhang Ruifang, another of the four actresses, a sign of the deep respect the Communist Party had for the women. He was the party secretary in Shanghai, not the mayor. The article also misstated the artistic background of Jiang Qing, a wife of Mao Zedong, who excoriated the “four great actresses” during the Cultural Revolution. Ms. Jiang, then known as Madame Mao, had been a Shanghai theater star, not an opera star.
match_headline: The Last Reservoir of Glamour From China’s ‘Four Great Actresses’

text: An article on Wednesday about a United Nations Security Council session intended to draw attention to the dire consequences of the war in Yemen misstated the size of a United States weapons deal with Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition trying to defeat Houthi insurgents in Yemen. The deal is worth $1.29 billion, not $129 million.
match_headline: Saudi-Led War in Yemen Frays Ties With the U.S.

text: An article on Tuesday about the artist Peter Blake and a new exhibition of his work in London omitted a co-designer of the cover of the Beatles album “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band.” Besides Mr. Blake, it was designed by his wife at the time, Jann Haworth.
ref_headline: Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band.
match_headline: Peter Blake, ‘Sgt. Pepper’ Artist, Still Going in and Out of Style

text: A picture on Page 26 this weekend in the special Lives They Lived issue, with a profile of Amelia Boynton Robinson, was published in error. It shows Gloria Richardson, not Ms. Boynton Robinson.

An obituary on Thursday about Fernande Grudet, who under the name Madame Claude operated a deluxe call-girl ring in Paris in the 1960s and ’70s, gave an incorrect conversion in some copies of francs into dollars. The equivalent of 100,000 francs in 1975 was about $20,000 — the amount she was said to take in monthly — not $500,000.
match_headline: Fernande Grudet, 92, Dies; Ran High-Society Call-Girl Ring as ‘Madame Claude’

text: An article on Dec. 13 about new scrutiny in criminal trials of bite-mark evidence misidentified the Mississippi court that in January will reconsider the sentence against Eddie Lee Howard Jr., who was convicted largely because of the testimony of a forensic dentist. It is a county circuit court, not the Mississippi Supreme Court.
match_headline: Lives in Balance, Texas Leads Scrutiny of Bite-Mark Forensics

text: An article last Sunday about a bill to overhaul the nation’s chemical safety system, and a separate measure to ban the use of tiny plastic beads in beauty products, misstated the name of a chemical safety statute that was enacted in 1976. It is the Toxic Substances Control Act, not the Toxic Chemicals Safety Act.
match_headline: Senate Votes to Overhaul Chemical Safety and Ban Beads in Beauty Products

text: A picture on Page 26 this weekend in the special Lives They Lived issue, with a profile of Amelia Boynton Robinson, was published in error. It shows Gloria Richardson, not Ms. Boynton Robinson.
An article on Dec. 13 about the history of flying in cinema misstated the rank of the character Robert Duvall plays in “Apocalypse Now.” The Character is Lt. Col. Bill Kilgore, not Lt. Bill Kilgore.
match_headline: The Art of Flying in the Movies

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an obituary about Kurt Masur, the music director emeritus of the New York Philharmonic, referred incorrectly to the Philharmonic musicians Rebecca Young and Cynthia Phelps, who were shown with Mr. Masur in 2002. They are violists, not violinists. The obituary also misstated the title of the East German leader Erich Honecker, whom Mr. Masur persuaded to build a new concert hall in Leipzig. He was general secretary of the Socialist Unity Party, not chancellor. And the obituary omitted a reporting credit in some editions. James R. Oestreich contributed.
match_headline: Kurt Masur, Conductor Who Transformed New York Philharmonic, Dies at 88

text: Because of an editing error, the Author’s Note feature on Dec. 13, about Geraldine Brooks’s novel based on the life of King David, misidentified the Prussian ruler most closely associated with the statesman Otto von Bismarck. He was William I, not Frederick II — who lived a century earlier than Bismarck.
match_headline: The King and I

text: A picture caption on Dec. 6 with a review of “Sinatra: The Chairman,” by James Kaplan, and “Sinatra’s Century,” by David Lehman, misstated the date of the photograph of Frank Sinatra. It is from 1957, not circa 1970.
match_headline: ‘Sinatra: The Chairman’ and ‘Sinatra’s Century’

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the artistic success but financial struggles of the Weinstein Company misidentified the Weinstein brother interviewed in the company’s Beverly Hills offices. The interview was conducted with Bob, not Harvey. The article also misidentified the prospective director of “The Six Billion Dollar Man.” He is Damián Szifrón, not Peter Berg.
match_headline: The Weinstein Brothers Have Oscar Gold. Now They Need Cash.

text: Because of an editing error, a report last Sunday on the Arena page about the British fashion designer Charlotte Hockin misidentified the person shown in the accompanying photo. She is a model wearing Ms. Hockin’s designs; she is not Ms. Hockin.
match_headline: A Young London Designer Who Doesn’t Want the Buzz

text: An article last Sunday about Jill Soloway, the writer and director of “Transparent,” misstated the name she now calls the parent whom she has described as the inspiration for that TV show. It is “Moppa” not “Mompa.”
match_headline: Jill Soloway of ‘Transparent’: A Daughter’s Story

text: An article last Sunday about the American Ballet Theater dancer Misty Copeland misidentified the theater in which the dance company performs. It is the David H. Koch Theater at Lincoln Center, not the neighboring Metropolitan Opera House.
match_headline: The Rise and Rise of Misty Copeland

text: A picture caption last Sunday on the Evening Hours page misidentified the honorees of Lincoln Center Corporate Fund’s gala at Alice Tully Hall on Dec. 7. They were the Valentino creative directors Maria Grazia Chiuri and Pierpaolo Piccioli, not Valentino Garavani.
match_headline: Debbie Harry, Keira Knightley and Diane Kruger at Lincoln Center to Honor Valentino Designers

text: A report in the Vows column last Sunday, about the marriage of Elise Morrissey and Joe Russo IV, incorrectly characterized the wedding site as a cathedral. It is a church.
match_headline: Me or My Mother? A Romantic Message Goes Astray

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 29 about the Islamic State’s control of the Libyan city of Surt, which Western agencies say may give it a fallback option in case it is ousted from its territories in Iraq and Syria, misstated the location of the city of Darnah, close to where Wissam Najm Abd Zayd al Zubaydi, an Iraqi leader of the Islamic State, was killed by an American airstrike in November. Darnah is in eastern Libya, not Syria.
match_headline: ISIS’ Grip on Libyan City Gives It a Fallback Option

text: An article on Nov. 30 about the potential discovery of the long-sought burial chamber of Queen Nefertiti, which would boost Egypt’s struggling tourism industry, quoted incorrectly from the paper “The Burial of Nefertiti?” by Nicholas Reeves, a noted Egyptologist. The paper referred to an “earlier royal interment,” not “internment.”
match_headline: Hope for Nefertiti’s Tomb, and Egypt’s Economy

text: An article on Friday about compensation for the Americans taken hostage at the United States Embassy in Tehran in 1979 misidentified, in some editions, the party affiliation of Gerald E. Connolly of Virginia, who promoted legislation for years to compensate the Americans. He is a Democrat, not a Republican.
match_headline: Americans Held Hostage in Iran Win Compensation 36 Years Later

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 13 about the first elections in Saudi Arabia to include women as voters and candidates misstated the number of Saudi citizens in some editions. There are roughly 20 million, not 28 million.
match_headline: Saudi Elections Are First to Include Women as Voters and Candidates

text: An article on Nov. 30 about Pope Francis’ visit to the Central African Republic, where Christian and Muslim militias have clashed since 2013, using information from a relative, misstated the fate of two local men who were in a Muslim neighborhood in Bangui, the capital, the day before the pope was scheduled to visit the neighborhood. The men were captured by Muslim militiamen, then handed over safely to United Nations peacekeepers; they were not killed.
match_headline: In Africa, Pope Francis Makes His First Visit to a War Zone

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Dec. 15 about a call by the United States for an international inquiry into human rights abuses in Burundi quoted incorrectly from a draft resolution before the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva. It called for a team of experts to be sent to Burundi “urgently and as soon as possible,” not within 45 days.
ref_headline: urgently and as soon as possible,
match_headline: U.S. Calls for Inquiry Into Rights Abuses in Burundi

text: An article on Dec. 21 about the governing party’s loss of its parliamentary majority in national elections in Spain misspelled, in some editions, the given name of an analyst at Open Europe, a political think tank, who said the results left Spain in “total uncertainty.” He is Vincenzo Scarpetta, not Vicenzo.
match_headline: Governing Party in Spain Loses Majority in Parliamentary Election

text: An article on Nov. 29 about Citizens, a rising political party in Spain that has broadened its appeal by opposing Catalan separatism, misstated the given name of a political-science professor at the National University of Distance Education who said the challenge for the party’s leader, Albert Rivera, is to turn “a one-dimensional party opposed to Catalan independence into something more sophisticated.” He is José Ignacio Torreblanca, not Juan.
ref_headline: a one-dimensional party opposed to Catalan independence into something more sophisticated.
match_headline: In Spain, New Political Party Makes Gains From Surprising Place — the Center

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 20 about Xavier Gabriel, a Spaniard whose lottery business has become a national emblem of luck and a formidable merchandising brand, misstated, in some editions, the timing of the crash of the Virgin Galactic space plane, on which Mr. Gabriel has booked a $200,000 seat. The crash was last year, not in July.
match_headline: A Spaniard Selling Lottery Fortune

text: An article on Saturday about the Yiddish New York festival misstated the given names of two performers. They are Shane Baker, not Shake, and Frank London, not Mike.
match_headline: A Festival of Language for the Good of Yiddish

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Tuesday with an article about Peter Mattaliano, who researched the history of century-old letters from two children to Santa that were found in his Hell’s Kitchen home, misidentified, in some editions, a cemetery where he was shown seeking information about the children, Mary and Alfred McGann. He was at Third Calvary Cemetery, not Mount St. Mary’s Cemetery.
match_headline: A Chimney’s Poignant Surprise: Letters Santa Missed, Long Ago

text: An article on Sunday about the drop in crime in New York City this year misstated the Brooklyn location where Christopher Henry was interviewed. It was East 18th Street near Caton Avenue in Flatbush, not 18th Street near Canton Avenue in East Flatbush.
match_headline: Anxiety Aside, New York Sees Drop in Crime

text: An article on Sunday about an Edgewater, N.J., man who the authorities say killed his wife and daughter and then himself misstated the prices of watches that the man, Michael Stasko, 53, sold online. While the retail prices were around $500 to $600 for some, the sales prices were, on average, about $200 cheaper.
match_headline: Man Kills Family and Then Shoots Himself in New Jersey

text: An article on Monday about the purchase of The Las Vegas Review-Journal from the New Media Investment Group by the family of Sheldon Adelson, the Las Vegas casino owner, misstated the given name of the editor of The Sarasota Herald-Tribune, another newspaper owned by New Media. He is Bill Church, not Jim.
match_headline: Questions on Direction of a Paper in Las Vegas

text: A picture caption on Monday with the continuation of an article about the challenges in getting Indians to pay for online streaming misspelled the surname of a man shown at the left and also misspelled the surname of another man pictured in the center. The men, who work on a YouTube series called “Pitchers,” are Viabhav Bundhoo, not Bandhu, and Amit Golani, not Gulani.
match_headline: India Offers Atypical Video Challenges

text: Because of an editing error, the Books of The Times review on Monday, about “Ardennes 1944: The Battle of the Bulge” by Antony Beevor, misattributed a statement about the training of regiments in the United States Army’s 106th Infantry Division, two of which surrendered in the battle. It was the reviewer, not the author of the book, who stated that the training was identical to that of most other American infantry.
ref_headline: Ardennes 1944: The Battle of the Bulge
match_headline: Review: In ‘Ardennes 1944: The Battle of the Bulge,’ Antony Beevor Is on Familiar Ground

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary in some copies on Monday about the artist Ellsworth Kelly misstated the surname of his husband, who survives him. He is Jack Shear, not Spear.
match_headline: Ellsworth Kelly, Who Shaped Geometries on a Bold Scale, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Monday about the cinematographer Haskell Wexler omitted the name of his collaborator on the 2000 documentary “Bus Riders Union.” He directed that film with Johanna Demetrakas.
match_headline: Haskell Wexler, Oscar-Winning Cinematographer, Dies at 93

text: A picture caption on Sunday with an obituary about the literary scholar Lewis M. Dabney omitted credit for the photograph of him. It was taken by Tess Steinkolk.
match_headline: Lewis M. Dabney, Who Devoted Life’s Work to Edmund Wilson, Dies at 83

text: Because of an editing error, an Upshot article on Tuesday about the limited predictive power of polls before the start of primary season misidentified the Democratic winner of the 2004 Iowa caucus. John Kerry came in first, not John Edwards.
match_headline: Are Primary Polls Finally Predictive? No, but This Is When the Fun Starts

text: A picture caption in some editions on Tuesday with an article about Henry Casilla, an immigrant from the Dominican Republic who has struggled while raising two sons in New York and who received money from the Children’s Aid Society, one of seven agencies supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, misstated the given name of one of the sons. As the article correctly noted, he is Hanle Casilla, not Hansle.
match_headline: Immigrant Father Hopes to Improve From His Mistakes

text: An article on Tuesday about the dismal 2015 returns for many hedge funds misstated the history of oil prices this year. While benchmark crudes in the United States and Europe are both trading below $40 a barrel now, that was not the case “for most of the year.”
match_headline: Hedge Funds Struggle With Steep Losses and High Expectations

text: An article on Saturday about for-profit companies started by the parents of children with rare diseases described incorrectly, in some copies, two children of John Crowley, who founded Novazyme Pharmaceuticals to research treatments for Pompe disease, a neuromuscular disease that affects both siblings. Mr. Crowley’s children are not twins.
match_headline: Parents of Children With Rare Diseases Find Hope in For-Profit Companies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the Carolina Panthers’ first loss of the N.F.L. season reversed the identities of the teams’ kickers in one instance in some editions. It was the Falcons’ Shayne Graham — not the Panther’s Graham Gano — who kicked a 54-yard field goal to give Atlanta a 20-13 lead.
match_headline: Panthers, Leading League in Wins and Dances, Have Their First Misstep

text: A picture credit last Wednesday with an article about a federal appeals court ruling that could bolster the Washington Redskins’ legal case to keep the registered trademarks to their name misidentified the photographer. The picture of the Slants, a band that sought to register a trademark for its name, was taken by Sarah Giffrow, not by Anthony Pigeon.
match_headline: Ruling Could Help Washington Redskins in Trademark Case

text: An article on Tuesday about lion conservation misstated the number of square miles devoted to hunting in Tanzania. It is just over 95,000 square miles, not 950,000. The article also misstated the behavior of male lions when confronted with a dark-maned stuffed lion during a study. The male lions avoided the dummies with dark manes; they did not challenge them.
match_headline: A Lion Expert Who Isn’t Inclined to Turn Tail

text: An article on Thursday about brain cancer referred incorrectly to a gene that, once activated, makes cells grow. It is PDGFRA, not PGDFRA.
match_headline: Brain Cancers Reveal Novel Genetic Disruption in DNA

text: A listing in the Transactions column in the Square Feet pages on Tuesday about a property for lease on Butler Place in Westchester Village, the Bronx, misstated the rent. It is $14.40 a square foot, not $30 a square foot. The approximate annual rent is $72,000, not $45,600.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Wednesday about the hiring of Jeffrey Siminoff as Twitter’s diversity chief misstated Mr. Siminoff’s role at Out Leadership, a lesbian, gay and transgender advocacy organization, using information from a Twitter message posted by the organization. He is a co-founder of Out Leadership’s Leadership Committee, not of the organization itself.
match_headline: Twitter Names Jeffrey Siminoff as New Diversity Chief

text: An article on Saturday about the Middle Eastern art and culture magazine Bidoun, which put its entire archive online this month, referred incorrectly to the artist and writer Sophia Al-Maria, whose work has appeared in Bidoun. She is half Bedouin Arab and half American, not half Bedouin Arab and half Norwegian.
match_headline: Bidoun, an Influential Magazine of the Middle East, Extends Its Reach

text: An article on Wednesday about notable deaths of 2015 misspelled the given name of an opera singer. He was Jon Vickers, not John. The article also referred incorrectly to the career of the basketball star Moses Malone. While he played for a number of N.B.A. teams, notably the Philadelphia 76ers and the Houston Rockets, he never played for the Utah Jazz. And the article referred incorrectly to Dr. Frances Oldham Kelsey, who helped expose the danger of thalidomide. While she worked in South Dakota for several years, she was not born there; she was from British Columbia.
match_headline: In 2015 Obituaries, Distant Eras Were Evoked

text: Because of an editing error, the Life as a Runway column last Thursday, about what some attendees wore to the Museum of Modern Art’s Free Friday night on Nov. 20, described imprecisely the milestone reached that night. The museum recorded its millionth visitor to Free Friday since Uniqlo started sponsoring the event in May 2013, not since the museum started admitting people free on Friday nights, which dates back to November 2004.
match_headline: What to Wear for Free Nights at MoMA

text: Because of an editing error, a picture credit on Thursday with an article about the filing of sexual assault charges against the comedian Bill Cosby misidentified the photographer. The picture of Mr. Cosby was taken by Matt Rourke of The Associated Press — not by Bryan Anselm, a freelancer, whose picture of Mr. Cosby leaving court appeared with the continuation of the article.
match_headline: Bill Cosby Charged in Sexual Assault Case

text: An article on Thursday about lobbying efforts by California farmers to get more irrigation water referred incorrectly in some editions to the location where the Sacramento and San Joaquin Rivers meet. It is east of San Francisco, not west.
match_headline: Farmers Try Political Force to Twist Open California’s Taps

text: An article on Dec. 22 about Apple’s resistance to government threats of crackdowns on encrypted communications after the jihadist-inspired attacks in San Bernardino, Calif., and Paris gave an outdated name for iPhone messaging software. It is now known as iMessage, no longer iChat.
match_headline: Apple Pushes Against British Talk of Softening Encryption

text: An article on Thursday about Amazon’s increasing dominance in American e-commerce misstated the number of items the company sold through its Prime subscription service during the holiday season. The company sold 200 million more items than in the same period last year, not 200 million items over all.
match_headline: It’s Amazon and Also-Rans in Retailers’ Race for Online Sales

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday in which the historian Lisa McGirr was interviewed about her new book, “The War on Alcohol: Prohibition and the Rise of the American State,” misidentified, in some editions, the state in which Cedar Rapids is located in citing cities where there are Prohibition-themed events or bars. It is in Iowa, not Michigan.
ref_headline: The War on Alcohol: Prohibition and the Rise of the American State,
match_headline: Lisa McGirr Discusses ‘The War on Alcohol’ and the Legacy of Prohibition

text: An article on Tuesday about an outbreak of Zika virus in Brazil misstated the relationship of the chikungunya virus to other mosquito-borne viruses. Chikungunya is an Alphavirus, while dengue, West Nile, yellow fever and Zika are members of the Flavivirus genus. They are not members of the same family.
match_headline: Zika Virus, a Mosquito-Borne Infection, May Threaten Brazil’s Newborns

text: A picture credit on Thursday with an article about flooding in Missouri misidentified the photographer in some editions. The picture, of Dawson Newbold taking a break from sandbagging, was taken by Michael Noble, not by Sid Hastings.
match_headline: Record Floods Affect Millions in the Midwest

text: A picture credit on Thursday with an article about New Year’s Eve activities in Coney Island misstated the given name of the photographer. The picture of a fire-breathing performer was taken by Norman Blake, not Norma.
match_headline: A Coney Island New Year’s Eve: Sword Swallowing. Fire Breathing. No Ball.

text: An article on Tuesday about obstacles facing Digital Asset Holdings, a start-up involved in virtual currency that was founded by Blythe Masters, a former top JPMorgan Chase executive, misstated the position of Beth Shah at the start-up. She is head of business development, not chief marketing officer.
match_headline: Start-Up With Bitcoin in Its DNA Stumbles on Fund-Raising Trail

text: A picture caption last Saturday with an article about the growth of the Rolex Sydney Hobart Race into a global sailing event misstated the name and type of boat shown racing Perpetual Loyal in Sydney Harbor. It is Rambler 88, an 88-foot maxi — not the Rambler, a 100-foot supermaxi.
match_headline: A Sailing Event Down Under Suddenly Gains a Global Reach

text: An article last Sunday about the counterterrorism experience of Gov. Chris Christie, a candidate for the Republican presidential nomination, misstated, in some editions, the surname of the special agent in charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Newark Division from 2005 to 2007. He is Leslie Wiser Jr., not Walker.
match_headline: Christie Spins His Version of Security Record on Trail

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Duke’s victory over Indiana in the Pinstripe Bowl at Yankee Stadium misstated the year the Duke football team last played in New York. It was 1953, not 1944.
match_headline: Duke Wins at Yankee Stadium (Attendance Isn’t Exactly Out of the Park)

text: An article last Sunday about the ways that artists are changing the narrative about what differences truly separate Mexico and the United States referred incorrectly to the comic strip La Cucaracha by Lalo Alcaraz, who is also a lead writer on the new Fox animated series “Bordertown.” The nationally syndicated strip, which focuses on Latino and political themes, appears daily, not weekly. The article also referred incorrectly to the college-educated man whom Bud’s activist daughter gets engaged to on the show. He is the nephew of the landscaper Ernesto, not his son.
match_headline: This Season’s Breakout Star: The Border

text: An article on Dec. 13 about the best theater of 2015 referred incorrectly to the play “Eclipsed,” written by Danai Gurira. The drama, about the brutal lives of women caught up in African conflicts, had its world premiere in 2009 by the Woolly Mammoth Theater Company in Washington; it was not originally staged at Yale Repertory Theater.
match_headline: The Best Theater of 2015

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Dec. 6 about Ada Calhoun’s “St. Marks Is Dead,” a history of St. Marks Place in Manhattan, misstated part of the terms of the tuition policy of nearby Cooper Union. Since 2014, when the college began charging about $40,000 in annual tuition, all incoming students have qualified for a scholarship to cover half the amount; qualification for the scholarship was never subject to an “option.” (Some students also receive additional need-based aid.)
match_headline: ‘St. Marks Is Dead,’ by Ada Calhoun

text: An article last Sunday about the economic effect of choosing mates of like income and education misstated, using statistics from a study that was later corrected, the effect on a standard measure of income equality of importing marriage patterns of 1960 into 2005. The mating patterns, combined with labor supply, marriage and divorce decisions, would account for a 33.3 percent rise in income inequality, not a drop in income inequality to 0.34 from 0.43 on a scale of zero to one.
match_headline: The Marriages of Power Couples Reinforce Income Inequality

text: An article on Oct. 4 about Donald Trump misidentified the source of several quotations about politics today. The comments that the political class had “rigged the game,” that “everyone knows that what you see in politics is fake or confected” and that “everyone’s O.K. with that, because it’s all been focus-grouped” came from an article by Louis Menand about Joan Didion; they did not come from Joan Didion’s book “Political Fictions.”
match_headline: Donald Trump Is Not Going Anywhere

text: An article last Sunday about new condo projects at 30 Warren Street and 12 Warren Street misspelled part of the name of the firm that designed 30 Warren Street. It is Post-Office Architectes, not Poste-Office Architectes. The article also misstated the number of units at 30 Warren Street in a second reference. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it has 23 units, not 22 units.
match_headline: New Condo Projects Dress Up TriBeCa

text: An article on Dec. 20 about the author Gareth Risk Hallberg referred incompletely to the number of copies his novel “City on Fire” has sold since being published in October 2014. While it has sold slightly in excess of 30,000 copies, as the article stated, that is just for the number of hardcover sales tracked by Nielsen BookScan; it has sold a total of 80,000, including e-books, according to Knopf, the book’s publisher.
match_headline: Garth Risk Hallberg, the Literary Wunderkind of 2015

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 20 about Rooney Mara’s red carpet looks during the current awards season misidentified the category in which the actress was nominated for a Golden Globe for her role in “Carol.” It is best actress, not best supporting actress.
match_headline: Lace With a Grimace: The Quirky Dresses of Rooney Mara

text: A picture caption last Sunday with the cover article, about searching for Vincent van Gogh’s inspirations, misidentified his painting shown. It is “Starry Night Over the Rhone,” painted in 1888 — not his “Starry Night,” from 1889.
match_headline: Touring Europe in the Footsteps of van Gogh

text: An article last Sunday about street art in Bristol, England, described incorrectly the location of Bristol in relation to London. It is west, not east, of the capital. And an accompanying picture caption omitted credit for an artist who contributed to a piece of street art shown. The face at the top of the image is by the artist Stinkfish. (As the caption correctly noted, the lettering at the bottom of that same image is by Tom Deams.)
match_headline: Art in Bristol, England, Moves Beyond Museum Walls

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about signs of increased collaboration by once-competitive jihadist groups in North Africa misstated the nationality of the troops manning a mud-brick fort in the Sahara and those accompanying French soldiers on their missions to cut jihadist smuggling routes across the desert. They are Nigerien, or from Niger, not Nigerian.
match_headline: Jihadists Deepen Collaboration in North Africa

text: An article on Dec. 27 about the failure of the Afghan legal system to provide justice in the case of Farkhunda Malikzada, a young Afghan woman who was beaten to death and set on fire after being falsely accused of burning a Quran, quoted incorrectly from comments by a Western lawyer who discussed efforts by Italian legal experts to rewrite the Afghan criminal procedure code. He said, “Why would they write a new one when the Afghans had a criminal procedure code” — not “penal code” — “that everyone knew?”
ref_headline: Why would they write a new one when the Afghans had a criminal procedure code
match_headline: Flawed Justice After a Mob Killed an Afghan Woman

text: An article on Nov. 21 about three Syrian women who joined the Islamic State in the Syrian city of Raqqa, married ISIS fighters and became widows, then fled to Turkey to escape ISIS’ brutality, referred imprecisely to the waiting period for remarriage that is mandatory for Muslim women, under nearly universal interpretations of Islam. The waiting period, called idaa, is three months for a divorced woman and four months and 10 days for a widow. (Although only one of the three women, Aws, whose husband abandoned her, was considered divorced, all three expected only a three-month idaa, as the Islamic State had refashioned the rules for its own purposes. This correction was delayed for research.)
match_headline: ISIS Women and Enforcers in Syria Recount Collaboration, Anguish and Escape

text: An article on May 4 about a promise by China’s leader, Xi Jinping, to heighten the country’s already robust presence in Antarctica referred incorrectly to a treaty that bans mining in Antarctica. It is expected to come up for review by 2048; it does not expire then.
match_headline: China, Pursuing Strategic Interests, Builds Presence in Antarctica

text: An article on Dec. 11 about the release of a document by the Vatican that advises Roman Catholics not to try to convert Jews but instead work with them to fight anti-Semitism erroneously attributed a distinction to Pope John Paul II. He was the first modern pope to pray in a synagogue, but not the first pope to do so. That distinction goes to St. Peter, considered by Catholics to be the first pope.
match_headline: Vatican Says Catholics Should Not Try to Convert Jews

text: An article on Dec. 18 about the ordering of a trial for Christine Lagarde, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, on charges of negligence that date back to when she served as France’s finance minister gave an outdated name for the law firm where Christopher Mesnooh, who said the charges were “a big deal,” is a partner in Paris. The firm is now Fieldfisher, no longer Field Fisher Waterhouse.
match_headline: I.M.F. Chief Faces Trial in Case Dating to Time as French Finance Minister

text: An article on Dec. 6 about a recent cut to a government program in Denmark that subsidizes green technology projects misstated the United States dollar equivalency for 2.5 million Danish krone, the amount of a grant received by one Dane to develop a prototype of a low-emissions furnace. The grant is worth $356,000, not $448,000.
match_headline: Denmark, a Green Energy Leader, Slows Pace of Its Spending

text: An obituary on Monday about the linguist John Holm misidentified the location of the University of Coimbra, where he was chairman of English linguistics. It is in Coimbra, Portugal — not Lisbon.
match_headline: John Holm, 72, Dies; Opened Linguistics to Creole and Pidgin Tongues

text: An obituary on Thursday about Frank Malzone, the All-Star third baseman for the Boston Red Sox, misstated the year in which he played 42 more games at third base than anyone else in the American League. It was 1957, not 1959.
match_headline: Frank Malzone, Star Fielder for Boston Red Sox, Dies at 85

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about James Burke, the former police chief of Suffolk County, N.Y., who is being held in jail on charges of violating a thief’s civil rights, referred incompletely in some copies to the area that Mr. Burke oversaw as police chief. It was all of Suffolk County, not just the East End.
match_headline: Ex-Suffolk County Police Chief’s Arrest Comes Amid a Broader Federal Inquiry

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the closing of a Broadway hangout rendered its name incorrectly. It is Angus’ Cafe Bistro, not Angus’s Cafe and Bistro. The article also misidentified the birthplace of the author Frank McCourt, an early investor in the restaurant. He was born in Brooklyn, not in Ireland.
match_headline: A Homey Hangout for Broadway Stars Closes After 14 Years

text: Because of an editing error, an article on the Personal Finance pages on Dec. 26, about long-term care insurance, described premium increases for a Genworth policy incorrectly. While premiums may rise during the life of the policy, they do not increase annually in line with health care inflation.
match_headline: Long-Term Care Insurance Can Be Costly but Effective

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with the On Pro Football column, about recent failures of Philadelphia’s pro sports teams, misstated the result of the Dec. 13 game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Buffalo Bills. The picture showed fans during the Eagles’ 23-20 win — not loss.
match_headline: Unbrotherly Feelings in Philadelphia

text: An article on Friday about Clemson’s 37-17 victory over Oklahoma in the Orange Bowl misspelled, in some editions, the given name of the Oklahoma running back who injured his ankle early in the second half. He is Samaje Perine, not Semaje.
match_headline: No. 1 Clemson Advances to National Championship Game

text: An article on Saturday about the Montreal Canadiens’ 5-1 victory over the Boston Bruins in the N.H.L.’s Winter Classic misstated, in some copies, the margin by which Montreal outshot Boston in the first period. It was 14-3, not 12-3.
match_headline: Canadiens’ Mike Condon, Inspired by a Boston-Area Hero, Stifles Bruins

text: An article on Saturday about Marceline Loridan-Ivens, who has written a memoir about her childhood experience in the Auschwitz-Birkenau death-camp complex, referred incorrectly to “La Petite Prairie aux Bouleaux” (“The Birch-Tree Meadow”), a film she started working on in 1993 that was released in 2003. Another movie, “Triumph of the Spirit,” was filmed at Birkenau in 1989; “La Petite Prairie aux Bouleaux” was not the first feature film shot there.
match_headline: Jewish Deportee on Persecution, Past and Present

text: An obituary on Dec. 10 about Fatema Mernissi, one of the founders of Islamic feminism, using information from her literary agent, misstated her marital history. She was divorced from the Ghanaian novelist Ayi Kwei Armah; it is not the case that she never married. The obituary also referred imprecisely to Professor Mernissi’s book “Dreams of Trespass: Tales of a Harem Girlhood.” Though it was described in many reviews as a memoir, it contained elements of both memoir and fiction.
ref_headline: Dreams of Trespass: Tales of a Harem Girlhood.
match_headline: Fatema Mernissi, a Founder of Islamic Feminism, Dies at 75

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the former New York Times fashion reporter Woody Hochswender referred incorrectly to the Times column Patterns. Mr. Hochswender wrote the column from 1988 to 1992, but he did not inaugurate it. The obituary also omitted the name of a survivor. Besides his sister and his girlfriend, Mr. Hochswender is survived by a daughter, Katharine Hochswender.
match_headline: Woody Hochswender, Fashion Reporter, Dies at 64

text: A Critic’s Notebook column last Wednesday in which Pete Wells reported on his blind tasting of chocolate bars misspelled the name of the cacao used in Dandelion chocolate. It is Mantuano, not Mantuana.
match_headline: A Taste Test of Chocolate Bars Made From Scratch

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Front Burner column last Wednesday about the tasting menu at Piora in the West Village misidentified the restaurant where Josep Roca is an owner. It is El Celler de Can Roca, near Girona in Spain — not Piora.
match_headline: Crisp Plantains for Party Dipping

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 17 about accusations that China continues to use prisoners’ organs for transplant despite a ban on the practice referred incompletely to one surgeon’s description of the effect of the ban. The surgeon, Dr. Chen Jingyu, noted that the supply of organs did not fall, as expected, but he attributed that to a surge in voluntary donations and said that in 2015, none of the lungs he transplanted came from convicts. Also because of an editing error, the article misstated the year that Dr. Huang Jiefu, who oversees China’s organ transplants, told The Beijing Times that voluntary organ donations from death row prisoners could be counted as donations from citizens. It was March 2014, not March 2015. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: China Bends Vow on Using Prisoners’ Organs for Transplants

text: An article on Wednesday about music sales in 2015 misstated the number of on-demand audio and video streams on streaming services in 2015. The number of songs streamed was 317.2 billion, not million, of which 114.9 billion, not million, were audio-only streams.
match_headline: Adele Album Resists the Streaming Trend in Music Sales

text: An article on Tuesday about airline passengers who pack their own meals misstated the Transportation Security Administration rules on carrying consumable liquids, pastes or gels onto flights. The 3.4-ounce limit on such substances applies to what may be carried through security checkpoints, not to what may be carried on board. (Once past security, passengers may purchase such items or fill drink containers to carry on board.)
match_headline: Fliers Go Their Own Way With Airline Meals

text: An article on Saturday about the disappointing ratings for the college football semifinals on Dec. 31 misstated the ratings for “Dick Clark’s New Year’s Rockin’ Eve With Ryan Seacrest” on ABC. Its prime-time audience increased 2 percent; it did not fall 23.4 percent and did not see “significantly lower viewership” as the college football semifinals did.
ref_headline: Dick Clark’s New Year’s Rockin’ Eve With Ryan Seacrest
match_headline: Before Ball Dropped, So Did Viewership of College Football Playoff Semifinals

text: An article on Tuesday about the exhibition “Thom Browne Selects,” which is to open at the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum in Manhattan in March, referred incompletely to the commission of a mirror by Jim Dine for the Biltmore Hotel in Los Angeles, a work that will be in the exhibition. It was a joint commission by the architect and Seagram heiress Phyllis Lambert and the architect Gene R. Summers, not solely Ms. Lambert.
match_headline: Thom Browne Brings a Designer’s Eye to Cooper Hewitt Show

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the artist Eugenie Schwartz misidentified the museum for which she and the artist George Dureau made a pair of bronze and steel gates in 1993. It is the New Orleans Museum of Art, not the Ogden Museum of Southern Art.
match_headline: Eugenie Schwartz, Artist From New Orleans, Dies at 64

text: An article on Thursday about a decision by Florida Atlantic University to fire a professor who repeatedly questioned the authenticity of recent mass shootings misidentified, in one instance, the person dismissed. He is James F. Tracy — not Lenny Pozner, who is the parent of a victim of the school shooting in Newtown, Conn., and had accused Mr. Tracy of harassment.
match_headline: Florida Professor Who Cast Doubt on Mass Shootings Is Fired

text: An article on Dec. 31 about a decision by the actress Tonya Pinkins to leave a production of Bertolt Bercht’s “Mother Courage and Her Children” over a creative dispute with the director referred incompletely to the setting for the play. It is in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Republic of Congo, not just the Republic of Congo.
match_headline: Star of ‘Mother Courage’ Quits in Creative Dispute

text: An article in some editions last Friday about a man who fell to his death while he and a friend tried to take pictures of the Manhattan skyline from a catwalk above the roof of the Four Seasons Hotel misspelled the man’s given name, using information from the Police Department. He was Connor Cummings, not Conner.
match_headline: Man Falls to His Death Climbing the Four Seasons Hotel

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision to redraw two school zones in Brooklyn misstated the timing of the vote. It took place on Tuesday, not on Monday.
match_headline: 2 Brooklyn Schools in Gentrifying Area Will Get New Zones

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about apps for keeping a journal misstated the price of the app Day One. It costs $5, not $1.
match_headline: Video Feature: Apps Give Journal Writers Inspiration, and Maybe a Nudge

text: An article on the Square Feet page on Wednesday about renovation plans for the historic Hotel Okura in Tokyo misstated when Airbnb announced that Japan was its fastest-growing market. It was in November, not “last month.”
match_headline: In a Renewed Hotel Okura, Japanese Historians Still See a Loss

text: An article on Monday about the Giants’ season-ending 35-30 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles misstated, in some copies, the number of seconds left in the game when the Giants began a last-ditch drive. It was 103 seconds, not 83.
match_headline: Giants Finish Quietly, and Tom Coughlin Has Little to Say About Future

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday about a concert Laurie Anderson played for dogs in Times Square on Monday night referred incorrectly to dogs from the Homeland Security Department that were there. While their training led them to sniff people’s bags, they were invited guests at the concert; they were not working.
match_headline: Laurie Anderson Puts on a Concert for Dogs in Times Square

text: An obituary on Thursday about Alan S. Gordon, the executive director of the American Guild of Musical Artists, omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to his wife, two daughters and a grandson, Mr. Gordon is survived by a sister, Karen Gordon Marrinan.
match_headline: Alan S. Gordon, Colorful Union Leader in Opera and Ballet, Dies at 70

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary in some copies on Tuesday about the cinematographer Vilmos Zsigmond omitted the given name of the director Woody Allen, who worked with Mr. Zsigmond on three films.
match_headline: Vilmos Zsigmond, Cinematographer, Dies at 85; Gave Hollywood Films a New Look

text: A map on Wednesday showing Sunni and Shiite populations erroneously included some areas among those with a predominant Wahhabi presence. In those areas — in parts of the United Arab Emirates like Dubai and Abu Dhabi — less conservative Sunni interpretations of Islam are actually more prevalent. In addition, the key with the map might have given the incorrect impression that Wahhabism is a separate branch of Islam; in fact, it is a movement linked to Sunni Islam. An updated version of the map can be found at nytimes.com/world .
match_headline: Saudi-Iran Feud Poses Threat to Iraq’s Effort to Combat ISIS

text: An article on Dec. 9 about challenges awaiting the political opposition in Venezuela, which rode discontent over a failing economy to an overwhelming majority in legislative elections, referred incorrectly to Henry Ramos, a leader of the opposition Democratic Unity coalition. He was elected — not re-elected — to the National Assembly.
match_headline: Opposition in Venezuela Now Has to Fix the Ills That Led to Its Victory

text: An article on Thursday about the election of Ken Griffey Jr. and Mike Piazza to the Baseball Hall of Fame misidentified, in some copies, the team from which the Mets acquired Piazza in a trade. He came from the Florida Marlins, not the Los Angeles Dodgers.
match_headline: Ken Griffey Jr. and Mike Piazza Trot Into Baseball Hall of Fame

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with the Sports of The Times column, about a common thread linking some of the key figures in an Al Jazeera documentary on doping in professional sports, misstated, in some editions, the origin of the picture of Charles Sly, a pharmacist featured in the documentary. It was from the YouTube video in which Sly retracted his assertions in the documentary, not from the documentary itself.
match_headline: Finding a Common Thread in the Al Jazeera Doping Report

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the final season of “American Idol” referred incorrectly to Simon Cowell’s involvement with “American Idol.” While he was a judge and a producer, he was not the creator. (As the article correctly noted elsewhere, the show was created by Simon Fuller.)
match_headline: How Pop Music Left ‘American Idol’ Behind

text: An article on Tuesday about a quarry pit in New Jersey that contains many fossils referred incorrectly to a fossilized specimen of a brachiopod, a sea creature. Although it resembled a clam, it was not a mollusk. The article also referred incorrectly to the nature of the element iridium that identifies the rock layer corresponding to the mass extinction. Natural iridium is not radioactive.
match_headline: Behind a Shopping Center in New Jersey, Signs of a Mass Extinction

text: A headline on Tuesday with an obituary about the actor Jason Wingreen overstated his involvement in the movie “The Empire Strikes Back.” He provided the voice of the bounty hunter Boba Fett, but another actor appeared on screen in the role; Mr. Wingreen alone did not play Boba Fett.
match_headline: Jason Wingreen, Actor Who Voiced Boba Fett, Dies at 95

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Light of Day Winterfest, a music festival with many events in Asbury Park that runs through Jan. 18 and raises money for research on Parkinson’s disease, misstated the age of Bob Benjamin, a longtime fixture on the Jersey Shore scene. He is 57, not 55.
match_headline: Rock Out for a Good Cause at Light of Day Winterfest

text: An article last Sunday in the Oscars special section about journalism in movies misspelled the surname of the actress who starred with Paul Newman in “Absence of Malice” in 1981. She is Sally Field, not Fields.
match_headline: When Journalism Catches Hollywood’s Eye

text: An article on Dec. 27 about the avant-garde filmmaker Andrew Noren misidentified the state he was living in when he died in May. It was North Carolina, not South Carolina.
match_headline: Andrew Noren, Avant-Garde Filmmaker, Fades to Black

text: An article on Dec. 27 about Marcy Borders, in the The Lives They Lived issue, referred imprecisely to how Stan Honda took a photograph of Borders minutes after she fled one of the towers on Sept. 11. The photographer did not stop her.

An article last Sunday about two people who moved from Astoria, Queens, to West 72nd Street in Manhattan misidentified the subway train one of them now takes to work in Brooklyn. It is the 2 or the 3, not the A.
match_headline: For a Better Commute, the Upper West Side

text: Because of an editing error, a report last Sunday about the marriage of Jessica Freireich and Geoffrey Mattson omitted part of the name of the Japanese company that employs the groom. It is SMBC Nikko Securities, not Nikko Securities.
match_headline: Jessica Freireich, Geoffrey Mattson

text: Because of an editing error, an article about diesel engines last Sunday misstated how diesel engine combustion works. Only diesel fuel is injected into each cylinder, not a fuel-air mix.
match_headline: The Dirty Truth About ‘Clean Diesel’

text: An article on Wednesday about analysts’ theories that Saudi Arabia’s executions of 47 prisoners was meant as a message to would-be militants and dissidents that the royal family would not tolerate any challenge to its rule misstated the length of time that Sheikh Nimr al-Nimr, a prominent Shiite cleric and outspoken critic of the government, and three other Shiite dissidents had been imprisoned before they were executed. It was less than four years, not less than three years.
match_headline: Saudi Executions Seen as Sending Message to All Dissenters

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about an 18-year-old woman who was raped by five people in Brooklyn referred incorrectly to the location of the crime, using information from the Police Department. It happened at the Osborn Playground, not in a park. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Woman Raped by 5 Men in Brooklyn Playground, Police Say

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about four teenagers being taken into custody in connection with the rape of an 18-year-old woman at a Brooklyn playground misspelled the surname of New York City’s mayor in some editions. He is Bill de Blasio, not de Balsio.
match_headline: 4 Suspects in Brooklyn Rape Are in Custody

text: An article on Sunday about a New York City police officer who was shot while breaking up a brawl in the Bronx misspelled the name of a nearby housing complex in some copies. It is the Mitchel Houses, not Mitchell Houses.
match_headline: New York Police Officer Is Shot Breaking Up a Brawl in the Bronx

text: An article on Saturday about the possibility of a public offering of shares in Saudi Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s giant state-owned oil company, misstated the proximity of Saudi Arabia to Syria. They are separated by Iraq and Jordan; they do not border each other.
match_headline: Saudi Aramco I.P.O. Prospect Reflects Kingdom Looking Beyond Oil

text: Because of an editing error, a music review on Monday about “Sága,” at National Sawdust in Brooklyn, referred incorrectly to a group that took part, Baroque Orchestration X. It is a Belgian ensemble, not Dutch.
match_headline: Review: Dez Mona’s ‘Sága,’ Acoustic Time Travel in a Song Cycle About Roots

text: Because of an editing error, schedule information on Friday with an article about immersive and participatory theater in New York City misspelled the name of the street in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, where one such production, “Then She Fell,” is playing. It is Maujer Street, not Mauger.
match_headline: Starring Me! A Surreal Dive Into Immersive Theater

text: An obituary on Friday about the character actor Pat Harrington Jr., using information from his manager, referred incorrectly to his survivors. He is survived by three sons and a daughter, not two sons and two daughters. (Terry Harrington is a son, not a daughter.)
match_headline: Pat Harrington, the Super on ‘One Day at a Time,’ Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Sunday by The Associated Press about the singer Nicholas Caldwell of the group the Whispers misidentified the location in California where the group was formed. It was in Los Angeles, not in the San Francisco area.
match_headline: California Beach City Enlists Private Partner to Rejuvenate Pier

text: An obituary on Saturday about the fashion designer André Courrèges misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the company where Jacques Bungert and Frédéric Torloting had been advertising executives before they bought the Courrèges brand in 2011. It is Young & Rubicam, not Young & Rubicon.
match_headline: André Courrèges, Fashion Designer Who Redefined Couture, Dies at 92

text: Because of an editing error, the On Pro Basketball column on Monday, about Mikhail D. Prokhorov’s handling of the Nets, misstated the surname of his business partner in some copies. He is Dmitry Razumov, not Ravumov.
match_headline: With Mikhail D. Prokhorov, a Distant Owner, the Nets Have Lost Their Way

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the college basketball roundup on Monday about South Carolina’s 83-58 victory over Missouri in a women’s game misstated the location of the game. South Carolina was at home, not on the road.
match_headline: A Way to Start Paying College Athletes

text: Because of an editing error, a television review on Thursday about “Angel From Hell,” on CBS, misstated the surname of Mary Tyler Moore’s character on “The Mary Tyler Moore Show” in comparing two characters in “Angel From Hell” to two on that show. Ms. Moore played Mary Richards, not Richardson.
match_headline: Review: Jane Lynch as the ‘Angel From Hell’ (With a Drink in Hand)

text: An article on Dec. 25 about expensive jewels and jeweled objects on display in Manhattan misidentified the owner of the Victory Diamond, which was sold at Christie’s in early December. The owner was a private collector — not the socialite and philanthropist Carroll Petrie, who died last year, and whose jewels were sold at the same time.
match_headline: All That Glitters, From Gems to Dazzling Crowns, to Behold in New York

text: A report in the In Brief column on Jan. 5 about psychotherapy as a treatment for irritable bowel syndrome erroneously included two symptoms in a list of those caused by the condition. Rectal bleeding and fever are not symptoms. (They may be symptoms of inflammatory bowel disease, a more serious condition.)
match_headline: U.S. Becomes More Vulnerable to Tropical Diseases Like Zika

text: An obituary on Sunday about George M. Elsey, who served in the White House during and immediately after World War II, referred incorrectly to a prediction President Harry S. Truman made to Mr. Elsey during the 1948 presidential campaign. The total of electoral votes Truman predicted he would receive, 340, was 74 more than he needed to win the election — not 71 more.
match_headline: George Elsey, One of the Last Survivors of World War II White House, Dies at 97

text: An article on Wednesday about a new broadcasting schedule for the second season of the podcast “Serial,” which this season is focusing on the story of the former Taliban prisoner Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl, misstated, in some editions, the year of his release from captivity. It was 2014, not last year. The article also referred incompletely to the interviews with Sergeant Bergdahl. The interviews were telephone conversations between Sergeant Bergdahl and the filmmaker Mark Boal, who gave “Serial” permission to use the recordings. The interviews were not with “Serial” itself.
match_headline: ‘Serial’ Podcast, Needing More Reporting Time, Goes Biweekly

text: An article on Tuesday about some of David Bowie’s best and most widely loved songs misidentified the producer of the song “Space Oddity.” While Tony Visconti produced the rest of the album it came from, that song was produced by Gus Dudgeon, not by Mr. Visconti.
match_headline: Listening to David Bowie: A Critic’s Tour of His Musical Changes

text: An article on Wednesday about Erin Markey and her new musical, “A Ride on the Irish Cream,” which is in previews at Abrons Arts Center in Manhattan, misspelled the surname of the guitar player in the show, who also co-wrote the score. As an accompanying picture caption correctly noted, she is Emily Bate, not Bait.
ref_headline: A Ride on the Irish Cream,
match_headline: A ‘Barbie From Outer Space’ Touches Down on a New Stage

text: An article on Tuesday about the first mention in The New York Times of using electricity to produce light misidentified the source of gas commonly used for residential lighting in the late 19th century. It was manufactured gas, which is produced from coal, oil and other feedstocks; the source was not natural gas.
match_headline: The Arrival of Electric Light

text: An article and a picture caption on Dec. 3 about the Pirelli calendar, using information from a publicist for Pirelli, referred incorrectly to the baby in a calendar photograph of the model Natalia Vodianova. The baby is not Ms. Vodianova’s child.
match_headline: The 2016 Pirelli Calendar May Signal a Cultural Shift

text: A picture caption last Thursday with an article about Shinola misspelled the given name and the surname of a worker shown at the company’s Detroit headquarters. He is Darrin Brouhard, not Darran Brossard. Another caption misidentified the leather goods shown. The picture was of dog collars produced by the factory, not belts.
match_headline: Shinola Takes Its ‘Detroit Cool’ Message on the Road

text: An obituary on Jan. 6 about the composer, writer and director Elizabeth Swados referred incompletely to her works on Jewish themes. She wrote a number of such works over the years, not just “The Haggadah: A Passover Cantata” and the oratorio “Jerusalem.”
match_headline: Elizabeth Swados, Creator of Socially Conscious Musicals, Is Dead at 64

text: An article on Dec. 10 about Marco Rubio’s efforts to undermine an element of the Affordable Care Act referred incorrectly to one element of the legislative history. While Mr. Rubio was the most prominent congressional opponent of the so-called risk corridor payments in the health law, and introduced measures to undermine them, other Republicans were ultimately responsible for inserting a provision into a 2014 spending bill that limited the payments. The error was repeated in a picture caption with the continuation of the article.
match_headline: Marco Rubio Quietly Undermines Affordable Care Act

text: An article on Dec. 21 about gay Nigerians’ contention that American support for gay rights in Africa has done more harm than good, using information from United States officials, misstated the amount of financing provided by the government to support gay rights globally since 2012. At least $41 million has been spent by the United States for that specific purpose, not more than $700 million. (Gay communities and causes have also received a portion of $700 million, which was spent on marginalized and “at-risk” groups, American officials said.) The article also misstated, in some editions, the given name of a Nigerian fashion blogger who said pushing too hard for gay rights could make things “bad or worse.” He is Abayomi Shoyinka, not Aboyani.
match_headline: U.S. Support of Gay Rights in Africa May Have Done More Harm Than Good

text: An article on Jan. 6 about policy changes sought by antigovernment protesters in Oregon misstated the year of a standoff in Nevada between another protester, Cliven Bundy, and the Bureau of Land Management over grazing fees for federal lands. It was 2014, not 2015.
match_headline: Protesters in Oregon Seek to End Policy That Shaped West

text: A picture credit on Wednesday with the continuation of an article about President Obama’s State of the Union address misidentified the photographer in some editions. The picture, of Mr. Obama and members of Congress, was taken by Stephen Crowley, not by Doug Mills. (A similar picture by Mr. Mills was in an earlier edition.)
match_headline: Obama Confronts Americans’ Fears in State of the Union Speech

text: An article on Sunday about a proposal by Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany for tougher laws regulating asylum seekers in the wake of New Year’s Eve assaults on scores of women in Cologne misstated part of the surname of a demonstrator at a rally in Cologne who urged Germany to preserve the rule of law. She is Irmgard Schenk-Zittlau, not Schenker-Zittlau.
match_headline: After Assaults in Cologne, Merkel Proposes Tougher Asylum Laws

text: An article on Wednesday about a suicide bombing in Istanbul that killed 10 foreign tourists misspelled, at one point and in some editions, the name of the historic district where the attack occurred. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is Sultanahmet, not Sultanahamet. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption in some copies.
match_headline: Istanbul Explosion Kills 10 Tourists, and ISIS Is Blamed

text: An article on Jan. 4 about the graphic novelist Gene Luen Yang, who was named by the Library of Congress as the national ambassador for young people’s literature, referred incorrectly to him. He is a second-generation American, not first-generation.
match_headline: Library of Congress Anoints Graphic Novelist as Ambassador for Young People’s Literature

text: An article on Friday about the Oscar nominations misstated the number Cate Blanchett has received in her career. It is seven, not six.
match_headline: Oscar Nominations 2016

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the Ghetto Film School and its collaboration with the Frick Collection, using information from a publicist, reversed the identities of two actors in the movie “The Progress of Love.” Grant Lancaster was on the left, and Max Woertendyke was on the right. In addition, a credit was omitted from another photograph. The shot of the actress Alfre Woodard and the director Baz Luhrmann was taken by Marion Curtis/Starpix.
match_headline: Young Moviemakers Meet Old Masters at the Frick

text: An article on Jan. 3 about the final season of “Downton Abbey” referred incompletely to the architecture of Highclere Castle, the mansion that serves as the set for the show. While the castle was once a classical Georgian mansion, as noted on its website, Highclere’s look has evolved over the many decades — buffeted by the winds of history and culture, much like the characters on the television series — and has assumed the characteristics of a range of architectural styles.
match_headline: ‘Downton Abbey’: Saying Farewell to All That
