text: An article on Jan. 3, about Richard Greenberg’s new play, “Our Mother’s Brief Affair,” using information from a publicist, misstated the number of his plays presented by the Manhattan Theater Club, which is also putting on this one. It is nine, not 10.
match_headline: Three Theater Stalwarts, Together at Last, Talk Mom

text: A picture caption on Jan. 3 with an article about the Atlantic coast of Morocco located a beach on the coast incorrectly. It is in Essaouira, not El Jadida.
match_headline: Morocco’s Other Coast Emerges as a Destination

text: An article on Dec. 3 about Molokai, Hawaii, misstated the travel options to Kalaupapa, a former leper colony on the island. It is accessible by charter flights, not just by mule rides or hikes.
match_headline: A Hawaiian Island Where Everybody Knows Your Name

text: An article last week about 52 places to go in 2016 misstated the timing of a visit Pope Francis will make to Mexico City. He will be there in February, not in the spring. Because of an editing error, the article misstated the name of a restaurant in Oakland. It is Ramen Shop, not Autological Ramen Shop. In addition, the article misidentified a wine museum that is opening this year in Bordeaux. It is La Cité du Vin, not the Bordeaux Wine and Trade Museum. And, because of an editing error, the article misstated the size of the waterfront expansion in Bordeaux. It is over 7,500,000 square feet, or about 700,000 square meters — not 700,000 square miles. And also because of an editing error, a report on the east coast of Sri Lanka, one of the recommended places, carried an erroneous credit. It was written by Daniel Scheffler, not by Shivani Vora.
match_headline: Robust 4th Quarter Couldn’t Redeem Market After an Anxious Year

text: An article last Sunday about anniversary events in 2016 erroneously included a character in discussing events commemorating the 150th birthday of Beatrix Potter. The character Mr. Toad was created by Kenneth Grahame and therefore not related to Ms. Potter. The article should have referred to her character Jeremy Fisher.
match_headline: Where History Buffs Should Go in 2016

text: An article last Sunday about the closing of the chain store Kitson referred incorrectly to legal action taken by Hudson Group, the company that operates Kitson’s stores at the Los Angeles International Airport. Hudson sued Kitson — not the store’s founder, Fraser Ross.
match_headline: Kitson, Where Kim Kardashian and Britney Spears Shopped, Sees the End

text: A headline on Jan. 8 with an article about a natural gas leak in California misstated the time frame for the leak to be halted. As the article correctly noted, the drilling of a release well is expected to be finished at the end of February; it will not take 30 to 45 days to fix the leak.
match_headline: No Short-Term Fix for California Methane Leak

text: A picture caption on Friday with an obituary about the rock impresario and record producer Giorgio Gomelsky referred incorrectly to the photograph of him at his rehearsal and performance space in Manhattan. It was taken in 2013; it is not undated.
match_headline: Giorgio Gomelsky, Impresario Who Gave the Rolling Stones Their Start, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Friday about the actor Alan Rickman omitted part of the name of the theater in London where he directed the play “My Name Is Rachel Corrie” in 2005. It is the Royal Court Theater, not merely the Court Theater.
match_headline: Alan Rickman, Watchable Villain in ‘Harry Potter’ and ‘Die Hard,’ Dies at 69

text: An article on Saturday about the Oscar nominations, in which all 20 contenders for acting awards are white and films with black themes were shut out of the best-picture category, misstated the timing of the awards campaign for one of those films, “Straight Outta Compton.” It began in August; it was not late getting started.
match_headline: Another Oscar Year, Another All-White Ballot

text: An article on Friday about federal support for the development of driverless cars referred incompletely to President Obama’s $4 billion request for research into autonomous car technology and infrastructure. While the request is included in his proposed budget for the next fiscal year, it would be spent over 10 years, not one year.
match_headline: U.S. Proposes Spending $4 Billion on Self-Driving Cars

text: An article on Wednesday about Volvo’s comeback as a Chinese-owned, Swedish-operated carmaker erroneously attributed a distinction to the company’s forthcoming plant in Ridgeville, S.C. It will be Volvo’s first plant in the United States, not the first in North America. (Volvo operated a manufacturing plant in Halifax, Nova Scotia, for several decades.)
match_headline: Volvo Makes a Comeback, With a Detour Through China

text: An article on Saturday about the United States stock market’s recent decline referred incorrectly to the Russell 2,000. It is an index of companies with small market capitalizations; it is not a broad measure of the stock market.
match_headline: Stock Market Ends Sharply Lower as Worries About Economy Surface

text: An article on the Personal Finance pages on Saturday about retirees who pursue outdoor adventures referred incorrectly to a hiking trail in California. It is the Pacific Crest trail, not the Pacific Coast.
match_headline: Goodbye, Golf Clubs. Hello, Hiking Boots and Kayak.

text: Because of an editing error, the Week Ahead column on Monday misstated the day the president of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, plans to hold a news conference. The news conference will take place on Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: China’s Growth Report and Oil Company Earnings

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about the NYC Winter Jazzfest Marathon misidentified the bass player in the band Mboko. He is Matt Brewer, not Matt Penman. A picture caption with the article, using information from a publicist, misidentified the bass player shown with the trumpeter Avishai Cohen. He is Tal Mashiach, not Tal Ronen.
match_headline: Hot Sets and Warm Chilly Nights at NYC Winter Jazzfest Marathon

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Wednesday about a dispute over a Picasso sculpture between the art dealer Larry Gagosian and the ruling family of Qatar misstated the history of Qatar’s founding and the family. While the Thani family’s status as local authorities over the area dates to the 19th century, Qatar did not become an independent country until 1971. Thus, the family has ruled the country since then, not since Qatar’s “founding in 1850.”
match_headline: Picasso Bust at Center of Custody Battle Between Gagosian and Qatar Royal Family

text: Because of an editing error, a news analysis article on Jan. 9 about the ability of the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, to play one big world power against another by testing a nuclear bomb misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the research organization in Seoul, South Korea, where Go Myong-hyun — who said, “This is exactly what North Korea wanted” — is a fellow. It is the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, not the Asian Institute for Policy Studies.
ref_headline: This is exactly what North Korea wanted
match_headline: With Nuclear Test, North Korea’s Leader Asserts Role of Instigator

text: An article on Monday about questions raised by subsidies for the planned Inner Harbor complex of hotels, upscale apartments and stores in Syracuse, N.Y., referred imprecisely to the relationship between the Onondaga County executive, Joanne M. Mahoney, and the Onondaga County Industrial Development Agency, which made the deal for the project. While Ms. Mahoney may hold sway over the agency, she does not “control” it. Appointment authority for agency members and its executive director rests with the Onondaga County Legislature.
match_headline: Questions on Subsidies and Local Hiring Surround Syracuse Project

text: An article on Saturday about a revitalization of Google’s robotics division misstated part of the background of Hans Peter Brondmo, who has been hired to help manage the unit, now part of the X research division of the Alphabet holding company. He graduated from M.I.T., not the M.I.T. Media Lab.
match_headline: Alphabet Shakes Up Its Robotics Division

text: An article in the Personal Finance pages on Saturday about a crackdown on so-called captive insurance companies, which are established by businesses ostensibly to protect against risk but that often also greatly reduce their owners’ tax bills, misstated the action such companies must now take to demonstrate they are entitled to a tax deduction of premiums. They must either prove that no more than 20 percent of the premiums come from one policyholder, or that an insured company is not wholly owned by one person and the captive by his or her heirs. They do not need to prove both of those things.
match_headline: Small, Private Insurers Face Increasing Scrutiny on Avoided Taxes

text: An article on Saturday previewing the N.F.L. playoff game between the New England Patriots and the Kansas City Chiefs misidentified the city in which the A.F.L.’s Texans played before moving to Kansas City and becoming the Chiefs. They were in Dallas, not in Houston.
match_headline: New England Is Abuzz (Oh, Is There a Game?)

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday and Sunday about Serena Williams’s health and frame of mind before beginning her tennis season misstated the month of the Hopman Cup exhibition event, at which Williams pulled out of two matches and failed to complete a third. It was this month, not in December.
match_headline: Serena Williams, Rejecting Health Doubts, Insists She’s Ready

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Saturday about the resignation of Ronald O. Perelman from the Carnegie Hall board this month gave an outdated title for him. He was no longer chairman when he resigned.
match_headline: Ronald Perelman Quits Carnegie Hall Board

text: A chart on Tuesday with an Upshot article about the distinctive nature of the 2016 presidential race omitted two Republican candidates in the 2008 race when comparing national polls conducted in the weeks before the Iowa caucuses. And because of that error, the chart misidentified the candidate leading an average of the polls. The chart should have included Rudolph Giuliani and Mitt Romney, with Mr. Giuliani averaging 20 percent and Mr. Romney 14 percent. That made Mr. Giuliani the leader — not Mike Huckabee, who averaged 18 percent.
match_headline: Why 2016 Is Different From All Other Recent Elections

text: An article on Friday about a lawsuit accusing the public defender’s office in New Orleans of putting clients on a “waiting list” misstated, in some instances, the source of the fees that support the program. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, the fees are assessed on traffic tickets, not on parking tickets. The article also misidentified the location of the federal court where the case was filed. It was in Baton Rouge, not New Orleans.
match_headline: New Orleans Puts Poor on ‘Waiting List’ for Lawyers, Suit Alleges

text: An article on Wednesday about a court battle over the estate of the radio drama creator Himan Brown misstated the given name of a lawyer for Radio Drama Network in some copies. She is Pamela A. Mann, not Patricia.
match_headline: Charity’s Suit Contests Will of Creator of ‘Dick Tracy’ and Other Radio Shows

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about a girl who died after falling from a Midtown Manhattan building misspelled her given name in some copies, using information from the Police Department. She was Natalia Jimenez, not Natalya.
match_headline: Girl, 15, Killed in Fall From Rooftop in Hell’s Kitchen

text: An article on Wednesday about IBM’s quarterly earnings misstated an estimate by analysts of the company’s revenue last quarter. The figure, compiled by Thomson Reuters, was $22.02 billion, not $20.02 billion.
match_headline: IBM Reports Declines in Fourth-Quarter Profit and Revenue Despite Gains in New Fields

text: An article on Monday about the Denver Broncos’ 23-16 victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers in the N.F.L. playoffs misstated, in some editions, the age Denver quarterback Peyton Manning will turn in March. He will be 40, not 39.
match_headline: Peyton Manning, the Broncos’ Flickering Star, Glows Just in Time

text: A report in the N.F.L. roundup on Monday about Green Bay Packers receiver Randall Cobb’s release from the hospital misstated the result of the catch that caused his injury. The catch was negated by a penalty; it did not move Green Bay to the Arizona 3-yard line.

An obituary on Tuesday about the guitarist, singer and songwriter Glenn Frey, a founder of the Eagles, misstated his contribution to the group’s song “Hotel California.” He, Don Henley and Don Felder wrote the words and music; Mr. Frey was not the sole lyricist. The obituary also misstated the year the album “Hotel California” was released. It was 1976, not 1977.
match_headline: Glenn Frey, Singer-Songwriter and Eagles Founding Member, Dies at 67

text: An article on Jan. 7 about the engagement of Pierre-Yves Roussel, the chairman and chief executive of the LVMH Fashion Group, and the fashion designer Tory Burch referred imprecisely to Mr. Roussel’s marital status. Although Mr. Roussel is in the process of getting a divorce from his first wife, the couple is not yet officially divorced.
match_headline: Tory Burch and Pierre-Yves Roussel Become Fashion’s Newest Power Couple

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Tuesday about first-round tennis matches at the Australian Open misidentified the home country of Timea Bacsinszky, the No. 11 seed who defeated Katerina Siniakova. She is from Switzerland, not Sweden.
match_headline: Zhang Shuai Breaks Through Against Simona Halep, a No. 2 Seed

text: An article on Saturday about the Ultimate Fighting Championship match between Dominick Cruz and T. J. Dillashaw misstated the day of the match. It was on Sunday, not Saturday. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Wrestlers Find Well-Worn Path to U.F.C. Title Bout

text: An article on Wednesday about the Norwegian producer and D.J. Kygo misidentified the nationality of another producer, Thomas Jack. Mr. Jack is Australian, not Norwegian.
match_headline: Kygo Delivers Dance Beats, With a Side Order of Pan Flute

text: An obituary on Thursday about the clothier Wilkes Bashford misspelled the given name of his father. He was Byaly Bashford, not Bialy.
match_headline: Wilkes Bashford, Clothier to Affluent San Franciscans, Dies at 82

text: An article on Friday about the killing of Dr. Robin Goldman of Scarsdale, N.Y., misspelled the given name of one of her daughters in some copies. She is Alyssa, not Elissa.
match_headline: Husband of Scarsdale Doctor Is Charged in Her Fatal Stabbing

text: An article on Thursday about efforts by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences to make its Oscar nominees more diverse misspelled the surname of an actor featured in “The Blind Side,” a film about a homeless black teenager that was nominated for best picture in 2010. He is Quinton Aaron, not Aron.
match_headline: Film Academy, Under Fire, Is Expected to Take Steps to Improve Oscar Diversity

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Thursday about the “Made in L. A.” biennial at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles later this year omitted the given name of an artist chosen for the show. He is Sterling Ruby.
match_headline: Courses for a New Year

text: Because of an editing error, schedule information on Friday with an art review of the Winter Antiques Show, at the Park Avenue Armory in Manhattan, misstated the website and telephone number for more information. The website is winterantiquesshow.com , not armoryonpark.org , and the telephone number is 718-292-7392.
match_headline: Winter Antiques Show Offers a Collection of Recent and Rare Works

text: An article on Wednesday about the Barcelona Sporting Club soccer team in Ecuador misspelled, in two instances, the name of a Brazilian soccer player who played for F.C. Barcelona in Spain and is expected to play in an exhibition for Barcelona Sporting Club. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Ronaldinho, not Ronaldhino.
match_headline: Sharing a Name With Barcelona, if Not Its Fortunes

text: An article on Tuesday about scientists who are undertaking a study of ancient bones and DNA to try to determine where and when dogs first appeared misspelled the given name of a scientist involved in the project and the city in France where she works. She is Allowen Evin, not Allowyn, and she is with the National Center for Scientific Research in Montpellier, not Montpelier.
match_headline: The Big Search to Find Out Where Dogs Come From

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about an indictment of two abortion opponents by a Houston grand jury misstated the age of David R. Daleiden, one of those indicted. He is 27, not 26.
match_headline: 2 Abortion Foes Behind Planned Parenthood Videos Are Indicted

text: An article on Thursday about problems in Detroit public schools misidentified the university where Camille Wilson, who commented on the problems, is an associate professor. It is the University of Michigan, not Wayne State University.
match_headline: Crumbling, Destitute Schools Threaten Detroit’s Recovery

text: A report in the World Briefing column on Jan. 14 about an avalanche in the French Alps that killed two students among a group from Lyon and a Ukrainian skier referred incorrectly to the students and misstated the number of students and school supervisors who were swept away by the avalanche. The students were in high school, not middle school, and the avalanche struck 10 students, killing two, and one supervisor, not 19 students and three supervisors.
match_headline: Avalanche in French Alps Leaves at Least 3 Dead

text: An article on Jan. 1 about a step toward a possible treatment for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which is caused by defects in a gene that encodes a protein called dystrophin, misstated which exon, or section of the gene, was targeted for editing in the new research. It is the 23rd exon, not the 21st.
match_headline: Gene Editing Offers Hope for Treating Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, Studies Find

text: An article on Monday about efforts in the Washington region to dig out from the weekend blizzard misidentified, in some editions, a restaurant worker who was the only person who showed up for work at a lunch spot near the White House. She is Lila Hertz, not Lisa Rein.
match_headline: Return to Normalcy Will Be Halting as Mid-Atlantic Starts Digging Out

text: An article in some copies on Thursday about the pending closing of the Ziegfeld Theater in Midtown Manhattan misstated the address of the theater. It is at 141 West 54th Street, not 1345 Avenue of the Americas at West 54th Street. (The latter was the address of the original Ziegfeld Theater, which was built in 1927 and was torn down in 1966.)
match_headline: Ziegfeld Theater in Midtown Is Closing to Become a Ballroom

text: An article on Saturday about the conductor and composer Esa-Pekka Salonen, who said he was too busy to consider becoming the next music director of the New York Philharmonic, misstated the call letters of the Chicago radio station whose website posted an interview with him in May in which he said he was happy with his life and career. The station is WFMT, not WMFT.
match_headline: Salonen Makes Clear He Won’t Lead New York Philharmonic

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the British adventurer Henry Worsley, who died after abandoning a solo trek across Antarctica, misstated, in some editions, the name of one of the explorers he commemorated on a trip to Antarctica in 2011. He was Robert Falcon Scott, not Robert Scott Falcon. The obituary also misstated, in some copies, the date of Mr. Worsley’s arrival at the South Pole on his last expedition and quoted incorrectly a description of the Antarctic snow from his audio diary. He reached the pole on Jan. 2, not Jan. 3, and he said the surface was “firm,” not “calm.”
match_headline: Henry Worsley, a British Adventurer Trying to Cross Antarctica, Dies at 55

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Marvin Minsky, a pioneer in artificial intelligence, misstated the year he received the Turing Award, computer science’s highest prize. It was 1969, not 1970.
match_headline: Marvin Minsky, Pioneer in Artificial Intelligence, Dies at 88

text: A review last Wednesday about La Chine restaurant, in the Waldorf Astoria, misstated the price of a whole duck. It is $70, not $90.
match_headline: Imagination Worth the Added Price at Midtown’s La Chine

text: An article on Wednesday about redesigning the $10 bill and putting a woman’s portrait on the front referred incorrectly to a proposal from Women On 20s — a group that supports putting a woman’s portrait on the front of the $20 bill — to keep Alexander Hamilton’s portrait on the $10 bill with a vignette of suffragists on the back. The group wants his portrait to appear on the front of the $10 bill alongside a portrait of a woman, not alone.
match_headline: A Woman on the $10 Bill, and Everyone Has 2 Cents to Put In

text: An article on Wednesday about new guidelines suggesting testing for the Zika virus in some newborns misstated the number of people who will develop symptoms if they are infected with the Zika virus. It is one out of five, not four out of five.
match_headline: Zika Testing Is Urged for Some Newborns

text: An article on Friday about a school shooting in northern Saskatchewan that killed four people misstated, in some editions, the number of people killed in Canada’s deadliest school shooting, at École Polytechnique, an engineering school in Montreal, in 1989. Fourteen students were killed, not 13.
match_headline: Four Killed in Saskatchewan School Shooting

text: An article on Monday about New England quarterback Tom Brady’s struggles in Sunday’s A.F.C. championship game misstated, in some copies, the length of the Patriots’ longest completion of the day. It was 40 yards to tight end Rob Gronkowski, not 31.
match_headline: Broncos’ Defense Keeps Patriots Off Rhythm

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Rangers’ 6-3 victory over the Buffalo Sabres misstated, in some copies, the number of points separating the Rangers from the Pittsburgh Penguins in the N.H.L.’s Eastern Conference standings after the game. The Rangers were 6 points ahead of Pittsburgh, not 5.
match_headline: Rangers Savor Win and a Week to Relax

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with an article about television and film actors who are voicing characters in video games misidentified the Batman game shown. It is Batman: Arkham City, not Batman: Arkham Asylum.
match_headline: Familiar Faces Lend Star Power to Video Game Voices

text: A report in the Observatory column on Tuesday about a 6,000-year-old tomb in Northern Spain referred incorrectly to bodies that were found in the upper layers of the burial site. While the remains there were manipulated and redistributed, there was no sign of violence or trauma or evidence that the individuals “encountered a more sinister demise” than the bodies closer to the bottom.
match_headline: In an Ancient Tomb, a Hierarchy of the Dead

text: Because of an editing error, the attribution for the Quotation of the Day on Tuesday, taken from a front-page article about El Salvador’s advice to women not to get pregnant until 2018 because of a mosquito-borne virus linked to brain damage in infants, misstated the name of the virus. As the article correctly noted, it is Zika, not Vika.
match_headline: Quotation of the Day

text: An article last Thursday about the return to elegance in Italian fashion misstated Bonnie Clearwater’s association with “Bellissima: Italy and High Fashion 1945-1968,” which opens at the NSU Art Museum next month. Although she is the chief curator of the museum, she is not the curator of this specific exhibition.
match_headline: For Italian Men, a Return to Elegance

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a demand by Haitian protesters that their president resign misstated, at one point, the day of the scheduled presidential runoff election, which was postponed. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it had been scheduled for this past Sunday, not last Friday.
match_headline: Protesters in Haiti Demand That President Quit

text: A headline on Thursday with an article about SunEdison’s agreeing to give Greenlight Capital, a hedge fund run by David Einhorn, a seat on its board misidentified the person who will hold that seat. Claire Gogel, a former Greenlight executive, will join the board — not Mr. Einhorn himself.
match_headline: Under Pressure, SunEdison Gives David Einhorn’s Fund a Board Seat

text: An article on Monday about investors’ withdrawing money from emerging-market funds misidentified the MFS investment management fund that had investor outflows of $1.4 billion last year. It is the Emerging Markets Debt fund, not a local currency fund.
match_headline: A Struggle to Quell Investor Fears Over Unsettled Emerging Markets

text: A report in the Observatory column on Tuesday about the number and type of bugs found in a typical home misstated the size of a gall midge, a type of fly. They are typically four-one hundredths of an inch long, not four-tenths of an inch.
match_headline: The Bugs Sharing Your Home (Get Out a Calculator)

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the glass artist Marvin Lipofsky misidentified the artist who set up glass programs at the University of California, Berkeley, and the California College of Arts and Crafts in Oakland. It was Mr. Lipofsky — not Harvey K. Littleton, with whom he had studied.
match_headline: Marvin Lipofsky, Ceramist Who Elevated Blown Glass to Fine Art, Dies at 77

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about Concepcion Picciotto, who maintained a peace vigil near the White House for more than 30 years, misstated plans being made after her death. A director of a women’s shelter said she expected Ms. Picciotto’s friends to make sure that she was not buried in a pauper’s grave, not that she was buried in one.
match_headline: Concepcion Picciotto, Who Kept Vigil by White House for Three Decades, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about divisions in Europe over the taxing of multinational corporations misidentified the recipients of written comments about European tax policies from Neal Todd, an international tax expert. They were sent to the news media, not to Mr. Todd’s clients.
match_headline: Taxing Google and Other U.S. Giants Is Dividing Europe

text: An obituary in some editions on Friday about Paul Kantner, a founding member of the rock band Jefferson Airplane, misstated when the band is to receive a Lifetime Achievement Grammy Award. It is Feb. 15, not “in the spring.” The obituary also referred incorrectly to the band Hot Tuna. It was formed by two former members of Jefferson Airplane, Jorma Kaukonen and Jack Casady, who are currently the only former members in the band; it is not “composed of several former members of Jefferson Airplane.”
match_headline: Paul Kantner, a Founder of Jefferson Airplane, Dies at 74

text: An article last Sunday about the United States’ reliance on Saudi Arabia to help financially support the Syrian rebels referred incorrectly to the beheading of a Shiite cleric, Sheikh Nimr al-Nimr. While the execution was not kept secret, it was not a public execution.
match_headline: U.S. Relies Heavily on Saudi Money to Support Syrian Rebels

text: An article last Sunday about the filing of terrorism charges in Bangladesh against 14 Bangladeshi construction workers deported from Singapore misstated the timing of their deportation. It was in December, not the middle of January.
match_headline: Terrorism Charges in Bangladesh for 14 Men Deported From Singapore

text: An article last Sunday about Arthur Miller’s life in Brooklyn referred incorrectly to Norman Mailer’s parents’ connection to 102 Pierrepont Street, where Mr. Miller moved in 1944. They rented an apartment there; they did not own the building.
match_headline: Arthur Miller’s Brooklyn

text: An article last Sunday about San Antonio Spurs center Boban Marjanovic misstated, in some copies, the record of the Golden State Warriors, the Spurs’ Western Conference rival, at the start of the season. The Warriors started the season 24-0, not 28-0.
match_headline: Boban Marjanovic Is Entering Fans’ Hearts, if Not the Spurs’ Lineup

text: A review in some editions last Sunday about “The Body of an American,” at Hartford Stage, misspelled the surname of the director of the production at one point. As the review correctly noted elsewhere, she is Jo Bonney, not Boney.
match_headline: Review: At Hartford Stage, Friendship Forged Through Somalia War

text: A picture caption in some editions last Sunday with the New York Panorama photograph misstated the name of the venue where the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Day Chess Tournament was held. The picture, of students playing matches, was taken at Mott Hall 2 in Manhattan, not at Moot Hall. The caption also misidentified the location of the matches. While students who took part were from all five boroughs of New York City, the matches were played only at locations in Manhattan.
match_headline: How New York's Shelters Keep Animals Alive

text: An article on Jan. 17 about the sociologist Alice Goffman misstated the academic affiliation of the sociologist Jamie Fader. She is at Temple University, not SUNY Albany.
match_headline: The Trials of Alice Goffman

text: An article last Sunday about the concept of purity in the singing of some early-music ensembles misstated the nationality of the conductor and Baroque-music specialist William Christie, who commented on vocal practices. He holds American and French dual citizenship; he is not English.
match_headline: Early-Music Ensembles: Praised as Pure, but Seeking More

text: An article last Sunday about the revival of “The X-Files” misstated the number of episodes David Duchovny appeared in during the original show’s final season. He was in a single episode, the series finale, not in half of the episodes that season.
match_headline: ‘The X-Files’: David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson Return to the Paranormal Beat

text: A subheading on Jan. 17 with a review of “The Love of Strangers: What Six Muslim Students Learned in Jane Austen’s London,” by Nile Green, misstated the century in which the students whose experiences the book describes studied in England. It was the 19th century, not the 18th.
ref_headline: The Love of Strangers: What Six Muslim Students Learned in Jane Austen’s London,
match_headline: ‘The Love of Strangers,’ by Nile Green

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Julia Groeblacher and Daniel Castillo misspelled the name of the location in Northern Virginia where the bride attended language training classes. It is an area known as Rosslyn, Va., not Rosyln.
match_headline: Julia Groeblacher and Daniel Castillo: They’ll Always Have Baghdad

text: A picture caption on Jan. 17 with an obituary about the racecar driver Maria Teresa de Filippis, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the car she was shown driving. It is a Stanguellini, not a Maserati.
match_headline: Maria Teresa de Filippis, Pioneer of Auto Racing, Dies at 89

text: An article on Saturday about the killing of Deven Black, 62, in a Harlem shelter misidentified the two people shown in a picture that Mr. Black had posted on Facebook. It was Mr. Black and his mother, not his wife and son. The article also misspelled, in some editions, the name of the store that employed Anthony White, the man accused of killing Mr. Black. It is J.C. Penney, not J.C. Penney’s.
match_headline: 2 Lives Collide in Fatal Night at a Harlem Shelter

text: An article on Jan. 4 about the basic differences between Shia and Sunni Islam referred incorrectly to the Prophet Muhammad’s succession. It is a matter of dispute; all Muslims do not agree that he died without appointing a successor. (Although Sunnis believe this, Shiites believe that he chose Ali, his cousin and son-in-law.) And because of an editing error, the article referred incorrectly to Ali at one point. The Sunnis believe that he and the three caliphs before him were all rightly guided and therefore entitled to succeed the prophet; Ali is not excluded from this list.
match_headline: How Do Sunni and Shia Islam Differ?

text: An article on Monday about Microsoft’s testing of underwater data centers misstated the title of Norman Whitaker, Microsoft’s managing director for special projects, when he was at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. He was a former deputy director of the agency’s Information Innovation Office; he was not the former deputy director of Darpa.
match_headline: Microsoft Plumbs Ocean’s Depths to Test Underwater Data Center

text: An article on Friday about the possibility that Volkswagen may need to buy back some diesel models sold in the United States because they cannot be modified to meet American emission standards misidentified a VW diesel sport utility vehicle sold in the United States. It is the Touareg, not the Tiguan.
match_headline: Volkswagen May Buy Back Diesel Cars It Can’t Fix

text: An article on Jan. 21 about John Scott, who was voted into the N.H.L. All-Star Game, then traded and demoted to the minor leagues, referred incorrectly to the twins his wife is expecting. They will be the couple’s third and fourth children, not their first. (They have two daughters.)
match_headline: Misnomer on Skates: John Scott, N.H.L. All-Star, Is Neither in N.H.L. Nor a Star

text: A report in the N.F.L. roundup on Saturday about a decision by the Chargers to stay in San Diego for the 2016 season misstated the given name of a San Diego County supervisor. He is Ron Roberts, not Dave.
match_headline: Chargers Will Play at Least One More Season in San Diego

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with an article about the Tampa Bay Lightning’s rebounding from a slow start to the N.H.L. season misstated, in some editions, the point at which the photograph of Lightning players was taken. It was during the first period of a 1-0 victory over the Maple Leafs last Wednesday, not after the game.
match_headline: Talking Out Their Problems, the Lightning Enter the Playoff Conversation

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Thursday about the Broadway debut of Cate Blanchett next season misstated the number of times she has been nominated for an Academy Award. It is seven, not six.
match_headline: Cate Blanchett to Make Broadway Debut in Play Directed by John Crowley

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about microcephaly, a condition in which babies are born with abnormally small heads, referred imprecisely to the number of cases in Brazil. While there have been more than 4,000 suspected cases since October, officials have not yet confirmed them so it is still unknown if “there are thousands of these children in Brazil.”
ref_headline: there are thousands of these children in Brazil.
match_headline: Microcephaly, Spotlighted by Zika Virus, Has Long Afflicted and Mystified

text: An article on Tuesday about the Zika virus and the declaration of an international public health emergency by the World Health Organization omitted part of the name of the institution at George Washington University where Dr. Ron Waldman is a professor. It is the Milken Institute School of Public Health, not the Milken School of Public Health.
match_headline: Zika Virus a Global Health Emergency, W.H.O. Says

text: An article on Tuesday about the Grammy Fund for Music Creators, a lobbying organization created by the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, misspelled the first reference to the surname of an official at the fund. As the article correctly noted in later references, he is Daryl P. Friedman, not Freidman. The article also erroneously included a performing-rights group among organizations that have political action committees. While Ascap has one, BMI does not. It dissolved its PAC in 2010.
match_headline: Organization Behind Grammys to Create Lobbying Group

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the increase in diagnosed concussions in the 2015 N.F.L. season misstated, in some copies, the percentage increase of concussions across preseason and regular-season games and practices from 2014. It was 31.6 percent, not 3.16 percent.
match_headline: Diagnoses of Concussions Increase by Nearly a Third Over Last Season

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the soprano Denise Duval misstated the year she made her professional debut, in “Cavalleria Rusticana” with the Bordeaux Opera, and the role she sang. It was in 1942, not 1943, and the role was Santuzza, not Lola.
match_headline: Denise Duval, French Soprano and Poulenc Interpreter, Dies at 94

text: An article on Wednesday about the stabbing death of a 13-year-old Virginia girl, Nicole Madison Lovell, misstated, in some editions, the given name of her youth pastor, who read part of a statement from Nicole’s mother. He is Josh Blankenship, not Joel.
match_headline: Virginia Girl Probably Died the Day She Vanished, Officials Say

text: An article on Wednesday about testimony at the manslaughter trial of Officer Peter Liang referred incorrectly in some editions to information provided by Officer Shaun Landau, Mr. Liang’s partner. Some parts of Officer Landau’s account, which was read in court, came from a police interview, not from grand jury testimony.
match_headline: Gun Tests and Tears at Officer Peter Liang’s Trial in Killing

text: An article on Wednesday about fabricated quotations in some articles written by a reporter for the news website The Intercept misstated the status of the case against Dylann Roof on charges of murdering nine people in a Charleston, S.C., church. He is awaiting trial; he has not been convicted.
match_headline: The Intercept Says Reporter Falsified Quotations

text: An obituary on Monday about the basketball player Kenny Sailors erroneously included one honor among those he received for his service with the Marines. He did not receive a Bronze Star.
match_headline: Kenny Sailors, a Pioneer of the Jump Shot, Dies at 95

text: An article on Thursday about reactions to the Zika virus by blood banks in the United States, using information from the American Red Cross, misstated the agency’s approach to potential blood donors who have traveled to regions affected by the virus. The American Red Cross is providing an information sheet about a 28-day waiting period for such travelers as recommended by the AABB, the group that represents most blood donation groups in the United States. The Red Cross is not quizzing prospective donors about recent travel. Because of the error, the headline overstated the blood banks’ new approach in saying they “scrutinize” travelers.
match_headline: Blood Banks Use Caution With Travelers From Zika Zones

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Darnell Earley, the former emergency manager of Flint, Mich., misidentified the individual who had declined to testify about Flint’s problems before a House committee. It was Mr. Earley — not his lawyer, A. Scott Bolden — who did not appear.
match_headline: Flint’s Former Manager Resigns as Head of Detroit Schools

text: An article on Thursday about a judge’s decision to allow a sexual assault case against Bill Cosby to proceed misstated the year when Andrea Constand, the woman he is charged with assaulting, and her mother contacted Mr. Cosby about the 2004 incident at his home. Ms. Constand’s lawyers have said the contact was in 2005, not in 2015.
match_headline: Judge Allows Bill Cosby Sexual Assault Case to Go Forward

text: An article on Thursday about the first issue of the redesigned Playboy magazine misstated when full-frontal nudity made its first appearance in Playboy. The first instance was in 1972; it was not part of the brand’s identity since its beginning in 1953.
match_headline: Playboy Puts On (Some) Clothes for Newly Redesigned Issue

text: An article on Thursday about Richard Anderson’s pending retirement in May as chief executive of Delta Air Lines misstated his employment circumstances in some copies. He is currently employed as chief executive without a contract; therefore, there is no contract “expiring soon.”
match_headline: Richard Anderson, Delta Chief Who Led Airline’s Rebound, Will Retire

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about General Motors’ annual earnings misidentified the Chevrolet model that was shown being unveiled at the event. It is a Chevrolet Bolt, not the company’s Volt model.
match_headline: G.M. Posts Record Profit of $9.7 Billion for 2015

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a television review of “Madoff” on ABC, using information from the network, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of Richard Dreyfuss, was taken by Eric Liebowitz — not by Eva Kaminsky, an actress in the show.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Madoff,’ What He Was Thinking

text: An article on Jan. 27 about an order by the Obama administration that state and local law enforcement agencies return federal surplus military equipment erroneously included two items on a list of equipment being sent back. Camouflage clothing and .50-caliber machine guns are not among the recalled items. (Both of those items are on a new list of prohibited material.)
match_headline: Some Officers Bristle at Recall of Military Equipment

text: An article on Wednesday about Boston Celtics point guard Isaiah Thomas, the lowest-drafted player to make an All-Star team since 1989, misstated the change in the N.B.A. draft that year. The draft contracted to two rounds; it did not expand to two rounds.
match_headline: Diminutive All-Star Isaiah Thomas Finds Shoulders to Stand On

text: An article in some editions on Jan. 28 about Serena Williams’s victory over Agnieszka Radwanska in the semifinals of the Australian Open misstated Williams’s age when she won her first Tier 1 title in 1999. She was 17, not 16.
match_headline: Serena Williams Routs Radwanska and Nears a 22nd Major Title

text: A listing of information on Page 17 this weekend with an article about racial issues on campus gives an outdated amount that Brown University has said it will spend on diversity initiatives. After the section had gone to press, the university increased its estimate to $165 million from $100 million.
match_headline: Student Demands: Who’s Resigned, What’s Renamed

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the N.B.A. roundup in some editions last Sunday about the Nets’ 105-103 loss to the New Orleans Pelicans misidentified the site of the game. It was at Smoothie King Center in New Orleans, not at the Barclays Center in Brooklyn.
match_headline: Barclays Center in Brooklyn Becomes a Classroom

text: Because of an editing error, a theater review in some editions last Sunday about a production of August Wilson’s “The Piano Lesson” at the McCarter Theater Center in Princeton, N.J., misidentified one of the two relatives of the character Berniece for whom a piano was traded. It was Berniece’s great-grandmother and grandfather, not her great-grandfather.
match_headline: In ‘The Piano Lesson,’ a Family Fight Over an Heirloom Rooted in Slavery

text: An obituary last Sunday about the Pakistani diplomat Sahabzada Yaqub Khan misidentified the United Nations secretary general who appointed him special representative for Western Sahara. The appointment was made by Boutros Boutros-Ghali, not by Javier Pérez de Cuéllar.
match_headline: Sahabzada Yaqub Khan, Pakistani Diplomat, Dies at 95

text: An article on Jan. 31 about the derailment of Amtrak 188 referred incorrectly to the ownership of the Amtrak network. Amtrak operates on more than 21,300 miles of routes, but does not own that entire network. The article also referred incorrectly to the length of Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor. It is 456 miles, not 225 miles.
match_headline: The Wreck of Amtrak 188

text: A headline last Sunday with an article about a revival of “Buried Child” by Sam Shepard referred incorrectly to the production. It is Off Broadway, by the New Group at the Pershing Square Signature Center. It is not a return to Broadway by Mr. Shepard.
match_headline: Sam Shepard Takes Stock of ‘Buried Child’ and the Writer’s Life

text: An article last Sunday about an exhibition by the journalist and filmmaker Laura Poitras at the Whitney Museum of American Art misspelled the surname of a hacker and computer-security expert who spoke at a program she organized at a Whitney Biennial. He is Jacob Appelbaum, not Applebaum.
match_headline: Laura Poitras Prepares ‘Astro Noise’ for the Whitney Museum

text: A review on Jan. 24 about “Russell Kirk: American Conservative,” a biography by Bradley J. Birzer, referred incorrectly to the aspect of America’s World War II internment of people of Japanese ancestry that particularly outraged Kirk. It was the internment of American citizens of Japanese ancestry, not the internment of Japanese citizens. (Though many Japanese citizens were indeed interned, a majority of the internees were American citizens.)
match_headline: ‘Russell Kirk: American Conservative,’ by Bradley J. Birzer

text: Because of an editing error, a cover article last Sunday about three Brooklyn properties offered for sale by the Jehovah’s Witnesses misstated the address of one of them, the Witnesses’ headquarters. As the caption correctly noted, it is 25-30 Columbia Heights — not 124 Columbia Heights, a residential building owned by the Witnesses and also for sale.
match_headline: Jehovah’s Witnesses’ Brooklyn Headquarters for Sale

text: An article on Jan. 10 about 52 places to go in 2016 misspelled part of the name of a winemaker organization in the Mosel area of Germany. It is the Bauernund Winzerverband Rheinland-Nassau, not Bauern und Winzerverbandes Rheinland-Nassau.
match_headline: How We Picked the 52 Places to Go in 2016

text: An article last Sunday about skiing in Mad River Glen, Vt., misidentified a position formerly held by Winthrop H. Smith Jr., the leader of a group that bought Sugarbush, a nearby resort. Mr. Smith was a chairman of Merrill Lynch International, not a chief executive of Merrill Lynch.
match_headline: In Vermont, the Lure of Skiing in the Mad River Valley

text: A report on Jan. 24 about the marriage of Elise Chang and Alastair Kusack referred incorrectly to one of the groom’s roles at Kammetal, a metal fabrication firm in Brooklyn. While he is a co-owner, he is not a co-founder. (His brother Sam Kusack is the sole founder.)
match_headline: Elise Chang, Alastair Kusack

text: An article on Jan. 11 about starvation in Madaya, a Syrian city controlled by rebels and besieged by government forces, referred imprecisely to the financing of the Syria Campaign, a group pushing for a no-fly zone over Syria. It comes chiefly from a private British foundation, not from Western governments.
match_headline: Starving Syrians in Madaya Are Denied Aid Amid Political Jockeying

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Jan. 16 about fears that the massacre of 17 civilians on a commercial street in Baghdad presaged a return to the guerrilla violence that plagued the city years ago referred incorrectly to the Islamic State’s connection to an attack earlier the same week, in Istanbul. Although the Turkish authorities say the Islamic State was behind the attack, the group itself did not claim responsibility for it.
match_headline: Gains Against ISIS Bring More Deaths Elsewhere in Iraq

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Monday about a Super Bowl reunion held at a hotel in West Point, N.Y., for Americans held hostage in Iran and their families 35 years after they watched another Super Bowl there just after being freed, misstated the given name of one of the hostages, who died in 1985 and whose daughter attended in his honor. He was William Keough, not Walter.
match_headline: A Super Bowl Reunion 35 Years After Iran Hostages’ American Homecoming

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Saturday about how the shooting of two police officers in the Bronx underscored the dangers of patrolling in public housing complexes misstated, in some copies, the number of police officers who were patrolling a stairwell on Thursday night. It was four, not two.
match_headline: Shootings in Public Housing Project Highlight Risks of Stairwell Patrols

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the Knicks’ 91-85 loss to the Memphis Grizzlies misspelled the given name of the Knicks player who hit a 3-pointer with 37.6 seconds left to cut the Knicks’ deficit to 2. He is Arron Afflalo, not Aaron. The article also misidentified, in some copies, the team the Knicks will face on Tuesday. It is the Washington Wizards, not the Boston Celtics.
match_headline: Without Carmelo Anthony, Knicks Put Up a Valiant Fight, Then Fade

text: An obituary on Saturday about the astronaut Edgar D. Mitchell misstated how far a golf ball hit on the moon by Capt. Alan B. Shepard Jr., his fellow Apollo 14 astronaut, was presumed to have gone. It was more than 800 yards, not more than 800 feet.
match_headline: Edgar D. Mitchell, Sixth Moonwalking Astronaut, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Sunday about the federal judge Miriam Goldman Cedarbaum, using information from her family, misstated her birthplace. She was born in Manhattan — not in Brooklyn, where she grew up.
match_headline: Miriam Cedarbaum, U.S. Judge, Dies at 86; Sentenced Martha Stewart

text: An obituary on Monday about the singer and songwriter Dan Hicks misstated the name of the college he attended in the late 1950s and early 1960s. At the time it was San Francisco State College — not San Francisco State University, the name it adopted in 1974.
match_headline: Dan Hicks, of the Hot Licks, Dies at 74; Countered the ’60s Sound

text: An obituary on Monday about the socialite and women’s rights advocate Robin Chandler Duke referred incorrectly to WCAU, the Philadelphia television station where she once worked. Although it is now an NBC station, it was a CBS affiliate at the time.
match_headline: Robin Chandler Duke, Philanthropist Who Championed Women’s Rights, Dies at 92

text: An article on Jan. 10 about the barriers that hamper the international fight against the illegal trafficking of antiquities, a crime that reached new heights as the Islamic State terrorist group plundered ancient sites in Syria and Iraq, misstated the year that the group declared its caliphate. It was 2014, not 2013.
match_headline: ‘Broken System’ Allows ISIS to Profit From Looted Antiquities

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the former New York Times reporter Arnold H. Lubasch misstated the outcome of a suit brought by Ariel Sharon against Time magazine, which Mr. Lubasch helped cover. Time was cleared of libeling Mr. Sharon in that case; the case was not settled out of court. (Another libel action, related to the same Time article and filed in Israel, was settled out of court.)
match_headline: Arnold Lubasch, Who Covered Crime for The Times, Dies at 83

text: An article on Thursday about how the Supreme Court’s decision to halt the carrying out of President Obama’s climate change regulations could weaken or even imperil the international global warming accord known as the Paris Agreement misidentified the court that would hear oral arguments in June on the regulations. It is the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, not a Federal District Court.
match_headline: Supreme Court’s Blow to Emissions Efforts May Imperil Paris Climate Accord

text: An article on Thursday about the conviction of Salvatore Perrone in the murders of three Brooklyn shopkeepers misidentified, in one instance, the weapon used in the killings. As stated elsewhere in the article, it was a .22-caliber rifle, not a shotgun.
match_headline: Man Convicted of Killing 3 Brooklyn Merchants in 2012

text: An article on Wednesday about Viacom’s quarterly earnings misspelled the given name of the author of “No Exit,” whose play was used as the title of an analyst’s research note. He is Jean-Paul Sartre, not Jen-Paul.
match_headline: Viacom Chief Is Defensive on Its Weak Earnings

text: An article on Wednesday about goaltender Martin Brodeur’s number retirement ceremony with the Devils misstated, in some copies, the number of regular-season victories he amassed in his career. It was 691, not 369.
match_headline: Martin Brodeur’s No. 30 Is Raised to Rafters as Devils Honor 3-Time Cup Champion

text: Because of an editing error, a headline with the men’s college basketball roundup in some editions on Wednesday misidentified the team that fell to Purdue. As the article correctly noted, it was Michigan State, not Michigan.
match_headline: Duke’s Absence From the Top 25 Is Likely to Be Brief

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the ballerina Violette Verdy misstated her age when she acted in the movie released in the United States as “Dream Ballerina.” She was 16, not 17.
match_headline: Violette Verdy, a ‘Theatrical’ Star of Balanchine’s City Ballet, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Thursday about the composer Leslie Bassett misidentified the orchestra that recorded his “Variations for Orchestra.” It was the Radio Zurich Symphony Orchestra under Jonathan Sternberg, not the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra under Sergiu Comissiona.
match_headline: Leslie Bassett, Pulitzer Prize-Winning Composer, Dies at 93

text: An article in some editions last Sunday that featured the Basilica of St. Patrick’s Old Cathedral in Manhattan, where a scene from “The Godfather” takes place, misstated the number of the Commandment that prohibits killing. While in certain other denominations it is the Sixth Commandment, in the Catholic Church it is the Fifth.
match_headline: An Old Cathedral and a Daily Aperitivo

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about “maker spaces” where students can tinker misstated the location of Rutgers University’s Livingston campus, where such a space is. It is in Piscataway, N.J., not Livingston.
match_headline: Wood Shop Enters the Age of High-Tech

text: An article on Feb. 7 about the editor Chris Jackson referred incorrectly to his college education. He attended Columbia University but did not graduate.
match_headline: How Chris Jackson Is Building a Black Literary Movement

text: An article on Jan. 24 about Syrian refugees and United States policy referred incorrectly to the type of visa with which one of the San Bernardino attackers legally entered the United States. It was a K-1 fiancée visa; the attacker did not enter through the visa-waiver program.
match_headline: Why Is It So Difficult for Syrian Refugees to Get Into the U.S.?

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the use of the assassination of John F. Kennedy as a plot element in television, books and film misidentified the actor shown in an episode of “The X-Files.” He is Chris Owens as the Smoking Man, not Morgan Weisser, who played Lee Harvey Oswald in that episode.
match_headline: In Movies, Books and TV, a Rabbit Hole of Kennedy Conspiracies

text: An article last Sunday about the artists Peter Fischli and David Weiss, whose work is the subject of a retrospective exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum in New York, misidentified the person described at the end of the article as walking through the installation of the exhibition and commenting on it. He is Mr. Fischli, not Mr. Weiss. As the article noted, Mr. Weiss died in 2012.
match_headline: Fischli and Weiss: Anarchy at the Guggenheim

text: An article last Sunday about the City Center Encores! revival of the 1940 musical “Cabin in the Sky,” which is choreographed by Camille A. Brown, misstated Ms. Brown’s history with musical-theater works. She has choreographed others; “Cabin in the Sky” is not her first.
match_headline: ‘Cabin in the Sky’: Translating a Dated Body Language

text: An article last Sunday about skiing in the Jizera Mountains of Central Europe misstated the point in 1938 at which Hitler annexed the German-speaking areas of Czechoslovakia. It was in the fall, not in the spring.
match_headline: Bohemia’s Secret Spot for Cross-Country Skiing

text: An article last Sunday about the resurgence of cover-cropping as an agricultural practice described incorrectly the effects of so-called no-till farming, in which farmers plant into the residue of a previous crop rather than tilling it in. It can reduce soil erosion; it does not increase it.
match_headline: Cover Crops, a Farming Revolution With Deep Roots in the Past

text: An article on Thursday about a Broadway production of an adaptation of Harper Lee’s novel “To Kill a Mockingbird,” produced by Scott Rudin and written by Aaron Sorkin, misspelled the given name of the play’s director. He is Bartlett Sher, not Barlett.
match_headline: ‘To Kill a Mockingbird’ Is Headed to Broadway

text: A picture with the Transactions column in the Square Feet pages on Wednesday was paired with the wrong property. The photograph should have been with the entry about 102 West 79th Street, a property for lease; it should not have illustrated the entry about 321 Malcolm X Boulevard, which recently sold.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about the Rangers’ 5-4 loss to the Los Angeles Kings misstated, in some copies, Dustin Brown’s role in the goal shown against Rangers goalie Antti Raanta. Brown was celebrating a teammate’s goal; he did not score the goal. Also because of an editing error, the byline misspelled the given name of the reporter in some editions. He is Allan Kreda, not Alan.
match_headline: On the Verge of Victory, the Rangers Let One Slip Away

text: An article last Thursday about the designer Jenny Packham and the celebrities who wear her gowns on the red carpet referred incorrectly to the client list of the stylist Jessica Paster. The actresses Sandra Bullock and Dakota Fanning are former clients of Ms. Paster. She does not currently work with them.
match_headline: Why Can’t Jenny Packham, a Red Carpet Success, Get More Respect?

text: An article last Thursday about a party to publicize a new clothing line from Kylie and Kendall Jenner that was attended by their mother, Kris Jenner, misstated the marital relationship between Ms. Jenner and her first husband, the lawyer Robert Kardashian. The two were divorced by 1995, the year of the O.J. Simpson trial, for which Mr. Kardashian was part of the legal team advising Mr. Simpson and which is the subject of a new TV series. They were not still married then.
match_headline: Kendall and Kylie Jenner Party for Their Fashion Brand

text: An article on Wednesday about an initiative by New York City’s Education Department aimed at maintaining a racial and socioeconomic balance at schools in fast-gentrifying areas included outdated information about Arthur Mattia’s connection to the Children’s School in Brooklyn, one of the seven schools taking part. Mr. Mattia is a former principal, not the current one. (He retired in January.)
match_headline: New York Schools Wonder: How White Is Too White?

text: An article on Thursday about a request by Cyrus R. Vance Jr., the Manhattan district attorney, to recuse himself from a criminal investigation into an allegation that former Gov. Eliot Spitzer assaulted a 26-year-old woman at the Plaza Hotel misstated the year that Mr. Spitzer appointed Mr. Vance to the New York State Commission on Sentencing Reform. It was 2007, not 2009.
match_headline: Manhattan Prosecutor Asks to Be Recused From Spitzer Inquiry

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on Feb. 4 about apps related to space exploration misidentified the dwarf planet visited by the spacecraft Dawn. It is Ceres, not Pluto.
match_headline: An Expanding Universe of Space Apps

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with a music review of the pianist Denes Varjon, at Zankel Hall in Manhattan, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of Mr. Varjon, was taken by Chris Smith, not by Chris Lee.
match_headline: Review: Denes Varjon, a Hungarian Pianist, at Zankel Hall

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Leo Van Munching Jr., whose company imported the Dutch beers Heineken and Amstel Light to the United States, misidentified the act signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1933 that taxed beverages containing no more than 3.2 percent alcohol. It was the Cullen-Harrison Act — not the Beer and Wine Revenue Act, a separate act passed several months later.
match_headline: Leo Van Munching Jr., Empire Builder for Heineken, Dies at 89

text: An editorial on Jan. 31 about the Republican primary race misstated the position of Gov. John Kasich on immigration reform. He supports a path to legalization, not citizenship, for undocumented immigrants.
match_headline: A Chance to Reset the Republican Race

text: An article on Wednesday about taunts and vandalism endured by a mosque in Tucson, Ariz., since University of Arizona students moved next door rendered incorrectly an anti-Muslim message scrawled on a wall at Virginia Tech, another university that has seen instances of Islamophobia. The message read, “I will be here 11/11/2015 to kill all muslims” — not “We will kill all the Muslims.”
ref_headline: I will be here 11/11/2015 to kill all muslims
match_headline: University of Arizona Students Hurl Insults, and Litter, at Mosque in Tucson

text: An article on Tuesday about the United States’ chances at a medal in rugby at the Rio de Janeiro Olympics misidentified one of the countries that is considered more likely to medal than the United States. It is Britain, not England. (England competes separately in other international rugby competitions, but is part of a combined Great Britain team at the Olympics.
match_headline: U.S. Rugby Sevens Team Emerges as Olympic Contender

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with a theater review of “The Humans,” at the Helen Hayes Theater in Manhattan, reversed the identities of two actors. Lauren Klein is in a wheelchair in a doorway, with Arian Moayed behind her.
match_headline: Review: ‘The Humans’ Depicts a Family, and a Country, Under Pressure

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with an art review of “Munch and Expressionism,” at the Neue Galerie in Manhattan, referred incorrectly to the version of Edvard Munch’s painting “Puberty” that was shown. While that version is dated from 1914-16, as noted in the caption, it was not painted “during Munch’s period in Berlin.” (He lived in Germany from 1892 to 1908.)
match_headline: Looking at Edvard Munch, Beyond ‘The Scream’

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about a Vietnam War-era helmet donated to the Intrepid Sea, Air and Space Museum by an aviation machinist who served on the aircraft carrier referred incorrectly to the Growler, a decommissioned submarine next to the Intrepid. It was diesel powered and carried missiles with nuclear warheads; it was not a nuclear submarine.
match_headline: Take Me to the Pilot

text: Because of an editing error, the Neighborhood Joint column in some editions last Sunday, about the 169 Bar in Manhattan’s Chinatown, misspelled the given name of a patron. She is Allison Clark, not Alison.
match_headline: At a Chinatown Bar, Libations Sipped by the Light of Disco Balls

text: A caption for a picture of a fashion model with the editor’s letter last Sunday misstated the brand and the price of the shoes the model was shown wearing. They are Achilles Ion Gabriel boots, not Céline, and they are price on request, not $1,250.
match_headline: Free Spirit

text: An article last Sunday about the dancer Eiko’s project “A Body in Places,” using information from Eiko, misstated the length of her dance solos in the East Village. They will run 40 to 50 minutes, not seven to eight minutes.
match_headline: Eiko Steps Away From One Dance Partner, to Take on Many More

text: An article last Sunday about George Washington’s distillery business misidentified its inheritors. The distillery was left to a granddaughter of Martha Washington’s and her husband, not a daughter and her husband.
match_headline: George Washington, the Whiskey Baron of Mount Vernon

text: An article last Sunday about the design firm Ideo, which is helping Ford Motor Company in multimodal product design, misstated the year Model T’s starting rolling off the assembly line. It was 1913 — not 1908, which was when the car was introduced but before Ford Motor started the integrated moving assembly line.
match_headline: The Commute of the Future? Ford Is Working on It

text: An article last Sunday about a condominium for sale in a mansion overlooking Gramercy Park gave an outdated name for the venture capital firm where the apartment’s owner is a partner. The firm is Benchmark, no longer Benchmark Capital.
match_headline: Half a Townhouse on Gramercy Park

text: A review last Sunday about Paul Kalanithi’s “When Breath Becomes Air” and four other books on death and dying misspelled the surname of the author of a 1991 book on the subject, “Final Exit.” He is Derek Humphry, not Humphrey.
match_headline: ‘The Good Death,’ ‘When Breath Becomes Air’ and More

text: An article last Sunday about the rise of art galleries in downtown Los Angeles misstated the age of the painter Sojourner Truth Parsons. She is 31, not 27.
match_headline: Art Scene Heats Up in Downtown Los Angeles

text: A subheading last Sunday for an essay about narcissism incorrectly described a figure of Greek mythology. Narcissus was a mortal, not a god.
match_headline: Narcissism Is Increasing. So You’re Not So Special.

text: An article on Monday about Zipongo, a start-up aimed at helping companies improve the eating habits of their employees, transposed the numbers in a quotation from Jason Langheier, Zipongo’s founder. He said that Japan spends about $3,200 per person on health care and $3,300 on food, not the reverse. Because of editing errors, the article also misstated the number of IBM employees who can use Zipongo and the year that Google introduced the service. IBM offers the service to tens of thousands of American employees, not to 10,000 workers worldwide, and Google started using Zipongo in 2013, not 2011.
match_headline: Wellness App Aims to Improve Workplace Nutrition

text: An article on Saturday about a study that found eBay customers tend to bid higher for items sold by men rather than women misidentified the journal that published the study. It is Science Advances, not Science.
match_headline: Male Sellers on eBay Have an Edge Over Women, Study Finds

text: An article on Monday about Harper Lee’s correspondence with the cartoonist Berkeley Breathed misstated her age at the time she wrote a letter to him comparing herself to a Charles Dickens character. She was in her early 80s, not her late 70s.
match_headline: When Harper Lee, of ‘Mockingbird,’ Corresponded With Opus the Penguin’s Creator

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with a theater review of “Nice Fish,” at St. Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn, misstated the given name of a co-writer of the play. As the review correctly noted, he is Louis Jenkins, not Simon. Schedule information with the review included an outdated address for the theater. It is at 45 Water Street; it is no longer at 29 Jay Street.
match_headline: Review: ‘Nice Fish,’ Mark Rylance and Louis Jenkins’s Quirky Ice Fishing Tale

text: An article on Saturday about the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s new logo referred imprecisely to the firm Wolff Olins, which designed it. While it has offices in London, as well as in other cities, it is not based there and the project was completed by the New York office.
match_headline: The Met and a New Logo

text: An obituary on Saturday about the author Umberto Eco referred to his novel “Foucault’s Pendulum” incorrectly. Although a pendulum devised by the 19th-century physicist Léon Foucault figures in the plot, Foucault himself is not a character in the novel, which is about an elaborate conspiracy and not about him.
match_headline: Umberto Eco, 84, Best-Selling Academic Who Navigated Two Worlds, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the actor George Gaynes misstated the surname by which his mother, Iya, became known. She was Lady Abdy, not Abny.
match_headline: George Gaynes, a Versatile Character Actor, Dies at 98

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Feb. 16 about the state of the economy in Japan misstated what trends in the value of the yen might encourage Japanese companies to cut costs, wages and investments. That could be a result of a stronger yen, not a weaker one.
match_headline: Rising Yen Adds to Abe’s Challenges as Japan’s Economy Contracts

text: An article on Tuesday about the government’s strategy in seeking to force Apple to help it open a terrorist’s iPhone misspelled the surname of one of Apple’s outside lawyers. He is Theodore B. Olson, not Olsen.
match_headline: Narrow Focus May Aid F.B.I. in Apple Case

text: Because of an editing error, the Sports of The Times column on Jan. 31, about Carolina Panthers quarterback Cam Newton’s confronting racism, misstated the given name of a reporter who covers the Panthers for The Charlotte Observer. He is Jonathan Jones, not Justin.
match_headline: Cam Newton Dances Around End Zones, Not Around Matters of Racism

text: An article on Feb. 16 about transgender patients who are facing health care challenges gave an outdated name for a health system with 21 hospitals in New York City, Long Island and Westchester that has a policy to treat transgender patients like any other patients. It is now Northwell Health, no longer North Shore LIJ Health System.
match_headline: Transgender Patients Face Challenges at the Hospital

text: An obituary on Tuesday about John E. Reinhardt, the first career diplomat to lead the United States Information Agency, misstated the surname of one of his daughters. She is Cecile Fenstermaker, not Fenstermarker.
match_headline: John E. Reinhardt, Ambassador and Head of U.S. Information Agency, Dies at 95

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an obituary about Michael Jaharis, a pharmaceutical industry executive and a philanthropist, misstated the year the photograph of Mr. Jaharis was taken. It was 1982, not 1962.
match_headline: Michael Jaharis, Pharmaceutical Executive and Philanthropist, Dies at 87

text: An article on Jan. 28 about President Obama’s nomination of Lt. Gen. John W. Nicholson Jr. to lead American military operations in Afghanistan misstated the rank of John F. Campbell, whom General Nicholson will succeed. He is a general, not a major general. (The Senate confirmed General Nicholson’s nomination on Feb. 4.)
match_headline: Change of U.S. Command Set in Afghanistan

text: An article on Wednesday about how Lin-Manuel Miranda, the creator of “Hamilton,” used Twitter to urge his followers to help the Drama Book Shop on West 40th Street after a burst pipe destroyed part of the store’s inventory misstated part of the name of a children’s theater company that rents space there. It is Story Pirates, not Story Pirate.
match_headline: Pipe Bursts at Drama Bookstore. Enter ‘Hamilton’ Creator to Drum Up Business.

text: An article on Wednesday about the packs that racers carry during the Arrowhead Ultra 135 misidentified the country of origin of Svetlana Vold, one of the competitors. She is from Belarus — not from “Belarus, Russia.” (They are both countries, of course.)
match_headline: To Carry the Day, Racers Must Fill Their Packs Carefully

text: An article on Feb. 8 about a controversy in China over a racy translation of some poems by Rabindranath Tagore misstated the number of years ago that Tagore died. It is nearly 75, not more than 80. (He died in August 1941.)
match_headline: Tagore Translation Deemed Racy Is Pulled From Stores in China

text: Because of an editing error, a dance review on Thursday about the Mariinsky Ballet, at the Kennedy Center in Washington, misstated the name of the Russian city where Oxana Skorik, a principal dancer in the company, trained. It is Perm, not Perma.
match_headline: Review: Mariinsky Ballet in ‘Raymonda,’ Searching About for a Perfect Suitor

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary by The Associated Press on Wednesday about the cinematographer Douglas Slocombe misspelled the given name of the actor who narrated the World War II documentary “Lights Out in Europe,” in which footage shot by Mr. Slocombe was used. He was Fredric March, not Frederic.
match_headline: Welsh Town Leads a British Revolt Against the Tax System and Corporations

text: An article on Page 40 this weekend about a start-up, Managed by Q, that tries to put cleaning-service workers on a professional path refers incompletely to the legal status of Guillermo Garcia, one of its employees. While he and his parents do not have formal legal status in the United States, he is permitted to work legally and is protected from deportation because of executive action taken by President Obama in 2012.
match_headline: Managed by Q’s ‘Good Jobs’ Gamble

text: A picture caption on Page 4 this weekend with the continuation of the Big City column, about the advertising campaign for Thinx underwear, misspells the name of the company’s chief executive officer. As the article correctly notes, she is Miki Agrawal, not Argawal.
match_headline: The Bohemian Capitalist

text: An article on Jan. 30 about the filing of corruption charges against Natalia Compagnon, the daughter-in-law of President Michelle Bachelet of Chile, misstated, in some editions, the amount of taxes that Ms. Compagnon and her business partner were accused of trying to avoid paying. It was $165,000, not $170 million. The error was repeated in some editions in a subheading with the article.
match_headline: Daughter-in-Law of Chile’s President Faces Corruption Charge

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about a portfolio of courtroom drawings acquired by the Library of Congress described incorrectly the illustration of Bernard Madoff, the former investment manager who spearheaded a multibillion-dollar Ponzi scheme. It shows him leaving a courtroom, but was not drawn at his trial. Mr. Madoff pleaded guilty and was not tried.
match_headline: Library of Congress Acquires Drawings of Courtroom Drama

text: An article on Friday about the “Orchidelirium” show at the New York Botanical Garden, and people who are obsessed with orchids, misstated the name of a British orchid fan who was captured by Marxist guerrillas while hunting for rare orchids on the Colombia-Panama border in 2000. He is Tom Hart Dyke, not Tom Van Dyke.
match_headline: ‘Orchidelirium’ Explodes With Color at New York Botanical Garden

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Feb. 1 about the revelation that four pebbles of moon dust the United States gave to Britain in 1970 had languished in a cupboard in the prime minister’s residence at 10 Downing Street for several years misstated the weight of the lunar dust in ounces. It weighed just over two-thousandths of an ounce, not less than one-thousandth.
match_headline: How Moon Dust Languished in a Downing Street Cupboard

text: An article on Saturday about an event in Queens honoring two retired Marines who were in the Battle of Iwo Jima misstated, in some copies, the name of the unit in which one of the two, Jack Seiferth, a retired Marine sergeant, served. It was the First Battalion, 24th Marines — not the First Battalion, Fourth Marine Division. Because of an editing error, the article misidentified the branch of the military in which Vincenzo Cerbone, the owner of Manducatis, the bar where the event was held, served. It was the Army, not the Marines.
match_headline: Marines Toast Iwo Jima Veterans on Anniversary of Flag Raising

text: An article on Friday about Alex Rodriguez’s first workout of spring training with the Yankees misstated the number of home runs Babe Ruth hit in his career, a number that is within the reach of Rodriguez, who has 687 home runs. Babe Ruth hit 714, not 713.
match_headline: Alex Rodriguez Embraces the Difference a Year Makes

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the New York Rangers star Andy Bathgate ended in midsentence in some copies. The final sentence, referring to Bathgate’s number, should have read, “Bathgate’s flew alongside the No. 9 jersey that had recently been retired to honor Adam Graves, who introduced him as ‘the greatest player ever to wear No. 9 for the New York Rangers.’ ” The obituary also erroneously included a Chicago Blackhawks player on a list of hockey players from Bathgate’s era who, like him, played right wing. Bobby Hull was not one of them; he played left wing.
ref_headline: Bathgate’s flew alongside the No. 9 jersey that had recently been retired to honor Adam Graves, who introduced him as ‘the greatest player ever to wear No. 9 for the New York Rangers.’
match_headline: Andy Bathgate, Standout on Dismal 1950s Rangers, Dies at 83

text: An obituary last Tuesday about the British test pilot Eric Brown referred incorrectly to an innovation he proposed to the United States Navy for easier takeoffs from aircraft carriers. It was angled decks, not upturned decks.
match_headline: Eric Brown, Record-Breaking British Aviator and World War II Combat Pilot, Dies at 97

text: An article on Tuesday about a nationwide push to test the emotional skills of students misidentified a school in New York that is discussed in the book “How Children Succeed,” which extols the efforts to teach such skills. It is Riverdale Country School, not Horace Mann.
match_headline: Testing for Joy and Grit? Schools Nationwide Push to Measure Students’ Emotional Skills

text: An article on Feb. 1 about a debate in Iran over whether foreign oil companies should have any new roles in developing Iran’s vast oil wealth now that economic sanctions have been relaxed misstated part of the name of one of the oil companies that had been active in Iran before the sanctions were imposed. It is Royal Dutch Shell, not Anglo-Dutch Shell.
match_headline: In Iran, New Battle Brews Over Contracts With Foreign Oil Giants

text: An article on Feb. 2 about the suicide of an award-winning French-Swiss chef, Benoît Violier, misstated, in some editions, the name of a cafe owned by Homaro Cantu, an American chef who also killed himself, in 2015. The cafe was Berrista, not Barrista.
match_headline: Benoît Violier’s Death Shines Light on High-Pressure Restaurant World

text: An article on Tuesday about the Republican presidential candidates’ final day of campaigning before the “Super Tuesday” voting misidentified the state that Jeff Sessions, who endorsed Donald Trump, represents in the Senate. It is Alabama, not Arizona.
match_headline: Slights, Gags and Vitriol as Rivals Target Donald Trump

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about concerns over the planned expansion of a natural-gas pipeline across the Indian Point nuclear power plant property in Buchanan, N.Y., misidentified, in some copies, one of three demonstrators shown.
