Jeanne Shaw, who was wearing a mask, is at left, not in the center. (The demonstrator in the center was not identified. The woman at right was correctly identified as Judy Allen.)
match_headline: Plan to Expand a Pipeline at Indian Point Raises Concern

text: An article on Wednesday about JPMorgan Chase’s efforts to reassure investors as its shares drop misstated the bank’s profit expectations. It envisions profits of $30 billion a year within the next few years, not this year, and that figure is an assumption based on the trajectory of earnings, not a prediction.
match_headline: JPMorgan Tries to Calm Investors on Its Outlook and Oil Defenses

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the reaction of Boston Globe staff members to the best-picture Oscar won by “Spotlight,” about the newspaper’s Pulitzer Prize-winning series on the Roman Catholic church’s cover-up of sexual abuse by Roman Catholic priests, gave an incorrect job title for one staff member, Sacha Pfeiffer. She is a reporter, not an editor. The article also misstated The Globe’s actions regarding its foreign and national bureaus. It eliminated all of them except for Washington; it did not make cuts in them.
match_headline: ‘Spotlight’ Oscar Warms Boston Globe, and Journalism

text: An article on Tuesday about a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation of the drug maker Valeant Pharmaceuticals International misidentified an investor in Valeant. It is Sequoia Fund, not Sequoia Capital.
match_headline: Valeant Pharmaceuticals Is Under S.E.C. Investigation

text: An article on Friday about Columbia basketball player Maodo Lo misstated his height. He is 6 feet 3 inches, not 6 feet.
match_headline: Maodo Lo, an ‘Artist With a Basketball’ at Columbia

text: An article on Tuesday about a program at the Pergamon Museum in Berlin to train refugees to be museum guides misidentified an Arabic-language tour guide there. She is Razan Nassreddine — not Zoya Masoud, another guide. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The article also misstated the religious affiliation of the Samaritans. (Ms. Nassreddine spoke of refugees’ emotional reactions to a 15th- or 16th-century object at the museum that is associated with the Samaritans.) They are a community related to Judaism, not a Christian minority.
match_headline: Berlin’s Museum Tours in Arabic Forge a Bridge to Refugees

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the architect Claude Parent misstated the year that the Ste. Bernadette du Banlay church in Nevers, France, designed by Mr. Parent and Paul Virilio, was consecrated. It was 1966, not 1968. Also because of an editing error, the obituary referred incorrectly in some copies to the height of an architectural project, devised by Mr. Parent and Mr. Virilio, that is suspended 10 meters in the air. That equals about 33 feet, not 330 feet.
match_headline: Claude Parent, Visionary Architect of the Oblique, Dies at 93

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a new study of Zika virus and its potential link to Guillain-Barré syndrome in French Polynesia misstated part of the results of the study. The researchers found that 11 percent of a control group of patients had IgM antibodies against Zika, but none against dengue fever; it did not find that 11 percent of the control group had the dengue antibodies.
match_headline: New Study Links Zika Virus to Temporary Paralysis

text: An article on Feb. 10 about an announcement that the United States Army would deploy hundreds of soldiers to the southern Afghan province of Helmand quoted incorrectly from a comment by a senior American military official discussing the deployment. The official said, “It’s part of what matters most right now for the future of the country,” not “ or the future of the country.”
ref_headline: It’s part of what matters most right now for the future of the country,
match_headline: U.S. to Send More Troops to Aid Afghan Forces Pressed by Taliban

text: An article on Feb. 14 about Britain’s plan to strengthen its northern cities, like Liverpool and Manchester, which are overshadowed by London’s economic might, misstated the year that Liverpool became a European Capital of Culture. It was 2008, not 2012.
match_headline: Britain Aims to Strengthen North’s Cities

text: A news analysis article on Feb. 8 about China’s struggle for balance in its response to North Korea’s provocations in its quest for ballistic missile technologies misstated the rank of Kim Yong-hyun, the head of operations for the South Korean military’s Joint Chiefs of Staff. He is a lieutenant general, not a major general.
match_headline: China Struggles for Balance in Response to North Korea’s Boldness

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the National Briefing column in some copies on Friday about a natural-gas leak at the Aliso Canyon storage facility in Los Angeles referred incompletely to its significance. The amount of methane released was the largest in terms of climate impact, but second to the natural gas released in a collapse in Moss Bluff, Tex., in 2004, because the methane burned off into a fireball in the Texas case.
match_headline: Texas Abortion Case

text: A picture caption on Monday in a photo essay about the lives of young technology workers in Silicon Valley misstated the name of an early-morning dance party held on a cruise ship in San Francisco. It is Daybreaker, not Daybreakers.
match_headline: The Silicon Valley Hustle

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the Knicks’ 98-81 loss to the Miami Heat misstated, in some copies, the Knicks’ progress in the 2013 playoffs. They reached the semifinals — not the finals — in the Eastern Conference.
match_headline: Amar’e Stoudemire Laments Knicks’ Decline, Then Helps Sustain It

text: An article on Wednesday about two German artists who secretly scanned a famous bust of Queen Nefertiti at the Neues Museum in Berlin and used the data to create copies and enable others to do so on 3-D printers included outdated information about Don Undeen, who commented on the project. He left the MediaLab at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York last August and thus is no longer its senior manager.
match_headline: Swiping a Priceless Antiquity ... With a Scanner and a 3-D Printer

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the actor George Kennedy misidentified the high school from which he graduated. It is Chaminade High School in Mineola, N.Y. — not W. C. Mepham High School in Bellmore, N.Y.
match_headline: George Kennedy Dies at 91; Versatile Actor Won Oscar for ‘Cool Hand Luke’

text: An article on Friday about the accuracy of candidates’ assertions at Thursday’s Republican presidential debate described the United States’ trade balance with Canada incorrectly in analyzing Donald J. Trump’s comments on trade. The United States has had a trade deficit with Canada for at least 25 years; the United States did not, as the article said, have a trade surplus with Canada last year for the first time since 1990. (Despite the deficit with Canada, Mr. Trump was not correct in saying that we have such a deficit with “every other country.”)
match_headline: They May Be Next to Lead the Country, but Can They Play Ball?

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a change in policy under which police officers in Manhattan will issue criminal summonses for certain minor offenses rather than making arrests described one aspect of the new policy incorrectly at one point. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, under the new practice officers will not make an arrest for those minor offenses unless there is a threat to public safety; it is not discretionary.
match_headline: Summonses, Not Arrests, for Small Crimes in Manhattan

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the exhibition “Jonathan Horowitz: Occupy Greenwich” misstated the name of the institution that will present it. It is the Brant Foundation Art Study Center, not the Peter Brant Foundation. (The art study center is part of the Brant Foundation; there is no “Peter Brant Foundation.”)
match_headline: A Rare Pollock Sculpture Gets a Home

text: A picture caption on Friday with a theater review of “Rimbaud in New York,” at the Brooklyn Academy of Music, misspelled a cast member’s surname. As the review and the listing of credits correctly noted, she is Jo Lampert, not Lambert.
match_headline: Review: ‘Rimbaud in New York’ Splices the Genes of the Original Outlaw Artist

text: An article on Monday about heroin addicts who use the drug in public places misstated the number of people who die each day from overdoses of heroin and painkillers. It is 78 — not 125, which is the total number of deaths daily from all drug overdoses.
match_headline: Heroin Epidemic Increasingly Seeps Into Public View

text: An article on Feb. 12 about the opening in Germany of the trial of Reinhold Hanning, 94, a former Nazi charged with being an accessory to the murder of at least 170,000 people at Auschwitz-Birkenau in Poland, referred imprecisely to the Sobibor camp, also in Poland. It was a death camp, established and used by the Nazis almost exclusively as a place to murder Jews; concentration camps served primarily as detention and labor centers, although many prisoners died there as well.
match_headline: Trial of Reinhold Hanning, Ex-Auschwitz Guard, Opens in Germany

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a decision by the president of Serbia, Tomislav Nikolic, to dissolve Parliament as the government seeks a new mandate to pursue an economic agenda it regards as essential to qualify for membership in the European Union misidentified the newest member of the union. It is Croatia, which joined in 2013 — not Bulgaria and Romania, both of which joined in 2007.
match_headline: Serbia Dissolves Parliament and Calls Early Elections

text: An article on Monday about the 25th volume of “The Complete Peanuts,” for which President Obama wrote the foreword, misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the creator of the comic strip “Calvin and Hobbes.” He is Bill Watterson, not Waterson.
match_headline: Obama Pays Tribute to Charlie Brown, Snoopy and the ‘Peanuts’ Gang

text: An article on Feb. 24 about the new documentary “The Big Beat: Fats Domino and the Birth of Rock ‘n’ Roll,” using information from its producer and director, Joe Lauro, referred incorrectly to time Mr. Lauro spent with Mr. Domino and the circumstances surrounding Mr. Domino’s approval of the project. Mr. Lauro now says that in fact he never played pool with Mr. Domino and that Mr. Domino did not sign a deal for the film in order to pay off a pool wager.
ref_headline: The Big Beat: Fats Domino and the Birth of Rock ‘n’ Roll,
match_headline: ‘The Big Beat’ Celebrates Fats Domino, Rock’s Reclusive Giant

text: An obituary in some editions on Saturday about the author Pat Conroy misstated the subject of his book “My Losing Season.” It is about his experience playing basketball at the Citadel in Charleston, S.C., not at his high school in Beaufort, S.C. The obituary also omitted seven of Mr. Conroy’s survivors. They include his daughters Jessica and Melissa Conroy and five stepchildren: Emily Conroy; Jake, James and Jason Ray; and Gregory Fleischer. And in some editions on both Saturday and Sunday, the obituary misstated the time period covered in Mr. Conroy’s last novel, “South of Broad.” It is 20 years, not two.
match_headline: Pat Conroy, Author of ‘The Prince of Tides’ and ‘The Great Santini,’ Dies at 70

text: A chart on Feb. 26 about Scott J. Kelly’s 340 days aboard the International Space Station, using information from NASA, misstated the number of sunrises and sunsets that occurred from the astronaut’s perspective. It was 10,880, not 10,944.
match_headline: Scott Kelly Poised to Set NASA Record for Consecutive Days in Space

text: An article on Saturday about two studies of the links between the Zika virus and serious birth defects misstated the academic affiliation of Dr. Ernesto T. A. Marques, who studies Zika. He is at the University of Pittsburgh Graduate School of Public Health, not the University of Pittsburgh Medical School.
match_headline: Two Studies Strengthen Links Between the Zika Virus and Serious Birth Defects

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Feb. 14 with a Q&A article about the battle for Aleppo, Syria, misstated the date of the picture, which showed Syrians seeking safety after airstrikes on the rebel-controlled side of the city. The picture was taken on Jan. 13, not on Feb. 13.
match_headline: Syrian War Could Turn on the Battle for Aleppo

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the first uterus transplant surgery performed in the United States referred incorrectly to one part of the operation. Because the patient was born without fallopian tubes, the surgeons could not have connected her fallopian tubes to the transplanted uterus. (The clinic announced on Wednesday that that transplant had failed.)
match_headline: Hopeful Start for First Uterus Transplant Surgery in U.S.

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with an article about federal prosecutors’ declining to bring charges against a New York City police officer who fatally shot a Bronx teenager, Ramarley Graham, reversed the identities, in some copies, of the two men shown. Mr. Graham’s father, Frank Graham, is at the right and the family’s lawyer, Royce Russell, is in the center. (Constance Malcolm, the victim’s mother, was correctly identified, at left.)
match_headline: Officer in Ramarley Graham Shooting Won’t Face U.S. Charges

text: An article on March 2 about the complexity of pricing on computer-driven stock markets misstated the price offered by the BATS-Y exchange, one of four stock exchanges run by BATS Global Markets, to traders of certain stocks. The prices are quoted in the hundredths of a cent, not in the thousandths of a cent.
match_headline: Stock Exchange Prices Grow So Convoluted Even Traders Are Confused, Study Finds

text: A listing in the Transactions column in the Square Feet pages on Wednesday about a property that was recently leased in Bushwick, Brooklyn, misstated the address. It is at 18 Stewart Street, not 8 Stewart Street.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Monday about the musician Emitt Rhodes, who released an album last month after abandoning a pop career 43 years ago, misidentified the fictional character whose story was reminiscent of Mr. Rhodes’s long unused home studio. He is Rip Van Winkle, not Rumpelstiltskin.
match_headline: Emitt Rhodes, a New Album Out, Emerges From His Slumber

text: An obituary on Monday about the conductor Nikolaus Harnoncourt misstated part of the name of the village where he died, and also misstated its location. It is St. Georgen im Attergau (not “in” Attergau), and it is east, not west, of Salzburg, Austria.
match_headline: Nikolaus Harnoncourt, Conductor and Early-Music Specialist, Dies at 86

text: An article on Thursday about a Google computer program’s victory over a South Korean master of the board game Go described the game’s composition incorrectly. Go, believed to be the most complex board game ever created, is played on a board made up of 19 lines by 19 lines, not 19 squares by 19 squares.
match_headline: Master of Go Board Game Is Walloped by Google Computer Program

text: An article on Thursday about the visit of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau of Canada to the United States described the visit incorrectly. It was an official visit, not a state visit. The error was repeated in the headline. And the article described incorrectly the length of a dress that his mother, Margaret, wore to a White House state dinner in 1977, when her husband, Pierre, was Canada’s prime minister. Instead of wearing a formal floor-length gown, Mrs. Trudeau caused a stir by wearing a dress that fell just below — not above — the knee. (The error about the dress was repeated in an article on Friday about Justin Trudeau’s meeting with President Obama on Thursday, and in an article on Friday about the state dinner for him.)
match_headline: Justin Trudeau, Canadian Prime Minister, Making Rare Official Visit

text: An article on Friday about a meeting between President Obama and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau of Canada misstated one of the elements of the formal arrival ceremony for Mr. Trudeau. It was a 19-gun salute, not a 21-gun salute. The article also rendered the name of his wife incorrectly. She is Sophie Grégoire Trudeau — not Grégoire-Trudeau.
match_headline: Obama and Canada’s Justin Trudeau Promote Ties and Climate Plan

text: An article and a headline on Thursday about an ethics investigation involving a New York State assemblywoman misstated an aspect of the findings. While the inquiry found that the assemblywoman, Angela M. Wozniak of Buffalo, had a sexual relationship with her director of legislation and retaliated against him when he tried to end it, the Ethics Committee did not find that she had in fact engaged in sexual harassment in violation of policy.
match_headline: New York Assemblywoman Is Punished After Sexual Relationship With Aide

text: An article on Thursday about the naming of the bassist Christian McBride as artistic director of the Newport Jazz Festival misstated the role of George Wein in the founding of the festival. He was a co-founder, along with Elaine and Louis Lorillard, not the sole founder.
match_headline: Christian McBride, Newport Jazz Festival Star, Becomes a Backstage Player

text: An entry in the Spare Times listings on Friday about the National Museum of the American Indian in Manhattan referred incorrectly to today’s program and misstated its time. “Crossing the Lines: Women and Ledger Art” runs from 11 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and includes in-gallery demonstrations and talks. It is not a discussion scheduled for 4:30 p.m.
ref_headline: Crossing the Lines: Women and Ledger Art
match_headline: Spare Times Listings for March 11-17

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about two exhibitions of work by the painter Louise Fishman, using information from a publicist, misstated the opening date of one at the Neuberger Museum of Art in Purchase, N.Y.. It is April 3, not April 29.
match_headline: How a Rembrandt Masterpiece Evolved

text: An article last Sunday about challenges facing the new president of New York University, Andrew Hamilton, misstated, in some editions, the size of endowments of Harvard and Yale. Harvard’s endowment is $37.6 billion, not $32 billion, and Yale’s is $25.6 billion, not $17 billion.
match_headline: Big Man on a Global Campus

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Joe Bataan, a leading figure of boogaloo, the fusion of Latin rhythm and soul music that he helped pioneer, referred incorrectly in some editions to “We Like It Like That,” a documentary about that music. It is now heading to streaming services after a successful run at film festivals; it is not currently touring the film festival circuit.
match_headline: The Return of Joe Bataan, the Boogaloo King

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions this weekend on Page 10 about a digital filmmaking program at Rutgers University omits the given name of a classics professor who comments on the program. He is T. Corey Brennan. And a picture caption with the article misstates part of the program’s name. As the article correctly notes, it is the Rutgers Film Bureau, not the Rutgers Film Institute.
match_headline: Amid Conflict, Rutgers Acquires a Noted Filmmaker

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Yale’s 71-55 victory over Columbia that secured the Ivy League men’s basketball championship misstated the game at which Yale’s Makai Mason hit a jump shot to force overtime in a crucial victory this season. It was on Feb. 27 against Dartmouth, not Feb. 26 against Harvard.
match_headline: Yale Finally Has an Ivy Title to Call Its Own

text: An article last Sunday about the Krishna devotee Roger Siegel and the Vedic Care Charitable Trust, an organization with roots in the International Society for Krishna Consciousness, misstated the number of core members who created the trust. It was created by Mr. Siegel and three others, not four others.
match_headline: Krishna Devotees Look to Provide for This Life

text: An article last Sunday about the need to set aside money in retirement for medical expenses gave an outdated title for Jean Setzfand, an AARP executive who commented on the matter. She is senior vice present of programs, no longer vice president for financial security.
match_headline: On Eve of Retirement, Savings for Medical Costs Can Fall Short

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the Italian architect Roberto Baciocchi’s idiosyncratic home in Tuscany misstated the year in which the pink metallic stand shown was designed by Achille Castiglioni. It was 1983, not in the 1960s.
match_headline: A Minimalist Architect’s Surprisingly Vibrant Tuscan Home

text: An article last Sunday about the Stephen Petronio Dance Company misstated a change the Trisha Brown Dance Company is planning for Ms. Brown’s proscenium works. It will reinvent the works through a site-specific series; it is not the case that the company will no longer focus on the works.
match_headline: The Stephen Petronio Company Goes Into the Wild

text: An article last Sunday about the anime film company Studio Ghibli misstated the number of Asian animated features at this year’s New York International Children’s Film Festival. It is four, not one. The article also misstated the title of a Studio Ghibli film. It is “The Tale of the Princess Kaguya,” not “Princess Kaguya.”
ref_headline: The Tale of the Princess Kaguya,
match_headline: Twilight in the House of Ghibli, as ‘The Boy and the Beast’ Roars

text: An article last Sunday about the CBS show “NCIS” misspelled the surname of a co-writer for the show. He is George Schenck, not Scheck. The article also misspelled the name of a character on “NCIS” played by Sasha Alexander. She is Caitlin Todd, not Caitlyn.
match_headline: ‘NCIS’: Meat and Potatoes TV, but Still Popular

text: A listing on the “On the Market” page last Sunday described a property at 320 East 57th Street incorrectly. It does not have a fireplace.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in Brooklyn and Manhattan

text: A picture caption on Feb. 14 with an article about travel to Iran misidentified a tourist destination in Isfahan. It is the Khaju Bridge and the Zayandeh River, not Iman Square.
match_headline: Sanctions Lifted, American Tourists Head to Iran

text: An article on Oct. 4 about a food and wine tour of Beaune, France, misstated the location of Mont Blanc in relation to Beaune. It is to the southeast, not north. The error was called to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Seduced by Beaune in Burgundy

text: An article last Sunday about traveling to the Jaffna region of Sri Lanka misspelled part of the Tamil name of the Queen of Jaffna train. It is Yarl Devi, not Yari Devi. The article also misstated the phone number for the Experience Travel Group, which organizes tours to the area. It is 44-20-79-24-7133.
match_headline: In Sri Lanka, Barriers Fall in a Land Marred by Bloodshed

text: An article last Sunday about an increase in visitors to the Trinity Church graveyard as a result of the popularity of the Broadway show “Hamilton” misstated one of the words on Eliza Hamilton’s headstone. It is “Widow,” not “Wife.”
match_headline: After the Broadway Show, a Trip to Hamilton’s Grave

text: An article last Sunday about sharply differing views in New Orleans regarding Airbnb and other short-term rental services misstated part of the name of a group that supports short-term rentals. It is the Alliance for Neighborhood Prosperity, not the Alliance for Neighborhood Progress.
match_headline: Airbnb Pits Neighbor Against Neighbor in Tourist-Friendly New Orleans

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the biotechnology evangelist Randal J. Kirk omitted an explanation of the importance of genetically modifying male mosquitoes rather than females to battle Zika and other mosquito-borne diseases. Unlike female mosquitoes, the males do not bite. Thus they cannot transmit the Zika virus; they can only mate with the females and pass on a gene that kills their offspring.
match_headline: A Biotech Evangelist Seeks a Zika Dividend

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Donald Trump’s views on American trade policy misidentified the location from which Carrier will be shifting its air-conditioner production. It is Indiana, not India. (It is expanding to Mexico.)
match_headline: On Trade, Donald Trump Breaks With 200 Years of Economic Orthodoxy

text: An article on Tuesday about Ambry Genetics’ decision to release genetic information from the people it has tested described the action incorrectly. Ambry is making the data publicly available; it is not putting the data in the public domain. (While the data is free to download and use, the company retains copyright.)
match_headline: Genetic Test Firm to Make Customers’ Data Publicly Available

text: An article last Monday about the final round of the World Golf Championships event at Trump National Doral, which was attended by Donald J. Trump, misstated his son Eric’s role at the tournament’s award ceremony. While he was present at the ceremony, he did not give Adam Scott the trophy.
match_headline: Adam Scott Wins at Doral as Rory McIlroy Falters After a Handshake From Donald Trump

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on March 3 about the Rendez-Vous With French Cinema series in Manhattan misidentified the nationality of the title character in “Fatima,” a film in the series. She is Algerian, not Moroccan.
match_headline: Big Issues (and, Yes, Amour) Hit Rendez-Vous With French Cinema

text: An article on Monday about the removal of a toxic chemical from the municipal water supply in Hoosick Falls, N.Y., misstated part of the name of a factory that once used the chemical in the making of Teflon products. It was Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics (not Plastic).
match_headline: Pollutant Is Removed From Water in Hoosick Falls, N.Y., Cuomo Says

text: An article on Monday about microbots developed by the Biomimetics and Dexterous Manipulation Laboratory at Stanford University misstated the position at Stanford of one of the developers, Srinivasan Suresh, in some copies. He is a graduate student, not a postdoctoral fellow.
match_headline: Modeled After Ants, Teams of Tiny Robots Can Move 2-Ton Car

text: An article on March 2 about Yankees reliever Aroldis Chapman’s accepting a 30-game suspension under Major League Baseball’s domestic violence policy misstated, in some editions, the amount of money he will lose during the suspension. It is $1.86 million, not $2.17 million.
match_headline: Aroldis Chapman’s Stance Changed From Defiance to Acceptance

text: An article on Wednesday about the double bill “Iolanta/The Nutcracker,” directed by Dmitri Tcherniakov at the Paris Opera, referred incorrectly to Mr. Tcherniakov’s involvement with his productions. While he does design his own sets, he does not design the lighting.
match_headline: In ‘Iolanta/The Nutcracker,’ a Director Unites Two Tchaikovsky Works

text: An obituary on Monday about the production designer Ken Adam misstated the surname of one of the people with whom he shared an Academy Award for his work on “Barry Lyndon.” He was Roy Walker, not Roy Scott. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Adam’s work as an assistant art director on “Around the World in 80 Days.” It was not uncredited. And the obituary described incorrectly the 1959 film “The Angry Hills,” on which he was production designer. It is a World War II drama, not a western.
match_headline: Ken Adam, Who Dreamed Up the Lairs of Movie Villains, Dies at 95

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary in some editions on Saturday about the keyboardist Keith Emerson misidentified the musician with whom he and the drummer Cozy Powell recorded an album before his band Emerson, Lake & Palmer reunited in 1991. He is Greg Lake — not Carl Palmer, another drummer.
match_headline: Keith Emerson, ’70s Rock Showman With a Taste for Spectacle, Dies at 71

text: An article on Monday about the importance of Ohio’s primary contest in the presidential race misidentified, in some copies, the state Ted Cruz represents in the Senate. It is Texas, not Florida.
match_headline: Ohio Looms Large in Both Races on Tuesday

text: An article on Saturday about the dismissal of two executives of the Wounded Warrior Project quoted incorrectly from a comment by Phillip Carter, a fellow at the Center for a New American Security, who discussed the value of the organization in helping other veterans groups. He called the Wounded Warrior Project “a fund-raising machine that is a grant-maker” — not a “rent-maker” — for other organizations.
ref_headline: a fund-raising machine that is a grant-maker
match_headline: After Complaints on Wounded Warrior Project, Pressure From Donors

text: An article on Tuesday about the shooting death of a Maryland police officer misstated part of the name of the county where the shooting took place. It is Prince George’s County, not St. George’s. The error was repeated in a capsule summary in the Inside The Times column.
match_headline: Gunman Intended to Die in Maryland Attack, Police Say

text: An article on Tuesday about growing optimism among investors that the energy market is poised for a rebound misstated the amount by which Iran has promised to increase its oil exports. The plan is for an additional 500,000 barrels a day, not 500 million.
match_headline: Investors Increasingly Bullish on Energy Sector

text: An article on Saturday about the closing of the hit play “War Horse” in London misidentified the milestone Queen Elizabeth II was celebrating when Joey, a life-size puppet horse in the play, reared up on the roof of the National Theater in salute. It was her Diamond Jubilee, celebrating 60 years on the throne — not her Golden Jubilee, which occurred 10 years earlier, in 2002. The article also referred incorrectly to the folk songs in the play. They were written for it by John Tams; they are not “ancient.”
match_headline: ‘War Horse’ Closes in Britain, but Its Influence Gallops On

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with a review of Lydia Johnson Dance, at the Ailey Citigroup Center in Manhattan, misidentified two of the three dancers shown performing. Audra Edwards is at the left, not Katie Martin-Lohiya. Ms. Martin-Lohiya is at the right — not Laura Di Orio, another member of the company. (The dancer in the center, Min-Seon Kim, was correctly identified.)
match_headline: Review: Lydia Johnson Dance Keeps Everything in Control

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about a woman who has been monitoring her pregnancy because of possible exposure to the Zika virus misspelled her surname. She is Ami Levy, not Levi.
match_headline: Women Who Brought Zika Fears Home With Them

text: Because of an editing error, the Books of The Times review on Tuesday, about a book on the Middle East by Richard Engel, the chief foreign correspondent for NBC News, misstated part of its title. It is “And Then All Hell Broke Loose,” not “And Then All Hell Breaks Loose.”
ref_headline: And Then All Hell Broke Loose,
match_headline: Review: ‘And Then All Hell Broke Loose,’ Richard Engel’s Memoir of Reporting From the Middle East

text: An entry in the Spare Times for Children listings in some editions on Friday misstated the closing date for the play “The Boy at the Edge of Everything,” at Lincoln Center. It is scheduled to close on Sunday, not Saturday.
ref_headline: The Boy at the Edge of Everything,
match_headline: Spare Times for Children Listings for March 11-17

text: An obituary on Friday about Clyde Lovellette, the first basketball player to win an N.C.A.A. championship, an Olympic gold medal and an N.B.A. title, referred incompletely to the players who later achieved that feat. There have been six — not just Bill Russell, Magic Johnson and Michael Jordan. (The other three are K. C. Jones, Jerry Lucas and Quinn Buckner.)
match_headline: Clyde Lovellette, Hall of Famer Who Brought Size and Skill to Basketball, Dies at 86

text: An article on Wednesday about John Kilgallon, a native of Far Rockaway who fought in the 1916 Easter Rising rebellion against the British, misidentified, in some editions, the branch of the United States military he joined after returning to America from Ireland. It is the Navy, not the Air Force.
match_headline: Student of Irish Language Brings to Life a Patriot of the Easter Rising

text: An article on Wednesday about a sharp drop in the value of Valeant Pharmaceutical International shares and the effect on a major investor, Pershing Square Capital Management, misstated the year Pershing Square’s founder, William A. Ackman, first began to buy Valeant shares. It was 2015 — not 2014, which is the year Mr. Ackman teamed up with the company in a joint takeover effort.
match_headline: Pressure on Valeant Puts William Ackman’s Image as Moneymaker at Risk

text: An article on the Square Feet page on Wednesday about the transformation of the decommissioned Quonset Air Naval Station in Rhode Island into a thriving industrial park misstated the size of a $5 million addition for Norad, an early tenant that imports and finishes cars. It is 35,000 square feet, not 230,000 square feet.
match_headline: Quonset Makes a New Name for Itself in Business

text: A listing in the Transactions column on the Square Feet page on Wednesday about a property for sale at 101 Seventh Avenue omitted part of the name of the company that owns it. It is 70 Grove L.L.C., not Grove L.L.C.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Wednesday about Sri Srinivasan, an Indian-born appeals court judge who was among President Obama’s candidates for the Supreme Court, misspelled, at one point, the name of the village in India where the judge has many relatives. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is Mela Thiruvenkatanathapuram, not Mela Thiruvenkanathapuram. (There is one syllable — “ta” — missing, between “ka” and “na.” With the additional letters, the town is pronounced MAY-la THEE-roo VEN-ka-ta NA-tha POO-ram. This correction, it should be noted, has been carefully proofread.)
match_headline: With Sri Srinivasan, Indian Town Prays for a ‘Son’ on Supreme Court

text: An article on the DealBook page on Wednesday about the financial troubles of the solar company SunEdison misidentified the SunEdison affiliate that the hedge fund Appaloosa Management claimed was forced to acquire assets from SunEdison. It is TerraForm Power, not TerraForm Global.
match_headline: The Financial Alchemy That’s Choking SunEdison

text: An article on Thursday about the J. Paul Getty Trust’s Pacific Standard Time initiative, which is developing exhibitions of art with Latin American and Latino themes in Southern California museums, misstated the surname of an artist-curator who is jointly preparing an exhibition about the Chilean-born artist Juan Downey. He is Robert Crouch, not Couch.
match_headline: The Pacific Standard Time Initiative Seeks to Rescue Fugitive Art

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the San Diego Comic Art Gallery in California misidentified the artist who painted a mural depicting various comic-book characters. He is Paul Mavrides, not Kevin Eastman.
match_headline: In San Diego, a Comics Confab That Never Ends

text: An article on Thursday about the advanced printing technologies used by art book publishers misstated the name of a publisher of art books and museum exhibition catalogs. It is D.A.P./Distributed Art Publishers, not D.A.P./Distributed Art Press.
match_headline: New Print Technologies Help Art Books Survive in a Digital World

text: A picture credit in some editions on Thursday with an obituary about the primate scientist Elwyn L. Simons, using information from Duke University, misidentified the source of the photograph of Dr. Simons with a lemur. It was taken by Patricia Wright of Stony Brook University, not Duke.
match_headline: Elwyn L. Simons, Who Discovered Early Human Forebears, Dies at 85

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Judge Merrick Garland’s judicial record and how it has earned him praise across the political spectrum referred imprecisely to his connection to the Citizens United campaign finance case. While he joined a panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in a campaign finance decision that built on Citizens United, he was not involved in the Citizens United case itself.
match_headline: Where Merrick Garland Stands: A Close Look at His Judicial Record

text: An article on Wednesday about new guidelines set by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on opioid prescriptions misstated the results of a study. According to the research, one in 32 patients whose treatment regimen on opioids was increased to very high doses died; they did not start on a high dosage. In addition, the study did not calculate the length of time between when patients received high doses and when they died; the study did not say that period was 2 1/2 years. The article also misstated legal actions taken by the Washington Legal Foundation. While the group has filed friend-of-the-court briefs supporting positions taken by pharmaceutical companies, it has not represented drug manufacturers in lawsuits.
match_headline: C.D.C. Painkiller Guidelines Aim to Reduce Addiction Risk

text: An article on Friday about President Obama’s move to declassify records that could reveal what the United States government knew about Argentina’s brutal war of the 1970s and ’80s misidentified the source of an account of a conversation in 1976 between Henry Kissinger, then secretary of state, and Cesar Augusto Guzzetti, the Argentine foreign minister. The account was in a document released in response to a Freedom of Information Act request by the National Security Archive; it did not come from documents the State Department declassified in 2002.
match_headline: Obama to Unseal Files on Argentina’s ‘Dirty War’

text: An article on Friday about an escalating disagreement between the government of Morocco and the United Nations — set off by Secretary General Ban Ki-moon’s characterization of the disputed territory of Western Sahara, claimed by Morocco, as an occupied region — referred imprecisely to efforts by the United Nations since 1991 to reach a political settlement between Morocco and the Polisario Front, an independence movement. Though the initial Security Council resolutions on the matter called for a referendum to decide the territory’s future, resolutions adopted since 2002 have called for a “mutually acceptable political solution,” without specifying a referendum. The article also misspelled the given name of a professor of international relations at McDaniel College in Westminster, Md., who was quoted in the article. He is Anouar Boukhars, not Anaouar.
match_headline: Morocco Orders U.N. to Cut Staff in Disputed Western Sahara Territory

text: An article on Friday about financial disclosures made by FIFA, soccer’s world governing body, misstated the amount of its cash reserves. It is $1.34 billion, not $1.34 million.
match_headline: FIFA’s Financial Disclosures Show That Scandal Has Affected Its Bottom Line

text: An article on Page 58 this weekend about new artistic steps taken by three design companies misstates the familial relationship between Pierre-Alexis, the chief artistic director of Hermès, and Axel Dumas, the company’s chief executive officer. They are cousins, not brothers.
match_headline: The New Direction of Three Storied Design Houses

text: A picture caption on Page 64 this weekend with an article about metallic-hued fashion misstates the price of Sophie Buhai earrings. They cost $340, not $170.
match_headline: Sophie Grégoire Trudeau: A Very Canadian ‘First Lady’

text: An article last Sunday about a tugboat that crashed into a barge near the Tappan Zee Bridge gave an incorrect age from the authorities for one of the crew members, Paul Amon, who was killed. He was 62, not 52.
match_headline: One Dead and Two Missing After Tugboat Hits Barge Near Tappan Zee Bridge

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about the Jay Heritage Center in Rye, N.Y., misstated the year that its mansion was built. It was constructed in 1838, not 1836.
match_headline: At the Jay Heritage Center in Rye: Young Americans

text: A picture with an article in some editions last Sunday about Carlin Isles, a standout in rugby as well as track and field for the United States, was published in error. It showed Isles’s rugby teammate Perry Baker — not Isles — being lifted during a match in January.
match_headline: Holding Their Noses, Louisiana Officials Act to Narrow State Budget Gaps

text: An article last Sunday about the play “The Effect” misstated its opening date. It is Sunday, March 20; it did not open on Wednesday.
match_headline: ‘The Effect,’ by Lucy Prebble, Comes to the Barrow Street Theater

text: An article last Sunday about the film “Fatima” misidentified the nationality of the title character. She is Algerian, not Moroccan.
match_headline: ‘Fatima’ Captures the Immigrant Experience in France

text: An article on Feb. 14 about Chirlane McCray, the wife of Mayor Bill de Blasio, misstated a recollection by McCray’s friend Stella Dong about Wellesley College in the 1970s. She said that a generation earlier it was not considered unusual for a student to drop out of the school to plan her wedding, not that it was common while she and McCray attended.
match_headline: Chirlane McCray and the Limits of First-Ladyship

text: An article last Sunday about cocktails in New Orleans misstated the timing of Krewe du Vieux, a parade. It is one of the first parades of the Mardi Gras season, not the first.
match_headline: What to Drink in New Orleans, Where Cocktail Is King

text: An article last Sunday about Nancy Reagan’s salutary effect on Ronald Reagan’s acting career misstated the profession of a Hollywood personality who aided the young Nancy Davis early in her acting career. Walter Huston was an actor, not a director.
match_headline: Nancy Reagan’s Abiding Role in her Husband’s Career

text: An article on Wednesday about the N.F.L.’s acknowledging the link between football and degenerative brain disorders gave an outdated name in some copies for the team of the physician Andrew Tucker, a member of the league’s concussion committee. It is the Baltimore Ravens, not the Baltimore Colts.
match_headline: N.F.L. Shifts on Concussions, and Game May Never Be the Same

text: An article on Jan. 13 about a divestment action against Israeli banks by the United Methodist Church pension board referred incorrectly to the Palestinian territories, where, the board said, the banks help finance Israeli settlement construction. While most of the world officially considers the territories to be occupied, and the settlements illegal, there is no consensus that the occupation itself is illegal. The error was brought to the attention of editors only this week.
match_headline: U.S. Church Puts 5 Banks From Israel on a Blacklist

text: An article on Thursday about waters off Long Island designated by the federal government as a possible site for a wind farm, using information from the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, misstated, in some editions, the number of groups that have expressed interest in developing an offshore wind site in the area. There are five, not two.
match_headline: Wind Farm May Be Built Off Long Island

text: An article last Monday about Sunrise Christian Academy, in Wichita, Kan., which has developed into a pipeline for basketball players from the Bahamas, including the Oklahoma star Buddy Hield, included outdated statistics for Hield in some editions. He was averaging 25.0 points per game, not 25.6, and shooting 46.4 percent from 3-point range, not 47 percent. And because of an editing error, the article misstated the day of an Oklahoma team shootaround, in which the Sooners prepared for the Big 12 Conference tournament quarterfinals. It was Wednesday, March 9 — not Thursday, March 10.
match_headline: For Buddy Hield and Other Bahamians, Talent Is Cultivated on the Great Plains

text: An article on Thursday about nicknames in men’s college basketball misspelled the surname of the Indiana University guard who is called Yogi. He is Kevin Ferrell, not Farrell.
match_headline: What’s in a Nickname? Ask Scoochie, Yogi or Tubby

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the history of major upsets in the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament reversed the opponents of two upset-minded No. 16 seeds — Princeton and East Tennessee State — in 1989. Princeton faced Georgetown and East Tennessee State played Oklahoma.
match_headline: In a Tournament Known for Upsets, There Is Always Hope

text: An article on Thursday about the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, which is named for the artists Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner and awards grants to artists, misspelled the given name of the foundation’s executive vice president. She is Kerrie Buitrago, not Kerry.
match_headline: Jackson Pollock, a Chance Encounter and a Multimillion-Dollar Foundation

text: Because of an editing error, an entry on Thursday in a listing of art exhibitions around the country this spring misstated the closing date for “This Is a Portrait if I Say So: Identity in American Art, 1912 to Today," at the Bowdoin College Museum of Art in Brunswick, Me. The exhibition runs from June 25 to Oct. 23, not Oct. 16.
ref_headline: This Is a Portrait if I Say So: Identity in American Art, 1912 to Today,
match_headline: A Nationwide Guide to Art Exhibitions This Spring

text: An article on Saturday about the primary elections in Arizona misstated projections for 2030 about the citizenship of Latinos living in the state. The study estimates that four in five — not one in five — Latinos will be United States citizens by then.
match_headline: Presidential Candidates Woo Arizona Voters on Immigration

text: An article on Saturday about a foster father who was charged with sexually abusing five boys on Long Island, all of them his adopted sons, misstated the title of Gerard Gigante in some copies. He is the chief of detectives with the Suffolk County Police Department, not the police chief.
match_headline: Foster Father Charged With Sexually Abusing 5 Boys on Long Island

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 14 about the recovery of the body of a crewman who was on a tugboat that crashed in the Hudson River described the term slack tide incorrectly. It is the time when the current subsides, not when the water recedes.
match_headline: Body of Second Crew Member Is Recovered From Tugboat Crash Near Tappan Zee Bridge

text: An article on Monday about Sherwin-Williams’s deal to buy a big rival, Valspar, misstated the acquisition price in some copies. It is $9.3 billion, not $8.9 billion.
match_headline: Sherwin-Williams to Buy Valspar for $9.3 Billion

text: An article on Monday about a proposal to stream movies into homes at the same time they arrive in theaters misstated part of the name of an industry trade group opposed to the idea. It is the National Association of Theater Owners, not the National Alliance of Theater Owners.
match_headline: Hollywood Divided Over Movie Streaming Service

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about the South by Southwest music festival, in Austin, Tex., misstated the number of acts there. It was more than 2,000, not more than 200.
match_headline: SXSW: From Exclusive Performances to Cellphone Souvenirs

text: An article on Monday about the theatrical production “The War of the Worlds” in London, produced by Bill Kenwright, misidentified the site where “Let the Right One In,” another of his productions, was performed when it transferred to New York from London last year. It went to St. Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn, not Broadway.
match_headline: ‘War of the Worlds’ Shape-Shifts Onto the London Stage

text: An article on Friday about “Dinosaurs Among Us,” at the American Museum of Natural History in Manhattan, misidentified the closest living relatives of dinosaurs. They are birds, not crocodiles. (Crocodiles do have a common ancestry with dinosaurs.)
match_headline: Fine Feathered Fiends: ‘Dinosaurs Among Us’ at the American Museum of Natural History

text: An article on Friday about seizures of antiquities by law enforcement officials during Asia Week New York, using information from the website of Leila A. Amineddoleh’s law firm, misstated the connection of Ms. Amineddoleh, who commented on Asian governments’ monitoring of antiquities, to the Lawyers’ Committee for Cultural Heritage Preservation. She is a former director, not the current one.
match_headline: Law Enforcement Focuses on Asia Week in Inquiry of Antiquities Smuggling

text: An article on Tuesday about the government’s decision to try to unlock a terrorist’s iPhone without Apple’s help misstated the surname of a Justice Department spokeswoman in some copies. She is Melanie Newman, not Newsom.
match_headline: U.S. Says It May Not Need Apple’s Help to Unlock iPhone

text: An article on Jan. 20 about victims of terrorist attacks, including one at a hotel and cafe in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, misidentified the organization that employed Ahmed Kéré, who was killed in the Burkina Faso assault. He worked for buildOn, an American nonprofit group — not the Sonder Project, another American nonprofit, for which Mr. Kéré was an unpaid consultant. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption. The error was only recently brought to the attention of editors.
match_headline: Week of Attacks, Scores of Civilian Deaths and a Question: Why Them?

text: An article on Tuesday about Yahoo’s challenges as it explores selling itself while preparing to battle an activist investor misidentified, in some copies, the corporation that has sought to renegotiate Yahoo’s relationship with Yahoo Japan. It is Yahoo Japan — not SoftBank, which is Yahoo Japan’s largest shareholder.
match_headline: No Respite for Yahoo, Battling on 2 Fronts

text: An article in some copies on Monday about Villanova’s 87-68 victory over Iowa in the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament misstated the number of points Iowa’s Adam Woodbury scored. He had 1 point; he was not held scoreless.
match_headline: Villanova Routs Iowa to Advance to Round of 16

text: An article on Saturday about Michigan State’s 90-81 loss to Middle Tennessee State in the first round of the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament misstated, in some copies, the number of shots Middle Tennessee State attempted from the field. It was 59 shots, not 39. (The team made 33 of them.)
match_headline: Michigan State, Poised for a Deep Run, Crashes Into Middle Tennessee

text: An article on March 12 about Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, which will be shared by the N.F.L.’s Rams and the University of Southern California football team, referred incorrectly in some editions to visits to Los Angeles by E. Stanley Kroenke, the Rams’ owner, and Kevin Demoff, their executive vice president for football operations. They had in fact visited the city since the league approved the team’s move from St. Louis in January; it is not the case that they had not visited.
match_headline: The Rams Can Go Home Again, to the 93-Year-Old Los Angeles Coliseum

text: An article on Thursday about the Home Sweet Home museum in East Hampton, N.Y., and how it had to revise its exhibits and tours after learning that John Howard Payne was not in fact born at the site, referred incompletely to DNA testing regarding a descendant of Sally Hemings, a slave of Thomas Jefferson. (His museum at Monticello also has had to revise historical references to him.) While DNA evidence confirmed that Ms. Hemings’s son Eston was fathered by a male descendant of the Jefferson family, the testing could not conclusively confirm that Thomas Jefferson was the father.
match_headline: Home Sweet Home Museum Changes Its Tune

text: Because of an editing error, a map last Wednesday with an article about Pittsburgh’s booming food scene misstated the address of a Primanti Brothers restaurant. It is 1832 East Carson Street — not 2100 Wharton Street, which is the address of the corporate office.
match_headline: Pittsburgh’s Youth-Driven Food Boom

text: An article on Tuesday about the introduction of several new Apple products misstated the price reduction for the Apple Watch. It is $50, not $100.
match_headline: Apple’s Modest Product Upgrades Take Back Seat to Worries on iPhone Encryption

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the reaction of Muslims in the New York region to a statement by Senator Ted Cruz that he wanted the police to “patrol and secure” Muslim communities in the United States because they might harbor terrorists misidentified, in some copies, one of the three men shown near the Council of Peoples Organization in Brooklyn. Muntaz Ali is in the center — not Ali Khan, who is at the right.
match_headline: New York Muslims Reject Ted Cruz’s Prescriptions for Monitoring

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a decision by the Brooklyn district attorney not to seek prison time for Peter Liang, a former police officer convicted of second-degree manslaughter in the shooting death of a man at a public housing complex, misspelled, in some copies, the given name of an officer who was found guilty of criminally negligent homicide in the 2003 shooting death of Ousmane Zongo. He is Bryan Conroy, not Brian.
match_headline: Prosecutor Won’t Seek Prison for Peter Liang, Ex-Officer Convicted in Killing

text: An article on Thursday about a decision by a judge to vacate the murder conviction of Richard Rosario, 40, who served 20 years in prison after being found guilty in the 1996 killing of Jorge Collazo in the Bronx, misstated, in some copies, the date that Mr. Rosario was sentenced. It was Dec. 17, 1998, not Dec. 19.
match_headline: Murder Conviction Vacated for Man Who Served 20 Years

text: An article on Thursday about the surprising number of small guards with outsize roles who are playing deep in the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament misstated the academic classification of one such guard for Kansas, Frank Mason III. He is a junior, not a sophomore.
match_headline: Don’t Sell These Point Guards Short

text: A review in the New Music column on Thursday about the album “A Cosmic Rhythm With Each Stroke” on the ECM label, by Vijay Iyer and Wadada Leo Smith, misidentified the most recent recording Mr. Smith made for ECM before the new album. It is “Kulture Jazz” from 1993, not “Divine Love” from 1979.
ref_headline: A Cosmic Rhythm With Each Stroke
match_headline: Review: Wadada Leo Smith and Vijay Iyer Share Their Influence Through Duets

text: An article on March 15 about environmentally sensitive construction of museums, using information from the Whitney Museum of American Art, referred incorrectly to its efforts to achieve gold status through the Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design program. While the Whitney is in fact pursuing the status, it will not be the first museum to receive it, as it had hoped. That distinction is already held by the Grand Rapids Art Museum, in Michigan, which achieved the status in 2008. The article also misstated the number of years that the University of California, Berkeley, Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive was propped up with temporary beams. It was 15 years, not more than 25. And the article misstated part of the name of a federal program that funded the building that has been renovated as the Berkeley museum’s new home. It was the Work Projects Administration, not the Works Project Administration.
match_headline: Art Museums Seek a Green Palette

text: An obituary on Thursday about the actor Ken Howard rendered incorrectly in some copies the name of the union that merged with the Screen Actors Guild to form SAG-Aftra, of which he was president. It was the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (not Radio and Television).
match_headline: Ken Howard, 71, Actor and SAG-Aftra Union President, Dies

text: An obituary in some editions on Tuesday and on Wednesday about Andrew S. Grove, the longtime chairman and chief executive of the Intel Corporation, misidentified the borough in which he lived with an aunt and uncle shortly after arriving in New York as a young man. Their apartment was in the Bronx, not in Brooklyn.
match_headline: Andrew S. Grove Dies at 79; Intel Chief Spurred Semiconductor Revolution

text: An article on March 15 about budget cuts that Alaska schools are facing because of lower oil prices referred incorrectly to science faculty departures at the University of Alaska. Ten biology faculty members who have left were from both the Fairbanks and Anchorage campuses, not just Fairbanks, creating a loss of 10 faculty members out of 60, not 10 out of 45.
match_headline: Alaska’s Schools Face Cuts at Every Level Over Oil Collapse

text: An article on Page 6 this weekend about a new permanent collection at the Museum of Modern Art that focuses on the 1960s misstates the opening date. It opens today; it is not scheduled to open next Saturday, April 2.
match_headline: MoMA Revisits the 1960s

text: An article last Sunday about the Zika virus in Puerto Rico misstated the role that Dr. Johnny Rullán has played in public health the last 31 years. Dr. Rullán has held several high-ranking public health roles in Puerto Rico and elsewhere, including two stints as the territory’s secretary of health, but he was not Puerto Rico’s secretary of health for 31 years.
match_headline: Puerto Rico Braces for Its Own Zika Epidemic

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the language of college basketball among players and coaches misstated the surname of the radio analyst for Virginia men’s basketball games. He is Ted Jeffries, not Jefferies.
match_headline: Foreign to Many, the Language of College Basketball Has Its Fluent Speakers

text: A picture in some editions last Sunday with the Connecticut calendar was published in error. It showed the musician Ornette Coleman, not the musician Ravi Coltrane.
match_headline: Things to Do in Connecticut, March 19 Through March 27

text: A picture caption in some editions last Sunday with the continuation of a cover article about the growing number of people practicing meditation in New York City misstated the surname of a class instructor shown at the Harlem branch of the New York Public Library. He is Benjamin Blythe, not Bythe.
match_headline: No Texts, Please, We’re Meditating

text: An article last Sunday about the Scottish opera director David McVicar misspelled part of the name of the production he is directing at the Metropolitan Opera. It is “Roberto Devereux,” not “Roberto Devereaux.” The article also misspelled the surname of a soprano in the production. She is Sondra Radvanovsky, not Radvanovksy. And an accompanying picture caption misidentified one of the three singers shown rehearsing. The singer at the right is Mariusz Kwiecien — not Matthew Polenzani, who is also in the production.
match_headline: Can David McVicar Bring Peace to the Opera Wars?

text: An article last Sunday about film portrayals of Hank Williams misstated the circumstances of his death. He died in West Virginia, in the back seat of a limousine on the way to a New Year’s Day show in Canton, Ohio, in 1953. He was not heading to a New Year’s Eve show in West Virginia.
match_headline: A New Map to Hank Williams’s Lost Highways

text: An article last Sunday about the architect Arno Brandlhuber’s concrete villa in Potsdam, Germany, misstated the inspiration behind the artwork of the sculptor Björn Dahlem, who rents space in Brandlhuber’s villa. Dahlem’s art is inspired by astronomy, not anatomy.
match_headline: A Former German Underwear Factory, Now an Elegant Concrete Villa

text: A picture caption on March 13 with an article about Sydney Bennett, leader of the band the Internet, misspelled the surname of the band’s bassist. He is Patrick Paige II, not Page.

An article on March 13 about the rapper Kendrick Lamar and his song “The Blacker the Berry” paraphrased incorrectly the lyrics of a song by Lauryn Hill. She criticized black women who wear hair weaves that look European; she did not say that they got the weaves from Koreans.
match_headline: Documenting Violence Against Women, Even if It’s Hard to Look

text: An article last Sunday about Natasha Gregson Wagner, the daughter of Natalie Wood, misstated her age. Although she told the reporter that she was 46, her husband pointed out to her after the article was published that she was still 45. 
match_headline: A Mother’s Death, a Daughter’s Life: Remembering Natalie Wood

text: An article on March 13 about the 50th anniversary of Jacqueline Susann’s “Valley of the Dolls” overstated what is known about the source of a quotation about Ms. Susann’s writing. While the author Barbara Seaman attributed the line “she doesn’t write, she types” to Gore Vidal in her biography of Ms. Susann, “Lovely Me: The Life of Jacqueline Susann,” it is more commonly associated with Truman Capote, who said it on a television talk show in 1959 when dismissing the work of Jack Kerouac, the author of “On the Road.”
match_headline: ‘Valley of the Dolls,’ Pitched to a New Generation

text: An article last Sunday about a new building at 251 First Street in Park Slope, Brooklyn, using information from a publicist for the development, misstated the name of one of the development partners. It is Vanke US, not China Vanke.
match_headline: Stroller Valet Service at a Park Slope Condo

text: An article last Sunday about a new cruise in the Dominican Republic misstated the status of Amber Cove, a port built by Carnival Cruise Line. It is fully built, not under construction.
match_headline: At a New Dominican Port, Cruising With a Conscience

text: A headline and an accompanying picture caption last Sunday with the Q&A column, featuring the chief executive of a worldwide expeditions company, misspelled his surname. As the column correctly noted, the executive is Sven Lindblad, not Linblad.
match_headline: Sven Lindblad Takes Passengers to the Wild Places

text: An entry on the young adult hardcover best-seller list last Sunday misstated the age range for the novel “This Is Where It Ends,” by Marieke Nijkamp. The book, a vivid depiction of a school shooting, is recommended for readers 14 and up, not 10 and up.
match_headline: A Coloring Book From the Garden

text: A review on March 13 about “For a Little While,” a story collection by Rick Bass, misidentified a highway that offers motorists driving up from the south of Florence, Mont., a ready view of environmental damage to the region’s forests. It is Route 93 — not I-90, which is an east-west road passing to the north of Florence.
match_headline: ‘For a Little While,’ by Rick Bass

text: An article last Sunday about the San Francisco office of Ellen Richey of Visa omitted part of Ms. Richey’s title. She is vice chairwoman of risk and public policy, not of public policy alone.
match_headline: Ellen Richey: Falcons Out the Window and the Whole World on a Screen

text: An article on Friday about the criticism of a North Carolina law that eliminates anti-discrimination protections misstated the surname of the mayor of Charlotte, who opposed the measure. She is Jennifer Roberts, not Rogers.
match_headline: North Carolina Gay Bias Law Draws a Sharp Backlash

text: An article on Friday about a congressional plan to address Puerto Rico’s financial crisis misstated, in some copies, when the island made its case to the Supreme Court. It was on Tuesday, not last week.
match_headline: Plan to Rescue Puerto Rico Advances, Led by House Republicans

text: An obituary on March 18 about the singer Frank Sinatra Jr. misstated his given name at birth. He was born Francis Wayne Sinatra, not Franklin.
match_headline: Frank Sinatra Jr., Singer Who Followed in His Father’s Footsteps, Dies at 72

text: An article in some editions last Tuesday about the Islanders’ 4-1 loss to the Philadelphia Flyers described incorrectly in some copies the Islanders’ position in the N.H.L. playoff race at the time. The Islanders led the Detroit Red Wings by 2 points for the first wild-card spot, not the second wild-card spot.
match_headline: Islanders, Listless in Loss, Allow Flyers to Close In

text: An article on Friday about Albert Camus’s visit to New York City 70 years ago misspelled the name of the theater where Camus spoke at Columbia University and omitted part of its name. It was the McMillin Academic Theater, not the McMillan Theater. (It is now the Miller Theater.) The article was accompanied by a picture that was published in error and whose caption misidentified the building shown. The photograph was of Buell Hall where Columbia’s Maison Française is housed, not the Miller Theater.
match_headline: Albert Camus, Stranger in a Strange Land: New York

text: A picture caption on Friday with an art review of “Edgar Degas: A Strange New Beauty” at the Museum of Modern Art, using information from the museum, omitted the name of one of the artists who created “The Ballet Master” (1876). Besides Degas, the work was also executed by Ludovic-Napoléon Lepic. (Lepic taught Degas the monotype technique featured in the work.)
ref_headline: Edgar Degas: A Strange New Beauty
match_headline: The Modern Degas You Haven’t Seen

text: An obituary on Friday about the Dutch soccer star Johan Cruyff misstated the year that he said, “There is no better medal than being acclaimed for your style,” after watching the Dutch national team compete in the World Cup. It was 1998, not 2008. (There was no World Cup in 2008.)
ref_headline: There is no better medal than being acclaimed for your style,
match_headline: Johan Cruyff, the High Priest of Dutch Soccer, Dies at 68

text: An obituary on Sunday about Robert Ebeling, an engineer who argued for a postponement of the launch of the space shuttle Challenger, rendered incorrectly the name of the university in San Luis Obispo, Calif., that he attended. It is California Polytechnic State University — not California State Polytechnic University, which is in Pomona.
match_headline: Robert Ebeling, Challenger Engineer Who Warned of Disaster, Dies at 89

text: An obituary on Wednesday by The Associated Press about Anker Jorgensen, a former prime minister of Denmark, misstated the year he stepped down as leader of the Social Democratic Party. It was 1987, not 1989.
match_headline: Florida Town Curbs Debauchery, and Pays the Price

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the increased abuse of the drug fentanyl referred incorrectly to the use of the drug in medical settings. While fentanyl was introduced in the 1960s to treat extreme pain, it did not appear in patches or as a lozenge until much later.
match_headline: Heroin Epidemic Is Yielding to a Deadlier Cousin: Fentanyl

text: An article on March 20 about the Islamic State’s preparations for last November’s Paris terrorist attacks misidentified the location of the Comptoir Voltaire bistro, the site of one of the attacks, a suicide bombing. The bistro is on Boulevard Voltaire, not Rue Voltaire.
match_headline: A View of ISIS’s Evolution in New Details of Paris Attacks

text: An article last Wednesday about Adelma Tapia Ruiz, a Peruvian woman who was killed in the terrorist attack at the Brussels airport, misstated the condition of Ms. Tapia’s husband, Christopher Delcambe. He was hurt in the attack; he was not unharmed. The article also included a quotation that misidentified the city in Peru the Tapia family came from. It is Pucallpa, not Iquitos.
match_headline: Alexander and Sascha Pinczowski, Siblings on Way to New York, Killed at Brussels Airport

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Israel’s relenting in a diplomatic dispute with Brazil over the Israeli government’s nomination of a former leader of Israel’s settler movement as its ambassador to Brasília misspelled, in one reference, the surname of the Brazilian president. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she is Dilma Rousseff, not Rouseff.
match_headline: Israel Changes Tack After Standoff With Brazil Over Dani Dayan

text: An article on Friday about the simmering frustrations of many Belgians over the country’s deep and longstanding divisions, which have been highlighted by last week’s terrorist attacks, misspelled the given name of a resident of the Molenbeek district of Brussels. He is Lieven Soete, not Leiven.
match_headline: In Belgium, a Country of Divisions, Patriotism Remains Subdued

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Andrew Auernheimer, a computer hacker who said he was behind a wave of anti-Semitic, racist fliers that appeared on printers at more than a dozen college campuses last week, including Princeton University, misstated, in some copies, the timing of a sit-in at Princeton that called for the removal of President Woodrow Wilson’s name from campus because of his racist positions. It was held in November, not earlier this year.
match_headline: Hacker Says He Printed Anti-Semitic and Racist Fliers at Colleges Across U.S.

text: An article on Saturday about the increasingly competitive “athleisure” apparel category — clothing, footwear and accessories that are suitable for work, workouts and leisure activities — misstated the size of the athleisure market in the United States. It is $97 billion annually — not $330 billion, which is the size of the entire apparel, footwear and accessories market.
match_headline: Products and Competition Stretch Market for ‘Athleisure’ Clothing

text: An obituary on Saturday about Santiago Erevia, a Vietnam War veteran who was found to have been denied the Medal of Honor for 45 years because he was Hispanic, misspelled the given name of his wife. She is Leticia Lopez Erevia, not Letica.
match_headline: Santiago Erevia, Once Denied Medal of Honor Over Ethnicity, Dies at 69

text: An article on Monday about a barrage of litigation against a Bangladeshi newspaper publisher at a time when criticism of the government has become risky referred incorrectly to the political leader Sheikh Hasina, whose 2007 arrest on corruption allegations was covered by the newspaper. Though she had been the nation’s prime minister and holds that office now, Ms. Hasina was not prime minister at the time of her arrest.
match_headline: Bangladesh Editor Faces 79 Court Cases After an Unusual Confession

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a party in Brazil’s governing coalition that withdrew its support from the embattled president, Dilma Rousseff, misstated the status of some of Ms. Rousseff’s cabinet ministers. Several ministers who belong to the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party have been asked by the party leadership to resign; they have not stepped down.
match_headline: Dilma Rousseff Loses Support From Key Part of Brazilian Coalition

text: An article on March 22 about Morocco’s request that the United Nations mission in Western Sahara close its military liaison office as part of an escalating quarrel between the Moroccan authorities and the United Nations secretary general, Ban Ki-moon, over the disputed territory of Western Sahara misspelled the name of the coastal city where the office is based. It is Dakhla, not Dhakla.
match_headline: Morocco Asks That U.N. Close Western Sahara Military Office

text: An article on Tuesday about Connecticut’s 86-65 victory over Texas in the quarterfinals of the N.C.A.A. women’s basketball tournament misstated the time span during which Connecticut has gone 120-1 with each victory in double digits. It is since a loss on March 12, 2013 — not “since their last regular-season loss on March 4, 2013.” (Connecticut’s last regular-season loss was actually on Nov. 17, 2014.)
ref_headline: since their last regular-season loss on March 4, 2013.
match_headline: Winning by Merely 21, UConn Makes 9th Straight Final Four

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about live broadcasting on Facebook misidentified the location of an interview with Wyclef Jean that was aired live by The Huffington Post. Mr. Jean was shown at the Brooklyn Bowl in Brooklyn, not at the one in Las Vegas.
match_headline: Facebook’s Live Videos Get Lots of Looks but No Money Yet

text: An article on Wednesday about the reclusive chairman of the Anbang Insurance Group of China, which has been pursuing deals for hotels and hotel chains in the United States, misstated the title of Chang Ping, a former employee of China’s Southern Weekend newspaper, who commented on the reason for an apology issued by that newspaper after it published an article identifying two directors of some of Anbang’s companies. He was its news department director, not its editor in chief.
match_headline: Starwood Bidder Is a Reclusive Chinese Insurer With Opaque Backing

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about tuberculosis in Vietnam referred imprecisely to the United States’ funding of The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. While the White House tried to reduce the American contribution to the fund in fiscal year 2016, the proposed cut was reversed by Congress.
match_headline: Vietnam’s Battle With Tuberculosis

text: A map in some editions on Friday with an article about the discovery of a possible new Viking settlement referred incorrectly to the location of the site. It is Point Rosee and is on the southwestern coast of Newfoundland, not Point Rosie on the southeastern coast.
match_headline: View From Space Hints at a New Viking Site in North America

text: An article on Tuesday about the rash of upsets at the Miami Open tennis tournament misidentified, in some editions, the country Andy Murray is from. It is Scotland, not England. The article also misidentified, in some editions, the tournament at which Serena Williams could have completed a Grand Slam. It was the 2015 United States Open, not the 2016 Australian Open. The article also misstated, in some editions, Williams’s finish at the 2015 United States Open. She lost in the semifinals; she did not win the tournament. Because of that error, the article misstated the timing of her last tournament victory. It was at an event a week before the United States Open, not at the Open.
match_headline: Serena Williams and Andy Murray Fall at Miami Open

text: An article on Thursday about the Mets’ eagerness to open the regular season against the Kansas City Royals with a clean slate after a poor spring misstated the game in the 2015 World Series that started with Mets pitcher Noah Syndergaard throwing high and inside to the Royals’ Alcides Escobar. It was Game 3, not Game 4.
match_headline: Mets Exit Camp, Eager to Be 0-0 Again

text: A review on Friday about “The Ranch,” on Netflix, was mislabeled. It was a television review, not a film review.
match_headline: Review: In ‘The Ranch,’ Ashton Kutcher and Danny Masterson Reunite as Cowboy Siblings

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the jazz musician and educator David Baker misstated his position at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. He was a distinguished professor, not a distinguished professor emeritus. The obituary also misstated his role in the introduction of the Smithsonian Jazz Masterworks Orchestra. He and Gunther Schuller were the original artistic directors of the orchestra, not the founders. And, using information from Mr. Baker’s biographer, the obituary erroneously attributed a distinction to him. When he was hired in 1966, he was the Indiana music school’s second African-American faculty member, not the only one.
match_headline: David Baker, Who Helped Bring Jazz Studies Into the Academy, Dies at 84

text: An article on March 20 about wave navigation in the Marshall Islands misstated part of the name of the organization that teaches students to build canoes using traditional methods and modern materials. It is Canoes of the Marshall Islands, not Canoes of Tese Islands. The article also misspelled part of the name of an organization in Norway. It is the Kavli Institute for Systems Neuroscience in Norway (not the Kavil).
match_headline: The Secrets of the Wave Pilots

text: An article on March 20 about Jan Baalsrud, a member of the Norwegian resistance in World War II, misstated the age of Tore Haug, an authority on Baalsrud. He is 74, not 75.
match_headline: The Fugitive

text: An article on March 20 about a 1968 North Pole expedition referred incorrectly to newspapers in Minneapolis in 1966. The city had two papers, the morning Minneapolis Tribune and the evening Minneapolis Star; there was no paper named The Minneapolis Star Tribune at the time. (The papers merged in 1982.)
match_headline: An Insurance Salesman and a Doctor Walk Into a Bar, and End Up at the North Pole

text: An article on March 20 about Sir John Franklin’s doomed expedition to find the Northwest Passage misstated the date in 1848 when Franklin and his crew abandoned their ships. It was April 22, not April 25. The article also misspelled the surname of the first explorer to navigate the Northwest Passage. He is Roald Amundsen, not Admunsen.
match_headline: Artifacts of a Doomed Expedition

text: An article on March 20 about the Chinese artist Cai Guo-Qiang’s exhibition of contemporary Chinese art in Qatar misspelled part of the name of the studio that provided a photograph of “Big Dog,” a piece that incorporates a fictional city made of dog chews. It is Liu Wei Studio, not Lui Wei Studio.
match_headline: Redefining Chinese Artists, in Qatar

text: An article last Sunday about the director Chantal Akerman referred incorrectly to the release of her final film, “No Home Movie.” It debuted at the Locarno Festival in August 2015 and at the New York Film Festival after her death, in October 2015, and was released this past Friday. It was not released last October.
match_headline: The Director’s Director: Chantal Akerman

text: A picture caption with an article on Feb. 8, 2015, about the musical “Hamilton” referred incorrectly to an image of Alexander Hamilton. It was a portrait of Hamilton, painted around 1806; it was not “Hamilton around 1806.” (He died in 1804.)
match_headline: Rapping a Revolution

text: An article last Sunday about Ultimate Fighting Championship’s efforts to bring mixed martial arts events to New York described a fight between two M.M.A. fighters, Conor McGregor and Nate Diaz, incorrectly. Mr. McGregor, who typically fights as a featherweight, was fighting as a welterweight; he was not competing for the welterweight title. The article also misstated the weight gain necessary for the match. Mr. McGregor gained 25 pounds, not 15.
match_headline: Fighting a Cage Match to Turn UFC Into a National Phenomenon

text: A review on March 20 about two books on the history of eugenics in America misspelled part of the name of the test on which authorities relied to assess the mental ability of Carrie Buck, a Virginia woman whose forced sterilization was upheld by the United States Supreme Court in 1927. It was the Binet-Simon Intelligence Test, not Benet-Simon.
match_headline: ‘Imbeciles’ and ‘Illiberal Reformers’
