text: An article last Sunday about a mountainous region of Bolivia rendered the name of an indigenous people incorrectly. As accompanying captions correctly noted, they are the Jalq’a, not the Jal’qa.
match_headline: In the Mountains of Bolivia, Encounters With Magic

text: An article last Sunday about travel and allergies misstated the number of hotels with hypoallergenic rooms reviewed on the site AllerPassMD.com . It is more than 1,200, not 200.
match_headline: Travel and Allergies: What to Do When Animals Are on Board

text: A news analysis on March 20 about mindfulness misstated the rate for a meditation class at Mndfl, aNew York studio. It is $20 for a 45-minute class, not for a 30-minute class.
match_headline: The Hidden Price of Mindfulness Inc.

text: A news analysis on March 20 about how Donald J. Trump might redecorate the White House misidentified its first architect. It was James Hoban, not Pierre L’Enfant.
match_headline: How Will Trump Redecorate the White House?

text: An article last Tuesday about the ways in which the Islamic State built its terrorist machine to attack Europe referred incorrectly to information about its planning that the group posted on Dar al-Islam, its online French magazine. As the Islamic State noted in its post, the information came from a study first published on the French security blog kurultay.fr ; it was not the Islamic State’s original explanation about its tactics in planning terrorist attacks.
match_headline: How ISIS Built the Machinery of Terror Under Europe’s Gaze

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Feb. 25 about Egypt’s first acknowledgment that terrorists had downed the Russian jetliner that broke up over the Sinai Peninsula in the fall omitted part of a quotation from President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. He said: “Those who downed the flight, what were they hoping for? Just to hit tourism? No, but also to hit relations. To hit relations with Russia, to hit relations with Italy. And if they could with the whole world, they would. So we would be alone and isolated.” While the error was promptly corrected online, editors failed to follow through on this print correction.
match_headline: In Reversal, Egypt Says Terrorists Downed Russian Jet Over Sinai

text: An article on Monday about roughly 11.5 million leaked documents from a Panama law firm that helped some of the world’s wealthiest people — including politicians, athletes and business moguls — establish offshore bank accounts misstated the year that Edward J. Snowden, a contractor for the National Security Agency, gave reporters documents from the N.S.A., and the number of documents he gave them. It was 2013, not 2014; and it was thousands of documents, not “at least 1.5 million.”
match_headline: Panama Law Firm’s Leaked Files Detail Offshore Accounts Tied to World Leaders

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about a bull that escaped from a holding area for livestock in Queens misstated, in some copies, the way in which the Animal Care Centers of NYC acquired the bull after it was captured. Staff members at the center started to collect money to buy the bull, which was taken to Farm Sanctuary’s shelter in Watkins Glen, N.Y., but the group ultimately did not have to pay for it. The error was repeated in a picture caption in some copies.
match_headline: Bull in Queens Is Captured, and Jon Stewart Chauffeurs It to Freedom

text: An article on Monday about the victims of an investment scheme operated by Andrew Casperson, a former Wall Street executive, misstated the amount of Mr. Caspersen’s bond in some copies. He posted a $5 million bond, not $5 billion.
match_headline: Victim in Wall St. Scheme Was a Classmate of Its Accused Architect

text: An article on March 28 about advertising campaigns by hotel chains seeking to get customers to book directly with them misstated the proportions of Americans who booked hotel rooms last year through online travel agencies and those who booked directly through a hotel website; 31 percent used online agencies, not 34 percent, and 28 percent booked directly, not 66 percent.
match_headline: Hotel Chains and Travel Websites in a Tug of War for Customers

text: A picture caption on Saturday with a music review of a tribute concert honoring David Bowie at Carnegie Hall misstated the surname of a musician shown performing. He is Matt Katz-Bohen, not Katz-Bohe.
match_headline: Review: Remembering David Bowie, With One Artist and One Song at a Time

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Cesar Gonzales-Mugaburu, a Long Island foster father charged with sexually abusing at least five children and endangering two others, misstated, in some editions, the current age of a man whom he adopted as a boy. The man turned 26 on Saturday; he is not 25.
match_headline: An ‘Exemplary’ Foster Father, a String of Suspicions and Sexual-Abuse Charges

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Feb. 21 about the re-election of Yoweri Museveni as president of Uganda referred incorrectly to his years in office. He is entering his fourth decade as president, not his third. The error was repeated in a picture caption. This correction was delayed because editors did not follow through after a reader pointed out the error in February.
match_headline: Yoweri Museveni, Uganda’s President, Wins a Widely Criticized Election

text: An article on Monday about a study of the drug evacetrapib that found it had no effect in preventing heart attacks, strokes or death from heart disease misstated the cost of a different class of cholesterol drugs known as PCSK-9 inhibitors. They can cost more than $14,000 a year, not a month.
match_headline: Dashing Hopes, Study Shows a Cholesterol Drug Had No Effect on Heart Health

text: An article on Monday about New Day, a new print-only daily publication in Britain, described incorrectly the publishing format of Politico, an American publication. Politico publishes a print newspaper and a magazine; it is not a digital-only publication.
match_headline: The New Day, a British Upstart, Casts Its Fate to the Newsstand

text: An article on Saturday about the potential hazards of engineered stone to workers who fashion it into so-called quartz countertops misidentified the natural stone material that has about half the amount of silica as engineered stone. It is granite, not marble.
match_headline: Popular Quartz Countertops Pose a Risk to Workers

text: An article on Saturday about the revival of the Pabst Brewing Company misspelled the surname of the billionaire investor who bought Pabst in 2010. He is C. Dean Metropoulos, not Metropolous. The article also misidentified the city from which Mr. Metropoulos moved the brewery’s headquarters. He moved it to Los Angeles from Chicago, not from Milwaukee.
match_headline: Pabst Raids Dad’s Beer Fridge as It Looks to the Future

text: An article in some copies on Friday about an agreement by the two largest daily fantasy sports sites, FanDuel and DraftKings, to indefinitely suspend contests involving college sports misstated the way the sites characterize themselves. They consider themselves to be games of skill, not of chance.
match_headline: FanDuel and DraftKings Suspend College Sports Contests

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Islanders forward Cal Clutterbuck misstated, in some editions, Frans Nielsen’s status with the Islanders during the 2006-7 season, when Clutterbuck and John Tavares were teammates with the Oshawa Generals of the Ontario Hockey League. Nielsen was in his first season with the Islanders, not his second.
match_headline: Cal Clutterbuck Churns Out Big Goals for Islanders

text: Because of an editing error, the byline for an article on Saturday about ice problems at Barclays Center for Islanders games misspelled the given name of the reporter. He is Allan Kreda, not Allen.
match_headline: Islanders Play for Home Ice, Be It Ever So Slushy

text: An article last Wednesday about the Indian cooking instructor Raghavan Iyer misidentified the source of his recipe for sambhar, a vegetable stew. It was his grandmother, not his mother-in-law.
match_headline: An Indian Spice Mix, Sambhar Masala, for All Seasons

text: An obituary on Sunday about the counterculture personality Coca Crystal misstated the month in 1977 that the conservative activist Phyllis Schlafly was hit with a pie, an act for which a group to which Ms. Crystal belonged took responsibility. It was April, not November.
match_headline: Coca Crystal, Avatar of Counterculture and Provocateur, Dies at 68

text: An article on Feb. 23 about Beijing’s plans to issue red alerts over air pollution in the city based on higher thresholds, despite government pledges to better address the toxic air, misstated, in some editions, the location of Shaanxi Province, which plans to build ventilation corridors to improve urban air circulation. It is in northwestern China, not northeastern China. While the error was promptly corrected online, editors failed to follow through on this print correction.
match_headline: Beijing to Raise Threshold on Red Alerts for Smog

text: An article on Wednesday about a backlash in the South against anti-gay laws misstated Duke Energy’s position regarding North Carolina’s law banning anti-discrimination protections based on sexual orientation. While Duke came out strongly in opposition to discrimination against gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people, it did not take a position on the law itself.
match_headline: Anti-Gay Laws Bring Backlash in Mississippi and North Carolina

text: An article on March 30 about a report on an increase in the amount of benefits denied to veterans misstated the year in which Joshua Bunn, who is trying to get permanent benefits, and his battalion saw the heaviest fighting in Afghanistan. It was 2008, not 2009.
match_headline: Report Finds Sharp Increase in Veterans Denied V.A. Benefits

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about an apparent New York Police Department tactic in which undercover officers target drug addicts for small-scale drug prosecutions misspelled the given name of a 21-year-old heroin addict who the police said bought drugs near a school for an officer on the Lower East Side. The man, who spoke on the condition that only the first initial of his surname be used, is Bryan L., not Brian. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Undercover Officers Ask Addicts to Buy Drugs, Snaring Them but Not Dealers

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the book “The Devil’s Diary: Alfred Rosenberg and the Stolen Secrets of the Third Reich,” using information from the book, misstated the setting of the picture of Rosenberg and Hitler and Friedrich Weber. They are shown at the groundbreaking of a World War I memorial in Munich in early November 1923 — not during the Munich Putsch, which occurred a few days later.
ref_headline: The Devil’s Diary: Alfred Rosenberg and the Stolen Secrets of the Third Reich,
match_headline: Tracking an Elusive Diary From Hitler’s Inner Circle

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Senator Bernie Sanders’s victory in the Wisconsin primary misstated the number of pledged delegates that preliminary results showed that Hillary Clinton had won in the contest. Those initial results gave her 31 delegates, not 13. (After the final tabulations, she won 38 to Mr. Sanders’s 48 .)
match_headline: Bernie Sanders Wins Wisconsin Democratic Primary, Adding to Momentum

text: An obituary on Thursday about the singer Merle Haggard misquoted one line in his song “Hungry Eyes.” The line is “And tried to feed my mama’s hungry eyes,” not “my mother’s.” The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Haggard’s recording of the song “That’s the Way Love Goes,” for which he won a Grammy Award in 1985. It was not a duet with Willie Nelson.
match_headline: Merle Haggard, Country Music’s Outlaw Hero, Dies at 79

text: A picture caption on Feb. 27 with an article about the 30th anniversary of the unsolved assassination of Olof Palme, Sweden’s prime minister, misidentified his political party. As the article correctly noted, it is the Social Democratic Party, not the Swedish Democratic Party. While the error was promptly corrected online, editors failed to follow through on this print correction.
match_headline: Questions Nag in Sweden 30 Years After Leader’s Assassination

text: An article on Thursday about the fatal beating of 17-year-old Ta’Jae Warner in Brooklyn misspelled, in some copies, the given name of one of her friends. She is Annastasia Elson, not Annastaisa.
match_headline: Brooklyn Girl, 17, Dies 4 Days After an Attack Outside Her Home

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about how the 1964 Kitty Genovese murder in Kew Gardens, Queens, still resonates in the neighborhood misidentified the location as shown that year. As the caption correctly noted for two other photographs, the picture showed a walkway behind Austin Street, not Austin Street itself.
match_headline: Queens Neighborhood Still Haunted by Kitty Genovese’s Murder

text: An article on Thursday about a suit filed against Volkswagen by the owner of three dealerships in the United States referred incorrectly to recent sales for the Volkswagen brands Audi and Porsche. In the first three months of the year, Audi sales in the United States rose 4.6 percent, and Porsche sales were up 7.1 percent; their sales did not drop steeply.
match_headline: Owner of 3 VW Dealerships Sues Carmaker Over Diesel Scandal

text: An article on Monday about a Gatorade advertising campaign on Snapchat described incorrectly a function of the Gatorade “sponsored lens.” It can overlay an animation of a bucket of Gatorade being dumped on a Snapchat user’s photos or video clips. It cannot do the same on photos or video clips of the user’s friends.
match_headline: As Messaging Apps Boom, Brands Tiptoe In

text: An article on Thursday about a program that encourages start-ups to address the problems of people without bank accounts misspelled the surname of the chief executive of Neighborhood Trust Financial Partners, which created PayGoal, a phone app that helps people make better financial decisions. She is Justine Zinkin, not Zinkine.
match_headline: Start-Ups Aim at Overlooked Demographic: The Unbanked

text: An article on Friday about the reasons certain immigrants in New York support Donald J. Trump misstated the status of lawsuits against the school board in the East Ramapo Central School District in Rockland County, where one resident said that he supported Mr. Trump because he believed the Democrats had not helped immigrants like himself and that he was fed up with the corruption and resulting lack of resources in the school district. The suits have been settled; the school board is not still facing them. The article also misstated the focus of an F.B.I. inquiry. The F.B.I. is investigating local religious schools, not the school district.
match_headline: Immigrants for Donald Trump? Some in New York Show Their Support

text: An article last Saturday about fans’ reactions to a crucial play at the plate during Game 5 of the 2015 World Series misspelled the given name of a woman who said: “I’m a Met fan. There is a shoe that’s gonna drop. I mean there has to be.” She is Debby Riegel, not Debbie.
ref_headline: I’m a Met fan. There is a shoe that’s gonna drop. I mean there has to be.
match_headline: Frenchman Plotting ‘Imminent’ Attack Is Charged With Terrorism

text: Because of an editing error, an Associated Press report in some copies of the N.B.A. roundup last Saturday about the Memphis Grizzlies signing guard Bryce Cotton misidentified the location of the April 1 game between the Grizzlies and the Toronto Raptors. It was in Memphis, not in Toronto.

An article last Sunday about unusual incidents in baseball history misidentified the team for which Hank Aaron played on Aug. 18, 1965, when he had a home run disallowed because the umpire ruled that he hit the pitch while out of the batter’s box. It was the Milwaukee Braves, not the Atlanta Braves. (The Braves moved from Milwaukee to Atlanta in 1966.)
match_headline: Baseball’s Enduring Oddities

text: A picture caption in some editions last Sunday with an article about Nyquist’s victory in the Florida Derby misspelled, in some copies, the surname of his jockey. As the article correctly noted, he is Mario Gutierrez, not Gutuerrez.
match_headline: Nyquist Wins in Florida, Establishing Himself as the Favorite in Kentucky

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Villanova’s 95-51 victory over Oklahoma in the national semifinals of the N.C.A.A. men’s college basketball tournament misstated Oklahoma’s margin of victory in its first meeting with Villanova this season. The Sooners won by 23 points, not 28.
match_headline: Villanova Wipes Out Oklahoma and a Record to Reach the Title Game

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about the Islanders’ 5-0 loss to the Pittsburgh Penguins misstated, in some copies, the score of the Islanders’ victory over the Columbus Blue Jackets a few days before. It was 4-3, not 4-1.
match_headline: Penguins Pour It On Against Islanders

text: An obituary in some editions last Sunday about the saxophonist Gato Barbieri misstated his given name. Though he went by Gato, he was born Leandro Barbieri, not Leonardo. The error was repeated in the headline and in a picture caption.
match_headline: Gato Barbieri, Latin Jazz Trailblazer With a Saxophone, Is Dead at 83

text: A review on March 27 about “The Abundance,” a collection of essays by Annie Dillard, referred incorrectly to luciferin, a naturally occurring chemical involved in a firefly’s glow. Luciferin is the substrate in a chemical reaction catalyzed by the enzyme luciferase — it is not itself an enzyme.
match_headline: ‘The Abundance,’ by Annie Dillard

text: An article last Sunday about Premier Cru, a Berkeley, Calif., wine store that is under investigation on suspicion of running a Ponzi scheme on futures contracts for French wines, erroneously included one person among the creditors or customers of the store. William Koch, of Medford, Ore., was in that group; William I. Koch, the Palm Beach, Fla., billionaire, was not.
match_headline: Claims of a Ponzi Scheme in the Collapse of a Rare-Wine Seller

text: An article last Sunday about Juicero, a Silicon Valley company that has developed a $700 cold-press juicer as well as packaged ingredients for it, described the Tovala, another high-tech kitchen appliance, incorrectly. It is a programmable oven that can bake, broil, steam or heat by convection in any sequence. It is not a combination microwave/toaster.
match_headline: A $700 Juicer for the Kitchen That Caught Silicon Valley’s Eye

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about the star of the Broadway show “Fully Committed” misstated his middle name. As the article correctly noted, he is Jesse Tyler Ferguson, not Taylor.
match_headline: Jesse Tyler Ferguson Skewers Food Culture on Broadway

text: An article last Sunday about a resurgence of art exhibitions featuring work by only women included an outdated title for an exhibition planned at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles next year. It is “Radical Women: Latin American Art, 1960-1985,” no longer “The Political Body: Radical Women in Latin America 1960-1985.”
match_headline: Female Artists Are (Finally) Getting Their Turn

text: A news analysis on March 27 about Radovan Karadzic misidentified the tribunal that convicted him. It is the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, not the International Criminal Court.
match_headline: A Case of Deadly Delusions

text: A picture caption with an opinion article last Sunday about slaves’ graves described incorrectly the statue in the photograph. It is in honor of a woman who was born into slavery; it is not a statue of that woman.
match_headline: Why Slaves’ Graves Matter

text: An article on March 29 about an assessment of the damage done by the Islamic State to the ancient Syrian city of Palmyra referred incorrectly to the second-century triple arch ISIS destroyed. The arches were decorative, not triumphal, and therefore were not built by the Romans to celebrate their victory over the Persians. The errors also appeared in another article on March 29, as well as in a picture caption, about efforts to create three-dimensional digital models of Palmyra’s threatened monuments in case the originals are damaged beyond repair, and the errors were repeated last Tuesday in a photo essay and in a caption by a Times photographer who visited Palmyra to document the destruction. The errors also appeared in an article and a picture caption on Oct. 6, 2015, about ISIS’ destruction of the arches.
match_headline: Scenes From Palmyra Indicate ISIS Slowed Assault on Treasures

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about a Bronx woman who was found guilty of killing her two children misstated the charges on which she was convicted. The woman, Lisette Bamenga, was convicted of two counts of manslaughter, not murder.
match_headline: Bronx Woman Convicted of Poisoning and Drowning Her Children

text: An article on Saturday about a visit by Bernie Sanders to his old neighborhood in Brooklyn to campaign referred incorrectly in some copies to Mr. Sanders’s departure from Brooklyn College. He left the school; he did not graduate from it. The article also misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a tenant of Mr. Sanders’s former apartment building in Midwood. She is Morgan McIlvain, not McIvain.
match_headline: Bernie Sanders Back in the Old Neighborhood to Make His Case

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about switching to an iPhone from an Android device misstated the content of a Google web page. It has tips for those switching from an Apple iPhone, not to it.
match_headline: How to Switch to iPhone From Android: Patience and Persistence

text: An article on Monday about a gathering of more than 200 female comedians in Brooklyn to have their picture taken together omitted a founder of a private Facebook group for female comedians in New York. Besides Selena Coppock, Katie Compa helped start the group.
match_headline: A Roomful of Funny Women, Bonding Over the New York Comedy Life

text: An obituary on Monday and in some editions on Sunday about the experimental filmmaker and musician Tony Conrad misspelled the surname of the New York Times film critic who praised Mr. Conrad’s film “Coming Attractions.” He is Roger Greenspun, not Greenspan. The obituary in some editions on Sunday misstated the year of Mr. Conrad’s first film, “The Flicker.” It was 1966, not 1965. It also referred incorrectly to Mr. Conrad’s wife, Paige Sarlin. She is his third wife, not his second. And it misstated the year in which Branden W. Joseph’s book “Beyond the Dream Syndicate: Tony Conrad and the Arts After Cage” was published. It was 2008, not 2007.
match_headline: Tony Conrad, Experimental Filmmaker and Musician, Dies at 76

text: An obituary on Monday about the former New York City chief medical examiner Dr. Charles S. Hirsch misspelled the given name of his wife, who died before him. She was Marie-Claude, not Marie-Calude.
match_headline: Charles S. Hirsch, New York’s Chief Medical Examiner on 9/11, Dies at 79

text: An article on Feb. 27 about Japan’s loss of nearly a million people in the last five years, an exceptional drop for a society not ravaged by war or other deadly crisis, referred imprecisely to the population decline. Although the term “inflection point” can be used colloquially to mean a “dramatic change,” in mathematics, the term means the point in a curve at which the shape changes concavity, bending up instead of down, for example. Under that definition, Japan’s inflection point occurred in the late 1970s, when its rate of growth slowed — not in 2015. While the error was promptly corrected online, editors failed to follow through on this print correction.
match_headline: Japan Lost Nearly a Million People in 5 Years, Census Says

text: An article on Feb. 25 about questions concerning the World Health Organization’s hiring of the wife of the deputy foreign minister of Syria — a powerful defender of the government’s war effort — to help assess the mental health of Syrians forced to flee their homes misstated the number of attacks on hospitals and health centers in Syria that Physicians for Human Rights has documented since the war began. It is 346, not 386. Because of an editing error, a picture credit with the article misidentified the photographer in some editions. The picture, of food aid delivered near Damascus, was taken by Abd Doumany, not Amer Almohibany. While the text error was promptly corrected online, editors failed to follow through on the print correction for that and the credit error.
match_headline: U.N. Agency Hires Wife of Top Figure in Syrian War to Assist the Displaced

text: An article last Wednesday about the questioning of top police officials in connection with an inquiry into two businessmen’s ties to Mayor Bill de Blasio misstated the connection between one of those men and a property at 23 Wall Street. JSR Capital L.L.C., a real estate company owned by Jona Rechnitz, one of the businessmen, was previously the owner’s representative and manager of 23 Wall Street, according to JSR’s website. It does not own the property.
match_headline: Police Leaders Questioned Amid Inquiry of Businessmen Linked to de Blasio

text: An article on April 1 about a changing of the guard at the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers described incorrectly a change in the role of John Doerr, who has been its day-to-day manager and will become its chairman. Mr. Doerr will continue to invest in new start-ups; it is not the case that he will not make such investments. However, he will no longer have fiduciary responsibility for the success of those investments.
match_headline: John Doerr to Step Aside and Become Chairman at Kleiner Perkins

text: An article on Saturday about a novel student loan program at Purdue University described the debt level of Purdue graduates incorrectly. The average graduate with debt emerges owing $28,000; that is not the debt level of average graduates over all.
match_headline: Getting a Student Loan With Collateral From a Future Job

text: An obituary on Saturday about the horse owner and breeder Ogden Mills Phipps omitted part of the name of his paternal grandmother. She was Gladys Livingston Mills Phipps, not Gladys Livingston Phipps.
match_headline: Ogden Mills Phipps, Horseman From a Leading Racing Family, Dies at 75

text: Because of an editing error, a report in some editions of the World Briefing column on March 15 about the reopening of a Paris restaurant that was the scene of an attack by Islamic State terrorists in November misstated part of the restaurant’s name at one point. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, it is Le Petit Cambodge, not La.
match_headline: France: A Restaurant Begins Again

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about ride-hailing services aimed at children whose parents cannot chauffeur them misstated part of the name of a service in Los Angeles. As the article correctly noted, it is HopSkipDrive, not HopSkipRide.
match_headline: Ride-Hailing Start-Ups Compete in ‘Uber for Children’ Niche

text: An article on Thursday about the broader economic questions behind the strike at Verizon misstated the day Verizon announced that it would expand its Fios service in Boston. It was Tuesday, not Monday.
match_headline: In Verizon Strike, Blue-Collar Stress Hits the Sidewalks

text: An article on Saturday about two recently added works at the Brooklyn Museum related to gentrification, including a video by the Illuminator collective, misstated part of the name of a tenants group with which the collective worked. It is the Crown Heights Tenant Union, not the Crown Heights Tenants Association. Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the article referred incorrectly to Alicia Boyd and to the exhibition “Agitprop!” Ms. Boyd helped create a work on display, not the overall exhibition. And while the exhibition includes the works on gentrification, it covers the way artists have used their work to press for political change; it is not solely about local gentrification.
match_headline: Brooklyn Museum Puts Artwork From Its Critics on Display

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a Critic’s Notebook article about the Tribeca Film Festival reversed the identities of the actors shown kissing in a scene from “Women Who Kill.” Sheila Vand is at the left and Ingrid Jungermann is at the right.
match_headline: How to Make Sense of the Tribeca Film Festival

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the furniture designer Vladimir Kagan, using information from a family member, referred incorrectly to a photograph of a Jewish boy in Germany wearing a coat with a Star of David on it. The picture is not of Mr. Kagan; the identity of the boy has not been determined. And the obituary referred incorrectly in some copies to Illya Kagan, one of Mr. Kagan’s survivors. Illya is Vladimir’s son, not his brother.
match_headline: Vladimir Kagan, Designer Whose Furniture Evoked Sensuality, Dies at 88

text: A picture caption on Friday with the continuation of an article about James Levine’s decision to step down as music director of the Metropolitan Opera misidentified the location where he was shown conducting in the early 1970s. He was in Kulas Hall at the Cleveland Institute of Music, not at the Met.
match_headline: James Levine, Transformative at the Met Opera, Is Stepping Down

text: An article on Thursday about how changes at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, the site of a debate that night between the Democratic presidential candidates, reflect an evolving economy misidentified a company that is building a motorcycle prototype there. It is FXE Industries, not Design Necessities Initiative.
match_headline: Presidential Debate Stage in Brooklyn Reflects Changing Economy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Yahoo’s reluctance to share financial details with prospective buyers misstated the amount the company hoped to raise by selling patents and real estate. The amount is $1 billion to $3 billion, not $1 billion to $35 billion.
match_headline: Yahoo’s Suitors Uncover Few Financial Details

text: An article on Page 120 this weekend about the increasing availability of specialty fruits refers incorrectly to a biological stage of development. The larval stage applies to the animal kingdom, not to plants. The article also describes several fruits incorrectly. The pink variegated lemon, the baby kiwi and the purple-fleshed dragon fruit are specialty fruits — not hybrids. And an accompanying picture caption also describes the fruits incorrectly. They are a mix of tropical, hybrid and specialty fruits, not just tropical and hybrid fruits.
match_headline: Strange Fruits

text: A subheading on Page 116 this weekend with an article about plans for the new Silicon Valley headquarters of Google and Apple, and the ways in which they are influenced by utopian-minded 1960s ideas, refers incorrectly to the design of one of the headquarters. It is the design of Google’s headquarters — not of Apple’s — that can be said to resemble larvae. The article also refers incorrectly to the technology company Silicon Graphics. Although the company went bankrupt in 2009, its assets were purchased by another company, and today it operates as Silicon Graphics International; it is not “long-defunct.”
match_headline: Google and Apple: the High-Tech Hippies of Silicon Valley

text: A picture credit on Page 69 this weekend with an article featuring a conversation between the cultural critic Leon Wieseltier and the comedian Chelsea Handler misstates the name of a hair and makeup agency whose services were used in styling Wieseltier. It is L’Atelier NYC, not L’atalier. The article also includes outdated information about Chelsea Handler’s talk show. After the article had gone to press, Handler announced that the show will be titled “Chelsea.” It is not untitled.
match_headline: When Chelsea Handler Met Leon Wieseltier

text: A picture caption on Page 60 this weekend with an article about the behind-the-scenes workers who make the Metropolitan Museum of Art function misstates the name of the main entry hall of the museum. It is the Great Hall, not the Grand Hall.
match_headline: Behind the Scenes at the Met

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the British playwright Arnold Wesker misstated the given name of the New York Times drama critic who reviewed Mr. Wesker’s play “Roots.” He was Howard Taubman, not Harold.
match_headline: Arnold Wesker, 83, Writer of Working-Class Dramas, Dies

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about how Brooklyn is the center of the next political contest between the Democratic presidential candidates Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders misspelled the surname of a senior designer on Hillary Clinton’s campaign who works at her Brooklyn headquarters and misstated her age. She is Meg Vazquez, not Vasquez, and she is 26, not 25.
match_headline: Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders Bring Their Battle to Brooklyn

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the third round of the Masters golf tournament misstated the number of bogeys Rory McIlroy had in his round. It was three, not two. The article also misstated the distance of Jason Day’s birdie putt at the 14th hole. It was 69 feet, not 60 yards.
match_headline: Jordan Spieth’s Lead Disappears

text: An obituary last Sunday about the lawyer Robert MacCrate omitted the name of the organization that gave him its Gold Medal in 1999. It is the New York State Bar Association. (He also received the American Bar Association’s highest honor, the ABA Medal, in 2001.)
match_headline: Robert MacCrate, Lawyer in My Lai Inquiry, Dies at 94

text: An article last Sunday about the Miami City Ballet misstated the role of Edward Villella in the troupe’s founding. He was the founding director, not the founder. (Toby Ansin was the ballet’s founder.)
match_headline: Miami City Ballet: Feeling That Warmth and Attack

text: A picture caption last Sunday with a cover article about the Wendels, a real estate dynasty in New York during the 19th and early 20th centuries, referred incorrectly to the Wendel mansion shown. The photograph was taken around 1905, not 1931, and the house was at the northwest corner of Fifth Avenue and 39th Street, not on Fifth Avenue between 38th and 39th Streets.
match_headline: Before the Trumps, There Were the Wendels

text: An article on Feb. 21 about the efforts taken by Palau to stop illegal fishing in its waters referred incorrectly to the percentage of illegally caught fish that is consumed. One in every five fish consumed globally — not in the United States — is caught illegally.
match_headline: Palau vs. the Poachers

text: An article on April 3 about a methane leak in Los Angeles misstated the amount by which the Aliso Canyon leak increased the rate of methane emissions in the Los Angeles Basin. The release of 58 metric tons per hour doubled the rate of emissions in the entire area; it was not double the rate.
match_headline: The Invisible Catastrophe

text: A review on April 3 about “The Dig,” by John Preston, referred incorrectly to the book. While it is now being published for the first time in the United States, it appeared in Britain in 2007; it is not Preston’s “new novel.”
match_headline: ‘The Dig,’ by John Preston

text: An article in the Mutual Fund Quarterly last Sunday about the role of junk bonds in an investment portfolio miscalculated the effect a 6 percent default rate would have on a broad junk bond portfolio. The loss would be 3.6 percentage points, not 2.4 percentage points. A further calculation based on that number misstated the return that would be left after that loss. It would be around 4 percent, not 5 percent or more.
match_headline: Junk Bonds: Never Stodgy and Steadier Than You Might Think

text: An article on Thursday about a confirmation by federal health officials that the Zika virus damages infant brains misstated the surname of the deputy director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She is Dr. Anne Schuchat, not Schucat.
match_headline: Zika Virus Causes Birth Defects, Health Officials Confirm

text: An article in some editions on Friday about a fire started by incense that killed two young sisters in a Bronx public housing complex misstated the surname of a spokeswoman for the New York City Housing Authority. She is Jean Weinberg, not Weisberg or Weisman.
match_headline: Incense Ignited Bronx Fire That Killed 2 Girls, Officials Say

text: An article in some editions on Friday about a decision by a nanny charged with murdering two children under her care to reject a plea deal that would have given her a sentence of 30 years to life in prison omitted the given name of the mother of the slain children. She is Marina Krim.
match_headline: Nanny Accused of Killing 2 Children in Manhattan Rejects a Plea Deal

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 19 about the Cheltenham Festival, a steeplechase event in horse racing, referred incorrectly to a nickname for the former Barclays executive Rich Ricci, the owner of the mare Annie Power. He earned the nickname Fat Cat in the Hat before Barclays paid a fine in 2012 for rigging interest rates and cheating its clients; the moniker did not arise after that. The article also misstated the amount that Barclays was fined. It was about $450 million, not $700 million.
match_headline: A Mix of Beer, Bragging Rights and Horse Races at the Cheltenham Festival

text: An article last Monday about Jordan Spieth’s collapse in the final round of the Masters misstated, in some editions, the spot from which he hit a wedge after his tee shot at the 12th hole went into a water hazard. He chose to drop his ball 80 yards from the hole; he was not in the designated drop area.
match_headline: Danny Willett Wins Masters as Jordan Spieth Folds

text: A report in the golf roundup on April 8 about Arnold Palmer’s not participating in the ceremonial first tee shot at the Masters misidentified, in some copies, one of the golfers who appeared in the interview room after the ceremony. Along with Jack Nicklaus, Gary Player was there — not Palmer.
match_headline: 9 Strokes, Then What? For Ernie Els, On to 2nd Hole

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the success of the U.S.A. Hockey National Team Development Program misstated, in some copies, the age of Jack Eichel, a program alumnus who led the N.H.L.’s Buffalo Sabres in goals this season. He is 19, not 18.
match_headline: U.S.A. Hockey Has No Need for Miracles Anymore

text: A picture in the Listings pages on Friday with an entry about a performance by the trio JF3 at the Harlem Stage Gatehouse, in Hamilton Heights, was published in error. It showed the vibraphonist Joel Ross, who has performed with JF3’s leader, the pianist James Francies; the picture was not of Mr. Francies.
match_headline: Jazz Listings for April 15-21

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about a new tree of life published by scientists referred incorrectly to Methanosarcina, the organism shown. It belongs to the domain archaea, not bacteria.
match_headline: Scientists Unveil New ‘Tree of Life’

text: An article on Saturday about a split on social issues between urban and rural parts of the South misstated the number of times that Houston has elected an openly gay mayor. It is three times, not two.
match_headline: Southern Cities Split With States on Social Issues

text: An article on Sunday about David Gowan, the speaker of the Arizona House, referred incorrectly in some editions to the location of Pinal County where Paul Babeu, a rival of Mr. Gowan’s for the United States House, is sheriff. It is near — not along — the Mexican border. The article also misstated the year in which Representative Ann Kirkpatrick, who is vacating her United States House seat, defeated Andy Tobin, a former Arizona House speaker. It was 2014, not 2012.
match_headline: Speaker David Gowan Reshapes Arizona House, From the Carpets on Up

text: An article in some editions on April 8 about a supporter of Mayor Bill de Blasio who began a 15-day jail sentence misstated the charges on which he was convicted. The supporter, Ari Noe, was found guilty of third degree sexual abuse and attempted forcible touching, not forcible touching.
match_headline: De Blasio Supporter Convicted of Sexual Abuse Begins Jail Term

text: An article on the DealBook page on April 6 about an activist campaign by the American asset manager BlackRock against the G-Resources Group, a Hong Kong company, misstated the timing of a recommendation by the proxy advisory firm Glass Lewis against a proposal by G-Resources to sell a gold mine. Glass Lewis issued its recommendation before — not after — BlackRock campaigned against the deal.
match_headline: An Activism-Shy BlackRock Throws a Surprise Punch

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about the Yankees’ 3-2 loss to the Seattle Mariners misidentified the Yankees player who made a heady defensive play in the fifth inning by throwing out Luis Sardinas at third base after he rounded the bag. The play was made by shortstop Didi Gregorius, not by second baseman Starlin Castro.
match_headline: Clutch Hitting Remains Elusive as Yankees Fall to the Mariners

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the death of a Cameroonian boy who was struck by a vehicle in a convoy carrying Samantha Power, the United States ambassador to the United Nations, to meetings with West African victims of the Islamist extremist group Boko Haram referred incorrectly to Mokolo, one of the cities she visited. It is a departmental capital in Cameroon, not the national capital. (That is Yaoundé.)
match_headline: Vehicle in Convoy of U.S. Ambassador to U.N. Kills Boy in Cameroon

text: An article on April 12 about a vote by a congressional panel in Brazil to impeach President Dilma Rousseff referred incompletely in some editions to the steps toward impeachment. Her suspension from office would only follow a Senate vote to put her on trial; a vote for impeachment by the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress, does not result in her immediate suspension. (She was impeached on Sunday.)
match_headline: Effort to Impeach Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff Clears Congressional Panel

text: An article on Tuesday about Gov. Rick Snyder’s plan to drink Flint tap water for a month referred incorrectly to the dismissal of Michigan state employees as a result of lead contamination. One state employee — not several — has been fired.
match_headline: Michigan Governor to Drink Flint Tap Water for a Month

text: An article on Thursday about the arrest of a suspect in a series of burglaries on Staten Island misstated part of the name of the city in New York where a detective provided information that led investigators from the New York Police Department to the suspect. It is Saratoga Springs, not Sarasota Springs.
match_headline: Official Says ‘Reign of Terror’ Is Over for the Ninja Burglar

text: An article on Thursday about the purchase of Lexmark, the American printing and software company, by a Chinese consortium misstated the period of time during which Chinese companies negotiated $106 billion worth of outbound deals. It was all of 2015, not just the first quarter of that year.
match_headline: Chinese Consortium Reaches Deal to Buy Lexmark

text: An article last Friday about an apology from the City of Philadelphia for the manner in which the Phillies treated Jackie Robinson when he began his baseball career misidentified a Philadelphia-based team that went to the Little League World Series in 2014. It was the Taney Dragons, not the Anderson Monarchs. (The two teams had several players in common, including Mo’ne Davis.)
match_headline: 69 Years Later, Philadelphia Apologizes to Jackie Robinson

text: A review in the New Music column on Thursday about the album “Always Strive and Prosper” by ASAP Ferg, on which he celebrates one of his grandmothers in a song, misidentified his relative who is heard on another song, “Beautiful People.” She is his other grandmother, not his mother. Another review in the column about the band The Strumbellas referred incorrectly to the release of the group’s album “Hope.” It is coming out this week; it was not released last year in Canada.
match_headline: Review: ASAP Ferg’s Big Heart Pulses on ‘Always Strive and Prosper’

text: An obituary on Thursday about the basketball player Pearl Washington misstated, in some copies, the year he received second-team all-American honors at Syracuse University. It was 1985 — 1986, not his final season.
match_headline: Pearl Washington, 52, Dies; Dazzling Guard Put Syracuse on Basketball Map

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about David Geffen’s $100 million gift to the Museum of Modern Art and financial problems at the Metropolitan Museum of Art referred incorrectly, in some editions, to a gift Mr. Geffen gave last year to the former Avery Fisher Hall. Though it was for $100 million, it was not his last donation in that amount before the gift to MoMA. He later gave $100 million to U.C.L.A. to build a middle school and a high school on its campus.
match_headline: 2 Art Worlds: Flush MoMA, Struggling Met

text: An article on Friday about an agreement by NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital to pay $2.2 million to federal regulators for allowing television crews to film two patients without their consent misidentified the person who filed a complaint with federal regulators in 2013 that led to the $2.2 million penalty. It was filed by Mark Chanko’s son Kenneth — not by his widow, Anita.
match_headline: New York Hospital to Pay $2.2 Million Over Unauthorized Filming of 2 Patients

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Volkswagen’s agreement to fix or buy back 500,000 diesel cars in the United States that are equipped with illegal emissions software misstated the number of states in a coalition that is investigating Volkswagen. It is 45, not six. Also because of an editing error, the article misstated the way the illegal software enabled cars to cheat on emissions tests. It increased the pollution controls; it did not reduce them.
match_headline: Volkswagen Reaches Deal in U.S. Over Emissions Scandal

text: An article last Saturday about Mets pitcher Jacob deGrom’s missing his scheduled start the following Tuesday misstated, in some copies, the day that Logan Verrett previously pitched in deGrom’s place. It was Wednesday, April 13 — not Thursday, April 14.
match_headline: Now Batting Third for Struggling Mets: Conforto, Not Cespedes

text: An entry in the Spare Times for Children listings in some editions on Friday about the Nitehawk Cinema’s Little Bookworm series, which is presenting the film “Chitty Chitty Bang Bang” Saturday and Sunday, misstated the cinema’s address. It is at 136 Metropolitan Avenue in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, not 36.
match_headline: Spare Times for Children Listings for April 22-28

text: Because of an editing error, a caption this weekend for two pictures with a cover article about older apartment buildings in New York that are adding amenities to stay competitive omits the description of the top photograph. It shows Monica Goel and her husband, Donal Burke, in the new bike room of the Carlton Regency, a co-op on East 36th Street.
match_headline: Insert a Gym, Then a Lounge: Older Buildings Add Amenities

text: An article last Sunday about the Coast Guard’s rescue of seven fishermen aboard the Carolina Queen III, a scalloping boat that ran aground on Rockaway Beach on Feb. 25 amid gusting winds, misstated, in some copies, the amount of ice that had been loaded onto the boat. It was 20,000 pounds, not 20,000 tons. The article also misstated the name of the muscle in the scallop that is eaten. It is the adductor, not abductor. And the article referred incorrectly to the helicopter that the Fire Department had planned to use during the operation. It is owned and operated by the New York Police Department, not by the Fire Department.
match_headline: Mayday on the Carolina Queen

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions last Sunday about the Rangers’ 4-2 victory over the Pittsburgh Penguins in Game 2 of their N.H.L. playoff series misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the Rangers player whose stick struck goaltender Henrik Lundqvist in the right eye in Game 1. He is Marc Staal, not Stall. The article also misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a Rangers defenseman who missed the game with an injury. He is Dan Girardi, not Giradri.
match_headline: Rangers Surge to Defeat Penguins

text: An article last Sunday about the artist Kay WalkingStick misidentified the location where she was raised. It was in Syracuse, not New Jersey.
match_headline: Kay WalkingStick’s American History

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the increasing number of celebrities who feature pictures of their young children on their social media accounts misidentified the woman and child shown in a photograph projected behind Mark Zuckerberg as he gave a speech at a Facebook conference earlier this year. They are not his wife and son.
match_headline: The Right to Privacy for Children Online

text: An article on April 10 about the rise of sororities on Ivy League campuses misidentified the college affiliation of Blair Wilson, one of the students interviewed. She is a sophomore at Columbia, not Barnard.
match_headline: When a Feminist Pledges a Sorority

text: An article last Sunday about the Berggruen Institute, the think tank operated by the billionaire investor Nicolas Berggruen, misstated, using information from the institute, the number of scholars it is currently funding. There are six scholars, not five.
match_headline: The Billionaire Who’s Building a Davos of His Own

text: A review last Sunday about “Ghetto: The Invention of a Place, the History of an Idea,” by Mitchell Duneier, misidentified the Michigan city that was the site of a debate between Democratic presidential candidates in March. It is Flint, not Detroit.
ref_headline: Ghetto: The Invention of a Place, the History of an Idea,
match_headline: ‘Ghetto,’ by Mitchell Duneier

text: An article on April 12 about a study of handwriting on pottery dating to 600 B.C. that was found in Arad, Israel — and could shed light on a long debate over when the main texts of the Bible were composed — misidentified the alphabet used in the handwritten texts. It was paleo-Hebrew, not Aramaic.
match_headline: New Evidence on When Bible Was Written: Ancient Shopping Lists

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Feb. 28 with an article about proposed legislation in Italy that would lower the penalties for counterfeiting in the commercial olive oil business referred incorrectly to the bottles of olive oil shown at the Colli Etruschi cooperative in Blera. They were awaiting labeling, not filling. Editors were alerted to the error immediately but failed to follow through on a correction. (The Italian Parliament approved the measure on March 1.)
match_headline: Italy Growers Wary of Olive Oil Fraud as New Law Is Weighed

text: An article on Feb. 27 about the sentencing of a Protestant pastor in China to a long prison term on corruption charges — part of a campaign in Zhejiang Province meant to limit the influence of Christian churches and groups — referred incorrectly to interactions between Zhang Kai, a Christian lawyer who has helped defend churches in Zhejiang, and Gu Yuese, leader of the Zhejiang Christian Council, which opposes the province’s practice of removing crosses from churches. The two did not discuss the possibility of suing local officials last year over the cross removals. While the error was promptly corrected online, editors failed to follow through on this print correction.
match_headline: Pastor in China Who Resisted Cross Removal Gets 14 Years in Prison

text: An article on Thursday about European Union antitrust charges against Google misstated the process though which Google receives revenue related to its Android operating system. Google earns revenue from, among other sources, advertising generated from services like mobile search that are included in the software. It does not receive fees from device makers.
match_headline: E.U. Charges Dispute Google’s Claims That Android Is Open to All

text: An article on Thursday about rancor at ABC over the move of the morning-show host Michael Strahan to “Good Morning America” rendered the name of his current show incorrectly. It is “Live With Kelly and Michael,” not “Live: Kelly and Michael.” The error also appeared in an article on Wednesday announcing the shift.
match_headline: Kelly Ripa’s Absence From ‘Live’ Points to Rancor at ABC

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about “An Early Clue to the New Direction: Queer Cinema Before Stonewall,” a series presented by the Film Society of Lincoln Center, misstated the number of short films in the series, which also has 23 feature films. It is 25, not 28.
ref_headline: An Early Clue to the New Direction: Queer Cinema Before Stonewall,
match_headline: Critic’s Notebook: Looking at Gay Movies Before Stonewall

text: An article on Friday in the Gallery Guide about art galleries on the Lower East Side of Manhattan, including the James Cohan Gallery, where a video from the collective the Propeller Group is being shown, misidentified the city in Vietnam where some members of the group are based. It is Ho Chi Minh City, not Hanoi.
match_headline: The Lower East Side as Petri Dish

text: An article on April 7 about a successful operation to separate conjoined Pakistani twins at a hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia — part of a Saudi program that helps poor families of such twins around the world — misstated the age of Dr. Abdullah al-Rabeeah, the surgeon who leads the program. He is 61, not 66.
match_headline: Conjoined Twins, a Trip to Saudi Arabia and a Risky Operation

text: An article on Thursday in which three Times writers discussed the coming changes to United States currency and some aspects of bills now in circulation misidentified the scene shown on the back of the $2 bill. It is a presentation of a draft of the Declaration of Independence, not the signing of it.
match_headline: Tubman’s In. Jackson’s Out. What’s It Mean?

text: An article on Saturday about the arrest of the Los Angeles art dealer Perry Rubenstein on embezzlement charges referred incorrectly to an artist who is among his creditors after his gallery filed for bankruptcy protection. The artist, Zoe Crosher, is a woman and thus not “Mr. Crosher.”
match_headline: Los Angeles Art Dealer Is Arrested on Embezzlement Charges

text: An article last Tuesday about Argentina’s return to the bond market misstated the currencies in which bond sales were made in emerging markets. The bonds were sold in several currencies, not just the dollar. The article also misstated the amount of Mexico’s bond sale in 1996. Mexico sold $18.1 billion of bonds, not $16 billion.
match_headline: Argentina Re-Enters International Bond Markets

text: An article on Monday about the settlement between Argentina and a group of disgruntled debt holders referred incorrectly to the returns received by hedge funds holding defaulted bonds. They were in the hundreds of percentage points, not hundreds of times, their original investments.
match_headline: How Argentina Settled a Billion-Dollar Debt Dispute With Hedge Funds

text: A headline on Monday with a music review of Mozart’s “Abduction From the Seraglio,” conducted by James Levine at the Metropolitan Opera, referred incorrectly to Mr. Levine’s tenure at the Met. While this run of performances will be his final appearances at the Met as music director, they are not scheduled to be his final appearances there. He will continue to conduct some performances after this season as music director emeritus.
match_headline: Review: James Levine Opens Last Run as Metropolitan Opera Music Director

text: Because of an editing error, a dance entry in the Listings pages on Friday about the Boogie Down Dance Series at the Bronx Academy of Arts and Dance included an outdated phone number for the academy. It is now 718-918-2110.
match_headline: Dance Listings for April 22-28

text: An obituary last Tuesday about Bill Campbell, an adviser to executives in the technology industry, misstated his history with the tablet computer company Go Corporation. While he was a former chief executive of the company, he did not help found it.
match_headline: Bill Campbell, Coach of Silicon Valley Stars, Dies at 75

text: An obituary on Monday about Elton Spitzer, who for many years ran the Long Island radio station WLIR, misspelled the surname of his stepdaughter, who survives him. She is Beverly Marchica, not Machica.
match_headline: Elton Spitzer, 84, Who Helped Turn WLIR Into a Radio Destination, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, a letter from Sonoma State University in California on Monday about Georgetown University’s role in the slave trade referred imprecisely to the Jesuit Plantation Project at Georgetown. Although it is no longer available, it has been replaced by a new website, the Georgetown Slavery Archive .
match_headline: The Slaves in Georgetown’s Past

text: An obituary on Friday about Prince referred imprecisely to which elements of the character he played in the movie “Purple Rain” were autobiographical and which were fictional. Although the character, known as the Kid, is biracial, Prince himself was not. (Both his parents were African-American.)
match_headline: Prince, an Artist Who Defied Genre, Is Dead at 57

text: An article on Tuesday about a donation to the University of California, San Francisco from the former Citigroup chairman Sanford I. Weill and his wife, Jane, misstated the portion of the university’s revenue that comes from state funds. It is 3 percent, not 97 percent.
match_headline: Sanford Weill and His Wife Donate $185 Million to U.C. San Francisco

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about start-ups that offer improved menstrual products described the material of the Lola tampon incorrectly. It is made of 100 percent cotton, but not organic cotton.
match_headline: Menstruation Joins the Economic Conversation

text: An article in some editions last Wednesday about the Yankees’ 3-2 loss to the Oakland Athletics misstated, in some copies, the given name of the Oakland player who drove in the winning run in the 11th inning. He is Mark Canha, not Stephen. The article also misstated, in some copies, the number of years Canha has been in the major leagues. He is a second-year player, not a rookie.
match_headline: Defensive and Offensive Lapses Haunt Yankees in Loss to A’s

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Wednesday about the success of the Islanders line of John Tavares, Kyle Okposo and Frans Nielsen during their playoff series against the Florida Panthers misstated, in some copies, the circumstances of Nielsen’s goal in Game 3. He scored late in the second period to tie the score, 3-3 — not two minutes after Ryan Pulock’s power-play goal made the score 2-1 early in the period.
match_headline: New Line’s Chemistry Fuels Islanders

text: An article on Monday about a new “super PAC” run by artists misspelled the given name of one who is among those contributing works that will be displayed. He is Bayeté Ross Smith, not Bayaté.
match_headline: A ‘Super PAC’ Where Art Meets Politics

text: A picture credit on Monday with a music review of a concert in the Trinity Wall Street Revolutionaries festival, using information from a publicist, misspelled the photographer’s surname. The picture, of the conductor Julian Wachner leading a performance, is by Saskia Kahn, not Khan.
match_headline: Review: Ginastera and Fauré, With a Nod to Prince

text: A picture caption on Friday with a report in the Antiques Column about 19th-century ledger books, which American Indians used to record tribal history in picture form, omitted a credit for the imprisoned Cheyenne warrior who produced an image of ledger art in the 1870s. He was Bear’s Heart.
match_headline: American Indian Narratives in Picture Form

text: Because of an editing error, a picture credit on Friday with a film review of the documentary “Keepers of the Game” omitted the photographer’s given name. The photograph of a girls lacrosse team chronicled in the documentary was taken by Peter Eliot Buntaine, not Eliot Buntaine.
match_headline: Review: ‘Keepers of the Game’ Sings of Young Women and Lacrosse

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article in the Gallery Guide about art galleries in the Chelsea neighborhood of Manhattan misstated the title of a series of works by Anne Collier on display at the Anton Kern Gallery. It is “Women Crying,” not “A Woman Crying.”
match_headline: Chelsea Galleries, Like a Box of Chocolates

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the bond investor William H. Gross overstated what is known about his exit from Pimco. The nature of his departure is the subject of litigation between Mr. Gross and Pimco; it has not been determined that “he was fired nearly two years ago.” (Mr. Gross contends that he was wrongfully terminated; the company says that Mr. Gross resigned and was not fired.)
ref_headline: he was fired nearly two years ago.
match_headline: For Bill Gross, Besting Pimco Is the Best Revenge

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some copies last Saturday about the Islanders’ 2-1 victory over the Florida Panthers in Game 5 of their N.H.L. playoff series misstated the time of Alan Quine’s winning goal. It came at 16:00 of the second overtime, not 15:58. The article also referred incorrectly to the Islanders playoff series in 1987 that ended with Pat LaFontaine’s goal in the fourth overtime of Game 7. It was the first-round series against the Washington Capitals, not the second-round series against the Philadelphia Flyers. In addition, the article misstated the margin by which the Panthers outshot the Islanders in the second period. It was 14-7, not 14-5. And the article referred imprecisely to the number of successive overtime losses by the Panthers. Entering the game, they had lost six straight overtime games in the playoffs — not over all.
match_headline: After Overtime Penalty Save, Islanders Prevail in a Goaltending Battle

text: A picture caption on Friday with a film review of the documentary “A Beautiful Planet” included an outdated credit. Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures is no longer associated with the film.
match_headline: Review: ‘A Beautiful Planet’ Shows a Dazzling Earth From Space

text: A map in some editions on April 25 with the continuation of an article about a report by an international panel of investigators that details the abduction of 43 missing Mexican students in the city of Iguala in September 2014 located incorrectly a town that is near Iguala, called Cocula. It is in Guerrero State, in southwest Mexico, as is Iguala; the Cocula that was labeled on the map is in Jalisco State, northwest of Guerrero.
match_headline: Missing Mexican Students Suffered a Night of ‘Terror,’ Investigators Say

text: An article on March 4 about President Xi Jinping’s remedy for China’s economic gloom, which has echoes of Reaganomics, misstated part of the name of an American credit-rating agency that lowered its outlook for China from stable to negative earlier that week. It is Moody’s Investors Service (not Investor). Although the error was corrected online shortly after publication, editors failed to follow through with this print correction.
match_headline: Xi Jinping’s Remedy for China’s Economic Gloom Has Echoes of Reaganomics

text: An article on March 14 about an attack by Al Qaeda’s North African affiliate that killed 16 people at three beach resort hotels near Abidjan in Ivory Coast referred incorrectly to Abidjan. It is the economic capital of Ivory Coast and its largest city — not the political capital, which is Yamoussoukro. Editors were alerted to the error the day of publication but failed to follow through promptly with online and print corrections.
match_headline: 16 Killed in Terrorist Attack on Resort Hotels in Ivory Coast

text: An article on Tuesday about proposals to require mandatory training for physicians who prescribe opioids misstated a summary by Dr. Darrell G. Kirch, president of the Association of American Medical Colleges, of the fears of medical school leaders. They feared that the federal mandate could lead to the imposition of additional legislative agendas that were not in the interest of patient care; they did not say the reverse, that such agendas were in the interest of patients.
match_headline: Opioid Prescribing Gets Another Look as F.D.A. Revisits Mandatory Doctor Training

text: An article last Wednesday about the effect of aging on elite runners misidentified the marathon at which Steve Spence won a bronze medal. It was the 1991 world championships, not the 1992 Olympics.
match_headline: Aging Runners Find Help for a Question: How Slow Will I Get?

text: Because of an editing error, the byline was omitted for an article on Tuesday about Scott Rothkopf, chief curator of the Whitney Museum of American Art. The article was by Robin Pogrebin. In addition, the article misidentified the institution where Yve-Alain Bois, Mr. Rothkopf’s thesis adviser at Harvard, is now an art history professor. It is the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J. — not Princeton University.
match_headline: For Scott Rothkopf, a Swift Ascendance in the Whitney Hierarchy

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the artist Marisol misstated the given name of an artist with whom she studied. He was Yasuo Kuniyoshi, not Kazuo. The obituary also misidentified the location of El Museo del Barrio, where the exhibition “Marisol: Sculptures and Works on Paper” was presented. It is in Manhattan, not in the Bronx.
ref_headline: Marisol: Sculptures and Works on Paper
match_headline: Marisol, an Artist Known for Blithely Shattering Boundaries, Dies at 85

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Wednesday about an accidental leak of confidential memos meant to temper news media criticism of the Egyptian government misstated the surname of a journalist who said the memos suggested that the government did not want to be held accountable. He is Mahmoud Elmamlouk, not Mahmoud El Mamluk Heba Habib. The article also misidentified Mr. Elmamlouk’s employer and his job title. He is the editor in chief of Innfrad, not a reporter for Youm7.
match_headline: Egypt’s Interior Ministry, in Error, Releases Memos on Restricting News Media

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 23 about survivors’ accounts of the Brussels terrorist attack misstated the day it occurred. It was on Tuesday, March 22 — not on Thursday, March 17. Although the error was promptly corrected online, editors failed to follow through with this print correction.
match_headline: Brussels Survivors Say Blasts Instantly Evoked Paris Attacks

text: An article on Tuesday about a second lawsuit filed by the former professional wrestler Hulk Hogan against Gawker Media misstated part of a claim in the suit. The suit contends that Gawker tried “to gain access to video and/or audio footage” of Mr. Hogan’s use of racial slurs, not that it had obtained that tape. (Gawker denies ever possessing it.)
ref_headline: to gain access to video and/or audio footage
match_headline: Hulk Hogan vs. Gawker, Round 2

text: An article on Wednesday about the growth of outside financing for law firms misstated the amount of capital held by Burford Capital, a litigation lender. It recently added capital, bringing its investment total to $1 billion. It does not have roughly half that of Gerchen Keller Capital’s $1.4 billion in assets. The article also misstated the position of Christopher P. Bogart, the chief executive of Burford, when he was at the law firm Cravath, Swaine & Moore. He was an associate, not a partner.
match_headline: Lack of Capital to Lead Law Firms to Seek Help, Survey Finds

text: A report in the N.B.A. roundup last Thursday about a meeting between Phil Jackson and David Blatt to discuss the Knicks’ coaching vacancy misstated the surname of the team’s general manager in some copies. He is Steve Mills, not Mill.

A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about the Lincoln Center Out of Doors festival this summer referred incorrectly to Patti Smith’s opening-night performance. She is headlining a double bill with Mariachi Flor de Toloache as the opening act; she is not being “honored.” The report also referred incorrectly to the salsa duo Richie Ray and Bobby Cruz, who will also appear at the festival. They perform songs; they are not dancers.
match_headline: Lincoln Center Announces Out of Doors Lineup, Including Patti Smith

text: An obituary on Monday and in some editions on Sunday about the Rev. Daniel J. Berrigan, the Jesuit priest and antiwar activist, misstated the year the movie “The Mission,” in which he had a small role, was released. It was 1986, not 1989.
match_headline: Daniel J. Berrigan, Defiant Priest Who Preached Pacifism, Dies at 94

text: An article on April 7 about revelations that at least three of the seven people on the Chinese Communist Party’s most powerful committee have relatives who have controlled secretive offshore companies gave an outdated title for Liu Lefei, whose wife was once a shareholder and director of a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, and whose father, Liu Yunshan, is a member of the committee. Although the younger Mr. Liu heads one of China’s leading private equity firms, he is no longer a vice chairman of Citic Securities.
match_headline: Panama Papers Tie More of China’s Elite to Secret Accounts

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the gala at the Metropolitan Museum of Art misidentified the entity that organized the exhibit about fashion in an age of technology. It is the Costume Institute, not the Anna Wintour Costume Center. The article also misstated Andrew Bolton’s title. He is head curator of the institute, not of the museum. Because of an editing error, the article misspelled, in some copies, the given name of the person who designed Madonna’s dress on first reference. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Riccardo Tisci, not Ricardo.
match_headline: At the Met Gala, Minimalism Is a Relative Term

text: A picture caption on Friday with an art review of Frieze New York, on Randalls Island in Manhattan, misstated the given name of an artist. He is François Morellet, not Nancy François Morellet.
match_headline: Frieze New York, a Visual Circus Under the Big Top

text: An article on Friday about recent changes made to the classic Brooks Brothers button-down shirt, including a more tapered fit — and not one tailored to the torso of the Tin Man in “The Wizard of Oz” — misidentified the actor who played that role. He was Jack Haley, not Ray Bolger.
match_headline: Brooks Brothers Revives the Preppiest Shirt Collar

text: An article on April 10 about the political ambitions of Boris Johnson, the departing mayor of London, referred incorrectly to a program offering free subway service for Londoners 60 and over. It was instituted in 1973 by the Greater London Council, not by Mr. Johnson.
match_headline: As Britain Contemplates Exit, Boris Johnson Prepares His Entrance

text: An article on April 27 about the confirmation by Colombia of two more cases of babies born with brain damage to mothers who had Zika during pregnancy misstated the year when researchers found Zika gene sequences in the blood of three children in Haiti. It was in December 2014, not 2015.
match_headline: Colombia Confirms More Birth Defects Linked to Zika

text: An article on Friday about a public hearing on options for shutting down the L Train tunnel during repairs misstated the name of a food market in Brooklyn. It is Smorgasburg, not Smorgasbord.
match_headline: L Train Riders Quiz Transit Officials on Shutdown

text: An article last Monday about the former Islanders goaltender Rick DiPietro’s new career as a television analyst misstated, in some copies, the status of the contract he signed with the team in 2006. It would have had several years remaining; this season would not have been its next-to-last season.
match_headline: Now Working Without a Net, an Ex-Islander Is Live on the Air

text: An article in some editions on April 15 about what the Pentagon called the failed launch of a ballistic missile by North Korea misstated the name of a South Korean news agency that reported the launch. It is Yonhap, not Yonghap.
match_headline: North Korea Ballistic Missile Launch a Failure, Pentagon Says

text: An article on Friday about fund-raising efforts in 2014 for New York Senate races overstated what Basil A. Smikle Jr., a leader of the New York State Democratic Party, knew about allegations that a group led by Mayor Bill de Blasio used earmarked funds through local county committees. While he cited published reports of such allegations, Mr. Smikle did not know of such an effort. The article also misstated the circumstances of Joseph Percoco’s departure from the Cuomo administration to run the governor’s re-election campaign. He resigned from the administration; he did not take a leave of absence. The error also appeared in an article on Wednesday.
match_headline: Cuomo Campaign’s Role in Scrutinized Senate Races Comes Into Focus

text: An article on the Automobiles page on Friday about the 2016 Chevrolet Camero omitted the writer’s byline. The article was by Tom Voelk.
match_headline: Video Review: A Sinewy Camaro, Still With Muscle Car Swagger

text: An obituary on Friday about Mark Lane, who concluded in the mid-1960s that Lee Harvey Oswald could not have acted alone in killing President John F. Kennedy, referred incorrectly to the origin of the term “grassy knoll” to describe a green expanse of Dealey Plaza in Dallas that Mr. Lane argued was the source of several shots fired at the president. While it is unclear who used the term first, it was not coined by Mr. Lane. (He himself said it was coined by Jean Hill, a witness to the Kennedy assassination; other sources credit the United Press International reporter Merriman Smith.) The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Lane’s college and postgraduate education. He received an undergraduate degree from Long Island University and a law degree from Brooklyn Law School; he did not “earn an undergraduate degree and a law degree at Brooklyn College.”
match_headline: Mark Lane, Early Kennedy Assassination Conspiracy Theorist, Dies at 89

text: An editorial on Wednesday about President Obama’s planned visit to Hiroshima failed to say Caroline Kennedy, the ambassador to Japan, was among the American officials who have visited Hiroshima in recent years. It also incorrectly described presidential visits to Cuba. The first sitting American president to visit was Calvin Coolidge, not Mr. Obama.
match_headline: What Mr. Obama Can Say at Hiroshima

text: An article in some editions last Saturday about criticism over the New York Police Department’s use of a restraint bag in an arrest misspelled the surname of a woman whose death led the police to re-evaluate its practices regarding emotionally disturbed people. She was Eleanor Bumpurs, not Bumpers.
match_headline: New York Police Criticized for Using Restraining Bag in Arrest

text: An article on Thursday about teenage sports champions misstated Martina Hingis’s age when she won the 1997 Australian Open. She was 16, not 15.
match_headline: Teenage Sports Stars, From Young Tom Morris to Max Verstappen

text: An article last Saturday about the visual artist and choreographer Yve Laris Cohen referred incorrectly to his study of Martha Graham technique at the University of California, Berkeley. He studied in the dance department founded by two former Graham company members; he did not study under them.
match_headline: Yve Laris Cohen, Melding Identities as Laborer and Artist

text: A picture caption on Friday with a film review of “Maggie’s Plan” carried a credit that misspelled the photographer’s given name. He is Jon Pack, not John.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Maggie’s Plan,’ Greta Gerwig Aspires to Motherhood on Her Terms

text: An article on Page 29 this weekend about Donald J. Trump’s improbable journey to the Republican nomination for president misstates the sequence of events by which Paul Manafort, a senior adviser, joined Trump’s presidential campaign. Manafort was referred to Trump by more than one person close to the campaign, not just by the former Trump adviser Roger Stone, and Manafort’s March 24 meeting with Trump occurred before, not after, Trump read a Wall Street Journal article describing Ted Cruz’s delegate strategy.
match_headline: Mr. Trump’s Wild Ride

text: An entry in the “This and That” feature on Page 32 this weekend about a new collaboration between the jeweler Brooke Garber Neidich and the fashion designer Duro Oluwo erroneously includes one person among those who are fans of the Sidney Garber jewelry line, which Garber Neidich designs. While Hillary Clinton might be a fan, as the article noted, that could not be confirmed. (She is, however, friends with Garber Neidich.) The article also refers incompletely to the fabrics Oluwo uses in his designs. They come from a variety of sources, not just African-printed fabrics.
match_headline: Duro Olowu and Sidney Garber’s Striking Jewelry Collaboration

text: An article on Page 110 this weekend about the British designer Chloe Lonsdale’s denim brand M.i.h. and her house in Sussex erroneously includes one person among those involved in Lonsdale’s London pop-up shop. While the boutique owner Alex Eagle was involved at one point, that is no longer the case. In addition, an accompanying picture caption misidentifies a collection to which a dress of Lonsdale’s design belongs. It is part of M.i.h. Jeans’s pre-fall 2016 collection, not the Cult Denim Project collection.
match_headline: At Home With a Cult Denim Designer (in a 400-Year-Old Boathouse)

text: A picture caption on Page 144 this weekend with an article about the cultural resilience of the people of Beirut in the face of continuing political strife misstates the time of day the photograph was taken. It was sunset, not sunrise.
match_headline: The Eternal Magic of Beirut

text: An obituary on Thursday about the historian Fritz Stern referred incorrectly to his work history and his tenure as provost at Columbia University. He taught at Cornell in the early 1950s; he did not spend his entire career at Columbia. And he was provost of Columbia from 1980 to 1983, not from 1980 to 1992.
match_headline: Fritz Stern, a Leading Historian on Modern Germany, Dies at 90

text: An article on March 11 about the grueling cleanup work that continues at Fukushima Daiichi, the radioactive nuclear power plant in northeastern Japan, five years after an earthquake and tsunami caused a meltdown referred imprecisely to the 2,000 tons of water that is released into the ocean every week after being scrubbed of most radioactive particles.
