It is groundwater that has seeped into the reactor buildings; it is not the water that is pumped through the reactor cores to keep melted fuel from overheating. A reader alerted The Times to the imprecision shortly after publication, but editors failed to follow up with a correction.
match_headline: Fukushima Keeps Fighting Radioactive Tide 5 Years After Disaster

text: A picture caption in some editions on Wednesday with an article about speculation over why dozens of law enforcement officials descended on a yeshiva in Kiryas Joel, N.Y., misspelled part of the name of the main synagogue there. It is Yetev Lev, not Yutev Lev.
match_headline: Sexual Abuse Questions Swirl Around Yeshiva Leader in Kiryas Joel

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about giant food companies’ investments in start-ups misstated, in some editions, the role of General Mills in an $18 million investment in Kite Hill. General Mills is the lead investor, not the sole investor.
match_headline: General Mills Adds Kite Hill to Food Start-Up Investments

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the success of Finland’s hockey teams at international tournaments this year described incorrectly the actions of Finland forward Sebastian Aho, using information from Agence France-Presse — Getty Images. He was reacting to a goal by a teammate; he had not scored the goal.
match_headline: Credit New Coaching Approach as Finland Hockey Seeks Triple Gold

text: An article on Thursday about the San Jose Sharks’ efforts to rejuvenate their fan base misstated, in some copies, the year in which the Sharks lost a playoff series to the Los Angeles Kings after winning the first three games. It was 2014, not 2013.
match_headline: San Jose Sharks Showing New Appreciation for Fans

text: An obituary on Friday about David King, a graphic designer who amassed one of the world’s largest collections of Soviet political art, misstated the original date of publication of his book “The Commissar Vanishes: The Falsification of Photographs and Art in Stalin’s Russia.” It was 1997, not 2014.
ref_headline: The Commissar Vanishes: The Falsification of Photographs and Art in Stalin’s Russia.
match_headline: David King, 73, Dies; Graphic Designer Amassed Trove of Soviet Political Art

text: A picture caption on April 26 with an article about the Afghan government’s cancellation of a planned visit by the first vice president of Afghanistan, Abdul Rashid Dostum, to the United States misidentified the location of the picture, which showed Mr. Dostum addressing a crowd in 2014. It was taken in Kunduz Province, not in Kabul.
match_headline: Afghanistan’s Vice President Is Barred From Entering U.S.

text: Because of an editing error, the Memo From Spain article on April 26, about political discord that is putting Spain at risk of a constitutional crisis, omitted the given name of Spain’s Socialist leader, who has criticized the acting government for its lack of accountability. He is Pedro Sánchez.
match_headline: Discord Pushes Spain Into Fifth Month With No Government

text: Because of an editing error, the Memo From China article on April 4, about the difficulty of determining whether carbon dioxide emissions in China are declining, misidentified the city in which the Natural Resources Defense Council has its headquarters. It is New York, not Washington. The error was corrected online shortly after the article was published, but editors failed to follow through with this print correction.
match_headline: China’s Carbon Emissions May Have Peaked, but It’s Hazy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the Transportation Security Administration’s replacing its top security official and adding new administrators at Chicago O’Hare International Airport misstated the time during which hundreds of passengers there missed flights because of long security lines. It was last week and over the weekend, not just on Sunday.
match_headline: T.S.A. Replaces Security Chief as Tension Grows at Airports and Agency

text: An article on Tuesday about the unionization of New York employees of the Babeland adult-toy stores misstated in some copies, using information from the union, the vote count that authorized the union. It was 21 to 4, not 24 to 1. The article also misstated the results of employees’ request for caller ID to help weed out threatening phone calls. Two of the three stores in New York now have caller ID; the push was not unsuccessful.
match_headline: Sex Shop Workers Welcome the Protections of a Retail Union

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a lawsuit filed by the chief executive and a director of Viacom, challenging their removal from a trust that controls the company, misidentified the city in which the suit was filed. It was Canton, Mass., not Norfolk.
match_headline: Redstone and Viacom Executives Go to Court Against Each Other

text: An article on Monday about online commenters in China who are paid to post messages favorable to the government misstated the university affiliations of two of the three authors of a study showing that most commenters are government employees. The study was not by “researchers at Harvard”; while Gary King is a professor there, Jennifer Pan is an assistant professor at Stanford, and Margaret E. Roberts is an assistant professor at the University of California, San Diego.
match_headline: In China, Government Workers Push Rosy, Diverting Views Online

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about movie box-office revenues, using information from Sony, misstated the amount Sony is to receive for distributing “Angry Birds,” which took in the most money in North America over the weekend. It is 8 percent of ticket sales, not 7 percent.
match_headline: ‘The Angry Birds Movie’ Nests Atop the Box Office

text: A picture caption on Friday with a film review of “Kaili Blues” was accompanied by an erroneous credit. The picture is by Grasshopper Film, not Grasshopper Films.
match_headline: Review: ‘Kaili Blues,’ a Dreamy Trek With Otherworldly Beauty

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Wednesday about the challenges facing home cooks in Cuba, where a dish called Moros y Cristianos is popular, misstated the period when Moors occupied parts of the Iberian Peninsula. It was the eighth century through the 15th century, not the first century.
match_headline: For Cuban Home Cooks, Ingenuity and Luck Are Key Ingredients

text: Because of an editing error, a recipe accompanying the Spirits of the Times column on May 15, for an almond-apricot tart, misstated the number of eggs required. It is two whole eggs for the tart filling and one yolk for the crust, not just two whole eggs. The complete recipe is at nytimes/cooking .
An obituary on Monday about the baritone saxophonist Joe Temperley omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to his wife, his sister and his stepson, Mr. Temperley is survived by his son, Stephen.
match_headline: Joe Temperley, Velvety Baritone Saxophonist in Big Bands, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Monday about the Italian politician Marco Pannella misstated the year he recruited Ilona Staller, an actress in pornographic films, to run for Parliament. It was 1987, not 2000.
match_headline: Marco Pannella, Italian Champion of Civil Liberties, Dies at 86

text: A subheading on Monday with an obituary about the North Korean nuclear negotiator Kang Sok-ju misstated how long it took for an agreement he negotiated with the United States in 1994 to fall apart. As the obituary correctly stated, the deal collapsed in 2002, or eight years later, not 18.
match_headline: Kang Sok-ju, Key Nuclear Negotiator for North Korea, Dies at 76

text: An article on April 28 about Germany’s struggle to integrate some of the million migrants who flooded the country last year — and to decide whom to deport — referred imprecisely to the handwritten grammar notes taped to the walls of a meeting room in Cologne where asylum interviews are conducted. They listed conjugations of German verbs, not declensions (that term is used in reference to nouns, adjectives and other parts of speech, but not verbs).
match_headline: Flooded With Migrants, Germany Struggles to Integrate Them

text: An article last Sunday about how two Manhattan buildings would look if they were built according to current codes misidentified the law that resulted in the development of so-called dumbbell tenements throughout New York City. It was the Tenement Law of 1879, not the Tenement Law of 1901.
match_headline: Which Buildings in Manhattan Couldn't Be Built Again Today?

text: An article on Friday about an appeals court’s rejection of an arbitration clause that prevented employees of Epic Systems, a Verona, Wis., health care software provider, from pursuing class actions misstated the location of the court, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, in some copies. It is in Chicago, not Madison, Wis.
match_headline: Court Rules Companies Cannot Impose Illegal Arbitration Clauses

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about an exhibition of work by the artist Simon Starling at Japan Society in Manhattan, using information from the society, referred incorrectly to the exhibition. It is the second solo exhibition there that features a non-Japanese artist, not the first. (Ansel Adams’s work was exhibited there in the 1980s.)
match_headline: A Fiery Splash in the Rockaways and Twists on Film at the Whitney

text: Because of an editing error, a list on Friday of noteworthy television premieres this summer misstated the starting date of Season 4 of “Survivor’s Remorse” on Starz. It is July 24, not June 24.
match_headline: More Reasons to Surf, Binge and Stream This Summer

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on May 20 with a television review of “Julian Fellowes Presents Doctor Thorne,” on Amazon Prime, misidentified an actor. He is Harry Richardson; Frank Gresham is the name of the character he plays. The caption also misspelled the given name of an actress. As the review correctly noted, she is Stefanie Martini, not Stefani.
match_headline: Review: Julian Fellowes Hosts ‘Doctor Thorne,’ a British Period Drama, on Amazon

text: A report in the Observatory column on Tuesday about Nile crocodiles in Florida misstated the distance that a tagged crocodile traveled between 2012 and 2014. It was 18 miles, not 29.
match_headline: Nile Crocodiles Found Really Far Out of Africa. In Florida.

text: Because of a production error, this weekend’s Travel section omits an article intended to accompany a cover article about Vladimir and Véra Nabokov’s cross-country journeys to the American West, during which the author researched “Lolita.” The omitted information, with suggested reading material and lodging for such a trip, can be found at nytimes.com/travel .
match_headline: On the Trail of Nabokov in the American West

text: An article on Saturday about a new study of African-American genetic diversity misstated the number of Africans brought to the United States as slaves. Though a precise figure is not known, scholars believe the number to be in the hundreds of thousands, not millions.
match_headline: Tales of African-American History Found in DNA

text: An article on Saturday about efforts by NASA to inflate a new room for the International Space Station misidentified the body of water in which SpaceX has landed four booster stages of rockets on a floating platform. It is the Atlantic Ocean, not the Pacific.
match_headline: NASA to Try Again to Inflate a Balloon-like Pod for the Space Station

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about the crash of a vintage warplane into the Hudson River misstated, in some copies, Albert J. Parisi’s title at the Army Air Forces Historical Association. He is its operations manager, not its operating officer. The article also misidentified, in some copies, the model of planes he described as being stalwarts of World War II. They were P-47s not P-40s.
match_headline: Pilot’s Body Recovered After Plane Crash in Hudson River, Officials Say

text: An article on Thursday about plans to close the Mount Sinai Beth Israel hospital in Manhattan misstated, in some editions, the number of beds at the hospital, using information from its website. It is 825, not 856. The error was repeated in a picture caption in some copies.
match_headline: Mt. Sinai Beth Israel Hospital in Manhattan Will Close to Rebuild Smaller

text: An article on Friday about books recommended for summer reading, using information from a publicist, referred incorrectly to Stuart Stevens’s coming novel, “The Innocent Have Nothing to Fear.” It is his second novel, not his first.
ref_headline: The Innocent Have Nothing to Fear.
match_headline: 12 New Books We’re Reading This Summer (and 6 Not So New)

text: An article on Tuesday about protecting salamanders in the United States from a deadly fungus misidentified the type of salamander that keeps its gills as adults. They are mud puppies, not hellbenders.
match_headline: How, and Why, to Hunt the Red-Spotted Newt

text: An obituary on Sunday about the political activist Hedy Epstein misstated part of the name of an organization for which she worked. It was Freedom of Residence, not Freedom of Resistance.
match_headline: Hedy Epstein, Rights Activist and Holocaust Survivor, Dies at 91

text: An article on Wednesday about efforts by state and federal officials to support existing nuclear plants misidentified the entities involved in trying to set above-market rates for power generated from some struggling coal and nuclear plants. The contracts would have been between AEP’s Ohio utility and its unregulated power-generation affiliate, and another contract would have been between FirstEnergy’s Ohio utilities and their unregulated generation affiliate; the contracts would not have been between AEP and FirstEnergy. The article also misstated the action taken by state regulators in Ohio. Regulators approved the rate plans — not the contracts — that would have allowed for above-market rates to go forward.
match_headline: Nuclear Plants, Despite Safety Concerns, Gain Support as Clean Energy Sources

text: An article on Monday about lessons that the national Democratic Party could learn from Gov. Jerry Brown and the California Democratic Party misidentified the type of religious facility where Mr. Brown spent time as a young man. It was a seminary, not a monastery.
match_headline: Success of Jerry Brown, and California, Offers Lesson to National Democrats

text: An article on May 10 about similarities between Rodrigo Duterte, then the Philippine presidential front-runner, and Donald J. Trump, the presumed Republican presidential nominee, referred incorrectly to Mr. Duterte’s political background. He served in the Philippine Congress from June 1998 to June 2001; it is not the case that he has “never held national office.” (Mr. Duterte is now the president-elect.)
match_headline: Rodrigo Duterte, Philippines Presidential Contender, Likened to Donald Trump

text: Because of an editing error, an article on May 11 about the Romanian government’s approval of legislation that would give priority to restitution claims by Holocaust survivors for property lost during World War II and under Communist rule referred incorrectly to Bucovina, all of whose Jews were deported in October 1941, according to a former resident. It is a northern region of Romania, not a city.
match_headline: Romania Takes Step Toward Restitution to Holocaust Survivors

text: An article on Wednesday about certain undocumented immigrants who are allowed to apply for professional teaching certificates and some professional licenses referred incorrectly to Dubai, home to some of these immigrants. Dubai is an emirate, not a country.
match_headline: For Undocumented Immigrants, a License to Teach

text: An article on Thursday about collaborations between the photographer Gordon Parks and the writer Ralph Ellison, including the project “Harlem Is Nowhere,” misstated a comment by Ellison in a letter to the author Richard Wright. He wrote that he hoped that the Harlem project would “make for something new in photo-journalism,” not that it would be a “new departure in photo reporting.” (That comment was made in a letter to Ellison from Richard E. Lauterbach, editor of the magazine in which the project was originally scheduled to appear.)
match_headline: Gordon Parks and Ralph Ellison, Artistic Giants of Postwar Harlem

text: An article on Monday about the Fandango Fronterizo, an annual event of Mexican music at the border between San Diego and Tijuana, misstated the name of an artist who performed. He is Tacho Utrera, not Tacho Utrera Laudería. The article also misspelled the surname of an assistant professor at Scripps College who commented on fandangos, and the name of the band in which she sings. She is Martha E. Gonzalez, not Gonzales, and the band is Quetzal, not Quetzel.
match_headline: Sharing Music Across the U.S.-Mexico Border’s Metal Fence

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Rick MacLeish, who played on the Philadelphia Flyers teams that won back-to-back Stanley Cups in the 1970s, reversed the positions played by two of his teammates. Gary Dornhoefer was a right wing and Ross Lonsberry was a left wing.
match_headline: Rick MacLeish, One of the Flyers’ Broad Street Bullies, Dies at 66

text: An article on April 23 about an executive order issued by Gov. Terry McAuliffe of Virginia that expanded voting rights for convicted felons, using information from the governor’s office, overstated the law’s effect on African-Americans. A subsequent analysis by the governor’s office showed that 45 percent — not a majority — of those affected were African-American. This correction was delayed because the error was not brought to the attention of editors until Thursday.
match_headline: Virginia Governor Restores Voting Rights to Felons

text: A headline on Friday for an article about Exelon’s plans to shut two nuclear power plants referred incorrectly in some editions to the timing of the closures. As the article correctly noted, one of the plants will be closed in June 2017 and the other in June 2018; they have not already closed.
match_headline: Exelon to Close 2 Nuclear Plants in Illinois

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the new oil minister in Saudi Arabia, Khalid al-Falih, misstated the time period during which the country issued a directive to diversify its economy. It was in April, not last month.
match_headline: Saudi Oil Chief Khalid al-Falih Tells OPEC Changes Are Coming

text: A picture caption in some copies last Saturday with an article about the Dodgers’ starting pitcher making his major league debut against the Mets misstated his surname. As the article correctly noted, he is Julio Urias, not Arias.
match_headline: Nostalgic Mets Fans Boo Chase Utley and Then Cheer a Walk-Off Win

text: An article on Monday about Shelby Rogers’s upset of Irina-Camelia Begu at the French Open misstated the set in which Rogers broke Begu when she was serving at 4-5. It was the second set, not the third. (As the article correctly noted elsewhere, they played only two sets.)
match_headline: Shelby Rogers Surprises Even Herself, Reaching French Open Quarterfinals

text: An article on Friday about Edgar Feuchtwanger, author of the memoir “I Was Hitler’s Neighbor,” misstated Hitler’s address in Munich when he moved into Mr. Feuchtwanger’s neighborhood in 1929. It was 16 Prinzregentenplatz (Prince Regent Square), not 16 Prinzregentenstrasse (Prince Regent Street).
match_headline: Edgar Feuchtwanger Bore Witness, Horribly Close to Hitler

text: An article on Page 12 this weekend about a family-friendly trip to New Orleans misstates part of the name of a green space in the French Quarter. It is Jackson Square, not Jackson Park. The article also refers incorrectly to a sightseeing carriage. It is led by a mule, not by a donkey. In addition, the article misstates part of the names of two streets. They are Frenchmen Street, not Frenchmen’s Street, and Washington Avenue, not Washington Street. And the article misidentifies the departure location for a jazz cruise. It is the Toulouse Street Wharf, not Canal Place. (The errors about Jackson Square, the carriage and Frenchmen Street also appear in an accompanying article on Page 11 about five vacation alternatives to Disney World.)
match_headline: New Orleans is a Party for Families Too

text: An article last Sunday about how subjects of last year’s Summer Love series have fared misstated the complications involved in the birth of a gorilla in the Bronx Zoo, where several gorillas were part of a mating program that was featured in the series. The birth was natural, followed by anesthesia to remove the placenta; it was not chemically induced.
match_headline: Summer Love, a Year Later

text: A picture in some editions last Sunday with an article about a rule change that extended the time college basketball players have to decide whether to enter the N.B.A. draft was published in error. It showed Oregon’s Elgin Cook taking a shot against Duke in the N.C.A.A. tournament — not his teammate Dillon Brooks, who recently chose to return to Oregon instead of entering the draft.
match_headline: College or the N.B.A? New Rule Gives Players More Time and Feedback

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Mets’ 9-1 loss to the Los Angeles Dodgers in which Mets pitcher Noah Syndergaard was ejected for throwing at Chase Utley misidentified the player Mets pitcher Shawn Estes tried and failed to hit in a 2002 game against the Yankees. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, the player was Roger Clemens — not Mike Piazza, who played for the Mets at the time.
match_headline: Chase Utley, Missed by a Pitch, Burns the Mets With Two Home Runs

text: A chart last Sunday about the longest hitting streaks for each Major League Baseball franchise misstated the nickname of the Cleveland team for which Napoleon Lajoie had a 31-game hitting streak in 1906. It was the Naps, not the Nips.
match_headline: With Mark Teixeira Out, Blue Jays End Yankees’ 6-Game Streak

text: An article on May 29 about a longtime journalist who wrote about restaurants frequented by civil rights activists made an outdated reference to Willie Bates, the owner of the Four Way restaurant in Memphis. Editors learned of Mr. Bates’s May 20 death after the section had gone to press.
match_headline: At Soul Food Restaurants, Activism Was on the Menu

text: An article on May 29 about attorney general Kamala Harris of California included an erroneous detail about her first race for attorney general, in 2010. While the outcome of that election took weeks to determine, there was no formal recount.
match_headline: Kamala Harris, a ‘Top Cop’ in the Era of Black Lives Matter

text: An article last Sunday about Paula Broadwell described imprecisely her academic record at the United States Military Academy at West Point. While Ms. Broadwell graduated in the top 5 percent of her class in fitness and military and in the top 10 percent in academics, she did not graduate “at the top of her class.”
ref_headline: at the top of her class.
match_headline: Paula Broadwell, David Petraeus and the Afterlife of a Scandal

text: An article on May 22 about the rock group Blue Öyster Cult misspelled the surname of the band’s guitarist and co-vocalist. Though he is known as Buck Dharma, he was born Donald Roeser, not Roesser.
match_headline: ‘(Don’t Fear) the Reaper’ Is a Creepy Tune, Even With the Cowbell

text: An article last Sunday about the authors Michael Marissen and Lauren Belfer misstated the area where Ms. Belfer grew up. It is Buffalo, not Greenwich Village.
match_headline: A Literary Couple Grapple With Bach and His God

text: An article last Sunday about the film “Popstar: Never Stop Never Stopping” misidentified part of the name of a concert film about Katy Perry. It is “Katy Perry: Part of Me” (not “All of Me”)
match_headline: Justin Bieber, They’re Coming for You

text: A picture credit last Sunday with an article about a documentary about the murder of Kitty Genovese misidentified the source of the photograph. It was supplied by The Witnesses Film LLC, not by FilmRise.
match_headline: Documentary Retries Kitty Genovese’s Neighbors

text: A subheading on May 22 with a review of “The Edge of the Empire. A Journey to Britannia: From the Heart of Rome to Hadrian’s Wall” misspelled the author’s given name. As the review correctly noted, she is Bronwen Riley, not Bronwyn.
ref_headline: The Edge of the Empire. A Journey to Britannia: From the Heart of Rome to Hadrian’s Wall
match_headline: ‘The Edge of the Empire,’ by Bronwen Riley

text: A review on May 8 about “Before the Wind,” by Jim Lynch, misstated the type of racing sailboat represented by the Star class. The Star is a keelboat, not a dinghy. (Instead of a fixed keel, a dinghy generally has a retractable centerboard.)
match_headline: ‘Before the Wind,’ by Jim Lynch

text: An obituary on Sunday and in some editions on Saturday about Muhammad Ali misstated the name of a Broadway show in which he appeared. It was “Buck White,” not “Big Time Buck White.” (“Buck White” was a musical version of the play “Big Time Buck White.”) The obituary also misstated the outcome of the 1963 fight between Ali, then still known as Cassius Clay, and Henry Cooper. The fight was stopped in the fifth round, after Cooper had knocked Clay down in the fourth; Cooper did not “go down in the fifth round ... after he had staggered Clay in the fourth.”
match_headline: Muhammad Ali Dies at 74: Titan of Boxing and the 20th Century

text: An article on Friday about the naming of Robert F. Smith as chairman of Carnegie Hall referred incorrectly to the National Museum of African American History and Culture, to which he has made substantial gifts. It is to open in September; it has not “recently opened.”
match_headline: At Carnegie Hall, a New Leader With a Son Named Hendrix

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in some copies on Wednesday with an article about the Toronto Blue Jays’ recent success against the Yankees misstated the day Toronto’s Jose Bautista was shown throwing an imaginary ball to Yankees fans was taken. It was during the Blue Jays’ 6-0 win on May 24 at Yankee Stadium — not during the Blue Jays’ 4-2 victory of May 30, which was played in Toronto.
match_headline: Not Many Teams Have Yankees’ Number, but the Blue Jays Are Memorizing It

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about this year’s Drama Desk Awards misstated the number of Tony nominations for “Hamilton,” which won seven Drama Desk Awards last year. It is 16, not 17.
match_headline: ‘The Humans’ and ‘Shuffle Along’ Take Top Honors at Drama Desk Awards

text: A picture credit on Monday with the Books of The Times review of “The Course of Love” by Alain de Botton and “Labor of Love” by Moira Weigel, using information from the publisher Farrar, Straus and Giroux, misidentified the photographer. The picture, of Ms. Weigel, is by Joni Sternbach, not Jean Ervasti.
match_headline: Review: ‘Labor of Love’ and ‘The Course of Love,’ on Finding and Keeping It

text: An article on Friday about Britain’s historic feeling of being apart from Europe as it considers whether to leave the European Union referred imprecisely to arrival protocols at British airports and to British passports. Only passengers from non-European countries are given British landing cards upon arrival, and they would not be directed to the line for British and European Union passport holders. Some holders of British passports — for example, citizens of overseas British territories like Bermuda and Turks and Caicos — do not hold European Union citizenship as well; it is not the case that “British passports are by definition European Union passports.”
ref_headline: British passports are by definition European Union passports.
match_headline: How Will ‘Brexit’ Vote Go? Monty Python May Offer Clue

text: An article on May 13 about the sagging fortunes of the Workers’ Party of Brazil, whose standard-bearer, President Dilma Rousseff, was suspended by the Brazilian Senate, misstated the amount of foreign debt that was hobbling the Brazilian economy in 1998, when Ms. Rousseff’s mentor, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, ran for president. It was $250 billion, not $250 million.
match_headline: Brazil Workers’ Party, Leaders ‘Intoxicated by Power,’ Falls From Grace

text: An article on Tuesday about a salary increase for first-year associates at Cravath, Swaine & Moore misstated the date the raises will take effect. It is July 1; they were not effective on May 1, and they will be reflected in paychecks starting July 8, not July 9.
match_headline: Law Firm Salaries Jump for the First Time in Nearly a Decade

text: An article on Monday about the effect of digital technology on productivity growth rendered incorrectly the name of a medical technology provider. It is Athenahealth, not Athena Health.
match_headline: Why the Economic Payoff From Technology Is So Elusive

text: An article on May 28 about the appointment of José Mourinho as the new manager of Manchester United misstated the year he was first appointed as manager of Chelsea. It was in 2004, not 2003.
match_headline: Manchester United Appoints José Mourinho: Here’s What Will Happen

text: An entry in the New Music column on Thursday about “Motown Gospel Presents 1 Mic 1 Take” misspelled the given name of a performer on that album. He is Brian Courtney Wilson, not Bryan.
match_headline: Review: ‘Motown Gospel Presents 1 Mic 1 Take’ Sells Simplicity

text: A recipe last Wednesday for chess pie squares, adapted from the new cookbook “Julia Reed’s South: Spirited Entertaining and High-Style Fun for All Year Long,” misstated the metric equivalent for the six ounces of butter used in both the shortbread crust and the filling. It is 170 grams, not 57.
ref_headline: Julia Reed’s South: Spirited Entertaining and High-Style Fun for All Year Long,
match_headline: A Nearly 12-Year-Long Vigil Ends, and a Massachusetts Church Closes

text: An article on May 20 about signs that some Vietnamese are eager for the American military to return to Cam Ranh Bay base, which the United States used in the Vietnam War, referred incorrectly to the use of the base during the war by American warplanes. While fighter jets took off from the base, B-52 bombers did not.
match_headline: Why Might Vietnam Let U.S. Military Return? China

text: A headline on Wednesday for the About New York column, about a lawsuit over subprime loans at Emigrant Savings Bank, referred incorrectly to those loans in the context of the bank’s history. The assertion by Howard Milstein, quoted in the column, that his family “saved” Emigrant referred to the family’s acquisition of the bank in the 1980s; it is not the case that the subprime loans, from the 2000s, “helped save” the bank.
match_headline: A Benefactor, His Home Loans, and Pain

text: An article on Thursday about Jona S. Rechnitz, a cooperating witness in a corruption case against the correction officers union leader and a central figure in one of the corruption investigations focused on Mayor Bill de Blasio’s fund-raising, misstated Mr. Rechnitz’s age. He is 33, not 26. The article also omitted a group of F.B.I. agents who are investigating some of the fund-raising issues. Besides the F.B.I. squad known as C14, a squad called C4 is also part of the inquiry.
match_headline: De Blasio Donor Emerges as Key Witness in Corruption Case. What Else Does He Know?

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the renaming of a Manhattan street for Norman Rockwell referred incorrectly to the length of time his family lived at 206 West 103rd Street, where the artist was born in 1894. It was until he was 2 years old, not until he was in his early 20s.
match_headline: Manhattan Street Is Renamed After Norman Rockwell

text: An article on Friday about a gift of artworks to the Menil Drawing Institute in Houston misstated the given name of an artist whose work is included in the gift. She was Eva Hesse, not Eve.
match_headline: 110 Pieces by Major Artists Go to Menil Drawing Institute

text: An article on May 29 about a funding crisis at the City University of New York misstated the academic discipline of Stephen Brier, a CUNY professor who spoke about the system’s financial straits. He specializes in urban education, not education. The article also omitted a word from the title of Mr. Brier’s forthcoming book. It is “Austerity Blues: Fighting for the Soul of Public Higher Education” (not merely “Public Education”).
ref_headline: Austerity Blues: Fighting for the Soul of Public Higher Education
match_headline: Dreams Stall as CUNY, New York City’s Engine of Mobility, Sputters

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about family-run Italian restaurants in Westchester County misstated the given name of a daughter of Maurice Giliberti, the owner of Sam’s in Dobbs Ferry. She is Melissa Giliberti, not Megan.
match_headline: Restaurants Where the Italian Family Tradition Endures

text: An article last Sunday about Garbiñe Muguruza’s victory over Serena Williams in the final of the French Open misstated, in some copies, the point in Williams’s career when she began working with her coach, Patrick Mouratoglou. It was in 2012 after losing in the first round of the French Open — not in 2014 after she lost at three major tournaments in a row.
match_headline: Garbiñe Muguruza Upsets Serena Williams in French Open Final

text: An article on May 29 about the economic costs of long security lines at airports gave an outdated figure for the fee that the Transportation Security Administration imposes on airline tickets. It is now $6.50 per flight leg, no longer $2.50. The article also referred incorrectly to a request for the T.S.A. to publish accurate data about lines at airport security checkpoints. It was a lobbying group, Airlines for America, not American Airlines, that made the request. Also, the group asked that the data be made more freely available. It did not specify how the T.S.A. should collect it.
match_headline: Waiting in Line for the Illusion of Security

text: An article last Sunday about signs of rising wages as the labor market tightens misspelled the surname of the Economic Policy Institute’s director of research and policy, who tracks wage trends. He is Josh Bivens, not Bevins.
match_headline: Workers’ Wages Rebound, While Wall Street Squirms

text: A picture caption on June 5 with an article about living in New York City at 800 feet described incorrectly the construction workers shown at 3 World Trade Center. They are workers who install rebar in concrete and create walls; they are not ironworkers.
match_headline: New York Above 800 Feet

text: A picture last Sunday with the Hunt column , about Richard Zoglin’s search for an Upper West Side apart-ment, was published in error. The photograph showed a building at 170 Amsterdam Avenue — not the Aire, an apartment building on West 67th Street that he considered. A picture of the Aire can be found at nytimes.com/realestate .
match_headline: Upper West Side: Prewar to Postwar

text: An article on May 22 about the remake of the mini-series “Roots” misstated the name of the ranch where the original series was filmed. It was Hunter Ranch — not Disney Ranch, which was used as a location for “Roots: The Next Generation.”
match_headline: ‘Roots,’ Remade for a New Era

text: An article last Sunday about the Performance Mix Festival misstated the surname of the festival curator. She is Karen Bernard, not Barnard.
match_headline: Performance Mix Festival Celebrates 30 Years With Tap, Tonics and More

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about recent and coming portrayals of Charles Manson in television and film misstated the title of Karina Longworth’s podcast about Hollywood. It is “You Must Remember This” — not “Charles Manson’s Hollywood,” which was the name of a 12-part series on the podcast. The article also misquoted Jeremy Rosen, a producer of the film “The Family.” He cited “Making a Murderer,” not “Making a Murder,” when talking about a recent surge in interest in shows about cult leaders and serial killers.
match_headline: In Hollywood, a Focus on Manson and His Women

text: A review on May 29 about “From the War on Poverty to the War on Crime,” by Elizabeth Hinton, re-ferred incorrectly to the Juvenile Delinquency and Youth Offenses Control Act of 1961. It was passed by Congress, as all federal acts must be; it was not established by John F. Kennedy’s executive order.
ref_headline: From the War on Poverty to the War on Crime,
match_headline: ‘From the War on Poverty to the War on Crime,’ by Elizabeth Hinton

text: Because of an editing error, a roundup review of cookbooks on June 5 misstated the surname of the author of “Vegan, Vegetarian, Omnivore” at one point. As the review correctly noted else-where, she is Anna Thomas, not Madison. (A book by Deborah Madison was mentioned in the same part of the review.)
match_headline: Cooking: Gwyneth Paltrow’s ‘It’s All Easy,’ and More

text: An article on June 5 about Berlin playgrounds misidentified the location of a local playground. It is behind the marketplace at Winterfeldt-platz, a square — not at Wittenbergplatz, an-other square where there is no playground.
match_headline: What Makes Berlin a Playground Paradise

text: A headline last Tuesday with a capsule summary about the jail sentence for a former Stanford University swimmer, Brock Turner, misidentified the crimes for which he was convicted. As the article correctly noted, the three felony counts were sexual assault of an unconscious person, sexual assault of an intoxicated person and sexual assault with intent to commit rape; the case did not involve a “rape sentence.”
match_headline: Light Sentence for Brock Turner in Stanford Rape Case Draws Outrage

text: An article on Thursday about a bill to create a federal control board to oversee a reboot of Puerto Rico’s economy referred incorrectly to the sovereign status of Puerto Rico. It is a commonwealth, not a country.
match_headline: Weighted by Debt, Puerto Ricans Divided Over Federal Oversight

text: A picture in some editions on Saturday with an article about the Environmental Protection Agency’s plan to install a sewage tank near a Brooklyn warehouse studio owned by Eastern Effects was published in error. The photograph was of one of the buildings for sale near Eastern Effects’s studio, not of the warehouse.
match_headline: Gowanus Canal Cleanup Could Evict Brooklyn Film Studio

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about the Human Rights Watch Film Festival in Manhattan, which includes the documentary “Sonita,” misidentified the school where the subject of the film is studying. It is Wasatch Academy in Mount Pleasant, Utah — not Utah Valley University. The article also misidentified the site of the university. The main campus is in Orem, Utah, not “Wasatch.” (While the university also has a Wasatch Campus, it is in Heber City, Utah; there is a Wasatch County in the state but no town of that name.)
match_headline: At the Human Rights Watch Film Festival, a Lot of the Humans Are Women

text: An article on Saturday about symbols used online by white extremists misspelled the surname of one who reverses a symbol used to designate Jewish heritage in order to signal that she is not Jewish. She is Lana Lokteff, not Lotkeff.
match_headline: For the Alt-Right, the Message Is in the Punctuation

text: Because of an editing error, the Quotation of the Day on Saturday, taken from an article about a wildfire that broke out last week in Yarnell, Ariz., and the memories it prompted of a devastating 2013 wildfire there, misidentified the person who said: “I was, like, a fire? We’re still recovering from a fire.” As the article correctly noted, the comment was by Chuck Tidey, president of the Yarnell-Peeples Valley Chamber of Commerce — not by Ben Palm, chief of the Yarnell Fire Department.
ref_headline: I was, like, a fire? We’re still recovering from a fire.

text: An obituary on Friday about the venture capitalist Thomas J. Perkins misstated part of the name of a company in which he invested. It was Tandem Computers, not Tandem Computer. The obituary also misstated, in some editions, the year that Hewlett-Packard, on whose board Mr. Perkins served, bought the computer company Compaq. It was 2002, not 2001.
match_headline: Thomas J. Perkins, Pioneering Venture Capitalist in Silicon Valley, Dies at 84

text: Because of an editing error, a news analysis article on May 18 about signs that the Islamic State is on the defensive in Iraq, but by no means in its death throes, carried an erroneous dateline. The reporter, Tim Arango, reported from Istanbul, not Baghdad.
match_headline: Yes, ISIS Is Losing in Iraq. No, It’s Not in Its Death Throes.

text: An article on May 17 about the Eurovision Song Contest, in which a singer from Ukraine unexpectedly upset the odds-on favorite, a Russian, referred incorrectly to changes in the contest this year. Contest organizers changed the way the votes were tabulated: Votes by viewer polls and by a five-member jury in each participating country were presented separately, instead of being combined. The popular vote/jury vote system was not introduced this year.
match_headline: Ukraine’s Eurovision Win Rouses a Chorus of Anger and Suspicion in Russia

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about expectations of a quieter Belmont Stakes this year misstated the projections for attendance that day. While 46,000 tickets had been sold as of Friday, more people were expected to attend; the number of attendees was not expected to be 46,000. (Officials later announced that paid attendance was just over 61,000; more than 100,000 have attended some years.)
match_headline: A Mellower Belmont Stakes Brings Out the Regulars

text: An article in some editions on Saturday about San Jose Sharks goaltender Martin Jones referred incorrectly to the playoff performances of his teammates Logan Couture and Joe Pavelski. Couture was the postseason leader in points and Pavelski was the leader in goals, not the other way around.
match_headline: A Humble Shield Safeguards the Sharks’ Net

text: A report in the Scoreboard column in some editions on June 4 about the United States men’s soccer team’s 2-0 loss to Colombia in the opening game of the Copa América tournament misstated the frequency of the tournament. While it has been played the past two years, it is not an annual event. (The tournament has been played at various intervals during its 100-year history.)
match_headline: United States Falls to Colombia in Copa América Opener

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about some museum-quality shows at art galleries in Manhattan misstated a date in the title of the show at the Edward Tyler Fine Art gallery. It is “Ed Ruscha: Ribbon Words: 1966-1973” (not “1967-1973”). The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Last Chance: Warhol, Basquiat and Other History Lessons

text: A picture credit on June 7 with an article about a new theory on black holes misstated the photographer’s middle initial. Two photographs, of several scientists, were taken by Anna N. Zytkow, not Anna M.
match_headline: No Escape From Black Holes? Stephen Hawking Points to a Possible Exit

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Joseph Percoco, a former aide to Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo who is under federal investigation, quoted incorrectly from comments by Blair Horner, the executive director of the New York Public Interest Research Group. Mr. Horner said that the actions of Mr. Percoco could cause harm if he was “gaming the system,” not “manipulating” it.
match_headline: How Joseph Percoco, Cuomo’s Problem-Solver, Became a Problem

text: An article on Saturday about the increasing presence of birds at Westchester County Airport, using information from government officials, misidentified birds that nest above hangar doors there. They are cliff swallows, not barn swallows. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: At Westchester Airport, Where Bald Eagles (and Their Friends) Dare

text: An article on Wednesday about Uber’s plans to raise as much as $2 billion through the use of leveraged securities described a leveraged loan incorrectly. It is issued by a company with heavy existing debt, not to that company.
match_headline: Uber Sets Sights on Leveraged Loans for Even More Money

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about “The Evidence Room,” an exhibition at the Venice Architecture Biennale that is a reconstruction of architectural elements of the Auschwitz death camp, misspelled the given name of a member of the team that worked on the project. She is Sascha Hastings, not Sacha.
match_headline: ‘The Evidence Room’: Architects Examine the Horrors of Auschwitz

text: An article on May 20 about the setback to Egypt delivered by the fatal crash of an EgyptAir Airbus A320 that was flying from Paris to Cairo omitted a reporting credit. Kareem Fahim and Nour Youssef contributed reporting from Cairo.
match_headline: EgyptAir Crash Blindsides a Nation That Thought It Was Recovering

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on May 20 about the inauguration of Tsai Ing-wen as president of Taiwan referred imprecisely to the “92 Consensus,” which Chinese state media outlets have called on Ms. Tsai to endorse. Under the consensus, the Kuomintang and China’s ruling Communist Party currently recognize Taiwan and mainland China as part of “one China,” but each has its own understanding of what that means; it is not the case that the parties have yet to reach the consensus and that doing so would bring them to a common understanding.
match_headline: Tsai Ing-wen Sworn In as Taiwan’s President, as China Watches Closely

text: An article on May 20 about the nomination of Binali Yildirim, a loyalist to the conservative president of Turkey, as the country’s new prime minister quoted incorrectly from comments by Mr. Yildirim about his opposition to the mixing of genders at Istanbul Technical University. He said, “I was taken aback by the sight of young people, girls and boys, sitting together on the lawn,” not “sitting on the together on the lawn.” (Mr. Yildirim was confirmed on May 22.)
ref_headline: I was taken aback by the sight of young people, girls and boys, sitting together on the lawn,
match_headline: Erdogan Loyalist Is Nominated to Be Turkey’s Prime Minister

text: An article on May 19 about an uproar in Iran prompted by a visit by Faezeh Hashemi, daughter of a prominent ayatollah, to a female leader of the persecuted Bahai religious minority misstated the number of Bahais worldwide. There are five million to seven million, not about 300,000.
match_headline: An Ayatollah’s Daughter Prompts a Debate on Religious Persecution in Iran

text: An article on May 18 about a decision by Australia’s national science agency to dismiss John Church, a pre-eminent scientist in the field of rising global sea levels, as part of deep cuts at the agency misstated part of the name of the San Diego research center where Dean Roemmich is a professor. Mr. Roemmich, who said the dismissal was “absolutely inconceivable,” is with the Scripps Institution of Oceanography (not “Institute”).
match_headline: Australia to Lay Off Leading Scientist on Sea Levels

text: An article on Tuesday about the victims of the Orlando nightclub massacre misidentified the country where the family of one victim, Jerald Arthur Wright, lives. It is Ecuador, not Colombia.
match_headline: 49 Lives Lost to Horror in Orlando: Mostly Young, Gay and Latino

text: An article on Monday about the sexual assault case at Stanford University referred incorrectly to the punishment for Brock Turner, the assailant in the case. Under California law, Mr. Turner will likely be released — not paroled — after three months in county jail. (There are no parole procedures for county terms.)
match_headline: Court Papers Give Insight Into Stanford Sex Assault

text: An article on Tuesday about global reaction to an attack on a gay nightclub in Orlando, Fla., that killed 49 people misspelled the given name of a Chinese lawyer who expressed concern about her daughter, a student at the University of Minnesota who was at the Shanghai airport when explosives were detonated there on Sunday. The lawyer is Gao Junlan, not Gao Junlian.
match_headline: Globally, Orlando Attack Strikes Now-Familiar Fault Lines

text: An article in some editions on Monday about a gathering at the Stonewall Inn in New York after the mass shooting in Florida misidentified a gay rights case that the Supreme Court decided a year ago. It was on the right to same-sex marriage — not the Defense of Marriage Act, which it struck down in 2013.
match_headline: At Stonewall Inn, a Gay Rights Landmark, a Vigil in Pride and Anger

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Friday about Molly Huddle’s competing in the New York City Marathon in November referred incorrectly to the events she is hoping to compete in at the Rio de Janeiro Olympics. They are the 5,000 meters or the 10,000 meters — not “middle-distance events.” (Middle distance typically refers to the 800 and 1,500.) The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: American Distance Star Plans to Run New York City Marathon

text: A map on Thursday with an article about a proposed expansion of ferry service in New York City omitted one of the proposed ferry terminals. One is planned for Roosevelt Island. The map also misidentified two proposed terminals in Manhattan and failed to label an existing one. The third stop from the bottom of the map, a planned stop, is Grand Avenue, not Stuyvesant Cove; the planned stop above that is Stuyvesant Cove, not East 34th Street; and the existing stop above that is East 34th Street. A corrected map can be found at nytimes.com/nyregion .
match_headline: De Blasio’s $325 Million Ferry Push: Rides to 5 Boroughs, at Subway Price

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about an outing on Long Island Sound that left two people dead after a kayak and paddleboard were swept far from shore transposed the given names of the two survivors, using information from the authorities. The mother is Delfina Reynoso of Hartford, and her daughter is Damaris.
match_headline: Sunset Ride Turns Deadly for 2 on Windy Long Island Sound

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a second vigil at the Stonewall Inn in New York for the 49 people who died in an attack on a gay nightclub in Orlando, Fla., misstated, in some editions, the surname of a 25-year-old man from Brooklyn who was one of those killed. He was Enrique Rios, not Ross.
match_headline: A Moment of Solidarity at the Stonewall Inn, a Gay Rights Landmark

text: A headline on Friday with an article about the appointment of Stacey Snider as chairman and chief executive at 21st Century Fox misstated Ms. Snider’s current job. As the article correctly noted, she is co-chairwoman of 20th Century Fox, the film studio — not its parent, 21st Century Fox.
match_headline: 21st Century Fox Names Stacey Snider Its Next Studio Chief

text: An article on the Square Feet page on June 8 about activist investors who are taking an interest in real estate investment trusts rendered incorrectly the name of the company with which New York REIT, a target of activist investors, plans to merge. It is JBG Companies, not JBP Companies.
match_headline: Activist Investors Have a New Favorite Target: REITs

text: A picture caption on Friday with the Antiques column misidentified the object shown. It is a vase made around 1895 at the Dorflinger glass factory in White Mills, Pa., not a wine ewer from 1899.
match_headline: A New Glass Museum Will Open in a Historic Factory

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about J. T. Rogers’s account of how his new play “Oslo” evolved misstates the circumstances under which he conceived the project. It was during a meeting with Terje Rod-Larsen, then a United Nations special envoy, who had been involved in the making of the Oslo Accords; it was not with Mr. Larsen and Mona Juul, an ambassador and representative to the United Nations Norway Mission. (Ms. Juul, who is married to Mr. Larsen, joined the project later.) A revised version of the article, in which Mr. Rogers clarifies his dealings with the diplomats, can be found at nytimes.com/arts.
match_headline: ‘Oslo’ and the Drama in Diplomacy

text: An obituary on Friday about Kenneth Walton, a top official in the New York office of the F.B.I. in the early 1980s, referred incorrectly to the 1981 robbery of a Brink’s armored truck in Rockland County. It was carried out by a coalition of groups that included members of the Weather Underground and the Black Liberation Army. It was not carried out solely by the Weather Underground.
match_headline: Kenneth Walton, F.B.I.’s Bold New York Face in the ’80s, Dies at 76

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Creator’s victory in the Belmont Stakes misattributed, in some copies, a quotation regarding the performance of Exaggerator, the Preakness Stakes winner who finished 11th. It was Kent Desormeaux, the horse’s jockey — not Keith Desormeaux, his trainer — who said, “I put him down for a mad drive and said, show me your stuff, but there was nothing there.”
ref_headline: I put him down for a mad drive and said, show me your stuff, but there was nothing there.
match_headline: Creator Wins the Belmont Stakes

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an essay about the death of the hockey great Gordie Howe reversed the identities of Howe’s sons shown with him and his wife, Colleen, during a Houston Aeros practice in 1974. Mark is at the left and Marty is second from right.
match_headline: Recalling a Time When Gordie Howe and His Sons Were the Power

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Detroit Tigers’ 6-1 victory over the Yankees referred imprecisely to the record of Tigers pitcher Justin Verlander at Yankee Stadium. Until his victory on Saturday, Verlander had never won a game at the new Yankee Stadium, which opened in 2009; it is not the case they he “had never won a start at Yankee Stadium.” (Verlander won his only start at the old Yankee Stadium, in 2007.)
ref_headline: had never won a start at Yankee Stadium.
match_headline: Once Bedeviled, Justin Verlander Conquers His Bronx Demons

text: An article last Sunday about “Oslo,” a new play by J.T. Rogers, referred incorrectly to one of two diplomats who set in motion the back-channel dealings that led to what became the Oslo peace accords. One is a woman; they are not both men.
match_headline: ‘Oslo’ by J.T. Rogers Looks Behind Rabin and Arafat’s Handshake

text: An article last Sunday about the Broadway musical “Hamilton” misstated the point at which the show’s performers began collectively pressing for profit-sharing. It was in August 2015, as the Broadway production was opening, not before the Off Broadway production opened.
match_headline: ‘Hamilton’ Inc.: The Path to a Billion-Dollar Broadway Show

text: An article on May 21 about Gaza residents’ fears that the rebuilding of attack tunnels to Israel puts Palestinians at risk referred incompletely to Israel’s suspension of cement deliveries to Gaza for reconstruction of homes destroyed in the 2014 war. The suspension affected only homes being rebuilt by private individuals; cement continued to flow to housing projects handled by foreign governments and international aid groups.
match_headline: As Hamas Tunnels Back Into Israel, Palestinians Are Afraid, Too

text: An article on May 22 about EgyptAir’s awareness of security threats to the Airbus A320 jetliner that crashed into the Mediterranean — including graffiti written in Arabic on the underside of the plane that said, “We will bring this plane down” — referred incorrectly in some editions to a cousin of the captain of the fatal flight. The cousin, Ezzat Shoukair, is a man.
ref_headline: We will bring this plane down
match_headline: EgyptAir Was Aware of Threats to Security, Including One Scribbled on Plane

text: An article on Monday about the transformation of Wyoming’s energy landscape to wind power from coal misstated the position of Bill Miller at the Anschutz Corporation. He is senior vice president of energy and land resources, not the president and chief executive. The article also misstated the number of acres on which the Anschutz Corporation will build the Carbon County wind farm. It will be on 2,000 acres, not 200.
match_headline: As Wind Power Lifts Wyoming’s Fortunes, Coal Miners Are Left in the Dust

text: An article on April 12 about two donors to Mayor Bill de Blasio and their connections with police officials who are under federal investigation misstated the rank of a former senior police commander. Philip Banks III, one of the officials under investigation, was once the highest ranking uniformed official in the New York Police Department, not the third-highest-ranking chief. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption. This correction was delayed because editors learned of the error only late last week.
match_headline: De Blasio Donors Took Pride in Connections With Top Police Officials

text: An article on Monday about allegations of conflict between Airbnb’s vow to eliminate bias in bookings and its policy of barring class actions by customers misidentified, in some editions, the university at which Jamila Jefferson-Jones, a law professor who commented on the issue, teaches. It is the University of Missouri, Kansas City — not Barry University School of Law.
match_headline: Airbnb Vows to Fight Racism, but Its Users Can’t Sue to Prompt Fairness

text: An article on Saturday about an installation on Italy’s Lake Iseo by the artist Christo misspelled, in one instance, part of the name of his wife and partner, who died in 2009. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she was Jeanne-Claude, not Jean-Claude.
match_headline: Christo’s Newest Project: Walking on Water

text: An obituary on Sunday about the costume and set designer Desmond Heeley rendered incorrectly the name of a magazine that published an interview with him in 2011. It is Lighting&Sound America, not Light & Sound America.
match_headline: Desmond Heeley, an ‘Alchemist’ of Theater Design, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Sunday about the writer Michelle Cliff misstated the century in which the social reformer Lillian Smith, a collection of whose writings Ms. Cliff edited, was active. It was the 20th century, not the 19th.
match_headline: Michelle Cliff, Who Wrote of Colonialism and Racism, Dies at 69

text: Because of a production error, the continuation of an article about a sit-in by House Democrats was omitted from some copies on Thursday. The complete article can be found at nytimes.com/us . Also because of a production error, Pages A4 and B4 were reversed in some copies. Though the continuation of an article about transgender bathroom rights in a town in Mexico appeared on Page A10 in all editions, the beginning of the article erroneously appeared in the Business section in some copies. The complete article can be found at nytimes.com/world .
match_headline: Mixed-Gender Bathroom Rights in Mexico

text: An article on Tuesday about the Orlando police department’s continuing defense of how it handled the nightclub massacre that left 49 people dead and 53 wounded misspelled the surname of a survivor who discussed law enforcement’s efforts the night of the shooting. He is Norman Casiano, not Caisano.
match_headline: Orlando Police Defend Actions as Clock Ticked in Massacre

text: A news analysis article on Thursday about politically inspired questioning of the Federal Reserve chairwoman, Janet L. Yellen, at a House hearing misstated the given name of a member of Congress from Washington State. He is Denny Heck, not Danny.
match_headline: On Capitol Hill, Yellen Finds Partisan Heat, Not Economic Light

text: An article on Thursday about resistance by insurers to payment for alternative pain treatments misidentified the medical specialty of Dr. Steven Feinberg, who commented on the issue. He is a specialist in physical medicine, not a psychiatrist.
match_headline: New Ways to Treat Pain Meet Resistance

text: An article on Monday about the performance of Minnesota Twins first baseman Joe Mauer this season overstated the significance of his three batting titles as a catcher. He was the first American League catcher to win multiple batting titles; it is not the case that “no catcher had won multiple batting titles” until Mauer did. (Ernie Lombardi won two National League batting titles, in 1938 and 1942.)
ref_headline: no catcher had won multiple batting titles
match_headline: Joe Mauer Fights to Stay Afloat Aboard a Sinking Twins Team

text: An article on Thursday about the financial performance of four Broadway shows misstated the cost of producing one of them. “American Psycho” cost $8.8 million to produce, not $9.8 million.
match_headline: Anatomy of a Broadway Flop: What Sank These 4 Shows?

text: Because of an editing error, a letter on Saturday about rape and intoxication misspelled the surname of the writer whose essay prompted the letter. She is Emily Bazelon, not Bazelton.
match_headline: Being Drunk Is No Excuse

text: An article on May 26 about the complex calculus behind President Obama’s decision to become the first sitting president to visit Hiroshima, Japan, referred incorrectly to one of the 11 presidents who have served since President Harry S. Truman’s decision to drop an atomic weapon on that city. That president, Gerald R. Ford, succeeded Richard M. Nixon after Nixon’s resignation; Ford was not elected.
match_headline: In Obama’s Visit to Hiroshima, a Complex Calculus of Asian Politics

text: Because of an editing error, an article on May 27 about a United Nations committee’s decision to suspend its investigation of torture allegations in Ukraine, citing a lack of cooperation from government security services, misidentified the United Nations agreement that allows its inspectors to make unannounced visits to any detention center in countries that have signed the agreement, as Ukraine has. It is the Optional Protocol, an addendum to the Convention Against Torture, not the torture treaty itself.
match_headline: U.N. Suspends Torture Inquiry in Ukraine

text: Because of an editing error, an article on May 25 about the barring of Vietnamese activists from a meeting with President Obama during his recent visit to Hanoi referred incorrectly to one of those barred, a prominent blogger and journalist. The journalist, Pham Doan Trang, is a woman.
match_headline: As Obama Presses Vietnam on Rights, Activists Are Barred From Meeting

text: An article on Thursday about free speech on campuses referred incorrectly to action taken by the board of trustees at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, Pa., on a faculty statement promoting free speech. While the board would not adopt the faculty’s language as part of a universitywide statement, it did permit the faculty to include the statement in its handbook; the faculty statement was not “vetoed” outright by the board.
match_headline: Studies in the First Amendment, Playing Out on Campus

text: An obituary in some copies on Friday about Ralph Stanley, the singer and banjo player who was a pivotal figure in the revival of interest in bluegrass music, omitted a survivor. Beside his wife, Jimmie; his daughters, Lisa Stanley Marshall and Tonya Armes Stanley; and a son, Ralph II, Mr. Stanley is survived by another son, Tim.
match_headline: Ralph Stanley, Whose Mountain Music Gave Rise to Bluegrass, Dies at 89

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Australian film director Paul Cox omitted a reporting credit. Michelle Innis contributed reporting from Sydney, Australia.
match_headline: Paul Cox, Independent Filmmaker Who Explored Postmodern Life, Dies at 76

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about letters by and about President Obama’s father, using information from officials in the 2008 presidential campaign, misstated the decade in which a picture of father and son was taken. It was the 1970s, not the 1960s.
match_headline: Words of Obama’s Father Still Waiting to Be Read by His Son

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about efforts to improve diversity in the Westchester Philharmonic included an incorrect figure from the League of American Orchestras for the percentage of Latinos in American orchestras. It is 2.5 percent, not 1.2 percent.
match_headline: Leading the Orchestra, an Outsider Invited In

text: An obituary last Sunday about the author Lois Duncan misidentified, in some copies, the city in Florida where she died. It is Bradenton, not Sarasota. The obituary also misstated, in some copies, the surname of one of her daughters, who survives her. She is Robin Burkin, not Robin Arquette.
match_headline: Lois Duncan, 82, Dies; Author Knew ‘What You Did Last Summer’

text: An article on June 12 about segregation in New York City schools misstated the number of buildings from the Farragut Houses, a public-housing project in Brooklyn, that were previously included in P.S. 307’s attendance zone. It was five of the 10 buildings, not seven.
match_headline: Choosing a School for My Daughter in a Segregated City

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the Ojai Music Festival misstated Scott Reed’s relationship to the festival. He resigned from the festival’s board in January; he is not a current board member.
match_headline: At Ojai, Peter Sellars Has a Personal Yet Global Playlist

text: An article last Sunday about the director Nicolas Winding Refn referred incorrectly to advertisements directed by Mr. Refn that feature the actor Matthew McConaughey. Mr. McConaughey appears in the advertisements, for Lincoln; they are not simply “voice-over commercials.”
match_headline: Nicolas Winding Refn Dissects His Bloody Confection

text: An article last Sunday about a fear of roller coasters misstated the surname of the editor of ThemeParkInsider.com . He is Robert Niles, not Miles.
match_headline: Don’t Like Roller Coasters? The View From Earth Is Fine

text: An article last Sunday about shrinking job prospects and mounting debt for law students misstated the timetable under which the government would forgive the debt incurred by John Acosta, a graduate of Valparaiso University Law School who is setting up his own criminal law practice. It would be forgiven in 20 years, not 25 years.
match_headline: An Expensive Law Degree, and No Place to Use It

text: An article on May 29 about the conviction and sentencing of former military officers for their roles in Operation Condor, in which South American military governments hunted down and eliminated leftist dissidents across national borders, misstated, in some editions, the number of officers convicted for their roles in killing, kidnapping and torturing more than 100 victims as part of the operation. Fourteen were convicted, not 15. (One other defendant was convicted on separate charges involving a different set of victims.) Because of an editing error, the article misstated, in some editions, the nationality of one defendant. He is from Uruguay, not Argentina. The article also misstated the decade during which Argentina passed amnesty laws, whose loopholes prosecutors exploited to proceed with the Operation Condor cases. It was the 1980s, not the 1990s. And also because of an editing error, an accompanying picture caption misidentified, in some editions, the site where victims and their relatives watched the sentencing. They were shown at the Argentine Embassy in Montevideo, Uruguay, watching a live feed — not at the sentencing itself, which was in a Buenos Aires courtroom.
match_headline: Argentine Court Confirms a Deadly Legacy of Dictatorships

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Mets’ 11-4 loss to the Washington Nationals referred incorrectly to Mets pitcher Noah Syndergaard’s walks in recent starts. His total of three walks on Monday equaled his total from his previous seven starts combined; it did not exceed it.
match_headline: Noah Syndergaard Exits Early, Putting Mets on Alert

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the track coach Sam Bell misspelled the surname of one of his daughters. She is Beth Ahearn, not Ahern.
match_headline: Sam Bell, Exacting Mentor of College Runners, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Saturday about the keyboardist Bernie Worrell misspelled the name of his 2007 solo album. It is “Improvisczario,” not “Improviscario.”
match_headline: Bernie Worrell, Whose Keyboards Left an Imprint on Funk and Hip-Hop, Dies at 72

text: An article on June 3 about torrential rains and flooding in central and northeastern France misstated the level the Seine reached in Paris on the evening of June 2. It rose to 18 feet, not 18 feet above its typical level. The article also misstated the level the Seine reached during a catastrophic flood in 1910. It rose to 26 feet, not 26 feet above its regular level.
match_headline: From Paris to Bavaria, Heavy Rains Cause Deadly Floods

text: An article on June 2 about a military advancement toward the Islamic State stronghold of Surt, Libya, by fighters aligned with the country’s United Nations-backed government misstated part of a comment by Frederic Wehrey, a Libya specialist at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace who visited the country recently. Referring to rival militias in Libya, he said, “Only a year ago, these two groups were battling for control of the so-called oil crescent, and lobbing” — not “lobbying” — “rockets and shells at one another.”
ref_headline: Only a year ago, these two groups were battling for control of the so-called oil crescent, and lobbing
match_headline: Militias in Libya Advance on ISIS Stronghold of Surt With Separate Agendas

text: A reporting credit on June 2 with an article about the Syrian government’s easing of some limits on humanitarian aid convoys in rebel-held areas misspelled, in some editions, the surname of a contributor from Beirut, Lebanon. She is Anne Barnard, not Bernard.
match_headline: Syria, Facing Deadline, Allows Limited Aid to Besieged Town of Daraya

text: An article on June 16 about a deadly 1980 attack on gay men at the Ramrod Bar in Greenwich Village, using information from Times news articles from that period, misspelled the surname and misstated the age of one of the victims. He was Vernon Kroening, not Koenig, and he was 32, not 21. (His surname was also misspelled in a picture caption with a collection of photographs on May 11.) The article, also using the earlier news reports, misidentified the intersection where the attacker initially opened fire. It is Washington and Charles Streets, not Washington and 10th Streets. A corrective article is on Page A15.
match_headline: New York’s Own Anti-Gay Massacre, Now Barely Remembered

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about a nine-hour film by the artist Cheng Ran that will be shown at the New Museum in Manhattan in the fall quoted incorrectly from comments about the film by the museum’s artistic director, Massimiliano Gioni. He said “The time that the viewer puts into seeing it — that is, to me, a form of sculpture,” not a form of “culture.”
ref_headline: The time that the viewer puts into seeing it — that is, to me, a form of sculpture,
match_headline: Auctioneer at Sotheby’s Confident in London as Art Hub

text: A picture caption in the Listings pages on Friday about Dusan Tynek Dance Theater, which performs next week at New York Live Arts in Manhattan, misstated the given name of the composer of the music for “Tethered Light,” a work on the program. He is Bryce Dessner, not Bruce.
match_headline: Dance Listings for July 1-7

text: An article on June 5 about Francesca Immacolata Chaouqui, the central protagonist at the “Vatileaks 2” trial in Vatican City, who has become a lightning rod of intrigue and criticism, misstated the given name of one of the two journalists to whom she is accused of leaking state secrets. He is Emiliano Fittipaldi, not Emanuele.
match_headline: Scapegoat or Spy? Vatican Consultant Commands Attention at Leaks Trial

text: An article on Monday about Antwun Shumpert’s fatal encounter with the police in Tupelo, Miss., misstated in some editions an office sought by Carlos Moore, a lawyer for the family of the victim. Mr. Moore ran for the State Senate, not the State House. The article also misstated in some editions part of a quotation from Mr. Moore. He said, “Make no mistake about it, I’m coming after you, Tupelo,” not, “Make no doubt about it, I’m coming after you, Tupelo.”
ref_headline: Make no mistake about it, I’m coming after you, Tupelo,
match_headline: Black Man’s Fatal Encounter With Police Splits Mississippi City Known for Harmony

text: An article on Thursday about a study in JAMA Dermatology of pubic hair grooming practices, based on the study’s results section, referred imprecisely to the percentage of women who remove all their pubic hair. Sixty-two is the percentage of women who reported ever having done so; smaller percentages reported having done it repeatedly. (The researchers have notified JAMA Dermatology of the need for a clarification.)
match_headline: Many Women Prefer to Groom, Citing Hygiene (and Baffling Doctors)

text: An article on Monday about the Yankees’ 6-3 victory over the San Diego Padres, in which Mark Teixeira hit two home runs, described incorrectly the injury that sidelined Teixeira last August. He fractured a shin; not an ankle.
match_headline: Mark Teixeira Hits 400th Home Run as Power Hitting Pushes Yankees Past Padres

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about the live streaming of the Broadway musical “She Loves Me” by BroadwayHD cited a Playbill report that a recording of the show would be released in theaters in November. A publicist for BroadwayHD says no theatrical release has been confirmed.
match_headline: Broadway Comes to a Laptop Near You

text: An obituary on Saturday about the British poet Geoffrey Hill misstated the name of the college from which he received a degree in English literature. It is Keble College, Oxford, not Kemble.
match_headline: Geoffrey Hill, Dense and Allusive British Poet, Is Dead at 84

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Abbas Kiarostami, often hailed as Iran’s greatest filmmaker, misstated the given name of one of his surviving sons. He is Ahmad, not Ahman.
match_headline: Abbas Kiarostami, Acclaimed Iranian Filmmaker, Dies at 76

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Michel Rocard, a former prime minister of France, misstated the year he joined François Mitterrand’s newly formed Socialist Party. It was 1974, not 1971.
match_headline: Michel Rocard, Former Prime Minister of France, Dies at 85

text: An article on Wednesday about Figment NYC, a free annual festival on Governors Island, misidentified the object represented by one of the miniature golf course holes. It is a key, not a keyhole.•
match_headline: On Governors Island, Family-Friendly Art With a Stroke of Whimsy

text: An article on Monday about the Silver Gull, a beach club in Queens, misstated, in some editions, the distance between it and the Breezy Point Surf Club, which is run by the same organization that operates Silver Gull. The clubs are about two miles apart, not one.
match_headline: A Beach Club in Queens Where Every Summer Is the Same

text: A picture with an article on Monday about the challenge of self-driving vehicles to the automobile insurance industry was published in error. The self-driving system shown was in a Continental test vehicle, not a Tesla.
match_headline: As Self-Driving Cars Hit the Road, Innovation Is Outpacing Insurance

text: An article on the DealBook page on Wednesday about Mondelez International’s $23 billion bid for the Hershey Company misidentified the location of the headquarters of Mondelez. The company is based in Deerfield, Ill., not Virginia, which is where it is incorporated.
match_headline: Another Hershey Deal May Come Unwrapped. Maybe It Should.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the consequences of a British vote to leave the European Union misstated the dollar equivalent of 150 million pounds, roughly the amount Britain was sending to the European Union each week. It is about $197 million, not $167 million.
match_headline: Welsh Reject E.U., but Its Money Will Be Missed

text: An article on Thursday about the fifth stage of the Tour de France misidentified the cyclist whom the stage’s winner, Greg Van Avermaet, left behind on the next-to-last climb of the day. It was Thomas De Gendt, not Rafal Majka.
match_headline: Belgian Takes Hilly Stage 5 and the Tour de France Overall Lead

text: A critic’s notebook article on Monday about the final broadcast of “A Prairie Home Companion” misstated, in some editions, the date the show was recorded. It was Friday, not Saturday.
match_headline: Garrison Keillor Turns Out the Lights on Lake Wobegon

text: An article on Page D3 about the basketball player Dwyane Wade and his interest in fashion design misstated the number of times he has made the National Basketball Association All-Star team. It is 12, not 10. The article also misidentified his team affiliation. Mr. Wade announced his intention to leave the Miami Heat for the Chicago Bulls on Wednesday, the day after the Men’s Style section went to press.
match_headline: Dwyane Wade’s Game Plan Includes Fashion Design

text: Because of an editing error, an article on June 10 about the conviction of Ahmed Adeeb, a former vice president of the Maldives, on charges of trying to assassinate the country’s president misstated, in some editions, the surname of a former Maldives prosecutor who had earlier refused to prosecute Mr. Adeeb and was convicted on terrorism charges. As noted correctly elsewhere in the article, he is Muhuthaz Muhsin, not Mushin. The article also referred incorrectly to actions taken by Mr. Muhsin before the government of Maldives brought charges against him. According to his lawyer, the charges were filed after Mr. Muhsin tried to obtain a warrant for President Abdulla Yameen’s arrest, not after Mr. Muhsin opened a corruption investigation into Mr. Yameen.
match_headline: Ex-Vice President of Maldives Convicted of Trying to Kill President

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a new arts complex in Athens referred incompletely to the project’s contractors. It is a joint venture of Salini Impregilo of Italy and Terna of Greece, not Salini Impregilo alone.
match_headline: Ancient Athens Neighborhood Pins Hopes on a Cultural Center

text: A picture with an article on Thursday about the decision of the former Fox anchor Gretchen Carlson to sue its chairman, Roger Ailes, omitted a credit. The portrait of Ms. Carlson was taken by Timothy Greenfield-Sanders and distributed by Stockland Martel.
match_headline: How Gretchen Carlson Took On the Chief of Fox News

text: An article on Thursday about Adam Warren, the former Yankees pitcher who now plays for the Chicago Cubs, misstated the given name of the Cincinnati Reds player who hit a three-run home run against the Cubs on Wednesday. He is Tucker Barnhart, not Trevor.
match_headline: On a Team That Values Versatility, Adam Warren Is Finding His Place
