text: An article on Wednesday about the impact of the baseball executive Theo Epstein on the rosters for this year’s All-Star Game described incorrectly the way the Boston Red Sox acquired shortstop Xander Bogaerts when Epstein was the team’s general manager. He was signed as an amateur free agent; he was not drafted.
match_headline: Theo Epstein’s Imprint Is Clear on All-Star Game Rosters

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about a new tour in the Tap City Festival contains outdated performance information. After the section went to press, the choreographer Brenda Bufalino withdrew from a July 14 dance performance at the Duke on 42nd Street, although she is still hosting the tour.
match_headline: Tap Treasures Takes Manhattan

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Page 20 this weekend about “You Are Having a Good Time,” by Amie Barrodale, concludes with a sentence containing an extraneous backslash in place of a word. The sentence should read, “And in all of this inefficiency, frustration and absurdity, Barrodale has captured something near to what it feels like to be confined to a human brain.”
ref_headline: You Are Having a Good Time,
match_headline: Stories Exploring the Misguided, the Unrequited and the Mortified

text: An obituary in some editions on Sunday and on Monday about the photographer Dave Heath misstated his marital history. He was briefly married to Angelika de Kornfeld in the early 1970s; it is not the case that he never married.
match_headline: Dave Heath, Photographer of Isolation, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Friday about the actor John McMartin referred incorrectly to a production of the Friedrich Dürrenmatt play “The Visit” in which he appeared on Broadway in the 1970s. It was not a musical. (He did appear in a later musical version of “The Visit,” although not on Broadway.) The obituary also misspelled the given name of an actor with whom Mr. McMartin appeared in the Broadway play “All the Way” in 2014. He is Bryan Cranston, not Brian.
match_headline: John McMartin, Versatile Mainstay on Broadway and TV, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Friday about the former New York deputy mayor Peter J. Powers misstated the given name of one of his brothers. He is Don, not Dan.
match_headline: Peter Powers, Mayor Giuliani’s Steady Right Hand, Dies at 72

text: An article last Sunday about do-it-yourself wine blending and other luxury experiences referred incompletely to V.I.P. tours that include lunch and a shoe-designing experience. The lunch is with Salvatore Ferragamo, the grandson and namesake of the founder of the Ferragamo shoe company, not the founder himself, who died in 1960. The shoe studio is owned by the Ferragamo company, not the younger Mr. Ferragamo, who is a winemaker.
match_headline: A Wine of One’s Own? They’ll Drink to That

text: An article last Sunday about complications arising from a set of Richard Avedon photographs that lack formal authentication referred incorrectly to the legal case Guggenheim v. Lubell, which may be a legal precedent for a lawsuit should the prints’ owner try to sell them. The case dealt with a work of art that had been stolen from the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum and then sold to a buyer unaware of the theft; it was not devised to retrieve art stolen by the Nazis. A picture caption with the article also misstated the year of a photo shoot in which Ruedi Hofmann was working with Mr. Avedon. The picture, of the men working to photograph a cowboy, was taken in 1983, not 1980.
match_headline: Avedon, Unsigned

text: Because of an editing error, an item in the Extra Bases column last Sunday about the rosters for the Major League Baseball All-Star Game misstated Oakland Athletics relief pitcher Ryan Madson’s saves total and earned run average. Through that Friday’s games, he had 15 saves — not 32 — and his E.R.A. was 3.00 — not 2.37.
match_headline: Call Adam Duvall the Louisville Power Hitter

text: An article last Sunday about the United States Olympic swimming trials in Omaha referred incorrectly, in some editions, to Katie Ledecky’s performance in the 800-meter freestyle race. It was the third fastest time ever in the event, not the 10th. (She owns the top 10 times in the event.)
match_headline: At the U.S. Olympic Trials, Katie Ledecky’s Biggest Rival Is Her Own World Record

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Wimbledon tennis tournament referred incorrectly to the timing of Madison Keys’s debut in the top 10 of the women’s rankings. It was two weeks ago, on June 20, not “during the week.”
match_headline: Upsets Open Field at Wimbledon as Rain Hinders It

text: Because of an editing error, an article on June 26 about female ballet choreographers misstated the year that Mikhail Baryshnikov made Twyla Tharp the artistic associate and resident choreographer of American Ballet Theater. It was 1988, not 1998.
match_headline: Breaking the Glass Slipper: Where Are the Female Choreographers?

text: An article last Sunday about the musician Dev Hynes referred incorrectly to the circumstances surrounding a work of art by Alex Da Corte and Jayson Musson. While they collaborated on the artwork, they are not an artist duo called Easternsports. (That is the title of the work.)
match_headline: Dev Hynes: New York’s Last Bohemian on the City and His New Album

text: A picture credit for a video still with an article last Sunday about an exhibition of Jonah Bokaer’s work misidentified the individual who created the image. It is Marisela La Grave, not Mr. Bokaer.
match_headline: Letting Beckett Seep Into a Hamptons Summer

text: Because of an editing error, a review on June 26 about “White Trash: The 400-Year Untold History of Class in America,” by Nancy Isenberg, referred incorrectly to Supreme Court Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, who wrote the majority opinion in Buck v. Bell, a 1927 forced-sterilization case. Though Holmes was the court’s acting chief justice for a brief period in 1930, he was never chief justice.
ref_headline: White Trash: The 400-Year Untold History of Class in America,
match_headline: A Look at America’s Long and Troubled History of White Poverty

text: An article on June 26 about the future of the Republican Party misspelled the given name of the governor of New Mexico. She is Susana Martinez, not Susanna.
match_headline: Will Trump Swallow the G.O.P. Whole?

text: An article on June 19 about patients’ trying to treat their own diseases with parasites misidentified a drug taken by a patient who had ulcerative colitis. It was mesalamine, not sulfasalazine.
match_headline: The Parasite Underground

text: A listing on the “On the Market” page last Sunday described incorrectly a property at 349 16th Street in Park Slope, Brooklyn. It is a one-flight walk-up, not a two-flight walk-up.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in Brooklyn and Manhattan

text: An article on Thursday about an investigation of an accident in Pennsylvania involving a Tesla vehicle being operated in Autopilot mode described incorrectly when Tesla made apparently inconsistent statements about an earlier accident, in Florida. In a company statement released June 30, immediately after the Florida investigation was disclosed, Tesla said it had informed the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration about the crash “immediately after it occurred.” In a statement issued on Tuesday, Tesla said that it did not tell the federal agency about the accident until nine days later. The statement issued on Tuesday did not contain both versions of when Tesla informed the safety agency of the Florida crash.
match_headline: U.S. Safety Agency Investigates Another Tesla Crash Involving Autopilot

text: An article on Thursday about Roger Federer and Andy Murray needing five sets to advance to the semifinals of the Wimbledon tennis tournament misstated, in some copies, Murray’s career record in five-set matches. Including the win on Wednesday, he is 23-7, not 22-7.
match_headline: Roger Federer and Andy Murray Need Five Sets to Reach Wimbledon Semifinals

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Mets pitcher Matt Harvey’s considering season-ending surgery misstated, in some copies, the date of Major League Baseball’s nonwaiver trade deadline this season. It is Aug. 1, not July 31.
match_headline: Matt Harvey Considering Season-Ending Surgery

text: Because of an editing error, a theater entry in the Listings pages on Friday about “Small Mouth Sounds,” which is in previews at the Pershing Square Signature Center in Manhattan, misidentified the play’s presenter. It is Ars Nova, not Signature Theater.
match_headline: Theater Listings for July 8-14

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s comments about Donald J. Trump’s presidential run referred incorrectly to Mr. Trump’s comments about Justice Ginsburg. He said that her involvement in the presidential campaign was “a disgrace to the court.” He did not say that Justice Ginsburg herself was “a disgrace.” The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Donald Trump Calls Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s Remarks a ‘Disgrace to the Court’

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the photographer Bill Jones referred incorrectly in some copies to Muhammad Ali, whom Mr. Jones photographed in London in 1966. He changed his name to Muhammad Ali in 1964; he was not still known as Cassius Clay at the time.
match_headline: Bill Jones, Photographer of the Black Glitterati, Dies at 81

text: An article on July 3 about Richard Petty’s reflections on racecar driving on his 79th birthday and the day of the Coke Zero 400 race in Daytona Beach, Fla., misstated the date of Dale Earnhardt’s death in 2001 in a crash at the Daytona 500. It was Feb. 18, not Feb. 22.
match_headline: At 79, Richard Petty, a Bastion of Nascar, Sticks to What He Knows

text: An article on Sunday about Strava, a data-driven social media site for cyclists, misspelled part of the name of a team that is looking at ways to profit from its riders’ race and training data. It is Giant-Alpecin, not Giant-Alpercin.
match_headline: Driven by Data, Pros and Joes Alike Vie for Cycling Crowns

text: An article on Wednesday about new research indicating that Vincent van Gogh cut off his entire left ear, not just part of it, omitted a co-author of the book “Van Gogh: The Life.” In addition to Steven Naifeh, who commented on the finding, it was also written by Gregory White Smith.
match_headline: New Evidence on van Gogh’s Ear Continues Debate on Painter’s Mental State

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Sicilian organized-crime figure Bernardo Provenzano, using information from his lawyer, misstated his date of birth. It is Jan. 31, 1933 — not Jan. 30.
match_headline: Bernardo Provenzano, Who Led Sicilian Mafia Clan, Is Dead at 83

text: An article Tuesday about concerns over visitors and protesters taking firearms to downtown Cleveland during the Republican National Convention misstated the position of Oath Keepers, a group of current and former members of the military that has shown up at other tense events heavily armed. Members of the group said in online postings they would travel to Cleveland ; the group itself did not say it plans to do so.
match_headline: Dallas Shooting and Open-Carry Laws Loom Over Cleveland Convention Plans

text: Because of editing errors, a caption on Friday for a picture of a funeral for a Dallas police officer misstated his surname in some editions and referred incorrectly to one of the officers who was killed the same night. The funeral was for Sgt. Michael Smith, not Michael Thomas, and one of the five officers killed was with the Dallas Area Rapid Transit; all five were not with the police department.
match_headline: Dallas Police Chief, David O. Brown, Is Calm at Center of Crisis

text: An article in some editions on Monday about the collapse of the Aerosmith guitarist Joe Perry during a performance in Coney Island erroneously attributed a song to the band. “I Don’t Want to Miss a Thing” was written by Diane Warren, not by members of Aerosmith, who only performed the song. In addition, a reporting credit for Joe Coscarelli was omitted.
ref_headline: I Don’t Want to Miss a Thing
match_headline: Joe Perry, Aerosmith Guitarist, Is Hospitalized After Staggering Off Stage in Coney Island

text: A report in the In Brief column on Tuesday about a study on replacing some saturated fat calories with another type of fat or carbohydrates reversed the effect of two fats in reducing total mortality. Switching to foods high in polyunsaturated fats reduced mortality by 27 percent and switching to foods high in monounsaturated fat reduced it by 13 percent.
match_headline: No Health Benefit to Replacing Fat With Carbs

text: An obituary on June 15 about the record producer and songwriter Chips Moman referred incorrectly at one point to his studio, American Sound. There was never a week when the studio accounted for a quarter of the songs on the Billboard Hot 100. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Chips Moman, Hit-Making Producer and Songwriter, Dies at 79

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about the history of the Four Seasons restaurant misstated the year Philip Johnson, the restaurant’s main architect, celebrated his 95th birthday. It was 2001, not 2005.
match_headline: Four Seasons, Lunch Spot for Manhattan’s Prime Movers, Moves On

text: A news analysis last Sunday, about the waning of major diseases in wealthy countries, misstated the number of deaths every year from heart disease in the United States, and its rate of decline. The number is more than 600,000 per year, not more than 300,000, which is the number of annual deaths from coronary heart disease. The rate of decline in heart disease deaths is nearly 70 percent from its peak, not 60 percent.
match_headline: A Medical Mystery of the Best Kind: Major Diseases Are in Decline

text: An article on July 10 about roadside drug tests described incorrectly one aspect of the procedure involving a closed drug-possession case. As was standard practice, the prosecutor — not the Houston Police Department — filed a motion to destroy the evidence.
match_headline: How a $2 Roadside Drug Test Sends Innocent People to Jail

text: An article last Sunday about funding for documentary films misstated the Ford Foundation’s policy regarding grant money for documentaries. Ford, through its JustFilms unit, continues to provide money to individual filmmakers; the organization has not stopped giving grant money to documentarians.
match_headline: Documentary Filmmakers Find That an Agenda Helps With Financing

text: An article last Sunday about the New York band the Frightnrs misstated part of the title of their forthcoming album on Daptone Records. It is “Nothing More to Say,” not “Nothing Left to Say.” The article also misstated part of the title of the Amy Winehouse album featuring the Dap-Kings as her backing band. It is “Back to Black,” not “Black to Black.”
match_headline: With Wounded Spirits, the Frightnrs Rally Around Their Frontman

text: A listing on the “ On the Market ” page last Sunday misstated the height of a tower at a house for sale in Rowayton, Conn. It is 20 feet, not 290 feet.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in New York and Connecticut

text: A picture caption with an article on July 3 about Johannes Vermeer’s Dutch hometown, Delft, misstated the name of the church whose interior is shown. It is the Oude Kerk, not the Nieuwe Kerk.
match_headline: In Vermeer’s Hometown, Seeking Clues to His Interior Life

text: An article on July 10 about items the actress Allison Janney packs when traveling misstated part of the name of an oil that she carries to ward off germs. It is Young Living Essential Oils (not Young Loving).
match_headline: What Allison Janney Can’t Travel Without

text: An article on July 9 about concerns at Yale after a professor, Thomas Pogge, was cleared of sexual misconduct included incorrect information from university officials about the role of Peter Salovey, the university’s current president, in the Pogge case. At the time he was provost, Mr. Salovey oversaw a committee that found insufficient evidence against the professor; he was not provost when Professor Pogge was hired and was not involved in that process. (Mr. Salovey became provost shortly after the hiring.)
match_headline: After a Professor Is Cleared of Sexual Harassment, Critics Fear ‘Cultural Silence’ at Yale

text: An article on Monday about the creation of little fairy houses in the woods of South Mountain Reservation in Millburn, N.J., misspelled the name of the place in Maine whose fairy homes helped influence Therese Ojibway to make similar creations in New Jersey. It is Monhegan Island, not Monehegan Island.
match_headline: Thumbelina’s Secret Architect, Creating Fairy Houses on a New Jersey Trail

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a new product introduction at Nest misstated the circumstances of the recent resignation of its chief executive, Tony Fadell. He resigned at a time of upheaval over his management style, not because of the upheaval.
match_headline: Nest Relies on New Outdoor Security Camera as Comeback

text: An article on Monday about a hiring cutback by Bridgewater Associates, the world’s largest hedge fund, referred incorrectly to access to the fund’s headquarters in Westport, Conn. The building has two entrances; it is not accessible only by a nondescript road.
match_headline: Bridgewater, World’s Biggest Hedge Fund, Is Said to Be Slowing Hiring

text: An article on Monday about political art during the current campaign season misidentified a location of the “Truth Booth” in Cleveland during the Republican National Convention. The booth — a video confessional where visitors finish the sentence that begins “The truth is” ...” — will be at the Transformer Station alternative art space among other sites, not at the Cleveland Museum of Art.
match_headline: Political Art in a Fractious Election Year

text: An article on Thursday about the first exhibition of artworks at the National September 11 Memorial Museum in Manhattan that were created as a response to the attacks of Sept. 11 referred incorrectly to the painting installation by Manju Shandler that will be shown. Some 840 pieces will be displayed, not all of the nearly 3,000 that make up the work. The article also misstated the number of works by Ejay Weiss that will be shown. It is four, not two. And the article misstated the number of items from the museum’s collection that are on display. While the museum has more than 11,000, about 1,000 are on display, not more than 11,000.
match_headline: 9/11 Museum to Open Its First Art Exhibition in September

text: An article on Friday about the Emmy nominations omitted a nominee for best actress in a drama. Besides Viola Davis, Robin Wright, Keri Russell, Tatiana Maslany and Claire Danes, the nominees also included Taraji P. Henson.
match_headline: Emmy Nominations 2016: ‘Game of Thrones’ Rules Again

text: An obituary on Monday about Alan Vega, the singer in the band Suicide, misspelled the surname of an artist with whom he studied at Brooklyn College. He was Kurt Seligmann, not Seligman.
match_headline: Alan Vega, Punk Music Pioneer and Artist, Dies at 78

text: A news analysis article on Tuesday about President Obama’s reaction to the killing of police officers in Baton Rouge, La., misstated the number of police officers who were killed in a shooting in Dallas. It was five, not six.
match_headline: In Aftermath of Baton Rouge Shooting, Obama Directs Message to His Successor

text: An article on Saturday about the homeless problem in San Diego referred incorrectly in some editions to the timing of the Major League Baseball All-Star Game that was played there. The game had already taken place; it was not coming up.
match_headline: Man Arrested in San Diego in Killings of Homeless People

text: An article on Monday about a virtual reality rendering of new headquarters for the chip maker Nvidia in Santa Clara, Calif., misstated the building’s expected opening date. It is late 2017, not late this year. The article also misstated the title of Debora Shoquist, an executive at Nvidia. She is the executive vice president for operations, not vice president for operations.
match_headline: Using Virtual Reality to Create a New Corporate Headquarters

text: An article on Tuesday about a proliferation of concussions in synchronized swimming misidentified the university that Mariya Koroleva was attending when she felt the effects of a concussion last October. She was at the University of San Francisco — not at Stanford, which she attended as an undergraduate.
match_headline: Synchronized Swimmers Find Danger Lurking Below Surface: Concussions

text: A chart accompanying Charles Blow’s column on Monday, about Donald Trump’s prospects for rebranding his campaign, misidentified the respondents to questions about Mr. Trump’s honesty and trustworthiness and their level of excitement about his candidacy. The respondents were Republicans only, not voters in general.
match_headline: Trump’s Chance to Reboot

text: An article on Wednesday about how recent police shootings have highlighted the inner tug of war that black officers experience regarding race relations and law enforcement paraphrased incorrectly from a Facebook post by Officer Montrell Jackson about the way he was seen when he was out of uniform. Officer Jackson, who was killed Sunday in Baton Rouge, wrote that he felt people considered him a threat, not that he felt threatened.
match_headline: Black Police Officers Feel the Inner Tug of a Dual Role

text: An article on Thursday about a speech by Senator Ted Cruz of Texas at the Republican National Convention referred incorrectly to Gerald R. Ford’s nomination for president at the 1976 Republican National Convention, at which Ronald Reagan made a memorable speech that set him up for his own nomination four years later. It was Ford’s first nomination; he was not “renominated.” (Though Ford was the incumbent, he became president when he succeeded Richard M. Nixon after Nixon’s resignation in 1974.)
match_headline: Ted Cruz Stirs Convention Fury in Pointed Snub of Donald Trump

text: Because of an editing error, the Memo From Barcelona article on June 24, about collaboration among rival political parties in Spain at the municipal and regional levels despite paralysis at the parliamentary level just before new national elections, omitted the name of one of Spain’s four main political parties. Besides Podemos, the Popular Party and the Citizens party, the Socialists are also a major party.
match_headline: Voting Again, Spain Faces Threat to Two-Party System

text: An article on June 23 about a declaration by North Korea that its test launch of an intermediate-range ballistic missile the day before was a success misspelled the name of the missile at several points, in some editions. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, the missile is the Musudan, not the Musadan. The error was repeating in an accompanying picture caption in some editions.
match_headline: North Korea’s Successful Missile Test Shows Program’s Progress, Analysts Say

text: An article on Monday about speakers at the Republican National Convention erroneously included an actor and model among Hispanics who were on the list. Antonio Sabato Jr., best known for his Calvin Klein underwear ads, is a native of Italy and a naturalized United States citizen; he is not Hispanic.
match_headline: Scrambling, Planners of the Republican Convention Put ‘Showbiz’ Off to the Wings

text: A picture caption on July 14 with an article about a police crackdown in Brooklyn after a rash of K2 overdoses misidentified Adrian Llewellyn’s position at Woodhull Medical and Mental Health Center. Mr. Llewellyn, who was shown working in the emergency department at Woodhull, is a physician assistant, not a doctor.
match_headline: Police Raid 5 Brooklyn Bodegas After Suspected K2 Overdoses

text: An article on Wednesday about efforts to revive the Glass-Steagall Act misstated the circumstances of JPMorgan Chase’s use of the Troubled Asset Relief Program. The bank took $25 billion from TARP at the government’s request; it did not seek the assistance.
match_headline: G.O.P. Joins Democrats Urging Glass-Steagall’s Revival. (Don’t Hold Your Breath.)

text: An article on the Square Feet page on Wednesday about the growing popularity of outdoor space in office buildings misidentified the owner of 2 Gansevoort Street, a former warehouse in the meatpacking district. It is the William Kaufman Organization, not the Kaufman Organization.
match_headline: Too Nice a Day to Stay in the Office? Then Don’t.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the political tract “Hindutva or Hind Swaraj,” by the Indian novelist and political commentator U. R. Ananthamurthy, referred incorrectly at one point to the plural nationalism originating from Indians’ struggle against British colonialism. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, “Hind Swaraj” is a text by Mohandas K. Gandhi, not a term for plural nationalism.
match_headline: In ‘Hindutva or Hind Swaraj,’ a Warning Against Hindu Nationalism

text: An article on Friday about reaction to a speech by Senator Ted Cruz of Texas at the Republican National Convention misstated, in some copies, the surname of the chief executive of the parent company of Hardee’s and Carl’s Jr. restaurants, who raised money for Mr. Cruz’s campaign. He is Andrew F. Puzder, not Pudzer.
match_headline: Ted Cruz Mounts the Convention Stage in the Role of Brutus

text: A map on Monday with an article about a subway extension in Los Angeles misidentified the location of the Farmers’ Market in Santa Monica, which can be reached by train. As the article correctly noted, the market is at Arizona and Second streets, not Main Street and Pico Boulevard.
match_headline: Los Angeles’ ‘Subway to the Sea’ Is Less About Play and More About Work

text: An article on Friday about a federal antitrust suit seeking to block two mergers of large health insurers rendered incorrectly part of the name of the law firm of which Matthew L. Cantor, who commented on the matter, is a partner. It is Constantine Cannon, not Constantine Cantor.
match_headline: U.S. Sues to Block Anthem-Cigna and Aetna-Humana Mergers

text: A picture caption in the Listings pages on Friday about the Museum of Modern Art film series Gaumont: Cinéma Pour Tout le Monde misspelled the surname of an actress. She is Danielle Darrieux, not Derrieux.
match_headline: Movie Listings for July 22-28

text: An obituary on June 4 about Mohammed Abdelaziz, the leader of the Polisario Front, referred imprecisely to that movement’s goal. It was to create an independent state for all the indigenous people of Western Sahara, not just Berber tribesmen. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Morocco’s annexation of Western Sahara. Morocco had already begun annexing the territory by the time the United Nations brokered a cease-fire between the Polisario Front and Morocco in 1991; it did not annex it that year. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Mohammed Abdelaziz, Advocate of an Independent Western Sahara, Dies at 68

text: An obituary on July 4 and in some editions on July 3 about the filmmaker Michael Cimino, using information from a friend and former lawyer, referred incorrectly to his survivors. They include two brothers, Peter and Edward; it is not the case that he left no immediate survivors.
match_headline: Michael Cimino, Director of ‘The Deer Hunter’ and ‘Heaven’s Gate,’ Dies at 77

text: An article on June 28 about the political muddle and rising economic fears that followed Britain’s vote to leave the European Union referred incorrectly to Prime Minister David Cameron’s communication with Enda Kenny, the Irish prime minister, meant to ensure that Britain’s exit would not endanger the fragile peace in Northern Ireland. Mr. Cameron spoke with Mr. Kenny; the two did not meet.
match_headline: Economic Fears Rising, Britain Hopes to Stay in E.U. Market

text: A picture on June 28 with the Memo From Bangladesh article , about Archer K. Blood, a United States diplomat who in 1971 became the first to use the State Department’s “dissent channel” to condemn Pakistan’s bloody assault on Dhaka at the start of Bangladesh’s war of independence, was published in error. The photograph, supplied by The Associated Press, showed a man The A.P. was unable to identify; it did not show Mr. Blood.
match_headline: To U.S. in ’70s, a Dissenting Diplomat. To Bangladesh, ‘a True Friend.’

text: An article on Friday about a heat dome moving over the New York area misstated the term for the release of water from plant leaves into the air. The process, which can add to a heat dome’s effects, is called transpiration, not evapotranspiration.
match_headline: A ‘Heat Dome’ Is Coming. Domes Are Bad.

text: An article on Friday about efforts by Chipotle’s Mexican-food rivals to capitalize on its stumbles in a series of food safety crises misstated the given name of a Harvard Business School professor who commented on Chipotle’s recovery strategy. He is Herman Leonard, not Herbert.
match_headline: Chipotle’s Rough Spell Is No Help for Its Rivals

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Apple’s quarterly earnings referred imprecisely to the company’s product upgrade schedule. While it makes major upgrades to its iPhone hardware and software every two years, it makes lesser upgrades annually.
match_headline: Apple’s iPhone Sales Drop Again, but Services Are a Bright Spot

text: An article last Thursday about a secret meeting of corporate leaders to discuss the sorry state of publicly traded companies described incorrectly mandatory retirement ages that apply to some corporate boards. The requirements are established by corporations, not by the New York Stock Exchange.
match_headline: C.E.O.s Meet in Secret Over the Sorry State of Public Companies

text: An article on the DealBook page on Wednesday about the high prices old-line consumer products companies are paying for disruptive start-ups misspelled the name of a technology website that reported on market share gains by small brands. It is TechCrunch, not TechCruch.
match_headline: $1 Billion for Dollar Shave Club: Why Every Company Should Worry

text: An article on Tuesday about new rules in the N.F.L.’s concussion protocol misstated, in some editions, the amount of money teams can be fined for violations of the rules after their first offense. It is a minimum of $100,000, not “up to $100,000.”
match_headline: N.F.L. Introduces New Rules to Back Its Concussion Protocol

text: An article on Monday about Michael Fishman, an assistant general manager for the Yankees who oversees their analytics staff, misstated the academic discipline of Ben Baumer, an assistant professor at Smith College who previously worked in analytics for the Mets. He is an assistant professor of statistical and data sciences, not data and sciences.
match_headline: Solving the Yankee Equation, One Number at a Time

text: An article on Saturday about the possibility that the Italian soccer federation will name Lazio a co-champion with Genoa of the 1914-1915 season misspelled the given name and misstated the position of the man who told the Genoese newspaper Il Secolo XIX, “Revisiting a decision of nearly a hundred years ago makes me smile.” He is Davide Traverso, not David, and he is president of the Genoa supporters club, not the team president.
ref_headline: Revisiting a decision of nearly a hundred years ago makes me smile.
match_headline: Lazio Inches Closer to an Italian Soccer Title ... From 1915

text: A caption in the Sports Briefing column on Tuesday with a picture of the Tall Ships’ Races in Lisbon misstated, in some copies, part of the name of the Italian Navy ship shown. It is Amerigo Vespucci, not Americo Vespucci.
match_headline: Dale Earnhardt Jr. Reveals a Slower Road to His Recovery

text: An article on Monday about the results of the New York City Triathlon misstated, in some copies, the time of Laurel Wassner, the fifth-place finisher in the women’s professional division. Her time was 2 hours 5 minutes 35 seconds, not 2:05:36.
match_headline: Boulder Man Wins New York City Triathlon

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about Sandy Pearlman, a record producer, lyricist, manager, and professor, misstated his date of birth. It is Aug. 5, 1943 — not Aug. 8.
match_headline: Sandy Pearlman, Producer, Manager and Lyricist for Blue Öyster Cult, Dies at 72

text: An article on Wednesday about the victims of terror attacks around the world during two weeks in March referred incorrectly to some of the perpetrators. The Kurdistan Freedom Falcons, a Marxist group in Turkey that broke off from the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, claimed responsibility for the bombing of a public square in Ankara, the capital, on March 13; not all of the perpetrators were Islamist extremists.
match_headline: Turkey ‘Almost Certain’ that Kurdish Militants Bombed Ankara, Premier Says

text: An article on Friday about Hillary Clinton’s acceptance of the Democratic Party’s presidential nomination referred incorrectly in some editions to coverage of her by Life magazine in 1969. While she was featured in the magazine, she was not on its cover.
match_headline: Hillary Clinton Warns of ‘Moment of Reckoning’ in Speech Accepting Nomination

text: An article on June 30 about reasons that the European Union seemed undemocratic to those leading the British campaign to leave it misidentified the body whose members are appointed by the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. It is the European Commission, not the European Council.
match_headline: The E.U. Is Democratic. It Just Doesn’t Feel That Way.

text: An article on July 1 about a military shake-up in Russia, which replaced the top commanders of its Baltic Fleet, misidentified, in some editions, the type of ship that was reported to have collided with a Russian submarine in April, one of several possible blunders that might have prompted the dismissals. The reports said it was a Polish military ship, but not a battleship.
match_headline: Russia Fires Dozens of Military Officers in Baltic Region

text: A chart on Thursday about the deaths of police officers in the line of duty misstated, in some editions, the date that two officers, Thomas Cottrell and Doug Barney, were killed. It was Sunday, Jan. 17 — not Jan. 18.
match_headline: 2 Police Officers Fatally Shot in Ohio and Utah, Officials Say

text: An article on Friday about the relationship between Donald J. Trump and Michael R. Bloomberg misstated the year that Mr. Trump said on Twitter that Mr. Bloomberg was doing a great job as mayor of New York. It was 2012, not 2007.
match_headline: For Trump and Bloomberg, Cordial Ties Have Soured

text: An article on Friday about Amazon’s quarterly earnings misstated the number of consecutive quarters in which Amazon has shown a record profit. It is three, not two.
match_headline: Amazon’s Profits Grow More Than 800 Percent, Lifted by Cloud Services

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a mock appeal hearing held in Venice for the character Shylock from “The Merchant of Venice” referred incorrectly to the disguise Portia adopts in the play. She is disguised as a lawyer, not a judge.
match_headline: Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg Presides Over Shylock’s Appeal

text: An article on Friday about plans by J. Tomilson Hill, vice chairman at the Blackstone Group private equity firm, to open a museum in Manhattan to display some of his art collection misspelled the given name of one of the artists on whom he and his wife, Janine, concentrated when they started collecting in depth. He is Brice Marden, not Bryce.
match_headline: A Billionaire Is Opening a Private Art Museum in Manhattan

text: A picture caption on Friday with a film review of the documentary “Gleason” referred incorrectly to the child of Steve Gleason, the subject of the film, and his wife, Michel Varisco. The child, Rivers, is their son, not daughter.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Gleason,’ a Devastating Diagnosis Prompts a New Mission

text: A report in the Observatory column on Tuesday about desert ants described their tripodal gait incorrectly. When they walk forward, the front and rear legs — not the hind and rear legs — on one side move in concert with the middle leg on the other.
match_headline: Ants March Differently, Depending on Direction

text: Because of an editing error, the Boten Journal article on July 7, about a remote Laotian town that is hoping a new development plan will bring back its once-thriving tourist business, misstated the imperial equivalent of the 1,640-hectare project. It is the equivalent of about 6.3 square miles, not 2.5 square miles.
match_headline: The Rise, Fall and Possible Renewal of a Town in Laos on China’s Border

text: An article on Page 10 this weekend about tensions on campus over the Palestinian-Israeli conflict misstates part of the name of a group critical of Israel. It is Jewish Voice for Peace (not Voices). The article also refers incorrectly to the position of Open Hillel, a national organization that is independent of Hillel. It says that it seeks open discourse; that it is not critical of Israel.
match_headline: Students and the Middle East Conflict

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 16 this weekend about Harvard final clubs misstates the academic degree held by Richard T. Porteus, president of the Fly Club’s graduate body. He has a bachelors in English and American literature and language, not a master’s in education.
match_headline: Are Final Clubs Too Exclusive for Harvard?

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about the Foundation for Individual Rights in Education misstates the professional status of Alan Kors, a co-founder. He is on leave from the University of Pennsylvania; he has not retired.
match_headline: Fighting for Free Speech on America’s Campuses

text: An article on Thursday about a study of barnyard dust and childhood asthma misstated the specialty of Dr. Brian Christman of Vanderbilt University, a volunteer spokesman for the American Lung Association. He is a pulmonologist, not an immunologist.
match_headline: Barnyard Dust Offers a Clue to Stopping Asthma in Children

text: Because of an editing error, an article on July 10 about Iran’s recent move to publicize its military activities in Iraq and Syria, instead of covering them up, referred incorrectly to the owner of an Instagram account who follows Hassan Shemshadi, a reporter for Iranian state television who posts pictures from the front lines in Syria. The owner of the account is a woman.
match_headline: Iran, Once Quiet About Its Casualties in Syria and Iraq, Now Glorifies Them

text: An article on Tuesday about the Zika virus in Florida included a quotation from Dr. Thomas Frieden of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in which he misstated the size of the area in Florida with active Zika transmission. The C.D.C. said on Tuesday that the area has a radius of 500 feet. It is not a 500-square-foot area, as Dr. Frieden said at a news conference. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Patch of Miami Is Ground Zero for the Zika Virus

text: An article on Tuesday about a movement toward treating mental illness with largely nonmedical approaches that are focused on holistic recovery rather than symptom treatment misidentified the location of Advocates, a center that runs such a program. It is in Framingham, Mass., not Worcester. And because of an editing error, a caption with a picture of Caroline White misidentified the location of Hearing Voices Network, where the photograph was taken. It is in Holyoke, Mass., not Worcester.
match_headline: An Alternative Form of Mental Health Care Gains a Foothold

text: An obituary on Monday, and in some editions on Sunday, about the jazz clarinetist Pete Fountain misstated the name of the hotel that housed his nightclub from 1977 to 2003. It is the Hilton New Orleans Riverside (originally the New Orleans Hilton), not the Hotel Riverside. The obituary, in some copies on Sunday, also misstated part of the name of a group Mr. Fountain led at Mardi Gras for many years. It is the Half-Fast Walking Club, not the Half-Fast Marching Club.
match_headline: Pete Fountain, 86, Dies; Clarinetist Popularized Spirited New Orleans Jazz

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actor David Huddleston misspelled the name of the character he played in the 1984 Broadway revival of “Death of a Salesman.” The character is Charley, not Charlie.
match_headline: David Huddleston, the Title Lebowski in ‘The Big Lebowski,’ Dies at 85

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Front Burner column last Wednesday referred incorrectly to the land on which Blake Arrowood, a former English teacher in Southeast Asia, began growing hops and brewing beer near New Paltz, N.Y. Mr. Arrowood acquired the rights to farm on 48 acres in the Hudson Valley; he did not purchase the land.
match_headline: A Hops Farm Turns to Brewing

text: An article on Wednesday about Donald J. Trump’s remarks about Hillary Clinton and gun control misidentified the position held by Al Baldasaro, a New Hampshire lawmaker who supports Mr. Trump, and who recently said that Mrs. Clinton deserved to face a firing squad over the use of a private email server. Mr. Baldasaro is a state representative, not a state senator.
match_headline: Donald Trump Suggests ‘Second Amendment People’ Could Act Against Hillary Clinton

text: An article on Wednesday about a Justice Department report on the Baltimore Police Department misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the organization led by Scott Thompson, who commented on the report. It is the Police Executive Research Forum (not Foundation). The article also misstated the surname of the president of the research forum in some editions. He is Scott Thomson, not Thompson.
match_headline: Justice Department to Release Blistering Report of Racial Bias by Baltimore Police

text: An article on Saturday about a decision by the State Department to suspend a teaching program in Turkey misidentified the program that was canceled. It is the Fulbright English Teaching Assistant Program, not the Fulbright Foreign Language Teaching Assistant Program.
match_headline: State Department, Citing Security, Suspends Teaching Program in Turkey

text: An article last Thursday about challenges awaiting James P. O’Neill, the incoming New York police commissioner, gave an incorrect date from city officials in some editions for the date of his final interview with Mayor Bill de Blasio. It was Saturday, July 30 — not Sunday, July 31.
match_headline: Tightrope Walk Awaits New York’s New Police Commissioner, and de Blasio

text: An article on the Square Feet page on Wednesday about development in a historic district of St. Paul misstated the century in which the Rayette building was built. It was the early 20th century, not the early 19th century.
match_headline: Downtown St. Paul Makes Room for New Settlers

text: A chart on Aug. 1 about first-time winners of all four golf major titles misstated the surname of the 1969 Masters champion. He was George Archer, not Arthur.
match_headline: Four Fresh Major Champions, but Still No Golf Savior

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a film review of “An Art That Nature Makes: The Work of Rosamond Purcell” carried an erroneous credit. The photographs are by Rosamond Purcell/BOND/360, not by Rosamond Purcell/BOND & 360.
ref_headline: An Art That Nature Makes: The Work of Rosamond Purcell
match_headline: Review: ‘An Art That Nature Makes,’ an Illuminating Look at Rosamond Purcell

text: An article on Wednesday about the erosion of support among Republican women for Donald J. Trump misidentified a Republican voter who said she did not trust the Republican nominee but would not vote for Hillary Clinton either. The comment was made by Laura Schrock of Delaware, not by Carol Hillenbrand of New York. (Ms. Hillenbrand, a Republican, says she will support Mrs. Clinton.)
match_headline: Donald Trump’s Support Among Republican Women Starts to Slide

text: Because of an editing error, an article on July 12 about the emergence of Theresa May as Britain’s new prime minister referred incorrectly in some editions to her place in British history. She is the second woman to serve as Britain’s prime minister, not the “second woman after Margaret Thatcher” to do so.
match_headline: Theresa May Is Poised to Be Britain’s Next Prime Minister

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on July 15 about a joy ride around Moscow taken by officers and recent graduates of the academy of the Federal Security Service, Russia’s top security agency, misidentified the agency once led by Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. It is the Federal Security Service, known as the F.S.B. — not the Soviet K.G.B., its predecessor.
match_headline: New Spies Went for a Joyride in Moscow. Russia Isn’t Happy.

text: An article on July 14 about Beijing’s protest of an international tribunal’s ruling rejecting its territorial claims in the South China Sea misstated, at one point and in some editions, the surname of a Japanese judge who appointed four of the five members of the tribunal. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Shunji Yanai, not Yensai. A Q.-and-A. article on July 11 about the ruling referred incorrectly to Indonesia’s maritime conflicts with China. Indonesia’s “exclusive economic zone” overlaps with China’s nine-dash line, which encircles up to 90 percent of the South China Sea, but Indonesia does not claim sovereignty over any part of the sea and was not a party to the ruling.
match_headline: Beijing Protests South China Sea Ruling With Modest Show of Strength

text: Because of an editing error, an article on July 14 about the no-nonsense working style of Theresa May, the new British prime minister, misstated the given name of one of her earlier challengers for the Conservative Party leadership. She is Andrea Leadsom, not Angela.
match_headline: Theresa May’s Style: Put Your Head Down and Get to Work

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an article in some editions about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s affordable-housing plan misstated the location of a proposed 62-unit condominium project. As the article correctly noted, it runs between 17th and 18th Streets near Avenue of the Americas; it is not on that avenue.
match_headline: Why, in One Case, the de Blasio Administration Opposes Affordable Housing

text: An article on Wednesday about reactions by female runners to the recent killings of two women who were jogging misidentified a jogger who said she carries safety pins as a possible weapon. She is Gisela Perez, not Melody Davis. The article also referred incorrectly to the area where the body of Vanessa Marcotte was discovered. She was found about a half-mile from her mother’s home in Princeton, Mass., not about a mile and a half from there.
match_headline: ‘It Absolutely Has Created Fear’: 2 Killings Prompt Female Joggers to Alter Routines

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the withdrawal of a lawsuit that had presented barriers to the construction of an office tower known as 1 Vanderbilt misstated the location of the planned building. It is across Vanderbilt Avenue from Grand Central Terminal, not across 42nd Street. And because of an editing error, the article referred incorrectly to the de Blasio administration’s position on the issue. It described the lawsuit — not the withdrawal of the suit — as having no merit.
match_headline: Owners of Grand Central Drop Lawsuit, Clearing Way for a 1,401-Foot-Tall Skyscraper

text: An article last Sunday about the cruise ship the United States men’s and women’s basketball teams are staying on during the Olympics misstated part of the name of the ship. It is the Silver Cloud, not the Sea Cloud.
match_headline: U.S.A. Basketball Is Already Cruising in Rio. Now, to Take the Court.

text: An article on July 14 about the appointment of new ministers by Prime Minister Theresa May of Britain referred imprecisely to soccer teams in Britain in relating a joking comment from a Northern Ireland lawmaker in Parliament to the departing prime minister, David Cameron, about vacant leadership roles he could fill. England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own teams (and the English manager position was open at the time), but outside of special events (like the 2012 Olympic Games), there is no soccer team for all of Britain.
match_headline: Theresa May, New British Prime Minister, Gives Boris Johnson a Key Post

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about a stylishly dressed newspaper vendor known for his bold colorful suits misspelled his given name and misstated his surname. He is Steeve Mackaya, not Steve Malek. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: The Ever-So-Stylish Newspaper Salesman

text: A report in the Extra Bases column last Sunday about the Milwaukee Brewers’ moves at the trade deadline misstated the earned run average of Phil Bickford, a Class A pitcher acquired from the San Francisco Giants. It was 2.58, not 2.97. An accompanying chart about the career statistics of Texas Rangers third baseman Adrian Beltre omitted the player who is second on the list of career home runs by a third baseman. He is Eddie Mathews, with 486 homers.
match_headline: Brewers, Like Yankees, Trade With Eye on Future

text: An article last Sunday about the Lincoln Square apartment of the choreographer Joshua Bergasse and the ballet dancer Sara Mearns described a revival of “Sweet Charity” incorrectly. The production will be staged Off Broadway, not on Broadway.
match_headline: Sara Mearns and Joshua Bergasse, Pirouetting on the 27th Floor

text: An article on Sunday, Aug. 31, about the actor Corey Stoll, misstated the opening date of “Troilus and Cressida” at Shakespeare in the Park, which Mr. Stoll stars in. After the section had gone to press, the opening date was changed. It was Aug. 9, not Aug. 3.
match_headline: Corey Stoll on Shakespeare Boot Camp and Killing Tiny Vampires

text: An article last Sunday about the composer Patrick Cowley referred imprecisely to his hospitalization in 1981. He went into the hospital for the first time that November, not into intensive care. (He went into intensive care a couple of months later.)
match_headline: Waking the Spirit of a Disco Innovator

text: An article on July 31 about the French island of Corsica misidentified the event that prompted a march through a largely North African quarter of Ajaccio, Corsica, on Christmas Day in 2015. The event was an attack in that neighborhood, not the terrorist attacks in Paris that November.
match_headline: Into Corsica, From Rustic Villages to Stony Cliffs

text: An article on July 31, about strife in the Hershey Trust Company, which controls Hershey, the candy dynasty, omitted a response from Robert F. Cavanaugh, the trust’s former chairman, to an internal memorandum written by the trust’s former chief compliance officer, Marc Woolley. In the memo, Mr. Woolley recounted a phone conversation in which Mr. Cavanaugh accused board members of running a “smear campaign” against him. Mr. Cavanaugh’s response disputed that memo, saying it contained “a number of errors, misstatements and omissions that were self-serving and significantly changed the context of the conversation.”
match_headline: Back-Stabbing and Threats of a ‘Suicide Parachute’ at Hershey

text: An article on Saturday about leadership changes at Fox News misstated what Bill Shine, who has been promoted to co-president of Fox News, said he knew about a relationship between Roger Ailes, the former chief executive and chairman of Fox News, and Laurie Luhn, a former Fox booker. Mr. Shine had told associates that he did not know that Mr. Ailes was in a relationship with Ms. Luhn; he did not say that he knew about it.
match_headline: Fox News Names 2 Insiders to Top Posts

text: An article on Monday about the reluctance of millennials to take on credit card debt misidentified the university from which one such person, Rebecca Liebman, graduated. She received a degree from Clark University, not Bentley University.
match_headline: How Millennials Became Spooked by Credit Cards

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article previewing that day’s events at the Rio Olympics referred incorrectly in some editions to Simone Biles, who was favored in the gymnastics individual all-around competition. Biles was the reigning world all-around champion, not the defending Olympic all-around champion. (Her American teammate Gabby Douglas won the Olympic all-around in 2012.)
match_headline: It’s Official: Simone Biles Is the World’s Best Gymnast

text: An article on Thursday in which The Times’s chief theater critic, Ben Brantley, answered questions from readers about the theater scene in London misidentified the director of “Oklahoma!” at the National Theater in the 1990s in discussing productions of classic Broadway musicals in London. He is Trevor Nunn, not Nicholas Hytner.
match_headline: Ben Brantley Answers Your London Theater Questions

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with an article about the collapse of a plan to bring Stefan Herheim’s acclaimed staging of Wagner’s “Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg” to the Metropolitan Opera in the 2019-20 season misidentified a singer shown in a 2013 production. He is Michael Volle — not Hans Sachs, the role Mr. Volle sang.
match_headline: On the Way to the Met, a ‘Meistersinger’ Is Stranded in Europe

text: An obituary on Aug. 6 about the chemist Ahmed H. Zewail, using information from a friend, referred incorrectly to Dr. Zewail’s health. He learned that he had cancer in 2013; he had not “been treated for spinal cancer for about 10 years.” (The cause of his death has not been released.)
ref_headline: been treated for spinal cancer for about 10 years.
match_headline: Ahmed H. Zewail, Nobel-Prize-Winning Chemist, Dies at 70

text: An article on Wednesday about a break on unpaid taxes that casinos founded by Donald J. Trump were given under the administration of Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey quoted incorrectly from comments the governor made about his family’s personal friendship with the Trumps. He said that he and his wife “Mary Pat” — not “Pat” — had been friends with the Trumps for more than a decade. In addition, the article misidentified an event where Mr. Christie also spoke about his close relationship with Mr. Trump. It was when he endorsed Mr. Trump in February, not at the Republican National Convention in July.
match_headline: Trump Casinos’ Tax Debt Was $30 Million. Then Christie Took Office.

text: An article on July 22 about the persistent secrecy in the race for the next secretary general of the United Nations, using information from diplomats speaking on the condition of anonymity, misidentified the candidate who came in last in a straw poll taken by the Security Council. She is Vesna Pusic of Croatia, not Christiana Figueres of Costa Rica.
match_headline: Secrecy Reigns as U.N. Seeks a New Secretary General

text: An article on May 26 about investors who are trying to get their money back from Mt. Gox, the Tokyo-based virtual currency exchange that collapsed into bankruptcy, misstated the legal and accounting costs for the investors claiming money from the Mt. Gox bankruptcy estate. It was $5.5 million, not $55 million. (It is now $5.9 million in current exchange rates.) A reader pointed out the error only recently.
match_headline: Mt. Gox Creditors Seek Trillions Where There Are Only Millions

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about the New York International Fringe Festival misstated the surname of an actress in “The 800th Annual Salvation Swing-Off.” She is Stacey Garbarski, not Gabarski.
match_headline: Finding Some Treasures at FringeNYC

text: An obituary on Wednesday about John McLaughlin, the host of the long-running television talk show “The McLaughlin Group,” referred incorrectly to the magazine National Review, where he worked in the 1980s. It is published biweekly, not weekly. The obituary also misstated the length of Mr. McLaughlin’s tenure there. He remained at National Review for a number of years after “The McLaughlin Group” made its debut in 1982; he did not begin the program “after a stint” at the magazine. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated the year Mr. McLaughlin was ordained a priest. It was 1959, not 1947.
match_headline: John McLaughlin, TV Host Who Made Combat of Punditry, Dies at 89

text: An article on Thursday about controversy surrounding the coming film “The Birth of a Nation” after the disclosure of new details about a nearly two-decade-old case in which the film’s director, writer and star, Nate Parker, was charged with rape misstated, in some editions, the year he was acquitted. It was 15 years ago — not 17 years ago, which was when he was initially charged, in 1999.
match_headline: ‘The Birth of a Nation,’ Nate Parker’s Heralded Film, Is Now Cloaked in Controversy

text: Because of an editing error, the Baishizhou Journal article on July 20, about the demolition of a tenement enclave called Baishizhou in Shenzhen, China, that long provided cheap housing for the migrant workers and immigrants who supported Shenzhen’s rapid economic growth, referred incorrectly to a professor of architecture at Hong Kong University who said Baishizhou’s ambiguous land ownership rights allowed it to survive for so long. The professor, Juan Du, is a woman. The article also misstated part of her title. She is an associate professor, not an assistant professor.
match_headline: Skyscrapers’ Rise in China Marks the Fall of Immigrant Enclaves

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Olympics Briefing column on Thursday about Germany’s victory over Nigeria in a men’s soccer game that set up a meeting with Brazil in the final misidentified the location of Germany’s 7-1 thrashing of host Brazil in the 2014 World Cup. It was at Estadio Mineirão in Belo Horizonte, not at Maracanã stadium in Rio de Janeiro. The article also misstated the round of the tournament when that game took place. It was a semifinal, not the final.
match_headline: After an Injury Scare, Neymar Strikes Back Against Honduras

text: An article on Tuesday about the United States’ 2-1 loss to Germany in the quarterfinals of the Olympics field hockey tournament misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the United States’ goal scorer. She is Katelyn Falgowski, not Falgowksi.
match_headline: Germany Eliminates U.S. Women’s Field Hockey in a Quarterfinal

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Aug. 8 with a Critic’s Notebook article about efforts by jazz musicians to promote racial justice through their music misstated the title of the trumpeter Ambrose Akinmusire’s major-label debut album. It is “When The Heart Emerges Glistening” — not “My Name Is Oscar,” which is the title of the track on which he pays tribute to Oscar Grant III, who was fatally shot by a transit police officer in Oakland in 2009.
match_headline: A Cri de Coeur From Jazz Musicians in a Black Lives Matter Age

text: An article on Thursday about Steven Korff, a Brooklyn resident who is a leading collector of contemporary Japanese ceramics, misstated the surname of an American artist whose work Mr. Korff bought when he started collecting ceramics. He was Robert Arneson, not Arnerson.
match_headline: An Obsessive Collector Who’s Drawn Royalty to Brooklyn

text: An obituary on Wednesday about João Havelange, the longtime head of FIFA, world soccer’s governing body, misstated the year he expanded the World Cup field to 32 nations from 24. It was 1998, not 1994.
match_headline: João Havelange, Who Built and Ruled World Soccer With Firm Hand, Dies at 100

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the political activities in Ukraine of Donald J. Trump’s former campaign chairman, Paul Manafort, misidentified the office once held by Yulia Tymoshenko, a rival of Mr. Manafort’s client, the former president Viktor F. Yanukovych. Ms. Tymoshenko served as prime minister of Ukraine, not its president.
match_headline: Ukraine Releases More Details on Payments for Trump Aide, Paul Manafort

text: An article on Friday about a federal judge’s decision to strike down a proposed class-action settlement between Uber and a group of current and former drivers referred incorrectly to the states in which some of Uber’s concessions would have applied. The company had agreed to recognize and speak with quasi-unions only in California and Massachusetts — not in “New York and other states.”
match_headline: Judge Overturns Uber’s Settlement With Drivers

text: An article in some editions on Friday about Usain Bolt’s victory in the 200 meters at the Rio Olympics referred incorrectly in some copies to the significance of his earlier victory in the 100 meters. He was the first person to win three consecutive Olympic gold medals in the 100 meters; he was not the first person to win three consecutive gold medals in any Olympic track and field event.
match_headline: 100? 200? Doesn’t Matter. They Still Can’t Catch Usain Bolt.

text: An article in some copies on Wednesday about two elbow injuries sustained by Yankees pitcher Nathan Eovaldi misstated the number of consecutive starts he won in May. It was five, not six.
match_headline: Yankees Drop Game to Blue Jays and Lose Pitcher Nathan Eovaldi

text: Because of an editing error, The Books of The Times review on Friday about “Blood in the Water: The Attica Prison Uprising of 1971 and Its Legacy,” by Heather Ann Thompson, misstated the number of hostages killed during the retaking of the prison on Sept. 13. It was nine, not 10.
ref_headline: Blood in the Water: The Attica Prison Uprising of 1971 and Its Legacy,
match_headline: ‘Blood in the Water,’ a Gripping Account of the Attica Prison Uprising

text: An article on Page 174 this weekend about the idea of waiting for things as a cultural trend misstates the English period when a lady-in-waiting could become the king’s mistress or wife. It was possible during the Tudor era in England, as well as other eras, but not during the Elizabethan period. (There were no kings of England during the Elizabethan era.)
match_headline: Has Waiting for Things Become the Ultimate Luxury?

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the killing of an imam and his friend near a mosque in Queens, using information from the Police Department, misstated the given name of the imam and the surname of his friend. They were Alauddin Akonjee and Thara Miah — not Maulama Aknonjee and Thara Uddin.
match_headline: Imam and His Assistant Killed in a Shooting Near a Mosque in Queens

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about a 1993 robbery in Rochester in which $7.4 million was stolen, an event that may become the subject of a Hollywood movie, omitted credit for a photograph of Ronnie Gibbons, a boxer who was linked to the case and was later killed. It was taken by Abbot Genser.
match_headline: A $7.4 Million Heist Made for Hollywood

text: A picture caption with an article on Aug. 7 about two men searching the sea for loved ones killed during a tsunami described the diver, Yasuo Takamatsu, incorrectly. He was shown surfacing after a practice dive; he had not been searching for his wife during the dive.
match_headline: ‘I Have No Choice but to Keep Looking’

text: An article last Sunday about the decline in repertory theaters misspelled the name of a character Lucy Peacock plays in “A Winter’s Tale.” It is Paulina, not Polina.
match_headline: In Praise of Repertory Theater: Macbeth at the Matinee, Miller at Night

text: An article last Sunday about Sergei Danilian, an Armenian theater impresario based in New York City, misstated the surname of a theater director that he worked with. He is Peter Brook, not Brooks.
match_headline: Meet the Impresario Who Makes Dance Happen

text: Because of an editing error, a listing on the “On the Market” page last Sunday misstated the common charges for a condo for sale at 11 Terrace Place in Brooklyn. The fee for #2B is $355 a month, not $355 a year.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in Brooklyn and Manhattan

text: An article last Sunday about a trip through Newfoundland misstated the name of a town where the author stopped on the way to St. John’s. It is Lumsden, not Lumberton. The article also misspelled the name of another town the author passed through. It is Frederickton, not Fredericton.
match_headline: I Lost My Job and My Husband. Then I Found Newfoundland.

text: An article on Aug. 7 about following in the footsteps of the Irish human-rights activist Roger Casement misstated the religion of his mother when he was born. She was Protestant, and later converted to Catholicism.
match_headline: In Ireland, Chasing the Ghost of the Rebel Roger Casement

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Amy Beamer and Charles Korschun included outdated information about one of the officiants. After the report had gone to press, Rabbi Bill Kraus had to cancel and was replaced by Lee Coopersmith, a cantor. The report also misidentified the year the couple met. It was 2013, not 2014.
match_headline: Amy Beamer, Charles Korschun

text: An article on July 26 about Peru’s efforts to protect the rain forest from illegal gold mining misstated part of the name of a park where forest rangers and marines conducted a raid in April. It is the Tambopata National Reserve (not “Nature”).
match_headline: Peru Scrambles to Drive Out Illegal Gold Mining and Save Precious Land

text: An article and a headline on July 25 about a fatal attack by a Syrian man on a woman in Reutlingen, Germany, misidentified the weapon he used, using information from the police. It was a kebab knife, not a machete. The error was repeated in a picture caption in some editions. The error also appeared in another article in some editions on July 25 about a suicide bomber who detonated his backpack near a music festival in Ansbach, Germany, and in two articles on July 26 — one about the suicide bomber’s profession of loyalty to the Islamic State and the second about the anxiety these attacks and others have fueled across Europe this summer.
match_headline: Syrian Refugee Arrested in Germany After Fatal Knife Attack

text: An article on July 29 about the disarray of Turkey’s military, long a pillar of the modern Turkish state, following a failed coup attempt referred incorrectly to a previous coup attempt, in 1960. It was carried out and supported only by lower-level officers; it was not supported up and down the chain of command, as the 1971 and 1980 coup attempts were.
match_headline: With Army in Disarray, a Pillar of Modern Turkey Lies Broken

text: An article on July 24 about confirmation by the Indonesian authorities that Abu Wardah, better known as Santoso — the country’s most wanted terrorism suspect and leader of the Mujahedeen of Eastern Indonesia — had been killed in a gun battle earlier in the week misstated his age and misidentified the Chinese region that the Uighurs in his terrorist group came from. He was 39, not 40, and the region is Xinjiang, not Ningxia.
match_headline: Indonesian Police Say DNA Confirms Most Wanted Terror Suspect Is Dead

text: An article on July 27 about the killing of a Roman Catholic priest in his church in St.-Étienne-du-Rouvray, France, an attack for which the Islamic State claimed responsibility, gave an outdated title for Dalil Boubakeur, a Muslim leader who condemned the attack. He is a former president of the French Council of the Muslim Faith, not the current president.
match_headline: ISIS Says Its ‘Soldiers’ Attacked Church in France, Killing Priest

text: An article on Friday about a decision by Goldman Sachs to name its new retail banking operation Marcus misidentified the business partner who originally started Goldman Sachs with Marcus Goldman. It is Samuel Sachs, not Joseph Sachs. (Joseph Sachs and Goldman were friends who met as youths in Germany.)
match_headline: Meet Marcus, Goldman Sachs’s Online Lender for the Masses

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about changes coming to the online music site Bandcamp, including an increase in the amount of editorial content it publishes, misspelled the given name of an electronic composer whose music is featured on the website. She is Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith, not Kaitlin.
match_headline: Is Bandcamp the Holy Grail of Online Record Stores?

text: An obituary on Saturday about the advertising executive Ronald DeLuca misspelled the name of the city in Pennsylvania where he was born and the railroad for which his father worked. They are both Reading, not Redding.
match_headline: Ronald DeLuca, Ad Man Who Helped Revive Iacocca’s Chrysler, Dies at 91

text: An editorial on Monday about accountability at the United Nations misstated the action of Anders Kompass, a former U.N. official. He leaked allegations of sex abuse by peacekeepers to French authorities, not to the news media.
match_headline: Dodging Accountability at the United Nations

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about Japan’s vast bet on aerospace misidentified the type of plane shown. It is a propeller plane, not a jet plane.
match_headline: Japan, Seeking to Regain Manufacturing Might, Bets on Aerospace

text: An obituary in some editions on Friday about Gen. John W. Vessey Jr., who was chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in the Reagan administration, referred incorrectly to the 241 victims of the truck bombing at a Marine barracks in Beirut in 1983. Eighteen sailors were among the dead; they were not all Marines and Army soldiers.
match_headline: John W. Vessey Jr., Who Was Chairman of Joint Chiefs, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Friday about Gerald Grosvenor, the Duke of Westminster and Britain’s richest landowner, misstated the amount of his founding gift for an armed forces rehabilitation center to open in 2018, as well as the cost of the center. The gift was 50 million pounds (roughly $65 million), not $50 million. And the cost of the center is 300 million pounds (roughly $392 million), not $300 million.
match_headline: Gerald Grosvenor, British Duke and Billionaire, Dies at 64

text: An article on Sunday about migrant children who represent themselves in immigration proceedings misstated part of the name of the appeals court where the federal government is contesting the immigration court’s authority. It is the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (not Ninth “District”).
match_headline: It’s Children Against Federal Lawyers in Immigration Court

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the Soviet discus thrower Nina Ponomareva misstated the year of the Tokyo Olympics, in which she finished 11th. They were in 1964, not 1960. (As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, the 1960 Games, in which she won a gold medal, were in Rome.) The obituary also misspelled the name of a city in Russia near the village where Ponomareva was born. It was Sverdlovsk, not Sverdlosk.
match_headline: Nina Ponomareva, Soviet Olympian Who Set Off a Diplomatic Crisis, Dies at 87

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the actor Steven Hill referred incorrectly to the 1981 movie “Rich and Famous,” in which he appeared. It was a remake of the 1943 movie “Old Acquaintance” — not of a movie also called “Rich and Famous.”
match_headline: Steven Hill, Who Starred on ‘Law & Order’ and ‘Mission: Impossible,’ Dies at 94

text: An article last Thursday about the former Whitney estate Joye Cottage, in one instance, omitted part of the title of a book by the mansion’s restorers, Gregory White Smith and Steven Naifeh. As the article correctly notes elsewhere, it is “How to Make Love to a Woman,” not “How to Make Love to Woman.”
ref_headline: How to Make Love to a Woman,
match_headline: Luck Unites a Couple for a Lifetime of Great Collaborations

text: An article last Thursday about the split between young Cuban-Americans who want to travel to the island and their parents who lived under Fidel Castro’s regime described incorrectly the American-born children of Cuban immigrants. They are second-generation Cuban-Americans, not first-generation.
match_headline: The Cuban-American Generation Gap

text: An article on Aug. 17 about the resignation of the chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley, amid criticism of his handling of sexual harassment complaints misstated the finding of a university investigation of the former law school dean. The report said the dean, Sujit Choudhry, violated the university’s policy on sexual harassment through conduct that was unwelcome and sexual in nature; it did not conclude that the conduct was forceful. The error first appeared in an article on March 25 about complaints about faculty conduct at the university.
match_headline: Nicholas Dirks Resigns as Chancellor of University of California, Berkeley

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a report that the New York Police Department had broken rules regarding the surveillance of Muslims described incorrectly in some editions the Office of the Inspector General for the New York Police Department, which issued the report. It is a law enforcement agency with oversight of the Police Department, not a civilian agency.
match_headline: New York Police Broke Surveillance Rules After 9/11, Inquiry Finds

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the auction of Charles M. Conlon’s archive of historical baseball images misidentified the team affiliation in 1925 of Nick Altrock, who was shown with Babe Ruth’s wife and daughter. At the time, Altrock was a coach for the Washington Senators, not a pitcher for the Chicago White Sox.
match_headline: Pictures of Baseball’s Golden Era, Yours for a Stack of Green

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a theater review of “The Good Earth,” at the Flea Theater in Manhattan, using information from a publicist, reversed the identities of two of the five actors shown. Gwenllian Higginson is third from left and Anni Dafydd is at the right.
match_headline: Review: A Welsh Family Clings to Native Soil in ‘The Good Earth’

text: An article on Thursday about a veteran who killed himself in the parking lot of a Veterans Affairs hospital in Northport, N.Y., referred incorrectly to the First Congressional District of New York, whose representative, Lee Zeldin, has been looking into complaints about the hospital. While it is on Long Island, it does not include Northport.
match_headline: Veteran Kills Himself in Parking Lot of V.A. Hospital on Long Island

text: An article on Aug. 19 about how a false report of a shooting at Kennedy International Airport provided officials with a case study in examining the airport’s security procedures misstated part of the name of an agency that has security officers at the airport. It is the Transportation Security Administration, not Transportation Safety Administration.
match_headline: False Reports of Gunfire at J.F.K. Airport Offer a Real Case Study in Security

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with an article about a rift in the music industry that was brought to light by the release of Frank Ocean’s new album “Blonde” misidentified the source of one music video image in some copies. The image, of Frank Ocean sitting next to a car with a drink in his hand, is from the video “Nikes,” not from the album “Endless.”
match_headline: Frank Ocean’s ‘Blonde’ Amplifies Discord in the Music Business

text: An obituary on Friday about Warren Hinckle, the editor who made Ramparts magazine a voice for the radical left, referred incorrectly to Mr. Hinckle’s marriage to the writer Susan Cheever. Although separated, they were still married; they were not divorced.
match_headline: Warren Hinckle, 77, Ramparts Editor Who Embraced Gonzo Journalism, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the Paris fashion designer Sonia Rykiel included an outdated title for Ms. Rykiel’s daughter, Nathalie. She is vice chairman of the fashion house her mother began; she is no longer artistic director.
match_headline: Sonia Rykiel, Fashion Designer for the ‘Fragile, but Strong,’ Dies at 86

text: An article last Sunday about a leading suicide researcher at Columbia University misstated the timing of a project to install fences on the sidewalks of the George Washington Bridge, from which people have jumped to their deaths. The project will begin next year, not in 2020. The article also misstated the number of years since Kevin Hines left a rehabilitation unit after his jump from the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco. It has been 15 years, not 11.
match_headline: A Suicidologist’s New Challenge: The George Washington Bridge

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Aug. 7 about the snowy egret, which can be seen in New York City during the summer, misidentified a document that was signed 100 years ago partly in response to excessive hunting of these birds. It is the Migratory Bird Treaty, not the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. (The act, which was passed in 1918, helped put the terms of the treaty into law.)
match_headline: Snowy Egrets, Once Fashion Victims, Always Elegant Predators

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the British runner Mo Farah’s victory in the 5,000 meters at the Rio Games misstated his finish in his 5,000-meter heat on Aug. 17. He was third, not second.
match_headline: Mo Farah Lands a Double-Double, Winning Gold in 5,000

text: An obituary last Sunday about the German historian Ernst Nolte referred incorrectly to the historians Andreas Hillgruber and Michael Stürmer. They were not among those who were “appalled” by Professor Nolte’s essay “The Past That Won’t Go Away.”
match_headline: Ernst Nolte, Historian Whose Views on Hitler Caused an Uproar, Dies at 93

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Edgar Ramírez included an erroneous description of comments he made when asked to compare politics in the United States and Latin America. While he criticized American politics, saying it was just as bad as in Latin America, he did not use an expletive in his comment.
match_headline: Edgar Ramírez Speaks Five Languages and Has One Peculiar Habit

text: Because of an editing error, a letter to the editor on Aug. 14 about “New England Bound,” by Wendy Warren, misspelled the given name of the letter writer. She is Nina Sankovitch, not Nine.
match_headline: Letters to the Editor

text: A review on Aug. 14 about “Face Value: The Hidden Ways Beauty Shapes Women’s Lives,” by Autumn Whitefield-Madrano, misspelled the surname of the author of “The Beauty Myth,” a 1991 book with a related theme. She is Naomi Wolf, not Wolfe.
ref_headline: Face Value: The Hidden Ways Beauty Shapes Women’s Lives,
match_headline: How the Pursuit of Beauty Affects Women’s Lives

text: An article on Aug. 14 about the fractured Arab world misstated the year that Iraq invaded Kuwait. It was 1990, not 1991.
match_headline: Fractured Lands: How the Arab World Came Apart
