text: A caption in last Sunday’s Scene City column , about the Trunks of Love benefit and Guild Hall’s gala, misspelled the surname of one of the subjects. She is April Gornik, not April Gornick.
match_headline: Christie Brinkley, Cindy Sherman and Chuck Close Take to the Hamptons Circuit

text: An article on Aug. 7 about the self-help guru James Altucher misstated the name of a website where people may learn basic web development. It is Codecademy.com, not Codeacademy.com .
match_headline: Why Self-Help Guru James Altucher Only Owns 15 Things

text: An article on Aug. 14 about bookstores in London summarized incorrectly the plot of the Jorge Luis Borges story “The Library of Babel.” It is about a place that contains every book ever written, or might be written — not just ever written.
match_headline: London Bookstores Go Rogue as No Wi-Fi Zones

text: An article last Sunday about visiting tourist-heavy sites misstated the surname of the lead park ranger for the Statue of Liberty National Monument. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Michael Amato, not Damato.
match_headline: How to Get the Most out of Visiting World-Famous Sites

text: An article and picture caption on July 29 about Indonesia’s execution of three foreigners and an Indonesian convicted of drug crimes misstated, in some editions, the nationality of one of the three foreigners, using information from The Associated Press. One was Senegalese; not all were Nigerian.
match_headline: Indonesia Executes 4 Prisoners Convicted of Drug Crimes

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about an advertising campaign for KLM, the Dutch airline, referred incorrectly to its official name. The airline is formally known as Royal Dutch Airlines, not “formerly” known as such.
match_headline: To Bolster KLM’s Identity, a ‘Charmingly Clueless Approach’ to Humor

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the draw for the United States Open misstated the reason Stan Wawrinka is seeded third at the tournament. He rose to No. 3 in the rankings last week; he is not seeded third because Roger Federer withdrew from the tournament.
match_headline: Williams Sisters Could Be in Step for Semifinal Showdown at U.S. Open

text: An article on Thursday about Hawaii’s road games in Australia and Michigan to begin the football season misidentified a conference that some sports teams at Hawaii compete in. It is the Big West, not the Big Sky. An accompanying picture caption also misstated, in some copies, the name of one of the Hawaii football players shown in Sydney, Australia. He is Makani Kema-Kaleiwahea, not Makan Kema-Kaleiwahia.
match_headline: Hawaii Is Redefining the Road Game

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the dwindling market for old master paintings omitted the given name and the title of an expert who commented on contemporary artists who talk with passion about the genius of old masters. He is Thomas P. Campbell, the director and chief executive of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
match_headline: Can the Old Masters Be Relevant Again?

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with the continuation of an article about a former recruiter for Al Qaeda who is now at George Washington University misstated his surname. As the article correctly noted, he is Jesse Morton, not Martin.
match_headline: Once a Qaeda Recruiter, Now a Voice Against Jihad

text: An article on Tuesday about a fatal explosion in Texas involving airbag propellant destined for a Takata airbag plant in Mexico misstated, in some copies, the title of Glenn P. Wicks of the Wicks Group, a law firm that specializes in hazmat transportation. He is its managing director, not its president.
match_headline: Airbag Propellant Bound for Takata Factory Detonates en Route

text: An article on Monday about the new Major League Soccer franchise in Minnesota, which was awarded to a group headed by the owner of the Minnesota United of the North American Soccer League, misstated, in some editions, the year in which Manny Lagos, United’s technical director, participated in the Olympics. It was 1992, not 1972.
match_headline: Duel of Suitors Yields an M.L.S. Franchise for Minnesota

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Friday with a review of “Mozart Dances” described incorrectly the musical composition to which the dance “Double” was set. It is a Mozart sonata, not a concerto.
match_headline: Review: Choreographers Should Stay Away From Mozart. Except Mark Morris.

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about tree deaths in California misidentified, in some copies, the type of fungus shown covering a dead tree. It is Phellinus gilvus , which developed after the tree died; it is not the pathogen that causes sudden oak death.
match_headline: Like Tens of Millions of Matchsticks, California’s Dead Trees Stand Ready to Burn

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the actor Gene Wilder referred incorrectly to the organization Gilda’s Club, which he helped found. It is a network of support centers for people with cancer, not just women with cancer.
match_headline: Gene Wilder Dies at 83; Star of ‘Willy Wonka’ and ‘Young Frankenstein’

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Antony Jay, a creator of the British television series “Yes Minister,” misstated the name of the fictional government agency depicted in that show. It was the Ministry of Administrative Affairs, not the Ministry of Administrative Public Affairs.
match_headline: Antony Jay, a Machiavelli Scholar and a Creator of ‘Yes Minister,’ Dies at 86

text: A review last Wednesday about the restaurant Bolivian Llama Party misspelled an ingredient in its cheese balls. It is yuca, not yucca.
match_headline: Overstuffed (and Underground) Pastry at Bolivian Llama Party

text: An article on Wednesday about primary elections in Florida and Arizona quoted incorrectly from comments by Senator Marco Rubio on whether he would serve a full term if Florida voters re-elect him to the Senate. Mr. Rubio declined to make the commitment, saying that “you don’t know what the future’s going to hold” — not that you “know now” what the future holds.
ref_headline: you don’t know what the future’s going to hold
match_headline: Marco Rubio and John McCain Win Primaries in Florida and Arizona

text: An article on Saturday about the relatively high proportion of cyclists killed in Brooklyn misidentified the road intersecting Avenue U in describing where a cyclist was killed on Jan. 19. It intersects with East Ninth Street, not Ninth Avenue. The article also referred incorrectly to the area where at least three cyclists have been killed this year. It is southern Brooklyn, not South Brooklyn.
match_headline: Brooklyn’s Bicycling Culture Doesn’t Ease Risks for Riders

text: An article on Aug. 18 about Pippa Middleton’s engagement misstated part of a quotation from Jo Elvin, editor in chief of British Glamour, about Kate Middleton, the duchess of Cambridge, and the news media. She said that Ms. Middleton is “heavily protected by certain guidelines upheld by press associations” — not that she is “heavily protected by the Press Association.” (The Press Association is a multimedia news organization. The guidelines she referred to are set by the Independent Press Standards Association.)
ref_headline: heavily protected by certain guidelines upheld by press associations
match_headline: Pippa Middleton Goes Out on Her Own. But She’s Not Alone.

text: An article last Thursday about the founder of a Hamptons-based publication called Whalebone Magazine misstated how many decades the Dock, a restaurant in Montauk, has been open. It has been open for four decades, not three.
match_headline: The Real Montauk? Ask This Native Surfer

text: A picture caption on Aug. 4 with the continuation of an article about the Emni, an intelligence unit of the Islamic State that is responsible for exporting terrorism abroad, mistranslated the Arabic writing shown on tanks that were captured by Kurdish militias in Syria last year. The writing says Jaysh al-Khilafa (or the Army of the Caliphate), not Jaysh al-Khalifa (or the Army of the Caliph).
match_headline: How a Secretive Branch of ISIS Built a Global Network of Killers

text: An article on Thursday about possible successors to the Islamic State strategist Abu Muhammad al-Adnani characterized incorrectly the views of Cole Bunzel, a doctoral candidate at Princeton. Mr. Bunzel provided biographical details about a senior Islamic State cleric, Turki al-Binali, but has not taken a position on whether Mr. Binali is a possible successor to Mr. Adnani.
match_headline: Spokesman’s Death Will Have Islamic State Turning to Its ‘Deep Bench’

text: An article on Aug. 2 about the Indian government’s efforts to support thousands of its citizens who have lost their jobs in Saudi Arabia with the drop in global oil prices misstated the price of oil in early August. It was about $40 a barrel, not $50.
match_headline: Thousands of Indian Workers Are Stuck in Saudi Arabia as Kingdom’s Economy Sags

text: An article on Wednesday about President Obama’s plans to campaign for Hillary Clinton misstated the date that early voting will start in North Carolina, one of the states he is expected to visit. It is Oct. 20, not Oct. 27.
match_headline: Stumping for Hillary Clinton, Obama Will Urge His Supporters to Get Out the Vote

text: An article on Thursday about a trans-Pacific trip by President Obama referred incorrectly to the creation of Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, which Mr. Obama plans to visit on his way to Asia. It was designated a national monument in 2006; Mr. Obama did not create it.
match_headline: Obama Heads to Asia Seeking Breakthrough on Trade and Climate Change

text: An article on Aug. 25 about how few workers at homeless shelters are trained to administer a heroin antidote referred incorrectly to the medication. It is naloxone, not Narcan. (Narcan is a brand name for naloxone.) The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Few Homeless Shelter Workers Are Trained to Administer Heroin Antidote

text: An article on Saturday about the injuries Serena Williams and Novak Djokovic carried into the U.S. Open misstated the number of consecutive weeks Williams had been No. 1 at the time. It was 184, not 183.
match_headline: Serena Williams and Novak Djokovic Sit Atop U.S. Open Draw, With Injuries Sharing Spotlight

text: An article on Aug. 25 about a decision by U.S. Soccer to terminate the contract of goalkeeper Hope Solo misstated the age of Alyssa Naeher, Solo’s backup at the Olympics. She is 28, not 27.
match_headline: U.S. Soccer Suspends Hope Solo and Terminates Her Contract

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Aug. 4 about the composer Einojuhani Rautavaara gave an incorrect guide for the pronunciation of his surname. It is ROW-ta-vah-ra, not row-ta-VAH-ra.
match_headline: Einojuhani Rautavaara, Composer, Dies at 87; His Lush Music Found Wide Appeal

text: An article on Thursday about the political problems of Gov. Paul LePage of Maine misstated the surname and the title of a legislative leader who discussed the turmoil. He is Justin Alfond, not Alford, and he is the Democratic leader of the Senate, not the majority leader of the House.
match_headline: Paul LePage, the Governor of Maine, Now Says He’s Not Quitting

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about a collision between kayakers and a ferry in the Hudson River, using information from Fire Department officials, misstated the approximate location of the accident in some copies. It was near West 39th Street, not 34th Street.
match_headline: 10 Kayakers Rescued From Hudson River After Collision With Ferry

text: Because of an editing error, a correction in this space on Friday for an article about a heroin antidote misspelled the name of the medication in some editions. It is naloxone, not naxolone.

Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a lawsuit filed against J.P. Morgan, accusing the financial services firm of conflicts of interest in advising Good Technology on its acquisition by BlackBerry, a company that J.P. Morgan also had a business relationship with, misstated the year Royal Bank of Canada was hired by Rural/Metro, an ambulance services company, looking to sell itself. (In that deal, Royal Bank of Canada was found liable for damages over banker conflicts.) It was 2011, not 2014.
match_headline: Good Technology Investors Sue J.P. Morgan, Claiming Conflicts

text: An article on Wednesday about Jared Donaldson’s upset of David Goffin at the United States Open misstated, in some editions, the way in which Donaldson made the field for the tournament. He won his qualifying matches; he was not given a wild card.
match_headline: Jared Donaldson, Unlikeliest of American Teenagers, Advances at the U.S. Open

text: An article on Tuesday about Rafael Nadal’s first-round victory at the United States Open misstated, in some editions, the day he first practiced in Arthur Ashe Stadium with the roof closed. It was Aug. 21, not Aug. 22.
match_headline: U.S. Open Today: John Isner Survives Five-Set Duel With Frances Tiafoe

text: An article on Aug. 21 about Flint’s water-contamination crisis referred incorrectly to Scott Smith’s relationship with Water Defense when he was named the group’s chief water scientist. He was appointed to the post and receives no compensation beyond expenses; he was not hired.
match_headline: Flint’s Water Crisis and the ‘Troublemaker’ Scientist

text: An article on Aug. 28 about 16 counties in America that have recently imposed a high number of death sentences misstated the year the governments of Duval County and the City of Jacksonville in Florida consolidated. It was 1968, not 1959.
match_headline: Where the Death Penalty Still Lives

text: An article last Sunday about the Dream Up Festival in New York City misstated the closing date. It runs through Sept. 18, not Sept. 28.
match_headline: Looking for Adventurous Theater? Try the Dream Up Festival

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the playwright Lisa Loomer misspelled the given name of an actress in Ms. Loomer’s play “Roe.” She is Sara Bruner, not Sarah.
match_headline: A Playwright Finds Drama, and Humor, in Roe v. Wade

text: An article last Sunday about recently reissued albums misstated the connection between the jazz historian and saxophonist Loren Schoenberg and Count Basie. Mr. Schoenberg, who provided the liner notes for an eight-CD boxed set of the music of Basie and Lester Young, played in bands led by Basie sidemen and alumni; he did not play in Basie’s band.
match_headline: Reissues: ’50s Moxie, ’60s Soul and ’90s Hip-Hop

text: An article on Aug. 21 about a trip on a freighter through the St. Lawrence Seaway referred incorrectly to the location of the ship as it headed toward LacSt.-Louis after leaving St. Lambert Lock in Montreal. The ship was north of the United States-Canada border; it was not sailing along the border. The article also gave outdated figures for the average ton-mile per gallon rate of freighters, trains and trucks. A freighter carries 576 ton-miles per gallon on average, not 514; a train carries 413, not 202; and a truck carries 155, not 59. The article also erroneously attributed a distinction to the farmers’ market in Hamilton, Ontario. It is the oldest indoor market in Canada, not the country’s oldest market. In addition, the article described imprecisely the ship’s passage through the Thousand Islands. Deer Island and Boldt Castle came into view nearly simultaneously; the ship did not pass Boldt Castle first.
match_headline: From Montreal to Minnesota, by Inland Sea

text: An article on Tuesday about a push by hotels to get guests to make reservations directly rather than through online travel services misstated the services provided by Preferred Hotels & Resorts. It provides sales and marketing for independent hotels; it does not manage them.
match_headline: With Occupancy High, Hotels Seek to Avoid Online Booking Services

text: An article on the Personal Finance pages on Saturday about caregiver burnout misstated the title of Mindi Golden at San Francisco State University, who commented on the matter. She is associate professor of communication studies, not communications studies.
match_headline: Love and Burnout: Caregivers, Too, Need Care

text: A picture caption last Wednesday with the About New York column, about how the bizarre is part of the daily experience on the subway, referred incorrectly to a man who was shown with a snake wrapped around his neck. He was a passenger who allowed a man carrying snakes to drape them on him; he was not “the snake guy.”
match_headline: Crickets, Snakes, Crabs: A Mix of Fact and Fraud in New York’s Subway

text: An article on Monday about drone sailboats that gather research data misidentified the variety of fish being counted off the coast of Alaska by boats deployed by a company called Saildrone. The drones are counting pollock, not haddock.
match_headline: No Sailors Needed: Robot Sailboats Scour the Oceans for Data

text: An article last Thursday about college football teams that schedule games far into the future misstated the nickname of teams representing Boston College, which recently announced that it would play Stanford in 2028 and 2029. It is the Eagles, not the Golden Eagles.
match_headline: Busy Schedule? Some College Football Games Give Fans More Than a Decade to Plan

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in the Sports Briefing column on Saturday showing the racecar drivers Dale Earnhardt Jr. and Jeff Gordon at Watkins Glen International racetrack misstated, in some copies, the day the photograph was taken. It was taken Aug. 5, not on Friday. Because of an editing error, a report in the column also described incorrectly, in some editions, Chicago Cubs pitcher Jon Lester’s performance in a win over the San Francisco Giants. He had a no-hitter until two were out in the seventh inning, not the eighth.
match_headline: I.O.C. Members Berate WADA Over Russia Scandal

text: Because of an editing error, the On College Football column on Monday, about the opening weekend of the 2016 season, misstated the nickname of the University of Houston’s teams. They are the Cougars, not the Tigers. The column also misidentified South Alabama’s college football affiliation. It is in the Football Bowl Subdivision, not “the lower-tier Football Championship Subdivision.”
match_headline: Business as Usual for Alabama Against a Nonconference Power

text: An article on Tuesday about the large number of Chicago Cubs fans who attended Monday afternoon’s game against the Brewers in Milwaukee, taking advantage of the teams’ proximity, misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a Cubs player who singled in the sixth inning. He is Jorge Soler, not Solar.
match_headline: It’s the Chicago Cubs’ Year, in the Milwaukee Brewers’ Park

text: An obituary on Saturday about the singer, guitarist and songwriter Fred Hellerman misstated the surname of the man with whom he wrote the song “I’m Just a Country Boy.” He was Marshall Barer, not Baker. It also erroneously credited Mr. Hellerman with the composition of two songs. He adapted “I Never Will Marry” and “Green Grow the Lilacs” for Harry Belafonte; he did not write either song. And the obituary, using information from Mr. Hellerman’s family, referred incorrectly to his mother, the former Clara Robinson. She was the daughter of Jewish immigrants from Riga, Latvia; she was not herself an immigrant.
match_headline: Fred Hellerman, Last of the Weavers Folk Group, Dies at 89

text: An article on Monday about accusations by the media mogul Barry Diller that the real estate tycoon Douglas Durst has secretly backed efforts to block a cultural pier on the West Side of Manhattan misstated the role of a Durst ally, Tom Fox, at New York Water Taxi, a ferry company now run by Mr. Durst’s daughter Helena. Mr. Fox was a co-owner of the company, not an employee.
match_headline: Clash of Titans? Opponents of Pier 55 Have Secret Backer, Media Mogul Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about no-ad scoring and other timesaving measures in tennis misstated the day Bob and Mike Bryan lost in the men’s doubles tournament at the United States Open. It was Tuesday, not Friday.
match_headline: Tennis Players Go Back and Forth on No-Ad Scoring

text: An article on Tuesday about Juan Martín del Potro’s victory in the fourth round of the United States Open misidentified the wrist of his that required three operations. It was his left wrist, not his right. (He also had one operation on his right wrist.)
match_headline: Juan Martín del Potro, Ranked No. 142, Reaches Quarterfinals in a Jimmy Connors Flashback

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some copies on Sept. 1 about the French tennis federation’s issuing suspensions to three top players misstated the timing of Benoit Paire’s suspension. It was announced after his loss at the Olympics, not after his loss at the United States Open.
match_headline: French Group Suspends Three Players for Unprofessional Behavior

text: An article on Thursday about films dealing with race being shown at the Toronto International Film Festival misspelled the given name of the author of the book on which the film “Hidden Figures” is based. She is Margot Lee Shetterly, not Margo.
match_headline: Toronto Film Festival: Just Don’t Call Them ‘Black Films’

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Namon O’Neal Hoggle, the last surviving defendant accused of killing a civil rights worker, the Rev. James J. Reeb, in Selma, Ala., in 1965, referred incorrectly to the slaying of Viola Liuzzo, another civil rights advocate. It occurred on March 25, 1965, two weeks after the killing of Mr. Reeb, not 10 days after his killing. The obituary also misstated the age of the Rev. Orloff Miller, one of Mr. Reeb’s companions when he was killed. He was 33 at the time, not 25. Because of an editing error, it also referred incorrectly to the civil rights march on March 7, 1965, known as Bloody Sunday. It was led by John Lewis and Hosea Williams, not the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King.
match_headline: Namon Hoggle, 81, Accused in a Civil Rights Killing, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Thursday about Anna Dewdney, whose “Llama Llama” picture books amused millions of preschool children, misstated the college she attended. It was Wesleyan University, not Wellesley College.
match_headline: Anna Dewdney Dies; Author of ‘Llama Llama’ Books Was 50

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the use of miniature donkeys as therapy animals in Ulster Park, N.Y., misstated the kind of cancer that Brittany Hill, a member of a donkey-walking group, has. She has leukemia, not bone-marrow cancer.
match_headline: The Miniature Donkey Therapy Meet-up

text: An article on Page 90 this weekend about the style preferences and career highlights of the professional surfer Kelly Slater erroneously includes one country among those where he has competed. While he surfs internationally, he does not compete in Morocco.
match_headline: From the Beach to the Runway, the World of Kelly Slater

text: An article on Aug 28 about user-generated websites referred incorrectly to fake reviews on Yelp. Businesses featured on the site — not Yelp itself — solicited the fake reviews.
match_headline: Turning Instagram Into a Radically Unfiltered Travel Guide

text: An article last Sunday about Cher’s political activism misstated the location of one of the Hillary Clinton’s fund-raising events attended by the singer. It was held in Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood, not Miami Beach.
match_headline: Cher’s Latest Road Show? The Campaign Trail

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Jack Gleeson misspelled the surname of a founding member of Collapsing Horse Theater. He is Matt Smyth, not Smythe.
match_headline: King Joffrey Is Coming. But Only to Act in a Play.

text: A listing on the On the Market page last Sunday misstated the down payment required for the apartment at 230 East 79th Street, #10F. It is 25 percent, not 75 percent.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in Brooklyn and Manhattan

text: A review on Aug. 28 about the Hotel Carlota in Mexico City misidentified the neighborhood where the hotel is located. It is in the Colonia Cuauhtémoc neighborhood, not the Colonia Juárez neighborhood.
match_headline: In Mexico City, a Modernist Hotel and Temple to High Design

text: A picture caption on Sept. 4 with an article about Boulder, Colo., described a house in the city incorrectly. The house was the setting of the “Mork and Mindy” TV show, not the residence of the poet Allen Ginsberg.
match_headline: In Boulder, Where Inner Peace Meets Outer Beauty

text: A picture caption on Sept. 4 with an article about Amsterdam misidentified the waterway into which a man was shown diving. It is the Noordhollandsch Kanaal, not the Amstel River.
match_headline: Amsterdam, Revisited

text: An article on Thursday about the differing business strategies of Michael Dell and Meg Whitman misquoted Mr. Dell in one instance. Referring to the prospects of Dell Technologies, the company formed by the merger of his computer business and the data storage company EMC, he said: “Things are going well on a relative basis,” not “Things are going well on a personal basis.”
ref_headline: Things are going well on a relative basis,
match_headline: Dell Gets Bigger and Hewlett Packard Gets Smaller in Separate Deals

text: An article on Thursday about the Yankees’ 2-0 victory over the Toronto Blue Jays misidentified the Yankees player who caught a high fly ball just in front of the right-field wall for the Jays’ final out of the eighth inning. He is Aaron Judge, not Tyler Austin. (Judge replaced Austin in right field in the seventh inning.)
match_headline: Yankees’ Bryan Mitchell Is Stellar in Long-Awaited Debut

text: An article on Sunday about Uber’s introduction of self-driving cars to Pittsburgh misstated the surname of the city’s assistant chief of police. He is Scott Schubert, not Schuster.
match_headline: No Driver? Bring It On. How Pittsburgh Became Uber’s Testing Ground

text: An article on Tuesday about the backlog of Zika tests in Florida misstated the surname of the medical director of Pathology Laboratories at Jackson Memorial Hospital. He is David Andrews, not Anderson.
match_headline: Pregnant Women Anxious as Florida’s Zika Test Results Take Weeks

text: An article on Aug. 14 about the flight of ISIS fighters from Manbij, Syria, misidentified the country that includes the nearby town of Jarabulus. It is Syria, not Turkey.
match_headline: U.S. Drones Record ISIS Fighters Fleeing Manbij in Northern Syria

text: An article on Monday about the EB-5 visa program referred incorrectly to one aspect of the process. The program allows foreign investors to gain permanent residency when they invest between $500,000 and $1 million in a business that creates 10 jobs directly or indirectly. They do not gain citizenship by doing so. (They can apply for full citizenship after five years.) The article also referred incorrectly to Angelique Brunner, a spokeswoman for the EB-5 Investment Coalition, which is made up of investors and developers. Ms. Brunner is the owner of a Washington-based center that raises capital through the EB-5 program; she is not a developer.
match_headline: Visa Program Up for Renewal Amid Allegations of Fraud

text: An article on Friday about efforts to clean up the Hudson River in a stretch running north from Albany misstated the surname of the mayor of Fort Edward. He is Matthew Traver, not Travers.
match_headline: G.E. Spent Years Cleaning Up the Hudson. Was It Enough?

text: An article on Monday about disparities in Connecticut schools omitted part of the name of a university in Atlanta that an honors student is considering attending. It is Clark Atlanta University, not Clark University.
match_headline: In Connecticut, a Wealth Gap Divides Neighboring Schools

text: An article on Monday about the junior titles at the United States Open tennis tournament misspelled, in some copies, the surname of the runner-up in boys’ singles. He is Miomir Kecmanovic, not Kecmnovic. The article also referred incorrectly in some editions to the performance of the girls’ singles champion, Kayla Day, in the women’s main draw. Day lost to Madison Keys in the second round — not the first — and the score was 6-1, 6-1 — not 4-6, 7-6 (5), 6-2.
match_headline: For Two Rising Prospects, a Day of Victory and Redemption

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the large number of Los Angeles Dodgers fans who watched their team play the Yankees on Monday night in a rare visit to the Bronx misstated the given name of an organizer of a Dodgers fan group. He is Alex Soto, not Danny.
match_headline: Dodgers, and Their Fans, Make Themselves at Home at Yankee Stadium

text: An article in some copies on Tuesday about the New England Patriots’ season-opening victory with Jimmy Garoppolo, who played in place of the suspended quarterback Tom Brady, misidentified the N.F.L. season in which Matt Cassel filled in for Brady as a starter. It was 2008, not 2007.
match_headline: Jimmy Garoppolo Rises From the Ashes of Deflategate

text: An article on Monday about “An Occupation of Loss,” a multidisciplinary artwork at the Park Avenue Armory in Manhattan by Taryn Simon that uses professional mourners, referred incorrectly to one, Aziz Tamoyan, who laments a massacre of members of the Yazidi community. Another man with that name is president of the Yazidi National Union, not Mr. Tamoyan. The article also misstated the number of concrete towers used in the work. It is 11, not 10.
match_headline: A Consolation of Voices: At the Park Avenue Armory, Mourning the World Over

text: A listing of credits on Monday with a theater review of “Bears in Space,” at 59E59 Theaters in Manhattan, misspelled a producer’s surname. He is Matt Smyth, not Smith.
match_headline: Review: ‘Bears in Space,’ an Interstellar Romp Through Winsome Silliness

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about a debate over whether a plaster cast of a dancer was made by Edgar Degas or his studio during his lifetime or was created afterward c arried an erroneous credit. The pictures, of the plaster cast and a cast bronze sculpture, are by Joseph Coscia Jr., not Joseph P. Coscia Jr./Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
match_headline: Did Degas Make This Plaster? An Expert Now Says Yes

text: An article on Aug. 15 about a Facebook friendship that ended up saving the life of an Afghan baby who received heart surgery through an Israeli charity, Save a Child’s Heart, misstated part of the name of a group led by Tony Laurance, who praised the outreach but criticized Israeli restrictions on medical care for Palestinians. The group is Medical Aid for Palestinians (not for Palestine). The article also overstated the impact of Israeli restrictions on travel and trade in the Gaza Strip, and overstated what is known about the financing of Save a Child’s Heart. Although the restrictions have made the import of some medical equipment difficult, the import of medicine is not restricted. According to the charity’s director, Simon Fisher, it receives money from the governments of Israel, the European Union and the United States, as well as Christian ministries, Jewish congregations, public and private foundations and individuals worldwide, but he said he did not know whether most of the money was from private Jewish donors.
match_headline: Unlikely Facebook Friendship Saves Afghan Baby With Heart Defect

text: An article on Aug. 15 about Afghan forces’ struggle to resist the Taliban outside the southern city of Lashkar Gah misstated part of the name of an Afghan Army unit that was trying to hold the line. It is the Third Regiment, 215 Corps, not the 2015 Corps.
match_headline: Afghanistan Forces Struggle to Hold Firm Against Taliban in South

text: An article on Wednesday about Museum Voorlinden, created by the Dutch chemical company executive and art collector Joop van Caldenborgh, misidentified the museum’s site. It is on the Netherlands’ west coast, not the north coast.
match_headline: How a Dutch Businessman Fulfilled His Dream to Open a ‘World-Class’ Museum

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the pastry chef Albert Kumin misstated the year his wife, Eva, died. It was 2012, not 2010. The obituary also misstated part of the name of the school where Nick Malgieri, a former colleague of Mr. Kumin’s, teaches. It is the Institute of Culinary Education (not “for” Culinary Education).
match_headline: Albert Kumin, Pastry Chef for Carter White House and Top New York Restaurants, Dies at 94

text: A picture caption last Thursday with an article about seating arrangements at New York Fashion Week misidentified one of the people sitting in the front row of the Halston fashion show in 1978. The woman on the far left, next to Andy Warhol, is D. D. Ryan, not the French Vogue editor Françoise de la Renta.
match_headline: The Front Row

text: An article on Aug. 16 about British Jews who have applied for German citizenship since Britain voted to leave the European Union, using information from the German Embassy in London, omitted an eligibility requirement for those seeking citizenship under a 1949 law. German citizenship passes down only through fathers for people born before April 1, 1953, and to a limited degree through mothers for people born through 1973, so it is not the case that all descendants are eligible for citizenship. The article also referred imprecisely to British suspicions about the Jews who arrived in Britain from Germany and Austria before 1939. They were seen as potential enemies and were held in internment camps because they were from enemy states, not because they were Jewish.
match_headline: Upset by Brexit, Some British Jews Look to Germany

text: An article on Thursday about workers who have been left behind despite the economic recovery misstated in one instance, and in some copies, the surname of a Colorado telecommunications analyst. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is David Pilot, not Platt.
match_headline: A Rebounding Economy Remains Fragile for Many

text: An article on Thursday comparing child-care plans put forth by Donald J. Trump and Hillary Clinton described incorrectly one aspect of the Trump proposal to allow pretax savings accounts for the care of a child. A match of $500 from the government would be available to low-income families, not to all families.
match_headline: How the Trump and Clinton Child Care Plans Stack Up

text: An article on Tuesday about a controversy at the Brisbane Writers Festival in Australia, where the American novelist Lionel Shriver’s keynote speech belittled the movement against cultural appropriation, referred incorrectly to information about Ms. Shriver’s appearance that was on the festival’s website. It was temporarily unavailable because of a technical malfunction, the festival said, not because it was censored. Because of an editing error, the article misstated the given name of the author of “Little Bee,” a Briton who has been criticized for writing that book from the point of view of a Nigerian girl. He is Chris Cleave, not Clive Cleave. The article also misspelled part of the title of a novel by Adam Johnson. It is “The Orphan Master’s Son” (not “Sun”).
match_headline: Lionel Shriver’s Address on Cultural Appropriation Roils a Writers Festival

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a theater review of “Blossom,” at Dixon Place in Manhattan, carried a credit that misstated the photographer’s surname. She is Maria Baranova, not Baranov.
match_headline: Review: ‘Blossom,’ a Puppet’s Tale of Alzheimer’s

text: An article on Friday about the fatal shooting of a 13-year-old boy in Columbus, Ohio, using information from the Columbus police, misspelled the teenager’s given name. He was Tyre King, not Tyree. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Black Child With BB Gun Is Shot by Police in Columbus, Ohio

text: An article on Wednesday about menthol cigarettes gave an outdated name for an antismoking research group. It is Truth Initiative, no longer the American Legacy Foundation.
match_headline: Black Health Experts Renew Fight Against Menthol Cigarettes

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Hillary Clinton’s pneumonia diagnosis misstated, in some editions, the year that Mrs. Clinton’s internist released a description of her health. It was July 28, 2015 — not July 28 this year.
match_headline: What Pneumonia Experts Say About Clinton’s Case

text: An article on Sept. 8 about a judge’s order that Connecticut overhaul its school system quoted incorrectly from part of the ruling. Judge Thomas Moukawsher wrote that the current system “has left rich school districts to flourish and poor school districts to flounder,” not “founder.”
ref_headline: has left rich school districts to flourish and poor school districts to flounder,
match_headline: Judge, Citing Inequality, Orders Connecticut to Overhaul Its School System

text: Because of an editing error, an art review on Sept. 9 about “Zao Wou-Ki: No Limits,” at Asia Society in Manhattan, using information from a 2013 New York Times obituary, misstated the year Zao was born. It was 1920, not 1921. (The obituary also misstated his birth date. It was Feb. 1, not Feb. 13.) In addition, the review misidentified the city in which he was born. While he spent his early years in Nantong, China, he was born in Beijing, not Nantong. The review also misstated the year of the earliest work in the exhibition. It is from 1943, not 1945. And it omitted a co-organizer of a show of Zao’s work at the Colby College Museum of Art. In addition to Ankeney Weitz, it was organized by Melissa Walt.
match_headline: Zao Wou-Ki, an Abstract Fusion Master

text: An article on Page 52 this weekend about efforts in the House of Representatives to reach a compromise on immigration reform misidentifies the birthplace of Representative Luis Gutiérrez, Democrat of Illinois, who helped draft legislation. He was born in Chicago, not Puerto Rico.
match_headline: How Republicans Lost Their Best Shot at the Hispanic Vote

text: An obituary on Friday about the director Jack Hofsiss misstated the name of a play he directed at the Public Theater in New York, and the surname of the playwright. It is “Rebel Women” by Thomas Babe, not “Rebel Woman” by Thomas Rabe. The obituary also misstated part of the name of a theater in Washington where Mr. Hofsiss acted early in his career. It is Arena Stage, not the Arena Theater.
match_headline: Jack Hofsiss, Stage Director of ‘The Elephant Man,’ Dies at 65

text: An editorial on Friday about Missouri’s gun law misstated the defense’s legal strategy in the George Zimmerman case. It did not rely on the “stand your ground” claim, but language from that law was contained in the jury instructions.
match_headline: Missouri: The Shoot-Me State

text: An article on Friday about efforts by Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, to block the administration’s plan to end federal oversight of the internet misstated part of the name of a government agency. It is the National Security Agency, not the National Security Administration.
match_headline: Ted Cruz Fights Internet Directory’s Transfer; Techies Say He Just Doesn’t Get It

text: An article on Saturday about six artworks that have been attributed to the 17th-century Dutch printmaker and painter Hercules Segers, by the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, misidentified the positions of two staff members there, Huigen Leeflang and Pieter Roelofs. They are curators, not conservators.
match_headline: Rijksmuseum Attributes Six Works to a Dutch Old Master

text: An obituary in some editions on Saturday and in some copies on Sunday about the playwright Edward Albee misstated the year that his “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” won the Tony Award for best play. It was 1963, not 1962. It also misstated the subject that Nick, a character in that play, teaches. It is biology, not math.
match_headline: Edward Albee, Trenchant Playwright Who Laid Bare Modern Life, Dies at 88

text: An article on Aug. 21 about the rise of political murders in Russia misidentified the airline whose flight Anna Politkovskaya, an opposition journalist, was aboard when she drank poisoned tea in 2004. The airline was Karat, not Aeroflot.
match_headline: More of Kremlin’s Opponents Are Ending Up Dead

text: Because of an editing error, the continuation of an article on Tuesday about the arrest of Ahmad Khan Rahami, a suspect in Saturday’s bombings in Manhattan and New Jersey, transposed two sections of type in some editions. The correct version can be found at nytimes.com/nyregion.
match_headline: Ahmad Khan Rahami Is Arrested in Manhattan and New Jersey Bombings

text: An article last Sunday about alternative therapies for post-traumatic stress syndrome misstated the academic credentials of Dr. Barbara Rothbaum, who runs a treatment program at Emory University in Atlanta. She is a psychologist, not a psychiatrist.
match_headline: Scuba, Parrots, Yoga: Veterans Embrace Alternative Therapies for PTSD

text: An article on Tuesday about JetBlue’s deal to buy 330 million gallons of biofuel over 10 years from the bioenergy firm SG Preston referred incorrectly to the company’s chief executive. As the article correctly noted, he is Randy Delbert LeTang, and therefore is not “Mr. Preston.”
match_headline: JetBlue Makes Biofuels Deal to Curtail Greenhouse Gases

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 13 about the trial of Oral Nicholas Hillary in the 2011 death of 12-year-old Garrett Phillips in Potsdam, N.Y., misidentified, in some editions, the location in New York of Clarkson University, where Mr. Hillary had coached soccer. It is in Potsdam, not Canton.
match_headline: Trial Over Potsdam Boy’s Killing Begins With Focus on Credibility

text: An article in some editions on Friday about the Jets’ 37-31 victory over the Buffalo Bills misidentified the Jets receiver whose fumble was returned for a touchdown. He is Jalin Marshall, not Brandon Marshall.
match_headline: Jets and Ryan Fitzpatrick Get Vindication Against Rex Ryan and Bills

text: An article on Sept. 3 about the noise level at Arthur Ashe Stadium since a retractable roof was added misspelled, in some copies, the given name of a vice president for ESPN, the broadcaster of the United States Open. He is Jamie Reynolds, not Jaime.
match_headline: U.S. Open Quieted Those Calling for a Roof. Now It Faces a Louder Problem.

text: Because of an editing error, the On Soccer column on Aug. 26 about goalkeeper Hope Solo misspelled, in some copies, the given name of the player who took over for Solo during the 2007 World Cup after she was benched. She is Briana Scurry, not Brianna.
match_headline: Hope Solo’s Behavior, and Play, Spells End With U.S. Team

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the writer D. Keith Mano misstated part of the title of his first novel. It is “Bishop’s Progress,” not “Bishop’s Watch.”
match_headline: D. Keith Mano, Novelist Who Tackled Christianity, Sex and More, Dies at 74

text: An article last Wednesday about food and cooking in the Umbria region of Italy misstated the century when Giotto painted frescoes in the Basilica of St. Francis in Assisi. It was the 14th, not the 15th. The article also misstated the church where some frescoes by Piero della Francesca are located. They are in the Basilica of St. Francis in Arezzo, Italy, not the basilica in Assisi.
match_headline: Umbria, Italy’s Best-Kept Culinary Secret, Is Budding

text: An article on Tuesday about John G. Stumpf, chief executive of Wells Fargo, whose company is facing a scandal over sham accounts set up by bank employees without customers’ knowledge, misidentified the industry trade group that Wells Fargo departed this year. It is the Financial Services Forum — not the Financial Services Roundtable, which lobbies for the financial industry.
match_headline: Wells Fargo’s John Stumpf Has His Wall St. Comeuppance

text: A report in the Inside Art column on Friday about the artist Cecily Brown’s joining the Paula Cooper Gallery, using information from the gallery, misidentified the Maccarone gallery where Ms. Brown has had a show since leaving the Gagosian Gallery. It is the one in New York, not Los Angeles.
match_headline: Curator From Menil Joins the Whitney

text: An obituary on Sept. 12 about the Jamaican performer and producer Prince Buster referred incorrectly to the rhythmic emphasis of the sessions he produced in the early 1960s that are widely credited as the first ska singles. The emphasis was on the upbeat, not the backbeat.
match_headline: Prince Buster, Trailblazer of Ska, Dies at 78

text: A picture caption on July 21 with an article about designers whose clothing addresses social problems misspelled the given name of one of the designers. She is Angela Luna, not Anglea.
match_headline: Fashion’s Newest Frontier: The Disabled and the Displaced

text: An article on Aug. 23 about the heroes that emerged from the terrorist attacks in France this year and last misstated the location of the kosher grocery store where Lassana Bathily, an immigrant from Mali, smuggled out shoppers after a terrorist attack in 2015. It was in Paris, not outside the city.
match_headline: ‘It Had to Be Stopped’: Heroes Rise Amid France Terror Attacks

text: An article on Thursday about the use of computer technology to unfurl a digital image of an ancient scroll misidentified the journal in which the research appears and misstated the date of publication. It was published in Science Advances on Wednesday, not in the Thursday issue of Science.
match_headline: Modern Technology Unlocks Secrets of a Damaged Biblical Scroll

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about a woman who was wounded in the bombing on West 23rd Street in Manhattan misidentified the workers pushing a gurney at the scene. They are emergency medical responders with the Fire Department, not firefighters.
match_headline: A Routine Night, Until an Explosion Lifted Her Off Her Feet

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 15 about jury selection in the trial over the George Washington Bridge lane closing scandal misstated, in some editions, the date a woman from the same town as Gov. Chris Christie’s was interviewed by the judge. It was Tuesday, Sept. 13 — not Wednesday, Sept. 14.
match_headline: Jurors Picked for Bridge Scandal Trial as Opinions About Chris Christie Are Aired

text: An article on Thursday about a federal insider trading suit against Leon G. Cooperman, founder of the hedge fund Omega Advisors, rendered incorrectly the name of another firm where a top manager was charged in June with insider trading. It is Visium Asset Management, not Visium Asset Manager.
match_headline: Leon Cooperman, a Billionaire Charged With Insider Trading, Prepares to Fight

text: An article on Monday about the Giants’ 16-13 victory over the New Orleans Saints misspelled, in some copies, the given name of the Giants defensive tackle who blocked a field goal in the second quarter. He is Johnathan Hankins, not Jonathan.
match_headline: Giants Beat Saints With a Field Goal That Ends a Lackluster Game

text: An article on Saturday about legislation that would shield artworks believed to have been plundered from seizure while on loan for exhibitions in the United States referred incorrectly to restitution groups’ response to the latest version of the bill. Some groups — not all — are satisfied that it exempts the descendants of owners of art looted in World War II because it will not shield works looted from 1933 to 1945 by the German military or its allies.
match_headline: Bill to Shield International Art Loans Gains in Senate

text: Because of an editing error, a dance entry in the Listings pages on Friday about Nichole Canuso, Geoff Sobelle and Lars Jan at New York Live Arts in Manhattan misstated the starting time of their performances, which will begin on Wednesday. It is 7:30 p.m., not 8 p.m.
match_headline: Dance Listings for Sept. 23-29

text: Because of an editing error, a classical music entry in the Listings pages on Friday about Momenta Festival II, which opens on Wednesday at the Tenri Cultural Institute in Manhattan, misstated the address. It is 43 West 13th Street in Manhattan, not 3 West 13th Street.
match_headline: Classical Music Listings for Sept. 23-29

text: An picture on Page 10 this weekend with an interview with the soprano Nina Stemme, in which she cites her favorite page from the score of Wagner’s “Tristan und Isolde,” was published in error. It shows Page 20; the picture should have been of Page 17, which she says is her favorite because it includes one of the few introverted moments for Isolde.
match_headline: Nina Stemme on a Love and Loss in ‘Tristan und Isolde’

text: An article on Page 167 this weekend about the architect Douglas Burnham misidentifies the city in California in which his office is located. It is Berkeley, not Oakland. And the article misstates Burnham’s role in the renovation of the restaurant the French Laundry. He collaborated on the design; he did not remodel the restaurant by himself.
match_headline: A Constellation of One-Room Cabins, Embedded in the Forest

text: A picture caption on Page 167 this weekend with an article about the artist Paulina Olowska and her interest in examining the lost utopian dreams of socialist Poland through her work misidentifies a building shown. It is Olowska’s Villa Kadenowka, where she hosts artists’ residencies in the Polish village of Rabka; it is not her home.
match_headline: Poland’s Most Optimistic, Backward-Looking Artist

text: A picture caption on Page 62 this weekend about the curator Matylda Krzykowski misstates part of the name of a designer of a blanket shown. It was made by Design Displacement Group, not by Design Displacement Studio.
match_headline: Contemporary Design That Upsets Our Perception of the Home

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about how two inmates spent their three weeks on the run after escaping from the state prison in Dannemora, N.Y., misidentified, in some editions, the prison job held by a female accomplice. She was an employee, but not a guard. The article also quoted incorrectly in some copies from comments by the surviving escapee, David Sweat. In describing the men’s preparations, he said, “You plan for the worst, hope for the best” — not “You plan for the best, hope for the worst.”
ref_headline: You plan for the worst, hope for the best
match_headline: Swamps, Marijuana, Moonshine: 2 Prison Escapees’ 3 Weeks on the Run in New York

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about bars where dogs are still welcome inside in violation of New York City’s health code misidentified the breed of a dog visiting a bar in Park Slope, Brooklyn. He is a yellow Labrador, not a golden retriever. The article also omitted part of the dog’s name. He is Captain William Trigger of Ludlow, not Captain Trigger of Ludlow.
match_headline: The Speakeasy Underworld of the Dog Bar

text: An article last Sunday about Paralympians’ mixed feelings about being called inspirational misstated, in some editions, the given name of a wheelchair rugby player for the United States. He is Kory Puderbaugh, not Kody.
match_headline: Paralympic Athletes’ Least Favorite Word: Inspiration

text: An article last Sunday about new developments in Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn, misstated a projected rise in sea level on the New York City coastline by midcentury. It is 11 to 21 inches, not 18 to 39 inches.
match_headline: Transformation on Brooklyn’s Southern Shore

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about online workout sessions offered by some boutique fitness companies misspelled the name of a cycling workout studio in one instance. It is Peloton, not Peleton.
match_headline: Spin Class Full? Feel the Burn From Your Living Room

text: An article last Sunday about the photographer Sean O’Neal misidentified the neighborhood in Manhattan where his father lives. It is the Upper West Side, not the Upper East Side.
match_headline: Sean O’Neal: An Activist Behind the Lens

text: A caption last Sunday with a picture of a model during New York Fashion Week misidentified the label of the clothing she was wearing. It is Naeem Khan, not Delpozo.
match_headline: The Best of Off the Runway

text: An article last Sunday about the Stanford University professors who teach the class Designing Your Life described incorrectly the $50,000 tuition that undergraduates at Stanford pay. That is full tuition, not in-state tuition. (Stanford is not a state university.) Because of an editing error, the article also misidentified the location in California of the Alpine Inn, where the professors discussed their ideas for the course. It is in Portola Valley, not Palo Alto.
match_headline: Want to Find Fulfillment at Last? Think Like a Designer

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Kiefer Sutherland misidentified the Canadian political party that Tommy Douglas, Mr. Sutherland’s grandfather, helped form. It is the New Democratic Party, not the National Democratic Party.
match_headline: Kiefer Sutherland Returns. This Time the Oval Office Is His.

text: An article last Sunday about four film actresses with breakout roles this fall misstated the release date for “The Handmaiden.” It is Oct. 21, not Oct. 14.
match_headline: Four Actresses Everyone Will Be Talking About This Fall

text: Because of an editing error, an entry in a listing of fall movie releases last Sunday about “The Ruins of Lifta” misspelled the surname of one of the film’s directors. He is Oren Rudavsky, not Rudavsk. And an entry about the documentary “The Anthropologist” misspelled the surname of the titular character. It is Susan Crate, not Crates.
match_headline: Fall Movie Release Schedule

text: An entry in the pop listings last Sunday for Bob Weir’s forthcoming album “Blue Mountain” misstated the given name of a musician who wrote the songs with Mr. Weir. He is Josh Kaufman, not John.
match_headline: Pop and Jazz Fall Preview: 105 Albums, Shows and Festivals

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about fall programs at Carnegie Hall misidentified the location where Jordi Savall was shown conducting. It was the Juilliard School, not Alice Tully Hall.
match_headline: Sounds of Venice’s Serene Republic Come to New York

text: An entry in the dance listings last Sunday for the series “Fall for Forsythe” misidentified a museum presenting the festival. It is the Los Angeles County Museum of Art — not the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles. And an entry for the Ballet Nacional de España included outdated information. After the section had gone to press, organizers announced that the troupe would not be performing at City Center.
match_headline: Dance This Season: Tap, Ballet and the Inexplicable

text: An entry in the art listings last Sunday for a coming exhibit of Jusepe de Ribera’s work at the Meadows Museum misstated the show’s title. It is “Between Heaven and Hell: The Drawings of Jusepe de Ribera” — not “Ribera: Master of Drawing.”
ref_headline: Between Heaven and Hell: The Drawings of Jusepe de Ribera
match_headline: Art Fall Preview: From East Coast to West Coast. From Concrete to Ethereal.

text: An article last Sunday about new cultural commissions in architecture around the world misspelled the surname of an architect and former I. M. Pei staffer who worked on the renovation of the East Building of the National Gallery of Art. He is Perry Chin, not Chen. The article also erroneously credited a distinction to the architect Steven Holl. He is not a Pritzker Prize winner.
match_headline: Millions of Square Feet, Billions of Dollars: An Arts Universe Expands

text: An article on Aug. 28 about the exhibition “Women of Abstract Expressionism” at the Denver Art Museum erroneously included one artist among those who did not become renowned for their work until after they had died. Joan Mitchell achieved critical and commercial success early in her career, as her work was regularly exhibited at galleries and purchased by museums and collectors.
match_headline: The Women Who Helped Create Abstract Expressionism

text: An article on Sept. 11 retracing a family rail trip from Chicago to San Francisco misstated part of the name of the passenger train on which the family rode in 1967. It is the California Zephyr, not the Silver Zephyr. The article also misidentified a railway that connects Russia and China. It is the Trans-Siberian Railway, not the Orient Express.
match_headline: Riding the Rails to the Summer of Love

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary in some editions on Wednesday about Shimon Peres, the former prime minister and president of Israel, misstated the year that a Franco-Israeli alliance led to Israel’s capture of Sinai. It was 1956, not 1967.
match_headline: Shimon Peres, an Enduring Pillar From Israel’s Founding Era, Dies at 93

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Aug. 29 about the Kremlin’s reliance on disinformation to sow doubt, fear and discord in Europe and the United States referred incorrectly to coverage of the Democratic National Convention by a Russian television outfit, RT. It devoted little time to the speeches, focusing instead on scattered demonstrations, on the day President Obama spoke — not throughout the entire convention.
match_headline: A Powerful Russian Weapon: The Spread of False Stories

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Aug. 29 about a crackdown by Israel’s culture ministry on immodest dress at government-sponsored musical events misidentified the strain of Judaism that is holding more influence in the current Israeli government. It is Orthodox Judaism, not Conservative Judaism.
match_headline: Israel Joins Bikini Fray, Ordering Concert Singer to Cover Up

text: An article on Tuesday about Lester Holt’s role as moderator of the presidential debate misspelled the given name of a noted CBS News correspondent. She is Lesley Stahl, not Leslie. And because of an editing error, the article erroneously attributed a distinction to Mr. Holt. Bernard Shaw of CNN — not Mr. Holt — is the first person of African-American descent to serve as the solo anchor of a weekday evening newscast. (Mr. Holt is the first to do so on a broadcast network.)
match_headline: Lester Holt, Given a Choice Assignment, Opted for Restraint

text: An article on Wednesday about reactions by women in Pennsylvania to Donald J. Trump’s performance in the presidential debate misspelled the surname of a Democrat who is a graduate student at Villanova University. She is Sarah Kelley, not Kelly.
match_headline: Suburban Women Find Little to Like in Donald Trump’s Debate Performance

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with an article about the effect the indictment of several of Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s associates on corruption charges could have on him misspelled, in some editions, the surname of one of the associates shown. He is Alain E. Kaloyeros (not Kalyeros).
match_headline: For Cuomo, Allies’ Graft Charges Are Best Bad Outcome

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Aug. 17 about an arrest by Brooklyn officials of a Gabonese man in a foreign bribery case referred incorrectly to the role played by African officials. They are said to have been the intended recipients of the bribes; they did not offer a view of the significance of the arrest. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Bribery Arrest May Expose African Mining Rights Scandal Tied to Och-Ziff

text: An article on Monday about one-click shopping on the internet misstated the fee structure of one online payment method. While Apple Pay charges a fee on each transaction, Samsung Pay does not.
match_headline: What if ‘One Click’ Buying Were Internetwide?

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with the Economic Scene column, about how Mexico might handle a Trump presidency, misspelled the surname of Mexico’s secretary of the economy in some editions. As the column correctly noted, he is Ildefonso Guajardo Villarreal, not Ildefonso Guajardo Villareal.
match_headline: What Can Mexico Do About Trump?

text: An article on Thursday about the Congressional override of a bill allowing families of those killed in the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks to sue Saudi Arabia for any role in the plot referred incorrectly in some editions to the attack on Pan Am Flight 103 in 1988, which prompted lawsuits against Libya. The flight was brought down by a bomb as it flew over Lockerbie, Scotland; it was not shot down.
match_headline: Congress Votes to Override Obama Veto on 9/11 Victims Bill

text: An article on Wednesday about Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s fast-track plan to create a train hall and retail space in the James A. Farley Building while renovating Pennsylvania Station misstated part of the name of the architecture firm that designed the Farley Building and the now-demolished train hall at Penn Station. It is McKim Mead & White (not Wright).
match_headline: Cuomo’s Vision for Revamped Penn Station: New Home for Amtrak and L.I.R.R.

text: An article in some editions on Aug. 26 about the dangers bicyclists still face on New York City streets, using information from an advocacy group, misstated the number of cyclist fatalities caused by a motor vehicle in 2015. It is 14, not 15. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Cyclist’s Death Shows Biking Perils Persist in New York

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a rise in bets against the stock of Deutsche Bank paraphrased incorrectly from a statement by Renee Calabro, a Deutsche Bank spokeswoman. She was referring to the bank’s clients, not its investors, in her remarks about weathering the current turmoil.
match_headline: Deutsche Bank Is the Darling of the Short-Sellers

text: An article on the Personal Tech pages on Thursday about apps for the new Apple Watch misspelled the name of a language-learning app. It is Babbel, not Babel.
match_headline: More Fun on Your Wrist With New Apps for the Apple Watch

text: A report in the Sports Briefing column on Monday about the firing of Les Miles, the football coach at Louisiana State University, misstated Ed Orgeron’s position with the team before being offered the job of interim coach. He was the defensive line coach, not defensive coordinator.
match_headline: L.S.U. Fires Les Miles After Failure Most Programs Would Love to Experience

text: An article on Thursday about a group of artists led by Mel Chin who provided artworks for the television show “Melrose Place” in the 1990s misidentified the position currently held at the College of Staten Island by Valerie Tevere, who at the time was a student of Mr. Chin at the California Institute of the Arts. She is a professor of media culture, not an associate professor of art. The article also referred incorrectly to the medication known as RU-486, the chemical symbol for which was put on a quilt made for a character in the show who became pregnant. It is an abortion pill, not a morning-after pill.
match_headline: The Plot to Put Conceptual Art on ‘Melrose Place.’ Yes, Really.

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about the Provincetown Tennessee Williams Theater Festival in Massachusetts, using information from the program, misspelled the surname of the actor who played Bill in “Small Craft Warnings,” one of the works presented. He is Joe Macdougall, not Macdougal.
match_headline: Tennessee Williams and Eugene O’Neill Side by Side, Under the Sun

text: An obituary on Thursday about the soap opera creator and writer Agnes Nixon misidentified which of her shows broadcast its last episode in January 2012. It was “One Life to Live” — not “All My Children,” which ended its run in September 2011. And because of an editing error, the obituary referred incorrectly to the cancellation of later online versions of those two shows. They ended in November 2013, not last November.
match_headline: Agnes Nixon, Who Infused Her Soap Operas With Social Relevance, Dies at 93

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the Yankees’ 6-4 victory over the Boston Red Sox misstated the number of games it took the Yankees’ Gary Sanchez to hit 20 home runs. It was 51, not 50. The error was repeated in a picture caption in some copies.
match_headline: Red Sox Are Riding High, but Yankees Fend Off Death Blow From David Ortiz

text: An article last Sunday about shortstop Asdrubal Cabrera’s contributions to the Mets this season misstated, in some copies, the period over which he had been the best hitter in the National League. It was the previous five weeks, not four.
match_headline: Beyond the Stats, Asdrubal Cabrera Is a Met Admired

text: An article last Sunday about the designer Pamela Shamshiri and her restoration of an iconic Los Angeles home by the architect R.M. Schindler rendered incorrectly the name of a Frank Lloyd Wright landmark, a scale model of which Shamshiri keeps in her house. It is Fallingwater, not Falling Water.
match_headline: Restoring a Run-Down Convent in Tuscany

text: A picture last week with the What’s Selling Now feature was published in error. It showed a Brooklyn apartment at 599 East Seventh Street, #5U, Kensington; it was not of 69-71 South Oxford Street, #2D, Fort Greene. A picture of the Fort Greene apartment can be found at nytimes.com/realestate .
match_headline: Homes That Sold for Around $1 Million

text: A picture caption on Sept. 18 with an article about Norah Jones, using information from The Associated Press, omitted part of the name of the newspaper whose photographer took the picture of Ms. Jones at the piano. It is The Newport Daily News, not merely The Daily News.
match_headline: Norah Jones Returns to Her Jazz Roots

text: An entry in the pop listings on Sept. 18 about Andrew Cyrille’s album “Proximity” misidentified the label that was scheduled to release it on Sept. 30. It is Sunnyside Records, not Palmetto Records.
match_headline: 10 Fall Pop and Jazz Albums (and One Festival) You Shouldn’t Miss

text: A review on Sept. 18 about “Man of the World: The Further Endeavors of Bill Clinton,” by Joe Conason, misspelled the surname of a former White House press secretary in the Clinton administration and rendered her first name incorrectly. She is Dee Dee Myers, not DeeDee Meyers.
ref_headline: Man of the World: The Further Endeavors of Bill Clinton,
match_headline: Joe Klein of ‘Primary Colors’ Reviews the Latest on Bill Clinton

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Sept. 18 about “Mischling,” a historical novel by Affinity Konar, referred incorrectly to “Children of the Flames: Dr. Josef Mengele and the Untold Story of the Twins of Auschwitz,” by Lucette Matalon Lagnado and Sheila Cohn Dekel, which Konar used as a source. It is a historical study, not “a collection of interviews.”
match_headline: A New Novel Draws on the Dark History of Josef Mengele

text: An entry on the children’s middle-grade hardcover best-seller list last Sunday misstated the given name of the hero of “The Last Kids on Earth and the Zombie Parade,” by Max Brallier. He is Jack Sullivan, not Zach.
ref_headline: The Last Kids on Earth and the Zombie Parade,
match_headline: The Best News You Don’t Know

text: An article last Sunday about one feminist’s waning opposition to cosmetic surgery overstated what is known about whether Gloria Steinem has used some of the cosmetic procedures mentioned. While the writer believed that she had, Ms. Steinem says she has not.
match_headline: Aging and My Beauty Dilemma

text: An article on Friday about Thomas Weaver, a former Marine who reported hazing during boot camp, misidentified the type of military discharge that he received. The other-than-honorable discharge was administrative, not punitive.
match_headline: Ex-Marine Describes Violent Hazing and the Lies That Covered It Up

text: A news analysis article in some editions on Sunday about strikes by three orchestras misstated, in some editions, the name of another orchestra that recently went through a 16-month lockout. It is the Minnesota Orchestra, not the Minneapolis Orchestra.
match_headline: For Orchestras in the U.S., So Much Depends on Their Communities’ Fortunes

text: An article on Monday about concerns over Deutsche Bank’s riskier assets misstated a comparison for the amount of derivatives on the German company’s books. The amount — about €42 trillion in derivatives — is equal to about 11 times the size of the German economy; it is not equivalent to the size of the country’s economy.
match_headline: Deutsche Bank’s Appetite for Risk Throws Off Its Balance

text: An article on Monday about a New York Review of Books article by Claudio Gatti saying that financial and real estate records “make a powerful case” that the best-selling author known as Elena Ferrante is actually the Italian translator Anita Raja included an erroneous reference to Ms. Raja’s earnings in 2015. Mr. Gatti wrote that the revenue of Ms. Ferrante’s publishing house in Rome, Edizioni E/O, grew to €7.6 million or about $8.4 million that year — not that Ms. Raja’s earnings were that amount. The article also misstated the title of Joe Klein’s book about Bill Clinton’s 1992 presidential campaign — another book that prompted a search for the author’s true identity. It is “Primary Colors,” not “Anonymous” — that was the “name” of the author shown on the cover.
match_headline: Who Is the Real Elena Ferrante? Italian Journalist Reveals His Answer

text: An article on Monday about the German singer Nena, who is on a mini-tour of the United States three decades after her 1984 hit song, misspelled the title of the song. It is “99 Luftballons,” not “99 Luftballoons.” The error was repeated in the headline and picture caption.
match_headline: Missed the ’80s? Nena, and ‘99 Luftballons,’ Alights Live in America

text: An article on Saturday about China’s manipulating its currency paraphrased incorrectly from a comment by Tony Gao, who helped found a start-up called Easy Transfer. Mr. Gao said the company’s growth — not its business — was down this year.
match_headline: China Manipulates Its Currency, but Not in the Way Trump Claims

text: An article on Tuesday about a rule governing the length of principal briefs submitted to federal appeals courts misstated the new word limit that takes effect on Dec. 1. It will be 13,000 words, not 13,500. (The current limit is 14,000 words.)
match_headline: Judges Push Brevity in Briefs, and Get a Torrent of Arguments

text: A picture caption on the Automobiles page on Friday with an article about the use of water-injection technology to turbocharge car engines misidentified the technology used in BMW’s M4GTS. It is BMW’s own version of water injection, not Bosch’s WaterBoost system.
match_headline: How Do You Make Turbo Engines More Efficient? Just Add Water

text: An article on Monday about the United States’ victory over Europe in the Ryder Cup misstated the final score in some copies. It was 17-11, not 17-10. The article also misstated, in some copies, Thomas Pieters’s record for the European team. It was 4-1-0, not 4-1-1. And an accompanying picture was published in error. It showed J.B. Holmes — not Ryan Moore, who clinched the United States’ victory with a singles win over Lee Westwood.
match_headline: U.S. Captures Ryder Cup, Ending Europe’s Streak

text: An obituary on Sunday about Oscar Brand, the folk singer and host of the long-running radio show “Folksong Festival,” misstated the origins of the name of the Weavers, a group that performed on his show. It was suggested by Fred Hellerman, a member of the group, who took it from the title of a play about a worker revolt; it was not suggested by one of Mr. Brand’s listeners.
match_headline: Oscar Brand, Folk Singer Whose Radio Show Twanged for Decades, Dies at 96

text: An article on Sept. 7 about Rashid Siddiqui, an American who survived a deadly crowd crush during the hajj in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, in 2015, misidentified his hometown. He lives in Marietta, Ga., not Atlanta.
match_headline: Hajj Prep: Search Soul, Buy Sturdy Shoes, Pay the Dentist

text: A headline on Sept. 7 with an article about a Unicef report on displaced children referred imprecisely to the nearly 50 million children described in the report. While all have been uprooted by conflict and poverty, not all are refugees. In addition, the article misstated, in some editions, the day the report was released. It was Tuesday, Sept. 6 — not Monday, Sept. 5.
match_headline: Conflict and Poverty Have Uprooted Nearly 50 Million Children, U.N. Says

text: An article on Wednesday about activist hedge funds and the gender gap on company boards referred incorrectly in some copies to efforts at the hedge fund Barington Capital Group more than a decade ago to change the practices of a company where a chief executive was deemed to be spending too much time on golf. Dianne McKeever, then a Barington partner — not the hedge fund itself — argued that the golf games were hurting the company’s stock price and that management changes were needed.
match_headline: Hedge Fund Targets Companies’ Weakness: The Gender Gap

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the 0-4 Cleveland Browns misstated, in some copies, the point differential through four games of the 2008 Detroit Lions, who also started 0-4. It was minus-81, not minus-71.
match_headline: At 0-4, the Browns Are Alone at the Bottom

text: Because of an editing error, the On Golf column on Tuesday about plans for France to host the next Ryder Cup misstated the year of the French golfer Jean Van de Velde’s infamous 18th-hole implosion at the British Open. It was 1999, not 1997.
match_headline: France’s Hope for 2018 Ryder Cup: If We Host It, They Will Come

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about the coming exhibition “The Institute Presents: Neurosociety” by David Byrne and Mala Gaonkar at the Pace Gallery’s branch in Menlo Park, Calif., included a quotation from Elizabeth Sullivan, the director of the branch, that misstated how the proceeds from ticket sales will be used. The money will go entirely toward production costs; not partly to Mr. Byrne and Ms. Gaonkar, and partly toward production costs.
match_headline: Next From David Byrne: Neuroscience in an Art Gallery

text: An obituary on Sunday about Curtis Roosevelt, who as a child lived in the White House with his sister, his mother and his grandparents Franklin D. and Eleanor Roosevelt, misidentified the position Dean Acheson held in the early days of the Roosevelt administration. It was under secretary of the Treasury, not assistant secretary of state. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated the name of the grandson of Winston Churchill with whom Mr. Roosevelt met in 2005. He was Winston S. Churchill, not Winston S. Churchill III. (His father was Randolph Churchill.)
match_headline: Curtis Roosevelt, a White House Charmer as a Child, Dies at 86

text: An article on Wednesday about the investigation of Mayor Bill de Blasio’s political nonprofit, the Campaign for One New York, misstated the organization’s history of disclosing its donors. The group said shortly after its formation in late 2013 that it would release the names of its donors and it began doing so about six months later; it did not release the names of donors in response to criticism.
match_headline: Ethics Panel Investigating de Blasio’s Nonprofit Is Said to Issue Broad Subpoena

text: An article on Thursday about the elimination of tollbooths at all Metropolitan Transportation Authority bridges and tunnels next year misstated the timing of new light shows planned for New York City bridges and tunnels, as well as for the George Washington Bridge. Light shows at each crossing will take place from dusk until dawn, not from dawn until dusk.
match_headline: New York State to Eliminate Cash Option for Paying Tolls

text: An article on Thursday about changes at Theranos, the embattled blood-testing business, misidentified the government agency that imposed sanctions against the company. It was the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, not the Food and Drug Administration.
match_headline: Theranos to Close Labs and Lay Off 340 Workers

text: An article on Thursday about Ava DuVernay’s new documentary, “13th,” referred incorrectly to Academy Award nominations for her movie “Selma.” It was indeed nominated for best picture.
match_headline: Ava DuVernay on Modern Slavery in America

text: An obituary on Sept. 27 about the country singer Jean Shepard erroneously attributed a distinction to her. At least two other women had joined the Grand Ole Opry before she did, in 1955; she was not the third woman to join after Minnie Pearl and Kitty Wells.
match_headline: Jean Shepard, a Female Country Voice With Muscle and Ambition, Dies at 82

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 10 about the rescue of nearly three dozen passengers from malfunctioning cable cars above the Mont Blanc glaciers in the French Alps misstated the height of the cable cars. They dangled at an altitude of 12,500 feet; they did not hang 12,500 feet above the glaciers.
match_headline: Stuck in a Cable Car High Above Mont Blanc, Waiting for Rescue

text: An article on Friday about Tony Granato, who had to agree to complete his undergraduate degree before becoming the University of Wisconsin’s new hockey coach, misstated, in some editions, the surname of an employee in the university’s athletics department. She is Tara Genske, not Genges.
match_headline: Former Badger Gives Team Fresh Start, While He Finishes His Degree

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about Harlem Cycle, the first boutique indoor cycling studio to open above 92nd Street in Manhattan, misstates the year of a business meeting between Tammeca Rochester, the owner, and Charles Tyler, a fitness instructor. Ms. Rochester and Mr. Tyler met in March 2016, not 2015.
match_headline: At Harlem Cycle, Fitness Classes That Speak to the Soul

text: A caption on Thursday with a picture of new products recommended by some interior designers and architects omitted one of the founders of JKC&D, a new custom hardware line. Jessica Kagan Cushman and Judy K. Dimon created the line, not just Ms. Cushman.
match_headline: Architects and Designers Pick Their Favorite New Textiles, Paints and Hardware

text: An obituary on Friday about Dr. Bertrand M. Bell, who was instrumental in reducing the grueling shifts worked by interns and residents in American hospitals, omitted the given name of his father. He was Samuel Harry Bell.
match_headline: Bertrand M. Bell, Who Strove to Reduce Medical Trainees’ Grueling Shifts, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Thursday about Phyllis Creore, whose radio show, “Canteen Girl,” was broadcast to soldiers during World War II, misstated the location of an art show where Ms. Creore exhibited sculptures and pastels. It was at the Broome Street Gallery, owned by the New York Artists Equity Association, not at the Art Studio Club of New York.
match_headline: Phyllis Creore, ‘Canteen Girl’ on Wartime Radio, Dies at 100
