text: An article on Sept. 25 about three design monographs that document the interiors of lavish European homes misidentified the English estate at which Prince Charles has been known to engage with tourists. It is Dumfries House, not Highgrove House.
match_headline: Rooms with a View

text: An article on Sept. 25 about the Impasse Ronsin, an alleyway in Paris in which a number of famed artists of postwar France lived and worked in the 1950s and 1960s, described incorrectly the career of the artist Niki de Saint Phalle and the artwork she is shown creating by shooting at it with a .22 rifle. These artworks are considered paintings, not pictures. And at the time the photograph was taken, in June 1961, de Saint Phalle had been making this type of work since February of that year; it was not the first time she had created such a painting. The article also misstated the role the artist Christo played in the marriage of the artists Yves Klein and Rotraut Uecker. Christo painted the couple’s wedding portrait; he did not serve as the photographer in the ceremony.
match_headline: The Artists and Their Alley, in Postwar France

text: An article last Sunday about the HBO series “Westworld” misstated the timing of a production shutdown for the show. It began in November 2015, not January 2016. The article also misstated the title of a film Jonathan Nolan, a showrunner for “Westworld,” worked on with his brother Christopher Nolan. It is “The Dark Knight Rises,” not “The Dark Knight Returns.”
match_headline: Is ‘Westworld’ HBO’s Next Big Hit?

text: A picture caption on Sept. 25 with a portfolio about Camino de Santiago, the Christian pilgrimage route in Spain, misidentified the location shown. The photograph was taken in Burgos, Spain — not in Santo Domingo de la Calzada.

An article last Sunday about the businessman Tom Clarke’s plan to cut carbon emissions by selling pollution credits with each ton of coal misstated the amount of time it takes an acre of trees to convert 156 tons of carbon. The process occurs over a period of 20 years, not in one year.
match_headline: A Curious Plan to Fight Climate Change: Buy Mines, Sell Coal

text: A review on Sept. 18 about “Indelible Ink: The Trials of John Peter Zenger and the Birth of America’s Free Press,” by Richard Kluger, misstated the legal impact of the Supreme Court’s ruling in the case of New York Times Co. v. Sullivan in 1964. The court ruled that a public official cannot prevail in a libel suit against a publisher without showing actual malice on the publisher’s part, even if the statements in question were false and defamatory. The ruling did not in fact “fully secure” the “principle that truth cannot be libel” — that principle has been part of American common law for well over a century.
ref_headline: Indelible Ink: The Trials of John Peter Zenger and the Birth of America’s Free Press,
match_headline: A Victory for Press Freedom in 1735 Set an Important Precedent

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about tubing in Laos referred incorrectly to an Australian backpacker. Para Pascoe is a woman.
match_headline: In Laos, a Haven for Tubing Offers More Peace, Less Partying

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the reaction of men to Donald J. Trump’s remarks about women referred incorrectly to his explanation that the comments were “locker room talk.” He used the description in a statement posted online; he did not say it in a video he released later.
match_headline: Men Say Trump’s Remarks on Sex and Women Are Beyond the Pale

text: An article on Monday about NBC’s being scooped on reporting a blockbuster video of Donald J. Trump that came from a syndicated entertainment program owned by NBCUniversal rendered the name of another syndicated entertainment show incorrectly. It is “Extra,” not “Extra!”
match_headline: How NBC Finished Second on the Trump Video Story

text: An article on Monday about the Pittsburgh Steelers’ 31-13 victory over the Jets misstated, in one instance and in some copies, the surname of the Jets quarterback. As the article and a picture caption correctly noted elsewhere, he is Ryan Fitzpatrick, not Fitzgerald.
match_headline: Ryan Fitzpatrick and Jets Avoid Turnovers but Can’t Evade Steelers

text: An obituary in some copies on Monday about Peter Allen, the longtime announcer of the Metropolitan Opera’s radio broadcasts, misidentified the housing complex in Manhattan where he lived. It is Peter Cooper Village, not Stuyvesant Town.
match_headline: Peter Allen, a Voice on the Radio for the Met Opera, Dies at 96

text: An obituary on Sunday about the graphic designer Elaine Lustig Cohen misstated the date of her birth in 1927. It was March 6, not March 26.
match_headline: Elaine Lustig Cohen, Designer Who Left Her Mark Everywhere, Dies at 89

text: An obituary in some copies on Monday about the mathematician Theodore W. Anderson misstated the surname of a mathematician who wrote about game theory. He was John von Neumann, not van Neumann.
match_headline: Theodore Anderson, Mathematician Who Advanced Data Analysis, Dies at 98

text: An obituary on Sunday about Brock Yates, who founded a cross-country road race and then fictionalized it in the script for the movie “The Cannonball Run,” misstated, at one point, the given name of the actor who starred in that movie. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, he is Burt Reynolds, not Bill.
match_headline: Brock Yates, Writer and Rebel Who Created the Cannonball Run, Dies at 82

text: An obituary in some editions on Monday about the Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda misstated the location of the Katyn Forest and referred incorrectly to the killing of Polish officers by Russians in 1940 that came to be known as Katyn, about which he made two films. The forest is in western Russia, not Ukraine, and the killings took place in several locations, not just in the Katyn Forest. The earlier version also misstated Mr. Wajda’s role at the Stary Theater in Krakow. While he directed many plays there, he was never the director of the theater.
match_headline: Andrzej Wajda, Towering Auteur of Polish Cinema, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Saturday about the scientist Dale B. Schenk, using information from a spokeswoman, referred incorrectly to two of his survivors. Mark Nagy is his half brother, not his stepbrother, and Linda Lopez is his sister, not his stepsister.
match_headline: Dale Schenk, Who Saw Immune System as Weapon Against Alzheimer’s, Dies at 59

text: An obituary on Oct. 3 about the artist Shirley Jaffe misidentified the degree she received from the Cooper Union in 1945. It was a certificate in art, not a bachelor’s degree. (The Cooper Union did not give bachelor’s degrees until 1963.)
match_headline: Shirley Jaffe, Geometric Artist of Joyful Forms, Dies at 92

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 13 about an eruption of violence in southern India after the Indian Supreme Court ordered the state of Karnataka to share water with a neighboring state, Tamil Nadu, referred incorrectly to the chief minister of Tamil Nadu. The minister, Jayalalithaa Jayaram, is a woman.
match_headline: Violence Erupts in Southern India Over Order to Share Water

text: An article on the Square Feet page on Wednesday about redevelopment in the Jewelers Row section of Philadelphia misstated part of the name of an economic development organization in the city. It is Center City District, not Center City Philadelphia.
match_headline: In Jewelers Row in Philadelphia, Condo Plan Worries Preservationists

text: Because of editing errors, picture captions on Monday with a Critic’s Notebook article about “Channel Zero: Candle Cove” on Syfy and “Freakish” on Hulu reversed their starting dates. As the article correctly noted, “Channel Zero” began on Tuesday, and “Freakish” on Monday.
match_headline: Hold Onto Your Teeth: 2 New Shows Herald the Creepy Season

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about Donn Fendler, whose disappearance in the wilds of Maine when he was a boy made headlines, misstated the year that the book “Lost on a Mountain in Maine,” which he wrote with Joseph B. Egan, was published. It was 1939, shortly after he was rescued — not 1978.
ref_headline: Lost on a Mountain in Maine,
match_headline: Donn Fendler, Who Was Lost in Wilds of Maine as a Boy, Dies at 90

text: An article on Thursday about America’s role in the war in Yemen referred incorrectly to the status of the aid group Doctors Without Borders in the country. It has pulled out of six hospitals in northern Yemen; it has not withdrawn from the country.
match_headline: U.S. Ship Off Yemen Fires Missiles at Houthi Rebel Sites

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 17 about an assertion by Edward J. Snowden, the former American intelligence contractor, that his leaking of documents about surveillance programs had improved individual privacy in the United States referred incorrectly to the revocation of his passport in 2013. It was revoked while he was in Hong Kong, not after he had traveled to Moscow.
match_headline: Edward Snowden Says Disclosures Bolstered Individual Privacy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 14 about a denunciation by Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein, the United Nations high commissioner for human rights, of what he called efforts to stop the United Nations Human Rights Council from monitoring abuses misidentified the agency that he leads. It is the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, not the Human Rights Council.
match_headline: Top U.N. Rights Official Denounces Growing Efforts to Block His Monitoring

text: An article on Tuesday about pipeline protests in North Dakota misspelled the surname of the chairman of the Morton County Commission, who discussed Washington’s response to the demonstrations. He is Cody Schulz, not Shulz.
match_headline: Ranchers Tote Guns as Tribes Dig In for Long Pipeline Fight

text: An article on Sept. 7 about geologists’ efforts to explain the Oklahoma earthquakes misstated the amount of energy represented by a one-point increase in the Richter scale. It is the equivalent of releasing 31 times as much earthquake energy, not 10 times.
match_headline: Geologist Sees Clues, and Further Dangers, in Puzzle of Oklahoma’s Earthquakes

text: An article on Wednesday about the influence of Latinos in Santa Ana, Calif., misstated the year in which the family of Miguel Pulido, who is the city’s mayor, immigrated from Mexico. It was 1961 — not 1984, which was the year they became citizens.
match_headline: This City Is 78% Latino, and the Face of a New California

text: An article on Thursday about the Washington Nationals’ bleak playoff history referred incorrectly to the current franchise. It is the third major league franchise to call the city home since the start of modern baseball, in 1901; it is not “the third incarnation of major league baseball in the city.” (Several major league clubs played there in the 1800s.) The article also misstated, in some copies, the margin of the lead squandered by closer Drew Storen in Game 5 of the team’s 2012 National League division series against the St. Louis Cardinals. The Nationals led by two runs, not four.
ref_headline: the third incarnation of major league baseball in the city.
match_headline: Cubs, Move Over: Washington’s Baseball Futility Is Second to None

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Scoreboard column on Saturday about qualifying for the 2018 World Cup misidentified, in some copies, the team that won the match between Sweden and Luxembourg. Sweden beat Luxembourg, 1-0, not the other way around.
match_headline: Kosovo: The Road Team

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an appraisal of Andrzej Wajda, the Polish film director who died on Sunday, misidentified the subject of his film “Katyn.” It is about a massacre by Soviet forces during World War II, not about the Warsaw Uprising. (That is the subject of his film “Kanal.”) And the appraisal misidentified the Soviet organization that carried out the massacre. It was the N.K.V.D. — the secret police — not the Red Army.
match_headline: Remembering Andrzej Wajda, Unflinching Observer of Modern Poland

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a film review of “Mascots,” using information from Netflix, misidentified the actor at the left. He is Don Lake — not Bob Balaban, another cast member.
match_headline: Review: ‘Mascots’ Suffers From Mockumentary Fatigue Syndrome

text: An obituary on Thursday about the documentarian Morton Silverstein misstated part of the title of a television series on which he worked. It is “Heritage: Civilization and the Jews,” not “Heritage: Civilization of the Jews.”
match_headline: Morton Silverstein, Documentarian Who Explored Social Ills, Dies at 86

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about Bob Dylan’s songwriting, citing a verse from the song “Isis,” quoted from the lyrics on Mr. Dylan’s website rather than the version Mr. Dylan recorded on the album “Desire.” On the recording, the second line of the verse ends “Well, I guess,” not “Well, not quite,” and the fourth line ends “If you want me to, yes!,” not “Yeah, I jes’ might.”
match_headline: Bob Dylan, the Musician: America’s Great One-Man Songbook

text: An article on Tuesday about damage from Hurricane Matthew in North Carolina misstated the name of the river that had flooded near the towns of Lumberton and Fair Bluff. It is the Lumber River, not the Lumberton.
match_headline: Fleeing the Coast Before the Storm, Only to Be Trapped Inland

text: An article on Tuesday about plans to build and launch a privately financed telescope to look for an Earthlike planet in the Alpha Centauri system misstated the size of the mirror of the ACESat telescope proposed by scientists at the NASA Ames Research Center. It is 18 inches in diameter, not 59.
match_headline: Telescope to Seek Earthlike Planet in Alpha Centauri System

text: Because of an editing error, the Sports Business column last Saturday, about whether the N.F.L.’s concussion settlement is good for all retired football players, described incorrectly, in some copies, the relationship between Alzheimer’s disease and head trauma. The disease has never been shown to be a product of head trauma.
match_headline: Is the N.F.L.’s Concussion Settlement Broken?

text: A picture caption last Saturday with an article about Ashley Bouder of New York City Ballet, who has returned to performing after having a baby in May, described Ms. Bouder incorrectly. She is shown removing her pointe shoes after a performance; she is not preparing for a performance.
match_headline: A Ballerina Goes From Baby Bump to High Jumps

text: An entry in the Spare Times for Children listings in some editions on Friday about a model Torah workshop at the Yeshiva University Museum in Manhattan misstated the day the program is to be held. It is at 1 p.m. Wednesday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Spare Times for Children Listings for Oct. 14-20

text: An obituary on Thursday about the civil rights lawyer Jack Greenberg referred incompletely to his years teaching law at Columbia University. Besides being an adjunct professor from 1970 to 1984, he was a professor from 1984 until retiring last year, including four years when he was also dean of Columbia College — not from 1993, when he stepped down as dean. The obituary also misspelled the given name of one of Mr. Greenberg’s children. She is Sarah Greenberg, not Sara. And the obituary omitted the name of a survivor. Besides his wife, children and grandchildren, Mr. Greenberg is survived by a brother, Daniel.
match_headline: Jack Greenberg, a Courthouse Pillar of the Civil Rights Movement, Dies at 91

text: An article last Sunday about efforts by the Abraaj Group to develop private health care systems in Africa rendered incorrectly the name of a medical device company that has invested in the group’s $1 billion health care fund. It is Medtronic, not Medtronics.
match_headline: An Investor’s Plan to Transplant Private Health Care in Africa

text: An article last Sunday about free markets and food banks described imprecisely the work of the late John Arnold, a director of a food bank in western Michigan. Despite his initial objections to the notion of free markets in food distribution, he pioneered practices like allowing clients to choose their own food in 1996. He did not do so as a result of food banks’ changing their distribution system in 2005.
match_headline: Sending Potatoes to Idaho? How the Free Market Can Fight Poverty

text: An article on Oct. 2 about chicken tetrazzini misstated part of the title of a play in which the actor Vincent Price appeared in the 1930s. It was “Victoria Regina,” not “Victor Regina.”
match_headline: Chicken Tetrazzini, the Casserole Even Snobs Love

text: An article on Oct. 2 about the conservative media’s reaction to Donald Trump’s presidential candidacy misstated the rank of Sean Hannity’s Fox News show among the highest-rated cable news shows. It is the third-highest, not the second. The article also misidentified the location in Florida of Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s estate-turned-club. It is Palm Beach, not West Palm Beach. (The Trump International Golf Club is in West Palm Beach.) And the article referred incorrectly to Ann Coulter’s book “¡Adios, America!” It is her 11th book, not her 10th.
match_headline: How Donald Trump Set Off a Civil War Within the Right-Wing Media

text: A listing in the What’s Selling Now feature last week misstated the location of the house in Westchester. It is in Somers, not in Heritage Hills.
match_headline: Homes That Sold for $450,000 and Under

text: A report on Oct. 2 about the wedding of Vicktery Sanchez and Justin Zimmerman misstated part of the name of the denomination in which the officiant was ordained. Pastor Will Grandberry was ordained at the Church of God in Christ, not the Church of God and Christ.
match_headline: Vicktery Sanchez, Justin Zimmerman

text: An article on Sept. 17 about the opening of an underground beer pipeline in Bruges, Belgium, overstated what is known about the history of the pipeline. It is the first legal beer pipeline, but perhaps not the first beer pipeline ever. (In 1930, 6,000 feet of hose was discovered under the streets of Yonkers, according to The Associated Press. It was believed to have been an illegal conduit for beer during Prohibition, but the historical record is inconclusive.)
match_headline: A Two-Mile Beer Pipeline Carries Belgium’s Lifeblood to Be Bottled

text: An article on Monday about chemical companies’ backing for some regulatory moves to curb climate change misidentified one company that supports a move away from HFCs as refrigerants. It is Chemours, a DuPont spinoff — not DuPont itself, though DuPont previously backed the agreement before spinning off its HFC business with Chemours. The article also misidentified, in some copies, one company that was criticized for lobbying against climate change rules. It is Exxon Mobil, not Enron.
match_headline: How the Chemical Industry Joined the Fight Against Climate Change

text: An obituary on Monday about Klaus Kertess, the curator and longtime director of the Bykert Gallery in Manhattan, referred incorrectly to the artist Billy Sullivan, who survives him. He is Mr. Kertess’s husband, not his companion.
match_headline: Klaus Kertess Dies at 76; Curator and Gallerist Gave Major Artists a Start

text: A picture caption in some editions on Thursday with an article about Tesla’s decision to install, but not yet activate, fully autonomous driving technology in its new vehicles misidentified the location of the Fontainebleau castle, in front of which a Tesla was shown. It is in France, not Monaco.
match_headline: Tesla Will Make Its Cars Fully Self-Driving, but Not Turn the System On Yet

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 23 about the resumption of aid convoys to besieged communities in Syria three days after a deadly attack on trucks loaded with supplies paraphrased incorrectly from a statement by Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei A. Ryabkov of Russia, which is fighting the opposition in Syria on behalf of the government. According to the RIA news agency, Mr. Ryabkov said the United States and other supporters of rebel groups trying to topple Syria’s president must ensure that they lay down their arms; he did not say the United States and the rebels must lay down their arms.
match_headline: Amid New Airstrikes in Syria, an Aid Convoy Arrives

text: An article on Friday about suspected email hacking by Russia’s foreign intelligence service misstated the name of one organization that first disclosed that a presidential counselor, John D. Podesta, was among those whose accounts were breached. The blog is Motherboard, not VICE Motherload.
match_headline: Private Security Group Says Russia Was Behind John Podesta’s Email Hack

text: An article in some copies on Friday about the Chicago Cubs’ 8-4 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 5 of the National League Championship Series, in which the Dodgers tried to force Cubs pitcher Jon Lester into throwing mistakes, misstated the year St. Louis Cardinals pitcher Rick Ankiel lost the ability to throw strikes in the playoffs. It was 2000, not 2001.
match_headline: Jon Lester, Unfazed by Antics, Brings Chicago Cubs to Cusp of World Series

text: An article on Thursday about the Cleveland Indians’ 3-0 victory over the Toronto Blue Jays in Game 5 of the American League Championship Series misstated, in some copies, the game in which the Blue Jays defeated the Indians, 5-1. It was Game 4, not Game 3.
match_headline: Indians Defeat Blue Jays and Reach First World Series Since 1997

text: An article on Page 174 this weekend about the artist Kerry James Marshall, who shows the writer Wyatt Mason around derelict areas of his Chicago neighborhood, gives an outdated name for the city’s Sears Tower. It was renamed the Willis Tower in 2009.
match_headline: Kerry James Marshall Is Shifting the Color of Art History

text: An article on Page 168 this weekend about Lady Gaga and her new album, “Joanne,” misstates the surname of her family. It is Germanotta, not Gemanotta. (She was born Stefani Joanne Angelina Germanotta.)
match_headline: Lady Gaga on Her New Album — and Everything That Came Before

text: An article on Page 132 this weekend about the journalist Ta-Nehisi Coates’s new foray into comic-book writing with the series “Black Panther” misspells the given name of a writer Coates has helped recruit to work on a companion series. She is Roxane Gay, not Roxanne.
match_headline: Sarah Jessica Parker and Ta-Nehisi Coates, on New Literary Paths

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the wealthy businessman Andrew E. Sabin’s contradictory stance of supporting both action to thwart climate change and the presidential aspirations of Donald J. Trump referred imprecisely to when Mr. Sabin joined the Army reserve. It was in the late 1960s, not “in the years after World War II.” The article also misidentified an environmental group that generally backs Democrats. It is the Natural Resources Defense Council Action Fund, not the N.R.D.C. itself.
ref_headline: in the years after World War II.
match_headline: Magnate’s Twin Goals: Fighting Climate Change and Electing Donald Trump

text: An article in the special Mutual Fund Quarterly section last Sunday about the strongest-performing mutual funds misstated the expense ratio for the institutional shares of the Hood River Small-Cap Growth Fund. It was 1.09 percent, a net figure that accounts for fee waivers and expense reimbursements by the fund company, not 1.49 percent, which is the gross expense ratio.
match_headline: How Three Strong-Performing Funds Pick Stocks

text: A column by Ross Douthat on the religious right last Sunday erroneously attributed a quotation to Ben Carson. Mr. Carson has argued that religion on occasion has to take a back seat to politics, but he did not say, “Sometimes you put your Christian values on pause to get the work done.”
ref_headline: Sometimes you put your Christian values on pause to get the work done.
match_headline: In Defense of the Religious Right

text: A review on Oct. 9 about “The Populist Explosion: How the Great Recession Transformed American and European Politics,” by John B. Judis, overstated George Wallace ’s performance in presidential polls when he was a third-party candidate in 1968. He drew close to the Democratic nominee, Hubert H. Humphrey, in late September (21 percent to Humphrey’s 28 percent, according to the Gallup Organization), but he did not lead Humphrey in the polls “until October” (or at any time).
ref_headline: The Populist Explosion: How the Great Recession Transformed American and European Politics,
match_headline: ‘The Populist Explosion’ Dissects the History of the Anti-Elite Worldview

text: An article on Oct. 2 about the Obama administration’s failure to take on corporate agriculture misattributed a quotation in the publication Agri-Pulse about the agriculture industry’s gearing up for “a pre-emptive strike against a long list of new regulations” expected from the Obama administration. A corn-industry spokesman — not Agri-Pulse — said: “We’ve seen so many attacks. We see Michael Pollan go on Oprah. What’s going to happen when those people . . . start to have an impact in Washington on policies and regulations?” The article also misstated the year Agri-Pulse published the quotation. It was 2010, not 2009.
ref_headline: a pre-emptive strike against a long list of new regulations
match_headline: Why Did the Obamas Fail to Take On Corporate Agriculture?

text: An article on Oct. 16 about Hillary Clinton misspelled the given name of the author of a book that she mentioned called “Amusing Ourselves to Death.” He is Neil Postman, not Neal.
match_headline: ‘I’m the Last Thing Standing Between You and the Apocalypse’

text: Because of an editing error, the Scene City column last Sunday, about the N.A.A.C.P.’s 80th anniversary benefit, referred incorrectly to Reginald Van Lee. He was one of the chairmen of the benefit, not its chairwoman.
match_headline: Autumn in New York, So Inviting

text: An article last Sunday about making (and unmaking) plans referred imprecisely to a study on scheduling leisure time. While it was conducted at Washington University in St. Louis, the study was by Gabriela Tonietto and Selin Malkoc, who were researchers there at the time; the study was not by the university’s Olin Business School.
match_headline: The art of making (and not making) plans

text: An article on Oct. 2 about Tiffany Trump transposed the given and last names of a reporter who once interviewed Ms. Trump. She is Carson Griffith, not Griffith Carson.
match_headline: The Other Trump

text: An article on Sept. 25 about Laura Wasser, the Los Angeles divorce lawyer hired by Angelina Jolie following her separation from Brad Pitt, misspelled the middle name of one of the Hollywood producer’s Brian Grazer’s former wives. She is Gigi Levangie Grazer, not Gigi Lavangie Grazer.
match_headline: Angelina Jolie Turns to Divorce Specialist Laura Wasser

text: An article on Oct. 9 about Art Deco Los Angeles quoted incorrectly from comments by the author Marlyn Musicant about the design of Union Station. She said that by utilizing bronze chandeliers, the architects wanted “a more modern influence,” not “a more Spanish influence.”
match_headline: Art Deco Los Angeles

text: An article last Sunday about a grand tour of Switzerland, using information from a guide, misidentified a village in the canton of Graubünden. It is Grevasalvas, not Maienfeld. The article also characterized incorrectly the relationship of the village to the book “Heidi.” Grevasalvas was a location for the TV show based on the book, not the inspiration for the book.
match_headline: A Grand Tour of Switzerland, Reluctant Son in Tow

text: A listing of highlights about the wedding of Cassandra Ilich and Shaun Reed, featured in the Vows column last Sunday, misstated the number of stones in her engagement ring. It has nine stones, not seven.
match_headline: The Gift of the Goat Sealed the Deal

text: A report on Oct. 9 about the wedding of Dyan Yu and Dong Joo Lee erroneously referred to Mr. Lee as “Mr. Yu” in one reference.
match_headline: Dyan Yu, Dong Joo Lee

text: An article on Friday about the online lending industry’s efforts to shape standards for itself, partly to stave off federal regulators, described the business of one online company, Fundera, incorrectly. It is a loan marketplace that connects borrowers with online lenders; it does not underwrite or make loans itself.
match_headline: Online Lenders Seek to Shape Industry Before Regulators Do

text: A subheading with an article on the Automobiles page on Friday about a father and son who leased a Porsche together misstated the pair’s geographic proximity. James Schembari, the father, lives in Connecticut and his son Sam lives in Michigan. They are not “in different time zones.” A picture caption with the article also misstated, in some editions, the two men’s reason for traveling to Porsche’s American headquarters in Atlanta. They were there to take the racing training that the company offers to new Porsche owners and lessees, not to take delivery of their car.
match_headline: A Father, a Son and the Porsche They Went In On Together

text: An article on Thursday about Silicon Valley’s unease with contributions to the Trump campaign by the billionaire investor Peter Thiel misstated the job title of Sam Altman at Y Combinator, an incubator for tech start-ups. He is president of the YC Group, not managing director of YC Research.
match_headline: How Silicon Valley Treats a Trump Backer: Peter Thiel

text: An article on Thursday about a fund-raising campaign by the Smithsonian Institution to repair a pair of Dorothy’s ruby red slippers worn by Judy Garland in “The Wizard of Oz” misstated the name of the museum being built by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in Los Angeles, where another pair of the slippers will be on display. It is the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures, not the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Museum.
match_headline: Smithsonian Seeks $300,000 to Save Dorothy’s Ruby Slippers

text: An obituary on Oct. 14 about the Italian playwright Dario Fo misstated the circumstances of his entry into the Italian army in World War II. He volunteered, he was not conscripted.
match_headline: Dario Fo, Whose Plays Won Praise, Scorn and a Nobel, Dies at 90

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about AT&T’s bid to acquire Time Warner misattributed a statement in some editions that expressed caution about the merger. The statement was from Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut — not Senator Edward J. Markey, a Democrat from Massachusetts.
match_headline: AT&T Agrees to Buy Time Warner for $85.4 Billion

text: An article on Monday about legal issues surrounding the inheritance of a brownstone, in which two longtime partners who never married lived for 55 years, attributed a quotation incorrectly. It was Tom Doyle — not his partner, Bill Cornwell — who recently said he is frightened by the ordeal. (Mr. Cornwell died two years ago.)
match_headline: A Brownstone and the Bitter Fight to Inherit It

text: An article on Monday about the Major League Soccer playoff matchups misstated, in some copies, the way the Eastern Conference semifinal opponents for the Red Bulls and New York City F.C. will be determined. The Red Bulls will play the lowest-seeded team remaining after the two first-round knockout games, and New York City F.C. will play the other winner. The Red Bulls will not play the winner of the Toronto F.C.-Philadelphia Union game, and New York City F.C. will not play the winner of the D.C. United-Montreal Impact game.
match_headline: New York’s M.L.S. Teams Finish Strong

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Satchel Paige and Larry Doby, who in 1948 with the Cleveland Indians became the first black players to be part of a major league championship, misstated the name of the Indians’ former stadium. It was Municipal Stadium, not Memorial Stadium.
match_headline: Cleveland Indians in 1948: A Story of Integration

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about the Swiss artist Pipilotti Rist, using information from the New Museum in Manhattan, where she is the subject of a retrospective that opens Wednesday, carried an incomplete credit. The picture, a video still from “Mercy Garden,” is from the Luhring Augustine gallery in addition to the artist and the Hauser & Wirth gallery.
match_headline: Pipilotti Rist, Provoking With Delight

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about rarities at the TEFAF New York art and antiques fair, at the Park Avenue Armory, misidentified the object shown. It is a 19th-century Lwalwa mask from Congo, not a figure from the Hemba tribe. The article referred incorrectly to a Ronald Phillips gallery offering and misstated its age. There are two dolphin tables made by Marsh and Tatham, not one, and they are from the 19th century, not the 18th. (The erroneous date was repeated in a picture caption.)
match_headline: 9 Rarities Appearing at a New York Art Fair’s Debut

text: A picture caption on Friday with an art review of “Wound: Mending Time and Attention,” at 41 Cooper Gallery, misstated the title of a work shown and carried an erroneous credit. The work is “Two Stage Transfer Drawing” by Taraneh Fazeli and Sick Time With Canaries — not “Sick Time With Canaries” by Ms. Faneli. The picture is from Marget Long and the Cooper Union, courtesy of the artist; the Murray Guy Gallery was erroneously included in the credit.
match_headline: What to See in New York Galleries This Week

text: An editorial on Sunday about the Senate race in Florida misstated Patrick Murphy’s tenure in the House of Representatives. He is in his second term, not his first.
match_headline: A Chance to Unseat Marco Rubio

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the writer and director Nicole Haran misstated the date of her death. It was Sunday, Oct. 16 — not this past Sunday, Oct. 23.
match_headline: Nicole Haran, 47, Who Helped Create a Theater Troupe and Web Series, Dies

text: An obituary in some copies on Sunday about David Bunnell, who helped create several magazines devoted to personal computers, misidentified the magazine of his where the computer columnist John C. Dvorak worked. It was PC World, not PC Magazine.
match_headline: David Bunnell, Whose Magazines Were Tech World Must-Reads, Dies at 69

text: An obituary on Oct. 16 about Joseph L. Birman, a physicist who worked to help dissident scientists from the Soviet Union and elsewhere, misstated the location of GTE Research Labs, where he worked until 1962. It was in Queens, not New Jersey.
match_headline: Joseph L. Birman, Physicist Who Aided Dissident Scientists, Dies at 89

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the comedian Kevin Meaney misstated the given name of the actor who starred in the 2016 version of “Uncle Buck,” the sitcom in which Mr. Meaney had starred earlier. He is Mike Epps, not Kevin.
match_headline: Kevin Meaney, Veteran Stand-Up Comedian, Dies at 60

text: An obituary on Sunday about Annemarie Huste, who was Jacqueline Kennedy’s private chef in the 1960s, misstated, in some copies, the year Mrs. Kennedy moved to New York from Washington. It was 1964, not 1966.
match_headline: Annemarie Huste, a Kennedy Chef Who Said Too Much, Dies at 73

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a decision by the Justice Department to replace its team of agents and lawyers in New York who were investigating the death of Eric Garner misidentified the location of another case it investigated involving a fatal police encounter. It occurred in north Minneapolis, not in Falcon Heights, Minn.
match_headline: Justice Dept. Shakes Up Inquiry Into Eric Garner Chokehold Case

text: A headline on Sept. 26 with an article about the killing of a Jordanian Christian writer, Nahed Hattar, after he posted a cartoon online deemed offensive to Islam overstated the case against him. He had been charged with insulting Islam, but not convicted of it. The article imprecisely translated a comment on Twitter by Abu Muhammad al-Maqdisi, one of Al Qaeda’s most influential ideologues, in response to Mr. Hattar’s apology. He said, “The apology and clarification from Hattar make him no less of an infidel” — not “is no less of an apostasy” — “than his caricature.”
ref_headline: The apology and clarification from Hattar make him no less of an infidel
match_headline: Writer Charged With Insulting Islam Is Killed as Extremism Boils Over in Jordan

text: An article on Sept. 26 about a gathering of secessionist movements in Russia, known for jailing its own separatists, misstated the surname of the self-proclaimed king of Hawaii, who did not attend but sent in a video statement calling for international solidarity against global warming. He is Edmund Keli’i Silva Jr., not Silver.
match_headline: Russia, Jailer of Local Separatists, Welcomes Foreign Secessionists

text: An article on Thursday about the shooting of Eleanor Bumpurs by the police in 1984 referred incorrectly to criminal charges in the case. The officer who shot her, Stephen Sullivan, was tried and acquitted of second-degree manslaughter and criminally negligent homicide in 1987. It is not the case that none of the officers were brought to trial.
match_headline: Fatal Police Shooting in Bronx Echoes One from 32 Years Ago

text: An article on Tuesday about concerns for CNN’s journalistic independence if AT&T buys Time Warner misidentified the buyer of The Washington Post in 2013. It was bought by Jeff Bezos, the chief executive of Amazon, not by Amazon itself.
match_headline: With AT&T-Time Warner Deal Brewing, a Focus on Preserving CNN’s Integrity

text: An article on Saturday about fan support for Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Yasiel Puig during the National League Championship Series misstated, in some copies, his postseason batting average at the time. It was .222, not .333.
match_headline: Yasiel Puig Has Cooled Down, but Dodgers Fans Don’t Seem to Care

text: An article on Tuesday about Gordon Hamilton, a climate scientist who died in Antarctica, described inaccurately an accident involving Lonnie G. Thompson, a glacier scientist. A colleague helped stop the slide of Dr. Thompson’s tent down a mountainside using an ax; Dr. Thompson did not stop the slide by himself. The article also misstated the circumstances of the death of one of Dr. Thompson’s graduate students. The student, Shawn Wight, died from a lung infection acquired after falling ill with altitude sickness on a Himalayan expedition. He did not die of altitude sickness.
match_headline: For Gordon Hamilton, a Life of Discovery and Danger

text: An article on Friday about the redevelopment of the Lambert Houses, a low-income housing complex in the Bronx, misstated the cost of the project. It is $600 million not $32 million.
match_headline: Rebirth of Bronx Housing Complex Aims to Cut Crime and Increase Homes

text: Because of an editing error, a picture credit on Friday with an article about a plane carrying Gov. Mike Pence of Indiana, the Republican vice-presidential nominee, misstated the surname of the Associated Press reporter who took the picture of Mr. Pence’s plane skidding off a runway at La Guardia Airport. He is Will Weissert, not Wessert.
match_headline: Plane With Mike Pence Aboard Skids Off La Guardia Runway

text: A picture caption on Friday with an article about the Carlyle Group’s decision to pivot away from hedge fund investments transposed the names of the Carlyle executives shown. William E. Conway Jr. is at the left, and David Rubenstein is at the right.
match_headline: Carlyle Group Turns Focus From Hedge Funds to Lending

text: Because of an editing error, an art entry in the Listings pages on Friday about an exhibition of work by Alma Thomas at the Studio Museum in Harlem misstated the closing date. It is tomorrow, not today.
match_headline: Museum & Gallery Listings for Oct. 28-Nov. 3

text: An obituary on Friday about Ewen Whitaker, an astronomer who helped select landing sites for unmanned NASA spacecraft and guided the footsteps of the Apollo 12 astronauts, referred incorrectly to the Pluto (Pipeline Under the Ocean), a gasoline pipeline project he worked on in World War II. The pipeline was built. It is not the case that the line was never laid.
match_headline: Ewen Whitaker, Who Guided NASA to the Moon, Dies at 94

text: A chart on Sunday with the continuation of an article about the unmet promises of genetically modified crops misstated the mode of action of Herculex I, a genetic trait developed by Dow AgroSciences and Pioneer. It breaks down the gut wall of insect larvae; it does not create a bacterium that does so.
match_headline: Doubts About the Promised Bounty of Genetically Modified Crops

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with an article about the concerns of voters in Philadelphia misstated the given name of a woman who volunteered at the Kitchen of Love food pantry in the Mount Airy neighborhood. She is Natalie Solomon, not Deborah. And also because of editing errors, a second picture caption misstated the surname of a founder of the food pantry and a third caption referred incorrectly to Raymond and Eric Melton, who were shown playing ball in the neighborhood. The founder of the pantry is Marlene Trice, not Price. And while the brothers live near the Kitchen of Love, they are not fed by the pantry.
match_headline: Black Voters, Aghast at Trump, Find a Place of Food and Comfort

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the bombing of a school compound in northern Syria referred incorrectly to the estimated range of 300,000 to 470,000 deaths in Syria since the conflict began in March 2011. Those are total deaths, not just civilian deaths.
match_headline: Airstrikes Hit a School in Syria, Killing Dozens

text: An article on Sept. 28 about Space X’s plans to send humans to Mars paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Elon Musk, founder of Space X, about the cost of future flights. He said only that initial prices would be fairly expensive — not that they would initially cost $500,000. (Mr. Musk said the aim would be for ticket prices to fall to less than $200,000.) The article also referred imprecisely to Mr. Musk’s relationship with PayPal when it was acquired by eBay. While he was still a board member and made money from the sale, he was not PayPal’s C.E.O. at the time and he did not sell it to eBay. This correction was delayed because editors did not follow through when the errors were pointed out.
match_headline: Elon Musk’s Plan: Get Humans to Mars, and Beyond

text: An article on Tuesday about Americans’ opinions on obesity misstated two findings of a survey. The research found that Americans believe obesity is now tied with cancer as the most serious health issue facing the nation; they do not see it as a bigger risk. And 68 percent of respondents said it was riskier — not safer — to remain obese than to have weight loss surgery.
match_headline: Americans Blame Obesity on Willpower, Despite Evidence It’s Genetic

text: An article on Oct. 22 about a hacking attack on Dyn, a company that manages part of the internet’s infrastructure, misstated the business of Verisign, a company that monitors such attacks. It is a registry of domain names, not a registrar of internet sites.
match_headline: Hackers Used New Weapons to Disrupt Major Websites Across U.S.

text: An article on Thursday about a ride on the Lake Shore Limited train from New York to Cleveland misidentified the Chicago train station that was Eva Marie Saint’s destination in “North by Northwest.” It was LaSalle Station, not Union Station.
match_headline: Can’t You Hear the 1948 Whistle Blowin’

text: Because of an editing error, the On College Football column on Tuesday about the role of The Associated Press college football poll in determining which teams play in the College Football Playoff misstated, in some copies, Notre Dame’s change in the A.P. poll after the release of the initial College Football Playoff rankings in 2014. It went from sixth to eighth, not the other way around.
match_headline: A.P. Poll About to Take a Back Seat to College Football Playoff Rankings

text: A review on Monday about the Mark Morris Dance Group, at the Gerald W. Lynch Theater of John Jay College in Manhattan, misidentified the attire worn by Dallas McMurray, one of the dancers. It was an Indian garment, a dhoti — not diapers.
match_headline: Review: Mark Morris Is a Citizen of the World at the White Light Festival

text: An article last Sunday about a woman in Brooklyn who owns many rabbits and is facing animal-cruelty charges described incorrectly the status of a civil lawsuit she filed. The suit was stayed, pending the outcome of her criminal trial, against at least six of the 12 defendants; it was not dismissed against most of the defendants.
match_headline: That’s a Lot of Rabbits

text: An article on Page 21 this weekend about obtaining a bachelor’s degree abroad misidentifies the alma mater of James Joyce. It is the University College Dublin, not Trinity College Dublin. The article also misidentifies the country that is home to the University of Liege. It is Belgium, not France. And the article misidentifies a university that ranks alongside Ivies. It is the University of Edinburgh, not Edinburgh College.
match_headline: Curly Putman, Writer of ‘The Green, Green Grass of Home,’ Dies at 85

text: Because of an editing error, a caption last Sunday with an article about institutions that are using social media to reach younger and global audiences carried an erroneous credit for a picture of “The Bedroom” by Vincent Van Gogh and for a picture of a recreation of it. Both were from The Art Institute of Chicago — not the Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam.
match_headline: Museums, the New Social Media Darlings

text: A picture caption last Sunday with a cover article about upgrades in co-ops reversed the identifications of the two men shown. Leon Geoxavier, the board president at Southridge Cooperative Section 1, in Jackson Heights, Queens, is at the left; his partner, Joshua Rotkin, is at right.
match_headline: Co-op Upgrades: Necessities or Frills?

text: An article on Oct. 23 about a house for sale in Colombia described incorrectly the town of Envigado, near Medellin. It was the hometown of the drug lord Pablo Escobar, not his birthplace.
match_headline: House Hunting ... in Colombia

text: An article last Sunday about the actor and comedian Patton Oswalt misstated part of the title of a stand-up special for which he won an Emmy. As an accompanying picture correctly noted, it is “Talking for Clapping,” not “Talking While Clapping.”
match_headline: Patton Oswalt: ‘I’ll Never Be at 100 Percent Again’

text: An article last Sunday about the theater troupe the Mad Ones misidentified the troupe member who commented on the setting for plays. It was Lila Neugebauer — not Stephanie Wright — who said, “Setting plays in other periods has been a way for us to examine questions that speak to us and inspire us, but with a distance that prevents us from taking anything for granted.”
ref_headline: Setting plays in other periods has been a way for us to examine questions that speak to us and inspire us, but with a distance that prevents us from taking anything for granted.
match_headline: For the Mad Ones, Bad Haircuts Make Good Theater

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the series “Brief Encounters” misstated the date that it began streaming. It was Oct. 31, not Nov. 1.
match_headline: Picture a Tupperware Party, but With Racier Products

text: An article last Sunday about the film “Night of the Living Dead” misstated the surname of the executive direc-tor of the nonprofit organization Film Foundation. She is Margaret Bodde, not Boddie.
match_headline: Guess What’s Back From the Grave? ‘Night of the Living Dead’

text: An article last Sunday about the Netflix series “The Crown” described a website incorrectly. The site, What’s on Netflix, is an unofficial fan site for the streaming service; it is not affiliated with Netflix.
match_headline: In ‘The Crown,’ a Young Queen, but a Young Woman, Too

text: An article on Oct. 16 about the film “Carrie,” based on the Stephen King novel, referred incorrectly to an advance manuscript of the book. Lawrence D. Cohen, who was later hired to write a screenplay after Paul Monash optioned the manuscript, first came across it while working for a producer in New York; Mr. Cohen did not pull it from a “slush pile.”
match_headline: ‘Carrie’ Is Back. Like a Bloody Hand From the Grave.

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Oct. 23 about a book by Ron Robin on the nuclear defense strategists Roberta and Albert Wohlstetter misstated part of the title. It is “The Cold World They Made,” not “The Cold War They Made.” The error was repeated in the table of contents in the same issue.
match_headline: Meet the Couple Who Helped Shape America’s Nuclear War Policy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 23 about Iceland misspelled the name of a town there. It is Keflavik, not Keflavk.
match_headline: Want to Explore Iceland? An Airline Has a Buddy Who Can Help

text: An article last Sunday about Italy misspelled the surname of a winemaker in Tuscany. He is Gabriele da Prato, not de Prato.
match_headline: The Italian Winemakers’ Cult

text: An article on Oct. 23 misstated the size of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. It is 1.1 million acres, not 1.1 million square miles. The error was repeated in a picture caption on Page A3.
match_headline: On the Water, and Into the Wild

text: An article last Sunday about the broken system of for-profit colleges described a recent action of the Education Department incorrectly. The department voted to revoke recognition of the main accreditor of for-profit colleges, the Accrediting Council for Independent Colleges and Schools, but the action is not final pending an appeal. The council is still recognized in the interim.
match_headline: A Conveyor Belt of Dropouts and Debt at For-Profit Colleges

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Bill Clinton’s efforts to secure the support of white working-class voters for Hillary Clinton misstated Mr. Clinton’s finish in the 1992 New Hampshire primary. While he achieved an unexpectedly strong showing, he placed second, not first.
match_headline: Bill Clinton Evokes Past, but From the Periphery of His Wife’s Campaign

text: An article on Thursday about the persistence of sexual harassment in politics referred incorrectly to complaints about the actions of State Senator Paul LeVota of Missouri. Only one intern — not “some” — complained to her college, and she did so in 2015, not in 2014.
match_headline: Why Sexual Harassment Persists in Politics

text: An article on Monday about campaign spending by super PACs in New York State misspelled the surname of the president of the Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union. He is Stuart Appelbaum, not Applebaum.
match_headline: ‘Super PACs’ Spend Freely as Control of New York Senate Hangs in Balance

text: An article on Thursday about the Chicago Cubs backup catcher David Ross, who played the final game of his major league career in Game 7 of the World Series, reversed, in some copies, the order in which he attended two colleges. He attended Auburn University first and then the University of Florida.
match_headline: David Ross, Oldest Player in World Series, Ends Career in Climactic Game 7

text: An obituary on Monday about the electronic music pioneer Jean-Jacques Perrey referred incorrectly to the composition “Baroque Hoedown.” Mr. Perrey wrote it with his longtime associate Gershon Kingsley; he was not the sole composer. The obituary also referred incorrectly in some editions to the composition “Flight of the Bumblebee.” Mr. Perrey adapted it for his album “Moog Indigo”; he did not write it. (It was composed by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.)
match_headline: Jean-Jacques Perrey, Electronic Music Pioneer, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Saturday about the Broadway producer Rick Steiner misidentified, in some editions, a show he produced and it misspelled the director’s surname. The show was “The Producers,” not “Jersey Boys,” and the director was Susan Stroman, not Strohman.
match_headline: Rick Steiner, Producer of Broadway Hits, Dies at 69

text: An obituary last Tuesday about the actress and singer Tammy Grimes misstated the name of the country club in Brookline, Mass., that her father managed. It is the Country Club, not the Brookline Country Club.
match_headline: Tammy Grimes, the Original ‘Unsinkable Molly Brown,’ Dies at 82

text: A picture caption on Oct. 9 with an article about “Era Mahathir,” an exhibition in Kuala Lumpur, the Malaysian capital, featuring artwork that was popular during the tenure of a former Malaysian prime minister, Mahathir Mohamad, misstated, in some copies, the patronymic of the artist whose self-portrait “Shhh!” is in the show. He is Ahmad Fuad Osman, not Osmand.
match_headline: Showing How Art Critical of Malaysian Premier Thrived During His Rule

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 9 about AT&T’s partnership with an Iranian company to provide voice and data service in Iran to AT&T’s customers with American phones referred incorrectly to a representative of AT&T who acknowledged the partnership. The representative was a spokeswoman, not a spokesman.
match_headline: Sign of Thaw With Iran: American Cellphones Ringing in Tehran

text: An article on the Automobiles page on Friday about high-end car sales in Russia misstated the origins of two makes of automobiles. The Trabant, made in East Germany, and the Tatra, made in Czechoslovakia, were products of the former Soviet Bloc, not the Soviet Union.
match_headline: In Russia, a Western Taste for High-End Auto Sales

text: Because of an editing error, the Common Sense column on Friday, about prospects for a tax code overhaul in the next administration, misidentified the political office held by Dan Coats. He is a senator from Indiana, not a representative. The error was repeated in a correction on Saturday, which also referred to Ron Wyden of Oregon as a representative, rather than a senator.
match_headline: A Rare Moment of Unity on Capitol Hill, Thanks to Trump’s Taxes

text: An article on Monday about the Montreal Impact’s 2-1 victory over the Red Bulls in the second leg of their Major League Soccer Eastern Conference semifinal misstated the given name of the midfielder who scored both Montreal goals. He is Ignacio Piatti, not Ianacio.
match_headline: Impact Top Red Bulls on Piatti’s Two Goals and Advance in M.L.S. Playoffs

text: An article on Oct. 27 about a portrait that was attributed to the Dutch painter Frans Hals but then was said by Sotheby’s to be a modern forgery erroneously included a group of experts among those who believed the portrait is by Hals. Curators from the Rijksmuseum did not join scholars who decided that he had made it.
match_headline: A Dubious Old Master Unnerves the Art World

text: An article on Tuesday about the Romanian artist Adrian Ghenie misstated the surname of the man with whom Mr. Ghenie started the Plan B gallery in Cluj, Romania. He is Mihai Pop, not Popin.
match_headline: How the Artist Adrian Ghenie Became an Auction Star

text: An article on Nov. 1 about key facts on donkeys described incorrectly a difficulty of interbreeding between horses and donkeys. It is most female donkeys that never conceive when bred to male horses, not most female horses when bred to male donkeys. (The latter pairing, as the article noted, is often successful and results in mules.)
match_headline: Of Jacks and Jennets: Facts About Donkeys

text: An article on Wednesday about the election of Donald Trump as president of the United States carried an erroneous byline in some editions. The article was by Matt Flegenheimer and Michael Barbaro — not by Patrick Healy and Jonathan Martin.
match_headline: Donald Trump Is Elected President in Stunning Repudiation of the Establishment

text: An article on Wednesday about news anchors’ reaction to the unfolding election results misspelled the given name of an MSNBC analyst. She is Nicolle Wallace, not Nicole.
match_headline: As Race Tightened, News Anchors Seemed as Stunned as Anyone

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about Kunlun Red Star, the Kontinental Hockey League team based in China, misidentified, in some copies, the Spartak Moscow player shown trying to score against Kunlun goaltender Andrei Makarov. He is Alexander Kuvayev, not Artem Voronin.
match_headline: China, Meet Hockey. Russia, Meet a Huge Untapped Market.

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the history of World Cup qualifying games between the United States and Mexico being played in Columbus, Ohio, misidentified the American player shown in the 2001 game. He is Clint Mathis, not Josh Wolff.
match_headline: U.S. Is Hosting Mexico Again? Road Trip to Columbus!

text: Because of an editing error, a Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about Emojicon, an event in San Francisco billed as a “celebration of all things emoji,” misidentified the job at Adobe held by the speaker who campaigned for more androgynous emojis. He is a typeface designer and font developer, not a software engineer.
match_headline: Secrets of the Emoji World, Now With Its Own Convention

text: An article last Thursday about election parties misstated the political position of Jacob Weisberg, the editor in chief of the Slate Group. Mr. Weisberg said that while he was “strongly anti-Trump,” he was not a Hillary Clinton supporter and had “never given money to a candidate, or campaigned for one.”
match_headline: The Worst Party of the Year? Election Night

text: An article on Oct. 11 about the town of Bojayá, Colombia, which was the scene of a devastating rebel attack in 2002 yet voted overwhelmingly for a peace deal between the government and the rebel group that the rest of the country rejected, mistranslated, in some editions, a comment by Rosa Mosquera, a resident of Bojayá who survived the attack. She said, “In order to live in peace, you have to disarm” — not “disassemble” — “your heart.” And, “But when you disarm” — not “rebuild” — “your heart, you can go on, you can give a lot of love.”
ref_headline: In order to live in peace, you have to disarm
match_headline: With Colombia’s Peace Deal in Doubt, a Battered Town Fears a Return to War

text: An article on Thursday about the billionaire investor Peter Thiel, one of the few leaders in the technology industry who backed Donald J. Trump, misidentified the politician Mr. Thiel backed in the presidential primaries in 2008 and 2012. It was Ron Paul, then a congressman from Texas — not his son Rand, who is a United States senator from Kentucky.
match_headline: Peter Thiel’s Bet on Donald Trump Pays Off

text: An article on Nov. 1 about Robert M. Bakish’s appointment as acting chief executive of Viacom misstated the year Mr. Bakish started at the company. It was 1997, not 1987.
match_headline: Viacom Names Its Second Acting C.E.O. as Tumult Continues

text: An article on Saturday about Air Time, the star bull on the Professional Bull Riders tour, misstated the way Bodacious, another famous bull, seriously injured two riders in 1995. He hit them in the face with his head, not his hoof.
match_headline: What Is Bull Riding’s Scariest Beast Afraid Of? You Name It

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about the Knicks’ 110-96 victory over the Nets misstated the number of points the Knicks outscored the Nets by during the second half. It was 19, not 21.
match_headline: ‘Embarrassed’ Knicks Roll Past the Nets in the Second Half

text: An article on Thursday about uncertainty over the fate of the new Museum of the Second World War in Gdansk, Poland, using information from the museum, misstated the amount by which the original budget grew. It was by more than about 90 million zlotys (about $22.4 million at the current exchange rate) not by more than 100 million zlotys (about $24.9 million). The article also misidentified the body that has filed a lawsuit to block the merger of the museum with another that has not been built yet. It is the Polish Ombudsman’s office, not the Polish branch of the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights.
match_headline: A Museum Becomes a Battlefield Over Poland’s History

text: A subheading on Tuesday with an image of the Nov. 7, 1888, front page of The New York Times, part of a collection of 42 front pages showing presidential coverage through the decades, misidentified the president elected that year. Benjamin Harrison won — not William Henry Harrison, his grandfather, who was elected in 1840 and died on April 4, 1841, his 32nd day in office.
An obituary on Thursday about the cinematographer Raoul Coutard misstated the title of a memoir he wrote. It is “L’Impériale de Van Su,” not “L’Imperiale Du Van.”
match_headline: Raoul Coutard, Cinematographer of the French New Wave, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Friday about the singer and songwriter Leonard Cohen misstated the name of one of his best-known compositions. Although a number of performers have recorded it as “Bird on a Wire,” the title he gave it is “Bird on the Wire.” The obituary also misidentified, in some editions, the awards show on which Tori Kelly sang Mr. Cohen’s composition “Hallelujah.” It was the 2016 Emmy Awards, not the Grammys. And in some editions the obituary erroneously included one person among Mr. Cohen’s survivors and omitted three others. The singer, songwriter and pianist Anjani Thomas had not been Mr. Cohen’s companion for some time. And in addition to his two children, he is survived by three grandchildren.
match_headline: Leonard Cohen, Epic and Enigmatic Songwriter, Is Dead at 82

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Donald J. Trump’s climate policy misspelled, in one instance and in some editions, the surname of the head of the president-elect’s transition team for the Environmental Protection Agency. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, he is Myron Ebell, not Ebel.
match_headline: Donald Trump Could Put Climate Change on Course for ‘Danger Zone’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the governor’s race in North Carolina misidentified, in some editions, the candidate that some members of the film workers’ union in Wilmington supported out of concerns for the industry. They backed the Democratic candidate for governor, Roy Cooper — not the incumbent governor, Pat McCrory, a Republican.
match_headline: Roy Cooper Holds Thin Lead Over Gov. Pat McCrory in North Carolina

text: Because of an editing error, the On Tennis column on Friday, about the battle for the No. 1 ranking between Andy Murray and Novak Djokovic, misstated, in some editions, the schedule for the ATP World Tour Finals. It opens tomorrow, Sunday, Nov. 13, and goes through Sunday, Nov. 20; it did not begin this past week.
match_headline: Andy Murray and Novak Djokovic: Old Friends in a Role Reversal

text: Because of editing errors, a jazz entry in the Listings pages on Friday about the McCoy Tyner Quartet included several errors. The group’s performances on Monday and Tuesday will be at the Blue Note, 131 West Third Street, Greenwich Village — not at Birdland, 315 West 44th Street, Clinton. The website is bluenote.net , not birdlandjazz.com , and the phone number is 212-475-8592.
match_headline: Jazz Listings for Nov. 11-17

text: An entry in the Spare Times for Children l istings in some editions on Friday about the film “Naledi: A Baby Elephant’s Tale” misstated the given name of one of the film’s directors. He is Ben Bowie, not Bob.
match_headline: Spare Times for Children Listings for Nov. 11-17

text: An entry on Page 36 in the “This and That” feature this weekend about the designer Jonathan Adler’s renovation of the Parker Palm Springs Hotel refers incorrectly to handbags by him. While Adler has designed them in the past, he no longer does so.
match_headline: A Very Jonathan Adler Hotel

text: An entry in the “This and That” feature on Page 40 this weekend about the increasing popularity of regional Japanese fare in America misstates one way in which an udon-noodle dish is served at TsuruTonTan. The noodles are served over a bed of ice, not a bed of rice.
match_headline: Regional Japanese Fare Comes to America

text: An article last Sunday about a ballot question in Massachusetts on charter schools misstated the academic affiliation for Prof. Parag Pathak, who discussed the issue. He teaches at M.I.T.’s Department of Economics, not its Sloan School of Management.
match_headline: Trump-Clinton? Charter Schools Are the Big Issue on Massachusetts’ Ballot

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about pro sports teams and players who have signed on with philanthropic causes misstated the year Bruce Edwards, Tom Watson’s former caddy, died of A.L.S. It was 2004, not 2005.
match_headline: Pro Teams and Players Sign On With Causes

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about internet memes and the presidential campaign misstated the debate that was shown. The photograph, of Hillary Clinton and Donald J. Trump, was taken at their second debate, not their third.
match_headline: Memes, Myself and I: The Internet Lets Us All Run the Campaign

text: An article last Sunday about the hip-hop group A Tribe Called Quest misstated the location of the home of the rapper Phife Dawg, who died in March before the group’s new album was completed. He lived near Oakland, Calif. — not in Oakland.
match_headline: Loss Haunts A Tribe Called Quest’s First Album in 18 Years

text: An article last Sunday about films featuring holiday office parties misstated the message scrawled on a corpse in the film “Die Hard.” It is “Now I have a machine gun. Ho ho ho,” not “Now have machine gun.”
match_headline: When the Office Holiday Party Goes Oh So Wrong, Onscreen

text: A picture caption on Oct. 30 with a review of “This Way Madness Lies: The Asylum and Beyond,” by Mike Jay, included an erroneous attribution for the engraving of Bedlam. Though it appeared in Jonathan Swift’s “A Tale of a Tub,” it was produced by Bernard Lens the Younger and John Sturt, not drawn by Swift himself.
ref_headline: This Way Madness Lies: The Asylum and Beyond,
match_headline: Six Centuries of Madness: An Asylum’s History

text: An article last Sunday about upscale Brooklyn referred incorrectly to Ebbets Field residences. It is an apartment complex, not a public housing complex.
match_headline: Adventures in Upscale Brooklyn

text: An article last Sunday about David F. Swensen, who manages Yale University’s endowment, misstated the role of a former colleague, Randy Kim, at the Conrad N. Hilton Foundation. Mr. Kim ran the investment department, not the foundation itself.
match_headline: The Money Management Gospel of Yale’s Endowment Guru

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Shari Silver and Evan Derrow misspelled the given name of the wedding officiant. She is Rabbi Mindy A. Portnoy, not Mindi.
match_headline: Shari Silver, Evan Derrow

text: An article on Monday about President-elect Donald J. Trump’s appointment of Reince Priebus to be his White House chief of staff misidentified the state where Mr. Priebus was born. He is a native of New Jersey, not of Wisconsin.
match_headline: Donald Trump Picks Reince Priebus as Chief of Staff and Stephen Bannon as Strategist

text: An article on Friday about Singles Day, an online discounting day in China, misspelled, in some editions, the name of a vendor who uses Alibaba’s sales platforms. He is Odyssey Cheng, not Chang.
match_headline: Alibaba, Amid Intense Hype, Confronts a Slowdown on Singles Day

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about how the first major art auctions after the presidential election may signal the market’s reaction to the result referred incorrectly to the sale of guaranteed works. External financiers typically receive part of the buyers’ fees; it is not the sellers who receive part of the fees. And while the profit can at times be minimal for auction houses, it is also not unusual for them to make a substantial profit on guarantees.
match_headline: The Art Market’s Reaction to Trump? Sales This Week Offer First Test

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Monday about the coming television series “Ocean Warriors,” on Animal Planet, misidentified the people the Swedish boat captain Peter Hammarstedt is shown chasing. They are icefish poachers, not whale hunters.
match_headline: Ocean Conservation Series Coming to Animal Planet

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the actor Robert Vaughn misstated when he received a doctorate from the University of Southern California. It was 1970, not in “the mid-1960s.” The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Vaughn’s tenure on the British television series “Hustle.” He was a member of the show’s cast from 2004 to 2012, not just in 2012.
match_headline: Robert Vaughn, Who Starred as Napoleon Solo in ‘Man From U.N.C.L.E.,’ Dies at 83

text: An obituary on Sunday about the digital media executive Cella Irvine misstated the name of a company acquired by the advertising agency Digitas when she was its chief administrative officer. It was Modem Media, not Modern Media.
match_headline: Cella Irvine, Digital Media Pioneer Who Led About.com, Dies at 59

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Sunday on the presidential voting process misidentified Phoenixville, Pa. It is a borough in Chester County, not a county.
match_headline: After a Fraught Election, Questions Over the Impact of a Balky Voting Process

text: An article on Monday about President-elect Donald J. Trump’s victory and House Republicans referred imprecisely to a group of Mr. Trump’s early supporters. Representative Lee Zeldin represents a district on Long Island, unlike the others mentioned, who are from the Rust Belt.
match_headline: In Twist, Trump Victory Could Defang Anti-Establishment G.O.P. Caucus

text: An article Thursday about Colson Whitehead’s winning the National Book Award for his novel “The Underground Railroad” was, in some copies, erroneously paired with a headline referring to a new discovery about Pluto. While the book has won out-of-this-world praise, word of its success has not traveled quite that far.
match_headline: Colson Whitehead Wins National Book Award for ‘The Underground Railroad’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 20 about a mutual ban on India’s and Pakistan’s film stars and TV shows, imposed after clashes in the disputed region of Kashmir, referred incorrectly to retaliatory military strikes by India and misstated the location where they occurred. They were “surgical strikes,” the army said, not airstrikes, and they took place in the Pakistani-controlled part of Kashmir, not within Pakistan itself.
match_headline: Bollywood Becomes India and Pakistan’s Latest Battleground

text: An article on Thursday about a new venture by Renaud Laplanche, former chief executive of Lending Club, referred incorrectly to disclosures about Mr. Laplanche’s investments in a fund that was purchasing Lending Club loans. He did inform one member of the board about those investments; it is not the case that no board members were informed.
match_headline: Former Lending Club Chief Is Creating a New Lending Site

text: An article on the Automobiles page on Friday about the heavy technology focus of the Los Angeles Auto Show misstated the name of the personal assistant in the Amazon Echo. It is Alexa, not Alexis. The article also gave an incorrect title for Detlev von Platen, who commented on autonomous driving technology. He is executive board member for sales and marketing at Porsche, not president and chief executive of Porsche Cars North America.
match_headline: At the Los Angeles Auto Show, an Industry Ponders Its Digital Future

text: A picture caption on Page 7 this weekend with an article about the director Christopher Bayes and his production of “The Servant of Two Masters,” at the Polonsky Shakespeare Center in Brooklyn, misidentifies the actor shown with Mr. Bayes. He is Liam Craig, not Andy Grotelueschen. The caption also reverses the identities of two actors shown in a picture with other cast members and Mr. Bayes. Mr. Grotelueschen is second from the left, and Mr. Craig is second from the right.
match_headline: Professor Pratfall: He Trains Actors in the Art of Silliness

text: An article last Sunday about Rudolph Giuliani’s support of Donald J. Trump referred incorrectly to the share of votes Mr. Trump won in the presidential election. He was supported by 47 percent of those who voted; 47 percent of the country did not vote for him.
match_headline: Rudy Giuliani, America’s Mayor, Rolls the Dice

text: An article on Oct. 14 about the perception among Yemen’s rebels that the United States has been the hidden hand behind Saudi Arabia’s devastating air war there misstated the location of the Red Sea strait of Bab el Mandeb. The strait separates Yemen from Eritrea and Djibouti, not from Somalia. While the error was promptly corrected online, an editor failed to follow through on this print correction.
match_headline: Yemen Sees U.S. Strikes as Evidence of Hidden Hand Behind Saudi Air War

text: An article on Oct. 16 about Prince Mohammed bin Salman, son of King Salman of Saudi Arabia and a potential rival with his cousin for the throne, misstated, in some editions, an achievement of another one of King Salman’s sons. The son, Sultan bin Salman, was the first Arab astronaut, not the only one.
match_headline: Rise of Saudi Prince Shatters Decades of Royal Tradition

text: An article on Oct. 19 about the execution of a Saudi prince for murder misstated the number of people Human Rights Watch said had been executed by Saudi Arabia so far this year. It is 134, not 143.
match_headline: Saudi Arabia Executes a Prince Convicted in a Fatal Shooting

text: An article on Oct. 19 about the devastation left behind in three Iraqi cities recaptured from the Islamic State — Ramadi, Tikrit and Falluja — misspelled the given name of the top United Nations aid coordinator in Iraq. She is Lise Grande, not Lisa.
match_headline: Retaking Mosul From ISIS May Pale to What Comes Next

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about India’s move to ban certain currency notes misstated an option available to Indians with the banned notes. They can deposit 250,000 rupees worth of notes, not exchange them. The article also misstated why people are lining up at A.T.M.s. They are seeking to withdraw the daily limit of 2,500 rupees, not 2,500-rupee notes (there is no such note).
match_headline: Indians Rush Frantically to Launder Their ‘Black Money’

text: An article on Saturday about the potential for conflicts of interest between President-elect Donald J. Trump and his family’s business ventures referred incorrectly to the office of the Japanese prime minister. He is the head of government, not the head of state.
match_headline: Ivanka Trump’s Presence at Meeting With Japan’s Leader Raises Questions

text: An article on Friday about how the presidential election played out in Seneca Falls, N.Y., the cradle of the national women’s rights movement, misstated, in some editions, the women who gathered there in 1848 to sign a “Declaration of Sentiments.” Elizabeth Cady Stanton was there, Susan B. Anthony was not.
match_headline: Election Themes Clash in Capra-esque Seneca Falls, Cradle of Women’s Rights

text: An article on Monday about New York City’s plan for new ferries misstated a criticism of the decision to have all boats the same size. The critics say there should be larger vessels for the trip to Rockaway, not that there should be smaller vessels for less popular routes.
match_headline: Bayou Shipyards Race Political Clock to Build New York’s Ferries

text: An obituary on Saturday about David Mancuso, who revolutionized night life in New York with weekly dance parties at his downtown loft, incorrectly attributed a statement made to Tim Lawrence, an author and professor of cultural studies at the University of East London. It was Mr. Mancuso who told Mr. Lawrence, “By the end of 1970 you couldn’t squeeze anyone else in, and it stayed like that for four and a half years, regardless” — not the D.J. David DePino. The obituary also omitted part of the name of a website that published an interview with Mr. Mancuso this year. It is Red Bull Music Academy Daily, not Red Bull Academy Daily. And an accompanying picture caption carried an erroneous credit. The photograph of Mr. Mancuso is by Pat Bates; it is not from the Tim Lawrence Collection.
ref_headline: By the end of 1970 you couldn’t squeeze anyone else in, and it stayed like that for four and a half years, regardless
match_headline: David Mancuso, Whose New York Loft Was a Hub of ’70s Night Life, Dies at 72

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the former All-Pro football player Bob Gain misstated the date of his death. It was Monday, Nov. 14 — not Monday, Nov. 21.

An article on Tuesday about investors’ exuberance over potential economic growth under the incoming administration misidentified whom Democrats broadly agree with on infrastructure spending. It is the president-elect, not the president.
match_headline: Investors Make Bullish Bet on Trump, and an Era of Tax Cuts and Spending

text: A picture caption on Oct. 23 with an article about Scotland’s enthusiastic embrace of diversity in sexuality in the space of a generation erroneously attributed a distinction to Susan and Gerrie Douglas-Scott. They were among the first gay Scots to marry under Scottish law, but not necessarily the first; several couples have claims to that distinction.
match_headline: Scotland Embraces Gay Politicians in a Profound Cultural Shift

text: An article on Oct. 16 about pressure on the police in south India to take action in the death of Aradhana Samdariya, a 13-year-old girl who went into cardiac arrest after a 68-day religious fast, misspelled, in some editions, the surname of her father. He is Laxmichand Samdariya, not Samdaria. While the error was corrected promptly online, an editor failed to follow through on this print correction.
match_headline: India Police Pressed to Act in Girl’s Death After Fast

text: An article on Oct. 23 about a new national understanding of sexual assault, apparently provoked by a recording in which Donald J. Trump brags about how his fame allows him to grope women, misidentified, using information from a Stanford historian, the century whose midpoint is regarded as the time when patriarchal attitudes toward sexual crimes began to change. Sexual assault and rape were viewed primarily as crimes against the honor of women’s husbands and fathers until the mid-19th century — not the mid-20th, according to the historian, Estelle B. Freedman.
match_headline: Trump Recording Narrows Divide on Sexual Assault

text: An article on Monday about a voting district in Milwaukee where many residents did not vote misstated the year of release for the documentary “Milwaukee 53206,” which examined problems in the same neighborhood.
