It was 2016, not 2015. The article also described incorrectly the turnout on Election Day. Nationally, about half of the eligible voters did not cast ballots, not half of registered voters.
match_headline: Many in Milwaukee Neighborhood Didn’t Vote — and Don’t Regret It

text: An article on Friday about an expansion of services offered by Airbnb referred imprecisely to the collection of local hotel taxes by Airbnb hosts. The hosts collect the taxes and turn the revenue over to Airbnb, which remits the taxes to local governments; Airbnb does not collect the taxes directly.
match_headline: Airbnb Broadens Its Business With Tours and Travel Experiences

text: An article on Tuesday about a new app to guide visitors at the American Museum of Natural History in Manhattan, which includes information about the museum’s large model of a blue whale, misstated the weight of a real blue whale. It can weigh as much as 400,000 pounds, not 85,200.
match_headline: Find the Whale and the Bathroom With the Natural History Museum App

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about A Tribe Called Quest’s new album being No. 1 on the Billboard chart misstated the given name of a member of the group. He is Jarobi White, not Jacobi.
match_headline: A Tribe Called Quest’s Comeback Album Debuts at No. 1

text: An article on Monday described a speech in Washington by Richard B. Spencer, president of the white-nationalist National Policy Institute. At the end of the speech, Mr. Spencer and audience members shouted versions of Nazi slogans, as some audience members raised their arms in the Nazi salute.
match_headline: Alt-Right Gathering Exults in Trump Election With Nazi-Era Salute

text: An article on Oct. 24 about Russia’s elastic boundary with Georgia referred imprecisely to the approximately 200 European Union monitors who are in Georgia to keep tabs on the agreement that ended the 2008 Russian-Georgian war. They are unarmed police officers, former and current military personnel and civilians; not all 200 are police officers.
match_headline: In Russia’s ‘Frozen Zone,’ a Creeping Border With Georgia

text: A news analysis article on Oct. 25 about China’s improved relationship with the Philippines, an important American ally, following a visit by the Philippine president to China referred incorrectly to an economist at Natixis Bank who discussed Chinese investments in the Philippines. The economist, Trinh Nguyen, is a woman.
match_headline: Rodrigo Duterte Gets Closer to China, and the Neighbors Notice

text: An article in some editions on Oct. 28 about an agreement to establish the world’s biggest marine reserve, in the Ross Sea in Antarctica, understated planned restrictions on commercial fishing in the reserve. It will be banned from the entire area, not just 72 percent of it.
match_headline: Coast of Antarctica Will Host World’s Largest Marine Reserve

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about a Children’s Health Fund study misspelled the surname of a doctor at a mobile clinic. He is Dr. Scott Ikeda, not Ikea.
match_headline: Many Insured Children Lack Essential Health Care, Study Finds

text: An article on Tuesday about overhauls at some big law firms that include reductions in the number of partners misstated the circumstances of some departures at Shearman & Sterling that preceded structural changes there. An antitrust specialist with Qualcomm as a client left, not three strategists whose clients also included Viacom. (Two of those strategists did not leave the firm, but went to another office.)
match_headline: Law Firms, Struggling Financially, Cull Partner Ranks

text: An article on Tuesday about President-elect Donald J. Trump’s position on education issues rendered imprecisely the name of the association run by Peter McPherson, who commented on some proposals. It is the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities, neither American nor Colleges is part of the name.
match_headline: Where Donald Trump Stands on School Choice, Student Debt and Common Core

text: An article on Nov. 15 about an auction of Impressionist and Modern art at Sotheby’s in Manhattan, using information from the auction house, erroneously attributed a distinction to the auctioneer, Helena Newman. Sotheby’s now says that Lorna Kelly, who came to Sotheby’s in the 1970s, was the first female auctioneer to lead an evening sale in New York, not Ms. Newman.
match_headline: Edvard Munch Brings $54 Million Amid ‘Thinner’ Sales at Sotheby’s

text: An article on Wednesday about a federal judge’s ruling that money invested in the Bernard Madoff fund from offshore accounts could not be made available to victims of the Madoff scheme misstated, in one instance and in some copies, when a judge made the ruling. It was Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Kochs and Other Madoff Investors Are Winners in Fight Over Profits Held Abroad

text: An article on Monday about a rally to protest anti-Semitic, pro-Trump graffiti found in a Brooklyn Heights playground misidentified one of the songs protesters sang. It was “This Land Is Your Land,” not “America the Beautiful.”
match_headline: Rally in Brooklyn Park Condemns Swastikas and ‘Go Trump’ Graffiti

text: Because of an editing error, an article this Sunday about the life and career of Robert. M. Morgenthau misstates the job that Mr. Morgenthau held when he indicted more than 100 Mafia figures. He was a United States attorney, not a district attorney.
match_headline: Robert Morgenthau on His Years as District Attorney: ‘I Don’t Look Back’

text: An article on Thursday about pitchers like Ralph Branca whose careers were overshadowed by one play misstated, in some copies, the day Branca died. It was Wednesday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Ralph Branca Wasn’t the Only One Branded by a Single Pitch

text: An article on Nov. 13 about a concert at Flushing Town Hall featuring five National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Masters misstated the age of one, the trumpeter Jimmy Owens. He is 72, not in his 80s.
match_headline: The Old (Jazz) Masters, They Keep Getting Better

text: A review on Nov. 13 about four children’s picture books referred incorrectly to the author of one, “A Small Thing . . . but Big.” The author, Tony Johnston, is a woman.
match_headline: Across the Generations: Four New Picture Books Celebrate the Power of Grandparents

text: A review last Sunday about the audiobook version of “Tales of the Peculiar,” by Ransom Riggs, misidentified the publisher. It is Listening Library, not Audible.
match_headline: What the Kids Are Listening To: New Children’s Audio

text: Because of a transcription error, an essay on Nov. 20 about the Latino vote in Florida quoted incorrectly from a comment by Helen Marrow, a sociologist at Tufts University who specializes in Latino immigration to the rural South. She said that when “racialized nativism” — not “radical” — rears its head, Latino citizens and legal residents tend to suffer its effects.
match_headline: Nepal Is Said to Detain 41 Tibetans Traveling to India

text: An article last Sunday about Charleston misidentified the capital of South Carolina. It is Columbia — not Charleston, which was the capital during much of the historical period discussed in the article. The article also misidentified the police department that an officer facing murder charges worked for. It is the police department of North Charleston, not of Charleston. The article also referred incorrectly to John Drayton, who built Drayton Hall. He was not a governor of South Carolina. (His grandson, of the same name, was once governor.)
match_headline: In Charleston, Coming to Terms With the Past

text: An article last Sunday about Martha’s Vineyard misstated part of the name of a road on the island. It is Edgartown-West Tisbury Road — not Edgartown-Airport Road.
match_headline: Martha’s Vineyard, Off-Season

text: An article on Monday about the World Chess Championship referred incorrectly, in some editions, to the television coverage in the United States of the 1972 match between Bobby Fischer and Boris Spassky. The match was covered in real time with live commentary, not broadcast live.
match_headline: At World Chess Championship, Familiar Overtones of East-West Politics

text: An article on Wednesday about the preparations for the N.H.L. expansion team in Las Vegas misstated, in some editions, one of the colors in the team’s new logo. In addition to black and gold, the logo contains steel gray, not blue.
match_headline: Vegas Golden Knights, N.H.L.’s New Team, Take Their Place on the Strip

text: An article on Thursday about Thomas Dooley, the head coach of the national men’s soccer team in the Philippines, misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a sports reporter for The Philippine Daily Inquirer. He is Cedelf Tupas, not Cedalf.
match_headline: Soccer in the Philippines Scrambles for a Toehold, With an American Leading the Way

text: An entry in the gift guide on Friday about the book “Alma Thomas” misstated the surname of one of its authors. He is Ian Berry, not Barry.
match_headline: Books and Museum Treats for Art Lovers

text: A column on Friday about decision-making misspelled the surname of a psychologist. He was Amos Tversky, not Twersky.
match_headline: Does Decision-Making Matter?

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor Ron Glass, best known for his work on the television show “Barney Miller,” misstated the number of Emmy Awards that show won for best comedy series. It was one, not two.
match_headline: Ron Glass, Who Played a Dapper Detective on ‘Barney Miller,’ Dies at 71

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor Fritz Weaver misidentified the actor who played the adversary to Mr. Weaver’s character in the 1970 Broadway drama “Child’s Play.” He was Pat Hingle, not Ken Howard. (Mr. Howard played a different character.)
match_headline: Fritz Weaver, Tony-Winning Character Actor, Dies at 90

text: An article on Monday about the way sports symbolized the strength and vulnerability of Cuban socialism under Fidel Castro misstated, in some editions, when baseball was discontinued as a sport at the Olympics. It was for the 2012 London Games, not the 2008 Games, which were in Beijing.
match_headline: Under Fidel Castro, Sport Symbolized Cuba’s Strength and Vulnerability

text: An article on Oct. 29 about a general strike in Venezuela, called by opposition parties trying to force a referendum to remove President Nicolás Maduro, misspelled the surname of a Venezuela expert at Drexel University in Philadelphia who said a referendum would give the winning side a more valid claim to represent the people’s voice. The expert is George Ciccariello-Maher, not George Ciccariello-Mahar.
match_headline: Venezuela Slowed by Strike in Campaign to Oust President Nicolás Maduro

text: An article on Sunday about the Louisiana Senate race misspelled the surname of the actor who donated money to the campaign of one candidate, Foster Campbell. He is David Skeist, not Skeits.
match_headline: For Democrats, a Last Faint Hope to Gain a Senate Seat

text: An article on Nov. 22 about falling dementia rates in the United States referred incorrectly to the number of dementia cases. Four million to five million is the number of Americans currently living with dementia, not the number of Americans who develop it each year.
match_headline: U.S. Dementia Rates Are Dropping Even as Population Ages

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about rising interest rates in recent weeks referred incorrectly to a real estate agent in Northern Virginia. The agent, Bic N. DeCaro, is a woman.
match_headline: Mortgage Rates’ Rise Catches Home Buyers — and Lenders — Off Guard

text: An article on Saturday about retirees who move to college towns erroneously included one big-box store among those a couple, Joe and Brenda Talley, travel to Tupelo, Miss., to shop at. There is no Costco there, though they sometimes go to one in Memphis.
match_headline: College Towns Can Be Attractive Later in Life

text: An article on Tuesday about technology companies’ role in developing self-driving vehicles misstated the number of operations per second that Nvidia’s Drive PX2 can compute. It is 24 trillion operations a second, not 24 million.
match_headline: Intel to Team With Delphi and Mobileye for Self-Driving Cars

text: An article on Thursday about the best games remaining in the N.F.L. season misstated the Indianapolis Colts’ history of making the playoffs. They have reached the postseason 12 of the past 14 seasons, not 13 seasons.
match_headline: The 10 Most Important N.F.L. Games (One of Them Is on Thursday)

text: An article in some editions on Wednesday about the Oakland Raiders’ success this season in the N.F.L. misidentified, in some copies, the team that was beaten by the Raiders, 35-34, during Week 1. It is the New Orleans Saints, not the Seattle Seahawks.
match_headline: In Turnaround, Raiders Close In on Winning Season, Maybe More

text: An entry in the What’s on Monday television highlights in some editions about the film “Dont Look Back” misstated the given name of the critic who reviewed the movie for The Times and was quoted in the entry. He was Donal J. Henahan, not Donald.
match_headline: What’s on TV Monday: Bob Dylan in ‘Dont Look Back’ and HBO Visits Cuba

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about France’s return of a 16th-century portrait to the descendants of a German-Jewish couple misstated the timing of the couple’s forced sale of the work. As the report correctly noted elsewhere, the couple, Hertha and Henry Bromberg, sold the painting in Paris in 1938 as they were fleeing Nazi Germany. Thus the sale was before World War II, not during it.
match_headline: France Returns 16th-Century Portrait to Descendants of Jewish Couple

text: An obituary on Thursday about the former Brooklyn Dodgers pitcher Ralph Branca misstated part of the name of an organization of which he had been president. It is the Baseball Assistance Team, not the Baseball Alumni Team.
match_headline: Ralph Branca, Who Gave Up ‘Shot Heard Round the World,’ Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Monday about the composer Pauline Oliveros misstated part of the name of the organization that presented her with the John Cage Award. It is the Foundation for Contemporary Arts, not the Foundation of Contemporary Arts.
match_headline: Pauline Oliveros, Composer Who Championed ‘Deep Listening,’ Dies at 84

text: An article on Oct. 7 about tougher laws in Pakistan against rape and the “honor killings” of women referred incorrectly to punishments for the rape of minors and the mentally and physically disabled. Laws against such acts were also toughened; it is not the case that the acts were just made punishable. A reader pointed out the error shortly after publication, but editors failed to follow through with a correction promptly.
match_headline: Pakistan Toughens Laws on Rape and ‘Honor Killings’ of Women

text: A picture caption with a column on Tuesday about President-elect Donald J. Trump’s business interests and his new job misidentified a building. The picture showed the Trump Building in Lower Manhattan, not Trump Tower.
match_headline: Dear President-Elect Trump: Here’s How to Fix Your Conflict-of-Interest Problem

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Saturday about the Islanders’ fondness for living on Long Island misstated, in some copies, the relationship of Brittany DaSilva to the Islanders’ Calvin de Haan. She is his girlfriend, not his fiancée.
match_headline: Islanders Moved to Brooklyn, but the Players and Their Dogs Stay on Long Island

text: Because of an editing error, the “ A Conversation With” column on Tuesday misstated the composition of the faculty of the Space Telescope Science Institute when C. Megan Urry got a staff position there in 1990. There were three other women, not one, and there were 52 faculty members in all, not “approximately 60 faculty members.”
match_headline: C. Megan Urry, Peering Into Universe, Spots Bias on the Ground

text: An article on Nov. 22 about Essure, a sterilization implant device from Bayer, referred incorrectly to a study the company is running to track 1,400 women implanted with the device. The company has submitted the study plan to the Food and Drug Administration and the first six-month report is due in March 2017; it is not the case that it is “already behind schedule.”
match_headline: Bayer’s Essure Contraceptive Implant, Now With a Warning

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the pianist and former Soviet chess champion Mark Taimanov referred incorrectly to a tournament in which he participated in 1953. Though the event, the Candidates tournament, which determines a challenger for the world championship of chess, was held in Zurich that year, it moved to other cities in other years. It was not always held in Zurich.
match_headline: Mark Taimanov, World-Class Chess and Piano Player, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Joe Esposito, Elvis Presley’s longtime road manager and friend, misspelled his mother’s maiden name. She was the former Antoinette Pecora, not Percora.
match_headline: Joe Esposito Dies at 78; Spent 20 Years Assisting Elvis Presley

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the photographer David Hamilton misstated the area of Paris where he lived. It is Montparnasse, not Montmartre. The obituary also misstated his marital history. He was married once, not twice. (The model Mona Kristensen used the surname Hamilton professionally when she worked with him, but they were never married.)
match_headline: David Hamilton, Photographer Known for Nude Images of Girls, Dies at 83

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about Cliff Barrows, the longtime musical director and program manager of the Rev. Billy Graham’s evangelistic crusades, misstated the year Mr. Graham’s book “Just as I Am” was published. It was 1997, not 1973.
match_headline: Cliff Barrows, Billy Graham’s Longtime Musical Director, Dies at 93

text: An obituary on Nov. 24 about the New Orleans restaurateur Edgar Chase Jr. misspelled his mother’s maiden name. She was the former Emily Tenette, not Tennette.
match_headline: Edgar Chase Jr., Purveyor of Creole Cuisine, Dies at 88

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a Transition Briefing item about Sarah Palin’s being considered by President-elect Donald J. Trump for the top job at the Department of Veterans Affairs misstated who won the Iowa caucuses. It was Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, not Mr. Trump.
match_headline: Sarah Palin for Veterans Affairs? A Wrestling Impresario for Small Business?

text: An article on Thursday about the federal government’s objection to road signs in New York State misidentified a town where the signs have had a mixed reception. It is North Hudson, not Hudson.
match_headline: ‘I Love N.Y.’ Signs Have a Lot to Say. The Government Says They’re Illegal.

text: An article on Thursday about reformulated sugar from Nestlé incorrectly described, in some issues, an attribute of the sugar. It delivers the same amount of sweetness as regular sugar; it is not sweeter. The error was repeated in a headline with a capsule summary.
match_headline: Nestlé Reformulates Sugar and Says It Will Use Less in Its Candy

text: An article on Thursday about the Sol Project, which aims to usher Latino artists into the mainstream of American theater and was conceived by Jacob G. Padrón after he attended a national meeting of the group Latina/o Theater Commons, referred incorrectly to a meeting currently being held in New York by the Commons. It is a regional gathering, not the national meeting.
match_headline: A Producer Spearheads a Collective to Help Hispanics in Theater

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the historian Bruce Mazlish omitted the name of one of his survivors. In addition to his wife, children, stepchildren and grandchildren, he is survived by a sister, Elaine Wyden. A picture with the obituary carried an incorrect credit. The most recent edition of Professor Mazlish’s book “In Search of Nixon,” the cover of which was pictured, was published by Transaction Publishers, not Penguin Random House. The obituary in some copies also misstated part of the title of another of Professor Mazlish’s books. It is “The Fourth Discontinuity: The Co-Evolution of Humans and Machines” — not “The Co-Evolution and Humans and Machines.”
match_headline: Bruce Mazlish, Who Fused Psychoanalysis and History in His Books, Dies at 93

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actress Florence Henderson misstated when she first hosted “The Tonight Show” and erroneously attributed a distinction to her. It was 1966, not 1962; and she was one of the first women to be a “Tonight Show” guest host, not the first.
match_headline: Florence Henderson, Upbeat Mom of ‘The Brady Bunch,’ Dies at 82

text: An article on Friday about President-elect Donald J. Trump’s campaign-style rally in Cincinnati misstated the size of the audience that greeted him. It numbered in the thousands, not the tens of thousands.
match_headline: Trump Kicks Off ‘Thank You’ Tour, Reveling in Crowd and Campaign Themes

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the continuation of an article about manufacturing jobs in the Midwest misstated in some editions the relationship between the women pictured. Arnita Gray and Carol Bigbee are co-workers at Carrier in Indiana; Ms. Gray is not Ms. Bigbee’s daughter.
match_headline: Trump Saved Jobs at Carrier, but More Midwest Jobs Are in Jeopardy

text: An article on Nov. 5 about the chaos of war in the government-held side of Aleppo, Syria — held out by President Bashar al-Assad as safer than the rebel-held side — misstated the surname of name of a man who died at Al Razi hospital in Aleppo while his mother wailed. He was Hazem Sharifa, not Sherif.
match_headline: ‘I Saw My Father Dying’: A View From Aleppo’s Government-Held Side

text: An article on Nov. 4 about the death of two American soldiers and more than 30 Afghans in heavy fighting in Kunduz misstated, in some editions, the month that Taliban insurgents nearly overran Kunduz for a second time. It was October, not November.
match_headline: 2 U.S. Soldiers and 30 Afghans Killed in Kunduz Battle

text: An article on Nov. 3 about fears in Hong Kong that Beijing would issue a rare interpretation of Hong Kong’s mini-constitution, the Basic Law, to effectively bar two newly elected separatist lawmakers from taking office referred incorrectly, in some editions, to four past interpretations of the Basic Law by China’s legislature. Only one of those interpretations came at the request of Hong Kong’s highest court; it is not the case that they “customarily” followed such a request. (Four days after the article was published, the Communist Party moved to bar the lawmakers.)
match_headline: Separatist Hong Kong Lawmakers Draw Fears of Intervention by China

text: An article last Sunday about New York’s disappearing diner culture misidentified the music club at 97th Street and Columbus Avenue that was replaced in the 1990s by the Central Park Cafe/Restaurant. It was Mikell’s, not Michael’s Pub. Michael’s Pub, where Woody Allen used to play clarinet, was on East 55th Street.
match_headline: More Than Coffee: New York’s Vanishing Diner Culture

text: An article on Thursday about China’s rethinking of its methods to fight counterfeit goods misstated the given name of a hunter of fake goods. He is Yu Fengxing, not Yu Fengsheng.
match_headline: Though Awash in Fakes, China Rethinks Counterfeit Hunters

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Thursday about Chris McCullough, who has bounced between the Brooklyn Nets and the Long Island Nets this season, misidentified him in some copies. He is in the center of the photo taken during a game between the Brooklyn Nets and the Los Angeles Clippers — not on the far left.
match_headline: He Works Day and Night for the Nets. And the Other Nets.

text: A picture caption with an entry in the “This and That” feature on page 66 this weekend about the pop-up events Petit h is hosting at Hermès’s Manhattan boutiques misspells the surname of a designer who works with the line. He is Christian Astuguevieille, not Astuguevielle.
match_headline: Crafting, the Hermès Way

text: An article last Sunday about the TV special “Mr. Neighbor’s House” misstated the circumstances of its appearance on Adult Swim. It was a one-time special on Friday, Dec. 2 — not a regular show on the late-night programming block.
match_headline: If He Asks You to Be His Neighbor, Don’t Do It

text: An article last Sunday about the British singer Kate Bush misstated the period in which her songs have reached the Top 10 in Britain. A 2012 remix of “Running Up That Hill” reached No. 6 on the British singles chart. It is not the case that her songs were in the Top 10 from 1978 to 2005.
match_headline: Kate Bush Is Running Up That Concert Stage for a Giant Live Album

text: A review on Nov. 20 about “They Can’t Kill Us All: Ferguson, Baltimore, and a New Era in America’s Racial Justice Movement,” by Wesley Lowery, misspelled the surname of an African-American man who was fatally shot by a police officer in Minnesota in July. He was Philando Castile, not Castille.
ref_headline: They Can’t Kill Us All: Ferguson, Baltimore, and a New Era in America’s Racial Justice Movement,
match_headline: Black Deaths Matter

text: A review of four children’s picture books on Nov. 13 referred incorrectly to the little penguin who is the main character of one of them, “Penguin Problems,” written by Jory John and illustrated by Lane Smith. In the book, he is un-named; he is not called Mortimer. (That is the name of another penguin in the book.)
match_headline: Is Life Fair? Four Picture Books Say No

text: Because of an editing error, a review of three children’s books on Nov. 13 misstated the publisher’s suggested age range for one of them, “In the Shadow of Liberty: The Hidden History of Slavery, Four Presidents, and Five Black Lives,” by Kenneth C. Davis. It is intended for readers ages 10 and up, not ages 8 to 12.
ref_headline: In the Shadow of Liberty: The Hidden History of Slavery, Four Presidents, and Five Black Lives,
match_headline: Black Lives Didn’t Matter: New Children’s Books Tell Slaves’ Real Stories

text: An article on Nov. 27 about the future of libel law in the Trump era misidentified Clara Jeffery. She is the editor in chief of Mother Jones magazine, not the co-editor.
match_headline: Billionaires vs. the Press in the Era of Trump

text: An article on Nov. 27 about Martin Scorsese referred incorrectly to his involvement with “Woodstock,” the 1970 documentary about the 1969 music festival. He was one of several editors on the film, not the sole editor. The article also misidentified the company that released the 1986 drama “The Color of Money.” It was released by Touchstone Pictures in association with Silver Screen Partners II, not Universal Pictures. The article also referred incorrectly to the title of a film. It is “The Bridge on the River Kwai,” not “Bridge Over the River Kwai.” The article also misstated the given name of a Jesuit poet. He was Gerard Manley Hopkins, not Gerald.
match_headline: The Passion of Martin Scorsese

text: A picture caption with an article on Nov. 27 about interracial marriages omitted the photographer’s credit. The picture was taken by Allison Shelley.
match_headline: For Interracial Couples, Growing Acceptance, With Some Exceptions

text: An article last Sunday about an effort to farm truffles in North America misspelled the term for the fungal relationships that assist in plant-to-plant communication, enabling truffles to grow. They are mycorrhizae, not mychorrizae.
match_headline: Has a Start-Up Found the Secret to Farming the Elusive Truffle?

text: An article last Sunday about a family trip to Hawaii misstated the location of Kona on the Big Island. It is on the island’s leeward, not windward, side.
match_headline: Looking for a Bargain Vacation? Don’t Rule Out Hawaii

text: An article last Sunday about Catskill, N.Y., gave an outdated reference to a performing arts organization. It is Lumberyard, no longer American Dance Institute.
match_headline: In the Hudson Valley, a New Mecca for Artisans

text: An article on Saturday about the Obama administration’s lifting of sanctions on Myanmar misstated the type of economic punishments that were removed. The restrictions that were lifted applied solely to United States government aid to the government of Myanmar, not to trade in jade and precious stones.
match_headline: Obama Lifts Some Sanctions Against Myanmar

text: An article on Sunday about a deadly warehouse fire in Oakland, Calif., misidentified the location in Rhode Island of a 2003 nightclub fire that killed 100 people. It was in West Warwick, not in Warwick.
match_headline: Fire at Warehouse Party in Oakland Kills at Least 9, With Dozens Missing

text: An article on Monday about a farm in Belvidere, N.J., that sells painted Christmas trees misstated, in some editions, the relationship between Jordan and Erin Yeisley, who were shopping there. Jordan is Erin’s daughter, not her son.
match_headline: At New Jersey Tree Farm, a White (and Blue and Purple) Christmas

text: Because of an editing error, a dance entry in the Listings pages on Friday about performances this week by students from the Juilliard School misidentified the location and misstated the phone number. The performances will be at the Peter Jay Sharp Theater at 155 West 65th Street in Manhattan — not at the Peter Jay Sharp Theater at 416 West 42nd Street — and the phone number is 212-769-7406. The entry also misidentified two compositions to which student dancers will be performing. A work for the freshman dancers was choreographed to a Schubert string quintet, not a quartet, and a work for the sophomore dancers was to a Chopin cello sonata, not a piano sonata.
match_headline: Dance Listings for Dec. 2-8

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Washington businessman C. Wyatt Dickerson misstated the year and the occasion of a party he and his wife, Nancy, gave for Lynda Bird Johnson, the daughter of President Lyndon B. Johnson. The party was in 1966, not 1968, and Ms. Johnson was returning to college at the University of Texas; she was not “college bound.”
match_headline: C. Wyatt Dickerson, Businessman and Man About Washington, Is Dead at 92

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actress Alice Drummond misidentified the director of the 1970 movie “Where’s Poppa?,” in which she had a small role. He is Carl Reiner, not Rob Reiner.
match_headline: Alice Drummond, Character Actress, Dies at 88

text: A picture caption on Tuesday for an article about a Sisterhood of Salaam Shalom conference misidentified one of the women shown. The woman at the left in the hijab is Erin El Idrissi, not Shabiha Sheikh. (The woman at right was correctly identified as Barbara Breitman.)
match_headline: Both Feeling Threatened, American Muslims and Jews Join Hands

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday attributed incorrectly an accusation against Gen. James N. Mattis, selected by President-elect Donald J. Trump to be defense secretary. Eric Blehm, author of “The Only Thing Worth Fighting For,” quoted a former Army Special Forces officer as saying that General Mattis was unwilling to help a group of Green Berets after they were hit by an American smart bomb in Afghanistan in 2001. Mr. Blehm did not make the accusation himself, and he is a civilian, not a past member of the Special Forces.
ref_headline: The Only Thing Worth Fighting For,
match_headline: James Mattis, Trump’s Choice for Defense, Favors Working With Allies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the continuing debate by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey over plans for a new bus terminal in Manhattan referred incorrectly to the timing of the agency’s decision to hold public hearings. It was after — not before — a steep toll increase was pushed through in 2011.
match_headline: Battle Over New Bus Terminal Threatens to Paralyze Port Authority’s Board

text: An article on Tuesday about a recent increase in hate crimes in New York City referred incorrectly to the executive director of the New York chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations. The director, Afaf Nasher, is a woman.
match_headline: Finding Hate Crimes on the Rise, Leaders Condemn Vicious Acts

text: An article on Nov. 10 about a new museum in the West Bank honoring Yasir Arafat misstated the year an assassin killed Yitzhak Rabin, the Israeli prime minister who shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize with Mr. Arafat and the Israeli foreign minister, Shimon Peres. Mr. Rabin was killed in 1995, not 1994.
match_headline: Museum Explores Arafat’s Legacy but Leaves Unanswered Questions

text: An article on Thursday about the surge in the dollar and its effects on emerging markets misstated a goal of quantitative easing. It is to combat deflation, not inflation.
match_headline: Surge in Dollar Provokes Jitters in Emerging Markets Around World

text: An obituary on Monday about Milt Moss, a comic actor who starred in a memorable Alka-Seltzer commercial, misstated the connection of Bob Pasqualina to that commercial. He was the art director, not the director. (George Gomes was the director.)
match_headline: Milt Moss, Actor in Classic Alka-Seltzer Ad, Is Dead at 93

text: An article on Tuesday reported on plans by Japan’s prime minister, Shinzo Abe, to visit Pearl Harbor. Using information from the Japanese government, the article and the headline stated that it would be the first such visit by a Japanese prime minister. However, according to accounts in 1951 by The Associated Press and by a Japanese newspaper, Prime Minister Shigeru Yoshida visited the site in September of that year, after signing a treaty in San Francisco to normalize relations. A follow-up article appears on Page A3.
match_headline: Shinzo Abe to Become First Japanese Leader to Visit Pearl Harbor

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a fake news article that led to a shooting at a pizza restaurant in Washington, D.C., misspelled, in some copies, the given name of the Florida lawyer who complained about the media. He is Jeffrey Marty, not Jeffery.
match_headline: In Washington Pizzeria Attack, Fake News Brought Real Guns

text: An article on Friday about the European Central Bank’s bond-buying program misstated the actions taken by investors in 2013 after the chairman of the Federal Reserve suggested that the American central bank would begin reducing asset purchases. Investors sold Treasury bonds; they did not buy them.
match_headline: E.C.B. Extends Bond-Buying Program to Protect Eurozone Economy

text: An article in some editions on Thursday about Connecticut’s 72-61 victory over Notre Dame in women’s basketball misstated the last time Notre Dame beat Connecticut in their rivalry. It was in the 2013 Big East tournament, not in the 2011 national semifinals.
match_headline: UConn Brushes Aside Notre Dame for 83rd Straight Victory

text: An article on Wednesday about the Polish Supreme Court’s rejection of a request by the government to extradite Roman Polanski to the United States referred incorrectly to a film project of Mr. Polanski’s about the Dreyfus Affair. The film is not yet in production, thus Mr. Polanski is not currently directing it. And the title is “An Officer and a Spy,” not “The Dreyfus Affair.”
match_headline: Roman Polanski Extradition Request Rejected by Poland’s Supreme Court

text: An article last Sunday about NBC’s live production of “Hairspray” misidentified an earlier live production by the network. It was “The Wiz,” not “The Wizard of Oz.”
match_headline: Back to Baltimore 1962, in ‘Hairspray Live!’

text: An article last Sunday about the Blue Man Group misstated the number of shows Joe Striedl, a program manager for a Baltimore aerospace company, said he had been to in 13 years. It is 20 to 30, not 2,000.
match_headline: How Blue Turned to Green: Blue Man Group at 25 Years

text: An article last Sunday about the portrayal of Muslim characters on television referred imprecisely to Howard Gordon’s role on the Fox show “24.” While he was an executive producer and eventually served as a showrunner, he was not “a creator” of the show. (The producers Joel Surnow and Robert Cochran are considered the original creators.)
match_headline: Can Television Be Fair to Muslims?

text: An article last Sunday about female composers throughout history misstated the reach of Hildegard of Bingen’s music. Around 1175, when several monks at a Cistercian abbey in Belgium wrote to her asking about theological matters, she responded by sending her music. It is not the case that none of her music “was ever heard outside her convent in her lifetime.”
ref_headline: was ever heard outside her convent in her lifetime.
match_headline: A History of Classical Music (The Women-Only Version)

text: Because of an editing error, an entry in the Paperback Row column on Nov. 20 referred incorrectly to “Imperium: A Fiction of the South Seas.” As indicated in the bibliographical note with the entry, the novel was written by Christian Kracht and translated by Daniel Bowles; it is not “Bowles’s novel.”
ref_headline: Imperium: A Fiction of the South Seas.
match_headline: Paperback Row

text: A review on Nov. 20 about “The Kid,” a novel by Ron Hansen, referred incorrectly to the origins of the historical Billy the Kid. There is no record of when and where he was born or who his biological father was. The idea that he was born William Henry McCarty in New York City in 1859 to a father who died at Chickamauga, reflecting various strands of conjecture, was adopted for the purposes of Hansen’s fiction. The review also referred incorrectly to the relationship between the historical Billy the Kid and Pat Garrett. They were acquaintances, not friends.
match_headline: Billy the Kid: The Novel

text: An article last Sunday about some financing by global lenders for projects that contribute to climate change misstated the number of countries involved in the Paris accord on planet-warming carbon emissions. It is 195, not 95.
match_headline: How Big Banks Are Putting Rain Forests in Peril

text: An article last Sunday about the author David Foster Wallace’s roots in Illinois misstated the legal age for drinking beer in Illinois during his adolescence. It was 19, not 18, and that legal drinking age lasted for seven years, not six.
match_headline: David Foster Wallace’s Peaceful Prairie

text: An article last Sunday about fearful flying rendered incorrectly the name of an airline in Europe. It is Ryanair, not Ryan Air. The article also referred incorrectly to an international airport serving London. It is London Stansted Airport, not Standsted.
match_headline: With an Arsenal of Apps, a Fearful Flier Faces the Skies

text: An article last Sunday about new ski lodging and programs misstated the number of resorts that a multiresort ski pass added for the 2016-2017 winter season. The M.A.X. Pass this season added an additional 17 resorts, not 10.
match_headline: 26 Ways That Skiing Gets Better This Season

text: An article on Friday about two toddlers who were burned to death by radiator steam in city-financed homeless housing in the South Bronx referred incorrectly to New York City’s efforts to shelter some homeless residents. Some of the people have been placed in hotel rooms paid for by the city instead of being placed in cluster apartments; the city has not moved people from cluster apartments to hotels.
match_headline: Sisters’ Deaths Reveal Strains in City’s Efforts to Tackle Homelessness

text: An entry in the Metropolitan Diary last Monday about letters the writer sent from an aircraft carrier off Korea in 1953 misstated the number of time zones in the world. It is 24, not 27.
match_headline: In a Box of More Than 300 Letters, a Godsend for a Broken Heart

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with the Mediator column, about rare examples of tough questions on TV news, misstated, in some copies, the given name of a CNN anchor. As the article correctly noted, he is Jake Tapper, not Jack. The column also misstated, in some copies, the month Mr. Tapper conducted his last interview with Hillary Clinton. It was in early June, not in May.
match_headline: In Trump Era, Uncompromising TV News Should Be the Norm, Not the Exception

text: An article on Monday about efforts to build safer batteries misidentified the work of Cyclotron Road. It is a project that supports energy innovators; it does not provide funding for start-ups.
match_headline: Designing a Safer Battery for Smartphones (That Won’t Catch Fire)

text: An article on Nov. 14 about an earthquake in New Zealand measuring 7.8 magnitude misidentified the tectonic plate that includes North Island and the northern part of South Island, both in New Zealand. They are on the Australian plate, not the Pacific one. The article also reversed the directions of the Australian and Pacific plates. The Australian is moving north and the Pacific, west.
match_headline: New Zealand Struck by Powerful Earthquake

text: An article on Tuesday about the proportion of American adults who have taken a psychiatric drug misstated the number of adults involved in a 2013 prescription drug survey done by the government. It was 37,421, not 242 million.
match_headline: One in 6 American Adults Say They Have Taken Psychiatric Drugs, Report Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the costs of delays in the completion of the Dakota Access Pipeline misidentified the nation’s largest pipeline operator. It is Kinder Morgan, not Energy Transfer Partners.
match_headline: North Dakota Could Be Biggest Loser in Ruling Against Oil Pipeline

text: An article on Friday about the Rule 5 draft in Major League Baseball contained an outdated figure for the minimum major league salary. It will be $535,000 in 2017, not $500,000. The article also misstated, in some copies, the year in which George Bell, a Rule 5 selection, was named the American League most valuable player. It was 1987, not 1985.
match_headline: Baseball Executives’ Idea of Gambling: The Rule 5 Draft

text: An article on Tuesday about Chicago Blackhawks forward Marian Hossa misstated, in some editions, his placement among the N.H.L.’s goal leaders at the time. With 15 goals, he was in a tie for fourth place, not fifth place.
match_headline: Blackhawks’ Marian Hossa, an Elder Statesman, Adapts to Run With a Younger Crowd

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the Olympic judo champion Kayla Harrison and her move to mixed martial arts misspelled, in some copies, the name of the city that hosted the 2016 Olympic Games. It is Rio de Janeiro, not Rio de Janiero.
match_headline: Entering Cage, Gold Medalist Kayla Harrison Helps a Show Become a Sport

text: An article on Friday about Montreal Canadiens forward Alexander Radulov misstated, in some copies, the number of days between the Canadiens’ signing of Radulov on July 1 and the trade in which Montreal sent P.K. Subban to the Nashville Predators for Shea Weber. The trade was two days before Radulov’s signing, not one.
match_headline: Alexander Radulov, Once a Disrupter, Grows Into a Leader for the Canadiens

text: An article on Tuesday about eight affordable theater shows with holiday themes misstated the website for “The Most Miserable Christmas Tree” at the Fort Hamilton Army Base Theater in Brooklyn. It is mostmiserablemusical.com .
match_headline: 8 Holiday Shows for Various Tastes

text: An article last Wednesday about new baking cookbooks misstated the price of “Golden,” by Itamar Srulovich and Sarit Packer. It is $30, not $39.
match_headline: The Year’s Best Baking Cookbooks: Radical Ideas, Classic Treats

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 16 about an Egyptian court’s annulment of the death sentence imposed on Mohamed Morsi, Egypt’s first democratically elected president, referred incorrectly to the actions of Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Mr. Morsi’s successor, in 2013. Mr. Sisi, who was then the commander of Egypt’s armed forces, took over as leader of the country after the military seized power amid a wave of popular anger at Mr. Morsi; Mr. Sisi did not lead an “uprising” that deposed Mr. Morsi.
match_headline: Court in Egypt Overturns Mohamed Morsi’s Death Sentence

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 15 about the renewal of a call by Israel’s right-wing politicians, in the wake of Donald J. Trump’s election victory, to abandon the two-state solution to the Palestinian conflict misstated, in some editions, the length of the delay the Israeli government requested to demolish an illegal Jewish settlement outpost in the West Bank. It was seven months, not six.
match_headline: Israel’s Right, Cheering Donald Trump’s Win, Renews Calls to Abandon 2-State Solution

text: Because of an editing error, the Books of The Times review on Wednesday about “Table Manners: How to Behave in the Modern World and Why Bother,” by Jeremiah Tower, misidentified the author of another book about etiquette, “Learning How to Behave.” He was Arthur M. Schlesinger Sr., not Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr.
ref_headline: Table Manners: How to Behave in the Modern World and Why Bother,
match_headline: Review: ‘Table Manners,’ Chef Jeremiah Tower’s Guide for All Dining Challenges

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about the fake snow used in “George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker” and “The Hard Nut” by Mark Morris misidentified the dancer shown between Ashley Hod and Lydia Wellington in a 2013 New York City Ballet performance of “The Nutcracker.” She is Mimi Staker, not Unity Phelan.
match_headline: It’s a Blizzard Onstage. Here’s All the Dirt.

text: Because of an editing error, bibliographic information on Dec. 6 with the Books of The Times review, about “The Revenge of Analog: Real Things and Why They Matter” by David Sax, rendered incorrectly the name of the publisher. It is PublicAffairs, not Public Affairs.
ref_headline: The Revenge of Analog: Real Things and Why They Matter
match_headline: ‘The Revenge of Analog’: See It. Feel It. Touch It. (Don’t Click)

text: An article on Nov. 16 about a leaked memo that said Britain was unsure of how to proceed on a plan to leave the European Union, and might need 30,000 more civil servants to deal with the task, referred imprecisely to the role of David Archer, the owner of an executive search firm, in supplying candidates for Civil Service jobs. Through his firm, he is recruiting lawyers and trade negotiators to suggest to the government; he is not working directly for the government. The article also omitted part of a comment by Robert Bourns, president of the Law Society of England and Wales. He said the number of lawyers capable of drafting legislation had fallen, not “the number of capable lawyers” over all.
match_headline: Leaked ‘Brexit’ Memo Says U.K. Is Unsure How to Proceed

text: Because of an editing error, a Congressional Memo article on Thursday about the dilemma faced by Republicans in deciding whether to support Rex W. Tillerson, Donald J. Trump’s selection for secretary of state, because of Mr. Tillerson’s connections to Russia misidentified, in some editions, the state that Senator Lindsey Graham represents. It is South Carolina, not Kentucky.
match_headline: For Republican Russia Hawks, a Dilemma Named Rex Tillerson

text: An article on Thursday about the conviction of Bernhard Laufer of Queens for hate crimes misstated one of the charges. It was second-degree attempted murder, not second-degree murder.
match_headline: Man Gets 20-Year Sentence for Hate Crimes at a Queens Mosque

text: An article on Thursday about a task force’s efforts to urge corporations to disclose climate risks voluntarily misstated the role of Myron Ebell. He is leading the president-elect’s transition team for the Environmental Protection Agency; he was not nominated to lead the agency itself. (Scott Pruitt, the attorney general in Oklahoma, is President-elect Donald J. Trump’s choice to head the agency.)
match_headline: Tell Investors of Climate Risks, Energy Sector Is Urged

text: An article on Dec. 7 about an MGM casino development opening at National Harbor near Washington misidentified the type of development that Disney had intended to build there before it changed its mind. It was to have been a hotel, not a theme park.
match_headline: From Sand to Shimmer: A Casino Resort Rises in Maryland

text: An article on Thursday about an increase in start-ups run by veterans in San Diego misstated part of the name of a federal agency. It is the Small Business Administration (not Association).
match_headline: Veterans Help Make San Diego a Hub for Start-Ups

text: An entry in the What’s on Thursday television highlights in some editions about the live streaming of a performance of Handel’s “Messiah” at Trinity Church in Manhattan misidentified the site of the performance on Sunday at 3 p.m. It is also at Trinity Church, at Broadway and Wall Street — not at Alice Tully Hall. (The performance there is on Monday at 7:30 p.m.)
match_headline: What’s on TV Thursday: ‘Nashville’ on CMT, and Jingle Ball 2016

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary by The Associated Press on Thursday about the football player James Elrod misidentified the location of the high school he attended. He went to school in Tulsa, Okla., not Memphis.
match_headline: Bereaved Texas Town Finds Comfort in a State High School Title Game

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about the failure, with few exceptions, of pictures and videos of suffering in the Syrian war to provoke much action overstated the death toll in Aleppo, the commercial capital of Syria, which fell to the government this week. While precise numbers are unavailable, tens of thousands have been killed in Aleppo — not “half a million,” which is the estimated death toll for all of Syria since the war began.
match_headline: Aleppo Close to Falling Under Complete Control of Syrian Government

text: A picture caption on Nov. 24 with the continuation of an article about the rising civilian death toll in Mosul, Iraq, six weeks after the Iraqi Army began a campaign to take the city back from the Islamic State referred incorrectly in some editions to the child whom Mustafa Muhammad was mourning in a field hospital. The child, Amira Omar, was his niece, not his nephew.
match_headline: Iraq Told Civilians to Stay in Mosul. Now They’re Paying With Their Lives.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 17 about an announcement by Mexico’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, following Donald J. Trump’s election, that it would provide more protection for Mexican immigrants in the United States quoted incorrectly in some editions from comments by Claudia Ruiz Massieu, the foreign minister. She said, “We want to inform you about possible migratory actions”; she did not say that the actions “could take effect starting in February.”
ref_headline: We want to inform you about possible migratory actions
match_headline: ‘Stay Calm,’ Mexican Officials Tell Fearful Immigrants in U.S.

text: An article on Wednesday about the signing of an abortion law in Ohio, using information from the governor’s office, referred incorrectly to the state’s current abortion law. Ohio currently bars abortion after 20 weeks unless doctors can prove the baby is not viable outside the womb — not after 24 weeks.
match_headline: John Kasich Signs One Abortion Bill in Ohio but Vetoes a More Restrictive Measure

text: An article on Friday about the recall of blades in more than eight million Cuisinart food processors misstated the number of daughters Karen Wolfe Haram has. Ms. Wolfe Haram, a retired food editor, has two daughters, not three.
match_headline: Cuisinart Recall ‘Just Screwed Up the Holidays for a Lot of People’

text: A review on Dec. 4 about “JFK and the Masculine Mystique: Sex and Power on the New Frontier,” by Steven Watts, misspelled the surname of an official who worked in the Defense Department during the Kennedy administration and who, like Kennedy and other figures of the era, has been associated with “manly panache.” He was Edward Lansdale, not Lonsdale.
ref_headline: JFK and the Masculine Mystique: Sex and Power on the New Frontier,
match_headline: Two New Books Shed Light on the Kennedy Mystique

text: An article last Sunday about European residents’ fighting back against Wall Street firms that have snapped up distressed housing debt referred imprecisely to notices that were given to some tenants. While the notices told them their leases were being terminated and that they would have to leave the property, they were not given eviction notices. The error was repeated in two accompanying picture captions. The article also referred incorrectly to a loan offered to one resident to help her buy her place. The County Council, not the developer, made the offer.
match_headline: Wall Street Is Europe’s Landlord. And Tenants Are Fighting Back.

text: An article last Sunday about destination bookstores described incorrectly the ownership of Munro’s Books, in Victoria, British Columbia. Jim Munro was the owner until he turned it over to a group of employees, in 2014; his first wife, the author Alice Munro, was never an owner.
match_headline: Temples for the Literary Pilgrim

text: An article last Sunday about several authors’ favorite bookstores referred incorrectly to items for sale in an Amsterdam bookstore. The Boekhandel Van Rossum does in fact sell calendars. An accompanying picture caption repeated the error. 

Because of an editing error, a listing last Sunday of Times critics’ favorite films of 2016 misstated the title of a film that Stephen Holden listed as a runner-up for his best movies of the year. It is “13th,” not “Thirteen.”
match_headline: Best Movies of 2016

text: A listing last Sunday of critics’ most memorable art shows of the year described imprecisely the first American exhibition of the British painter Denzil Forrester. His show at the gallery White Columns has improvisational depictions of people at reggae clubs, not jazz clubs.
match_headline: The Best Art of 2016

text: A listing last Sunday of Times critics’ top albums of 2016 misstated the name of the performer previously known as Antony Hegarty. She is now Anohni, not Anonhi.ds
match_headline: The Best Albums of 2016

text: An article on Tuesday about pardons issued by President Obama erroneously attributed a distinction to his use of clemency during his two terms. His decision to pardon or commute the sentences of a total of 1,324 people is one of the largest uses of clemency by a president — not “by far the largest.” (Several presidents exceeded that number when both pardons and commutations were counted.) The article also referred incorrectly to the timing of presidential pardons and commutations. Clemency has often been granted throughout presidential terms, not solely at the end of those terms.
match_headline: Obama’s 78 Pardons and 153 Commutations Extend Record of Mercy

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the restoration of the 15th-century Ghent Altarpiece misidentified the photographer of the restored exterior panels, depicting the Annunciation. He is Dominique Provost, not Hugo Maertens.
match_headline: A Master Work, the Ghent Altarpiece, Reawakens Stroke by Stroke

text: A review and an accompanying 360 video last Wednesday about Pete Wells’s favorite new restaurants of 2016 misspelled the name of the seventh restaurant on his list. It is Hao Noodle and Tea by Madam (not Madame) Zhu’s Kitchen. The review also misidentified the restaurant’s neighborhood. It is Greenwich Village, not the West Village.
match_headline: Top New York Restaurants of 2016

text: An article on Nov. 26 about a diaspora of poorer Venezuelans fleeing poverty and hunger omitted the names of two of the three Caribbean islands that a fleet of the Dutch Caribbean Coast Guard patrols for refugees. Besides Curaçao, the fleet also patrols Aruba and Bonaire. In addition, the article paraphrased incorrectly from comments by Rob Jurriansen, a coast guard officer who heads the fleet. Mr. Jurriansen said his fleet had intercepted just 5 percent to 10 percent of the illegal immigrants — not boats — coming to those three islands from all countries, not only Venezuela.
match_headline: Hungry Venezuelans Flee in Boats to Escape Economic Collapse

text: An article on Nov. 21 about a decision by Angela Merkel, the German chancellor, to seek a fourth term referred incorrectly to the population of Germany. It has the largest population in the European Union, not in all of Europe. (Russia’s population is larger.)
match_headline: Angela Merkel to Seek 4th Term as Germany’s Leader

text: An article on Sunday about efforts to tamp down the raucous party atmosphere on the streets of Miami Beach misstated the surname of the executive vice president of Brio Investment Group, which oversees the Cleveland Hotel. He is Mike Palma, not Palmer.
match_headline: Miami Beach Tries to Tame Its Most Raucous Street (but the Fishbowl Drinks Can Stay)

text: An article on Tuesday about the cost and effectiveness of widening the 405 freeway to ease traffic congestion in Los Angeles misstated part of the name of the institute of which Brian D. Taylor is director. It is the U.C.L.A. Institute of Transportation Studies (not of Traffic Studies).
match_headline: Los Angeles Drivers on the 405 Ask: Was $1.6 Billion Worth It?

text: An article on Wednesday about the process the actor Alec Baldwin goes through to portray President-elect Donald J. Trump on “Saturday Night Live” misidentified which of Mr. Baldwin’s brothers he feuds with about politics on Twitter. He is Stephen Baldwin, not Billy.
match_headline: A Tangerine Wig and a Tightrope Walk: Alec Baldwin as Donald J. Trump

text: An entry in the What’s on Wednesday television highlights in some editions about “Joe’s Pub Presents: A Holiday Special,” on IFC, misstated the surname of a performer. She is Bridget Everett, not Evans.
ref_headline: Joe’s Pub Presents: A Holiday Special,
match_headline: What’s on TV Wednesday: ‘Surprise! Instant Xmas Carol’ and Lin-Manuel Miranda

text: An article last Thursday about apps for planning dinner parties misspelled the surname of the executive director of OneTable, an organization that encourages millennials to host Sabbath dinners. She is Aliza Kline, not Klein.
match_headline: How to Have a Dinner Party: Friends Not Required

text: An article on Nov. 25 about an F.B.I. program that has identified and killed about a dozen members of an Islamic State cell that exhorts online followers to carry out attacks in the West misstated, in some editions, the age of Munir Abdulkader, an Ohio college student who was recruited but arrested before he could strike. He is 22, not 21.
match_headline: One by One, ISIS Social Media Experts Are Killed as Result of F.B.I. Program

text: An article on Wednesday about the issue of ride-hailing apps in upstate New York misstated, in some editions, part of the name of the organization run by John Tomassi. He is the president of the Upstate Transportation Association, not the Upstate Transportation Coalition.
match_headline: Ride-Hailing Gains Prominence for Any Special Session in Albany

text: An article on Thursday about efforts by video game makers and publishers to increase diversity in esports misidentified the city in California where the TwitchCon convention took place this year. It was in San Diego, not in San Francisco.
match_headline: Esports Sees Profit in Attracting Female Gamers

text: An article on Friday about an experimental Ebola vaccine that has been shown to be effective against the lethal virus rendered the name of the vaccine incorrectly. It is rVSV-ZEBOV, not rVSV-EBOV. The article also misstated the number of people killed by the virus outside Africa during the epidemic in 2014. One person died, not a “handful.”
match_headline: New Ebola Vaccine Gives 100 Percent Protection

text: An article on Dec. 13 about investments by the venture capital firm Union Square Ventures in a hedge fund powered by ideas from anonymous contributors misstated the role of Fred Wilson. He co-founded Union Square Ventures, but does not lead it. (Albert Wenger and Andy Weissman are its managing partners.)
match_headline: Hedge Fund Driven by Anonymous Ideas Gets New Investments

text: An article on Monday about a dispute over a 1914 baseball card of Guy Zinn, a Jewish major leaguer, quoted incorrectly from comments by John Thorn, the official historian of Major League Baseball. He said the interest surrounding the card illustrates “the acquisitiveness about the fan” — not the inquisitiveness.
match_headline: A Jewish Player’s 1914 Baseball Card Triggers a $125,000 Dispute

text: An obituary on Friday about Sidney D. Drell, a physicist who was a top adviser to the United States government on military technology and arms control, omitted two of his survivors. Besides two daughters and three grandchildren, he is also survived by his wife, the former Harriet Stainback, and his son, Daniel. The obituary also misstated his position at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center. He was deputy director, not the director.
match_headline: Sidney Drell, Who Advised Presidents on Nuclear Weapons, Dies at 90

text: An article last Sunday about the director Pablo Larraín misstated the surname of the screenwriter for the film “Jackie.” He is Noah Oppenheim, not Oppenheimer.
match_headline: Pablo Larraín on His Latest Films, ‘Jackie’ and ‘Neruda’

text: A subheading on Dec. 18 with an article about lodging and tours in Africa misidentified the country to which Thanda Island belongs. It is Tanzania, not South Africa.
match_headline: From Botswana to Zambia, New Lodges, Resorts and Tours

text: A review on Dec. 4 about “Al Capone: His Life, Legacy, and Legend,” by Deirdre Bair, misidentified the violent political campaign in Chicago that became known as the “pineapple primary.” It was the 1928 primary for a range of offices, not the 1927 mayoral campaign of William (Big Bill) Thompson.
ref_headline: Al Capone: His Life, Legacy, and Legend,
match_headline: Why the Legend of Al Capone Still Fascinates

text: A review on Dec. 11 about “Nonstop Metropolis: A New York City Atlas,” edited by Rebecca Solnit and Joshua Jelly-Schapiro, misidentified the designer who oversaw the creation of the atlas’s maps and brought them to completion. She is Lia Tjandra — not the book’s principal artist, Alison Pebworth, who contributed the cover logo and title page artwork.
ref_headline: Nonstop Metropolis: A New York City Atlas,
match_headline: What Makes a City: A Highly Subjective, Idiosyncratic New York Atlas

text: A map on Nov. 27 with an article about the struggles of the Houthis, a rebel group that has seized the Yemeni capital, Sana, and many other parts of the country, misidentified the country east of Iran in some editions. It is Pakistan, not Afghanistan. In addition, a reporting credit with the article misstated, in some editions, the given name of a contributor. He is Shuaib Almosawa, not Shuab.
match_headline: Plight of Houthi Rebels Is Clear in Visit to Yemen’s Capital

text: An article on Thursday about businesses that sell Hanukkah-themed products misstated, in some copies, the given name of the wife of Michael Patchen, a creator of the Menorah Tree. She is Jenny, not Mary.
match_headline: From Yamaclaus to Menorah Bong: Hanukkah Goods That Can Hold a Candle

text: A picture caption on Dec. 2 with an article about Tiger Woods’s return to golf with his appearance in the Hero World Challenge misstated the shot Woods was shown watching in the first round. It was his third shot at the 13th hole, not his second shot at the 18th hole.
match_headline: Tiger Woods Shows Some Magic, Then Shows Some Rust

text: An article on Dec. 18 about ice swimming competitions described incorrectly two people in Ireland, who in February, swimming in 40 degrees, lasted 2.05 miles in 57 minutes 45 seconds and 2.06 miles in 54:49. The swimmers were a man and a woman, not two men.
match_headline: For Swimmers With Ice Water in Their Veins, an Event to Match

text: An obituary on Friday about the playwright and screenwriter David Berry misstated how he entered the Army. He enlisted; he was not drafted.
match_headline: David Berry, Playwright and Screenwriter, Dies at 73

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about sign-ups for insurance under the Affordable Care Act referred incorrectly to a letter obtained by Politico and addressed to Republicans in Congress. Gov. Susana Martinez of New Mexico did not authorize or send the letter, which was drafted for her consideration by the staff of the state’s health insurance exchange, an independent public corporation.
match_headline: Health Exchange Enrollment Jumps, Even as G.O.P. Pledges Repeal

text: An article on Nov. 28 about the defiance of South Korea’s president, Park Geun-hye, in the face of threats of impeachment and prosecution misstated, in some editions, the time frame for nuclear tests conducted by North Korea, against which Ms. Park has taken a hard line. It has conducted five tests over the last decade, not just this year. (The South Korean Parliament voted to impeach her Dec. 9.)
match_headline: South Korean Leader Digs In Against Rising Calls for Impeachment

text: An article on Nov. 29 about an outpouring of Arab-Jewish cooperation amid suspicions of arson after wildfires raged across Israel misstated the surname of the chef of Rama’s Kitchen, a restaurant in the Israeli village of Nataf that was burned by one of the wildfires. He is Tomer Niv, not Ziv.
match_headline: Amid Flames and Suspicions in Israel, Acts of Jewish-Arab Cooperation

text: An article on Nov. 27 about the appointment of Lt. Gen. Qamar Javed Bajwa as the new commander of Pakistan’s Army misstated, in some editions, the surname of another senior general who was passed over for the promotion. He is Lt. Gen. Ishfaq Nadeem Ahmad, not Ashfaq Nadeem.
match_headline: Pakistan Names New Military Leader

text: An article on Friday about a ruling by the Florida Supreme Court that vacated more than 100 death penalty sentences referred incorrectly to the writing of the decision. It was written by the court as a group, not solely by Chief Justice Jorge Labarga.
match_headline: Florida Ruling Upends More Than 100 Death Sentences

text: An article on Monday about a new program for international entrepreneurs misidentified the educational institution that partnered with New York City’s Economic Development Corporation. It is the City University of New York, not the City College of New York.
match_headline: First Crop of Foreign Entrepreneurs Setting Up Shop at CUNY

text: A picture credit on Tuesday with an article about the theft of fur coats from a Dennis Basso store in Manhattan referred incorrectly in some editions to the source of the photographs. They were provided by Dennis Basso store management, not by the New York Police Department.
match_headline: Thieves With Discriminating Taste Steal Sable Furs From New York Shop

text: An article on Dec. 12 about benefits that Google has brought to Pryor, Okla., by building a data center in the small town erroneously included one college that Pryor students have recently attended. Although several students have gone on to prestigious universities, Brown is not one of them. The article also gave an outdated name for a major company based in Bartlesville, Okla. It is now ConocoPhillips, no longer Phillips 66.
match_headline: Google Effect Rubs Off on Schools in One Rural Oklahoma Town

text: An article on Dec. 20 about the 35th anniversary of the Broadway opening of “Dreamgirls” erroneously included an actor among the original cast. David Alan Grier replaced Cleavant Derricks; he was not in the original cast. The article also misidentified the area of Manhattan where the director Michael Bennett’s rehearsal studios were located. It is the Flatiron district, not Chelsea.
match_headline: Sheryl Lee Ralph and Ben Harney on the Long Reach of ‘Dreamgirls’

text: An article on Tuesday about five long-running Broadway shows that will be closing in the coming weeks misstated the closing date for “The Color Purple.” It is Sunday, Jan. 8 — not this Sunday. The article also misspelled the given name of a cast member in “Jersey Boys.” She is Sara Schmidt, not Sarah.
match_headline: After Thousands of Broadway Performances, 5 Shows Take Their Bows

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington referred incorrectly to an auction block that was shown. Andrew Jackson and Henry Clay spoke from it in Hagerstown, Md., in 1830; it was not used in 1880. (Slavery had been abolished by then.)
match_headline: Visiting the African-American Museum: Waiting, Reading, Thinking, Connecting, Feeling

text: An obituary on Monday about the singer and songwriter George Michael misspelled, in some copies, the surname of his bandmate in the duo Wham! He is Andrew Ridgeley, not Ridgely.
match_headline: George Michael, Pop Superstar, Is Dead at 53

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 29 about President-elect Donald J. Trump’s threat to roll back President Obama’s détente with Cuba referred imprecisely to the Akerman law firm, where an adviser on Cuba, Matthew D. Aho, said a reversal would be legally complicated. Although Akerman has an office in New York, its main office is in Miami; it is not the “New York law firm Akerman.” The same imprecision appeared in an article on March 3 about a proposal by Major League Baseball to allow Cuban ballplayers to sign directly with league franchises, and in an article on March 16 about new federal work rules that allow that.
match_headline: Donald Trump’s Threat to Close Door Reopens Old Wounds in Cuba

text: An obituary on Dec. 20 about the supermodel China Machado erroneously attributed a distinction to her. While she is believed to have been the first non-Caucasian to appear on the cover of a major American glossy magazine, she was not the first to appear on the inside pages of a magazine. (At least one other non-Caucasian — Adrienne Fidelin, a dancer and model from Guadeloupe — was featured inside a magazine, the September 1937 issue of Harper’s Bazaar.)
match_headline: China Machado, Breakthrough Model Until the End, Dies at 86

text: An article on Dec. 2 about residents of Nova Scotia who are fighting to be recognized as Indians, which would entitle them to tax breaks and other privileges, gave an outdated name for the department that oversees Indian affairs. It is Indigenous and Northern Affairs Canada, no longer Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada.
match_headline: In Canada, Feeling ‘Robbed’ of Indian Identity, and Benefits

text: An article on Dec. 1 about calls by a Saudi prince, Alwaleed bin Talal, to lift Saudi Arabia’s ban on women driving misidentified the body that enforces the ban. It is the Interior Ministry, not the religious police.
match_headline: Let Women Drive, a Prince in Saudi Arabia Urges

text: An article on Wednesday about challenges facing Rick Perry, President-elect Donald J. Trump’s nominee to run the Energy Department, erroneously included a position that an earlier energy secretary, Bill Richardson, had held before heading the department for President Bill Clinton. While Mr. Richardson had been the United States ambassador to the United Nations and, before that, a congressman from New Mexico, he had not yet served as governor of New Mexico. (He held that post after leaving the Energy Department.)
match_headline: Rick Perry, as Energy Secretary, May Be Pressed to Resume Nuclear Tests

text: An article on Tuesday about a report by the Civil Complaint Review Board on the use of Tasers by the New York Police Department misstated a change from the draft of the report to the final version. The recommendation that the Police Department create an annual report on the use of the stun guns was moved to the last page of the report; it was not removed entirely.
match_headline: Complaint Board Softened Report on Police Use of Tasers

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the astronomer Vera Rubin referred incorrectly to the Vassar College class of 1948, of which she was a member. It was not “immortalized by Mary McCarthy in the novel ‘The Group.’” (That novel was about the Vassar class of 1933.) The obituary also misstated the number of days it takes the planet Mercury to orbit the sun. It is 88 days, not 84.
ref_headline: immortalized by Mary McCarthy in the novel ‘The Group.’
match_headline: Vera Rubin, 88, Dies; Opened Doors in Astronomy, and for Women

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Gordie Tapp, a longtime regular on the television variety series “Hee Haw,” referred incorrectly to the death of his fellow cast member Don Harron. He died in January 2015, not this past January.
match_headline: Gordie Tapp, ‘Hee Haw’ Regular of ‘Pfft! You Was Gone’ Fame, Dies at 94

text: A picture caption last Thursday with the Scene City column, about a party for the film “Fences,” misidentified the woman shown with the actress Phylicia Rashad. She is Janet League-Katzin — not her mother, Vivian Ayers-Allen.
match_headline: Michèle Morgan, the First ‘Best Actress’ at Cannes, Dies at 96

text: An obituary in some editions on Thursday about the actress Debbie Reynolds misstated the occupation of Harry Karl, her second husband. He was a shoe retailer, not a shoe manufacturer. The obituary also referred imprecisely to Ms. Reynolds’s role in the 1950 movie “The Daughter of Rosie O’Grady.” It was her first credited movie role, not her movie debut. (She had a small uncredited part in “June Bride” in 1948.)
match_headline: Debbie Reynolds, Wholesome Ingénue in 1950s Films, Dies at 84

text: An article on Dec. 1 about a pilots’ strike at Lufthansa, the latest German company in distress, referred imprecisely to fines sought by the United States against Deutsche Bank, a German institution accused of financial malfeasance. Although the authorities have threatened fines of $14 billion, that amount is the starting point in negotiations — not the final amount, which is expected to be lower. The article also misstated the location, relative to Istanbul, of a new airport expected to compete for passengers with traditional European hubs like Berlin. It will be about 22 miles northwest — not northeast — of the Turkish city. And because of an editing error, the article referred incorrectly to Istanbul. It is the commercial capital of Turkey, not the administrative capital.
match_headline: Lufthansa Joins Germany’s List of Companies in Distress

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 1 about reports that a jet carrying members of a Brazilian soccer team that crashed had run out of fuel misspelled, at one point and in some editions, the surname of a defender for the team, Chapecoense, who was in critical condition. As correctly noted elsewhere in the article, he is Alan Ruschel, not Rushel.
match_headline: Doomed Jet Carrying Brazilian Team Reportedly Ran Out of Fuel

text: An article on Wednesday about clean tech companies referred incorrectly to spending by Genomatica. It has devoted most of the $200 million it has raised to industrial chemicals; it has not spend $300 million on biofuels.
match_headline: Clean Tech Rises Again, Retooling Nature for Industrial Use

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Friday about pitcher Ivan Nova’s re-signing with the Pittsburgh Pirates misstated, in some editions, the minor-league level of the two players the Yankees acquired for Nova in an August trade. They were at Class A, not Class AAA.
match_headline: Ivan Nova Is Said to Agree to 3-Year Deal to Stay With Pirates

text: An article in some editions last Friday about Anthony Stolarz, the Philadelphia Flyers’ backup goaltender, misstated, in some copies, the number of consecutive games in which he did not play after a shutout victory over the Detroit Red Wings. It was four, not five.
match_headline: Anthony Stolarz, First N.H.L. Goalie From New Jersey, Excels With Flyers

text: An article on Thursday about the designation of lands in Utah and Nevada as national monuments misstated the total area of public lands and waters protected by President Obama. He has designated about 553 million acres, not 553 acres, as national monuments; that figure does not include other newly protected lands and waters.
match_headline: Obama Designates Two New National Monuments, Protecting 1.65 Million Acres

text: An article on Dec. 21 about Medicare’s considerations as it weighs paying for outpatient knee replacement surgery misstated the amount patients would pay for such procedures. Medicare covers inpatient hospital stays, aside from a $1,288 deductible; it does not cover them at 100 percent. The outpatient cost for the procedure itself would be capped at the same amount as the inpatient deductible, but could involve additional fees and would include no coverage for aftercare at a skilled nursing facility, which, if needed, would add up to thousands of dollars; it is not the case that an outpatient procedure’s 20 percent co-payment would easily add up to thousands of dollars.
match_headline: Should Medicare Allow Outpatient Knee Replacement? Doctors Are Deeply Split

text: An article last Saturday about the strength of New Jersey men’s college basketball teams this season misstated, in some copies, the surname of the player who gave Seton Hall a 54-53 lead in a 72-61 victory over Rutgers. He is Ismael Sanogo, not Songo. The article also misstated, in some copies, the name of the Northeast Conference team that is seen as a favorite to win the league title. It is Fairleigh Dickinson, not Farleigh Dickson.
match_headline: Seton Hall Rally Beats Rutgers as a New Jersey Basketball Renaissance Blooms

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about role debuts by members of New York City Ballet in “George Balanchine’s The Nutcracker” erroneously included a dancer as one who made her debut in the role of Marzipan this year. The dancer, Olivia MacKinnon, made her Marzipan debut in 2014. (She made her debut in the role of Coffee this year.)
match_headline: Fresh Dewdrops for New York City Ballet’s ‘Nutcracker’

text: An obituary on Friday about LaVell Edwards, the former Brigham Young University football coach, using information the family released through the university, omitted some survivors. Besides his wife, the former Patti Louise Covey, and his daughter, Ann Cannon, and sons Jim and John, he is also survived by his sisters Ruby Cameron, Norma Brady, Alene Felix, Shirley Maag and Colleen Healey; his brothers Lewis and Wayne, 14 grandchildren and 11 great-grandchildren.
match_headline: LaVell Edwards, Coach Who Led B.Y.U. to a Football Title, Dies at 86

text: An article on Dec. 4 about anti-corruption efforts in Panama referred incorrectly to leaked documents known as the “Panama Papers.” They were obtained by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, not the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists.
match_headline: Panama Struggles to Shed Its Image as a Magnet for Shady Deals

text: An article last Sunday about the actors Cate Blanchett and Richard Roxburgh misstated the number of characters Ms. Blanchett plays in the video installation “Manifesto.” It is 13, not 12.
