match_headline: Cate Blanchett and Richard Roxburgh, in Love and Battle

text: A picture credit on Dec. 18 with a review of “A Woman Looking at Men Looking at Women” misspelled the surname of the photographer. The picture of the book’s author, Siri Hustvedt, was taken by Marion Ettlinger, not Ettinger.
ref_headline: A Woman Looking at Men Looking at Women
match_headline: Siri Hustvedt Views the Human Condition Through Art and Science

text: An article last Sunday about the women who met Hillary Clinton early in her political career misstated the relationship of the National Women’s Education Fund to the National Women’s Political Caucus. The education fund is an unofficial training arm of the caucus, with no formal affiliation. It is not an official training arm.
match_headline: The Women Who Met Hillary, and Spotted a Future Political Star

text: An article last Sunday about restaurants in Los Angeles strip malls misidentified the street in Hollywood where two neighboring restaurants are. Petit Trois and Trois Mec are on Highland Avenue, not Vine Street.
match_headline: 6 Standout Restaurants in Los Angeles Strip Malls

text: An obituary last Sunday about the singer Léo Marjane misidentified the person who insisted that she adopt Léo as her first name. It was a record producer, not her manager.
match_headline: Léo Marjane, a Music Hall Star in Occupied France, Dies at 104

text: An article on Dec. 3 about the discovery, in Norway, of a wrought-iron gate believed to have been stolen from the Dachau concentration camp in Germany referred imprecisely to the gate, which bears the phrase “Arbeit Macht Frei.” It is a replica of the original, not the original itself.
match_headline: ‘Arbeit Macht Frei’ Gate Thought to Be Stolen From Dachau Is Found

text: An article on Thursday about Ed Whitlock, a record-setting 85-year-old marathoner, misstated the given name of a co-founder of the Association of Road Racing Statisticians. He is Ken Young, not Ed.
match_headline: 85-Year-Old Marathoner Is So Fast That Even Scientists Marvel

text: An article on Nov. 21 about age verification for the oldest competitors at the World Masters Athletics Championships misidentified the type of medical equipment the 97-year-old John Gilmour wore at the 2016 event. It was a urostomy bag, not a colostomy bag. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Still Running at 119? Not So Fast

text: A picture caption on Friday with an art review of “Simon Starling: At Twilight,” at Japan Society in Manhattan, referred incorrectly to one of Mr. Starling’s works. The work, “Project for a Masquerade (Hiroshima),” is not part of the Japan Society show.
match_headline: Simon Starling: Modernism Gazing Into the Past

text: An article on Dec. 4 about China’s likely re-evaluation of President-elect Donald J. Trump after his telephone call to Taiwan’s president, Tsai Ing-wen, referred incompletely to the presidential candidacy of Hung Hsui-chu of the Kuomintang party. Favored by China, she initially challenged Ms. Tsai, but later dropped out of the race.
match_headline: China Sees New Ambiguity With Donald Trump’s Taiwan Call

text: An article on Dec. 4 about admiration on both sides of the Atlantic for Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president, among white ethnocentrists, nationalists, populists and neo-Nazis misspelled, in some editions, the given name of President-elect Donald J. Trump’s new chief strategist, an alt-right figure who has not wholly embraced Mr. Putin. He is Stephen K. Bannon, not Steven.
match_headline: Extremists Turn to a Leader to Protect Western Values: Vladimir Putin

text: An article on Monday about some of the victims of a terror attack on an Istanbul nightclub misidentified the occupation of one of those killed, Haykal Mousallem of Lebanon. He was a fitness trainer, not a businessman.
match_headline: Victims in Istanbul New Year’s Attack Came From Across the World

text: An article on Dec. 10 about the conviction of Geert Wilders, a Dutch far-right leader, on charges of inciting discrimination and insulting a group misstated the action that led to that conviction. He led an anti-Moroccan chant at a political rally in the Netherlands; although he had previously said the country would be safer with fewer Moroccans, he was acquitted of hate-speech charges in connection with that statement.
match_headline: Geert Wilders, Dutch Far-Right Leader, Is Convicted of Inciting Discrimination

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 4 about the Mentawai people of Indonesia, who have resisted government policies for decades but now face a generational divide as their children embrace the modern world, referred incorrectly in some editions to Teu Kapik Sikalabai, the wife of Teu Kapik Sibajak, a Mentawai elder. Mr. Kapik is a Sikkerei, a special class of shamans and forest healers, but Ms. Kapik is not; only men can be in that class.
match_headline: Modern World Tugs at an Indonesian Tribe Clinging to Its Ancient Ways

text: An article on Nov. 27 about homeowners who refused to sell their property to the Trump International Golf Links in Balmedie, Scotland — and lost their sea view when Mr. Trump’s workers built a wall — referred incorrectly to a contest won by Sarah Malone, a vice president of the golf course. It was a regional marketing campaign, not a beauty pageant. (Ms. Malone sent an email pointing out the error shortly after publication; this correction was delayed because editors did not follow through on the complaint.)
match_headline: In Scotland, Trump Built a Wall. Then He Sent Residents the Bill.

text: An article on Saturday about a decision by Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo to commute the sentence of the driver of the getaway car in the infamous 1981 robbery of a Brink’s armored car in Rockland County, N.Y., misstated the given name of the guard who was killed. He was Peter Paige, not Paul Paige.
match_headline: Cuomo Commutes Sentence of Judith Clark, Driver in Deadly Brink’s Robbery

text: A chart on Dec. 28 with article about potential conflicts of interest among members named to a biotechnology panel of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine, using information erroneously posted on the website of the Engineering Biology Research Consortium, referred incorrectly to Mary Maxon and David Rejeski, two of the 13 members of the panel. They do not have any connection to the consortium. As a result, seven of the members of the panel have potential conflicts of interest, not nine. The article, using the same information from the website, misstated the number of people connected to the consortium who are also members of the biotechnology panel. It is three, not five.
match_headline: National Biotechnology Panel Faces New Conflict of Interest Questions

text: An article on Saturday about the deaths of major figures in 2016 misstated the cause of death of the basketball coach Pat Summitt. It was Alzheimer’s disease, not cancer.
match_headline: Among Deaths in 2016, a Heavy Toll in Pop Music

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Archbishop Hilarion Capucci, who as the head of the Greek Catholic Church in Jerusalem was arrested in 1974 and charged with aiding Palestinian militants, described the location of Nazareth incorrectly. It is in northern Israel, not in the West Bank.
match_headline: Hilarion Capucci, Archbishop Jailed for Aiding Palestinian Militants, Dies at 94

text: An article last Wednesday about American sheep’s milk cheeses misspelled the name of the Wisconsin city where Hidden Springs Creamery is located. It is Westby, not Wesby.
match_headline: Sheep’s Milk Cheeses in U.S. Earn Ribbons but Little Profit

text: An article last Wednesday about the forecasters of food trends misspelled the surname of a popular musician. She is Alanis Morissette, not Morrisette.
match_headline: The Dark (and Often Dubious) Art of Forecasting Food Trends

text: A review last Wednesday about the Odeon restaurant in TriBeCa misstated the location of the wheelchair-accessible restroom. It is downstairs (and reached by elevator), not on the sidewalk level. The review also misstated the relationship between Lynn Wagenknecht and Keith McNally when they opened the Odeon in 1980. They were not married until more than three years later.
match_headline: The Odeon’s Not-So-Bright Lights Still Beckon

text: An article on Nov. 23 about the likelihood that President Obama will leave office with a federal prison population smaller than when he was sworn in misidentified the last president who did so. The most recent time this happened was with President Jimmy Carter, not President Lyndon B. Johnson.
match_headline: After Obama Push for Clemency, Hints of Reversal Likely to Come

text: An article on Tuesday about the strong views against torture held by James N. Mattis, President-elect Donald J. Trump’s nominee for secretary of defense, misstated the rank held by General Mattis when he commanded a Marine division in Iraq. He was a major general then, not a lieutenant general.
match_headline: Inside Trump Defense Secretary Pick’s Efforts to Halt Torture

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the United States’ assisting Baltic militaries misidentified the position held by Lt. Gen. Jonas Vytautas Zukas in Lithuania. He is the country’s chief of defense, not chief of Special Operations forces.
match_headline: U.S. Lending Support to Baltic States Fearing Russia

text: An article on Wednesday about the political ramifications of drastic changes to the newspaper industry in New Jersey referred incorrectly to the journalist Bob Ingle. At the time he retired in 2015, he was a senior political columnist for Gannett NJ, not a columnist for The Asbury Park Press. (Mr. Ingle’s column appeared in the Asbury paper, which is owned by Gannett.)
match_headline: In New Jersey, Only a Few Media Watchdogs Are Left

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday highlighting tools and techniques to retune your career referred incorrectly to the writer of the App Smart column. The writer, Kit Eaton, is a man.
match_headline: The Best Time to Retune Your Career? It’s Probably Right Now

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Monday about N.F.L. coaching changes misstated the record for the San Francisco 49ers this season. They were 2-14, not 1-15.
match_headline: Gary Kubiak, Denver Broncos Coach Who Led Team to a Title, Is Expected to Retire

text: An article on Saturday about Canadian soldiers from the 228th Overseas Battalion who played professional hockey during World War I misidentified the championship the Montreal Canadiens won in 1917. It was the N.H.A. championship, not the Stanley Cup. An accompanying picture caption also misidentified an officer shown with one of the battalion teams. He was George McNamara — not Howard McNamara, who was George’s brother.
match_headline: A Quirk of Canadian History: When War and Hockey Shared the Ice

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with a report in the Scoreboard column on Tuesday about the Winter Classic hockey game between the Chicago Blackhawks and the St. Louis Blues misidentified the Blues player shown vying with the Blackhawks’ Michal Kempny. He is Kyle Brodziak — not Corey Crawford, who is the Chicago goaltender pictured in the background.
match_headline: St. Louis Blues Defeat Chicago Blackhawks in Winter Classic

text: An article on Tuesday about a carbon capture plant in Texas misstated the driving distance that would produce 1.6 million tons of carbon dioxide. It is 3.5 billion miles, not million.
match_headline: Can Carbon Capture Technology Prosper Under Trump?

text: An obituary on Dec. 25 about the costume designer Willa Kim referred imprecisely to the 1961 show “Red Eye of Love,” for which she did the costumes. While it was a comedy with music, it was not a musical. (A musical version of the play was staged in 2014.) The obituary also referred incorrectly to the 1963 show “Have I Got a Girl for You!” It was not the first show on Broadway for which Ms. Kim received sole credit for the costumes. (“Are You With It?” was the first, in 1945.)
match_headline: Willa Kim, Designer of Fanciful Costumes, Dies at 99

text: An obituary in some editions on Sunday about Allan Williams, the Beatles’ first manager, misidentified one of the people he enlisted to paint murals at his Liverpool nightclub, the Jacaranda. Rod Murray, an art student, worked on the murals — not Rod Davis, a former member of John Lennon’s first band, the Quarrymen.
match_headline: Allan Williams, First Manager of the Beatles, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Sunday about the artist Tyrus Wong referred imprecisely at one point to “Water to Paper, Paint to Sky,” a retrospective of his work. As correctly noted elsewhere in the obituary, it was mounted at the Walt Disney Family Museum in San Francisco, which is independent of the Walt Disney Company; it was not “Disney’s own retrospective.”
ref_headline: Water to Paper, Paint to Sky,
match_headline: Tyrus Wong, ‘Bambi’ Artist Thwarted by Racial Bias, Dies at 106

text: An editorial on Thursday about Gov. Andrew Cuomo’s free college tuition plan misstated the estimated cost of a free-tuition program for New York City community colleges. It is $232 million, not $232 billion.
match_headline: A Promising Proposal for Free Tuition

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about team camaraderie at the world junior hockey championship misidentified, in some editions, the location of the semifinal game between Canada and Sweden. It was in Montreal, not in Toronto.
match_headline: At World Junior Hockey Championship, Team Camaraderie Overcomes Club Rivalries

text: An article on Page T3 this weekend about saving on travel in 2017 misstates the conversion rate of the British sterling pound to the dollar, both two years ago and in October 2016. Two years ago, it was exchanging at over $1.60; it was not valued at 1.6 to the dollar. And in October, it plunged to around $1.16; it did not plunge to 1.17 to the dollar.
match_headline: Eight Ways to Save on Travel in 2017

text: A headline last Sunday for a capsule summary about the obituary of Justice Antonin Scalia, listed among the year’s most read New York Times articles, misstated the justice’s age. He was 79, not 69.
match_headline: New York Today: Jackie-Michelle Martinez, a New Yorker of the Year

text: An article on Dec. 25 about the astronaut Edgar Mitchell described inaccurately the past employment of one of Mitchell’s ex-wives. She was a cocktail waitress at a Playboy Club, not a Playboy Playmate.
An article on Dec. 25 about Sirdeaner Walker, an anti-bullying activist, transposed her son’s surname. He was Carl Walker-Hoover, not Hoover-Walker.

An article last Sunday about efforts by the United States government to seize assets from corrupt officials gave an outdated title for Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue of Equatorial Guinea, who has agreed to give up valuables he amassed in the United States. He is now the country’s vice president, no longer the second vice president. (He is the son of the nation’s president, Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo.)
match_headline: Shielding Seized Assets From Corruption’s Clutches

text: A picture credit on Dec. 25 with an article about the landscape architect Lawrence Halprin, using information from the Cultural Landscape Foundation, misspelled the photographer’s surname. He is Jeremy Bittermann, not Bitterman.
match_headline: Celebrating a Rugged Vision of Landscape Architecture

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Lauren Pully and Dylan Graham misspelled the bride’s surname in one instance as Pulley.
match_headline: Lauren Pully, Dylan Graham

text: An article on Thursday about the Rockefeller Foundation’s naming Rajiv Shah as its new president, using information from the organization, erroneously attributed a distinction to him. At age 43, Mr. Shah is one of the youngest people to lead the foundation, not the youngest. (At least two of his predecessors were younger.)
match_headline: Rockefeller Foundation Picks Rajiv J. Shah, a Trustee, as President

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the Giants’ 38-13 loss to the Green Bay Packers in the N.F.L. playoffs misstated Aaron Rodgers’s postseason history against the Giants. While the Packers had lost their previous two playoff games against the Giants, Rodgers was the quarterback for only one of those games; he had not lost to the Giants in their two previous playoff matchups.
match_headline: Giants Bare Their Chests and Get Exposed by the Packers

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the many injuries the Rangers have endured during the first half of the N.H.L. season misspelled, in some copies, the given name of a player the Rangers traded to Ottawa in the off-season. He is Derick Brassard, not Derrick.
match_headline: Rangers Face Blue Jackets. Then It’s Break Time.

text: An article on Saturday about Bruce Reznick, the Nets’ fan known as Mr. Whammy who has an antagonistic relationship with Cleveland Cavaliers star LeBron James, misstated Reznick’s former profession. He was a lawyer, not a dentist.
match_headline: Even With Mr. Whammy, Nets Are No Match for LeBron James and the Cavs

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about Ayatollah Ali Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, a former president of Iran, misstated the age at which he left home to study theology in Qum, Iran. He was 14, not 4.
match_headline: Ayatollah Ali Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Ex-President of Iran, Dies at 82

text: An article on Tuesday about the planned Women’s March on Washington referred imprecisely to Gloria Steinem’s role in a town hall meeting planned during the march. She will be a participant, not the host, of the event. (The National Domestic Workers Alliance will host the meeting.)
match_headline: Women’s March on Washington Opens Contentious Dialogues About Race

text: An article on Dec. 13 about a report from the Committee to Protect Journalists that said a record number of journalists had been jailed around the world in 2016 misstated the overall total and the totals in Eritrea and Ethiopia. The overall total was 259, not 257; Eritrea’s was 17, not 16; and Ethiopia’s was 16, not 14.
match_headline: Record Number of Journalists Jailed in 2016, Press Advocacy Group Says

text: An article on Dec. 11 about Turkey’s crackdown on Kurdish politicians, schools, news outlets and charities omitted part of a comment by Feleknas Uca, a member of Parliament from the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party, explaining why so many young Kurds had fled to the mountains. They did so to avoid curfews imposed this year in parts of eastern Turkey, she said, not just since the arrests of Selahattin Demirtas, the party co-chairman, and Figen Yuksekdag, the co-chairwoman.
match_headline: As Turkey Cracks Down, Kurdish Mayors Pack Bags for Jail

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the changing role of the New York City Fire Deparment, due in part to a decline in fire-related deaths, misidentified the workers loading a fire victim into an ambulance. They are emergency services workers, not firefighters.
match_headline: New York City’s Fire Deaths Reach Lowest Point in Over 100 Years

text: An article on Monday about the Modern Language Association erroneously attributed a distinction to the organization. It is not the largest scholarly group in the United States. (It has about 25,000 members worldwide; by comparison, the American Chemical Society has about 157,000 members.)
match_headline: Modern Language Association Moves to Reject Academic Boycott of Israel

text: An article on Friday about 15 standout television shows omitted the name of an executive producer responsible for the show “Sneaky Pete” on Amazon. He is Graham Yost.
match_headline: 15 TV Shows to Watch This Season

text: An article on Wednesday about prominent people who have been hired at the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, a philanthropic effort started by Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, referred incorrectly to one person who was previously appointed. Although Cori Bargmann joined the initiative as president of science, she continues her work as a neuroscientist at Rockefeller University; she has not left that post.
match_headline: Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Builds Political Muscle for Philanthropic Work

text: An obituary on Jan. 2 about the scholar of religion Huston Smith referred incorrectly to his book “The World’s Religions,” published in 1991. It was a revised and expanded — not abridged — version of his 1958 book, “The Religions of Man.” The obituary also characterized Central Methodist University, where Professor Smith studied, incorrectly. It is a liberal arts college affiliated with the United Methodist Church; it is not a Bible college. In addition, the obituary misstated the year Professor Smith met Aldous Huxley. It was 1947, not 1948.
match_headline: Huston Smith, Author of ‘The World’s Religions,’ Dies at 97

text: An article on Tuesday about cities that are dealing with problems of homelessness misstated the type of communication the Justice Department had with officials in Boise, Idaho, over a local law challenged by advocates for the homeless. It was a statement of interest, made as part of a legal filing, not a letter.
match_headline: Rights Battles Emerge in Cities Where Homelessness Can Be a Crime

text: An article on Thursday about Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s agenda for 2017 misstated part of his proposal for wind farms. He proposed generating 2,400 megawatts of power from wind projects off Long Island by 2030, not from an offshore wind farm near Montauk. (A proposed wind farm off Montauk would generate 90 megawatts of power.)
match_headline: As State Tour Ends, Fate of Cuomo’s Agenda Lies With Restive Legislature

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the continuation of an article about the publishing industry’s struggles with polarizing right-wing authors misstated, in some copies, the year the mass shooting at the Pulse nightclub in Orlando, Fla., occurred. It was last June, not June 2015.
match_headline: Publishers Encounter Political Storms in Turn to Right

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about Clemson’s 35-31 victory over Alabama in the college football national championship game misstated the day the game ended. It was early Tuesday, not late Monday.
match_headline: Clemson Upsets Alabama to Win the College Football Championship

text: Because of an editing error, the On Soccer column on Tuesday, about plans to expand the World Cup to 48 teams, misstated, in some copies, the year the expansion would take place. As an accompanying picture caption correctly noted, it is 2026, not 2028.
match_headline: Seeing the Upside as FIFA Votes on Expanding the World Cup

text: An article on Page D2 today about the only female writer for the watch website Hodinkee misstates the percentage of Hodinkee’s readership that is male. It is 93 percent, not 95.
match_headline: Breaking Into the Boys’ Club of Watches

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an obituary about Jill Saward, an advocate for rape victims, misspelled the name of the city in England where the photograph of Ms. Saward was taken. It is Lichfield, not Litchfield.
match_headline: Jill Saward, Advocate for Victims of Sexual Assault, Dies at 51

text: An article on Dec. 18 about the European Union’s crisis of legitimacy, which is fueling right-wing, nationalist politics, misidentified an area of France where the right-wing National Front party is popular. It is southeast France, not southwest.
match_headline: E.U. Faces Its Next Big Test as France’s Election Looms

text: An article on Dec. 17 about ambivalence toward the European Union even in countries that have prospered under the bloc, like Slovakia, misstated the number of seats in Parliament that the People’s Party-Our Slovakia won in March. The party won 14 seats, not 13.
match_headline: Not Even a Prosperous Slovakia Is Immune to Doubts About the E.U.

text: An article on Friday about a meeting between Donald J. Trump and AT&T’s chief executive, Randall Stephenson, misstated the nature of CNN’s reporting this week that brought criticism from Mr. Trump, as AT&T aims to buy Time Warner, which owns CNN. CNN broke news of a briefing by intelligence officials to the president and the president-elect about an unverified report linking Mr. Trump to a Russian campaign to influence the election; CNN did not break the news about the report’s existence.
match_headline: AT&T Chief Visits Trump With Time Warner Deal Looming Large

text: An article on Wednesday about Maria Sharapova’s scheduling her return to tennis misstated the overall length of her doping suspension after it was reduced by the Court of Arbitration for Sport. It is 15 months, not 16.
match_headline: Maria Sharapova to Return From Suspension at April Event in Germany

text: An obituary on Friday about John M. Richman, a former chief executive and chairman of Kraft Inc., misstated part of the name of the company, a precursor of Kraft, that he joined in 1954. It was the National Dairy Products Corporation (not Product).
match_headline: John M. Richman, Chief of Kraft Who Oversaw Merger With Philip Morris, Dies at 89

text: A map on Dec. 18 with the continuation of an article about sad times in the Turkish town that is the birthplace of St. Nicholas, the fourth-century bishop who was an inspiration for Santa Claus, misspelled the name of the town in some editions. As noted correctly in the article, it is Demre, not Demri.
match_headline: In Turkey’s Home of St. Nick, Far From North Pole, All Is Not Jolly

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about that day’s N.F.L. wild-card playoff games misidentified the home team for the game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Miami Dolphins on Oct. 16. It was Miami.
match_headline: N.F.L. Sunday Wild-Card Matchups: Who We Think Will Win

text: An article on Jan. 1 retracing the steps of the main characters in the film “When Harry Met Sally” misstated a word that Harry said in a nonsensical voice at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. It is paprikash, not poppycosh.
match_headline: In the Footsteps of Harry and Sally

text: An article last Sunday on how the 52 Places to Go list was picked omitted the hashtag used for the feature on Instagram. It is #52Places2017.
match_headline: How We Put Together Our 52 Places to Go List

text: A picture caption on this page on Dec. 25 for the 36 Hours column, about Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, described incorrectly the musical group shown playing on a beach there. It is an acoustic-style norteño troupe, not a mariachi band.
match_headline: 36 Hours in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico

text: An article on Dec. 25 about Matthew Bourne’s new production of “The Red Shoes” misstated part of the name of a film that Bernard Her-rmann composed the score for. It is “Hangover Square,” not “Hanover Square.”
match_headline: ‘The Red Shoes’ Takes the Stage

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about TV shows that examine the black middle class misstated the surname of an actor on “The Jeffersons.” He was Sherman Hemsley, not Helmsley.
match_headline: What TV Says About Race and Money

text: An article last Sunday about the playwright Tarell Alvin McCraney and the director Barry Jenkins, the creators of the film “Moonlight,” misstated the age Mr. McCraney was when his screenplay of “Moonlight” was sent to Mr. Jenkins. It arrived on Mr. McCraney’s 31st birthday, not his 34th.
match_headline: From Bittersweet Childhoods to ‘Moonlight’

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about a new, technologically advanced version of Shakespeare’s “The Tempest” referred incorrectly to efforts by the company Intel to change perceptions of its brand. It is taking on high-visibility projects in entertainment, music, sports and gaming (not gambling).
match_headline: At This ‘Tempest,’ Digital Wizardry Makes ‘Rough Magic’

text: An article last Sunday about the conductor and scholar Nikolaus Harnoncourt misidentified Gustav Leonhardt’s ensemble. It was the Leonhardt Consort, not the Amsterdam Baroque Orchestra.
match_headline: An Austrian Maestro’s Career, Seen Through His Recordings

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a gathering of world leaders in Paris for an Israeli-Palestinian peace conference that neither the Israelis nor the Palestinians attended referred incorrectly to the two-state solution endorsed at the conference. Those attending reiterated their support for the existing two-state solution; there is no new proposal.
match_headline: World Leaders Push Israel and Trump to Forge a 2-State Deal

text: An article on Saturday about the grocery spending habits of households receiving food stamps misstated the portion of spending used to purchase soft drinks. Households receiving food stamps spent 9.3 percent of their bills on “sweetened beverages,” a category that includes soft drinks, juices, and energy drinks, among others; they did not spend that percentage on soft drinks alone. In addition, the article misidentified the location of a Walmart store that was used as an example of prices in California. The store is in San Leandro, Calif., which neighbors Oakland; it is not in Oakland.
match_headline: In the Shopping Cart of a Food Stamp Household: Lots of Soda

text: An article on Friday about Iowa voters’ views of Donald J. Trump since the election misstated the pattern on the overalls worn by the man in the “American Gothic” painting by the artist Grant Wood, who was born in Jones County, Iowa. They are solid blue denim, not pinstriped.
match_headline: In Iowa, Trump Voters Are Unfazed by Controversies

text: An article on Dec. 19 about Margot Wallstrom, Sweden’s foreign minister, referred incorrectly to her country’s position on Palestinian statehood. Sweden is one of the few European countries that recognize statehood — not “one of a few countries” that recognize it. (Worldwide, 136 countries recognize Palestinian statehood).
match_headline: Margot Wallstrom on Feminism, Trump and Sweden’s Future

text: An article on Dec. 19 about an attack by a gunman in southern Jordan that killed nine Jordanians and a Canadian tourist misidentified, in some editions, the son whom the tourist, Linda Vatcher, had been visiting in Jordan. He is Christopher Vatcher, not David Vatcher. (Christopher was among the injured in the attack.)
match_headline: Gunmen in Jordan Kill 10, Including 7 Officers and a Canadian Tourist

text: An article on Monday about the Martin Luther King Jr. parade in Lexington, Va., using information from a retired professor at Washington and Lee University, misidentified the location of a statue of General Robert E. Lee. It is in Lee Chapel on the university campus, not at R.E. Lee Memorial Episcopal Church. (The article also referred incorrectly to the church as Robert E. Lee Memorial Episcopal Church.)
match_headline: A New Martin Luther King Jr. Parade Divides a Virginia Town

text: An article on Saturday about a closed-door session on Capitol Hill with James B. Comey, the director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, misspelled the given name of a congressman from New York who attended. He is Representative Jerrold Nadler, not Jerold.
match_headline: Democrats Confront F.B.I. Chief at Closed-Door Intelligence Briefing

text: An article on Monday about President Obama’s final days in office misidentified the state that is home to four sites he designated as the Reconstruction Era National Monument. They are in South Carolina, not Alabama.
match_headline: One Hand on Light Switch, Obama Isn’t Flipping to ‘Off’ Just Yet

text: An obituary on Monday about the conservationist Bud Lilly omitted several survivors. A stepson, Chris Lilly; a stepdaughter, Alisa Flores; and two step-grandchildren also survive him. In addition, the obituary misidentified the author of a 2016 Facebook post inviting people to visit Mr. Lilly. It was his stepson, Chris — not his son Gregory.
match_headline: Conservationist Bud Lilly, ‘a Trout’s Best Friend,’ Dies at 91

text: An earlier version of the front page correction misidentified Mr. Wood’s birthplace as Monticello, Iowa.

An article on Wednesday about a speech by Prime Minister Theresa May of Britain in which she charted the country’s course toward a clean break with the European Union misstated the timing of her call to “get on with it.” It came late in the speech, not early.
match_headline: In ‘Brexit’ Speech, Theresa May Outlines Clean Break for U.K.

text: An article on Jan. 9 about the propensity of inexperienced drone owners to crash their new machines misstated one part of the federal guidelines regarding drone use, based on information from a spokesman. Drone hobbyists are governed by community-based safety guidelines, which permit night flights with proper equipment, according to the Federal Aviation Administration; hobbyists are not prohibited from flying drones in the dark.
match_headline: Santa Delivered the Drone. But Not the Safety and Skill to Fly Them.

text: An article on Dec. 25 about Russia’s cultivation of far-right extremist groups in other countries to destabilize the European Union referred imprecisely to the political party of a Hungarian legislator who proposed a parliamentary investigation into Russian meddling in Hungary. While it is a green party, its official name is Politics Can Be Different, not the Green Party.
match_headline: Intent on Unsettling E.U., Russia Taps Foot Soldiers From the Fringe

text: An article on Friday about the arrival of foreign troops in Gambia with orders to dislodge Yahya Jammeh — the loser of last month’s presidential election, who refuses to step down — misstated the given name of a spokesman for the new president, Adama Barrow, who was inaugurated in neighboring Senegal for his own safety. The spokesman is Halifa Sallah, not Halif. The article also misquoted part of the new president’s inauguration pledge. Mr. Barrow promised to serve his country “without fear or favor,” not “without fear or failure.”
match_headline: Troops Enter Gambia as New President Is Sworn In

text: An article on Friday about a copyright lawsuit over KinderGuides, a series of books that aims to make literary classics accessible to young readers, misstated the relationship between the creators, the author Fredrik Colting and Melissa Medina. Mr. Colting and Ms. Medina are a couple and business partners; they are not married. (The error also appeared on Thursday in an article about the couple’s endeavor.)
match_headline: Author Who Turns Classics Into Children’s Books Is Sued

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about the results of Netflix’s global expansion misidentified an actor in the Netflix series “The Crown.” He is Jeremy Northam, not Pip Torrens.
match_headline: Netflix Goes Global and Its Profit Soars

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about bookmakers’ predictions for Sunday’s N.F.L. conference championship games misidentified, in some copies, the home city of the 2000 Rams, who were a participant in the regular-season game with the highest over-under. While they now play in Los Angeles, the Rams played in St. Louis in 2000.
match_headline: In N.F.L. Betting, Patriots Are Closest to Being a Sure Thing

text: An article on Friday about artists considered to be standouts at this year’s Outsider Art Fair, which is at the Metropolitan Pavilion through Sunday, misstated the surname of one of the artists. He is Frank Walters, not Wilson.
match_headline: Outsider Art 2017: A Top 10

text: An article on Friday about three television programs worth watching this weekend misstated the number of episodes in the PBS series “Secrets of the Six Wives,” airing Sundays at 10 p.m. It has three parts, not six.
match_headline: How Much Watching Time Do You Have This Weekend?

text: An article on Jan. 8 about surveillance software erroneously included one company among those that sell so-called ethical malware. The Israeli company Nice no longer sells such software; it sold its intelligence division in May 2015.
match_headline: Cyberwar for Sale

text: An article on Dec. 25, 2016, about the biologist Ruth Hubbard, the first woman to gain tenure in the biology department at Harvard University, in 1974, misstated how long it took for another woman to be awarded tenure in biology . It was one year, not 10.
match_headline: UConn Women Say ‘Nah’ to Rebuilding Year

text: An article on Jan. 15 about President Rodrigo Duterte of the Philippines included an erroneous description of a fire truck parked outside the office of Alvin Mañalac, a local elected official from a district in northern Manila. While Mañalac’s name and logo were painted on the truck, his face was not.
match_headline: President Duterte’s List

text: An article last Sunday about living in Washington referred incorrectly to Donald J. Trump’s impending move to the White House. He will be the 45th president, but not the 45th tenant.
match_headline: Where I Live: Washington, D.C.

text: A review on Jan. 8 about “The Secret Life of Fat,” by Sylvia Tara, misstated the bodily source of the hormone ghrelin. It is secreted primarily by the stomach, not by fat cells.
match_headline: Is Fat Really All That Bad? A Biochemist Explains.

text: A review last Sunday about “The Atheist Muslim,” using information from the publisher’s website, misstated the medical specialty of the book’s author, Ali A. Rizvi. He is an oncologic pathologist, not a surgical oncologist.
match_headline: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar on Two Books About Muslim Identity

text: A review on Jan. 1 about “The Moravian Night” referred imprecisely to the parentage of the novel’s author, Peter Handke, and incorrectly to the military service of his father. Both Handke’s biological father and his stepfather served in the Wehrmacht, but both survived World War II by many years; it is not the case that “Handke’s father died as a soldier in the Wehrmacht.”
match_headline: Peter Handke’s Time-Traveling Tale of a Europe in Flux

text: An article last Sunday about the playwright August Wilson misstated the amount of time between John Douglas Thompson’s first seeing Wilson’s play “Joe Turner’s Come and Gone” and when he was asked to star in a production of it. He was asked by Phylicia Rashad to star in it more than 25 years after first seeing it, not 35 years later. The article also misstated the year that Ruben Santiago-Hudson directed Wilson’s play “Jitney.” He is directing the current run on Broadway; he did not direct a version in 2007.
match_headline: From Nosebleed Seats to the Stage, Actors Discuss August Wilson

text: An article last Sunday about the portrayal of rape and sexual violence in recent TV shows and movies misstated Jennifer Kaytin Robinson’s title on the MTV show “Sweet/ Vicious.” She is the creator and co-executive producer, not the showrunner. (The showrunner is Amanda Lasher.)
match_headline: How Movies and TV Address Rape and Revenge

text: An article last Sunday about efforts by Southern California utilities to use big batteries as power sources misidentified the city in Virginia that is the headquarters for AES, which installs storage systems. It is Arlington, not Alexandria. The article also misstated the status of an installation of batteries near Chino, Calif., for the utility Southern California Edison. It has been built by Tesla; it is not being built. In addition, an accompanying picture caption omitted part of the surname of a resident in the area of the Aliso Canyon storage facility, where a gas leak occurred in 2015. He is George Chang, not Gorman-Chang.
match_headline: A Big Test for Big Batteries

text: An article on Thursday about lawsuits against Navient, the nation’s largest servicer of student loans, using information from the Washington State attorney general’s office, erroneously included one defendant in that state’s lawsuit. The Washington attorney general’s office filed a lawsuit against Navient; Sallie Mae is not charged in that suit. (Navient and Sallie Mae split into two companies in 2014.)
match_headline: Student Loan Collector Cheated Millions, Lawsuits Say

text: An article on Dec. 23 about Anis Amri, the suspect in an attack on a Christmas market in Berlin, who despite brushes with the law slipped through the fingers of German law enforcement, misstated, at one point, the given name of one of his sisters. As noted correctly elsewhere in the article, she is Najwa Amri, not Najma.
match_headline: Ordered Deported, Berlin Suspect Slipped Through Germany’s Fingers

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 19 about leadership of the Tata Group in India erroneously included one type of contract among those no-bid contracts granted to companies belonging to Mehli Mistry, a friend of Tata’s patriarch, Ratan Tata. Shipping contracts were not among them. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: In India, a Clash at the Top of the Tata Empire Gets Ugly

text: An article on Wednesday about Indianapolis’s supporting technology businesses as a way to make up for diminished manufacturing misstated part of the name of the location of Salesforce’s new regional headquarters there. It is Monument Circle, not Monument Square. The article also misstated the year that David Becker, an Indiana native, founded First Internet Bank. It was 1998, not 1986.
match_headline: How Indianapolis, Long Known as a Manufacturing Center, Is Luring Tech Talent

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Monday about the Green Bay Packers’ 34-31 victory over the Dallas Cowboys in the N.F.L. playoffs misidentified, in some editions, the Packers player who quarterback Aaron Rodgers was waiting on to run downfield on the second-to-last play of the game. It was tight end Jared Cook, not receiver Randall Cobb.
match_headline: Packers Thwart Cowboys as Time Expires to Make N.F.C. Title Game

text: An article on Tuesday about physician aid in dying misstated the American Medical Association’s stance on the practice. At its 2016 annual meeting, the association commissioned its Council on Ethical and Judicial Affairs to “outline the current landscape surrounding the issue of physician-assisted suicide.” That report, expected in June, will not recommend any policy. The Association did not agree to study whether to shift from its position opposing physician participation in aid in dying to a neutral position.
ref_headline: outline the current landscape surrounding the issue of physician-assisted suicide.
match_headline: Physician Aid in Dying Gains Acceptance in the U.S.

text: An article on Monday about the future of the protest movement, using information from Planned Parenthood, referred incorrectly to a training session for 2,000 organizers. Several groups — not just Planned Parenthood — conducted the training.
match_headline: After Success of Women’s March, a Question Remains: What’s Next?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Jan. 14 about an uproar over a calendar cover photo in India that shows Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a setting that evokes an iconic image of the father of independent India misspelled his surname at one point. As noted correctly elsewhere in the article, he is Mohandas K. Gandhi, not Ghandi.
match_headline: Photo of Narendra Modi at the Spinning Wheel Invokes Gandhi, and Some Cry Blasphemy

text: An article on Dec. 28 about the British government’s announcement of plans to crack down on voter fraud by tightening voting regulations referred incorrectly to new rules affecting students. Once automatically registered by their schools, students now have to register individually; the new regulations do not prohibit students from voting where they go to school, as long as they are registered there.
match_headline: As U.K. Tightens Voting Rules, Critics Say Labour and the Poor Will Suffer

text: An article on Dec. 26 about the Islamic State’s continuing power to inspire terrorist mayhem around the world despite its recent string of military defeats misstated the surname of a political scientist who examined 315 suicide bombings for a book he wrote, and misstated the year of publication. The author is Robert Pape, not Paper, and his book was published in 2005, not 2003.
match_headline: Weakened Militarily, ISIS Still Has Power to Sow Deadly Mayhem

text: An article on Saturday about financial disclosures of Betsy DeVos, the education secretary nominee, misstated the name of the Michigan publication that reported on one company, Neurocore, that Ms. DeVos and her husband back. It is MiBiz, not West Michigan Business News and Information.
match_headline: Betsy DeVos Won’t Shed Stake in Biofeedback Company, Filings Show

text: A subheading in the Week Ahead column on Monday about Alibaba misstated, in some copies, the quarter for which the company will be reporting earnings this week. It is its third quarter, not its fourth.
match_headline: Retrial for Law Executives, U.S. Economic Growth Findings and Auto Industry and Trump

text: An obituary on Saturday about the former corporate chief executive Brenda Barnes, using information from her family, misstated the cause of her death. It was complications of a recent stroke, not of a stroke she suffered in 2010.
match_headline: Brenda Barnes, Pepsi Chief Who Spurred a Work-Life Debate, Dies at 63

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the longtime Village Voice columnist Wayne Barrett misstated the location of The Voice’s offices in some copies. The paper is based in the Financial District, no longer in Greenwich Village, where it had offices for many years.
match_headline: Wayne Barrett, Fierce Muckraker at The Village Voice, Dies at 71

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about supporters of President Trump and their views of his executive order on immigration omitted a key phrase about killings that involved immigrants from the seven countries included in the 90-day visa ban. Since Sept. 11, 2001, no one in the United States has been killed “in a terrorist attack” by an immigrant, or the son or daughter of an immigrant, from any of the seven countries.
match_headline: In Ban on Migrants, Trump Supporters See a Promise Kept

text: An article on Wednesday about the business dealings of Anthony Scaramucci, a former campaign fund-raiser for President Trump, described incorrectly a Manhattan building that was the subject of investment negotiations between Anbang Insurance Group, a Chinese financial colossus, and the family business of Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. It is an office tower, not an apartment building.
match_headline: Trump Aide’s Deal With Chinese Firm Raises Fear of Tangled Interests

text: An article on Jan. 5 about the rescheduling of the trial of a son of the president of Equatorial Guinea on embezzlement and money-laundering charges transposed two of the son’s names. He is Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue (not Obiang Nguema). The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Accused of Looting Millions, Son of African Leader Stalls Trial

text: An article and a picture caption on Friday about a court ruling that South Korea could keep a statue stolen from a Japanese temple in 2012, on the grounds that it had been taken from Korea centuries earlier by Japanese pirates, misidentified the subject of the statue. It represents a bodhisattva, a person on the path to enlightenment, who is known as Kanzeon in Japan and Gwaneum in South Korea; it is not a statue of Buddha.
match_headline: South Korea Can Keep Buddhist Statue Stolen From Japan, Court Says

text: An article on Tuesday about a legal fight of many technology firms against President Trump’s executive order on immigration referred imprecisely to the Iranian revolution, which led Dara Khosrowshahi, Expedia’s chief executive, to flee the country with his parents. Although Mr. Khosrowshahi left Iran in 1978, when there was unrest against the shah, the revolution was not over at that point. (Iran did not become an Islamic republic until 1979.)
match_headline: Tech Companies Fight Trump Immigration Order in Court

text: An article on Jan. 24 about a lawsuit filed against the federal government regarding the tribal school in Supai, Ariz., referred imprecisely to the actual filing. It was by several members of the Havasupai Tribe, not by the tribe itself.
match_headline: Barely Two R’s Are Taught at School That Led Tribe to Sue U.S.

text: An entry in the Metropolitan Diary on Monday about encountering famous people on the streets of New York misspelled the surname of one celebrity the writer and his wife had spotted. He is Richard Meier, not Meyer.
match_headline: Famous People Encountered on the Street

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the rock musician John Wetton, using information from his manager, misspelled the maiden name of Mr. Wetton’s wife and misstated the month they were married. She is the former Lisa Nojaim, not Nojain, and they married in November 2016, not December.
match_headline: John Wetton, Rocker With King Crimson and Asia, Dies at 67

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the record producer Max Wilcox referred incorrectly to his performance in 1973 with Arthur Rubinstein and the Liverpool Philharmonic. He conducted the orchestra; he did not play piano.
match_headline: Max Wilcox, Grammy-Winning Record Producer, Dies at 88

text: An article last Thursday about the actress Marlo Thomas applied an erroneous distinction to Ms. Thomas’s fashion line. It is not the first commercial product to bear her name; her given name appeared on a sewing pattern sometime in the 1970s.
match_headline: Fashion From Marlo Thomas: ‘That Girl’ Shifts to ‘That Woman’

text: An article last Thursday about the men’s wear designer turned unisex shoemaker Simon Spurr misspelled another designer’s given name. He is Patrik Ervell, not Patrick.
match_headline: Simon Spurr Returns to Fashion

text: Because of an editing error, the On Pro Football column in some editions on Monday about watching the Super Bowl through a political prism misstated the name of the song Lady Gaga was singing when she hugged a woman in the audience during the halftime show. It is “Million Reasons,” not “Stay.”
match_headline: A Super Bowl Awash in Politics, on Social Media and Off the Field

text: An article in some editions on Tuesday about the Knicks’ 121-107 loss to the Los Angeles Lakers misstated, in some copies, the Lakers’ position in the N.B.A. standings entering the game. They had the third-worst record in the league, not the second-worst record.
match_headline: Pounded by Lowly Lakers, Knicks Fall Further From Playoff Field

text: An editorial on Tuesday about President Trump’s ban on travelers and refugees from seven predominantly Muslim nations incorrectly described attacks in the United States by people from those nations. There have been no such fatal attacks in more than two decades, but there have been nonfatal attacks.
match_headline: President Trump’s Real Fear: The Courts

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Jacksonville Jaguars owner Shahid Khan’s opposition to President Trump’s executive order temporarily banning visits by citizens from seven predominantly Muslim countries erroneously attributed a distinction to Khan in some copies. While he is the only Muslim owner in the N.F.L., he is not also the only immigrant in the group.
match_headline: Jaguars Owner Shahid Khan Opposes Trump’s Immigration Ban

text: An article last Sunday about undocumented students at the University of California, Merced, misstated a requirement for Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, known as DACA, a renewable waiver from deportation for the undocumented who arrived as minors. DACA recipients can be in school or have a G.E.D. certificate; they do not have to be a high school graduate.
match_headline: Creating a Safe Space for California Dreamers

text: An article last Sunday about using data analytics in student advising overstated the capabilities of a Stanford tool to help students choose courses. It does not recommend courses, or have an alert system in response to choices a student makes.
match_headline: Will You Graduate? Ask Big Data

text: An article on Jan. 29 about Alexa, Amazon’s home assistant, misstated the total number of marshmallows offered to subjects of the “marshmallow test,” which measured the ability of preschoolers to delay gratification. If the subjects could resist the temptation of a single marshmallow, they were rewarded with one more — not two more.
match_headline: How Alexa Fits Into Amazon’s Prime Directive

text: An article on Feb. 5 about the Oklahoma City Thunder basketball player Russell Westbrook misspelled part of the name of a rapper. He is Flavor Flav, not Flava Flav.
match_headline: The Misunderstood Genius of Russell Westbrook

text: A review on Jan. 29 about “Earning the Rockies: How Geography Shapes America’s Role in the World,” by Robert D. Kaplan, referred incorrectly to the voting results of last year’s presidential election. Of the nearly 137 million Americans who actually cast ballots, 48.1 percent voted for Hillary Clinton, 46 percent for Donald J. Trump and nearly 6 percent for other candidates. It is not the case that “just over half of America” voted for Clinton.
ref_headline: Earning the Rockies: How Geography Shapes America’s Role in the World,
match_headline: September’s Book Club Pick: ‘Earning the Rockies,’ by Robert D. Kaplan

text: A review on Jan. 29 about “A House Full of Females: Plural Marriage and Women’s Rights in Early Mormonism, 1835-1870,” by Laurel Thatcher Ulrich, misstated the year that Wilford Woodruff, as president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, signed the “Official Declaration” ending the church’s practice of polygamy. It was 1890, not 1889.
ref_headline: A House Full of Females: Plural Marriage and Women’s Rights in Early Mormonism, 1835-1870,
match_headline: How the Women of the Mormon Church Came to Embrace Polygamy

text: A map on Jan. 15 with the Surfacing column , about Montreal, misspelled part of the name of a street in the Petite-Patrie district. It is Rue Beaubien, not Rue Baubien.
match_headline: Five Places to Go in Montreal

text: An article last Sunday about an essay contest to win a house in the Catskills misspelled the given name of the lawyer handling the competition. She is Sara F. Hawkins, not Sarah.
match_headline: Write an Essay, Win This House

text: Because of an editing error, a workplace advice article last Sunday misstated the surname of a letter writer who commented on an earlier article about a female worker’s “revulsion” toward a male colleague. She is Dr. Virginia Collings, not Collins. 
match_headline: When a Job Is Temporary, but the Company Doesn’t Know It

text: An article last Sunday about a doctor with a rare disease who used himself as his own test subject misspelled the surname of another medical researcher who experimented on himself. He is Dr. Werner Forssmann, not Forssman.
match_headline: His Doctors Were Stumped. Then He Took Over.

text: A picture with the continuation of a front-page article on Thursday about the decaying facilities from the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro was published in error. It showed a closed community pool, not the closed pool that was used for the Olympic canoe slalom course.
match_headline: Legacy of Rio Olympics So Far Is Series of Unkept Promises

text: An article in some editions on Jan. 26 about a report by a New Delhi nonprofit organization on the lack of transparency in India’s political financing misstated, at one point, the percentage of contributions to the country’s political parties in which the source was disclosed to the Election Commission. As noted correctly elsewhere in the article, it was 31 percent, not 69 percent.
match_headline: Pressure Builds for Modi to Overhaul Indian Campaign Finance

text: An article on Jan. 29 about a growing conviction among Japanese that a woman should be allowed to inherit the Chrysanthemum Throne misidentified the member of the royal family who is next in line to Crown Prince Naruhito. He is Naruhito’s younger brother, Prince Akishino, not Prince Hisahito. (Hisahito is Akishino’s son, and would be next in line after him.)
match_headline: Many Japanese Look for a Shift to Female Heirs to the Throne

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Feb. 11 about familial searching, a new crime-solving technique, misstated the name of the organization that held a public meeting on the issue. It was the New York State Commission on Forensic Science, not the National Commission on Forensic Science.
match_headline: Conflicting Views on a Wider Police Use of DNA

text: An article on Friday about an update to Facebook’s mission statement misstated, in some copies, the location of a nightclub massacre last year. It was in Florida, not Paris. (A nightclub massacre in Paris occurred in 2015.)
match_headline: Facebook’s Zuckerberg, Bucking Tide, Takes Public Stand Against Isolationism

text: A column on Thursday misstated the time left in President Trump’s term of office. It is three years, 48 weeks.
match_headline: Well, Trump Watchers, Things Could Be Worse

text: An obituary in some copies on Sunday about Norma McCorvey, the anonymous plaintiff in Roe v. Wade, the 1973 Supreme Court ruling that legalized abortion in the United States, misattributed a passage about abortion. It was Justice Byron White, who dissented in a companion ruling, Doe v. Bolton — not Justice Harry A. Blackmun, who wrote the majority opinion in Roe v. Wade — who said: “At the heart of the controversy in these cases are those recurring pregnancies that pose no danger whatsoever to the life or health of the mother but are nevertheless unwanted for any one or more of a variety of reasons — convenience, family planning, economics, dislike of children, the embarrassment of illegitimacy, etc. The common claim before us is that for any one of such reasons, or for no reason at all, and without asserting or claiming any threat to life or health, any woman is entitled to an abortion at her request if she is able to find a medical adviser willing to undertake the procedure. The Court for the most part sustains this position: during the period prior to the time the fetus becomes viable, the Constitution of the United States values the convenience, whim or caprice of the putative mother more than life or potential life of the fetus.”
match_headline: Norma McCorvey, ‘Roe’ in Roe v. Wade, Is Dead at 69

text: An article on Tuesday about statements from Russian officials regarding contacts with aides to President Trump before the election erroneously stated that Mr. Trump visited Israel during the campaign trip. While he did announce plans to visit, the trip was canceled.
match_headline: Contradicting Trump on Russia: Russian Officials

text: A headline in some editions on Monday with a report in the Sports Briefing column about Kelsey Plum, who moved into second place on the N.C.A.A.’s women’s career scoring list, misidentified her college. As the article correctly noted, she plays for Washington, not for U.C.L.A.
match_headline: An Indoor Football Team Has Its Fans Call the Plays

text: A review on Friday about “Seurat’s Circus Sideshow,” an exhibition of works by the painter Georges Seurat and other artists at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, misstated the number of life-size figures in Fernand Pelez’s “Grimaces and Misery — The Saltimbanques.” There are 11, not nine. Because of an editing error, the review also referred incorrectly to Susan Alyson Stein’s work at the museum. She curates European painting from the 19th Century, not the ninth.
match_headline: Cirque du Seurat at the Metropolitan Museum of Art

text: An article on Feb. 14 about depression in teenagers misstated part of the title of Dr. Benjamin Shain. He is the head of the division of child and adolescent psychiatry — not psychology — at NorthShore University Health System.
match_headline: Is a Teen Depressed, or Just Moody?

text: An article on March 2 about the first leg of a monthlong tour of Asia by King Salman of Saudi Arabia, who brought an entourage worth billions of dollars, referred incorrectly to the 506 tons of cargo that arrived with his entourage aboard half a dozen Boeing jets and a C-130 Hercules. That amount was spread across all of the aircraft; it was not carried only by the Hercules, whose cargo limit is 22 tons.
match_headline: Austerity? Not on This Saudi Itinerary

text: An article and a picture caption on March 4 about the privileges and wealth enjoyed by Brazil’s richest and most powerful citizens at a time when much of the country is enduring a harrowing economic decline misidentified the recipients of a raise in the country’s public sector. Civil servants in the judicial branch, not judges, received a 41 percent raise.
match_headline: Brazil’s Leaders Tout Austerity (Just Not for Them)

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Feb. 27 about Taiwan’s commemoration of the 70th anniversary of the uprising known as the “2/28 Incident,” which led to the massacre of 28,000 Taiwanese by Chiang Kai-shek’s troops, misidentified the authors of a book in which Chou Ching, a journalist, describes the 1947 protests. It was written by Tai Kuo-hui and Yeh I-i, not by Mr. Chou.
match_headline: Taiwan Commemorates a Violent Nationalist Episode, 70 Years Later

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Sunday with an article about the Inuit who harvest mussels in ice caves that form during unusually large tides in northern Quebec misstated, in some editions, the given name of one of the Inuit. As noted correctly in the article, he is Tiisi Qisiiq, not Tilsi.
match_headline: Burrowing Under Luminous Ice to Retrieve Mussels

text: An article on Tuesday about Republican senators’ desire to quickly confirm Judge Neil M. Gorsuch to the Supreme Court described incorrectly the subject of a case currently before the court, Lee v. Tam. It concerns trademarks, not copyrights.
match_headline: Will Gorsuch Join Justices in Time to Matter This Term?

text: A picture caption on March 11 with an article about improved food options at gas stations carried an erroneous credit. The two pictures of Thai Pan, a restaurant at a gas station in Leesburg, Va., were taken by Andrew Mangum, not by Hiroko Masuike.
match_headline: Honey, Please Pick Up Some Grilled Tilapia at the Gas Station

text: An article on Feb. 18 about stand-up comedians at open mike events misspelled the surname of one comic who hosts an open mike at a cabaret and jazz club in the Flatiron district. She is Teresa DeGaetano, not Dagaetano.
match_headline: Inside the Brutal World of Comedy Open Mikes

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Thursday with an article about efforts to create a place that would comprehensively chronicle the AIDS tragedy referred incorrectly to the names that are included at the National AIDS Memorial Grove in San Francisco. The names are of people who died from AIDS or who were affected by the epidemic, not just the ones who died. The article also misstated the year in which Congress designated the site a national memorial. It was 1996, not 1999.
match_headline: An AIDS Museum: The Challenges Are Huge, but the Timing Is Right

text: Because of an editing error, a letter on Sunday, about dealing with offensive ideas on campus, omitted part of a foundation’s name in an identification note. The writer, Robert Weisbuch, is a former president of the Woodrow Wilson National Fellowship Foundation.
match_headline: Dealing With Offensive Ideas on Campus

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Monday about the evolution of the National Front party in France misstated, at one point, the number of candidates opposing Marine Le Pen in the French presidential race. There are 11 candidates on the ballot, not four. (Four are considered to be the major opponents of Ms. Le Pen.)
match_headline: As French Election Nears, Le Pen Targets Voters Her Party Once Repelled

text: A picture caption last Monday with an article about the rise of neo-fascist groups in Europe misidentified Robert Svec, the leader of the Slovak Revival Movement. He was shown second from the right, not third.
match_headline: Once in the Shadows, Europe’s Neo-Fascists Are Re-emerging

text: An article on Thursday about a vaccine for rotavirus referred incorrectly to another vaccine used in Africa. The cholera vaccine typically used there is a liquid; it does not need reconstitution.
match_headline: New Vaccine Could Slow Disease That Kills 600 Children a Day

text: An article on Thursday about open-access publications that publish articles for a fee misspelled the given name of a scholarly communications librarian at the University of Colorado, Denver. He is Jeffrey Beall, not Jeffery. The error was repeated on Friday in a correction about Mr. Beall’s credentials.
match_headline: A Scholarly Sting Operation Shines a Light on ‘Predatory’ Journals

text: An article on Feb. 15 about Intel’s pulling back from its sponsorship of science fairs misstated the time period over which Intel had said it would spend $300 million to diversify its work force. In 2015, it said the money would be spent by 2020, not over three years. The error previously appeared in an article on Jan. 7, 2015, about Intel’s plans to diversify its work force. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Intel Drops Its Sponsorship of Science Fairs, Prompting an Identity Crisis

text: A picture caption on Monday with the On College Basketball column, about factors that led to Gonzaga’s reaching the national championship game, misidentified the Gonzaga player shown with Przemek Karnowski. He is Killian Tillie, not Zach Collins.
match_headline: Gonzaga Earns Chance to Prove It Belongs Among Basketball’s Elite

text: An article in some editions on Monday about South Carolina’s winning the N.C.A.A. women’s basketball title misstated the number of N.C.A.A. titles Geno Auriemma has won at Connecticut. It is 11, not eight.
match_headline: South Carolina Defeats Mississippi State to Win Women’s Title

text: An article in some editions on Monday about a controversial penalty against Lexi Thompson at the ANA Inspiration golf tournament misstated her age in some copies. She is 22, not 21.
match_headline: Lexi Thompson Loses L.P.G.A. Major After Surprise Four-Stroke Penalty

text: An article on Wednesday about the composer Julia Wolfe erroneously included one location where her choral work “Anthracite Fields” will be presented. While it will be performed in Trenton, Amsterdam and Athens, it will not be a part of the Bang on a Can Marathon at the Brooklyn Museum.
match_headline: As Trump Tries to Revive Coal, a Composer Confronts Mining’s Past

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Wednesday about this summer’s Public Theater production of “Julius Caesar” misidentified the character that one of the actors portrays on the television show “Homeland.” Elizabeth Marvel plays the president-elect, not the president.
match_headline: ‘House of Cards’ Stars Join ‘Julius Caesar’ at Shakespeare in the Park

text: An obituary on Saturday about the television producer Noreen Fraser, who led a national campaign against breast cancer, misstated her age when she learned she had the disease. She was 47, not 46.
match_headline: Noreen Fraser, Who Led a Public Fight Against Cancer, Dies at 63

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a poison gas attack in Syria misstated when the government of President Bashar al-Assad renounced chemical weapons. It was nearly four years ago, not nearly five.
match_headline: Worst Chemical Attack in Years in Syria; U.S. Blames Assad

text: An article on March 29 about a decision by the White House staff to skip the White House Correspondents Dinner this year misstated the role that a celebrity or comedian typically plays at the event. A celebrity or comedian typically provides entertainment; that person is neither the host nor the master of ceremonies. (The host is the White House Correspondents’ Association, and the master of ceremonies is the association’s president.)
match_headline: Like Trump, White House Staff Will Skip Correspondents Dinner

text: An article on Tuesday about a ruling by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration in the case of a Wells Fargo whistle-blower misstated, in some references in some editions, the surname of an OSHA regional administrator. She is Barbara Goto, not Gato.
match_headline: Wells Fargo Whistle-Blower Wins $5.4 Million and His Job Back

text: An article on Saturday about the accent and colloquialisms of Roy Williams, coach of North Carolina men’s basketball, misstated the given name of his high school basketball coach. He is Buddy Baldwin, not Buzzy.
match_headline: Roy Williams? ‘He Doesn’t Have an Accent. You Have an Accent.’

text: An article on Saturday about victories by Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer in the semifinals at the Miami Open misstated, in some editions, the round in which Federer defeated Nadal in their previous tournament, the BNP Paribas Open. It was the fourth round, not the third.
match_headline: Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal Will Meet for Miami Open Title

text: An article on page D3 today about new products for men misstates the release date of the Berluti bomber jacket. It is April 18, not April 8.
match_headline: Crystal Creatures, Mr Porter’s California Collection and the Return of PF Flyers

text: A picture on Page D7 today with the On Time column, about the noteworthy watches from Baselworld 2017, was published in error. It is a watch from the Slim d’Hermés collection, but not the Slim d’Hermés L’heure Impatiente described in the article. In addition, a subheading with the article misstates the price of the Hublot MP-09 Tourbillon Bi-Axis watch. It costs $211,000 — not $169,000, which is the price of the titanium model.
match_headline: 16 Noteworthy Watches From Baselworld 2017

text: An article on Thursday about a warning by the American ambassador to the United Nations, Nikki R. Haley, that the United States might take unilateral military action against the Syrian government referred incorrectly to pledges of humanitarian aid made at international donor conferences in 2016 and 2017. The 2016 pledges of more than $12 billion in Syrian relief were for a five-year period, while the 2017 pledges of $6 billion were for a single year. (The 2017 figures did not indicate that donors had pledged at less than half the rate of the previous year.)
match_headline: Nikki Haley Says U.S. May ‘Take Our Own Action’ on Syrian Chemical Attack

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about Gonzaga’s 77-73 victory over South Carolina in the semifinals of the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament misstated Gonzaga’s lead at halftime. It led by 45-36, not 42-36.
match_headline: Gonzaga Beats South Carolina in Final Four for Shot at Another First

text: An article on Thursday about President Trump’s infrastructure plans erroneously included one state among those where operators of toll roads have faced bankruptcy. While operators in Alabama and Virginia have had problems, that is not the case in Michigan because the state has no toll roads. (The operator of a tunnel connecting Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, did have financial problems.)
match_headline: Trump Cuts Leave Bridge and Rail Projects Hanging

text: An obituary on March 24 about the educator Mary Maples Dunn misstated her position at Radcliffe College. She was acting president when Radcliffe merged with Harvard, and she became acting dean of the newly created Radcliffe Institute after the merger; she was not interim dean at the time of the merger.
match_headline: Mary Maples Dunn, Advocate of Women’s Colleges, Dies at 85

text: An article last Sunday comparing streaming services misstated prices for the streaming service Mubi. It is $5.99 a month, not $4.99, and offered a $34.99 yearly subscription only as part of a Black Friday promotion.
match_headline: Cut the Cord, but Keep the Films? Here Are 3 Ways

text: An article last Sunday about choral music attributed incorrectly the statement from 1571 that “in the choir no more shall be used in song that shall drown any word or syllable.” Robert Horne, bishop of Winchester, made the statement, not Archbishop Cranmer.
ref_headline: in the choir no more shall be used in song that shall drown any word or syllable.
match_headline: Nico Muhly on Why Choral Music Is Slow Food for the Soul

text: A picture caption on Feb. 26 with a review of “Jonathan Swift: The Reluctant Rebel,” by John Stubbs, included an erroneous date with the engraving of Swift. The engraving represents him circa 1740, not circa 1800. (Swift died in 1745.)
match_headline: A Life of Jonathan Swift, Beyond Satire

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 26 about Hawaii gave an incorrect English translation of the Hawaiian word “Kilauea.” It is “much spreading,” not “mush spreading.”
match_headline: The Hawaii Cure

text: An article last Sunday about airline fee transparency under the Trump administration misstated the Travel Technology Association’s position on the Transportation Department’s proposal on baggage fees. The group said the proposal did not address whether consumers can purchase add-ons for checked baggage on third party travel websites, not that they could not view them.
match_headline: Trump’s Moves on Airline Fees Prompt Transparency Questions

text: An article last Sunday about the Festival International de Louisiane in Lafayette, La., misspelled the surname of a radio host who commented on the instrumentation in zydeco, a southwest Louisiana musical tradition that is featured in the festival. He is Herman Fuselier, not Fusilier. The article also referred imprecisely to the cultural significance of gumbo. The stew is representative of south Louisiana culture in general, not specifically Acadiana culture.
match_headline: Accordions, Étouffée and Nonstop Dancing in a Zydeco Capital

text: An article last Sunday about the New York real estate heiress Isabel Rose and her daughter’s gender transition misidentified the university that Ms. Rose’s husband, Jeffrey Fagen, attended. It is the University of Pennsylvania, not Dartmouth.
match_headline: My Son, My Daughter: A Mother’s Evolution

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the threat of rising waters on China’s cities as breakneck development collides with climate change carried an erroneous byline. The article was by Michael Kimmelman — not by both Mr. Kimmelman and Josh Haner, who was the photographer.
match_headline: Rising Waters Threaten China’s Rising Cities

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about an attack in Stockholm that killed four people erroneously included one country among those that make up NATO. Sweden is not a member.
match_headline: Stockholm Truck Attack Kills 4; Terrorism Is Suspected

text: An article on Friday about delayed flights on Delta Air Lines referred incorrectly to a press officer for the company. The official, Morgan Durrant, is a man.
match_headline: For Delta Passengers Facing Delays, No Calm After the Storm

text: A picture caption on Saturday with a classical music review about a performance of works by the contemporary Italian composer Salvatore Sciarrino, at Columbia University, misspelled the given name of a member of the ensemble shown. She is Kelley Barnett, not Kelly.
match_headline: Review: Skittering, Creeping Music That Had Me Seeing Things

text: An obituary on Monday about the investor and philanthropist Eugene M. Lang, using information from his family, omitted the name of a survivor and misstated the number of his great-grandchildren. In addition to a daughter and two sons, he is survived by a sister, Barbara Lang, and by eight great-grandchildren, not five.
match_headline: Eugene Lang, Investor Who Made College Dreams a Reality, Dies at 98

text: An article last Wednesday about Matthew Pottinger, who has been advising the Trump Administration on relations with China, referred incorrectly to China’s currency policy. In recent years the country has been intervening to slow the decline of its currency’s value, not allowing the currency to rise.
match_headline: A Veteran and China Hand Advises Trump for Xi’s Visit

text: An article on Tuesday about commercial aircraft sales to Iran misstated the middle initial of the Florida senator who co-wrote a letter to President Trump urging him to suspend licenses for those sales. He is Marco A. Rubio, not Marco J.
match_headline: Iran May Get First New Boeing Jetliner a Year Ahead of Time

text: An article on Monday about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s moving his office to Staten Island for the week misspelled the surname of a former Staten Island borough president. He is Guy V. Molinari, not Molanari.
match_headline: With ‘Listening Tour,’ de Blasio Tries Courting Staten Island. Again.

text: An article on Tuesday about legislation that changes the way in which New York State deals with 16- and 17-year-old defendants, diverting the majority of those cases to Family Court, referred incorrectly to the death of Kalief Browder, a minor who was held with adult prisoners. He died at his home, in the Bronx — not at the jail complex on Rikers Island.
match_headline: ‘Raise the Age,’ Now Law in New York, Is Still a Subject of Debate

text: An obituary on Sunday about the actress and dancer Chelsea Brown misspelled the given name of one of her fellow performers on the television show “Rowan & Martin’s Laugh-In.” She is Jo Anne Worley, not Jo Ann. The obituary also included a quotation from George Schlatter, the executive producer of “Laugh-In,” that misidentified the cast member who played chess with Ms. Brown in a sketch on the show. It was Ms. Worley, not Arte Johnson.
match_headline: Chelsea Brown, of ‘Laugh-In,’ Dies at 74

text: A news analysis article on Wednesday about President Trump’s relationship with Russia misspelled the surname of a former acting director of the Central Intelligence Agency. He is Michael Morell, not Morrell.
match_headline: Trump’s Shift on Russia Brings Geopolitical Whiplash

text: An article on Sunday about a legal dispute in China over a large meteorite found in 1986 by a Kazakh herder, Juman Reamazhaen, paraphrased incorrectly from Mr. Reamazhaen’s account of his discovery. He said he had not noticed the meteorite before that day; he did not say that it had appeared overnight.
match_headline: Meteorite Finder Fights China’s (Mostly Terrestrial) Property Law

text: An article on Thursday about a new Hungarian law apparently intended to shut down the Central European University in Budapest misspelled the given name of the acting spokesman for the State Department. He is Mark C. Toner, not Marc.
match_headline: Hungary Law That Could Close Soros-Backed University Faces Uncertainty

text: An article on Thursday about the death of Sheila Abdus-Salaam, an associate judge on the New York State Court of Appeals and the first African-American woman to serve on that bench, erroneously included one job among her legal accomplishments. Judge Abdus-Salaam never worked for the New York City Law Department.
match_headline: Sheila Abdus-Salaam, Judge on New York’s Top Court, Is Found Dead in Hudson River
