text: An article on Thursday about anger at United Airlines after a passenger was dragged off a flight before it left Chicago for Louisville, Ky., misstated the surname of a spokeswoman for the Chicago Department of Aviation. She is Karen E. Pride, not Price.
match_headline: United Airlines Offers Refunds as Outrage at a Violent Removal Continues

text: An article on Saturday about Patrick Ewing’s first days as the men’s basketball coach at Georgetown University erroneously included one coach among former N.B.A. players who went directly from the pro game to college coaching. Bobby Hurley was a coach at three colleges before taking over at Arizona State.
match_headline: Patrick Ewing’s Slip Shows Need to Learn N.C.A.A. Recruiting Rules

text: An article in some editions on April 6 about the Mets’ 3-1 loss to the Atlanta Braves misstated the number of pitches the Mets’ Jacob deGrom threw during the 2016 season. It was 2,353 — not 1,549, which is the number of strikes he threw.
match_headline: Jacob deGrom Displays His Old Form, but the Mets Sputter

text: An article in some editions on April 5 about the Yankees’ 5-0 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays misstated, in some copies, the number of home runs Yankees shortstop Didi Gregorius hit last season. It was 20, not 21.
match_headline: Small in Stature, Yankees’ Ronald Torreyes Makes a Towering Statement

text: An article on Monday about a home run by Tim Tebow in his first at-bat for the Columbia Fireflies, the Mets’ Class A affiliate, misspelled the hometown of Jeff Reed, a fan who attended a recent game. It is Blythewood, S.C., not Blythwood.
match_headline: Tebow’s 2nd Act Has South Carolina Giving Him the 1st-Class Treatment

text: An obituary on Thursday about the children’s-book author Patricia McKissack misspelled the given name of her husband, who was also her collaborator, and that of one of their sons. Her husband was Fredrick, not Frederick, as is the son named for him. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Patricia McKissack, Prolific Author Who Championed Black Heroes, Dies at 72

text: An obituary on Thursday about the former federal prosecutor and judge Frederick B. Lacey misstated the name of a bank that was part of an investigation he conducted. It is Banca Nazionale del Lavoro, not Lavora.
match_headline: Frederick B. Lacey, Who Prosecuted Corruption in New Jersey, Dies at 96

text: An obituary on Monday about Masha Leon, the longtime society columnist for the Jewish newspaper The Forward, misstated the name of another publication that published her work. It is Tablet, not The Tablet.
match_headline: Masha Leon, Society Columnist and Holocaust Survivor, Dies at 86

text: A picture caption on Friday with the continuation of an article about the battle over public lands in the West misstated Monument Valley’s relationship to the Bears Ears National Monument. While Monument Valley is near Bears Ears, it is not part of the national monument.
match_headline: Siege Has Ended, but Battle Over Public Lands Rages On

text: An obituary on Saturday about the computer scientist Robert W. Taylor misidentified the institution from which he earned a bachelor’s degree. It is the University of Texas at Austin (where he also did graduate work), not Southern Methodist University in Dallas.
match_headline: Robert Taylor, Innovator Who Shaped Modern Computing, Dies at 85

text: An article on Friday about Immigration and Customs Enforcement requirements for jails that will house detained immigrants misstated the frequency with which bedsheets must be changed. It is once a week, not once a day. The article also referred incorrectly to a requirement for the thickness of trash bags. Only bags used for blood and bodily fluid cleanup must be 1.5 millimeters thick; that requirement does not include all trash bags.
match_headline: Trump Plan Would Curtail Protections for Detained Immigrants

text: An article on Saturday about the artist Kenyatta A.C. Hinkle misstated the closing date of her current exhibition, “The Evanesced,” at the California African American Museum in Los Angeles. The show runs through June 25, not June 2.
match_headline: One Artist’s Melancholy Look at Missing African-American Women

text: Because of an editing error, a picture on Friday with a film review of “Little Boxes” carried an erroneous caption in some editions. The caption named three actors — Nelsan Ellis, Melanie Lynskey and Armani Jackson, but Mr. Jackson was not shown. A picture showing all three of the actors can be found at nytimes.com/movies .
match_headline: Review: In ‘Little Boxes,’ a Biracial Family Meets a White Town

text: An article on Friday about the new Museum of the American Revolution, which opens in Philadelphia on Wednesday, misstated the name of the historic Philadelphia building that is a few blocks away. It is Independence Hall, not Constitution Hall.
match_headline: A New Museum of the American Revolution, Warts and All

text: An article on Friday about donors to President Trump’s inauguration described incorrectly Fertitta Entertainment, which contributed $500,000. The company owns casinos and restaurant chains, not the Ultimate Fighting Championship. (A company also named Fertitta Entertainment owns the UFC.)
match_headline: From N.F.L. Owners to Florida Retirees, a Who’s Who of Inaugural Donors

text: An article last Saturday about financial aid appeals for college students misstated at one point, in some editions, the surname of the chief executive of the Independent Educational Consultants Association. He is Mark Sklarow, not Skarlow.
match_headline: To Trim the Tuition Bill, Haggle (or Hire a Haggler)

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about the exhibition “Calder/Miró: Constellations,” using information from Acquavella Galleries, misstates the number of paintings by Miró in the show. It is 22, not 23. (One painting that was to have been on loan to Acquavella was withdrawn and the gallery substituted a print; The Times discovered the change after the section had gone to press.)
match_headline: Miró, Calder and a Convergence of ‘Constellations’

text: An article on Page 114 this weekend about the quirky, unconventional work of the French artist Sophie Calle, which blurs the distinction between art and life, misidentifies the medium in which her “The Birthday Ceremony” series and her “Voir la mer” series were made. “The Birthday Ceremony” is comprised of sculptures, not photographs, and “Voir la mer” is comprised of digital films, not photographs. The article also omits part of the title of a Calle show. It is “My Mother, My Cat, My Father, in that order” — not merely “My Mother, My Cat, My Father.” In addition, the article misstates the year a show by Calle will open at the Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature. It will be shown starting in October 2017, not 2018. The article also misstates part of the name of the organization curating Calle’s upcoming show “Sophie Calle: Missing.” It is Ars Citizen, not Arts Citizen. And, finally, the article refers incorrectly to Calle’s connection to a burial plot at Green-Wood cemetery in Brooklyn. She was offered the plot as part of a site-specific project she is making there; she has not bought a burial plot there.
match_headline: The Fertile Mind of Sophie Calle

text: An obituary on April 1 about the lawyer and former transportation secretary William T. Coleman erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He was one of first black members of the Harvard Law Review, not the first. (Charles Hamilton Houston had served on the board in the early 20th century.) The obituary also misstated the year Mr. Coleman graduated from Harvard Law School. It was 1946, not 1947. In addition, the obituary referred imprecisely to Mr. Coleman’s military service in World War II. He joined the Army Air Forces — not the Army Air Corps, which was a component of the Army Air Forces.
match_headline: William T. Coleman Jr., Who Broke Racial Barriers in Court and Cabinet, Dies at 96

text: An article last Sunday about efforts to investigate and prosecute cases of war crimes committed in Syria referred incorrectly to a case against Syrian officials that has been filed in a court in Spain. It is one of such cases pending, but not the only one. (Investigations are also open in France and Germany.)
match_headline: As Atrocities Mount in Syria, Justice Seems Out of Reach

text: An article last Sunday about the hacking group Shadow Brokers’ release of a trove of highly classified hacking tools used to break into Microsoft systems, which may have been used by the National Security Agency, referred incorrectly to software that was not affected by N.S.A. hacking tools. It is Windows 10, not Microsoft 10. (There is no such software by that name.)
match_headline: Hacking Group Claims N.S.A. Infiltrated Mideast Banking System

text: An article last Sunday about political television shows in the Trump era misspelled, on first reference, the name of a “House of Cards” showrunner. She is Melissa James Gibson, not Melissa Jane Gibson.
match_headline: How to Write TV in the Age of Trump: Showrunners Reveal All

text: An article on April 9 about CNN misidentified the news outlet that first reported the existence of an intelligence dossier containing private information that Russia was said to have collected on Donald Trump. It was reported by the magazine Mother Jones, not by CNN. (CNN later broke the news that United States intelligence officials had briefed President-elect Trump on the possibility that Russia had compromising information about his activities.)
match_headline: CNN Had a Problem. Donald Trump Solved It.

text: An article on April 16 about Japanese photography after the 2011 earthquake, tsunami and nuclear disaster misidentified the medium in which Shimpei Takeda made photograms from radioactive soil. He exposed the soil to photosensitive film, not photosensitive paper.
match_headline: Pictures in the Aftermath

text: An article last Sunday about French influences in Harlem misidentified the birthplace of Fabrice Warin, owner of Barawine Harlem. He was born in Bordeaux, not in Alsace.
match_headline: Harlem’s French Renaissance

text: An article last Sunday about drinking in Brno, Czech Republic, referred incorrectly to the city’s location. It is southeast of Prague, not southwest.
match_headline: In Brno, Drinks for Morning, Noon and Night

text: An article on April 9 about southern Laos rendered the name of a local beer incorrectly. It is Beerlao, not Beer Lao.
match_headline: Along the Mekong River, a Timeless Place Where Time Marches On

text: A review on April 9 about Paul Watson’s “ Ice Ghosts: The Epic Hunt for the Lost Franklin Expedition ” misstated the role that Jim Balsillie, one of the participants in the hunt, played at Research in Motion, the makers of the BlackBerry smartphone. He is a former co-chief executive of the company, not one of its founders.
ref_headline: Ice Ghosts: The Epic Hunt for the Lost Franklin Expedition
match_headline: The Hunt for Ships Trapped in the Canadian Ice Nearly 170 Years Ago

text: An article last Sunday about Maureen Chiquet, a former executive with Chanel, misspelled the surname of an artist whose work decorates Ms. Chiquet’s home. She is Alice Neel, not Neal.
match_headline: Maureen Chiquet’s Move From Chanel to Self-Empowerment

text: An article in the Mutual Fund Quarterly last Sunday about the growth in inflows to the index fund giant Vanguard misspelled the given name of the executive who oversees its retail investor group. She is Karin A. Risi, not Karen. (The error was repeated in a picture caption.)
match_headline: Vanguard Is Growing Faster Than Everybody Else Combined

text: An article last Sunday about financial abuse of older people referred incorrectly to systems for complaints and intervention in suspected cases. Though the federal government has no such system, each state has its own; it is not the case that there is no government-run system.
match_headline: Declaring War on Financial Abuse of Older People

text: An article last Monday about Slack Technologies and the competition it faces from larger companies misstated the number of employees at R/GA, whose chief technology officer commented on the use of Slack’s software. It is 2,000, not 1,000.
match_headline: Slack, an Upstart in Messaging, Now Faces Giant Tech Rivals

text: An article on Wednesday about Goldman Sachs’s earnings misstated, in some copies, the position that R. Martin Chavez, Goldman’s incoming chief financial officer, previously held with the company. He was chief information officer, not chief technology officer.
match_headline: Goldman’s Dim Trading Results Raise Eyebrows on Wall St.

text: An article on Tuesday about a potential walkout by the Writers Guild of America misstated the year of a previous strike. It was 1988, not 1998.
match_headline: With a Hollywood Writers’ Strike Looming, Here’s What to Know

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an article about the Boston Marathon misspelled the surname of the winner of the men’s race in some copies. As the article correctly noted, he is Geoffrey Kirui, not Kiriu.
match_headline: First Woman to Enter Boston Marathon Runs It Again, 50 Years Later

text: Because of an editing error, an article on April 5 about N.H.L. players’ reactions to a decision by the league that they could not participate in the 2018 Winter Olympics referred incorrectly in some copies to games being played in Sweden next season. They are regular-season games, not preseason games.
match_headline: N.H.L.’s Olympics Stance Leaves Players Cold

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the influence of the real-estate industry on tax issues referred incorrectly to the makeup of Congress when it approved a 1986 tax overhaul. Republicans were in the majority in the Senate and Democrats controlled the House; there was not a “Democratic Congress” then.
match_headline: Trump's Industry, Real Estate, Poses Hurdle to Tax Overhaul

text: An article on Sunday about people outside the White House whose advice is sought by President Trump referred incorrectly to one such informal adviser, Robert Kraft, the owner of the New England Patriots. Mr. Kraft’s loyalty to the president dates partly to Mr. Trump’s thoughtfulness when Mr. Kraft’s wife died, not when his father died. The article also referred imprecisely to the legal credentials of Sheri A. Dillon. While she has advised President Trump on ethics issues, she specializes in tax law; she is not an “ethics lawyer.”
match_headline: Trump Reaches Beyond West Wing for Counsel

text: A picture caption on Sunday with an article about an Afghan woman with dementia who has been ordered deported from Denmark misidentified the woman, Zarmena Waziri, in some copies. In the 1989 photograph of her family, she is the second woman from the right, not from the left.
match_headline: Old, Ill and Ordered Deported From Denmark to Afghanistan

text: An article on Thursday about three Americans now being detained in North Korea misstated the age of one of them, Otto F. Warmbier. He is 22, not 21.
match_headline: Imprisoned in North Korea: The Cases of 3 Americans

text: A listing on the Square Feet page on Wednesday misstated the surname of a landlord broker at 535 Zerega Avenue in the Bronx. He is Josh Gopan, not Gopa.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: A picture caption with an article on the Square Feet page on April 19 about the West Kowloon Cultural District and coming M+ museum of visual culture referred incorrectly to the construction site shown. It is the future location of the West Kowloon Cultural District Art Park, not the M+ museum itself.
match_headline: Amid Delays, Hong Kong’s Ambitious Museum Plan Takes Shape

text: An article on Monday about Yankees catcher Austin Romine misstated, in some copies, the Yankees’ record in games that he had started this season. At the time, they had won eight of 10 games, not nine of 11.
match_headline: Before Crouching Behind Yankees’ Plate, Austin Romine Brushes Away Adversity

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Armand Duplantis, a top high school pole-vaulter, misstated, in some copies, the world record held by the French pole-vaulter Renaud Lavillenie. It is 20 feet 2 1/2 inches, not 20 feet 1/2 inch.
match_headline: At 17, ‘the Tiger Woods of Pole Vaulting’ Soars Ahead of His Time

text: An article on Saturday about Latrobe Country Club’s first golf season after Arnold Palmer’s death misstated the surname of a member of Palmer’s regular golf group at the club. He is Marty Newingham, not Newington.
match_headline: Arnold Palmer’s Hometown Golf Course Adjusts to Life Without Him

text: A picture caption on Thursday with the continuation of a review of “Der Fliegende Holländer,” at the Metropolitan Opera, misidentified the performer shown with Amber Wagner, who sings the role of Senta. He is Franz-Josef Selig, portraying the character Daland; not AJ Glueckert, who performs the part of Erik.
match_headline: Review: Met Opera’s Next Music Director Captains a Blazing ‘Dutchman’

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Robert M. Pirsig, the author of “Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance,” referred incorrectly to a New York Times review of that book. The review, written by Christopher Lehmann-Haupt, did not compare Mr. Pirsig to Thoreau.
ref_headline: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance,
match_headline: Robert M. Pirsig, Author of ‘Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance,’ Dies at 88

text: An article on Sunday, about demonstrations in Russia, misquoted an outspoken critic of the Kremlin, Aleksei A. Navalny. In a recent video, Mr. Navalny said that four charities had spent $66 million to maintain luxury residences for Prime Minister Dmitri A. Medvedev, not $66 billion.
match_headline: Thousands of Russians Present Letters of Protest in Demonstrations

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about a threat to the street-food culture in Southeast Asia misidentified a Vietnamese dish shown in a bowl in the photo. It is banh da cua, not bun cha.
match_headline: Efforts to Ease Congestion Threaten Street Food Culture in Southeast Asia

text: A picture with an article on Sunday, about a judge overturning part of the bail system in Houston, was published in error. It showed a building that was once the Harris County jail, it is no longer used for that purpose.
match_headline: Judge in Houston Strikes Down Harris County’s Bail System

text: An article on Saturday about the Los Angeles riots in 1992 misstated the makeup of the jury that acquitted four white police officers in the beating of Rodney King. It included an Asian juror and a Hispanic juror, it was not all-white.
match_headline: The L.A. Riots 25 Years Later: A Return to the Epicenter

text: A listing in The Conversation on April 20 of most-read articles, about the suicide of the former N.F.L. player Aaron Hernandez, misstated the prevalence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy among former N.F.L. players. While it has been found in dozens of former players, research is continuing and it is not known to be “extremely common.”
match_headline: Aaron Hernandez’s Brain Will Be Donated to C.T.E. Research Center

text: An article in the Gallery Guide on Friday about art galleries on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, including the Craig F. Starr Gallery, where an exhibition of paintings by John Baldessari is on view, misstated the city in California depicted in some of his artworks. It is National City, not Los Angeles.
match_headline: 11 Galleries to Visit Now on the Upper East Side and in Harlem

text: An obituary on Saturday, about the performance artist Vito Acconci, misstated his date of birth. It was Jan. 24, 1940, not Jan. 4.
match_headline: Vito Acconci, Performance Artist and Uncommon Architect, Dies at 77

text: An article on Tuesday about calls by President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela to rewrite his country’s Constitution misstated the timing of a Supreme Court decision to strip power from the National Assembly. It was handed down in March, not April.
match_headline: Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela President, Calls for a Rewrite of the Constitution

text: An article on April 25 about a United Nations commission investigating possible war crimes in Syria misstated the number of witnesses and victims it has interviewed. The number is now more than 5,200, not more than 1,400.
match_headline: U.N. Documents Syrian War Crimes, but Prosecution Moves Slowly

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s plan to end the federal deduction for state and local taxes misstated a reason some taxpayers can deduct sales taxes from their federal returns. In Nevada and Washington, it is because the states have no state income taxes, not “low” income taxes.
match_headline: State and Local Tax Deduction: An Item Blurring Party Lines

text: An article on Saturday about Theo Epstein’s return to Boston after winning a World Series with the Chicago Cubs misidentified the highway he crossed on his walk to Fenway Park on Friday. It is I-90, not I-95.
match_headline: Theo Epstein, Conquering Hero, Returns With Chicago Cubs to Fenway Park

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about soccer clubs changing their logos misstated the year the Liverpool Football Club was founded. As an accompanying picture correctly showed, it was 1892, not 1872.
match_headline: In Soccer, Teams Change Logos at Their Peril

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the American diplomat Malcolm Toon referred incorrectly to the fate of SALT II, an arms agreement with the Soviet Union that Mr. Toon took part in negotiating. President Jimmy Carter withdrew it from Senate consideration; it was not the case that “the Senate voted not to ratify it.” Because of another editing error, the obituary misstated the distance between Boston and Northborough, Mass., where Mr. Toon grew up. It is about 35 miles, not about 50.
ref_headline: the Senate voted not to ratify it.
match_headline: Malcolm Toon Made Waves as a Diplomat, but His Death Went Largely Unreported

text: An article on Sunday about American far-right activists who promoted a hacking attack on Emmanuel Macron, the centrist candidate for president of France, erroneously attributed a distinction to Marie Antoinette, to whom Mr. Macron was compared in some internet memes. She was the last queen of France before the French Revolution; she was not France’s last queen. (That was Maria Amalia of Naples and Sicily, wife of Louis-Philippe I.)
match_headline: U.S. Far-Right Activists Promote Hacking Attack Against Macron

text: An article on Tuesday about Taiwan’s efforts to gain inclusion in the World Health Assembly’s annual meeting misstated the year the United Nations ejected Taiwan, known formally as the Republic of China, and turned its former seat over to the People’s Republic of China instead. It happened in 1971, not 1979.
match_headline: Blocked by China, Taiwan Presses to Join U.N. Agency’s Meeting

text: A news analysis article on Monday about policy debates on social issues like health care and hunger misidentified the administration in which Ron Haskins, who commented on the war on poverty, was an adviser. He served under President George W. Bush, not Mr. Bush’s father.
match_headline: On Health and Welfare, Moral Arguments Can Outweigh Economics

text: An article on April 18 about a major reorganization of Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s second-term administration, using information from the governor’s office, erroneously attributed a distinction to Melissa DeRosa, secretary to the governor. At 34, she is not in fact the youngest person to hold that job. (At least one other person, Gerald C. Crotty, was younger when he was appointed to it in 1985, at age 33.)
match_headline: Cuomo Promotes Chief of Staff, Melissa DeRosa, to Be His Secretary

text: An article on Monday about plans by the Sinclair Broadcasting Group to buy Tribune Media misstated the share of television station ownership that the company would achieve with the acquisition. It would own about 15 percent of local commercial stations, not more than a third of them.
match_headline: Sinclair Is Said to Be Near a Deal for Tribune Media

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an obituary about the former East German defense minister Heinz Kessler misidentified the former East German leader Erich Honecker, who was shown with Mr. Kessler in a 1949 photograph. Mr. Honecker was at the right, not in the center. (Information supplied with the photograph did not identify the man in the center.)
match_headline: Heinz Kessler, Who Led East Germany’s Military, Dies at 97

text: A review last Wednesday about Loring Place misidentified the firm that designed the restaurant’s interior. It is Cycle Projects, not Cycle Architecture & Planning.
match_headline: ‘Vegetable Forward’ Chef Gets His Own Patch at Loring Place

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s dismissal of James B. Comey as director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation misstated Mr. Comey’s tenure in that position. He was in his fourth year when he was fired, not in his third. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption. The error was also repeated on Wednesday in an article about the historical context of the dismissal.
match_headline: F.B.I. Director James Comey Is Fired by Trump

text: Because of an editing error, an article on April 17 about Hispanic clergy in the Southwest who support the preservation of the Colorado River referred incorrectly at one point to the Rev. Helia Martinez, who explained how the area was dependent on the water. Rev. Martinez is a woman.
match_headline: To These Pastors, Saving the Colorado River Is a Divine Command

text: An article on Tuesday about the Synchrotron-light for Experimental Science and Applications in the Middle East, or Sesame, project erroneously included one country on a list of those participating as members. While Bahrain was involved in the project initially, it is not currently a member.
match_headline: A Light for Science, and Cooperation, in the Middle East

text: An article last Thursday about the style of Emmanuel Macron misstated the name of the school where Anja Aronowsky Cronberg, an expert on fashion semiotics, is a senior research fellow. It is London College of Fashion, not London School of Fashion.
match_headline: The Look of the French Election

text: An article on Friday about ticket sales for a Yankee game at which Derek Jeter’s number will be retired misidentified the job that Kevin Burke holds at StubHub. He is a spokesman for the ticket site, not a senior vice president there.
match_headline: Yankee Fans May Be Looking Forward, but Jeter Is Still a Draw

text: A picture credit on Friday with an article about the singer Harry Styles, using information from a publicist, misidentified the photographer. The picture, of Mr. Styles, is by Jamie-James Medina, not by Harley Weir.
match_headline: Harry Styles Opens Up, Slightly, About Going Solo With a Rock Edge

text: An obituary on Friday about Stan Weston, the creator of the action figure G.I. Joe, using information from his family, omitted the name of one of his survivors. They also include a half sister, Ann Sowers.
match_headline: Stan Weston, 84, Dies; Sent G.I. Joe Marching Into Childhoods of Millions

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the band At the Drive-In, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the band that Omar Rodríguez-López and Cedric Bixler-Zavala performed with in 2001. It was De Facto, not the Mars Volta. (The two also formed the Mars Volta.)
match_headline: At the Drive In Rekindles Its Manic Inferno

text: An article last Sunday about the Metropolitan Opera’s 50th anniversary at Lincoln Center misspelled the given name of a performer in the 1966-67 season. She is Birgit Nilsson, not Brigit.
match_headline: Is the Met Opera Too Big? And Other Questions as Its Home Turns 50

text: An article last Sunday about different film stars’ audition experiences misspelled part of the title of the coming “Transformers” film. It is “Transformers: The Last Knight,” not “The Last Night.”
match_headline: Actors Share How They Got the Job

text: An entry on the hardcover fiction best-seller list on April 30 misidentified the sport coached by one of the characters in Lisa Scottoline’s “One Perfect Lie.” It is baseball, not basketball. The error was repeated on the combined print and ebook fiction list.

A review on April 23 about “Falstaff,” by Harold Bloom, misquoted an observation by Samuel Johnson, one of Bloom’s favorite critics on the Shakespearean character who is the subject of his book. Johnson wrote, “Men more frequently require to be reminded than informed” — not “People need to be reminded more often than they need to be instructed,” which is a paraphrase of Johnson by C.S. Lewis in his book “Mere Christianity.”
match_headline: Shakespeare’s Hot Mess: What We Can Learn From Falstaff

text: An article on April 30 about a young woman who was disoriented and vomiting misidentified the university that she and her older sister attended. It is the University of Arizona, Tucson, not Banner University, which does not exist. Banner University Medical Center Tucson, a hospital on the campus of the University of Arizona, Tucson, is where the woman was treated.
match_headline: What Caused This College Student’s Stomach Pain and Vomiting?

text: Because of a transcription error, an article on April 30 about a new Netflix series based on “Anne of Green Gables” included an incorrect word in dialogue from the series. The character Anne Shirley says, “Shouldn’t we hold hands over a running stream and pledge ourselves to each other as Cuthberts forever, or prick our fingers and mingle our blood as a symbol of our lasting devotion?” The character does not say “break our fingers.”
match_headline: The Other Side of Anne of Green Gables

text: An article last Sunday about Manhattan natives who cannot afford to live there as adults but are finding that there is life in other boroughs misidentified, in some editions, the birthplace of Michelle Bar, who now lives in NoHo, and misstated the surname of her boyfriend. Ms. Bar was born on the Upper East Side, not the Upper West Side, and her boyfriend is Alex Gumer, not Grommer.
match_headline: Growing Up in, and Outgrowing, Manhattan

text: A picture credit last Sunday with an article about the Court Square section of Long Island City, Queens, using information from a developer, misstated the surname of a photographer. He is Ed Lederman, not Lederer.
match_headline: Long Island City Grows Ever Skyward

text: A picture caption accompanying an article last Sunday about St. Croix misidentified a former plantation on the island. It is Estate Whim Museum, not Estate Cane Garden.
match_headline: The West Indian Island That Shaped Alexander Hamilton

text: An article on April 30 about millennials in Mexican wine country misspelled the name of a food truck offering. The truck parked at Adobe Guadalupe serves duck tortas, not tortes.
match_headline: Millennials Answer the Call of Mexican Wine Country

text: Because of an editing error, the Check In column last Sunday, about the Meliá Braco Village resort in Jamaica, omitted the byline. The article was by Steve Knopper.
match_headline: Beachside in Jamaica, Where the Frills Are the Sun and Sea

text: An article on April 30 about Warm Showers, an online hospitality organization for bicyclists, misidentified the state where the Warm Showers host Phillip Michael Long offered lodging. It was in Kelso, Wash., not Kelso, Ore. An accompanying picture caption misidentified a person sitting at a dining table in Santa Rosa, Calif. It is Alex Corcoran, not Chris Lang.
match_headline: For Road-Weary Cyclists, a Room, a Couch, Maybe Even a Meal.

text: An article last Sunday about the Marciano Art Foundation, one of several new Los Angeles institutions making use of existing buildings, described incorrectly the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, which gave its name to the foundation’s home on Wilshire Boulevard. The Scottish Rite is a series of degrees awarded by Masonic groups; it is not the Scottish branch of the Masons.
match_headline: L.A. Reincarnation: New Art Spaces in Vintage Settings

text: An article last Sunday about Robert Rauschenberg described incorrectly the role that he filled for a decade with the Merce Cunningham Dance Company. He was its resident designer, not its artistic director.
match_headline: For Robert Rauschenberg, No Artist Is an Island

text: Because of an editing error, a review on May 14 about “Survivors Club: The True Story of a Very Young Prisoner of Auschwitz,” by Michael Bornstein and Debbie Bornstein Holinstat, misidentified the country in which Chiune Sugihara, a Japanese diplomat, was serving when he issued thousands of transit visas for Jews to flee to Japan during World War II. It was Lithuania, not Poland.
ref_headline: Survivors Club: The True Story of a Very Young Prisoner of Auschwitz,
match_headline: A Moving Holocaust Memoir for Younger Readers, and Older Ones Too

text: A review on May 14 about “Yvain the Knight of the Lion,” by M. T. Anderson, erroneously attributed a distinction to the 12th-century poet Chrétien de Troyes, who wrote the poem on which the book is based. He was not “the original source” of the King Arthur stories; elements of the legend appear in various sources that predate Chrétien’s work.
ref_headline: Yvain the Knight of the Lion,
match_headline: A Knight’s Epic Quest, and the Perils of Chivalry

text: Because of an editing error, a review on May 14 about “Mighty, Mighty Construction Site,” by Sherri Duskey Rinker, misspelled the surname of the book’s illustrator. He is Tom Lichtenheld, not Lichenheld.
match_headline: New Picture Books for Young Vehicle Lovers

text: An article on May 14 about open marriages described incorrectly a detail about child care in one marriage. Blake Wilson and Joe Spurr are equally involved in the day-to-day care of Spurr and Zaeli Kane’s child; Wilson does not do more of it.
match_headline: Is an Open Marriage a Happier Marriage?

text: An article last Sunday about the prominent Buddhists Nena and Robert Thurman referred incorrectly to Mr. Thurman’s vision. He lost sight in his left eye, not his right.
match_headline: 50 Years of Marriage and Mindfulness With Nena and Robert Thurman

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Simone Matthew and Joseph McElroy misidentified the city where Brenda L. Hughes, the bride’s mother, lives. It is Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago — not Port-au-Prince, Haiti.
match_headline: Simone Matthew and Joseph McElroy: A Cat Named Mehitabel, a Lowercase Cockroach and Love

text: An article last Sunday about 10 waterside destinations in Europe described the location of the Guggenheim Bilbao, in Bilbao, Spain, incorrectly. It is about 60 miles east of the city of Santander, not west .
match_headline: East Meets West, and Cafe Becomes Sake Bar, at Hi-Collar

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Russian proxy support for fringe political figures in Central and Eastern Europe referred incorrectly to requests made to the office of a Russian billionaire for money to finance pro-Russian politicians in Polish elections. The requests came directly from Alexander Usovsky, a Belarus-born writer and agitator, not from an assistant.
match_headline: Foot Soldiers in a Shadowy Battle Between Russia and the West

text: An article on Tuesday about Representative Rodney Frelinghuysen, Republican of New Jersey, omitted part of the reporting credit. The writer, Nancy Solomon, is a reporter for WNYC and New Jersey Public Radio.
match_headline: Political Winds Leave New Jersey Lawmaker Caught Between Party and Home

text: An article on Tuesday about the box-office success of the Broadway musical “A Bronx Tale” misstated the gross receipts in a recent week for another musical, the revival of “Hello, Dolly!” starring Bette Midler. “Hello, Dolly!” brought in $1.93 million, not $1.64 million. The article also misstated the week in which those sales occurred. It was the week of May 15, not last week.
match_headline: The ‘Bronx Tale’ Strategy: Win Suburban Love, Not Broadway Prestige

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a bombing at an ice cream shop in Baghdad misstated the trend in the number of terrorist attacks in the city. Such attacks have declined this year, compared with 2016; they have not increased.
match_headline: ISIS Blasts Kill Dozens at Family Gatherings, This Time in Iraq

text: A news analysis article on Monday about American-Iranian diplomacy misidentified one country among a group of nations, known as the P5+1, involved in negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program. Besides Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States, the group also included Germany, but not Iran.
match_headline: As Iran and U.S. Leaders Trade Barbs, Big Deals Proceed

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about transgender graduates at the military academies misstated the medical procedure being done by one of the graduates, Blake Dremann. He is transitioning from female to male, not the other way around.
match_headline: Loophole in Rules on Transgender Troops Denies 2 Their Commissions

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the sportswriter Frank Deford referred incorrectly to the career of the sportswriter Tony Kornheiser. He was not one of the journalists hired by The National Sports Daily, edited by Mr. Deford, in the early 1990s.
match_headline: Frank Deford, a Literary Storyteller of Sport, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on May 20 about the costume designer Jeanne Button, using information from a family member, misspelled the given name of her second husband, who died in 2013. He was MacDonald Eaton, not McDonald.
match_headline: Jeanne Button, Designer of Whimsical Costumes, Dies at 86

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the novelist and memoirist Ann Birstein misstated part of the title of a book by her former husband, Alfred Kazin. It is “An American Procession,” not “The American Procession.”
match_headline: Ann Birstein, Memoirist and Novelist, Dies at 89

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the novelist Denis Johnson misstated one of the call letters of a Santa Monica radio station whose podcast “Bookworm” interviewed him. The station is KCRW, not WCRW.
match_headline: Denis Johnson, Who Wrote of the Failed and the Desperate, Dies at 67

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump’s growing discontent with Attorney General Jeff Sessions summarized incorrectly comments that Alan M. Dershowitz made during the 2016 election. Mr. Dershowitz, a professor emeritus at Harvard Law School, regularly defended the civil liberties of Donald J. Trump and Hillary Clinton. He did not regularly defend Mr. Trump.
match_headline: Trump Grows Discontented With Attorney General Jeff Sessions

text: An article on Monday about the Navy’s plans to name a warship after Gabrielle Giffords, a former Democratic member of Congress from Arizona, misidentified the previous Navy warship to be named after a living woman. It is the Lady Washington, not the Harriet Lane.
match_headline: Warship Named for Giffords Is Close to Being Ready for Sea

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption and a subheading on Tuesday with an article about a United States senator’s decision to cancel an appearance on “Real Time With Bill Maher” misstated the senator’s surname in some editions. As the article correctly noted, he is Al Franken, not Franklin.
match_headline: Al Franken Cancels Appearance on ‘Real Time With Bill Maher’

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Monday with the “What’s on TV” listings misidentified the actor shown with Audrey Hepburn in a scene from “Roman Holiday.” He was Gregory Peck, not Gary Cooper.
match_headline: What’s on TV Monday: ‘The Bachelorette’ and ‘If You’re Not in the Obit, Eat Breakfast’

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about animal farms in Southeast Asia misstated part of the name of a park in Chiang Mai, Thailand, where tourists were shown posing with a tiger. It is Tiger Kingdom, not Tiger World.
match_headline: Asia’s Illegal Wildlife Trade Makes Tigers a Farm-to-Table Meal

text: A picture on Thursday with an obituary about the author Juan Goytisolo was published in error. The man shown in a scene from the film “Notre Musique” was Jean-Christophe Bouvet, not Mr. Goytisolo. (The picture was also published with three different articles in 2004, the year the film was released, and each time Mr. Bouvet was misidentified as Mr. Goytisolo.)
match_headline: Juan Goytisolo, Novelist Who Took Aim at Spanish Conservatism, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the arms trader Adnan Khashoggi erroneously attributed a distinction to a yacht that he owned. Though quite large at 282 feet long, it was not “the world’s largest yacht.”
match_headline: Adnan Khashoggi, High-Living Saudi Arms Trader, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on May 29 and in some editions on May 28 about Jim Bunning, the Hall of Fame pitcher who became a United States senator, misidentified the legislative job he once held in the Kentucky State Senate. He was the minority leader of the Republicans, not the majority leader.
match_headline: Jim Bunning, Hall of Fame Pitcher and Blunt-Spoken Senator, Dies at 85

text: An article on Monday about American combat deaths in Afghanistan referred incorrectly to some of the six soldiers who have been killed so far in 2017. The three who died in an apparent insider attack on Saturday were Army paratroopers; the three who died in April, not all six, were members of the Special Operations forces.
match_headline: All 6 U.S. Combat Deaths in Afghanistan in 2017 Were in Fight Against ISIS

text: An article on Monday about an American drone strike in Somalia misidentified the branch of military service of three Americans wounded or killed last month while accompanying Somali forces on a raid against Shabab militants. They were Navy SEALs, not Marines.
match_headline: U.S. Strikes Shabab, Likely a First Since Trump Relaxed Rules for Somalia

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the election in Kosovo on Sunday referred imprecisely at one point to the role that Ramush Haradinaj, whose coalition won the most votes, once played in the Kosovo Liberation Army, which fought a war for independence from Serbia in the 1990s. As noted correctly elsewhere in the article, Mr. Haradinaj was one of the group’s leaders, but not its overall head.
match_headline: Ex-Rebel Leader Is Poised to Win Kosovo Election

text: An article on Monday about plans by Attorney General Jeff Sessions to testify before the Senate Intelligence Committee misidentified a leadership position held by Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina. He chairs a subcommittee examining Russian interference in the election; he is not the chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee.
match_headline: Senate Democrats Call for Sessions’s Russia Testimony to Be Public

text: An article on Monday about the Yankees’ 14-3 win over the Baltimore Orioles misstated, in some copies, the number of relief pitchers the Yankees used in the game. It was four, not five.
match_headline: Aaron Judge Hits Two Homers, One Very Long, as Yankees Crush Orioles

text: An article on Saturday about a decision by the International Olympic Committee to award the 2024 and 2028 Summer Games at the same time misstated the year the most recent London Olympics were held. It was 2012, not 2010.
match_headline: I.O.C. Paves Way for Paris and Los Angeles to Host Summer Games

text: A picture on Wednesday with an obituary about the ballet master Sergei Vikharev was published in error. The photograph, supplied by Getty Images, showed Dmitri Korneyev in a Kirov Ballet production of “Romeo and Juliet” — not Mr. Vikharev in the same production.
match_headline: Sergei Vikharev, Russian Ballet Master Who Revived the Past, Dies at 55

text: An editorial on June 12 about terrorists’ trying to take advantage of more lenient gun control in the United States misstated identification requirements for buying guns online or at gun shows. Private sellers are not required to follow federal mandates on background checks of buyers. Dealers must do so.
match_headline: Shunning Gun Control, Helping Terrorists

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about reform at Uber misstated part of the name of the law firm that investigated sexual harassment and other wrongdoing at the ride-hailing company. As correctly noted later in the article, it is Covington & Burling (not Burlington).
match_headline: Uber Embraces Major Reforms as Travis Kalanick, the C.E.O., Steps Away

text: An article on Friday about the arrest of the longtime fugitive Masaaki Osaka referred incorrectly in some copies to the target of the 1971 protest where the crime Mr. Osaka was wanted for — throwing a homemade firebomb that killed a police officer — took place. The protest was against the terms of a treaty under which the United States returned to Japan sovereignty over Okinawa, not Osaka.
match_headline: Japan Arrests Longest-Sought Fugitive After Nearly 46 Years

text: An article on Wednesday about the effects on climate change of the retirement of several nuclear power plants omitted an affiliation of John Hanger, who commented on the possible closure of a reactor at Three Mile Island. While Mr. Hanger is a former Pennsylvania environmental secretary, he is also an outside adviser to Exelon, the utility that operates Three Mile Island.
match_headline: How Retiring Nuclear Power Plants May Undercut U.S. Climate Goals

text: An article on Saturday about the removal of slides from some New York City playgrounds described incorrectly federal safety rules for playground equipment. They are guidelines, not regulations.
match_headline: New Question on the Playground: Where Are the Slides?

text: An article on Tuesday about the U.S.S. Ling, a World War II-era submarine, compared incorrectly the length of the vessel to a football field . At 312 feet, the submarine is shorter — not longer — than a football field, which is 360 feet.
match_headline: A Submarine Is Stuck in the Muck in Hackensack

text: An article last Thursday about the comedian Lee Camp, host of the comedy news show “Redacted Tonight” on the RT America network, described incorrectly the departure of an employee at the network, Liz Wahl. She was a journalist for the network during the gestation of “Redacted Tonight,” but quit the network before — not after — the show’s premiere. The article also described incorrectly two comedians who performed with Mr. Camp at a stand-up show at the Cutting Room last month. Only one was a correspondent for “Redacted Tonight,” not both.
match_headline: An American Comic on a Russian Channel: What He Avoids Speaks Volumes

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Saturday about the New York bookstore Books of Wonder misidentified the store that served as an inspiration for the bookstore in the romantic comedy “You’ve Got Mail.” It was Eeyore’s, a children’s bookstore on the Upper West Side that closed in 1993 — not Books of Wonder.
match_headline: Books of Wonder to Open Upper West Side Location

text: A report in the Extra Bases column last Sunday about baseball franchises that have had a pitcher throw a perfect game and a player who hit four or more home runs in a game misidentified one of the teams. The Dodgers, not the Braves, have had both.
match_headline: Before Scooter Gennett, a Slugging Show on a Smaller Stage

text: A review on the cover this weekend about two books on China misstates part of the title of one of the books, by Graham Allison. As an accompanying listing correctly notes, it is “Destined for War: Can America and China Escape Thucydides’s Trap?” — not “America, China and Thucydides’s Trap.”
ref_headline: Destined for War: Can America and China Escape Thucydides’s Trap?
match_headline: America’s Collision Course With China

text: An entry in the Paperback Row column on May 28 about “The Sport of Kings,” by C.E. Morgan, misstated the equestrian job held by a man who was hired by Henrietta, one of the novel’s characters, in defiance of her father’s wishes. He is a groom, not a jockey.
match_headline: Shetland Pony Grand National

text: A review on June 4 about Dennis Lehane’s “Since We Fell” misstated, at one point, the relationship between the novel’s protagonist and her handsome colleague at the television network where they work. At the time he leaves her, he is her husband, no longer her fiancé.
match_headline: Dennis Lehane’s Latest Follows a Woman in a Downward Spiral

text: An obituary last Sunday about the educator Samuel DuBois Cook misidentified the position for which he was hired by Duke University. It was associate professor, not assistant professor.
match_headline: Samuel D. Cook, Educator Who Pierced Campus Color Barriers, Dies at 88

text: An article last Sunday about dance partnerships reversed the ages of the dancers Sara Mearns and Jared Angle. She is 31, and he is 36.
match_headline: How Dance Partners Create Chemistry Onstage

text: An article last Sunday about Times film critics’ picks for the 25 best films of the 21st century so far included a quotation from the director Guillermo del Toro that described incorrectly a scene in “Puss in Boots.” The scene was animated by the Japanese anime master Hayao Miyazaki and Otsuka Yasuo, not by Isao Takahata.
match_headline: The 25 Best Films of the 21st Century So Far.

text: An article last Sunday about the Apostle Islands in Wisconsin misidentified the launching point for the writer’s kayak trip. It is Little Sand Bay, not Sand Point.
match_headline: On Wisconsin Islands, a Warm Welcome and Brisk Waters

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about Cumberland Island, Ga., misspelled the surname of a culinary gardener shown at Greyfield Inn. He is Ryan Graycheck, not Greycheck.
match_headline: On a Georgia Island, a Lot of Good Food and Plenty of Nothing

text: An article last Sunday about the NBC correspondent Katy Tur, whose mother founded the Los Angeles News Service, referred incorrectly to the Los Angeles riots of 1992. They were ignited by the acquittal of four white police officers after they were tried for the use of excessive force on Rodney King, a black taxi driver. The riots were not ignited by a later episode, the assault of Reginald Denny, a white truck driver who was beaten by a group of rioters.
match_headline: ‘You Can’t Rattle Her’: Katy Tur on the Rise

text: An article on Monday about a collision off Japan between a container ship and an American destroyer, using information from the Japanese Coast Guard, misstated the time of the collision. After further investigation, the Coast Guard said on Monday that the accident occurred around 1:30 a.m. local time on Saturday, not around 2:20 a.m. as initially estimated. The article also misstated, in some copies, how long Cmdr. Bryce Benson has been in command of the destroyer, the U.S.S. Fitzgerald. Commander Benson became the ship’s captain in May after serving as its executive officer from November 2015 to March 2017; he has not been its captain for more than a year, as a Navy news release incorrectly indicated.
match_headline: Sleeping Sailors on U.S.S. Fitzgerald Awoke to a Calamity at Sea

text: An obituary on Saturday about Helmut Kohl, the former chancellor of Germany, omitted credit for two reporters. The obituary was written by Craig R. Whitney and Alan Cowell, not just by Mr. Whitney; and Melissa Eddy contributed reporting from Berlin.
match_headline: Helmut Kohl, Chancellor Who Reunited Germany, Dies at 87

text: An article on Monday about United Nations estimates of the total number of people forcibly displaced from their homes around the world referred incorrectly to the record set in 2016. The figure of 65.6 million was the highest since World War II, not the highest in all of history.
match_headline: Displaced Population Hit Record in ’16, U.N. Says

text: An article on Saturday about the appointment of a longtime associate of President Trump’s family to be head of the Department of Housing and Urban Development’s New York and New Jersey office misstated the role of another Trump associate, Keith Schiller, the president’s longtime bodyguard, in the firing of James Comey as F.B.I. director. Mr. Schiller hand-delivered the dismissal papers to F.B.I. headquarters, not to Mr. Comey personally.
match_headline: Trump Family Wedding Planner to Head New York’s Federal Housing Office

text: An article on Saturday about how the Russia investigation entangled Rick Gates, a protégé of Paul Manafort, the former Trump campaign chairman, referred incorrectly to work Mr. Gates and Richard Holht did on behalf of President-elect Trump. They worked on his inaugural committee; they were not part of the presidential transition team.
match_headline: How the Russia Investigation Entangled Rick Gates, a Manafort Protégé

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about Bill Cosby’s trial misstated the medical specialty of Cliff Huxtable, the character portrayed by Mr. Cosby on “The Cosby Show.” He was an obstetrician, not a pediatrician.
match_headline: How to Think About Bill Cosby and ‘The Cosby Show’

text: An article on Saturday about mowing lawns gave the incorrect square mileage of turf grass planted in the United States. It is 62,000 square miles, not 60 million.
match_headline: Beyond Blades of Grass

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about knife attacks in the Old City section of East Jerusalem referred incorrectly to a claim of responsibility for the attacks by the Islamic State. It was not the group’s first for attacks on territory internationally recognized as part of Israel; the status of East Jerusalem is disputed.
match_headline: Israeli Dies as Palestinian Attackers Stage Assaults in Jerusalem

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about federal spending on Medicaid and the opioid epidemic misstated, in some editions, the position of Senator Pat Toomey, Republican of Pennsylvania, on a proposal to spend $45 billion over 10 years for opioid abuse treatment and prevention costs. Mr. Toomey has not discussed that proposal with its supporters and said he is considering plans to increase funding for substance abuse programs; he has not opposed the $45 billion plan.
match_headline: G.O.P. Rift Over Medicaid and Opioids Imperils Senate Health Bill

text: An article on Tuesday about the results of the French legislative election misstated the share of victorious candidates for the National Assembly who are women. It is 39 percent, not 36 percent.
match_headline: For Emmanuel Macron, Fight for France Is Just Beginning

text: A picture caption on June 4 with the continuation of an article about a secret Israeli contingency plan to use a nuclear weapon to ward off defeat in the 1967 war misstated the location and the date of the photograph supplied by Agence France-Presse. The Israeli fighter jets shown were flying over Israel on March 1, 1967 — not over the Sinai Peninsula on June 5, the first day of the war.
match_headline: ‘Last Secret’ of 1967 War: Israel’s Doomsday Plan for Nuclear Display

text: An article on Tuesday about the head of the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office, Keith Hall, who is under fire from Republicans, misstated the action that President Richard M. Nixon took on the Congressional Budget Act of 1974, which created the C.B.O. Nixon signed it on July 12 of that year; he did not veto it.
match_headline: C.B.O. Head, Who Prizes Nonpartisanship, Finds Work Under G.O.P. Attack

text: An article on June 13 about the death of a Penn State student, Timothy Piazza, at a fraternity party misspelled the surname of a lawyer for the Piazza family. He is Tom Kline, not Klein.
match_headline: Penn State Student’s Dying Hours Play Out in Courtroom Video

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with a Critic’s Notebook article about dance performances in the River to River festival misidentified one of the dancers in “Paramodernities.” He is Nicholas Leichter, not Jeremy Jae Neal.
match_headline: Dance for the People (by the Pros) at the River to River Festival

text: An article last Thursday about Gwyneth Paltrow’s “In Goop Health” conference misspelled the surname of one person who attended. She is Logan Brendt, not Brent.
match_headline: Meet the Goopies

text: An obituary on Friday about the musicologist Philip Gossett misstated his role in producing the critical edition of the score of Verdi’s “Rigoletto.” While he was the general editor of the Verdi series, the editor of that score was Martin Chusid, not Mr. Gossett.
match_headline: Philip Gossett, Scholar Who Brought Operas Back to Life, Dies at 75

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the former New York Jets linebacker Larry Grantham omitted a credit. Daniel E. Slotnik contributed reporting.
match_headline: Larry Grantham, Defensive Captain of Champion Jets, Dies at 78

text: An article on Thursday about President Trump’s rally in Cedar Rapids, Iowa on Wednesday, referred incorrectly to his return to the state. The trip was his first since the inauguration, not since the election.
match_headline: Trump Turns an Iowa Rally Into a Venting Session

text: An article on Thursday about the producer and D.J. Laurel Halo misidentified the nationality of the producer Klein, one of her collaborators on the album “Dust.” She is British, not Nigerian.
match_headline: Laurel Halo Shakes Up Her Sound After Partnering With a Humanoid Pop Star

text: An obituary on Sunday about the anthropologist Ben Finney referred incorrectly to the crowd that greeted the arrival of the Hokulea, the sailing canoe whose construction he oversaw, in Papeete Harbor in Tahiti in 1976. The crowd, of some 17,000 people, was more than half the population of the city of Papeete — not of all Tahiti.
match_headline: Ben Finney, Anthropologist Who Debunked Theory on Island Settlement, Dies at 83

text: An article on Friday about exaggerations and falsehoods that President Trump stated during a recent rally in Iowa misstated the value of a proposed arms deal with Saudi Arabia. The package of weapons offered the Saudis totals $110 billion, not $110 million.
match_headline: In One Rally, 12 Inaccurate Claims From Trump

text: An article on Friday about the firing of a Wall Street Journal reporter, Jay Solomon, referred incompletely to communications within the Journal newsroom about Mr. Solomon’s departure. While no staffwide memo or other communication had been issued by Thursday night, the firing was discussed at the Thursday morning news meeting attended by top editors, bureau chiefs and other staff members.
match_headline: Wall Street Journal Fires Reporter With Ties to Iranian-Born Magnate

text: An article on Thursday about Nick Bowers, who shoots drone videos for sailing races, referred incorrectly to Oracle Team USA’s finishing first in the qualifying rounds of the America’s Cup. Oracle earned a one-point advantage in the finals; it did not clinch a place in the finals. (As the defending champion, Oracle was guaranteed a spot in the finals.) The article also misstated Leandro Spina’s role with the Corfu Challenge, a race in Greece. He works for the race and will compete in it; he did not organize the race.
match_headline: The Kiwis’ Edge in America’s Cup: Drones

text: An article in some editions on Monday about Brooks Koepka’s victory in the United States Open misspelled the given name of his caddie in some copies. He is Ricky Elliott, not Rickie.
match_headline: Brooks Koepka Wins U.S. Open for His First Major Title

text: Because of an editing error, the “On This Day in History” feature on Friday about Joe Louis’s victory over James J. Braddock for the world’s heavyweight championship, misstated, in some copies, the date on which a New York Times headline about the event appeared. The headline — “Louis Knocks Out Braddock in 8th, Wins World Title” — was published on June 23, 1937, not on June 23, 1925.

A review on the cover this weekend about four books on the rise of Uber and other transformative start-ups includes outdated information about Travis Kalanick, one of Uber’s founders. After the section had gone to press, Mr. Kalanick resigned as the company’s chief executive; he is no longer merely on an indefinite leave of absence from that position. In addition, an accompanying picture caption also includes the outdated reference.
match_headline: How Uber and Airbnb Became Poster Children for the Disruption Economy

text: An obituary on Friday about Pete Flynn, the New York Mets’ longtime groundskeeper, misspelled, in some editions, the given names of his daughters and misstated which of them he lived with in Clinton, Conn. They are Eileen Flynn, not Aileen, and MaryAnne Poeschl, not Mary Anne; and he lived with Ms. Poeschl, not with Ms. Flynn.
match_headline: Pete Flynn, Mets Groundskeeper for Almost 50 Years, Dies at 79

text: An article in some editions on May 28 about the Yankees’ 3-2 victory over the Oakland Athletics misstated, in some copies, the number of at-bats over which Chase Headley had two hits after the game. It was 28, not 27. The article also misstated, in some copies, the numbers of at-bats over which Aaron Judge hit 13 home runs from the beginning of the season. It was 88, not 92. And the article misstated the dates Aroldis Chapman and Greg Bird were put on the disabled list. Chapman was put on the list on May 14, not May 2, and Bird on May 2, not May 13.
match_headline: With the Offense Still on Hiatus, the Yankees Eke Out a Win

text: A picture caption last Sunday with the continuation of an article about Jonathan Williams, the pastor of Forefront church in Brooklyn, whose father recently came out as a transgender woman, referred incorrectly to the man in the center of the photograph shown wearing a plaid shirt. He is a member of the congregation; he is not Mr. Williams.
match_headline: Faith and Family, in Transition

text: An article last Sunday about the Lower East Side development known as Essex Crossing referred incompletely to one aspect of the project. Besides the Market Line bazaar, a Trader Joe’s is also planned for Essex Crossing.
match_headline: Essex Crossing, a Renewal Project 60 Years in the Making

text: An article last Sunday about Staubitz Market, a 100-year-old butcher shop in Brooklyn, misidentified its neighborhood. The shop is in Cobble Hill, not in Boerum Hill.
match_headline: Staubitz Market in Brooklyn: 100 Years of Sawdust, Steaks and Chops

text: A review on May 7 about “Notes of a Crocodile,” by Qiu Miaojin, erroneously referred to the author by her given name in subsequent references. Her surname is Qiu, not Miaojin. (Qiu, who was Taiwanese, observed the usual Chinese convention in which a personal name consists of the family name followed by a given name.)
match_headline: A Taiwanese Classic Now Available in English

text: An article last Sunday about the painter Andrew Wyeth misstated the day of the week that a new exhibition of his work was to open at the Brandywine River Museum. It was Saturday, June 24, not Sunday.
match_headline: Unclothed in Andrew Wyeth’s Art

text: An article last Sunday about the expansion of television programming with African-American themes misstated the name of a BET series debuting on Tuesday, June 27. It is “Tales,” not “Flags.”
match_headline: A ‘Queen Sugar’ Rush Heralds a ‘Silver Age’ for African-American TV

text: An article on June 11 about a short-seller referred incorrectly to Daraprim, the drug whose price was increased 56-fold by Turing Pharmaceuticals. The company bought the marketing rights, not the patent, to the drug.
match_headline: The Bounty Hunter of Wall Street

text: An article last Sunday about an effort to sell a family business, Wild West Town theme park, misidentified the state where a shuttered theme park, Ponderosa Ranch, is located. It is on Lake Tahoe in Nevada, not California.
match_headline: When Mom and Pop Can’t Sell the Farm (or in This Case, the Theme Park)

text: An article on Wednesday about how a warming climate may affect air travel in the future referred incorrectly in some editions to the recent American Airlines policy allowing passengers traveling to or from Phoenix on several days to change their trips without a fee. It applied to flights arriving at or departing from the airport between 3 and 6 p.m., not to all flights.
match_headline: Too Hot to Fly? Climate Change May Take a Toll on Air Travel

text: A picture caption on Monday with an article about the loss of retail jobs misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a jewelry store owner and the name of the business in Johnstown, Pa., that carries his name. He is Tom Apryle IV of Apryle’s jewelry store (not Arpyle).
match_headline: In Towns Already Hit by Steel Mill Closings, a New Casualty: Retail Jobs

text: An article and an accompanying illustration on Sunday about the fire that destroyed the Grenfell Tower housing block in London misstated the time of the first call to the fire department. It was made at 12:54 a.m., not 12:45 a.m.
match_headline: Why Grenfell Tower Burned: Regulators Put Cost Before Safety

text: An article on Monday about the origin of the Confederate battle flag referred incorrectly to its design. As correctly noted elsewhere in the article, the flag has a pattern of stars and bars, but it is not known as the Stars and Bars flag. (That was the name given to the first national flag of the Confederate states.)
match_headline: Which Is the Real Confederate Flag?

text: An article on June 15 about the Trump administration’s review of Obama administration rules intended to crack down on predatory for-profit colleges referred incorrectly to part of an Education Department action involving such schools. The department said that it would reconsider provisions involving the “gainful employment” rule, which cuts off loans to colleges if graduates’ earnings cannot meet their debt burden, not move immediately to halt the loans.
match_headline: U.S. Halts New Rules Aimed at Abuses by For-Profit Colleges

text: An article on Monday about a number of art galleries that are closing erroneously included one New York gallery. While Team Gallery did recently shutter a location on Wooster Street, its main gallery on Grand Street — and its business — remain open. In addition, an accompanying picture of the Wooster Street gallery should not have been used to represent gallery businesses that are shutting down.
match_headline: Art Gallery Closures Grow for Small and Midsize Dealers

text: An obituary on Sunday about Dr. John E. Sarno, the author of books on the psychological origins of chronic pain, gave an outdated reference in some editions to Dr. Christopher Gharibo’s title at the Langone Medical Center at New York University. He is a pain management specialist there, no longer the medical director of pain medicine at the Hospital for Joint Diseases.
match_headline: Dr. John Sarno, 93, Dies; Best-Selling Author Tied Pain to Anxieties

text: An article on Tuesday about the products at the center of the deadly London fire referred incorrectly to Whirlpool’s connection to the refrigerator that caught fire. Whirlpool bought the company that made the refrigerator, sold under the Hotpoint brand, after the appliance was made; Whirlpool did not make the refrigerator.
match_headline: Products at Center of London Fire Faced Tougher Rules in U.S.

text: An article on June 14 about the investor David Bonderman’s resignation from Uber’s board misidentified the region for which Wan Ling Martello, another board member, is the executive vice president at Nestle. It is Asia, not South Asia.
match_headline: David Bonderman Resigns From Uber Board After Sexist Remark

text: An article on Saturday about the firm of Kenneth R. Feinberg and the role of an employee, Camille Biros, in devising ways to compensate disaster victims misstated the low end of the range of awards to clients of Robert Hilliard from the General Motors ignition switch fund. The awards ranged from about $10,000 to close to $40 million, not from about $10 million to close to $40 million.
match_headline: From 9/11 to Orlando, Ken Feinberg’s Alter Ego in Compensating Victims

text: An article on June 16 about Spotify’s annual report on its financial data misstated its revenue in euros in 2016. It was 2.9 billion euros (about $3.3 billion), not 2.9 million euros.
match_headline: Spotify Is Growing, but So Are Its Losses

text: An article on June 5 about Palmer Luckey, a founder of Oculus VR who is working on a new start-up, misidentified the county where he grew up. It is Los Angeles County, not Orange.
match_headline: Oculus Founder Plots a Comeback With a Virtual Border Wall

text: An article on Tuesday about DNA fingerprinting of biopsies to ensure samples do not get mixed up misstated the percentage of blood samples, out of 6,733, that were switched in a clinical trial in 2011. It was 0.5 percent, not 0.05 percent.
match_headline: The Lab Says It’s Cancer. But Sometimes the Lab Is Wrong.

text: An article on April 19 about President Trump’s “Hire American” order referred incorrectly to the application process for employers seeking to hire H-1B workers. The employers must attest that they are paying the foreign workers prevailing wages and that the working conditions of existing workers will not be adversely affected. They do not have to attest that they tried to find an American first. This correction was delayed because the error was pointed out to editors only recently.
match_headline: How Trump’s ‘Hire American’ Order May Affect Tech Worker Visas

text: An article on Thursday about the search for a motive behind a recent cyberattack that spread around the world misstated the name of a cybersecurity firm based in Tel Aviv. It is IntSights, not Insight.
match_headline: Mystery of Motive for a Ransomware Attack: Money, Mayhem or a Message?

text: An obituary on Thursday about the jazz pianist Geri Allen referred incorrectly to Nathan Davis, with whom she worked at the University of Pittsburgh. He is a saxophonist, not a pianist.
match_headline: Geri Allen, Pianist Who Reconciled Jazz’s Far-Flung Styles, Dies at 60

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the new prime minister of Serbia, Ana Brnabic, referred incorrectly to her political affiliation. She is backed by the Serbian Progressive Party, but she is not a member of any party.
match_headline: Serbia Gets Its First Female, and First Openly Gay, Premier

text: An article on May 11 about concerns over pro-Nazi soldiers in the German armed forces referred incorrectly to Lippe, the location of an army barracks named for Erwin Rommel, the World War II field marshal. Lippe is a district in western Germany, not a city. This correction was delayed because the error was only recently called to the attention of editors.
match_headline: Pro-Nazi Soldiers in German Army Raise Alarm

text: An article on June 21 about travel companies’ bracing for weaker growth this year referred incorrectly to cancellations in bookings reported this summer by Loews Hotels. The company said it had seen an increase in cancellations by groups that have international attendees, but this increase is not especially concentrated in New York City.
match_headline: As Travel Industry Awaits Slowdown, Travelers Pack Bags — for Now

text: An article on Friday about the qualifying tournament for Wimbledon omitted one way people can get Center Court tickets for the main event. Besides paying a high price or waiting overnight, they can also win a lottery.
match_headline: Wimbledon’s Qualifying Tournament Is 3½ Miles and a World Away

text: An article on June 18 about the Manhattan office of Karl Frey gave an outdated name of the company he works for. It is iStar, not iStar Financial. (The company’s name was changed in 2015.)
match_headline: A Sleek Manhattan Office, Softened by Family Mementos

text: An article last Sunday about colleges that offer courses in embracing failure misidentified the position that Amy Jordan holds at the University of Pennsylvania. She is the associate dean for undergraduate studies in the school of communication, not for the entire university.
match_headline: On Campus, Failure Is on the Syllabus

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Addison Schultz and Tal Hirshberg misstated the relationship of the bride’s father, Howard D. Schultz, to the coffee company Starbucks. Mr. Schultz has been the company’s longtime leader and is now its executive chairman, but was not its founder. Gordon Bowker, Jerry Baldwin, and Zev Siegl founded Starbucks in 1971.
match_headline: Addison Schultz and Tal Hirshberg: A Coffee Scion, and a Grande Love Story

text: An article on Sunday about the influence of Scott Pruitt, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, erroneously reported a meeting between Mr. Pruitt and Andrew Liveris, the chief executive of the Dow Chemical Company. While a meeting was scheduled for March 9 at an energy conference in Houston, both the E.P.A. and Dow said it was later canceled and did not take place.
match_headline: Counseled by Industry, Not Staff, E.P.A. Chief Is Off to a Blazing Start

text: An article on Saturday about Germany’s new law to crack down on hate speech in social media misstated the surname of a member of the Global Public Policy Institute who criticized the legislation. He is Alexander Pirang, not Pirant.
match_headline: Delete Hate Speech or Pay Up, Germany Tells Social Media Companies

text: An article on Sunday about Pope Francis’ removal of a conservative cardinal, Gerhard Ludwig Müller, from a prominent Vatican post included an imprecise translation of a papal document’s Latin title, Amoris Laetitia. It means Joy of Love, not Joy of the Family.
match_headline: Pope Francis Ousts Powerful Conservative Cardinal

text: An article on Sunday about summer reading selections for college freshmen misidentified an author whose work was assigned. Susquehanna University’s reading list included a work by the poet Ross Gay, not Roxane Gay. The article also misstated part of the name of a group that opposes some of the reading choices. It is the National Association of Scholars, not the National Academy of Scholars.
match_headline: Summer Reading Books: The Ties That Bind Colleges

text: An article on Friday about a jury’s decision to let the federal government seize a Midtown Manhattan skyscraper it says is controlled by Iran overstated Iran’s responsibility for the Sept. 11 attacks. While a federal court found that Iran had some culpability for the Sept. 11 attacks as a state sponsor of terrorism, it has not been established that Iran sponsored the attacks, which were planned and executed by Al Qaeda. (A similar error occurred in a Sept. 25, 2013 article in The Times .)
match_headline: Manhattan Skyscraper Linked to Iran Can Be Seized by U.S., Jury Finds

text: An article on Sunday about the life of the gunman who shot former colleagues at Bronx-Lebanon Hospital misstated the location and management of a homeless shelter. It is on East 30th Street in Manhattan, not at Bellevue Hospital Center, and is run by the the New York City Department of Homeless Services, not the hospital.
match_headline: For Gunman at Bronx Hospital, Fleeting Success and Persistent Strife

text: An article on Monday about two military veterans who recently received robotic arms transposed how the men were injured. It was Fred Downs who stepped on a land mine in Vietnam; Artie McAuley was injured in a car accident in New York.
match_headline: For Two Veterans, a Freedom Restored for Independence Day

text: An article on June 11 about an annual fund-raising auction to have lunch with the billionaire investor Warren Buffett misidentified the person who said that it did not matter whether bidders see the lunch as a business opportunity or a job interview. It was Pete Budlong, the first winner of the lunch in 2000, not Janice Mirikitani, a founder of the nonprofit group Glide, which benefits from the auction.
match_headline: The Cost of Dining With Warren Buffett? This Year, It’s $2,679,001

text: An obituary on Monday about the lawyer Norman Dorsen misstated the year that Justice William J. Brennan Jr. delivered a tribute to him. It was 1992, not 2001. (Justice Brennan died in 1997.) Because of an editing error, the earlier version also misspelled, at one point, the surname of Senator Joseph R. McCarthy’s chief counsel. As noted correctly elsewhere in the obituary, he was Roy Cohn, not Cohen.
match_headline: Norman Dorsen, Tenacious Civil Rights Advocate, Dies at 86

text: An article on Thursday about President Trump’s scheduled talks with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia misidentified a committee on which Senator Jack Reed, Democrat of Rhode Island, serves. He is the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, not of the House panel.
match_headline: Trump Aides’ Biggest Worry About Europe Trip: Meeting With Putin

text: A news analysis on Thursday exploring the likely casualties from a military strike on the Korean peninsula misstated in one passage some forecasts from the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability. The figures of nearly 3,000 fatalities from a North Korean artillery attack on military targets, and 30,000 for one on civilian targets, were for an initial barrage, not for the initial hours of fighting.
match_headline: In North Korea, ‘Surgical Strike’ Could Spin Into ‘Worst Kind of Fighting’

text: An article on Tuesday about Republican tax-cut proposals misstated the percentage of households that would get a tax cut of $250,000. It is the top 0.1 percent, not the top 1 percent.
match_headline: Five Misleading Republican Claims About Health Care

text: Because of an editing error, an article in some editions on Saturday about Archibald Wright Graham, a baseball player who played in one game for the New York Giants in 1905, misstated the part of the inning when he was on deck. It was in the top of the ninth inning, not the bottom.
match_headline: Dustin Fowler’s Injury Evokes Another Brief Call-Up, 112 Years Later

text: An obituary on Monday about the yacht designer Doug Peterson mistranslated the name of his yacht, Ganbare. It is a Japanese word of encouragement roughly equivalent to “good luck” or “do your best”; it does not mean “go fight wind.”
match_headline: Doug Peterson, Trailblazer in the Design of Racing Yachts, Dies at 71

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on June 30 about the theologian and sociologist Peter L. Berger misstated when he served in the United States Army. It was in the 1950s, not during World War II.
match_headline: Peter Berger, Theologian Who Fought ‘God Is Dead’ Movement, Dies at 88

text: An article on Friday about the Egyptian police detaining and deporting Chinese citizens of the Uighur ethnic group referred imprecisely to Lucia Parrucci, a spokeswoman for the World Uyghur Congress. She is associated with the Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization, which represents the congress; she does not work directly for the congress.
