The article also misstated the congress’s estimate of the number of Uighurs detained in Cairo. Eighty was how many congress estimated were being held, not how many had been arrested since July 1.
match_headline: Egyptian Police Detain Uighurs and Deport Them to China

text: An article on Monday about the Mets’ 7-1 loss to the Philadelphia Phillies misstated the given name of the Mets relief pitcher who gave up three runs in the eighth inning. He is Chasen Bradford, not Chase.
match_headline: Momentum Deserts the Mets Amid Wave of Misplays

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the growing problem of players quitting tennis matches at Grand Slam tournaments misstated, in some editions, the number of Grand Slam events in the past 10 years in which the men’s singles draw has had eight or more retirements. It is 11, not 12.
match_headline: Players Pull Out at Wimbledon, and Calls for Reform Flood In

text: An article this weekend about a collection of essays by Durga Chew-Bose misstates the title. The book is “Too Much and Not the Mood,” not “Too Much and Not in the Mood.” The article also misstates the publisher of the book. It is FSG Originals, not FSB Originals.
ref_headline: Too Much and Not the Mood,
match_headline: New Sentences: From ‘Too Much and Not the Mood,’ by Durga Chew-Bose

text: An article this weekend about Marine recruits at Parris Island misspells the name of the town where Jake Weaver, a former Marine, grew up. It is Interlachen, Fla., not Interlaken.
match_headline: How the Death of a Muslim Recruit Revealed a Culture of Brutality in the Marines

text: An article on July 2 about Bridge International Academies, a chain of international schools, referred incorrectly to a comment that Shan-non May, a founder of the chain, made about notifying the police about unescorted visits to Bridge schools. She said Bridge staff members acted responsibly in contacting the police; she was not referring to her own actions.
match_headline: Can a Tech Start-Up Successfully Educate Children in the Developing World?

text: A review last Sunday about “The Imagineers of War: The Untold History of DARPA, the Pentagon Agency That Changed the World” included outdated information about the book’s author, Sharon Weinberger, relying in part on her website. While she was indeed the national security editor for The Intercept in March, when the book was published, she subsequently left that position and is now an executive editor at Foreign Policy.
ref_headline: The Imagineers of War: The Untold History of DARPA, the Pentagon Agency That Changed the World
match_headline: How an Agency of Oddballs Transformed Modern War and Modern Life

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about helping hoarders misstated the publishing frequency of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. It has gone through multiple editions, but it is not updated annually.
match_headline: Helping Those Who Hoard

text: A news analysis article on Sunday about President Trump’s trip to Europe misstated the timing of his meeting in Hamburg, Germany, with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. It took place on Friday, not on Thursday. The article also misstated the middle initial of Mr. Trump’s national security adviser in some copies. He is Lt. Gen. H. R. McMaster, not H.W.
match_headline: Despite Deep Policy Divides, Europe Trip Seen by Buoyant Trump as High Point

text: An article on Saturday about the visit of four senior Trump administration officials to the American wartime prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, misidentified the location of two deadly terror bombings in 2002 and 2003. They were in Indonesia, not Malaysia.
match_headline: Administration Officials, Including Sessions, Tour Guantánamo

text: A picture credit on Wednesday with an article about two airlines that have been exempted from an American ban on laptops and other electronic devices in the passenger cabins of flights from eight predominantly Muslim countries misstated the photographer’s surname. The picture, of an Emirates plane, was taken by Adam Schreck, not Scheck.
match_headline: Emirates and Turkish Airlines Say Laptop Ban Is Lifted on Their U.S. Flights

text: A picture on Wednesday with a Critic’s Notebook article about the pop groups Hey Violet and Terror Jr was published in error. It showed Terror Jr’s 2016 album, “Bop City” — not the new album, “Bop City 2: TerroRising,” which was the focus of the article.
match_headline: Hey Violet and Terror Jr: The New Female Pop Rebels

text: An article on Saturday about the opera-in-concert series Bel Canto of Caramoor’s move to Purchase College next summer and reinvention as Teatro Nuovo referred incorrectly to two works that will be performed as part of Teatro Nuovo’s first season. They are Rossini’s “Tancredi” and Johann Simon Mayr’s “Medea in Corinto”; the works are not yet to be announced.
match_headline: At Caramoor, an Operatic Milestone That’s Both Farewell and Beginning

text: A picture credit on Friday with a film review of the documentary “City of Ghosts” omitted a source of the image. The photograph, of a scene from the movie, is from Amazon Studios/A&E Indie Films, IFC Films, not just IFC Films.
match_headline: Review: In ‘City of Ghosts,’ Fighting ISIS With Journalism

text: An obituary on Saturday about Spencer Johnson, the author of the best-selling book “Who Moved My Cheese?”, erroneously included a name among Mr. Johnson’s survivors in some copies. Lesley Bostridge, his second wife, does not survive him; she died in 2009.
match_headline: Spencer Johnson, ‘Who Moved My Cheese?’ Author, Dies at 78

text: An article on Tuesday about the election of Avi Gabbay to lead the Labor Party in Israel included a quotation that referred incorrectly to participation in the leadership election. Tal Schneider, who writes for an independent political blog, said there were 52,000 voters, not 62,000; the figure was for the number eligible to cast ballots, not the number who actually did.
match_headline: Israeli Labor Party Tries a New Leader: Gabbay, Self-Made Millionaire

text: An article on Monday about a protest march in Istanbul referred incorrectly to Die Zeit, a German newspaper that published an interview with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Die Zeit is a weekly, not a daily.
match_headline: ‘March for Justice’ Ends in Istanbul With a Pointed Challenge to Erdogan

text: An article on Tuesday about hotels that are training workers to improve their hospitality skills misstated the name of Philadelphia’s tourist bureau. It is the Philadelphia Convention and Visitors Bureau, not Discover Philadelphia.
match_headline: Hotels Train Workers in the Personal Touch

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a performance of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony at the Group of 20 summit meeting in Hamburg, Germany, misidentified the king to whom Beethoven dedicated the symphony. He was Frederick Wilhelm III of Prussia, not Frederick III.
match_headline: At G-20, Beethoven Sends a Mixed Message to Trump

text: An obituary last Thursday about Gene Conley, who won a World Series with the Milwaukee Braves and three N.B.A. titles with the Boston Celtics, erroneously attributed a distinction to him and to Otto Graham, who played for the Cleveland Browns of the National Football League and the Rochester Royals of the National Basketball League. They were not the only athletes to win championships in two major American professional sports. (At least one other athlete, Hinkey Haines, did so, winning a World Series with the New York Yankees in 1923 and a professional football championship with the New York Giants in 1927.)
match_headline: Gene Conley, Dual-Sport Threat With World Series and N.B.A. Titles, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the longtime F.B.I. agent Neil J. Welch misstated the year of his birth. He was born on Aug. 9, 1926 — not 1927. (As the obituary correctly noted, he was 90.) Because of an editing error, the obituary also misidentified the state for which Mr. Welch served as justice secretary. It is Kentucky, not Kansas.
match_headline: Neil Welch, F.B.I. Mastermind in Abscam Sting Operation, Dies at 90

text: An article last Thursday about up-and-coming creative talents omitted part of the name of the museum located near the landscape designer Lily Kwong’s most recent project. It is the Parrish Art Museum, not the Parrish Museum. The article also misspelled the surname of a prominent artist and curator. He is Jeffrey Deitch, not Dietsch.
match_headline: Lily Kwong, a Model and Landscape Designer Sought by Fashion Brands

text: An article last Thursday about e-commerce companies that let customers try products before they pay for them contained outdated information about two companies. Try.com now works for any online store, not just 30; and Rockets of Awesome’s boxes can contain as few as eight items, which customers may consider for five days, not 10.
match_headline: Try, Then Buy? Amazon’s Move Is Part of a Shopping Trend

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the sentencing of David Wildstein in New Jersey’s George Washington Bridge scandal misstated the year Bridget Anne Kelly and Bill Baroni were sentenced. It was this year, not last year.
match_headline: David Wildstein, Ex-Christie Ally, Gets Probation for Lane Closings

text: An article on Thursday about procedures known as fat freezing that enhance physiques misstated the number of treatments necessary to get a “gross profit” of $200,000 a year for CoolSculpting, one of the procedures, according to an investor presentation. It would take an average of two patients a week receiving four treatments each, not two treatments each.
match_headline: Fat Freezing Helps Doctors Enhance Physiques, and Their Revenue

text: A picture caption on Page D4 today with an article about the home of the author Don Winslow refers incorrectly to some of his possessions shown. Only the binoculars — not all of the objects — are from his days as a safari guide.
match_headline: A Tour of Don Winslow’s Ranch in Southern California

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Jon Underwood, the founder of the Death Cafe movement, misstated the profession of Sue Barsky Reid, his mother. She is a psychotherapist, not a psychiatrist.
match_headline: Jon Underwood, Founder of Death Cafe Movement, Dies at 44

text: An article on Wednesday about Natalia Veselnitskaya, the lawyer who met with Donald Trump Jr. in 2016 to discuss possible compromising material about Democrats, misspelled in one passage the given name of the father of Denis P. Katsyv, whom Ms. Veselnitskaya represented in a money-laundering case. He is Pyotr Katsyv, not Petr.
match_headline: Natalia Veselnitskaya, Lawyer Who Met Trump Jr., Seen as Fearsome Moscow Insider

text: An article on Wednesday about an inquiry into how contaminated blood in the 1970s and 1980s resulted in the deaths of at least 2,400 people in Britain included an out-of-date reference to the preferred treatment for hemophilia. At the time, the disease was usually controlled using blood plasma products that encouraged clotting, but that is no longer the case. Since the late 1990s, synthetic clotting factor proteins have been the preferred treatment.
match_headline: U.K. Orders New Inquiry Into Contaminated-Blood Scandal

text: Because of an editing error, a news analysis article on Friday about how the issue of human rights has receded in Western diplomatic contacts with China misstated the year Xi Jinping became president of China. It was in 2013, not 2012. (He became general secretary of the Communist Party, effectively the country’s leader, in 2012.)
match_headline: Liu Xiaobo’s Fate Reflects Fading Pressure on China Over Human Rights

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about efforts by California to make its bar exam easier to pass referred incorrectly in some editions to the public information officer for the California Supreme Court. The officer, Cathal Conneely, is a man.
match_headline: California Supreme Court Moves to Make Bar Exam Easier to Pass

text: An article on Monday about the Mets’ season before the All-Star break misstated, in some copies, the month in which their mascot, Mr. Met, made an obscene gesture at a fan. It was May, not “last month.”
match_headline: Mets, Once ‘All In,’ Are More Than 10 Games Out at Break

text: A picture on Friday with an art review about Condo New York, an exhibition in which galleries from around the world are paired with galleries in Manhattan, was published in error. It showed an installation view of “All That Glitters” at Rachel Uffner Gallery, with art works by Ebony G. Patterson, Derek Fordjour and Maria Berrio; it was not a view of the installation, presented by Koppe Astner and Sandy Brown, that is part of the Condo New York exhibition, which also has works on view at Rachel Uffner. In addition, the review misidentified the exhibition that is showing a lapidary model of Antonio Vega Macotela’s work. It is Documenta 14, not the Venice Biennale.
match_headline: Out-of-Town Galleries Arrive, Bearing Art

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about deals made with N.B.A. restricted free agents misspelled, in some copies, the given name of a player the Nets tried to sign last summer. He is Allen Crabbe, not Allan.
match_headline: It’s Official: Tim Hardaway Jr. Is Back With the Knicks

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the severe knee injury sustained by Bethanie Mattek-Sands during a second-round match at Wimbledon misstated the surname of her opponent in the match in some copies. She is Sorana Cirstea, not Cristea.
match_headline: Bethanie Mattek-Sands to Have Surgery on Injured Knee

text: An article last Sunday about Maria Balshaw, the new director of Tate, misstated the title of a 1973 painting by Emma Amos. It is “Eva the Babysitter,” not “Eve.”
match_headline: Tate’s New Leader Has ‘Fresh Eyes and a Lot of Energy.’ Is That Enough?

text: An entry on the children’s middle-grade hardcover best-seller list last Sunday omitted the name of the co-author with whom James Patterson wrote “Pottymouth and Stoopid.” He is Chris Grabenstein.

A review last Sunday about “Love, Africa: A Memoir of Romance, War, and Survival” referred incorrectly to conversations that presented the author, the New York Times correspondent Jeffrey Gettleman, with the question of how free he should be with familiar African stereotypes in his reporting from the region. The book recounts two such conversations, both in New York before the author left for the continent. One was with an editor, the other with “a former Africa hand.” Neither conversation took place with “old Africa hands” in Nairobi.
ref_headline: Love, Africa: A Memoir of Romance, War, and Survival
match_headline: Stories of a Lifelong Fascination With Africa

text: An article last Sunday about Amy Pascal, the film producer, misidentified a producer of “Molly’s Game.” He is Mark Gordon, not Scott Rudin.
match_headline: Amy Pascal’s Hollywood Ending, Complete With Comeback Twist

text: A picture credit last Sunday with a report about the wedding of Elizabeth O’Boyle and John Gavin III misspelled the surname of the photographer. She is Beth Dixson, not Dixon.
match_headline: Elizabeth O’Boyle, John Gavin III

text: An article on July 2 about new efforts to contact extraterrestrials misstated the impact a few kilograms traveling half the speed of light would have if they collided with Earth. The impact would be less than that of the asteroid that killed off the dino-saurs, not more.
match_headline: Greetings, E.T. (Please Don’t Murder Us.)

text: An article on Monday about Cosmo DiNardo, who has been charged in the murders of four men in Pennsylvania, misidentified the source of a statement by Mr. DiNardo that he had killed two other people when he was 15. A person with knowledge of Mr. DiNardo’s confession — not the Bucks County prosecutor’s office — provided the information. The article also described incorrectly Solebury Township, Pa., the location of the farm to which the men were lured. Solebury Township is in central — not northern — Bucks County.
match_headline: Cosmo DiNardo Took a Dark Turn Before Bucks County Killings, Friends Say

text: An article on Monday about frictions between Qatar and its Arab neighbors in the Gulf referred incorrectly to the offshore gas field that Qatar shares with Iran. It is the world’s largest gas field, not the third-largest.
match_headline: Qatar Opens Its Doors to All, to the Dismay of Some

text: Because of an editing error, the Saturday Profile article on July 8 about Letizia Battaglia, a photojournalist known for her work chronicling organized crime in Sicily, omitted the given name of the filmmaker in whose 2016 documentary she appeared. He is Franco Maresco.
match_headline: A Sicilian Photographer of the Mafia and Her ‘Archive of Blood’

text: An article on Friday about the Annual Greenhouse Gas Index published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration misstated what the index measures. The index records the impact of the emissions of five greenhouse gases on the warming of the planet. It does not measure the absolute level of those emissions.
match_headline: Climate-Altering Gases Spiked in 2016, Federal Scientists Report

text: An article on Monday about Roger Federer’s victory at Wimbledon misstated the round in which Roger Federer upset Pete Sampras at Wimbledon in 2001. It was the round of 16, not the quarterfinal.
match_headline: Roger Federer Wins Record-Breaking Eighth Wimbledon Title

text: An obituary on Monday about the mathematician Maryam Mirzakhani, using information from Stanford University, where she was a professor, misstated the date of her death. It was Friday, July 14 — not Saturday, July 15.
match_headline: Maryam Mirzakhani, Only Woman to Win a Fields Medal, Dies at 40

text: An obituary on Monday about Hootie Johnson, a former chairman of Augusta National Golf Club in Georgia, misidentified his immediate predecessor in that position. He was Jack Stephens, an Arkansas financier — not Clifford Roberts, the club’s first chairman, who founded Augusta National with the golfer Bobby Jones in the early 1930s.
match_headline: Hootie Johnson, Who Opposed Letting Women Into Augusta National, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Monday about the filmmaker George A. Romero misstated the name of the university from which he graduated in 1960. It was the Carnegie Institute of Technology — not Carnegie Mellon University, which was established in 1967 when the Carnegie Institute of Technology merged with the Mellon Institute of Industrial Research.
match_headline: George Romero, Father of the Zombie Movie, Dies at 77

text: An article on Tuesday about missing paperwork for private student loans referred imprecisely to how debt collectors may garnish federal benefits like Social Security from borrowers. The collectors can in some circumstances take benefits after they are deposited in a bank account; they cannot garnish the benefits directly.
match_headline: As Paperwork Goes Missing, Private Student Loan Debts May Be Wiped Away

text: An article on Saturday about accusations that playlists on Spotify, the streaming music service, are dotted with hundreds of supposedly “fake” artists misstated the number of times videos using music by Epidemic Sound have been viewed. It is 10 billion a month, according to the company, not 10 billion total.
match_headline: While Some Cry ‘Fake,’ Spotify Sees No Need to Apologize

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts by the investor Nelson Peltz to gain a seat on the board of Procter & Gamble misstated the name of the company that bought beauty brands from Procter & Gamble last year. It is Coty, not Cody.
match_headline: Struggles at Procter & Gamble Draw Scrutiny of Nelson Peltz

text: An article last Wednesday about the baker Pascal Rigo’s plan to start a chain of boulangeries in France misstated the surname of an executive of Starbucks, which bought a business from Mr. Rigo. She is Sharon Rothstein, not Rothman.
match_headline: A Baker’s Crusade: Rescuing the Famed French Boulangerie

text: An article last Thursday about a gene-altering leukemia treatment referred incorrectly to the availability of gene therapy. If the Food and Drug Administration approves the leukemia treatment, it will be the first gene therapy approved in the United States, but not the first anywhere; other forms of gene therapy have already been approved and marketed in Europe and China.
match_headline: F.D.A. Panel Recommends Approval for Gene-Altering Leukemia Treatment

text: An article on Monday about the life one Connecticut prisoner, Erroll Brantley Jr., has experienced since being paroled misstated the relationship between his aunt, who was murdered, and the man who killed her. He was her former boyfriend, not her former husband.
match_headline: She’s His Rock. His Parole Officer Won’t Let Him See Her.

text: An article on Tuesday about corrupt officials and organized-crime groups profiting from refugee reception centers in Italy included an outdated figure for the number of migrants and refugees reaching the country in 2017. As of Tuesday, it was more than 93,000, not 83,000.
match_headline: Mafia in Italy Siphons Huge Sums From Migrant Centers

text: An article on Wednesday about infighting among members of the royal family in Saudi Arabia misstated the relationship between Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Prince Mohammed bin Nayef. Mohammed bin Salman is Mohammed bin Nayef’s cousin, not his nephew.
match_headline: Saudi King’s Son Plotted Effort to Oust His Rival

text: An article on Wednesday about United Airlines’ earnings for the latest quarter referred incorrectly to Delta Air Lines’ profit in the second quarter compared with United’s profit during the same period. Delta’s profit was about 30 percent higher, not twice as high.
match_headline: United Airlines Profit Rises Despite Boycott Threats Over Passenger Treatment

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on July 12 about the Global Jukebox, an interactive web portal with recordings of more than 6,000 folk songs collected by Alan Lomax, misstated the year of his death. It was 2002, not 2001.
match_headline: The Unfinished Work of Alan Lomax’s Global Jukebox

text: An article on Monday about a storm that killed nine people in Arizona misstated the date on which the state’s monsoon season started. It began on June 15, not July 15.
match_headline: Flash Floods in Arizona Kill at Least 9

text: An article on Tuesday about drilling and soil samples being taken by the Army Corps of Engineers in preparation for building a border wall erroneously included one city among the locations where work is taking place. It has not yet begun in the San Diego area. (The Corps is scheduled to start work in August.)
match_headline: Engineers Begin Preparatory Work for Border Wall Construction

text: An article on Thursday about the identification of one of the victims of John Wayne Gacy, a 1970s serial killer, misstated part of the name of the lab that provided DNA testing. The Center for Human Identification is at the University of North Texas, not the University of Northern Texas.
match_headline: John Wayne Gacy Victim Is Identified After Four Decades

text: An article on Wednesday about comic books that address political subjects omitted the name of Representative John Lewis’s co-author of the March trilogy of graphic novels. Andrew Aydin also wrote the books. (Nate Powell is the artist.)
match_headline: Comic Books That Put the Pow in Political Power

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with a music review about a performance of the Boston Symphony Orchestra at Tanglewood misstated the day on which the violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter was shown performing. It was Sunday, not Saturday.
match_headline: Review: Nelsons Turns Tanglewood Into Bayreuth-in-the-Berkshires

text: An article on Friday about communities of drug users on the online forum Reddit misstated the year the website banned a section containing provocative images of teenagers. It was banned in 2011, not “about two years ago.”
match_headline: On Reddit, Intimate Glimpses of Addicts in Thrall to Opioids

text: A listing in the “Newspaper And Beyond” feature on Friday about “Morning Joe” on MSNBC misspelled the surname of the show’s co-host. She is Mika Brzezinski, not Brzenzinski.

An article in some editions last Saturday about a decision by the Boston Red Sox to designate third baseman Pablo Sandoval for assignment misstated the number of days the Red Sox had to trade him or else be responsible for the nearly $48 million remaining on his contract. It was seven days, not 10.
match_headline: Red Sox Designate Third Baseman Pablo Sandoval for Assignment

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about Josh Adams, who is making a pro basketball comeback after a car accident, misstated his height. He is listed at 6 feet 2 inches, not 5 feet 9 inches.
match_headline: N.B.A. Hopeful’s Scar Tells a Tale of Determination

text: An obituary on July 13 about the artist Ilya Glazunov referred incorrectly to the subject of one of his paintings, Zinaida Sohlman. While she was the wife of a Swedish ambassador, as the obituary noted, she was not the former Princess Obolenskaya.
match_headline: Ilya Glazunov, Painter Entranced by Russia’s Past, Dies at 87

text: An article last Sunday about the director Christopher Nolan misstated the number of times the actor Cillian Murphy had worked with him before their latest film, “Dunkirk.” He has been in four of Mr. Nolan’s previous films — “Batman Begins,” “Inception,” “The Dark Knight Rises” and “The Dark Knight” — not two.
match_headline: Christopher Nolan’s Latest Time-Bending Feat? ‘Dunkirk’

text: An article last Sunday about the director David Lynch misstated the availability of some of his short films. Three of them are available on the Criterion Channel of the streaming service Filmstruck. It is not the case that all of Mr. Lynch’s short films are available only from bootleg sources.
match_headline: David Lynch Weaves Film History Into ‘Twin Peaks: The Return’

text: A review on July 9 about the novel “Standard Deviation,” by Katherine Heiny, misstated part of the title of a 2015 story collection by the same author. It is “Single, Carefree, Mellow,” not “Single, Careful, Mellow.”
match_headline: A Debut Novel Asks, What if His First Wife Was the One?

text: An article on July 16 about Washington politics misidentified the location where John Boehner, the former Republican speaker, called the Trump administration “a complete disaster.” The comment was made in Houston, not Colorado.
match_headline: This Town Melts Down

text: An article last Sunday about homes in the Hamptons that blur the distinction between indoors and out misstated part of the name of an interior design firm that has worked on outdoor spaces in the area. It is Gachot Studios, not Gachot Design.
match_headline: Hamptons Homes Blur the Line Between Inside and Out

text: An article on June 25 about homemade slime referred incorrectly to the characters who did the sliming in the movie “Ghostbusters.” Bill Murray’s character, Dr. Peter Venkman, was hit by green goo by the ghostly blob Slimer; Dr. Venkman and his crew did not do the sliming.
match_headline: Feel the Noise: Homemade Slime Becomes Big Business

text: An article last Sunday about lawyers and drug addiction misstated the period during which Wil Miller, a former sex crimes prosecutor, was addicted to methamphetamines. It was the last six months of his tenure, not the entire 10 years he was in the job. The article also misspelled Mr. Miller’s given name as Will.
match_headline: The Lawyer, the Addict

text: An article last Sunday about universal college admission tests misstated the percentage of students nationwide who used a fee waiver for the SAT in 2017. It was 25 percent, not 10 percent.
match_headline: Simple Way to Help Low-Income Students: Make Everyone Take SAT or ACT

text: An article on June 18 about celebrating anniversaries and other festive occasions in various destinations referred incorrectly to the accessibility of the Caribbean island of St. Barts from the United States. The island is generally only reachable by regional or charter flights; there are currently no nonstop flights on major airlines.
match_headline: How to Have a Destination Celebration

text: An article last Sunday about digging for prehistoric fossils in North Dakota misstated the name of a city in the state. It is Marmarth, not Marmath.
match_headline: When Dinosaurs Roamed North Dakota

text: An article on Sunday about the relationship between Coca-Cola and Dr. Brenda Fitzgerald, the new director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, misstated the amount of money Coke donated to the C.D.C. Foundation between 2010 and 2012. It was $1.1 million, not $1.4 million.
match_headline: New C.D.C. Chief Saw Coca-Cola as Ally in Obesity Fight

text: An article on Monday about the risks of a maritime disaster in the Arctic described the United States Coast Guard’s ice breaking capabilities incorrectly. The Coast Guard currently has two operating large icebreakers, but only one is classified as “heavy,” capable of breaking through the thickest ice. A second heavy icebreaker is no longer operating.
match_headline: With More Ships in the Arctic, Fears of Disaster Rise

text: An article on Tuesday about a decision by President Andrzej Duda of Poland to veto two bills that would have placed his country’s courts under political control translated imprecisely part of the name of the country’s leading opposition party. It is usually rendered in English as Civic Platform, not Civil Platform.
match_headline: Poland’s President Vetoes 2 Proposed Laws Limiting Courts’ Independence

text: An article on Monday about an opinion by the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court that limits the authority of local law enforcement officials to detain people at the request of federal immigration authorities referred incorrectly to the authorship of the opinion. The ruling was issued by the full court; it was not written by Associate Justice Barbara Lenk.
match_headline: Court Officers Can’t Hold People Solely Under ICE Detainers, Massachusetts Justices Rule

text: An article on Saturday about political spending by the drugmaker Mallinckrodt misstated the global sales of the drug H.P. Acthar in the 2014 fiscal year. It was $951 million, not $123 million.
match_headline: A Drug Maker Spends Big in Washington to Make Itself Heard

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the basketball coach John Kundla misspelled the surname of an N.B.A. coach who, like Kundla, was named one of the 10 best in the league’s history in 1996. He was Jack Ramsay, not Ramsey.
match_headline: John Kundla, Winning Coach of Fledgling Lakers, Dies at 101

text: An article on Wednesday about problems at the University of Southern California erroneously attributed a distinction to the university. It is the largest private employer in Los Angeles, not the largest overall.
match_headline: At a Moment of Success, U.S.C. Is Rocked by Scandal

text: An article on Monday about Jeffrey L. Bewkes, the chief executive of Time Warner, erroneously attributed a distinction to the company. It introduced a weekly magazine, but not the first one. (The Saturday Evening Post and other magazines started before the company was founded.)
match_headline: Leader Who Rebuilt Time Warner Empire Prepares an Exit

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about the film producer Will Parker misstated part of the name of the hotel in Miami where he was shown standing. It is the Mandarin Oriental Hotel, not the Mondrian Oriental Hotel. (Mondrian Hotels owns a boutique hotel in Miami.)
match_headline: Will Packer Starting Production Company With Backing From Discovery and Universal

text: An article on Wednesday about shared working spaces described the business Jones Lang LaSalle incorrectly. It is a real estate services company, not a real estate developer.
match_headline: Shared Work Spaces Spread, Mixing Styles and Services

text: An article last Thursday about the transgender night-life fixture Amanda Lepore misidentified her place of residence. She lives at Hotel 17 in the Gramercy neighborhood of Manhattan, not at the Gramercy Park Hotel.
match_headline: Amanda Lepore, Transgender Club Diva, Tells All About Her Plastic Surgery

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on July 18 about the scholar Wm. Theodore de Bary misstated the time frame in which he visited Eleanor Roosevelt at the White House with other student leaders. He did so as a college student; he was not a teenager at the time. The obituary also misstated a position Professor de Bary held during student protests at Columbia University in 1968. He was a member of a faculty committee that studied the university’s relations with outside agencies; he was not the chairman of the university senate executive committee. In addition, the obituary referred incorrectly to two courses taught at Columbia. They are Contemporary Civilization and Humanities — not a single course, Western Civilization and Humanities. And the obituary, using information from Professor de Bary’s family, referred incompletely to his survivors. They include three step-grandchildren, not one, and a step-great-grandson.
match_headline: Wm. Theodore de Bary, Renowned Columbia Sinologist, Dies at 97

text: A headline on May 21 with an obituary about the balloonist David Levin misstated his age in some editions. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 68, not 88. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only this week.
match_headline: David Levin, the Only Triple Crown Balloonist, Dies at 68

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the mathematician Marina Ratner referred incorrectly to her teaching career at the University of California, Berkeley. She supervised one doctoral student; it was not the case that she “taught only one graduate student.”
match_headline: Marina Ratner, Émigré Mathematician Who Found Midlife Acclaim, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on July 7 about Sheila Michaels, who campaigned for the use of the honorific “Ms.,” misspelled the given name of a woman who helped inspire that campaign. She was Mary Hamilton — not Mari, the spelling Ms. Michaels used in several references over time.
match_headline: Sheila Michaels, Who Brought ‘Ms.’ to Prominence, Dies at 78

text: An article last Friday about mounting tensions between Turkey and Germany referred incorrectly to a provision of the German Constitution. It requires Parliament’s approval for military missions abroad; it does not require lawmakers to visit troops stationed abroad.
match_headline: Turkey’s Arrest of German Activist Heightens Nations’ Tensions

text: An article last Friday about the Mets’ 3-2 victory over the St. Louis Cardinals misidentified the Cardinals’ first baseman who fielded Jose Reyes’s winning hit. He is Matt Carpenter, not Luke Voit.
match_headline: Mets Say Asdrubal Cabrera May Have More Suitors as a Third Baseman

text: An article in some editions last Friday about the restricted choices for uniform numbers that new Yankees players face misstated the given name of the player LaTroy Hawkins wanted to honor by wearing No. 21. He was Roberto Clemente, not Robert.
match_headline: No No. 21 for Todd Frazier. Instead, He’ll Settle for No. 29.

text: An article on Tuesday about England’s ambitious effort to treat depression, anxiety and other common mental illnesses misstated the name of one type of therapy included in the National Health Services’ guidelines. It is interpersonal therapy, not intrapersonal therapy.
match_headline: England’s Mental Health Experiment: No-Cost Talk Therapy

text: An entry in the What’s Streaming column on Friday about the show “The Rich and the Ruthless,” which was created by the actress Victoria Rowell, misstated part of the title of the soap opera on which Ms. Rowell played Drucilla from 1990 through 2007. It was “The Young and the Restless,” not “The Youth and the Restless.”
match_headline: What’s on TV Friday: ‘The Incredible Jessica James’ and ‘The Last Tycoon’

text: An article on Page 2 this weekend about the redesign of South Street Seaport misidentifies the ship adjacent to Pier 17. It is the Wavertree, not the Peking.
match_headline: Reclaiming South Street Seaport for New Yorkers

text: An article last Sunday about a new exhibition of work by the painter Cristóbal de Villalpando reversed the action taking place at the top and bottom in his 1683 “Moses and the Brazen Serpent and the Transfiguration of Jesus.” The top portrays the transfiguration of Jesus into light; the bottom is Moses using the image of the brazen serpent to heal Israelites.
ref_headline: Moses and the Brazen Serpent and the Transfiguration of Jesus.
match_headline: De Villalpando’s Holy Canvases Arrive at the Met

text: An article last Sunday about adaptations of works by F. Scott Fitzgerald misstated the title of his second novel, published in 1922. It is “The Beautiful and Damned,” not “The Beautiful and the Damned.”
match_headline: Amazon Tackles Hollywood’s F. Scott Fitzgerald Obsession

text: A chart on July 16 with an article about how data science can be used to analyze the vocabulary in Jane Austen’s novels misstated the number of works by other British authors being compared with Austen’s. There were 125, not 127.
match_headline: The Word Choices That Explain Why Jane Austen Endures

text: An essay on July 16 about Jane Austen’s handling of the subject of death misstated a plot sequence in “Sense and Sensibility.” Marianne Dashwood contracts a virulent fever after walking in the wet after a period of heavy rain, not in the rainstorm itself.
match_headline: In Jane Austen’s Pages, Death Has No Dominion

text: An article on July 16 about how to protect your home while you’re on vacation misspelled part of the name of a smart bulb. It is Philips Hue, not Phillips Hue.
match_headline: How to Protect Your House When You’re on Vacation

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Erik Gensler and Ryan Donovan reversed the identities of the spouses in the accompanying photo. Mr. Gensler was shown on the left and Mr. Donovan on the right.
match_headline: Ryan Donovan, Erik Gensler

text: An article on Saturday about the stresses of air travel described incorrectly the change to a seat reserved by the conservative columnist Ann Coulter. She paid for a seat in Delta Air Line’s Comfort+ section and was reassigned to a seat in the same section; she was not moved to a coach seat.
match_headline: Airport Checklist: Boarding Pass, ID, Stress

text: An obituary on Saturday about John G. Morris, the distinguished picture editor for Life magazine, The New York Times and other publications, as well as for the Magnum Photos agency, misidentified the mother of his two deceased daughters. Their mother was his first wife, the former Mary Adele Crosby — not his second, the former Marjorie Smith.
match_headline: John G. Morris, Renowned Photo Editor in the Thick of History, Dies at 100

text: An article on Tuesday about large Russian military exercises near the eastern edge of NATO territory described one area, Kaliningrad, incorrectly. It is an exclave of Russia, not an enclave.
match_headline: Russia’s Military Drills Near NATO Border Raise Fears of Aggression

text: An article on Tuesday about the short tenure of Anthony Scaramucci as White House communications director misstated the number of children he has. He is the father of five children, not two. (He has two with his second wife; she gave birth to a boy just days after Mr. Scaramucci became communications director.)
match_headline: Scaramucci’s Brief, but Volatile, Tenure

text: An article on Friday about the Thirty Meter Telescope that astronomers hope to build atop Hawaii’s Mauna Kea mountain misstated the location of the Canary Islands, their second choice if the Hawaii location is not approved. The islands, which are an autonomous region of Spain, are situated off the coast of Africa, not Spain.
match_headline: Giant Telescope Atop Hawaii’s Mauna Kea Should Be Approved, Judge Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about plans by Foxconn to build a factory in Wisconsin misstated, in some copies, the average number of jobs the economy added per month in the first half of 2017. It was an average of 180,000 jobs, not 80,000 jobs.
match_headline: Foxconn Says It Plans to Build Factory in Wisconsin, Adding 3,000 Jobs

text: An article on July 11 about a study of cycling and air pollution in New York City misstated the role of the radio station WNYC in the study. It helped start the study with scientists at Columbia University; it did not merely air announcements to recruit participants.
match_headline: On Your Bike, Watch Out for the Air

text: An article on Wednesday about ways in which war veterans are seeking serenity misspelled, in some copies, the given name of a former National Guard sergeant who is riding a bicycle across the United States. She is Sarah Lee, not Sara.
match_headline: Finding Some Peace After War

text: An article on Wednesday about France’s economy erroneously attributed a distinction to the Meraviglia cruise liner, built by the shipyard STX France, which an Italian competitor is trying to take over. At 171,598 tons, the Meraviglia is the world’s biggest luxury cruise ship built in 2017; it is not the biggest over all. (The 226,963-ton Harmony of the Seas, also built by STX France, holds that distinction.)
match_headline: Macron Vowed to Be Business Friendly. Now He Faces a Protectionist Uproar.

text: An article on Tuesday about a hotel boom in SeaTac, Wash., misidentified the company that employs Yogi Hutsen, an executive in SeaTac. He is executive vice president of Columbia Hospitality, not of Cedarbrook Lodge. (Cedarbrook Lodge is managed by Columbia Hospitality.)
match_headline: Hotel Boom in SeaTac Is Unfettered by $15 Minimum Wage

text: Because of an editing error, the DealBook column on Tuesday, about Starbucks’s expansion plans in China, referred incorrectly to China Central Television, known as CCTV. It has not changed its name to China Global Television Network, or CGTV.
match_headline: While Other U.S. Companies Flee China, Starbucks Doubles Down

text: An article on Tuesday about the Mets’ moves at the trading deadline misspelled, in some editions, the given name of a prospect acquired by the Mets in exchange for pitcher Addison Reed. He is Gerson Bautista, not Gershon.
match_headline: As Addison Reed Departs the Mets, Prospects Are on Their Way

text: A picture credit on Monday with an article about the National Baseball Hall of Fame induction ceremonies misidentified the photographer who took the picture of the former Montreal Expos Andre Dawson and Tim Raines, an inductee. It was by Jean Fruth of the National Baseball Hall of Fame — not by Vladimir Guerrero, another former Expo. The error was repeated in the picture caption, which noted that Dawson was posing for a former teammate.
match_headline: Tim Raines Is Enshrined as an Expo, and He’s Happy About It

text: An article on Monday about the Yankees’ acquiring pitcher Jaime Garcia in a trade misstated the number of career at-bats Yankees third baseman Todd Frazier has against Garcia. It is 23, not 26.
match_headline: Yankees Acquire Starter Jaime Garcia From Twins, Then Lose to Rays

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the Discovery Channel show “Manhunt: Unabomber” misstated the surname of the F.B.I. profiler portrayed by Sam Worthington. He is James R. Fitzgerald, not Fitzpatrick.
match_headline: Will Shark Lovers Love ‘Unabomber’? Asking for a Cable Network.

text: An article on Tuesday about solar eclipses misidentified the location where Bobby Powell, a physicist at the University of West Georgia, will be performing an experiment with students during the eclipse on Aug. 21. The experiment will be near Lexington, S.C. — not Lexington, Ky.
match_headline: The Eclipse That Revealed the Universe

text: An article on Wednesday about the capture of escaped prisoners in Alabama misstated the time that one of them, Brady Andrew Kilpatrick, was caught. It was 6:30 p.m. Central time on Tuesday, not Eastern time.
match_headline: Inmates Who Used Peanut Butter, and Guile, to Escape an Alabama Jail Are Caught

text: An article on Tuesday about conflicts between members of Stuyvesant High School’s alumni groups misstated the voting procedures of the board of the school’s alumni association. Members can vote for a candidate or abstain; they cannot vote a candidate down.
match_headline: At Competitive Stuyvesant, Alumni Are Waging a Bitter Contest

text: An article on Thursday about a new chief executive for the snack giant Mondelez misidentified the company that Nelson Peltz, an activist investor and member of Mondelez’s board, criticized for “slow growth” in its beverage unit. He was referring to PepsiCo, not to Mondelez.
match_headline: Snack Giant Mondelez, Facing Changing Tastes, Names a New C.E.O.

text: An article on Thursday about Amazon’s Job Fair misstated the hourly pay that one of the event’s attendees, Victor Salgado, makes at an aerosol company. It is $9 per hour, not $10.75.
match_headline: Amazon’s Jobs Fair Sends Clear Message: Now Hiring Thousands

text: An article on Friday about the arrest of a British security researcher misstated the year in which the Federal Bureau of Investigation arrested a Russian encryption expert in his Las Vegas hotel room. It was in 2001, not 2002.
match_headline: He Won Praise for Halting a Global Cyberattack. Then He Was Arrested.

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about students with developmental disabilities in special college programs refers incorrectly to a legislative act passed in 1975 that opened the way for such students to attend mainstream classes. When it became law, it was the Education for All Handicapped Children Act (and was later reauthorized as the Individuals With Disabilities Education Act); it was not known as the Individuals With Disabilities Act in 1975 or at any other time.
match_headline: Developmentally Disabled, and Going to College

text: An article on Page 12 this weekend about New World School of the Arts misspells part of the name of one of the Broadway shows orchestrated by Alex Lacamoire, an alumnus. It is “Dear Evan Hansen” (not Hanson). The error is repeated on Page 14 in an interview with Mr. Lacamoire.
match_headline: Where All the School’s a Stage, and the List of Success Stories Is Long

text: An article last Sunday about poems by contemporary American poets that inspired photographers misspelled the given name of one poet. She is Katy Lederer, not Katie.
match_headline: How Poems Inspire Pictures

text: An article last Sunday about a soccer match in Miami between Barcelona and Real Madrid and the festivities around it misspelled the given name of a former Barcelona star who competed in a small exhibition game with Patrick Kluivert. He is Carles Puyol, not Carlos.
match_headline: Soccer’s El Clásico Comes to Miami. So Does the Circus.

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about Claire Smith’s receiving the J. G. Taylor Spink Award at the National Baseball Hall of Fame misspelled, in some copies, the surname of a previous winner. He was Damon Runyon, not Runyan. (He was born Runyan but later began using the alternative spelling professionally.)
match_headline: Claire Smith, a Pioneer in Sports Writing, Is Honored at Cooperstown

text: A picture credit last Sunday with a review of the novel “Less” misspelled the given name of the photographer who took the picture of the author, Andrew Sean Greer. He is Kaliel Roberts, not Caliel.
match_headline: June’s Book Club Pick: ‘Less,’ by Andrew Sean Greer

text: An article last Sunday about Berryessa Snow Mountain National Monument in California misstated the height of Snow Mountain. It is 7,056 feet, not 3,057 feet.
match_headline: At Berryessa National Monument, Wildflowers and Rebirth

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about choreographed performances of classical music misstated the given name of a cellist shown. She is Beth Root Sandvoss, not Ruth.
match_headline: Concert Choreography: When Musicians Get Up and Move

text: A caption accompanying Maureen Dowd’s column last Sunday misidentified the work shown. It was inspired by Hieronymus Bosch’s The Last Judgment, but was painted by another, unidentified artist.
match_headline: President Trump’s Really Weak Week

text: An article on Monday about fictional characters in advertisements misstated the name of the manicurist in Palmolive commercials. The character was Madge, not Marge.
match_headline: The Potential and Peril of Giving a Brand a Human Face

text: An article on Monday about deals being considered by Sprint misstated the timing of two statements about possible deals. Charter Communications said last week — not this week — that it had no interest in buying Sprint. And Sprint’s chief executive also said last week — not this week — that an announcement on any deal could be coming in the near future.
match_headline: Sprint, Looking to Get Bigger to Survive, Weighs Deal-Making

text: Because of an editing error, the Global Sports column on Monday about medal reallocation ceremonies at the world track and field championships misstated the given name of the son of Kara Goucher, who received a new silver medal on Saturday night. He is Colt, not Cole.
match_headline: An Awkward and Bittersweet Righting of Doping’s Wrongs

text: An article on Tuesday about a sweeping federal climate change report referred incorrectly to the availability of the report. While it was not widely publicized, the report was posted by the nonprofit Internet Archive in January; it was not first made public by The New York Times.
match_headline: Scientists Fear Trump Will Dismiss Blunt Climate Report

text: An article on Monday about presidents who have been caught in lies gave an incorrect date for the height of the Watergate scandal, when President Richard M. Nixon was accused of lying, obstructing justice and finally resigned. It was 1974, not 1972.
match_headline: Many Politicians Lie. But Trump Has Elevated the Art of Fabrication.

text: Because of an editing error, schedule information on Tuesday with a review of Anna Netrebko’s first performance in the title role of “Aida” at the Salzburg Festival misidentified the location of the performance. The opera is in Salzburg, Austria — not in Vienna.
match_headline: Review: Anna Netrebko Sings Her First ‘Aida’ in Salzburg

text: An article last Wednesday about the 40-year history of the River Café in Brooklyn misstated the decade when its owner, Michael O’Keeffe, first visited the restaurant La Grenouille. It was the 1960s, not the 1950s.
match_headline: View From the River Café: 40 Years of Feasts and Firsts

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the former Philadelphia Phillies catcher Darren Daulton omitted a reporting credit. Daniel E. Slotnik contributed.
match_headline: Darren Daulton, Catcher for the 1993 Pennant-Winning Phillies, Dies at 55

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s endorsement of Senator Luther Strange in the special Senate election in Alabama misidentified the position that Mitch McConnell of Kentucky holds in the Senate. He is the majority leader, not the minority leader.
match_headline: Trump Rewards Loyalty in Alabama Senate Race by Tweeting Endorsement

text: An article on Tuesday about a recent surge of initial coin offerings referred incorrectly to Patrick Murck, a lawyer who commented on the regulatory oversight of such offerings. He is special counsel at Cooley, not a partner in the law firm.
match_headline: Despite S.E.C. Warning, Wave of Initial Coin Offerings Grows

text: An article last Sunday about Wired magazine’s Colophon note from its August issue misstated the city where the Saigon Sandwich shop mentioned in the note is located. It is San Francisco, not New York.
match_headline: Wired Thanks Women. Twitter Reacts.

text: An article on Thursday about the Democratic Party in California misidentified the presidential candidate that Kimberly Ellis, a Bay Area activist, supported in the presidential primary last year. She backed Hillary Clinton, not Senator Bernie Sanders. The article also referred incorrectly to Ms. Ellis’s association with Emerge California. She is a former executive director, not the current one.
match_headline: Democratic Fight in California Is a Warning for the National Party

text: An article on Thursday about new fossil discoveries that show that prehistoric “squirrels” glided through forests at least 160 million years ago referred imprecisely to what is shared between placental mammals and their mothers. While nutrients and oxygen from the mother’s blood are transferred to fetal blood through the placenta, the growing mammals do not draw blood from their mothers.
match_headline: When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth, Mammals Took to the Skies

text: An obituary on July 24 about the actor John Heard misstated his full name and the name of his son. He was John Heard Jr., not John Matthew Heard Jr., and his son is John Matthew Heard, not John M. Heard III.
match_headline: John Heard, the Frazzled Father in ‘Home Alone,’ Dies at 71

text: An obituary on Thursday about the graphic designer Alan Peckolick erroneously included a famous movie poster among his noted designs. It was Saul Bass, not Mr. Peckolick, who designed the poster for the Alfred Hitchcock movie “Vertigo.” (Mr. Bass also designed the movie’s title sequence.)
match_headline: Alan Peckolick, a Leading Logo Designer, Dies at 76

text: An article on July 21 about O.J. Simpson’s parole, using information from the Nevada parole commission, misstated Mr. Simpson’s criminal history. He pleaded no contest in 1989 to misdemeanor battery of his wife; it is not the case he had no criminal record before his 2008 conviction for armed robbery in Las Vegas. An article about the commission’s error is on Page A11.
match_headline: O.J. Simpson Wins Parole, Claiming He Has Led a ‘Conflict-Free Life’

text: An article last Saturday about the playwright Sam Shepard’s early years in New York misidentified one of Mr. Shepard’s friends who found him a job at the Village Gate nightclub. He is the artist Charles Mingus III — not Mr. Mingus’s father, who was a jazz musician.
match_headline: How Sam Shepard Hit Downtown New York and Reinvented Himself

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on July 31 about the Cajun singer and songwriter D. L. Menard referred incorrectly to one of his children. Doris Menard is a son, not a daughter.
match_headline: D.L. Menard, ‘the Cajun Hank Williams,’ Is Dead at 85

text: A picture caption on July 28 with an obituary about the voice actress June Foray misspelled the surname of a composer who recorded with her. He was Walter Schumann, not Schuman.
match_headline: June Foray, Virtuoso of Cartoon Voices, Notably Rocky’s, Dies at 99

text: An obituary on July 30 about the guitar maker Bill Collings referred incorrectly to the Gibson C-1 guitar. Elvis Presley did not play one on “The Ed Sullivan Show.”
match_headline: Bill Collings, Maker of Sought-After Guitars, Dies at 68

text: An article last Sunday about the artist Julie Mehretu misstated Jason Moran’s role at the Kennedy Center. He is the artistic director for jazz, not the artistic director of the entire center.
match_headline: In an Unused Harlem Church, a Towering Work of a ‘Genius’

text: An article on July 30 about turning games and other nonnarrative intellectual property into movies misspelled the surname of an actress. She is Anna Faris, not Farris.
match_headline: How to Make a Movie Out of Anything — Even a Mindless Phone Game

text: An article on Aug. 6 about prosecutorial misconduct omitted part of the name of a law school. It is Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law, not Southern Methodist University Dedham.
match_headline: She Was Convicted of Killing Her Mother. Prosecutors Withheld the Evidence That Would Have Freed Her.

text: A headline last Sunday with an article about Qualcomm’s efforts in China misidentified the location of the company’s headquarters. It is based in San Diego, not Silicon Valley.
match_headline: How This U.S. Tech Giant Is Backing China’s Tech Ambitions

text: An article last Sunday about efforts by Diane Hendricks to remake Beloit, Wis. misidentified the company led by Brent Fox, one of Ms. Hendricks’s sons. It is Hendricks Holding Company, not ABC Supply. The article also referred incorrectly to Ms. Hendricks’s ranking among the richest women in the United States. She is the second-richest self-made woman, according to Forbes magazine, not the second-richest woman.
match_headline: In Weary Wisconsin Town, a Billionaire-Fueled Revival

text: An article on Monday about Sinclair Broadcast Group referred imprecisely to the results of an investigation by the Federal Communications Commission involving the company, the nation’s largest owner of television stations. Sinclair agreed to pay $9.5 million to settle the case, without admitting wrongdoing; it was not fined that amount by the F.C.C.
match_headline: How a Conservative TV Giant Is Ridding Itself of Regulation

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about West Virginia’s efforts to focus on vocational training as a way to help its flagging economy described Donald J. Trump’s victory margin in that state incorrectly. While Mr. Trump won his highest percentage of the vote in West Virginia, the state did not give him his greatest victory margin. (That was Wyoming.)
match_headline: Seeing Hope for Flagging Economy, West Virginia Revamps Vocational Track

text: An article on Thursday about artifacts from a Syrian prison for an exhibition at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum described incorrectly plans to preserve the material. The items could be held in plexiglass containers that protect from ultraviolet rays, not in containers fitted with ultraviolet lights.
match_headline: On Cloth Scraps, Syrian Names Are Immortalized in Rust and Blood

text: An article on Thursday about the naming of a new president by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences misstated the occupation of Michael Tronick, a vice president of the Academy. He is a film editor, not a music editor.
match_headline: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Names New President

text: A listing of information with a review last Wednesday about the Middle Eastern restaurant Nur, on East 20th Street, misidentified the cross street. It is Park Avenue South, not Park Avenue.
match_headline: At Nur, an Open-Armed Approach to Middle Eastern Flavors

text: An article on Saturday about the Yankees putting pitcher C.C. Sabathia on the disabled list misspelled the surname of the Yankees’ trainer in some copies. He is Steve Donohue, not Donahue.
match_headline: C.C. Sabathia Goes on D.L., but Hopes to Miss Only One Start

text: An article last Thursday about a decision by Major League Baseball to allow players to put nicknames on their uniforms as part of Players Weekend this month misspelled, in some copies, the name of a player from the Netherlands national team who is known for his bat flip in the World Baseball Classic. He is Wladimir Balentien, not Balantien.
match_headline: Nicknames on Yankees’ Backs? What Would the Bambino Think?

text: An article last Friday about an inflatable chicken that was displayed near the White House misidentified the city where Taran Singh Brar, the artist who installed the chicken, lives. He is in Ladera Ranch, Calif., not Laredo.
match_headline: This Is Why a Trump Chicken Was Near the White House

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about efforts by Democrats to reconnect with working class voters erroneously included one state among those with right-to-work laws. Though Michigan and Wisconsin have the laws, California does not.
match_headline: On Four-State Tour, Democratic Leaders Try to Reconnect With Workers

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about an effort by Rajat K. Gupta to restore his reputation after serving a prison term for divulging confidential corporate information to Raj Rajaratnam referred incorrectly to Mr. Rajaratnam’s prison sentence. At 11 years, it is not the longest for insider trading; Matthew Kluger was sentenced to 12 years in 2012.
match_headline: For Rajat Gupta, Returning Is a Hard Road

text: An article on Monday about museum exhibitions in Detroit focused on the city’s 1967 riots misidentified a mock military vehicle that is displayed at the Detroit Historical Museum. It is an armored personnel carrier, not a tank. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Detroit Museums Examine the Riots That Changed the City

text: An article on Thursday about tensions between President Trump and military and business leaders over his remarks about protesters in Charlottesville, Va., misidentified, in some editions, the location of a statue of Robert E. Lee that was the focus of the protests. It is in a public park in Charlottesville — not on the University of Virginia campus, where protesters first gathered. The article also referred incorrectly to a military leader whose post on social media condemned racism. The post was by the chief of the National Guard Bureau, not the Coast Guard.
match_headline: Trump Comments on Race Open Breach With C.E.O.s, Military and G.O.P.

text: An article on Tuesday about plans for additional marches by white supremacists and right-wing extremists referred incorrectly to the conservative lawyer running for Senate from Florida who attended the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Va. His name is Augustus Sol Invictus, legally changed from Austin Gillespie; it is not a pseudonym.
match_headline: Far Right Plans Its Next Moves With a New Energy

text: An article on Friday about the left-wing faction of counter-protesters known as antifa misidentified the location of the 2008 Republican National Convention. It was in St. Paul, not in Minneapolis.
match_headline: ‘Antifa’ Grows as Left-Wing Faction Set to, Literally, Fight the Far Right

text: An article on Thursday about a newly discovered daguerreotype image of President John Quincy Adams misspelled the given name of a photographer who created a daguerreotype of Vice President John C. Calhoun. He was Mathew Brady, not Matthew.
match_headline: Found: Oldest Known Photo of a U.S. President (Socks and All)

text: An article on Friday about the artist Kara Walker reversed the second and third columns of type. The correct version can be found at nytimes.com/art .
match_headline: Kara Walker, ‘Tired of Standing Up,’ Promises Art, Not Answers

text: An obituary on Friday about the blues historian Paul Oliver misspelled the given name of a blues artist. He was Son House, not Sun House.
match_headline: Paul Oliver, Pre-eminent Authority on the Blues, Dies at 90

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the Yankees’ 10-5 loss to the Boston Red Sox misspelled the surname of the Red Sox catcher who drew third-inning walk. He is Christian Vazquez, not Vasquez.
match_headline: After Yankees’ Montgomery Is Struck in the Ear, Severino Is Hit Hard in Loss

text: Because of an editing error, a report in the Extra Bases column last Sunday about Freddie Freeman’s role with the Atlanta Braves this season misstated, in some copies, the number of wins the team had last season. It was 68, not 63.
match_headline: Braves’ Freddie Freeman Sets a Moving Example

text: An article last Sunday about the streaming channel Heera referred incompletely to its availability, as well as to that of the series “Inside Edge.” Besides being available in the United States, Heera is also available in Britain. And the series itself is available worldwide because it is on Amazon Prime; it is not available just on Heera.
match_headline: Wade Into the Deep Bollywood Pool With Amazon’s Heera

text: A review on July 30 about “Pretend We Are Lovely” referred incorrectly to the book. It is not Noley Reid’s debut novel. She is also the author of “In the Breeze of Passing Things,” published under the name Nicole Louise Reid in 2003. The error was repeated in a subheading with the review.
match_headline: A Novel Spirals Through Loss, Desire and Longing

text: An article on Aug. 6 about the Voyager space probes misstated the title of Tom Krimigis. He is the emeritus head of the Space Department at the Applied Physics Laboratory at Johns Hopkins University, not the emeritus head of the entire laboratory.
match_headline: The Loyal Engineers Steering NASA’s Voyager Probes Across the Universe

text: An article on Sunday about the departure of Stephen K. Bannon from the White House senior staff referred incorrectly to President Trump’s pending decision on American troop strength in Afghanistan. The president is expected to add nearly 4,000 troops, not keep the number at nearly 4,000. (The United States currently has about 8,400 troops there.)
match_headline: Will Bannon’s White House Agenda Survive Without Him?

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on June 27 with an article about obscure soccer teams that qualified for the Champions League misspelled part of the name of the team shown playing Heart of Midlothian in 2016. It is Infonet Tallinn, not Tallin. The caption also misidentified the competition in which the teams were playing. It was Europa League, not Champions League. This correction was delayed because an email from a reader pointing out the error went astray at The Times.
match_headline: A Welcome Payday for Obscure Teams in the Champions League

text: An article on Monday about Jerry Lewis’s influence on other entertainers misspelled the surname of one of the hosts of the “Tonight Show.” He was Jack Paar, not Parr.
match_headline: For Jerry Lewis, Few Statuettes but Lots of Influence

text: An article on Monday about a Russian immigrant who met last summer with senior Trump campaign officials referred incorrectly to the location of Kazan, Russia. It is 500 miles east of Moscow, not west.
match_headline: Lobbyist at Trump Campaign Meeting Has a Web of Russian Connections

text: An article on Saturday about the shooting death in Tanzania of a wildlife conservationist referred incorrectly to Dar es Salaam, where the conservationist, Wayne Lotter, was killed. While Dar es Salaam is the largest city in the East African nation, it is not the capital. (That is Dodoma.)
match_headline: Crusader Who Saved Elephants From Poachers Is Shot Dead in Tanzania

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the rockabilly singer Sonny Burgess misspelled the given name of a musician with whom he recorded. He is Garry Tallent, not Gary.
match_headline: Sonny Burgess, Rockabilly Wild Man, Is Dead at 88

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Aug. 3 about the former Notre Dame football coach Ara Parseghian misstated a reason that he initially hesitated to take the Notre Dame job. It was because his father had formed a dislike of Catholics, not Christians.
match_headline: Ara Parseghian, Coach Who Returned Notre Dame Football to Greatness, Dies at 94

text: An article last Wednesday about tomato jam referred incorrectly to the process for canning tomatoes. It requires the addition of an acid, like lemon juice, lime juice or vinegar. It is not the case that no acid is needed in canning the tomatoes. The error was repeated in an accompanying recipe. A tablespoon of either white distilled or red wine vinegar should be added at the beginning of cooking.

An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s rally in Phoenix referred incorrectly in some copies to the destroyer John S. McCain. It was named for Senator John McCain’s grandfather and father — John S. McCain Sr. and John S. McCain Jr., both Navy admirals; it was not named after the Arizona senator.
match_headline: At Rally, Trump Blames Media for Country’s Deepening Divisions

text: An article on Wednesday about similarities between President Trump’s strategy on Afghanistan and proposals made by former Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. quoted incorrectly from Mr. Trump’s speech on Monday night about Afghanistan. In a reference to terrorists, he said, “These killers need to know they have nowhere to hide,” not “no place” to hide.
ref_headline: These killers need to know they have nowhere to hide,
match_headline: The Forerunner of Trump’s Plan for Afghanistan: Joe Biden’s

text: An article on Wednesday about the future of Fiat Chrysler quoted incorrectly from comments by Kristin Dziczek, an analyst at the Center for Automotive Research. Referring to Fiat Chrysler’s debt, she said, “That does not bode well for investing in future product.” She did not say that the debt does bode well for future investments.
ref_headline: That does not bode well for investing in future product.
match_headline: Fiat Chrysler Is at a Crossroads. It’s Looking to China for a Solution.

text: An article on Wednesday about a partnership between Walmart and Google misstated the role of the Google Assistant, the artificially intelligent software assistant, in the relationship with Walmart. The eventual plan is for Walmart customers to be able to buy products using the Google Assistant; customers cannot do that now.
match_headline: Google and Walmart Partner With Eye on Amazon

text: An article on Tuesday about Sempra Energy’s winning the bidding for Energy Future Holdings misstated an outcome for a losing bidder, Berkshire Hathaway. It is not entitled to a $270 million breakup fee.
match_headline: Sempra Bid Tops Buffett and Singer in Race for Energy Future

text: An article on Tuesday about the accomplishments of the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 space missions misstated the date on which the PBS documentary “The Farthest” was broadcast. It was shown Wednesday night; it had not already aired at the time the article was published.
match_headline: A Reverie for the Voyager Probes, Humanity’s Calling Cards

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the playwright, novelist and screenwriter Janusz Glowacki, using information from his family, misstated the year of his marriage to Olena Leonenko. It was 2014, not 2015. Because of an editing error, an accompanying picture caption misspelled the original surname of Mr. Glowacki’s first wife, Ewa. As the obituary correctly noted, it is Zadrzynska, not Zadrzyska. And the obituary misstated, in some copies, the year of the Andrzej Wajda film “Walesa: Man of Hope,” for which Mr. Glowacki wrote the screenplay. It was 2013, not 2003.
match_headline: Janusz Glowacki, Polish Playwright of Terror and Dark Humor, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on Sunday about the architect Gunnar Birkerts omitted an architect whose work inspired Mr. Birkerts. Besides Eero Saarinen, Mr. Birkerts was also inspired by Eliel Saarinen, the father of Eero.
match_headline: Gunnar Birkerts, Architect, Dies at 92; Gave Shape to the Unexpected

text: An article on Thursday about thawing permafrost in Alaska misspelled the surname of a researcher at the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. He is Vladimir E. Romanovsky, not Ramonovsky.
match_headline: Alaska’s Permafrost Is Thawing

text: An article on Thursday about the Yankees’ 10-2 victory over the Detroit Tigers misidentified, in some editions, the Detroit outfielder who caught a Chase Headley line drive. He is Andrew Romine — not Kevin Romine, who is Andrew’s father and a former major leaguer.
match_headline: Chase Headley Is at Peace in His Place, No Matter Where That Is

text: An article on Friday about the Yankees’ brawl-filled 10-6 loss to the Detroit Tigers misspelled, in some editions, the surname of the Detroit pitcher who hit Gary Sanchez in the fifth inning. He is Michael Fulmer, not Fullmer.
match_headline: Punches and Ejections Mar a Yankees Loss in Detroit

text: An article on Aug. 12 about casting and other changes to “The Great British Bake Off” referred incorrectly to efforts to reach Love Productions, which created the program. It did not respond to an email seeking comment because the message was misdirected. (The production company subsequently declined to answer questions.)
match_headline: ‘The Great British Bake Off’ as We Know It Is Over. What Comes Next?

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about Tony A. de Brum, a Marshall Islands political leader who fought for his country’s survival in the face of climate change, referred incorrectly to the Paris climate accord’s call for limiting a global temperature increase by 2011. It said temperatures should rise by no more than 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (or 1.5 degrees Celsius, as the obituary correctly noted), not 34.7 degrees Fahrenheit.
match_headline: Tony de Brum, Voice of Pacific Islands on Climate Change, Dies at 72

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the automotive engineer Roy Lunn, who oversaw development of the Ford GT40, misidentified the models of the GT40 cars that finished first, second and third at Le Mans in 1966. They were GT40 Mark II models, not Mark IV.
match_headline: Roy Lunn, Pioneering Engineer of Celebrated Cars, Dies at 92

text: An article last Sunday about the streaming service Crunchyroll misidentified Colin Decker’s position at the company. He is chief operating officer, not chief executive.
match_headline: Crunchyroll Cultivates a Streaming Community With a Novel Idea: Film Screens

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption last Sunday with an article about a PBS “Nova” special on the solar eclipse last week misstated part of the name of the show. The eclipse is generally called “Eclipse Across America,” but the show is “Eclipse Over America.”
match_headline: Ready for the Solar Eclipse? ‘Nova’ on PBS Has You Covered

text: An article on Aug. 13 about a fraternity hazing death misstated the name and location of a public school in New York City. It is Junior High School 185 in Flushing, Queens; there is no Middle School 185 in Bayside.
match_headline: What a Fraternity Hazing Death Revealed About the Painful Search for an Asian-American Identity

text: An article on Aug. 20 about Breitbart News misstated the religious affiliation of a British anti-extremist activist named Maajid Nawaz. He is a former Islamist, not an ex-Muslim.
match_headline: Down the Breitbart Hole

text: An article last Sunday about hostility toward women in economics misstated the current views of George Borjas, a Harvard professor, about Economics Job Market Rumors, an online forum, after he received a copy of a paper by Alice H. Wu, who will be starting doctoral studies at Harvard next year, about the forum. Mr. Borjas said, “While there is some value in that forum, there is also a great deal that is offensive and disturbing. The problem is I’m not sure exactly where to draw line.” He did not say that all his views about the forum were unchanged.
ref_headline: While there is some value in that forum, there is also a great deal that is offensive and disturbing. The problem is I’m not sure exactly where to draw line.
match_headline: Evidence of a Toxic Environment for Women in Economics

text: An article last Sunday about heirs who do not want all of their parents’ belongings misstated the job held by Jennifer Lacker. She is an antiques appraiser, not an antiques dealer.
match_headline: Aging Parents With Lots of Stuff, and Children Who Don’t Want It

text: An article on Saturday about the growing outcry against a wider array of monuments misstated ESPN’s reasoning for not having a sportscaster named Robert Lee broadcast a University of Virginia football game. ESPN said the decision was a mutual one, made to avoid becoming a distraction; it was not to avoid offending viewers.
match_headline: Far From Dixie, Outcry Grows Over a Wider Array of Monuments

text: An article on Thursday about a ruling by a federal appeals panel to uphold the insider trading conviction of Mathew Martoma referred incorrectly to an insider trading case involving Todd Newman and Anthony Chiasson, which was ultimately thrown out. The two men were casual acquaintances of some of the later sources of the information, not the original sources.
match_headline: Mathew Martoma’s Insider Trading Conviction Is Upheld

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Aug. 9 about the singer Barbara Cook erroneously attributed a distinction to her. While her 2006 performance at the Metropolitan Opera was the first full concert by a female pop singer there under the Met’s auspices, she was not the first female pop singer to perform there. (Judy Garland appeared at the Met for seven nights in 1959, though those shows were produced independently.)
match_headline: Barbara Cook, Broadway Star Who Became a Cabaret Mainstay, Dies at 89

text: An obituary on Saturday about Cecil D. Andrus, who was secretary of the interior under President Jimmy Carter, referred incorrectly to his marriage to Carol May in 1949. They married before he fought in the Korean War — not after he returned.
match_headline: Cecil D. Andrus, 85, Carter’s Preservationist Interior Secretary, Dies

text: An obituary on Sunday about the polar explorer Charles R. Bentley misstated the time he spent in Greenland in the 1950s. It was two summers, not two years.
match_headline: Charles R. Bentley, 87, Pioneer of Polar Science, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Aug. 21 about Jerry Lewis referred imprecisely to his use of video assist, which allows directors to review their work immediately on a movie set. While he is widely acknowledged as the first major director to use it, he did not invent it. (He may have conceived the idea independently, but at least three patents for a form of video assist predate Mr. Lewis’s first use of it.)
match_headline: Jerry Lewis, a Jester Both Silly and Stormy, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a Food and Drug Administration crackdown on stem cell clinics omitted comments from two of the companies cited — StemImmune in San Diego and California Stem Cell Treatment Centers in Rancho Mirage, Calif., and Beverly Hills. It is not the case that the companies did not respond to requests for comment. The article reported that the F.D.A. had serious concerns about how StemImmune obtained hundreds of doses of small pox vaccine containing live Vaccinia virus for use in an unapproved and potentially dangerous stem cell treatment. A statement from StemImmune said the company had lawfully obtained the drug. The article also reported that patients at the California Stem Cell Treatment Centers received the treatment made with the smallpox vaccine. In response, Dr. Mark Berman, one of the founders of the centers, said that the F.D.A. had not accurately interpreted a cancer pilot study that the centers conducted with StemImmune. Dr. Berman, who is also a director of StemImmune, said that none of the patients had experienced serious adverse effects or died as a result of the treatment, which he noted was free.
match_headline: F.D.A. Cracks Down on ‘Unscrupulous’ Stem Cell Clinics

text: An article last Wednesday about the chef Tom Colicchio’s decision to change the name of his restaurant Fowler & Wells because of its connections to phrenology misidentified the members of the Fowler family who helped Samuel Wells found the Fowler & Wells publishing company in the 19th century.
