They were Lorenzo and Orson Fowler, not Edward Fowler. The article also misidentified which Fowler family member wrote a passage suggesting that African-Americans were racially inferior. It was by Orson, not Edward.
match_headline: Tom Colicchio Changes His Restaurant’s Racially Tinged Name

text: An article on Wednesday about the construction of weapons factories in Lebanon and Syria misspelled the given name of the Israeli defense minister. He is Avigdor Lieberman, not Avidgor.
match_headline: Iran Building Weapons Factories in Lebanon and Syria, Israel Says

text: An article on the Square Feet page on Wednesday about the Upper Peninsula neighborhood in Charleston, S.C., misidentified a company located in the Half Mile North development in the city. It is SIB Fixed Cost Reduction, not SIB Development and Consulting.
match_headline: A Vibrant Turnaround for a Neglected Charleston Neighborhood

text: An article on Tuesday about the seasonal fluctuations of gut bacteria described mucins incorrectly. They are carbohydrates produced in the mucus lining of the intestines; they are not enzymes.
match_headline: Gut Bacteria Can Fluctuate With the Seasons

text: An article on Thursday about the legacy of Diana, Princess of Wales, misstated the nationality of Meghan Markle, an actress who is dating Prince Harry. She is American, not Canadian.
match_headline: Diana’s Legacy: A Reshaped Monarchy, a More Emotional U.K.

text: An article on Thursday about thousands of Rohingya who have fled from Myanmar to Bangladesh because of violence referred incorrectly to the city of Yangon. It is no longer the capital of Myanmar. (Naypyidaw is.)
match_headline: Violence in Myanmar Pushes at Least 18,500 Rohingya Into Bangladesh

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the future of the New York City subway misidentified the person who said that “the city was pleased to shed the responsibility for operating and financing the transit system.” The comment was by Mitchell L. Moss, a professor at New York University — not by Robert Moses, the noted New York City builder. (Mr. Moses died in 1981.)
ref_headline: the city was pleased to shed the responsibility for operating and financing the transit system.
match_headline: They Have a Say Over the Subways, From Hundreds of Miles Away

text: An article on Thursday about New York City’s new director of night life erroneously included one European city on a list of those with similar positions, commonly known as “night mayors.” Berlin does not have a night mayor.
match_headline: What Europe’s ‘Night Mayors’ Can Teach New York

text: An article on Friday about the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau quoted incorrectly from comments by Richard Hunt of the Consumer Bankers Association. Mr. Hunt described the bureau’s chief, Richard Cordray, as “definitely ideological.” He did not say Mr. Cordray is “doggedly ideological.”
match_headline: Republicans Want to Sideline This Regulator. But It May Be Too Popular.

text: An article on Friday about explosions at a flood-damaged chemical plant in Crosby, Tex., misidentified the site of an explosion at a fertilizer factory in 2013 that killed 15 people. It was in the town of West, Tex. — not in Texas City. The article also referred incorrectly to fines the owner of the Crosby plant, Arkema, has paid for health and safety violations since 2010. It has paid $1.2 million in fines for its United States plants, not just the one in Crosby.
match_headline: New Hazard in Storm Zone: Chemical Blasts and ‘Noxious’ Smoke

text: An article on Friday about a labor overhaul in France misstated part of the name of a research institute. It is the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, not the Organization for Cooperation and Economic Development.
match_headline: France Unveils Contentious Labor Overhaul in Big Test for Macron

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about an operation to retake the Iraqi city of Tal Afar referred incorrectly to a deal involving Islamic State fighters. The deal was reached with the Kurdish pesh merga forces, not the Iraqi military.
match_headline: ISIS Loses Another City to U.S.-Backed Iraqi Forces

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a film adaptation of the book “Lord of the Flies” misstated the year that an earlier adaptation was released. It was 1990, not 2000.
match_headline: In ‘Lord of the Flies’ Remake, Girls Survive Instead

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the artist Justin Brice Guariglia misstates part of the name of a film festival he attended and the year he was there. It is the Telluride Mountainfilm Festival, not the Telluride Film Festival, and he attended in 2017, not 2016. The article also misidentifies the location of the Norton Museum of Art, where Mr. Guariglia’s new exhibition is opening on Monday. It is in West Palm Beach, Fla., not Palm Beach.
match_headline: A Man on an Eco-Mission in Mixed Media

text: An article in some editions last Sunday about the fight between Floyd Mayweather Jr. and Conor McGregor described incorrectly the condition of McGregor’s face at the end of the bout. While late punches turned his face red, it was not bloodied.
match_headline: Mayweather, a Defensive Mastermind, Beats McGregor With His Fists

text: An obituary last Sunday about the author Brian Aldiss referred incorrectly to Helliconia, on which three of his science fiction novels are set. It is a planet where the cycle of seasons lasts more than 2,000 years, not where a day lasts a millennium.
match_headline: Brian Aldiss, Author of Science Fiction and Much More, Dies at 92

text: A review on Aug. 20 about “Freud: The Making of an Illusion” misidentified the birthplace of Sigmund Freud. He was born in Moravia, not Galicia; his parents were from Galicia.
ref_headline: Freud: The Making of an Illusion
match_headline: The Curious Conundrum of Freud’s Persistent Influence

text: An article on Aug. 20 about what the mystery writer Sue Grafton packs when traveling for work misstated the surname of a British writer whose work she reads. He is Lee Child, not Childs.
match_headline: What the Mystery Writer Sue Grafton Can’t Travel Without

text: A news analysis article on Monday about the motives of Kim Jong-un, North Korea’s leader, who oversaw the detonation of the country’s sixth nuclear bomb over the weekend, misspelled the given name of the Chinese president. He is Xi Jinping, not Jingping.
match_headline: Motives of North Korea’s Leader Baffle Americans and Allies

text: An article on Friday about Karolina Pliskova’s victory over Nicole Gibbs in the second round of the United States Open misstated, in some copies, Pliskova’s career record against Gibbs before the match. They had played three times before Thursday, not two. And Pliskova had won two of those matches; Thursday’s victory was not her first over Gibbs.
match_headline: U.S. Open Results: Federer Struggles Again; Dimitrov Loses

text: An article in some editions on Sunday about Karolina Pliskova’s third-round victory over Zhang Shuai at the United States Open misstated, in some copies, the score for the second set. Pliskova won it 7-5, not 6-5.
match_headline: Uneven Pliskova Battles Back to Advance to 4th Round Against Brady

text: An article on Aug. 28 about Alexander Zverev and his rising expectations in tennis misstated the age of his fellow player Nick Kyrgios. He is 22, not 24.
match_headline: The Rise of Alexander Zverev

text: An article on Friday about Roger Federer’s second-round victory over Mikhail Youzhny at the United States Open misstated, in some copies, the result of the first set. Federer won it 6-1; he did not lose it by that score.
match_headline: Though Federer Survives 2nd 5-Set Match, His Play Invites Questions

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Nick Kyrgios’s loss to John Millman in the first round of the United States Open misstated the score in the fourth set. Millman won 6-1, not 6-4.
match_headline: Nick Kyrgios, With a Long-Suffering Mother Watching, Crashes Out of U.S. Open

text: An article on Aug. 26 about the United States Open qualifying match between Allie Kiick and Victoria Duval misstated the given name of Kiick’s mother in some copies. She is Mary, not Kathy.
match_headline: Allie Kiick, No. 633, Qualifies for Main Draw of U.S. Open

text: A headline on Friday with an obituary about the actor Richard Anderson misstated his age in some copies. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 91, not 89.
match_headline: Richard Anderson, of ‘Six Million Dollar Man’ and ‘Bionic Woman,’ Dies at 91

text: An article on Monday about North Korea’s latest nuclear test misstated the location of the Punggye-ri underground test site. As correctly shown on an accompanying map, it is in northeastern North Korea, not northwestern.
match_headline: North Korean Nuclear Test Draws U.S. Warning of ‘Massive Military Response’

text: A picture on Wednesday with an article about a report retracted by CNN was published in error. It showed Thomas Frank, a political analyst, historian and author — not the former CNN reporter Thomas Frank, who wrote the CNN article.
match_headline: At CNN, Retracted Story Leaves an Elite Reporting Team Bruised

text: An article on Wednesday about the United States Open misstated the score for the second set of Pablo Carreño Busta’s victory over Diego Schwartzman. Carreño Busta won 6-4, 6-4, 6-2. (The second set was not 7-4.)
match_headline: U.S. Open Results: Pablo Carreño Busta and Sloane Stephens Reach Semifinals

text: A picture caption on Aug. 27 with the Sports of The Times column, about the last United States Open at Forest Hills, in 1977, misspelled the surname of the man shown painting the scoreboard there. The competitors’ names were being painted by Edward Perline, not Perlime.
match_headline: The U.S. Open’s Last Day at Forest Hills

text: An article on Thursday about deaths of C.I.A. paramilitary operatives in Afghanistan misidentified the home state of Brian R. Hoke, one of the operatives killed. Mr. Hoke was from the town of Park River, in North Dakota — not South Dakota.
match_headline: A Funeral of 2 Friends: C.I.A. Deaths Rise in Secret Afghan War

text: An article on Monday about negotiations on the future of the North American Free Trade Agreement misstated the United States’ goal for a system of independent arbitration under the agreement. The White House wants to overhaul the system, not end it.
match_headline: Nafta Negotiations: What’s at Stake in the Second Round

text: An article on Tuesday about the television show “American Horror Story” referred incorrectly to the actress Lena Dunham’s role. She will portray the writer and feminist activist Valerie Solanas, who may be best known for trying to assassinate Andy Warhol; Ms. Dunham’s role is not a mystery.
match_headline: ‘American Horror Story’ Sets Scares in Postelection America

text: An article last Friday about Legend Holdings’ acquisition of a controlling stake in Banque Internationale à Luxembourg misstated Legend’s relationship with the computer manufacturer Lenovo Group. It is Lenovo’s largest shareholder, not its owner.
match_headline: Chinese Firm With Big Stake in Lenovo to Buy Control of Luxembourg Bank

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a European court ruling on employers’ monitoring of their workers’ email misidentified the court that issued the ruling. It is the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights, not the European Court of Justice.
match_headline: European Court Limits Employers’ Right to Monitor Workers’ Email

text: An article on Monday about the singer Taylor Swift, who previewed a new song, “Ready for It?,” during the broadcast of the Alabama-Florida State college football game, misidentified the television network that showed the game. It is ABC, not ESPN.
match_headline: Now on Stage: The Countdown to a New Taylor Swift Album

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Hurricane Irma’s destruction in the Caribbean misstated the number of people in Haiti who have died from cholera since the disease’s outbreak there in 2010. It is more than 10,000 people, not 104. (That is the number who have died this year, government records show.)
match_headline: Caribbean Devastated as Irma Heads Toward Florida

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Hurricane Harvey relief efforts led by the football star J. J. Watt and his mother, Connie, misstated the distance between Pewaukee and Janesville, Wis., two locations where relief supplies were stored. They are about 50 miles apart, not 30 miles.
match_headline: J.J. Watt Appealed for Donations. Then His Mom Got to Work.

text: An obituary on Monday about the guitarist and songwriter Walter Becker, who founded the band Steely Dan with Donald Fagen, referred incorrectly to the band China Crisis, whose album “Flaunt the Imperfection” Mr. Becker produced. It is English, not Scottish.
match_headline: Walter Becker, Guitarist, Songwriter and Co-Founder of Steely Dan, Dies at 67

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about the victims of Hurricane Harvey misstated the relationship between Belia and Manuel Saldivar and four children who were found dead with them after the storm. As the article correctly noted, the couple were the children’s great-grandparents, not their grandparents.
match_headline: Human Toll of Harvey Comes Into View as Waters Recede

text: An article on Aug. 27 about the restoration of a tennis court where generations of African-American players got their start, using information from the Women’s Tennis Association website, misstated the ranking that one of those players, Leslie Allen, reached in 1983. She was No. 17, not No. 21.
match_headline: Restoring a Landmark for African-American Tennis Stars

text: A chart last Sunday with the Calculator column, about increased ownership of rental units by institutional investors, mislabeled the percentages shown with vertical bars. The percentages were for the “Share of Rental Properties,” not the “Share of Rental Units.”
match_headline: Mom and Pop Own Fewer Rental Units

text: An article on Sept. 3 about photography tours referred incorrectly to the type of camera used on a tour offered by andBeyond Kichwa Tembo Tented Camp. It is a camera equipped with a Nikon 600-millimeter lens, not a Nikon 600-millimeter camera. (There is no such camera.)
match_headline: 10 Tours to Turn Travelers Into Photographers

text: A review on Aug. 6 about “Poetry Will Save Your Life,” by Jill Bialosky, referred incorrectly to the author’s responsibilities at W. W. Norton & Company. She oversees the trade poetry list there, but she is not involved with the Norton anthologies.
match_headline: Exploring the Sources and Consolations of Poetry, in Prose

text: Because of an editing error, a listing of information with a music review on Saturday about a combined performance by two orchestras at Alice Tully Hall misspelled part of the names of both groups. They are the orchestras from Helsinki’s Sibelius Academy, not the Siblius Academy; and the Juilliard School, not the Juliard School.
match_headline: Review: Celebrating Sibelius and His Slowly Imparted Secrets

text: An article on Monday about the commercial success of the new horror film “It” misstated the given name of the film’s director. He is Andy Muschietti, not Anthony.
match_headline: ‘It’ Breaks September Records, Supercharging the Box Office

text: A picture on Saturday with an article about Major League Baseball’s decision to move the Yankees’ three-game series in St. Petersburg, Fla., against the Tampa Bay Rays to Citi Field was published in error. It showed the Yankees warming up for a 1998 regular-season game at Shea Stadium against the Mets, not the team warming up before a 1998 game that was moved to Shea Stadium because a beam had fallen at Yankee Stadium.
match_headline: Hurricane Irma Forces Yankees to Play Tampa Bay Rays at Citi Field

text: An article on Friday about the Yankees’ 9-1 victory over the Baltimore Orioles referred incorrectly to the Yankees’ results in the series in Baltimore. It was their first series win — not sweep — in Baltimore since 2013.
match_headline: ‘This One Was for Stick’: Yankees Do Gene Michael’s Legacy Proud

text: An article on Friday about the women’s semifinals at the United States Open misstated Sloane Stephens’s results at major tournaments since reaching the semifinals of the 2013 Australian Open. She advanced past the fourth round once, at Wimbledon in 2013; it is not the case that “she had not advanced past the fourth round in a major tournament” until this year’s U.S. Open.
ref_headline: she had not advanced past the fourth round in a major tournament
match_headline: Sloane Stephens and Madison Keys Reach U.S. Open Final

text: An article on Saturday about the men’s semifinals at the United States Open misidentified the last man representing South Africa to reach a Grand Slam final before Kevin Anderson at this year’s U.S. Open. The last to do so was Kevin Curren, at the 1984 Australian Open — not Johan Kriek, at the 1981 Australian Open.
match_headline: Rafael Nadal and Kevin Anderson Advance to U.S. Open Final

text: An article on Thursday about the men’s quarterfinals at the United States Open misstated the given name of Rafael Nadal’s opponent. He is Andrey Rublev, not Andrew.
match_headline: Juan Martín del Potro Upends Roger Federer and Disrupts an Anticipated Showdown

text: An obituary on Monday about the documentary filmmaker Jeffrey Tuchman misstated the name of the county in England where he attended school. It is Hertfordshire, not Hersfordshire.
match_headline: Jeffrey Tuchman, 62, Dies; Directed Clinton ‘Man From Hope’ Film

text: An editorial on Sunday misstated the background of Representative Jim Bridenstine, President Trump’s choice to run NASA. Mr. Bridenstine is on the House Science, Space and Technology Committee and previously was executive director of the Tulsa Air and Space Museum and Planetarium. It was not correct that he had no science or space background.
match_headline: President Trump’s War on Science

text: An article on Wednesday about a resolution passed unanimously by Congress urging the president to denounce hate groups misidentified the location of a statue of the Confederacy’s top general, Robert E. Lee, that was at the center of controversy in Charlottesville, Va., last month, when violence erupted as white supremacists protested its removal. The error also appeared in the New York pages on Wednesday in an article about a statue of Christopher Columbus in Central Park that was vandalized. As previous corrections in this space have noted, the statue is in the City of Charlottesville, not on the University of Virginia campus there.
match_headline: Congress Passes Measure Challenging Trump to Denounce Hate Groups

text: An article on Wednesday about Apple’s newly released iPhone models described incorrectly a phone call made during Apple’s product announcement at its headquarters in Cupertino, Calif. An executive onstage at headquarters demonstrated Apple Watch capabilities by calling an employee on a paddle board in a lake; the employee did not initiate the call.
match_headline: Apple Unveils iPhone X and 8 Models as It Upgrades TV Set-Top Box

text: An article on Wednesday about the second game of the Yankees-Tampa Bay Rays series misspelled the surname of the Rays’ No. 9 hitter. He is Adeiny Hechavarria, not Hechevarria. The article also misspelled the given name of the Yankees player in an 0-for-14 slump. He is Starlin Castro, not Starling.
match_headline: Rays Make Themselves at Home, Beating the Yankees and Sonny Gray

text: An article on Wednesday about plans for the Oakland Athletics’ new stadium misspelled the given name of one player and the surname of another. They are Rickey Henderson, not Ricky, and Ryan Madson, not Madsen.
match_headline: The Oakland A’s Are Trying to Solve Their Stadium Problem. Still.

text: An article on Wednesday about structures designed to protect art from extreme weather quoted incorrectly from comments by the director of the Pérez Art Museum in Miami. He said that the Mark di Suvero sculpture outside the museum could survive a Category 5 storm because of its cement base, not that the museum could survive.
match_headline: Irma-Proof Armor and Nights at the Museum: Shielding Florida’s Arts

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the theater director Peter Hall misidentified the play in which he directed Dustin Hoffman in 1989. It was “The Merchant of Venice,” in which Mr. Hoffman played Shylock — not “Death of a Salesman,” in which he played Willy Loman. (The 1984 Broadway production of “Death of a Salesman,” in which Mr. Hoffman played Willy Loman, was directed by Michael Rudman.)
match_headline: Peter Hall, British Theater Director and Founder of Royal Shakespeare Company, Dies at 86

text: An article on Sept. 2 about investigations into election tampering in several states referred incorrectly to problems with voter rolls in three North Carolina counties that included the cities of Raleigh, Winston-Salem and Charlotte. The problems involved paper rolls, not e-poll books.
match_headline: Russian Election Hacking Efforts, Wider Than Previously Known, Draw Little Scrutiny

text: A headline on Thursday with an article about Bitcoin manufacturing in China misstated the location of a Bitcoin factory. As the article correctly noted, it is in the Inner Mongolia region of China, not in Mongolia.
match_headline: In China’s Hinterlands, Workers Mine Bitcoin for a Digital Fortune

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a review of “For Peter Pan on Her 70th Birthday” misidentified one of the two actors shown. Lisa Emery, not David Chandler, was pictured with Kathleen Chalfant.
ref_headline: For Peter Pan on Her 70th Birthday
match_headline: Review: Reimagining ‘Peter Pan’ for the Lipitor Demographic

text: A review on Wednesday about the documentary film “Ex Libris: The New York Public Library” misstated the month the New York Public Library opened in 1911. It was May, not March.
ref_headline: Ex Libris: The New York Public Library
match_headline: Review: We the (Library-Card Carrying) People of ‘Ex Libris’

text: An article on Page D4 today about the musician Alex Zhang Hungtai, whose work was featured in the recent remake of the television series “Twin Peaks,” misidentifies the entertainment company that is producing the series. It is Showtime, not Netflix.
match_headline: Dispatches From the Nomad Musician Alex Zhang Hungtai

text: An obituary on Thursday about the former New Mexico senator Pete V. Domenici, using information from a spokesman, misstated the number of great-grandchildren who survive him. There are three, not two.
match_headline: Pete Domenici, Long a Powerful Senate Voice on Fiscal Policy, Dies at 85

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s relationship with Democrats in Congress misidentified the leadership position held by Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York. He is the minority leader — not the majority leader, the post held by Senator Mitch McConnell, Republican of Kentucky. The article also described incorrectly the preparation of a dinner at the White House. The food was prepared by the White House chef, not ordered from a restaurant.
match_headline: Why Did Trump Work Again With Democrats? ‘He Likes Us,’ Schumer Says

text: A review on Friday about “Deadeye Dick: Richard Bellamy and His Circle,” at Peter Freeman, Inc., misspelled the surname of an artist whose work is featured in the exhibit. She is Jean Follett, not Follet. The article also misstated the number of artists Richard Bellamy represented at the time of his death. He represented several, not just one.
ref_headline: Deadeye Dick: Richard Bellamy and His Circle,
match_headline: When Dealers, Too, Were Romantics

text: Because of an editing error, a theater entry in the Listings pages on Friday about the play “Tiny Beautiful Things,” at the Public Theater, misstated its opening date. It is Oct. 2, not Sept. 25.
match_headline: What’s New in NYC Theater

text: A review on Page 11 this weekend about “Blurred Lines: Rethinking Sex, Power and Consent on Campus,” by Vanessa Grigoriadis, refers incorrectly to her reporting on the issues. She does in fact write about Department of Justice statistics that say college-age women are less likely than nonstudent women of the same age to be victims of sexual assault; it is not the case that Grigoriadis was unaware of the department’s findings. In addition, the review describes incorrectly Grigoriadis’s presentation of statistics from the Rape, Abuse and Incest National Network. She showed that there is disagreement over whether the data are sound; it is not the case that she gave the reader “no reason to believe” the statistics are wrong.
ref_headline: Blurred Lines: Rethinking Sex, Power and Consent on Campus,
match_headline: Shining a Light on Campus Rape

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about the growing prominence of gender-fluid artists refers incorrectly to Diamond Stingily, an artist. Ms. Stingily is not transgender. The article also refers incorrectly to Sadie Benning’s series of photographs. They are portraits, but not self-portraits.
match_headline: Gender-Fluid Artists Come Out of the Gray Zone

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Edith Windsor, whose landmark case led the Supreme Court to grant same-sex married couples federal recognition, misstated the surname of the man she married in 1951. Although he used the surname Windsor in divorce papers filed the next year, and she herself went by that name for the rest of her life, his name when they married was Saul Wiener, not Saul Windsor. (This error also appeared in an article in 2012.) Because of an editing error, the obituary also referred incorrectly at one point to Ms. Windsor’s wife, Judith Kasen-Windsor. She is the only immediate family member who survives Ms. Windsor, not her only survivor. (Several cousins, a niece and a nephew also survive her.)
match_headline: Edith Windsor, Whose Same-Sex Marriage Fight Led to Landmark Ruling, Dies at 88

text: A review on Sept. 3 about two books by Walt Whitman misstated the academic status of Zachary Turpin, who wrote the books’ introductions. He is an assistant professor of English at the University of Idaho; he is no longer a graduate student at the University of Houston.
match_headline: Two New Old Books That Show Walt Whitman’s Different Selves

text: An article last Sunday about Shakespeare plays coming this season misspelled the surname of the director of “Arden/Everywhere” at the Baruch Performing Arts Center. She is Jessica Bauman, not Baumann.
match_headline: Reinventing Shakespeare, According to the Gospel of Joseph Papp

text: An article last Sunday about revivals of “gay plays” misstated the year for the original production of “M. Butterfly.” It had its premiere in 1988, not 1998.
match_headline: Will the Old Gay Play Have Something New to Say?

text: An article last Sunday about an uptick in flawed heroines on television referred incorrectly to the marital status of the main character in “Ten Days in the Valley.” She is single, not divorced, and she was not married to her daughter’s father, whom she suspects in the girl’s abduction.
match_headline: When the TV Heroine Is Less Than Perfect

text: An article last Sunday about Unesco heritage sites referred incorrectly to the Indian city of Ahmedabad. It is the former capital of Gujarat state — not the current capital, which is Gandhinagar.
match_headline: Unesco World Heritage Sites 2017 Picks Range From Eritrea to England

text: An article last Sunday about the social media entrepreneur Jake Paul, using information from a publicist, misstated the name of Mr. Paul’s company. It is TeamDom, not TeenDom. The article also referred incorrectly to the nature of a YouTube video featuring Justin Bieber, in which he appears to be reacting to Mr. Paul’s video “It’s Everyday Bro.” The video was a parody that used footage from an interview that Mr. Bieber gave about Selena Gomez’s video “Hands to Myself,” in which he refers to her video co-star as “a chump.” Mr. Bieber did not call Mr. Paul “a chump.”
match_headline: How Jake Paul Set the Internet Ablaze

text: An article last Sunday about the fashion designer Ralph Lauren’s vintage car collection described incorrectly a comment by Mr. Lauren about his personal net worth. When he said he set his worth higher than Forbes magazine’s estimate, he was referring to the value of his company, not his personal net worth. The article also referred incorrectly to the departure of Stefan Larsson as the chief executive officer of Ralph Lauren. The designer did not abruptly remove Mr. Larsson; the departure was mutually agreed upon.
match_headline: Ralph Lauren Is Still Behind the Wheel

text: An article last Sunday about the airport-security screening company Clear referred incorrectly to its record on data security. It has never had problems on that front. (An early iteration of the company, Verified Identity Pass, which was under different ownership, had a single problem with data security.)
match_headline: Passing Through Airport Security With the Touch of a Finger

text: A news analysis last Sunday about Hillary Clinton’s new book and role in public life misspelled the surname of the executive director of the Barbara Lee Family Foundation. She is Adrienne Kimmell, not Kimmel.
match_headline: Well, What Should Hillary Clinton Do Now?

text: An article on Monday about the effect on Facebook and other technology companies of government efforts around the world to regulate online activity misspelled the surname of Facebook’s head of public policy in Europe. He is Richard Allan, not Allen.
match_headline: Facebook Faces a New World as Officials Rein In a Wild Web

text: An article on Saturday about a lawsuit against the virtual reality start-up Upload misstated the age of Elizabeth Scott, the plaintiff in the case. She is 26, not 27.
match_headline: Lurid Lawsuit’s Quiet End Leaves Silicon Valley Start-Up Barely Dented

text: An article on Friday about a new federal rule designed to protect hospital patients and nursing home residents during natural disasters misidentified a position once held by Keith Myers of MorseLife Health System. He was a member of the Florida Board of Nursing Home Administrators; he was never the board’s chairman.
match_headline: Nursing Home Deaths in Florida Heighten Scrutiny of Disaster Planning

text: An article on Saturday about the Trump administration’s refusal to release the names of visitors to the Trump family’s Mar-a-Lago resort misstated the nature of a federal court order related to the visitors. The court ordered the release of all related records subject to the Freedom of Information Act, not a log of all presidential visitors to Mar-a-Lago. The article and an accompanying picture caption also misstated the amount of time the president has spent at the resort in the first months of his presidency. He has been there a total of 25 days; he has not visited 25 times.
match_headline: Trump Declines to Release List of His Mar-a-Lago Visitors

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about accusations of sexual harassment at Rochester University referred incorrectly to Dr. T. Florian Jaeger, who was accused of sexual harassment and then cleared by the university. He is not facing a federal lawsuit. (A federal discrimination complaint has been filed against the university.)
match_headline: Sexual Harassment Charges Roil Elite University Department

text: An article on Saturday about insurance companies that cater to high-net-worth individuals misstated the estimated cost of cleaning up after Hurricane Irma in Florida. It is $50 billion, not $50 million.
match_headline: Protecting Andy Warhol From Flood, Fire and Quake

text: An article last Tuesday about Tesla’s decision to extend the range of vehicles owned by individuals in Florida described incorrectly criticism of the decision. Critics said that the ability to make the upgrade raised questions of corporate greed, not that the upgrade itself was an act of greed.
match_headline: Tesla Boosts Car Battery Power During Irma, Raising Questions of Control

text: An article on Wednesday about the collapse of the British public relations firm Bell Pottinger misstated the connection of one of the firm’s former clients, Aleksandr G. Lukashenko, to Belarus. He is the current president and dictator of the country; he is not a former dictator.
match_headline: Bell Pottinger, British P.R. Firm for Questionable Clients, Collapses

text: An article on Monday about highlights from the weekend’s N.F.L. matches misstated the ways in which the Minnesota Vikings scored 9 points in their most recent game. They had a field goal and a touchdown with a missed extra point, not three field goals.
match_headline: N.F.L. Highlights: Here’s What We Learned in Week 2

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Rev. René Laurentin, a Roman Catholic theologian who devoted his career to investigating reports of supernatural religious visions, omitted part of the name of a journal in which he explained the church’s guidelines for discerning an apparition. It is The Call of Heaven: The Journal of Messengers and Apparitions — not simply The Journal of Messengers and Apparitions.
match_headline: René Laurentin, Investigator of Celestial Visions, Dies at 99

text: An obituary on Monday about Penny Chenery, the owner and breeder of the racehorse Secretariat, misspelled part of the name of the racing stable owned by Elizabeth Arden Graham. It was Maine Chance Farm, not Main Chance Farm.
match_headline: Penny Chenery, Owner of the Triple Crown Winner Secretariat, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Monday about the gallery owner, collector and writer Greg Escalante misstated the name of a store in Laguna Beach, Calif., where he once worked. It was the Pottery Shack, not the Pottery Shed.
match_headline: Greg Escalante, Champion of ‘Lowbrow’ Art, Dies at 62

text: An article on Monday about the role of insurers in the opioid crisis misidentified the source of a recent study on opioid use and addiction. The study was conducted by researchers at the University of Arkansas and published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; it was not done by the C.D.C.
match_headline: Amid Opioid Crisis, Insurers Restrict Pricey, Less Addictive Painkillers

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts to ban corporate and union donations in provincial elections in British Columbia, Canada, misstated the amount of money raised by the British Columbia Liberal Party in 2016. The party raised 13.1 million Canadian dollars, not just 13.1.
match_headline: British Columbia Proposes Ban on Corporate and Union Donations in Elections

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about protests in St. Louis following the acquittal of a former police officer in a murder case misidentified the defendant at one point. He is Jason Stockley, not Anthony Lamar Smith. (Mr. Smith was the victim).
match_headline: St. Louis Protests: Police Say They ‘Owned’ the Night After 80 Arrests

text: An article on Saturday about China’s plans to ban gasoline-powered cars misstated the mileage range for plug-in gasoline-electric hybrid vehicles like the Chevrolet Volt when running on battery power alone. It is slightly more than 50 miles, not 100 miles or more.
match_headline: G.M. Chief, in China, Challenges Planned Bans of Gasoline Cars

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about a recent global health report by Bill and Melinda Gates misidentified the location of a speech the couple gave concerning the report’s findings. It was in Manhattan, not at the Seattle headquarters of the Gates Foundation.
match_headline: Bill and Melinda Gates Grade the World’s Health

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an obituary about the architect Gin Wong, whose projects included the Transamerica Pyramid in San Francisco, misstated Ron Wagley’s position with Transamerica. He was chief executive of Transamerica Insurance — not of the Transamerica Corporation, its parent company.
match_headline: Gin Wong, Who Designed Futuristic Buildings in Los Angeles, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Sept. 12 about the computer scientist Lotfi Zadeh referred imprecisely to the status of Azerbaijan when he was born there in 1921. While it officially became a Soviet Socialist republic in 1920, it was not yet part of the Soviet Union, which was established in late 1922.
match_headline: Lotfi Zadeh, Father of Mathematical ‘Fuzzy Logic,’ Dies at 96

text: A news analysis article on Wednesday about President Trump’s speech at the United Nations General Assembly described incorrectly Elliott Abrams’s work during the George W. Bush administration. He was a senior diplomat and policy maker under Presidents Reagan and Bush, but not a senior State Department official under Mr. Bush.
match_headline: Trump Offers a Selective View of Sovereignty in U.N. Speech

text: An article on Wednesday about the Washington Nationals’ joining the ranks of teams that have won their league or division by 20 or more games misstated the number of teams in the Cleveland Indians’ division in 1995. There were five, not four.
match_headline: Nationals Join Elite Teams Who Have Crushed Their Divisions

text: A report in the “Arts, Briefly” column on Tuesday about Billboard’s new No. 1 album, Thomas Rhett’s “Life Changes,” using information from Nielsen, reversed the albums that are No. 2 and No. 3. The National’s “Sleep Well Beast” is No. 2 and Odessa’s “A Moment Apart” is No. 3.
match_headline: Thomas Rhett’s ‘Life Changes’ Is Country’s First No. 1 Album in 2017

text: An article last Thursday about Toronto’s influence on this season’s red carpet trends misstated the surname of an up-and-coming actress. She is Tatiana Maslany, not Malsany. In addition, the article misspelled the surname of the director of “Gaga: Five Foot Two.” He is Chris Moukarbel, not Mourkarbel. The article also misspelled the surname of the director of “The Gospel According to André.” She is Kate Novack, not Novak. And, finally, the article misspelled the given name of a designer. He is Markus Lupfer, not Marcus.
match_headline: Who Knew? For Red Carpet Trends, Look North

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an article about President Moon Jae-in of South Korea misidentified an official shown at the United Nations General Assembly listening to President Trump’s speech. He is Cho Tae-yul, South Korea’s ambassador to the United Nations, not President Moon.
match_headline: South Korea’s Leader Will Be Odd Man Out in Meeting With Trump and Shinzo Abe

text: An obituary on Sept. 14 about the author J. P. Donleavy misstated his birth name and his father’s name. He was born James Patrick Dunleavy, not James Patrick Donleavy Jr., and his father was Patrick John Dunleavy, not James Donleavy. (The spelling of the family name was later changed.) The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Donleavy’s survivors. He did not have grandchildren. And the obituary misstated the name of a manuscript on which he had been working. It was “The Dog on the 17th Floor,” not “The Dog That Fell From the 17th Floor.” Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated the surname of the college classmate who inspired the title character of Mr. Donleavy’s novel “The Ginger Man.” He was Gainor Steven Crist, not Cris.
match_headline: J.P. Donleavy, Acclaimed Author of ‘The Ginger Man,’ Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Thursday about the boxer Jake LaMotta misspelled part of the name of the character he played in a 1965 production of “Guys and Dolls.” The character is Big Jule, not Big Julie.
match_headline: Jake LaMotta, ‘Raging Bull’ in and Out of the Ring, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Sept. 15 about the actor Gastone Moschin misidentified the street festival during which Don Fanucci, the character he played, is killed in “The Godfather Part II.” It is the festival of San Rocco, not San Gennaro.
match_headline: Gastone Moschin Dies at 88; Played a Doomed Don in ‘Godfather Part II’

text: An article last Saturday about Harvard University’s withdrawal of a fellowship granted to Chelsea Manning misstated the credentials of Pranav Reddy, a student, who commented on the decision. He is in his fourth year of medical school; he does not yet have his medical degree.
match_headline: With Chelsea Manning Invitation, Harvard Got a Discussion It Didn’t Want

text: A picture caption on Friday with The Shift column, about scandals plaguing Facebook, which, like Victor Frankenstein, may have created something it cannot fully control, misidentified the actor shown playing the scientist in the movie “The Curse of Frankenstein.” He was Peter Cushing, not Christopher Lee.
match_headline: Facebook’s Frankenstein Moment

text: Because of an editing error, a music entry in the Listings pages on Friday about the concert “Band Together: A Concert Against Hate” at Knockdown Center misspelled part of the name of the event. It is “Band Together: A Concert Against Hate” (not “Hat”).
ref_headline: Band Together: A Concert Against Hate
match_headline: Pop, Rock and Jazz in NYC This Week

text: An obituary on Friday about the football player, actor and painter Bernie Casey misstated the month of his birth. He was born on June 8, 1939 — not on Sept. 8.
match_headline: Bernie Casey, Who Glided From Football to Hollywood, Dies at 78

text: An article last Sunday about Secretary of State Rex W. Tillerson’s decision to reduce the size of the United States delegation to the United Nations General Assembly referred incorrectly to his diplomatic travel. Though Mr. Tillerson uses a smaller airplane than his predecessors in order to travel with fewer people and cut costs, there is no evidence that the smaller plane has forced him to spend extra time in Honolulu in order to rest his flight crew, or has otherwise interfered with his travel to crucial diplomatic meetings.
match_headline: With Cost-Cutting Zeal, Tillerson Whittles U.N. Delegation, Too

text: A review on Sept. 10 about “Black Detroit,” by Herb Boyd, misstated the name of the publishing company led by the poet Dudley Randall. It was Broadside Press (now Broadside Lotus Press), not Blackside Press.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Detroit,’ Black Lives Caught in a Prehistory of the Alt-Right

text: An article on Sept. 10 about Michigan charter schools misstated part of the name of an organization that examined the fi nancial eff ects of school choice on Michigan school districts. It is the Education Policy Center, not the Education Policy Institute.
match_headline: Michigan Gambled on Charter Schools. Its Children Lost.

text: An article on Sept. 10 about the photographer Marie Cosindas misidentified the neighborhood in which she was raised. It is Boston’s South End, not South Boston.
match_headline: Still Lives That Won’t Hold Still

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Amber Brandes and Elana Caplan misidentified Ms. Brandes in an accompanying picture. She was at the right, with Ms. Caplan at the left — not the other way around.
match_headline: Amber Brandes, Elana Caplan

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Shauna Woods and Alexander Smith included outdated information about the officiant. After the section had gone to press, Judge Willam B. Shubb, senior district judge of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of California, substituted for Chief Judge Virginia A. Phillips of the United States District Court for the Central District of California, because of an emergency.
match_headline: Shauna Woods, Alexander Smith

text: An article on Wednesday about the civil rights pioneer Alberta Jones erroneously attributed a distinction to her. She was the first female black prosecutor in Louisville, Ky. — not the city’s first black prosecutor. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: A ‘Quest for Justice’ for a Murdered Civil Rights Pioneer, 52 Years Later

text: An article on Saturday about the stabbing deaths of a Syrian activist and her daughter misstated Suzanne Barakat’s relationship to the 2015 shooting victim Deah Barakat. He was her brother, not her cousin.
match_headline: Syrian Activist and Her Daughter Are Fatally Stabbed in Turkey

text: A picture caption on Sunday with an article about the latest Republican-sponsored health bill in the Senate misspelled the given name of the senator from South Carolina who drafted the measure. He is Lindsey Graham, not Lindsay.
match_headline: Why the Latest Health Bill Is Teetering: It Might Not Work

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about blue-collar jobs in Dortmund, Germany, misidentified a piece of equipment shown on display at the former site of a ThyssenKrupp steel-making complex. It is a Bessemer converter, not a blast furnace.
match_headline: In Germany, Blue-Collar Jobs Provide Bulwark to Populism

text: A picture caption on Sunday with an obituary about the playwright Myrna Lamb misspelled the surname of the woman shown with Ms. Lamb in a 1974 photograph. She is Marnie Mueller, not Muller.
match_headline: Myrna Lamb, Feminist Playwright in an Unwelcoming Era, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Friday about Liliane Bettencourt, the heiress to the L’Oréal cosmetics fortune, referred incorrectly to anosognosia, from which a psychologist said she suffered. It is a condition in which a patient does not seem aware of his or her disorder — not in which he or she does.
match_headline: Liliane Bettencourt, L’Oréal Heiress Vexed by Swindling Case, Is Dead at 94

text: An obituary on Saturday about the record producer and engineer Johnny Sandlin misstated the name of an Allman Brothers album on which he worked. It is “At Fillmore East,” not “Live at Filmore East.”
match_headline: Johnny Sandlin, 72, Allman Brothers Band Producer, Is Dead

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about changes in the government’s policies on campus sexual assault referred imprecisely to the background of an advocacy organization. While the organization, the Foundation for Individual Rights in Education, has received support from conservative donors, it describes itself as a nonpartisan organization that works on behalf of individuals holding a range of political viewpoints. The article also referred incorrectly to the participants in an investigation at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. While the victim had assistance from an academic adviser, she did not have a lawyer.
match_headline: Betsy DeVos Reverses Obama-era Policy on Campus Sexual Assault Investigations

text: An article on Tuesday about the findings of a study on Wisconsin’s voter identification laws misstated the number of registered voters in two Wisconsin counties who were kept from the polls in November by the law. It was 16,800, not 25,800. The error was repeated in a capsule summary.
match_headline: Wisconsin Strict ID Law Discouraged Voters, Study Finds

text: An entry on Monday in the What’s on TV highlights erroneously included one option for streaming the film “The Double,” starring Jesse Eisenberg. While it is available on iTunes and Hulu, it cannot be streamed on Netflix. (A 2011 film by the same name, starring Richard Gere, is available on Netflix.)
match_headline: What’s on TV Monday: ‘Young Sheldon’ and ‘The Opposition w/ Jordan Klepper’

text: An article on Sept. 15 about the actor Nat Wolff misidentified a film in which Mr. Wolff is the leading man. It is “Paper Towns” — not “The Fault in Our Stars,” in which he has a smaller role.
match_headline: Nat Wolff, a Movie Star on the Rise, Likes a Uniform

text: An editorial on Monday about President Trump’s criticism of football players’ protests against police brutality referred incorrectly to the network where Rex Ryan, who criticized Mr. Trump, works as a commentator. It is ESPN, not CBS.
match_headline: The Day the Real Patriots Took a Knee

text: An article on Sunday about gambling in Britain misstated the percentage increase in “problem gamblers” cited in a report by the country’s Gambling Commission. The report said the number rose by more than 53 percent from 2012 to 2015, not by almost 50 percent.
match_headline: 42 Minutes, £2,600 Lost: The U.K.’s Growing Gambling Problem

text: An article on Wednesday about a visit by Mayor Bill de Blasio to the High Line for the first time misstated the number of boroughs the mayor and his top commissioners have visited as part of their “City Hall in Your Borough” program. The visit to Manhattan this week was the fourth stop, not the fifth. (Brooklyn will be the last borough they visit.)
match_headline: Mayor Visits the High Line and Becomes One in Seven Million, Finally

text: An article on Monday about the FedEx Cup misstated Xander Schauffele’s final round score. He shot a 68, not a 66.
match_headline: Rookie Claims a Title, but Justin Thomas Clinches the FedEx Cup

text: An entry on Wednesday in the What’s on TV highlights described the plot of the season premiere of “The Blacklist” incorrectly. The criminal mastermind Raymond Reddington planned to deliver a new Blacklister to the Task Force, not send one to infiltrate the Task Force.
match_headline: What’s on TV Wednesday: ‘Liar’ and ‘The Blacklist’

text: An article on Thursday about a North Korean textile plant suspected of producing rocket fuel misstated part of the name of the educational institution affiliated with the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies. It is Middlebury College, not Middlebury University.
match_headline: Remote Textile Plant May Secretly Fuel North Korea’s Weapons

text: An article on Aug. 16 about plans by the artist Yayoi Kusama to open her own museum in Tokyo misstated the given name of the museum’s director. He is Akira Tatehata, not Tensei Tatehata. (The museum officially opens on Sunday.) This correction was delayed because the error was called to the attention of editors only this week.
match_headline: Yayoi Kusama to Open Her Own Museum in Tokyo

text: An article on Friday about efforts by Stephen K. Bannon to create a political coalition to challenge the Republican establishment misidentified the home state of Harold Hamm, a billionaire oilman who expressed interest in the plan. He is from Oklahoma, not from Texas.
match_headline: Alabama Victory Provides Blueprint for New Bannon Alliance

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the likely effects of President Trump’s tax plan misidentified a tax expert who criticized the president’s proposed tax cuts. It was Robert Willens — not Mark A. Weinberger, the chief executive of the financial services firm EY — who said, “This isn’t good for tax professionals.”
ref_headline: This isn’t good for tax professionals.
match_headline: In Trump Tax Plan, a Windfall for Businesses Large and Small

text: An editorial on Thursday about a scandal involving college basketball referred incorrectly to the University of Louisville coach, Rick Pitino. Mr. Pitino has not been “a master” of the one-and-done, in which high school stars play at universities for just a year before moving on to professional careers.
match_headline: The Corruption at the Heart of March Madness

text: A picture caption last Sunday with a profile of the architect Rafael de Cárdenas referred incorrectly to the fabric used to cover the Grete Jalk chair he reinterpreted. It was inspired by the designs of Christian Lacroix; it was not made by him.

An article last Sunday about sites to visit in Reykjavik, Iceland, referred incorrectly to the country’s location in relationship to the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. Iceland is situated at a divergent boundary between the plates, not at their point of collision. (There is no such point along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.)
match_headline: A Guide to Reykjavik, as Wonderfully Weird as Ever

text: An article last Sunday about oil-industry middlemen quoted incorrectly from comments by a spokesman for Britain’s Serious Fraud Office about its success in bringing cases under the country’s Bribery Act. He said the office had secured successful outcomes in “all foreign bribery cases” brought under the act, not in “all cases.”
match_headline: Deals in Code, Arrests in Raids: The Risky Stakes of Oil Middlemen

text: An article last Sunday about the making of the film “Mother” misstated the year that Susan Griffin’s book “Woman and Nature” was published. It was 1978, not 1979.
match_headline: Making ‘Mother!,’ the Year’s Most Divisive Film

text: An article last Sunday about a new generation of male country music stars misstated the number of albums Thomas Rhett has released. “Tangled Up” is his second album, not his debut; and “Life Changes” is his third album, not his second.
match_headline: In Country Music, Nice Guys Finish First (for Now)

text: An article last Sunday about Andrea Incontri’s favorite sites in Milan, including the Teatro Gerolamo, misstated Luisa Pisano’s title at the theater. She is the director of events, not the director.
match_headline: A City of Secrets

text: An article last Sunday about Donatella Versace’s tribute to her brother Gianni misidentified the location of the house where he was shot and killed. It is in Miami Beach, not Miami.
match_headline: The Inside Story of Donatella Versace’s Homage to Gianni: Classic Prints and Your Favorite ’90s Supermodels

text: A picture last Sunday with the Living In column , about Pelham, N.Y., was published in error. The picture with the description of 55 Witherbee Avenue did not show that property. The correct photograph is online at nytimes.com/realestate .
match_headline: Pelham, N.Y.: Close to the City, but With a Friendly Vibe

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Ingrid Louise Price and Rahul Prabhakar misspelled the maiden name of the bride’s mother and, because of an editing error, the report rendered the given name of the groom’s father incorrectly. The bride’s mother is Berit Stroemme Price, not Stoemme; the groom’s father is Sunil Prabhakar, not SunilI.
match_headline: Ingrid Price, Rahul Prabhakar

text: An article on Saturday about China’s trade boom with South Korea misidentified the location of the headquarters for the electronics maker Foxconn. The company is based in Taiwan — not in mainland China, where it has extensive operations.
match_headline: China’s Harsh Words Mask a Trade Boom With South Korea

text: An article on Sunday about the N.F.L. announcer Tony Romo misspelled the surname of one of Mr. Romo’s critics. He is the broadcaster Brent Musburger, not Musberger.
match_headline: Answer to N.F.L. Viewers’ Prayers: Tony Romo, the Play Predictor

text: A headline on Saturday with a report in the “Arts, Briefly” column about a new book on Woody Allen misidentified the book’s author. As the article correctly noted, the book, “Start to Finish: Woody Allen and the Art of Moviemaking,” is by Eric Lax, not by a son of Mia Farrow.
match_headline: New Book About Woody Allen Alleges Abusive Parenting by Mia Farrow

text: An article on Sept. 30 about the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates misidentified an audience member who asked him a question at an event in Harlem. The question was from Adrian Hopkins, not from the filmmaker Barry Jenkins. (Mr. Hopkins works for The New York Times, but was not reporting on the event.)
match_headline: Ta-Nehisi Coates and the Making of a Public Intellectual

text: An article on Monday about bike-sharing programs in Washington, D.C., misstated the pace at which automated traffic signals allow bicycles to travel in several European cities. It is about 12 miles per hour, or 20 kilometers per hour, not 20 miles per hour.
match_headline: Bike-Sharing Is Flourishing in Washington. Can the City Handle It?

text: An article last Wednesday about new immigration rules proposed by the White House described incorrectly one aspect of an online verification system. It is used by employers to screen the immigration status of people who have been hired, not employment applicants.
match_headline: White House Considers Tougher Rules as Part of Immigration Overhaul

text: An obituary on Monday about S. I. Newhouse, the owner of The New Yorker, Vogue, Vanity Fair and other magazines, referred incorrectly to his dismissal of Robert Gottlieb as editor of The New Yorker. Mr. Gottlieb already knew he was being let go before he received a call from a reporter asking for comment about his firing; he did not learn about it from that phone call. The obituary also misstated Harold Evans’s position at the book publisher Random House under Mr. Newhouse. He ran the company’s trade division, not the entire company.
match_headline: S.I. Newhouse Jr., Who Turned Condé Nast Into a Magazine Powerhouse, Dies at 89

text: An article on Tuesday about hospitals overtaxed by the mass shooting in Las Vegas described the location of the Sunrise Hospital & Medical Center incorrectly. It is about six miles from the site of the shootings, not within walking distance.
match_headline: Controlled Chaos at Las Vegas Hospital Trauma Center After Attack

text: An article on Wednesday about an algae bloom in Lake Erie misidentified a toxin produced by algae blooms. It is microcystin, not microcystis.
match_headline: Miles of Algae Covering Lake Erie

text: An article on Saturday about a teacher with a rare form of amnesia who went missing in the Virgin Islands referred incorrectly to the academic affiliation of Dr. David Spiegel, who commented on the case. He is the associate chairman of Stanford University’s department of psychiatry — not psychology — and behavioral sciences.
match_headline: A Teacher Vanishes Again. This Time, in the Virgin Islands.

text: An article last Thursday about the Andy Warhol muse Janet Susan Mary Hoffmann, also known as Viva, misidentified the event where Ms. Hoffmann’s memoir was distributed in June. It was Kunsthalle Basel, not Art Basel.
match_headline: Viva: A Warhol-Era Superstar Wants the Last Word

text: An article last Thursday about the new fashion exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art included a quotation that misstated the name of a hat worn by Israeli Jews. It is a tembel hat, not a temple hat.
match_headline: Van Gogh on Five, Wonderbra on Six: A Tour of MoMA’s New Fashion Exhibit

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Jalal Talabani, the first president of Iraq under its postwar Constitution, misstated the status of Iraq when Mr. Talabani joined a Kurdish student movement in the 1940s. It was an independent monarchy at that time; it was not under British rule.
match_headline: Jalal Talabani, Kurdish Leader and Iraq’s First Postwar President, Is Dead at 83

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the singer, songwriter and guitarist Tom Petty misstated the surname of one of the members of his band Mudcrutch. He is Randall Marsh, not March.
match_headline: Tom Petty, a Mainstay of Rock With the Heartbreakers, Dies at 66

text: An obituary on Sept. 27 about Joseph M. McDade, a Republican congressman from Pennsylvania who was a champion of the coal industry, referred incorrectly to anthracite coal. It has a low — not high — sulfur content.
match_headline: Joseph M. McDade, 18-Term Pennsylvania Congressman, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Sept. 18 about the opera singer Brenda Lewis misidentified the television network that broadcast the City Opera production of “Lizzie Borden,” in which she sang the title role, in 1967. It was National Educational Television — not PBS, which replaced NET in 1970. The obituary also referred incorrectly to a tour in which Ms. Lewis sang the role of Rosalinde in “Die Fledermaus.” She alternated in the role with Laura Castellano, and therefore sang it fewer than eight times a week (though she claimed in a 1999 interview that she did all eight).
match_headline: Brenda Lewis, Versatile American Soprano, Is Dead at 96

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the father of Stephen Paddock, the man the police identified as the gunman in the mass shooting in Las Vegas, misidentified Mr. Paddock’s youngest sibling. Eric Paddock is his youngest brother, not Patrick Paddock II.
match_headline: Las Vegas Gunman’s Criminal Father Vanished From Sons’ Lives

text: An article on Thursday about Marilou Danley, the girlfriend of the Las Vegas gunman, Stephen Paddock, misidentified the country where she worked as a tour guide. It is the Philippines, not Australia.
match_headline: Marilou Danley, Gunman’s Girlfriend, Says She Was Unaware of His Plans

text: An article on Thursday about the Yankees’ first postseason game in Cleveland since 2007 misstated the number of regular-season appearances Joba Chamberlain made in that year. It was 19 — not 24, which was the number of innings he threw that year.
match_headline: The Yankees Are Back in Cleveland. Will the Bugs Return, Too?

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the Cambodian architect Vann Molyvann referred incorrectly to Norodom Sihanouk, who was deposed in a coup in 1970. Though he was the country’s head of state and had once been king, he was a prince at the time he was ousted, not the king.
match_headline: Vann Molyvann, Architect Who Shaped Cambodia’s Capital, Dies at 90

text: An article on Friday about Stephen Paddock’s uncertain motive for killing 58 people in Las Vegas misstated the circumstances of the death of Charles Whitman, the gunman in the 1966 University of Texas massacre. He was killed by the police; he did not kill himself.
match_headline: No Manifesto, No Phone Calls: Las Vegas Killer Left Only Cryptic Clues

text: An article on Friday about a Spanish court’s move to pre-empt the Catalan independence declaration misspelled the surname of the Catalan leader. He is Carles Puigdemont, not Puidgemont.
match_headline: Spanish Court Moves to Pre-empt Catalan Independence Declaration

text: An article on Sept. 26 about efforts by the governor of Puerto Rico to secure more federal aid to deal with the destruction wrought by Hurricane Maria misspelled the surname of the Republican chairman of the House Appropriations Committee. He is Rodney Frelinghuysen, not Frelinghusyen.
match_headline: In Battered Puerto Rico, Governor Warns of a Humanitarian Crisis

text: An obituary on Thursday about John Thompson, who was exonerated after spending 14 years on death row in the Louisiana State Penitentiary, referred incorrectly to his scheduled execution in 1999. It was to be by lethal injection, not electrocution. (Louisiana began using lethal injection for its executions in the early 1990s.) The obituary also omitted the name of a lawyer who represented Mr. Thompson without fee. He is Nicholas Trenticosta. And the obituary misstated the role of the Innocence Project in Mr. Thompson’s case. It handled his claim for state compensation; it did not help represent him in his appeals. In addition, the obituary misstated the number of stepchildren who survive Mr. Thompson. There are four, not five. And, finally, the obituary misspelled his mother’s surname. She is Josephine Casby, not Casey.
match_headline: John Thompson, Cleared After 14 Years on Death Row, Dies at 55

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Arthur Janov, the creator of primal scream therapy, referred incorrectly to “My Mummy’s Dead,” a song on the album “John Lennon/Plastic Ono Band.” While many songs on that album, a reflection of John Lennon’s primal therapy, were “half-sung, half-screamed,” “My Mummy’s Dead” was not.
match_headline: Arthur Janov, 93, Dies; Psychologist Caught World’s Attention With ‘Primal Scream’

text: A headline last Sunday with an article about the influence of opera on Walt Whitman misstated the title of his magnum opus. It is “Leaves of Grass,” not “Leaves of the Grass.”
match_headline: How Opera Inspired Walt Whitman’s ‘Leaves of Grass’

text: A picture caption on Sept. 24 with an article about Hurricane Irma’s effect on Caribbean tourism, using information from The Associated Press, misidentified the area shown. It is a section of the British Virgin Islands, not the United States Virgin Islands.
match_headline: After Maria and Irma: Caribbean Tourism, Island by Island

text: A graphic on Sept. 3 with an article about gerrymandering misstated the political affiliation of two representatives who served in the Wisconsin State Assembly in 2008. District 58 was represented by a Republican, not a Democrat, and the representative for District 67 was an independent, not a Republican. The chart also misstated the percentage of votes the Republican and Democratic Parties won in the Assembly elections in Wisconsin in 2008. The Democrats won 56 percent, not 57 percent, and the Republicans won 44 percent, not 43 percent.
match_headline: With Primary Days Away, de Blasio Rolls Out First TV Ad

text: An article on Sept. 17 about the best way to pull down a statue in a public square referred incorrectly to the material used in many of the Lenin statues that were toppled in Ukraine. They were made of concrete, not cement.
match_headline: How to Pull Down a Statue

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about a reviewer’s accusations of plagiarism in a memoir by the poet Jill Bialosky included an outdated description of the response by the book’s publisher, Atria Books, and its editor in chief, Peter Borland. It was not the case that Mr. Borland failed to respond to requests for comment. After a version of the article was published online Wednesday evening, Atria’s parent company, Simon & Schuster, made a statement on Thursday night: “Jill Bialosky is a highly regarded editor and author who, in ‘Poetry Will Save Your Life,’ has written a unique and critically acclaimed memoir. We stand by the book and are ready to work with the author to make any necessary corrections for future editions of the book.”
match_headline: Jill Bialosky Says Plagiarism Claims ‘Should Not Distract’ From Her Poetry Memoir

text: An article on Monday about Sheriff Joseph Lombardo of the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department misstated the surname of the chairwoman of the Clark County Black Caucus, who credited Mr. Lombardo for improved relations between the African-American community and the police. She is Yvette Williams, not Thompson.
match_headline: After Las Vegas Shooting, a Tight-Lipped Sheriff Faces a Maddening Case

text: An article on Monday about the construction of a new shelter for three peacocks at the Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine misstated the surname of the manager of the cathedral’s soup kitchen. He is Robert Finn, not Flynn.
match_headline: Construction Project at a Cathedral: A New Home for Its Peacocks

text: An article on Monday about The Forward, a Jewish publication that has been aggressively reporting on so-called alt-right and white nationalist groups, misidentified Dan Friedman’s position at the magazine. He is The Forward’s executive editor, not managing editor.
match_headline: Anti-Semitism’s Rise Gives The Forward New Resolve

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about challenges facing Germany’s clean energy industry misspelled the surname of a farmer in Betzigau, Germany, who, with his wife, has installed solar panels on his property. He is Norbert Bechteler, not Bechtelier.
match_headline: Germany’s Shift to Green Power Stalls, Despite Huge Investments

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sept. 30 about Joe Louis Barrow Jr. referred incorrectly to stadiums and arenas in the four biggest North American professional sports leagues named after an athlete. After the closing of the Joe Louis Arena in Detroit there remains one such stadium named for a former athlete; it is the not the case that there are none. (Lambeau Field, home to the N.F.L.’s Green Bay Packers, is named for Curly Lambeau, who coached and played for the team.)
match_headline: A Lasting Influence in Golf Descends From a Boxing Legend

text: An article on Thursday about rally towels and their popularity at baseball games erroneously included a team among those with orange colors that made the playoffs last season. While Baltimore and San Francisco reached the postseason, Houston did not.
match_headline: As Baseball Playoffs Begin, a Question Looms: Are There Enough Red Towels?

text: An article on Monday about the baseball manager Dusty Baker misstated the year the Washington Senators won the World Series. It was 1924, not 1925. (The Senators lost the World Series in 1925.)
match_headline: Dusty Baker Is Back at Wrigley Field, Still Looking for a Ring of His Own

text: An obituary on Saturday about the mathematician Vladimir Voevodsky referred imprecisely to his tenure at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J. He was named a professor there in 2002, but he had become a member several years earlier; it was not the case that he “moved to” the Institute in 2002.
match_headline: Vladimir Voevodsky, Revolutionary Mathematician, Dies at 51

text: A picture caption on Sunday with an article about female drivers in Saudi Arabia misidentified a Saudi town in which women are allowed to drive. It is Dhahran, not Dammam. The caption also misstated the oil company Aramco’s relationship to the area. The company owns a residential compound there, not the entire town.
match_headline: Once Shunned as ‘Drivers,’ Saudi Women Who Fought Ban Now Celebrate

text: An article on Sunday about scandals in Ukraine included a quotation from a Harvard professor who is an expert on Ukrainian history that failed to include all of the post-Soviet nations that have become democracies. Georgia is among the states that have established a democratic government; the distinction is not exclusive to Ukraine and the Baltic States.
match_headline: Schooled in Scandal: What Makes Ukraine a Hotbed of Intrigue

text: An entry on Monday in the What’s on TV highlights misidentified the writer of the film “Harold and Maude.” He is Colin Higgins, not Hal Ashby. (Mr. Ashby was the film’s director.)
match_headline: What’s on TV Monday: ‘The Islands and the Whales’ and ‘Valor’

text: An article on Tuesday about attempts to use facial recognition software to detect sexual orientation misstated the name of a school where Rebecca Jordan Young is chairwoman of women’s, gender and sexuality studies. It is Barnard College, not Barnard University.
match_headline: Why Stanford Researchers Tried to Create a ‘Gaydar’ Machine

text: An obituary on Sunday about the comedian Ralphie May, using information from a spokeswoman, misspelled the given name of one of his sisters and omitted the names of three other survivors. His sister is Camellia May, not Camilia. And in addition to those named, his survivors include his stepmother, Gayle May; a half sister, Carrie May Ezell; and a stepbrother, Gary Gilley. The obituary also misstated, in some editions, the year of Mr. May’s birth. He was born on Feb. 17, 1972, not 1971. (As the obituary correctly noted, he was 45.)
match_headline: Ralphie May, 45, Comedian ‘Who Happens to Be Fat,’ Dies

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the fashion designer Hervé L. Leroux misidentified the movie for which Hilary Swank won an Academy Award in 2005, the year she wore a dress he designed to the ceremony. It was “Million Dollar Baby,” not “Boys Don’t Cry” (for which she won the award in 2000).
match_headline: Hervé Leroux, Creator of the Hervé Léger Bandage Dress, Dies at 60

text: An article on Wednesday about an admission by the Japanese company Kobe Steel that it had falsified data about the quality of metals it sold described incorrectly one way that quality is measured. A metal’s “tensile strength” is its ability to withstand a load without breaking when being stretched; it is not a measure of the metal’s stiffness.
match_headline: Kobe Steel’s Falsified Data Is Another Blow to Japan’s Reputation

text: An article on Sunday about unusual profit-making ventures of North Korean embassies around the world misstated the status of a youth hostel operating in what was originally North Korean diplomatic quarters in Berlin. Although it was ordered shut down by the German government and has stopped paying rent, it remains open; it has not closed.
match_headline: Hosting Proms and Selling Cows: North Korean Embassies Scrounge for Cash

text: A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about the former child soldier Joseph Duo who is seeking political office in Liberia misidentified the location of one of his campaign rallies. It was in Grand Bassa County — not Little Bassa, his hometown.
match_headline: He Was the Face of Liberia’s Endless War. Now He Wants to Govern.

text: An article on Wednesday about reactions to allegations of sexual harassment against the film producer Harvey Weinstein misspelled his spokeswoman’s surname. She is Sallie Hofmeister, not Hoffmeister.
match_headline: Disney, Hillary Clinton and the Obamas Condemn Weinstein

text: An article on Wednesday about the slowing growth of Yale University’s endowment misstated part of the name of an organization that tracks investment returns in the nonprofit sector. It is Cambridge Associates, not Cambridge Associations.
match_headline: Yale Endowment, Often a Pacesetter, Is a Laggard This Time

text: An article and its headline on Wednesday about contemporary Israeli dance referred incorrectly at one point to military service in Israeli. Not “everyone serves.” As correctly noted elsewhere in the article, there are a variety of exemptions.
match_headline: Soldier Dances, From a Land Pervaded by the Military

text: An article last Thursday about the photographer Mark Sharkey’s “Queer Kids” exhibition misidentified the type of surgery that his subject Mars underwent. It is a female-to-male transition, not male-to-female.
match_headline: Style That Demands to Be Seen

text: An article on Sept. 13 about Singapore’s process for selecting its new president paraphrased incorrectly a comment made by a potential presidential candidate, Mohamed Salleh Marican. Mr. Marican told local media that he would work to enforce a zero-tolerance policy on corruption, not that he would open a corruption investigation against Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong. The article also described imprecisely how criteria to determine a candidate’s eligibility to stand for election as president was established. The prime minister formed a commission that set the requirements and the Parliament approved them, not the government.
match_headline: Singapore Has a New President, No Election Needed

text: An article on Thursday about the House Intelligence Committee’s plans to make public the thousands of Facebook ads linked to Russia misidentified the state where Representative Adam B. Schiff’s district is. It is in California, not Massachusetts.
match_headline: Lawmakers Say They Plan to Release Facebook Ads Linked to Russia

text: An article on Thursday about a backlash over the American Jewish Historical Society’s decision to cancel two events referred incorrectly to the professional status of David Myers, the executive director of the Center for Jewish History in Manhattan. He is on the faculty of the University of California, Los Angeles; he is not a former professor of Jewish history there. The article also referred incorrectly to a fictional family in Dan Fishback’s play “Rubble Rubble.” The modern-day Jewish settlers live in the West Bank; they do not live in Israel.
match_headline: Jewish Center Faces Backlash After Canceling Play Criticized as Anti-Israel

text: An article on Friday about the reinstatement of the Cowboys running back Ezekiel Elliott’s six-game suspension over domestic violence allegations misstated the Cowboys’ record last season. It was 13-3, not 14-2.
match_headline: Ezekiel Elliott’s 6-Game N.F.L. Suspension Reinstated by Court

text: An article on Friday about three television programs worth watching this weekend misspelled the given name of a contestant on “Top Chef Jr.” She is Rahanna, not Rahana.
match_headline: How Much Watching Time Do You Have This Weekend?

text: A picture caption on Oct. 1 with the Long View Column, about books by losing presidential candidates, included an erroneous date for a photograph of Gerald and Betty Ford. The photograph was taken in 1973, not 1974.
match_headline: ‘What Happened’? They Lost. With Her Memoir, Hillary Clinton Joins a Haunted Club

text: An article on Sept. 24 about traveling in Guinea for the Muslim festival Eid al-Adha misidentified which son, according to Islamic tradition, Abraham was willing to sacrifice. The son was Ishmael, not Isaac.
A listing on the “On the Market” page last Sunday misstated the year in which the brownstone at 26 Eighth Avenue, in Park Slope, Brooklyn, was built. It was 1883, not 1937.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in New York City

text: An article last Sunday about Madison Cox, the legal heir to the Yves Saint Laurent archive, misstated the profession of his associate Konstantin Kakanias. Mr. Kakanias is primarily an illustrator and visual artist, not a cartoonist.
match_headline: For Madison Cox, Widower of Pierre Bergé, C’est Compliqué

text: An article last Sunday about automation in the food-service industry misstated the estimated amount of time required for Sally the Salad Robot to make a salad. It ranges from 45 seconds to two minutes, not less than one minute.
match_headline: A Robot Makes a Mean Caesar Salad, but Will It Cost Jobs?

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Meredith Truesdale and Patrick Mullane misstated the title of the officiant, John Shea. He is a Roman Catholic deacon, not a priest.
match_headline: Meredith Truesdale, Patrick Mullane

text: An article on Monday about people who have contributed to The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, an annual campaign that provides assistance to those struggling in New York and beyond, misstated, at one point, the surname of a New Jersey woman who started giving to the fund in the late 1950s. She is Ruth Queen, not Queens. The article also referred incorrectly to her family’s contributions to the fund. Her father — not Ms. Queen — began giving in the 1950s.
match_headline: Tradition of Helping Neediest Cases Inspires Readers to Give Back

text: An obituary on Monday about the chess grandmaster William Lombardy, using information from a family member, referred incorrectly to one survivor and omitted the name of another. Natalie Pekala is Mr. Lombardy’s younger sister, not his older sister; and he is also survived by another younger sister, Vickie Lombardy.
match_headline: William Lombardy, Chess Grandmaster Turned Priest, Dies at 79

text: An article on Monday about the detection of a collision of neutron stars misidentified the journal in which a paper written by thousands of authors describing the event appeared. It was in Astrophysical Journal Letters, not Physical Review Letters.
match_headline: LIGO Detects Fierce Collision of Neutron Stars for the First Time

text: An article last Wednesday about Cody Bellinger’s performance for the Los Angeles Dodgers during the postseason misstated the hand on which Bellinger wears his mitt. It is his right, not his left.
match_headline: Cody Bellinger Goes Deep, and Upside Down, for Dodgers

text: An obituary on Monday about the poet Richard Wilbur referred incorrectly to his military service in World War II. Although he served for three years, he did not spend that entire time as a combat soldier in Europe.
match_headline: Richard Wilbur, Poet Laureate and Pulitzer Winner, Dies at 96
