text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about the drummer and vocalist Grady Tate referred incompletely to his work on the television series “Twin Peaks.” He played drums on the soundtrack of both the original series and the recent “Twin Peaks: The Return” — not just the original series.
match_headline: Grady Tate, Jazz Drummer Turned Vocalist, Dies at 85

text: An article on Tuesday about reaction on social media to sexual harassment allegations against Harvey Weinstein quoted incorrectly from comments the HBO comedy host John Oliver made about the actor Casey Affleck. Mr. Oliver said Mr. Affleck would present Best Actress at the next Academy Awards, not Best Picture.
match_headline: Harvey Weinstein’s Fall Opens the Floodgates in Hollywood

text: Because of an editing error, an article about Iraqi security forces’s retaking control of oil fields from Kurdish separatists misidentified the location of the National Defense University. It is in Washington, not Baghdad.
match_headline: Iraqi Forces Retake All Oil Fields in Disputed Areas as Kurds Retreat

text: An article on Tuesday about Bill de Blasio’s impact on public health in New York City during his mayoralty referred incorrectly to James R. Tallon Jr.’s work with the United Hospital Fund of New York. He is a former president of the fund, not the current one. (Anthony Shih took over after Mr. Tallon retired in August.)
match_headline: On Health, de Blasio Focuses on Crises and Inequality

text: An article on Thursday about an investigation into a possible misappropriation of funds at a subsidiary of Samsung Electronics described incorrectly the 2008 conviction of Lee Kun-hee, chairman of Samsung Electronics. He was convicted of inheriting money from his father in a way that avoided taxes, not for money his son, Lee Jae-yong, inherited. The article also misspelled the name of Lee Kun-hee’s father. He was Lee Byung-chull, not Lee Byung-chul. In addition, the article also misstated the reason for Lee Jae-yong’s conviction earlier this year. It was for bribing South Korea’s former president, not for bribing multiple government officials. And the article misstated Lee Jae-yong’s title at Samsung Electronics. He is vice chairman, not deputy chairman.
match_headline: Samsung Is Under Scrutiny Again as South Korean Police Raid Offices

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the Los Angeles Dodgers’s win over the Chicago Cubs in Game 5 of the National League Championship Series carried an incorrect dateline. It was written from Chicago, not Los Angeles. The article also referred incorrectly to Enrique Hernandez’s two first-pitch home runs in his first two at-bats. While the first was off Cubs starter Jose Quintana, the second was against the reliever Hector Rondon; both were not off Quintana.
match_headline: Dodgers Crush the Cubs and Reach Their First World Series Since 1988

text: An article on the cover this weekend about the singer Kelly Clarkson refers incorrectly to Julie Greenwald and Craig Kallman, two executives at Atlantic Records, Ms. Clarkson’s record label. While they are both married, they are not married to each other.
match_headline: Kelly Clarkson Is Nobody’s Puppet

text: An article on Page 8 about the Metropolitan Opera’s production of Thomas Adès’s “The Exterminating Angel” misstates the highest note written for Audrey Luna’s character in the opera “The Exterminating Angel.” It is an A, not an F, above high C.
match_headline: Your Guide to the Met Opera’s ‘Exterminating Angel’

text: An obituary on Friday about the French actress and singer Danielle Darrieux referred incorrectly to the title character of the 1963 movie “Landru,” in which she appeared. The character, a serial killer, was similar to Bluebeard, a fictional French murderer — not to Blackbeard, a notorious British pirate.
match_headline: Danielle Darrieux, French Film Star Over 8 Decades, Is Dead at 100

text: An obituary on Oct. 10 about Liam Cosgrave, a former prime minister of Ireland, gave an incorrect guide for the pronunciation of “taoiseach,” the Gaelic word for prime minister. It is commonly pronounced TEA-shock, not TAY-shuss.
match_headline: Liam Cosgrave, Irish Premier Who Helped End Violence, Dies at 97

text: An article on Oct. 15 about early efforts to bring clean drinking water to New York City misstated the location of the source of water in the Croton Aqueduct. It is in Westchester County, not the Catskills. (The Catskill Aqueduct was completed in 1917.)
match_headline: The Drinking Water Woes of Early New York

text: An article on Oct. 1 about Mayor Bill de Blasio’s pledge to bring more transparency to disciplinary actions taken against police officers misstated the age of a man who officer Francis X. Livoti was accused of choking to death. He was 29 years old, not a teenager.
match_headline: What Happened to Police Accountability? The Mayor’s Not Saying

text: An article on Oct. 8 about the actor David Patrick Kelly misidentified the location in Manhattan of the club where he introduced Bob Marley, Charles Mingus and Bruce Springsteen. The club, Max’s Kansas City, was in Gramercy Park, not on the Lower East Side.
match_headline: David Patrick Kelly, a Character Actor Vibrating on His Own Plane

text: An article on Oct. 15 about the battle over copper-nickel mining near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in Minnesota misstated the time of the formation of iron- ore- rich sedimentary rock in the region. It formed nearly two billion years ago, not two million years ago.
match_headline: In Northern Minnesota, Two Economies Square Off: Mining vs. Wilderness

text: An article on Sept. 17 about amenities in rental buildings, using information from a developer, misstated the type of business that will be opening at Henry Hall, at 515 West 38th Street. It will be a wine store, not a liquor store.
match_headline: Dog Yoga and Electric Guitars: Amenities, at a New Level

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about a cottage for sale in the Cotswolds, England, misidentified the cottage in the photo. The picture showed a street scene in the village of Biddestone, not the cottage for sale.
match_headline: House Hunting in ... the Cotswolds, England

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about style in Dakar, Senegal, misidentified the animal pictured. It is a sheep, not a goat.
match_headline: Looking for Surprises in Senegal

text: A map on Sept. 17 with an article about New Orleans gave an incorrect location for the restaurant Superior Seafood & Oyster Bar. It is at the corner of St. Charles and Napoleon Avenues, not Claiborne and Napoleon Avenues.
match_headline: We Wanted a Carefree Family Trip. So We Invited a Second Family.

text: Because of an editing error, a report last Sunday about the marriage of Julie Kohn and Bradley Cohen misstated the degree Ms. Kohn received from George Washington University. She has an undergraduate degree, not a law degree.
match_headline: You Say Cohen. I Say Kohn. Let’s (Not) Call the Whole Thing Off!

text: An article on Saturday about the uncertain future of the panel investigating chemical weapons use in Syria misstated the findings of its work so far. The panel concluded that Syrian government forces used chlorine-filled bombs on at least three occasions, not two. The article also misidentified the group that the panel found responsible for using mustard poison at least once. It is Islamic State militants — not Syrian rebels.
match_headline: Russia-U.S. Diplomatic Dispute Could Endanger Syria Investigation

text: An article on Saturday about the outcry over the killing of an investigative journalist in Malta misspelled the surname of a former opposition leader. He is Simon Busuttil, not Busutti.
match_headline: Malta in an Uproar Over Killing of an Investigative Journalist

text: An article on Sunday about an ambush in Egypt quoted incorrectly a security researcher’s comments about militants’ use of homemade bombs. The researcher, Ahmed Kamel El-Beheiri, was describing improvised explosive devices, not improved explosives devices.
match_headline: Militants Kill Egyptian Security Forces in Devastating Ambush

text: An article on Saturday about tax penalties associated with the Affordable Care Act misstated the exemption for the cost of coverage. People are exempt if the lowest-priced coverage available costs more than 8.16 percent of their household income, not 2.5 percent of their adjusted gross income.
match_headline: I.R.S. Says It Will Reject Tax Returns That Lack Health Insurance Disclosure

text: An article on Saturday about guidelines for science education in New Mexico misstated part of the name of a group that studies climate change. It is the Intergovernmental — not International — Panel on Climate Change.
match_headline: New Mexico Wavered on Evolution and Climate Change in Science Education

text: An article on Saturday about the trial of the man charged with the 2015 murder of Officer Brian Moore in eastern Queens misstated the given name of the assistant district attorney. He is Daniel Saunders, not David.
match_headline: Officer’s Question Drew Deadly Response in Queens, Prosecutor Says

text: An article on Oct. 11 about the trial of the man accused of planting a bomb in Chelsea last year, misstated the date on which Judge Richard M. Berman ruled that a Dumpster could be used as evidence. It was Tuesday, Oct. 3, not Thursday, Oct. 5.
match_headline: Smelly and Dirty and, in Bombing Trial, Suddenly a Star

text: An article on Friday about the Los Angeles Dodgers’ victory over the Chicago Cubs misstated Justin Turner’s position with the Dodgers. He is the team’s third baseman, not second baseman.
match_headline: A Reinvented Swing Solves the Dodgers’ Leadoff Problem

text: An article on Saturday about a diplomatic dispute between the United States and Turkey misspelled the name of a Turkish city where a consulate employee’s wife and daughter were detained for more than a week. It is Amasya, not Asmaya.
match_headline: U.S.-Turkey Visa Standoff Disrupts Business and Tourism

text: An article on Friday about the liquefaction of human remains as an alternative to burials and cremations referred incorrectly to how alkali salts can be derived. They can come from both alkaline earth metals and alkali metals, not alkaline earth metals alone.
match_headline: An Alternative to Burial and Cremation Gains Popularity

text: An article on Tuesday about the history of the two teams that will meet in this year’s World Series — the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Houston Astros — misstated the year of Al Gionfriddo’s catch off Joe DiMaggio in a previous World Series. It was in 1947, not 1949.
match_headline: My Field of Memories: I See the New Dodgers and Summon the Old

text: An article on Tuesday about the singularly strong winning records of both teams playing in the 113th World Series misidentified the team for which Josh Fields currently plays. It is the Dodgers, not the Astros.
match_headline: World Series Preview: A Matchup With No Underdog

text: A review on Saturday about the documentary “Too Funny to Fail” misstated the surname of the actress on the cast of “The Dana Carvey Show.” She is Heather Morgan, not Heather Logan.
match_headline: Review: ‘The Dana Carvey Show’ Was Doomed. ‘Too Funny to Fail’ Explains Why.

text: A report in the Playlist column on Monday about Fever Ray misstated the surname of the Swedish vocalist who records under that name. She is now known as Karin Elisabeth Dreijer, not Karin Elisabeth Dreijer Andersson.
match_headline: The Playlist: Taylor Swift Has a Miserable Crush and 12 More New Songs

text: An entry on Tuesday in the “What’s on TV” highlights misstated the name of a category on the game show “Snoop Dogg Presents Joker’s Wild.” It is “Primpin’ Ain’t Easy,” not “Pimpin’ Ain’t Easy.” (Sorry, Big Daddy Kane.)
match_headline: What’s on TV Tuesday: ‘At Home With Amy Sedaris’ and ‘Snoop Dogg Presents Joker’s Wild’

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the author and artist Marian Cannon Schlesinger referred incorrectly to Alice B. Toklas, whom Mrs. Schlesinger visited in Paris when she was 17. It was Toklas’s partner, Gertrude Stein — not Toklas herself — who had been a classmate of Mrs. Schlesinger’s mother at Radcliffe.
match_headline: Marian Cannon Schlesinger, Author and Eyewitness to History, Dies at 105

text: Because of an editing error, a letter on Oct. 11 in defense of the poet Jill Bialosky over charges of plagiarism in her recent memoir misspelled the given name of a signer. She is Roxana Robinson, not Roxanne.
match_headline: 72 Friends of Literature, in Defense of the Poet Jill Bialosky

text: An article on Tuesday about cities and regions bidding to host Amazon’s proposed second headquarters incorrectly described Yukon Territory in Canada. It is a territory, not a province.
match_headline: Amazon Counts Its Suitors: 238 Want to Be Home for 2nd Headquarters

text: An article on Wednesday about the Los Angeles Dodgers’ win in the first game of the World Series misstated the given name of a Dodgers player. He is Andre Ethier, not Andrew. The article also referred incorrectly to Dallas Keuchel’s ground-ball-to-fly-ball rate. It is the highest among starting American League pitchers, not the lowest.
match_headline: Dodgers Overcome Heat, and Astros, in World Series Game 1

text: An article last Thursday about the Canadian singer-songwriter Gord Downie’s farewell tour misidentified which of Mr. Downie’s brothers performed percussion on the song “You Me and the B’s” using hockey sticks. It was Patrick, not Mike.
match_headline: Gord Downie, a Canadian Rock Legend, Sings Goodbye

text: An article last Thursday about a book that explores the estate that inspired “The Philadelphia Story” misstated the honor that Katharine Hepburn received for her performance in the film. She was nominated for an Academy Award for her role; she did not win the award.
match_headline: Inside the Estate that Inspired ‘The Philadelphia Story’

text: An article on Thursday about the White House chief of staff, John F. Kelly, misidentified the branch of the armed forces in which his son, who was killed in combat, served. He was a Marine, not a soldier.
match_headline: Pitched as Calming Force, John Kelly Instead Mirrors Boss’s Priorities

text: An article on Thursday about the revelation that Stephen Paddock had removed the hard drive from at least one computer in his possession in Las Vegas misidentified the location of Mr. Paddock’s home in Nevada. It was in Mesquite, not Henderson.
match_headline: Stephen Paddock’s Missing Hard Drive Complicates Las Vegas Case

text: An article on Oct. 14 about efforts by Japanese companies to create more gay-friendly work environments misstated the amount of prize money won by Kento Hoshi in a business contest. He won 1 million yen, not 10 million. The article also paraphrased incorrectly comments made by a representative for the brokerage firm Nomura about cash benefits offered to gay couples after marriage. While the benefit is offered by some Japanese companies, it is not offered by Nomura.
match_headline: To Court Workers, Japanese Firms Try Being More Gay-Friendly

text: An article on Wednesday about the history of the Houston Astros’ league affiliation misidentified the division of the Astros and the Texas Rangers. They are in the A.L. West, not the A.L. Central.
match_headline: How the Astros Became an American League Team

text: A picture last Friday with a film review of Todd Haynes’s “Wonderstruck” carried an erroneous credit. The photograph, of the actress Millicent Simmonds, was taken by Myles Aronowitz, not by Mary Cybulski.
match_headline: Review: ‘Wonderstruck,’ Todd Haynes’s Imitations of Life

text: An article on Thursday about unpublished works by J. D. Salinger referred incorrectly to the relationship between him and his daughter, Margaret. While they had a difficult relationship, she had not been disowned.
match_headline: So Where Are the New J. D. Salinger Books We Were Promised?

text: A report in “Arts, Briefly” on Friday about the defacement of the Theodore Roosevelt statue outside the American Museum of Natural History described incorrectly one of the figures standing next to Roosevelt. The figure represents an African man, not an African-American. Because of an editing error, the article also misidentified which figure in a statue of the composer Stephen Foster was depicted playing a banjo. It was the African-American figure, not the figure of Foster.
match_headline: Protesters Deface Roosevelt Statue Outside Natural History Museum

text: An article on Page 28 this weekend about the forthcoming show “Alexis Rockman: The Great Lakes Cycle” misidentified the location of the crash of a Northwest Orient plane in 1950. It was Lake Michigan, not Lake Ontario.
ref_headline: Alexis Rockman: The Great Lakes Cycle
match_headline: Alexis Rockman Portrays the Great Lakes in Glory and Decline

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 26 about the artist Mary Kelly misspells part of the title of one of her works. It is “Circa Trilogy,” not “Circa Triology.”
match_headline: Art Lurks in an Unlikely Place for Mary Kelly: the Dryer

text: An article on Page 8 about Dia: Chelsea misspells the surname of an artist represented at the gallery. He is Michael Heizer, not Heiser.
match_headline: Women Take Center Stage in the Reimagining of Dia Galleries

text: An obituary on Friday about Tom Mathews, a promoter of liberal causes and candidates, misstated the position he held at the State Department in the Kennedy administration. He was a deputy assistant secretary of state for congressional relations, not a deputy secretary of state for congressional affairs.
match_headline: Tom Mathews, Promoter of Liberal Causes and Candidates, Dies at 96

text: An article last Sunday about “The Walking Dead” referred imprecisely to Robert Kirkman and Frank Darabont. They are not the cocreators of “The Walking Dead”; there are technically no creator credits on the TV series. Mr. Kirkman is an executive producer, and the show is based on his series of graphic novels. Mr. Darabont developed the series for television.
match_headline: ‘The Walking Dead’ at 100: Still a Hit, but for How Much Longer?

text: An article last Sunday about the Russian Revolution, “10 Days Still Shaking the World,” misstated the name of the author of “The Anatomy of Revolution.” He was Crane Brinton, not Brinton Crane.
match_headline: Condoleezza Rice on the 10 Days Still Shaking the World

text: A review on Oct. 15 about “The Ordinary Virtues,” by Michael Ignatieff, misstated the author’s academic affiliation. He is the rector of Central European University in Budapest; he no longer teaches at Harvard.
match_headline: Is Globalization Drawing Us Together or Tearing Us Apart?

text: An article on Oct. 22 about the social psychologist Amy Cuddy referred incorrectly to the number of social psychologists who participated in a survey assessing their perceptions of the influence of social media on their careers. It was 350, not 700. The article also quoted incorrectly from a response Cuddy wrote to a blog that criticized a paper she helped write on power posing. She said she was looking forward to “more progress on this important topic,” not “more research.” And the article misstated part of the name of a professional organization of social psychologists. It is the Society for Personality and Social Psychology, not the Society of.
ref_headline: more progress on this important topic,
match_headline: When the Revolution Came for Amy Cuddy

text: An article last Sunday about the Teachers Insurance and Annuity Association referred incorrectly to the method some former employees used to make whistle-blower accusations against the company. It was a complaint filed with regulators, not a lawsuit.
match_headline: The Finger-Pointing at the Finance Firm TIAA

text: A picture caption on Oct. 15 with an article about a road trip along the Mississippi River misidentified a bridge near Vicksburg, Miss. It is the Old Vicksburg Bridge, not the Vicksburg Bridge.
match_headline: Along the Mississippi

text: An article on Sunday about Japan and South Korea reconsidering establishing their own nuclear arsenals referred incorrectly to Charles D. Ferguson’s role with the Federation of American Scientists. He is the group’s former president, not its current one. The article also misstated the amount of plutonium Japan stores overseas. It is 37 tons, not 37 million tons.
match_headline: North Korea Rouses Neighbors to Reconsider Nuclear Weapons

text: An article on Sunday about the response of Carles Puigdemont, Catalonia’s ousted leader, to the move by Spain’s central government to take control of the restive region misstated the location from which he delivered a televised address on Saturday. Mr. Puigdemont spoke from Girona, not Barcelona.
match_headline: Catalonia’s Ousted Leader Calls for Peaceful Defiance

text: An article on Monday about the ideological dilemma facing Catalan civil servants in the wake of Catalonia’s independence movement referred incorrectly to Joan Maria Sentís’s role at the Catalan branch of the Workers’ Commissions. He is its public sector coordinator, not the coordinator.
match_headline: Catalonia Civil Servants Must Decide: Resist or Obey Madrid’s Rule

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about allegations of sexual assault against a renowned Islamic scholar in France misspelled the surname of one of the lawyers for the French activist and author Henda Ayari. He is Grégoire Leclerc, not Leclercq or Leclerq.
match_headline: 2 Frenchwomen Accuse Prominent Islamic Scholar of Sexual Assault

text: An article on Saturday about Saudi Arabia’s ambitious business development plans misspelled the surname of the chief executive of the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He is Kirill Dmitriev, not Dimitriev.
match_headline: Saudi Arabia Is Open for Business, but Not Everybody’s Buying

text: An article on Monday about abuses of Facebook’s services in various countries rendered incorrectly the name of a government-run telecom company in Myanmar. It is MPT, not MTP.
match_headline: Forget Washington. Facebook’s Problems Abroad Are Far More Disturbing.

text: An article on Saturday about an apology from Houston Texans owner Bob McNair over insensitive comments he made about N.F.L. players who sit or kneel during the national anthem referred incorrectly to the setting where Mr. McNair made the comment about “inmates running the prison.” McNair was speaking with other N.F.L. owners at a New York hotel, not among players and owners during a meeting at N.F.L. headquarters. A caption on an accompanying picture repeated part of the error.
match_headline: Texans Owner Bob McNair Apologizes for ‘Inmates’ Remark

text: An article on Oct. 17 about the choice of Kehinde Wiley and Amy Sherald to paint portraits of Barack and Michelle Obama for the Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery misidentified the painter of a portrait of King Philip II. It was Peter Paul Rubens, not Velázquez.
match_headline: Why the Obamas’ Portrait Choices Matter

text: An article on Saturday about a coming health care referendum in Maine misstated the surname of a man in Bangor, Me. He is James Klemenz, not James Smith. (A picture caption gave his correct name.) The article also described incorrectly the insurance status of Mr. Klemenz’s partner, Kirsten Reed. She is not uninsured.
match_headline: The Governor Blocked Medicaid Expansion. Now Maine Voters Could Overrule Him.

text: An article on Tuesday about the Trump campaign’s interactions with Russia misstated the steps that prosecutors took in connection with George Papadopoulos. Prosecutors unsealed Mr. Papadopoulos’s guilty plea on Monday; he was not indicted on Monday. (Mr. Papadopoulos pleaded guilty on Oct. 5 to making a false statement to the F.B.I.)
match_headline: Trump Campaign Got Early Word Russia Had Democrats’ Emails

text: An article on Sunday about the investigation surrounding the killing of a Honduran land rights activist referred incorrectly to investors in the proposed dam project. They are members of the Atala Zablah family, not “the Atala family” (no members of the Atala Faraj family have been investors in Desa or the Agua Zarca project).
match_headline: Who Ordered Killing of Honduran Activist? Evidence of Broad Plot Is Found

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the best and worst N.F.L. performances in Week 8 misspelled the surname of the Vikings player who caught a touchdown pass from Case Keenum against the Browns. He is Adam Thielen, not Thielan. The article also misstated C. J. Beathard’s position with the 49ers. He is a quarterback, not a running back.
match_headline: More Monteverdi: The Week’s 8 Best Classical Music Moments on YouTube

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about a surge in restaurant openings fueled by financing from banks and private equity firms misidentified an area along Illinois Highway 59. It is in Aurora, Ill., not Plainfield.
match_headline: Thanks to Wall St., There May Be Too Many Restaurants

text: An article on Tuesday about Franco Moretti’s data-driven approach to literary analysis misstated the number of research pamphlets collected in “Canon/Archive.” It is 11, not a dozen. The article also misstated part of the title of a book by Mr. Moretti. It is “The Bourgeois: Between History and Literature,” not “Between Literature and History.”
match_headline: Reading by the Numbers: When Big Data Meets Literature

text: An article last Thursday about enduring fandom for the singer Sade referred incorrectly to a scene in the TV show “Big Little Lies” in which Reese Witherspoon’s character hears Sade. It is at a dinner party, not in the car.
match_headline: Sade’s Quiet Storm of Cool

text: An obituary on Wednesday about June Robles Birt, whose abduction when she was 6 years old was national front-page news, misstated the surname of one of her sons. He is James Birt, not James Robles.
match_headline: June Robles Birt, Whose Abduction at 6 Gripped the Nation, Is Dead at 87

text: An article on Page D10, about the Presidents Cup golf event, misstates the given name of a participant in the tournament. He is Mike Weir, not Bob. The article also misstates his role in the tournament. He was a captain’s assistant, not a player.
match_headline: What 8 Golfers and Fans Wore to the Presidents Cup

text: An obituary on Thursday about the pianist and composer Muhal Richard Abrams misspelled the surname of a disc jockey who organized a 1957 album on which he played. He was Daddy-O Daylie, not Dailey.
match_headline: Muhal Richard Abrams, 87, Individualistic Pianist and Composer, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Thursday about the author Jane Juska misidentified the city in California where she died. It is Chico, not Chino.
match_headline: Jane Juska, 84, Who Drew Notice Writing of Late-Life Sex, Dies

text: An article on Friday about the 100th anniversary of the Balfour Declaration misstated the number of years between the writing of the declaration and the creation of Israel. It was three decades, not four.
match_headline: Balfour Declaration of Support for Jewish Homeland Still Divisive at 100

text: An article on Friday about the evolution of the Big Ten college hockey league over its five-year history misstated Wisconsin’s postseason results in its first season under Coach Tony Granato. It lost in the Big Ten championship game; it did not reach the N.C.A.A. tournament.
match_headline: Big Ten Hockey, at Age 5, Learns That Rivalries Are Hard to Manufacture

text: An article on Tuesday about enthusiasm surrounding the playing style of the Philadelphia Eagles quarterback, Carson Wentz, misstated the Cleveland Browns’ opinion of Wentz before the 2016 N.F.L. draft. They thought he would not be a top-20 N.F.L. quarterback; it is not the case that the Browns “did not even think Wentz was among the top 20 quarterbacks in the draft.”
ref_headline: did not even think Wentz was among the top 20 quarterbacks in the draft.
match_headline: Carson Wentz Is Fueling Eagles’ Hype. Not That He’s Noticed.

text: An article on Wednesday about the New York Knicks’ performance this season, playing without Carmelo Anthony, rendered incorrectly a part of the name of the agency that represents Kristaps Porzingis. It is ASM Sports, not ASA.
match_headline: Carmelo Anthony Is Gone, and Perhaps the Knicks Don’t Miss Him

text: An article on Oct. 27 about the Mountrigi Management Group, a Swiss company that secured exclusive broadcast rights for the World Cup through 2030, mischaracterized legal action taken by a company whose former chief executive bribed soccer officials. The company, Torneos y Competencias, entered a deferred prosecution agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice and paid a settlement; it did not plead guilty.
match_headline: How Did a Tiny Swiss Company Quietly Secure Valuable World Cup TV Rights?

text: A picture caption with a film review about “My Friend Dahmer,” using information provided by the film studio, misidentified one of the actors in the photograph. The picture shows the actor Ross Lynch with the actress Sydney Meyer, not the actress Katie Stottlemire.
match_headline: Review: ‘My Friend Dahmer,’ the Boy Who Became a Cannibal

text: An article this weekend on Page 22 about opioid usage by college students misstates the release date of a preliminary report from the federal task force examining the problem. It was released in July, not in the fall.
match_headline: Opioids on the Quad

text: An article on Page 4 on home intrusions by inebriated Penn State students misstated the surname of a woman who found such a student on her couch. She is Barbara Nilsen, not Nilson.
match_headline: What to Do When an Inebriated Stranger Stumbles Into Your Home?

text: An article on Page 7 about college subsidies of internships misidentified the Pace University director who spoke about making students aware of different economic sectors. It was Rebecca Tekula, executive director of the Wilson Center for Social Entrepreneurship, not Phyllis Mooney, executive director of career services.
match_headline: When Internships Don’t Pay, Some Colleges Will

text: An article last Sunday about Kerala, India, misstated the type of Christianity introduced by the Portuguese to the region. It was Latin Catholicism, not Catholicism; other forms of Catholicism had been practiced previously. The article also misstated the number of states in India. There are 29 states, not 36. (There are 36 states and union territories, combined.)
match_headline: In Spice-Laden Kerala, a Break From Urban India

text: A review on Oct. 22 about “Stalin: Waiting for Hitler, 1929-1941,” by Stephen Kotkin, misstated Winston Churchill’s position in 1939. He was first lord of the Admiralty; he was not yet prime minister.
match_headline: A Portrait of Stalin in All His Murderous Contradictions

text: An article last Sunday about the photographer Terry Richardson’s suspended relationship with magazines misstated Joanna Coles’s title. She is the chief content officer of Hearst Magazines, not Hearst.
match_headline: ‘Terry Richardson Is Just the Tip of the Iceberg’

text: An article last Sunday about the growing virtual-reality sex industry misspelled, in two instances, the surname of the C.E.O. and creative director of Realbotix. As correctly noted elsewhere in the article, it is McMullen, not McCullen. The article also mischaracterized the company VRTube.xxx. It makes technology; it does not employ performers.
match_headline: Virtual Reality Gets Naughty

text: An article on Saturday about a federal report linking human activities to climate change misstated the number of global heat records established over the last 17 years. Sixteen of the last 17 years have been the warmest years on record for the globe, not six of the last 17.
match_headline: U.S. Report Says Humans Cause Climate Change, Contradicting Top Trump Officials

text: An article on Monday about Facebook’s efforts to monitor fake accounts on its social platform’s misstated at one point the most recent report of its monthly average users. It is 2.07 billion, not 2.3 billion. The article also misstated the company’s estimate of fake accounts on its site. Facebook estimates that about 60 million — not 200 million — accounts are fake. The company estimates that about 200 million accounts are duplicate, used by real people.
match_headline: Facebook Says It’s Policing Fake Accounts. But They’re Still Easy to Spot.

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about Google’s new machine learning technology misstated the surname of a researcher for Google. He is Sergey Levine, not Levin. The caption also included an outdated credential for him. He is an assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley, not a postdoctoral researcher there.
match_headline: Building A.I. That Can Build A.I.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the costume designer John Mollo misspelled the name of the county in England where he died. It is Wiltshire, not Wilshire.
match_headline: John Mollo, Whose Costumes Made ‘Star Wars’ Seem Real, Dies at 86

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about the family therapist Salvador Minuchin misidentified his birthplace in Argentina. He was born in San Salvador, not San Salvador de Jujuy.
match_headline: Salvador Minuchin, a Pioneer of Family Therapy, Dies at 96

text: An article on Thursday about the economic policies of the president of France, Emmanuel Macron, misspelled the surname of a firebrand of France Unbowed, a leftist party. He is François Ruffin, not Rufin.
match_headline: Emmanuel Macron’s Unwanted New Title: ‘President of the Rich’

text: A report in the Playlist column on Monday about Brian Blade and the Fellowship Band referred incompletely to Myron Walden’s contributions to the group’s new album. He plays bass clarinet on the track “Within Everything,” not only on other tracks.
match_headline: The Playlist: The Return of the Real Boy Band and 10 More New Songs

text: An article on Saturday about new artwork on display in New York by the artist Yayoi Kusama misstated the age of Yayoi Kusama. She is 88, not 89.
match_headline: Yayoi Kusama and the Amazing Polka-Dotted, Selfie-Made Journey to Greatness

text: An article on Tuesday about sanctuaries that take in chimpanzees once used for laboratory research misidentified a university that owns one such chimpanzee. It is Georgia State University, not the University of Georgia.
match_headline: Lab Chimps Are Moving to Sanctuaries — Slowly

text: A headline on Wednesday with an article about Russia’s reaction to the findings of United Nations chemical arms investigators on a lethal sarin attack on the Syrian village of Khan Sheikhoun misstated the year of the attack. As the article correctly noted, the attack occurred in April, not in 2016.
match_headline: Russia Assails Investigators Who Faulted Syria in Sarin Attack

text: An article on Tuesday about the aspirations of the new Louvre Abu Dhabi museum misstated the reason the labor specialist Andrew Ross was traveling to the United Arab Emirates when he was barred from entering that country. Mr. Ross, a New York University professor, was planning to do research there, but he did not have a relationship with the school’s satellite campus in Abu Dhabi. The article also misstated the age of a Quran in the museum’s collection. It is from the seventh century, not the sixth.
match_headline: Louvre Abu Dhabi, a Cultural Cornerstone Where East Meets West

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Thursday about a book on Joan Rivers misstated her red carpet catchphrase. It was “Who are you wearing?” not “What are you wearing?”
match_headline: The Last of Joan Rivers

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the astronaut Richard Gordon misstated the size of Mr. Gordon’s family. He was one of five children, not six.
match_headline: Richard Gordon, Astronaut Who Reached for Moon and Very Nearly Made It, Dies at 88

text: An article on Thursday about efforts to unlock the iPhone used by the gunman who killed 26 people in a Texas church referred imprecisely to the circumstances under which an iPhone automatically wipes itself clean. A phone’s data will be erased after 10 incorrect login attempts only if the owner has enabled its data-erase function. It is not the case that 10 unsuccessful logins alone will result in erasure.
match_headline: Why Texas Shooting Could Draw Apple Back Into Security Debate

text: An article on Thursday about the uncertain future of the Joint Investigative Mechanism, an independent panel created to determine responsibility for chemical weapons use in Syria, misstated a precedent set by its report on the April 4 sarin attack in Khan Sheikhoun, Syria. It was the first time the panel had determined the Syrian government was responsible for an attack using sarin, a lethal nerve agent. It was not the first time that conclusion had been reached by an independent panel. (A United Nations Human Rights Council panel investigating abuses in Syria made that conclusion in a September report.)
match_headline: Leader of Chemical Weapons Panel Is Not Optimistic About Its Future

text: An article on Friday about the photojournalist Pete Souza, who covered much of Barack Obama’s presidency, misidentified an individual for whom Mr. Obama helped select a ring. He helped Mr. Souza choose an engagement ring for Patti Lease; he did not help select Mr. Souza’s wedding band.
match_headline: Pete Souza Photographed the Obama Presidency. Now He Helps People Remember It.

text: An article on Thursday about a debate in Congress over the proposed elimination of a tax credit for research into rare-disease treatments misstated the relationship between the National Organization for Rare Disorders and Philip English, a former Republican congressman and now a lobbyist representing drug companies. Mr. English did not lobby on behalf of the organization.
match_headline: Congress Weighs Repeal of Tax Credit for Rare Disease Drugs

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 1 erroneously attributes a distinction to Letitia James. Ms. James became the first African-American woman to hold citywide office when she was elected public advocate in 2013, not when she was elected to City Council in 2003. The councilwoman position is not a citywide office.
match_headline: David Dinkins Doesn’t Think He Failed. He Might Be Right.

text: An article on Thursday about the detention of three U.C.L.A. men’s basketball players in China described incorrectly Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s trip to the country in 2011. Though he attended a Georgetown game there, he did not attend the game at which a brawl broke out.
match_headline: LiAngelo Ball and Two Other U.C.L.A. Players Reportedly Detained in China

text: An article on Wednesday about the Royal Ballet’s new triple bill in London misspelled the given name of the actress in the ballet “The Wind.” She was Lillian Gish, not Lilian.
match_headline: Review: A Triple Bill at the Royal Ballet Comes Up Two-Thirds Short

text: An article on Page 6 about two millionaires’ perspectives on inherited and earned wealth misspells the surname of Mitzi Perdue’s second husband. He is Frank Perdue, not Purdue.
match_headline: How Wealth Shaped Mitzi Perdue and Blaine Vess

text: An essay by Maria Bamford last Sunday misstated the date of her wedding. It was on March 14, 2015 — not April 13, 2015.
match_headline: Maria Bamford: The First Time Someone Loved Me for Who I Really Am

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Oct. 29 about “The Apparitionists,” by Peter Manseau, referred incorrectly to Abraham Lincoln’s political career. Lincoln never served as a United States senator.
match_headline: The Man Who Photographed Ghosts

text: An article on Oct. 22 about the Russian Revolution, “The Temptations of Totalitarianism,” misstated the geographical location of Stalingrad. The city, now Volgograd, is hundreds of miles from the Ural Mountains; it is not in the Urals.
match_headline: Stalin, Hitler and the Temptations of Totalitarianism

text: An article on Oct. 29 about a dinner in 1908 honoring Henri Rousseau erroneously included a writer in the list of invitees to the event. Alfred Jarry was not invited; he died the previous year.
match_headline: The Dinners That Shaped History

text: An article on Nov. 5 about Democrats and the 2018 midterm elections included an erroneous figure for the number of times a president’s party suffered no electoral losses midway into the president’s first term. It is two times, not three.
match_headline: A Post-Obama Democratic Party in Search of Itself

text: Because of an editing error, a listing in the “On the Market” column last Sunday about a house at 247 Palmer Avenue in Sleepy Hollow, N.Y., misstated the number of bathrooms in the home. It has four-and-a-half bathrooms, not three-and-a-half bathrooms.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in New York and Connecticut

text: An article last Sunday about the housing market in Detroit misstated the number of mortgages that Quicken Loans wrote for home purchases in the city last year. It was 170, not 90.
match_headline: Detroit: From Motor City to Housing Incubator

text: An article last Sunday about millennial parenting misspelled the given name of Sara Mauskopf’s daughter. She is Bryn, not Brynn.
match_headline: App Time for Nap Time: The Parennials Are Here

text: Because of a production error, an article last Sunday about the former United States attorney Preet Bharara attending the opening-night performance of the play “Junk” appeared with the fourth and fifth columns of text reversed. The correct version of the article can be found at nytimes.com/styles.
match_headline: Preet Bharara Goes to the Theater and Sees a Familiar World on Stage

text: An article on Monday about the lawsuit brought by families of victims killed in the 2012 mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School misstated the number of people killed by a gunman in Las Vegas last month. It was 58, not 59.
match_headline: Appeal Offers Hope for Newtown Families in Suit Against Gun Companies

text: A picture caption on Sunday with an article about Vietnam and its relations with the United States and China misidentified two ships shown in the South China Sea. A U.S. Navy cruiser is the vessel in the foreground, and a Chinese frigate is in the distance — not the other way around.
match_headline: Vietnam, in a Bind, Tries to Chart a Path Between U.S. and China

text: A chart on Nov. 6 listing the top finishers in the New York City Marathon misidentified the countries that several competitors represented. Mamitu Daska is from Ethiopia, not the United States. Allie Kieffer is from the United States, not Switzerland. Diane Nukuri is from Burundi, not the United States. And Fikadu Girma Teferi is from Ethiopia, not the United States.
match_headline: Right and Left React to the New York Attack and Trump’s Call to End the Green Card Lottery

text: An entry on Sunday in the “What’s on TV” highlights about “AMC Visionaries: Robert Kirkman’s Secret History of Comics” misstated the length of the series. It is a six-part series that began on Sunday with a second episode on Monday, not a two-night special.
match_headline: What’s on TV Sunday: Joe Biden and the MTV Europe Awards

text: A review on Friday of the documentary “No Stone Unturned” misstated the film’s setting. It is Northern Ireland, not “Northern Island.”
match_headline: Review: ‘No Stone Unturned’ Explores an Attack in Northern Ireland

text: A headline with an obituary on Monday about the folk singer Katie Lee, who tried to stop construction of the Glen Canyon Dam, referred incompletely to the location of the canyon. It is in Arizona and Utah, not just in Arizona.
match_headline: Katie Lee, Folk Singer Who Fought to Protect a Canyon, Dies at 98

text: An obituary on Nov. 8 about Irv Refkin, who worked as a spy for the United States and Britain during World War II, said that “according to his account, his parents were killed in an auto accident when he was 3 or 4, and for the next 10 years he was raised in a German Lutheran orphanage.” This account was taken from an interview Mr. Refkin gave to the Office of Strategic Services Society.
ref_headline: according to his account, his parents were killed in an auto accident when he was 3 or 4, and for the next 10 years he was raised in a German Lutheran orphanage.
match_headline: Irv Refkin, Brash Accidental Spy in World War II, Dies at 96

text: An article on Tuesday about the Beirut Marathon misstated the year in which the American Embassy in Beirut was bombed. It was 1983, not 1982.
match_headline: A Missing Prime Minister Is the Antihero of Beirut’s Marathon

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 7 about Roza Livshits, who received assistance from an agency supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, misstated, at one point, the location of Minsk. It is in Belarus, not Russia.
match_headline: For Holocaust Survivor, America Is the ‘Reason I Can Smile’

text: An article on Tuesday about the Cleveland Cavaliers’ win over the New York Knicks on Monday misstated the number of assists and rebounds that LeBron James had against the Knicks. He had 12 assists and 9 rebounds, not 12 rebounds and 9 assists. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Cavaliers Erase 23-Point Lead to Beat Feisty Knicks

text: An article on Monday about forthcoming high-value art auctions misstated the date of Sotheby’s evening contemporary art auction. It will be held on Thursday, Nov. 16. It was not held on Tuesday evening.
match_headline: Contemporary Art Sales: Do I Hear $100 Million?

text: An article on Tuesday about a fund-raising event held by Arts in the Armed Forces, using information provided in advance by a publicist, erroneously included an actor among the cast members at the event. John Leguizamo did not perform at the event on Monday.
match_headline: Adam Driver’s Nonprofit Seeks Soldiers for the Stage

text: An article on Sunday about how lottery winners manage their winnings described incorrectly the lump sum payment received by Amanda Spiller, who won $1 million in the Virginia Lottery. It was about $688,000 after taxes, not before taxes.
match_headline: I Won the Lottery and I Need Help. No, Really!

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about different perspectives on income inequality in the United States misstated the year CNN arrived in Atlanta. It was 1980, not 1986.
match_headline: They’re Rich but Trying to Reach Beyond the Money Bubble

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Oct. 29 about exhibits of art from the Hudson River School misstated the location of the Catskill Mountain House. It was on the eastern escarpment of the Catskill Mountains, not on Catskill Creek.
match_headline: ‘Scenes of Solitude’ From Hudson River School Artists

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Korean War hero Thomas J. Hudner Jr. misstated the year he graduated from the Naval Academy. It was 1947, not 1946.
match_headline: Thomas Hudner, War Hero in a Civil Rights Milestone, Dies at 93

text: An article on Wednesday about Irene Rosenfeld, the chief executive of the snack food maker Mondelez International, misstated the year that Philip Morris agreed to acquire General Foods. It was 1985, not 1989.
match_headline: A Big Deal in Big Food, Irene Rosenfeld Retires From Mondelēz

text: An article on Tuesday about genetic keys to longevity misidentified the Massachusetts town in which Goldie Michelson resided. She lived in Worcester, not Gloucester.
match_headline: The Secret to Long Life? It May Lurk in the DNA of the Oldest Among Us

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the Hall of Fame second baseman Bobby Doerr misstated the year that David Halberstam’s book “The Teammates,” about Doerr and three of his fellow Boston Red Sox players, was published. It was 2003, not 2007.
match_headline: Bobby Doerr, 99, Red Sox Hall of Fame Second Baseman, Is Dead

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the tentative decision of Charles G. and David H. Koch to support Meredith Corporation’s efforts to purchase Time Inc. misidentified the speaker at an Americans for Prosperity event in August. It was Wilbur L. Ross, the commerce secretary, not Vice President Mike Pence.
match_headline: Meredith Bid for Time Inc. Said to Be Backed by Koch Brothers

text: An article on Wednesday about a new Barbie doll modeled on the Muslim Olympic fencer Ibtihaj Muhammad misstated when the doll was revealed. It was first put on display on Monday afternoon at the summit portion of the annual Glamour Women of the Year event, not during the awards show on Monday night.
match_headline: New Barbie Is Modeled After American Olympian Who Wears a Hijab

text: An article on Page F10 of today’s paper about an Iraqi man’s efforts to resettle his family in the United States misstates when his wife was granted a reunification petition. It was granted in December, not January. The article also refers imprecisely to a memo announcing an indefinite pause on the “follow-to-join” immigration program. The memo was issued jointly by the State Department, the Department of Homeland Security and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, not by the State Department alone.
match_headline: ‘Happiness Is Incomplete’: A Refugee Couple’s Scattered Lives

text: An editorial on Wednesday about Attorney General Jeff Sessions’ inaccurate descriptions of contacts he and other officials of Donald Trump’s presidential campaign had with Russians incorrectly described communications Mr. Sessions had with one official, Carter Page. Mr. Page told Mr. Sessions he was traveling to Russia, but not that he would be meeting with Russian government officials there.
match_headline: Attorney General Jeff Sessions Doesn’t Recall

text: A picture caption on Nov. 1 with an obituary about the mountaineer Fred Beckey omitted credit for the photograph of Mr. Beckey on an expedition to Mount Seattle in Alaska in 1966. It was taken by Jim Stuart.
match_headline: Fred Beckey, Conqueror of North American Peaks, Dies at 94

text: An article on Friday about the State Department’s possible willingness to remove Sudan from its list of state sponsors of terrorism misidentified the location of the province of Darfur. It is in the southwestern part of Sudan, not the southeastern.
match_headline: U.S. Is Open to Removing Sudan From Terrorism List, Diplomat Says

text: An article on Friday about the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s declining ridership misspelled the surname of the chief regional economist with the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It is Martin Kohli, not Kohl.
match_headline: In the Best of Times, the Worst of Rides

text: Because of an editing error, a jazz entry in the music listings on Friday about Jason Moran and the Bandwagon misstated how long the band has been playing a Thanksgiving-period gig at the Vanguard. It has been performing over the holiday for five years, not “over a decade.”
match_headline: Pop, Rock and Jazz in NYC This Week

text: An entry in the art listings on Friday about “Michelangelo: Divine Draftsman and Designer,” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, misstated how tickets to the show would be sold. The exhibition is free with the museum’s suggested admission; admissions will not be by a timed ticket.
match_headline: Art and Museums in NYC This Week

text: An article on Page 20 about the forthcoming album “Utopia” by Björk includes an erroneous transcription of part of an interview with the article. She described thinking about her new album as “a city in the clouds,” not “graffiti in the clouds.”
match_headline: Björk’s New Album Is a Love Letter to Optimism

text: A picture caption with a round-table conversation last Sunday about rap on TV and in film misstated the given name of an actor in “The Get Down” on Netflix. He is Shameik Moore, not Shaolin Moore. (The character he plays is named Shaolin Fantastic.)
match_headline: Rap Disrupted Music First. Now It’s TV and Film.

text: An article last Sunday about exhibitions commemorating the World War I battle at Ypres, Belgium, misstated the given name of the polar explorer whose expedition the photographer Frank Hurley accompanied. He was Sir Ernest Shackleton, not George.
match_headline: How to Remember a War Without Glory?

text: A review on Nov. 5 about “We Were Eight Years in Power,” by Ta-Nehisi Coates, misspelled the name of a writer and recording artist. She is Sister Souljah, not Sistah Souljah.
ref_headline: We Were Eight Years in Power,
match_headline: Between the Presidency and Him

text: A picture caption on Nov. 5 with a review about “Revolution Song,” by Russell Shorto, misspelled the middle name of a painter whose portrait of George Washington accompanied the review. He was Charles Willson Peale, not Wilson.
match_headline: The War of Independence, Seen Through Six Sets of Eyes

text: A review on Oct. 29 about “After the Eclipse,” by Sarah Perry, misstated the timing of a partial solar eclipse. It occurred two days before the murder of the author’s mother; it did not occur two nights before the murder.
match_headline: In ‘After the Eclipse,’ a Daughter Mourns Her Murdered Mother

text: An article on Nov. 5 about a new translation of the “Odyssey” misstated part of the name of a scholar who translated the Bible into English. His name was William Tyndale, not William York Tyndale.
match_headline: The First Woman to Translate the ‘Odyssey’ Into English

text: An article last Sunday about the absence of child care professionals on Instagram referred imprecisely to the presence of celebrity nannies in paparazzi shots. The nannies of Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt, as well as the royal nanny Maria Borrallo, have been photographed by paparazzi, though they seldom appear in photographs with their employers.
match_headline: Where Are All the Nannies on Instagram?

text: An article last Sunday about the shutdown of the Cone Denim White Oak plant in Greensboro, N.C., misstated the timing of an article by Michael Williams about the plant. The article was published two years ago, not two months ago.
match_headline: No Room for America Left in Those Jeans

text: An article last Sunday about new resorts and attractions in the Caribbean misstated the opening date of the Nikki Beach club in Barbados. It is scheduled to open in early 2018, not in December.
match_headline: What’s New in the Caribbean

text: An article on Saturday about the migration of tens of thousands of Puerto Ricans to Florida in the wake of Hurricane Maria misstated the area where the Puerto Rican population has recently risen from 479,000 to well over one million, according to the Pew Research Center. That figure refers to Puerto Rican migrants throughout Florida, not just those in Orlando.
match_headline: A Great Migration From Puerto Rico Is Set to Transform Orlando

text: An article on Thursday about the $450.3 million sale of the Leonardo da Vinci painting “Salvator Mundi” misstated the given name of Christie’s head of old master paintings. He is Francois de Poortere, not Francis.
match_headline: Leonardo da Vinci Painting Sells for $450.3 Million, Shattering Auction Highs

text: An article on Saturday about a Belgian Malinois military dog that was awarded Britain’s highest award for animal bravery, misstated the date of the Battle of Pelusium, in which cats and other animals are said to have aided a Persian victory over the Egyptians. It was the sixth century B.C., not the sixth century A.D.
match_headline: Dog Earns Special Treat: British Award for Bravery

text: An article on Saturday about the search for a missing Argentine Navy submarine misstated the number of military ships searching for the vessel. There were three, not two.
match_headline: Search Underway for Argentine Navy Submarine With 44 Aboard

text: An article on Monday about the popularity of the ABC series “The Good Doctor” misstated the date the show will wrap the first half of its debut season. It is Dec. 4, not Nov. 20.
match_headline: How ABC Found a Surprise Hit in ‘The Good Doctor’

text: An article on Monday about Ben McAdoo’s future as the coach of the New York Giants following the team’s upset victory over the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday misstated the place on the field from which the Giants converted a fourth-and-5 play during overtime. It was the Chiefs’ 36-yard line, not the Giants’.
match_headline: Giants Salvage Win Over Chiefs. But Is It Too Late for Ben McAdoo?

text: An article on Friday about an exhibit surveying the filmmaker Dara Friedman’s experimental films erroneously included a work in the exhibition. The film “DARA I” is not part of the show, although it is featured in its catalog.
match_headline: An Artist Turns Her Lens on a New Art City: Miami

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Saturday about the dancer and choreographer Gemze de Lappe misstated the role of Tommy Rall in the 1959 Broadway musical “Juno,” for which he was pictured rehearsing with Miss de Lappe and the choreographer Agnes de Mille. He was a member of the cast, not a choreographer.
match_headline: Gemze de Lappe, 95, Dies; Keeper of the Agnes de Mille Flame

text: An obituary on Monday about the country singer and songwriter Mel Tillis referred incorrectly to his composition “Ruby, Don’t Take Your Love to Town.” It was sung from the perspective of a disabled veteran of the Korean War, not the Vietnam War.
ref_headline: Ruby, Don’t Take Your Love to Town.
match_headline: Mel Tillis, Country Star Known for His Songs and His Stutter, Dies at 85

text: A picture caption on Tuesday with an article about faltering efforts by Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany to form a new government misidentified a man accompanying the chancellor. He is Stephan Steinlein, head of the federal presidential office, not Frank-Walter Steinmeier, Germany’s president.
match_headline: In Crisis, Angela Merkel Prefers Elections to Minority Rule

text: An article on Tuesday about a political stalemate in Northern Ireland misidentified the head of a homeless charity who meets with lawmakers at the Northern Ireland Assembly’s building in Stormont. She is Ricky Rowledge, not Ricky Routledge.
match_headline: Northern Ireland Is Sinking Into a ‘Profound Crisis’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 15 about plans for a mixed-use waterfront project in Long Island City, Queens, misstated the length of Anable Basin. It is 1,000 feet long, not 500.
match_headline: A 700-Foot Tower Is Proposed for Queens

text: An article last Wednesday about the decision by Toys “R” Us to file for bankruptcy in a Virginia court misidentified the city where the law firm Kirkland & Ellis is based. It is Chicago, not New York.
match_headline: Why Companies Like Toys ‘R’ Us Love to Go Bust in Richmond, Va.

text: A recipe on Nov. 8 for sweet potato and Gruyère gratin misstated how much butter should be used, and how. It is 3 tablespoons, all used to butter the pan and foil; no more is needed in the recipe.

An article on Wednesday about a new oversight panel set up by 21st Century Fox to address concerns over workplace sexual harassment misspelled the surname of one of the independent members of the panel. She is Sylvia Ann Hewlett, not Hewett.
match_headline: Fox Establishes Workplace Culture Panel After Harassment Scandal

text: An article on Tuesday about effective business tactics of the sports merchandise company Fanatics misidentified the operator of the Pittsburgh Steelers’ website. It is the team itself, not the sports apparel maker Fanatics.
match_headline: Fanatics, Maker of Sports Apparel, Thrives by Seizing the Moment

text: An article on Wednesday about the Boston Celtics’ winning streak misstated the date on which the team could win its 33rd straight game. It is Dec. 21 against the Knicks, not Dec. 18 against the Indiana Pacers.
match_headline: Celtics’ Winning Streak Adds Significance With Each Game

text: An article last Thursday about the actress Tatum O’Neal misspelled the name of a Hollywood star whom she befriended at a young age. She is Anjelica Huston, not Angelica Houston.
match_headline: Now Pass the Mic to Tatum O’Neal

text: An article last Thursday about Bulletin Broads, a feminist concept store, misstated the address of Bulletin Mini Mall, another store opened by its founders. It is 927 Broadway, not 926.
match_headline: A Feminist Collective, Not Just a Store in NoLIta

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the singer and actor David Cassidy misstated the surname of his mother. She was Evelyn Ward, not Wood.
match_headline: David Cassidy, Heartthrob and ‘Partridge Family’ Star, Dies at 67

text: An article on Friday about the conservative speaker and podcast host Ben Shapiro referred imprecisely to the tweets received by Mr. Shapiro. He received 38 percent of all anti-Semitic tweets aimed at journalists in 2016; not of tweets over all.
match_headline: Ben Shapiro, a Provocative ‘Gladiator,’ Battles to Win Young Conservatives

text: An entry in the Pop listings on Friday included a concert on Saturday by David Crosby & Friends at the New York Society for Ethical Culture. Mr. Crosby canceled the event because of laryngitis.
match_headline: Pop, Rock and Jazz in NYC This Week

text: An article this weekend on Page 32 about Spike Lee misidentifies the location of the 1963 church bombing that was the subject of his movie “4 Little Girls.” The bombing occurred at the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Ala., not in Little Rock, Ark.
match_headline: The Culture Caught Up With Spike Lee — Now What?

text: An obituary on Nov. 16 about the economist Uwe Reinhardt referred incorrectly to the hand-to-hand combat between American and German soldiers in 1944 in the Hürtgen Forest, near where he was raised in Germany. It lasted about three months, not four.
match_headline: Uwe Reinhardt, 80, Dies; a Listened-to Voice on Health Care Policy

text: An article on Friday about a couple who married despite their long-distance relationship misstated the given name of a man who received assistance from the Neediest Cases Fund, an annual campaign that helps those struggling in New York and beyond. He is Abdulaziz Marwan Hussin Mohammed, not Andulaziz. The article also misstated a surname of his wife. She is Hind Sirelkhatim Hamid Mukhtar, not Siralkhatim. (The errors were repeated in a picture caption.)
match_headline: From Afar, He Confessed His Love. Via an App, He Attended His Wedding.

text: An article on Nov. 14 about the media company Barstool Sports, relying on information from company representatives, misstated the circumstances under which one of its bloggers, Chris Spagnuolo, left the company last spring. Following a brief suspension, his departure occurred when the company and Spagnuolo could no longer agree on the terms of his continued employment. He was not fired.
match_headline: Spurned by ESPN, Barstool Sports Is Staying on Offense

text: A review on Nov. 12 about Philipand Erin Stead’s “The Purloining of Prince Oleomargarine,” in-spired by one of Mark Twain’s bedtime stories, misstated the children’s book award that theSteads received. They won theCaldecott Medal for “A Sick Dayfor Amos McGee”; they did notwin the Newbery Medal.
match_headline: A Mark Twain Tale, Brought Back From the Dead

text: An article last Sunday about the sex toy company Doc Johnson misstated the year Missy Elliott’s song “Toyz” was released. It was 2003, not 2012.
match_headline: For the First Family of Pleasure Products, Toys Are Us

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday on style in South Sudan misidentified the nationality of the musician Diamond. He is Tanzanian, not Ugandan.
match_headline: What War Can’t Destroy

text: An article last Sunday on the play “Torch Song Trilogy” misstated the title of a play by Robert Patrick. It is “The Haunted Host,” not “The Haunted Coast.”
match_headline: ‘Torch Song Trilogy’ and Me: A 35-Year Love Affair

text: An article on Monday about a proposed bipartisan resolution in Congress to confront sexual harassment misspelled the given name of a senator. She is Kirsten Gillibrand, Democrat of New York, not Kirstin.
match_headline: Congress Returns to Intense Pressure to End Secrecy Over Sex Harassment

text: An article on Saturday about a C.I.A. base operating in the Australian outback misstated the name of an advocacy group. It is the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, not the International Campaign for the Abolition of Nuclear Weapons.
match_headline: An American Spy Base Hidden in Australia’s Outback

text: An article on Monday about communities in Northern Canada affected by receding sea ice gave the incorrect age for Derrick Pottle when he moved to Happy Valley-Goose Bay from Rigolet as a child. He was 11 years old, not 9.
match_headline: Trudeau Apologizes for Abuse and ‘Profound Cultural Loss’ at Indigenous Schools

text: An article on Saturday about the challenges faced by major retail companies such as Sears gave an incorrect name for a video game store at the Phillipsburg Mall in New Jersey. It is GameStop, not Game Stopper.
match_headline: Scenes From Sears: 2 Locations Tell a Story of Struggle in a Tight Retail Market

text: An article on Monday about a New York Times Twitter account being accidentally locked referred incorrectly to the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador. It is a single province, not two separate provinces.
match_headline: Twitter Says Blocking a New York Times Account Was ‘an Error’

text: Because of an editing error, a subheading in the Scoreboard column on Saturday about a fine for an Arizona Cardinals receiver misstated his surname. As the article correctly noted, he is Larry Fitzgerald, not Fitzpatrick.

Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the European soccer club A.C. Milan’s financial troubles under its new Chinese owner, Li Yonghong, misstated the nation where another club, CSKA Sofia, plays. It is Bulgaria, not Hungary.
match_headline: At UEFA, Mounting Concern About A.C. Milan’s Murky Finances

text: A picture caption with an art entry in the Listings pages on Friday, using information supplied by the Center for Italian Modern Art, translated incorrectly the title of an Alberto Savinio painting exhibited at the center. The title of his “Le Songe d’Achille,” in English, is “The Dream of Achilles,” not “The Song of Achilles.”
match_headline: Art and Museums in NYC This Week

text: Because of an editing error, a film entry in the Listings pages on Friday for “La Belle Noiseuse” at the Quad Cinema misstated the year “The Last Emperor” was released. It was in 1987, not 1986.
match_headline: Film Series in NYC This Week

text: An obituary on Friday about Edward Herman, an economist known for his work with Noam Chomsky, referred incorrectly to the two men’s arguments about genocide in Rwanda and, during the Bosnia war, Srebrenica. Those arguments did not appear in their book “Manufacturing Consent,” which was published several years before those genocides.
match_headline: Edward Herman, 92, Critic of U.S. Media and Foreign Policy, Dies

text: An obituary on Sunday about the composer and music critic Eric Salzman misspelled the given name of the actor heard on the recording of his work “The Nude Paper Sermon.” He is Stacy Keach, not Stacey.
match_headline: Eric Salzman, Composer Who Championed Avant-Garde, Dies at 84

text: An article on Tuesday about Pope Francis’ visit to Myanmar incorrectly described a present given to the pope by General Min Aung Hlaing, who has ambitions to run the country. It was a harp in the shape of a boat, not in the shape of a goat. The article also erroneously attributed a distinction to the pope’s visit to Myanmar. It was not Francis’ first papal visit to a majority-Buddhist nation; Francis visited Sri Lanka in 2015.
match_headline: Pope Francis Arrives in a Myanmar Tarnished by Rohingya Crackdown

text: An article on Tuesday about the announcement of Prince Harry’s engagement to Meghan Markle referred incorrectly to Henry VIII’s relationship to Prince Harry. Henry VIII is a distant relative of Prince Harry, not an ancestor.
match_headline: Prince Harry, Meghan Markle and News of a Royal Wedding

text: An article on Tuesday about accusations of rape against the Moroccan pop star Saad Lamjarred described incorrectly an escape from a Paris hotel room made by his accuser, Laura Prioul. She was partly, not completely, naked.
match_headline: She Accused a Moroccan Pop Star of Rape. Online, She Was Vilified.

text: An article on Sunday about a yacht once owned by the Yugoslav leader Josip Broz Tito, which is now being restored as part of an effort to transform the Croatian city of Rijeka into a cultural hub, referred incorrectly to the creation of Yugoslavia. While Tito is credited with establishing the modern state of Yugoslavia in 1945, the country was formed after World War I.
match_headline: Banking on Tito’s Yacht to Steer a Cultural Renaissance

text: An article on Nov. 16, about a ruling by a Brooklyn judge that the police must obtain a warrant to track the cellphones of criminal suspects, misstated the court in Washington, D.C., that overturned a sexual assault suspect’s conviction. It was the District of Columbia Court of Appeals, a local court — not a federal appeals court.
match_headline: Brooklyn Judge’s Ruling Raises Bar for Covert Cellphone Tracking

text: An article on Tuesday about the legal dispute between Waymo and Uber misstated the circumstances surrounding the departure of David Drummond, a top Alphabet executive, from Uber’s board. He resigned from the company’s board; he was not asked to leave.
match_headline: Waymo Seeks Delay in Court Fight With Uber Over Trade Secrets

text: An article on Tuesday about the painter Kehinde Wiley, whose portrait of Barack Obama will be displayed at the Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery in Washington, misidentified the country in which Mr. Wiley’s father was born. He was born in Nigeria, not Kenya.
match_headline: Kehinde Wiley on Painting the Powerless. And a President.

text: An article on Wednesday about the reported suicide of Zhang Yang, a senior Chinese general who was under investigation for bribery, misstated the title of the political scientist Steve Tsang. He is director of the China Institute at the School of Oriental and African Studies in London, not head of contemporary Chinese studies at the University of Nottingham.
match_headline: Chinese General Being Investigated for Bribery Kills Himself

text: Because of an editing error, an appreciation of the designer Azzedine Alaïa misstated how old he was when he died this month. He was 82, not 77.
An obituary on Tuesday about the singer Wayne Cochran misstated part of the name of a nightclub in Bossier City, La., where he once performed. It was Sak’s Boom Boom Room, not Sax’s.
match_headline: Wayne Cochran, Singer With High Energy and Big Hair, Dies at 78

text: An article on Nov. 20 about the search for an Argentine Navy submarine missing off the coast of Patagonia misstated the size of the area being searched. It is 186,000 square miles, not 186 square miles. The error was repeated in a subsequent article about the search on Nov. 21.
match_headline: Search for Missing Argentine Submarine Raises Grim Scenarios

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about the film “Wonder” misspelled part of the title of the film based on Roald Dahl’s book “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.” It is “Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory,” not Willie.
match_headline: Why ‘Wonder,’ the Movie, Can’t Best the Book It’s Based On

text: An article on Nov. 24 about the search for an Argentine Navy submarine missing off the coast of Patagonia misstated the last major deadly submarine accident. It was in 2003, when 70 sailors died on a Chinese vessel during a training mission, not in 2000, when the Russian submarine Kursk was brought down by a misfired weapon, killing 118 sailors. The error was repeated in an article on Friday.
match_headline: Hopes Dashed, Relatives of Argentine Submarine Crew Turn to Grief and Anger

text: An article on Thursday about Harvey Weinstein’s legacy and its impact on this year’s Academy Awards celebrations misstated the awards strategist Tony Angelotti’s relationship with Mr. Weinstein. Mr. Angelotti did not work at Mr. Weinstein’s companies, though the two men did work closely together over the years.
match_headline: How Can the Oscars Celebrate in Weinstein’s Long Shadow?

text: Because of a reporting error, a comedy entry in the Listings pages on Friday about “Air Punch” at the Peoples’ Improv Theater Striker, misstated the number of performers reuniting at the venue. There will be about 25, not four.
match_headline: Comedy in NYC This Week

text: An article on the cover this weekend about the film “The Disaster Artist” omits the co-author of the book on which the film is based. The book was written by Tom Bissell along with the actor Greg Sestero, not solely by Mr. Sestero.
match_headline: When Your Movie Is a Hit for All the Wrong Reasons

text: An article on Page 16 about the MTV series “Floribama Shore” misstates the number of spinoffs in which family members featured in “Keeping Up With the Kardashians” have starred. It is 10, not seven.
match_headline: MTV Searches for ‘Jersey Shore’ Magic on the Florida Panhandle

text: An article on Page 6 about a Théâtre du Soleil production coming to Park Avenue Armory misstates the visa status of three Afghan actors in the production. The actors’ applications are no longer pending; they were approved after the article went to press, and the production will proceed as planned.
match_headline: A Theater Visionary ‘Nourished by the World’

text: A review on Nov. 19 about “Adults in the Room,” by Yanis Varoufakis, misspelled the surname of the prime minister of Greece. He is Alexis Tsipras, not Sipras.
match_headline: Why the Greek Bailout Went So Wrong

text: A review on Nov. 19 about “A Brief History of Everyone Who Ever Lived,” by Adam Rutherford, misstated the location where Richard III’s body was unearthed in 2012. It was found in Leicester, not London.
ref_headline: A Brief History of Everyone Who Ever Lived,
match_headline: A History of Humanity Told Through Genetics

text: Because of an editing error, a listing on last Sunday’s On the Market page misstated the number of bathrooms at 99A Clinton Street, Brooklyn, No. 1. The home has two and a half bathrooms, not one and a half bathrooms.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in New York City

text: An article last Sunday about Fiona the hippo misstated the weight of Bibi, Fiona’s mother. She weighs about 3,300 pounds, not 8,000 pounds. The article also referred imprecisely to the care Fiona received at the Cincinnati Children’s Hospital during a bout of dehydration. She was cared for by nurses, not doctors.
match_headline: Hooray for Fiona the Hippo, Our Bundle of Social-Media Joy

text: An article on Monday about an Arab-Israeli peace plan presented by Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman referred incorrectly to comments made by Ahmad Tibi, a Palestinian member of the Israeli Parliament. He described a set of ideas that he said the Palestinians had received from the Israelis and the Americans; he did not confirm the main points of the Saudi proposal.
match_headline: Talk of a Peace Plan That Snubs Palestinians Roils Middle East

text: An article on Sunday about corporate tax benefits and loopholes in the new tax bills passed by the Senate and House misstated Kinder Morgan’s current status. It has been a corporation since 2014, not a pass-through entity that would benefit from a provision in the Senate tax bill aimed at pass-through income from gas and oil operators. The article also misstated the status of limits on how much interest companies can deduct from their taxes. The limits would be imposed by the Senate tax bill that was approved last week, but would not apply to interest paid by car dealerships. They are not included in the existing tax code.
match_headline: Tax Bill Offers Last-Minute Breaks for Developers, Banks and Oil Industry

text: An article last Wednesday about Throwdown Fitness’s 10-year lease at 3 East 17th Street in Manhattan misstated the name of the building’s landlord. It is Yjl 3 East Street, not Yjl East 17th Street. The article also misspelled the name of the landlord’s broker. It is Okada & Company, not Okado.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Saturday about the draw sorting countries into groups for the 2018 World Cup misspelled the given names of a Senegalese player and a Nigerian one. The player from Senegal is Cheikhou Kouyate, not Cheikou, and the Nigerian player is Wilfred Ndidi, not Wilfried.
match_headline: 2018 World Cup: 32 Teams, 1 Goal

text: An article last Tuesday about the decision to redevelop a housing complex in France containing the former home of James Baldwin misstated what would happen to structures at the site. They will be developed into a luxury apartment complex, not demolished.
match_headline: James Baldwin’s Former Home in France Is Set to Be Developed

text: An article on Sunday about Republicans’ plans to reduce federal spending following the tax cut legislation quoted incorrectly from comments made by Senator Marco Rubio of Florida about entitlements and the deficit. He said the driver of the federal debt is Social Security and Medicare but did not specify “instituting structural changes.”
match_headline: Heading Toward Tax Victory, Republicans Eye Next Step: Cut Spending

text: An article on Tuesday about statute of limitations laws brought up in cases of past sexual misconduct at various U.S. prep schools misstated the location of the Pingry School in the 1970s. The school did not open its campus in Basking Ridge until 1983. The article also misidentified the school where Thad Alton, a teacher accused of abusing students, allegedly perpetrated certain acts of abuse. Some of these acts allegedly took place while Mr. Alton was a teacher at Short Hills Country Day School, which merged with the Pingry School in 1974.
match_headline: In Sex Abuse Cases, an Expiration Date Is Often Attached

text: An article on April 19 about a Bronx murder case referred incorrectly to the time frame in which a witness identified Steven Odiase as taking part in the murder of Juan Jerez. The witness first identified Mr. Odiase days after the shooting, not two years later, but the witness then disappeared for two years before being arrested by the police on an unrelated charge; he then again identified Mr. Odiase.
match_headline: The Case of the Missing Murder Witness

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about high profile investors looking for opportunities in inland regions of the United States misstated the name of the city where the company 75f is based. It is Burnsville, not Burnside, Minn.
match_headline: From Bezos to Walton, Big Investors Back Fund for ‘Flyover’ Start-Ups

text: An obituary on Nov. 22 about the scientist Lilli Hornig misspelled part of the current name of Aussig, the city in Czechoslovakia (now the Czech Republic) where she was born. It is Usti Nad Labem, not Laben.
match_headline: Lilli Hornig, 96, Dies; A-Bomb Researcher Lobbied for Women in Science
