text: An obituary on Nov. 26 about Mary Adelman, who for decades ran a typewriter-repair shop in Manhattan, misidentified the mystery novel by David Handler in which she is a character. It is “The Man Who Loved Women to Death,” not “The Girl Who Ran Off With Daddy.”
ref_headline: The Man Who Loved Women to Death,
match_headline: Mary Adelman, 89, Fixer of Broken Typewriters, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Tuesday about John B. Anderson, the former Republican congressman who ran for president as an independent in 1980, misstated the degree of support he received when he initially ran for the Republican presidential nomination. He was endorsed by Representative Jim Jeffords, Republican of Vermont, and some state and local elected officials; it was not the case that “no elected officials, not even his friends in the House, endorsed him.”
ref_headline: no elected officials, not even his friends in the House, endorsed him.
match_headline: John Anderson, Who Ran Against Reagan and Carter in 1980, Is Dead at 95

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Saturday about Mitch Margo of the singing group the Tokens, using information from Getty Images, misidentified one of the members of the group. Stephen Friedland is standing at left in the photograph, not Eddie Rabkin.
match_headline: Mitch Margo, an Original Member of the Tokens, Dies at 70

text: An article on Wednesday about a gathering of 45 mayors held to discuss city-level policies to address climate change misstated the day of an interview with Mayor Rahm Emanuel of Chicago. It was on Tuesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: 4 Takeaways From a Gathering of Mayors on Climate Change

text: An article on Wednesday about a defamation lawsuit brought against President Trump in New York State Supreme Court misstated an argument made by a lawyer in the case. Mariann Meier Wang, a lawyer for the plaintiff, argued that a federal ruling in a similar case against former president Bill Clinton allows a state court to hear a lawsuit against a sitting president — so long as it does not concern his official conduct. Ms. Wang did not argue that a state court could hear the case “so long as it concerns his official conduct.”
ref_headline: so long as it concerns his official conduct.
match_headline: New York Judge Is Asked to Toss Defamation Suit Against Trump

text: An article on Wednesday about an increase in official disputes between the New York City Police Department and the Civilian Complaint Review Board misstated the percentage of board recommendations the police commissioner modified in the first six months of 2016. It was 21 percent, not 18 percent.
match_headline: New York Police Rejecting More of Watchdog’s Findings, Report Says

text: An article on Wednesday about a redesigned rendition of “The Nutcracker” performed by Miami City Ballet misidentified the production of Balanchine’s “Nutcracker” for which Karinska and Rouben Ter-Arutunian designed the scenery. It was the 1964 production, not the 1954 original.
match_headline: A ‘Nutcracker’ Dressed in Bon Bons, With a Pineapple Throne

text: An article last Thursday about anthurium flowers, using information from a florist, referred imprecisely to the flowers in Emily Weiss’s wedding bouquet. It included roses, but not orchids.
match_headline: An ‘It’ Flower for a Feminist Moment

text: An article last Thursday about anxious New Yorkers turning to pottery and crafts as a balm and a corrective misspelled the surname of Bkln Clay’s co-founder. She is Jennifer Waverek, not Wavereck.
match_headline: Pottery Is the New Pilates, and Macramé Takes Away the Crazy

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Christine Keeler, who in the early 1960s was at the center of the political scandal known as the Profumo affair, misspelled the surname of the actor who played the British politician John Profumo in the 1989 movie “Scandal,” in which Joanne Whalley played Ms. Keeler. He is Ian McKellen, not McKellan.
match_headline: Christine Keeler, Central Figure in British ‘Scandal of the Century,’ Is Dead at 75

text: An obituary on Wednesday about King Michael of Romania misspelled the given name of one of his daughters. She is Margareta, not Margarita.
match_headline: King Michael of Romania, Who Ousted a Hitler Puppet, Dies at 96

text: An obituary on Saturday about the architecture historian Vincent Scully referred incorrectly to his childhood. While he did grow up in New Haven, he did not grow up under East Rock, which rises above New Haven’s harbor.
match_headline: Vincent Scully, 97, Influential Architecture Historian, Dies

text: An article on Thursday about Democratic senators’ calls for Senator Al Franken to resign incorrectly described Representative Joe Barton’s ranking among the Texas delegation. He is the state’s senior Republican, not the state’s senior senator.
match_headline: A Democratic Chorus Rises in the Senate: ‘Franken Should Resign’

text: An article on Thursday about wildfires in Southern California misstated the relative location of a large fire threatening the city of Ventura, Calif. The fire is 40 miles to the northwest of another fire threatening Los Angeles, not to the northeast. The article also misstated the number of children in a family that lost its home to the fire in Ventura. The Gonzales family has five children, not seven.
match_headline: California Fires Enter the Heart of Los Angeles

text: An article on Thursday about a rare decision to block the appointment of a right-leaning politician to the committee that awards the Nobel Peace Prize misstated the year in which the populist Progress Party entered Norway’s government for the first time, in a coalition with the Conservative Party. It was 2013, not this year (in which it entered a second coalition with the Conservatives).
match_headline: Right-Wing Populist Is Blocked From Joining Nobel Peace Prize Committee

text: An article on Thursday about an announcement from President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia that he will seek a fourth presidential term described incorrectly the extension of Russia’s presidential term limit to six years from four. It was extended in 2008, while Dmitri A. Medvedev was president; it was not Vladimir V. Putin who extended the term, though he is the first to take advantage of the longer term (and to seek another one).
match_headline: Putin Confirms He Is Running for President

text: An article on Wednesday about U.S. radio broadcasters being labeled “foreign agents” by the Russian government referred incorrectly to the status of the Russian government-run Sputnik news agency. While Sputnik was not required to register, its partner, Reston Translator, which transmits Radio Sputnik on FM frequencies, was.
match_headline: Russia Designates U.S.-Backed Broadcasters as ‘Foreign Agents’

text: An article on Thursday about the resignation of Lorin Stein, the editor of The Paris Review, amid an investigation into his behavior toward the publication’s female employees, omitted the name of a previous editor of the magazine. Brigid Hughes succeeded the magazine’s founder and editor, George Plimpton, after his death in 2003. Philip Gourevitch succeeded Ms. Hughes in 2005.
match_headline: Paris Review Editor Resigns Amid Inquiry Into His Conduct With Women

text: An article on Thursday about efforts by district attorneys in New York to crack down on fraud and wage theft misstated the amount of unpaid wages the state Department of Labor has recovered since 2011. It was nearly $150 million, not nearly $30 million.
match_headline: New York Officials Battle Wage Theft in Construction Industry

text: An article on Thursday about controversy surrounding the Amazon series “Transparent” referred imprecisely to the distinction achieved by Jeffrey Tambor, when he won a 2015 Golden Globe best actor award for his role on “Transparent.” It was not the first Golden Globe given to an actor for a transgender role; Hilary Swank won a best actress award in 2000 for her performance in “Boys Don’t Cry.”
match_headline: For ‘Transparent,’ Accusations Against Jeffrey Tambor Burst an Idealistic Bubble

text: An article on Page D3 of today’s paper about the skier Bode Miller refers incorrectly to the child Mr. Miller welcomed in 2016. His fourth child — a daughter — was born, not his first son.
match_headline: What’s Next for Bode Miller After Skiing? Hint: Think Fashion

text: A picture caption on Thursday with an obituary about Maurice Carroll, a former reporter for The New York Times and other newspapers and a former pollster, reversed the identifications of him and the man he was shown talking to, Carter Burden, a New York City councilman, in 1971. Mr. Carroll was in the foreground at left; Mr. Burden was at right.
match_headline: Maurice Carroll, Political Reporter and Pollster, Dies at 86

text: An article on Friday about former Gov. Phil Bredesen, who will run for the Senate seat being vacated by Senator Bob Corker of Tennessee, misstated the day on which Mr. Bredesen announced his entry into the race. It was Thursday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Ex-Governor’s Run Gives Democrats a Bit More Hope of Retaking the Senate

text: An article on Page 20 about the most notable art of 2017 misstates the number of paintings in the “Ad Reinhardt: Blue Paintings” show. It was 28, not 37. Additionally, a list of notable deaths with the article erroneously includes an artist who died before this year. Tony Conrad died in 2016, not 2017.
match_headline: The Best Art of 2017

text: An article on Dec. 3 about the Fox News host Sean Hannity referred incorrectly to the terms of his contract. It is not the case that he can leave the network with no notice.
match_headline: How Far Will Sean Hannity Go?

text: An article last Sunday about drag queens misstated the surname of a drag historian. He is Joe E. Jeffreys, not Jeffries.
match_headline: Beyond the Drag Event Horizon

text: Because of an editing error, last week’s cover story about ferry service misstated the percentage change in the number of rentals near ferry terminals that advertise ferry service. The percentage is 30 percent, up from 23 percent last year, not an increase of 23 percent from last year.
match_headline: How the Ferry Is Changing the Brooklyn-Queens Waterfront

text: An article on Monday about planned legal and tax reforms in France misspelled the given name and surname of the chief executive of Luxembourg for Finance. He is Nicolas Mackel, not Nicholas Mackal. The article also misstated where the Shard building is located. While it is in central London, it is not specifically in the financial district.
match_headline: As Brexit Looms, Paris Tries a Business Makeover

text: An article on Monday about Nikki R. Haley’s comments that women who have accused President Trump of sexual misconduct “should be heard” misstated the year in which Juliet Huddy, a former Fox News anchor, said that Mr. Trump kissed her on the lips in an elevator. Ms. Huddy said the incident occurred in 2005 or 2006, not in 2011.
match_headline: Nikki Haley Says Women Who Accuse Trump of Misconduct ‘Should Be Heard’

text: An article on Sunday about differences in the way similar workers are taxed under the new House and Senate tax plans misidentified a tax-reduction move made in 2003 under President George W. Bush. It was the tax rate on dividends, like long-term capital gains, that was lowered, not the rate on short-term capital gains.
match_headline: Tax Plans May Give Your Co-Worker a Better Deal Than You

text: An article on Sunday about President Trump’s speech at the opening of the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum described incorrectly the murder of Emmett Till, a 14-year-old African-American boy who was killed in 1955. He was killed by two men, not a white mob.
match_headline: Trump, Rejecting Calls to Stay Away, Speaks at Civil Rights Museum

text: An article on Saturday about the firefighters managing widespread wildfires in California misstated the number of fire departments in the state. There are 1,100, not 11,000.
match_headline: In Scorched California, a Year of ‘Epic Firefighting’ Is Testing Limits

text: An article on Dec. 2 about economic development in historically poorer and isolated regions of China misspelled the given name of a deputy researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. He is Hu Bingchuan, not Binchuan.
match_headline: China’s Next Potential Boom Spot: The Places People Overlook

text: An article on Monday about the growing popularity of fly fishing among women misstated the river that the St. Johns Bridge spans. It is the Willamette, not the Columbia.
match_headline: Fly Fishing Targets Women as a Source for Growth

text: An article on Tuesday about a failed terrorist bombing in Times Square misstated the location of an explosion in Chelsea in September 2016. The blast occurred on 23rd Street, not 27th Street, where a second undetonated device was found hours later.
match_headline: Bomber Strikes Near Times Square, Disrupting City but Killing None

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Vladimir V. Putin’s recent trip to the Middle East referred incorrectly to the resumption of air travel between Russia and Egypt. The two countries are in talks to resume direct flights from Russia to Cairo, but not elsewhere in Egypt.
match_headline: Whirlwind Putin Tour Highlights Moscow’s New Reach in Mideast

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about escalated attacks against the news media by President Trump misspelled the name of a spokeswoman for The New York Times. She is Danielle Rhoades Ha, not Danielle Rhodes Ha.
match_headline: Trump Escalates His Criticism of the News Media, Fueling National Debate

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Kenneth Dillard Jr., who received assistance from an agency supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, misstated the kind of housing lottery that Mr. Dillard won. It was run by Catholic Charities Brooklyn and Queens; it was not a city housing lottery. (The error was repeated in a picture caption.)
match_headline: Working in Philanthropy, Then Finding Himself in Need

text: An article on Tuesday about Broadcom’s $100 billion bid for the rival chip maker Qualcomm misstated where Broadcom is based. Although the company announced its intention to move to the United States, it is still based in Singapore.
match_headline: More American Jobs? Broadcom Deal Might Mean the Opposite

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the longtime New York Times reporter Roy Reed misspelled the name of a fellowship that he received. It is the Nieman fellowship, not Neiman.
match_headline: Roy Reed, Times Reporter Who Covered the Civil Rights Era, Dies at 87

text: An article on Wednesday about sexual harassment allegations against the restaurateur Ken Friedman misstated the year in which Mr. Friedman sent Carla Rza Betts, then a wine director at his restaurant the Breslin, a series of texts seeking nude pictures of her. It was 2010, not 2009.
match_headline: Ken Friedman, Power Restaurateur, Is Accused of Sexual Harassment

text: An article on Wednesday about apparently biased text messages sent between F.B.I. agents investigating Donald J. Trump misidentified the F.B.I. official who wrote that Hillary Clinton “has to win.” It was Lisa Page, not Peter Strzok.
match_headline: In Texts, F.B.I. Officials in Russia Inquiry Said Clinton ‘Just Has to Win’

text: An article on Wednesday about the tunnel in Times Square that was the target of a recent unsuccessful terrorist attack misstated the cost of a subway ride in 1932. It was 5 cents, not 10 cents. It also misstated that the tunnel spared commuters from paying an additional fare when transferring between lines. An additional fare was required.
match_headline: ‘The Tunnel.’ Depressing, Claustrophobic and Now a Terror Target.

text: An article on Wednesday about planned repairs on the East River subway tunnel misstated when a shutdown of the Canarsie Tunnel will begin. It is April 2019, not next April.
match_headline: Subway Tunnel Will Be Closed Entirely in Week After Christmas

text: An article on Monday about net neutrality rules in Europe included a quotation that misstated the availability of internet access in Cuba. It is severely restricted there, not totally unavailable.
match_headline: Net Neutrality’s Holes in Europe May Offer Peek at Future in U.S.

text: An obituary on Monday about Mickey Gurdus, who monitored the airwaves for Israel Radio, misstated where his parents settled after fleeing Warsaw in 1939. It was the British mandate of Palestine — not the state of Israel, which did not exist until 1948.
match_headline: Mickey Gurdus, Who Eavesdropped on the World, Dies at 73

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the filmmaker Bruce Brown misidentified the writer who reviewed his surfing documentary “The Endless Summer” for The New Yorker. It was Susan Lardner, not Pauline Kael.
match_headline: Bruce Brown, 80, Dies; His ‘Endless Summer’ Documented Surfing

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a deal to unify two tax bills drafted by Republicans in the House and the Senate referred incorrectly to one provision of the new proposal. The agreement would retain a provision allowing graduate students to avoid paying taxes on tuition waivers, not tuition stipends.
match_headline: Republican Tax Bill in Final Sprint Across Finish Line

text: An article on Thursday about Unesco’s recognition of the cultural importance of Neapolitan pizza making misstated the location of Mr. Sorbillo’s new pizzeria in New York. It is on Bowery Street, not Mulberry Street.
match_headline: It’s Official: Naples Pizza Is One of Civilization’s Glories

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the city’s plans to reroute commuters when part of the L train line is closed for repairs misstated the dollar amount of the emergency plan for the subway. It is a multimillion dollar plan, not a multibillion dollar plan.
match_headline: Rerouting Thousands: City Plans for L Train Closure

text: An article on Sunday about the most recent Army-Navy college football game misidentified the team that went ahead by 7-0 on Darnell Woolfolk’s 3-yard run. It was Army, not Navy.
match_headline: Leading Army’s Running Game, Two Years After He Nearly Walked Away

text: An article on Dec. 3 about the ongoing success of the Trisha Brown Dance Company after its founder’s death misstated the year Trisha Brown retired. It was 2013, not 2009.
match_headline: The Persistence of Vision (Trisha Brown’s, That Is)

text: An obituary on Friday about the equestrian Bill Steinkraus misstated the location of the equestrian events at the 1956 Summer Olympics, at which his team finished fifth. It was Stockholm — not Melbourne, Australia, where the rest of the Olympics was held that year. (The equestrian events could not be held in Australia because of quarantine regulations.)
match_headline: Bill Steinkraus, Equestrian Who Made Olympic History, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Thursday about Pat DiNizio, the songwriter and lead singer for the rock ’n’ roll band the Smithereens, misidentified one of the colleges Mr. DiNizio attended. It was Union County College in Cranford, N.J., not Union College in Schenectady, N.Y.
match_headline: Pat DiNizio, Singer and Songwriter for the Smithereens, Dies at 62

text: An article on Thursday about rape accusations against the music mogul Russell Simmons referred incorrectly to Mr. Simmons’s relationship with the media company Global Grind. While Mr. Simmons’s company Rush Communications oversaw Global Grind until 2014, it no longer has ties to the company.
match_headline: Music Mogul Russell Simmons Is Accused of Rape by 3 Women

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about a new report on the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, using information from The Associated Press, overstated what was known about the people shown in the image. While they were fleeing Gitarama, Rwanda, their ethnicity is not known.
match_headline: Rwanda Accuses France of Complicity in 1994 Genocide

text: An article on Friday about the increased probability of a Democrat takeover of the Senate after Alabama’s special election misidentified a state in which a Democrat won re-election to the Senate by a large margin in 2006. It was North Dakota, not South Dakota.
match_headline: Once Unthinkable, Now Possible: Senate Looks Like a Tossup in 2018

text: An article on Thursday about a federal criminal investigation into Uber’s business practices misstated Richard Jacobs’s relationship to the company, which he has said secretly gathered intelligence on competitors. Mr. Jacobs is a former Uber employee, not a former security contractor for the company.
match_headline: Uber Under Criminal Investigation, Justice Dept. Confirms in Letter to Court

text: An article last Sunday about Marriott International’s acquisition of Starwood Hotels misstated which company operates the Homewood Suites brand. It is Hilton Worldwide, not Marriott.
match_headline: Can Marriott Keep Starwood’s Culture of Cool, and Its Customers?

text: A picture caption with an article on Dec. 3 about high-speed internet service coming to Point Hope, Alaska, misstated the location of a home seen at twilight. It is in Nome, not Point Hope.
match_headline: Melting Arctic Ice Makes High-Speed Internet a Reality in a Remote Town

text: An article on Dec. 10 about Luke Bryan misspelled the middle name of a country-music artist. He is David Allan Coe, not Allen.
match_headline: From Farm to Farm With the King of ‘Bro-Country’

text: Because of an editing error, the Our Back Pages column on Dec. 3 omitted a clause that identified Charles Dickens’s “friend and eventual biographer.” That person was John Forster, not Jane Carlyle. 
match_headline: Notes From the Book Review Archives

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Dec. 3 about “Sticky Fingers,” by Joe Hagan, misidentified one of the celebrities whose children attended a Southern California boarding school with Jann Wenner. She was Judy Garland, not Liza Minnelli; Minnelli, Garland’s daughter, was one of Wenner’s classmates. 
match_headline: The Licentious Life and Times of Jann Wenner

text: A review on Dec. 3 about “Sense of Occasion,” by Harold Prince, misstated the performance record of “The Phantom of the Opera.” It is the longest-running show ever on Broadway; it is not the longest-running show ever in New York. 
match_headline: Rolling Merrily Along With Hal Prince

text: An article on Thursday about living conditions in villages in Myanmar’s Rakhine State referred incompletely to an estimate by relief agencies about the state’s population. The agencies estimate that about 300,000 Muslims remain in Rakhine State, not that the state’s total population is 300,000.
match_headline: In Myanmar’s Divided Villages, Fear Prevails and ‘Life Has Stopped’

text: An article on Dec. 10 about conditions in Ojai, Calif., during recent wildfires in the region gave an incorrect derivation for the name Ojai. It comes from the Chumash word for “moon”; it does not derive from the word for “nest.”
match_headline: Ojai, Calif., Ringed by Flames, Is an Ash-Covered Shangri-La

text: Because of an editing error, an N.B.A. report in the Scoreboard column, about Oklahoma City’s 119-117 victory over Philadelphia, referred incorrectly to Andre Roberson’s game-winning basket. He hit a three-footer with nine seconds left, not a 3-pointer.

A picture caption with an article on Sunday about Pep Guardiola’s success as the coach of Manchester City misidentified a player to whom Coach Pep Guardiola was giving directions. He is Bernardo Silva, not Sergio Agüero.
match_headline: Another Tough Test? Not for Manchester City and Pep Guardiola

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about the contemporary artist Beth Rudin DeWoody misstated the given name of an artist. He is Alec Egan, not Alex.
match_headline: Mar-a-Lago Has a Feisty New Neighbor

text: An article on Sunday about a meeting of far-right European leaders misstated the size of the Muslim population in the Czech Republic. Muslims make up less than 0.2 percent of the country’s population, not less than 0.02 percent.
match_headline: European Far-Right Leaders, Meeting to Condemn the E.U., Are Greeted With Boos

text: An article on Tuesday about the victory of Sebastián Piñera in Chile’s recent presidential election incorrectly described the political alignment of Alejandro Guillier. He is center-left, not center-right.
match_headline: Chile’s Election Consolidates Latin America’s Rightward Shift

text: A chart with an article on Sunday about changes in the tax code under the new Republican tax bill described incorrectly the rates for a one-time repatriation tax in the G.O.P. bill. The rate would be 8 percent (15.5 percent for cash), not 7.5 percent (14.5 percent for cash).
match_headline: Listen to ‘The Daily’: A Tax Deal, and Net Neutrality

text: An article on Dec. 8 about the Ford Motor Company’s plans to build electric vehicles in Mexico compared incorrectly the range of a small, battery-powered sport-utility vehicle that Ford plans to begin building in Mexico in 2020 and the ranges of electric cars now on the market. The Ford vehicle, which is supposed to go 300 miles before needing recharging, would have a greater range than many such cars, not all such cars.
match_headline: Ford Will Build Electric Cars in Mexico, Shifting Its Plan

text: An article on Monday about Jerry Richardson’s decision to sell the Carolina Panthers referred incorrectly to the relationship between NFL Network and the six men who were suspended from their jobs after a former wardrobe stylist for the network leveled accusations of sexual harassment and sexual assault. Three were current employees of the network, not all six. (The other three were former employees of the network and were suspended by their current employers.)
match_headline: Jerry Richardson, Facing Misconduct Allegations, Will Sell Panthers

text: An article on Tuesday about the absence of precision tracking technology in the N.F.L. misstated the technology used to track tennis balls in some competitions. The Hawk-Eye system relies on cameras, not chips attached to tennis balls.
match_headline: Why Doesn’t the N.F.L. Use Tracking Technology for First-Down Calls?

text: An article on Sunday about an Italian nonprofit that organizes soccer matches inside the country’s prisons rendered incorrectly the organization’s name. It is BambiniSenzaSbarre, not BambiniSenzasBarre.
match_headline: Bars on the Windows, Laughter Between the Lines

text: An obituary on Dec. 5 about the graphic designer Ivan Chermayeff referred imprecisely to his role in the design of two corporate logos. The blue Pan Am globe was designed by Charles Forberg and Edward Larrabee Barnes, not by Mr. Chermayeff, although he probably had some input (and later, with Tom Geismar, designed a modified version). The updated NBC peacock introduced in 1986 was designed by Steff Geissbuhler, a partner at Chermayeff & Geismar, not by Mr. Chermayeff himself. The earlier version also referred incorrectly to the facade of 9 West 57th Street, the Manhattan building for which Mr. Chermayeff designed the sidewalk sculpture. It is concave, not convex.
match_headline: Ivan Chermayeff, 85, Eminent Designer of Familiar Logos, Dies

text: An obituary on Friday about the filmmaker Anthony Harvey misstated the name of a short film that he directed and the play by LeRoi Jones on which it was based. It is “Dutchman,” not “The Dutchman.”
match_headline: Anthony Harvey, ‘Lion in Winter’ Director and Kubrick Editor, Dies at 87

text: An article on Sunday about Republican lawmakers marshaling enough votes to pass sweeping tax legislation misstated the types of taxes that taxpayers would be prohibited from prepaying under the new law. It would bar taxpayers only from prepaying next year’s state and local income taxes, not property taxes.
match_headline: Republicans’ $1.5 Trillion Tax Plan Appears on Track to Pass Next Week

text: An article on Wednesday about France’s decision to designate an original manuscript of Marquis de Sade’s “120 Days of Sodom” as a national treasure misstated the length of the scroll on which the work was written. It was 39 feet long, not three feet long.
match_headline: Halting Auction, France Designates Marquis de Sade Manuscript a ‘National Treasure’

text: A review on Tuesday about the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum referred incorrectly to the early history of the slave trade in Mississippi. The state had thriving slave markets in towns across the state in the decades before the Civil War — but it did not have markets in its big cities, including Jackson, when it was admitted to the Union in 1817. (Jackson was founded later, in 1821.)
match_headline: The New Mississippi Civil Rights Museum Refuses to Sugarcoat History

text: An article last Thursday about Finch College misstated the title of a Jefferson Airplane song. It is “Somebody to Love,” not “Don’t You Want Somebody to Love?”
match_headline: ‘Where Out-of-Town Girls Could Come Feel Safe in New York’

text: An obituary on Saturday about the drummer Sunny Murray referred incompletely to a story he had told about winning an award from DownBeat magazine. Although he told an interviewer that he took the award to the magazine’s office and burned it, Dan Morgenstern, who was DownBeat’s editor at the time, denies that this happened.
match_headline: Sunny Murray, Influential Free-Jazz Drummer, Is Dead at 81

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the longtime M&T Bank chief executive Robert G. Wilmers, using information from the bank, omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to those named, Mr. Wilmers is survived by his sister, Mary-Kay Wilmers, the editor of The London Review of Books.
match_headline: Robert G. Wilmers, Bank Chief and Buffalo Philanthropist, Dies at 83

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Prime Minister Justin Trudeau of Canada and the country’s conflict-of-interest laws gave an incorrect conversion to American dollars for the Canadian government’s contribution to the Aga Khan Foundation Canada. The contribution of 49 million Canadian dollars is worth about $38 million at current exchange rates, not $63 million.
match_headline: Trudeau Holiday on Aga Khan’s Island Broke Ethics Law, Report Says

text: An article on Thursday about passenger railroads’ failure to universally implement congressionally mandated safety devices misidentified the train involved in a fatal crash in Philadelphia two years ago. It was a Northeast Regional Amtrak train, not an Acela.
match_headline: Law Requires Life-Saving Braking Device. Most Trains Don’t Have It.

text: An article on Dec. 13 about Kristian Hidalgo, who received help from the Community Service Society, one of the eight organizations supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, referred incorrectly to Mr. Hidalgo’s employer from June to September. He was employed by Green City Force, which hired him to work in energy management as a contractor, not Ameresco, an energy management company.
match_headline: Carrying a Load of Debt and Pain, and Determined to Get Stronger

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 15 about James Polite, who received assistance from Children’s Aid, one of the eight organizations supported by The New York Times Neediest Cases Fund, referred incompletely to the type of youth whom Josh Waletzky and Jenny Levison sought to foster. The couple sought to help an L.G.B.T.Q. youth on the brink of aging out of the system, not merely a gay youth. The article also gave outdated information about a monthly stipend that Mr. Polite receives for college, based on incorrect information from a source. He no longer receives $300 a month for college from Children’s Aid.
match_headline: After Years in Foster Care, Intern ‘Adopted’ by City Hall Catches a Break

text: An article on Thursday about reports that Turkish prosecutors were seeking to jail the New York Knicks player Enes Kanter for remarks he made on Twitter misspelled the surname of the Turkish president in some instances. He is Recep Tayyip Erdogan, not Erdrogan.
match_headline: Enes Kanter Shrugs Off News That Turkey Wants to Jail Him

text: An entry on Thursday in the “What’s on TV” highlights misstated the title of a horror series on Shudder. It is “Black Lake,” not “Blake Lake.”
match_headline: What’s on TV Thursday: ‘Peaky Blinders’ and ‘Great News’

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Cardinal Bernard F. Law misidentified the branch of the military in which his father served. It was the Army Air Corps — not the Air Force, which did not exist at the time. (It was established in 1947.)
match_headline: Bernard Law, Powerful Cardinal Disgraced by Priest Abuse Scandal, Dies at 86

text: An article on Friday about the end of the individual mandate as legislated by the Republican tax bill misstated the name of a public policy think tank. It is the American Enterprise Institute, not the American Enterprise Institution.
match_headline: Requiem for the Individual Mandate

text: An article on Friday about the atmosphere in Memphis after the removal of several monuments to Confederate soldiers referred inaccurately to the membership of the Memphis City Council. The council is made up of seven black and six white members, not six black and three white members.
match_headline: How Memphis Hopes to Move On, Now That Statues Are Down

text: An article on Friday about regulators’ approval of plans to continue building the only two nuclear reactors still under construction in the country gave an incorrect title for a member of the Georgia Public Service Commission. The member, Chuck Eaton, is one of the group’s commissioners, not its chairman.
match_headline: Georgia, Facing ‘Difficult Dilemma,’ Keeps Nuclear Project Alive

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about interactive toys’ vulnerability to many hacking threats misstated the year when a cyberattack at VTech Holdings exposed the data of more than 6.4 million people. The attack occurred in 2015, not last year.
match_headline: A Cute Toy Just Brought a Hacker Into Your Home

text: A picture caption with a television review of “The Last Post” on Friday reversed the identifications of the women shown in the image. Jessica Raine is on the left, and Jessie Buckley is on the right.
match_headline: Review: ‘The Last Post’ Shows an Empire Awash in Adultery and Gin and Tonics

text: A review on Dec. 3 about “GenerationWealth,” by the photographer Lauren Greenfield, referred incorrectly to one of the book’s conclusions. Greenfield does refer to the media’s influence on people’s obsession with wealth and fame; it is not the case that “she never mentions” that influence. The review also misstated the provenance of some of the book’s images; many of them accompanied reports that appeared in major publications, not “most” of them.
match_headline: Capturing a Lost Generation in Photographs

text: A picture caption on Dec. 10 with a review about “Ramp Hollow,” by Steven Stoll, misidentified the West Virginia community where a photograph showing a coal miner’s wife and three children in 1938 was taken. It was Scotts Run, not Arthurdale.
match_headline: What the People of Appalachia Want

text: An article on Dec. 10 about changes to Title IX rules on university campuses misstated the findings of a ruling issued by the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit in a case involving the University of Cincinnati. The court found that the university violated an accused student’s rights by failing to let him submit questions to his accuser, not by failing to let him cross-examine his accuser.
match_headline: The Takedown of Title IX

text: An article last Sunday about uphill skiing misstated the date for the America’s Uphill race on Aspen Mountain. It is March 10, 2018, not March 30.
match_headline: For Some Skiers, It’s Uphill All the Way

text: An article on Sunday about widespread sexual harassment at Vice Media referred incorrectly to the agency with which a female Vice employee filed a complaint involving the company’s president, Andrew Creighton. It is the United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, not the United States Equal Opportunity Commission.
match_headline: At Vice, Cutting-Edge Media and Allegations of Old-School Sexual Harassment

text: An article on Sunday about the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, which is closing after 24 years, misattributed a comment about defendants’ facing “a presumption of guilt.” The remark, during a discussion in a university hall in The Hague, was made by someone in the audience, not the lawyer Marie O’Leary.
match_headline: Yugoslavia Tribunal Leaves Rich Legacy, but ‘Immense’ Challenges Remain

text: An article on Saturday about an impeachment motion in Peru misstated the legal scholar Cesar Landa’s judicial background. He is a former president and magistrate of Peru’s Constitutional Court; he did not serve on the Supreme Court.
match_headline: Peru’s President Hangs On to Power, but at What Cost?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the Cavaliers-Warriors matchup misstated the number of N.B.A. games scheduled for Christmas Day. There were five, not four.
match_headline: Who’s Fresher Than the Warriors?

text: An article on Sunday about women in the Lucasfilm story group misspelled the surname of a producer at Lucasfilm. He is John Swartz, not Schwartz.
match_headline: The Women Who Run the ‘Star Wars’ Universe

text: An article on Tuesday about a new fungal disease that threatens snake species worldwide misspelled the fungus’s name. It is Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola, not Ophidiomyces ophidiodiicola.
match_headline: Researchers Warn of a Spreading Fungus Deadly to Snakes

text: An article on Friday about a skating exhibit at the Museum of the City of New York, using information supplied by the museum, misidentified the site of the colonial-era canal used by skaters. It was on what is now Broad Street, not Canal Street.
match_headline: Where Winter’s Silver Skates Warmed the Soul

text: An obituary on Monday about Jerry Yellin, who as a fighter pilot flew the last combat mission of World War II, misstated his full given name. It was Jerome, not Jeffrey.
match_headline: Jerry Yellin, 93, Dies; Flew the Last World War II Combat Mission

text: An obituary on Saturday about the sportscaster Dick Enberg omitted part of the name of the college, now known as California State University, Northridge, where he was a teacher and an assistant baseball coach. It was San Fernando Valley State College, not San Fernando State College.
match_headline: Dick Enberg, Veteran Sportscaster, Is Dead at 82

text: An article on Saturday about rising obesity rates in Malaysia misstated the name of an application that grades various foods in terms of their health value. It is Fooducate, not Food Educate.
match_headline: In Asia’s Fattest Country, Nutritionists Take Money From Food Giants

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the continuation of an article on Friday about the victory of Catalonia’s separatist parties in a recent election misidentified flags being displayed in Girona, Spain. They are Catalan flags, not pro-independence flags.
match_headline: Catalonia Election Gives Separatists New Lift

text: An article on Nov. 19 about the history of problems with New York’s subway system overstated compensation figures for subway workers and managers, based on a Times analysis of federal data. Subway workers, including administrative personnel and managers, make an average of about $155,000 a year in salary, overtime and benefits, not $170,000 (the higher figure includes some labor-related overhead costs). The average figure for managers alone, not including overhead costs, is $240,000 a year, not $280,000 (and not “nearly $300,000,” as the article said in one reference).
match_headline: How Politics and Bad Decisions Starved New York’s Subways

text: A review on Monday of “All the Money in the World” referred incorrectly to a speech by the character Portia in “The Merchant of Venice.” Although she tried to persuade Shylock not to take a pound of flesh with her appeal to his mercy, she did not succeed.
ref_headline: All the Money in the World
match_headline: Review: Christopher Plummer Dominates ‘All the Money in the World’

text: An article on Thursday about the ticketing service MoviePass described incorrectly attendance trends at North American cinemas in recent years. While sales were flat in 2016, they increased 3.9 percent in 2015.
match_headline: MoviePass Adds a Million Subscribers, Even if Theaters Aren’t Sold on It

text: An article on Wednesday about progress made by unions representing employees of digital media companies misstated Slate’s position with regard to the Writers Guild of America East. While most members of Slate’s staff have signed cards with the guild, the company’s management has not recognized the union.
match_headline: Unions Are Gaining a Foothold at Digital Media Companies

text: An article on Thursday about Clemson University’s football coach Dabo Swinney misstated the given name of the school’s coach during the mid-2000s. He is Tommy Bowden, not Terry Bowden.
match_headline: Dabo Swinney Creates the Un-Alabama at Clemson

text: An article on Thursday about Liverpool’s acquisition of Virgil van Dijk misidentified the team from which Benjamin Mendy was transferred. It was Monaco, not Tottenham.
match_headline: Liverpool’s Price for Van Dijk? A Wait, an Apology and $100 Million

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the trombonist Roswell Rudd misstated the year that the bassist Charlie Haden’s album “Liberation Music Orchestra,” on which Mr. Rudd performed, was released. It was 1970, not 1969.
match_headline: Roswell Rudd, 82, Trombonist With a Wide-Open Approach, Is Dead

text: An article on Friday about a fatal fire in a Bronx apartment building misidentified the City Council member who represents the Bronx neighborhood where the fire occurred. He is Ritchie Torres, not Rafael Salamanca Jr.
match_headline: Bronx Fire, City’s Deadliest in Decades, Kills at Least 12 and Injures More

text: An article on Thursday about subway access across the city misstated the findings of a report about the number of New Yorkers who live beyond walking distance to a subway. The report said less than two-thirds of the city’s population lives within walking distance of a subway station, not that two-thirds of New Yorkers live beyond walking distance.
match_headline: Left Behind by the Nation’s Largest Subway System

text: An article on Friday about prepaying property taxes misstated whether Quicken Loans notes property tax payments on forms they submit to the government. The company does report the payments. The article also misstated where on the tax form the company reports such payments. It is on the second page of the form, not on Line 10.
match_headline: Prepaying Property Taxes? Your Bank May Make You an Audit Risk

text: An article on the cover this weekend about prominent cultural battles in 2017 misstates part of the title of a Carrie Underwood song. It is “Before He Cheats,” not “Before He Sleeps.”
match_headline: 10 Cultural Battles That Ruled 2017

text: An entry in the Listings pages on Friday about a performance by Television and Eleanor Friedberger referred incorrectly to Television’s current band members. The guitarist Richard Lloyd no longer plays with the group; he has been replaced by Jimmy Rip.
match_headline: New Year’s Eve 2017: A Guide to Music and Comedy Events

text: An article last Sunday about what happens to the rest of the country when certain “global cities” thrive misstated a type of ship that was assembled in the Bay Area during World War II. Military ships were built there during that period, but battleships were not among them.
match_headline: What Happens When the Richest U.S. Cities Turn to the World?

text: An article on Dec. 24 about Ammar al-Baluchi, who is accused of running money for the Sept. 11 attacks, used an outdated figure from 2008 for the number of counts of murder faced by each of the Sept. 11 defendants. It is 2,976, not 2,973.
match_headline: Alka Pradhan v. Gitmo

text: An article on Dec. 24 about Carter Page, a Trump campaign foreign-policy adviser, described incorrectly Page’s statements about his interactions with Russia’s deputy prime minister Arkady Dvorkovich. Page vacillated on whether he met with any Russian government officials. It is not the case that until his November 2017 testimony, he maintained that he hadn’t met with any Russian government officials on a 2016 trip to Moscow.
match_headline: What (if Anything) Does Carter Page Know?

text: A review on June 19, 2016, about the novel “Barkskins,” by Annie Proulx, misstated the background of one character. The “wife who at her death is revealed to have been a man” is Scandinavian (probably Danish), not Dutch. A reader recently pointed out the error in an email.
match_headline: ‘Barkskins,’ by Annie Proulx

text: An article on Monday about a veterans hospital in Oregon misidentified the university where Dr. Michael Mann is a professor of surgery. He is a professor at the University of California, San Francisco, not the University of San Francisco.
match_headline: At Veterans Hospital in Oregon, a Push for Better Ratings Puts Patients at Risk, Doctors Say

text: An article on Sunday about acceptance for openly gay, lesbian and transgender people in Lebanon referred incorrectly to the country’s exceptionality in the Middle East. While Lebanon’s tolerance is an exception in the Arab world, it is not an exception in the Middle East; in Israel, gay, bisexual and transgender people have widespread rights and freedoms.
match_headline: Coming Out in Lebanon

text: An article on Sunday about Barry Singer, owner of Chartwell Booksellers in Midtown Manhattan, misidentified the author of the book “Five Days in London: May, 1940.” The author was John Lukacs, not Winston Churchill.
match_headline: Running an Indie Bookstore, With Churchillian Resolve

text: An article on Thursday about a drug-treatment center in California misstated the number of years since Gary Benefield’s death. Mr. Benefield died seven years ago, not 11.
match_headline: The Club No Parent Wants to Join

text: An article on Monday about the New Year’s address by Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany misstated the number of votes the Alternative for Germany party won in parliamentary elections in 2017. It was about 5.8 million votes, not more than one million.
match_headline: Merkel’s Wishes for 2018: More Empathy and a New Government

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday with the Keeping Score column, about whether LeBron James is better at age 33 than he was five years ago, misstated the year he faced Tim Duncan in the N.B.A. finals. It was 2013, not last season.
match_headline: Is LeBron James, at 33, Better Than He Was 5 Years Ago?

text: An article on Sunday about memorable sports moments in 2017 misstated the number of consecutive women’s college basketball championships Connecticut had won. In 2017, they were going for their fifth straight title, not their fourth.
match_headline: The Year in Sports

text: An article on Saturday about Ohio State University’s victory over the University of Southern California in the Cotton Bowl misstated Northwestern’s record. It is 10-3, not 10-4.

An article on Monday about popular GIFs around the world misidentified a soccer player who is featured in a GIF that is popular in Italy. Graziano Pelle is pictured giving his teammate a kiss, not Giorgio Chiellini.
match_headline: Where Athletes in the Premier League, the N.B.A. and Other Sports Leagues Come From, in 15 Charts

text: A listing on Tuesday about performance festivals misstated the closing date of the American Realness festival. It runs Jan. 9-16, not Jan. 9-15.
match_headline: Five Festivals for the Open-Minded Theater and Dance Lover

text: An obituary on Dec. 26 about the former corporate executive William Agee misstated the current name of the company once known as Allied Corporation. It is Honeywell, not Allied Signal. (That company merged with Honeywell and took its name in 1999.)
match_headline: William Agee, ’70s C.E.O. Whose Star Was Dimmed, Dies at 79

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a Turkish banker convicted of taking part in a billion-dollar scheme to evade American sanctions against Iran misstated the gender of a former banker and political analyst. Selva Tor is a woman.
match_headline: Banker From Turkey Is Convicted in U.S. Over Plot to Evade Iran Sanctions

text: An article on Saturday about false or misleading statements made by President Trump in an impromptu interview with The New York Times misstated when Brown University published an assessment of how much the United States has spent on wars in the Middle East. The assessment for the 2017 fiscal year was published in September 2016, not this past September.
match_headline: 10 Falsehoods From Trump’s Interview With The Times

text: An article on Wednesday about the popular Chinese news app Jinri Toutiao, relying on comments made by the head of the company’s artificial intelligence lab, referred incorrectly to which content Bytedance screens before uploading it to the app. All content is screened by a basic computer algorithm, even if it is seen by only a handful of people.
match_headline: A Saucy App Knows China’s Taste in News. The Censors Are Worried.

text: An article on Dec. 28, about findings that the F.D.A. is not moving quickly enough to ensure that contaminated food is removed from store shelves, misspelled the surname of an F.D.A. official. He is Douglas Stearn, not Stearns.
match_headline: F.D.A. Leaves Tainted Foods on Shelves Too Long, Report Finds

text: An article on Saturday about efforts to lure sports teams and tourists to Fukushima, Japan, referred incorrectly to the death toll after the 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami and the following meltdown at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant. An estimated 16,000 people died across Japan — not solely in Fukushima Prefecture — and those deaths were caused only by the earthquake and tsunami, not by radiation from the damaged nuclear facility.
match_headline: Would You Play Ball at Fukushima?

text: An article on Wednesday about the possibility that a hip injury may keep Andy Murray out of the Australian Open tennis tournament misstated Kei Nishikori’s injury. It is a wrist injury, not an elbow injury.
match_headline: Andy Murray’s Australian Open Is in Doubt Because of Lingering Hip Problem

text: A report in the Playlist column on Dec. 18 misstated the surname of a member of the duo Her. He is Victor Solf, not Victor Soif.
match_headline: The Playlist: Black Thought Freestyles for 10 Minutes and 11 More New Songs

text: An obituary on Monday about Dan Talbot, an operator of Lincoln Plaza Cinemas in Manhattan and a founder of the film distribution company New Yorker Films, misspelled the maiden name of his wife and the first name of his mother. His wife is the former Toby Tolpen, not Tolpern; and his mother was the former Jean Charak, not Jeanne.
match_headline: Dan Talbot, Impresario of Art Films, Is Dead at 91

text: An article on Friday about Albert Schultz’s departure from the Soulpepper Theater Company amid sexual misconduct accusations misstated part of the name of Canada’s public radio and TV broadcaster. It is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, not the Canadian Broadcasting Company.
match_headline: Toronto Theater Director Resigns Amid Sexual Misconduct Accusations

text: An article on Friday about self-driving technology misspelled the surname of a researcher at the Virginia Department of Transportation. He is Noah Goodall, not Goodhall.
match_headline: Competing With the Giants in Race to Build Self-Driving Cars

text: A picture with an article on Thursday about accusations that FIFA is stalling an inquiry of failed doping tests by Russian soccer players was published in error. It showed Gianni Infantino, the head of FIFA, not Vitaly Mutko, Russia’s deputy prime minister.
match_headline: Critics Say FIFA Is Stalling a Doping Inquiry as World Cup Nears

text: Because of developments after the magazine went to press, the clue to 114-Down in this weekend’s puzzle — “Only N.F.L. team ever to go 0-16 for a season” — is no longer correct. The clue, which has been corrected online, should read: “First N.F.L. team to go 0-16 for a season, in 2008.” (The Cleveland Browns this season became the second.)
ref_headline: Only N.F.L. team ever to go 0-16 for a season
match_headline: When We Can No Longer Pass Through the Giant Sequoia

text: An article on this weekend’s cover about a development battle over the Marx Brothers Playground in Manhattan refers incorrectly to Melissa Mark-Viverito’s role in city government. While Ms. Mark-Viverito served as the City Council speaker from 2014 through 2017, she is no longer in that position. Corey Johnson was elected to the post on Wednesday.
match_headline: Park or Playground? Semantics Dispute Illuminates Preservationists’ Fight

text: An article on Page 4 misstates the quantity of raw sewage released into New York’s waterways each year. It is just under 20 billion gallons, not 27 billion.
match_headline: From Bicycles to Wooden Beams: The Weird Stuff Found in City Sewage

text: An article last Sunday about the inventor Nikola Tesla misstated who named the carmaker Tesla after him. It was Martin Eberhard, one of the company’s founders, not Elon Musk, another founder and the current chief executive.
match_headline: Tesla the Car Is a Household Name. Long Ago, So Was Nikola Tesla.

text: An article on Dec. 24 about competition dance misstated the location of a dance studio. Angel DiMartino Palladino, a 12-year-old dancer, was part of a studio in Ontario, Canada, not Orlando, Fla.
match_headline: Inside the High-Drama World of Youth Competition Dance

text: An article last Sunday about Ronald S. Baron, the founder of Baron Funds, misstated the performance of iShares Russell 2000 Growth fund over a five-year period. It was up 15 percent, not 96 percent.
match_headline: Why Are Mutual Fund Fees So High? This Billionaire Knows

text: A news analysis last week about U.F.O.s misspelled the surname of the director of Mutual U.F.O. Network. It is Jan Harzan, not Harden.
match_headline: Dad Believed in U.F.O.s. Turns Out He Wasn’t Alone.

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about President Trump’s move to expand offshore drilling, using information from the photo agency, misidentified a Chevron offshore platform. The platform pictured is a semisubmersible production facility, not a drilling platform.
match_headline: Trump Moves to Open Nearly All Offshore Waters to Drilling

text: An article on Saturday about debate in the United Nations Security Council over protests in Iran referred imprecisely to the nature of a cocktail reception held by the United States Mission to the United Nations. It was for countries that did not vote in favor of a General Assembly resolution denouncing the United States’ decision to recognize Jerusalem as Israel’s capital, not solely for the nine countries that voted against it.
match_headline: The U.S. Wanted to Discuss Iran. Russia Brought Up Black Lives Matter.

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the effects of climate change on coral reefs, relying on information from a research organization, misidentified a fish on a bleached coral. It is a blenny, not a goby.
match_headline: Global Warming’s Toll on Coral Reefs: As if They’re ‘Ravaged by War’

text: An article on Sunday about the artist Harry Bertschmann misidentified a museum that recently acquired a travel poster made by Mr. Bertschmann for its permanent collection. It was the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, not the Los Angeles Museum of Contemporary Art.
match_headline: The Struggling Artist at 86

text: Because of an editing error, the Square Feet column on Wednesday about rebuilding the Salt Lake City International Airport described incorrectly the location of Tribune Company’s shuttered printing plant in Orange County, Calif. It is west of the South Coast Plaza shopping center, not south of it.
match_headline: Building a Modern Airport in Salt Lake City From One Well Past Its Prime

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the success of the Los Angeles Rams in the team’s first year since its relocation misspelled the first name of the Rams’ kick returner. He is Pharoh Cooper, not Pharaoh.
match_headline: The Rams Bank on Playoff Football to Win Over Los Angeles

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about a ballet exhibition at the Miriam and Ira D. Wallach Art Gallery misidentified the individual the exhibition celebrates. He is Arthur Mitchell, not Miller.
match_headline: Arthur Mitchell, Ballet’s ‘Grandfather of Diversity’

text: An obituary on Sunday about the astronaut John Young referred incorrectly to his role in the Apollo mission that preceded the first moon landing. He was the command module’s pilot, not the mission commander.
match_headline: John Young, Who Led First Space Shuttle Mission, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Sunday about the actor Jerry Van Dyke misidentified the company that produced the movie “Chitty Chitty Bang Bang,” in which his brother, Dick Van Dyke, starred. It was Warfield Productions, not Disney.
match_headline: Jerry Van Dyke, ‘Coach’ Actor and Foil for His Brother, Dick, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actress Peggy Cummins misstated the surname of the person who confirmed her death. She is Dee Kirkwood, not Kirkman.
match_headline: Peggy Cummins, Seductive Star of a Cult Film, Dies at 92

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the former New Jersey governor Brendan T. Byrne referred incorrectly to a recorded telephone conversation between mobsters in which one said that Mr. Byrne, who was Essex County prosecutor at the time, “couldn’t be bought.” It was a mobster’s phone that was tapped, not Mr. Byrne’s.
match_headline: Brendan Byrne, Former New Jersey Governor, Is Dead at 93

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sept. 29 about Hugh Hefner, the creator of Playboy magazine, misstated when he edited the Playboy book “The Century of Sex.” It was after he and Kimberley Conrad separated in 1998, not after they divorced in 2010. The author of the book, James R. Petersen, pointed out the error recently in an email.
match_headline: Hugh Hefner, Who Built the Playboy Empire and Embodied It, Dies at 91

text: An article on Tuesday about natural disasters in the United States in 2017 misstated the name of an American scientific agency. It is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, not the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration.
match_headline: These Billion-Dollar Natural Disasters Set a U.S. Record in 2017

text: An article on Monday about the potential impact that the new tax law and President Trump’s position on trade could have on farmers misstated the tariff that South Korea could impose on United States beef. It could raise its tariffs to 40 percent on beef, not 27 percent.
match_headline: As Trump Appeals to Farmers, Some of His Policies Don’t

text: An article on Monday about Dr. Mitchell H. Katz, the incoming president of NYC Health & Hospitals, described incorrectly the services offered by Healthy San Francisco. It provides health care to uninsured people; it does not provide health insurance.
match_headline: City’s New Public Hospitals Chief Will Focus on Primary Care

text: A recipe on Jan. 3 for pork stew with pears and sweet potatoes misstated the amount of country-style pork ribs to use. It is 2½ pounds boneless or 3 pounds bone-in ribs, not 3 pounds boneless or 2½ pounds bone-in ribs. The recipe also omitted an item from the ingredient list: The ribs should be seasoned with 2 teaspoons black pepper before they’re browned.
match_headline: The Kindest Cut of All: A Pork Rib With Slow-Cooked Comforts

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Wednesday with an article about a meeting of President Trump and members of Congress on immigration referred incorrectly to the televising of much of the session. It was not shown live.
match_headline: 6 Dramatic Moments in Trump’s Unusual Immigration Session

text: An article on Wednesday about protests in Tunisia misstated the education level of Mohamed Bouazizi, a produce vendor whose self-immolation in December 2010 set off protests that toppled the government of Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali in early 2011. He was a high school dropout, not a college graduate.
match_headline: ‘You Can’t Survive Anymore’: Tunisia Protests Rising Prices and Taxes

text: An article on Wednesday about lawsuits filed against Fusion GPS and BuzzFeed by President Trump’s lawyer, Michael D. Cohen, misstated when Mr. Cohen said he was suing BuzzFeed. It was Tuesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Trump’s Longtime Lawyer Sues BuzzFeed and the Firm Behind Russia Dossier

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s meeting with congressional leaders to discuss immigration misidentified the room of the White House where the meeting was held. It was the Cabinet Room, not the Roosevelt Room.
match_headline: Trump’s Negotiation on Immigration, Unfolding on Camera

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about President Trump’s first comprehensive physical examination as president misstated the year in which a doctor said Mr. Trump would be the “healthiest individual ever elected” to the office of the president. It was 2015, not 2016.
match_headline: Trump’s First Full Physical Is Approaching. What He Discloses Is Up to Him.

text: An article on Wednesday about the end of the college football championship game misstated when Tua Tagovailoa first drove Alabama to a touchdown in the game. It was his second possession, not his first.
match_headline: How Tua Tagovailoa Stepped Up, Dropped Back, and Saved Alabama

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about efforts to scan and read a damaged biblical text misstated the given name of an individual aiding with the effort. He is Seth Parker, not Sean.
match_headline: Scanning an Ancient Biblical Text That Humans Fear to Open

text: An article on Wednesday about a dispute over ownership of the playwright Arthur Miller’s estate misidentified the publisher of a forthcoming volume of selections from Mr. Miller’s diaries. It is Viking Books, not Penguin Press. (Both are imprints of the Penguin Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House.)
match_headline: Inside the Battle for Arthur Miller’s Archive

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the French pop singer France Gall misstated the year her husband, the songwriter Michel Berger, died. It was 1992, not 1991.
match_headline: France Gall, Adaptable French Singing Star, Is Dead at 70

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday, about a criminal inquiry opened in Egypt over a New York Times article, misstated the number of countries that imposed a boycott against Qatar in June. It is four, not five.
match_headline: Egypt Opens Criminal Inquiry Over New York Times Article

text: An article on Tuesday about outdoor ice skating spots along the East Coast during the recent cold snap described incorrectly the location near the Chain Bridge on the Chesapeake & Ohio Canal where people were skating. It is along the Potomac, northwest of the National Mall. It is not across the Potomac.
match_headline: The Reflecting Pool Isn’t a Skating Rink, Washington Tells Visitors

text: An article on Thursday about a lawsuit by the de Blasio administration against five oil companies misstated how much money New York City has already divested from fossil fuel companies and private prisons. It is $60 million, not $100 million. The article also misstated the last time that legislation to combat climate change was introduced by city government. A bill relating to energy efficiency in buildings was proposed in the City Council; the administration’s September 2017 proposal to increase energy efficiency in large buildings was not the last legislation introduced.
match_headline: To Fight Climate Change, New York City Takes On Oil Companies

text: An article on Thursday about the gap in salaries paid to actors in the film “All the Money in the World” referred incorrectly to Michelle Williams’s compensation for the reshoots of the film after the replacement of Kevin Spacey. She received a per diem of $80, not 80 pounds.
ref_headline: All the Money in the World
match_headline: Purge of Kevin Spacey Gives ‘All the Money in the World’ a Pay Problem

text: An article on Thursday about President Trump’s recent renewal of past pledges to strengthen United States libel laws referred incorrectly to the attendees at a meeting the president held on Tuesday that was broadcast on television. They were lawmakers, not members of Mr. Trump’s cabinet.
match_headline: Trump Renews Pledge to ‘Take a Strong Look’ at Libel Laws

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the spread of chronic wasting disease among deer populations in North America misidentified a game warden. He is Keith Knighton, not Zac Norris.
match_headline: States Confront the Spread of a Deadly Disease in Deer

text: An article on Friday about the benefits of receiving the flu shot described incorrectly how the effectiveness of the flu vaccine is gauged. When a vaccine was considered effective, 3.9 percent of unvaccinated people contracted the flu. It is not the case that when a vaccine was considered effective, 3.9 percent of people did not contract the flu.
match_headline: Why It’s Still Worth Getting a Flu Shot

text: An article on Friday about diverging decisions by federal judges in cases related to partisan gerrymandering referred incorrectly to the makeup of a three-judge panel that threw out North Carolina’s congressional map. The panel included district court judges, not solely appellate judges.
match_headline: Is Partisan Gerrymandering Legal? Why the Courts Are Divided.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about concerns that a forthcoming article in Harper’s Magazine would reveal the identity of a woman who compiled a list of sexual harassment allegations against men in media erroneously included a magazine among the publications for which the essayist Katie Roiphe has written. Ms. Roiphe’s work has not been published in Dissent magazine.
match_headline: ‘Media Men’ List Creator Outs Herself, Fearing She Would Be Named

text: An article on Wednesday about proposals by electric companies in several states to pass their tax cuts on to customers through lower rates misstated the nature of returns available to utility shareholders. Such returns are authorized, not guaranteed.
match_headline: Power Companies Got a Tax Cut. Will Your Bill Reflect It?

text: An article on Thursday about the International CES trade show this week in Las Vegas misidentified one of the robots on display at the trade show. It is Loomo that doubles as a hoverboard and a companion that can take photos, not Nimbo, a different robot that works as an intelligent security system that can be programmed to patrol specific routes.
match_headline: CES 2018: What the Gadget Fest Looks Like in ‘the Year of A.I.’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about initial steps taken by the file storage company Dropbox to go public misstated which companies may file plans for public offerings confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Any company can make such a filing; the option is not limited to companies that generate less than $1 billion a year in revenue.
match_headline: Dropbox Is Said to Be Planning to Go Public This Year

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the artist and educator Tim Rollins misstated the date of his death. It was Dec. 22, not Dec. 26. The obituary also referred incompletely to the founders of Group Material, an organization Mr. Rollins helped create. The five people named in the obituary were not the group’s sole founders; several others helped establish it.
match_headline: Tim Rollins Dies at 62; Turned Bronx Teenagers Into Art Stars

text: An article on Tuesday, about the differing goals that have emerged among women’s groups since the 2017 protests that followed President Trump’s inauguration, misspelled the surname of a sociology professor at Oakland University. She is Jo Reger, not Roger.
match_headline: One Year After Women’s March, More Activism but Less Unity

text: A map with an article on Sunday about uranium mining near the Bears Ears National Monument showed an incorrect location for the Daneros Mine. As the article correctly noted, the mine is outside the current boundaries of protected land, not inside.
match_headline: Uranium Miners Pushed Hard for a Comeback. They Got Their Wish.

text: An article on Sunday about Haitian migrants in Canada described incorrectly regulations on face veils in Quebec. While the government in 2017 barred people wearing face coverings from using public services or working in government jobs, it did not ban full-face veils in public spaces.
match_headline: Migrants Fleeing to Canada Learn Even a Liberal Nation Has Limits

text: An article on Monday about reaction among black churchgoers to President Trump’s disparaging comments on immigrants misidentified the church leader at the Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal Church in Washington who led worshipers in the song “We Shall Overcome.” It was the church’s music director, Marty Austin Lamar, not the pastor, the Rev. William H. Lamar IV (the two men are brothers).
match_headline: In Trump’s Remarks, Black Churches See a Nation Backsliding

text: A Critic’s Notebook on Saturday about a review of public monuments misidentified the city where protesters pulled down a Confederate statue in the wake of a white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Va., last August. It was in Durham, N.C., not Charlottesville.
match_headline: Half-Measures Won’t Erase the Painful Past of Our Monuments

text: An article on Jan. 10 about a memo to the Trump administration written by Robert E. Murray, the head of the country’s largest coal mining company, misstated the number of suggested actions in his memo. It had 16 recommendations, not 14.
match_headline: How a Coal Baron’s Wish List Became President Trump’s To-Do List

text: An article on Sunday about Nice Leng’ete, a young woman who started a program in Kenya to create new rites of passage to replace female genital cutting, misstated how many girls she has helped. It is 15,000, not 50,000. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: She Ran From the Cut, and Helped Thousands of Other Girls Escape, Too

text: An article on Monday about the recent false missile alert in Hawaii misstated the time between the 1983 downing of a Korean Airlines jet and a false alert by the Soviet early warning system. It was 25 days, not three months.
match_headline: Hawaii False Alarm Hints at Thin Line Between Mishap and Nuclear War

text: An article on Monday about the outlook for the United States automobile industry in 2018 misstated the corporate title of Dan Ammann of General Motors. He is G.M.’s president; he is no longer its chief financial officer.
match_headline: Detroit Auto Show May Be Celebrating an Era About to End

text: An obituary on Monday about the museum curator Kynaston McShine misstated part of the name of a feminist collective that was founded in response to the low number of women in his 1984 exhibition “An International Survey of Recent Painting and Sculpture.” Although they are known for wearing gorilla masks in public, they are the Guerrilla Girls, not the Gorilla Girls.
ref_headline: An International Survey of Recent Painting and Sculpture.
match_headline: Kynaston McShine, Curator of Historic Art Exhibitions, Dies at 82

text: An article on Thursday about Democratic senators positioning themselves for their party’s 2020 presidential nomination misstated the name of a liberal advocacy group. It is the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, not the Democratic Change Campaign Committee.
match_headline: Senate Democrats Make Hard Turn Left in Warming Up for 2020 Race

text: An article on Saturday about a letter signed by the actress Catherine Deneuve and other women that criticized the #MeToo movement referred incorrectly to the accusations made by a journalist against Eric Brion, the former head of a French television channel. The journalist said the disrespectful conduct involved an encounter she had with Mr. Brion in Cannes, not a text message.
match_headline: Response to French Letter Denouncing #MeToo Shows a Sharp Divide

text: An article on Thursday about the United States’ decision to withhold $65 million in aid from the United Nations Relief and Works Agency misstated the number of Palestinian refugees registered at camps administered by the agency in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. It is 1.7 million, not 5.2 million.
match_headline: U.S. Funding Cut Reignites Debate on Palestinian Refugee Agency

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about a plan by a group of hospitals to create a nonprofit generic drug company erroneously named the new company. The company does not yet have a name; it is not called Project Rx.
match_headline: Fed Up With Drug Companies, Hospitals Decide to Start Their Own

text: An article on Jan. 12 about how automobile companies name different car models referred incorrectly to Robert Pyrah’s position at Oxford University. He is a member of the university’s history faculty, not a lecturer on branding.
match_headline: How Car Companies Decide You’ll Ride a Mustang or Catch a Tiguan

text: An article on Sept. 30 about technological improvements to aircraft onboard recorders, in describing the Asiana Airlines crash in San Francisco in 2013 that left three people dead, misstated the circumstances of the deaths. One of the three died of injuries onboard, while the other two were ejected from the plane; it is not the case that all three were ejected.
match_headline: New Black Boxes Will Be Easier to Track in Plane Crashes at Sea

text: An article on Friday about a crackdown on a Chinese Mafia ring in Italy misspelled the surname of a professor of sociology at Florence University. He is Stefano Becucci, not Bocucci.
match_headline: Police Bust a Chinese Mafia in the Country That Invented the Term

text: An article on Friday about a shuffling of top aides to the president of Egypt, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, referred incorrectly to the relationship between the General Intelligence Service and the public relations agency Weber Shandwick. The agency said it stopped doing work for the service in July; it is not currently representing the service.
match_headline: Egypt’s Sisi Fires Spy Chief as Shuffle of Top Aides Continues

text: An article on Thursday about efforts to save an endangered herd of caribou referred incorrectly to Gordon Eason, a retired biologist. He does not hold a Ph.D. and therefore is not Dr. Eason.
match_headline: Trapped on an Island With Wolves, the Only Way Out for These Caribou Was Up

text: An article on Friday about a lawsuit against the city government brought by a city official referred imprecisely to comments made about the case by the plaintiff’s lawyer. While the lawyer, Samuel O. Maduegbuna, acknowledges that he has no “direct evidence” that a supervisor offered favorable testimony to protect the mayor during a federal investigation, he says there is strong circumstantial evidence. He did not say he had “no evidence.”
match_headline: Official Sues City Claiming Retaliation Tied to Inquiry of Mayor

text: An article on Thursday about predictions surrounding developments in the N.B.A. misidentified the team Steve Sax played for in 1989. It was the Yankees, not the Chicago White Sox.
match_headline: 8 Fearless N.B.A. Predictions: LeBron, Boogie and the Blazers’ Backcourt

text: An article on Friday about the Outsider Art Fair misstated the David Lewis Gallery’s involvement with the estate of the outsider artist Thornton Dial. While the gallery is showing Dial’s work, it does not represent the estate. The article, using information from the Fleisher/Ollman gallery, also incorrectly stated that P. M. Wentworth and Martín Ramírez were in a mental hospital in Northern California at the same time. Mr. Ramírez was a patient at the hospital, not Mr. Wentworth. The article also misspelled the surname of an artist at the ZQ gallery. She is Anne Grgich, not Grgrich.
match_headline: The Outsider Fair Once More Confirms That Art Is Everywhere

text: An obituary on Friday about Stansfield Turner, who ran the Central Intelligence Agency under President Jimmy Carter, referred incorrectly to part of his education. He received a single degree in politics, philosophy and economics from Oxford University — not separate degrees in each subject.
match_headline: Stansfield Turner, C.I.A. Director Who Confronted Communism Under Carter, Dies at 94

text: A picture caption on Jan. 7 with a review of two books about how literature has shaped human society misstated the location of the Anna Amalia Library. It is in Weimar, Germany, not Leipzig.
match_headline: We Are What We Read

text: An article last Sunday about new lodging options around the world misidentified the country where Quito is. It is Ecuador, not Peru.
match_headline: New Hotels to Check Out in 2018

text: An article last Sunday about Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon, misstated his age. He is 54, not 53.
match_headline: Jeff Bezos, Mr. Amazon, Steps Out

text: Because of an editing error, two picture captions with an article last Sunday about the radioisotope Molybdenum-99 referred incorrectly to its role in medical diagnostics. It is used to make an imaging agent that is injected into patients; it is not injected directly into patients.
match_headline: Inside the Global Relay Race to Deliver Moly-99

text: An article on Dec. 31 about the comedian and activist Dick Gregory referred incorrectly to the status of Chicago’s Playboy Club in the 1960s. It is not the case that the club was racially segregated at that time.
match_headline: The Things They Loved: Inside Dick Gregory’s Pockets

text: An article on Jan. 7 about the New York City subway referred incorrectly to an October 2017 service change made after a Yankees game. Trains moved from the N to the Q line, not from the M to the Q. And a picture caption with the article overstated what is known about the food that a rat picked up on the tracks at 125th Street. It was not a Moon Pie.
match_headline: The Case for the Subway

text: An article on Jan. 14 about the online trivia contest Learned League misspelled the name of the author of “The Decameron.” It is Boccaccio, not Bocaccio.
match_headline: Letter of Recommendation: Learned League

text: A picture caption with the Inside The Times article on Saturday about the retiring of the 747 airliner fleet misidentified the location shown in the image. It was Marana, Ariz., not Atlanta.
match_headline: Say So Long to a Runway Career: Reporting From an Aircraft Boneyard

text: An article on Dec. 18 about the global outlook for electric vehicles misstated the rough cost of operating one. It is around 4 cents per mile depending on the local cost of electricity and fuel, not 1 cent per mile.
