match_headline: What Needs to Happen Before Electric Cars Take Over the World

text: An article on Monday about the closing of the Actors Company Theater misstated the opening date of its final production, “Three Wise Guys.” It is Feb. 28, not Feb. 9.
match_headline: The Actors Company Theater Set to Close This Year

text: An article on Saturday about the circumstances of the musician Tom Petty’s death misstated the number of concerts Tom Petty performed at the Hollywood Bowl in his final tour. It was three, not two.
match_headline: Tom Petty Died From Accidental Drug Overdose Involving Opioids, Coroner Says

text: An obituary on Friday about the business consultant William Bain Jr. misstated his role at the firm Bain Capital. Although he was involved in its founding, he did not have a management role there.
match_headline: William Bain Jr., 80, Business Consultant and Romney Mentor, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Jan. 16 about the racecar driver and builder Dan Gurney erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He was one of the most successful Americans to compete in Grand Prix races, not the most successful.
match_headline: Dan Gurney, Driver and Builder of Racecars, Is Dead at 86

text: An article on Tuesday about Turkey’s military offensive against Kurds in Syria misattributed a statement to Metin Gurcan, a security analyst and columnist. While Mr. Gurcan said Russia was managing the tempo of the Turkish operation in Syria, he did not say that Turkey’s senior security officials had visited Moscow the day before it began.
match_headline: As Turkey Attacks Kurds in Syria, U.S. Is on the Sideline

text: An article on Tuesday about the potential long-term benefits of new tax legislation in the United States misstated the dollar amount of recent stock grants for Apple employees. It is $2,500, not $2,000.
match_headline: Bonuses Aside, Tax Law’s Trickle-Down Impact Not Yet Clear

text: An article on Monday about Qatar’s competition with neighbors in the Middle East referred incorrectly to the status of Abd al-Rahman al-Nuaymi. He is under arrest in Qatar, not living openly there. The article also misstated the given name of a former energy minister. He is Abdullah bin Hamad al-Attiyah, not Ahmed. In addition, the article misstated Rex W. Tillerson’s position at Exxon Mobil when Qatar built a gas liquefaction plant in 1996. He was an executive with the firm, but not yet the company’s chief executive.
match_headline: Tiny, Wealthy Qatar Goes Its Own Way, and Pays for It

text: An article on Thursday about a lawsuit alleging that the New Orleans district attorney’s office deliberately covered up evidence in a criminal prosecution misspelled the surname of a former judge of the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. He is Alex Kozinski, not Kosinski.
match_headline: Prosecutors Had the Wrong Man. They Prosecuted Him Anyway.

text: An article on Tuesday about a discussion among centrist senators in the office of Senator Susan Collins of Maine, using information from Ms. Collins, referred incorrectly to a wooden talking stick the lawmakers used to keep order in the meeting. It is a Masai tribal talking stick; it is not of Native American origin.
match_headline: With Talking Stick in Hand, Moderate Senators Broke the Shutdown

text: An article on Sunday about residents of cohousing communities misstated the given name of the director of social impact initiatives at the National Cooperative Bank. He is Robert Jenkens, not Richard.
match_headline: There’s Community and Consensus. But It’s No Commune.

text: An article on Wednesday about the Teesside Airport rail station in England misidentified a railway stop near the station. It is Chester-le-Street, not Chester-le-Track.
match_headline: At England’s Loneliest Rail Station, a Train Comes Just Once a Week

text: An article on Wednesday about a recent overhaul of French labor rules misquoted a statement from Philippe Martinez, the secretary general of the General Confederation of Labor. He said, in part, “This is a means for companies to get rid of employees with seniority,” not “This is a means for companies to get rid of low-cost employees with seniority.”
ref_headline: This is a means for companies to get rid of employees with seniority,
match_headline: French Companies Have Newfound Freedom … to Fire

text: An article on Wednesday about the resignation of Barry Lubin, who performed as Grandma the clown in the Big Apple Circus, misstated where he first met a young performer whom he acknowledged pressuring to pose for pornographic photos. Mr. Lubin met the performer while she was participating in Circus Smirkus’s touring youth troupe, not at its camp in Vermont.
match_headline: The #MeToo Movement Hits the Circus: ‘Grandma’ the Clown Resigns

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the Philadelphia Eagles’ victory in the N.F.C. championship game misidentified an Eagles player pictured. He is Jalen Mills, not Patrick Robinson.
match_headline: Eagles March Past Vikings to Super Bowl, Just as They Predicted

text: Because of an editing error, picture captions with an article on Tuesday about the photographer Nan Goldin’s struggles with opioid addiction omitted the titles of four of her photographs. They are “In My Room, Paris”; “Oxy Script, 2017”; “Pain/Sackler, Royal College of Art, London, 2017” and “My Room, Berlin, 2016.”
match_headline: Don’t Call Her a Victim: After Surviving Opioids, Nan Goldin Goes After the Makers

text: An article on Wednesday about extrajudicial killings by police in Pakistan incorrectly listed the number of terrorism suspects reported to have been killed by the Karachi police in 2017. The police said that 73 had been killed, not 7,373.
match_headline: The Slain ‘Militant’ Was a Model, and a Karachi Police Commander Is Out

text: An article on Thursday about disagreement between the Justice Department and the House Intelligence Committee concerning the release of a classified memo misidentified the F.B.I. official who made reference to a “secret society” in a text message the day after the election. It was Lisa Page, not Peter Strzok.
match_headline: F.B.I. Texts and Dueling Memos Escalate Fight Over Russia Inquiry

text: An article on Tuesday about the possible security risks posed by adding elevators to the subway system misstated the name of an online publication. It is The Tribeca Trib, not The TriBeCa Tribune. The article also misattributed the quote: “For someone to use terrorism as an excuse not to provide access to people is a huge stretch.” It was said by Susan M. Dooha, the executive director of the Center for Independence of the Disabled, New York, not Christi Gehrisch, the chief operating officer of the Cerebral Palsy Foundation.
ref_headline: For someone to use terrorism as an excuse not to provide access to people is a huge stretch.
match_headline: In New Proposed Subway Elevators, Some See a Terrorism Risk

text: An article on Thursday about a dispute between Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo and Mayor Bill de Blasio over a plan to renovate 33 subway stations, using information from the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, misstated one of the uses of New York City payroll and other taxes. That money accounts for about 70 percent of the $16 billion of the M.T.A. operating budget, not of the state’s transit capital plan.
match_headline: Mayor Forces Delay of Cuomo’s Plan to Renovate 33 Subway Stations

text: An article on Jan. 15 about a meeting of Sherlock Holmes devotees referred incorrectly to a costume worn by a woman attending a costume ball. She was dressed as the Grimpen Mire, not a Scottish moor.
match_headline: It’s Elementary: Sherlockians Take Manhattan

text: An article on Wednesday about perjury charges against the former superintendent of Baltimore County Public Schools misstated where state officials are scrutinizing the relationships between school superintendents’ and the Education Research and Development Institute, or ERDI. It is in Ohio and Maryland specifically, not around the country.
match_headline: Former Baltimore County Schools Leader Charged With Perjury

text: An article on Thursday about the N.C.A.A.’s inquiry into Michigan State University over the crimes of Dr. Lawrence G. Nassar misstated the circumstances that put Jerry Sandusky in prison. He was convicted by a jury of abusing 10 boys; he did not plead guilty to abusing more than a dozen boys. The article also misstated the punishment of the Penn State officials involved in the scandal surrounding Mr. Sandusky. They were sentenced to prison time; thus far they have not all served prison time.
match_headline: In Michigan State Investigation, N.C.A.A. Moves Beyond Its Comfort Zone

text: An article on Thursday about advocacy by the N.B.A. for legal sports gambling nationwide described incorrectly the association’s position in a New Jersey lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of a 1992 law that set the legal status of sports betting. The N.B.A. is a plaintiff in the suit, not a defendant.
match_headline: N.B.A. Pushes for Legal Sports Gambling Nationwide and a Cut of the Bets

text: An article on Friday about a campaign to remove Rebekah Mercer from the board of the American Museum of Natural History misstated the stance of the Becket Fund, a religious freedom group, on abortion. While the fund has litigated on behalf of groups that oppose abortion, it does not take a formal position on the practice.
match_headline: A Science Denier at the Natural History Museum? Scientists Rebel

text: An article on Dec. 28 in the special Addiction Inc. section about fraud schemes related to urine testing and rehabilitation for recovering prescription drug abusers misidentified the plaintiff in a lawsuit against UnitedHealthcare. It is Living Tree Laboratories, not A New Start, a rehab clinic. The two companies are separate but have common ownership. Dr. Michael Ligotti oversaw urine tests for John Baker, a client at A New Start, through an unrelated company.
match_headline: The Giant, Under Attack

text: An article this weekend on page 14 about a coming horror movie gave an incorrect title for the film. It is “Winchester,” not “Winchester: The House That Ghosts Built.”
match_headline: This Horror Movie Is Based on a True Story. Sort Of.

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Soviet dissident Valery N. Chalidze referred incorrectly to a Russian translation of the Kama Sutra. His company, Chalidze Publications, published it; it is not the case that “it is not clear if it was ever published.”
ref_headline: it is not clear if it was ever published.
match_headline: Valery Chalidze, Soviet Dissident Forced Into Exile, Dies at 79

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the author Ursula K. Le Guin misstated part of her mother’s name. She was Theodora Kracaw Kroeber, not Theodora Quinn Kroeber. The obituary also misspelled the surname of the social anthropologist who wrote “The Golden Bough.” He was James Frazer, not Frazier.
match_headline: Ursula K. Le Guin, Acclaimed for Her Fantasy Fiction, Is Dead at 88

text: An article last Sunday about the choreographer Dean Moss’s new project, “Petra,” misidentified the board he served on at Danspace Project. It was the artists advisory board, not the board of directors.
match_headline: That Obscure, Unattainable Object of Desire: Your Own Art

text: An article last Sunday about the artist Derrick Adams misidentified the location of the exhibition “Derrick Adams: Patrick Kelly, the Journey.” It is on view at the Countee Cullen Library in Harlem, not at the Studio Museum in Harlem. (The Studio Museum is presenting the exhibition.)
ref_headline: Derrick Adams: Patrick Kelly, the Journey.
match_headline: How an Artist Learned About Freedom From ‘The Negro Motorist Green Book’

text: An article last Sunday about the MSNBC anchor Nicolle Wallace mischaracterized the significance of her being named solo anchor of a network news show. She was not the first former White House aide since George Stephanopoulos to achieve that distinction. Karen Finney, a former aide to President Bill Clinton, anchored “Disrupt With Karen Finney” on MSNBC from 2013 to 2014.
match_headline: Nicolle Wallace’s Road From the White House to 30 Rock

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about Dana Loesch, the N.R.A. spokeswoman, misstated the name of a gun. It is a Black Rain Ordnance AR-15, not a Black Range Ordinance AR-15.
match_headline: The National Rifle Association’s Telegenic Warrior

text: An article on Monday about a female Kurdish fighter who carried out what appeared to be a suicide bombing attack on the Turkish military in Syria misidentified the area where Turkey fears an autonomous semi-state is being carved out by the Syrian Democratic Forces. It is in northeastern Syria, not northeastern Turkey.
match_headline: Female Kurdish Fighter Kills Turkish Troops in Likely Suicide Bombing in Syria

text: An article on Friday about the Doomsday clock misstated the timing of the first thermonuclear weapons tests by the Americans and the Soviets. They were within 10 months of each other, not within six months.
match_headline: Doomsday Clock Is Set at 2 Minutes to Midnight, Closest Since 1950s

text: An article on Wednesday about legal loopholes reportedly used by Afghan security forces who committed human rights violations referred incorrectly to 5,753 cases from 2010 to 2016 involving the United States and Afghan militaries. Those were cases in which the American military asked to review Afghan units to see if there were “gross human rights abuses,” not the number of times the American military reported such abuses.
match_headline: Afghan Pedophiles Get Free Pass From U.S. Military, Report Says

text: An article on Monday about children operating machines on family farms misspelled the name of a Wisconsin city where a child was killed in a farm accident. It is Loyal, Wis., not Royal.
match_headline: 5-Year-Olds Work Farm Machinery, and Injuries Follow

text: An article on Saturday about a public list identifying Russian oligarchs with ties to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia misspelled the surname of the former F.B.I. director who is leading the investigation of Russian meddling in the 2016 election. He is Robert S. Mueller III, not Muller.
match_headline: Coming U.S. List of Oligarchs Linked to Putin Alarms Russia’s Rich

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Meryl Streep joining the cast of the HBO series “Big Little Lies” misstated when Ms. Streep last won an Emmy for her television work. She received an Emmy last year for outstanding narrator for the Netflix documentary “Five Came Back”; it was not in 2004 for the HBO mini-series “Angels in America.”
match_headline: Meryl Streep Joins the Cast of ‘Big Little Lies’

text: An article on Monday about the African Nations Championship misstated the role of Kalusha Bwalya in Zambia’s soccer federation. He is a former federation president, not the current one.
match_headline: At African Soccer Event, Games of Cat and Mouse

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the basketball prospect Robert Bobroczkyi misidentified the place where Robert Bobroczkyi trains. It is the Spire Institute, not the Spire Academy.
match_headline: A Teenager’s Basketball Dream Is Size XXXXXL

text: An article on Saturday about talented Grammy nominees misstated the title of the Le’Andria album nominated for best gospel album. It is “Bigger Than Me,” not “Better Days.”
match_headline: The Grammy Gems You Won’t Hear on ‘Music’s Biggest Night’

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Jan. 8 about the runner Horace Ashenfelter misstated the number of hurdles in the 3,000-meter steeplechase, the event in which he set a world record at the 1952 Olympic Games. There are 35, not 28. The obituary also referred incorrectly in part to the race in which he set the record. The Russian runner Vladimir Kazantsev was not “far ahead” for most of that race; he and Ashenfelter were neck and neck going into the last lap before Kazantsev pulled into a big lead. In addition, a picture caption with the obituary misstated what the photograph depicted. It showed Ashenfelter and Kazantsev during the race; it did not show Ashenfelter winning the race.
match_headline: Horace Ashenfelter, Olympic Victor of a Cold War Showdown, Dies at 94

text: An article on Saturday about popular support for Turkey’s military offensive in Syria misquoted Mehmet Akif Perker, a representative of the Republican People’s party. He said his party is “against war,” not “against the war” in Syria.
match_headline: On Turkey’s Border With Syria, Many Are Eager for War

text: An article on Tuesday about energy savings associated with Americans spending more time at home misspelled the surname of the lead author of a study in the journal Joule. He is Ashok Sekar, not Seka.
match_headline: Americans Are Staying Home More. That’s Saving Energy.

text: An entry on Monday in the “What’s on TV” highlights misidentified the Avett brother quoted. He is Seth Avett, not Scott.
match_headline: What’s on TV Monday: Avett Brothers Documentary and ‘Between 2 Shores’

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about design breakthroughs allowing apparel to fit people across larger size ranges misstated the surname of one of the designers who coined the term “super normal.” He is Jasper Morrison, not Meyerson.
match_headline: How Design for One Turns Into Design for All

text: An obituary on Saturday about William J. McDonough, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, referred incompletely to that institution. It is responsible for regulating financial institutions in the Second District of New York — not for regulating all financial institutions in the country.
match_headline: William McDonough, Who Guided New York Fed Through Crises, Dies at 83

text: An article on Tuesday about Melania Trump’s reaction to reports that her husband had an affair with the adult film star Stormy Daniels misstated the time period in which the affair reportedly occurred. It is reported to have occurred after President Trump’s son Barron was born, not while his wife, Melania Trump, was pregnant.
match_headline: Melania Trump, Out of Sight Since Report of Husband’s Infidelity, to Attend State of the Union

text: An article on Tuesday about partisan gerrymandering of electoral districts misstated the title of Mark Gersh. He is the former president of NCEC Services, not its current one.
match_headline: Just How Bad Is Partisan Gerrymandering? Ask the Mapmakers

text: An article on Tuesday about Representative Rodney Frelinghuysen’s decision to retire from Congress when his term expires referred incorrectly to Representative Frank LoBiondo’s status in office. Mr. LoBiondo announced in November that he would not seek re-election; he has not yet left office.
match_headline: Rodney Frelinghuysen, Powerful House Republican, Announces He Will Not Seek Re-Election

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about a new provision in the tax code that encourages investment in areas with high poverty and sluggish job and business growth referred incorrectly to Baltimore’s location. The city is in the Mid-Atlantic region, not New England.
match_headline: Tucked Into the Tax Bill, a Plan to Help Distressed America

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Jan. 21 about the writer Julius Lester misstated the consequences of his public criticism of James Baldwin during his tenure at the University of Massachusetts. He was moved from the department of Afro-American studies to the department of Judaic and Near Eastern studies; he did not lose his professorship.
match_headline: Julius Lester, Chronicler of Black America, Is Dead at 78

text: An article on Thursday about Britain’s use of private contractors to provide social services misstated the amount of debt held by Four Seasons. It is $700 million, not $700 billion.
match_headline: Britain Was a Pioneer in Outsourcing Services. Now, the Model Is ‘Broken.’

text: An article on Thursday about a ban on ivory sales in Hong Kong partly misquoted Peter Shiu, a Hong Kong lawmaker. He said, “To expect ivory artisans” — not “traders” — “in their 60s to change industries is impractical.”
match_headline: Hong Kong Moves to Ban All Ivory Sales, Closing a Loophole

text: An article on Friday about polar bears’ metabolism misstated the amount of weight lost by some bears in the study. The bears that scavenged or fasted lost as much as 10 percent of their body mass, not 20 percent
match_headline: What Cameras on Polar Bears Show Us: It’s Tough Out There

text: An article on Thursday about the Trump administration’s suspension of a major Obama-era clean water regulation misstated part of the name of an environmental group. It is the Natural — not National — Resources Defense Council.
match_headline: E.P.A. Blocks Obama-Era Clean Water Rule

text: An obituary on Friday about Andre Surmain, the founder of the Manhattan restaurant Lutèce, misidentified the critic who gave the restaurant its first four-star rating in The New York Times and misstated the year it was bestowed. Raymond A. Sokolov, not Mimi Sheraton, did so, in a review in 1972. Ms. Sheraton renewed the rating in 1980.
match_headline: Andre Surmain, Who Fed the Elite in Luxe Style at Lutèce, Dies at 97

text: An essay on Jan. 28 about gentrification misstated the year an article on the “tiny house” phenomenon appeared in BuzzFeed. It was 2016, not 2015.
match_headline: When ‘Gentrification’ Isn’t About Housing

text: A review on Jan. 21 in the Crime column about “A Map of the Dark,” by Karen Ellis, misidentified one of the novel’s characters. The girl dropping a trail of jewelry in the forest is named Hope; she is not the missing girl, Ruby.
match_headline: Keep Watch Over Your Children: Danger Lurks Everywhere

text: An article last Sunday about Marfa, Tex., misstated the highest point in the state. It is Guadalupe Peak, not the Davis Mountains.
match_headline: Marfa Road Trip: Thelma and Louise, With a Happier Ending

text: An article on Monday about a settlement between Wells Fargo and the Federal Reserve misstated when Elizabeth A. Duke became Wells Fargo’s chairwoman. It was January, not last summer.
match_headline: How Wells Fargo and Federal Reserve Struck Deal to Hold Bank’s Board Accountable

text: An article on Monday about Turkey’s military offensive in Syria misstated the location of the Syrian city of Manbij. It is about 80 miles east of Afrin, not west of it.
match_headline: Turkey’s Worst Day Yet in Syria Offensive: At Least 7 Soldiers Killed

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about lawsuits related to the estate of the singer James Brown paraphrased incorrectly a quote from a lawyer for his widow, Tommie Rae Hynie. The lawyer, Robert Rosen, said he and Ms. Hynie have “full confidence in the appellate courts of South Carolina to decide” the issue of whether Ms. Hynie and Mr. Brown were legally married. He did not say that he and Ms. Hynie had “full confidence” that the appellate court would uphold a lower court ruling that had found the marriage legal.
ref_headline: full confidence in the appellate courts of South Carolina to decide
match_headline: Why Is James Brown’s Estate Still Unsettled? Ask the Lawyers

text: An obituary on Monday about the former television executive Lin Bolen referred incorrectly to Lisa Demberg, who confirmed Ms. Bolen’s death. Ms. Demberg is a producer, not a former producer.
match_headline: Lin Bolen, a Trailblazing TV Executive, Dies at 76

text: An obituary on Friday about the journalist and author Nicholas von Hoffman misidentified the Chicago newspaper at which he began his career in 1963. It was The Daily News, not The Sun-Times.
match_headline: Nicholas von Hoffman, Provocative Journalist and Author, Dies at 88

text: An article on Sunday about delays in the F.B.I. inquiry into sexual assault allegations against Lawrence G. Nassar referred incorrectly to Dr. Nassar’s association with Holt High School. He worked there, but it was not his alma mater. The article also misstated the number of medals Aly Raisman won at the Rio Olympics. It was three, not six (she has six Olympic medals over all).
match_headline: As F.B.I. Took a Year to Pursue the Nassar Case, Dozens Say They Were Molested

text: An article on Monday about an annual ceremony to memorialize four chaplains who died in World War II misidentified one of the four. He was Rabbi Alexander D. Goode, not Alexander B. Goode.
match_headline: Remembering the Four Chaplains and Their Ultimate Sacrifice

text: An article on Tuesday about the reasons behind the most recent downturn in the stock market misstated the context of a comment from Scott Minerd, the chief investment officer of Guggenheim Partners. His comment was given in an interview with Reuters, not written in a note to investors.
match_headline: Investors Fear the Tax Cuts Will Work Too Well

text: An article on Saturday about a report by Exxon Mobil predicting strong demand for oil and gas despite renewed global efforts to reduce carbon emissions misstated the portion of Exxon Mobil’s business that the company estimates would be affected by strict climate policies. It is undeveloped resources representing less than 5 percent of the company’s property by value, not less than 5 percent of its reserves.
match_headline: Exxon Studies Climate Policies and Sees ‘Little Risk’ to Bottom Line

text: An article on Tuesday about Michigan State athletes who said they were sexually abused by Lawrence G. Nassar misidentified the sports team on which these athletes competed. It was the women’s rowing team, not the women’s volleyball team.
match_headline: For Nassar Accusers From Michigan State Teams, Feelings of a Trust Betrayed

text: A map with an article on Sunday about a secret agreement between Egypt and Israel to allow Israeli strikes against Islamist militants in Egypt’s Northern Sinai omitted the boundaries of the West Bank.
match_headline: Secret Alliance: Israel Carries Out Airstrikes in Egypt, With Cairo’s O.K.

text: An article on Wednesday about new business strategies being pursued by the Walt Disney Company misstated the price of Disney’s shares following after-hours trading. The price was $109.28, not $106.17.
match_headline: Disney Reports Mixed Earnings and a Full Project Pipeline

text: An article on Tuesday about a planned $300 million solar farm in Saudi Arabia misstated the number of homes the farm would be able to power. It would power around 40,000, not up to 200,000.
match_headline: From Oil to Solar: Saudi Arabia Plots a Shift to Renewables

text: An article on Tuesday about protests over a lack of Hispanic characters in Hollywood films misidentified in one instance the name of the hotel where a lunch for Academy Award nominees took place. As stated elsewhere in the article, it was the Beverly Hilton, not the Beverly Hills Hotel.
match_headline: Hispanic Group Protests at Oscars Luncheon

text: An article on Monday about a trick play by the Philadelphia Eagles in the Super Bowl misstated the result of a pass from Danny Amendola to Tom Brady in a game between the Patriots and the Eagles in 2015. The pass gained 36 yards; it was not a touchdown pass.
match_headline: How Nick Foles and the Eagles Tricked the Patriots

text: An article on Thursday about an extended speech given by Representative Nancy Pelosi in opposition to the budget deal misspelled the surname of an immigrant who once worked as an aide to former Representative Michael M. Honda. He is Carlos Gonzalez, not Gonzales.
match_headline: Pelosi Held House Floor in Advocacy of ‘Dreamers’ for More Than 8 Hours

text: An article on Thursday about reactions to the resignation of Steve Wynn from the Wynn Resorts casino conglomerate misidentified the chairman of the Massachusetts Gaming Commission. He is Stephen Crosby, not David Crosby.
match_headline: Without Steve Wynn, Casino Empire Risks Losing More Than a Name

text: An entry on Thursday in the “What’s on TV” highlights misstated the airtime for “Happy Ending With Nando Vila” on Fusion. It is 10 p.m., not 9.
match_headline: What’s on TV Thursday: The Winter Olympics and the Brit Awards

text: An obituary on Thursday about the physicist Joseph Polchinski misstated the day he died. It was Friday, Feb. 2, not Saturday, Feb. 3. The obituary also misspelled the given name of one of his sons. He is Steven, not Stephen.
match_headline: Joseph Polchinski, 63, Leading Theorist on Multiple Universes, Dies

text: An article on Thursday about New York Fashion Week and what designers choose to wear on the runway during their shows included an erroneous quotation that misrepresented Tory Burch’s comments. While Ms. Burch said social media posts that feature her have an impact on retail sales, she did not say those posts drove items to “No. 1” in her stores.
match_headline: ‘I Try Not to Look as if I’m Trying Too Hard’

text: An article last Sunday about online divorce services referred imprecisely to a scene in the film “The Women,” in which divorce is far less convenient. The characters traveled to Reno, Nev., by train for their divorces, not by plane.
match_headline: Angelina Jolie’s Lawyer Now Offers Quickie Divorces Online

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about Representative Nancy Pelosi’s difficulty uniting the Democratic Party misstated the circumstances depicted in the photo. Ms. Pelosi was photographed walking to her office on Friday after the House voted to fund the federal government, not on Wednesday after her eight-hour speech on “Dreamers.”
match_headline: Nancy Pelosi Wants to Take Back the House. But She Faces a More Urgent Test.

text: An article on Sunday, about a plan in Kentucky to require Medicaid recipients to work or volunteer, misstated the insurance status of Sarah and Matt Burress before getting Medicaid. They had insurance through a job Mr. Burress had before he started his own business, although their coverage did not cover vision care. Additionally, the article misstated Mr. Burress’s medical diagnosis. He learned he had glaucoma, not advanced glaucoma, after getting Medicaid. Finally, the article also misstated when he and his wife enrolled in Medicaid. They enrolled in 2016, not 2015.
match_headline: Kentucky Rushes to Remake Medicaid as Other States Prepare to Follow

text: An article on Monday about the crash of a Russian plane that killed 71 passengers misspelled the name of another Russian plane that crashed in December 2016. It was a Tupolev TU-154, not Tupulov.
match_headline: Russian Plane Crash Kills All 71 Aboard

text: An article on Friday about a fight club in Chengdu misidentified an amateur boxer. He is Li Guowei, not Li Weiguo.
match_headline: First Rule of Chinese Fight Club: No Karaoke

text: An article on Saturday about Colombian rebels suspending an election campaign misstated the timing of the coming congressional elections in Colombia. They are scheduled for March, not May.
match_headline: Colombian Rebels Suspend Election Campaign, Putting Peace Into Limbo

text: An obituary on Monday about the longtime Los Angeles Dodger outfielder Wally Moon misstated the year the Los Angeles Coliseum, where the Dodgers played from 1958 until 1962, opened. It was 1923, not 1932.
match_headline: Wally Moon, Whose Homers Helped the Dodgers Win a World Series, Dies at 87

text: An article on Tuesday about a move by Mayor Bill de Blasio to strengthen campaign finance laws misspelled the given name of the Manhattan borough president. She is Gale Brewer, not Gail.
match_headline: Mayor Wants City Charter Revision to Tackle Campaign Finance

text: An article on Tuesday about the coincidence of Valentine’s Day and Ash Wednesday this year misstated the holy obligations of Ash Wednesday. They include fasting and abstaining from eating meat, not receiving ashes.
match_headline: Eat, Pray, Love: An Ash Wednesday and Valentine’s Day Dilemma

text: A picture caption with an article misidentified an instructor of a class at Butler University in which students run an insurance company. He is Kevin Thompson, not Zach Finn.
match_headline: Insurance 101: Butler Undergrads Write Coverage for Dogs and Pianos

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about dominant performances by Russian figure skaters competing in the Olympics misidentified a pair of skaters who competed on Sunday. They are Natalia Zabiiako and Alexander Enbert, not Evgenia Tarasova and Vladimir Morozov.
match_headline: Russian Figure Skaters Dominate Despite Olympic Ban

text: An obituary on Monday about the Pakistani rights activist Asma Jahangir contained an incomplete list of her survivors. In addition to her husband, two daughters and a son, she is survived by two sisters and a brother.
match_headline: Asma Jahangir, Fearless Pakistani Rights Activist, Dies at 66

text: An article on Tuesday about the contingent of North Korean cheerleaders at the Olympics misstated the title of an Avril Lavigne song that South Korea’s cheerleaders danced to. It is “Girlfriend,” not “Boyfriend.”
match_headline: A Night Out With North Korea’s Cheerleaders: Matching Snowsuits, Military Discipline and Chaperoned Bathroom Trips

text: An article on Wednesday about Rohingya refugee camps that are vulnerable to flooding, quoting the United Nations high commissioner for refugees, misstated the start of the monsoon in Bangladesh. It begins in June, not March. (March is the start of cyclone season, which can also produce severe flooding.)
match_headline: Besieged Rohingya Face ‘Crisis Within the Crisis’: Deadly Floods

text: An article on Wednesday about state legislatures’ attempts to punish courts for controversial rulings misstated the date that the United States Supreme Court refused to review a lower court ruling on the drawing of a Pennsylvania congressional district. It was Feb. 5, not Feb. 12.
match_headline: Judges Say Throw Out the Map. Lawmakers Say Throw Out the Judges.

text: An obituary on Feb. 7 about the actor John Mahoney referred incorrectly to the relocation of his family during World War II. The family was relocated from Manchester to Blackpool, not to Lancashire. (Both Manchester and Blackpool were in Lancashire County at that time.)
match_headline: John Mahoney, Actor Best Known for ‘Frasier,’ Dies at 77

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a case of bank fraud at India’s Punjab National Bank described incorrectly the relative impact of a 10 percent share price drop on the bank’s market value. It was $1.77 billion in fraudulent transactions, not the drop in share prices, that equaled nearly one-third of the bank’s market value.
match_headline: $1.8 Billion in India Bank Fraud Raises Fears of Ripple Effects

text: Because of an editing error, two picture captions with an article on Monday about facial recognition software misstated the number of photos used by researchers to study the accuracy of artificial intelligence in identifying two groups of people by gender. There were 385 photos of lighter-skinned men, not 296, and 296 of lighter-skinned women, not 385.
match_headline: Facial Recognition Is Accurate, if You’re a White Guy

text: An article on Wednesday about the New York Philharmonic’s efforts to strengthen ties to its local audience misstated the extent of a planned tour next season. It was to have been a domestic tour, not an international one.
match_headline: The New York Philharmonic’s Fresh Start: A Season Spent at Home

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the actor and diplomat John Gavin misstated his birth name and misidentified his father. He was born Juan Vincent Apablasa, not John Anthony Golenor, and his father was Juan Apablasa, not Herald Golenor. (His mother later divorced his father and married Herald Golenor, who adopted him and changed his name.)
match_headline: John Gavin, Actor and Ambassador to Mexico Under Reagan, Dies at 86

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the decision of the Securities and Exchange Commission to block the acquisition of the Chicago Stock Exchange by a Chinese company misstated the political affiliation of Jay Clayton, the chairman of the S.E.C. He is politically independent, not a Republican.
match_headline: S.E.C. Blocks Chinese Takeover of Chicago Stock Exchange

text: An article on Wednesday about injuries suffered by some snowboarders misstated the part of the halfpipe that Kevin Pearce hit when he sustained a traumatic brain injury before the 2010 Olympics. He hit his head about halfway down the wall of the halfpipe, not on the edge of the halfpipe.
match_headline: Shaun White, Amid Bolder Tricks, Keeps Up and Wins Another Olympic Gold

text: An article on Friday about ticket sales at the Olympics misspelled the surname of a German biathlete. She is Laura Dahlmeier, not Dahlheimer.
match_headline: Olympic Organizers Say Tickets Are Sold, but Where Are the People?

text: A picture caption with an entry in the dance listings on Friday misidentified a dancer. He is Darrell Jones, not Darren Jones.
match_headline: 5 Dance Performances to See in NYC This Weekend

text: An article last Sunday about the artist Jasper Johns omitted one of the creators of the exhibition “Something Resembling Truth” at the Broad. Edith Devaney, a curator at the Royal Academy in London, helped conceive of the show.
match_headline: Jasper Johns Still Doesn’t Want to Explain His Art

text: An article last Sunday about older artists turning to online sales to supplement or replace their gallery ties misstated how Kalisher, a company that places art in businesses, found Matthew Dibble’s artwork. It found Mr. Dibble’s art directly online and by visiting Cleveland and talking to local artists, not by scouting the online outlet Saatchi Art.
match_headline: A Lifetime of Making Art, but New to Selling It Online

text: An article on Feb. 4 about skeleton racing referred imprecisely to the composition of the sled used in the sport. It is made up of a metal frame with a carbon-fiber underside, not just carbon fiber.
match_headline: Why Skeleton Racing Is So Brutal on the Body

text: An article last Sunday about the television anchor Joy-Ann Reid misidentified the birthplace of Ms. Reid’s mother. It is the country of Guyana, not British Guiana, which was a colony. The article also misidentified the channel on which Lou Dobbs is a host. It is Fox Business Network, not Fox News.
match_headline: How Joy Reid of MSNBC Became a Heroine of the Resistance

text: An essay on Jan. 28 about the 50th anniversary of Edward Abbey’s book “Desert Solitaire” misstated the location of the Comb Ridge area in Utah. It is east of the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument; it is not in the Grand Staircase-Escalante.
match_headline: President Trump, Please Read ‘Desert Solitaire’

text: An article last Sunday about Tijuana, Mexico, referred incorrectly to violent crime trends in the city. While crimes like kidnapping have decreased, homicides have recently increased.
match_headline: Through a Tijuana Turnstile and Into Tacos and Tortas

text: An article on Feb. 4 about travel networks misstated the name of one of them. It is American Express Travel, not Fine Hotels & Resorts. A picture caption with the article also misidentified a building in Quito. It is the San Francisco Cathedral, not the Casa Gangotena hotel.
match_headline: Meet the New Travel Agents (a.k.a. Travel Networks)

text: An article on Tuesday about state election officials’ concerns about election threats misspelled the surname of the Department of Homeland Security’s deputy assistant secretary for infrastructure protection. He is Robert Kolasky, not Kulasky.
match_headline: State Officials Say They Are Told Too Little About Election Threats

text: An article on Saturday about students speaking out about gun violence misstated the number of students killed in the shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School. The gunman killed 17 people: 14 students and three faculty members. He did not kill 17 students.
match_headline: A ‘Mass Shooting Generation’ Cries Out for Change

text: An article on Tuesday about political rivalries in Kenya misspelled the name of the town where the Kenya Land Alliance is located. It is Nanyuki, not Nyanyuki.
match_headline: Kenya’s Political Turmoil Is a Tale of Fathers and Sons

text: An article on Monday about concerns about the institutional health of NATO misspelled the surname of a defense expert with the European Union Institute for Security Studies. He is Daniel Fiott, not Flott.
match_headline: U.S. Revives Concerns About European Defense Plans, Rattling NATO Allies

text: An article on Sunday about retaliatory strikes by Israel in various parts of Gaza misstated the response of the Popular Resistance Committees, a militant offshoot of Fatah, to a bombing that wounded four Israeli soldiers. The group did not claim responsibility for planting the explosive device, but praised the attack as a “heroic operation.”
match_headline: 4 Israelis Hurt by Bomb Set in Flag at Gaza Fence, Igniting Night of Fighting

text: An article on Tuesday about the admission by the South Korean director Lee Youn-taek that he sexually abused actresses misstated his age. He is 65, not 66.
match_headline: A Director’s Apology Adds Momentum to South Korea’s #MeToo Movement

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Sunday about the reaction of North Koreans to the global perspective the Olympics provides misstated the names of two North Korean figure skaters. They are Ryom Tae-ok and Kim Ju-sik, not Tae Ok-ryom and Ju Sik-kim.
match_headline: Seeing Bounty Abroad, Will North Koreans Change Their Homeland?

text: An article on Saturday checking facts about gun violence and mental illness misstated the location of an accidental weapons discharge. It occurred in Minnesota, not Michigan.
match_headline: Checking Facts and Falsehoods About Gun Violence and Mental Illness After Parkland Shooting

text: An article on Friday about two Bronx men arrested on bomb-making charges misidentified the school where one of the men, Christian Toro, worked. It is Harlem Prep High School, not Democracy Prep High School. Democracy Prep Public Schools is the charter network that operates Harlem Prep High School.
match_headline: Two Bronx Brothers Arrested in Bomb-Making Scheme

text: An article on Friday about the anticipation surrounding the superhero movie “Black Panther” misstated the middle initial of Disney’s movie chairman. He is Alan F. Horn, not Alan H.
match_headline: ‘Black Panther’ Poised to Shatter a Hollywood Myth

text: A picture caption on Monday about team pairs figure skaters misidentified the skaters shown. They were Miu Suzaki and Ryuichi Kihara of Japan, not Yu Xiaoyu and Zhang Hao of China.
match_headline: The 22nd-Largest Team at the Olympics: Zamboni Drivers

text: An article on Tuesday about a new conservation effort in Peru misstated the corner of the country in which Yaguas National Park is found. It is in the country’s northeast, not its northwest.
match_headline: Peru Moves to Protect ‘One of the Last Great Intact Forests’

text: A recipe last Wednesday for Limpin’ Susan, an okra stir-fry with rice, misstated the amount of cooking oil in the first step. It is ¼ cup, not ½ cup.
match_headline: Finding a Lost Strain of Rice, and Clues to Slave Cooking

text: An article on Feb. 11 about the selection of Mary Lou McDonald as the new president of the Irish political party Sinn Fein overstated the significance of the move. While Ms. McDonald is the first woman to lead the modern incarnation of the party, she is not the first female leader in its history.
match_headline: Sinn Fein Gets a New Leader, Mary Lou McDonald

text: An article on Wednesday about a fund-raising raffle held by the Kent Volunteer Fire Department that included several guns as prizes referred imprecisely to new raffle prizes that were ultimately used in place of the guns. The new prizes are gift certificates from a gun shop — in the value of the two guns that were to be raffled off — not the cash value of the guns.
match_headline: Raffle Off an AR-15? A N.Y. Fire Department Reconsiders

text: An article on Wednesday about the recent success of the South Korean women’s curling team misstated the nickname of Kim Chohi, a team member. It is ChoCho, not Cookie.
match_headline: Garlic Girls Take Over the Olympics, and Their Hometown Is Loving It

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision from the N.C.A.A. to strip the Louisville’s men’s basketball team of a past championship as a penalty for a sex scandal involving prostitutes misstated Louisville’s record in the A.C.C. this season. It is 8-6, not 14-4.
match_headline: Louisville Must Forfeit Basketball Championship Over Sex Scandal

text: An article on Thursday about the immigration status of Melania Trump’s parents misstated President Trump’s plans for family-based immigration. Mr. Trump’s policy would allow American citizens to petition for residency for their spouses and children under 21, but not for their parents.
match_headline: Questions Swirl as Melania Trump’s Parents Obtain Green Cards

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the molecular biologist Günter Blobel misstated the name of one award he won and referred incorrectly to another. The award he received from Columbia University was the Horwitz Prize, not the Horowitz Prize. The Albert Lasker award he received was for basic medical research, not public service.
match_headline: Günter Blobel, Nobel Laureate Who Found Cell ‘ZIP Codes,’ Dies at 81

text: An article on Friday about new fraud charges filed against Paul Manafort in the special counsel investigation misidentified Donald Trump Jr. He is President Trump’s son, not his son-in-law.
match_headline: Mueller Files New Fraud Charges Against Paul Manafort and Rick Gates

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the intimate nature of public broadcasting misstated the location of a recording studio where Garrison Keillor was shown working. He was in a studio in St. Paul, but it was not a Minnesota Public Radio studio.
match_headline: What Makes Public Radio ‘Very Personal’ Magnifies Its #MeToo Cases

text: A review on Friday about “Jerry Springer — The Opera” misstated the name of an accolade won by a previous production of the same show. It is the Olivier Award, not the Oliver Award.
match_headline: Review: ‘Jerry Springer,’ Sacred and Profane, Triumphantly Sings Again

text: An article on Page 8 about the outlook for J. K. Rowling’s Broadway debut incorrectly describes the sales of the book “Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.” More than 5 million copies have been sold in North America, not only in the United States.
ref_headline: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.
match_headline: How Much Magic Can ‘Harry Potter and the Cursed Child’ Make on Broadway?

text: Because of an editing error, the Personal Health column on Tuesday about teenagers’ incorrect and inconsistent use of contraception misstated the findings of a report by the Guttmacher Institute. Many states explicitly allow certain categories of minors to consent to contraceptive services; it is not the case that 24 states prohibit the distribution of contraception to minors without parental permission.
match_headline: Contraception for Teenagers

text: Because of a production error, a paragraph on Pages 9 and 10 of this weekend’s special section appears with an incomplete sentence. It should read: The state’s leadership initially viewed the levee authority lawsuit as a direct assault.
match_headline: Read the Special Counsel’s Indictment Against the Internet Research Agency and Others

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about new organs for Trinity Church Wall Street and its St. Paul’s Chapel omitted the given name of a former music director there. He is Owen Burdick. Also because of an editing error, the article mischaracterized the cost of the new organ for St. Paul’s Chapel. The $1 million cost included the instrument’s purchase and its installation, not just its purchase. The article also misstated the joking label on an organ stop that makes a bird song imitation. The label says “Byrds,” after the Elizabethan organist and composer William Byrd, not “Brass.”
match_headline: An Organ — and Soon Another — Lands on Broadway

text: An article last Sunday about Veena Sud, the showrunner for “Seven Seconds” on Netflix, misspelled the surname of a man who sustained a fatal spinal cord injury while in police custody. He is Freddie Gray, not Grey.
match_headline: Another Killing for Veena Sud, Both Familiar and New

text: An article last Sunday about the American Psychoanalytic Association’s annual conference misstated the age of one of its members, Jamie Steele. She is 33, not 36. The article also misstated the degree Ms. Steele was pursuing before she shifted to psychoanalytic theory. It was a master’s degree in political theory, not a Ph.D. in philosophy.
match_headline: Still Talking After All These Years

text: A review last Sunday about the novel “Asymmetry,” by Lisa Halliday, misspelled the surname of one of the main characters. He is Amar Jaafari, not Jaafarri.
match_headline: Three Lives, and the Tenuous Ties That Bind Them

text: A review on Feb. 4 about Paul Kix’s book “The Saboteur,” whose subject is Robert de La Rochefoucauld, a member of the French Resistance, misstated La Rochefoucauld’s age in early 1944. He was 20, not 19.
match_headline: One of the Men Who ‘Set Europe Ablaze’

text: A review on Jan. 28 about “The Last Man Who Knew Everything,” David N. Schwartz’s biography of the physicist Enrico Fermi, misstated the year for which a German peace activist, Carl von Ossietzky, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. It was 1935, not 1936 (though he did not receive the prize until 1936).
ref_headline: The Last Man Who Knew Everything,
match_headline: A Remarkable Man Among Remarkable Men and Women

text: A news analysis about United States involvement in foreign elections misidentified a recipient of grants from the National Endowment for Democracy. An organization employing Aleksei Navalny, who has become a political opponent of President Vladmir Putin of Russia, received a $23,000 grant from the endowment in 2006; Mr. Navalny himself was not a recipient.
match_headline: Russia Isn’t the Only One Meddling in Elections. We Do It, Too.

text: An article on Saturday about Rick Gates, a former top adviser to Donald J. Trump who pleaded to charges brought by Robert S. Mueller III, incorrectly described Mr. Gates’s employment after the election. He worked for the presidential inaugural committee, not the transition team. The article also misstated how long Mr. Gates traveled on the Trump campaign plane. He traveled with the candidate through the end of August, not Election Day.
match_headline: Rick Gates, Trump Campaign Aide, Pleads Guilty in Mueller Inquiry and Will Cooperate

text: An article on Sunday about Warren Buffett’s annual letter to Berkshire Hathaway’s shareholders misstated the book value for Berkshire Hathaway in 2017. The value rose to $348 billion, not $358 billion.
match_headline: Buffett’s Annual Letter: Berkshire Records $29 Billion Gain From Tax Law

text: An article on Saturday about the corruption trial of Joseph Percoco misidentified the lawyer for Joseph Gerardi. He is Milton L. Williams Jr., not Milton J. Williams.
match_headline: Defense Case in Percoco Trial Begins With a Whimper, Not a Bang

text: An article on Sunday about campaign contributions from state appointees to Gov. Andrew Cuomo misstated the circumstances of Kenneth A. Manning’s appointment to a state position by Mr. Cuomo. The governor appointed Mr. Manning to a state judicial screening committee, not the Roswell Park Cancer Institute. Mr. Manning was appointed to the cancer institute by the State Assembly leader. The article also misstated the timing of Howard Zemsky’s donations and appointments. Mr. Zemsky was appointed chairman of the Niagara Frontier Transportation Authority in 2012; all of his donations came before then, not before 2015, and all of his wife’s donations came after 2012, not 2015.
match_headline: In Spite of Executive Order, Cuomo Takes Campaign Money From State Appointees

text: An article on Saturday about an Instagram post by Jonathan Martin, a former N.F.L. offensive lineman, misidentified the type of weapon pictured in his post. It was a shotgun and shells, not a rifle and bullets.
match_headline: Ex-Dolphin Jonathan Martin Is Detained After Social Media Post Shuts School

text: A report in “Arts, Briefly” on Wednesday included an erroneous credit for Rammellzee. He did not have a cameo in the music video for Blondie’s “Rapture.”
match_headline: A Rammellzee Exhibition Is Coming to New York

text: An article on Saturday about tips submitted to various law enforcement agencies warning about Nikolas Cruz’s mental state misstated how Mr. Cruz was said to have bought weapons in one 911 call. The caller said he had used money from his mother’s account, not from a life insurance policy.
match_headline: Tipster’s Warning to F.B.I. on Florida Shooting Suspect: ‘I Know He’s Going to Explode’

text: An article on Friday about the death of Kavous Seyed Emami, an environmental activist, in Iran’s Evin Prison misidentified the official who showed images of Mr. Seyed Emami’s autopsy on his phone. It was a deputy prosecutor, not the prosecutor general.
match_headline: Iran Finally Let Her See Her Husband. He Was Dead.

text: An article on Tuesday about a federal appeals court ruling that a major civil rights law protects employees against discrimination based on sexual orientation misstated when Donald Zarda died. It was in 2014, not 2015.
match_headline: Civil Rights Act Protects Gay Workers, Appeals Court Rules

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a novel strategy adopted by the Food and Drug Administration to encourage new treatments for opioid addiction misstated the number of people who died from drug overdoses in 2016. Roughly 64,000 people were killed by drug overdoses, including from prescription opioid painkillers and heroin, not by opioid and heroin overdoses alone.
match_headline: F.D.A. to Expand Medication-Assisted Therapy for Opioid Addicts

text: An article on Feb. 12 about Broadcom’s $1.2 billion takeover bid of Qualcomm omitted the name of one agency involved in a report estimating the indirect economic effects of Qualcomm’s employment on San Diego. In addition to the San Diego Workforce Partnership, the study was also written by the San Diego Regional Economic Development Corporation.
match_headline: With Qualcomm in Play, San Diego Fears Losing ‘Our Flag’

text: An article on Monday about an intensive, two-week study of Vermeer’s “Girl With a Pearl Earring” using new exploratory technologies misstated the name of the company that created a high-resolution, three-dimensional reproduction of the painting. It is Océ, not OC.
match_headline: Uncovering the Secrets of the ‘Girl With a Pearl Earring’

text: An article on Wednesday about a political standoff between the National Rifle Association and Delta Air Lines, using information provided by a consulting firm working for Delta, misstated the airline’s estimate of its economic impact on Georgia. It is $43.5 billion, not $435 billion.
match_headline: In N.R.A. Fight, Delta Finds There Is No Neutral Ground

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a rally staged by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey misstated the status of a 6-year-old girl who appeared onstage with Mr. Erdogan at the event. While she wore a military-style uniform, she is not a cadet.
match_headline: Erdogan Tells a Weeping Girl, 6, She’d Receive Honors if Martyred

text: An article last Thursday about the street style star Anna dello Russo misstated when Franca Sozzani, who was the editor of Italian Vogue, died. It was December 2016, not this past December.
match_headline: Doug Jones ‘Outraged’ by Russian-Style Tactics Used in His Senate Race

text: An article on Thursday about the International Olympic Committee lifting its ban on Russia misstated the event in which Ekaterina Bobrova won a silver medal at the 2018 Winter Games. It was ice dancing, not pairs figure skating.
match_headline: I.O.C. Reinstates a Russia That Is Defiant and Eager to Move On

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the forthcoming exhibition “Heavenly Bodies: Fashion and the Catholic Imagination,” at the Costume Institute of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, misstated the location of the Chapel of the Rosary. It is in Vence, France, not Venice, Italy.
ref_headline: Heavenly Bodies: Fashion and the Catholic Imagination,
match_headline: Fashion Meets the Vatican at a Met Costume Institute Preview

text: An article on Friday referred incorrectly to a Günther Förg retrospective at the Dallas Museum of Art. It will open this year, not in 2019.
match_headline: They Built a Home, and With It, a Collection

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday referred incorrectly to Tony Conigliaro’s move to the California Angels in 1971. It was the only time that he was traded to the team; it was not the case that he was “traded back” to the Angels.
match_headline: Jack Hamilton, Who Hurled a Fateful Pitch, Dies at 79

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the Chinese government’s detention of relatives of at least five reporters who covered an extensive crackdown on ethnic Uighurs in the Xinjiang region misstated the day that Radio Free Asia released a statement about the detention. It issued the statement on Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: After U.S.-Based Reporters Exposed Abuses, China Seized Their Relatives

text: An article on Friday about the exploitation of nuns in the Vatican misstated the surname of a sociologist. She is Paola Lazzarini Orrù, not Lattanzi.
match_headline: In Vatican Magazine Exposé, Nuns Reveal Their Economic Exploitation

text: An article on Thursday about an Amnesty International report accusing Egypt of using American-made cluster munitions referred imprecisely to the position held by Middle East countries regarding the treaty that bans such weapons. While many in the region, like Egypt, have not signed the treaty, others including Lebanon and Iraq have signed.
match_headline: Egypt Is Using Banned U.S.-Made Cluster Munitions in Sinai, Rights Group Says

text: An article on Thursday about China’s dispatch of the economic adviser Liu He to the United States to help prevent a trade war misstated which U.S. Chamber of Commerce executive attended the meeting with Mr. Liu on Wednesday. It was Myron Brilliant, executive vice president at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, not Thomas J. Donohue.
match_headline: China Envoy Seeks to Defuse Tensions With U.S. as a Trade War Brews

text: An article on Tuesday about retirement plans and index funds that have gun company stocks in their portfolios referred imprecisely to the gun that Smith & Wesson manufactures. It makes AR-15-style rifles, not the AR-15.
match_headline: You Might Be Giving Gun Companies Money, Even if You Don’t Own a Gun

text: An article on Thursday about Marc Maron’s decision to close his podcast studio, famously situated in his garage, included an erroneous name among the celebrities he interviewed there. Mr. Maron spoke with Robin Williams at the actor’s home in Marin County, Calif., not in his garage.
match_headline: Tour Marc Maron’s Garage Before He and His Podcast Move

text: An article on Feb. 21 about the artist Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, a grandson of the former prime minister of Pakistan, misspelled the title of Mr. Bhutto’s mixed-media series. It is “Mussalmaan Musclemen,” not “Musaalmaan Muscleman.”
match_headline: The Scion of a Pakistani Political Dynasty Comes Out

text: An article on Friday about possible Oscar winners omitted part of the name of an actor who appears in “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.” He is Caleb Landry Jones, not Caleb Landry.
match_headline: Our Expert Predicts the Oscar Winners

text: A review on Friday about the film “Midnighters” misidentified the presidential administration in which Alston Ramsay worked. He served as a speechwriter for George W. Bush, not Bill Clinton.
match_headline: Review: A Cover-Up Turns Terrifying in ‘Midnighters’

text: An article on Page 11 about Lafayette Anticipations, an art center in Paris, misspells the last name of Lafayette Anticipations’ managing director. He is François Quintin, not Quentin.
match_headline: A Newcomer in the Paris Art Scene Jostles for Position

text: An article on Page 4 about spending strategies for middle-income workers with limited retirement savings misstates the age at which a person who has saved $400,000 for retirement must take a minimum distribution of about $14,600. It is 70, not 71.
match_headline: No Pension? You Can ‘Pensionize’ Your Savings

text: An obituary on Friday about the former Gen. Luciano Benjamín Menéndez of Argentina misstated the given name of the president whose election ended years of military rule in Argentina. He was Raúl Ricardo Alfonsín, not Ricardo Alfonsín.
match_headline: Luciano Menéndez, Army Chief in Brutal Argentine Era, Dies at 90

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about William H.T. Bush, the brother of President George H. W. Bush, misidentified the location of the Hotchkiss School, which Mr. Bush attended. It is in Lakeville, Conn., not Lakeview.

Because of an editing error, a profile of the actress Glenda Jackson last Sunday failed to include the role that Ms. Jackson described as an “awful” experience. She was referring to her work in a 1989 production of “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” in Los Angeles, directed by the playwright, Edward Albee, not to her role in the current revival of Mr. Albee’s “Three Tall Women.”
match_headline: Glenda Jackson on Quitting Parliament, Playing Lear and Returning to Broadway

text: An article on Feb. 4 about a curling club in Tampa misidentified the teammate who found the squad’s uniform online and who described watching Olympic team trials on TV. It was Jason Wagner, not Sean Moats.
match_headline: What Winter Olympic Sports Are You Most Excited About Watching?

text: An article on Monday about primaries testing the divide in the Democratic Party, misspelled the name of a Chicago suburb. It is Lemont, not Lamont.
match_headline: As Primaries Begin, Divided Voters Weigh What It Means to Be a Democrat

text: An article on Friday about a carbon tax proposed by Gov. Jay Inslee of Washington misstated the origins of Microsoft. The company was started in New Mexico, not Washington. It later moved to Washington.
match_headline: In a Gamble to Make Climate Change a Political Win, a Governor Pursues a Carbon Tax

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the death of a man who went missing in 1990 misstated his name. He is Kevin Germany, not German.
match_headline: A Lost Son, a Mother’s Search, and Too Late, the Truth

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Saturday misstated the result of the spring training game Friday between the Yankees and the Braves. The Yankees won, 5-4; they did not lose by that score.
match_headline: After Yankees Exile ‘Goose’ and Then the Geese, Who’s Next?

text: A picture with an article on Friday about a community health program for soccer fans battling memory issues was published in error. It showed the 1967-68 Everton team that lost the F.A. Cup to West Brom, not the West Brom team that won.
match_headline: Seeking Solace, and Finding Strength, in Shared Soccer Memories

text: A review on Saturday about a performance of the ballet “Giselle” at the Royal Opera House in London misstated the date when Mr. Hallberg is next scheduled to perform in the show. It is March 9, not May 9.
match_headline: Review: ‘Giselle’ Reunited Hallberg and Osipova, but Only for an Act

text: An article on Friday about free and low-cost museums in New York misstated the address of the American Folk Art Museum. It is 2 Lincoln Square, on Columbus Avenue near 65th Street, not 2 Columbus Avenue.
match_headline: NYC Museums to Visit for $12 or Less

text: An article last Tuesday about the concern in the public health industry over “fat acceptance” misstated how many adults are overweight or obese. It is two in three, not one in three.
match_headline: More Fitness, Less Fatness

text: An obituary on Sunday about Harvey Schmidt, a commercial artist who wrote the music for “The Fantasticks,” the world’s longest-running musical, misstated the number of years “The Fantasticks” played continuously at the Sullivan Street Playhouse in Greenwich Village. It was 38 years, not 18.
match_headline: Harvey Schmidt, Co-Creator of ‘The Fantasticks,’ Is Dead at 88

text: An article on Feb. 28 about a shake-up in Saudi Arabia’s military and security leadership misidentified one of the three princes who were named deputy governors in a series of royal decrees. The appointed princes are the descendants of Princes Talal, Sultan and Muqrin, not princes Talal, Ahmed and Muqrin. A son of Prince Ahmed, Prince Sultan bin Ahmed, was appointed as an adviser to the royal court.
match_headline: Saudi King Shakes Up Military and Security Leadership

text: An entry on Sunday in the “What’s On TV” highlights about the Cartoon Network series “Mike Tyson Mysteries” misstated which season Sunday’s episode of “Mike Tyson Mysteries” was part of. It was the second half of the show’s third season, not the start of its fourth season.
match_headline: What’s on TV Sunday: The Oscars

text: An article on Sunday about the popularity of the AR-15 assault rifle referred incorrectly to government data on rifle manufacturing. The most recent data from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives is from 2016, not 2015.
match_headline: Once Banned, Now Loved and Loathed: How the AR-15 Became ‘America’s Rifle’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a deal reached to end a statewide teachers’ strike in West Virginia referred incorrectly to the lower house of the West Virginia legislature. It is the House of Delegates, not the House of Representatives.
match_headline: West Virginia Raises Teachers’ Pay to End Statewide Strike

text: An article on Wednesday about a budding movement among young Republican groups to support a carbon tax misspelled the surname of a former secretary of state in several instances. He is George P. Shultz, not Schultz.
match_headline: College Republicans Propose an Unusual Idea From the Right: A Carbon Tax

text: An article on Tuesday about James Pitaro’s appointment as ESPN’s next president misstated Bill Grimes’s work history before he became ESPN’s president in 1982. Mr. Grimes had previously worked for the company; he had not, like Mr. Pitaro, become president of ESPN without having previously worked at the sports network.
match_headline: James Pitaro, a Disney Digital Veteran, Is Named ESPN President

text: An article last Thursday about the actor John Boyega misstated the title of a Caribbean folk tale. It is “Anansi the Spider,” not “Ansari the Spider.”
match_headline: How John Boyega Went From ‘Star Wars’ Stormtrooper to Sci-Fi Producer

text: An article last Thursday about rugs misstated the decade when ABC Carpet and Home ushered in the trend of dyed Oriental rugs. It was the early 2000s, not the 1990s.
match_headline: The Rich Have Abandoned Rich-People Rugs

text: An article on Sunday about the benefits of retaining aging workers gave an imprecise description of PKF O’Connor Davies. It is part of a network of independent accounting and advisory firms in 440 cities and 150 countries, not the network itself. The article also misstated the location of Thomas F. Blaney’s office. It is New York City, not Woodcliff Lake, N.J.
match_headline: Reaping the Benefits of an Aging Work Force

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the former major league pitcher Sammy Stewart misstated who managed the Baltimore Orioles in 1978, when the team called Stewart up from the minors. It was Earl Weaver, not Joe Altobelli.
match_headline: Sammy Stewart, Pitcher Whose Life Took a Downturn, Dies at 63

text: An obituary on Jan. 26 about the former New York Times fashion writer Bernadine Morris, using information from her family, omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to her daughter, her son and two granddaughters, Ms. Morris is survived by a brother, Harvey Taub.
match_headline: Bernadine Morris, Veteran Observer of Fashion, Dies at 92

text: An article on Thursday about a lawsuit claiming California’s immigrant-protection laws violate federal law misquoted Attorney General Jeff Sessions’s remarks about Mayor Libby Schaaf of Oakland. He said Ms. Schaaf’s actions to alert residents about a planned immigration raid “support those who flout the law and boldly validates” — not “invalidates” — “illegality.”
ref_headline: support those who flout the law and boldly validates
match_headline: Jeff Sessions Scolds California in Immigration Speech: ‘We Have a Problem’

text: An article on Thursday about how Republican tax cuts are affecting working-class voters in Ohio misstated the number of times Matt Kazee voted for Barack Obama. He voted once for him, in 2008.
match_headline: Blue-Collar Trump Voters Are Shrugging at Their Tax Cuts

text: An obituary on Saturday about the architect and urban planner Richard Weinstein omitted part of the name of the school at the University of California, Los Angeles, where he was dean from 1985 to 1995. It was the Graduate School of Architecture and Urban Planning — not the School of Architecture and Urban Planning.
match_headline: Richard Weinstein, Public-Minded Urban Planner, Dies at 85

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the Italian soccer star Davide Astori misspelled the name of the team now coached by Diego Lopez, a former coach of Astori’s. It is Cagliari, not Caligari.
match_headline: In Fight for Equality, U.S. Women’s Soccer Team Leads the Way

text: An article on Wednesday about George Nader, an adviser to the United Arab Emirates with ties to current and former aides to President Trump, referred imprecisely to the way in which the United Arab Emirates invested in Russian projects. The U.A.E. co-invested in projects together with the Russian Direct Investment Fund, or RDIF; it did not invest in the RDIF itself.
match_headline: Adviser to Emirates With Ties to Trump Aides Is Cooperating With Special Counsel

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Page 14 about the NBC drama “Rise” misidentified the character played by Josh Radnor. As the article correctly noted, he plays Lou Mazzuchelli, a fictional character based on the visionary real-life drama teacher Lou Volpe; he does not play Lou Volpe.
match_headline: With ‘Rise,’ a ‘Friday Night Lights’ for Theater Kids

text: An article on Page 12 about the comic book artist Billy Graham described incorrectly Mr. Graham’s initial involvement with the Black Panther comics and his role in designing Wakanda, the Black Panther’s homeland. Marvel assigned Mr. Graham to the title; his friend Don McGregor did not ask him to collaborate on it. Mr. McGregor and Alex Simmons designed the maps of Wakanda; Mr. Graham was not involved.
match_headline: Black Panther, Luke Cage and the First Black Artist to Draw Both

text: A profile of Ida B. Wells on Page 4 referred imprecisely to voting rights during Reconstruction. Black men were able to vote. Women did not get the right to vote until 1920.
match_headline: Ida B. Wells, Who Took on Racism in the Deep South With Powerful Reporting on Lynchings

text: An obituary on Friday about the former Nestlé chief executive Hans O. Maucher, using information from a company spokeswoman, misstated the number of sons who survive him. It is two, not three.
match_headline: Helmut Maucher, Executive Who Transformed Nestlé, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Feb. 27 about the real estate magnate George S. Kaufman, who was chairman of Kaufman Astoria Studios in Astoria, Queens, incorrectly included one title on a list of television shows that have used those studios. The police procedural “Blue Bloods” is not produced there.
match_headline: George S. Kaufman, Who Revived Astoria Studios, Dies at 89

text: An article on this weekend’s cover misstates the name of a police union. It is the Sergeants Benevolent Association, not the Sergeant’s Benevolent Organization.
match_headline: Al Sharpton, Reconsidered

text: An article last Sunday about the actress Olivia de Havilland’s lawsuit against FX and Ryan Murphy Productions over her portrayal in a docudrama rendered incorrectly the name of a video game. It is Band Hero, not Hero Band.
match_headline: At 101, Olivia de Havilland Sued Hollywood — Again

text: An article last Sunday about the final party at the editor George Plimpton’s apartment mischaracterized the circumstances under which the previous editor of The Paris Review departed. Lorin Stein resigned; he was not fired. The article also misspelled the surname of a former managing editor of the literary magazine. She is Jeanne McCulloch, not McCullough.
match_headline: Last Call at George Plimpton’s Party Pad

text: A column on Feb. 25 about South Korea’s aging population misspelled the given name of a professor at Wellesley College. She is Katharine H.S. Moon, not Katherine.
match_headline: South Korea’s Most Dangerous Enemy: Demographics

text: An article last Sunday about expedited security lanes at airports referred incorrectly to 11 airports participating in the Global Entry expedited customs clearance program. The program in November made it easier to join upon arrival at those 11 airports; it did not add them (the airports were already part of the Global Entry network).
match_headline: How to Bypass Airport Lines With the Tips of Your Fingers

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Montgomery, Ala., misstated when the Civil Rights Memorial opened. It was in 1989, not 2005; a Civil Rights Memorial Center was added in 2005.
match_headline: The 52 Places Traveler: In Montgomery, a City Embedded With Pain, Finding Progress

text: An essay on Feb. 25 about Iceman, a gay Marvel superhero, misidentified the author of a scene depicting a conversation between Iceman and another character, Kyle. The author is Christos Gage, not Marjorie Liu.
match_headline: The Iceman Cometh Out

text: A review on Feb. 18 about “Hippie Food,” by Jonathan Kauffman, misidentified the owners of Stonyfield Farm. It is now a subsidiary of Lactalis, the French dairy company; it is no longer owned by Danone.
match_headline: How We Got From Twinkies to Tofu

text: An article on Monday about a sweeping anti-corruption campaign in Saudi Arabia misstated when Salman became king of the country. It was in 2015, not 2005.
match_headline: Saudis Said to Use Coercion and Abuse to Seize Billions

text: An article on Monday about Martin Selmayr, a German lawyer who was recently promoted to the job of deputy secretary general of the European Commission, misstated Alexander Italianer’s title. He was the secretary general of the European Commission, not the chief of staff.
match_headline: A Sudden Promotion Raises Questions in the Brussels Bubble

text: An article on Monday about a helicopter that crashed into the East River misstated the number of people who died in a 2011 episode in which another helicopter crashed into the river. It was three, not one. (Two died from injuries in the following weeks.)
match_headline: East River Helicopter Crash Kills 5 in New York; Pilot Survives

text: An article on Monday about SoftBank’s ambitions to build an elite private equity firm misstated the amount of assets that Kohlberg Kravis Roberts has under its management. It is $168 billion, not $148 billion.
match_headline: SoftBank Looks to Invade Wall Street’s Turf

text: An article on Saturday about the possible effects of tariffs proposed by President Trump on rural voters in the Midwest misstated the age of Davie Stephens, vice president of the American Soybean Association. He is 52, not 67.
match_headline: Trade War Prospect Shakes Part of Trump Base: Midwest Farmers

text: An article on Saturday about an antitrust case centering on AT&T’s efforts to buy Time Warner misstated the surname of a research analyst at Macquarie Group. She is Amy Yong, not Young.
match_headline: AT&T Backs Off Political Argument in Antitrust Case

text: An article on Monday about the nuances in Jake Arrieta’s new contract with the Phillies misstated Andy MacPhail’s title with the Phillies. He is the team president, not the president of baseball operations.
match_headline: Jake Arrieta Heads to the Phillies for 2-5 Years

text: An article on Thursday about the dearth of practice space for the 25 men’s college basketball teams that competed in concurrent tournaments in New York misstated part of the name of the school at which Miami practiced. It is Léman Manhattan Preparatory School, not Academy.
match_headline: When College Basketball Teams Invade New York, an Empty Gym Is Hard to Find

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 10 about the music of Gyorgy Ligeti and teaching listeners to like difficult music did not fully identify a composer quoted in the article. The composer who said “I have no desire to explain any work of art” is Gerard McBurney, the organizer of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra series Beyond the Score from 2005-16.
ref_headline: I have no desire to explain any work of art
match_headline: How Do You Teach People to Love Difficult Music?

text: An article on Saturday about the production of a Barbie doll modeled after the Mexican artist Frida Kahlo misstated Ms. Kahlo’s age at the time of her death in 1954. She was 47, not 44. Although Ms. Kahlo said she was 44, it was subsequently determined that she was born in 1907, not 1910.
match_headline: Frida Kahlo Is a Barbie Doll Now. (Signature Unibrow Not Included.)

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about ballet companies in Philadelphia misstated the year that Matthew Neenan’s “Increasing” had its premiere. It was in 2014, not 2016.
match_headline: In Philadelphia, Ballet Neighbors Divided by Style

text: A review on Friday about the film “Shining Moon” misspelled the surname of the movie’s director. It is Letelier, not Leteiler. The error was repeated in a capsule summary.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Shining Moon,’ Two Gay Chilean Actors Confront the Past

text: A map with an article on Monday about tipping in the restaurant industry misstated New York State’s highest hourly minimum wage for tipped workers. It is $8.65, not $2.90.
match_headline: Wage Theft in Restaurants

text: An article on Tuesday about complaints filed against White House officials for apparent violations of the Hatch Act described incorrectly the process by which such violations are punished. The decision to punish White House officials for violating the Hatch Act is made by the president or the Office of Special Counsel, which can request that the Merit Systems Protection Board take disciplinary action. It is not the case that cabinet secretaries play a role in deciding how and whether to discipline violators of the law.
match_headline: White House Aides Blur the Legal Lines Between Partisans and Public Servants

text: An article on Tuesday about self-piloted electric planes being tested in New Zealand misstated the wingspan of the Cora aircraft. It is 36 feet, not 12 feet.
