match_headline: Larry Page’s Flying Taxis, Now Exiting Stealth Mode

text: An article on Tuesday about teams capable of causing upsets in the N.C.A.A. tournament misstated the surname of a Loyola player. He is Clayton Custer, not Cluster.
match_headline: Here Are 6 N.C.A.A. Bracket Busters. You’ve Been Warned.

text: An article on Tuesday about the electronic music duo Mouse on Mars misspelled the given name of the leader of the band Beirut. He is Zach Condon, not Zac.
match_headline: Mouse on Mars at M.I.T.: A Symposium Becomes a Dance Party

text: An article on Monday about the early arrival of spring misspelled the title of a book by Ernest Hemingway. It is “A Moveable Feast,” not “A Movable Feast.”
match_headline: The Dark Warning of an Early Spring

text: An article on Wednesday about a Chinese reporter whose exasperated expression went viral in China referred incorrectly to Jason Quin, the president of American Multimedia Television U.S.A. Mr. Quin is also the president of the Confucius Institute of Education, which is unrelated to the Confucius Institutes supported by the Chinese government; he is not the president of a Los Angeles Confucius Institute.
match_headline: A Reporter Rolled Her Eyes, and China’s Internet Broke

text: An article on Wednesday about a history professor’s critique of National Geographic’s coverage of race over the years misstated how many years the magazine has been publishing. The magazine began publishing 130 years ago, not 120.
match_headline: National Geographic Acknowledges Its Racist Past Coverage

text: An article on Monday about pervasive myths related to picking winners in the N.C.A.A. tournament misidentified the team that won the tournament for the first time before Florida did in 2006. It was Syracuse in 2003, not Maryland in 2002.
match_headline: March Madness Myths: N.C.A.A. Bracket Traps to Avoid

text: An article on Monday about the children’s book author Andy Griffiths misstated Mr. Griffiths’s age. He is 56, not 57.
match_headline: Andy Griffiths, the Down-Under Kids’ Author Known for His Butt Jokes, Now Builds and Builds on His Hit ‘Treehouse’ Series

text: An article on Page 14 about Barbara Haskell, a longtime curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art, omits the current owner of works in two photo credits. “The Midnight Ride of Paul Revere” (1931) is Figge Art Museum, Estate of Nan Wood Graham/VAGA, New York, NY, via The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
ref_headline: The Midnight Ride of Paul Revere
match_headline: At the Whitney, a Champion of American Art

text: An article on Page 18 about art museums in Puerto Rico misstates the name of a federal agency. It is the National Endowment for the Humanities, not the Endowment for the Humanities.
match_headline: Art Museums in Puerto Rico Face Long and Expensive Recovery

text: An entry on Page 42 in a listing of art exhibitions around the country this spring gives an incorrect location for the Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art (MASS MoCA). It is North Adams, Mass., not West Adams.
match_headline: From 12th Century B.C. to 2017, Art in Startling Variety

text: An article on Page 43 about new strategies museums are using to improve gift shop sales misspells the surname of the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s vice president of merchandising. He is Rich Pedott, not Perdott.
match_headline: You Can Take It With You, and Museums Hope You Will

text: A picture caption on Page 10 about the digital art immersion space Artechouse in Washington, D.C., misspelled the name of an experience design company that created “IceNeon.” It is Noirflux, not Noriflex.
match_headline: Artechouse Lights Up Washington’s Museum Scene

text: An article on Thursday about voters’ support for Conor Lamb in a special congressional election on Tuesday referred incorrectly to the voting history of the 18th Congressional District while paraphrasing two voters at a Starbucks. They said that their region had not supported a Democrat in years, not that it had not voted for a Republican.
match_headline: In Pennsylvania Election Shaped by Trump, Candidates Still Mattered

text: An article on Wednesday about the effects that steel and aluminum tariffs could have on Boeing misstated the Export-Import Bank’s relationship to Boeing. It lends to Boeing’s customers, not Boeing itself.
match_headline: Boeing May Become a Target in a Trade War Over Trump’s Tariffs

text: A review on Thursday about the New Jersey indie-rock band Yo La Tengo misstated which member of the band sings “Why cry? Why try? It’s all the same” on the song “Dream Dream Away.” It is James McNew, not Ira Kaplan.
ref_headline: Why cry? Why try? It’s all the same
match_headline: Music Is a Sanctuary From Chaos on Yo La Tengo’s ‘There’s a Riot Going On’

text: An article on Feb. 21 about this year’s flu vaccine misstated a figure describing its effectiveness. It is 36 percent effective overall, not 39 percent.
match_headline: The Flu Vaccine Is Working Better Than Expected, C.D.C. Finds

text: An article on Tuesday about attacks on antismoking activists misstated the number of years ago that the activist Akinbode Oluwafemi’s home was invaded. It was six, not eight.
match_headline: In Poor Countries, Antismoking Activists Face Threats and Violence

text: An article on Thursday about the National Museum of the Marine Corps misstated the involvement of the Marines on D-Day. No Marines participated in storming the beaches of Normandy.
match_headline: In the Marines, a Connection Between Art and Combat

text: Because of an editing error, a headline with the Encounters column last Sunday, about a British actor who will appear in “My Fair Lady” on Broadway, misspelled his surname. As the article correctly noted, he is Harry Hadden-Paton, not Haddon-Paton.
match_headline: Shopping for Marmite With Harry Hadden-Paton

text: An article on Page 7 about the use of profanities in theater paraphrases imprecisely the comments of the playwright Stephen Adly Guirgis. While Mr. Guirgis said that he may use racial epithets in his dialogue, he does so sparingly and did not suggest that the title of his play, “The _______ With the Hat,” includes a profanity as a stand-in for a racial epithet.
match_headline: Curses! And Why They Work So Well Onstage (Sometimes)

text: An article on Page 12 about the new romantic comedy “Love, Simon” included an outdated name for Glaad. It no longer calls itself the Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation.
match_headline: A Romantic Comedy About a Gay Teenager? What Took So Long?

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the playwright Tony Kushner and “Angels in America” misidentified which part of the play one image was from. It showed Nathan Lane and Nathan Stewart-Jarrett in Part 2, not Part 1.
match_headline: Tony Kushner, at Peace? Not Exactly. But Close.

text: An article last Sunday about a new app that matches users with professional skiers and skateboarders misstated the name of one of the towns where it is available for skateboarding. It is Oceanside, Calif., not Oceanville, Calif.
match_headline: An App That Helps You Ride Like a Pro — by Riding With a Pro

text: A review on Feb. 25 about the novel “The Boat People,” by Sharon Bala, misstated the status of the Canadian Tamil Congress under the United Nations Security Council. The Security Council has not designated them a terrorist group.
match_headline: Seeking Asylum but Finding Heartbreak

text: A news analysis last week about women, power and money misspelled the surname of a BBC editor who resigned in protest over pay inequality. She is Carrie Gracie, not Grace. The article also misidentified the actress who plays Naomi Bishop in “Equity.” She is Anna Gunn, not Anita.
match_headline: Money Is Power. And Women Need More of Both.

text: An article on Monday about Syrian rebels taking control of the city Afrin misstated the given name of an assassinated politician. He was Mashaal Tammo, not Michel Tammo.
match_headline: Syrian Rebels, Backed by Turkey, Seize Control of Afrin

text: An article on Friday about a dispute over the sale of a rare beer at a Dutch supermarket chain referred incorrectly to the price of the beer. It was several times higher than the original price, not 10 times higher. Because of an editing error, the article also referred incorrectly to the chain’s marketing manager. The marketing manager, Gineke Wilms, is a woman.
match_headline: An Unholy Fight Over a Saintly Beer

text: An article on Saturday about developments in the men’s N.C.A.A. tournament misstated the score at halftime of Virginia’s loss to U.M.B.C. It was tied at 21, not 31. The article also misidentified Texas A&M’s conference. The Aggies are in the Southeastern Conference, not the Big 12. (Texas A&M left the Big 12 in 2012.)
match_headline: March Madness: UMBC Delivers Historic Upset Over No. 1 Virginia

text: An article on Monday about the results of the Arnold Palmer Invitational misstated the hole in which Rory McIlroy made a chip-in birdie. It was No. 15, not No. 13.
match_headline: Masters Preview? Rory McIlroy Wins at Bay Hill, and Tiger Woods Makes a Run

text: An obituary on Friday about the former Met third baseman Ed Charles erroneously attributed a distinction to him. He received no votes for the American League Rookie of the Year award in 1962; he did not finish second. It also misstated his relationship to Sarah Lou Parker, a relative whose apartment in Queens he inherited. She was a cousin, not an aunt. And because of an editing error, it misstated the given name of Charles’s brother, who survives him. It is Charlie, not Elder.
match_headline: Ed Charles, Infield Sage of the Miracle Mets, Is Dead at 84

text: An article on Tuesday about the appointment of the British designer Kim Jones as the new artistic director of Dior Homme misstated overall revenue last year at Christian Dior Couture. It was 2.23 billion euros, or $2.7 billion, not €43.7 billion.
match_headline: Dior Confirms Kim Jones as Men’s Wear Artistic Director

text: A Critic’s Notebook last Wednesday about a new style of casual Indian restaurants in Manhattan misspelled the given name of the chef at Old Monk. He is Navjot Arora, not Navjut.
match_headline: For Casual Indian Restaurants, It’s Party Time

text: An article on Tuesday about a geneticist at Harvard Medical School whose team is retrieving DNA from ancient bones to trace the prehistoric migrations of our species misstated the given name of a mathematician. He is Nick Patterson, not Neil.
match_headline: David Reich Unearths Human History Etched in Bone

text: An article on Tuesday about predatory birds and the spread of wildfires misstated the name of a federal territory in Australia. It is the Northern Territory, not the Northern Territories.
match_headline: In Australia, Arsonists May Have Wings

text: Because of an editing error, the headline with an obituary on Tuesday about the comedian Mike MacDonald misstated his age. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 63, not 62.
An obituary on Thursday about the physicist Stephen Hawking misstated the year of a meeting at the Vatican that he attended. It was 1981, not 1982.
match_headline: Stephen Hawking Dies at 76; His Mind Roamed the Cosmos

text: An article on Wednesday about Macedonia’s struggles to keep its name in a long-running cultural dispute with Greece gave the incorrect year in which the country agreed to temporarily call itself the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. That compromise was reached in 1995, not 1993.
match_headline: What’s in a Name? For Macedonia, the Key to Peace and Security

text: An article on Tuesday about a worker in the French Consulate in Jerusalem charged with smuggling guns into the West Bank misidentified the newspaper for which Yossi Melman is a columnist. It is Maariv, not Haaretz.
match_headline: French Consulate Worker Is Accused of Smuggling Guns From Gaza

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the challenges Ford Motor has faced in the sport-utility vehicle market referred imprecisely to the vehicle shown and omitted mention of another. According to Ford, a high-performance Explorer ST was under wraps in the background and a different sport-utility vehicle, the Edge, was in the foreground; a Ford Expedition S.U.V. was not shown in the image.
match_headline: Ford, Once a Leader in the S.U.V. Race, Aims to Catch Up

text: A picture caption with a review on Saturday about the documentary series “Wild Wild Country” misidentified the women shown in two side-by-side photographs. The photograph on the left was an image of Jane Stork; Ma Anand Sheela was in the image on the right.
match_headline: Review: On Netflix, a Wild Story of Guns, Sex and a Guru

text: A review on Friday about the comedy “Love, Simon” referred imprecisely to the Motion Picture Association of America’s PG-13 rating for the film. The rating was for “thematic elements,” which the organization says “may include coming-of-age issues, illness, accidents, family discord, suicidal thoughts, bullying, acting out, crises in faith, sibling rivalry, death, betrayals or difficulties in friendship.” The rating does not reference sexual orientation.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Love, Simon,’ a Glossy Teen Romance, the Hero Has a Secret

text: An obituary on Thursday about Millie Veasey, who served in an all-black, all-women’s battalion in World War II, misstated the year that Ms. Veasey’s unit arrived in Scotland. It was 1945, not 1944.
match_headline: Millie Veasey, Part of Trailblazing Unit in WWII, Dies at 100

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the financier and philanthropist Peter G. Peterson misstated the reason Mr. Peterson left M.I.T. for Northwestern University. He was expelled; he did not transfer.
match_headline: Peter G. Peterson, a Power From Wall St. to Washington, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about President Trump’s selection of John R. Bolton to replace Lt. Gen. H. R. McMaster as his national security adviser misstated the duration of a sexual relationship with Mr. Trump as described by Karen McDougal in her CNN interview. She said it lasted 10 months, not nine.
match_headline: Trump Chooses Bolton for 3rd Security Adviser as Shake-Up Continues

text: Because of a production error, an article on Thursday, about attorneys general from Democratic states filing environmental lawsuits against the Trump administration, was missing two paragraphs and failed to fully identify the attorney general of West Virginia. He is Patrick Morrissey.
match_headline: Borrowing G.O.P. Playbook, Democratic States Sue the Government and Rack Up Wins

text: An article on Friday about new technology that could make car speakers obsolete misspelled the name of the sound system developed by Continental. It is called Ac2ated Sound, not Ac2ate Sound or Ac2uate Sound. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Speakers Might Be the Next Thing in Your Car to Go the Way of the 8-Track

text: An article on Page F3 about crafting legal documents to minimize friction between individuals inheriting an estate misspells the given name of the chief wealth advisory officer at Ballentine Partners. It is Coventry Edwards-Pitt, not Covington.
match_headline: Here’s How to Maintain Peace Among Your Heirs

text: A news analysis last week about populists’ admiration of Vladimir Putin misidentified a political office once held by Silvio Berlusconi. He was the prime minister of Italy, not its president.
match_headline: The Poison Putin Spreads

text: An article last Sunday about “Prurience,” at the Guggenheim Museum, misidentified the designer of the Wright restaurant at the museum. The restaurant was designed by Andre Kikoski — not by Frank Lloyd Wright, who designed the museum.
match_headline: They Talk About Porn in This Show. Audience Participation Is Encouraged.

text: An article on Feb. 25 about three young people to watch in theater this spring misstated the name of a character played by Andrew Burnap in “The Inheritance.” He is Toby Darling, not Harry Darling.
match_headline: 3 Young People to Watch in Theater This Spring

text: A review on March 11 about “Behemoth,” by Joshua B. Freeman, misspelled the given name of the wealthy Boston merchant for whom Lowell, Mass., was named. He was Francis Cabot Lowell, not Frances.
match_headline: In ‘Behemoth,’ Manufacturing Still Looms Large

text: A review last Sunday about “The Which Way Tree,” by Elizabeth Crook, misstated the number of novels the author has written.“The Which Way Tree” is her fifth, not her first.
match_headline: The Good, the Bad and the Panther

text: An article on March 4 about color forecasting described incorrectly the ownership of Pantone. Pantone is a subsidiary of X-Rite, Inc.; it is not a privately owned company.
match_headline: What Is the Perfect Color Worth?

text: An article on March 11 about Jason Isbell misstated a lyric from his song with the 400 Unit “If We Were Vampires.” The line is “If we were vampires and death was a joke,” not "If we were vampires and life was a joke.”
match_headline: In Death as in Life, Women Count. Here’s How The Times Counted Them.

text: An article on March 18 about recovery literature incorrectly states that D.T. Max attributed an anonymous testimonial to David Foster Wallace. Though other writers have made this attribution, Max has not.
match_headline: Does Recovery Kill Great Writing?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the sale of marijuana in the Netherlands referred imprecisely to Nicole Maalsté, who represents Dutch coffee shops that sell marijuana. She is an academic, not an activist.
match_headline: Solving the Dutch Pot Paradox: Legal to Buy, but Not to Grow

text: An article on Monday about obstacles that opposition parties are facing in their bid to challenge Viktor Orban, Hungary’s far-right prime minister, omitted the middle initial and misstated the surname of a candidate who represents a pair of socialist parties. She is Marta V. Naszalyi, not Szakaly.
match_headline: In Hungary, Disunity and Gerrymandering Frustrate Anti-Orban Voters

text: An article on Sunday about a plan to drill natural gas reserves in the Great Australian Bight, off the nation’s south coast, referred incorrectly to the origins of the region’s name. “Bight” is a nautical term referring to the characteristic bend of the bay; the name does not arise from its bitelike shape.
match_headline: Drilling the Great Australian Bight: Hoping for Jobs, but Fearing a Spill

text: An article on Saturday about the trial of a nanny who fatally stabbed two children in her care misstated the year the children were killed. It was 2012, not 2013.
match_headline: ‘It Was Not Herself That Killed Them,’ Sister Testifies in Nanny Trial

text: An article on Wednesday about researchers’ use of individuals’ Facebook behavior to build algorithms that predict and potentially manipulate their political views misstated the title of Michal Kosinki, a researcher who helped develop the model that created personality profiles from Facebook “likes.” He is a professor of organizational behavior, not a professor of computer science.
match_headline: How Researchers Learned to Use Facebook ‘Likes’ to Sway Your Thinking

text: An obituary on Saturday about the broadcast news executive Lawrence K. Grossman misstated the year the 13-part television series “Vietnam: A Television History” was broadcast. It was 1983, not 1981.
match_headline: Lawrence K. Grossman, Head of PBS and Then NBC News, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Monday about the jazz bassist Buell Neidlinger misstated the given name of the guitarist on the album “The Happenings: Music of Herbie Nichols.” He is Howard Alden, not Harold.
ref_headline: The Happenings: Music of Herbie Nichols.
match_headline: Buell Neidlinger, Acclaimed Genre-Crossing Bassist, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Monday about Eli Leon, a scholar of African-American quilts, misstated the location of Black Mountain College. It was in Black Mountain, N.C., not Ashland, N.C.
match_headline: Eli Leon, 82, Dies; Champion of African-American Quilt Makers

text: An obituary on Saturday about Zell Miller, a former Democratic governor and Senator from Georgia who departed from his party to support George W. Bush’s 2004 presidential bid, misstated the dollar amount of President Bush’s tax-cut measure in early 2001. It was $1.6 trillion, not $1.6 billion.
match_headline: Zell Miller, Feisty Democrat Who Sided With G.O.P., Is Dead at 86

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the European Union’s response to the recent poisoning of a former Russian spy and his daughter misstated when a chemical agent was last used on European soil. The poisoning marked the first use of a chemical agent on European soil since — not before — the Second World War.
match_headline: How an Outraged Europe Agreed to a Hard Line on Putin

text: A review on Monday about a double bill of two Pygmalion operas by Donizetti and Rameau misstated the surname of the conductor of the Rameau production. He is Gil Rose, not Gil French.
match_headline: Review: Ahead of ‘My Fair Lady,’ Two Operatic Pygmalions

text: An article on Monday about the television series “Silicon Valley” included a quotation from Mike Judge that misstated Google’s Gmail ad policy. Google stopped scanning its consumer, or free, email accounts for the purpose of targeted ads in 2017.
match_headline: Mike Judge on ‘Silicon Valley,’ T.J. Miller’s Exit and How ‘Idiocracy’ Endures

text: An article on Monday about the rise of childhood obesity in the U.S. misstated the definition of a severely obese youth. It is at or above 120 percent of the 95th percentile of body mass index for age and gender, not 120 percent above the 95th percentile.
match_headline: American Adults Just Keep Getting Fatter

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Tony-winning actor Sammy Williams misstated the title of a Broadway play in which Mr. Williams performed. It was “The Happy Time,” not “The Happy Times.” A picture caption with the obituary misstated the given name of an actress who won a Tony Award for her performance in “A Chorus Line.” She is Kelly Bishop, not Carole.
match_headline: Sammy Williams, Tony Winner in ‘A Chorus Line,’ Dies at 69

text: A picture with an obituary on Tuesday about Linda Brown was published in error. The photograph, released by The Associated Press, misidentified the woman in the image. The image showed another student, not Linda Brown.
match_headline: Linda Brown, Symbol of Landmark Desegregation Case, Dies at 75

text: An article on Wednesday about the Trump administration’s efforts to add a question on citizenship to the 2020 census referred incorrectly to the American Community Survey. It is a mandatory poll; it is not voluntary.
match_headline: At Least Twelve States to Sue Trump Administration Over Census Citizenship Question

text: An article on Tuesday referred incorrectly to services provided by the gay dating app Hornet. The app has offered H.I.V.-testing reminders to its users since 2012; it is not the case that it has yet to offer such a service.
match_headline: Grindr App to Offer H.I.V. Test Reminders

text: An article on Thursday about a new arrest tied to a $20 million heist in Britain misspelled the name of one of the robbery’s ringleaders. He is Brian Reader, not Brain Reade.
match_headline: New Arrest in $20 Million Heist, Britain’s Biggest Burglary

text: An article on Thursday about the working conditions and wages for food workers on City University of New York campuses misspelled the surname of the president of the Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union. He is Stuart Appelbaum, not Applebaum.
match_headline: CUNY Food Workers Complain of Poor Conditions and Low Wages

text: An article on Thursday about a merger between Daimler and BMW misstated when the companies said they would merge their car-sharing businesses. It was Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: BMW and Daimler, Once Rivals, Join Forces to Fend Off Silicon Valley

text: A column on Thursday about social media’s recent decline in popularity among Americans misstated the number of registered users on Mastodon. It is more than a million, not more than 140,000.
match_headline: Can Social Media Be Saved?

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Sunday about college basketball coaches straying beyond the limits of the coach’s box misidentified a coach pictured. He is Bill Self of Kansas, not John Calipari of Memphis.
match_headline: College Coaches Cannot Be Contained

text: An article on March 18 about the N.A.I.A. basketball tournament in Kansas City attributed an erroneous distinction to Clarence Walker’s appearance in the 1948 N.A.I.A. tournament. He was the first black player to appear in a national association’s postseason basketball tournament; Walker did not break the color barrier for “all college basketball tournaments.”
match_headline: 32 Teams, 7 Days, 1 Gym

text: An article on Thursday about the funding needed to build the International African American Museum in Charleston, S.C., referred imprecisely to the status of a statue of Robert E. Lee. There has been a proposal to remove it; it has not yet been taken down.
match_headline: Charleston Needs That African American Museum. And Now.

text: An article on Tuesday about a clot-busting drug treatment for stroke patients misstated Dr. Jerome Hoffman’s involvement in a business venture. Dr. Hoffman contributed to informational tapes; he did not sell them.
match_headline: For Many Strokes, There’s an Effective Treatment. Why Aren’t Some Doctors Offering It?

text: An obituary on Thursday about the historian Arnold R. Hirsch misstated the affiliation of the historian Thomas J. Sugrue. He is a professor at New York University; he is no longer at the University of Pennsylvania.
match_headline: Arnold R. Hirsch, Historian of Housing Segregation, Dies at 69

text: An article on Wednesday about Kim Jong-un’s train misstated how many people are believed to have died in a 2004 train disaster in Ryongchon, North Korea. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies concluded that 161 people were killed, with 1,300 injured; it is no longer thought that 3,000 people died, though early news reports estimated that there had been 3,000 casualties.
match_headline: Bulletproof, Slow and Full of Wine: Kim Jong-un’s Mystery Train

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the poisoning of the Russian ex-spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter incorrectly described Det. Sgt. Nick Bailey, who was exposed to the nerve agent. He is a policeman, not an emergency medical worker.
match_headline: Russian Ex-Spy Sergei Skripal Was Poisoned via Front Door, U.K. Says

text: An article on Friday about the Lithuanian capital city of Vilnius misspelled the name of the Holocaust remembrance center in Israel. It is Yad Vashem, not Yad Vesham. The article also misspelled the name of a human rights organization. It is the Simon Wiesenthal — not Weisenthal — Center.
match_headline: Where the Genocide Museum Is (Mostly) Mum on the Fate of Jews

text: An article on Friday about the lawsuit to preserve the DACA program misspelled the surname of the spokeswoman for the New York attorney general. She is Amy Spitalnick, not Spitalnik.
match_headline: Citing Trump’s ‘Racial Slurs,’ Judge Says Suit to Preserve DACA Can Continue

text: A column on Friday about Rusty Staub, who died on Thursday, erroneously included a player in a group of those who had reached base at least 4,000 times and become eligible for induction into the Baseball Hall of Fame. While Pete Rose reached base over 4,000 times in his career, he was barred permanently from Major League Baseball in 1989 and has never been eligible for induction into the Hall.
match_headline: 4,050 Reasons to Appreciate Rusty Staub

text: An article on Friday about the departure of the music executive Charlie Walk from the Republic Group amid harassment accusations misstated the number of women, in addition to Tristan Coopersmith, who said in a Rolling Stone story that they were sexually harassed by Mr. Walk. It was four, not five.
match_headline: Charlie Walk, Record Executive Accused of Harassment, Is Out at Republic

text: An article on Friday about film series and special screenings in New York City misstated the title for the series highlighting Lynne Ramsay’s films at BAM. It is “Tough Love: Cinema by Lynne Ramsay,” not “Tough Love: The Cinema of Lynne Ramsay.”
ref_headline: Tough Love: Cinema by Lynne Ramsay,
match_headline: 4 Film Series to Catch in NYC This Weekend

text: An article on Thursday about Boyd’s clothing store in Philadelphia misspelled the name of a men’s clothing store. It is Morvilles, not Morevilles.
match_headline: The Last Great Clothing Store

text: An article on Thursday about the remains of a baby girl discovered in Chile misstated the distance between La Noria, Chile, and the Atacama Desert. La Noria is within the desert, not 450 miles north of it. The article also misstated the surname of a biologist. She is Cristina Dorador, not Dorado.
match_headline: Chile and Its Scientists Protest Research on Tiny Mummy

text: An obituary on Friday about the writer Russell Freedman misspelled the name of a children’s literature award. It is the Newbery Medal, not Newberry. The obituary also misstated the title of Mr. Freedman’s first novel. It is “Teenagers Who Made History,” not “Teenagers Who Changed History.”
match_headline: Russell Freedman, 88, Writer of History for Young Readers, Dies

text: An article about Cuba on March 18 misstated the year in which President Barack Obama visited that country. It was 2016, not 2015.
match_headline: Havana’s Symphony of Sound

text: An article on March 25 about Aleksander Doba, who kayaked across the Atlantic Ocean three times, misstated the date of a National Geographic Society award ceremony and described incorrectly the clothing Doba wore to it. The ceremony was in June, not February, and Doba wore jeans, not shorts.
match_headline: Why He Kayaked Across the Atlantic at 70 (for the Third Time)

text: An article in the March 18 issue about efforts to save threatened species in Hawaii misidentified an organization that works on environmental issues. It is the Natural Resources Defense Council, not the National Resources Defense Council.
match_headline: Should Some Species Be Allowed to Die Out?

text: A review on March 18 about “Victorians Undone,” by Kathryn Hughes, misstated the book’s American publisher. It is Johns Hopkins University Press, not HarperCollins.
match_headline: A Corporeal History of the 19th Century

text: A review on March 11 about the graphic novel “The Prince and the Dressmaker,” by Jen Wang, misstated the nationality of one of the main characters. He is Prince Sebastian of Belgium, not France.
match_headline: Secrets, Lies and a Murder (or Three) in the Latest Y.A. Crossover Novels

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the privacy concerns surrounding digital assistants misstated Jeff Bezos’s role in Amazon’s Super Bowl ad. He was trying to figure out what to do when Alexa lost her voice; he did not fill in for her.
match_headline: Hey, Alexa, What Can You Hear? And What Will You Do With It?

text: An article on Dec. 7 about a macabre curtain of reindeer skulls strung up outside Norway’s parliament in Oslo as part of a protest of the country’s reindeer reduction policy misstated the name of an anthropologist who used the term “welfare colonialism.” He is Robert Paine, not Richard. (A reader doing research on a thesis pointed out the error in an April 2 email to The Times.)
match_headline: In Norway, Fighting the Culling of Reindeer With a Macabre Display

text: An article on Saturday about a discussion between Pope Francis and Eugenio Scalfari regarding the existence of hell misidentified Pope Francis’ predecessor. He was Benedict XVI, not Benedict XI.
match_headline: Does Hell Exist? And Did the Pope Give an Answer?

text: An article on March 26 about family-based immigration and low-skilled workers misstated the provenance of an immigration bill that has been introduced in Congress. It was introduced by two Republican senators, Tom Cotton of Arkansas and David Perdue of Georgia, not by Representative Bob Goodlatte.
match_headline: When the Elderly Call for Help, a ‘Chain’ Immigrant Often Answers

text: An article on Saturday about a residence rented by Scott Pruitt, the head of the Environmental Protection Agency, misstated the role of Jeffrey Lagda, who commented on whether the E.P.A.’s inspector general might open an investigation. Mr. Lagda is a spokesman for the Office of Inspector General, not the inspector general.
match_headline: Scott Pruitt, E.P.A. Chief, Rented Residence From Wife of Energy Lobbyist

text: An article on Monday about the midterm election campaign in Pennsylvania misspelled the surname of the chairman of the Pennsylvania Republican Party. He is Val DiGiorgio, not DiGregorio.
match_headline: How Will the Midterm Elections Play Out? Watch Pennsylvania

text: An article on Saturday about an uproar among employees at Facebook over a leaked 2016 memo misstated Adam Mosseri’s position at the company. He is the head of news feed, not the head of news.
match_headline: Facebook Employees in an Uproar Over Executive’s Leaked Memo

text: An article on Saturday about Walmart’s partnership talks with Humana referred incorrectly to the relationship between CVS Health and Aetna. While CVS agreed last year to acquire Aetna, it has not yet done so; the deal is not expected to close until the second quarter of 2018.
match_headline: Walmart in Talks to Strengthen Ties to Health Insurer Humana

text: A picture caption with a review on Saturday of a performance by the Seattle Symphony of John Luther Adams’s “Become Desert” referred incorrectly to the piece being performed. It was the piece discussed in the review, not an earlier work by Mr. Adams, “Become Ocean.”
match_headline: Review: A Pulitzer Sequel for Orchestra, Packed With Drama in Microcosm

text: An article on Saturday highlighting five standout jazz performances from the past month misspelled the surname of the DIVA Jazz Orchestra’s bandleader. She is Sherrie Maricle, not Miracle. The article also incorrectly described Noriko Ueda’s role in the band; she is the bassist, not the pianist.
match_headline: March in Live Jazz: 5 Standout Shows

text: An obituary on Saturday about the specialty-foods retailer Andrew Balducci misstated the date of Mr. Balducci’s birth in 1925. It was Aug. 3, not Aug. 23. It also misidentified who conceived a mail-order catalog. It was Mr. Balducci’s wife, not his mother.
match_headline: Andrew Balducci, Who Turned a Market Into a Food Mecca, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Canadian gold-mining magnate Peter Munk misspelled the name of a company he controlled. It is Trizec Properties, not Trizac.
match_headline: Peter Munk, 90, Dies; Built World’s Biggest Gold Mining Company

text: An obituary on Monday about the cowboy poet Elizabeth Ebert misstated the location of Lemmon, S.D., relative to Thunder Hawk, S.D. It is about 10 miles west of Thunder Hawk, not east.
match_headline: Elizabeth Ebert, ‘Grand Dame of Cowboy Poetry,’ Dies at 93

text: An earlier version of a headline with these corrections misstated the date on which the corrections appeared in print. They appeared on April 3, 2018, not March 3. (Go ahead. Snicker.)
match_headline: Corrections: March 31, 2018

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a recent surge in the popularity of e-cigarettes misstated the proportion of high school seniors who told the 2017 Monitoring the Future survey on adolescent drug use that they vaped daily. The survey found that 11 percent of seniors had vaped nicotine in the previous 30 days and that 24 percent of those students reported vaping daily. The survey did not find that 24 percent of high school seniors overall reported vaping daily.
match_headline: ‘I Can’t Stop’: Schools Struggle With Vaping Explosion

text: An article on Monday about how a Times photographer captured the cover picture of Defense Secretary Jim Mattis for Sunday’s Magazine misstated the official with whom Mr. Mattis was meeting when the photograph was taken. It was the defense minister of Estonia, not Montenegro.
match_headline: How a Photographer Got a Rare Shot of James Mattis

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a New York State effort to create a state-run retirement plan for private sector workers misidentified one of the states creating a similar program. It is Vermont, not Virginia.
match_headline: New York Envisions a State-Run Retirement Plan for Private Workers

text: An obituary on Monday about the corporate raider Samuel Belzberg misstated the name of a brother with whom Mr. Belzberg founded First City Financial in 1963. He is William, not Robert.
match_headline: Samuel Belzberg, Corporate Raider in a Family Dynasty, Dies at 89

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s plan to deploy the National Guard to the southern border misstated part of the immigration strategy described by Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the White House spokeswoman. She urged closing legal loopholes, not passing them.
match_headline: Trump Plans to Send National Guard to the Mexican Border

text: An article on Monday about the New York Mets’ Sunday game against the St. Louis Cardinals misstated the number of innings Steven Matz pitched. It was four, not five.
match_headline: Mets Off to a Roaring Start, With a Tinge of Sadness

text: Because of an editing error, a book review on Wednesday about Asne Seierstad’s “Two Sisters,” which chronicles the story of two Norwegian girls who joined the Islamic State, misstated the given name of the author of “SCUM Manifesto.” She was Valerie Solanas, not Valeria.
match_headline: ‘Two Sisters,’ About Teenage Girls Who Left Norway to Fight With ISIS

text: An editorial on Tuesday about voting rights misstated the length of time between the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments to the Constitution and the passage of the Voting Rights Act. It was 97 years, not more than a century.
match_headline: What the Supreme Court Doesn’t Get About Racism

text: An editorial on Wednesday about Gaza misstated when Israel will celebrate the 70th anniversary of its independence. It will begin on the evening of April 18, not on May 14.
match_headline: Israel Courts Catastrophe in Gaza Protests

text: An article on Sunday about the bail bond industry misstated the amount of bonds underwritten by AIA Bail Bond Insurance Company in 2016. It was more than $800 million, not more than $800 billion.
match_headline: When Bail Feels Less Like Freedom, More Like Extortion

text: An article on Thursday about economic conditions in Hungary referred incorrectly to the number of Hungarians who have found work in the European Union. It is as many as 350,000, not roughly 350,000.
match_headline: An Economic Miracle in Hungary, or Just a Mirage?

text: An article on Wednesday about cities and states that are mounting a court challenge to the federal government’s plan to add a citizenship question to the 2020 census misattributed a quotation criticizing the Trump administration. It was Representative Jerrold Nadler, Democrat of New York, who called the move “a brazen attempt by the Trump administration to cheat on the census,” not Ellen F. Rosenblum, Oregon’s attorney general.
ref_headline: a brazen attempt by the Trump administration to cheat on the census,
match_headline: Cities and States Mount Court Challenge to Census Question on Citizenship

text: An article on Thursday about challenges to Representative Paul D. Ryan, the speaker of the House, in his home district in Wisconsin referred incorrectly to the occupation of Cathy Myers, a Democratic candidate. She is currently a schoolteacher, not a former schoolteacher.
match_headline: Can Paul Ryan Be Defeated? Maybe Not, but His Race Is ‘a Circus’

text: Because of a production error, the solutions in Wednesday and Thursday’s paper for the mini crossword were incorrect. The correct solutions appear on Page A3.

An article on Wednesday about a plan to build a “smart city” near Boston called Union Point described incorrectly the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s involvement. M.I.T. has discussed participating in the project but there is no formal agreement in place.
match_headline: Building a Connected City From the Ground Up

text: An article on Thursday about Minnesota Duluth’s unlikely run in the N.C.A.A. hockey tournament misidentified the interstate that connects St. Paul and Duluth. It is Interstate 35, not 95.
match_headline: From Thin Ice to Frozen Four: The Unlikely Saga of Minnesota Duluth

text: A chart with an article on March 25 about the benefits of setting up a trust implied incorrectly that revocable trusts can protect assets against claims in divorce. Irrevocable trusts can potentially protect assets; revocable trusts can be set up for a wide variety of purposes, but do not protect against such claims.
match_headline: Life After Your Death? Here’s Why You Should Have a Trust

text: An obituary on Thursday about Janka Nabay, a singer, songwriter and bandleader from Sierra Leone, misstated the name of the country’s lingua franca. It is Krio, not Kiro.
match_headline: Janka Nabay, 54, Dies; Carried an African Dance Music Worldwide

text: An article on March 29 about efforts under Ben Carson, the secretary of housing and urban development, to roll back Obama administration attempts to enforce fair housing rules referred incorrectly to a provision inserted into a 2018 spending bill. The provision barred HUD — not local governments — from using federal funding to create plans to integrate racially divided neighborhoods.
match_headline: Under Ben Carson, HUD Scales Back Fair Housing Enforcement

text: An article on Friday about the safety of Tesla’s Autopilot system misidentified the Alfa Romeo model that was named the 2018 Motor Trend Car of the Year. It is the Giulia, not the Giulietta.
match_headline: With Tesla in a Danger Zone, Can Model 3 Carry It to Safety?

text: An article on Friday about charges brought against Conor McGregor, the Ultimate Fighting Championship lightweight champion, misstated the type of event at which Mr. McGregor jumped into a cage to celebrate a friend’s victory. It was a Bellator — not a U.F.C. — event.
match_headline: Conor McGregor Is Charged With Assault Before UFC 223

text: An article on Page 17 about a new documentary focused on the musician Grace Jones omitted part of the title of the film. It is “Grace Jones: Bloodlight and Bami,” not “Bloodlight and Bami.”
match_headline: Grace Jones on a Lifetime of Doing Whatever She Pleases

text: An article on Page 4 about new social and financial challenges facing colleges and universities misstates the number of countries in which Northeastern University has students working overseas. It is 136, not 36.
match_headline: With Changing Students and Times, Colleges Are Going Back to School

text: An article on Page 6 about the growing popularity of pop-up classes misspells the city in which James Madison University is located. It is Harrisonburg, Va., not Harrisburg.
match_headline: Pop-Ups Offer Classes on Today’s Hot Topics

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the influential Republican fund-raiser Anna Chennault misstated the type of dress Ms. Chennault was wearing in her memoir photographs where she appeared with her husband. It was a cheongsam, not an ao dai.
match_headline: Anna Chennault, Behind-the-Scenes Force in Washington, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on March 30 about the Renaissance scholar Barbara Lewalski misstated where Ms. Lewalski earned a master’s degree. It was from the University of Chicago, not from Kansas State Teachers College.
match_headline: Barbara Lewalski, 87, Milton Scholar and Barrier Breaker, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Friday about the bridal gown designer Amsale Aberra misstated Ms. Aberra’s relationship to a relative who lived in Boston when she moved there. It was her half sister, not her stepsister.
match_headline: Amsale Aberra, Trendsetting Bridal Gown Designer, Is Dead at 64

text: An article on Monday about a bus crash that killed 15 members of a Canadian hockey team misspelled the name of a former coach of the team. He is Dean Brockman, not Bookman. It also misstated the given name of a resident who has hosted the team’s players in the past. He is Devin Cannon, not David. The article, relying on incorrect information from the chief coroner of Saskatchewan, also misidentified one of the victims killed in the crash. He was Parker Tobin, not Xavier Labelle.
match_headline: A Town That Lives for Hockey Is Devastated by Humboldt Broncos’ Deaths

text: An article on Thursday about gains made in solar power capacity worldwide overstated the amount by which solar energy has increased. Solar accounted for more than a third of all net new power capacity added worldwide in 2017, not more than a third of all electricity generated.
match_headline: Solar Power Is Burning Bright. But It’s Hardly Twilight for Fossil Fuels.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Central American migrants traveling through Mexico incorrectly rendered the name of the group that organized the caravan. The group is Pueblo Sin Fronteras, not People Without Borders.
match_headline: Inside an Immigrant Caravan: Women and Children, Fleeing Violence

text: An article on Saturday about recent protests by Palestinians misstated the number of Palestinians killed in demonstrations in Gaza on Friday as well as the number who died in a demonstration a week earlier. Nine people died in the protest on Friday, not 10, and 22 people died in the previous week, not 21.
match_headline: Nine Killed in Gaza as Palestinian Protesters Face Off With Israeli Soldiers

text: An article on Saturday about President Trump’s resistance to fire his Environmental Protection Agency administrator, Scott Pruitt, misstated the day on which 64 House Democrats called for Mr. Pruitt’s resignation. It was Friday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Chief of Staff Advised a Resistant Trump to Fire the E.P.A. Chief

text: An article on March 30 about a crash that killed a family in Northern California, using information provided by the Mendocino County Sheriff’s Office, incorrectly stated Sierra Hart’s age at the time of the crash. She was 15 years old, not 12.
match_headline: Devonte Hart, Boy in Famous Photo, Feared Dead With Family in S.U.V. Plunge

text: An article on Sunday about George Parros, the N.H.L.’s senior vice president for player safety, misquoted Mr. Parros’s comments comparing the way hockey is played now to how it was during his career. He said, “There was a lot more headhunting going on, head shots, perhaps more reckless behavior.” He did not say there is more reckless behavior in current games.
ref_headline: There was a lot more headhunting going on, head shots, perhaps more reckless behavior.
match_headline: George Parros Used to be an N.H.L. Enforcer. Now He’s in Charge of Player Safety.

text: An article on Sunday about restrictive rules governing personal conduct faced by cheerleaders in the N.F.L. misstated the surname of a radio host who recently wrote a column in The Boston Globe. She is Margery Eagan, not Evan.
match_headline: Is It Time to Rethink the Rules for N.F.L. Cheerleaders?

text: An article on Saturday about a star-studded Passover Seder referred incorrectly to the writers of the song “Over the Rainbow.” They were children of Jewish immigrants to America; they were not immigrants themselves.
match_headline: There’s No Seder Like a Showbiz Seder

text: An obituary on Sunday about the sportswoman and firearms authority Sheila Link misspelled the name of the company where Mrs. Link’s father was an executive. It is Aramco, not Aramaco.
match_headline: Sheila Link, Sportswoman and Firearms Authority, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Saturday about the jazz pianist Cecil Taylor misspelled the given name of one of the composers whose music Mr. Taylor enjoyed. It is Gyorgy Ligeti, not Gyorgi.
match_headline: Cecil Taylor, Pianist Who Defied Jazz Orthodoxy, Is Dead at 89

text: An obituary on Friday about the actress Susan Anspach misidentified the writer of the play “The Journey of the Fifth Horse.” It was written by Ronald Ribman, not Turgenev. (The play was an adaptation of Turgenev’s short story, “The Diary of a Superfluous Man.”) It also misstated when Ms. Anspach’s all-nude final scene in “Hair” took place. It was at the end of the first act, not at the end of the show.
ref_headline: The Journey of the Fifth Horse.
match_headline: Susan Anspach, 75, Dies; Daring Actress in Maverick Films

text: An obituary on Saturday about Daniel Akaka, a former Democratic senator from Hawaii, misidentified the unit Mr. Akaka served in during World War II. He served in the 100th Infantry Battalion, not the 100th Infantry Division.
match_headline: Daniel Akaka, Former Democratic Senator From Hawaii, Dies at 93

text: An article on Saturday about medical devices made in China that a Trump administration proposal is targeting for a potential 25 percent tariff erroneously included Pfizer among a group of manufacturers that declined to comment on the proposal. Pfizer was not contacted for comment by The New York Times.
match_headline: Why Trump’s Tariffs Could Raise the Cost of a Hip Replacement

text: An article on Tuesday about privacy and free online content misstated Google’s policy on scanning the content of its Gmail service as a way of directing advertising to specific users. It no longer scans emails for advertising purposes; it discontinued that practice last year.
match_headline: Failed by Facebook, We’ll Return to the Scene of the Crime. We Always Do.

text: An article on Tuesday about accusations of plagiarism against a member of the National Academy of Medicine misspelled the surname of the dean of the F. Edward Hébert School of Medicine at the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences. He is Dr. Arthur Kellermann, not Kellerman.
match_headline: Doctors Urge Elite Academy to Expel a Member Over Charges of Plagiarism

text: A review on Tuesday about the play “This Flat Earth” incorrectly described the musical recording being played on stage. It is a Bach cello suite, not a cello concerto.
match_headline: Review: ‘This Flat Earth’ Traces Childhood Fears No Parent Can Allay

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the choreographer Donald McKayle misidentified the actor who starred in the 1999 Broadway show “It Ain’t Nothin’ but the Blues.” It was Gregory Porter, not Gregory Hines.
ref_headline: It Ain’t Nothin’ but the Blues.
match_headline: Donald McKayle, 87, Broadway and Modern Dance Choreographer, Dies

text: An article on Tuesday about evidence that Syrian forces led by President Bashar al-Assad targeted foreign journalists misidentified a group that aims to build war-crimes cases against the Syrian government. It is the Commission — not Committee — for International Justice and Accountability.
match_headline: Syrian Forces Aimed to Kill Journalists, U.S. Court Is Told

text: An article on Thursday about the inquiry into the cause of a highway accident in Saskatchewan misstated the name of a Canadian federal department. It is Transport Canada, not Transpost Canada.
match_headline: A Fateful Crossroads: What Caused the Crash That Killed 16 Canadians?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Mike Pompeo’s ascent to the role of secretary of state misstated Mr. Pompeo’s role on the House Intelligence Committee after the Benghazi attacks in 2012. He was a member of the committee, not its chairman.
match_headline: Pompeo Vows to Embrace Diplomacy, but Pledges Tougher Line on Russia

text: An article on April 5 about candidates running for Paul D. Ryan’s seat in Congress misstated the support the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee provided to Randy Bryce, a candidate seeking the party’s nomination in the race. The committee has targeted Mr. Ryan’s district, but has not endorsed in the Democratic primary.
match_headline: Paul Ryan Is Leaving. Who’s Running for His Seat?

text: An article on April 4 about Nasim Najafi Aghdam, the woman who shot three people at YouTube’s headquarters, misquoted a comment made by Ms. Aghdam in one of her YouTube videos. She said, “This is what they are doing to vegan activists and many other people who try to promote healthy, humane and smart living,” not “what they are doing to weekend activists.” The article also misspelled the name of the city in California containing Ms. Aghdam’s last known address. It is Menifee, not Menefee.
ref_headline: This is what they are doing to vegan activists and many other people who try to promote healthy, humane and smart living,
match_headline: Police Identify Woman Who Wounded 3 at YouTube and Killed Herself; Motive Is Unclear

text: An article on Thursday about a raid of the International Biathlon Union misstated the location of the organization’s headquarters. It is in Salzburg, not Vienna.
match_headline: In Austria, Police Raids Stemming From Russian Sports Corruption Inquiries

text: A review on Wednesday of the book “Natural Causes” by Barbara Ehrenreich misstated the profession of Helen Vendler. She is a critic, not a poet.
match_headline: Barbara Ehrenreich Urges Us to Accept, Accept the Dying of the Light

text: An obituary on Thursday about the writer and actress Lois Wheeler Snow misstated, at one point, the number of years between Ms. Snow’s first and last visits to China. It was 30, not 50. (As correctly noted elsewhere in the obituary, her first visit was in 1970 and her last in 2000.)
match_headline: Lois Wheeler Snow, Critic of Human Rights Abuses in China, Dies at 97

text: A review on Friday about the HBO documentary “Elvis Presley: The Searcher” misstated the year of a film Elvis starred in. The movie, “King Creole,” was released in 1958, not 1956.
match_headline: Review: A Reverent Elvis Doc Separates the Trailblazer From His Tragedy

text: A review on Friday about the 1983 film “Liquid Sky” misstated the status of a club that was part of the club scene in Lower Manhattan in the late 1970s and early 1980s. The Pyramid Club is still open; it has not closed.
match_headline: Revisiting the Downtown Scene Through Alien Eyes in ‘Liquid Sky’

text: A review on Friday about the documentary “‘Grace Jones: Bloodlight and Bami” misstated the title of one of Ms. Jones’ hit singles. It is “Pull Up to the Bumper,” not “Pull Up to My Bumper.”
match_headline: Review: ‘Grace Jones: Bloodlight and Bami’ Finds the Model, Singer, Actress, Person

text: An obituary on Thursday about the aviator Fran Bera referred incorrectly to the Piper Aztec plane that Ms. Bera flew when she broke an altitude record. The Piper Aztec she flew had two piston engines; not a turboprop.
match_headline: Fran Bera, Competitive, Record-Breaking Aviator, Is Dead at 93

text: An article about the musical culture at American Legion Post 398 in Harlem misspells the surname of one of the organists in the Harlem Groove Band. He is Judd Nielsen, not Judd Neilsen.
match_headline: Hot Jazz in a Veterans Club Basement in Harlem

text: An article on April 8 about Senator Lisa Murkowski gave the incorrect name of the law school she attended. It is Willamette University College of Law, not Willamette University Law School
match_headline: How Lisa Murkowski Mastered Trump’s Washington

text: An article last Sunday about the importance of writing a will misstated the percentage of Americans who are subject to the federal estate tax. It is less than 0.2 percent, not 4 percent.
match_headline: What It Was Like to Finally Write My Will

text: An article on Sunday about an abortion rights bill in Argentina misstated the given name of a researcher at the Center for the Study of the State and Society. She is Mariana Romero, not Marcela. It also misstated the given name of a sociologist. She is Dora Barrancos, not Nora.
match_headline: Legal Abortion in Argentina? A Long Shot Is Suddenly Within Reach

text: An article on Sunday about a village in the Netherlands that added musical rumble strips to a newly paved section of highway misstated the length of the section. It is about 16 miles long, not 124 miles.
match_headline: Dutch ‘Singing Road’ Silenced After Villagers Complain: ‘I’m Going Nuts’

text: An article on Sunday about Russia’s reaction to limited American-led airstrikes in Syria misstated part of the name of a Russian current affairs magazine. It is Yezhednevny Zhurnal, not Yezhenedelny Zhurnal.
match_headline: In Moscow, a Sense of Relief After a Limited Syria Attack

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about regulators’ apparent lack of understanding of Facebook misidentified a member of the Senate attending a hearing with Mark Zuckerberg. It was Senator Roy Blunt, Republican of Missouri, not Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana.
match_headline: Knowledge Gap Hinders Ability of Congress to Regulate Silicon Valley

text: An article on Thursday about the resignation of Paymon Rouhanifard as superintendent of schools in Camden, N.J., based on incorrect information from the Camden school district, misstated test scores and the years they were achieved at the Bonsall Elementary School. Four percent of students scored proficient in English and 3 percent scored proficient in math at the school the year before it was taken over by Uncommon Schools. It is not the case that no students scored proficient on either test the year after Uncommon took over.
match_headline: Camden Superintendent Who Led Turnaround Is Stepping Down

text: An article on Monday about an effort by Maurice R. Greenberg, the former chairman of A.I.G., to curtail financial regulations misstated the name of an organization led by Joseph P. Borg. It is the North American Securities Administrators Association, not the National American Securities Administrators Association. The article also misidentified the law used to challenge Richard A. Grasso, the onetime head of the New York Stock Exchange, over his pay. It was the state’s Not-for-Profit Corporation Law, not the Martin Act.
match_headline: Wall Street Titan Takes Aim at Law That Tripped Him Up

text: An article on Saturday about tips for filing tax returns misstated the contribution limit for a Simplified Employee Pension plan, known as an SEP I.R.A., in 2017. It is $54,000, not $55.000.
match_headline: Tax Dawdlers, It’s the Last Minute. Here Are Tips on Filing.

text: An article on Saturday about public pushback against a proposed donation by the billionaire Stephen A. Schwarzman to the high school he attended misstated the date on which Mr. Schwarzman, while speaking to a gathering of school superintendents in Nashville, announced the donation. It was Feb. 15, not Feb. 14.
match_headline: A Public Outcry Against a Wall Street Titan’s Name on a High School

text: An article last Tuesday about technologies used in astronomy now being applied to prevent poaching misstated the animal order to which Riverine rabbits belong. They are lagomorphs, not rodents.
match_headline: How Do You Count Endangered Species? Look to the Stars

text: A review on Monday about Beyoncé’s performance at Coachella misstated the song recorded by Nina Simone that Beyoncé featured during her set. It was “Lilac Wine,” not “Strange Fruit.”
match_headline: Review: Beyoncé Is Bigger Than Coachella

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump’s decision to reject new sanctions against Russia, relying on information provided by a senior official at the Department of Homeland Security, referred incorrectly to an increase of Russian online trolling activity that occurred around the time the United States launched airstrikes against Syria. The increase was noted among Russian hashtags, not bots. Additionally, the information should not have been attributed to the department’s spokesman, Tyler Q. Houlton.
match_headline: Trump Declines to Add Sanctions Against Russians, Contradicting Haley

text: An article on Tuesday about the 2018 Pulitzer Prizes misspelled the surname of the editor of pictures for Reuters. He is Ahmad Masood, not Maood.
match_headline: 2018 Pulitzer Prize Winners: Full List

text: An article on Tuesday about a Senate bill that would have exempted businesses on tribal lands from federal labor standards misstated how many more votes were needed to end a filibuster blocking a package of bills that included the Tribal Labor Sovereignty Act. The number was five, not six.
match_headline: Senate Bill to Curtail Labor Rights on Tribal Land Falls Short

text: An article on Tuesday about the results of the Boston Marathon misidentified the runner who said, “I was in third or fourth, and I thought, ‘I probably shouldn’t drop out.’” It was Desiree Linden, not Shalane Flanagan. Ms. Linden went on to win the women’s race.
ref_headline: I was in third or fourth, and I thought, ‘I probably shouldn’t drop out.’
match_headline: Desiree Linden and Yuki Kawauchi Pull Off Upsets in Rainy Boston Marathon

text: A review on Saturday about the Massenet opera “Cendrillon” referred incorrectly to the history of the word “carosse,” which means royal coach. It is an archaic French word, not a word from the Old French language.
match_headline: Review: The Stepchild of Cinderella Operas Finally Makes It to the Met

text: An obituary on Monday about the filmmaker Milos Forman misstated where he shot the film “Amadeus.” It was Czechoslovakia — not the Czech Republic, which did not exist until 1993, nine years after “Amadeus” was released. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Forman’s biological father. He moved from Czechoslovakia to Ecuador, not Peru, but he was not living in South America when Mr. Forman found him in the 1960s; he had moved again, to New York, in 1945.
match_headline: Milos Forman, 86, Dies; Won Oscars for ‘Cuckoo’s Nest’ and ‘Amadeus’

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the actor R. Lee Ermey described incorrectly an action by Mr. Ermey’s character, Gunnery Sergeant Hartman, in the film “Full Metal Jacket.” Sgt. Hartman punches a recruit in the gut; he does not knee him in the groin.
match_headline: R. Lee Ermey, Harsh Drill Instructor in ‘Full Metal Jacket,’ Dies at 74

text: An article on Wednesday about Russia’s defiance in the face of pressure from Western countries misstated the date of a BBC interview with Sergei V. Lavrov, Russia’s foreign minister. It was broadcast Tuesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: The Fight With the West Is Isolating Russia. But That Isn’t Stopping Putin.

text: An article on Wednesday about an announced one-day shutdown of 8,000 Starbucks locations misstated the annual revenue of all of Starbucks’s stores in the United States, Canada and Latin America. Those stores generated $14 billion in revenue in the company’s most recent fiscal year, not $1.3 billion.
match_headline: Starbucks to Close 8,000 U.S. Stores for Racial-Bias Training After Arrests

text: An article on Tuesday about public school classrooms referred incorrectly to the base salary of teachers in North Las Vegas, Nev. While Kelsey Pavelka earned roughly $33,000 for an academic year, after leaving her job with the district in June 2017, the current base salary for teachers in North Las Vegas is $40,900, not $33,000.
match_headline: 25-Year-Old Textbooks and Holes in the Ceiling: Inside America’s Public Schools

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the strong performance of the Marlins’ pitcher Jarlin Garcia against the Yankees described incorrectly the circumstances of Garcia’s second major league start. His first start was a home game in Miami against the Mets; he was not “back on a New York mound on Tuesday” when he faced the Yankees. The article also misstated Garcia’s pitching hand. He is a left-hander, not a right-hander.
ref_headline: back on a New York mound on Tuesday
match_headline: Marlins’ Jarlin Garcia Stifles the Yankees With Ease

text: An article on Wednesday about the Mets’ first losing streak of the season described incorrectly Jose Reyes’s hitless streak. He is hitless in 11 games, not 11 at-bats. (He is hitless in 17 at-bats.)
match_headline: Nationals Send the Mets to (Gasp!) Their First Losing Streak

text: An article on Tuesday about the Mets’ late loss to the Nationals misstated the circumstances of Asdrubal Cabrera’s being thrown out at the third base in the bottom of the ninth inning. He was trying to advance to third on a wild pitch; he was not trying to stretch a double into a triple.
match_headline: Mets’ Bullpen Collapses, Wasting Jacob deGrom’s Strong Night

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the sculptor Hans Van de Bovenkamp described incorrectly a lamp depicted in the photo. It was an Arco floor lamp by Flos, not a Knoll piece.
match_headline: From Doodling on Napkins to Acres of Art

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Bill Nack, a sportswriter who wrote frequently about horse racing, misstated the date of the 1973 Belmont Stakes. It was June 9, not June 10.
match_headline: Bill Nack, Who Covered the Horses From Up Close, Dies at 77

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Mary Regula, the founder of the National First Ladies’ Library, misspelled her maiden name. It was Rogusky, not Rugosky.
match_headline: Mary Regula, Founder of Library Saluting First Ladies, Dies at 91

text: An article on Thursday about the impact of a trade dispute between the United States and China on the computer chip manufacturer Qualcomm misstated the title of Guan Zhisheng. He is an associate professor at Sun Yat-sen University, not an assistant professor.
match_headline: Qualcomm May Be Collateral Damage in a U.S.-China Trade War

text: An article on Thursday about Judge Kimba M. Wood, who presided over a hearing related to President Trump’s attorney Michael D. Cohen, described incorrectly Judge Wood’s marital history. Michael Kramer was her second husband, not her first. The article also misstated the connection between her current husband, Frank E. Richardson, and George Soros’s Quantum Industrial Holdings. Mr. Richardson once served as an unpaid member of an investment advisory committee for the group; he did not sit on its board.
match_headline: Hearing the Cohen Case: A Soft-Spoken Judge Who ‘Carries a Big Stick’

text: A review on Saturday about works by the Martha Graham Dance Company misstated the name of an award the company grants. It is the Martha Graham Award, not the Martha Graham Award for Lasting Impact to the Field of Dance.
match_headline: Review: For the Martha Graham Company, Opposites Attract

text: An obituary on Thursday about Jean McFaddin, who as Macy’s events planner was in charge of the store’s Thanksgiving Day parade, misstated the name of a college in Missouri that she attended. It is Stephens College, not St. Stephen’s College.
match_headline: Jean McFaddin, Who Made the Macy’s Parade What It Is, Dies at 75

text: An article on Friday about Puerto Rico’s financial situation since Hurricane Maria misstated the amount of debt the country has accumulated. It is more than $70 billion, not more than $70 million.
match_headline: Hurricane Aid Has Eased Puerto Rico’s Finances. It May Not Be Enough.

text: An article on Friday about memos made by the former F.B.I. director James Comey documenting his interactions with the president rendered a date incorrectly in quoting one of Mr. Comey’s notes. He wrote that he typed the notes “upon exiting Trump Tower on 1/6/17,” not 1/5/17.
match_headline: Comey Memos Provide Intimate Look Into Trump Presidency

text: An article on Thursday about a settlement between American Media Inc. and Karen McDougal, a former playboy model, described incorrectly one provision of the agreement. Under the deal’s terms, A.M.I. has the right to up to $75,000 of the profits from any deal Ms. McDougal makes in the next year for her story about an affair she claims to have had with Donald J. Trump before he became president. The provision does not apply to any deal made after that.
match_headline: Ex-Playboy Model, Freed From Contract, Can Discuss Alleged Trump Affair

text: An article on Friday about damaged engines on multiple Southwest Airlines planes misstated the type and frequency of inspections of the engine of an American Airlines Boeing 767 that failed in 2016. According to a National Transportation Safety Board report, the inspections used eddy current and fluorescent penetrant techniques; they were not visual inspections. The article also misstated the last time an inspection of the engine was conducted. According to the report, the last inspection was conducted in 2011, not between flights.
match_headline: Engine on Southwest Jet Not the Only One to Develop Cracks

text: An article on Friday about the Yankees’ win over the Blue Jays misstated the direction of Aaron Judge’s seventh-inning homer. He hit it to left field, not right.
match_headline: Giancarlo Stanton Is Bumped Down, and Yankees Edge Blue Jays

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the N.B.A. playoffs misidentified the team the San Antonio Spurs played on Thursday. It was the Warriors, not the Nuggets.
match_headline: Gregg Popovich Is Absent for Game 3 After Wife’s Death

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the sex assault trial of Bill Cosby misstated the legal teams for which two toxicologists testified. Dr. Timothy P. Rohrig testified for the prosecution, not the defense. Dr. Harry A. Milman was the toxicologist for the defense.
match_headline: Toxicologists Clash on Drug in Cosby Sex Assault Trial

text: An article on Page 14 about different renditions of the tale of Orpheus misstates the name of a chorus presenting “Orfeo ed Euridice.” It is MasterVoices, not Masterworks Chorale.
match_headline: Past and Present, the Orpheus Myth Makes Us Rethink Music

text: A picture with an article on Page 121 about people who have died of AIDS-related illnesses was published in error. The image showed David Wolfe, the retired fashion consultant, not David Wolfe, the stage manager.
match_headline: Rue St. Denis, Longtime Outfitter to TV and Chic People, Is Closing

text: An article on Page 88 about New York Times writers revisiting pieces they wrote in the 1980s refers incorrectly to the job title of Ben Brantley; he is the co-chief theater critic, not the chief theater critic.
match_headline: This Season’s Leather Pieces, Inspired by ’80s New York

text: An article on Page 102 about the art scene in the East Village in the early 1980s misspells the surname of a film director; he is John Cassavetes, not Cassevetes.
match_headline: That Humble Object of Desire

text: An article on Page 116 about the AIDS crisis in New York City in the 1980s gave an incorrect subtitle for a memoir by Paul Monette; the book is “Becoming a Man: Half a Life Story,” not “Becoming a Man: Half a Lifetime.”
ref_headline: Becoming a Man: Half a Life Story,
match_headline: New York Today: A Look Back at a Grittier City

text: A picture caption with an article on April 8 about a national identification system being developed by India misstated what was being scanned during a security check. It was a man’s irises, not his retinas.
match_headline: ‘Big Brother’ in India Requires Fingerprint Scans for Food, Phones and Finances

text: An article last Sunday about investing in bonds misquoted Peter Chiappinelli, a member of the asset allocation team at the investment management firm GMO. He said that investing in a portfolio of bonds that is increasing its duration when interest rates are “at historic lows is the exact opposite of prudence.” He did not say that adding more duration when “rates are rising is the exact opposite of prudence.”
ref_headline: at historic lows is the exact opposite of prudence.
match_headline: Warren Buffett Isn’t a Fan of Bonds. But They May Be Good for You.

text: An article last Sunday on street food in Bangkok misstated the name of the organization that announced it would ban street food vendors. It is the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration, not Authority.
match_headline: Where to Find Bangkok’s Best Street Food While You Can

text: An article on April 8 about China’s attempts to crack down on sellers of banned books in Hong Kong described incorrectly recent changes to media control. The Communist Party’s Central Propaganda Department will have oversight of all print media, not all media. A new government administration will have control of radio and TV outlets.
match_headline: The Case of Hong Kong’s Missing Booksellers

text: A review on April 8 about “I Got It!,” a picture book by David Wiesner, misstated the number of illustrators who have won three Caldecott Medals. In addition to Wiesner, Marcia Brown won three; he is not “the only three-time winner.”
match_headline: If Graphic Novels Are Hip for Adults, Why Not Picture Books?

text: An article on Monday about the number of women and Afro-Cubans chosen to serve under Cuba’s new president referred incorrectly to research about the racial balance among college students in Cuba and the United States in the 1980s. A study by Alejandro de la Fuente found that the proportion, not the number, of black Cubans with degrees compared with white Cubans was close, and that the proportion, not the number, of white college degree holders in the United States was twice that of African-Americans. The study also referred to graduation rates, not attendance.
match_headline: More Black Officials in Power in Cuba as Leadership Changes

text: An article on Monday about protests against social security changes in Nicaragua misstated the legal changes that allowed Daniel Ortega to win a presidential election in 2007. He was allowed to win by a plurality, not a simple majority.
match_headline: With Death in Streets, Nicaragua Cancels Social Security Revamp

text: An article on Sunday about the reception of Miguel Díaz-Canel Bermúdez, Cuba’s new president, described incorrectly adjustments to immigration policy under the Obama administration. President Barack Obama ended “wet foot dry foot,” a rule that allowed Cubans who arrived without visas to remain in the United States. He did not end the Cuban adjustment act.
match_headline: Cubans Doubt a Change at the Top Will Bring Change at the Bottom

text: An article on Saturday about the actress Natalie Portman’s decision to skip the Genesis Prize ceremony in Jerusalem referred incorrectly to Scarlett Johansson’s departure from the charity Oxfam. She resigned as a spokeswoman; she was not dropped.
match_headline: Natalie Portman Backs Out of Israeli Award Ceremony

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about an auction to sell historical objects in Heathrow Airport misstated how many passengers Heathrow’s Terminal 1 could accommodate when it was dedicated in 1969. It was nine million passengers a year, not a day.
match_headline: Sale at Heathrow Terminal 1. Everything Must Go.

text: An article on Sunday about Campbell Brown’s role as Facebook’s head of news partnerships erroneously included a reference to Palestinian actions as an example of the sort of far-right conspiracy stories that have plagued Facebook. In fact, Palestinian officials have acknowledged providing payments to the families of Palestinians killed while carrying out attacks on Israelis or convicted of terrorist acts and imprisoned in Israel; that is not a conspiracy theory.
match_headline: Is Facebook’s Campbell Brown a Force to Be Reckoned With? Or Is She Fake News?

text: An article on Saturday about President Trump’s criticism of OPEC and rising oil prices misstated, in one reference, a recent increase in gasoline prices. They have risen 33 cents in the last year, not the last month.
match_headline: Trump Criticizes OPEC, Calling Oil Prices ‘Artificially’ High

text: An article on Wednesday about budget airlines reinvigorating smaller airports on the outskirts of major cities misstated the distance between Seattle Tacoma International Airport and Paine Field. They are about 37 miles apart, not 12.
match_headline: Stewart Airport Adopts a New Identity: New York Area’s Budget Flight Hub

text: An article on Friday about the hesitance of the International Association of Athletics Federations to allow Russian athletes to compete in major track and field events misstated Sebastian Coe’s title within the organization during an extortion scheme. He was vice president, not senior vice president.
match_headline: Inside the Deadlock Over Russia’s Track and Field Athletes

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about the Actors’ Equity Association’s decision to retire the term “Gypsy Robe” misidentified the “Cats” cast member wearing the garment. He is Jeremy Davis, not Jeremy Ford.
match_headline: Term of Affection? Ethnic Slur? Theater Union Decides That ‘Gypsy’ Must Go.

text: An editorial on Monday about what the special counsel’s investigation has revealed about business misconduct referred imprecisely to the reason prosecutors were able to persuade a judge to allow them to seize documents from the president’s lawyer Michael Cohen. The prosecutors had to show the judge that Mr. Cohen’s files probably contained evidence of criminal activity, not that he himself had committed a crime, although he is under criminal investigation.
match_headline: Mueller Guides Us Through the Swamp

text: An obituary on Friday about the record producer and songwriter Ronald Dunbar omitted the name of one of his survivors. In addition to those named, he is survived by a daughter, Ginger Atherton.
match_headline: Ronald Dunbar, 78, Producer and Grammy-Winning Songwriter, Dies

text: An obituary on April 15 about the actor Tim O’Connor misidentified the county in New Jersey where Glen Wild Lake, the site of an island where he and his wife lived for many years, is located. It is Passaic, not Essex.
match_headline: Tim O’Connor, Complex Resident of ‘Peyton Place,’ Dies at 90

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the confirmation hearing for Mike Pompeo misstated when President Trump said that Senator Rand Paul has “never let us down” and that “he’s a good man.” It was last week, not Monday.
match_headline: After Late Vote Switch, Senate Panel Approves Pompeo for Secretary of State

text: An article on April 4 misstated, in one instance, the name of the group that compared fuel economy standards for different countries. It is the International Council on Clean Transportation, not the International Center on Clean Transportation.
match_headline: Calling Car Pollution Standards ‘Too High,’ E.P.A. Sets Up Fight With California

text: An article on Tuesday about Darius Bazley, a young N.B.A. prospect, attributed an erroneous distinction to Bazley. He was the first player since Latavious Williams to join the N.B.A.’s development league directly out of high school; he was not the first player to do so.
match_headline: Darius Bazley Charts Yet Another Path to the N.B.A.: The Development League

text: An obituary on April 2 about Gen. Efraín Ríos Montt, the former dictator of Guatemala who was convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity in 2013, misstated the length of his trial. It was about two months, not five. The obituary also misstated the year General Ríos Montt’s son Homero died — it was 1984, not 1982 — and overstated what is known about the helicopter crash in which he was killed.
