Most reports at the time said that the helicopter experienced mechanical failure; it has not been determined that guerrillas shot it down.
match_headline: Efraín Ríos Montt, Guatemalan Dictator Convicted of Genocide, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Monday about Carolyn Jacobson, a champion of women’s union rights, misstated the year she graduated from the School of Industrial and Labor Relations at Cornell University. It was 1972, not 1975.
match_headline: Carolyn Jacobson, Champion of Women’s Union Rights, Dies at 67

text: An obituary on Monday about the Mexican author Sergio Pitol referred incorrectly to the Polish writer Witold Gombrowicz, whose works Mr. Pitol translated. While he was nominated for a Nobel Prize, he was not a Nobel laureate.
match_headline: Sergio Pitol, Inventive and Honored Mexican Author, Dies at 85

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the beginning of jury deliberations in a retrial of Bill Cosby mistakenly stated that the testimony of Marguerite Jackson had been read out to the jury. It was not.
match_headline: Bill Cosby’s Fate Rests With Jury as It Begins Deliberations

text: An article on Thursday about the sports talk radio host Mike Francesa misidentified a newspaper to which Mr. Francesa recently gave an interview. It was Newsday, not The New York Post.
match_headline: Jeering, at Least From the Press Box, as Mike Francesa Returns

text: An article on Thursday about the Yankees’ win over the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday misstated the number of home runs Didi Gregorius has hit and his position among the major league leaders. He has hit nine, not 10, and is one behind the league lead, not tied with Mike Trout for the lead. The article also misstated the location on the field where Tyler Austin made a sliding catch in the seventh inning. It was down the right-field line, not the left-field line.
match_headline: Another Middling Outing by Sonny Gray Is Enough for the Yankees

text: An article on Wednesday about Matt Harvey’s performance in the Mets’ win over the St. Louis Cardinals misspelled the surname of a player for the Cardinals. He is Dexter Fowler, not Flower.
match_headline: Matt Harvey, Demoted to Bullpen, Shows Little Growth in Mets’ Win

text: An article on Tuesday about the impact of the Brexit vote on fishermen in Britain misstated the population of Grimsby, England. It is around 88,000, not 27,000.
match_headline: In Brexit Vote, Town’s Nostalgia for Seafaring Past Muddied Its Future

text: An article on Friday about the arraignment of Andre Braddy, a middle school teacher facing sexual abuse charges, misspelled the surname of the lawyer representing Mr. Braddy. He is Andrew Stoll, not Stahl.
match_headline: Brooklyn School Grapples With Teacher’s Arrest on Sex Abuse Charges

text: An article on Friday about the Yankees victory over the Minnesota Twins misidentified the player who hit a sacrifice fly in the seventh inning. It was Aaron Hicks, not Aaron Judge.
match_headline: After a Wild Twist, Yankees Walk Off With a Series Sweep

text: An article last Sunday about the American retailer Brooks Brothers misstated where the company’s made-to-measure suits are manufactured. It is at the company’s factory in Haverhill, Mass., not in Italy.
match_headline: With a Glance Backward, Brooks Brothers Looks to the Future

text: An article on April 8 about the Arlee Warriors, Montana’s championship- winning high-school basketball team, misstated the year that Arlee, a chief of the Salish tribe, agreed to government demands that his tribe relocate. It was 1872, not 1871.
match_headline: What the Arlee Warriors Were Playing For

text: A review on April 15 about “A Dangerous Woman: American Beauty, Noted Philanthropist, Nazi Collaborator — The Life of Florence Gould,” using information taken from the book, referred incorrectly to the Associated Press war correspondent Edward Kennedy. He was not the son of Joseph Kennedy.
ref_headline: A Dangerous Woman: American Beauty, Noted Philanthropist, Nazi Collaborator — The Life of Florence Gould,
match_headline: The Amazing Life of a Robber Baron’s Daughter-in-Law, With Caveats

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a merger plan announced by Sprint and T-Mobile omitted mention of a previous merger effort by the two firms. In addition to a deal that was not completed in 2014, the two companies negotiated over a potential merger last year but failed to agree on terms. The omission was repeated in the article’s headline.
match_headline: Sprint and T-Mobile to Merge, in Bid to Remake Wireless Market

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about a new soccer stadium that will host Los Angeles F.C. misstated the color of the stadium’s seats. They are gray, not black.
match_headline: A Shiny New Front in the Battle for L.A.’s Soccer Soul

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about the outcomes of two games in the first round of the N.B.A. playoffs misidentified a Raptors player. He is DeMar DeRozan, not Kyle Lowry.
match_headline: N.H.L. Playoff Preview: Penguins and Capitals Get Reacquainted

text: An article on Sunday about the musical “Once on This Island” referred incorrectly to a natural disaster portrayed in the performance. The island depicted is suffering the effects of a hurricane, not an earthquake.
match_headline: Ravaged but Resilient: Creating ‘Once on This Island’

text: An article on Saturday about a consecutive screening of 12 Marvel movies at a movie theater in Times Square misidentified the love interest of Steve Rogers (Captain America). She is Peggy, not Betty.
match_headline: 12 Marvel Movies in 31 Hours. It Didn’t Feel Like Infinity.

text: An obituary on Sunday about Larry Harvey, the driving force behind the Burning Man festival, referred incorrectly to his former girlfriend Janet Lohr, with whom he moved to San Francisco in the 1970s. She is not an executive of Burning Man.
match_headline: Larry Harvey, the Man Behind Burning Man, Is Dead at 70

text: An obituary on Saturday about Charles Neville, the saxophonist in the New Orleans band the Neville Brothers, misstated the date of his birth. It was Dec. 28, 1938 — not 1939. (As the obituary correctly noted, he was 79.)
match_headline: Charles Neville of the Neville Brothers Is Dead at 79

text: An article on Oct. 22, 2017, about moves by Iran’s president to contain the influence of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, offered an incomplete account of the case of Reza Golpour, who the state newspaper Kayhan reported was arrested and accused of cooperating with Israeli intelligence. At the time, Mr. Golpour could not be reached for comment. From prison, where he is awaiting trial, Mr. Golpour now says that he is facing a lesser charge of “passing information to nonrelevant people,” and that no accusations against him have been proved in court.
match_headline: Iran Saps Strength of Revolutionary Guards With Arrests and Cutbacks

text: A review on April 20 about an exhibition of work by Adrian Piper at the Museum of Modern Art misstated the year Ms. Piper created “Self-Portrait as a Nice White Lady.” It was 1995, not 1985.
ref_headline: Self-Portrait as a Nice White Lady.
match_headline: Adrian Piper: The Thinking Canvas

text: A Critic’s Notebook last Wednesday about the new version of the Danish restaurant Noma misspelled the name of the section of Copenhagen where it has opened. It is Christiania, not Christiana.
match_headline: The New Noma: Frequently Asked Questions

text: An article on April 28 about Palestinians protesting along the fence between Gaza and Israel referred imprecisely to the fence. While the fence is fitted with electronic sensors to detect infiltrators, it is not an electrified fence.
match_headline: Plan to Storm Fence Gets Bloody Preview in Gaza

text: An article on Wednesday about the Armenian opposition leader, Nikol Pashinyan, referred incorrectly to Mr. Pashinyan’s party affiliation. He is a member of a small opposition alliance called Yelq; it is not the case that he has no political affiliation.
match_headline: Denied Power, Armenian Opposition Leader Urges Nationwide Strikes

text: An article on Wednesday about a lawsuit brought by Texas and six other states to end the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals described incorrectly the lawsuit’s request. The suit states that the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas has the power to “immediately rescind and cancel all DACA permits currently in existence”; it does not ask the court to do so.
ref_headline: immediately rescind and cancel all DACA permits currently in existence
match_headline: Seven States, Led by Texas, Sue to End DACA Program

text: An article on Tuesday about the Houston Astros’ pitching lineup referred incorrectly to the Boston Red Sox’ earned run average. After the Astros, the Red Sox have the next best E.R.A. in the American League, not in baseball.
match_headline: How Is the Astros’ Pitching So Good? Trevor Bauer Has Theories

text: An article on Tuesday about the musical “Hair” misstated the location of its premiere in 1967. It was at the Public Theater, not the New York Shakespeare Festival.
match_headline: ‘Hair’ 50 Years Later: Readers Tell Us When They Let the Sunshine In

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the artist Gerson Leiber, using information from a family spokesman, omitted the names of two of his survivors. In addition to his brother, Dr. Joseph Leiber, he is survived by two sisters, Martha Dermer and Sarah Stachel.
match_headline: Gerson Leiber, 96, Dies; Artist Created Museum With Designer Wife

text: An article on Thursday about the former lobbyist Matthew Freedman misstated the title of Kevin Chmielewski before he was removed from his position at the Environmental Protection Agency this year. He was deputy chief of staff, not chief of staff.
match_headline: Ex-Lobbyist for Foreign Governments Helped Plan Pruitt Trip to Australia

text: An article on Wednesday about protests over austerity measures in Puerto Rico misidentified the party that ratified the tuition increase at the University of Puerto Rico. The university ratified the increase, not the federal board that oversees Puerto Rico’s finances.
match_headline: Protest in Puerto Rico Over Austerity Measures Ends in Tear Gas

text: An article on Wednesday about the disproportionately small amount of hurricane aid Puerto Rico has received from the Department of Education described imprecisely how New York University used hurricane relief funds from the Department of Education. N.Y.U. was given funds to defray the costs of Puerto Rican students it had enrolled at the university, not to enroll Puerto Rican students temporarily.
match_headline: In Devastated Puerto Rico, Universities Get Just a Fraction of Storm Aid

text: An editorial on Wednesday about anti-Semitic comments by the Palestinian Authority president, Mahmoud Abbas, misidentified the signers of the Oslo Accords in 1993. They were Mr. Abbas, then the foreign policy aide for the Palestine Liberation Organization, and Shimon Peres, the foreign minister of Israel. The Palestinian leader Yasir Arafat and Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin of Israel attended the ceremony but did not sign the pact.
match_headline: Let Abbas’s Vile Words Be His Last as Palestinian Leader

text: An article on Thursday misidentified the inning in which Yankees pitcher Luis Severino confronted his “only trouble spot.” It was in the seventh inning, not the sixth. The article also misquoted the team’s manager, Aaron Boone. He said, “Hopefully we are proficient at helping guys develop at a better and maybe in some cases a more rapid pace,” not a “more rapid case.”
match_headline: Following Old Masters, Luis Severino Throws a Gem for the Yankees

text: An obituary on Thursday about the artist Marcia Hafif misstated her age. She was 88, not 89. The error was repeated in the headline. (As the obituary correctly noted, she was born on Aug. 15, 1929.)

An article on Friday about the nerve agent in an attack in Britain on a former Russian spy and his daughter, using information provided by the director general of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, gave an incorrect estimate for the amount used. The organization later said in a statement that the amount should be measured in milligrams, not grams, and that in any case it would not be able to estimate how much was used in the attack. (The director general originally gave an estimate of 50 to 100 grams.)
match_headline: Weapons Watchdog Corrects Estimate of Nerve Agent Used in U.K. Attack

text: An article on Wednesday about the resignation of two aides erroneously included a former policy adviser to Scott Pruitt among the people Mr. Pruitt blamed in congressional testimony for the public criticism he has faced. He did not publicly blame the adviser Samantha Dravis.
match_headline: Two Top Aides to Scott Pruitt Quit the E.P.A. Unexpectedly

text: An article on Friday about new sexual harassment rules issued by the Department of Justice misattributed a statement regarding a report on sexual harassment within the department. It was a Justice Department employee who stated that officials responded to the report by saying that the episodes it covered all occurred under the Obama administration, not Michael E. Horowitz, the department’s inspector general. The article also misstated how Mr. Horowitz believed the department would begin to respond to sexual harassment. He said that he believed the department would fire more people than it had in the past and that people who receive harsher punishments often push back, not that he believed the department would not fire more people and would be sued.
match_headline: Justice Department Releases New Sexual Harassment Guidelines

text: An article on Friday about a coming I.P.O. for the hardware company Xiaomi misstated the relationship between Alibaba and Ant Financial. They are both controlled by Jack Ma; Alibaba does not own Ant Financial. The article also misstated the given name of the chief executive of Hong Kong’s stock exchange. He is Charles Li, not Richard Li.
match_headline: Xiaomi, Chinese Gadget Maker, Opens Floodgates for Hong Kong I.P.O.s

text: An article on Friday about two projects highlighting female artists from Africa misstated the age of the artist Alka Dass. She is 25, not 23.
match_headline: Two Projects Helping Female Artists in Africa Find Their Voices

text: An article on Page 1 about the comedian Ali Wong misstates Ms. Wong’s status with the series “Fresh Off the Boat.” She used to write for it; she is not currently a writer on it. The article also refers incorrectly to Justin Hakuta’s position at a tech company. He is a vice president, but not the sole vice president.
match_headline: The Strategic Mind of Ali Wong

text: An article on Page 38 about the actor Ryan Reynolds misstates the title of Mr. Reynolds’s sitcom. It was “Two Guys, a Girl and a Pizza Place,” not “Two Girls and a Guy and a Pizza Place.”
ref_headline: Two Guys, a Girl and a Pizza Place,
match_headline: This Story Has Already Stressed Ryan Reynolds Out

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 28 about the artist Dorothea Rockburne omits the name of the artwork using conté crayon, pencil, oil, gessoed and painted white on folded linen. It is “Egyptian Painting: Sahura.”
match_headline: Dorothea Rockburne’s Ephemeral Art and Enduring Legacy

text: An article on Page 26 about the actor Benedict Cumberbatch misstates the name of a work by the writer David Nicholls. It is “One Day,” not “One Fine Day.”
match_headline: Benedict Cumberbatch Just Crossed the Last Role Off His Bucket List

text: An article on March 25 about Maui’s upcountry referred incorrectly to the reign of King David Kalakaua; he was the second-to-last reigning royal of Hawaii, not the last one. The article also misstated the location of two small towns, Lahaina and Kapalua; they are on the island’s northwest coast, not in the south.
match_headline: Where to Stay (and What to Eat) in Maui’s Upcountry

text: An obituary on April 26 about Dr. Samuel S. Epstein, an authority on carcinogens, referred incorrectly to cyclamates and nitrites. Cyclamates are used as sweeteners, not preservatives; nitrites are used to cure hot dogs, not to dye them.
match_headline: Dr. Samuel Epstein, 91, Cassandra of Cancer Prevention, Dies

text: An article on Sunday about Albert Pujols’ three thousandth hit erroneously included Roberto Clemente among the list of foreign-born players to get 3,000 hits. Clemente, who was born in Puerto Rico, was not “foreign-born.”
match_headline: Overlooked No More: Julia de Burgos, a Poet Who Helped Shape Puerto Rico’s Identity

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a traveling exhibition centered on the show “Hamilton” misspelled the name of that musical’s director. He is Thomas Kail, not Kale.
match_headline: For Those Still Hungering for ‘Hamilton,’ a New Indulgence

text: An article on Sunday about summer movie releases, using information from the film’s representatives, misstated the release date for “McQueen.” It is July 20, not July 13.
match_headline: Summer Movies 2018: Here’s What’s Coming Soon to Theaters

text: A review on Friday about an exhibition of pre-Columbian art at the Metropolitan Museum misidentified the institution where the curator Joanne Pillsbury worked before joining the Met. She was with the Getty Research Institute, not the Getty Museum.
match_headline: At the Met, All That Dazzles Is Not Just Gold — It’s Feathers, Too

text: An obituary on Saturday about Ninalee Allen Craig, the subject of the well-known photograph “American Girl in Italy,” misstated how her marriage to R. Ross Craig ended. It ended with his death, not in divorce.
match_headline: Ninalee Allen Craig, at the Center of a Famous Photograph, Dies at 90

text: An article on Tuesday about mounting pressure on President Trump to fire Scott Pruitt misstated the home state of Representative Kevin Cramer, who advised the Trump campaign and is running for Senate. Mr. Cramer represents North Dakota, not South Dakota.
match_headline: White House Aides Are Urging President Trump to Fire Scott Pruitt, the E.P.A. Chief

text: An article on Saturday about new artificial intelligence labs launched by Facebook misstated Ed Lazowska’s position at the University of Washington. He is the Bill and Melinda Gates professor of computer science, not the chairman of the computer science and engineering department.
match_headline: Facebook Adds A.I. Labs in Seattle and Pittsburgh, Pressuring Local Universities

text: An article on Tuesday about the excavation of colonial-era ships in Old Town Alexandria, Va., referred incorrectly to the research specialist leading the conservation team at Texas A&M. He is Dr. Peter Fix, not Dr. Peter Nix.
match_headline: Ships Unearthed in Virginia Offer Glimpse of Colonial Era

text: An article on Page 6 about a calendar of upcoming design-related events erroneously includes an entry about the East Midtown Partnership Spring Design Pop-up on May 15. The event has been canceled because its location, Tramway Plaza, has been closed for construction.
match_headline: New York Design Destinations You Can’t Miss This Month

text: An article on Page 10 about different styles of home lighting misstates the available finishes for Lindsey Adelman’s Drop System lighting. They are verdigris, tarnished silver and mottled brass; a pewter finish is not available. It also misstated the price of a Drop System unit with a verdigris finish that was shown in an accompanying photo. The price is $13,310, not $12,100.
match_headline: What’s Hot (and Cool) in Home Lighting

text: An article on Page 20 about the renovation of the Greenwood Baptist Church in Kansas City, Mo., misspells the surname of the carpenter who renovated the church. He is Jamie Jeffries, not Jefferies. It also misstates who did the renovation work. Mr. Jeffries renovated the building; the artist Peregrine Honig did not work on the renovation with him. Further, the article also misspells the surname of a singer who performed at Greenwood Social Hall. She is Julia Haile, not Hale.
match_headline: The Pews Went, but the Spirit Stayed in a Kansas City Church

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Wednesday about the former two-term California governor George Deukmejian misstated the nationality of his parents. As the obituary correctly stated, they were Armenian, not Turkish.
match_headline: George Deukmejian, 2-Term California Governor in the ’80s, Dies at 89

text: An article on Thursday about a lawsuit against the consulting firm McKinsey & Company misstated Jay Alix’s current role with AlixPartners. He is a board member; he is not co-chairman.
match_headline: McKinsey Hid Conflicts of Interest From Courts, Lawsuit Says

text: An article on Wednesday about a proposed pardon for the boxer Jack Johnson described incorrectly the school lunch Linda Haywood, who has campaigned to clear Mr. Johnson’s name, received from her impoverished mother. It often included pieces of bread and an egg, beans or a leftover pork chop; it was not only pieces of bread.
match_headline: A Relative Wages Jack Johnson’s Biggest Fight: To Clear His Name

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the singer Françoise Hardy misstated the year in which Ms. Hardy learned she had cancer. It was 2004, not 2014.
match_headline: Françoise Hardy, a French National Treasure, Is Back from the Brink

text: An article on Friday about Tammie Jo Shults, the pilot who landed the plane damaged on Southwest Airlines Flight 1380, misstated the reason that Ms. Shults and her husband switched work schedules. They changed schedules so that Ms. Shults — not her husband — could attend their son’s track meet.
match_headline: Southwest Pilot Who Landed Fatal Flight Wasn’t Supposed to Be On It

text: An article on Friday about a man who pleaded guilty to promoting prostitution, using information from the Brooklyn district attorney’s office, misstated the misdemeanor charge to which a co-defendant, Keisia Atkins, pleaded guilty. It was endangering the welfare of a child, not fourth-degree promoting prostitution.
match_headline: Brooklyn Man Pleads Guilty to Promoting Prostitution of 3 Teenagers on Backpage.com

text: An article on May 4 about art fairs in Brooklyn misstated the title of a Moniker art fair leader. Tina Ziegler is the fair’s director, not its founder.
match_headline: Anti-Frieze Art Fairs Abound in Brooklyn

text: An article on Friday about the opening of the 71st Cannes Film Festival misstated the number of the Cannes main jury members. It is nine, not eight. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: The Cannes Film Festival Opens Amid Disruptions

text: A picture caption with a review on Aug. 4, 2017, about the film “The Battleship Island” misidentified the two actors seen standing in the background. So Ji-sub is at left; Hwang Jung-min is in the center. This correction was delayed because the error was called to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Review: ‘The Battleship Island’ Is a Violent War Spectacle

text: An obituary on Friday about the jazz pianist and Duke Ellington authority Brooks Kerr misstated his full name. It is Chester Brooks Joseph Kerr Jr., not Chester Monson Brooks Joseph Kerr III.
match_headline: Brooks Kerr, Piano Prodigy and Ellington Expert, Dies at 66

text: An obituary on Thursday about the author Daniel Cohen, using information from his wife, misstated the surname of his sister, who survives him. She is Jean Cohen, not Jean Fuller.
match_headline: Daniel Cohen, 82, Dies; Sought Justice for Pan Am Bombing Victims

text: An article last Sunday about Stephen A. Schwarzman misidentified the part of the National Library of Israel that will be named after him. It is the library’s education center, not the entire library.
match_headline: The Man Who Bought New York

text: An article last Sunday about the Vatican’s role in shaping the Met Gala misspelled the surname of an artist. She is Katarina Jebb, not Jedd.
match_headline: How the Met Got the Vatican’s Vestments

text: Because of a production error, an article on April 29 about the playwright Caryl Churchill omitted part of a sentence. The full sentence should have read: This collaborative method is part of what appeals to James C. Nicola, the longtime artistic director of New York Theater Workshop, about Ms. Churchill’s writing.
match_headline: Prepare to Be Provoked. Caryl Churchill Is Back.

text: A review on April 29 about “Make Trouble,” by Cecile Richards, misidentified the first woman governor of Texas. She was Miriam (Ma) Ferguson, not Ann Richards, the author’s mother.
match_headline: A Professional Troublemaker’s Guide for Young Activists

text: A news analysis last Sunday about teachers unions and strikes misidentified the role of one union official in Racine, Wis., when the union fought for the continuation of key contract elements. The official, Peter Knotek, was the former president, not the president.
match_headline: Can Weak Unions Get Teachers More Money?

text: A chart with an article on Sunday about the effects of the federal tax overhaul on different states misstated how Idaho, Oregon and Vermont define income when calculating state taxes. Idaho and Oregon use the federal government’s definition of taxable income, not adjusted gross income; Vermont uses adjusted gross income, not taxable income.
match_headline: Federal Tax Cuts Leave States in a Bind

text: An article on Saturday about a strategy by the United States to train former members of Iranian-backed militias in Iraq misstated the middle initial of the American ambassador to Iraq. He is Douglas A. Silliman, not Douglas J.
match_headline: U.S. Takes a Risk: Old Iraqi Enemies Are Now Allies

text: An article on Sunday about the arrest of Peter Dalglish in Nepal on charges of child rape misstated when the British charity Oxfam disciplined workers for misbehavior in Haiti. It was in 2011, not February.
match_headline: Noted Humanitarian Charged With Child Rape in Nepal, Stunning a Village

text: An article on Saturday about Peter Galbraith Kelly Jr.’s admission that he lied about hiring the wife of a former top aide to Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo misstated the date that Mr. Kelly is to be sentenced. It is Sept. 28, not June 11.
match_headline: Energy Executive Admits Lying About ‘Low-Show Job’ for Percoco’s Wife

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a federal indictment involving widespread insurance fraud in slip-and-fall cases misstated whose lawsuits litigation-finance firms support with large cash advances. It is plaintiffs’ suits, not defendants.
match_headline: How a Web of Slip-and-Fall Cases Puts a New Spin on an Old-Fashioned Scheme

text: An article on Friday about Elaine Wynn’s efforts to remove John J. Hagenbuch from the board of Mirage and Wynn Resorts referred imprecisely to a painting that Elaine Wynn bought for $142 million. It is a triptych of Lucian Freud by Francis Bacon. It was not painted by Lucian Freud.
match_headline: With Steve Wynn Gone, ‘Queen of Las Vegas’ Does Boardroom Battle

text: An article on Sunday about Tiger Woods’ performance at the Players Championship misstated the number of greens that he made in regulation. It was 15, not 16.
match_headline: Tiger Woods Climbs Leaderboard With a 65 at the Players Championship

text: An article on Sunday about Brett Gardner’s performance in the Yankees’ win over the Athletics misstated the team that Domingo German held hitless for six innings during his first major league start. It was the Cleveland Indians, not the Los Angeles Angels.
match_headline: Neil Walker Delivers a Yankees Win, but Give Brett Gardner the Save

text: An article on Sunday about the Mariners’ pitcher James Paxton, who threw a no-hitter against the Blue Jays last Tuesday, misstated Harry Brecheen’s position in the Orioles’ organization. He was a major-league coach, not a minor-league coach.
match_headline: A No-Hitter Brings Out Canadian Pitching Pride

text: An entry on Monday in the “What’s on TV” highlights described incorrectly the sitcom “Superior Donuts.” Although it is based on a play by Tracy Letts, it did not win a Pulitzer Prize. (Mr. Letts’s play “August: Osage County” did win a Pulitzer.)
match_headline: What’s on TV Monday: ‘Royal Wedding Watch’ and ‘What Haunts Us’

text: An article on Sunday about a demonstration against gender inequality staged by woman at the Cannes Film Festival misstated the name of the film by Jane Campion that won the Palme d’Or. It is “The Piano,” not “The Piano Teacher.”
match_headline: Women Rally on Cannes Red Carpet to Highlight Gender Inequality

text: A review on Friday about the documentary “Always at the Carlyle” misspelled the given name of one actor who speaks about the hotel in the film. She is Anjelica Huston, not Angelica.
match_headline: Review: ‘Always at the Carlyle’ Hints at Scandal, Chooses Discretion

text: An obituary on April 27 about the actor, playwright and director Gertrude Jeannette referred incorrectly to Dunbar High School in Little Rock, Ark., which she attended. It was not a one-room schoolhouse.
match_headline: Gertrude Jeannette, Actor, Director and Cabdriver, Dies at 103

text: An article on Monday about risks associated with keyless-ignition vehicles, using information from a company spokesman, referred incorrectly to the availability of an automatic shut-off feature in Fiat Chrysler cars. One model, the 2018 Chrysler Pacifica hybrid, shuts off the engine after a certain period of idling; it is not the case that no Fiat Chrysler vehicle does so.
match_headline: Deadly Convenience: Keyless Cars and Their Carbon Monoxide Toll

text: An article on Sunday about the process of preparing a horse called Quip for the Preakness misstated Quip’s status for the Kentucky Derby. While Quip qualified for the Derby, the horse was never entered in the race.
match_headline: How to Prepare a Horse for the Preakness

text: An obituary on Sunday about the physicist David Pines misstated where he met his wife, Suzy. It was at the University of California, Berkeley, not Princeton. The obituary — using information from the Santa Fe Institute in New Mexico, which Dr. Pines had helped establish — also omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to his daughter, son and grandchildren, Dr. Pines is survived by a sister, Judith Fried.
match_headline: David Pines, 93, Insightful and Influential Physicist, Dies

text: An article on April 13 about Pasquale Perrotta, the head of the protective detail for Scott Pruitt, the E.P.A. administrator, erroneously included Mr. Perrotta among those who gathered for beers at an event at the Elephant and Castle in Washington that was attended by Patrick Sullivan, the assistant inspector general who oversees investigations at the E.P.A. Mr. Sullivan said that Mr. Perrotta had been invited but did not attend that gathering and that he has never met for drinks with Mr. Perrotta, though he acknowledged that the two men met for lunch several months later at another restaurant near the E.P.A. headquarters.
match_headline: At E.P.A., Pruitt’s ‘Sheriff’ Clashed With Critics of Spending

text: An article on Saturday about Dimitrij Chpakov, a Jewish rapper, referred incorrectly to the location of Osnabrück, Germany. It is north of the Ruhr Valley; it is not in the valley itself.
match_headline: Jewish Rapper Takes On Germany’s Hip-Hop Scene

text: An article on Monday about Mark Dubowitz, the chief executive of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, and his perspective on nuclear negotiations with Iran referred imprecisely to Mr. Dubowitz’s salary as compared with those of leaders of other Washington think tanks. Mr. Dubowitz’s $560,221 compensation in 2016 was determined by the foundation’s board of directors and is commensurate with the average annual salary of other think-tank leaders in Washington in recent years. It is not nearly twice as much as the salaries of his counterparts. The article also inaccurately linked the foundation to Israel’s Likud party. While the think tank does align with some of Likud’s positions, it is not directly involved with the party. The article also referred imprecisely to the funding of conferences held by the foundation and the Hudson Institute. While Elliott Broidy provided $2.7 million in funds for consulting, marketing and other services, the foundation says it received only $360,000 from Mr. Broidy for one conference.
match_headline: He Was a Tireless Critic of the Iran Deal. Now He Insists He Wanted to Save It.

text: A review on May 7 about a reimagination of Aristophanes’ “The Birds” misidentified the presenter of an avian-themed festival. It is presented by the Onassis Cultural Center New York, not the Onassis Cultural Center-Athens. (The play was presented by the Onassis Cultural Center-Athens.)
match_headline: Review: Building the Wall (Not That One) in Aristophanes’ ‘The Birds’

text: An article on May 5 about endorsements by Emily’s List referred incorrectly to the timing of the group’s endorsement of Aruna Miller in a Maryland Democratic Primary. The organization endorsed Ms. Miller before Nadia Hashimi became a candidate; it did not endorse Ms. Miller over Ms. Hashimi.
match_headline: Tough Choices, and Criticism, for Emily’s List as Democratic Women Flood Primaries

text: An article on Monday about Jerry West’s role with the Los Angeles Clippers misidentified the course where Mr. West recently shot two under-80 rounds of golf. He played them at the Virginia Country Club in Long Beach, Calif., not the Bel-Air Country Club.
match_headline: Jerry West Just Wants to Feel Wanted

text: An article on Tuesday about a Broadway adaptation of the 1959 film “Some Like It Hot” misstated the company that released the film. It was United Artists, not MGM; United Artists was purchased by MGM in 1982.
match_headline: New Musical Version of ‘Some Like it Hot’ Is Headed for Broadway

text: An article on Friday about the departures of many prominent Republican congresswomen misidentified the organization Lea Márquez-Peterson runs. She is the president of the Tucson Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, not the Tucson Chamber of Commerce.
match_headline: As Democratic Women Surge, Ranks of Republican Women May Shrink

text: A review on Friday about the opening of Paul Simon’s farewell tour misstated the live performance history of two songs. Paul Simon has previously performed “Rene and Georgette Magritte With Their Dog After the War” and “Can’t Run, But” onstage. (Onstage at this concert, Mr. Simon introduced the songs saying he did not recall previously performing them live.)
ref_headline: Rene and Georgette Magritte With Their Dog After the War
match_headline: Review: Paul Simon, Still Evolving, Is Saying Goodbye

text: An article on Page 59 about the Louisiana house of Robert E. Smith refers incorrectly to the craftsmen who performed a crackle finish on the trim inside his house; they were painters, not carpenters. The article also misspelled the name of a French porcelain; it is Comte d’Artois, not Comte d’Artios. The article misstated the era of the crystal that Smith uses for entertaining guests; it is 19th-century, not 18th. And it gave an incorrect measurement for the octagonal rooms in the house; they are 548 square feet, not 26 square feet.
match_headline: In the Heart of Louisiana, One Man’s Impossibly Ornate Home

text: An article last Sunday about Daniel Kramer and the English National Opera misstated Matthew Epstein’s title at the Welsh National Opera. He was general director, not artistic director.
match_headline: A Newcomer to Opera Tries to Tame a Tempest

text: An article on April 1 about the writer Gerald Murnane misspelled the surname of an Australian journalist. He is Imre Salusinszky, not Saluszinksy.
match_headline: Is the Next Nobel Laureate in Literature Tending Bar in a Dusty Australian Town?

text: An article on May 6 about a bank heist misstated an area that was affected by cyberattacks in 2017 that Kaspersky Lab claims were linked to North Korea. In addition to Europe, the attacks occurred in Central America, not the United States.
match_headline: China Moves to Steady Ties With North Korea Before Trump-Kim Meeting

text: An article last Sunday about the Silicon Valley Community Foundation misstated which foundations in the United States are larger. The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and the Open Society Foundations are both larger than the Silicon Valley Community Foundation; the Gates Foundation is not the only one that is larger.
match_headline: Inside a Powerful Silicon Valley Charity, a Toxic Culture Festered

text: An article last Sunday about high-end sneaker resellers omitted the given name of the co-founder and chief executive of one of those resellers, GOAT. He is Eddy Lu.
match_headline: How Much Is That Sneaker in the Window?

text: An article last Sunday about shopping like British royalty misidentified the royal family member who bestowed an honor on Fortnum & Mason, a purveyor of tea and fine provisions. It was Queen Elizabeth II who granted the business a royal warrant, not Prince Philip.
match_headline: A Road Map to Shopping Like a Royal in London

text: A picture of an architect with an article on Monday about the diminishing number of rent-regulated apartments in New York City was published in error. The man shown in the image, Ken Hudes, was not associated with work at 1578 Union Street in Brooklyn, which was pictured adjacent to his photograph.
match_headline: The Eviction Machine Churning Through New York City

text: An article on Sunday about a semifinal match between Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic in the Italian Open misstated the number of titles Nadal had won at the Italian Open. He was trying to win his eighth, not his sixth.
match_headline: In Rome, a Semifinal Win for Rafael Nadal and a Big Step Forward for Novak Djokovic

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the actress Patricia Morison misstated the day she died. It was Sunday, not Saturday.
match_headline: Patricia Morison, 103, Dies; Broadway’s First Kate to Be Kissed

text: An obituary on Monday about the artist Per Kirkeby misstated the number of outdoor brick structures he created. It was more than 60, not more than 20. The obituary also described Mr. Kirkeby’s family incorrectly. He was the oldest of three children, not an only child.
match_headline: Per Kirkeby, Painter Inspired by Nature, Is Dead at 79

text: An article on Sunday about efforts in Germany to regulate Facebook misstated the name of a prolific right-wing group that uses the social network. It is Alternative for Germany, not Alternative of Germany.
match_headline: Germany Acts to Tame Facebook, Learning From Its Own History of Hate

text: An article on Sunday about African-American cultural influence at the royal wedding misspelled the surname of a Twitter user who wrote that the Most Rev. Michael Curry’s address at the ceremony was a moment “hundreds of years in the making.” She is Andrea L. Pino, not Pinto.
ref_headline: hundreds of years in the making.
match_headline: Meghan Markle Introduces the British Monarchy to the African-American Experience

text: An article on Friday about high-quality engineering in Cadillac sedans, relying on information from Cadillac, misstated the source of data on the average sale price of its vehicles. The source was J.D. Power, not R.L. Polk.
match_headline: Cadillac Makes Great Cars. Too Bad Americans Want S.U.V.s.

text: An article on Tuesday about innovations in cancer research described incorrectly Dr. Amy Abernethy’s role at Flatiron Health. She is its chief medical officer, not its founder. In addition, the article misstated the number of medical records obtained by the company. The figure is 2.2 million, not 1 million.
match_headline: New Cancer Treatments Lie Hidden Under Mountains of Paperwork

text: An article on Tuesday about the genetic condition mosaicism misstated the year in which Theodor Boveri died. It was 1915, not 1914.
match_headline: Every Cell in Your Body Has the Same DNA. Except It Doesn’t.

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the artist Robert Indiana misidentified Maxwell Anderson, who in 2008 called Mr. Indiana “an artist of consequence who gets mistaken for a one-hit wonder.” He is the former director of the Indianapolis Museum of Art and the Dallas Museum of Art; he is not currently the director of the Dallas Museum.
ref_headline: an artist of consequence who gets mistaken for a one-hit wonder.
match_headline: Robert Indiana, 89, Who Turned ‘Love’ Into Enduring Art, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the lawyer Dovey Johnson Roundtree referred incorrectly to the United States District Court in Washington. It was not the case that Ms. Roundtree, a black woman, was “not allowed to use the law library, cafeteria or restroom” there when she defended a man accused of murder in 1965 (although those were obstacles that she had faced at other times in her career).
ref_headline: not allowed to use the law library, cafeteria or restroom
match_headline: Dovey Johnson Roundtree, Barrier-Breaking Lawyer, Dies at 104

text: An article on Wednesday about a partial rollback of the 2010 Dodd-Frank law misstated the name of the think tank where John Berlau is a senior fellow. It is the Competitive Enterprise Institute, not the Conservative Enterprise Institute.
match_headline: Congress Approves First Big Dodd-Frank Rollback

text: An article on Saturday about candidates vying for Senator Dianne Feinstein’s role as an ideological leader within the Democratic Party misstated Kevin de León’s age at the time Ms. Feinstein was entering politics. He would have been 3, not 4. The error was repeated in a photo caption.
match_headline: Running Uphill: The Challenge of Unseating Dianne Feinstein

text: An article on Wednesday about a new sociolinguistics study surrounding expressions of thanks in different languages, based on a draft of the study given to a reporter, misstated the study’s title. It is “Universals and Cultural Diversity in the Expression of Gratitude,” not “Universality and Cultural Diversity in Social Reciprocity.”
ref_headline: Universals and Cultural Diversity in the Expression of Gratitude,
match_headline: Think You Always Say Thank You? Oh, Please

text: An entry in the Metropolitan Diary on Monday about being swindled in New York misspelled the given name of the author. She is Isabelle Fitzgerald, not Isabel.
match_headline: Swindled Again

text: An entry in the “Of Interest” section on Monday misidentified the person who worked at Macy’s. As the article correctly noted, Maureen Corrigan, a professor at Georgetown University, once worked at the department store. Zelda Fitzgerald did not work at Macy’s.
match_headline: Finding the Backdrop of ‘Gatsby’ in Connecticut, Not Long Island

text: An obituary on May 15 about the Russian chess grandmaster Evgeni Vasiukov misstated the difference in age between him and the former world chess champion Mikhail Tal, to whom he was sometimes compared. Mr. Vasiukov was three years older than Mr. Tal, not three years younger.
match_headline: Evgeni Vasiukov, Russian Chess Grandmaster, Is Dead at 85

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the author Philip Roth misspelled the surname of a character in his novel “American Pastoral.” He is Swede Levov, not Lvov. It also misstated part of the name of Mr. Roth’s alma mater. It is Bucknell University, not College. And it misstated, at one point, the year Mr. Roth’s novel “Everyman” was published. As correctly noted elsewhere, it was 2006, not 2005.
match_headline: The Liberation in Roth’s American Berserk
