Ms. Sandberg and Mr. Schrage first worked together at Google; Ms. Sandberg did not work with him at the Council on Foreign Relations.
match_headline: Facebook’s Head of Communications and Policy Is Leaving Company

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about Las Chicas Locas, a weekly salsa dancing party in New York, misidentified a dancer shown with Fernando Polanco. She is Jessica Churgin, not Maria-Fernanda Mendez.
match_headline: Watch These Captivating Salsa Dancers, and Try Not to Break a Sweat

text: An article on Page 1 about Snapchat’s forays into augmented reality misspells the surname of the author of “Augmented Human.” She is Helen Papagiannis, not Pappagiannis.
match_headline: How Snapchat Makes Mini Movies in Augmented Reality

text: An article on Page 18 about Mara Brock Akil’s show “Love Is ___,” misstates the title of a television drama. It is “This Is Us,” not “All of Us.”
match_headline: The Black Sitcom Steps Out of the ’90s and Gets Real

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the fashion designer and illustrator Michael Vollbracht misstated his age. He was 70, not 71. (As the obituary correctly stated, he was born on Nov. 17, 1947.) The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Michael Vollbracht, Fashion Designer and Illustrator, Dies at 70

text: An article on June 3 about the self-help organization Nxivm and its founder, Keith Raniere, misspelled the name of a Mexican newspaper company. It is Grupo Reforma, not Groupo Reforma.
match_headline: Inside Nxivm, the ‘Sex Cult’ That Preached Empowerment

text: An article on June 3 about blood-spatter evidence included an outdated affiliation for Toby Wolson. He is no longer a criminalist in the Miami-Dade Police Department; he retired from that position in 2015.
match_headline: Blood Will Tell, Part 2: Did Faulty Evidence Doom Joe Bryan?

text: A review on June 3 about the Y.A. novel “Bruja Born,” by Zoraida Córdova, misstated the protagonist’s given name in two instances. She is Lula Mortiz, not Lulu.
match_headline: Dark Magic and Other Escapes in These Summer Y.A. Novels

text: An article on Saturday about senior staff members at the Environmental Protection Agency who said they frequently felt pressured by Scott Pruitt to help in nonwork matters included an item that erroneously described Mr. Pruitt’s use of his position for personal matters. While a Virginia lawmaker, William Howell, said he wrote a letter of recommendation to the University of Virginia Law School on behalf of Mr. Pruitt’s daughter, McKenna, he actually wrote it while Mr. Pruitt was the attorney general of Oklahoma. After publication of the article, additional research by a legislative aide, Mr. Howell said, showed he had incorrectly stated the date of the letter, which he said was actually written on Nov. 1, 2016, more than three months before Mr. Pruitt was confirmed as E.P.A. administrator, in February 2017. The law school, which had declined to comment for the article because of privacy concerns, issued a statement on Saturday saying Ms. Pruitt had given the school permission to confirm that she had been offered early admission in late November 2016 and that the “application was evaluated according to our usual admissions procedures.”
ref_headline: application was evaluated according to our usual admissions procedures.
match_headline: For Pruitt Aides, the Boss’s Personal Life Was Part of the Job

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about Jalal Mansur Nuriddin, who helped establish the foundation for hip-hop as a member of the Last Poets, misidentified, using information from Getty Images, the member of the group shown with Mr. Nuriddin and Umar Bin Hassan. He is Nilaja Obabi, not Abiodun Oyewole.
match_headline: Jalal Mansur Nuriddin, ‘Grandfather of Rap,’ Is Dead at 73

text: A headline with an article on Saturday about President Trump’s reaction to a Justice Department inspector general report described incorrectly Mr. Trump’s trip back from Asia. He began reacting to the report after returning to the United States from a conference in Singapore, not North Korea.
match_headline: Justice Dept. Watchdog Will Be Tested in Next Chapter of Clinton Investigation Firestorm

text: An article on Monday about Turning Point USA’s Young Women’s Leadership Summit, a conservative conference, misspelled the surname of a woman who attended the event. She is Maggie Anders, not Andrews. The article also described incorrectly the March for Our Lives. It was a demonstration against gun violence, not gun control.
match_headline: Trumpism Finds a Safe Space at Conservative Women’s Conference

text: An article on June 7 about a petition to rename Boston’s Faneuil Hall misstated the occupation of a tourist who was asked to comment on the proposal. Matt Birch, the tourist, is an online editor, not a social media editor.
match_headline: Boston Grapples With Faneuil Hall, Named for a Slaveholder

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about The Colorado Sun, a publication started by former employees of The Denver Post, misidentified Ethereum. It is a virtual currency and blockchain database platform, not a company.
match_headline: Goodbye, Denver Post. Hello, Blockchain.

text: An article on Saturday about the playwright Ayad Akhtar misstated the given name of a theater director. She is Karin Beier, not Katrin Beier.
match_headline: Ayad Akhtar Gets a European Welcome, With Conditions

text: An obituary on Saturday about the rare-book seller William Reese misstated the title of a guidebook he wrote in his final years. It is “The Best of the West: 250 Classic Works of Western Americana,” not “The Western 100.”
ref_headline: The Best of the West: 250 Classic Works of Western Americana,
match_headline: William Reese, Leading Seller of Rare Books, Is Dead at 62

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about immigration issues and populist movements in Europe referred incorrectly to the role of Janez Jansa in Slovenian politics. As the article correctly notes elsewhere, his party is now the largest in Slovenia but is struggling to form a coalition. It is not the case that he “rode the migrant issue back into power.”
ref_headline: rode the migrant issue back into power.
match_headline: As Europe’s Liberal Order Splinters, Trump Wields an Ax

text: An article on Tuesday about the role of conservative hard-liners in making federal immigration policy misstated the name of an organization that tracks white nationalists and other hate groups. It is the Southern Poverty Law Center, not the Southern Policy Law Center.
match_headline: How Anti-Immigration Passion Was Inflamed From the Fringe

text: Because of a production error, an article on Tuesday about the restoration of the Mariposa Grove in Yosemite National Park was missing from some editions. To read the article and enjoy photos of the majestic sequoias, visit nytimes.com.
match_headline: A Renewed View of Some of the World’s Oldest Trees

text: An article on Tuesday about Juan Soto’s performance in the Nationals’ win over the Yankees misstated the number of days between the beginning and the conclusion of the game, which was rain-delayed. It was 34 days, not 33.
match_headline: 34 Days Later, the Yankees Lose a Game That Was Halted by Rain

text: An article on Sunday about golfers’ unconventional accommodations at the United States Open misstated the location of Sag Harbor. It is northeast of Shinnecock Hills, not northwest.
match_headline: By Land or by Sea, U.S. Open Golfers Got Creative About Their Lodging

text: An article on Tuesday about a spate of Guinea worm infections in dogs described incorrectly the size of Hoplobatrachus occipitalis, the bullfrogs occasionally consumed by villagers in Chad. They can weigh as much as a half-pound, not as much as five pounds. (Another species consumed in Chad, Pyxicephalus edulis, can weigh as much as three pounds.)
match_headline: Nearly Eradicated in Humans, the Guinea Worm Finds New Victims: Dogs

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about Walter Bahr, a soccer coach and star player in the 1950 World Cup, included outdated information about the National Soccer Hall of Fame. It is scheduled to reopen this year in Frisco, Tex.; it is no longer in Oneonta, N.Y.
match_headline: Walter Bahr, a Star of a World Cup Upset, Is Dead at 91

text: An article on Sunday about Afghan refugees deported upon reaching Turkey misstated the year in which the number of migrants arriving in Europe via Turkey by sea dropped to 173,000. That occurred in 2016, not last year.
match_headline: Their Road to Turkey Was Long and Grueling, but the Short Flight Home Was Crueler

text: An article on Tuesday about the race for governor of Texas misstated which gay rights group did not endorse Lupe Valdez, the Democratic nominee. It was the youth branch of Houston’s Stonewall Democrats that declined to endorse Ms. Valdez, not the Stonewall Democrats.
match_headline: In Texas Governor’s Race, Lupe Valdez Faces Resistance From Fellow Democrats

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a report on coordination between scientists and the alcohol industry misstated the type of study to which an acronym refers. An R.C.T. is a randomized controlled trial, not a randomized clinical trial.
match_headline: It Was Supposed to Be an Unbiased Study of Drinking. They Wanted to Call It ‘Cheers.’

text: An obituary on May 23 about the political adviser and author Richard N. Goodwin misstated his role in the concession speech that Vice President Al Gore delivered after the Supreme Court halted the Florida recount in the 2000 presidential election. Mr. Goodwin contributed to the writing of the speech; he did not write the entire speech himself.
match_headline: Richard N. Goodwin, Adviser to Democratic Presidents, Dies at 86

text: An article last Friday about the sentencing of a group of human traffickers in Hungary misstated the number of people transported by the network into Germany and Austria. The smuggling network transported groups of up to 100 people daily, not groups of three or four people daily.
match_headline: They Let 71 People Die in a Stifling Truck. They Got 25 Years.

text: An article on Wednesday about a carbon tax plan proposal by Americans for Carbon Dividends erroneously included an environmental group among its supporters. While the group, the Nature Conservancy, signed on as a founding member of the Climate Leadership Council, it has not endorsed the specific proposals of the group’s carbon tax and dividend plan.
match_headline: New Group, With Conservative Credentials, Plans Push for a Carbon Tax

text: An article on Thursday about Giancarlo Stanton’s performance in the Yankees’ win over the Mariners described incorrectly the situation Stanton faced before he hit a game-ending home run. There were two outs in the bottom of the ninth; since the score was tied, 5-5, the Yankees were not “down to their final out.”
match_headline: With Walk-Off Homer, Giancarlo Stanton Finally Gets His Moment at Yankee Stadium

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about a performance of “Romeo and Juliet” at the American Ballet Theater misstated when Stella Abrera made her debut as Juliet. It was in February in Detroit, not June 14 in New York.
match_headline: 4 Buzzy ‘Romeo and Juliet’ Debuts, 1 Fainthearted Production

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the opera singer Bonaldo Giaiotti misstated the role in Verdi’s “Nabucco” in which he made his debut at the Metropolitan Opera. It was the High Priest, not Zaccaria.
match_headline: Bonaldo Giaiotti, Stalwart Operatic Bass, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Thursday about the philosopher Stanley Cavell misidentified one of the movies he discussed in his book “Pursuits of Happiness: The Hollywood Comedy of Remarriage.” It is “The Lady Eve,” not “All About Eve.”
ref_headline: Pursuits of Happiness: The Hollywood Comedy of Remarriage.
match_headline: Stanley Cavell, Prominent Harvard Philosopher, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the veteran NBC News correspondent Richard Valeriani misstated the original surname of his mother. She was Christina Camerota, not Camarito.
match_headline: Richard Valeriani, Veteran NBC News Correspondent, Dies at 85

text: An article on Friday about a plan to house migrant children on United States military bases misspelled the given name of the director of Migrant Rights and Justice at the Women’s Refugee Commission. She is Michelle Brané, not Michele.
match_headline: U.S. Prepares to House Up to 20,000 Migrants on Military Bases

text: An article on Friday about countervailing tariffs imposed on the United States by the European Union misstated the day of President Trump’s speech in Duluth, Minn. He spoke there on Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Europe Retaliates Against Trump Tariffs

text: A picture with an article on Friday about the use of material witness warrants was published in error. The building shown in the photograph was the State Court of Appeals in Albany, not the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.
match_headline: Court Warns City About Misuse of Material Witness Warrants

text: An article on Friday about the Yankees’ sweep of their series with the Mariners misstated the length of the Yankees’ longest losing streak this season. It is two games, several times; they did not have a three-game losing streak from May 15 to May 17 that involved a rain-suspended game with the Nationals. Because of an editing error, the article also misidentified the player who homered off Yankees pitcher Luis Severino. It was Kyle Seager, not Nelson Cruz.
match_headline: Yankees Sweep the Mariners With a Pair of Homers and a Couple of Breaks

text: An editorial on Friday included outdated data on defense spending by NATO members. Eight members, not four, now spend at least 2 percent of their gross domestic product on defense.
match_headline: How Should Europe Respond to Trump’s Bullying?

text: An obituary on Monday about the movie producer Martin Bregman referred incorrectly to a court case involving the actor Alec Baldwin. A woman was prosecuted for harassment after Mr. Baldwin accused her of stalking him; Mr. Baldwin did not sue her.
match_headline: Martin Bregman, Producer of ‘Scarface’ and ‘Serpico,’ Dies at 92

text: A picture caption with an article on June 10 about Jewish history in Egypt, India and other countries misidentified a building in Cairo. It is the Church of St. George, not Ben Ezra Synagogue.
match_headline: From Cairo to Kolkata, Traces of a Vibrant Jewish Past

text: A review last Sunday about the novel “Kudos,” by Rachel Cusk, misidentified the source for a quotation from one of the author’s two previous books in her fictional trilogy. The novel in which the narrator wonders if it is possible “that one forges one’s own destiny by what one doesn’t notice or feel compassion for” is “Outline”; the quotation does not appear in “Transit.”
match_headline: Rachel Cusk Strips the Novel Down to Its Frame. Again.

text: A review on May 20 about “The Burning Shores: Inside the Battle for the New Libya,” by Frederic Wehrey, misstated the target of the Benghazi attack in 2012. The attack was directed against an American diplomatic mission, not an embassy.
ref_headline: The Burning Shores: Inside the Battle for the New Libya,
match_headline: Why Libya Continues to Burn

text: An article on May 20 about retro cellphones misstated the amount raised by Jelly on Kickstarter and Indiegogo. It was $1.7 million, not close to $3 million.
match_headline: Is a Dumber Phone a Better Phone?

text: An article on June 3 about using 3-D modeling to reconstruct the killing of protesters in Kiev, Ukraine, included an erroneous detail about the laser scanning of Instytutska Street. The scanning was independently organized by Evelyn Nefertari; it was not done by Nefertari at the behest of SITU, an architecture firm and research lab in Brooklyn.
match_headline: Who Killed the Kiev Protesters? A 3-D Model Holds the Clues

text: An article on June 17 about new thinking in cancer research included an incomplete definition of the word “genome.” A genome is the complete set of all genetic material present in an organism or cell, not solely the set of genes.
match_headline: The Search for Cancer Treatment Beyond Mutant-Hunting

text: An article on Monday about the seizure of email records from a Times reporter and her relationship with an intelligence aide misstated where President Trump described the aide as “a very important leaker.” The president made the statement to reporters, not in a tweet.
match_headline: How an Affair Between a Reporter and a Security Aide Has Rattled Washington Media

text: An article on Saturday about a waterworks employee in Kobe, Japan, who was fined for leaving his desk minutes before his lunch break began referred incorrectly to a Dentsu worker who jumped from the roof of an employee dormitory in 2015. The worker, Matsuri Takahashi, was a woman, not a man.
match_headline: He Left Work for 3 Minutes Before His Lunch Break. Now His Pay Is Docked.

text: An article on Sunday about a Guatemalan woman who was reunited with her son after being separated from him in May at the United States border with Mexico described incorrectly the relationship between Nexus Services Inc. and the law firm representing Beata Mariana de Jesus Mejia-Mejia. The company funds the law firm; it does not own it.
match_headline: ‘No One Is Going to Separate Us Again’: Guatemalan Mother Reunites With Son

text: An article on Monday about appearances by Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo and Cynthia Nixon at the Pride parade in Manhattan misstated the amount of money Cynthia Nixon’s campaign had on hand. It was just over $400,000, not $1 million.
match_headline: At Pride Parade, Few Paid Attention to the Candidates

text: An article on Saturday about Shaun Leonardo’s “Primitive Games” at the Guggenheim Museum referred incorrectly to some of the young adults and juveniles in the Assembly program. They have been charged with nonviolent crimes, not convicted of them.
match_headline: Can an Artist Shift the Gun Debate?

text: An article on Saturday about the summer solstice event Make Music New York misspelled the surnames of two musicians playing at Riverside Park. One is Emily Tong, not Trong, and the other is Ethan Liang, not Lang.
match_headline: A Musical Solstice Spectacle Sprawls Across New York

text: An article on Friday about stand-up, improv and variety shows misidentified the creator of “Am I a Terrible Person?” Chelsea Stoutenburgh is the producer of the show, not Chelsea White. (Chelsea White is the show’s host.) The article also referred incorrectly to Ms. Stoutenburgh’s treatment at Mount Sinai. She received outpatient therapy for obsessive-compulsive disorder; she was not an inpatient at Mount Sinai.
match_headline: 6 Comedy Shows to Catch in N.Y.C. This Weekend

text: An article on Monday about educators’ efforts to find appropriate ways to present gunfire in theatrical performances amid students’ fears about school shootings misspelled the given name of a theater teacher at Fishers High School in Fishers, Ind. He is Jon Colby, not John.
match_headline: When the Actors Are Students, and They’re Armed

text: An article on Tuesday about the financial crisis faced by the United Nations Relief and Works Agency misstated the United States contributions to the agency in 2018 and 2017. The United States has contributed about $60 million this year, not $125 million, compared with more than $360 million last year, not $300 million.
match_headline: Head of U.N. Agency for Palestinian Refugees Warns of Cuts

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump’s reaction to a Virginia restaurant’s refusal to serve the White House press secretary, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, misspelled the name of the comedian who hosted this year’s White House Correspondents’ Association dinner. She is Michelle Wolf, not Michele Wolff.
match_headline: Trump Takes His Time Supporting Sanders After Restaurant Rejects Her

text: An article on Tuesday about primary elections in New York incorrectly stated that James Felton Keith was challenging Representative Adriano Espaillat in Tuesday’s primary. He withdrew his candidacy in the spring.
match_headline: Only in New York: Where Primary Day Comes Twice a Year

text: An article last Wednesday about artificial intelligence systems built to interact with humans misquoted the IBM Debater, a computer program that participated in a debate with an Israeli college senior on June 18. During an exchange, the IBM Debater said, “It is very easy to say there are more important things to spend money on, and I do not dispute this,” not “and I dispute this.”
ref_headline: It is very easy to say there are more important things to spend money on, and I do not dispute this,
match_headline: IBM Unveils System That ‘Debates’ With Humans

text: An article on Tuesday about spider ballooning misstated the diameter of a human hair. It is 80,000 to 100,000 nanometers, not just under 100 nanometers. It also misstated the country where Moonsung Cho, a scientist, first saw spiders ballooning. It was Denmark, not Australia.
match_headline: How Spiders Fly

text: An obituary on Monday about the poet Donald Hall referred incorrectly to the years the English-born poet W. H. Auden, a literary influence on Mr. Hall, lived in the United States. He had a home in Manhattan until the early 1970s; he did not return to England in the late 1950s.
match_headline: Donald Hall, a Poet Laureate of the Rural Life, Is Dead at 89

text: An article on Wednesday about Argentina’s victory over Nigeria in a World Cup match misspelled the given name of an Argentina striker. He is Gonzalo Higuaín, not Ganzalo.
match_headline: Argentina Finds World Cup Salvation in Thriller Over Nigeria

text: A picture caption for the answer to the “Spot the Ball” quiz on Wednesday misspelled the surname of Costa Rica’s goalkeeper. He is Keylor Navas, not Nava.
match_headline: In World Cup, Serbia Holds On Against Costa Rica

text: An article on Wednesday about primary elections and President Trump’s endorsement of his preferred candidates misidentified the opponent who defeated David Trone in a Maryland House race in 2016. Mr. Trone lost to Jamie B. Raskin, not John Delaney.
match_headline: Trump Helps Boost Two Preferred Candidates While Progressive Democrats Gain

text: An article on Wednesday about Croatia’s victory over Iceland in a World Cup match misidentified a Croatian star player who did not start but later came on as a substitute. He is Ivan Rakitic, not Luka Modric.
match_headline: Croatia Crushes Iceland’s World Cup Dream

text: An entry on Thursday in the “What’s on TV” highlights, using information from a publicist, misstated the guests appearing on “Desus and Mero” on Thursday. Awkwafina is not on the show.
match_headline: What’s on TV Thursday: ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race’ and ‘CMT Crossroads’

text: An article on Thursday about the annual United Nations report that says more than 10,000 children were killed or maimed in armed conflicts in 2017 misstated a detail in the description of Graça Machel, a Mozambican politician whose 1996 report about the impact of armed conflict on children helped create the basis for the annual list of countries that fail to protect children. She was the third wife of Nelson Mandela, the South African leader, not the second.
match_headline: U.N. Reports Sharp Increase in Children Killed or Maimed in Conflicts

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the risks climate change poses to South Asia misstated the rate at which annual average temperatures rose in western Afghanistan and southwestern Pakistan. Temperatures rose 1 degree Celsius to 3 degrees total between 1950 and 2010, not per year.
match_headline: Global Warming in South Asia: 800 Million at Risk

text: An article on Friday about budget negotiations in the New Jersey state legislature and the threat of a potential shutdown of the state government misstated which parks and beaches would be affected by a shutdown. Sandy Hook would not be closed.
match_headline: Feud Over Millionaire’s Tax Inches New Jersey Closer to Shutdown

text: A review on June 17 about “The Death of Democracy: Hitler’s Rise to Power and the Downfall of the Weimar Republic,” by Benjamin Carter Hett, misstated the year of Hitler’s attempted coup. It was 1923, not 1924.
ref_headline: The Death of Democracy: Hitler’s Rise to Power and the Downfall of the Weimar Republic,
match_headline: How Did the Nazis Gain Power in Germany?

text: A review on June 10 about “How to Change Your Mind,” by Michael Pollan, misstated the legal history of LSD in the United States. It was outlawed by the federal government in 1968 and declared a Schedule 1 substance in 1970, when the drug schedule system was created; LSD had not been declared a Schedule 1 substance “by 1966.”
match_headline: Michael Pollan Drops Acid — and Comes Back From His Trip Convinced

text: An article on June 24 about the Heritage Foundation did not fully identify two employees who left the foundation soon after the departure of Jim DeMint, its president. Th ey are James Wallner, who was a research executive, and Wes Denton, who was a communications executive.
match_headline: How One Conservative Think Tank Is Stocking Trump’s Government

text: An article on June 17 about U.S.-Canadian relations was accompanied by an image of President Trump and Prime Minister Trudeau that did not credit its source. Th e image was based on an iconic photo illustration by Bob Gill that was published on the cover of the Art Directors Club Annual in 1986, and it was meant as a homage to Gill’s work.
match_headline: First Canada Tried to Charm Trump. Now It’s Fighting Back.

text: An article on Sunday about Bavaria’s growing challenge to Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany misspelled the surname of a man who runs a cultural institute in Munich. He is Klaus Reichold, not Reichhold.
match_headline: Bavaria: Affluent, Picturesque — and Angry

text: An article on Monday about the burial of Simone Veil in the Panthéon misstated the amount of time that passed between Marie Curie’s death and her Panthéon burial. It was 61 years, not 34.
match_headline: ‘Merci Madame’: Simone Veil Is Honored With Panthéon Burial

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about a budget agreement to avert a state shutdown in New Jersey misstated the location of Island Beach State Park. It is in Ocean County, not in Seaside Heights, N.J.
match_headline: Last-Minute Budget Deal Averts Shutdown in New Jersey

text: An article on Sunday about the Yankees’ need for starting pitchers misstated the earned run average for Sonny Gray at home this year. It is 8.25, not 7.75.
match_headline: Sonny Gray Is Battered by Red Sox, Emphasizing Yankees’ Need for Rotation Help

text: An article on Monday about LeBron James’s decision to leave the Cleveland Cavaliers for the Los Angeles Lakers incorrectly stated how George Mikan joined the Minneapolis Lakers. He was acquired by the team when another league folded and was not homegrown.
match_headline: The Lakers Got Their Man. (That’s What the Lakers Do.)

text: A picture caption on Thursday with a review of “Carmen Jones” misstated an actress’s surname. She is Anika Noni Rose, not Jones.
match_headline: Review: Bad Girl Makes Good in a Glorious ‘Carmen Jones’

text: An article on Monday about a new policy in Denmark requiring children living in low-income immigrant neighborhoods to receive mandatory instruction in Danish culture gave an incorrect estimate of the number of Muslims in the country. There are half a million non-Western immigrants and descendants in Denmark; the Danish government does not provide statistics on religious groups.
match_headline: In Denmark, Harsh New Laws for Immigrant ‘Ghettos’

text: An article on Tuesday about political pressure compelling Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany to shift her stance on migration policy described incorrectly the negotiations by Ms. Merkel’s conservatives to form a government. The talks involved four other parties, not six.
match_headline: Merkel, to Survive, Agrees to Border Camps for Migrants

text: An article on Tuesday about the Braves’ win over the Yankees misstated the base the Yankees’ Gleyber Torres advanced to in the third inning. On a wild pitch that strayed no more than five feet from Atlanta catcher Kurt Suzuki, Torres advanced to third base, not second.
match_headline: Fly Ball Escapes Aaron Judge’s Glove, and a Win Eludes the Yankees

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about awards for pitching excellence in Japan and the United States misstated the name of the team with which Don Newcombe won the first Cy Young Award. At the time, they were the Brooklyn Dodgers, not the Los Angeles Dodgers.
match_headline: A 50-Year-Old Japanese Baseball Record Unites Two American Pitchers

text: An article on Tuesday about the discovery of personal notes written by Jacqueline Kennedy misstated the city in which the Kennedys rode in a white Lincoln during their November 1963 trip to Texas. It was Fort Worth, not Dallas.
match_headline: Jacqueline Kennedy’s Notes for Dallas Are Found, Starting a Quiet Tug of War

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about the scientist Arvid Carlsson misstated the given name of his wife. As the obituary correctly stated, it is Ulla-Lisa, not Ula.
match_headline: Arvid Carlsson, Who Discovered a Treatment for Parkinson’s, Dies at 95

text: An article on Thursday about changing admissions policies in New York’s elite high schools mistakenly referred to a Harvard policy of using personality traits and other intangible measures to limit the number of Asian-Americans it admits. Such a policy has been alleged in a lawsuit against the university; its existence has not been confirmed.
match_headline: ‘A Huge Blind Spot’: Why New York Asians Feel Overlooked

text: An article on Thursday about smart TVs capable of mining users’ viewing data misidentified one of the investors that contributed venture funding to Samba TV. It was Time Warner, not Time Warner Cable.
match_headline: How Smart TVs in Millions of U.S. Homes Track More Than What’s On Tonight

text: An article on Wednesday about a court ruling protecting companies like Yelp from liability for statements written by users misstated a lower court action in the case brought by Dawn Hassell. A San Francisco Superior Court judge ordered one of Ms. Hassell’s clients and Yelp to remove a post from the site. The judge did not issue a second order asking Yelp to remove the post.
match_headline: Yelp Can’t Be Ordered to Remove Negative Posts, California Court Rules

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Benjamin Pavard’s upbringing and soccer career misstated the score of the World Cup match between France and Argentina after Gabriel Mercado redirected Lionel Messi’s shot past French goalkeeper Hugo Lloris. Argentina led by 2-1, not 1-0. The article also misstated the time of that goal. It was in the 48th minute, not the 57th minute.
match_headline: Benjamin Pavard, and His World Cup Highlight, Came Out of Nowhere

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the French journalist and magazine editor Philippe de Baleine misstated the name of the character in the comic-book series “The Adventures of Tintin” said to be based on him. He is Jean-Loup de la Batellerie, not Jean-Baptiste de la Battellerie.
match_headline: Philippe de Baleine, Editor and Worldly Writer, Dies at 96

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the relaxation of vaccination requirements in Italy misstated Matteo Salvini’s decision about his children. He said they had been vaccinated; he did not say they had not been.
match_headline: Proof of Children’s Vaccinations? Italy Will Now Take Parents’ Word for It

text: An article last Saturday about the outlook for female candidates in light of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s victory misstated the percentage of male challengers who won elections for the Virginia House of Delegates. It was 12 percent, not 7 percent.
match_headline: Is This the Year Women Break the Rules and Win?

text: An article on Wednesday about Imran Awan, a former congressional technology worker who pleaded guilty to bank fraud, referred incorrectly to a transfer of money by Mr. Awan. According to his lawyer, Mr. Awan sent money to Pakistan to help his father; he did not send it to his father directly. The article also misstated where his father was living when the transfer was made. Before his death in January 2017, his father had been living in Virginia, not Pakistan.
match_headline: Imran Awan, Ex-Congressional I.T. Worker, Pleads Guilty to Bank Fraud

text: An article on Friday about the trial of Alain Kaloyeros and his ties to Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo misstated the given name of a former deputy director for state operations in New York. He is Andrew Kennedy, not Anthony.
match_headline: Culture of Fear and Ambition Distorted Cuomo’s Economic Projects

text: An article on June 29 about “Ocean Wonders: Sharks!,” a new display at New York Aquarium in Coney Island, omitted one of the firms that consulted on the project. In addition to the architects of record, Edelman Sultan Knox Wood, the Portico Group of Seattle contributed.
match_headline: Coney Island’s Newest Wonder: Sharkitecture!

text: An article on June 15 about the novelist Sayaka Murata misstated when her “Of Bones, of Body Heat, of the White-Colored City” won the Yukio Mishima Prize. It was five years ago, not four. And it was only last year that Ms. Murata quit her part-time job at a convenience store to pursue writing full time.
ref_headline: Of Bones, of Body Heat, of the White-Colored City
match_headline: For Japanese Novelist Sayaka Murata, Odd Is the New Normal

text: A column on Page 7 about three dark documentaries available on Netflix mischaracterizes a farm attached to Jacob’s Ladder, a rehab facility. It is not a dairy farm. The column also misstates the given name of the founder of Jacob’s Ladder. He is Kevin Blankenship, not Keith.
match_headline: 3 Sobering Documentaries on Netflix, Fandor and Field of Vision

text: An obituary on Thursday about the sprinter and long jumper Irena Szewinska misspelled the given name of one of her sons. He is Andrzej, not Andrezj.
match_headline: Irena Szewinska, Champion Polish Sprinter, Is Dead at 72

text: An article on June 24 about the Getty family misstated Mark Getty’s role in the founding of Getty Images. He was co-founder, with Jonathan Klein; he was not the sole founder.
match_headline: Growing Up Getty

text: An article last Sunday about how to alleviate stress in airports incorrectly included Chad as part of President Trump’s travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries. Chad was taken off the list of banned countries earlier this year.
match_headline: 18 Ways to Navigate Stress at the Airport

text: An article on June 24 about statutes of limitations for sexual-assault cases included incorrect details of one woman’s case. Danielle Tudor reported her assault the day it happened, not after six years. The article also misstated Oregon’s statute of limitations when her attacker was arrested. It was three years, not six.
match_headline: Should Statutes of Limitations for Rape Be Abolished?

text: A review on June 24 about “Tyrant: Shakespeare on Politics,” by Stephen Greenblatt, misidentified the play that features the rebel leader Jack Cade. It is “Henry VI, Part II,” not “Part III.”
match_headline: What Would Shakespeare Have Made of Donald Trump?

text: A review on June 24 about the picture book “Tiny, Perfect Things,” written by M.H. Clark, misspelled the illustrator’s given name. She is Madeline Kloepper, not Madeleine.
match_headline: Grandmas and Grandpas Are a Kid’s Natural Allies in These Books

text: An article on Friday about the recovery of a watch belonging to the Israeli spy Eli Cohen misidentified the watch model. It is an Eterna-Matic Centenaire 61, not an Omega.
match_headline: Israel’s Secret Operation to Recover the Watch of a Legendary Spy

text: An article on Thursday about the death in France of Wang Jian, one of China’s richest businessmen, misstated the rank of Hubert Mériaux of the Gendarmerie. He is a lieutenant colonel, not a colonel.
match_headline: Wang Jian, Co-Founder of Chinese Giant HNA, Dies in France

text: A review on Monday about the pianist Lang Lang’s first concert since injuring a hand over a year ago misidentified the oboe and flute players in the Mozart piano concerto. They were Mark McEwen and Elizabeth Ostling, not John Ferrillo and Elizabeth Rowe.
match_headline: Review: Lang Lang, Classical Music’s Superstar, Returns Quietly

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Jean-Marc Vallée, the director of the new HBO series “Sharp Objects,” misstated Mr. Vallée’s role in the production of Season 2 of “Big Little Lies.” He is executive producer, not director.
match_headline: ‘Sharp Objects’: Jean-Marc Vallée on the Series Premiere and Underdog Storytelling

text: An article on Tuesday about Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s new term as the president of Turkey misstated the title of a book about Mr. Erdogan by Soner Cagaptay. It is “The New Sultan,” not “The Last Sultan.”
match_headline: Erdogan Begins New Term and Names His Son-in-Law Finance Minister

text: An article on Tuesday about declining orca populations misstated Brad Hanson’s position at the Northwest Fisheries Science Center. He is the team leader for research, not recovery efforts. The article also misstated the acronym for polybrominated diphenyl ethers, widely used in fire retardants. It is PBDE, not PPDE.
match_headline: Orcas of the Pacific Northwest Are Starving and Disappearing

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about an experimental medical procedure involving mitochondria transplants referred incorrectly to the source of the mitochondria infused into Georgia Bowen. They were taken from neck muscle, not abdominal muscle.
match_headline: Dying Organs Restored to Life in Novel Experiments

text: An article on Tuesday about two plays in London featuring strong performances by female leads misidentified the director of the play “Machinal.” She is Natalie Abrahami, not Nathalie Armin, who is an actress in the production. The article also misstated Tina Turner’s original name. It was Anna Mae Bullock, not Anna Mae Bullard.
match_headline: Women Set London’s Stages Ablaze

text: An article on Friday about the novelist Anne Tyler misstated Ms. Tyler’s age. She is 76, not 75.
match_headline: Attention, Please: Anne Tyler Has Something to Say

text: An article last Wednesday about a Maryland agricultural official who is training dogs to detect bacteria harmful to beehives misstated the breed of one dog, Mack. He is a Labrador retriever, not a golden Labrador.
match_headline: With a Sniff and a Signal, These Dogs Hunt Down Threats to Bees

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the composer Oliver Knussen, using information from his publisher, omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to his daughter, Sonya, and his brother, Kenneth, Mr. Knussen is survived by a sister, Susan MacQuarrie.
match_headline: Oliver Knussen, ‘Where the Wild Things Are’ Composer, Dies at 66

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Sunday about Steve Ditko, the comic-book artist best known for his role in creating Spider-Man, referred incorrectly to the images shown. They are two full pages from The Amazing Spider-Man No. 33, not one.
match_headline: Steve Ditko, Influential Comic-Book Artist Who Helped Create Spider-Man, Dies at 90

text: An article on Tuesday about Israel’s response to a spate of fires caused by incendiary devices flown into Israel from Gaza on kites misidentified the newspaper for which Ben-Dror Yemini writes a column. It is Yediot Ahronot, not Maariv.
match_headline: Unable to Stop Flaming Kites, Israel Moves to Choke Off Gaza Commerce

text: An article on Tuesday about increased funding for an emergency food program in New York misstated the name of a Brooklyn church. It is St. Mary, Mother of Jesus Roman Catholic Church, not Our Mary Mother of Jesus Church.
match_headline: New York’s Emergency Food Program Gets More Funding, but Will It Be Enough?

text: An article on Saturday about Martina Navratilova’s first time winning Wimbledon misstated the significance of Navratilova’s mixed doubles match with Leander Paes in 2003. It was her last Wimbledon final, not her last Wimbledon match. It also misstated the amount of time that passed between Navratilova’s mother coming to Wimbledon in 1979 and the whole family being reunited. It was several months, not several years.
match_headline: 40 Years Later, Martina Navratilova Remembers 1st Wimbledon Win

text: An article on Friday about a ruling giving Transportation Security Administration agents immunity in civil suits over misconduct misstated the surname of a woman who sued the group, saying that its employees had mistreated her. She is Nadine Pellegrino Waldman, not Pellegrino Walden.
match_headline: Court Gives T.S.A. Screeners Immunity From Abuse Lawsuits

text: An article on Friday about the Chinese tennis player Li Na misspelled the surname of one of China’s junior players. She is Zheng Qinwen, not Zhang.
match_headline: Years After Retiring, Li Na Wields Major Influence in Tennis

text: An article on Friday about soccer fans and World Cup celebrations in Europe misstated the name of the train station in Paris that was to be renamed in honor of Eden Hazard if Belgium had defeated France. It is Saint-Lazare, not Saint-Hazard.
match_headline: Four Countries. Two Games. One Goal.

text: A review on Thursday about the Batsheva dance company’s performance of “Naharin’s Virus” misstated, in one instance, the name of the play by Peter Handke that is adapted in the performance. The play is “Offending the Audience,” not “Offering the Audience.”
match_headline: Review: With Batsheva, Politics Inside and Outside the Joyce Theater

text: An article on Friday about a federal appeals court’s decision in a case regarding California’s royalty laws described incorrectly a provision involving a 90-day grace period. The provision gives sellers 90 days to identify and pay royalties to artists, not the California Arts Council.
match_headline: California Tried to Give Artists a Cut. But the Judges Said No.

text: A review on Friday about the American artist David Wojnarowicz misstated, in one instance, the year Mr. Wojnarowicz received an H.I.V.-positive diagnosis. As correctly noted elsewhere in the review, it was 1988, not 1990.
match_headline: He Spoke Out During the AIDS Crisis. See Why His Art Still Matters.

text: An article on Page 1 about controversy over an exhibit at the Art Gallery of Ontario misstates when the Denver Art Museum was founded. It was 1893, not during the 1920s. (The museum established a Native arts department in the 1920s.)
match_headline: A Canadian Museum Promotes Indigenous Art. But Don’t Call It ‘Indian.’

text: An article on Page 15 about cast changes ahead of the new season of “Suits” misidentifies an actor who left “M*A*S*H*” during its run. It was Wayne Rogers, who played Trapper John McIntyre, not Alan Alda, who played Hawkeye Pierce.
match_headline: With Meghan Markle and Patrick J. Adams Gone, ‘Suits’ Retailors Itself

text: An article on Page 26 about Michael Avenatti, the lawyer representing Stormy Daniels, describes incorrectly the investment firm Columbus Nova. The firm’s biggest client is a company controlled by Viktor Vekselberg; Vekselberg does not control the firm itself. The article also misidentifies Richard Gephardt, for whom Avenatti worked in 1989. He was a representative, not a senator.
match_headline: The Fast and Furious Michael Avenatti

text: An obituary on Friday about the runner Lindy Remigino misstated the cause of his death. It was pancreatic cancer, not prostate cancer.
match_headline: Lindy Remigino, Olympic Champion Runner, Is Dead at 87

text: An obituary on Thursday about the trombonist and bandleader Bill Watrous misstated the date of his death. He died on July 2, not July 3. It also misstated the surname of the co-author of Mr. Watrous’s book “Trombonisms.” He is Alan Raph, not Ralph.
match_headline: Bill Watrous, Trombonist and Bandleader, Is Dead at 79

text: An article on July 1 about the artist Adrian Piper referred imprecisely to her performance in her doctoral program. Piper graduated at the top of her class, not near the top. Th e article also misstated how she exhibited her work; it is not the case that she regularly exhibited exclusively with other artists of color. In addition, the article misstated which shows she decided not to participate in. She will not exhibit her work in all- black shows, not shows with other artists of color.
match_headline: Adrian Piper’s Show at MoMA is the Largest Ever for a Living Artist. Why Hasn’t She Seen It?

text: An article last Sunday about intimate selfies included an anecdote about a married man who received a selfie from a woman who was not his wife; the article also included comments from others about the selfie.
match_headline: The Selfie That Dares to Go There

text: An article last Sunday about Kansas City, Mo., described incorrectly the location of the city in relation to the Mississippi River. It is west of the river, not east.
match_headline: The Perfect Way to Explore Modern Kansas City? A Streetcar, Believe It or Not

text: An article on Sunday about a provocative art project in Beijing highlighting water pollution in rural areas misstated the number of water bottles seized by the police. It was 7,000, not 9,000.
match_headline: With 9,000 Bottles of Dirty ‘Spring Water,’ a Chinese Artist Gets Results

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the nationalist appeal of Brexit misstated the affiliation of Sean Hannity’s radio show. Although his television show is on Fox News, his radio show is not affiliated with the network.
match_headline: In Brexit, Trump Finds a British Reflection of His Own Political Rise

text: An article on Saturday about a United Nations agreement concerning ways to manage migration flows misattributed quotations from a Swiss envoy about the United States’ withdrawal from negotiations over the global migration pact. The remarks were from Jürg Lauber, Switzerland’s ambassador to the United Nations in New York, not Valentin Zellweger, its ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva.
match_headline: U.N. Agrees on Migration Pact, but U.S. Is Conspicuously Absent

text: An article on June 28 about applications of blockchain technology omitted partners in the land registry pilot in Cook County, Ill. They were the New York office of the law firm Hogan Lovells, the Chicago law firm Goldberg Kohn, and Onyx Electronics of Valparaiso, Ind., all of which joined velox.RE in doing the work for free. The article also described incorrectly the scope of the pilot. The pilot included work on research and encryption; it is not the case that it involved only creating blockchains for parcels of land.
match_headline: Governments Explore Using Blockchains to Improve Service

text: An article on Monday about Democrats believed to be preparing for 2020 presidential campaigns misstated the age of Representative Kyrsten Sinema. She is 42, not 41.
match_headline: Warren Is Preparing for 2020. So Are Biden, Booker, Harris and Sanders.

text: An article on Monday about Cardinal Theodore E. McCarrick’s pattern of sexual abuse over the course of his life misidentified the seminary where Richard Sipe was a professor in the 1980s. He worked at St. Mary’s Seminary and University in Baltimore, not Mount St. Mary’s Seminary, which is in Emmitsburg, Md.
match_headline: He Preyed on Men Who Wanted to Be Priests. Then He Became a Cardinal.

text: An article on Monday about cows around the campus of the University of Cambridge described incorrectly the weight of a full-grown steer. Full-grown steers can yield about 450 pounds of meat; they do not weigh about 450 pounds.
match_headline: Parks Give Cambridge a Rural Vibe. ‘But Cows Do It Better.’

text: An article on Tuesday about dubious claims made at the joint news conference held by President Donald J. Trump and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia misstated the name of the publicist who brokered a June 2016 meeting between the Trump campaign and a Kremlin-connected lawyer. He is Rob Goldstone, not Gladstone.
match_headline: Trump Seeks Meeting With Putin Even as Allies Seek to Isolate Russia

text: An article on Tuesday about a slowdown in venture capital in China misspelled the given name of the founder of the asset management company Jinfuzi. He is Zhang Kaixing, not Kaixin.
match_headline: Latest Sign of China’s Slowdown: A Technology Cash Crunch

text: An article on Monday about a new Broadway production of “West Side Story” misstated the family background of a character, Tony. He is Polish-American, not Italian-American. The article, using information from a producer, also attributed an erroneous distinction to the new production. At least one production currently running, at the Guthrie Theater in Minneapolis, is using original choreography; the Broadway production is not the first in the United States not to base choreography on the original Jerome Robbins dances. (It is the first production on Broadway to do so.)
match_headline: New ‘West Side Story’ From Ivo van Hove and Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker

text: An article on Saturday about reactions to the 2018 Emmy nominations misstated the category in which Netflix’s “Last Chance U” was submitted. The docu-series was nominated for a Sports Emmy for outstanding serialized sports documentary; it was not under consideration for an Emmy for best documentary.
match_headline: Our TV Critics on the 2018 Emmy Nominations

text: An article on July 5 about a series built around the Marvel Entertainment character Iceman misstated when the character was first depicted in an animated series. It was in “The Marvel Super Heroes” in 1966, not “Spider-Man and His Amazing Friends” in 1981.
match_headline: Iceman Came Out. Now He’s Coming Back in His Own Series.

text: A review on Friday about the 1986 film “The Rise and Fall of a Small Film Company” referred incorrectly to the history of Jean-Pierre Léaud’s working relationship with Jean-Luc Godard. They worked together on “Détective” in 1985; the 1986 film did not reunite them for the first time since 1969.
ref_headline: The Rise and Fall of a Small Film Company
match_headline: Review: A Godard Film About Making Movies Arrives in New York

text: An article last Wednesday about making Chinese-style ribs at home misidentified Guangzhou and Guangdong, in China. Guangzhou is the capital of Guangdong province, not vice versa.
match_headline: Mastering Chinese-Style Ribs at Home

text: An editorial on Tuesday about President Trump misstated the action taken to charge a Russian woman as a foreign agent. She was charged in a criminal complaint, not an indictment.
match_headline: Why Won’t Donald Trump Speak for America?

text: An article on Saturday about the indictment of Russian intelligence officers referred incorrectly to an area of mathematics cited in a 2003 thesis presented to Russia’s domestic intelligence agency. It is nonlinear Boolean algebra, not “nonlinear, or Boolean, equations.”
match_headline: G.R.U., Russian Spy Agency Cited by Mueller, Casts a Long Shadow

text: An article on Saturday about hostile comments posted on science-themed videos hosted by women on YouTube misspelled the given name of a science communication researcher. She is Inoka Amarasekara, not Inoaka.
match_headline: Women Making Science Videos on YouTube Face Hostile Comments

text: An article on Thursday about new misinformation standards at Facebook misstated the social media platforms owned by Facebook that are subject to the new rules. The rules apply to Instagram, but not WhatsApp.
match_headline: Facebook to Remove Misinformation That Leads to Violence

text: An article on Thursday about the first mountain stage of the Tour de France misstated the year that Team Sky backed Bradley Wiggins over Chris Froome. It was 2012, not 2013.
match_headline: A Burst Through the Mountains Breaks Open the Tour de France

text: A review on Thursday about the production of “Coriolanus” at the Stratford Festival misstated the city where Ex Machina is based. It is Quebec City, not Montreal.
match_headline: Review: At Stratford, ‘Coriolanus’ Is Riveting and Troubling

text: An article on Friday about sweeping changes to the Endangered Species Act misstated the title of Robert Gordon. He is an adjunct fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute, not the director of the National Wilderness Institute.
match_headline: Law That Saved the Bald Eagle Could Be Vastly Reworked

text: An article on Friday about the health insurer Anthem’s denial of claims for emergency room visits misstated the name of a doctors trade group. It is the American College of Emergency Physicians, not the American College of Emergency Room Physicians.
match_headline: A Health Insurer Tells Patients It Won’t Pay Their E.R. Bills, but Then Pays Them Anyway

text: An article on Page 7 about a rare production of Anton Rubinstein’s 1871 opera “Demon” includes a picture caption that misstated the name of a character in the opera. He is Prince Sinodal, not Prince Gudal.
match_headline: It Was Russia’s Most Popular Opera. Then It Disappeared.

text: An obituary on Thursday about the jockey Manny Ycaza misstated the number of children his parents had. He was one of nine children, not 10.
match_headline: Manny Ycaza, Hall of Fame Jockey, Is Dead at 80

text: An article last Sunday about retirees who return to their former employers misstated how long a nurse, Ilana Benet, worked at Montefiore Health System in the Bronx. It was 40 years, not 26. The article also misstated the status of Montefiore retirees who returned. They are working in a series of informal arrangements, not in a formal program.
match_headline: In a Tight Labor Market, Retirees Fill Gaps Their Previous Employers Can’t

text: An article last Sunday about the lamp designer Margit Wittig referred incorrectly to the museum where Ms. Wittig once spent time. It was the Art Institute of Chicago, not the Chicago Institute of Art.
match_headline: Lighting the Way Toward a New Career

text: An article about buying a home sight unseen misidentified the school where Alan D. Kaye is chairman of the anesthesiology department. It is Louisiana State University Medical School, not Tulane University.
match_headline: Buying a Home Sight Unseen

text: An article about planned bans of For Sale signs included a caption that misidentified the location pictured. It is New Canaan, Conn., not Darien.
match_headline: Does a For Sale Sign Help Sell a House?

text: An article on June 24 about how to barricade a door misstated the position of a member of the Fort Lauderdale Police Department’s SWAT team. Steven Smith is a team leader, not the team leader.
match_headline: How to Barricade a Door

text: An article on July 8 about how to throw out a ceremonial first pitch described incorrectly the direction of the ball. The ball bounced before reaching the catcher, not the pitcher.
match_headline: How to Throw Out a Ceremonial First Pitch

text: A recipe on July 8 about a Roman breakfast cake specified an incorrect tube-pan size. It should be a 10-inch tube pan, not 9-inch.

An article on Tuesday about newsroom layoffs at The Daily News misstated Sarah Ryley’s role in a series of articles about the New York Police Department’s abuse of eviction rules. She was the reporter on the series, not the editor.
match_headline: Daily News Newsroom Cut in Half by Tronc as Top Editor Is Ousted

text: An article on Friday about the impact of Robert G. Mugabe’s 37-year rule in Zimbabwe misidentified an American organization that has raised concerns about Zimbabwe’s elections. It is the International Republican Institute, not the International Research Institute.
match_headline: Mugabe Has Left, but His Legacy Haunts Zimbabwe’s Election

text: An article on Tuesday about a lawsuit over curriculums in ultra-Orthodox Jewish schools in New York misstated how many children attend ultra-Orthodox yeshivas that do not meet secular state standards. It is not all 115,000 students, but many of them.
match_headline: A Law Tailored for Orthodox Jewish Schools Is Unconstitutional, Lawsuit Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a woman’s allegations of sexual abuse against a former diving coach at Ohio State University referred imprecisely to which abuse cases were brought to the attention of university officials long before school officials took action. Officials are said to have failed to respond to abuse allegations involving Dr. Larry Nassar at Michigan State University, Dr. George Tyndall at the University of Southern California and Dr. Richard H. Strauss at Ohio State University; however, as the article noted elsewhere, Ohio State says it took immediate action in response to Eszter Pryor’s complaint against her diving coach.
match_headline: ‘I Didn’t Know How to Stop Him’: Ohio State Abuse Scandal Widens

text: An article on Tuesday about the return of an ancient limestone relief to Iran misquoted David Schoen, a lawyer for the Safani Gallery. Mr. Schoen said that investigators had found his client’s efforts to research the provenance of the piece commendable, not that he had.
match_headline: Judge Orders Return of Ancient Limestone Relief to Iran

text: A recipe for peach polenta cake last Wednesday misstated the amount of all-purpose flour. It is a half-cup plus a tablespoon of all-purpose flour, not a quarter-cup plus a tablespoon.
An obituary on July 18 about the cancer researcher Alan S. Rabson misstated the name of the university where he did biology research. It is the University of Rochester, not Rochester University.
match_headline: Dr. Alan S. Rabson, Influential Cancer Researcher, Is Dead at 92

text: An obituary on Saturday about the screenwriter Shinobu Hashimoto misstated the year the movie “Seven Samurai,” which he helped write, was released. As a picture caption with the obituary correctly noted, it was 1954, not 1950. The obituary also contained incorrect information about Mr. Hashimoto’s survivors, provided by the United States publisher of his memoir. In addition to two daughters and a grandson, he is survived by two granddaughters and a great-grandson. And his son, Shingo, was mistakenly listed as a survivor; he is no longer alive.
match_headline: Shinobu Hashimoto, Writer of Towering Kurosawa Films, Is Dead at 100

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the shuttering of Ivanka Trump’s namesake brand misstated the name of a watchdog organization. It is Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, not Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics.
match_headline: Ivanka Trump Is Shutting Down Her Fashion Brand

text: An article last Thursday about nontraditional summer parties misstated the status of a Texas bill to restrict transgender bathroom use. The bill was not passed.
match_headline: The Ultimate Guide to This Fabulous Summer

text: An article on Thursday about Republican representatives’ move to impeach the deputy attorney general, Rod J. Rosenstein, referred incorrectly to the impeachment process. A group of House Republicans would need the support of a majority of the House to impeach and two-thirds of the Senate to convict the deputy attorney general, not to impeach him.
match_headline: House Republicans Mount a Long-Shot Bid to Impeach Rod Rosenstein

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the impact of strikes on the discount carrier Ryanair misstated Michael O’Leary’s role at Ryanair. He is the airline’s chief executive, not its founder.
match_headline: Ryanair, Long Opposed to Unions, Grapples With Strikes in Europe

text: An editorial on Thursday about legislation to reform the Congressional Accountability Act suggested incorrectly that the law allows for punitive damages. It allows for compensatory and other damages.
match_headline: Why Does Congress Make Taxpayers Pay Hush Money?

text: An article on Monday about attacks on Roman Catholic clergy in Nicaragua by supporters of President Daniel Ortega referred imprecisely to comments made by Jaime Wheelock, a Sandinista commander in the 1979 revolution. While Mr. Wheelock suggested that the Ortega government might decide that the church is not a constructive mediator between the government and its opponents, Mr. Wheelock fully supports the church’s role in the dialogue and condemns the paramilitaries’ attacks on protesters.
match_headline: Nicaragua Clergy, Siding With Protesters, Becomes ‘Terrible Enemy’ of Ortega

text: A headline with an article on Friday about a ruling in a case in which Enrichetta Ravina, an assistant professor at Columbia University, claimed she had been harassed and retaliated against misstated the result of the lawsuit. The jury found in Ms. Ravina’s favor on a claim of retaliation; she did not “win” the “harassment suit.”
match_headline: Former Assistant Professor Wins Retaliation Claim Against Columbia

text: An article on Friday about the tradition of “tour hostesses” at the Tour de France misstated the number of stages Peter Sagan won at this year’s Tour de France. He had won three stages, not five.
match_headline: The Tour de France Loves Its ‘Podium Girls’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the Sexual Offenders Assessment Board’s psychological evaluation of Bill Cosby overstated what is known about the board’s process in making the assessment. The board does not publicly reveal details about its evaluation; it is unclear whether Mr. Cosby met with a board psychologist.
match_headline: Panel Finds Bill Cosby to Be a Sexually Violent Predator

text: An article on Thursday about “Sharkwrecked” misstated the year that Paul de Gelder lost a hand and a leg to a bull shark attack. It was 2009, not 1999.
match_headline: 43 Hours, Circling Fins, No Boat: All for the Shark Week Glory

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about Iceland Airwaves, a musical festival that committed to booking female artists for at least half of its lineup, misidentified a performer at a Fever Ray show. She is Helena Gutarra, not Karin Dreijer.
match_headline: Some Music Festivals Balk at Booking 50% Female Acts. One Just Did It.

text: A review on Friday about the exhibition “Mary Corse: A Survey in Light” misstated the number of children Mary Corse had. It is two, not one.
ref_headline: Mary Corse: A Survey in Light
match_headline: Bands of Paint and Light Shimmer. But Do They Still Shock?

text: An article on Page 1 about the comedian Hannah Gadsby misstated whom Ms. Gadsby’s show, “Nanette,” was referencing. The title refers to a barista the comedian had been observing; it is not a reference to an ex-girlfriend.
match_headline: The Comedy-Destroying, Soul-Affirming Art of Hannah Gadsby

text: An obituary on Thursday about Oksana Shachko, the founder of the women’s rights group Femen, misstated the nationality of the director Alain Margot, with whom Ms. Shachko had worked on a documentary film about Femen. He is Swiss, not French.
match_headline: Oksana Shachko, a Founder of Feminist Protest Movement, Dies at 31

text: An obituary on Thursday about the veteran Staten Island politician Guy V. Molinari misstated where in New York City he was born. It was Manhattan, not Staten Island.
match_headline: Guy V. Molinari, Power Broker in New York and Beyond, Is Dead at 89

text: An article last Sunday about emerging musicians in Baltimore misidentified where the artist Al Rogers Jr.’s earliest foray in club music took place. It was at The ’Dox (a nickname for a club that was called the Paradox), not the Patapsco River docks. A picture caption with the article also misstated the name of a rap collective. It is Refugee, not Modern Refugees.
match_headline: The Changing Sound of Baltimore

text: An article last Sunday about women who faced media scrutiny while in college misidentified a gallery in New Haven. It is ArtSpace, not ArtSpaceOne. The article also incompletely described the college major of Aliza Shvarts. It was art as well as English.
match_headline: There Is Life After Campus Infamy

text: An article on July 1 about the singer-songwriter Carly Simon’s family and friends at home on Martha’s Vineyard misstated the age of one of the guests, Sophie Hiller. She is 28, not 30.
match_headline: Carly Simon and Her Family, on Martha’s Vineyard

text: An article last Sunday about multigenerational households misstated where Diana Limongi’s father was born. He is from Ecuador, not Colombia.
match_headline: What to Know Before Buying a Home With Your Parents

text: An article on July 15 about a patient who had a bone disorder referred incorrectly to Dr. David Gorson’s actions after the patient was given a diagnosis. It is not the case that Dr. Gorson was unsure what to do. The article also misstated how the patient found Dr. Karl Insogna, a bone specialist. Dr. Gorson suggested that the patient contact Dr. Insogna; the patient did not find Dr. Insogna on her own.
match_headline: The Young Woman Was a Healthy and Avid Runner. Now She Could Barely Walk. Why?

text: A review on July 8 about “Kicks: The Great American Story of Sneakers,” by Nicholas Smith, misidentified the killer in a 1989 murder involving a pair of Nike Air Jordans. He was James David Martin. He was not Michael Eugene Thomas; Thomas was the victim.
ref_headline: Kicks: The Great American Story of Sneakers,
match_headline: How Sneakers Intersect With Recent American History

text: A review on July 15 about the novel “That Kind of Mother,” by Rumaan Alam, misstated the title of the author’s first novel. It is “Rich and Pretty,” not “Pretty and Rich.”

match_headline: Glen Roven, Emmy-Winning Composer and Conductor, Dies at 61

text: An article on Friday about the discovery of a plane wreck from 1946 in Switzerland referred incorrectly to the organization that operated the crashed plane. It was a division of the United States Army, not the Air Force, which was established in 1947.
match_headline: Melting Ice Uncovers 1946 Wreckage of U.S. Plane in Swiss Glacier

text: A review on Friday about art shows in Los Angeles misspelled the surname of an artist. She is Christina Quarles, not Quales.
match_headline: 3 Knockout Art Shows to See in Los Angeles Right Now

text: An obituary on Friday about the convicted drug dealer Herbert Sperling misstated the year the James Cagney crime film “Angels With Dirty Faces” was released. It was 1938, not 1932.
match_headline: Herbert Sperling, Drug Kingpin Tied to French Connection Case, Dies at 79

text: An obituary on Friday about Aretha Franklin referred incorrectly to the shooting of her father, the Rev. C. L. Franklin, in 1979. He was shot in the knee and the groin, and one bullet severed an artery, limiting the flow of blood to his brain; he was not shot in the head.
match_headline: Aretha Franklin, Indomitable ‘Queen of Soul,’ Dies at 76

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about people who use frightening visuals on social media to challenge a beauty standard misspelled the middle name of Steven Bhaskaran. It is Raj, not Taj. The article also misstated this person’s preferred honorific. It is the gender-neutral Mx., not the masculine Mr.
match_headline: Latte Art Begone! Here Come the Bold Freaks of Instagram

text: Because of an editing error, three pictures with an article on Aug. 5 about the legacy of the artist Robert Indiana were published with incomplete credits. The credit for Mr. Indiana’s work “Amor” is 2018 Morgan Art Foundation Ltd./Artists Rights Society (ARS), NY; Paul Marotta/Getty Images; for “Ahava” it is 2018 Morgan Art Foundation Ltd./Artists Rights Society (ARS), NY; DeAgostini/Getty Images; and for “One Through Zero (The Ten Numbers)” it is 2018 Morgan Art Foundation Ltd./Artists Rights Society (ARS), NY; Corbis via Getty Images.
match_headline: Nicole Eisenman Wins $200,000 Artist Prize

text: An article on Aug. 5 about “Madeline’s Madeline” misidentified the director of Jackie Sibblies Drury’s play “We Are Proud To Present a Presentation…” at Soho Rep. Eric Ting was the director, not Sarah Benson, who is the artistic director of the theater.
match_headline: Learning Lines. And Crossing Them.

text: An article on July 29 about the science of meat allergy described the hormone epinephrine inaccurately. Epinephrine is another term for adrenaline, not a different form of adrenaline.
match_headline: What the Mystery of the Tick-Borne Meat Allergy Could Reveal

text: An article on Aug. 5 about one decade in the history of climate-change activism misstated the type of solar panels installed by President Jimmy Carter on the White House roof. They were solar-thermal panels, not photovoltaic panels. The article also misstated the number of acres that burned in Yellowstone National Park in 1988. Yellowstone lost 793,880 acres, not four million.
match_headline: Bison-Taunting Man at Yellowstone Is Arrested, Park Officials Say

text: An article on Thursday about evidence against Paul Manafort in his fraud trial misstated the day on which closing arguments were made. They took place on Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: Evidence Against Manafort Is ‘Overwhelming,’ Prosecutors Say

text: An editorial on Saturday about the process to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court mischaracterized the rationale that President George W. Bush’s lawyer, William Burck, gave for withholding large numbers of documents pertaining to Judge Kavanaugh from the Senate Judiciary Committee. Mr. Burck has told the National Archives that they are personal to President Bush. He’s not withholding the documents “for no clear reason.”
match_headline: Why Are Republicans Covering Up Brett Kavanaugh’s Past?

text: An obituary on Monday about the socialist activist David McReynolds misidentified the publication in which an interview with him appeared in 2015. It is The Villager, not The Village Voice.
match_headline: David McReynolds, Socialist Activist Who Ran for President, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on April 9 about Lillias Campbell Davidson, an early women’s cycling advocate, erroneously attributed a distinction to the Campbell’s Lady Cyclists’ Association. It was one of the earliest groups for female bicyclists; it was not the first. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Overlooked No More: Lillias Campbell Davidson, an Early Advocate for Women’s Cycling

text: An article on Monday about advertising in sports radio misstated which electronics retailer has a longstanding relationship with Mike Francesa of WFAN-FM. It is P.C. Richard & Son, not Adorama.
match_headline: To Reach Men, Advertisers Dial In to Sports Radio

text: An article last Wednesday about restaurants that describe their food as organic misstated the type of beef the Bareburger chain is currently using. The company says that for now, it is serving only 100 percent organic beef, not a blend that is part organic. (A picture caption repeated the error.)
match_headline: When the Menu Says ‘Organic,’ but Not All the Food Is

text: An article on Wednesday about Mark Gordon’s victory in the Republican primary for governor of Wyoming misspelled the name of the Democratic nominee. She is Mary Throne, not Thorne. It also misstated her political status. She is a former member of the state House of Representatives, not a current member.
match_headline: Wyoming Republicans Snub Trump-Endorsed Candidate for Governor

text: An article on Wednesday about Giancarlo Stanton’s reception in Miami as a Yankee misstated the value of his contract with the Miami Marlins. It was $325 million, not $275 million.
match_headline: Giancarlo Stanton Takes His Scorching Bat to a Miami Homecoming

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the actress Barbara Harris misidentified the director of the 1976 movie “Freaky Friday,” in which she appeared. It was Gary Nelson, not Mark Waters. (Mr. Waters directed the 2003 remake.)
match_headline: Barbara Harris, Stage, Screen and Improv Actress, Dies at 83

text: An article on Thursday about Ammar Campa-Najjar, a congressional candidate in California, misstated his age. He is 29, not 28.
match_headline: Duncan Hunter’s Indictment in California Opens the Door for a Long-Shot Challenger

text: An obituary on Thursday about the producer Craig Zadan referred imprecisely to the television series “Smash,” of which he and Neil Meron were executive producers. They were involved for only 15 episodes, but the show was canceled after 32 episodes, not 15. Because of an editing error, the obituary also referred incorrectly to Rob Marshall, the director of the movie version of the musical “Chicago.” Although the film won the best-picture Oscar, Mr. Marshall did not win an Oscar for directing it.
match_headline: Craig Zadan, 69, Dies; Produced Musicals for Stage, Screen and TV

text: An obituary on Sunday about the former United Nations secretary general Kofi Annan omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to his wife and children, Mr. Annan is survived by a brother, Kobina, a former Ghanaian ambassador to Morocco.
match_headline: Kofi Annan, Who Redefined the U.N., Dies at 80

text: An obituary on Thursday about George Andrie, a defensive end who played for the Dallas Cowboys from 1962 to 1972, misstated the given name of the man who was the Cowboys’ team physician in those years. He was Marvin Knight, not Melvin.
match_headline: George Andrie, Pillar of Cowboys’ Doomsday Defense, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Thomas B. Hofeller, a Republican master of redistricting strategy, misstated his role in Thornburg v. Gingles, a 1986 Supreme Court case that effectively made the creation of black-majority districts a consideration in drawing electoral maps. He was part of a Republican National Committee team that drafted an amicus brief supporting black plaintiffs in the case; he was not an expert witness for them.
match_headline: Thomas Hofeller, Republican Master of Political Maps, Dies at 75

text: An article on Thursday about the current bull market misstated the duration of the current upward trend. It is nearly 10 years, not 10 years. The article also referred imprecisely to the share of stocks owned by the wealthiest 10 percent of households in the United States. It is 84 percent of the value of shares owned by households, not 84 percent of all outstanding shares.
match_headline: Bull Market Hits a Milestone: 3,453 Days. Most Americans Aren’t at the Party.

text: An article on Thursday about declining consumer spending in China misstated the name of the province where Wu Xiaoqiong, a young woman who has decided to remain childless, is from. It is Anhui, not Hefei. Hefei is the capital of Anhui province.
match_headline: China’s Consumption Downgrade: Skip Avocados, Cocktails and Kids

text: An entry on Friday in the “What’s on TV” highlights misstated the opening date of the movie “What Men Want.” It is slated to open on Feb. 8, 2019, not Jan. 11.
match_headline: What’s on TV Friday: ‘The Road’ and ‘Trolls: The Beat Goes On’

text: An article on Page 8 about Leonard Bernstein misspells the given name of a Harvard professor. She is Carol J. Oja, not Carole.
match_headline: Brash, Confident and Democratic: How Leonard Bernstein Symbolized America

text: A picture with an entry on Page 2 about an exhibition of propaganda postcards was published in error. The photograph shows a group of men walking on a road, not a postcard illustration by Giuseppe Scalarini.
match_headline: This Week in Arts: Drake, ‘Carousel’ and Propaganda Postcards

text: An article on Page 11 about regulations on tennis courts in New York misstates where Oscar Hijuelos, a novelist who played at the Riverside Clay Tennis Association, died. He had a heart attack while playing on the association’s courts, not while playing elsewhere. The article also misstates the location of the tennis court at Washington Market Park. The court is next to the Tribeca Bridge, not under it.
match_headline: The Courts of New York City

text: An article on Aug. 5 about “Madeline’s Madeline” gave an incorrect distinction for the Soho Rep production of Jackie Sibblies Drury’s play “We Are Proud to Present a Presentation….” The play was first presented in April 2012 at the Victory Gardens Theater in Chicago; Soho Rep did not stage its premiere.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Madeline’s Madeline,’ Hazy Boundaries Between Life and Art

text: A review on Aug. 12 about “Conservatism,” by Roger Scruton, misstated the book’s publisher. It is All Points Books, not St. Martin’s Press.
match_headline: Defending Conservatism, and Seeking Converts

text: An article in the July 29 kids section about how words get into the dictionary gave the incorrect hometown for Levi Budd, who coined the word “levidrome.” He lives in Victoria, British Columbia, not Vancouver.
match_headline: Facebook Is Failing to Aid Inquiry Into ‘Fake News,’ British Lawmakers Say

text: An article last Sunday about restaurants in London misstated the name of a neighborhood in the city. It is Mayfair, not Mayfield. The article also misstated the rating of the One Aldwych hotel. It is a five-star hotel, not four-star. And the article misstated the phone number for the Eneko restaurant. It is 44-20-7300-0300, not 44-20-7300-0700.
match_headline: Beyond Porridge and Boiled Mutton: A Taste of London

text: An article last week about children and chores misstated the values that 80 percent of students in a survey ranked more highly than caring for others. They were happiness and achievement, not only happiness.
match_headline: Happy Children Do Chores

text: An article on Monday about enrollment at the European University at St. Petersburg referred incorrectly to Vladimir Y. Gelman. He is a political scientist, not a political theorist.
match_headline: In Russia, a Top University Lacks Just One Thing: Students

text: An article on Monday about Joe Arpaio misstated the first name of the Democrat who was elected Maricopa County sheriff in 2016. He is Paul Penzone, not Peter.
match_headline: In Arizona Primary, Joe Arpaio Is Making His Last Stand

text: An article on Monday about the surge in female politicians winning primaries misspelled the name of a congressional candidate in New York. It is Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, not Alexandra.
match_headline: Let’s Get New York to the Polls

text: An entry in the Week Ahead report on Monday about a review of Volkswagen since its emissions scandal referred incorrectly to the review. It is expected to detail the extent to which the carmaker has complied with the terms of a civil settlement with the United States, not the terms of a plea agreement in a criminal case.
match_headline: Report on VW Progress After Emissions Scandal, and Consumer Spending Data

text: An article on Monday about legacy brands marketing to younger generations misidentified the business unit that SunnyD merged with when it was acquired by Brynwood Partners in 2016. It is Harvest Hill, not Heritage Hill.
match_headline: Brands Try to Convince New Generations Products Aren’t Just for Their Parents
