text: An article on Thursday about a suspected hacking of the Democratic National Committee misstated what cybersecurity officials said about hackers’ efforts to gain access to the organization’s voter database. The officials said the hackers may have sent so-called spearphishing emails to D.N.C. officials, not that they did send such emails.
match_headline: Democratic Party Says It Thwarted Attempted Hack of Voter Database

text: An article on Aug. 18 about economic stress in Turkey misstated Ugur Dalbeler’s position with the Turkish Steel Exporters’ Association, an industry group. He is a board member, not the president.
match_headline: Life in Turkey Now: Tough Talk, but Fears of Drug Shortages

text: An obituary on Monday about the playwright Neil Simon contained an incomplete credit for the original Broadway production of the musical “Little Me,” for which he wrote the book. It was directed by Cy Feuer and Bob Fosse, not just by Mr. Fosse. In addition, a picture caption with the obituary, using information from Getty Images, misidentified one of the writers pictured with Mr. Simon and Sid Caesar. The second man standing from the left is Joseph Stein, not Gary Belkin.
match_headline: Neil Simon, Broadway Master of Comedy, Is Dead at 91

text: An article on Tuesday about a federal ruling finding North Carolina’s congressional district map to be unconstitutional misstated the usual number of Supreme Court justices whose assent is required for the court to hear a case. It is four, not five.
match_headline: North Carolina Is Ordered to Redraw Its Gerrymandered Congressional Map. Again.

text: An article on Monday about the efficacy of Job Corps referred incorrectly to Mathematica Policy Research. It is an employee-owned company, not a nonprofit organization.
match_headline: $1.7 Billion Federal Job Training Program Is ‘Failing the Students’

text: An article on Friday about the deportation of Jakiw Palij, a former member of Hitler’s Schutzstaffel, misstated the number of Jews who were killed in Poland during the Holocaust. It was 3 million, not 1.7 million.
match_headline: How the Nazis Got to New York: Immigration Fraud

text: An article on Tuesday about the effect of the new tax law on housing prices misstated the number of tax filers who claimed the mortgage interest deduction last year and the number expected to claim it this year. About 14 million are expected to claim it this year versus about 32 million last year, not 14,000 this year versus 32,000 last year.
match_headline: The Trump Tax Cuts Were Supposed to Depress Housing Prices. They Haven’t.

text: An article on Tuesday about a new monograph by Françoise Gilot misstated the length of time that Ms. Gilot has been with the Mac-Gryder Gallery. It has been since 2017, not 1972, but Jill McGaughey, the owner of that gallery, has represented her for 10 years.
match_headline: In a New Book of Sketches, Françoise Gilot Clears Her Mind of the Past

text: Because of a production error, a recipe last Wednesday by Nasim Alikhani, the owner of Sofreh restaurant in Brooklyn, omitted the final five ingredients for Persian cod with herbs and tamarind. They are 3 tablespoons fresh lemon juice; 2½ teaspoons kosher salt, plus more as needed; sugar, as needed; 6 thick fillets of cod (6 to 8 ounces each) or another meaty white fish; and cooked basmati rice, for serving. The correct recipe is at nytcooking.com.
match_headline: At 59, a Gutsy Chef Makes Her Restaurant Debut

text: An article last Wednesday about the sudden disappearance of red salmon in many parts of Alaska misstated the year when the smolt, or young salmon, for this year’s red-salmon runs headed to the sea. It was 2015, not 2014. A picture caption with the article also misidentified the body of water in Anchorage where many people were shown fishing. It is Ship Creek, not Fish Creek.
match_headline: A Dwindling Catch Has Alaskans Uneasy

text: An obituary on Sunday and Monday about Senator John S. McCain referred incorrectly to the fire onboard the aircraft carrier Forrestal, on which he served, that killed 134 people. It was not the worst noncombat incident in American naval history; there were several other incidents with higher death tolls. The obituary also misstated Mr. McCain’s position on the Senate Select Committee on P.O.W./M.I.A. Affairs. He was a member, not a co-chairman. Because of an editing error, the obituary misstated the league in which the 1996 Republican vice-presidential nominee Jack Kemp had been a star before entering politics. It was the American Football League, not the National Football League. And it omitted the name of one of Mr. McCain’s survivors. In addition to his wife, children and grandchildren, he is survived by his mother, Roberta McCain.
match_headline: John McCain, War Hero, Senator, Presidential Contender, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Saturday about the architect Costas Kondylis misspelled the given name of his mother and the middle name of one of his daughters. His mother was Vassiliki Kondylis, not Vassilikis; his daughter is Katherine Cary Kondylis, not Kary.
match_headline: Costas Kondylis, Go-To Architect in a High-Rise Town, Dies at 78

text: An article on Saturday about C.I.A. informants in Russia falling largely silent misstated when President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia spoke publicly against former intelligence agents he viewed as traitors. It was in 2010, not shortly before the assassination attempt on a former Russian intelligence officer, Sergei V. Skripal. The article also referred incorrectly to the public comments Mr. Putin made. They were menacing, but not direct threats.
match_headline: Kremlin Sources Go Quiet, Leaving C.I.A. in the Dark About Putin’s Plans for Midterms

text: An article on Saturday about an announcement by the Trump administration that it would cut aid for Palestinians referred incorrectly to the Israel Project. The organization identifies itself as nonpartisan, not right-leaning.
match_headline: Trump Administration Cuts More Than $200 Million in Aid for Palestinians

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about deteriorating relations between the United States and North Korea referred incorrectly to the South Korean foreign minister. Kang Kyung-wha is a woman.
match_headline: North Korean State Media Denounce U.S. as Diplomacy Stalls

text: An article on Wednesday about a proposal to rename the Russell Senate Building misstated the position of a senator from Georgia on the proposal. Senator Johnny Isakson supports the formation of a committee to consider how to honor Senator John McCain; he did not say he supported renaming the building after Mr. McCain.
match_headline: Replace Richard Russell’s Name With McCain’s? Senate Debates a Segregationist’s Legacy

text: An article on Wednesday about a federal court ruling declaring that North Carolina’s congressional district map was unconstitutional misstated the middle initial of an election-law scholar at the Moritz College of Law at Ohio State University. He is Edward B. Foley, not Edward F.
match_headline: University of North Carolina Chancellor Explores New Spot for ‘Silent Sam’

text: An article on Wednesday about the 1968 Democratic National Convention misstated the age of a press organizer for the National Mobilization Committee to End the War in Vietnam. The organizer, Don Rose, was 37 at the time of the convention, not 29.
match_headline: ‘The Whole World Is Watching’: The 1968 Democratic Convention, 50 Years Later

text: An article on Tuesday about a $500 million investment in Uber made by Toyota, using information from Uber, misstated the valuation of the ride-hailing company. It is $76 billion, not $72 billion.
match_headline: In a Shift in Driverless Strategy, Uber Deepens Its Partnership With Toyota

text: An article on Wednesday about the extreme heat policy at the United States Open misstated the length of the new serve clock. It is 25 seconds, not 20 seconds.
match_headline: U.S. Open Highlights: Heat Is the Big Winner on Day 2

text: An article on Tuesday about Pierre Hache, a French D.J., misstated when the ballroom scene originated. It was in Harlem in the 1920s, not the 1980s.
match_headline: ‘Son of Immigrants, Black and Gay’: A D.J. Breaks Barriers in France

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about John McCain’s funeral misidentified Mr. McCain’s sons. James McCain is shown at left, and John is at right.
match_headline: The Schedule of Tributes to John McCain: When and How He Will Be Remembered

text: An article on Thursday about ethnic diversity among recently nominated Democratic candidates misspelled the first name of the Republican candidate for governor in Colorado. He is Walker, not Walter, Stapleton.
match_headline: Democratic Embrace of Diverse Candidates Collides With Barbed Politics of Trump Era

text: An article on Thursday about a debate between the two Democratic candidates for lieutenant governor misspelled the given name of the mayor of Rochester. She is Lovely Warren, not Lovey.
match_headline: Want to Be the Governor’s No. 2? Debate Offers Opposing Views of Job

text: An article on Friday about Colin Kaepernick’s collusion case against the N.F.L. misstated the amount in compensatory damages he would receive if he were to win his case in a full hearing. He would receive two times the amount of compensatory damages, not three times (which is for a second offense).
match_headline: Colin Kaepernick’s Collusion Case Against the N.F.L. Will Advance

text: An article on Thursday about classic jazz recordings planned for release misstated the type of material onto which William Savory pressed bootleg recordings of radio broadcasts. He used acetate and metal discs, not shellac.
match_headline: Unreleased Jazz Treasures Are Arriving: Here’s a Guide

text: An obituary on Aug. 8 about the Hall of Fame hockey player Stan Mikita misidentified the country where he was born. At the time of his birth, in 1940, it was the Slovak Republic, not Czechoslovakia.
match_headline: Stan Mikita, 78, Dies; Hockey Hall of Famer Lifted Blackhawks

text: A picture caption with a review last Sunday about “The Husband Hunters: American Heiresses Who Married Into the British Aristocracy,” by Anne de Courcy, misstated the name of Winston Churchill’s maternal grandmother. She was Clarissa Jerome, not Mrs. Jerome Martin.
ref_headline: The Husband Hunters: American Heiresses Who Married Into the British Aristocracy,
match_headline: Titles and Troubles: American Heiresses Abroad

text: Because of an editing error, the By the Book feature on Aug. 12 misstated a word in the title of a biography by Selina Hastings. It is “The Secret Lives of Somerset Maugham,” not “The Secret Life.”
ref_headline: The Secret Lives of Somerset Maugham,
match_headline: Anne de Courcy: By the Book

text: An article on Aug. 5 about one decade in the history of climate-change activism erroneously cited a 1974 C.I.A. study. The study was about climate change; it was not specifi cally about global warming caused by carbon dioxide.
match_headline: Inquiry Ends Into Exxon Mobil’s Accounting Tied to Climate Change

text: An article on Aug. 26 about presidential judicial appointments misidentifi ed which Widener University law school Donald F. McGahn attended. He graduated from Widener University Commonwealth Law School in Pennsylvania, not in Delaware.
match_headline: How the Trump Administration Is Remaking the Courts

text: An article on Sunday about the funeral for Senator John McCain misstated the surname of the friend and classmate next to whom Mr. McCain was to be buried. He was Adm. Charles R. Larson, not Lawson. The article also misquoted a line from Robert Louis Stevenson’s poem “Requiem.” It is “Home is the sailor, home from the sea,” not “Here is the sailor, home from the sea.” A picture caption with the article also referred incorrectly to Mr. McCain’s daughter, Meghan McCain. She is the eldest of his children with his widow, Cindy McCain, not his eldest daughter. (Sidney McCain, Mr. McCain’s daughter from an earlier marriage, is older.)
match_headline: In McCain Memorial Service, Two Presidents Offer Tribute, and a Contrast to Trump

text: An article last Wednesday about China’s successful modernization of its navy misstated the number of submarines in China’s naval fleet in 1995. There were 83, not three, according to Pentagon figures cited in a report from Congressional Research Service, though it noted that the figure included obsolete models.
match_headline: With Ships and Missiles, China Is Ready to Challenge U.S. Navy in Pacific

text: An article on Sunday about concerns surrounding the Vatican’s oversight of bishops accused of sexual abuse misstated the age of Pope Benedict. He is 91, not 90.
match_headline: If Cardinal Was Under Pope’s Sanctions, Why Was He Allowed at Gala Events?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a dispute between NBC News and Ronan Farrow over reporting on Harvey Weinstein misstated a position held by Andrew Lack, the chairman of NBC News. He was previously NBC’s chief operating officer, not its chief executive.
match_headline: NBC News and Ronan Farrow Trade Jabs Over Weinstein Reporting

text: An article on Tuesday about the unmasking of Barbara Rae-Venter as the genetic genealogist who helped identify Joseph DeAngelo as the Golden State Killer referred incorrectly to the individuals Mr. DeAngelo is charged with killing. They include 13 women and men, not 13 women.
match_headline: She Helped Crack the Golden State Killer Case. Here’s What She’s Going to Do Next.

text: An article last Wednesday about Devon, a Manhattan restaurant and cocktail bar to be opened this fall by Oliver Zabar, misidentified Ken Addington. He is the consulting chef, not the chef.
match_headline: Out From Under the Family Name

text: A review on Friday about the documentary “Inventing Tomorrow” misstated the kind of paint invented by teenage scientists. It is photocatalytic paint, not photosynthetic.
match_headline: Review: Teenagers Tackle Environmental Enemies in ‘Inventing Tomorrow’

text: An obituary on Saturday about the economist Martin Shubik misspelled the surname of a Nobel-winning economist with whom he collaborated. He was Lloyd S. Shapley, not Shapely.
match_headline: Martin Shubik, Economist and Game Theory Pioneer, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Aug. 24 about the historian Robert H. Ferrell, who wrote a number of books about Harry S. Truman, misstated when Truman met Bess Wallace, his future wife. They met when he was 6 years old and she was 5 — not in 1910, when they were both in their mid-20s.
match_headline: Robert H. Ferrell, 97, Truman Authority Inspired by Diaries, Dies

text: An article on Wednesday about the confirmation hearings for the Supreme Court nominee Brett M. Kavanaugh referred imprecisely to the number of documents from Mr. Kavanaugh’s time in the White House Counsel’s Office that have been made available to the Senate Judiciary Committee. The committee was given 445,000 of 663,000 total documents, not a small portion of the total.
match_headline: Kavanaugh Portrayed as a Hopeless Partisan as Hearings on Supreme Court Nominee Open

text: An article on Aug. 29 about recent real estate transactions misidentified the tenant that signed a lease at 383 Third Avenue. It is Zeta 383, not Blue Haven NYC. The article also described incorrectly the tenant’s plans for the building. Zeta 383 plans to open a cocktail lounge in the building this fall, not a pub.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An editorial on Tuesday about California’s new standard for electrical generation misstated how that standard could be reached. The law requires that by 2045, all the state’s electricity come from sources that don’t produce carbon emissions, including wind, solar, hydro and nuclear power. It does not require that power be produced only by renewable sources like wind, solar and hydro power.
match_headline: In California, Facts and Science Still Matter

text: Because of an editing error, a subheading with an article on Thursday about British detectives’ use of surveillance footage to identify two Russian men linked to the poisoning of a former Russian spy misstated the status of the two suspects. As the article correctly noted, Interpol red notices and warrants have been issued, but the men have not been arrested. Also, a picture caption referred incompletely to a bottle that detectives said was used to transport the nerve agent used in the poisoning. It was a counterfeit — not genuine — Nina Ricci bottle.
match_headline: From Mountain of CCTV Footage, Pay Dirt: 2 Russians Are Named in Spy Poisoning

text: An article on Aug. 30 about a study in China suggesting a link between air pollution and reduced language and math skills referred imprecisely to a type of pollutant analyzed in a study on air pollution and cognitive performance in China. The pollutant, known as PM10, was defined in the study as particulate matter smaller than 10 micrometers in diameter, not between 2.5 and 10 micrometers.
match_headline: Pollution May Dim Thinking Skills, Study in China Suggests

text: An article on Thursday about a heated exchange between Alex Jones and Senator Marco Rubio referred incorrectly to Laura Loomer’s affiliation with Project Veritas. She left the group in 2017; she is not currently a member.
match_headline: Alex Jones Takes His Show to the Capitol, Even Tussling With a Senator

text: An article on Thursday about “Have a Nice Day,” a new play by Billy Crystal and Quinton Peeples, misstated which actor will read the part of the president of the United States in the piece. It is Kevin Kline, not Billy Crystal.
match_headline: Billy Crystal Brings Stars to Read His New Play Live for Audible

text: A listing of televised sports on Friday misstated the channel that will broadcast Game 2 of the WNBA Finals on Sunday. It is ABC, not ESPN2.
match_headline: W.N.B.A. Finals 2018: When Her Game is Your Game, Too

text: A picture caption with the On Pro Basketball column on Thursday about the career of Steve Nash misstated the location of the Naismith Hall of Fame. It is in Springfield, Mass., not Springfield, Ill.

An article on Thursday about Alexandra Waterbury’s suit against New York City Ballet and the dancer Chase Finlay, using information from legal filings, misstated Ms. Waterbury’s age. She is 20, not 19. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The article also described incorrectly the nature of the images Mr. Finlay was accused of exchanging with Zachary Catazaro, another male dancer. The lawsuit does not specify what type of images they were.
match_headline: City Ballet and Chase Finlay Sued by Woman Who Says Nude Photos of Her Were Shared

text: An article on Page 8 about the premiere of Missy Mazzoli’s opera “Proving Up” misstated the company that produced it. It was Washington National Opera, in January, not Opera Omaha, which gave the second performances in April.
match_headline: After Two Hit Operas, a Composer Takes on the Bleak Prairie

text: Because of a technical error, the combined print and e-book nonfiction best-seller list in this weekend’s Book Review duplicates the print hardcover nonfiction list. The correct rankings for the combined list can be found at nytimes.com/best-sellers .
match_headline: He Wrote a Memoir About Infiltrating the Ku Klux Klan. Then Spike Lee Turned It Into a Film.

text: An editorial on Friday about President Trump and the Constitution incorrectly attributed critical statements about the president in Bob Woodward’s new book, “Fear.” It is not the case that the people said to have made the statements were unnamed.
match_headline: There Oughta Be a Law …

text: An obituary on Aug. 29 about the makeup artist Heidi Morawetz referred imprecisely to the nail polish worn by Uma Thurman in the movie “Pulp Fiction.” Although some people in the makeup industry say it was Vamp, the shade Ms. Morawetz helped create, others say it was a different if similar shade created for the movie.
match_headline: Heidi Morawetz, Creative Force in Makeup Industry, Is Dead at 79

text: An obituary on Sunday about the printmaker and sculptor Krishna Reddy referred incorrectly to his time at the printmaking workshop Atelier 17. Both Alexander Calder and Alberto Giacometti had left Atelier 17 before Mr. Reddy joined; he and they were not members at the same time.
match_headline: Krishna Reddy, Master Printmaker and Indian Modernist, Dies at 93

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Simone Leigh erroneously attributed a distinction to her sculpture “Brick House,” for the High Line in Manhattan. It is not her first public project; she previously displayed sculptures in Marcus Garvey Park in Manhattan from 2016 to 2017.
match_headline: An Artist Ascendant: Simone Leigh Moves Into the Mainstream

text: A review on Aug. 5 about “Metamorphica,” by Zachary Mason, misidentified the author’s last book. It was “Void Star,” published in 2017; it was not “The Lost Books of the Odyssey” (2010).
match_headline: Classical Myths Filtered Through a Modern Prism

text: An article on Sept. 2 about the actor Riz Ahmed misspelled the given name of a British musician. She is Susheela Raman, not Shusheela.

Because of a production error, an article on Sept. 2 about flooding in Houston during Hurricane Harvey referred incorrectly in a highlighted quotation to the time of Wayne Dailey’s fourth call to 911. As the article correctly stated, it took place at 10:15 a.m., not 10:15 p.m.
match_headline: Lost in the Storm

text: An article on Saturday about Harley Rouda’s race against Representative Dana Rohrabacher in California referred incorrectly to Mr. Rohrabacher’s tenure in the House of Representatives. He is serving his 15th term, not his eighth. It also misstated when the real estate brokerage set up by Mr. Rouda’s father was sold; it was in 2007, not 2016.
match_headline: He’s a Former Republican Taking On Dana Rohrabacher. Can He Win?

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the Blue School misidentified the two men in the image. David Rockwell is on the left and Matt Goldman is on the right. In another caption, the designer of the cafeteria was misidentified. The designer was Mr. Rockwell.
match_headline: He Designed Restaurants, Hotels and Stage Sets. Now He Tackles a Middle School.

text: An article on Monday about the race for New York Attorney General misstated the title of Christina Greer. She is an associate professor at Fordham University, not an assistant professor.
match_headline: Diversity in Attorney General’s Race Is Celebrated: Whoever Wins Will Make History.

text: An article on Saturday about tension between the Trump administration and immigration courts misstated which employees of the U.S. Department of Justice must submit extensive documentation for foreign travel. All executive branch employees with security clearances must adhere to the new rules, not all Department of Justice employees.
match_headline: In Immigration Courts, It Is Judges vs. Justice Department

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about websites offering ways to set up estate plans described incorrectly the estate plan for the actor James Gandolfini. He did have a will; he did not die without one. He did not, however, have a trust, which would have kept private the contents of his estate.
match_headline: Making Wills Easier and Cheaper With Do-It-Yourself Options

text: An article on Aug. 28 about museum conservators’ efforts to preserve modern artworks and historical objects that are disintegrating misidentified a substance described by Dr. Odile Madden. She referred to opacifiers — not pacifiers — as a type of additive used to make materials opaque.
match_headline: These Cultural Treasures Are Made of Plastic. Now They’re Falling Apart.

text: An article on Sunday about the work behind a special section on Central Park referred incorrectly to the photographers who contributed to the report. There were 11 photographers, not 10, and all were freelancers on assignments made by The Times Magazine’s photo department, not staff members.
match_headline: How to Talk to Strangers in Central Park

text: An article on Thursday about Mary Boone, a veteran gallerist, pleading guilty to filing false federal income tax returns misidentified the year of an exhibition at her gallery that led to her arrest. It was 1999, not 1990.
match_headline: Gallerist Mary Boone Pleads Guilty to Filing False Tax Returns

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor Bill Daily referred incorrectly to Howard Borden, the character he played on “The Bob Newhart Show.” He was originally an airline navigator and later in the show’s run became a co-pilot; he was not a pilot.
match_headline: Bill Daily, a Regular on ‘I Dream of Jeannie’ and ‘The Bob Newhart Show,’ Dies at 91

text: An article on Wednesday about the economic outlook in Elkhart County, Ind., misidentified the head of economic development in the county. He is Mark Dobson, not Mark Babson.
match_headline: As Elkhart, Ind., Goes, So Goes the Nation, and Elkhart Is Nervous

text: An article on Wednesday about David Wright’s recovery from a series of injuries misstated the date Wright had faced pitching before his batting practice on Saturday. It was Aug. 29, not Oct. 29.
match_headline: David Wright Is Getting Better. But Will the Mets Allow His Return?

text: An article on Aug. 30 about fertility companies misattributed a statistic about egg freezing. The source was Gina Bartasi, not the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology.
match_headline: These Companies Really, Really, Really Want to Freeze Your Eggs

text: An obituary on Monday about the artist Irving Petlin, using information from his family, omitted two survivors. In addition to his wife, his son and his daughter Alessandra Petlin, he is survived by another daughter, Yaelisa Petlin, and by five grandchildren, not four.
match_headline: Irving Petlin, Artist Who Recorded Injustice, Dies at 83

text: An article on Thursday about the challenges presented by Hurricane Florence misspelled the surname of a spokesman for the Edison Electric Institute, an industry group. He is Brian Reil, not Riel.
match_headline: Hurricane Florence Is a Formidable Test for FEMA and Trump

text: A map with an article on Sunday about disputed government statements regarding the United States’ military presence in Afghanistan erroneously included more districts among those considered contested than military analysts had said. The figure of 61 percent of districts considered contested that appeared with the map was correct, not the percentage implied by the map.
match_headline: How the U.S. Government Misleads the Public on Afghanistan

text: An article on Thursday about a government study’s findings that a large U.S. initiative to help Afghan women has accomplished little misstated when Rajiv Shah left United States Agency for International Development. He left the agency in 2015, not after the Obama administration ended.
match_headline: U.S. Aid Program Vowed to Help 75,000 Afghan Women. Watchdog Says It’s a Flop.

text: An article on Thursday about the arrest of seven New York City police officers on prostitution, corruption and misconduct charges misidentified the area in Queens through which Roosevelt Avenue runs. It is Corona, not Crotona.
match_headline: 7 New York Police Officers Arrested in Prostitution and Gambling Investigation, Authorities Say

text: An article on Sept. 2 about bullish stock market forecasts misstated the return of the Standard & Poor’s 500-stock index from the beginning of the year through Aug. 30. It was 9.9 percent, not 15.5 percent.
match_headline: What if the Economy and Markets Are Even Better Than They Look?

text: An article on Saturday about the composer Anton Reicha described incorrectly the circumstances in which several other major composers studied with him. All studied with him in Paris, but only Berlioz did so at the Paris Conservatory. The other three studied privately with Reicha. (Although two of them subsequently enrolled at the conservatory.)
match_headline: A Friend of Beethoven, Now Rediscovered in His Own Right

text: A review on Tuesday about the mixed-media show “The Unwritten Law” misquoted a passage from the show’s script. The scene described eyes that “swelled with misty rain.” They did not “mist” and “rain.”
match_headline: Review: A Beatboxer Climbs Up and Out in ‘The Unwritten Law’

text: An entry in the Theater Listings on Page 40 refers incorrectly to the late journalist Anna Politkovskaya, whose story is told the play “Intractable Woman.” She was Russian, not Polish.
match_headline: 72 Plays and Musicals to See This Fall and Beyond

text: An article on Page 62 about the 19-year-old actress Amandla Stenberg misstates the nationality of Ms. Stenberg’s father. He is Danish, not Dutch.
match_headline: The Education of Amandla Stenberg

text: An entry in the Film Listings on Page 72 gave an outdated title for the film “Ralph Breaks the Internet.” It is no longer titled “Wreck-It Ralph 2.”
match_headline: Fall Movies 2018: Dive Into an Ocean’s Worth of Offerings

text: An entry in the Art Listings on Page 98 misstates the title of an exhibition at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. It is “Rauschenberg: The 1/4 Mile,” not “Robert Rauschenberg: The 1/4 Mile or 2 Furlong Piece.”
match_headline: Art Fall Preview: Over 100 Not-to-Miss Shows From East Coast to West

text: An article on Page 108 about a new album by the French pop singer Hélöise Letissier misidentifies the host of “The Daily Show” when Christine and the Queens performed. It was Trevor Noah, not Jon Stewart.
match_headline: Gender Is a Construct. Christine and the Queens Built a Bulldozer.

text: An entry in the Pop Listings on Page 109, using information provided by a record publicist, misidentifies two artists on a Muscle Shoals compilation. Alicia Keys and Demi Lovato are not on the album.
match_headline: Pop and Jazz Fall Preview: 70 Albums, Shows and Festivals

text: An article last Sunday about men’s oversize coats mistakenly inverted the directionals for four picture captions. On both Page 58 and Page 62, the fashion credits listed for the left picture correspond to the picture on the right, and vice versa.
match_headline: What Jack Dorsey and Sheryl Sandberg Taught Congress and Vice Versa

text: An essay last Sunday about public libraries included outdated information about a policy at the libraries in San Jose, Calif. Patrons are prohibited from borrowing books and using computers once their overdue fees surpass $20, not $10.
match_headline: To Restore Civil Society, Start With the Library

text: An essay last Sunday about the Rio Grande incorrectly described an aspect of the Yukon River. It originates in Canada; it does not run wholly in the United States.
match_headline: The Rio Grande Is Dying. Does Anyone Care?

text: An article on Monday about a deal that would allow Macedonia to join NATO gave an incorrect title for Jens Stoltenberg of NATO. He is the organization’s secretary general, not its general secretary.
match_headline: In the Balkans, Russia and the West Fight a Disinformation-Age Battle

text: An article on Sunday about Boris Johnson’s political tactics misspelled the surname of the European Union’s Brexit negotiator. He is Michel Barnier, not Bernier.
match_headline: Boris Johnson, Eyes on Downing Street, Sets Political Fires

text: An article on Saturday about President Trump’s record on protecting Medicare and Social Security misstated the state that Senator Claire McCaskill represents. It is Missouri, not Indiana.
match_headline: Taking Page From 2016, Trump Claims Democrats Will Destroy Safety Net

text: An article on Monday about Simcha Felder, a Brooklyn Democrat who caucuses with Republicans in the New York State Senate, misidentified the language of sample ballots that were given to voters in Borough Park. They were in Yiddish, not Hebrew.
match_headline: How a Brooklyn Democrat Who Votes With the G.O.P. Defied the Progressive Wave

text: An article on Monday about investors betting against Tesla misstated the role of Gabe Hoffman at the hedge fund Accipiter Capital Management. He is general partner, not a partner.
match_headline: Betting Against Tesla: Short-Sellers Make Their Case

text: An article on Monday about trends in the N.F.L. through the second week of the season misidentified the winner of a game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Arizona Cardinals. The Rams won by a score of 34-0, not the Cardinals.
match_headline: Calm Before the Season: The Week in Classical Music

text: An article on Tuesday about fund-raising letters disguised as legal summonses sent to voters by Senator Ted Cruz’s re-election campaign misstated the name of a newspaper. It is The San Antonio Express-News, not the News-Express.
match_headline: Ted Cruz’s Campaign Marked a Fund-Raising Letter an Official ‘Summons.’ It Wasn’t Against the Rules.

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the Emmy Awards, using information from a photo agency, misidentified a woman presenting the award for outstanding lead actress in a comedy series. The woman was Angela Bassett, not Omarosa Manigault Newman.
match_headline: Don’t Look at Trevor Noah

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actor Peter Donat referred incorrectly to an award he received for his work in the play “The First Gentleman” in 1957. While he did win a Theater World Award, it was not for best supporting actor; the Theater World Awards are given for New York stage debuts and do not distinguish between lead and supporting performances.
match_headline: Peter Donat, Actor Who Played a Panoply of Roles, Dead at 90

text: An article on Wednesday about accusations against Judge Brett M. Kavanaugh referred incorrectly to the 1992 elections. That year was a presidential election year, not a midterm election year.
match_headline: On Kavanaugh, a Changed America Debates an Explosive Charge

text: An article on Wednesday about a settlement between the Diocese of Brooklyn and men who were sexually abused as children at a Brooklyn church misstated the location of the Dorothy Bennett Mercy Center. It is next to St. Lucy’s-St. Patrick’s Church in Clinton Hill, not in Fort Greene.
match_headline: Brooklyn Diocese Is Part of $27.5 Million Settlement in 4 Sex Abuse Cases

text: An article on Wednesday about a television interview with two Russian men accused of poisoning Sergei V. Skripal, a former Russian spy, referred incorrectly to the nerve agent Novichok. It is a chemical weapon, not a biological one.
match_headline: Tragedy? Farce? Confusion? The Method Behind That Russian Poisoning Interview

text: An article on Wednesday about the increasing severity of damage from hurricanes in the Carolinas referred incorrectly to Garland, N.C. Garland is a town in Sampson County; there is no Garland County in the state.
match_headline: ‘It’s Back’: Underwater Yet Again, the Carolinas Face a New Reality

text: An article on Friday about an exhibition of Russian avant-garde art at the Jewish Museum rendered incorrectly in several instances the surname of an artist whose work appears in the exhibition. He is El Lissitzky, not Lissitsky.
match_headline: Flying Goats and Black Squares, Charging Into the Future

text: A headline with an article on Friday about an exclusive deal between an artificial intelligence company and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center referred imprecisely to the venture. As the article correctly noted, the company will be given exclusive access to images of the hospital’s trove of patient tissue slides, not the tissue slides themselves.
match_headline: Sloan Kettering’s Cozy Deal With Start-Up Ignites a New Uproar

text: An article on Tuesday about the discovery of three new species of snailfish misstated how scientists lowered a camera and other gear in the Atacama Trench. The equipment went into the trench in a free fall; it was not lowered on a cable.
match_headline: They’re Blue, Pink and Purple, and No One Has Ever Seen Them Before

text: An article on Page 91 about the architect Bruce Goff refers incorrectly to the Nicol House. The house’s shingles are pale green and hexagonal, not white and fish scale.
match_headline: Presidential Lying Is Contagious

text: An obituary on Thursday about the architect Robert Venturi misstated the year he appeared on the cover of Architecture magazine proclaiming, “I am not now and never have been a postmodernist.” It was 2001, not 1991. The obituary also misstated the year Guild House, a retirement home in Philadelphia that Mr. Venturi designed, was completed. It was 1966, not 1964.
ref_headline: I am not now and never have been a postmodernist.
match_headline: Robert Venturi, Architect Who Rejected Modernism, Dies at 93

text: An article on Page 91 about the architect Bruce Goff refers incorrectly to the Nicol House. The house’s shingles are pale green and hexagonal, not white and fish-scale.
match_headline: The Man Who Made Wildly Imaginative, Gloriously Disobedient Buildings

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Amina Claudine Myers misstated the words she sang at the Community Church of New York in 2016. They were “Ain’t nobody ever gonna hear us/ Ain’t nobody hearing us now,” not “Ain’t nobody ever gonna hear nobody hearing us now.”
ref_headline: Ain’t nobody ever gonna hear us/ Ain’t nobody hearing us now,
match_headline: Amina Claudine Myers, a Singer Who Still Needs No Words

text: An article last Sunday about women in architecture described incorrectly the curriculum at a school designed by the architect Toshiko Mori in the Senegalese village of Fass. The school will serve all of its students at once; it will not separate them by religion.
match_headline: Architecture Is No Longer Just a ‘Gentleman’s Profession’

text: A picture caption on Page 6 on Sunday with the continuation of an article about The Village Voice misidentified the given name of a former mayor of New York. His name is William O’Dwyer, not Paul O’Dwyer.
match_headline: Seven Ways The Village Voice Made New York a Better Place

text: An article on Saturday about efforts by Prime Minister Stefan Lofven of Sweden to form a new government by luring smaller parties away from the center-right alliance misstated when the leadership of the Sweden Democrats eliminated the repatriation plank of their platform. It was 19 years ago, not seven. The article also misstated when the party’s youth group was kicked out. It was three years ago, not seven.
match_headline: To End Stalemate, Will Sweden Include Far-Right Party in Government?

text: An article on Monday about the possible impact that tariffs on Chinese goods might have on American tech and telecom companies misidentified the location of Nokia’s headquarters. The company is based in Finland, not Sweden.
match_headline: Trump’s China Fight Puts U.S. Tech in the Cross Hairs

text: An article on Sept. 14 about an exhibition of previously unseen photographs by Diane Arbus misstated the number of photographs that will be included in the exhibit. It is five, not 11. The error was repeated in a headline.
match_headline: Five Diane Arbus Photographs to Go on Public Display for First Time

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the impact of a deal between China and the Vatican on Chinese Christians described incorrectly the early spread of Christianity in China. While it gained a permanent presence in China in the 16th century, it was not the only foreign faith to gain a permanent foothold in China since the arrival of Buddhism two millenniums ago.
match_headline: With Vatican Talks and Bulldozers, China Aims to Control Christianity

text: An article on Tuesday about Michael Kors nearing a deal to buy Versace referred imprecisely to the amount earned by Versace in 2017. The amount, €44.6 million, or $52.5 million, reflects earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, but not before appreciation.
match_headline: Michael Kors Nears Versace Purchase in Challenge to European Luxury Groups

text: An article last Wednesday about the runaway popularity of ranch dressing misstated the origins of Ranch, a pizzeria in Portland, Ore. It started as a pop-up restaurant, not a food truck.
match_headline: Ranch Nation

text: Because of an editing error, a brief report in the Off the Menu column last Wednesday misstated the surname of a chef at 10 Corso Como, a new restaurant in the Seaport District of New York City. He is Danilo Galati, not Galafi.
match_headline: La Vara Chefs Open Saint Julivert Fisherie in Cobble Hill, Brooklyn

text: An obituary on Sept. 13 about Diane Leather, the first woman to run a mile in less than five minutes, referred imprecisely to the recognition she received for that accomplishment. The International Amateur Athletics Federation acknowledged it, but as a “world’s best” rather than a world record, because at the time the federation did not acknowledge records for women’s distances greater than 800 meters. It was not the case that her accomplishment “was not recognized by the track and field establishment.” The obituary also misstated the date of Leather’s death. It was Sept. 5, not Sept. 6.
match_headline: Diane Leather, 85, First Woman to Run Mile in Under 5 Minutes, Dies

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Hall of Fame wide receiver Tommy McDonald misstated the location of Roy, the town where he was born. It is in New Mexico, not Oklahoma.
match_headline: Tommy McDonald, Fleet Hall of Famer for the Eagles, Dies at 84

text: An article on Wednesday about Prime Minister Stefan Lofven of Sweden losing a vote of confidence referred incorrectly to Mr. Lofven’s government before the elections. He was the head of a minority coalition; he did not have a majority.
match_headline: Walmart, Patagonia and Lyft Make Push to Increase Voter Turnout

text: An article on Tuesday about upsets in college football referred incorrectly to a game between Virginia Tech and Old Dominion. Virginia Tech was the road team, not the home team.
match_headline: A Showdown in South Bend, and Clear Sailing for Clemson

text: An article on Tuesday about the Yankees’ win over the Rays referred incorrectly to Yankees pitchers J.A. Happ, Luis Severino and Masahiro Tanaka. While one of those pitchers is expected to face Oakland in the wild-card playoff game, they were not the Yankees’ “next three starters against the Rays.”
ref_headline: next three starters against the Rays.
match_headline: By Starting a Reliever, the Yankees Imitate and Eliminate the Rays

text: An article on Sunday incorrectly described how Anat Hazan, an Orthodox Jewish woman, decided to hide her hair when she was 21. Ms. Hazan placed a wig over her hair; she did not shave it.
match_headline: A Glimpse Inside the Hidden World of Hasidic Women

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about President Trump’s comments regarding the timeline for North Korea to give up its nuclear arms misquoted part of the president’s statement. He said, “If it takes two years, three years or five months,” not “If it takes two years, five years or five months.”
ref_headline: If it takes two years, three years or five months,
match_headline: North Korea Nuclear Deal Could Take ‘Years,’ Trump Suggests

text: An article on Monday about the Metropolitan Opera commissioning new works misstated the title of an opera by Jake Heggie. It is “Dead Man Walking,” not “Dead Men Walking.”
match_headline: The Met Is Creating New Operas (Including Its First by Women)

text: An obituary on Thursday about the anthropologist Constance Sutton misstated the surname of her parents. It was Woloshin, not Sutton.
match_headline: Constance Sutton, Feminist Anthropologist, Is Dead at 92

text: An obituary on Sept. 6 about Jan Ellen Lewis, a historian who wrote extensively about Thomas Jefferson, referred imprecisely to the results of DNA analysis of Jefferson’s living descendants. While it showed that it was likely he had fathered at least one child with Sally Hemings, one of his slaves, it did not establish this with absolute certainty.
match_headline: Jan Ellen Lewis, Expert on Jefferson’s Other Family, Dies at 69

text: An obituary on Thursday about David Wolkowsky, the developer who helped transform Key West, Fla., into a bohemian haven and a tourist destination, misstated the name of the unfinished novel Truman Capote wrote in Mr. Wolkowsky’s trailer there. It is “Answered Prayers,” not “Unanswered Prayers” or “Unfinished Prayers.” The obituary also erroneously included Ernest Hemingway on the list of literary figures Mr. Wolkowsky befriended in Key West.
match_headline: David Wolkowsky, Developer Hailed as Mr. Key West, Dies at 99

text: An article on Friday about expedited efforts by the United Nations Human Rights Council to prosecute Myanmar military commanders misidentified the European Union’s ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva. He is Walter Stevens, not Carl Hallergard.
match_headline: Human Rights Council Ratchets Up Pressure on Myanmar

text: An article on Friday about planned spaces that would improve New York City’s ability to absorb rainwater, using information from the city’s Department of Environmental Protection, misstated the amount of money the city is spending to reduce flooding in southeastern Queens. It is $1.9 billion, not $1.9 million.
match_headline: New York’s Next Nickname: The Big Sponge?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a lawsuit filed by the Securities and Exchange Commission against Elon Musk, Tesla’s chief executive, misidentified the body style of Tesla’s Model 3 car. It is a sedan, not a roadster.
match_headline: Tesla Chief Elon Musk Is Sued by S.E.C. in Move That Could Oust Him

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a vote to allow Russian athletes to return to international sports competitions misstated the World Anti-Doping Agency position from which Beckie Scott resigned. She resigned from her post on WADA’s compliance review committee, not from her position as chairwoman of the athlete committee.
match_headline: Vote to Reinstate Russia Exposes Rifts in Antidoping Community

text: An article on Friday about the N.F.L. safety Eric Reid signing with the Carolina Panthers misspelled the given name of the team’s general manager. He is Marty Hurney, not Mary.
match_headline: Eric Reid, Who Knelt With Colin Kaepernick, Signs With Carolina Panthers

text: An article on Thursday about changes in Tiger Woods’ playing style misstated the number of major tournaments won by Ernie Els. It is four, not five.
match_headline: Playing Golf Alongside Tiger Woods Feels Different Now

text: An article on Friday about seven new art exhibitions in New York misstated the year of a Gary Snyder Gallery exhibition. It took place in 1998, not 1988.
match_headline: At 7 Art Galleries, the Ecstatic Flow of Paint and the Stories It Can Tell

text: An article on Page 44 about felon disenfranchisement includes an erroneous description of Amendment 4, a Florida referendum to restore former felons’ voting rights. If the amendment becomes law, it is not the case that it would allow former felons to serve on juries and run for public office. And a picture caption in the article misstates the affiliation of Neil Volz. He is the political director of the Florida Rights Restoration Coalition, not the Amendment 4 campaign.
match_headline: Will Florida’s Ex-Felons Finally Regain the Right to Vote?

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Charles Kuen Kao, a Nobel laureate in physics in 2009, misstated part of the work he and a colleague did in the late 1960s. They outlined fiber optic cables’ potential capacity for transmitting information, not for storing it.
match_headline: Charles Kao, Nobel Laureate Who Revolutionized Fiber Optics, Dies at 84

text: An article last Sunday about Alabama misidentified the lead designer of the National Memorial for Peace and Justice and the Legacy Museum. The Equal Justice Initiative created and designed both, not Local Projects, which was apartner.
match_headline: For Roy Wood Jr., Alabama Is Painful History, New Hope and Home

text: A picture caption with an article last Sundayabout Akagera National Park in Rwanda misidentified a monkey. It is a vervet monkey,not a velvet monkey.
match_headline: A Rwandan Game Park Defying the Odds

text: An item in the television listings on Sept. 16 misspelled the surname of the creator of the show “I Feel Bad.” She is Aseem Batra, not Bhatra.
match_headline: What’s on TV Wednesday: ‘The Greatest Showman’ and ‘I Feel Bad’

text: An article on Sept. 9 about teaching in the age of school shootings misquoted Robert Pynoos, a director of the National Center for Child Traumatic Stress. He said: “For teachers, the duty to educate students is primary. But the urge to protect those students is deeper than that.” He did not say, “It’s primal.”
ref_headline: For teachers, the duty to educate students is primary. But the urge to protect those students is deeper than that.
match_headline: Readers Respond to the 9.16.18 Issue

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Justin Theroux misidentified the location of the Flower Shop, a bar in Manhattan. It is on Eldridge Street, not Orchard Street. 
match_headline: Justin Theroux Is on the Prowl

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Norah Lewin and Georges Rouan misstated the name of a business owned by the groom’s mother. It is Transfer Plus, not Transfer Pluf. The report also misstated the hometown of the groom’s father. It is Montpellier, France, not Aix-en-Provence, France.
match_headline: Norah Lewin, Georges Rouan

text: An essay last Sunday about the effects of #MeToo on female aides on Capitol Hill misstated Christine Blasey Ford’s profession. She is a professor of psychology, not sociology.
match_headline: The Long Year of #MeToo on Capitol Hill

text: An essay last Sunday about anger at this political moment misspelled the given name of the author of “The Life and Loves of a She-Devil.” She is Fay Weldon, not Faye Weldon.
ref_headline: The Life and Loves of a She-Devil.
match_headline: The Patriarchy Will Always Have Its Revenge

text: An article on Friday about the appointment of Marcello Foa as chairman of Italy’s state broadcaster RAI referred incorrectly to the web team of Luca Morisi. The team has been compared to Casaleggio Associates, a company closely linked with the League’s coalition partner, the Five Star Movement, but there is no evidence that alumni of Casaleggio Associates work in Mr. Morisi’s team.
match_headline: Journalist Who Spread Conspiracy Theories Will Oversee Italy’s State TV

text: An article on Sunday about angry reactions to Judge Brett M. Kavanaugh’s testimony misstated Cleta Mitchell’s party affiliation. She is a former Democratic state legislator, not a Republican.
match_headline: Kavanaugh Borrows From Trump’s Playbook on White Male Anger

text: An article on Saturday about The Simpsons episodes over the last thirty years misstated the title of an early comic series by Matt Groening. It is “Life in Hell,” not “Life is Hell.”
match_headline: ‘The Simpsons’ at 30: Six Era-Defining Episodes

text: An obituary on Sunday about Martin Balin, a founder of the band Jefferson Airplane, misspelled the surname of the spokesman who provided information about his death. He is Ryan Romenesko, not Romanesco.
match_headline: Marty Balin, a Founder of Jefferson Airplane, Dies at 76

text: An article on Tuesday about widespread delays affecting British train companies misidentified the organization that owns the United Kingdom’s railroad infrastructure and handles timetables. It is Network Rail, not National Rail.
match_headline: British Rail Companies Have a Message: We’re Sorry. Very Sorry. Apologies.

text: An article on Tuesday about President Andrés Manuel López Obrador of Mexico and changes in his stance on trade referred imprecisely to Canada’s leadership. Canada has a prime minister, not a president.
match_headline: Mexico’s New Leader, Once a Nafta Foe, Welcomes New Deal

text: A chart with an article on Feb. 13 about drinking water safety across the United States represented incorrectly the scale of the y-axis. The chart shows violations of water quality regulations per 10 water systems in rural areas, not per 100 systems. The correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Here Are the Places That Struggle to Meet the Rules on Safe Drinking Water

text: An article on Monday about a proposal by the Trump administration to weaken regulations on mercury emissions referred incorrectly to the initial estimate of direct health benefits from the mercury rule. The Obama administration estimated those benefits to be worth $6 million per year, not $6 billion.
match_headline: Trump Administration Prepares a Major Weakening of Mercury Emissions Rules

text: A review on Tuesday about “Girl From the North Country” misidentified the London theater where the musical had its premiere. It was the Old Vic Theater, not the National Theater.
match_headline: Review: ‘Girl From the North Country’ Sets the Darkness Aglow

text: An obituary on Monday about the blues singer and guitarist Otis Rush incorrectly explained a quotation from him that began, “When you play lefty, you’re pulling that vibrato down to the floor.” He was referring to a manual technique executed without the use of an external mechanical device, not to the tremolo bar of an electric guitar.
ref_headline: When you play lefty, you’re pulling that vibrato down to the floor.
match_headline: Otis Rush, Influential Blues Singer and Guitarist, Is Dead at 83

text: An article on Wednesday about a refugee camp outside Moria in Greece misspelled the surname of Doctors Without Borders’ lead psychiatrist on Lesbos, Greece. He is Dr. Alessandro Barberio, not Barbiero.
match_headline: ‘Better to Drown’: A Greek Refugee Camp’s Epidemic of Misery

text: An article on Saturday about a vote in Canada’s House of Commons to revoke honorary citizenship from Myanmar’s civilian leader misstated the number of people who have received honorary citizenship in Canada. The total is six, not seven.
match_headline: Canada’s Parliament Moves to Strip Honor for Myanmar’s Leader

text: An article on Wednesday about financial trouble facing the British business Marks & Spencer misstated how far the English national soccer team reached in the 2018 World Cup championship. The team reached the semifinals, not quarterfinals. The article also misspelled the surname of a British celebrity who has collaborated with Marks & Spencer. She is Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, not Rosie Huntingdon Whitely.
match_headline: Marks & Spencer Is Struggling. Can Knickers, Candy and Colin the Caterpillar Cakes Save It?

text: An article on Tuesday about patients’ difficulties in obtaining new cholesterol drugs misidentified the manufacturers of two medications. The drug Praluent is manufactured by Regeneron and Sanofi, not Amgen. Repatha, not Praluent, is made by Amgen. In addition, the article misstated the given name of Amgen’s executive vice president. He is Tony Hooper, not Tom.
match_headline: These Cholesterol-Reducers May Save Lives. So Why Aren’t Heart Patients Getting Them?

text: An article on Tuesday about the “NY Quadrille” season at the Joyce Theater misstated the year that “Dearest Home” was first staged. It was in 2017, not 2016.
match_headline: At the Joyce, a Rearranged Theater Brings Mystery and Orthodoxy

text: An article on Wednesday about the race for the Tennessee Senate seat being vacated by Bob Corker, using information from the United States attorney’s office, misstated the age of Thomas Walter Gillen. He is 24, not 34.
match_headline: Four California Men Accused of Inciting Riots in Charlottesville Violence

text: An article on Friday about fake academic papers published in several scholarly journals misidentified the Twitter account that publicized a fraudulent academic article about dog parks. The account is called New Real Peer Review, not Real Peer Review, which was the name of an account that was closed. The article also described incorrectly the status of one of the hoax papers. The paper, “When the Joke’s on You,” had been accepted by the journal Hypatia, but it had not yet been published.
match_headline: Hoaxers Slip Breastaurants and Dog-Park Sex Into Journals

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Erik Prince’s presence in Afghanistan misstated the timing of planned parliamentary elections in the country. They are scheduled for this month, not next month.
match_headline: As Afghanistan Frays, Blackwater Founder Erik Prince Is Everywhere

text: An article on Friday about the effort by the United States women’s soccer team to qualify for the World Cup misstated the team that the United States lost to in the 2010 Concacaf championship. It was Mexico, not Canada.
match_headline: U.S. Women Begin World Cup Qualifying Tournament With 6-0 Win

text: An article on Friday about an exhibition at the New-York Historical Society misstated the date of the oldest artifacts on display. They date as far back as 1600-1046 B.C., not A.D. 700.
match_headline: Spellbound by Harry Potter and the Museum of Magic

text: An article on Page 10 about Rufus Wainwright’s new opera, “Hadrian,” misstates the inspiration for Daniel MacIvor’s libretto for the opera. It is an original story, not based on the Marguerite Yourcenar novel “Memoirs of Hadrian,” though that book did get Mr. Wainwright interested in the subject of Hadrian.
match_headline: Rufus Wainwright’s First Opera Was ‘a Nightmare.’ He’s Trying Again.

text: An article on Thursday about the artist Tara Donovan misstated Robbie Crawford’s role at Standard Architects when he met Ms. Donovan. He was a designer, not an intern.
match_headline: In Williamsburg, Designing for Work-Life Balance

text: An article last Sunday about a mini-recesssion in the United States in 2015 and 2016 that went largely unnoticed misstated the year when the price of a barrel of West Texas Intermediate crude oil was around $106. It was 2014, not 2015.
match_headline: The Most Important Least-Noticed Economic Event of the Decade

text: An article last Sunday about the National Cowboy Poetry Gathering in Nevada incorrectly described Kristin Windbigler’s childhood. It was in rural Northern California, not on a logging operation in the state. The article also misstated the topic of her 2005 film. It was about her experience making cowboy boots, not her involvement in the family business. And the article misspelled the given name of the poet who performed at the 1985 gathering. He is Waddie Mitchell, not Waddy.
match_headline: At the Cowboy Poetry Gathering, Tall Tales, Resonant Rhymes

text: An article on Sept. 30 about the vulnerability of electronic voting systems described incorrectly a 2007 Florida law involving direct-recording electronic machines, or D.R.E.s. Th e law mandated the use of voter-marked paper ballots, not the use of paper trails for D.R.E.s.
match_headline: The Crisis of Election Security

text: An article on Sunday about advice given to Brett M. Kavanaugh by the White House counsel, Don McGahn, misstated when Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, had dinner with three Republican senators who were undecided on Judge Kavanaugh’s confirmation. The dinner was Friday, Sept. 28, not Thursday, Sept. 27.
match_headline: Show How You Feel, Kavanaugh Was Told, and a Nomination Was Saved

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about representatives of vaping technology companies attending the World Health Organization’s tobacco treaty negotiations misstated the terms of Israel’s regulation of Juul vaping products. The country has banned only Juul’s 5% nicotine pod, not all Juul products.
match_headline: Flashy Science Hub and Vaping Parties Fail to Win Friends at W.H.O. Tobacco Talks

text: An article on Saturday about political friction between Ukraine and Hungary misspelled the name of a Hungarian far-right group. It is Jobbik, not Jobbick.
match_headline: At War With Russia in East, Ukraine Has Worries in the West, Too

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a proposed future investigation into accusations of sexual misconduct and perjury against Brett M. Kavanaugh misspelled the given name of Christine Blasey Ford’s lawyer. She is Debra Katz, not Deborah.
match_headline: House Democrat Promises Kavanaugh Investigation if Party Wins Control

text: An article on Sept. 30 about a 6-year-old boy overcoming an unusual speech pathology misidentified the person who left the operating room to speak with the boy’s parents during the procedure. It was Dr. Luedemann-Lazar’s assistant, not the doctor herself.
match_headline: Texas Boy Speaks Clearly for First Time After Dentist Discovered He Was Tongue-Tied

text: An article on Sept. 27 about a statement by President Trump in which he declined to fire the deputy attorney general, Rod J. Rosenstein, misquoted the president. Speaking about Mr. Rosenstein, Mr. Trump said: “We’ve had a good talk. He said he never said it, he said he doesn’t believe it. He said he has a lot of respect for me, and he was very nice, and we’ll see”; not “he gets a lot of respect from me.” The error was repeated in an article on Friday.
ref_headline: We’ve had a good talk. He said he never said it, he said he doesn’t believe it. He said he has a lot of respect for me, and he was very nice, and we’ll see
match_headline: Trump Says He’s Open to Keeping Rod Rosenstein at Justice Dept.

text: A headline with the On Soccer column on Monday about the 0-0 draw between Liverpool and Manchester City misidentified the team that missed a penalty kick late in the game. As the article correctly noted, it was Manchester City, not Liverpool.
match_headline: Liverpool and Manchester City Leave Everyone Hungry for More

text: An article on Saturday about the rivalry between the Yankees and the Red Sox misspelled the surname of the player inextricably linked with Ralph Branca. He was Bobby Thomson, not Thompson.
match_headline: In the Yankees-Red Sox Rivalry, History’s Echoes Are Everywhere

text: An article on Sept. 30 about former N.F.L. cheerleaders speaking out about workplace harassment misstated the surname of a lawyer representing several of the cheerleaders. She is Sara Blackwell, not Davis.
match_headline: Former N.F.L. Cheerleaders Hope to Quicken Change by Shedding Their Anonymity

text: An obituary on Sept. 30 about the diabetes researcher Dr. Lois Jovanovic, using information from a spokeswoman, misstated her parents’ occupations and omitted the name of a survivor. Her parents, Arnold and Alice (Dechter) Blaustone, were both pharmacists; it was not the case that her father was a neuropsychiatrist and her mother a homemaker. And in addition to her two children and four grandchildren, Dr. Jovanovic is survived by a sister, Beryl Blaustone.
match_headline: Dr. Lois Jovanovic, 71, Dies; Helped Diabetic Women Have Babies

text: An article on Tuesday about threats facing Australia’s coral reefs misidentified the location of Edith Cowan University. It is in Western Australia, not Queensland.
match_headline: Australia’s Other Great (and Threatened) Coral Reefs

text: An article on Monday about venture capital financing for electronic cigarette companies referred incorrectly to the Food and Drug Administration’s description of an event in which officials seized documents from Juul’s office. It was a surprise inspection, not a surprise raid.
match_headline: Silicon Valley Investors Shunned Juul, but Back Other Nicotine Start-Ups

text: An article on Monday about technology workers raising concerns about the use of their work misstated the timing of the real estate company Redfin’s addition of context to the school test score information it publishes online. It plans to add that context early next year; it has not already added it.
match_headline: Tech Workers Now Want to Know: What Are We Building This For?

text: An article on Monday about the Red Sox’ decisive win over the Yankees referred incorrectly to Andrew Benintendi’s hit that cleared the bases on the fourth inning. It was a double, not a triple, and it made the score 7-0, not 8-0.
match_headline: Red Sox Thrash Yankees in a Humiliating Home Defeat

text: An article last Wednesday about the Food section’s favorite new cookbooks misidentified the publisher of “The Noma Guide to Fermentation.” It is Artisan, a division of Workman Publishing, not Workman.
match_headline: The 19 Best Cookbooks of Fall 2018

text: An article on Tuesday about Aasif Mandvi’s play “Sakina’s Restaurant,” using information from the audiobook publisher and retailer Audible, misstated the position of Kate Navin at the company. She is artistic producer, not artistic director.
match_headline: For Aasif Mandvi, a 20-Year-Old Play Now Feels Like ‘Political Resistance’

text: An obituary on Sept. 26 about the South Street Seaport historian John Putnam misidentified the Massachusetts high school from which he graduated. It was Belmont High School, not Belmont Hill School (which he had attended earlier).
match_headline: John Putnam, the Melville of the South Street Seaport, Dies at 82

text: An article on Monday about violence in Afghanistan misstated the number of civilians killed daily in the conflict there. It is at least 10, not at least 13.
match_headline: 17 Years to the Day the U.S. Invaded, 54 Are Killed Across Afghanistan

text: An article on Wednesday about the global environmental outlook in light of new climate change forecasts misstated the year when China’s emissions are expected to peak. It is 2030, not 2050.
match_headline: The Climate Outlook Is Dire. So, What’s Next?

text: An article on Tuesday about the biomechanics behind frogs’ jumps misstated the affiliation of Chris Richards. He is at the Royal Veterinary College at the University of London, not at Harvard.
match_headline: What a Frog Needs to Make That Leap

text: An editorial on Wednesday about a new United Nations report on climate change referred incorrectly to a provision of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Countries pledged to limit increases in global warming to 3.6 degrees (2 degrees Celsius) above preindustrial levels, not below preindustrial levels.
match_headline: Wake Up, World Leaders. The Alarm Is Deafening.

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about Alex Spanos, the owner of the Chargers of the National Football League, misstated the location of Stockton, Calif., where he was born. It is about 80 miles east of San Francisco, not west. Because of another editing error, the obituary also misstated part of the Chargers’ history. The team was originally in Los Angeles but moved after one season to San Diego, where it remained for more than 50 years; it was not originally in San Diego.
match_headline: How the Los Angeles Chargers Can Make the N.F.L. Playoffs

text: An article on Thursday about the congressional candidate Nate McMurray misidentified the organization that Tom Perez leads. He is chairman of the Democratic National Committee, not the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.
match_headline: He’s Running for Congress. It Doesn’t Hurt That His Opponent Is Out on Bail.

text: An article on Thursday about the actress Tilda Swinton misspelled the “Suspiria” makeup artist’s first name. He is Mark Coulier, not Marc.
match_headline: How ‘Suspiria’ Transformed Tilda Swinton Into an 82-Year-Old Man

text: An article last Sunday about dancers who have been invited to coach New York City Ballet dancers in the roles that were made for them by George Balanchine referred imprecisely to one former baller master, Sean Lavery, suggesting that he is still alive. Mr. Lavery, who retired in 2011, died in February.
match_headline: At City Ballet, Learning From Dancers Who Learned From Balanchine

text: An article last Sunday about a fraud scheme against Denmark’s tax agency misidentified the city where Lenny Kravitz performed a fund-raising concert for autism research. It was London, not Dubai.
match_headline: Where in the World Is Denmark’s $2 Billion?

text: An article last Sunday about the Ghetto Film School, which is focused on increasing ethnic and racial diversity in the movie industry, misidentified one the school’s donors. It is 21st Century Fox, not 20th Century Fox.
match_headline: Ghetto Film School Trains Its Lens on Hollywood’s Diversity Problem

text: An article last Sunday about Eugene O’Neill’s life in Northern California misstated, in one instance, the designation of his former home there. It is a national historic site, not a national park.
match_headline: Discovering Eugene O’Neill’s San Francisco

text: An article on Sept. 30 about the New York Mets’ broadcast trio, Gary Cohen, Keith Hernandez and Ron Darling, misidentified the company that produces “The Michael Kay Show.” It is a production of WEPN, an ESPN Radio affiliate, and is simulcast on YES; it is not a YES Network show.
match_headline: Gary Keith and Ron, the Magi of Mets Nation

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about search-and-rescue crews’ efforts in the aftermath of Hurricane Michael misidentified a dog used by rescue workers. It is Dexter, who is trained to sniff out human life, not Luna, who is trained to sniff out human remains.
match_headline: With Sniffer Dogs and Hope, Rescue Teams Comb Through Hurricane Michael Damage

text: An obituary on Sunday about Sidney Shachnow, who escaped a Nazi labor camp in Lithuania as a boy and went on to become a major general in the United States Army, misstated the surname of one of his daughters. She is LeeAnne Keister, not Meister.
match_headline: Sidney Shachnow, 83, Is Dead; Holocaust Escapee and U.S. General

text: An article on Sunday about a limousine crash in which 20 people died misstated the location of the Ommegang brewery. It is in Cooperstown, N.Y., not in the Finger Lakes region.
match_headline: Death at the Crossroads: A Ragged Limo, an Anxious Driver and 17 Friends

text: An article on Monday about different views on affirmative action among Asian-Americans misspelled the name of a pharmaceutical researcher who attended a rally in Cambridge, Mass., supporting Harvard. He is Chaoyang Dai, not Changyang. The article also misstated Mr. Dai’s gender. He is a man, not a woman.
match_headline: On Eve of Harvard Bias Trial, Dueling Rallies Show Rifts Among Asian-Americans

text: An article on Tuesday about James A. Wolfe, a former Senate Intelligence Committee aide who pleaded guilty to lying to the F.B.I. about his contacts with a reporter, misspelled the surname of a lawyer for Ali Watkins. He is Mark MacDougall, not MacDougal.
match_headline: Ex-Senate Aide Pleads Guilty to Lying to F.B.I. About Contacts With Reporter

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about significant events in the history of Sears misstated the year that the company opened its first store. It was 1925, not 1915.
match_headline: Sears Went From Gilded-Age Boom to Digital-Age Bankruptcy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a play by Breeland Speaks that might have led to the Chiefs’ loss to the Patriots misstated the score of the game after Tom Brady’s touchdown. The Patriots led 37-33 after it, not 40-30.
match_headline: How Fear of a Penalty Might Have Cost the Chiefs the Game

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Paul G. Allen, a founder of Microsoft, misspelled his middle name. It is Gardner, not Gardener.
match_headline: Paul G. Allen, Microsoft’s Co-Founder, Is Dead at 65

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the tenant activist Marie Runyon referred incorrectly to Berea College in Kentucky, which she attended. Although it had been founded as an interracial school just before the Civil War, it was required by law to become racially segregated in 1904; it was not interracial in the 1930s, when she studied there.
match_headline: Marie Runyon, a Liberal Firebrand Into Her 90s, Dies at 103

text: An obituary on Saturday about the former South African foreign minister Pik Botha misspelled his middle name. His full name was Roelof Frederik Botha, not Frederick.
match_headline: Pik Botha, South Africa’s Last Apartheid Foreign Minister, Dies at 86

text: An article on Wednesday about recent commercial real estate transactions in New York misstated the asking price of a six-story building at 441 Ocean Avenue in Flatbush, Brooklyn. It is $25.5 million, not $11.226 million.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Tuesday about new guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics about caring for transgender patients included a quote that misstated a statistic. People who grow up gender diverse experience triple the rate of suicide attempts; it is not known whether they experience triple the rate of suicide.
match_headline: Helping Pediatricians Care for Transgender Children

text: An article on Saturday about landlords in booming housing markets turning away tenants with Section 8 vouchers included an incorrect explanation of the subsidy formula for the Section 8 program. A voucher from the housing program provides tenants a guaranteed subsidy limiting their rent payments to 30 percent of their income. It is not a guaranteed subsidy paying 70 percent of the rent.
match_headline: With Market Hot, Landlords Slam the Door on Section 8 Tenants

text: An article on Wednesday about a provision in the tax code that allows Congress to retrieve tax returns referred imprecisely to the disclosure of two pages of President Trump’s 2005 federal tax return. While the pages were discussed on “The Rachel Maddow Show,” they were obtained and initially disclosed by David Cay Johnston at DCReport.org.
match_headline: With a House Takeover, Democrats Could Get Trump’s Tax Returns. Would They?

text: An article on Thursday about coastal military bases’ vulnerability to climate change misstated in one instance the surname of the retired Air Force lieutenant general who discussed the political sensitivities that military leaders may face in addressing the threat posed by climate change. He is General Jameson, not General Arlen.
match_headline: Exposed by Michael: Climate Threat to Warplanes at Coastal Bases

text: An article on Saturday about Brandon Woodruff’s performance in the first game of the National League Championship Series misstated the order in which Woodruff appeared in the game. He pitched first, then batted.
match_headline: A Brewers Reliever Bests a Dodgers Ace, With a Homer, in an N.L.C.S. Game 1 Win

text: An article on Friday about the sale of Marilyn Monroe’s personal prayer book misstated the surname of the rabbi who presided over Ms. Monroe’s conversion to Judaism. He was Robert Goldburg, not Goldberg.
match_headline: Auction of Marilyn Monroe’s Jewish Prayer Book Puts Her Conversion Story on Display

text: A picture caption with a film review on Friday about “Can You Ever Forgive Me?” misstated the name of the character played by Richard E. Grant. As the review correctly states, the character’s name is Jack Hock, not Jack Hockey.
match_headline: Review: Melissa McCarthy Is Criminally Good in ‘Can You Ever Forgive Me?’

text: A review on Friday about the Sarah Lucas retrospective at the New Museum omitted the name of a curator of the exhibit. She is Margot Norton.
match_headline: Is Sarah Lucas Right for the #MeToo Moment?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 1 about Tiffany Haddish refers incorrectly to the marriage of Ms. Haddish’s mother and stepfather. It was her mother’s first marriage; she wasn’t remarrying.
match_headline: Tiffany Haddish: ‘My Career Is a Delicious Roasted Chicken’

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the interior decorator Mario Buatta misstated the year he became chairman of the annual antiques and design fair in Manhattan now known as the Winter Show. It was 1977, not 1975.
match_headline: Mario Buatta, Interior Designer and ‘Prince of Chintz,’ Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Thursday about Walter D. Huddleston, a former United States senator from Kentucky who lost his bid for a third term to Mitch McConnell in 1984, misstated Mr. McConnell’s position at the time. As the head of the executive branch of a Kentucky county, he held the title of judge executive; he was not a judge and executive of the county.
match_headline: Walter Huddleston, Senator Toppled by Mitch McConnell, Dies at 92

text: An article last Sunday about investing in energy master limited partnerships misspelled the given name of a Goldman Sachs portfolio manager. He is Kyri Loupis, not Kiri Loupis.
match_headline: Energy Partnerships Rebound as U.S. Oil and Gas Output Rise

text: An article last Sunday about Lexington, Ky., misidentified the farm where the horse Secretariat was born. Secretariat was born at the Meadow farm in Virginia, not at Claiborne in Kentucky, where Secretariat retired. The article also misstated Christa Marrillia’s title. She is the chief marketing officer at Keeneland, not the marketing director.
match_headline: In Lexington, Selfies With American Pharoah, Then ‘Bourbon and Branch’

text: An article last Sunday about the local creative scene in Marrakesh, Morocco, misstated Abdellatif Ait Ben Abdallah’s relationship to the riad Dar Cherifa. He rents the space; he does not own it. (He does own seven other properties, six in Marrakesh and one in Fez.)
match_headline: A New Taste of Marrakesh

text: An article on Sunday about Saudi Arabia’s account of the circumstances of Jamal Khashoggi’s death misstated the name of the German foreign minister. He is Heiko Maas, not Meiko Mass.
match_headline: Saudi Explanation of Jamal Khashoggi’s Killing Fails to Squelch Skepticism

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about discontent and infighting at the Justice Department misstated who Justice Department leaders consulted in stripping protections for transgender people. They spoke to departmental experts, though not to the head of the civil rights appellate division and her team.
match_headline: Justice Dept. Rank-and-File Tell of Discontent Over Sessions’s Approach

text: An article on Monday about the policies of Senator Joe Donnelly of Indiana misspelled the surname of a lawyer who spoke about the Indiana candidates for Senate. She is Gaya Boyers, not Bowers.
match_headline: Joe Donnelly Runs to the Middle and Tries to Not Get Run Over

text: An article on Saturday about American and European companies’ ties to Saudi Arabia misidentified the leader of the Saudi-French Business Council. He is Dr. Mohammed bin Laden; he is not the leader of the Saudi Binladin Group or the father of Osama bin Laden.
match_headline: C.E.O.s May Avoid Riyadh Conference but Not Saudi Money

text: An article on Saturday about the relationship between the Knicks and the Nets misstated the number of times the two teams have played each other, and the record between them. They have met 192 times, not 184. The article also misstated the teams’ historical record. The record between the two franchises is 98-94, Knicks, not a 92-92 tie.
match_headline: What Will It Take for the Knicks and Nets to Have a Real Rivalry?

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Sunday about the Seattle Seahawks’ recent trip to London for an N.F.L. game misidentified the players at a Top Golf center. Doug Baldwin was on the left, not the near right; Jaron Brown was on the right.
