match_headline: ‘Four Thousand Miles for the W’

text: An article on Sunday about college hockey coaches moving into jobs in the N.H.L. misstated the number of years between Wayne Gretzky’s departure from the Edmonton Oilers and the Calgary Flames’ victory in the Stanley Cup Finals. It was one year, not two.
match_headline: College Hockey Alumni Rise in Prominence in the N.H.L.

text: An article on Monday about American Ballet Theater’s fall season misstated the surname of the set designer for “Garden Blue.” She is Sarah Crowner, not Sarah Crowden. The article also misspelled the given name of a pianist. He is Jacek Mysinski, not Yacek Misinski.
match_headline: Too Many Cooks at American Ballet Theater?

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the investigation into the disappearance of the Saudi dissident Jamal Khashoggi misstated the location that a Turkish investigator was searching in Istanbul. He was at the residence of the Saudi consul, not at the Saudi consulate.
match_headline: Aide to Saudi Crown Prince, Suspect in Khashoggi Case, Is Shown Walking Into Consulate

text: An article on Monday about the trade group Safer Phosphates and its influence in Europe rendered incorrectly the academic affiliation of Erik Smolders, a soil scientist. He is affiliated with K.U. Leuven, not Catholic University of Leuven. (The university changed names and now identifies itself as K.U. Leuven).
match_headline: A Push for Safer Fertilizer in Europe Carries a Whiff of Russian Intrigue

text: Because of an editing error, a headline for the classical music highlight in the Weekend Listings misidentified Igor Levit. He is a pianist, not a violinist.
match_headline: Review: A Pianist’s Profound Vision of ‘Life,’ in Just 2 Hours

text: An article on Tuesday about Bill Cosby’s large defense team referred incorrectly to Mr. Cosby’s sentencing. His sentencing date was set before a new lawyer, Joseph P. Green was hired; it was not pushed back in order to give Mr. Green additional time to review the evidence.
match_headline: Bill Cosby, Appealing Conviction, Hires 12th Firm and 20th Lawyer

text: An article on Tuesday about the first portrait generated by an algorithm misstated where AI work will be exhibited for sale in Miami. It will be shown at Scope Miami Beach, not Art Basel Miami Beach.
match_headline: Up for Bid, AI Art Signed ‘Algorithm’

text: An article on Friday about the next generation of home robots misstated the name of a robot being developed at Stanford. It is JackRabbot, not Jackrobbot. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: What Comes After the Roomba?

text: Because of an editing error, a headline with the obituary about a 19th-century Nebraska schoolteacher who ushered schoolchildren to safety during a blizzard misspelled her surname. As the obituary correctly noted, she is Minnie Mae Freeman Penney, not Penne.
Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the translator Anthea Bell misstated the location of Suffolk, where she was born. It is in eastern England, not western.
match_headline: Anthea Bell, Translator of Freud, Kafka and Comics, Dies at 82

text: An article on Wednesday about David Freese’s performance in the postseason referred incorrectly to Texas Rangers pitcher Neftali Feliz. He was in his second full season in 2011; he was not a rookie.
match_headline: The Dodgers’ David Freese Is the Guy Who Owns the Postseason

text: An article on Wednesday about the Boston Red Sox’ victory in the opener of the 2018 World Series misidentified the Dodgers pitcher who yielded a double to Andrew Benintendi in the seventh inning. He is Julio Urias, not Pedro Baez.
match_headline: World Series: Red Sox Outmaneuver Dodgers, and Finally Outdistance Them

text: A picture caption with the Critic’s Notebook column on Wednesday misidentified an actor shown in a scene from “What Price Hollywood?” He was Gregory Ratoff, not Neil Hamilton.
match_headline: In ‘A Star Is Born,’ Equality Is Deadly

text: An article on Thursday about a judgment that found two former Adidas employees guilty of fraud misstated Robert S. Khuzami’s title. He is the deputy United States attorney for the Southern District of New York, not the United States attorney for the Southern District of New York.
match_headline: Three Found Guilty in N.C.A.A. Basketball Recruiting Scheme

text: An obituary on Thursday about the fashion entrepreneur Wanda Ferragamo misstated the age of her husband, Salvatore, when he died in 1960. He was 62, not 63. It also misstated the location of Fiesole, the village where Mr. and Mrs. Ferragamo had a villa. It is on a hilltop, not on the banks of the Arno River. The obituary misspelled in one instance the name of one of Mrs. Ferragamo’s sons. He is Ferruccio, not Ferrucio. It also misspelled in one instance part of the name of the palace in Florence that is the company’s headquarters. It is the Palazzo Spini Feroni, not Spina.
match_headline: Wanda Ferragamo, 96, Dies; Reigned Over Family’s Luxury Goods Empire

text: An obituary on Thursday about Osamu Shimomura, who shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2008, misidentified one of his survivors. Dr. Shimomura is survived by his sister Sumiko Sawayama but not by his sister Setsuko, who died before him.
match_headline: Osamu Shimomura, 90, Dies; Won Nobel for Finding a Glowing Protein

text: An article on April 28 about a proposal in San Diego for a government-run electricity program misstated the name of a group opposed to the proposal. It is the Clear the Air Coalition, not the Clean Air Coalition. This correction was delayed because the error was only recently called to the attention of editors.
match_headline: Can San Diego Ditch the Power Company? Not Without a Fight

text: An article on Friday about the fifth installment of Tefaf New York misstated the length of the fair. It opens on Saturday, Oct. 27, and runs through Wednesday.

text: A picture caption with the Streaming column on Page 13 about “The Black Cat” reverses the identities of two actors. Bela Lugosi is on the left, and Boris Karloff is on the right.

Mr. Biegun has met senior North Korean officials since his appointment, but he has not held working-level talks with his designated North Korean counterpart.
match_headline: North Korean Nuclear Shell Game

text: An article on Saturday about the C.I.A.’s conclusion that the Saudi crown prince ordered the killing of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi misstated when Prince Khalid bin Salman last communicated with Mr. Khashoggi. It was in October 2017, not this October.
match_headline: C.I.A. Concludes That Saudi Crown Prince Ordered Khashoggi Killed

text: An article on Monday about President Trump’s reaction to the C.I.A.’s conclusion regarding the death of Jamal Khashoggi incorrectly attributed as a direct quotation that the national security adviser, John R. Bolton, said an audio recording of the killing of Mr. Khashoggi “does not, in any way, link the crown prince to the killing.” A reporter posed that to him as a question, and Mr. Bolton responded, “I have not listened to the tape myself, but in the assessment of those who have listened to it, that’s right.”
ref_headline: does not, in any way, link the crown prince to the killing.
match_headline: Despite Evidence on Khashoggi, Trump Sticks With the Crown Prince. Why?

text: An article on Saturday about discrepancies in Florida’s vote counts in the midterm election referred incorrectly to mail-in ballots that were tallied as part of a statewide recount. Only domestic mail-in ballots that arrived by Election Day were considered valid and counted; votes that arrived late were not included in the recount.
match_headline: Nearly 3,000 Votes Disappeared From Florida’s Recount. That’s Not Supposed to Happen

text: An article on Friday about signs of drinking water contamination in Detroit misidentified the elementary school that Roslyn Markhal’s daughter attends. She attends Mann Elementary School, not Chrysler.
match_headline: Not Far From Flint, Contamination Has Left Detroit School Taps Dry

text: An article on Monday about a $1.8 billion donation to Johns Hopkins University made by Michael R. Bloomberg described incorrectly how Mr. Bloomberg’s donation would expand the university’s endowment. It would increase by more than 40 percent, not by almost 30 percent.
match_headline: Bloomberg Gives $1.8 Billion to Johns Hopkins for Student Aid

text: An article on Sunday about ushers at the Metropolitan Opera House misspelled the surname of a married couple, both of whom are ushers. They are Peter and Mercedes Valdes, not Valdez.
match_headline: The Met Reinvents Itself, Yet the Ushers Remain the Same

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Lexi Thompson’s performance at the CME Group Tour Championship misstated Thompson’s age. She is 23, not 25.
match_headline: Lexi Thompson Takes a 3-Shot Lead at the CME Group Tour Championship

text: An article on Tuesday about ethnic and nationalist divisions in Bosnia misspelled the name of a river that the Bosnian wartime front runs along. The river is the Neretva, not the Nirveta.
match_headline: In Bosnia, Entrenched Ethnic Divisions Are a Warning to the World

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about forensic laboratories that analyze bullet components from crime scenes misidentified the object shown in a tray at the National Laboratory of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. It was a bullet, not a cartridge case.
match_headline: Catching Killers by Matching Tiny Marks on Bullets

text: An article on Sunday about Ron DeSantis’s subdued approach in navigating a recount in Florida misidentified the office held by Joe Gruters in the Florida Legislature. While he formerly was a member of the House of Representatives, he is now a state senator.
match_headline: Trump Cried ‘Fraud’ in Florida. Ron DeSantis Said, Tone It Down.

text: An article on Tuesday about the death of Conrado Juárez misstated the status of the prosecution’s effort to have a reporter testify at trial in the “Baby Hope” case. An appeals court in Manhattan ruled last month that she must testify in the case, not that she would not have to testify.
match_headline: Man Charged With Killing ‘Baby Hope’ Dies in Custody

text: An article on Tuesday about the difficulties of developing vaccines misstated the name of a vaccine against pneumonia. The shot that protects against 23 strains of one bacterium is Pneumovax 23, not Prevnar 23.
match_headline: Why Don’t We Have Vaccines Against Everything?

text: Because of an editing error, a recipe on Nov. 7 for Roast Turkey With Garlic and Anchovies did not include instructions for how to use the tarragon in making gravy. It is optional, and can be added to the pan with the stock in Step 6.

An obituary on Monday about Ramona Ripston, the longtime executive director of the A.C.L.U. of Southern California, misstated the position held by Daryl F. Gates when Ms. Ripston called for his resignation. He was the chief of the Los Angeles Police Department, not the city’s police commissioner.
match_headline: Ramona Ripston, California Civil Liberties Champion, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Nov. 13 about the conservative academic, social critic and politician Herbert London misstated two details of his years at Columbia College. He did not receive a basketball scholarship, and he graduated with a bachelor’s degree in sociology, not social studies. In addition, according to the National Basketball Association, he was not drafted by the Syracuse Nationals.
match_headline: Herbert London, Conservative Savant and Social Critic, Dies at 79

text: An article on Tuesday about a recent slide in technology and banking stocks misidentified the company of which Alphabet is the parent. It is Google, not Apple.
match_headline: Amazon, Apple and Facebook Once Led the Market. Now They Are Driving It Down.

text: An article on Tuesday about public nuisance charges brought against the leaders of a Hong Kong protest movement misstated the goal of students who went on strike before joining forces with the Occupy movement in 2014. They were seeking democratic reforms, and at the time were not protesting against “patriotic education.”
match_headline: Hong Kong Activists Face Trial Over 2014 Pro-Democracy Protests

text: An article on Wednesday about the conclusion of the trial of the man accused of murdering Karina Vetrano misstated when Ms. Vetrano was attacked in 2016. It was in early August, not late August.
match_headline: Hung Jury in Murder Trial Over 2016 Death of Jogger Karina Vetrano

text: An article on Tuesday about the athlete William Reilly misstated part of the name of a race that Mr. Reilly completed in the Bronx. It was the Riverdale Ramble, not the Riverside Ramble.
match_headline: A Little Help, a Connection Rekindled and a Forward Trajectory

text: An article on Nov. 14 about reinterpretations of Norman Rockwell’s “Four Freedoms” series misstated the state in which the town of Hillsdale is located. It is New York, not Massachusetts.
match_headline: Reimagining Norman Rockwell’s America

text: An article last Sunday about food halls in Miami misspelled the surname of the chief executive of Goldman Properties. She is Jessica Goldman Srebnick, not Sbrenick.
match_headline: Latest Sizzle in Miami? Food Halls

text: A review on Nov. 11 about the graphic novel “Zenobia,” written by Morten Dürr and illustrated by Lars Horneman, misstated the name of the book’s protagonist. Her name is Amina, not Zenobia.
match_headline: Stories for Kids About Heroic Young Refugees

text: An article on Nov. 11 about the growth of right-wing extremism misstated the percentage of the federal budget that is spent on counterterrorism. It is 15 percent of discretionary spending, not 16 percent of the overall federal budget. Th e article also misstated the number of additional participants in a meeting between P. W. Singer and senior Trump administration officials. It was Singer and one colleague who met with the officials. It was not Singer and several other analysts.
match_headline: U.S. Law Enforcement Failed to See the Threat of White Nationalism. Now They Don’t Know How to Stop It.

text: An article on Nov. 18 about the study of proteins to help diagnose diseases misstated one step in the protein-measurement process. Light is passed through fluorescent tags, not fluorescent aptamers.

An article on Sunday about nationality law in Ireland referred incorrectly to an Irish organization that promotes migrants’ rights. It is the Immigrant Council of Ireland, not the Irish Council for Immigrants.
match_headline: In Ireland, Bid to Restore Birthright Citizenship Gains Ground

text: An article on Saturday about the impact of tourism on the Hong Kong suburb of Tung Chung referred incorrectly to a Hong Kong tourism authority. It is the Hong Kong Tourism Association, not the Hong Kong Travel Association.
match_headline: For Some in Hong Kong, New Bridge Has a Downside: ‘That Kind of Tourist’

text: An article on Friday about a makeshift Thanksgiving dinner at a relief kitchen in California misstated when a caravan of fire evacuees departed Paradise, Calif. It was two weeks before Thanksgiving, not one week before.
match_headline: Devastated by California Fire, Paradise Finds a Way to Give Thanks

text: An article on Friday about the circumstances of suspicious killings in New Jersey misidentified one of the children who was killed. He is Jesse Caneiro, 11, not James.
match_headline: Lawyer Defends New Jersey Man Over Arson Charge and His Brother’s Death

text: An article on Sunday about the Giving Tuesday event organized by the 92nd Street Y misstated the former title of Aaron Dean on the Brooklyn Community Services board. He was chairman, not president. A picture caption with the article also misstated the given name of Mr. Dean’s daughter. She is Cydney, not Cyndey.
match_headline: On Giving Tuesday, ‘No Act of Giving Is Too Small’

text: An article on Monday about ratings trends over the first months of the new television season misidentified the network that broadcasts the program “Shark Tank.” It is ABC, not NBC.
match_headline: The New TV Season: Reboots and Reality Shows Are Sinking. Fallon Counters a Move by Colbert.

text: An article on Monday about Kristine E. Guillaume, the first black woman to be elected president of the Harvard Crimson, misstated the French city in which Ms. Guillaume had a stint as a reporter. It was in Lyon, not Léon.
match_headline: For the First Time, a Black Woman Will Lead The Harvard Crimson

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a meeting between the chief executive of Goldman Sachs and Jho Low, a financier charged with looting billions from a Malaysian investment fund, misstated the year that the fund 1 Malaysia Development Berhad was created. It was founded in 2009, not 2008.
match_headline: Goldman Chairman Met Privately With Fugitive Accused in Malaysian Fraud

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the acquisition of the toy company F.A.O. Schwarz by ThreeSixty misidentified the location of an F.A.O. Schwarz store where shoppers were shown looking in a window. It was 745 Fifth Avenue, not the General Motors building, which is elsewhere on Fifth Avenue.
match_headline: The F.A.O. Schwarz Piano Is Back — but With a Different Tune

text: An article on Saturday about Joan Graves, a chairwoman of the Motion Picture Association, misstated when Ms. Graves will retire. She will leave in the coming months, not by the end of the year.
match_headline: Filling Their Lives With Art, and Not Just One Piece at a Time

text: An article on Tuesday about House Democrats who have worked to block Representative Nancy Pelosi’s effort to win the speakership misstated when Ms. Pelosi will propose new rules governing how legislation is considered in Congress. She plans to propose those rules when the new Congress convenes in January, not on Wednesday, when she plans to unveil rules for the Democratic caucus.
match_headline: Ringleader of Democratic Rebels Softens Tone on Pelosi

text: An article on Monday about Major League Baseball’s request that Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith return a contribution to her campaign misstated the manner in which a Giants owner, Charles Johnson, and his wife also donated to Ms. Hyde-Smith’s campaign. The donation was made to the campaign directly, not through a super PAC. The article also published statements from Mr. Johnson and the Giants in error. The statements referred to a different donation by Johnson, not his contribution to Ms. Hyde-Smith’s campaign. The article also misstated the timing of M.L.B.’s donation to Ms. Hyde-Smith. It came about two weeks after video of her comments invoking public hangings emerged, not two weeks after she made the comments.
match_headline: M.L.B. Asks Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith to Return $5,000 Donation

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts to return art stolen by the Nazis during World War II misstated the title of Stuart E. Eizenstat, who is helping the State Department monitor compliance with the Washington Principles, a 1998 international accord on the return of Nazi-looted art. He is an expert adviser to the department, not a special envoy. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The article also referred imprecisely to plans for a report about such compliance for the department. Department officials will write that report and it will focus on international compliance with the Terezin Declaration, a 2009 follow-up agreement to the Washington Principles; it will not be prepared by Mr. Eizenstat and it will not focus on the Washington Principles.
match_headline: Five Countries Slow to Address Nazi-Looted Art, U.S. Expert Says

text: An article on Nov. 12 about Dirk Hannema, who ran one of the most influential Dutch museums during World War II and has been accused of collaborating with Nazis, misstated when 30 works from the museum’s collection recently listed as having “questionable provenance” were acquired. Museum officials say they were acquired after Mr. Hannema left the museum in 1945, not during his tenure as director.
match_headline: In a Netherlands Museum Director, the Nazis Found an Ally

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about Willie Naulls, one of pro basketball’s early black stars, misstated the position he played. As the obituary correctly stated, he was a forward, not a guard.
match_headline: Willie Naulls, Knicks All-Star and Celtics Champion, Dies at 84

text: A headline with an obituary on Monday about the magician, actor and author Ricky Jay misstated his age. He was 72, not 70. The obituary said that Mr. Jay was believed to be 70 but that some sources say he was 72; information learned from birth records after the obituary was published established his correct age and birth date. The obituary also referred incorrectly in part to Mr. Jay’s wife, Chrisann Verges. While she is a producer, she was never a location manager.
match_headline: Ricky Jay, Gifted Magician, Actor and Author, Is Dead at 72

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about tensions between President Emmanuel Macron’s focus on a long-term vision for France and its citizens’ short-term needs misspelled the surname of a candidate in the French presidential election last year. He is François Fillon, not François Fallon.
match_headline: Macron Has a Long-Term Vision. But the French Have Urgent Needs.

text: An article on Tuesday about firefighters working to contain the Camp Fire misspelled the name of the town Capt. Osh Ahmad is from. He is from Fremont, Calif., not Freemont.
match_headline: California Firefighters Recount Historic Blaze: ‘There Wasn’t Anything That Wasn’t on Fire’

text: An article on Wednesday about the reasons for General Motors’ recent cutbacks referred incorrectly to Tesla’s electric car sales. Tesla is the only company to have sold more than 200,000 electric vehicles in the United States; it is not the only company to have sold 200,000 over all.
match_headline: What’s Behind the G.M. Cutbacks, and Why Trump Is Angry

text: An article on Thursday about the public art project New Monuments for New Cities misstated the month that the show starts, in Houston. It is February, not April.
match_headline: What Should Monuments Look Like Now? 25 Artworks Reveal Some Ideas

text: An article on Wednesday about winning films of the IFP Gotham Awards misstated the reason Chloé Zhao missed the Gotham Awards. She is at work now on a small-budget film, not a Marvel movie, which she will direct later.
match_headline: ‘The Rider’ and ‘First Reformed’ Top the Gotham Awards

text: An entry on Thursday in the “What’s on TV” highlights referred incorrectly to Thursday’s episode of “Law & Order: SVU.” It is the fall season finale, not the 20th season finale; Season 20 will resume in January.
match_headline: What’s on TV: ‘Coco’ and ‘Law & Order: SVU’

text: A picture caption with an article on Oct. 28 about the “Syria Matters” exhibit in Qatar, using information from the Museum of Islamic Art, misidentified a painting by Louis-François Cassas. It is “View of the Ancient City of Palmyra From the Necropolis,” not “The Great Caravan at Palmyra.”
match_headline: Exhibitions in Qatar Celebrate Syria Before the War

text: An obituary on Wednesday, reprinted on Thursday, about the former New York City schools chancellor Harold O. Levy misstated his father’s given name. He was Hugo Levy, not Hugh.
match_headline: Harold O. Levy, Progressive New York City Schools Chief, Dies at 65

text: An article on Friday about the convictions of seven men in the 2016 assassination of an indigenous environmental leader in Honduras misspelled the given name of the environmentalist who was killed. She was Berta Cáceres, not Bertha.
match_headline: Seven Convicted in Killing of Prominent Honduran Environmentalist

text: An article on Page 20 about the rapper Offset misstates the relationship between Offset’s mother, Latabia, and his father-figure, Kevin. Kevin is Latabia’s ex-husband, not her husband.
match_headline: Emerging From Migos as His Own Man: The Metamorphosis of Offset

text: An obituary on Nov. 12 about the writer Louise A. DeSalvo misstated the name of the college at Rutgers University from which she graduated in 1963. It was Douglass College, not Douglass Residential College. (Douglass Residential College replaced Douglass College after it was merged with Rutgers’s other undergraduate liberal arts colleges to form the School of Arts and Sciences in 2007.)
match_headline: Louise DeSalvo, Memoirist and Virginia Woolf Scholar, Dies at 76

text: An article on Monday about Omar Abdulaziz, a Saudi dissident who claims his conversations with Jamal Khashoggi were surveilled, overstated what is known about a report by McKinsey & Company describing Mr. Abdulaziz. Although the report identified him as an influential driver of dissent on social media, it is not clear whether that evaluation was shown to the royal court.
match_headline: Israeli Software Helped Saudis Spy on Khashoggi, Lawsuit Says

text: An article on Monday about fallout from the “Yellow Vest” protests in France misspelled the name of a French city where protests turned violent on Sunday. It is Bordeaux, not Bourdeaux.
match_headline: Macron Returns to Turmoil, as France Weighs State of Emergency

text: An article on Saturday about damage from an earthquake in Alaska misstated the given name of a man who experienced the earthquake at his condo near the University of Alaska. His name is Tim Woody, not Todd.
match_headline: Earthquake Shreds Highways and Sows Panic in South Central Alaska

text: An article on Nov. 8 about the size of Democrats’ gains in midterm elections overstated or misstated the shift — the amount that a district voted more for Democrats or Republicans in 2018 versus 2016 — for 20 districts. Because of an inconsistency in how the shift was calculated for races where there was only one major party candidate running, the blue shift was overstated in 17 districts by six to 28 percentage points. In two districts, the shift should have been red instead of blue. And in one district, the red shift was overstated by 46 percentage points.
match_headline: Two Years and Hundreds of Inflammatory Ads Later, the G.O.P. Is the Party of Trump

text: An article on Friday about Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Manhattan townhouse misstated the office held by Calvin Coolidge when he defeated John W. Davis in the presidential election of 1924. He was president, not vice president.
match_headline: Remembering the House F.D.R. Built (Well, His Mother Did)

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about cases of violent behavior by N.F.L. players outside of games misidentified the player who was suspended for the first two games of the season. It was Reuben Foster, not Kareem Hunt.
match_headline: The N.F.L. Was Soaring. Then a Familiar Demon Reared Its Ugly Head

text: An obituary on Oct. 13 about Carol Hall, who wrote the music and lyrics for the hit Broadway musical “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas,” misstated the year of her marriage to Leonard Majzlin. It was 1978, not 1973. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.
ref_headline: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas,
match_headline: Carol Hall, ‘Best Little Whorehouse’ Composer, Is Dead at 82

text: An article on Monday about riots in France misidentified a Paris street that suffered damage during the protests. It is Boulevard Haussmann, not Avenue Haussmann.
match_headline: ‘Yellow Vests’ Riot in Paris, but Their Anger Is Rooted Deep in France

text: An article on Tuesday about President George Bush’s correspondences misstated the year that Mr. Bush’s plane was shot down over the Pacific. It was 1944, not 1943. An earlier version also misstated the office for which Geraldine Ferraro was the Democratic nominee in 1984. She was running for vice president, not president. An earlier version also incorrectly identified the recipient of a 1982 letter from President George Bush. He wrote the actress Katharine Hepburn, not Audrey.
match_headline: George Bush: A Life Through Letters

text: An article on Tuesday about a trip by Paul Manafort to discuss the release of Julian Assange referred incorrectly to an investigation of Mr. Assange. While he was pursued by Swedish prosecutors over a rape accusation, he was never charged with the crime.
match_headline: Manafort Discussed Deal With Ecuador to Hand Assange Over to U.S.

text: An article on Tuesday about the jukebox show “Summer: The Donna Summer Musical” misstated which actresses received Tony Award nominations for their roles in the show. Ariana DeBose and LaChanze were nominated for Tony Awards, not Storm Lever and LaChanze. The article also misstated a date involving “The Cher Show.” The show opened on Monday; it did not start previews then.
match_headline: ‘Summer: The Donna Summer Musical’ to Close in December

text: An article on Nov. 14 about the history of turkey brining misstated who the food editor of The Los Angeles Times was in 2006. It was Leslie Brenner, not Russ Parsons, who was food editor from 1999 to 2002 and from 2008 to 2014.
match_headline: The Rise and Fall of Turkey Brining

text: A recipe last Wednesday for burekas with spinach or eggplant filling misidentified the equipment needed to mix the dough in Step 2. It is a food processor fitted with a metal blade, not a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment.
A picture caption with an obituary on Sunday about George Bush referred incorrectly to the room in which Mr. Bush was shown standing. It was the old Senate chamber, not the official Senate chamber.
match_headline: George H.W. Bush: A Life of Public Service

text: An article on Wednesday about the Bush family misidentified President George Bush’s attorney general. He is Bill Barr, not Bob Barr.
match_headline: ‘A Mixture of Sad and Joyful’: The Old Bush Gang Gathers for a Final Send-Off

text: An article on Tuesday about a deal to end nationwide strikes against Marriott International, relying on information from a union representative, misstated which provisions were included in Marriott’s contracts with its hotel workers. While a provision allowing people with low-level nonviolent drug convictions to obtain union jobs was proposed, it was not included in the final contract.
match_headline: Deal in San Francisco Ends Nationwide Marriott Strikes

text: A review on Wednesday about the film “The Charmer” omitted the name of a screenwriter for the film. In addition to Milad Alami, Ingeborg Topsoe contributed to the script.
match_headline: ‘The Charmer’ Review: Desperate Man Seeks Willing Lover. Watch Out.

text: A listing on Friday about “If Beale Street Could Talk” misstated its opening dates. It opens in limited release in New York and Los Angeles on Dec. 14, not nationwide; the movie will expand to more theaters on Dec. 25.
match_headline: ‘If Beale Street Could Talk’ Review: Trusting Love in a World Ruled by Hate

text: An article on Nov. 27 about the Chinese researcher He Jiankui, using information provided by two sources, including an organizer of a conference on genome engineering, misstated the year in which Dr. He spoke at that conference. He spoke about his work on human embryo editing at a conference at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in 2017, not 2018. Because of that error, the premise of a quote by Fyodor Urnov was incorrect. Dr. He was speaking in 2017 before a woman in China was carrying twins whose genes had been edited; he was not concealing that he had already completed the procedure.
match_headline: Chinese Scientist Claims to Use Crispr to Make First Genetically Edited Babies

text: An article on Thursday about Republicans in Wisconsin limiting the power of the governor misstated the day on which a North Carolina judge struck down part of a series of legislative changes. It was Wednesday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Wisconsin, Limiting Governor, Borrows a Page From North Carolina’s Book

text: An obituary on Thursday about the longtime New York Public Library art curator Robert Rainwater misstated the name of a French printmaker whose work he exhibited. He was Félix Buhot, not Puhot. The obituary also misstated the name of the club in Manhattan where Mr. Rainwater celebrated Christmas with friends. It is the Century Association, not the Century Club.
match_headline: Robert Rainwater, Influential Art Curator, Is Dead at 75

text: A review on Nov. 18 about the audio version of “The Tattooist of Auschwitz,” a novel by Heather Morris, misidentified one of the historical figures who appear in the book. He is the Auschwitz commandant Rudolf Höss, not Rudolf Hess, who was deputy leader of the Nazi Party.
match_headline: A Novel About the Death Camps, Brought to Vivid Life in Audio

text: An article on Nov. 25 about the effect of biofuel policy and palm-oil productionon climate change included an erroneous description of a 2008 article in the jour-nal Science. The article noted that when the ripple effects of land use were included, corn-based ethanol — not the use of biodiesel — would nearly double the greenhouse-gas emissions of conventional fuels.
match_headline: Palm Oil Was Supposed to Help Save the Planet. Instead It Unleashed a Catastrophe.

text: An article on Dec. 2 about the decline of insect populations misidentified, on first reference, the location of Radboud University. It is inthe Netherlands, not Denmark. The article also misspelled the name of an extinct species.It is Steller’s sea cow, not Stellar’s.
match_headline: The Insect Apocalypse Is Here

text: An article on Nov. 25 about the Shetland Islands described incorrectly the municipal services on the smaller islands of Yell and Unst. Both have a school, a health clinic and a police station; it is not the case that they are lacking them. The article also misspelled surnames of a writer who set a series of murder mysteries on the Shetland Islands and the owner of Uradale Farm. The author is Ann Cleeves, not Cleaves, and the farm owner is Ronnie Eunson, not Euston.
match_headline: Shetland Islands: Scenery, Sheep and Knitters Galore on Britain’s Northern Tip

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about Senator Cory Booker referred incorrectly to Cindy Rosenwald. She is a State Senator in New Hampshire, not a senator-elect.
match_headline: Cory Booker Dips a Toe Into New Hampshire as 2020 Decision Nears

text: An article on Saturday about Atlantic City’s mayor, Frank M. Gilliam Jr., included a caption that misstated the position of Mr. Gilliam at a ribbon cutting in June. He is third from the right, not third from the left. The article also misstated the surname of the real-life political boss romanticized in HBO’s “Boardwalk Empire.” He was Enoch “Nucky” Johnson, not Thompson.
match_headline: The Mayor and the F.B.I. Raid: Atlantic City Is Stained Once Again

text: An article on Sunday about recent N.B.A. games misstated the Nets’ win-loss record. It is 10-18, not 10-8.

An article on Nov. 27 about inexperienced backup quarterbacks in the N.F.L. referred incorrectly to the ratings of the bottom eight quarterbacks. Those quarterbacks have an average — not median — rating of 77.6.
match_headline: N.F.L. Is Full of Quarterbacks Who Are Off the Mark, or Even Off the Street

text: An article on Wednesday about Urban Meyer misstated the relationship between Meyer and Earl Bruce. Meyer was Bruce’s protégé, Bruce was not Meyer’s protégé.
match_headline: Urban Meyer to Retire From Ohio State Following Tumultuous Season

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the final of the 2018 Copa Libertadores misidentified the city where the police were out in force. It was Buenos Aires, not Madrid.
match_headline: In a Transplanted Final, Even the Copa Libertadores Is Sanitized

text: An article on Tuesday about a Dutch church misstated the geographic location of Katwijk, a seaside town in the Netherlands. Katwijk is southwest of Amsterdam, not north of it.
match_headline: To Protect Migrants From Police, a Dutch Church Service Never Ends

text: An article on Tuesday about Baghdad’s Green Zone misidentified the people standing beside the idle checkpoints on Monday. They were armed Americans in civilian clothes, not American soldiers.
match_headline: Baghdad’s Fortified Green Zone Opens to Public After 15 Years

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the gunman who killed 26 people at Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012 misidentified the town where the gunman’s home was located. It was in Newtown, Conn., not Sandy Hook.
match_headline: Newly Released Documents Detail Sandy Hook Shooter’s Troubled State of Mind

text: An article on Tuesday about the former World Cup winner who bought the soccer club Real Valladolid misspelled the player’s name. He is Ronaldo Luís Nazário de Lima, not Ronaldo Luíz Nazário de Lima.
match_headline: The Original Ronaldo Adjusts to the Owner’s Box

text: An obituary on Monday about the longtime Tour de France commentator Paul Sherwen misidentified the French king he would sometimes refer to in jest in his commentary. He was Louis XIV, not Louis IV.
match_headline: Paul Sherwen, 62, Who Became a Voice of the Tour de France, Dies

text: An editorial on Sunday about tax breaks given to corporations for providing jobs referred incorrectly to an incentive New Jersey gave to Honeywell. Honeywell, which is moving its headquarters from New Jersey to North Carolina, is eligible for a total of $40 million in New Jersey tax credits over 10 years if it keeps enough jobs in the state. It has not already gotten the full $40 million credit.
match_headline: Taxpayers Always Lose Industry’s Shell Game With Jobs

text: An article on Monday about an area of Syria occupied by Islamic State fighters misstated the date cited by officials when referring to the bombing strikes by the American-led coalition in its “Operation Roundup” campaign that began in May. They were for the week ending Dec. 1, not Dec. 5.
match_headline: Battered ISIS Keeps Grip on Last Piece of Territory for Over a Year

text: An article on Tuesday about natural selection among coral reef populations referred incorrectly to Melissa Roth’s position at the University of California, Berkeley. She is an assistant research biologist, not a postdoctoral fellow.
match_headline: Scientists Find Some Hope for Coral Reefs: The Strong May Survive

text: An article on Wednesday about three women who filed lawsuits against CBS over Charlie Rose’s behavior misidentified the women’s employers. Two of the women worked for Mr. Rose, and one for CBS, when the lawsuit was filed; it is not the case that all three women were CBS employees.
match_headline: CBS Settles With Women Who Accused Charlie Rose of Sexual Harassment

text: An article on Sunday about Evo Morales’s efforts to seek a fourth term as president of Bolivia misstated an action on tax policy taken by his predecessor, Gonzálo Sánchez de Lozada. While Mr. Sánchez de Lozada proposed a tax increase that would have affected the poor, the tax plan was not implemented during his tenure.
match_headline: In Bolivia, Morales’s Indigenous Base Backtracks on Support

text: An article on Saturday about immigration in Japan misspelled the surname of a contributor who helped in the reporting. He is Shunta Takino, not Tashino.
match_headline: Bucking a Global Trend, Japan Seeks More Immigrants. Ambivalently.

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about cities facing future natural disasters misidentified animals that were being herded through floodwaters west of Houston after Hurricane Harvey. They were cattle, not horses.
match_headline: Cities Prepare to Face New Disasters

text: An article on Friday about Canada’s role in the trade war between the United States and China misspelled the surname of one of the Canadians detained by China. He is Michael Spavor, not Spovar.
match_headline: Who’s in the Middle of a Spat Between the U.S. and China? Canada

text: An article on Friday about modeling the brain’s genome misstated the number of people whose cells were analyzed in a study. It was dozens of people of all ages, not exactly 1,866 people. Additionally, the article misstated the source of single cells examined for patterns of gene expression. The people the cells came from did not have a particular disorder.
match_headline: Mapping the Brain’s Genetic Landscape

text: An article on Friday about the disrupted lives of students at Paradise High School misspelled the surname of a student who lost her home in the Camp Fire. She is Elie Wyllie, not Wylie.
match_headline: Their Plans Derailed by a Wildfire, Seniors at Paradise High School Wonder What’s Next

text: Because of an editing error, the Q. and A. column last Sunday, about the comic actor Billy Eichner, misstated the location of Provincetown, one of Mr. Eichner’s favorite vacation spots. It is in Massachusetts, not Rhode Island.
match_headline: Billy Eichner Has Never Been to Paris

text: An article on Nov. 25 about the director Yorgos Lanthimos misstated Lanthimos’s relationship with the ad agency where he met Efthimis Filippou, a playwright and co-writer on four of Lanthimos’s films. Lanthimos did not work for the agency.
match_headline: Yorgos Lanthimos’s Polarizing Visions

text: A review on Dec. 2 about “My Big Wimmelbook,” a series of large-format board books, misspelled the surname of one of the authors. He is Max Walther, not Walth. The review also misstated the publishing history of the series. The volumes published in the United States this year are new books; they were not “originally published in Germany.”
match_headline: Big, Beautiful Books to Catch the Eye of Every Child

text: A review on Dec. 2 about the novel “Jeeves and the King of Clubs,” by Ben Schott, misstated the nickname of P.G. Wodehouse’s recurring character Hildebrand Glossop. It is Tuppy, not Tubby.
ref_headline: Jeeves and the King of Clubs,
match_headline: New Sentences: From ‘Jeeves and the King of Clubs’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Jared Kushner’s role in criminal justice reform contained a truncated quote from Van Jones, a CNN host. The full quote is: “The person who made it safe for everyone is Donald Trump, and that is an insane outcome.”
ref_headline: The person who made it safe for everyone is Donald Trump, and that is an insane outcome.
match_headline: The Senate Passed the Criminal Justice Bill. For Jared Kushner, It’s a Personal Issue and a Rare Victory.

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the ethics inquiries surrounding Ryan Zinke misidentified the national park near which new mining claims are now banned. It is Yellowstone National Park, not Yosemite.
match_headline: Ryan Zinke’s Legal Troubles Are Far From Over

text: An article on Sunday about the artist Judy Chicago misspelled the surname of the astronaut who later painted lunar landscapes. It was Alan L. Bean, not Beam.
match_headline: A Museum Honoring Judy Chicago, Star of Feminist Art? Not in This ‘Sleepy Little Town’

text: An article on Wednesday about the failed legal effort to make disciplinary records of police officers available to the public misstated the name of the independent city agency that investigates allegations of police abuse in New York City. It is the Civilian Complaint Review Board, not the Civilian Complaint Control Board.
match_headline: Discipline Records of New York Police to Stay Secret, Court Rules

text: An article on Saturday about increased arrests and deportations of undocumented immigrants misstated the number of undocumented immigrants who were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in the 2018 fiscal year. The number is 159,000, not 59,000.
match_headline: Immigration Arrests and Deportations Are Rising, I.C.E. Data Show

text: An article on Monday about advertising and traffic jams misstated the location of the advertising technology company Intersection. It is in Manhattan, not Brooklyn.
match_headline: Digital Data Gives Billboard Owners More Reason to ‘Love a Good Traffic Jam’

text: An article on Saturday about former athletes at the University of North Carolina who signed a letter opposing a history center that would house a confederate monument incorrectly stated that Jerry Stackhouse played for the Tar Heels’ 1993 national championship team. His college career started the next season.
match_headline: Former Tar Heel Players Derail New Home for ‘Silent Sam’ Confederate Statue

text: An article on Saturday about Association of Tennis Professionals’ decision not to remove Justin Gimelstob misstated the given name of the acquaintance Mr. Gimelstob is accused of beating. He is Randall Kaplan, not Ronald.
match_headline: ATP Board Votes Not to Remove Justin Gimelstob

text: An article on Friday about Bill Cosby referred imprecisely to the handling of appeals by Pennsylvania’s Superior Court. The court considers all appeals that are filed.
match_headline: Bill Cosby’s Appeal Cites 11 ‘Errors’ by Trial Judge

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actress Sondra Locke misstated the name of a film website on which a biographical sketch of Ms. Locke appears. It is the Internet Movie Database, not the International Movie Database.
match_headline: Sondra Locke, 74, Is Dead; Oscar-Nominated Actress

text: An obituary on Sunday about the lawyer John Gibbons referred incorrectly to the role played by Joseph Margulies in the effort to win due process rights for detainees at Guantánamo Bay. He was the lead counsel in one of two cases — Rasul v. Bush — not in the consolidated cases, which Judge Gibbons successfully argued before the Supreme Court.
match_headline: John Gibbons Dies at 94; Argued for Rights for Guantánamo Detainees

text: An article on Thursday about extreme weather misstated the findings of a report by Munich Re, a reinsurance company, on damages caused by tropical storms in 2018. The company reported that tropical cyclones had caused $51 billion in losses worldwide, not that the hurricane season caused $51 billion in losses in the United States. Additionally, the long-term annual average of $34 billion in losses, as calculated by the company, is for tropical cyclones worldwide, not hurricanes in the United States.
match_headline: More Floods and More Droughts: Climate Change Delivers Both

text: An article on Tuesday about a new birth control program referred incorrectly to a change in the estimated rate of unintended pregnancy among low-income women in the Title X family program in Delaware. The rate is estimated to have dropped 24 percent between 2014 and 2017; it is not expected to result in a 24 percent decline this year.
match_headline: Set It and Forget It: How Better Contraception Could Be a Key to Reducing Poverty

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about legislation aimed at protecting Israel from boycotts referred imprecisely to the status of Gaza. Israel withdrew from Gaza and does not consider it occupied. Hamas, which governs Gaza, does consider it occupied because Israel still controls most of its borders.
match_headline: Lawmakers Consider Adding Measure Protecting Israel to Languishing Spending Bills

text: An article on Saturday about withdrawing money from retirement accounts referred imprecisely to the tax benefits of qualified charitable distributions. The distributions are excluded from taxable income, but taxpayers cannot also take a deduction for the same gift on their tax return.
match_headline: Of a Certain Age? You May Need to Withdraw Money From a Retirement Account

text: An article on Tuesday about television programming, using information from NBC’s website, misstated who will perform on Tuesday’s episode of “The Voice.” Halsey and John Legend are among the performers; Cher is not.
match_headline: What’s on TV Tuesday: ‘Ellen DeGeneres: Relatable’ and ‘Terrace House’

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the singer Nancy Wilson misstated the first name of a credited co-writer of the song “Face It Girl, It’s Over,” which was a hit for Ms. Wilson in 1968. He was identified on the label as Andy Badale, not Angelo.
match_headline: Nancy Wilson, Singer Who Bridged Jazz and Pop, Is Dead at 81

text: An article on Wednesday about the disclosure of data by Facebook to other companies misstated the year that Yahoo ended a feature on its website that incorporated Facebook user data. The feature was discontinued in 2012, not 2011.
match_headline: As Facebook Raised a Privacy Wall, It Carved an Opening for Tech Giants

text: An article on Thursday about reaction to President Trump’s order to withdraw American troops from Syria referred imprecisely to the scope of violence by the Islamic State. A researcher estimated that the group is still carrying out 75 terrorist attacks a month in Iraq, not 75 attacks a day.
match_headline: U.S. Exit Seen as a Betrayal of the Kurds, and a Boon for ISIS

text: An article on Sunday about a group of childhood friends reuniting in Chinatown misidentified the location of Taishan. It is in southeastern China, not southwestern China.
match_headline: The Return of the ‘Bad Boys’ of Chinatown

text: An article on Thursday about Aziz Ansari and Louis C.K. misstated the kind of dress that inspired a cultural appropriation uproar. It was a cheongsam, not a kimono, that a white girl wore to her prom.
match_headline: Should Aziz Ansari and Louis C.K. Talk About Accusations Onstage?

text: A review on Thursday about “Mary Poppins Returns” misstated the surname of the actress playing a housekeeper. She is Julie Walters, not Waters.
match_headline: ‘Mary Poppins Returns’ Review: A Truck Full of Sugar Can’t Make This Uplift Go Down

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s proposal to withdraw about 7,000 troops from Afghanistan misstated the number of NATO troops deployed in the country. It is 8,000, not 16,000.
match_headline: U.S. to Withdraw About 7,000 Troops From Afghanistan, Officials Say

text: An article on Friday about Zachary Fuentes, the deputy White House chief of staff, misstated the length of Mr. Fuentes’s active duty service. In July 2019, it will be 15 years, not 19 years.
match_headline: A Top Aide’s Exit Plan Raises Eyebrows in the White House

text: An article on Friday about a Manhattan music school for the visually impaired misstated how The New York Times obtained a letter sent to the school’s students by Dr. Alan Morse, the president of Lighthouse Guild International. The letter was provided by Jillian Raquet, a student at the school, not by Leslie Jones, the school’s director.
match_headline: Why a School for Blind Musicians Is Being Evicted at Christmastime

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 8 about suggestions for new characters in a Spider-Man sequel misstates the first name of one of the Spideys. He is Miles — not Milo — Morales.
match_headline: More Spideys for a ‘Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse’ Sequel

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the actress and director Penny Marshall misstated the year she and Rob Reiner divorced. It was 1981, not 1979. .
match_headline: Penny Marshall, ‘Laverne & Shirley’ Star and Movie Director, Dies at 75

text: A review on Dec. 2 about “Mad Scenes and Exit Arias: The Death of the New York City Opera and the Future of Opera in America,” by Heidi Waleson, misidentified City Opera’s inaugural production after the company’s move to the New York State Theater at Lincoln Center in 1966. It was Alberto Ginastera’s “Don Rodrigo,” which opened on Feb. 22 that year; it was not Handel’s “Giulio Cesare,” which opened on Sept. 27.
ref_headline: Mad Scenes and Exit Arias: The Death of the New York City Opera and the Future of Opera in America,
match_headline: How ‘A Mad Love’ of Opera Has Played Out From 17th-Century Mantua to 21st-Century New York

text: A picture caption on Dec. 2 with a review of Christine Otten’s novel “The Last Poets,” using information from Getty Images, misidentified a member of the hip-hop forerunners known as the Last Poets. He was Nilaja Obabi, not Abiodun Oyewole.
match_headline: Rap’s Radical First Act

text: Because of an editing error, the Ethicist column on Dec. 9 misquoted the philosopher Harry Frankfurt. He wrote that love “creates reasons,” not “generates reasons.”
match_headline: Should a Nonprofit Splurge on Management?

text: An article on Dec. 16 about the war in Yemen misstated one aspect of the involvement of the United States in the war in Yemen. In 2015, the United States Navy began assigning warships to the region to prevent weapons shipments from reaching Yemen. The United States did not send warships to help Saudi Arabia enforce a blockade.
match_headline: From Arizona to Yemen: The Journey of an American Bomb

text: An article last Sunday about training feral cats to kill mice for homeowners misstated the full name of the A.S.P.C.A. It is the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, not the Animal Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.
match_headline: Got Mice? Time for a Working Cat

text: An article on Friday about a couple sentenced for their membership in National Action, a far-right group banned in Britain, misstated the location of Birmingham Crown Court. It is in central England, not northwest England.
match_headline: Couple Who Named Their Child After Hitler Are Sentenced for Neo-Nazi Membership

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday referred imprecisely to the representation of Muslims and Christians in Lebanon’s population. They make up most of the country’s 18 officially recognized sects, not just two.
match_headline: Christmas in Lebanon: ‘Jesus Isn’t Only for the Christians’

text: An article on Wednesday about a new law that will put an end to the “bread-and-water” punishment — a disciplinary practice left over from the era of sailing ships — referred incorrectly to the Supreme Court review process for disciplinary cases. Reviews to the Supreme Court are handled by the United States Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces, not by the military itself.
match_headline: No More Bread and Water: U.S. Navy Scraps an Age-Old Penalty

text: An article on Thursday about reaction to reports of Facebook’s failure to disclose data-sharing deals misattributed a statement made to Fox News about Facebook. The statement was made by Senator John Kennedy, the Louisiana Republican, not Senator Roy Blunt, the Missouri Republican.
match_headline: Facebook Rebuked for Failing to Disclose Data-Sharing Deals

text: An article on Saturday about Chun Hsin Tseng, the top-ranked male junior tennis player, misspelled his father’s name. He is Yu Te Tseng, not Yu Tu.
match_headline: Mom Sells Tomatoes as Her Son Seeks Tennis Titles

text: An obituary on Saturday about the basketball star Mel Hutchins misspelled, at one point, the surname of one of his teammates on the Brigham Young University basketball team. He is Roland Minson, not Minton.
match_headline: Mel Hutchins, B.Y.U. All-American and N.B.A. All-Star, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Sunday about James E. Rogers, a former chief executive of Duke Energy, referred incorrectly to his stint as a reporter at The Lexington Herald-Leader. He worked there while attending the University of Kentucky, not after he graduated.
match_headline: James Rogers, 71, Dies; Utility Chief and Clean Energy Advocate

text: An obituary on Sunday about Peter Masterson, who co-wrote and co-directed the Broadway musical “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas” and directed the movie “The Trip to Bountiful,” referred incorrectly to Sterling Van Wagenen of the Sundance Institute, who produced “The Trip to Bountiful.” His cousin was married to Robert Redford, the institute’s founder, at the time; he was not Mr. Redford’s father-in-law.
ref_headline: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas
match_headline: Peter Masterson, 84, a ‘Best Little Whorehouse’ Creator, Is Dead

text: An article on Wednesday about New York City housing department policies misspelled the surname of a supervising attorney with the National Housing Law Project. She is Deborah Thrope, not Thorpe.
match_headline: Leaks, Mold and Rats: Why New York City Goes Easy on Its Worst Landlords

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo misidentified the aid organization administering care to a patient in a “bio-secure” plastic cube. It is the nonprofit Alima, not Doctors Without Borders.
match_headline: Texas’ One-Stop Shopping for Judge in Health Care Case

text: An article on Wednesday about Lora Safir, a survivor of the World War II invasion of Ukraine, using information from a source, misstated the monthly amount that Mrs. Safir receives in Blue Card funds. It is $100, not $50.
match_headline: A Daughter’s Death Leaves a Mother Struggling

text: An article on Thursday about the impact that Amazon’s planned headquarters is having on real estate prices in Long Island City misspelled the surname of a condo owner. He is Gary Hirshfield, not Gary Hirschfield.
match_headline: An ‘Amazon Effect’ on Queens Real Estate? Here’s Why Brokers Say It’s Real

text: An article on Thursday about the effects of environmental deregulation under the Trump administration misstated the location of the John E. Amos Power Plant. It is downstream from Charleston, W.Va., not upstream.
match_headline: The Real-Life Effects of Trump’s Environmental Rollbacks: 5 Takeaways From Our Investigation

text: An article on Friday about the partial government shutdown misquoted Senator Pat Roberts discussing the shutdown. Mr. Roberts’s full quote was, “In Dodge City, Kansas, they say a horse divided against itself cannot stand,” putting a Kansas twist on an aphorism made iconic by a former Senate candidate from Illinois.
ref_headline: In Dodge City, Kansas, they say a horse divided against itself cannot stand,
match_headline: With No Votes Scheduled, a Government Shutdown Will Greet the Democratic House

text: An article on Friday about the effects of a transformer explosion in Queens misspelled the surname of an Astoria resident. She is Yiota Androtsakis, not Androtsokis.
match_headline: New York Sky Turns Bright Blue After Transformer Explosion

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the long-term value of Vespa scooters misidentified the manufacturer of three scooters. Only one of the scooters pictured is a Vespa, not all four; the others are Lambrettas.
match_headline: A 72-Year-Old Italian Star Barely Showing Its Age

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about Turkish television misidentified the actor in the series “Fatmagul.” He is Engin Akyurek, not Kerim Ilgaz, the name of the character he plays.
match_headline: Can Netflix Take Turkey’s TV Dramas to the World?

text: A Critic’s Notebook on Page 10 about the #MeToo movement and the film “If Beale Street Could Talk” misstates the relationship between the characters Fonny and Sharon. Fonny is engaged to Sharon’s daughter, Tish; he is not Sharon’s son.
match_headline: How #MeToo Changes ‘If Beale Street Could Talk’

text: An article on Dec. 16 about a warehouse fire i n Oakland misidentified a woman who gave a statement at a sentencing hearing and misidentified the victim she spoke of. She is Linda Regan, who spoke about her daughter, Amanda Kershaw, not Susan Slocum, who spoke about her daughter Donna Kellogg. The article also misidentified the college that Peter Wadsworth, who died in the fire, attended. He graduated from Reed College, not Reed University.
match_headline: He Helped Build an Artists’ Utopia. Now He Faces Trial for 36 Deaths There.

text: An article on Monday about the Jets’ firing of coach Todd Bowles gave an incorrect date for the resignation of Bill Parcells as Jets coach. He stepped down in January 2000, after the 1999 season, not in 1999.
match_headline: Todd Bowles Is Fired by Jets After Rout by the Patriots

text: An article on Sunday about Liverpool’s undefeated record in the Premier League misstated the timing of the most recent Merseyside derby. It was in December, not November.
match_headline: What Pressure? Liverpool Allows Itself to Smile and Its Fans to Believe

text: An article on Friday about Jessica Springsteen’s career in professional show jumping referred incorrectly to her Olympic experience. She aspires to compete in future Olympic Games; she was not an alternate for the United States team for the London Games in 2012.
match_headline: Another Springsteen, Starring Way Off Broadway

text: A review on Dec. 14 about the film “Bird Box” misstated a character’s role in the movie. The character Douglas is a neighbor, not the owner of the home in which some of the characters hide.
match_headline: ‘Bird Box’ Review: The End of the World Is Riveting. Sometimes.

text: An article on Tuesday about a looming schism between the Orthodox Christian churches in Ukraine and Russia misstated the title of the senior Moscow Patriarchate priest in Rivne, Ukraine. He is Bishop Pimen, not Archbishop Pimen.
match_headline: As Ukraine and Russia Battle Over Orthodoxy, Schism Looms

text: An article on Wednesday about Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s inaugural address referred incorrectly to the Cuomo family’s time in power. For those born in 1980, a Cuomo — either Mario or Andrew Cuomo — served as governor of New York for a majority of their life; this is not true of everyone born since 1980.
match_headline: At Inauguration, Cuomo Rallies State Against Trump

text: An article on Tuesday about new laws going into effect in 2019 misstated the legal age for buying cigarettes in New York City. It is 21, not 18.
match_headline: A Long-Awaited Ban on Foam, and Other New Laws in New York in 2019

text: An article on Wednesday about Netflix’s decision to pull an episode of “Patriot Act With Hasan Minhaj” from its platform in Saudi Arabia misstated the name of an organization that has documented a crackdown on Saudi journalists. It is the Committee to Protect Journalists, not the Committee to Project Journalists.
match_headline: Netflix Blocks Show in Saudi Arabia Critical of Saudi Prince

text: A picture with an article on Tuesday about six athletes who transformed their sports in 2018 was published in error. It showed Amos Kipruto, the runner-up at the Berlin Marathon — not Eliud Kipchoge, the winner.
match_headline: Ravens and Eagles Claw Their Way to the N.F.L. Playoffs

text: An article on Tuesday about Serena Williams and Roger Federer facing off in a doubles exhibition gave an incomplete list of players who have won 20 or more Grand Slam singles titles in the Open Era. They are Serena Williams, Roger Federer and Steffi Graf, not only Williams and Federer.
match_headline: Serena Williams and Roger Federer to Face Off for First Time Ever

text: An article on Tuesday about the impact of hearing loss described incorrectly how insurance companies cover hearing aids. Insurance plans typically do not cover hearing aids, though some do; it is not the case that hearing aids are never covered.
match_headline: Hearing Loss Threatens Mind, Life and Limb

text: An article last Thursday about the artist Theaster Gates referred incorrectly to the ownership of the photographs featured in an installation by Mr. Gates. He licensed the images from the Johnson Publishing Company; he did not buy them.
match_headline: Theaster Gates Is a Toast of the Fashion and Art Circuit

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the lyricist Norman Gimbel misstated the year of the Broadway musical “The Conquering Hero,” for which Mr. Gimbel wrote the lyrics and Moose Charlap wrote the music. It was 1961, not 1967.
match_headline: Norman Gimbel, 91, Grammy and Oscar-Winning Lyricist, Is Dead

text: An article on Thursday about the exodus of Turkey’s academics and business elite misidentified the university in the Netherlands where Ilker Birbil took up a position after leaving Turkey. It is Erasmus University Rotterdam, not Utrecht University.
match_headline: Spurning Erdogan’s Vision, Turks Leave in Droves, Draining Money and Talent

text: An article on Wednesday about how Native Americans have been affected by the government shutdown referred incorrectly to the impact of the shutdown on a Department of Agriculture food program. The program will be funded through January, but will be curtailed if the shutdown continues beyond that date.
match_headline: Shutdown Leaves Food, Medicine and Pay in Doubt in Indian Country

text: An article on Friday about Paul N. Whelan’s arrest in Russia described incorrectly his university education. Mr. Whelan attended Northern Michigan University from the fall semester of 1988 until the fall semester of 1990 but did not complete his bachelor’s degree, according to the school; he did not graduate from the University of Michigan. (The information came from Mr. Whelan’s Russian social media account, where he said he studied at the University of Michigan.)
match_headline: Spy or Not? American Who Loves Russia Ensnared in New Cold War

text: An article on Friday about recommended winter TV series misstated the premiere date for the third season of “High Maintenance.” It will debut on Jan. 20, not Jan. 19.
match_headline: Winter TV Preview: ‘True Detective,’ ‘Carmen Sandiego’ and 19 More Shows to Watch

text: An article on Page 1 about the artists Gillie and Marc Schattner, using information from the artists and the MetroTech BID, misidentifies the organization that secured “The Last Three” sculpture in Brooklyn’s MetroTech Commons. While MetroTech Commons is a privately operated space within the MetroTech BID, the BID did not secure the work. The error is repeated in a picture caption. The article also misstates Jennifer Lantzas’s position with the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. She is its deputy director of public art, not its public arts coordinator.
match_headline: How Paparazzi Dogs and Rabbitgirl Conquered New York City Streets

text: An article on Page 1 about Jada Yuan’s experiences traveling the world for The New York Times misstates the surname of a woman who was murdered in Washington last year. She was Wendy Martinez, not Marina. The article also misidentifies a farmer in Puerto Rico who told her and a friend about a party. He is Elmer Sánchez, not Rafael.
match_headline: Try to Keep Up With Australia’s Fastest 92-Year-Old Woman

text: An obituary on Friday about Herb Kelleher, the co-founder of Southwest Airlines, misstated his middle name. It was David, not Dwight.
match_headline: Herb Kelleher, Whose Southwest Airlines Reshaped the Industry, Dies at 87

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Dec. 23 about the Dead Sea misstated the amount of money in dollars that the Israeli tourism ministry recently spent on improvements at the Ein Bokek resort area. It was $135 million, not $13 million.
match_headline: The Otherworldly Beauty of a Dying Sea

text: An article on Dec. 16 about a patient who had a rare autoimmune disorder misstated the location of a Toronto hospital. While North York General Hospital is in Toronto, it is not in the downtown section of the city.
match_headline: Why Was the Woman Having Trouble Seeing, if Her Eyes Were Fine?

text: A picture caption with the Inside The Times feature on Thursday about reporting on a volunteer medic who was killed in Gaza misidentified the woman being interviewed by Iyad Abuheweila and David M. Halbfinger. She is Eslam Abu Dagga, not Eslam al-Najjar.
match_headline: How Times Reporters Froze a Fatal Moment on a Protest Field in Gaza

text: An article on Wednesday about the Chinese photographer Li Zhensheng referred incorrectly to the publication of the first Chinese-language edition of “Red-Color News Soldier.” It was published in July, not October.
match_headline: A Photographer’s Quest to Reverse China’s Historical Amnesia

text: An article on Saturday about pet insurance policies, using information supplied by Healthy Paws Pet Insurance, misstated how a pet’s age affects premiums for the company’s policies. The pet’s age affects the premium at the time of enrollment and as the pet gets older, not just at enrollment.
match_headline: More Pet Insurance Policies Are Being Sold. But Are They Worth the Cost?

text: An article on Dec. 6 about a concert with blues and soul stars at President George Bush’s 1989 inauguration party misspelled the surname of the lawyer who helped produce the concert. He is Howell Begle, not Beagle. This correction was delayed because an editor was only recently notified of the error.
match_headline: George Bush, Soul Man? Footage From an Inauguration Concert Is Restored

text: An article on Tuesday about the impact of the government shutdown on workers misidentified the agency that approves new beer labels for craft brewers. It is the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, not the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.
match_headline: As Government Shutdown Persists, Americans Feel the Bite

text: An article on Tuesday about a televised speech delivered by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel in which he attacked a corruption investigation into his dealings with Israeli media tycoons misstated the length of his address. It lasted seven minutes, not 20.
match_headline: Netanyahu, Feeling Heat, Grabs Spotlight to Assail ‘Witch Hunt’ Investigation

text: An article on Tuesday about a coup attempt in Gabon, using information provided by the government, misstated who was among those killed in the episode. Lt. Kelly Ondo Obiang, the leader of the self-declared Patriotic Movement of the Defense and Security Forces of Gabon, announced the coup but was not one of the plotters killed in the attempt.
match_headline: Coup Attempt in Gabon Is Thwarted, Government Says

text: An article on Tuesday about Income Sharing Agreements as an alternative to traditional tuition models misstated the year that Lambda School was founded. It was 2017, not 2016.
match_headline: No Tuition, but You Pay a Percentage of Your Income (if You Find a Job)

text: An article on Tuesday about the opportunities for smaller soccer clubs competing in the F.A. Cup misstated Coventry’s status at the time of its loss to Sutton United in the 1989 F.A. Cup. Coventry won the Cup in 1987; it was not the holder at the time of its loss to Sutton United.
match_headline: The Fleeting Magic of the F.A. Cup

text: A review on Tuesday about the play “Blue Ridge” by Abby Rosebrock misstated the title of a Tennessee Williams play. It is “Summer and Smoke,” not “Summer in Smoke.”
match_headline: Review: Marin Ireland Brings Down the Halfway House in ‘Blue Ridge’

text: An article about the Undiagnosed Diseases Network misspelled the surname of a genetic counselor at Stanford University. She is Chloe Reuter, not Chloe Richter.
match_headline: When the Illness Is a Mystery, Patients Turn to These Detectives

text: An obituary on Saturday about the singer Christine McGuire omitted a reference to one of her marriages. She was married five times, not four; her fourth marriage, to George Rosenfeld, a restaurateur, lasted from 1993 until his death in 1996, and her marriage to David Mudd was her fifth, not her fourth. The obituary also misstated the surname of Ms. McGuire’s son who died in 2015. He was Asa Ashcraft, not McGuire.
match_headline: Christine McGuire, Eldest of the Singing Sisters, Is Dead at 92

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about the retail scion Blake W. Nordstrom misidentified the family member at left in the photo. He is Jamie — not Peter — Nordstrom.
match_headline: Blake W. Nordstrom, Scion of Retail Family, Dies at 58

text: An article on Wednesday about a court filing indicating that Paul Manafort shared polling data with a contact tied to Russian intelligence misidentified the people to whom Mr. Manafort wanted the contact to send the data. Mr. Manafort wanted the data sent to two Ukrainian oligarchs, Serhiy Lyovochkin and Rinat Akhmetov, not to Oleg V. Deripaska, a Russian oligarch close to the Kremlin.
match_headline: Manafort Accused of Sharing Trump Polling Data With Russian Associate

text: An article on Wednesday about the increasing number of women over 60 achieving senior roles in business and government misidentified the university where Susan Douglas is a professor of communication studies. It is the University of Michigan, not Michigan State University. The article also misstated the age of Representative Maxine Waters. She is 80, not 79.
match_headline: I Am (an Older) Woman. Hear Me Roar.

text: An article on Wednesday about inquiries into claims of physical and sexual abuse by R. Kelly misstated the year a Buzzfeed report about R. Kelly was published. It was 2017, not last year.
match_headline: Investigators Looking Into Accusations From R. Kelly Documentary

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the physicist Roy J. Glauber misspelled the surname of his daughter, who survives him. She is Valerie Glauber Fleishman, not Fleischman.
match_headline: Roy J. Glauber, 93, Dies; Nobel Laureate Explored Behavior of Light

text: An article on Thursday about Bill Shine’s White House role misstated the location and theme of a poster displayed by President Trump. It was present at a cabinet meeting, not in the Oval Office, and it was related to sanctions on Iran, not the government shutdown.
match_headline: Trump Thinks He’s His Own Best Messenger. Where Does That Leave Bill Shine?

text: An article on Monday about an expected teachers’ strike in Los Angeles misstated the causes behind the disproportionate numbers of black and Latino students in the Los Angeles school district. While white students’ enrollment in private schools and surrounding districts has contributed to the demographic shift, charter school enrollment has not. (The demographics of the city’s charter schools, over all, generally match those of the city’s traditional district schools.)
match_headline: Los Angeles Braces for Major Teachers’ Strike

text: An article on Thursday about the economic strategy devised by President Moon Jae-in of South Korea misstated Mr. Moon’s approval rating in the most recent Gallup poll. It was 45 percent, not 46 percent.
match_headline: South Korea Raised Taxes in Bid for Growth. So Far, It’s Not Working.

text: A headline with the Corner Office column last Sunday, about Julie Sweet of Accenture, referred imprecisely to her title with the company. She is the chief executive for North America, not the company’s overall chief executive. A subheading misstated the number of employees she oversees. It is 57,000, not 500,000, which is the number of employees in the entire company.
match_headline: Julie Sweet of Accenture Could See Her Future. So She Quit Her Job.

text: An article last Sunday about people referring to pit bulls as “pibbles” misstated the year Rebecca Corry organized the One Million Pibble March. It was 2013, not 2015.
match_headline: The Pit Bull Gets a Rebrand

text: A news analysis last Sunday about Julián Castro misidentified where Erica Lira Castro, his wife, teaches. It is the Harlandale Independent School District, not the Harlingen Consolidated Independent School District.
match_headline: Is America’s Political Future in San Antonio?

text: An essay last Sunday about the decline of Apple in China misstated when the author replaced her iPhone with a phone made by Xiaomi. It was in late 2015, not early 2014.
match_headline: Why My Chinese Dad Switched From an iPhone to a Huawei

text: An article on Saturday about the political stalemate over funding of a border wall misstated the amount of money in emergency aid the Army Corps of Engineers has been directed to study as a possible source of funding for a border barrier. It is $13.9 billion, not $13.9 million.
match_headline: Trump Pulls Back From Declaring a National Emergency to Fund a Wall

text: An article on Monday about President Trump’s continuing conflicts with Congress misstated Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s schedule during the weekend. Her staff said she was in Washington; she had not, as the article stated, left town.
match_headline: Trump Confronts the Prospect of a ‘Nonstop Political War’ for Survival

text: An article on Monday about statements from three Democratic House committee chairmen about Michael Cohen misstated Mr. Cohen’s business relationship with his father-in-law. They were never business partners; Mr. Shusterman owned seven taxi medallion corporations.
match_headline: Top Democrats Warn Trump Over Comments on Michael Cohen

text: An article on Saturday about new members of the New York State Senate, relying on information provided by the Senate Democrats’ press office, misstated Julia Salazar’s age. She is 28, not 27.
match_headline: They Won Senate Seats. Now Comes the Hard Part: Adjusting to Albany.

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an obituary on Saturday about the musician Joseph Jarman, best known for his work with the Art Ensemble of Chicago, misidentified the members of the ensemble. Pictured in the photograph, from left, are Roscoe Mitchell, Mr. Jarman, Famoudou Don Moye and Malachi Favors — not Mr. Favors, Mr. Mitchell, Mr. Jarman and Mr. Moye. In addition, the obituary misidentified the venue in Manhattan where Mr. Jarman made his last public appearance, in 2017. It is the Lenfest Center for the Arts, not the Miller Theater.
match_headline: Joseph Jarman, 81, Dies; Mainstay of the Art Ensemble of Chicago

text: An article on Tuesday about a teachers’ strike in Los Angeles overstated the scale of the demonstration. The strike was the largest in a single district in the past year, not the largest in the United States.
match_headline: Los Angeles Teachers Strike, Disrupting Classes for 500,000 Students

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about new biometric data on American men miscalculated the height of someone who is 69.4 inches tall. He is about 5 feet 9 inches, not 5 feet 8 inches. In addition, the article misstated the average height of Mexican-American men in 2016. The figure was 66.5 inches, not 61.5 inches.
match_headline: You’re Not Getting Much Taller, America. But You Are Getting Bigger.

text: An obituary on Sunday about Lamin Sanneh, a world-renowned scholar of Christianity and Islam, referred incorrectly to Rowan Williams, who was quoted as calling Dr. Sanneh “probably the most significant theologian of mission in the English-speaking world today.” While he was the archbishop of Canterbury when he made that statement, he has not held that position since 2012.
ref_headline: probably the most significant theologian of mission in the English-speaking world today.
match_headline: Lamin Sanneh, Scholar of Islam and Christianity, Dies at 76

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the author Francine du Plessix Gray misspelled the surname of an author who reviewed her novel “Lovers and Tyrants” for The New York Times. He was Julian Moynahan, not Moynihan.
match_headline: Francine du Plessix Gray, Searching Novelist and Journalist, Is Dead at 88

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about an early step taken by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency toward surveilling a far-right party misidentified the position from which Hans-Georg Maassen was removed. He was the head of Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, not interior minister.
match_headline: German Intelligence Agency Puts Far-Right Party on Warning

text: An article on Sunday about the arrest of an employee of the Chinese telecommunications company Huawei in Poland misstated the given name of the chief financial officer of Huawei. She is Meng Wanzhou, not Wangzhou.
