match_headline: Huawei Fires Employee Arrested in Poland on Spying Charges

text: An article on Tuesday about the second season of “True Detective” misidentified the show’s music director. It is T Bone Burnett, not the Haxan Cloak (the stage name of the musician and producer Bobby Krlic).
match_headline: The Second Season of ‘True Detective’ Wasn’t as Bad as You Think. Here’s Why.

text: An article last Thursday about sick days misstated a company’s policy on sick time. The company, Skillcrush, does not have a firm limit on sick time; it does permit employees to take paid days off for illness or other circumstances that could prevent them from working.
match_headline: The Death of the Sick Day

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article last Thursday about Gov. Jared Polis of Colorado misstated the relationship between Mr. Polis and Marlon Reis. As the article and a caption on the front page of the section correctly noted, they are partners; they are not married.
match_headline: Colorado’s Got a Gay Governor. Who Cares?

text: An article last Thursday about magazines focused on marijuana misspelled part of the title of one such publication; it is Dope Girls, not Girlz. The article also misstated the name of another publication; it is Kitchen Toke, not Toke Kitchen. The article misstated the slogan of Miss Grass; it is “Welcome to the High Road,” not “High Minded.” And because of an editing error, the publishing history of Miss Grass, an online publication, was described incorrectly. It started last year; it does not have individual issues.
match_headline: High Times Has Some Glossy New Competition

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Saturday about the botanical artist Jessica Tcherepnine, using information from the Shepherd Gallery in Manhattan, misidentified the subject of one of her paintings. It is an ackee, not a magnolia. And the obituary misstated part of the name of a museum in London whose collection includes paintings by Ms. Tcherepnine. It is the Natural History Museum, not the National History Museum. (The error was repeated in a picture caption.) In addition, another picture caption with the obituary misstated Ms. Tcherepnine’s given name as Josephine.
match_headline: Jessica Tcherepnine, Exacting Botanical Artist, Is Dead at 80

text: An article on Thursday about British Prime Minister Theresa May misidentified the party affiliation of Stewart McDonald. He is a member of the Scottish National Party, not the Scottish Labour Party.
match_headline: Theresa May, Britain’s Lady of Perpetual Crisis

text: A review on Jan. 9 of the television series “You’re the Worst” referred incorrectly to an episode in which the character Gretchen takes a trip home. It was in Season 4, not Season 5.
match_headline: Review: ‘You’re the Worst’ Heads Toward Happily Ever After. Maybe.

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Wednesday about the actress Carol Channing, using information from the photo agency Photofest, misstated when the photograph of her as Dolly Levi in “Hello, Dolly!” was taken. It was in 1978, when she returned to the role in a Broadway revival — not during the show’s original Broadway run.
match_headline: Carol Channing Dies at 97; a Larger-Than-Life Broadway Star

text: An article on Friday about the debate over charter schools amid a teachers’ strike in Los Angeles misstated the share of students at Citizens of the World, a charter school, who qualify for free or reduced-price lunch. It is 45 percent of students, not 15 percent.
match_headline: At Los Angeles Teachers’ Strike, a Rallying Cry: More Funding, Fewer Charters

text: An article on Jan. 11 about doubts surrounding elections in the Democratic Republic of Congo misidentified the candidate who counts Limete as a stronghold. It is Felix Tshisekedi, not Martin Fayulu.
match_headline: Disputed Congo Election Result Leaves Country on Edge

text: An article on Page 6 about the 16-year-old actor Andrew Barth Feldman misstates Evan Hansen’s year in high school in the play “Dear Evan Hansen.” The character is a senior, not a junior.
match_headline: He’s 16 Going On Stardom: Meet Broadway’s Next ‘Evan Hansen’

text: An obituary on Jan. 7 about Georges Loinger, who saved hundreds of Jewish children from deportation to concentration camps during World War II, referred incorrectly to Strasbourg, where he was born. It was ceded by France to Germany in 1871 and was part of the German Empire when Mr. Loinger was born there in 1910; it was not “Strasbourg, France” at the time.
match_headline: Georges Loinger, Wartime Rescuer of Jewish Children, Dies at 108

text: An article in last Sunday’s special section on mutual funds and exchange-traded funds about the investing strategies of three mutual funds that outperformed the market in the fourth quarter of 2018 misstated the process for allocating the assets of the MFS Diversified Income Fund. The fund starts with allocations of 25 percent of assets to high-yield bonds and 15 percent to emerging-markets bonds, not with allocations of 20 percent to both those categories.
match_headline: How 3 Funds Sidestepped a Market Thumping

text: An article last Sunday about Puglia, Italy, as part of the 52 Places to Go in 2019 misstated who has been attracted to the region and its winemaking. It is the Antinori family, which operates the Tormaresca bistro in Lecce, not the owners of the London restaurant Bocca di Lupo.
match_headline: Five Places to Visit in London

text: An article on Jan. 6 about Jada Yuan’s experiences traveling the world for The New York Times described incorrectly the status of Puerto Rico. It is a territory of the United States; it is not its own country.
match_headline: U.S. Downgraded E.U.’s Diplomatic Status (but Didn’t Say Anything)

text: An article on Dec. 23 about hotels that have music events planned this year misstated who will be promoting the Beat Hotel festival in Marrakesh. The promoters are the group behind the Beat Hotel at Glastonbury, England, festival, not the promoters of the entire Glastonbury festival.
match_headline: 5 Hotels Booking Live Music Events

text: A review on Dec. 30 about “Tell Them of Battles, Kings, and Elephants,” by Mathias Énard, describedincorrectly the terminal points of a bridge in that novel. Michelangelo designs the bridge to cross the Golden Horn in Constantinople; it is not “a bridge that will join Asia to Europe.” The review also misspelled the surname of the book’s translator; she is Charlotte Mandell, not Mandel. These errors were repeated in the Editors’ Choice column on Jan. 6.
ref_headline: Tell Them of Battles, Kings, and Elephants,
match_headline: Three French Novels You Should Read

text: An article on Sunday about scrutiny that the website Buzzfeed is facing over an investigative article about President Trump and Michael Cohen misstated the month that Mark Schoofs, BuzzFeed’s longtime investigative editor, left the organization. It was October, not August.
match_headline: BuzzFeed News Faces Scrutiny After Mueller Denies a Dramatic Trump Report

text: An article on Saturday about the handling of a sexual assault accusation against a top official in the administration of Gov. Philip D. Murphy of New Jersey misidentified the lawmaker who asked a question of Mr. Murphy’s chief counsel during a hearing. It was Assemblywoman BettyLou DeCroce, not Assemblywoman Holly T. Schepisi.
match_headline: N.J. Lawmakers Question if Governor’s Inner Circle Took Sexual Assault Complaint Seriously

text: An article on Sunday about a plan to protect the Lower East Side from flooding misspelled the given name of a member of Community Board 3. She is Vaylateena Jones, not Vaylateeba.
match_headline: To Save East River Park, the City Intends to Bury It

text: An article on Monday about the tennis player Frances Tiafoe misstated the given name of the Italian player beaten by Tiafoe. He is Andreas Seppi, not Andrea.
match_headline: Reintroducing Frances Tiafoe, the New Mr. Upset of the Australian Open

text: An obituary on Saturday about John E. Merow, a former chairman of the Wall Street law firm Sullivan & Cromwell, misstated the date of his birth. It was Dec. 20, 1929 — not 1919. (As the obituary correctly noted, he was 89.)
match_headline: John E. Merow, Former Head of Sullivan & Cromwell, Dies at 89

text: An article on Tuesday about the government shutdown’s impact on the Department of Housing and Urban Development and nonprofit groups dedicated to helping low-income renters misidentified the location of an apartment complex. It is in Newport, Ark., not Newton, Ark.
match_headline: Shutdown’s Pain Cuts Deep for the Homeless and Other Vulnerable Americans

text: An article on Jan. 9 about the possibility of a “no-deal” Brexit quoted Martin Thornton, who was described as a driver for the Eddie Stobart trucking company. The company has since said it did not have a driver with that name. The Times was unable to confirm Mr. Thornton’s employment information and has removed his comments from the digital version of the article.
match_headline: U.K.’s Mixed Signals on a No-Deal Brexit: A Calamity, and All Is Well

text: An article Thursday about the confirmation hearing for Andrew Wheeler, President Trump’s nominee to lead the Environmental Protection Agency, misstated Molly Rauch’s position with Moms Clean Air Force. She is public health policy director for the group, not a volunteer.
match_headline: Andrew Wheeler, at E.P.A. Confirmation Hearing, Walks a Fine Line on Climate Change

text: An article on Tuesday about the complexities of airlines’ frequent-flier perks misstated the medallion status that Delta Air Lines passengers achieve by flying 25,000 qualifying miles. It is silver, not platinum.
match_headline: These Days, ‘You Practically Need a Ph.D.’ to Figure Out Frequent-Flier Status

text: An article on Tuesday about the navigational strategies of ants misstated the surname of a researcher. He is Ryan W. Draft, not Dash.
match_headline: How Ants Sniff Out the Right Path

text: A recipe last Wednesday for Sumac-Scented Eggplant and Chickpeas omitted the addition of the eggplant. After being browned in a skillet and cooled on a baking sheet, the eggplant should be stirred back into the tomato mixture, in Step 3, with the chickpeas, scallions, mint and water, and simmered.
match_headline: As Government Pulls Back, Charities Step In to Help Released Migrants

text: An obituary on Thursday about John C. Bogle, the founder of the Vanguard Group of Investment Companies, misstated both the original name and the current name of the fund he established shortly after founding Vanguard. It was originally called the First Index Investment Trust, not the Vanguard Index Trust (that was a later name); and it is now known as the Vanguard 500 Index Fund, not the Index 500 Fund. The obituary also omitted part of the name of the heart condition for which Mr. Bogle had been treated for more than 30 years. It is arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia, not right ventricular dysplasia.
match_headline: John C. Bogle, Founder of Financial Giant Vanguard, Is Dead at 89

text: An article on Wednesday about a territorial dispute between Japan and Russia misidentified the affiliation of a group of protesters who held up a large banner at a demonstration. They were members of The Other Russia, not the Left Front.
match_headline: Putin Quashes Japanese Hopes of End to Island Dispute

text: An article on Wednesday about the effects of the government shutdown on F.B.I. operations incorrectly described the F.B.I. Agents Association. It is a professional association, not a union.
match_headline: Report Says Shutdown Is Impeding F.B.I.’s Law Enforcement Efforts

text: An article on Wednesday about cryptocurrency mining in Georgia misstated the nation where Bitfury, a blockchain technology company, is based. It is incorporated in Britain, not the United States. The error was repeated in a photo caption. The article also misstated the position that George Kikvadze holds at Bitfury. He is the executive vice chairman, not the vice president.
match_headline: Despite Bitcoin’s Dive, a Former Soviet Republic Is Still Betting Big on It

text: An article on Monday about the Showtime comedy “Black Monday” described incorrectly the car owned by Don Cheadle’s character. It is known as a “Limbo,” not a “Lambo.”
match_headline: ‘Black Monday’ Mines ’80s Excess for Comedy and Commentary

text: A review on Saturday about the Outsider Art show referred incorrectly to the dealer Phyllis Kind. She was an original exhibitor at the Outsider Art Fair. She was not one of the fair’s founders.
match_headline: Outsider Art of the Moment: 66 Exhibitors, 7 Countries, 1 Fair

text: An editorial on Wednesday about the murder of Pawel Adamowicz, the mayor of Gdansk, Poland, incorrectly stated that Jaroslaw Kaczynski, leader of the conservative Law and Justice Party, had attended Mr. Adamowicz’s funeral on Saturday.
match_headline: In Poland, the Limits of Solidarity

text: An obituary on Monday about the singer, guitarist, record producer and label executive Bonnie Guitar misstated the location of Auburn, Wash., which is near the farm where she and her siblings were raised. It is about 10 miles east of the Puget Sound, not 70 miles south.
match_headline: Bonnie Guitar, Music Industry Trailblazer, Is Dead at 95

text: An article on Tuesday about the Supreme Court’s decision to hear a case related to vulgar trademarks referred incorrectly to the etymology of the “most versatile” curse word. It is of Middle English origin, not Anglo-Saxon.
match_headline: Trademark Fight Over Vulgar Term’s ‘Phonetic Twin’ Heads to Supreme Court

text: An article on Wednesday about the 91st Academy Awards referred imprecisely to the filming of “The Artist.” Although it was a French film, and production took place in France, it was filmed in the United States.
match_headline: Oscar Nominations 2019: ‘Roma,’ ‘The Favourite’ and ‘Black Panther’ Break Ground

text: An article on the cover on Tuesday about increasing noise levels in the oceans from shipping and oil exploration misstated the decibel levels of underwater seismic blasts, and miscalculated the comparison to sounds in the atmosphere made by container ships. Underwater, the seismic blast would register at about 200 decibels, not 260 decibels. By comparison, that seismic blast would then be 10 times more intense than the sound of a container ship, not 10 million times more intense.
match_headline: Oceans Are Getting Louder, Posing Potential Threats to Marine Life

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the filmmaker, curator, archivist and critic Jonas Mekas misstated the original location of Anthology Film Archives, which Mr. Mekas and several others founded. Although it has been on Second Avenue in Lower Manhattan for many years, it opened in 1970 at the Public Theater in the East Village; it did not open on Second Avenue.
match_headline: Jonas Mekas, ‘Godfather’ of American Avant-Garde Film, Is Dead at 96

text: An article on Friday about the most expensive residential sale in United States history described incorrectly the gift Kenneth Griffin gave to Harvard. Mr. Griffin’s $150 million gift to Harvard University in 2014 was, at the time, the largest gift in the school’s history; the university has since received larger donations.
match_headline: The $238 Million Penthouse, and the Hedge Fund Billionaire Who May Rarely Live There

text: Because of an editing error, an article about layoffs at BuzzFeed and other media companies misstated Gannett’s reason for reducing the size of its work force. It is to shore up its shrinking profits, not to attract a buyer.
match_headline: BuzzFeed Plans Layoffs as It Aims to Turn Profit

text: An article this weekend about Mitch McConnell misstated the number of American troops in Afghanistan and the number of troops that President Trump said he would withdraw from the country. Seven thousand of 14,000 American troops in Afghanistan were going to be pulled out. It is not the case that only 7,000 troops were still deployed to Afghanistan.
match_headline: Mitch McConnell Got Everything He Wanted. But at What Cost?

text: An obituary on Thursday about Mary Boyd Higgins, the psychoanalyst Wilhelm Reich’s trustee, using information from a family member, misstated the year she moved to Lexington, Ky., where she died. It was 2018, not 2001.
match_headline: Mary Boyd Higgins, Wilhelm Reich’s Devoted Trustee, Is Dead at 93

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Roger Stone’s career misidentified the organization that disputed characterizations of Mr. Stone as a Nixon campaign aide or adviser. It was the Nixon Foundation, not the Nixon Library.
match_headline: Roger Stone’s Dirty Tricks Put Him Where He’s Always Wanted to Be: Center Stage

text: An article on Saturday about layoffs at BuzzFeed misspelled the surname of the national editor of BuzzFeed News. She is Tina Susman, not Sussman.
match_headline: BuzzFeed’s First Round of Layoffs Puts an End to Its National News Desk

text: An article on Monday about the Juilliard School’s Focus Festival misidentified the public radio broadcaster for which Harry Vogt runs the new music program. It is the WDR (Westdeutscher Rundfunk), not the NDR (Norddeutscher Rundfunk).
match_headline: In Focus Festival, Juilliard Salutes Public Broadcasters

text: A review on Monday about the mini-series “I Am the Night” misstated the year of the Black Dahlia killing in Los Angeles. It was 1947, not 1945.
match_headline: Review: ‘I Am the Night’ Stitches Together Los Angeles Neo-Noir Clichés

text: An entry on Saturday in the “What’s on TV” highlights reversed the parenthetical descriptions about Amanda Seales’s HBO special. It should be “differentiates a ‘Hannah’ (a person who happens to be white) from a ‘Becky’ (a white person),” not the reverse.
match_headline: What’s on TV Saturday: Amanda Seales and ‘Austin City Limits’

text: An article on Saturday about a unionization effort by workers at the New Museum overstated what is known about which groups a future union might represent. The final terms are still being negotiated; it is not the case that associated curators will definitely be represented.
match_headline: Workers at New Museum in Manhattan Vote to Unionize

text: An article on Sunday about the Trump administration’s efforts to block an expansion by the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei described incorrectly the official status of two Canadian citizens detained by the Chinese government since a Huawei executive was arrested in Canada in December. Only one of the two was a diplomat. They were not both diplomats.
match_headline: In 5G Race With China, U.S. Pushes Allies to Fight Huawei

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the reaction to a lack of diversity among the 2019 class of partners with the law firm Paul, Weiss misidentified the previous position of one of the firm’s partners. Jeh Johnson is a former Homeland Security secretary, not a former defense secretary.
match_headline: Elite Law Firm’s All-White Partner Class Stirs Debate on Diversity

text: An article on Saturday about a Chicago prosecutor who encouraged people with allegations of sexual assault against R. Kelly to come forward misstated Mr. Kelly’s academic history at Kenwood Academy. Mr. Kelly attended the high school, but did not graduate.
match_headline: Meet the Woman Asking R. Kelly’s Accusers to Come Forward

text: Because of an editing error, a brief report in the Front Burner column last Wednesday about brisket cooked by Truth BBQ in Brenham, Tex., ran with a picture of meat that was not from the company.
match_headline: Texas Barbecue for Your Super Bowl Party

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the dancer Patricia McBride Lousada misidentified the company with which she performed in George Balanchine’s “The Four Temperaments” in 1946. It was Ballet Society — not New York City Ballet, the name by which the company became known in 1948.
match_headline: Patricia McBride Lousada, One of Balanchine’s Originals, Dies at 89

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Wednesday about the former United States senator Harris Wofford misstated his place in the photograph taken at a White House meeting in 1961. He is to the left of President John F. Kennedy, not the right.
match_headline: Book by Former Staff Member Describes a White House ‘Out of Control’

text: An article on Sunday about experimental therapies for sickle-cell disease misidentified a patient who received treatment. He is Manny Johnson, not Manny Hernandez. The article also misstated his age. He is 21, not 20. Because of an editing error, the article also described incorrectly the trial conducted by Bluebird Bio. The researchers are attempting to restore a functional adult hemoglobin gene, not to restart a fetal hemoglobin gene.
match_headline: These Patients Had Sickle-Cell Disease. Experimental Therapies Might Have Cured Them.

text: A picture with The White House Memo article on Wednesday was published in error. The photograph, supplied by The Associated Press, showed a man The A.P. was unable to identify; it did not show Archer Blood.
match_headline: Why Did Soviets Invade Afghanistan? Documents Offer History Lesson for Trump

text: An article on Tuesday about the police reaction to “Yellow Vest” protesters in France referred incorrectly to police use of rubber balls against demonstrators in Western Europe. It is authorized in France, Northern Ireland and Spain. It is not the case that only France and Northern Ireland use such tools.
match_headline: Use of Force in France’s ‘Yellow Vest’ Protests Fuels Anger

text: An article on Wednesday about ways that Bitcoin could help Iran undermine sanctions misstated the name of the Chinese computers used to mine Bitcoin at the site visited in the Iranian desert. They are Antminer V9s, not A9Antminers.
match_headline: How Bitcoin Could Help Iran Undermine U.S. Sanctions

text: An article on the cover about the history of fur misstates the price of fur storage at Saks Fifth Avenue in Chicago. It is $175 per year, not $70. The article also misstates the temperature of the storage unit. It is 55 degrees Fahrenheit, with 50 percent humidity, not between 48 and 52 degrees Fahrenheit, with 30 percent humidity.
match_headline: A Year Into the Overlooked Project, Widening the Lens

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the New York City labor leader Stanley Hill misidentified the high school where he played basketball. It was the High School of Commerce, not Central Commercial High School.
match_headline: Stanley Hill, 82, Dies; Led New York City’s Biggest Public Union

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about Charles Kettles, who as an Army helicopter commander in the Vietnam War led a rescue operation that saved the lives of dozens of troops, misidentified the craft in which he was shown. It is an Army L-19 aircraft, not a helicopter.
match_headline: Charles Kettles, Who Rescued Dozens of Troops in Vietnam, Dies at 89

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Peter Magowan, the longtime owner of the San Francisco Giants, using information from his wife, misstated the surnames of his daughters Kimberley, Margot and Hilary. They all use the surname Magowan.
match_headline: Peter Magowan, Giants Fan Turned Giants’ Owner, Is Dead at 76

text: An article on Thursday about the Canadian government’s decision to withdraw some of its diplomatic staff from its embassy in Cuba misstated when the Trump administration expelled Cuban diplomats from the United States. It was in October 2017, not October 2018.
match_headline: Canada Slashes Diplomatic Staff in Cuba After Another Mystery Illness

text: A review on Thursday about the play “God Said This” misstated Leah Nanako Winkler’s age. She is 33, not 34.
match_headline: Review: In ‘God Said This,’ a Hot Mess of a Daughter Heads Home

text: A review last Friday about a survey at the American Folk Art Museum of the artist John Dunkley misstated the closing date of the exhibition. The show closes on Feb. 24, not Feb. 20.
match_headline: John Dunkley, an Outsider Artist Deep in the Heart of Jamaica

text: An article on Friday about a campaign by anti-abortion advocates in New York misstated Gov. Ralph Northam’s medical specialty. He is a pediatric neurologist, not a pediatric surgeon.
match_headline: Trump, Pence Lead G.O.P. Seizure of Late-Term Abortion as a Potent 2020 Issue

text: An article on Friday about an internet outage in Tonga referred incorrectly to internet speeds there. When a fiber-optic cable was installed in 2013, they rose to 10 gigabits from 20 to 30 megabits per second, not to 10 gigabytes from 20 to 30 megabytes.
match_headline: Could You Last 11 Days Without the Internet? Tonga Finds Out the Hard Way

text: An article on Friday about the agreement to appoint a federal monitor to oversee the New York City Housing Authority referred imprecisely to Donald Nesbit’s role in District Council 37. He is a vice president and a member of its executive board; he is not its executive director.
match_headline: De Blasio Cedes Further Control of Nycha but Avoids Federal Takeover

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts in Taiwan misstated the center’s size in comparison to New York’s Central Park. As the article correctly states, the municipal park adjoining the center is roughly one-seventh the size of Central Park, not the arts center itself.
match_headline: Trump National Golf Club in N.Y. Fires Undocumented Workers, Lawyer Says

text: An article on Page 10 about the challenges of contemporary opera performance misstates the subtitle of a Robert Ashley opera being revived in New York. The full title is “Improvement (Don Leaves Linda),” not “Improvement (Don Meets Linda).”
An article last Sunday about changes at the Alta ski resort in Utah referred incorrectly to the Snowpine Lodge. It is the first luxury hotel at Alta, not the first in Little Cottonwood Canyon.
match_headline: Big Change in Little Cottonwood Canyon

text: An article on Page 10 about the challenges of contemporary opera performance misstates the subtitle of a Robert Ashley opera being revived in New York. The full title is “Improvement (Don Leaves Linda),” not “Improvement (Don Meets Linda).”

An article on Sunday about the impact of child care on Japanese women’s careers described incorrectly employment statistics for women in Japan. The proportion of working women employed part time is close to half, not more than half, and the proportion on temporary contracts is more than half, not about a third.
match_headline: Japan’s Working Mothers: Record Responsibilities, Little Help From Dads

text: A headline with an article on Monday about the discovery of the wreckage of the aircraft that crashed carrying the Argentine soccer striker Emiliano Sala referred incorrectly to the plane. As the article correctly stated, it was a single-engine, propeller-driven airplane, not a jet.
match_headline: Video Shows Undersea Wreck of Plane that Carried Soccer Star Emiliano Sala

text: An entry on Monday in the “What’s on TV” highlights described incorrectly the debut episode of “Elvis Goes There.” It opens with a visit to London with the actor and director Paul Feig, not a visit to Oakland, Calif., with the director Ryan Coogler.
match_headline: What’s on TV Monday: ‘Black Memorabilia’ and ‘Experimenter’

text: An article on Sept. 21 about Maroon 5’s scheduled appearance in Sunday’s Super Bowl halftime show misstated the name of the band’s song with Cardi B. It is “Girls Like You,” not “Girls Like Us.” (The correction was delayed, because it was only recently brought to the attention of the editor.)
match_headline: Maroon 5 to Headline Super Bowl Halftime Show

text: An article on Monday about calls for the resignation of Gov. Ralph Northam of Virginia referred incorrectly to the state’s response to the Supreme Court order to send white and black children to the same schools in the 1950s. Some counties closed their schools, rather than follow the order; the state did not close its schools.
match_headline: As Calls Mount for Ralph Northam to Resign, Some Virginians Mull a Second Chance

text: An article on Thursday about shifting plans for a proposed Foxconn factory in Wisconsin misstated how land designated for the site was acquired. It was through voluntary agreements, not eminent domain. The article also misstated what portion of the initial 1,200 acres meant for the project had been acquired by December. It was 99 percent, not 85 percent.
match_headline: Foxconn Reconsidering Plans for a Wisconsin Factory Heralded by Trump

text: An article on Monday and two others on Tuesday about a fatal shooting at the 90th Street-Elmhurst Avenue subway station in Queens, using information from the New York Police Department, referred incorrectly to the murder and to the one recorded murder that took place on the subway in 2018. The killing in Queens was the first recorded murder in just over six months, not a year. The 2018 incident was a murder-suicide that occurred in July at the Broadway Junction station in Brooklyn, not in January at the Jay Street station.
match_headline: A Man Was Shot at a Queens Subway Station. He Died on the Platform.

text: An article on Tuesday about the increasing use of machine-generated journalism misstated the name of a tool that Forbes is testing for reporters. It is Bertie, not Birdie.
match_headline: The Rise of the Robot Reporter

text: An article on Monday about the recurring song on the new Netflix series “Russian Doll” referred incorrectly to the finances of the singer and composer Harry Nilsson. Nilsson had a lucrative recording career in the late 1960s and early 1970s before facing financial troubles toward the end of his life. It is not the case that he struggled financially throughout his career.
match_headline: This Is That Song From ‘Russian Doll’

text: An article last Wednesday about Atlanta dining misstated some ingredients in the fried chicken at the original Watershed restaurant. The chicken was fried in lard and sweet butter, not peanut oil.
match_headline: A Game Plan for Eating Well in Atlanta

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the Navy pilot and commander Rosemary Mariner misstated the surname of her former husband. He is Douglas Hugh Conatser, not Conaster.
match_headline: U.S. Navy Performs Its First All-Female Flyover to Honor Rosemary Mariner

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s message at the State of the Union speech misstated the year in which President George Bush delivered a State of the Union address following devastating midterm losses for the Republicans. It was in 2007, not 2011, when he was no longer in office.
match_headline: A Call for Bipartisanship With a Familiar Partisan Sting

text: An article on Tuesday about events celebrating the Lunar New Year misidentified the host of a discussion on the lion dance. Stephen Gong, the co-founder of Luen Hing Lion Dance, hosted the event, not Stephen Gong, the executive director of the Center for Asian American Media.
match_headline: 7 Cultural Events Celebrating the Lunar New Year

text: A map with an article on Tuesday about fluctuations in the location of Earth’s north magnetic pole misspelled the name of an island. It is Ellesmere Island, not Ellsmere.
match_headline: The North Magnetic Pole’s Mysterious Journey Across the Arctic

text: A picture caption with the No Regrets column last Thursday, about a Sotheby’s auction of old masters by female artists, misidentified a woman shown at the event. She is Lilah Ramzi, not Lauren McCarthy.
match_headline: Partying During the Polar Vortex

text: An editorial on Monday calling for American forces to withdraw from Afghanistan misstated the number of foreign troops serving there. There are about 16,000 troops from 39 nations in NATO’s Afghanistan force; about 8,000 are from nations other than the United States, not 2,000. While there are about 14,000 American troops in Afghanistan, only about 8,500 are under NATO command, not all of them.
match_headline: Before Trump’s State of the Union, a Look at How Last Year’s Promises Fared

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the longtime Manhattan Democratic leader James R. McManus misstated the middle initial of his great-uncle Thomas McManus. It was J, not R. It also misspelled the maiden name of Mr. McManus’s mother, Helen. It was Kearney, not Kerney.
match_headline: James R. McManus, 84, Last of the Hell’s Kitchen Bosses, Dies

text: An article on Page 8 about the costume designer Montana Levi Blanco misidentifies the theater where “‘Daddy’” is being staged. The show, a coproduction from the New Group and the Vineyard Theater, will be staged at the Pershing Square Signature Center, not at the Vineyard.
match_headline: A Costume Designer With Low Budgets and High Style

text: An obituary on Friday about Frank Robinson, the slugging outfielder who became the first black manager in the major leagues, misstated when he was traded by the Baltimore Orioles to the Los Angeles Dodgers. It was after the 1971 season, not before. The obituary also misstated when Larry Doby, who like Robinson went on to be a manager, became the first black player in the American League. It was 1947, not 1948.
match_headline: Frank Robinson, Hall of Fame Slugger and First Black Manager, Dies at 83

text: An article last Sunday about Graydon Carter’s new weekly digital newsletter, Air Mail, misstated a source of funding for the endeavor. It is TPG Growth, a private equity firm where James Coulter is one of the chief executives — not Mr. Coulter himself.
match_headline: Firm That Sold Social Media Bots Settles With New York Attorney General

text: An article last Sunday about a surfing resort in Costa Rica misspelled the given name of a New Hampshire resident who was visiting the resort. She is Abby Hutchinson, not Abbie.
match_headline: At Surf Camp 2.0, Data Rules

text: An article on Jan. 20 about ancient-DNA research misstated the number of peer reviewers who evaluated the 2016 Nature paper “Genomic Insights Into the Peopling of the Southwest Pacific” before publication. It was four, not three; a fourth reviewer was added to evaluate the paper after the original submission was revised. The article also misstated the geographic area where migrants from the steppes of eastern Ukraine and southern Russia signifi cantly replaced existing communities of huntergatherers and early farmers, as reported in an academic paper on the migration. It was Central and Northern Europe, not the entire continent.
ref_headline: Genomic Insights Into the Peopling of the Southwest Pacific
match_headline: Is Ancient DNA Research Revealing New Truths — or Falling Into Old Traps?

text: An article on Feb. 3 about sports gambling misidentifi ed the source for the estimate that a fully developed sports-gambling industry would take in close to $400 billion in bets. It was the congressional National Gambling Impact Study Commission, not the American Gaming Association.
match_headline: No Kneeling During Super Bowl LIII National Anthem, but Still Plenty of Talk

text: Because of an editing error, a review last Sunday about the thriller “As Long as We Both Shall Live” misspelled the author’s name. She is JoAnn Chaney, not Joann Cheney.
ref_headline: As Long as We Both Shall Live
match_headline: Murderous Husbands, Flapper-Era Gun Molls and Korean Assassins: The Best Winter Thrillers

text: An article on Sunday about a protest at the Guggenheim Museum over donations made to the museum by the Sackler family misstated the name of a museum in London. It is the Victoria and Albert Museum, not the Albert and Victoria Museum.
match_headline: Guggenheim Targeted by Protesters for Accepting Money From Family With OxyContin Ties

text: An article on Monday about so-called rental goalies serving the needs of amateur hockey teams in Toronto misspelled the surname of a commercial airline pilot who is also a rental goalie. He is Dan Medeiros, not Madeiros.
match_headline: The Goalie Is a Hired Gun, and He’s Yours for $50 a Game

text: An article on Saturday about a $3.5 million gift to the Baltimore Museum of Art misstated the position held by Asma Naeem at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery. She was the curator of prints, drawings and media arts, not the associate curator.
match_headline: Baltimore Museum of Art Gets $3.5 Million to Endow Chief Curator

text: An obituary on Monday about the children’s author Jan Wahl misstated the surname of the Chilean cartoonist who illustrated Mr. Wahl’s book “Lorenzo Bear & Company.” He was Fernando Krahn, not Krahl.
match_headline: Jan Wahl, Children’s Writer Who Attracted Top Artists, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Saturday about the radical black nationalist Nehanda Abiodun misstated the source of a quotation from her. Her statement that she had little sympathy for the police officers killed after the botched robbery of a Brink’s armored truck in 1981 came from an interview with The Miami New Times in 2000 — not with the website The Talking Drum, which later reprinted the interview. The earlier version also misstated the location of the prison from which Assata Shakur, who had been convicted in the killing of a state trooper, escaped. It was in New Jersey, not upstate New York.
match_headline: Nehanda Abiodun, 68, Black Revolutionary Who Fled to Cuba, Dies

text: An article on Friday about Britain’s chief medical officers calling for restrictions on children’s use of screens and social media misidentified the organization that set guidelines for children’s use of media in the United States. It is the American Academy of Pediatrics, not the American Association of Pediatrics.
match_headline: U.K. Doctors Call for Caution in Children’s Use of Screens and Social Media

text: An article on Jan. 31 about Russian influence in Venezuela referred incompletely to the countries in Latin America that support President Nicolás Maduro. In addition to Nicaragua and Cuba, Bolivia and Suriname also support him.
match_headline: For the Kremlin, Venezuela Is Not the Next Syria

text: An article on Monday about a prosecutor’s decision to drop an abortion charge in a Queens murder case misspelled the surname of Anthony Hobson’s defense lawyer. He is Steven Questore, not Questlore.
match_headline: Prosecutor Drops Abortion Charge in Queens Murder Case, Stirring Debate

text: An article on Saturday about a new business venture by Les Moonves, the former chief executive of CBS, referred imprecisely to the payment of legal fees incurred by Mr. Moonves. Although CBS paid some of Mr. Moonves’s legal fees, it is not paying them amid an arbitration fight over his severance.
match_headline: Les Moonves, Fired by CBS, Sets Up Shop in Hollywood

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about federal prosecutors’ investigation of Jeff Bezos’ extortion claims against American Media Inc. misspelled the name of the crown prince of Saudi Arabia. He is Mohammed bin Salman, not Salmans.
match_headline: Jeff Bezos’ Extortion Claim Said to Be Under Review by Prosecutors

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the illustrator and author Tomi Ungerer misstated when Maurice Sendak began working with the book editor Ursula Nordstrom. She had already published work by Mr. Sendak before she published Mr. Ungerer’s first children’s book, “The Mellops Go Flying”; she did not work with Mr. Ungerer first.
match_headline: Tomi Ungerer, Brash Illustrator for Young and Older, Dies at 87

text: An article on Wednesday about a plan among BuzzFeed News employees to unionize misstated the size of the BuzzFeed News national security team before BuzzFeed made layoffs last month, and also misstated how many members of the team lost jobs in the layoffs. The team had nine members, not seven; six were laid off, not seven.
match_headline: ‘Not All Fun and Memes’: BuzzFeed News Employees Plan to Form a Union

text: An article on Wednesday about new rules enforced by the United States Golf Association misstated the number of strokes Rickie Fowler was penalized for hitting a ball into the water during the Phoenix Open. It was one stroke, not two.
match_headline: Golf’s New Rules: Few Players Know Them, Fewer Understand Them

text: An article on Jan. 31 about employer insurance covering in vitro fertilization misstated the interval one must work at Starbucks before receiving I.V.F. benefits. It is three months, not one month.
match_headline: I.V.F. Coverage Is the Benefit Everyone Wants

text: An article on Sunday about the collapse of a mining dam in Brumadinho, Brazil, misstated the number of mining dams in the country built like the structure that collapsed. There are 87 — not 88 — mining dams in the country that are similar to the Brumadinho dam, and 27 — not 28 — are estimated to sit above cities or towns.
match_headline: Brumadinho Dam Collapse: A Tidal Wave of Mud

text: An article on Thursday about the reach of Mexican drug cartels into the United States misstated the global production of cocaine in 2016. It was 1,410 tons, not 1,140. The error was repeated in the “Of Interest” section on Page A3.
match_headline: El Chapo Is Behind Bars, but Drugs Still Flow From Mexico

text: An obituary on Thursday about the dancer Mel A. Tomlinson misstated the surname of one of his fellow dancers. She is Karen Brown, not Karen Black.
match_headline: Mel A. Tomlinson, 65, Ballet Star and ‘Agon’ Interpreter, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a photojournalist’s concern over President Trump’s use of her photo without permission misstated Yalda Moayeri’s recollection of the scene when she shot the photograph. Police officers, not students, blasted the fire extinguishers that had filled the air with white fumes, she said.
match_headline: Trump Tweeted a Photo of Iranian Protest. He Didn’t Ask the Journalist Who Took It.

text: An article on Thursday about Burke Mountain Academy misstated the year Diann Roffe won a gold medal at the world championships while still enrolled at the academy. It was 1985, not 1987.
match_headline: At Shiffrin’s Alma Mater, Future Ski Champions for $58,000 a Year

text: Because of an editing error, a summary on Page 1 misspells the surname of the writer and actress whose one-woman play “Fleabag” is headed to Off Broadway. As the article correctly notes, she is Phoebe Waller-Bridge, not Waller-Bridges.
match_headline: Phoebe Waller-Bridge Will Make You Laugh So Hard It Hurts

text: An article on Page 48 about Climeworks, a company that has developed technology to remove carbon dioxide from the air, misstates the abbreviation of the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology. It is E.T.H. Zurich not E.C.H.
match_headline: The Tiny Swiss Company That Thinks It Can Help Stop Climate Change

text: An article on Page 38 about women coders misidentifies the institution Ellen Spertus was affiliated with when she published a 1991 report on women’s experiences in programming classes. Spertus was at M.I.T. when she published the report, not Mills College, where she is currently a professor. The article also misstates Akshaya Dinesh’s current age. She is 18, not 19.
match_headline: The Secret History of Women in Coding

text: An article on Page 189 about British interior designers referred imprecisely to Martin Brudnizki’s work on two projects. He designed all the interiors of the Beekman hotel in Manhattan, not just its reception area, and he designed the Coral Room at the Bloomsbury hotel in London, not the entire hotel.
match_headline: Long Live Eccentric English Design

text: An article on Page 214 about the Hermès ateliers misstates how long Véronique Nichanian has designed the Hermès men’s wear collection. She has designed it for more than 30 years, not more than 10. A picture caption with the article misstates the year Nichanian began designing the collection; it was 1988, not 2009.
match_headline: Hermès’s Refusal to Change Is Its Most Radical Gesture Yet

text: A picture caption on Page 13 with a review of “Walk This Way,” by Geoff Edgers, misidentifies a member of Run-DMC. He is Run, not Jam Master Jay.
match_headline: Run-DMC, Aerosmith and the Song That Changed Everything

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Feb. 5 about the former secretary of the Army John O. Marsh Jr., using information from Getty Images, misstated his location in a photograph of President Gerald R. Ford and his senior advisers. Mr. Marsh was second from the left, not second from the right.
match_headline: John O. Marsh Jr., Ex-Army Chief and Presidents’ Adviser, Dies at 92

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Erykah Badu misstated the release date for her new movie, “What Men Want.” It was Feb. 8, not Feb. 15.
match_headline: Erykah Badu Helped Define ‘Wokeness.’ Now She’s a Target.

text: An article last Sunday on the problems tourism is bringing to the Galápagos Islands misstated the cost of a suite at the Finch Bay Galápagos hotel. It is $800 a night, not $950.
match_headline: Going to the Galápagos Is Easier and Cheaper Than Ever. That Might Not Be a Good Thing.

text: Because of an editing error, The Fix column last Sunday about finding decorative accessories for a living room was published with the wrong byline. The column was written by Tim McKeough, not Michelle Higgins.
match_headline: Bringing the Living Room to Life

text: A picture caption on Page 13 with a review of “Walk This Way,” by Geoff Edgers, misidentifies a member of Run-DMC. He is Run, not Jam Master Jay.

An article on Friday about a fire in 2017 at a government-run group home in Guatemala that killed 41 girls rendered the name of the home incorrectly. It is Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción, not Virgin de Asuncion Hogar Seguro.
match_headline: A Locked Door, a Fire and 41 Girls Killed as Police Stood By

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about an Afghan cafe owner and activist misspelled the activist’s surname. It is Laila Haidari, not Hairdari.
match_headline: She’s a Force of Nature, and She Just Declared War on Peace With the Taliban

text: An article on Sunday about the changing character of tourism in the Indian state of Goa misstated the title of Stafford Braganza. He is the head of makeup and technique for L’Oreal in India, not the head of education.
match_headline: ‘The Pirate Days Are Over’: Goa’s Nude Hippies Give Way to India’s Yuppies

text: An article on Saturday about the ways in which President Trump’s national emergency on the border could be undone in the courts misstated the name of a group that is joining El Paso County in a lawsuit over the emergency declaration. The group is Protect Democracy, not Project Democracy.
match_headline: Trump Declared a Border Emergency. Here’s How It Could Be Undone in Court.

text: An article on Monday about controversies surrounding the growing field of “embryo adoption” misspelled in some editions the given name, in one instance, of a woman who gave birth after receiving a donated embryo. She is Monika Broecker, not Monica. It also misstated the location of the clinic that provided the embryo. It is in Sacramento, not Palo Alto, Calif.
match_headline: Embryo ‘Adoption’ Is Growing, but It’s Getting Tangled in the Abortion Debate

text: An article on Monday about Anthony D. Weiner’s release from prison misstated where the former congressman is living since his release. Federal records show he is assigned to the Brooklyn re-entry field office, which oversees sites throughout New York City, and records do not specify where he is housed. It is not known that he is living in a re-entry center in Brooklyn.
match_headline: Anthony Weiner Is Out of Prison and in a Halfway House in New York

text: An article on Monday about Wall Street banks’ plans to move to other parts of Europe from London ahead of the anticipated British withdrawal from the European Union misstated the given name of a lawyer specializing in corporate lending. She is Susan Whitehead, not Susanne.
match_headline: For Wall Street Banks in London, It’s Moving Time

text: An article on Friday about an audit that found slipshod oversight of federal student loan servicers misstated how much in student loans the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency handles. It is more than $340 billion, not more than $340 million.
match_headline: Student Loan Servicers’ Frequent Mistakes Went Unpunished, Audit Finds

text: An article on Friday about the American Kennel Club’s Museum of the Dog misidentified the word on the cup of a beggar’s terrier in the painting “Pug and Terrier” (1875) by John Sargent Noble. It is “charity,” not “pity.”
match_headline: A Museum of Man’s Best Friend, From Fossils to Virtual Reality

text: An article on Monday about the York Theater Company’s “Lolita, My Love,” based on information from the publicist, mischaracterized the role of the therapist in the musical. The character, Dr. Ray, will appear onstage; she will not be unseen.
match_headline: An Infamous ‘Lolita’ Musical Gets a Belated New York Debut

text: An article on Tuesday about House scrutiny of the Education Department misstated the name of a piece of legislation. It is the Individuals With Disabilities Education Act, not the Individuals With Disabilities Act.
match_headline: House Democrats Prepare to Scrutinize DeVos’s Education Department

text: An article on Feb. 1 about the art of Pierre Puvis de Chavannes misspelled the given name of another artist. He is Auguste Rodin, not August.
match_headline: A French Painter, Fallen From Fame, Gains Historical Weight

text: A picture caption accompanying the Out There column on Tuesday misspelled the surname of a scientist. He is David Reitze, not Reitzein.
match_headline: In Science, as in Sports, the Sidelines Matter

text: An article last Thursday about Frieze Los Angeles misstated how art, memorabilia and other objects from regulars at the nightclub Max’s Kansas City would be distributed at the fair. They were sold, not auctioned. The article also misidentified, using information from the sale’s organizer, a musician who played the French horn. It was David Amram, not Bob Dylan.
match_headline: Max’s Kansas City Reborn for Los Angeles Art Fair

text: An article on Thursday about the Jussie Smollett case misstated who approved the charges against the actor. He was charged with staging his own assault by prosecutors; he was not indicted by a grand jury.
match_headline: Accused of Faking Own Assault, Jussie Smollett Arrested on Felony Charge

text: An article on Feb. 14 on the sighting of a rare black panther in Africa referred incorrectly to the animals. They are not a distinct species, but a melanistic color variant of the African leopard subspecies.
match_headline: Africa’s Black Panthers Emerge From the Shadows

text: An article on Thursday on concerns about a top Veterans Affairs official’s travel expenses misstated the circumstances in which the official, Darin Mr. Selnick, left the department. He had clashed with the former secretary of Veterans Affairs, Dr. David Shulkin; he was not fired by Dr. Shulkin or forced out at his request. It also referred incorrectly to the timing of his return to the department; it occurred just before President Trump replaced Dr. Shulkin, not afterward.
match_headline: Critic of Waste at Veterans Affairs Now Faces Questions About His Travel Costs

text: An article on Thursday about the latest smartphone technology misstated the circumstances of the release of a new Samsung foldable phone. The phone is expected to be available in the United States on April 26 and in Europe on May 3; the release dates are not unknown.
match_headline: What’s Next for Smartphones? Samsung’s New Galaxy Line Offers a Few Answers

text: An article on Thursday about the Time’s Up initiative misstated the connection between Time’s Up and a commission headed by Anita Hill. The commission was formed by Time’s Up, but the two are no longer affiliated. The article also mischaracterized Time’s Up’s initial staffing. There were a few paid employees; it was not all-volunteer.
match_headline: Time’s Up a Year Later: Hollywood Women Test Their Clout

text: An obituary on Sunday about the actor Bruno Ganz misstated the occupation of his partner, Ruth Walz, who survives him. She is a theatrical photographer, not a film-industry photographer. It also misstated the nationality of the protagonist of “Radegund,” one of Mr. Ganz’s last films. He is Austrian, not German.
match_headline: Bruno Ganz, Who Played an Angel and Hitler, Is Dead at 77

text: An obituary on Thursday about the psychoanalyst and author Theodore Isaac Rubin misstated part of the name of an organization with which he had a long association. It is the Institute for Psychoanalysis, not the Institute of Psychoanalysis. The obituary also omitted a survivor. In addition to those named, Dr. Rubin is survived by a great-grandson.
match_headline: Theodore Isaac Rubin Is Dead at 95; Popularized Psychotherapy

text: An obituary on Feb. 14 about the wrestler Pedro Morales misstated the year he won the World Wide Wrestling Federation championship. It was 1971, not 1970.
match_headline: Pedro Morales, 76, First to Win Three Major Wrestling Titles, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a fire in Bangladesh misstated the number of people killed. According to officials’ accounts at the time, the toll was at least 70, not 110.
match_headline: Scores Dead in Bangladesh Fire: ‘This Isn’t About Poverty, It’s About Greed’

text: An article on Friday about divisions in the British Labour Party over accusations of anti-Semitism misidentified the organization with which Jonathan Goldstein is affiliated, and his role in it. He is the chairman of the Jewish Leadership Council, not the editor of The Jewish Chronicle.
match_headline: For U.K.’s Labour, Anti-Semitism and Corbyn Are as Divisive as Brexit

text: An article on Wednesday about the young climate activist Greta Thunberg misstated the day of her first protest at the Swedish Parliament. While the protest was on Aug. 20, it was a Monday, not a Friday.
match_headline: Becoming Greta: ‘Invisible Girl’ to Global Climate Activist, With Bumps Along the Way

text: An item on Page 6 misstates the length of time that HB Studio will be celebrating the Broadway star Uta Hagen. It will be a monthslong celebration, not monthlong.
match_headline: The Week in Arts: A Renaissance Gem, Isabelle Huppert, Uta Hagen

text: An article on Feb. 14 about Annie Leibovitz’s early years referred incorrectly to the book “Photographs Annie Leibovitz 1970-1990.” It was not Ms. Leibovitz’s first book.
match_headline: Annie Leibovitz Revisits Her Early Years

text: An article on Page 28 about the National Domestic Workers Alliance misstates the relationship between Care in Action and the National Domestic Workers Alliance. They are allied, but separate organizations. Care in Action is not a group within N.D.W.A. And a picture caption with the article misstates aspects of Edith Mendoza’s work history and relationship to N.D.W.A. She cleaned offices for the past two and a half years, not four. And she joined an N.D.W.A. affiliate in 2016, not last year.
match_headline: The New Labor Movement Fighting for Domestic Workers’ Rights

text: An article last Sunday about the annual Jane Austen Evening misstated the subject of the celebrations in 2017. It was the 200th anniversary of Austen’s death, not of her birth. A caption with the article misstated the occupation of one of the people participating in the evening. Sydney Stechmann is a commodities clerk at a cemetery and mortuary, not a tutor.
match_headline: Dancing to Jane Austen’s Beat

text: An article last Sunday about wealthy Americans unhappy about tax cuts misstated an aspect of Senator Elizabeth Warren’s tax proposal. Ms. Warren has called for a 2 percent annual tax on assets above $50 million in a household, not on all assets owned by a household with a net worth of $50 million or more. The same error appeared in a Jan. 24 article about Ms. Warren’s tax proposal.
match_headline: They’re Rich and They’re Mad About Taxes (Too Low!)

text: An essay last Sunday about feminism and a Catholic education misidentified the process by which women become nuns. They take vows; they are not ordained.
match_headline: Everything I Know About Feminism I Learned From Nuns

text: A news analysis last Sunday about the Equal Rights Amendment misstated the proportion of states needed to ratify a constitutional amendment. It is three-fourths of the states, not two-thirds.
match_headline: What Is the Equal Rights Amendment, and Why Are We Talking About It Now?

text: An article on Jan. 27 about Manuel Gomez, a private investigator in New York City, referred imprecisely to one way Gomez receives payment from clients. It is not the case that he is paid a fee only if the city settles a lawsuit. Gomez says he is never paid on a contingency basis.
match_headline: A Private Investigator Wanted to Prove His Clients Innocent. Will His Methods Be His Own Undoing?

text: An article on Feb. 3 about a rare cancer of white blood cells called POEMS syndrome misstated the outcome of treatment with stem-cell transplants. While durable remission rates have been shown to reach nearly 100 percent with stem-cell transplants, there is no known permanent cure for POEMS. It is not the case that stem-cell transplants used to treat the disorder result in a nearly 100 percent cure.
match_headline: China Investigates Reports of H.I.V.-Tainted Blood Plasma Treatment

text: An article on Feb. 10 about women and big-wave surfing referred incorrectly to Mira Manickam-Shirley’s role at Brown Girl Surf, a community organization in Oakland, Calif. She is a co-founder, not the founder.
match_headline: The Fight for Gender Equality in One of the Most Dangerous Sports on Earth

text: A review on Feb. 3 about the memoir “I Am Yours,” by Reema Zaman, misstated the nationality of the author’s mother. She is Bangladeshi, not Thai.

A review on Feb. 10 about Siddharth Dube’s “An Indefinite Sentence,” a memoir that centers on the ravages of AIDS in India, misstated the year a group of prostitutes were arrested in Madras and tested for H.I.V. without their knowledge. It was 1986, not 1996.
match_headline: A Personal Fight for the Dignity of L.G.B.T. People in India

text: An article on Monday about a deal between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and the extremist party Otzma Yehudit, or Jewish Power, misstated Moshe Kahlon’s position in Mr. Netanyahu’s government. He is the finance minister, not the foreign minister. The article also misstated the name of a nonprofit organization that criticized the pact. It is Americans for Peace Now, not Americans for Peace.
match_headline: Netanyahu Sparks Outrage Over Pact With Racist Party

text: An article on Thursday about white supremacism in the United States military misstated where Carter F. Smith teaches criminal justice. It is at Middle Tennessee State University, not Austin Peay State University.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the epidemiologist Bill Jenkins, who tried to expose the unethical Tuskegee syphilis study in the 1960s, misspelled the given name of the director of the National Center for Bioethics in Research and Health Care at Tuskegee University. text: An article on Thursday about the Mexican government’s approval of a new 60,000-member National Guard to tackle the nation’s public security crisis misstated the given name of a former Mexican president. He is Felipe Calderón, not Ernesto.

text: An article on Wednesday about black-run numbers businesses omitted a source on the historical fight in the State Legislature over the numbers game and the daily lottery.
