match_headline: Juventus Survives, as the Improbable Becomes Real Again

text: An article on Wednesday about the indictment of the actresses Felicity Huffman and Lori Loughlin in an alleged college admissions scandal misstated the name of a charity cited in the indictment. It is the Key Worldwide Foundation, not the Key World Foundation.
match_headline: Felicity Huffman and Lori Loughlin: How College Admission Scandal Ensnared Stars

text: A picture caption with a film review on Wednesday about “Rezo” misidentified the film shown in the picture. It was a frame from “Tale of Tales,” not “Rezo.”

An obituary on Wednesday about the drummer Hal Blaine, who played on countless hit records, misstated the given name of a guitarist who was one of his fellow studio musicians. He was Tommy Tedesco, not Tony.
match_headline: Hal Blaine, Wrecking Crew Drummer, Is Dead at 90

text: An obituary on Feb. 25 about the opera singer Hilde Zadek referred incorrectly to the production of “Aida” in which she made her debut with the Vienna State Opera in 1947. It was sung in German, not Italian. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Stettin, where Ms. Zadek’s family moved in 1920. It was part of Germany at the time — not the German Empire, which ended when Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated in 1918.
match_headline: Hilde Zadek, Mainstay of the Vienna State Opera, Dies at 101

text: An article on Thursday about five family members who died in the crash of Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 misstated the total number of people who perished in the crash. It was 157, not 159. The article also misstated the location of the island of Bermuda. It is in the Atlantic Ocean, not the Caribbean Sea.
match_headline: ‘My Heart Is on Fire’: Ethiopian Airlines Victims Embodied Kenya’s Ambitions

text: An article on Thursday about China blocking a United Nations Security Council measure misidentified the country that proposed designating Masood Azhar a terrorist. It was the United States, not France.
match_headline: China Blocks U.N. Vote to Blacklist Pakistani Militant Leader

text: An article on Thursday about major figures in finance and law involved in a college admissions scandal misstated the amount of assets that the investment firm TPG has under management. It is $103 billion, not $70 billion.
match_headline: College Admission Scandal’s Other Big Names Are Titans of Finance and Law

text: An article on Wednesday about the New York Giants trade of Odell Beckham Jr. to the Cleveland Browns misstated the terms of Landon Collins’s contract with the Washington Redskins. It is a six-year deal worth $84 million — not three years worth $45 million.
match_headline: Giants Trade Odell Beckham Jr. to the Browns

text: An article on Wednesday about coaches involved in a college admissions scandal misstated William Ferguson’s position at U.S.C. He was the men’s volleyball coach, not the women’s volleyball coach.
match_headline: The Coaches Connected to the College Admissions Fraud Case

text: An article on Wednesday about the soccer player Arjen Robben’s signature move referred incorrectly to Shanti Ganesh. She is a woman.
match_headline: Arjen Robben Has Been Cutting Left His Entire Career. So Why Can’t Anyone Stop Him?

text: An article on Page F16 about the exhibition “Gender Bending Fashion” at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston misstates the city in which the designer Rad Hourani is based. It is Paris, not Los Angeles.
match_headline: Looking Beyond the Fashion Binary

text: An article on Page F34 about the National Churchill Museum at Westminster College in Missouri misquotes Tim Riley, the director and chief curator of America’s National Churchill Museum at Westminster College, when he talked about Winston Churchill’s speech at the college. The speech was 50 minutes, not 15 minutes. It also misstates the century in which the Church of St. Mary the Virgin, Aldemanbury was built. It was the 17th century, not the 16th.
match_headline: The Missouri Museum That Churchill Built

text: An article on Page F36 about museum exhibitions related to climate change misstates the name of a museum in New York City. It is the Climate Museum, not the Climate Change Museum. The article also misstates the name of an exhibition. It is “Nature’s Nation: American Art and Environment,” not “Nature’s Nation: America’s Art and Environment.” The article also misstates the name of a work by Sam Van Aken. It is “Tree of 40 Fruit,” not “The Tree of 40 Fruits.” The article also omits the name of an artist involved with the “smell series” at Cooper Hewitt. She is Christina Agapakis.
ref_headline: Nature’s Nation: American Art and Environment,
match_headline: Can Art Help Save the Planet?

text: An article on Page F38 about new art exhibitions in the United States and Europe misstates the date on which the Norton Museum of Art in West Palm Beach, Fla., reopened after a major expansion. It was Feb. 9, not Feb. 19. The article also misstates the collective name for a commemoration at the New-York Historical Society. It is “Stonewall 50 at New-York Historical Society,” not “Stonewall 50.” A New-York Historical Society exhibition is also misidentified. It is “By the Force of Our Presence: Highlights From the Lesbian Herstory Archives,” not “By the Force of Our Presence: Highlights From the Lesbian Herstory.” It also misstates the conditions under which the subject of “Sara Berman’s Closet” left her husband and then decided to start wearing only white. She was 60 and living in Israel, not 40 and living in New York.
match_headline: Mark These Dates: A Wave of Art Is Coming Your Way

text: An article on Friday about the firing of the lawyer Morris Dees by the Southern Poverty Law Center misstated the year in which Mr. Dees won $7 million in damages on behalf of the family of Michael Donald. It was 1987, not 1981.
match_headline: Morris Dees, a Co-Founder of the Southern Poverty Law Center, Is Ousted

text: An article on Thursday about the death of the mob boss Francesco Cali misstated the name of a street used as a location in the film “The Godfather.” It was Longfellow Avenue, not Road.
match_headline: Reputed Gambino Mob Boss Is Shot and Killed on Staten Island

text: An article on Thursday about the tennis player Naomi Osaka’s adjustment to stardom misstated when Belinda Bencic beat Ms. Osaka in straight sets at the Hopman Cup. It was in December 2018, not January 2019.
match_headline: A Wiser Naomi Osaka Adjusts to Stardom, Even as She Briefly Stumbles

text: An article on Friday about a ban on drugs and whips on racing days at Santa Anita Park misstated the period during which 22 horses died. The first of the horse deaths occurred on Dec. 26, not six weeks before the publication of the article.
match_headline: Santa Anita Bans Drugs and Whips After Spate of Horse Deaths

text: An article on Page 14 about the actress and comedian Amy Schumer refers imprecisely to the video Ms. Schumer made about Beyoncé’s “Lemonade.” It was a tribute, not a spoof.
match_headline: Amy Schumer Doesn’t Care What You Think (That Much)

text: An article on Friday about Roz Chast and Patricia Marx misstated the title and publication date of their new book. It is “Why Don’t You Write My Eulogy Now So I Can Correct It? A Mother’s Suggestions” with a release date of April 2, not “Why Don’t You Write My Eulogy So I Can Correct It? A Mother’s Suggestions” with a release date of April 1.
ref_headline: Why Don’t You Write My Eulogy Now So I Can Correct It? A Mother’s Suggestions
match_headline: Roz Chast and Patricia Marx Mine the Mother Lode

text: An article on March 3 about the photographer James Van Der Zee’s pictures of Harlem omitted a credit for the photographs. The credit should have read: James Van Der Zee and Donna Mussenden Van Der Zee, courtesy of Howard Greenberg Gallery in New York.
match_headline: A View of Historic Harlem That’s Not on the Walking Tour

text: A review on March 3 from Paris Fashion Week misstated the given name of a designer. He is Mariano Fortuny, not Mario.
match_headline: The Glamour Cure

text: An article last Sunday about living in Long Valley, N.J., misstated the sale price of a home sold by the Klaassen family. The home sold for $582,000, or 16 percent less than the owners paid in late 2005, not $575,000, or 17 percent less.
match_headline: Long Valley, N.J.: Verdant and Occupationally Diverse

text: An article on March 3 about places in Venice to find cicchetti, the Venetian version of tapas, misidentified a white wine served at Cantine del Vino già Schiavi and its place of origin. The wine is Orto di Venezia, not Orto di Venezia St. Venissa, and its grapes are grown on the island of Sant’Erasmo, not Mazzorbo. The article also misspelled the given name of an owner of the restaurant All’Arco. He is Matteo Pinto, not Mateo. And the article misstated the name of a gondola station near the Osteria Bancogiro. It is the Traghetto Santa Sofia, not San Sofia.
match_headline: When in Venice, Eat Like a Venetian

text: An article on Feb. 10 about the French writer Éric Zemmour described incorrectly Breton, Basque and Occitan. They are languages, not dialects.
match_headline: The Right-Wing Pundit ‘Hashtag Triggering’ France

text: Because of a production error, an article on Monday about similarities in data recovered from “black boxes” of a jetliner that crashed in Ethiopia and one involving the same Boeing model in Indonesia five months earlier, was missing part of a sentence. Because of the error, the sentence misstated the number of people who died in the Ethiopia crash. It was 157, not 57.
match_headline: Boeing Black Box Data Shows Similarities Between Ethiopian and Lion Air Crashes

text: An article on Saturday about student reactions to a college admissions scandal misstated the number of articles that the Yale Daily News published this week about the university’s connection to the scandal. It was three, not one.
match_headline: ‘So Disheartening’: At Colleges Embroiled in Scandal, a Sense of Outrage and Sadness

text: An article on Monday about so-called opportunity zones created in the 2017 tax law, misstated the surname of the chief executive of Virtua Partners. She is Quinn Palomino, not Palombo. The surname of the mayor also was misspelled. He is Kenn Weise, not Weiss.
match_headline: Investors Eagerly Await Trump Rules on Opportunity Zones

text: An article on Monday about the box office numbers for “Captain Marvel” omitted the name of a distributor of “Five Feet Apart.” The movie is distributed by Lionsgate and CBS Films, not just Lionsgate.
match_headline: ‘Captain Marvel’ Climbs the List of Superhero Hits

text: An article on Dec. 14 about The Times’s art critics’ favorite art books of 2018 misidentified the publisher of “Hairy Who? 1966-1969.” It is the Art Institute of Chicago, not Yale University Press. This correction was delayed because it was only recently brought to the attention of the editors.
match_headline: The Best Art Books of 2018

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the police response to the Christchurch, New Zealand, mosque attacks referred incorrectly to which side of the gunman’s vehicle he was pulled from by two arresting officers. It was the passenger side, not the driver’s side.
match_headline: Quick Action, Near Miss and Courage in New Zealand Attacks

text: An article on Friday about activist movements that have formed in the wake of the killing of the Brazilian activist Marielle Franco misidentified the office to which three women were elected last year. Renata da Silva Souza, Dani Monteiro and Mônica Francisco were elected to the Rio de Janeiro State Assembly, not the City Council.
match_headline: A Year After Her Killing, Marielle Franco Has Become a Rallying Cry in a Polarized Brazil

text: An article on Tuesday about a dead whale beached in the Philippines misstated, in one reference, the amount of plastic found inside the whale’s body. As noted in the headline and elsewhere in the article, it was 88 pounds, not 40 pounds.
match_headline: Dead Whale Found With 88 Pounds of Plastic Inside Body in the Philippines

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the former White House counsel Gregory B. Craig misstated the dates of Mr. Craig’s tenure as White House counsel. As the article correctly noted, he served from 2009 to 2010, not after 2012.
match_headline: Lobbying Case Against Democrat With Ties to Manafort Reaches Key Stage

text: An article on Tuesday about the legacy of Levi Strauss & Company misstated, based on information included in Levi’s’ public offering filing, when Beyoncé performed at Coachella. It was April 2018, not 2017.
match_headline: Levi’s, Whose Jeans Are a Rugged Symbol of Americana, Prepares to Go Public

text: An article on Tuesday about the political contributions of executives misidentified the positions of three researchers. Although the study was conducted through a Harvard Law School program, Moshe Hazan is a professor at Tel Aviv University, David Weiss is a lecturer at Tel Aviv University, and Roberto Tallarita is an associate director of the Harvard program. They are not Harvard professors.
match_headline: How Executives Vote With Their Wallets

text: An article on Tuesday about the New York International Antiquarian Book Fair misstated the words above the portrait of Qiu Jin in the pamphlet published soon after Qiu’s death. Though she is referred to as “woman warrior” elsewhere in the pamphlet, those are not the words that appear on the page with her portrait.
match_headline: At a Rare Book Fair, the Prices Are Steep but the Lore Is Free

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the economist Alan B. Krueger misstated the year he graduated from Cornell. It was 1983, not 1985.
match_headline: Alan B. Krueger, Economic Aide to Clinton and Obama, Is Dead at 58

text: An article on Wednesday about the decline in German military spending misstated the name of the organization where the analyst Julianna Smith is a senior fellow. It is the Robert Bosch Academy, not the Robert Bosch Foundation.
match_headline: German Defense Spending Is Falling Even Shorter. The U.S. Isn’t Happy.

text: An article on Wednesday about the resignation of President Nursultan Nazarbayev of Kazakhstan misidentified a possible successor to Mr. Nazarbayev. She is Dariga Nazarbeyeva, his oldest daughter, not Dinara Kulibaeva, his second daughter.
match_headline: Longtime President of Kazakhstan Surprises Region by Resigning

text: An article on Tuesday about the spread of a conspiracy theory based on the idea that white women are not having enough children reported certain comments by the Fox News host Tucker Carlson out of context. The quotation — “This is why important science is no longer being conducted. It’s why art isn’t being made and comedy is dying.” — referred to the criticism Mr. Carlson had received for saying on his television program that women out-earning men was a major cause of the collapse of families. The quotation was not describing his views of the effects of women out-earning men.
ref_headline: This is why important science is no longer being conducted. It’s why art isn’t being made and comedy is dying.
match_headline: ‘Replacement Theory,’ a Racist, Sexist Doctrine, Spreads in Far-Right Circles

text: An article on Tuesday about NASA’s successful MarCO mission referred imprecisely to how far a cubesat had traveled when it reached Mars. It had traveled 300 million miles, not 90 million miles (Earth and Mars were about 90 million miles apart at the time the cubesat flew past Mars). The article also provided an erroneous distinction to a picture a cubesat took. It was the first picture taken of Mars by a cubesat, not the first in deep space.
match_headline: Space Is Very Big. Some of Its New Explorers Will Be Tiny.

text: An article on March 7 about coffee-table books on the subject of design misstated the price of the facsimile edition of the Bauhaus Journal. It is $80, not $91. It also misidentified the publisher of “Home Futures: Living in Yesterday’s Tomorrow.” It is Design Museum, not D.A.P.; the latter is the book’s distributor.
ref_headline: Home Futures: Living in Yesterday’s Tomorrow.
match_headline: Design Books That Explore History in the Making

text: An obituary on Sunday about the writer and editor Al Silverman misstated the surname of a former executive editor of the Book-of-the-Month Club, where Mr. Silverman was an executive for many years. He is Larry Shapiro, not Jacobs.
match_headline: Al Silverman, Writer Behind ‘Brian’s Song,’ Is Dead at 92

text: An article on Saturday about the massacre at two mosques in New Zealand transposed the first and second guns used by the accused gunman in the Al Noor mosque shooting. The first was a semiautomatic shotgun, not a rifle. The second was a semiautomatic rifle, not a shotgun.
match_headline: Two New Zealand Mosques, a Hate-Filled Massacre Designed for Its Time

text: An article on Wednesday about the indictment of eight Cambodian opposition leaders misidentified a vice president of the Cambodia National Rescue Party. He is Eng Chhai Eang, not Eng Chhai.
match_headline: Exiled Cambodian Opposition Leaders Are Indicted as Prime Minister Tightens Grip

text: An article on Wednesday about the victims of the mass shooting in New Zealand, relying on information from the police, erroneously included an individual among the victims who were killed in the attack. That profile has been removed from the digital version of the article.
match_headline: The New Zealand Shooting Victims Spanned Generations and Nationalities

text: An article on Wednesday about a plan for seven Western states to reduce water use amid a 19-year drought stated incorrectly the decade that Lake Mead began to fill. The lake began to fill in the 1930s, not the 1960s.
match_headline: Amid 19-Year Drought, States Sign Deal to Conserve Colorado River Water

text: An article on Thursday about the philanthropist Michael Steinhardt misspelled the given name of Sheila Katz’s lawyer. She is Debra Katz, not Deborah.
match_headline: Michael Steinhardt, a Leader in Jewish Philanthropy, Is Accused of a Pattern of Sexual Harassment

text: An article on Wednesday about soil shipped overseas for Major League Baseball games described incorrectly the significance of games between the Cubs and the Mets in Japan in 2000. They were the first regular-season games played outside North America, not the first played outside the United States and Canada.
match_headline: As the M.L.B. Season Opens in Japan, at Least the Dirt Is Familiar

text: An article on Tuesday about the struggle to build a transit line between Durham, N.C., and Chapel Hill, N.C., attributed an erroneous distinction to Mark-Anthony Middleton, a Durham City Council member. He attended Duke Divinity School, but he does not hold a degree from the university.
match_headline: Durham Dreamed of a Transit Line. Duke University All but Killed It.

text: An article on Friday about the “Jexodus” movement said that Elizabeth Pipko attends the Harvard Extension School, not Harvard University. The extension school is part of the university. She does not attend Harvard College.
match_headline: From a Swimsuit Model to the Trump Megaphone: The Genesis of ‘Jexodus’

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about former Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s response to concerns about his age as a factor in a possible presidential run misstated his age. He is 76, not 78.
match_headline: Vice President Season Starts Early for 2020 Democrats

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 1 about the mental health initiative ThriveNYC misidentifies the location of a community class. It took place at the Metropolitan College of New York, not Manhattan College.
match_headline: Chirlane McCray, de Blasio’s Wife, Is Questioned Over His ‘Revolutionary’ $1 Billion Mental Health Plan

text: An article on March 13 about lower-profile sports at the center of the college admissions scandal misstated the profession of William Singer. He worked in the college counseling business; he is not an intellectual property lawyer.
match_headline: Lower-Profile Sports Are at Center of Admissions Cheating Scandal

text: An article on Friday about the 50th anniversary of the novel “Slaughterhouse-Five” omitted one of Kurt Vonnegut’s children. In addition to children from his first marriage, Vonnegut had a daughter, Lily, from his second.
match_headline: From Dresden on the 50th Anniversary of ‘Slaughterhouse-Five’

text: An article on Friday about the comics publisher Artists, Writers & Artisans misidentified Bill Jemas’s roles at Marvel and AWA. He was chief operating officer and publisher at Marvel, not a vice president; and he is the chief executive and publisher of AWA, not the chief operating officer and publisher.
match_headline: A Comic Book Publisher Creates Its Own Origin Story

text: An article on Page 19 about the exhibition “Broken Nature: Design Takes on Human Survival” in Milan misstates the end year of the data represented in “Room of Change.” It is 2400, not 2040.
ref_headline: Broken Nature: Design Takes on Human Survival
match_headline: The End Is Nigh. Can Design Save Us?

text: An earlier version of a picture caption with an article on Page 17 about band reunion tours, using information from the source, misstates the year the picture was taken and one of the band members on stage. The photo was of the band Kiss in 1982, not 1984, and the picture included Ace Frehley, not Tommy Thayer.
match_headline: Reunion Tour! The Band Is Back! Wait, Who Are These Guys?

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the author Rachel Ingalls referred incorrectly to her graduation from Radcliffe. She graduated in 1964, not 1962, and she did not graduate cum laude.
match_headline: Rachel Ingalls, 78, Rediscovered Author of ‘Mrs. Caliban,’ Dies

text: An article last Sunday about Lawrence Ferlinghetti’s San Francisco misstated the middle initial of a poet. He is D.A. Powell, not D.
match_headline: Lawrence Ferlinghetti’s Enduring San Francisco

text: A review last Sunday about “Truth in Our Times,” by David E. McCraw, misspelled the given name of a New York Times reporter. She is Megan Twohey, not Meghan.
match_headline: The Truth Is Hard. But for a New York Times Lawyer, Defending It Is Fun.

text: A review on March 10 about “El Norte,” by Carrie Gibson, misspelled the surname of a Mexican writer. She is Carmen Boullosa, not Bullosa.
match_headline: Anglos, Hispanics and the Formation of America

text: A review last Sunday about the story collection “Elsewhere, Home,” by Leila Aboulela, misstated the author’s publishing history. Previous books of hers have appeared in the United States; “Elsewhere, Home” is not her American debut. The subheading with the review repeated the error.
match_headline: Stories of the Muslim Immigrant Experience, From a Sudanese Writer Now Living in Scotland

text: A review on March 10 about “Nobody’s Looking at You,” by Janet Malcolm, misspelled the surname of the journalist who wrote the book “Fatal Vision.” He was Joe McGinniss, not McGinness.
match_headline: In the Hands of Janet Malcolm, Journalism Becomes Art

text: An article on March 10 about the singer Kacey Musgraves misstated the name of a venue where she performed in 2013. It is the Ryman Auditorium, not the Ryman Theater.
match_headline: Kacey Musgraves Is Not Your Usual Kind of Outlaw

text: An article on Sunday about black artists finding success after 70 included an erroneous distinction about the artist McArthur Binion’s education. While he earned a graduate degree from the Cranbrook Academy of Art, he was not the first African-American student to do so.
match_headline: Discovered After 70, Black Artists Find Success, Too, Has Its Price

text: An article on Sunday about the effect of Medicare for All on private health insurance companies misidentified the state Senator Cory Booker represents. It is New Jersey, not California.
match_headline: Medicare for All Would Abolish Private Insurance. ‘There’s No Precedent in American History.’

text: An article on Friday about authoritarian governments that hire hackers from the private market misidentified the source of a valuation for the market of so-called lawful intercept spyware. The $12 billion market estimate cited by Moody’s originated from the company NSO, not Moody’s.
match_headline: A New Age of Warfare: How Internet Mercenaries Do Battle for Authoritarian Governments

text: An article on Saturday about Italy’s decision to join China’s One Belt One Road project misspelled part of the Chinese prime minister’s name. He is Li Keqiang, not Kequiang.
match_headline: Italy Gives Xi, and China’s Vast Infrastructure Project, a Royal Welcome

text: An article on Sunday about a march in London to protest Brexit misidentified where in New York the protester Olivia Leydenfrost grew up. It was in Nyack, not Manhattan.
match_headline: Angry Over Brexit Stalemate, Huge Crowds March in London to Demand Second Vote

text: A picture with an article on Saturday about the acquittal of the police officer who shot Antwon Rose II, using information from The Associated Press, was published in error. The framed photograph it showed, displayed as part of a memorial in front of the Allegheny County Courthouse, was not of Antwon Rose II.
match_headline: Antwon Rose Shooting: White Police Officer Acquitted in Death of Black Teenager

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the annual Aipac conference referred incorrectly to Senator Amy Klobuchar. It is not the case that she will be speaking this year at the annual conference of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
match_headline: Israel Lobby Convenes in Washington Amid Fraying Bipartisanship and Rising Tension

text: An article on Saturday about Attorney General William P. Barr misstated his age. He is 68, not 69.
match_headline: Who Is William Barr: He Will Decide What Happens With Mueller’s Report

text: An article on Monday about a video made by members of Tau Kappa Epsilon fraternity at the University of Georgia included a quotation from a University of Georgia student that referred incorrectly to Richard B. Russell Jr. While he was a segregationist, he was not a slave owner.
match_headline: ‘Pick My Cotton’: Video of Mock Whipping Prompts Fraternity to Expel 4 Students

text: An article on Saturday about the Gambino murder suspect Anthony Comello misidentified the origin of the QAnon conspiracy theory. It was born on the 4chan message board, not on Reddit.
match_headline: A Conspiracy Theorist, Anthony Comello, and a Mystery Motive in Gambino Murder

text: An article on Sunday about Boeing’s competition with Airbus misstated the number of 737 Maxes that Boeing makes a month. It is making a record 52 737s a month, but not all of them are Maxes.
match_headline: Boeing Was ‘Go, Go, Go’ to Beat Airbus With the 737 Max

text: An article on Monday about why people procrastinate referred incorrectly to the university at which Judson Brewer is employed. He is the director of research and innovation at Brown University’s Mindfulness Center, not the director of research at the Center of Mindfulness and associate professor of medicine at the University of Massachusetts Medical School.
match_headline: Why You Procrastinate (It Has Nothing to Do With Self-Control)

text: An article on Saturday about the University of Southern California athletic administrator Donna Heinel misstated one of Ms. Heinel’s titles at U.S.C. She was the senior woman administrator, not the senior women’s administrator.
match_headline: A Supposed Stickler for the Rules, Now at the Center of a U.S.C. Scandal

text: An obituary on Feb. 27 about the documentarian Perry Wolff misstated his involvement in the CBS News documentaries “Hunger in America,” “The Selling of the Pentagon” and “You and the Commercial.” He was executive producer, not producer.
match_headline: Perry Wolff, Award-Winning TV News Documentarian, Dies at 97

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump’s response to the end of the Mueller investigation misstated a remark the president made about his critics. He said that some were guilty of “evil things,” not “evil deeds.” The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Trump and Republicans Seek to Turn the Tables in Post-Mueller Washington

text: An article on Tuesday about activists urging warnings about the connections between breast implants and disease misspelled the given name of a woman who testified at the hearing on breast implants. She is Christina Avila, not Christine Avila.
match_headline: Women at Breast Implant Hearing Call for Disclosure of Safety Risks

text: An article on Tuesday about the second weekend of the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament erroneously attributed a distinction to Houston. It is one of two teams, along with Gonzaga, still in the tournament from outside college basketball’s six power conferences; it is not the only one.
match_headline: What’s Next in the N.C.A.A. Tournament? Let’s Look Ahead

text: An article on Thursday about a diorama at the American Museum of Natural History depicting a meeting between Peter Stuyvesant and members of the Lenape tribe overstated what is known about the weapon a soldier is carrying in the scene; it is not a rifle. The article also described incorrectly the skirts worn by the Lenape women depicted in the diorama. They fell to mid-calf; they did not brush the ground.
match_headline: What’s Wrong With This Diorama? You Can Read All About It

text: A picture caption with an article on March 1 about the Los Angeles art scene misidentified the title of an artwork. It is “Ground Transposition,” not “Ground Transportation.”
match_headline: The Los Angeles Art Scene Looks to the World

text: An article last Wednesday about a resurgent local-food movement in Puerto Rico misspelled the surname of a lawyer turned farmer. She is Natalia Quiles Deyá, not Deya. The article also misspelled the name of a native herb that Ms. Quiles grows. It is oregano brujo, not bruja. Additionally, the article misstated the Vietnamese name for the herb recao, or culantro. It is ngo gai, not rau ram. And the article misidentified the two women who founded the restaurant El Departamento de la Comida. They are not sisters.
match_headline: Local Food in Puerto Rico Finds Energy in Recovery

text: A review last Wednesday of the Japanese restaurant Odo misidentified a spirit used in the mikan-orange cocktail. It is Japanese shochu, not its Korean counterpart, soju. The article also misidentified the sauce brushed over some of the sushi. It is nikiri, not nishiki. And it misidentified the rice used by a Brooklyn brewery for one of its sakes. It is Yamada Nishiki from California and Arkansas, not koshihikari from New Jersey.
match_headline: Kaiseki, Straight Up With a Twist

text: An obituary on Monday about the Israeli spymaster Rafi Eitan referred incorrectly to the disappearance in the late 1960s of enriched uranium from a nuclear fuel plant in the Pittsburgh area. Though many believed that Israeli agents had stolen the material and diverted it to their country to help its nuclear weapons program, that allegation was never proved. And though Mr. Eitan visited the plant around the time of the disappearance, it was never shown conclusively that he had had an important role in it.
match_headline: Rafi Eitan, 92, Israeli Spymaster Who Caught Eichmann, Is Dead

text: An obituary on March 4 about the Chinese historian Li Xueqin misstated when he wrote an article critical of his mentor, Chen Mengjia. It was in 1957 — not after the start of the Cultural Revolution in 1966.
match_headline: Li Xueqin, Key Historian in China’s Embrace of Antiquity, Dies at 85

text: An editorial on Friday misstated the academic affiliation of Jennifer Lawless. She is a professor of politics at the University of Virginia; she is no longer director of the Women and Politics Institute at American University.
match_headline: The Outspoken Women of the House

text: An article on Tuesday about five Taliban officials who were jailed at the American detention camp in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, misidentified the source of a transcript of Mullah Mazloom’s remarks to an initial tribunal hearing at Guantánamo. The transcript was obtained by The New York Times in a Freedom of Information Act request; it was not released by WikiLeaks.
match_headline: Once Jailed in Guantánamo, 5 Taliban Now Face U.S. at Peace Talks

text: An article on Tuesday about an N.F.L. rule change that will allow challenges on pass interference described incorrectly the way the challenges will be used. Coaches may use them for the first 28 minutes of each half, not in the first 58 minutes of the game. In the last two minutes of each half, only replay officials may challenge a call, not just in the final two minutes of the game.
match_headline: N.F.L. Will Experiment With Replay Reviews of Pass Interference

text: An article on Tuesday about a settlement between MoMA PS1 and a curator who accused the museum of discrimination misidentified the position that Nikki Columbus was offered. It was associate curator of performance, not curator of performance.

text: An editorial on Wednesday referred imprecisely to the source of a report that found that over 80 percent of Americans addicted to opioids were not getting treatment with medications that could help. text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the decision by the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office to drop charges against the actor Jussie Smollett paraphrased inaccurately part of a prosecutor’s explanation for dropping the charges. The prosecutor, Joe Magats, said that Mr. Smollett had no previous criminal record of violence or felonies; he did not say that Mr. Smollett had no criminal record. text: An article on Wednesday about Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s comments on the implications of President Trump recognizing Israel’s sovereignty over the Golan Heights misstated the West Bank’s Palestinian population. It is 2.8 million, not 1.8 million.

text: An article on Thursday about a judge blocking Medicaid work requirements in Arkansas and Kentucky misstated the surname of the Arkansas governor. He is Asa Hutchinson, not Asa Huckabee.
match_headline: Judge Blocks Medicaid Work Requirements in Arkansas and Kentucky

text: An article on Thursday about religious exemptions to vaccines misidentified an organization that has made the elimination of nonmedical vaccination exemptions a priority. It is the American Academy of Pediatrics, not the American Association of Pediatrics.
match_headline: Measles Outbreak: What Are Religious Exemptions for Vaccinations?

text: An article on Monday about women in the Marines referred incorrectly to the Parris Island recruit training facility. While it is the only site where women can become enlisted Marines, there are other training sites that offer paths for women to become officers in the Marine Corps.
match_headline: Women Becoming Marines: ‘I’ Will No Longer Be in Your Vocabulary

text: An article on Wednesday about the choreographer Martha Graham’s piece “El Penitente” referred incorrectly to self-flagellating religious traditions of the American Southwest as belonging to Native Americans. They were in fact inculcated by Spanish colonists in that area.

text: An article on Thursday about the collapse of an effort to legalize marijuana in New Jersey misstated one of Nia Gill’s former positions. She was president pro tempore of the State Senate, not speaker of the assembly.
match_headline: Why the Plan to Legalize Marijuana in New Jersey Suddenly Unraveled

text: An article on Friday about a rally held by President Trump in Grand Rapids, Mich., misstated the last year a Republican won Michigan in a presidential election before 2016. George Bush won Michigan in 1988; President Trump was not the first Republican to win the state since 1984.

text: An article on Thursday about a decision made by McDonald’s officials not to lobby against minimum-wage increases misstated the given name of a McDonald’s worker in Kansas City. He is Terrance Wise, not Terrence.
match_headline: McDonald’s Will No Longer Lobby Against Federal, State and Local Minimum-Wage Increases

text: An article on Thursday about Vincent van Gogh’s time in London described incorrectly which museums van Gogh visited there. He saw paintings now in the Wallace Collection, then on display elsewhere, but did not go to the museum of that name, which opened in 1900.
match_headline: Van Gogh the Wild Man? Try Van Gogh the Suburban Professional

text: An article on Friday about the balletomane Lincoln Kirstein misspelled the name of one of the artists featured in the exhibition “Lincoln Kirstein’s Modern,” at the Museum of Modern Art. It is Jay Leyda, not Jan Leyda.
match_headline: Lincoln Kirstein: A Modern Tastemaker With Some Iffy Taste

text: An article on Page 14 about the film “10 Things I Hate About You” misstates what it cost to make the film. It was made for $11.2 million, not $16 million.
match_headline: ‘10 Things I Hate About You’: When Heath Ledger Was Just Breaking Through

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the Mets’ 1962 season, using information from The Associated Press, misstated the team the Mets were playing at the Polo Grounds. It was the San Francisco Giants, not the Los Angeles Dodgers.
match_headline: 1962: The Bumbling Beginning

text: An article last weekend about Castello di Potentino in southern Tuscany misspelled the title of Ned Lambton. He is the seventh Earl of Durham, not of Dunham.
match_headline: Reviving a Centuries-Old Abandoned Castle and, With It, a Way of Life

text: An article last weekend about Victoire de Castellane’s opal collection misstated how she stores her opals. She keeps them in a box with a glass of water, not in a glass of water.
match_headline: A Jewelry Designer’s Opals, Illustrated

text: An item in the With Interest article last Sunday misstated the model of Boeing plane that was involved in two recent fatal crashes. It was the 737 Max 8, not the 787 Max 8.
match_headline: The Week in Business: Boeing Plays It Safe, and Lyft Kicks Off Tech I.P.O.s

text: An article last Sunday about Batsheva Dance Company misstated the year that the work “Venezuela” had its premiere. It was in 2017, not 2016.
match_headline: Batsheva: A New Era, a New Role for Ohad Naharin

text: An article last weekend about Modernist architecture in Chile misidentified the client who commissioned Le Corbusier to design a house on the coast of Chile; it was Matías Errázuriz Ortúzar, not Eugenia Errázuriz. It also misstated the year of the commission; it was 1929, not 1930. And the article misidentified the location of a Benedictine monastery; it is in Las Condes, on the outskirts of Santiago, not Los Leones.
match_headline: In Chile, Homes as Extreme as the Landscape Itself

text: An essay last week about online friendships misidentified the country in which the funeral of the disabled gamer Mats Steen was held. It was Norway, not the Netherlands.
match_headline: This Friendship Has Been Digitized

text: An item in the “Of Interest” article on Sunday about financial schemes carried out by far-right extremists misidentified a database run by researchers who track the crimes. It is the United States Extremist Crime Database, not the U.S. Extremist Financial Crime Database.
match_headline: White House Blames Fed for Slowing Economic Growth

text: An article on Sunday about violence in American prisons misidentified the location of the Equal Justice Initiative, a nonprofit civil rights organization. It is in Montgomery, Ala., not Birmingham.
match_headline: Inside America’s Black Box: A Rare Look at the Violence of Incarceration

text: An article on Monday about a man who claims to have found part of the stage from the 1969 Woodstock festival misspelled the name of the lumber manufacturer that made the boards used for the stage. It is Weyerhaeuser, not Weyerhauser.
match_headline: He Says He Found a Souvenir From the ’60s: The Stage at Woodstock

text: A headline with an article on Monday about Nigeria’s efforts to recoup money that was looted from the country’s coffers decades ago by a handful of high-ranking government officials misstated the amount the country is seeking from JPMorgan Chase. As the article correctly noted, it is seeking $900 million, not $900 billion.
match_headline: Ben Ray Luján, High-Ranking House Democrat, Will Run for Senate in New Mexico

text: An article on Friday about the N.C.A.A. Division I men’s hockey tournament misstated the number of teams in this year’s field that have won a national championship. It is six, not five.
match_headline: College Hockey’s Depth Is Reflected in Men’s Tournament Field

text: An article on Friday about Michigan State’s victory against Duke misstated the game that Cam Reddish missed. It was the Virginia Tech game, not the Louisiana State game.
match_headline: Michigan State Heads to Final Four After Banding Together to Shock Duke

text: An article on Tuesday about a judge’s decision to temporarily seal Stephen Moore’s divorce records misstated the Federal Reserve’s recent actions on interest rates. It increased rates. It did not cut them.
match_headline: Trump Fed Pick’s Divorce Records Are Put Under Temporary Seal

text: An article on Sunday about once-dominant N.H.L. teams adjusting to an evolving league misstated the number of conference finals appearance by the Kings, the Ducks and the Blackhawks since 2009. It is 10, not nine. Because of an editing error, an earlier version also misstated the number of playoff appearances by those teams in that span. It is 24, not 27.
match_headline: Longtime N.H.L. Powers Adjust to the View From the Bottom

text: An article on March 23 about a lawsuit against Harvard over the rightful ownership of photos of slaves described incorrectly the daguerreotype technology around 1850. Exposure times did not require that subjects sit still for as much as an hour.
match_headline: Your Ancestors Were Slaves. Who Owns the Photos of Them?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Americans who belong to Generation Z misstated the age of Shanaya Stephenson. She is 23, not 19.
match_headline: Generation Z: Who They Are, in Their Own Words

text: An article on Thursday about security vulnerabilities at President Trump’s Florida resort Mar-a-Lago misstated the ownership of hotels that have been subject to cyberattacks. They are owned by the Trump Organization, not the Trump administration. An earlier version of a picture caption with the article misidentified a property visited by President Trump in Florida. The president’s motorcade was entering the Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, not the resort Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach.
match_headline: Malware Arrest Exposes Security Gaps at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Club

text: An article on Thursday about extradition laws between Hong Kong and mainland China referred incorrectly to Taiwan’s position on China’s territorial claims. Taiwan’s Ministry of Justice has said it would not go along with an extradition agreement that declares Taiwan to be part of China’s territory. It did not address one that declares Hong Kong to be part of its territory.
match_headline: Despite Fears About China, Hong Kong Pushes Ahead on Extradition Bill

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Pacific Gas and Electric’s announcement of a new C.E.O. and 10 new board members referred incorrectly to Progress Energy’s nuclear plant in Crystal River, Fla. It was the utility’s only nuclear plant in Florida, not its only nuclear plant anywhere.
match_headline: PG&E Reveals New C.E.O. and a Revamped Board of Directors

text: An article on Tuesday about new content available to stream this month misstated the given name of Lakeith Stanfield’s character in “Someone Great.” The character is Nate, not Nick.
match_headline: The Best Movies and TV Shows New to Netflix, Amazon and More in April

text: An obituary on Thursday about the private investigator David Fechheimer misspelled the surname of an executive who was at the center of one of his cases. He was Larry Hillblom, not Hillbloom. Because of an editing error, the obituary also referred incorrectly to a scene from the novel “The Maltese Falcon” involving the private eye Sam Spade and his secretary. It was included in the screenplay for the 1941 movie adaptation but was not in the movie itself.
match_headline: David Fechheimer, a Reserved but Adroit Sam Spade, Dies at 76

text: An article on Friday about the psychology of personal space misstated when former Vice President Joe Biden released a video on the importance of respecting it. It was Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Beyond Biden: How Close Is Too Close?

text: An article on Tuesday about a plague that kills frogs, using information provided by a researcher, misstated the extent of the spread of a fungus that kills frogs. It has spread to Madagascar; it is not the case that the island country remains free of the fungus.
match_headline: The Plague Killing Frogs Everywhere Is Far Worse Than Scientists Thought

text: Because of a production error, this weekend’s KenKen puzzle is a duplicate of the March 31 puzzle. New KenKen puzzles will resume in the April 14 issue.
match_headline: Tea Set

text: An item in the Week Ahead column last Sunday misstated the location of the opening of the film “Peterloo.” It was New York and Los Angeles, not New York and London.
match_headline: The Week in Arts: Martha Graham, ‘Ink’ and More

text: An article on March 24 about the travel expert Rick Steves misstated the size of a bus he used in his early tours through Europe. It was a nine-seat minibus, not a nine-foot minibus.
match_headline: Rick Steves Wants to Save the World, One Vacation at a Time

text: Because of a production error, a map of the United States with an article on Saturday about white extremist attacks showed the incorrect locations of attacks. A map with the correct locations appears online at nytimes.com.
match_headline: Scrutinizing White House Security Clearances, House Panel Subpoenas Ex-Official

text: An article on Saturday about the implementation of mindfulness in militaries across the world referred incorrectly to the All Blacks. The phrase describes a prominent rugby team in New Zealand, not the national air force.
match_headline: The Latest in Military Strategy: Mindfulness

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about opposition to gay rights in Poland’s Law and Justice party misspelled the surname of the mayor of Gdansk, who was stabbed and killed this year. He was Pawel Adamowicz, not Adamkiewicz.
match_headline: Poland’s Populists Pick a New Top Enemy: Gay People

text: An article on Monday about an attempt by Democratic lawmakers in Albany to obtain Trump’s tax returns referred incorrectly to the committees allowed to seek tax returns under a proposed bill from the New York Legislature. They are the House Ways and Means Committee, the Senate Finance Committee and the Joint Committee on Taxation.
match_headline: To Get Trump’s Tax Returns, N.Y. Democrats Try a New Strategy

text: An article on Saturday about the “Seven Day Book Cover Challenge” misstated the publication date of a catalog from an exhibition devoted to the fashion designer Rudi Gernreich. It was 2001, not 2010.
match_headline: What Your Book Covers Say About You

text: An obituary on Saturday about the singer Kim English misstated the surname of a producer who worked with her. He is Maurice Joshua, not Maurice Johnson.
match_headline: Kim English, Who Blended Gospel With Dance Music, Dies at 48

text: An article on Tuesday about a bomb blast near the Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan, citing an official report from the Defense Department, misstated the number of casualties in the attack. Three American service members were killed in the attack, and a contractor was wounded; the contractor was not killed in the attack.
match_headline: Three Americans Killed in Afghan Blast, Despite Continuing Peace Talks

text: An article on Saturday about three church fires in a Louisiana parish referred incorrectly to the congregation of a church in Caddo Parish that suffered a fire. It is a predominantly white church, not a predominantly black one.
match_headline: 3 Black Churches Have Burned in 10 Days in a Single Louisiana Parish

text: Because of an editing error, an article on April 2 about horse fatalities at Santa Anita Rocks misstated the date of this year’s Kentucky Derby. It is May 4, not May 2.
match_headline: Death of Another Horse at Santa Anita Rocks the Racing Industry

text: A review last Wednesday of Standard Grill misspelled the surname of its maître d’hôtel. He is Michael Cecchi-Azzolina, not Cecchi-Azzolini.
match_headline: The TV Chef Rocco DiSpirito Returns, With a Quieter Touch

text: An article last Wednesday about Villa Deevena, a restaurant and hotel in Costa Rica, misstated the type of surf break at a nearby beach, Playa Negra. It is a right-hand break, not a left-hand break.
match_headline: A Chef’s Dream Villa in Costa Rica

text: An obituary on Saturday about the biologist Sydney Brenner misstated his age when he viewed the model of DNA constructed by Francis H.C. Crick and James D. Watson. He was 26, not 22.
match_headline: Sydney Brenner, a Decipherer of the Genetic Code, Is Dead at 92

text: An obituary on April 1 about the human rights lawyer Tejshree Thapa misstated the number of years she spent at the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia and at Human Rights Watch. She was with the tribunal for 13 years, not 15, and with Human Rights Watch for 11 years, not 15.
match_headline: Tejshree Thapa, Defender of Human Rights in South Asia, Dies at 52

text: Because of a translation error, an article on Wednesday about the Bialowieza Forest in Poland inaccurately rendered a quote attributed to Adam Bohdan. He said, “In the natural forest, there is two times more dead wood than in the managed part of the forest,” not that “there is two times more dead wood than living.”
ref_headline: In the natural forest, there is two times more dead wood than in the managed part of the forest,
match_headline: Life and Death in an Ancient Polish Forest

text: An article on Tuesday about Israel’s elections referred incorrectly to the Institute for Middle East Understanding. It is an American nonprofit educational group that promotes Palestinian viewpoints. It is not a Palestinian group.
match_headline: Israel Elections: How the Country Chooses a Leader and What’s at Stake

text: An article on Wednesday about a drug that increases bone density misspelled the name of an older drug used to treat osteoporosis. It is alendronate, not aldendronate.
match_headline: Most Osteoporosis Drugs Don’t Build Bone. This One Does.

text: An article on Sunday about renovations on a residential block on the Upper West Side misidentified a cat that had taken to overgrooming because of the construction noise. Its name is Titania of the Grey, not Titania of the Greil.
match_headline: That Noise? The Rich Neighbors Digging a Basement Pool in Their $100 Million Brownstone

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Thursday about the cost of groceries at Whole Foods misstated what types of produce were included in a test of the company’s new prices. Romaine lettuce was also among the items purchased to test the new prices; strawberries were not the sole produce item tested.
match_headline: Whole Foods Cut Prices. It Saved Us 5 Cents.

text: An article on Sunday about the New York Rangers’ rebuilding period misstated the number of overtime losses the Rangers had since the trade deadline on Feb. 25. It was five, not four.
match_headline: David Quinn’s Rangers Get Many Teachable Moments, but Few Wins

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about the musicians Ben Monder and David Torn erroneously included a band among the artists Ben Monder covers on “Day After Day.” He does not perform a song by Pixies.
match_headline: Ben Monder and David Torn, Jazz Guitarists Unafraid to Wrestle With Darkness

text: An article on Friday about art exhibitions to view in New York last weekend misstated the nature of the presentation of “Bridge Over Tree,” a sculpture by Siah Armajani currently at Brooklyn Bridge Park. The sculpture is not part of Armajani’s exhibition at the Met; it is being presented by the Public Art Fund to coincide with the Met show.
match_headline: 18 Art Exhibitions to View in N.Y.C. This Weekend

text: An article on Friday about the Palestinian novelist Isabella Hammad misspelled the surname of a Palestinian writer. She is Susan Abulhawa, not Susan Albuhawa.
match_headline: A Debut Novelist Explores Her Family’s History, and Palestine’s

text: An obituary on Saturday about Dan Robbins, who helped conceive what became known as paint by numbers, misspelled the surname of the character who was depicted in paint-by-numbers style on the cover of Mad magazine. He is Alfred E. Neuman, not Newman.
match_headline: Dan Robbins, Who Made Painting as Easy as 1-2-3 (and 4-5-6), Dies at 93

text: An article on Tuesday about a promise by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, to annex part of the West Bank referred incorrectly to a passage in the Oslo accords, the 1993 agreement between the Israelis and Palestinians. The Oslo accords called for a negotiated settlement, but did not commit both sides to a two-state solution.
match_headline: Netanyahu’s Talk of West Bank Annexations Is a Blow to Peace but No Surprise, Palestinians Say

text: An article on Thursday about two actresses involved in the college admissions scandal incorrectly described Felicity Huffman and William H. Macy as Oscar winners. They have both been Oscar nominees, but neither has been a winner.
match_headline: Lori Loughlin and Felicity Huffman: 1 Scandal, 2 Actresses, Diverging Paths

text: An article on Thursday about an economic plan laid out by the Turkish government misstated the exchange rate for the lira on Wednesday. It cost 5.7 lira to buy $1, not 1 lira to buy $5.70.
match_headline: Turkey’s Plan for Economy Is Seen as Tepid Response to Downturn

text: A headline accompanying an article on Thursday about a fire that destroyed the Shakespeare Theater in Stratford, Conn., misstated the number of arrests that were made. As the article stated correctly, three teenagers were arrested in connection with the fire, not two.
match_headline: Teenagers Charged With Setting Fire to Shakespeare Theater in Connecticut

text: An article this weekend on Page 7 about Taylor Knapp, a Long Island chef who became a certified snail farmer, attributes an erroneous distinction to the Peconic Escargot snail farm. It is not the only snail farm certified by the U.S.D.A.; there is at least one other snail farm located in the United States with the same certification.

text: An article on Thursday about Amazon employees and climate change referred imprecisely to Chris Page’s role at Amazon. She ran a part of the company’s sustainability work, not all of it.

text: An article this weekend on Page 46 about investing and climate change refers incorrectly, in one instance, to G.M.O., the asset-management company. It is a firm, not a fund. And the article misstates Jeremy Grantham’s role at the firm. He does not manage the firm; he helps oversee it. The article also misstates the title of a speech by Grantham. It was “The Race of Our Lives,” not “Protect the Planet, Profit From Green Causes.”
match_headline: Climate Change: Debating the Best Fix

text: An item in the table of contents this weekend on Page 34 misspells a photographer’s given name; he is Bon Duke, not Ben Duke.

The photos were taken at a few different places in Chicago, including the Illinois Institute of Technology College of Architecture and Anthony Overton Elementary School, both of which Abloh attended. They were not taken only at Anthony Overton Elementary.

text: A headline with an article on Friday about safety reviews of the Boeing 737 Max referred imprecisely to the F.A.A.’s actions. While the administration did not review the changes to the aircraft’s software, it is not the case that the jet bypassed safety reviews by the F.A.A.
match_headline: Changes to Flight Software on 737 Max Escaped F.A.A. Scrutiny

text: An item on Friday in the “Of Interest” article misspelled the given name of the most productive shot-blocking N.B.A. guard. He is Dwyane Wade, not Dwayne.
match_headline: Dwyane Wade Bows Out: Once, Again and Always a Heat Player

text: An article on Page 46 about investing and climate change referred incorrectly, in one instance, to G.M.O., the asset-management company. It is a firm, not a fund. And the article misstated Jeremy Grantham’s role at the firm. He does not manage the firm; he helps oversee it. The article also misstated the title of a speech by Grantham. It was “The Race of Our Lives,” not “Protect the Planet, Profit From Green Causes.”
match_headline: Climate-Change Funds Try to Profit From a Warming World

text: Because of a transcription error, an article on March 31 about the boycott, divestment and sanctions (B.D.S.) movement misstated a quotation from the inaugural campaign speech of Benny Gantz, the leader of the center-left bloc in Israel. It should have read: “We will strengthen the settlement blocs” and “retain control of security in the entire land of Israel.” The article also misspelled the surname of a participant in the black-Palestinian solidarity video “When I See Them, I See Us.” She is Noura Erakat, not Erekat.
ref_headline: We will strengthen the settlement blocs

text: A review on March 31 about “Bending Toward Justice,” by the United States senator Doug Jones, misstated the involvement of the Jones campaign in deceptive tactics employed during the 2017 Alabama senatorial race. There is no evidence that Jones or his campaign was aware of a project using Russian social media techniques to influence the election.
match_headline: Moving Alabama Into the Modern Age

text: Because of an editing error, the Crime column last Sunday misspelled the given name of the publisher of Philip Kerr’s novel “Metropolis.” She is Marian Wood, not Marion.
match_headline: Philip Kerr’s Last Novel and a New Series From Alexander McCall Smith

text: An article on March 31 about women and the dangers they face when traveling abroad alone referred incorrectly to Cassie DePecol’s Guinness World Record. It is for the fastest time to visit all sovereign nations, not merely the first woman on record to travel to all countries.
match_headline: Adventurous. Alone. Attacked.

text: An item in the table of contents this weekend on Page 34 misspells a photographer’s given name; he is Bon Duke, not Ben Duke.

An article on Sunday about a presidential campaign rally for Senator Cory Booker misidentified the year that the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. wrote “Letter From a Birmingham Jail.” It was 1963, not 1969.
match_headline: Cory Booker, Citing a Rising Newark, Pitches a Campaign of ‘Justice’

text: An article on Monday about Pete Buttigieg’s official announcement to run for president misstated the number of veterans among the 2020 presidential candidates. Both Mr. Buttigieg and Representative Tulsi Gabbard are veterans; Mr. Buttigieg is not the only one.
match_headline: Pete Buttigieg Announces Official Start to 2020 Campaign

text: An article on Friday about the Senate’s confirmation of David Bernhardt as secretary of the interior misspelled the given name of a Democratic senator who supported Mr. Berhardt’s nomination. She is Kyrsten Sinema, not Krysten.
match_headline: Senate Confirms Bernhardt as Interior Secretary Amid Calls for Investigations Into His Conduct

text: An article on Friday about a bill passed by the New York City Council that will bar marijuana drug tests for job applicants misspelled the last name of the City Council’s minority leader. He is Steven Matteo, not Mateo. It also misidentified the borough that Mr. Matteo represents. It is Staten Island, not Queens.
match_headline: Marijuana Testing of Job Applicants Is Barred by City in Groundbreaking Measure

text: An article on Friday about the baseball player C.C. Sabathia’s final season misstated the year in which Aaron Boone had open-heart surgery. It was in 2009, not 2003.
match_headline: With a Patched-Up Heart, C.C. Sabathia Returns for One Final Run

text: An article on Sunday about the New York Islanders and the Pittsburgh Penguins’ captain Sidney Crosby misstated Crosby’s playoff history at PPG Paints Arena in Pittsburgh. He has played postseason games there every year except the 2010-11 season, not every year since his rookie season.
match_headline: Islanders Keep Sidney Crosby in Check as They Put Penguins in a 2-0 Hole

text: An article on Monday about female directors in Hollywood misidentified the actress who will star in a “Shaft” sequel. She is Regina Hall, not Regina King.
match_headline: As Hollywood Embraces Diversity, Jobs for Female Directors Remain Sparse
