text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about President Trump’s history of using the Sept. 11 attacks in political jabs misstated the publication timing of Rick Reilly’s book on Mr. Trump. It was published in April; it is not due out in May.
match_headline: Trump’s History of Using 9/11 for Political Attacks

text: An article on April 4 about a planned lawsuit against Boeing over the Ethiopian Airlines crash misstated the relationship of one of the victims to Ralph Nader, the consumer rights advocate. She was his grandniece, not his niece.
match_headline: Family of Ralph Nader’s Grandniece, Killed in Crash, Plans to Sue Boeing

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the Carolina Hurricanes coach Rod Brind’Amour misstated a player’s age. Andrei Svechnikov is 19, not 18.
match_headline: To Lead a Young Team, the Hurricanes Turn to Rod the Bod

text: A picture caption with an article about how Times reporter Paul Mozur covered surveillance in Kashgar, China, referred incorrectly to the spread of surveillance cameras. There are about 200 million surveillance cameras across China, not in Shanghai alone.
match_headline: Being Tracked While Reporting in China, Where ‘There Are No Whys’

text: An article on Wednesday about elections in Indonesia misstated the location of Yogyakarta. It is 250 miles southeast of the capital, Jakarta, not 250 miles southwest.
match_headline: In Indonesia’s Election Campaign, a Dictator’s Son-in-Law Rails Against ‘Elites’

text: A column on Monday about Tiger Woods’s victory at the 2019 Masters misstated when he first went into the lead at the tournament. He shared the lead at times during the first and third rounds; he was not tied for the lead for the first time at 12:44 p.m. Sunday.
match_headline: Tiger Woods Showed He Was Back Not With a Shot, but With a Stare

text: An article on Tuesday about great athletic comebacks referred incorrectly to Jack Nicklaus’s win at the 1986 Masters at age 46. It made him the oldest man to win the Masters, not the oldest man to win a golf major. (Julius Boros was 48 when he won the 1968 P.G.A. Championship.)
match_headline: Tiger Woods’s Masters Win Joins the Ranks of Great Sports Comebacks

text: A picture caption with an article about Roberto Clemente misidentified the woman pictured with his teammate Willie Stargell in 1973. The woman accompanying Mr. Stargell was his first wife, Dolores, not his second wife, Margaret.
match_headline: For Many Latino Players, Roberto Clemente’s Number Is Off Limits, Too

text: A review on Monday about Handel’s “Semele” at Carnegie Hall misspelled the surname of a countertenor. He is Christopher Lowrey, not Lowery.
match_headline: Review: The English Concert Brings a Marvelous ‘Semele’

text: An article on Wednesday about the Youth America Grand Prix ballet competition misstated the given name of Melanie Hamrick’s co-choreographer. She is Joanna DeFelice, not Jenn DeFelice.
match_headline: Ballet’s Biggest Matchmakers (Student, Meet Scholarship)

text: An obituary on Monday about the neuroscientist Paul Greengard referred imprecisely to his research. Though the paradigm-shifting work that led to his Nobel Prize extended from the late 1960s to the mid-1980s, he was an active researcher until his death, not just for that period.
match_headline: Paul Greengard, 93, Nobel Prize-Winning Neuroscientist, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Mirjana Markovic, the wife of the Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic, misstated the status of Mr. Milosevic’s war-crimes trial when he died in 2006. He was awaiting the conclusion of the trial; he was not awaiting the trial itself.
match_headline: Mirjana Markovic, the ‘Lady Macbeth’ of War-Torn Serbia, Dies at 76

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the International Criminal Court’s decision to abandon an Afghanistan war-crimes investigation misspelled the surname of a Swiss scholar who said the court’s decision was self-destructive to its own authority. He is Guenael Mettraux, not Metraux.
match_headline: Hague Court Abandons Afghanistan War Crimes Inquiry

text: An article on Thursday about the suicide of Alan García misstated when Ollanta Humala was president of Peru. His presidency was from 2011 to 2016, not 2006 to 2011.
match_headline: Alan García, Ex-President of Peru, Is Dead After Shooting Himself During Arrest

text: An article on Thursday about the Rev. Jean-Marc Fournier’s efforts to save the relics in Notre-Dame from being destroyed by fire misidentified one of two objects recovered by Father Fournier. It was the Blessed Sacrament, not a statue of Jesus.
match_headline: The Chaplain, the Cathedral Fire and the Race to Rescue Notre-Dame’s Relics

text: An article on Thursday about Pinterest’s I.P.O. misstated the value of the shares held by Ben Silbermann, the founder and chief executive of Pinterest. He stands to make about $981 million in the I.P.O., not $1.5 billion.
match_headline: Pinterest Prices I.P.O. at $19 a Share, for a $12.7 Billion Valuation

text: An article on Thursday about the Knicks and the Nets returning to the N.B.A. playoffs misstated the Knicks’ record in the 2014-15 season. They were 17-65, not 17-63.
match_headline: Four Forgettable Years Later, Playoff Basketball Returns to New York

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s behavior during the Mueller investigation misidentified the person for whom Annie Donaldson served as chief of staff. It was Donald F. McGahn II, not Attorney General Jeff Sessions.
match_headline: A Portrait of the White House and Its Culture of Dishonesty

text: An article on Sunday about N.B.A. photographers in the age of social media referred imprecisely to Nelson Campana’s job. He photographs the Toronto Raptors as an employee of Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment, which owns the team; he is not the team photographer.
match_headline: N.B.A. Photographers ‘Do It for the Gram,’ Too

text: An article on Friday about sport events to watch this weekend misstated the date of the next Nascar auto race. Nascar is at Talladega Superspeedway for the Geico 500 on April 28, not Sunday.
match_headline: 8 Things to Do With Your Kids in N.Y.C. This Weekend

text: An article on Friday about plays and musicals to see in New York this weekend misstated one of the cast members in “Gary: A Sequel to Titus Andronicus.” Andrea Martin was injured and left the production; Kristine Nielsen has taken over her role.
ref_headline: Gary: A Sequel to Titus Andronicus.
match_headline: 15 Plays and Musicals to Go to in N.Y.C. This Weekend

text: An article on Friday about kid-friendly activities in New York this weekend misstated the day of one of Margaret Leng Tan’s performances at the New York Botanical Garden. It is Sunday, April 21, not Saturday, April 20.
match_headline: 8 Things to Do With Your Kids in N.Y.C. This Weekend

text: An article last Sunday about a dispute between the bankruptcy adviser Jay Alix and McKinsey & Company described incompletely a hearing before the bankruptcy court Judge David R. Jones. In addition to saying that allegations Mr. Alix made against McKinsey, if true, could constitute a crime, the judge told Mr. Alix that it could be a crime if he had lied to the court about McKinsey’s conduct. The article also misstated when the hearing took place. It was in January, not December.
match_headline: One Man vs. McKinsey: A Billionaire Says the Consultancy Has Rigged the Bankruptcy System

text: An article last Sunday about the increasing appeal of the Catskills for people buying second homes omitted a credit for the picture of the house in Kerhonkson, N.Y. The picture was taken by Deborah DeGraffenreid for The New York Times.
match_headline: Is the Hudson Valley Turning Into the Hamptons?

text: An article on April 7 that looked back at Avicii’s death and at the release of his new music misstated when the Avicii documentary “True Stories” came out. It was before his death, not after.
match_headline: Avicii’s Death Left Many Questions. Will His New Music Provide Answers?

text: An article last Sunday about the artist community of Prince Albert, South Africa, misstated the surname of a local artist. He is J.P. Meyer, not Martin.
match_headline: An Artist Colony Thrives in the South African Desert

text: An article on April 7 about Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response, or A.S.M.R., misidentified the force that causes the universe to expand. It is dark energy, not dark matter.
match_headline: How A.S.M.R. Became a Sensation

text: An article on Sunday about the shortage of international aid in Mozambique misstated when a tropical cyclone made landfall there last month. It was March 14, not March 4.
match_headline: Mozambique Cyclone Wiped Out the Nation’s Food. Now Aid Is in Short Supply.

text: An article on Monday about the re-election of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and its possible impact on Palestinians in the West Bank misstated the given name of a man who runs a wedding-planning business with his daughter. He is Hasan Teeti, not Samar. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: For Palestinian Families, ‘No Light at the End of the Tunnel’

text: An editorial on Sunday about adding a citizenship question to the 2020 census misstated the office Kris Kobach held in Kansas. He was secretary of state, not attorney general.
match_headline: Will the Census Count All of America?

text: An obituary on April 10 about Richard E. Cole, the last survivor of the 1942 bombing raid on Japan in retaliation for its attack on Pearl Harbor, referred incorrectly to his life after he retired from the Air Force in 1967 and moved to Texas. He first went into the citrus business and many years later had a small farm in the town of Comfort; he did not initially settle in Comfort and own a citrus farm there.
match_headline: Richard Cole, 103, Last Survivor of Doolittle Raid on Japan, Dies

text: An article on Monday about the deadly bombings in Sri Lanka described incorrectly the three churches that were attacked by suicide bombers on Sunday. Not all of them are Roman Catholic; one is evangelical. The error was repeated in an article on Tuesday.
match_headline: Blasts Targeting Christians Kill Hundreds in Sri Lanka

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Monday about the financial struggles of Kenyan long-distance runners misspelled the surname of one of the runners. He is Robert Kipkoech Cheruiyot, not Cheruyiot. The caption also misstated who received advice from a lawyer to avoid the pitfalls encountered by many champions. As the article correctly stated, it was Robert Kiprono Cheruiyot, not Robert Kipkoech Cheruiyot, who was shown in the photo.
match_headline: For Kenyan Runners, Winning Can Be a Road to Ruin

text: An article on Tuesday about a deal between the W.N.B.A. and CBS misstated the title of Lisa Borders at the W.N.B.A. She was the president, not the commissioner.
match_headline: W.N.B.A. Games to Air on CBS Sports Network in New Deal

text: An article on Tuesday about the nutritional value of eggs misstated the amount of sodium in a large egg. It is 71 milligrams, not 71 grams.
match_headline: Should You Be Eating Eggs?

text: Because of an editing error, a picture and map caption with an article on Tuesday about an emerging warm spot at Yellowstone National Park misidentified the park shown. It was Yellowstone, not Yosemite National Park, of course.
match_headline: It’s Warm and Stealthy, and It Killed Yellowstone Trees and Turned Soil Pale

text: A review last Wednesday of Niche, a new restaurant on the Lower East Side, misidentified an ingredient in the avocado salad. It is tempura flakes, not puffed rice. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Ramen Without Broth? A Chef Doubles Down on a Sidelined Dish

text: An article last Thursday about Judith Clark, the getaway driver in a deadly Brink’s heist in 1981, misstated where Marilyn Jean Buck died. She died at home in Brooklyn in August 2010, not in prison.
match_headline: Judith Clark, Getaway Driver in Deadly Brink’s Heist in 1981, Is Granted Parole

text: An article on Saturday about Pete Buttigieg’s firing of the police chief of South Bend, Ind., misstated the history of gay presidential candidates. Mr. Buttigieg is the first openly gay presidential candidate to gain national recognition and support; he is not the first openly gay man to run for president.
match_headline: Pete Buttigieg Fired South Bend’s Black Police Chief. It Still Stings.

text: An article on Tuesday about the lawsuit filed by President Trump and his businesses to sue the chairman of the House Oversight and Reform Committee misquoted the lawsuit. It stated that the “The Democrat Party,” not “The Democratic Party,” had weaponized subpoenas for political use. (The party’s official name is the Democratic Party.)
match_headline: Trump and His Businesses Sue House Democrats to Hide Accounting Records

text: An article on Wednesday about the professional gambler and “Jeopardy!” champion James Holzhauer misstated the amount of the lowest-value clues on the “Jeopardy!” game. They are worth $200, not $100.
match_headline: ‘Jeopardy!’ Phenom James Holzhauer Smashes Through $1 Million Mark

text: An article on Wednesday about Julia Angwin’s departure from The Markup misstated, based on information provided by The Markup’s new editor in chief, Jeff Larson, how many reporters the site had hoped to have in place by early 2019. It is 24, not almost 36.
match_headline: Julia Angwin Is Out as Editor of New Tech Watchdog Site The Markup

text: An article on Wednesday about the retired tennis player Justin Gimelstob referred imprecisely to the area where Mr. Gimelstob lives. His home is in the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles, not in Brentwood, Calif.
match_headline: Justin Gimelstob’s Criminal Case Is Settled. Now He Awaits a Verdict From His Tennis Peers.

text: An article on Thursday about a sting operation aimed at catching people seeking sexual encounters with minors misstated the day on which The New York Times attempted to reach Roger Arroyo and Jason Keizer. It was Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: They Arranged to Meet Underage Teens for Sex. Instead the Police Were Waiting.

text: An article on Thursday about Tesla’s quarterly loss misstated the availability of the $35,000 Model 3. It is being offered now; it is not the case that Tesla plans to begin selling it next month.
match_headline: Tesla Posts Big Quarterly Loss as Its Electric-Car Sales Lag

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the Islanders after their first-round playoff series misstated how many more suites Barclays Center has than Nassau Coliseum. It is 89, not 81.
match_headline: The Islanders Are Happy to Wait for Their Next Playoff Opponent

text: An article on Thursday about the New Orleans Jazz Fest misstated the relationship between Art Neville and Ivan Neville. Art is Ivan’s uncle, not his father.
match_headline: Jazz Fest at 50: The Stubbornness and Joy of New Orleans

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about the Hulu series “Ramy” misstated the ancestries of the titular character’s parents. They are Palestinian and Egyptian, not Palestinian by way of Egypt.
match_headline: Review: ‘Ramy’ Is a Soulful, Funny Leap of Faith

text: An article on Sunday about a web-based learning platform rolled out by public schools in Kansas mistakenly linked a recurrence of Megan Jackson’s epileptic seizures to her middle school’s use of the Summit Learning platform. While her school uses some of the same web-based tools that are used by Summit, the school is not on the Summit platform. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Silicon Valley Came to Kansas Schools. That Started a Rebellion.

text: An article on Friday about Anita Hill’s reaction to a phone call from Joe Biden misquoted one part of Ms. Hill’s response. She said, “There needs to be an apology to the other witnesses, and there needs to be an apology to the American public.” She did not say that “he needs to give an apology to the other women and to the American public.”
ref_headline: There needs to be an apology to the other witnesses, and there needs to be an apology to the American public.
match_headline: Joe Biden Expresses Regret to Anita Hill, but She Says ‘I’m Sorry’ Is Not Enough

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Saturday referred incorrectly to Jesus’s background. While he lived in an area that later came to be known as Palestine, Jesus was a Jew who was born in Bethlehem.
match_headline: As a Black Child in Los Angeles, I Couldn’t Understand Why Jesus Had Blue Eyes

text: An article on Friday about a cyclone in Mozambique misidentified the city from where Déborah Nguyen spoke. It was Johannesburg, not Beira.
match_headline: Weeks After Deadly Storm, Cyclone Kenneth Hits Mozambique

text: An article on Friday about Joe Biden’s chances of winning the Democratic Party’s nomination for president misstated the number of Democratic candidates in the race. With his entry in the race, there are 20 candidates, not 19.
match_headline: 5 Questions That Will Determine if Joe Biden Can Succeed

text: An article on Friday about Anna Sorokin’s conviction on grand larceny charges misidentified a hotel that lost $11,000 to Ms. Sorokin. It was the Beekman Hotel, not the Beacon Hotel.
match_headline: Fake Heiress Who Swindled N.Y.’s Elite Is Found Guilty

text: An article on Page 20 about new operas in Berlin misspells a composer’s given name. It is Detlev Glanert, not Detlef.
match_headline: 4 New Operas in 4 Months? Only in Berlin

text: An article on Tuesday about a possible ban on the international trade of Asian small-clawed otters included a quotation from a biologist that described incorrectly an increase in the popularity of pet otters. The increase has been exponential, not logarithmic.
match_headline: These Otters Are Popular Pets in Asia. That May Be Their Undoing.

text: An obituary on April 20 about James W. McCord Jr., who led the burglars in the Watergate break-in, referred incorrectly to the disposition of the cases against Mr. McCord and E. Howard Hunt. Mr. McCord, not Mr. Hunt, was convicted in a federal trial; Mr. Hunt, not Mr. McCord, pleaded guilty.
match_headline: James W. McCord Jr., Who Led the Watergate Break-In, Is Dead at 93

text: An obituary on Thursday about Verena Wagner Lafferentz, the last surviving grandchild of Richard Wagner, misstated the difference in age between her and Adolf Hitler, with whom she was romantically linked. He was three decades older than her, not two.
match_headline: Verena Lafferentz, 98, Last of Wagner Grandchildren, Is Dead

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about the organist Marilyn Mason, using information from the University of Michigan, misstated when the photograph of Dr. Mason there was taken. It was in the 1960s, not the 1950s.
match_headline: Marilyn Mason, Globe-Trotting Organist and Teacher, Dies at 93

text: An obituary on Thursday about Grand Duke Jean of Luxembourg misstated the nature of his participation in the Allied invasion of France in 1944. He arrived in Normandy in the days after D-Day, when troops first landed on the beaches there — not on D-Day itself. In addition, the headline with the obituary misstated his age. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 98, not 88.
match_headline: Grand Duke Jean of Luxembourg Is Dead at 98

text: Because of a production error, the cover story last Sunday, about new developments opening in historic former bank buildings, omitted several paragraphs. The full version of the article is at nytimes.com/realestate.
match_headline: Historic Bank Buildings Get a Second Act

text: A picture caption with the Scene City article last Sunday misstated the name of the group that performed at the Food Bank for New York City awards dinner. It is the Four Tops, not the Four Steps.
match_headline: On the Market in New York City

text: An article last Sunday about the Central Cemetery in Vienna misstated when the Habsburg reign in Austria ended. It was in the early 20th century, not the late 18th century.
match_headline: Tombstone Tourism’s Last Stop, a Plot of Your Own in Vienna

text: Because of a transcription error, an article on April 21 about the prison abolitionist Ruth Wilson Gilmore misquoted the activist Mariame Kaba. The quote is: “Similarly I know that our ancestors, who were slaves, could not have imagined my life,” not “Similarly I know that my ancestors, who were slaves, could not have imagined my life.”
ref_headline: Similarly I know that our ancestors, who were slaves, could not have imagined my life,
match_headline: Is Prison Necessary? Ruth Wilson Gilmore Might Change Your Mind

text: An article on Saturday about the relationship between Barack Obama and Joseph R. Biden Jr. misstated the role that Mr. Biden had on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in 2005 when Mr. Obama arrived in Congress. He was the committee’s ranking Democrat, not its chairman.
match_headline: Biden and Obama’s ‘Odd Couple’ Relationship Aged Into Family Ties

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Saturday about saffron as an alternative to traditional crops in Afghanistan misidentified the province where workers were harvesting saffron flowers. It was Balkh Province, not Herat Province.
match_headline: Hashim Aslami Has Just One Word for Afghan Farmers: Saffron

text: An article on Tuesday about the ongoing measles outbreak in the United States misidentified one of the states permitting exemptions from vaccination only on medical grounds. It is West Virginia, not South Carolina.
match_headline: Measles Outbreak Infects 695, Highest Number Since 2000

text: An article on Saturday about the conviction of a white supremacist in Oregon misstated the number of additional years that the convict could have faced in prison if an Oregon law had allowed him to be charged with a felony hate crime, rather than a misdemeanor. It is five years, not 20 years.
match_headline: In Oregon, a Murder Conviction Adds to Calls for Tougher Hate Crime Punishments

text: An obituary on Monday about the photographer Michael Wolf misstated his age. He was 64, not 65. (As the obituary correctly stated, he was born on July 30, 1954.) The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Michael Wolf, Who Photographed Skyscrapers Minus the Sky, Dies at 64

text: An article on Monday about the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner misstated the origin of a quote that the historian Ron Chernow shared during his remarks at the event. While Mr. Chernow attributed the remark to Mark Twain, there is no evidence that Twain ever said, “Politicians and diapers must be changed often, and for the same reason.”
ref_headline: Politicians and diapers must be changed often, and for the same reason.
match_headline: Perspective, Not Parody, at a Subdued Correspondents’ Dinner

text: An article on Tuesday about Tesla’s decision to significantly reduce the prices of its solar panels misstated the national average price for residential solar systems. The average is $2.98 per watt, according to the Solar Energy Industries Association, not $2.85. Because of that error, the story also misstated how much Tesla would be slashing prices for its solar systems. The company’s system will cost up to 41 percent less than the national average, not up to 38 percent.
match_headline: Tesla Looks to Regain Its Luster in Solar Energy by Slashing Prices

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Tuesday about the singer Jo Sullivan Loesser referred incorrectly to her marriage to the composer Frank Loesser. They were married when he died; they did not divorce.
match_headline: Jo Sullivan Loesser, Singer and Guardian of a Legacy, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the Venezuelan opposition leader’s moves to push President Nicolás Maduro to resign misidentified the CNN program on which Secretary of State Mike Pompeo made his remarks about plans for Mr. Maduro to fly to Cuba. It was “The Situation Room With Wolf Blitzer,” not “State of the Union.”
ref_headline: The Situation Room With Wolf Blitzer,
match_headline: Venezuelan Opposition Leader Steps Up Pressure, but Maduro Holds On

text: A map with an article on Tuesday about the measles outbreak in the United States misstated the number of measles cases reported in New York in 2019. There were 493 cases in the state this year as of April 29, not 659, which is the total number reported since September 2018.
match_headline: Measles Cases Surpass 700 as Outbreak Continues Unabated

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s threat to place a full embargo on Cuba misspelled the name of the opposition leader in Venezuela. He is Juan Guaidó, not Juan Guiadó. The article also misstated the day on which Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said that President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela had planned to flee to Cuba and the day that President Trump threatened a tougher embargo. Both statements were made on Tuesday, not Monday.
match_headline: Trump, Seeking to Put Pressure on Maduro, Threatens a Full Embargo on Cuba

text: An article on Tuesday about the historical data stored in tree rings misstated when a cosmic ray event described as the strongest found in the tree ring record happened. It occurred from 774 to 775, not in the year 744.
match_headline: Chronicles of the Rings: What Trees Tell Us

text: An article last Thursday about the International Furniture Fair in Milan misstated the type of garments that Eileen Fisher uses to make wall hangings. They are recycled, not unsold.
match_headline: The Most Wondrous Things at the Milan Furniture Fair

text: An article last Thursday about audiophile bars in New York described imprecisely the status of the nightclub Analog Brooklyn. Although a sound system was removed, the club remains open.
match_headline: No Noise Complaints Here

text: An article on Monday about support in Pennsylvania for Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s presidential bid in Pennsylvania referred incorrectly to his event in Pittsburgh. It was the first public appearance of Mr. Biden’s campaign, but not his first campaign appearance over all.
match_headline: In Pennsylvania, Joe Biden Finds Support Where He Most Needs It

text: A picture with an article on Monday about an abuse victim who recorded a conversation with his accused abuser was published in error. It was not an image of Sterling Van Wagenen.
match_headline: How an Abuse Victim’s Nerve and a Hidden iPhone Led to the Arrest of a Sundance Founder

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about two Estonian lawmakers making a hand gesture that many interpreted as a white power symbol transposed the positions of two government officials. Mart Helme is the interior minister, and Martin Helme is the finance minister.
match_headline: Estonia Ministers’ Gesture Raises Fears of Support for White Supremacy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the science behind high levels of testosterone and their impact on athletes’ performance misidentified the city in which the Court of Arbitration for Sport is located. It is Lausanne, Switzerland, not Zurich.
match_headline: Does Testosterone Really Give Caster Semenya an Edge on the Track?

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about Japan’s royal family misstated when the image was taken. Women in the imperial family posed in photos with Japan’s new emperor, Naruhito, and his wife, Masako, after the ascension ceremony at the Imperial Palace on Tokyo, not during it. (Only adult male members of the royal family are permitted to witness the rites.)
match_headline: One Image of Japan’s Royals Tells a Story of Demographic Crisis

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the Shalimar Diner in Queens misstated the year that the Moondance Diner closed. It was 2007, not 2017.
match_headline: What We Know About the Measles Outbreak in N.Y.

text: A subheading in a review of the Frieze Art Fair on Friday misstated the name of a gallery in the Frame section of the fair. It is Various Small Fires, not Very Small Fires.
match_headline: At Frieze New York, Islands of Daring

text: An article on Page 64 about the acquisition of Remington by Cerberus misstates the birthplace of Stephen Feinberg, a founder of Cerberus. He was born in the Bronx, not Spring Valley, N.Y., which is where he grew up.

An article on Page 54 about Meow Wolf, an art collective that creates immersive and interactive experiences, refers imprecisely to Creative Startups. It is a start-up accelerator, not a business incubator.
match_headline: Can an Art Collective Become the Disney of the Experience Economy?

text: An obituary on Monday about the former United States senator Richard G. Lugar referred incorrectly in part to his service in the Navy. He enlisted in 1956, not 1957, and he was commissioned an ensign, not a second lieutenant. It also misstated when he married Charlene Smeltzer. It was after he studied at Oxford on a Rhodes scholarship, not before. In addition, the obituary referred incorrectly to the Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction Program, a program to help destroy surplus stocks of nuclear weapons. Congress passed it shortly after it was proposed by Mr. Lugar and Senator Sam Nunn in 1991; it did not take “almost a decade” to persuade Congress of the need for the program. The obituary also mistakenly included one item on a list of issues addressed by the Lugar Center, which Mr. Lugar established after leaving office. The center has not sponsored studies of education.
match_headline: Richard Lugar, G.O.P. Senator and Foreign Policy Force, Dies at 87

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about the fashion designer Corinne Cobson misstated where she was in the photograph. She was in the center, not second from the right.
match_headline: Corinne Cobson, Designer With a Rock ’n’ Roll Edge, Dies at 62

text: An article on Page 64 about the acquisition of Remington by Cerberus misstates the birthplace of Stephen Feinberg, a founder of Cerberus. He was born in the Bronx, not Spring Valley, N.Y., which is where he grew up.

An article on April 21 about gender-discrimination lawsuits against the Salk Institute misstated the location of the institute’s annual faculty retreat. It is in Borrego Springs, Calif., not Palm Springs.
match_headline: ‘I Want What My Male Colleague Has, and That Will Cost a Few Million Dollars’

text: An article last Sunday about the Museum of Italian Judaism and the Shoah in Ferrara, Italy, misstated the name of a powerful family that lived in Ferrara for about three centuries. It is Este, not Estes.
match_headline: A New Museum Explores 2,000 Years of Jewish Life in Italy

text: An article on Monday about concerns of online censorship in Europe misstated the location of Malsch. It is in western Germany, not eastern Germany.
match_headline: Europe Is Reining In Tech Giants. But Some Say It’s Going Too Far.

text: An article last Friday about the accused gunman in a shooting at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte misspelled the suspect’s first name. He is Trystan Andrew Terrell, not Tristyn.
match_headline: U.N.C. Charlotte Shooting Suspect Was ‘Withdrawn,’ but Motive Is Still a Mystery

text: An article on Saturday about injured Yankees players returning to the field referred incorrectly to Gio Urshela. He is in his first season with the Yankees; he is not a rookie. The article also misstated the length of the Yankees’ current homestand. It is seven games, not 10.
match_headline: With Miguel Andujar Returning, Yankees’ Injury Nightmare Starts to Fade

text: An article on Saturday about the Hurricanes victory over the Islanders in the N.H.L. playoffs misstated the surname of the Islanders player who scored the team’s second goal. He is Brock Nelson, not Turner. The article also misstated the given name of a Hurricanes player involved in the team’s third goal. He is Brett Pesce, not Brad.
match_headline: Islanders on Wrong End of Sweep This Time

text: An article on Monday about the weekend’s box office totals misidentified one of the voice stars of the movie “UglyDolls.” It is Nick Jonas, not Joe Jonas.
match_headline: ‘Avengers: Endgame’ Muscles Out Competition to Maintain Box Office Lead

text: An obituary on April 30 about the film and television producer Steve Golin misstated the surname of his sister. She is Susan Dickson, not Dickinson.
match_headline: Steve Golin Is Dead at 64; Producer Built a Small Hollywood Empire

text: An article on Monday about President Trump’s decision to present Tiger Woods with the Presidential Medal of Freedom referred incorrectly to a car accident Mr. Woods had in Florida in 2009. The accident occurred inside his gated community near Orlando, not outside.
match_headline: In Tiger Woods, Trump Finds a Hero and a Business Opportunity

text: An article on Tuesday about Riley Howell misstated the name of a bluegrass band that played at Mr. Howell’s funeral on Sunday. It is Balsam Range, not Balsam Ridge.
match_headline: Riley Howell’s Parents Say He Was Shot 3 Times While Tackling the U.N.C. Charlotte Gunman

text: A chart accompanying a list of questions and answers about food and climate change last Wednesday misidentified the journal where a scientific study by Aleksandrowicz et al about climate-friendlier diets appeared. It was in PLoS One, not Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
match_headline: Your Questions About Food and Climate Change, Answered

text: An article on April 24 about Marsala wine misspelled three Italian terms used to describe the wine. They are dolce (sweet), not dolci; secco (dry), not seco; or semisecco (semi-dry), not semiseco.
match_headline: The Case for Marsala

text: An article on Wednesday about black middle-class voters in South Africa misstated the percentage of South Africa’s population that is black. It is about 80 percent, not 90 percent.
match_headline: South Africa’s Middle Class Sours on Mandela’s Party, Tainted by Corruption

text: An article on Wednesday about Secretary of State Mike Pompeo’s visit to Iraq misidentified the country to which the Trump administration gave a waiver to buy Iranian electricity without incurring American penalties. It was Iraq, not Iran.
match_headline: Pompeo Makes Unscheduled Trip to Iraq to Press U.S. Concerns About Iran

text: An article on May 2 about the increasing diversity in neighborhoods in the United States misstated the university affiliation of Japonica Brown-Saracino. She is a sociologist at Boston University, not Brown University.
match_headline: All-White Neighborhoods Are Dwindling as America Grows More Diverse

text: An article on Wednesday about the revision of debt-collection rules by federal regulators misidentified a consumer advocacy organization by its previous name. It is Consumer Reports, not Consumers Union.
match_headline: Consumer Bureau Moves to Cap Debt Collectors’ Calls, and Allow Texts and Emails

text: An article on Tuesday about the former minor-league baseball manager Wally Backman misstated the location of the Long Island Ducks’ stadium. It is in Central Islip, not Bethpage.
match_headline: Wally Backman, a Throwback in Baseball’s Testing Ground, Waits for Another Chance

text: An article last Thursday about new underwear options for transgender people used incorrect pronouns when referring to the brand director Christian Dominique and the designer Sky Cubacub. They are nonbinary and use the pronouns “they,” not “he” or “she.”
match_headline: There Are New Options in Trans Underwear

text: An article on Tuesday about skin infections acquired while traveling misstated how leishmaniasis is spread. The disease is spread by sand flies, not sand fleas.
match_headline: When Travelers Bring Skin Infections Back as Souvenirs

text: An article on Page 18 about imaginative vases misstates the name of a vase by Esque Studio. As a picture caption with the article notes correctly, it is Pushmepullme, not Pushmepulleme.
match_headline: You Call That a Vase?

text: An entry on Page 26 about events at NYCxDesign includes an outdated list of participants in “The Chair” at The Future Perfect. Max Lamb is no longer part of the exhibition.
match_headline: Design Destinations in a Citywide Festival

text: An article on Wednesday about the testimony of a former member of the cultlike group Nxivm misstated when Marc Agnifilo asked the court for a mistrial. It was on Tuesday, not last week.
match_headline: Former Member of Sex Cult Describes How She Became ‘Slave’

text: An article on Monday about the installation of sandbags in Lower Manhattan to protect against storm surges referred imprecisely to the flip-up flood gates the city plans to install north of the Brooklyn Bridge. The gates may rise up beneath the elevated Franklin D. Roosevelt Drive, but they will not attach to it.
match_headline: 6 Years After Hurricane Sandy, Here’s What They Came Up With: Really Big Sandbags

text: An article on April 12 about Uber’s I.P.O. filing misstated how many drivers Uber has said it intends to award cash bonuses to, where those drivers are and which ones can buy shares in the company’s public offering. Uber plans to award the bonuses to more than 1.1 million drivers around the world, not more than 1.1 million drivers in the United States. Only Uber drivers in the United States will have the option to buy stock, not all drivers.
match_headline: Uber, Losing $1.8 Billion a Year, Reveals I.P.O. Filing

text: An article on Friday about North Korea’s second missile launch in a week misquoted John C. Demers, the head of the Justice Department’s national security division. He said, “This sanctions-busting ship is now out of service,” not “This sanctions business ship is now out of service.”
ref_headline: This sanctions-busting ship is now out of service,
match_headline: New North Korea Concerns Flare as Trump’s Signature Diplomacy Wilts

text: An article on Friday about Ekrem Imamoglu’s findings as the 17-day mayor of Istanbul misstated how long Mr. Imamoglu served as a district mayor of an Istanbul suburb. It was five years, not 10.
match_headline: Cars, Contracts and Debt: What Istanbul’s Mayor Found in 17 Days

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 1 about Amazon Go’s first New York location misstates the number of cities in which Amazon tested its cashierless store. It was tested in three cities before New York, not 11.
match_headline: After a Messy Breakup With New York, Amazon Is Back With a Cashierless Go Store

text: An article on Friday about Blue Origin’s new moon lander misstated the amount the cargo version of the spacecraft could land on the moon. It could land 8,000 pounds, not tons.
match_headline: Jeff Bezos Unveils Blue Origin’s Vision for Space, and a Moon Lander

text: An article on Friday about a proposal by soccer clubs to restructure the Champions League misstated how many of the top teams would qualify automatically for the next season’s event under the new proposal. It is 24 teams, not 21.
match_headline: Proposal to Restructure Champions League Leaves Out Most of Europe

text: A picture caption with a film review on Friday about “Charlie Says,” using information from IFC Films, misidentified the actors. They are, from left, Julia Schlaepfer, Hannah Murray, Dayle McLeod, Sosie Bacon, Suki Waterhouse, Marianne Rendón and Kayli Carter. A second picture caption, again using information from IFC Films, also misidentified the actors. They are, from left, Marianne Rendón, Hannah Murray and Sosie Bacon.
match_headline: ‘Charlie Says’ Review: Complicating Those Manson Family Values

text: An article on Page 18 about the eight artists participating in the Whitney biennial describes incorrectly the scene in a Calvin Marcus painting. The figure lifting weights is the older man, not the younger one, who is hovering.
match_headline: The Whitney Biennial Called. How Will They Answer?

text: An article on Friday about the government response to sexual assault misidentified, in some editions, the chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee during the Kavanaugh hearings. It was Charles Grassley, not Lindsey Graham.
match_headline: Anita Hill: Let’s Talk About How to End Sexual Violence

text: A picture caption with the Economic View column last Sunday misstated the name of the agency that employed workers on a construction job in 1943. It was the Work Projects Administration, not the Works Progress Administration, which had been renamed in 1939.
match_headline: Manufacturing Can’t Create Enough Jobs. Infrastructure Can.

text: An article last Sunday about Uber misstated the timing of the decision by the current chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi, to keep Travis Kalanick, his predecessor, from taking part in a celebration this past Friday at the New York Stock Exchange of the company’s initial public offering. The decision was made on the evening of May 2, not on May 3.
match_headline: With Uber’s I.P.O., Dara Khosrowshahi Is Taking Travis Kalanick’s Company Public

text: An article last Sunday about riot grrrl misstated the name of a performer in Team Dresch. He is Marcéo Martinez, not Marci Martinez.
match_headline: Riot Grrrl United Feminism and Punk. Here’s an Essential Listening Guide.

text: Because of an editing error, the Q. and A. article last Sunday, about the Black Mamba Anti-Poaching Unit, referred incorrectly to its makeup. The group is predominantly female, not all-female.
match_headline: ‘Wild Animals Belong to All of Us’

text: An article last Sunday about the Nobu Ryokan hotel in Malibu, Calif., misstated the name of the designer of the bed linens. It is Anichini, not Anichi.
match_headline: The Anxiety of the $2,300-a-Night Hotel Room

text: An article on Saturday about the French adventurer Jean-Jacques Savin referred imprecisely to the vessel that picked up Jean-Jacques Savin. It was the tanker Maritime Kelly Anne, not the maritime tanker Kelly Anne.
match_headline: He Crossed the Atlantic in a Barrel. We Asked Him About Dodging Ships and Using ‘La Toilette.’

text: An article on Thursday about a proposal that will require pharmaceutical companies to include the price of prescription drugs in television advertisements misstated the amount of money spent by the drug industry on advertisements, including television commercials. According to Kantar, which tracks media spending, the drug industry spent nearly $5.9 billion, not $5 billion, on all advertising in 2018. Of that, about $4.5 billion, not $4 billion, was spent on television ads.
match_headline: Drug Prices Will Soon Appear in Many TV Ads

text: An article on Sunday about the removal of two Harvard deans from their positions at an undergraduate house misstated the month when Harvey Weinstein is scheduled to face trial. It is September, not June.
match_headline: Harvard’s First Black Faculty Deans Let Go Amid Uproar Over Harvey Weinstein Defense

text: An article on Saturday about Anna Sorokin’s statements from prison following her sentencing of four to 12 years in prison misspelled the name of a television show created by Shonda Rhimes. It is “Grey’s Anatomy,” not “Gray’s.”
match_headline: A Fake Heiress Called Anna Delvey Conned the City’s Wealthy. ‘I’m Not Sorry,’ She Says.

text: An article on Monday about New Zealand’s efforts to build global support for measures to curb online violence misstated Australia’s expected position on a nonbinding pledge called the “Christchurch Call.” It is among the countries expected to sign the pledge.
match_headline: New Zealand Seeks Global Support for Tougher Measures on Online Violence

text: A picture caption with a dance review on Saturday about Stephen Baynes’s “Unspoken Dialogues” misidentified the dancer shown on the floor. He is Callum Linnane, not Nathan Brook.
match_headline: Review: Australian Ballet Returns With Homegrown Talent, Humdrum Program

text: An article on Tuesday about an investigation of Michael Steinhardt’s behavior toward members of the N.Y.U. faculty, staff and student body referred incorrectly to a $10 million gift from Mr. Steinhardt and his wife. It was the largest gift that N.Y.U.’s graduate school of education had ever received, not the largest that the university had ever received.
match_headline: N.Y.U. Hires Law Firm to Investigate Behavior of Steinhardt, a Prominent Donor

text: An article on Tuesday about a WhatsApp security flaw misidentified the country from which a lawyer received telephone calls at odd hours. It was Sweden, not Norway.
match_headline: WhatsApp Rushes to Fix Security Flaw Exposed in Hacking of Lawyer’s Phone

text: An article on Tuesday about a $2 billion jury verdict against Monsanto misstated the reduced amount of a verdict against Monsanto last year. A judge reduced an award of $289 million to $78 million, not to $89 million.
match_headline: $2 Billion Verdict Against Monsanto Is Third to Find Roundup Caused Cancer

text: A chart accompanying a Q, and A. article on May 1, about the greenhouse gas impacts of various foods, misstated a value for milk. The 1.6 kilograms of carbon dioxide resulting from milk production is per half-liter of milk, not per 50 grams of protein.
match_headline: In a Switch, Some Republicans Start Citing Climate Change as Driving Their Policies

text: A recipe accompanying the Good Appetite column last Wednesday, for skillet greens with runny eggs, peas and pancetta, omitted instructions for adding the ramp or scallion greens. They should be added with the chard leaves in Step 3.
match_headline: Google’s Sundar Pichai: Privacy Should Not Be a Luxury Good

text: An article on May 4 about restrictions in Florida that will require felons to fully pay back fines in order to regain their voting rights referred incorrectly to the number of states that have laws prohibiting anyone with a felony record from voting. In addition to Iowa and Kentucky, Virginia has a similar law, but it permits the governor to restore voting rights in individual cases.
match_headline: Floridians Gave Ex-Felons the Right to Vote. Lawmakers Just Put a Big Obstacle in Their Way.

text: An article on Wednesday about Google’s plans for online commerce misstated the name of a marketing analytics firm. It is Jumpshot, not Jumpstart. The article also misstated what grew 39 percent on sites like Google and YouTube, according to quarterly results announced by Alphabet last month. It was paid clicks on ads, not ads themselves.
match_headline: Attention, Amazon Shoppers: Google Wants Some of Your Spending Money

text: An article on Wednesday about a funeral home where several minor league baseball players have lived misspelled the surname of a pitcher. He is Cale Coshow, not Coshnow. Because of an editing error, the article also misspelled the surname of Bob Gillette’s neighbor. He is Pat Revello, not Rovello.
match_headline: For These Minor Leaguers, the Living Is Good if You Don’t Mind the Dead Below

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the economist Alice M. Rivlin misstated her parents’ surname. It was Mitchell, not Rivlin. (As the obituary correctly stated, Rivlin was the surname of her first husband.) Because of another editing error, it also misstated the given name of Ms. Rivlin’s husband, who survives her. He is Sidney G. Winter, not Signey.
match_headline: Alice M. Rivlin, 88, a Leading Government Economist, Is Dead

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the struggles of women running for Parliament in India misstated the number of women contesting a seat in Haryana. As the article correctly stated, Swati Yadav is one of two women in the race. She is not the only woman candidate.
match_headline: A Whitewashed Monument to Women’s Suffrage

text: An article on Thursday about Tiger Woods’s spinal fusion surgery misstated Tony Delitto’s position at the University of Pittsburgh. He is the dean of the School of Health and Rehabilitation Sciences, not the chairman of physical therapy.
match_headline: How Tiger Woods Won the Back Surgery Lottery

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the cancellation of the “Jeremy Kyle Show” referred incorrectly to the relationship between Steve Dymond and his former partner. She was his girlfriend, not his wife.
match_headline: ‘Jeremy Kyle Show’ Canceled After Death of Guest

text: An article on Friday about Israel’s position on Iran misstated the name of the port near which four oil tankers were reportedly sabotaged. It is Fujairah, not Jubairah.
match_headline: Israel Presses the Case Against Iran, but Not for War

text: An article on Wednesday about a man accused of killing one person and injuring another on the Appalachian Trail misspelled the name of a hiker who encountered the attacker on the trail. She is Madeline Gosse, not Madeline Gossee.
match_headline: Hikers Take to the Appalachian Trail to Escape the Real World. This Time, They Couldn’t.

text: An article on Friday about House Democrats’ hope that Robert S. Mueller III will testify before the House Judiciary Committee misstated which version of the special counsel’s report was read aloud. The redacted version of Mr. Mueller’s report was read aloud, not the unredacted report, which has not been released. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Frustrated House Democrats Pin Their Hopes on Mueller

text: An article on May 4 about the loosening of regulations on offshore drilling equipment misidentified the petroleum industry group led by Barry Russell. He is chief executive of the Independent Petroleum Association of America, not the Independent Petroleum Producers of America.
match_headline: Interior Dept. Loosens Offshore-Drilling Safety Rules Dating From Deepwater Horizon

text: An article on Friday about the record set by Brooks Koepka at Long Island’s Bethpage State Park Black Course misstated the timing of Mr. Koepka’s three major titles. He won them over the last eight major tournaments, not the last seven. The article also misstated the number of birdies Danny Lee had in the first round. He had eight, not seven.
match_headline: Brooks Koepka, Happily in the Shadows, Sets Bethpage Black Record

text: An article on Page 37 about the choreographer Alexei Ratmansky misspells the given name of a pianist. It is Jacek Mysinski, not Yacek.
match_headline: ‘More Than Pretty Dances’: Alexei Ratmansky’s Alliance With Ballet Theater

text: An article on Page 35 about the musician Kevin Parker misstates the given name of the A&R manager at Universal Music Australia who first signed Tame Impala. It is Glen Goetze, not Greg.
match_headline: Tame Impala Makes Music for Loners. But Now Kevin Parker Plays the World’s Biggest Stages.

text: An article on Page 18 about Annette Bening refers incorrectly to the category for which Ms. Bening was nominated for a Tony Award this year. It is for best actress in a play, not featured actress in a play.
match_headline: How Annette Bening Puts It All Onstage. But Keeps Something for Herself.

text: An article on Page 101 about sour foods misstates the nationality of the historian Herodotus; he was Greek, not Roman.
An article on Page 112 about site-specific art refers incorrectly to the location of the Cranbrook Art Museum; it is in Bloomfield Hills, Mich., not Detroit.

An obituary on Friday about the architect I. M. Pei misstated the current name of the firm originally known as I. M. Pei & Associates. It is Pei Cobb Freed & Partners — not Pei, Cobb and Freed. The obituary also misspelled the surname of the former president of France who invited Mr. Pei to update and expand the Louvre Museum. He was François Mitterrand, not Mitterand.

text: An obituary on Dec. 31 about Nancy Grace Roman, NASA’s first chief of astronomy, misstated the date of her death. It was Dec. 25, not Dec. 26. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of editors only recently.

text: An essay last Sunday about ethics and museum money misquoted part of a letter that the Whitney’s director, Adam Weinberg, sent to the museum’s staff. He wrote that “trustees do not hire staff, select exhibitions, organize programs or make acquisitions,” not that trustees do not “remove board members.”
ref_headline: trustees do not hire staff, select exhibitions, organize programs or make acquisitions,

text: An article on Page 101 about sour foods misstates the nationality of the historian Herodotus; he was Greek, not Roman.
An article on Page 112 about site-specific art refers incorrectly to the location of the Cranbrook Art Museum; it is in Bloomfield Hills, Mich., not Detroit.

text: A review on March 10 about “An American Summer,” by Alex Kotlowitz, misspelled the given name of a teenage girl who was shot and killed in Chicago in 2012. Her name was Shakaki Asphy, not Shakiki.
match_headline: Growing Up With Murder All Around

text: An essay last Sunday about America’s founders misstated where Lois Peters, the wife of an Army captain, lived during the Revolutionary War. It was Connecticut, not Massachusetts.
match_headline: Why We Still Care About America’s Founders

text: An article on Thursday about new details of an attack on Camp Bastion in Afghanistan misspelled the given name of the acting Afghan secretary of defense. He is Asadullah Khalid, not Atiqullah.
match_headline: Spies, Stealth and Threats: How Militants Infiltrated a Vital Army Base

text: An article on Thursday about Iraq’s concerns about another war with the United States referred incorrectly to Canada’s support for the Bush administration’s decision to invade Iraq in 2003. While Canada was a close ally during the Bush administration, it did not support the war in Iraq.
match_headline: Iraq, Fearing Another U.S. War, Warns Militias Against Provocation

text: An article on Sunday about the momentum of the anti-abortion movement referred incorrectly to Mary Elizabeth Coleman of Missouri. She is a state representative, not a state senator.
match_headline: ‘This Is a Wave’: Inside the Network of Anti-Abortion Activists Winning Across the Country

text: An article on Sunday about President Trump’s indication that he may pardon servicemen accused of war crimes misstated the given name of the attorney general. He is William P. Barr, not Robert Barr.
match_headline: Trump May Be Preparing Pardons for Servicemen Accused of War Crimes

text: An article last Monday about the prosecutor John H. Durham’s assignment to examine the origins of the Russia investigation referred incorrectly to the status of George Papadopoulos and Carter Page, two Trump campaign advisers, at the time when law enforcement officials assigned an informant to gather information about them. Mr. Papadopoulos and Mr. Page were members of the campaign at the time.
match_headline: Barr Assigns U.S. Attorney in Connecticut to Review Origins of Russia Inquiry

text: An article on Wednesday about new projects in Times Square misidentified the location of the planned entrance to the Palace Theater. It will be on West 47th Street, not East 47th Street.

text: An article on Monday about making yourself less available misstated the name of the business school at the University of Michigan. It is the University of Michigan Ross School of Business, not Michigan Ross University.
match_headline: Why You Should Try to Be a Little More Scarce

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the graffiti artist Brian Donnelly’s effect on the art market referred incorrectly to sales of postwar and contemporary art at the three auction houses that totaled $981 million. That figure was for evening sales alone, not the spring sales.
match_headline: Contemporary Art Evening Sales Bring $981 Million, Led by Koons and KAWS

text: An article on Monday about the art dealer Robert Mnuchin misspelled the surname of an artist whose work was collected by Robert Mnuchin’s father. He is Franz Kline, not Klein.
match_headline: Robert Mnuchin Would Rather Not Discuss His Client (or His Son)

text: An obituary on Saturday about Fleming Begaye Sr., a code talker in World War II, misstated the date of his death. He died on May 10.
match_headline: Fleming Begaye, Navajo Code Talker Honored at White House, Dies at 97

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the re-election of Australia’s conservative coalition misspelled the name of a town in New South Wales, Australia. It is Narrabri, not Narrabi.
match_headline: It Was Supposed to Be Australia’s Climate Change Election. What Happened?

text: An article on Tuesday about criticism of President Trump’s demands for investigations into his political opponents misstated Mark Rozell’s role at George Mason University. He is the dean of the Schar School of Policy and Government, not a law professor.
match_headline: Trump’s Demands for Investigations of Opponents Draw Intensifying Criticism

text: An article on Tuesday about job cuts at Ford Motor misstated the timing of layoffs that Ford plans in the United States. The company said that there would be 500 layoffs this week and an unspecified number over the next several weeks, and that its domestic job cuts, including those already made, would total 800 by August. Ford did not say 800 employees would be laid off over the next several weeks.
match_headline: Job Cuts at Ford Motor to Total 7,000 by August

text: An article on Tuesday about the Golden State Warriors’ victory over the Portland Trail Blazers on Monday night misstated the number of rebounds by Stephen Curry. He had 13, not 12.
match_headline: Warriors Sweep Blazers to Reach Their 5th Straight N.B.A. Finals

text: An article on Tuesday about seating arrangement mishaps at the upcoming FIFA Women’s World Cup misstated when Dawn Bauman was trying to pair up friends and families at the event. It happened Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Going to the Women’s World Cup? You Might Not Sit With Your Family and Friends

text: A picture with an article last Wednesday about Persian cooking was published in error. The correct picture of khoresh-e ghormeh sabzi (Persian herb, bean and lamb stew) is at nytimes.com/food.
match_headline: Samin Nosrat’s 10 Essential Persian Recipes

text: An article on Wednesday about the release of John Walker Lindh misstated the family member through which he was able to gain Irish citizenship. It was his paternal grandmother, not his paternal great-grandmother.
match_headline: John Walker Lindh, Known as the ‘American Taliban,’ Is Set to Leave Federal Prison This Week

text: A chart with an article on Wednesday about the rural-urban political divide in the United States referred incorrectly to the votes cast for Hillary Clinton in the 2016 presidential race. She received more votes than Donald J. Trump, not the votes of most Americans.
match_headline: How the Rural-Urban Divide Became America’s Political Fault Line

text: An article on Wednesday about fund-raising methods for Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s campaign misstated which years Leah Daughtry ran the Democratic National Convention. They were 2008 and 2016, not 2008 and 2012.
match_headline: As Biden Rakes In Big Money, Will There Be a Political Cost?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the opening of the W.N.B.A. season omitted one of the 12 teams in the W.N.B.A. The digital version of the article has been updated to include the Dallas Wings.
match_headline: W.N.B.A. Season Preview: Does a Ring Await Elena Delle Donne?

text: An editorial on Tuesday about a financier’s promise to pay off all student loans for this year’s graduates of Morehouse College referred imprecisely to the average debt load of recent college graduates. Recipients of bachelor’s degrees in 2016 who left school with debt owed an average of about $30,301. That was not the average debt of all bachelor degree recipients in 2016.
match_headline: We Are Applauding the ‘Gift’ of an Affordable Education. Something Has Gone Wrong.

text: An obituary on May 11 about the German actress Hannelore Elsner misstated her age when her brother died in an air raid. She was 2, not 3.
match_headline: Hannelore Elsner, Compelling German Actress, Is Dead at 76

text: An article on Thursday about the decision to delay putting Harriet Tubman’s image on the $20 bill misstated the party affiliation of Representative John Katko of New York. He is a Republican, not a Democrat.
match_headline: Harriet Tubman $20 Bill Is Delayed Until Trump Leaves Office, Mnuchin Says

text: Because of an editing error, a digital headline with an article about the Brexit Party misspelled the given name of the party’s leader. As the article correctly noted, he is Nigel Farage, not Neil.
match_headline: How Farage’s Brexit Party Is Crushing Its Opponents

text: An article on Wednesday about a police raid of a freelance journalist’s home misidentified the union where Kat Anderson holds a position. She is interim executive officer at the Pacific Media Workers Guild, not Guild Freelancers.
match_headline: After Police Raid and a Hearing, a San Francisco Freelancer Will Get His Property Back

text: An article on Thursday about top amateur baseball players who sign with foreign professional leagues instead of with Major League Baseball misidentified the school attended by Carter Stewart. It is Eastern Florida State College, not Eastern Florida State University.
match_headline: Carter Stewart, 19, Chooses Japan Over the M.L.B. Draft

text: An article on Thursday about bookshelves as a design staple misstated the surname of a used-book seller. He is Chuck Roberts, not Chuck Wonder.
match_headline: A Room Without Books Is Just Very Sad

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the Kenyan author Binyavanga Wainaina referred incorrectly to the Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie. She is a woman.
match_headline: Binyavanga Wainaina, Pioneering Voice in African Literature, Dies at 48

text: An obituary on Thursday about Jake Black of the band Alabama 3, using information from a representative, omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to his two sisters and his brother Robert, he is survived by another brother, Steven.
match_headline: Jake Black, a Composer of the ‘Sopranos’ Theme, Dies at 59

text: An article on Friday about new requirements considered by New York State health officials to prevent the spread of the drug-resistant fungus Candida auris misspelled the given name of a trade group official. She is Zeynep Sumer King, not Zyenep.
match_headline: To Fight Deadly Candida Auris, New York State Proposes New Tactics

text: An entry in the Listings pages on Friday about kid-friendly activities in New York this weekend misspelled the surname of one of the creators of “Pip’s Island.” He is Walter Krudop, not Kudrop.
match_headline: 7 Things to Do With Your Kids in N.Y.C. This Weekend

text: An article on Friday about television shows to watch this summer misidentified where “Los Espookys” was made. It was filmed in Chile, not Mexico City.
match_headline: Here’s What to Watch on TV This Summer

text: An article on Page 10 this weekend about 2019 summer movies, using information provided by the film’s representatives, misstates the release date of “21 Bridges.” It is now opening in September, not the summer. Using information provided by Sony, the article also misstates the release date for “Spider-Man: Far From Home.” It is July 2, not July 5.
match_headline: Summer Movies 2019: Here’s What’s Coming Soon to Theaters

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about the fashion designer Virgil Abloh misspells the name of the director of AMO. He is Samir Bantal, not Bental.
match_headline: Virgil Abloh Has Designs on High Culture

text: An article on Page 26 this weekend about ABC’s “The View” misstates Lis Smith’s role in Mayor Pete Buttigieg’s campaign. She is his communications adviser, not his campaign manager.
match_headline: How ‘The View’ Became the Most Important Political TV Show in America

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the racecar driver Niki Lauda misstated the results of the 1977 Formula One world championship. Lauda defeated Jody Scheckter by 17 points; he did not defeat James Hunt by a single point.
match_headline: Niki Lauda, Formula One Champion Who Pushed Limits, Dies at 70

text: An article last Sunday about the Verde Valley wine region in Arizona misstated the status of Maynard Keenan, the lead singer of the alt-metal band Tool. Mr. Keenan remains active in the band.
match_headline: In the Arizona High Desert, Taking the Temperature of a Wine Boom

text: Because of a production error, a picture caption with an article last Sunday about the market for home sales in the Hamptons misidentified who was shown in the top images. It was Keith Baltimore and his house, not Jon Vaccari and Steve Fleming and their house.
match_headline: In the High-Flying Hamptons, Real Estate Is in a Rut

text: Because of an editing error, a review on May 5 about Julie Orringer’s novel “The Flight Portfolio” — which is based on the story of Varian Fry, who helped rescue thousands of anti-Nazi and Jewish refugees in Vichy France — quoted a phrase that does not appear in the finished book. In the author’s note that appeared in advance reading copies, Orringer, discussing Fry’s sexuality and his sensitivity to those who suffered persecution, said she “made that a part of his character.” But the sentence containing that phrase was deleted in the final version of the book.

text: A review on May 12 about “Our Man: Richard Holbrooke and the End of the American Century,” by George Packer, misstated Anthony Lake’s connection to Barack Obama. He was an adviser on foreign policy during the 2008 presidential campaign; he was not the national security adviser in the Obama administration. (He did serve as national security adviser in the Clinton administration.)
ref_headline: Our Man: Richard Holbrooke and the End of the American Century,

text: An article on May 18 about Aleksandr Gorbunov, the creator of the online persona StalinGulag, misstated the age of Mr. Gorbunov’s mother. She is 65, not in her 80s.
match_headline: Putin’s Toughest Online Critic Brings His Name, and Wheelchair, Into the Light

text: An article on Sunday about the 10th climber to die on Mount Everest this season referred incorrectly to the death toll for the 2019 climbing season on Everest. Seventeen have died in the Himalayas so far this season, not on Mount Everest alone.
match_headline: British Climber Dies on Everest as Traffic Jam’s Toll Rises to 10

text: An article on Friday about traffic near the summit of Mount Everest misspelled the given name of one of the mountain guides interviewed for this story. His name is Thupden Sherpa, not Phupden.
match_headline: On Everest, Traffic Isn’t Just Inconvenient. It Can Be Deadly.

text: An article on Monday about killings by the police in Rio de Janeiro misstated the given name of the governor of the state of Rio de Janeiro. He is Wilson Witzel, not William.
match_headline: ‘They Came to Kill.’ Almost 5 Die Daily at Hands of Rio Police.

text: An article on Tuesday about the European Parliament elections misstated the given name of Mr. Macron’s parliamentary majority leader. He is Gilles Le Gendre, not Gilbert.
match_headline: European Vote Reveals an Ever More Divided France

text: An article on Monday about Senator Cory Booker’s recent visit to Iowa misspelled the surname of one of the candidates for the Democratic presidential nomination. He is Mayor Pete Buttigieg, not Buttitgieg.
match_headline: Cory Booker Says Beating Trump Should Be ‘the Floor, Not the Ceiling’

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about animal rescue operations in Oklahoma misspelled the surname of a man who was helping to rescue a cat from a flooded house. He is Corie Rybak, not Rybuk.
match_headline: Saving Charlie: A Rush to Rescue Stranded Cats and Dogs from Oklahoma Floods

text: An article on Friday about the former White House communications director Hope Hicks misidentified the individual who appointed Robert S. Mueller III as special counsel. It was Rod Rosenstein, not Jeff Sessions.
match_headline: Hope Hicks Left the White House. Now She Must Decide Whether to Talk to Congress.

text: An article on Sunday about a fact-check on Senator Bernie Sanders’s campaign trail misspelled the surname of a moderator at a Fox News town hall in which Mr. Sanders participated in April. She is Martha MacCallum, not McCallum.
match_headline: Fact-Checking Bernie Sanders on the Campaign Trail

text: An article on Tuesday about a couple attacked in their Brooklyn home misidentified the street where the couple lived. It is Garden Street, not Garden Avenue. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: 71-Year-Old Woman Is Killed, and Her Husband Is Wounded, in Stabbing Attack

text: An article on Saturday about a security failure on a title insurance provider site misstated the day when Moody’s, the ratings agency, cut its outlook on Equifax. The agency made the change on May 17, not Wednesday, May 22.
match_headline: Security Gap Leaves 885 Million Mortgage Documents Exposed

text: An article on Monday about Sunday’s game between the New York Yankees and the Kansas City Royals misstated the final score. It was 8-7, not 7-6.
match_headline: A Rare Defensive Lapse by Gio Urshela Dooms Yankees to Defeat

text: An article on Saturday about the president of the Oakland Athletics misstated the reason for an A’s celebration last year. The team was celebrating the 50th anniversary of its first season in Oakland in its 51st season there; it was not celebrating its 50th season in Oakland.
match_headline: Can This Man Keep the A’s in Oakland?

text: An article on Monday about Saturday’s game between the Toronto Raptors and the Milwaukee Bucks misstated the final score of Game 6 of the Eastern Conference finals. The Raptors beat the Bucks, 100-94, not 100-96.
match_headline: With Kawhi Leonard, the Raptors Find Success That Endures

text: An article on Monday about writer-actress-producer Emerald Fennell misstated the awards that the first season of “Killing Eve” received. It was nominated for Emmys; it did not win them.
match_headline: ‘Killing Eve’ Showrunner: ‘All Obsession Is Sexual’

text: A review on Saturday about the New York Philharmonic’s “Music of Conscience” series misstated the dates that John Corigliano’s Symphony No. 1 will be performed. It will be May 30 and June 1, not May 30 and 31.
match_headline: John Corigliano and David Lang: Two Paths to Political Music

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about what’s on TV that day, using information from HBO, misidentified one actor. He is Joe Dempsie, not Daniel Portman.
match_headline: What’s on TV Sunday: ‘Vida’ and ‘Game of Thrones: The Last Watch’

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Bill Buckner, the major league baseball player whose historic error in Game 6 of the 1986 World Series led to a Mets victory, misstated the score when the Mets outfielder Mookie Wilson came to the plate in the bottom of the 10th inning. It was 5-4, not 5-5. (The tying run was scored on a wild pitch during his at-bat. He then hit the game-winning ground ball that passed through Buckner’s legs.)
match_headline: Bill Buckner, All-Star Shadowed by World Series Error, Dies at 69

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the biographer Edmund Morris misstated the subject of a biography by Sylvia Jukes Morris, his wife. It is Edith Kermit Roosevelt, Theodore Roosevelt’s second wife, not Eleanor Roosevelt. Based on information supplied by the family, the obituary also misstated the given name of Mr. Morris’s surviving brother. It is Roy, not Eric.
match_headline: Edmund Morris, Reagan Biographer Who Upset Conventions, Dies at 78

text: An article on Monday about Ireland’s vote to ease divorce restrictions referred imprecisely to the country’s 2015 vote to approve same-sex marriage. While it was the first nation to approve gay marriage by popular vote, it did not hold the world’s first popular vote on the issue.
match_headline: Ireland Votes Overwhelmingly to Ease Divorce Restrictions

text: An article on Wednesday about Representative Justin Amash, Republican of Michigan, misidentified an attendee at a town-hall-style meeting who was reconsidering her support for him. She is Cathy Garnaat, not Teena Quinn.
match_headline: Justin Amash, Under Attack for Impeachment Talk, Finds Mixed Support at Home

text: An article on Sunday about paying reparations to black Americans for suffering under slavery referred imprecisely to former President Barack Obama’s eligibility for compensation. Mr. Obama could qualify for a reparations program based on his maternal ancestry; it has not been determined that he would not qualify.
match_headline: What Reparations for Slavery Might Look Like in 2019

text: An article on Wednesday about the decision in some states to include a nonbinary gender option on government documents misspelled the surname of a longtime advocate for progressive causes in Hawaii. She is Jocelyn Doane, not Doan.
match_headline: Which Box Do You Check? Some States Are Offering a Nonbinary Option

text: An article on Thursday about a boat sinking in the Danube River misidentified the Hungarian news outlet that reported that 14 people had been brought to shore and other details. It was the state television news broadcaster M1, not the state news agency MTI.
match_headline: Boat Sinks in Danube, Killing at Least 7 on Tour of Budapest

text: An article on Thursday about Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s delay on scheduling a vote on an updated North American trade deal misidentified the chairman of the House Ways and Means subcommittee on trade. It is Representative Earl Blumenauer, not Bill Pascrell Jr.
match_headline: Pelosi Slow-Walks Trump’s New Nafta Deal

text: An article on Thursday about the game Pokémon Sleep misspelled the name of a Pokémon species. The creatures are Eevees, not Eevies.
match_headline: Pokémon Sleep Wants to Make Snoozing a Game Too

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about a queer Muslim character who appeared on CBS misspelled the surname of one actor. He is Ben Sprunger, not Ben Springer.
match_headline: Queer Muslims Are Still Rare on TV. One Writer Wants to Change That.

text: An article on Thursday about the mini-series “Good Omens” misstated the title of a movie directed by Terry Gilliam. It is “12 Monkeys,” not “13 Monkeys.”
match_headline: ‘Good Omens’ Unites an Angel and a Demon for Judgment Day

text: An article on Friday about a bombing campaign in the last rebel-held province in Syria misstated Dr. Zaher Sahloul’s affiliation. He is the president of MedGlobal, not the Syrian American Medical Society. (Dr. Sahloul formerly headed that organization.)
match_headline: Huge Wave of Syrians Flee Intensified Bombing on Last Rebel-Held Province

text: An article on Friday about the execution of North Korean officials, as reported by a South Korean daily, misidentified Kim Yo-jong’s brother. It is Kim Jong-un, not Kim Jong-il.
match_headline: North Korea Executed and Purged Top Nuclear Negotiators, South Korean Report Says

text: An article on Friday about the measles outbreak in the United States misstated the number of confirmed cases of measles in New York City from September 2018 through May 29. It is 550, not 500.
match_headline: Measles Cases Reach Highest Level in More Than 25 Years, C.D.C. Says

text: Because of an editing error, a graphic with an article on Thursday about how tariffs on products made in China would affect an American bicycle maker misstated the cost to consumers. The new 25 percent tariff applies to the wholesale cost of the company’s bikes, not their retail price.
match_headline: This Boutique Bike Shop Shows How Trump’s Tariffs Can Hit the Little Guy

text: An article on Friday about three exhibitions in New York that are marking Walt Whitman’s 200th birthday misstated when a marathon reading of “Song of Myself” will take place in Brooklyn Bridge Park. It is Sunday, not Monday.
match_headline: On Walt Whitman’s Big Birthday, 10 Glorious Relics

text: An article on Saturday about tariff threats to Mexico misidentified the official at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce who said, “Given the gravity of the situation we have to explore all our options.” It was Neil Bradley, the chief policy officer at the chamber, not John G. Murphy, the senior vice president of international affairs. The article also misspelled the surname of Mexico’s foreign minister. He is Marcelo Ebrard, not Ebrand.
ref_headline: Given the gravity of the situation we have to explore all our options.
match_headline: Trump’s Tariff Threat Sends Mexico, Lawmakers and Businesses Scrambling

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about Leah Chase, the nation’s pre-eminent Creole chef, referred incorrectly to the time when Mrs. Chase stopped Barack Obama from putting hot sauce in his gumbo. It was during his presidential run in 2008; not during his presidency.
match_headline: Leah Chase, 96, Creole Chef Who Fed Presidents and Freedom Riders, Dies

text: An article on Sunday about a murder trial in Vancouver misstated the location of Pym Island. It is near Vancouver Island, not Victoria Island.
match_headline: A Tale of Murder, Revenge and a Canadian Immigrant Dream Gone Wrong

text: An article on Monday about an investigation into an airstrike killing in Afghanistan misspelled the surname of a spokesman for the American forces in Afghanistan. He is Bob Purtiman, not Puritman.
match_headline: Caught Between U.S. and Taliban, a Family Dies and the Survivor Seeks Justice

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about American aid funds in Guatemala misspelled the given name of the former secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. She is Kirstjen Nielsen, not Kristjen.
match_headline: U.S. Promises Security Aid, but No Funds, to Guatemala to Curb Migration

text: A map with an article on Sunday about the Democratic primary schedule reversed the labels for Vermont and New Hampshire. Vermont is west of New Hampshire, not east.
match_headline: ‘You Don’t Have to Be in Des Moines.’ Democrats Expand Primary Map, Spurred by Social Media.

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the suspect in a Virginia Beach shooting on Friday misstated the location of the police officers pictured. They were outside Princess Anne Middle School in Virginia Beach, not the Virginia Beach Municipal Center.
match_headline: Suspect in Virginia Beach Shooting Was a Longtime City Employee

text: An article on May 26 about an outdoors enthusiast with cancer attributed an erroneous distinction to Aconcagua. It is the highest summit outside Asia, not the Himalayas.
match_headline: She Had Stage 4 Lung Cancer, and a Mountain to Climb

text: An article on Saturday about Friday’s French Open match between Karolina Pliskova and Petra Martic misidentified Polona Hercog’s home country. She is from Slovenia, not Slovakia.
match_headline: 2019 French Open: Upset of No. 2 Karolina Pliskova Opens Up the Women’s Draw Some More

text: An article on Saturday about Figment NYC misstated the number of people who attended Roosevelt Island’s annual cherry blossom festival in 2018. It was around 10,000, not 1,000.
match_headline: Art Festival Is Welcome, but Not the Huge Crowds

text: An obituary on May 25 about the physicist Murray Gell-Mann overstated a law about the conservation of a quantity in physics called strangeness.
