It is conserved in strong interactions and electromagnetic interactions but not in weak interactions. It is not the case that “like energy, strangeness must always be conserved.”
ref_headline: like energy, strangeness must always be conserved.
match_headline: Murray Gell-Mann, Who Peered at Particles and Saw the Universe, Dies at 89

text: An article on May 19 about Generation X and the fragrance CK One misidentified the font of the “CK” initials on the earliest bottles. The font was a serif in the Didone family; it was not a version of Futura Light.
match_headline: It Smelled Like Gen X Spirit

text: An article last Sunday about the dwindling number of diners across New York City misstated how many had been sold in Queens since 2014. It was six, not seven.
match_headline: New York’s Vanishing Diners

text: An article on May 19 about CBD referred incompletely to the professional affiliation of a neurologist who ran trials using CBD. Eric Marsh has positions at both the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania.

An article on Monday about the Trump Organization’s development project in Uruguay misstated the responsibilities of real estate developers in the country. Developers in Uruguay are subject to legal requirements to perform due diligence on the origins of funding for purchases.
match_headline: Inside a Flashy Trump Project in Uruguay: Cash Shortages and Mismanagement

text: An article on Tuesday about Mexico’s crackdowns on migrants referred incorrectly to Nuevo León. It is a state in Mexico, not a city.
match_headline: Mexico Cracks Down on Migrants, After Pressure From Trump to Act

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the “Tank Man” of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown described incorrectly a film that recreated the scene. While the film was promoting Leica cameras, the company says it did not commission the film.
match_headline: 30 Years After Tiananmen, ‘Tank Man’ Remains an Icon and a Mystery

text: An article on Tuesday about a Hollywood producer raising funds for a legal anti-abortion battle misspelled the surname of the author of the “Fear Street” novels. He is R.L. Stine, not Stein.
match_headline: Hollywood Producer Seeks to Raise Funds to Battle Anti-Abortion Laws

text: A chart with an article on Monday about the Arizona Diamondbacks’ draft picks misidentified the team that Gerrit Cole plays for. It is the Houston Astros, not the Pittsburgh Pirates. The chart also misstated how Cole entered Major League Baseball via the draft. While he was selected by the Yankees in 2008 — with the 28th overall pick, not the No. 1 pick — he did not enter M.L.B. until after he was the No. 1 overall pick by the Pirates in 2011.
match_headline: In M.L.B. Draft, Diamondbacks Hope a Wealth of Picks Pays Off

text: An article on Tuesday about endurance exercise and its benefits to heart health referred incorrectly in several instances to the risk posed by marathon running. Studies examined the risk of cardiac arrest, not heart attacks.
match_headline: Does Marathon Running Increase the Risk of Cardiac Arrest?

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Wednesday about Sancerre wines misidentified Sancerre. It is a wine region, not a grape.
match_headline: Despite Eye Rolls, Good Sancerres Rise Above the Sniping

text: An article last Wednesday about tupelo honey included an assertion by Vaughn Bryant, director of the palynology laboratory at Texas A&M University, that referred incorrectly to honey samples from Georgia. After publication, Dr. Bryant said he had sampled honey from Georgia that was shown in tests to be more than 90 percent tupelo, not that he had never sampled honey from Georgia that was more than 52 percent tupelo.
match_headline: On the Trail of Tupelo Honey, Liquid Gold From the Swamps

text: An obituary on May 7 about the dancer Norma Miller referred incorrectly to the troupe the Lindy Hoppers, of which she was the last survivor. Although it was primarily black, it is not the case that it had only black members.
match_headline: Norma Miller, Lindy-Hopping ‘Queen of Swing,’ Is Dead at 99

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about the art dealer Virginia Zabriskie misstated her mother’s surname. It was Marshall, not Zabriskie. (As the obituary correctly states, Ms. Zabriskie was born Virginia Marshall.)
match_headline: Virginia Zabriskie, 91, Art Dealer Who Promoted the Overlooked, Dies

text: An article on Wednesday about a police raid on the Australian Broadcasting Corporation referred incorrectly to a comment by Prime Minister Scott Morrison, “It never troubles me that our laws are being upheld.” He made the remark on Tuesday when asked about the raid on Annika Smethurst’s home, not on Wednesday in regard to two recent raids targeting journalists.
ref_headline: It never troubles me that our laws are being upheld.
match_headline: Australian Police Raids Target News Media Over Leaked Documents

text: An article on Wednesday about the possible collapse of the Palestinian Authority referred incorrectly to the exclusivity of the interview with Mr. Shtayyeh. It was one of his earliest interviews with a major Western news organization; it was not the first.
match_headline: New Palestinian Premier Warns of a ‘Very Hot Summer’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about eight people accused of using fake parking placards misstated the age of Adrian Ramprasad. He is 27, not 47.
match_headline: Charged With Stealing a Scarce Urban Asset: The Parking Space

text: An article on Monday about the arrest of the estranged husband in the disappearance of his wife incorrectly described the couple’s five children. There are three boys and two girls, not four boys and three girls.
match_headline: Estranged Husband Arrested in Disappearance of Connecticut Mother of 5

text: An article on Saturday about the actor Richard Madden misidentified the actress he previously dated. It was Ellie Bamber, not Jenna Coleman.
match_headline: It’s Going Great for Richard Madden. That’s What Worries Him

text: An article last Thursday about the author Elizabeth Gilbert misspelled the surname of a writer for The New Yorker. He was Alexander Woollcott, not Wolcott. The article also referred imprecisely to Ms. Gilbert’s travels in “Eat Pray Love.” She went to Italy, India and the Indonesian island of Bali; not to Italy, Indonesia and Bali.
match_headline: Eat, Pray, Love, Lose, Write a Book, Repeat

text: An article on Thursday about the families of American World War II veterans misspelled the surname of a researcher at the National World War II Museum in New Orleans. He is Dan Olmsted, not Olmstead.
match_headline: Their Fathers Never Spoke of the War. Their Children Want to Know Why.

text: An article on Wednesday about a protest in Prague demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Andrej Babis misstated the name of Mr. Babis’s political party. It is Ano, not Anos.
match_headline: Protesters Fill Prague Square Again, in New Struggle for Country’s Soul

text: An article on Thursday about President Trump’s visit to Ireland referred incorrectly to a comment made about Mr. Trump’s policies on climate change. It was Ireland’s president, Michael D. Higgins, not Prime Minister Leo Varadkar, who criticized Mr. Trump’s policies. The article, citing an Irish reporter, also rendered the comment incorrectly. Mr. Higgins called the policies “regressive” — not reckless — “and pernicious.”
match_headline: On Trump’s Ireland Visit, Talk of Brexit and Border Walls

text: An article on Thursday about new S.E.C. broker rules misidentified the political affiliation of the commissioner who voted against the new rules. Robert Jackson is an independent, not a Democrat.
match_headline: S.E.C. Adopts New Broker Rules That Consumer Advocates Say Are Toothless

text: An article on Thursday about a viral video in China misstated which officials in Minnesota declined to file charges against Richard Liu, the Chinese e-commerce billionaire. It was the prosecutor’s office, not the police.
match_headline: In China, a Viral Video Sets Off a Challenge to Rape Culture

text: An article on Thursday about Women’s World Cup teams misstated the best World Cup finish by Sweden’s women’s team. It was second place in 2003, not third place in 1991 and 2011.
match_headline: Women’s World Cup Preview: Meet the Teams

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Judge Ellen Bree Burns misspelled part of the name of a foundation involved in a 1992 case in which she presided. It is the Stewart B. McKinney Foundation, not Stuart. Because of an editing error, the obituary also erroneously credited Judge Burns with a distinction. Although she was the first woman to be appointed to the federal bench in Connecticut and the first woman to serve on its Superior Court, she was not the first female state judge in Connecticut history; she was the second.
match_headline: Ellen Bree Burns, Barrier-Breaking Connecticut Judge, Dies at 95

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s D-Day speech misstated the location of a Trump golf course in Ireland. It is Doonbeg, not Doonberg.
match_headline: Trump Honors D-Day Sacrifices, With Some Legacies Unspoken

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the New York police commissioner’s apology for the department’s actions during the 1969 Stonewall riots, using information from a film distributor, misidentified the event shown. The picture captured an arrest during a protest of the film “Cruising” in 1979, not during the Stonewall uprising in 1969.
match_headline: Stonewall Riot Apology: Police Actions Were ‘Wrong,’ Commissioner Admits

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about an Australian doctor who invented an implant to help block opioid effects misidentified the scientific equipment shown in the image. The containers shown in the image are flasks, not test tubes.
match_headline: An Australian Doctor’s Dream: Curing America’s Opioid Curse

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about Amanda Anisimova’s victory in the French Open quarterfinals misidentified the players shown in a group of images. Anisimova was shown at top and left, and her opponent, Simona Halep, was at right.
match_headline: Amanda Anisimova and Ashleigh Barty Reach French Open Semifinals

text: An article on Friday about an anonymous donation to the Philadelphia Orchestra misstated the length of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra’s strike earlier this year. It lasted 47 days, not 128.
match_headline: A $55 Million Gift Aims to Ensure the Philadelphia Orchestra’s Recovery

text: An article on Aug. 19, 2018, about the architect Le Corbusier’s influence in Japan referred incorrectly to Nicholas Fox Weber’s book “Le Corbusier: A Life.” The book discusses both the National Museum of Western Art in Tokyo and Le Corbusier’s blending of Modernism with Japanese traditions in his design for the building. It is not devoid of any reference to the museum or the association between Le Corbusier and Japan. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the editors’ attention only recently.
match_headline: How Le Corbusier Became Big in Japan

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the New Orleans musician Dr. John misstated his birth date. He was born on Nov. 20, 1941 — not Nov. 21, 1940. (As the obituary correctly states, he was 77.)
match_headline: Dr. John, of Voodoo Beads, Feathers and New Orleans Sound, Dies at 77

text: A picture caption with an article on May 26 about Shakespeare & Company misstated the location of Trevor Day School. It is on the Upper East Side, not in Harlem.
match_headline: 3 Days in a Van With a Shakespeare Troupe: Daggers and Dunkin’ Donuts

text: Because of an editing error, a review last Sunday about “Hot, Cold, Heavy, Light,” by Peter Schjeldahl, misstated the year that the author became The New Yorker’s art critic. It was 1998, not 1988.
match_headline: The Penetrating Gaze of One of America’s Most Brilliant Art Critics

text: Because of an editing error, an Opinion essay last Sunday about the British writer Letitia Elizabeth Landon described the poet Shelley incorrectly. He published his works in the 1810s and after, not in the 1790s.
match_headline: The Cautionary Tale of the ‘Female Byron’

text: An article on Thursday about a $500 million contribution by Michael R. Bloomberg, the former mayor of New York City, to a new campaign to close every coal-fired power plant in the United States included incorrect information about the roughly 280 coal plants that have shut down in the United States since 2010. Those closings represent about 40 percent of the country’s coal-fired power capacity, not 40 percent of all coal plants.
match_headline: Michael Bloomberg Promises $500 Million to Help End Coal

text: An article on Saturday about a proposal to demolish Columbine High School, the site of a horrific shooting in 1999, referred incorrectly to a plan to preserve the school’s library. The proposal concerns the Hope Columbine Memorial Library, which was built after the 1999 shooting; the school’s former library, where 10 students were killed, has been demolished.
match_headline: Columbine High School Could Be Torn Down to Deter Copycats

text: An article on Saturday about the trial of Thomas Gilbert Jr., a Princeton graduate accused of killing his father, misstated the year of his father’s murder. It was Jan. 4, 2015, not 2014.
match_headline: How a Princeton Graduate Accused of Killing His Father Got the Gun

text: An article on Monday about a deal between Fiat Chrysler Automobiles and Aurora Innovation on self-driving technology misstated the investment that Aurora announced in February that it had received from Amazon and others. It was $530 million, not $350 million.
match_headline: Fiat Chrysler in Deal for Self-Driving Car Technology

text: An article on Tuesday about the Supreme Court’s refusal to hear the appeal of a man who has been held in wartime detention at Guantánamo Bay prison for 17 years referred incorrectly to an opinion issued by Justice Stephen Breyer. It was a statement, not a dissenting opinion.
match_headline: Justice Breyer Raises Specter of Perpetual Detention Without Trial at Guantánamo

text: Because of an editing error, an article about a judicial ruling empowering the Food and Drug Administration authority to regulate a stem-cell treatment referred incorrectly to a company that made a blood product contaminated with bacteria. It was Genetech, not Genentech.
match_headline: A Judge Rules Against One Stem-Cell Clinic. There Are Hundreds of Them.

text: A picture caption with this article on Sunday about gay knitting circles incorrectly described how a blue piece was made. It was knitted, not crocheted.
match_headline: Trading the Noisy Gay Bar Scene for the Knitting Circle

text: A picture credit with a brief report in the Off the Menu article last Wednesday about the reopening of the restaurant Pastis misidentified the photographer. He is Emon Hassan, not Sara Naomi Lewkowicz.
match_headline: Pastis Reopens After a Five-Year Hiatus

text: An obituary on June 6 about the architect Stanley Tigerman misstated the location of the Power House energy museum his firm created. It is in Zion, Ill., not Indiana.
match_headline: Stanley Tigerman, Architect of Puckish Postmodernism, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Sunday about the drug dealer Nicky Barnes misstated the date this year that another drug dealer, Frank Lucas, died. It was May 30, not May 31.
match_headline: Nicky Barnes, ‘Mr. Untouchable’ of Heroin Dealers, Is Dead at 78

text: A picture caption with an article on June 2 about a luxurious Manhattan apartment listed for sale at $85 million misidentified an apartment shown in an image. It was a model apartment in the building, not the apartment being offered for sale.
match_headline: Perk for the Ultrarich: Buy an $85 Million Apartment, Get a Trip to Space

text: An article on Wednesday about the posting of a doctored video of Mark Zuckerberg as a challenge to Facebook’s rules misstated the surname of one of the artists behind the fake video. He is Bill Posters, not Powers.
match_headline: A Fake Zuckerberg Video Challenges Facebook’s Rules

text: An obituary on Saturday about the cookbook author Maida Heatter misstated the dates of two deaths. Ms. Heatter’s daughter, Toni Evins, died in 1989, not 1994; and her third husband, Ralph Daniels, died in 1991, not “a few months” after Ms. Evins.
match_headline: Maida Heatter, Cookbook Writer and the ‘Queen of Cake,’ Dies at 102

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the use of YouTube in Russia described incorrectly the material performed by Danila Poperechny, a Russian comedian. While Mr. Poperechny’s act is provocative, it is not filled with “blatant misogyny.” (The description of his act was based on brief video clips; longer versions of those videos showed the description to be inaccurate.)
match_headline: Looking for Free Speech in Russia? Try YouTube

text: An article on Thursday about an animal cruelty investigation of a New Jersey couple misspelled the surname of one of the dog breeders. He is Martin Strozeski, not Strozenski.
match_headline: 188 Sickly Dogs Hoarded by a One-Time Top Breeder at Westminster

text: An article on Thursday about business leaders’ concerns about street protests in Hong Kong gave an incorrect title for Fred Hu’s former position at Goldman Sachs. He was the chairman of its Greater China business, not its head.
match_headline: As Protesters Fill Hong Kong’s Streets, Businesses Are Alarmed, Too

text: An obituary on May 31 about Claus von Bülow, the socialite who was convicted and later acquitted of twice trying to murder his wife, overstated what is known about his father, Svend Borberg. Although he was arrested as a Nazi collaborator after World War II and sentenced to prison, it is not clear that he was “an admirer of the Third Reich.” The obituary also omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to those named, Mr. von Bülow is survived by a half brother, Henrik Borberg.
ref_headline: an admirer of the Third Reich.
match_headline: Claus von Bülow, Society Figure in High-Profile Case, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on May 31 about the singer Leon Redbone referred incorrectly to the Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem, where his parents lived before moving to Cyprus in the late 1940s. It was under the control of Jordan at the time, not Israel.
match_headline: Leon Redbone, Idiosyncratic Throwback Singer, Is Dead at 69

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s statement that he would accept campaign help from Russia misstated the given name of a senator from Iowa. It is Joni Ernst, not Jodi.
match_headline: Trump Is Assailed for Saying He Would Take Campaign Help From Russia

text: An article on Page 4 about an after-school program that invites students to build small sailboats from scratch refers incorrectly to a student. Kawthar Alsahqani is a girl. The article also misstates the location of the college from which Jovon Ferguson graduated. He graduated from Wheaton College in Massachusetts, not from Wheaton College in Illinois.
match_headline: How Middle Schoolers Built ‘Pizza Sail’ (Hint: Without Their Phones)

text: A picture credit with a photograph of Chuck Berry on Page 26 omits the name of the photographer. He is Jeff Lowenthal.
match_headline: The Day the Music Burned

text: An article on Page 40 about the U.S. women’s national soccer team refers incorrectly to past victories in the Women’s World Cup. It is not the case that no team has ever won back-to-back titles. Germany won the 2003 Cup and the following one in 2007.
match_headline: The Best Women’s Soccer Team in the World Fights for Equal Pay

text: An article on Page 22 about the 2020 Democratic presidential candidates misstates the number of bills Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota has sponsored or contributed to that became law under President Trump. It is 34, not 6.
match_headline: 23 Democrats Are Running for President. Do Any of Them Know What They’re Doing?

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the former United States ambassador to Cambodia John Gunther Dean referred incorrectly to the languages he knew when he was in the Army. He was skilled in German, English and French, but not Dutch.
match_headline: John Gunther Dean, U.S. Ambassador as Cambodia Fell, Dies at 93

text: An obituary on Thursday about the actress Sylvia Miles misstated the names of her parents and her first husband. Her parents were Reuben and Bella (Feldman) Scheinwald, not Reuben and Belle (Fellman) Lee; her first husband was William Myers, not Miles. The obituary, using information from a friend, also misstated where Ms. Miles died. It was in a hospital, not in an ambulance. And it misstated the role she played in the Off Broadway production “A Chekhov Sketchbook.” She played a woman whose husband thinks she’s a witch; she did not play a witch.
match_headline: Sylvia Miles, Actress With a Flair for the Flamboyant, Dies at 94

text: An article last Sunday about Hootie & the Blowfish misstated the name of one of the band’s songs. It is “Not Even the Trees,” not “Alone.”
match_headline: Hootie & the Blowfish, Great American Rock Band (Yes, Really)

text: A review on June 2 about Richard Roper’s novel, “How Not to Die Alone,” referred incorrectly to the book’s protagonist. His name is Andrew Smith. It is not the case that he has “no last name.”
match_headline: Turning a Bad Day at the Office Into Cubicle Comedy

text: An article on Saturday about the market for medical equipment in China misstated the prices of two M.R.I. machines that Siemens sold to public hospitals in China. They were $2.8 million and $4.7 million, not $2,800 and $4,700.
match_headline: Bribes and Backdoor Deals Help Foreign Firms Sell to China’s Hospitals

text: An article on Saturday about New York City’s allocation of $250,000 to support abortion access misstated which expenses will be paid directly by the New York Abortion Access Fund. The fund will refer women who need assistance with transportation costs to groups that pay those costs; it is not the case that the fund pays those costs directly.
match_headline: New York City Allocates $250,000 for Abortions, Challenging Conservative States

text: An article on Tuesday about Germany’s investigation into the killing of a regional councilman who was found dead earlier this month misspelled the councilman’s given name. He was Walter Lübcke, not Werner.
match_headline: Killing of German Politician Is Treated as Possible Terrorist Act

text: An article on Monday about Lucas Silverio, a teenager who died after rescuing a child from an apartment fire in the Bronx, misstated the surname of Mr. Silverio’s cousin. He is Jeury Tineo, not Jeury Martinez.
match_headline: A Teenager Had Nearly Escaped a Raging Fire. Then He Heard a Little Girl’s Cries.

text: An article on Saturday about the passage of a sweeping package of rent laws misstated a former rule under which an apartment in New York City could be deregulated. Both income and rent thresholds needed to be met for a unit to be deregulated, not only an income or a rent threshold. The article also misstated the amount of the rent threshold. It was $2,774, not $2,733.
match_headline: New Rent Laws Pass in N.Y.: ‘The Pendulum Is Swinging’ Against Landlords

text: An article on Sunday misidentified one of the five golfers who has achieved a modern career Grand Slam. Along with Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Jack Nicklaus and Tiger Woods, it was Gary Player — not Bobby Jones — who did it. (Jones’s Grand Slam predated the Masters tournament and golf’s modern professional era.)
match_headline: U.S. Open: Time Is Becoming Even Less on Phil Mickelson’s Side

text: An article on Saturday about Masai Ujiri’s altercation with a California sheriff’s deputy included outdated information about Mr. Ujiri. While he continues to be the Toronto Raptors’ team president, he is no longer the team’s general manager.
match_headline: Masai Ujiri Could Be Charged in Altercation After Raptors’ Title Win, Authorities Say

text: An article on Tuesday about No. 2 N.B.A. draft picks misstated the number of players who had become All-Stars after being chosen No. 2 in the draft this decade. Victor Oladipo and D’Angelo Russell both did it, not only Oladipo.
match_headline: Why Picking Second in the N.B.A. Draft Might Be a Bad Thing

text: An article on Tuesday about the Museum of Modern Art’s last official day open to the public before its planned renovation misstated the age of Chet Gold, a security supervisor at the Museum of Modern Art. He is 32, not 42.
match_headline: What 7 Visitors (and One Guard) Cherished on MoMA’s Closing Day

text: An article on March 29 about J.C. Penney ending its partnership with “Project Runway All Stars” misidentified the recent season of “Project Runway.” It had its 17th season, not its 18th. This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to editors’ attention.
match_headline: How ‘Project Runway All Stars’ Became an Ad for Nothing

text: An article last Wednesday about a new wave of Taiwanese cuisine in the United States misspelled the name of the steamed buns filled with braised pork belly, cilantro, chopped peanuts and pickled greens. They are gua bao, not guo bao.
match_headline: A New Generation of Chefs Reframes Taiwanese Cuisine in America

text: An obituary on Sunday about the film and opera director Franco Zeffirelli misstated part of the title of a Mozart opera. It is “Così Fan Tutte,” not “Così Fan Tutti.” The obituary also misstated the year of a production of “Tosca” with Maria Callas that Mr. Zeffirelli staged in London. It was 1964, not 1962.
match_headline: Franco Zeffirelli, Italian Director With Taste for Excess, Dies at 96

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about street protests in Hong Kong described incorrectly the circumstances in which a protester died late Saturday. The man fell to his death after unfurling a protest banner and remaining perched on scaffolding for several hours; he did not fall while hanging the banner.
match_headline: Carrie Lam, Hong Kong’s Leader, Retreats, but Her Critics Want More

text: An article on Wednesday about House Democrats’ consideration of a panel to develop proposals and a “national apology” to repair the lingering effects of slavery misidentified a candidate campaigning for president in 2020. He is Julián Castro, not his twin brother, Joaquin Castro.
match_headline: House Democrats, With Pelosi’s Support, Will Consider a Commission on Reparations

text: An article on Tuesday about the death of Everett Palmer Jr. at York County Prison misstated who wrote the autopsy report for the York County Coroner’s office. It was Dr. Rameen Starling-Roney, not Pamela Gay. It also misstated the news organization that first reported his death. It was The York Daily Record, not NY1.
match_headline: A Prison Death, a Mysterious Autopsy and Official Silence

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about William Kentridge and Faustin Linyekula’s Holland Festival misidentified the city in the Democratic Republic of Congo where Faustin Linyekula’s Studios Kabako is located; it is in Kisangani, not Kinshasa.
match_headline: A Festival at the Intersection of Amsterdam and Africa

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Charles A. Reich, the author of “The Greening of America,” misspelled the given name of a scholar who wrote about Mr. Reich’s book in 2007. He is Rodger D. Citron, not Roger. The obituary also omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to his nephew, Daniel Reich, Mr. Reich is survived by a niece, Alice Reich.
match_headline: Charles Reich, Who Saw ‘The Greening of America,’ Dies at 91

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s comments about working with segregationist senators in the 1970s misidentified the man shown at a Watergate hearing in 1973. He was former Attorney General John N. Mitchell, not Senator Herman E. Talmadge of Georgia.
match_headline: Joe Biden and Democratic Rivals Exchange Attacks Over His Remarks on Segregationists

text: An article on Thursday about Hope Hicks’s appearance before the House Judiciary Committee on Wednesday referred incorrectly in one instance to the proceedings. The hearing was held in private, not in public.
match_headline: Hope Hicks Declines to Answer Lawmakers’ Questions on Transition and White House

text: An article on Friday about Oregon Republicans’ efforts to prevent a vote on a climate change bill misstated the name of an organization that interviewed the Oregon senate minority leader. It is Oregon Public Broadcasting, not Oregon Public Radio.
match_headline: A Climate Bill Sets Off Tumult: Republicans Flee, Police Follow

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Friday about Slack’s first day of public trading misstated the stock’s closing price. It was $38.62, not $38.50.
match_headline: Slack Stock Soars, Putting Company’s Public Value at $19.5 Billion

text: An article on Friday about outdoor art installations in New York City misstated the closing date of Matt Keegan’s installation in Long Island City, Queens. The work, “what was & what is,” will be on view through Aug. 18, not Aug. 19.
match_headline: 11 Outdoor Installations to See in New York This Summer

text: An article on Friday misstated the position of Susanna V. Temkin. She is curator of El Museo del Barrio, not chief curator.
match_headline: Is El Museo del Barrio Forsaking Its Roots, or Expanding Them?

text: An article on Friday about a show at The New York Botanical Garden misidentified a green and pink plant. The plant was a bromeliad, not a staghorn fern. Also, a picture caption with the article misidentified the title of a painting by Roberto Burle Marx. It is “Untitled,” from 1970; not Calcáreo, from 1966.
match_headline: Roberto Burle Marx and His Leafy Vision of the Tropics

text: An article on Page F6 about pivotal court cases on L.G.B.T.Q. rights misstates the year that the Connecticut Supreme Court ruled in Kerrigan v. Commissioner of Public Health. It was 2008, not 2006. Also, because of an editing error, the article misstates the name of a government agency in one instance. It is the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, not the Equal Opportunity Employment Commission.
match_headline: The Court Cases That Changed L.G.B.T.Q. Rights

text: An article on Page 24 about Senator Elizabeth Warren refers imprecisely to contributions made to the Senate campaigns of Joseph R. Biden Jr. These contributions came from individuals who worked for MBNA, not from the company itself. The article also misstates the number of years between Senator Warren’s divorce and her marriage proposal to her current husband, Bruce Mann. The proposal came one year after her divorce, not two.
match_headline: Elizabeth Warren Is Completely Serious

text: An article on Page 30 about fertility and obesity misidentifies the nationalities of the authors of a 2017 study in the journal Patient Education and Counseling. They are American, not Australian. The article also misstates Sharon Bernecki DeJoy’s position at West Chester University. She is an associate professor of health, not the director of public health.
match_headline: When You’re Told You’re Too Fat to Get Pregnant

text: An article on Page 36 about Judith Sheindlin, the star of “Judge Judy,” misstates the title of David Theodosopoulos. He is the executive producer of “Hot Bench,” a legal show, not a CBS executive producer. The article also misstates the titles of two executives on the “Judge Judy” show. Randy Douthit is the executive producer, not an executive producer. Amy Freisleben is the co-executive producer, not an executive producer.
match_headline: Judge Judy Is Still Judging You

text: An article last Sunday about less-crowded European travel destinations included outdated information about the American Embassy in The Hague. It was formerly next to the museum Escher in Het Paleis, but has moved.
match_headline: What’s Next for Europe?

text: An article on June 9 about the revival of the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland misspelled the surname of the co-author of “Where the River Burned: Carl Stokes and the Struggle to Save Cleveland.” He is David Stradling, not Stradlin.
ref_headline: Where the River Burned: Carl Stokes and the Struggle to Save Cleveland.
match_headline: A Cleveland River Once Oozed and Burned. It’s Now a Hot Spot.

text: An article on Saturday about state climate change policies misidentified a Republican governor who was one of three vowing to uphold the Paris climate agreement. He is the governor of Vermont, not Puerto Rico.
match_headline: Blue States Roll Out Aggressive Climate Strategies. Red States Keep to the Sidelines.

text: An article on Saturday about Jane O’Meara Sanders misstated the given name of a Burlington College donor. She is Corinne Bove Maietta, not Corrine.
match_headline: Jane Sanders and the Messy Demise of a Vermont College

text: An item in “On This Day in History” on Friday about a Times article from 1945 misstated the title of former Emperor Akihito of Japan when he visited Okinawa in the 1970s. He was the crown prince; he was not yet the emperor.
match_headline: Rui Hachimura Is Ready to Make History for Japan in the N.B.A.

text: An article on Friday about bone spurs in the necks of young people mischaracterized the pool of study participants whose X-rays were examined for bone spurs. Some, but not all, of the participants had neck trouble.
match_headline: About the Idea That You’re Growing Horns From Looking Down at Your Phone …

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about decriminalization of marijuana in New York misstated the previous law governing smoking marijuana in public. It was considered a misdemeanor, not a violation, which is a lesser offense.
match_headline: Marijuana Decriminalization Is Expanded in N.Y., but Full Legalization Fails

text: A report in the Digest on Saturday about a lawsuit over a fire that destroyed thousands of archived recordings misidentified one of the plaintiffs. A former wife of Tom Petty, who owns rights in some of his music, is suing; his estate is not a party to this lawsuit.
match_headline: Artists Sue Universal Music Group Over Losses in 2008 Fire

text: An article on Monday about independent bookstores misstated the surname of the owner of McNally Jackson Independent Booksellers. She is Sarah McNally, not Jackson.
match_headline: Bookstores Find Growth as ‘Anchors of Authenticity’

text: An article on Sunday about milestones in L.G.B.T.Q. history misstated the title of a novel by John Rechy. It is “City of Night,” not “City at Night.”
match_headline: What Was Your Stonewall? Pivotal L.G.B.T.Q. Moments Across the U.S.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the University of Connecticut’s possible return to the Big East misstated the year the UConn men’s basketball team won its fourth national title. It was 2014, not 2015.
match_headline: UConn May Return to the Big East and Some Familiar Rivals

text: An article on Saturday about Aaron Judge misstated the year he won the American League Rookie of the Year Award. It was in 2017, not 2016.
match_headline: Aaron Judge Enters Camp Smiling, as Usual, and Healthy, for a Change

text: An article on Monday about the SailGP sailing race misstated the type of boat used in the race. It is an F50, not a GP50.
match_headline: Sailing Into Uncharted Waters

text: An article on Feb. 27 about a performance by Les Arts Florissants misidentified a dance student of Jean-Georges Noverre. He was Antoine Bournonville, not Antoine’s son, August Bournonville.
match_headline: ‘Everyone Danced in France’: A Baroque Bourrée Comes to BAM

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the chemist George Rosenkranz misspelled the name of the town in California where Dr. Rosenkranz lived. It is Atherton, not Atheron.
match_headline: George Rosenkranz, 102, a Developer of the Birth Control Pill, Is Dead

text: An article on Tuesday about the confessed Qaeda courier Majid Khan omitted a credit to the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting, which produced the article in partnership with The Times.
match_headline: Hidden Document Reveals N.Y. Was Warned of Looming Taxi Loan Crisis

text: An article on Monday about covering the Nxivm trial mischaracterized a photograph used in the trial. Camila, a young woman with whom the Nxivm co-founder Keith Raniere struck up a sexual relationship, did not send him a photo of herself on all fours, with her hands and legs in restraints. Mr. Raniere sent that photo, of another woman, to Camila.
match_headline: What It Was Like to Report on the Nxivm Sex Cult Trial

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump’s response to accusations that he sexually assaulted E. Jean Carroll misstated that Monday was the first time she spoke publicly since an excerpt from her new book was published. It was not.
match_headline: ‘She’s Not My Type’: Accused Again of Sexual Assault, Trump Resorts to Old Insult

text: An article on Tuesday about finch-singing contests misstated the location of Phil “Scooter” Rizzuto Park. It is in Queens, not Brooklyn.
match_headline: Illegal Bird Smuggling Is Fueled by Finch-Singing Contests in New York

text: An article on Tuesday about how President Trump’s feud with the Fed compares to the actions of past presidents misstated the year that Jerome H. Powell’s term will expire. It is 2022, not 2021.
match_headline: Trump’s Feud With the Fed Is Escalating, and Has a Precedent

text: Because of a transcription error, an article on June 13 about the movie “Rocketman” misstated Elton John’s description of Bernie Taupin. John said Taupin “really was the brown dirt cowboy,” not “the Brando cowboy.”
match_headline: Elton John and Bernie Taupin on How ‘Rocketman’ Captures an R-Rated Life

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the painter Joyce Pensato, using information supplied by a publicist, misstated Ms. Pensato’s age at her death and her birth date. She was 77, not 78, and she was born on Aug. 20, 1941, not Aug. 29, 1940. The age error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Joyce Pensato, Who Made Cartoon Characters Complex, Dies at 77

text: An article on Wednesday about Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s record on criminal legislation described incorrectly his comments to his hometown newspaper in 1977 about an amendment he had proposed. Mr. Biden said he wanted equitable sentences for defendants “who don’t meet the middle-class criteria of susceptibility to rehabilitation.” He did not say he wanted to prevent such defendants from being set free.
ref_headline: who don’t meet the middle-class criteria of susceptibility to rehabilitation.
match_headline: ‘Lock the S.O.B.s Up’: Joe Biden and the Era of Mass Incarceration

text: An article on June 16 about a dog pageant misidentified the name of a Weeknd song used in a dance number in the pageant. It is “Earned It (Fifty Shades of Grey),” not “Worth It.”
match_headline: The Real Dog Moms of New York City

text: An article on Monday about streaming classical music misstated the name of one of the musical groups that the composer William Brittelle enlisted in the recording of his latest album, “Spiritual America.” It is the Metropolis Ensemble, not the Metropolitan Ensemble.
match_headline: In Streaming Age, Classical Music Gets Lost in the Metadata

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the Republican lawmaker Jan Meyers erroneously credited her with a distinction. She was the first Republican woman from Kansas elected to the United States House of Representatives, not to Congress. (Nancy Kassebaum, elected earlier to the Senate, was the first.)
match_headline: Jan Meyers, a Kansas Republican ‘First’ in Congress, Dies at 90

text: An article on Monday on the deaths of tourists in the Dominican Republic misstated the given name of the tourism minister of the country. It is Francisco Javier García, not Fernando.
match_headline: Crisis Hits Dominican Republic Over Deaths of U.S. Tourists

text: An article on Wednesday about the damage from a 2004 Taylor Energy oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico misstated the amount of oil that flowed into the gulf in the Deepwater Horizon accident in 2010. While an estimated 4.9 million barrels’ worth was released in the spill, an emergency response team collected or burned 810,000 barrels before the oil hit the water.
match_headline: New Estimate for an Oil Leak: A Thousand Times Worse Than Rig Owner Says

text: An article on Thursday about the email app Superhuman misstated the time period in which 300 billion emails are sent and received. It is a day, not a year.
match_headline: Would You Pay $30 a Month to Check Your Email?

text: An article on Tuesday about a satellite launch by SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket misstated the size of mylar sails used by one of the satellites. The sails are 344 square feet in size, not nearly 20 miles.
match_headline: SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy Deploys Dozens of Satellites to Orbit

text: An article on June 18 about the company Mindstrong, which seeks to flag mental distress, misidentified the California proposition that set aside funding for technology innovation in mental health care. It was Proposition 63, not Proposition 30.
match_headline: California Tests a Digital ‘Fire Alarm’ for Mental Distress

text: An article on Sunday about mass protests in Prague misstated Czechoslovakia’s relationship with the Soviet Union in 1989. While Czechoslovakia was a part of the Soviet bloc and emerged from Kremlin domination that year, it was never a part of the Soviet Union.
match_headline: In the Largest Protests in Decades, Czechs Demand Resignation of Prime Minister

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 1 about the Flatiron Building misstates the given name of the architect who designed it. He was Daniel H. Burnham, not Henry.
match_headline: End of an Era for the Flatiron Building

text: An article on Friday about the publisher Judith Gurewich misspelled the given name of the author of “My Brother Moochie.” It is Issac, not Isaac.
match_headline: The Editor Will See You Now

text: An article on Friday about Joel Grey’s photography misstated the surname of the artist in the first interview question. It is Tuttle, not Rauschenberg.
match_headline: Joel Grey’s Other Love, Art, Is Not So Far From the Stage

text: An article on Page 13 about a new dance piece that mixes ballet and shibari misstates the artist Brendan Fernandes’s role at Northwestern University. He was hired to teach art theory and practice, not dance.
match_headline: The Impresario of ‘Ballet Kink’

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the author Judith Krantz misstated her mother’s married name. It was Tarcher, not Gittel.
match_headline: Judith Krantz, Whose Tales of Sex and Shopping Sold Millions, Dies at 91

text: An article last Sunday about the latest in Europop misspelled the surname of one member of the duo IC3PEAK. He is Nikolay Kostylev, not Kostylov or Kostylyov.

An article on June 16 about San Francisco’s hotel bar revival included an outdated reference to a chef’s position at Ayala, a restaurant and bar. Bill Montagne is no longer its chef partner and has left the restaurant.
match_headline: In San Francisco, the Revival of the Hotel Bar

text: A map with the Living In article last Sunday, about South Williamsburg, Brooklyn, misidentified a waterway. It is the East River, not the Hudson River.
match_headline: South Williamsburg, Brooklyn: Where Families Are Out in Force

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Sarah Franklin and Ariel Peikes described inaccurately a place that houses one of the music schools in Manhattan where the bride teaches. The Kaufman Music Center is a separate performing arts complex; it is not affiliated with Lincoln Center.
match_headline: Sarah Franklin, Ariel Peikes

text: An article on June 23 about hypersonic missiles misattributed a quotation. The remark, which discussed how U.S. actions cause concerns in other countries, was made by the former senior adviser to President Obama who also spoke about Obama’s desire for better options to hold North Korean missiles at risk; it was not made by another Obama-administration official.
match_headline: Hypersonic Missiles Are Unstoppable. And They’re Starting a New Global Arms Race.

text: An article on Sunday about a faux Biden web page misstated CNBC’s coverage of the page. CNBC reported on the website but did not link to it.
match_headline: Trump Consultant Is Trolling Democrats With Biden Site That Isn’t Biden’s

text: An article on Sunday about Belarusians’s use of national identity to resist Russian annexation misstated the color scheme of the 1918 Belarusian flag. It was white-red-white, not red-white-red.
match_headline: As Putin Pushes a Merger, Belarus Resists With Language, Culture and History

text: An article on Saturday about Mayor Pete Buttigieg’s response to a police shooting in South Bend, Ill., misattributed a quotation. It was E-Lexus Thornton who said, “To me it’s all been a big dumpster fire,” not Jordan Geiger.
ref_headline: To me it’s all been a big dumpster fire,
match_headline: Buttigieg’s Debate Remarks on Police Shooting Don’t Satisfy Some Back Home

text: An article on Saturday about the decision by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints to drop the name “Mormon” misstated the surname of the president of the Mormon History Association. He is W. Paul Reeve, not Reeves.
match_headline: ‘Mormon’ No More: Faithful Reflect on Church’s Move to Scrap a Moniker

text: An article on Saturday about where Senator Kamala Harris stands on private health insurance misquoted Ms. Harris. She told “Morning Joe” on Friday, “The question was would you give up your private insurance for that option.” She did not say, “The question was would you give up private insurance for that option.”
match_headline: Where Is Kamala Harris on Medicare for All vs. Private Insurance?

text: An article on Sunday about the celebration of the 1969 Mets team misstated the placement of patches on the uniforms of former Mets players. They were on the right sleeves, not the left.
match_headline: With Little to Celebrate, Mets Honor a Title-Winning Team

text: An obituary on Sunday about the former New York City detective Luis G. Alvarez misstated his birthplace. He was born in Havana, not in Queens. It also referred incorrectly to his retirement in 2010. He did not retire on a disability.
match_headline: Luis Alvarez, Champion of 9/11 Responders, Dies at 53

text: An article on Tuesday about Ivanka Trump’s diplomacy described incorrectly the attendees of a closed-door meeting between President Trump and Kim Jong-un, the North Korean leader. While Ivanka Trump met Mr. Kim, she did not attend the meeting; the White House declined repeated requests to reveal who was there.
match_headline: Ivanka Trump Tests Her Diplomatic Chops and Riles a Legion of Critics

text: Because of an editing error, the headline on an article on Tuesday about a visit to a detention facility by members of Congress mischaracterized their remarks. Lawmakers called Border Patrol officers’ behavior toward them toxic and called the detention system broken; they did not describe the migrant holding sites as toxic or broken.
match_headline: ‘It Feels Like a Jail’: Lawmakers Criticize Migrant Holding Sites on Border

text: An article on Sunday about the box office success of “Toy Story 4” misstated a plot point in “Yesterday.” The main character wakes up in bed after a traffic accident; he does not fall out of bed.
match_headline: ‘Toy Story 4’ Is Bigger Than the Beatles

text: An article last Wednesday about the South African restaurant Wolfgat misspelled the name of the local fish that Wolfgat wraps in seaweed and serves with tomato broth. It is snoek, not snook. The article, using information from a publicist, also misidentified the organization that in February named Wolfgat the world’s No. 1 Off-Map Destination. It is the World Restaurant Awards, not the World Restaurant Awards, IMG.
match_headline: Wolfgat, a Far-Flung Destination for South African Coastal Cuisine

text: A picture caption with an obituary on June 15 about Pat Bowlen, the longtime owner of the Denver Broncos, using information from Reuters, misidentified the woman in the photograph with Mr. Bowlen and the Broncos quarterback John Elway. She is Mr. Bowlen’s wife, Annabel — not Mr. Elway’s wife, Janet.
match_headline: Pat Bowlen, Influential Owner of the Denver Broncos, Dies at 75

text: An article on Wednesday about a Taliban attack on a school in Kabul misattributed a quotation. It was Henrietta Fore, Unicef’s executive director — not Erica Vogel, a Unicef spokeswoman — who said, “Schools should be havens of peace.”
ref_headline: Schools should be havens of peace.
match_headline: A Taliban Attack on Children Causes Outrage, Everywhere but at Peace Talks

text: An article on Wednesday about a fire on a Russian Navy deep-sea vessel misstated where the Russian submarine the Kursk, which sank in 2000, was based. It was based in Vidyayevo, a port of Russia’s Northern Fleet, not in Severomorsk.
match_headline: Russian Deep-Sea Military Vessel Catches Fire, Killing 14

text: An article on Monday about Glaad, the L.G.B.T advocacy organization, omitted one aspect of the history of a proposed L.G.B.T.-inclusive amendment. The ERA Coalition first brought the concept to Glaad in 2016.
match_headline: Glaad’s Bold New Campaign: an L.G.B.T. Constitutional Amendment

text: An article on Wednesday about the New York Mets game against the New York Yankees misstated when it took place. It was Tuesday night, not Monday.
match_headline: Mets Win With a Late Rally and End the Yankees’ Homer Streak

text: An article on Tuesday about the closing of the West End production of “Les Misérables” referred imprecisely to the period in which the play is set. It is set in the years leading up to and after the Paris Uprising of 1832, not “revolutionary France.”
match_headline: The ‘Les Misérables’ Revolving Stage Is Going. Fans Are in a Spin.

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about Lee Iacocca, the former Chrysler leader, misidentified two of the three men shown riding in a Mustang at the New York World’s Fair in 1965. Mr. Iacocca is in the center and Henry Ford II is at right, not the reverse.
match_headline: Lee Iacocca, Visionary Automaker Who Led Both Ford and Chrysler, Is Dead at 94

text: An obituary on Thursday about Stewart Greene, a founder of the advertising agency Wells Rich Greene, misspelled part of the name of a company that was a client of the agency. It is Procter & Gamble, not Proctor.
match_headline: Stewart Greene, Who Helped Shape TV Advertising, Dies at 91

text: An item in the Week Ahead column last Sunday misspelled the surname of the director of “Three Peaks.” He is Jan Zabeil, not Zabiel.
match_headline: The Week in Arts: Sarah Jessica Parker Back for More ‘Divorce’; a Farewell to ‘My Fair Lady’

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about how tours of historic houses in the South are talking about the slaves who built them misstated the surname of a historical interpreter at the Owens-Thomas House in Savannah, Ga. As was correctly stated in the article, she is Lacey Wilson, not Williams.
match_headline: Enslaved People Lived Here. These Museums Want You to Know.

text: A picture caption with the cover story last Sunday, about kitchen counters, misidentified the location of a home. It is in Palm Beach, Fla., not Palm Springs, Calif.
match_headline: The Kitchen Counter Challenge

text: A review on June 23 of books about the first moon landing misstated when Alan Shepard became the first American in space. It was May 5, 1961, not May 7.
match_headline: Fifty Years Ago We Landed on the Moon. Why Should We Care Now?

text: An article on June 23 about the show “Fleabag” misstated the episode in which a certain scene occurs. The protagonist says “I’m not obsessed with sex” in the first season’s second episode, not its first.
match_headline: How ‘Fleabag’ Seduces Us, Then Accuses Us

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Ursula von der Leyen, who was recently nominated as the next president of the European Commission, referred incorrectly to a defense expert at the European Council on Foreign Relations. The expert, Ulrike Franke, is a woman.
match_headline: E.U.’s Top Pick: Too Pious for Feminists, Too Feminist for Conservatives

text: An article on Tuesday about commercial whaling in Japan misstated the availability of whale meat in school lunches in Japan after 1987. It decreased substantially; it did not end entirely.
match_headline: Japan Resumes Commercial Whaling. But Is There an Appetite for It?

text: An article on Sunday about a theatrical production of the 1980 Wimbledon match between Bjorn Borg and John McEnroe misstated the year in which United States Open offered fans an augmented reality experience that made them feel as if they were stepping onto the court at Arthur Ashe Stadium. It was 2016, not 2018.
match_headline: McEnroe-Borg Redux: This Time With Actors

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Tuesday about vertigo misstated the location of the “stones” that help maintain balance. The “stones” are present on the ends of hair cells, not follicles.
match_headline: How Do You Treat Positional Vertigo?

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an obituary on Saturday about the orchestrator, arranger and composer Sid Ramin identified two of the people in the photograph of a rehearsal for the Broadway show “Gypsy” in reverse order. Mr. Ramin is at the far left and the composer Jule Styne is second from the left, not vice versa.
match_headline: Sid Ramin, ‘West Side Story’ Orchestrator and a Composer, Dies at 100

text: An article on Tuesday about the indictment of the financier Jeffrey Epstein on sex-trafficking charges misstated the given name of a government lawyer. He is Alexander Rossmiller, not Andrew.
match_headline: Jeffrey Epstein Is Indicted on Sex Charges as Discovery of Nude Photos Is Disclosed

text: An article on Friday about the ways in which personal identity shaped the lives of people in the L.G.B.T.Q. community referred incorrectly to AIDS. It is an acquired immunodeficiency disease, not an autoimmune disease.
match_headline: When ‘Black Lives Matter’ Is Invoked in the Abortion Debate

text: An article on Sunday about the lack of lesbian-themed shows on Broadway misstated the year “The Children’s Hour” was last seen on Broadway. It was last seen on Broadway in 1953, not 1936.
match_headline: The Boys in the Band Get to Broadway. Why Not the Girls?

text: An obituary on Saturday about Barry Kowalski, the Justice Department lawyer who won the convictions of two Los Angeles police officers in 1993 for the beating of Rodney G. King, misstated the month in 1991 when that beating happened. It was March, not June.
match_headline: Barry Kowalski, Prosecutor in Rodney King Case, Is Dead at 74

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the lyricist and director Martin Charnin omitted part of the name of a television special starring Anne Bancroft that he won an Emmy Award for producing. It was “Annie, the Women in the Life of a Man” — not “Annie, the Women in the Life.”
ref_headline: Annie, the Women in the Life of a Man
match_headline: Martin Charnin, Who Brought ‘Annie’ to the Stage, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on June 5 about the ophthalmologist and inventor Dr. Patricia Bath, using information from the National Library of Medicine and the United States Patent and Trademark Office, referred incorrectly to the influence of the apparatus Dr. Bath patented for the treatment of cataracts by laser. Her method is in use worldwide — not her device, which was never commercially marketed. And it is the method, not the specific device, that helped to “restore or improve vision to millions of patients worldwide.” This correction was delayed for research.
ref_headline: restore or improve vision to millions of patients worldwide.
match_headline: Dr. Patricia Bath, 76, Who Took On Blindness and Earned a Patent, Dies

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Janne E. Nolan, an expert on international affairs and arms-control issues, misidentified the university from which she received a master’s degree in law and diplomacy. It was Tufts, not Stanford.
match_headline: Janne E. Nolan, Principled Adviser on World Affairs, Is Dead at 67

text: An article on Wednesday about France Télécom executives facing “moral harassment” charges after a wave of worker suicides misstated France Télécom’s past financial performance. By 2005, the company was over $50 billion, not $50 million, in debt.
match_headline: 35 Employees Committed Suicide. Will Their Bosses Go to Jail?

text: An article on Wednesday about the discovery of U.S. missiles in a rebel camp in Libya misstated the day that the United Nations issued a statement on the death toll from the conflict in Libya. It was issued on Tuesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: U.S. Missiles Found in Libyan Rebel Camp Were First Sold to France

text: An article on Monday about a Republican primary runoff in North Carolina referred incorrectly to robocalls recorded by former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin for Joan Perry, a North Carolina congressional candidate. While the group WFW Action, the political arm of Winning for Women, has funded robocalls by Newt Gingrich, the former House speaker, the group said it did not pay for calls recorded by Ms. Palin. The article also misidentified a voter who said that Dr. Perry’s gender was a factor in his choice of candidates. He is Tommy Moore, not Tommy Jones.
match_headline: A Battle of the Sexes in North Carolina Fuels a Wider Republican Clash

text: An article on July 3 about a recent spate of cyclist deaths, using information from the New York City Department of Transportation, misstated the number of cycling fatalities in Brooklyn this year. It is 11, not 10.
match_headline: Cyclist Killed by Cement Truck and 2 Other Deaths Spur ‘Emergency’

text: An article on Wednesday about incentives offered to developers to incorporate affordable housing into mixed-use projects misstated the nature of an effort in Minneapolis to encourage construction of multifamily housing. The city eliminated single-family zoning, it did not ban single-family homes. The article also misstated the nature of certain efforts by Houston and Austin, Tex., to add more affordable housing. The cities have introduced measures to encourage the development of such housing, not to require it.
match_headline: Cities Need Affordable Housing, but Builders Want Big Profits. Can It Work?

text: An article on Wednesday about what to watch on television reversed the fates of two characters at the end of Season 2 of “Harlots.” Lydia Quigley (Manville) was sent to a mental institution and Margaret Wells (Morton) was sent to America, not the other way around.
match_headline: What’s on TV Wednesday: ‘Snowfall’ and ‘Harlots’

text: An article on Saturday about New Zealand’s efforts to combat online hate misidentified the platform on which an online threat against a mosque was first posted. The post originated on 4Chan, not Reddit.
match_headline: As New Zealand Fights Online Hate, the Internet’s Darkest Corners Resist

text: An article on June 14 about digital assistants and privacy concerns misstated who was involved in the creation of the “Knowledge Navigator” video. It was a group of Apple employees that included Bud Colligan, Hugh Dubberly, Mike Liebhold and Doris Mitsch. The computer scientist Alan Kay did not have a role in the video’s development.
match_headline: Stanford Team Aims at Alexa and Siri With a Privacy-Minded Alternative

text: A picture caption with a collection of photos of the United States women’s soccer team on Thursday misidentified the player shown. It was Tobin Heath, not Ali Krieger.
match_headline: The Women’s World Cup Team Is the Most American Thing Out There

text: An article on Thursday about the music in Season 3 of the Netflix series “Stranger Things” attributed an erroneous distinction to Aimee Mann’s song “Save Me.” While it was nominated for an Oscar in 1999, it did not win.
match_headline: ‘Stranger Things’ Season 3 Is a Portal to 1985. Here’s What It Sounded Like.

text: An obituary on Monday about the record producer Mickey Kapp, using information from a family member, misstated his academic history. While he attended Stanford University, he did not graduate from the school.
match_headline: Mickey Kapp, Who Made Mixtapes for Astronauts, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Thursday about the architect Philip G. Freelon misstated the publication for which Siddhartha Mitter wrote about the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum in Jackson, which Mr. Freelon designed. It was Artforum, not The Village Voice.
match_headline: Philip Freelon, African-American Museum Architect, Dies at 66

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s plan to lower prescription drug prices misstated the day on which Mr. Trump killed a proposal that would have reduced out-of-pocket drug costs for older consumers. It was Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Trump’s Efforts to Rein In Drug Prices Face Setbacks

text: An article on Wednesday about the strain that the wave of migrant families and unaccompanied children is putting on school districts misstated the surname of a woman who leads a team of early-learning specialists from the Guatemalan-Maya Center. She is Amanda Escalante, not Escobar.
match_headline: Schools Scramble to Handle Thousands of New Migrant Families

text: An article on Friday about two taxi industry titans in New York accused of carrying out a bribery scheme described incorrectly an Instagram post from Tony Georgiton. The post, which has since been removed, showed Mr. Georgiton and Mayor Bill de Blasio with Basil Messados, not Alan S. Kaufman.
match_headline: A Super Bowl Trip, a Bribery Indictment and the Taxi Industry’s Corruption

text: An article on Friday about a move by California lawmakers to create a fund to cover fire claims gave an incorrect figure for the death toll in the Camp Fire. Eighty-five people were killed, not 84.
match_headline: California Lawmakers Give Utilities a Backstop on Wildfire Liability

text: An article on July 5 about Brandi Chastain’s 1999 World Cup celebration and the debate on how female athletes are depicted and treated misstated the name of the television show hosted by David Letterman. It was “The Late Show,” not “Late Night.”
match_headline: The Sports Bra Seen Round the World Has New Meaning 20 Years Later

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the former New York Jets coach Walt Michaels misstated the year that the Jets’ record under him was 10-5-1. It was 1981, not 1982.
match_headline: Walt Michaels, Outspoken Coach of the Jets, Is Dead at 89

text: An article last Sunday about the state of vineyards in Sonoma County, Calif., after the 2017 wildfires misidentified Jared Childress’s employer. It is the Audubon Canyon Ranch, not the Audubon Canyon Reserve. The article also misidentified a type of grass growing in the Bouverie Preserve. It is bear grass, not deer grass.
match_headline: How Sonoma’s Vineyards Survived a Siege of Fire, Smoke and Ash

text: A review on June 30 about “Never a Lovely So Real: The Life and Work of Nelson Algren,” by Colin Asher, misidentified the cemetery where Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir are buried. It is Montparnasse Cemetery, not Montmartre Cemetery. The review also misstated the timing of an earlier biography of Algren. “Algren: A Life,” by Mary Wisniewski, was published shortly before the election of Donald Trump in 2016; it did not appear “in the immediate aftermath” of his election.
ref_headline: Never a Lovely So Real: The Life and Work of Nelson Algren,
match_headline: What Counts as a Democracy? And Other Questions. …

text: An article on June 30 about Russia’s foreign-policy goals misspelled the name of a retired Egyptian military officer. He is Nasr Salem, not Nassr Salem. The article also misstated Condoleezza Rice’s title in 2002. She was national security advisor, not secretary of state. And the article misidentified the nationalities of two academics who wrote a 2016 article in the journal Russia in Global Affairs. They are American, not Russian.
match_headline: What Does Putin Really Want?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about extravagant spending by the cabinet of President Emmanuel Macron of France referred incorrectly to François de Rugy. He is the former president of the National Assembly, not the current president. (The current president is Richard Ferrand.) The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: 5 Lobster Tails and a $560 Bottle of Wine, at Taxpayers’ Expense, Give Macron a Headache

text: An article on Monday about Bethany Vierra’s, an American woman who lost a custody battle for her daughter in Saudi Arabia, referred incorrectly to the court testimony of Ms. Vierra’s husband. He did say that she did not speak Arabic very well, but he did not accuse her of being an atheist.
match_headline: American Woman Loses Custody Battle for Daughter in Saudi Arabia

text: An article on Sunday about the silencing of investigative journalists in China misstated the given name of a participant in a training camp for aspiring journalists. She is Cheng Xinyu, not Yuxin.
match_headline: ‘We’re Almost Extinct’: China’s Investigative Journalists Are Silenced Under Xi

text: An article on Sunday about flooding in Louisiana misspelled the given name of a woman at the First Baptist Church in Denham Springs, La. She is Ashleigh Green, not Ashley.
match_headline: Still Menaced by Flooding, Louisiana Dodges a Storm’s Worst Blows

text: An article on Sunday about a crash that killed the several members of a motorcycle club of ex-Marines misstated when black regiments known as the Buffalo Soldiers were formed. They were formed after the Civil War; they did not fight in that war.
match_headline: 7 Died in a Motorcycle Crash. How Their Club of Former Marines Is Mourning Them.

text: An article on Monday about the effort by Joseph R. Biden Jr. to end court-ordered busing misstated the party affiliation of the governor of Delaware who sent the National Guard to Wilmington. The governor, Charles L. Terry Jr., was a Democrat, not a Republican.
match_headline: How Joe Biden Became the Democrats’ Anti-Busing Crusader

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump’s decision to send a delegation to Geneva for nuclear talks with Russia misstated a security agency that will send representatives to the arms control discussions. It is the National Nuclear Security Administration, not the National Security Agency.
match_headline: Trump Sends Negotiators to Geneva for Nuclear Talks With Russians and Also Seeks to Limit Chinese Warheads

text: An article on Tuesday about Ghislaine Maxwell’s relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, the financier accused of sexually trafficking and abusing girls, misidentified the university that the investment banker Euan Rellie attended. He studied at Cambridge, not Oxford.
match_headline: The ‘Lady of the House’ Who Was Long Entangled With Jeffrey Epstein

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the cause of a blackout in Manhattan on Saturday misidentified the location in the image. It showed a darkened area just north of Columbus Circle, not Columbus Circle itself.
match_headline: A Burning 13,000-Volt Cable Touched Off Manhattan Blackout, Con Edison Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the astronaut Michael Collins and his role on the Apollo 11 mission misstated the year in which his book “Carrying the Fire” was first published. It was 1974, not 1979.
match_headline: For Apollo 11 He Wasn’t on the Moon. But His Coffee Was Warm.

text: An article on Tuesday about a growing trade in lion bones misstated the quota for exports of lion skeletons enacted by South African authorities in 2018. The quota was 800, not 1,500; the latter was the number first announced by officials but later reduced.
match_headline: Lion Bones Are Profitable for Breeders, and Poachers

text: An obituary on Saturday about the chef Elka Gilmore misstated the name of the restaurant she ran at the Miyako Hotel in San Francisco. It was Elka, not Elka’s. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Elka Gilmore, Chef Who Blended the Old and the New, Dies at 59

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about the union leader Hector Figueroa misspelled his wife’s given name. She is Deidre McFadyen, not Deirdre.
match_headline: Hector Figueroa, Union Leader With Impact, Dies at 57

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Tuesday about the art scholar and curator Douglas Crimp misstated the year that the photograph of Mr. Crimp with the artists Cindy Sherman and Robert Longo was taken. It was 1979, not 1977.
match_headline: Douglas Crimp, Scholar, Curator and Art World Disrupter, Dies at 74

text: An article on Tuesday about a new rule imposed by the Trump administration that would further restrict migrant asylum applications misstated the number of migrant family members from Honduras, El Salvador and Guatemala the Border Patrol has arrested at the southwestern border so far in fiscal year 2019. It is 363,300, not 510,412.
match_headline: Most Migrants at Border With Mexico Would Be Denied Asylum Protections Under New Trump Rule

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump’s attacks on Twitter against four Democratic congresswomen of color referred incorrectly to the election of Representative Ilhan Omar. Ms. Omar is one of the first two Muslim women elected to Congress, not one of the first two Muslims.
match_headline: After Trump Accuses Four Democratic Congresswomen of Hating U.S., They Fire Back

text: An article on Tuesday about protest in Puerto Rico demanding the resignation of Gov. Ricardo Rosselló misstated the year that Puerto Ricans began holding protests against the military presence on the island of Vieques. It was 1999, not 1989.
match_headline: Tear Gas Fired at Puerto Rico Protesters Amid Calls for Governor’s Resignation

text: An article on Tuesday about an email error that resulted in reports of child abuse going unread referred incorrectly to an email account set up for Colorado government employees to report abuse claims to a statewide hotline. It was created for internal use by state and county employees and was not released to the public.
match_headline: Child Neglect Reports Sat Unread for 4 Years Because of an Email Mix-up

text: An article on Tuesday about Christine Lagarde, the nominee to be the next president of the European Central Bank, misstated action taken by Mario Draghi in 2011. Mr. Draghi lowered interest rates shortly after taking office; he did not raise them.
match_headline: Christine Lagarde Faces a New Challenge in Europe

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the former W.N.B.A. star Cappie Pondexter misidentified the player who committed a hard foul in a W.N.B.A. game in 2010. It was Pondexter who fouled Penny Taylor, not the other way around.
match_headline: Cappie Pondexter Goes from W.N.B.A.’s ‘Unstoppable’ to Retired

text: An article on July 5 about fans who translate the lyrics of the Korean pop band BTS referred incorrectly to Janet Hong’s translation work. While she has done work for the Center for the Art of Translation, she is not on the center’s staff.
match_headline: As BTS’s Reach Expands, an Army of Dedicated K-Pop Translators Grows

text: An editorial on Wednesday about the Justice Department’s decision not to charge the New York City police officer who applied a chokehold that led to the death of Eric Garner, and the city’s delay in taking disciplinary action against him, misstated where Mr. Garner’s family met with federal prosecutors. It was in Brooklyn, not Lower Manhattan.
match_headline: ‘The D.O.J. Has Failed Us’: Eric Garner’s Family Assails Prosecutors

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the former Supreme Court justice John Paul Stevens misstated the vote in the 1976 Supreme Court case Gregg v. Georgia. It was 7 to 2, not 5 to 4. The obituary also referred incorrectly to the length of Justice Stevens’s tenure on the Supreme Court. It was the third-longest in history, not the second-longest. And it misstated how many justices President Dwight D. Eisenhower appointed to the Supreme Court. It was five, not four. Because of an editing error, the obituary omitted part of the title of one of Justice Stevens’s books. It is “The Making of a Justice: Reflections on My First 94 Years” — not “The Making of a Justice: My First 94 Years.”
ref_headline: The Making of a Justice: Reflections on My First 94 Years
match_headline: Supreme Court Justice John Paul Stevens, Who Led Liberal Wing, Dies at 99

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the South African musician Johnny Clegg misstated the name of an album released by his band Savuka in 1993. It is “Heat, Dust and Dreams,” not “Heat and Dust.”
match_headline: Johnny Clegg, South African Singer Who Battled Apartheid With Music, Is Dead at 66

text: An obituary on June 30 about the museum curator Peter Selz misspelled the given name of his wife, who survives him. She is Carole Schemmerling, not Carol.
match_headline: Peter Selz, an Art Museum Force on Two Coasts, Dies at 100

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about urinary tract infections and their increasing resistance to antibiotics misspelled the name of a drug. It is ciprofloxacin, not ciproflaxacin.
match_headline: Urinary Tract Infections Affect Millions. The Cures Are Faltering.

text: An article on Thursday about Heydi Gámez García, a Honduran girl who was depressed that her father was unable to migrate to the United States, misstated the night on which she shut herself in her room and tried to hang herself. It was July 2, not one night last week.
match_headline: A Border Kept Him From His Daughter. He Came Only in Time to Say Goodbye.

text: An article on Wednesday about a deadly train derailment and explosion in Quebec in 2013 misstated when Lisa Raitt was transport minister. She became minister nine days after the crash; she was not the minister at the time of the disaster.
match_headline: A Runaway Train Explosion Killed 47, but Deadly Cargo Still Rides the Rails

text: An article on Friday about President Trump disavowing a chant shouted by his supporters at a campaign rally misquoted Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota. She said, “A lot of people are trying to distract us now. But I want you all to know that we are not going to let them,” not, “We are not going to back down.”
ref_headline: A lot of people are trying to distract us now. But I want you all to know that we are not going to let them,
match_headline: Trump Disavows ‘Send Her Back’ Chant After Pressure From G.O.P.

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about the Staten Island district attorney’s office and the borough’s reluctance to join the progressive wave of criminal justice reforms misidentifies the city agency that provided data on cash bail. It is the New York City Criminal Justice Agency, not the Criminal Justice Authority.
match_headline: Where Law-and-Order Justice Still Reigns in New York City

text: An article on Friday about the scheduled closing of the crowd-pleasing Broadway musical “Waitress” misstated the number of new Broadway musicals from the 2015-2016 season that were ultimately profitable. Three musicals went into the black, not two.
match_headline: ‘Waitress’ to Close in January 2020

text: An article on Friday about the art collection of Trey and Jenny Laird misspelled the name of an artist. He is Do Ho Suh, not Doh Ho Suh.
match_headline: When You Display Ai Weiwei, Beware of Cats

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about Poul Ruders and his most recent opera, “The Thirteenth Child,” misstates the dates and order of two of Mr. Ruders’s other operas. “The Handmaid’s Tale” was his second opera and debuted in 2000, not 2005; “Kafka’s Trial” was his third and debuted in 2005, not 1990.
match_headline: A Rarity for Poul Ruders: A Feel-Good Opera

text: An article last Sunday about the play “Mojada” misspelled the name of the churro vendor character. She is Luisa, not Louisa.
match_headline: Rewriting Greek Tragedies as Immigrant Stories

text: An article last Sunday about the increasing popularity of sparkling water misspelled the surname of a co-founder of Bevi, a carbonation machine company. He is Sean Grundy, not Gundy.
match_headline: The Seltzer Bubble

text: An article last Sunday about Delphi, Greece, misspelled the name of an ancient water source in Delphi. It was the Castalian Spring, not the Castilian Spring.
match_headline: Voyage to the Center of the World

text: An article on July 7 about the revival of an industrial Toronto street misspelled the surname of the president and publisher of the House of Anansi publishing company. She is Sarah MacLachlan, not McLachlan. The article also attributed an incorrect distinction to Ms. MacLachlan. She is not a founder of the company.
match_headline: In Toronto, an Industrial Stretch Has Its Breakout Moment

text: A picture credit last Sunday with the On the Market article misidentified the photographer of the townhouse in Greenwood Heights, Brooklyn. It is Emily Gilbert for The New York Times, not Katherine Marks for The New York Times.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in Manhattan, Brooklyn and Staten Island

text: An article on July 14 about streaming services misstated the platform that carries the show “Russian Doll.” It is Netflix, not HBO.
match_headline: The Great Race to Rule Streaming TV

text: An article on Monday about residents of a former warehouse in Manhattan who paid a developer $11 million not to build a tower that would have darkened their windows and blocked their views misstated the name of the former warehouse. It is City Prairie, not Chelsea Prairie.
match_headline: How Much Is a View Worth in Manhattan? Try $11 Million

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about presidential administrations and space exploration misidentified the object in the image taken from the Apollo 11 spacecraft. It showed a view of Earth, not the moon.
match_headline: For 50 Years Since Apollo 11, Presidents Have Tried to Take That Next Giant Leap

text: An article on Friday about the decision by Andrew R. Wheeler, the E.P.A. administrator, to allow the use of the pesticide chlorpyrifos, which has been linked to serious health problems in children, misquoted Angela Logomasini, a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute. Ms. Logomasini used the term “junk science” to refer to the studies upon which the Obama administration based its proposed ban on chlorpyrifos, not to a later review by the E.P.A. Science Advisory Board.
match_headline: E.P.A. Won’t Ban Chlorpyrifos, Pesticide Tied to Children’s Health Problems

text: An article on Monday about Democratic candidates’ responses to President Trump’s incendiary language on race misstated what the crowd chanted at President Trump’s rally in North Carolina. It was “send her back,” not “send her home.”
match_headline: Trump Sets the Terms on Racial Division. Do Democrats Know What to Do?
