text: An article on July 14 about Hurricane Barry misstated the surname of the president of Louisiana’s Plaquemines Parish. He is Kirk Lepine, not Kirk Lenin.
match_headline: Hurricane Barry Spares New Orleans (So Far), as Inland Cities Brace for Floods

text: An article on Thursday about Netflix’s second-quarter loss of subscribers misstated the order in which the company signed Shonda Rhimes and Ryan Murphy to production deals. Ms. Rhimes, not Mr. Murphy, was signed first.
match_headline: Netflix Stock Tumbles as U.S. Subscribers Decrease After Price Increases

text: An article on Monday about the revival of “Veronica Mars” on Hulu misstated which character joined Veronica to binge watch “Harlots.” It was Logan, not Keith.
match_headline: Review: ‘Veronica Mars’ and the One-Great-Season Debate

text: An entry on Monday in the What’s on TV highlights misspelled the surname of a filmmaker of “The Great Mother.” He is Chad Walker, not Walke.
match_headline: What’s on TV Monday: ‘The Great Mother’ and ‘Time Freak’

text: An essay about gender bias in American space exploration misstated the genders of people involved in testing of the SpaceX’s Crew Dragon capsule. The testing included both men and women, not only men. It also incorrectly stated that an astronaut had completed a spacewalk. Cady Coleman qualified for a spacewalk, she did not perform one.
match_headline: To Make It to the Moon, Women Have to Escape Earth’s Gender Bias

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about the journalist Lucette Lagnado misstated the year her memoir “The Man in the White Sharkskin Suit” was published. It was 2007, not 2008.
ref_headline: The Man in the White Sharkskin Suit
match_headline: Lucette Lagnado, Memoirist of Jews in Old Cairo, Dies at 62

text: An obituary on Saturday about the socialite and philanthropist Marylou Whitney misstated, at one point, the state where Mrs. Whitney was born and grew up. It is Missouri, not Kansas. The earlier version also misstated part of the name of the village in New York State where she and her husband Sonny Whitney had a ski lodge. It is Lake Placid, not Mount Placid.
match_headline: Marylou Whitney, Social Queen of the Racing World, Dies at 93

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the discovery of a shipwreck from the Renaissance era misstated the vessel’s location. It was found in Baltic waters, not Balkan waters.
match_headline: A Shipwreck, 500 Years Old, Appears on the Baltic Seabed

text: An article on Saturday about inmates released as part of the First Step Act rendered a word incorrectly in a quotation from Veda Ajamu, Robert Shipp’s sister. Referring to his early release, she said it was not “a small feat,” not “a small piece.”
match_headline: For Inmates Released Under New Criminal Justice Reforms, ‘Every Day Counts’

text: Because of an editing error, a timeline last Sunday with an article about the career of the Yankees closer Mariano Rivera misstated the significance of the team’s World Series championship in 1996. It was the Yankees’ first title since 1978, not 1981.
match_headline: Covering the Closer: Two Decades of Writing on Mariano Rivera

text: An article last Wednesday about 16 influential black American chefs misstated the number of consecutive years that the James Beard award winners for best chef or outstanding restaurant did not include black chefs. It was 14 years, not 17.
match_headline: Killing of Sadie Roberts-Joseph, African American Museum Founder, Stuns Baton Rouge

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about Robert M. Morgenthau misidentified the queen for whom he roasted hot dogs in 1939 at the Hudson Valley home of Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt. She was Queen Elizabeth, not the future Queen Elizabeth II, her daughter.
match_headline: Robert Morgenthau, Longtime Manhattan District Attorney, Dies at 99

text: An obituary on Monday about Paul Krassner, the editor of the magazine The Realist and a founder of the Yippies, referred incorrectly to his association with Ken Kesey. While Mr. Krassner knew Mr. Kesey, he did not join Mr. Kesey and the Merry Pranksters on their bus trip across America.
match_headline: Paul Krassner, Anarchist, Prankster and a Yippies Founder, Dies at 87

text: An article on Wednesday about Boris Johnson, the new Conservative Party leader and incoming prime minister of Britain, referred incorrectly to Frans Timmermans, the European Commission vice president. Mr. Timmermans is a man.
match_headline: Boris Johnson to Take Leadership of a Britain in Deep Crisis

text: An article on Wednesday about North Carolina’s approval of a settlement that prohibits the state government from banning transgender people from using bathrooms in state buildings that match their gender identity misidentified the part of the North Carolina “bathroom bill” case that is on hold until the Supreme Court addresses whether a federal ban on sex discrimination includes gay and transgender people. It is the part dealing with whether people can claim damages, not the portion dealing with limits on local anti-discrimination laws.
match_headline: North Carolina Reaches Settlement on ‘Bathroom Bill’

text: An article on Wednesday about the deployment of the solar sail LightSail 2 misstated the source of propulsion for a solar sail. It is photons from the sun, not solar winds. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: LightSail 2 Unfurls, Next Step Toward Space Travel by Solar Sail

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Christopher C. Kraft Jr., the founder of NASA’s mission control, erroneously credited the American astronaut Edward H. White 2d with a distinction. He was the first American to walk in space, not the first person to do so. The Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov holds that distinction.
match_headline: Christopher Kraft, NASA Mission Control’s Founding Father, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on July 11 and 12 about Jim Bouton, the author of the baseball memoir “Ball Four,” omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to those listed, he is survived by a brother, Robert.
match_headline: Jim Bouton, Author of Tell-All Baseball Memoir ‘Ball Four,’ Dies at 80

text: An article on Thursday about an intense heat wave in Europe incorrectly described the level of air conditioning on London’s Tube network. Some trains are air-conditioned; it is not the case that none are.
match_headline: Europe Suffers Heat Wave of Dangerous, Record-High Temperatures

text: An article on Thursday about Boris Johnson’s first moments as prime minister of Britain misquoted Mr. Johnson. He said, “The people who bet against Britain are going to lose their shirts,” not “The people who bet against Brexit are going to lose their shirts.”
ref_headline: The people who bet against Britain are going to lose their shirts,
match_headline: Boris Johnson Becomes U.K. Prime Minister, Replacing Theresa May

text: An article on Wednesday about a battle for the leadership of the National Socialist Movement, one of the country’s oldest neo-Nazi groups, misspelled the surname of a former official of the group. He is Matthew Heimbach, not Heinbach.
match_headline: Why a Black Preacher Is Fighting for Control of a Neo-Nazi Group

text: An obituary on Thursday about Dr. Joel Filártiga, a Paraguayan who won a landmark case in the United States that extended universal law against torture, misidentified the author of the 2004 book “Breaking Silence: The Case That Changed the Face of Human Rights.” It is Richard Alan White, a specialist on Latin America, not Robert E. White, a former United States ambassador to Paraguay.
ref_headline: Breaking Silence: The Case That Changed the Face of Human Rights.
match_headline: Dr. Joel Filártiga, 86, Dies; Won Human Rights Ruling in Son’s Death

text: An article on Friday about the drowning deaths of about 150 migrants in a shipwreck off the coast of Libya misstated the name of the United Nations refugee agency. It is the High Commissioner for Refugees, not the High Commission for Refugees.
match_headline: About 150 Migrants Drown in Shipwreck Off Libya

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the consulting firm McKinsey & Company’s advice to Johnson & Johnson on driving the sales of opioids erroneously attributed a quotation to McKinsey. A lawsuit filed in New Jersey, not McKinsey, stated that McKinsey advised a pharmaceutical company to “get more patients on higher doses of opioids” and study techniques “for keeping patients on opioids longer.”
ref_headline: get more patients on higher doses of opioids
match_headline: McKinsey Advised Johnson & Johnson on Increasing Opioid Sales

text: An article on Page 16 about sunscreens described melanoma incorrectly. It is not the most common form of skin cancer; it is the most lethal. Basal-cell carcinoma is the most common type.
match_headline: Should Black People Wear Sunscreen?

text: An article on Page 38 about the purge of academics in Turkey misidentified the Turkish writer and sociologist Ismail Besikci. He is not Kurdish.

A picture caption with an article last Sunday about “The Lion King,” using information provided by Photofest, misstated the timing of a scene from the original “Lion King.” The image was from the film’s closing sequence, not the opening.
match_headline: What Disney Risked to Make ‘The Lion King’ in 1994

text: An article last Sunday about the actor and podcast host Marc Maron misspelled the surname of a writer. He is Kurt Andersen, not Anderson.
match_headline: Marc Maron on ‘GLOW,’ His Podcast and ‘Sword of Trust’

text: An article last Sunday about day trips from New York City misstated the price of a round-trip train ride from the city to Philadelphia. The off-peak fare is $52, not $33.50.
match_headline: 8 Day Trips From New York, No Car Needed

text: An article on July 14 about elephants in captivity misstated a position of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums. It has raised questions about the suitability of animal sanctuaries that it has not accrredited; it does not disapprove of sanctuaries in general. The article also referred incorrectly to Lisa Faust. She is an expert in captive-animal viability, not captive-animal reproduction.
match_headline: Zoos Called It a ‘Rescue.’ But Are the Elephants Really Better Off?

text: An article on Page 16 about sunscreens described melanoma incorrectly. It is not the most common form of skin cancer; it is the most lethal. Basal-cell carcinoma is the most common type.
match_headline: When You Wear Sunscreen, You’re Taking Part in a Safety Study

text: An article on Page 38 about the purge of academics in Turkey misidentified the Turkish writer and sociologist Ismail Besikci. He is not Kurdish.
match_headline: ‘The Era of People Like You Is Over’: How Turkey Purged Its Intellectuals

text: An article on July 11 about Jeffrey Epstein’s personal wealth misstated how Mr. Epstein came to the attention of Alan Greenberg, the chairman of Bear Stearns. A parent of a student at the Dalton School recommended Mr. Epstein to Mr. Greenberg. Mr. Epstein did not tutor Mr. Greenberg’s son.
match_headline: Jeffrey Epstein’s Fortune May Be More Illusion Than Fact

text: An article on Saturday about Jeffrey Epstein’s yearslong relationship with Leslie H. Wexner misstated the name of an arts center in Columbus, Ohio. It is the Wexner Center for the Arts, not the Wexner Arts Center.
match_headline: How Jeffrey Epstein Used the Billionaire Behind Victoria’s Secret for Wealth and Women

text: An article on Saturday about Congo’s new plan to fight Ebola referred incorrectly to David Gressly’s role in the Ebola relief effort. He is coordinating the security and humanitarian response in Congo, not all of the U.N. efforts. The W.H.O., part of the U.N., continues to lead the health response, in partnership with the Democratic Republic of Congo.
match_headline: In Congo, a New Plan to Fight Ebola Follows a Government Power Struggle

text: An article on Sunday about violence against gay men and lesbians in Poland misspelled the surname of the United States ambassador to Poland. She is Georgette Mosbacher, not Mossbacher.
match_headline: Anti-Gay Brutality in a Polish Town Blamed on Poisonous Propaganda

text: An article on Monday about Democratic voters’ perspective on impeaching President Trump misspelled the surname of a New Hampshire Democratic activist. He is Terry Shumaker, not Shoemaker.
match_headline: Why Aren’t 2020 Democrats Talking About Impeachment? Because Voters Aren’t Asking

text: An article on Sunday about the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions campaign to boycott Israel referred imprecisely to the position that the World Council of Churches in Europe has taken on the boycott. While some members of the organization publicly support the movement, the organization itself is not among the groups leading the charge for B.D.S.
match_headline: Is B.D.S. Anti-Semitic? A Closer Look at the Boycott Israel Campaign

text: An article on Tuesday about protests in Puerto Rico included a remark by René Pérez, the rapper known as Residente, that misstated the origins of Puerto Rico’s Constitution. It was written by a Puerto Rican constitutional assembly, then amended and approved by the United States Congress; it was not written by officials in Washington.
match_headline: Protests Are Still Erupting in Puerto Rico. This Time, It’s Over Wanda Vázquez as Governor

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the trial of several men connected to a far-right group called the Proud Boys on charges of riot and attempted assault misidentified a city in which far-right groups have clashed with opponents. It is Portland, Ore., not Portland, Me.
match_headline: Far-Right Proud Boys Go on Trial, but Anti-Fascists Are Boycotting

text: An article on Friday about a House panel’s hearing on claims that the e-cigarette maker Juul Labs paid schools and youth organizations for the opportunity to talk with children incorrectly included Dwight School in New York City among schools that were offered $10,000 by Juul Labs. Dwight School was not offered money by the company in exchange for access to students in classrooms or after school.
match_headline: Juul Targeted Schools and Youth Camps, House Panel on Vaping Claims

text: An article on Saturday about the lack of applicants for tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs in France misstated Agnès Pannier-Runacher’s title. She is France’s secretary of state for economy and finance, not the country’s economy minister. The article also misstated the given name of the president of Groupe Pernoud. He is Gilles Pernoud, who is also the company’s chief executive, not Georges, who is the company’s founder.
match_headline: In an Industrial Corner of France, 18,000 Jobs Are On Offer. Why Aren’t People Taking Them?

text: An article on Monday about Amazon’s investments in the grocery industry misstated the name of a grocery store chain. It is Kroger, not Krogers.
match_headline: Amazon Wants to Rule the Grocery Aisles, and Not Just at Whole Foods

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the Mets’ acquisition of the All-Star pitcher Marcus Stroman referred incorrectly to Jason Vargas. He is a left-hander, not a right-hander.
match_headline: Marcus Stroman Arrives as Jason Vargas Departs in Mets Shuffle

text: An article about chimney swifts misidentified the journal in which a study of chimney swifts appeared. It was Avian Conservation & Ecology, not Aviation Conservation & Ecology.
match_headline: Wanted: Old Chimney, Suitable for Roosting

text: An article on July 19 about the appointment of an American to the top NATO intelligence post referred incorrectly to the number of Americans currently serving as assistant secretary-general in NATO. There are two, not one. (In addition to John Manza, Wayne Bush is an assistant secretary-general until his term ends in October.)
match_headline: American to Lead NATO Intelligence as Iraq-War-Era Concerns About U.S. Linger

text: An article on Tuesday about the introduction of legislation that would increase oversight of the Olympic committee and national sports governing bodies to protect athletes from abuse misstated the amount of the United States Olympic Committee’s current contribution to SafeSport. It is $6.2 million, not $3.1 million.
match_headline: Senators Will Push for Increased Oversight of Olympic Sports

text: An article on Tuesday about an algorithm that identifies which patients are most likely to become infected with H.I.V. misidentified the institution at which Julia Marcus works. She is now at Harvard Medical School, not Kaiser Permanente.
match_headline: Would You Want a Computer to Judge Your Risk of H.I.V. Infection?

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the football star Keith Lincoln misstated the number of seasons he played for the San Diego Chargers. It was six, not three. As the obituary noted later, he began playing for the team in 1961, was traded to the Buffalo Bills in 1967 and returned to San Diego the next season for one game.
match_headline: Keith Lincoln, San Diego Chargers Star in the A.F.L., Dies at 80

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Broadway producer and director Hal Prince misstated Mr. Prince’s role in the 1978 Broadway musical “On the Twentieth Century.” He directed it; he did not produce it. (The production had several producers.) A photo caption with an image from a performance of his remake of “Show Boat” misstated the year of the performance. It was 1994, not 1998.
match_headline: Hal Prince, Giant of Broadway and Reaper of Tonys, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the All-Pro linebacker Nick Buoniconti misstated an achievement of the Miami Dolphins in 1971. They were champions of the American Football Conference, not the American Football League. (The A.F.L. and N.F.L. merged in 1970.)
match_headline: Nick Buoniconti, 78, Dies; All-Pro Linebacker Championed Medical Research

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the Hungarian philosopher Agnes Heller included a quotation from a statement by Judith Friedlander, a former dean of the New School for Social Research in New York, that conveyed imprecisely Dr. Friedlander’s thoughts about Ms. Heller’s death. While some of Ms. Heller’s colleagues and friends expressed skepticism about the circumstances of her death, Dr. Friedlander did not. The quotation has been removed from the obituary.
match_headline: Agnes Heller, 90, Hungarian Philosopher and Outspoken Dissident, Is Dead

text: An article on Friday about Representative Will Hurd of Texas and his decision to retire referred incorrectly to a FiveThirtyEight analysis predicting which party would win control of Congress in the 2020 elections. The article said a composite of polls found that 40 percent of voters favored Republicans, not that the Republican Party has a 40 percent chance of winning control of Congress.
match_headline: Will Hurd, Only Black Republican in House, Is Retiring From Congress

text: An article on Thursday about the series finale of “Jane the Virgin” misidentified the character who was “back in everyone’s good graces.” She was Luisa, not Rose.
match_headline: ‘Jane the Virgin’ Ended Much Like It Began

text: An article on Page 22 about the Spanish writer Javier Marías misstated the year in which Spain announced that Generalissimo Francisco Franco’s remains would be exhumed. It was 2018, not 2019.
match_headline: Spain’s Most Celebrated Writer Believes the Fascist Past Is Still Present

text: An obituary on Friday about Vivian Paley, a pioneering educator and author, using information provided by a family member, misstated Ms. Paley’s date of death. It was July 26, not July 19.
match_headline: Vivian Paley, Educator Who Promoted Storytelling, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Monday about Ben Kinchlow, a co-host of “The 700 Club,” referred incorrectly to Mr. Kinchlow’s wife, Vivian Carolyn Jordan. She died in 2014; she did not survive him.
match_headline: Rev. Ben Kinchlow, Co-Host of TV’s ‘The 700 Club,’ Dies at 82

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Corbin Gwaltney, the founder of the Chronicle of Higher Education newspaper, referred incorrectly to an editorial policy at The Chronicle under which the title Dr. would be used only for medical doctors, not recipients of Ph.Ds. The policy was in force only while Mr. Gwaltney ran the publication; it did not continue afterward. The Chronicle has since dispensed with honorifics altogether.
match_headline: Corbin Gwaltney, Chronicle of Higher Education Founder, Dies at 97

text: An article last Sunday about Charles Manson and pop culture referred imprecisely to the timing of events of the summer of 1969. The Woodstock music festival took place the week after the Manson family murders, not beforehand.
match_headline: Why Pop Culture Still Can’t Get Enough of Charles Manson

text: An article on Monday about an algae bloom that is contaminating Lake Hopatcong misstated the requirements for septic tanks in Jefferson Township, N.J. The tanks must be pumped out every three years, not yearly. It also misidentified the administration that revived the Lake Hopatcong Commission. It was renewed under former Gov. Chris Christie’s administration, not Gov. Philip D. Murphy’s.
match_headline: Algae Bloom Fouls N.J.’s Largest Lake, Indicating Broader Crisis

text: An article on Friday about the Rev. LaKeesha Walrond, who recently became president of New York Theological Seminary, referred incorrectly to her presidency’s distinction. She is the first African-American woman and the first woman to serve as its president in a permanent capacity, but not the first African-American.
match_headline: A First at a Century-Old Seminary: A Black Woman Takes Charge

text: An article on Thursday about the accused sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein and his fascination with eugenics misstated the name of a group to which a charity established by Mr. Epstein donated $20,000 in 2011. It was the World Transhumanist Association, not the Worldwide Transhumanist Association.
match_headline: Jeffrey Epstein Hoped to Seed Human Race With His DNA

text: An article on Friday about the complications that the adoption of self-driving cars could pose for communities and urban planners misstated the name for a transportation standards-setting organization. It is SAE International, not the Society of Automotive Engineers.
match_headline: How Jaywalking Could Jam Up the Era of Self-Driving Cars

text: An article on Friday about the South African musician Abdullah Ibrahim referred incorrectly to his marriage to Sathima Bea Benjamin. They were divorced in 2011; they did not remain married until her death in 2013.
match_headline: Abdullah Ibrahim: A Lifetime of Dreams and Resistance at the Piano

text: An article on Tuesday about combating domestic terrorism referred incorrectly to the attacks on mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand. The attack involved a single gunman, not multiple.
match_headline: Shootings Renew Debate Over How to Combat Domestic Terrorism

text: An article on Tuesday about a 1996 law meant to protect young internet companies from liability misidentified the law that protects hate speech. It is the First Amendment, not Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Legal Shield for Websites Rattles Under Onslaught of Hate Speech

text: A picture caption with a critic’s notebook on Tuesday about the Mostly Mozart Festival misidentified the composers who were included in the program conducted by Gianandrea Noseda. They were Beethoven and Schubert, not Beethoven and Brahms.
match_headline: Guests Artists Enliven the Mostly Mozart Festival

text: An article on Wednesday about international reaction to the El Paso shooting misspelled the given name of a writer for the German newsmagazine Der Spiegel. He is Marc Pitzke, not Mark.
match_headline: World Reacts to El Paso Shooting and the Hate That Fueled It

text: An article on Wednesday about new sanctions placed on Venezuela by the United States, relying on a transcript of prepared remarks, misquoted John R. Bolton, President Trump’s national security adviser. At his meeting in Lima, Peru, Mr. Bolton said, “now is the time for action,” not “the time for dialogue is over.”
ref_headline: now is the time for action,
match_headline: With Tougher U.S. Sanctions on Venezuela, Bolton Says ‘Now is the Time for Action’

text: An article on Wednesday about the limit of free speech in European countries misstated the year in which a gunman killed 77 people in Norway. It was 2011, not 2001.
match_headline: The El Paso Shooting Revived the Free Speech Debate. Europe Has Limits.

text: An article on Wednesday about the Democratic Socialists of America misstated the given name of a member from the chapter in Providence, R.I. The member is Thea Riofrancos, not Theo.
match_headline: Is ‘Bernie or Bust’ the Future of the Left?

text: An article on July 27 about Roman Polanski’s latest film, “J’accuse,” misidentified the country where Mr. Polanski was born. It was France, not Poland.
match_headline: Roman Polanski’s New Film Will Compete at Venice Film Festival

text: An article on Wednesday about anxiety among Latinos following the mass shooting at a Walmart store in El Paso misstated the size of the Latino population in the United States. There were about 59.9 million as of July 2018, not 56.5 million now.
match_headline: ‘It Feels Like Being Hunted’: Latinos Across U.S. in Fear After El Paso Massacre

text: An article on Saturday about the growing number of young voters, including conservatives, who identify climate change as a top priority described incorrectly one of the findings of a report by the Republican polling firm Public Opinion Strategies. The conclusion that “climate change is their most important issue” referred to younger voters in general, not only to younger Republicans.
ref_headline: climate change is their most important issue
match_headline: Climate Could Be an Electoral Time Bomb, Republican Strategists Fear

text: An article on Sunday about the closing of The Warroad Pioneer, a local newspaper in Minnesota, described incorrectly the song passage referred to by the publisher of The Warroad Pioneer. It is from a traditional Christian hymn; not a contemporary song.
match_headline: Dying Gasp of One Local Newspaper

text: An article on Thursday about the arrests in Mississippi of hundreds of workers in raids by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents misidentified the organization for which Tom Super is a spokesman. It is the National Chicken Council, not Koch Foods, which ran of the poultry plants raided.
match_headline: ICE Arrests Hundreds in Mississippi Raids Targeting Immigrant Workers

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about food in ancient Pompeii misidentified the date of a mosaic showing the sea life of the Mediterranean. It is from circa 100 B.C.- A.D. 79, not 1000 B.C.
match_headline: Stuffed Dormouse and Fish Gut Sauce: The Flavors of Pompeii

text: An article on Thursday about the effect of climate change on the global food supply misquoted and misattributed comments about proposals to address a possible food crisis. Those comments were made by Pamela McElwee, not Cynthia Rosenzweig. In addition, part of the quote was rendered incorrectly. Dr. McElwee said, “What some of these solutions do require is attention, financial support, enabling environments.” She did not say, “But what some of these solutions do require is attention, financial support, enabling environments.”
ref_headline: What some of these solutions do require is attention, financial support, enabling environments.
match_headline: Climate Change Threatens the World’s Food Supply, United Nations Warns

text: An article on Wednesday about Beijing’s need for private businesses to boost the economy misstated the increased use by RiseSun Real Estate Development of notes issued in China by companies and banks in lieu of cash. The developer said its use of commercial acceptance notes, which are issued by companies, and similar notes backed by banks had increased by nine times last year, not 13 times. Its use of commercial acceptance notes alone increased by 13 times over that period.
match_headline: Circulating in China’s Financial System: More Than $200 Billion in I.O.U.s

text: An article on Friday about a baseball game next summer at Iowa’s Field of Dreams misidentified the stadium in Omaha that hosted a major league game in June. It was TD Ameritrade Park, not Rosenblatt Stadium. (Rosenblatt was closed in 2010.)
match_headline: Yankees Will Play White Sox at Iowa’s Field of Dreams

text: An article on Thursday about a study that suggests baseball players live longer than the average man misstated a finding of Harvard researchers in a study about baseball players’ long-term health. Scientists determined that at any given age, major leaguers are 24 percent less likely to die than men in the general population; they did not determine that “major leaguers live 24 percent longer than the average male.”
ref_headline: major leaguers live 24 percent longer than the average male.
match_headline: Another Baseball Mystery: Why Do Players Seem to Live Longer?

text: An article on Tuesday about the ancient burning of a Maya city misidentified the translator of text on a stone column in an ancient Maya site. Alexandre Tokovinine, a specialist in Mayan writing at the University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, translated the text, not Francisco Estrada-Belli, the archaeologist at Tulane University who excavated the site. Additionally, a picture caption in the article incorrectly described the stone column. It included the name of a city, Bahlam Jol; it did not describe the burning of that city.
match_headline: Burning of Maya City Said to Be Act of Total Warfare

text: An article on Page 4 about playgoers’ different perceptions of the play “Fairview” misidentifies the London theater that will be presenting the play. It is the Young Vic, not the Old Vic.
match_headline: ‘Fairview’: Watching a Play in Black and White

text: An article on Page 9 about viral campaign ads misidentifies the ad maker for M.J. Hegar and Amy McGrath. They both use Putnam Partners, not Mark Putnam.
match_headline: How the Viral Campaign Ad Became a Political Trap

text: An obituary on Friday about the Indian politician Sushma Swaraj misidentified the body to which she was elected at age 25. It was the state legislative assembly in Haryana, not the lower house of India’s Parliament.
match_headline: Sushma Swaraj, 67, Popular Indian Minister and Modi Ally, Dies

text: An article last Sunday about sustained demand for waterfront property referred incorrectly in one instance to the area around the house listed in Glen Arbor, Mich. It is Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore, not Sleepy Bear Dunes National Lakeshore.

An article last Sunday about Lana Wood’s search for answers in the unexplained 1981 death of her sister, the actress Natalie Wood, misstated the person responsible for the casting of the Wood sisters in the film “The Searchers.” It was John Ford, not John Huston. The article also misidentified the law enforcement organization that employs Detective Ralph Hernandez. It is the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, not the Los Angeles Police Department. And the article paraphrased incorrectly one of Detective Hernandez’s statements. He said that the coroner could not rule out that Natalie Wood was unconscious before entering the water, not that he could not rule out that she was dead before entering the water.
match_headline: Lana Wood, Natalie’s Little Sister, Has Plenty to Say

text: An article on Sunday about the rise of far-right nationalism in Sweden included an inaccurate detail about speakers hosted by Sweden Democrats, a political party with neo-Nazi roots. The party has not hosted the American white nationalist Richard Spencer.
match_headline: The Global Machine Behind the Rise of Far-Right Nationalism

text: An article on Monday about an explosion that released radiation off the coast of northern Russia last week misstated the location of Chernobyl. It is in present-day Ukraine, which was part of the Soviet Union at the time of the nuclear accident. It is not in Russia.
match_headline: U.S. Officials Suspect New Nuclear Missile in Explosion That Killed 7 Russians

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about an attack on a mosque in Norway misidentified the message board on which the suspect in the attack posted messages. While it was an online message forum, it was not 8chan.
match_headline: After Attack on Norway Mosque, Body Found at Home Tied to Assailant

text: An article on Thursday about a new study that suggests gulls take behavioral cues from people when foraging in urban environments misidentified a type of gull in Britain. It is the lesser black-backed gull, not the lesser black-billed gull.
match_headline: Want to Stop Gulls From Stealing Your Food? Stare Them Down, Study Says

text: An article on Monday about Karen Bermudez Rodriguez, a nanny who was killed along with her employer in New Jersey, misstated the given name of the man accused of killing them. His name is Joseph Porter, not Joshua Porter.
match_headline: How a Nanny’s Adventure in the U.S. Ended in Bloodshed

text: An article on Saturday about “Blinded by the Light,” a film based on a memoir by Sarfraz Manzoor, misspelled the surname of the film director’s husband and collaborator. He is Paul Mayeda Berges, not Burges.
match_headline: Finding Salvation in Springsteen From a London Suburb

text: An article on Saturday about the pop star Sho Madjozi misstated the media executive Alex Okosi’s job title. He is an executive vice president of the channel that oversees the BET awards, not the director. The article also misstated the nationality of Sho Madjozi’s father. He is South African, not Swedish.
match_headline: Sho Madjozi’s Mixed Up, Pan-African Rap

text: An article on Wednesday about Toni Basil and her work as the choreographer for the film “Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood,” misstated the title of a hit song. It is “Mickey,” not “Hey Mickey.”
ref_headline: Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood,
match_headline: Quentin Tarantino’s Goddess of Go-Go

text: An article on Sunday about Woodstock artifacts referred incorrectly to an album recorded by one of its performers. Ravi Shankar’s “At the Woodstock Festival” was recorded in a studio, with crowd noise added in; it was not recorded at the festival.
match_headline: How to Relive Woodstock From the Comfort of Your Couch

text: An obituary on Saturday about the jazz clarinetist and saxophonist Bob Wilber omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to his wife, the singer Pug Horton, Mr. Wilber is survived by a daughter, Elizabeth Wilber Gongde.
match_headline: Bob Wilber, Champion of Jazz’s Legacy, Is Dead at 91

text: An obituary on Sunday about the inventor Sherm Poppen, using information from a family member, misstated his mother’s original surname. It was Fowlie, not Fowler.
match_headline: Sherm Poppen, a Dad Who Fathered the Snowboard, Dies at 89

text: An article on Monday about an attack on a mosque in Norway misstated the number of victims in a 2011 bombing and mass shooting in Norway. An attacker killed 77 people, not 92.
match_headline: Norway Police Investigate Mosque Attack as Attempted ‘Act of Terrorism’

text: An article on Saturday about documents that offer disturbing details about Jeffrey Epstein’s activities at his Florida mansion misidentified the job that Virginia Giuffre held at the spa at Mar-a-Lago. She was an attendant, not a masseuse.
match_headline: ‘Massage’ Was Code for ‘Sex’: New Epstein Abuse Revelations

text: An article on Friday about LiveWire, the first production electric vehicle from Harley-Davidson, misstated the LiveWire’s charging speeds. It can be charged with a regular wall outlet for a normal charge and with a DC Fast charger. A Level 2 charger, while compatible, will not charge it any faster than a standard outlet.
match_headline: An Electric Harley Loses the Growl but Still Aims to Turn Heads

text: Because of a production error, several sentences were missing from an article about technology companies’ newly patriotic posturing as a tactic to fend off government regulation. The full article is available online at nytimes.com.
match_headline: The Phony Patriots of Silicon Valley

text: An obituary on Thursday about the artist Marisa Merz referred incompletely to the 2017 retrospective “Marisa Merz: The Sky Is a Great Space.” It was organized by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles — not just by the Metropolitan Museum.
ref_headline: Marisa Merz: The Sky Is a Great Space.
match_headline: Marisa Merz, Bold Explorer When Art Was a Man’s World, Dies at 93

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about Henri Belolo, a founder of the disco group the Village People, referred incorrectly to the song “Back Stabbers.” It was written by Leon Huff, Gene McFadden and John Whitehead — not by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff.
match_headline: Henri Belolo, a Founder of the Village People, Dies at 82

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s reaction to the protests in Hong Kong misidentified a nationalist Chinese newspaper that is seen as reflecting the views of government hard-liners. It is The Global Times, not The Daily Times.
match_headline: ‘Hong Kong Thing’ Is ‘Very Tough,’ but Trump Doesn’t Criticize China

text: An article on Thursday about an ethics investigation into Prime Minister Justin Trudeau of Canada misstated where Jagmeet Singh spoke to reporters. He was in Victoria, British Columbia, not Vancouver.
match_headline: Trudeau Violated Ethics Law in SNC-Lavalin Case, Watchdog Finds

text: An article on Thursday about grass-roots efforts to bar gerrymandering in Wisconsin misstated the size of the Lincoln County board of supervisors. It has 22 members, not 27.
match_headline: In the War Against Gerrymandering, an Army of Voters Meets a Dug-in Foe

text: An article on Thursday about efforts in Ocean City, N.J., to tame aggressive gulls, misspelled one New Jersey town’s name. It is Marlton, not Marleton.
match_headline: Flying Assassins Are Called In to Combat Aggressive Gulls

text: An article on Aug. 3 about the merger of the kosher food companies Kayco and Manischewitz referred imprecisely to Wise potato chips. They are kosher, but they are not certified for Passover.
match_headline: ‘Man, Oh Manischewitz’: Kosher Food Merger Opens New Chapter for Famous Name

text: An article on Thursday about a website that displays private art collections described incorrectly a type of magazine advertising spending that has seen a sharp decline between 2007 and 2017. It was magazine ad spending over all, not home magazine spending.
match_headline: Art Disappears in Private Hands. Can Social Media Resurface It?

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s cautious distance from Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement misidentified the state that Senator Lindsey Graham represents. It is South Carolina, not North Carolina.
match_headline: Trump’s Hong Kong Caution Isolates Him From Congress, Allies and Advisers

text: An article this weekend on Page 5 about the new popularity of New Jersey boardwalk towns among New Yorkers misstates the location of a hotel. The Seaview, A Dolce Hotel, is in Galloway, not Stone Harbor.Also, it omitted a buyer of Pier Village. A partnership of Kushner Companies and Extell Development Company purchased the complex, not just Kushner. Additionally, Kushner was responsible for five restaurants, not six, on the Long Branch boardwalk, and Extell commissioned the carousel there, not Kushner.
match_headline: The New Yorkers Are Coming. Can Springsteen’s Jersey Shore Survive?

text: An article on Friday about a rule proposed by the Labor Department that would allow more federal contractors to base employment decisions on religion misstated the name of a group that opposes government-funded religion. It is the Baptist Joint Committee for Religious Liberty, not the Baptist Joint Committee for Religious Freedom.
match_headline: Labor Dept. Moves to Expand Religion Exemption for Hiring and Firing

text: An article on Aug. 9 about sexual abuse allegations against the equestrian coach George H. Morris referred incorrectly to the time Michael D. Cintas spent with Mr. Morris in 1964. text: An editorial on Sept. 1 about the Trump administration’s approach to conservation and environmental regulation used outdated information to describe the storage of wastes from the proposed Twin Metals copper and nickel mine in Minnesota. The company announced in July that it would store mining wastes using a dry stack system, which it says greatly reduces the risk of leakage of hazardous mine waste, not in tailings ponds.
match_headline: Trump to Miners, Loggers and Drillers: This Land Is Your Land

text: An article on Saturday about the matchup between Serena Williams and Bianca Andreescu at the United States Open tennis tournament referred incorrectly to Andreescu’s title last month at the Rogers Cup, or Canadian Open. She is the first Canadian woman to win it since 1969, not the first Canadian woman to win it.
match_headline: Serena Williams vs. Bianca Andreescu: An Intergenerational Duel at the U.S. Open

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Antonio Brown, the seven-time Pro Bowl receiver who was released from the Oakland Raiders to sign with the New England Patriots, misidentified the city where the Raiders will open their season on Monday. They will be playing at home, not in Denver.
match_headline: Antonio Brown, Released by the Raiders, to Sign With the Patriots

text: An entry on Saturday in the What’s on TV highlights misstated how many comedy specials Gary Owen has done for Showtime. “#DoinWhatIDo” is his fourth, not his second.
match_headline: What’s on TV Saturday: ‘Mary Queen of Scots’ and ‘WOW’

text: An article on Monday about the acclaimed film director Gus Van Sant and his first solo exhibition of paintings in New York misstated his age. He is 67, not 66.
match_headline: Gus Van Sant’s Next Picture Will Be a Watercolor

text: An obituary on Saturday about Robert Mugabe, the first prime minister and later president of independent Zimbabwe, misspelled the surname of a former vice president of Zimbabwe. She is Joice Mujuru, not Majuru.
match_headline: Robert Mugabe, Strongman Who Cried, ‘Zimbabwe Is Mine,’ Dies at 95

text: An article on Sunday about an Iranian oil tanker anchored off the coast of Syria incorrectly described the release of satellite images of the Adrian Darya 1. The images were released by the space technology company Maxar Technologies, not by two companies.
match_headline: Images from Space Show Released Iranian Oil Tanker Near Syrian Coast

text: An article on Tuesday about Nigeria’s plans to airlift its citizens out of South Africa misstated the name of the airline that has volunteered to help Nigerians leave. It is Air Peace, not Peace Air.
match_headline: Nigeria Plans to Airlift Its Citizens Out of South Africa After Xenophobic Riots

text: An article on Monday about the decision by Mark Sanford, the former governor and representative from South Carolina, to challenge President Trump for the Republican presidential nomination misstated the year Bill Weld was a nominee on the Libertarian ticket for president. It was 2016, not 2012.
match_headline: Mark Sanford Will Challenge Trump in Republican Primary

text: An article on Tuesday about a possible threat that the beams of light projected in Lower Manhattan each year in tribute to the victims of the Sept. 11 attacks pose to migratory birds misstated part of the name of a program that monitors the streets for birds that have died after crashing into buildings. It is N.Y.C. Audubon’s Project Safe Flight, not Safelight.
match_headline: The 9/11 Tribute Lights Are Endangering 160,000 Birds a Year

text: An article on Tuesday about Daniel Markovits’s book “The Meritocracy Trap” misspelled the given name of one graduate of Yale Law School — and the newest Supreme Court justice. He is Brett Kavanaugh, not Bret.
match_headline: The Meritocrat Who Wants to Unwind the Meritocracy

text: An article on Sept. 3 about thousands of lawsuits filed by Carlsbad Medical Center in New Mexico against patients referred incorrectly to the government agency regulating consumer financial products. It is the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, not the Consumer Credit Protection Bureau.
match_headline: The Mysterious Vaping Illness That’s ‘Becoming an Epidemic’

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about the filmmaker Alice Guy Blaché misstated the year that her film “My Madonna” was released. It was released in 1915, not 1951.
match_headline: Overlooked No More: Alice Guy Blaché, the World’s First Female Filmmaker

text: An article on Tuesday about a C.I.A. informant extracted from Russia referred incorrectly to the timing of the initial reporting of the C.I.A.’s 2016 exfiltration offer to the informant. An offer that appears to be the same one described in the Times article was reported by Bob Woodward in his 2018 book “Fear.”
match_headline: C.I.A. Informant Extracted From Russia Had Sent Secrets to U.S. for Decades

text: An article on Wednesday about Margrethe Vestager, the European Union’s competition commissioner, erroneously presented some paraphrased comments by Joe Kennedy about Ms. Vestager’s work on tech industry regulation as a direct quotation. While Mr. Kennedy expressed the idea that Ms. Vestager is at the vanguard of tougher tech industry regulation on both sides of the Atlantic, those were not his exact words.
match_headline: E.U.’s New Digital Czar: ‘Most Powerful Regulator of Big Tech on the Planet’

text: An article on Wednesday about possible replacements to succeed John Bolton as President Trump’s national security adviser misspelled the surname of the diplomat who became the ambassador to the United Nations. She is Kelly Knight Craft, not Kraft.
match_headline: Who Could Replace John Bolton?

text: An article on Wednesday about a bill to stem rising rents in California misstated one provision of the bill approved by the State Senate. It exempts dwellings built within the last 15 years from rent caps, not buildings older than that.
match_headline: California Rent Control Bill Advances, Fueled by Housing Crisis

text: An article on Wednesday about Canada’s approach to flood-prone areas as a guide for communities in the United States misstated the number of “severe repetitive loss properties” in North Carolina. It is more than 1,100, not roughly 10,000.
match_headline: Canada Tries a Forceful Message for Flood Victims: Live Someplace Else

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about dance Instagram accounts misstated Dava Huesca’s academic credentials. She is a graduate of Purchase College, not a senior.
match_headline: Five Dance Instagram Accounts You Should Follow

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about Miles Davis’s album “Rubberband” misspelled the given name of Davis’s third wife. She is Cicely Tyson, not Cecily.
match_headline: What ‘Rubberband’ Reveals About Miles Davis’s Final Act

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the photographer Robert Frank misstated how old his daughter, Andrea, was when she died. She was 20, not 21.
match_headline: Robert Frank Dies; Pivotal Documentary Photographer Was 94

text: An article on Thursday about Kamala Harris’s presidential campaign referred imprecisely to the organization She the People. It is an organization for women of color, not a black women’s organization.
match_headline: What Kamala Harris Needs to Do at the Debate Tonight

text: A picture with this weekend’s cover article about the divorce of Rudolph W. and Judith Giuliani was published in error. The image showed Jennifer LeBlanc walking with Mr. Giuliani, not Judith Giuliani.
match_headline: Giuliani Divorce: It’s Ugly, It’s Operatic. What Did You Expect?

text: An article on Wednesday about soaring pork prices in China referred incorrectly to Xu Shufang. She is a woman.
match_headline: China’s Pork Prices Soar, Adding to Beijing’s Troubles

text: An article on Brown University putting an official tied to Jeffrey Epstein’s Massachusetts Institute of Technology gifts on leave misstated the surname of M.I.T.’s president. He is L. Rafael Reif, not Reid.
match_headline: Brown University Puts Official Tied to Jeffrey Epstein’s M.I.T. Gifts on Leave

text: An article on Friday about a proposed ban on flavored vaping products misstated the number of countries outside the United States where Juul’s products are sold. It is 19, not 20.
match_headline: A Ban on Flavored E-Cigarettes Would Sharply Cut Sales

text: An article on Page 8 about “Slave Play” misstates the date of its opening night. The show, which is now in previews, will open Oct. 6, not Oct. 10.
match_headline: Is Broadway Ready for ‘Slave Play’?

text: An article on Page 86 about modernist art shows misstates the years of Abby Weed Grey’s birth and death. She was born in 1902 and died in 1983, not in 1922 and 1978.
match_headline: Modernism Reboots at the Museums

text: An article on Page 54 about classical music concerts scheduled for the fall, using information from the publicist, misstated the title of Christopher Cerrone’s new piano concerto. It is “The Air Suspended,” not “Dissolving Margins.” (That was a working title.) It also misstates the date on which the Detroit Symphony Orchestra will open a celebration of the centennial of its Orchestra Hall with a re-creation of its first concert there. It is Oct. 4, not Oct. 23. (Oct. 23 is the actual anniversary.) And misstates the role of Daniela Candillari in the new chamber opera “Desire.” She is the music director, not the conductor. (The work is performed without a conductor.)
match_headline: 10 Months of Classical Concerts You Won’t Want to Miss

text: An entry about “Between Two Ferns: The Movie” in the Fall TV preview article on Page 28 misspells the surname of the actress in the Netflix film. She is Tiffany Haddish, not Hadish.
match_headline: Theater This Season: A Show (or 10) for Every Mood

text: An article on Page 106 about outdoor architectural projects misspells the name of the landscape architecture firm that worked on Roberto Clemente State Park in the Bronx. It is Mathews Nielsen, not Matthews Nielsen.
match_headline: The New Architecture: Sky Parks, Tidal Pools and ‘Solar Carving’

text: An article on Page 88 about 19 art shows that highlight a new focus on inclusion referred incorrectly to a museum in Washington. It is the National Gallery of Art, not the National Art Gallery.
match_headline: At 19 Art Shows, From Los Angeles to Manhattan, All Eyes Are on Inclusion

text: An article on Page 120 about albums, shows and festivals coming this fall, using information from a representative of the artist Vagabon, misstates some of the lyrics to one of the songs on her album “Vagabon.” The lyric is “All the women I meet are tired” not “All the women in me are tired.”
match_headline: 77 Pop and Jazz Albums, Shows and Festivals Coming This Fall

text: An article on Sunday about legislation that would effectively bar a Chinese state-owned company called CRRC from competing for new contracts in the United States referred incorrectly to one of the manufacturers that American cities have bought subway cars from. Hyundai is a South Korean manufacturer, not a Japanese manufacturer.
match_headline: Fearing ‘Spy Trains,’ Congress May Ban a Chinese Maker of Subway Cars

text: An article on Monday about Tunisia’s presidential election misspelled the given name of the wife of the candidate Nabil Karoui. She is Salwa Smaoui, not Salma.
match_headline: Tunisia Votes for a President as It Struggles to Build Democracy

text: An article on Saturday about Representative Liz Cheney’s combative style in Congress referred incorrectly to Representative Rashida Tlaib. She is a congresswoman representing Michigan, not Minnesota.
match_headline: Liz Cheney, Tart-Tongued Fighter, Is Warring With Rand Paul Over Who’s Trumpier

text: An article on Sunday about the American team’s seventh-place finish in the FIBA World Cup basketball tournament misspelled the name of a German basketball team. It is Ratiopharm Ulm, not Radiopharm Ulm.
match_headline: U.S. Defeats Poland at Basketball World Cup. But for 7th Place.

text: An article on Thursday about making long-term care choices described imprecisely government coverage for nursing homes. While Medicare does cover some care in nursing homes under certain conditions, it is Medicaid that can help pay for long-term nursing home care after a patient’s other assets are depleted.
match_headline: What Are My Long-Term Care Options?

text: An article on Sunday about a planned cable-car network to Jewish holy sites erroneously attributed a distinction to the Western Wall in Jerusalem. It is one of the holiest sites in Judaism, not the holiest.
match_headline: Cable Cars Over Jerusalem? Some See ‘Disneyfication’ of Holy City

text: An article on Sept. 9 about Maggy Hurchalla, an environmental activist in Florida who was successfully sued by a mining company, referred incorrectly to the account that had been taken over to pay a legal judgment against her. It was a joint bank account that held savings for her and her husband’s retirement, not a retirement account belonging solely to her husband.
match_headline: The Florida Activist Is 78. The Legal Judgment Against Her Is $4 Million.

text: An article on Sunday about predictions for the second week of the N.F.L. season misstated the Vikings’ won-lost record entering the week. They were 1-0, not 0-1.
match_headline: N.F.L. Week 2 Predictions: Our Picks Against the Spread

text: An article on Monday about the reopening of the Théâtre du Châtelet in Paris misstated the date and location of the premiere of Stravinsky’s “Rite of Spring.” It was at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in 1913, not the Théâtre du Châtelet in 1911.
match_headline: After a Renovation, a Storied Theater Hopes to Entice Paris

text: An article on Tuesday about species of salmon and steelhead trout in the Columbia River basin that are listed as threatened or endangered misstated the origin of a plan to kill sea lions along the Columbia River. The plan was proposed by Native American tribes and state officials in Oregon, Washington and Idaho, not by the National Marine Fisheries Service. (The agency is responsible for approving the plan.)
match_headline: How Long Before These Salmon Are Gone? ‘Maybe 20 Years’

text: An obituary on Friday about Alison Cheek, the first female priest to celebrate the Eucharist in an Episcopal service, misstated when she and 10 other women were ordained as priests in a ceremony not authorized by the Episcopal Church’s leadership. It was July 29, 1974 — not June 29.
match_headline: Alison Cheek, Pioneering Episcopal Priest, Is Dead at 92

text: An article on Wednesday about five candidates under consideration to serve as President Trump’s national security adviser misspelled the surname of a former director of national intelligence. He is Dan Coats, not Dan Coates. It also misstated the name of a foundation. It is the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, not the Foundation for Defense of Democracy.
match_headline: Trump Names 5 Candidates for National Security Adviser

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s focus on California’s homelessness problem misstated the proportion of people in the United States who live in California. The state is home to 12 percent of the country’s population, not one-twelfth, which is a little more than 8 percent.
match_headline: Trump and California See Same Homeless Problem, but Not the Same Solutions

text: An article on Wednesday about Amazon offering improved audio for 50 million songs referred incorrectly to FLAC files, which Amazon uses to stream music. FLAC files are a compressed, not an uncompressed, format.
match_headline: Amazon Offers Millions of Songs in High-Quality Audio. Even Neil Young Approves.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the reporter Paul Ingrassia misstated when he began working at Thomson Reuters. It was 2011, not 2007.
match_headline: Paul Ingrassia, Prizewinning Auto Industry Reporter, Dies at 69

text: An article on Sept. 13 about the Trump administration’s plan to repeal a clean water regulation aimed at the use of chemicals near streams, wetlands and other water bodies misstated the scope of the 1972 Clean Water Act and the 2015 clean water regulation issued under President Obama. The Clean Water Act gave the federal government broad authority to limit pollution in major water bodies as well as smaller bodies that drain into them. It is not the case that the Obama administration extended federal authority to smaller bodies of water.
match_headline: Trump Administration Rolls Back Clean Water Protections

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about a French mayor who banned pesticides misattributed a quotation beneath a photo of Daniel Cueff, the mayor of Langouët. As the article correctly states, it was Bertrand Astic, the mayor of Boussières, not Mr. Cueff, who commented on dying trees and other signs of climate change.
match_headline: A Revolution in Brittany: Mayors Defy French State to Ban Pesticides

text: An article on Wednesday about a Spanish court’s refusal of a request from the United States to extradite Hugo Carvajal, the former intelligence chief of Venezuela, described incorrectly Juan Guaidó’s claim to Venezuela’s presidency. Mr. Guaidó called the last presidential election fraudulent, and as president of the legislature swore himself in as the head of an interim government. He did not claim to win a presidential election.
match_headline: Spanish Court Calls U.S. Extradition Request Politically Motivated

text: An article on Thursday about Greta Thunberg, a Swedish teenager and climate activist, misstated the name of a television news program that interviewed her. It is “CBS This Morning,” not “Good Morning.”
match_headline: Greta Thunberg, on Tour in America, Offers an Unvarnished View

text: An obituary on Sept. 12 about Frederic Pryor, who was jailed in East Germany on suspicion of espionage but later freed as part of a prisoner exchange between the United States and the Soviet Union, misidentified one of the cities connected by the Glienicke Bridge, where the exchange of the prisoners Francis Gary Powers and Rudolf Abel took place in 1962. It connected West Berlin with Potsdam, not East Berlin.
match_headline: Frederic Pryor, Player in ‘Bridge of Spies’ Case, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the television reporter Sander Vanocur misstated the subject in which he received a degree from Northwestern University. It was communications, not political science. It also misstated part of the name of one of Mr. Vanocur’s employers. It is the Public Broadcasting Service, not System. And it misstated the years of the movie “Dave,” in which Mr. Vanocur played a newsman, and “The Kingdom and the Power,” Gay Talese’s book about The New York Times. The movie was released in 1993, not 1983; the book was published in 1969, not 1966.
match_headline: Sander Vanocur, TV Newsman Who Covered Kennedy, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the musician, photographer, filmmaker and musicologist John Cohen incorrectly included a name on a list of musicians he photographed. He did not photograph the banjo player Charlie Poole. The obituary also referred incompletely to the 1959 film “Pull My Daisy,” whose production Mr. Cohen photographed. It was directed by Robert Frank and Alfred Leslie, not just by Mr. Frank.
match_headline: John Cohen, Champion of Old-Time Music, Is Dead at 87

text: An article on Friday about concerns that outstanding state lawsuits against the Sackler family and Purdue Pharma could jeopardize the family’s pledge to contribute $3 billion to a national opioids settlement misstated the name of a law school. It is the University of Georgia Law School, not George.
match_headline: Purdue Pharma Warns That Sackler Family May Walk From Opioid Deal

text: A picture caption with this weekend’s cover article about the production of Gershwin’s “Porgy and Bess” opening the Metropolitan Opera’s season misstates the year it was taken. It was from a 1953 performance, not a 1935 performance.
match_headline: The Complex History and Uneasy Present of ‘Porgy and Bess’

text: An article on Page 36 about the Boeing 737 Max misstates the date of the crash of Air France Flight 447. It occurred in June 2009, not January 2015. The article also describes incorrectly a mechanism used to retrim the Boeing 737 Max airplane. It is electric, not electrohydraulic. And the article misstates a detail about the National Transportation Safety Board. Though the board was denied full access to cockpit audio from Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, N.T.S.B. representatives were allowed to listen to recordings.
match_headline: What Really Brought Down the Boeing 737 Max?

text: An article last Sunday about the mattress seller Casper’s ambitions described incorrectly the product of one of the company’s competitors. The competitor, Saatva, does not imitate Casper’s mattress-in-a box concept; it ships uncompressed mattresses.
match_headline: Casper Dreams of Being Bigger Than Mattresses

text: An article on Sept. 8 about Bauhaus described incorrectly the Heinrich Neugeboren Bach monument. While it was never realized in his lifetime, it was constructed, and is still standing, in Leverkusen, Germany.
match_headline: At the Bauhaus, Music Was More Than a Hobby

text: A map with an article last Sunday about the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge misidentified a river that goes through it. The river is the Porcupine, not the Yukon.
match_headline: Exploring a Timeless Wilderness, Before the Drilling Begins

text: An article on Sept. 8 about a swim in the Willamette River in Portland, Ore., misstated the type of traffic permitted on the Marquam Bridge. It is open only to cars, not to cyclists and pedestrians.
match_headline: Following the Lead of the Diving Girl

text: An article on Monday about a lawsuit centering on Europe’s “right to be forgotten” law misstated the court to which the journalist Alessandro Biancardi has appealed a verdict to delete an article he wrote about a stabbing. It is the European Court of Human Rights, not the European Court of Justice.
match_headline: One Brother Stabbed the Other. The Journalist Who Wrote About It Paid a Price.

text: An article on Sunday about an effort to sell a vacant lot of land in Inwood misidentified the geologic origin of the Cooper Street Rock. It is Inwood Marble, formed more than 500 million years ago; it was not deposited by glaciers. The error was repeated in a headline.
match_headline: How a Paleozoic Rock Became a $3 Million Real Estate Prospect

text: An article on Tuesday about a pledge by energy companies to take action on climate change misstated the terms of a plan for a tax on carbon dioxide. While an initial draft of that proposal would have protected oil companies from lawsuits holding them accountable for climate change, the current plan does not contain that provision.
match_headline: Oil Giants, Under Fire From Climate Activists and Investors, Mount a Defense

text: An article on Tuesday about an antibiotic regimen shown to prevent tuberculosis incorrectly described a diagnostic test for tuberculosis. It is a test of sputum, not saliva.
match_headline: A Simple Regimen Can Prevent TB. Why Aren’t More People on It?

text: An article on Friday about an increase in the number of vaping-related lung illnesses referred incorrectly to the federal classification of the drug fentanyl. It is a Schedule 2 drug, not Schedule 1.
match_headline: Vaping Illnesses Increase to 530 Probable Cases, C.D.C. Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Vice President Mike Pence using a motorcade during a visit to Michigan’s Mackinac Island — where cars have been banned for more than a century — referred imprecisely to Ron Fournier. He is a public relations executive who, according to his firm, was registered as a lobbyist in the past but did no lobbying; he is not a lobbyist.
match_headline: A Motorcade on Mackinac Island? Pence’s Visit Breaks a Long Tradition

text: An article on Wednesday about an ex-soldier seeking a military funeral misstated the age of Onida Mayers. She is 54, not 55.
match_headline: On His Deathbed, a Black Ex-Soldier Makes a Plea to Clear His Name

text: An article on Friday about details disclosed in a whistle-blower complaint about the transcript of a call between President Trump and the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelensky referred incorrectly to a classification given to documents in a secret system accessible only to select White House aides, among others. It is Sensitive Compartmented Information, not Sensitive Compartmentalized Information.
match_headline: Whistle-Blower Shines Light on Super-Secret N.S.C. Computer System

text: An article on Friday about the South African golfer Lee-Anne Pace misspelled the surname of her sister in one instance. She is Simone Krog, not Krug.
match_headline: For One L.P.G.A. Golfer, a Million-Dollar Prize Is Worth the Pain

text: An article on Friday about weekend television highlights misidentified the coming season of “Bob’s Burgers.” It is the 10th, not the ninth.
match_headline: How Much Watching Time Do You Have This Weekend?

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about the New York Film Festival misstated the period in which “First Cow” takes place. It is the 19th century, not the 18th century. The error was repeated in picture caption.
match_headline: Around the Movie World in 17 Days at the New York Film Festival

text: An article on Page 30 about Namibia includes an erroneous reference to the country’s geographic location. As correctly noted in the article, it is in southwestern Africa, not in West Africa.
An obituary on Sept. 20 about Maurice Ferré, the first Hispanic mayor of Miami, misstated part of the name of one of his sons. He is José Luis, not José Antonio.
match_headline: Maurice Ferré, Miami’s First Hispanic Mayor, Dies at 84

text: An article on Page 30 about Namibia includes an erroneous reference to the country’s geographic location. As correctly noted in the article, it is in southwestern Africa, not in West Africa.

A news analysis on Sept. 15 about the expertise of meteorologists misstated the height of the Citicorp Center in relation to other buildings worldwide. When it opened in 1977, it was the 11th tallest in the world, not the seventh tallest.
match_headline: Trust Our Weather Forecasters, Not Trump

text: A chart with an article on Sunday about the increase in online photos and videos of children being sexually abused omitted the unit of measurement of federal funding for U.S. law enforcement agencies. The figures were in millions of dollars.

An article on Sunday about the founding fathers’ concerns about foreign influence on an American president misstated the year William Blount was expelled from the Senate. It was 1797, not 1787. The article also misstated the number of years since his expulsion. It is 222, not 232.
match_headline: Impeachment Battle to Turn for First Time on a President’s Ties to a Foreign Country

text: An article on Saturday about the resignation of Kurt D. Volker, the State Department’s special envoy for Ukraine, misspelled the surname of the ambassador to the European Union. He is Gordon Sondland, not Sandland.
match_headline: Kurt Volker, Trump’s Envoy for Ukraine, Resigns

text: An article on Monday about Democrats in battleground districts balancing the impeachment inquiry against President Trump and potential backlash from constituents misspelled the surname of a Democratic pollster. He is Zac McCrary, not Zac McCray.
match_headline: Back Home, House Democrats Tread Carefully on Impeachment and 2020

text: An article on Monday about Sebastian Kurz, who came in first in a snap election in Austria, misstated the threshold to earn representation in Parliament. It is 4 percent, not 5 percent.
match_headline: Kurz Wins Austria Election. Will He Turn to Far Right or Greens to Govern?

text: An article on Friday about the White House’s first knowledge of a whistle-blower’s allegations about President Trump’s dealings with Ukraine misspelled the surname of the C.I.A. general counsel. She is Courtney Simmons Elwood, not Ellwood.
match_headline: In Trump’s Ukraine Phone Call, Alarmed Aides Saw Trouble

text: An article on Saturday about the world track and field championships described incorrectly the race Allyson Felix was scheduled to run the following day. It was the 4 x 400-meter relay, not the 4 x 100. (She and her teammates won the event in world-record time.)
match_headline: At Track’s World Championships, Heat and a Hunt for Stars

text: An article on Monday about the four teams headed to the Major League Baseball playoffs misstated the number of home runs hit in 2019. There were 6,776, not 6,773.
match_headline: M.L.B.’s Juggernauts Set to Clash After a Season of Extraordinary Numbers

text: An article on Sunday about the midnight running of the marathon at the track and field world championships in Doha, Qatar, misstated the name of the stadium hosting the event. It is Khalifa International Stadium, not Khalid International Stadium.
match_headline: A Marathon at Midnight, to Beat the Heat at the World Championships in Doha

text: An article on Sunday about the chefs and owners of more than two dozen of New York City’s best restaurants misspelled the given name of Michelle Puyane’s husband. He is Ramon, not Raymond.
match_headline: Finding the Deliciousness in New York City

text: An obituary on Sunday about the ventriloquist Jimmy Nelson misstated the name of one of the characters the ventriloquist Señor Wences used in his act. He was Pedro, not Johnny.
match_headline: Jimmy Nelson, Star of the Golden Age of Ventriloquism, Dies at 90

text: A headline with an obituary about Myron Bloom, a revered French horn player, misstated Mr. Bloom’s age when he died. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 93, not 94.
match_headline: Myron Bloom, Revered French Horn Player, Is Dead at 93

text: An article on Page 4 about properties developed on desert scrub land near Pioneertown, Calif., misstates the final prices for three lots sold by Dave McAdam. The lots were sold for $150,000 each, not for a total of $150,000.
match_headline: In the Desert With Jackrabbits and Clint Eastwood

text: An article on Friday about the tradition of major film stars appearing in space films described incorrectly the recognition Sandra Bullock received for her performance in the film “Gravity.” She was nominated for an Oscar; she did not win.
match_headline: You’re a Movie Star. Congrats, Here’s Your Space Movie.

text: An article on Page 18 about the reopening of the newly expanded Museum of Modern Art omits the name of one of the architectural firms that collaborated on the museum’s expansion. It was planned by Diller Scofidio + Renfro in collaboration with Gensler, not just by Diller Scofidio + Renfro.
match_headline: The New MoMA Is Here. Get Ready for Change.

text: An article on Page 30 about the N.B.A.’s expansion efforts in India misstates a valuation. The N.B.A.’s business operations in China are valued at more than $4 billion, not the professional basketball league in China.
match_headline: Can the N.B.A. Find a Basketball Superstar in India?

text: An article last Sunday on the wedding of Christa Marie Orsino and Marcel Anthony Martino misstated the location of Francis Marion University, where the groom’s father was a professor. It is in Florence, S.C., not Marion, S.C.
match_headline: When the Timing Is Finally Right

text: An article on Sept. 15 about college enrollment referred incompletely to “tuition discounts.” The term applies to merit and need-based institutional aid, not just merit aid.
match_headline: New Mexico Announces Plan for Free College for State Residents

text: An article on Sept. 15 about Puerto Rico’s disappearing public schools referred incompletely to the types of lawsuits that Puerto Rico is protected from. The commonwealth is protected from lawsuits filed by creditors seeking repayment, not from any lawsuit. The article also described incorrectly an aspect of the Financial Oversight and Management Board. It has the authority to propose debt restructuring or cancellation plans to the federal judge in charge of overseeing Puerto Rico’s bankruptcy process; it cannot forgive or cancel Puerto Rico’s debt.
match_headline: The Disappearing Schools of Puerto Rico

text: An article on Saturday about steps taken by Saudi Arabia and Iran to ease tensions misidentified the affiliation of Martin Indyk. He is a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, not the executive vice president of the Brookings Institution.
match_headline: Saudi Arabia and Iran Make Quiet Openings to Head Off War

text: An article on Sunday about a conference on forensic genealogy misstated Department of Justice guidelines as described by Ted Hunt, senior adviser to the attorney general on forensic science at the Department of Justice. He said he was referring to publicly available records used to conduct genealogy research, not specifically to uploads to genealogy databases, when discussing the Department of Justice’s role in providing guidance to investigators.
match_headline: Playing Catch a Killer With a Room Full of Sleuths

text: An article on Sunday about the difficulties that Qatar has faced in hosting the track and field world championships referred incorrectly to the company sponsorships in Qatar’s bid to host the event. There were millions of dollars in sponsorships, not millions of sponsorships.
match_headline: In Qatar, Track and Field’s Championships Limp to the Finish

text: An article on Friday about the Yankees pitcher James Paxton misstated his performance at the end of the season. He won his final 10 decisions, not his final 10 starts.
match_headline: How a Midseason Revelation Revived James Paxton’s Season

text: An article on Friday about a looted Ethiopian crown misidentified the Ethiopian ambassador to the Netherlands. He is Million Samuel Gebre, not Abay Weldu Hagos.
match_headline: Looted Ethiopian Crown Resurfaces in the Netherlands

text: An article on Friday about the new CW television drama “Nancy Drew” misstated the surname of the showrunner for the series. She is Melinda Hsu Taylor, not Melinda Hsu.
match_headline: Nancy Drew and the Mystery of Her Enduring Relevance

text: An editorial on Saturday about the Trump administration’s hostility to California misstated California’s regulatory authority under the Clean Air Act. The state sets its own vehicle emissions rules, not fuel efficiency standards.
match_headline: Trump Governs by Grudge in California

text: An obituary on Sept. 27 about the lawyer Plato Cacheris referred incompletely to the circumstances under which the former National Security Agency contractor Edward J. Snowden received asylum in Russia. He had been traveling to Latin America from Hong Kong but was stopped and detained at a Moscow airport before boarding a connecting flight when authorities learned that his United States passport had been revoked. Although Russia eventually granted him asylum, it is not the case that he “fled to asylum” there.
match_headline: Plato Cacheris, Washington ‘Super Lawyer’ in Headline Cases, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Friday about the lawyer Jerome Facher referred incorrectly to his military service. Although he was in the Army, he did not serve in the Korean War.
match_headline: Jerome Facher, 93, Dies; Won Acquittal in Noted Pollution Case

text: An article on Tuesday about fallout from a comment about the Hong Kong protests posted to Twitter by Daryl Morey, the general manager of the Houston Rockets, described his tweet incorrectly. Mr. Morey shared an image that read, “Fight for Freedom. Stand with Hong Kong”; he did not write those words in a tweet.
ref_headline: Fight for Freedom. Stand with Hong Kong
match_headline: Hong Kong Protests Put N.B.A. on Edge in China

text: An article on Monday about Russian oligarchs’ roles as arts patrons described incorrectly how the Fort Ross Conservancy decided to stop taking money from the Renova Group. The conservancy says it made the decision after reading a Justice Department memo; the conservancy was not, it says, contacted by the Justice Department directly.
match_headline: Oligarchs, as U.S. Arts Patrons, Present a Softer Image of Russia

text: An article on Tuesday about Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s request that the wife of an American diplomat involved in a crash that killed a teenager be returned to Britain referred incorrectly to the location of the town of Brackley. It is 60 miles northwest of London, not northeast.
match_headline: Britain Demands Return of American Woman Who Fled After Fatal Crash

text: An article on Sunday about popular restaurants for fund-raising events in Washington, D.C., misstated where Representative Scott Tipton spent $21,000, according to spending data from the F.E.C. He spent that amount at the Capitol Hill Club, not the Capital Grille.
match_headline: Jumbo Shrimp and Lobster Tails: D.C.’s Fund-Raising Hot Spots

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about leadership changes at the digital publication Quartz misstated the timing of Kevin Delaney’s departure. He will step down as Quartz’s editor in chief at the end of the month and remain an adviser; he did not leave on Monday.
match_headline: Quartz Editor in Chief Steps Down in Shake-Up

text: A picture credit with an article on Tuesday about China’s pork reserve misidentified the photographer who took the photo of a wholesale meat market in Beijing. It was Lam Yik Fei, not Gilles Sabrié.
match_headline: Swine Fever? Trade War? China Turns to Strategic Pork Reserve

text: An article on Tuesday about conservationists’ concerns that recreational mountain biking and e-bikes on public lands lead to unsafe conditions for humans and wildlife misstated the scope of a decision by the Trump administration to allow electric bikes on trails on federal lands. The e-bikes are permitted in national parks and other lands under the jurisdiction of the Interior Department, but not national forests under the Department of Agriculture.
match_headline: When Biking and Bears Don’t Mix

text: An article on Wednesday about Israelis’ reactions to President Trump’s decision to withdraw American troops from Syria misstated when Mr. Trump said on Twitter that the United States had not abandoned the Kurds. He did so on Tuesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Israelis Watch U.S. Abandon Kurds, and Worry: Who’s Next?

text: An article on Monday about misconduct among top executives at the Japanese automaker Nissan misspelled the surname of a former assistant to Hari Nada. Her name is Kathryn Carlile, not Carlisle.
match_headline: Nissan’s Crisis Goes Much Deeper Than Carlos Ghosn

text: An article on Tuesday about Stuart Copperman, a pediatrician who faced a stream of sexual abuse complaints before being stripped of his medical license, misidentified a town in which Mr. Copperman maintains a home.
