It is Boca Raton, Fla., not Delray Beach, Fla. The article also misidentified a water feature at The Greens at Half Hollow. It is an artificial pond, not a river.
match_headline: These Women Say a Trusted Pediatrician Abused Them as Girls. Now They Plan to Sue.

text: A subhead with an article on Thursday about a book that has inspired organizing efforts among Google workers and Uber drivers misstated its original authorship. The 1978 edition of the book, “Labor Law for the Rank and File,” was by Staughton Lynd; it was later revised with a collaborator, Daniel Gross. Mr. Lynd did not have a co-author on the 1978 edition.
ref_headline: Labor Law for the Rank and File,
match_headline: The Radical Guidebook Embraced by Google Workers and Uber Drivers

text: An article on Tuesday about the liquidation of the French design brand Sonia Rykiel misstated the timing of Eric Langon’s dismissal as its managing director. It was July 2018, not a few months after a January 2018 brand celebration. It also misstated where the brand’s chairman, Jean-Marc Loubier, moved after leaving the Rykiel headquarters. It was to a new office on the Right Bank, not to the Left Bank headquarters of the French shoemaker Robert Clergerie. Also, a picture caption with the article misstated Mr. Loubier’s title at Rykiel. It was chairman, not chief executive.
match_headline: What Really Happened at Sonia Rykiel

text: An article on Wednesday about the Minnesota Twins’ loss to the New York Yankees in their division series misidentified one of three 100-loss teams the Twins played often in their final 55 games. Besides the Kansas City Royals and the Miami Marlins, it was the Detroit Tigers, not the Chicago White Sox. (The White Sox lost 89 games this season.)
match_headline: For All Their Slugging, Twins-Yankees Came Down to Pitching

text: An article on Friday about the deadly shooting at a synagogue in Germany misspelled the surname of the gunman. He is Stephan Balliet, not Balliert.
match_headline: Only a Locked Door Stopped a Massacre at a German Synagogue

text: An article on Friday about the announcement by President Trump that United States forces had killed a Qaeda bomb maker Ibrahim Hassan al-Asiri misstated the year in which a suicide bomber tried to assassinate Saudi Arabia’s crown prince. It was 2009, not 2014.
match_headline: Trump Confirms 2017 Killing of Feared Bomb Maker for Al Qaeda

text: An article on Page 22 about the actress Kathryn Hahn misstated the number of years that Hahn and her husband, Ethan Sandler, have been married. It is more than 16 years, not more than 25 years. (They have been a couple for more than 25 years.)
match_headline: Kathryn Hahn’s Funny, Sensual Portrayals of Female Desire

text: An article on Page 76 about the writer Ben Lerner misstated the years when he played football. It was in middle school, not high school. And the article misstated the location of an anti-ICE protest in Lerner’s most recent novel, “The Topeka School.” It was Manhattan, not Brooklyn.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in Brooklyn, Manhattan and the Bronx

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 2 about campus news misspelled the name of the student newspaper at the University of Kentucky. It is The Kentucky Kernel, not Kernal.
match_headline: ABC Apologizes for Showing Video From U.S. Gun Range in Report on Syria

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 2 about Pell Grants misspelled the surname of the managing director of policy at the National Skills Coalition. He is Kermit Kaleba, not Kermit Kalebaof.

An article last Sunday about the director Pedro Almodóvar and his new film, “Pain and Glory,” described incorrectly the timing of La Movida Madrileña. While there were cultural movements roiling Madrid when Mr. Almodóvar arrived there in 1969, this movement began later.
match_headline: Why Pedro Almodóvar’s Newest Film Frightened His Friends

text: An article on Page 22 about the actress Kathryn Hahn misstated the number of years that Hahn and her husband, Ethan Sandler, have been married. It is more than 16 years, not more than 25 years. (They have been a couple for more than 25 years.)

Because of an editing error, an article on Page 2 about Pell Grants misspelled the surname of the managing director of policy at the National Skills Coalition. He is Kermit Kaleba, not Kermit Kalebaof.

A column by Ross Douthat last Sunday misstated the post of the Ukrainian leader whose phone call with President Trump has become a subject of the impeachment inquiry. The leader, Volodymyr Zelensky, is the president of Ukraine, not the prime minister.
match_headline: When Trump Gets His Alligator

text: Because of a production error, the Mini Crossword on Monday included an incorrect clue for 8 across. is the correct emoji for nerd, not .

An article on Oct. 7 about several significant cases before the Supreme Court misstated the month the court granted a last-minute request to block a law restricting abortion in Louisiana. The request was granted in February, not November.
match_headline: As the Supreme Court Gets Back to Work, Five Big Cases to Watch

text: An article on Oct. 6 about prominent conservatives whose opposition to President Trump has softened over time described imprecisely the views of former Homeland Security secretary Tom Ridge on Mr. Trump. While Mr. Ridge has supported policies such as the border wall and at times declined to criticize the president when asked, he has also said his concerns “have not diminished over time.”
match_headline: The ‘Never Trump’ Coalition That Decided Eh, Never Mind, He’s Fine

text: An article on Oct. 5 about the recent crash of a World War II-era plane in Connecticut misstated the material that makes up the interior of the B-17. It is aluminum, not steel.
match_headline: What We Know About the Victims of the B-17 Bomber Crash

text: An obituary on Sunday about the naturalist and philanthropist Robert Goelet misstated the surname of the first person in Mr. Goelet’s family to immigrate to the United States. He was Jacobus Goelet, not Gardiner.
match_headline: Robert Goelet, New York Grandee and Naturalist, Dies at 96

text: An article on Oct. 7 about farmers growing hemp attributed an erroneous distinction to the work of Andy Huston. While he was the only person in Illinois last year to successfully harvest hemp as part of a research project with Western Illinois University, he was not the only person to grow it.
match_headline: Amid Trade War, Farmers Lean on a New Crop: Hemp

text: An article on Sunday about the impeachment inquiry misspelled the surname of a constitutional law professor at the University of Texas. He is Stephen Vladeck, not Vladek.
match_headline: Fact-Checking 5 Claims About the Impeachment Inquiry

text: An article on Sunday about the thriving Halloween industry in Sleepy Hollow and neighboring towns misspelled the name of the Georgia town where the Sleepy Hollow Experience began in 2013. It started in Chattahoochee Hills, not Chatahoochee Hills.
match_headline: The Headless Horseman Industrial Complex

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the gymnast Simone Biles becoming the most decorated gymnast in world championship history misstated the difference between her record medal count at the world gymnastics championships and the previous high, held by Vitaly Scherbo. With 25, Biles has two more than Scherbo, not one more.
match_headline: Simone Biles Becomes World Championships’ Most Decorated Gymnast

text: An obituary on Monday about the poet and artist John Giorno misstated when he moved into his longtime home on the Bowery. It was 1966, not 1962.
match_headline: John Giorno, Who Moved Poetry Beyond the Printed Page, Dies at 82

text: An article on Wednesday about political upheaval in Peru referred incorrectly to a Peruvian government publication that issues administrative regulations. It is a national register, not a federal register.
match_headline: Who’s in Charge in Peru? Peruvians Can’t Agree

text: An article on Saturday about Justice Sylvia G. Ash of State Supreme Court in Brooklyn, who was charged with obstruction of justice in a $10 million corruption case, misstated the financial threshold for cases to be heard in the Commercial Division of State Supreme Court. It is $150,000, not $500,000.
match_headline: Judge Obstructed Justice in $10 Million Corruption Case, U.S. Says

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the search for the missing plane of the aviator Amelia Earhart misstated when the photo was taken. The photo was released in December 1937; it was not taken then. Because of an editing error, the article also misspelled the given name of the mother of the ocean explorer Robert Ballard, who led an expedition in search of the plane. She was Harriett Ballard, not Hariett. It also misstated the reason Ms. Ballard had cited for dropping out of college. It was to care for her three children, not for her sister.
match_headline: The Amelia Earhart Mystery Stays Down in the Deep

text: An article on Wednesday about the Washington Nationals’ four-game sweep of the National League Championship Series misstated the number of teams currently in Major League Baseball. It is 30, not 32. And the Nationals are the 29th of those franchises — not the 31st — to reach the World Series.
match_headline: Finally, the Nationals Are in the World Series

text: An article on Sept. 25 about a production of Rameau’s “Les Indes Galantes” at the Paris Opera referred incorrectly to Bintou Dembélé, the choreographer of the production. While she is believed to be the first black female and first black French choreographer to be engaged by the company, she is not the first black choreographer in the history of the Paris Opera. (Alvin Ailey, who created “Au Bord du Précipice” for the Paris Opera Ballet in 1983, is believed to be the company’s first black choreographer.)
match_headline: Vogue Dancers Subvert a Baroque Spectacle at the Paris Opera

text: An article on Thursday about Chelsea Clinton’s announcement that she would not run for Congress misidentified the source of the law that requires members of Congress to live only in the state they seek to represent. It is the United States Constitution, not New York law.
match_headline: Chelsea Clinton Says She Won’t Run for Congress in 2020

text: An article on Wednesday about a virtual-reality tour of Leonardo da Vinci’s “Mona Lisa” at the Louvre, using information from a publicist, misstated the number of virtual reality stations for viewing the masterpiece. It is 11, not 15.
match_headline: Meeting the ‘Mona Lisa’ for an Intimate (Virtual) Rendezvous

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about “Swan Lake/Loch na hEala” misidentified the dancer portraying a swan in the production. She is Rachel Poirier, not Anna Kaszuba.
match_headline: Review: A Startling ‘Swan Lake’ That’s Hard to Recognize

text: An article on Wednesday about the discussion of foreign policy during the Democratic debate on Tuesday night misstated the state Senator Amy Klobuchar represents. It is Minnesota, not Michigan.
match_headline: Unified Against Trump on Syria, Democrats Struggle to Define Alternate Strategy

text: An article on Oct. 11 about the Equality Town Hall, a forum focusing on gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender issues, referred incorrectly to Pete Buttigieg, the mayor of South Bend, Ind., as the first openly gay candidate for president. He is the first top-tier candidate for president who is openly gay.
match_headline: Highlights From the L.G.B.T.Q. Town Hall, Where Protesters Took the Spotlight

text: An article on Friday about mourning in Baltimore over the death of Representative Elijah E. Cummings misquoted Bishop Walter Thomas, the pastor of New Psalmist Baptist Church. He said Mr. Cummings touched lives all over the world “in his own inimitable way,” not “in his own inimical way.”
match_headline: ‘He Was Loved by All’: Friends in Baltimore Mourn Elijah Cummings

text: An article on Friday about CBS’s announcement that it had extended Stephen Colbert’s contract to host “The Late Show” through August 2023 misstated the ratings for Jimmy Fallon and Mr. Colbert this season among adults under 50. They are tied in these ratings; Mr. Fallon does not have a slim lead.
match_headline: Stephen Colbert Signs a New ‘Late Show’ Deal Through 2023

text: An article on Sunday about the relationship between Bill Gates and Jeffrey Epstein referred imprecisely to the time Melanie Walker, an associate of Mr. Epstein, spent in New York City. Ms. Walker traveled to the city and stayed there but did not move there.
match_headline: Bill Gates Met With Jeffrey Epstein Many Times, Despite His Past

text: An article on Thursday about a musical adaptation of “Mrs. Doubtfire” that is coming to Broadway misidentified the film studio behind “The Notebook.” It was released by New Line Cinema/Warner Bros., not 20th Century Fox.
match_headline: ‘Mrs. Doubtfire’ Musical Is Coming to Broadway

text: An article on Page 14 about a new adaptation of the graphic novel “Watchmen” misstates how long Richard Nixon was president in the book. It was 17 years, not 30.
match_headline: ‘Watchmen’ Is Coming. (Actually, It Never Left.)

text: An article on Page 8 about Herman Cornejo’s 20th anniversary at American Ballet Theater, using information from a publicist, misidentifies the piece that Twyla Tharp’s “A Gathering of Ghosts” is set to. It is Brahms’s second string quintet, not his second quartet.
match_headline: Herman Cornejo: A Ballet Hero’s Milestone

text: An article on Page 7 about the stage actress Elaine Stritch misstates the name of a song from the musical “Anyone Can Whistle” that Stritch often performed. It is “Everybody Says Don’t,” not “Everyone Says Don’t.”
match_headline: Love Elaine Stritch? Thank the Parts She Didn’t Get

text: An article on Page 40 about Maria Ressa, the editor of a popular news site in the Philippines, reverses the given names of two Filipino political figures. They are Ramon Revilla and Ronald dela Rosa, not Ronald Revilla and Ramon dela Rosa.
match_headline: The Journalist vs. the President, With Life on the Line

text: An obituary on Thursday about the fashion designer Sophia Kokosalaki misstated her age. She was 46, not 47. (As the obituary correctly stated, she was born on Nov. 3, 1972.) The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: Sophia Kokosalaki, Who Gave London Fashion a Grecian Spin, Dies at 46

text: An obituary on Friday about Representative Elijah E. Cummings of Maryland misstated what office he considered running for in 1996 before deciding to run for the House of Representatives in a special election. It was a seat in the United States Senate, not the Maryland Senate.
match_headline: Elijah Cummings, Powerful Democrat Who Investigated Trump, Dies at 68

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the 20th anniversary of the film “Boys Don’t Cry” described incorrectly the character played by Hilary Swank. The character is a transgender man, not a teenage girl passing for a boy.
match_headline: ‘Boys Don’t Cry’ 20 Years Later: For Trans Men, a Divisive Legacy

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Stephanie Yarbrough and John Few misstated the affiliation of the officiant, the Rev. Brian McGreevy. He is a minister of the Anglican Church of North America, not an Episcopal priest (he was ordained in the Episcopal Diocese of South Carolina).
match_headline: Stephanie Yarbrough, John Few

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Oct. 6 about “A State at Any Cost: The Life of David Ben-Gurion,” by Tom Segev, omitted the name of the book’s translator. He is Haim Watzman.
ref_headline: A State at Any Cost: The Life of David Ben-Gurion,
match_headline: Israel’s First Prime Minister Was Complicated. So Is This Book About His Life.

text: An article on Saturday about the acting White House chief of staff, Mick Mulvaney, misstated the amount of military aid to Ukraine that the Trump administration withheld. It was $391 million, not $490 million.
match_headline: Defiant Mulvaney Rides Out Storm Over His Ukraine Comments

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a career State Department official who told House impeachment investigators that he raised concerns about Hunter Biden in 2015 referred incorrectly to the investigation that Mick Mulvaney, the acting White House chief of staff, referred to in a televised news briefing on Thursday. The investigation in question was related to unsubstantiated allegations related to the 2016 election, not regarding Joseph R. Biden Jr. and his son Hunter.
match_headline: Diplomat Told House Investigators He Raised Alarm About Hunter Biden in 2015

text: An article on Sunday about the loss of small newspapers across the country referred incorrectly in some instances to the closing of The Ann Arbor News’s daily print operation. It transitioned from a daily print and online newspaper to a twice-a-week print publication with stories published on MLive.com . It did not shutter its print edition and end its online presence.
match_headline: When the Student Newspaper Is the Only Daily Paper in Town

text: An article on Sunday about Chinese state-run television’s reaction to comments made by the N.B.A. commissioner, Adam Silver, referred incorrectly to the The South China Morning Post. It is an English-language newspaper based in Hong Kong; it is not a “Chinese media outlet.”
match_headline: Chinese State Television Vows ‘Retribution’ Against N.B.A.’s Adam Silver

text: An obituary on Sunday about the author and literary critic Samuel Hynes misattributed a quotation. It was Malcolm Bradbury, not Professor Hynes, who wrote that criticism is “not a way of reading and explaining literature, but a way of rewriting it.”
ref_headline: not a way of reading and explaining literature, but a way of rewriting it.
match_headline: Samuel Hynes, Professor Whose Books Taught Lessons of War, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Monday about the artist Ed Clark referred incorrectly to his father. It was not the case that he did not support his family. The obituary also misstated the given name of Mr. Clark’s daughter, who survives him. She is Melanca Clark, not Melcanca. In addition, the headline referred imprecisely to Mr. Clark’s work. Although he was an abstract painter, his art was not Abstract Expressionist.
match_headline: Ed Clark, Pioneering Abstract Painter, Dies at 93

text: An Editorial Observer on Monday about Trump administration officials who spoke up about what they saw as abuses or violations of the law, misstated when Joel Clement, an Interior Department official, filed a whistle-blower complaint. It was July 2017, not July of this year.
match_headline: They Are Not the Resistance. They Are Not a Cabal. They Are Public Servants.

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about Beverly Sackler, the matriarch of the family that owns Purdue Pharma, referred incorrectly to the relationship between the company and her husband, Raymond Sackler. As the obituary correctly stated, he and his brothers acquired the company that became Purdue Pharma; they did not found it.
match_headline: Beverly Sackler, 95, Dies; Philanthropist and Purdue Pharma Director

text: An obituary on Saturday about William G. Milliken, who was governor of Michigan from 1969 until 1983, referred imprecisely to the Arab oil embargo of the 1970s. It began in 1973 and ended in 1974; it was not “the 1974 Arab oil embargo.”
match_headline: William G. Milliken, Michigan Governor in a Transformative Era, Dies at 97

text: An obituary on Monday about the breast cancer researcher Dr. Bernard Fisher misstated part of the name of the high school in Pittsburgh he attended. It is Taylor Allderdice High School, not Taylor Allerdice.
match_headline: Dr. Bernard Fisher, Who Revolutionized Breast Cancer Treatment, Dies at 101

text: An article on Wednesday about the testimony by the diplomat William B. Taylor Jr. in the House impeachment inquiry into President Trump misstated the state that Representative Sean Patrick Maloney represents. It is New York, not Massachusetts.
match_headline: Ukraine Envoy Testifies Trump Linked Military Aid to Investigations

text: An article on Tuesday about an effort by the Jeff Bezos start-up Blue Origin to build the next spacecraft that will land American astronauts on the moon misstated the amount of time the Apollo 17 astronauts stayed on the moon. It was just over three days, not six.
match_headline: Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to Partner With 3 Companies on NASA Moon Lander

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the conductor Raymond Leppard misstated when the Italian composer Francesco Cavalli lived. It was the 17th century, not the 18th.
match_headline: Raymond Leppard, Versatile Maestro Who Led Baroque Revival, Dies at 92

text: An article on Wednesday about Democrats questioning the chances of the current Democratic presidential field to prevail in 2020 misstated H. Ross Perot’s party affiliation when he ran for president in 1992. He ran as an independent, not as a Reform Party candidate. (Mr. Perot founded the Reform Party in 1995.)
match_headline: Anxious Democratic Establishment Asks, ‘Is There Anybody Else?’

text: An obituary on Thursday about the saxophonist and arranger Ray Santos misstated part of the name of an album by Eddie Palmieri for which he wrote arrangements. It is “Mi Luz Mayor,” not “Mi Luz Amor.”
match_headline: Ray Santos, a Pillar of Latin Jazz, Is Dead at 90

text: An obituary on Thursday about Hildegard Bachert, the longtime co-director of the Galerie St. Etienne in Manhattan, misstated the year the gallery was founded. It was 1939, not 1940.
match_headline: Hildegard Bachert, 98, Dies; Championed Klimt, Schiele and Grandma Moses

text: An article on Feb. 27 about allegations of sexual abuse against the French film director Luc Besson by the actress Sand Van Roy referred inaccurately to the complaints Ms. Van Roy filed against Mr. Besson. She filed two complaints with the police; she did not file any lawsuits against him. The article also misstated her age. She was 31 at the time of publication, not 28. Publication of this correction was delayed because the errors were brought to the attention of editors only recently.
match_headline: Luc Besson, French Director, Won’t Be Charged After Rape Accusation

text: An article on Page 4 about “Agatha Raisin & the Haunted House” misstates the URL for the streaming platform carrying it. It is Acorn.tv, not acorntv.com.
match_headline: The Week in Arts: Sleater-Kinney, Paul Taylor and ‘Synonyms’

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 18 about museums in the Netherlands grappling with the history of colonialism misidentifies the photographer. The work is “José Montoya as Jean Rabo” by Milette Raats, not by Humberto Tan.
match_headline: A Dutch Golden Age? That’s Only Half the Story

text: An article on Page 30 about the editor Mary-Kay Wilmers misidentified the family member who diagnosed familial dysautonomia in her son. It was her father’s sister, not her mother’s.
match_headline: How Mary-Kay Wilmers Became Britain’s Most Influential Editor

text: An article on Page 4 about Japan’s imprint on Mexico City describes incorrectly a relative of the Tijuana-born restaurateur Edo Lopez. His great-grandfather who was born in Japan was on the maternal side of the family, not paternal.
match_headline: In Mexico City, a Blossoming of All Things Japanese

text: An article on Page 8 about an exhibition on indigenous Canadian women misstates the amount of clay that the special projects director at the Museum of Indian Arts and Culture ordered to help make the piece “Every One.” It was 300 pounds, not three pounds.
match_headline: Illuminating the Plight of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women

text: An article on Page 34 about Meleko Mokgosi misstates the closing date for his “Bread, Butter, and Power” installation at the Smart Museum of Art at the University of Chicago. It is Dec. 15, not Dec. 29.
match_headline: Meleko Mokgosi Wants You to See the Politics of Everyday Life

text: An article on Page 32 about an artist colony in Paris misspells the name of a Paris center for exiled artists. It is L’Atelier des Artistes en Exil, not Exile.
match_headline: A Paris Colony for Exiled Artists Needs a New Home

text: An article on Page 2 about how some museums are working to incorporate the impact of slavery in exhibitions and permanent collections misspells the surname of the woman who was the mother of at least six of Thomas Jefferson’s children. She was Sally Hemings, not Hemmings.
match_headline: Displaying, not Hiding, the Reality of Slave Labor in Art

text: An article last Sunday about appliances and finishes that developers say will make new condos stand out misspelled the surname of an interior designer. He is Ryan Korban, not Korbin.
match_headline: Six Must-Haves Needed to Seduce Buyers

text: A review on Oct. 13 about “Transaction Man,” by Nicholas Lemann, misspelled the surname of the main author of “The Lonely Crowd.” He was David Riesman, not Reisman.
match_headline: The Forces That Are Killing the American Dream

text: A review on Oct. 13 about “We Are the Weather,” by Jonathan Safran Foer, misstated the year of the Master Settlement Agreement, which was signed by major American tobacco companies and 46 states. It was 1998, not 1988.
match_headline: Meat Is Murder. But You Know That Already.

text: A picture caption with an essay last Sunday about a pilgrimage misidentified the Italian town where the church in the photograph, San Geminiano, is situated. It is Vicofertile, not San Gimignano.
match_headline: One Cure for Malnutrition of the Soul

text: An article on Monday about an American commando raid in Syria this past weekend that President Trump said culminated in the death of Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, the leader of the Islamic State, misstated the name of a group of Kurdish fighters. It is the Syrian Democratic Forces, not Syrian Defense Forces.
match_headline: ISIS Leader al-Baghdadi Is Dead, Trump Says

text: An article on Sunday about John R. Bolton, President Trump’s former national security adviser, misstated the name of the university where John Yoo works. It is the law school at the University of California, Berkeley, not the University of Berkeley.
match_headline: Waiting for Bolton: A Capital Speculates on What He Will Say

text: An article on Saturday about some of the factors contributing to wildfires in California misstated the surname of Park Williams, an assistant research professor at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory at Columbia University, in one instance. He is Dr. Williams, not Dr. Park.
match_headline: California Emerged From Drought and Is Still Catching Fire

text: An article on Saturday about the fatal shooting of a man at a Brooklyn nail salon misidentified which officer fired six shots at the man during an altercation in the salon. It was the officer who the police say the man attacked with a chair, not a second officer at the scene.
match_headline: Brooklyn Shooting: Police Kill Man After He Critically Injures Officer

text: An article on Monday about Disney’s marketing approach for its new streaming service Disney Plus misspelled the name of a planned “Star Wars” series. It is “The Mandalorian,” not “The Mandelorian.”
match_headline: Disney Is New to Streaming, but Its Marketing Is Unmatched

text: An article on Saturday about the MSNBC anchor Rachel Maddow confronting the network’s leadership over its handling of Ronan Farrow’s reporting on Harvey Weinstein and its investigation of Matt Lauer’s behavior with colleagues misstated the timing of NBC Universal’s release of the results of the investigation of Mr. Lauer. The results were released several months after NBC fired Mr. Lauer, not seven months.
match_headline: Rachel Maddow Confronts Her NBC News Bosses Live, on the Air

text: An article on Saturday about the potential risks and benefits of purchasing a franchise misstated a service that Jeff Rahn provides through his franchises in the Minneapolis area. It is plumbing, not home cleaning.
match_headline: How to Get Rich by Buying a Franchise (Really)

text: A picture caption with a theater review on Saturday about “What if They Went to Moscow?” misidentified an actress in the image. Julia Bernat is seated on the far right of the stage, not in the water tank. (Isabel Teixeira is in the tank.)
ref_headline: What if They Went to Moscow?
match_headline: ‘What if They Went to Moscow?’ Review: Chekhov, Sliced and Spliced

text: An obituary on Monday about John Conyers, the longest-serving African-American in the history of Congress, misstated the year the Supreme Court ruled that the vote by the House of Representatives to deny Adam Clayton Powell Jr. his seat was unconstitutional. It was 1969, not 1967.
match_headline: John Conyers Jr., Longest-Serving African-American in Congressional History, Dies at 90

text: An article on Friday about strategies for dealing with environments prone to experiencing an increasing number of wildfires misstated which fire was the largest in Kansas’ history. It was the Starbuck fire in 2017, not the 2016 Anderson Creek fire, which until then had been the state’s largest fire in the state’s history.
match_headline: A Forecast for a Warming World: Learn to Live With Fire

text: A news analysis on Tuesday about the differences between a photo of the Situation Room from the Obama administration and another from the Trump administration misstated the state of the raid when the image of President Trump in the Situation Room was taken. The raid was not over; it was in progress, the White House said.
match_headline: 2 Photos of Tense White House Moments: Note the Differences

text: An article on Wednesday about the firing of a Deadspin editor misstated the tagline of the website Deadspin. It is Sports News Without Access, Favor, Or Discretion, not Sports News Without Access, Fear or Favor.
match_headline: Deadspin Editor Fired Amid Pushback Over ‘Stick to Sports’ Memo

text: An article on Friday about the artist Shi Guorui referred incorrectly to the workings of the camera obscura. It projects a reverse and inverse image, not a negative and inverse image. Then, photographic paper — not the optical device — produces the negative image.
match_headline: Staring Into the Soul of the Catskills Through a Pinhole

text: An article on Wednesday about migrants found dead in a truck in Britain last week referred incorrectly to Yen Thanh, Vietnam. It is a district, not a province.
match_headline: Britain Hasn’t Named 39 Dead in a Truck. But in Vietnam, They Know.

text: An article on Thursday about the decision by several carmakers to back President Trump in his battle with California over auto emissions misstated Honda’s affiliation with an auto manufacturer’s organization. Honda is a member of the Association of Global Automakers, not the Alliance of Automobile Manufacturers.
match_headline: White House Pressed Car Makers to Join Its Fight Over California Emissions Rules

text: Because of an editing error, the On Pro Basketball column on Wednesday about the Golden State Warriors’ outlook for this season misspelled the first name of their All-Star guard. He is Stephen Curry, not Stephon Curry. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Don’t Worry About Stephen Curry and the Warriors

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about student lunch debt described incorrectly the location of Cherry Hill, N.J. The township is 10 miles east of Philadelphia, not west.
match_headline: First, the Tuna Fish ‘Badge of Shame.’ Next, Banned From the Prom?

text: Because of an editing error, a music entry in the Listings Pages on Friday misstated the nationality of Jeffrey Milarsky, a conductor. He is American, not British, and he is not visiting from Britain. He is leading a program on Friday that includes a piece by the British composer Harrison Birtwistle.
match_headline: 5 Classical Music Concerts to See in N.Y.C. This Weekend

text: An article on Page 28 about Greta Gerwig and the film “Little Women” misstates the title of Noah Baumbach’s forthcoming film. It is “Marriage Story,” not “A Marriage Story.”
match_headline: What Greta Gerwig Saw in ‘Little Women’: ‘Those Are My Girls’

text: Because of an editing error, a listing of forthcoming holiday films on Page 39 misstates the writing credit for the drama “Queen & Slim.” The screenplay is by Lena Waithe, not Waithe and James Frey. The story is by the two of them.
match_headline: Five Holiday Movies Worth Bingeing This Season

text: An article on Page 11 about a revival of the documentary solo show “Fires in the Mirror” misquotes the actor Michael Benjamin Washington when he describes his experience with excerpts from the play in high school debate competitions. He observed the excerpts; he did not perform them himself. The error was repeated in a caption.
match_headline: He Took Her Parts in ‘Fires in the Mirror.’ All 25 of Them.

text: An article on Page 32 about the mental health crisis in Iraq misstates the name of an academic conference held in Duhok. It is the International Conference on Genocide and Trauma, not the International Conference on Trauma and Genocide.
match_headline: How Does the Human Soul Survive Atrocity?

text: An obituary on Oct. 25 about the Filipino politician Aquilino Pimentel Jr. referred incorrectly to his son Aquilino Pimentel III. He is the former president of the Philippines Senate, not the president. It also misidentified the founder, with Mr. Pimentel, of the opposition party PDP-Laban. He was Benigno Aquino Jr., not Benigno Aquino.
match_headline: Nene Pimentel, 85, Dies; Filipino Politician Stood Up to Marcos

text: An obituary on Oct. 15 about the literary critic Harold Bloom misspelled the name of an epic poem by Edmund Spenser. It is “The Faerie Queene,” not “The Fairie Queen.”
match_headline: Harold Bloom, Critic Who Championed Western Canon, Dies at 89

text: Because of an editing error, a listing of forthcoming holiday films on Page 39 misstates the writing credit for the drama “Queen & Slim.” The screenplay is by Lena Waithe, not Waithe and James Frey. The story is by the two of them.
match_headline: ‘Queen of Hearts’ Review: A Gut-Wrenching Family Drama

text: An article on Monday about the finance industry’s hostility toward Senator Elizabeth Warren’s campaign misspelled the surname of the former fund-raiser for Barack Obama. He is Mitch Draizin, not Draizen.
match_headline: As Warren Gains in Race, Wall Street Sounds the Alarm

text: An article on Saturday about Senator Elizabeth Warren’s campaign in Iowa misquoted part of a speech she delivered there. She said, “Hope and courage wins elections,” not “Hope and courage do not win elections.”
match_headline: Warren Laces Into Rivals as Iowa Campaign Grows Combative

text: An article on Sunday about the latest New York Times/Siena College Iowa poll referred incorrectly to the group of voters who said they believe big banks and tech companies should be broken up. It was 43 percent of likely Iowa Democratic voters, not 43 percent of Americans.
match_headline: 5 Takeaways From the Latest Iowa Poll

text: An article on Sunday about the Daylight Saving Doughnut misstated how Washington State proposes to end the time changes associated with daylight saving time. It is seeking to stay permanently on daylight saving time, not on standard time.
match_headline: Have an Extra Hour? Try Passing Through the ‘Daylight Saving Doughnut’

text: An article on Sunday about the decision by the Trump administration to reduce the number of Iraqi refugees entry into the United States referred incorrectly to the number admitted during President Obama’s last year in office. Although 110,000 Iraqi refugees were authorized to enter, not all of the slots were filled.
match_headline: Under Trump, Iraqis Who Helped U.S. in War Are Stalled in Refugee System

text: An article on Saturday about the exodus of staff members from the website Deadspin misstated the timing of Megan Greenwell’s resignation. It was three weeks after a critical post, not three days.
match_headline: Deadspin’s Last Staff Member Quits. But Deadspin Is Not Dead, the Boss Says.

text: An article on Friday about the appeal of Japanese cars to collectors erroneously attributed a distinction to Nissan’s R382 racecar. It was not the first car to be equipped with a Japanese V12 engine.
match_headline: ‘Japanese Cars Are Getting to Be Full-Fledged Collectibles’

text: An article on Friday about the Ultimate Fighting Championship misstated the ethnicity of the fighter Jorge Masvidal. He is of Cuban and Peruvian descent, not of Cuban and Puerto Rican descent.
match_headline: Diaz a Reminder of U.F.C.’s Star Challenge

text: An obituary on Friday about the author Ed Cray misstated the name of the record company that released a collection of Woody Guthrie’s music for which he and Bill Nowlin wrote the liner notes. It is Rounder Records, not Rounders.
match_headline: Ed Cray, Biographer of Woody Guthrie and Earl Warren, Dies at 86

text: An article on Monday about transgender children and school sports referred imprecisely to a child at the center of a custody dispute in Texas. The child’s gender is contested by the parents.
match_headline: A Conservative Push to Make Trans Kids and School Sports the Next Battleground in the Culture War

text: An article on Tuesday about an effort by Republicans to flood the phone lines of House Democrats misattributed a quotation. It was Adav Noti, not Joe Birkenstock, who said, “They can use campaign and R.N.C. funds for impeachment-related work, including legal and advocacy.”
ref_headline: They can use campaign and R.N.C. funds for impeachment-related work, including legal and advocacy.
match_headline: Republicans Seek to Swamp Democratic Offices With Anti-Impeachment Calls

text: An article on Monday about the dismissal of Steve Easterbrook from McDonald’s misstated the role of John Hamburger at the Franchise Times. He is the publication’s president, not its editor.
match_headline: McDonald’s Fires C.E.O. Steve Easterbrook After Relationship With Employee

text: An article on Tuesday about the Ethiopian runner Girma Bekele Gebre misstated the amount of money he collected after he finished the New York City Marathon. It was $55,000, not $40,000. (He won a $15,000 bonus for finishing faster than 2:09.)
match_headline: The Couch Surfer Who Made the N.Y.C. Marathon Podium

text: An article on Saturday about Deborah F. Rutter, the president of the Kennedy Center, misspelled the surname of the chairman of the Kennedy Center’s board. He is David M. Rubenstein, not Rubinstein.
match_headline: She’s Putting Her Mark on the Kennedy Center

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the results of the New York City Marathon misstated where the runners on the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge were headed. It was Brooklyn, not Manhattan.
match_headline: Kenyan Runners Dominate in N.Y.C. Marathon

text: An obituary on Saturday about the biologist Victoria Braithwaite, who maintained that fish feel pain, misquoted a passage from Ian McEwan’s novel “Saturday.” The novel’s protagonist, who is debating how much empathy to have for the creatures for sale at a fish market, says that being “selective in your mercies” is the key to human success, not “selected in your mercies.”
match_headline: Victoria Braithwaite, Researcher Who Said Fish Feel Pain, Dies at 52

text: An obituary on Sunday about the baseball player turned broadcaster Ron Fairly referred incorrectly at one point to the three World Series won by the Los Angeles Dodgers when he was on the team. As correctly noted elsewhere in the obituary, they were in 1959, 1963 and 1965; they were not all in the 1960s.
match_headline: Ron Fairly, Dodger Star Turned Broadcaster, Dies at 81

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the dominance of Egyptian women in professional squash, using information from a photo agency, misidentified the player in the image. It is Amanda Sobhy, not her sister Sabrina.
match_headline: Overlooked No More: Annie Londonderry, Who Traveled the World by Bicycle

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the former New York State senator Jerome L. Wilson misstated the given name of one of his daughters. She is Emma Wilson, not Ella.
match_headline: Jerome Wilson, Key in Revamping New York Divorce Law, Dies at 88

text: An article on Wednesday about Russia’s involvement in Libya’s civil war misspelled the surname of the United Nations secretary general. He is António Guterres, not Gutteres.
match_headline: Russian Snipers, Missiles and Warplanes Try to Tilt Libyan War

text: An article on Monday about a Ukrainian oligarch’s plans for a ski resort included a map of Ukraine, suggesting that it was separate from Crimea. The map should have indicated the area, annexed by Russia in 2014, with a dashed border line.
match_headline: A Disgraced Ukrainian Oligarch’s Bizarre Ski Resort Plan

text: An article on Monday about the New York Jets’ lack of success under new leadership misstated the number of points by which the Jets trailed the Dolphins with under seven minutes remaining in the game. It was 9 points, not 8.
match_headline: A Supposed Renovation Reveals the Same Old Jets

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the violinist Marya Columbia, who played for rescue workers after the New York City terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, referred imprecisely to the sequence of events in those attacks. The North Tower of the World Trade Center was struck first, not the South Tower. The obituary also misspelled the given name of the niece who wrote about Ms. Columbia for The New Yorker and misstated when her article was published. She is Caroline Lester, not Carolyn, and the article was published this year, not last year.
match_headline: Marya Columbia, Whose Music Soothed on 9/11, Dies at 63

text: An article on Friday about the relationship between President Trump and Attorney General William P. Barr amid the impeachment inquiry misstated the president under whom Harry Litman worked as a deputy assistant attorney general. It was President Bill Clinton, not President Barack Obama.
match_headline: Impeachment Inquiry Tests Ties Between Barr and Trump

text: An article on Friday about sports leagues’ restrictions on how players can customize their uniforms misstated the surname of the man who regularly designs cleats for Minnesota Vikings receiver Stefon Diggs and Giants receiver Golden Tate. He is Daniel Gamache, not LeMache.
match_headline: LeBron James Can Play in Whatever Shoes He Wants. Why Can’t Odell Beckham Jr.?

text: A picture caption in the Listings pages on Friday misspelled the surname of a dancer in Martha Graham Dance Company’s upcoming performance of “Appalachian Spring.” She is Leslie Andrea Williams, not Leslie Andrea William.
match_headline: 8 Dance Performances to See in N.Y.C. This Weekend

text: An article on Page 8 about Philip Glass misidentifies the choreographer of the original production of Mr. Glass’s opera “Einstein on the Beach.” It was Andrew de Groat, not Lucinda Childs; Ms. Childs, who appeared in “Einstein” and performed her own solo dance, remade the group choreography for later revivals. The article also mischaracterizes the arrangement by which “Einstein” came to the Metropolitan Opera in 1976. It was a co-presentation with the Met, not a rental of its theater. The article also carries an incorrect dateline. It was reported from Stanford University, which is in Stanford, Calif., not Palo Alto.
match_headline: Philip Glass Is Too Busy to Care About Legacy

text: An article on Page 16 about the artist and filmmaker Lynn Hershman Leeson misstates the location of Ms. Leeson’s ZKM retrospective in 2014. It was at ZKM in Germany, not in Switzerland.
match_headline: With ‘Shadow Stalker,’ Lynn Hershman Leeson Tackles Internet Surveillance

text: An article last Sunday about the landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted misstated the name of the fund that supported the restoration of the Derby Arboretum. It was the National Lottery Heritage Fund, not the National Heritage Lottery Fund. The article also misstated the year when the Chirk Castle was sold. It was 1978, not 1981. And a picture with the article was published in error. The image shows Olmsted’s son Frederick Law Olmsted Jr., not Olmsted himself.
match_headline: The Parks That Made the Man Who Made Central Park

text: An article on Oct. 27 about hotel programs that help place dogs with new owners misstated the name of the city near the Westin Mission Hills hotel. It is Palm Springs, Calif., not Palm Springs Valley.
match_headline: Forget the Cookie. I Want a Dog at Check In.

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Kaytlin Bailey and Tre Jones misstated the name of the company where the groom is the head of marketing. It is Dotdash, not DotDah.
match_headline: Kaytlin Bailey, Tre Jones

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Cheryl Ann McCullagh and Conor Cassidy misstated the groom’s surname in one instance. He is Mr. Cassidy, not Mr. McCullagh.
match_headline: Cheryl Ann McCullagh, Conor Cassidy

text: An article on Friday about the impeachment inquiry testimony of George P. Kent misstated the timing of a conversation between Vice President Mike Pence and President Trump as described in the testimony of Jennifer Williams, a longtime State Department employee. It was in early September, when Mr. Pence met in Warsaw with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, not the day Mr. Trump spoke with Mr. Zelensky.
match_headline: Top State Dept. Official Complained of Trump’s Politicization of Ukraine Policy

text: An article on Sunday about the deputy interior secretary David Bernhardt misstated the relationship between Edward McDonnell and Mr. Bernhardt at the Interior Department during the George W. Bush administration. While Mr. McDonnell worked under Mr. Bernhardt for about two years, he did not report directly to Mr. Bernhardt.
match_headline: Interior Chief’s Lobbying Past Has Challenged the Agency’s Ethics Referees

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about the Huntsman family’s $150 million gift for mental health research and care misstated a philanthropist’s given name. As the article correctly notes, he is Peter Huntsman, not Paul.
match_headline: A New Generation Stakes Out a New Path for Charitable Giving

text: An article on Sunday about this week’s business events misstated the number of listings by Airbnb. It is more than seven million, not six million.
match_headline: The Week in Business: Spies at Twitter

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about L.S.U.’s college football victory over Alabama referred imprecisely to the touchdowns that Clyde Edwards-Helaire of L.S.U. scored. He rushed for three and caught one.
match_headline: L.S.U. Survives Alabama’s Second-Half Push for a Big Win

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Tua Tagovailoa, Alabama’s star quarterback, misidentified a doctor who performed close to a dozen “tightrope” surgeries on Alabama football players. It is Norman Waldrop, not Thomas Clanton.
match_headline: Tua Tagovailoa’s Return From Injury for Alabama-L.S.U. Comes With Risk

text: An article on Thursday about the 1811 Slave Rebellion Re-enactment organized by the New York artist Dread Scott included an outdated name for an organization that contributed funds for the project. It is now the Open Society Foundations, not the Open Society Institute.
match_headline: With a Slave Rebellion Re-enactment, an Artist Revives Forgotten History

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about Robert C. Norris, who portrayed the Marlboro Man in television commercials, misspelled his mother’s given name. She was Dellora Norris, not Delora.
match_headline: Robert Norris, Marlboro Man Who Didn’t Smoke, Dies at 90

text: An article on Monday about the 1811 Slave Rebellion Re-enactment organized by the New York artist Dread Scott described incorrectly the attack on a plantation owner and his son by about two dozen slaves near New Orleans. The son was killed, but the plantation owner survived; both men were not killed.
match_headline: A Slave Rebellion Rises Again

text: An article on Tuesday about the dismissal of the Canadian hockey broadcaster Don Cherry misstated the significance of wearing a poppy in the days leading up to Remembrance Day. It is worn in Canada to honor all of the country’s war dead, not only those who died in World War I.
match_headline: Don Cherry, a Hockey Institution in Canada, Is Fired After Divisive Comments

text: An article on Saturday about Plácido Domingo’s withdrawal from an event at the Tokyo Olympics misstated the reason for an anniversary concert at La Scala in 2020. It will celebrate the 50th anniversary of Mr. Domingo’s first performance there, not the 50th anniversary of the opera house.
match_headline: Plácido Domingo Withdraws From Tokyo Olympics Performances

text: An article on Tuesday about the Swedish musician Ludwig Goransson misidentified the flutist on the Fula flute. It was Amadou Ba, not Baaba Maal.
match_headline: How Ludwig Goransson Became Directors’ Secret Musical Weapon

text: An article on Saturday about an increase in lawsuits filed by hospitals against patients misidentified the source of the medical debt that led to the garnishment of an Oregon cashier’s wages. It was debt owed to a doctor’s office, not to the hospital where she worked. The article also misstated the number of hours the cashier worked in the pay period when she was left with 54 cents in take-home pay. It was 61 hours, not 80.
match_headline: With Medical Bills Skyrocketing, More Hospitals Are Suing for Payment

text: An article on Monday about a murder-suicide in Brooklyn, relying on information from the police, misspelled the given name of one of the victims. It is Jened Duncan, not Janed.
match_headline: 2 Die in Jealous Rampage, New York City’s Third Murder-Suicide in Days

text: An article on Tuesday about the “Groundbreakers Lunch” at the annual DealBook conference in New York contained multiple errors. It misspelled the given name of the founder and executive chairman of ClassPass; she is Payal Kadakia, not Payel. It misspelled the surname of the founder of littleBits; she is Ayah Bdeir, not Bedir. It misspelled the surname and misstated the title of an official at First Draft: She is Claire Wardle, not Wardel, and she is the executive director, not the founder. It misstated the title of Wes Moore of Robin Hood; he is chief executive, not the founder. It misstated the name of Harpreet Rai’s company; it is Oura Ring, not Oura.
match_headline: Business Leaders on Capitalism, Challenges and Their 8-Year-Old Selves

text: An article on Page 3 about offensive Halloween decorations in the window of a Brooklyn townhouse misspells the given name of a man who moved to Brooklyn from South Carolina after World War II. He is Curives Lorick Sr., not Corives. The article also misstates when the Rev. Kirsten Foy was the head of the Brooklyn chapter of the National Action Network. He is the previous head, not the current one.
match_headline: She Hung Nooses on Halloween. What Happened Next Was Surprising.

text: An article on Page 8 about the casting of disabled actors in the role of Tiny Tim in a Broadway production of “A Christmas Carol” misstates Talleri McRae’s relationship to the National Disability Theater. She is a co-founder, not the artistic director.
match_headline: Rethinking Tiny Tim: Should a Disabled Actor Play the Role?

text: An article on Page 84 about teenagers and identity misspells the name of a video game. It is Fortnite, not Fortnight.
match_headline: What Do Teenagers Learn Online Today? That Identity Is a Work in Progress

text: An obituary on Oct. 14 about Mitsuye Endo, the lead plaintiff in a Supreme Court case that successfully challenged mass internment of American citizens during World War II, referred imprecisely to an opinion expressed by Justice Frank Murphy in the case, referring to the detention of Japanese-Americans as “racial discrimination.” Justice Murphy was writing in a concurring opinion, not the majority opinion.
match_headline: Overlooked No More: Mitsuye Endo, a Name Linked to Justice for Japanese-Americans

text: An article last Sunday about artwork from the Burning Man festival misstated part of the name of a sculpture. It is “All Power to All People,” not “All Power to the People.” The article referred incorrectly to the sculpture’s size. It is 24 feet by 10 feet, not 20 feet tall. And the article misstated which version of the sculpture is on display in Portland, Ore. It is a smaller version, not the one that appeared at Burning Man (that larger version will tour the United States in 2020).
match_headline: Missed Burning Man? Burning Man, or at Least Its Art, Is Coming to You

text: An article last Sunday about home surveillance technology described incorrectly the security camera service provided by Flock Safety. Flock Safety can view or access the footage from security cameras with the consent of its customers, but it does not monitor all footage.
match_headline: Are My Neighbors Spying on Me?

text: An article last Sunday about smart home technology misstated the address of One United Nations Park. It is at 695 First Avenue, not 689 First Avenue.
match_headline: How Smart Is Your Home?

text: A review last Sunday about the middle-grade novel “Beverly, Right Here” misstated the number of times the author, Kate DiCamillo, has won the Newbery Medal for children’s literature. She has won it twice, and she has also received a Newbery Honor. She is not a “three-time Newbery medalist.”
match_headline: Kate DiCamillo’s New Novel May Be Her Finest Yet

text: An article on Page 84 about teenagers and identity misspells the name of a video game. It is Fortnite, not Fortnight.
match_headline: Google Stadia Wants You to Replace Your Video Game Console. Don’t.

text: An article on Sept. 26 about President Trump’s long preoccupation with Ukraine misstated an element of what he told President-elect Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine during a phone call on April 21. While the original White House summary of the call said the two men discussed corruption, a reconstructed transcript released by the White House on Friday indicated only that Mr. Trump congratulated Mr. Zelensky on his election victory; he did not urge Mr. Zelensky to coordinate with Rudolph W. Giuliani, his personal lawyer, to pursue investigations of corruption as he did in a July 25 call.
match_headline: Phone Call Showed Only a Slice of Trump’s Obsession With Ukraine

text: An article on May 2 about the overlap between Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s diplomacy and his son’s work for a Ukrainian gas company misstated the date of a trip to Kiev during which Mr. Biden urged the firing of a Ukrainian prosecutor. The trip occurred in December 2015, not March 2016. (The mistake was brought to the attention of The Times by a tweet from Glenn Kessler of The Washington Post, who had also pointed out the error in a previous fact-checking article.)
match_headline: Biden Faces Conflict of Interest Questions That Are Being Promoted by Trump and Allies

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about President Trump’s tweet that attacked Marie L. Yovanovitch misstated who was questioning Ms. Yovanovitch when the president tweeted. It was Daniel Goldman, the chief Democratic lawyer, not Representative Adam Schiff.
match_headline: The President Bursts Through the Virtual Courtroom Doors

text: An article on Friday about the shooting at Saugus High School in Santa Clarita, Calif., relying on information from the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, misstated the age of a girl who was killed in the shooting at Saugus High School. She was 15, not 16.
match_headline: Santa Clarita Shooting Is Another Nightmare Made Real

text: An article on Saturday about Iran’s sudden increase in gasoline prices referred incorrectly to the price increase that Iran imposed for purchases over the monthly ration limit. The increase was 200 percent, not 300. The error was repeated in a headline.
match_headline: Iran Abruptly Raises Fuel Prices, and Protests Erupt

text: An article on Friday about the Makah tribe and whaling described incorrectly the treaties between Native American tribes and the United States government. More than one tribe has treaty rights to hunt whales; the Makah tribe is not the only one. (Although their treaty explicitly allows it, a different treaty protects the rights of other tribes to take fish, which a court has ruled includes whales and seals.)
match_headline: A Native Tribe Wants to Resume Whaling. Whale Defenders Are Divided.

text: An article on Saturday about three people convicted of charges in connection with a gas explosion in the East Village misstated the charges that the defendants were convicted of. They were found guilty of manslaughter and related offenses, but not criminally negligent homicide. The article also misstated the occupation of the person to whom Maria Hrynenko sent a text message. It was a real estate broker, not a restaurant worker. In addition, the article misstated the month in which Andrew Trombettas pleaded guilty. It was January, not March.
match_headline: An Illegal Gas Line, a Deadly Explosion and Now Guilty Verdicts

text: An article on Saturday about the Adam Driver film “The Report” misattributed a quotation to John O. Brennan, a former C.I.A. director. It was Mr. Brennan’s aide Nick Shapiro who said the film “fictionalizes much of what happened.” Mr. Brennan declined to comment.
match_headline: ‘The Report’ and the Untold Story of a Senate-C.I.A. Conflict

text: A picture caption with an art review on Friday of a Rachel Harrison exhibit at the Whitney misstated the dates for an art installation. The work “Should home windows …” was from 1996/2019, not 1996/2009. The review and a picture caption also misstated the number of artworks inside a circle of chairs. There are 15 sculptures, not 10.
match_headline: Peas, Socks and Sidewalk-Trash Sculptures: Just Keep Looking

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the HBO series “Our Boys” misidentified one of the actors photographed. He is Yoram Toledano, not Tzahi Grad.
match_headline: ‘Our Boys’ Explores the Anatomy of Hate Crimes

text: An article on Monday about Ford Motor’s new electric Mustang S.U.V. misidentified one of the two companies where Ford customers will be able to charge electric vehicles. The company is Greenlots, not ChargePoint.
match_headline: Ford Wants to Sell You an Electric S.U.V. It’s Called a Mustang.

text: An article on Sunday about a chemical fire in France misstated the amount of chemicals that went into the air on the night of the Lubrizol factory fire. It was more than 9,000 tons, not more than nine tons.
match_headline: Fear Has Yet to Be Extinguished After Chemical Fire in France

text: An article on Tuesday about a Tennessee woman’s efforts to have DNA tests conducted to determine whether her father committed a 1985 murder, for which he was executed in 2006, misspelled the surname of the Shelby County district attorney general. She is Amy Weirich, not Weyrich. The article also misidentified April Alley’s legal representation. It includes lawyers in Tennessee, not the Tennessee Innocence Project.
match_headline: DNA Tests Could Clear an Executed Man. Why a Judge Said No.

text: An article on Tuesday about Rutgers University’s football program described incorrectly reporting from NJ.com about conversations that Greg Schiano, the former Rutgers coach, has had about returning to coach the university’s football team. The website reported that Schiano met with the athletic director, Patrick Hobbs, and Greg Brown, a member of the Rutgers Board of Governors, not that Schiano met with the board of governors itself. The website also reported that Schiano spoke by phone with Phil Murphy, the governor of New Jersey, not that Schiano and Murphy had met.
match_headline: In the Gilded Big Ten, Rutgers Is Still a Have-Not

text: An article on Wednesday about testimony in the House impeachment inquiry misstated the country that was said to have conspired with Democrats in 2016, a theory that has been debunked. It was Ukraine, not Russia.
match_headline: Officials Testify Trump Call Was Inappropriate; One ‘Couldn’t Believe’ It

text: An article on Wednesday about North Macedonia’s bid to join the European Union misstated Aleksandar Vucic’s title. He is the president of Serbia, not prime minister.
match_headline: ‘I Am Breaking Inside’: Balkan Leader Fears Conflict After E.U. Snub

text: An article on Wednesday about cities opting to leave flood-prone land undeveloped, using information provided by Michele Braun, the former zoning official, misstated the amount of property value for tax revenue that was lost in Northfield, Vt., when the town bought out homes and built a park to help mitigate risks from climate change. It was $2.2 million, not $2.7 million.
match_headline: As Climate Risk Grows, Cities Test a Tough Strategy: Saying ‘No’ to Developers

text: An article last Thursday about women who avoid fashion trends misstated the age of Olivia Jackson, who was window shopping on Madison Avenue. She is 28, not 38.
match_headline: Fashion? They’re Over It

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Jack O’Dell, a former aide to the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., misstated the date of the 1963 March on Washington, at which Dr. King gave his “I Have a Dream” speech. It was Aug. 28, not Aug. 29.
match_headline: Jack O’Dell, King Aide Fired Over Communist Past, Dies at 96

text: An article on Thursday about a conference for the Arab Council for Regional Integration misidentified a sponsor of the event. It was the Center for Peace Communications, not the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
match_headline: Arab Thinkers Call to Abandon Boycotts and Engage With Israel

text: An article on Wednesday about life in the West Bank misstated the surname of Jewish settlers in the Israeli-occupied territory. They are Yossi and Michal Leibovitz, not Berkovitz.
match_headline: On West Bank, No One Rests Easy, No Matter What U.S. Says About Settlements

text: An obituary on Thursday about the publisher Walter J. Minton misstated part of the name by which the 18th-century novel “Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure,” which he published, is popularly known. It is “Fanny Hill,” not “Fannie Hill.”
ref_headline: Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure,
match_headline: Walter J. Minton, Publisher Who Defied Censors, Dies at 96

text: An article on Friday about a family in India who masqueraded for decades as Oudh royalty misstated the dollar value of 10,000 rupees in 1975. It was about $1,200, not $90,000.
match_headline: The Jungle Prince of Delhi

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Senate passage of a stopgap spending bill misstated the participation of several lawmakers. Senators who are running for the Democratic presidential nomination and the Republican Senator Bill Cassidy were absent.
match_headline: Senate Approves Spending Bill to Avoid Shutdown, and Trump Signs It

text: An article on Thursday about Patrick W. Carlineo Jr., who threatened Representative Ilhan Omar, misstated where Mr. Carlineo entered his guilty plea. It was in Federal District Court in Rochester, not Buffalo.
match_headline: Man Who Threatened to ‘Put a Bullet’ in Rep. Omar Pleads Guilty

text: An obituary on Friday about the historian William Loren Katz misstated the year “Gay American History,” a book written by Mr. Katz’s stepbrother, Jonathan, was published. It was 1976, not 1978.
match_headline: William Loren Katz, Historian of African-Americans, Dies at 92

text: An article on Nov. 10 about ancient Puebloan civilization in the American Southwest misspelled part of the name of a mission church in New Mexico. It is San Estevan del Rey Mission Church, not San Estaban del Rey Mission Church.
match_headline: Searching for the Ancestral Puebloans

text: An essay on Nov. 3 about Edith Wharton’s novel “The Age of Innocence” misstated the given name of one character. He is Julius Beaufort, not Julian.
match_headline: The Age of ‘The Age of Innocence’

text: A review on Nov. 10 about the picture book “The Perfect Seat” misspelled the author’s surname. He is Minh Le, not Li.
match_headline: What’s So Funny, Kid?

text: A review on Nov. 10 about the graphic novel “White Bird,” by R.J. Palacio, misidentified a character who has polio. He is Julien, not Vincent (Julien’s antagonist).
match_headline: A New Book From the Creator of ‘Wonder’ Tells a Holocaust Story

text: An article on Sunday about the presidential election occurring in the wake of the impeachment inquiry misstated the given name of a former Republican member of the House of Representatives from Florida. He is Carlos Curbelo, not Chris.
match_headline: A Split Decision From Congress Will Leave Voters With Final Say on Trump

text: An article on Saturday about children from the former Islamic State territory in Syria who will be repatriated as British citizens misspelled the given name of a senior research fellow at King’s College in London. She is Joana Cook, not Joanna.
match_headline: U.K. Takes Back Children From Former ISIS Territory

text: An article on Monday about a student in France who set himself on fire in a political protest misstated the surname of a friend of the student who was a member of his student union. She is Sophie Lapoix, not La Toix.
match_headline: Student Sets Himself on Fire, Highlighting Broader Distress in France

text: An article on Sunday about polling issues in the 2016 presidential election that could happen again in 2020 misstated the name of a university. It is Vanderbilt University, not the University of Vanderbilt.
match_headline: Four Problems With 2016 Trump Polling That Could Play Out Again in 2020

text: An article on Sunday about climate change activists at a Yale-Harvard football game misstated part of the title of a John Denver song. It is “Take Me Home, Country Roads,” not “Country Road.”
match_headline: Climate Change Protesters Disrupt Yale-Harvard Football Game

text: Because of a production error, a Metropolitan Diary entry on Sunday about a coffee date misspelled the surname of the author. He is Jason Hack, not Hac.
match_headline: ‘We Had Hardly Taken a Sip When I Heard a Voice Behind Me’

text: An article on Sunday about Ohio State’s football victory over Penn State misstated the given name of an Ohio State center. He is Josh Myers, not Jake.
match_headline: Ohio State Passes Its First Test of the Season by Beating Penn State

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about Fred Cox, a place-kicker for the Minnesota Vikings and one of the inventors of the Nerf Football, referred incorrectly to the footballs he was shown holding. Only one of them was a Nerf Football, not all of them.
match_headline: Fred Cox, Vikings Kicker and an Inventor of Nerf Football, Dies at 80

text: An article on March 6, 2018, about Judge Dan Aaron Polster’s strategy for addressing hundreds of lawsuits tied to the opioid crisis, gave an incomplete description of Dr. Anna Lembke’s role at a court session with Judge Polster. Dr. Lembke was giving testimony as an expert witness in support of plaintiffs in the opioid cases; she was not speaking solely as an addiction specialist.
match_headline: Can This Judge Solve the Opioid Crisis?

text: An article on Tuesday about the acquisition of Tiffany & Company by LVMH misstated the change in Tiffany’s net income in the fiscal year that ended Jan. 31 from the previous year. It rose 58 percent, not 9 percent.
match_headline: Luxury Giant LVMH to Buy Tiffany for $16.2 Billion

text: An article on Tuesday about Charles Schwab’s acquisition of TD Ameritrade referred incorrectly to the types of accounts that make up the customer count of the company. It is retail and adviser accounts, not retail accounts only.
match_headline: Charles Schwab to Buy TD Ameritrade as Free Trading Takes Over

text: An article about Susan Sontag’s “Duet for Cannibals” misspelled the given name of an actor. He is Gosta Ekman, not Gost Ekman.
match_headline: Susan Sontag’s Mind Games

text: An article on Sunday about handling holiday meals with family members misstated the occupation of Parisa Parsa. She is the chief executive at Cortico, not the executive director at Essential Partners. (She is the former executive director at Essential Partners.)
match_headline: The Family Meal: Tips for Staying Sane and Sated

text: An article on Friday about a British climate debate that was skipped by Prime Minister Boris Johnson referred incorrectly to Michael Gove’s role in the government. He formerly served as environment secretary; he no longer holds that position.
match_headline: Ice Sculpture Steals Show at U.K. Climate Debate That Boris Johnson Skips

text: An article on Thursday about M.R.I.s and breast cancer detection misstated the proportion of women over the age of 40 who have dense breasts. It is just under half, not more than half.
match_headline: M.R.I.s Can Better Detect Cancer in Women With Dense Breasts, Study Finds

text: An obituary on Sept. 14 about the civil rights activist Juanita Abernathy misstated her age. She was 87, not 88. The error was repeated in the headline. (As the obituary correctly states, she was born on Dec. 1, 1931.)
match_headline: Juanita Abernathy, a Force in the Civil Rights Movement, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Nov. 22 about the Japanese-American basketball player Wat Misaka referred incompletely to the communities of people of Japanese descent that were subject to internment during World War II. It was not the case that “relocation was confined to people of Japanese descent who lived on the West Coast”; some of those interned lived elsewhere.
ref_headline: relocation was confined to people of Japanese descent who lived on the West Coast
match_headline: Wat Misaka, 95, First Nonwhite in Modern Pro Basketball, Dies

text: An article last Sunday about the new 17-mile Crosstown Trail in San Francisco misspelled the surname of the man who spearheaded the path’s creation. He is Bob Siegel, not Seigel.
match_headline: A 17-Mile Hike to Unite San Francisco

text: A picture caption with last Sunday’s cover story , about the restoration of a Brooklyn building facade, misstated the date of an etching of the Abraham & Straus department store. It was not made in 1880. (The store itself was established in 1893.)
match_headline: Restoring Brooklyn’s Queen of Department Stores

text: An article about “three-parent babies” in a special section on fertility Nov. 10 misstated the year and place of birth of the first such child. Several babies have been born with the DNA of three people, through various techniques, since the 1990s; the first was not born in 2016 overseen by the New Hope Fertility Center. The error was repeated in a timeline.
match_headline: Two Times Editors on Creating a Special Section About Fertility

text: Because of an editing error, an opinion article last week about the Ukraine scandal rendered incorrectly an account by one of the authors of his history of travel to Ukraine. The article should have said that the author, Glenn R. Simpson, says it is true that he has never visited Ukraine, not the opposite.
match_headline: The Double-Barreled Dream World of Trump and His Enablers

text: An article on Tuesday about the detention of José Daniel Ferrer García, a Cuban human rights activist, misstated the year when President Obama met with dissidents in Cuba. It was 2016, not 2015.
match_headline: Activist’s Case Hints at What Changes and What Stays the Same in Cuba

text: An article on Tuesday about the possible election impact of the recent terror attack on London Bridge misquoted David Wilson, an emeritus professor of criminology. He referred to a “one-size-fits-all, tick-box course,” not a “one-size-fits-all kickbox course.”
match_headline: For Boris Johnson, a Perilous Week Negotiating Terrorism and Trump

text: A map with an article on Monday about life inside a South Korean village in the Demilitarized Zone incorrectly located the town of Munsan. As the article states, the town is near the Demilitarized Zone, not in it.
match_headline: Life Inside the DMZ? Scary, but There’s 5G and a Great School

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about packages disappearing across the country misidentified the people in the photograph. Gabriel Cepeda, the founder of Pickups Technologies, was wearing the Pickups shirt, at right, while Douglas Grant, accepted packages at his home in Brooklyn, not the reverse.

An article on Monday about climate change’s impact on Iceland’s fishing industry misspelled the surname of the Rutgers associate professor in some instances. His name is Malin Pinsky, as correctly stated in the first instance, not Pinksy.
match_headline: Warming Waters, Moving Fish: How Climate Change Is Reshaping Iceland

text: A picture caption in an article on Saturday about “Rembrandt-Velázquez,” an exhibition at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, misidentified the painting to the right of Francisco de Zurbarán’s “Agnus Dei.” It is “Interior of the Sint-Odulphuskerk in Assendelft” by Pieter Saenredam, not “View of the Gardens of the Villa Medici” by Diego Velázquez.
An article last Wednesday about Thanksgiving table settings from around the country omitted the byline. The article is by Christine Muhlke.
match_headline: How Six Different Cooks Set Striking Thanksgiving Tables

text: An obituary on Nov. 28 about the literary critic Clive James misstated the year he left Australia for England. It was 1961, not 1962.
match_headline: Clive James Dies at 80; Literary Critic Took His Wit to TV

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about Adm. James L. Holloway III misidentified his predecessor as chief of naval operations, a post he assumed in 1974. He was Elmo R. Zumwalt Jr., not Elmo R. Zumwalt III.
match_headline: James Holloway III, 97, Dies; Navy Chief Under Three Presidents

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about Seymour Siwoff, the longtime president and chief executive of the Elias Sports Bureau, referred incorrectly to St. John’s University, which he attended. Although it is now in Queens, it was in Brooklyn when he was a student there.
match_headline: Seymour Siwoff, Master of Sports Statistics, Is Dead at 99

text: An article on Wednesday about Rudolph W. Giuliani’s call records, because of an error in the Democrats’ impeachment report, gave an incorrect date for a conversation between Secretary of State Mike Pompeo and Mr. Giuliani. The call was on March 29, not March 28.
match_headline: A Mysterious ‘-1’ and Other Call Records Show How Giuliani Pressured Ukraine

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about a Senate committee’s vote to advance the nomination of an oncologist to lead the Food and Drug Administration misspelled the given name of the nominee. He is Stephen Hahn, not Steven.
match_headline: F.D.A. Nominee Clears Senate Panel

text: A graphic with an article on Friday about Randal K. Quarles, the Federal Reserve’s vice chairman for supervision and regulation, misstated the source of data about Mr. Quarles’s meetings. It was from the Federal Reserve, not a Freedom of Information Act disclosure.
match_headline: Meet the Man Loosening Bank Regulation, One Detail at a Time

text: An article on Tuesday about the screenwriter Lena Waithe described incorrectly the work Melina Matsoukas did on Beyoncé’s “Lemonade.” She directed “Formation,” which was a part of “Lemonade,” but did not direct the whole film.
match_headline: Lena Waithe’s Art of Protest

text: An article on Thursday about accelerating climate change omitted part of the name of a research organization in Germany. It is the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, not the Potsdam Institute for Climate Research.
match_headline: Climate Change Is Accelerating, Bringing World ‘Dangerously Close’ to Irreversible Change

text: An article on Wednesday about a lawsuit filed by the City of Newark against New York City, arguing that New York pressured vulnerable people to accept substandard housing, misstated the news outlet that first reported the lawsuit. It was WCBS-TV, not The Star-Ledger.
match_headline: They Ended Up in Decrepit Housing in Newark. Is New York to Blame?

text: An article on Thursday about Steven A. Cohen’s interest in purchasing a controlling stake of the Mets from the Wilpon family misstated the amount Fred Wilpon paid in 2002 to buy out a partner’s 50 percent stake in the Mets. The deal cost about $135 million, not $391 million. It was repeated in a timeline caption.
match_headline: Steve Cohen in Talks to Buy Majority of Mets From Wilpons

text: An obituary on Thursday about the environmentalist Carolyn Konheim misstated her original surname. It was Salminen, not Salminem.
match_headline: Carolyn Konheim, Foe of All That Befouled a City, Dies at 81

text: An article last Sunday about the slow rise of lesbianism on TV misstated which season of “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” featured a scene in which the characters Willow and Tara are shown in bed together. The scene occurred in the show’s sixth season, not its final season. The article also referred incorrectly to the scene. It was not the first lesbian sex scene shown on broadcast television; it showed the characters in bed together, but not engaged in sex. A later scene in that episode with the characters Willow and Kennedy was the first lesbian sex scene on broadcast television.
match_headline: The Very (Very) Slow Rise of Lesbianism on TV

text: An article last Sunday about a father who finally saw value in the movie “Frozen” misstated the title of a Hayao Miyazaki film. It is “My Neighbor Totoro,” not “My Friend Totoro.”
match_headline: Achieving Transcendence on the Millionth ‘Frozen’ Viewing

text: An article last Sunday about Frederick Douglass and Savannah, Ga., referred incorrectly to the museum at Savannah College of Art and Design. It is the SCAD Museum of Art, not the museum of the Savannah College of Art and Design.
match_headline: Looking for Frederick Douglass in Savannah

text: An article last Sunday about the growing popularity of uphill skiing misspelled the surname of a partner creating the Bluebird Backcountry ski area in Colorado. He is Jeff Woodward, not Woodworth.
match_headline: Uphill Skiing: Subtract Crowds and Lift Lines, Add Cardio

text: An article last Sunday about skiing in the Italian Dolomites misidentified the colors used to denote the difficulty of the slopes. Intermediate slopes are red and the easiest are blue, not the reverse.
match_headline: Hut Skiing in the Dolomites: Storybook Scenery and Grappa Included

text: An article last Sunday about the photographer Raven B. Varona misstated how Ms. Varona connected with Jay-Z. It was a producer for Jay-Z who responded to her Twitter message, not Jay-Z himself.
match_headline: A Photographer Who Toured With Beyoncé and Jay-Z

text: An article on Page 11 about a father and son watching “Jeopardy!” together misstates how long Alex Trebek has been the host of “Jeopardy!” It is 35 years, not 25.
match_headline: How Watching ‘Jeopardy!’ Together Helped Me Say Goodbye to My Father

text: An article on Page 32 about the writer and translator Ken Liu misspells the name of a Chinese self-publishing platform. It is Douban, not Daoban.
match_headline: How Chinese Sci-Fi Conquered America
