text: An article on Page 58 about rage in Asian cinema misidentifies the country of origin of the novel “The Vegetarian”; it is South Korean, not Vietnamese.
match_headline: Why Does Rage Define ‘Parasite’ and Other Popular East Asian Movies?

text: An article on Page 124 about the artist Andrea Fraser misspells her husband’s surname. He is Andy Stewart, not Steward.
match_headline: Have We Finally Caught Up With Andrea Fraser?

text: An article on Monday about Amazon’s plans to lease office space in Midtown Manhattan for more than 1,500 employees misstated Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s connection to the area where Amazon had considered building a large campus. She represents an area in Queens near where the campus was to be built. She does not represent the area where the campus was to be built.
match_headline: Amazon Grows in New York, Reviving Debate Over Abandoned Queens Project

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the Knicks’ decision to fire Coach David Fizdale misidentified the Knicks assistant coach who was also fired. It was Keith Smart, not Keith Smith. The article also misstated the location of one of the Knicks’ last losses before firing Fizdale. The loss to Milwaukee was on the road, not at home.
match_headline: Knicks Fire Coach David Fizdale

text: An article on Monday about the Patriots loss to the Chiefs misidentified the Patriots receiver who was ruled out of bounds before an apparent touchdown. He is N’Keal Harry, not Jakobi Meyers.
match_headline: Patriots Run Out of Comebacks in Testy Rematch Against Chiefs

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about Maurizio Cattelan’s installation “Comedian” referred incorrectly to the relationship between Banksy and an auction house that sold his self-destructing artwork. A spokesperson for Banksy has said the auction house had no foreknowledge of the prank.
match_headline: A (Grudging) Defense of the $120,000 Banana

text: An article on Saturday about the television series “Crisis on Infinite Earths” misstated when The Flash and Supergirl died in the Crisis on Infinite Earths comic book. The Flash died in Issue No. 8, not No. 7, and Supergirl died in Issue No. 7, not No. 8.
match_headline: A ‘Crisis’ Brings Together Many DC Comics Heroes

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the Parisian landscape architect Arnaud Casaus misidentified a plant; the image featured gaura and Verbena bonariensis, not Mexican feather grass.
match_headline: On the Rooftops of Paris, a New Kind of Urban Garden

text: An obituary on Nov. 2 about the television sports impresario Barry Frank, using information from his family, misstated his full name and part of his mother’s name. He did not have a middle name, and his mother was Miriam (Fisher) Frank, not Miriam (Wiseman) Frank. The earlier version also referred imprecisely to where Mr. Frank lived. While he had a home in New Canaan, Conn., he no longer had another home in Manhattan. This correction was delayed because the errors were brought to the editors’ attention only recently.
match_headline: Barry Frank Dies at 87; Sports Agent, Negotiator and Programmer

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the actor Ron Leibman referred incorrectly to the character he played in the movie “Norma Rae.” He was a labor organizer, not a labor lawyer. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Ron Leibman, Tony Winner for ‘Angels,’ Is Dead at 82

text: An article on Wednesday about incarcerated journalists in China misstated the time period in which the Committee to Protect Journalists helped win the early release of 80 imprisoned journalists worldwide. It was over the past year, not since the group’s founding in 1981.
match_headline: China Displaces Turkey as Top Jailer of Journalists in 2019

text: An article on Wednesday about the divorce between Rudolph and Judith Giuliani misstated the capacity in which Jeffrey R. Cohen represented the singer Marc Anthony in a legal case. He represented him in a family law case, not in his divorce from Jennifer Lopez.
match_headline: Giulianis Settle Ugly Divorce Case, Avoiding a Public Trial

text: An article on Tuesday about the comet 2I Borisov described incorrectly the Las Cumbres Observatory in California. It consists of a worldwide network of small robotic optical telescopes. It does not include radio antennas.
match_headline: The Interstellar Comet Has Arrived in Time for the Holidays

text: An article on Thursday about the political climate in Britain amid the election campaign misstated the age of Queen Elizabeth II. She is 93 years old, not 95.
match_headline: Photos of the U.K. in the Shadow of Brexit

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the growing number of Americans choosing to die at home instead of in hospitals misstated the year that a picture was taken. The image of Dwight and Margaret Peterson was taken in 2013, not 2016.
match_headline: More Americans Are Dying at Home Than in Hospitals

text: An article on Wednesday about a potential delay in tariffs on Chinese imports gave an incorrect figure for the rate that President Trump will impose on $160 billion worth of Chinese goods on Dec. 15. He has threatened to impose a 15 percent tariff, not a 10 percent one.
match_headline: Signs Point to China Tariff Delay, but Decision Rests With Trump

text: An article on Thursday about a new N.Y.P.D. special unit created to investigate far-right extremists misstated the name of one of the analysts. It is Katherine Sizemore, not Katherin Sizemoer.
match_headline: With Rise of Far-Right Extremists, N.Y.P.D. Creates Special Unit

text: An article on Thursday about 10 definitive jazz moments of this decade misstated one of the musicians who paid tribute to Ornette Coleman in 2014. Lou Reed did not perform at the concert (he died in 2013), but his wife, Laurie Anderson, played a song in Coleman’s honor.
match_headline: The Decade in Jazz: 10 Definitive Moments

text: An obituary on Monday about the puppeteer Caroll Spinney misstated the name of the high school he attended. It was Acton High School — not Acton-Boxborough, its current name. The obituary also referred incompletely to Mr. Spinney’s college education. Although he did drop out of the Art Institute of Boston to join the Air Force, he later returned and graduated in 1958.
match_headline: Caroll Spinney, Big Bird’s Alter Ego on ‘Sesame Street,’ Is Dead at 85

text: An article on Page 4 about a New York Times project to photograph the record number of women in the 116th Congress misstates how many participated. Most female representatives and senators took part, not all of them.
match_headline: Women Made Them. Viewers and Critics Liked Them. No One Nominated Them.

text: An article on Friday about the Culinary Workers Local 226, a union in Nevada, misquoted former Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. He described the “incredible pain” caused by deportations during the Obama administration. He did not say, “I understand the pain that comes from those deportations.” And he started a sentence by saying “If I end up being your president.” He did not say “If I am your president.”
match_headline: Where Housekeepers, Bartenders and Cooks Wield Vast Political Clout

text: An article on Friday about a divide in Jewish communities following President Trump’s executive order to combat anti-Semitism misstated the location of the Jewish Community Center of Harrison. It is in New York, not Connecticut.
match_headline: Trump’s Order to Combat Anti-Semitism Divides Its Audience: American Jews

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the demand for Danish television misstated the title of a Norwegian television show. It is “Lilyhammer,” not “Lillehammer.”
match_headline: The World Wants More Danish TV Than Denmark Can Handle

text: An article on Saturday about Senator Mitch McConnell’s approach to the impeachment case misstated the leadership role of Tom Daschle in the Senate when President Bill Clinton was impeached. He was the Democratic minority leader, not the Democratic majority leader.
match_headline: McConnell, Coordinating With White House, Lays Plans for Impeachment Trial

text: An article on Sunday about Representative Jeff Van Drew’s plans to leave the Democratic Party for the Republican Party described incorrectly the loss of three legislative seats in New Jersey as part of a slate associated with Mr. Van Drew. The loss resulted in the seats flipping from blue to red, not from red to blue.
match_headline: Representative Jeff Van Drew, Anti-Impeachment Democrat, Plans to Switch Parties

text: An article on Monday about the inability of presidential campaigns to adequately combat disinformation misstated when Twitter announced plans to forbid all political ads. It was in October, not last month.
match_headline: 2020 Campaigns Throw Their Hands Up on Disinformation

text: An article on Friday about the former N.B.A. commissioner David Stern’s emergency surgery for a brain hemorrhage misstated the year that David Stern implemented a dress code in the N.B.A. It was in 2005, not 2015.
match_headline: David Stern Has Surgery for Brain Hemorrhage

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Dec. 10 about the former Federal Reserve Board chairman Paul A. Volcker misstated the equivalent in today’s money of $89,500, his salary in 1987, his final year at the Federal Reserve. It is about $203,000, not $312,000.
match_headline: Paul A. Volcker, Fed Chairman Who Waged War on Inflation, Is Dead at 92

text: An obituary on Dec. 4 about the rock climber Wayne Merry misspelled the surname of another climber. He was William Feuerer, not Feurer.
match_headline: Wayne Merry, Climber Who Conquered El Capitan, Dies at 88

text: An article on Monday about the resources allocated by different states for the 2020 census referred incorrectly to an online Census Bureau map related to response rates: It shows the predicted likelihood of a low response rate in 2020 for most census tracts, not the actual rate for 2010. It also misstated the total number of census tracts: There are 73,057, not 66,000. And it gave an outdated title for Ann Beeson at the Center for Public Policy Priorities: She is now chief executive, not executive director.
match_headline: In 2020 Census, Big Efforts in Some States. In Others, Not So Much.

text: An article on Tuesday about Croilot Semexan, a nonprofit worker who helps parents pursue education, misstated the scope of the program that Mr. Semexan leads. His program offers bonding activities and workout sessions for the men, but not swimming. The article also referred incorrectly to a poetry club he was part of during college. He did not create a poetry club at the college that went on to nationwide competitions; he created a club outside college that participated in competitions.
match_headline: He Helps Parents Get a Second Chance at Learning

text: An article on Nov. 29 about the best places to eat in New York museums described incorrectly the service at Petrie Court restaurant at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. It is self-serve; there is no waiter service.
match_headline: Where to Eat and Drink at 14 N.Y.C. Museums Right Now

text: An article on Tuesday about the large amount of prescription and nonprescription drugs taken by older people misstated the name of an organization. It is the American Society of Consultant Pharmacists, not the American Association of Consultant Pharmacists.
match_headline: The Hidden Drug Epidemic Among Older People

text: An obituary on Dec. 9 about the college football star and coach Bump Elliott misidentified the starting quarterback on the University of Michigan’s undefeated 1947 team, on which he played halfback. It was Howard Yerges — not Elliott’s brother Pete, who was on the team but not a starter. The same error appeared in Pete Elliott’s obituary in 2013.
match_headline: Bump Elliott, College Football Star and Coach, Dies at 94

text: An article on Wednesday about a $1.7 billion settlement reached between PG&E and California regulators described incorrectly the trial involving the company’s role in the Tubbs Fire that was delayed by a state judge. It was a civil trial, not a criminal trial.
match_headline: PG&E Reaches Deal With Regulators but Faces More Hurdles

text: Because of editing errors, an article on Wednesday about the N.H.L.’s lack of popularity with Canadian youth misstated the positions played by Joel Ward and, in an accompanying picture caption, Wayne Simmonds. Simmonds is a forward, not a defenseman, as was Ward, who is retired.
match_headline: Amid Blackface and Abuse Allegations, Hockey Wonders Why Young Canadians Don’t Play

text: An article on Thursday about the sexual exploitation and abuse of women and girls by U.N. peacekeepers in Haiti misstated Sienna Merope-Synge’s affiliation. She is a staff attorney at the Institute for Justice and Democracy in Haiti, but she is not a legal director of the Bureau des Avocats Internationaux.
match_headline: U.N. Peacekeepers in Haiti Said to Have Fathered Hundreds of Children

text: An article on Thursday about the political views of voters in Bucks County, Pa., described incorrectly the Bucks County government. It is the Board of Commissioners, not the County Council.
match_headline: Where Impeachment Crosses Party Lines, but Fixates on Trump

text: An article on Thursday about toaster ovens, using incorrect information from the company, misstated the price of the Brava smart oven. It costs $1,095, not $995.
match_headline: Gadget of the Year: The Toaster Oven

text: An article on Wednesday about recent commercial real estate transactions misidentified the landlord of the building at 463 Seventh Avenue in Manhattan. It is the Arsenal Company, not Ten West Thirty Third Associates.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An obituary on Saturday about the editor and publisher Elisabeth Sifton misstated when she began exploring the derivation of the Serenity Prayer. It was 1998, not 2008.
match_headline: Elisabeth Sifton, Editor and Tamer of Literary Lions, Dies at 80

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the former commerce secretary Frederick B. Dent misstated his role in the organization Citizens Against Government Waste. Although he was a member, he was not a past president.
match_headline: Frederick B. Dent, 97, Commerce Secretary and Nixon Ally, Dies

text: An article on Friday about the haggling and eventual agreement between congressional Democrats and the Trump Administration over the new North American trade deal misstated the stance of Representative Terri A. Sewell of Alabama on past trade deals. It is not true that she had never voted on a trade deal. The article also misstated the timing of a conversation Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office had with Robert Lighthizer, the country’s top trade negotiator, and when Ms. Pelosi told the Democratic caucus “We ate their lunch.” Ms. Pelosi’s office informed Mr. Lighthizer of a news conference late Monday, not Tuesday, and the speaker talked to her caucus on Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: How a Trump Trade Pact Won Over Democrats

text: Because of an editing error, a concert entry in the Listings pages on Friday about the choir Blue Heron misstated the ensemble’s home country. It is based in the United States, not England.
match_headline: 5 Classical Music Concerts to See in N.Y.C. This Weekend

text: An obituary on Dec. 15 and 16 about the financier Felix Rohatyn misidentified Frank G. Wisner, whom President Bill Clinton had considered naming ambassador to France before appointing Mr. Rohatyn. He was the son of Frank Wisner, who helped found the C.I.A.; he himself was not a founder. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Mr. Rohatyn’s friendship with President François Mitterrand of France. It began before Mr. Rohatyn was named ambassador, not during his tenure. (Mr. Mitterrand died before Mr. Rohatyn was appointed.) In addition, the obituary misstated when Mr. Rohatyn first wrote for The New York Review of Books. It was in 1980, not after his return to the United States from Paris in 2000. And it referred incorrectly to two deals on which Mr. Rohatyn worked. One was an attempted takeover by The Limited, the clothing retailer, of the company that operated Bergdorf Goodman and Neiman Marcus — not the purchase of The Limited by that company. The other was an attempted takeover by International Nickel of the battery manufacturer ESB — not by Morgan Stanley of International Nickel.
match_headline: Felix G. Rohatyn, Financier Who Piloted New York’s Rescue, Dies at 91

text: A review on Nov. 10 about the picture book “Encyclopedia of Grannies” misspelled the surname of the author and illustrator. He is Eric Veillé, not Viellé.
match_headline: Grandparents Are Heroes, and Also Totally Normal People

text: A review on Dec. 1 misstated the name of the cartooning school that produced the graphic biography “Charlotte Brontë Before Jane Eyre,” by Glynnis Fawkes. It is the Center for Cartoon Studies, not Stories.
match_headline: Charlotte Brontë and Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Before the World Knew Them

text: An article on Sunday about the losses that communities suffer when local newspapers close misstated the status of The Birmingham News. A print edition publishes three days a week; it has not ceased publication. A picture caption with the article referred imprecisely to the building shown in the photo. It was the former headquarters of The Los Angeles Times, not its current location.
match_headline: More Than 1 in 5 U.S. Papers Has Closed. This Is the Result.

text: An article on Sunday about swimming pools in Kabul, Afghanistan, that allow women access misspelled the given name of the director of the female committee at Afghanistan’s swimming federation. She is Helena Saboori, not Haleena. A picture caption also misidentified Ms. Saboori. She is on the left in the photo, preparing to enter the pool, not in the center.
match_headline: For Women in Kabul, ‘It Is Just Me and the Water’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Edward Durham’s struggles with student loan debts misstated the amount Americans collectively owe in student loans. It is $1.6 trillion, not $11.6 trillion.
match_headline: Decades Later, His Student Debt Came Back to Haunt Him

text: An article on Monday about the arrest of Drita D’Avanzo, a star of the television show “Mob Wives,” misstated the given name of an infamous mob turncoat known as Sammy the Bull. He is Salvatore Gravano, not Sammy.
match_headline: Drita D’Avanzo, Hot-Tempered Star of ‘Mob Wives,’ Is Arrested

text: An article on Saturday about Daniel Fish’s production of “The Most Happy Fella” described incorrectly the meeting of Frank Loesser and his wife, Jo Sullivan Loesser. They met when she starred as Rosabella in the original production of “The Most Happy Fella,” not afterward.
match_headline: Daniel Fish’s Post-‘Oklahoma!’ Musical: ‘The Most Happy Fella’

text: An obituary on Saturday about Herman Boone, the high school football coach portrayed in the film “Remember the Titans,” using information from Mr. Boone’s family, misstated the field in which he earned a master’s degree. It was physical education, not biology. Because of an editing error, the obituary misstated the year the coach Bill Yoast died. It was 2019, not 1994. (Mr. Yoast was 94 at his death.)
match_headline: Herman Boone, Coach Portrayed in ‘Remember the Titans,’ Dies at 84

text: A picture caption with an article last Friday about pushback from members of the Sackler family against Tufts University’s decision to remove the Sackler name from buildings and programs misidentified the location of buildings that had the name removed. They were on the Tufts University campus, not the Tufts Medical Center campus.
match_headline: Sackler Family Members Fight Removal of Name at Tufts, Calling It a ‘Breach’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a house party in Chicago where 13 people were shot described the party incorrectly. It was a memorial for a carjacker who was killed, not for the victim of the carjacking.
match_headline: Chicago House Party Shooting Leaves 13 Wounded, 4 Critically, Police Say

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the hip-hop party D’ussé Palooza misspelled the surname of its chief operating officer. He is Benner Hall, not Hal.
match_headline: How a Hip-Hop Party Went From a Harlem Basement to Packing Barclays

text: An article on Sunday about the banker Felix G. Rohatyn misspelled the given name of one of his sons. He is Nicolas Rohatyn, not Nicholas.
match_headline: How a Banker Helped Save N.Y. (and Why It Will Never Happen Again)

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a Christmas card with a message said to be from prisoners forced into labor in China misspelled the name of a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman. He is Geng Shuang, not Gene.
match_headline: Inside Christmas Card, Girl Finds Plea From Chinese Prison Laborers

text: An article on Monday about a decline in movie ticket sales in 2019 misspelled the name of the director of “The Farewell.” She is Lulu Wang, not Wong.
match_headline: Not Even ‘Star Wars’ Can Save This Year’s Box Office

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about The Learning Network, a New York Times section dedicated to creating resources for instructors and students to teach and learn using The Times, referred incorrectly to Michael Gonchar’s tenure as head of The Learning Network. He has been in the position since January 2019; it is not the case that he will begin in January 2020.
match_headline: How The Learning Network Transforms Classrooms Across America

text: An article on Wednesday about Australia’s volunteer firefighting force referred incorrectly to Balmoral. It is a village southwest of Sydney, not a coastal area of suburban Sydney.
match_headline: Australia’s Volunteer Firefighters Find It Hard to Pause, Even for Christmas

text: An article on Wednesday about recent commercial real estate transactions misstated the cross streets nearest to the property at 228 Seventh Avenue in Brooklyn. They are Third and Fourth Streets, not West 23rd and West 24th Streets.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: A chart on the “Evolution of the N.F.L.” with the “N.F.L. at 100” package on Sunday described incorrectly some links between A.F.L. teams in the 1960s and current N.F.L. teams. The old Boston Patriots should have been linked to the New England Patriots. The old Houston Oilers did not become the Houston Texans; they eventually became the Tennessee Titans, as was noted elsewhere in the chart. And the Dallas Texans/K.C. Chiefs franchise should have been linked to the Kansas City Chiefs, not the Dallas Cowboys.
match_headline: The Patriots Beat the Bills (Again) Behind Julian Edelman

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Sunday in a grid of photographs with the “N.F.L. at 100” package erroneously attributed a distinction to Wally Triplett. He was the first black player to play for an N.F.L. team, not the first black player drafted in the N.F.L. (That was George Taliaferro.)
match_headline: Beautiful. Violent. American. The N.F.L. at 100.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Marshawn Lynch’s move to the Seattle Seahawks misstated the day of the coming Seahawks-49ers game. As the article noted elsewhere, it is on Sunday night, not Monday night.
match_headline: Marshawn Lynch Arrives to Give Seattle a Playoff Push

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the songwriter Allee Willis misstated the given name of her collaborator on the song “Boogie Wonderland.” He is Jon Lind, not Bob.
match_headline: Allee Willis, 72, Dies; ‘Friends’ Theme and ‘September’ Songwriter

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the journalist Karl E. Meyer misstated who at The New York Times decided not to report in early 1961 that the Bay of Pigs invasion was imminent and that it was being financed and directed by the Central Intelligence Agency. It was the publisher, not the reporter Tad Szulc’s editors. The obituary also misstated the given name of Mr. Meyer’s paternal grandfather and part of his mother’s name. His grandfather was Georg Meyer, not George, and his mother was Dorothy (Narefsky) Meyer, not Narevsky.
match_headline: Karl E. Meyer, 91, Reporter, Editorialist and Author, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a hunger strike in Nicaragua included an erroneous byline. It was written by Frances Robles, not by Ms. Robles and Cesar Rodriguez. (Mr. Rodriguez was the photographer for the article.)
match_headline: Nicaragua Has a Simple Message for Protesters: Don’t

text: Because of an editing error, the Surfacing article on Page 32, about photographs of clouds, includes an erroneous byline. The text is by Josephine Sedgwick.
Because of an editing error, a review on Page 22 about the Y.A. novel “Jackpot,” by Nic Stone, refers incorrectly to the author. She is a woman.
match_headline: The Explosive Y.A. Novels Fans Have Been Waiting For

text: An obituary on Nov. 28 about the director Jonathan Miller referred imprecisely to Jeremy Hillary Boob, a character in the animated Beatles film “Yellow Submarine.” Although the character may have been based in part on Mr. Miller, it is generally accepted that he is based primarily on the historian Jeremy Adams.
match_headline: Jonathan Miller, Bold Director of Theater and Opera, Is Dead at 85

text: An obituary on Friday about the college football coach Hayden Fry misstated the name of one of the universities at which he coached. It was North Texas State University, not North Texas University.
match_headline: Hayden Fry, Who Made Iowa a Football Powerhouse, Dies at 90

text: Because of an editing error, the Surfacing article on Page 32, about photographs of clouds, includes an erroneous byline. The text is by Josephine Sedgwick.

An article last Sunday about the musical “Cats” misidentified the Tony Award that Betty Buckley won for her performance in the show in 1983. It was the prize for best featured actress in a musical, not for best actress. (Natalia Makarova was named best actress in a musical for her performance in “On Your Toes.”)
match_headline: ‘Cats’: What to Know Before You See It

text: A map with an article last Sunday about sailing around the Exuma Islands misidentified an island. It is Andros Island, not Grand Bahama Island.
match_headline: On a Bahamas Sail, 8 Friends Get a Taste of Robinson Crusoe

text: A review on Dec. 8 about “Listening for America,” by Rob Kapilow, misstated the length of the first chorus in the Kern and Hammerstein song “All the Things You Are.” It is 36 measures, not 32.
match_headline: What Makes a Popular Song Great?

text: A review on Dec. 8 about “The Europeans,” by Orlando Figes, misstated the mid-19th-century location of the spa town of Baden (also known as Baden-Baden). It was in the Grand Duchy of Baden, not Prussia.
match_headline: How Modernity Came to Europe

text: An article on Tuesday about the United States losing its competitive edge in astronomy misstated the circumference of the Large Hadron Collider. It is about 17 miles around, not 27. Also, because of an editing error, the article misstated the collider’s dimensions. Seventeen miles is its approximate circumference, not its diameter.
match_headline: Will the United States Lose the Universe?

text: An article on Tuesday about the portrayal of theater in film, television and literature misidentified the play directed by the character Charlie Barber in “Marriage Story.” It is “Electra,” not “Medea.”
match_headline: Is Theater Ridiculous? Movies, TV and Books Seem to Think So

text: An article on Tuesday about Carlos Ghosn’s escape from Japan misstated the total amount Carlos Ghosn paid in bail. It was 1.5 billion yen, or about $13.8 million, not $9 million. The error was repeated in two other articles on Wednesday.
match_headline: Carlos Ghosn, Fallen Nissan Boss, Flees Japan to Escape ‘Political Persecution’

text: An article on Wednesday about concerns expressed by scientists on an E.P.A. advisory panel over the rollback of three significant environmental regulations misstated the name of the state environmental agency in Texas. It is the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, not the Texas Council on Environmental Quality.
match_headline: Science Panel Staffed With Trump Appointees Says E.P.A. Rollbacks Lack Scientific Rigor

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the end of Pete Buttigieg’s term as mayor of South Bend, Ind., included an erroneous distinction. He is not the youngest mayor ever of a city of more than 100,000 residents.
match_headline: He’s Not ‘Mayor Pete’ Anymore: Buttigieg’s Successor Is Sworn In

text: An article on Tuesday about building facade violations discovered in surprise inspections described incorrectly the number of Class 1 violations issued by the city Department of Buildings in 2019. Thousands of Class 1 violations were issued in 2019, not 345. The 345 Class 1 violations referred specifically to those that were issued for failure to address unsafe facade issues that had previously been reported.
match_headline: After Death From Falling Debris, Violations Found at 220 Buildings

text: An article on Wednesday about Ron Rivera’s new position with the Washington Redskins referred incorrectly to the Carolina Panthers’ Super Bowl appearance in the 2015 season. It was their second Super Bowl appearance, not their first. (The first came in the 2003 season.)
match_headline: Ron Rivera, Cast Out of Carolina, Lands With the Washington Redskins

text: An entry on Wednesday in the What’s on TV highlights misidentified the setting of “The Shawshank Redemption.” It was set in Maine, not Ohio.
match_headline: What’s on TV Wednesday: A Linda Ronstadt Doc and ‘Doctor Who’

text: An article on Page 8 about an apprentice program for young adults recovering from substance abuse run by luthiers from the Appalachian Artisan Center in Kentucky misspells the name of Kentucky’s capital. It is Frankfort, not Frankfurt.
match_headline: In Appalachia, Crafting a Road to Recovery With Dulcimer Strings

text: An article on Page 3 about the director and writer Simon Stone misstated the relationship of the actors Bobby Cannavale and Rose Byrne. They are partners, but they are not married.
match_headline: Simon Stone Faced the Unthinkable. He Thinks You Should Too.

text: An article last Sunday about culinary podcasts included outdated information about the producer of one podcast, “The Sporkful.” It is now part of Stitcher, not WNYC.
match_headline: 6 Podcasts to Feed Your Inner Gourmand

text: An article last Sunday about Réunion Island misstated the year that it became an overseas department of France. It was 1946, not 1960.
match_headline: Why Hiking Beats Surfing on Réunion Island (Hint: Sharks!)

text: A map with the Living In article last Sunday, about Midtown South, misidentified an avenue shown on the east side of Manhattan. It is Park Avenue, not Park Avenue South.
match_headline: Midtown South, Manhattan: A Commercial Neighborhood Sees an Influx of Residents

text: An article on Saturday about the decision by President Trump to order the killing of Maj. Gen. Qassim Suleimani misspelled the given name of the defense secretary. He is Mark T. Esper, not Marc.
match_headline: For Trump, a Risky Decision on Suleimani Is One Other Presidents Had Avoided

text: An article on Saturday about threats exchanged between the United States and Iran after the death of General Suleimani described incorrectly the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force. It was approved by Congress to grant legal authority to wage war in Iraq, not to enable military action against Al Qaeda.
match_headline: U.S. and Iran Exchange More Threats as Democrats Question Timing of Strike

text: An article on Sunday about the effect the conflict with Iran will have on the fight against ISIS misstated the occupation of the American whose killing helped precipitate the United States’ strike on Maj. Gen. Qassim Suleimani. The American was a civilian contractor, not a soldier.
match_headline: Conflict With Iran Threatens Fight Against ISIS

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the Department of Homeland Security’s assessment of potential threats from Iran misstated the name of the department’s transportation agency. It is the Transportation Security Administration, not the Transportation Security Agency.
match_headline: Homeland Security Sees ‘No Specific, Credible Threat’ From Iran, but Warns of Cyberattacks

text: An article on Saturday about the endurance of the car-buying boom in the United States misidentified the Michigan hometown of Pete Krupsky, a used-car buyer. It is Rockwood, not Rosewood.
match_headline: Low Rates, Cheap Gas and Deeper Debt Sustain Car Buying Boom

text: An entry in the Listings pages on Friday about television to watch this winter misstated the director of the “68 Whiskey” pilot. It is Michael Lehmann, not Ron Howard; Howard is an executive producer.
match_headline: The 50 TV Shows You Need to Watch This Winter

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Sunday about a new rule that will allow federal agencies to disregard climate change when assessing the environmental impact of infrastructure projects misidentified a pipeline in Walsh County, N.D. While the pipeline in the photo is part of the Keystone system, it is not a part of the Keystone XL phase.
match_headline: Trump Rule Would Exclude Climate Change in Infrastructure Planning

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about the United Methodist Church’s plan to split over same-sex marriage misstated the location of two churches shown in a collection of images. The church in the top-right image is in Winona, Minn., not Homer, Ark.; the church in the bottom right photo is in Highland Falls, N.Y., not High Falls, N.Y. The caption also referred incorrectly to the United Methodist Church. It is the second-largest Protestant denomination in the United States, not in the world.
match_headline: United Methodist Church Announces Plan to Split Over Same-Sex Marriage

text: An article on Monday about Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo’s assistance in roadside emergencies misidentified the hurricane in Puerto Rico for which he helped in recovery efforts. It was Hurricane Maria, not Hurricane Irene.
match_headline: Driver in Distress? It’s Cuomo to the Rescue (Again)

text: An article on Tuesday about super-thin materials misidentified the location where the craze for two-dimensional chemistry began. It was the University of Manchester, not the University of Liverpool.
match_headline: The Superpowers of Super-Thin Materials

text: An article on Wednesday about the Trump administration’s justification for the killing of Maj. Gen. Qassim Suleimani referred incorrectly to an intelligence briefing given to lawmakers on Tuesday. It was not given by Gina Haspel, the C.I.A. director.
match_headline: Pressed for Details on Suleimani Strike, Trump Administration Gives Few

text: An article on Sunday about tech companies’ expansion in New York referred imprecisely to a Wall Street Journal report on Facebook’s negotiations to lease office space in the James A. Farley Building. While the Journal was among the first to report on the deal, it was not the first.
match_headline: Silicon Valley’s Newest Rival: The Banks of the Hudson

text: An article on Wednesday about the partial removal of NATO trainers in Iraq misidentified the country in which NATO will continue to maintain a presence. It is Iraq, not Iran.
match_headline: Some NATO Troops Begin Leaving Iraq

text: An article on Wednesday about the use of the word “assassination” in relation to the killing of Maj. Gen. Qassim Suleimani misstated the surname of a University of Virginia law professor who said many legal issues were unsettled concerning the killing. She is Ashley Deeks, not Ashley Meeks.
match_headline: A One-Word Accusation Swirls Around Trump’s Deadly Strike: Assassination

text: An article on Tuesday about racism and sexism in the field of economics misstated the methodology of a study about differences in the questioning of male and female economists at seminars. The study was based on direct study of the seminars; it did not involve video.
match_headline: A Year After a #MeToo Reckoning, Economists Still Grapple With It

text: An obituary on Jan. 1 about Sonny Mehta, the chairman of the Knopf Doubleday Publishing Group,using information from a Knopf spokesman, misstated where in Manhattan he died. It was at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital/Weill Cornell Medical Center, not at his home. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated where the Alfred A. Knopf offices were located when Mr. Mehta was hired as president and editor in chief in 1987. They were on Third Avenue, not Park Avenue.
match_headline: Sonny Mehta, Venerable Knopf Publisher, Is Dead at 77

text: An obituary on Dec. 17 about the composer Gershon Kingsley incorrectly included one name on a list of artists who have recorded his composition “Pop Corn.” It was never recorded by Kraftwerk.
match_headline: Gershon Kingsley, Master of Electronic Sounds, Dies at 97

text: An article on Thursday about a decision by the Duke and Duchess of Sussex to withdraw from royal duties misidentified the place in Canada where Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, spent the holidays. It is Vancouver Island, not Vancouver. The article also referred incorrectly to the son of Prince Harry and Meghan. He is Master Archie Mountbatten-Windsor — or Archie — not Prince Archie.
match_headline: Prince Harry and Meghan to ‘Step Back’ From Royal Duties in Extraordinary Retreat

text: An article on Thursday about the obscurity around the reasons for the crash of Ukraine International Flight 752 misstated the direction the plane appeared to be flying after its transponder stopped working. It went northeast, not northwest.
match_headline: Little Clarity, Many Theories in Ukraine Airline Crash in Iran

text: An article on Wednesday about pedestrian fatalities, relying on information provided by the Police Department, misstated the number of pedestrians killed in traffic accidents on Tuesday. It was two, not three. The person erroneously reported as dead, a man hit by a bus in Manhattan, was critically injured. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: 2 Dead After Sanitation and Concrete Trucks Hit Pedestrians in N.Y.C.

text: An article on Wednesday about the Seke language described incorrectly the length of a civil war in Nepal. It lasted a decade, not three decades. The article also misstated which party currently leads the Nepalese government. The government is led by the Nepal Communist Party, not by a coalition of moderate Communists and former Maoists. The coalition had ruled, but then merged their parties to form the Nepal Communist Party.
match_headline: Just 700 Speak This Language (50 in the Same Brooklyn Building)

text: An article on Thursday about Rupert Murdoch’s influence on a debate concerning the wildfires in Australia misidentified the owner of the Bairnsdale Advertiser as one of the many small regional papers owned by News Corp. It is owned by Yeates Media, not News Corp.
match_headline: How Rupert Murdoch Is Influencing Australia’s Bushfire Debate

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Broadway producer Adela Holzer misstated part of the name of a play by Murray Schisgal that she produced. It was “All Over Town,” not “All Around Town.” It also misstated the date that another Holzer production, “Something Old, Something New,” opened and closed. It was Jan. 1, 1977 — not Oct. 1.
match_headline: Adela Holzer, Whose Fall From Grace Was Theatrical, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Jan. 1 about the historian Gertrude Himmelfarb mistakenly included one name on a list of immigrants who influenced her when she attended the University of Chicago. The historian Louis Gottschalk was not an immigrant; his parents immigrated from Poland, but he was born in Brooklyn.
match_headline: Gertrude Himmelfarb, Conservative Historian of Ideas, Dies at 97

text: An article on Friday about intelligence that says an Iranian missile brought down Flight 752 in Tehran misstated the name of the airline. It was Ukraine International Airlines, not Ukrainian Airlines.
match_headline: Iranian Missile Accidentally Brought Down Ukrainian Jet, Officials Say, Citing Early Evidence

text: An article on Dec. 30 about a California law that requires public companies in the state to include more women on their boards misstated the name of a company that recently added a woman to its board. It is OSI Systems, not OSI Securities.
match_headline: California Companies Are Rushing to Find Female Board Members

text: An article on Oct. 13 about the use of images from the photo-sharing site Flickr in facial-recognition technology misstated a goal of the CyberPatriot program. It encourages young people to pursue careers in fields like cybersecurity, not just careers in intelligence and the military. This correction was delayed, because the error was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: Facebook Bans Content About Holocaust Denial From Its Site

text: A picture caption with an article about the Trump administration’s actions over the course of a week that pushed the U.S. and Iran to the brink of war was duplicated. The image showed Iranian rockets being fired at Al Asad Air Base in Iraq, not the funeral procession for Maj. Gen. Qassim Suleimani.
match_headline: Seven Days in January: How Trump Pushed U.S. and Iran to the Brink of War

text: An article on Friday about Canadians who died on Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752 misstated the day of the crash. It was Wednesday, not Friday.
match_headline: Plane Crash Leaves Iranian Diaspora in Canada Grief-Stricken

text: An article on Jan. 5 about the suicide of a professor at Dartmouth misstated the number of Dartmouth students who attempted suicide amid what they called an abusive culture fueled by their professors. Two made suicide attempts, according to their legal complaint, not one.
match_headline: He Was Accused of Enabling Abuse. Then Came a Downward Spiral.

text: An article on Thursday about security vulnerabilities found in TikTok’s mobile app misstated Luke Deshotels’s position with the company. He is a member of TikTok’s security team, not the head of the team.
match_headline: Major TikTok Security Flaws Found

text: An obituary on Friday about the writer and actor Buck Henry misidentified the television show on which he appeared in a sketch as a member of the Frightened family. It was “The New Show,” not “Saturday Night Live.”
match_headline: Buck Henry, Who Helped Create ‘Get Smart’ and Adapt ‘The Graduate,’ Dies at 89

text: An obituary on Thursday about Bob Wade, an artist known for his outsize public sculptures, misidentified the university where he had been a professor of art. It was North Texas State University (now the University of North Texas), not Texas State University.
match_headline: Bob Wade, Sculptor of the Outlandishly Large, Dies at 76

text: An article on Sunday about far-right trolls in Germany misspelled the surname of North-Rhine-Westphalia’s governor. He is Armin Laschet, not Lashet.
match_headline: Far-Right Trolls, Not Grannies, Drive Outrage Over German Satire

text: An article on Tuesday about a new Iowa poll by Monmouth University misstated Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s result. He earned 24 percent support, not 25 percent.
match_headline: New Iowa Poll Shows Tight Race, With Joe Biden Jumping Ahead

text: An article on Thursday about misleading statements made by President Trump described incorrectly a provision of the Iran nuclear deal. The deal placed limits on the use of centrifuges for research and development, but did not bar it outright.
match_headline: Trump’s Inaccurate Statements About the Conflict With Iran

text: An article on Tuesday about the 2020 Oscar nominations misstated the name of the country where “Honeyland” takes place. It is now the Republic of North Macedonia, not Macedonia.
match_headline: Oscar Nominations 2020: ‘Joker’ Leads With 11 Nods; Three Others Get 10

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about art stolen by the Nazis paraphrased incorrectly a comment by Magda Mielnik, a curator at the National Museum in Gdansk, Poland. She said that she and her colleagues at the museum are working to identify the provenance of all the works in the collection. She did not mention having a role in any decision on whether to return those found to have been stolen by the Nazis.
match_headline: Poland Urged to Look for Nazi-Looted Art Still Held in Its Museums

text: An article on Tuesday about the Vera C. Rubin Observatory misidentified the astronomer who discovered a relationship between the luminosities and periodicities of variable stars. It was Henrietta Leavitt, not Henrietta Swope.
match_headline: Vera Rubin Gets a Telescope of Her Own

text: An article on Wednesday about Nissan’s financial troubles misstated the decline in Nissan sales in the United States last year. It was 10 percent, not 11 percent.
match_headline: Nissan Is in Trouble. Carlos Ghosn May Deserve the Blame.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the civic leader and former congressman Frederick W. Richmond, who helped save Carnegie Hall from demolition, referred incorrectly to a developer’s plan for replacing the hall when it was torn down. The plan was to build an office building on the site, not an apartment building.
match_headline: Frederick Richmond, 96, Dies; Congressman Undone by Corruption

text: An obituary on Sunday about Sultan Qaboos bin Said of Oman at one point misstated his date of birth. As the obituary later stated correctly, it was Nov. 18, 1940, not Oct. 18.

A picture caption on Wednesday with an article about a clash between the Democratic presidential candidates Senator Bernie Sanders and Senator Elizabeth Warren misidentified the city where Mr. Sanders was photographed campaigning on Saturday. It was Davenport, Iowa, not Newton, Iowa.
match_headline: Tonight’s Democratic Debate in Iowa: Will Sanders and Warren Clash or De-Escalate?

text: An article on Friday about a report that said the White House violated a law by withholding aid to Ukraine described incorrectly the legislative history of the Impoundment Control Act. The bill was signed into law in 1974 by President Richard M. Nixon after being passed in Congress; it is not the case that the bill was passed over the veto of Mr. Nixon.
match_headline: G.A.O. Report Says Trump Administration Broke Law in Withholding Ukraine Aid

text: An article on Wednesday about a new contract between the W.N.B.A. and its players’ union, using information from a league official, described incorrectly the teams that will play for the title in the Commissioner’s Cup. The top team in each conference with the best record in Cup games will play for the title, not the top two teams over all.
match_headline: W.N.B.A. Makes ‘Big Bet on Women’ With a New Contract

text: An article on Page 48 about split-jury verdicts misstates the number of people the Innocence Project New Orleans says have been exonerated in Louisiana since 2000. It is 43, not 56.

text: An article on Page 42 about the staging of sex scenes for film and theater misstates Siobhan Richardson’s title. She is an intimacy director, not an intimacy coordinator. text: An article last Sunday about Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s decision to “step back” from royal duties misidentified one of the sources of Harry’s inheritance. It was his great-grandmother’s estate, not his grandmother’s.

text: An article on Jan. 5 about the marketing of hydration misstated the surname of a dermatologist. He is Dr. Joshua Zeichner, not Zeigler.

text: An article on Jan. 5 about the Norwegian archipelago Svalbard misstated its location. It is 1,200 miles north of Oslo, not from mainland Norway. The article also referred incorrectly to the makeup of Svalbard’s population. Its inhabitants are mostly from Russia and Scandinavia — not Russia, Scandinavia and Canada.
match_headline: Greeting the New Year in Earth’s Northernmost Settlement

text: An article on Page 48 about split-jury verdicts misstates the number of people the Innocence Project New Orleans says have been exonerated in Louisiana since 2000. It is 43, not 56.
match_headline: A Painter Resurrects Louisiana’s Vanished Creole Culture

text: An article on Aug. 18, 2019, about the legacy of racial myths in modern medicine misstated the proportion of medical students and residents surveyed who believed that black skin is thicker than white skin. It was a third of those surveyed, not a majority. The article also misidentified the medical condition of children described in a 2013 review. They had conditions that required adenoidectomies or tonsillectomies; they did not have appendicitis.

text: An article on Monday about the challenges presidential candidates face in earning the support of black voters misstated when Booker T. Washington made his argument for black self-help. It was the late 19th century and early 20th century, not the early 19th century.
match_headline: The Big Ask of Black Voters: Trust the Government

text: An article on Tuesday about ground rules laid out by Senator Mitch McConnell for President Trump’s impeachment trial referred incorrectly to Representative Lee Zeldin. He is the representative of a district in New York, not Texas.
match_headline: McConnell Pushes to Speed Impeachment Trial as Trump Requests Swift Acquittal

text: An article on Monday about a pledge by multiple countries to end military involvement in Libya’s civil war misstated the year that the United Nations Security Council first agreed to an arms embargo. It was 2011, not 1970.
match_headline: International Powers Call for Cease-Fire in Libya’s Long Civil War

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about a conspiracy theory spread by President Trump involving the Democratic Party and Bernie Sanders’s campaign misidentified the leadership position held by Representative Kevin McCarthy, Republican of California. He is the House minority leader, not the majority leader.
match_headline: How Trump Is Spreading a Conspiracy Theory About Pelosi, Biden and Sanders

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about a congressional hearing in Boulder, Colo., at which executives of some technology companies said their big rivals hindered their business, misidentified the congressman pictured. He is Representative Ed Perlmutter, Democrat of Colorado, not Representative David Cicilline, Democrat of Rhode Island.
match_headline: Please Stop Big Tech, Small Rivals Tell Lawmakers

text: An article on Tuesday about Davos through the years misidentified the profession of Samuel Huntington, who coined the term “Davos Man.” He was a political scientist, not an economist.
match_headline: A Look at Davos Through the Years

text: An article on Sunday about the successful season for the San Francisco 49ers misstated how many seasons it had been since the 49ers made the playoffs when General Manager John Lynch and Coach Kyle Shanahan received six-year contracts in 2017. It had been three seasons, not six.
match_headline: A Rival’s Advice Put the 49ers on a Super Bowl Path

text: An article on Tuesday about Michael Sheen’s role in “Prodigal Son” misstated the status of a potential second season of the show. It had not been ordered at the time the article was published.
match_headline: On ‘Prodigal Son,’ Michael Sheen’s Father Knows, and Kills, Best

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the singer-songwriter Dave Olney misstated the year Bob Dylan first performed at the Newport Folk Festival, a performance Mr. Olney witnessed. It was 1963, not 1964.
match_headline: David Olney, 71, Singer-Songwriter, Dies Onstage

text: An article on Wednesday about the defense team’s strategy in Harvey Weinstein’s rape trial misstated the composition of the jury. It includes five women, not six.
match_headline: Weinstein’s Lawyers Say Accusers ‘Bragged’ About Sex With Him

text: An article on Monday about the Kansas City Chiefs’ victory against the Tennessee Titans in the A.F.C. championship game on Sunday misidentified the Titans’ home city. It is Nashville, not Memphis.
match_headline: The Kansas City Chiefs Waited 50 Years for This Super Bowl Date

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the 2020 SAG award winners misidentified the “Parasite” cast member on the far right. She is Lee Jung Eun, not Chang Hyae Jin.
match_headline: SAG Award Winners 2020: ‘Parasite’ Pulls Off Huge Victory

text: An obituary on Monday about the jazz saxophonist and composer Jimmy Heath misspelled the surname of the co-author of his autobiography, “I Walked With Giants.” He is Joseph McLaren, not McLarin.
match_headline: Jimmy Heath, 93, Jazz Saxophonist and Composer, Is Dead

text: An article on Thursday about a new white supremacist group called the Base misstated the name of a Georgia county where three men cased a house of Antifa members. It is Bartow County, not Barstow County.
match_headline: A New Face of White Supremacy: Plots Expose Danger of the ‘Base’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a fire in Brooklyn that killed an 11-year-old girl referred incorrectly to Shomrei Hadas. Madelyn Novitsky, a substitute teacher, would sometimes take Shirr Teved to synagogue, but that synagogue was not Shomrei Hadas. Shomrei Hadas is the funeral home where Shirr’s funeral services were held.
match_headline: Girl, 11, Dies in Unexplained Fire in Brooklyn

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the soccer player Javier Hernández misstated the timing of David Beckham’s first season with the Los Angeles Galaxy of Major League Soccer in relation to Landon Donovan’s. Beckham joined the team after Donovan did, not before.
match_headline: Mexico’s ‘Chicharito,’ Javier Hernández, Joins Los Angeles Galaxy in M.L.S.

text: An article on Friday about an invitation extended to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to visit the White House misstated President Trump’s itinerary when he spoke to reporters aboard Air Force One. He was en route from Joint Base Andrews to Doral, Fla., to speak at the Republican National Committee’s winter meeting, not on his way back from the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.
match_headline: Trump Invites Netanyahu to White House to Discuss Middle East Peace Plan

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Thursday about the closing of a beloved shop in Paris misstated the store’s name. As the article (and a sign in the image) correctly noted, the shop is Au Marché du Marais, not Au Marché du Paris.
match_headline: Review: Shrinking Lives at a Big Box Store in ‘Paris’

text: An article on Tuesday about testimony at Guantánamo Bay regarding the C.I.A.’s use of torture misstated the scheduled start date for the trial of the accused plotters of the Sept. 11 attacks. It is Jan. 11, 2021, not Jan. 22.
match_headline: Psychologist Who Waterboarded for C.I.A. to Testify at Guantánamo

text: An article on Friday about the conditions that led to Fairway’s bankruptcy filing described imprecisely the relationship between Village Super Market and ShopRite. Village Super Market operates some ShopRite locations, not all. It also misstated which company could end up buying fewer Fairway locations. It is Village Super Market, not ShopRite. The article also misstated the locations of Fairway’s Manhattan stores. The locations include its first store on Broadway on the Upper West Side, and also those in Chelsea, Harlem, Kips Bay and the Upper East Side. There is not a second location on the Upper West Side.
match_headline: Fairway Is So Crowded! How Can It Be in Bankruptcy?

text: An article on Jan. 17 about a Grolier Club exhibition that explores the history of working women misstated the date of an artwork by Martha Maxwell. The stereograph “Mrs. Maxwell and Her Pets” was from around 1879, not 1876. The article also misidentified one of the animals seen in a stereographic image of Mrs. Maxwell. It is a pronghorn, not a deer.
match_headline: The Overlooked History of Women at Work

text: An article on Page 16 about “Before Sunrise” misstates the film’s box office take. It made about $5.9 million domestically, not worldwide. It took in an additional $17.2 million internationally.
match_headline: ‘Before Sunrise’: The Making of an Indie Classic

text: An article on Jan. 12 about Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, as part of the 52 Places to Go in 2020 special issue, misstated the location of Aksum, the city which, according to Ethiopian tradition, was the home of the Queen of Sheba. Aksum is in northern Ethiopia, hundreds of miles from Addis Ababa; it is not within Addis Ababa.
match_headline: For Prince Harry, No Special Treatment in Canada

text: Because of an editing error, the Living In article last Sunday, about Hyde Park, N.Y., omitted the given name and misstated the courtesy title in the attribution for a quotation about the town’s location. The speaker was Aileen Rohr, the town supervisor.
match_headline: Hyde Park, N.Y.: A Gilded Age Getaway With a Friendly Vibe

text: A picture caption with the Shopping Guide article last Sunday, about coasters, was duplicated and misidentified a set of coasters with animal images on them. It was the Party Animals Needlepoint Coaster Set, made by Smathers & Branson, not the Table Tiles set by Bower.
match_headline: Shopping for Coasters

text: An article on Dec. 22 about home funerals referred incorrectly to a result of a lawsuit brought by Rabbi Daniel Wasserman against the Pennsylvania board of funeral directors. The board agreed that clergy members may conduct “religious” burial services without a funeral director. The Funeral Director Law was not amended.
match_headline: The Movement to Bring Death Closer

text: A review on Dec. 29 about the picture book “While Grandpa Naps” misspelled the given name of its illustrator. She is Junghwa Park, not Jungwa.
match_headline: Helping Children Understand Death

text: An article on Monday about the purchase of newspapers by hedge funds misstated the name of the institution where Ann Marie Lipinski is the curator. It is the Nieman Foundation for Journalism at Harvard University, not the Nieman Center for Journalism.
match_headline: Worried Reporters Make a Plea: Please Buy Our Paper

text: An article on Friday about the rivalry between Connecticut and Tennessee’s women’s basketball teams described incorrectly the 1997 N.C.A.A. tournament game in which Tennessee beat Connecticut. It was in Iowa City, not Cincinnati, and the game was a regional final, not a national semifinal.
match_headline: UConn, Tennessee and the Gamesmanship of Auriemma and Summitt

text: An article on Sunday about Kobe Bryant’s legacy with the Los Angeles Lakers described incorrectly LeBron James’s team affiliation at the time of Mr. Bryant’s Oscar acceptance speech in March 2018. James was in his final season with the Cleveland Cavaliers; he was not “already a Laker.”
match_headline: For Decades, Kobe Bryant Defined the Lakers. He Shaped Their Future, Too.

text: An Editorial Observer on Sunday about the Supreme Court agreeing to hear two cases involving the voting obligations of members of the Electoral College said no Republican electors had joined the Democratic-led effort to keep Donald Trump from taking the White House in 2016. One elector, from Texas, did.
match_headline: Why Do We Have an Electoral College Again?

text: An obituary on Jan. 17 about Christopher Tolkien, the son of the writer J.R.R. Tolkien, using information from the Tolkien Society, misstated the day he died. It was Thursday, Jan. 16 — not Wednesday, Jan. 15.
match_headline: Christopher Tolkien, Keeper of His Father’s Legacy, Dies at 95

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the death of Kobe Bryant misspelled the surname of the chief medical examiner for Los Angeles County. He is Jonathan Lucas, not Luca.
match_headline: Kobe Bryant, Transformational Star of the N.B.A., Dies in Helicopter Crash

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about Michael R. Bloomberg’s ad campaign that criticizes President Trump referred incorrectly to Joe Torre’s position with the Yankees in 2008. He was the team’s former manager, not its manager.
match_headline: Bloomberg Is Taunting Trump, and Trump Is Taking the Bait

text: An article on Tuesday about California politicians who are playing pivotal roles in the impeachment proceedings misstated the length of Ken Starr’s time as dean of the Pepperdine University School of Law. It was six years, not two.
match_headline: In Impeachment Battle, California Stands on the Front Lines

text: An article on Saturday about protests in the United States misspelled the surname of a man who attended an anti-abortion march in Washington. He is Jim Rowland, not Roland.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Broadway producer Margo Lion omitted the name of a writer of the Broadway musical “Hairspray,” of which she was the lead producer. The show’s book was written by Mark O’Donnell and Thomas Meehan, not just by Mr. O’Donnell.

text: An article last Wednesday about the chef Iliana Regan misidentified the fruit she foraged in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. They were crab apples, not cranberries.

text: An article on Saturday about sewage contracts between U.S. cities and the Environmental Protection Agency misstated the status of one city’s consent decree. Louisville, Ky., is not known to have renegotiated its decree with the Environmental Protection Agency.

text: An article on Tuesday about the helicopter crash that killed Kobe Bryant and eight others misspelled the surname of a pastor who heard the impact while leading Sunday school. He is Bob Bjerkaas, not Bjerkas.

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about dogs on the campaign trail referred incorrectly to Bailey, Senator Elizabeth Warren’s golden retriever. Bailey is male.

text: An article on Wednesday about Goldman Sachs’s “investment day” misstated the amount of money the investment bank planned to commit to environmental and other initiatives. The commitment was for $750 billion, not $750 million.

text: An article on Tuesday about the sexual assault case against Kobe Bryant in 2003 described incorrectly the Lakers’ playoff status going into the 2003-4 season. The team was chasing its fourth title in five years, not a fourth straight championship.

text: An article on Thursday about a dispute between protesters in India and the Modi government over the legacy of Mohandas K. Gandhi misidentified the Bharatiya Janata Party lawmaker who edited a pamphlet about the citizenship law. He is Prabhat Jha, not Shiv Shakti Bakshi.

text: An article on Thursday about newly released images of the sun’s surface captured by the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope in Hawaii misstated the temperature of the sun’s surface. It is about 5,000 degrees Celsius, not Fahrenheit.
match_headline: These Images Show the Sun’s Surface in Greater Detail Than Ever Before

text: An article on Wednesday about the testimony of James E. Mitchell, a former C.I.A. contract psychologist, misidentified two sons of Khalid Shaikh Mohammed. His lawyers said they are Hamza, who was 9 when seized by Pakistani security forces in 2002, and Zaid, 7 at the time. text: An article on Thursday about an event in a black community in Cleveland that promoted Trump administration policies and gave cash prizes to attendees misidentified the news outlet that first reported about the event. It was Cleveland.com, not Politico.
match_headline: Trump Ally Held Event Handing Out Cash in a Black Community

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about how the Republican Party attracted white blue-collar voters misstated part of a remark by Dean Lacy, a political scientist at Dartmouth College. He said many blue-collar voters felt they had been left without an economic champion; he did not say white college-educated voters felt that way. text: An article on Thursday about Kryptos, a courtyard sculpture at C.I.A. headquarters, misstated the decryption at the end of Passage Two. The decryption of those letters is “XLAYERTWO,” not “LEVELTWO.”

text: An article on Friday about proposed tweaks to the Volcker Rule misstated the name of a trade group. It is the Independent Community Bankers of America, not the Independent Community Bankers Association.

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 7 misspelled the surname of a dancer. He is Max Westwell, not Westwall. It also misstated his age. He is 34, not 33.
match_headline: Boys Will Be Swans: ‘What Is That Show, and How Do I Do It?’

text: An article on Page 17 about the final season of “Homeland” misspelled the given name of an actor in the series. He is Damian Lewis, not Damien.

text: An article last Sunday about the Benin Bronzes misstated the weight of a sculpture of a leopard’s head. It was 20 pounds, not 40 pounds.
match_headline: This Art Was Looted 123 Years Ago. Will It Ever Be Returned?

text: A picture caption with an article on Jan. 19 about Pina Bausch’s dance-theater production “Bluebeard” misidentified the dancer with Jan Minarik. She is Marion Cito, not Ulli Weiss. (Ulli Weiss took the picture.)
match_headline: When Pina Bausch Made Tanz Into Tanztheater

text: An article last Sunday about the actor David Corenswet misspelled the name of an airplane manufacturer. It was Cessna, not Cesna.

text: Because of an editing error, the Hunt article last Sunday described incorrectly the apartment seeker’s bedroom. The room is not windowless; there are two windows that face the front of the apartment.

An article on Jan. 12 about Mohammed bin Zayed, the ruler of the United Arab Emirates, misidentified the descendant of Richard Wagner who appears in a photograph with Zaki Nusseibeh. She is Katharina Wagner, not Cosima Wagner.
match_headline: Mohammed bin Zayed’s Dark Vision of the Middle East’s Future

text: An article last Sunday about the Caneel Bay Resort in the United States Virgin Islands misstated the price of a golf-cart ride to Honeymoon Beach. A round-trip fare is $10, not $20. The article also referred imprecisely to the room rate at the resort during the holidays. text: Because of an editing error, a review last Sunday about the novel “Little Gods,” by Meng Jin, misstated the reviewer’s estimation of the protagonist, a woman named Su Lan. The review should have said that Su Lan is a “compellingly complex” character, not that she is “as complex a protagonist as any I can recall.”
match_headline: For a Successful Chinese Woman, Can Motherhood Be Her Undoing?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the helicopter crash that killed NBA star Kobe Bryant and eight others described incorrectly the minimum visibility requirements for flight under federal visual flight rules. They require a helicopter flying at low altitude in daylight to have at least a half-mile of visibility and visual reference to the ground, not at least three miles of visibility and a cloud ceiling no lower than 1,000 feet above the ground.
match_headline: Helicopter in Kobe Bryant Crash Wasn’t Legal to Fly in Poor Visibility

text: An article on Saturday about Senator Lamar Alexander’s decision to vote against having witnesses at President Trump’s impeachment trial misstated the middle initial of former Senator Howard Baker of Tennessee. He is Howard H. Baker Jr., not Howard R. Baker Jr.
match_headline: Alexander Says Convicting Trump Would ‘Pour Gasoline on Cultural Fires’

text: An article on Saturday about Secretary of State Mike Pompeo’s visit with President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv misspelled the surname of the director of the New Europe Center in Kyiv, Ukraine. She is Alyona Getmanchuk, not Gemantchuk.
match_headline: Amid Trump’s Trial, Pompeo Visited Ukraine. Here’s How It Went.

text: An article on Saturday about Latino culture and Super Bowl LIV misstated the surname of the owner of Martha of Miami. She is Martha Valdes, not Ochoa.
match_headline: A Super Bowl With a Latino Flair in Miami

text: An article on Tuesday about the fraught relationship between Gov. Andrew Cuomo and Andy Byford misstated Mr. Byford’s age. He is 54, not 55.
match_headline: How a Clash of Egos Became Bigger Than Fixing the Subway

text: An article on Sunday about the Chinese government’s handling of the coronavirus outbreak misstated the reason that a market tied to the outbreak closed. It was for an environmental and hygienic cleanup, not for renovations.
match_headline: As New Coronavirus Spread, China’s Old Habits Delayed Fight

text: An article last Wednesday about the Trump administration’s Middle East peace plan referred incorrectly to proposed adjustments to Israeli boundaries. The plan proposes significant changes to Israel’s pre-1967 borders; the borders in question were not drawn in 1967.
match_headline: Trump Releases Mideast Peace Plan That Strongly Favors Israel

text: An article on Saturday referred incorrectly to the role that the Department of Homeland Security played in the review of an app used in the Iowa caucuses. Homeland Security officials did an exercise for Iowa officials to run through their caucus processes, but they did not vet the app.
match_headline: Iowa Will Be the First Test Case for 2020 Election Security

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about people who confuse Kansas City, Kan., and Kansas City, Mo., exhibited similar confusion. Both pictures of fans cheering the Kansas City Chiefs were from Kansas City, Mo.; the picture of fans in front of a light-filled background was not in Kansas City, Kan. (We were just testing you.)
match_headline: Trump Mistakenly Congratulates Kansas City, Kan., on Its Super Bowl Win

text: An article on Friday about the widespread acceptance of the Super Bowl despite controversies surrounding football misstated the role of the former player Aaron Hernandez in the killing of two men in 2012. While he was charged in 2014 with the shooting deaths of the men, he was found not guilty of those charges.
match_headline: The Super Bowl Is Problematic. Why Can’t We Look Away?

text: An article on Tuesday about the new Taylor Swift documentary misidentified the film that Lana Wilson made directly before “Miss Americana.” It was “The Departure” — not “After Tiller,” which was her first film.
match_headline: The Newly Self-Aware Taylor Swift

text: An article last Wednesday about pop-up dinners described incorrectly the group that Rachel Branson organized to attend a dinner by the chef Omar Tate. It was a group of friends, not her mother and her mother’s friends. The article also rendered incorrectly a quotation by Ms. Branson. She said, “I’m glad we’re here, because there aren’t many other black people here,” not “any other black people here.”
ref_headline: I’m glad we’re here, because there aren’t many other black people here,
match_headline: Pop-Up Dinners That Share a Culture, Course by Course

text: An article on Wednesday about a debate over a new bail law described incorrectly the recorded number of serious crimes in New York City in January 2020 and January 2019 by reversing the figures. The police recorded a total of 8,437 serious crimes in January 2020, compared to 7,215 in January 2019.
match_headline: Spike in Crime Inflames Debate Over Bail Law in New York

text: An article on Tuesday about subversive politics in Super Bowl XIV misstated the location of the Super Bowl in 2016. It was in Santa Clara, Calif., not in New Orleans.
match_headline: At the Super Bowl, the Political Was Debatable

text: An obituary on Jan. 30 about the skier Rhona Wurtele referred incorrectly to Westmount, where she and her identical twin sister and fellow skier, Rhoda, grew up. It is a neighborhood of Montreal; it is not a “community outside Montreal.”
match_headline: Rhona Wurtele, One of Canada’s ‘Flying Twins’ Ski Champions, Dies at 97

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Hall of Fame defensive back Willie Wood misstated his middle name. It was Vernell, not Verrell.
match_headline: Willie Wood, Star Defensive Back With the Green Bay Packers, Dies at 83

text: An article on Thursday about the effect of the coronavirus on carmakers’ supply chains in China described incorrectly the distribution of the Volvo XC60 sport utility vehicle. While the car is still made in China, it is no longer available for export to the United States.
match_headline: Virus Exposes Cracks in Carmakers’ Chinese Supply Chains

text: An article on Thursday about the return of the XFL misspelled the name of an XFL player. He is Matt McGloin, not Matt McGlouin.
match_headline: This Is Not Your Crazy Uncle’s XFL

text: An obituary on Thursday about the actor Kirk Douglas misstated the branch of the military to which the colonel he played in the movie “Seven Days in May” belonged. It was the Marines, not the Air Force.
match_headline: Kirk Douglas, a Star of Hollywood’s Golden Age, Dies at 103

text: An article on Monday about a teenager who jumped to his death from the Vessel at Hudson Yards misidentified the publication where Audrey Wachs formerly worked. She was the associate editor of The Architect’s Newspaper, not of ArchDaily.
match_headline: Suicide at Hudson Yards Vessel: Teenager Jumps Over Railing

text: An obituary on Jan. 30 about the disc jockey Harry Harrison misstated the year he joined the New York radio station WMCA. It was 1959, not 1958. It also referred incorrectly to the disc jockeys Dan Daniel and Jack Spector. They were not yet with WMCA when Mr. Harrison was hired; they both joined the station in 1961. And it incorrectly included Scott Muni on a list of disc jockeys who were at WABC when Mr. Harrison moved to that station in 1968; he had left in 1965. In addition, the obituary misidentified the song “May You Always,” which Mr. Harrison performed every holiday season. It was a different song from the one of the same name that was a hit for the McGuire Sisters.
match_headline: Harry Harrison, ‘Good Guy’ Radio D.J., Is Dead at 89

text: An article last Sunday about the Everglades in Florida misspelled the name of a river that was straightened by the Army Corps of Engineers. It is the Kissimmee River, not Kissimee.
match_headline: Tears for the Magnificent and Shrinking Everglades, a ‘River of Grass’

text: An article on Jan. 26 about skiing and presidential campaigning in New Hampshire this time of year included an erroneous distinction for Mount Washington. It is the highest mountain in the Northeastern United States, not in the East; that is Mount Mitchell, in North Carolina. The article also misstated the name of a popular skiing location in New Hampshire. It is Tuckerman Ravine, not Tuckerman’s.
match_headline: It’s Primary Season in New Hampshire. Time to Go Skiing!

text: An article on Jan. 12 about La Paz, Mexico, as part of the 52 Places to Go in 2020 special issue, misstated the year in which the city passed a ban on single-use plastic. It was 2018, not 2019.
match_headline: And the Winners Are, Part 2: The ‘Alphabetrivia’ Contest

text: An article on Saturday about the Trump Administration’s decision to relax Obama-era restrictions on the U.S. military’s use of anti-personnel land mines, currently banned by 160 countries, misidentified the former country in which Quang Tri Province was located. It was South Vietnam, not North Vietnam.
match_headline: 160 Nations Ban These Weapons. The U.S. Now Embraces Them.

text: An article on Sunday about precautions travelers can take to avoid disease misattributed a recommendation about the use of hand sanitizers. It was Dr. Philip M. Tierno who said to make sure sanitizer dries, not Dr. Vicki Hertzberg.

An article on Monday about the Women Riders World Relay attributed an erroneous distinction to the Van Buren sisters and their 1916 motorcycle trip across the United States. They were among the first women to make such a trip, not the first.
match_headline: 3,500 Women, 6 Continents and a Year of Riding High

text: An article on Sunday about the length of the film “The Irishman” and an average baseball game misstated the average number of hits in a major league game in 2019. It was 17.3, not 8.65.
match_headline: Enjoy ‘The Irishman’? Baseball Offers Much of the Same, 162 Times a Year

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the intense competition on the United States women’s national soccer team for Olympic roster spots, using information from Getty Images, misidentified a player who was celebrating a goal by Lindsey Horan. She is Tobin Heath, not Carli Lloyd.
match_headline: U.S. Women’s Team Qualifies for Olympic Soccer Tournament

text: A review on Feb. 4 about Nordic television misidentified an actor who plays a detective in “All the Sins.” He is Johannes Holopainen, not Matti Ristinen.
match_headline: Here’s the Latest in Nordic TV, Noir and Otherwise

text: An obituary on Feb. 4 about the literary critic George Steiner misstated the year his “My Unwritten Books” was published. It was 2008, not 2009. It also misstated his daughter’s surname. She is Deborah Tarn Steiner, not Deborah Tarn. And it referred imprecisely to his tenure at the University of Geneva. He was a professor there from 1974 to 1994.
match_headline: George Steiner, Prodigious Literary Critic, Dies at 90

text: An article on Tuesday about racial identity in Puerto Rico misstated the location of Isla Verde, a popular tourist area in Puerto Rico. It is near San Juan, not in San Juan.
match_headline: Why Some Black Puerto Ricans Choose ‘White’ on the Census

text: An article on Monday about the intense competition on the United States women’s national soccer team for Olympic roster spots misidentified one of the United States goal scorers in the game. In addition to Megan Rapinoe and Lindsey Horan, Lynn Williams — not Christen Press — scored.
match_headline: ‘It’s Cutthroat’: U.S. Women Beat Canada in Soccer, With Fight Ahead

text: An obituary on Sunday about the actor Orson Bean misidentified the Massachusetts high school from which he graduated in 1946. It was Cambridge High and Latin School — not Cambridge Rindge and Latin School, which was created by a merger of that school and the Rindge Technical School in 1977.
match_headline: Orson Bean, Free-Spirited Actor of Stage and Screen, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the neuroscientist Bruce S. McEwen overstated the findings by Dr. McEwen and his research team in the 1960s on the effects of long-term stress on the brain. While his studies demonstrated, as the obituary correctly stated, that toxic stress atrophied neurons near the hippocampus, the brain’s memory and learning center, his research did not demonstrate that stress expanded neurons near the amygdala, the area of the brain that promotes vigilance toward threats; that discovery was made by others, including former collaborators with Dr. McEwen, although his laid the foundation for it.
match_headline: Bruce McEwen, 81, Is Dead; Found Stress Can Alter the Brain

text: An obituary on Sunday about Greta Beer, whose search for her father’s Swiss bank account helped force banks in Switzerland to pay compensation to Holocaust victims and their heirs, misstated the name of the city in Romania where she was born. It is Cernauti, not Cermauti.
