match_headline: Greta Beer, Who Fought Swiss Banks for Family Assets, Dies at 98

text: An editorial on Monday about the Chinese military theft of personal information from the credit bureau Equifax misstated the developer of Apache Struts software. Apache Struts is an open source project of the Apache Struts Foundation, not a product of the software giant Adobe.
match_headline: Chinese Hacking Is Alarming. So Are Data Brokers.

text: An article on Wednesday about the resignation of four prosecutors following the Justice Department’s intervention in the case against Roger J. Stone Jr. misstated the action that a prosecutor took on a memo supporting probation for Michael T. Flynn. Brandon L. Van Grack signed the memo; it is not the case that he did not sign it.
match_headline: Prosecutors Quit Roger Stone Case After Justice Dept. Intervenes on Sentencing

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Joseph Shabalala, the founder of the South African choral group Ladysmith Black Mambazo, referred incorrectly to the group’s current tour. It is continuing; it was not canceled when the group learned that Mr. Shabalala, who retired in 2014, had died.
match_headline: Joseph Shabalala, Ladysmith Black Mambazo Founder, Dies at 78

text: An article on Wednesday about Lawrence V. Ray, who is charged with sex trafficking and abusing students at Sarah Lawrence College, misspelled the name of a dormitory where Mr. Ray had installed himself. It is Slonim, not Slomin.
match_headline: Sarah Lawrence Parent Accused of Sex Trafficking and Abusing Students

text: An article on Wednesday about recent commercial real estate transactions misidentified the landlord of the building at 460 Bergen Street in Brooklyn. It is Michael Pintchik, not TerraCRG.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Thursday about James Murdoch’s interest in sustainable investments misidentified Gary Knell as the president of the National Geographic Society. Mr. Knell was president when the society created a joint venture with 21st Century Fox, but he is no longer in the role.
match_headline: James Murdoch Plans Big Bets on Sustainable Businesses

text: An article on Friday about Attorney General William P. Barr’s rebuke of President Trump’s attacks on the Justice Department misstated who informed Mr. Trump of what Mr. Barr planned to say in an ABC News interview. The attorney general’s office, not Mr. Barr himself, sent word to a White House official.
match_headline: Barr Says Attacks From Trump Make Work ‘Impossible’

text: An article on Tuesday about the pangolin as a possible animal source of the coronavirus misspelled the surname of a scientist. He is Benjamin Neuman, not Neumann.
match_headline: Pangolins Are Suspected as a Potential Coronavirus Host

text: An article on Wednesday about Pakistani students told to stay in Wuhan amid the coronavirus outbreak misstated the status of Nepalis in the city. They were awaiting evacuation; they had not been evacuated.
match_headline: As Foreigners Flee China, Pakistan Tells Its Citizens to Stay

text: An article on Thursday about a Chinese student in South Korea facing prejudice because of coronavirus fears misstated the name of the disease caused by the virus. It is COVID-19, not CORVID-19.
match_headline: For a Chinese Traveler, Even Paradise Comes With Prejudice

text: An article on Friday about an American citizen living with his mother in a locked down Chinese town misspelled the name of the place. It is Zhicheng, not Zhichang. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: An American in a Locked Down Chinese Town: ‘Everyone Here Is So Bored’

text: An article on Page 4 about whether to stick with TV shows with mediocre pilots describes incorrectly the online availability of the series “Murder, She Wrote.” The first five seasons were streaming on Amazon Prime Video at the time of publication; it was not unavailable on all three so-called Big 3 streamers.
match_headline: The Pilot Is Mediocre. Do You Stick With It? Sometimes.

text: An article on Page 12 about a sequel to the film “To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before” misidentifies Jenny Han’s debut novel. It is “Shug,” not “To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before.” The article also misstates the source of the yogurt brand used in the film. It is from Japan, not Korea.
ref_headline: To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before
match_headline: ‘To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before’ … and to Fans Hungry for More

text: An article on Page 16 about the actress Zoë Kravitz misidentifies the song she sang as a child. It was “The Boy Is Mine” by Brandy and Monica, not “The Girl Is Mine.”
match_headline: Sooner or Later, Zoë Kravitz Was Going to Be a Star

text: An article on Page 54 about the ultrarunner Jim Walmsley misspells the name of the Athenian herald said to have run the original marathon. It is Philippides, not Phillipedes. The article also omits one of the men who qualified for the Olympic team trials in the marathon with times below 2 hours and 10 minutes. In addition to Scott Fauber, Galen Rupp and Leonard Korir, Jared Ward qualified with a time of 2:09:25 at the 2019 Boston Marathon.
match_headline: Can the King of Ultrarunning Conquer a Race as Short as the Marathon?

text: An article last Sunday about tourism in Hawaii misstated the cost of groceries in the state. They cost 60 percent more than the national average, not more than 50 percent of the national average.
match_headline: Hawaii Is a Paradise, but Whose?

text: An article on Feb. 2 about a coffee-tasting trip to Costa Rica referred incorrectly to chicharrón. It is fried pork belly or pork rinds, not a form of sausage.
match_headline: Savoring Costa Rica, Sip By Sip

text: An article on Jan. 26 about the new Broadway production of “West Side Story” misstates a lyric to “Cool.” The lyric is “get cool, boy,” not “stay cool, boy.”
match_headline: How ‘West Side Story’ Was Reborn

text: An article on Saturday about Iranian rebels living in Albania misspelled in two instances the name of a woman who is a member of the Mujahedeen Khalq group. As the article correctly noted elsewhere, she is Somayeh Mohammadi, not Mohammedi. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Highly Secretive Iranian Rebels Are Holed Up in Albania. They Gave Us a Tour.

text: An article on Saturday about Yigit Aksakoglu, a child development specialist accused of trying to overthrow the Turkish government, described incorrectly the place where Mr. Aksakoglu was born. It is a city, not a small village.
match_headline: He Observed a Protest. Now He Faces a Possible Life Sentence.

text: An article on Friday about the possibility that some states will broaden parole misstated Gov. Ralph Northam’s position on a related bill. He has said he would sign a measure that would grant parole eligibility to prisoners who are older than 50.
match_headline: ‘It Didn’t Work:’ States That Ended Parole for Violent Crimes Are Thinking Again

text: An article on Saturday about the conviction of Michael Avenatti for extortion against Nike misstated the length of prison time that Mr. Avenatti could face in the Nike extortion case. It is 42 years, not up to 40 years.
match_headline: Michael Avenatti Is Convicted in Nike Extortion Trial

text: An article on Tuesday about a 6-year-old girl who spent 48 hours in a mental health center referred incorrectly to a representative for Duval County Public Schools. The official, Tracy A. Pierce, is a man.
match_headline: 6-Year-Old Held in Mental Health Center for 2 Days Without Mother’s Consent

text: An article on Sunday about junior varsity basketball teams misidentified the junior varsity team Roy Williams once coached. It was at North Carolina, not Kansas.
match_headline: Did You Know There Are College Junior Varsity Basketball Teams? North Carolina Has One

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s decision to grant clemency to several white-collar criminals misstated the year in which Edward J. DeBartolo Jr. was elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. It was 2016, not 2014.
match_headline: Trump Grants Clemency to Blagojevich, Milken and Kerik

text: An article on Tuesday about an application for clemency by the Air Force veteran Reality Winner referred incorrectly to the process. Clemency can include a sentence commutation or a pardon. It is not different from a pardon.
match_headline: Reality Winner, Imprisoned for Leaking Russian Hacking Report, Seeks Clemency

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Feb. 9 about the biochemist Stanley Cohen misspelled the surnames of three of his fellow Nobel laureates. They are Gerd Binnig, not Bennig; Heinrich Rohrer, not Rohr; and Dudley R. Herschbach, not Hersbach.
match_headline: Stanley Cohen, Nobelist, Dies at 97; Made Breakthrough on Cell Growth

text: A map with an article on Sunday about the philanthropic contributions of Michael R. Bloomberg misidentified the location of one recipient, EngenderHealth. It is based in Washington, D.C., not Vermont.
match_headline: Moderates Search for a Savior

text: An article on Thursday about an increase in airline flight delays misstated part of the reason given by the trade group Airlines for America for tarmac delays last year. It said airport maintenance and construction work, not poor airport maintenance, was a factor.
match_headline: Airline Flight Delays Got Worse in 2019. Here’s a Scorecard.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the author Charles Portis referred incorrectly to Indian Territory, where his novel “True Grit” was set. It was defined as “all of that part of the United States west of the Mississippi, and not within the states of Missouri and Louisiana, or the territory of Arkansas”; no part of it was in Arkansas. The obituary also mistakenly included one name on a list of Mr. Portis’s former colleagues at The New York Herald Tribune. Nora Ephron did not work there.
match_headline: Charles Portis, Elusive Author of ‘True Grit,’ Dies at 86

text: An article on Thursday about Pete Buttigieg’s struggle to attract voters of color described incorrectly the votes cast in the 2016 Democratic caucuses in Elko County. There were 88 county delegates selected in the county, not 88 total votes recorded.
match_headline: Pete Buttigieg Hoped to Win Over Voters of Color. It Still Hasn’t Happened.

text: An article on Friday about the planned sale of Donald Marron’s art collection misstated the terms of Mr. Marron’s will. The will stated that Mr. Marron’s collection could be sold at a “public or private sale,” not that it should be sold at Sotheby’s or Christie’s auction houses.
match_headline: Donald Marron’s Art Collection to Be Sold Privately

text: An article on Friday about the artist Brian Donnelly, known as KAWS, misspelled the surname of an artist admired by Mr. Donnelly. She is Helen Rae, not Helen Ray.
match_headline: KAWS Looks to the Fringes for Inspiration

text: An article on Friday about a new children’s book by Dan Brown misstated part of the name of a classical musical work. It is “The Carnival of the Animals,” not “The Carnival and the Animals.”
match_headline: Dan Brown … Children’s Book Author?

text: An article on Friday about Caroline Baumann’s first public remarks after resigning as director of the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum misstated the timing of a nonprofit’s meetings held at the museum. The LongHouse Reserve held a board meeting at the museum several months before Ms. Baumann married, and it held another board meeting two months after the wedding; it did not hold two meetings in the months after the wedding.
match_headline: Ousted Cooper Hewitt Director Calls Investigation a ‘Sham’

text: An article last Sunday about Jordan Casteel and her show at the New Museum misstated the profession of Jiréh Breon Holder, who posed for Ms. Casteel. He is a writer and playwright, not an actor.
match_headline: Jordan Casteel Won’t Let You Look Away

text: An article last Sunday about unique lodging options misstated the location of the Anantara Golden Triangle Elephant Camp & Resort. It is in Chiang Rai, Thailand, not Bangkok.
match_headline: Treehouses, Glass Igloos and Other Out-of-This-World Spots to Lay Your Head

text: An article on Saturday about the direction of the National Security Council under Robert O’Brien, President Trump’s national security adviser, misspelled the surname of a former director of national intelligence. He is Dan Coats, not Coates.
match_headline: Under O’Brien, N.S.C. Carries Out Trump’s Policy, but Doesn’t Develop It

text: An article on Monday about tensions between the Justice Department and the U.S. attorney’s office in Washington attributed an erroneous distinction to the U.S. attorney’s office. The office has handled many high-profile cases such as the conviction of the main suspect in the 2012 Benghazi, Libya, attacks, but it did not handle the corruption scandal involving the lobbyist Jack Abramoff.
match_headline: D.C. Prosecutors’ Tensions With Justice Dept. Began Long Before Stone Sentencing

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Andy Byford’s last day as subway chief misstated the location of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s headquarters. It is in Manhattan, not Brooklyn.
match_headline: Who’s Your ‘Train Daddy’? On Byford’s Last Day, N.Y. Leaves No Doubt

text: An article on Wednesday about Michael R. Milken’s legacy referred imprecisely to the timing of Mr. Milken’s release. He left federal prison in January 1993, a month before he said his cancer was detected. He was released from federal custody in March of that year.
match_headline: Pardon Closes the Book on Michael Milken’s Case but Can’t Rewrite It

text: An article on Monday about a pullback in tech start-up investments misstated the surname of the chief executive officer of the cannabis producer Tilray. He is Brendan Kennedy, not Kenney.
match_headline: As the Start-Up Boom Deflates, Tech Is Humbled

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the hockey player Alex Ovechkin’s 700th career goal misstated the timing of the goal in Saturday’s game. It came about five minutes into — not remaining in — the third period.
match_headline: Alex Ovechkin Scores Goal No. 700 in a Loss to the Devils

text: An article on Sunday about the high cost of Canadian youth hockey in Canada included an extraneous word in a quotation by Ryan Compton. It should have read, “When you see that your child is playing with a peer group and you hear about all the other things they are doing on the side, it’s easy to feel, ‘If I don’t do the same, my child is not going to continue in the next level’” — he did not say, in part, “and you don’t hear about all the other things.”
ref_headline: and you don’t hear about all the other things.
match_headline: In Canada, the Cost of Youth Hockey Benches the Next Generation

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about an all-star team of female racecar drivers misstated an accomplishment by Simona De Silvestro. She has a podium finish in the IndyCar series, not a win. It also misstated, because of an editing error, the year the W Series began racing. It was last year, not this year.
match_headline: Behind the Wheel, Behind the Eight Ball

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the exhibitions that Chirlane McCray has spearheaded at Gracie Mansion during her husband’s tenure as mayor of New York City misstated the name of an artwork by Devra Freelander. It is “Late Capitalist Relic,” not “Late Capitalistic Relic.”
match_headline: With Final Gracie Mansion Show, First Lady Aims to Secure Arts Legacy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a claim by Eyal Weizman that the U.S. blocked his entry into the country described inaccurately the action Mr. Weizman said was taken by U.S. officials. Mr. Weizman, the director of the investigative group Forensic Architecture, was not denied a visa; his right to travel under a visa-waiver program was revoked.
match_headline: Forensic Architecture Founder Says United States Prevented His Visit

text: An obituary on Feb. 16 about the Rev. George V. Coyne, the longtime director of the Vatican Observatory, misstated his middle initial. It is V, not C. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, his middle name was Vincent. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The obituary also misstated the name of the city in Maryland where Loyola High School, which Father Coyne attended, is located. It is Towson, not Blakefield. (The school is now known as Loyola Blakefield, but there is no Blakefield, Md.)
match_headline: George Coyne, 87, Vatican Astronomer and Galileo Defender, Dies

text: An article on Tuesday about the spread of the coronavirus in Iran misstated the first name of a health ministry adviser who disputed claims of a high number of virus-related deaths in Qom. He is Iraj Harirchi, not Ahmad Harirchi.
match_headline: ‘Recipe for a Massive Viral Outbreak’: Iran Emerges as a Worldwide Threat

text: An article on Tuesday about the possibility that the Trump administration will block congestion pricing in New York misstated the amount the Metropolitan Transportation Authority spent on a contract related to the implementation of congestion pricing. The contract was for $507 million, not $570 million.
match_headline: Could the Trump Administration Block Congestion Pricing in New York?

text: An article on Tuesday about the debut of The Markup, a website devoted to reporting on technology, misstated the position previously held by The Markup’s new president, Nabiha Syed. Ms. Syed was BuzzFeed’s associate general counsel, not general counsel.
match_headline: After Long Wait, The Markup Is Ready to ‘Show Our Work’

text: An article on Tuesday about the debate surrounding the necessity of prostate cancer screenings referred incorrectly to a study author at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. He is Dr. James Eastham, not Eastman.
match_headline: Debating the Value of PSA Prostate Screening

text: An article last Wednesday about the British chefs Margot and Fergus Henderson misstated the year that the restaurant Black Axe Mangal opened. It was 2015, not 2019.
match_headline: The Culinary Couple Who Built a British Empire

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about President Trump’s demand that two Supreme Court justices recuse themselves from cases that involve him described incorrectly a judge whom Mr. Trump called “an Obama judge.” He is a federal judge, not a Supreme Court justice.
match_headline: Trump, in India, Demands 2 Liberal Justices Recuse Themselves From His Cases

text: An article on Tuesday about a group working to influence the Trump administration on personnel decisions referred incorrectly to an individual contacted for comment. The person was a former employee of the Heritage Foundation, not a current employee.
match_headline: Among Those Pressing Trump to Weed Out Disloyalty: Clarence Thomas’s Wife

text: An article on Wednesday about a surveillance system used by the National Security Agency misidentified which 2016 Ohio machete attack investigation was cited in the report as having made use of the Freedom Act phone logs system. It referred to a February 2016 attack at a restaurant, not a November 2016 attack at Ohio State University.
match_headline: N.S.A. Phone Program Cost $100 Million, but Produced Only Two Unique Leads

text: An article on Wednesday about the conditions Harvey Weinstein could face in prison misstated which medical facility at Rikers Island has private cells with features like showers. It is the West Facility, not the North Infirmary Command.
match_headline: Inmate No. 3102000153: What Awaits Harvey Weinstein Behind Bars

text: A headline with the Wheels column on Friday, about road trips in foreign countries, misstated the age of a vehicle driven from London to Singapore. The 1954 Land Rover would have been about 62 years old, not 48, during the 2015-2016 trip. A picture caption with the article misstated the given name of the adventurer who took the trip. He is Ray Hyland, not Roy.
match_headline: London to Singapore in a Tiny Truck, and Other Road Trip Adventures

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the artist Jack Youngerman misstated the given name of the director of the film “Last Year in Marienbad,” whose cast included Mr. Youngerman’s ex-wife, Delphine Seyrig. He was Alain Resnais, not Louis.
match_headline: Jack Youngerman, Distinctively Abstract Artist, Dies at 93

text: An obituary on Monday about the restaurateur and lifestyle entrepreneur B. Smith misstated the surname of her first husband, who died in 2018. He was Don Anderson, not Henderson.
match_headline: B. Smith, Model Turned Restaurateur and Lifestyle Guru, Dies at 70

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Mafia underboss John Franzese misstated the name of one of his surviving daughters. She is Maryanne Shinn, not Marianne Chin.
match_headline: John Franzese, Mafioso Who Consorted With Celebrities, Dies at 103

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Chilean lawyer José Zalaquett, who investigated human rights abuses during Augusto Pinochet’s regime, referred incorrectly to Chile’s return to democracy. It occurred in 1990, when Patricio Aylwin took office as president, not in 1981. Pinochet had established a constitutional framework that allowed for democracy in 1981, but he continued his autocratic rule throughout the ’80s.
match_headline: José Zalaquett, Leader in Chile’s Search for Truth, Dies at 77

text: An article on Monday about the architect Rem Koolhaas described incorrectly Zaha Hadid’s involvement in the Office for Metropolitan Architecture. She was an early member, but she was not a founder of the firm.
match_headline: Why Rem Koolhaas Brought a Tractor to the Guggenheim

text: An obituary on Saturday about the computer scientist Lawrence Tesler misstated his mother’s maiden name. She was Muriel (Krechmer) Tesler, not Krechman.
match_headline: Lawrence Tesler, Who Made Personal Computing Easier, Dies at 74

text: An article on Friday about a patient who exhibited symptoms associated with the coronavirus, but was not tested for days because she did not meet the strict federal criteria, misspelled the county in California where she lives. It is Solano, not Solana.
match_headline: Coronavirus Diagnosis in California Highlights Testing Flaws

text: An article on Friday about the stock market entering a correction misstated the number of coronavirus cases in Italy. It was 650, not 14.
match_headline: Coronavirus Fears Drive Stocks Down for 6th Day and Into Correction

text: An article on Friday about a proposal that would increase the fee to challenge a deportation order misstated the impact of the proposal on fees for green cards and naturalization. Fees for permanent residence permits, known as green cards, would increase by $990, to a total of $2,750, and the cost for naturalization of new citizens would increase by $445, to $1,170; it is not the case that a green card and naturalization would cost $990 and $445.
match_headline: Immigrants Could Face Nearly $1,000 Charge to Appeal Deportation Orders

text: An article on Thursday about Deontay Wilder’s entrance costume for his fight with Tyson Fury misstated the given name of Mr. Wilder’s opponent in a match last November. He is Luis Ortiz, not Victor.
match_headline: Deontay Wilder’s Costume Was Heavyweight Camp

text: An article on Page 18 about the play “Help” by Claudia Rankine describes incorrectly the production of “The White Card.” It was an American Repertory Theater production at ArtsEmerson; it was not at American Repertory Theater.
match_headline: Claudia Rankine Looks at White Privilege From 35,000 Feet

text: An article this weekend on Page 20 about medical examiners erroneously includes one location in a list of places where chief medical examiners have resigned in protest over intolerable caseloads and insufficient funding and resources. New Hampshire’s former chief medical examiner did not resign in protest; he retired.
match_headline: Piled Bodies, Overflowing Morgues: Inside America’s Autopsy Crisis

text: An article this weekend on Page 26 about originalism and textualism on the Supreme Court misstates an aspect of a dissent written by Justice Clarence Thomas in a Second Amendment case from 2015. It was not a solo dissent. (It was joined by Justice Antonin Scalia.)
match_headline: How Will Trump’s Supreme Court Remake America?

text: An obituary on Feb. 18 about the golfer Mickey Wright omitted a name from a list of golfers who have won four consecutive major events. In addition to Wright in 1961 and 1962 and Tiger Woods in 2000 and 2001, Bobby Jones achieved this feat in 1930.
match_headline: Mickey Wright, One of the Greatest Players in Women’s Golf, Dies at 85

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about a parrot’s escape in Midtown Manhattan misstated the surname of the author’s husband. He is Chris Reese, not Flitter.
match_headline: The Day Frankie Flew Away

text: An article last Sunday about Montreal’s Nordic spas misstated the name of a documentary being made about sweat-bath culture. It is “Perfect Sweat,” not “Sweet Sweat.”
match_headline: Napping Away Winter in Montreal’s Nordic Spas

text: An article on Saturday about the coronavirus and the Zuoling neighborhood of Wuhan, China, misattributed a quote by a local resident. It was Deng Zhi’an who said, “We’ve lost confidence. Nobody in the neighborhood took charge,” not Zhang Jin, another resident.
ref_headline: We’ve lost confidence. Nobody in the neighborhood took charge,
match_headline: In China’s War on the Coronavirus, a Community Is Besieged

text: An article on Monday about an Interior Department official who has pressed scientists to include misleading climate language in their work misstated the month when President Trump signed a memo relaxing regulations that have limited the flow of water to irrigate farms in California’s Central Valley. It was February, not March.
match_headline: A Trump Insider Embeds Climate Denial in Scientific Research

text: An article on Monday about a possible return to dangerous factory conditions in Bangladesh despite efforts to strengthen safety rules after the 2013 Rana Plaza disaster misstated the legal obligations for members of the Ready Made Garments Sustainability Council. The strictures will not be legally binding. It also misspelled the given name of the chief executive of Nirapon. He is Moushumi Khan, not Moushoumi Khan.
match_headline: After Factory Disaster, Bangladesh Made Big Safety Strides. Are the Bad Days Coming Back?

text: An article on Monday about the lessons Michael R. Bloomberg is learning during his presidential campaign misstated Mr. Bloomberg’s age. He is 78, not 77.
match_headline: Michael Bloomberg, a Billionaire Learning on the Job

text: An article on Monday about media consolidation and The Times’s dominance in the industry misstated Janice Min’s role at Us Weekly. She is a former Us Weekly editor, but she did not create it.
match_headline: Why the Success of The New York Times May Be Bad News for Journalism

text: An article on Saturday about right-wing pundits who claim the coronavirus is being politicized by Democrats to hurt President Trump misstated Dr. Nancy Messonnier’s title. She is the head of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, not the head of the Centers for Disease Control. (The center she heads is part of the CDC.)
match_headline: Right-Wing Media Says Virus Fears Were Whipped Up to Hurt Trump

text: An article on Thursday about the documentary “We Are the Dream” referred incorrectly to its development. It was the producer Diane Kolyer who proposed focusing on the Oakland Unified School District’s contest, not the executive producer Julie Anderson.
match_headline: In ‘We Are the Dream,’ Oakland Students Channel Dr. King

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts to increase testing for the coronavirus in the United States, relying on remarks by Dr. Stephen Hahn, the commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration, referred imprecisely to the availability of coronavirus testing in the United States. Dr. Hahn intended to say that the administration could have the capacity for approximately one million tests by the end of the week, not that one million tests could be administered by the end of the week. (The error was repeated in a separate article on Tuesday about missteps by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that left the potential for the virus’s spread.)
match_headline: Close to a Million Coronavirus Tests Could Be Ready in U.S. This Week

text: An article on Thursday about the Tohono O’odham Nation misstated the pronunciation of its name. It is To-HO-no Aw-aw-tham, not To-HO-no AW-tham.
match_headline: Tribal Nation Condemns ‘Desecration’ to Build Border Wall

text: An article on Sunday about leap days on Mars misstated the name of a mission to the planet. The Curiosity rover is part of the Mars Science Laboratory, not the Mars Exploration Rover project.
match_headline: Why Mars Needs Leap Days, Too

text: An obituary on Friday about the cartoonist Claire Bretécher, using information supplied by Ms. Bretécher’s publisher, referred incorrectly to her marital history. Her first husband, a photographer, is still alive. It is not the case that she was “widowed twice.”
match_headline: Claire Bretécher, Satirical French Cartoonist, Dies at 79

text: An obituary on Monday about Charles Friedgood, a doctor convicted of killing his wife, referred incorrectly to the medical school from which Dr. Friedgood graduated in 1946. At the time, it was part of Wayne University, not Wayne State University. The university did not add “State” to its name until 1956.
match_headline: Dr. Charles Friedgood, Paroled Wife Killer, Is Dead at 99

text: An obituary on Saturday about the technologist Freeman Dyson referred imprecisely to positrons in a description of a problem in theoretical physics that Dr. Dyson sought to solve. They are the antimatter equivalent only of electrons, not of both electrons and photons.
match_headline: Freeman Dyson, Math Genius Turned Technological Visionary, Dies at 96

text: An article on Wednesday about a Supreme Court case challenging the independence of the director of a government agency created as part of the Dodd-Frank Act misstated the agency’s name. It is the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, not the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau.
match_headline: Supreme Court Divided on Trump’s Power to Fire Head of Consumer Bureau

text: An article on Wednesday about an annual town meeting in Jericho, Vt., misstated the number of delegates Senator Bernie Sanders won in Vermont. It was 10, not 16. The article also misstated the age of Deborah Waterman, a town resident. She is 71, not 77.
match_headline: In Bernie Sanders Country, It’s Super Tuesday. It’s Also ‘Town Meeting Day.’

text: An article on Wednesday about recent commercial real estate transactions misstated the street in the address of the medical/dental co-op where office space was sold. It is East 60th Street, not East 61st Street.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Wednesday about Chinese factories whose production has been affected by the coronavirus outbreak referred incorrectly to the relationship between Fitch Ratings and India Ratings and Research. The companies are independently operating parts of Fitch Group; India Ratings and Research is not a unit of Fitch Ratings.
match_headline: As Coronavirus Disrupts Factories, India Curbs Exports of Key Drugs

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal misidentified the university where she was chairwoman of the department of art practice. It was the University of California, Berkeley — not the University of California, Los Angeles.
match_headline: A Painter and Social Activist With an ‘Unruly Nature’

text: An article on Thursday about a record number of parliamentary seats won by Arab-led parties in Israel’s election referred incorrectly to the number of Israelis who are of Arab ethnicity. It is about one in five, not two in five. The article also misstated Arab turnout in Israeli elections. It fell below 50 percent in the April election, but it is not the case that turnout has been below that level historically.
match_headline: Israel’s Right Had a Good Election. So Did Israeli Arabs. That May Be No Coincidence.

text: An article on Thursday about the future of Senator Elizabeth Warren’s presidential bid after her campaign’s losses on Super Tuesday misstated Maurice Mitchell’s title with the Working Families Party. He is the national director, not the national political director.
match_headline: After Mounting Losses, Elizabeth Warren Reviews Her Options

text: An article on Thursday about a report by the House Financial Services Committee that asserted that an appointee in the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau promised special favors to Wells Fargo referred incorrectly to correspondence between two executives at the bank. Michael Loughlin, the chief risk officer, wrote an email to Timothy J. Sloan that proposed a resolution for customers harmed by fake accounts. Mr. Sloan did not write to Mr. Loughlin.
match_headline: Wells Fargo Was Promised Soft Handling by Trump Appointee, Democrats Say

text: An obituary on Thursday about Rosalind P. Walter, the inspiration for “Rosie the Riveter” and a prominent benefactor of PBS programming, misidentified the town in which Ms. Walter grew up. It was Fairfield, Conn., not Centre Island, N.Y., where her family later settled.
match_headline: Rosalind P. Walter, 95, First ‘Rosie the Riveter’ and a PBS Funder, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the hockey player Mika Zibanejad’s five-goal game for the Rangers misstated the status of his contract. He is in the third of its five years, not the second.
match_headline: Mika Zibanejad’s 5 Goals for the Rangers Help Bring the Playoffs Into View

text: An article on Page 14 about a growing number of women who direct films misstates the surname of a director. It is Janicza Bravo, not Brown.
match_headline: Five Short Films by Women, About Women

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about Javier Pérez de Cuéllar, the former secretary of the United Nations, referred incorrectly to Mr. Pérez de Cuéllar’s wife, Marcela Temple Seminario, whom he married in 1975. She died in 2013; she does not survive him.
match_headline: Javier Pérez de Cuéllar Dies at 100; U.N. Chief Brokered Peace Pacts

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about movie monsters referred incorrectly to the character played by Boris Karloff in the 1931 film “Frankenstein.” It was the monster, not Frankenstein. The article also misidentified a character in the Universal horror franchise. It is Frankenstein’s monster, not Frankenstein.
match_headline: There’s No Dark Universe Anymore, Just One Monster After Another

text: An article last Sunday about the preponderance of quotations from men in U.S. passports misstated the year that Anna Julia Cooper died. It was 1964, not 1974.
match_headline: There Are 13 Quotations in a U.S. Passport. Guess How Many Are From Men?

text: An article on Saturday about the detention of three members of the Saudi royal family by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman misstated the date of arrests. They were arrested Friday morning, not Thursday evening.
match_headline: Saudi Prince Detains Senior Members of Royal Family

text: An article on Monday about the Trump campaign’s success in gaining control of the Republican Party misidentified a client of Convergence Media. The firm works for the National Republican Congressional Committee, not the Republican National Committee.
match_headline: How the Trump Campaign Took Over the G.O.P.

text: An article on Monday about the Democratic presidential primary in Michigan misstated Mike Duggan’s title. He is the current mayor of Detroit, not the former mayor.
match_headline: Bernie Sanders Won Michigan in 2016. Tuesday’s Primary Looks Much Tougher.

text: An article on Sunday about contact between Erik Prince and spies associated with Project Veritas misstated the age of Marisa Jorge, a Project Veritas operative. She is 25, not 23. A headline with the article misstated the origin of information about Erik Prince’s role in recruiting a former spy to help infiltrate a local teachers union. As the article stated, the information came from source interviews, not documents in a lawsuit.
match_headline: Erik Prince Recruits Ex-Spies to Help Infiltrate Liberal Groups

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about a new audio guide offering at the Armory Show misspelled the surname of two artists. They are Nancy and Ed Kienholz, not Keinholz.
match_headline: Welcome to the Armory Fair. It’s Huge. It’s Hectic. Would You Like an Audio Guide?

text: An obituary on Saturday about Troy Collings, who ran Young Pioneers Tours, referred incorrectly to a 2018 interview with Mr. Collings. It was posted on his company’s website, not on the website NK News.
match_headline: Troy Collings, 33, Who Took Travelers Into North Korea, Dies

text: An article on Friday about a temporary disruption in communications between NASA and a robotic probe, Voyager 2, misstated the probe’s distance from Earth. Voyager 2 is more than 11 billion miles from Earth, not 13 billion. (Voyager 1, the spacecraft’s twin, is more than 13 billion miles from Earth.)
match_headline: When Voyager 2 Calls Home, Earth Soon Won’t Be Able to Answer

text: An article on Tuesday about the Supreme Court’s decision to consider a case on the constitutionality of the harshest punishments for youthful offenders referred incorrectly to Jim Hood. He is the former attorney general of Mississippi, not Alabama.
match_headline: Supreme Court to Consider When Juveniles May Get Life Without Parole

text: An article on Tuesday about Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s latest health care proposal misstated the year the House passed its version of the Affordable Care Act. It was 2009, not 2019.
match_headline: Pelosi, Seeking to Insulate House Majority, Presses Plan to Lower Health Costs

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Tuesday about traffic deaths in New York City misstated where Dr. Daniel Cammerman was biking when he was killed in December. He was on the 96th Street transverse road through Central Park, not on Fifth Avenue.
match_headline: More Pedestrians and Cyclists are Dying in N.Y.C. Drivers are Often to Blame.

text: An article on Tuesday about Prince Andrew’s refusal to cooperate with federal prosecutors who are investigating sex trafficking misstated his age. He is 60, not 59.
match_headline: Prince Andrew Is Stonewalling in Epstein Case, Prosecutor Says

text: An article on Tuesday about a D.J. in Kazakhstan misidentified the language in which the word “zvuk” means “sound.” It is Russian, not Kazakh.
match_headline: A D.J. Shows How to Let Go in Authoritarian Kazakhstan

text: An article on Feb. 11 about a trick to make quadratic equations easier to solve referred incompletely to the role played by coefficients in the quadratic function, y = ax2 + bx + c. Both a and b can shift a parabola’s axis of symmetry, not just b.
match_headline: This Professor’s ‘Amazing’ Trick Makes Quadratic Equations Easier

text: An article on Tuesday about the geneticist Nancy Wexler’s announcement that she has Huntington’s disease misidentified the owner of the drug manufacturing facility that Dr. Wexler was filmed touring. It is owned by Ionis Pharmaceuticals, not Roche. The article also implied that the video segment was part of an upcoming documentary, “The Gene.” The segment will not be in the documentary.
match_headline: Haunted by a Gene

text: An article on Thursday about Harvey Weinstein’s sentencing misstated the date of his conviction. It was Feb. 24, not Feb. 25.
match_headline: Harvey Weinstein’s Stunning Downfall: 23 Years in Prison

text: An article on Thursday about the album “We Are Sent Here by History” described incorrectly the genre of music played by the band Batsumi. The group performs songs sung in southern African languages and includes influences from ethnic groups other than Zulu. It is not simply a Zulu jazz-rock band.
ref_headline: We Are Sent Here by History
match_headline: Shabaka and the Ancestors Are Making Their Own Jazz History

text: An article on Page 32 about museums in New York that focus on immigration misstates the location of the Tenement Museum’s food stall. It is in the Market Line, under the Essex Market; it is not in the Essex Market itself.
match_headline: New York City Museums Teach the History of Immigration

text: An article on Page 2 about a reunited series of panels by the artist Jacob Lawrence misspells the surname of a curator. She is Austen Barron Bailly, not Bailey.
match_headline: Lost, and Now Found, Art From the Civil Rights Era

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 36 about the Feminist Art Coalition misidentifies the people in the photograph. Anne Ellegood is on the right, and Rita Gonzalez is in the center, not the reverse.
match_headline: Feminists Arm Themselves With Art

text: An article on Page 28 about the way Holocaust and Jewish museums use history to combat bigotry misattributes a quote about an exhibit at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, D.C. The comment was from Sara J. Bloomfield, the museum director, not Sarah Campbell, the program coordinator.
match_headline: From Swastika Selfies to Lessons on Nazism

text: An article on Page 18 about the exhibition “Displaced” at SITE Santa Fe misstates the contribution of the Irish artist Richard Mosse. He will show still images from his three-channel video installation, “Incoming,” not the installation itself.
match_headline: Bringing Human Migration Closer to Home

text: An article on Page 26 about the art form known as figuration misstates the subjects primarily depicted by the Pakistani-born artist Salman Toor. They are gay men of South Asian descent, not Southeast Asian descent.
match_headline: Two Artists, Two Views of the Human Figure

text: An article on Thursday about a secret extrajudicial location where the Greek government is detaining migrants referred incompletely to the nationality of Somar al-Hussein. While Mr. al-Hussein is a Syrian Kurd, he is also one of a small minority of Syrian exiles to recently receive a Turkish passport.
match_headline: ‘We Are Like Animals’: Inside Greece’s Secret Site for Migrants

text: An article on Friday about the effects of the coronavirus on the 2020 presidential campaign misidentified the Brazilian officials who had, as of Thursday morning, tested positive for the coronavirus. An aide to President Jair Bolsonaro tested positive, not both the aide and the president.
match_headline: How the Coronavirus Changed the 2020 Campaign

text: An article on March 6 about a heart procedure performed on Harvey Weinstein described incorrectly the nature of the procedure. He had angioplasty to alleviate a blockage, but did not have a stent installed.
match_headline: Weinstein Undergoes Heart Procedure Before Transfer to Jail

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the N.B.A.’s decision to suspend the 2019-20 season referred incorrectly to a masked spectator, Michael Clayton. He is a Knicks fan, not a member of the team.
match_headline: From Rocky Season to No Season, Inside the N.B.A.’s Decision to Freeze

text: An article on Page 10 about the project “02020” at Performance Space New York misspelled the surname of an artist in the cohort running Performance Space New York. She is Monica Mirabile, not Mirable.
match_headline: The Artists Are in Charge. Step 1: Upend the Status Quo.

text: An article on Page 12 about Stephen Sondheim’s body of work misstated the relationship of the character George to Georges Seurat in “Sunday in the Park With George.” George is Seurat’s great-grandson, not his grandson.
ref_headline: Sunday in the Park With George.
match_headline: Now You Know: A Critic’s Guide to Sondheim

text: An article on Page 14 about the emotional complexity of Stephen Sondheim’s musicals misidentifies the theater where the original production of “Follies” played. It was the Winter Garden, not the Palace Theater.
match_headline: Stephen Sondheim, the Man Who Felt Too Much

text: An article on Page 8 about maker studios at the Brooklyn Navy Yard misstates the name of a side table designed by Jessica Banks. It is the Float, not the Matrix.
match_headline: At the Brooklyn Navy Yard It’s Full Steam Ahead

text: An article on Friday about an exhibition at the Eli and Edythe Broad Art Museum at Michigan State University misstated a connection between John Lucas and Claudia Rankine, the producers of the “Situations” video series, and Yale University. Ms. Rankine teaches at Yale; Mr. Lucas does not.
match_headline: At Michigan State, Bold Statements About Big Issues

text: An article on Sunday about Trump supporters’ unwavering trust in the president misstated the surname of a Tennessee state legislator representing Jonesborough. He is Micah Van Huss, not Jones.
match_headline: Trump Supporters Know Where to Turn in a Crisis: To Him

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about R. Kelly knowingly exposing women to herpes referred incorrectly to the court in which he appeared in Chicago. It was Cook County Criminal Court, not federal court.
match_headline: R. Kelly Knowingly Exposed Sex Partners to Herpes, Prosecutors Say

text: An article on Sunday about the transformation of Little Italy in the Bronx misidentified the region that includes Albania. It is among the Balkan States, not the Baltic States.
match_headline: How Little Italy Became Little Albanian-Mexican Italy

text: An article on Monday about the basketball player Danilo Gallinari misspelled the last name of his friend. He is Filippo Curti, not Filippo Conti.
match_headline: For Danilo Gallinari, the N.B.A. Shutdown Wasn’t So Sudden

text: An article on Friday about the vocalist Angélique Kidjo misidentified the organization for which Ms. Kidjo is a goodwill ambassador. It is UNICEF, not UNESCO.
match_headline: It’s Angélique Kidjo’s Birthday, and Her Country’s Too

text: An article on Monday about the temporary closure of the New York Public Library misstated the title of a retired librarian, Daniel Winocour. He was a reference librarian at the Queens Public Library, not a research librarian.
match_headline: At the Library, Last Call for Beauty and Books

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about recordings of classical music misidentified the type of saxophone being held by the composer and musician Anthony Braxton. It is a soprano saxophone, not an alto.
match_headline: Charles Wuorinen, Uncompromising Modernist Composer, Dies at 81

text: An article on Tuesday about the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on the U.S. economy misspelled the surname of the owner of Helix Rotation Services, a cleaning service in Atlanta. He is Steve Coffie, not Coffle.
match_headline: America’s Economy Begins to Shut Down as Pandemic Measures Take Hold

text: An article on Monday about the U.S. food supply, using information from a chicken supplier, misstated the time it takes a chicken to incubate and hatch. It is about three weeks, not 10 days.
match_headline: ‘There Is Plenty of Food in the Country’

text: An article on Sunday about cheating in chess erroneously attributed a distinction to the chess player Leinier Domínguez. He is ranked No. 3 in the United States, not No. 1. (No. 1 is Fabiano Caruana.) The article also misstated part of the name of the I.B.M. computer that defeated the world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997. It was Deep Blue, not Big Blue.
match_headline: Think Cheating in Baseball Is Bad? Try Chess

text: An article on Tuesday about a woman facing charges of embezzling $1.5 million from the Kirov Academy of Ballet paraphrased incompletely from remarks by Pamela Gonzales de Cordova about the leadership team that is addressing concerns at the ballet academy. Ms. de Cordova said Tatiana Moon, the academy’s board president, and the school’s artistic director, Runquiao Du, had also played critical roles.
match_headline: A Ballet School Rehired an Embezzler. Then $1.5 Million Vanished.

text: An article on Wednesday about the decline in pollution caused by the shutdowns of countries around the world misspelled the surname of the Greenpeace East Asia coordinator. He is Minwoo Son, not Minwoo Sun. Additionally, one of a pair of maps that showed the drop in northern Italy was labeled incorrectly in print. The map on the left showed pollution over northern Italy from Feb. 22 to March 14, 2019, not 2020.
match_headline: Outbreak in Northern Italy Poses National Challenge

text: An article on Wednesday about research that examines the life span of the new coronavirus in different environments misstated the length of time that it is found to survive on cardboard. It can live about 24 hours, not 8 hours.
match_headline: How Long Will Coronavirus Live on Surfaces or in the Air Around You?

text: An article on Tuesday about the postponement of the Kentucky Derby referred incorrectly to the 1901 Derby, which was run in April that year. The Derby has twice before been run on dates other than the first Saturday in May. It is not the case that 1901 is the only other year it did not take place on the first Saturday in May. (The 1945 Derby was run in June.)
match_headline: Kentucky Derby Is Postponed Until September Because of Coronavirus

text: An article on Tuesday about an appeal by astronomers for the funding of two telescope projects misstated the name of an organization. It is the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, not American Universities for Research in Astronomy.
match_headline: American Astronomy’s Future Goes on Trial in Washington

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the actor Stuart Whitman misstated part of the title of a movie in which he appeared. It is “Those Magnificent Men in Their Flying Machines,” not “and Their Flying Machines.”
ref_headline: Those Magnificent Men in Their Flying Machines,
match_headline: Stuart Whitman, Leading Man on Big and Small Screens, Dies at 92

text: An article on Thursday about federal bailouts for companies amid different financial crises misstated which of the Big Three automakers accepted a federal bailout and went through Chapter 11 bankruptcy after the economic crisis in 2008 and 2009. General Motors and Chrysler did, not Ford. The article also misstated which type of bankruptcy involves business liquidation. It is Chapter 7, not Chapter 13.
match_headline: A Taxonomy of Bailouts: Comparing the Coronavirus Rescues With Rescues Past

text: An article on Thursday about the quarterback Tom Brady’s potential move to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers misstated the number of interceptions Jameis Winston threw last season in comparison with Brady’s 36 over the last five seasons. Brady’s five-year total was six more than Winston’s 2019 total, not six fewer.
match_headline: Tom Brady in Tampa Bay? It’s Not as Weird as It Sounds

text: An article on Wednesday about a researcher in Germany who tracked down art looted by the Nazis misstated the limits of the Washington Principles on the restitution of such works. Experts say they are meant to encourage nations and museums, both state-owned and privately operated, to identify art confiscated by the Nazis and to find just solutions that address those losses. The principles do not apply only to public collections.
match_headline: She Tracked Nazi-Looted Art. She Quit When No One Returned It.

text: An obituary on Monday about the Balinese dancer Ni Gusti Ayu Rak attributed an erroneous distinction to her dance troupe’s 1952 tour. While the tour helped popularize Balinese dance in the West, it was not the first to present Balinese dance to audiences in the West in more than 20 years. There had been several such performances.
match_headline: Overlooked No More: Ni Gusti Ayu Raka Rasmi, Balinese Dancer

text: An article on Friday about voters who want to hear former Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. speak more about climate change misidentified the group that Collin O’Mara leads. It is the National Wildlife Federation, not the National Wildlife Foundation.
match_headline: Climate Voters Still Want More From Biden

text: An article on Page 4 about the lack of diversity in Atlanta’s theater scene misspells the surname of the artistic director of the Out of Hand theater company. It is Ariel Fristoe, not Fristo.
match_headline: 54% of the People. 12% of the Plays. Atlanta, Do We Have a Problem?

text: An article on Page 60 about the designer Faye Toogood misstates the month for the opening of her show at New York’s Friedman Benda gallery; it will open in September, not next month.
match_headline: ‘I Don’t Know How I’m Going to Pay Rent Next Month’

text: An article on Page 124 about the furniture designer George Nakashima refers incorrectly to Japanese torii gates; they are commonly found at Japanese shrines, not temples.
match_headline: How Two Children Are Keeping Their Father’s Design Legacy Alive

text: An article on March 1 about cultural events in New York City this spring misidentified the book writer for the musical “Assassins.” He is John Weidman, not Jerome Weidman — who was his father.
match_headline: What to See and Experience in New York City This Spring

text: An article on Page 60 about the designer Faye Toogood misstates the month for the opening of her show at New York’s Friedman Benda gallery; it will open in September, not next month.
match_headline: For Faye Toogood, the Rough Draft Is Also the Final Product

text: A review on March 8 about Jerry Mitchell’s “Race Against Time” misstated the surname of the man who killed the civil rights leader Medgar Evers. Byron De La Beckwith’s last name was Beckwith, not De La Beckwith.
match_headline: The Journalist and the Murderers

text: An article on Tuesday about congressional negotiations on an emergency economic stimulus package to respond to the coronavirus pandemic misstated the day Speaker Nancy Pelosi returned to Washington from San Francisco. It was Saturday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Top Senate Democrat and Treasury Secretary Say They Are Near a Stimulus Deal

text: An article on Tuesday about a decision by the drug maker Gilead to abruptly shut down its emergency access program misstated the title of Jack Allard, a New Jersey resident who has coronavirus. He is an associate at Bank of America, not an analyst.
match_headline: Coronavirus Patients in Limbo as Gilead Suspends Emergency Drug Access

text: An article on Sunday about efforts by the Bureau of Land Management to control the mustang population misstated the name of an area near Challis, Idaho. It is Spar Canyon, not Spur Canyon.
match_headline: A Mustang Crisis Looms in the West

text: An article on Tuesday about the use of thalidomide in the United States misstated the regulatory status of the drug. It was approved in the 1990s for leprosy and cancer treatment; it is not the case that it was never approved in the United States. (Approval in this country for use as a morning sickness treatment was rejected in earlier decades.) The error was repeated in an article about the F.D.A.’s investigation of thalidomide during the 1960s.
match_headline: The Unseen Survivors of Thalidomide Want to Be Heard

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Eric Weissberg, the multi-instrumentalist best known for the hit single “Dueling Banjos,” referred incorrectly to the father and uncle of Toshi Aline Ohta, Pete Seeger’s future wife. They were members of the staff of Camp Woodland in Phoenicia, N.Y., which Mr. Weissberg attended; they did not run the camp.
match_headline: Eric Weissberg, ‘Dueling Banjos’ Musician, Dies at 80

text: An obituary on Friday about the obstetrician and gynecologist Catherine Hamlin contained an incomplete list of her survivors. In addition to those listed, she is survived by two great-grandchildren.
match_headline: Catherine Hamlin, 96, Dies; Pioneering Doctor Treated Childbirth Injury

text: An obituary on Friday about the flutist Doriot Anthony Dwyer misspelled the given name of her daughter, who survives her. She is Arienne Dwyer, not Adrienne.
match_headline: Doriot Anthony Dwyer, Flutist and Orchestral Pathbreaker, Dies at 98

text: An article on Friday about the global competition for a coronavirus vaccine misstated the relationship of one company, Sanofi, to others working in the field. It is working independently on a vaccine, not with Eli Lilly, Johnson & Johnson, Roche and Takeda.
match_headline: Search for Coronavirus Vaccine Becomes a Global Competition

text: An article on Wednesday about the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on countries with vulnerable economies referred incorrectly to the co-owner of a hot-air balloon company in the Cappadocia region of Turkey. The co-owner, Deniz Turgut, is a woman.
match_headline: In World’s Most Vulnerable Countries, the Pandemic Rivals the 2008 Crisis

text: An article on Wednesday about the effects of an Olympics postponement on athletes’ training schedules described incorrectly the Olympic medal won by the gymnast Laurie Hernandez in balance beam at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro. She won silver, not bronze.
match_headline: Olympians Have Another Year to Prepare for Tokyo. It’s a Blessing and a Curse.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the French actress and singer Suzy Delair misstated part of the name of one of her movies. It is “L’Assassin Habite … au 21,” not “… sur 21.”
match_headline: Suzy Delair, French Star of Movies and Music Halls, Dies at 102

text: An obituary on March 11 about the translator Jamey Gambrell rendered incorrectly the English transliteration of the surname of a poet whose work she translated. She was Marina Tsvetaeva (sometimes rendered as Tsvetayeva), not Svetaeva.
match_headline: Jamey Gambrell Dies at 65; Made Russian Writing Sing, in English

text: An obituary on March 17 about the architect Vittorio Gregotti misstated the name of an architecture and design studio where he had worked. It was B.B.P.R., not B.P.P.R.
match_headline: Vittorio Gregotti, Modernist Architect, Dies in Pandemic at 92

text: An article on Thursday about the retirement of Col. W. Shane Cohen, the military judge presiding in the Sept. 11 death penalty trial at Guantánamo Bay, misstated the target start date of the trial. It is Jan. 11, 2021, not Jan. 22, 2021.
match_headline: Military Judge in 9/11 Trial at Guantánamo Is Retiring

text: An obituary on March 10 about the real estate executive Charles Urstadt referred incorrectly to the championship he won in a swimming tournament when he was 72. It was a national championship, not a world championship.
match_headline: Charles Urstadt, Who Eased N.Y. Rent Controls, Dies at 91

text: An article on Tuesday about public health experts’ plea to the federal government to take over the nation’s ventilator supply referred imprecisely to a study’s estimate of the need for ventilators in the United States. The study, by the Society of Critical Care Medicine, projected that there may be as many as one million people in the United States who need treatment with a ventilator over the course of the pandemic, not that the country will need 1 million ventilators over the course of the pandemic.
match_headline: Amid Desperate Need for Ventilators, Calls Grow for Federal Intervention

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about the painting “Saint Rosalie Interceding for the Plague-stricken of Palermo” at the Met refers incorrectly to the first location of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. It was 681 Fifth Avenue, not 128 West 14th Street. The West 14th Street address was the museum’s second location.
ref_headline: Saint Rosalie Interceding for the Plague-stricken of Palermo
match_headline: The Saint Who Stopped an Epidemic Is on Lockdown at the Met

text: An article on Friday about “Top Gun” incorrectly defined the term RIO. It stands for radar intercept officer, not radio intercept officer.
match_headline: Who’s Your Wingman Now? Pushing the Envelope With ‘Top Gun’

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 32 about the Stellenbosch Triennale misidentified a member of the Asafo Black collective from Ghana. He is Jeffrey Otoo, not Daniel Mensah.
match_headline: Stellenbosch Triennale, a Bold Experiment

text: An article on March 8 about the Chinese gay dating app Blued misspelled the given name of a Taiwanese writer. He is Bai Xianyong, not Bai Xinyong. And the article misstated the name of China’s Legislature. It is the National People’s Congress, not the National Party Congress.
match_headline: How a Dating App Helped a Generation of Chinese Come Out of the Closet

text: An article on Friday about the murky science behind the theory that the coronavirus was transferred to humans through pangolins misstated the name of a bat species in which the RaTG13 virus is found. It is an intermediate horseshoe bat, not a Chinese horseshoe bat.
match_headline: Significance of Pangolin Viruses in Human Pandemic Remains Murky

text: An article on Saturday about criticism of Dr. Deborah L. Birx, the coronavirus response coordinator, misstated the estimated need for ventilators in the United States as described in a study by the Society of Critical Care Medicine. The study projected that there may be as many as one million people in the United States who need treatment with a ventilator over the course of the pandemic, not that the country would need up to 1 million ventilators.
match_headline: For Dr. Deborah Birx, Urging Calm Has Come With Heavy Criticism

text: An article on Monday about President Trump’s struggle to ramp up the production of ventilators referred incorrectly to General Motors. It is the largest carmaker in the United States, not the largest in the world.
match_headline: Trump Said He Was the President of Manufacturing. Then Disaster Struck.

text: An article on Sunday about a tornado in Jonesboro, Ark. misspelled the name of a department store. It is J.C. Penney, not Penny.
match_headline: A City Hunkered Down to Survive an Outbreak. That Helped in a Tornado, Too.

text: An article on Saturday about the $23.5 billion in assistance to farmers included in the $2 trillion relief package passed to support the U.S. economy amid the coronavirus pandemic misidentified Ken Goldman’s employer. He is an analyst at JPMorgan, not Goldman Sachs.
match_headline: For Farmers, Stimulus Bill Means Subsidies Continue to Flow

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the Trump administration’s plans to roll back automobile fuel efficiency standards misstated the auto industry’s position on fuel economy. Although the industry has recently improved fuel economy by 2.4 percent annually, it has never said it would strengthen fuel economy standards by 2.4 percent per year.
match_headline: U.S. to Announce Rollback of Auto Pollution Rules, a Key Effort to Fight Climate Change

text: An article on Tuesday about the New York attorney general looking into the privacy practices of the video conferencing platform Zoom misstated the given name of the executive director of the Campaign for a Commercial-Free Childhood. He is Josh Golin, not John.
match_headline: New York Attorney General Looks Into Zoom’s Privacy Practices

text: An article on Tuesday about restaurants delivering meals to hospitals misspelled the surname of the founder of the New York company Scott’s Pizza Tours. He is Scott Wiener, not Weiner.
match_headline: Restaurants Find Hope in Delivering Donated Meals to Hospitals

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday misstated the date the 2020 Paralympic Games were scheduled to begin. They were planned to start on Aug. 25, not Aug. 24.
match_headline: Summer Olympics in Tokyo to Start on July 23, 2021

text: An article on Saturday about niche films being aired online misstated the source of the shorts being posted by the Tribeca Film Festival. Most of them are by alumni of the festival, not all.
match_headline: Select Film Festivals and Indie Movies Figure Out Online Access

text: An article on Tuesday about movies that depict viral outbreaks misstated the origins of the film “Outbreak.” It had an original screenplay. It was not based on the Richard Preston novel “The Hot Zone.” The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: ‘Outbreak’ Was a Hit in 1995. Now We’re Living the Sequel.

text: An article last Wednesday about restaurant suppliers losing business in the coronavirus crisis misstated what Heather Shouse did at Bottle & Branch in Chicago. She furloughed nine of her year-round employees and put the 10th on part-time status; she did not lay off all 10.
match_headline: Restaurant Closings Inflict Collateral Damage on Other Businesses

text: An article last Wednesday on making crumb cake using staple ingredients omitted the temperature at which to set the oven. It is 350 degrees.

An article on Wednesday about asymptomatic coronavirus cases and potential changes to federal guidelines on wearing masks misstated the location of a choir that developed many cases of coronavirus infection. It was in Mount Vernon, Wash., north of Seattle, not in Seattle.
match_headline: Infected but Feeling Fine: The Unwitting Coronavirus Spreaders

text: An article on Tuesday about people making medical equipment at home misidentified the platform on which Trevor Smale started a project to share ventilator designs. He started it on GitLab, not GitHub.
match_headline: D.I.Y. Coronavirus Solutions Are Gaining Steam

text: An article last Thursday about the online presence of New York’s nightlife during the coronavirus pandemic misspelled the given name of a clubgoer. She is Masami Hosono, not Masanni.
match_headline: New York Nightlife Goes Online

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the physicist Philip W. Anderson misspelled his mother’s middle name. She was Elsie Eleanor Anderson, not Elinore.
match_headline: Philip W. Anderson, Nobel Laureate in Physics, Is Dead at 96

text: An obituary on Monday about the composer Krzysztof Penderecki misstated the source of a 2013 interview with him. It was the Louisiana Channel, an online video channel run by the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Denmark — not “a Louisiana television station.”
match_headline: Krzysztof Penderecki, Polish Composer With Cinematic Flair, Dies at 86

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on March 26 about the science journalist Daniel S. Greenberg referred incorrectly to the Wilmington, Del., newspaper The Journal-Every Evening, which he joined in 1955. It changed its name to The Evening Journal in 1960; it did not cease publication that year.
match_headline: Daniel S. Greenberg, Science Journalist and Iconoclast, Dies at 88

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on March 25 about the saxophonist Manu Dibango misstated his birth date. He was born on Dec. 12, 1933 — not Feb. 10, 1934.
match_headline: Manu Dibango, Soulful Ambassador of African Music, Dies at 86

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on March 26 about the restaurateur and chef Floyd Cardoz misstated the month in which the Swiss chef Gray Kunz, with whom Mr. Cardoz once worked, died. It was March, not February.
match_headline: Floyd Cardoz, 59, Dies; Gave American Fine Dining an Indian Flavor

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s support for a possible oil deal between Saudi Arabia and Russia misstated the amount of the recent stimulus package. It was $2.2 trillion, not $2.2 billion.
match_headline: Trump Promotes Oil Deal That May Not Exist

text: An article on Friday about cruise ships docking in Florida misidentified the company that will pay for the passengers to fly home on charter flights. The cruise line will pay for the flights, not the airline.
match_headline: Ships With Coronavirus-Stricken Passengers Dock in Florida

text: An article on March 28 about Denmark’s response to the economic decline triggered by the coronavirus pandemic misspelled the surname of a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. He is Jacob F. Kirkegaard, not Kierkegaard.
match_headline: The Nordic Way to Economic Rescue

text: An obituary on Friday about the jazz pianist and educator Ellis Marsalis misstated how many grandchildren survive him. There are 15, not 13.
match_headline: Ellis Marsalis, Jazz Pianist and Music Family Patriarch, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Thursday about the author and illustrator Tomie dePaola misstated part of the name of a reviewer who wrote about his book “Strega Nona.” She is Norma Malina Feld, not Norma Mauna Feld.
match_headline: Tomie dePaola, ‘Strega Nona’ Author and Illustrator, Dies at 85

text: An article last Sunday about the poet John Keats and the typhus epidemic in Naples in 1820 misspelled the surname of a woman Keats wrote to. It is Brawne, not Brawn. The article also included several misquotations from Keats’s writings. A corrected version is at nytimes.com/travel.
match_headline: When the World Stops, Traveling in John Keats’s ‘Realms of Gold’

text: A picture caption with a photo essay on Monday about social distancing in New Orleans misspelled a woman’s surname. She is Li Yaffe, not Yaffee.
match_headline: Our ‘Digital Selves’ Are No Less Real

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the Bacillus Calmette-Guerin vaccine described incorrectly its earliest form. It contained a weakened version of the TB bacterium, not a weakened virus.
match_headline: Can an Old Vaccine Stop the New Coronavirus?

text: An article on March 31 about data that suggests government-mandated restrictions are slowing the rate of coronavirus infections misstated an event that occurred on March 20. A stay-at-home order in New York was announced, it did not take effect (it took effect on March 22).
match_headline: Restrictions Are Slowing Coronavirus Infections, New Data Suggest

text: An article on Monday about economic research focused on the coronavirus pandemic misidentified the academic institution at which Filipe Campante is a political economist. He is at Johns Hopkins University, not Princeton. The article also rendered one word incorrectly in the name of a research institute with which Olivier Blanchard is affiliated. It is the Peterson Institute for International Economics, not Finance.
match_headline: How Economists Are Trying to Answer Coronavirus Questions

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about virtual NASCAR races misidentified the site of the first NASCAR Cup Series race postponed because of the coronavirus pandemic. It was the Atlanta Motor Speedway, not Homestead-Miami Speedway. Because of an editing error, the article also misstated the duration of postponements for the series. Races are currently postponed through — not until — May 3.
match_headline: The Best Thing About NASCAR’s Virtual Races Might Be the Real Competition

text: An article on Friday about performers whose practice regimens have changed because of the coronavirus pandemic referred incorrectly to the partner with whom Constance Stamitiou is learning new choreography on TikTok. It is her daughter, not her daughters.
match_headline: Dancing With Myself: How Artists Stay in Shape Without a Stage

text: An article on Monday about the Museum of the Bible in Washington misstated the nature of the team of conservators and scientists that examined the fragments of the fake Dead Sea Scrolls. The team was assembled and managed by Art Fraud Insights, a research and consulting firm; they were not employees of Art Fraud Insights.
match_headline: Bible Museum, Admitting Mistakes, Tries to Convert Its Critics

text: An article last Tuesday about an underwater cypress grove exposed by Hurricane Ivan misstated the age of the grove. It is about 50,000 to 70,000 years old, not two ice ages old. The article also referred imprecisely to the size of the forest. The exposed portion of the forest is about one half mile square, it is not two football fields by five feet wide (that was the size of the area to be explored by a group of scientists).
match_headline: A Forest Submerged 60,000 Years Ago Could Save Your Life One Day

text: An obituary on Friday about Dr. John Murray, an expert in pulmonology, misspelled his mother’s maiden name. She was Dorothy (Hanna) Murray, not Hannah.
match_headline: Dr. John Murray, Pioneering Lung Expert, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Saturday about the author and former actress Patricia Bosworth misstated part of the title of the 1959 movie in which she appeared alongside Audrey Hepburn. It is “The Nun’s Story,” not “A Nun’s Story.” The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Patricia Bosworth, Actress-Turned-Author, Dies at 86

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump’s aggressive advocacy of a malaria drug for the treatment of coronavirus patients incorrectly described a financial firm. Fisher Asset Management is an investment company, not a mutual fund company.
match_headline: Trump’s Aggressive Advocacy of Malaria Drug for Treating Coronavirus Divides Medical Community

text: An article on Monday about the relationship between the Cuomo brothers and the public misstated the year that the broadcast journalist Edward R. Murrow delivered a report from a London roof. It was 1940, not 1941.
match_headline: Americans Don’t Trust the Media Anymore. So Why Do They Trust the Cuomos?

text: An article on Tuesday about the departure of Matthew Belloni from The Hollywood Reporter misstated the year that Matthew Belloni took over for Janice Min. It was 2017, not 2016.
match_headline: Hollywood Reporter’s Top Editor Exits After Dispute With Publisher

text: An article on Tuesday about an indictment charging three media executives and a sports marketing company with crimes in connection with bribes to secure television and marketing rights for international soccer tournaments described incorrectly an accusation in the indictment against a Guatemalan soccer official, Rafael Salguero. The indictment said Salguero was promised $1 million to vote for Russia to host the 2018 World Cup; it did not say he received it.
match_headline: U.S. Says FIFA Officials Were Bribed to Award World Cups to Russia and Qatar

text: Because of an editing error, a Good Question article on Tuesday about pulsars misstated the spin rate of the pulsar PSR J1748–2446. It is 43,000 miles per second, not 43,000 miles per hour.
match_headline: How’s the View From a Spinning Star?

text: An article on Wednesday about the resignation of Thomas B. Modly, the acting Navy Secretary, misstated when Defense Secretary Mark T. Esper accepted Mr. Modly’s resignation. It was Tuesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Acting Navy Secretary Resigns After Outcry Over Criticism of Virus-Stricken Crew

text: An article on Wednesday about Kayleigh McEnany, the new White House press secretary, misstated the year Ms. McEnany graduated from Harvard Law School. It was 2016, not 2017.
match_headline: Trump Has a New Press Secretary Who Knows How to Defend Him

text: An article on Wednesday about Wisconsin Republicans’ push for an election to take place during a pandemic described incorrectly the identification requirements for Wisconsin voters. They may have a photo ID with a current address or an ID and acceptable proof of residency; it is not the case that only a photo ID with a current address is acceptable.
match_headline: Why Wisconsin Republicans Insisted on an Election in a Pandemic

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about new material released on TikTok by Drake misstated which Drake song has become the soundtrack to a recent TikTok challenge. It is “Nonstop,” not “Flip the Switch,” which features Quavo.
match_headline: It’s a TikTok! No, It’s a Song! Drake and the Viral Feedback Loop

text: An obituary on Friday about the chess master Arianne Caoili misstated her mother’s nationality and her father’s profession. Her mother was Australian, not Dutch, and her father was an engineer, not a minister. It also misstated the location in Spain of the 1996 World Youth Chess Championship. It was held in Minorca, not Las Palmas.
match_headline: Arianne Caoili, Chess Master, Is Dead at 33

text: An article on Thursday about coronavirus conspiracy theories referred imprecisely to statements by Senator Tom Cotton about the origins of the coronavirus. Mr. Cotton has suggested it might have been produced as a bioweapon by a Chinese laboratory, but he did not rule out other explanations.
match_headline: Why Coronavirus Conspiracy Theories Flourish. And Why It Matters.

text: An article on Thursday about a selection of John Prine recordings misidentified the album that includes the track “You Never Can Tell.” It is “Common Sense,” not “Sweet Revenge.”
match_headline: John Prine, Who Chronicled the Human Condition in Song, Dies at 73

text: An article on Friday about an introduction to silent comedies described incorrectly the newspaper a woman is reading in “Seven Chances.” The paper uses Hebrew lettering; it is not entirely in Hebrew.
match_headline: Now’s a Good Time to Give Silents a Try. Start With These Comedies.

text: An article on Friday about “Saturday Night Seder,” a streaming Passover event, misspelled part of the title of a television show. It is “Madam Secretary,” not “Madame.”
match_headline: What Can You Do for People in Crisis? Put on a Seder Show

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the former federal judge John G. Davies misstated his age when he won a gold medal in the 200-meter breaststroke at the 1952 Olympics. He was 23, not 20. (As the obituary correctly states, he was born in May 1929.)
match_headline: John G. Davies, Rodney King Judge and Olympic Medalist, Dies at 90

text: An article on March 29 about Estonia misstated two dates. Estonia adopted the euro in 2011, not 2004. Lennart Meri stepped down as president in 2001, not 1997.

An article on Monday about the spread of the coronavirus by Biogen employees referred incorrectly to Jie Li, a statistician who fell ill with flulike symptoms and who was traveling to China. She told flight attendants she was unwell; she did not conceal her health condition from them.
match_headline: How a Premier U.S. Drug Company Became a Virus ‘Super Spreader’

text: An article on Sunday about the political relationship between former Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo of New York misidentified the keynote speaker at the Democratic National Convention in 1988. It was Ann Richards, not Bill Clinton.
match_headline: Biden and Cuomo: Friends, Allies and Supporting Players No Longer

text: A headline with a Coronavirus Update column on Saturday misstated the global death toll. More than 100,000 people had died to date, not in the previous week.
match_headline: How Many People Have Actually Died From Coronavirus in New York?

text: An article on Saturday about ways the coronavirus pandemic could aid the re-election campaigns of Democratic governors in conservative states misidentified the youngest governor in the United States. He is the Republican Ron DeSantis of Florida, not the Republican Chris Sununu of New Hampshire. The article also misstated the amount of money the Democratic Party’s Senate campaign finance arm plans to invest in the North Carolina Senate race. It is $25.6 million, not $16.6 million.
match_headline: How the Virus Crisis Could Help a Red-State Democrat Stay in Office
