text: An article on Friday about the concerns of hospital employees over their working conditions referred incorrectly, based on information from a doctor’s union, to a situation involving a doctor at Lincoln Medical and Mental Health Center in the Bronx. While the union cited a news report in which the doctor spoke about conditions there, it now says the incident did not result in a reprimand or any disciplinary proceeding.
match_headline: Nurses and Doctors Speaking Out on Safety Now Risk Their Job

text: An article on Saturday about the potential hurdles that minority business owners could face in securing federal aid described Fundera incorrectly. It is an online marketplace that helps small businesses find loans, not a nonbank lender.
match_headline: Black-Owned Businesses Could Face Hurdles in Federal Aid Program

text: An article on Monday about the negative effects of the coronavirus pandemic on media companies referred incorrectly to recent layoffs at Bustle Digital Group. Six employees lost their jobs as part of the folding of The Outline, and 18 other employees were also laid off; the company did not lay off 24 employees of The Outline.
match_headline: News Media Outlets Have Been Ravaged by the Pandemic

text: An article on Monday about the ultrarunner Michael Wardian misstated the name of the company that put on the Quarantine Backyard Ultra. It is Personal Peak, not Peak Performance.
match_headline: How to Run for 2.5 Days

text: An article on Saturday about theater productions streamed online misstated the day that National Theater Live productions are uploaded on its YouTube channel. It is Thursday, not Friday.
match_headline: Where to Find Drama Now? All the Internet’s a Stage

text: An article on Sunday about different ways to help the medical community misidentified the borough of the hospital where Lynne Hewett has been treating coronavirus patients. It is Manhattan, not the Bronx.
match_headline: How to Help the Helpers

text: An obituary on Friday about the Mad magazine cartoonist Mort Drucker referred incorrectly to the actress Louise Lasser, whom Mr. Drucker caricatured as part of a parody of the movie “Hannah and Her Sisters.” She was Woody Allen’s second wife, not his first.
match_headline: Mort Drucker, Master of the Mad Caricature, Is Dead at 91

text: An article on Tuesday about a liberal candidate’s upset victory over a conservative incumbent endorsed by President Trump in the Wisconsin Supreme Court race referred incorrectly to the elections in Wisconsin won by a margin of about 30,000 votes or fewer. The most recent contests for president, governor and the State Supreme Court had such margins, not all races in the last four years.
match_headline: Upset Victory in Wisconsin Supreme Court Race Gives Democrats a Lift

text: An editorial Tuesday about the global coronavirus crisis misidentified the location of secessionists in Ukraine. They are in the east, not the west.
match_headline: The Global Coronavirus Crisis Is Poised to Get Much, Much Worse

text: An article last Wednesday about corned ham, a popular North Carolina dish, misstated the year the restaurant Crook’s Corner opened. It was 1982, not 1985.
match_headline: The Lure and Lore of Corned Ham, a Salty Slice of North Carolina

text: An article on Wednesday about the widespread rejection of President Trump’s claim that his office wields total authority misstated, in one instance, the type of equipment that the Trump administration urged General Motors to manufacture under the Defense Production Act. It was pushed to make ventilators, not masks.
match_headline: Trump’s Claim of Total Authority in Crisis Is Rejected Across Ideological Lines

text: An article on Wednesday misstated which sports and business leaders President Trump neglected to mention in his news conference on Tuesday. Mark Cuban, the billionaire entrepreneur and outspoken critic of Mr. Trump, was cited during the briefing. The president did not omit him.
match_headline: Trump Announces His ‘Opening the Country’ Council

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the students who are learning from home because of the pandemic misidentified the location of Delia and Delilah’s play date. It was in Gallatin County, Mont., not Poulsbo, Wash.
match_headline: ‘I Can’t Believe I Am Going to Say This, but I Would Rather Be at School’

text: An article on Wednesday about new laws in Virginia that reflect the Democratic control of the Legislature referred incompletely to one of Gov. Ralph S. Northam’s recent changes to the state’s voting requirements. He removed a photo ID requirement, not the requirement of identification altogether.
match_headline: Virginia’s New Laws on L.G.B.T. Protections, Guns and Marijuana Reflect a Shift in Power

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Craig Gilbert, the creator of the television series “An American Family,” misidentified the organization he joined during World War II. It was the American Field Service, not the American Red Cross.
match_headline: Craig Gilbert, 94, Dies; Created Groundbreaking ‘American Family’

text: An article on Thursday about people commuting to work on a Detroit bus line misstated the age of Valerie Brown’s mother. She is 42, not 46.
match_headline: Shoulder-to-Shoulder, These Detroit Workers Have No Choice but to Ride the Bus

text: An article on Thursday about a field hospital in Central Park misstated the name of a nonprofit organization that works to maintain Central Park. It is the Central Park Conservancy, not Conservatory.
match_headline: Treating Coronavirus in a Central Park ‘Hot Zone’

text: An obituary on April 8 about the ballet teacher Wilhelm Burmann misstated his birthplace in Germany and misspelled his sister’s name. He was born in Oberhausen, North Rhine-Westphalia, not Oberhausen, Rheinland-Pfalz; and his sister is Christel Weidemann, not Chrystal Weideman.
match_headline: Wilhelm Burmann, Teacher of Ballet’s Brightest, Dies at 80

text: An obituary on April 10 about the arts patron Anne Bass misstated the name of a museum of which she had been a trustee. It is the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth, not the Fort Worth Art Museum.
match_headline: Anne Bass, 78, Arts Patron and Peerless Gardener, Dies

text: An obituary on April 7 about the actress Honor Blackman misidentified the character she played in a British tour of the musical “A Little Night Music” in the 1980s. It was Desiree Armfeldt — not Madame Armfeldt, Desiree’s mother.
match_headline: Honor Blackman, a Memorable James Bond Adversary, Dies at 94

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about protests against stay-at-home orders misidentified the location of a protest in Michigan. It was in Lansing, at the State Capitol, not in East Lansing.
match_headline: ‘You Have to Disobey’: Protesters Gather to Defy Stay-at-Home Orders

text: An article on Friday about banks that are withholding stimulus checks from customers who have overdrawn accounts referred incorrectly to the status of Minnesota day care service during the pandemic. Some day care centers have closed, but the state did not order all child care facilities to shut down.
match_headline: Some Banks Keep Customers’ Stimulus Checks if Accounts Are Overdrawn

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 58 misstates Alberta Ferretti’s title with Aeffe. She is the vice president and creative director, not the product director. The caption also misstates Stefano Canali’s title with Canali. He is the president and chief executive officer, not the general manager. And it misidentifies the brand for which Andrea Molteni is the director of product development. It is Molteni & C Dada, not Molteni & C.
match_headline: On Politics: Vice-Presidential Chatter

text: An article on Page 70 about alumni of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp misstates the years that the Belgian artist Luc Tuymans studied painting there. It was from 1978 to 1979, not 1980 to 1982.
match_headline: This Artist Proposes a Community Space ‘to Dream, to Imagine’

text: An article last Sunday about the FX series “Mrs. America” misstated the publication status of the historian Rick Perlstein’s book “The Invisible Bridge: The Fall of Nixon and the Rise of Reagan.” It has been published; it is not forthcoming.
match_headline: ‘Mrs. America’ Depicts a Different Kind of Feminist: The Anti- Kind

text: An article last Sunday about remote wine tastings misstated the starting time of a session on Thursdays held by the St. Supéry Estate Vineyards and Winery. It is 8:30 p.m. Eastern time, not 8:50 p.m.
match_headline: Raising a Glass, Remotely

text: An article last Sunday about the lack of assistance for cruise companies in the $2 trillion federal coronavirus relief package misstated the name of a trade group. It is the Cruise Lines International Association, not the Cruise Line Industry Association.
match_headline: Cruise Lines Were Shut Out of the Stimulus. Here’s Why.

text: Because of an editing error, the Calculator article last Sunday, about real estate television shows, misstated the given name of one of the stars of “Property Brothers.” He is Drew Scott, not Dave.
match_headline: How Long Does It Take to Binge-Watch Every Real Estate TV Show?

text: An article on Page 70 about alumni of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp misstates the years that the Belgian artist Luc Tuymans studied painting there. It was from 1978 to 1979, not 1980 to 1982.
match_headline: ‘#blackAF’ Review: A Second Portrait of the Artist, With More Scars

text: Because of an editing error, a letter to the editor on April 5 about voter representation in the United States Senate misstated the relative populations of California and Wyoming. California has more than 65 times as many people as Wyoming, not “almost four” times as many.
match_headline: Freddy the Pig and the Electoral College: Readers Respond

text: Because of an editing error, a review on April 5 about “A History of Islam in 21 Women,” by Hossein Kamaly, referred incorrectly to the schism that occurred after the death of Muhammad. It was the Shiites, not the Sunnis, who supported Muhammad’s daughter Fatima and her husband, Ali; the Sunnis did not believe that Fatima “should inherit leadership of the faith.”
ref_headline: A History of Islam in 21 Women,
match_headline: These Are the Faces of Muslim Women Throughout History

text: An article on Thursday about the way the coronavirus pandemic will be seen by history misstated the name of a Smithsonian museum in one instance. It is the National Museum of American History, not the Natural Museum of American History.
match_headline: What Historians Will See When They Look Back on the Covid-19 Pandemic of 2020

text: An article on Saturday misstated the age of Noah Bendig. It is 6, not 7. The article also misidentified the surname of Noah’s father. He is Jesper Hansen, not Bendig. (Noah uses his mother’s surname.)
match_headline: In Denmark, the Rarest of Sights: Classrooms Full of Students

text: An article on Monday about the 10th anniversary of the explosion on the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig referred incorrectly to Sandy Day. He is a man. Because of an editing error, the article also misidentified one of the positions held by Terry D. Garcia, a former deputy administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. He was also a member of the National Commission on the BP Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill and Offshore Drilling, not the United States Arctic Research Commission.
match_headline: Ten Years After Deepwater Horizon, U.S. Is Still Vulnerable to Catastrophic Spills

text: An article on Monday about the repercussions of the State Department’s expulsion of about 60 employees from five Chinese state media outlets misspelled the surname of a Washington Post journalist. She is Emily Rauhala, not Ruahala. The article also described incorrectly the departure of the Times reporter Chris Buckley from China. He was asked to leave after his visa expired; he was not expelled.
match_headline: The U.S. Tried to Teach China a Lesson About the Media. It Backfired.

text: An article on Saturday about the removal of Native American imagery from Land O’Lakes products misstated the name of the city where Land O’Lakes is based. It is Arden Hills, Minn., not Alden Hill.
match_headline: Land O’Lakes Removes Native American Woman From Its Products

text: An article on Monday about the impact of Hollywood’s shutdown on film workers misstated the name of the studio producing the film “Nightmare Alley.” It is Searchlight Pictures, not Fox Searchlight.
match_headline: Hollywood’s Specialized Backstage Workers Try to Soldier On

text: An article on Monday about Eva Holland’s book “Nerve” misstated the subtitle of the book as it appears in the edition published in the United States. It is “Adventures in the Science of Fear,” not “A Personal Journey Through the Science of Fear.”
match_headline: In ‘Nerve,’ Facing Up to Fears With an Assist From Science

text: Because of an editing error, a Metropolitan Diary entry on April 12 about a postal worker misspelled a contributor’s surname. He is Andrew Marotta, not Marrotta.
match_headline: ‘I Was Only Able to Enjoy My Daily Walks With a Pair of Hiking Poles’

text: An obituary on Friday about the actor Brian Dennehy misstated the year he and his first wife, Judith Scheff, divorced. It was 1987, not 1974. The obituary, using information from Mr. Dennehy’s agency, also misstated the year he married his second wife, Jennifer Arnott. It was 1988, not 1989.
match_headline: Brian Dennehy, Tony Award-Winning Actor, Dies at 81

text: An article on Tuesday about Israeli hospitals’ decision to allow family members to visit coronavirus wards misspelled part of the name of a coronavirus patient and her daughter. The patient is Batsheva Vita, not Zita, and her daughter is Rinat Vita-Dishlo, not Zita-Dishlo.
match_headline: ‘It’s Really a Gift’: Israeli Hospitals Let Relatives Say Goodbye Up Close

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about a $450 billion economic relief package misattributed a quotation to Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin. It was Senator Chuck Schumer who said on Sunday, “I’m very hopeful we could come to an agreement tonight or early tomorrow morning,” not Mr. Mnuchin.
ref_headline: I’m very hopeful we could come to an agreement tonight or early tomorrow morning,
match_headline: White House and Democrats Near Deal on Aid for Small Businesses

text: An article on Monday about the 25th anniversary of the bombing in Oklahoma City that killed 168 people misstated the military rank of Timothy McVeigh. He was an Army gunner with the rank of sergeant, not a gunnery sergeant, which is a Marine Corps rank.
match_headline: Oklahoma City Marks 25 Years Since America’s Deadliest Homegrown Attack

text: An article last Wednesday about Native Americans’ strategies for dealing with a food crisis gave an incomplete title for Denisa Livingston. She is the Slow Food International Indigenous councilor of the Global North, not a counselor with Slow Food International.
match_headline: How Native Americans Are Fighting a Food Crisis

text: An article on Tuesday about a unity government formed in Israel by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Benny Gantz referred imprecisely to West Bank territory that Mr. Netanyahu would like to annex. The land is occupied by Israel. The Palestinians want it for a future state, but do not have sovereignty over it.
match_headline: Netanyahu’s Power Is Extended as Rival Accepts Israel Unity Government

text: An article on Wednesday about the problems many independent restaurateurs have had in getting federal small-business relief misidentified the advocacy group that Thomas Keller and other chefs have formed to get insurance companies to pay claims for Covid-related shutdowns. It is the Business Interruption Group, not the Business Interruption Organization.
match_headline: Help Is On the Way, Restaurants Are Told. But Will It Work?

text: An article on Wednesday about the effects of President Trump’s decision to suspend some green cards misstated the position that Brad Smith holds at Microsoft. He is the company’s president, not its chief executive. It also misstated the number of employment-based green cards granted in 2018. It was 140,000, not 14,000.
match_headline: New Immigration Limits Cause Anxiety in Families and Businesses

text: An article on Wednesday about a new Senate report that undercuts claims by President Trump that Obama-era officials sought to undermine him while investigating Russia’s meddling in the 2016 election misstated the day the Senate Intelligence Committee released a report. It was Tuesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Republican-Led Review Backs Intelligence Findings on Russian Interference

text: An article on Monday about the effects of the coronavirus pandemic on the meat industry misstated the amount of meat in cold storage. There are hundreds of millions of pounds of beef, chicken and pork in storage, not hundreds of millions of tons.
match_headline: The Meat Business, a Big Contributor to Climate Change, Faces Major Tests

text: An article on Saturday about a public act of racism directed at the New York Rangers player K’Andre Miller described incorrectly the preparation leading up to a videoconference call on April 4 that included Renee Hess and Kim Davis, an N.H.L. executive. Hess asked Davis about her thoughts on the harassment of Miller for the first time while on a call organized by the Black Girls Hockey Club; Hess did not reach out by email ahead of the call to ask if Davis would address the Miller incident during it.
match_headline: A Black Hockey Player Faced Racial Taunts. Some Fans Aren’t Surprised.

text: An article on Tuesday about misinformation that arises from scientific research posted on preprint servers and read by the nonscientific community referred imprecisely to the posting of and subsequent revisions to a paper that studied how the new coronavirus endures on surfaces and in aerosols. While language in an introductory paragraph to the paper posted on medRxiv was revised, the authors did not back away from the central conclusions of their research.
match_headline: Coronavirus Tests Science’s Need for Speed Limits

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the restaurateur Sirio Maccioni, using information from a family friend, misstated the number of grandchildren who survive him. There are five, not two.
match_headline: Sirio Maccioni, Whose Le Cirque Drew Manhattan’s Elite, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Monday about the former Treasury secretary Paul H. O’Neill misstated the name and location of the school where he studied for a doctorate in economics. It was Claremont University College, not Claremont Graduate University (its name only since 1998), and it is in Claremont, Calif., not Pomona.
match_headline: Paul O’Neill, Treasury Secretary Who Clashed With Bush, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on April 9 about Linda Tripp, whose secret audiotapes of Monica Lewinsky led to the impeachment of President Bill Clinton, referred incorrectly to a grant of immunity that she received. Although she was granted federal immunity by Kenneth Starr, the independent prosecutor handling the Clinton investigation, a county judge in Maryland ruled that she was not protected from prosecution on state wiretapping charges. (Maryland’s chief state prosecutor nonetheless later dropped those charges.)
match_headline: Linda Tripp, Key Figure in Clinton Impeachment, Dies at 70

text: An article on Thursday about President Trump’s statement contradicting health officials’ projections about the likely return of coronavirus in the fall misstated what season it is in the Southern Hemisphere. It is autumn, not summer.
match_headline: Trump’s Scientists Push Back on His Claim That Virus May Not Return This Fall

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Thursday about the actress Shirley Knight misstated the category in which she won a Tony Award in 1976. It was best performance by a featured actress in a play, not best actress.
match_headline: Shirley Knight, Tony- and Emmy-Winning Actress, Dies at 83

text: An article on Friday about how President Trump is spending his time in the White House misstated which position with the Federal Reserve that Mr. Trump had proposed for his outside economic adviser Stephen Moore. The president had chosen him to serve on the Federal Reserve Board, not to serve as its chairman.
match_headline: Home Alone at the White House: A Sour President, With TV His Constant Companion

text: An article on Wednesday about women who are pregnant during the pandemic described incorrectly the legal status of home births in different states. Three-quarters of the country’s states allow licenses for midwives to practice out-of-hospital deliveries, including home births. Some states, like West Virginia and Georgia, do not offer licenses, making midwifery essentially illegal. Home births themselves are not illegal.
match_headline: Pregnant and Scared of ‘Covid Hospitals,’ They’re Giving Birth at Home

text: An article on Wednesday about unproven treatments for coronavirus patients mentioned by President Trump referred incorrectly to William N. Bryan. He is a science administrator in the federal government, not a scientist. It also misstated the substance consumed by a man and his wife in Arizona. They ingested a cleaning product that contained chloroquine, not a chemical found in the related compound hydroxychloroquine.
match_headline: Trump Muses About Light as Remedy, but Also Disinfectant, Which Is Dangerous

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the environmental victories and failures of the past 50 years, because of incorrect information supplied by the photo agency, misstated the time period. The initial picture of the New York City skyline was from the 1930s or 40s, not 1973.
match_headline: On the Market in New York City

text: An article on Wednesday about the Tenement Museum in Manhattan misidentified the family whose apartment is depicted with a table set for Shabbat dinner. It is the apartment of the Rogarshevsky family, not the Levines. It also misstated the year the Moore family lived in a building that is now part of the museum. It was in 1869, not in the 1890s.
match_headline: A Museum Devoted to Survivors Now Faces Its Own Fight to Live

text: An article on Aug. 25 about early country music recordings in southern Appalachia misstated the location of Jonesborough, Tenn., in relation to Johnson City, Tenn. It is about six miles west of Jonesborough, not east.
match_headline: In Southern Appalachia, Searching for the ‘Big Bang’ of Country Music

text: An article this weekend on Page 24 about Afghanistan referred imprecisely to the country’s reliance on foreign funding. Afghanistan relies on foreign funding for 75 percent of its public spending, not for its annual budget.
match_headline: No Fight Over Red Ink Now, but Virus Spending Will Force Tough Choices

text: An obituary on April 13 about the racecar driver Stirling Moss referred incorrectly to three cars he beat in 1961 to win the Monaco Grand Prix. They were six-cylinder Ferraris, not eight-cylinder. It also misstated the record he set in 1957. It was the Class F land speed record, not the world land speed record. And it referred incorrectly to the Austin he was given as a present when he was a boy. Although it is uncertain how much horsepower it had, it was more than seven.
match_headline: Stirling Moss, One of the Greatest Drivers of All Time, Dies at 90

text: An article last Sunday about the artwork of the chef Ficre Ghebreyesus misidentified the area where he spent his childhood. It was in Eritrea, in East Africa, not in North Africa.
match_headline: The Inventive Chef Who Kept His 700 Paintings Hidden

text: An article last Sunday about loudness in classical music misspelled the given name of a former music director of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. He was Georg Solti, not George.
match_headline: Loud, Louder, Loudest: How Classical Music Started to Roar

text: An article last Sunday about food tours misstated the food writer Diana Kennedy’s country of origin. She is British, not American.
match_headline: A Food Snob’s Food Tour Conversion

text: A review on April 12 of two novels about Mary Pinchot Meyer referred incorrectly to the C.I.A. history of Cord Meyer Jr., her former husband. He held management positions at the agency; he was not the chief of counterintelligence.
match_headline: A Real-Life J.F.K. Lover, Murdered in 1964, Stars in Two New Novels

text: A review on April 12 of “Thinking Inside the Box,” by Adrienne Raphel, misstated the surname of the first crossword tournament champion. She was Ruth von Phul, not van Phul.
match_headline: Here’s Looking at You, Grid: A History of Crosswords and Their Fans

text: An article in the April 5 issue about the cannabis industry misidentified Jack Herer. Herer was a cannabis activist, not a grower. (He did not grow commercial-scale cannabis.)
match_headline: Cannabis Scientists Are Chasing the Perfect High

text: An article in the April 12 issue about Weird Al Yankovic misstated part of a lyric from his song “White & Nerdy.” It is: “First in my class there at M.I.T.,” not “here at M.I.T.”
match_headline: The Weirdly Enduring Appeal of Weird Al Yankovic

text: An article on April 19 about life during the next year of the pandemic misidentified the source of an epidemiological model that estimated the United States would suffer 100,000 to 240,000 deaths during the coronavirus epidemic. The estimate was made by the White House, not the University of Washington’s Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation.
match_headline: The Coronavirus in America: The Year Ahead

text: An article on Monday about Yuri Dmitriev, who discovered a mass grave in Karelia from the Stalin era, misstated when a municipal court extended the detention of Mr. Dmitriev. It was late last month, not last week.
match_headline: He Found One of Stalin’s Mass Graves. Now He’s in Jail.

text: An article on Friday about Syrian officers on trial in Germany misstated the timing of Anwar Raslan’s defection to the opposition. He defected less than two years into the Syrian war, not less than a year into the conflict.
match_headline: Germany Takes Rare Step in Putting Syrian Officers on Trial in Torture Case

text: An article on Thursday about scammers taking advantage of the stimulus fund referred incorrectly to a figure given by Eva Velasquez of the Identity Theft Resource Center. Last month, the center experienced an 850 percent increase in total traffic, including calls, emails and website visits, and not in calls alone.
match_headline: ‘Pure Hell for Victims’ as Stimulus Programs Draw a Flood of Scammers

text: An article on Monday about people with disabilities who have been hired by call centers misstated the countries in which Alorica, an outsourcing company, closed its call centers. The company did not close its sites in the Philippines.
match_headline: Needing At-Home Workers, Call Centers Turn to People With Disabilities

text: An article on Saturday about the revelations gleaned from the N.F.L. draft misstated the number of players from the Southeastern Conference drafted in the first round. There were 15 players, not 17. It also misstated Clemson’s conference affiliation. Clemson is in the A.C.C., not the SEC.
match_headline: 2020 N.F.L. Draft: What We Learned

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the cast album of “Hair,” using information from Getty Images, misidentified the cast shown in the image. The cast pictured belonged to an Off Broadway staging, not the Broadway production.
match_headline: A Cast Album I Love: ‘Hair’

text: An obituary on Saturday about the former Federal Communications Commission official Henry Geller misstated the surname of the man whose letter to the commission inspired Mr. Geller to begin the process that led to the end of cigarette advertising on television and radio. He is John Banzhaf III, not Banzaf.
match_headline: Henry Geller, Who Helped Rid TV of Cigarette Ads, Dies at 96

text: An obituary on Friday about the photographer John Pfahl misstated Lisa Hostetler’s title at the George Eastman Museum in Rochester, N.Y., which has a large collection of Mr. Pfahl’s work. She is the curator in charge of the museum’s department of photography, not in charge of the museum.
match_headline: John Pfahl, Photographer Who Played With Landscapes, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Monday about the climate scientist Eunice Foote misstated the first name of the scientist who presented Ms. Foote’s work at the annual meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1856. He was Joseph Henry, not John.
match_headline: Overlooked No More: Eunice Foote, Climate Scientist Lost to History

text: An article on Tuesday about lawmakers and state officials who want more flexibility in spending federal emergency aid misstated the amount of money that bipartisan legislation provided for state and local governments. It was $500 billion, not million.
match_headline: Officials Say Limits on Virus Relief Funds for States Are Too Tight

text: An article on Tuesday about the lack of enforcement of the General Data Protection Regulation misstated which states have passed similar laws. New York is not among them.
match_headline: Europe’s Privacy Law Hasn’t Shown Its Teeth, Frustrating Advocates

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the former NASA administrator James M. Beggs misidentified the president under whom he served as under secretary of transportation. It was Richard M. Nixon, not Lyndon B. Johnson.
match_headline: James Beggs, 94, Is Dead; NASA Chief Championed Space Shuttle

text: An article on Saturday about some states that are allowing businesses to reopen misidentified the location of a drive-by protest in Atlanta. It was outside the Governor’s Mansion, not the governor’s office.
match_headline: Businesses Tiptoe Into a World of Masks, Gloves and Wary Customers

text: An article on Thursday about the suspension of Maggie Haney, a gymnastics coach, misspelled the surname of a lawyer who represented gymnasts involved in the case against Ms. Haney. She is Judie Saunders, not Sanders.
match_headline: Maggie Haney, Elite Gymnastics Coach, Is Suspended for 8 Years

text: An article on Sunday about Tim Duncan’s signature bank shot included a quote that implied John “Hot Rod” Williams was still alive. He died in 2015.
match_headline: Tim Duncan to Springfield? Take It to the Bank

text: An article on Wednesday about the legacy of the D.J. and producer Mike Huckaby misstated one of the Detroit dance-music figures that worked at Record Time. Mike Servito did not work at the store.
match_headline: Remembering Mike Huckaby, a Towering Figure in Detroit House Music

text: An article on Friday about the overnight closing of New York’s subway referred imprecisely to the city’s public transit schedule. It is the only system in the United States that runs all of its train lines 24 hours a day; it is not the only system in the country to operate 24 hours a day.
match_headline: N.Y.C.’s Subway, a 24/7 Mainstay, Will Close for Overnight Disinfection

text: An article on Page 6 about the filmmaker Alice Wu misstates the given name of her firefighter friend. It is CJ, not TJ.
match_headline: Alice Wu’s Lesbian Rom-Com Was Influential, but Her Follow-Up Wasn’t Easy

text: An article on Page 15 about the future of art biennials misstates the titles of Natasha Ginwala and Defne Ayas at the Gwangju Biennale. They are co-artistic directors, not co-curators. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Art Biennials Were Testing Grounds. Now They Are Being Tested.

text: An article on April 12 about the first Covid-19 survivor in New Jersey referred incorrectly to chloroquine: It is an antimalarial drug, not an antiviral drug.
match_headline: How New Jersey’s First Coronavirus Patient Survived

text: Because of a production error, a cover article on Saturday about the effects of the coronavirus on the production of oil in the Permian Basin included columns of type that were out of order.
match_headline: ‘This Feels Very Different’

text: An article on Sunday about couples who have died from Covid-19 misspelled the North Carolina town in which Lois King was raised. It is Ahoskie, not Ohaskie.
match_headline: After a Lifetime Together, Coronavirus Takes Them Both

text: An article on Sunday about Shady Habash, a filmmaker who died in an Egyptian prison, misstated his age. He was 24, not 22.
match_headline: Filmmaker Who Mocked Egypt’s President Dies in Prison

text: An article on Thursday about a virtual tour of Midtown’s skyscrapers with the engineer Guy Nordenson, using information from Mr. Nordenson, misidentified the structural engineer in charge of 432 Park and referred incorrectly to the project’s influences. The structural engineer in charge was Silvian Marcus of WSP, not Ahmad Rahimian, a colleague at the same firm. And the work was not influenced by Bill Baker from Skidmore, Owings & Merrill.
match_headline: The Hidden Feats That Built New York’s Towering Skyscrapers

text: An article on Monday about a lawsuit brought by Howardena Pindell against the N’Namdi family misstated the year Garth Greenan began representing Howardena Pindell. It was 2012, not 2014. (2014 was the year he had his first exhibition of her work).
match_headline: Helping Black Artists, But at What Price?

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Sunday about the Motown Records executive Barney Ales misstated the year that a picture of Mr. Ales and Marvin Gaye was taken. It was taken sometime after 1968, not in 1961.
match_headline: Emissions Declines Will Set Records This Year. But It’s Not Good News.

text: An article on Friday about an increase in global poverty misstated how many people were lifted from poverty in India from 2006 to 2016, according to the United Nations. The number was 271 million people, not 210 million.
match_headline: Millions Had Risen Out of Poverty. Coronavirus Is Pulling Them Back.

text: An article on Tuesday about a fund-raising conference organized by the European Union misstated the given name of the director of Chatham House, the think tank. He is Robin Niblett, not Robert.
match_headline: World Leaders Join to Pledge $8 Billion for Vaccine as U.S. Goes It Alone

text: An article on Tuesday about a study’s finding that billions could live in extreme heat zones within decades misidentified the university where Timothy A. Kohler is employed. He is an archaeologist at Washington State University, not the University of Washington.
match_headline: Billions Could Live in Extreme Heat Zones Within Decades, Study Finds

text: An article on Monday about the effect of activists on the media industry referred incorrectly to the circumstances in which a union official recalled coaching newly organized journalists about picketing. It was during a demonstration for a contract with the legal news site Law360, not during an organizing drive.
match_headline: How a New Breed of Union Activists Is Changing the Rules (and Newsrooms)

text: An article on Monday about Rich Jackson, the former editor of The Herald-Times, misstated when he was laid off. It was April 24, not April 29.
match_headline: Newspaper’s Top Editor Is Now a ‘Homeless’ Blogger

text: An article on Tuesday about wastewater that could provide localized data about the rise and fall of coronavirus levels misspelled the name of a company that tracks pathogens in wastewater. It is BioBot, not BioBiot.
match_headline: Is It Safe to Come Out of Lockdown? Check the Sewer

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Tuesday about the football coach Don Shula misstated the year that he and the Baltimore Colts lost to the Jets in Super Bowl III. It was 1969, not 1971.
match_headline: Don Shula, N.F.L. Coach Who Won, and Won, and Won, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Thursday about the artist Norman Gulamerian misstated the name of the school in Brooklyn that inspired the name of the art supply company he and his brother founded. It is New Utrecht High School, not Utrecht High School.
match_headline: Norman Gulamerian, Artist With a Grand Passion, Dies at 92

text: An article on Wednesday about an increase in coronavirus cases in U.S. cities beyond New York misspelled the surname of the wife of an imam who has counseled workers at meatpacking plants. She is Qudsia Hussaini, not Hussein.
match_headline: With New Hot Spots Emerging, No Sign of a Respite

text: An article on Tuesday about an announcement from the Carnival Corporation that some of its ships may begin sailing again as soon as August misidentified the spokeswoman for Norwegian Cruise Line. She is Maria Elena Monasterios, not Maria Elena.
match_headline: Carnival Plans to Sail Again in August, Maybe

text: An article on Wednesday about the pandemic’s impact on companies’ first-quarter results misstated the month when Starbucks’ fiscal fourth quarter ends. It is the end of September, not October.
match_headline: After a Terrible First Quarter, Executives Offer Some Hope

text: An obituary on April 11 about the art dealer Paul Kasmin misidentified the photographer Aaron Rose, whose work Mr. Kasmin exhibited at his gallery in SoHo. He is not the same Aaron Rose who owned the downtown gallery Alleged.
match_headline: Paul Kasmin, Gallerist Who Ruled a Mini-Empire of Art, Dies at 60

text: An article on Thursday about the risks of gathering in cooling centers during the pandemic misstated the number of people sleeping without shelter in Phoenix. A survey in January counted almost 4,000 in all of Maricopa County, which includes Phoenix, not in the city of Phoenix alone.
match_headline: Coronavirus Makes Cooling Centers Risky, Just as Scorching Weather Hits

text: An article on Friday about countries’ efforts to safely reopen their economies misstated the surname of the director of the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University. He is Tom Inglesby, not Tom Inglesbury.
match_headline: Reopenings Mark a New Phase: Global ‘Trial-and-Error’ Played Out in Lives

text: An article on Thursday about a letter to the National Archives by President Obama misquoted the letter. It said that Mr. Obama’s office would offer the records the Senate had requested “in the interest of countering the misinformation campaign,” not “undermining the misinformation campaign.”
ref_headline: in the interest of countering the misinformation campaign,
match_headline: Obama Says G.O.P.’s Biden Inquiry Promotes ‘Russian Disinformation’

text: An obituary on Thursday about the mezzo-soprano Rosalind Elias misidentified the opera company that mounted the premiere of “The Grapes of Wrath” in 2007, in which she sang. It was the Minnesota Opera, not the Michigan Opera Theater.
match_headline: Rosalind Elias, a Popular American Mezzo-Soprano, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Friday about the poet Michael McClure misstated part of the name of the school, now the San Francisco Art Institute, where he had once hoped to study. It was the California School of Fine Arts, not the California Institute of Fine Arts. The obituary, using information from Mr. McClure’s family, also misstated the year of his marriage to Amy Evans. It was 1997, not 1998.
match_headline: Michael McClure, Present at Beat Poetry’s Birth, Dies at 87

text: A headline with an article on Saturday about court records related to Tara Reade’s work in Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s Senate office misstated what Ms. Reade told her ex-husband during the 1990s, according to court records. As the article correctly noted, Ms. Reade, according to the records, said that she had been a victim of sexual harassment while working in Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s Senate office, not that Mr. Biden himself had harassed her.
match_headline: In Court Document, Tara Reade’s Ex-Husband Said She Spoke of Harassment

text: An article on March 22 about the co-working space Wing described incorrectly a married couple’s connection to it. The two women were engaged at a Wing location; they did not meet there.
match_headline: The Wing Is a Women’s Utopia. Unless You Work There.

text: An article on Sunday about a claim by President Trump’s supporters that federal guidelines are coaching doctors to inflate the pandemic’s death toll misidentified the Fox-affiliated television station where Chris Berg as a host. It is West Dakota Fox, not KX4. While KX4 also carries Mr. Berg’s program, it is a CBS affiliate.
match_headline: Fight Over Virus’s Death Toll Opens Grim New Front in Election Battle

text: An article on Sunday about the debate on spending recovery funds to quickly restore the old economy or invest in a greener one misspelled the last name of a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. He is Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, not Kierkegaard.
match_headline: Will the Coronavirus Crisis Trump the Climate Crisis?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about murder charges filed against two men for the fatal shooting of Ahmaud Arbery in Georgia misspelled the given name of Mr. Arbery’s mother. She is Wanda Cooper, not Wander.
match_headline: 2 Suspects Charged With Murder in Ahmaud Arbery Shooting

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about race relations in Brunswick, Ga., misstated the surname of Georgia’s attorney general. He is Chris Carr, not Chris Cox.
match_headline: In Ahmaud Arbery’s Hometown, Pain, Anger and Pride in a Shared Racial History

text: An article on Monday about money in dependent care accounts described incorrectly a consequence of forfeiting unspent money from such an account. Individuals will not be required to pay taxes on the amount.
match_headline: There’s Money Stuck in Your Dependent Care Account. Now What?

text: An article on Friday about musicals from the 1940s misspelled the given name of one of Hollywood’s leading actors of the era. He was Cary Grant, not Gary.
match_headline: Escape With Me Into the Delirious World of 1940s Musicals

text: An obituary on Saturday about the artist Satish Gujral misstated the name of the publication that published a tribute to him by the artist Krishen Khanna. It is The Indian Express, not India Express.
match_headline: Satish Gujral, Versatile Indian Artist, Is Dead at 94

text: An obituary on Saturday about the singer Millie Small misstated the name of the newspaper that Chris Blackwell, the producer of her hit “My Boy Lollipop,” told she had suffered a stroke. It is The Jamaica Observer, not The Jamaican Observer.
match_headline: Millie Small, ‘My Boy Lollipop’ Singer, Is Dead at 73

text: An article on Tuesday about the soccer player Andrés Iniesta misidentified the location of his childhood home. It is Albacete, Spain, not Asturias.
match_headline: Andrés Iniesta Plots a Return to Barcelona, Where the Beauty Is Gone

text: An article on Sunday about the end of past pandemics misstated the name of a prominent influenza doctor in 1918. He was Victor Vaughan, not William Vaughan.
match_headline: How Pandemics End

text: An article on Tuesday about surfers who were found dead on a Dutch beach inaccurately rendered a quote attributed to Yannick de Jager. He said the North Sea is “a fickle bitch,” not “a thicker beach.”
match_headline: Several Surfers Are Found Dead in the Netherlands

text: Because of an editing error, a book review on Tuesday of “Rodham” described incorrectly the relationship between Thomas Haden Church’s character in “Sideways” and a woman in the movie. He failed to tell her that he was engaged to be married, he did not cheat on her.
match_headline: Reader, She Didn’t Marry Him. Curtis Sittenfeld’s ‘Rodham’ Reimagines Hillary.

text: An article on Wednesday about the comic actor Jerry Stiller’s legacy misstated where he worked with the Compass Players. It was in St. Louis, not Chicago.
match_headline: In Jerry Stiller, the Rage of Jewish Fathers Found a Hilarious Outlet

text: An obituary on Sunday about Little Richard misidentified the producer of his first session for Specialty Records. It was Bumps Blackwell — not Art Rupe, the founder of the company. The obituary also misspelled the name of a street in Atlanta where Little Richard performed early in his career. It is Decatur Street, not Decautur.
match_headline: Little Richard, Flamboyant Wild Man of Rock ’n’ Roll, Dies at 87

text: An article on Wednesday about the potential impacts that Manhattan would face if companies decide to let their employees work from home permanently misspelled the name of the owner of Aux Epices restaurant. She is Mei Chau, not Mei Cahu.
match_headline: Manhattan Faces a Reckoning if Working From Home Becomes the Norm

text: An article on Thursday about the reopening of European countries before the summer travel season misstated what had been the projected value of cross-border travel in Europe in 2020. It was 1.3 trillion euros, or $1.4 trillion, not 1.3 billion euros.
match_headline: Across Europe, Reopening Borders in Time for Summer

text: An article on Thursday about the response by Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany to a Russian hack misattributed responsibility for a 2016 cyberattack in which 900,000 Germans lost access to internet and telephone services. The attack was carried out by a British citizen, not Russia. The article also misstated when the attack took place. It was in November, not December.
match_headline: Merkel Is ‘Outraged’ by Russian Hack but Struggling to Respond

text: An article on April 30 about newly revealed court documents that unveiled private exchanges between President Trump’s longtime friend Roger Stone and the WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange referred incorrectly to Mr. Assange’s response to the special counsel investigation by Robert S. Mueller III. He did not refuse to cooperate; his lawyers said that investigators on that team never contacted him.
match_headline: Roger Stone Was in Contact With Julian Assange in 2017, Documents Show

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about shortages of staple items at grocery stories in New York lacked context and could have left readers with the impression that Morton Williams stores have been emptied of their inventory. The image was taken in March, shortly after the city’s shutdown began. It does not reflect the current situation at Morton Williams stores.
match_headline: Gone From Grocery Shelves, Now There’s a Mad Dash to Find Them

text: An article on Friday about threats to the movie theater industry and innovations that might revive it misstated the expected release date of the film “Jurassic World: Dominion.” It is the summer of 2021, not this summer.
match_headline: Movie Theaters Are on the Brink. Can Wine and Cheese Save Them?

text: An article on Tuesday about concerns in the scientific community about a quick reopening of the U.S. economy relied on outdated figures to compare testing in New York, California and Texas. At the time the article was published, New York had tested more than three times as many people as had Texas on a per capita basis, not five times as many.
match_headline: As States Rush to Reopen, Scientists Fear a Coronavirus Comeback

text: An article on Page 13 about the TNT series “Snowpiercer” misstates the class status of Andre Layton, the character played by Daveed Diggs. Layton is a member of the bottom class, known as tailies, not the third class, which is higher.
match_headline: On Track for the Apocalypse, ‘Snowpiercer’ Comes to Television

text: A map on Page 22 accompanying the editor’s letter reverses the placement of two Chinese cities. Tianshui is east of Zhangye, not west.
match_headline: A Poetic Journey Through Western China

text: An article on Page 57 about depictions of the Buddha misstates the century during which the monk Kumarajiva lived. It was the fourth century A.D., not the fourth century B.C.
match_headline: How the Buddha Got His Face

text: An article last Sunday about artist residencies misstated the relationship between Coady Brown and Pat Phillips. She is his partner, not his wife.
match_headline: Alone With Their Muses, Artists in Retreat Wonder if It’s Too Much

text: An article on May 3 about “I Know This Much Is True,” using information from a publicist, misstated the surname of a person whom Mark Ruffalo consulted during the development of the series. He is Richard Wiedeman, not Wheaton.
ref_headline: I Know This Much Is True,
match_headline: Mark Ruffalo Fights (and Comforts) Himself for ‘I Know This Much Is True’

text: Because of an editing error, a review on May 3 about Ann Clare LeZotte’s historical novel “Show Me a Sign” referred incorrectly to Martha’s Vineyard Sign Language. It preceded and influenced the development of American Sign Language; it is not a combination of A.S.L. and “home sign.”
match_headline: A Deaf Girl Finds Her Voice on Martha’s Vineyard in the 19th Century

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the coronavirus pandemic prompting people to move from New York City to the suburbs misidentified a street in Weston, Conn. It is Lyons Plain Road, not Blueberry Road.
match_headline: Travel From New York City Seeded Wave of U.S. Outbreaks

text: An article on Saturday about the allocation of coronavirus relief funds to private and religious schools by Education Secretary Betsy DeVos misstated a school’s action on money allocated for it. The Wright Graduate University for the Realization of Human Potential was allocated about $495,000, but it did not claim it.
match_headline: DeVos Funnels Coronavirus Relief Funds to Favored Private and Religious Schools

text: An article on Saturday about tensions between the United States and China over the handling of the pandemic misspelled the surname of the scholar at Harvard’s Weatherhead Center for International Affairs. He is Julian Gewirtz, not Gerwirtz.
match_headline: From ‘Respect’ to ‘Sick and Twisted’: How Coronavirus Hit U.S.-China Ties

text: An article on Saturday about the threats and violence retail workers have encountered when attempting to enforce face mask rules misstated the name of a Trader Joe’s customer. She is Genevieve Peters, not Powers.
match_headline: Who’s Enforcing Mask Rules? Often Retail Workers, and They’re Getting Hurt

text: An article on Sunday about closed New York City beaches misspelled the surname of a spokeswoman for Mayor Bill de Blasio. She is Jane Meyer, not Mayer.
match_headline: Summer Is Coming. Don’t Count on N.Y.C.’s Beaches for Relief.

text: An article on Thursday about an outbreak among a choir in Washington misstated Lea Hamner’s academic credentials. Ms. Hamner has a master’s degree in public health, not a doctorate.
match_headline: Coronavirus Ravaged a Choir. But Isolation Helped Contain It.

text: An article on Monday about weaknesses in some of Ronan Farrow’s reporting misstated the month of Harvey Weinstein’s conviction. It was in February, not January.
match_headline: Is Ronan Farrow Too Good to Be True?

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor Fred Willard misspelled the surname of the playwright whose play “Little Murders” was produced Off Broadway with Mr. Willard in the cast. He is Jules Feiffer, not Pfeiffer.
match_headline: Fred Willard, Who Played Characters ‘Gloriously Out of Their Depth,’ Dies at 86

text: An article on Monday about a possible connection between air pollution and Covid-19 referred incorrectly to Chevron’s air-monitoring efforts around the Richmond refinery. According to Braden Reddall, a company spokesman, Chevron monitors 10 chemical compounds at three fence-line locations at the refinery and tracks additional compounds at three other locations in the community. It does not monitor five chemical compounds at three locations.
match_headline: In the Shadows of America’s Smokestacks, Virus Is One More Deadly Risk

text: An article on Tuesday about the lack of federal aid distributed to minority-run businesses described incorrectly the findings from a survey of minority-owned businesses that had sought federal pandemic aid. The survey asked them about all Small Business Administration relief efforts, not just the Paycheck Protection Program.
match_headline: Few Minority-Owned Businesses Got Relief Loans They Asked For

text: An article on Tuesday about countries that are unable to repay debts to China misstated the name of Chen Long’s research firm. It is Plenum, not Primus.
match_headline: Poor Countries Borrowed Billions from China. They Can’t Pay It Back.

text: An article on Tuesday about Fred Willard’s most memorable roles referred incorrectly to the streaming availability of the film “Best in Show.” It is no longer available on the streaming service Sundance Now.
match_headline: Best in Show: Watch Fred Willard’s Most Memorable Roles

text: An article on April 26 about Road Scholar, a nonprofit travel organization, misspelled the surname of one of its frequent clients. His name is Ken Gallaher, not Gallagher.
match_headline: Amid a Sea of Vouchers, Road Scholar Offers Cash

text: An article on Wednesday about difficulties faced by Prime Minister Boris Johnson of Britain in Parliament misspelled the given name of the speaker of the House of Commons. He is Lindsay Hoyle, not Lyndsey Hoyle.
match_headline: For Boris Johnson, Parliament Is Becoming a House of Horrors

text: An article on Tuesday about the career outlook for young adults entering the job market in an economic downturn misstated the graduation years of the subjects of a study by Lisa B. Kahn of the University of Rochester. She studied white men who left college between 1979 and 1988, not in 1979 and 1980.
match_headline: Facing Adulthood With an Economic Disaster’s Lasting Scars

text: An article on Wednesday about what to watch on television referred incorrectly to the streaming availability of the film “How to Build a Girl.” It is not available on the streaming service IFC Films Unlimited.
match_headline: What’s on TV Wednesday: Ben Platt Live and ‘At Home With Amy Sedaris’

text: An article last Thursday about Melissa DeRosa, who is the top aide to Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo of New York, misstated Matt Wing’s role at Uber in 2015. He was a senior communications officer there at that time; he was not among the company’s lobbyists as it sought expansion in the state.
match_headline: Who Can Say ‘No’ to Cuomo? His Top Aide, Melissa DeRosa

text: An article on Wednesday about virtual dance performances and classes misstated the name of Bill T. Jones’s company. It is the Bill T. Jones/Arnie Zane Company, not the Bill T. Jones/Arnie Zane Dance Company.
match_headline: DanceAfrica, Dormeshia and Contact Improvisation (for One)

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a grant given to the drug company AstraZeneca misstated the partial results announced by the biotech company Moderna from a first-phase trial of a vaccine it is developing. The vaccine candidate produced an immune response in the first 45 study participants, the company said, not just in 8.
match_headline: $1.2 Billion From U.S. to Drugmaker to Pursue Coronavirus Vaccine

text: An article on Friday about missed commercial rent payments misstated the name of one of the city’s biggest commercial landlords. It is Vornado Realty Trust, not Vornado Property Trust.
match_headline: New Threat to New York City: Commercial Rent Payments Plummet

text: An article on May 17 about a business mogul in Norway who was charged with murdering his wife misstated the age of Tommy Broske, a police officer. He is 42, not 48.
match_headline: A Mogul’s Wife Vanishes. Now Norway Has a National Obsession.

text: An article on Feb. 22 about the Shincheonji Church of Jesus, a church at the center of a coronavirus outbreak in South Korea, referred imprecisely to church gatherings. At meetings, former members say, they were discouraged from wearing glasses or face masks; they were not forbidden to wear them.
match_headline: Shadowy Church Is at Center of Coronavirus Outbreak in South Korea

text: An article on Friday about the future of Hong Kong misstated when Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese leader who was the architect of the “one country, two systems” formula for the city, guaranteed the former British colony’s way of life for 50 years after its handover. It was in 1984, when China and Britain negotiated the handover agreement, not when the 1997 handover took place. (Deng died on Feb. 19, 1997, more than four months before the July 1 handover.)
match_headline: What Happens to Hong Kong Now?

text: An article on Friday about the effect of global warming on dams misstated one aspect of designing dams as the climate changes. Spillways may need to be designed to handle larger volumes of water over long time periods, not lesser volumes.
match_headline: ‘Expect More’: Climate Change Raises Risk of Dam Failures

text: An article on Page 5 about the choreographer Bill T. Jones misstated the name of his company. It is the Bill T. Jones/Arnie Zane Company, not the Bill T. Jones/Arnie Zane Dance Company.
match_headline: Bill T. Jones Knows Life Will Change, and His Art Too

text: An article this weekend on Page 34 about living in France during the pandemic misstated the date of Pierre Mendès-France’s book “Liberté, liberté chérie.” It was published in 1943, not 1977.
match_headline: Adopting a Pet in California During a Pandemic

text: An article on Page 5 about the choreographer Bill T. Jones misstated the name of his company. It is the Bill T. Jones/Arnie Zane Company, not the Bill T. Jones/Arnie Zane Dance Company.
An article on May 10 about voting during the pandemic referred incorrectly to one aspect of judicial elections in Wisconsin. Only one — not four — of the judicial seats up for election was statewide.
match_headline: Will Americans Lose Their Right to Vote in the Pandemic?

text: An article on Monday about the implications of China’s move to control Hong Kong misstated the timing of the recent arrests of pro-democracy leaders in Hong Kong. They were arrested in April, not a week ago.
match_headline: Why China’s Move to Rein In Hong Kong Is Just the Start

text: An article on Tuesday about campaigning for president during the 2008 financial crisis misstated what term John McCain was serving as a senator from Arizona when the 2008 campaign started. It was his fourth, not his sixth. (He ultimately served for six terms in the Senate.)
match_headline: Campaigning in a Crisis: Obama, McCain and the 2008 Meltdown

text: An article on Monday about Tristan da Cunha, a volcanic island that sits in the remote waters of the South Atlantic, misspelled one of the seven family names shared among the island’s inhabitants. It is Hagan, not Hagen.
match_headline: A Visual Dispatch From One of the World’s Most Remote Islands

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about antigovernment protests in Baghdad misstated the month in which the picture was taken. It was November, not October.
match_headline: U.N. Documents Abductions and Torture Of Iraqi Protesters

text: An article on Monday about a 20-year prison sentence given to President Desi Bouterse of Suriname, who was convicted of murder, misstated the years that Mr. Bouterse was elected and re-elected to the presidency. They were 2010 and 2015, not 2000 and 2005.
match_headline: Suriname’s President Shrugs Off Murder Sentence in Re-election Bid

text: An article on Monday about a recreation of the Aston Martin from the classic film “Goldfinger” misstated the name of a “continuation” model built by Jaguar. The automaker built a car called XKSS, not XJSS.
match_headline: James Bond’s Car Comes to Life With Oil-Slick Sprayer, but No Ejector Seat

text: An article on Monday about new ways that technology has allowed celebrities to monetize their brand misstated the title of a podcast run by Sofia Franklyn and Alexandra Cooper. It is “Call Her Daddy,” not “Call Your Daddy.”
match_headline: The New Model Media Star Is Famous Only to You

text: A picture caption with an article on May 15 about the literary festival Afrolit Sans Frontieres misspelled the name of a writer. She is Ayesha Harruna Attah, not Ayesha Harunna Atta.
match_headline: An African Literary Festival for the Age of Coronavirus

text: An article on Wednesday about the conclusion of a Justice Department inquiry into the stock transactions of three senators misstated the number of senators who were under investigation and up for election this year. Both Senator Kelly Loeffler of Georgia and Senator James M. Inhofe of Oklahoma are running to hold their seats, not just Ms. Loeffler.
match_headline: Justice Dept. Ends Inquiries Into 3 Senators’ Stock Trades

text: An article on Wednesday about Charlatan, a racehorse and Belmont Stakes contender that tested positive for lidocaine, misspelled the surname of a managing partner of Starlight Stables. He is Jack Wolf, not Jack Wolfe.
match_headline: Charlatan, a Belmont Stakes Contender, Tests Positive for a Banned Substance

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about plans by the N.H.L. to resume its season with a playoff format omitted one of the cities under consideration to host the playoffs. Vancouver is among them.
match_headline: N.H.L. Announces Plan to Return Straight Into the Playoffs

text: An article on Saturday about Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s struggle to adapt to a virtual campaign misidentified the state President Trump was visiting when the song “Live and Let Die” was playing during his visit to a factory. It was Arizona, not Pennsylvania.
match_headline: Biden’s Online Campaign Is Still Loading

text: An article on Friday about the activation of the National Guard amid protests in Minneapolis referred incorrectly to Kirsten Delegard’s employer. She works for the Mapping Prejudice project at the University of Minnesota, but she is not a professor there or at Augsburg University.
match_headline: National Guard Called as Minneapolis Erupts in Solidarity for George Floyd

text: An article on Friday about the prospect of a cutoff of coronavirus-related government aid programs misstated the city where Julie Glasser was laid off from a vacation-rental start-up. It is Portland, Ore., not Seattle.
match_headline: Millions Relying on Pandemic Aid Can See Its End, and They’re Scared

text: An item about cats in The Conversation on Friday misidentified the breed of a cat in a photo. It was a Bengal cat, not a toyger.
match_headline: You Thought Your Cat Was Fancy?

text: An article on Friday about Prime Minister Mark Rutte of the Netherlands misspelled the surname of a former Dutch Labor Party leader. He is Diederik Samsom, not Samson.
match_headline: Playing by the Rules: Dutch Leader Offers a Sober Contrast in a Brash Era

text: An article on Friday about the pandemic’s effect on partisanship in the United States misstated the size of the stimulus bill adopted in late March. It was $2.2 trillion, not $2.2 billion.
match_headline: Does a Crisis Spur Political Unity? Not This Pandemic

text: An article this weekend on Page 12 about the Netflix series “The Baby-Sitters Club” refers imprecisely to Lucia Aniello’s role. She is one of several executive producers; she is not its sole executive producer. It also misstated when Aniello and Rachel Shukert met. They met during the development of “The Baby-Sitters Club,” not while working together on the wrestling comedy “GLOW.”
match_headline: ‘The Baby-Sitters Club’ Is Back: Help Yourself to the Fridge

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 14 about new television shows coming this summer misidentified Jonathan Zaccaï and Mathieu Amalric. Mr. Zaccaï is at left and Mr. Amalric is at the right, not the reverse.
match_headline: 15 Summer TV Shows We’re Looking Forward To

text: An obituary on May 6 about the artist Zarina Hashmi misstated who organized the exhibition “Zarina: Dark Roads” at New York University. It was Alexandra Chang and Ms. Hashmi, not Sarah Burney. The obituary also neglected to credit Ms. Burney as the co-author of Ms. Hashmi’s memoir, “Directions to My House.”
match_headline: Zarina Hashmi, Artist of a World in Search of Home, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Thursday about the motivational speaker and author Barbara Sher misstated part of the name of a company she founded in the 1970s. It was Women’s Success Teams, not Women Success Teams.
match_headline: Barbara Sher, 84, Dies; Prescribed Self-Help With a Dose of Humor

text: A picture caption with an article on May 17 about a funeral home adapting to the pandemic misstated what is shown in the image. Sal Farenga, an owner of the funeral home, was taking a casket into the funeral home; he was not taking in the body of a Covid-19 victim.
match_headline: How Do You Maintain Dignity for the Dead in a Pandemic?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about interactions between George Floyd and Derek Chauvin, the officer now charged with Mr. Floyd’s death, misidentified the individual who sometimes acted aggressively while working at a nightclub. It was Mr. Chauvin, not Mr. Floyd.
match_headline: What Happened in the Chaotic Moments Before George Floyd Died

text: An article on Sunday about the resistance faced by efforts to hold police officers accountable misspelled the surname of an expert on police training and discipline at the John Jay College of Criminal Justice in New York. She is Maria Haberfeld, not Haberman.
match_headline: Thousands of Complaints Do Little to Change Police Ways

text: An article on Saturday about Senator Amy Klobuchar’s record as a Minnesota prosecutor misstated when Ms. Klobuchar called for charges against Mr. Cauvin. She first mentioned the need for charges on Tuesday, not Friday.
match_headline: Protests in Minnesota Renew Scrutiny of Klobuchar’s Record as Prosecutor

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the American priest who founded the Knights of Columbus omitted his given name. He was the Rev. Michael J. McGivney.
match_headline: Knights of Columbus Founder, Who Died in a Pandemic, Moves Closer to Sainthood

text: An article on May 25 about the Bugatti Chiron misspelled a make of car. It is a McLaren, not a McClaren.
match_headline: This Car’s Yearly Tune-Up Costs as Much as a Civic

text: A recipe for carne asada cheese fries, accompanying an article last Wednesday about 12 popular American restaurants, omitted the ingredients for serving. They are 1/2 cup finely chopped yellow or white onion, 1/2 cup chopped fresh cilantro leaves and 1 tablespoon fresh lime juice, mixed together for a garnish, and 1 1/2 pounds homemade French fries or any fresh or frozen fried potato variety, such as home fries, waffle fries, curly fries or Tater Tots. Finally, the dish is served with extra lime wedges and an optional Crema Mexicana or sour cream.
match_headline: That Dish, That Restaurant: Vivid Memories to Savor

text: An obituary on Saturday about the Jamaican record producer Bobby Digital misstated at one point part of the name of a performer he worked with. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, he is Bounty Killer, not Bounty Hunter.
match_headline: Bobby Digital Dies at 59; His Reggae Rhythms Spread Worldwide

text: An obituary on Sunday about the wheelchair athlete Margaret Maughan misspelled the surname of the neurologist who is considered the father of the Paralympic movement. He was Ludwig Guttmann, not Guttman.
match_headline: Margaret Maughan, Medal-Winning Wheelchair Athlete, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Monday about the former congressman Sam Johnson, using information from his family, misstated the year he received a master’s degree from the Elliott School of International Affairs at George Washington University. It was 1974, not 1976.
match_headline: Sam Johnson, Congressman and Former P.O.W., Is Dead at 89

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about the artist Christo misstated the year that the photo of him at the site of his work “The Floating Piers,” on Lake Iseo in Italy, was taken. It was 2015, not 2016.
match_headline: Christo, Artist Who Wrapped and Festooned on an Epic Scale, Dies at 84

text: An article on Wednesday about protests against police brutality evolving into a nationwide movement with diverse interests and tactics misidentified the location of an episode at a protest in Baltimore. It was outside City Hall, not outside the governor’s mansion.
match_headline: March Peacefully or ‘Take the Streets’? Protesters Debate What Comes Next

text: An article on Tuesday about similarities between the current demonstrations in the United States and those of the Arab Spring referred incorrectly to the involvement of the Egyptian writer and activist Ahdaf Soueif in a recent street protest in Cairo. She participated in the protest; she did not lead it.
match_headline: In Egypt, Images From American Protests Evoke a Lost Revolution

text: An article on Wednesday about the Pennsylvania primaries viewed as a “dry run” for the election in November described incorrectly a Pennsylvania law that aims to make it easier for voters to receive mail-in ballots for the November election. Anyone who voted by mail in the state’s June 2 primary election was able to check a box to request a mail-in ballot for November; the law did not mandate that those voters would automatically be sent a November ballot.
match_headline: What Pennsylvania’s ‘Dry Run’ Election Could Reveal About November

text: An article on Wednesday about the closing of the Metropolitan Opera for the rest of the season misidentified the director of a canceled production of “Fidelio.” He was Jürgen Flimm, not Herbert Wernicke.
match_headline: Crowds Define Opera. They’re Also Keeping It From Returning.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the photographer Elsa Dorfman misstated the status of the 20x24 Studio, a Massachusetts company that acquired the Polaroid materials she used. It remains open; it did not close.
match_headline: Elsa Dorfman, Who Made Art With Giant Polaroids, Dies at 83

text: An obituary on May 27 about the author Anthony Bailey misstated the surname of a priest about whom he wrote in the 1950s. He was Ivan Illich, not Ilyich.
match_headline: Anthony Bailey, Biographer With Restless Literary Spirit, Dies at 87

text: An article on Wednesday about the shortcomings of the C.D.C. exposed by the pandemic, in describing the institution’s data practices, referred incorrectly to DVDs as a tool it uses to back up information. Though the agency is in the midst of a multiyear effort to modernize its data network and move to cloud computing, it does not use DVDs as a storage system.
match_headline: The C.D.C. Waited ‘Its Entire Existence for This Moment.’ What Went Wrong?

text: An article on Thursday about the importance of the events at Tiananmen Square in 1989 for the people of Hong Kong misstated the year that the Berlin Wall fell. It was 1989, not 1988.
match_headline: For Hong Kong, Tiananmen Looms Over the Future

text: An article on Wednesday about the construction of skyscrapers during the pandemic misidentified the distinction of a 55-story tower at 110 North Wacker Drive in Chicago. It is the tallest office building erected in the city since 1990, not the tallest building.
match_headline: Office Towers Are Still Going Up, but Who Will Fill Them?

text: An editorial on Tuesday about police brutality misstated the age of a boy holding a sign at a Tampa protest. He is 3, not 5.
match_headline: America’s Protests Won’t Stop Until Police Brutality Does

text: An obituary on Saturday about the artist Emma Amos misstated the date of her death. It was May 20, not May 21.
match_headline: Emma Amos, Painter Who Challenged Racism and Sexism, Dies at 83

text: An article on Thursday about a drop in the number of visits to emergency rooms during the coronavirus pandemic misstated in one instance the professional affiliation of Dr. William Jaquis. He is affiliated with the American College of Emergency Physicians, not Yale. The article also misattributed a quotation to him. It was Dr. Thomas Balcezak, the chief clinical officer for Yale New Haven Health, not Dr. Jaquis, who said: “It’s made the access to care even harder. We’re not seeing them in the emergency department.”
ref_headline: It’s made the access to care even harder. We’re not seeing them in the emergency department.
match_headline: E.R. Visits Drop Sharply During Pandemic

text: An article on Thursday about films that had been scheduled to premiere at the Cannes Film Festival this summer misidentified the director of the film “Heaven: To the Land of Happiness.” It is Im Sang-soo, not Hong Sang-soo.
ref_headline: Heaven: To the Land of Happiness.
match_headline: Cannes 2020: What Films Would Have Premiered at the Film Festival?

text: An article on Page 16 about the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on Native American artists and artisans misstates the name of a New Mexican pueblo. It is Kewa Pueblo, not Tewa Pueblo.
match_headline: On Tribal Lands, a Time to Make Art for Solace and Survival

text: An article this weekend on Page 5 about the cellist Sheku Kanneh-Mason misidentifies the location of an elementary school in Baltimore where he gave a master class. It is on the west side of the city, not the east side.
match_headline: The Sheku Effect: A Classical Music Star Rises

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about doctors protesting the killing of George Floyd misidentified the location of one of the demonstrations. It was Atlanta, not Decatur, Ga.
match_headline: George Floyd Protests Add New Front Line for Coronavirus Doctors

text: An article on Friday about a call by global leaders for the United States to protect journalists misstated the given name of a CNN reporter arrested while reporting live from Minneapolis. He is Omar Jimenez, not Oscar.
match_headline: In Turnabout, Global Leaders Urge U.S. to Protect Reporters Amid Unrest

text: An article on Friday about Russia’s response to the killing of George Floyd misquoted Ivan Kurilla, an expert on Russian-American relations in St. Petersburg. He said the Russian authorities were “enjoying” the opportunity provided by the unrest in the United States to get across their own propaganda message, not that “Russia is really enjoying this.”
match_headline: Russia Jumps on Floyd Killing as Proof of U.S. Hypocrisy

text: An article on Saturday about the debate over content moderation in the tech industry misidentified the law school where Nadine Strossen is an emerita professor. It is New York Law School, not New York University Law School.
match_headline: The Complex Debate Over Silicon Valley’s Embrace of Content Moderation

text: An article on Monday about political disruption in American newsrooms misstated the news organization Trymaine Lee was working for in 2014. It was MSNBC, not The HuffPost. In addition, an earlier version of a picture caption with the article misattributed credit for the image of the reporter Yamiche Alcindor in Ferguson, Mo. It was taken by Curtis Compton of The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, not Christine Conetta.
match_headline: Inside the Revolts Erupting in America’s Big Newsrooms

text: An article on June 2 about a world tour of “The Phantom of the Opera” that has continued its run despite the pandemic described incorrectly how audiences for a Seoul production were notified by public health authorities about a coronavirus outbreak among the cast. The notification was sent by text alert, not through an app. The article also implied incorrectly that a second announcement describing safety measures at the theater was a public announcement made by authorities. It was made by the production and was sent only to audience members.
match_headline: How ‘Phantom of the Opera’ Survived the Pandemic

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the art activism following the killing of George Floyd misstated the number of people who are on the curatorial staff at the Whitney. There are 30 members on the curatorial staff, not 14; but 14 of them are curators.
match_headline: Floyd Case Forces Arts Groups to Enter the Fray

text: An obituary on Friday about the runner Bobby Morrow misstated the circumstances that led to his absence from the 1960 Summer Olympics. He failed to qualify for the United States track and field team during the Olympic trials; it was not the case that a groin injury kept him from competing in the trials.
match_headline: Bobby Morrow, Who Ran to Stardom at the 1956 Olympics, Dies at 84

text: An article on Monday about flawed data concerning Bolivia’s election in 2019 misspelled the surname of a professor at the University of Miami. She is Dr. Calla Hummel, not Hullum.
match_headline: A Bitter Election. Accusations of Fraud. And Now Second Thoughts.

text: An article on Monday about the connection between the civil unrest in the United States and racial disparities exposed by the coronavirus crisis misidentified the academic institution where Professor Nickolas Zaller teaches. It is the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, not the University of Arkansas.
match_headline: ‘Pandemic Within a Pandemic’: Coronavirus and Police Brutality Roil Black Communities

text: An article on Tuesday about the stock market’s positive upturn for the year misidentified the position of James Montier at Grantham, Mayo, Van Otterloo & Company. He is a member of the firm’s asset allocation team, not its asset management team.
match_headline: Despite Recession, Stock Markets Turn Positive for the Year

text: An article on Monday about the conductor Michael Tilson Thomas misspelled the surname of a composer. He is Henry Brant, not Brandt.
match_headline: After 25 Years, San Francisco’s Maverick Conductor Moves On

text: An article last Wednesday about the restaurant-quality ingredients now available to home cooks from farmers and other suppliers misstated where Jessica Kramer has been living in Newport, R.I. She lives in a hotel, not a condominium.
match_headline: Your Kitchen Can Be as Well Stocked as Restaurants Now

text: An article on Monday about the lasting power of the worldwide protests in favor of racial justice misstated the former job title of Nekima Levy Armstrong. She was a professor of law at the University of St. Thomas, not an associate professor.
match_headline: Other Protests Flare and Fade. Why This Movement Already Seems Different.

text: An article on Tuesday about an Iranian law that significantly expands legal protection for children and adolescents described incorrectly the state of Iranian law on the protection of children. A law adopted in 2002 had provided limited protection; the new measure is not the first to protect children.
match_headline: Iran Criminalizes Child Abuse After Outrage Over Killing of Teenage Girl

text: An article last Friday about offshore wind farming referred incorrectly in several instances to devices used by the offshore wind power industry. They are wind turbines, not windmills.
match_headline: A New Weapon Against Climate Change May Float

text: An obituary on May 31 about the defense lawyer Albert Krieger misstated the given name of the author of the book “Gangland: The Lawyers.” He is James Morton, not John. And a picture caption with the obituary, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the man shown with Mr. Krieger in a 1992 photograph. He is Jackie D’Amico, not John D’Amato.
match_headline: Albert Krieger, a Bulldog of the Criminal Defense Bar, Dies at 96

text: An article on Thursday about a retired federal judge who called the Justice Department’s reversal of the case against Michael T. Flynn a “gross abuse of prosecutorial power” misstated when conversations between Michael Flynn and Sergei Kislyak took place.
