The men spoke in December 2016, a year before Mr. Flynn first pleaded guilty to lying to the F.B.I. about those conversations, not a month before his guilty plea.
match_headline: Outsider Tapped in Flynn Case Calls Justice Dept. Reversal a ‘Gross Abuse’ of Power

text: An article on Thursday about a strike in the scientific community in support of minority researchers misstated the name of an astronomy organization. It is the American Astronomical Society, not the American Astronomical Association. The article also misidentified the location of the group’s headquarters. It is Washington, D.C., not College Park, Md.
match_headline: For a Day, Scientists Pause Science to Confront Racism

text: An article on Friday about the renewed scrutiny of European police that has followed the demonstrations against police brutality in the United States misstated the given name of the Human Rights Watch director in France. She is Bénédicte Jeannerod, not Béatrice.
match_headline: George Floyd Protests Inspire Fresh Scrutiny of Policing in Europe, Too

text: An article on Page 8 about Bob Dylan misspelled a name in a lyric in “Key West (Philosopher’s Pirate).” It is “Ginsberg, Corso and Kerouac,” not “Ginsburg, Corso and Kerouac.”
match_headline: Bob Dylan Has a Lot on His Mind

text: An article this weekend on Page 28 about the future of remote work misspelled the surname of GoNoodle’s chief executive. He is K.C. Estenson, not Estensen.
match_headline: What If Working From Home Goes on … Forever?

text: An obituary on Nov. 28 about William D. Ruckelshaus, who resigned as deputy attorney general in 1973 rather than carry out President Richard M. Nixon’s order to fire the independent special Watergate prosecutor, misstated in part the action taken by Robert H. Bork, the solicitor general, after Mr. Ruckelshaus and Attorney General Elliot L. Richardson resigned. While Mr. Bork did fire Archibald Cox as special prosecutor, he did not also abolish the special prosecutor’s office; he appointed Leon Jaworski to replace Mr. Cox. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the attention of the obituary editors only recently.
match_headline: William Ruckelshaus, Who Quit in ‘Saturday Night Massacre,’ Dies at 87

text: An article on May 31 about how the coronavirus epidemic is affecting meatpacking workers in Nebraska misstated Tyson Foods’ policy for administering $30 daily bonuses. Workers receive the bonus for each day they work; it is not contingent on continuous attendance. And the article included an erroneous detail about the mother of an advocate for workers at the Tyson plant in Lexington. The mother ceased working at the local Walmart after her fever began; she did not continue working.
match_headline: When Going to Work Means Taking a Calculated Risk

text: An article on May 31 about Amazon misstated at what stage Amazon selects a seller when a customer clicks on the “Buy Now” button. The seller is selected when the customer loads the product page, not when the customer clicks the “Buy Now” button.

A review on May 31 about “Ornette Coleman,” by Maria Golia, misattributed a quotation. It was the musician John Wallace Carter, not Ornette Coleman, who said: “As I search my experiences now, looking for areas to call upon for thematic material … I go back often to the scenes of my early childhood. I wish I could capture the raw power of my baptizing pastor.” The review also misstated the given name of Coleman’s sister Trudy Coleman, a blues singer; it was Truvenza, not Trudenza.
match_headline: Lighting Out for the Territories With Ornette Coleman

text: An article last Sunday about things to do in the coming week misstated the name of a museum in Washington, D.C. It is the National Museum of Women in the Arts, not the Women in the Arts Museum. The same article also misstated the producer of the Sunday night performances by Arturo O’Farrill. It is the nonprofit Afro Latin Jazz Alliance, not the Manhattan jazz club Birdland.
match_headline: Let a Week of the Arts Offer Uplift

text: An article on Monday about efforts to undermine climate science research by federal employees who are wary of the scrutiny of senior officials misstated the timing of the resignation Marcy Rockman, a former climate change adaptation coordinator for the Park Service. Ms. Rockman resigned in November 2018, not last November.
match_headline: A War Against Climate Science, Waged by Washington’s Rank and File

text: An article on Sunday about large tech companies that are taking advantage of the reeling economy described incorrectly Apple’s finances. Apple has $193 billion in cash and debt, not $192 billion in cash.
match_headline: The Economy Is Reeling. The Tech Giants Spy Opportunity.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about demonstrations against racism in Europe and the emergence of far-right counterdemonstrators misstated part of a quote by Prime Minister Boris Johnson of Britain in response to the protests in London on Saturday. He said “racism has no part in the U.K.,” not “racism has no place in the U.K.”
ref_headline: racism has no part in the U.K.,
match_headline: Far-Right Groups Push Back as Protesters Rally in Europe

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a video of a police officer in Canada beating an Indigenous leader misidentified the motto of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Their motto is “maintiens le droit,” the French equivalent of “maintain the right” or “uphold the law,” not “to serve and protect.”
match_headline: Video of Arrest of Indigenous Leader Shocks Canada

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Sunday about Juneteenth misstated the year the photo was taken. The parade pictured was in 2018, not last year.

An article on Friday about a push by lawmakers to invest billions of dollars in the semiconductor industry misstated the amount of funding Taiwan unveiled in an effort to attract foreign semiconductor companies. It was more than $300 million, not $300 billion.
match_headline: Lawmakers Push to Invest Billions in Semiconductor Industry to Counter China

text: An obituary on May 19 about the actor Michel Piccoli referred imprecisely to his education. While he did earn what was called a bachelor’s degree at the Collège Sainte-Barbe in Paris, that degree would be considered the equivalent of a high school diploma in the United States.
match_headline: Michel Piccoli, Star of French Stage and Screen, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Thursday about the writer Albert Memmi referred incorrectly to his novel “The Scorpion.” It is about a writer who has disappeared; it is not about a mixed marriage.
match_headline: Albert Memmi, a ‘Jewish Arab’ Intellectual, Dies at 99

text: An article on Sunday about the lack of policy change following the 2014 demonstrations against racism in Ferguson, Mo., described incorrectly the oversight of the San Francisco Police Department. It is in a voluntary reform program overseen by the California Department of Justice; it is not under a federal consent decree.
match_headline: Rage and Promises Followed Ferguson, but Little Changed

text: An article on Sunday about calls for racial justice across seemingly all aspects of American life misstated the title of a play by Jeremy O. Harris. It is “Slave Play,” not “The Slave Play.” It also described incorrectly the timing of an apology by the television host Jimmy Fallon for performing in blackface in a 2000 comedy sketch. He apologized on camera the week after a video of the sketch resurfaced online, not the following day.
match_headline: From Cosmetics to NASCAR, Calls for Racial Justice Are Spreading

text: An article on Friday about Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s hair misstated the name of the Canadian government benefit referenced by its acronym, CERB, in a quote by Katy Jean, a mother from Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. It is the Canada Emergency Response Benefit, not the Canada Emergency Relief Benefit.
match_headline: Counting the Days Under Virus Lockdown by the Length of Trudeau’s Hair

text: A picture with an article on Tuesday about cultural references in the film “Da 5 Bloods” was published in error. The image showed Morehouse students on a field trip, not Morehouse College.
match_headline: A Pop-Culture Glossary for ‘Da 5 Bloods’

text: An obituary on Saturday about Julio Guzman, the founder of an evangelical church in New Jersey, misstated his birth date. It was Sept. 24, 1955, not Sept. 20. It also misspelled the given name of his goddaughter. She is Mayra Amaya, not Myra.
match_headline: Julio Guzman, Salvadoran Refugee Who Started a Church, Dies at 64

text: An article on Wednesday about an attempt by the Trump administration to delay the publication of John R. Bolton’s memoir misidentified the person who sent a letter to Mr. Bolton’s lawyer, Charles J. Cooper. It was John A. Eisenberg, a deputy White House counsel, not Michael Ellis.
match_headline: Trump Administration Sues to Try to Delay Publication of Bolton’s Book

text: An article on Wednesday about dexamethasone, a steroid believed to help save severely ill coronavirus patients, described incorrectly the subjects of a trial conducted in Spain. They had acute respiratory distress, but were not infected with the coronavirus.
match_headline: Common Drug Reduces Coronavirus Deaths, Scientists Report

text: An article on Monday about Sweden’s relations with China misstated a Chinese executive’s title and referred incorrectly to the corporate entities involved in a proposed merger involving the Swedish automaker Volvo. Li Shufu is chairman — not president — of both Zhejiang Geely Holding and its subsidiary Geely Auto Group. It was Zhejiang Geely Holding that purchased Volvo Cars in 2010, not the Geely Auto Group, and it announced plans to merge Volvo Cars with Geely Auto, not with itself. The article also misidentified the company in which Zhejiang Geely Holding became a major stakeholder in late 2017. It was AB Volvo, not its subsidiary Volvo Truck.
match_headline: Fears for Volvo Expose Sour Turn in Sweden’s Ties With China

text: An article on Tuesday about masks and respiratory health misidentified the nerve that innervates the diaphragm. It is the phrenic nerve, not the vagus nerve.
match_headline: Looking at Masks and Respiratory Health

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Rupert Hine, a synth-pop music producer, misstated where he died. It was at his home in Wiltshire, England — not in London.
match_headline: Rupert Hine, Synth-Pop Music Producer, Dies at 72

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Harry Anderson, who helped shape American sailboat racing, misspelled the surname of Mr. Anderson’s biographer. He is Roger Vaughan, not Vaughn.
match_headline: Harry Anderson, ‘M.V.P. of American Sailing,’ Is Dead at 98

text: An article on Wednesday about Pacific Gas & Electric’s guilty plea to 84 counts of manslaughter in the devastating 2018 wildfire that destroyed the town of Paradise, Calif., referred incorrectly to the changes Gov. Gavin Newsom asked the utility to make. He asked the company to implement a new “leadership structure,” not to replace its chief executive.
match_headline: PG&E Pleads Guilty to 84 Counts of Manslaughter in Camp Fire Case

text: An article on Thursday about college football cancellations described incorrectly the cancellation of four games. They were the first for major college football programs, not the first for college football.
match_headline: First Cancellations Emerge for Major College Football

text: An article on Wednesday about orchestral music that can be performed by a reduced symphonic ensemble referred imprecisely to the number of players who remain playing at the end of Haydn’s “Farewell” Symphony. Two violinists are playing, not one.
match_headline: So You Want to Be a Socially Distanced Orchestra

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Thomas F. Freeman, the longtime Texas Southern University debate coach, misstated the surname of his successor. She is Gloria Batiste-Roberts, not Baptise-Roberts.
match_headline: Thomas Freeman, Debate Coach With Broad Influence, Dies at 100

text: An article on Thursday about the Chinese government’s effort to collect DNA samples from males across China misstated comments from Dr. Zhong Chang, a researcher at the U.S. firm Thermo Fisher. When speaking about genetic testing kits the company was marketing to Chinese law enforcement, Dr. Zhong said the kits are calibrated so that they can effectively gather DNA information from China’s ethnic minorities like Uighurs and Tibetans, not that they could distinguish ethnic minorities from other groups. (A spokesman for Thermo Fisher said the kits lack that capability.)
match_headline: China Is Collecting DNA From Tens of Millions of Men and Boys, Using U.S. Equipment

text: An article on Thursday about the decline in handwritten correspondence included part of a letter from Pat Parker to Audre Lorde that referred incorrectly to the oil tycoon and conservative activist H.L. Hunt. He had no family or business connections to Hunt’s ketchup.
match_headline: Mourning the Letters That Will No Longer Be Written, and Remembering the Great Ones That Were

text: An article on Page 6 about the first Pride march refers incompletely to the event’s organizers. They included Brenda Howard, Craig Rodwell, Fred Sargeant, Ellen Broidy and Linda Rhodes; Ms. Howard was not the sole organizer. The article also omitted a word from the title of a book by Chiké Frankie Edozien. The title is “Lives of Great Men: Living and Loving as an African Gay Man,” not “Lives of Great: Living and Loving as an African Gay Man.”
ref_headline: Lives of Great Men: Living and Loving as an African Gay Man,
match_headline: How the Pride March Made History

text: An essay on June 7 about Wallace Stegner misstated the title of one of his books. It is “Wolf Willow,” not “Wolf Hollow.” The essay also misstated the name of a town in Saskatchewan where Stegner spent part of his childhood. It is Eastend, not Eastview.
match_headline: Wallace Stegner and the Conflicted Soul of the West

text: An article on June 7 about Attorney General William Barr misstated the location of the visitors’ entrance to the main Department of Justice building in Washington. It is on Constitution Avenue, not Independence Avenue.
match_headline: William Barr’s State of Emergency

text: An article on June 7 about ICE detainees and Covid-19 misstated the date of a hearing regarding a habeas petition on behalf of immigrants held by ICE in Georgia. Th e hearing was on May 28, not May 24.
match_headline: Fear, Illness and Death in ICE Detention: How a Protest Grew on the Inside

text: An article on Sunday about tight Democratic primary races in New York misspelled the surname of a congressional candidate in the Democratic primary against Representative Carolyn B. Maloney. She is Lauren Ashcraft, not Ashcroft.
match_headline: ‘This Is a Change Election’: Will 2 Entrenched House Members Fall?

text: An article on Saturday about social media companies with products that undermine supportive statements about racial justice misstated the circumstances of the death of a black man, Ahmaud Arbery. Two white Georgia men have been charged in the shooting; Mr. Arbery was not the victim of police brutality.
match_headline: Social Media Giants Support Racial Justice. Their Products Undermine It.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about onscreen depictions of transgender people misstated Chaz Bono’s profession. He is an actor, not a writer-musician.
match_headline: Transgender Lives Onscreen: Seen, but Not Always Believable

text: An article on Saturday misidentified the screenwriter of “You Should Have Left.” It was adapted from the Daniel Kehlmann novel by David Koepp; it was not by Koepp and Kehlmann.
match_headline: ‘You Should Have Left’ Review: This Haunted House Is Familiar

text: An article on Friday about digital museum exhibitions for kids misidentified the cultural background of an immigrant whose story is featured in upcoming programming at the Tenement Museum. Victoria Confino was a Sephardic Jewish teenager who immigrated from what is now Greece, not a teenage Italian immigrant.
match_headline: Digital Field Trips: Museum Adventures Abound for Kids

text: An obituary on June 14 about the racecar driver Vicki Wood referred incorrectly to the loss of her driver’s license when she was 99. It was taken away by the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles — not by the state police.
match_headline: Vicki Wood, Who Broke Car-Racing Gender Barriers, Dies at 101

text: An obituary on June 8 about the gymnast Kurt Thomas misstated his finish in the all-around at the 1979 world gymnastics championships. He won a silver medal; he did not finish sixth. (He had finished sixth in that event the year before.)
match_headline: Kurt Thomas, Trailblazing Champion Gymnast, Dies at 64

text: An obituary on May 23 about Harold Blake, a longtime associate of the urban planner Robert Moses, referred incorrectly to Mr. Moses’s tenure as chairman of the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority. He continued to hold that position while also serving as president of the 1964-65 World’s Fair in New York; he was not ousted.
match_headline: Harold Blake, Loyal to Robert Moses Until the End, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on May 3 about the inventor Takuo Aoyagi referred imprecisely to the mathematical formula he developed that underpins the operation of pulse oximeters. It accounts for “pulsatile noise” in blood flow to measure oxygen levels; it does not cancel them out. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Takuo Aoyagi, an Inventor of the Pulse Oximeter, Dies at 84

text: An article on May 24 about the lives that were lost to the coronavirus pandemic misstated the age and city of Melita Baker. She was 86, not 89, and of Norwell, Mass., not Irvington, N.Y.
match_headline: What We Can Learn From Endurance Athletes About Getting Through This Pandemic

text: An article on Monday about the Serbian president, Aleksandar Vucic, misstated whom he will meet with at the White House this week. He is scheduled to meet Richard Grenell, the United States envoy to the Balkans, but not with President Trump.
match_headline: Serbia’s Strongman Wins Big in Election Boycotted by the Opposition

text: An article on Monday about an effort to preserve music composed in Nazi concentration camps misstated the name for a series of recordings made by Francesco Lotoro. It is KZ Music, not K2 Music.
match_headline: Music From the Death Camps: Alive and Being Readied for a New Home

text: An article last weekend about an infamous brawl involving Yankees players at the Copacabana club in 1957 referred incorrectly to one of them. Not all of the players involved are dead; Whitey Ford is still alive.
match_headline: 63 Years Later, a Confession in a Legendary Yankees Scandal

text: An article last Wednesday about New York City bars doing takeout business in the pandemic misstated the date the city lifted its recent curfew. It was June 7, not June 6.
match_headline: New York’s New Bar Stool: The Sidewalk

text: An article last Wednesday about swordfish au poivre misstated the name of the museum where the restaurant Veronika is located. It is Fotografiska New York, not the Fotografiska Museum.

Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the dance critic and historian Sally Banes misidentified the institution at the University of Wisconsin at Madison where she was director in 2001 and 2002. It is the Institute for Research in the Humanities, not the Center for the Humanities.
match_headline: Sally Banes, Distinguished Dance Critic and Historian, Dies at 69

text: An obituary on Monday about the filmmaker Joel Schumacher misstated the location of the Henri Bendel department store in Manhattan when he was a window dresser there. It was on West 57 Street at the time, not Fifth Avenue. (It relocated to Fifth Avenue later.)
match_headline: Joel Schumacher, Director of ‘St. Elmo’s Fire,’ Is Dead at 80

text: An obituary on May 9 about Ji Chaozhu, a longtime interpreter for top Chinese officials, including Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, misstated where he attended high school. It was the Horace Mann-Lincoln High School in Manhattan, not the Horace Mann High School in the Bronx. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Ji Chaozhu, Interpreter for China During Nixon’s Trip, Dies at 90

text: An article on Wednesday about testimony before the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the new surge in coronavirus cases misspelled the given name of one of the doctors testifying. He is Adm. Brett P. Giroir, not Brent.
match_headline: Fauci, Citing ‘Disturbing Surge,’ Tells Congress the Virus Is Not Under Control

text: An article on Tuesday about Nordic countries that have closed their borders to Sweden because of concerns about the coronavirus misspelled the given name of the editor in chief of Altinget, a political website, and incorrectly rendered a portion of a quote from him. The editor is Jakob Nielsen, not Jacob. Mr. Nielsen referred to the divide between Denmark and Sweden as the “deepest since the Second World War,” not the deepest since “the First World War.”
ref_headline: deepest since the Second World War,
match_headline: Sweden Tries Out a New Status: Pariah State

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about a German league’s sequestered competition during the pandemic, misstated the given name of a player on the N.B.A.’s Washington Wizards​. He is John Wall, not Kevin.
match_headline: China’s Man in Washington, Named Trump

text: An article on Wednesday about a letter to the director of the Guggenheim from the museum’s curators calling for greater diversity in its staff, board and exhibitions misstated the timing of the Guggenheim Museum’s decision to hire Ashley James as a curator. It was days after a panel discussion in November 2019, not several months later.
match_headline: Curators Urge Guggenheim to Fix Culture That ‘Enables Racism’

text: An article last Thursday about recent online jewelry auctions misstated the clarity of a diamond being auctioned by Christie’s. As stated elsewhere in the article, it is graded VVS1; it is not flawless.
match_headline: Meanwhile, Some People Are Stress-Shopping Diamond Bracelets

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the movie producer and financier Steve Bing referred incorrectly to his relationship with Lisa Bonder, the mother of his daughter. It was not the case that they had been married and were divorced. The obituary also included an incomplete list of Mr. Bing’s survivors. In addition to those named, he is survived by his parents.
match_headline: Steve Bing, Hollywood Producer and Financier, Is Dead at 55

text: An article on Thursday about the indictment of the President Hashim Thaci of Kosovo for war crimes committed during Kosovo’s battle for independence from Serbia misstated the year that the Kosovar Parliament founded a special judicial system to investigate possible war crimes carried out by guerrilla groups. It was 2015, not 2016.
match_headline: Kosovo President Is Indicted for War Crimes for Role in War With Serbia

text: An article on Wednesday about new CARES Act grants from the National Endowment of the Humanities described incorrectly the location of the cultural institutions receiving some of the N.E.H. grants. There are 52 cultural organizations in New York State receiving grants, not 52 in New York City.
match_headline: National Endowment for the Humanities Announces New CARES Act Grants

text: A map with an article on May 31 about a clash in the Himalayas between India and China included outdated boundaries for Jammu and Kashmir. The India-controlled area just west of the Line of Actual Control is the territory of Ladakh, not Jammu and Kashmir.
match_headline: China and India Brawl at 14,000 Feet Along the Border

text: An article on Sunday about the police killing of Elijah McClain misstated the description of Mr. McClain given by a person who called 911. The person reported that Mr. McClain looked “sketchy,” not “suspicious.”
match_headline: Elijah McClain Died After He Was Detained. Now He’s Being Remembered.

text: An article on Friday about “Jurassic Park” misidentified the actor who plays the businessman behind the theme park. He is Richard Attenborough, not David Attenborough.
match_headline: Viewing Party! Let’s all Watch ‘Jurassic Park’

text: An article on Saturday about a heat wave in Britain referred incorrectly to one of the areas where crowds had formed during hot weather. People flocked to parks, beaches and streams, not swamps.
match_headline: Lockdown? What Lockdown? Heat Wave Brings Britons Out in Droves

text: An article on Sunday about black trans activists referred imprecisely to the role of transgender women of color in the Stonewall Inn uprising, suggesting they were the sole leaders of the event. Trans women of color were leaders in L.G.B.T.Q. activism before, during and after the uprising, but they were among many activists who led at Stonewall.
match_headline: Black Trans Women Seek More Space in the Movement They Helped Start

text: An article on Monday about the effect of the pandemic on college towns misidentified the month that the University of California, Davis, held its virtual graduation. It was in June, not May.
match_headline: ‘We Could Be Feeling This for the Next Decade’: Virus Hits College Towns

text: An obituary on Saturday about Lester C. Crystal, the longtime executive producer of the PBS program “NewsHour,” omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to those named, Mr. Crystal is survived by a sister, Elaine Hallfin.
match_headline: Lester Crystal, Guiding Force Behind ‘NewsHour,’ Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Friday about the Afrikaans writer Elsa Joubert misidentified the location of Leiden University, whose African Studies Center compiled a list of the best African books of the 20th century that included her novel “The Long Journey of Poppie Nongena.” It is in the Netherlands, not Belgium.
ref_headline: The Long Journey of Poppie Nongena.
match_headline: Elsa Joubert, 97, Dies; Afrikaans Writer Explored Black Reality

text: An article on Saturday about the European Union’s decision to bar most U.S. citizens from entry misstated Greece’s position on allowing visitors from outside the bloc. Greece has allowed visitors from outside the E.U. but has considered them authorized travelers. It did not ignore E.U. recommendations.
match_headline: E.U. Plans to Bar Most U.S. Travelers When Bloc Reopens

text: An article on Monday about the activist history of an Indigenous chief in Canada who was beaten by the police misspelled the surname of the well-known climate activist who offered praise for the First Nations leader Allan Adam. She is Greta Thunberg, not Thunburg.
match_headline: Chief Beaten by Police Is Longtime Fighter for Indigenous Rights

text: An article on Monday about measures taken at Houston Methodist Hospital to cope with a surge in coronavirus cases misstated Texas Medical Center’s location within Houston. It is outside the downtown area; it is not downtown.
match_headline: ‘Feeling Like Death’: Inside a Houston Hospital Bracing for a Virus Peak

text: An article on Monday about a surge in coronavirus cases in Florida referred incorrectly to the number of patients admitted to Miami’s main public hospital who tested positive for the coronavirus. About a quarter of all patients over the past two weeks tested positive for the virus, including those who came in from car crashes, heart attacks and other problems; it is not the case that a third of the people who were admitted from the emergency room tested positive.
match_headline: Florida’s Covid Cases Up Fivefold in 2 Weeks: ‘The Numbers Are Scary’

text: An article on Tuesday about candidates of color poised to defeat incumbents in congressional primaries in New York described incorrectly the lead that Ritchie Torres holds over his closest competitor, Michael Blake. Mr. Torres leads Mr. Blake by 4,516 votes; he does not have twice as many votes.
match_headline: Insurgent Wave in New York Pushes Old Guard Democrats Aside

text: An obituary on June 24 about the civil rights lawyer Shirley A. Siegel erroneously credited her with a distinction. She was not New York State’s first female solicitor general; Ruth Kessler Toch was appointed to that position in 1966, 13 years before Ms. Siegel.
match_headline: Shirley Siegel, Leading New York Civil Rights Lawyer, Dies at 101

text: An article on Wednesday about calls for the founding director of the Southern Foodways Alliance, John T. Edge, to resign referred imprecisely to the dinner series Brown in the South. It was a benefit for the Southern Foodways Alliance and included a dinner at the James Beard Foundation; it was not sponsored by the alliance and the James Beard Foundation.
match_headline: A White Gatekeeper of Southern Food Faces Calls to Resign

text: An article on Thursday about troubles faced by Britain’s cultural sector because of the pandemic lockdown partially misattributed a statement about protecting the arts in Britain. Several prominent voices in British classical music, including the conductor Simon Rattle, urged that the government not let arts “fall by the wayside”; it was not from Mr. Rattle alone.
match_headline: Cultural Life Is Back in Europe. In the U.K., They Talk of Collapse.

text: An article on Friday about planned congressional testimony by Geoffrey S. Berman, the former top federal prosecutor in Manhattan, referred incorrectly to his role at the time of his dismissal. He was the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York; he was no longer the acting U.S. attorney.
match_headline: U.S. Attorney Ousted by Barr Will Testify Privately Before Congress

text: An article this weekend on Page 20 about the screenwriter and author Charlie Kaufman misspells the surname of an actor. He is Steve Carell, not Carrell.
match_headline: This Profile of Charlie Kaufman Has Changed

text: An article last Sunday about mocktails misspelled the name of a Brazilian cocktail. It is a caipirinha, not a caipiriña.
match_headline: Make It the Summer of the Mocktail

text: An article on Friday about professional athletes who are also social justice activists misstated the kind of school LeBron James is financially supporting in Akron, Ohio. It is a public school, not a charter school.
match_headline: W.N.B.A. Star’s Role in Freeing Man From Prison Shows Female Athletes at Forefront

text: An article on Sunday about Hong Kong’s new reality after China imposed a new security law misspelled the given name of a 22-year-old recent college graduate who worries that the law could be used to clamp down on dissent. He is Xu Zhe, not Ze.
match_headline: Hong Kong, Changed Overnight, Navigates Its New Reality

text: An article on Monday about the diplomatic style of Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. misstated the party affiliation of John P. Hannah, who has worked under three presidents. While he was a national security aide for Vice President Dick Cheney, he is not a Republican.
match_headline: ‘Strategic Empathy’: How Biden’s Informal Diplomacy Shaped Foreign Relations

text: Because of a production error, the final paragraphs were missing from an article on Monday on about the flooding of a Turkish valley filled with relics of bygone civilizations. The full article can be found online at nytimes.com .
match_headline: ‘An Empty Presence in My Chest’: Vanessa Guillen’s Family Calls for Change in the Military

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the vice-presidential vetting process misspelled the given name of the Democratic presidential nominee in 2016. She is Hillary Clinton, not Hilary.
match_headline: Let the Delegates Help Choose Biden’s V.P.

text: An article on Sunday about evictions during the coronavirus pandemic misstated the source of research on potential evictions tied to job losses. It was from Amherst Capital Management, not Amherst College.
match_headline: Sleeping Outside in a Pandemic: Vulnerable Renters Face Evictions

text: An article on Monday about Netflix’s Black programming misstated a detail about the 2019 documentary “The Black Godfather,” a portrait of the Black entertainment industry deal maker Clarence Avant. The film states that Mr. Avant’s daughter, Nicole, is married to Netflix’s chief content officer, Ted Sarandos; it is not the case that it does not reveal the connection.
match_headline: How Netflix Beat Hollywood to a Generation of Black Content

text: An article on Saturday about jobless benefits for students misidentified the gender of the sibling who benefited from Walter Cortina’s earnings from a carwash. The money supported his brother, not his sister. (He does not have a sister.)
match_headline: Students May Qualify for Special Jobless Benefits

text: An obituary on June 19 about the former United States ambassador to Ireland Jean Kennedy Smith misstated the reason she was reprimanded by Secretary of State Warren M. Christopher. It was for retaliating against two senior staff members who disagreed with her views, not for removing them.
match_headline: Jean Kennedy Smith Dies at 92; Helped Forge Peace in Northern Ireland

text: An obituary on Sunday about the author Rudolfo Ayana misstated the surname of one of his stepdaughters. She is Melissa Morris, not Messec.
match_headline: Rudolfo Anaya, a Father of Chicano Literature, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on June 26 about the computer programmer, educator and musician Michael Hawley erroneously included a name on the list of his survivors. He was formerly Choki Lhamo’s guardian; she is not his daughter.
match_headline: Michael Hawley, Programmer, Professor and Pianist, Dies at 58

text: An article on Tuesday about the lack of coronavirus testing capacity in U.S. cities described incorrectly the details of recent testing in Wuhan, China. The rapid testing of 6.5 million people was part of a campaign to screen the city’s entire population, not in response to a new outbreak. And the testing took place in May, not June.
match_headline: Months Into Virus Crisis, U.S. Cities Still Lack Testing Capacity

text: An article on Monday about a spike in gun violence in Chicago described incorrectly the homicide toll there in 2016. The 778 deaths that year were the most in the city since the mid-1990s, not a record. The error was repeated in an article on Tuesday about gun violence in New York in the national pages.
match_headline: Chicago Gun Violence Spikes and Increasingly Finds the Youngest Victims

text: An article on Friday about rising coronavirus cases in Kansas misidentified the party affiliation of the state’s governor, Laura Kelly. She is a Democrat, not a Republican.
match_headline: What to Know About California’s ‘Dimmer Switch’ Reopening

text: An article on Saturday about coronavirus tests at airports misstated part of the name of a newspaper that reported on slow results in Alaska. It is The Anchorage Daily News, not The Alaska Daily News.
match_headline: How Infrared Images Could Be Part of Your Daily Life

text: An article on Tuesday about New York City’s reopening of its beaches for swimming misidentified the day Rodney Jackson, 21, went to the beach for the first time in his life. It was Thursday, not Friday.
match_headline: New York City’s Biggest Decision: How to Safely Reopen Schools

text: An article on Tuesday about families coping with rare diseases misstated the brain illness that Sonia Vallabh’s mother died of, and which Dr. Vallabh also carries a mutation for. It is a genetic prion disease, not specifically Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome.
match_headline: ‘It Will Consume Your Life’: 4 Families Take On Rare Diseases

text: A Critic’s Notebook last Wednesday about reasons not to dine out in the coronavirus pandemic misstated an order issued in June by Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida. It banned drinking inside bars but did not close all of them. They can sell takeout alcohol and food if they have a proper license.
match_headline: I’m Not Ready to Go Back to Restaurants. Is Anyone?

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an obituary on Sunday about the photographer Margaret Morton misstated when the photograph of her at an exhibition of her work was taken. It was 2015, not 1995.
match_headline: Margaret Morton, Photographer at Home With the Homeless, Dies at 71

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the singer, songwriter and bandleader Charlie Daniels misspelled the surname of a musician who performed at Volunteer Jam, the festival hosted by the Charlie Daniels Band. He was Stevie Ray Vaughan, not Vaughn.
match_headline: Charlie Daniels, Fiddling Force in Country and Rock, Dies at 83

text: An article on Wednesday about Mary L. Trump’s reasons for writing a memoir about President Trump, her uncle, misstated the birth order of Ms. Trump and her brother, Fred Trump III. She is younger than him, not older. The article also misidentified a member of the Trump family who sued over an estate. The quote referred to Fred Trump III, not Fred Trump Jr.
match_headline: The Inside Story of Why Mary Trump Wrote a Tell-All Memoir

text: An article on Wednesday about the strength of the case against Amy Cooper, a white woman who called 911 on a Black birder, misidentified the name of the school where Alvin Bragg is a professor. It is New York Law School, not New York University.
match_headline: Case Against Amy Cooper Lacks Key Element: Victim’s Cooperation

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the decision to proceed with the Women’s British Open without spectators misstated the name of the organization that conducts the tournament. It is the R&A, not the Royal and Ancient Golf Club.
match_headline: Women’s British Open Will Proceed Without Fans

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the film composer Ennio Morricone referred incorrectly to his American concert tour of 2007. He had made at least one previous visit to the United States; it was not his first. The obituary also referred imprecisely to Mr. Morricone’s composition “The Ecstasy of Gold.” While it is heard in the movie “The Good, the Bad and the Ugly,” it is not the movie’s theme song.
match_headline: Ennio Morricone, Oscar-Winning Composer of Film Scores, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the cartoonist Henry Martin misspelled his wife’s original surname. She was Edith Matthews, not Mathews.
match_headline: Henry Martin, Wry New Yorker Cartoonist, Is Dead at 94

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on June 30 about the philanthropist and hostess Ruth Buchanan referred incorrectly to Wiley T. Buchanan Jr., her first husband. He was not a descendant of James Buchanan, the 15th president of the United States. (James Buchanan had no children.) The obituary also referred incorrectly to Juan Carlos, the future king of Spain, who attended a gala in 1962 for the reopening of Beaulieu, the mansion owned by Mr. and Mrs. Buchanan in Newport, R.I. He was the son of Don Juan, widely regarded at the time as the pretender to the Spanish throne; he was not a crown prince.
match_headline: Ruth Buchanan, Philanthropist and Hostess Extraordinaire, Is Dead at 101

text: An article on Monday about corporate lobbying in Washington misstated the timing of a meeting between Secretary of State Mike Pompeo and the chief executive of the arms maker Raytheon. David Urban, a lobbyist close to Mr. Pompeo and President Trump, requested the meeting more than two weeks before Mr. Pompeo issued an emergency waiver in May 2019 allowing Raytheon to proceed with arms sales to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, but according to the State Department the meeting took place in June, after the waiver was issued, not a few months before.
match_headline: Trump Vowed to ‘Drain the Swamp,’ but Lobbyists Are Helping Run His Campaign

text: An article on Friday about rising coronavirus infections misidentified the state where Chris Sununu is the governor. It is New Hampshire, not Vermont.
match_headline: Hogan, Maryland Governor, Plans Book Tour as He Eyes 2024 White House Run

text: An article on Friday about the critically endangered status of northern right whales misstated the name of the government agency that focuses on oceans and the atmosphere. It is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, not the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association.
match_headline: Northern Right Whales Are on the Brink, and Trump Could Be Their Last Hope

text: An article on Thursday about the Puerto Rican economy during the pandemic misidentified the location of the headquarters of the Puerto Rico Financial Oversight and Management Board. It is now meeting in San Juan, P.R., not New York.
match_headline: Pandemic Plunges Puerto Rico Into Yet Another Dire Emergency

text: An article on Friday about the W.N.B.A. and the Black Lives Matter movement misstated Layshia Clarendon’s team. It is the New York Liberty, not the Connecticut Sun.
match_headline: A W.N.B.A. Owner Clashes With Players on Protests

text: An article last Sunday about falling real estate prices in New York misspelled the surname of the regional president of the brokerage Compass. He is Rory Golod, not Gold.
match_headline: Real Estate Prices Fall Sharply in New York

text: An article on June 28 about economic justice misspelled the surname of a 25-year-old Black man who was pursued by armed white residents of a South Georgia neighborhood and killed. He was Ahmaud Arbery, not Aubrey.
match_headline: The Enormous Black-White Wage Gap

text: A feature on June 14 about the death of Charles Dickens misidentified Shakespeare’s burial site. He was buried at Holy Trinity Church in Stratford-upon-Avon; he was not buried at Westminster Abbey.
match_headline: When Dickens Died, America Mourned. Our Archives Tell the Story.

text: A review last Sunday about the anthology “The Faking of the President,” edited by Peter Carlaftes, misidentified the editor of an earlier anthology from the same publisher. “The Obama Inheritance” was edited by Gary Phillips; it was not edited by Carlaftes.
match_headline: Can Political Satire Outpace Reality? 3 Books Toss Their Hats in the Ring

text: An article last Sunday about essential oils had an incorrect byline. Its author is Caitie Kelly, not Caitlin Kelly.
match_headline: 4 Body Scrubs to Slather On

text: An article on Saturday about students who have been defrauded by their schools misstated how an accepted borrower-defense claim would have affected David Boyer’s student loans. It would have refunded his federal loans; it would not have affected his G.I. Bill benefits.
match_headline: The Students Are Victims of Fraud, but the Government Won’t Help

text: An entry in the Listings Pages on Friday about things to do last weekend erroneously included Vaughn Monroe among the performers in comedy clips recently posted to “The Ed Sullivan Show” YouTube channel. Monroe was a singer, not a comedian.
match_headline: 7 Things to Do This Weekend

text: An article on Monday about the Metropolitan Opera’s live streams referred incompletely to the beneficiaries of an emergency relief fund set up by the Met’s chorus. The fund benefits a range of Met artists, not only members of the chorus.
match_headline: Metropolitan Opera Will Livestream Its Biggest Stars

text: An article on Saturday about the reluctance of public health experts to speak about the dangers of attending protests during a pandemic when the protests are against racism misstated the difference in life expectancy between Black Americans and white Americans. It is a difference of three and a half years, not two years.
match_headline: Are Protests Dangerous? What Experts Say May Depend on Who’s Protesting What

text: An article on Tuesday about two Shiite protesters in Bahrain who are sentenced to die, relying on an outdated report provided by a rights group, referred incorrectly to the treatment of one of the men facing execution. Husain Moosa said he was beaten by his interrogators, but he was not hanged from the ceiling for three days.
match_headline: Bahrain to Execute 2 Shiite Protesters After Years of Desperate Appeals

text: An article on Sunday about the risk of deportation for undocumented immigrants who are arrested at protests misidentified the Republican state senator who was the lead proponent of the anti-immigration measure Senate Bill 1070 in Arizona. It is Russell Pearce, not Russell Pierce.
match_headline: After an Arrest at a Black Lives Matter Protest: Deportation Proceedings

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Cyrus R. Vance Jr., the Manhattan district attorney, misstated the former job title of Tali Farhadian Weinstein. She was a general counsel to the Brooklyn district attorney, not a former Brooklyn prosecutor.
match_headline: He Beat Trump and Weinstein. Why Is This D.A.’s Standing Still Shaky?

text: An article on Monday about organizations that received loans from the Paycheck Protection Program misstated the amount of money received by Carolina FC, a youth soccer organization. It received thousands, not a “multimillion-dollar loan.”
match_headline: For Sports Halted at the Outbreak’s Onset, Loans Saved Staff

text: An article on Tuesday about activists who protest offensive sports mascots misidentified an organization Suzan Shown Harjo worked for and her title at the organization. The organization is the National Congress of American Indians, not the National Council of American Indians. She was its executive director, not president.
match_headline: For Native American Activists, Washington Name Change Was ‘a Long Time Coming’

text: An article on Tuesday about violin vigils honoring the memory of Elijah McClain, who died in police custody, misspelled the given name of an organizer of a violin vigil in New Jersey. He is Zach Brock, not Zack.
match_headline: Violin Vigils Honor the Memory of Elijah McClain

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Judy Dyble, a singer who was in the first recorded lineup of the British band Fairport Convention, misstated the name of the village in England where the band holds an annual music festival. It is Cropredy, not Copredy.
match_headline: Judy Dyble, Singer in Fairport Convention and Beyond, Dies at 71

text: An article on Monday about oil and gas companies that are heading toward bankruptcy misidentified the scientific agency where Claus Zehner works. It is the European Space Agency, not the SRON Netherlands Institute for Space Research.
match_headline: Fracking Firms Fail, Rewarding Executives and Raising Climate Fears

text: An article on Wednesday about a new Cold War between the United States and China misstated the name of the group that James A. Lewis writes for. It is the Center for Strategic and International Studies, not the Center for Strategic Studies.
match_headline: Caught in ‘Ideological Spiral,’ U.S. and China Drift Toward Cold War

text: An article on Saturday about a decree that will allow the Hagia Sophia to operate as a mosque misstated Cevdet Yilmaz’s role in the Justice and Development Party. He is the party’s deputy chairman responsible for foreign affairs, not its spokesman.
match_headline: Erdogan Signs Decree Allowing Hagia Sophia to Be Used as a Mosque Again

text: An article on Wednesday about the effect of the latest surge in coronavirus cases on automakers described incorrectly General Motors’ policy on masks, social distancing and frequent hand washing at its plants. Those practices are required by the company, not simply encouraged.
match_headline: Automakers Are Making Cars, but Virus Surge Puts That at Risk

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the South African activist and poet Zindziswa Mandela misstated her husband’s surname and omitted the name of another survivor. He is Molapo Motlhajwa, not Motlhawa. And in addition to the survivors named, she is survived by a half sister, Makaziwe Mandela-Amuah.
match_headline: Zindzi Mandela, Activist in South Africa and Ambassador, Dies at 59

text: An obituary on Friday about Ola Mae Spinks, who helped organize an archive of interviews with former slaves, misstated how old she was when her family left Louisiana for the all-Black town of Vernon, Okla. She was 7 or 8, not 2.
match_headline: Ola Mae Spinks, Who Helped Preserve a Slave Archive, Dies at 106

text: An article on Thursday about TikTok’s lobbying efforts in Washington misstated the name of the news program that hosted Peter Navarro’s interview. It was Fox News Channel’s “Sunday Morning Futures,” not Fox Business.
match_headline: TikTok Enlists Army of Lobbyists as Suspicions Over China Ties Grow

text: An article on Monday about a Navy warship that caught fire in San Diego, using information from the Navy, attributed an erroneous distinction to the original Bonhomme Richard. It was not the first Navy vessel to defeat an enemy ship in combat; the U.S.S. Ranger, also commanded by Capt. John Paul Jones, captured the H.M.S. Drake in 1778.
match_headline: Navy Ship Continues to Burn Off San Diego After Fire Injures 57

text: An obituary on June 26 about the inventor John J. Mooney misspelled the name of the company where he worked for 43 years. It is the Engelhard Corporation, not Englehard.
match_headline: John J. Mooney, an Inventor of the Catalytic Converter, Dies at 90

text: An article on Sunday about the relationship between China and Iran misstated the location of the academic institution where an Iranian energy researcher is based. The researcher, Ali Gholizadeh, is at the University of Science and Technology of China in Hefei, not in Beijing.
match_headline: Defying U.S., China and Iran Near Trade and Military Partnership

text: An article on Thursday about scrutiny of a contract to run a centralized Covid-19 database for the Trump administration, using information posted to the federal contract site USASpending.gov, referred incorrectly to the contract awarded to TeleTracking Technologies. The Department of Health and Human Services said Friday that TeleTracking Technologies was one of six bids, not the sole bidder. (The Department said the error on the federal website was being corrected.)
match_headline: ‘Sole Source’ Contract for Covid-19 Database Draws Scrutiny From Democrats

text: An entry in the Listings Pages on Friday about the NYC Math Festival from the National Museum of Mathematics included outdated information about the time of the event. After the entry was published, the museum announced that the festival would end at 8:30 p.m., not 8:15.
match_headline: 7 Things to Do This Weekend

text: An article this weekend on Page 40 about the lead-up to the invasion of Iraq in 2003 refers incorrectly to the United Nations chamber where Colin Powell delivered a speech in February 2003. It was the Security Council, not the General Assembly.
match_headline: Colin Powell Still Wants Answers

text: An article this weekend on Page 30 about the U.S. public health system and the pandemic misspells the given name of a public health professor at Johns Hopkins University. She is Shelley Hearne, not Shelly.
match_headline: Why We’re Losing the Battle With Covid-19

text: An article last Sunday about artists in Newark amid the pandemic and protests misstated the name of a museum. It is the Newark Museum of Art, not the Newark Museum.
match_headline: Newark Artists, Thriving Amid Crisis and Catharsis

text: An article last Sunday about the Dance on Camera festival misspelled the surname of a dancer in “Bend.” She is Troy Ogilvie, not Ogilive.
match_headline: The Dance on Camera Festival, When Dance Is Only on Camera

text: An article last Sunday about Harvard’s reopening plan and its effect on low-income students referred incorrectly to Dumebi Adigwe. She is not the first person in her family to attend college.
match_headline: What’s the Value of Harvard Without a Campus?

text: An essay last Sunday about Ann M. Martin’s Baby-Sitters Club books misstated the year that Raina Telgemeier began publishing her graphic novel adaptations of the series. It was 2006, not 2015, which was the year the color editions debuted.
match_headline: The Baby-Sitters Club Taught Me Everything I Needed to Know About Literary Fiction

text: An article July 5 about things to do in the coming week misstated the year that the Mexican Revolution began. It started in 1910, not 1920.
match_headline: Visit the Louvre and Christina Tosi’s Kitchen

text: An article on Sunday about the effects of the Nicaraguan government’s response to the coronavirus outbreak misstated the name of a top police official who died in May. He was Olivio Hernández Salguera, not Olivio Salguera Hernández.
match_headline: Nicaragua’s Ruling Sandinistas Fall Victim to Covid-19, Highlighting the Disease’s Spread

text: An article on Saturday about a Tunisian woman who was sentenced to prison for posting a joke alluding to the Quran on social media referred incorrectly to a sura in the Quran. A sura is a chapter, not a verse.
match_headline: Tunisian Woman Sentenced to Prison Over Joke Alluding to the Quran

text: An article on Sunday on plans for Representative John Lewis to lie in state misidentified the location where former Representative Elijah E. Cummings, Democrat of Maryland, had lain in state. It was Statuary Hall, not the Capitol Rotunda.
match_headline: Amid a Pandemic, Supporters Hope John Lewis Can Still Lie in State in the Capitol

text: An article on Sunday about the negative reaction by some conservatives to President Trump’s attacks on Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. referred incorrectly to the LaPorte County government’s history of resolutions regarding Supreme Court rulings. The County Commission adopted one resolution in support of a ruling last month, Bostock v. Clayton County, Ga., in which the decision was written by Justice Neil M. Gorsuch; it is not the case that the County Council occasionally adopts resolutions either hailing or denouncing Chief Justice Roberts’s rulings.
match_headline: Why Trump’s Attacks on John Roberts Aren’t Working With Some Conservatives

text: An article on Saturday about newly declassified documents connected to the investigation of Trump-Russia ties described incorrectly the involvement of the former F.B.I. agent Peter Strzok in the interview of a source for a former British spy, Christopher Steele. Mr. Strzok was not present for that interview, although he appeared to be aware of aspects of it.
match_headline: F.B.I. Agent in Russia Inquiry Saw Basis in Early 2017 to Doubt Dossier

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the future of the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors misstated the name of a former Fed governor. She is Sarah Bloom Raskin, not Boom.
match_headline: Trump’s Hot-Button Fed Pick Faces Senate Committee Vote This Week

text: An article on Saturday about the World Surf League’s canceled 2020 season misstated the world governing body of the sport. It is the International Surfing Association, not the World Surf League.
match_headline: World Surf League Cancels 2020 Season and Revamps Future Tours

text: An article on Sunday about the bike trails in Los Dinamos National Park in Mexico City misstated the size of the park. It is 6,000 acres, not “more than 1,000 acres.”
match_headline: Hardcore Cyclists Head for the Hills … Mexico City’s

text: An article on Sunday about the Toronto Blue Jays referred incorrectly to the minor league classifications of the ballparks in Buffalo and Rochester, N.Y. They are Class AAA, not Class AA.
match_headline: Blue Jays Can’t Play Games in Canada Because of Pandemic

text: An article on Saturday about the Washington N.F.L. franchise’s harassment report described incorrectly the gender makeup of hiring by the N.F.L. In 2019, 36.8 percent of the people hired at the N.F.L.’s headquarters were women; it is not the case that women hold 36.8 percent of jobs at the N.F.L.’s headquarters. (At the N.F.L. headquarters in New York, 45 percent of employees are women.)
match_headline: Washington N.F.L. Harassment Report Shocked Many, but Not Women

text: An article last Friday about the N.H.L.’s reworked playoff format described incorrectly the Bruins’ margin of loss in Game 7 of last year’s Stanley Cup finals against the Blues. They lost the game, 4-1; Boston was not “a one-goal loser.”
match_headline: The Boston Bruins Had Home Ice. Now They’ve Got a Hub.

text: An article on Monday about Japan’s reality TV hit “Terrace House” misspelled the surname of a computer science professor at the Kitami Institute of Technology in Hokkaido. He is Michal Ptaszynski, not Ptaszynsky.
match_headline: The Fall of ‘Terrace House’

text: An article on Monday about the The Metropolitan Opera’s venture into the realm of paid digital content misstated to whom the opera singer Jonas Kaufmann was donating $5,000. It was for musicians who are out of work, not specifically those at the Metropolitan Opera.
match_headline: The Met Opera Tries to Find Paying Customers in a Pandemic

text: An article on Saturday about WNYC’s presentation of “Richard II” misstated the number of characters bearing the title of King Henry in the Henriad. It is three, not two.
match_headline: ‘Richard II’ Review: A Radio King With a Tottering Crown

text: An article last Tuesday about the climate scientist Maureen Raymo relying on data in a Columbia University publication, misstated the share of white faculty members in the university’s department of earth and environmental sciences. It is at least 95 percent, not 88 percent.
match_headline: She’s an Authority on Earth’s Past. Now, Her Focus Is the Planet’s Future.

text: An obituary on July 11 about the actor Earl Cameron referred incorrectly to the character he played in the James Bond movie “Thunderball.” He played an intelligence agent based in the Bahamas who helps Bond — not Bond’s chauffeur.
match_headline: Earl Cameron, Barrier-Breaking British Actor, Is Dead at 102

text: An article on Tuesday about the anti-feminist lawyer suspected in the deadly attack on a judge’s family misstated the age of the suspect, Roy Den Hollander, who was later found dead. He was 72, not 69.
match_headline: ‘Anti-Feminist’ Lawyer Is Suspect in Killing of Son of Federal Judge in N.J.

text: An article on Saturday about street demonstrations in Portland, Ore., misidentified the object that a protester was holding when he was struck in the head by an impact munition. It was a speaker, not a sign.
match_headline: Federal Agents Unleash Militarized Crackdown on Portland

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the decision by the New York Giants and New York Jets not to admit fans for regular-season games, misidentified the location of the Jets’ training camp. It is located in Florham Park, N.J., not New York.
match_headline: Jets and Giants Are N.F.L.’s First to Say They’ll Play Without Fans

text: An article on Tuesday about N.B.A.-linked social media accounts misidentified the N.B.A. team that Meyers Leonard plays for. It is the Miami Heat, not the Portland Trail Blazers.
match_headline: Who Is Behind Those N.B.A. ‘Bubble Life’ Tweets?

text: A Reporter’s Notebook on Saturday about plans for the release of Christopher Nolan’s film “Tenet” overstated what is known about Christopher Nolan’s compensation for the film. While it has been reported that Nolan will receive 20 percent of the film’s first-dollar gross, both Nolan and Warner Bros. dispute that figure and have not disclosed details about Nolan’s compensation.
match_headline: Christopher Nolan Says ‘Tenet’ Will Come Out This Summer. Should It?

text: An article on Saturday about Adam Greenfield’s plans to present four plays directed by women in Playwrights Horizons’ next season misstated the number of years that Tim Sanford was artistic director of Playwrights Horizons. It was nearly 25 years, not 35.
match_headline: Playwrights Horizons Details First Season Under New Leadership

text: An article on July 8 about the scarcity of Black-owned restaurants in the Twin Cities, misstated the racial heritage of Dawn Drouillard, a co-owner of Fabulous Catering. She is partly of Anishinaabe heritage, and a Grand Portage tribal descendant.
match_headline: In the Twin Cities’ Robust Dining Scene, Few Black-Owned Businesses

text: An article on Wednesday about a study that suggested that coronavirus infections may be much higher than reported in parts of the United States misstated the journal in which the new study was published. It is JAMA Internal Medicine, not JAMA.
match_headline: Coronavirus Infections Much Higher Than Reported Cases in Parts of U.S., Study Shows

text: An article on Wednesday about the resignation of Jide Zeitlin, the chief executive of Tapestry, misstated the number of Black chief executive officers in the Fortune 500. With Mr. Zeitlin, there were five, not four.
match_headline: Tapestry C.E.O. Resigns, Acknowledging Past Relationship

text: An obituary on Saturday about the Rev. Vickey Gibbs misstated the name of the town in Texas where Sandra Bland was found hanged in a jail cell in 2015. It is Hempstead, not Hampstead.
match_headline: Rev. Vickey Gibbs, Activist in a Progressive Church, Dies at 57

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the singer and songwriter Emitt Rhodes referred incorrectly to Hawthorne, where he lived. It is a city in Los Angeles County, not an area of Los Angeles.
match_headline: Emitt Rhodes, 70, Dies; Singer-Songwriter Vanished After a Splash

text: An article on Thursday about the return of the N.B.A. during the pandemic misstated Montrezl Harrell’s role on the Los Angeles Clippers. He usually is a reserve, not a starter.
match_headline: The N.B.A. Is Back. This Is What Pandemic Basketball Looks Like.

text: An article on July 16 about a debate over plans to redesign the sculpture garden at the Hirshhorn Museum omitted an aspect of the debate. After publication, museum officials indicated that they had received letters of support from prominent figures in the world of museums and architecture for the design.
match_headline: At the Hirshhorn, a Battle Over Plans for Its Sculpture Garden

text: An obituary on July 15 about the Brazilian society figure Thereza de Orléans e Bragança misstated her age. She was 91, not 93. (As the obituary correctly stated, she was born on Jan. 11, 1929.) This error was repeated in the headline. The obituary also misstated the year that Dom João Maria de Orléans e Bragança, her second husband, moved to Brazil from France. It was 1935, not 1925.
match_headline: Thereza de Orléans e Bragança, Brazilian Society Doyenne, Dies at 91

text: An article on Friday about a large DNA study that traced the violent history of American slavery referred imprecisely to some historical research. Historical records do exist showing that enslaved people were shipped directly from Nigeria to the United States, but not to the extent indicated by the new genetic evidence.
match_headline: Large DNA Study Traces Violent History of American Slavery

text: An article on Friday about a new Pentagon U.F.O. unit inaccurately rendered remarks attributed to Harry Reid, the retired Senate majority leader from Nevada. Mr. Reid said he believed that crashes of objects of unknown origin may have occurred and that retrieved materials should be studied; he did not say that crashes had occurred and that retrieved materials had been studied secretly for decades. The article also misstated the frequency with which the director of national intelligence is supposed to report on unidentified aerial phenomena. It is 180 days after enactment of the intelligence authorization act, not every six months.
match_headline: No Longer in Shadows, Pentagon’s U.F.O. Unit Will Make Some Findings Public

text: An article on Thursday about the 18th-century composer Joseph Boulogne, using information from a 1990 journal article, misidentified the Boulogne violin concerto that has similarities to a Mozart work. It is Op. 7, No. 1, not Op. 7, No. 2.
match_headline: His Name Is Joseph Boulogne, Not ‘Black Mozart’

text: An article this weekend on Page 5 about the director Krzysztof Warlikowski, who is staging “Elektra” at the Salzburg Festival, misspells the surname of a Polish actor. He is Jacek Poniedzialek, not Pondiezialek.
match_headline: A Director Brings Cerebral, Sexy Style to Opera Classics

text: An article on July 12 about the new Starz drama “P-Valley” described incorrectly the extent to which the actress Brandee Evans performed her character’s moves in the show’s dance sequences. She did many of them, not all; body doubles performed many as well.
match_headline: ‘P-Valley’ Dances to a Different Tune

text: Because of an editing error, the Calculator feature last Sunday misspelled a street name of a property in Pickering, Ontario. The home is at 429 Tonavale Road, not 429 Yonavale Road.
match_headline: The Most Popular Listings of June

text: An article on Monday about coronavirus antibodies referred incorrectly to a clinical testing company. It is Quest Diagnostics, not Quest Labs.
match_headline: Your Coronavirus Antibodies Are Disappearing. Should You Care?

text: An article on Sunday about the W.N.B.A. dedicating its season to Breonna Taylor, who was fatally shot by police in Louisville, Ky., misstated the length of the 2020 W.N.B.A. season. It will be 22 games (for each team), not weeks.
match_headline: ‘We Will Be a Voice for the Voiceless’: The W.N.B.A. Season Is Dedicated to Breonna Taylor

text: An article on Saturday about the actor Johnny Depp’s lawsuit against a British newspaper misstated the reasons that Winona Ryder and Vanessa Paradis did not testify at the trial. It was because Depp’s team decided not to call them, not because the defense team chose not to challenge their testimony.
match_headline: Johnny Depp and Amber Heard’s Courtroom Face-Off: An Explainer

text: An obituary on Thursday about the singer and actress Annie Ross referred incorrectly to her son, Kenny Clarke Jr. He died in 2018; he does not survive her.
match_headline: Annie Ross, Jazz Vocalist of ‘Twisted’ Renown, Dies at 89

text: An article on Tuesday about Confederate identity in Lexington, Va., misspelled the given name of a member of the Lexington City Council. She is Marylin Alexander, not Marilyn.
match_headline: A Liberal Town Built Around Confederate Generals Rethinks Its Identity

text: An article on Saturday about Jacksonville’s brief time as the future home of the Republican National Convention described incorrectly the size of Jacksonville, Fla. It is the largest city by land area in the contiguous United States, not the continental United States.
match_headline: Thanks to Trump, Jacksonville Becomes Political Roadkill

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a postponed game between the Yankees and the Philadelphia Phillies described incorrectly the Major League Baseball summer camp. Every team had workouts at their home stadiums, not all teams except Toronto.
match_headline: After Marlins’ Outbreak, Yankees Stay Inside and Wait for Phillies

text: An article on Tuesday about the 1980 Olympic boycott described incorrectly the circumstances in which Vice President Walter Mondale apologized for the boycott. He made the statement during an interview with The Wall Street Journal, not during a town hall event with athletes.
match_headline: That Almost Apology for the 1980 Olympic Boycott Helps. A Little.

text: An article on Wednesday about similarities between the public personas of President Trump and his father described incorrectly the illness that afflicted Donald Trump’s mother when he was two and a half years old. The illness she suffered from, peritonitis, is an inflammation of the peritoneum, a tissue lining the abdominal cavity, not the stomach lining.
match_headline: Like Father, Like Son: President Trump Lets Others Mourn

text: A picture caption with an article on July 4 about the use of deepfakes in a documentary, based on information from a publicist, misidentified a volunteer whose face was used to cloak one of the documentary’s subjects. He is Miguel Grisanti, not Matias Alvial.
match_headline: Deepfake Technology Enters the Documentary World

text: A headline with an article last Thursday about the decline of Brooks Brothers referred imprecisely to Lisa Birnbach’s contribution to “The Official Preppy Handbook.” She was the book’s editor and an author, not its sole author.
match_headline: Save Brooks Brothers!

text: An obituary on Friday about Tony Elliott, the founder of the Time Out global publishing empire, misspelled the name of the town in England where he was born. It is Reading, not Redding.
match_headline: Tony Elliott, Whose Time Out Clued Readers In, Dies at 73

text: An obituary on July 4 about the marijuana scholar Lester Grinspoon misstated the year that the movie “Reefer Madness,” originally known as “Tell Your Children,” was released. It was either 1938 or 1939 — not, despite what many sources say, 1936.
match_headline: Lester Grinspoon, Influential Marijuana Scholar, Dies at 92

text: An article on Thursday about Representative Louie Gohmert of Texas testing positive for the coronavirus misidentified the state that Raúl M. Grijalva represents. It is Arizona, not New Mexico.
match_headline: Anti-Mask Louie Gohmert Tests Positive, Sending Shudders Through Congress

text: An article on Thursday about Belarus accusing Russian mercenaries of trying to interfere in the country’s election described incorrectly what 33 arrested Russians were said to be carrying when they came to Belarus. They were carrying three heavy suitcases altogether, according to a report by Belta, Belarus’s official news agency; they were not each carrying three heavy suitcases.
match_headline: Belarus Says Russian Mercenaries Planned to Disrupt August Election

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Bahrain’s investment in Paris F.C. misstated the reason for Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei’s arrest. He was arrested for participating in pro-democracy protests, not antidemocracy protests.
match_headline: Bahrain Buys Into Paris F.C., With Plans to Use It as a Billboard

text: An article on Page 10 about the Netflix documentary series “Last Chance U” refers imprecisely to coach John Beam. He identifies as multiracial, not white.
match_headline: ‘Last Chance U’ Travels to Oakland, Just Like the Players

text: An article on Monday about the teenager who recently hacked Twitter misattributed a quote to Colby Meeds and referred incorrectly to his relationship with Graham Ivan Clark. Referring to Mr. Clark, Mr. Meeds said, “He scammed me for a little bit of money when I was just a kid,” not that Mr. Clark “would do anything for money.” Also, Mr. Meeds was a fellow player of Minecraft, not a friend of Mr. Clark’s.
ref_headline: He scammed me for a little bit of money when I was just a kid,
match_headline: From Minecraft Tricks to Twitter Hack: A Florida Teen’s Troubled Online Path

text: An article on Saturday about signs of economic recovery in Europe misstated the total value of the bonds to be sold under an agreement reached by European Union members this month. The countries agreed to sell 750 billion euros’ worth of bonds, not 750 million.
match_headline: Despite Historic Plunge, Europe’s Economy Flashes Signs of Recovery

text: An article on Saturday about a heat wave in the Middle East misspelled the surname of the director of the World Weather Research Program. It is Paolo Ruti, not Rutti.
match_headline: Scorching Temperatures Bake Middle East Amid Eid al-Adha Celebrations

text: An article on Saturday referred incorrectly to the political affiliations of Cass and Samantha Mattison of Texas. They are Republican, but they are not registered Republicans. (In Texas, voters do not register by party affiliation.)
match_headline: Alienated by Trump, Suburban Voters Sour on G.O.P. in Battle for the House

text: An article on Monday about remakes and remasters of popular video games misstated the plans of the publisher Capcom for the game Resident Evil 4. The company has not announced plans to remake the game.
match_headline: Like Old Hollywood Movies, Video Games Get a Polish for New Audiences

text: An article on Monday about Beyoncé’s “Black Is King” referred incorrectly to the contribution by the musician Tekno. He performs background vocals on the album, but he does not appear in the visual album.
match_headline: Beyoncé’s ‘Black Is King’: Let’s Discuss

text: An article on Sunday about a far-right network in Germany misstated one of the uses of quicklime. It can be used to mask the stench of decomposing bodies, not to decompose organic material.
match_headline: Body Bags and Enemy Lists: How Far-Right Police Officers and Ex-Soldiers Planned for ‘Day X’

text: An article on Saturday about an inquiry by the House Foreign Affairs Committee into reports that the U.S. ambassador to Brazil framed negotiations over ethanol tariffs in partisan terms misstated the date of Brazil’s municipal elections. They are scheduled to take place in November, not September.
match_headline: Lawmakers ‘Alarmed’ by Reports U.S. Envoy Told Brazil It Could Help Re-elect Trump

text: An article on Monday about the new Genoa San Giorgio bridge misstated the location of Genoa, Italy. It is in the country’s northwest, not northeast.
match_headline: As Genoa Inaugurates New Bridge, the Feeling Is Bittersweet

text: An article on Tuesday about a minor-league baseball team that chose to keep its name despite a reference to Native Americans misstated the month that a football team said it would change its name. The Washington N.F.L. Team abandoned its nickname last month, not earlier this month.
match_headline: Why One Team Named the Indians Won’t Be Changing Its Name

text: An article on Jan. 8 about Usha Prabakaran, the Indian author of a classic cookbook on pickling, described incorrectly the soup known as rasam. It is often vegetarian, but not always. (This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to editors’ attention.)
match_headline: India’s ‘Pickle Queen’ Preserves Everything, Including the Past

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about plasma infusions as a coronavirus treatment misstated the network that runs “Lou Dobbs Tonight.” It is Fox Business Network, not Fox News.
match_headline: As Trump Praises Plasma, Researchers Struggle to Finish Critical Studies

text: An article on Wednesday about discoveries made by scientists by studying the worst cases of coronavirus misstated the name of a scientific journal that published a recent study. It was Nature, not Nature Medicine.
match_headline: Scientists Uncover Biological Signatures of the Worst Covid-19 Cases

text: An article on Tuesday about Turkey’s aggressive foreign policy referred incorrectly to part of the remarks made by Amanda Sloat, a former State Department official. Ms. Sloat said the European Union had no clear policy on Turkey or Libya. While the United Nations lacks a policy on competing claims for drilling rights in the Eastern Mediterranean, Ms. Sloat said, she did not say the U.N. had no policy on the countries as a whole.
match_headline: Turkish Aggression Is NATO’s ‘Elephant in the Room’

text: An article on Wednesday about state primary results announced this week misstated the winner of a Missouri House race. Cori Bush defeated William Lacy Clay Jr., not the reverse.
match_headline: Kris Kobach Loses Kansas Senate Primary, Easing Republican Worries

text: An article on Wednesday about a ruling by a federal appeals court that blocked the Trump administration’s efforts to deny permanent residency to legal immigrants misidentified the judge who affirmed the ruling and misstated the timing of his decision. It was affirmed by a Manhattan judge in 2019, not by Judge George P. Daniels of the U.S. District Court in Manhattan last week.
match_headline: Appeals Court Blocks Immigrant Wealth Test in the Northeast

text: A picture with an article on Wednesday about BP’s $16.8 billion quarterly loss, relying on information from Reuters, misidentified a BP site in Cambridgeshire, Britain. The image was of a ground-mounted Lightsource BP site, not a floating installation at the Queen Elizabeth II Reservoir.
match_headline: BP Reports a Huge Loss and Vows to Increase Renewable Investment

text: An article on Wednesday about Sotheby’s 2019 art sales misspelled the surname of the chief executive of Pi-eX. She is Christine Bourron, not Bouron.
match_headline: Sotheby’s Reports $2.5 Billion in Sales

text: An article on Tuesday about the effect of the global response to the coronavirus on the prevalence of diseases other than Covid-19 referred imprecisely to the region where 90 percent of annual malaria deaths occur. They occur across Sub-Saharan Africa, not only in West Africa.
match_headline: ‘The Biggest Monster’ Is Spreading. And It’s Not the Coronavirus.

text: An article last Thursday about the soprano Renée Fleming referred incorrectly to the vocal range of Susan Graham. She is a mezzo-soprano, not a soprano.
match_headline: Renée Fleming, Songbird in Seclusion

text: An obituary on July 27 about the actress Olivia de Havilland, one of the stars of “Gone With the Wind,” referred incorrectly to the production of that movie. It was produced by Selznick International Pictures and distributed by MGM; it was not an “MGM production.” The obituary also misstated the cause of the death of Ms. de Havilland’s son, Benjamin Goodrich. It was heart disease, not Hodgkin’s disease.
match_headline: Olivia de Havilland, a Star of ‘Gone With the Wind,’ Dies at 104

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor Wilford Brimley described incorrectly the character he played in the movie “Absence of Malice.” He was an assistant U.S. attorney, not a district attorney. The obituary also referred incorrectly in part to Mr. Brimley’s musical talents. While he was an accomplished singer, he was not known to play the guitar.
match_headline: Wilford Brimley, ‘Cocoon’ Star and Quaker Oats Pitchman, Is Dead at 85

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the pianist Leon Fleisher misstated the year he had planned to tour the Soviet Union with the Cleveland Orchestra before bowing out. It was 1965, not 1964.
match_headline: Leon Fleisher, 92, Dies; Spellbinding Pianist Using One Hand or Two

text: An article on Friday about Sahar Fares, a paramedic who died in the explosion in Beirut, misstated her age. She was 27, not 24.
match_headline: Paramedic Who Died in Beirut Explosion Is a Symbol of Lebanon’s Grief

text: An article on Friday about allegations of sexual abuse against the Olympian George Morris misstated part of the name of one of the places where an equestrian athlete said she was abused. It was the Flintridge Riding Club, not Academy.
match_headline: Top Equestrians Accused of Sex Abuse in Lawsuits

text: An article on Thursday about the future of Henrik Lundqvist’s career misstated the number of Mr. Lundqvist’s career wins and shutouts. He has won 459 games in his career, not 449, and has 64 shutouts, not 63.
match_headline: Henrik Lundqvist’s Rangers Future Is in Doubt After Elimination

text: An article on Friday about street art on boarded-up storefronts in New York misattributed the words on a sign created by an anonymous artist on Wooster Street. The words were taken from Frederick Douglass’s 1852 speech “The Meaning of July Fourth for the Negro”; it was not poetry by the unnamed artist. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
ref_headline: The Meaning of July Fourth for the Negro
