match_headline: New York’s Sidewalk Prophets Are Heirs of the Artisans of France’s Lascaux Caves

text: An article on Page 20 about Covid-19 treatment research misstates Lynn Schnapp’s position at the University of Wisconsin medical school. She is chair of the department of medicine, not chair of the medical school. It also refers incorrectly to the participants in a conference call. Dr. Stella Hahn was not in the conference room with her colleagues during the call.
match_headline: The Covid Drug Wars That Pitted Doctor vs. Doctor

text: An article last Sunday about fraternity brothers and sorority sisters who are working to get Greek organizations off campus misidentified the sorority that the Emory student Emma Pinto left. It was Zeta Tau Alpha, not Kappa Kappa Gamma. The article also misspelled the surname of a student at Vanderbilt. He is Jared Bauman, not Baumann.
match_headline: The War on Frats

text: A headline with a wedding report last Sunday misstated the given name of the man who married Jennifer Soffen. As the article correctly noted, he is Harrison Marks, not Douglas — which is his middle name.
match_headline: A Perfect Spot for Running, or Proposing

text: An article on July 26 about the Kariba Dam, on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe, misstated an aspect of the dam. Erosion threatens the foundation; it is not the case that the foundation is eroded. The article also misstated the location of a future dam. It will be on a tributary of the Zambezi River, not on the Zambezi River. And the trees in Lake Kariba are dead trees; they do not continue to grow.

A review on July 19 about Maggie O’Farrell’s “Hamnet: A Novel of the Plague” overstated what is known about the death of Shakespeare’s son, Hamnet. The circumstances of his death were not recorded; it is not known that he “died of plague.”
ref_headline: Hamnet: A Novel of the Plague
match_headline: Shakespeare’s Son Died at 11. A Novel Asks How It Shaped His Art.

text: An article last Sunday about taking mass transit safely misstated the academic credentials of Sarah M. Kaufman. She has a degree in urban planning but does not have a Ph.D.
match_headline: How to Stay Safer on Mass Transit

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the harsher impacts that the world’s poorest communities face with the rise in global temperatures misstated the findings of a study on heat in Athens since the late 1800s. The city experienced fewer than 20 hot days in total in the decade from 1897 until 1906, not fewer than 20 hot days per year. Similarly, there were fewer than 50 hot days in total from 1987-96, not per year; and more than 120 in total from 2007-16, not per year.
match_headline: Kenya’s Unusual Solution to the School Problem: Cancel the Year and Start Over

text: Because of an editing error, an Op-Ed column about the diplomatic career of Susan Rice omitted part of a sentence in some copies on Tuesday. The full sentence should have read: The former New York Times correspondent Howard French noted that Rice seems to have taken the view that the best U.S. policy was to “look the other way” as Rwanda and Uganda went to war.
match_headline: Susan Rice Was a Diplomatic Disaster

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the N.B.A. star Stephen Curry misidentified the employer of John Hollinger. He works for The Athletic, not ESPN.
match_headline: Stephen Curry Has ‘Major FOMO’ in Life Outside the N.B.A. Bubble

text: An article last Wednesday about making empanadas using popcorn misstated the place in Colombia where empanadas de pipián originated. They are from Popayán, not Bocayá.
match_headline: A Colombian Chef Shares His Secret to Better Empanadas

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about James Powers, the owner of an art gallery in Brooklyn, misstated the year the jazz pianist Geri Allen died. It was 2017, not this year.
match_headline: James Powers, Brooklyn Gallerist Who Nurtured Black Artists, Dies at 80

text: An article on Saturday about the re-election challenge faced by President Aleksandr G. Lukashenko of Belarus misspelled the surname of one of his supporters. She is Lyudmila S. Krokhaleva, not Khrokhaleva.
match_headline: Europe’s ‘Last Dictator,’ Facing Re-Election, Is Increasingly in Peril

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s search for a running mate misidentifieda former Florida lawmaker who served with Mr. Biden in the Senate. He is Bill Nelson, not Ben.
match_headline: In Tennessee, Bill Hagerty Wins Senate Primary

text: An article on Monday about composting in New York described incorrectly the status of compost collection at GrowNYC farmers’ markets. Most of the sites have paused collection, not all of them.
match_headline: Composting Has Been Scrapped. These New Yorkers Picked Up the Slack.

text: An article on Monday about UCONN’s decision to cancel its football season included an outdated job description for Gretchen Snoeyenbos Newman. She is now an assistant professor of infectious disease at Wayne State University, not an infectious disease fellow at the University of Washington.
match_headline: Players to UConn Coach: ‘There’s No Way That We Can Play’

text: An article on Friday about a suffragist statue that will be placed in Central Park referred incorrectly to its funding sources. While the group behind the statue, Monumental Women, raised the bulk of the funding, it did receive some money from the city. A total of $135,000 came from the Manhattan borough president, Gale Brewer, and Councilwoman Helen Rosenthal.
match_headline: For Three Suffragists, a Monument Well Past Due

text: An obituary on Saturday about the former Yankee second baseman Horace Clarke misstated the number of major league players, including Clarke, who had 150 or more stolen bases and 1,200 or more hits from 1965 to 1974. It was 11, not 10.
match_headline: Horace Clarke, Standout in a Dismal Yankee Era, Dies at 82

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about pro-democracy protests in Thailand misidentified a subject in the image. Benjamaporn Nivas is second from the left in the image; she is not being interviewed.
match_headline: In Thailand, Students Take on the Military (and ‘Death Eaters’)

text: An article last Thursday about the comforts of home that Americans abroad miss at a time of international travel restrictions referred incorrectly to a newborn member of Nicole Trilivas’s family. The baby is her nephew, not her niece.
match_headline: Peanut Butter and Ranch Dressing: What Americans Abroad Miss From Home

text: An obituary on July 11 about Helen O’Hagan, the longtime publicity director of Saks Fifth Avenue, erroneously credited the store’s former in-house designer Sophie Gimbel with a distinction. She was credited with introducing culottes to the American market — not with inventing them.
match_headline: Helen O’Hagan, Fashion Executive Who Personified Saks, Dies at 89

text: An article on Thursday about the closing of The Daily News’s Manhattan newsroom misidentified the newspaper where Jen Sheehan works. Ms. Sheehan works for The Morning Call, not The Orlando Sentinel.
match_headline: The Daily News Is Now a Newspaper Without a Newsroom

text: An article on Tuesday about a request for discovery filed by Daniel Snyder, the owner of the Washington Football Team, misstated Tracy Schar’s role at Comstock Holding Companies. She is its senior vice president for marketing and brand management, not a member of its board of directors.
match_headline: Washington N.F.L. Team Owner Files Claims Hinting at a Conspiracy

text: An article on Thursday about a track coach at Wesleyan University who fostered a culture of body shaming and eating disorders misstated the Wesleyan University women’s cross-country program’s results. The team has made two Division III championship appearances since 2009, not in 2009 alone.
match_headline: ‘Fat Talks,’ an Investigation, and a Reckoning: How Collegiate Runners Forced Reform

text: An obituary on July 23 about the civil rights leader Charles Evers referred incorrectly to Fayette, Miss., where he was elected mayor in 1969. While it is near the Mississippi River, it is not in the Mississippi Delta.
match_headline: Charles Evers, Businessman and Civil Rights Leader, Dies at 97

text: An article on Friday about the promotion of a theory by President Trump that questions Senator Kamala Harris’s eligibility to run for vice president misspelled the name of the University of California school from which Ms. Harris’s parents received doctorates. It was the University of California, Berkeley, not Berkley.
match_headline: Trump Encourages Racist Conspiracy Theory About Kamala Harris

text: An article on Friday about a tennis match between Venus and Serena Williams at the Top Seed Open misstated the score of the Williams sisters’ match on Thursday. Serena Williams beat Venus Williams, 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, not 6-3, 3-6, 6-4.
match_headline: With No Fanfare, Williams Sisters Give It Their All

text: An article on Friday about new exhibitions on the Lower East Side misspelled the surname of the owner of the Karma gallery. He is Brendan Dugan, not Duggan. A picture caption with the article, using information from Tibor de Nagy gallery, misstated the title of an artwork by Ann Toebbe. It is “Sheila’s House,” not “Antique Dealers.” Also, a picture caption omitted the title of an artwork shown. It is Zenzaburo Kojima’s “Roses,” 1960, at Karma in the East Village.
match_headline: A Bouquet of Group Art Shows Near Houston Street

text: An article last Sunday about the author H. P. Lovecraft’s legacy misidentified the setting of the film “Re-Animator.” It is the fictional town of Arkham, Mass., in the 1980s, not contemporary Chicago.
match_headline: Gods, Monsters and H.P. Lovecraft’s Uncanny Legacy

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about New York City and the pandemic misstated the number of coronavirus cases and deaths in New York in mid-April. At that time, there were more than 100,000 cases and over 6,000 deaths, not more than 420,000 cases and 30,000 deaths.
match_headline: A Season of Grief and Release: 5 Months of the Virus in New York City

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Lauren Maillian and Robert Palmer misstated Mr. Palmer’s marital history. He had previously been married.
match_headline: Between Reps at the Gym, a Strong Connection

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about choosing the right New York City suburb misstated the property tax amount for a one-bedroom condo in Mahopac, N.Y. The taxes are $2,797 a year, not $2,797 a month.
match_headline: Leaving New York: How to Choose the Right Suburb

text: Because of a production error, an obituary about Robert S. Trump, President Trump’s younger brother, was missing from some editions of Sunday’s paper. It is reprinted today.
match_headline: President Trump Visits Younger Brother in Hospital in New York

text: An article on Sunday about an increased demands for tuition rebates as colleges move to online instruction referred incorrectly to a petition to the University of North Carolina system that has attracted more than 40,000 signatures. It is a plea to the university to refund student housing charges in the event of another Covid-19 related shutdown, not to house students in that event. The article also misstated the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s reopening plans; the university will begin the fall semester with some classes held in person but most held remotely; it will not be relying entirely on remote classes.
match_headline: As Colleges Move Classes Online, Families Rebel Against the Cost

text: An article on Monday about protests in Belarus referred incorrectly to NATO’s spokesperson. The spokesperson, Oana Lungescu, is a woman .
match_headline: Belarus Protests Eclipse Rally in Defense of Defiant Leader

text: An article on Saturday about President Trump visit to see his dying brother, Robert S. Trump, in a Manhattan hospital misstated Robert Trump’s age. He was 71, not 72.
match_headline: Robert S. Trump, the President’s Younger Brother, Dies at 71

text: An article on Saturday about the Marxist scholar Adolph Reed misstated the connection of Keeanga-Yamahtta Taylor to the Democratic Socialists of America. She has given talks to D.S.A. chapters, but she is not a member.
match_headline: A Black Marxist Scholar Wanted to Talk About Race. It Ignited a Fury.

text: An article on Sunday about notable political moments that occurred the previous week misquoted a portion of President Trump’s comments at a briefing last week about what he believes will happen if Joseph R. Biden Jr. is elected. He said, “They’re going to, in my opinion, destroy suburbia. And just so you understand, 30 percent-plus of the people living in suburbia are minorities. African-American, Asian-American, Hispanic-American — they’re minorities. Thirty percent. The number is even higher, it’s — they say 35, but I like to cut it a little bit lower. You know why? That way I can never get myself in too much trouble with the fake news.” He did not say: “They’re going to destroy suburbia. And 30 percent of the people in suburbia are minorities. They say 35 percent, but I like to cut it lower.”
ref_headline: They’re going to destroy suburbia. And 30 percent of the people in suburbia are minorities. They say 35 percent, but I like to cut it lower.
match_headline: Kamala Harris Changes the Race While Trump Tells on Himself

text: An article on Monday about Bhutanese immigrants who have occupied themselves during the pandemic with archery misstated the distance between the archery targets during the matches. They are 145 meters, or about 475 feet, apart, not 145 feet apart.
match_headline: These Uber Drivers Are Stressed. Archery Soothes Them.

text: An article on Monday about new music to explore misstated the surname of the violinist on Slow Pulp’s song. She is Molly Germer, not Gemer.
match_headline: Drake’s GIF-a-Thon, and 9 More New Songs

text: An article on Tuesday about the Great American Outdoors Act misidentified the lawmaker who introduced the Great American Outdoors Act in the House. It was Representative Joe Cunningham, not the late Representative John Lewis.
match_headline: Trump Signs Landmark Land Conservation Bill

text: An obituary on July 31 about the former Republican presidential candidate Herman Cain referred incorrectly to the Burger King franchises he oversaw when he was an executive at Pillsbury. They were in the Philadelphia area; they were not all in the city of Philadelphia.
match_headline: Herman Cain, Former C.E.O. and Presidential Candidate, Dies at 74

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the effects of President Trump’s restrictions on Chinese tech companies misstated the name of the company celebrating its 2018 I.P.O. It is Tencent Music Entertainment, not Tencent.
match_headline: Trump’s Attacks on TikTok and WeChat Could Further Fracture the Internet

text: An article on Monday about the opening night of the Democratic National Convention misstated the circumstances of Sandra Bland’s death. She was found hanged in a Texas jail cell; she was not slain by the police.
match_headline: Democrats Begin Virtual Convention, Hailing Biden and Denouncing Trump

text: An article on Tuesday about an increase in coronavirus infections in France misstated the coronavirus case numbers in three European countries. In the past week, about 16,000 new cases, not 20,000, were reported by France; 7,000, not 3,000, by Britain; and 3,000, not 7,000, by Italy, according to data collected by The New York Times.
match_headline: Beaten Back, the Coronavirus Regains Strength in France

text: An article on Tuesday about a legal settlement that requires automakers to comply with emissions standards in California misstated the number of automakers that reached the agreement. It was five, not four.
match_headline: Defying Trump, 5 Automakers Lock In a Deal on Greenhouse Gas Pollution

text: An article on Tuesday about two conflicting measurements for the foot misstated the number of original signatories of the Treaty of the Metre in 1875. There were 17, not 16.
match_headline: America Has Two Feet. It’s About to Lose One of Them.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the newspaper executive turned screenwriter Kurt Luedtke misstated the scope of the landmark 1964 Supreme Court ruling in New York Times v. Sullivan. The court held that the First Amendment protects a publication from libel suits by public officials, even when it prints false statements, as long as the publication did not act with “actual malice.” The ruling did not protect publications from all libel suits.
match_headline: Kurt Luedtke, Newspaperman Turned Screenwriter, Dies at 80

text: An obituary on Aug. 12 about the singer Trini Lopez misstated the name of the town in central Mexico where his parents lived before moving to Dallas. It is Moroleón, not Morolean.
match_headline: Trini Lopez, Singing Star Who Mixed Musical Styles, Dies at 83

text: An article on Friday about Beirut’s Shiite community misstated when Lebanon’s power-sharing system was put in place. It was in existence before the country’s civil war; it was not adopted after the war. The article also overstated what is known about the country’s demographic composition. No reliable census data on the current population is available; it is not clear whether Shiites represent the largest sect of Islam in the country.
match_headline: Beirut’s Shiites Like the Idea of Change, but Like Hezbollah More

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a sharp increase in the cost of U.S. naturalization misstated the amount by which fees for naturalization applications could rise under a proposed plan. They would rise to $1,170, or $1,160 for online applications, not vice versa.
match_headline: Looming Fee Increase Could Thwart Many U.S. Citizenship Applications

text: An article last Friday about President Trump’s weakening of an Obama-era regulation on methane referred incorrectly to the organization where Lee Fuller is a vice president. It is the Independent Petroleum Association of America, not the Independent Petroleum Producers of America.
match_headline: Trump Eliminates Major Methane Rule, Even as Leaks Are Worsening

text: An article on Wednesday about the complexities surrounding transgender athletes and women’s sports misspelled the given name of a Brazilian volleyball player. She is Tifanny Abreu, not Tiffany.
match_headline: Who Should Compete in Women’s Sports? There Are ‘Two Almost Irreconcilable Positions’

text: An article on Thursday about the reopening of two New York museums, using information from the publicist, misstated the Brooklyn Museum’s reopening days that are reserved for members. Members can visit Sept. 10 and 11, not Sept. 9 through Sept. 11.
match_headline: Two Museums Announce September Reopenings

text: An article on Thursday about the reopening of Florida schools referred incorrectly to Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach Counties. They are the three largest counties in Florida; they do not have the state’s three largest school districts.
match_headline: ‘All In, All the Time’: Reopening Florida Schools Is Likened to Military Operation

text: An article on Friday about Ron Rivera’s cancer diagnosis misstated the playoff record of the Washington Football Team under Dan Snyder’s ownership. The franchise has won two playoff games, not zero.
match_headline: Washington N.F.L. Team Coach Ron Rivera Says He Has Cancer

text: An article this weekend on Page 8 about a ballet school in Lagos, Nigeria, misidentifies a ballet school in Birmingham, England. It is the Elmhurst Ballet School of Birmingham Royal Ballet, not of Birmingham Royal Academy.
match_headline: In Lagos, a Homegrown Ballet Academy Leaps Into the Spotlight

text: An article this weekend on Page 9 about the photographer Gregory Crewdson misspells the surname of Mr. Crewdson’s studio manager and partner. She is Juliane Hiam, not Haim.
match_headline: For Gregory Crewdson, Truth Lurks in the Landscape

text: An article last Sunday about immersive theater for children misidentified one of the actors in “The Wizards of Oakwood Drive.” He is Jonathan Randell Silver, not Jonathan Randell.
match_headline: How I Got My Kids Into Theater: Online Shows That Put Them to Work (and Play)

text: An article on Sunday about a widespread crackdown on parties on college campuses misstated the day that the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill began remote classes for undergraduates. It was last Wednesday, not last Thursday.
match_headline: Stop Campus Partying to Slow the Virus? Colleges Try but Often Fail

text: An article on Thursday about the corruption marring South Africa’s coronavirus relief effort described incorrectly South Africa’s coronavirus outbreak. The country has the fifth-highest number of confirmed cases globally, not the fifth-highest infection rate.
match_headline: South Africa’s Big Coronavirus Aid Effort Tainted by Corruption

text: An article on Monday about the choice of Erin O’Toole as Canada’s Conservative Party leader misidentified the premier of Ontario, Canada. He is Doug Ford, not Rob Ford, his brother, who died in 2016.
match_headline: Canada’s Conservatives Pick a Leader to Rival Scandal-Scarred Trudeau

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s attacks on former Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. during a trip to Pennsylvania misspelled the last name of a voter in Pennsylvania. He is Joe Vadala, not Joe Vidala.
match_headline: Trump Shows Up in Biden’s Home Region, and a Turf War Begins

text: An article on Friday about top Republican officials who endorsed former Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. referred incorrectly to the party affiliation of Fiona Hill, who served in the Trump Administration for several years as its top Russia expert on the National Security Council. Ms. Hill says she is neither a Republican nor a Democrat.
match_headline: Top Republican National Security Officials Say They Will Vote for Biden

text: An article on Saturday about Robert Trump’s funeral referred incorrectly to Elizabeth Trump Grau’s relationship with President Trump. She is his older sister, not his younger sister.
match_headline: Trump Holds a Rare White House Funeral for His Younger Brother, Robert

text: An article on Saturday about David Pecker’s departure from The National Enquirer misidentified the locations of Pace University. It has campuses in Manhattan and Westchester County, not the Bronx.
match_headline: National Enquirer Chief David Pecker Loses Top Job in Company Merger

text: An article on Wednesday about recent commercial real estate transactions in New York misstated the sales price for the building at 39-30 59th Street in Queens. It was $9.5 million, not $20.5 million.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about Aesha Ash, the first Black female member of the School of American Ballet’s permanent faculty, misidentified the dancers and the performance. The photo showed Ms. Ash with Benjamin Wardell and Brett Conway in a performance by Alonzo King’s company, Lines, at the Joyce Theater in 2007. It did not show Ms. Ash with Sebastien Marcovici in New York City Ballet’s production of Albert Evans’s “Haiku” in 2002.
match_headline: On the Market in New York City

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the eradication of the wild poliovirus in Africa referred incorrectly to the World Health Organization’s director for the continent. The director, Matshidiso Moeti, is a woman.
match_headline: Africa Celebrates the End of the Wild Poliovirus (but Not the End of All Polio)

text: An article on Tuesday about the effects of years of wildfires on residents in Northern California misidentified the tallest mountain in the Bay Area. It is Mount Hamilton, not Mount Diablo.
match_headline: 4 Years of Catastrophic Fires in California: ‘I’m Numb’

text: An article on Monday about Hollywood’s return to the box office misstated the planned release date for the next James Bond movie “No Time to Die.” It will open in November, not next year.
match_headline: With ‘Unhinged,’ Hollywood Cautiously Returns to Movie Theaters

text: An article on Thursday about the impact that the unrest in Wisconsin is having on voter preferences misstated the surname of a waitress at a pizza restaurant in Kenosha, Wis. She is Priscella Gazda, not Gazza.
match_headline: How Chaos in Kenosha Is Already Swaying Some Voters in Wisconsin

text: An article on Thursday about outdoor comedy in New York misstated the given name of a comedian. He is Matthew Broussard, not Zach Broussard.
match_headline: Live Comedy Is Back in New York! But Outdoors. Is This a Good Thing?

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Page 4 about the golden age of televised theater misidentifies the production company for “Twelve Angry Men.” It was Studio One, not Playhouse 90.
match_headline: A Beginner’s Guide to the Golden Age of Live Theater on TV

text: An obituary on Thursday about the tennis player Angela Buxton misspelled the surname of the author of “The Match: Althea Gibson and a Portrait of a Friendship” (2005). He is Bruce Schoenfeld, not Schoenfield.
ref_headline: The Match: Althea Gibson and a Portrait of a Friendship
match_headline: Angela Buxton, Half of an Outcast Duo in Tennis History, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Thursday about the jazz impresario Joe Segal misspelled the given name of a big-band leader. He was Benny Goodman, not Bennie. The obituary also misspelled the name of a theater in Philadelphia that presented big-band music. It was the Earle Theater, not Earl. The obituary also misidentified the military branch into which Mr. Segal was drafted in 1944. It was the Army Air Corps, not the Air Force. (The Air Force was not created until after the war.)
match_headline: Joe Segal, Impresario of Live Jazz for 70 Years, Dies at 94

text: An article last Sunday about short-term rentals once occupied by celebrities referred incorrectly to Willem Dafoe’s acting honors. He has been nominated for an Academy Award four times but has not yet won an Oscar.
match_headline: Frank Sinatra Slept Here, and So Can You

text: An article last Sunday about a home for sale in Málaga, Spain, misspelled the given name of a partner at Diana Morales Properties. She is Pia Arrieta Morales, not Pam.
match_headline: House Hunting in Spain: Mediterranean Views on the Costa Del Sol for $1.5 Million

text: An article on canning tomato sauce in last Sunday’s edition omitted an ingredient and also incorrectly used ingredients and procedures that can be dangerous for home canning. Adding lemon juice to the tomato sauce helps ensure safety in canning, and carrots, celery, basil and other low acidic vegetables should not be included in the sauce for canning; they can be added when the sauce is reheated for use. Finally, new jars should be used for canning.
match_headline: Make and Jar Pomodoro to Last All Year Long

text: An article on Monday about the fossil fuel industry’s demands for a trade deal that weakens Kenya’s rules on plastics and imports of American trash misidentified a group formed by the plastics industry to address the issue of waste. It is the Alliance to End Plastic Waste, not the Alliance to End Public Waste.
match_headline: Big Oil Is in Trouble. Its Plan: Flood Africa With Plastic.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the sentencing of Brendan Tarrant, a man convicted of murdering 51 Muslims at two mosques in New Zealand in 2019, misspelled the given name of a woman who spoke at the hearing. She is Maysoon Salama, not Maysson.
match_headline: New Zealand Gives Christchurch Killer a Record Sentence

text: An article on Thursday about a repurposed convent that was damaged during Hurricane Katrina misstated the title of Mary Kincaid. She is a senior project manager for the city of New Orleans, not the director of the city’s Office of Resilience and Sustainability.
match_headline: Flood and Sacrifice: How an Old Convent Could Help Save New Orleans

text: An article on Saturday about race-based housing policies that left some neighborhoods hotter than others described incorrectly a highway that was built through Jackson Ward. While the route that isolated Gilpin later became part of the national Interstate highway system, it was not a federal highway when it was built.
match_headline: ‘My Mind Is My Own,’ Daniel Cameron Says, Backing Trump

text: An article on Friday about the singles draws for the United States Open described incorrectly the performance of Kim Clijsters in the 2012 United States Open. She played in the singles tournament but did not win it.
match_headline: U.S. Open Draw Lacks Some Stars, but Not Story Lines

text: A picture caption on Monday with the On Tennis column , about Grand Slam events that like the current United States Open lacked the best players of the day, misstated the year Ken Rosewall won the U.S. Championships as an amateur. It was 1956, not 1955.
match_headline: Attach an Asterisk to This U.S. Open? Tennis History Mocks That Idea

text: An article on Aug. 26 about Black male voters overstated what is known about Kenny Paskel’s voting eligibility in Wisconsin. The state allows adults convicted of felonies to vote if they have finished their sentence, including parole.
match_headline: Biden Wants Black Voter Turnout Similar to Obama’s. He’ll Need Black Men.

text: An article on Aug. 5 about Johnny Alf, a Black pianist whose pioneering role in bossa nova has been largely overlooked, misidentified the organizer of the “Bossa Nova at Carnegie Hall” concert in 1962. It was Sidney Frey, not Aloisio de Oliveira, who served as a mediator between the artists and the production.
match_headline: A Black Pianist Helped Birth Bossa Nova. His Story Is Rarely Told.

text: An article on Saturday about changes made to the British Museum to clarify its links to slavery and colonialism misstated the year in which the Benin Bronzes were taken during a raid by British forces. It was 1897, not 1879.
match_headline: The British Museum Reopens to a World That Has Changed

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the scientist Myriam Sarachik misstated the year in which City College of New York offered Myriam Sarachik a job. It was 1964, not 1967.
match_headline: Myriam Sarachik Never Gave Up on Physics

text: A Critic’s Notebook on Aug. 5 about the reopening of restaurants in Manhattan’s Chinatown misidentified one of them, Shanghai 21. It is not also known as 21 Shanghai House; that is the name of a different restaurant. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to editors’ attention only recently.
match_headline: Chinatown Is Coming Back, One Noodle at a Time

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actress Linda Manz misspelled the surname of an actress with whom she starred on the television series “Dorothy.” She was Dorothy Loudon, not Louden.
match_headline: Linda Manz, Young Star of ‘Days of Heaven,’ Dies at 58

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the lack of progress in countering violent extremism by the Department of Homeland Security described incorrectly the police encounter with Jacob Blake. He was shot, but not killed.
match_headline: Trump Administration Promise to Focus on Extremism Remains Unfulfilled

text: An article on Wednesday about professional gamblers leaving the United States to play poker during the pandemic misspelled the surname of a professional poker player. He is Phil Hellmuth, not Helmuth.
match_headline: To Play Poker in a Pandemic, Americans Flee the U.S.

text: An article on Tuesday about John Thompson’s success as a basketball coach at Georgetown University misstated the day that Mr. Thompson died. It was Sunday, not Monday.
match_headline: John Thompson’s Success at Georgetown Made Him Ahead of His Time

text: An obituary on Aug. 6 about the journalist and author Pete Hamill referred incorrectly to his hiring as editor in chief of The New York Post in 1993. It was not “his first crack at running a newsroom”; he had been the editor of The Mexico City News from late 1986 to early 1987.
ref_headline: his first crack at running a newsroom
match_headline: Pete Hamill, Quintessential New York Journalist, Dies at 85

text: An article on Thursday about the Democrats’ efforts to plan a response to a scenario in which President Trump declares his own election victory prematurely misstated the number of states that do not allow mail-in ballots to be processed before Election Day. It is 11, not 12; New Hampshire changed its rules this year to allow some processing.
match_headline: This Is Democrats’ Doomsday Scenario for Election Night

text: An article on Thursday about new virus tests, using information from the National Institutes of Health, misstated the amount of money the N.I.H. said it would provide to nine additional companies developing coronavirus tests. It said it is providing $129.3 million, not $123.3 million.
match_headline: Backed by Federal Funds, New Virus Tests Are Hitting the Market

text: An article on Thursday about President Trump’s move to cut funding to certain cities controlled by Democrats misstated the title of Russell T. Vought. He is the director of the Office of Management and Budget, not the acting director.
match_headline: Trump Moves to Cut Federal Funding From Democratic Cities

text: An article on Sunday about the basketball player Angel McCoughtry’s activism misstated where Breonna Taylor was when she was shot by the police in Louisville, Ky. Taylor had gotten out of bed before she was shot; she was not shot while she was asleep in bed.
match_headline: Why Does the W.N.B.A. #SayHerName? Ask Angel McCoughtry

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the lawyer, banker and entrepreneur Barbara Judge at one point misstated when she took time off from work to help her son deal with dyslexia. As correctly noted elsewhere in the obituary, it was in the 1990s; it was not after Ms. Judge gave a speech in 2016 in which she said she opposed long maternity leaves.
match_headline: Barbara Judge, Who Shattered Many Glass Ceilings, Dies at 73

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Hall of Fame college basketball coach John Thompson Jr. referred incorrectly to Georgetown’s record in the N.C.A.A. championship tournament under his son John III. Georgetown reached the Final Four under John Thompson III in his third season as coach, not his first, and his teams went beyond the first round three other times; it was not the case that they “never made it beyond the first round afterward.” The obituary also misstated when Georgetown lost in the 1943 N.C.A.A. tournament, its only other appearance there before Thompson was hired in 1972. It was the final round, not the first.
ref_headline: never made it beyond the first round afterward.
match_headline: John Thompson, Hall of Fame Basketball Coach, Dies at 78

text: An article on Friday about spit hoods, a device used by to prevent people from biting or spitting, misspelled the surname of a professor of police science at John Jay College of Criminal Justice. She is Maria Haberfeld, not Haberfield.
match_headline: What Are ‘Spit Hoods,’ and Why Do the Police Use Them?

text: An article on Page 9 about the limitations of institutional jazz as a form of Black resistance music includes a quotation that misstates the number of students and faculty members at the New England Conservatory who identify as Black. There are now five such students and six faculty members, not three and three.
match_headline: Jazz Has Always Been Protest Music. Can It Meet This Moment?

text: A picture caption on Page 28 misidentifies one of Jennifer Villa’s children. The seated child is Armani Rodriguez, 8, not Troy Rodriguez, 6, who was not pictured.
match_headline: It’s Not Easy to Get a Coronavirus Test for a Child

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump’s dwindling campaign funds misstated the magazine on which Jared Kushner appeared after the 2016 election. It was Forbes, not Fortune.
match_headline: How Trump’s Billion-Dollar Campaign Lost Its Cash Advantage

text: An article on Sunday about a backlash among some tech workers against benefits companies are offering to parents in the face of the coronavirus pandemic misstated the name of Professor Erin Kelly’s school. It is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management, not the school of business.
match_headline: Parents Got More Time Off. Then the Backlash Started.

text: An article on Saturday about the results of Massachusetts’ Sept. 1 elections misstated the race won by Representative Seth Moulton. Mr. Moulton easily won his primary, not the general election.
match_headline: Jake Auchincloss Wins Massachusetts Primary for Joe Kennedy’s House Seat

text: An article on Monday about preparations for in-person voting across the country misstated the early voting schedule in North Carolina. While the state has begun mailing out absentee ballots, in-person voting will not begin until next month.
match_headline: In Year of Voting by Mail, a Scramble to Beef Up In-Person Voting, Too

text: An article on Aug. 30 about concerns over coronavirus testing, using information provided by a laboratory spokesman, misstated the number of positive coronavirus tests in July processed by Wadsworth Center, New York’s state lab. It was 872 tests, not 794. Based on that error, the article also misstated the number of tests that would no longer qualify as positive with a C.T. value of 35 cycles. It is about 43 percent of the tests, not about half of them. Similarly, the article misstated the share of tests that would no longer qualify as positive if cycles were limited to 30. It is about 63 percent, not about 70 percent.
match_headline: Your Coronavirus Test Is Positive. Maybe It Shouldn’t Be.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the number of Black players in professional tennis described incorrectly the racial makeup of the men’s and women’s singles tennis rankings. There is one Black player from the United States in the men’s top 100 and 10 in the women’s top 200; they do not account for all Black players in the rankings.
match_headline: With More Black Women, U.S. Open Shows Serena and Venus Legacy

text: An article on Friday with viewing suggestions for the weekend misidentified the actor pictured from the Starz series “Power Book II: Ghost.” He is Lovell Adams-Gray, not Michael Rainey Jr.
match_headline: How Much Watching Time Do You Have This Weekend?

text: An article on Friday about the struggles of various artists and workers misspelled the given name of the wife of Phil LaDuca, the founder of LaDuca Shoes in Manhattan. She is Fon LaDuca, not Ton. The article also misidentified the location of Mr. LaDuca’s shop in Manhattan. It is on 45th Street, near 10th Avenue; not Eighth Avenue and 47th Street.
match_headline: This Labor Day, These Workers Are Trying to Stay Afloat

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about films by Yasujiro Ozu misidentified an actress appearing with Setsuko Hara, the star of “Early Summer.” The actress is Kuniko Miyake, not Chikage Awashima.
match_headline: Ready to Try an Ozu Film? Watch These Two Family Tales.

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Wednesday about ghost kitchens misidentified SBE’s virtual kitchen operation. It is C3, not Virtual Kitchen Co., which is a separate company unaffiliated with SBE. The article also misstated when CloudKitchens was founded. It was in 2016, not in the past year.
match_headline: As Food Deliveries Boom, So Do Ghost Kitchens

text: An article on Sunday about the racism faced by Black soldiers returning to America from World War II misstated the role of John Rankin, a Mississippi politician. He was a member of the House of Representatives, not the Senate.
match_headline: Returning From War, Returning to Racism

text: An obituary on Aug. 19 about Dr. Charles V. Wetli, the medical examiner best known for investigating the crash of Trans World Airlines Flight 800 in 1996, referred imprecisely to the journalist Christine Negroni and misstated the title of a book she wrote. Although she was a correspondent for CNN at the time of the crash, she is not currently “a CNN journalist.” And her book is “Deadly Departure,” not “The Deadly Departure of Flight 800.”
match_headline: Charles Wetli, Medical Examiner for T.W.A. Flight 800 Crash, Dies at 76

text: An article on Wednesday about helicopter rescue missions during the California wildfires misattributed two quotations. It was Chief Warrant Officer Kipp Goding, not Chief Warrant Officer Joseph Rosamond, who said, “Every piece of vegetation as far as you could see around that lake was on fire.” It was also Mr. Goding who said: “I’ve been flying for 25 years. We get occasionally shot at overseas during missions. It’s definitely by far the toughest flying that I’ve ever done.”
ref_headline: Every piece of vegetation as far as you could see around that lake was on fire.
match_headline: ‘You Couldn’t See Anything’: Harrowing Helicopter Rescues as California Wildfires Rage

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s statements about fair housing policies in Westchester County, N.Y., incorrectly described Briarcliff Manor. It is a village, not a town.
match_headline: How Trump Is Using Westchester to Stir Up Suburban Fears

text: An article on Wednesday about the resignation of U. Reneé Hall, the Dallas police chief, misstated the status of the police chief in Tucson, Ariz. Although the chief offered his resignation, the city manager did not accept it.
match_headline: Dallas Police Chief Resigns in Wake of Policing Protests

text: An article on Tuesday about the Nigerian musician Tiwa Savage misidentified Ms. Savage’s ex-husband. He is her former manager; he is not the same Tunji Balojun who was an A&R representative at Interscope Records.
match_headline: Tiwa Savage, Queen of Afrobeats, Makes a New Start

text: An article on Thursday about a reassurance from health officials that a coronavirus vaccine will meet safety standards before approval included incorrect information on school requirements for vaccination. Schools no longer require smallpox vaccinations, and many schools require skin testing, not vaccination, for tuberculosis.
match_headline: Health Official Tries to Reassure Public That Science Will Set Vaccine Approval

text: An article on Thursday about President Trump’s encounters with Black leaders misstated the month George Floyd was killed by the police. It was May, not June.
match_headline: In Encounters With Black Leaders, Trump Has Chosen Photo Ops Over Substance

text: An article on Thursday about predictions for the first week of the 2020 N.F.L. season described incorrectly the professional connection between Josh McDaniels and Tim Tebow. McDaniels drafted the quarterback, but was no longer coach of the Denver Broncos when Tebow led the team to the playoffs after the 2011 season.
match_headline: N.F.L. Week 1 Predictions: Our Picks Against the Spread

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the 146th Kentucky Derby incorrectly described the stage of the race shown. Authentic, the eventual winner, was taking the lead in the middle of the race, not “capping his victory.”
match_headline: Pull Out of the Kentucky Derby? Pressure on a Black Owner Mounts

text: An article on Tuesday about the dangers of taking inappropriate prescriptions misstated the anti-diarrheal medication Lisa McCarthy said some patients use to counter the effects of metformin. It is loperamide, not Lomotil.
match_headline: The Risks of the Prescribing Cascade

text: An article on Page 40 about homeless families in New York City misstates the estimated shelter population if the goals of Mayor Bill de Blasio’s Turning the Tide plan are met. The Institute for Children, Poverty and Homelessness estimates that city shelters will have a population of 57,500 homeless individuals, not 65,000 homeless families.
match_headline: The Children in the Shadows: New York City’s Homeless Students

text: An obituary on Friday for the actress Diana Rigg misquoted a line from the critic John Simon’s New York magazine review of the 1971 Broadway production of “Abelard and Heloise,” in which she starred. Mr. Simon, who was notorious for criticizing actors’ looks, wrote that Ms. Rigg was “built like a brick basilica with insufficient flying buttresses” — not “a brick mausoleum.” Because of an editing error, the obituary also misspelled the surname of one of Ms. Rigg’s former husbands. He is Archibald Stirling, not Sterling.
match_headline: Diana Rigg, Stylish Emma Peel of ‘The Avengers,’ Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Thursday about the painter Ron Gorchov misstated the date of his birth in 1930. It was April 5, not April 15. The obituary, using information from Mr. Gorchov’s family, also omitted the name of one of his former wives. He married Sharma Bennett in 1979.
match_headline: Ron Gorchov, Painter Who Challenged Viewers’ Perceptions, Dies at 90

text: An article last Sunday about Kehinde Wiley and how he is riding out the pandemic misidentified the gallery that is home to his portrait of former President Barack Obama. It is the National Portrait Gallery, not the National Gallery.
match_headline: Kehinde Wiley on Protests’ Results: ‘I’m Not Impressed Yet’

text: An article last Sunday about sculpture gardens around the country misspelled the name of a sculptor exhibiting at the Grounds for Sculpture in Hamilton, N.J. It is Autin Wright, not Austin. It also incorrectly identified the location and size of the grounds at the Crystal Bridges Museum. It is in the northwestern corner of Arkansas, not the northeastern, and has 120 acres of grounds, not 20. A photo caption also misidentified the sculptor of an artwork at the Nasher Sculpture Center in Dallas. It is by Tony Cragg, not Tony Brown. Separately, an article about the rise in injuries among people working from home misidentified the “Peanuts” character who plays the piano. It is Schroeder, not Linus.
match_headline: 7 Sculpture Gardens that Merge Art With the Landscape

text: An article on Page 24 about homeless families in New York City misstates the estimated shelter population if the goals of Mayor Bill de Blasio’s Turning the Tide plan are met. The Institute for Children, Poverty and Homelessness estimates that city shelters will have a population of 57,500 homeless individuals, not 65,000 homeless families.
match_headline: The Sunday Read: ‘The Children in the Shadows’

text: An article on Aug. 23 about the migrant route to the United States through the Sonoran Desert referred incorrectly to a road in the Tohono O’odham Nation. It is Federal Route 15, not State Route 15.
match_headline: How U.S. Policy Turned the Sonoran Desert Into a Graveyard for Migrants

text: An article on Sunday about President Trump’s nominations for the Nobel Peace Prize by two Scandinavian politicians misidentified the year for which he was nominated. He was nominated for the 2021 prize, not this year’s.
match_headline: Mandela, Gorbachev, Trump? A Disruptive President Plays Peacemaker

text: An article on Friday about the effect of La Niña on drought conditions in the southwestern United States this winter misstated the direction of Pacific trade winds. They move from east to west, not west to east.
match_headline: La Niña May Worsen Southwest Drought This Winter

text: An article on Monday about Dominic Thiem’s win at the U.S. Open misidentified the men’s singles champion at Wimbledon in 2002. It was Lleyton Hewitt, not Goran Ivanisevic. (Ivanisevic was the 2001 champion.) The article also misspelled the surname of a Swedish player. He is Thomas Johansson, not Johanson.
match_headline: Dominic Thiem Comes Back From Down 2 Sets to Win U.S. Open Final

text: An article on Monday about the sound of N.F.L. games without fans referred imprecisely to the number of fans the Kansas City Chiefs will welcome right away for home games during the pandemic. The Chiefs’ stadium capacity for each game to start the season has been limited to about 22 percent, or just under 17,000, not “tens of thousands.”
match_headline: What Will N.F.L. Games Sound Like?

text: An article on Monday about the 50th anniversary of “Right On Be Free,” the debut album by the African-American youth choir Voices of East Harlem, misstated the instrument Wayne Shorter plays. It is the saxophone, not the piano.
match_headline: 50 Years Ago, They Did Something Rare in Gospel: Tied Music to Protest

text: An article on Monday about Israel’s second lockdown misstated the distance that citizens are allowed to stray from their homes. It is 500 meters, not 500 yards.
match_headline: Israel to Celebrate Jewish New Year Under a Second Lockdown

text: An article on Tuesday about an Israeli settler who firebombed a Palestinian family described incorrectly the findings of a December report by a human rights group, Yesh Din, about investigations of crimes by Israeli civilians against Palestinians or their property in the West Bank. The group reported that only 8 percent of 1,252 cases of violence, property crime, seizure of Palestinian land and other offenses that it monitored between 2005 and 2019 had resulted in indictments. It did not report that only 8 percent of violent crimes — which the group said amounted to 36 percent of all the cases it monitored — had led to indictments.
match_headline: Israeli Settler Gets 3 Life Sentences for Firebomb Attack on Family

text: An article on Sunday about SoftBank’s potential sale of the chip designer Arm to Nvidia referred incorrectly to the difference in the current valuation of Nvidia compared with that of Arm in 2016. Nvidia’s valuation is about 12 times bigger than Arm’s, not 260 times.
match_headline: SoftBank Said to Be Near Deal to Sell British Chip Designer Arm

text: An article on Monday about a scandal that led to a fallout in The Intercept’s newsroom described incorrectly a copy of a document that an Intercept reporter sent to the National Security Agency for verification. The copy contained a crease, not markings showing where and when it had been printed. The column also referred incorrectly to demands for a more thorough investigation of The Intercept’s handling of the document. They were made privately, not publicly.
match_headline: The Intercept Promised to Reveal Everything. Then Its Own Scandal Hit.

text: An article on Tuesday about restrictions imposed by the United States on Chinese apparel and tech importsmisstated the penalties imposed against Changji Esquel Textile Co. Ltd., a subsidiary of Esquel Group. The Commerce Department placed Esquel Group on an entity list, which restricts its access to American products over accusations of forced labor. It is not subject to a withhold release order.
match_headline: U.S. Restricts Chinese Apparel and Tech Products, Citing Forced Labor

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the sale of the New York Mets misstated the name of the buyer, Steven Cohen’s previous hedge fund. It is SAC Capital Advisors, not S.A.C. Capital Partners.
match_headline: Steven Cohen Agrees to Buy the Mets, Again

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor Kevin Dobson referred incorrectly to the character he played on the prime-time soap opera “Knots Landing.” He was a lawyer, not a detective.
match_headline: Kevin Dobson, ‘Kojak’ and ‘Knots Landing’ Actor, Dies at 77

text: An obituary on Friday about the sculptor Siah Armajani misspelled the surname of a Persian poet who was the subject of one of his works. He was Neema Yooshij, not Yooshiji. (His given name is sometimes rendered as Nima and his surname as Yushij.)
match_headline: Siah Armajani, Sculptor of Communal Spaces, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Sunday about the reggae singer Toots Hibbert misstated the title of a song by Bob Marley that Mr. Hibbert and his group, the Maytals, recently recorded with Mr. Marley’s son Ziggy. It is “Three Little Birds,” not “Three Birds.”
match_headline: Toots Hibbert, a Father of Reggae, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Monday about Florence Howe, a founder of the Feminist Press, referred incorrectly to “The Defiant Muse,” one of the titles published by that company. It is a series of anthologies of verse by women from countries around the world, including Vietnam. It is not solely a collection of Vietnamese poems.
match_headline: Florence Howe, ‘Mother of Women’s Studies,’ Dies at 91

text: An article on Saturday about coronavirus transmission outbreaks on college campuses misstated the age of Megan Bernstein, who grew up in Oxford, Ohio. She is 45, not 47.
match_headline: How Colleges Became the New Covid Hot Spots

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the New York Philharmonic’s “Soundwalk” misidentified a body of water in Central Park our critic visited as part of the walk. It was the Pool, near West 101st Street, not Lasker Pool, a swimming pool near the north end of the park.
match_headline: Over Headphones and in a Truck, the Philharmonic Stays Alive

text: An article on Thursday about an experimental monoclonal antibody used to treat coronavirus patients, using information from a Pfizer scientist, misstated where DNA was inserted. It is inserted into hamster ovary cells, not E. coli bacteria. Using the same information, it also misstated the time required to produce the antibodies. It takes two to four months, not weeks.
match_headline: An Experimental Drug Protects Covid-19 Patients, Eli Lilly Claims

text: An article on Thursday about a suggestion by Attorney General William P. Barr that prosecutors charge violent protesters with sedition overstated what is known about the origin of Justice Department discussions about possible charges against Mayor Jenny Durkan of Seattle. While lawyers in the civil rights division discussed potential charges, a department spokesman said that Attorney General William P. Barr did not direct them to the explore the idea.
match_headline: Barr Told Prosecutors to Consider Sedition Charges for Protest Violence

text: An article on Thursday about the initial public offering of the data storage and analytics provider Snowflake misspelled the surname of the author of “The Lean Startup.” He is Eric Ries, not Reis.
match_headline: Snowflake More Than Doubles in Debut as Wall Street Embraces Tech IPOs

text: An article on Wednesday about the 20th anniversary of Tiger Woods’s first U.S. Open win misstated the number of Masters Tournament wins the golfer had before 2006. Woods had won the tournament four times and failed to win his fifth that year, not his fourth.
match_headline: Tiger Woods Would Like to Remind You That He Dominated the U.S. Open 20 Years Ago

text: An obituary on Aug. 24 about Mercedes Barcha, the wife and muse of the novelist Gabriel García Márquez, referred imprecisely to García Márquez’s travel to the United States. The government denied him an unrestricted visa until 1995, but he was not denied a visa entirely; for many years he was able to obtain a waiver to travel to the U.S. whenever he wanted. This error also appeared in García Márquez’s New York Times obituary, in 2014.
match_headline: Mercedes Barcha, Gabriel García Márquez’s Wife and Muse, Dies at 87

text: An article on Friday about plans for coronavirus vaccine trials misstated the number of points at which an outside panel reviews data before a drug trial is complete at the drugmaker Pfizer. There are four such points, not three.
match_headline: Moderna and Pfizer Reveal Secret Blueprints for Coronavirus Vaccine Trials

text: An article on Thursday about Julian Assange’s extradition hearing described incorrectly Eric Lewis’s role in the hearing. He is a witness for the defense, not for the prosecution.
match_headline: At Assange’s Extradition Hearing, Troubled Tech Takes Center Stage

text: An article on Friday about A’ja Wilson winning the W.N.B.A.’s Most Valuable Player Award described incorrectly the draft position of Chennedy Carter of the Atlanta Dream. Ms. Carter was drafted No. 4 overall, not No. 2.

An article on Wednesday about the meditative installation, “Our Labyrinth,” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art misspelled the given name of one of the performers. He is DeAngelo Blanchard, not D’Angelo.
match_headline: Dancing With Rice: A Meditative Pas de Deux at the Met

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 4 about the archive of rehearsal tapes of the choreographer Trisha Brown, using information provided by the publicist, misidentified the dancer with Brown in “Leaning Duets II.” She is Carol Goodden, not Sylvia Palacios.
match_headline: Watching a Choreographer Build: Trisha Brown’s Unusual Archive

text: An article on Page 46 about Ed Buck, a West Hollywood political donor, and two men who died of meth overdoses at his home misstated the increase in deaths in Los Angeles County related to meth overdoses from 2007 to 2017. The increase was from 43 to 347, not from 50 to 320.
match_headline: What Happened Inside Ed Buck’s Apartment?

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the critic and author Stanley Crouch misstated the year his book “Kansas City Lightning: The Rise and Times of Charlie Parker” was published. It was 2013, not 2003.
ref_headline: Kansas City Lightning: The Rise and Times of Charlie Parker
match_headline: Stanley Crouch, Critic Who Saw American Democracy in Jazz, Dies at 74

text: An article on Monday about former world leaders demanding the ratification of a nuclear arms ban treaty misidentified the nationality of Willy Claes, a former NATO secretary-general. He is from Belgium, not the Netherlands.
match_headline: Former World Leaders Urge Ratification of Nuclear Arms Ban Treaty

text: An article on Monday about Judge Amy Coney Barrett, based on the recollection of a family friend, referred incorrectly to the Down syndrome diagnosis of the Barretts’ son. In fact, the Barretts did not learn of that diagnosis through prenatal testing, according to a family member.
match_headline: To Conservatives, Barrett Has ‘Perfect Combination’ of Attributes for Supreme Court

text: An article on Sunday about leading candidates for the Supreme Court vacancy left by the death of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg misstated the court on which Judge Amy Coney Barrett sits. It is the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, not the Sixth Circuit. The article also misstated the given name of another judge under consideration. He is Amul Thapar, not Amal Thapar.
match_headline: Leading Candidates to Fill Supreme Court Vacancy

text: An article on Sunday about letters sent to the White House and local law enforcement agencies containing the lethal substance ricin, using information from a source, referred incorrectly to the agencies in Texas that received the letters. text: An article on Monday about Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s childhood ties to Brooklyn misstated the name of a resident of Prospect Lefferts Gardens. She is Becky Celestina, 26, not Becky Celestine, 24.

text: An article on Sunday about yoga studios in New York misstated the year a prominent yoga studio closed. Jivamukti Yoga closed in 2019, not 2017.

text: An article on Wednesday about the Billboard album chart misstated the title of the rapper Pop Smoke’s posthumous album. It is “Shoot for the Stars Aim for the Moon,” not “Aim for the Stars Shoot for the Moon.”
ref_headline: Shoot for the Stars Aim for the Moon,

text: An article on Saturday about the challenges that ephemeral works of art present for curators incorrectly gave the length of time that an artwork by Yoko Ono was exhibited by the Museum of Modern Art. It was almost four months, not four weeks.

text: An article on Tuesday about a friendship with Ruth Bader Ginsburg misstated the justice’s age in 2002. She was 69, not 70.

text: Because of an editing error, a recipe with David Tanis’s column last Wednesday for panna cotta misstated the metric equivalent for two cups of half-and-half. It should be 475 milliliters, not 240.

text: An article on Tuesday about the Portland, Ore., protests moving into suburb neighborhoods referred incorrectly to Jessie Burke, a business owner in Portland. She is a woman.

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about Paul Rusesabagina, the hero behind the film “Hotel Rwanda,” using information from Getty Images, misidentified the location of a refugee camp photographed in 1994. It was in Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo, not Rwanda.

text: An article on Sunday about a Danish children’s television show aimed at countering body shaming misstated medical treatment received by Rei, one of the adults featured on the program. Rei did not have a vasectomy.
match_headline: A Danish Children’s TV Show Has This Message: ‘Normal Bodies Look Like This’

text: A headline on a chart with the Keeping Score column on Tuesday about the career of the Los Angeles Angels slugger Albert Pujols described incorrectly the exclusive baseball club his statistics put him. match_headline: Albert Pujols Passes Willie Mays in Home Runs, if Not Dominance

text: An article on Tuesday about a study of corporate efforts to address social justice concerns referred incorrectly to the inclusion of the British insurance company Willis Towers Watson PLC in a Business Roundtable statement on the purpose of a corporation. The company was part of the academic study the article explored, but it was not a signatory to the Business Roundtable statement.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a proposal to handle asylum seekers in Europe misstated the number of member states in the European Union. There are 27, not 26.

text: An article on Sunday about the pandemic’s impact on housekeepers misquoted Ai-jen Poo, the executive director of the National Domestic Workers Alliance. Ms. Poo said that in surveys of members, unemployment had plateaued at 40 percent, not that employment had peaked at that figure.

text: An article on Thursday about Gillian Flynn and the new series “Utopia” misstated the number of episodes in the series. The show has eight episodes, not 10.
match_headline: Gillian Flynn Takes Her Paranoia to Television

text: An article in today’s paper about a series of killings on Long Island nearly a decade ago misstated the status of Thomas J. Spota’s sentencing for conspiracy. He has been convicted, but has not yet been sentenced or served time in prison.

text: An article on Friday about the reissue of the Prince album “Sign O’ the Times” referred incorrectly to the gender identity of one of Prince’s alter-egos. Camille was male.

text: An article on Friday about art made by incarcerated people misstated the year the artist Ronnie Goodman was released from prison. It was 2010, not 2016.
match_headline: Making Art When ‘Lockdown’ Means Prison

text: An article this weekend on Page 15 about Lenny Kravitz’s new memoir, “Let Love Rule,” refers imprecisely to Prince’s race. Both of his parents were African-American, he was not biracial.
match_headline: How Lenny Kravitz Keeps His Cool

text: An article this weekend on Page 4 about a mini-series based on former F.B.I. director James Comey’s memoir, misidentifies the surname of Mr. Comey’s wife. She is Patrice Comey, not Failor; Failor was her maiden name.
match_headline: ‘The Comey Rule’: Why Watching Jeff Daniels Ruined James Comey’s Day

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the most popular listings of August misidentified the listing broker of the property at 251 Seaman Avenue in Manhattan. It was listed by New Heights Realty, not Right at Home Realty Inc.
match_headline: The Most Popular Listings of August

text: An article on Sunday about the pandemic’s impact on women in the work force misidentified the university at which the economist Claudia Olivetti is employed. Dr. Olivetti is a professor at Dartmouth College, not the University of Chicago.
match_headline: Pandemic Will ‘Take Our Women 10 Years Back’ in the Workplace

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the trial of suspects in the 2015 terror attacks in Paris misidentified the location where Jewish tombstones were defaced. It was the Alsace region, not the city of Alsace.
match_headline: At Trial, Jewish Victims of 2015 Paris Attack Ask: Why the Hatred?

text: An article on Monday about Fox News and its election night staff misstated the title for Suzanne Scott. She is the chief executive of Fox News, not its president.
match_headline: Trump Wants to Discredit the Election. This Nerd Could Stop Him.

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about what to watch on television this week reversed the identities of two actors shown in a still from the film “You Can’t Take It With You.” Lionel Barrymore was on the left; Edward Arnold was on the right.
ref_headline: You Can’t Take It With You.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Saturday Night Live’ and the First Presidential Debate

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Hall of Fame football player Gale Sayers referred incorrectly in part to his survivors. He had seven grandchildren, not two; and his son Scott was adopted, not his son Timothy.
match_headline: Gale Sayers Dies; Elusive Hall of Fame Running Back Was 77

text: An article on Monday about President Trump’s strategy for the presidential debate misstated the given name of a Republican congressman who claimed Joseph R. Biden Jr. had dementia. He is Greg Murphy, not Joe Murphy.
match_headline: By Lowering the Debate Bar for Biden, Has Trump Set a Trap for Himself?

text: An article on Saturday about the Miami Marlins clinching a playoff spot misstated the given name of one of the Marlins’ pitchers. He is Pablo Lopez, not Jorge.
match_headline: In a Season of Challenges, the Marlins Finally Break Through

text: An article on Tuesday about historians who are interested in statues that depict more accurate portrayals of U.S. history misstated the title of Hilary Green of the University of Alabama. It is in Louisiana, not Mississippi.

text: An obituary on Friday about Donald Kendall, the longtime chief executive of PepsiCo, referred imprecisely to one of the company’s acquisitions during his tenure. PepsiCo bought only the international division of 7Up in 1986, not the entire company.
match_headline: Donald Kendall, Pepsi’s Chief During the Cola Wars, Dies at 99

text: An article on Sept. 24 about a real estate project that would have led to the expansion of the Industry City complex in Brooklyn referred imprecisely to the relationship between Chelsea Market and its developer, Jamestown. Jamestown created Chelsea Market and owns the rights to the Chelsea Market brand, but Google bought the complex in 2018.
match_headline: Progressives Defeat Brooklyn Project That Promised 20,000 Jobs

text: An article on Monday about the relationship between Arab countries and Israel referred imprecisely to the status of a lawsuit by 9/11 victims against Sudan. They do not intend to sue Sudan. They already have.
match_headline: Sudan Is Focus of U.S. Efforts to Improve Ties With Israel

text: An article on Wednesday about rising coronavirus cases in Quebec misstated the title of David Buckeridge of McGill University in Montreal. He is a professor, not an assistant professor.
match_headline: As Cases Surge, Pandemic Restrictions Again Descend on Quebec

text: An article on Tuesday about the rise in opioid deaths during the pandemic misstated the county seat of Windham County in Vermont. It is Newfane, not Brattleboro (which is the largest town in the county).
match_headline: ‘The Drug Became His Friend’: Pandemic Drives Hike in Opioid Deaths

text: An article on Wednesday about layoffs at Disney’s theme parks attributed information about a food bank for furloughed workers to the wrong person. text: An article on Wednesday about streaming classical concerts, relying on outdated information from the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, provided an incorrect date for Gilles Vonsattel’s recital. It will be streamed live on Oct. 27, not Oct. 6.

text: An article on Thursday about uncommitted voters’ reaction to the presidential debate on Tuesday described incorrectly a tally of interruptions in the debate that was compiled by the online tracker Factba.se. text: An article on Thursday about the death of a gang rape victim misstated the date of the hanging of four men convicted of raping and murdering a young woman on a bus in 2012. It was in March, not late last year.
match_headline: Woman Dies in Delhi After Gang Rape, Fueling Outrage Again in India

text: An article on Friday about the precautions that President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia is taking to protect himself from the coronavirus misspelled the surname of Brazil’s president. He is Jair Bolsonaro, not Jair Balsonaro.
match_headline: Russians Were Urged to Return to Normal Life. Except for Putin.

text: An article this weekend on Page 4 about pop-up comedy shows in the city misspelled the surname of a comedian and activist in New York. Her name is Kambri Crews, not Krews.
match_headline: Why New York Comedy Has Gone Underground (and Onto the Rooftops)

text: An article on Friday about the popular YouTube personality Doug DeMuro included outdated information about the online auction site Bring a Trailer. The site lists an average of 335 cars a week, not 275, and sells 80 percent, not 70 percent.

text: An article this weekend on page 37 about the increasing number of older people among Phoenix’s homeless misstated a statistic. Thirty percent of 65-74-year-olds will be in the work force by 2026; they will not make up 30 percent of the work force overall.

text: A report last Sunday about the marriage of Julie-Ann Hutchinson and Dr. Kyle Burton misstated the year the couple met. It was 2017, not 2016.

text: An article on Sept. 13 about the legacy of Milton Friedman misstated an equation from the 1976 paper “Theory of the Firm.” In the paper, the manager’s indifference curve is tangent to a line with slope equal to -α , not — u.

text: An article on Saturday about the facts surrounding President Trump’s coronavirus infection misstated the health procedure that President Ronald Reagan underwent when he briefly turned over power in 1985. It was a colectomy, not a colonoscopy.
match_headline: Trump Infected: What We Know and Don’t Know

text: An article on Saturday about tapes from the grand jury hearing about Breonna Taylor’s death overstated what was known about a remark heard in the audio. text: An article on Monday about the influence of the far right in Delaware referred incorrectly to Pierre Samuel du Pont IV’s activity in presidential politics. He ran for the Republican nomination in 1988; it is not the case that he only considered a run.

text: An article on Friday about a bankruptcy declaration by the Diocese of Rockville Centre misstated the number of the other dioceses in the state that had filed for bankruptcy protection. It was three, not two.

text: An article on Thursday about the initial public offering of Palantir Technologies misstated the company’s closing share price on its first day of trading, on Sept. 30. It closed at $9.50, not $9.73.
match_headline: Palantir Shares Go Up in Wall Street Debut

text: An article on Sunday about the results of the Preakness Stakes referred incorrectly to Authentic’s betting odds in the Preakness. While he was the betting favorite, he was not the “odds-on” favorite. (Authentic went off at 3-2 odds, not at less than even odds.)

text: An article on Monday about a project by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation that will reimagine monuments referred incorrectly to the status of four monuments in New Orleans that were removed in 2017, when Mitch Landrieu was mayor. They were four prominent Confederate monuments, not the city’s four last Confederate monuments. The error was repeated in a picture caption.

text: An obituary on Monday about the playwright Murray Schisgal misspelled the given name of an actress who appeared in Mr. Schisgal’s plays. She was Anne Jackson, not Ann.
match_headline: Murray Schisgal, Who Brought the Absurd to the Mainstream, Dies at 93

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about fading hopes for political change in Algeria following last year’s popular uprising described incorrectly the Algerian revolt against the French 58 years ago. The revolt was hampered because of the lack of a clear leader; it did not fail.

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the future of California’s economy misidentified a bridge in the Bay Area. It is the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge, not the Golden Gate Bridge.

text: An obituary on Sept. 26 about the author Sam McBratney misstated the location of County Antrim, where he lived. It is in Northern Ireland, not Ireland.
match_headline: Sam McBratney Dies at 77; Wrote ‘Guess How Much I Love You’

text: An obituary on Sept. 30 about the former major league outfielder Jay Johnstone misspelled the name of the area in California where he died and described it incorrectly. It is Granada Hills, not Grenada Hills, and it is a neighborhood in Los Angeles, not a separate city.

text: A chart with an article on Wednesday about President Trump’s decision to cut off talks on an economic stimulus deal misstated the day that the S&P 500 dropped. It fell at the end of the day on Tuesday, not Monday.

text: An article on Tuesday about suicides among Japanese celebrities inaccurately suggested that a tweet questioning Ms. Takeuchi’s suicide was a judgment of her as a mother. text: An obituary on Monday about the pioneering suffragist, scholar and educator Lucy Diggs Slowe erroneously included a school in Washington among the existing sites honoring her legacy. While there was a Lucy D. Slowe elementary school in Washington, it has closed and been renamed.

text: An article on Thursday about the topics covered during the vice-presidential debate misstated Senator Kamala Harris’s accusation about President Trump’s record on Black judges. text: A headline with an article on Wednesday about the Trump administration’s family separation policy for undocumented immigrants misstated a directive given by Attorney General Jeff Sessions to federal prosecutors in 2018. text: An article on Wednesday about the first overall pick of this year’s N.H.L. draft described incorrectly the format for the N.H.L. draft lottery. text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s criticism of his top officials for not prosecuting or implicating his political enemies referred incorrectly to a video of the president speaking on the White House lawn. text: An article on Friday about a 2016 Trump campaign fund-raiser accused of evading foreign lobbying laws misspelled his given name. He is Elliott Broidy, not Elliot. The error was repeated in two picture captions.

text: An article on Friday about Judge Amy Coney Barrett’s faith community misstated the status of Arthur Wang’s medical training when he was torn about prescribing contraceptives. He was a medical resident, not a medical student.

text: An article on Oct. 1 about the Indian Health Service’s challenges in addressing the pandemic misstated the year Rear Adm. Michael D. Weahkee was appointed to lead the health service. He was appointed to lead the agency on an acting basis in June 2017, not in 2015. (He was confirmed by the Senate in April.)

text: An article on Friday about stock market gains made by executives during the economic downturn sparked by the pandemic misstated the month that Stéphane Bancel, the chief executive of Moderna, received an option award. It was in February, not January.

text: A review on Friday of painting shows at galleries in Chelsea misspelled the surname of an artist showing at Berry Campbell gallery. He is Edward Avedisian, not Avesidian.

text: A picture caption with an opinion article on Sept. 27 about blackface in film and television misidentified an actor. He is Mark Proksch, not Rainn Wilson.

text: An article on Friday about protests in Indonesia described incorrectly a jobs bill that was passed by Indonesia’s Parliament. Although the bill contained a provision allowing companies to eliminate paid maternity and menstrual leave, it was removed before final passage.

text: An article on Thursday about preparation by election officials anticipating unrest at the polls misstated the increase in volunteers recruited by the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law. text: A chart with an article on Thursday about polls of likely voters in Nevada and Ohio mislabeled the responses that voters could choose. To the question, “How should politicians campaign in person?” the responses were “Large crowds” and “Small crowds,” not “Yes” and “No.”

text: An article on Wednesday about the arrest of the software engineer John McAfee referred incorrectly to the potential prison terms he faces. The five counts of failure to file taxes each carry a maximum one-year sentence, while the five tax evasion counts each carry a maximum of five years.

text: An obituary on Sept. 23 about the activist and adventurer Henrietta Boggs referred incorrectly to the civil war after which José Figueres Ferrer, her husband at the time, became president of Costa Rica in 1948. text: An obituary on Friday about Stephen Barnes of the law firm Cellino & Barnes referred incorrectly to his niece Elizabeth D. Barnes, who died in the same plane crash that killed Mr. Barnes. text: An article on Friday about a foiled plot to kidnap Gov. text: An article on Saturday about Hurricane Delta’s impact on the Louisiana region where it made landfall misstated a distinction associated with the storm. It set a record by being the 10th named storm this year to make landfall in the continental United States, not the entire nation.

text: An article on Saturday about a spike in coronavirus cases in ultra-Orthodox Jewish communities referred incorrectly to the Hasidic community of New Square, N.Y. It is an enclave of Skvirer Hasidim, not Squarer Hasidim.

text: An article on Saturday about an increase in applications to private schools misstated the increase in enrollment in private schools in New England. Thirty-six percent of the schools reported a rise in enrollment from last year; the schools did not report a 36 percent increase in enrollment.

text: An article last Wednesday about bakers in the Sahrawi refugee settlements had an incorrect byline. Its author and photographer is Matteo de Mayda, not Matteo de Maya.

text: Because of a production error, an article on Tuesday about reasons for optimism in the coronavirus pandemic included columns of type that were out of order. The article, with the headline “A Dose of Optimism, as the Pandemic Rages On,” can be read at nytimes.com .
ref_headline: A Dose of Optimism, as the Pandemic Rages On,
match_headline: A Dose of Optimism, as the Pandemic Rages On

text: An article on Saturday about fading hopes of an economic recovery in Europe misstated how long cafes and bars in Paris have been ordered shut in response to a surge in coronavirus cases. They have been ordered shut for two weeks, not two months.

text: An article on Monday about Judge Amy Coney Barrett, President Trump’s Supreme Court nominee, misstated the page on which a high school yearbook image Judge Barrett appeared.
