text: An article on Wednesday about a call by Dr. Anthony Fauci for the Trump campaign to take down an ad that he said was misleading misidentified the profession of Dr. Jay Bhattacharya. He is an economist, not an epidemiologist.

text: An article on Monday about Amazon’s expansion to France misstated the unemployment rate in the Gard region of France. It is 9.8 percent, not nearly 17 percent, which was the rate in 2017.

text: An article on Wednesday about the flutist Brandon Patrick George misspelled the name of a modern-music ensemble based in Paris. It is the Ensemble Intercontemporain, not Intercomporain.

text: An article on Wednesday about a new philanthropic award misstated Edafe Okporo’s connection to the RDJ Refugee Shelter. He is its director, not its founder.

text: An article on Friday about efforts to reopen a high school in Manhattan during the coronavirus pandemic misspelled the name of a parent of a Hunter College High School student. She is Meika Mustrangi, not Mika Mustrungi.
match_headline: This Elite School Is in a Brick Fortress. Can It Handle a Pandemic?

text: An article on Thursday about ​false accusations made by ​Amy Cooper​ against a Black bird-watcher in Central Park, citing courtroom statements, ​referred incorrectly ​to Ms. Cooper​’s second conversation with a 911 dispatcher. text: An article last Sunday about James Murdoch misstated the criticism that British regulators leveled at Mr. Murdoch in the wake of a phone hacking scandal involving British tabloids. text: An article on Monday about the two children Judge Amy Coney Barrett and her husband adopted from Haiti misstated the school that Libien Becker attends. It is Montana Technological University, not Montana Technical University.

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misidentified the characters played by Imelda Staunton and Francesca Annis in “Flesh and Blood.” Staunton is the neighbor and Annis is the widow, not the other way around. text: A Critic’s Notebook on Saturday about the Montpellier Danse festival misspelled the surname of the festival director. He is Jean-Paul Montanari, not Montenari. The article also misspelled the given name of an Israeli choreographer. He is Emanuel Gat, not Emmanuel.

text: An earlier version of a picture caption with an article on Monday about Bruce Springsteen’s new album, using information provided by the artist’s representatives, misidentified a musician. He is Charlie Giordano, not Benjamin Newberry.

text: An article on Tuesday about a teacher killed in a Paris suburb misidentified the type of school where the victim had taught. It was a middle school, not a high school.

text: An article last Wednesday about the Seattle dining scene, using information from Canlis restaurant, reported incorrectly that the restaurant had retained all 115 of its employees through the pandemic. After publication, the restaurant said that in late September, it had laid off or furloughed 77 employees, with plans to bring them back later this year.
match_headline: The News Cycle Is Crushing Seattle’s Vibrant Restaurant Scene

text: An article on Wednesday about President Trump’s business dealings in China attributed an erroneous distinction to Tony Tiah Thee Kian. He is one of the richest men in Malaysia, not the richest man in Malaysia.
match_headline: Trump Records Shed New Light on Chinese Business Pursuits

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday referred incompletely to a 2010 episode during which Ahmed Luqman Talib was shot. He was on a ship that was part of a flotilla trying to carry aid to Gaza, but the particular vessel he was aboard was not carrying aid.
match_headline: U.S. Imposes Sanctions on Qaeda Financier Who Trades in Gems

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Mexico’s defense secretary being identified as “El Padrino,” Godfather to a drug cartel, misstated the name of a U.S. agency. It is the Drug Enforcement Administration, not the Drug Enforcement Agency.
match_headline: Who Was ‘El Padrino,’ Godfather to Drug Cartel? Mexico’s Defense Chief, U.S. Says

text: An article on Wednesday about a joint effort by the United States Cyber Command and technology firms to disrupt a Russian network that they fear could sabotage election systems misstated the day a CyberScoop article was published. It was Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: As Election Nears, Government and Tech Firms Push Back on Russia (and Trump)

text: An article on Wednesday about the film “The Trial of the Chicago 7” referred imprecisely to the film style of “Chicago 10,” a 2008 release. It is animated with a style that mimics the look of a rotoscoping, a technique involving tracing over existing film, but it did not involve actual rotoscoping.
match_headline: The Chicago 7 Trial Onscreen: An Interpretation for Every Era

text: An article on Thursday about efforts by Richard Grenell, a close ally of President Trump, to persuade President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela to give up power referred incorrectly to Juan Guaidó. He remains the current leader of Venezuela’s Parliament; he is not its former leader.
match_headline: Grenell Pursued Talks Over Change of Power in Venezuela

text: An article on Thursday about Quentin State Prison in California being ordered to release or move half of its prisoners because of the pandemic described incorrectly the crime for which Isauro Aguirre received a death sentence. He was convicted of killing his girlfriend’s 8-year-old son, not his girlfriend and her son. (She was sentenced to life in prison in the case.)
match_headline: San Quentin Ordered to Reduce Prison Population by Half Over Virus Fears

text: An article on Friday about the #MeToo movement in Iran misidentified the position of Elnaaz Mohammadi at Abuse Watch, an education and advocacy group in Tehran. She is a member, not a co-founder. The article also imprecisely paraphrased her comments regarding the recipient of student complaints about Aydin Aghdashloo’s behavior. Ms. Mohammadi said she had received the complaints, not Abuse Watch.
match_headline: A #MeToo Awakening Stirs in Iran

text: An article on Friday about winter sports in Europe during the pandemic misspelled the surname of an American ski racer. He is Ryan Cochran-Siegle, not Ryan Cochrane-Siegle.
match_headline: Winter Sports Athletes Are Crisscrossing Europe for Races. Is That a Good Idea?

text: An article on Page 6 about the Asia Society Triennial misstates Michelle Yun’s role at the Asia Society Museum. She is the senior curator of modern and contemporary art, not only of contemporary art.
match_headline: A First-Time Survey of Asian Art Gets a Second Chance to Dazzle

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 14 about a four-decade retrospective on the work of Sue Coe misstates the status of Peter Eleey, who organized “Sue Coe: It Can Happen Here.” He is the chief curator at MoMA PS1, not the former chief curator.
ref_headline: Sue Coe: It Can Happen Here.
match_headline: Casting a Critical Eye, From the Slaughterhouse to the White House

text: An article on Page 22 about the chef Gaggan Anand misstates the location of the Don’t Tell Aunty restaurant. It is in Sydney, Australia, not Melbourne.
match_headline: The Fed-Up Chef

text: An article on Page 26 about the tech company Palantir omits part of the name of a German pharmaceutical company. It is Merck K.G.a.A., not simply Merck, which is the name of an American company.
An obituary on Oct. 6 about Mike Foster, a former two-term governor of Louisiana, misstated the year he was elected to the Louisiana State Senate. It was 1987, not 1986.
match_headline: Mike Foster, Louisiana Governor During a Lull, Dies at 90

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Oct. 13 about the Hall of Fame second baseman Joe Morgan misstated the number of World Series the Cincinnati Reds, for whom Morgan played in the 1970s, appeared in from 1970 to 1977. It was four, not three. The obituary also misstated the name of the college from which Morgan received a bachelor’s degree. It is California State University, Hayward, not the University of California, Heyward.
match_headline: Joe Morgan, Hall of Fame Second Baseman, Is Dead at 77

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Samantha McCluskey and Louis Keleher misstated the year of the couple’s first date. It was in 2016, not 2018.
match_headline: An Argument for Loving ‘Devil’s Advocate’

text: A report last Sunday about the wedding of Roxann Belle and Gaspar Stinfil misstated the location of the ceremony. It was at the San Francisco Palace of Fine Arts, not at City Hall, where they had originally planned to wed.
match_headline: Winning at the Game of Love

text: An article last Sunday about design trends in new luxury condos misspelled the surname of a partner at Concrete, an Amsterdam-based architecture and design firm. He is Erikjan Vermeulen, not Bermeulen.
match_headline: Understatement Is the New Luxury

text: An article on Page 26 about the tech company Palantir omits part of the name of a German pharmaceutical company. It is Merck K.G.a.A., not simply Merck, which is the name of an American company.
An article on Sunday about partnerships between Apple and Google misstated a term for cooperation between competitors. It is co-opetition, not co-optation.
match_headline: Apple, Google and a Deal That Controls the Internet

text: A headline with an article last Tuesday about early data on coronavirus cases in New York City public schools misstated the number of positive test results. As the article correctly stated, there were 28 positive test results, not 18.
match_headline: Surprising Results in Initial Virus Testing in N.Y.C. Schools

text: A chart with an article on Sunday about coronavirus outbreaks in rural areas of the United States was mislabeled. The chart on the right showed new reported deaths in the United States, not new reported cases.
match_headline: The Worst Virus Outbreaks in the U.S. Are Now in Rural Areas

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about activists in Hong Kong who are fleeing to the West misstated when Vicky Xiao traveled to Hong Kong to join the protests. It was in August of 2019, not last August.
match_headline: As China Clamps Down, Activists Flee Hong Kong for Refuge in the West

text: An article on Monday about a clash between supporters of President Trump and counterprotesters in Manhattan misstated Rudolph W. Giuliani’s connection to a convoy of Trump supporters. He encountered the convoy in Manhattan but was not riding in one of its cars.
match_headline: Fights Erupt During ‘Jews for Trump’ Rally in Manhattan

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the Sports of The Times column on Monday about Charles Adams, an African-American high school football coach and former police officer in Minneapolis, included an outdated figure for the enrollment at the high school Minneapolis North. As the column stated, enrollment was about 100 10 years ago; it is not about 100 currently. (Current enrollment is 403 students.)
match_headline: As a Coach and a Cop in Minneapolis, Where Would He Draw the Line?

text: An article on Monday about a surge in coronavirus cases in Wisconsin misidentified the court that blocked an emergency order by Gov. Tony Evers. It was a state appeals court, not the Wisconsin Supreme Court.
match_headline: Game Day in Green Bay: Empty Sports Bars, Full Hospitals

text: An article on Tuesday about the Georgia’s emergence as a battleground state misstated the amount of time between Jason Carter’s campaign for governor and that of Stacey Abrams. It was four years, not six years. (As the article correctly noted, Mr. Carter lost in 2014, and Ms. Abrams in 2018.)
match_headline: Georgia, Once Reliably Red, Is Suddenly a Battleground. What Happened?

text: An article on Tuesday about endangered lemurs in Madagascar misstated the name of a conservation group. It is Lemur Conservation Foundation, not Lemur Conservation International.
match_headline: In Madagascar, Endangered Lemurs Find a Private Refuge

text: An article on Wednesday about the reasons that New York’s indie movie theaters may survive the pandemic, using information from the theater owner Nick Nicolaou, misidentified the month when he began offering the documentary “The Booksellers” online. It was in June, not April.
match_headline: How New York’s Small Cinemas Are Hanging On

text: An article on Wednesday about the use of conservative judicial appointments as an incentive for people to vote Republican misstated the number of vacancies in the federal appellate courts. Several hours before Justice Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed by the Senate, a judge from the First Circuit, Juan Torruella, died. The courts now have two vacancies, not one.
match_headline: ‘Fat and Happy’ With a Conservative Court, Are Republicans Losing a Winning Issue?

text: An article on Thursday about Hurricane Zeta misstated the Greek letters that would be used to identify the next three named storms of the 2020 Atlantic cyclone season. They are Eta, Theta and Iota, not Eta, Iota and Kappa.
match_headline: Hurricane Zeta Lashes Louisiana Coast in a Storm Season to Remember

text: An article on Thursday about the expected guilty plea of David Correia, a business partner of Lev Parnas, an associate of Rudolph W. Giuliani who was indicted on federal campaign finance charges, misstated Mr. Correia’s age. He is 45, not 50.
match_headline: Business Partner of Giuliani Associate Is Expected to Plead Guilty

text: An article on Saturday about the expulsion of non-Mexican children to Mexico by the United States, using information provided by the Women’s Refugee Commission, referred incorrectly to the number of children expelled in the past eight months who were not accompanied by a parent or other adult. The Mexican government has not specified the number of unaccompanied children; it is unknown if the number exceeded 200.
match_headline: U.S. Expels Migrant Children From Other Countries to Mexico

text: An article on Saturday about women who protested Poland’s abortion ban misspelled the name of a newspaper. It is Gazeta Wyborcza, not Gazeta Wyborca.
match_headline: Women Converge on Warsaw, Heightening Poland’s Largest Protests in Decades

text: An article on Sunday about the impact of race on the 2020 election in Georgia misstated the year that Joe Biden dropped out of the presidential race. It was 2008, not 2007.
match_headline: In This Strange Election Year, Foreign Embassies Find Little Access to Democrats

text: An article on Monday about the intimidating tactics used by President Trump’s supporters misstated the day that an incident involving Trump supporters and a bus for Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s campaign occurred. It was Friday, not Saturday.
match_headline: Trump Backers Block Highways as Election Tensions Play Out in the Streets

text: An article on Saturday about the approval of Steven Cohen as owner of the Mets referred incorrectly to the relationship of the singer and actor Jennifer Lopez and the former baseball star Alex Rodriguez. They are engaged; they are not married.
match_headline: Steven Cohen Is Approved as Mets Owner After Clearing 2 More Hurdles

text: An article on Oct. 27 about malaria misstated the origin of “sticky” proteins in red blood cells infected with malaria. They are generated by the malaria parasite, not by the cells. The article also misspelled the given name of a researcher. It is Silvia Portugal, not Sylvia Portugal.
match_headline: A Malaria Mystery, Partly Solved: What Happens When the Rains End?

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the biblical scholar Virginia Ramey Mollenkott referred incorrectly to her marriage to J. Suzannah Tilton. They married shortly after the United States Supreme Court overturned a law that denied federal benefits to same-sex couples, but before the court ruled that the Constitution guarantees a right to same-sex marriage.
match_headline: Virginia Mollenkott, 88, Dies; Feminist Found Liberation in the Bible

text: An obituary on Thursday about the restaurateur Cecilia Chiang referred incorrectly to the six-part PBS series “The Kitchen Wisdom of Cecilia Chiang.” It was broadcast nationally in 2016, not just by the San Diego station KPBS.
ref_headline: The Kitchen Wisdom of Cecilia Chiang.
match_headline: Cecilia Chiang, Who Brought Authentic Chinese Food to America, Dies at 100

text: An article on Tuesday about the final hours before Election Day misstated the surname of a construction worker in Los Angeles. He is Fernando Casas, not Fernando Salas.
match_headline: Undeterred by Pandemic, Americans Prepare to Deliver Verdict on Trump

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about The Associated Press’s role in the presidential election reversed the identities of two A.P. journalists. Ashley Thomas was at center, and Julie Pace on the right.
match_headline: In a Hot Election, the Cool-Headed Associated Press Takes Center Stage

text: A picture with an article on Tuesday about a project by Leonard Bernstein, Stephen Sondheim and Jerome Robbins that was never produced was published in error. The photo showed Mike Stoller, not Jerry Leiber. (Stoller was Leiber’s frequent collaborator.)
match_headline: A Golden Team, a Terrible Title and a Show That Vanished

text: An article on Tuesday about the television show “How To With John Wilson” misstated the day new episodes are released. It is Friday, not Sunday.
match_headline: The Best Half-Hour of Comedy in 2020 Is About … Scaffolding?

text: An obituary on Saturday about the Hall of Fame cornerback Herb Adderley misstated his mother’s given name. She was Reva Adderley, not Rene.
match_headline: Herb Adderley, a Packers Hall of Fame Cornerback, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Monday about the industrial designer Enzo Mari misstated part of the name of a museum in Milan that is presenting a retrospective of his work. It is the Triennale Milano Museum, not the Triennale Design Museum. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated the surname of Mr. Mari’s first wife. She was Gabriela Ferrario, not Ferrariol.
match_headline: Enzo Mari, Industrial Designer Who Kept Things Simple, Dies at 88

text: An article on Wednesday about calls for voters to exercise patience during the election process misstated the name of a Minneapolis man who said he planned to vote for President Trump. He is Justin Salzl, not Salz.
match_headline: How Long Is This Going to Take? Americans Settle In to Wait

text: An obituary on Oct. 25 about the costume designer and art director Robert DeMora misstated his role in the production of the 1996 film “The Birdcage.” He was an associate costume designer for the film, not the chief costume designer. (Ann Roth was the chief designer.) And a photograph of a scene from that film was published in error. It showed Nathan Lane and Robin Williams wearing outfits designed by Ms. Roth, not by Mr. DeMora.
match_headline: Robert DeMora Dies at 85; Helped Make Bette Midler Look Divine

text: An article on Thursday about the Democrats’ inability to gain a majority in the Senate misstated the length of time Joseph R. Biden served in the Senate. He was a senator for more than 35 years, not 45.
match_headline: A Split Decision for Democrats

text: An article on Thursday about disinformation targeting Latinos misstated whom QAnon adherents falsely believe is part of a global cabal. It is Joseph R. Biden Jr., not President Trump. (They believe, also falsely, that the president is battling such a cabal.)
match_headline: False News Targeting Latinos Trails the Election

text: An article on Thursday about lawsuits pursued by President Trump in states that he lost in the election misidentified one of the Supreme Court justices who signaled an openness to reconsidering an extension of Pennsylvania’s deadline for counting ballots. Justice Neil M. Gorsuch was one of the three justices taking that position, not Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh.
match_headline: With His Path to Re-election Narrowing, Trump Turns to the Courts

text: An article on Sunday about President Trump’s first-term promises misstated the affiliation of the Tax Policy Center. It is a joint partnership between the Brookings Institution and the Urban Institute, it is not run by the Brookings Institution.
match_headline: Did President Trump Keep His First-Term Promises? Let’s Look at 5 of Them

text: An article on Oct. 31 about tax loopholes in the real estate industry that have benefited President Trump misstated the effect of 2017 changes to a tax break for rehabilitating historic structures. The law limited the tax break to 4 percent a year, but allowed it to be credited in five consecutive years for a total of 20 percent of the project’s cost. It did not lower the tax credit to 4 percent from 20 percent. The article also misstated the timing of an exemption for the tax break. The exemption applied to projects started before mid-2018, not before 2017.
match_headline: How a Century of Real-Estate Tax Breaks Enriched Donald Trump

text: An article on Thursday about key races in Washington State misstated the position of Kim Wyman, the Republican secretary of state, on the state’s mail-in voting policy. Ms. Wyman does not agree with President Trump’s voiced opinion and attacks on mail-in voting; she is a defender of the procedure.
match_headline: ‘I feel very good,’ President Trump tells campaign workers during an Election Day visit to a Republican office.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 12 about the composer Osvaldo Golijov misidentified the person who programmed the 2006 Ojai Music Festival. It was Robert Spano, not Thomas W. Morris.
match_headline: After a Decade of Silence, a Composer Reappears

text: An article this weekend on Page 24 about the folk singers Gillian Welch and David Rawlings misstates the title of Gillian Welch’s new three-volume collection of songs. It is “Boots No. 2: The Lost Songs,” not “Boots 2: Lost Songs.”
match_headline: How Gillian Welch and David Rawlings Held Onto Optimism

text: An obituary on Sunday about the actor Sean Connery misidentified the tartan he wore when he was knighted in 2000. It was a MacLean tartan, not MacLeod.
match_headline: Sean Connery, Who Embodied James Bond and More, Dies at 90

text: A picture caption in an article on Oct. 18 about free speech and online disinformation referred incorrectly to the pictured protest in Skokie, Ill. It was against a proposed Nazi march; it was not a counterprotest. A neo-Nazi group successfully petitioned to hold a march in Skokie, but held it elsewhere.
match_headline: The Problem of Free Speech in an Age of Disinformation

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about Latin plant names misidentified two plants in an illustration. The Camellia flower is at top, and the Magnolia cambelli is at bottom.
match_headline: Yes, You Can Learn to Speak the Language of Plants

text: An article on Wednesday about Maricopa County, Ariz., misidentified which elected positions in the county are held by Democrats. Positions held by Democrats include the county recorder and sheriff, not the assessor and school superintendent.
match_headline: Why Arizona’s Storied Conservative Stronghold Could Flip for Biden

text: An article on Sunday about Ballina, the ancestral Irish town of President-elect Joseph R. Biden Jr., misstated the vintage of a cherry red Buick Electra with Elvis cushions. It was from 1959; the Electra was not made in 1957. The article also misspelled the name of a teacher in Ballina. She is Aileen Horkan, not Horkin.
match_headline: Irish Home of Biden’s Great-Great-Great Grandfather Cheers His Victory

text: An article on Sunday about the Eataly executive Dino Borri misstated the name of a restaurant. It is La Pizza e La Pasta, not La Pizza e La La Palla.
match_headline: How an Eataly Executive Spends His Sundays

text: An article on Saturday about Nannette Streicher, the prominent keyboard manufacturer, misstated her age at her death, in 1833. She was 64, not 70.
match_headline: The Woman Who Built Beethoven’s Pianos

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about negotiations for a trade agreement between Britain and the European Union misstated the reason for Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s appearance at a ceremony at the Cenotaph. He was commemorating the anniversary of the end of World War I, not honoring coronavirus victims.
match_headline: Trump’s Defeat Weakens Boris Johnson in Urgent Brexit Talks

text: An article on Tuesday about the storming of a football field after a game by thousands of Notre Dame students who broke virus protocol described incorrectly the reason that Notre Dame’s president apologized in August after posing for photos with students who were returning to campus. He apologized for not properly following the university’s social distancing guidelines, not for posing without a mask.
match_headline: Trading Blame and Worry, Notre Dame Grapples With Celebration’s Fallout

text: An article on Sunday about the impact of Black Lives Matter protests on the U.S. election referred incorrectly to Crystal Daddario. She identifies as Hispanic, not white.
match_headline: Voters Say Black Lives Matter Protests Were Important. They Disagree On Why.

text: An article on Monday about divisions in the United States following last week’s election misstated the day that a World War II sailor spontaneously kissed a woman in a nurse’s uniform in Times Square. It was V-J Day, not V-E Day.
match_headline: The Election Is Over. The Nation’s Rifts Remain.

text: An article on Saturday about Steven A. Cohen’s first day as the new owner of the Mets misstated part of the name of a hedge fund group that he founded and owned. It was SAC Capital Advisors, not SAC Capital Partners.
match_headline: A Friday Full of M.L.B. News and Mercy

text: An article on Tuesday about the potential for several affirmative action cases to reach the Supreme Court described incorrectly a vote regarding California’s ban on affirmative action. About 56.5 percent of voters supported maintaining the ban; the vote was not narrow.
match_headline: Affirmative Action Cases May Reach Supreme Court Even Without Trump

text: An article on Wednesday about coronavirus hospitalizations in El Paso misspelled the name of a vehicle ridden by El Paso officers. It is a Segway, not a Segue.
match_headline: As Hospitalizations Soar, El Paso Brings In New Mobile Morgues

text: An article on Wednesday about a doctor in Connecticut who overcharged patients for coronavirus tests referred incorrectly to Darien, Conn. It is a town, not a city.
match_headline: These Towns Trusted a Doctor to Set Up Covid Testing. Sample Patient Fee: $1,944.

text: An article on Wednesday about the lingering followers of Keith Raniere, the leader of Nxivm, misstated the profession of Janja Lalich, a cult expert. She is a sociologist, not a psychologist.
match_headline: Nxivm’s Leader Is Guilty of Ugly Crimes. These Die-Hards Stand by Him.

text: An article on Thursday about new officials at the Pentagon and the National Security Agency misstated Ezra Cohen-Watnick’s role in preparing intelligence reports for Representative Devin Nunes of California. A lawyer for Mr. Cohen-Watnick said he did not provide the material to Mr. Nunes, although he did help compile it. The article also misidentified Kashyap Patel’s hometown. He is from Garden City, N.Y., not New Jersey.
match_headline: Who Are the Senior Officials at the Pentagon and the N.S.A?

text: An obituary on Saturday about Marguerite Littman, the inspiration for Holly Golightly of Truman Capote’s “Breakfast at Tiffany’s” and an early force in the fight against AIDS, misstated the number of friends Ms. Littman contacted to request funding for what would become the AIDS Charitable Trust. She wrote to 300 friends, not 100.
match_headline: Marguerite Littman, the Inspiration for Holly Golightly, Dies at 90

text: An article on Thursday about contenders for the cabinet of President-elect Joseph R. Biden Jr. misstated one of Michael J. Morell’s past government positions. He is a former C.I.A. analyst, not a former Foreign Service officer.
match_headline: Who Will Fill Biden’s Cabinet?

text: An article on Friday about canceled and postponed sports in the Ivy League misstated the season in which a sport is played. Soccer is a fall sport, not a spring sport.
match_headline: Ivy League Cancels Winter Sports and Stalls Spring Sports Over Coronavirus

text: An article on Thursday about the filmmaker John Waters’s donation to the Baltimore Museum of Art, using information supplied by the museum, misspelled the name of a work by Karin Sander. It is “Gebrauchsbild,” not “Gebrauschsbild.”
match_headline: John Waters, Droll Bard of Baltimore, Promises Art to Hometown Museum

text: An article on page 44 about the artist Senga Nengudi misstates the title of one of her works. It is “Ceremony for Freeway Fets,” not “Ceremony for Freeway Fetes.”

An article last Sunday about the musical “Lone Star Love,” relying on information from one of the show’s producers, described incorrectly the timing and purpose of an $81,000 payment. The producers Ed and Eleanor Burke made the payment as severance to members of the show’s company before it closed, not to pay a fine by Actors’ Equity against Randy Quaid.
match_headline: A Not-So-Merry Mix: Shakespeare, Bluegrass and Randy Quaid

text: An article last Sunday about voter support for drug decriminalization ballot initiatives referred imprecisely to a statistic in a recent report by the American Civil Liberties Union. Black people are over three and a half times more likely to be arrested for marijuana possession than white people, not three and a half times.
match_headline: This Election, a Divided America Stands United on One Topic

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about co-ops that are increasing residential fees to make up for lost commercial rent misidentified the woman shown with Fernando Andrade at Andrade Shoe Repair. She is Nilda Andrade, his wife, not Carolina Conigliaro, his daughter.
match_headline: Maintenance Fees for Some Co-ops Rise to Cover Lost Commercial Rent

text: An article on page 44 about the artist Senga Nengudi misstates the title of one of her works. It is “Ceremony for Freeway Fets,” not “Ceremony for Freeway Fetes.”

An article on Sunday about the ways houses of worship in New York are serving their communities during the pandemic misstated the surname of a deacon at St. Agatha’s Roman Catholic church in Brooklyn who died of Covid-19. He was Emilio Arteaga, not Artea. It also misstated the “zone” St. Agatha’s was placed in. It was an orange zone, not red.
match_headline: Staying Apart, But Praying Together

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about American students who lack reliable internet access misstated the given name of a student in rural North Carolina. As the article correctly stated, she is Orlandria Lennon, not Orlandrie.
match_headline: No signal: Internet ‘dead zones’ cut rural students off from virtual classes.

text: An article on Wednesday about charges faced by Ace Magashule, the secretary general of the governing African National Congress, misidentified a personal assistant to Mr. Magashule. The assistant, who has become a witness for the state, is Moroadi Cholota, not Refiloe Mokoena. Because of an editing error, the article also referred incorrectly to an unnamed businessman accused of once paying a $3,431 bribe to Mr. Magashule. The businessman has since died; he is not facing court charges.
match_headline: Top A.N.C. Official Charged With Corruption in South Africa

text: An article on Saturday about the newest members of Congress misstated the significance of Nancy Mace’s election as a representative for South Carolina. She is the first Republican woman to represent the state in Congress, but not the first woman to do so.
match_headline: A More Subdued Orientation on Capitol Hill as Newest Members of Congress Arrive

text: An article on Saturday about the likelihood that Republican-led state legislatures will choose members of the Electoral College to cast votes for President Trump in states won by President-elect Joseph R. Biden Jr. misstated the year that the Electoral Count Act was enacted. It was 1887, not 1876.
match_headline: Mr. President, Pack Your Bags and Be Gone

text: An article on Saturday about Bryson DeChambeau’s poor performance on the third hole at Augusta National on Friday misstated his score on the hole. He carded a triple bogey, not a double bogey.
match_headline: Bryson DeChambeau’s Ball Search Pushes Him Out of Masters Hunt

text: An article on Friday about the Super Bowl halftime show this coming February misstated the number of followers that the musical artist the Weeknd has on Instagram. It is 25 million, not 2.5 million.
match_headline: N.F.L. Announces the Weeknd for Its Super Bowl Halftime Show

text: An article on Saturday about a musical history project led by Rhiannon Giddens included a statement from Ms. Giddens that misidentified the topic of a traditional song. It is the Swannanoa Tunnel, not the Cumberland Gap.
match_headline: Rhiannon Giddens Aims at 1800s America in Her Silkroad Plans

text: An article on Monday about a visit by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey to northern Cyprus described incorrectly the U.N. peacekeeping mission there. It is one of the organization’s longest-serving peacekeeping missions, not its longest-serving one.
match_headline: Erdogan’s Visit to Northern Cyprus Stokes Decades-Long Dispute

text: An article on Friday about the handling of the pandemic by pubs in Britain misstated the home base of the pub chain Greene King. The company is based in Suffolk, England, not in Scotland.
match_headline: Uneasy Under Lockdown, Pubs in England Count the Days Till Christmas

text: An article on Tuesday about current events in theater performances transposed the names of the actors playing the writers James Baldwin and Nikki Giovanni in a segment of “Lessons in Survival.” In that segment, Kyle Beltran portrays Giovanni and Nana Mensah is Baldwin.
match_headline: When Political Theater Ditches the Disguises of Fiction

text: A recipe last Wednesday for mixed apple pie misstated the gram amount for the granulated sugar in the filling. It is 130 grams, not 65 grams.
A Critic’s Notebook last Wednesday about cooking burnout misspelled the given name of a home cook in San Francisco. She is Christina Samala, not Christine.
match_headline: For Home Cooks, Burnout Is a Reality This Holiday Season

text: An article on Wednesday about Dana Remus, who has been named White House Counsel for the Biden administration, misstated when Eric Schultz began working for President Barack Obama. It was 2011, not 2008.
match_headline: Dana Remus Has Taken an Unlikely Path to the White House Counsel’s Office

text: An article on Wednesday about the firing of Christopher Krebs, misstated when Defense Secretary Mark T. Esper was fired. It was last week, not two weeks ago.
match_headline: Trump Fires Christopher Krebs, Official Who Disputed Election Fraud Claims

text: An article on Wednesday about a plan by President Trump to sell oil leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge misspelled the surname of a lawyer who works on environmental issues. She is Ann Navaro, not Navarro.
match_headline: Trump Plan to Sell Arctic Oil Leases Will Face Challenges

text: An article on Tuesday about self-inflicted gun deaths misstated the name of a suicide-prevention organization. It is the National Action Alliance for Suicide Prevention, not the National Action Alliance to Prevent Suicide.
match_headline: ‘How Did We Not Know?’ Gun Owners Confront a Suicide Epidemic

text: An article last Thursday about the safety measures “dive bars” are taking during the pandemic misstated the age of My Brother’s Bar in Denver. It is 147 years old, not 167.
match_headline: Dive Bars Bring in the Light

text: An article on Thursday about a threat by Mexico to expel American drug agents misstated Senator Bob Menendez’s role on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. He is its top Democrat, not its chairman.
match_headline: Mexico, Outraged at Arrest of Ex-Official, Threatened to Toss U.S. Agents

text: An article on Thursday about possible cuts to the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s budget misstated McKinsey & Company’s best-case scenario for ridership. It projected that by 2024 ridership would reach 90 percent of pre-pandemic levels, not 80 percent.
match_headline: Subway Service Could Be Cut 40% if No Federal Aid Arrives

text: An article on Thursday about the language used by lawyers supporting President Trump misstated the circumstances in which they claimed that the election was stolen. They were in court, but they were not under oath at the time.
match_headline: Giuliani in Public: ‘It’s a Fraud.’ Giuliani in Court: ‘This Is Not a Fraud Case.’

text: An article on Wednesday about the acquisition of Kind North America by Mars misstated the year that Kind was founded. It was 2004, not 2005.
match_headline: Kind Bars to Be Acquired by Maker of Snickers

text: An article on Thursday about the N.B.A. draft misstated when the Knicks moved up. It was Wednesday, not Monday.
match_headline: Anthony Edwards Drafted No. 1 by the Minnesota Timberwolves

text: An article on Friday about the political system in Bosnia 25 years after the Dayton Accords misspelled the given name of a woman whose husband was killed during the fighting in Prijedor. She is Zdravka Karlica, not Zvadka.
match_headline: Under a Divisive Peace, Wartime Rifts Hobble Hope in Bosnia

text: An article on Friday about the certification process for the U.S. election misstated the final certification deadlines in Nevada and Ohio. The deadline in Nevada is Nov. 24, not Dec. 1, and the deadline in Ohio is Nov. 28, not Nov. 24.
match_headline: The G.O.P. bungles its final stand to stop Pennsylvania’s election certification.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the International Swimming League’s bubble in Budapest misstated the distance of a short-course event in which Caeleb Dressel set a world record. It was 100 meters, not yards.
match_headline: Swimming in a Bubble, Free From the Tyranny of Times

text: An article on Friday about the winner of the 2020 Booker Prize misstated Douglas Stuart’s citizenship. It is British and American, not Scottish and American.
match_headline: Douglas Stuart Wins Booker Prize for ‘Shuggie Bain’

text: An article this weekend on Page 34 about President Trump’s potential legal liabilities misstates the given name of a former secretary of Housing and Urban Development under President Obama. He is Julián Castro, not Raúl. And the article refers incorrectly to the agency that oversees federal campaign law. It is the Federal Election Commission, not the Federal Elections Committee. The article also misstates where Attorney General Eric Holder used the phrase “the criminalization of policy differences.” It was during a 2009 congressional hearing, not during House confirmation hearings.
match_headline: Can America Restore the Rule of Law Without Prosecuting Trump?

text: An article this weekend on Page 22 about N95 masks misstates 3M’s federal contract to expand domestic production of N95 masks. The company received two contracts in April worth $201 million, not a $1 billion contract.
match_headline: Inside the Chaotic, Cutthroat Gray Market for N95 Masks

text: An obituary on Thursday about the South Korean women’s rights activist Lee Hyo-jae misstated her role in the trip a delegation of activists took into North Korea in 2015. She helped organize the group; she did not take part in the crossing.
match_headline: Lee Hyo-jae, Champion of Women’s Rights in South Korea, Dies at 95

text: An article last Sunday about the political correspondent Abby Phillip misstated the year CNN hired her. It was 2017, not 2018.
match_headline: Abby Phillip Is Next-Gen CNN

text: An article on Nov. 8 about the recycling of discarded compact discs described imprecisely the new game consoles from Sony and Microsoft. While the companies are releasing editions of the PlayStation and the Xbox without disc drives, they will also offer versions of the consoles with a disc drive. (The consoles with a disc drive cost more.)
match_headline: The Uneasy Afterlife of Our Dazzling Trash

text: An article on Saturday about President Trump’s setbacks in his efforts to undo the election results in Michigan and Georgia misstated the number of uncounted ballots discovered during a recount in Georgia. There were more than 5,000, not several hundred.
match_headline: Georgia and Michigan Deliver Blows to Trump’s Efforts to Undo the Election

text: An article on Sunday about the race between Pfizer and Moderna to develop a coronavirus vaccine misstated the age of a daughter of Moderna’s chief executive, Stéphane Bancel. She is 18, not 19. A picture caption in the article also misstated the academic degree of Mr. Bancel. He does not hold a doctorate.
match_headline: Politics, Science and the Remarkable Race for a Coronavirus Vaccine

text: An article on Sunday about an experimental antibody treatment granted emergency authorization by the Food and Drug Administration misstated the amount of Eli Lilly’s deal with the government. The company received $375 million, not $375,000.
match_headline: F.D.A. Grants Emergency Authorization of Antibody Treatment Given to Trump

text: An article on Monday, based on information from AdvaMed, misstated the rate that AdvaMed’s member companies were producing ventilators. The output before the pandemic was 700 per week and by summer reached 10,000 per week; the tallies were per week, not per month.
match_headline: Now the U.S. Has Lots of Ventilators, but Too Few Specialists to Operate Them

text: An article on Saturday about the backlash from President Trump’s allies that followed Tucker Carlson’s criticisms of arguments made by Sidney Powell, a lawyer for the president, referred incorrectly to the location of the bombing raid that killed Iran’s top general, Qassim Suleimani. The raid was in Iraq, not Iran.
match_headline: Tucker Carlson Dared Question a Trump Lawyer. The Backlash Was Quick.

text: An article on Saturday about the Republican resistance that awaits nominees to the Biden administration misspelled the given name of a longtime foreign policy adviser to President-elect Joseph R. Biden Jr. He is Antony Blinken, not Anthony.
match_headline: Republican Resistance Looms in the Senate for Biden’s Nominees

text: An article on Saturday about a congressional investigation into the Pebble Mine project in Alaska described incorrectly the proposed daily production from the mine. It would process 160,000 metric tons of ore per day, not 160,000 metric tons of gold and other mineral concentrates.
match_headline: Congress Seeks Answers on Alaskan Mine Project

text: An article on Sunday about the return of Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner to New York misidentified the real estate agency a broker is affiliated with. She is with Brown Harris Stevens, not Warburg.
match_headline: Will Manhattan’s Elite Really Spurn Ivanka and Jared (and Their Money)?

text: An obituary on Nov. 12 about the art collector Sindika Dokolo misstated part of the name of an organization that tracked the actions of his wife, Isabel dos Santos, that led to charges of money laundering and embezzlement. It is the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, not the International Coalition of Investigative Journalists.
match_headline: Sindika Dokolo, Crusader for Return of African Art, Dies at 48

text: An obituary on Nov. 16 about the singer and actress Lynn Kellogg misspelled the maiden name of her mother, Maxine Kellogg. It was Goeres, not Goekes. It also referred incorrectly to Sheila, the character Ms. Kellogg played in the musical “Hair.” She was a student protester, not a debutante turned hippie. The obituary also referred incompletely to the creation of “Hair.” While James Rado and Gerome Ragni conceived the show and wrote the book and lyrics, the music was written by Galt McDermot. And it misstated the date on which Ms. Kellogg appeared on the TV series “The Johnny Cash Show” in 1969. The episode was broadcast on July 26, not July 20, the day American astronauts landed on the moon.
match_headline: Lynn Kellogg, Who Found the Spotlight in ‘Hair,’ Dies at 77

text: An obituary on Sunday about the interior designer François Catroux misstated the nationality of the tycoon Antenor Pritiño, on whose apartment Mr. Catroux worked. He was Bolivian, not Chilean.
match_headline: François Catroux, Decorator of Choice for Aristocrats, Dies at 83

text: An article on Monday about the possible disruption of Vermont’s ski season by the state’s quarantine rules misstated the occupancy rate in the Stowe area in August. It was 36 percent, not 69 percent.
match_headline: Vermont’s Ski Season, on the Brink

text: An editorial on Sunday about the coronavirus’s spread in prisons and jails misstated the timing of virus-related deaths at Sanand jails misstated the timing of virus-related deaths at San Quentin State Prison in California. Twenty-eight inmates had died by September, not by August.
match_headline: America Is Letting the Coronavirus Rage Through Prisons

text: An article on Monday about ski patrollers shaving their beards during the pandemic misspelled the name of the ski patrol supervisor in Killington, Vt. He is Mike O’Hare, not Mike O’Hara.
match_headline: To Wear Their Masks, the Beards (and a Tradition) Had to Go

text: An article last Wednesday about Native Americans and Thanksgiving misstated the location of the first Thanksgiving celebration in the United States. It was in Plymouth, Mass., not on Cape Cod.
match_headline: The Thanksgiving Myth Gets a Deeper Look This Year

text: An article on Nov. 11 about chocolate preferences in India and its diaspora misstated the location of Dwaar Chocolate. It is in West Bloomfield Township, Mich., not East Township.
match_headline: Indians Love Cadbury Chocolate. These Rivals Would Love to Woo Them Away.

text: An article on Sunday about the Kolyma Highway in Russia misstated the surname of a rocket scientist who survived political imprisonment and later helped put the first man in space. He is Sergei Korolev, not Kovalyov.
match_headline: Along Russia’s ‘Road of Bones,’ Relics of Suffering and Despair

text: An article on Wednesday about real estate transactions in New York City, using information provided by the real estate broker Marcus & Millichap, misidentified the buyer and seller of the building at 210 Prospect Park West in Brooklyn. The buyer is Alchemy Ventures, not Sam Kooris, who is a principal at Alchemy. The seller is Slope Realty, not 573 11th St. LLC.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Aug. 13 about Scott Borgerson, a maritime expert who is an associate of Ghislaine Maxwell, misstated the degree Mr. Borgerson received from Fletcher, the graduate school of global affairs at Tufts University. It was a master of arts in law and diplomacy, not arts and diplomacy. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to editors’ attention only recently.
match_headline: How Did Scott Borgerson Get Mixed Up With Ghislaine Maxwell?

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s exchange with reporters in the White House on Thursday misstated the last time a Democrat won Georgia in a presidential election. It was 1992, not 1996.
match_headline: Trump, Still Claiming Victory, Says He Will Leave if Electors Choose Biden

text: An article last Sunday about dividend payouts misstated the amount that American corporations have sold in bonds this year. Through Nov. 10, they sold $1.6 trillion, not billion.
match_headline: Dividends Are Down, but They Are Vastly Better Than Expected

text: A review on Nov. 8 about “The Mystery of Charles Dickens,” by A. N. Wilson, misstated where the young David Copperfield is sent to work. He washes, labels and corks bottles at a wine and spirits warehouse; he is not “sent to labor in a boot-blacking factory.” The review also misstated David’s age at the time; he is 10, not 12. (The 12-year-old Charles Dickens did work in a boot-blacking factory.)
match_headline: Robert Gottlieb on Dickensworld — the Great Novelist’s Grand Universe

text: An article on Nov. 15 about insomnia misspelled the given name of the director of the Center for Sleep & Wake Disorders. She is Helene Emsellem, not Helen.
match_headline: Break the Cycle of Insomnia

text: An article on Saturday about down-ballot losses for Democrats in the 2020 U.S. election misstated the name of a G.O.P. group. It is the Republican State Leadership Committee, not the Republican Legislative Leadership Committee.
match_headline: How Democrats Suffered Crushing Down-Ballot Losses Across America

text: An article on Wednesday about the clinical trial results of AstraZeneca’s coronavirus vaccine misstated how many clinical trial protocols AstraZeneca and Oxford have made public. They have released protocols for the trials in Britain and in the U.S., not only for the U.S. trials.
match_headline: What We Know About AstraZeneca’s Head-Scratching Vaccine Results

text: An article on Sunday about teaching during the pandemic misstated the shape of students’ desks at Walter P. Carter Elementary/Middle School in Baltimore. They are trapezoidal, not triangular, as the students there undoubtedly learn in geometry.
match_headline: Plastic Dividers and Masks All Day: What Teaching in a Pandemic Looks Like

text: An article on Monday about struggling drivers working for food delivery apps misstated New York City’s current unemployment rate. The most recent rate, from October, is 13.2 percent, not 14.1 percent.
match_headline: Food Delivery Apps Are Booming. Their Workers Are Often Struggling.

text: An article on Monday about online competition among luxury brands misstated the ownership of the watch brand Patek Philippe. It is owned by the Stern family, not by Richemont.
match_headline: The Luxury E-Commerce Wars Heat Up

text: An article on Sunday about the first woman to play football in a Power 5 conference game misidentified the first woman to score in a Division I football game. It was Ashley Martin of Jacksonville State in the Football Championship Subdivision, not Katie Hnida of New Mexico, who was the first woman to score in the Football Bowl Subdivision.
match_headline: Sarah Fuller, With a Kickoff, Is the First Woman to Play Football in a Power 5 Game

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Argentine soccer star Diego Maradona misstated the round of the 1990 World Cup in which he scored the only goal in a win against Brazil. It was the round of 16, not the quarterfinals.
match_headline: Diego Maradona, One of Soccer’s Greatest Players, Is Dead at 60

text: A headline with an obituary about the recording engineer Bruce Swedien misstated his age. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 86, not 66.

An article on Saturday about a ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit that rejected a request by President Trump’s legal team to block Pennsylvania’s certification of its vote misidentified the Chicago mayor referenced by Rudolph W. Giuliani. It was Richard J. Daley, who served as mayor from 1955 to 1976, not Richard M. Daley, his son, who served as mayor from 1989 to 2011.
match_headline: In Harsh Rebuke, Appeals Court Rejects Trump’s Election Challenge in Pennsylvania

text: A picture caption with an article on Nov. 24 about Canada’s attempt to keep schools open during a second lockdown misstated Scarborough’s relationship with Toronto. It is a section of Toronto. It is not outside it.
match_headline: In Canada, a Push to Keep Schools Open in Second Lockdown

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the decision in many European countries to keep schools open during the pandemic referred imprecisely to the number of new coronavirus cases in France in November. The country as of Nov. 30 had seen a daily average of more than 80 new cases per 100,000 people over the previous seven days, not on average in early November.
match_headline: How Toronto Plans to Keep Schools Open Amid Its Second Lockdown

text: An article on Saturday about poor security in the Demilitarized Zone between North and South Korea misstated the length of the DMZ. It is about 155 miles long, not 255.
match_headline: How Did the North Korean Defector Cross the Border? Loose Screws

text: An entry in the Listings pages on Friday about classical concerts to stream this month misstated the Brooklyn venue that has presented the trumpeter and composer Nate Wooley’s “For/With” series in recent years. It is Issue Project Room, not Roulette.
match_headline: 10 Classical Concerts to Stream in December

text: An article on Monday about the music in Steve McQueen’s “Small Axe” anthology misstated the first name of a musician. He is Augustus Pablo, not August.
match_headline: The Beat at the Heart of ‘Lovers Rock’

text: An obituary on Friday about the actress Dena Dietrich misidentified the advertising agency that created the Chiffon Margarine commercials in which she portrayed Mother Nature. It was Cunningham & Walsh, not D’Arcy Masius Benton & Bowles.
match_headline: Dena Dietrich, Who Found TV Fame as Mother Nature, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Oct. 8 about Lyon Gardiner Tyler Jr., a grandson of John Tyler, the 10th president of the United States, referred incorrectly to President Tyler’s role in the annexation of Texas. While he supported annexation, and signed a congressional resolution agreeing that Texas could become a state under certain conditions, he was not “the president who annexed Texas.” Texas was annexed during the administration of Tyler’s successor, James K. Polk. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Lyon Gardiner Tyler Jr., Grandson of the 10th President, Dies at 95

text: An article on Tuesday about epidemiologists’ projections that the pandemic’s toll will worsen drastically during the next three months misspelled the name of an American infectious disease epidemiologist. It is David L. Heymann, not David L. Heyman. The article also misstated the role of Mitchell Warren with the AIDS advocacy group AVAC. He is its executive director, not its founder.
match_headline: As Hiking Surges During the Pandemic, So Do Injuries

text: A map with an article on Sunday about China’s construction of a Himalayan village in territory claimed by Bhutan misidentified a river shown. It is the Brahmaputra River, not the Ganges.
match_headline: Beijing Takes Its South China Sea Strategy to the Himalayas

text: An article on Wednesday about the resignation of Jozsef Szajer, a member of Hungary’s conservative Fidesz party, referred incorrectly to the origin of the country’s ban on same-sex marriage. It was written into the constitution adopted after Prime Minister Viktor Orban came to power a decade ago; it was not recently proposed. (A recent proposal could restrict adoptions by same-sex couples.)
match_headline: Hungarian Politician Resigns After Brussels Party Is Raided by Police

text: An article on Wednesday about the need to shore up the Social Security program misstated the amount that the Social Security Administration will pay this year in benefits. In 2020, the agency will distribute more than $1 trillion in retirement, disability and survivor benefits, not nearly $70 billion, which is how much it paid retired workers in June 2020.
match_headline: Social Security Seemed Like a Future Problem. The Virus Changed That.

text: An article on Wednesday about the N.F.L.’s efforts to keep the season going amid the pandemic misstated the number of teams in the league. It is 32, not 30.
match_headline: Do We Need Football in America This Badly?

text: An obituary on Friday about the neuropathologist Dr. Mary Fowkes referred imprecisely to the findings of autopsies on patients who died of Covid-19 early in the pandemic. The autopsies suggested that the coronavirus traveled through a patient’s blood vessels and damaged the endothelial cells, which line the interior of blood vessels — not that the virus traveled through the body in those cells.
match_headline: Dr. Mary Fowkes, 66, Dies; Helped Science Understand the Pandemic

text: An article on Thursday about Iran’s response to the assassination of its top nuclear scientist misspelled, in two instances, the surname of the Iranian nuclear scientist who was assassinated on Friday. He was Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, not Fakrizadeh or Fakhirizadeh.
match_headline: Iran Moves to Increase Uranium Enrichment and Bar Nuclear Inspectors

text: An article on Wednesday about the impact of the coronavirus on criminal trials in New York City misstated the location of the first virtual criminal jury trial in Texas. It was held in Austin, not in McKinney.
match_headline: Only 9 Trials in 9 Months: Virus Wreaks Havoc on N.Y.C. Courts

text: An article on Thursday about the investigation of an instructor at France’s national soccer academy misstated the first name of the president of a French soccer club. He is Yves Jacquier, not Yann.
match_headline: Young Players, Blurred Boundaries and a Coach on the Move

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Tuesday about the golf photographer Leonard Kamsler reversed the identities of two players at the 1968 United States Open. Arnold Palmer was on the right, and Jack Nicklaus on the left.
match_headline: For the World Economy, a Grim Slog Tempered by New Hopes

text: An article on Friday about contenders for energy and climate positions in the Biden administration misstated the name of the organization that Heather McTeer Toney leads. It is Moms Clean Air Force, not Mom’s Clean Air Task Force.
match_headline: Meet Biden’s Energy and Climate Cabinet Contenders

text: An article on Thursday about the election of a new board by an elite wine organization, the Court of Master Sommeliers, misstated the nature of four new seats added to the board. They will be held by people outside the organization, not by candidates for the title of master sommelier. The article also misstated a new provision in the court’s code of ethics. Relationships are now prohibited between master sommeliers and candidates they are mentoring, not between master sommeliers and any candidates.
match_headline: Amid Sexual Harassment Scandal, Elite Wine Group Elects New Board

text: An article on Friday about the singer Selena misstated which Michael Jackson song Selena covered at a 1987 performance. It was “Billie Jean,” not “Beat It.”
match_headline: Selena’s Special Genius

text: Because of a transcription error, an article last Sunday about cannabis farms facing a devastating wildfire season misidentified the location of Sweet Creek Farm. It is in Guerneville, Calif., not Greenville.
match_headline: Can Cannabis Farms Weather Wildfire Season?

text: An article last Sunday on Indigenous podcasts referred incorrectly at several points to the podcast host Sterlin Harjo. He is a man. An article in the same issue about the new rules for this year’s ski season misstated the price of renting out the entire Eagle Point resort in Utah. It is $15,000 a day, not $10,000. Another article in the issue, about writing a form of poetry called a cento, misstated the century that the word cento came into use. It was the third century, not the 16th. And an article about bar trivia games moving online misspelled the name of a founder of the Learned League trivia site. He is Shayne Bushfield, not Busfield.
match_headline: Listen to Indigenous People

text: An article on Nov. 26 by Pope Francis misidentified the source of a quoted line by Friedrich Hölderlin. It is “Patmos,” not “Hyperion.”
match_headline: Pope Francis: A Crisis Reveals What Is in Our Hearts

text: An article on Monday about mass transit spending cuts across the United States described incorrectly the Bay Area Rapid Transit System. It operates heavy rail, like subways. It is not a light-rail system.
match_headline: ‘Existential Peril’: Mass Transit Faces Huge Service Cuts Across U.S.

text: An article on Monday about a push by the Trump administration to distribute vaccines by mid-January referred incorrectly to the new restrictions taking effect in much of California. They do not require schools to close.
match_headline: Trump Officials Push Ambitious Vaccine Timeline as California Locks Down

text: An article on Monday about Wilmington, Del., misstated the year the city was founded. It was 1638, not 1683.
match_headline: After Centuries of Obscurity, Wilmington Is Having a Moment

text: An article on Sunday about President Trump’s behavior since he lost the election referred incompletely to a letter signed by Republican legislators in Pennsylvania disavowing their own election and calling on Congress to reject the state’s electors for Joseph R. Biden Jr. While the letter initially had 75 signatures, a revised version was issued late Friday evening with only 64 signatures.
match_headline: Trump’s Final Days of Rage and Denial

text: An article on Friday about New York Representative Sean Patrick Maloney’s new role as the chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee referred imprecisely to Representative Cheri Bustos’s status as chairwoman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. She did not resign from the post; she announced she would not seek another term.
match_headline: Democrats Pick Campaign Chief for Uphill Bid to Protect House Majority

text: An article on Sunday about a fire in the East Village in Manhattan, using information from the Fire Department, misstated the address of the vacant building where the fire started. It is 48 East 7th Street, not 47 East 7th Street.
match_headline: East Village Fire Damages 128-Year-Old Church

text: A picture with an article on Saturday about 50 million pounds of paper money that has gone missing from the Bank of England was published in error. The building shown in the photograph was the Royal Exchange, not the Bank of England.
match_headline: Bank of England Rebuked Over ‘Missing’ $67 Billion of Cash

text: An article on Monday about last week’s N.F.L. news misstated the score by which the Cleveland Browns were outscored by the Tennessee Titans in the second half after taking a 38-7 lead at halftime. It was by 28-3, not 32-3.
match_headline: What We Learned From Week 13 of the N.F.L. Season

text: An article on Monday about virtual theater productions misstated the location of the college in “Heroes of the Fourth Turning.” It is in Wyoming, not Montana.
match_headline: How ‘Wolves’ and ‘Heroes’ Are Saving Pandemic Theater

text: An obituary on Saturday about the poet and publisher Naomi Long Madgett misstated the first part of a quotation from her about her poem “Midway.” She said, “I know what’s wrong with it, but I don’t know how to fix it” — not “I don’t know what’s wrong with it.”
match_headline: Naomi Long Madgett, Champion of Black Poets, Is Dead at 97

text: An article on Tuesday about a global update on the coronavirus pandemic misidentified the country where ski lifts were opening. It is Austria, not Australia.
match_headline: ‘Is Exxon a Survivor?’ The Oil Giant Is at a Crossroads.

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about a plan to keep schools in New York City safe as they reopen misstated the location of a school in Brooklyn. Public School 189 is on the border of Crown Heights and East Flatbush in Brooklyn, not in East New York .
match_headline: How New York City Plans to Keep Children Safe as Schools Reopen

text: A article on Tuesday about protests in Poland over an abortion ban described incorrectly Pope John Paul II’s position before his papacy. He was the archbishop of Krakow, and a cardinal, but he was not the leader of the Roman Catholic Church in Poland.
match_headline: In Poland, Protests Over Abortion Ban Could Revolutionize Politics

text: An article on Dec. 2 about recent commercial real estate transactions in New York, using information provided by the broker, misstated the date the building designed by the architect Rafael Guastavino at 124 West 78th Street in Manhattan was built. It was built in 1886, not 1881.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Tuesday about an Israeli soccer team co-owned by an Emirati royal misidentified the team against which a Chechen striker, Zaur Sadayev, scored his first goal for Beitar Jerusalem. It was against Maccabi Netanya, not Maccabi Tel Aviv.
match_headline: Israeli Soccer Team, Infamous for Anti-Arab Fans, Has New Co-Owner: a Sheikh

text: An article on Tuesday about the negative effects of family rifts misidentified the person a woman blocked from seeing her children. He was not her father-in-law.
match_headline: When a Family Is Fractured

text: An obituary on Saturday about Betsy Wade, the first woman to edit news copy for The New York Times, misidentified one of the journalism schools for which scholarships for women are endowed by the Anne O’Hare McCormick Memorial Fund, of which Ms. Wade was a board member. It is the City University of New York journalism school, not City College of New York.
match_headline: Betsy Wade, First Woman to Edit News at The Times, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Aug. 1 about the filmmaker Alan Parker referred incorrectly to “The Evacuees,” a 1974 BBC Television movie he directed. It was about Jewish children being evacuated from Manchester during World War II, not from London. This correction was delayed, because the error was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: Alan Parker, Versatile Film Director, Is Dead at 76

text: An obituary on Nov. 21 about the writer Jan Morris misidentified the leader of the first ascent of Mount Everest, which she covered for The Times of London in 1953. The expedition was led by Col. John Hunt — not by Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, the climbers who reached the summit.
match_headline: Jan Morris, Celebrated Writer of Place and History, Is Dead at 94

text: An obituary on Tuesday about former Senator Paul S. Sarbanes misstated several dates. George J. Mitchell was the Senate Democratic majority leader from 1989 to 1995, not 1987 to 1994; Thomas A. Daschle was the Democratic leader until 2005, not 2006; and Senator Charles McC. Mathias retired in 1987, not 1984.
match_headline: Paul Sarbanes, 87, Dies; Maryland Senator Fought Accounting Fraud

text: An article on Tuesday about the sale of Bob Dylan’s song catalog to Universal misstated the number of songs that he owned the copyrights to but did not write. It was not only “The Weight,” as recorded by the Band, but several other tracks associated with that group as well.
match_headline: Bob Dylan Sells His Songwriting Catalog in Blockbuster Deal

text: An article on Wednesday about AT&T’s influence on the decision by Warner Bros. to release its 2021 movies on HBO Max misstated the percentage of customers who are worth $100 million to AT&T. Every 0.01 percent of customers who stay glued to AT&T are worth about $100 million to the company, not every 1 percent of customers.
match_headline: Who’s Behind the Fight Between Warner Bros. and Hollywood? It’s AT&T

text: An article on Tuesday about ways to help count and conserve native bees misstated a taxonomist’s affiliation. Zach Portman is with the University of Minnesota, not Minnesota State University.
match_headline: How You Can Help Count and Conserve Native Bees

text: An obituary on Sunday about Irina Antonova, the longtime director of the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts in Moscow, misstated the day of her death. It was Monday, Nov. 30 — not Tuesday, Dec. 1.
match_headline: Irina Antonova, Grande Dame of Russian Museum World, Dies at 98

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor David L. Lander, who played Squiggy on the sitcom “Laverne & Shirley,” misstated the number of seasons the show was on the air. It was eight, not seven.
match_headline: David L. Lander, Squiggy on ‘Laverne & Shirley,’ Dies at 73

text: An article on Tuesday about the latest lockdown in California misstated the capacity at which supermarkets can operate under new coronavirus restrictions. They can operate with 35 percent capacity, not 20 percent, after the state modified the original stay-at-home order.
match_headline: Most of California Locks Down Again as Coronavirus Strains Hospitals

text: An article on Wednesday about restaurant apps misstated the surname of a Maryland restaurant owner. He is Ashish Alfred, not Arnold.
match_headline: Apps Are Helping to Gut the Restaurant Industry

text: An article last Sunday about the actress Candice Bergen, who lived in the house on Cielo Drive later occupied by the director Roman Polanski, misidentified the actress who shared it with him. She was Sharon Tate, not Sharon Stone.
match_headline: Candice Bergen, Woman Who’s Had It All

text: An article last Sunday about the motion picture industry in New York misstated the share of film production costs eligible for tax credits in the city, as well as the year in which the credits will expire. Twenty-five percent of film production costs are eligible for tax credits through 2025, not 30 percent through 2022.
match_headline: Lights, Camera, Construction!

text: Because of a production error, a portion of the review of Barack Obama’s memoir “A Promised Land” on Nov. 29 included columns of type that were misordered.
match_headline: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie on Barack Obama’s ‘A Promised Land’

text: A review on Nov. 29 about “The National Road,” by Tom Zoellner, misidentified the city where the first highway built by the federal government ended. It stretched from Cumberland, Md., to Vandalia, Ill., not Joliet, Ill.
match_headline: Crisscrossing the Country on Highways Big and Small

text: An article last Sunday about books over 500 pages omitted a word in the description of “Bleak House.” It is known for spontaneous combustion, not just combustion. An article in the same issue about holiday movies misstated the setting of “White Christmas.” The film takes place after World War II, not during. Another article , about donating frequent-flier miles, misstated the number of donated miles Hawaiian Airlines will match. Typically it matches up to 500,000 miles per organization annually; it doesn’t cap the number at 100,000. And a Calendar item referred incorrectly to where a performance by the MacArthur fellow Taylor Mac was streaming. It was available from 18 venues, not just the Center for the Art of Performance at the University of California, Los Angeles.
match_headline: Geek Out Over Christmas Films

text: An article on Friday about a panel of experts formally recommending that the Food and Drug Administration authorize Pfizer’s Covid-19 vaccine misstated the name of an organization. It is the National Women’s Health Network, not the National Women’s Health Center.
match_headline: F.D.A. Advisory Panel Gives Green Light to Pfizer Vaccine

text: An article on Thursday about Gen. Lloyd J. Austin III’s military career referred incorrectly to Henry O. Flipper. He was the first Black officer to lead Buffalo Soldiers of the 10th Cavalry; he was not a noncommissioned officer.
match_headline: ‘Is Austin on Your List?’: Biden’s Pentagon Pick Rose Despite Barriers to Diversity

text: An article on Sunday about the Electoral College’s 538 electors referred incorrectly to the military service of Alan Kennedy, a presidential elector in Denver. He is a captain in the Colorado Army National Guard, not a former Marine.
match_headline: Meet the Electoral College’s Biggest Critics: Some of the Electors Themselves

text: An article on Saturday about the pandemic’s impact on students in M.B.A. programs misstated the location where Megan Reichert worked remotely as an intern for Chewy. It was her parents’ home in Virginia, not Berkeley, Calif., where she attends business school.
match_headline: Zoom Classes. No Chance Meetings. Is Virtual Business School Worth the Cost?

text: An article on Monday about setbacks faced by the musical “Six” during the pandemic referred incompletely to productions of the show in Chicago. A production that debuted in 2019 was set to return; it was not in the works when the pandemic began.
match_headline: ‘Six’ Tries to Get Back Onstage. Again, and Again, and Again.

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the Electoral College’s affirmation of Joe Biden’s victory misidentified an elector. He is Calvin Smyre, not Van Johnson.
match_headline: Biden’s 306 Electoral College Votes Make His Victory Official

text: An article on Sunday about a woman in Mexico who stalked her daughter’s killers referred imprecisely to the significance of Sept. 15. It is the eve of Mexican Independence Day, when Mexicans celebrate, not Mexican Independence Day, Sept. 16.
match_headline: She Stalked Her Daughter’s Killers Across Mexico, One by One

text: An article on Sunday about Rebekah Jones, a Florida scientist whose home was raided by state agents, misstated whom Ms. Jones had been charged with cyberstalking. It was one of her former students at Florida State, not a current student.
match_headline: A State Scientist Questioned Florida’s Virus Data. Now Her Home’s Been Raided.

text: An article on Tuesday about Norman Pearlstine’s new role at The Los Angeles Times misspelled the given name of a co-owner of The Los Angeles Times. She is Michele B. Chan, not Michelle.
match_headline: Norman Pearlstine, Top Editor of Los Angeles Times, Takes Adviser Role

text: An article on Tuesday about issues faced by the unemployed without government aid included an outdated affiliation for Stephen A. Wandner, an expert on unemployment insurance. He is a senior fellow at the National Academy of Social Insurance; he is no longer at the Upjohn Institute for Employment Research.
match_headline: What Happens to the Unemployed When the Checks Run Out

text: An article on Tuesday about a decision to change the mascot of Cleveland’s baseball team misstated the location of the Tulalip tribes. They are in western — not eastern — Washington State.
match_headline: Cleveland Makes Name Removal Official, Saying It Is ‘Moving Forward’

text: An article on Monday about the financial devastation the pandemic has brought the sports industry misidentified an employer at a Milwaukee arena and how many furloughs it announced this summer. Levy Premium Foodservice — not Delaware North — employs vendors at Fiserv Forum; it announced furloughs that affected 475 people, not more than 1,000 people.
match_headline: Just How White Is the Book Industry?

text: A headline with an article on Monday about a growing interest in chess among women and girls misspelled the title of the Netflix series that is driving the interest. It is “The Queen’s Gambit,” not “Queens Gambit.”
match_headline: The Women Faced Off to Play Soccer. One Team Lost Because of Hair Dye.

text: An article on Tuesday about setbacks to affordable hearing aids misstated the name of a hearing aid made in 2018 by Bose. It is unnamed; it is not the Hearphone.
match_headline: Hearing Aids Could Use Some Help

text: An article on Saturday about an open letter signed by German cultural leaders rejecting the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel misstated the reason that Achille Mbebe did not address the Ruhrtrienniale festival. He was not disinvited; the festival was canceled because of the coronavirus pandemic, after lawmakers and officials called for Mr. Mbebe to be removed from the program.
match_headline: German Cultural Leaders Warn Against Ban on Israel Sanctions Movement

text: An article on Thursday about revelations about Johns Hopkins’s life misstated the name of the grandniece of Mr. Hopkins who wrote a biography. She is Helen Hopkins Thom, not Alice Thom.
match_headline: Johns Hopkins Reveals That Its Founder Owned Slaves

text: An obituary on Nov. 25 about the Australian senator and cabinet minister Margaret Guilfoyle erroneously credited her with a distinction. She was the first woman in Australia to hold a cabinet-level portfolio — not the first woman to run a government department. (Annabelle Rankin ran the housing department from 1966 to 1971, but she was not a cabinet minister.) Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated the year in which the Guilfoyle family moved to Melbourne, Australia, when Ms. Guilfoyle was young. It was 1928, not 1948.
match_headline: Margaret Guilfoyle, a Multiple ‘First’ in Australia Politics, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the dancer and actor Ann Reinking referred imprecisely to the length of her Broadway performing career. That career, which began in 1969, essentially ended in 1997, but she returned to Broadway in 2001 for a few performances of the revue “Fosse,” which she choreographed, so she performed for more than three decades, not “nearly three decades.”
match_headline: Ann Reinking Dies at 71; Dancer, Actor, Choreographer and Fosse Muse

text: An article on Thursday about the East Coast snowstorm misstated the surname of a boy enjoying his first major snowstorm in Philadelphia. He is Lucas Coyle, not Lucas Whiffen.
match_headline: Storm Dumps Snow on East Coast, Shutting Schools and Virus Testing

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about opposition to President Trump’s potential move to Mar-a-Lago misidentified the location of the Florida resort. It is Palm Beach, not West Palm Beach.
match_headline: President Trump still shows no sign he will concede.

text: An article on Wednesday about tougher oversight of the tech industry in Europe misstated the name of a landmark European law governing online privacy. It is the General Data Protection Regulation, not the European Data Protection Regulation.
match_headline: Big Fines and Strict Rules Unveiled Against ‘Big Tech’ in Europe

text: A headline with an obituary on Thursday about the banker Joseph Safra misstated his age. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 82, not 52.
match_headline: Joseph Safra, Banker Who Was the Richest Brazilian, Dies at 82

text: Because of an editing error, the Crime column on Dec. 6 misstated the surname of the author of the novel “Hard Cash Valley.” He is Brian Panowich, not Pavovich. The column misstated the surname of another mystery writer. She is Louise Penny, not Perry. The column also misstated the title of a novel by John McMahon. It is “The Evil Men Do,” not “The Evil That Men Do.”
match_headline: The 10 Best Crime Novels of 2020

text: An article on Sunday about new Sesame Street characters based on Rohingya Muslims, using information provided by a publicist, misspelled the surname of the president of social impact for Sesame Workshop. She is Sherrie Westin, not Weston.
match_headline: ‘R’ is for Rohingya: Sesame Street Creates New Muppets for Refugees

text: An article on Oct. 31 about the band Salem misspelled the surname of the artist whose painting appears on the cover of the album “Fires in Heaven.” She is Nicole Besack, not Nicole Bessek.
match_headline: A Decade Later, Salem Returns to an Even Darker World

text: An obituary on Sunday about Karen Killilea, whose life with cerebral palsy was the subject of two best-selling books written by her mother, Marie, misstated the year that Marie Killilea’s book “Wren,” a version of her “Karen” for children, was published. It was 1954, not 1981.
match_headline: Karen Killilea, 80, Dies; Turned Disability Into Triumph
