text: An article on Sunday about criticism of the Vatican’s Christmas Nativity scene in St. Peter’s Square misstated the year that the Nativity scene was sculpted from beach sand. It was 2018, not last year.
match_headline: In a Tough Year, a Nativity Scene ‘That Has Had Problems’

text: An article on Aug. 4 about the departure of Trump administration appointee, Merritt Corrigan, from the United States Agency for International Development included an imprecise description of comments by another U.S.A.I.D. official, Tera Dahl. In discussing Islam, she has made statements against extremist groups; she has not made public statements against Islam itself.
match_headline: Trump Appointee With History of Anti-L.G.B.T.Q. Remarks Leaves Aid Agency

text: A picture caption with a photo essay on Monday about the pandemic’s effect on holiday traditions misspelled part of the name of a city in Michigan. It is Grosse Pointe, not Point.
match_headline: The New York City Sheriff’s Office has a crucial role during the pandemic.

text: An obituary on Saturday about the composer and pianist Harold Budd misstated the names of two colleges. The college Mr. Budd attended before joining the Army was Los Angeles City College, not Los Angeles Community College. The college he attended after returning to civilian life was known at the time as San Fernando Valley State College — not California State University, Northridge, the name it adopted in 1972.
match_headline: Harold Budd, Composer of Spaciousness and Calm, Dies at 84

text: An article on Tuesday about presidential pardons misstated the status of a meeting between Erik Prince and a Russia-sanctioned banker in the Seychelles. The meeting took place during the 2017 presidential transition; it was not the case that it did not occur.
match_headline: Trump Pardons Two Russia Inquiry Figures and Blackwater Guards

text: An article on Wednesday about provisions in a U.S. stimulus bill that aid the rich described incorrectly one provision. It would make permanent some lower tax rates levied on distillers, brewers and vintners; it would not lower taxes on alcoholic beverages.
match_headline: Buried in Pandemic Aid Bill: Billions to Soothe the Richest

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Ioannis Lagos, a leader of the neo-fascist political party Golden Dawn in Greece, misstated the number of Golden Dawn adherents who were convicted in a trial that lasted for five years. It was 58 people, not 68.
match_headline: Greece Wants Him in Prison. Instead, He’s in the E.U. Parliament.

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Wednesday for Chad Stuart, a member of the British pop duo Chad & Jeremy, misattributed a quotation. As the article correctly noted, it was Jeremy Clyde, not Mr. Stuart, who said that becoming a star in America in the 1960s “was a young man’s dream come true.”
ref_headline: was a young man’s dream come true.
match_headline: Chad Stuart, of the Hit British Duo Chad & Jeremy, Dies at 79

text: An article on Wednesday about the decline of the New England Patriots misstated the round in which quarterback Jarrett Stidham was drafted. It was the fourth round, not the sixth.
match_headline: The Fall of the House of Belichick

text: An article on Page 4 about the online variety show “Stars in the House” misstates the date of its first livestream. It was March 16, not March 17. The article also misstates when the number of shows per week was reduced. It was in June, not May.
match_headline: An Online Show that Runs and Runs (and Runs)

text: A review on Dec. 6 about Robert Harris’s novel “V2” misstated the name of an award that the aerospace engineer Wernher von Braun received in 1975. It was the National Medal of Science, not the National Medal of Honor.
match_headline: The Plot to Stop the Nazis’ Missiles With Slide Rules

text: An article on Saturday about unemployment in the arts misstated one of the performers in the Local Honeys. She is Montana Hobbs, not Monica Hobbs.
match_headline: A ‘Great Cultural Depression’ Looms for Legions of Unemployed Performers

text: Because of a production error, an article on Sunday about the explosion in Nashville, described in a front-page capsule summary, was omitted from some editions.
match_headline: A Warning, Then a Blast: Nashville Explosion Was Deliberate, Police Say

text: An article on Monday about the Vienna Philharmonic misidentified the airline that recently flew the orchestra to Japan. It was All Nippon Airways, not Austrian Airlines.

An article on Dec. 22 about a plan by Eastern states to cap tailpipe emissions misstated the given name of the current governor of New Hampshire. He is Christopher Sununu, not John. (John H. Sununu, the father of Christopher, was governor of the state from 1983 to 1989.)
match_headline: A Plan by Eastern States to Cap Tailpipe Emissions Gets Off to a Slow Start

text: A headline with an article on Wednesday about the latest stimulus package misstated an alternative to a Social Security number for noncitizens. It is an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number, not an Employer Identification Number.
match_headline: Saving at Work for Retirement: A Perk Coming to More States in 2021

text: An article on Monday about Heather Cox Richardson, a historian who has become the most successful individual author on the newsletter platform Substack, described incorrectly the targeted audience for Capital B, a nonprofit publication. It will target Black audiences when it launches in 2021; it will not be specifically aimed at Black women.
match_headline: Heather Cox Richardson Offers a Break From the Media Maelstrom. It’s Working.

text: An obituary on Monday about the art historian and critic Barbara Rose misspelled the name of New York University’s art gallery. It is the Grey Art Gallery, not Gray.
match_headline: Barbara Rose, Critic and Historian of Modern Art, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Monday about the author Barry Lopez misstated where he and his wife, Debra Gwartney, had lived until recently. It was along the McKenzie River, near Finn Rock, Ore. — not in McKenzie, Ore. (There is no such town.)
match_headline: Barry Lopez, Lyrical Writer Who Was Likened to Thoreau, Dies at 75

text: An obituary on Dec. 15 about the science fiction writer and editor Ben Bova referred incorrectly to a 1977 issue of the magazine Analog, which he edited. The issue consisted almost entirely of work by female writers, not entirely. (It also included the third part of a serial by George R.R. Martin.)
match_headline: Ben Bova, Science Fiction Editor and Author, Is Dead at 88

text: An article on Tuesday about challenges faced by Nashville in 2020 misidentified one of the Nashville restaurants run by Trey Cioccia. It is the Farm House, not the Treehouse.
match_headline: A Tornado, a Pandemic and Now a Bombing: ‘Nashville Strong’ Is Tested

text: An article on Tuesday about a German officer who faces terrorism charges described incorrectly the location of Baustarring, a Bavarian hamlet. It is 250 miles east of Franco A.’s former army base, not 250 miles west.
match_headline: A Far-Right Terrorism Suspect With a Refugee Disguise: The Tale of Franco A.

text: An article on Wednesday about the first case of a highly contagious coronavirus variant found in the United States included outdated information about a couple in Canada who tested positive for the variant. Health officials there said on Sunday that the couple had been in contact with a visitor from the United Kingdom; it is not the case that they had no known exposure.
match_headline: First U.S. Case of Highly Contagious Coronavirus Variant Is Found in Colorado

text: An article on Dec. 22 about Google’s response to the Justice Department’s accusations that it violated antitrust laws misstated the number of states that had sued Facebook on antitrust claims. It was 46, not 40.
match_headline: Google Denies Antitrust Claims in Early Response to U.S. Lawsuit

text: A headline with an article on Thursday about cases of a more contagious form of the coronavirus in Colorado and California referred incorrectly to the virus. The new cases show a new variant of the virus, not a new strain.
match_headline: Discovery of Virus Variant in Colorado and California Alarms Scientists

text: An article on Thursday about the influence of Jon Ossoff’s 2017 campaign on the Democratic resistance to President Trump referred incorrectly to Angelika Kausche’s family. She has two daughters, not two sons.
match_headline: The ‘Resistance’ Formed Because of Trump, With an Assist From Jon Ossoff

text: An article on Wednesday about the struggle by Black homeowners to get insurers to pay claims misstated the location of Inglewood. It is a city in Los Angeles County, not a neighborhood in Los Angeles.
match_headline: Black Homeowners Struggle to Get Insurers to Pay Claims

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the bluegrass guitarist and singer Tony Rice misstated the day he died. It was Friday, Dec. 25 — not Saturday, Dec. 26.
match_headline: Tony Rice, Bluegrass Innovator With a Guitar Pick, Dies at 69

text: An article this weekend on Page 16 about a patient who had hereditary angioedema refers incorrectly to a protein that blocks swelling and inflammation. It is C1-inhibitor, not C1.
match_headline: Her Stomach Hurt Unbearably. Her Doctors Were Baffled.

text: An article this weekend on Page 22 about the runoff elections in Georgia refers incorrectly to a lawsuit asking for 200,000 people who had been purged from voter rolls to be restored. A judge denied an injunction that would have allowed them to vote in the runoffs. The suit was not dismissed.
match_headline: Knocking on Two Million Doors in Georgia

text: An article on Dec. 27 about Konrad Steffen, a Swiss glaciologist, misstated a prediction made by Dr. Steffen. He predicted the melting of the ice sheet covering Greenland could pass a threshold of irreversibility in as little as 50 years, which would eventually result in a global sea-level rise of 16 feet. He did not say that the ice sheet would disappear in 50 years, resulting in a global sea-level rise of 16 feet.
match_headline: New Year’s Resolutions for the Planet

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the sportscaster Jeannie Morris misstated when in 1935 she was born. It was Dec. 2, not Feb. 2. Using information from Ms. Morris’s family, the earlier version also misstated where she was born and the year she married her second husband, Johnny Morris. She was born in Visalia, Calif., not Walla Walla, Wash., and married Mr. Morris in 1962, not 1960.
match_headline: Jeannie Morris, Trailblazing Chicago Sportscaster, Dies at 85

text: An article last Sunday about problems in learning pods misidentified the number of children in a pod in Oakland, Calif. There were four, not six.
match_headline: Learning Pods Show Their Cracks

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Stephanie Williams and LaMarr Coles III misstated the name of the restaurant in Washington where the couple met for their first date. It is Rosa Mexicano, not Rosa Mexicana.
match_headline: The Start of a New Chapter in Their Favorite Bookstore

text: An article on Saturday, about New York’s moratorium on evictions, incorrectly reported that the wife of Diba Gaye, a 65-year-old immigrant facing eviction, had died of Covid-19 in April, based on information that Mr. Gaye provided to The Times and to his lawyer. After the article was published, Mr. Gaye acknowledged to The Times and to his lawyer that his wife had died of heart disease, and had not contracted the coronavirus.
match_headline: New York Halted Evictions. But What Happens When the Ban Ends?

text: An article on Sunday about coronavirus deaths in Africa misquoted part of a statement by the demographer Stéphane Helleringer. He said that very few countries in Africa try to estimate mortality “based on death records,” not “death rates.”
match_headline: A Continent Where the Dead Are Not Counted

text: An article on Friday about Vilseck, Germany, misstated the volume of a “mass” of beer. It is a little more than a quart, not slightly less.
match_headline: A German Town Warily Considers a Future Without a Deep U.S. Presence

text: Because of a production error, a map of Chicago in Saturday’s paper was misprinted in some editions. Parts of the map, which showed voting shifts from 2016 to 2020, were duplicated and overprinted on other parts of the map.
match_headline: This Rescue Moose Was Also 2020

text: An obituary on Saturday about the director Joan Micklin Silver misstated how much money her film “Crossing Delancey” grossed worldwide. It was about $16 million, not more than $116 million.
match_headline: Joan Micklin Silver, Director of ‘Crossing Delancey,’ Dies at 85

text: An article on Dec. 28 about challenges that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey is facing amid the country’s economic crisis misspelled the surname of a tobacco shop owner. He is Ozgur Aybas, not Akbas.
match_headline: Battered Turkish Economy Puts a Powerful Erdogan to the Test

text: An article on Dec. 30 about a man who was arrested because of a bad facial recognition match, using information from a Woodbridge Police Department report, said that the New York State Intelligence Center and New Jersey’s Regional Operations Center helped make a facial recognition match of a suspect in a shoplifting case in New Jersey. Both agencies denied that. The matches were made by the Rockland County Sheriff’s Office and Palisades Interstate Parkway Police.
match_headline: Another Arrest, and Jail Time, Due to a Bad Facial Recognition Match

text: An article on Wednesday about the potential sale of a mural by Diego Rivera misidentified the institution that owns the Diego Rivera mural. It is the San Francisco Art Institute, not the University of California.
match_headline: San Francisco’s Top Art School Says Future Hinges on a Diego Rivera Mural

text: An article on Thursday about a growing push for cyclists’ safety in Las Vegas misstated the name of a popular cycling destination in Nevada. It is Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area, not Red Rock National Park.
match_headline: A Push for Cyclists’ Safety After 5 Die Near Las Vegas

text: An article on Tuesday about the importance for older individuals to maintain their vaccinations during the pandemic misstated the average cost to Medicare Part D beneficiaries of the two-dose Shingrix shingles vaccine. It is $50 per dose, not $50 for the pair.
match_headline: Don’t Let the Pandemic Stop Your Shots

text: An obituary on Dec. 6 about the economist Walter Williams referred incorrectly to the basketball star Julius Erving. He was not a neighbor of Mr. Williams and his family during Mr. Williams’s childhood in Philadelphia. (He was born 14 years after Mr. Williams.)
match_headline: Walter E. Williams, 84, Dies; Conservative Economist on Black Issues

text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s allies in media and politics after the storming of the National Capitol by a pro-Trump mob referred incorrectly to the police shooting of Jacob Blake. Mr. Blake was seriously injured; he did not die.
match_headline: How Trump’s Allies Are Still Defending Him: Denial, Deflection, Disinformation

text: An article on Page 9 about the Royal Academy of Dance misstates in several instances the surname of the archives and records manager at the academy. She is Eleanor Fitzpatrick, not Fitzgerald.
match_headline: From the Music Hall to Ballet Royalty: A British Tale

text: An article on Jan. 3 about monoliths referred incorrectly to the monoliths in “2001: A Space Odyssey.” While they appear four times in the film, only one appears after the “vortex of light” sequence.
match_headline: A New Theory About the Monolith: We’re the Aliens

text: Because of a production error, obituaries on pages B11 and B12 were omitted from some of Friday’s editions. They can be read online at nytimes.com/obituaries .
An article last Sunday about the composer John Sheppard and his “Media vita” misstated the number of commercial recordings of the work. There are nine, not eight.
match_headline: From a 1550s Pandemic, a Choral Work Still Casts Its Spell

text: An article on Dec. 20 about the film “Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom” described incorrectly the awards for the show’s original Broadway run. It was nominated for three Tonys, but it did not win them.
match_headline: Viola Davis and Company on ‘Ma Rainey’ and Chadwick Boseman’s Last Bow

text: An article last Sunday about Jeanie Buss, the controlling owner of the Los Angeles Lakers, misstated the amount of time Becky Hammon led the San Antonio Spurs against the Lakers. It was the entire second half of the game as well as 3 minutes 56 seconds in the first half, not just the time in the first half.
match_headline: Lady of the Lakers

text: An article last Sunday about Tillett Textiles misidentified the print of a fabric Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis used to upholster a sofa. It was Large Feather, not Fish Head Plaid. The article also misstated the closing date of Design Works of Bedford-Stuyvesant. It was 1979, not 1978.
match_headline: Some of Jackie O.’s Favorite Fabrics are Back on the Market

text: An article on Dec. 20 about the Trump campaign’s attempts to overturn the election results in Pennsylvania referred incorrectly to a lawsuit. It was brought by two Democrats trying to keep the Green Party off the ballot in Pennsylvania, not by the Green Party trying to get on the ballot.
match_headline: He Wanted to Count Every Vote in Philadelphia. His Party Had Other Ideas.

text: A review last week about “Conservatism: The Fight for a Tradition,” by Edmund Fawcett, misstated the decade when the politician Enoch Powell served in the British cabinet. It was the early 1960s, not the early 1970s.
ref_headline: Conservatism: The Fight for a Tradition,
match_headline: Andrew Sullivan on the War Within Conservatism and Why It Matters to All of Us

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the riot at the Capitol misattributed a quotation. “We had enough people, we could have tore that building down brick by brick” was said by Eric Dark, not Brian Hobbs.
ref_headline: We had enough people, we could have tore that building down brick by brick
match_headline: These Are the Rioters Who Stormed the Nation’s Capitol

text: An article on Monday about a chaotic vaccine rollout in Florida misstated the age group receiving vaccines first in Hawaii. It is those 75 and older, not 65 and older.
match_headline: ‘It Became Sort of Lawless’: Florida Vaccine Rollout Turns Into a Free-for-All

text: An article on Monday about the use of lies as a political tool misstated the date when Janez Jansa became prime minister of Slovenia. It was March 2020, not in 2018.
match_headline: The Art of the Lie? The Bigger the Better

text: An article on Saturday about Suriname’s vice president, Ronnie Brunswijk, transposed the name of a former rebel commander. He is Petrus Adam, not Adam Petrus. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Guerrilla Leader, Drug Baron, Gold Magnate … and Now Social Reformer?

text: An article on Saturday about the departures of officials in the Trump administration misstated the cabinet position of Elaine Chao. She is stepping down as transportation secretary, not labor secretary.
match_headline: Bravery or Self-Preservation? Resignations of Trump Officials Draw Skepticism

text: An article on Saturday about Democrats’ preparedness to bring impeachment charges against President Trump for a second time described incorrectly the setting in which Richard Barnett was photographed in Nancy Pelosi’s office. He was seated at an aide’s desk, not at the desk belonging to Ms. Pelosi. The error was repeated in an article about Mr. Barnett.
match_headline: Democrats Ready Impeachment Charge Against Trump for Inciting Capitol Mob

text: An article on Saturday about the Republican National Committee’s endorsement President Trump to lead the party forward misspelled the given name of a committee woman from Nevada. She is Michele Fiore, not Michelle.
match_headline: Ronna McDaniel is re-elected to lead the Republican National Committee.

text: An article on Sunday about the archives of the journalist Robert Caro misidentified the location of a typewriter repair shop. Gramercy Typewriter Co. is in Chelsea, not Gramercy Park.
match_headline: What We Found in Robert Caro’s Yellowed Files

text: An article on Monday about the beginning of the professional tennis season misidentified Naomi Osaka’s nationality. She is Japanese, not American. It also misstated Andy Murray’s age. He is 33, not 31.
match_headline: Tennis Players Mull Competition or Rest at Start of New Season

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Sunday about the filmmaker Michael Apted misidentified two of the three women in the photo from his movie “49 Up.” Lynn Johnson is in the center and Susan Davis is on the right, not vice versa.
match_headline: Michael Apted, Versatile Director Known for ‘Up’ Series, Dies at 79

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about infighting among Republicans over the future direction of their party misidentified the home state of Representative Mo Brooks. It is Alabama, not Arkansas.
match_headline: Facing Backlash, Republicans Confront Trump’s Effect on Their Party

text: An article on Monday about business rules the Trump administration is trying to finish before Jan. 20 described incorrectly the risks of a new regulation to the Federal Deposit Insurance Fund. The fund is now at greater risk from having to cover failures of vulnerable banks that rely on “hot money” deposits. Its coverage of deposits has not been expanded.
match_headline: The Business Rules the Trump Administration Is Racing to Finish

text: An article on Tuesday about an accusation by the social media platform Parler that Amazon broke antitrust laws by suspending its service referred incorrectly to the practice of a lawyer representing the social media company Parler. David J. Groesbeck is a sole practitioner and does not specialize in intellectual property law.
match_headline: Parler Accuses Amazon of Breaking Antitrust Law in Suspending Hosting Services

text: An article last weekend about how Dr. Stephanie Sterling, an infectious disease expert, spends her Sundays referred incorrectly to a coffee machine. It is the Moka Express, not the mocha express.
match_headline: How the Head of a Vaccine Research Clinic Spends Her Sundays

text: An article on Tuesday about the storming of the U.S. Capitol last week as seen through television and social media misstated the name of a news site. It is HuffPost, not The Huffington Post.
match_headline: The Attack on the Capitol Was Even Worse Than It Looked

text: An obituary on Saturday about Carol Johnson, a landscape architect whose firm designed John F. Kennedy Park in Cambridge, Mass, misstated the date of Kennedy’s birth in 1917. It was May 29, not May 17.
match_headline: Carol Johnson, Leading Landscape Architect, Dies at 91

text: An article on Wednesday about Ireland’s mother and baby homes referred incorrectly to the Roman Catholic Church’s role in managing the homes. The church ran most of the homes, not all.
match_headline: Report Gives Glimpse Into Horrors of Ireland’s Mother and Baby Homes

text: An article on Wednesday about a memo from the Joint Chiefs of Staff re-asserting the armed forces’ obligation to defend the Constitution and reject extremism misstated the day when a Pentagon spokesman told reporters that the department did not “tolerate extremists” in its ranks. It was Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Military Chiefs Remind Troops of Their Oath After Fallout From Assault on Capitol

text: An article last Thursday about buyer’s remorse in 2020 incorrectly described the playable characters in Animal Crossing: New Horizons, a game for the Nintendo Switch, which many people bought during quarantine. The playable characters are human, not anthropomorphic animals.
match_headline: The Year of Buyer’s Remorse

text: An obituary on Dec. 30 about the fashion designer Pierre Cardin misspelled the given name of a New York Times reporter who interviewed him in 1969. She was Marylin Bender, not Marilyn.
match_headline: Pierre Cardin, Designer to the Famous and Merchant to the Masses, Dies at 98

text: An obituary on Monday about Nancy Bush Ellis, the sister of President George Bush and aunt of President George W. Bush, using information from her family, misidentified the town where she was born. It was Greenwich, Conn., not Milton, Mass. (George Bush was born in Milton.)
match_headline: Nancy Bush Ellis, Sister and Aunt of Presidents, Dies at 94

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about mass gatherings that turn violent misstated the location of a 1971 protest. It was held at the Capitol steps, not the Lincoln Memorial.
match_headline: Making Sense of the ‘Mob’ Mentality

text: An article on Friday about a lawsuit against the New York Police Department for its handling of protests last summer described incorrectly the political views of Commissioner Dermot Shea and Chief of Department Terence A. Monahan. They are registered Republicans, but have not said publicly whether they supported President Trump.
match_headline: N.Y. Attorney General Sues N.Y.P.D. Over Protests and Demands Monitor

text: An article on Friday about the state of the Capitol Police in the wake of the storming of the Capitol last week referred incompletely to an episode involving the response by police officers to a woman who made a U-turn at a White House checkpoint in 2013. While she was ordered to stop and instead turned around and led officers on a chase toward the Capitol, the firing of 26 shots by the officers on public streets later came under criticism.
match_headline: The Capitol Police Had One Mission. Now the Force Is in Crisis.

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about Thomas Girardi, one of the country’s premier “toxic tort” lawyers who is accused of misappropriating money from clients, misspelled the surname of his wife who filed for divorce in November. She is Erika Jayne, not James.
match_headline: A Hall of Fame Lawyer, a ‘Real Housewife’ and a Stunning Fall

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 5 about rape-revenge films misspells the given name of the actress who plays the protagonist in “Promising Young Woman.” She is Carey Mulligan, not Carrie.
match_headline: Rape-Revenge Tales: Cathartic? Maybe. Incomplete? Definitely.

text: A picture caption with an essay this weekend on Page 30 about the Jan. 6 riot at the Capitol misidentifies as a rioter a shirtless man shown outside a broken door at the Capitol. He was a videographer who removed his shirt after being pepper-sprayed while covering the event for The Daily Caller, a right-wing website, not one of the Trump supporters who stormed the Capitol. The original caption stated that he had punched the door; in fact, he said he was attempting to retrieve his phone, with which he had been documenting the event. The error did not come to light until after the magazine went to press.
match_headline: The American Abyss

text: Because of a production error, an article last Sunday about Beethoven’s “Für Elise” mislabeled several sections of a score.
match_headline: Beethoven’s ‘Für Elise’ Doesn’t Deserve Your Eye Rolls

text: An article on Dec. 20 about salsa macha misspelled the surname of an owner of the restaurant Taco María. She is Emilie Coulson Salgado, not Coulson Selgado.
match_headline: The Most Valuable Condiment of 2020: Salsa Macha

text: An article on Saturday about a man in Dallas looking for partners to play catch with a baseball referred incorrectly to bluebird eggs. While they are occasionally white, they are most often blue.
match_headline: He Just Wanted to Play Catch. They Got Relief From Troubled Times.

text: An article on Tuesday about the 1776 Commission misstated when George Floyd was killed by a police officer in Minneapolis. It was in May, not June. It also misspelled the surname of a conservative activist. He is Ned Ryun, not Ryan.
match_headline: Trump’s 1776 Commission Critiques Liberalism in Report Derided by Historians

text: An article on Tuesday about speeches made by the New York mayoral candidates at the Rev. Al Sharpton’s headquarters on Martin Luther King’s Birthday misquoted Andrew Yang. He said that the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was fighting for a guaranteed minimum income when he was assassinated; Mr. Yang did not say that he was assassinated because he was fighting for a universal basic income.
match_headline: On King Holiday, New York’s Mayoral Hopefuls Vie for Attention

text: An article on Tuesday about new attempts to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere misstated the name of the process that Project Vesta is using for removal. It is known as enhanced weathering, not weatherization.
match_headline: Businesses Aim to Pull Greenhouse Gases From the Air. It’s a Gamble.

text: An article on Monday about wearable sensors used by some businesses to prevent coronavirus outbreaks misstated the distance, in feet, that would prompt sensors worn by factory workers to go off if they came within 1.5 meters of one another for more than five seconds. The equivalent distance is roughly five feet, not six feet.
match_headline: On Factory Floors, a Chime and Flashing Light to Maintain Distance

text: An article on Tuesday about unemployed college graduates from China choosing to attend graduate school misstated the gender of Hong Dayong, an official with China’s Ministry of Education. He is a man.
match_headline: China’s College Graduates Can’t Find Jobs. The Solution: Grad School.

text: An article on Thursday about this year’s likely nominees for the Oscar for best actor misstated the date of the Oscars ceremony. It will be held on April 25, not April 28.
match_headline: Can Anyone Beat Chadwick Boseman for the Best-Actor Oscar?

text: An obituary on Jan. 12 about Pat Loud, a star of the early reality TV show “An American Family,” misstated when she told her husband, Bill, that she wanted a divorce. It was late in the show’s 12-episode run, but not in the final episode.
match_headline: Pat Loud, Reality Show Matriarch of ‘An American Family,’ Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Thursday about Barbara Weisberger, the founder of the Pennsylvania Ballet, misstated her date of birth in 1926. It was Feb. 28, not Oct. 28. The obituary also misstated her father’s association with a well-known dress store in Wilkes-Barre, Pa. He owned the business; he did not only manage it.
match_headline: Barbara Weisberger, a Force in American Ballet, Dies at 94

text: An article on Saturday about a coronavirus variant found in Britain misidentified one of the parameters used in the C.D.C. model. It assumed that one million people were vaccinated each day, not each week.
match_headline: C.D.C. Warns the New Virus Variant Could Fuel Huge Spikes in Covid-19 Cases

text: An article on Wednesday about the actress Javicia Leslie, who plays the lead role in “Batwoman,” misidentified the character Ali Finer, played by Ms. Leslie in “God Friended Me.” The character is the churchgoing sister of an atheist, not the atheist.
match_headline: Javicia Leslie on Becoming TV’s First Black Batwoman

text: An article last Thursday about the closing of the Brooklyn boutique Bird referred incorrectly to Jennifer Mankins’s tenure at Bird. She took over the store in 2004; she did not open the store in 1999.
match_headline: Saying Goodbye to Bird

text: An article on Thursday about President Biden’s actions on environmental and climate policy misstated a generally accepted time frame for achieving emissions reductions. Most experts say the United States can cut emissions 40 to 50 percent below 2005 levels by 2030, not 2035.
match_headline: Biden Cancels Keystone XL Pipeline and Rejoins Paris Climate Agreement

text: An article on Thursday about the career of pitcher Don Sutton misstated Mike Mussina’s first season with the Yankees. It was 2001, not 2002.
match_headline: Don Sutton Had an ‘Easy Job’ Thanks to a Lifetime of Hard Work

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Hall of Fame pitcher Don Sutton misstated the name of a newspaper that quoted him about leaving the Atlanta Braves’ broadcast team after missing the 2019 season. It is The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, not The Atlanta Constitution. The obituary also rendered the quotation incorrectly. Sutton said, “This ball club is amazing, and I feel left out because I’m not there to watch it firsthand” — not “The ball club is amazing, and I feel left out because I’m not there to watch firsthand.”
ref_headline: This ball club is amazing, and I feel left out because I’m not there to watch it firsthand
match_headline: Don Sutton, Hall of Fame Right-Hander, Is Dead at 75

text: An article on Page 4 about the actress Hunter Shafer misstates her age. She is 22, not 21.
match_headline: Hunter Schafer’s Week: A New York Whirlwind

text: An article on Page 10 about the musician and painter John Lurie misidentifies which Jack Smith was intended in a reference by John Lurie. He was the American director and artist Jack Smith, not the British artist.
match_headline: John Lurie Doesn’t Paint Happy Trees

text: An article on Page 12 about the conductor and keyboardist Karl Richter misstates the location of a Silbermann organ. It is in the Freiberg Cathedral, not the Freiburg Cathedral.
match_headline: Playing Bach, Was He a Pioneer or a Reactionary?

text: An article last Sunday about the art collective Tim Rollins and K.O.S. (Kids of Survival) misspelled the surname of the author of “Amerika.” He was Franz Kafka, not Kakfa.
match_headline: The Kids of Survival Are Middle-Aged — and Transforming Yet Again

text: An article on Page 1 about the effects Zoom has on free speech on college campuses refers imprecisely to comments made by Andrew Ross about Leila Khaled. Mr. Ross noted that Ms. Khaled is revered in the Arab world and elsewhere as a “role model” and “freedom fighter”; he did not refer to her that way himself.
match_headline: What Zoom Does to Campus Conflicts Over Israel and Free Speech

text: An article last Sunday about living in Larchmont, N.Y., misidentified the location of the homes of several families, a restaurant and a school. It also misstated the number of students served by a school district and who can join a beach. The homes of the Laschewer and the Raved families, Billy & Pete’s Social, and Saints John and Paul School are in the Town of Mamaroneck, not the Village of Larchmont; the Mamaroneck Union Free School District serves 5,554 students, not 1,800; and Manor Beach is open to the residents of the Village of Larchmont but is not public.
match_headline: Larchmont, N.Y.: An Affluent Suburb on Long Island Sound

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Mariann Channell and Benson Woo misstated where Mr. Woo lives. It is Bloomfield Hills, Mich., not West Bloomfield. The article also misstated the location of the wedding. It was the Grosse Pointe Yacht Club, not the Bayview Yacht Club in Detroit.
match_headline: Finding Their Second Wind

text: A review on Jan. 10 about “Icebound,” by Andrea Pitzer, referred incorrectly to the Antarctic explorer Ernest Shackleton and the fate of the crew on his ship, the Endurance. In 1916, all of the crew members were rescued; it is not the case that “all but three” were rescued. (Three crew members from the Aurora, another ship that was part of Shackleton’s Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, did die.)
match_headline: ‘Icebound’ Takes Us Back to the Arctic, in All Its Terror and Splendor

text: A review on Jan. 10 about “Himalaya,” by Ed Douglas, misstated the geographical size of India relative to the United States. India is one-third the size of the United States; it is not “a third smaller than the United States.”
match_headline: Climbing the Himalaya With Soldiers, Spies, Lamas and Mountaineers

text: An article on Monday about Jeffrey Clark’s actions regarding President Trump’s efforts to overturn the presidential election results described incorrectly a meeting among the Justice Department’s top leaders on New Year’s Eve. While Mr. Clark, the acting head of the civil division, was a topic of discussion, he was not in attendance.
match_headline: Jeffrey Clark Was Considered Unassuming. Then He Plotted With Trump.

text: An article on Jan. 17 about Fiji’s new position as president of the United Nations’ top human rights body misstated President-elect Biden’s position in regard to the U.N. Human Rights Council. He promised during the presidential campaign that the United States would return to the council. It is not the case that he had taken no public position.
match_headline: Fiji Will Lead U.N. Rights Body, Over Russian and Chinese Opposition

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about location data used by intelligence analysts without warrants referred imprecisely to X-Mode’s sale of location data. While the broker has sold data to defense contractors that work with the U.S. military, a publicist for the company said it did not sell data to the military directly.
match_headline: Intelligence Analysts Use U.S. Smartphone Location Data Without Warrants, Memo Says

text: An article on Saturday about the best ways to navigate the prospect of higher taxes under a Biden administration misstated the amount of income of self-employed people and business owners that is subject to the Medicare tax. All of their income is subject to the tax, not only the first $142,800. The article also misstated the rate of the tax on Medicare. It is 2.9 percent, not 2.8 percent.
match_headline: With Higher Taxes Possible, Here’s What to Do Now

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Jan. 18 about Shirley Abrahamson, the first female chief justice of the Wisconsin Supreme Court, misstated her parents’ surname. It was Schlanger, not Abrahamson. (As the obituary states, Abrahamson was the surname of her husband, whom she married after graduating from college.)
match_headline: Shirley Abrahamson, Trailblazing Wisconsin Judge, Dies at 87

text: An article on Sunday about the effects of marijuana legalization in Canada on social justice issues misstated the time period during which 1,548 people died of opioid overdoses in British Columbia. The deaths occurred from January through November 2020, not January through October 2020.
match_headline: 2 Years After Legalizing Cannabis, Has Canada Kept Its Promises?

text: A graphic with an article about the lifetime costs of electric cars misidentified one of the vehicles evaluated. It was the Chevrolet Spark, not the Chevrolet Bolt.
match_headline: G.M.’s Electric Car Push Could Put China in the Driver’s Seat

text: An article on Saturday about small foundations that take on environmental issues misstated the given name of the president of the Campbell Foundation. She is Samantha Campbell, not Sarah.
match_headline: Small Donations Aiming to Make a Big Splash

text: An article on Jan. 20 about the first climbers to reach the summit of K2 in winter used an outdated ratio for deaths to ascents on the mountain. It is nearly one to six, not one to four. (By comparison, on Mount Everest, it is about one to 34.)
match_headline: How Climbers Reached the Summit of K2 in Winter for the First Time

text: An article on Wednesday about the decision by Senate Republicans to drop their demand for a promise from Democrats that the filibuster would remain intact misspelled the surname of a spokesman for Fix Our Senate. He is Eli Zupnick, not Zupnik.
match_headline: Filibuster Fight Subsides, for Now, as Democrats Assume Full Senate Control

text: An article on Monday about the resignation of the board chairwoman for the San Francisco Art Institute referred incorrectly to the type of funds the board voted to use on Dec. 17 to address the school’s financial issues. The vote approved the spending of $1.5 million in endowment funds, not purpose restricted endowment funds. The college says there was no requirement for approval by the attorney general or the original donors for the expenditure of those funds, as critics questioned in the article. The article also incorrectly described the disbursement from the endowment as a bridge loan. Although the school plans to repay the money back into the endowment, it said the disbursement did not technically constitute a bridge loan.
match_headline: Chairwoman of San Francisco Art School Facing Budget Issues Resigns

text: An article on Friday about a school district in the Atlanta suburbs referred imprecisely to attendance at athletic events in the Cherokee County schools. The district says it limited attendance to 25 percent capacity, and that football games were not packed. The article also misstated which students were permitted to participate in sports. The district says its policy allowed all students to participate, and says students who opted for remote learning were not prohibited from participating.
match_headline: A School District Vowed to Stay Open, Until Its Staffing Ran Out

text: An article on Tuesday about studies showing a significant drop in infections and hospitalizations in Israel following initial vaccination doses misstated the percentage of the Israeli population that had received a first dose of the vaccine. More than 30 percent of population had gotten a first dose, not more than 40 percent.
match_headline: Israel’s Early Vaccine Data Offers Hope

text: An article on Friday about protests in Poland over a ban on abortions in cases of fetal abnormalities misstated the name of an L.G.B.T. group protesting the laws. It is Queer Tour, not Queen Tour.
match_headline: ‘Declaration of War’: Protesters in Poland Vow to Fight Abortion Ban

text: An article on Thursday about the Cheech Marin Center for Chicano Art described incorrectly the votes of the Riverside City Council to approve plans and funding for the museum. One member abstained and two others recused themselves; three members did not abstain.
match_headline: Cheech Marin’s Chicano Art Museum Is to Open This Fall

text: An article this weekend on Page 28 about armed militias protesting in Virginia misidentified the person wearing a Black Lives Matter patch. It was worn by a demonstrator, but not by Mike Dunn, a member of the Last Sons of Liberty militia.
match_headline: They’re Breaking Glass and Criticizing Biden. From the Left.

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the drama “The Dig” referred imprecisely to the helmet shown. It was a reconstruction of what the original Anglo-Saxon helmet might have looked like, not the original.
match_headline: Recreating an Archaeological Discovery From the Ground Down

text: An article last Sunday about Robert Bigelow and his financing of research about afterlife experiences and paranormal events misstated his age. He is 76, not 75.
match_headline: Can Robert Bigelow (and the Rest of Us) Survive Death?

text: An article last Sunday about sponsored pregnancy announcements on social media misstated the surname of a Los Angeles hairdresser. She is Elizabeth Gress, not Cordero (Cordero is her maiden name). The article also misstated how long her child lived. It was seven weeks, not seven days. And the article referred imprecisely to Queen Elizabeth II at the time she announced her first pregnancy, in 1948. She was a princess; she had not yet become the queen.
match_headline: Celebrity Pregnancy Is Big Business

text: An article on Jan. 17 about kelp as a food source referred incorrectly to the relationship between Patagonia and Eat More Kelp. There is no partnership between the companies.
match_headline: Why Isn’t Kelp Catching On?

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about people making friends with their neighbors during the pandemic misidentified the women in the image. Caroline Marks was pictured on the left and Cornelia Holzbauer on the right, not the reverse.
match_headline: My Neighbor, My Pandemic Pal

text: Because of an editing error, the Crime column on Jan. 10 omitted the name of the author of the new novel “Hard Times.” He is Les Edgerton.
match_headline: Murder, Murder Everywhere: the Woods, the Hospital, the Market Square

text: An article on Thursday about an effort by the Biden administration to oust Trump loyalists from government agencies described incorrectly the Environmental Protection Agency employee Charlotte Bertrand. She is a career agency employee, not a Trump official.
match_headline: Biden’s Treasury will seek to put Harriet Tubman on the $20 bill, an effort the Trump administration halted.

text: An article on Saturday about the controversy around Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia misstated when a 40-minute video in which Ms. Greene questioned the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, said former President Barack Obama was a Muslim and suggested the Clintons were guilty of murder was first reported. Media Matters for America reported on the video in August; it was not newly unearthed.
match_headline: Marjorie Taylor Greene’s Controversies Are Piling Up. Republicans Are Quiet.

text: An article on Monday about the Trump campaign’s attempt to subvert the election misidentified the state where D. John Sauer is solicitor general. It is Missouri, not Mississippi.
match_headline: Trump Raised $255.4 Million in 8 Weeks as He Sought to Overturn Election Result

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the refurbishment of the Louvre during a lockdown misidentified artwork in one of the photographs. It showed a frieze of the “Magnesie Du Meandre from the Temple of Artemis” near the statue of “Melpomene, Muse of Tragedy,” not “The Winged Victory of Samothrace.”
ref_headline: Magnesie Du Meandre from the Temple of Artemis

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about high-level job vacancies in newsrooms misstated the title of Lydia Polgreen when she left The New York Times. She was an associate masthead editor, not a deputy managing editor.
match_headline: Washington Post, Reuters and Los Angeles Times Search for New Top Editors

text: An article on Monday about methods to learn if facial recognition systems have used your photos described incorrectly Liz O’Sullivan’s role in the Exposing.AI tool. She was a collaborator, not one of its creators.
match_headline: Here’s a Way to Learn if Facial Recognition Systems Used Your Photos

text: An obituary on Jan. 23 about the Hall of Fame baseball star Hank Aaron misstated the total number of home runs hit by two teammates that he and Eddie Mathews surpassed on Aug. 20, 1965. It was 772, not 722. The obituary also misstated the significance of that figure. It did not make Aaron and Mathews “the No. 1 home run tandem in major league history,” although they did eventually set that record; Major League Baseball believed at the time that it did, because 772 was thought to be the total number hit by Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig of the Yankees, but that figure was later changed to 859. (The original calculation did not include the 1923 and 1924 seasons, when Ruth was playing regularly but Gehrig saw limited action.)
ref_headline: the No. 1 home run tandem in major league history,
match_headline: Hank Aaron, Home Run King Who Defied Racism, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Jan. 25 about the screenwriter Walter Bernstein omitted part of the name of the high school in Brooklyn he attended. It was Erasmus Hall, not Erasmus. The obituary also misstated the name of the college newspaper for which he was the film critic. It is The Dartmouth, not The Daily Dartmouth. And it referred imprecisely to Mr. Bernstein’s work on the movies “The Wonderful Country” and “The Couch Trip.” Although he did contribute to the screenplays of both, they were technically not “among his film credits” because he did not receive screen credit for either one.
match_headline: Walter Bernstein, Celebrated Screenwriter, Is Dead at 101

text: An obituary on Jan. 18 about the record producer Phil Spector referred incorrectly to the Paris Sisters, a group he produced. They were from San Francisco, not Los Angeles.
match_headline: Phil Spector, Famed Music Producer and Convicted Murderer, Dies at 81

text: An article on Thursday about vaccine shortages in the European Union misstated the percentage of the Israeli population that had received a first dose of the vaccine. More than 30 percent of the population had gotten a first dose, not more than 40 percent.
match_headline: E.U. Pushes for AstraZeneca to Provide More Vaccines

text: An article on Monday about the upcoming redrawing of congressional maps misstated the year that Democrats in New York last held total control over redistricting. It was 1911, not 1991.
match_headline: A 10-Year-Old GameStop Investor Cashed In. His Return? Over 5,000%.

text: An article on Jan. 26 about President Biden’s efforts to combat climate change misstated the scope of President Biden’s conservation plans. Mr. Biden aims to set aside 30 percent of all land and water in the United States for conservation, not 30 percent of federal land and water.
match_headline: Biden Sets in Motion Plan to Ban New Oil and Gas Leases on Federal Land

text: An article on Tuesday about the James Webb Space Telescope misstated Eric Smith’s title. He is a program scientist, not a project manager. It also misstated the temperature the telescope needs to be. It is less than 45 degrees Celsius above absolute zero, not Fahrenheit.
match_headline: The Webb Telescope, NASA’s Golden Surfer, Is Almost Ready, Again

text: An obituary on Jan. 4 about the United Nations diplomat Brian Urquhart misstated the year U.N. peacekeepers were sent into the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights. It was 1973, not 1972. The earlier version also incorrectly included southern Africa among the areas where Mr. Urquhart deployed peacekeeping forces. Such forces were not deployed in that region until 1989, three years after Mr. Urquhart retired.
match_headline: Brian Urquhart, Troubleshooter for the U.N., Dies at 101

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the American refugee resettlement system misstated Barbara L. Strack’s comments. Ms. Strack, a former chief of the refugee affairs division at Citizenship and Immigration Services, said President Biden was likely to cite a global need for resettling refugees, not unlikely.
match_headline: Biden to Welcome More Refugees, but Far From All Will Get In

text: An article on Jan. 31 that fact-checked the accuracy of President Biden’s comments during his first week in office described incorrectly the increase in the value of federal government contracts awarded directly to foreign companies under the Trump administration. They rose from about $11.9 billion in the 2017 fiscal year to about $13.2 billion, not from $11.9 million.
match_headline: Fact-Checking Biden’s First Week in Office

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the South African singer Sibongile Khumalo misstated the day she died. It was Thursday, Jan. 28 — not Thursday, Feb. 4.
match_headline: Sibongile Khumalo, South Africa’s ‘First Lady of Song,’ Dies at 63

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a boost given to companies endangered by the pandemic by rising stock prices described incorrectly one of the ways that companies can borrow money. Borrowing involves selling bonds to investors, not equity.
match_headline: How the Stock Market’s Relentless Rise Saved Companies

text: An article on Sunday about a call for safety measures in professional cycling paraphrased imprecisely comments made by Laura Mora, the secretary general of the Cyclistes Professionnels Associés, who talked about the difficulty of enforcing safety rules in cycling races. Ms. Mora said she meant her group had threatened legal action against race organizers, not against the Union Cycliste Internationale, cycling’s governing body.
match_headline: How a Horrifying Cycling Crash Set Up a Battle Over Safety

text: An article on Friday about events in New York City this weekend misspelled the surname of the artist whose controversial death is the subject of a dance dialogue. She is Ana Mendieta, not Mandieta. The article also misstated the time for the performance of Boom.Diwan and Nduduzo Makhathini. The show will stream at 11 a.m. Eastern time on Saturday, not 8 p.m.
match_headline: 5 Things to Do This Weekend

text: An article on Page 12 about whether showrunners will incorporate the pandemic into new seasons misidentifies the TV network that broadcasts the legal series “All Rise.” It is CBS, not ABC.
match_headline: How the Pandemic Is Coming to Prime Time (or Not)

text: An article on Page 11 about documentary photography on view at the International Center of Photography misidentifies a “Sesame Street” character doll. It is Elmo, not Cookie Monster.
match_headline: Photographing Life as It’s Seen, Not Staged

text: An article on Page 36 about Dan-el Padilla Peralta, a professor of classics at Princeton University, omits part of the identification of the person who said “Dan-el has galvanized a lot of people.” She is Rebecca Futo Kennedy, a professor at Denison University.
ref_headline: Dan-el has galvanized a lot of people.
match_headline: He Wants to Save Classics From Whiteness. Can the Field Survive?

text: An article on Page 12 about whether showrunners will incorporate the pandemic into new seasons misidentifies the TV network that broadcasts the legal series “All Rise.” It is CBS, not ABC.
match_headline: Do viewers want TV that reflects a shared pandemic reality, or that distracts from it?

text: An article on Jan. 24 about the artist Gordon Hookey, using information from the gallery, misstated the title and date of a painting of his. It is “Victory, Solidarity, Peace and Freedom” (2016), not “Victor, Solidarity, Peace and Freedom” (2017).
match_headline: Two Artists, Continents Apart, and a Shared Language of Struggle

text: An article last Sunday about nitrous oxide as a casual party drug misspelled the given name of a professor of medical engineering at M.I.T. He is Dr. Emery Brown, not Emory.
match_headline: Nitrous Nation

text: An essay on Jan. 24 about “The Custom of the Country” by Edith Wharton misstated the location of the fictional town of Apex City in the novel. It is in an unspecified Midwestern state; the book does not place it in Iowa.
match_headline: How Can We Read Edith Wharton Today?

text: An article on Monday about political unrest in Haiti misidentified the source of a statement saying that Haiti was “on the verge of explosion.” It was from a collection of the country’s Roman Catholic bishops, not Episcopal bishops.
match_headline: Haiti Braces for Unrest as a Defiant President Refuses to Step Down

text: An obituary on Friday about George McDonald, the founder of the nonprofit Doe Fund, using information from the fund and Mr. McDonald’s family, misstated the number of grandchildren who survive him. It is four, not three.
match_headline: George McDonald, Power Broker for the Powerless, Dies at 76

text: An article on Monday about steps Senator Chuck Schumer of New York is taking to head off a primary challenge misstated the year that Mondaire Jones defeated David Carlucci in a House primary in New York. It was 2020, not 2018.
match_headline: Why Chuck Schumer Is Cozying Up to the A.O.C. Wing of His Party

text: An article on Wednesday about Joe Allen, who owned restaurants in New York’s theater district, described incorrectly the actor Justin Ross Cohen. He joined the original production of “A Chorus Line” after it opened. He was not a member of the original cast.
match_headline: ‘He Missed Nothing’: Nathan Lane, Chita Rivera and Others on Joe Allen

text: An article on Thursday about the impeachment proceedings against Donald J. Trump misstated the number of Republicans that Democrats need to achieve a two-thirds majority necessary to convict Mr. Trump. It is 17, not 34.
match_headline: House Lays Out Case Against Trump, Branding Him the ‘Inciter in Chief’

text: An article on Feb. 5 about the pattern of people crossing state lines to obtain the coronavirus vaccine misstated Dr. Francisco García’s position with Pima County, Ariz. He is its chief medical officer, not its health director.
match_headline: Can’t Get a Shot? Thousands of ‘Vaccine Hunters’ Are Crossing State Borders to Get Theirs

text: An editorial on Thursday about relaxing indoor restrictions on restaurants included outdated information about the day that indoor dining is set to resume in New York City. It will return on Friday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Governors Are Easing Restrictions at Exactly the Wrong Time

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Thursday about the Washington Post columnist Maxine Cheshire misidentified President Richard M. Nixon’s dance partner at an inaugural ball in 1973. It was not Ms. Cheshire.
match_headline: Maxine Cheshire, Who Chronicled Beltway Scandals, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Feb. 5 about the Watergate burglar Eugenio Martínez misidentified the magazine that published a reminiscence by him. It was Harper’s Magazine, not Vanity Fair.
match_headline: Eugenio Martínez, Last of the Watergate Burglars, Dies at 98

text: An article on Friday about the possible effects of delayed census data on elections misstated the years in which census delays raised the prospect of Virginia holding state legislative elections three years in a row. They are 2021, 2022 and 2023, not 2022, 2023 and 2024.
match_headline: A New Delay for Census Numbers Could Scramble Congressional Elections

text: An article on Friday about historical adventures for Presidents’ Day misstated the location of the Morris-Jumel Mansion. It is in Washington Heights, not the Bronx.
match_headline: Presidents’ Day: 5 Ways to Make It Meaningful This Year

text: Because of a production error, a chart with an article on Feb. 7 about a decrease in the rate of new coronavirus cases nationwide displayed outdated figures. The chart reflected data collected through Feb. 4, not Feb. 5.
match_headline: Vaccines Could Blunt U.K. Epidemic in Weeks

text: An article last Sunday about a Super Bowl advertisement featuring Dolly Parton and an update of her classic song “9 to 5” referred incorrectly to one of the actors in the ad. She is Puerto Rican and identifies as Latina, not Black.
match_headline: The Working Woman’s Anthem ‘9 to 5’ Needed an Update. But This?

text: An article last Sunday about a new shade of blue called YInMn referred imprecisely to a scientific discovery by the French chemist Louis Jacques Thénard. He discovered the chemical composition of cobalt pigment; he did not discover cobalt.
match_headline: It’s Not Every Day We Get a New Blue

text: Because of an editing error, the Letters column on Jan. 31 misidentified the address of a letter writer, Stephen Schlesinger. He lives in New York, not Toledo, Ohio.
match_headline: What’s a Best Book? And What Isn’t?

text: An article on Feb. 6 about a decision by the International Criminal Court that states it has jurisdiction over territories occupied by Israel in 1967 referred imprecisely to the dissenting opinion of Judge Péter Kovács. Judge Kovács did not completely reject the court’s jurisdiction in the case, but in what the court called a “partly dissenting opinion,” he argued that the court had geographical jurisdiction over some parts of the occupied territories, not all. The article also overstated what is known about whether Israel, which is not a member of the International Criminal Court and did not participate in the process, can appeal the court’s ruling. International law experts say Israel’s standing to appeal this ruling is uncertain.
match_headline: I.C.C. Rules It Has Jurisdiction to Examine Possible Israel War Crimes

text: An article on Monday about new restrictions placed by China on the Utsuls, a Muslim community on the island of Hainan, misstated Ma Haiyun’s title at Frostburg State University. He is an associate professor, not an assistant professor.
match_headline: China’s Crackdown on Muslims Extends to a Resort Island

text: An article on Sunday about the extradition to Japan of two Americans tied to Carlos Ghosn’s escape misidentified the man who worked in private security and had helped with international escape operations. It was Michael Taylor, not his son Peter Taylor.
match_headline: 2 Americans Tied to Carlos Ghosn’s Escape to Be Extradited to Japan

text: An article on Monday about a foiled Iranian plot in Ethiopia against diplomats from the United Arab Emirates misidentified the location of a missile attack on American forces in January 2020. It occurred in Iraq, not Iran.
match_headline: In a Dangerous Game of Cat and Mouse, Iran Eyes New Targets in Africa

text: A subheading with an article on Tuesday about lawsuits big tech firms are facing from smaller competitors erroneously named one company. While the article details lawsuits faced by Google, it does not mention Apple.
match_headline: Big Tech’s Next Big Problem Could Come From People Like ‘Mr. Sweepy’

text: An article on Saturday about Michael Jordan’s NASCAR team misidentified the person who discovered a noose in the garage stall assigned to Darrell Wallace Jr. at Talladega Superspeedway last June. It was a member of Mr. Wallace’s racing team, not Mr. Wallace himself.
match_headline: Bubba Wallace Needed NASCAR Help. Michael Jordan Took It Personally.

text: An article on Saturday about movies to watch for Valentine’s Day misstated the year “Kramer vs. Kramer” was released. It was 1979, not 1977.
match_headline: Lesson of the Day: ‘Watch This Billion-Year Journey of Earth’s Tectonic Plates’

text: An article on Feb. 10 about the possibility that Iran may revoke its commitment to never seek a nuclear weapon referred imprecisely to a restriction on nuclear inspections that Iran said it will impose on Feb. 21 if American sanctions are not lifted. While international inspectors will be barred from visiting undeclared nuclear facilities and conducting unannounced inspections, which Iran agreed to allow as part of the 2015 nuclear accord, inspections of the sites that Iran declared under the Non-Proliferation Treaty will continue. (The error also appeared in articles published in the print editions of Feb. 3 and Jan. 28 .)
match_headline: Iran Suggests It May Seek Nuclear Weapons, in New Escalation of Threats

text: An article on Wednesday about Oregon’s halting efforts to return children to public school classrooms misidentified the grade levels that Seattle had proposed for in-person learning before later scrapping the program. They were prekindergarten through first grade; second grade was initially considered for inclusion but not part of the official proposal.
match_headline: Oregon Is Vaccinating Teachers. It Might Not Be Enough to Reopen Schools.

text: An article on Thursday about Democrats’ public anger at Texas Republicans’ response to the collapse of the state’s power grid misstated the name of the operator of the state’s grid. It is the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, not the Electricity Reform Council of Texas.
match_headline: ‘Now It’s Coming Back to Bite Them’: Democrats See an Opening in G.O.P. Oversight of Texas Grid

text: An article on Thursday about a New York City restaurant that fired a waitress for refusing to get vaccinated misstated the day that the waitress got a message from her employer informing her that she would be required to get a Covid-19 vaccine to continue working there. It was Friday, Feb. 12, not Sunday, Feb. 14.
match_headline: N.Y. Restaurant Fires Waitress Who Wouldn’t Get Covid-19 Vaccine

text: An article on Tuesday about the virus surveillance system pilot program, Global Immunological Observatory, misstated the number of people who died in a 2018 measles outbreak in Madagascar. It was 1,000, not 10,000. The article also misspelled the name of a plasma donation company. It is Octapharma, not Octopharma.
match_headline: Scientists Are Trying to Spot New Viruses Before They Cause Pandemics

text: An article on Page 6 about the conceptual artist Lorraine O’Grady misstates the date of Manet’s painting, “Olympia.” While first displayed in Paris in 1865, it was painted in 1863. The article also described incorrectly the subject of the painting as aristocratic. While the model herself was a Parisian artist, the character she portrays is a courtesan.
match_headline: Lorraine O’Grady, Still Cutting Into the Culture

text: An article on Friday about the successful landing of the new robotic rover Perseverance on Mars misstated the year the Spirit and Opportunity rovers landed on Mars. It was 2004, not 2003.
match_headline: NASA’s Perseverance Rover Lands on Mars to Renew Search for Extinct Life

text: An article on Friday about the distribution of stockpiled coronavirus vaccines described incorrectly the percentage of nursing home workers who did not receive vaccinations. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said that 63 percent of workers were not initially vaccinated; it did not say that 63 percent had refused.
match_headline: Short of Vaccine, States Find Hidden Stashes in Their Own Backyards

text: An article on Friday about the Federal Reserve’s warning on the possible effects of climate change on financial institutions misstated the number of Federal Reserve governors serving who were appointed by President Barack Obama. In addition to Lael Brainard, Jerome H. Powell was also appointed by Mr. Obama before being elevated to Fed chair by President Donald J. Trump.
match_headline: As Winter Sweeps the South, Fed Officials Focus on Climate Change

text: An article on Friday about car collecting during the pandemic misstated the role of McKeel Hagerty at the Hagerty insurance firm in Traverse City, Mich. He is the chief executive officer, not the chairman.
match_headline: How Car Collecting Powered Through the Pandemic

text: An article on Friday about content to stream this weekend misstated the number of “Muppet Show” episodes that were being withheld because of legal rights issues. One is being held for that reason, not two.
match_headline: How Much Watching Time Do You Have This Weekend?

text: An article on Thursday about the Marfa Invitational described incorrectly the Chinati Foundation. It receives public funding; it is not a private museum.
match_headline: A New Arts Destination Near Marfa Quietly Takes Shape

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the astronaut Millie Hughes-Fulford described incorrectly NASA’s advertisement in Family Circle magazine. It announced NASA’s efforts to send the first American woman to space, not to send the first woman to space. (The cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman to travel into space, in 1963.)
match_headline: Millie Hughes-Fulford, NASA Shuttle Scientist, Dies at 75

text: An article on Saturday about the winter storms and extreme cold that killed 58 people in storm-affected areas misidentified the facility in Texas where a dialysis patient died. The patient died at a local medical facility, not at Hendrick Medical Center.
match_headline: Extreme Cold Killed Texans in Their Bedrooms, Vehicles and Backyards

text: An article on Wednesday about the widespread theft of catalytic converters misstated federal rules on pollution control. Tighter standards introduced in 1975 meant that the vast majority of new vehicles would, in practice, need catalytic converters. Those standards did not explicitly require catalytic converters.
match_headline: Thieves Nationwide Are Slithering Under Cars, Swiping Catalytic Converters

text: An article on Saturday about a talk among President Biden and European leaders misidentified the role of Prime Minister Boris Johnson of Britain at a virtual conference on Feb. 19. He was the host of a closed meeting of the Group of 7 on the same day, not the Munich Security Conference.
match_headline: Biden Tells Allies ‘America Is Back,’ but Macron and Merkel Push Back

text: An article on Saturday about the reaction by Israel and Persian Gulf nations to the pursuit by the United States of a nuclear deal with Iran misspelled the name of a spokeswoman for China’s foreign ministry. She is Hua Chunying, not Hua Chuying.
match_headline: In Israel and the Gulf, Reaction to U.S. Push for Iran Talks Is Muted but Wary

text: An article on last Tuesday about a decision not to renew the contract of a female philosopher at the University of St. Andrews misstated Jonathan Ichikawa’s position at the University of British Columbia. He is a professor, not an associate professor.
match_headline: Scottish University Draws Ire for Dismissing Female Gender Studies Lead

text: An article on Monday about the limiting of travel in Europe because of coronavirus variants mistranslated remarks the German interior minister, Horst Seehofer, made to the newspaper Bild about the European Commission’s stance regarding cross-border movement in the bloc during the pandemic. Mr. Seehofer said the commission should “not put a monkey wrench in the works with cheap advice.” He did not say “put spokespeople in our wheels with cheap advice.”
ref_headline: not put a monkey wrench in the works with cheap advice.
match_headline: Virus Variants Deliver Fresh Blow to Europe’s Open Borders

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about Judge Merrick B. Garland’s history with domestic terrorism cases misspelled the surname of a former Justice Department counsel. She is Amy Jeffress, not Jeffries.
match_headline: Garland Says as Attorney General He Would Combat Domestic Extremism

text: Because of a production error, some copies of the weekend Book Review were printed with the cover for the Feb. 28 issue.

An obituary on Feb. 4 about the architectural historian Barry Lewis misstated the name of a university and stated incorrectly that he had studied there. It is the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, not the University of Jerusalem. The earlier version also partly misstated the name of a university where Mr. Lewis did study. It is the New School for (not of) Social Research.
match_headline: Barry Lewis, Beloved Guide to New York City, Dies at 75

text: An obituary on Jan. 25 about the Hockey Hall of Fame forward George Armstrong erroneously credited him with a distinction. He was not the first player of Indigenous descent to score a goal in the N.H.L.; at least two others had done so before him.
match_headline: George Armstrong, Who Led Toronto to 4 Stanley Cup Titles, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Feb. 6 about the author Sharon Kay Penman misstated the name of the company that published her first novel, “The Sunne in Splendour.” It was Holt, Rinehart & Winston, not Henry Holt & Company.
match_headline: Sharon Kay Penman, Whose Novels Plumbed Britain’s Past, Dies at 75

text: An article on Wednesday about a car crash involving Tiger Woods and his subsequent surgery misstated when Mr. Woods recently underwent a procedure on his spine called a microdiscectomy. It was in December, not January.
match_headline: Tiger Woods Out of Surgery and ‘Recovering’ After Serious Car Crash

text: An article on Wednesday about Afghanistan’s vaccination campaign misstated the timing of the World Health Organization’s emergency approval for a vaccine against the polio virus variant. The emergency approval was granted last November, it is not expected by year’s end. (Rollout is expected by year’s end.)
match_headline: Where a Vaccination Campaign Faces Skepticism, War and Corruption

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the sale of vaccines by Israel to other countries referred imprecisely to the West Bank. The land is occupied by Israel. The Palestinians want it for a future state but do not have sovereignty over it.
match_headline: Israel Gives Vaccine to Far-Off Allies, as Palestinians Wait

text: An article on Wednesday about a digital firewall in Myanmar misspelled the name of one of the foreign-owned telecom operators that have complied with demands from the military to limit online access. The company is Ooredoo, not Ooredo.
match_headline: A Digital Firewall in Myanmar, Built With Guns and Wire Cutters

text: An article last Thursday about hair loss during the pandemic referred incorrectly to the phase during which hair grows. It is the anagen phase, not antigen.
match_headline: You’re Not Imagining It: The Pandemic Is Making Your Hair Fall Out

text: An article on Monday about revised rates for flood coverage misstated rules governing rates for home insurance policies. Federal Emergency Management Agency rules allow buyers for whom a property is a primary residence to assume the previous owner’s policy. It is not always the case that new owners of homes must pay full rates for insurance immediately.
match_headline: Climate Threats Could Mean Big Jumps in Insurance Costs This Year

text: An article about New Jersey’s spending plan misstated the amount New Jersey borrowed in November. It borrowed $3.67 billion, not $4.29 billion.
match_headline: How New Jersey Averted a Pandemic Financial Calamity

text: An article on Saturday about “Judas and the Black Messiah” and the filmmaker Shaka King misstated Niija Kuykendall’s title. She is executive vice president of feature production at Warner Bros. Pictures, not senior vice president of feature production.
match_headline: Shaka King Goes to Hollywood

text: An article on Wednesday about the architect David Adjaye’s mural in a former union headquarters building misstated Mr. Adjaye’s birthplace. He was born in Tanzania, not Ghana. It also referred imprecisely to his project for the Studio Museum of Harlem. It is a new building, not an expansion of an existing structure.
match_headline: The Union Moved. The Beloved Mosaic Mural Couldn’t.

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about Shlomo Hillel, a former Israeli diplomat and minister who smuggled Jews out of Iraq, referred incorrectly to the Mossad in describing an operation organized by Mr. Hillel in 1947. It was a clandestine arm of the Haganah; it was not Israel’s intelligence service. It also misstated the year Mr. Hillel received the Israel Prize. It was in 1998, not 1988.
match_headline: Shlomo Hillel, Who Helped 120,000 Jews Flee Iraq, Dies at 97

text: An article on Friday about the future of the coronavirus described incorrectly vaccination efforts in Kazakhstan. About 20,000 health care workers received their first vaccine shot this month, according to the country’s health ministry; it is not the case that no one in the country has been immunized.
match_headline: The Coronavirus Is Threatening a Comeback. Here’s How to Stop It.

text: An article on Wednesday about Thomas Webster, a retired New York police officer charged in the riot at the Capitol, misidentified the landscaping business owned by him. It is Semper Fi Landscaping in Goshen, N.Y., not Semper Fi Landscape and Design in Florida, N.Y.
match_headline: Retired N.Y.P.D. Officer Who Guarded City Hall Charged in Capitol Riot

text: An article on Thursday about Silas Farley’s new position as head of the dance academy at the Colburn School in Los Angeles described incorrectly the relationship between Mr. Farley and Darleen Callaghan. Ms. Callaghan was the director of the ballet school Mr. Farley joined at age 9; she was not his first ballet teacher when he was 8.
match_headline: Silas Farley to Lead Dance Academy in Los Angeles

text: An article on Feb. 21 about a delivery-app worker referred imprecisely to whether such workers receive compensation if they are injured or fall ill. They are not legally entitled to compensation. It is not the case that they necessarily receive no compensation.
match_headline: Don’t Look Away From Amazon Workers’ Latest Union Drive

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Lenore Janis, the founder of Professional Women in Construction and of Era Steel, named after the Equal Rights Amendment, misstated the number of states needed to ratify an amendment to the Constitution. It is three-fourths of the states, not two-thirds.
match_headline: Lenore Janis, Who Broke Construction Industry Barriers, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Friday about the voice teacher Florence Birdwell misstated when her husband, Robert, died. It was 2003, not 2013.
match_headline: Florence Birdwell, Singing Teacher to Broadway Stars, Dies at 96

text: An article last Sunday about lab-made foods misidentified the company that makes sake without rice. It is Endless West, not Perfect Day. It also misidentified the ingredient used to make ice cream. It is microflora, not yeast. And it misstated a role that a company, Geltor, has in the making of face cream with fermented spider silk proteins. Geltor produces the proteins; it does not make the cream.
match_headline: Could This Be the Lab-Made Dinner Party of Our Future?

text: An article last Sunday about socializing as Covid-19 vaccines are introduced misstated Ingrid Katz’s job title at Harvard Medical School. She is an associate professor, not an assistant professor.
match_headline: When Can I Be a House Guest Again?

text: An article on Thursday about the arrest of Georgia’s opposition leader misidentified the vice president of the Atlantic Council of Georgia. The position is held by Batu Kutelia, not Shota Utiashvili. It also incorrectly attributed quotations stating that “Georgia has been labeled as a beacon of democracy in the region” and that “Georgia has never been a perfect democracy.” They were said by Mr. Kutelia, not Mr. Utiashvili.
ref_headline: Georgia has been labeled as a beacon of democracy in the region
match_headline: Arrest of Opposition Leader in Georgia Raises Fear of Growing Instability

text: An article on Sunday about the firing of Myanmar’s envoy to the United Nations referred incorrectly to the U.N. General Assembly meeting at which U Kyaw Moe Tun spoke. It was in New York, not Geneva.
match_headline: Myanmar Military Fires U.N. Envoy Who Spoke Against Its Coup

text: An article on Sunday about a proposal to name a lake in Kosovo after President Donald J. Trump misstated the dates of the war in Kosovo. It began in 1998 and ended in 1999, not 1988 and 1989.
match_headline: How to Unite a Deeply Divided Kosovo? Name a Lake After Trump

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a debate in the Republican Party around an increase in the federal minimum wage misstated the equivalent of today’s $7.25 to 2009 buying power, adjusted by consumer price inflation. It is $5.97, not $5.85.
match_headline: Republicans Grapple With Raising the Minimum Wage

text: An article on Monday about two plays from London that tackle racism misidentified a character in the play “Hymn.” The actor Adrian Lester portrayed Gil, not Gus.
match_headline: Making Black Lives, Not Just Black Deaths, Matter Onstage

text: An obituary on Friday about the sculptor Barry Le Va misspelled his wife’s surname and misstated the year of an exhibition of his work at the New Museum in Manhattan. She is Lisa Rubenstein, not Rubinstein; the exhibition was in 1979, not 1973. Using information from Mr. Le Va’s gallery, the earlier version also misstated his parents’ names. His mother was Muriel (McCollon) Leva, not Muriel (McCullinan) Le Va, and his father was Arthur C. Leva Jr., not Le Va. (Mr. Le Va later changed the spelling of his surname.)
match_headline: Barry Le Va, Whose Floor-Bound Art Defied Boundaries, Dies at 79
