text: An obituary on Sunday about Shelia Washington, who helped exonerate the Scottsboro Boys, misspelled her given name as Sheila. The error was repeated in the headline and a picture caption. (The error also appeared in a Times article published in November 2013.)
An article on Monday about winners at the Golden Globes misstated the nationality of Chloé Zhao, who won the award for best director for the drama “Nomadland.” She is Chinese, not American.
match_headline: Chloé Zhao becomes the first Asian woman to win the Golden Globe for best director.

text: An article last Wednesday about the chef Gregory Gourdet misstated the composition of the kitchen staff at Kann Winter Village, his pop-up restaurant in Portland, Ore. Seven of the nine staff members are people of color, not all of them.
match_headline: Under Fire, a Portland Chef Tries to Build a Fairer Workplace

text: An article last Wednesday about households with more than one refrigerator misstated the surname of a Utah man who owns two. He is Phillip Smith, not King.
match_headline: When One Fridge Is Not Enough

text: An article on Feb. 3 about new producers of applejack referred imprecisely to Du Nord Craft Spirits, which opened in Minneapolis in 2013, as the first Black-owned urban distillery in the United States. Jack From Brooklyn, a distillery in New York City, began producing a liqueur in 2012.
match_headline: America’s First Moonshine, Applejack, Returns in Sleeker Style

text: An article on Feb. 4 about the photographer Gordon Parks misidentified a memoir by Mr. Parks and described incorrectly the sequence of events in a recollection in the book. The memoir is “A Hungry Heart,” not “Voices in the Mirror”; and he photographed a gown whose color reminded him of the blood of a murdered gang member after he had photographed the gang member, not before. The article also misidentified the setting of a photograph Mr. Parks took in 1956. It was at a theater in Mobile, Ala., not a department store (Mr. Parks titled the work “Department Store”). And the article, using information from the Gordon Parks Foundation, misstated the year he bought his first camera. It was 1938, not 1937.
match_headline: Gordon Parks Was the Godfather of Cool

text: An article on Wednesday about three journalists killed in Afghanistan misidentified or did not fully name the victims. They were Mursal Wahidi, Sadia Sadat and Shahnaz Raofi, not Mursal Hakimi, Sadia and Shanaz.
match_headline: Three Women Working for a News Outlet Are Gunned Down in Afghanistan

text: An article last Thursday about rising tensions at Smith College after a student claimed she was racially profiled referred imprecisely to a summer camp program at Smith College. It served high school students, not young children. The article also misstated students’ ability to obtain a social justice minor at the college. A minor has been proposed but cannot currently be obtained.
match_headline: Inside a Battle Over Race, Class and Power at Smith College

text: An article on Friday about investigations awaiting Judge Merrick B. Garland when he assumes leadership of the Justice Department misstated the U.S. Attorney’s office responsible for indicting members of a white supremacist group involved a plot to kidnap Gov. Gretchen Whitmer of Michigan. It was the office of U.S. Attorney Andrew Birge, not Matthew Schneider.
match_headline: Justice Dept. Backs Away From Trump Era but Is Still Expected to Test Garland

text: An article on Thursday about wind farms in Wyoming misstated the governing body where Terry Weickum once held a seat. It is the Carbon County Commission, not the Carbon County Commissioners Association. It also described imprecisely one of President Biden’s environmental actions. Mr. Biden imposed a moratorium on new drilling leases on federal land. He did not impose a general moratorium on all drilling on federal land.
match_headline: Wyoming Coal Country Pivots, Reluctantly, to Wind Farms

text: An article last Sunday about snitch culture referred incorrectly to the recipient of a selfie from inside the Capitol Rotunda on Jan. 6. He was the brother of the sender’s girlfriend, not the sender’s brother-in-law.
match_headline: The Season of the Snitch

text: An article last Sunday about a property for sale in the Dominican Republic misstated the annual property tax on the featured home. It is $24,950, not $2,495.
match_headline: House Hunting in the Dominican Republic: A Tropical Compound for $2.5 Million

text: An article last Sunday about D.I.Y. home renovation misstated the distance from West Orange, N.J., to Manhattan. It is about 15 miles, not 40 miles.
match_headline: Extreme D.I.Y. for Home Decor

text: A picture with an article last Sunday about homes that sold for around $600,000 showed the wrong house with the description of 2599 Gregory Street in Yorktown Heights, N.Y.
match_headline: Homes That Sold for Around $600,000

text: A review on Feb. 21 about “Bugsy Siegel,” by Michael Shnayerson, referred incorrectly to the Beverly Hills residence where Siegel was killed in 1947. It was the home of his longtime girlfriend, Virginia Hill; it was not Siegel’s home.
match_headline: Was Bugsy Siegel the ‘Supreme Gangster’? A Biography Makes the Case

text: An article on Sunday about the effect of the pandemic on global shipping misstated the freight rate that Peter Baum said his company, Baum-Essex, had paid for a recent shipment. It was $6,000 to $7,000, not $67,000.
match_headline: ‘I’ve Never Seen Anything Like This’: Chaos Strikes Global Shipping

text: An article on Sunday about the coronavirus in Rhode Island included remarks from Dr. Ashish Jha, dean of the School of Public Health at Brown University in Providence, that misidentified the state with the highest poverty rate in New England. It is Maine, not Rhode Island.
match_headline: How Rhode Island Fell to the Coronavirus

text: An article on Sunday about the possibility of a Democrat winning another Senate seat in Ohio misidentified an Ohio state lawmaker who is under indictment on corruption charges. It is a former House speaker, Larry Householder, not the current speaker.
match_headline: Democrats Want a Stronger Edge in the Senate. Ohio Could Be Crucial.

text: An article on Monday about new independent print media from the Lower East Side referred incorrectly to the ownership of Dimes restaurant in Lower Manhattan. The restaurant’s owners are not models.
match_headline: They Had a Fun Pandemic. You Can Read About It in Print.

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about victims of violence by Myanmar’s military misstated the date of a protest at which officers were shown lined up in a security cordon. It took place on Feb. 9, not on Tuesday.
match_headline: As Bullets and Threats Fly, Myanmar Protesters Proudly Hold the Line

text: An article on Tuesday about Prince Harry’s racial awakening misstated the title of a book. It is “The Souls of Black Folk,” not “The Souls of Black Folks.”
match_headline: Prince Harry Finally Takes On White Privilege: His Own

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Senator Chuck Schumer’s challenges as the Senate majority leader misstated the year that he could face a possible primary challenge from Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. It is 2022, not 2024.
match_headline: For Chuck Schumer, a Dream Job Comes With Tall Orders

text: An obituary on March 3 about the civil rights leader and Washington power broker Vernon E. Jordan Jr. referred incorrectly to his choice of college. He enrolled in DePauw University although his mother had urged him to attend the historically Black school Howard University; he did not attend DePauw “at his mother’s urging.”
match_headline: Vernon Jordan, Civil Rights Leader and D.C. Power Broker, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on March 4 about the academic and activist Joseph D. Duffey misstated the position he held at American University in Washington. It was president, not chancellor.
match_headline: Joseph D. Duffey, 88, Dies; Apostle of Liberalism and Humanities

text: An article on Thursday about vaccine misinformation prevalent in Black and Latino communities misstated the year that the Tuskegee syphilis study began. It started in 1932, not 1943.
match_headline: Black and Hispanic Communities Grapple With Vaccine Misinformation

text: An article on Wednesday about athletes’ accusations that coaches in synchronized swimming subjected them to emotional abuse misstated the age of Viktoria Reichova, a swimmer. She is 19, not 23.
match_headline: Complaints of Emotional Abuse Roil Synchronized Swimming

text: An article on Thursday about designer Stuart Weitzman’s stamp collection misstated the year that Weitzman sold his company to Coach. Although Weitzman remained affiliated with the company he founded, he had sold it before its sale to Coach in 2015. The article also referred incorrectly to the quartet of stamps as the only block of four “Inverted Jennies.” There are other blocks of four, but only one — the Weitzman block — that bears the original plate number.
match_headline: He Owns World Famous Stamps and a Prized Coin. Now He’s Selling.

text: An obituary on Thursday about the historian Walter LaFeber misspelled, at one point, the middle name of a historian of whom he was a disciple. He was William Appleman Williams, not Appelman. The obituary also misspelled, at one point, the surname of the co-author of an article about Professor LaFeber. He is Frank Costigliola, not Cosigliola.
match_headline: Walter LaFeber, Historian Who Dissected Diplomacy, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Thursday about Charles Hill, a detective known for his investigations of art thefts, misstated the given name of the leader of a gang that stole 18 paintings from a mansion in Ireland in 1986. He was Martin Cahill, not Guy.
match_headline: Charles Hill, Detective Who Found ‘The Scream,’ Dies at 73

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about Norton Juster, the author of the children’s book “The Phantom Tollbooth,” misidentified the source of a quotation from the author and illustrator Maurice Sendak. It was an introductory essay in a 1996 edition of “The Phantom Tollbooth” — not of Mr. Sendak’s “Where the Wild Things Are.”
match_headline: Norton Juster, Who Wrote ‘The Phantom Tollbooth,’ Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Allan J. McDonald, an engineer who warned of possible problems with the space shuttle Challenger, misspelled the given name of one of his daughters. She is Lora McDonald, not Laura.
match_headline: Allan McDonald Dies at 83; Tried to Stop the Challenger Launch

text: An obituary on Sunday about Henry Goldrich of the Manhattan store Manny’s Music referred incompletely to the ownership of the store before it was sold to Sam Ash in 1999. Mr. Goldrich and his sister, Helen Goldrich Burgauer, were co-owners from 1978 to 1991, when she sold him her share; he was not the sole owner in those years.
match_headline: Henry Goldrich, Gear Guru to Rock Stars, Is Dead at 88

text: An article on Thursday about the passage of the stimulus bill by Congress misattributed the quotation “The American people are going to see an American comeback this year, but it won’t be because of this liberal bill.” It was from Representative Kevin McCarthy of California, not Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.
ref_headline: The American people are going to see an American comeback this year, but it won’t be because of this liberal bill.
match_headline: Congress Clears $1.9 Trillion Aid Bill, Sending It to Biden

text: An article on Friday about a gun control bill passed by the House referred imprecisely to regulations on online gun purchases. Online buyers of firearms from private sellers are not required to undergo background checks, while other online purchasers are.
match_headline: House Passes Gun Control Bills to Strengthen Background Checks

text: An article on Tuesday about the Cy Twombly Foundation’s lawsuit against the Louvre over repainted walls in the room where Twombly created a ceiling mural included remarks from the Louvre’s president, Jean-Luc Martinez, that misstated the museum’s interactions with the foundation. It is not the case that the museum had no contact with the foundation before or after Twombly completed the mural in 2010.
match_headline: Palace Intrigue at the Louvre, as a Paint Job Leads to a Lawsuit

text: An obituary on March 4 about the photographer Benedict J. Fernandez misstated the given names of his mother and daughter. His mother was Palma (Perella) Fernandez, not Pamela; his daughter is Tiina Polvere, not Tina.
match_headline: Benedict J. Fernandez, Photojournalist and Mentor, Dies at 84

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Feb. 14 about “Let Me Tell You What I Mean,” by Joan Didion, misstated the criminal offenses that Martha Stewart was convicted of in 2004. Though she was investigated for insider trading, Stewart was found guilty of other related charges. She was not “sentenced to prison for insider trading.”
ref_headline: Let Me Tell You What I Mean,
match_headline: Joan Didion Revisits the Past Once More

text: An article on Saturday about steps President Biden took to address the global vaccine shortage misstated which countries are receiving Russia’s vaccine, Sputnik V. Though the Czech Republic is seeking the vaccine from Moscow, it has not yet received it.
match_headline: Biden Takes First Tentative Steps to Address Global Vaccine Shortage

text: An article on Saturday about the Desert X biennial misstated who read passages from Catherine Venn’s homesteading diary in a project by the artist Kim Stringfellow. It was the musician Claire Campbell, not Stringfellow.
match_headline: Desert X Artists Dig Beneath the Sandy Surface

text: An article on Monday about lessons learned by Democrats from President Barack Obama’s 2009 stimulus package misidentified the Democratic leader who Senator Susan Collins said showed “absolutely no interest” in reaching a bipartisan agreement on the stimulus package. She was speaking of Senator Chuck Schumer, not President Biden.
match_headline: Democrats, Pushing Stimulus, Admit to Regrets on Obama’s 2009 Response

text: An article on Sunday about far-right politics in Perpignan, France, referred incorrectly to polling results on the expectation that Marine Le Pen will be France’s next leader. The number of respondents who said she would probably be France’s next president was up seven percentage points compared with half a year ago, not 7 percent.
match_headline: Can France’s Far Right Rise to Power? One Mayor Shows How.

text: An article on Jan. 10 about a phone conversation between President Trump and a Georgia election investigator incorrectly attributed two direct quotations to President Trump. While Mr. Trump pressed the investigator to find “dishonesty” in Georgia’s voting and said she would win praise if she did, he did not use the phrase “find the fraud” or say she would be “a national hero.” Those erroneous quotations were originally provided by a state elections official, who now says they were the investigator’s description of what Mr. Trump said.
match_headline: Georgia Officials Reveal Third Trump Call Seeking to Influence Election Results

text: An article on Monday about the Stanford women’s basketball team earning the top seed in the N.C.A.A. women’s basketball tournament described incorrectly a portion of Stanford’s season after Santa Clara County, Calif., restricted sports participation because of the coronavirus pandemic. The team went on a nine-week road trip with its first stop in Las Vegas; it did not spend nine weeks practicing and playing in Las Vegas.
match_headline: Stanford Earns the Top Seed in the Women’s N.C.A.A. Tournament

text: An article on Monday about the cancellation of the artist Judy Chicago’s “Living Smoke” artwork included remarks from Ms. Chicago that misstated the planned work’s distance from the developed area of the Living Desert Zoo and Gardens. The artwork would have been just under one mile from some animals’ enclosures, according to a spokeswoman for the Living Desert, not 1.5 miles.
match_headline: Smoky Artwork by Judy Chicago at Desert Zoo Is Canceled

text: An article on Tuesday about the suspension of the AstraZeneca vaccine by some European governments misspelled the surname of Spain’s health minister. The minister is Carolina Darias, not Dorias.
match_headline: Europe’s Vaccine Suspension May Be Driven as Much by Politics as Science

text: A map with an article about Lake Baikal in Russia misspelled the name of a national park. It is Zabaykalsky National Park, not Zaybaykalsky.
match_headline: For Russians in a Pandemic, Lake Baikal Is the Place to See and Be Seen

text: An article on March 12 about rules imposed by Beijing that would make it more difficult for democracy advocates in Hong Kong to run for chief executive or the legislature described incorrectly charges faced by Martin Lee. Mr. Lee is a barrister known as the “father of democracy” in Hong Kong. He is facing charges related to unauthorized assembly, not national security.
match_headline: How China Plans to Control Hong Kong’s Elections and Elevate ‘Patriots’

text: An article on Thursday about a vote in the House to remove a deadline for ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment misstated how the House voted on the measure in 2020. The House voted to drop the deadline, rather than extend it.
match_headline: The Roadblocks to Equal Rights for Women, a Century Later

text: An article on Thursday about increasing homelessness in the United States referred incorrectly to data supplied by ChildTrends, a research organization based in Bethesda, Md. It was analyzed last month; renters and homeowners were not interviewed last month.
match_headline: Homelessness in U.S. Rose for 4th Straight Year, Report Says

text: An article on Wednesday about protests by arts workers in France and whether workers on Broadway should follow suit misidentified the year in which a production of “1984” was canceled at the Alley Theater in Houston. It was 2020, not this year.
match_headline: Should the American Theater Take French Lessons?

text: An obituary on Friday about Dr. Carola Eisenberg, a founder of Physicians for Human Rights, misstated part of her birth name. She was born Carolina Blitzman, not Caroline.
match_headline: Carola Eisenberg Dies at 103; Helped Start Physicians for Human Rights

text: An article on Sunday about an alliance of lawyers, lobbyists and Orthodox Jewish leaders that influenced clemency grants by President Donald J. Trump misstated the recommendation made by Rabbi Sholom D. Lipskar at the 2014 sentencing of Eliyahu Weinstein. Rabbi Lipskar sought a punishment of five years in prison plus five years of house arrest, not five years of house arrest.
match_headline: Access, Influence and Pardons: How a Set of Allies Shaped Trump’s Choices

text: An article on March 16 about housing bias in New York City misstated the year in which Section 8 was enacted. It was signed into law in 1974, not 1978.
match_headline: ‘She Wants Well-Qualified People’: 88 Landlords Accused of Housing Bias

text: An article on Monday about a $29 billion deal to link the United States, Mexico and Canada by rail referred incorrectly to the Surface Transportation Board. It is an independent federal agency, not a division of the U.S. Department of Transportation.
match_headline: $29 Billion Railroad Merger to Connect U.S., Mexico and Canada

text: An obituary on Thursday about President John Magufuli of Tanzania referred imprecisely to his birthplace. He was born in the district of Chato in what was then known as Tanganyika. The area later became part of Tanzania.
match_headline: John Magufuli, Tanzania Leader Who Played Down Covid, Dies at 61

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the conductor James Levine misstated his age when he made his Metropolitan Opera debut. It was a few weeks before he turned 28, not 29. (As correctly noted elsewhere in the obituary, he was born on June 23, 1943, and made his Met debut on June 5, 1971.)
match_headline: James Levine, Former Met Opera Maestro, Is Dead at 77

text: An article on Thursday about a shift in U.S. policy toward China incorrectly placed in quotation marks conclusions from an article in Foreign Affairs by Kurt Campbell and Ely Ratner that was studied closely by Chinese leaders. The conclusions were paraphrases from the Foreign Affairs article, not direct quotations.
match_headline: As Biden and Xi Begin a Careful Dance, a New American Policy Takes Shape

text: An article on Monday about slow delivery by the U.S. Postal Service misspelled the surname of the president of the American Postal Workers Union. He is Mark Dimondstein, not Diamondstein.
match_headline: Postal Service Struggles to Speed Up Delivery, Compounding Its Troubles

text: An article on March 13 about a prolonged lack of drinkable water in Jackson, Miss., after a storm included remarks from Chokwe Lumumba, the mayor of Jackson, in which he described incorrectly the state’s payment for local water resources. The state does pay for the water that its agencies use; it is not the case that the city receives no payment from the state.
match_headline: ‘You Can’t Bathe. You Can’t Wash.’ Water Crisis Hobbles Jackson, Miss., for Weeks

text: A chart on Saturday that included a preview of a first-round matchup between Oregon and Virginia Commonwealth in the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament described incorrectly the outcome of the Atlantic 10 Conference tournament. St. Bonaventure won the tournament, not Virginia Commonwealth, which lost in the championship game.
match_headline: Virginia Commonwealth was forced out of the N.C.A.A. tournament by the coronavirus.

text: An article on Saturday about the anti-populist, Pan-European youth party Volt misstated the year in which it was founded. It was established in 2017, not 2016. An earlier version also referred imprecisely to its founders. It was established by Andrea Venzon, Colombe Cahen-Salvador and Damian Boeselager, not by Mr. Venzon alone.
match_headline: A Pro-Europe, Anti-Populist Youth Party Scored Surprising Gains in the Dutch Elections

text: A picture with an article on Wednesday about the game that a Times columnist’s father played against the basketball star Elgin Baylor was published in error. The player shown in the image wearing jersey No. 52 is Happy Hairston, not Baylor.
match_headline: Elgin Baylor, Acrobatic Hall of Famer in N.B.A., Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Monday about the investor and philanthropist Richard H. Driehaus misstated the surname of one of his sisters. She is Elizabeth Driehaus, not Elizabeth Mellin.
match_headline: Richard H. Driehaus, Champion of Classic Architecture, Dies at 78

text: An article on Thursday about the Israeli election misstated the turnout. It was 67.4 percent, not 66.7 percent.
match_headline: Israel’s Election Ends in a Stalemate, Final Results Show

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 7 about digital interactions between Broadway stars and fans misidentifies the digital event attended by the “Beetlejuice” actor Alex Brightman. It was a birthday party that included actors from other shows, not a “Beetlejuice” event.
match_headline: Can You Autograph a Playbill Through Your Screen?

text: A graphic feature on Page 3 with an article highlighting data that show how the pandemic hurt the travel industry last year misstates a decline in revenues for Carnival Corporation. As the article correctly notes, revenues dropped 99.5 percent during the third quarter of 2020 compared with the same period in 2019 — not 99.5 percent for all of 2020.
match_headline: Shadowed by Pandemic, Olympic Torch Relay Begins in Japan

text: An article on Page 43 about Marie-Louise Sciò’s apartment in Rome misspells the name of her lifestyle website. It is Issimo, not Issima.
An obituary on Thursday about the actor George Segal misstated the year the movie “Fun With Dick and Jane,” in which he starred with Jane Fonda, was released. It was 1977, not 1979.
match_headline: George Segal, Veteran of Drama and TV Comedy, Is Dead at 87

text: An article last Sunday about the art of Rohingya survivors misstated the nationality of refugees in the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in northern Uganda. They are South Sudanese, not Syrians.
match_headline: For Rohingya Survivors, Art Bears Witness

text: An article last Sunday about the soaring value of rare collectibles referred incorrectly to an Android and iPhone app that sells fractional shares of those items. As stated elsewhere in the article, it is Rally, not Valley Road.
match_headline: Here’s How Bored Rich People Are Spending Their Extra Cash

text: An article on Page 43 about Marie-Louise Sciò’s apartment in Rome misspells the name of her lifestyle website. It is Issimo, not Issima.

Because of an editing error, some of the photographs with a list on Sunday of the first 20 prisoners at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, were misplaced. In the third column of that article, each prisoner photograph should have been placed with the name immediately above. Ridah bin Saleh al Yazidi, listed at the bottom of the column, was not shown in a photograph.
match_headline: They Were Guantánamo’s First Detainees. Here’s Where They Are Now.

text: An article on March 23 about the state of the coronavirus pandemic misspelled the given name of the president of Lithuania. He is Gitanas Nauseda, not Gitranas. It also misspelled the given name of the speaker of the legislature. She is Viktorija Cmilyte-Nielsen, not Viktoria.
match_headline: How the Pandemic Changed Your Politics

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about deadly protests in Bangladesh misidentified the city where the Baitul Mokarram mosque is located. It is Dhaka, not Brahammanbaria.
match_headline: At Least 10 Killed in Protests Against Modi’s Visit to Bangladesh

text: An article on Monday about the revival of hunting and trapping certain predators in Montana misstated an aspect of Montana’s trapping regulations. It is illegal — not legal — to use snares on black bears.
match_headline: In Montana, Bears and Wolves Become Part of the Culture Wars

text: An article on Friday about Black figure skaters who use skating as a platform to speak out about social justice issues referred incorrectly to Joel Savary’s professional relationship to Kaitlyn Saunders. He is her former coach, not her current one.
match_headline: Black Figure Skaters See Performing as Their Best Way to Speak Out

text: An article on Monday about the advancement of Gonzaga and U.C.L.A. to the round of 8 in the N.C.A.A. Men’s basketball tournament misstated Alabama’s performance from the free-throw line in its loss to U.C.L.A. It was 11 for 25, not 11 for 27.
match_headline: As Gonzaga Dominates, U.C.L.A. Tops Alabama in an N.C.A.A. Thriller

text: An article on Monday about the standing of each Major League Baseball team ahead of opening day misstated the given name of one of three Most Valuable Player Award winners on the Dodgers’ roster. He is Cody Bellinger, not Clay. (Clay Bellinger is a former major league player.)
match_headline: A Ballpark Half Full and Another Half Empty for All 30 Teams

text: An article on Tuesday about the difference between the “green jobs” stimulus package that Joe Biden oversaw as vice president and the environmental goals of his stimulus plan as president misstated the amount of greenhouse gases emitted by the United States each year. It is five billion tons, not five million tons.
match_headline: Biden’s Lesson From Past Green Stimulus Failures: Go Even Bigger

text: A headline with an article on Tuesday about the freeing of the Ever Given in the Suez Canal misstated the nature of the ship. The Ever Given is a container ship, not a tanker. The error also occurred in a headline for a picture caption on the front page.
match_headline: The Freeing of the Ever Given

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the vulnerability felt by retail workers as states lift mask mandates misspelled the given name of a Kroger employee. As the article correctly stated, her name is Marilyn Reece, not Marylin.
match_headline: As Mask Mandates Lift, Retail Workers Again Feel Vulnerable

text: An article on Tuesday about Houston’s victory over Oregon State in the men’s N.C.A.A. basketball tournament misstated the interval between Houston’s N.C.A.A. tournament wins. Its 2018 victory was its first in the tournament in 34 years, not 38.
match_headline: Houston Hangs On and Reaches the Final Four

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the former NASA flight director Glynn S. Lunney misstated the middle initial of the Apollo 13 astronaut James Lovell Jr. It is A, not L.
match_headline: Glynn S. Lunney Dies at 84; Oversaw NASA Flights From Mission Control

text: An article on Tuesday about the challenges faced by House Democrats in order to pass President Biden’s infrastructure bill misstated the number of Democratic House votes that Mr. Biden can currently afford to lose on his spending proposal. It is three, not eight.
match_headline: Democrats Look to Smooth the Way for Biden’s Infrastructure Plan

text: An article last Thursday about brooches misstated the surname of the fine jeweler designing as JAR. He is Joel Arthur Rosenthal, not Rosenfeld.
match_headline: The Brooch Is Back, Baby

text: An article last Thursday about a rise in popularity for the cold-shoulder top misstated the surname of a jewelry designer. She is Wendy Brandes, not Brande.
match_headline: How the Cold-Shoulder Top Became a Vaccine Fashion Trend

text: An obituary on Wednesday about G. Gordon Liddy, the mastermind of the Watergate burglary, misstated the location of the burglars’ lookout across the street from the Watergate complex. It was in a motel, not an apartment.
match_headline: G. Gordon Liddy, Mastermind Behind Watergate Burglary, Dies at 90

text: A picture caption with an obituary on March 18 about the wine merchant Steven Spurrier misstated when the photo of him in his wine shop was taken. It was about two years after he had held a blind tasting of California versus French wines — not “several years” later.
match_headline: Steven Spurrier, Who Upended Wine World With a Tasting, Dies at 79

text: An obituary on March 22 about Nawal el Saadawi, an advocate for women in the Arab world, misstated her age when she divorced her third husband, Sherif Hetata. She was in her late 70s, not her early 80s.
match_headline: Nawal el Saadawi, Advocate for Women in the Arab World, Dies at 89

text: An article on Thursday about a citizen’s arrest bill approved in Georgia misstated the middle initial of a law professor at American University. He is Ira P. Robbins, not Ira R.
match_headline: Georgia to Weaken Citizen’s Arrest Law Cited in Ahmaud Arbery’s Death

text: An article on Thursday about the man charged in a violent attack on a Filipino immigrant near Times Square, relying on information from the Bronx district attorney’s office, misstated the timing of a guilty plea. The man, Brandon Elliot, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder in 2003, not 2002.
match_headline: Man Arrested in Anti-Asian Attack Was on Parole for Killing His Mother

text: An article on Wednesday about the expansion of the N.F.L. regular season to 17 games misstated how many teams were in the playoffs last season. It was 14, not 16.
match_headline: With 17 Games, the N.F.L. Evolves for Streaming Generation

text: An article on Thursday about planned concerts and the reopening of music venues for the summer and fall misstated the location of Jungle’s planned New York concert. It is Avant Gardner, not Brooklyn Steel. The article also misstated the amount of federal relief money available through the Shuttered Venue Operators Grant fund. It is $16 billion, not $10 billion.
match_headline: Itchy to Perform Again, Musicians Eye Return to Touring

text: An article on Page 22 about a pediatric H.I.V. outbreak in Ratodero, Pakistan, misstates the number of countries that have not eradicated polio. It is two, not three.
match_headline: The City Losing Its Children to H.I.V.

text: An obituary on Friday for Paul G. Feinman, the first openly gay judge on New York State’s highest court, misstated the occupation of his husband, Robert Ostergaard, and the year they married. He is digital communications director at Montclair State University in New Jersey; he is no longer senior editorial director of NickJr.com. And they married in 2013, not 2003.
match_headline: Paul Feinman, First Openly Gay Judge on N.Y. High Court, Dies at 61

text: An article last Sunday about the pandemic’s effect on our friendships misstated where Rachel Stevens works as a radio producer. It is Seattle, not Bozeman, Mont.
match_headline: We Want Our Friends Back! (But Which Ones?)

text: An article last Sunday about Millerton, N.Y., misstated the status of a Westerlind apparel store in Manhattan after the company opened a shop in Millerton. The Manhattan store remains open. The article also misstated the number of homes for sale in Millerton, and included a picture of a home that is not in the village. There were two homes for sale in the center of Millerton, not in the entire village.
match_headline: Millerton, N.Y.: Unspoiled Beauty With a New Youthful Energy

text: An article last Sunday misstated the square footage of a house for sale in Cresskill, N.J. It has 3,353 square feet, not 2,038 square feet.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in Connecticut and New Jersey

text: An article on Saturday about the arrest of high-profile figures in Jordan misstated the role of Sharif Hassan bin Zaid. Although he is a member of the Jordanian royal family, he was not an envoy to Saudi Arabia. The error was repeated in an article on Sunday.
match_headline: Jordan Arrests High-Profile Figures, and Ex-Crown Prince Cries Foul

text: An article on Sunday about negotiations between the U.S. and the Taliban misidentified the news outlet that first reported the Taliban’s proposal for a reduction in violence. It was Voice of America, not Tolo News.
match_headline: U.S. Looks to Build on Secret Portions of Taliban Deal to Reduce Violence

text: An article on Saturday about the release of a video that shows the police shooting of a 13-year-old boy in Chicago referred incorrectly to the violence in the city in the first quarter of 2021. There were 131 homicides in Chicago, not shootings.
match_headline: Chicago to Release Video of Deadly Police Shooting of a 13-Year-Old

text: An article on Thursday about shifting politics in Virginia referred incorrectly to an early voting location in Virginia Beach. The City Council there did not move the polling place to a building that was at least a mile away from the nearest bus stop; such a move was discussed but ultimately did not occur.
match_headline: Virginia, the Old Confederacy’s Heart, Becomes a Voting Rights Bastion

text: An article on Saturday about the challenges faced by President Biden in his push for public transit through his new infrastructure plan described incorrectly the Bay Area Rapid Transit system. It is a heavy-rail system, not a light-rail system.
match_headline: America Has Long Favored Cars Over Trains and Buses. Can Biden Change That?

text: An article on Saturday about Gonzaga’s victory over U.C.L.A. misstated the number of teams that had reached the semifinals of the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament without a loss since Indiana did so in 1976. In addition to Kentucky in 2015 and Nevada-Las Vegas in 1991, Indiana State did it in 1979.
match_headline: Gonzaga Was Finally, Truly Tested. It Passed With a Buzzer-Beater Over U.C.L.A.

text: An article on Sunday about white evangelicals who do not intend to get vaccinated erroneously included a photograph of an anti-vaccine protest in Atlanta. Although some protesters carried signs featuring Bible verses, the event was organized by a group with no religious affiliation.
match_headline: White Evangelical Resistance Is Obstacle in Vaccination Effort

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about virus tests at an elite high school misstated the federal agency to which SafeGuard had applied for lab certification. Such certifications are reviewed by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, not the Food and Drug Administration.
match_headline: Why Virus Tests at One Elite School Ran Afoul of Regulators

text: A column on Monday about violence against Black Americans described incorrectly what Emmett Till’s killers did with his body. They tied to his neck a fan from a cotton gin, not a cotton gin. It also used an outdated title for Daina Ramey Berry at the University of Texas, Austin. She is a professor of history and African diaspora studies, not an associate professor.
match_headline: Lessons From Lynchings

text: An article on Sunday about rezoning in SoHo referred incorrectly to applications submitted in a lottery for affordable apartments. New York City’s housing lottery site received over 25 million applications; 25 million people did not submit applications. The article also misidentified the street where jazz performer Ornette Coleman lived. He lived on Prince Street, not Grand Street.
match_headline: Does SoHo, Haven for Art and Wealth, Have Room for Affordable Housing?

text: An article on Tuesday about 16 players and a coach from the N.H.L.’s Vancouver Canucks that tested positive for the coronavirus misidentified a Vancouver radio station. It is Sportsnet 650, not 360.
match_headline: Vancouver Canucks Brought to a Standstill by the Pandemic

text: An article on Tuesday about the four-part series “Exterminate All the Brutes” on HBO described incorrectly a phrase from the character Kurtz in the Joseph Conrad novella “Heart of Darkness.” The words “Exterminate all the brutes!” are in a postscript written by Kurtz at the end of a report; they are not the final words we hear from him. (His final words are: “The horror! The horror!”)
match_headline: In ‘Exterminate All the Brutes,’ Raoul Peck Takes Aim at White Supremacy

text: An obituary on Monday about the China scholar Kristofer Schipper misstated where he was born. Although he grew up in Schardam, the Netherlands, he was born in Varmland County, Sweden. The obituary also misstated part of the name of Mr. Schipper’s wife, who survives him. She is Yuan Bingling, not Yang.
match_headline: Kristofer Schipper, Influential China Scholar, Dies at 86

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a triple homicide in Brooklyn misstated the length of time that Joseph McCrimon was in prison after a manslaughter conviction. It was five years, not 15 years.
match_headline: Her Dad Came to Her Birthday Party. Then He Killed Her Family.

text: An article on Wednesday about a $212 billion budget agreement reached by New York State leaders described incorrectly state lawmakers’ response to a lawsuit over school aid. The Legislature committed to the financial obligations set out in the lawsuit once before, in 2007, before canceling the funding; it is not the case that it was the first time it agreed to the funding.
match_headline: New York Reaches Deal on $212 Billion Budget to Jump-Start Recovery

text: An article on Friday about a 9-year-old boy who was killed in a Southern California shooting misidentified the organization that determined that in 2020, there were more than 600 shootings in which at least four people were shot by one person, compared with 417 in 2019. It is the Gun Violence Archive, not the Violence Project.
match_headline: A 9-Year-Old Boy Is Among 4 Killed in Southern California Shooting

text: An obituary on Sunday about Malcolm Cecil, who helped to create a synthesizer prominently featured on four Stevie Wonder albums in the 1970s, misstated part of the name of a song by Mr. Wonder. It is “Living for the City,” not “Living in the City.”
match_headline: Malcolm Cecil, Synthesizer Pioneer, Is Dead at 84

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the Florida congressman Alcee Hastings referred incorrectly to his chief of staff, Lale Morrison. She is a woman.
match_headline: Alcee Hastings, Longtime Florida Congressman, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the theologian Hans Küng misstated the middle initial of the priest and author Andrew Greeley, who wrote about Dr. Küng in his book “The Making of the Popes 1978.” It was M, not W.
match_headline: Hans Küng, Catholic Theologian Critical of the Church, Dies at 93

text: An article this weekend on Page 7 about the impact of the pandemic on food pantries misstates the role the National Guard played in helping the Rev. Emaeyak Ekanem run a food pantry in the Bronx. Last year, the National Guard helped Mr. Ekanem set up his pantry for increased demand. It did not provide Mr. Ekanem with training before the pandemic, as he was never part of the National Guard.
match_headline: How Covid Turned Food Pantries Into ‘Mini-Costcos’

text: An obituary on Friday about Sharon Matola, who became a fixture in the society of Belize, her adopted country, after opening a zoo there, referred imprecisely to mycology, which she was studying at one point. It is the study of all fungi, not just mushrooms.
match_headline: Sharon Matola, Who Opened a Zoo in the Jungle of Belize, Dies at 66

text: An article last Sunday about the singer Brandi Carlile misstated the year she performed alongside Judy Collins at the Newport Folk Festival. It was 2019, not 2017.
match_headline: Brandi Carlile Has Always Seen Herself Clearly. Now It’s Our Turn.

text: An article on Wednesday about a tax break for the wealthy in Hong Kong misstated the status of Michael Tien, a Hong Kong lawmaker. He is a current a member of the city’s Legislative Council, not a former one.
match_headline: Hong Kong Courts the Rich as China Tightens Its Grip

text: An article on Saturday about plans for Prince Philip’s funeral misidentified the mother of Queen Elizabeth II. Her name was also Elizabeth, not Mary.
match_headline: For Prince Philip, Royal Family Plans Pandemic-Muted Honors

text: An article on Saturday about a city’s response to the shooting deaths of a family by ex-N.F.L. player Phillip Adams misstated the given name of the football coach of Rock Hill High School. He is Joe Montgomery, not Jim.
match_headline: The Mystery of Why a Foundering Football Player Killed a Family

text: An article on Sunday about the Padres’ first no-hitter, Joe Musgrove, misstated the year Gaylord Perry won a Cy Young Award while pitching for the San Diego Padres. It was 1978, not 1972. (In 1972, he won the award while pitching for Cleveland.)
match_headline: A ‘San Diego Kid’ Gives the Padres Their First No-Hitter

text: An article on Sunday about the New York budget calculated the tax burden on a couple hypothetically making $2.5 million a year based on the understanding that new increases to New York State tax codes were marginal. In fact, they apply to total income.
match_headline: New York, Finally, Taxes the Rich

text: An article on Monday about the secrecy surrounding “Salvator Mundi” at the Louvre quoted incorrectly a portion of comments by Robert Simon, a New York art dealer. He said, “It is sullied in a way,” not “It is soiled in a way.”
match_headline: A Clash of Wills Keeps a Leonardo Masterpiece Hidden

text: A review on March 26 about David Hammons’s work misstated David Hammons’s academic background. He took classes at Otis Art Institute. He did not graduate from or attend the Chouinard Art Institute.
match_headline: David Hammons, Body and Soul, at the Drawing Center

text: An article on Saturday about a project producing sign language covers of musical works recorded by Black female artists misidentified the type of sign language used as part of the “Global Ode to Joy” celebration last year. It was Egyptian Arabic Sign Language, not Arabic Sign Language.
match_headline: Making Music Visible: Singing in Sign

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the causes of India’s most recent wave of coronavirus infections misstated India’s Covid-19 mortality rate. The country recorded 0.04 deaths per 100,000 people for the past seven days as of April 9. The figure did not represent a rate for total deaths since the pandemic began.
match_headline: Complacency and Missteps Deepen a Covid-19 Crisis in India

text: A chart with an article on Tuesday about reasons a government might take for delaying the second vaccine shots misstated the number of coronavirus deaths per resident in the United States and Britain. The chart depicts deaths per 10 million residents in Britain and the U.S., not deaths per 1,000 residents.
match_headline: Johnson & Johnson Vaccinations Paused After Rare Clotting Cases Emerge

text: An article on Tuesday about Chris Magnus, President Biden’s choice to be the commissioner of Customs and Border Protection, misquoted Mr. Magnus. He said, “I like a challenge. I genuinely care,” not “I generally care.”
ref_headline: I like a challenge. I genuinely care,
match_headline: Not Your Usual Police Chief: Biden Picks Trump Critic to Run Border Agency

text: An article on Tuesday about Valdosta High School in Georgia misstated when the school hired the football coach Rush Propst. It was more than a year, not three weeks, after the previous coach was fired.
match_headline: Trouble in Titletown

text: An obituary on Saturday about Prince Philip, the husband of Queen Elizabeth II, misidentified the ship he was on in Tokyo Bay when the Japanese surrendered there on Sept. 2, 1945. It was the British destroyer H.M.S. Whelp, not the American battleship Missouri, where the ceremony took place.
match_headline: Prince Philip, Husband of Queen Elizabeth II, Is Dead at 99

text: An obituary on Monday about Benita Raphan, who made short experimental films about well-known people, misstated the title of her most recent film, about Emily Dickinson. It is “Up to Astonishment,” not “Up From Astonishment.”
match_headline: Benita Raphan, Maker of Lyrical Short Films, Is Dead at 58

text: An article on Tuesday about the end of Britain’s lockdown misstated the location of the Carlton Tavern. It is in the Maida Vale area of London, not in the Kilburn area.
match_headline: U.K. Rejoices and Asks: Are Lockdowns Finally Finished?

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the dancer Mary Ellen Moylan misstated her age at her death. She was 94, not 95. (As the obituary correctly states, she was born in August 1925 and died in April 2020.) The error was repeated in the headline. The obituary also referred incorrectly to the ballerina Maria Tallchief. She was George Balanchine’s third wife, not his second. And it misspelled the surname of the composer of the musical “The Day Before Spring,” in which Ms. Moylan appeared. He was Frederick Loewe, not Lowe.
match_headline: Mary Ellen Moylan, Acclaimed Balanchine Dancer, Is Dead at 94

text: An article on Thursday about Coinbase’s stock market arrival misspelled the name of a blockchain platform. It is Ethereum, not Ethererum. The article also may have implied incorrectly that Bitcoin is likely to shift to a proof-of-stake model. While some critics say Bitcoin will eventually need to make the switch, there are no plans to do so, and the idea is broadly unpopular within the Bitcoin community.
match_headline: In Coinbase’s Rise, a Reminder: Cryptocurrencies Use Lots of Energy

text: An article on Sunday about Hideki Matsuyama’s lead in the third round of the 2021 Masters misstated Hideki Matsuyama’s finish at the 2019 Masters. He finished tied for 32nd; he was not the runner-up to Tiger Woods. The article also misstated Jordan Spieth’s result at No. 15. He had a birdie, not an eagle.
match_headline: Hideki Matsuyama Charges Into the Lead at the Masters

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about New Yorkers whose houses were flooded with sewage in 2019 misstated the percentages of homeownership among New Yorkers of different ethnic and racial groups in 2018. The percentages given referred to homeownership within those communities, not to homeownership in the city over all. That year, 44 percent of Asian households and 43 percent of white households owned their homes, while the same was true for just 27 percent of Black households and 17 percent of Latino households.
match_headline: Raw Sewage Flooded Their Homes. They’re Still Waiting for Help.

text: An article on Friday about a noose being removed from the logo of Placerville, Calif., misstated the given name of the man who discovered flecks of gold in a streambed in early 1848, touching off the California gold rush. He was James Marshall, not John Marshall.
match_headline: A Gold Rush Town Removes a Noose From Its Logo

text: An article on Sunday about the professor Carl L. Hart referred incorrectly to his position at Columbia University. Jennifer Manly, a professor of neuropsychology, was the first tenured African-American science professor granted tenure at Columbia, not Professor Hart.
match_headline: This Heroin-Using Professor Wants to Change How We Think About Drugs

text: An article on Friday about a former alt-right YouTuber misstated the name of the group that the video producer Caolan Robertson runs. It is Future Freedom, not Future of Freedom.
match_headline: Feeding Hate With Video: A Former Alt-Right YouTuber Explains His Methods

text: An article on Friday about the acquisition of the basketball player Charli Collier by the Dallas Wings misstated the first Finnish player in the W.N.B.A. It is Taru Tuukkanen, not Awak Kuier.
match_headline: Charli Collier Is the No. 1 Pick in the W.N.B.A. Draft

text: An article on Page 15 this weekend about play reading groups describes incorrectly the type of work that donors to the Playwrights Realm could pay to act in. They could commission new plays or pay a smaller fee to act in a previously written play.
match_headline: Put Down Your Book. It’s Time to Act Out.

text: An article on Page 46 this weekend about Jo van Gogh-Bonger, Vincent van Gogh’s sister-in-law, misstates the surname of an artist. He is Richard Roland Holst, not Roland-Horst.
match_headline: The Woman Who Made van Gogh

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the use of informants in terrorism-related cases misstates the filing date of a lawsuit about the constitutionality of Communications Management Units brought by several prisoners against the Justice Department. It was 2010, not 2011.
match_headline: The ‘Herald Square Bomber’ Who Wasn’t

text: An article on Page 19 this weekend about drying your laundry in the sun misstates Joe Wachunas’s position at an electric-transportation advocacy group. He is a program manager, not a program director.
match_headline: How to Hang Your Laundry

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 56 this weekend about friends who create together misspells the surname of a model and journalist. They are Trey Gaskin, not Gaskins.
match_headline: Friends Who Create Together

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about music in Boston in the 1970s referred incorrectly to the term the composer Gunther Schuller coined to describe music that drew from both classical contemporary and jazz genres. It is “third stream,” not “third wave.”
match_headline: When Boston Ruled the Music World

text: An article last Sunday about Alexis Feacher, a.k.a. YungBBQ, who creates freestyle dance routines, referred incorrectly to an outfit that Ms. Feacher wore in some of her videos. It was a work uniform, not a high school uniform.
match_headline: YungBBQ Can Be Almost Anyone. Just Watch.

text: An obituary on April 10 about the author Peter Manso referred incorrectly to his academic career. Though he studied for a doctorate in American literature at the University of California, Berkeley, it was not the case that he earned one there. He had advanced far along toward receiving the degree but never fulfilled the requirement of submitting a dissertation.
match_headline: Peter Manso, Biographer of Brando and Mailer, Dies at 80

text: An article on Monday about a red flag gun law in Indiana that failed to prevent the mass shooting in Indianapolis last week misidentified the university where a study was conducted on Indiana’s law, and where Aaron J. Kivisto is a professor. It is the University of Indianapolis, not Indiana University.
match_headline: In Indianapolis Shooting, a Red Flag That Never Flew

text: An article on Saturday about laws used by police to stop drivers who have air fresheners hanging from their rearview mirrors described incorrectly a conclusion from the Open Policing Project regarding racial bias in traffic stops. Data shows that Hispanic drivers are stopped at similar or lower rates as white drivers; they are not more likely to be stopped.
match_headline: How a Common Air Freshener Can Result in a High-Stakes Traffic Stop

text: An article on Saturday about the way down-ballot Democrats helped elect President Biden misstated the seat in the Georgia General Assembly that Ebony Carter ran for last year. It was a seat in the State House, not the State Senate.
match_headline: How Democrats Who Lost in Deep-Red Places Might Have Helped Biden

text: An article on Friday about the trial of Derek Chauvin and his decision to invoke his Fifth Amendment privilege described incorrectly his posture seen on video as he knelt on George Floyd. His hands were resting on his thighs, not in his pockets.
match_headline: Derek Chauvin Declines to Testify as His Defense Ends After 2 Days

text: An article on Tuesday about migrants’ nighttime crossings of the U.S.-Mexico border misidentified the person who slashed an inflatable boat as it neared the shore. It was a Texas state trooper, not a U.S. Border Patrol agent. The error was repeated in a photo caption.
match_headline: Night Crossings: Scenes From the U.S.-Mexico Border

text: An article on Tuesday about an end to talks between Tribune Publishing and Newslight for a potential offer misstated the nature of the agreement made between Tribune and Alden Global Capital. It was binding, not nonbinding.
match_headline: Tribune signals a preference for a sale to a New York hedge fund.

text: An article on Tuesday about Catherine Russell and her performance in the play “Perfect Crime” misstated the date of the play’s first performance. It was April 18, 1987, not April 14. The article also described incorrectly Ms. Russell’s association with the building where the show is playing. She is the general manager, not the owner.
match_headline: A Tireless Actress, Back at the Scene of the ‘Crime’

text: An article on Tuesday about the science of climate change misidentified the authors of The Debunking Handbook. It was written by social scientists who study climate communication, not a team of climate scientists.
match_headline: The Science of Climate Change Explained: Facts, Evidence and Proof

text: An article on Wednesday about reactions across the United States to the verdict in the Derek Chauvin trial misspelled the surname of a woman who lamented that businesses in downtown Chicago had been boarded up before the verdict. She is Lucy Putlak, not Putluk.
match_headline: ‘We Matter’: A Moment of Catharsis After the Derek Chauvin Verdict

text: An article last Thursday about the resentment some wealthy New Yorkers may face upon their return to the city after the pandemic misstated Cheryl Dunn’s age. She is 60, not 63.
match_headline: Some New Yorkers Don’t Want the Superrich to Return

text: An article on Thursday about safety flaws at a Baltimore plant that led to the disposal of up to 15 million possibly contaminated doses of Johnson & Johnson’s coronavirus vaccine misquoted a line in the F.D.A. report about the Emergent vaccine plant. The report said there was no assurance that other batches “have not been subject to cross-contamination.” It did not say: “have not been contaminated.”
ref_headline: have not been subject to cross-contamination.
match_headline: Federal Inspectors Fear More Vaccines Were Exposed to Contamination

text: An article on Thursday about a new boxed set of recordings from John Lennon’s “Plastic Ono Band,” his first post-Beatles solo album, misspelled the surname of a musician who played on the album. He is Klaus Voormann, not Voorman.
match_headline: Half a Century Later, John Lennon’s ‘Plastic Ono Band’ Still Hits Hard

text: An article on Thursday about a collaboration effort between Judson, Los Angeles’s oldest stained glass studio, and local artists described incorrectly the UNESCO status of Frank Lloyd Wright houses in Los Angeles. Wright’s Hollyhock House is a UNESCO site, but not the Ennis House.
match_headline: Stained Glass That Breaks All the Rules

text: An article on Friday about President Biden’s commitment to halving U.S. climate emissions misspelled the given name of the French president. He is Emmanuel Macron, not Emanuel.
match_headline: Biden, Calling for Action, Commits U.S. to Halving Its Climate Emissions

text: An article on Friday about the electric vehicle developer Arrival misstated UPS’s stake in the company. UPS has a stake of less than 1 percent in the company, not 4 percent.
match_headline: An E.V. Start-Up Backed by UPS Does Away With the Assembly Line

text: A headline with a film review on Friday about a Sesame Street documentary misstated the title. It is “Street Gang: How We Got to Sesame Street,” not “Street Gang: The Complete History of ‘Sesame Street.’”
ref_headline: Street Gang: How We Got to Sesame Street,
match_headline: ‘Street Gang: How We Got to Sesame Street’ Review: Making of a Sunny Day

text: An article on Page 9 this weekend about Marianne Faithfull misstates the occupation of her husband, John Dunbar. He is an artist, not a writer. It also mistakenly referenced the armistice in relation to Ms. Faithfull’s year of birth. She was born a year after the end of World War II, not World War I.
match_headline: She’s Marianne Faithfull, Damn It. And She’s (Thankfully) Still Here.

text: An obituary on April 16 about the economist John Williamson misstated the year he graduated from the London School of Economics. It was 1958, not 1951.
match_headline: John Williamson, 83, Dies; Economist Defined the ‘Washington Consensus’

text: An article last Sunday about the Paula Cooper Gallery referred incorrectly to an artist it represents. It represents Carl Andre, who is 85, not Andre’s estate.
match_headline: Art of the Dealer: Paula Cooper Shores Up Her Legacy

text: An article last Sunday about celebrities and gardening misidentified where the series “Inside Out” will be shown. It is HGTV, not Discovery+.
match_headline: Americans Have Discovered the Garden, and Celebrities Want In

text: Because of an editing error, the third crossword puzzle on April 11 listed an incorrect clue. For 1-Down, the clue should have been “Scale,” for the answer CLIMB, not “Deli counter device.”
match_headline: Minor Performer

text: An article on Sunday about C.E.O. compensation during the pandemic misstated the reason Robert A. Iger’s compensation fell in 2020. It was entirely because of the difficult year at the Walt Disney Company. His move from chief executive to executive chairman was not a factor.
match_headline: C.E.O. Pay Remains Stratospheric, Even at Companies Battered by Pandemic

text: An article on Monday about a 1985 Supreme Court case, Tennessee v. Garner, misstated the year that Tamir Rice was shot and killed by a Cleveland police officer. It was 2014, not 2015.
match_headline: Split-Second Decisions: How a Supreme Court Case Shaped Modern Policing

text: An article on Monday about the sending of vaccine materials to India from the United States referred imprecisely to a ban on the export of coronavirus vaccines and vaccine components, a term India’s government has used. While legal impediments stand in the way of such exports, they are not banned.
match_headline: U.S. to Send Virus-Ravaged India Materials for Vaccines

text: An article on Sunday about the history and politics surrounding the killing of 1.5 million Armenians by Turks in the early 20th century referred incorrectly to the region that is modern-day Armenia. It was once part of the Russian Empire, not the Ottoman Empire. The article also contained an outdated reference to a precedent thought to have been set by the Armenian genocide. While many historians once considered it the first genocide of the 20th century, many now regard the German Empire’s 1904-1907 campaign of killings and persecution of the Herero and Nama people of Namibia, then known as German South West Africa, to be the first.
match_headline: The Armenian Genocide, in History and Politics: What to Know

text: A picture caption with an article on April 14 about the final moments of Daunte Wright’s life misspelled the given name of Daunte Wright’s father. He is Arbuey Wright, not Aubrey.
match_headline: Daunte Wright Spent Final Moments Talking With His Mother

text: An article on Saturday about methane emissions misstated the amount of time needed for a reduction in carbon dioxide emissions to produce results in the climate. It would take until the second half of the century, not until the end of the century.
match_headline: Halting the Vast Release of Methane Is Critical for Climate, U.N. Says

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about Allon Schoener, the curator who organized the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s 1969 show “Harlem on My Mind,” referred incorrectly to the 1995 edition of the exhibition’s catalog. It was published by the New Press, not the Met.
match_headline: Allon Schoener, 95, Dies; Curator Caught in Furor Over ‘Harlem’ Show

text: An item on Tuesday about the capture of Benito Mussolini misspelled the given name of the Nazi dictator of Germany. It is Adolf Hitler, not Adolph.

An article on Tuesday about an Apple update that allows users to decide whether or not an app can track them, using information from Apple, misstated how the Siri voice assistant previously worked with Apple Music. Siri was capable of playing music through other services, but asking it to do so required extra effort; it did not work only with Apple Music.
match_headline: To Be Tracked or Not? Apple Is Now Giving Us the Choice.

text: An article on Saturday about money market funds misstated Pennsylvania Republican Senator Patrick J. Toomey’s position on the Banking Committee. He is the ranking member, not the chair.
match_headline: Biden Will Seek Tax Increase on Rich to Fund Child Care and Education

text: An article on Tuesday about endometriosis misstated the institutional affiliation of two researchers; it is Northwell Health’s Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research, not Northwestern’s Feinstein Institute. It also misstated the stage of Linda Griffith’s cancer at one point in time; it was stage 2, not stage 4. Finally, the article misidentified the make of Linda Griffith’s motorcycle in graduate school. It was a Kawasaki, not a Bugatti.
match_headline: They Call It a ‘Women’s Disease.’ She Wants to Redefine It.

text: An obituary on Thursday about the filmmaker Monte Hellman misstated the name of a television series on which he worked as a film editor. It was “Medic,” not “The Medic.”
match_headline: Monte Hellman, Cult Director of ‘Two-Lane Blacktop,’ Dies at 91

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about the radio personality Bob Fass, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the man shown talking to Mr. Fass during the “sweep-in” Mr. Fass organized in the East Village in 1967. He was Samuel J. Kearing Jr., the New York City sanitation commissioner — not Joseph F. Periconi, Mr. Kearing’s predecessor.
match_headline: Bob Fass, Pioneer of Underground Radio, Dies at 87

text: An article on Wednesday about the aggressive approach said to have been taken by federal prosecutors to root out conspirators following the attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6 erroneously included a senior Justice Department official among those who denied prosecutors’ request for a search warrant of Stewart Rhodes. That official, Matthew S. Axelrod, was not involved. It also misstated the date on which the political operative Roger J. Stone Jr. spoke at a rally. It was Jan. 5, not Jan. 6.
match_headline: Prosecutors Are Said to Have Sought Aggressive Approach to Capitol Riot Inquiry

text: An article on Tuesday about the loss of a congressional seat in New York misspelled the surname of a former state assemblyman. He is Jack McEneny, not McEnany.
match_headline: New York Loses House Seat After Coming Up 89 People Short on Census

text: An article on Wednesday about the ways data collection is changing the workplace misstated the timing of a $60 million fund-raising round by the tech start-up HqO. It was this month, not last year.
match_headline: How Data Is Changing the Way Offices Are Run

text: An article on Tuesday about the purchase of the podcast “99% Invisible” by SiriusXM misstated the surname of the host of “Connections.” He is James Burke, not Brooks.
match_headline: SiriusXM Is Buying ‘99% Invisible,’ and Street Cred in Podcasting

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Ole Anthony, the leader of an organization that worked to expose fraud committed by televangelists, misstated the date of his death. It was April 16, not April 13.
match_headline: Ole Anthony, Scourge of Televangelists, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on March 31 about Dennis Mileti, an expert on planning for disasters, misstated the given name of his brother, who survives him. He is Richard, not Dennis.
match_headline: Dennis Mileti, Expert on Preparing for Disasters, Dies at 75

text: An obituary on April 15 about the architect Donald P. Ryder misstated the location of the Frederick Douglass Houses, which were designed by Mr. Ryder’s firm, Bond Ryder & Associates. They are on the Upper West Side of Manhattan, not in Harlem.
match_headline: Donald P. Ryder, Architect of Black Heritage Sites, Dies at 94

text: An article on Friday about the expansion of a law in Germany aimed at reducing carbon emissions misstated the title of Peter Altmaier. He is the economy minister, not the finance minister.
match_headline: German High Court Hands Youth a Victory in Climate Change Fight

text: An article on Friday about a deadly stampede in Israel misstated the date that the Bar Kokhba revolt against the Romans took place. It was in the second century A.D., not the first.
match_headline: Stampede at Israel Religious Celebration Kills at Least 45

text: An article on April 25 about Representative Liz Cheney of Wyoming referred incorrectly to her presence at a Feb. 3 Republican conference meeting. She stood for the duration of the meeting; she did not sit. The article also misidentified a country she served in while working at U.S.A.I.D. She served in Eastern Europe, not China. The article also misidentified Jackson Hole, Wyo. It is a resort area surrounding the town Jackson, not a resort town.
match_headline: Liz Cheney vs. MAGA

text: An article on Monday about Republican efforts to restrict voting misstated which Florida city State Representative Angela Nixon is from. It is Jacksonville, not Tampa.
match_headline: Florida Republicans Pass Voting Limits in Broad Elections Bill

text: An article on Wednesday about two people who modeled for Norman Rockwell paintings and reunited after reading a New York Times article misspelled the given name of the daughter of one of the models. She is Kristin Sorenson, not Kristen.
match_headline: Nearly 70 Years Later, Reunited by Norman Rockwell (and The Times)

text: An article on Sunday about a special election for Texas’ Sixth Congressional District referred incorrectly to a referendum in Austin. Voters favored reinstating a ban on public camping, not ending one. It also misstated the number of terms Mayor Ron Nirenberg of San Antonio has served. He was re-elected to his third term, not his second.
match_headline: With 23 Candidates, Special Election in Texas Is Headed for Runoff

text: An article on Monday about the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles referred incorrectly to in-depth, in-person interviews of Klaus Biesenbach since he became director of the museum. The interview was his first since the pandemic, not, as information from the museum stated, the first since he became director.
match_headline: Amid Signs of Trouble, Can MOCA Find Its Footing?

text: An essay on Saturday about deceptive digital practices referred incorrectly to an action by the Federal Trade Commission concerning the parent company of ABCmouse. The F.T.C. reached a settlement with the company; it did not issue the company a fine.
match_headline: Schumer Readies Plan B to Push Immigration Changes Unilaterally

text: A headline with an obituary on Saturday about the microbiologist Thomas Brock misstated a distinction about his work. His discovery of heat-resistant bacteria led to creation of the polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, which earned Kary B. Mullis a share of the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Mr. Brock did not share in the Nobel Prize for his work.

An article on Wednesday about support for Jordi Cuixart, an imprisoned Catalan separatist leader, incorrectly described the eight other people who were jailed for sedition along with Mr. Cuixart. Six other men and two women were jailed; they were not all men.
match_headline: Criminal or Martyr? Prisoner Poses a Political Dilemma for Spain.

text: An article on Tuesday about a lawsuit by Epic Games against Apple misidentified the judge who will decide a lawsuit. The case will be heard by Judge James Donato, not Judge Yvonne Gonzales Rogers.
match_headline: Apple and Epic Trial Opens With a Tour of the Fortnite ‘Metaverse’

text: An article on Tuesday about an exhibition in Philadelphia of monuments to local heroes misstated the number of formerly incarcerated women depicted in the artwork “When They Come Home.” Four women were incarcerated, not five.
match_headline: They Are Their Own Monuments

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the chemist Helen Murray Free, using information from her family, misspelled the surname of one of her daughters. She is Penny Moloney, not Maloney.
match_headline: Helen Murray Free Dies at 98; Chemist Developed Diabetes Test

text: An article on Wednesday about a Mississippi student who has struggled with remote learning during the pandemic misstated his brother’s age. Jayciyon Coleman is 15, not 16.
match_headline: ‘I Used to Like School’: An 11-Year-Old’s Struggle With Pandemic Learning

text: An article on Tuesday about Australia’s decision to temporarily bar Australian citizens from re-entering the country from India referred incorrectly to the ban. It is not the case that no other democratic nation had banned all arrivals from India; New Zealand blocked its citizens from returning from India for a time in April.
match_headline: Australia Tells Its Citizens in India Amid Covid Crisis: Don’t Come Home

text: An article on April 24 about the slander industry described incorrectly the process that Anytime Mailbox uses in handling its clients’ mail. The company scans the mail and uploads it to a secure server, but does not email it to its customers.
match_headline: The Slander Industry

text: An article on Wednesday about families separated at the U.S. border misstated who paid for the counseling sessions of a migrant child. The counseling sessions were paid for by Seneca Family of Agencies, and not through the settlement of a government lawsuit related to migrant families separated at the border.
match_headline: Many Families Torn Apart at Southern U.S. Border Face a Long and Uncertain Wait

text: An article on Sunday about Dana Beal, a longtime advocate for the legalization of marijuana, misstated the date when marijuana was legalized in New York. It was March 31, not March 30.
match_headline: He Fought for Decades to Make Marijuana Legal. Now What?

text: An article on Thursday about the recall of Peloton treadmills misstated the reason for the recall of one of the models. The Peloton Tread was recalled because of risk of injury from falling touch screens; it has not been associated with serious injuries to children. (The Tread+ model was recalled because it posed a risk of injury or death to children and adult users.) The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Peloton Recalls Treadmills After Injuries and a Child’s Death

text: An article on Thursday about Edmonton Oilers player Connor McDavid’s noteworthy season described incorrectly the N.H.L. experience of Jack Hughes of the Devils. He is a second-year player, not a rookie.
match_headline: Connor McDavid Is Having a (Shortened) N.H.L. Season for the Ages

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Willie Mays’s baseball career erroneously attributed a distinction to Mays in the 1962 season. He played in 162 of the Giants’ 165 regular-season games that year, not in “every one” of their regular-season games.
match_headline: Willie Mays Carries the Torch for His Generation

text: An article this weekend on Page 6 about a cohort of prizewinning theater directors who are questioning the norms of their industry misattributes a comment by one of the directors interviewed. The quotation, “This has been an indescribably devastating time for our community, so I feel like we must say that very clearly. But I think, occasionally, with great hardship comes growth,” was said by Tyne Rafaeli, not Danya Taymor.
ref_headline: This has been an indescribably devastating time for our community, so I feel like we must say that very clearly. But I think, occasionally, with great hardship comes growth,
match_headline: These Four Stage Directors Know Just What Needs to Change

text: An article this weekend on Page 7 about the effects of streaming on the music industry describes incorrectly a figure of 5.6 million artists that Spotify referred to. Those artists have never released more than 10 tracks in total, but some may have drawn more than 1,000 listeners at some point in 2020.
match_headline: Musicians Say Streaming Doesn’t Pay. Can the Industry Change?

text: An article on Page 34 this weekend about the Republican Party in Texas describes incorrectly The Houston Chronicle’s report of voter-fraud cases prosecuted by Ken Paxton, the attorney general of Texas, in 2020. The 16 cases described in the report included prosecutions related to the 2018 election; the cases did not all involve 2020.
match_headline: The G.O.P. Won It All in Texas. Then It Turned on Itself.

text: An article on Page 40 this weekend about gymnastics misstates the country for which the Olympic vaulter Oksana Chusovitina competes. It is Uzbekistan, not Germany.
match_headline: What If Everything We Know About Gymnastics Is Wrong?

text: An article this weekend on Page 8 about an inn in New Orleans misstates the status of property provided by Travelers New Orleans for artists to use as studio space. The property was leased, not purchased. The article also misstates who built the hotel’s reception desk. It was a local woodworker, not an architecture professor at Tulane University.
match_headline: In New Orleans, an Art Break Hotel

text: An article this weekend on Page 9 about a tennis pavilion on Long Island misstates the birthplace of the interior designer Ghislaine Viñas. She was born in the Netherlands, not South Africa, where she grew up.
match_headline: A Tennis Pavilion With a Throwback Vibe

text: An obituary on Friday about David Swensen, who oversaw Yale University’s endowment, misstated the size of the loss the endowment sustained in fiscal 2009. It was 24.6 percent, not 30 percent.
match_headline: David Swensen, Who Revolutionized Endowment Investing, Dies at 67

text: An article on Monday about Eric Adams described incorrectly a branch of Service Employees International Union. The branch, 32BJ SEIU, represents private sector workers; it is not New York City’s largest municipal union.
match_headline: Eric Adams Says He Has Something to Prove. Becoming Mayor Might Help.

text: A map with an article on May 3 about the unlikelihood of herd immunity understated the willingness of residents to be vaccinated, according to Department of Health and Human Services estimates.
match_headline: Reaching ‘Herd Immunity’ Is Unlikely in the U.S., Experts Now Believe

text: An article on Saturday about the Biden administration’s policy toward Ukraine described incorrectly John F. Tefft’s ambassadorship. He served as the American ambassador to Russia from 2014 to 2017, not 2009 to 2013.
match_headline: For Biden, Ukraine Is a ‘Déjà Vu’ Problem That’s Hard to Fix

text: An article on Monday about the Champions League final misstated the date of the F.A. Cup final. It is May 15, not May 17.
match_headline: Champions League Final Could Move to London or Portugal

text: An article on Monday about the death of Bo, the Obamas’ Portuguese water dog, using information from the White House Historical Association, misstated the breed of President Ronald Reagan’s dog, Rex. He was a Cavalier King Charles spaniel, not a King Charles spaniel.
match_headline: Bo, the Obamas’ Portuguese Water Dog, Dies

text: Because of an editing error, a Metropolitan Diary item on Sunday about a bad fall at Brooklyn College misidentified the author. It was written by Karen Widman, not Mikki Shaw. (Ms. Shaw submitted the item on behalf of Ms. Widman, her sister.)
match_headline: ‘The Older Man Was Standing by the Doors and Waiting to Exit the Train’

text: An article on Monday about a Chinese-controlled alternative to the global news media, using information from a report by the International Federation of Journalists, misstated the origins of a media group that fired a columnist. A media group from South Africa, not Kenya, fired the journalist.
match_headline: When Covid Hit, China Was Ready to Tell Its Version of the Story

text: An article on May 5 about the musician Dodie misstated the surname of the vlogger that inspired a Dodie song. He is Charlie McDonnell, not McConnell.
match_headline: Dodie Can’t Resist Sharing. It’s Made Her Music Soar.

text: An article on Saturday about preparations by “Saturday Night Live” for an episode hosted by Elon Musk misquoted a tweet by Senator Bernie Sanders. It was “the 50 wealthiest people in this country own more wealth than some 165 MILLION Americans,” not “the 50 wealthiest people in America in this country.”
match_headline: ‘Saturday Night Live’ Gets Ready for Elon Musk

text: An article on Tuesday about the rap supergroup Mount Westmore misstated the year that the album “Doggystyle” was released. It was in 1993, not 1992.
match_headline: One Surreal Night With the Rap Veterans of Mount Westmore

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about the architect Helmut Jahn misidentified the building that had been criticized as “squished foil.” As correctly stated in the article, a critic dismissed Mr. Jahn’s 70-story CitySpire in Midtown Manhattan as “squished foil to the irrepressible upward thrust of the Chrysler Building,” not his One Liberty Place in Philadelphia.
match_headline: Helmut Jahn, ‘Convention-Busting’ Architect, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Saturday about Nancy Lassalle, a longtime patron of New York City Ballet and its school, referred incorrectly to the photographer Alfred Stieglitz, who was her mother’s mentor and lover. He was born in 1864 and died in 1946; he was not a “postwar cultural figure.”
match_headline: Nancy Lassalle, Longtime Promoter of Ballet, Dies at 93
