text: An obituary on Monday about Pete du Pont, the former governor of Delaware, misstated his place in his family’s birth order. He was the oldest of three children of Pierre S. du Pont III and Jane Holcomb du Pont, not the youngest.
match_headline: Pete du Pont, Ex-Delaware Governor Who Ran for President, Dies at 86

text: An article on Monday about the use of psychedelic drugs in psychiatric treatment misstated where Field Trip Health, a two-year-old Canadian company, is traded. It is listed on the Canadian Securities Exchange and the OTC Markets Group, not the New York Stock Exchange.
match_headline: The Psychedelic Revolution Is Coming. Psychiatry May Never Be the Same.

text: An article last Thursday about knitwear designers misspelled the surname of one designer. She is Hope Macaulay, not Macauley. The error was repeated in two picture captions.
match_headline: The Designers Who Are Making Knitwear Cool

text: An obituary on Friday about the journalist Lucinda Franks erroneously credited her with a distinction. She was one of the first female reporters in United Press International’s London bureau, but not the first; at least one other woman, China Altman, was a reporter there before her. It also referred incorrectly to the Ohrdruf concentration camp, where Ms. Franks’s father, an American secret agent during World War II, was once flown. It was the first camp liberated by United States troops — not the first liberated by the Allies. (Soviet troops had earlier liberated another camp, Majdanek.)
match_headline: Lucinda Franks Dies at 74; Prize-Winning Journalist Broke Molds

text: An article on Thursday about Senator Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and her possible infrastructure deal with the White House misstated the size of President Biden’s plan. It is $2.3 trillion, not $2.3 billion.
match_headline: In Infrastructure Talks With Biden, Capito Faces Fraught Path to Deal

text: An article on March 29 about climate change and steel companies referred incompletely to the gases converted by bacteria into useful chemicals in pilot programs by ArcelorMittal. Both carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide are converted, not carbon dioxide alone.
match_headline: How to Clean Up Steel? Bacteria, Hydrogen and a Lot of Cash.

text: An article last weekend about plans for development on a $180 million parking lot in Manhattan misidentified the years that Catherine McVay Hughes was the chairwoman of Community Board 1. She held the position from 2005 to 2012; she was not the chairwoman on Sept. 11, 2001.
match_headline: How a $180 Million Parking Lot Could Change N.Y.C.’s Historic Character

text: A picture caption last Sunday with an article about pandemic reopening protocols in residential buildings misstated an address at which packages were being sanitized. It was 150 West 56th Street, not 58th.
match_headline: In New York, a Wait-and-See Attitude Even With a Reopening

text: An article on Sunday about incidents that led to the current Israeli-Palestinian crisis misstated the planned date of Palestinian legislative elections. They had been scheduled for May 22, not March.
match_headline: After Years of Quiet, Israeli-Palestinian Conflict Exploded. Why Now?

text: An article on Sunday about a police shooting of a Black man from South Africa in Hawaii referred incorrectly to the case of Rodney King. Mr. King was beaten by police officers in Los Angeles in 1991, but not killed.
match_headline: A Police Shooting in Hawaii Has South Africans Demanding Justice

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Leslie Moonves’s exit package from CBS omitted a reference to Mr. Moonves’s private settlement with an unidentified CBS contractor that was noted in a joint statement from the company and Mr. Moonves.
match_headline: Leslie Moonves Receives Nothing From CBS Exit Package

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about “American Experience” misidentified the year of Billy Graham’s death. It was 2018, not 2008.
match_headline: Sarah Colt on Why 2021 Is the Right Time for a Film About Billy Graham

text: An article on Saturday about the New York mayoral candidates after their first debate misidentified the location of a campaign stop by Maya Wiley. It was the Roberto Clemente Family Guidance Center, not the Clemente Cultural and Educational Center.
match_headline: N.Y.C. Mayoral Candidates Keep Focus on Crime After a Feisty Debate

text: An article on Thursday about efforts by the United States and Europe to stop the Israel-Gaza conflict misspelled the surname of Germany’s foreign minister. He is Heiko Maas, not Mass.
match_headline: New Political Pressures Push U.S. and Europe to Stop Israel-Gaza Conflict

text: An article on Wednesday about the threats that hackers and climate change pose to U.S. oil pipelines and grids referred imprecisely to a move barring oil exports to the United States in 1973. It was an embargo imposed by Arab oil producers, not by all members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.
match_headline: Hackers and Climate Change Threaten U.S. Energy Independence

text: An article on Wednesday about Jordan Ellenberg’s book “Shape” misstated the name of the poet who wrote: “Euclid alone has looked on Beauty bare.” She was Edna St. Vincent Millay, not Edna St. Millay.
match_headline: ‘Shape’ Makes Geometry Entertaining. Really, It Does.

text: An obituary on Thursday about the winemaker Jim Clendenen misspelled the surname of the author of the book “Vines & Visions: The Winemakers of Santa Barbara County.” He is Matthew Dennis Kettmann, not Kettman.
ref_headline: Vines & Visions: The Winemakers of Santa Barbara County.
match_headline: Jim Clendenen, Santa Barbara Winemaking Pioneer, Dies at 68

text: An obituary on April 30 about the opera impresario Paul Kellogg, using information from the Glimmerglass Festival, misstated the year he was hired as a French teacher by the Allen-Stevenson School in Manhattan. It was 1960, not 1967.
match_headline: Paul Kellogg, New York City Opera Impresario, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on May 12 about the television journalist Bill McCreary misstated the year he became the managing editor and anchor of “The McCreary Report” on Channel 5 in New York and was named a vice president of Fox 5 News. It was 1987, not 1978.
match_headline: Bill McCreary Dies at 87; Blazed Trail for Black Journalists on TV

text: Because of an editing error, an article this weekend on Page 12 about Maya Lin’s “art landscapes” in the Pacific Northwest describes her work “Bird Blind” incorrectly. The structure’s slats are engraved with the common and scientific names of the 134 species Lewis and Clark noted in their journey, not only bird species. The article also misidentifies the creator of the model of the Vancouver Land Bridge that is the centerpiece of the exhibition “Along the Columbia River: Maya Lin and the Confluence Project.” It was created by Johnpaul Jones and his architectural firm, not Ms. Lin.
match_headline: Along the Columbia River, Making a Monument of the Land

text: An article this weekend on Page 29 about a collection of works by Jean-Michel Basquiat on display at the Broad museum in Los Angeles misstates the background of the artist’s parents. Basquiat’s mother was of Puerto Rican descent and his father was an immigrant from Haiti, not the reverse.
match_headline: The Broad Museum Reopens With a Celebration of Basquiat

text: An article last weekend about the dramatization of addiction in films referred incorrectly to the setting of “Trainspotting.” While the movie was shot primarily in Glasgow, the story is set in Edinburgh.
match_headline: Hollywood Has a New Way to Dramatize Addiction

text: An article last weekend about botanical oils misspelled the surname of a makeup artist. He is Hung Vanngo, not Vanggo.
match_headline: How Botanical Oils Won Over the West

text: An article last weekend about fragrances referred incorrectly to the academic Edward Said. He was Palestinian-American, not French-Palestinian.
match_headline: The Fragrances That Changed the Field

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the actor Charles Grodin misstated which of his performances was praised as “impeccable” by the critic Walter Kerr. Mr. Kerr used the word in a 1975 piece about Mr. Grodin’s work in the play “Same Time, Next Year” — not, as Mr. Grodin recalled in a 1990 article, in a 1962 review of the play “Tchin-Tchin.” The obituary also misidentified the newspaper in which Mr. Kerr’s 1962 review appeared. It was The New York Herald Tribune, not The Times.
match_headline: Charles Grodin, Star of ‘Beethoven’ and ‘Heartbreak Kid,’ Dies at 86

text: A review last Sunday about “Notes on Grief,” by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, misidentified the Beyoncé album that included part of Adichie’s 2012 TED Talk, “We Should All Be Feminists.” It was featured on the 2013 album “Beyoncé,” in the song “Flawless.” It was not on “Lemonade.”
match_headline: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie: ‘My Madness Will Now Bare Itself’

text: An article last Sunday about Indigenous cultural sites misidentified the construction material of the Desert View Watchtower at Grand Canyon National Park. The tower is made of sandstone and limestone, not granite.
match_headline: Immerse Yourself in Indigenous Culture

text: An article on Sunday about a leaked still-classified document that sheds new light on the Taiwan Nuclear War crisis of 1958 misspelled the last name of a former Air Force general. He is Laurence S. Kuter, not Kutner.
match_headline: Risk of Nuclear War Over Taiwan in 1958 Said to Be Greater Than Publicly Known

text: An article on Monday about President Biden’s climate plan misstated the year by which Mr. Biden committed to cutting carbon emissions by half. It is 2030, not 2035.
match_headline: It’s Crunch Time and Biden’s Climate Gambit Faces Steep Hurdles

text: An article on Monday about a house-party shooting in New Jersey misspelled the surname of the Cumberland County prosecutor. She is Jennifer Webb-McRae, not Webb-McCrea.
match_headline: Arrest Made in N.J. House-Party Shooting That Killed 2 and Injured 12

text: An article on Saturday about the ways Americans used their wealth during the pandemic misstated the release date of a survey from the Charles Schwab Corporation. It was released in May, not March.
match_headline: How the Pandemic Has Changed Attitudes Toward Wealth

text: An obituary on Saturday about the psychologist Jerome Kagan misstated his daughter’s given name. She is Janet, not Jane. It also misspelled his mother’s original surname. She was Myrtle (Lieberman) Kagan, not Liebermann.
match_headline: Jerome Kagan, Who Tied Temperament to Biology, Dies at 92

text: An article on Sunday about a bill in Congress that would ban kangaroo products misstated the Australian politician Mark Pearson’s status as an elected representative of the Animal Justice Party. He is one of the few elected members from the party; he is not the party’s sole elected member.
match_headline: U.S. Activists Try to Halt an Australian Way of Life: Killing Kangaroos

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about calls to ban flights to Belarus misstated a detail of the scene inside the passenger cabin of Ryanair Flight 4978 as it was descending toward Vilnius, Lithuania, its scheduled destination, before the plane was abruptly rerouted to Minsk, Belarus. The seat backs on this model of aircraft are stationary and do not recline. They were not “returned to their upright positions.”
match_headline: Belarus Is Isolated as Other Countries Move to Ban Flights

text: An article on Monday about the author Shoshana Zuboff misspelled the surname of a New York Times technology correspondent. He is Mike Isaac, not Issac.
match_headline: Shoshana Zuboff Explains Why You Should Care About Privacy

text: A chart with an article on Monday that listed the golfers with the most titles at major tournaments omitted a golfer. Gary Player won nine, the last in 1978.
match_headline: Four Major Tournaments in Four Months Is a Lot of Important Golf

text: An article last weekend about a major interior expansion at the Philadelphia Museum of Art misspelled the name of the hill on which the Philadelphia Museum of Art sits. It is Fairmount, not Fairmont.
match_headline: Rethinking What It Means to Be a Philadelphia Artist

text: An article on Wednesday about umpires misstated an incident umpired by Bruce Froemming. Jason Varitek shoved his glove into Alex Rodriguez’s face; Rodriguez did not slap at Varitek’s glove.
match_headline: A History of Baseball’s Modern Era in Four Umpires

text: An article on Tuesday about poets in Myanmar overstated what is known about the origin of lines from a poem read by Ko Khet Thi at another poet’s funeral. While he recited the poem, it is unknown if he wrote it.
match_headline: Where Poets Are Being Killed and Jailed After a Military Coup

text: An article on Friday about unexamined intelligence possessed by the United States related to the origins of the coronavirus misstated the day that Gen. Mark A. Milley told reporters he had not seen any conclusive evidence about the cause of the pandemic. It was Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: U.S. Is Said to Have Unexamined Intelligence to Pore Over on Virus Origins

text: An article on Page 26 this weekend about the scholar Andrea Smith omits the location of the University of Wisconsin campus from which her sister, Justine, received an undergraduate degree. It is the University of Wisconsin, Milwaukee.
match_headline: The Native Scholar Who Wasn’t

text: An obituary on Friday about the gay rights activist and photographer Kay Tobin Lahusen misstated where she grew up. It was Cincinnati, not Cleveland. It also referred incorrectly to a 1993 interview with Ms. Lahusen. Although it appears on the website OutHistory.org, it was not done for the website; it was done by the historian Marc Stein for his University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. dissertation.
match_headline: Kay Tobin Lahusen, Gay Rights Activist and Photographer, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an article on May 16, adapted from Barry Meier’s book “Spooked: The Trump Dossier, Black Cube, and the Rise of Private Spies,” imprecisely summarized the book’s description of the hiring of Fusion GPS by lawyers for Theranos. As noted in the book, the firm was hired around the time Theranos learned that a Wall Street Journal reporter was looking into Theranos.
ref_headline: Spooked: The Trump Dossier, Black Cube, and the Rise of Private Spies,
match_headline: Secret Sharers: The Hidden Ties Between Private Spies and Journalists

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Emily Shakeshaft and Izaak Theo Adu-Watts misstated the full name of the groom’s mother, the singer Sade. She is Helen Folasade Adu, not Helen Fuller Adu.
match_headline: A Wedding in Hawaii for Sade’s Son

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Elizabeth Conway and Kyle Manley misstated the SEAL team where Mr. Manley was stationed in Virginia Beach. It was SEAL Team 8, not 18.
match_headline: A Clear Connection Leads to Marriage

text: An article last Sunday about how to prepare to help aging parents while visiting misspelled the surname of an expert on aging issues at Guardian Life Insurance and misstated his position. He is Ivan Watanabe, not Watannabe, and he is a financial representative, not a managing partner.
match_headline: If You Plan to Visit Aging Parents, Bring a To-Do List

text: An essay on May 9 about young parenthood, in discussing a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention study on the ages of first-time mothers by race and Hispanic national origin, erroneously characterized one category of mothers. “Mexican” describes national origin, not a race.
match_headline: I Became a Mother at 25, and I’m Not Sorry I Didn’t Wait

text: A picture with an article on May 28 about children killed in the Israel-Hamas war was published in error. The child in the photograph was not Rahaf al-Masri, who was among those killed. The photograph has been replaced online with a photograph supplied by Rahaf’s family.
match_headline: China Says It Will Allow Couples to Have 3 Children, Up From 2

text: A headline with an article on May 21 about the conflict between Israel and Hamas overstated the death toll in the conflict. As the article correctly stated, more than 240 people were killed in Gaza and Israel, not more than 250, according to local officials, and it is not known whether most of those killed were civilians.
match_headline: The Toll of Eight Days of Conflict in Gaza and Israel

text: An obituary on Thursday about the former C.I.A. officer Janine Brookner misstated the surname of another former C.I.A. official. He is Thomas Twetten, not Tweedon. The earlier version also misstated part of the name of a government agency. It is the Agency for International Development, not the Agency for Industrial Development.
match_headline: Janine Brookner, Punished C.I.A. Officer Who Got Revenge, Dies at 80

text: An article on Saturday about Ebrahim Raisi’s path to Iran’s presidency misstated the year that Mr. Raisi lost the presidential election in a surprise victory by Hassan Rouhani, the outgoing president. It was 2017, not 2013.
match_headline: Iran Clears Way for Hard-line Judiciary Chief to Become President

text: An article about New Delhi’s reopening described incorrectly figures provided by the Indian government. Government officials estimated that India’s gross domestic product shrank by at least 7.3 percent during the previous fiscal year, which ended March 31; they did not forecast that gross domestic product would shrink during the current fiscal year, which began April 1. It also described incorrectly comments by Sunil Kumar Sinha. He said the estimate for the previous fiscal year was the lowest recorded. He was not referring to a forecast for the current fiscal year.
match_headline: America’s Record-Setting Stimulus Could Power a Rebound in Other Countries

text: An article on Monday about Dominic Thiem referred incorrectly to Der Standard. It is an Austrian newspaper, not a German one.
match_headline: What Has Happened to Dominic Thiem? He Has No Idea.

text: An article on Monday about Rafael Nadal misstated the given name of a professional soccer player. He is Lionel Messi, not Leonardo.
match_headline: The First of Nadal’s 100 French Open Victims Has His Say

text: An article on Tuesday about Naomi Osaka’s exit from the French Open misspelled the surname of a former tennis player who is now an ESPN analyst. She is Rennae Stubbs, not Stubs.
match_headline: Naomi Osaka Skips News Conference, Drawing Tennis Officials’ Ire

text: An obituary on Monday about Sister Margherita Marchione, known as “the fighting nun” for her defense of Pope Pius XII against allegations that he had not done enough to save the Jews from Nazi atrocities during World War II, included an outdated reference to a display about Pius in a museum operated by Yad Vashem, the memorial in Israel to victims of the Holocaust. A panel beneath a photograph of him says that he “did not publicly protest” the deportation of Jews from Rome. It no longer says that “he did not intervene” to try to stop the deportation; that language was revised in 2012.
match_headline: Sister Margherita Marchione, Defender of Pius XII, Dies at 99

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Sunday about Mary Beth Edelson, a feminist art pioneer, misidentified an artwork. The work in the image is “Public Ritual,” not “Shape Shifter.”

An article on Saturday about evidence of a mass grave of Indigenous children on the grounds of a British Columbia school described incorrectly the reaction of the Roman Catholic Church to revelations of abuse within Canada’s residential schools for Indigenous children. While Pope Francis rejected a direct appeal for an apology from Prime Minister Justin Trudeau of Canada in 2018, the archbishop of Vancouver, J. Michael Miller, apologized on behalf of his archdiocese for the church’s role.
match_headline: ‘Horrible History’: Mass Grave of Indigenous Children Reported in Canada

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a cargo ship burning off the coast of Sri Lanka referred incorrectly to Dr. Asha de Vos, a marine biologist. She is a woman.
match_headline: Sri Lanka, Facing ‘Worst’ Marine Disaster, Investigates Cargo Ship Fire

text: An article on Wednesday about a cyberattack on the world’s largest meat processor misstated the name of a cattle industry publication. It is Daily Livestock Report, not Daily Livestock Observer.
match_headline: Ransomware Disrupts Meat Plants in Latest Attack on Critical U.S. Business

text: An article on Thursday about Serena Williams and Roger Federer at the French Open misstated the years when Marin Cilic lost to Roger Federer in Grand Slam finals. He lost at Wimbledon in 2017, not 2018; and he was defeated at the Australian Open in 2018, not 2019.
match_headline: At the French Open, Serena Williams Wins While Roger Federer Waits

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the singer and lesbian activist Alix Dobkin referred imprecisely to Ms. Dobkin’s album “Lavender Jane Loves Women.” It was arguably the first lesbian album, not the first lesbian record. (A single of lesbian songs written and sung by Edythe Eyde under the name Lisa Ben was released by the organization the Daughters of Bilitis 13 years earlier.)
match_headline: Alix Dobkin, Who Sang Songs of Liberation, Dies at 80

text: An article on Thursday about a mass shooting at a San Jose Rail Yard misidentified the area of San Jose, Calif., where Samuel Cassidy lived. His house was several blocks west of Highway 101, not in the Evergreen neighborhood. The error was repeated in an article on Friday about the gunman.
match_headline: Gunman Kills 9 People at San Jose Rail Yard

text: Because of an editing error, a Metropolitan Diary item this weekend about a bike ride in Riverdale misstates the author’s surnames. He is Malcolm-Wiley Floyd, not Ford.
match_headline: ‘She and Her Roommate Had Bought a Sofa From a Woman in Queens’

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about the diversity of young assistant conductors incorrectly describes the status of Black music directors of top-tier American orchestras. James DePreist was the music director of the Oregon Symphony from 1980 to 2003; it is not the case that there have been no Black music directors in this group.
match_headline: Want More Diverse Conductors? Orchestras Should Look to Assistants.

text: An article on Tuesday about an Arctic station that keeps satellites connected misstated the relationship between the paths of orbiting satellites and the location of ground stations. Because of Earth’s rotation, a station at the Equator, which might have been aligned with a satellite’s orbit when the satellite was crossing the pole, would have rotated far to the east, not the west, by the time it passed overhead.
match_headline: Here’s the Arctic Station That Keeps Satellites Connected

text: An article on June 8 on Page D1 about diversity and inclusivity in JAMA journals incorrectly described Dr. Mary Bassett’s recollection of her experience submitting a study to the journal JAMA. The editor asked for a series of revisions to the paper and then rejected it; he did not remove the word “racism” from the text.
match_headline: Medical Journals Blind to Racism as Health Crisis, Critics Say

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about a deli valued at $113 million misspells the surname of a Bloomberg journalist. He is Joe Weisenthal, not Wiesenthal.
match_headline: The Mystery of the $113 Million Deli

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the Brooklyn Nets incorrectly describes the playoff history of the Nets before the team signed Kevin Durant. The team made the playoffs in 2019, not two years in a row.
match_headline: Kevin Durant and (Possibly) the Greatest Basketball Team of All Time

text: An article on May 30 about the Black Keys misidentifies a defunct music venue in Cleveland. It was called Speak in Tongues, not Speaking in Tongues.
match_headline: Are the Black Keys Still Underdogs?

text: An essay on May 23 about Daniel Patrick Moynihan misstated the middle initial of an American psychologist. He was Kenneth B. Clark, not Kenneth D.
match_headline: Daniel Patrick Moynihan Was Often Right. Joe Klein on Why It Still Matters.

text: An article on June 1 about heat deaths linked to climate change misstated in one instance the scope of the increase in deaths. The study found that an average of 37 percent of the heat-related deaths in warm seasons could be linked to climate change, not that climate change had boosted heat deaths by 37 percent.
match_headline: More Than a Third of Heat Deaths Are Tied to Climate Change, Study Says

text: An obituary on May 22 about the evolutionary biologist David Wake, an authority on salamanders, referred incorrectly to plethodontids. They are a family of species of lungless salamanders, not a single species.
match_headline: David Wake, Expert on Salamanders and Evolution, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on June 1 about the lawyer Thomas Sullivan misstated the given name of his sister. She is Mary Comstock, not Nancy.
match_headline: Thomas Sullivan Dies at 91; Investigated Corruption in Chicago’s Courts

text: An obituary on June 1 about the children’s book author and illustrator Lois Ehlert misstated the year her book “Color Zoo” was published and the year it received a Caldecott Honor, and also described the book’s original format incorrectly. It was first published in 1989, not 1997 — in hardcover, not as a board book — and the prize was awarded in 1990, not 1997.
match_headline: Lois Ehlert, Creator of Boldly Colored Children’s Books, Dies at 86

text: A chart on Saturday showing employment gains since the beginning of the pandemic misstated the scale of the recovery. As of May, the U.S. economy had recovered two-thirds of the pandemic job losses; the economy is not “at two-thirds of its prepandemic work force.” (In fact, the economy is at 95 percent of its prepandemic work force.)
ref_headline: at two-thirds of its prepandemic work force.
match_headline: The U.S. Economy Is Sending Confusing Signals. What’s Going On?

text: An article on Monday about Ban Ki-moon’s memoir included comments from the book that misstated details of a lawsuit filed on behalf of Haitians affected by the cholera epidemic that ravaged the country after the 2010 earthquake. It was a class-action lawsuit that named five plaintiffs, filed in federal court in 2013, that sought unspecified damages from the United Nations and Mr. Ban, who was then the United Nations secretary general. The suit was not, as Mr. Ban recalled in the book, filed in 2011 by 500 plaintiffs who sought $40 billion.
match_headline: Cholera ‘Forever Destroyed’ U.N.’s Image in Haiti, Ban Ki-moon Says

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about pushback in the Senate against legislation that would change the way the military handles sexual assault cases reversed the names of two senators. Senator Jack Reed is on the left, and Senator James M. Inhofe is on the right.
match_headline: Old-Guard Senators Defy Changes in How Military Treats Sex Assault Cases

text: An obituary on Monday about the theologian Richard Rubenstein misstated his date of birth. He was born on Jan. 8, 1924, not Jan. 28.
match_headline: Richard Rubenstein, 97, Dies; Theologian Challenged Ideas of God

text: An article on Thursday about the restoration of clean-water protections by the Biden administration misidentified the state that Senator John Boozman represents. It is Arkansas, not Montana.
match_headline: Biden Administration to Restore Clean-Water Protections Ended by Trump

text: An article on Thursday about the closing of Crook’s Corner, a restaurant in Chapel Hill, N.C., misspelled the surname of a founder. He is Gene Hamer, not Hammer.
match_headline: Crook’s Corner, a Landmark North Carolina Restaurant, Has Closed

text: An article on Friday about a photo project for The Times Magazine misstated the relationship between a woman and the relative she was meeting for the first time when she was photographed. It was her great-grandchild, not her grandchild.

An article on Tuesday about Democrats in West Virginia referred imprecisely to the political survival of Senator Joe Manchin III. No other member in the House or Senate other than Mr. Manchin represents constituents, in either their state or district, who voted for the other party’s presidential candidate by more than 16 points — not just constituents in their state.
match_headline: How Joe Manchin Survives as a Democrat in West Virginia

text: An article on March 20 about Facebook’s difficulty distinguishing satire from misinformation referred imprecisely to the Babylon Bee, a right-leaning satirical website, and a controversy regarding the handling of its content by Facebook and the fact-checking site Snopes. While both Facebook and Snopes previously have classified some Babylon Bee articles as misinformation, rather than satire, they have dropped those claims, and the Babylon Bee denies that it has trafficked in misinformation.
match_headline: For Political Cartoonists, the Irony Was That Facebook Didn’t Recognize Irony

text: An article on Page 11 this weekend about the (Un)Known Project in Louisville, Ky., misattributes a line in Hannah Drake’s poem “Dawn.” Drake, in an asterisk, attributes the line in her poem to Anne Lamott. (It is from Lamott’s book “Bird by Bird.”) It also misidentifies the year Drake’s video won millions of views and praise from Ava DuVernay. DuVernay’s comments and millions of views occurred in 2019, not 2017, when Drake made the video.
match_headline: On a Kentucky Riverbank, a Path to Remembrance

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about post-pandemic New York City describes incorrectly an action taken by the Interboro Community Land Trust. Interboro purchased the land beneath the homes of two Brooklyn families, not the homes themselves.
match_headline: New York City Can’t Just Gentrify Its Way Back to Normal

text: An essay on Wednesday about the U.S. tax system described taxable income inaccurately. Shares of stock received as compensation must be reported as taxable income when they are granted, not when they are sold, and taxes must be paid on capital gains when those shares are sold.
match_headline: The Real Tax Scandal Is What’s Legal

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Lauren Thomas and Charles Finkel misstated the location of the Timber Cove Resort. It is in Jenner, Calif., not Sonoma, Calif.
match_headline: Making a Good Impression With Flowers, Street Art and Dog Treats

text: An article on May 16 about cryptoart and NFTs misstated the year that the artist Coldie first sold his art for $1,000. It was in 2019, not 2020.
match_headline: The Untold Story of the NFT Boom

text: An article on Monday about a meeting between the Group of 7 leaders in England misstated the year of the group’s last in-person meeting. It was in France in 2019, not in Canada in 2018.
match_headline: G7 Leaders Offer United Front as Summit Ends, but Cracks Are Clear

text: An article on Monday about President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey and his country’s membership in NATO rendered incorrectly a remark from Soner Cagaptay of the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. He said President Biden “knows he may have to choose between Erdogan and democracy,” not “between Turkey and democracy.”
ref_headline: knows he may have to choose between Erdogan and democracy,
match_headline: As Biden Meeting Nears, Erdogan Softens His Stance

text: An article on Sunday about failures at a southeastern Baltimore plant producing doses of the Johnson & Johnson coronavirus vaccine misstated the date that the report detailing the problems was published. It was published on Saturday, not Friday.
match_headline: F.D.A. details failures at a Baltimore plant that led to unusable vaccine doses.

text: An article on Monday about a labor dispute at The New Yorker misidentified a New Yorker writer who attended a meeting to discuss union issues. She is Jane Mayer, not Jane Kramer.
match_headline: Why The New Yorker’s Stars Didn’t Join Its Union

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about student protests over tuition hikes at Juilliard School implied incorrectly that Juilliard had regularly used an acting workshop in which students were asked to pretend they were slaves. The workshop was held only once at the school.
match_headline: Juilliard Students Protest Tuition Increase With Marches and Music

text: An article on Monday about television shows to watch this week misidentified the actor who voices the character of Morty as an adult in “Rick and Morty.” It is Justin Roiland, the co-creator of the show, not Maurice LaMarche.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘The Celebrity Dating Game’ and a Father’s Day Special

text: An obituary on Thursday about Jessica Morris, who turned her experience with the brain cancer glioblastoma into a crusade for more research and a patient-directed approach to treatment, misstated the year Senator John McCain died of the disease. It was 2018, not 2017.
match_headline: Jessica Morris, Whose Brain Cancer Was Her Cause, Dies at 57

text: An obituary on June 3 about the producer Jerome Hellman misstated John Schlesinger’s involvement in the film “Promises in the Dark” (1979), which Mr. Hellman directed. He had planned to direct a different film with the same name; he did not plan to direct this film and then back out.
match_headline: Jerome Hellman, Producer of ‘Midnight Cowboy,’ Dies at 92

text: An article on Thursday about a report in ProPublica that detailed how the richest Americans avoid paying taxes, referred incorrectly to a Democratic tax proposal on inheritances. They want to strengthen the tax on inherited estates by taxing the unrealized capital gains on a person’s assets, not by fixing the price of inheritances at their value when a wealthy person dies.
match_headline: An Exposé Has Congress Rethinking How to Tax the Superrich

text: An article on Saturday about the challenges that police departments are facing in retaining and recruiting officers misstated Maria Haberfeld’s position at the John Jay College of Criminal Justice in New York. She is a professor of police science, not a professor of political science.
match_headline: Departures of Police Officers Accelerated During a Year of Protests

text: An article on Friday about Yugo enthusiasts misstated the model year of a Yugo GV that had been listed for sale by Hollywood Motors. It was from 1988, not 1998.
match_headline: They Love the Car That People Love to Hate

text: An obituary on Thursday about the landscape architect Cornelia Hahn Oberlander misstated the relationship of Walter Gropius, a leader of the Bauhaus movement, to Harvard’s Graduate School of Design. He taught there; he was not its founder.
match_headline: Cornelia Oberlander, a Farsighted Landscape Architect, Dies at 99

text: An obituary on June 4 about the behavioral psychologist Arthur Staats misstated the name of the journal that reported on a survey of how many parents relied on the time out, a concept he developed, to moderate the behavior of their children. It is Academic Pediatrics, not American Pediatrics.
match_headline: Arthur Staats Dies at 97; Called ‘Time Out’ for Unruly Kids

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Richard Baron, the former publisher of the Dial Press, misstated the surname of an author whose work he published. He was Frank Yerby, not Yerba. It also rendered incompletely the name of a novel by Mr. Yerby. It is “The Foxes of Harrow,” not “Foxes of Harrow.”
match_headline: Richard Baron, Who Published Baldwin and Mailer, Dies at 98

text: An article on Tuesday about the impact of recently passed voting legislation on people with disabilities misstated the given name of a Wisconsin state senator. He is Rob Cowles, not Ron Cowles. The article also included outdated descriptions of two bills in Wisconsin that had since been amended. The amended proposals would restrict who could return voters’ ballots on their behalf and weaken accommodations for “indefinitely confined” voters, but would not forbid voters with family in-state to have a person outside of their family return their ballot or require indefinitely confined voters to provide photo identification in all cases.
match_headline: G.O.P. Bills Rattle Disabled Voters: ‘We Don’t Have a Voice Anymore’

text: An article on Wednesday about Texas’ power grid referred incorrectly to the Comanche Peak nuclear power plant. Comanche Peak is one of several nuclear power plants in Texas; it is not the only one.
match_headline: Texas Power Grid, Strained Last Winter, Now Faces an Early Heat Wave

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about President Biden’s selection of Chesley B. Sullenberger III as the country’s aviation ambassador misstated which body is composed of 36 member states. It is the Council of the International Civil Aviation Organization, not the International Civil Aviation Organization.
match_headline: Biden Selects Sullenberger for Aviation Ambassadorship

text: An article on Wednesday about a trade deal between Britain and Australia referred incorrectly to the increase in gross domestic product the deal would yield for Britain’s economy. It would be an increase of about $700 million, not $700 billion.
match_headline: Britain Signs Its First Major Post-Brexit Trade Deal With Australia

text: An article on Saturday about leak investigations involving Apple and Google, using information from Apple, misstated the number of times the Justice Department renewed a gag order on its subpoena. The order was renewed twice, not three times.
match_headline: In Leak Investigation, Tech Giants Are Caught Between Courts and Customers

text: An article last Thursday about Phexxi, a new form of birth control, misstated the surname of a founder and the chief executive of LOOM. She is Erica Chidi, not Chidu.
match_headline: Menstrual Cups in Museums? It’s Time.

text: An article on Thursday about an affordable housing crisis in the United States misstated the surname of the managing director of the Legal Aid Society of Columbus, Ohio. She is Melissa Benson, not Melissa Dutton.
match_headline: The U.S. Averted One Housing Crisis, but Another Is in the Wings

text: An article on Friday about a space launch in China referred incorrectly to senior political and military leaders who watched the launch on Thursday. Some were in Beijing; not all were at the space launch center near Jiuquan.
match_headline: As Astronauts Dock, China Takes Up Long-Term Residence in Orbit

text: An article on Thursday about Juneteenth becoming a federal holiday misstated the number of border states that were not affected by the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863. There were four, not three.
match_headline: House Passes Bill to Make Juneteenth a Federal Holiday, Sending It to Biden

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a potential pill to treat Covid-19 misstated the availability of Tamiflu in the United States. Although its maker has secured the rights to sell it over the counter, it still requires a prescription.
match_headline: A Pill to Treat Covid-19? The U.S. Is Betting on It.

text: An article on Thursday about the Southern Baptist Convention described incorrectly one of the votes at the convention. Messengers voted to reject proposed revisions to governing documents, not to the budget.
match_headline: Southern Baptist Vote Signals Further Fractures in American Evangelicalism

text: An article on the cover this weekend about efforts to draw tourists to Roosevelt Island misidentifies the bridge that goes to the island. It is the Roosevelt Island Bridge, not the Queensboro Bridge.
match_headline: Why This Overlooked Residential Island in N.Y.C. Wants Tourists

text: An article on Friday about the return of in-person theater misstated the title of a forthcoming musical by Michael R. Jackson. It is “White Girl in Danger,” not “White Girls in Danger.”
match_headline: A Guide to Theater Festivals in New York and the Berkshires

text: A picture caption this weekend on Page 13 with an interview with the sprinter Allyson Felix misidentifies two members of the 4x400 team from the Rio de Janeiro Olympics in 2016. They are, from left to right, Phyllis Francis, Natasha Hastings, Courtney Okolo, and Ms. Felix.
match_headline: Allyson Felix Knows What Really Makes the Olympics Run

text: An essay on Thursday about corporate contributions to members of Congress described incorrectly contributions by Morgan Stanley’s PAC. It indefinitely suspended contributions to the 147 Republicans who voted to overturn the 2020 presidential election results; it never suspended contributions entirely.
match_headline: Corporate America Forgives the Sedition Caucus

text: An article on June 6 about the Venice Architecture Biennale included comments from the curator Hala Wardé that described incorrectly a structure in Lebanon’s Pavilion. That work uses new glass to evoke the destruction from the blast that devastated Beirut in 2020, not glass from the blast.
match_headline: Solving the World’s Problems at the Venice Architecture Biennale

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about unusual baby names misstated the date Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, announced the birth of their second child. It was June 6, not May 6.
match_headline: Lilith, Lilibet … Lucifer? How Baby Names Went to ‘L’

text: An article last Sunday about a property for sale in the West Village misspelled the name of the fashion brand that designed Jill Biden’s inauguration outfit. It is Markarian, not Makarian.
match_headline: A West Village Home With a Gated Courtyard Is Up for Sale

text: An article on May 2 about the human life span misidentified Norman Heatley’s professional field. He was a biochemist by training, not an engineer.
match_headline: How Humanity Gave Itself an Extra Life

text: An article on Tuesday about the increasing irrelevance of the Republican Party in some major U.S. cities referred incorrectly to Darrell Issa’s departure from his House seat in 2018. He declined to run for re-election; he was not defeated.
match_headline: When It Comes to Big City Elections, Republicans Are in the Wilderness

text: An article on Sunday about money laundering in art deals omitted attribution in a discussion of a legal dispute between Dmitry E. Rybolovlev and Yves Bouvier as to whether Mr. Bouvier was acting as an art adviser or independent seller of art works. Mr. Rybolovlev’s position was drawn from court filings.
match_headline: As Money Launderers Buy Dalís, U.S. Looks at Lifting the Veil on Art Sales

text: An article on Tuesday about the Supreme Court’s decision in National Collegiate Athletic Association v. Alston to allow relatively modest payments to student-athletes misstated the role that the economist Andy Schwarz played in the case. He consulted with Shawne Alston’s legal team; he did not testify in support of Mr. Alston.
match_headline: Ruling Dings N.C.A.A., but It Keeps Rule-Making Power

text: An article last Wednesday about the chef Martin Yan described incorrectly the television stations on which the shows “Yan Can Cook” and “Simply Ming” aired. They were public television stations, which include PBS member stations, and not solely PBS member stations. In addition, the article misstated the station KQED’s relationship to PBS. It is a member station, not an affiliate.
match_headline: Four Decades on, Martin Yan Faces a New Audience and a New World

text: An article on Wednesday about documents revealing that four Saudis who participated in the killing of Jamal Khashoggi received paramilitary training in the United States referred imprecisely to Louis Bremer’s nomination for a Pentagon position. Mr. Bremer’s nomination never received a Senate vote and expired at the end of President Donald J. Trump’s term; it was not withdrawn.
match_headline: Saudi Operatives Who Killed Khashoggi Received Paramilitary Training in U.S.

text: An article on Wednesday about the shift away from mass vaccination centers misidentified the city in which the Federal Emergency Management Agency is beginning a pilot program to offer coronavirus vaccinations at a disaster recovery center. The program is in Lake Charles, part of Calcaseiu Parish, where only 38 percent of the adult population has had at least one shot, not St. Charles Parish, La., where 51 percent has.
match_headline: With Mass Vaccination Sites Winding Down, It’s All About the ‘Ground Game’

text: An article on Wednesday about Alvin Bragg’s lead in the Democratic primary for Manhattan district attorney referred incorrectly to a court on which Tali Farhadian Weinstein clerked. It was the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, not the Washington, D.C., Court of Appeals.
match_headline: Bragg Holds Lead in Manhattan District Attorney Primary

text: An article on Tuesday about Lordstown Motors, an electric-vehicle start-up, misstated Ford Motor’s plans for an electric F-150 pickup truck. The model is expected to go into production next year, not this year.
match_headline: Lordstown Motors Opens Up Its Electric Truck Factory to Show Progress

text: An article on Wednesday about the U.S. seizure of websites linked to Iran misidentified the language displayed alongside English on a banner announcing the seizure of Press TV’s website. It was Arabic, not Persian.
match_headline: U.S. Seizes Iran-Linked Websites at Key Point in Nuclear Talks

text: An article last Thursday about Paul Skallas, a proponent of the Lindy Effect, a current way of living based on wisdom of the ancient past, misstated the century in which Petrarch wrote. It was the 14th century, not the 13th. The article also misspelled the surname of a Harvard professor. He is Joseph Henrich, not Heinrich.
match_headline: The Lindy Way of Living

text: An article last Thursday about the runway show for Ferrari’s first high-fashion collection misspelled the name of one of the companies where Rocco Iannone, the creative director of Ferrari, worked previously. It is Pal Zileri, not Zilieri.
match_headline: Ferrari Is Racing Into Fashion

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Richard Stolley, the founding editor of People magazine, misstated the name of the Illinois newspaper where he worked as a teenager. It is The Pekin Daily Times, not The Pekin Sun Times.
match_headline: Richard Stolley, Founding Editor of People Magazine, Dies at 92

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the chemist Ei-ichi Negishi misstated when the chemist Herbert C. Brown, of whom Dr. Negishi said, “In terms of research, he is my only mentor,” won the Nobel Prize. It was 1979, not 2004.
ref_headline: In terms of research, he is my only mentor,
match_headline: Ei-ichi Negishi, Nobel Prize Winner in Chemistry, Dies at 85

text: An article on Monday about parliamentary elections in Ethiopia misstated the time in November when Senator Chris Coons of Delaware warned Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed of Ethiopia about the perils of using military force in Tigray. Senator Coons said he had spoken to Mr. Ahmed in late November, not early November.
match_headline: From Nobel Hero to Driver of War, Ethiopia’s Leader Faces Voters

text: An article on June 20 about the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention misidentified the act of Congress that funded electronic medical-record systems. It was the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, not the Affordable Care Act of 2010.
match_headline: Covid Proved the C.D.C. Is Broken. Can It Be Fixed?

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the chef and restaurateur Mark Peel misstated the year he and his wife, Daphne Brogdon, separated. It was 2019, not 2017.
match_headline: Mark Peel, Who Helped Forge a New Culinary Path, Dies at 66

text: An article last Sunday about a lawsuit claiming that Subway’s tuna sandwiches do not contain tuna referred incorrectly to the preparation of pale tuna. It is seared and left raw in the middle; the middle is not thrown out. The article also described incorrectly the manner by which a P.C.R. test identifies an organism. It is by its DNA, not its protein.
match_headline: The Big Tuna Sandwich Mystery

text: An article last Sunday about Gerald Stratford, a gardener in England who has built a large Twitter following, misidentified the vegetable pictured in one of Mr. Stratford’s tweets. It is a bundle of rocket potatoes, not arugula.
match_headline: Gerald Stratford Knows How to Garden

text: An article on Saturday about Manhattan landmarks that honor Chinese Americans and Native Americans misidentified the city department that maintains the Kimlau War Memorial and the similarly named plaza. It is the parks department, not the police department.
match_headline: City Approves Landmarks Honoring Chinese Americans and Native Americans

text: An article on Saturday about the violinist Randall Goosby misstated the name of the composer who wrote the version of “Deep River” on the album “Roots.” He is Samuel Coleridge-Taylor, not Samuel Taylor-Coleridge.
match_headline: For a Major Debut, a Young Violinist Gets Personal

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the art curator Diego Cortez referred incorrectly at one point to his work with the singer-songwriter and poet Patti Smith. He mounted shows of her drawings and photographs in the early 2000s, not in the late ’70s and early ’80s.
match_headline: Diego Cortez, a Scene Shaper in Art and Music, Dies at 74

text: An article on Tuesday about a federal judge’s decision to throw out two antitrust lawsuits against Facebook misspelled the surname of a former chairman of the Federal Trade Commission. He is William E. Kovacic, not Kovacich.
match_headline: Judge Throws Out 2 Antitrust Cases Against Facebook

text: An article last Wednesday about American Chinese food misstated the location of the New York City restaurant Nice Day Chinese Takeout. It is in Greenwich Village, not the West Village.
match_headline: More Than ‘Just Takeout’

text: An article on Wednesday about the decision by Representative James Clyburn of South Carolina to endorse Shontel Brown for Congress misstated which House Democratic leaders had agreed to vacate their posts after this Congress. Although Speaker Nancy Pelosi initially considered a deal with limits on all three of the top Democratic leaders, the deal ultimately applied only to her, not all three.
match_headline: No. 3 House Democrat Steps Into Ohio Race to Head Off a Sanders Acolyte

text: An article on Tuesday about what to expect as ranked-choice results were released for the New York City mayoral election described incorrectly the lawmaker who Jean Quan defeated in the 2010 mayoral race in Oakland, Calif. While he was indeed the front-runner, he was not the incumbent.
match_headline: What to Expect as Early Ranked-Choice Results Are Released in New York

text: An article on last Thursday about the group stage of Euro 2020 referred incorrectly to potential quarterfinal opponents of three teams. England and Germany could have played Sweden or Ukraine in the quarterfinals, not Croatia. Belgium could have faced Italy or Austria, not France.
match_headline: The Euro 2020 Group Stage Is Over: Here’s What We Learned

text: An article last Thursday about photographs of abandoned houses misidentified the state where Margaret Dewar’s husband grew up. It was Minnesota, not Michigan.
match_headline: The Abandoned Houses of Instagram

text: An obituary on June 20 about Madeline Davis, the first openly lesbian delegate to a national political convention in the United States, misquoted a line from “Stonewall Nation,” a song she wrote. It is “You can take your tolerance and shove it” — not “your intolerance.”
match_headline: Madeline Davis, Who Spoke to the Nation as a Lesbian, Dies at 80

text: An article on Thursday about Chow Po Chung, a Hong Kong professor and political philosopher who has seen several of his students jailed for political activism, referred incorrectly to the status of Gwyneth Ho’s case. She is waiting for her trial, not her sentencing.
match_headline: Hong Kong Philosopher Taught Life’s Meaning. Now He Visits Students in Jail.

text: An article on June 22 about teenagers on the U.S. Olympic swim team participating in the Tokyo Games erroneously attributed a distinction to Lydia Jacoby. While she is the first Olympic swimmer to be born in Alaska, she is the 10th Summer Games participant — not the second — who was born there.
match_headline: U.S. Swim Team Will Take 11 Teenagers to Tokyo Olympics

text: A review on Thursday of “America: The Motion Picture” misidentified the document George Washington signed. It was the Constitution, not the Declaration of Independence.
match_headline: ‘America: The Motion Picture’ Review: In Bros We Trust

text: An article on Monday about a meeting between Israel’s foreign minister, Yair Lapid, and Secretary of State Antony J. Blinken incorrectly described management of the Temple Mount. The area is administered by an Islamic trust known as the Waqf, funded and controlled by Jordan. It is not managed by Israel.
match_headline: Meeting Blinken, Israel’s Top Diplomat Aims to Fix Netanyahu ‘Mistakes’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about an inquiry delayed by Joseph V. Cuffari, the inspector general in the Department of Homeland Security, misstated Mr. Cuffari’s former position at the Justice Department. He worked for 20 years in the department’s Office of Inspector General; he was not an inspector general for 20 years.
match_headline: Homeland Security Watchdog Delayed Inquiry, Complaint Says

text: A picture caption with a cover story this weekend about visitors returning to the city misidentifies a park. The image shows people seated on the grass in North Fifth Street Pier and Park, not Domino Park.
match_headline: How Basquiat and Street Artists Left Their Mark on Hip-Hop Culture

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 38 this weekend about state laws regulating education refers imprecisely to the prisoners held at Perm-36, a notorious “special regime” camp for political prisoners in Russia. The population of prisoners was disproportionately Ukrainian, not just mostly Ukrainian.
match_headline: The War on History Is a War on Democracy

text: An article on June 27 about childhood obesity and the pandemic misstated the number of children between the ages of 2 and 17 who had their body mass index measured during visits to the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia Care Network. It was about 300,000, not more than 500,000.
match_headline: The Pandemic Seems to Have Made Childhood Obesity Worse, but There’s Hope

text: An article on June 27 about the potential for wind-powered cargo ships referred incorrectly to the views of the International Chamber of Shipping. The chamber endorses a carbon tax. It is not the case that it supports a levy instead of a carbon tax.
match_headline: Can Massive Cargo Ships Use Wind to Go Green?

text: An article on Friday about President Biden’s plan to increase electric car sales referred imprecisely to the mileage rating of the Ford F-150. While the hybrid version gets roughly 25 miles to the gallon, the basic model gets only about 20 miles per gallon.
match_headline: Here’s How Biden Aims to Increase Electric Car Sales

text: An article last Sunday about the cryonics industry misspelled the name of a Russian cryopreservation company. It is KrioRus, not KryoRus.
match_headline: The Cryonics Industry Would Like to Give You the Past Year, and Many More, Back

text: An article last Sunday about moneymaking pandemic hobbies misstated the name of a gardening company. It is PlantParenthood, not PlantParent.
match_headline: My Pandemic Hobby? Making Money.

text: An article on Wednesday about a gun violence emergency in New York State declared by Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo misstated the number of jobs available at the start New York City’s summer jobs program this year. It is 75,000, not 7,500.
match_headline: Cuomo Declares a Gun Violence Emergency in New York State

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the reopening of cabaret venues in New York City misstated the surname of a performer. He is George Salazar, not George Lazarus.
match_headline: With Venues Reopening Across New York, Life Is a Cabaret Once Again

text: An article on Thursday about an attack in Afghanistan by the Taliban misstated the day on which the Taliban broke into a jail in Badghis Province. It was Wednesday, as noted elsewhere in the article, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Taliban Attack a Provincial Capital in Afghanistan’s North, Freeing Prisoners

text: An article on Thursday about an antitrust suit filed against Google misidentified the given name of the company’s director of public policy. He is Wilson White, not William.
match_headline: Dozens of States Sue Google Over App Store Fees

text: An obituary on Sunday about the singer and guitarist Ellen McIlwaine referred incorrectly to her parents. They were Southern Presbyterian missionaries, not Methodist missionaries.
match_headline: Ellen McIlwaine, Slide Guitarist With a Power Voice, Dies at 75

text: An article on Friday about Pope Francis’s surgery misstated Francis’s age when he became pope. He was 76, not 78.
match_headline: Will Surgery Slow Down (or Speed Up) a Pope Who’s in a Hurry?

text: An article on Thursday about former President Donald J. Trump’s lawsuit against Facebook, Twitter and Google misidentified the legal provision that lets social media companies remove posts that violate their standards. It is the First Amendment, not Section 230.
match_headline: Trump sues tech firms for blocking him, and fund-raises off it.

text: An article on Thursday about the musical “Waitress” returning to Broadway misstated the given name of the book writer for the musical “Waitress.” She is Jessie Nelson, not Jennie.
match_headline: ‘Waitress’ Is Returning to Broadway. So Is Sara Bareilles.

text: An article on Page 40 this weekend about for-profit autopsy services misstates how Jay Eisinger heard the verdict in his son Christopher’s case. He listened via cellphone. He was not sitting in the courtroom.
match_headline: The Police Called It an Accident. She Turned to 1-800-Autopsy.

text: An article on June 27 about Hurricane Dorian’s impact on the Bahamas described incorrectly the building of domes to temporarily house people whose homes were destroyed by the storm. The National Emergency Management Agency contracted the construction of the domes, and the Disaster Reconstruction Authority oversaw the construction of some of them. The authority did not contract the construction of the domes. And the cost of building the domes was part of a $6.4 million relief package. The domes did not cost $6 million to build.
match_headline: Climate Change Is Destroying My Country. The Nations Causing It Must Help.

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the geneticist Richard C. Lewontin misstated the percentage of genetic variability between human populations determined by research conducted by Dr. Lewontin and other scientists in 1972. It is 7 percent, not 15 percent.
match_headline: Richard C. Lewontin, Eminent Geneticist With a Sharp Pen, Dies at 92

text: An article last Sunday about masks as a signifier of social class misspelled the surname of a public relations strategist who was recently shopping in Hudson Yards. He is Mark Pasetsky, not Pasektsky.
match_headline: Are Masks a New Signifier of Social Class?

text: An article last Sunday about a couple seeking an apartment in Manhattan misstated the net-effective rent for the one-bedroom apartment in Chelsea. It was $4,511 a month, not $4,060.

An article on Saturday about a group of scientists who argue against the theory that the coronavirus was leaked from a lab misspelled the city with the first known SARS cases. It is Shenzhen, not Shenzen.
match_headline: A Group of Scientists Presses a Case Against the Lab Leak Theory of Covid

text: An article on Friday about an agreement between 15 states and Purdue Pharma misstated Pennsylvania’s position on the new agreement, in one instance. The state is among the 15 supporting the deal; it is not among the states opposing it.
match_headline: 15 States Reach a Deal With Purdue Pharma, Advancing a $4.5 Billion Opioids Settlement

text: An article on Saturday about the retirement of Brig. Gen. Mark S. Martins, who has led war crimes prosecutions at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, misstated the position that Michael O’Sullivan is serving in the military commissions system. It is acting chief prosecutor, not acting chief defense counsel. The article also misstated when the defendants in the case stemming from the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks were arraigned. It was May 2012, not May 2011.
match_headline: Chief Guantánamo Prosecutor Retiring Before Sept. 11 Trial Begins

text: An article on Sunday about questions surrounding guardianship spurred by Britney Spears’s legal case misstated the number of guardians certified by the Center for Guardianship Certification. It is 1,500, not 15,000.
match_headline: Britney Spears’s Case Calls Attention to Wider Questions on Guardianship

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about the men’s singles semifinals at Wimbledon misstated an achievement by Matteo Berrettini. As the article correctly noted, he became the first Italian, man or woman, to reach a Wimbledon singles final, not any Grand Slam final.
match_headline: Novak Djokovic Wins Wimbledon, and His 20th Career Grand Slam Title

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a chant popular among protesters in Cuba misspelled the surname of Cuba’s president. He is Miguel Díaz-Canel, not Díaz-Canal.
match_headline: ‘Patria y Vida’ — Homeland and Life — Watchwords in Cuba’s Protests

text: An article on Wednesday about a defaced mural of the soccer player Marcus Rashford misspelled the name of a Manchester suburb cited by Mr. Rashford in a statement posted to Twitter. It is Wythenshawe, not Wythershawe.
match_headline: A Manchester Mural Was Defaced by Racist Graffiti. Soccer Fans Rushed to Fix It.

text: An article on Wednesday about the Texas legislature’s battle over a Republican-sponsored bill that would overhaul the state’s election system misstated the legislative chamber from which Texas Democrats walked out of to block the bill. It was the House, not the Senate.
match_headline: Texas Lawmakers, Dueling 1,300 Miles Apart, Map Out Next Voting Moves

text: An article on Wednesday about New York City’s plan to move the homeless misidentified the federal court district where Judge Gregory Howard Woods sits. It is the Southern District of New York in Manhattan, not the Eastern District of New York in Brooklyn.
match_headline: N.Y.C.’s Plan to Move Homeless People From Hotels Is Blocked by a Judge

text: An article on Wednesday about Germany’s plan for autonomous vehicles misidentified one of the cities where Volkswagen is testing Moia, a ride-hailing service. It is Hanover, not Berlin.
match_headline: How Germany Hopes to Get the Edge in Driverless Technology

text: An article on Tuesday about Game 3 of the N.B.A. finals misstated the outcome of Game 4 of the Milwaukee Bucks’ semifinal series against the Nets. Milwaukee won that game and lost Game 5.
match_headline: In Game 3, Antetokounmpo Didn’t Do All of the Work

text: An article on Wednesday about the artist Keioui Keijaun Thomas misstated part of a quotation by the curator Shehab Isis Awad. She said, “We’re not gonna wait any longer for someone to throw a party for us,” not “give a party for us.”
ref_headline: We’re not gonna wait any longer for someone to throw a party for us,
match_headline: For Keioui Keijaun Thomas, the Body Becomes a Vessel

text: A picture caption with an obituary on June 24 about the Native American spiritual leader Leonard Crow Dog misidentified the two people in a photograph with him. His father, Henry Crow Dog, is on the right, and Chief Frank Fools Crow is in the center — not vice versa.
match_headline: Leonard Crow Dog, Spiritual Leader at Wounded Knee, Dies at 78

text: An article on Friday about “Hansken, Rembrandt’s Elephant,” an exhibition at the Rembrandt House Museum in Amsterdam, referred imprecisely to the food in the biblical story of Adam and Eve. It was a forbidden fruit, not a poisoned apple.
match_headline: When Rembrandt Met an Elephant

text: An article this weekend on Page 6 about the ballerina Georgina Pazcoguin misstates one of her distinctions. She was New York City Ballet’s first female Asian American soloist, not the first Asian American soloist.
match_headline: A ‘Rogue Ballerina’ Gives a Candid Account of Ballet Culture

text: An essay last Sunday on recreational drug use in the United States described Portugal’s and Switzerland’s policies on it incorrectly. Portugal has decriminalized the use of recreational drugs, and Switzerland has done the same in some circumstances. Neither country has legalized the drugs themselves.
match_headline: How Should We Do Drugs Now?

text: A headline last Sunday referred incorrectly to recent fashion shows in Paris. They were part of the first post-pandemic in-person couture week, not fashion week.
match_headline: Falling for Couture’s Gravitational Pull

text: Because of an editing error, the Letters column on July 4 misidentified the address of a letter writer, Arthur Caplan. He lives in Ridgefield, Conn., not Rockville, Md.
match_headline: Cicadas, Average Human Lifespan and Other Letters to the Editor

text: An article on Friday about a new policy to increase diversity in the Boston school system misspelled the surname of a man who recently graduated from Boston Latin School. He is Ben Hofmann, not Hoffman.
match_headline: Boston Overhauls Admissions to Exclusive Exam Schools

text: An article on Monday about Collin Morikawa’s victory at the British Open misstated the number of major tournaments Tiger Woods has won in his golf career. It is 15, not 14.
match_headline: Collin Morikawa Wins the British Open in His First Appearance

text: An obituary on July 13 about Edwin W. Edwards, the former four-term governor of Louisiana, misstated the number of times he lost an election. It was twice, in 1987 and 2014, not once. The obituary also misstated when Mr. Edwards said he could not lose an election unless he was “caught in bed with either a dead girl or a live boy.” It was in 1983, before he was elected to a third term as governor — not in 1991, after he won a fourth team by defeating David Duke.
ref_headline: caught in bed with either a dead girl or a live boy.
match_headline: Edwin Edwards, Flamboyant Louisiana Governor, Is Dead at 93

text: An article on Monday about the effects of climate change on winemaking in Napa Valley misidentified a site where tanker trucks take on treated wastewater for use in vineyards. It is a Napa Sanitation District facility, not a City of Napa sanitation department facility. (The Napa Sanitation District is run jointly by the city and the county, and covers the city as well as several adjacent county areas.)
match_headline: Scorched, Parched and Now Uninsurable: Climate Change Hits Wine Country

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the Bootleg Fire in Oregon misstated the size of the Carr Fire in California in 2018. It burned about 230,000 acres, not 130,000 acres.
match_headline: How Bad Is the Bootleg Fire? It’s Generating Its Own Weather.

text: An article on Monday about volunteers in Germany leading the recovery from a devastating flood there misstated the name of a German relief agency. It is the Technisches Hilfswerk, not the Technisches Helfswerke. The article also misspelled the given name of the operator of the Caspari Hotel. She is Stefanie Nelles, not Stephanie.
match_headline: Neighbor Helping Neighbor, German Volunteers Lead Flood Recovery

text: An article on Tuesday about Peru’s presidential election misstated the amount of time that passed between the second round and the announcement of the results. It was more than a month, not nearly a month. The article also undercounted the final vote tally of the winning candidate, Pedro Castillo, by 100 votes. Mr. Castillo was 44,263 votes ahead of the losing candidate, with a total of 8,836,380 votes.
match_headline: Pedro Castillo, Leftist Political Outsider, Wins Peru Presidency

text: An article on Saturday about ruling by a federal judge in Texas that found the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program unlawful misidentified the method President Barack Obama used to create it. He did so through an executive action, not an executive order. Because of an editing error, the article also described incorrectly how current DACA recipients are affected by a court ruling. The judge allowed renewals to proceed; he did not temporarily bar their approval.
match_headline: Judge Rules DACA Is Unlawful and Suspends Applications

text: An article on Sunday about disagreement in the Asian American community over strategies to address bias crimes misstated the number of bias crimes against African Americans in California last year. According to a report released by the state attorney general’s office, there were 456, not 875.
match_headline: Fear, and Discord, Among Asian Americans Over Attacks in San Francisco

text: An article on Tuesday about the history of Indigenous boarding schools misidentified the location of Grand Junction Indian School. It was in western Colorado, not central Colorado. Because of an editing error, the article described imprecisely the location of Fort Lewis College. While the school was outside Durango when it opened, its current campus is within the city.
match_headline: Lost Lives, Lost Culture: The Forgotten History of Indigenous Boarding Schools

text: An article on Sunday about a focus on climate policy in Germany following major flooding misspelled the surname of the governor of Rhineland-Palatinate State. She is Malu Dreyer, not Dryer.
match_headline: Floods Thrust Climate Change to Center of German Campaign as Toll Mounts

text: An article on Wednesday about a climate law passed in France misstated when the Yellow Vest protests, which prompted President Emmanuel Macron to convene a climate convention, first started. It was 2018, not 2019.
match_headline: France Passes Climate Law, but Critics Say It Falls Short

text: An article on Monday about a renewed mask mandate misstated the percentage of Los Angeles County residents who were fully vaccinated against the coronavirus. Fifty-two percent were, not 61 percent.
match_headline: Wary and Weary, Los Angeles Largely Accepts Restored Mask Mandate

text: An article last Thursday about the debut of the Pyer Moss couture collection, using information from the company, misstated where the creations will be sold. Negotiations with an art gallery are still in progress.
match_headline: A Black American Designer Disrupts the French Couture

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the author Carol Easton misstated the disease that ended the career of the cellist Jacqueline du Pré, whose biography Ms. Easton wrote. It was multiple sclerosis, not cerebral palsy.
match_headline: Carol Easton, Biographer of Arts Figures, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Tuesday about John P. McMeel, the founder of the newspaper syndicate Andrews McMeel Universal, misstated when the company changed its name from Universal Press Syndicate. It was the late 1990s, not the late 1980s. (This error also appeared in May in an obituary about the Andrews McMeel executive Kathleen Andrews.)
match_headline: John P. McMeel, Newspaper Syndicator With a Difference, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on July 14 about the artist Jane Kaufman misstated what degree she received from Hunter College in 1965. It was an M.A., not an M.F.A.
match_headline: Jane Kaufman, Artist Who Celebrated Women’s Work, Dies at 83

text: An article on Thursday about Martine Moïse’s return to Haiti after being wounded in the attack that killed her husband, President Jovenel Moïse, misstated Ms. Moïse’s remarks about her husband’s funeral. As the article correctly pointed out elsewhere, she said that her family would pay for the funeral and that public funds would not be sought. She did not say that public money would be used.
match_headline: Mourning Haitians Console Martine Moïse, Widow of the Slain President

text: An article on Thursday about the questions on coronavirus testing raised by positive tests for dozens of people with Olympic credentials misstated the number of vaccinated Texas legislators who were infected with the coronavirus in Washington. It is six, not five.
match_headline: Olympics Virus Cases Raise Tricky Questions About Testing

text: An article on Tuesday about the idea of restoring the human intestinal microbiome to an ancestral state misstated a researcher’s chronic medical condition. It is ulcerative colitis, not irritable bowel disease (the medical term is irritable bowel syndrome).
match_headline: You’re Missing Microbes. But Is ‘Rewilding’ the Way to Get Them Back?

text: An article on Friday about flooded subways misidentified the nonprofit organization where Bernardo Baranda Sepúlveda works as a researcher. It is the Institute for Transportation and Development Policy, not the Institute for Transport Development.
match_headline: Climate Crisis Turns World’s Subways Into Flood Zones

text: An article on Friday about a libel case defeat for the British far-right activist Tommy Robinson misstated the age of the plaintiff, Jamal Hijazi. He is now 18, not 17.
match_headline: Teen Wins Libel Case Against Tommy Robinson, U.K. Far-Right Activist

text: An article on Friday about a New York police sergeant who faces criminal charges for attacking two handcuffed suspects misstated, based on inaccurate information from the Manhattan district attorney’s office, the surname of an assistant district attorney who appeared in court. She is Carolina Nevin, not Nevins.
match_headline: An Officer Was Taunted and Spit At. Now He Faces Criminal Charges.

text: An article on Friday about a delay by Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon in scheduling a hearing for President Biden’s nominee to run U.S. Customs and Border Protection referred incorrectly to George Floyd’s death. He died after being pinned to the ground under the knee of a police officer; he was not shot by the police.
match_headline: A Democratic senator is bottling up Biden’s Customs and Border Protection nominee.

text: An article on Friday about the music scene in Ditmas Park misstated the given name of a musician involved in the music programs. He is Aidan Scrimgeour, not Aaron.
match_headline: The Music Scene in This Brooklyn Neighborhood Is Here to Stay

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about a staging of “Don Giovanni” refers incorrectly to the orchestra MusicAeterna’s recent activities at the Salzburg Festival in Austria. The ensemble did not play both Mozart’s “La Clemenza di Tito” and “Idomeneo”; it played only “La Clemenza di Tito.” The Freiburg Baroque Orchestra performed “Idomeneo.”
match_headline: At Salzburg, Don Giovanni Gets No Pleasure From Seducing

text: An article on Page 10 this weekend about auctioned items from Carol Channing’s estate misstates the year that David Turner listened obsessively to the “Free to Be You and Me” album. It was 1977, not 1972, the year the album was released.
ref_headline: Free to Be You and Me
match_headline: Goodbye, Dolly: With Their Bids, Fans Hold Onto Carol Channing

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 12 this weekend about the Chilean photographer Sergio Larrain misspells the name of a location in Chile. It is Puerto Montt, not Puerto Monti.
match_headline: Stumbling Upon Greatness: Discovering Sergio Larrain

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 28 this weekend about genetically modified foods refers imprecisely to glyphosate. It is a herbicide, a type of pesticide.
match_headline: Learning to Love G.M.O.s

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about Toyota’s resistance to electric vehicles, using information from a photo agency, misidentified a Toyota vehicle outfitted for the Tokyo Olympics. It is a Prius, not a Mirai.
match_headline: Toyota Led on Clean Cars. Now Critics Say It Works to Delay Them.

text: An article on Friday about Svetlana Tikhanovskaya, the exiled Belarus opposition leader, misstated the action taken against the opposition politician Valery Tsepkalo before the election in Belarus last year. While he was barred from running, he was not jailed.
match_headline: Pulling Levers in Exile, Belarus Opposition Leader Works to Keep Her Influence Alive

text: An article on Sunday about Big Oil in Nigeria misstated the surname of a spokesman for the Gbaramatu Kingdom. He is Godspower Gbenekama, not Benekama.
match_headline: The Fisherwomen, Chevron and the Leaking Pipe

text: An article on Saturday about Dr. Joseph Mercola, an osteopathic physician, referred incorrectly to the outcome of regulatory actions against Dr. Mercola. He paid millions of dollars in refunds to customers as a result of a settlement with the Federal Trade Commission; he was not fined millions of dollars by the Food and Drug Administration.
match_headline: The Most Influential Spreader of Coronavirus Misinformation Online

text: An article on Monday about fatal car crashes in the New York area misspelled the surname of two brothers killed in a collision on the Hamptons this weekend. They were Michael and James Farrell, not Farell.
match_headline: 5 Dead in Hamptons Crash That Is Blamed on Speeding

text: An article on Saturday about the completion of the human genome misstated when scientists determined the correct number of human chromosomes. It was in the 1960s, not a century ago.
match_headline: Scientists Finish the Human Genome at Last

text: An article on Monday about Phil Valentine, a conservative radio host who contracted the coronavirus, misidentified the date when Mr. Valentine announced his Covid-19 diagnosis. It was July 11, not June 11.
match_headline: After Covid Diagnosis, a Conservative Radio Host Sends a New Message

text: An article on Monday about a declining interest in investment banking as a career choice among young professionals misidentified the class of a university student. Armen Panossian is a rising senior at Rutgers University, not a rising junior.
match_headline: Rookie Bankers Sour on Wall Street’s Pitch of Big Pay and Long Hours

text: An obituary on July 17 about William H. Regnery II, a reclusive heir to a textile fortune who bankrolled a number of people and organizations behind the rise of the alt-right, referred incorrectly to four of his children. He adopted Robert and William T. Regnery, two of his wife’s children; William F. and David Regnery are his sons from a previous marriage.
match_headline: William H. Regnery II, 80, Dies; Bankrolled the Rise of the Alt-Right

text: An obituary on July 3 about Gen. Tran Thien Khiem, who was second in command to President Nguyen Van Thieu of South Vietnam during the last six years of the Vietnam War, misstated when and where he died. He died on June 23 in the Irvine, Calif., area — not on June 24 in Santa Ana.
match_headline: Tran Thien Khiem, 95, Dies; a Power in South Vietnam Before Its Fall
