text: An article on Tuesday about extreme weather in England misstated part of a warning issued by the Fire Brigade. The Fire Brigade warned that generators used to dry out old buildings could have released carbon monoxide, not carbon dioxide.
match_headline: Floods, Heat, Then Floods Again: England Is Battered by Wild Weather

text: An article on Tuesday about cybersecurity companies that have profited from recent cyberattacks misstated the amount of venture capital raised by a cloud security start-up since its founding. Lacework, the start-up, has raised $558 million across all rounds of funding, not $625 million. The article also misstated the title of a Lacework executive. Andy Byron is the company’s chief revenue officer and president, not its chief resource officer.
match_headline: As Cyberattacks Surge, Security Start-Ups Reap the Rewards

text: An article on Tuesday about the lunar rovers put on the moon during the Apollo missions misspelled the surname of the first American to travel in space. He was Alan Shepard, not Shepherd.
match_headline: 50 Years Ago, NASA Put a Car on the Moon

text: An article on Tuesday about atrial fibrillation described incorrectly the effects of Coumadin and Xarelto, two anticoagulants. Coumadin stays in the system longer and may help to avert a stroke if a patient misses a dose or two, not Xarelto.
match_headline: A Common Heart Problem That’s Easy to Miss

text: An obituary on July 1 about Frieda Fritzshall, who created a Holocaust museum in Illinois, misstated how old she was when she, her mother and two brothers were sent to the Auschwitz concentration camp. She was 14, not 13.
match_headline: Frieda Fritzshall, 91, Dies; Survived to Create a Holocaust Museum

text: An obituary on Monday about the physicist Steven Weinberg, a Nobel laureate, referred incorrectly to a lecture series, titled “On the Shoulders of Giants,” in which he was the inaugural speaker. It was held in 2011, not 2015, and the event, produced by the World Science Festival, took place at New York University, not Columbia University.
match_headline: Steven Weinberg, Groundbreaking Nobelist in Physics, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Friday about the newspaper editor Harry Rosenfeld referred incorrectly to a news conference in which President Richard M. Nixon, in response to a question, famously said, “I’m not a crook.” The question was asked by a member of the White House press corps, not by Mr. Rosenfeld. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated the year Mr. Rosenfeld became editor of the Hearst Corporation’s two newspapers in Albany, The Times Union and the afternoon Knickerbocker News. It was 1978, not 1988.
match_headline: Harry Rosenfeld, Who Saw News in a ‘Third-Rate Burglary,’ Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Sunday and in some copies on Monday about the comedian Jackie Mason contained a number of errors. It referred incorrectly to the circumstances in which he was reported to have used a Yiddish word, considered to be a racial slur, in talking about David N. Dinkins, at the time a Black candidate for mayor of New York City. The comment came in 1989 during a luncheon with Newsweek reporters, not during a banquet at the Plaza hotel in Manhattan. The obituary misstated where Mr. Mason pursued rabbinical studies; he did so at Mesivtha Tifereth Jerusalem of America, a yeshiva in Manhattan, not Yeshiva University, also in Manhattan. It overstated the number of times that Mr. Mason had appeared on the “The Ed Sullivan Show” before his contract with it was canceled after Mr. Mason made what Mr. Sullivan regarded as an obscene gesture onstage; he had appeared on the show about 20 times before then, not “dozens of times.” The obituary omitted two of Mr. Mason’s survivors: a sister, Gail Schulman, and a brother, Rabbi Gabriel Maza. And it was not the case that Mr. Mason’s two younger sisters had married rabbis.
match_headline: Jackie Mason, 93, Dies; Turned Kvetching Into Comedy Gold

text: An article on Tuesday about flooding in China misstated the location of the Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University in China. It is in Suzhou, not Xi’an.
match_headline: As China Boomed, It Didn’t Take Climate Change Into Account. Now It Must.

text: An article on Sunday about Spain’s rejection of some applications for citizenship by descendants of Sephardic Jews expelled during the Spanish Inquisition described incorrectly Sephardim within the context of Europe. They are one of the continent’s main Jewish ethnic divisions, not one of the two Jewish ethnic divisions of Europe.
match_headline: Spain Pledged Citizenship to Sephardic Jews. Now They Feel Betrayed.

text: An article on Monday about a cyclist from the Netherlands who mistakenly thought she won a road race misspelled her given name. She is Annemiek van Vleuten, not Annamiek.
match_headline: She celebrated as if she had won a gold. Except she hadn’t.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the musician and conductor Elliot Lawrence misstated the number of Broadway musicals for which he served as musical director after his work on “How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying.” It was seven, not eight. It also erroneously included “1776” among them. Peter Howard was the musical director of that show, not Mr. Lawrence.
ref_headline: How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying.
match_headline: Elliot Lawrence, Award-Winning Conductor, Dies at 96

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about efforts to revive nuclear talks between the United States and Iran misattributed a remark to Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. While Mr. Khamenei characterized the approach to the nuclear deal by Iran’s outgoing president, Hassan Rouhani, as naïve, he did not call Mr. Rouhani naïve.
match_headline: Khamenei Adds to Doubts on Iran Nuclear Deal Talks

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about deported members of the United States military misstated the name of a mural. It is the Playas de Tijuana Mural Project, not the “Leave No One Behind” mural.
match_headline: Deported Veterans Long to Return From Exile. Some Will Get the Chance.

text: An article on Thursday about the Detroit Pistons misstated the length of Tom Gores’s ownership of the N.B.A. team. He has been the owner since 2011, not 2015.
match_headline: Not ‘Bad Boys’ Anymore, the Pistons Just Want to Be Good Again

text: An article last Sunday about the vogue legend Archie Burnett misspelled the name of a performer. She is Princess Lockerooo, not Princess Lockeroo. The article also referred imprecisely to Burnett. While he has been referred to as the father of the House of Ninja, he now prefers to be known as the grandfather of the house.
match_headline: A Vogue Legend, Still Enlarging Circles of Pleasure

text: An article last Sunday about the increasing popularity of Springs, a hamlet in the Hamptons, misspelled the surname of a homeowner. He is Ross Matsubara, not Mastubara.
match_headline: Is the Hamptons Party Moving to Springs?

text: An essay on July 18 about the Democratic Party in Texas misstated the state’s policy on firearms. Texans have been barred since 1896 from carrying unlicensed handguns in public, not from carrying any unlicensed firearm. It also described incorrectly how some voters in the state receive mail-in ballots. Organizations in Texas may send unsolicited ballot applications, not unsolicited ballots.
match_headline: Texas Should Be a Warning to Democrats Everywhere

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the admiration across Venezuela’s political spectrum for Dr. José Gregorio Hernández, a doctor recently beatified by the Vatican, referred incorrectly to his status in the church. While he has been beatified (putting him on the path to sainthood), he has not yet been canonized and is not yet a saint. The error was repeated in a front page summary.
match_headline: Even the Pope Has Prayed to Venezuela’s Beloved ‘Doctor of the Poor’

text: An article on Saturday about the Government Accountability Office’s rejection of Jeff Bezos’s challenge of NASA’s decision to award a $2.9 billion contract to SpaceX to build the next lunar lander for astronauts misstated the status of Bezos’s bid. His rocket company will not be flying astronauts to the moon at this time; it is not the case that it will.
match_headline: Bezos’ Rocket Company Loses Challenge to NASA SpaceX Moon Contract

text: An article on Saturday about the U.S. military’s efforts to get more service members vaccinated without issuing a mandate misstated when soldiers and their families started a letter-writing campaign against a smallpox vaccine. It was during World War I, not in 1911.
match_headline: Short of the Mandate They Crave, Military Leaders Race to Vaccinate Troops

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the vulnerability of tenants as a federal eviction moratorium ends misspelled the given name of one of Migreldi Lara’s children. Her eight-year-old daughter’s name is Julmeiris, not Julmeiri.
match_headline: For Tenants Nationwide, a Scramble to Pay Months of Rent or Face Eviction

text: An article on Sunday about who will pay for Covid tests as more companies and institutions require them misstated the types of unvaccinated people at Rhodes College who will have to cover the costs of testing. Unvaccinated students without a religious or medical exemption will have to pay a fee, but not faculty or staff.
match_headline: New Rule Raises Question: Who’ll Pay for All the Covid Tests?

text: An article on Saturday about start-up alternatives to banks, relying on information from a station biography, misstated Dave Davies’s job description. He is a fill-in host on “Fresh Air” but is no longer a senior reporter at WHYY.
match_headline: We Asked Daves About Dave, Marcus and Other First-Name Money Apps

text: An article on Monday about influencers recruited by the White House to promote coronavirus vaccines misspelled the name of one of the counties where officials are working with local influencers to broadcast vaccine information. It is Guilford County, N.C., not Guildford.
match_headline: To Fight Vaccine Lies, Authorities Recruit an ‘Influencer Army’

text: An article on Sunday about Elaine Thompson-Herah’s victory in the 100-meter dash included outdated information about Sha’Carri Richardson. She recently served her one-month suspension, which began on June 28; she is not currently serving the suspension.
match_headline: Elaine Thompson-Herah of Jamaica wins the 100-meter dash.

text: An obituary on Saturday about Ruth Pearl, the mother of the murdered reporter Daniel Pearl, misstated the previous name of the New Jersey Institute of Technology. It was the Newark College of Engineering, not the Newark Institute of Technology. It also misstated a previous name of the Tandon School of Engineering at New York University. It was the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn, not New York Polytechnic.
match_headline: Ruth Pearl, Mother of Murdered Reporter Daniel Pearl, Dies at 85

text: An article on Tuesday about the allocation of funds in President Biden’s $1 trillion infrastructure bill misstated the amount of money Mr. Biden had sought to try to bring high-speed internet access to every American. It was $100 billion, not $100 million. The article also misstated the amount the bill would spend on restoring the Great Lakes. That figure is $1 billion, not $1 million.
match_headline: What’s in the $1 Trillion Infrastructure Bill

text: An essay on Monday about the effects of people’s opposition to vaccination against Covid described incorrectly a treatment for RSV, a virus that poses a threat to premature infants. The treatment is a medication that protects against the virus, not a vaccine that prevents infection.
match_headline: Unvaxxed, Unmasked and Putting Our Kids at Risk

text: An article on Saturday about the archaeologist Kisha Supernant misspelled the surname of the professor of archaeology who collaborates with her. He is Andrew Martindale, not Martin.
match_headline: The Indigenous Archaeologist Tracking Down the Missing Residential Children

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts by the White House to protect renters from the end of the eviction moratorium referred incorrectly to President Biden’s request of Dr. Rochelle Walensky, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention director, to explore the possibility of extending the eviction moratorium to areas hit especially hard by the Delta variant of the coronavirus. While he called on her to do so, he did not call her directly.
match_headline: Administration Seeks to Blunt Effects From End of Eviction Moratorium

text: An article on Tuesday about the speedskater and baseball player Eddy Alvarez referred incorrectly to the year of the Nagano Olympics. They were in 1998, not 1996.
match_headline: He Has a Speedskating Medal. Can He Get One in Baseball, Too?

text: An article on Wednesday about the runner Christine Mboma described incorrectly the questions raised by her performance. The questions around physiological advantage gained by intersex athletes begins after 399 meters; it does not end at 399 meters.
match_headline: Barred From 400 Meters, Namibia’s Mboma Wins Silver in the 200

text: An article on Wednesday about the effects of heat and humidity in Tokyo on sport climbing misspelled the name of a South Korean climber. He is Jongwon Chon, not Jongwong.
match_headline: Sport Climbers Add a New Worry (Heat) to an Old One (Gravity)

text: A headline with an article on Wednesday about the Olympic sprinter Elaine Thompson-Herah’s gold medal in the women’s 200 meters misidentified her nationality. She is from Jamaica, not the United States.
match_headline: Elaine Thompson-Herah wins her second gold in Tokyo.

text: A picture caption with a music review on Tuesday about Bang on a Can’s LOUD Weekend festival misidentified the violinist seated in the center of the image. She is Annaliese Kowert, not Philippa Thompson.
match_headline: As Bang on a Can Returns, a New Generation Rises

text: An article on Thursday about the Squirrel Comedy Theater misstated the name of an annual event held by the Upright Citizens Brigade. It is the Del Close Marathon, not the Del Close Festival.
match_headline: A New Improv Theater Tries to Be the Anti-U.C.B. Is That a Trap, Too?

text: A picture caption in an article last weekend about Muammar el-Qaddafi’s son Seif misidentified pieces of ammunition found in Ain Zara, Libya. They are mortar shells, not artillery shells.
match_headline: Qaddafi’s Son Is Alive. And He Wants to Take Libya Back.

text: An article on Thursday about a debate over presidential war powers misidentified which Senate committee voted on legislation repealing two authorizations for use of military force. It was the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, not the Senate Armed Services Committee.
match_headline: Debate Over Presidential War Powers Sets Up Test for a Divided G.O.P.

text: An article on Friday about the response by Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo of New York after women accused him of sexual harassment described incorrectly Roberta A. Kaplan’s connection to the Time’s Up Legal Defense Fund. Ms. Kaplan is a founder of the fund, but does not run it.
match_headline: How Cuomo and His Team Retaliated Against His Accusers

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the restoration and strengthening of tailpipe emissions regulations from the Obama era described incorrectly Washington State’s timeline for transitioning to low-emissions vehicles. While the state’s legislature set 2030 as the year when only the sale of low-emissions vehicles would be permitted, the measure was vetoed by Gov. Jay Inslee. State officials are currently drafting new requirements.
match_headline: Biden, in a Push to Phase Out Gas Cars, Tightens Pollution Rules

text: An article on Wednesday about the return of 17,000 looted artifacts to Iraq referred imprecisely to the Gilgamesh epic. While the saga has similarities to the stories of the Great Flood and the Garden of Eden, it does not specifically mention them.
match_headline: Iraq Reclaims 17,000 Looted Artifacts, Its Biggest-Ever Repatriation

text: An article on Sunday about wildfires in Greece misstated the day a 38-year-old volunteer firefighter from Ippokrateios Politeia died. It was Friday, not Thursday.
match_headline: Greek Fires Force Thousands More to Evacuate

text: An article on Monday about a report regarding the cause of the so-called Havana syndrome misstated the surname of an ambassador. She is Pamela Spratlen, not Spartan.
match_headline: Mystery Attacks on Diplomats Leave Scores of Victims but Still Little Evidence

text: An article on Aug. 3 about irritable bowel syndrome misstated the name of the journal in which an article about the diagnosis and treatment of I.B.S. appeared. It is JAMA, not JAMA Network.
match_headline: Solving the Mystery of I.B.S.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the singer, guitarist and songwriter Paul Cotton rendered incorrectly the name of a website that published an interview with him in 2000. It is Sound Waves, not soundwaves. The obituary also misstated the website’s address. It is swaves.com, not soundwaves.com.
match_headline: Paul Cotton, Mainstay of the Country-Rock Band Poco, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on Monday about the former Florida State football coach Bobby Bowden referred incorrectly to the former Penn State assistant coach Jerry Sandusky. He retired from the Penn State staff after the 1999 season; he was no longer an aide to the head coach, Joe Paterno, when he was indicted on child sex abuse charges in 2011. And he had been Paterno’s defensive coordinator at the time, not his top assistant. (Paterno also had an offensive coordinator.)
match_headline: Bobby Bowden, Coach Who Led Florida State to Greatness, Dies at 91

text: An article on Tuesday about the spread of the Delta variant of the coronavirus and families with unvaccinated high-risk children misstated the portion of the eligible Utah population that is fully vaccinated. It is about 58 percent, not 45 percent.
match_headline: Families of High-Risk Children Despair Over Covid Resurgence

text: An article on Wednesday about attacks on Brazil’s voting system by President Jair Bolsonaro referred incorrectly to Florianópolis. It is a city in southern part of Brazil not a state.
match_headline: Bolsonaro Prompts Fears of a Power Grab With Attacks on Brazil’s Voting System

text: An article on Saturday about the film “Chernobyl 1986” misstated the region in which it is available to watch on Netflix. It is available in Britain and elsewhere in parts of Europe, not the United States.
match_headline: Dramatizing the Chernobyl Disaster, for Its Survivors

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the actor and director Arthur French referred incorrectly to the 2010 production of the play “Pecong.” It was not the last play Mr. French directed; he went on to direct at least one other, “Deep Are the Roots,” in 2016.
match_headline: Arthur French, Negro Ensemble Company Pioneer, Dies at 89

text: An article on Wednesday about the death of Julissia Batties misidentified the relative with whom she went to live last year. It was her mother, Navasia Jones, not her grandmother, Yolanda Davis.
match_headline: A 7-Year-Old Dies in the Bronx, and Records Show a History of Abuse

text: Because of an editing error, an essay on Thursday about the gubernatorial recall election in California misstated the year Chief Justice Earl Warren retired from the Supreme Court. It was 1969, not 1968.
match_headline: There Is a Problem With California’s Recall. It’s Unconstitutional.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the theoretical physicist Toshihide Maskawa misstated the name given to the type of particle known as a quark that was discovered in 1974. As correctly stated elsewhere in the obituary, it is known as a charm quark, not charmed.
match_headline: Toshihide Maskawa, 81, Dies; Nobelist Helped Unlock a Cosmic Mystery

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about Pine Bluff, Ark., misstated Census figures for the city. It now has about 41,250 residents, down from just over 49,000 a decade ago, not 87,500, down from just over 100,000. (The larger population figures are for the Pine Bluff metropolitan area as a whole.)
match_headline: The census data tells Pine Bluff, Ark., what it already knew: It’s shrinking, quickly.

text: An article on Friday about “Showstoppers! Spectacular Costumes From Stage and Screen” misidentified the creator of the Medusa costume in “Dragus Maximus.” It was designed by Miodrag Guberinic, not Fabian Fidel Aguilar.
ref_headline: Showstoppers! Spectacular Costumes From Stage and Screen
match_headline: Velvet, Organza and Vipers: Stage Costumes Dazzle

text: An article on Page 6 this weekend about David Lat, one of the first patients to be put on a ventilator while hospitalized with Covid-19, misspells the surname of Mr. Lat’s husband. He is Zach Shemtob, not Shamtob.
match_headline: Catching Up With One of the First Covid Patients to Be Put on a Ventilator

text: A review on July 18 about S. A. Cosby’s novel “Razorblade Tears” misidentified the setting of the author’s previous novel, “Blacktop Wasteland.” It takes place mostly in Virginia, not Louisiana.
match_headline: A Brawling, Go-for-Baroque Pulpfest

text: Because of an editing error, an essay last Sunday about online fandom misstated which season of “Star Trek” was saved by a fan letter-writing campaign. The campaign persuaded NBC to air a third season of the show, not a second season.
match_headline: From ‘Loki’ to ‘Brooklyn Nine-Nine,’ Fans Are Calling the Shots

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about police killings in rural America misspelled the given name of a niece of Bradley Grant, a man who was shot in 2018 by a Kentucky detective. It is Natilee, not Natalie.
match_headline: Where Police Killings Often Meet With Silence: Rural America

text: An article on Sunday about Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina misidentified President Barack Obama’s first appointee to the Supreme Court. It was Sonia Sotomayor, not Elena Kagan.
match_headline: Tap Dancing With Trump: Lindsey Graham’s Quest for Relevance

text: An article on Saturday about nine moderate Democrats in the House who say that they will not vote for a budget resolution until an infrastructure bill is signed into law misstated the year that Representative Josh Gottheimer flipped a seat in New Jersey’s 5th congressional district. It was 2016, not 2018.
match_headline: House Moderates Say They Won’t Back Budget Vote Until Infrastructure Bill Passes

text: An article on Friday about hydrogen as a next-generation fuel described incorrectly the steam reforming process, a method of making hydrogen fuel. The process uses high heat and pressure to break down methane into hydrogen and carbon monoxide, not carbon dioxide.
match_headline: For Many, Hydrogen Is the Fuel of the Future. New Research Raises Doubts.

text: An article on Friday about universities that cannot require vaccinations because of state restrictions misstated the coronavirus positivity rate last year at Cleveland State University. It was 0.36 percent, not 3.6 percent. Because of an editing error, the article also misspelled the given name of the governor of Texas. He is Greg Abbott, not Gregg.
match_headline: Campuses Are Virus Incubators, but These Colleges Can’t Require Vaccines

text: An article on Sunday about a court ruling on an eviction moratorium imposed to aid tenants struggling during the coronavirus pandemic misstated the name of a law that prohibits courts from evicting tenants who experienced financial hardship from accrued rent during the pandemic. It is the Tenant Safe Harbor Act, not the Tenant Safety Harbor Act.
match_headline: Landlords and Tenants Worry About Effects of Ruling on Eviction Moratorium

text: A headline with an article on Aug. 10 about the release from prison of two men who were wrongly convicted three decades ago misstated the reasons for their release. A picture caption with the article also misstated which of the men was exonerated. As the article correctly noted, only Carlton Roman was exonerated. Though Christopher Ellis’s conviction was vacated, he may face a retrial.
match_headline: Get a Covid-19 Vaccine or Face Prison, Judges Order in Probation Cases

text: An article on Saturday about a philanthropist’s decision to put more money and resources into a mentoring program for young people misstated the age of Manyi Ngu, a high school senior in Jacksonville, Fla. She is 17, not 18.
match_headline: A Donor Makes a Long-Term Investment: In Mentoring Teens

text: An obituary on Saturday about the singer and songwriter Nanci Griffith misstated part of the name of an award that she won in 2008. It is the Lifetime Americana Trailblazer Award, not American. It also misstated the name of a condition she had that limited the mobility of her fingers. It is Dupuytren’s contracture, not Dupuyten’s. And it misstated how old she was when she began performing in nightclubs in Austin, Texas. She was 12, not 14.
match_headline: Nanci Griffith, Singer Who Blended Folk and Country, Dies at 68

text: An obituary on July 25 about the sailboat designer Bruce Kirby referred incorrectly to the use of his Laser sailboat in men’s and women’s single-handed events in Olympic competition. Men sail the craft in the Laser class, women in the Laser Radial class. It is not the case that they both compete in a class whose name was changed to ILCA, for International Laser Class Association.
match_headline: Bruce Kirby, Who Transformed Sailing With a ‘Doodle,’ Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Monday about James C. Hormel, the first openly gay person to represent the United States as an ambassador, misstated the position he held at the University of Chicago Law School from 1961 to 1967. He was dean of students, not dean of the school.
match_headline: James Hormel, America’s First Openly Gay Ambassador, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Sunday about the historian Leon Litwack misstated at one point the given name of his mother. As correctly noted elsewhere, she was Minnie (Nitkin) Litwack, not Millie.
match_headline: Leon Litwack, 91, Dies; Changed How Scholars Portray Black History

text: An article on Wednesday about the history and motives of the Taliban misstated the age of the Great Buddhas of Bamiyan, which the Taliban destroyed in 2001. The statues were about 1,500 years old, not 800.
match_headline: 50 Years After Vietnam, Thousands Flee Another Lost American War

text: An article on Friday about care home residents in Toronto leaving their buildings after nearly a year in lockdown misspelled the surname of a care home resident who had his first outing. He is Ted Freeman-Attwood, not Freeman-Atwood.
match_headline: A Return to Freedom, After Nearly a Year Trapped Indoors Under Lockdown

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas testing positive for the coronavirus referred incorrectly to guidance recently issued by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The guidance said that everyone, including fully vaccinated people, should wear masks in public indoor settings, not that the fully vaccinated did not need to do so.
match_headline: Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas has tested positive for the coronavirus.

text: An article on Wednesday about a vow by the Sackler family to withdraw from a $4.5 billion pledge to help communities unless a judge grants the family immunity from all current and future civil claims associated with Purdue Pharma described incorrectly Purdue’s marketing efforts for OxyContin. While the campaign drastically downplayed the drug’s addictive qualities, it did not say the drug was nonaddictive.
match_headline: Sacklers Threaten to Pull Out of Opioid Settlement Without Broad Legal Immunity

text: An article on Tuesday about Naomi Osaka’s struggle to return to news conferences misstated the round of the Olympics in which she lost to Marketa Vondrousova. It was the third round, not the second.
match_headline: Naomi Osaka Struggles in Return to Tournament News Conferences

text: An article on Tuesday about Christopher Massimine, a theater executive who faced questions about errors on his résumé, misstated when Massimine accepted the job as managing director of the Pioneer Theater Company in Utah. He was still employed by the National Yiddish Theater in New York when he accepted the Pioneer job; he did not leave before accepting it.
match_headline: Theater Director With Exaggerated Résumé Quits, Citing Mental Illness

text: An article on Thursday about a new digital tool called Disney Genie that allows line-skipping privileges at Walt Disney World misstated the status of its FastPass service in California in 2017. The park kept FastPass while introducing the MaxPass app; it did not eliminate FastPass that year. In addition, an earlier version of a picture caption with the article misstated the location of the park shown. The photograph was taken at Disneyland Paris, not in the United States.
match_headline: To Skip the Line at Disney, Get Ready to Pay a Genie

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about the project Theater in Quarantine by Joshua William Gelb, using information provided by a publicist, misstates the composer Heather Christian’s age. She is 39, not 29.
match_headline: He Invited Us Into His Closet for Theater. And It Was Astonishing.

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about the producer and musician Aaron Dessner includes a photograph of a man playing guitar that was published in error. It pictured Mr. Dessner’s twin brother, Bryce, not Mr. Dessner.
match_headline: How Aaron Dessner Found His Voice (With an Assist From Taylor Swift)

text: An obituary on Thursday about Bill Davis, the longtime premier of Ontario, referred incorrectly to an aide of Mr. Davis and misstated his surname. He is Clare Westcott, not Wescott, and he is a man. The obituary also misstated part of the name of the political party that merged with the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada In 2003. It was the Canadian Alliance, not the Conservative Alliance.
match_headline: Bill Davis, Pragmatic Ontario Premier, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Friday about the artist Chuck Close misspelled the surname of a painter who, like Mr. Close, was a practitioner of Photorealism. He was Robert Bechtle, not Bechtel.
match_headline: Chuck Close, Artist of Outsized Reality, Dies at 81

text: An article on Sunday about disorder in the U.S. exit from Afghanistan misidentified the date of a meeting among national security officials at the Pentagon. It was April 24, not April 28.
match_headline: Miscue After Miscue, U.S. Exit Plan Unravels

text: An article on Wednesday about recent commercial real estate transactions in Brooklyn, using incorrect information from a real estate broker, misstated the number of bedrooms in the apartments in a Bushwick building. The building at 416 Melrose Street has eight two-bedroom apartments, not eight four-bedroom apartments.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Sunday about the actress Dorinda Medley of “The Real Housewives of New York City” implied that Soho House was in the Manhattan neighborhood of SoHo. It is in the Meatpacking District, not SoHo.
ref_headline: The Real Housewives of New York City
match_headline: How a Former ‘Real Housewife’ of NYC Spends Her Sundays

text: An article on Friday about the artist Peter Bradley described incorrectly the group of artists represented in a seminal, racially integrated show of abstract art. An artist of Mexican heritage was included in the show; it was not made up only of white and Black artists.
match_headline: Is Peter Bradley Ready for Round 2 in the Limelight?

text: An article on Sunday about the prices hospitals negotiate with private insurers erroneously included a hospital among those that had posted little or no data about their negotiated rates or cash prices. Methodist Hospital (San Antonio) has posted some required information. The article referred incorrectly to the hospital’s response for a request for comment; the requests for comment were mistakenly sent to another hospital with the same name.
match_headline: Hospitals and Insurers Didn’t Want You to See These Prices. Here’s Why.

text: An article on Monday about flooding in Tennessee misspelled the given name of a relative of Lily Bryant, a girl who has been missing since the flood. She is Tarri Lynn Gillinger Holderman, not Tarry.
match_headline: ‘Our People Need Help’: Devastation in Tennessee, as Experts Warn of Flooding Risks

text: An article on Monday about a decision by the United States in 2001 to ignore the Taliban’s offer to surrender misstated Donald Rumsfeld’s cabinet position at the time. He was secretary of defense, not secretary of state.
match_headline: Did the War in Afghanistan Have to Happen?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Aug. 18 about racial inequities in health care described incorrectly the journals that Dr. Phil B. Fontanarosa, interim editor in chief of JAMA, said had published more than 850 articles related to racial disparities. They were published in a variety of journals associated with JAMA, not only in JAMA itself.
match_headline: Racial Inequities Persist in Health Care Despite Expanded Insurance

text: An article on Tuesday about the rainiest hour on record in the history of New York City misidentified the park in Brooklyn where a deluge turned a staircase into a waterfall. It was Mount Prospect Park, not Prospect Park (the parks are adjacent).
match_headline: 2 Months of Rain in a Day and a Half: New York City Sets Records

text: An article on Aug. 17 about the study of cat genomics misstated the profession of Leslie Lyons. She is a geneticist, not a veterinarian.
match_headline: The Unappreciated Importance of Cats (to Medical Science)

text: An obituary on Thursday about Ellen Havre Weis, a creator of the Museum of Modern Mythology in San Francisco, misstated the given name of the author of the essay collection “Mythologies,” from which she took inspiration. He was Roland Barthes, not Ronald.
match_headline: Ellen Havre Weis, Whose Museum Put Pop Into Mythology, Dies at 64

text: An article on Tuesday about Jews praying at the Temple Mount misspelled the name of the president of the board of the Temple Institute, which supports the construction of a new Jewish temple at the site. He is Rabbi Yisrael Ariel, not Israel Arieli.
match_headline: In Shift, Israel Quietly Allows Jewish Prayer on Temple Mount

text: An article on Tuesday about sentences that were commuted by Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo of New York on his last day in office misidentified one of the left-wing radical groups involved in the 1981 robbery of a Brink’s truck. It was the May 19th Communist Organization, not its predecessor, the Weather Underground.
match_headline: Cuomo Commutes Sentences of 1981 Brink’s Robbery Participant and 4 Others

text: An article on Wednesday about Donald H. Rumsfeld’s funeral misstated how David Hume Kennerly came to work in the White House. President Gerald R. Ford brought him on to his staff, not Mr. Rumsfeld.
match_headline: Donald Rumsfeld, Architect of War in Afghanistan, Is Laid to Rest

text: An article on May 20 about the devastating costs of invasive pests on the agricultural sector in Nigeria and other African countries, because of errors in the study cited in the article, overstated those costs. A revised version of the study estimates those costs at $65.58 billion per year, not $3.66 trillion. The error was repeated in the headline. (The errors in the study arose from the fact that the authors calculated weeding costs based on square kilometers when, in fact, the data reflected costs per hectare.)
match_headline: Intruder Pests May Drain Trillions From Africa’s Economies, Study Finds

text: An article on Wednesday about the musician Larry Harlow misstated the name of a song by the Mars Volta. It is “L’Via L’Viaquez,” not “L’Via L’Vasquez.”
match_headline: Larry Harlow, a Salsa Revolutionary

text: An article last Thursday about the reality TV star Kathy Hilton misstated the day of the week that “The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills” airs on Bravo. It is Wednesday, not Tuesday.
ref_headline: The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills
match_headline: Kathy Hilton’s Calling

text: An article last Thursday about luxury car customization referred incorrectly to a 2021 Aston Martin model. It is a DBX, not a UBX.
match_headline: Hypebeasts Hit the Road

text: An article on Monday about Tropical Storm Henri misstated the name of a village in Rhode Island. It is Point Judith, not Port Judith.
match_headline: Tropical Storm Henri Brings Power Outages and Record Rain to Northeast

text: An article on Aug. 20 about New Braunfels, Texas, misstated the financial figure that has jumped to $90,000 from $65,000 in Comal County, Texas, over the past decade. It was the median household income, not the median salary.
match_headline: How This Texas Town Became One of America’s Fastest-Growing Cities

text: An article on Monday about the installation of roomier seats in San Francisco’s War Memorial Opera House described incorrectly the venue’s 12 bariatric seats. They were designed to hold up to 600 pounds, not 300 pounds.
match_headline: ‘The Opposite of Airlines’: When Larger Audiences Require Fewer Seats

text: An obituary on Friday about the pianist, bandleader and record producer Larry Harlow referred incorrectly to his marriage to Wendy Caplin. It ended with her death in 2013; it did not end in divorce.
match_headline: Larry Harlow, Influential Figure in Salsa, Dies at 82

text: An article last Sunday about Anne Bredin and JF Brandon’s wedding misstated when the bride’s family farmhouse was built in New Ipswich, N.H. It was built in the 1840s, not 100 years ago, which was when the bride’s maternal great-grandparents moved into the farmhouse. The article also misidentified the church where the bride’s parents were married. Her parents were married at the New Ipswich Congregational Church, not the Temple Congregational Church in Temple, N.H., where the couple were married.
match_headline: Taking the Plunge After a Farmhouse Sauna

text: An article on July 25 about the Americans With Disabilities Act referred incorrectly to A.D.A. claims filed in federal court. It is not the case that $75,000 was the minimum demand claim needed to get Albert Dytch’s case into federal court. The article also misstated the amount of Dytch’s expenses that were covered by insurance. Dytch paid $10,000 for his power wheelchair out of pocket; the remaining cost was covered by insurance; it is not the case that only $10,000 of his accessibility expenses were covered by insurance.
match_headline: The Man Who Filed More Than 180 Disability Lawsuits

text: An article on Sunday about U.S. veterans who are acting as digital guides to Americans and Afghans trying to flee Afghanistan misidentified a project manager from North Carolina who had served in the Marines. He is Rich Porter, not Phil.
match_headline: A Digital Dunkirk: Veterans Online Scramble to Get People Out of Afghanistan

text: An article on Saturday about the lack of a firm conclusion by American intelligence agencies on the origins of the coronavirus described incorrectly a position taken by the Asian American Foundation. The foundation said that it was concerned that the debate over the origins of the virus could intensify hatred against Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders. It did not question the intelligence community’s entire effort to examine the origins of the pandemic.
match_headline: Intelligence Review Yields No Firm Conclusion on Origins of Coronavirus

text: An article on Tuesday about college students stranded in Afghanistan misstated comments by the president of the American University of Afghanistan about attempts to evacuate students. He said that the university had shared the students’ names with the U.S. military, and that the military’s protocol was to share that information with the Taliban to coordinate access to the airport. He did not say the U.S. military had shared with the Taliban a list of students trying to leave Afghanistan.
match_headline: American University of Afghanistan students and relatives trying to flee were sent home.

text: An article on Monday about some hotels requiring guests to be vaccinated against the coronavirus misstated the policy at the Equinox Hotel in New York. On-site Equinox employees are required to be vaccinated; they are not exempted from the policy.
match_headline: Some Hotels Are Mandating Vaccines. Will Others Follow?

text: An article on Tuesday about a natural gas power plant’s failure to power New Orleans after Hurricane Ida, using information from his wife, misstated the age of Bob Smith, a New Orleans resident. He is 73, not 71.
match_headline: Hurricane Ida Exposes Grid Weaknesses as New Orleans Goes Dark

text: An article on Tuesday about lawmakers who sought to help the U.S. evacuation effort in Afghanistan misstated the circumstances of the evacuation from Kabul of a pair of Afghan orphans. A contact of Senator Jon Ossoff called an ex-military officer to help them at the airport, not Mr. Ossoff himself. The orphans had encountered difficulties getting on a U.S. government plane, but were not lost.
match_headline: ‘We Have to Try’: Lawmakers Rush to Assist in Afghanistan Evacuations.

text: An item on Tuesday about the U.S. Open schedule misspelled the surname of a tennis player. He is Alex de Minaur, not de Minuar.
match_headline: 2021 U.S. Open: What to Watch on Tuesday

text: An article on Wednesday about the consolidation of four prominent art dealers, using information provided by Salon 94, misstated the artist Luis Flores’s relationship with the gallery; he is no longer represented by Salon 94.
match_headline: Four Powerful Art Dealers Join Forces, Upending Traditional Model

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the record producer Lee Perry misspelled the name of the town in Jamaica where he died. It is Lucea, not Lucca.
match_headline: Lee (Scratch) Perry, Bob Marley Mentor and Reggae Innovator, Dies at 85

text: An article on Tuesday about a rise in demand for the drug ivermectin misattributed a quote from an author of an ivermectin study. She is Maria Popp, not Maria-Inti Metzendorf.
match_headline: Demand Surges for Deworming Drug for Covid, Despite Scant Evidence It Works

text: An article on Tuesday about changes to diversity practices on Broadway misstated the number of theater owners and operators who signed a pact developed by Black Theater United. The pact was signed by the owners and operators of 39 Broadway theaters, not all 41.
match_headline: Broadway Power Brokers Pledge Diversity Changes as Theaters Reopen

text: An obituary on Saturday about William G. Clotworthy, the longtime in-house censor for “Saturday Night Live,” referred incorrectly to the television show “Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood,” which Eddie Murphy parodied as “Mister Robinson’s Neighborhood” on “Saturday Night Live.” Mister Rogers, unlike Mister Robinson, did not have a “word of the day.” It also misidentified the studio from which the NBC show “Texaco Star Theater” was broadcast when Mr. Clotworthy worked as an NBC page. It was Studio 6B, not 8H. And it misstated the year Mr. Clotworthy retired. As a picture caption with the obituary correctly states, it was 1991, not 1990. The obituary also referred imprecisely to Jamestown, Va., to which Mr. Clotworthy traced his roots in America. It was the first permanent English settlement in North America, not the first such settlement of any kind.
match_headline: William G. Clotworthy, ‘Saturday Night Live’ Censor, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Aug. 22 about the singer and songwriter Tom T. Hall misstated the name of the man who was the inspiration for his song “The Year That Clayton Delaney Died.” He was Lonnie Easterly, not Floyd Carter.
ref_headline: The Year That Clayton Delaney Died.
match_headline: Tom T. Hall, Country Music’s ‘Storyteller,’ Is Dead at 85

text: An obituary on Aug. 21 about Gustave M. Hauser, the former chairman and chief executive of Warner Cable Communications, erroneously credited Warner’s QUBE cable television system with a distinction. At least two companies had introduced set-top boxes and remote control devices for cable before QUBE did in 1977; it is not the case that QUBE was the first to do so. The error was repeated in the “Of Interest” section on A3.
match_headline: Gustave M. Hauser, an Early Force in Cable TV, Dies at 91

text: An article on Friday about the deaths of four Louisiana nursing home residents misspelled the parish that was home to a 77-year-old man who died. He was from Terrebonne Parish, not Terrebone.
match_headline: Louisiana Nursing Home Residents, Evacuated Before the Storm, Died in New Facility, State Says

text: An article on Friday about a settlement between Renaissance Technologies and the Internal Revenue Service referred incorrectly to media reports about the compensation of Robert Mercer. His annual pay as co-chief executive of Renaissance was between $125 million and $135 million, according to the reports. They did not say he had an estimated fortune of $125 billion.
match_headline: Hedge Fund’s Insiders Agree to Pay as Much as $7 Billion to I.R.S.

text: A review on Friday of a retrospective of the painter Joan Mitchell’s work at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art misstated the nationality of Jean-Paul Riopelle. He was French Canadian, not French.
match_headline: The Roots of Joan Mitchell’s Greatness

text: An article on Page 9 this weekend about how the film “Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings” avoided Asian stereotypes misstates the heritage of Destin Daniel Cretton. He is Japanese American, not Chinese American.
ref_headline: Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings
match_headline: How Shang-Chi, Master of Kung Fu, Knocked Down Stereotypes

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about Terry Albury, a former F.B.I. special agent who leaked information to journalists, misspells the surname of a Black man who was killed by the police in Milwaukee. He was Dontre Hamilton, not Hamiton. The article also misspells the given name of a Black teenager who was killed by the police in Chicago. He was Laquan McDonald, not Lacquan. Additionally, it misspells the surname of the former Subway spokesman who is serving 15 years in prison for sex acts with minors and distribution of child pornography. He is Jared Fogle, not Fogel.
match_headline: ‘I Helped Destroy People’

text: An article on Page 34 this weekend about the writer Maggie Nelson describes incorrectly the man who was convicted of murdering her aunt. The man was not a serial killer.
match_headline: Maggie Nelson Wants to Redefine ‘Freedom’

text: An obituary on Aug. 12 about Elka Schumann, who ran the Bread and Puppet Theater in Vermont with her husband, Peter, misidentified the author of the manifesto “Why Cheap Art,” distributed by the Bread and Puppet Press, which she managed. It was Peter Schumann, not Elka Schumann.
match_headline: Elka Schumann, Matriarch of the Bread and Puppet Theater, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Aug. 10 about Sergei A. Kovalev, a Kremlin adversary during the Soviet era who went on to campaign against the post-Communist leaders Boris A. Yeltsin and Vladimir V. Putin, misstated when Ivan Kovalev, his son, was arrested and charged with “undermining and weakening the Soviet Union.” It was August 1981, not August 1982.
ref_headline: undermining and weakening the Soviet Union.
match_headline: Sergei Kovalev, Longtime Kremlin Adversary, Dies at 91

text: An article last Sunday about Black composers in Europe misstated part of the history of the Berlin Philharmonic. Rudolph Dunbar was not the first foreign musician to lead the orchestra after World War II.
match_headline: When Europe Offered Black Composers an Ear

text: An article last Sunday about the gatherings known as salons misstated the name of a university that hosts some of these events. It is the University of California, San Francisco; it is not the University of Southern California, San Francisco. The article also misidentified the source of funding for a June salon about the human microbiome that was hosted by Susan MacTavish Best. It was funded by Ms. Best, not the Templeton World Charity Foundation.
match_headline: Smarty Party

text: An article on Aug. 22 about plans to develop a spaceport on Cumberland Island in Georgia referred imprecisely to requirements for operating motor vehicles on the island. People need permits to drive in some protected areas, not all parts of the island. The article also misstated the starting rate for a room at the Greyfield Inn. It is about $865, not $855.
match_headline: Last Stop on the Way to the Cosmos? No Thanks.

text: An article last Sunday about searching for a home on the Upper West Side of Manhattan misstated the configuration of the apartment in Lincoln Terrace on Amsterdam Avenue. It was a one-bedroom converted from a studio, not a studio converted from a one-bedroom. Two pictures with the article were misidentified. Lincoln Towers on West End Avenue was on the left, and Schwab House on Riverside Drive was in the middle.
match_headline: A First-Time Buyer Took His $500,000 to the Upper West Side. Which Home Would You Choose?

text: An article on Aug. 1 about the film “Old” misstated the given name of an actor. He is Gael García Bernal, not Gabriel.
match_headline: I’m Obsessed With ‘Old.’ The Twist: I Won’t See It.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the actor Michael K. Williams described incorrectly Vanderveer Estates in Brooklyn, N.Y., now called Flatbush Gardens, where Michael Williams’s family lived. It was a privately owned housing complex, not public housing.
match_headline: Michael K. Williams, Omar From ‘The Wire,’ Is Dead at 54

text: An article on Friday about New York colleges that require vaccinations misstated the mask policies at Vassar College and St. John’s University. Vassar issued an indoor mask mandate in August that applies to everyone with exceptions for private settings, and masks are required at St. John's inside campus buildings, regardless of vaccination status. It is not the case that fully vaccinated students and staff may go unmasked in the schools’ indoor facilities.
match_headline: Most N.Y. Colleges Require Vaccination. Students Are Fine With That.

text: An article on Sunday about an oil spill off Louisiana’s coast misstated when two boats appeared to join the cleanup effort. It was by Saturday morning, not late Saturday.
match_headline: Satellite Images Find ‘Substantial’ Oil Spill in Gulf After Ida

text: An article on Saturday about the squalid conditions at a warehouse in Louisiana that housed evacuees from nursing homes during Hurricane Ida misstated the middle initial of the businessman who owns the nursing homes. He is Bob G. Dean Jr., not Bob J. Dean Jr.
match_headline: Louisiana Nursing Home Residents Describe Squalor at Warehouse

text: An article on Friday about concessions made by Apple to developers in regards to the App Store misstated the name of the entity that prompted Apple’s policy change for some companies. It is the Japan Fair Trade Commission, not the Japanese Fair Trade Commission.
match_headline: Apple Gives Ground in a Strategic Retreat From Strict App Store Rules

text: A crossword puzzle on Friday provided an erroneous clue for 37-Down, seeking the answer “Hellcat.” The clue should have read “W.W. II fighter plane that flew off an aircraft carrier,” not “W.W. II aircraft carrier.”
match_headline: On the Up-and-Up

text: A crossword puzzle on Monday provided an erroneous clue for 17-Across, seeking the answer for “Chloe Zhao.” The clue should have read “Chinese national who became only the second woman to win the Oscar for Best Director,” not “Asian American who became only the second woman to win the Oscar for Best Director.”
match_headline: We Know How to Teach Kids to Read

text: A review last Wednesday of the Japanese restaurant Nakaji, in Manhattan’s Chinatown, misstated the origin of the scallops used in some nigiri. They are from Hokkaido, not Hokkaido Bay.
match_headline: A Sushi Hideaway Where There’s Always Something New to Taste

text: An obituary on Friday about the biochemist Edmond H. Fischer misstated the year Edwin G. Krebs, with whom he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, died. It was 2009, not 2006.
match_headline: Edmond H. Fischer, 101, Who Helped Discover How Cells Talk, Dies

text: An obituary on Friday about the Greek composer and political activist Mikis Theodorakis misstated when he began an international campaign of concerts and contacts with world leaders that helped topple Greece’s military government. It was 1970, not 1968. Because of an editing error, the obituary also referred incorrectly to the actress Melina Mercouri. She became Greece’s minister of culture in 1981, seven years after the military junta that ruled the country was ousted — not while the junta was in power.
match_headline: Mikis Theodorakis, ‘Zorba’ Composer and Marxist Rebel, Dies at 96

text: An article on Tuesday about an 11-year prison sentence handed to Maria Kolesnikova, a leading Belarus opposition leader, misstated her status in last year’s presidential election. She was active in the campaign of Svetlana Tikhanovskaya, but was not a presidential candidate herself.
match_headline: Belarus Opposition Leader Sentenced to 11 Years in Prison

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the future of Sept. 11 documentaries misstated the number of parts in the series “9/11: One Day in America.” It has six, not four.
match_headline: Is 9/11 a Day, or Is It an Era?

text: Because of a production error, a part of an article on Tuesday about a rise in lawsuits over food labels was missing. The full article is at nytimes.com .
match_headline: Lawsuits Over ‘Misleading’ Food Labels Surge as Groups Cite Lax U.S. Oversight

text: An article on Thursday about a surge in coronavirus cases in South Korea misidentified the head epidemiologist of South Korea’s Central Disease Control Headquarters. He is Lee Sang-won, not Bang Dae-bon, which is a shortened form of his agency’s name in Korean.
match_headline: South Korea’s surge in Covid cases threatens its plans for reopening.

text: An article on Monday about the singer and songwriter Yebba misspelled the name of an artist. He is Sean Shrum, not Shawn.
match_headline: The Secret to Yebba’s Debut Album? A Big Voice and Lots of Time.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the actor Jean-Paul Belmondo misstated the age of his former wife Nathalie Tardivel when they married in 2002. She was 37, not 24. The obituary also misstated the surname of the director of the 1960 film “Moderato Cantabile,” in which Mr. Belmondo starred with Jeanne Moreau. He is Peter Brook, not Brooks.
match_headline: Jean-Paul Belmondo, Magnetic Star of the French New Wave, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the novelist Stephen Vizinczey referred incorrectly to the 1978 movie based on his novel “In Praise of Older Women.” It was a Canadian production; it was not made in Hollywood.
match_headline: Stephen Vizinczey, ‘In Praise of Older Women’ Author, Dies at 88

text: An article on Friday about security trading in 2020 by Federal Reserve officials misstated the timing of stock disclosures by Randal K. Quarles and Jerome H. Powell. Mr. Quarles’s disclosure was made in 2020, for 2019 transactions. His transactions were not made last summer. And Mr. Powell’s disclosures of 41 transactions were for 2019, not 2020.
match_headline: Fed Officials’ Trading Draws Outcry, and Fuels Calls for Accountability

text: An article this weekend on Page 13 about Kelly Clarkson misstates which Coldplay song her children were brought out to hear Chris Martin perform. It was “Yellow,” not “Green Eyes.”
match_headline: As a Daytime Host, Kelly Clarkson Has No Fear of Being Vocal

text: A picture caption with an article this weekend on Page 92 about the 1928 narrative poem “The Wild Party” misstates the website for a Maximilian top. It is brownsfashion.com , not browns.com . The mistake is repeated in the On the Covers credit in the table of contents.
match_headline: A Cautionary Tale for the New Roaring Twenties

text: An article last Sunday about Monica Lewinsky and the new FX series “Impeachment: American Crime Story” described incorrectly a book that Beanie Feldstein read as she prepared to play Lewinsky. The book, “Monica’s Story,” is an authorized biography written by Andrew Morton, not an autobiography.
match_headline: Monica Lewinsky Is (Reluctantly) Revisiting ‘That Woman’

text: An article last Sunday about farms in the Pacific Northwest coping with extreme weather conditions misstated the size of the room in which six bunk beds were stacked for workers at a farm in southern Oregon. The room is 20 feet by 20 feet, not 20 square feet.
match_headline: When Hard Jobs Turn Hazardous

text: An article last Sunday about office work and chance encounters at water coolers misstated the type of firm the researcher Kristie McAlpine studied. It was a tech firm, not a tax firm.
match_headline: When Chance Encounters at the Water Cooler Are Most Useful

text: An article on Aug. 29 about the fashion of Charlie Watts, the late Rolling Stones drummer, referred incorrectly to the shopping habits of Mr. Watts and Keith Richards. Mr. Watts bought suits at Tommy Nutter, not Mr. Richards. The article also described incorrectly the signage of some Savile Row tailors in the 1970s. The businesses had small plaques on their storefronts; they were not unmarked.
match_headline: The Uniform Cool of Charlie Watts

text: An article last Sunday about the revival of motels as vacation destinations in the Catskills misstated the age of Anthony Nelson, an owner of the Terrace Motel in Ellenville, N.Y. He is 38, not 28.
match_headline: Upstate Motels Make a Comeback, With an Aim to Captivate

text: An article on Wednesday about the end of pandemic-related federal programs in New York City misstated the city’s unemployment rate in July. It was 10.5 percent, not 10.2 percent.
match_headline: 800,000 New Yorkers Just Lost Federal Unemployment Benefits

text: An article on Monday about Rivian, an electric-vehicle maker, misidentified the location of its headquarters. The company is based in California, not Michigan.
match_headline: Can a Green-Economy Boom Town Be Built to Last?

text: An article on Friday about a Democratic proposal for a Civilian Climate Corps misstated the given name of the father of Representative Marcy Kaptur of Ohio. It is Steve, not Joseph.
match_headline: Democrats Want a ‘Climate Corps.’ They Just Can’t Agree How to Create It.

text: An article on Sunday about parents of young children seeking coronavirus vaccine trials misstated the number of children participating in Pfizer’s vaccine trial for children under 12. It is 4,500 overall now in a single trial, not an additional 4,500 in later phases. The article also referred incorrectly to Kit Longley. He is a man.
match_headline: Parents of Young Children Desperately Seek Vaccine Trials

text: An article on Sunday about N.F.L. week one predictions misstated the ranking of the Las Vegas Raiders defense in 2020. It ranked 25th in the N.F.L., not 30th.
match_headline: N.F.L. Week 1 Predictions: Our Picks Against the Spread

text: An obituary on Friday about the actor Michael Constantine referred imprecisely to his appearances on the television series “Hey, Landlord.” He played a recurring role, not a guest role.
match_headline: Michael Constantine, Father in ‘My Big Fat Greek Wedding,’ Dies at 94

text: An article on Monday about the German politician Armin Laschet misstated the month he defeated Markus Söder to become the leader of the Christian Democrats. It was April, not January.
match_headline: Germany’s Election Was His to Lose, and He Might Just Do That

text: An article on Sept. 8 about a return to work for Broadway’s costume shops described incorrectly Sally Ann Parsons’s milestone as a Tony Award winner. She is the first costume shop proprietor to receive a Tony, not the first costume maker.
match_headline: With a Mess of Fabrics, Broadway’s Costume Shops Return to Work

text: An article last Wednesday about new restaurants opening soon in New York City misstated the opening date for Yoshino New York. It is Sept. 23, not Sept. 25. The article also misspelled the surname of a partner in Cherry on Top; he is Mohan Kumar, not Jumar. And it incorrectly included Dani García on a list of chefs making their debuts in New York. Casa Dani, Mr. García’s new restaurant, is not his first in the city.
match_headline: Fall Restaurant Preview: A Reboot for New York

text: An obituary on Sept. 5 and 6 about Willard Scott, the longtime weather forecaster on the “Today” show, misstated when he began playing Bozo the Clown on WRC-TV in Washington. It was 1959, not 1952. The obituary also referred incompletely to Mr. Scott’s replacement of the meteorologist Bob Ryan on “Today.” Mr. Ryan did lose the “Today” job to Mr. Scott, but he went on to take over Mr. Scott’s previous job covering weather at WRC.
match_headline: Willard Scott, TV’s Clown Prince of Sun and Showers, Is Dead at 87

text: An article on Wednesday about proposed changes to California’s recall law referred incompletely to the threshold of signatures needed for triggering a recall election for elected officials in California. While the threshold for the governor’s office is 12 percent of voters in the previous election, it can range up to 20 percent for other offices.
match_headline: As California Votes, It Rethinks Its Tradition of Direct Democracy

text: An article on Sunday about religious exemptions for vaccinations erroneously included a company among a list of major private employers who announced this summer that they would require at least some of their workers to be vaccinated. Apple is not among that group.
match_headline: Vaccine Resisters Seek Religious Exemptions. But What Counts as Religious?

text: An article on Sunday about the film “Legend of Destruction” referred imprecisely to the time periods when Jews enjoyed sovereignty in the land in ancient times. While the first period of unified sovereignty some 3,000 years ago is believed to have lasted for less than a century, separate kingdoms remained sovereign for hundreds of years.
match_headline: For a Fractured Israel, a Film Offers Ominous Lessons From Ancient Past

text: An article on Tuesday about a vaccine mandate for N.B.A. referees misstated the position Marc Davis holds in the referees’ union. He is a member of its executive board, not its president.
match_headline: For Basketball Refs, Agreeing to a Vaccine Mandate Was ‘Not That Difficult’

text: An article on Tuesday about a company that aims to genetically resurrect the woolly mammoth misstated a philosopher’s name. She is Heather Browning, not Heather Bushman.
match_headline: A New Company With a Wild Mission: Bring Back the Woolly Mammoth

text: An article on Aug. 19 about the popularity and risks of the cosmetic procedure known as a Brazilian butt lift misidentified, in the print edition, a business in Florida associated with shoddy practices and patient deaths. Clinics run by Dr. Ismael Labrador have had eight patients die, four from botched Brazilian butt lifts; none of those cases were associated with Mia Aesthetics, which has no connection to Dr. Labrador. The Times regrets the error.
match_headline: Brazilian Butt Lifts Surge, Despite Risks

text: An article about the Inspiration4 mission misstated the distance of the Inspiration4 crew from Earth. They are farther from Earth than anyone since space shuttle crews visited the Hubble telescope in the 1990s, not farther than anyone since the Apollo missions ended in the 1970s.
match_headline: SpaceX Launches Astronaut Crew Like No Other on Orbital Adventure

text: An article on Friday about an appeal by the Justice Department to block a bankruptcy plan that would grant broad legal immunity to Purdue Pharma misstated the timing of OxyContin’s introduction to the market. It was 25 years ago, not 15 years ago.
match_headline: U.S. Seeks to Block Bankruptcy Plan That Would Free Sacklers From Opioid Claims

text: A picture with a film review of “In Balanchine’s Classroom” was published in error. The man pictured with a student was Jacques D’Amboise, not George Balanchine.
match_headline: ‘In Balanchine’s Classroom’ Review: Teaching the Ineffable

text: An article on Page 44 this weekend about dance events this fall misstates the last name of a founder of FLOCK. He is Florian Lochner, not Lockner.
match_headline: All the Ways to Fall for Dance Again Onstage and Beyond

text: An article on Page 68 this weekend about new movies being released this fall misstates where “The Drummer” will be released. It will be on demand, not in theaters.
match_headline: New Fall Movies 2021: Here Are More Than 125 Coming Soon

text: An article on Page 87 this weekend about three new indie albums coming out this fall misstates the release date for the new Parquet Courts album. “Sympathy for Life” is due Oct. 22, not Oct. 20.
match_headline: Fall Brings a Bounty of New Albums. Watch for These 3.

text: An article on Page 90 this weekend about new pop and jazz albums and events to anticipate this fall misstates the instruments that Billy Strings plays on his new album, “Renewal,” and the number of albums he has released. He plays guitar, not guitar and mandolin. “Renewal” is his fourth album, not his fifth.
match_headline: 66 Pop and Jazz Albums, Shows and Festivals Coming This Fall

text: An article on Page 94 this weekend about new exhibits at museums this fall refers incorrectly to “Just Above Midtown: 1974 to the Present,” a forthcoming show at the Museum of Modern Art. It will run from Oct. 9, 2022, to Feb. 18, 2023, not from Oct. 9, 2021, to Feb. 18, 2022.
ref_headline: Just Above Midtown: 1974 to the Present,
match_headline: Counting New Art Blessings Amid the Uncertainty

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Newport Jazz Festival impresario George Wein omitted the name of a survivor. Mr. Wein is survived by his partner, Glory Van Scott. The obituary also referred incompletely to the leadership of the festival. Although Danny Melnick was named producer in 2016, he left the next year.
match_headline: George Wein, Newport Jazz Festival Trailblazer, Is Dead at 95

text: An article last Sunday about the return of Berlin’s club scene misstated the surname of a clubgoer. She is Sanne van ’t Walderveen, not vand’t Walderveen.
match_headline: Berlin Clubs Return With a Vengeance

text: An article last Sunday about the diver Tom Daley misstated the title of a medical journal. It is The British Journal of Occupational Therapy, not The British Journal of Occupational Health.
match_headline: Tom Daley Is All-Around Gold

text: An article on Monday about the role played by Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia in shaping U.S. climate policy misidentified the type of firearm he used to shoot a hole through President Barack Obama’s climate plan. It was a rifle, not a shotgun.
match_headline: This Powerful Democrat Linked to Fossil Fuels Will Craft the U.S. Climate Plan

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the second week of the N.F.L. season misidentified the location of the Dallas Cowboys’ 20-17 victory. It was in Inglewood, Calif., against the Los Angeles Chargers — not in Seattle.
match_headline: N.F.L. Week 2 Predictions: Our Picks Against the Spread

text: An article on Monday about N.F.L. teams in the New York City area misidentified the location of the Patriots-Jets game on Sunday. It was in East Rutherford, N.J., not Foxborough, Mass.
match_headline: Are the Jets and Giants Watchable Yet?

text: An obituary on Monday about Bishop John Shelby Spong attributed an erroneous distinction to him. He was one of the first Episcopal bishops in the United States to ordain a woman into the clergy; he was not the first.
match_headline: John Shelby Spong, 90, Dies; Sought to Open Up the Episcopal Church

text: An article on Tuesday about a bill introduced in the House to impose checks on executive authority misstated the number of days presidential campaigns would wait before starting transitions into office as part of proposed legislation. If the General Services Administration makes no determination of the president-elect, the campaigns can start transitions five days after the election, not 10.
match_headline: Democrats Begin Effort to Curb Post-Trump Presidential Powers

text: An article on Monday about the removal of racist language from the Alabama Constitution described incorrectly the document’s text. Language banning interracial marriage was removed after a statewide vote in 2000. It is not in the state’s current Constitution.
match_headline: Alabama Begins Removing Racist Language From Its Constitution

text: An article on Tuesday about the expansion of The Washington Post’s newsroom misstated the timing of The Post’s plan to add breaking news hubs in London and Seoul. The plan was announced in December, not June.
match_headline: The Washington Post is adding 41 new editing jobs as part of its expansion.

text: An article on Sept. 7 about the bend and twist of scorpions’ tails misstated the location of a fictional movie scene. The character Elle Woods in “Legally Blonde” introduced the bend and snap, a foolproof method of catching someone’s attention, to a nail technician named Paulette in the Boston area, not Los Angeles.
match_headline: How Scorpion Tails Do the Bend and Twist

text: An article on Aug. 18 about the West African-influenced costumes in the Shakespeare in the Park production of “The Merry Wives of Windsor” described incorrectly an outfit worn by one of the characters, Madam Ford, at the top of the show. It is a blouse and wrapper ensemble, not a dress. The article also misstated when the costume designer Dede Ayite settled in Harlem. It was 10 years ago, not 20.
match_headline: Ankara Print Dresses? These Aren’t Shakespeare’s ‘Merry Wives.’

text: An article on Aug. 26 about the effects of air pollution on skin misstated Dr. Karen Burke’s title at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York. She is a professor, not an assistant professor.
match_headline: Wildfire Smoke Is Damaging Your Skin

text: An article on Sept. 9 about the counterfeit market for vintage punk clothing misstated the stage name of Grant Champkins-Howard. It is Grant Dell, not Grant Lee.
match_headline: Anarchy, and $$$, in the Vintage Punk Clothing Market

text: An article on Wednesday about President Biden’s address at the United Nations General Assembly misquoted the Chinese leader Xi Jinping. He said international disputes must be handled “on the basis of equality and mutual respect,” not “on the basis of quality and mutual respect.”
ref_headline: on the basis of equality and mutual respect,
match_headline: At U.N., Biden Calls for Diplomacy, Not Conflict, but Some Are Skeptical

text: An obituary on Thursday about the filmmaker, author and actor Melvin Van Peebles misstated the year he graduated from Ohio Wesleyan University. It was 1953, not 1954.
match_headline: Watching the Films of Melvin Van Peebles

text: An article this weekend on Page 11 about Mo Abudu, the head of EbonyLife Media, describes incorrectly the status of more than 30 deals between Abudu’s media company and others. Some of those deals have been made public; they were not all unreported.
match_headline: Mo Abudu Isn’t Waiting for Permission

text: An article this weekend on Page 132 about the architect Valerio Olgiati misidentifies the location of Muharraq. It is in Bahrain, not Dubai.
match_headline: An Architect Who’s Known for Aesthetic Purity and Counts Kanye West as a Client

text: An obituary on Friday about the theater and film director Roger Michell misstated the name of the London theater where he was an assistant director early in his career. It is the Royal Court Theater, not the Royal Theater Company.
match_headline: Roger Michell, Director of ‘Notting Hill,’ Is Dead at 65

text: An editorial last Sunday on problems with the generic prescription drug supply misstated the number of foreign pharmaceutical plants inspected by the F.D.A. in 2020. It was 206, not three.
match_headline: Our Drug Supply Is Sick. How Can We Fix It?

text: An article on Monday about German election results misstated the effect that the election results would have on the formation of a government. It will be the first time since the 1950s that at least three parties will be needed to form a coalition; it is not the first time ever.
match_headline: German Election Heralds Messier Politics and Weaker Leadership After Merkel

text: An article on Sunday about a Sikh officer in the Marines who was allowed to wear a turban misidentified the deputy Marine Corps commandant for manpower and reserve affairs. It was Lt. Gen. David A. Ottignon, not Lt. Gen. Michael A. Rocco.
match_headline: The Marines Reluctantly Let a Sikh Officer Wear a Turban. He Says It’s Not Enough.

text: An article on Monday about how accounting giants craft favorable tax rules from inside government misstated in a photo caption the length of time Pamela Olson served as assistant Treasury secretary for tax policy. It was more than 16 months, not less than a year.
match_headline: How Accounting Giants Craft Favorable Tax Rules From Inside Government

text: An article on Monday about vaccine mandates for health care workers misstated a vaccination requirement for some health care workers in Connecticut. The deadline for workers at nursing homes and long-term care facilities to get one dose of a coronavirus vaccine was extended to Sept. 27. It did not go into effect on Sept. 7.
match_headline: These Health Care Workers Would Rather Get Fired Than Get Vaccinated

text: An article on Wednesday about the women’s basketball pioneer Seimone Augustus described incorrectly the relationship of LaTaya Varner and Augustus. They are divorced, not married.
match_headline: Seimone Augustus Found Her Voice Long Before Coaching

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the Tony Awards winners misstated Matthew López’s relationship to “The Inheritance,” which won the award for Best Play. He is its playwright, not director.
match_headline: Tonys Winners List: ‘Moulin Rouge!’ Gets 10 Awards

text: An obituary on Friday about Barbara Campbell Cooke, the widow of the singer Sam Cooke, referred incorrectly to Mr. Cooke’s death in a shooting. A coroner’s jury ruled that the death was justifiable homicide — not murder.
match_headline: Barbara Campbell Cooke, 85, Widow of the Slain Sam Cooke, Is Dead

text: An obituary on Monday about the press agent Bobby Zarem misspelled the surname of the author of the true-crime book “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil.” He is John Berendt, not Behrendt.
ref_headline: Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil.
match_headline: Bobby Zarem, ‘Superflack’ and Maker of Stars, Dies at 84

text: An article on Sept. 24 about France’s influence in global affairs misstated the status in the past of Lebanon under French administration. It was a protectorate, not a colony.
match_headline: An Uncomfortable Question in France: Are We Still a Great Power?

text: An article on Saturday about charges the utility company Pacific Gas & Electric faces in connection to a wildfire in California last year misstated the company’s history of convictions. The company was found guilty in 1997 of criminal negligence in a 1994 wildfire; a 2016 verdict was not its first criminal conviction.
match_headline: PG&E Faces Criminal Charges Over Fatal 2020 Wildfire in California

text: A column on Sunday about a proposed deal between the investment bank Goldman Sachs and the digital media company Ozy misstated what is known about the source of a fake email address that was provided to the bank. Carlos Watson, Ozy’s chief executive, said he was not the source. The column also misstated the national origin of Mr. Watson’s parents. Only his father was Jamaican; his mother was from Virginia.
match_headline: Goldman Sachs, Ozy Media and a $40 Million Conference Call Gone Wrong

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about “Convergence Station,” an immersive art installation by the company Meow Wolf, misidentified the location of some visitors. They were in the Macarenia section and heading toward the Parlour Birds exhibit. They were not in the Parlour Room.
match_headline: Paranormal Play in Denver From Meow Wolf

text: An article on Saturday about this year’s winners of the Lasker awards transposed the institutional affiliations of two researchers. Peter Hegemann is with Humboldt University of Berlin and Dieter Oesterhelt is with Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry, not the other way around.
match_headline: Covid Vaccine Pioneers and Others Win 2021 Lasker Awards in Medicine

text: An article on Tuesday about cancer patients forgoing chemotherapy misstated the annual deaths caused by lung cancer. It kills about 132,000 Americans each year, not 69,000. The article also referred incorrectly to annual breast cancer deaths. Each year, 43,000 women die because of it. That is not the total number of all American breast cancer fatalities.
match_headline: Cancer Without Chemotherapy: ‘A Totally Different World’

text: An article on Saturday about an effort by Senate Democrats to draft a tax on carbon dioxide pollution misstated the size of the Democrats’ proposed budget bill in one instance. It is $3.5 trillion, not $3.5 billion.
match_headline: Democrats Consider Adding Carbon Tax to Budget Bill

text: An article on Wednesday about lip-syncing referred incorrectly to the arts organization that released the short film “The Island We Made.” It is Opera Philadelphia, not the Philadelphia Opera.
match_headline: How Lip-Syncing Got Real

text: An article on Page 26 this weekend about “The Sopranos” misstates the title of a book about the mafia by Selwyn Raab. It is “Five Families,” not “The Five Families.”
match_headline: Why Is Every Young Person in America Watching ‘The Sopranos’?

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about George Frayne, the musician known professionally as Commander Cody, misstated the given name of the director who made the video for Mr. Frayne’s 1980 song “Two Triple Cheese, Side Order of Fries.” He is Joe Dea, not John.
ref_headline: Two Triple Cheese, Side Order of Fries.
match_headline: George Ferencz, Innovative Theater Director, Dies at 74

text: An article on Wednesday about New York unions and the vaccine mandate wrongly included a category of workers among those represented by Local 32BJ of the Service Employees International Union. It does not represent health care aides. It also misstated the affiliation of Local 2507, which represents the city’s emergency medical workers. It is a part of District Council 37, not the Teamsters.
match_headline: ‘If You’re Not Vaccinated, Don’t Come to Work’

text: An article last Sunday about the Bushwig festival in New York referred incorrectly to two performers who have strained relationships with gay and trans communities because of their social media posts. While Azealia Banks performed at Bushwig, Nikita Dragun did not. The article also misstated the compensation options for local drag queens. Performers with experience could negotiate their rates; their compensation was not set at $60 or a pass to one of the festival days.
