match_headline: Bushwig Grows Up

text: An article last Sunday about “cheer moms” misspelled the given name of a parent of a cheerleader. She is Kristen Wheeler, not Kristin. The article also misstated the age of her daughter Abby. She is 17, not 14.
match_headline: The Highs and Lows of the ‘Cheer Mom’

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Jared Polis and Marlon Reis misstated the Hebrew verse that Mr. Polis, who is the governor of Colorado, had inscribed in the engagement ring that he gave to Mr. Reis. It was Isaiah 11:6, not Isaiah 11:16.
match_headline: A Wedding 18 Years in the Making for Colorado Governor

text: An article on Sunday about the perilous Darién Gap route many migrants take to reach the United States misstated the geographical definition of the Darién Gap. The Darien makes up part of the Isthmus of Panama, not its entirety.
match_headline: Perilous, Roadless Jungle Becomes a Path of Desperate Hope

text: An article on Sunday about an experiment to make Paris a cycling capital of Europe misspelled the name of a Danish cultural institute in Paris. It the Maison du Danemark, not the Maison de Danmark.
match_headline: As Bikers Throng the Streets, ‘It’s Like Paris Is in Anarchy’

text: An article on Sunday about abortion rights marches misspelled the surname of a woman who attended a march in Washington, D.C. Her name is Liz Field, not Fields.
match_headline: Supporters of Abortion Rights, at Nationwide Marches, Try to Regain Momentum

text: An article on Sunday about the turbulence President Biden has faced while pushing for transformative policies described incorrectly how President Biden has proposed to pay for his domestic policy proposals. He has called for tax hikes on the rich, not tax cuts.
match_headline: Biden’s Big Vision Collides With His Small Majorities

text: An article on Saturday about the Bedlam theater company’s adaptation of Jane Austen’s “Persuasion” misstated the era in which Jane Austen’s “Persuasion” takes place. It is the Regency era, not the Victorian era.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Persuasion,’ How to Lose Lovers and Influence People

text: An article on Saturday about the documentary “Karen Dalton: In My Own Time” misstated the era in which Karen Dalton was born. She was born before World War II, not after.
ref_headline: Karen Dalton: In My Own Time
match_headline: Karen Dalton, a Musical Mystery That Doesn’t Need to Be Solved

text: An article on Sept. 28 about health care for transgender youth misstated the name of a transgender health association. It is the World Professional Association for Transgender Health, not the World Professional Organization for Transgender Health.
match_headline: For Transgender Youth, Stigma Is Just One Barrier to Health Care

text: An article on Tuesday about leaked confidential financial records referred to as the Pandora Papers misstated the position held by the Czech Republic leader whose purchase of a French Riviera property was described in the Pandora Papers. He is prime minister, not president.
match_headline: Pandora Papers: A Money Bomb With Political Ripples

text: An article on Tuesday about four new Ford Motor factories misstated the conditions under which workers at planned Ford Motor factories in Tennessee and Kentucky could come under union jurisdiction. For the United Auto Workers contract to apply at a Ford electric-truck assembly plant in Tennessee, a majority of eligible workers there would need to sign cards backing the union. At three battery plants that would be a joint venture between Ford and another company, unionization efforts would need to start from scratch. The first provision reflects the U.A.W. contract with Ford, and the second reflects federal labor law; neither stems from those states’ right-to-work laws.
match_headline: Ford Will Build 4 Factories in a Big Electric Vehicle Push

text: An article on Monday about week four of the N.F.L. season omitted the given name of the Dallas Cowboys’ defensive coordinator. He is Dan Quinn.
match_headline: What We Learned From Week 4 of the N.F.L. Season

text: An article on Tuesday about artist Alan Michelson’s new installation, “Midden,” at MoMA PS1 misidentified the location of the Grand River. It is wholly, not partially, in Ontario. The artist’s video piece “Two Row II” was shot on the northern and southern shorelines of the river, not only on its northern shore.
match_headline: Oyster Shoreline at ‘Greater New York’ Has a Pearl of a Message

text: An article on Sunday about a photo studio in Pakistan, using information from the studio, misidentified the couple in a 1940 photo. They were Mansoor and Nuzhat Muzaffar, not Mr. and Mrs. Mohammad Abbas. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Saving a Vibrant History, One Frame at a Time

text: An article on Saturday about Greenland’s deposits of rare elements needed for electric cars and wind turbines described two substances incorrectly. Neodymium and dysprosium are elements, not minerals. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: The World Wants Greenland’s Minerals, but Greenlanders Are Wary

text: An article on Wednesday about the M.L.B’s wild-card game misstated the number of teams that have used the wild-card game to begin a run to the World Series. It is three (the 2019 Nationals, the 2014 Royals and the 2014 Giants), not four.
match_headline: ‘Is it Fair? No, It’s Not Fair. Is It Fun? Absolutely.’

text: An article on Sunday about rappers shopping at Icebox described incorrectly a scene in a video in which Lil Durk views one of Icebox’s safes in a video. He looks in from outside, but does not enter the safe.
match_headline: Rappers Come Shop for Jewelry. Icebox Turns the Cameras On.

text: An article on Wednesday about the winners of the Nobel Prize in Physics misstated the dollar amount of the monetary part of the Nobel Prize. It is approximately $1.1 million, not $10 million.
match_headline: Nobel Prize in Physics Awarded for Study of Humanity’s Role in Changing Climate

text: An article on Thursday about recommended single doses of the coronavirus vaccine for children in some countries described incorrectly the actions taken by regulators in Sweden and Denmark. They have halted use of the Moderna vaccine in children; they have not begun offering single doses. The article also misstated the number of Covid hospitalizations in U.S. children. It is more than 63,000 from August 2020 to October 2021, not 900,000 since the beginning of the pandemic. In addition, the article misstated the timing of an F.D.A. meeting on authorization of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine for children. It is later this month, not next week.
match_headline: A New Vaccine Strategy for Children: Just One Dose, for Now

text: An article on Wednesday about the New York Film Festival misidentified the color film process used for “Giant.” It was in Warnercolor, not Technicolor.
match_headline: The Future of Movies Collides With the Past at the New York Film Festival

text: An article on Friday about the new malaria vaccine in Africa referred incorrectly to malaria in one instance. It is caused by a parasite, not a virus.
match_headline: Africans Welcome New Malaria Vaccine. But Is It a ‘Game Changer'?

text: An article on Thursday about the Biden administration’s proposed changes to the National Environmental Policy Act misidentified a key environmental law in one instance. It is the National Environmental Policy Act, not the National Environmental Protection Act.
match_headline: Biden Administration to Restore Climate Criteria to Landmark Environmental Law

text: An article on Friday about negotiations to overhaul the international tax system misspelled the given name of Ireland’s prime minister. He is Micheal Martin, not Michael.
match_headline: A Global Deal Aimed at Ending Tax Havens Gains Momentum

text: Because of an editing error, a review on Friday of the reinstallation “Companions in Solitude: Reclusion and Communion in Chinese Art” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art misstated the position held by Joseph Scheier-Dolberg at the museum. He is associate curator of Chinese painting and calligraphy, not assistant curator. The review also misspelled the surname of the Chinese artist who painted “Famous Women.” He is Gai Qi, not Gia Qi.
ref_headline: Companions in Solitude: Reclusion and Communion in Chinese Art
match_headline: Looking Close at the Fragile Beauty of Chinese Painting

text: A review on Friday of “Greater New York,” a survey at MoMA PS1, misstated the surname of an artist featured in Marie Karlberg’s video “The Good Terrorist.” She is Nicole Eisenman, not Eisenberg.
match_headline: ‘Greater New York,’ a Show of the Moment, Dwells in the Radical Past

text: A review on Friday of the documentary “The Rescue” misidentified the cave diver who, when he finds the children in a cave, repeats the word “believe.” It is John Volanthen, not Rick Stanton.
match_headline: ‘The Rescue’ Review: Going All In on a Risky Mission

text: An article on Page 26 this weekend about the legal battle between the writers Dawn Dorland and Sonya Larson misstates the GrubStreet writing center’s action after Dorland’s initial questions about potential plagiarism. It did reply; it’s not the case that she received no response. The article also misstates Dorland’s thoughts on what could happen if she loses the court case. Dorland said she fears that Larson would be able to sue her for copyright infringement should she publish her letter to the end recipient of the kidney donation chain, not that she fears that Larson might be able to sue her for copyright infringement should she write anything about organ donation.
match_headline: Who Is the Bad Art Friend?

text: An obituary on Sept. 26 about the former Republican congressman Sherwood Boehlert referred imprecisely to the district he represented. It included parts of Cornell University, but not the central campus.
match_headline: Sherwood Boehlert, a G.O.P Moderate in the House, Dies at 84

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sept. 26 about Penny Harrington, the first woman to head a major American city’s police department, omitted the given name of her second husband. He is Gary Harrington.
match_headline: Penny Harrington, Who Broke a Blue Ceiling, Dies at 79

text: An obituary on Sept. 30 about the jazz organist Lonnie Smith, using information from his record company, omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to those named, Mr. Smith is survived by a son, Lonnie Jr.
match_headline: Lonnie Smith, Soulful Jazz Organist, Is Dead at 79

text: An article last Sunday about the safety of New York City’s new supertall towers misstated the occupancy status of Trump World Tower. It received a final certificate of occupancy from the New York Department of Buildings in 2005; it is not among a number of properties operating under a temporary certificate of occupancy.
match_headline: New Supertalls Test the Limits, as the City Consults an Aging Playbook

text: An article on Sept. 19 about metabolism overstated what is known about the number of labs that perform a method to measure metabolism during daily life called “doubly labeled water.” A small number of labs — not only nine — employ it regularly.
match_headline: The New Science on How We Burn Calories

text: An editorial last Sunday about reforming federal election law misstated the party affiliations of the presidents who appointed the Supreme Court justices who served on the electoral commission of 1877. Two of the justices were aligned with Democrats and three with Republicans; they were not appointed by two Democrats and three Republicans.
match_headline: Jan. 6 Was Worse Than We Knew

text: An article on Saturday about security agreement negotiations between the United States and Mexico misstated to whom 16 senators addressed a letter urging that Haitian migrants be protected. It was addressed to the Homeland Security secretary, Alejandro N. Mayorkas, and Secretary of State Antony J. Blinken, not to Mr. Mayorkas and President Biden.
match_headline: At Mexico-U.S. Security Talks, Migration Question Is Largely Avoided

text: An article on Sunday about the parliamentary election in the Czech Republic misstated the day that the election concluded. It was Saturday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Populist Leader of Czech Republic Narrowly Defeated in Election

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about Seattle voters’ support for President Biden’s domestic agenda referred incorrectly to Green Lake Park in Seattle. It is a city park, not a state park.
match_headline: ‘Long Overdue’: Liberal Voters Hold Firm to Biden’s Stronger Safety Net

text: An article on Thursday about General Motors’ plans to double its annual revenue by 2030 misstated Tesla’s market capitalization. It is nearly $800 billion, not $800 million.
match_headline: G.M. Hopes Electric Cars and New Businesses Will Help Double Its Revenue

text: An article on Thursday about the actor Adrian Lester misstated the name of the alias of the character he portrayed on the television series “Hustle.” It is Mickey Bricks (an alias of Michael Stone), not Mickey Rocks.
match_headline: Adrian Lester Finally Arrives on Broadway, via Wall Street

text: A review on Friday of Carnegie Hall’s reopening misidentified the inspiration for the composer Valerie Coleman’s “Seven O’Clock Shout.” The work, which was played by the Philadelphia Orchestra at Carnegie Hall on Oct. 6, was inspired by the 7 p.m. cheers for frontline workers during the pandemic, not by Boccaccio’s “Decameron,” which was mentioned in the program notes.
match_headline: Review: Carnegie Hall Reopens With a Blaze From Philadelphia

text: An article on Tuesday about Iraq’s parliamentary elections referred incorrectly to the party that made the biggest gains in the Iraqi elections. It is the Sadrist Bloc, not Sairoun (as the party was previously known).
match_headline: In Iraq Election, Shiite Cleric Who Fought U.S. Strengthens Power

text: An article on Friday about gas price surges in Europe and claims that Russia is manipulating the flow of gas misstated Aleksandr Novak’s role in the Russian government. He is a deputy prime minister, not the energy minister (a position he held previously).
match_headline: As Europe Faces a Cold Winter, Putin Seizes on the Leverage From Russia’s Gas Output

text: An article on Tuesday about the recently reopened trial of 14 men accused of plotting the 1987 assassination of Thomas Sankara misstated the language of Burkina Faso’s largest ethnic group. It is Moore, not Mossi (which is the name of the ethnic group).
match_headline: Who Killed African Icon Thomas Sankara? Trial Opens, 34 Years After His Death.

text: An article on Monday about French actress Léa Seydoux misstated the title of a forthcoming Mia Hansen-Love movie. It is “One Fine Morning,” not “One Fine Day.”
match_headline: Bonding With Léa Seydoux

text: An article on Tuesday about the actress Maryann Plunkett’s final performance in Richard Nelson’s “Rhinebeck Panorama” cycle misspelled the given name of an actor. He is Jon DeVries, not John.
match_headline: Maryann Plunkett Says Goodbye to Her Lives in Rhinebeck

text: An article on Friday about tennis player Emma Raducanu misstated the date of the U.S. Open women’s final. It was Sept. 11, not Sept. 12.
match_headline: Emma Raducanu, After U.S. Open Win, Keeps Her Feet on the Ground

text: An obituary on Saturday about the artist Billy Apple misstated his age in 1966, when city inspectors put restrictions on an exhibition of his neon works in New York. He was 30, not 27. (As the obituary correctly noted, he was born in December 1935.)
match_headline: Billy Apple, Artist Who Was His Own Life’s Work, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the actress Cynthia Harris misstated the day she died. It was Sunday, Oct. 3 — not Monday, Oct. 11.
match_headline: Cynthia Harris, the Mother on ‘Mad About You,’ Dies at 87

text: An article on Thursday about how U.S. antigovernment groups are influencing the French far right incorrectly implied the nature of the extremist cells that a French official said had been broken up by French authorities. Six Islamist cells have been broken up in the last five years and accused of plotting attacks. No right wing extremist cells have been broken up.
match_headline: U.S. Antigovernment Groups Are Influencing the French Far Right

text: An article on Thursday about guidelines from the Food and Drug Administration to reduce salt in foods misstated the year of a White House nutrition conference that involved a discussion about reducing salt consumption. It was held in 1969, not 1968.
match_headline: F.D.A. Issues Guidelines to Reduce Salt in Foods

text: An obituary on Thursday about Paddy Moloney, the frontman of the Irish band the Chieftains, misspelled the name of a group that recorded with the Chieftains in 2012. They are the Decemberists, not the Decembrists.
match_headline: Paddy Moloney, Piper Who Led Revival of Irish Music, Dies at 83

text: An article last Sunday about the changing nature of California suburbs referred incorrectly to the architectural style of the houses in the Clairemont Villas development. They are ranch-style houses, not Craftsman.
match_headline: Where the Suburbs End

text: An article this weekend on page 11 about tango dancers in New York describes incorrectly the movement of dancers around a statue of William Shakespeare in Central Park. They went in a counterclockwise direction, not clockwise. It also misstates how many people tested positive for the coronavirus after a dance event in July. It was two, not one.
match_headline: Dancing Cheek to Cheek Again: New York’s Tango Scene Rebounds

text: An article last Sunday about the footwear designer Salehe Bembury misstated the name of a private school in Manhattan that he attended. It is the Calhoun School, not Calhoun High School.
match_headline: A Day in the Studio With Salehe Bembury

text: An article last Sunday about off-the-grid living on Oak Island, N.Y., misidentified a shellfish restoration project. It is the Suffolk Project in Aquaculture Training, not the Billion Oyster Project.
match_headline: An Island of Off-the-Grid Homes, Just 50 Miles From Times Square

text: An article this weekend on Page 54 about the director Denis Villeneuve and his adaptation of “Dune” misspells the surname of an actor in Denis Villeneuve’s adaptation of “Dune.” His name is Stellan Skarsgard, not Starsgard.
match_headline: The Man Who Finally Made a ‘Dune’ That Fans Will Love

text: An article on Page 40 this weekend about the artist Mickalene Thomas misspelled part of the title of one of her paintings. It is “Racquel Reclining Wearing Purple Jumpsuit” not “Raquel Reclining Wearing Purple Jumpsuit.”
match_headline: Mickalene Thomas Is Reinventing Nudes

text: A review on June 20 about Yan Lianke’s novel “Hard Like Water” referred incorrectly to the book’s setting. It begins in China in 1967, soon after the Cultural Revolution has started. It does not begin “in the wake of the Revolution.” This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: Cheat on Your Partner or Change the World: In This Novel, It’s All the Same

text: An article on Page 48 about Black artists’ collectives misspells the surname of an artist; she was Barbara Jones-Hogu, not Jones-Hobu.
match_headline: ‘Fighting for Change’: Life as a Black Artist

text: An article on Saturday about an offer made by the Pentagon to pay the family members of the 10 civilians mistakenly killed by the U.S. military in a drone strike on Aug. 29 misstated the groups represented by the American Civil Liberties Union in the deaths. It is currently representing only Nutrition & Education International, not both that group and Zemari Ahmadi’s family.
match_headline: U.S. Pledges to Pay Family of Those Killed in Botched Kabul Drone Strike

text: An article on Saturday about the testimony of Adam Laxalt, a Republican candidate for governor of Nevada, in the trial of Lev Parnas described incorrectly a 2018 donation to the campaign of Mr. Laxalt. The donation was $10,000, not $2,700, and, according to prosecutors, it was made in the name of Igor Fruman, not using Mr. Fruman’s credit card.
match_headline: Testimony at Lev Parnas Trial Offers Peek at His Place in Trump’s Orbit

text: An article on Monday about Christian Aid Ministries, using information from the group’s website, described incorrectly the 17 missionaries who were abducted in Haiti on Saturday. There were six men, six women and five children were taken, not five men, seven women and five children. It also omitted part of the name of a program at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary. It is the Center for the Study of Global Christianity, not the Study of Global Christianity.
match_headline: For Missionary Group in a Fragile Haiti, Charity Turns to Chaos

text: An article on Monday about Republican concerns about the 2022 midterm elections described incorrectly a survey conducted by Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene. The internal survey found that 4 percent of Republican voters in her district said they did not think elections were secure in Georgia and would not vote in future elections, and 6 percent said they were unsure whether their votes would be counted. It did not specifically ask about Georgia conducting an audit of the 2020 election.
match_headline: As Trump Thunders About Last Election, Republicans Worry About the Next One

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the environmental sustainability of products made by plant-based food companies misstated the disclosure of sustainability measures by Beyond Meat and Impossible Foods. The companies disclose some data on greenhouse gas emissions, but not the total amount across all of their operations.
match_headline: Plant-Based Food Companies Face Critics: Environmental Advocates

text: An article on Wednesday about the N.H.L. player Connor McDavid misidentified a Calgary Flames defenseman. He is Christopher Tanev, not Brandon Tanev, who is his brother and who is a forward for the Seattle Kraken.
match_headline: Connor McDavid Is Ready for a Stanley Cup Championship

text: An article on Monday about an exhibition at the Jewish Museum in Manhattan based on a book by the artist and writer Edmund de Waal described incorrectly the experiences of Elizabeth Diller’s mother, Anna, upon her return to Poland after World War II. The man whom Anna married before the war, and who had been presumed dead and then reappeared after the war, was Anna’s first husband; he was not Elizabeth’s father. And it was Anna from whom Elizabeth said she had never been able to get the whole story of what happened during that period, not Anna’s first husband. The article also misidentified where the photographer Iwan Baan is based. He is in Amsterdam, not in Paris.
match_headline: Elizabeth Diller Is Retelling Edmund de Waal’s Story — and Her Own

text: An article on Saturday about the sale of Banksy’s “Love Is in the Bin” misidentified the previous record for a sale of Banksy’s work at auction. It was $23.2 million, given at Christie’s in London in March for the painting “Game Changer.” It was not the $12.1 million given at Sotheby’s in 2019 for his painting “Devolved Parliament.”
match_headline: Banksy’s Shredding Artwork Is Auctioned for $25.4 Million at Sotheby’s

text: An article on Sunday about “scripted homicide” clubs in China misstated the amount of money made by Wang Yihan from running games based on a script she altered. It was $31,000, not $3,100.
match_headline: China’s Latest Craze: Scripted Murders, With Real Tears and Piracy

text: An article on Saturday about the confession of a man accused of killing five people and wounding two others with a bow and arrow in Norway misspelled the suspect’s middle name. He is Espen Andersen Brathen, not Espen Anderson Brathen. The error was repeated in a subheading.
match_headline: Suspect Confesses in Bow-and-Arrow Rampage in Norway

text: An article on Monday about the video at the center of the trial of the men accused of killing Ahmaud Arbery in Georgia misstated Gregory McMichael’s statement to the police. He said he had seen Mr. Arbery running down the street, not inside a house under construction.
match_headline: In the Trial of Ahmaud Arbery’s Accused Killers, Unsettling Video Will Have a Starring Role

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the rosters of the Los Angeles Lakers and the Golden State Warriors misstated the season in which Stephen Curry missed all but five games because of an injury. As the article correctly noted, it was the 2019-20 season, not last season.
match_headline: LeBron James and Stephen Curry Test Different Paths Back to N.B.A. Peak

text: An article last Wednesday about Food staff recommendations of 50 restaurants around the country misstated the given name of a co-owner of Atomix, in New York City. She is Ellia Park, not Ella.
match_headline: There Is Shadow Inflation Taking Place All Around Us

text: An obituary on Sunday about Brian Goldner, the president of Hasbro, misstated the number of movies based on the Hasbro property G.I. Joe on which he was a producer. It was three, not two. A picture caption with the obituary misstated the surname of the Paramount Pictures executive shown with Mr. Goldner at the premiere of a G.I. Joe movie in 2013. He is Adam Goodman, not Goldman.
match_headline: Brian Goldner, Hasbro Executive With Hollywood Vision, Dies at 58

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the former secretary of state and national security adviser Colin L. Powell misstated when his tenure as secretary of state ended. It was January 2005, not January 2004.
match_headline: Colin Powell, Who Shaped U.S. National Security, Dies at 84

text: An article on Tuesday about a group of U.S. veterans working to rescue Afghan allies after the American withdrawal referred imprecisely to J. Kael Weston’s background. Mr. Weston is a former State Department official, not a former foreign service officer.
match_headline: These U.S. Veterans Won’t Rest Until They’ve Kept a Wartime Promise

text: An article on Wednesday about a Christian aid group kidnapped in Haiti referred incorrectly to the abduction of relatives of the businessman Eric Jean-Jacques. His cousin was held hostage by a gang called 5 Segonn, and his aunt was kidnapped by another gang that he could not identify. They were not both taken by 5 Segonn.
match_headline: Kidnappers in Haiti Demand $17 Million to Free Missionary Group

text: An article on Tuesday about a statue by stone carver William Edmondson found on a St. Louis couple’s front lawn referred incorrectly to the scene in which Mary and Martha are depicted. It is Jesus’s meal in Bethany, not the Last Supper.
match_headline: A ‘Holy Grail’ of American Folk Art, Hiding in Plain Sight

text: An article last Thursday about the debate over temporary tattoos referred imprecisely to Jewish law on tattooing. Some rabbis interpret verses in the Torah as prohibiting tattoos, but others do not.
match_headline: Why Do You Tattoo?

text: An article on Wednesday about the reporting behind the The New York Times Magazine article “Who Is the Bad Art Friend?” referred imprecisely to a letter Dawn Dorland had written about her kidney donation and posted to a Facebook group. She wrote the letter to the person at the end of the surgical chain, not directly to the organ recipient.
ref_headline: Who Is the Bad Art Friend?
match_headline: How Bad Art Friend Became Twitter’s Favorite Parlor Game

text: An article on Sunday about 17 missionaries that were kidnapped in Haiti, relying on information from a former field director for Christian Aid Ministries, misstated the age of one of the children who was abducted. The child is 3, not 2.
match_headline: Missionaries With an American Christian Group Kidnapped in Haiti

text: An article on Wednesday about former combatants seeking veterans’ benefits for fighting to overthrow South Africa’s apartheid regime misstated the racial makeup of the country’s apartheid-era army. Battalions of Black soldiers were recruited to fight for the army. It was not all white.
match_headline: They Fought Apartheid in South Africa. Now They Want Veterans’ Benefits.

text: An article on Friday about an announcement by the National Institutes of Health that a nonprofit group had failed to promptly report findings from studies on how well bat coronaviruses grow in mice misstated the year in which the P3CO framework for research on certain potential pandemic pathogens was introduced and misidentified the government organization that introduced it. It was introduced in 2017, not 2019, and by the Department of Health and Human Services, not the N.I.H.
match_headline: Bat Research Group Failed to Submit Virus Studies Promptly, N.I.H. Says

text: An article on Friday about the federal prosecutor Breon S. Peace misstated the year that Dr. M. Marquette Peace Jr. retired. It was 2020, not 2000.
match_headline: Can Brooklyn’s New U.S. Attorney Help Restore Faith in Law Enforcement?

text: An article on Page 11 this weekend about the documentary “American Veteran” misspelled the given name of the writer and director. He is Stephen Ives, not Steven.
match_headline: ‘American Veteran’ Honors the Many Faces of the U.S. Soldier

text: An article on Page 10 this weekend about an exhibit at the Jewish Museum based on a book by Edmund de Waal, relying on outdated information from a publicist, misstates how many netsuke, Japanese decorative carvings, will be displayed in an exhibition at the Jewish Museum of New York. It is 168, not 157.
match_headline: Tracing a Family History Through the Journey of a Tiny Figurine

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 20 about the artist Robert Lugo misspells the surname of an artist collaborating in the “Back and Forth: Red and Meth” exhibition at the Wexler Gallery in Philadelphia. The artist is Ashley Porrini, not Porini. The article also misstates the ending date of an exhibition at the Arthur Ross Gallery at the University of Pennsylvania. It is Dec. 19, not Dec. 1. Additionally, because of outdated information from a publicist, it misstates when “Before Yesterday We Could Fly: An Afrofuturist Period Room” will open at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. It is Nov. 5, not Nov. 1.
ref_headline: Back and Forth: Red and Meth
match_headline: His First Art Was Graffiti. Now His Pottery Is in the Met.

text: An article on Page 30 about climate exhibits misspells the surname of the director of the Chrysler Museum of Art. He is Erik Neil, not Neill. It also misstates Jane Winchell’s title. She is the director of the Peabody Essex Museum’s Art & Nature Center, and a leader of its Climate + Environment Initiative; she is not the director of the Climate + Environment Initiative.
match_headline: Climate Exhibitions Look Beyond Declarations of Calamity

text: An article on Page 36 about a variety of art shows across the United States misstates the title of an exhibition by the Dutch designer-artists known as Drift. It is “Fragile Future,” not “Fragile Futures.”
match_headline: At Museums and Auctions, Paintings, Posters and a Magician’s Treasures

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts by Amazon employees on Staten Island to form a union misstated the expected timing of a hearing where Amazon can contest which jobs should be included in the bargaining unit and the terms of the election. The hearing is expected in mid-November, not mid-May.
match_headline: Amazon workers on Staten Island show they have enough support to hold a union election.

text: An article last weekend about artist residencies misspelled the name of a residency program in New Hampshire. It is MacDowell, not McDowell.
match_headline: Despite Covid Challenges, Some Artist Residencies Are Thriving

text: An obituary on Monday about the singer Jay Black misstated the surname of his sister, who survives him. She is Gail Denker, not Decker.
match_headline: Jay Black, Soaring Lead Singer of the Americans, Dies at 82

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about modern Israeli identity misidentified a cafe in Haifa. It is Rai, not Fattoush. Both are known for welcoming Jews and Arabs.
match_headline: Whose Promised Land? A Journey Into a Divided Israel

text: An article on Monday about mistakes that Amazon made in handling paid and unpaid leave, using information provided by Amazon, misstated the status of the company’s efforts to identify and repay workers who had been shortchanged while on leave. The company finished this year, it is not still repaying them.
match_headline: Inside Amazon’s Worst Human Resources Problem

text: An article on Monday about a shortage of sanitation workers in U.S. cities misstated the recent pay increases for some sanitation workers in Dallas. Contract employees received a bump to $15.21 an hour, not $13.12 an hour, which was up from $12.38 an hour, not $12.28 an hour. The article also misstated the previous base pay rate for truck drivers employed by the city. It was $16.50 an hour, not $12.28 an hour.
match_headline: An Unexpected Pandemic Consequence Frustrates Florida’s Biggest City

text: An article on Wednesday about Claudette Colvin, a civil rights pioneer, erroneously attributed a distinction to Calvin L. Williams, the judge hearing Colvin’s case. He is not the first Black judge to serve on Alabama’s 15th Judicial Circuit Court.
match_headline: A Civil Rights Pioneer Seeks to Have Her Record Cleared

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the second New York City mayoral debate described incorrectly a 19th-century opera referenced by Curtis Sliwa. Pagliacci is the name of the opera and means “clowns” in Italian; it is not the name of a character in the opera.
match_headline: Final New York Mayoral Debate Descends Into Exchange of Personal Insults

text: An item on Wednesday about recent real estate transactions in New York, relying on information supplied by the broker, misstated the construction date of the building at 23-15 Astoria Boulevard in Queens. It was built in 2016, not 2013.
match_headline: Recent Commercial Real Estate Transactions

text: An article on Sunday about the basketball player Kris Wilkes, relying on information from Mr. Wilkes, described incorrectly his insurance coverage. It was permanent total disability, not loss of value.
match_headline: His N.B.A. Dream Was Right There. Then He Couldn’t Move His Legs.

text: An article on Wednesday about possible replacements for Mark Zuckerberg as the chief executive of Facebook misstated the given name of Facebook’s next chief technology officer. He is Andrew Bosworth, not Adam.
match_headline: Beyond Zuckerberg

text: An article on Thursday about the return to school for some girls in Afghanistan misspelled the name of the high school in Mazar-i-Sharif. It is Fatima Balkhi High School, not Balkh.
match_headline: Taliban Allow Girls to Return to Some High Schools, but With Big Caveats

text: An article on Thursday about bans faced by transgender athletes misstated the party affiliation of the governors of Kansas and Louisiana. They are Democrats, not Republicans.
match_headline: Transgender Athletes Face Bans From Girls’ Sports in 10 U.S. States

text: An article on Thursday about the Boston mayoral candidate Michelle Wu attributed an erroneous distinction to her election to the Boston City Council. She was not the youngest person ever elected to the council. It also misstated the year she was first elected to the Council. Ms. Wu was 28 when she was elected in 2013, not 2012; Lawrence DiCara was elected at age 22 in 1971.
match_headline: Michelle Wu Makes Her Play for Power in Boston

text: An article on Friday about coronavirus infections in children misstated the timing of a meeting at which advisers to the Food and Drug Administration debated use of the Pfizer-BioNTech Covid-19 vaccine in children ages 5 to 11. The meeting took place on Tuesday, Oct. 26, not the previous week.
match_headline: Has the Virus Infected Huge Numbers of Younger Children?

text: An article on Friday about art galleries in TriBeCa referred incorrectly to Mother Gallery. It did not relocate from Beacon, N.Y. It opened a new location in TriBeCa.
match_headline: TriBeCa Gallery Guide: New York’s Most Vibrant Art Scene

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 8 about Abba misidentifies two of the group’s members. Bjorn Ulvaeus is at left, not right, and Benny Andersson is at the right, not left.
match_headline: After 40 Years, Abba Takes a Chance With Its Legacy

text: An article on Page 2 this weekend about the Guild Gallery in New York, relying on information from a publicist, described incorrectly the work that the architecture and design firm Roman and Williams had done for Goop. The firm designed two Goop stores, not Goop’s offices.
match_headline: Journey to a Center of the Earth

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 8 this weekend about an apartment makeover in Paris converts incorrectly the measurement of half a square meter. It is five square feet, not two.
match_headline: In Paris, a Straight Road to the Past

text: An article on Page 9 this weekend about designer delis misstates the status of the newest location of Zucker’s deli. It is the second in Midtown Manhattan, not the first; there is also a location at 370 Lexington Avenue, near 41st Street. It also misstates which location of the deli Vicki Bodwell, an internet retail executive, was discussing when she described its interior. She was discussing the TriBeCa location, not the Midtown one.
match_headline: The Rise of the Designer Deli

text: An obituary on Friday about the psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi misstated at one point where he was born. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, he was born in Italy to Hungarian parents, not in Hungary.
match_headline: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, the Father of ‘Flow,’ Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Thursday about Arnold Hano, the author of “A Day in the Bleachers,” a book about Game 1 of the 1954 World Series, referred incorrectly to the circumstances under which Vic Wertz of Cleveland hit a long fly ball that was caught by Willie Mays. There were no outs at the time, not one out. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misstated where Mr. Hano went to college. It was Long Island University in Brooklyn, not Queens. (There is no L.I.U. campus in Queens.)
match_headline: Arnold Hano, Author of a Bleachers’ View Baseball Classic, Dies at 99

text: An article on Page 4 about where the New York City mayoral candidates stand on the issues misidentified the candidate who said, “I believe we can save at least $500 million annually through strategic civilianization of N.Y.P.D. units.” It was Eric Adams, not Curtis Sliwa.
ref_headline: I believe we can save at least $500 million annually through strategic civilianization of N.Y.P.D. units.
match_headline: Eric Adams and Curtis Sliwa prepare for final showdown in New York City mayor’s race.

text: An article on Sunday about parents who are reluctant to consent to vaccinating their children against the coronavirus referred imprecisely to myocarditis. It is an inflammation of the heart, not a weakening of the heart muscle. (The condition can sometimes lead to a weakening of the heart muscle.)
match_headline: Covid Shots Are a Go for Children, but Parents Are Reluctant to Consent

text: An article on Sunday about the Tip column in The New York Times Magazine referred incorrectly to the klezmer clarinet player Giora Feidman. Mr. Feidman is a man.
match_headline: Advice You Don’t Need, but Might Want

text: An article on Friday about scrutiny of the production team of the Alec Baldwin film “Rust” misstated the relationship between Nathan Klingher and Ryan Winterstern and the Highland Film Group. They used to work for the company; they do not currently work there.
match_headline: Producers of Alec Baldwin Film Scrutinized After Shooting

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about a new book of unpublished writings by Rachel Held Evans, who died in 2019, misstated the timing of the book’s release. It is this week, not next week.
match_headline: The Last Words of Rachel Held Evans

text: An article on Saturday about the role of Richmond, Va., and its suburbs in the Virginia election misspelled the surname of a candidate for the Virginia House of Delegates. He is Mark Earley Jr., not Early.
match_headline: Why a Changing Richmond and Its Suburbs Are Key to Virginia’s Vote

text: An article on Monday about Alvin Bragg, a Democratic candidate for Manhattan district attorney, misstated the institution where Jessica Roth directs a center for ethics. It is Cardozo Law School, not Cardozo University.
match_headline: Manhattan’s Likely Next D.A. Questions Police Over Eric Garner’s Death

text: An article on Monday about an opportunity for Congress to pass legislation that would lower drug costs misstated the conclusion of a Congressional Budget Office report on the possible decline of new drug development related to a 2019 House bill intended to reduce drug costs. The report said about eight fewer drugs could be expected to be developed over the next decade, not 30. (The estimate of 30 was for the 2030s, not the 2020s.)
match_headline: This May Be Democrats’ Best Chance to Lower Drug Prices

text: An article on Sunday about weekly N.F.L. predictions misspelled the surname of the quarterback for the Arizona Cardinals. He is Kyler Murray, not Murry.
match_headline: N.F.L. Week 8 Predictions: Our Picks Against the Spread

text: An article on Sunday about a golf match between Columbia and Yale misidentified the college that has won 11 national golf titles in the sport’s N.C.A.A. era since 1939. It is Oklahoma State University, not the University of Oklahoma.
match_headline: 125 Years After the First College Golf Match, a Rematch

text: An article last Thursday about the reconstructured Alexander Palace, czar Nicholas II’s former home that opened to the public as a museum, misspelled the surname of a private benefactor of the museum. He is Bob Atchison, not Atchinson.
match_headline: Russia Reopens the Last Czar’s Palace, a Century After His Execution

text: An obituary on Sunday about the author Richard Hammer misstated the number of premeditated killings of civilians of which Lt. William L. Calley Jr. was convicted in connection with the My Lai massacre during the Vietnam War, which Mr. Hammer wrote about in his book “One Morning in the War: The Tragedy of Son My.” Lieutenant Calley was convicted of “not less than” 22 of these premeditated killings, not “several hundred,” though as many as 500 people died in the incident.
ref_headline: One Morning in the War: The Tragedy of Son My.
match_headline: Richard Hammer, Who Illuminated the My Lai Massacre, Dies at 93

text: An article on Thursday about the Republican strategy to turn education into a potent wedge issue misstated Representative Kevin McCarthy’s title. He is the House minority leader, not its majority leader.
match_headline: Republicans Seize on Schools as a Wedge Issue to Unite the Party

text: An article on Monday about electric vehicles from China that are sold in Europe misstated the given name of an auto dealer in Bietigheim-Bissingen, Germany. He is Julius Emrich, not Julian.
match_headline: China’s Popular Electric Vehicles Have Put Europe’s Automakers on Notice

text: An article on Thursday about soccer documentaries misstated the name of a holding company that has invested in several Italian soccer teams. It is North Sixth Group, not North Six Group.
match_headline: When the Soccer Is Just a Story Line

text: An obituary on Thursday about the scholar Richard M. Ohmann misstated part of the name of a website for which he wrote an article in 2017. It is Inside Higher Ed, not Insider Higher Ed.
match_headline: Richard M. Ohmann, 90, Dies; Brought Radical Politics to College English

text: An article on Friday about an increase in rates on some government savings bonds misstated the URL for the website Treasury Direct. It is TreasuryDirect.gov, not TreasuryDirect.com.
match_headline: Inflation Bonds Are Getting a Big Rate Bump

text: An article on Page 10 this weekend about the new Empire State Trail misstates the relationship between Seneca Falls and the movie “It’s a Wonderful Life.” The town was the inspiration for the film’s fictional Bedford Falls; it was not the site of filming.
match_headline: ‘Dune’ May Be Set in a Distant Time and Place, but the Film Has Canadian Roots

text: An obituary on Friday about the historian Pamela McCorduck misstated at one point the title of her history of artificial intelligence. As correctly noted elsewhere in the obituary, it is “Machines Who Think,” not “Computers Who Think.”
match_headline: Pamela McCorduck, Historian of Artificial Intelligence, Dies at 80

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the effect of supply-chain issues on the availability of Halloween costumes referred incorrectly to the history of the Salem witch trials. People suspected of witchcraft there were typically hanged, not burned or drowned.
match_headline: How the Supply Chain Stole Halloween

text: A review on Oct. 17 about “You Bet Your Life,” by Paul A. Offit, referred incorrectly to the first public demonstration of ether anesthesia. The operation was performed by the surgeon John Collins Warren, and it was Warren who is said to have declared afterward, “Gentlemen, this is no humbug.” It was not William Morton, the dentist who administered the ether but did not perform the operation.
match_headline: A History of Medical Innovation That Doesn’t Ignore the Side Effects

text: An article on Sunday about Democratic losses in rural Virginia misstated the origin of The Homestead in Hot Springs, Va. It is believed to have been founded as a lodge in 1766, not in the late 1800s. (Its operation as a luxury resort dates to when it was rebuilt in the late 1800s.) Because of an editing error, the article also misstated the location of a monument to Confederate soldiers. It is in Warm Springs, not Hot Springs, Va.
match_headline: Democrats Thought They Bottomed Out in Rural, White America. It Wasn’t the Bottom.

text: An article on Saturday about the conviction of Alexandre Benalla — a former aide to President Emmanuel Macron of France — misstated the dollar equivalent of his fine. It is about $578, not about $460.
match_headline: Ex-Macron Aide Convicted of Assault and Posing as a Police Officer

text: An article on Saturday about the planned execution of Nagaenthran Dharmalingam, a mentally disabled man, misidentified the group that called the planned execution a breach of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons With Disabilities. It is the Divisions of Social Justice of the American Psychological Association, not the American Psychiatric Association.
match_headline: Rights Groups Urge Singapore Not to Execute Man With Mental Disability

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the German politician Awet Tesfaiesus misstated Germany’s ranking as a destination country for migrants. It is the second-largest destination country among the 38 members of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, not the second-largest in the world.
match_headline: First Black Woman in Bundestag Wants to Change Image of ‘Germanness’

text: An article on Saturday about an investigation into how Ashley Biden’s diary came to be publicly disclosed referred incorrectly to the steps that Project Veritas said it took in dealing with the diary. In a video, the group’s founder, James O’Keefe, said Project Veritas had returned the diary to law enforcement and had attempted to return it to a lawyer for Ms. Biden. He did not say that the group had attempted to return it to the Justice Department and a lawyer for Ms. Biden.
match_headline: People Tied to Project Veritas Scrutinized in Theft of Diary From Biden’s Daughter

text: An article on Sunday about the $47 billion in the infrastructure bill designated for climate resilience misstated the spending dedicated to climate measures in a larger spending bill still on Capitol Hill. The climate provisions in that bill are worth $555 billion, not trillion. The article also misquoted Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana speaking about flooding in his state in 2016. Describing the effects of the floods, he referred to people living in Livingston Parish, not Lexington. There is no Lexington Paris in Louisiana.
match_headline: Infrastructure Bill Makes First Major U.S. Investment in Climate Resilience

text: An article on Saturday about a review of classified documents in the Sept. 11 case misstated the number of classified cables and other documents James G. Connell III, a defense lawyer for Ammar al-Baluchi, said he had obtained through the Freedom of Information Act. The C.I.A. had agreed to release to his team 3,165 pages of such cables and other documents. He had not obtained 1,025 pages of once-classified cables and other documents.
match_headline: Some Sept. 11 Trial Secrets May Not Be Secrets Anymore

text: An article on Monday about the lawyer Steven Donziger misspelled the surname of an environmental activist. He is Bill McKibben, not McKibbon.
match_headline: An Environmental Hero or Outlaw? Can It Be Both?

text: An article on Wednesday about the organist Jeanne Demessieux misspelled the surname of an organist who was active in the early 20th century. She was Renée Nizan, not Nazin.
match_headline: She Was an Organist for the Ages

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the top finishers in the New York City Marathon reversed the identities of two of the runners. Mohamed El Aaraby of Morocco, who came in second place, was on the left, and Eyob Faniel of Italy, the third-place finisher, was on the right.
match_headline: How to Track Runners in the New York City Marathon

text: An article on Monday about autocratic rule in Nicaragua described imprecisely the presence of campaign advertisements in Managua, Nicaragua’s capital. While the vast majority of advertisements featured President Daniel Ortega, some opposition candidates were featured on banners in the city.
match_headline: Nicaragua Descends Into Autocratic Rule as Ortega Crushes Dissent

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about an appeal from the Justice Department that argued in favor of a vaccination mandate for large employers described incorrectly a case involving a vaccination mandate before a Federal District Court judge in the District of Columbia. That case, in which the judge declined to block the mandate, concerned vaccinations of federal civilian and military employees, not an Occupational Safety and Health Administration rule for private workers.
match_headline: U.S. Urges Court Not to Block Vaccine Mandate on Employers

text: An article on Tuesday about anti-vaccination rhetoric used by the quarterback Aaron Rodgers, who tested positive for the coronavirus, misstated the N.F.L.’s protocol for an unvaccinated player who has tested positive. Rodgers must be cleared by a team doctor before returning to the field, not provide two negative tests.
match_headline: Scientists Fight a New Source of Vaccine Misinformation: Aaron Rodgers

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about six different television and film depictions of Princess Diana described incorrectly the director Oliver Hirschbiegel. His 2005 film “Downfall” was nominated for an Oscar; he is not an Oscar winner.
match_headline: Remaking Diana: Six Faces of a Princess to Stream Online

text: An obituary on Monday about the gun control advocate Mark Glaze misstated the year he received a law degree from the George Washington University. It was 1999, not 1996.
match_headline: Mark Glaze, Influential Gun Control Advocate, Dies at 51

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Pfizer’s request to the Food and Drug Administration to authorize its coronavirus vaccination booster shots for those 18 and older misstated the month that the Israeli vaccination campaign began. It was December 2020, not July 2021.
match_headline: Pfizer Asks F.D.A. to Expand Booster Eligibility to All Adults

text: An article on Wednesday about rising energy costs in Montargis, France, misstated the surname of a homemaker who heads a local association against wind power. She is Magalie Pasquier, not Pasquet. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: In France, the People the Climate Summit Forgot

text: An article on Tuesday about the stand-up comic Joe Pera misspelled the name of a tree. It is Old Tjikko, not Old Chico.
match_headline: Joe Pera and the Surprising Pleasures of Gentle Humor

text: An article last Thursday about the comedian Aida Rodriguez misstated the age of another comedian, Glory Mora. She is 31, not 33.
match_headline: Aida Rodriguez Wants You to Laugh at the Pain

text: An article on Thursday about the making of a 3-D reconstruction of the Dixie fire’s thunderclouds misattributed comments about the process of animating the data. It was Noah Pisner, not Nick Bartzokas, who described the process.
match_headline: Using Radar Data to Build a 3-D Model

text: An article on Thursday about the murder conviction of Yacine Mihoub misstated the day on which the French court announced its verdict. It was Wednesday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: French Court Convicts Man in the Murder of a Holocaust Survivor

text: An article on Thursday about an initial public offering by the electric-vehicle maker Rivian misstated the availability of Tesla service in Michigan. Tesla has a service center near Detroit; it is not the case that the nearest service centers are in Cleveland or Chicago.
match_headline: Rivian I.P.O. Is Embraced by Investors Looking for Another Tesla

text: An article on Thursday about Tesla shares sold by Elon Musk misstated the day on which he sold $1.1 billion in shares to cover tax obligations. It was Monday, not Wednesday. (He sold an additional $3.9 billion in shares this week unrelated to the exercise of his stock options.)
match_headline: Elon Musk sells $5 billion in Tesla shares, partly to cover taxes on stock options.

text: An article on Thursday about interest payments made by China Evergrande misstated the amount that China Evergrande needed to pay on Wednesday. It was $150 million, not $150 billion.
match_headline: China Evergrande meets another interest payment deadline.

text: An article on Friday about the confrontation between Poland and Belarus over an influx of migrants misstated the first name of a fascist leader of Spain. He was Francisco Franco, not Federico.
match_headline: Migrants in Peril, and Raw Emotions, in a Volatile European Border Standoff

text: An article on Friday about calls for climate reparations at COP26 misstated Nicola Sturgeon’s title. She is the first minister of Scotland, not the prime minister.
match_headline: Calls for Climate Reparations Reach Boiling Point in Glasgow Talks

text: An article on Nov. 6 about Marvel’s “Eternals” described incorrectly the character Ikaris and the Greek mythological story of Icarus, as portrayed in the movie. In the movie, the Icarus myth is said to be based on the character Ikaris, but Ikaris does not say he created the story.
match_headline: ‘Eternals’ Review: When Super Franchises Walk the Earth!

text: An article on Page 46 this weekend about the 1619 Project and the battle over U.S. history refers incompletely to early critics of the 1619 Project. The World Socialist Web Site, which published numerous articles about the project and interviewed historians with objections to its conclusions, was among them.
match_headline: The 1619 Project and the Long Battle Over U.S. History

text: An obituary on Friday about F.W. de Klerk, the former president of South Africa, misstated the country that hosted the ceremony at which he and Nelson Mandela were given the Nobel Peace Prize. It was Norway, not Sweden.
match_headline: F.W. de Klerk, South Africa President Who Ended Apartheid, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Friday about John Artis, the co-defendant of the prizefighter Rubin (Hurricane) Carter in a highly publicized murder case, omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to his sister, Deborah Artis Chibar, Mr. Artis is survived by a stepsister, Cinda Wallace.
match_headline: John Artis, Convicted With Rubin (Hurricane) Carter, Dies at 75

text: A picture caption on Friday with an obituary about the former Mets relief pitcher Pedro Feliciano misstated one of his career distinctions. As the obituary correctly noted, he led the major leagues for three seasons in games pitched, not innings pitched.
match_headline: Pedro Feliciano, Durable Relief Pitcher for the Mets, Dies at 45

text: An obituary on Monday about Julie Green, the creator of an art project that documented the last meals of death row prisoners around the country, misstated the location and year one prisoner asked for pecan pie for his last meal and, because he didn’t understand the concept of execution, said he intended to save it to eat later. It was in Arkansas in 1992, not Georgia in 2009.
match_headline: Julie Green, Artist Who Memorialized Inmates’ Last Suppers, Dies at 60

text: An article last Sunday about the renewed popularity of “Attached,” a book on relationship styles published in 2010, gave incomplete credentials for the co-author Rachel Heller. She is a psychologist, not only a writer. The article also misspelled the name of the book’s publisher. It is TarcherPerigee, not TarcherPedigree.
match_headline: Are You Anxious, Avoidant or Secure?

text: An article on Friday about staff shortages in schools referred imprecisely to remarks Kim Anderson made about teacher shortages. She said the new lower standards for substitute teachers are shortchanging students, not that substitute teachers are shortchanging students.
match_headline: Substitute Teachers Never Got Much Respect, but Now They Are in Demand

text: An article on Saturday about a federal appeals court’s decision to uphold a block against a federal mandate on vaccinations for large employers referred incorrectly to the circumstances that led a number of large companies to impose vaccine mandates on their workforces. They did not all decide to do so on their own. At least one, 3M, did so in response to a requirement for federal contractors.
match_headline: Appeals Court Extends Block on Biden’s Vaccine Mandate for Employers

text: An article on Monday about the labor shortage in Vietnam misstated the title of an official. Adam Sitkoff is executive director of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hanoi, not of the American Chamber of Commerce in Vietnam.
match_headline: As Holidays Near, Bosses Try to Coax Vietnam’s Workers Back to Factories

text: An obituary on Sunday about Graeme Edge, a co-founder of the British rock band the Moody Blues, misstated the town in England where he was born. It was Rocester, a village near Birmingham — not Rochester, a city in the southeast.
match_headline: Graeme Edge, Drummer and Co-Founder of the Moody Blues, Dies at 80

text: An article on Monday about the implications of the infrastructure bill for New York described incorrectly the families who were displaced by the construction of the Cross-Bronx Expressway in the 1950s and 1960s. It was a diverse group of lower-income families, not mainly Black communities.
match_headline: What the Infrastructure Bill Means for the New York Region

text: An obituary on Friday about the playwright and food columnist Jonathan Reynolds omitted the names of two survivors. In addition to those named, he is survived by a sister, Nancy Reynolds, and a half brother, Donald Reynolds Jr.
match_headline: Jonathan Reynolds, Playwright and Food Columnist, Dies at 79

text: An obituary on Monday about the artist Bettina Grossman misstated the name of the city in Italy where she traveled to select marble for her sculptures. It is Carrara, not Carrera. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Bettina Grossman, an Artistic Fixture at the Chelsea Hotel, Dies at 94

text: An article on Thursday about the censure of Representative Paul Gosar by the House of Representatives misstated the date of the first censure by the legislative body, which was meted out to Representative William Stanbery. It was 1832, not 1842.
match_headline: House, Mostly Along Party Lines, Censures Gosar for Violent Video

text: An article on Thursday about mask rules and coronavirus testing in the N.F.L. misstated the number of positive coronavirus cases in the United States in the 14-day period that ended Tuesday. There were more than 85,000 positive cases per day on average, not total.
match_headline: N.F.L. Requires Masks and Increases Coronavirus Testing for Thanksgiving

text: An article on Thursday about the Chilean songwriter who goes by Mon Laferte misspelled her last name. It is Bustamante, not Bustamente.
match_headline: Mon Laferte Wants to Give You Goose Bumps

text: An article on Thursday about the death of the 36-year-old rapper Young Dolph misstated the make of the car said to belong to him. It was a Corvette, not a Lamborghini.
match_headline: Young Dolph, Promising Memphis Rapper, Shot and Killed at 36

text: An article on Friday about the civil trial in the deadly 2017 rally in Charlottesville, Va., described incorrectly a request for damages that was made during closing arguments. A lawyer for the nine plaintiffs suggested that the jury should award each plaintiff between $3 million and $10 million for “pain and suffering,” not for punitive damages. No sum has been specified for punitive damages.
match_headline: Charlottesville Rally Trial: What We’ve Learned as the Case Goes to the Jury

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the “Fearless Girl” statue near the New York Stock Exchange described an image of the installation “The Girl Puzzle” incorrectly. It is a photograph, not a rendering.
match_headline: The ‘Fearless Girl’ Statue Is in Limbo

text: An article on Nov. 14 about the real estate market in Austin, Texas, misspelled the names of two of that city’s suburbs. They are Pflugerville and Buda, not Pfluggerville and Butta.
match_headline: Will Real Estate Ever Be Normal Again?

text: An article last weekend about the artist Agnieszka Kurant misidentified a department of Google. It is the Artists and Machine Intelligence program, not Artificial and Machine Intelligence.
match_headline: An Artist Who Disavows the Possibility of Individual Agency

text: An article last weekend about rice in Senegal referred incorrectly to the Négritude movement in the 1930s. It was an offshoot of Pan-Africanism, which preceded it, not one of its ideological forebears.
match_headline: In Senegal, a Return to Homegrown Rice

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the graphic designer Bob Gill misspelled the original surname of his mother. She was Frieda (Gothelf) Gill, not Gotthelf.
match_headline: Bob Gill, Graphic Designer Who Elevated the ‘Message,’ Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Cuban poet and journalist Raúl Rivero misstated when he died. It was Nov. 6, not Nov. 14.
match_headline: Raúl Rivero, Disenchanted Poet of the Cuban Revolution, Dies at 75

text: An article last week about skin tone and raising children of color misstated the timing of the events described. They happened over the late summer and early fall of 2021, not in October and November.
match_headline: How to Teach a Little Girl to Love Her Brown Skin

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about roundabouts in Carmel, Ind., misspelled the given name of a songwriter honored by a sculpture at one of the roundabouts. He was Hoagy Carmichael, not Hoagie.

An article on Monday about the killing of an Israeli tour guide near the entrance of the Temple Mount described incorrectly the Western Wall. It is one of the last remaining parts of an ancient Jewish temple compound, not the last remaining part of an ancient Jewish temple.
match_headline: Israeli Is Killed by Palestinian Near Holiest Site in Jerusalem

text: An article on Friday about the prosecutor’s cross-examination of the defendant Travis McMichael in the Ahmaud Arbery killing trial misstated part of the prosecutor’s description of Mr. McMichael’s conversation with a neighbor on social media. When a neighbor stated that her father “doesn’t care about jail,” the prosecutor said that Mr. McMichael responded that his father, fellow defendant Gregory McMichael, was “the same way,” not that his father “doesn’t care about going to jail.”
match_headline: Prosecutor Challenges Assailant on Whether Arbery Posed a Threat

text: An article on Monday about a tech gadget shortage referred incorrectly to the role of Matt Swider, a tech journalist. He is the former editor in chief of TechRadar; he no longer leads the blog.
match_headline: The Tech Gifts That Are Hard to Buy This Holiday Season

text: An article on Saturday about the silence from the International Olympic Committee in the disappearance of Peng Shuai misstated the United Nations’ characterization of China’s treatment of Muslim minorities in Xinjiang. While the United States and lawmakers in several other nations have called it genocide, the United Nations has not.
match_headline: The Question the I.O.C. Is Too Weak to Ask

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Rev. W. Sterling Cary, the first Black president of the National Council of Churches, misstated when he was elected conference minister of the Illinois conference of the United Church of Christ. It was 1974, not 1994.
match_headline: Rev. W. Sterling Cary, Pioneering Black Churchman, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Sunday about the singer Philip Margo of the Tokens misstated the name of the owner of the Warwick label, which released the Tokens’ first hit, “Tonight I Fell in Love.” He is Morty Craft, not Marty Kraft.
match_headline: Philip Margo of the Tokens, Who Sang of a Snoozing Lion, Dies at 79

text: An article on Saturday about the $555 billion climate package passed by the House misstated the position of the National Ocean Industries Association on the $2.2 trillion spending bill passed by the House. The association objected to the oil and gas provisions, not the full legislation.
match_headline: House Passes the Largest Expenditure on Climate in U.S. History

text: An article on Tuesday about a mammoth tusk found in the Pacific Ocean misstated which scientist used a saw to slice a chunk of a tusk. It was Daniel Fisher, not Katherine Louise Moon.
match_headline: Why Was This Ancient Tusk 150 Miles From Land, 10,000 Feet Deep?

text: A headline with an article on Tuesday about the trial of organizers of the 2017 far-right rally in Charlottesville, Va., misstated the number of people held liable for injuries to counterprotesters. Jurors ordered 12 individuals and five white nationalist organizations to pay damages; they did not find nine individuals liable. (The case was brought by nine people seeking compensatory and punitive damages for injuries they suffered.)
match_headline: Jury Finds Rally Organizers Responsible for Charlottesville Violence

text: An article on Wednesday about rezoning proposals in New York misidentified the height of a proposed new building that the New York Blood Center can build. It is 13 floors, not 16.
match_headline: New York Targets Affluent Neighborhoods in Push for Affordable Housing

text: An article last Thursday about private dog parks in New York City misstated the name and location of a private dog space in Manhattan. It is School for the Dogs, not the School Yard, and it is in the East Village, not on the Lower East Side.
match_headline: Does Your Dog Deserve a Private Park?

text: An article last Thursday about the clothing brand Von Dutch referred incorrectly to Ed Boswell, an art collector who is often cited as the brand’s founder. The Times did not reach him for comment before publication; it is not the case that he declined to comment.
match_headline: The Untold Story of Von Dutch

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the threats that climate change and flooding pose to the Smithsonian museums in Washington misidentified the maker of the original Star Spangled Banner, which hangs in the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History. It was made by Mary Pickersgill, not Betsy Ross.
match_headline: Saving History With Sandbags: Climate Change Threatens the Smithsonian

text: An article on Thursday about a government minister’s successful defamation suit misidentified the source of mistaken reports that Andrew Laming, a Liberal member of Parliament, had taken a photo of a woman in a skirt and had been accused of “upskirting.” The mistaken report was from social media users, not news outlets.
match_headline: Australia Defamation Case Signals a Crackdown on Ordinary Citizens, Critics Say

text: An article on Friday about Don Johnson reprising the title role in a “Nash Bridges” revival misidentified the creators of the new TV movie. Johnson wrote it with Bill Chais, based on the work of Carlton Cuse. Cuse said he was not involved in the revival.
match_headline: Don Johnson Is Back as ‘Nash Bridges.’ Why?

text: An article on Page 28 this weekend about risks associated with e-cigarettes misstates which products were approved by the Food and Drug Administration. It approved two tobacco-flavored products. No menthol flavor was approved.
match_headline: Vaping Is Risky. Why Is the F.D.A. Authorizing E-Cigarettes?

text: An article last Sunday about a film-production company focused on teen comedies misstated the given name of the 24-year-old man who now manages a team of script readers. He is Matt Sacca, not Will.
match_headline: How Do You Make Teen Comedies Today? Buy a High School.

text: An article last Sunday about maternal health in the United States used an incorrect courtesy title for one of its authors, Jordan Downey. She is Ms. Downey, not Mr. Downey.
match_headline: Want More Affordable Housing and Health Care? Here’s a Fix.

text: A picture caption with the Scene City article last Sunday misidentified an artist at the Guggenheim International Gala. He is Tavares Strachan, not Titus Kaphar.
match_headline: Lorde Performs at Guggenheim Gala

text: An article last Sunday about the musical “Flying Over Sunset” misstated the vaccination status of an understudy for the role of Archie Leach. The understudy had been vaccinated as the show went into previews; he was not waiting to be vaccinated.
match_headline: Up, Up and Away: The Trippy Tales Behind ‘Flying Over Sunset’

text: An article last Sunday about looted artifacts seized by the Manhattan district attorney’s office misstated the age of the Harihara statue. It dates from the ninth century A.D., not the eighth century B.C.
match_headline: Looking for a Stolen Idol? Visit the Museum of the Manhattan D.A.

text: An article on Friday about Republican gerrymandering in four battleground states referred incorrectly to the status of Pennsylvania’s new maps for its legislature. A state legislative commission is designing them and they will then become official; it is not the case that the state’s Democratic governor is likely to force the process to be completed by the courts.
match_headline: G.O.P. Cements Hold on Legislatures in Battleground States

text: An article on Friday about a new coronavirus variant detected by South African scientists referred incorrectly to a receptor found on some human cells known as ACE2, an abbreviation for angiotensin-converting enzyme 2. The ACE2 is part of a human cell, not part of the spike protein on the surface of the coronavirus.
match_headline: South Africa detects a new variant, prompting new international travel restrictions.

text: An article on Saturday about racist incidents in Pittsford, N.Y., misidentified the high school that Ameera Duarte attends and that State Senator Samra G. Brouk attended. It is Pittsford Mendon High School, not Pittsford Sutherland.
match_headline: In a Picture-Postcard New York Town, Racist Incidents Rattle Schools

text: An article on Monday about the road to 100 percent clean energy in New York described incorrectly the representation of the administration of New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, at the global climate conference in Glasgow. Representatives of her administration attended the conference, not the governor herself.
match_headline: Can New York Really Get to 100% Clean Energy by 2040?

text: An article on Thursday about graduate student workers on strike at Columbia University described incorrectly a strike at Harvard University. A tentative agreement was reached in November after the strike ended in late October; it was not reached while the strike was still going on.
match_headline: Why Columbia Student Workers Are Back On Strike

text: An article on Saturday about the declining number of Quebec-born professional hockey players misstated the length of Maurice Richard’s career with the Canadiens. It was 18 years, not 28. It also misstated Eddie Johnston’s, in the N.H.L. It was from 1962 — not 1958 — to 1978. The article also misidentified the Canadiens’ opponent in a game in 1955 in which Richard punched a linesman. It was Boston, not Detroit. And it misstated the decade in which the Canadiens won four consecutive Stanley Cups, to go along with five straight from 1956 to 1960. It was in the 1970s, not the 1940s.
match_headline: In Canada, the Premier of Quebec Worries About the State of Hockey

text: An article on Saturday about a woman named Abigail who was enslaved by John Jay misstated the given name of the author of “Les Chaînes de L’Esclavage” (“The Chains of Slavery”). It is Jean-Paul Marat, not Jean-Pierre.
match_headline: Enslaved to a Founding Father, She Sought Freedom in France

text: An article on Sunday about a potential comeback for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the former president of Brazil, misstated the title of Spain’s head of government. It is prime minister, not president.
match_headline: Brazil’s President Lula Is Staging a Comeback. Can He Bring the Country Along?

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about Guantánamo Bay misstated the name of the radio station at the Guantánamo Bay Naval Base. It is known as Radio GTMO, not Radio Gitmo.
match_headline: Guantánamo Bay: Beyond the Prison

text: An article on Monday about work by Stephen Sondheim available to stream misspelled the surname of an actor in the “American Playhouse” filming of “Into the Woods.” She is Joanna Gleason, not Gleeson.
match_headline: Stream These 7 Productions That Celebrate Stephen Sondheim’s Work

text: An article on Thursday about art studios at a Los Angeles law office misstated the South Bay town where the parents of Edgar Ramirez have a home. It is in Wilmington, not Torrance.
match_headline: Cultivating Art, Not Argument, at a Los Angeles Law Office

text: A headline with an article on Nov. 10 about the television show host Padma Lakshmi and her preparations for Thanksgiving referred imprecisely to her status as a home cook. Though she is not a professional chef, she is the host of the Bravo reality cooking competition “Top Chef” and the culinary travel show “Taste the Nation,” and the author of several cookbooks.
match_headline: Padma Lakshmi’s Thanksgiving Turkey: Slow Roasted and Richly Sauced

text: A headline with an article on Wednesday about an appearance by Jerome H. Powell, the Federal Reserve chair, before the Senate Banking Committee described his testimony incorrectly. As the article correctly noted, he signaled that the Fed could hasten the end of its bond-buying program, which is one piece of the Fed’s monetary policy that currently supports the economy. He did not signal an end to support altogether, nor did he address fiscal policy — taxes and spending — which the Fed does not set.
match_headline: Jerome Powell pivots, suggesting quicker reduction in economic help as high inflation persists.

text: An article on Saturday about quarreling between Britain and France over migrants crossing the English Channel misstated the timing of France’s presidential elections next year. They will be in April, not May.
match_headline: France-U.K. Acrimony Impedes Progress on Channel Crossings

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the prosecutor Philip B. Heymann misidentified the associate justice of the Supreme Clark for whom Mr. Heymann clerked as a young law school graduate, and it described incorrectly the justice’s reputation on the bench. He was John M. Harlan II, not Justice Harlan’s grandfather, John M. Harlan. And it was the elder Justice Harlan, not the grandson, who was noted for his many dissents in cases that restricted civil liberties.
match_headline: Federal Scrutiny of Cuomo Widens to His Office’s Treatment of Women

text: An article last Thursday about the Yeezy Gap jacket misspelled the surname of a self proclaimed Kanye West superfan. He is Pergrin Pervez, not Pervec. The article also misstated the name of a sneaker store. It is Flight Club, not Fight Club.
match_headline: Feeling Rich in the Yeezy Gap Jacket

text: An article on Friday about the efficiency of boosters across different brands misstated the given name of a statistician. She is Merryn Voysey, not Merry.
match_headline: Most Covid Vaccines Will Work as Boosters, Study Suggests

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about prairie fires in Montana misstated the given name of a farmer and volunteer firefighter in Denton, Mont. He is Brock Linker, not Brandon.
match_headline: Prairies on Fire in Montana Amid a Record December Heat Wave

text: An article on Friday about efforts to find a cause of the chronic ailments referred to as the Havana syndrome reported by intelligence officers and diplomats misstated which branches of the military had administered cognitive tests to Mark Lenzi, a State Department official. It was the Air Force and the Navy, not the Army and the Navy.
match_headline: Review Finds No Answers to Mystery of Havana Syndrome

text: An article on Nov. 21 about George Gascón, the district attorney of Los Angeles, misstated how much the nationwide state prison population had increased since the 1970s. The fivefold increase was to roughly 1.2 million, not 1.4 million.
match_headline: He’s Remaking Criminal Justice in L.A. But How Far Is Too Far?

text: An obituary on Nov. 27 about the composer and lyricist Stephen Sondheim misspelled the surname of the director of “Stavisky,” a 1974 film whose score was written by Mr. Sondheim. He was Alain Resnais, not Renais.
match_headline: Stephen Sondheim, Titan of the American Musical, Is Dead at 91

text: An obituary on Thursday about the composer Alvin Lucier misstated the year he and his first wife, the artist Mary Lucier, divorced. It was 1974, not 1972.
match_headline: Alvin Lucier, Probing Composer of Soundscapes, Is Dead at 90

text: An article last Sunday about the spiritual adviser Carissa Schumacher described incorrectly the biblical name Yeshua. It refers to multiple people, including Joshua; it does not refer solely to Jesus Christ. The article also referred incorrectly to the Old Testament. While the name Yeshua appears in it, Jesus Christ does not.
match_headline: In Good Spirits
