text: An article last Sunday about the British composer Malcolm Arnold misidentified the composer of the Concerto for Group and Orchestra, a collaboration between the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra and the rock band Deep Purple. It was Jon Lord, Deep Purple’s organist, not Arnold.
match_headline: The Hilarious, Heartbreaking Life and Music of Malcolm Arnold

text: An article on Saturday about a surge in Covid cases in upstate New York misstated Kathy Parrinello’s position with the UR Medicine health care system. She is an executive vice president with UR Medicine, not its chief executive officer.
match_headline: Upstate New York Hospitals Are Overwhelmed as Covid Cases Surge

text: An article on Saturday about a financial dispute between SoftBank executives misstated the entity that had invested roughly $9 billion in WeWork. SoftBank and its Vision Fund invested the money; the money did not come from the fund alone.
match_headline: A Top SoftBank Executive Wants $2 Billion in Pay. His Boss Disagrees.

text: An article on Monday about the University of Michigan football team’s victory in the Big Ten championship game misstated Michigan’s record under Coach Jim Harbaugh against Ohio State entering this season. It was 0-5, not 0-6.
match_headline: Michigan Rolls to a Playoff Spot With Big Ten Title

text: An article on Friday about holiday events in New York City erroneously included an event on the performance calendar for the Brooklyn Academy of Music. The Mark Morris Dance Group is not performing “The Hard Nut” at the venue this season.
match_headline: A Guide to New York Holiday Events: Trains, Nutcrackers and a 79-Foot Tree

text: A picture caption with a television review on Monday about “Landscapers” misspelled the surname of an actress. She is Olivia Colman, not Coleman.
match_headline: Review: ‘Landscapers’ Is Not Your Typical True-Crime Love Story

text: An article on Friday about the political artist Andrea Bowers misspelled the surname of an artist whose socially engaged work Bowers admired. She was Kate Ericson, not Kate Eriksen.
match_headline: Andrea Bowers: Her Activism Animates Her Art

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor Antony Sher misspelled the surname of a British drama critic who reviewed his performance in Shakespeare’s “Richard III.” He was Sheridan Morley, not Morely.
match_headline: Antony Sher, Actor Acclaimed for His Versatility, Dies at 72

text: An article on Monday about TikTok’s algorithm misstated the title of the document that was produced by TikTok’s engineering team in Beijing. It is titled “TikTok Algo 101,” not “TikTok Algo 100.”
match_headline: How TikTok Reads Your Mind

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about takeaways from Week 13 of the N.F.L. season misstated the field position of the Washington Football Team’s Antonio Gibson. He is a running back, not a receiver.
match_headline: What We Learned From Week 13 in the N.F.L.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Fred Hiatt, the longtime editorial page editor of The Washington Post, misstated the surname of a New York Times editor. She is Katie Kingsbury, not Kingsley.
match_headline: Fred Hiatt, Washington Post Editorial Page Editor, Dies at 66

text: An article on Tuesday about the Omicron variant misstated the new coronavirus testing rule for air passengers traveling to the United States. Passengers must be tested no earlier than the day before departure, not 24 hours.
match_headline: Omicron Is Fast Moving, but Perhaps Less Severe, Early Reports Suggest

text: An article on Tuesday about the Summit for Democracy misstated the percentage of U.S. debt held by China. It is about 3.5 percent, not about 14 percent.
match_headline: Biden’s Democracy Conference Is About Much More Than Democracy

text: An article on Wednesday about redistricting in California referred imprecisely to Paul Mitchell’s work in demographics. He is a leading demographer in California, but he is not a state employee.
match_headline: Redistricting Makes California a Top House Battlefield for 2022

text: An article on Thursday about David Banks, who is set to become the next chancellor of New York City’s public school system, misstated a distinction of the first Eagle Academy school, which was founded by Mr. Banks. It was the first public single-sex boys’ school — not the first public single-sex school — to open in New York City in roughly 30 years.
match_headline: David Banks, Educator and Adams Ally, Is Next N.Y.C. Schools Chancellor

text: An article on Dec. 3 about the impact of new travel restrictions announced by the United States misstated South Korea’s capacity for administering P.C.R. tests. It was an average of 680,000 P.C.R. tests a day in November, not 68,000.
match_headline: Travelers to U.S. Count the Hours: Can They Get Their Tests Back in Time?

text: An article on Thursday about a student worker strike at Columbia University misidentified one of the union locals whose members joined the picket line. It was Teamsters Local 804, not 104.
match_headline: Tensions Rise at Columbia as Strikers Fear Retaliation From University

text: An article on Thursday about Ali Alexander, who helped organize the gathering that drew Trump supporters to Washington on Jan. 6, described incorrectly what is known about Mr. Alexander’s whereabouts and actions during the riot. While it is not clear what he was doing during large portions of the riot, he posted a video of himself watching the crowd march on the Capitol from a terrace a few blocks away.
match_headline: Rally Planner With Ties to G.O.P. Is Cooperating in Jan. 6 Inquiry

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Pro Football Hall of Fame defensive end Claude Humphrey misstated one of his accomplishments. He twice forced opponents into safeties; he did not twice recover fumbles for safeties.
match_headline: Claude Humphrey, Pillar of N.F.L. Falcons’ ‘Grits Blitz,’ Dies at 77

text: An article on Friday about a plan to ban cigarette sales in New Zealand misidentified the academic affiliation of Janet Hoek, a public health expert. She is a professor at the University of Otago, not the University of Auckland.
match_headline: New Zealand Plans to Eventually Ban All Cigarette Sales

text: An article on Friday about the passing of the Protecting Our Democracy Act in the House misstated, in one instance, how Republicans voted on changes to rules on presidential power. One Republican voted in favor; Republicans did not vote unanimously.
match_headline: House Approves Post-Trump Curbs on Presidential Power

text: An article on Wednesday about a change in the workweek in the United Arab Emirates referred incorrectly to the normalization of ties between Arab countries and Israel. Both Bahrain and U.A.E did so last year; it is not the case that U.A.E. was the only Persian Gulf state to do so.
match_headline: Sundays Off: U.A.E. Changes Its Weekend to Align With West

text: An article on Wednesday about the New York Giants’ risk-averse offense misstated the type of conversion the Los Angeles Chargers have attempted 21 times this season. They were fourth-down conversions, not third-down ones.
match_headline: For the Giants, It’s Always Fourth-and-Too-Far

text: An article on Friday about holiday album releases misstated the day Kat Edmonson will perform a livestream. It is Sunday, Dec. 12, not Saturday, Dec. 11.
match_headline: 13 Albums That Revisit (and Redefine!) Holiday Classics

text: An article this weekend on Page 24 about the best art exhibitions of 2021 misidentifies the object Jaune Quick-To-See Smith manipulates at Garth Greenan. It is the American map, not the American flag.
match_headline: Best Art Exhibitions of 2021

text: An article on Dec. 5 about a patient who had a bone disorder misidentified, in two instances, the name of a medical center. It is UW Health in Madison, not the University of Wisconsin Health Center and not the University of Wisconsin Medical Center.
match_headline: The Toddler Was Bowlegged, Her Gait Awkward. What Was It?

text: An article last weekend on Page 64 about the architect Lisa Van Dusen’s family home in Savannah, Ga., misspelled the name of a style of sofa. It is Sheraton, not Sheridan.
match_headline: A Savannah Home Melds Georgian Architecture With ’60s Flair

text: An article last weekend on Page 99 about the filmmaker Hayao Miyazaki, relying on information from Citroën, misstated the engine power of Miyazaki’s Citroën 2CV. It is nine horsepower, not two.
match_headline: Hayao Miyazaki Prepares to Cast One Last Spell

text: An obituary on Thursday about the critic and journalist Greg Tate misstated the year his first book, “Flyboy in the Buttermilk: Essays on Contemporary America,” was published. It was 1992, not 1993. The obituary also referred incompletely to the poet and playwright Thulani Davis, who recommended in the early 1980s that Mr. Tate submit material to Robert Christgau, the music editor of The Village Voice. She was also an editor at The Voice at the time; she did not simply know Mr. Christgau.
ref_headline: Flyboy in the Buttermilk: Essays on Contemporary America,
match_headline: Greg Tate, Influential Black Cultural Critic, Dies at 64

text: An obituary on Dec. 3 about the Hall of Fame football player Curley Culp misstated the number of future Hall of Famers who were in the defensive unit he joined when he was traded to the Kansas City Chiefs in 1968. There were five, not four. (The safety Johnny Robinson’s name was missing from the list.)
match_headline: Curley Culp, Defensive Anchor of Two Football Teams, Dies at 75

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about Denzel Washington misstated the year “Training Day” was released. It was 2001, not 2004.
match_headline: Denzel Washington, Man on Fire

text: An article on Nov. 21 about Iman and her life with and after the death of her husband, David Bowie, misstated the year that the couple acquired a property in the Catskills. It was 2011, not a few years after 2002. The article rendered Iman’s name at birth incompletely. She was named Zahra Muhammed Abdulmajid, not Iman Abdulmajid. It also misstated the year in which Iman established her cosmetics business. She established it in 1994, several years after she met Mr. Bowie, not before. The article described incorrectly a meeting between Iman and Diana Vreeland, the former editor of Vogue. Ms. Vreeland was no longer at Vogue when they met. The article also misstated the period when Iman began spending most of her time in the Catskills. It was March 2020 in the early weeks of the pandemic, not immediately after Mr. Bowie’s death in 2016.
match_headline: Getting Personal With Iman

text: An article on Nov. 17 about Refaat Alareer, a Palestinian professor who includes a discussion of Israeli poetry in his literature classes, gave an inaccurate portrayal of the professor.
match_headline: In Gaza, a Contentious Palestinian Professor Calmly Teaches Israeli Poetry

text: An article on Sunday about vaccination efforts in Africa misidentified the country that first identified the Omicron variant of the coronavirus. It was identified by scientists in Botswana, not South Africa. (The discovery was first publicly reported by scientists in South Africa.)
match_headline: As Vaccines Trickle Into Africa, Zambia’s Challenges Highlight Other Obstacles

text: An article on Saturday about rising consumer prices misstated when Jennifer Callahan’s house burned down. It was earlier this year, not in 2020.
match_headline: Consumer Prices Rose at Fastest Pace Since 1982, Pressuring Washington

text: An article on Monday about a boat of migrants sinking in the English Channel misspelled the name of a man who witnessed the incident from another boat. He is Zana Hamawandi, not Hamawandani.
match_headline: ‘Our Boat Was Surrounded by Dead Bodies’: Witnessing a Migrant Tragedy

text: An article on Saturday about the prosecutor Karen D. McDonald misstated the prison sentences that James and Jennifer Crumbley would face if convicted of involuntary manslaughter. They would each face a maximum of 15 years, not 60.
match_headline: In the Michigan School Shooting, the Prosecutor Asks, What About the Parents?

text: An article on Thursday about President Biden’s plan to make the federal government carbon neutral by 2050 misstated the energy plan’s requirements of the Defense Department. While purchases related to war-fighting are exempt, the plan sets carbon neutral requirements for much of the department’s support infrastructure, such as office buildings.
match_headline: Biden Orders Federal Vehicles and Buildings to Use Renewable Energy by 2050

text: An article on Saturday about the closing of the Metro Pictures gallery in Manhattan misspelled the given name of an artist whose work was displayed at MoMA PS1. She is Niki de Saint Phalle, not Nikki.
match_headline: As Metro Pictures Closes, Its Founders Look Back

text: An obituary on Monday about the novelist Anne Rice misspelled the given name of her daughter, who died of leukemia at the age of 5. She was Michele, not Michelle.
match_headline: Anne Rice, Who Spun Gothic Tales of Vampires, Dies at 80

text: An article on Tuesday about a meeting between Prime Minister Naftali Bennett of Israel and Prince Mohammed bin Zayed of the United Arab Emirates misstated the title of Mohammed bin Zayed. He is crown prince of the emirate of Abu Dhabi, not crown prince of the United Arab Emirates.
match_headline: Israeli Leader Holds Historic Meeting With Emirati Crown Prince

text: An article on Dec. 2 about the Supreme Court’s consideration of a Mississippi law that would ban abortions after 15 weeks of pregnancy misattributed a response to an assertion by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. about the cutoff line for abortions used by other countries. The response came from Julie Rikelman of the Center for Reproductive Rights, a lawyer for the challengers, not from Elizabeth Prelogar, the solicitor general.
match_headline: Roberts Searches for Middle Ground in Abortion Case

text: An article on Tuesday about the Federal Reserve’s handling of inflation mischaracterized inflation over the past year. It grew by 6.8 percent, not to 6.8 percent.
match_headline: We Need to Do Hard but Necessary Things to Tackle Inflation

text: An article on Monday about the donation of scripts, props and other artifacts from the television series “Dickinson” to the Emily Dickinson Museum and Harvard University misidentified the place where Emily Dickinson’s sister, Lavinia, found hand-sewn books after the poet’s death. They were in a chest of drawers, not a trunk.
match_headline: A 21st-Century Emily Dickinson Finds a Home in the Archives

text: An item in the Listings pages on Monday about the animated film “Ron’s Gone Wrong” misstated the name of the robot companion voiced by Zach Galifianakis in “Ron’s Gone Wrong.” It’s Ron, not Bubble. It also misstated the name of the boy voiced by Jack Dylan Grazer. It is Barney, not Ben.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘American Auto’ and ‘MTV Unplugged’

text: An article on Thursday about President Biden’s visit to Kentucky following a series of deadly tornadoes misstated the location of two communities affected by the storms. Mayfield and Dawson Springs are in the southwestern corner of the state, not southeastern.
match_headline: Touring Kentucky, Biden Vows ‘Whatever It Takes’ to Recover From Storms

text: An article on Thursday about Fox News hosts who sent text messages on Jan. 6 to Mark Meadows, misstated the commentator Juan Williams’s relationship with Fox News. While he left the program “The Five,” he did not leave the channel entirely.
match_headline: Fox News Hosts Take the Offensive About Texts to Meadows

text: An article on Wednesday about new uses for former Sears stores misstated the cost of a Sears site on Chicago’s West Side that Novak Development Company acquired in 2020. It was $14.8 million, not $2.4 million.
match_headline: Sears, Struggling to Sell Goods, Markets a Valuable Asset: Real Estate

text: An article this weekend on Page 13 about the Westcoast Black Theater Troupe misspells the surname of a choreographer. He is Donald Frison, not Frisson.
match_headline: For This Theater Leader, a Mission That Goes Beyond the Stage

text: An article this weekend on Page 17 about a Times reporter’s experience growing up with parents in the carnival business misstates the release date of the original film adaptation of “Nightmare Alley.” It was 1947, not 1949.
match_headline: See the Real Live Man Who Grew Up in a Carnival

text: A picture caption on Page 9 this weekend misspells the given name of the photographer shown in her Brooklyn studio. She is Deana Lawson, not Deanna.
A review on Dec. 5 about Alex Danchev and Sarah Whitfield’s “Magritte: A Life,” using information from the book, misstated René Magritte’s age at the time of his death. He was 68, not 69.
match_headline: Magritte, Surrealism and the Pipe That Is Not a Pipe

text: A picture caption on Page 9 this weekend misspells the given name of the photographer shown in her Brooklyn studio. She is Deana Lawson, not Deanna.

An article on Sunday about an investment in grass-roots programs by the city of Indianapolis to reduce violence misstated the surname of a criminologist at Indiana University-Purdue University of Indianapolis. It is Eric Grommon, not Grommer. It also misstated the given name of a sociology professor at Princeton University. His name is Patrick Sharkey, not Paul.
match_headline: To Stem a Homicide Surge, Indianapolis Invests $45 Million in Grass-Roots Programs

text: An article on Saturday about actions to take if you test positive for the coronavirus while traveling misspelled the first name of a writer for The Atlantic magazine. It is Katherine J. Wu, not Katharine.
match_headline: What Happens if You Test Positive While Traveling?

text: An obituary on Nov. 30 about the golfer Lee Elder referred incorrectly to the death of his father. He died in Dallas in 1942; he was not killed in Germany during World War II.
match_headline: Lee Elder, Who Broke a Golf Color Barrier, Dies at 87

text: An article on Dec. 14 about Richard Gottfried, the longest-serving state lawmaker in New York’s history, misidentified the New York State lawmaker who first introduced a same-sex marriage bill. It was Thomas K. Duane, who introduced such a bill in the State Senate in 2001; not Mr. Gottfried, who introduced a bill in the State Assembly two years later.
match_headline: A Champion of Liberal Causes in New York to Retire After 52 Years

text: An article on Monday about confusion over vaccine mandates described incorrectly a mental health company’s employee vaccine policy. In August, Spring Health mandated vaccines for employees who work in person, not for all of its employees.
match_headline: Whiplash on U.S. Vaccine Mandate Leaves Employers ‘Totally Confused’

text: An article on Monday about Tiger and Charlie Woods at the PNC Championship misidentified the tools used to extract the elder Woods from his vehicle after a crash. Responders used a Halligan tool and an ax, not the Jaws of Life.
match_headline: Charlie Woods Dazzles While Tiger, in Return, Grimaces and Grinds

text: Because of a production error, the Brain Tickler puzzle on Monday included an incorrect answer to a puzzle that appeared on Saturday. The answer to Saturday’s Wit Twister is “housecat, chase out, hot sauce,” not “warden, warned, wander.”
An article on Tuesday about two piano recitals in New York misstated the location of the University of British Columbia. It is in Vancouver, not near Vancouver.
match_headline: Two Pianists, Two Recitals, Two Deeply Personal Statements

text: A picture caption on Dec. 11 with an obituary about the bassist Robbie Shakespeare reversed the identifications of Mr. Shakespeare and his longtime musical partner, Sly Dunbar. Mr. Shakespeare was on the left, Mr. Dunbar on the right.
match_headline: Robbie Shakespeare, Prolific Reggae Bassist, Is Dead at 68

text: An obituary on Sunday about Rosalie Trombley, the longtime music director of the Canadian AM radio station CKLW, misidentified the source of several quotations about her. They are from “Radio Revolution,” a documentary feature about CKLW; they are not from a video series produced by the organization Radio Trailblazers.
match_headline: Rosalie Trombley, Who Picked Hits and Made Stars, Dies at 82

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the rise of e-sports at the expense of traditional youth sports misidentified the brothers David and Matthew Grimes. David, 13, is at left, and Matthew, 11, is at right, not the reverse.
match_headline: Step Aside, LeBron and Dak, and Make Room for Banjo and Kazooie

text: An article on Wednesday about the Biden administration’s approval of two large solar projects in California misstated the estimated cost to build them. It is $689 million, not billion.
match_headline: Biden Administration Approves Two Big Solar Projects

text: An article on Tuesday about cryptocurrency start-ups misidentified the person who created the software tool used to build a block-headed avatar. It was Julius Tarng, an independent software designer, not Jack Dorsey.
match_headline: The New Get-Rich-Faster Job in Silicon Valley: Crypto Start-Ups

text: An article on April 24 about investments in family businesses referred incorrectly to Family Legacy Capital’s dealings with a group of hotels in the Pacific Northwest. While the fund had considered investing in the hotels, it never did. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the editors’ attention only recently.
match_headline: Wealthy Families Look to Help Family Businesses in the Pandemic

text: An article on Dec. 16 about hundreds of artifacts seized by the Manhattan district attorney’s office from museums, galleries and private collections misstated the disposition of an Italian criminal investigation of an antiquities dealer, Edoardo Almagià. The case was dismissed in 2012; he was not acquitted.
match_headline: A Trove of Artifacts Officials Call ‘Stolen’ Are Returned to Italy

text: An obituary on Dec. 15 about the ballerina Marjorie Tallchief misidentified the ballet by Bronislava Nijinska that she performed with the Grand Ballet du Marquis de Cuevas in New York in 1950. It was “Les Biches,” not “Le Train Bleu.”
match_headline: Marjorie Tallchief, Acclaimed Ballerina, Is Dead at 95

text: An article last Thursday about Your Friends in New York, a fashion collective designed to support designers of color, using information from the organization, omitted the name of a Facebook entity involved in supporting the collective. In addition to Instagram, We the Culture, a program started by Facebook to support Black creators, is supporting Your Friends in New York.
match_headline: Meet the Next Big Fashion Group

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Thursday about the auction of a digital replica of the patchwork JW Anderson cardigan that became a hit when Harry Styles wore it misstated the date of the sale. It was Dec. 14, not Dec. 13.
match_headline: That Viral Harry Styles Cardigan Just Got Auctioned as an NFT

text: An article on Dec. 9 about legal strategies for lawyers that represent defendants charged in the assault on the Capitol on Jan. 6 misspelled the given name of a lawyer. He is Steven Metcalf, not Stephen Metcalf.
match_headline: Some Jan. 6 Rioters May Use Police Brutality as a Defense

text: An article on Wednesday about the effectiveness of monoclonal antibodies in treating the Omicron variant misidentified Dr. Bruce Muma. He is president of the Henry Ford Physician Network, not the Henry Ford Health System, which is the parent organization.
match_headline: Hospitals Scramble as Antibody Treatments Fail Against Omicron

text: An article on Thursday about a special hearing next month by the Supreme Court to assess the legality of President Biden’s vaccine mandates misstated when the court had asked for responses to emergency applications in two sets of cases regarding vaccine mandates. The court requested the responses by Dec. 30, not Jan. 30.
match_headline: Supreme Court to Hold Special Hearing on Biden Vaccine Mandates

text: An article on Page 38 this weekend about Colin Powell misstates the name of a school associated with the former secretary of state who died in October. It is the Colin Powell School for Civic and Global Leadership, not the Colin Powell School for Global and Civic Leadership.
match_headline: Defense Contractor Tried to Give Classified Information to Russia, U.S. Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the actor David Arquette’s mission to improve the image of clowns misstated the name of a wrestling organization. It is World Championship Wrestling, not World Champion Wrestling.
match_headline: David Arquette Spray Paints Bozo in Brooklyn

text: A review on Dec. 5 about “Little Women: The Complete Novel, Featuring the Characters’ Letters and Manuscripts,” using information from the publisher, was accompanied by an incorrect photograph. It showed pages and a letter from “Pride and Prejudice,” not “Little Women.”
ref_headline: Little Women: The Complete Novel, Featuring the Characters’ Letters and Manuscripts,
match_headline: Holiday Gift Books for Children

text: An article on Sunday about pandemic politics in Enid, Okla., referred incorrectly to the state of the coronavirus in the community in the fall of 2020. While cases were spiking, they were not attributed to the Delta variant.
match_headline: First They Fought About Masks. Then Over the Soul of the City.

text: An article on Monday about Dr. Mehmet Oz misstated the position of Jeff Bartos, a Senate candidate, on the 2020 presidential election. While Mr. Bartos has called for a full audit of votes in the state, he has acknowledged that President Biden won the election.
match_headline: ‘Magic’ Weight-Loss Pills and Covid Cures: Dr. Oz Under the Microscope

text: An article on Monday about hotel wellness programs misidentified a program that Miraval Resorts & Spas partnered with the National Alliance on Mental Illness to create. It was Sensory Journeys, a meditation and soundscape series available for free on the Miraval website; it was not Journeys With Intention, which is a separate program created by Miraval.
match_headline: Travel as Healing

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about Justin Peck’s choreography in the new film adaptation of “West Side Story” misidentified the writer of the screenplay for the 1961 film. Ernest Lehman wrote the screenplay, not Arthur Laurents. (Mr. Lehman's screenplay was based on the stage book by Mr. Laurents.)
match_headline: What Is ‘West Side Story’ Without Jerome Robbins? Chatty.

text: An article on Monday about the increasingly vital role of understudies during the pandemic misidentified the name for stage performers who take over principal roles for a number of performances on a predetermined basis. They are alternates, not standbys. The article also described incorrectly Kathy Voytko’s history with the character Marian Paroo in “The Music Man.” The night Ms. Voytko first went on in place of Sutton Foster, she had first rehearsed the part that afternoon; she had not performed without rehearsing the role.
match_headline: On Broadway, Newly Vital Understudies Step Into the Spotlight

text: An article on Dec. 15 about the best new restaurants of the year misstated the name of a restaurant that opened in 2018. It is Adda Indian Canteen, not Adda Indian Cuisine.
match_headline: New York’s Top 10 New Restaurants of 2021

text: An article on Dec. 22 about how to eat oysters misspelled the surname of the author of “The Essential Oyster.” He is Rowan Jacobsen, not Jacobson.
match_headline: To Eat Oysters Better, Treat Them Like Wine

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Dec. 25 about Carlos Tejada, the deputy Asia editor of The New York Times, misstated the day of his death. It was Friday, Dec. 17, not Friday, Dec. 24.
match_headline: Carlos Tejada, Deputy Asia Editor for The Times, Dies at 49

text: An article on Tuesday about Saudi Arabia’s efforts to become a cultural capital described imprecisely the size of its population. Saudi Arabia’s population is about 35 million, not 22 million, which refers only to its citizens.
match_headline: As Other Arab States Falter, Saudi Arabia Seeks to Become a Cultural Hub

text: An article on Monday about Joan Didion movies to stream described incorrectly Mission San Juan Bautista in California, where Ms. Didion and John Gregory Dunne were married and where a scene in the movie “Vertigo” is set. The couple did marry under the same bell tower from which Kim Novak’s character in “Vertigo” leaps to her death; although the mission has a tower, the one in the movie was added using studio effects.
match_headline: Five Joan Didion Movies You Can Stream Right Now

text: An article on Tuesday about testing for sickle cell disease misstated the affiliation of Dr. Richard Olney. He is chief of the Genetic Disease Screening Program at the California Department of Public Health, not head of a program at the Sickle Cell Disease Foundation.
match_headline: Sickle Cell Math Is Brutally Simple, but Not Widely Taught

text: An obituary on Monday about Archbishop Desmond Tutu erroneously credited him with a distinction. He was the first Black Anglican bishop of Johannesburg — not the first Anglican bishop.
match_headline: Desmond Tutu, Whose Voice Helped Slay Apartheid, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the ecologist Thomas Lovejoy misstated the surname of the deputy director for climate and environment in the White House’s office of science and technology policy. She is Jane Lubchenco, not Lobchenco.
match_headline: Thomas Lovejoy, Wide-Ranging Ecologist and Amazon Rescuer, Dies at 80

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about companies and schools that are setting new requirements for booster shots misspelled the name of a New York investment bank in one instance. It is Jefferies, not Jeffries.
match_headline: As Omicron Spreads, Officials Ponder What It Means to Be ‘Fully Vaccinated’

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about a Marine’s return to Afghanistan included an incorrect credit with an image of the 2010 battle in Marja, Afghanistan. The photograph was taken by Goran Tomasevic for Reuters, not by Jim Huylebroek for The New York Times.
match_headline: 11 Years After Trying to Kill Each Other, a Marine and a Talib Meet Again

text: An article this weekend on Page 15 about the painter and illustrator Doris Lee misstates her birth year. It was 1904, not 1905 (although the artist went by 1905). It also misstates the surname of Milton Avery’s wife. She was Sally Michel, not Michael. And it misstates the year the dealer Deedee Wigmore began representing Doris Lee’s estate. It was 1990, not 1991.
match_headline: Doris Lee, Unjustly Forgotten, Gets a Belated but Full Blown Tribute

text: An article this weekend on Page 46 about privacy issues associated with DNA tests misstates the web address of a genealogy website. It is FamilySearch.org, not FamilySearch.com.
match_headline: Your DNA Test Could Send a Relative to Jail

text: An article on Dec. 19 about “Nightmare Alley” misstated the occupation of Cate Blanchett’s character. She plays a psychologist, not a psychiatrist.
match_headline: The 1947 ‘Nightmare Alley’: A Dark View of Class as Destiny

text: An article on Friday about the “Jeopardy!” contestant Amy Schneider misstated the year in which Ken Jennings won 74 consecutive games on “Jeopardy!” It was 2004, not 2014.
match_headline: Amy Schneider Wins the Most Consecutive ‘Jeopardy!’ Games of Any Female Contestant

text: An article on Monday about the Audrey Irmas Pavilion in Los Angeles misstated the name of the firm founded by Rem Koolhaas. It is the Office for Metropolitan Architecture, not the Office for Metropolitan Art.
match_headline: Boldface Names Give Los Angeles a New Cultural Center

text: An article on Monday about term limits for Supreme Court justices mischaracterized the purpose of a report by the Presidential Commission on the Supreme Court. It was to consider reforms to the court, not call for reforms to it.
match_headline: Why the Supreme Court Needs (Short) Term Limits

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an obituary on Saturday about the Hall of Fame Boston Celtics guard Sam Jones misidentified the team the Celtics were playing in the 1965 game shown. It was the Philadelphia 76ers, not the Philadelphia Warriors. (The Warriors moved to San Francisco in 1962; the Syracuse Nationals moved to Philadelphia and were renamed the 76ers in 1963.)
match_headline: Sam Jones, Sharpshooting Celtics Star of the 1960s, Dies at 88

text: An article on Tuesday about an inquiry into a large Colorado wildfire misstated when the fire began. It started on Dec. 30, not just before Christmas.
match_headline: Colorado Wildfire Inquiry Focuses on Christian Sect

text: An article on Tuesday about two new chief executives at the hedge fund Bridgewater misstated in two instances the surname of an associate professor at the University of Michigan Ross School of Business. She is Lindy Greer, not Green or Ross. The article also misstated the surname of Bridgewater’s departing chief executive in one instance. He is David McCormick, not Cormick.
match_headline: Bridgewater, World’s Largest Hedge Fund, Names New Chief Executives

text: An obituary on Dec. 21 about the sex therapist Shirley Zussman misstated her connection to the sex researchers William H. Masters and Virginia E. Johnson. Though she and her husband, Leon Zussman, attended a workshop led by Dr. Masters and Ms. Johnson, they did not train with them.
match_headline: Shirley Zussman, Indefatigable Sex Therapist, Is Dead at 107

text: An article on Friday about prominent people who died in 2021 misstated the author Donald Cozzens’s status in the Roman Catholic Church. Mr. Cozzens, who challenged the church on its protection of child-molesting clerics, was an active priest at his death, not a former priest.
match_headline: Deaths in 2021: Headline Names Against the Backdrop of Pandemic

text: An article on Tuesday about 12 things The Times’s critics are looking forward to in 2022 misstated the title of the debut stand-up special from Taylor Tomlinson. It is “Quarter-Life Crisis,” not “Quarter-Life Special.”
match_headline: 12 Things Our Critics Are Looking Forward to in 2022

text: An article last Thursday about the resurgence of Murano glass misspelled the surname of the editorial director at 1stdibs. He is Tony Freund, not Fruend.
match_headline: Inspired by Murano, Glassware Goes Wild

text: An article on Sunday about tracking climate change misidentified the country where Kuomboka is practiced. It is Zambia, not Zimbabwe.
match_headline: Tracking Climate Change in 193 Countries

text: An article on Dec. 26 about nonprofit groups that helped families during the holiday season misstated part of the name of a city in South Dakota. It is Sioux Falls, not Sioux City.
match_headline: Celebrations and Gifts That Embody the Holiday Spirit

text: An article on Sunday about the Governors Island Winter Village misstated the given name of an artist who works on the island. His name is Josef Pinlac, not Joseph Pinlac.
match_headline: A Summer Hot Spot Is Now a Winter Village. But Will New Yorkers Visit?

text: An obituary on Thursday about the racehorse trainer Billy Turner, using information from his family, omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to those named, Mr. Turner is survived by a stepdaughter, Jessica Rich.
match_headline: Billy Turner, Trainer of a Triple Crown Winner, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Monday about the investment banker James Cayne, using information from his family, misstated the surname of one of his daughters. She is Jennice Cayne Nienkerk, not Jennice Schenker.
match_headline: James Cayne, Who Ran the Ill-Fated Bear Stearns, Dies at 87

text: An article on Sunday about the inaccuracy of some prenatal tests for rare disorders misstated the location of the company Sequenom. It is based in San Diego, not Silicon Valley. Although many of the noninvasive prenatal blood tests currently in use were developed in Silicon Valley, not all of the testing firms have current headquarters there. The article also referred imprecisely to projected numbers from the test maker Natera’s newest algorithms. Natera said those figures were included in its clinical studies.
match_headline: When They Warn of Rare Disorders, These Prenatal Tests Are Usually Wrong

text: An article on Friday about an effort by Virginia Democrats to block Andrew Wheeler, the former chief of the Environmental Protection Agency, from taking a similar role in Virginia’s administration described incorrectly one of the positions held by Michael Catanzaro. Although Mr. Catanzaro has worked as a lobbyist, he is no longer registered to do so.
match_headline: Virginia Democrats Aim to Block Trump’s E.P.A. Chief From State Agency

text: An article on Friday about Alice Childress’s play “Trouble in Mind” erroneously attributed a distinction to LaChanze and her daughter Celia Rose Gooding. LaChanze and Gooding were not the first mother and daughter to perform on Broadway as leading actors in the same season. (Jennifer Ehle and Rosemary Harris both starred in Broadway productions in 2000.)
match_headline: LaChanze on Alice Childress’s Timeless Words in ‘Trouble in Mind’

text: An article this weekend on Page 28 about the Capitol Police and the Jan. 6 riots refers imprecisely to the British assault on the Capitol in 1814. The building was severely damaged; it did not burn to the ground.
match_headline: The Capitol Police and the Scars of Jan. 6

text: An article this weekend on Page 2 misstates Jona Tajonera’s ethnicity. She is Filipino, not Latino.
match_headline: How a Mobile Covid Tester Spends Her Sundays

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Marti Ladd and the folk singer Arlo Guthrie referred incompletely to the 50th anniversary associated with Mr. Guthrie’s November 2019 performance at Carnegie Hall. It was the anniversary of the 1969 movie inspired by the 1967 song “Alice’s Restaurant.”
match_headline: They Could Be Anything They Want (Together)

text: Because of an editing error, the On the Market feature last Sunday misstated the year in which the house at 37 Old Post Lane in Mamaroneck, N.Y., was built. It was 1996, not 1986.

A review on Dec. 19 about “Master of the Game: Henry Kissinger and the Art of Middle East Diplomacy,” by Martin Indyk, referred imprecisely to Tel Aviv, implying that it was the seat of Israel’s government. Israel’s government is in Jerusalem, not Tel Aviv.
ref_headline: Master of the Game: Henry Kissinger and the Art of Middle East Diplomacy,
match_headline: Henry Kissinger and the Puzzle of the Middle East

text: An article on Dec. 23 about Minnesota’s deployment of National Guard members to short-staffed nursing homes misstated Gov. Tim Walz’s efforts to increase pay for nursing assistants. He has sought to use federal coronavirus relief funds for bonus pay for nursing home staff; he has not sought to raise reimbursement rates for those nursing homes.
match_headline: National Guard Empties Bedpans and Clips Toenails at Nursing Homes

text: An article on Friday about a North Korean man who crossed the Demilitarized Zone incorrectly rendered part of the name of a Seoul-based human rights group. It is the Database Center for North Korean Human Rights, not the Data Center for North Korean Human Rights.
match_headline: To Reach South Korea, He Risked His Life. To Leave It, He Did It Again.

text: An article on Sunday about Harry Reid’s memorial service misstated the number of sons he had. He had four sons, not three.
match_headline: ‘Goodbye, Harry’: Reid’s Memorial Draws Warm Testimonials From Biden and Obama

text: An article on Monday about Week 18 in the N.F.L. misstated the score at the beginning of the fourth quarter in the Jaguars-Colts game. It was 23-3, not 23-10.
match_headline: What We Learned From Week 18 in the N.F.L.

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about a Sherlock Holmes mystery at the Grolier Club misstated the year that Frederic Dorr Steele created an illustration showing the actor William Gillette portraying Sherlock Holmes. It was 1933, not 1903.
match_headline: A Sherlock Holmes Mystery at the Grolier Club

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the lyricist Marilyn Bergman misstated the age difference between her and her husband and co-lyricist, Alan Bergman. He was born a little more than three years before her, in 1925 — not four.
match_headline: Marilyn Bergman, Half of an Oscar-Winning Songwriting Duo, Dies at 93

text: An article on Friday about China’s latest pandemic lockdown strategy referred incorrectly to the university that Zhang Shengzi attends. It is a university in Xi’an, not the University of Xi’an.
match_headline: China’s Latest Lockdown Shows Stubborn Resolve on Zero-Covid

text: A map with an article on Tuesday about the potential impact of the Omicron variant misstated the date through which vaccination rates among older Americans were recorded. The data was current through Jan. 7, 2022, not 2021.
match_headline: Early Data Hints at Omicron’s Potential Toll Across America

text: An article on Tuesday about civil suits against Donald J. Trump seeking damages for the Jan. 6 Capitol attack misspelled the surname of a former Justice Department official and University of Minnesota Law School professor in one reference. He is Alan Rozenshtein, not Rozenshstein.
match_headline: Civil Suits Against Trump Seek Damages for Jan. 6 Attack

text: An article on Dec. 29 about forecasts of American food trends in 2022 misstated the surname of the associate director of food and drink at the research firm Mintel. She is Jennifer Zegler, not Zigler.
match_headline: How Will Americans Eat in 2022? The Food Forecasters Speak.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the author F. Sionil Jose omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to those listed, Mr. Jose is survived by a son, Alex Jose.
match_headline: F. Sionil Jose, 97, Novelist Who Saw Heroism in Ordinary Filipinos, Dies

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about Dan Reilly, the original Mr. Met, misstated when a publicity photograph of him was taken. It was in the late 1980s — not during his tenure as Mr. Met in the 1960s. A headline with the obituary misstated Mr. Reilly’s age. As the obituary correctly noted he was 83, not 93.
match_headline: Dan Reilly, the Original Mr. Met, Is Dead at 83

text: An article on Saturday about efforts by airlines to ease some European Union airport rules during the pandemic referred incompletely to the Federal Aviation Administration’s waiver of slot limits at Kennedy and La Guardia in New York and Ronald Reagan National in Washington. It extended them through March for international operations, not for domestic travel.
match_headline: Airlines push the E.U. to ease airport rules as Omicron rages.

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the actor and comedian Bob Saget misstated when he was cast in the Richard Pryor movie “Critical Condition.” It was before he worked on “The Morning Program” on CBS-TV, not after.
match_headline: Bob Saget, Comic Who Starred in the Sitcom ‘Full House,’ Dies at 65

text: An article on Thursday about a meeting between Russia and NATO referred incorrectly to NATO allies bordering Russia. Poland and the Baltic countries share a border with Russia, but Turkey does not.
match_headline: NATO and Russia Talk Frankly, but Past One Another for Now

text: An article on Monday about heavy rain and snowfall in Washington misstated the location of Rainier, Wash. It is southeast of Olympia, not southwest.
match_headline: Record Rain and Snow Shut Down Roads and Schools in Washington State

text: An article on Thursday about the actor John Cariani referred imprecisely to Cariani’s roles as a father. His role in “Caroline, or Change” marks the second time he has played a father in a Broadway role, not the first.
match_headline: After Its Odds-Defying Run, John Cariani Says Bye to ‘Caroline, or Change’

text: An article on Wednesday about a pay increase for security guards at the Met misstated the new wage for existing guards at the museum who were earning $15.51 an hour. They are now being paid $16.50 an hour, not $17.
match_headline: The Met Increases Its Pay to Guards to Address Covid-Related Shortages

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a rejected bid in the Senate to impose sanctions on a Russian natural-gas pipeline misstated the tally of the vote. It was 55 to 44, not 55 to 43.
match_headline: New Sanctions for Russian Gas Pipeline Fall Short in Senate

text: An article on Tuesday about a federal lawsuit in which 16 private universities and colleges are accused of conspiring to reduce financial aid misstated the day the lawsuit was filed. It was Sunday, not Monday.
match_headline: Lawsuit Says 16 Elite Colleges Are Part of Price-Fixing Cartel

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about lemon-pepper wings misstates Lou Williams’s relationship with the Atlanta Hawks. He was traded to the team, not drafted by it.
match_headline: Lemon Pepper Makes Everything Better — Especially Wings

text: An article last Sunday about the billionaire Ronald O. Perelman referred imprecisely to a get. It is a written document obtained from a Jewish rabbinical court that grants permission to divorce; it is not a religious tradition by which men leave their wives without leaving the faith. The article also misstated the resolution of a lawsuit that Samantha Perelman filed against her uncle, James Cohen. It went to trial, where she lost; it was not dismissed. And the article referred imprecisely to a meeting sought by the investor Chris Mittleman. He has sought a meeting with executives at Revlon, not specifically with Mr. Perelman.
match_headline: The Debt King

text: An article on Sunday about the eruption of an underwater volcano near the South Pacific island of Tonga referred incorrectly to New Zealand’s location relative to Tonga. It is southwest, not northeast, of Tonga.
match_headline: Underwater Volcano Erupts, Setting Off Tsunami Warnings Across Pacific

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about efforts by colleges to adapt campus rules as the pandemic persists, misspelled the given name of a woman at Rice University. She is Talia Andris, not Thalia Andris.
match_headline: Some Colleges Loosen Rules for a Virus That Won’t Go Away

text: An article on Saturday about Democrats’ calls for a shift in strategy ahead of the midterm elections misstated Bradley Beychok’s role with American Bridge 21st Century, a Democratic group. He is a senior adviser with the organization, not its president.
match_headline: Frustrated Democrats Call for ‘Reset’ Ahead of Midterm Elections

text: An article on Monday about the Arizona Cardinals’ championship drought referred incorrectly to Charles Bidwill Jr., a former president of the Cardinals. He is the uncle, not the grandfather, of the current team owner, Michael Bidwill.
match_headline: Is the Arizona Cardinals’ Title Drought the Result of a Curse?

text: An article on Monday about the Buffalo Bills’ defeat of the New England Patriots described incorrectly the third-seeded Bills’ opponent in the next round of the N.F.L. playoffs. They are playing the second-lowest remaining seed in the A.F.C., not the lowest.
match_headline: Josh Allen’s Bills Nearly Perfect in Dismantling the Patriots

text: An article on Wednesday about a guaranteed income program for New York City mothers misidentified the college where Daniela Gutierrez was working when the pandemic hit. It was the New York City College of Technology in Brooklyn, not Queens College in Queens, where she had worked previously.
match_headline: How $1,000 a Month in Guaranteed Income Is Helping N.Y.C. Mothers

text: An article on Tuesday about Naomi Osaka’s return to tennis misidentified the home country of Camila Osorio. She is from Colombia, not Spain.
match_headline: Naomi Osaka Returns, Ready or Not

text: An article on Wednesday about triathlete training in Norway misspelled the middle name of the engineer and serial entrepreneur who worked with Norway’s national team. He is Olav Aleksander Bu, not Alexander.
match_headline: Why Do They Swim-Bike-Run So Fast? Data.

text: A column on Wednesday about Russia’s President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine misspelled the surname of the chairman of the Center for Liberal Strategies. He is Ivan Krastev, not Kratsev.
match_headline: Putin to Ukraine: ‘Marry Me or I’ll Kill You’

text: An obituary on Dec. 31 about Lee Kaufman, who appeared with her husband, Morty, in advertising spots for Swiffer products when they were in their 90s, misstated how many children she had with her first husband, Bernard Allen. It was two, not three.
match_headline: Lee Kaufman, Who Cleaned Her Way to Late-Life Stardom, Dies at 99

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Jan. 13 about Stephen Lawrence, the music director for the album and television special “Free to Be … You and Me” and a longtime composer for “Sesame Street,” misidentified one of his collaborators. He was David Axlerod, who wrote lyrics for many “Sesame Street” songs — not the composer, arranger and producer David Axelrod.
ref_headline: Free to Be … You and Me
match_headline: Stephen Lawrence, Whose Music Enriched ‘Sesame Street,’ Dies at 82

text: Because of an editing error, a summary accompanying a graphic on Saturday about temperature records set in 2021 described incorrectly the period over which the weather data were gathered. Weather stations included in the analysis had data for 30 to 65 years or more, not two decades.
match_headline: We Mapped a Year of Extreme Weather

text: A picture with an article on Thursday about interference between 5G signals and radio altimeters was published in error. The image showed a pressure altimeter, not a radio altimeter. The article incorrectly described the fighter planes used in World War II. Most were not jets.
match_headline: How 5G Clashed With an Aviation Device Invented in the 1920s

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Alan Scott, the doctor behind the medical use of Botox, referred incorrectly to Clostridium botulinum. It is a microbe that produces the toxin botulinum; it is not itself a toxin.
match_headline: Alan Scott, Doctor Behind the Medical Use of Botox, Dies at 89

text: An article on Friday about President Biden’s concession on his social safety net and climate package misidentified a senator from Alabama. He is Richard C. Shelby, not Richard J. Shelby.
match_headline: With Broad Safety Net Bill Stalled, Democrats Weigh What to Salvage

text: Because of an editing error, the Big City column on Page 3 misstates when the Costume Industry Coalition was formed. It was May 2020, not last May.

An article on Friday about Taylor Mack’s “Fever Dream” misspelled the surname of a jazz vocalist in one instance. The vocalist is Kat Edmonson, not Edmondson. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Taylor Mac’s ‘Fever Dream’: Exploring the Philosophy of the Hang

text: An article on Page 10 this weekend about two operas by Ricky Ian Gordon misstates the premiere date of “Intimate Apparel.” It opens Jan. 31 not Jan. 27.
match_headline: Review: In ‘Intimate Apparel,’ Letting the Seamstress Sing

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about the conflict in eastern Ukraine misidentifies the origins of the far-right group C-14. It is Ukrainian, not Russian.
match_headline: In the Trenches of Ukraine’s Forever War

text: An obituary on Friday about the German-born actor Hardy Kruger referred incorrectly to two actors who told him stories about Nazi crimes when he met them while shooting the Nazi propaganda film “Young Eagles.” in 1944. They were not Jewish. And a picture caption with the obituary, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the actress shown with Mr. Kruger in a scene from the movie “Sundays and Cybèle.” She is Patricia Gozzi, not Nicole Courcel.
match_headline: Hardy Kruger, German-Born Hollywood Star, Is Dead at 93

text: An obituary on Monday about the songwriter Dallas Frazier referred imprecisely to his composition “Beneath Still Waters.” While it did become a hit for Emmylou Harris, he did not write it for her; it was first recorded by George Jones in 1967, more than a decade earlier.
match_headline: Dallas Frazier, Who Wrote Hits for Country Stars, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Charles E. McGee, one of the last surviving Tuskegee Airmen, misstated the day in 1944 that he shot down a German fighter plane. It was Aug. 24, not Aug. 23.
match_headline: Charles E. McGee, Honored Tuskegee Airman, Dies at 102

text: An article on Thursday about Silvio Berlusconi’s presidential campaign misspelled the given name of a lawmaker formerly with the anti-establishment Five Star Movement. He is Cristian Romaniello, not Christian.
match_headline: Silvio Berlusconi Angles for Italy’s Presidency, Bunga Bunga and All

text: An article Friday about a new constitution for the N.C.A.A. misstated Betsy Mitchell’s position at Caltech. She is the athletic director, not the president.
match_headline: N.C.A.A. Reorganizes Around New Constitution That Shifts Power to Universities

text: Because of an editing error, the Big City column on Page 3 misstates when the Costume Industry Coalition was formed. It was May 2020, not last May.

An article last Sunday about a picture of a personal library that is repeatedly shared on social media referred incorrectly to the nationality of Paul de Man. He was Belgian, not French. The article also referred incorrectly to Mr. de Man’s lecture at Johns Hopkins University. It was not his first stateside lecture; he had lectured at Bard and Harvard before 1966.
match_headline: A Library the Internet Can’t Get Enough Of

text: An article on Dec. 26 about Janet Malcolm misstated Ingrid Sischy’s age in 1986. She was 34, not 27.

A review on Jan. 9 about “Chasing History,” by Carl Bernstein, misidentified the newspaper that the reporter Will Fowler worked for when he was covering the Black Dahlia murder. It was The Los Angeles Examiner, not The Los Angeles Times.
match_headline: Carl Bernstein’s Eulogy for the Newspaper Business

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the areas of Tonga that bore the brunt of the tsunami referred incorrectly to the areas that were hardest hit. The three islets of Mango, Fonoifua and Nomuka were most devastated by the tsunami, not Nomuka alone.
match_headline: Three Tiny Islands Have Borne the Brunt of Tonga’s Tsunami

text: An article on Saturday about a free speech ruling involving the University of Florida misstated the year that Judge Mark E. Walker was appointed to a U.S. District Court in Florida. It was 2012, not 2018.
match_headline: Judge Issues Stinging Free Speech Ruling Against University of Florida

text: An article on Sunday about abortion laws around the world misstated the position of Michael New at the Catholic University of America. He is a research associate, not a law professor.
match_headline: On Abortion Law, the U.S. Is Unusual. Without Roe, It Would Be, Too.

text: An article on Monday about the firing of the top staff investigator for the House committee scrutinizing the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol misstated a previous position of Eric K. Shinseki. He is the retired chief of staff of the Army, not the secretary.
match_headline: Top Jan. 6 Investigator Fired From Post at the University of Virginia

text: An article on Saturday about the impact of a volcanic eruption on Tonga’s communication networks referred incorrectly to Tonga’s location. It is northeast of New Zealand, not northwest.
match_headline: Heard, Felt but Barely Seen: How a Volcano Severed Tonga From the World

text: An article on Tuesday about Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI’s presence at a meeting concerning a priest accused of pedophilia misidentified part of the location of the archdiocese where Benedict was once archbishop. It is the archdiocese of Munich and Freising, not Freiburg.
match_headline: Benedict Admits Being at Meeting About Priest Accused of Abuse

text: An article on Sunday about a wildfire in Big Sur misstated the rank of a Cal Fire official. George Nuñez is an assistant chief, not a captain.
match_headline: Wildfire in Big Sur Forces Residents to Evacuate

text: An article on Tuesday about the James Webb Telescope misstated the amount the Webb telescope’s mirrors will be fine-tuned. Engineers will aim for alignments as accurate as one-10,000th of a hair, not a hair follicle.
match_headline: After Million-Mile Journey, James Webb Telescope Reaches Destination

text: An article on Tuesday about the death of a gunman accused of shooting two New York City police officers described incorrectly the handgun that officials say was used in the shooting. It was a Glock 45, not a .45 caliber gun.
match_headline: Gunman Accused of Shooting 2 N.Y.P.D. Officers Dies

text: An article on Tuesday about a study on the impact that cash stipends to poor mothers had on the brain activity of babies misstated the name of the scientific journal where the new study was published on Monday. It is the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, not the Proceedings of the National Academies of Sciences.
match_headline: Cash Aid to Poor Mothers Increases Brain Activity in Babies, Study Finds

text: An article on Tuesday about Trump administration documents turned over by the National Archives to a House panel investigating the Jan. 6 riot at the Capitol misstated the response by John Ratcliffe, the former director of national intelligence, to the panel’s request for a report. Because of a disagreement in the intelligence community, Mr. Ratcliffe’s report about foreign influence in the election, which was scheduled to be submitted on Dec. 18, was delayed until Jan. 7; it is not the case that is was never submitted.
match_headline: What the Trump Documents Might Tell the Jan. 6 Committee

text: An article last Wednesday about ambitious chefs opening restaurants in the suburbs misstated the location of some of Peter Chang’s restaurants. Most are in suburban settings in Virginia and Maryland, not just in the suburbs of Washington, D.C.
match_headline: America’s Next Great Restaurants Are in the Suburbs. But Can They Thrive There?

text: An obituary on Monday about Dennis Smith, the New York City firefighter who became a best-selling author, misspelled part of the name of the Bronx high school he attended. It is Cardinal Hayes High School, not Hays.
match_headline: Dennis Smith, Firefighter Who Wrote Best Sellers, Dies at 81

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about Dale Clevenger, the longtime solo French horn of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, referred incorrectly at one point to Daniel Barenboim. He was Riccardo Muti’s predecessor as the orchestra’s music director, not his successor.
match_headline: Dale Clevenger, Chicago Symphony’s Fearless Horn Master, Dies at 81

text: An article on Wednesday about Germany’s hesitation to take forceful measures to bolster Ukraine in its standoff with Russia misidentified Artis Pabriks. He is Latvia’s minister of defense, not its foreign minister.
match_headline: Where Is Germany in the Ukraine Standoff? Its Allies Wonder.

text: An article on Saturday about a pair of films about the Jane Collective misstated the release status of a 2018 film. The movie, “Ask for Jane,” was shown in theaters; it did not play only in festivals.
match_headline: At Sundance, Two Films Look at Abortion and the Jane Collective

text: An article last Thursday about the artist Françoise Gilot described incorrectly the painting “Paloma à la Guitare.” It is a portrait of Ms. Gilot’s daughter; Ms. Gilot is not in it with her.
match_headline: Françoise Gilot: ‘It Girl’ at 100

text: An article on Thursday about President Biden’s promise to nominate a Black woman to the Supreme Court referred incorrectly to the first appointment of a Black woman to serve as a federal appeals court judge. The appointment was made by President Jimmy Carter in 1979, not by President Gerald R. Ford in 1975.
match_headline: Biden Expected to Nominate a Black Woman to the Supreme Court

text: An article on Wednesday about a motion to temporarily block a ruling that had struck down New York’s mask mandate misstated the next steps in the case. The state appeals court judge set a Friday deadline for papers to be submitted; he did not schedule an additional hearing for Friday.
match_headline: New York Mask Mandate Back in Effect After Judge Grants Stay

text: An article on Thursday about Sean Caddle, a political consultant who pleaded guilty to hiring two men to kill a longtime associate, misstated the status of his sentencing. It is scheduled for June 7, 2022; it is not the case that it had not been scheduled.
match_headline: Political Consultant Admits Hiring 2 Men to Kill Longtime Associate

text: An article on Wednesday about Fashion Nova, a clothing site accused of hiding bad reviews, described incorrectly the outcome of a dispute between Fashion Nova and the Federal Trade Commission. Fashion Nova agreed to a $4.2 million settlement; it was not a fine.
match_headline: A fashion brand agrees to pay $4.2 million after F.T.C. says it suppressed negative reviews online.

text: An article on Saturday about a new chip manufacturing complex in Ohio funded by Intel described incorrectly the presence of semiconductor manufacturing in the state. While there has not been a major chip maker in Ohio recently, related businesses there include a former RCA semiconductor plant that was bought by Harris Corporation in 1988 and later closed.
match_headline: Intel to Invest at Least $20 Billion in New Chip Factories in Ohio

text: An article on Friday about school closures in India misspelled the surname of the head of the Population Foundation. She is Poonam Muttreja, not Poonam Mattreja.
match_headline: India Schools Stay Closed, and Hopes Fade for a Lost Generation

text: An article on Monday about the recent resignation of Mark B. Rosenberg as president of Florida International University in Miami misspelled the surname of the man named to serve as the school’s interim president. He is Kenneth Jessell, not Jessel.
match_headline: Former President of Florida International University Explains Sudden Exit

text: An article on Page 7 this weekend about Michael Fanone, a Metropolitan Police officer who defended the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, refers imprecisely to the timing of Fanone’s interview with Molly Ball, a Time magazine reporter. It took place shortly before he returned to work in September, not after.
match_headline: To Hell and Back, Then to CNN

text: An article on Jan. 23 about coronavirus transmission between animals and humans misstated the number of European countries that banned or began phasing out fur farming following coronavirus outbreaks on mink farms in 2020. Three European countries, not 12, did so after the outbreaks. Additionally, legislation to ban fur farming in Poland is still pending.
match_headline: Animals That Infect Humans Are Scary. It’s Worse When We Infect Them Back.

text: An obituary on Aug. 31 about the wine exporter Rebecca Wasserman-Hone, using information from her family, misstated the name of her first husband. He was Denison Andrews, not Dennis Andrew. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the editors’ attention only recently.
match_headline: Rebecca Wasserman-Hone, Who Put Burgundy on the U.S. Map, Dies at 84

text: An article on Saturday about efforts to aid Tonga following the recent volcanic eruption and tsunami misspelled the name of a Tongan community leader living in Melbourne, Australia. She is Mele Makelesi Facci, not Mele Malekesi Facci.
match_headline: Tonga’s Proud Diaspora Confronts Daunting Challenge of Disaster Response

text: An article on Sunday about the ban of a Native American mascot in an upstate New York high school district referred incorrectly to a reference to a different mascot by Duane Honyoust. Mr. Honyoust was critical of the Cleveland baseball team’s now-discontinued use of the Chief Wahoo logo, not the “tomahawk chop” cheer, which is associated with a different baseball team.
match_headline: Facing a Ban, a School District Fights to Keep ‘Indian’ Nickname

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the funeral for Detective Jason Rivera of the New York Police Department misstated the type of flag draping his coffin. It was a department flag, not an American flag.
match_headline: Mourners Remember N.Y.P.D. Officer Killed in Shooting: ‘He Was Joy’

text: An article on Saturday about Rafael Nadal and Daniil Medvedev’s Grand Slam men’s singles title tournament misstated the amount that the Canadian player Denis Shapovalov was fined. It was $8,000, not 8,000 Australian dollars.
match_headline: Rafael Nadal and Daniil Medvedev Will Meet in Australian Open Final

text: An article on Monday about the N.F.L.’s Conference Championships misidentified the Bengals’ defensive coordinator. He is Lou Anarumo, not Brian Callahan.
match_headline: What We Learned From the N.F.L.’s Conference Championships

text: An article on Saturday about Joe Burrow and Patrick Mahomes’s gap in N.F.L. experience misstated the Chiefs’ record at the start of this season. They were 3-4 (then 4-4); they were never 3-5.
match_headline: The Gap Year Between Mahomes and Burrow Is Closing

text: An article on Monday about the Cincinnati Bengals’ victory over Kansas City misidentified the location of the high school Joe Burrow attended. The school, Athens High School, is in The Plains, Ohio, not Athens, Ohio.
match_headline: How the Bengals Beat Kansas City to Advance to the Super Bowl

text: An obituary on Jan. 22 about the Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh misidentified an institution where he studied in the early 1960s. It was Princeton Theological Seminary, not Princeton University. It also referred incorrectly to his name before he was ordained a monk. The earliest record of his name, on a school registration, is Nguyen Dinh Lang. It was later changed to Nguyen Xuan Bao; that was not his birth name.
match_headline: Thich Nhat Hanh, Monk, Zen Master and Activist, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor and comedian Howard Hesseman misstated Mr. Hesseman’s birthplace. It was Lebanon, Ore., not Salem, Ore.
match_headline: Howard Hesseman, 81, the D.J. Johnny Fever in ‘WKRP in Cincinnati,’ Dies

text: An obituary on Saturday about the legal reformer Edgar S. Cahn misstated the name of the journal that published a paper by Mr. Cahn and his wife, Jean Camper Cahn, concerning the War on Poverty. It was The Yale Law Journal, not The Yale Law Review.
match_headline: Edgar S. Cahn, Legal Reformer in Defense of the Poor, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Sunday about jazz pianist Beegie Adair misspelled the surname of a country singer. He was Porter Wagoner, not Waggoner.
match_headline: Beegie Adair, a Jazz Master in Country Music’s Capital, Dies at 84

text: An article on Tuesday about tax breaks driving a rush to buy property in Puerto Rico misstated the benefits for a new investor buying a primary residence in Puerto Rico under Act 60. The purchase qualifies the investor for zero capital gains tax, but not for corporate income tax relief.
match_headline: The Rush for a Slice of Paradise in Puerto Rico

text: An article on Friday about Vice President Kamala Harris’s trip to Honduras misstated the name of Taiwan’s vice president. He is William Lai, not Tai.
match_headline: Harris Seeks Ally in Honduras as She Revisits Central America

text: An article on Tuesday about a meeting of populist leaders in Madrid called “Defend Europe” misstated the year Poland became a full member of NATO. It was 1999, not 2009.
match_headline: For Some of Ukraine’s Neighbors, ‘Defend Europe’ Has Another Meaning

text: An article on Sunday about the 50th anniversary of Bloody Sunday referred incorrectly to the rifles fired by British soldiers on protesters in Northern Ireland. They were semiautomatic, not automatic.
match_headline: 50 Years On, Bloody Sunday’s Wounds Are Still Felt

text: An article on Sunday about 16 men who died in New York City jails last year described incorrectly a ruling made by the New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner in the death of a detainee, Esias Johnson. The cause of Mr. Johnson’s death was still pending. It also misstated the month in which Amanda Velasco told police that her husband, Javier Velasco, broke into her apartment, stole property and sent her threatening text messages. She made that report in September 2020, not February 2021. (Mr. Velasco was jailed and released in February 2021, when he sent her more threatening texts and was jailed again.)
match_headline: 16 Men Died in New York City Jails Last Year. Who Were They?

text: An article on Monday about inequality in China misstated the source of data showing that the top 10 percent of income earners control 68 percent of China’s wealth and that the bottom half control about 6 percent. It was the World Inequality Database, not the World Bank.
match_headline: Migrant Worker’s Tale of Inequality Grips China, Then Is Erased

text: An article on Tuesday about the troubles facing Prime Minister Boris Johnson of Britain misquoted an emailed invitation to a gathering organized by one of his aides. It read, “Bring your own booze,” not “Bring your own bottle.” The article also misstated the number of coronavirus deaths in Britain as of April 16, 2021. The government had registered 127,457 by that date, not more than 150,000.
match_headline: The Next Few Days Are Critical for Boris Johnson

text: An obituary on Monday about the veteran State Department officer Phyllis Oakley misstated the year the department lifted its unofficial ban on married women in the foreign service. It was 1971, not 1974.
match_headline: Phyllis Oakley, Female Pioneer at the State Department, Dies at 87

text: An article on Tuesday about Brian Houston, the former leader of the megachurch Hillsong, misidentified the Australian city in which members of the church sang and danced at a youth camp, seemingly in violation of pandemic restrictions. It was Newcastle, not Sydney.
match_headline: Leader of Australian Megachurch Steps Down After Charge Over Father’s Sexual Abuse

text: An article on Wednesday about China’s expanding ties in the Middle East described incorrectly a top Turkish diplomat’s trip to China in January. He discussed opportunities for economic cooperation, not reports targeting China in the Turkish news media.
match_headline: As the U.S. Pulls Back From the Mideast, China Leans In

text: An article on Wednesday about Tom Brady’s legacy misstated when he won his fifth Super Bowl. It was in 2017, not 2015. It also misstated the Patriots’ opponent in the A.F.C. championship game following the 2014 season. They faced the Indianapolis Colts, not the Baltimore Ravens.
match_headline: Tom Brady’s Impact Was Best Measured in Goose Bumps

text: An article last Thursday about the “Jeopardy!” champion Amy Schneider misstated her age. She is 42, not 43.
match_headline: ‘Jeopardy!’ Hasn’t Had a Player Like Amy Schneider

text: A headline with an obituary about the dancer and choreographer Donald Mahler referred imprecisely to his work. While Mr. Mahler staged the dark ballets of Antony Tudor, he was not known as the choreographer of such ballets.
match_headline: Donald Mahler, Prolific Ballet Choreographer, Dies at 88

text: An article on Thursday about memos from lawyers working with the Trump campaign after the 2020 election that proposed putting in place alternate electors misstated the number of counties in Wisconsin in which the Trump campaign did not seek to invalidate votes in a 2020 lawsuit. It was 70 counties, not 72. The article also misidentified one of the jurisdictions where the campaign did seek to invalidate results. It was Milwaukee County, not just the city of Milwaukee.
match_headline: Memos Show Roots of Trump’s Focus on Jan. 6 and Alternate Electors

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Thursday about the film series “Dames, Janes, Dolls and Canaries” at the Museum of Modern Art misidentified the film starring Dolores del Río and Joel McCrea. It was “Bird of Paradise,” not “Night World.”
match_headline: These Talkies Star Complicated Women You Might Well Recognize

text: An article on Friday about the resignations of senior aides to Prime Minister Boris Johnson of Britain misstated the surname of Mr. Johnson’s chief of staff. It is Dan Rosenfield, not Rosenfeld.
match_headline: Top Aides to Boris Johnson Quit, Adding to Downing Street Turmoil

text: A headline with an article on Thursday about a subscription goal reached at The New York Times Company misstated the milestone. The company reached 10 million subscriptions, not subscribers. (One subscriber may hold multiple subscriptions.)
match_headline: The Times hits its goal of 10 million subscriptions with the addition of The Athletic.

text: Because of a production error, an article on Jan. 27 about CNN’s efforts to bolster its streaming service included words that were run together and columns of type that were out of order.
match_headline: The Best Brain Foods You’re Not Eating

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the purchase of two islands by Colby College from foundations owned by the Wyeth family misstated the age of a young woman memorialized in the painting “Pentecost” by Andrew Wyeth. She was 19 when she died, not 15.
match_headline: New Life for the Wyeth Legacy Five Miles Out to Sea

text: An article on page 12 this weekend about a production of “Swan Lake” by Miami City Ballet misidentifies the character that Nathalia Arja referred to as “almost not there” in the lakeside pas de deux. It was Benno, not Siegfried.
match_headline: In Miami, Climbing Ballet’s Everest: ‘Swan Lake’

text: An article on page 9 this weekend about Hugh Jackman and Sutton Foster in the Broadway production of “The Music Man” misstates Kate Horton’s title. She is a producer of the musical, not an executive producer. (She was originally brought in as an executive producer.)
match_headline: How Hugh Jackman, Sutton Foster and ‘The Music Man’ Withstood Covid

text: A subheading with an obituary on Monday about Jeremiah Stamler, a cardiovascular researcher who in 1965 was subpoenaed to testify by the House Committee on Un-American Activities, misstated Joseph McCarthy’s relationship to the committee. He did not found it and was not a member.
match_headline: Jeremiah Stamler, Who Found Ways to Curb Heart Disease, Dies at 102

text: An article last Sunday about the late designer Thierry Mugler misspelled the given name of one of Mr. Mugler’s onetime models. She is Patty Hearst, not Patti. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The article also misidentified a model who walked for Mr. Mugler. She is Elizabeth Jagger, not Bianca Jagger.
match_headline: Mugler, Remembered by His Crowd

text: An article last Sunday about preserving Bronx train stations designed by Cass Gillbert, using information from Amtrak, misstated the status of the Morris Park station. It is currently used by a gun club; it is not vacant.
match_headline: In the Bronx, a Push to Save Cass Gilbert’s Train Stations

text: An article last Sunday about efforts to ban books from libraries and school curriculums misstated the year “Close Quarters” by Larry Heinemann was published. The novel was published in 1977, not 1974, which is when a chapter from the work in progress appeared in Penthouse.
match_headline: My Young Mind Was Disturbed by a Book. It Changed My Life.

text: Because of an editing error, a recipe on Feb. 4 for chocolate cream pie with an Oreo crust misstated the American equivalent of 720 milliliters of whole milk. It is 3 cups, not ¼ cup.

An article on Saturday about methane leak sites around the world misstated the rate of methane emissions from leaks that are categorized as ultra emitters. They emit more than 25 tons an hour, not more than 55 pounds an hour.
match_headline: Seen From Space: Huge Methane Leaks

text: An article on Sunday about President Biden’s opposition to sending U.S. troops into Ukraine misspelled the given name of a former National Security Council director for Russia in the Obama White House. He is Jeffrey Edmonds, not Jeffery Edmonds. The article also misstated the title of a book about the war between Russia and Georgia in 2008. It is “A Little War That Shook the World,” not “The Little War That Shook the World.”
ref_headline: A Little War That Shook the World,
match_headline: All Options Are Not on the Table as Biden Moves Troops Closer to Ukraine

text: An article on Monday about the possibility of a catastrophic tsunami striking the Pacific Northwest misstated the year in which an earthquake in Alaska led to tsunami deaths in California. It was in 1964, not 1962.
match_headline: The Tsunami Could Kill Thousands. Can They Build an Escape?

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misidentified the performer who voices the mayor of Fairview on the Comedy Central series “Fairview.” It is Marina Cockenberg, not Blair Socci. Socci voices an outspoken mother.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: The Super Bowl and an Oscar Micheaux Documentary

text: An article on Feb. 1 about practicing healthy eating habits inappropriately referenced research in which fasting shoppers bought higher-calorie, less healthful foods. The studies, from 2012 and 2013, have since been retracted.
match_headline: Savor, Celebrate and Pay Attention: 8 Lessons From the Eat Well Challenge

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about protests by truckers in Canada against coronavirus restrictions incorrectly implied that the protest shown was in Ottawa, Canada’s capital. The image showed a protest in Toronto, not Ottawa.
match_headline: ‘This Is Not My City’: Protesters Turn a Quiet Capital Upside Down

text: An article on Saturday about efforts to rescue a 5-year-old boy who was trapped in a well in Morocco for days misstated the location of the village of Ighrane. It is about 60 miles from the city of Chefchaouen, not about 125 miles.
match_headline: Rescuers in Morocco Race to Save 5-Year-Old Stuck in Well for Days

text: An article on Tuesday about the resignation of Dr. Eric S. Lander, President Biden’s top science adviser, referred incorrectly to an editorial published in Scientific American urging Mr. Biden to name someone else to the post. It was written by the grass-roots organization 500 Women Scientists, not by 500 female scientists.
match_headline: Biden’s Top Science Adviser Resigns After Acknowledging Demeaning Behavior

text: An obituary on Feb. 1 about Maj. Gen. John K. Singlaub, who waged clandestine warfare for the United States Army and the C.I.A., referred incorrectly to the Office of Strategic Services, the C.I.A.’s World War II forerunner. It was a civilian agency; it was not part of the Army.
match_headline: John K. Singlaub, 100, General Who Clashed With Jimmy Carter, Dies

text: An article on Wednesday about the dropping of mask mandates by Democratic governors misattributed a quotation about being photographed without a mask at an N.F.L. playoff game.
