It was Eric Garcetti, the mayor of Los Angeles, who said he held his breath during a photo, not Gov. Gavin Newsom of California.
match_headline: Dropping Indoor Mask Mandate, New York Joins Blue States Easing Covid Rules

text: An article on Saturday about a Pentagon report that said a lone Islamic State suicide bomber carried out the Aug. 26 attack at Kabul’s international airport misstated the surname of a senior officer who said the bombing had not been preventable. He is Brig. Gen. Lance Curtis, not Lance Clark.
match_headline: Lone ISIS Bomber Carried Out Attack at Kabul Airport, Pentagon Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about diplomacy over the crisis in Ukraine misidentified the city where President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine met with Emmanuel Macron, France’s president. They met in Kyiv, not Berlin.
match_headline: Europe Calls for Peace, but Not at Any Price

text: An article on Monday about the figure skater Kamila Valieva of Russia misattributed a distinction to Vincent Zhou. He is the only skater since March 2018 to win a gold medal over Nathan Chen, not beat him. (When Zhou won Skate America in 2021, the second-place finisher Shoma Uno also beat Chen, who was third.)
match_headline: Led by a 15-year-old, Russia’s team glides past the U.S. in figure skating.

text: An article last Thursday about a secondhand clothing boom in Malaysia, misstated the age of Amirul Ruslan, a fan of Malaysia’s thrift stores. He is 31, not 21.
match_headline: How Malaysia Got in on the Secondhand Clothing Boom

text: An article on Jan. 27 about Hugo Boss’s reinvention as a brand described incorrectly a look worn by Gigi Hadid in a Hugo Boss fashion show. She wore gym shorts, not sweatpants. The article also misstated the stock performance of Hugo Boss. It began to decline in 2018 and then rose again in November 2020; it has not consistently fallen since 2018. And the article described incorrectly Daniel Grieder’s employment history at Tommy Hilfiger. He was at the company for 23 years, seven of them as its chief executive; he was not the chief executive for 23 years.
match_headline: Can Hugo Boss Actually Be Cool?

text: An obituary on Saturday about Arnie Kantrowitz, an early champion of gay rights, misstated the year the first Christopher Street Gay Liberation Day Parade was held. It was 1970, not 1969.
match_headline: Arnie Kantrowitz, Pioneer of Gay Liberation, Dies at 81

text: An article on Thursday about a clash in Syria at a detention camp for family members of Islamic State fighters described incorrectly the nature of a shooting there. It was the first time that guards had fatally shot a child at the camp, according to aid workers, not the first time that guards had fired on children there.
match_headline: Violence Erupts at Syrian Camp for ISIS Families, Leaving a Child Dead

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about strategies used at New York City hospitals to manage this winter’s Omicron wave misstated that day that saw the peak death toll in New York during the surge. It was Jan. 11, not Jan. 1.
match_headline: How New York City’s Hospitals Withstood the Omicron Surge

text: An article on Thursday about Uber’s earnings report misstated the number of users Lyft had in the fourth quarter. It had 18.7 million users, not 18,728.
match_headline: Uber says its business is bouncing back from a pandemic-induced slump.

text: An article on Thursday about the new director of the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art misstated the middle initial of one of the museum’s board members. She is Pamela J. Joyner, not Pamela L. Joyner.
match_headline: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art Names New Director

text: Because of a production error, an article on Friday about President Biden’s prediction that he would have Republican support for his Supreme Court nominee included columns of type that were out of order.
match_headline: Biden Predicts His Supreme Court Nominee Will Get Republican Support

text: An obituary on Friday about the virologist Luc Montagnier, who shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the virus that causes AIDS, misstated the surname of the Nobel committee member who introduced the winners of that award at a ceremony in Sweden that year. He is Prof. Björn Vennström, not Bennström.
match_headline: Luc Montagnier, Nobel-Winning Co-Discoverer of H.I.V., Dies at 89

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Beatriz Rivera and Edgar Alonzo misspelled the surname of the owner of Acme Bar & Company. She is Jennifer Seidman, not Sied­man.
match_headline: On Paper, They Were All Wrong. But in Time, Just Right.

text: An article last Sunday about home buyer’s remorse in the pandemic misidentified the year in which Stephanie DiSantis noticed a price reduction on the Seattle house she later purchased. It was in October 2020, not 2021.
match_headline: They Rushed to Buy in the Pandemic. Here’s What They Would Change.

text: An article on Sunday about a lawsuit in which a Pennsylvania police department is being accused of misconduct in a murder case misstated, in several instances, the surname of one of the men accusing the police in Allegheny County, Pa., of misconduct. He is Cheron Shelton, not Selton.
match_headline: Pennsylvania Police Are Sued After Murder Cases Collapse

text: An article on Tuesday about Jamie Anderson’s failure to advance to the women’s big air snowboarding final in the Winter Olympics misidentified the event in which the freestyle skier Marin Hamill was injured. It was the freeski slopestyle qualifying event, not the snowboard big air qualifying event.
match_headline: U.S. snowboarder Jamie Anderson fails to qualify for the big air final.

text: An article on Sunday about the Olympic snowboarders Lindsey Jacobellis and Nick Baumgartner erroneously attributed a distinction to Jacobellis. She is the oldest American woman to win a gold medal at the Winter Olympics, not the Olympics overall.
match_headline: Golden years: Jacobellis, 36, and Baumgartner, 40, win in team snowboard cross.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about how exercise may enhance the effects of a Covid or flu vaccine misstated the substance in the blood that can prompt the creation of immune cells. It is interferon alpha, not interferon alfa, a drug form of the substance.
match_headline: Exercise May Enhance the Effects of a Covid or Flu Shot

text: An article on Wednesday about challenges faced by U.S. intelligence agencies in deciphering the moves of President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia described incorrectly John Sipher’s role with the C.I.A. in Moscow. He served there as a C.I.A. officer, not as the station chief.
match_headline: U.S. Intelligence Agencies Face Crucial Test in Deciphering Putin’s Motives

text: An article on Tuesday about Zimbabwe’s prosecution of a freelancer for The New York Times misstated the surname of an official with the Zimbabwe Media Commission who testified in the trial. He is Academy Chinamhora, not Chimamora.
match_headline: Zimbabwe Abruptly Closes Prosecution of Reporter for New York Times

text: An article on Wednesday about a decision by Representative Kathleen Rice of New York misstated Representative Nancy Pelosi’s role in the House in 2016. She was running for minority leader, not speaker.
match_headline: Rice Announces Retirement, the 30th House Democrat to Plan an Exit

text: An article on Tuesday about the Swedish curler Niklas Edin misidentified the host city of the 1998 Winter Olympics. It was Nagano, Japan, not Vancouver, British Columbia.
match_headline: A Curler Chases Gold, While He Still Can

text: A review on Monday of the Super Bowl halftime show misstated the location of the event. It was in Inglewood, not South Los Angeles.
match_headline: Rap Takes Over Super Bowl Halftime, Balancing Celebration and Protest

text: An article on Wednesday about a settlement between the gun maker Remington and families of nine Sandy Hook school shooting victims misstated the year that a string of sniper shootings occurred in Washington, Maryland and Virginia. It was 2002, not 2001.
match_headline: Sandy Hook Families Settle With Gunmaker for $73 Million Over Massacre

text: An article on Monday about Indian cotton misstated the name of the organic cotton label certified by Textile Exchange. It is the Organic Content Standard, not the Organic Cotton Standard.
match_headline: That Organic Cotton T-Shirt May Not Be as Organic as You Think

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Thursday about Harriet S. Shapiro, the first female lawyer hired in the office of the U.S. Solicitor General, misstated Ms. Shapiro’s given name as Helen.
match_headline: Harriet S. Shapiro, Groundbreaker in Solicitor General’s Office, Dies at 93

text: An article on Monday about the history of lox misstated the clue for LOX in the Feb. 7 crossword. The clue is “bagels and ___,” not “Schmear topper.” The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: The Lox Story: From Scandinavia to New York

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a proposal by Mayor Eric Adams of New York to suspend the expansion of New York’s composting program misattributed a statement on a mayoral campaign platform that claimed that methane from organic waste was “destroying our environment and speeding climate change.” It was part of Mr. Adams’s platform, not Bill de Blasio’s.
ref_headline: destroying our environment and speeding climate change.
match_headline: New York Was Set to Expand Composting. Now It’s on the Chopping Block.

text: An article on Friday about John H. Durham, the Trump-era special counsel scrutinizing the investigation into Russia’s 2016 election interference, and his reaction to false characterizations of his recent filing by right-wing media outlets, misquoted a portion of the filing. It said a member of the defense team for a cybersecurity lawyer, Michael Sussmann, had worked for the White House “during relevant events that involved” the White House, not “during the relevant events that involved” the White House.
match_headline: Durham Distances Himself From Furor in Right-Wing Media Over Filing

text: An article on Friday about the possible need for a fourth coronavirus shot referred imprecisely to the status of Israel’s booster shot program. The nation began offering fourth shots to a test group of medical workers in late December and has progressively broadened eligibility; it has not limited the shots to only medical workers.
match_headline: Will Adults Need a Fourth Dose of Covid Vaccine? It’s Too Soon to Know.

text: An article on Page 2 this weekend about the novelist Marlon James misstates the title of his new book. It is “Moon Witch, Spider King,” not “Moon Witch, Spider Kingdom.”
match_headline: How Marlon James, Novelist, Spends His Sundays

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about the actor Sam Waterston misspells the given name of one of his daughters. It is Elisabeth, not Elizabeth. It also misstates the availability of “Law & Order” reruns; old episodes of the show no longer air on TNT.
match_headline: Sam Waterston Is Still the Face of ‘Law & Order’

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about the surge in the number of people quitting their jobs misstates Google’s position regarding the formation of a union by its engineers. Google does not recognize the union as formal or official. The article also misstates the name of a publication. It is Insider, not Business Insider (its former name). Also, a reference to the movie “Office Space” misidentifies a piece of office equipment being destroyed in a scene. It is a printer, not a computer.
match_headline: The Age of Anti-Ambition

text: An article on Page 48 this weekend about parents working at home misstates the age of a child pictured. Inez just turned 1, not 2.
match_headline: Babies Have Entered the Chat

text: An article on Page 116 about Black psychedelia refers to the funk singer and songwriter Betty Davis. She died a few weeks after the article went to press.
match_headline: Jurors to Weigh Fate of Officers Who Restrained George Floyd as He Died

text: An article on Page 138 about painted chapels in Michoacán, Mexico, misidentifies a church in Tupátaro. It is the church of Santiago Apóstol, not Santo Santiago. The error is repeated in several photo captions.
match_headline: In Mexico, Ornately Painted Churches Enshrine Years of Indigenous Resilience

text: A column on Thursday about gerryman­dering misstated the reason New York is losing a seat in the House of Representa­tives. The state grew in population from 2010 to 2020 but less than some other states did; its population did not decline.
match_headline: Who’s to Blame for Sneaky Partisan Line-Drawing?

text: An article last Sunday on inflation misstated the change in the monthly Consumer Price Index inflation rate for October. It rose 0.9 percent, not 0.09 percent.
match_headline: Inflation May Have Already Peaked. The Fed Needs to Step Gingerly.

text: An article last Sunday about segmented sleep misstated the title of a book by A. Roger Ekirch. It is “At Day’s Close: Night in Times Past,” not “The Great Sleep Transformation,” which is a collection of essays in French based on Professor Ekirch’s research. The article also misstated the point in history when segmented sleep was first documented in literary writing. It has been traced to ancient civilization (via the writings of Homer and others), not the late Middle Ages.
ref_headline: At Day’s Close: Night in Times Past,
match_headline: Meet Me at 3 A.M. for a Cup of Coffee.

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Jafreen Uddin and Shakil Rabbi misstated the attendance of the groom’s parents. His mother attended in person, not via video; his father is deceased.
match_headline: A Muslim Dating App Powered Their Connection

text: An article on Jan. 23 about a proposal to defend the southern U.S. border with drones referred imprecisely to a patent granted to Blake Resnick. He provisionally applied for a patent in 2017 and was awarded one in 2020.
match_headline: Trump’s Dream of a Border Wall, Twisted Into a Sci-Fi Nightmare

text: An article on Page 116 about Black psychedelia refers to the funk singer and songwriter Betty Davis. She died a few weeks after the article went to press.
match_headline: Remembering Betty Davis, a Futuristic Funk Force

text: An article on Feb. 10 about evolving Eng­lish language rules mischaracterized the guidance in Strunk and White’s “The El­ements of Style” on whether to use sub­ject or object pronouns after linking verbs. It advises that writers use good judgment; it does not insist on using object pronouns after all linking verbs.
match_headline: English Is a Living Language — Period

text: An obituary on Saturday about the author Valerie Boyd misstated the subject of the program she instituted at the University of Georgia. It was narrative nonfiction, not creative nonfiction. The obituary also misspelled the middle name of a writer Ms. Boyd brought to the university. She is Melissa Fay Greene, not Faye. In addition, the obituary contained outdated information about Ms. Boyd’s brother Michael. While he did survive her, he died on Friday, six days after she did.
match_headline: Valerie Boyd, Biographer of Zora Neale Hurston, Is Dead at 58

text: An article on Tuesday about President Biden’s efforts to prevent armed conflict in Ukraine misstated the location where the President’s Daily Brief is normally held. It is in the Oval Office, not the Situation Room.
match_headline: Wooing Allies, Publicizing Putin’s Plans: Inside Biden’s Race to Prevent War

text: An article on Friday about the Trump administration’s “public charge” immigration policy, relying on inaccurate information from the Department of Homeland Security, misstated the reason it was creating a regulation that could make it harder for future presidential administrations to restore the policy. The department started drafting the rule after a court vacated the Trump administration regulation, not because it was under a court order to create the rule.
match_headline: Biden Rule Could Help Prevent Revival of Key Trump Immigration Policy

text: A graphic with an article on Sunday about who is behind QAnon misstated the year that a tweet by Paul Furber was posted. The tweet included in the article was from 2019, not 2018.
match_headline: Who Is Behind QAnon? Linguistic Detectives Find Fingerprints

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about the impact of congressional gerrymandering on Nashville, Tenn., misidentified the legislator shown in the image. He is Jeff Yarbro, the State Senate’s Democratic leader, not Representative Jim Cooper.
match_headline: In Nashville, a Gerrymander Goes Beyond Politics to the City’s Core

text: An article on Thursday about the ice makers of Olympic curling described incorrectly the ice conditions that technicians have to provide at the Olympics. A stone should be able to travel the length of the sheet in roughly 25 seconds, with four to five feet of curl, not move four to five feet in roughly 25 seconds.
match_headline: Beijing Got All Ready for Olympic Curling. But About the Ice …

text: An article on Monday about seven Winter Olympians to watch in 2026 misstated how old Elvira Oeberg would be at the time of the 2030 Winter Games. She will be 30, not 32.
match_headline: Coming Attractions: Seven Winter Olympians to Watch in 2026

text: An article on Saturday about P.J. O’Rourke misstated the date of the critic Terry Teachout’s death. He died on Jan. 13, not in February.
match_headline: P.J. O’Rourke Wrote With High, Cranky Style in a Shrinking Tradition

text: An obituary on Friday about the former Air Force pilot Gail Halvorsen misstated the locations of Rigby, where his parents had a small farm, and Garland, where they later farmed sugar beets. Rigby is in Idaho, not Utah, and Garland is in Utah, not Idaho.
match_headline: Gail Halvorsen, ‘Candy Bomber’ in Berlin Airlift, Dies at 101

text: An obituary on Feb. 4 about Sister Janet Mead, the nun whose recording of “The Lord’s Prayer” was a pop hit in the 1970s, misstated her status with the Sisters of Mercy when she made that record. She was no longer a novice.
match_headline: Janet Mead, Nun Whose Pop-Rock Hymn Reached the Top of the Charts, Dies

text: A picture caption with an article on Feb. 17 about supply chain complications in the home-building industry misstated the material used to board up a garage. It’s oriented strand board, not plywood.
match_headline: 4 Bed, 3 Bath, No Garage Door: The Unlikely Woes Holding Up Home Building

text: An article on Feb. 17 about a men’s basketball game between Providence and Villanova misstated the Providence men’s basketball team’s performance history. It has never won a Big East regular-season title; it is not the case that it has never won a conference title. (It won the Big East tournament in 1994 and 2014.)
match_headline: Against Villanova, Providence Gets a Taste of the Big Games Ahead

text: An article on Wednesday about the dance piece “An Untitled Love” by the dancer and choreographer Kyle Abraham misstated the given name of the production’s lighting designer. He is Dan Scully, not Joe. It also misspelled the name of the Royal Ballet’s smaller theater. It is the Linbury Studio Theater, not the Lindbury.
match_headline: ‘A Black Love Sitcom Dance’: Kyle Abraham’s D’Angelo Moves

text: A picture caption on Feb. 15 with an obituary about the filmmaker Ivan Reitman, using information from Getty Images, misstated where a photograph of him was taken. It was on the set of “Delta House,” the television spinoff of the movie “National Lampoon’s Animal House,” which he produced (he was also an executive producer of “Delta House”); it was not on the set of the movie.
match_headline: Ivan Reitman, Director of ‘Ghostbusters,’ Is Dead at 75

text: An article on Sunday about the importance of the crisis in Ukraine referred imprecisely to the outcome of President Donald J. Trump’s first impeachment trial. While the House voted to impeach him, the Senate acquitted him of all charges.
match_headline: The Ukraine Crisis: What to Know About Why Russia Attacked

text: An article on Thursday about a delay in the bribing and money-laundering trial of a former Goldman Sachs executive misstated the amount of the bonds Goldman Sachs was trying to underwrite for a Malaysian fund. It was $6.5 billion, not million.
match_headline: 1MDB Trial Will Take a Break So the Defense Can Study New Documents

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about the rapper Tariq Trotter misstates his age and year of birth. He is 48, not 50, and he was born in 1973, not 1971.
match_headline: Is There Such a Thing as Black Thought?

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about Clarence and Virginia Thomas misstates her birthday. She will be 65 on April 25; she did not turn 65 on Feb. 23. The article also refers imprecisely to the Council for National Policy’s “action steps” memo. The document was shared by Brent Allpress with the Center for Media and Democracy, which posted it in November 2020; it is not the case that its existence had never been reported.
match_headline: The Long Crusade of Clarence and Ginni Thomas

text: An article on Monday about the impact that congressional redistricting is having on political races across the United States misidentified the job formerly held by Phill Cady, a Texas resident. He was an airline mechanic, not a pilot.
match_headline: ‘Blood Red’: How Lopsided New District Lines Are Deepening America’s Divide

text: An article on Monday about a case before the Supreme Court that challenges the extent of the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority to regulate power plant emissions misspelled the surname of the West Virginia attorney general. He is Patrick Morrisey, not Morrissey.
match_headline: Supreme Court Will Hear Biggest Climate Change Case in a Decade

text: An article on Saturday about an interview between members of the House committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol and Kimberly Guilfoyle, the fiancée of former President Donald J. Trump’s eldest son, misstated which committee members participated in the interview. Representative Liz Cheney, Republican of Wyoming, was not on the call.
match_headline: Jan. 6 Panel Threatens to Force Guilfoyle to Testify After She Ends Interview

text: A review on Monday of the play “sandblasted” misstated in one instance the name of the character whose arm falls off. It is Odessa, not Angela.
match_headline: Review: In ‘sandblasted,’ Seizing the Day. Also the Nose.

text: An article Sunday about live performances to see in New York this spring described incorrectly two characters in Dominique Morisseau’s upcoming play “Confederates.” Both women are Black, not just one.
match_headline: What to See and Experience Live in New York This Spring

text: An article on Sunday about Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s role in the vaccine resistance movement described incorrectly the length of time a member of the Kennedy family has served in Congress. This is not the first time without a Kennedy in Congress since Edward M. Kennedy was elected in 1962; there was one such stretch last decade.
match_headline: A Kennedy’s Crusade Against Covid Vaccines Anguishes Family and Friends

text: An article on Sunday about right-wing support for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia rendered the name of a German newspaper incorrectly. It is Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung, not Neuer Osnabrücker Zeitung.
match_headline: Putin’s Aggression Leaves His Right-Wing Fan Club Squirming

text: An article on Thursday about the trial of an officer involved in the police raid that killed Breonna Taylor misspelled the surname of Brett Hankison’s lawyer. He is Stew Mathews, not Stew Matthews.
match_headline: Officer Accused of Recklessly Firing in Breonna Taylor Raid Goes on Trial

text: An article on Sunday about the acceptance of Ukrainian refugees in many European countries misstated the day that Linda Thomas-Greenfield, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said that a Russian assault on Ukraine could uproot as many as five million people. It was Wednesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: For Ukraine’s Refugees, Europe Opens Doors That Were Shut to Others

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the return of Major League Soccer misidentified the league in which the soccer club Swansea City plays. It has competed since 2018 in the English Championship, not the Premier League.
match_headline: M.L.S. Returns With New Team, New Faces and a New York Champion

text: An article on Feb. 16 about questions surrounding the authenticity of some artworks attributed to Jean-Michel Basquiat at an Orlando Museum of Art exhibition described incorrectly Jordana Moore Sagghese’s work. While she attributed some of the 25 artworks to Basquiat, she said she was unable to attribute nine of the paintings to him.
match_headline: In Orlando, 25 Mysterious Basquiats Come Under the Magnifying Glass

text: An article on Tuesday about Russian artists’ opposition to the war in Ukraine misstated the date on which Ragnar Kjartansson’s performance piece “Santa Barbara” was scheduled to end in Moscow. It was March 13, not March 22.
match_headline: Russian Artists Speak Out Against War, but Fear Reprisals

text: An article on Tuesday about the Belgian singer-songwriter Stromae misstated the name of Stromae’s brother. He is now known as Luc Van Haver, not Luc Junior Tam.
match_headline: Stromae’s Music Delves Into Dark Topics. His Return Is Right on Time.

text: An article on Tuesday about a new paper suggesting the Tyrannosaurus rex should be split into three different species misstated the year in which the book “Predatory Dinosaurs of the World” was published. It was 1988, not 1998.
match_headline: They Want to Break T. Rex Into 3 Species. Other Paleontologists Aren’t Pleased.

text: An article last Wednesday about people who feed their pets human-style diets misquoted Dr. Leah Reilly, a veterinarian in Clinton Hill, Brooklyn, in her comparison of fresh and dry pet food. Dr. Reilly referred to the dry food as “extruded kibble,” not “excreted kibble.”
match_headline: The Diet Worked For Them. Now Their Pets Are on It.

text: An article on Wednesday about President Biden’s State of the Union address misstated the colors on the Ukrainian flag. They are blue and yellow, not blue and white.
match_headline: Biden says Putin ‘badly miscalculated’ in invading Ukraine.

text: An article on Feb. 21 about the Munich Security Conference misstated a quotation by the British prime minister Neville Chamberlain. He declared “peace for our time” in 1938, not “peace in our time.”
match_headline: A Subdued Munich Conference Hears a Troubling Word: Appeasement

text: An article on Wednesday about Gov. Greg Abbott’s victory in the Texas primaries misstated the public office previously held by David Perdue in Georgia. He was a U.S. senator, not the state’s governor.
match_headline: Abbott and O’Rourke win their Texas primaries.

text: A picture with an article on Wednesday about the tennis star Serena Williams and the $111 million-fund that her venture capital firm has raised was published in error. The image showed her sister, Venus Williams.
match_headline: Serena Williams raises $111 million for new venture fund.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the former New York Times photo editor Michele McNally erroneously attributed a distinction to her. She was not the first photo editor at The Times to be promoted to the newsroom’s top management as an assistant managing editor; the first was Carolyn Lee, in 1990.
match_headline: Michele McNally, Who Elevated Times Photography, Dies at 66

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about John Landy, the Australian who became the second man to run the mile in under four minutes, misstated the location of a statue commemorating the so-called Mile of the Century race between Landy and Roger Bannister, the first to run the mile in under four minutes, held at Empire Stadium in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1954. The statue stands in Hastings Park in Vancouver, near the former site of the stadium — not “outside the stadium,” which was torn down in the early 1990s.
match_headline: John Landy Dies at 91; Dueled Roger Bannister in ‘Mile of the Century’

text: An obituary on Feb. 17 about Walter Dellinger, one of the top legal figures in the Clinton administration, misstated his role in the Supreme Court case District of Columbia v. Heller in 2008, when he was in private practice. He argued for the government, not against it.
match_headline: Walter Dellinger, 80, Scholar and Top Legal Aide Under Clinton, Dies

text: An article on Thursday about Eastern Europe’s reaction to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine misspelled the first name of Lithuania’s foreign minister. He is Gabrielius Landsbergis, not Gabrielus.
match_headline: Putin’s War to Bring Ukraine to Heel Unites Eastern Europe in Alarm

text: An article on Thursday about coronavirus in New York City misstated the day Mayor Eric Adams announced that he was preparing to eliminate some virus-related mandates. He made the announcement on Sunday, not Monday.
match_headline: New York City’s Next Chapter

text: An article on Wednesday about unifying moral outrage over Russia’s war in Ukraine referred incorrectly to a TikTok video that gave instructions on how to drive abandoned Russian military vehicles. The video was posted by a Russian woman, not by a Ukrainian woman.
match_headline: A Surge of Unifying Moral Outrage Over Russia’s War

text: An article on Thursday about mask mandates in New York public schools, relying on outdated information from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website, misstated the centers’ latest guidance for school masking. As of last week, school masking is recommended in communities experiencing high levels of the virus; it is no longer the case that it is recommended in all school settings.
match_headline: As New York Students Shed Masks, Elation Mixes With Trepidation

text: An article on Thursday about canceled Major League Baseball games misstated the number of games that were canceled by Commissioner Rob Manfred. At least 75 games have been canceled, not 150.
match_headline: M.L.B. Canceled Games. What Happens Now?

text: An article on Wednesday about basketball player Wilt Chamberlain erroneously attributed a distinction to Al Attles. In the 1974-75 season, he coached the Warriors to their first N.B.A. title since their move to California, not to their first title. (While in Philadelphia, the Warriors won in 1955-56; they also won in 1946-47, when the N.B.A. was known as the Basketball Association of America.)
match_headline: Wilt Chamberlain’s 100-Point Game Changed the N.B.A.

text: An article on Thursday about the conductor Herbert Blomstedt misstated where he was born. It was Massachusetts, not Illinois.
match_headline: A Conductor Brings Nearly a Century of Experience to Beethoven

text: An article on Page 1 this weekend about the Brooklyn enclave Red Hook misspells the surname of the real estate mogul for whom a pool in Red Hook was named. He was Sol Goldman, not Goodman.
match_headline: Everybody Loves Red Hook. Or So They Say.

text: An article on Friday about the New York-based artist Josh Kline misstated his age. He is 42, not 43. The review also misstated the number of Kline’s artworks at the 2019 Whitney Biennial. There were eight, not 12.
match_headline: Josh Kline: Living in the Ruined World

text: An article on Feb. 27 about the Epstein-Barr virus and multiple sclerosis described imprecisely how the virus spreads. It replicates itself; it does not only produce proteins which its host sheds.
match_headline: The Strange Connection Between Mono and M.S.

text: An article on Monday about arms being sent to Ukraine from the United States and Europe misidentified the city that was overrun by Russian tanks in 1956. It was Budapest, not Prague.
match_headline: Arming Ukraine: 17,000 Anti-Tank Weapons in 6 Days and a Clandestine Cybercorps

text: A subheading with an article on Sunday about a meeting between Prime Minister Naftali Bennett of Israel and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia referred imprecisely to Tel Aviv, implying that it was the seat of Israel’s government. Israel’s government is in Jerusalem, not Tel Aviv.
match_headline: Israeli prime minister visits Moscow for talks with Putin on Ukraine.

text: An article on Sunday about U.S. veterans joining the fight in Ukraine misstated the last name of an Iraq war veteran. He is Daniel Gade, not Daniel Gale.
match_headline: ‘I Just Can’t Stand By’: American Veterans Join the Fight in Ukraine

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misstated when NBC’s “The Thing About Pam” and HBO’s “Undercurrent: The Disappearance of Kim Wall” will air. They are both set to debut on Tuesday, not Monday.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘The Thing About Pam’ and the Critics Choice Awards

text: An obituary on Saturday about Monique Hanotte, who smuggled Allied airmen out of Belgium during World War II, using information from the government of Nivelles, Belgium, misstated when she died. It was Feb. 20, not Feb. 19.
match_headline: Monique Hanotte, Savior of Allied Airmen, Dies at 101

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about internet blockages in Russia misspelled the surname of an Oxford University researcher. He is Aliaksandr Herasimenka, not Herasmenka.
match_headline: Russia, Blocked From the Global Internet, Plunges Into Digital Isolation

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about horror television shows misstated which crew members of the TV series “From” had also worked on “Lost.” John Griffin, the creator of “From,” is not among them.
match_headline: A Hot Time in the Haunted House

text: An obituary on Monday about the civil rights lawyer Dennis Cunningham misidentified the lawyer he called for advice after two leaders of the Black Panther Party in Illinois were killed in a police raid in 1969. He is Gerald B. Lefcourt, not Gerald L. Shargel.
match_headline: Dennis Cunningham, Civil Rights Lawyer for Varied Causes, Dies at 86

text: An article on Monday about the upcoming trial of Lawrence V. Ray, who is accused of abusing students at Sarah Lawrence College, misidentified the dormitory where he lived on campus. It was Slonim Woods, not Slonim House.
match_headline: Accused Leader in Sarah Lawrence Cult Case Is Set to Stand Trial

text: An article on Wednesday about what students in New York think about the end of the school mask mandate misspelled the given name of a high school student. He is Otzar Jaffe, not Oscar.
match_headline: What Young New Yorkers Think About the End of the School Mask Mandate

text: An article on Tuesday about the end of school mask mandates in New York described incorrectly a policy regarding public transportation in New York City. While riders are required to wear masks, they are not required to show proof of vaccination against the coronavirus.
match_headline: New York’s Students Shed Their Masks, Warily, in Pandemic Milestone

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the former mayor of Atlanta and civil rights activist Andrew Young, using information from The Associated Press, misidentified a person standing with Mr. Young and the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. It was the Rev. Hosea Williams, not Ralph D. Abernathy.
match_headline: A Lion of the Civil Rights Era Is Still Preaching Optimism

text: An article on Thursday about Awol Erizku’s exhibition at Gagosian, using information from the artist, described incorrectly his representation. He is still represented by Ben Brown, abroad, but currently has no representation in the United States.
match_headline: Beyond Beyoncé Fame, Awol Erizku Expands What Black Art Can Be

text: A column on Thursday about former Gov. Andrew Cuomo of New York misstated Grover Cleveland’s history in the state. He was a mayor of Buffalo, not New York’s first governor born and raised in Buffalo.
match_headline: Cuomo? Oh, No!

text: An obituary on March 3 about the art conservator Barry Bauman misstated who contacted him in 2011 about cleaning a portrait that was wrongly believed to be of Mary Todd Lincoln. It was the curator of the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum — not descendants of Abraham Lincoln. (Descendants of Lincoln had once owned the painting, but they later donated it to the museum. The last descendant died in 1985.)
match_headline: Barry Bauman, Restoration Artist and Detective, Dies at 73

text: An obituary on Thursday about Evgeny Maslin, a Russian general who worked with the United States to secure his country’s nuclear arsenal, misstated part of the name of a program sponsored by Senators Sam Nunn and Richard Lugar. It was the Cooperative Threat Reduction Program, not the Comprehensive Threat Reduction Program. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misidentified the president under whom Dick Cheney served as defense secretary. He was George H.W. Bush, not George W. Bush.
match_headline: Evgeny Maslin, Russian General Who Secured Nuclear Arsenal, Dies at 84

text: An article on Friday about a collective bargaining agreement between Major League Baseball’s club owners and its players’ union misstated the amount that the M.L.B.’s luxury tax threshold will increase to in 2026. It is $244 million, not $242 million.
match_headline: Play Ball! Lockout Ends as M.L.B. and Union Strike a Deal

text: An article on Friday about the new leader of the Islamic State misstated the day that the group announced its new leader. It was Thursday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: ISIS Names a New Leader, but Says Little About Him

text: An article on Friday about residents of Berkeley, Calif., leveraging state environmental laws to accuse the University of California, Berkeley, campus of congesting neighborhoods by admitting more students than the city can handle misstated the court-ordered enrollment cap for the university. It is 42,347 students, not 42,357.
match_headline: Berkeley vs. Berkeley Is a Fight Over the California Dream

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about the movie “The Godfather” and its similarities to the real life mafia misspells the name of the author of “The Five Families: The Rise, Decline, and Resurgence of America’s Most Powerful Mafia Empires.” He is Selwyn Raab, not Rabb. The article also describes incorrectly a recording of two mobsters in 2005. The recordings were made in person, not over the telephone.
match_headline: With ‘The Godfather,’ Art Imitated Mafia Life. And Vice Versa.

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 16 this weekend about seven quotes from “The Godfather” misidentifies the actor sitting with Richard Castellano in a car in the film. He is John Martino, not Tom Rosqui.
match_headline: ‘The Godfather’ Explained in Seven Quotes

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about the play “King James” refers incorrectly to Kenny Leon’s role with the True Colors Theater Company, which he co-founded. He is now the company’s artistic director emeritus, not its artistic director.
match_headline: LeBron Fandom, and the Making of a Friendship in ‘King James’

text: An article on March 6 about a patient who had an unusual case of irritable-bowel syndrome referred incorrectly to the location of Mexico. It is part of North America, not Central America.
match_headline: Her I.B.S. Was Misery. But What If She Actually Had Something Else?

text: An article on March 6 about Representative Rashida Tlaib misstated the timing of her parents’ arrival in Detroit. They arrived there before 1976, not in 1976, the year Tlaib was born.
match_headline: What Rashida Tlaib Represents

text: An article last Sunday about an increase in muscle dysmorphia among some teenage boys as a result of social media images referred imprecisely to orthorexia. The condition may include, among other behaviors, counting calories; that is not the only behavior associ­ated with it.
match_headline: What Is ‘Bigorexia’?

text: A review on Feb. 13 about Harley Rustad’s “Lost in the Valley of Death” misidentified the city where the subject of the book, the adventurer and trekker Jus­tin Alexander Shetler, had once led a punk band. It was San Francisco, not Seattle.
ref_headline: Lost in the Valley of Death
match_headline: Seeking Enlightenment, He Disappeared Into a Hiker’s Bermuda Triangle

text: An article on Sunday about Democrats urging President Biden to sharpen campaign messaging ahead of midterm elections misstated the cost of the American Rescue Plan. It is $1.9 trillion, not $1.9 billion.
match_headline: House Democrats Push Biden to Build a Better Midterm Message

text: An article on Monday about a growing number of Californians using solar power misstated the drop in the cost of solar over the last two decades. The price dropped to less than $4 a watt, from about $11.40 in 2000, not to less than 4 cents, from about 11.4 cents.
match_headline: Frustrated With Utilities, Some Californians Are Leaving the Grid

text: An article on Saturday about the cult of Saint Brigid in Ireland misstated Mary Condren’s position at Trinity College Dublin’s Center for Gender and Women’s Studies. She is a visiting research fellow, not the director.
match_headline: As Ireland’s Church Retreats, the Cult of a Female Saint Thrives

text: An article on Friday about a child custody battle in Dallas and its impact on an effort to roll back transgender protections in state houses across the country misspelled the given name of a candidate for the Texas House. He is Jeffrey Younger, not Jeffery.
match_headline: How Medical Care for Transgender Youth Became ‘Child Abuse’ in Texas

text: An article on Sunday about possible changes to the next U.S. census included a comment from Kenneth Prewitt, who oversaw the 2,000 census, in which he misidentified the person he urged to use more samples of data in the census. It was the former House Speaker J. Dennis Hastert, not the former House Speaker Thomas P. (Tip) O’Neill Jr.
match_headline: One More Census Takeaway: The End of an Era of Counting the Nation?

text: An obituary on March 8 about the philosopher Alice von Hildebrand misstated the educational status of the author and philosopher Ronda Chervin when she was inspired to convert to Catholicism after seeing Ms. von Hildebrand and her husband, Dietrich, on television. She was a graduate student at Johns Hopkins University, not an undergraduate.
match_headline: Alice von Hildebrand, Conservative Catholic Philosopher, Dies at 98

text: An article on Tuesday about the ways that China could benefit from the war in Ukraine misspelled the surname of the German chancellor. He is Olaf Scholz, not Sholz.
match_headline: China Sees at Least One Winner Emerging From Ukraine War: China

text: An article on Saturday about how a line of Russian tanks became a target for Ukrainians misspelled the surname of a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Defense Research Establishment. He is Tor Bukkvoll, not Bukkvol.
match_headline: How a Line of Russian Tanks Became an Inviting Target for Ukrainians

text: An article on Sunday about the Village to Village volunteer network referred incorrectly to a support village for older people in North Carolina. It is Fearrington Village, not Fearrington Cares. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Generation X Volunteers Want to Help You, and One Day Themselves, Age at Home

text: An article on Tuesday about brackets for the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament listed an impossible Final Four prediction. U.C.L.A. would play Texas Tech, not Wisconsin, and Villanova would play Wisconsin, not Texas Tech.
match_headline: Picking an N.C.A.A. Tournament Bracket? Read This First.

text: An article on Tuesday about historically Black universities’ struggle to compete in N.C.A.A tournaments described incorrectly one of Norfolk State’s opponents. Xavier, like Norfolk State’s other opponents, did not make the N.C.A.A. tournament; it was not the only one that did.
match_headline: When You’re in the N.C.A.A. Tournament, but Not Fully In

text: An article on Tuesday about a revival of the musical “The Life” directed by the actor Billy Porter described incorrectly Porter’s directing role in the Encores! production of “The Life.” It is his directorial debut with Encores!, not his directorial debut. The article also misstated Clint Ramos’s title. He is the producing creative director of Encores!, not its producing artistic director.
match_headline: Comedy Undercut ‘The Life.’ Billy Porter Looks for Its Humanity.

text: An article on Monday about how actress Rita Moreno made Oscar history omitted one of the filmmakers of “West Side Story.” Jerome Robbins was a director along with Robert Wise.
match_headline: Oscars Rewind: When Rita Moreno Made History and Thanked No One

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about Autherine Lucy Foster, the first Black student to attend the University of Alabama, misstated the location of her birthplace in Alabama. She was born in the community of Shiloh in the state’s southwest, not in the town of Shiloh in the state’s northeast corner. (There are several municipalities named Shiloh in Alabama.)
match_headline: Autherine Lucy Foster, First Black Student at U. of Alabama, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Saturday about the cultural historian Leo Marx misstated when he left the faculty of Amherst College for the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. It was 1977, not 1971.
match_headline: Leo Marx, 102, Dies; Studied Clash of Nature and Culture in America

text: An obituary on Monday about the documentary filmmaker Brent Renaud, using information from his family, misstated the day he was born in 1971. It was Oct. 2, not Oct. 13.
match_headline: Brent Renaud, Crusading Filmmaker, Is Killed at 50

text: An article on Monday about series of recent defamation lawsuits against right-wing news outlets misstated which court’s judge ruled that the Smartmatic case against Fox could go forward. It was a New York State judge, not a federal judge.
match_headline: First Amendment Scholars Want to See the Media Lose These Cases

text: A picture caption with an article on March 7 about strategies to prevent violence against Asian Americans misidentified a woman sitting next to Zhanxin Gao, whose wife died after an attack. She is his lawyer, Jennifer H. Wu, not his interpreter.
match_headline: Asian Americans Grapple With Tide of Attacks: ‘We Need Our Safety Back’

text: An article on Sunday about the declining number of bilingual street signs in Manhattan’s Chinatown misidentified who was first petitioned to create the bilingual signs. It was the New York City traffic commissioner, not the New York City Transit Authority. The article also misstated the name of the president of the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association. It is Li Libo, not Li Boli.
match_headline: Manhattan’s Chinese Street Signs Are Disappearing

text: An article last Thursday about Guinevere van Seenus and her career as a model and a photographer misspelled the surname of a photographer. She is Yelena Yemchuk, not Yemcheck

An obituary on Saturday about the transgender educator and activist Rusty Mae Moore omitted the names of two of the editors of the book “GenderQueer: Voices From Beyond the Sexual Binary,” which included an essay by her. It was edited by Joan Nestle, Clare Howell and Riki Anne Wilchins — not just by Joan Nestle.
ref_headline: GenderQueer: Voices From Beyond the Sexual Binary,
match_headline: Rusty Mae Moore, Transgender Educator and Activist, Dies at 80

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the lawyer Bernard W. Nussbaum contained outdated information about his daughter, Emily Nussbaum. She is a staff writer for The New Yorker; she is no longer the magazine’s television critic.
match_headline: Bernard W. Nussbaum, Clinton Counsel and Defender, Dies at 84

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the search for Ernest Shackleton’s ship Endurance, using information provided by the photo agency, misidentified the location shown. The cross atop a stone cairn in Grytviken on the island of South Georgia is a memorial to Shackleton. His grave is elsewhere in the settlement.
match_headline: 106 Years, 4 Weeks, 1 Wreck: How Shackleton’s Ship Was Found

text: An article on Thursday about Ukraine’s plea for stricter restrictions from the United States at Russian ports referred incompletely to the current value of Russian oil exports. The country’s producers were earning about $700 million a day from exports of both oil and gas before the invasion of Ukraine; they are not necessarily earning that much now.
match_headline: Citing a Chevron Tanker, Ukraine Seeks Tougher Restrictions at Russian Ports

text: An obituary on March 5 about the singer Joni James erroneously credited her with a distinction. She was not the first American to record at Abbey Road Studios in London.
match_headline: Joni James, 91, Heartfelt Chanteuse of the 1950s, Dies

text: An article on Friday about Russia’s $117 million interest payments on two U.S. bonds misstated the amount of foreign currency debt accumulated by corporations in Russia. JPMorgan estimates the amount at $100 billion, not $100 million.
match_headline: Russia appears to have avoided default as it makes a $117 million bond payment.

text: An article on Friday about the abstract painter Bridget Riley misidentified the collection from which a small work by Eugène Delacroix was chosen. It is from the Yale University Art Gallery, not the Yale Center for British Art.
match_headline: Bridget Riley, Through Her Own Eyes

text: An article on Friday about the poet and filmmaker Jonas Mekas misidentified one of the organizations that Mekas helped found. It was the Film-Makers’ Cooperative, not Film Forum.
match_headline: The Avant-Garde Filmmaker Who Tried to Tell the Truth

text: An article on Thursday about “The Nurse Antigone,” a dramatic reading of a translation of Sophocles’ “Antigone” presented on Zoom by Theater of War Productions misstated the employer of the nurse Charlaine Lasse. It is Anne Arundel Medical Center in Maryland, not Johns Hopkins Hospital.
match_headline: Confronting Grief, With Margaret Atwood, in ‘The Nurse Antigone’

text: An article on Page 5 this weekend about composer Heather Christian’s choral piece “Oratorio for Living Things” misstates Christian’s age. She is 40, not 41.
match_headline: Heather Christian’s Choral Work Is a Study of Time. Patience, Too.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 8 this weekend about the movie comedy “The Lost City” starring Sandra Bullock, Channing Tatum and Daniel Radcliffe misstates the film’s release date. It is scheduled to be in theaters on March 25, not this weekend.
match_headline: A ‘Lost City’ Group Chat With Sandra Bullock, Channing Tatum and Daniel Radcliffe

text: An article last Sunday about the Colombian pop star Maluma’s move into fashion misstated his age. He is 28, not 26. The article also misstated the name of his clothing collection. It is Royalty by Maluma, not Royalty.
match_headline: Maluma, Fashion Chameleon

text: An article on Monday about Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson’s academic career at Harvard misstated Barack Obama’s job when Judge Jackson met him in 1996. He was a lawyer, not a community organizer.
match_headline: At Harvard, a Confederate Flag Spurred Ketanji Brown Jackson to Act

text: An article on Friday about an investigation of Mark Meadows’s absentee ballot in 2020 misidentified which area of North Carolina Mr. Meadows represented in Congress. He served a district in the western part of the state, not eastern.
match_headline: Mark Meadows’s 2020 Vote Is Under Investigation in North Carolina

text: An article on Friday about the Spanish pop singer Rosalía misstated the nationalities of two pop stars. The Weeknd is from Canada and James Blake is from England. They are not Americans.
match_headline: Rosalía Reserves the Right to Transform

text: An obituary on Friday about the hockey player Jean Potvin misspelled the name of the city in Florida where he died. It is Weston, not Westin.
match_headline: Jean Potvin, Part of the 1980s Islanders’ N.H.L. Dynasty, Dies at 72

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on March 7 about the production designer Tony Walton misstated the location in England of Radley College, which he attended. It is in Oxfordshire, not “near Oxfordshire.” The obituary also referred imprecisely to two of Mr. Walton’s credits. The productions of “Guys and Dolls” and “Anything Goes” on which he worked were revivals, not the original productions.
match_headline: Tony Walton, Award-Winning Stage and Screen Designer, Dies at 87

text: An article on Saturday about Russian war tactics before its invasion of Ukraine mischaracterized an essay by Alexei Arbatov, a former Russian lawmaker. Mr. Arbatov was describing views held by the Russian leadership, not by himself.
match_headline: Russia’s Brutality in Ukraine Has Roots in Earlier Conflicts

text: An article on Sunday about demand for a psychedelic toad toxin misidentified the secretions of the Sonoran desert toad. They are a poison, not a venom.
match_headline: Demand for This Toad’s Psychedelic Toxin Is Booming. Some Warn That’s Bad for the Toad.

text: A review last Wednesday of the Manhattan restaurant Commerce Inn misstated the location of the Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village. It is in New Gloucester, Maine, not Gloucester.
match_headline: Going Back to the Time of the Shakers at Commerce Inn

text: An article on March 17 about the risk of nuclear war misquoted António Guterres, the U.N. secretary general, who commented on the escalation of Russia’s attack on Ukraine. Mr. Guterres said the prospect of “nuclear conflict” was within the realm of possibility, not “nuclear war.”
match_headline: As Russia Digs In, What’s the Risk of Nuclear War? ‘It’s Not Zero.’

text: An article on Tuesday about Gov. Eric Holcomb of Indiana, who vetoed legislation that would have blocked transgender girls from playing school sports, misstated the timing in which 11 states enacted bills blocking transgender girls from competing in girls’ sports. Those approvals came in recent years, not only during this year.
match_headline: Bucking Republican Trend, Indiana Governor Vetoes Transgender Sports Bill

text: An article last Thursday about the photographer Campbell Addy referred imprecisely to one of the magazines where Mr. Addy’s work has been published. It has appeared inside British Vogue, not on the cover. The article also misstated the country where Mr. Addy’s partner is from. It is Lithuania, not Latvia.
match_headline: Campbell Addy Up Close

text: An article on Sunday about the Russian military’s move toward Kyiv, Ukraine’s capital, misidentified Lt. Tetiana Chornovol’s car model. It is a Chevy Aveo, not a Volt.
match_headline: The Battle for Kyiv Looms as a Long and Bloody Conflict

text: An article on Sunday about ice skating trails in Ottawa misstated the position played by the former National Hockey League player Chris Neil. He was a forward, not a defenseman.
match_headline: Ice Skating at a Rink Is Fun. Gliding Through a Forest? Glorious.

text: A column on Wednesday about a new nu­clear deal with Iran misstated the name of one of Iran’s military branches. It is the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, not the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps.
match_headline: A New Iran Deal Leaves Us Meeker and Weaker

text: An obituary on Saturday about the Talmudic scholar Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky misstated the number of times he determined that the name of Moses was mentioned in the Torah. It is 614, not 97.
match_headline: Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, Venerated Talmudic Scholar, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the longtime Democratic representative Victor Fazio misstated the name of a foundation that granted him a fellowship. It is the Coro Foundation, not Caro.
match_headline: Victor Fazio, Longtime Democratic Leader in the House, Dies at 79

text: An article on Friday about the Supreme Court confirmation hearing of Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson misstated the role of Senator Mitch McConnell, Republican of Kentucky. He is Senate the minority leader, not the majority leader.
match_headline: The Respectful Supreme Court Hearing That Wasn’t

text: An article on Thursday about Germany’s military readiness referred imprecisely to the rank and title of Lt. Gen. Alfons Mais. He is a lieutenant general, not a general, and is chief of the German army, not Germany’s defense chief.
match_headline: Germany Is Ready to Lead Militarily. Its Military Is Not.

text: An article on Friday about the Biden administration’s plan to accept 100,000 Ukrainian refugees misstated the countries outside the European Union that have created private sponsorship programs. They are Britain and Canada, not Ireland, which is a member of the union.
match_headline: United States Will Welcome Up to 100,000 Ukrainian Refugees

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about Halle Berry’s 2002 Oscar win for best actress incorrectly describes the achievements of Hattie McDaniel and Sidney Poitier at the Academy Awards. They were two of the Black performers to earn acting Oscars before Halle Berry; they were not the only two.
match_headline: Oscars Rewind: For Halle Berry, a Bittersweet Breakthrough

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about Shaina Taub’s musical “Suffs” misquotes lyrics in the song “Find a Way.” They are “How will we do it when it’s never been done?,” not “when it hasn’t been done?” and “How will we find a way where there isn’t one?,” not “when there isn’t one?” The article also misstates the title of a song in the musical. The error was repeated in a picture caption. It is “Watch Out for the Suffragette,” not “Watch Out for the Suffragist.”
match_headline: Friendship, Betrayal and the Fight: ‘Suffs’ Tells the Suffragist Tale in Song

text: An obituary on March 19 about the television producer and filmmaker Jack Willis misstated the given name of one of his collaborators on the documentary “The Streets of Greenwood.” He was Fred Wardenburg, not Phil.
match_headline: Jack Willis, TV Producer and Empathetic Filmmaker, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the lifestyle author and personality Chris Madden misstated the name of a magazine of hers published by Hearst and the year it was first published. It was Your Good House, not At Home With Chris Madden, and the first issue was in 2006, not 2005. (At Home With Chris Madden, shown in a photograph with the obituary, was a different magazine, published by Hachette.) It also misstated the year Ms. Madden’s HGTV program “Interiors by Design” ended. It was 2002, not 2003.
match_headline: Chris Madden, Lifestyle Author and Personality, Dies at 73

text: An obituary on Thursday about the former secretary of state Madeleine Albright misidentified the high school in Denver that she attended. It was the Kent School for Girls, not the Kent Denver School. (The Kent School for Girls merged with Denver Country Day School to become the Kent Denver School in 1974.)
match_headline: Madeleine Albright, First Woman to Serve as Secretary of State, Dies at 84

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the actress Marin Hinkle misstated the location of the kitchen where she made truffles. It is on the Upper West Side of Manhattan, not the Upper East Side.
match_headline: Marin Hinkle of ‘The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel’ Melts Chocolate

text: A review on May 10, 2020, about Cho Nam-­Joo’s novel “Kim Jiy­oung, Born 1982” referred incor­rectly to the book’s protagonist, Jiyoung. She has a daughter, not a son. This correction was de­layed because the error was brought to the attention of edi­tors only recently.
match_headline: In This Korean Best Seller, a Young Mother Is Driven to Psychosis

text: An editorial last Sunday about freedom of speech mischaracterized a Tennessee law banning the teaching of critical race theory. It prohibits promoting the concept that “an individual should feel discomfort, guilt, anguish or another form of psychological distress solely because of the individual’s race or sex.” It does not ban lesson plans that could cause students distress.
ref_headline: an individual should feel discomfort, guilt, anguish or another form of psychological distress solely because of the individual’s race or sex.
match_headline: America Has a Free Speech Problem

text: An article on Sunday about the first streaming service film to win an Oscar misstated the year that the film “Parasite” won the Oscar for best picture. It was 2020, not 2021.
match_headline: Streaming Took Over Hollywood. Will It Take Best Picture, Too?

text: An article on Sunday about Afghan refugees in the U.K. misidentified the deputy director of West London Welcome. She is Leyla Williams, not Leyla Ferguson.
match_headline: Afghan Refugees in U.K. Are Still in Limbo as Ukrainians Arrive

text: An article on Sunday about an influx of federal funds to New York during the pandemic misstated the dollar amount of the infrastructure bill. It is $1 trillion, not $1 billion.
match_headline: Federal Covid Cash Kept New York State Afloat. That Could End Soon.

text: An article on Sunday about investors across the country buying mobile home parks and driving up rents misstated when residents of the San Souci mobile home park became aware that the park had been sold. Many learned of the sale after the new owners distributed notifications of new park rules, according to a resident, not when maintenance crews appeared a few weeks later and began cutting down bushes and flowers.
match_headline: Investors Are Buying Mobile Home Parks. Residents Are Paying a Price.

text: An article on Sunday about mask mandates for young children in New York City schools described imprecisely the C.D.C.’s current guidance on the use of masks for children in day-care and preschool settings. The C.D.C. now recommends that those centers and schools align their protocols with those of the broader community and not require masks in all settings.
match_headline: Cases Are Rising in Schools. So Why Are Masks Off?

text: An article on Monday about Will Smith’s onstage altercation with Chris Rock at the Academy Awards ceremony misstated the year Hans Zimmer won his Oscar for “The Lion King.” It was in 1995, not 1989.
match_headline: Onstage Slap Rattles Oscars, Before ‘CODA’ Triumphs

text: An article on March 21 about Edward Holmes, a biologist at the center of the debate over the origins of the coronavirus, attributed an erroneous distinction to the coronavirus genome sequenced by the Chinese virologist Yong-Zhen Zhang’s team. It was not the first one to be posted online; others had been posted a day earlier.
match_headline: ‘He Goes Where the Fire Is’: A Virus Hunter in the Wuhan Market

text: A column on Monday about Gov. Ron De­ Santis mischaracterized a Florida bill that would ban the teaching of critical race theory. It would prohibit promoting the concept that people “must feel guilt, anguish or other forms of psychological distress because of actions, in which the individual played no part, committed in the past by other members of the same race, color, sex or national origin.” It would not ban lesson plans that may make people feel guilt.
match_headline: DeSantis Is Trump 2.0

text: A headline with an obituary on Monday about the physical chemist Martin Pope misstated his age. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 103, not 106.
match_headline: Martin Pope, Whose Research Led to OLEDs, Dies at 103

text: An article on Wednesday about Ukrainian counterattacks against Russian forces misstated the amount of money that Prime Minister Mario Draghi of Italy said his country had frozen in Russian assets. It was 800 million euros, which is the equivalent of about $900 million, not $900 billion.
match_headline: Ukrainians Try to Push Back Russian Forces Pummeling Their Cities

text: An article on Saturday about Representative Jeff Fortenberry of Nebraska, who was accused of lying to F.B.I. agents investigating illegal foreign donations, misidentified the speaker in a conversation who said that an illegal campaign donation “probably did come from Gilbert Chagoury,” a Lebanese Nigerian billionaire; a fund-raiser identified by prosecutors as Individual H said that to Mr. Fortenberry; Mr. Fortenberry did not say that to the fund-raiser.
ref_headline: probably did come from Gilbert Chagoury,
match_headline: Nebraska Congressman Faces Calls to Step Down After Convictions

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the Oscars misspelled the title of a film. It is “Minamata,” not “Minimata.”
match_headline: Does the Academy Hold Movies in Contempt? Our Critics Wonder.

text: A picture caption with an article last Wednesday about the food writer Emily Nunn misstated the readership for her newslet­ ter, The Department of Salad. It is the sixth­most­popular paid food newsletter on Substack, not among the top 10 of all newsletters on the platform.
match_headline: How Emily Nunn Turned Salad Into a Soapbox

text: A picture with an obituary on March 13 about the novelist Bruce Duffy misidentified the photographer who took the picture of Mr. Duffy. It was taken by Steve McCurry, not Michel Le Gall.
match_headline: Bruce Duffy, Hailed for His Ambitious First Novel, Dies at 70

text: An obituary on Thursday about John Roach, who helped introduce the Tandy TRS-80 personal computer, referred incorrectly to one of the components of the prototype that he and his team assembled. It was a cassette recorder, not a videocassette recorder.
match_headline: John Roach, Pioneer of the Personal Computer, Is Dead at 83

text: An article on Wednesday about people fleeing the Ukrainian city of Chernihiv misstated the city’s location. It is on the left bank of the Desna River, not the Dnieper River.
match_headline: A Vow to Ease Bombing Is Too Late for Many in Ukraine City Near Kyiv

text: An article on Wednesday about President Donald J. Trump’s call logs both before and during the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol misspelled the name of a former Republican senator from Georgia and misidentified the opponent who defeated him last year. The former senator is David Perdue, not Purdue, and he lost to Senator Jon Ossoff, not Senator Raphael Warnock.
match_headline: Call Logs Underscore Trump’s Efforts to Sway Lawmakers on Jan. 6

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about changes to the N.F.L.’s postseason overtime rule misstated what the original proposal would have affected. It would have been the regular season and postseason in 2022, not 2021.
match_headline: N.F.L. to Change Postseason Overtime Rule After Bills’ Playoff Loss

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the women’s softball sensation Joan Joyce earlier misstated the time frame in which she appeared on the television game show “To Tell the Truth.” She did so in 1974, not during “the 1960s.”
match_headline: Joan Joyce, a Sensation in Softball and More, Is Dead at 81

text: An article on Thursday about pro-Russian Serbians misstated the given name of a Belgrade-based psychotherapist. She is Aurelija Djan, not Arijan.
match_headline: Bound by a Sense of Victimhood, Serbia Sticks With Russia

text: An article on Thursday about a large study’s conclusion that the anti-parasitic drug ivermectin showed no sign of alleviating Covid-19 misstated the name of the spokeswoman for The New England Journal of Medicine. She is Julia Morin, not Morins.
match_headline: Ivermectin Does Not Reduce Risk of Covid Hospitalization, Large Study Finds

text: An obituary on Thursday about the author Richard Lipez misstated when his former wife, Hedy Harris, died. It was 2021, not this January.
match_headline: Richard Lipez, Who Reimagined the Gay Detective Novel, Dies at 83

text: An article on Friday about Syrian fighters deployed to join Russian forces in Ukraine paraphrased incorrectly comments by John Kirby, a Pentagon spokesman. He said that the Wagner Group is believed to recruit Syrians, not that Syrians are among the 1,000 mercenaries who are believed to be focused on the Donbas region of Ukraine.
match_headline: Putin’s War Is Complicating India’s Middle Path Among Powers

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 4 about the many books returned after New York’s public library systems ended late fees misstates the author and title of a work shown. It is “Ninon de Lenclos” by Emile Magne, not “Magne” by Ninon de Lenclos.
match_headline: The Library Ends Late Fees, and the Treasures Roll In

text: An article this weekend on Page 6 about the return of the play “For Colored Girls” to Broadway omits the given name and the title of a representative from the Shange estate. Donald Sutton is the literary trustee for the estate.
match_headline: ‘Told It Like It Was’: Ntozake Shange’s Tales of Black Womanhood

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about Adriana Hoffmann, a botanist who fought to protect Chile’s forests, misspelled her given name as Adrianna.

An article last Sunday about Sheila Bridges’s Harlem Toile de Jouy wallpaper misstated the job title of Lisa Silverman Meyers. She is the global head of retail licensing at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, not the global head of retail.
match_headline: The Wallpaper That Is Also a ‘Reminder That My Ancestors Had My Back’

text: An article on March 13 about the singer Doja Cat misspelled her surname. She is Amala Dlamini, not Dlamani.

A column last Sunday about the Senate and the Supreme Court misidentified which court Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson joined last year. It was the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, not the District of Columbia Court of Appeals, which is Washington’s equivalent of a state’s highest court.
match_headline: Real Justice: Justice Jackson

text: An article on Sunday about the Minverva Virgo, a tanker loaded with Russian oil that was forced to change course after its buyer fell through, misstated the tanker’s country of registry. The ship is Greek-flagged, not Croatian-flagged.
match_headline: A Tanker’s Giant U-Turn Reveals Strains in the Market for Russian Oil

text: An article on Sunday about intractable problems of homelessness in New York 30 years after the Tompkins Square riots misspelled the given name of a volunteer coordinator with North Brooklyn Essentials. He is Benjamin Adam, not Benjamim.
match_headline: Decades After the Destruction of Homeless Camps, What Have We Learned?

text: An article on Monday about the Rally Jameel in Saudi Arabia misstated the person who conceived and sponsored the motor rally event. It was Hassan Jameel, not Mohammed Abdul Latif Jameel, his father.
match_headline: Women Drive Off-Road in Saudi Desert for Fun and Bragging Rights

text: A headline with an article on Saturday about the movie “Deep Water” misstated the surname of its director. As the article correctly noted, he is Adrian Lyne, not Lane.
match_headline: When the Master of the Erotic Thriller Fails to Thrill

text: An obituary on Friday about the poet Richard Howard referred incorrectly to the novelist Sir Walter Scott, the subject of a poetic monologue by Mr. Howard in his collection “Untitled Subjects.” Scott lived during the Georgian era in Britain; he was not among “the Victorians and Edwardians” whose monologues by Mr. Howard also appear in the book.
match_headline: Native Hawaiian Hula Teacher Among Five Women Who Will Appear on Quarters

text: An obituary on Sunday about the fashion photographer Patrick Demarchelier misstated the year that Vogue magazine published its 100th anniversary issue. It was 1992, not 1999.
match_headline: Patrick Demarchelier, Fashion Photographer, Dies at 78

text: An article on Monday about a wave of new legislation intensifying already marked differences liberal- and conservative-led parts of the country misstated the number of states in which control of the legislative chambers is split between parties. Such a split exists in two states — Minnesota and Virginia — not one.
match_headline: Flurry of New Laws Move Blue and Red States Further Apart

text: An article on Sunday about moments of courage and kindness on the ground in Ukraine amid the war misidentified the city from which Clare Toeniskoetter was reporting. She was in Przemyśl, Poland, not Kraków.
match_headline: Surrounded by War, Compassion Endures

text: Because of an editing error, an article on March 29 about a meeting of diplomats from Israel, the United States and four Arab countries in Israel misstated the location of Morocco. It is in North Africa, not the Middle East.
match_headline: Israeli Summit Mixes Historic Symbolism With Sharp Disputes

text: An article on Sunday about a Delta airplane that had to make an emergency landing because of a cracked windshield, using information from the F.A.A., misstated the approximate time of the flight’s emergency landing in Denver. It was around 11 a.m. local time, not 11:15 p.m.
match_headline: Delta Plane Makes Emergency Landing After Windshield Cracks Mid-Flight

text: An article on Saturday about the impact of unemployment benefits on families’ financial aid eligibility described incompletely the FAFSA filing deadline. The form can be filed to seek aid retroactively, but it generally must be filed and processed by the last day of the student’s academic term or June 30 — whichever comes first. It cannot be filed after the academic year has ended for aid for that particular year. The article also referred incorrectly to SwiftStudent. It is a free tool for financial aid appeals, not a nonprofit organization.
match_headline: Jobless Benefits’ Unintended Fallout: Reduced College Financial Aid

text: An article on Monday about a judge’s decision that a California law requiring diversity on corporate boards was unconstitutional described incorrectly the decision by Judge Terry Green of Los Angeles County Superior Court. Judge Green issued a filing on his ruling; it was not the case that he did not provide an explanation for his decision.
match_headline: California Law Requiring Board Diversity Is Struck Down

text: An article on Sunday about the Kansas versus Villanova game referred incorrectly to Kansas guard Ochai Agbaji. He is a natural senior, not a fifth-year senior. The article also referred incorrectly to Kansas’ loss to Villanova in the 2018 Final Four. While Kansas also lost to Villanova in the 2016 tournament, it was in the round of 8; the 2018 game was not Kansas’ second consecutive loss in the Final Four to Villanova.
match_headline: Kansas Runs Past Villanova to Get to the N.C.A.A. Final, Avenging a 2018 Loss

text: An article on Monday that previewed the baseball season with a team-by-team look at each American League club misstated the position of Grayson Rodriguez, a prospect for the Baltimore Orioles. He is a pitcher, not a catcher.
match_headline: American League Has an East Coast Bias

text: An article on Tuesday about the best and worst moments from the 2022 Grammys misstated the title of the song performed by Ledisi. It is “Ne Me Quitte Pas,” not “Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien.”
match_headline: Best and Worst Moments From the 2022 Grammys

text: An article last Wednesday about the growth of culinary programs at community colleges misstated the location of the cooking schools that Le Cordon Bleu has closed. It closed all of its outposts in the United States, not in North America.
match_headline: A Fast, Frugal Track to a Cook’s Career? Community College.

text: A report in the Off the Menu column last Wednesday, using information from a publicist, misstated the phone number for the new restaurant Momoya Soho. It is 646-429-9315.
match_headline: L’Abeille, Serving French Fare With Casual Elegance, Opens in TriBeCa

text: An article on Wednesday about Elon Musk joining Twitter’s board after becoming the company’s biggest shareholder misstated the year that he mused in a tweet about taking Tesla, the electric car company he founded, private. It was 2018, not 2016.
match_headline: Elon Musk Joins Twitter’s Board, Pitching Ideas Big and Small

text: An article on Wednesday about attempts in certain states to restrict abortion pills and criminalize medication abortions referred incorrectly to the circumstance under which the Texas law requires a doctor to offer to administer Rh immunoglobulin to a pregnant woman. It is when she tests Rh negative, not Rh positive.
match_headline: Abortion Pills, Once a Workaround, Are Now a Target

text: An article on Wednesday about the expansion of the vertical farming industry misstated Jason Green’s position at Upward Farms, a vertical farming start-up. He is the chief executive and a co-founder of the company, not the president.
match_headline: Vertical Farms Expand as Demand for Year-Round Produce Grows

text: An article on Tuesday about protests in Sri Lanka demanding that President Gotabaya Rajapaksa resign misstated President Rajapaksa’s U.S. citizenship status. While he was once a dual citizen with the United States, he no longer holds U.S. citizenship.
match_headline: Sri Lanka Protesters Defy President, Rejecting a Cabinet Shuffle

text: An article on Wednesday about the Biden administration’s extension of a pandemic relief measure allowing millions of federal student loan borrowers to freeze their payments until Aug. 31 misstated the number of extensions the federal government has granted. This was the seventh, not the sixth.
match_headline: Biden’s Student Loan Plan Sets Off Fierce Debate Among Economists

text: An article on Tuesday about the UConn’s women’s basketball team’s failure to win a title since 2016 erroneously attributed a distinction to some players on this year’s team. While it is a rarity in the Geno Auriemma era that some players will graduate without having won a national title, they won’t be the first group to do so since 2008.
match_headline: Is UConn’s Dynasty Done? Auriemma Likes the Outlook for Next Year.

text: An article on Page 7 this weekend about the director Lileana Blain-Cruz’s Broadway directing debut with “The Skin of Our Teeth,” in one instance, misstates her given name. It is Lileana, not Lily; she does not use the nickname Lily.
match_headline: ‘Not Understanding Is Really Satisfying’: A Director Keeps You Thinking

text: An article on Page 28 this weekend about billionaire entertainers misstates the number of Black American entertainers included in a Forbes list of billionaires. There were four, not five.
match_headline: The Psychic Contortions of the Black Mogul-Entertainer

text: An article on April 3 about a man’s episodes of exhaustion defined “acephalgic” incorrectly. It means without head pain, not without a head.
match_headline: For Decades, He Had Strange Episodes of Utter Exhaustion

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about the growing number of billionaires incorrectly includes Forbes India in a list of internationally licensed editions whose reporters contribute to the magazine’s billionaires list. Reporters at Forbes India do not conduct research for the list.
match_headline: How Many Billionaires Are There, Anyway?

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Terry Wallis, who regained the ability to speak after a traumatic brain injury left him virtually unresponsive for 19 years, misstated his birth date. It was April 7, 1964, not Feb. 4.
match_headline: Terry Wallis, 57, Dies; Awoke 19 Years After a Traumatic Brain Injury
