text: An article last Sunday about divorced and separated couples who still live together misstated the surname of a professor of clinical psychology at Clark University in Worcester, Mass., in one refer­ence. She is Abbie E. Goldberg, not Greenberg.
match_headline: Separated but Under the Same Roof

text: An article on Sunday about efforts to save Florida’s starving manatees misstated where some of them went for the winter. It was northwest of the Indian River Lagoon, not northeast of it.
match_headline: Trying Everything, Even Lettuce, to Save Florida’s Beloved Manatees

text: An article on Sunday about the ouster of Prime Minister Imran Khan of Pakistan misstated who met with him late Saturday night. It was the country’s intelligence chief, not the army chief.
match_headline: Pakistan Parliament Ousts Imran Khan as Prime Minister

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about two shootings in the Bronx misstated statistics about gun violence in the city this year. More than 330 people have been shot so far, not killed.
match_headline: As Police Make Arrests in One Bronx Shooting, Teen Is Slain in Another

text: An article on Sunday about the Covid-19 death rate in Ocean County, N.J., misidentified how the state’s death rate compares to other states. New Jersey now has the sixth highest death rate, not the fifth highest.
match_headline: Why This Coastal County Has the Highest Covid Death Rate in Its State

text: A review on Friday of Michael Bay’s film “Ambulance” misidentified the actor who played one of the villains in “The Rock.” It was Ed Harris, not Sean Connery.
match_headline: ‘Ambulance’ Review: Michael Bay Is Our Emergency Movie Technician

text: An article on Sunday about rents in New York City rising from early pandemic lows misstated the vacancy rates in Manhattan. It was 1.3 percent in February 2022, not 2021. That figure was down from the record high of 11.8 percent in February 2021, not 2020.
match_headline: The New York Dream of Cheap Rent and No Roommates? It’s Over.

text: An article on Sunday about the master tap dancer Ayodele Casel misnamed a tap dancer who appeared in films in the 1930s and 1940s. She is Eleanor Powell, not Ellen Powell.
match_headline: Ayodele Casel Is on Tap for ‘Funny Girl’

text: An obituary on April 5 for the baseball player Tommy Davis misstated Al Campanis’s position with the Dodgers when he persuaded Davis to sign with the team in 1956. He was a scout, not the general manager.
match_headline: Tommy Davis, Batting Star With the ’60s Dodgers, Dies at 83

text: An article on Tuesday about tensions at Twitter after Elon Musk became the company’s largest shareholder described incorrectly the role of Rich Greenfield. He is an analyst for the research firm LightShed Partners, not the venture capital investment fund LightShed Ventures.
match_headline: Twitter Grapples With an Elon Musk Problem

text: An article on Sunday about residents in Puerto Rico who remained without electricity days after a power outage misidentified the company that controls the power plant in Puerto Rico where a fire broke out. It is the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority, not Luma Energy.
match_headline: Power Returning to Puerto Rico, but Frustrations Remain

text: An article on Tuesday about Miya Ponsetto, a California woman who tackled a Black teenager at a SoHo hotel after falsely accusing him of stealing her cellphone, described incorrectly Ms. Ponsetto’s guilty plea. She can enter a new plea to a lesser charge — a misdemeanor — if she abides by the plea’s terms, but it is not the case that the lesser charge will not include a hate crime element.
match_headline: Woman Pleads Guilty to Tackling Black Teen at SoHo Hotel

text: An article on Tuesday about a temporary permit from New York City officials allowing the “Fearless Girl” statue to remain outside the New York Stock Exchange for 11 months described incorrectly the work of State Street Global Advisors. It is an asset management arm of State Street Corporation, not a hedge fund.
match_headline: New York Lets ‘Fearless Girl’ Hold Her Ground, for Now

text: An article last Wednesday about Black American Jews misstated a finding from the Pew Research Center’s 2021 report on Jewish Americans. The group found that 1 percent of adult Jewish Americans identify as Black, not that 1 percent of Black Americans identify as Jewish. The article also misstated the age of Rabbi Sandra Lawson. She is 52, not 53.
match_headline: ‘Blackness Deserves a Seat at the Seder’

text: An obituary on March 28 about Vera Gissing, who in 1939 was one of the many Jewish children evacuated from Czechoslovakia by the stockbroker Nicholas Winton, misstated the surnames of her parents. They were Karel Diamant and Irma Diamantova, not Karel and Irma Diamontova.
match_headline: Vera Gissing, Who Was Rescued by ‘Britain’s Schindler,’ Dies at 93

text: An article on Friday about key facts concerning France’s presidential election referred imprecisely to the election of 1965. That was the first time that a president was elected in a direct ballot; it was not the case that a candidate was elected without a runoff. That has not happened yet.
match_headline: Even Before France Votes, the French Right Is a Big Winner

text: An article on Tuesday about the selection of Shehbaz Sharif by the Pakistani Parliament to become the country’s prime minister misstated the date of the coup that cut short his brother Nawaz Sharif’s second term in office. It occurred in 1999, not 1998.
match_headline: Shehbaz Sharif Becomes Pakistan’s New Prime Minister Amid Turmoil

text: An article on Wednesday about Germans’ doubts concerning Chancellor Olaf Scholz’s recent foreign policy plan in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine misattributed the remark “Cheap Russian energy has been the basis of our industry’s competitiveness.” It was made by Martin Brudermüller, the chief executive of BASF, not by Michael Heinz, the chief executive of BASF Corporation in North America.
ref_headline: Cheap Russian energy has been the basis of our industry’s competitiveness.
match_headline: Ukraine War Pushes Germans to Change. They Are Wavering.

text: An article on Sunday about the dance artists Eiko Otake and Bill T. Jones described incorrectly a production that was choreographed by Jones. The production, “Black No More,” was an Off Broadway play; it was not on Broadway.
match_headline: Bill T. Jones and Eiko Otake: Opposites Guided by ‘Too-Much-Ness’

text: An article on Tuesday about how the shift to remote work has affected New York City misstated the percentage of New York workers who went into the office before the pandemic. It is more than 90 percent, not 80 percent.
match_headline: As Remote Work Becomes Permanent, Can Manhattan Adapt?

text: An article on Wednesday about protests in Sri Lanka calling for the resignation of President Gotabaya Rajapaksa misstated the post held by Mr. Rajapaksa’s brother Chamal. He is the state minister of defense — effectively an assistant cabinet minister — not the minister of defense.
match_headline: An Angry Public Wants Sri Lanka’s President Gone

text: An article on Thursday about meetings between two Trump White House lawyers and the House committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol described the meetings incorrectly. They met in person, not virtually.
match_headline: Two Trump White House Lawyers Meet With Jan. 6 Investigators

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about House Republicans’ withdrawal of support for a bill to name a federal courthouse after Justice Joseph W. Hatchett, the first Black man to serve on the Florida Supreme Court, attributed an erroneous distinction to him. Justice Hatchett was the first Black judge to be appointed to a federal appeals court in the Deep South, not the first Black judge to be appointed to a State Supreme Court south of the Mason-Dixon line.
match_headline: House G.O.P., Banding Together, Kills Bid to Honor Pioneering Black Judge

text: An article on Friday about a Soviet-era air defense system sent to Ukraine by Slovakia misspelled the given name of the mayor of Dobra, Slovakia. He is Mikulas Csoma, not Mikolas.
match_headline: Hiding in Plain Sight, a Soviet-Era Air Defense System Arrives in Ukraine

text: An article on Friday about a man charged with setting a fire at an L.G.B.T.Q. club in Brooklyn misstated, in some editions, the date of his initial appearance in federal court. It was Thursday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Man Is Charged With Arson in Fire at an L.G.B.T.Q. Club in Brooklyn

text: An article on Friday about the Nashville Stars, a children’s baseball team named in honor of a Negro leagues team, misstated the age group of the youth team’s first players. They were 17 and under, not 15 and under. The article also misstated, in some editions, the name of an organization that worked with the Nashville Stars. It is Music City Baseball, not Music Baseball.
match_headline: Honoring the Past by Focusing on the Future

text: An article this weekend on Page 1 about the rise in popularity of electric cargo bikes in New York City as a way for parents to get children places misidentifies the Instagram account of Madeleine Novich. It is Cargobikemomma, not CargoBikeMama.
match_headline: The Smallest New Yorkers Join the Pandemic Biking Surge

text: An article this weekend on Page 8 about the actor Alexander Skarsgard misstates the role he plays in the series “Generation Kill.” His character is a Marine, not a member of the Navy SEALs.
match_headline: Alexander Skarsgard’s Viking Dream

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the comedian Gilbert Gottfried misstated the name of a movie in which he appeared. It is “Look Who’s Talking Too,” not “Look Who’s Talking II.”
match_headline: Gilbert Gottfried, Comedian With a Distinctive Voice, Dies at 67

text: Because of an editing error, the Of Interest section on Friday referred incorrectly to Jackie Robinson. While Robinson was the first Black player in the modern era of Major League Baseball after decades of segregated play, there were a small number of Black players in the major leagues in the 1800s.
match_headline: ‘This Is American History’: The Hall of Fame Reconsiders Race

text: An article on Friday about European officials drafting plans for an embargo on Russian oil products misstated the date that Easter fell on this year. It was April 17, not April 16.
match_headline: Europe Reluctantly Readies Russian Oil Embargo

text: An obituary on Saturday about the molecular biologist Sidney Altman, who shared the 1989 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, misstated the name of his first wife, who is also a molecular biologist. She is Ann M. Körner, not Anne Korner.
match_headline: Sidney Altman, Who Stumbled on a Breakthrough in Genetics, Dies at 82

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about retracted or challenged studies linked to Cassava Sciences’ Alzheimer’s drug misstated Dr. David Bredt’s employment status. He is no longer with MPM Capital.
match_headline: Scientists Question Data Behind an Experimental Alzheimer’s Drug

text: An article on Tuesday about guidelines to follow when someone in your household tests positive for coronavirus misstated the name of a type of mask that is highly protective against the virus. It is the KF94 mask, not KN94 mask.
match_headline: When Covid Enters the House, What Should We Do?

text: An article on Monday about Ford Motor’s new electric F-150 pickup truck and the company’s efforts to catch up to Tesla misstated the age of the Ford Motor Company. It was founded 118 years ago, not 113. It also misstated the weight of Ford’s electric F-150 pickup truck. It is 6,000 pounds, not 4,000.
match_headline: Jim Farley Tries to Reinvent Ford and Catch Up to Elon Musk and Tesla

text: An article on Tuesday about the effect that the pandemic has had on people’s feet misspelled the given name of an associate professor at the University of Southern California. She is Jacquelyn M. Dylla, not Jacqueline.
match_headline: The Pandemic Has Been Hard on Our Feet

text: An article on Saturday about homeless­ness misstated the number of hotels in New York City under consideration for conversion to permanent supportive housing. There are more than 700 hotels in the city; the number under considera­tion for conversion is not known.
match_headline: On Homelessness, Mayor Eric Adams Needs a Little Religion

text: An article on Wednesday about a $50 million donation from the estate of H.F. Lenfest to The Museum of the American Revolution described incorrectly a bronze relief at the museum. It depicts the presentation of the Declaration of Independence to the Continental Congress by the drafting committee, not the signing of the Declaration of Independence.
match_headline: The Museum of the American Revolution Receives $50 Million

text: A column on Tuesday about the current social and political climate misstated the jurisdiction of a gun control case before the Supreme Court. It is New York State, not New York City.
match_headline: This Is Not the Year of the Optimist

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about Michael F. Neidorff, the longtime chief executive of the Centene Corporation, misidentified the institution where he earned a master’s degree. It was Saint Francis University in Loretto, Pa. — not St. Francis College in Brooklyn.
match_headline: Michael F. Neidorff, 79, Dies; His Company Was an Obamacare Stalwart

text: An article on Thursday about Bohus Garbar, a donor to the far-right political parties in Slovakia and a Russian spy, misspelled the surname of the founder and editor of Main News. He is Robert Sopko, not Supko. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The article also misspelled the surname of the director of the Strategic Policy Institute. He is Matej Kandrik, not Kendrik.
match_headline: He Was a Penniless Donor to the Far Right. He Was Also a Russian Spy.

text: An article on Thursday about Brian D. North, a Connecticut trooper charged in the fatal shooting of Mubarak Soulemane, misstated the offense that George Floyd was accused of committing. He was accused of attempting to pass a counterfeit bill, not shoplifting.
match_headline: White Connecticut Trooper Charged in Killing of Black Man During Stolen Car Chase

text: An article on Thursday about former President Barack Obama’s new effort to fight disinformation misstated his age. He is 60, not 61.
match_headline: Barack Obama Takes On a New Role: Fighting Disinformation

text: An article on Thursday about Chancellor Olaf Scholz of Germany and the debate over sending heavy weapons to Ukraine misstated the name of a German infantry-fighting vehicle. It is the Marder, not the Mardar.
match_headline: Calls to Give Heavy Weapons to Ukraine Divide Germany’s Government

text: An article on Tuesday about the economic policies of President Macron and Marine Le Pen and their impact in the French presidential election misstated Ms. Le Pen’s wage proposals. She has pledged tax cuts for companies that raise salaries, not to increase the minimum wage.
match_headline: French Candidates’ Economic Programs Hold Key to the Election

text: An article on Friday about an alert issued by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for a cluster of hepatitis cases in children misstated the day the alert was issued. It was Thursday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: C.D.C. Issues Alert Over Cluster of Hepatitis Cases in Children

text: An article on Friday about the National Women’s History Museum and journal entries the museum collected about women’s experiences during the pandemic misstated the name of the city in Ohio where the occupational therapist Alexis Misko lives. The city is Columbus, not Columbia. The article also article misstated when Asya Aizman, a creative technologist in Somerville, Mass., gave birth to her child. It was in May, not June, of 2020.
match_headline: The Caretakers of Women’s Pandemic Stories

text: An article on Page 13 this weekend about a new production of Donizetti’s “Lucia di Lammermoor” misstates the setting of the opera in the original libretto. It takes place in the 16th century, not the 18th century.
match_headline: Risking Boos, the Met Opera Puts Present-Day America Onstage

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about Chiwetel Ejiofo and the Showtime series “The Man Who Fell to Earth” misidentifies the number of episodes of “The Man Who Fell to Earth” that were directed by Alex Kurtzman. It was four, not two.
ref_headline: The Man Who Fell to Earth
match_headline: Chiwetel Ejiofor Was Asked to Play a Space Alien. He Knew What to Do.

text: An article on Page 2 this weekend about how design has been shaped by the pandemic misstates Todd Bracher’s involvement in the design of a fabric for the Path chair by Humanscale. Mr. Bracher was not the sole creator of the fabric; the fabric was co-created with Humanscale.
match_headline: A Panorama of Design

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about the impact of the pandemic on the careers of architects misstates the conditions under which Elisabeth Johs moved into a house in Mexico City. She rented the house; she did not buy it.
match_headline: The Upside of a Lockdown

text: An article on Page 11 this weekend about redesigning libraries to include outdoor spaces misidentifies the architecture firm where Annie Barrett is a principal. It is BAS Architecture, not Aalso Architects.
match_headline: Why Libraries May Never Stop Being People Places

text: An article on April 17 about a diagnosis of chronic diarrhea misstated the name of the institution where Dr. Tarek Sawas works. It is the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, not the University of Texas Southwestern.
match_headline: He Was Remarkably Healthy Until Chronic Diarrhea Nearly Killed Him

text: An article on Page 90 this weekend about the rapper Saweetie misidentifies two rings. The Completedworks ring is worn on her left hand, and the Darius ring is worn on her right hand, not vice versa.
An obituary on April 11 about the biochemist Arthur D. Riggs misstated part of his mother’s name. She was Nelly (Caulkins) Riggs, not Calkins.
match_headline: Arthur D. Riggs, 82, Dies; Led Team That Invented Artificial Insulin

text: An article last Sunday about Beta, a company in Burlington, Vt., that is developing battery-powered aircraft, misstated Blain Newton’s role at the company. He is chief operations officer, not chief finance officer and chief operating officer. The article also overstated what is known about Ver­mont’s use of nuclear power relative to other states. According to the Vermont Department of Public Service, the state’s power consumption is approximately 26 percent nuclear in origin, but state­-by-­state rankings of nuclear power usage are unreliable, and it is not clear whether Vermont had a higher use of nuclear power than any other state.
match_headline: The Battery That Flies

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about how infidelity can affect retirement sav­ings included a description of credit card debt accumulated during a marriage. One member of the couple contacted The New York Times after publication and disputed the account.
match_headline: Their Cheating Heart, Your Damaged Retirement Plan

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Joel Grey misidentified a chair in Mr. Grey’s West Village loft. It was designed by Alvar Aalto, not Jens Risom.
match_headline: Joel Grey, on Making a Space for Art and Dreams

text: An article last Sunday about a young transgen­der man preparing to become a gondolier in Venice referred incorrectly to Alex Hai, who runs a private gondola service under the auspices of a hotel. Mr. Hai is a transgender man, not a transgender woman.
match_headline: In Venice, a Young Boatman Steers a Course of His Own

text: An article on Page 90 this weekend about the rapper Saweetie misidentifies two rings. The Completedworks ring is worn on her left hand, and the Darius ring is worn on her right hand; not vice versa.

An article on Saturday about the slowing of momentum of the World Health Organization’s goal to vaccinate the world against Covid-19 misspelled the surname of the chief executive of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. He is Dr. Seth Berkley, not Berkeley.
match_headline: The Drive to Vaccinate the World Against Covid Is Losing Steam

text: An article on Monday about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his plans for a solar plant in the village of Palli referred incorrectly to Samita Devi, who said that because of a new solar plant, “We are very, very happy.” Ms. Devi is a woman.
match_headline: Modi Stresses Growth, Sidestepping Politics, in Visit to Restive Territory

text: An article on Saturday about a Texas National Guard soldier who is feared dead in Rio Grande misstated the day that Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas issued a statement about the missing member of the National Guard. It was Friday, not Monday.
match_headline: Texas National Guard Soldier Feared Drowned in Rio Grande

text: An article on Monday about the success of the New Orleans Pelicans without Zion Williamson referred incorrectly to the Phoenix Suns. They are the reigning N.B.A. Western Conference champions, not the champions.
match_headline: The Pelicans Are Finding Their Way Without Zion Williamson

text: An obituary on April 14 about the photographer Jerry Uelsmann misspelled the surname of one of his former wives. She is Diane Farris, not Faris.
match_headline: Jerry Uelsmann, Surreal Image-Maker, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Sunday about Peter Swales, whose research challenged received wisdom on Sigmund Freud, misstated the year Freud’s daughter Anna died. It was 1982, not 1989.
match_headline: Peter Swales, Who Startled Freud Scholarship, Dies at 73

text: An article on Sunday about first-time homeowners in Charlotte, N.C., misstated the monthly rent increase that Jameisha Wilkes was facing. The proposed increase was $88, not $150.
match_headline: Why the Road Is Getting Even Rockier for First-Time Home Buyers

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about a three-alarm house fire in Canarsie, Brooklyn, misstated the given name of the firefighter who died in the blaze. He was Timothy Klein, not Kevin.
match_headline: Firefighter Is Killed When Ceiling Collapses in Brooklyn House Fire

text: An article on Tuesday about Jacob and Karsten Kirk and their morel mushrooms growth method misstated the Kirk brothers’ yield of morels last year. It was about 20 pounds per square yard per year, not 22 pounds per square yard.
match_headline: Cultivating Coveted Morels Year-Round and Indoors

text: A review on Tuesday of the production of “The Skin of Our Teeth” misstated the New Jersey town in which the play is set. The Antrobus family’s home is in Excelsior, N.J., not Edison.
match_headline: ‘The Skin of Our Teeth’ Review: A Party for the End of the World

text: An article on Monday about Randy Rainbow and his new memoir misstated the name of a song in the musical “Gypsy.” The song is “If Momma Was Married,” not “If Mama Got Married.”
match_headline: Your Son Will Come Out Tomorrow: Randy Rainbow’s Memoir of Love, Turmoil and Trump

text: An obituary on Thursday about the pianist Radu Lupu misidentified the newspaper that conducted a rare interview with him in 1994. It was The Orange County Register, not The Chicago Tribune. (The Tribune later reprinted the interview.)
match_headline: Radu Lupu, Pianist Who Awed Listeners, Is Dead at 76

text: An article on Wednesday about a small town located on the front lines of the Russian and Ukrainian war misidentified the mayor of Orikhiv, Ukraine. He is Anatoliy Khvorostyanov, not Kostyantin Denisov.
match_headline: Standing in the path of war, a small Ukrainian town braces as Russians advance.

text: An article on Sunday about a judicial inquiry’s conclusion that corruption at South Africa’s tax agency was tied to “collusion” between Bain & Company and South Africa’s former president, Jacob Zuma, misstated the length of time that Bain was under contract with the South African Revenue Service. Bain was under contract with SARS from January 2015 until May 2017, not for four years.
match_headline: An American Consulting Firm Became a Power Broker, and Then a Pariah, in South Africa

text: An article on Tuesday about a criminal court in Texas that halted the execution of Melissa Lucio, a mother convicted of killing her child more than a decade ago attributed an erroneous distinction to Ms. Lucio. If she had been executed, she would have been the first Hispanic woman executed in Texas since the Civil War, not the first in the state’s history.
match_headline: Texas Court Halts Execution of Mother Convicted of Killing Child

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about NFTs for children described incorrectly a cartoon dog created by the company Invisible Universe for Jennifer Aniston. Clydeo is meant to be a cousin of Aniston’s real-life dog, Clyde; he is not an animated version of Clyde.
match_headline: Does a Toddler Need an NFT?

text: An article on Thursday about fears in Washington and European capitals that the conflict in Ukraine may soon escalate into a wider war misidentified Seth G. Jones’s position at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. He is the director of the International Security Program, not the European Security Program.
match_headline: Fears Are Mounting That Ukraine War Will Spill Across Borders

text: An article on Sunday about an Israeli military operation in the West Bank referred imprecisely to Israel’s comments on the shooting death of Mohammad Zakarneh. While the military declined to comment to The Times directly, it released a statement describing an incident the same day and place as his death in which soldiers shot someone who had first shot at them.
match_headline: Israel and Gaza Militants Exchange Fire in Worst Fighting in Months

text: An article on Friday about Holocaust survivors fleeing to Germany from Ukraine misstated the age of Galina Ploschenko. She is 88, not 90.
match_headline: They Survived the Holocaust. Now, They Are Fleeing to Germany.

text: An article on Friday about the Michigan Republican Party and its candidates for attorney general and secretary of state misstated Richard M. DeVos’s relationship to Betsy DeVos. He was her father-in-law, not her father.
match_headline: Revolt Brews in Michigan G.O.P. After Elevation of Trump Allies

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about the use of natural Black hairstyles in TV and film misstates the given name of one of the stars of “Coming 2 America.” She is Bella Murphy, not Bria Murphy.
match_headline: In Films and on TV, a New Openness to Natural Black Hairstyles

text: An article this weekend on Page 37 about smaller museums that are using podcasts to broaden their audiences misstates Jeff Martin’s job title at the Philbrook Museum of Art. It is assistant director of communications, not online communities manager.
match_headline: Using Podcasts to Broaden the Reach of Smaller Museums

text: An article this weekend on Page 30 about the Guggenheim Museum’s first poet in residence, relying on incorrect information from a publicist, describes incorrectly the program “Poetry of the Senses” and misstates when it is set to take place. It is an immersive experience, not a panel, and it is being organized primarily by Cecilia Vicuña, not by Taylor Johnson. It is scheduled for the first week of the exhibition “Cecilia Vicuña: Spin Spin Triangulene,” which opens on May 27, not in August.
match_headline: Coming Soon to the Guggenheim: Words, Words, Words

text: An article this weekend on Page 39 about Florida and the expansion of the art scene on the Gulf Coast misstates the name of an art fair. It is Art Basel Miami Beach, not Art Basil Miami.
match_headline: In Florida, It’s ‘Go West’ for Arts Donors and Patrons

text: A headline with an article on Saturday about national security surveillance of people on domestic soil misidentified the agency that conducts such surveillance. It is the F.B.I., not the National Security Agency.
match_headline: National Security Surveillance on U.S. Soil Dropped Again in 2021, Report Says

text: An article on Sunday about children of temporary visa holders who age out of green card eligibility in the United States misstated the citizenship of Barathimohan Ganesan. While he was born in India, he is a citizen of Singapore, not India.
match_headline: They Grew Up Legally in the U.S., but Can’t Stay After They Turn 21

text: An obituary on Thursday about Cynthia Albritton, who became famous for making sculptures of rock musicians’ genitals, misstated the surname of the friend who confirmed her death. He is Chris Kellner, not Hellner.
match_headline: Cynthia Albritton, Rock’s ‘Plaster Caster,’ Is Dead at 74

text: An obituary on April 22 about the quarterback Daryle Lamonica misstated two aspects of the play in a 1972 playoff game between Lamonica’s Oakland Raiders and the Pittsburgh Steelers that became known as the “immaculate reception.” A pass from the Pittsburgh quarterback Terry Bradshaw ricocheted off the Raider defensive back Jack Tatum in a collision with the Steelers’ Frenchy Fuqua and was caught by Pittsburgh’s Franco Harris, who ran it back for a touchdown; it did not ricochet off Fuqua. And although there were only a few seconds left on the clock when Harris scored, his touchdown was not “the game’s final play.”
match_headline: Daryle Lamonica, Hard-Throwing Quarterback, Is Dead at 80

text: An obituary on Saturday about the French actor and director Jacques Perrin misidentified his co-star in the 1967 movie “All the Other Girls Do.” She was Rosemarie Dexter, not Natalie Wood.
match_headline: Jacques Perrin, Soft-Spoken Film Star and Producer, Is Dead at 80

text: An article on Tuesday about the midterm primaries in Indiana and Ohio misidentified the candidate in an Indiana prosecutor’s race who was endorsed by former Vice President Mike Pence. It was Greg Garrison, not D. Lee Buckingham.
match_headline: 5 Takeaways From Ohio’s Primary Elections

text: An article on Saturday about an offer from Jim Ratcliffe to purchase the Premier League soccer team Chelsea misspelled the surname of the chairman of Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment. He is Larry Tanenbaum, not Tenenbaum.
match_headline: Billionaire’s Late Bid Upends Sale of Chelsea F.C.

text: An article on Wednesday about reactions to the leaked draft opinion from the Supreme Court on Roe v. Wade misstated the surname of a Louisiana dance instructor. She is Yvette Ware, not Clark.
match_headline: Leaked Threat to Roe v. Wade Stuns, Then Energizes Americans

text: An article on Wednesday about protesters who gathered at the steps of the Supreme Court after the leak of a draft opinion that supported overturning Roe v. Wade misspelled the surname of an activist with Pro-Life San Francisco. He is Robert Byrd, not Robert Buird.
match_headline: Demonstrators Gathered at Supreme Court Lament, and Celebrate, Leaked Draft

text: An article last Thursday about New York residents traveling to New Jersey to buy marijuana legally misstated the location of a New Jersey dispensary that did not apply to expand to recreational sales. It is in Secaucus, not Hoboken.
match_headline: No, New Yorkers Aren’t Flocking to New Jersey for Legal Weed

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the actor David Birney misstated when he died. It was Wednesday, April 27 — not Friday, April 29.
match_headline: David Birney, Who Starred on TV’s ‘Bridget Loves Bernie,’ Dies at 83

text: An article on Thursday about rising violence by separatists in Pakistan misstated the timing of an assault on the Pakistan Stock Exchange by Baluchistan Liberation Army militants. The stock exchange assault in Karachi occurred in 2020, not the year after the group’s 2018 attack on the Chinese consulate there. The article also misstated part of the name of an Islamabad-based think tank. It is the Pak Institute for Peace Studies, not the Pak Institute of Peace Studies.
match_headline: Rising Violence by Separatists Adds to Pakistan’s Lethal Instability

text: An article on Friday about Bad Bunny’s fourth album, “Un Verano Sin Ti,” misquoted Buscabulla’s Luis Alfredo Del Valle. He said “It’s pretty noble” that Bad Bunny brings other artists into his music, not “It’s pretty notable.”
match_headline: Behind Bad Bunny’s Summery Surprise, ‘Un Verano Sin Ti’

text: An article on Page 28 this weekend about the squash player Amanda Sobhy misstates when she was ranked 17th in the world. It was before she attended college, not when she began college. And, because of a transcription error, the article misstated what Sobhy said after a match in Chicago in February. She said, “I love performing, I love grinding it out, I love putting on a show,” not, “I love performing, grinding it out, putting on a show.”
ref_headline: I love performing, I love grinding it out, I love putting on a show,
match_headline: No American Has Ever Been No. 1 in Squash. Amanda Sobhy Can Change That.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the photographer Ron Galella referred incorrectly in part to a 1982 case involving his photographs of Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis. While Mr. Galella had violated a 1972 order to stay away from Mrs. Onassis and her children, he was cited for violating the order 12 times — not “hundreds of times.” And while he did agree never to photograph Mrs. Onassis or her children again, he later reached an agreement with her son, John F. Kennedy Jr., that permitted Mr. Galella to photograph him under certain conditions; it was not the case that “he never did.”
match_headline: Ron Galella, Celebrity-Hounding Photographer, Dies at 91

text: An article on April 24 about George Pele­canos and “We Own This City” described incorrectly his role as showrunner. It is not his first time to serve as showrunner of a series.
match_headline: ‘We Own This City’ Brings George Pelecanos Back to Baltimore

text: An article last Sunday about the Fire Island Pines Historical Preservation Society, relying on incor­rect information from a tour guide, referred imprecisely to the house at 482 Tarpon Walk, also known as the Kodak House. The house was designed by the architect Horace Gifford for Robert Evans and Scott DePass, not for Mr. Gifford’s own use.
match_headline: Saving the History of the Pines on Fire Island

text: Because of an editing error, the Crime column on April 24 referred incorrectly to Joe Brody, the pro­tagonist of David Gordon’s novel “The Wild Life.” He is a veteran of the war in Afghanistan; he is not a Vietnam veteran.
match_headline: Solving a Garden-Party Murder in 1920s India

text: An article on Saturday about Republican lawmakers’ silence concerning a draft opinion that would eliminate the constitutional right to an abortion misstated the method by which morning-after pills prevent pregnancy. They prevent ovulation, not implantation.
match_headline: G.O.P. Lawmakers Recast Abortion Stance, Wary of Voter Backlash

text: An article on Thursday about feminist movements outside the United States that may change their strategies to support abortion rights in light of the recent leaked Supreme Court opinion that would overturn Roe v. Wade misstated the given name and area of study of a scholar in Colombia: She is Julia Zulver, not Julie, and she is a political sociologist, not a political anthropologist.
match_headline: Roe Inspired Activists Worldwide, Who May Be Rethinking Strategy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the duality of Russia’s Victory Day and Western Europe’s Europe Day celebrations misstated the location of the Katyn Forest. It is in Russia, not Poland.
match_headline: Two Europes Confront Each Other Over the Glory, or Shame, of War

text: An article on Sunday about Charles W. Herbster’s bid for governor in Nebraska misspelled the given name of a former adviser to President Donald J. Trump. He is Stephen Moore, not Steven.
match_headline: In Nebraska, a Trump-Inspired Candidate Cracks Open Divide in the G.O.P.

text: An article on Sunday about reviews released by the state of Florida that led to the rejection of dozens of math textbooks misidentified the publisher for the math textbook “Thinking Mathematically.” It is Pearson, not Savvas Learning Company.
match_headline: Florida Releases Reviews That Led to Rejection of Math Textbooks

text: An article on Saturday about the sale of the Premier League soccer team Chelsea F.C. to a U.S. consortium led by Todd Boehly misstated the name of an investment firm he founded. It is Eldridge Industries, not Eldridge Investments.
match_headline: Chelsea F.C. Says It Will Sell to U.S.-Led Group

text: An article on Friday about a Russian law under which individuals are labeled “foreign agents” referred incorrectly to the law’s passage. The measure was enacted in several stages, starting with organizations; news media and individuals were included after amendments. The law was first adopted in 2012, not 2020.
match_headline: Anti-Putin Russians Are Leaving, With a Push From the Kremlin

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the closure of Lincoln College in Illinois misidentified the college as a historically Black college. It is a predominantly Black college, not a Department of Education-listed H.B.C.U.
match_headline: Lincoln College to Close, Hurt by Pandemic and Ransomware Attack

text: An article on Monday about the psychedelic history of the Hotel Catalina Beach Resort in Zihuatanejo, Mexico, misstated the name of Timothy Leary’s consciousness-expansion organization. It was the International Federation for Internal Freedom, not the International Foundation for Internal Freedom.
match_headline: A Return Trip to Timothy Leary’s Psychedelic, Day-Glo Mexico

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the Netflix Is a Joke Fest misstated the title of the Netflix executive Robbie Praw. He is vice president of stand-up and comedy formats, not director of original stand-up.
match_headline: In Comedy, Timing Is Everything, Especially at Netflix’s Festival

text: An article on Tuesday about the Jazz Bassist Ron Carter misidentified a Rochester jazz club. It was the Ridge Crest Inn, not the Red Creek Inn.
match_headline: At 85, the Jazz Bassist Ron Carter Still Seeks ‘A Better Order of Notes’

text: An article on Monday about obstacles to expanding access to Covid antiviral pills in poor nations referred imprecisely to the arrival of generic Covid pills in low- and middle-income countries. Most of those nations, but not all of them, will likely have to wait until 2023 for the pills to be available.
match_headline: As Poor Nations Seek Covid Pills, Officials Fear Repeat of AIDS Crisis

text: An article on Wednesday about increased layoffs, stock dumps and decreases in revenue affecting the start-up market referred incorrectly to a start-up business. Knock is a home-loan start-up, not a home-buying one. The article also misidentified the city of the company’s headquarters. It is based in New York City, not Austin, Texas.
match_headline: Fear and Loathing Return to Tech Start-Ups

text: An article on Wednesday about the Netflix adaptation of the webcomic and graphic novel “Heartstopper” misstated the age of the character Charlie in a scene described from Episode 2. He is 14 in the scene, not 15.
match_headline: ‘Heartstopper’ Is a TV Love Story With the Soul of a Comic

text: An article on Thursday about a police chase in the Bronx misstated when Officer Dennis Vargas joined a Bronx public safety team. It was in October, not in December.
match_headline: Man Dead and Officer Wounded After a Chase in the Bronx

text: An article on Thursday about a new Bloomberg Media UK venture misstated Bloomberg’s revenue in the first quarter of 2022. It was up 26 percent, not 21 percent, compared with the same period in 2021.
match_headline: Bloomberg Aims to Compete Directly With British Press

text: An article on April 30 about the auction of a dinosaur skeleton that inspired the “Jurassic Park” raptor, using incorrect information from Christie’s, misidentified the excavator of the specimen. The excavators were Jack and Roberta Owen, not Jared Hudson, who bought and prepared the specimen. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Christie’s to Sell a Dinosaur That Inspired the ‘Jurassic Park’ Raptor

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about a crackdown on gang violence in El Salvador that led to the imprisonment of more than 25,000 people misidentified the woman shown with Irvin Antonio Hernández and his girlfriend after he was arrested. She is his sister, not his mother.
match_headline: Outside the Walls of a Salvadoran Prison, ‘We’re All Crying Mothers’

text: An article on Sunday about five men who were wrongly convicted of murder and how they banded together to get out of prison misidentified the television studio that plans to produce “The Sing Sing Chronicles.” It is NBC News Studios, not NBC Studios.
match_headline: How 5 Convicted Murderers Banded Together to Get Out of Prison

text: An article on Thursday about the auction of Toscha Seidel’s Stradivarius violin misstated the 1974 auction price of the “da Vinci” violin in today’s dollars. It would be over $300,000, not over $3 million.
match_headline: A Violin From Hollywood’s Golden Age Aims at an Auction Record

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the 100th anniversary of the interfaith marriage comedy “Abie’s Irish Rose” on Broadway misidentifies the play that overtook “Abie’s Irish Rose” as the longest-running show in Broadway history. It was “Tobacco Road” (1933), not “Life With Father,” which became the longest-running play later on.
match_headline: The Smart Set Sneered, but the Play Won the Day

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about a new production of Anthony Davis’s pathbreaking Malcolm X opera misspells the surname of a composer. He is John Adams, not Adam.
match_headline: ‘It’s Anthony’s Time’: A Composer Gets His Due

text: An article on Page 36 this weekend about phalloplasty misstates the location of the N.Y.U. Langone transgender-surgery program. It is on the seventh floor of an office building, not the sixth. And the article describes incorrectly an achievement of Dr. Eduardo Rodriguez. He performed the world’s most extensive face transplant, not the first.
match_headline: How Ben Got His Penis

text: An article on Page 42 this weekend about the architect and artist Gaetano Pesce refers incorrectly to the genesis of his upcoming installation at the Aspen Art Museum. The museum first approached Salon 94 Design, Pesce’s New York gallery, about mounting an exhibition in 2020; the gallery did not approach the museum with the idea.
match_headline: In All That He Does, Gaetano Pesce Looks to Counteract Sameness

text: An article on May 1 about the artists Bronwyn Katz and Igshaan Adams referred incorrectly to their first U.S. shows. Katz’s work was first exhibited at the Arts Club of Chicago, not at the New Museum Triennial. Adams had his first U.S. museum exhibition at the SCAD Museum of Art in Savannah, Ga., not at the Art Institute of Chicago.
match_headline: Art That Finds Clarity in South Africa’s Fraught Terrain

text: A picture caption in the In the Garden column last Sunday incompletely described an image of mulch piled against the bark of a tree trunk. As the article correctly stated, the practice, known as volcano mulching, is to be avoided as it promotes bark decay and causes roots to grow up, rather than down into the soil.
match_headline: Why Your Garden Needs Mulch (Assuming You Do It Right)

text: An article on Monday about Sweden and Finland embracing NATO amid the ongoing war in Ukraine misspelled the last name of the director of the Institute for International Affairs. She is Nathalie Tocci, not Tucci.
match_headline: In Rebirth for NATO, Europe Unites in Face of Putin’s Ambition

text: An article on Monday about the use of social media platforms by the suspect in the Buffalo, N.Y., mass shooting misidentified a site as one of the sources that he said had inspired him. He cited 4chan, the writings of the gunman in the Christchurch mass shootings, and The Daily Stormer, not Reddit.
match_headline: After Buffalo Shooting Video Spreads, Social Platforms Face Questions

text: An article on Sunday about Mohammed bin Zayed and his influence in Washington and the Middle East misstated the timing of Bahrain’s formal opening of relations with Israel. It followed the move by the United Arab Emirates; it was not on the same day.
match_headline: Mohammed bin Zayed, an Ambitious U.S. Partner, Rises to Lead the U.A.E.

text: An article on Saturday about student loan debt misstated the name of a government form for students seeking financial aid for college. It is the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, not the Free Application for Financial Aid.
match_headline: Student Loan Borrowers Don’t Deserve ‘Forgiveness.’ They Deserve an Apology.

text: An article on Sunday about youth hockey and ranking teams misstated an age group affected by a change by the MYHockey Rankings website. The site will no longer rank teams of players under age 11, not 12.
match_headline: Youth Hockey Site Rethinks Ranking Teams of Children

text: An obituary on May 9 about the civil rights lawyer Johnnie A. Jones Sr. referred incorrectly to Thurgood Marshall’s age when he argued cases involving sit-ins before the Supreme Court in 1961. He was in his early 50s; he was not “a young civil rights lawyer.”
match_headline: Johnnie A. Jones Sr. Dies at 102; a Civil Rights Lawyer Early On

text: An article on Thursday about Cardinal Joseph Zen and his involvement with a legal aid group that helped protesters in Hong Kong referred imprecisely to the cardinal. He was formerly the Roman Catholic bishop of Hong Kong; as a cardinal, he is a leading bishop in the church, not a former bishop.
match_headline: Hong Kong Police Arrest Cardinal in National Security Case

text: An article on Tuesday about Representative Elise Stefanik of New York and her campaign advertisements that play on themes of the white supremacist “great replacement” theory referred imprecisely to a tweet in which she attacked Democrats and used the phrase “pedo grifters.” Her posting, borrowing language from the baseless pro-Trump QAnon conspiracy theory, referred to “Democrats and the usual pedo grifters.” It did not describe Democrats as “pedo grifters.”
match_headline: Racist Attack Spotlights Stefanik’s Echo of Replacement Theory

text: An article on Tuesday about the study of gene variants as they relate to kidney transplants misstated which donated kidneys are downgraded by risk calculations. Kidneys from only deceased Black donors are downgraded, not living and deceased donors.
match_headline: What a Gene and Its Risks Could Mean for Kidney Transplants

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about Robert C. McFarlane referred incorrectly to his tenure as President Ronald Reagan’s national security adviser. He replaced William P. Clark Jr. as the third person, not the second, to hold that title under Reagan. Richard V. Allen had preceded Mr. Clark in the role. An earlier version of this obituary also misstated the year that Mr. McFarlane made a secret diplomatic trip to Iran at President Ronald Reagan’s request. It was in 1986, not 1987.
match_headline: Robert C. McFarlane, Top Reagan Aide in Iran-Contra Affair, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Indian musician Pandit Shiv Kumar Sharma misstated part of his father’s name. He was Pandit Uma Dutt Sharma, not Pandit Uma Devi Sharma.
match_headline: Pandit Shiv Kumar Sharma, Master of the Santoor, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Friday about the actor Bruce MacVittie misstated the name of a television series on which he appeared. It is “When They See Us,” not “The Way They See Us.”
match_headline: Bruce MacVittie, Ubiquitous Character Actor, Dies at 65

text: An article on Wednesday about the decline of Russia’s energy industry misstated the status of oil shipments by an oil project operated by Exxon Mobil on Sakhalin Island in Russia’s Far East. The project has shipped no oil so far in May, according to Kpler, a tracking firm; it is not the case that it shipped no oil in April.
match_headline: Omens of Decline for Russia’s Once World-Leading Energy Industry

text: An article on Tuesday about what to expect when the Miami Heat plays the Boston Celtics in the N.B.A. Eastern Conference finals this week misstated Max Strus’s playoff role. He has been starting, not coming off the bench.
match_headline: What to Expect as the Heat and Celtics Battle to Win the N.B.A.’s East

text: An article on Wednesday about Tiger Woods and his recent comments about his rivalry with Phil Mickelson misidentified the golfer currently ranked No. 1 in world. He is Scottie Scheffler, not Jon Rahm (who is No. 2).
match_headline: ‘I Believe in Legacies’: Woods Chides Mickelson on the Eve of a Major

text: An article last Thursday about the return of the Robot Heart party and its debut in New York City misquoted Nana Meriwether’s comment about her pageant history. She said that she won the Miss USA pageant in 2012, not that she was first runnerup. (Ms. Meriwether earned the title after the initial winner also won the Miss Universe pageant.)
match_headline: Festival Devotees Migrate East

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the writer Larry Woiwode misspelled the given name of an author who wrote in The Times in 1974 about the long wait for the publication of Mr. Woiwode’s novel “Beyond the Bedroom Wall.” He was Wilfrid Sheed, not Wilfred.
match_headline: Larry Woiwode, Who Wrote of Family, Faith and Rural Life, Dies at 80

text: An article on Thursday about rare phallic-shaped carnivorous plants in the mountains of Cambodia misspelled the name of a spokesman for Cambodia’s ministry of environment. He is Neth Pheaktra, not Neth Sopheaktra.
match_headline: Selfies Further Endanger Rare Phallic Plant, Conservationists Fear

text: An article on Thursday about India’s ban on alcohol in Bihar State and the ban’s effects on neighboring Nepal misspelled the name of the chief minister of Bihar. He is Nitish Kumar, not Nitesh.
match_headline: An Indian State Banned Alcohol. The Drinking Moved to Nearby Nepal.

text: An article on Thursday about House legislation aimed at bulking up the federal government’s efforts to combat domestic terrorism misstated the number of people killed by a gunman in El Paso in 2019. It was 23, not 22.
match_headline: House, Acting After Buffalo Rampage, Moves to Combat Domestic Terrorism

text: An article on Thursday about an event in Montauk that became a coronavirus superspreader event misstated the location of the event. It was at Gurney’s Star Island, not Gurney’s Montauk Resort and Seawater Spa.
match_headline: 70 N.Y. Judges Went on a Montauk Retreat. 20 Came Down With the Virus.

text: An article on Thursday about the economic outlook in Russia referred incorrectly to Vladimir V. Putin’s role in Rosatom, the Russian State Nuclear Energy Corporation. He signed the law that founded the company; he was not listed by Rosatom as a founder.
match_headline: In Russia, as Prices Soar, the Outlook for Its Economy Grows ‘Especially Gloomy’

text: An article on Tuesday about an Emergency World Voices Congress of Writers meeting at the United Nations misidentified the relative in Leila Slimani’s family whom she said had never learned to read or write. It was her grandmother, not her mother and grandmother.
match_headline: We, the Writers? A Global Literary Congress Meets in New York.

text: An article on Thursday about Christian Cooper and his birding series for National Geographic misstated the status of “Extraordinary Birders.” Six episodes are planned; they have not been completed. A picture caption with the article referred incorrectly to the scope of the show. The episodes will be set in multiple locations in America, not all over the world.
match_headline: A Birder Is Back in the Public Eye, Now on His Own Terms

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the L.G.B.T.Q. activist Urvashi Vaid misstated at one point the name of a Boston newspaper where she worked while attending college. As correctly noted elsewhere in the obituary, it was Gay Community News, not Gay City News.
match_headline: Urvashi Vaid, Pioneering L.G.B.T.Q. Activist, Is Dead at 63

text: An article on Friday about the Senate’s approval of a $40 billion aid package for Ukraine misstated the status of a proposed spending bill to address the baby formula crisis. Republicans voted against it this week; they did not block it.
match_headline: The Senate overwhelmingly approves $40 billion in aid to Ukraine, sending it to Biden.

text: An article on Friday about the possibility of a recount in a Republican primary election in Pennsylvania referred incorrectly to a filing made by Bruce Marks in 2020 on Donald Trump’s behalf in Pennsylvania. It was a petition for a writ of certiorari, not an amicus brief.
match_headline: A Pennsylvania Election Storm Brews Again, This Time in a G.O.P. Primary

text: An article on Tuesday about the shooting at a Taiwanese congregation in Laguna Woods, Calif., referred incorrectly to Dr. John Cheng, a physician who was killed while helping to disarm the gunman in the attack. While Dr. Cheng was not a member of the church, friends and family described him as an observant Christian.
match_headline: California Church Shooting Was ‘Hate Incident,’ Sheriff Says

text: An article this weekend about New York City’s push for local control over street traffic regulations includes outdated information. After the article went to press on Thursday, the State Legislature reached a tentative agreement to extend the speed camera program in the city for three years and to keep the cameras on 24 hours a day, seven days a week, pending a vote and official support from the City Council.
match_headline: Why New York City Traffic Cameras Are Off When Drivers Speed the Most

text: An article on Friday about the new arrangements of Latin American ballads by the saxophonist Miguel Zenón and the pianist Luis Perdomo misstated Adrian Quesada’s role in the Black Pumas. He is a guitarist and songwriter, but not a singer.
match_headline: The Bolero Is Timeless. Miguel Zenón Is Giving It a Jazzy Tinge.

text: An article on Page 21 this weekend about Billy Eichner and his romantic comedy “Bros” misstates Judd Apatow’s title on the project. He is a producer of the film, not an executive producer.
match_headline: Crafting a Rom-Com That’s True to 21st-Century Gay Life

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Haiti’s history with slavery and the price that France made generations of Haitians pay for their freedom referred imprecisely to the period in which the colony of Saint-Domingue absorbed nearly 40 percent of the entire trans-Atlantic slave trade. That was the portion between 1785 and 1790, not the cumulative share of the slave trade to that point.
match_headline: The Root of Haiti’s Misery: Reparations to Enslavers

text: An article on Wednesday about reactions to the Uvalde school shooting by the parents of children killed at Sandy Hook elementary school misstated the location of a previous school shooting. It was at Santa Fe High School in Texas, not New Mexico.
match_headline: ‘It’s almost like an instant replay.’ Newtown parents grapple with another school shooting.

text: An article on Wednesday about George Miller’s next film “Furiosa” misstated the number of films in the “Mad Max” series. “Furiosa” would be the fifth in the series, not the fourth.
match_headline: George Miller Is at the Cannes Film Festival Making ‘Furiosa’ (That’s Right)

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about Kristine Gebbie, the first national AIDS policy coordinator in the United States, misstated the number of children from her first marriage who survive her. It is three, not four. (One daughter, Sharon Eileen Gebbie, is known by both Sharon and Eileen.) The obituary also misstated Dr. Gebbie’s last year as director of the Columbia University School of Nursing’s Center for Health Policy. It was 2008, not 2000.
match_headline: Kristine Gebbie, the First U.S. AIDS Czar, Dies at 78

text: An article on Sunday about the discovery of human remains exposed by dropping water levels in Lake Mead described incorrectly the deaths of Gus Greenbaum and his wife, Bess, in their Phoenix home. They were beaten and stabbed, not fatally shot.
match_headline: Bodies Pulled From Parched Lake Mead Stir Wise-Guy Ghosts of Las Vegas

text: An article on Tuesday about the resignation of the mayor of Anaheim, Calif., amid a corruption investigation referred incorrectly to a political consultant who provided information to authorities in the investigation. Melahat Raffiei was a cooperating witness, not a confidential informant.
match_headline: Anaheim Mayor Resigns as F.B.I. Investigates Angel Stadium Deal

text: An article on Tuesday about the singer Oliver Sim misstated the text on Sim’s T-shirt. An allusion to the serial killer in “Silence of the Lambs,” the text reads “Buffalo Bill’s Body Lotion,” not “Buffalo Bill’s Skin Lotion.”
match_headline: The Horror and Happiness of Oliver Sim

text: An article on Saturday about the pop star Harry Styles misstated his age when One Direction went on hiatus. He was in his early twenties, not 24.
match_headline: Harry Styles Is Still a Dreamy Cipher on His Third LP, ‘Harry’s House’

text: An obituary on May 9 about the drummer Ric Parnell, using information from his partner, referred incorrectly to two of his survivors, Emma Parnell and Sarah Currie. They are his half sisters, not his stepsisters.
match_headline: Ric Parnell, Real Drummer in a Famous Fake Band, Dies at 70

text: An obituary on Sunday about the composer and synthesizer player Vangelis misstated the name of the book of the Bible that inspired “666,” an album by his band Aphrodite’s Child. It is the Book of Revelation, not Revelations.
match_headline: Vangelis, Composer Best Known for ‘Chariots of Fire,’ Dies at 79

text: An article on Sunday about an experimental psychedelic therapy that some female veterans are undergoing in Mexico to treat post-traumatic stress disorder misidentified one of the institutions where researchers intend to study the treatment protocols later this year. It is Baylor College of Medicine, not Baylor University.
match_headline: ‘I Want to Reset My Brain’: Female Veterans Turn to Psychedelic Therapy

text: An article on Saturday about President Biden’s five-day visit to South Korea and Japan misstated the day when Rahm Emanuel, Mr. Biden’s ambassador to Japan, gave remarks to reporters about the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework. He made them on Thursday, not Friday.
match_headline: In South Korea, Biden Seeks to Rebuild Economic Ties Across Asia

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the assassination of a senior member of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps misstated part of the meaning of the phrase “defend the shrine” in Iran. It is used to justify Iran’s presence in the war in Syria, and to identify those fighting against the Islamic State, not fighting for it.
match_headline: A Senior Member of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Is Killed in Tehran

text: An item in the Metropolitan Diary column on Sunday misstated the name of a museum on the Upper West Side. It is the American Museum of Natural History, not the American Museum of National History.
match_headline: ‘It Was My First Visit to the City and I Had an Interview Lined Up’

text: An article on Friday about the development 40 years ago of the Off Off Broadway show “Little Shop of Horrors” and the play’s lasting influence misidentified the Manhattan neighborhood in which the WPA Theater was located when the play opened there in 1982. It was in the Flatiron district, not the East Village.
match_headline: ‘Little Shop of Horrors’ at 40: The Plant That Conquered the World

text: An obituary on Saturday about the writer Roger Angell referred incorrectly to his book “This Old Man.” Although the essay that gave the book its title was about aging, the book itself was a collection of various kinds of writing, not of essays on that subject. The earlier version also misidentified the kind of fox terrier Mr. Angell loved. It was smooth, not wire-haired.
match_headline: Roger Angell, Who Wrote About Baseball With Passion, Dies at 101

text: An obituary on Saturday about the art critic Suzi Gablik misstated where in Blacksburg, Va., she died. She died at her home, not in a hospice facility.
match_headline: Suzi Gablik, Art Critic Who Took Modernism to Task, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on May 13 about the columnist John Leo referred incorrectly to columns he wrote that appeared on the opposite page from those of the writer Garry Wills. They appeared in The National Catholic Reporter, not Commonweal.
match_headline: John Leo, Columnist Who Took Aim at Liberal Pieties, Dies at 86

text: An article on Thursday about the musician Brian Jackson referred imprecisely to Peter Adarkwah’s role at the music label Barely Breaking Even. He is the sole head of the label, not one of several. The article also misstated when Mr. Jackson decided to start a podcast with the activist and death row prisoner Keith LaMar. It was after learning about his cause, not after appearing on a benefit album.
match_headline: Brian Jackson, a Key Gil Scott-Heron Collaborator, Reintroduces Himself

text: An obituary on Thursday about Thomas S. Murphy, the businessman who led the purchase of the American Broadcast Company, referred incorrectly to the ABC News programs “20/20” and “Nightline.” They both began before Capital Cities acquired ABC, not after.
match_headline: Thomas S. Murphy, Broadcasting ‘Minnow’ Who Swallowed ABC, Dies at 96

text: An article on Friday about Léolia Jeanjean and Fernanda Contreras Gomez’s path to their first Grand Slam tournament at the French Open misstated the year that Gómez met Christo van Rensburg as he was coaching players in Austin. It was in 2020, not 2001.
match_headline: Two Outsiders Get Career Boosts at the French Open

text: An article this weekend on Page 16 about a new documentary focused on the all-female band Fanny misstates Rick Danko’s role in the Band. He was a singer in the group, not the lead singer.
match_headline: The All-Female Band Fanny Made History. A New Doc Illuminates It.

text: An article this weekend on Page 14 about the fourth season of the Danish series “Borgen” misstates the distance between Ilulissat, Greenland, and Copenhagen. They are 2,000 miles apart, not 5,000.
match_headline: A Darker ‘Borgen’ Returns, and Heads to Greenland

text: An article this weekend on Page 4 about seven great biking cities includes a photo caption that misidentifies a location. It is a bridge on Île Saint-Louis in Paris, not Place de la République. The article also misspells the name of the “Godfather of Rollerskating” in San Francisco. It is David Miles, not David Mills. The article also misidentifies the status of the C & O Canal in Washington, D.C., and Maryland. All 184.5 miles of the canal have been preserved, not some of it. The article also refers incompletely to a bike route through Washington, D.C. The bike lane in Rock Creek Park is temporarily closed between P Street and Shoreham Drive. (It will reopen in June.)
match_headline: 7 Great Biking Cities (and Which Trails to Ride)

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the anti-vaccine movement misstates one publication in which Brian Deer’s multipart investigation into Andrew Wakefield’s 1998 Lancet paper was published. It appeared in The BMJ and The Sunday Times of London, but not in The Times of London. The article also misstates the number of segments from Deer’s investigation that appeared in The BMJ; it was five, not two. Finally, the article refers imprecisely to the timing of Deer’s investigation. It began before, not after, 10 of 12 co-authors of the Lancet paper issued a partial retraction in March 2004.

A column on Friday about mass shoot­ings and civil virtue misattributed the suggestion that families could keep their children safe by home-­schooling them. It was made by a writer for the online pub­lication The Federalist, not by the Feder­alist Society.
match_headline: The G.O.P. War on Civil Virtue

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor Kenneth Welsh misidentified the play in which he acted alongside Glenn Close. It was “The Real Thing,” not “The Little Foxes.” It also misstated what his last stage performance was. It was a reading of “A Christmas Carol,” not a production of ‘Under Milk Wood.” And it misstated the name of the town in Ontario where he lived. It is Sandford, not Sanford. In addition, the obituary referred incorrectly to Mr. Welsh’s son, Devon. He is from Mr. Welsh’s third marriage, not his first.
match_headline: Kenneth Welsh, Memorable as a Villain on ‘Twin Peaks,’ Dies at 80

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about Baz Luhrmann and his new Elvis Presley film misidentified a subject. The person on the left is Schuyler Weiss, Mr. Luhrmann’s producing partner, not an assistant. Another caption misidentified a poster shown. It was for John Huston’s film “Moulin Rouge” from 1952, not the film “Moulin Rouge” from 2001.
match_headline: Baz Luhrmann Is Ready for Rhinestones, Cadillacs, Dr. Feelgood and a Svengali

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the anti-vaccine movement misstates one publication in which Brian Deer’s multipart investigation into Andrew Wakefield’s 1998 Lancet paper was published. It appeared in The BMJ and The Sunday Times of London, but not in The Times of London. The article also misstates the number of segments from Deer’s investigation that appeared in The BMJ; it was five, not two. Finally, the article refers imprecisely to the timing of Deer’s investigation. It began before, not after, 10 of 12 co-authors of the Lancet paper issued a partial retraction in March 2004.

An article on Tuesday about a draft of an agreement by the European Union to ban most Russian oil imports misstated the E.U.’s previous actions against Russia for the invasion of Ukraine. It has not barred imports of Russian natural gas, but individual nations have.
match_headline: Europe’s Russian Oil Ban Could Overhaul Global Energy Market

text: An article on Monday about Turkey and NATO misstated when France sent ships in support of Greece. It was in 2020, not 2019.
match_headline: For NATO, Turkey Is a Disruptive Ally

text: An article on Sunday about renovations of Old Library at Trinity College Dublin misspelled the name of a nearby library where two reading rooms will be relocated during the work. It is the Ussher Library, not Usher.
match_headline: An Irish National Treasure Gets Set for a Long-Needed Restoration

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about how some veterans have started businesses that draw from their experiences in Iraq and Afghanistan misidentified a manufacturing facility. A contractor makes rubber soles for Combat Flip Flops, not a Combat Flip Flops factory.
match_headline: They Served. Now, Inspired by What They Saw, They Sell.

text: An article on Monday about the Carolina Hurricanes’ Game 7 against the Rangers attributed an erroneous distinction to the Carolina Hurricanes. They became the first N.H.L. team to lose their first six road playoff games, not the first to lose six road playoff games.
match_headline: Rangers Aim to Give the Hurricanes an Unhappy Homecoming

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misidentified the actress who played a drama student in the Alfred Hitchcock film “Stage Fright.” She was Jane Wyman, not Marlene Dietrich. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Julia’ and the MTV Movie & TV Awards

text: An article on Tuesday about a retrospective at the Museum of the Moving Image that looks at the career of the cinematographer James Wong Howe misidentified an actor and a shot in “The Prisoner of Zenda.” The image shows Douglas Fairbanks Jr. and Ronald Colman; it is not a split-screen shot showing just Colman.
match_headline: James Wong Howe: A Gutsy Cinematographer Finally Gets His Due

text: A review last Wednesday of Inga’s Bar misstated the year in which another Brooklyn Heights bar, Jack the Horse Tavern, closed. It was 2020, not 2021.
match_headline: The Food at Inga’s Bar Is Far From Bar Food

text: A column on Sunday about mass shoot­ings misspelled the surname of the prime minister of New Zealand. She is Jacinda Ardern, not Arden.
match_headline: America’s Human Sacrifices

text: An obituary on Sunday about the theologian Rosemary Radford Ruether, who brought feminist, antiracist and environmental perspectives to bear on the teachings of the Roman Catholic Church, misstated the location of Scripps College, the Claremont Graduate School (now Claremont Graduate University) and the Claremont School of Theology, all of which granted her degrees. They are in Claremont, not Pomona, Calif.
match_headline: Rosemary Radford Ruether, Feminist Theologian, Dies at 85

text: An article on Sunday about the manufacturer of the military-style rifle used in the recent Texas elementary school shooting misstated the name of the school in Florida where a mass shooting occurred in 2018. It is Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, not Parkland High School.
match_headline: Gun in Texas Shooting Came From Company Known for Pushing Boundaries

text: An article on Saturday about David Kertzer, a man who has spent decades excavating the Vatican’s hidden history, misstated the title of one of his books. It is “The Popes Against the Jews,” not “The Pope Against the Jews.”
match_headline: Deep in Vatican Archives, Scholar Discovers ‘Flabbergasting’ Secrets

text: An article on Wednesday about the theft of a Brooklyn church’s tabernacle misstated its contents. It held only communion wafers, not wafers and wine. It also mischaracterized the work being done on the church. The work was being done on the church’s exterior, not on its sanctuary.
match_headline: Theft of a Church’s Tabernacle Leaves More Than a Physical Void

text: An article on Saturday about how the decline in illegal immigration has affected California farms misstated the origin of “high rise” varieties of broccoli. They were developed through conventional plant breeding; they are not genetically modified. The article also referred incompletely to a statistic on average California farm employment. The decline from 170,000 in 2010 to 150,000 in 2020 counts only workers hired directly by farms for crop production, not those employed by farm labor contractors, who include foreign workers on temporary H-2A visas.
match_headline: Illegal Immigration Is Down, Changing the Face of California Farms

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the golfer Michelle Wie West mischaracterized the men’s U.S. Open. The tournament is operated by the United States Golf Association, not the PGA Tour.
match_headline: At the U.S. Women’s Open, Michelle Wie West Reflects on an ‘Amazing Journey’

text: An article on Tuesday about French officials’ response to chaos at the Champions League Final in Paris misstated the given name of a British lawmaker who was in Paris to support Liverpool. It is Ian Byrne, not Liam.
match_headline: Under Fire for Chaos at Soccer Final, France Rejects Blame for Failures

text: An article on Wednesday about Rafael Nadal’s tennis match with Novak Djokovic at the French Open misstated the score when Djokovic served for the fourth set. He was ahead, 5-3, not 5-4. (Rafael Nadal broke his serve to make it, 5-4.)
match_headline: Nadal and Djokovic Meet Again, With Gen Z Breakout in Wings

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the television series “Pistol” on Hulu and the television series “Angelyne” on Peacock misspelled Johnny Rotten’s real name. He is John Lydon, not John Lyndon.
match_headline: Rock ’n’ Roll Swindles, Revisited

text: An article on Friday about the first Hindi novel to win the International Booker Prize incorrectly described the partition of British India. It was partitioned into India and Pakistan; India was not partitioned from Pakistan.
match_headline: Hindi Novel Wins International Booker Prize for the First Time

text: An article last Thursday about the unconventional fashion sense of John Fetterman, the Democratic nominee for a Senate seat from Pennsylvania, misstated the degree that he received from Harvard. It was a master’s degree in public policy, not business administration.
match_headline: John Fetterman and the Remaking of Political Image

text: An obituary on Sunday about Andy Fletcher, who played synthesizers in the British band Depeche Mode, misstated the year that the group released its popular album “Violator.” It was 1990, not 1989.
match_headline: Andy Fletcher, a Founder of Depeche Mode, Dies at 60

text: An article on Wednesday about civilian deaths in Mali that have been linked to a Russian militia misspelled the surname of the Sahel director for Human Rights Watch. She is Corinne Dufka, not Dukfa.
match_headline: ‘The Killings Didn’t Stop.’ In Mali, a Massacre With a Russian Footprint.

text: An article on Thursday about the U.S. decision to send advanced weapons to Ukraine misspelled the surname of a founder of the Silverado Policy Accelerator. He is Dmitri Alperovitch, not Alperovich. The article also misstated the title of NATO’s leader. He is the secretary general, not the director general.
match_headline: The U.S. Is Sending Advanced Weapons to Ukraine. But Conditions Apply.

text: An article on Thursday about the Trump-era prosecutor John H. Durham and the loss of his case against Michael Sussmann misspelled the given name of the manager of Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign. He is Robby Mook, not Robbie. The article also misstated when the Justice Department’s inspector general issued its report on the Russia inquiry. It was December 2019, not November 2019.
match_headline: Sussmann Acquittal Raises Question: What Is Durham Actually Trying to Do?

text: An article on Monday about a new documentary from Trump allies claiming the 2020 election was stolen misstated the location of Fred Eshelman, who donated $2.5 million to a group called True the Vote. He is in North Carolina, not Texas.
match_headline: A Big Lie in a New Package

text: A map with an article on Thursday about the Q23 bus route in Queens misstated the scale. The distance is ½ mile, not five miles.
match_headline: When the Only Way to Get to Work Is This Slow Bus

text: An article on Wednesday about how Lviv, Ukraine, is changing its architecture to house war refugees misstated the city’s population. It is 800,000, not 400,000.
match_headline: To House Refugees, Lviv Wants to Make Beautiful Buildings That Last

text: An article on March 23 about a potential deal among six groups of victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks to divide Afghan central bank assets misstated the first name of a member of a group of Sept. 11 plaintiffs, known as the Ashton case. He is Brett Eagleson, not Brian. This correction was delayed because editors were only recently made aware of the error.
match_headline: Rival Sept. 11 Victims Near Potential Deal to Divide Afghan Central Bank Assets

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about a hub for Inuit artistry in arctic Canada misspells the name of the Indigenous First Nations people of Canada and the United States with whom Wanda Nanibush is identified. The people are Anishinaabe, not Anishabee.
match_headline: Making Art on Top of the World

text: An article on Friday about what television shows to watch this weekend misspelled the title of a CBS political drama. It is “Madam Secretary,” not “Madame Secretary.”
match_headline: How Much Watching Time Do You Have This Weekend?

text: An article on Page 2 this weekend about highlights of Milan Design Week misstated the name of the exhibition space in Milan showing work by the design company Studiopepe. It is Baranzate Ateliers, not Baranzate Studios. The article also misstated the name of the space in Milan exhibiting products by the lighting company Flos. It is Fabbrica Orobia, not Fabricca Orobia.
match_headline: A Panorama of Design

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 13 this weekend about nature-based patterned household goods misstates the price of Bloom fabric by Brook Perdigon Textiles. The fabric is $216 per yard, not $9 per yard.
match_headline: Nothing but Flowers (and Some Creatures, Too)

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about the reasons people come to New York misspells the name of a woman who moved from Newtown, Pa. Her name is Susan Carey Dempsey, not Susan Cary Dempsey.
match_headline: 5 Things to Do This Weekend

text: A column on Friday about voters’ re­sponses to inflation misstated the month of the Eurostat inflation estimate re­leased on May 30. It was a preliminary estimate for May, not March.
match_headline: The Perverse Politics of Inflation

text: An article on Monday about mass shootings in several U.S. cities during the same weekend misstated the name of an anti-violence group. It is Moms Demand Action, not Mom Demands Action.
match_headline: Mass Shooting in Philadelphia Kills at Least 3 on Weekend of Gun Violence

text: An item in the Conversation feature on Friday misstated the number of generations of royals standing beside Queen Elizabeth II at the Platinum Jubilee. Three generations stood by her, not four.
match_headline: How to Watch Queen Elizabeth II’s Platinum Jubilee Events

text: An article on Sunday about talented Russian goalies in the N.H.L. misspelled the given name of the head coach of the Tampa Bay Lightning. He is Jon Cooper, not John.
match_headline: In the N.H.L., Russian Goalies Grab the Spotlight

text: An article on Tuesday about the Mets split series with the Dodgers during their West Coast trip referred incorrectly to Mets starter David Peterson’s performance on Saturday against the Dodgers. He allowed four runs, one of which was an earned run; he did not allow one run.
match_headline: The Mets Keep the Doors Open, the TV On and Opponents on Edge

text: An article on Monday about Joel Kim Booster, the writer and star of the movie “Fire Island,” misstated the name of Booster’s boyfriend. While he uses John-Michael Kelly on some social media, his name is John-Michael Sudsina.
match_headline: For Joel Kim Booster, Making ‘Fire Island’ Was a Real Trip

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the lyricist Paul Vance misidentified the television show on which Brian Hyland performed Mr. Vance’s song “Itsy Bitsy Teenie Weenie Yellow Polka Dot Bikini.” It was “The Dick Clark Show,” also known as “Dick Clark’s Saturday Night Beechnut Show” — not “American Bandstand.”
ref_headline: Itsy Bitsy Teenie Weenie Yellow Polka Dot Bikini.
match_headline: Paul Vance, Lyricist Behind an ‘Itsy Bitsy’ Bikini, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Sunday about the talent manager George Shapiro referred incorrectly to Beverly Hills, Calif., where he lived. It is a city in Los Angeles County, not a section of Los Angeles.
match_headline: George Shapiro, Talent Manager Who Pushed for ‘Seinfeld,’ Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on June 1 about the author Walter Abish misidentified a college where he had taught. It was Wheaton College in Massachusetts, not Wheaton College in Illinois.
