An obituary on Wednesday about the educator Charlotte Frank misstated in one instance the given name of one of her sons. As the obituary correctly noted elsewhere, he is Harley Frank, not Harlan.
match_headline: Charlotte Frank, Shaper of New York City Curriculums, Dies at 93

text: An obituary on Saturday about the professor and psychiatric social worker Sophie Freud misspelled a form of currency used in Vienna when she was a girl there. Her grandfather Sigmund Freud would often give her eight schillings, not shillings, to buy a ticket to the theater.
match_headline: Sophie Freud, Critic of Her Grandfather’s Gospel, Dies at 97

text: An obituary on June 2 about the C.I.A. whistle-blower David C. MacMichael misspelled the surname of a former secretary of state. He was George Shultz, not Schultz. It also misspelled the surname of Dr. MacMichael’s wife. She is Barbara Jentzsch, not Jentsch.
match_headline: David C. MacMichael, C.I.A. Whistleblower, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Friday about the Colombian drug lord Gilberto Rodríguez Orejuela misstated the location of Mariquita, the town in Colombia where he was born. It is northwest of Bogotá, the nation’s capital, not southeast.
match_headline: Gilberto Rodríguez Orejuela, Colombian Drug Lord, Dies at 83

text: An article on April 29 about 16 states that sued the Postal Service for failing to properly vet clean alternatives to gas-powered mail trucks misstated the agency that brought to light the poor gas mileage of new Postal Service vehicles. It was the Postal Service itself, not the Environmental Protection Agency, that found that the trucks would achieve only 14.7 miles to the gallon, or 8.6 miles per gallon when using air conditioning.
match_headline: States Sue Postal Service Over New Gas-Powered Mail Trucks

text: An article on Wednesday about New Jersey centrists’s efforts to topple the state’s ban on fusion voting misstated the timing of a 1997 Supreme Court decision on the issue. It was more than 25 years ago, not nearly. It also included a paraphrase of the court’s opinion that was incorrectly presented as a direct quotation. While the court’s opinion expressed a preference for the political stability of a two-party system, the text of the decision referred to the “perceived benefits of a stable two-party system.”
ref_headline: perceived benefits of a stable two-party system.
match_headline: New Jersey Centrists Seek to Legalize Their Dream: The Moderate Party

text: An article on Thursday about a Game 4 tie between the New York Rangers and Tampa Bay Lightning hockey teams misstated how long Ondrej Palat, Steven Stamkos and Nikita Kucherov have been on the Lightning together. The three have played together since the 2013-14 season, not 2015.
match_headline: Rangers Head Home to the Garden, Where They Always Seem to Win

text: An article on Friday about Naasón Joaquín García, the head of the church La Luz del Mundo, who was sentenced to more than 16 years in prison for sexually abusing minors referred incorrectly to Alondra Ocampo. She is a woman.
match_headline: Leader of Mexican Church Is Sentenced to 16 Years for Sex Crimes

text: An article on Friday about Representative Liz Cheney and her role in the Jan. 6 hearings misstated the number of children that Ms. Cheney has. She has five children, not four.
match_headline: Liz Cheney Takes On Trump, and Her Own Party

text: An article on Page 7 this weekend about the Paul Taylor Dance Company and its upcoming performance at the Joyce Theater misstates the program’s end date at the Joyce. It runs until June 19, not June 18. It also incorrectly includes “Fibers” among the dances with designs by Robert Rauschenberg. Additionally, it describes incorrectly an evening of the choreographer Paul Taylor’s works in 1957. It was one of his first evening-length performances, not the first time he showed original works.
match_headline: The Everyday Avant-Gardist: Paul Taylor’s First Principles

text: An article on June 5 about roommates in New York City misstated the city where Ivana and Kalina Popova lived before moving to New York City. It was Kansas City, Kan., not Kansas City, Mo.
match_headline: Their Solution to the Housing Crisis? Living With Strangers.

text: An obituary on May 28 about the Holocaust survivor Margot Heuman misstated her age when she and her family were deported to the Jewish “transit” ghetto Theresienstadt. She was 15, not 14. It also misstated how much time elapsed between when Ms. Heuman and her family were sent to Auschwitz and when Dita Neumann and her family were sent there. It was a few days, not a month.
match_headline: Margot Heuman, Who Bore Witness to the Holocaust as a Gay Woman, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Thursday about the computer designer Dave Smith misstated the source of the quotation from him that began, “If we had done MIDI the usual way.” It was from an interview with the Red Bull Music Academy, not with Waveshaper Media.
ref_headline: If we had done MIDI the usual way.
match_headline: Dave Smith, Whose Synthesizers Shaped Electronic Music, Dies at 72

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the political cartoonist Ranan Lurie misstated the location in Israel of the Herzliya Gymnasium, where he attended high school. It is in Tel Aviv, not in the town of Herzliya.
match_headline: Ranan Lurie, Political Cartoonist With a Global Pen, Dies at 90

text: An article May 29 about the role of Times Square in New York City’s economic recovery misstated the history of 1 Times Square. It was one of the former headquarters of The New York Times. It was not the original one.
match_headline: Times Square at Its Overcrowded, Dizzying Worst Is Exactly What N.Y.C. Needs

text: An article last Sunday about the hosts of the podcast “The Ion Pod” misstated the role of a production company in the New People’s Cine­ma film festival in October 2021. Play Nice was a sponsor; it did not finance the festival.
match_headline: Who Is the Ion Pack?

text: An article last Sunday about parents who are upset with the Gerber Photo Search contest misstated the given name of the winner’s mother. She is Meredith Slish, not Melissa. The article also included outdated information about Ann Turner Cook, whose image was used as the original Gerber baby. She died on June 3 at age 95.
match_headline: There’s a New Gerber Baby and Some Parents Are Mad

text: An article in the Arena feature last Sunday about the artist Wangechi Mutu misstated the title of an artwork by her. It is “Nywele,” not “Nywele I.”
match_headline: Wangechi Mutu Brings Her Sculptures to Storm King

text: An article last Sunday about New York City’s priciest residential closings misstated the location of Estanne Fawer’s new apartment on the Upper West Side. It is on West 86th Street and West End Avenue, not near 61st Street and Riverside Park.
match_headline: A Bird’s-Eye View of Central Park and Beyond, for $70.5 Million

text: An article on Sunday about fashion giants’ efforts to promote synthetic materials in garments misstated the share of global carbon dioxide emissions produced by the fashion industry. It is as much as 8 percent, not 8 to 10 percent.
match_headline: How Fashion Giants Recast Plastic as Good for the Planet

text: An article on Saturday about a warning from the United States to China about activity near Taiwan misquoted Defense Secretary Lloyd J. Austin III. He said, “The stakes are especially stark in the Taiwan Strait,” not, “Mistakes are especially stark in the Taiwan Strait.”
ref_headline: The stakes are especially stark in the Taiwan Strait,
match_headline: U.S. Warns China on Taiwan as Defense Officials Meet to Cool Tensions

text: An article on Saturday about the removal of the names of Confederate generals from schools in Shenandoah County, Va., misspelled the last name of a man who spoke at a school board meeting. He is Stuart Didawick, not Didiwick.
match_headline: Stonewall Jackson’s Name Fell Fast, and a Fury Quickly Followed

text: Because of an editing error, a photo caption with an article on Sunday about the quest of a Long Island seaweed farmer to make kelp the next kale misstated the location of Newtown Creek, a Superfund site. It is in Brooklyn, not the Bronx.
match_headline: The Johnny Appleseed of Sugar Kelp

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about player trades that the Boston Celtics did not make misstated the Celtics’ seed in the Eastern Conference playoffs. They were the No. 2 seed, not No. 3.
match_headline: The Celtics Got Lucky by Not Getting What They Wanted

text: An article on Monday about The Tampa Bay Lightning hockey team going to three Stanley Cup finals referred incorrectly to the Islanders’ four consecutive Stanley Cup victories. They were from 1980 to 1983, not to 1984. The article also referred incorrectly to Tampa Bay players’ postseason experience. They have combined to play 204 games in Stanley Cup finals, not in the playoffs overall.
match_headline: Lightning Will Go for a Third Straight Stanley Cup Against the Avalanche

text: An article on Saturday about the possible impact of abortion laws on the future of college softball misstated the academic class of the Oklahoma University softball player Tiare Jennings. She is a sophomore, not a freshman.
match_headline: Oklahoma’s Abortion Law Raises Questions About N.C.A.A.’s Softball World Series

text: An article on Saturday about a new garden adjacent to the landmark McKim building in Manhattan misstated the cost of building J. Pierpont Morgan’s library. It cost just over $1 million (about $32 million today), not $50,000.
match_headline: Manhattan’s New Green Space Was J.P. Morgan’s Side Yard

text: An article on Monday with a list of the Tony Award winners for 2022 misspelled the name of the Regional Theater Tony Award winner. It is the Court Theater, not Cort.
match_headline: Tony Award Winners 2022: Complete List

text: An article on Sunday about transforming shopping malls mischaracterized North­ Park Center in Dallas. It is an enclosed shopping mall, not an outdoor mall. The article also misspelled the surname of a landscape architect who worked with Lawrence Halprin. He was Richard Vignolo, not Vignola.
match_headline: Get In. We’re Going to Save the Mall.

text: An article on Tuesday about testimony from Day 2 of the Jan. 6 hearings misstated Chris Stirewalt’s role in Fox News’s election night projection that Joseph R. Biden Jr. won Arizona in the 2020 election. While Mr. Stirewalt was part of the team that made the decision, he did not make the call himself.
match_headline: 4 takeaways from Day 2 of the Jan. 6 hearings.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Andrew Giuliani’s campaign for New York governor and his father’s spotlight at his campaign events misstated the location of Hauppauge, a hamlet in Long Island. It is in central Long Island not eastern.
match_headline: The Main Draw at Andrew Giuliani’s Campaign Events? His Father.

text: An article on Monday about fine art inspired by the sport of basketball misstated the middle name of an artist who built a bronze sculpture of the arm of the Philadelphia 76ers star Joel Embiid. The artist is Hank Willis Thomas, not Hank Williams Thomas.
match_headline: The Art World Loves Basketballs. And Hoops and Jerseys and Backboards.

text: An article on Sunday about declining numbers of officers in urban police de­partments misstated the location of the fatal shooting of Philando Castile by a po­lice officer in 2016. It was Falcon Heights, Minn., not St. Paul.
match_headline: Violent Crime Is Up as Cities Lose Police Officers. What Now?

text: Because of a production error, the Off the Menu column last Wednesday duplicated menu items for the restaurant 53 and omitted items for the Noortwyck. The correct list can be found at nytimes.com/food.
match_headline: Building a Juneteenth Menu for the 21st Century, One Recipe at a Time

text: An article on Tuesday about Ukraine’s resistance to Russia’s invasion and its impact on Taiwan’s military strategy misstated the rank of Sun Li-fang, the spokesman of Taiwan’s defense ministry. He is a major general, not a colonel.
match_headline: As China Rattles Sabers, Taiwan Asks: Are We Ready for War?

text: An article on Sunday about an environmental rating system used in the apparel industry included in some editions an outdated affiliation for Simon Hall, a quoted expert. Mr. Hall is a senior manager for sustainability at Walmart; he is no longer a director at the National Wildlife Federation. (Because Mr. Hall is now working for one of the companies that is a subject of the article, his quote was removed.)
match_headline: Nicole McLaughlin’s Designs Are No Joke

text: An article on Sunday about demonstrations in hundreds of cities by supporters of gun control legislation misquoted Frank Ruiz, one of the protesters at the rally in San Antonio. He said that he was “scared and tired of gun violence,” not “scared and tired of guns.”
ref_headline: scared and tired of gun violence,
match_headline: ‘Scared and Tired’: Thousands Across the U.S. Rally Against Gun Violence

text: A column on Wednesday about Saudi Arabia and a new pro golf tour mis­spelled the surname of a professional golfer. He is Chi Chi Rodriguez, not Ro­driquez.
match_headline: Saudi Arabia Should Take a Mulligan on Golf. Here’s What It Can Do Instead.

text: An article on Thursday about flooding in Yellowstone National Park and climate change’s expected impact on U.S. national parks misstated where 1.3 million Joshua trees were destroyed by a wildfire in 2020. The tree deaths occurred in the nearby Mojave National Preserve, not in Joshua Tree National Park.
match_headline: Flooding Chaos in Yellowstone, a Sign of Crises to Come

text: An article on Thursday about money laundering schemes exposed in the province of British Columbia, Canada, described incorrectly the actions that the Cullen commission report said provincial government officials took to address money laundering in the gaming industry. The report said that some officials took actions that were insufficient and that one official took no action, not that all officials took no action.
match_headline: Lavish Money Laundering Schemes Exposed in Canada

text: An article on Tuesday about liberal district attorneys’ reactions to the ouster of the district attorney of San Francisco in a recall vote misstated the year Larry Krasner was elected to a second term as district attorney of Philadelphia. It was 2021, not 2020.
match_headline: The Lessons Liberal Prosecutors Are Drawing From San Francisco’s Backlash

text: An article on Saturday about a group of billionaires behind a push to reinvigorate computer chip-making in the United States referred imprecisely to the White House’s relationship with the America’s Frontier Fund. While it is engaged with the fund, it did not direct the fund to lead the Quad Investor Network; it announced the network’s launch at the fund’s request.
match_headline: The Billionaires Behind a Push to Reinvigorate U.S. Chip-Making

text: An article on Thursday about “Downtown Stories,” a series of interactive theater staged in downtown Manhattan, omitted one of the writers of “Uncovering Downtown.” The work was written by Mona Mansour and the director Jessica Holt, not only Mansour.
match_headline: In ‘Downtown Stories,’ Theater That Uses New York as Its Stage

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about a TikTok account dedicated to New York’s publicly accessible bathrooms misidentifies the profession of an author of a study on public bathrooms in New York City. Boyeong Hong is a data analyst, not an urban planner.
match_headline: Need to Find a Bathroom in New York City? Try TikTok.

text: An article on Page 6 this weekend about the play “Corsicana” by Will Arbery misspells the surname of an actor. He is Will Dagger, not Daggett. The article also refers incorrectly to the age difference between Will Arbery and his sister Julia. She is two years older, not three.
match_headline: In ‘Corsicana,’ Will Arbery Puts Art, Family and Down Syndrome Onstage

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about the clay artist Rose B. Simpson misidentifies the location of the Fabric Workshop and Museum. It’s in Philadelphia, not Pittsburgh.
match_headline: Rose B. Simpson Thinks in Clay

text: A profile on Page 13 this weekend of the actor-director Cooper Raiff misattributes a line of dialogue from the film “Lars and the Real Girl.” It was the character of Gus who spoke about growing into maturity, not the title character.
match_headline: Adams Announces Plan to Fix New York City’s Growing Housing Crisis

text: An article on Page 28 this weekend about transgender therapy refers incorrectly to the comprehensive assessment that Grace Lidinsky-Smith said she wished she had received. It was the last Standards of Care endorsed for adults by the World Professional Association for Transgender Health, not for adolescents. And the article refers incorrectly to Colt St. Amand’s role at the Mayo Clinic. He is a family medicine physician at Mayo and works as a clinical psychologist in private practice.
match_headline: The Battle Over Gender Therapy

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about a woman diagnosed with acromegaly misstates the location of the pituitary gland in relation to the optic nerves. The gland is below the nerves, not above.
match_headline: What if This Wasn’t Menopause After All?

text: An article on June 12 about the Indonesian art collective Ruangrupa misstated the number of beds in a dormitory at Documenta’s Fridericianum. Thirty-eight are planned, not 16.
match_headline: A Radical Collective Takes Over One of the World’s Biggest Art Shows

text: An article last Sunday about the revival of the roadside franchise Stuckey’s misstated the name of an almond brand. It is Blue Diamond, not Diamond.
match_headline: The Pralines, Pecan Log Rolls and Nostalgia Fueling the Stuckey’s Revival

text: An article last Sunday about Milan Design Week misstated the surname of a designer. She is Audrey Large, not Range.
match_headline: Color, Craft and Comfort at Milan Design Week

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Edna Tafari Makonnen and Jamal Akil Rob­inson misquoted Ms. Makonnen’s description of her time in high school with Mr. Robinson. She said, “He didn’t know me,” not, “He didn’t even remember me.”
match_headline: Fitting Into His Schedule, Then Into Her Royal Family

text: A review on June 5 about Eliza­beth Day’s novel “Magpie” mis­quoted a sentence in the book. It is “But nothing stayed perfect for­ ever, did it?” It is not “But nothing stayed perfect together, did it?”
match_headline: Welcome to ‘Single White Female’ With a Maternal Twist

text: An article on Sunday about a project documenting Black family heirlooms referred incorrectly to a book written by the historian Tiya Miles. Her book “All That She Carried” traces the story of one cotton sack, not a cotton dress.
match_headline: Discovering Black Family Heirlooms and the Stories Behind Them

text: An article on Friday about tourist towns affected by the floods at Yellowstone National Park misquoted Patrick Sipp, the owner of an adventure tours company. He said, “This is the best crew I have ever been part of,” not “the best career I have ever been part of.”
ref_headline: This is the best crew I have ever been part of,
match_headline: Yellowstone Towns Had Big Summer Plans Until Floods Struck

text: An article on Sunday about the Juneteenth holiday, using incomplete information from the Congressional Research Service, misstated the number of states that have adopted it as an official paid holiday. It is 24 states and the District of Columbia, not 18 states. It also misstated the length of time between the Emancipation Proclamation and Gen. Gordon Granger’s arrival in Galveston, Texas, where he informed enslaved African Americans of their freedom. It was nearly — not more than — two and a half years.
match_headline: Juneteenth Is a Federal Holiday, but in Most States It’s Still Not a Day Off

text: An article on Thursday about Emma Thompson’s new movie, “Good Luck to You, Leo Grande,” misstated how often she had appeared naked on camera. It was a few times, not just once. Asked to clarify, she said: “One forgets,” before adding, “No body doubles here.”
ref_headline: Good Luck to You, Leo Grande,
match_headline: Emma Thompson and the Challenge of Baring All Onscreen at 63

text: An article on Sunday about the declining price of Bitcoin misstated the last time the price was $20,000. It was December 2020, not November 2020. It passed its previous record of $19,738 in November 2020.
match_headline: Bitcoin Plummets Below $20,000 for First Time Since Late 2020

text: An article on Saturday about the basketball player Stephen Curry’s long list of accomplishments included an incorrectly worded passage about criticism Curry had received entering this season. The criticism was that Curry’s previous championships had come when opponents were not at full strength or when Kevin Durant was one of his teammates; it was not that he had neither helped his team win a title without Durant nor defeated a finals opponent who was at full strength.
match_headline: Stephen Curry Left His Critics With Nothing Else to Say

text: An article on Tuesday about a wave of rising stars in boys’ basketball from New Jersey included an outdated reference to Elliot Cadeau. He will be transferring to Link Academy in Missouri and is no longer a star at Bergen Catholic High School.
match_headline: ‘Jersey Is Taking Over’: N.J. Hoopers Outshine the Shadow of New York

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the college basketball star Lennie Rosenbluth misstated where Tommy Kearns, one of his teammates on the University of North Carolina team, went to high school. It was St. Ann’s Academy in Manhattan (which later became Archbishop Molloy High School in Queens), not St. Ann’s in Brooklyn.
match_headline: Lennie Rosenbluth, Who Led North Carolina to a Title, Dies at 89

text: An article on Wednesday about a rent increase of at least 3.25 percent for rent-stabilized homes in New York City misstated how Christina Smyth, a representative of landlords on the Rent Guidelines Board, voted. She voted in favor of the proposal that passed, not against it.
match_headline: Rents Will Rise by at Least 3.25 Percent for 2 Million New Yorkers

text: An article last Thursday about Artbag, a shop that repairs luxury handbags, misstated the location of Coral Springs in Florida. It is between Miami and Palm Beach, not Miami and Fort Lauderdale.
match_headline: Who Will Repair Their Birkins Now?

text: A column on Wednesday about Prime Minister Naftali Bennett of Israel impre­cisely quoted him regarding the killing of Shireen Abu Akleh. He said, “What I do know is that Israeli soldiers definitely do not shoot intentionally. Never will Israeli soldiers intentionally target reporters.” He did not say, “What I do know is that Israeli soldiers did not shoot intention­ally.”
ref_headline: What I do know is that Israeli soldiers definitely do not shoot intentionally. Never will Israeli soldiers intentionally target reporters.
match_headline: Naftali Bennett’s Exit Interview

text: An article on Thursday about subpoenas issued by the Justice Department in investigation of the Trump fraudulent electors plan misspelled the name of a Trump campaign aide who received a subpoena. The aide is Shawn Flynn, not Sean.
match_headline: Justice Dept. Issues More Subpoenas in Trump Electors Investigation

text: An article on Thursday about testimony by Republican witnesses at the House committee panel investigating the Jan. 6. attack on the Capitol misidentified the role of Jessica Post at the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee. She is the committee’s president, not its executive director.
match_headline: G.O.P. Testimony at Jan. 6 Panel Exposes a Party Torn Between Truth and Trump

text: An article on Thursday about a broader trend of Democrats switching their party preference in primary elections to defeat far-right Republicans misidentified Jenny Wilson’s position. She is the mayor of Salt Lake County, not Salt Lake City.
match_headline: In Boebert’s District, as Elsewhere, Democrats Surge Into G.O.P. Primary

text: An article on Monday about people who are living in recreational vehicles and their creative efforts to mitigate high gas prices misstated the approximate starting price of a new van. The price starts around $45,000, not $100,000.
match_headline: When #Vanlife Meets the $300 Tank

text: An article on Thursday about Red Wings defenseman Moritz Seider’s strong rookie season misattributed two quotations. “There’s definitely a buzz around the team; this is the most excited I’ve seen the fan base in quite some time” and “When he was picked at six overall, it was pure shock and disappointment” were said by Ryan Hana of the “Winged Wheel Podcast,” not Evan Lobsinger, his co-host.
ref_headline: There’s definitely a buzz around the team; this is the most excited I’ve seen the fan base in quite some time
match_headline: The Rookie Some Didn’t Want Now Has a Fan Base Feeling Optimistic

text: An article on Wednesday about the roller-skating experience DiscOasis in Central Park misstated the DiscOasis’s hours. Skating sessions are available from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. Wednesdays through Sundays, not daily.
match_headline: How New York Got a Glorious Throwback Roller-Skating Extravaganza

text: An obituary on June 15 about the novelist A.B. Yehoshua rendered the name of his sister incorrectly. She is Tzila Petrushka, not Pzila Petroshka.
match_headline: A.B. Yehoshua, Politically Engaged Israeli Writer, Dies at 85

text: An article on Tuesday about a risk of bias in death examinations misstated the amount of time Jocelyn McLean wrongly spent in jail after the death of her daughter. It was almost a year, not more than a year. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Failed Autopsies, False Arrests: A Risk of Bias in Death Examinations

text: An article on Page 1 about crisis pregnancy centers in New York City includes an outdated reference to Roe v. Wade. After the section went to press, the Supreme Court handed down a decision that overturned Roe.
match_headline: Fifty Years On, Title IX’s Legacy Includes Its Durability

text: An item in the “Queue” article on Page 2 this weekend misstates the given name of an Iranian singer. He is Shahram Shabpareh, not Shabnam.
An article on Friday about a Luis Buñuel film misstated its title. It is “The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie,” not “The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeois.”
ref_headline: The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie,
match_headline: Still Charming at 50: Luis Buñuel’s Greatest Hit

text: A picture with an article on Monday about a national Juneteenth museum in Fort Worth, relying on incorrect information from Bjarke Ingels Group, was published in error. The image showed a rendering of the project against the skyline of Austin, not Fort Worth.
match_headline: National Juneteenth Museum Takes Shape in Fort Worth

text: An article on Page 28 about the push to diversify the book business misspells the surname of a writer. She is Audre Lorde, not Lourde. The article also incorrectly renders the name of another writer. He is Chang-rae Lee, not Chang Rae-Lee.
match_headline: Inside the Push to Diversify the Book Business

text: An article on Page 36 this weekend about the use of raptors in pest-animal abatement on the Jersey Shore misstates the year the U.S. Department of Agriculture killed 17,633 gulls in the name of wildlife control, along with 2,664 hawks, 510 falcons and 359 owls. It was 2021, not 2018.
match_headline: The Ancient Art of Falconry at the Jersey Shore

text: An article on June 19 about the Native American artist Cannupa Hanska Luger misidentified the buyer of the sculpture “Nature.” Though it is in the collection of the Denver Art Museum, it was sold to a private collector, not to the museum. And the article attributed an erroneous distinction to the curator Patricia Marroquin Norby. She is the first Native American curator at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, not the first Indigenous curator there.
match_headline: Cannupa Hanska Luger Is Turning the Tables on the Art World

text: An item in the “Queue” article on Page 2 this weekend misstates the given name of an Iranian singer. He is Shahram Shabpareh, not Shabnam.
An article last Sunday about Dyke Day LA, an annual Pride celebration, misstated the age of Romy Hoffman, a musician. She is 41, not 42.
match_headline: Not Your Average Pride Event

text: An article last Sunday about lemonade stands misstated the amount of money raised by Aria York, 8, and her father, Michael York. It was $1,275, not $280.
match_headline: When the World Gives You Lemons … Make a Stand

text: An article last Sunday about a New York insurance law on dogs misidentified the name of the group dedicated to telling the stories of those hurt or killed by dogs. It is DogsBite.org, not DogBite.org. The article and a picture caption with the article also misstated the name of the shelter in Menands, N.Y. It is the Mohawk Hudson Humane Society, not the Hudson Mohawk Humane Society.
match_headline: Love Your Dog, but Beware of Your Homeowners’ Insurance

text: A review on June 5 about “La Nijinska,” by Lynn Garafola, referred incorrectly to the dancer Vaslav Nijinsky’s career. It has been documented by many re­ports and photographs of his performances, but there is no known film footage.
match_headline: The Woman Who Was Written Out of the History of Dance

text: Because of an editing error, a review on June 12 about “Fire Island,” by Jack Parlett, referred incorrectly to Fire Island. It is 32 miles long, not 9.6 miles. (The land area of Fire Island is 9.6 square miles.)
match_headline: Paradise by the Patchogue Ferry: A Hundred Years on Fire Island

text: An article on Monday about a county clerk in Colorado who was indicted in a breach of voting machines and is now the Republican nominee for secretary of state misstated the sum spent by a super PAC in Colorado, Citizens for Election Integrity, on ads attacking Pam Anderson, one of Tina Peters’s opponents for the Republican nomination. It has spent roughly $100,000, not $198,000.
match_headline: The Strange Tale of Tina Peters

text: An article on Sunday about the methodical strategy to eventually overturn Roe v. Wade laid out by Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. decades ago misstated the name of a law journal. It is The Yale Law Journal, not The Yale Law Review.
match_headline: Decades Ago, Alito Laid Out Methodical Strategy to Eventually Overrule Roe

text: An article on Sunday about Devon Allen’s shift from track to playing professional football for the Philadelphia Eagles misstated the timing of Allen’s third-fastest time in the history of the 110-meter hurdles. It came in a race after he switched to a seven-step approach to the first hurdle, not in his first race after doing so.
match_headline: An N.F.L. Rookie’s Back-up Plan: A Track World Championship

text: An obituary on Thursday about James Rado, who created the rock musical “Hair” with Gerome Ragni, misidentified the director of the 1965 Chicago production of the comedy “The Knack,” whose cast included Mr. Rado and Mr. Ragni. It was Brian Bedford, not Mike Nichols. (Mr. Nichols directed the New York production of the play, in which Mr. Bedford starred.)
match_headline: James Rado, Co-Creator of the Musical ‘Hair,’ Is Dead at 90

text: An obituary on Saturday about the architect Harry Gesner misstated the nationality of Jorn Utzon, the architect who won the competition to design the Sydney Opera House. He was Danish, not Swedish.
match_headline: Harry Gesner, Architect of Soaring California Style, Dies at 97

text: An obituary on Friday about the concert promoter Meghan Stabile misstated the name of a Manhattan concert venue where she booked a show. It was the Highline Ballroom, not the Highland Ballroom.
match_headline: Meghan Stabile, Who Linked Jazz and Hip-Hop, Dies at 39

text: An obituary on June 20 about the Civil War-era diarist William B. Gould misstated the year Gould contracted measles. It was 1863, not 1865.
match_headline: Overlooked No More: William B. Gould, Escaped Slave and Civil War Diarist

text: An article on June 20 about a Republican-led drive to tilt courts against climate action misstated the number of Republican-appointed judges on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. There are eight, not nine. The article also stated incorrectly that Patrick Morrisey, the West Virginia attorney general, had argued West Virginia v. E.P.A. before the Supreme Court. He did not.
match_headline: Republican Drive to Tilt Courts Against Climate Action Reaches a Crucial Moment

text: An article on Saturday about Romania’s efforts to meet demands for grain exports in Europe misstated the name of a Romanian farmer. He is Mircea Chipaila, not Chipaila Mircea.
match_headline: As Russia Chokes Ukraine’s Grain Exports, Romania Tries to Fill In

text: An article on Tuesday about Eric Hechtman, a club professional from Miami, who has signed on to help Serena and Venus Williams with their career misstated Evan Zeder’s role at New Balance. He is head of global tennis sports marketing, not head of global sports marketing.
match_headline: How a Tennis Nerd Gave Serena and Venus Williams a New Lease on the Game

text: An article on Tuesday about the 10th anniversary of the gene-editing technology CRISPR and how it has led to innovations in multiple fields misstated the nature of the CRISPR patent dispute. The University of California initiated the court challenge, not the Broad Institute.
match_headline: CRISPR, 10 Years On: Learning to Rewrite the Code of Life

text: An article on Tuesday about the uses of the gene-editing technology CRISPR gave an erroneous context for a quote from Dr. Ed Stadtmauer. When he said, “Patients that had very dismal prognoses are now doing much better, and some are being cured,” he was referring to a CAR T-cell trial involving genetically modified cells, not a CAR T-cell trial that used CRISPR.
ref_headline: Patients that had very dismal prognoses are now doing much better, and some are being cured,
match_headline: The Many Uses of CRISPR: Scientists Tell All

text: An article on Wednesday about growing safety concerns as New York City pools open amid a swim lesson shortage misstated the name of a nonprofit group offering free swim lessons. It is Friends of + POOL, not Plus Pools.
match_headline: N.Y.C. Pools Open Amid a Swim Lesson Shortage, Raising Safety Fears

text: An article on Wednesday about Turkey’s decision not to Bar Sweden and Finland from NATO referred incorrectly to Finland. It is a Nordic not a Scandinavian country.
match_headline: In Blow to Putin, Turkey Won’t Bar Sweden and Finland From NATO

text: An article on Thursday about rising unrest across India after the killing of a Hindu man who expressed support for Nupur Sharm, a politician who made remarks that were condemned by Muslims, misstated when Ms. Sharm made the remarks. She did so in May, not in June.
match_headline: Religious Unrest Spreads in India With Killing of Hindu Man

text: An article on Thursday about Unilever’s decision to sell Ben & Jerry’s business after controversy surrounding the company’s pledge to discontinue sales in the occupied West Bank described incorrectly the Israeli occupation of the West Bank. While most of the world officially considers the West Bank to be occupied, and the settlements there illegal, there is no consensus that the occupation itself is illegal.
match_headline: Unilever Sells Ben & Jerry’s Business in Israel, Defusing Dispute

text: An article on Thursday about a Black man who was left paralyzed after being transported in a New Haven police van without a seatbelt misstated the rank of one of the police officers involved in the episode. It is a sergeant, not a lieutenant.
match_headline: A Black Man Is Paralyzed, and New Haven Police Are Investigated

text: An article on Wednesday about the shrinking coupon market misstated the plans of Quotient, a company formerly known as Coupons.com , for printable coupons. It is scaling back, not phasing out, their use.
match_headline: As Prices Skyrocket, Coupons Are Harder to Find Than Ever

text: An article on Wednesday about the collaboration between the composer David Lang and the choreographer Pam Tanowitz included a comment from Tanowitz that referred imprecisely to the choreographer Hanya Holm. Holm was not Jewish.
match_headline: Pam Tanowitz’s Next Act: ‘I Need to Make a Jewish Dance’

text: An article on Wednesday about the pos­sible legal consequences of Cassidy Hutchinson’s testimony before the Jan. 6 committee mischaracterized a federal le­gal case referred to in discussions of Sec­tion 3 of the 14th Amendment. It was a post­-Civil War case, not an antebellum case.
match_headline: Cassidy Hutchinson Changes Everything

text: An obituary on Monday about the record producer, arranger and engineer Patrick Adams misspelled part of the name of an act he worked with. It is Eric B. & Rakim, not Erik.
match_headline: Patrick Adams, Master of New York’s Underground Disco Scene, Dies at 72

text: An article on Friday about the Supreme Court ruling that allows the Biden administration to end a Trump-era immigration program that forces asylum seekers at the southwestern border to await approval in Mexico described incorrectly the history of immigration legislation. Congress has made changes to immigration law since 1986, but it has not passed any law to legalize undocumented immigrants since that year.
match_headline: Supreme Court Sides With Biden’s Efforts to End ‘Remain in Mexico’ Program

text: An article on Thursday about violent threats that election workers continue to face despite federal efforts to deter them misstated Claire Woodall-Vogg’s job title. She is the executive director of Milwaukee’s election commission, not the city clerk.
match_headline: Violent Threats to Election Workers Are Common. Prosecutions Are Not.

text: An article on June 11 about guidance on opening a Roth I.R.A. account for your child misstated the age of a person in a hypothetical example who would have accumulated about a million dollars less than someone starting at age 15. The age is 25, not 20.
match_headline: You’re Never Too Young for a Roth I.R.A.

text: An article on June 26 about the documentary film “George Michael: Freedom Uncut” misstates the location of Michael’s childhood home. It was in the Edgware area of North London, not East Finchley.
match_headline: George Michael Preferred Music to Fame. The Doc He Made Does, Too.

text: An article on Page 26 this weekend about moderate Democrats misstates the given name of a New York state senator. She is Alessandra Biaggi, not Alexandra. The article also refers incorrectly to Representative Matt Cartwright’s electoral track record. He is not the only Democrat to win in a Trump district in 2016, 2018 and 2020 (he is one of three), but he is the only one running for re-election.
match_headline: The Vanishing Moderate Democrat

text: An article on June 19 about Serbian nationalism misstated the outcome of Slobodan Milosevic’s trial at The Hague. He died before a verdict could be handed down; he was not convicted of war crimes.
match_headline: Bosnia on the Brink

text: An article last Sunday about forever renters in New York City described incorrectly the growth in the city’s population in comparison with the number of new homes built. Between 2000 and 2020, there were 438,088 apartments and single­-family homes built. The city grew by more than 800,000 residents in that same time period, not 600,000.
match_headline: ‘Rent, Forever’: The Price of Living in New York City

text: An article on Monday about American Special Operations veterans training Ukrainians near the front lines in the fight against Russia mischaracterized the group that helps evacuate Americans from Ukraine. It is a nonprofit organization, not a volunteer group.
match_headline: In Ukraine, U.S. Veterans Step In Where the Military Will Not

text: An article on Sunday about young women who oppose abortion rights misspelled the surname of a philosopher who defended abortion. She was Judith Jarvis Thomson, not Thompson.
match_headline: ‘The Pro-Life Generation’: Young Women Fight Against Abortion Rights

text: An article on Saturday about Xi Jinping’s ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of Hong Kong’s return to China referred incorrectly to Tian Feilong of Beihang University in Beijing. He is an associate professor of law, not an assistant professor of law.
match_headline: Xi Tells a Muted Hong Kong That Political Power Is for Patriots

text: An article on Sunday about a request by the Supreme Court’s chief security officer that state officials enforce laws that would prohibit protests outside the homes of justices, in one instance, misstated where Marc Elrich serves as county executive. It is Montgomery County, not Fairfax County. The article also misstated the status of a bill to extend police protection to the immediate families of Supreme Court justices. It is not awaiting President Biden’s signature; he has signed it.
match_headline: Supreme Court Marshal Asks Officials to End Protests at Justices’ Homes

text: An article on Thursday about Spirit Airlines’ decision to put off a shareholder vote on a merger with Frontier Airlines after JetBlue emerged as a rival suitor misstated the airline offering a $350 million payment if regulators block the deal. It is Frontier, not Spirit.
match_headline: Spirit calls off vote on Frontier bid as talks with JetBlue continue.

text: An article on Sunday about how racial gaps in equity persist in sports despite Title IX misstated the year that Carolyn Peck’s Purdue women’s team won the national basketball championship. It was 1999, not 1998.
match_headline: Equity in Sports Has Focused on Gender, Not Race. So Gaps Persist.

text: An article on Sunday about the baseball player Justin Verlander misstated the significance of Verlander’s age. He is the second oldest active player in the American League, not the second oldest active player in the major leagues.
match_headline: Circling the Bases as Baseball Nears Its Midpoint

text: A Critic’s Pick article on Monday about the show “Water Memories” at the Metropolitan Museum misspelled the name of an Indigenous community member who wrote a personal response to an artwork in “Water Memories.” He is Nick Estes, not Nick Estates.
match_headline: At the Met, Protest and Poetry About Water

text: A picture caption with a theater review on Monday of “Dom Juan” misidentified an actress in the play. It was Kirsten Harvey as Charlotte, not Zuzanna Szadkowski as Sganarelle.
match_headline: ‘Dom Juan’ Review: The Perks of Being a Professional Hypocrite

text: An article on Tuesday about foods that keep you hydrated mischaracterized the hormone vasopressin. Vasopressin does not differ from antidiuretic hormone, or ADH; they are the same hormone.
match_headline: The Foods That Keep You Hydrated

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about the musicologist Richard Taruskin misstated part of the current name of the High School of Music & Art, which he attended. It is the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts — not of Music & the Arts.
match_headline: Richard Taruskin, Vigorously Polemical Musicologist, Dies at 77

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about Martin C. Dreiwitz, the founder of the Long Island Youth Orchestra, misstated part of the current name of the High School of Music & Art, which he attended. It is the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts — not of Music & the Arts.
match_headline: Directing the Beatles Was Just One Part of His Long and Winding Career

text: An article on Wednesday about the Justice Department’s lawsuit against Arizona because of a new state voting law misstated the number of times the department, under Attorney General Merrick B. Garland, has challenged a state’s voting law. It is four times, not three.
match_headline: Justice Dept. Sues Arizona Over Voting Restrictions

text: An article on Tuesday about the Nathan’s Famous International Hot Dog Eating Contest incorrectly described Joey Chestnut’s victory in the contest on Monday. While it was his 15th victory, it was not his 15th win in a row.
match_headline: At Nathan’s Hot Dog Contest, One Champion Keeps His Title and Another Reclaims Hers

text: An article on Sunday about wealthy na­tions’ broken promises to asylum seek­ers worldwide referred imprecisely to an arrangement European Union nations made with Turkey to reduce the flow of migrants from the Middle East. Those nations agreed to allow visa-­free travel of Turkish nationals to E.U. countries if Turkey met certain criteria. They did not unconditionally allow visa-­free travel.
match_headline: Let’s Not Pretend We’re Keeping Our Promises on Asylum

text: An article on Tuesday about widespread claims of 2020 election fraud on right-wing radio shows referred incorrectly to the Sinclair Broadcast Group as a syndicator of radio shows. The company does not syndicate radio shows.
match_headline: On Conservative Radio, Misleading Message Is Clear: ‘Democrats Cheat’

text: An article on Thursday about Representative Mayra Flores incorrectly described the history of Republican representation of the Rio Grande Valley. Ms. Flores is the second Republican to represent parts of the region in Congress, not the first.
match_headline: The Rise of the Far-Right Latina

text: An article on Wednesday about Highland Park’s reputation as Chicago’s “Mayberry” misstated the old location of Bob’s Deli in Highland Park, Ill. It is several miles from the city’s Fourth of July parade route, not one block away.
match_headline: Before Shooting, Highland Park Was Considered Chicago’s ‘Mayberry’

text: An article on Thursday about conflicts of interest that arise when accounting firms simultaneously help clients avoid taxes and audit their finances referred incorrectly to the firms considering a split of auditing and consulting arms into separate companies. The move is being explored by officials at EY, not at Deloitte.
match_headline: Officials Balked at a Drug Company’s Tax Shelter. Auditors Approved It Anyway.

text: An article on Wednesday about Mike Grier’s becoming the N.H.L.’s first Black general manager described incorrectly his father Bobby Grier’s football career. He was a college running back, not an N.F.L. running back.
match_headline: Sharks Hire Mike Grier as N.H.L.’s First Black General Manager

text: An article on Thursday about a fight between Jake Paul and Tommy Fury being canceled for the second time in eight months misstated the venue for their past matchup that was canceled. That fight was to be held in December in Tampa, Fla., not at Madison Square Garden.
match_headline: Jake Paul Gets New Opponent After Tommy Fury’s Travel Troubles

text: An article on Tuesday about Maybelle Blair, a former pitcher for the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League and inspiration for the movie “A League of Their Own,” misstated part of the name of the bomber Blair worked on in her 37-year-career. It was the Northrop B-2 bomber, not Northman.
match_headline: She Inspired ‘A League of Their Own.’ At 95, She’s Far From Done.

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about the ever-changing character of Sherlock Holmes misstated the year Arthur Conan Doyle’s story “The Final Problem” was published. It was 1893, not 1883.
match_headline: The Shape-Shifting Sherlock Holmes, Now Playing the Villain

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about areas of eastern Ukraine that Russia’s invasion has left largely devoid of people and industry misstated the location of the conference where Ukraine’s prime minister, Denys Shmyhal, described the cost of rebuilding his country. It was in Switzerland, not Italy.
match_headline: As Russia Moves on Another Province, Ukrainians Leave Ghost Towns Behind

text: An article on July 2 about the director of the Chinati Foundation in Marfa, Texas, stepping down, using information from the Chinati Foundation, described imprecisely the work done on 23 sculptures by John Chamberlain. The sculptures were cleaned for the installation’s reopening, but Chinati did not conduct a full conservation of the sculptures.
match_headline: Director of the Chinati Foundation in Marfa to Step Down

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about the new host of NPR’s “Code Switch” misidentifies the platform that hosts “This American Life.” It is delivered to stations by Public Radio Exchange, not NPR.
match_headline: B.A. Parker Can’t Get Enough of K-Dramas

text: An article on Page 13 this weekend about the self-taught artist Dr. Charles Smith’s African-American Heritage Museum and Black Veterans Archive misstates the location of Sheboygan. It is in Wisconsin, not Michigan.
match_headline: A Self-Taught Artist Takes His Roadside Acropolis North

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about the singer-songwriter Lili Trifilio misstates where Trifilio and her family live. It is in Chicago, not the Chicago suburbs.
match_headline: Beach Bunny Is Building an Indie-Rock Career in a Time of TikTok

text: An article on Page 7 this weekend about podcasts run by professional athletes describes incorrectly Tommy Alter’s professional background. He produces and hosts a podcast with a former N.B.A. player but he was not a player himself.
match_headline: The Rise of the Professional-Athlete Podcast

text: An obituary on June 9 about Ken Bode, a former moderator of the PBS program “Washington Week in Review,” misstated his role at the Center for Contemporary Media at DePauw University in Indiana. He was the center’s director from 1989 to 1994, not its founder. This correction was delayed because the error was brought to the editors’ attention only recently.
match_headline: Ken Bode, Erudite ‘Washington Week’ Host on PBS, Dies at 83

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the vegan hamburger chain Monty’s Good Burger misstated the surname of actress who had been pictured. She is Rooney Mara, not Marae.
match_headline: The Burger That Instagram Built

text: An article on Friday about Boris Johnson’s downfall misstated the role of Conrad Black at the Spectator magazine. He was its owner, not its editor.
match_headline: Johnson’s Lies Worked for Years, Until They Didn’t

text: An article on Friday about the end of Boris Johnson’s political career misquoted part of Mr. Johnson’s resignation speech. He said, “I want to tell you how sad I am to be giving up the best job in the world,” not, “I want to tell you how sorry I am to be giving up the best job in the world.”
ref_headline: I want to tell you how sad I am to be giving up the best job in the world,
match_headline: For Boris Johnson, a Tumultuous Tenure Ends With a Messy Exit

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a judge’s ruling clearing the way for Prince Harry to pursue a libel claim against the newspaper The Mail on Sunday misstated where Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, live in Southern California. Their home is in Montecito, not Los Angeles.
match_headline: High Court Sides With Prince Harry in Libel Claim

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the shooting of John Edwards, a beloved fixture on his Bronx block, and the eroding sense of safety in New York City misstated when Cesar Lebron was interviewed. It was last week, not this week.
match_headline: A Random Killing Erodes a New York Block’s Sense of Stability

text: An article on Sunday about an ant species from Europe that is invading New York City apartments misstated the location of Kennesaw State University. It is in central Georgia, not southern Georgia.
match_headline: In N.Y.C. Apartments, the Ants Go Marching Up

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a Louisiana judge who allowed state laws banning nearly all abortions to take effect misspelled the given name of the administrator of Hope Medical Group for Women. She is Kathaleen Pittman, not Kathleen.
match_headline: Louisiana Judge Allows Abortion Ban to Take Effect

text: An article on Monday about Brazil’s 40-year rise to global surfing dominance misidentified the politician who created a set of stabilizing policies for Brazil’s economy in the early 1990s. It was Fernando Henrique Cardoso, a finance minister, not Fernando Collor de Mello.
match_headline: Inside Brazil’s 40-Year Rise to Global Surfing Dominance

text: An article on Monday about the Jan. 6 committee’s decision to hold an emergency public hearing of testimony from the former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson referred incorrectly to the dress code at Christopher Newport University. While the university previously required students to follow a dress code, according to student handbooks, it did not during the period when Ms. Hutchinson was a student there.
match_headline: Cassidy Hutchinson: Why the Jan. 6 Committee Rushed Her Testimony

text: An article on Tuesday about Representative Jamie Raskin’s role in the Jan. 6 committee hearing to examine the role of far-right groups in the Jan. 6, 2021, assault at the Capitol referred imprecisely to his father’s affiliation with the Institute for Policy Studies. His father, Marcus Raskin, was a co-founder of the institute, not the founder.
match_headline: Raskin Brings Expertise on Right-Wing Extremism to Jan. 6 Inquiry

text: An article on Tuesday about the afterlife of public artworks misidentified the gallery that represented Diana Al-Hadid and helped her sculpture go on tour. It was Marianne Boesky Gallery, not Kasmin Gallery. Because of an editing error, the article also described imprecisely an artwork by Pamela Council. It was a monument to survivors in general, not just survivors of the pandemic.
match_headline: Does Public Art Have an Afterlife?

text: An obituary on Saturday about Shinzo Abe, Japan’s longest-serving prime minister, omitted the given name of the current prime minister of Japan. He is Fumio Kishida, whom Mr. Abe eventually supported as his successor after Mr. Abe resigned in 2020.
match_headline: Shinzo Abe, Japan’s Longest-Serving Prime Minister, Dies at 67

text: An obituary on Monday about Dr. Joyce C. Lashof, the first woman to head a state public health department and the first to serve as dean of the School of Public Health at the University of California, Berkeley, misstated part of the name of a college where she did graduate work. It was the Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania, not Women’s.
match_headline: Joyce C. Lashof, Doctor Who Shattered Glass Ceilings, Dies at 96

text: An obituary on Friday about the artist Harvey Dinnerstein misstated where the painter Jerry Weiss studied with him. It was at the National Academy of Design, not the Art Students League.
match_headline: Harvey Dinnerstein, Proudly Realistic Painter, Is Dead at 94

text: An article on March 9 about the discovery of the wreck of the Endurance, which sank in the Antarctic in 1915 during an expedition by the explorer Ernest Shackleton, misstated the point at which Shackleton joined Endurance on what would be the ship’s final voyage. He came aboard in Argentina; he was not on the ship when it left England. This correction was delayed, because the error was only recently brought to the attention of editors.
match_headline: At the Bottom of an Icy Sea, One of History’s Great Wrecks Is Found

text: An article on Tuesday about Delaware’s Court of Chancery and its role in Elon Musk’s Twitter deal misstated who founded SolarCity, a solar panel energy company. It was founded by Mr. Musk’s cousins Lyndon and Peter Rive, with help from Mr. Musk, not by Mr. Musk himself.
match_headline: What Is Delaware’s Court of Chancery and Its Role in Elon Musk’s Twitter Deal?

text: Because of an editing error, a column on Saturday about Brittney Griner’s complicated path to release from Russia after facing drug charges for bringing hashish oil into the country misstated the time served by Paul Whelan of his 16-year sentence on espionage charges that he has denied. He has served three and a half years, not two.
match_headline: Glimpses of Brittney Griner Show a Complicated Path to Release

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about this summer’s Aix-en-Provence Festival misspelled the surname of a singer in “L’Incoronazione di Poppea.” He is Paul-Antoine Bénos-Djian, not Bénos-Dijan.
match_headline: At This Summer’s Aix Festival, the Only Laughter Is Bitter

text: An article on Wednesday about the premiere of the musical “Notre Dame de Paris” in New York misstated the theater where the musical “Notre Dame de Paris” had its 1998 Paris run. It was at the Palais des Congrès, not the Palais des Sports.
match_headline: A Global Hit, ‘Notre Dame de Paris’ Finally Lands in New York

text: An obituary on July 5 about the actor Joe Turkel referred imprecisely to the similarities between him and the director Stanley Kubrick, with whom he worked on three movies. While both men grew up as secular Jews in New York, Mr. Kubrick was the son of a doctor; unlike Mr. Turkel, he did not grow up “working-class.”
match_headline: Joe Turkel, the Spectral Bartender in ‘The Shining,’ Dies at 94

text: An article on Thursday about the first Black American to be represented with a state statue in the National Statuary Hall at the United States Capitol misstated the milestone represented by Mary McLeod Bethune’s statue. She is the first Black American to have a state statue in Statuary Hall, not the first Black American to have a statue there.
match_headline: Statue of Black Educator Replaces Confederate General in U.S. Capitol

text: An article on Wednesday about a legal scion expected to be charged with the murders of his wife and son said that a gunshot fired at Alex Murdaugh did not hit him. The man who fired the gun said the shot did not strike him, but Mr. Murdaugh’s lawyers subsequently produced evidence that it did.
match_headline: Alex Murdaugh Is Expected to Be Charged With Killing Wife and Son, Lawyer Says

text: A picture caption with an article on July 5 about the impact that Western sanctions have had on the travel of Russia’s superrich, using information from Aviation-Images.com, misidentified the type of aircraft shown. It is a Beechjet 400, not a Cessna.
match_headline: An American’s Murky Path From Russian Propagandist to Jan. 6

text: An obituary on June 28 about the artist Sam Gilliam misstated the occupation of his mother, Estery Gilliam. She was a teacher, not a seamstress.
match_headline: Sam Gilliam, Abstract Artist of Drape Paintings, Dies at 88

text: An article on Friday about the story of a 10-year-old girl in Ohio who crossed state lines to get an abortion and became a flash point in the national abortion debate misstated Bill O’Reilly’s connection to The First, a conservative media outlet. He is a host for the outlet, not the owner.
match_headline: Facts Were Sparse on an Abortion Case. But That Didn’t Stop the Attacks.

text: An article on Wednesday about Tadej Pogacar’s tight lead in the Tour de France misidentified the mountains that include the Super Planche des Belles Filles. They are the Vosges, not the Alps.
match_headline: Chasing Precious Seconds, Pogacar Holds Tight to Tour de France Lead

text: An article on Thursday about the delay of the British Open at St. Andrews to ensure that it could host the 150th edition misstated the given name of a former owner of the Dunvegan Hotel. He is Jack Willoughby, not Tom. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Beauty of the Old Course Upstages LIV Golf Angst, for Now

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about planting trees to fight climate change refers imprecisely to an action taken by Elon Musk. He changed his Twitter display name to “Treelon,” not his Twitter handle.
match_headline: Can Planting a Trillion New Trees Save the World?

text: An obituary on June 27 about Vivian Hewitt, who with her husband, John Hewitt Jr., amassed one of the largest private collections of paintings by Black artists in the United States, misstated when NationsBank acquired the core of that collection. It was 1998, not 2009.
match_headline: Vivian Hewitt, Who Amassed a Major Collection of Black Art, Dies at 102

text: An article on Monday about the Biden administration's stalled climate change legislation misstated the amount of NextGen’s planned spending to mobilize college students. The group says it will spend $15.1 million, not $1.5 million.
match_headline: As the Planet Cooks, Climate Stalls as a Political Issue

text: An article on Wednesday about the strain that the oil competition set off by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is putting on Russia’s allies described incorrectly Iran’s calendar year. It is not lunar.
match_headline: Putin’s Oil War With the West Comes at His Allies’ Expense

text: An article on Saturday about a woman in Nepal who was worshiped as a goddess as a child but still made time to study misstated the relationship between the last king of Nepal and the perpetrator of a royal massacre. The last king of Nepal, Gyanendra, was the assassin’s uncle, not his brother.
match_headline: Ex-Goddess Works to Reform 700-Year Tradition. Her M.B.A. Helps.

text: An article on Saturday about Ivana Trump’s status in the New York City social scene of the 1980s and 1990s misidentified the actress who starred on the television program “Green Acres.” It was Eva Gabor, not Zsa Zsa Gabor.
match_headline: Ivana’s New York

text: An article on Monday about Rory McIlroy’s letdown at this year’s British Open misidentified McIlroy’s most recent win at a major championship. It was at the 2014 P.G.A. Championship, not the 2014 British Open.
match_headline: At the British Open, Another Letdown for Rory McIlroy

text: An article on Monday about a new Netflix show based on the author Michael Pollan’s book “How to Change Your Mind” misstated the year the drug LSD was made illegal in California. It was 1966, not 1967.
match_headline: With ‘How to Change Your Mind,’ Taking a Trip With Michael Pollan

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week described incorrectly the events at the end of Season 4 and beginning of Season 5 of “Grown-ish.” Season 4 ended with a college graduation, not a high school graduation, and in Season 5, the returning characters are exploring post-college life, not entering college.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Grown-ish’ and ‘The Old Man’

text: An obituary on Sunday about the actor L.Q. Jones referred incorrectly in part to the 1955 movie “Battle Cry,” in which he made his first screen appearance. It is about Marine recruits, not Army recruits.
match_headline: L.Q. Jones, Who Played Heavies With a Light Touch, Dies at 94

text: An article on July 13 about the recovery of timbers from the so-called Beeswax Wreck omitted a credit to the news organization that first reported how researchers identified the Beeswax Wreck as the Santo Cristo de Burgos, a 17th-century Spanish galleon. The findings were reported on June 16 by National Geographic.
match_headline: Timbers From 17th-Century Shipwreck Recovered Off Oregon Coast

text: A review on July 29, 2021, of the documentary “Sabaya,” about Yazidi women who had been sexually enslaved by ISIS, deemed the film a Critic’s Pick, largely because of a scene showing the rescue of a woman named Leila from a Syrian detention camp. The director recently admitted that he wasn’t present for that rescue and that he substituted footage of another woman’s rescue. Had the circumstances surrounding filming been clear, The Times would have noted the director’s use of the misleading footage in the review and the documentary would not have been named a Critic’s Pick.
match_headline: ‘Sabaya’ Review: Light Breaking Through Darkness

text: An article on Thursday about the arrest of the owner of a tavern in South Africa where 21 teenagers died misstated the location of East London, South Africa. It is on the country’s southeastern coast, not southwestern coast.
match_headline: Police Arrest Owner of South African Tavern Where 21 Teenagers Died

text: An article on Monday about Cameron Smith’s win at the 150th British Open incorrectly stated the significance of the British Open that Kel Nagle won in 1960. It was the 100th anniversary of the tournament’s first year, not the 100th edition of the tournament.
match_headline: Cameron Smith Overtakes Rory McIlroy to Win the 150th British Open

text: An article on Wednesday about the House’s passage of bill to protect same-sex marriage at the federal level misstated when the Supreme Court overturned the Defense of Marriage Act. It was overturned in 2013 in the case of the United States v. Windsor, not in 2015 in Obergefell v. Hodges.
match_headline: House Moves to Protect Same-Sex Marriage From Supreme Court Reversal

text: An article on Thursday about Turkey’s attack on a resort in northern Iraq misstated the type of military equipment involved in the attack. The strikes were from artillery, not warplanes.
match_headline: Turkey Strikes Iraq Resort, Killing at Least 8, Officials Say

text: An article on Wednesday about Democrats’ concerns about the 2022 midterm elections referred incorrectly to an action that Jocelyn Benson, the Michigan secretary of state, took during the 2020 election. She sent mail-in ballot applications to every registered voter in the state, not mail-in ballots themselves.
match_headline: The Midterm Races That Give Democrats Nightmares

text: An article on Thursday about surprising bipartisan support for a same-sex marriage bill in the House referred imprecisely to the protections for same-sex couples in the legislation passed by the House on Tuesday. While the bill would require the federal government and states to recognize same-sex marriages that were legally performed under state law, it does not codify the entirety of the Supreme Court’s decision in Obergefell v. Hodges.
match_headline: Same-Sex Marriage Bill, Considered Dead on Arrival, Gains New Life

text: An article on Wednesday about shifting demographics in senior housing complexes misstated the amount of volunteer work that Opus Newton requires of its residents. It is 10 hours a month, not 10 hours a week.
match_headline: What Baby Boomers Want (Options!), Senior Housing Delivers

text: An article on March 23 about a Donatello exhibit in Florence misstated the century in which Vasari wrote a biography of Donatello. It was in the 16th century, not the 17th. This correction was delayed, because the error was only recently brought to the attention of editors.
match_headline: Donatello Gets His Due

text: An article on Friday about Amazon’s acquisition of One Medical clinics misstated the year that Amazon acquired PillPack, an online pharmacy. It was 2018, not 2019. The article also misstated the plan used by patients of Iora Health, a company acquired last year by One Medical. Iora serves senior patients enrolled in Medicare, not Medicaid.
match_headline: Amazon to acquire One Medical clinics in latest push into health care.

text: An article on Thursday about the difficulty of adapting Jane Austen for plays, television, movies and other novels misspelled the surname of an author. She is Emmeline Clein, not Cline.
match_headline: Why Is It So Hard to Adapt Austen? The Fans Play a Part.

text: An article on July 24 about election conspiracies taking root in the American right misstated the source of a statistic on Republican candidates for secretary of state who claim that the 2020 election was illegitimate. The group responsible for the statistic is States United Action, not the States United Democracy Center, a sister organization.
match_headline: How ‘Stop the Steal’ Captured the American Right

text: An obituary on Monday about the Talmudic scholar David Weiss Halivni misstated part of the current name of a movement he co-founded. It is the Union for Traditional Judaism, not the Union of Traditional Judaism.
match_headline: David Weiss Halivni, Controversial Talmudic Scholar, Dies at 94

text: An article last Sunday about the perform­ance of municipal bonds this year referred incorrectly to the state tax deductibility of income from nationwide municipal bond funds for residents of California. For Califor­nia residents, the deductibility depends on the amount that a particular fund invests in California municipal bonds and U.S. Treas­uries; California residents would not get a deduction in every case.
match_headline: It’s Been a Poor Year So Far for Municipal Bonds

text: An article last Sunday about Christine Quinn of the reality TV show “Selling Sunset” misspelled the surname of a server at Caviar Russe. He is John Gergeos, not Gergeous.
match_headline: Christine Quinn of ‘Selling Sunset’ Has Caviar for Breakfast

text: An article on Saturday about a deal between Russian and Ukraine that would allow grain shipments misstated the price of wheat futures on Friday, July 22. Prices fell by more than 5 percent to around $7.60 per bushel, not $760 per bushel.
match_headline: Russia Agrees to Let Ukraine Ship Grain, Easing World Food Shortage

text: An article on Sunday about President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey and his role in the negotiation of a trade deal between Russia and Ukraine misstated where Dana Stroul spoke this month. It was at the Middle East Institute, not the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
match_headline: Turkey’s Leader Remains a Headache for Biden Despite Aiding in Ukraine Deal

text: An article on Monday about a French university’s Nazi past and medical crimes committed at the school referred incompletely to the Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp. It was the only German concentration camp, not the only concentration camp, on French soil.
match_headline: A French University Confronts Medical Crimes and Its Nazi Past

text: An article on Sunday about the care of pregnant women with cancer in states where women are unable to terminate pregnancies referred incorrectly to abortion in Michigan. The procedure is criminalized by a law in the state that has not been implemented; it has not been banned.
match_headline: After Roe, Pregnant Women With Cancer Diagnoses May Face Wrenching Choices

text: An article on Sunday about Elizabeth Holtzman, the pathbreaking former congresswoman who is running for Congress again at 80-years-old, misstated whom Holtzman walked with at Brooklyn’s Pride parade. She was joined by a former state lawmaker and an aide; she did not walk alone.
match_headline: Liz Holtzman Wants Another Crack at Congress, 50 Years Later

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the artist Claes Oldenburg referred incorrectly to an ice cream cone sculpture. It was not a soft sculpture.
match_headline: Claes Oldenburg Captured a Carefree (and Consumerist) America

text: A column last Wednesday about the U.S. affordability crisis misstated the increase in parents’ average spending per child for child care from 1972 to 2007 as calculated by a 2012 study. The increase was about 200 percent, not 2,000 percent.
match_headline: Why a Middle-Class Lifestyle Remains Out of Reach for So Many

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about Russia’s decision to reduce gas deliveries to Germany misstated the sea under which the Nord Stream 1 pipeline runs. It is the Baltic Sea, not the North Sea.
match_headline: Russia Cuts Gas Flow to Europe, Intensifying Fears It Is Weaponizing Fuel

text: An article on Tuesday about increased pressure on Attorney General Merrick B. Garland to move more quickly in the Justice Department’s investigation of former President Donald J. Trump referred incorrectly to Mr. Garland’s tenure as a judge of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. He served on the court for nearly 23 years, not seven.
match_headline: Sharp Contrasts With Other Jan. 6 Inquiries Increase Pressure on Garland

text: An obituary on July 2 about Dr. Vladimir Zelenko, whose controversial treatments for Covid-19 gained White House support in the early days of the pandemic, referred incorrectly to quercetin, which Dr. Zelenko promoted as one of those treatments. It is an anti-inflammatory plant pigment, or flavonoid; it is not “a drug.”
match_headline: Vladimir Zelenko, 48, Dies; Promoted an Unfounded Covid Treatment

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the British actor David Warner misstated the titles of two screen productions in which he had roles. They were the 1968 movie “The Bofors Gun,” not “The Borfors Gun,” and the 1960s television mini-series “The Wars of the Roses,” not “The War of the Roses.”
match_headline: David Warner, Actor Who Played Villains and More, Dies at 80

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the actor Paul Sorvino described incorrectly the character he played in the movie “Reds.” He portrayed an Italian American Communist leader, not a Russian American Communist leader.
match_headline: Paul Sorvino, Master of the Mild-Mannered Mobster, Dies at 83

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about six American authors nominated for this year’s Booker Prize misstated the former eligibility criteria for the prize. Before 2014, it was open to authors from Britain, Ireland, the Commonwealth and Zimbabwe, not only to authors from Britain and Ireland.
match_headline: U.S. Authors Dominate Booker Prize Nominees

text: An article on July 22 about the sentencing of a former Minneapolis police officer who held down George Floyd’s legs included an outdated reference to the upcoming state trial of two other officers, J. Alexander Kueng and Tou Thao. It is now scheduled to begin in October, not in January.
match_headline: Ex-Officer Who Held George Floyd’s Legs Sentenced to 30 Months in Prison

text: An article on Tuesday about productions of “Hamlet” and “Oresteia” misstated the title of the director Robert Icke when he worked at London’s Almeida Theater. He was the associate director, not the artistic director.
match_headline: A Rebound for a Summer Pairing of ‘Hamlet’ and ‘Oresteia’ at the Armory

text: An article on Friday about President Biden’s health secretary’s suggestion that states bear responsibility for a flawed response to a rise in monkeypox cases incorrectly attributed a comment about the challenges of coordinating a national response to monkeypox. Adriane Casalotti, the chief of public and government affairs for the National Association of County and City Health Officials, spoke about the issues, not Theresa Spinner, a spokeswoman for the group.
match_headline: Health Secretary Says States ‘Need to Work With Us’ on Fighting Monkeypox

text: An article on July 13 about Senator Joe Manchin III’s opposition to government incentives for electric vehicles described incorrectly the role of methane in hydrogen production. Much of the hydrogen produced today is extracted from natural gas in a process that consumes methane, not a process that produces it. (The production and transportation of natural gas itself do result in large releases of methane.)
match_headline: Manchin, Playing to the Home Crowd, Is Fighting Electric Cars to the End

text: An article on Wednesday about a generation of Australia’s defiant female filmmakers left an incorrect impression about the background of Jane Campion. Although her work is included in the series “Pioneering Women in Australian Cinema,” she is from New Zealand.
match_headline: Rediscovering Australia’s Generation of Defiant Female Directors

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about Barbados includes an outdated reference to the country’s publicly traded debt. BlackRock is one of the largest holders of the debt; it is no longer the largest holder of the debt. A picture caption with the article misstates the volume of coconuts a recycling center receives each week. The facility receives more than 100 tons each week, not eight. Another picture caption with the article misstates part of the name of a research center. It is the Walkers Institute for Regenerative Research, Education and Design, not the Walkers Institute for Regenerative Research and Design.
match_headline: Judith Schiff, Who Roamed Yale’s Vast Archive, Dies at 84

text: A picture caption with the Most Dressed article last Sunday misidentified a person wearing Fendace. He is Chris Henry, not Jonathan Cohen.
match_headline: It’s Getting Hot in Here

text: An article on Thursday about default tech settings that share more personal data than consumers may realize misstated, in one instance, the name of a line of Amazon products. It is Ring, not Nest.
match_headline: The Default Tech Settings You Should Turn Off Right Away

text: A picture caption with an article on July 11 about Jazz Camp for Girls, a program that aims to encourage girls to play rhythmic instruments, misidentified the type of guitar held by the student Ella Hargreave. It is a six-string electric guitar, not a bass guitar.
match_headline: Girls Are Outnumbered in Jazz. At This Summer Camp, They Run the Show.

text: An article on Tuesday about a promise from Democratic leaders and the White House to complete a highly contested 304-mile gas pipeline in West Virginia in exchange for Senator Joe Manchin III’s support of climate legislation misstated the timing of Mr. Manchin’s announcement on the agreement. It was Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Manchin Won a Pledge From Democrats to Finish a Contested Pipeline

text: An article on Monday about changes in the United Auto Workers union prompted by a corruption scandal misstated the title of a union official running for re-election whose name was embroidered on backpacks to be given to members. He is secretary-treasurer, not a vice president. The article also misstated a compensation move approved by the union’s executive board. It increased pensions for staff members at union headquarters; it did not increase their pay, or the pay and pensions of the board members.
match_headline: United Auto Workers Seek to Shed a Legacy of Corruption

text: An article on Tuesday about the difficulties smokers may soon face after the Food and Drug Administration said that it would move toward slashing nicotine levels in cigarettes misstated the number of vaping products approved so far by the Food and Drug Administration. It is nearly two dozen, not six.
match_headline: Breaking Nicotine’s Powerful Draw

text: An article on July 28 about the plan to reverse the outcome of the 2020 election by creating slates of electors pledged to Donald Trump in states he had lost referred incorrectly to the origins of the Jan. 6 date for certifying the final count of the Electoral College. The date is set by federal law, not by the Constitution.
match_headline: The Fake Electors Scheme, Explained

text: An entry on Wednesday in the calendar of remaining midterm primary elections contained outdated information about candidates in Wisconsin. Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes now has a clear path to winning the Democratic nomination for Senate; he no longer faces a difficult primary. In the Republican primary for governor, the former Lt. Gov. Rebecca Kleefisch’s main opponent is Tim Michels; it is no longer Kevin Nicholson.
match_headline: In Senate Battle, Democrats Defy Biden’s Low Standing (for Now)

text: An article on Monday about the impact that the pandemic had on parents’ political views reversed the ages of Natalya Murakhver’s two children. Violet is 9, and Clementine is 5.
