match_headline: How Some Parents Changed Their Politics in the Pandemic

text: An article on Friday about the Washington Commanders’ owner, Daniel Snyder, agreeing to appear before a congressional committee investigating his team’s workplace culture misstated Snyder’s estimated net worth. His fortune has been valued at $4 billion, not $40 billion.
match_headline: Will Anyone Hold Daniel Snyder Accountable?

text: An article and a photo caption on Tuesday about the ways in which dams imperil environments that depend on floodwaters described incorrectly the Yellowstone River. It is among the longest undammed U.S. rivers, not the longest.
match_headline: A Silver Lining: Giant Floods Not Only Destroy, They Renew

text: An article on Thursday about Ukrainian refugees temporarily housed on a cruise ship leased by the Estonian government misstated the name of a group that issued a report on the refugees. It is the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, not the Organization for Economic Development and Cooperation.
match_headline: When Home Is a Ferry Ship: An Influx From Ukraine Strains Europe

text: An article on Thursday about a Trump lawyer who suggested looking for voting irregularities in Georgia misstated the arrangement that John Eastman, the lawyer advising Mr. Trump, had with Bruce Marks, another lawyer whose firm was working with the Trump campaign. Mr. Eastman was paid by Mr. Marks’s firm for work he did with the firm on the campaign’s behalf, according to Mr. Marks. Mr. Eastman did not have a private arrangement to be paid by Mr. Marks for other work he did on Mr. Trump’s behalf.
match_headline: Trump Lawyer Proposed Challenging Georgia Senate Elections in Search of Fraud

text: An article on Wednesday about Twitter’s efforts to obtain information related to Elon Musk’s efforts to finance his purchase of the company misidentified the university at which Eric Talley works as a professor of corporate law. It is the Columbia Law School, not the Columbia Business School.
match_headline: What Twitter’s Subpoenas Say About Its Plan to Fight Elon Musk in Court

text: An article on Page 9 this weekend about six podcasts about political scandals and upheaval refers incorrectly to the producers of “The Fault Line: Bush, Blair and Iraq.” They are Somethin’ Else and Sony Music Entertainment, not the BBC.
ref_headline: The Fault Line: Bush, Blair and Iraq.
match_headline: 6 Podcasts About Political Scandals and Upheaval

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about the physical and emotional risks theater performers face misstates the name of an organization helping to shape performances of physical contact onstage. It is Intimacy Directors & Coordinators, not Intimacy Directors & Choreographers.
match_headline: Shutting the Door on the Hard-Knock Life

text: An article on Page 13 this weekend about five classic sci-fi summer movies from 1982 misstated which Philip K. Dick work “Blade Runner” was adapted from. It was adapted from Dick’s novel “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” not from one of his short stories.
match_headline: Five Sci-Fi Classics, One Summer: How 1982 Shaped Our Present

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about New York’s teen punk bands in the 1970s misstates the name Arthur Brennan adopted when he ran away to New York City to join a band. It was Darvon Staggard, not Darvon Stagger.
match_headline: In the Late ’70s, Teen Punks Ruled New York. These Are Their Stories.

text: An article on July 31 about fracking misstated the type of companies that funded America’s fracking boom. They were private-equity companies, not venture-capital companies.
match_headline: Hardly Anyone Talks About How Fracking Was an Extraordinary Boondoggle

text: An obituary on Friday about the artist Jennifer Bartlett omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to her daughter and her sister Julie Losch Matsumoto, Ms. Bartlett is survived by another sister, Jessica Ann Losch.
match_headline: Jennifer Bartlett, Conceptual Painter on Vast Scale, Is Dead at 81

text: A picture caption with an obituary on July 4 about the stage director Peter Brook referred imprecisely to a photograph of his 1953 production of “Faust” at the Metropolitan Opera. The photograph was taken during a rehearsal, not a performance. Another picture caption with that obituary misidentified the actress pictured with Laurence Olivier in Mr. Brook’s production of “Titus Andronicus.” She is Maxine Audley, not Vivien Leigh.
match_headline: Peter Brook, Celebrated Stage Director of Scale and Humanity, Dies at 97

text: A review on July 24 about “A Way Out of No Way,” by Senator Raphael G. Warnock of Georgia, misspelled the given name of the other United States senator from Georgia. He is Jon Ossoff, not John.
ref_headline: A Way Out of No Way,
match_headline: Civil Rights Memoirs

text: An article last Sunday about seasonal Native American celebrations and competitions across the country incorrectly described Grand Entry. It is the beginning of the competition, not the beginning of the season.
match_headline: Tim Giago, Native American Newspaperman, Is Dead at 88

text: Because of an editing error, the On the Market feature last Sunday misspelled the surname of a contributing reporter. She is Claudia Gryvatz Copquin.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in New York and New Jersey

text: An article on Sunday about safety fears over fighting around a nuclear power plant in southern Ukraine misspelled the name of the Ukrainian state nuclear company. It is Energoatom, not Enerhoatam.
match_headline: Fighting Around Ukrainian Nuclear Plant Heightens Safety Fears

text: An article on Friday about the arrest of former Puerto Rico Governor Wanda Vázquez for corruption charges misattributed this quotation: “Not even the indictment alleges that she was enriched one cent.” Ignacio Fernández, a lawyer for Ms. Vázquez, made the remark, not Luis Plaza.
ref_headline: Not even the indictment alleges that she was enriched one cent.
match_headline: Former Puerto Rico Governor Arrested on Corruption Charges

text: An article on Saturday about Indiana’s restrictive new abortion law misidentified the institution at which Jennifer Drobac is a law professor. It is Indiana University’s McKinney School of Law in Indianapolis, not Indiana University Bloomington.
match_headline: Indiana Governor Signs First Post-Roe Abortion Ban, With Limited Exceptions

text: A review on July 29 about the survey of the life and art of Raphael Montañez Ortiz at El Museo del Barrio misidentified an animal depicted in the work “The Memorial to the Sadistic Holocaust Destruction of Millions …” (2019-20). It is a jaguar, molded in plastic, not a stuffed cheetah.
ref_headline: The Memorial to the Sadistic Holocaust Destruction of Millions …
match_headline: How to Decolonize a Museum? Try an Ax.

text: A column on Monday about the defamation case against Alex Jones incompletely described a data file several hundred gigabytes in size that his lawyers sent a lawyer for the plaintiffs. It contained some of Mr. Jones’s cellphone records and other data, not only his cellphone records.
match_headline: For Alex Jones, a Moment of Truth in a Flood of Lies

text: An obituary on Aug. 1 about Fidel V. Ramos, a former president of the Philippines, misstated the date in 1986 when he publicly broke with the dictatorship of Ferdinand E. Marcos. It was Feb. 22, not Nov. 22. The obituary also misstated the position of Corazon C. Aquino, Mr. Ramos’s predecessor, on his campaign for president. Ms. Aquino endorsed Mr. Ramos; it was not the case that she did not endorse him.
match_headline: Fidel Ramos, Philippine President Who Broke With Marcos, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on July 24 about the singer and actress Shonka Dukureh, who played Big Mama Thornton in the movie “Elvis,” misstated the year Elvis Presley’s version of “Hound Dog,” a song first recorded by Ms. Thornton, was released. It was 1956, not 1953.
match_headline: Shonka Dukureh, Actress Who Sang ‘Hound Dog’ in ‘Elvis,’ Dies at 44

text: An obituary on Aug. 1 about Nichelle Nichols, the actress best known for playing Lieutenant Uhura on “Star Trek,” misspelled the surname of one of the astronauts NASA said were inspired to join the American space program by Ms. Nichols’s role. She was Judith Resnik, not Resnick.
match_headline: Nichelle Nichols, Lieutenant Uhura on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 89

text: A picture caption with an obituary on July 8 about the actor James Caan, using information from Getty Images, misidentified both of the women shown in a photo with him. They are Frances Stark and Connie Kreski, not Lilyan Chauvin and Sheila Ryan.
match_headline: James Caan, Actor Who Won Fame in ‘The Godfather,’ Dies at 82

text: A profile on Saturday about Mechai Viravaidya, known as “Captain Condom” for his campaigns to promote safe sex and family planning, misstated the average number of children a Thai family had in the early 1970s. It was five, not seven.
match_headline: ‘Captain Condom’ Turned the Tide in Thailand’s War on AIDS and Overpopulation

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the singer Olivia Newton-John referred incorrectly to the song “Summer Nights,” which she sang with John Travolta in the movie “Grease.” It reached No. 5 on the Billboard pop singles chart, not No. 1.
match_headline: Olivia Newton-John, Pop Singer and ‘Grease’ Star, Dies at 73

text: An article on Wednesday about the search at former President Donald J. Trump’s home in Florida described incorrectly how the National Archives retrieved 15 boxes of material that Mr. Trump had improperly taken with him when he left the White House. The agency said it arranged to have the boxes picked up from Mr. Trump’s home at Mar-a-Lago. It did not fly an official to Florida to collect them.
match_headline: F.B.I. Search of Trump’s Home Pushes Long Conflict Into Public View

text: An obituary on Aug. 2 about the actress Pat Carroll referred incompletely to her education. In addition to attending Immaculate Heart College in Los Angeles, she later studied drama at the Catholic University of America in Washington.
match_headline: Last Conviction in Salem Witch Trials Is Cleared 329 Years Later

text: An obituary on Monday about Dee Hock, the longtime chief executive of Visa, erroneously credited him with a distinction. He oversaw the development of one of the first electronic authorization systems for a credit card, not the first.
match_headline: Dee Hock, Credit Card Visionary, Is Dead at 93

text: An obituary on July 28 about the ecologist James Lovelock misstated part of the name of his autobiography. It is “Homage to Gaia: The Life of an Independent Scientist,” not “Home to Gaia: The Life of an Independent Scientist.”
ref_headline: Homage to Gaia: The Life of an Independent Scientist,
match_headline: James Lovelock, Whose Gaia Theory Saw the Earth as Alive, Dies at 103

text: An article on Page 11 this weekend about HBO’s new “Game of Thrones” prequel “House of the Dragon” misidentifies the last Targaryen monarch. He was Aerys II, not Aegon IV. It also describes in error the relationship between Jaehaerys Targaryen and Viserys. Viserys is Jaehaerys’s grandson, not his son. (Miraculously, we managed to spell all of the characters’ names correctly.)
match_headline: Near Castle Ruins, a Wedding with a Dash of ‘Game of Thrones’

text: An article on Aug. 7 about the Claremont Institute misspelled the surname of a U.S. representative. She is Marjorie Taylor Greene, not Green.
match_headline: How the Claremont Institute Became a Nerve Center of the American Right

text: An article on Page 11 this weekend about Afghan refugees includes an outdated reference to the Afghan Adjustment Act. After the section went to press, Congress took up the legislation.
match_headline: Five Decades in the Making: Why It Took Congress So Long to Act on Climate

text: An article last Sunday about L.G.B.T.Q. museums referred incorrectly to Oscar Wilde’s criminal conviction. He was jailed for “gross indecency,” not sodomy.
match_headline: What Should an L.G.B.T.Q. Museum Be? Approaches Vary.

text: An article on Saturday about files seized from Donald Trump’s Florida residence misstated the number of sets of top secret documents that federal agents had collected. Five sets of top secret documents were collected, not four.
match_headline: Files Seized From Trump Are Part of Espionage Act Inquiry

text: An article on Aug. 6 about Germany’s reconsideration of its use of nuclear power because of the war in Ukraine referred incorrectly to the role of nuclear power in Europe. Nuclear reactors provide France with about 70 percent, and Germany with about 6 percent, of their electricity, not their total energy.
match_headline: Facing Energy Crisis, Germans, Warily, Give Nuclear a Second Look

text: An article on Sunday about a clash between parents and police over a school lockdown in Arizona misstated the month in which the Uvalde, Texas, school shooting occurred. It was May, not March.
match_headline: Relatives Clash With Police Over School Lockdown in Arizona

text: An article on Sunday about a string of resignations of young male executives in Silicon Valley misstated the year that Adam Neumann was forced out as the chief executive of WeWork. It was 2019, not 2018.
match_headline: The Boy Bosses of Silicon Valley Are on Their Way Out

text: An article on Saturday about a credibility crisis at the Orlando Museum of Art following an authenticity scandal surrounding paintings attributed to Jean-Michel Basquiat described incorrectly the departure of a former director of the museum in 2020. The director, Glen Gentele, resigned after a special museum board meeting to discuss reports of workplace harassment; he was not fired.
match_headline: After Basquiat Raid, Orlando Museum Faces Crisis of Credibility

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the 1947 partition of India, using information from Getty Images, misstated the location of a throng of people celebrating the end of British rule. They were at the Secretariat in New Delhi, not at the Constituent Assembly in Karachi.
match_headline: India’s Partition: A History in Photos

text: An earlier version of a picture caption with a profile on Saturday about the Communist mayor of Graz, Austria, described incorrectly the iconic building shown in the image. It is a clock tower, not a bell tower.
match_headline: In Wealthy City, a Marxist Mayor Wins Over Voters

text: An article on Monday about the threat of a radiation leak near a Ukrainian nuclear plant because of fighting around it misidentified the type of reactors at the Fukushima nuclear plant in Japan. They were boiling water reactors, not pressurized water reactors.
match_headline: Threat to Ukraine Nuclear Plant Increases as Fighting Rages

text: An article on Sunday about the experiences of Afghan refugees misstated the names of Omar Ahmadi’s brothers. They are Bilal and Shabir, not Bilal and Yalda.
match_headline: ‘We Can’t Claim Mission Accomplished’: A Long Road for Afghan Refugees

text: An article on Friday about the new scripted series on Apple TV+ “Five Days at Memorial” described imprecisely the call status of Dr. Anna Pou during Hurricane Katrina and its aftermath. Although she was given the option of assigning her patients to other doctors and evacuating before the storm, she was nonetheless on call the weekend leading into the storm and, after declining to evacuate, was expected to continue caring for her patients until another doctor could replace her. It is not the case, as was described in a quotation, that she was “not on the call sheet.”
match_headline: ‘Five Days at Memorial’ Tells the Harrowing Story of a Deadly Choice

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Nicholas Evans, the author of the novel “The Horse Whisperer,” misstated the surname of the book’s protagonist. He is Tom Booker, not Brooker.
match_headline: Nicholas Evans, Author of ‘The Horse Whisperer,’ Dies at 72

text: An article on Wednesday about the conflict surrounding Russian diamonds and their role in funding the war in Ukraine misstated the given name of the Alrosa chief executive. He is Sergey S. Ivanov, not Serge. An earlier version also described incorrectly the U.S. policy on the Russian diamond industry. The U.S. import ban applies to nonindustrial diamonds, not rough diamonds.
match_headline: Russia Fights Efforts to Declare It an Exporter of ‘Blood Diamonds’

text: An article on Wednesday about a tuberculosis vaccine from the early 1900s and the possibility that it might protect people from Covid-19 incorrectly described the percentage represented by the 1 in 96 people who received B.C.G. tuberculosis vaccine doses and developed Covid. It is slightly more, not less, than 1 percent.
match_headline: Why a Century-Old Vaccine Offers New Hope Against Pathogens

text: An article on Monday about Southern California residents beginning to accept that lush lawns are unsustainable because of drought misstated, in one instance, the given name of a resident’s daughter. She is Sienna Kochakji, not Sierra.
match_headline: In Los Angeles, the Grass Isn’t Always Greener This Year

text: An article on Wednesday about carbon capture and storage technology misspelled in some copies the name of a carbon capture project. It is Petra Nova, not Petro Nova.
match_headline: Every Dollar Spent on This Climate Technology Is a Waste

text: An article on Thursday about Mary Peltola, who could become the first Alaska Native in Congress, misstated Ms. Peltola’s tenure in the Alaska Legislature. She served from 1999 to 2009, not from 2009 to 2019.
match_headline: The Democrat Who Could Become the First Alaska Native in Congress

text: An obituary on March 17 about the former New York State Supreme Court justice Thomas A. Demakos misstated the makeup of the jury that in 1974 acquitted the New York City police officer Thomas J. Shea of murder, a case handled by Mr. Demakos when he was an assistant district attorney. It consisted of 11 white men and one Black woman; it was not all white. This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: Thomas Demakos, Judge in Howard Beach Murder Case, Dies at 98

text: An article on Tuesday about French soldiers pulling out of Mali after nine years misstated the change to Germany’s role in the United Nations’ peacekeeping operation in Mali. Germany has suspended parts of its involvement, not ended it.
match_headline: French Soldiers Quit Mali After 9 Years, Billions Spent and Many Lives Lost

text: An article on Thursday about Mexico’s future in fossil fuels, relying on data from 2019, misstated the amount of energy Mexico generates from fossil fuels versus other sources. As of 2021, the country generated about 70 percent of its energy from fossil fuels, not 80 percent, with renewables, nuclear power and other low-emission sources making up the rest, according to government figures.
match_headline: Mexico Sees Its Energy Future in Fossil Fuels, Not Renewables

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the Parkland school shooting survivors’ embrace of activism misidentified a participant in a meeting that included relatives of victims of the Uvalde school shooting. The image shows Brett Cross, not David Hogg.
match_headline: Impatient With Gun Debate, Parkland Survivors Embraced Activism

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the history of the polio vaccine, using information from The Associated Press, referred incorrectly to an anti-polio inoculation campaign in Elmira, N.Y., in 1953. The image showed children lined up to receive gamma globulin shots, not the polio vaccine. (The vaccine was not widely available until 1955.)
match_headline: Was I Vaccinated Against Polio? Young Adults Wonder.

text: An article on Tuesday about the Mets pitching duo of Max Scherzer and Jacob deGrom attributed erroneously a distinction to Randy Johnson. Johnson and Greg Maddux have each won four Cy Young Awards in a row; Johnson is not the only pitcher to have done so.
match_headline: Scherzer and deGrom Are Great. But How Great?

text: An article on Aug. 14 about women who escaped the Taliban and are in their first year at U.S. universities misstates the location of a gathering hosted by a student at Arizona State University. It was in a dorm room, not in a hotel room adjacent to the campus.
match_headline: She’s at Brown. Her Heart’s Still in Kabul.

text: An article on Aug. 14 about the musician Connie Converse misspelled the given name of her younger brother. He was Philip Converse, not Phillip.
match_headline: The Art of Disappearance

text: An article on Page 146 this weekend about collectors of artworks by gay artists misstates the medium of a 1990 portrait of Paul Monette by Don Bachardy. It is acrylic on paper, not watercolor.
match_headline: Resurrecting the Forgotten Art of the AIDS Era

text: An obituary on Thursday about the inventor Raymond Damadian referred incorrectly to the first commercial M.R.I. scanner, which was produced by his company in 1980. It was based on his own scientific work; it did not incorporate the work of Paul C. Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield, who later shared a Nobel Prize for the science behind the scanner. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misidentified the court that affirmed a lower court’s ruling in favor of Dr. Damadian in his patent infringement suit against General Electric. It was the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, not the Second Circuit.
match_headline: Raymond Damadian, Creator of the First M.R.I. Scanner, Dies at 86

text: An article last Sunday about the designer Eileen Fisher misstated the given name of her daughter. She is Sasha, not Emily.
match_headline: The Queen of Slow Fashion on the Art of a Slow Exit

text: An article on Monday about Kremlin-controlled news media misspelled the surname of a man who broadcasts a Russian press review on YouTube for an organization founded by the Kremlin critic Aleksei A. Navalny. He is Ilya Shepelin, not Shelepin.
match_headline: What Russians See in the News: A War Over Western Plans to Subjugate Them

text: An article on Sunday about the killing of a student in a national forest in Alabama misstated the location of the shooting. It occurred east of Birmingham, Ala., not west.
match_headline: Student Fatally Shot by Woman He Stopped to Help

text: An obituary on Sunday about the stuntman Gene LeBell misstated the original surname of his mother. It was Goldstein, not Moss.
match_headline: Gene LeBell, 89, Judo Champion, Wrestler and Star Stuntman, Dies

text: An obituary on Sunday about Ann McGuiness, a fund-raiser for Planned Parenthood and other organizations, misspelled the surname of a former United States senator from Colorado. He is Tim Wirth, not Worth.
match_headline: Ann McGuiness, Major Fund-Raiser for Women’s Health, Dies at 65

text: An article on Tuesday about the search for hundreds of sensitive documents at Mar-a-Lago, former President Donald J. Trump’s home in Florida, misstated the classification of a set of documents recovered in the search. They were marked top secret/sensitive compartmented information, not top secret/secret compartmented information.
match_headline: Trump Had More Than 300 Classified Documents at Mar-a-Lago

text: An article on Tuesday about language in the Inflation Reduction Act that gives the Environmental Protection Agency the authority to regulate greenhouse gases misstated the date of a meeting between Democratic and Republican aides in the Lyndon Baines Johnson Room of the U.S. Capitol. It took place on Aug. 3, not on Aug. 5.
match_headline: Democrats Designed the Climate Law to Be a Game Changer. Here’s How.

text: An obituary on Saturday about Dr. Nafis Sadik, a former executive director of the United Nations Population Fund, misstated the given name of the fund’s current executive director. She is Natalia Kanem, not Natalie.
match_headline: Nafis Sadik, U.N. Official and ‘Proud Champion of Choice,’ Dies at 92

text: An article on Wednesday about Nicaragua’s attacks on church leaders referred incorrectly to the murders of dozens of priests and nuns in the 1980s civil wars in El Salvador and Guatemala. They were killed by security forces and paramilitaries aligned with the government, not both sides.
match_headline: Nicaragua Silences Its Last Outspoken Critics: Catholic Priests

text: An article on Sunday about the challenge of welcoming more migrants, relying on a witness account from the scene, described incorrectly the actions of Mayor Eric Adams’s team distributing food at a volunteer event for migrants. They took boxes of food donated by volunteers from a table, not out of the hands of volunteers.
match_headline: A Migrant Wave Tests New York City’s Identity as the World’s Sanctuary

text: An article on Sunday about the financial implications of attending college misstated the percentage of people from the New England Conservatory of Music who were earning more than high school graduates six years after enrolling there. According to a study of federal data by Third Way, 48 percent of the people were earning more, not 57 percent.
match_headline: Some Colleges Don’t Produce Big Earners. Are They Worth It?

text: An article on Wednesday about the growing usage of cannabis and hallucinogenic compounds misstated the time period in which people age 19-30 had used cannabis. It was 20 or more times over the previous year, not month.
match_headline: Use of Marijuana and Psychedelics Is Soaring Among Young Adults, Study Finds

text: An article on Aug. 19 about a sculptural billboard on Sunset Boulevard in West Hollywood designed by the architect Tom Wiscombe referred to Wiscombe as a professor at Southern California Institute of Architecture in downtown Los Angeles; while he remains a professor there, he has been placed on paid leave. The institute declined to comment on Wiscombe’s leave, which came after students’ criticism of internships at his firm.
match_headline: There’s a New Billboard in Town, and You Can Walk in

text: An article on Thursday about the Public Works musical adaptation of “As You Like It,” relying on incorrect information from a source, misstated the age range of the community members taking part in “As You Like It.” It is 7 to 81, not 87.
match_headline: With ‘As You Like It,’ Public Works Aims for a Reflection of Humanity

text: An article on Thursday about California’s plan to ban the sale of gasoline-powered cars featured a quotation that misstated the distinction of the California measure. While California is the first U.S. state government to mandate zero-emission vehicles, it is not the only government to have done so. (British Columbia has similar rules in place.)
match_headline: California to Ban the Sale of New Gasoline Cars

text: An article on Tuesday about the expansion of government loans and loan guarantees for clean energy misidentified the energy market in which the Palisades Power Plant in Michigan is situated. It is the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, not PJM.
match_headline: Expansion of Clean Energy Loans Is ‘Sleeping Giant’ of Climate Bill

text: An article on Page 36 this weekend about the artist Cecilia Vicuña misstates the date of her painting “Leoparda de Ojitos.” It is 1977, not 1976.
match_headline: Cecilia Vicuña’s Desire Lines

text: An article on Aug. 21 about the Arizona Republican Party referred imprecisely to Selina Bliss’s performance in the Republican primary for an Arizona House seat. She came in second and so will appear on the general-election ballot along with Quang Nguyen, the G.O.P. incumbent, and two Democratic candidates. She was not eliminated from the race.
match_headline: The Arizona Republican Party’s Anti-Democracy Experiment

text: An obituary on Aug. 9 about the historian David McCullough referred incorrectly to the performance of his book “Truman” on The New York Times’s best-seller list. While it was on the list for 43 weeks, it never “topped” the list.
match_headline: David McCullough, Best-Selling Explorer of America’s Past, Dies at 89

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Hall of Fame quarterback Len Dawson misstated the circumstances under which he joined the Dallas Texans of the American Football League (who would become the Kansas City Chiefs). He had been released by the Cleveland Browns of the N.F.L. after going unclaimed by the league’s other teams in the waiver process; the Texans did not take part in that process, because they were in a rival league.
match_headline: Len Dawson, Who Took Kansas City to a Championship, Dies at 87

text: An article on Friday about the sale of the art collection of the Microsoft co-founder Paul G. Allen omitted a material used for “Small False Start.” It was encaustic, acrylic and paper collage, not just acrylic and paper collage.
match_headline: Christie’s to Sell Paul G. Allen’s $1 Billion Art Collection

text: An article on Sunday about the benefits of dialectical behavior therapy on suicidal or self-harming teens misidentified the profession of Michele Berk. She is a psychologist, not a psychiatrist.
match_headline: ‘The Best Tool We Have’ for Self-Harming and Suicidal Teens

text: An obituary on Saturday about the convicted fraudster Steven Hoffenberg referred incorrectly to Sutton Place, where he once lived. It is just south of the Upper East Side of Manhattan; it is not “on Manhattan’s Upper East Side.”
match_headline: Steven Hoffenberg, Debt Baron Who Ran a Vast Fraud, Dies at 77

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a potential protracted standoff between Ukraine and Russia referred imprecisely to Ukraine’s military attacks on Russia. While Ukraine is using long-range, precision-guided rockets provided by the United States against Russian forces, there is no evidence that they have been used to strike Crimea.
match_headline: Ukraine Weighs a Risky Offensive to Break Out of a Stalemate

text: An article on Tuesday about Ukraine’s counteroffensive to retake territory seized by Russia misstated the name of a rocket launcher provided to Ukraine by the United States. It is the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, not the High Mobility Rocket Artillery System.
match_headline: Ukraine Launches Southern Offensive, as Inspectors Head to Nuclear Plant

text: An article on Saturday about the federal government’s 20-month effort to retrieve documents from former President Donald J. Trump misstated which documents Mr. Trump’s team had sought to find lawyers who had the appropriate clearance to review. They were documents already retrieved by the National Archives, not ones remaining at Mr. Trump’s home in Florida.
match_headline: Inside the 20-Month Drive to Get Trump to Return Presidential Material

text: An article on Sunday about the growing number of teenagers using powerful psychiatric drugs misidentified the journal that published an analysis citing a “significantly increased diagnosis” of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder after the requirement for impairment was dropped. It was the journal JAMA Network Open, not The Journal of the American Medical Association.
match_headline: This Teen Was Prescribed 10 Psychiatric Drugs. She’s Not Alone.

text: An article on Tuesday about Serena Williams’s first-round U.S. Open match misspelled a player’s given name. It is Frances Tiafoe, not Francis.
match_headline: Serena Williams Keeps Focus Amid the Fanfare

text: An obituary on Aug. 17 about the filmmaker Wolfgang Petersen misidentified the interviewer to whom he said, “When I was 11, I decided I wanted to become a film director.” It was André Müller, not Elfriede Jelinek. And a picture caption with the obituary misidentified an actor shown in a scene from Mr. Petersen’s movie “Das Boot.” He is not Jürgen Prochnow.
ref_headline: When I was 11, I decided I wanted to become a film director.
match_headline: Wolfgang Petersen, Director of ‘Das Boot,’ Is Dead at 81

text: An article on Wednesday about the rescheduling of the Artemis I mission launch because of an engine problem misspelled the given name of the launch weather officer. He is Mark Burger, not Marc Berger.
match_headline: NASA Plans to Retry Its Moon Rocket Launch on Saturday

text: An article last Thursday about Khristianne Uy, a private chef known as Chef K, who has worked with the Kardashians, misstated where she was catering for Philip Sarofim. It was Pebble Beach, Calif., not Miami.
match_headline: The Public Life of the Kardashians’ Private Chef

text: An article on Sunday about colonial reparations misstated the timing of a visit by King Philippe of Belgium to the Democratic Republic of Congo. It was in June, not last month.
match_headline: The Long Road Ahead for Colonial Reparations

text: An article on Wednesday about Confederate symbols at U.S. military sites, including a hooded K.K.K. figure at West Point, misstated the location of the three bronze plaques at the Bartlett Hall Science Center at West Point. They are located beside the entrance to the hall, not above the entrance.
match_headline: Plaque Bearing Image of Hooded K.K.K. Figure Hangs at West Point

text: An article on Thursday about Coco Gauff’s win against Elena-Gabriela Ruse of Romania at the U.S. Open misstated the year that Gauff was ousted from the U.S. Open in the first round. It was 2020, not 2021.
match_headline: Coco Gauff Warms Up the Court for Serena Williams, and Gets a Win

text: An article last Sunday about “quiet quitting” misstated the primary occupation of Carolyn Chen, the author of “Work Pray Code.” She is a sociologist, not a journalist.
match_headline: How Quitting a Job Changed My Relationships

text: An obituary on Thursday about the civil rights activist Esther Cooper Jackson misstated the number of grandsons who survive her. It is one, not three.
match_headline: Esther Cooper Jackson, Civil Rights Pioneer, Dies at 105

text: An article this weekend on Page 12 about the disc jockey Zach Sang misstates the arrangement surrounding the ownership of his content and his plans for a new studio. Sang is building a studio in conjunction with a production partner, OBB Media, not alone. OBB Media will have partial ownership of his content for a period of time; he does not retain sole ownership.
match_headline: Zach Sang, the Ryan Seacrest of the Youth, Wants to Save Radio

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about the football kicker Justin Tucker misstates the location of the game where he made his 66-yard field goal. It took place at Ford Field in Detroit on artificial turf, not at the Baltimore Ravens’ home field on grass.
match_headline: How Justin Tucker Became the Greatest Kicker in N.F.L. History

text: An article this weekend on Page 6 about grilling in city parks misstates the type of home that Roy and Ida White’s family moved to in East Harlem in 1938. It was an apartment building, not a brownstone.
match_headline: New York’s Communal Summer Ritual: Grilling

text: An article on Aug. 21 about farms that host social events misstated the New York county where the Hudson Valley CSA Coalition is based. It is Putnam, not Westchester.
match_headline: The Hottest Party Is at … the Farm

text: An article on Aug. 21 about the wedding of Denise Pyfrom and Daniel White misstated where Mr. White was deployed in 2014. It was Kuwait, not Iraq or Jordan.
match_headline: After She Gave an Inch, He Took Her Heart

text: An article about new home goods, relying on information from a publicist, misstated the starting price for individual clusters of glass pieces that are used in chandeliers made to order for Dolce & Gabbana’s Casa furniture line. Each cluster starts at 175,000 euros (about $175,300), not $300,000.
match_headline: From Ralph Lauren to Louis Vuitton, Who Dressed Your Living Room?

text: An article on Tuesday about one million migrants awaiting asylum hearings in the United States misstated the name of a think tank that analyzed data on migrants who were allowed to stay in the United States to face removal proceedings. It is the Migration Policy Institute, not the Migrant Policy Institute.
match_headline: Biden Administration Has Admitted One Million Migrants to Await Hearings

text: An article on Monday about plans to revive regular loudspeaker broadcasts in Vietnam referred incorrectly to Dan Doan. He is a man, not a woman.

text: An article on Page 42 this weekend about climate change paraphrases incorrectly comments by the author and activist Bill McKibben about the pace of energy transition. When noting that the transition is accelerating at once-unimaginable speeds, he expressed a concern that it still would not come fast enough; he was not predicting that that would be the case. The article also misstates the number of deaths from natural disasters. There are about 50,000 deaths each year today, from as much as an average of 500,000 deaths each year a century ago. It is not the case that there are about 50,000 deaths each decade today from as much as 500,000 deaths each decade a century ago. And the article referred incorrectly dates to the origins of the Non-Aligned Movement. It began in the early years of the Cold War, not in the last decades of the Cold War. And a picture caption with this article misidentified plants grown by Upward Farms. They are microgreens, not sprouts.
match_headline: Some good news on energy

text: An obituary on Friday about the literary agent Lucianne Goldberg misstated when she was hired by an adviser of President Richard M. Nixon to pose as a reporter. It was 1972, not 1973.
match_headline: Lucianne Goldberg, Who Helped Expose Clinton Affair, Dies at 87

text: An article last Sunday about the rivalry between tennis and pickleball misstated a statistic about tennis participation in 2020. According to the Physical Activity Council, some 21 million Americans played the sport that year; not all 21 million were playing it for the first time.
match_headline: Pickleball Is Expanding. Tennis Is Mad.

text: An article on Aug. 21 about living in Stone Ridge, N.Y., and another from Oct. 2 about living in Athens, N.Y., misstated the school year associated with enrollment data. In both cases it was the 2020-­21 school year, not 2021-­22.
match_headline: Stone Ridge, N.Y.: Antique Homes and Welcoming Neighbors

text: An article on Oct. 2 about a woman with facial drooping misidentified the institution with which the Facial Paralysis and Reanimation Center is affiliated. It is N.Y.U. Langone Health, not New York University.
match_headline: Her Face Started Drooping. What Was Wrong?

text: An article on Saturday about Giorgia Meloni, Italy’s new prime minister, and what her ascent has meant to her far-right followers misstated when the Italian Social Movement was first formed. It was 1946, not 1948.
match_headline: Italy’s Hard Right Feels Vindicated by Giorgia Meloni’s Ascent

text: An obituary on Saturday about Jerry Lee Lewis misstated the first name of the artist who had a hit with the song “Drinkin’ Wine Spo-Dee-O-Dee,” which Mr. Lewis performed when he was 14. He was Stick McGhee, not Sticks.
match_headline: Jerry Lee Lewis, a Rock ’n’ Roll Original, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Oct. 20 about the former energy secretary Charles W. Duncan Jr. misstated the name of a school he attended. It was Sewanee Military Academy — not Sewanee Academy, which became its name in 1971.
match_headline: Charles W. Duncan Jr., Energy Secretary in Oil Crisis, Is Dead at 96

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about Roz Wyman, who as a member of the Los Angeles City Council helped bring the Brooklyn Dodgers to Los Angeles, misstated how long Major League Baseball had 16 teams. It was until 1961, not until 1958. The obituary also misidentified the westernmost city with a Major League Baseball team before the Dodgers and Giants moved to California for the 1958 season. It was Kansas City, Mo., not St. Louis. (The Philadelphia Athletics moved to Kansas City in 1954.)
match_headline: Roz Wyman, Who Helped Bring the Dodgers to Los Angeles, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Oct. 16 about Robert Toll, the longtime chairman and chief executive of the home-building company Toll Brothers, misstated the country of origin of Albert Toll, his father. He had immigrated from what was then part of Russia but is now part of Ukraine; it is not the case that he was “a Ukrainian immigrant.”
match_headline: Robert Toll, Who Mass-Produced ‘McMansions,’ Is Dead at 81

text: An obituary on Monday about the poet Gerald Stern misstated his surname. As the obituary noted correctly, it is Stern, not Stein.
match_headline: Gerald Stern, Poet of Wistfulness, Anger and Humor, Dies at 97

text: An article on Tuesday about a correction officer who was stabbed while working at Rikers Island prison complex misstated the number of people who died either in or shortly after being released from New York City’s jails in 2013. It was 23, not 21.
match_headline: Correction Officer Is Stabbed in Head by Rikers Detainee

text: An article on Tuesday about inflation reaching a record high in Europe misstated the annual inflation rate for Britain in September. It was 10.1 percent, not 8.8 percent.
match_headline: Inflation in Europe Reaches a Record 10.7% as Officials Face Hard Options

text: An article on Sunday about the Penn State football team incorrectly described quarterback Sean Clifford’s success against Ohio State and Michigan, two of the team’s main rivals. He will end his college career with two victories against them, not one. (Both were against Michigan.)
match_headline: Penn State’s Football Team Isn’t Bad. It Isn’t Good Enough, Either.

text: An article on Tuesday about entertainment mogul David Geffen and how he is building his legacy as a philanthropist described incorrectly part of David Geffen’s career. While he was an agent for Janis Joplin, the Doors and Peter, Paul and Mary, he was not their manager early in their careers.
match_headline: One More Project for David Geffen: Building His Legacy

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Sunday about the impact of Western weapons on the war in Ukraine misidentified the location where Ukrainian soldiers were inspecting a rocket system. They were in the Mykolaiv region, not the Kherson region.
match_headline: With Western Weapons, Ukraine Is Turning the Tables in an Artillery War

text: An article on Tuesday about the growing acceptance of digital artists from major museums misstated the dates of the exhibition “Refik Anadol: Unsupervised.” It will run at the Museum of Modern Art through March 5, not Jan. 30.
match_headline: A Smithsonian zoo and museum are set to reopen seven days a week with masks optional.

text: An article last Thursday about the revival of J. Crew misspelled the given name of a fashion director and the publication where he works. He is Mobolaji Dawodu, not Mobilaji, and he is the fashion director at large of GQ, not GQ Style.
match_headline: Can Hypebeast Magic Revive J. Crew?

text: An article on Thursday about the Democratic Party’s long struggle to build a cohesive approach to immigration misstated the title of Carolina Rodriguez-Greer at the voter outreach group Mi Familia Vota. She is the group’s Arizona state director, not a co-executive director.
match_headline: Democrats Twist and Turn on Immigration as Republicans Attack in Waves

text: An article on Thursday about “The Age of Roe,” a new exhibition at Harvard on the broad impact of the Supreme Court’s 1973 decision in Roe v. Wade, misstated the name of the library hosting the exhibition. It is the Schlesinger Library on the History of Women in America, not the Schlesinger Library for the History of Women. The article also referred incorrectly to the college to which the suffragist Maud Wood Park donated her women’s rights collection. It was Radcliffe College, not Harvard.
match_headline: How Do You Tell the Story of Roe v. Wade?

text: An obituary on Thursday about the cartoonist George Booth misstated the date of the issue of The New Yorker that contained his two-page spread “Ip Gissa Gul.” It was Jan. 20, 1975, not Jan. 12. Because of an editing error, the obituary also referred incorrectly to Lee Lorenz. He was The New Yorker’s art editor from 1973 to 1993 and cartoon editor from 1993 to 1997; he is not currently the art editor.
match_headline: George Booth, New Yorker Cartoonist of Sublime Zaniness, Dies at 96

text: An article on Friday about the refugee crisis in Europe caused by the war in Ukraine misstated Sasha Kovtutskyi’s marital status. He and his partner are being hosted in Munich, but they are not married.
match_headline: A New Refugee Crisis Stirs Uncomfortable Issues for Europe

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the attempt by Kremlin proxies to broker a deal with Trump campaign officials to partition Ukraine refers imprecisely to a declassified report’s findings about Russian intelligence attempts to promote the idea of the Bidens’ corruption in Ukraine. The report strongly suggested that Rudolph W. Giuliani was among the Americans associated with this attempt; it did not say so outright.
match_headline: A government-connected Kremlin critic’s flight from Russia raises questions about who is still safe.

text: An article on Oct. 30 about climate change referred incorrectly to the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s prediction on warming. It predicts that warming could surpass 1.5 degrees Celsius as soon as the next decade, not 2 degrees Celsius.
match_headline: War in Ukraine Likely to Speed, Not Slow, Shift to Clean Energy, I.E.A. Says

text: An article on Page 17 this weekend about some favorite holiday movies of a select few celebrities misspells the surname of an actor. He is Macaulay Culkin, not Caulkin. The article also misspelled the name of a character in “How the Grinch Stole Christmas.” She is Cindy Lou Who, not Cindy Lou Hoo.
match_headline: The Stars Have Holiday-Movie Favorites, Too

text: An article on Saturday about Russians engaged in a grass-roots effort to find missing sons, husbands, brothers and other loved ones who fought for Russia misstated the location of Rostov-on-Don. It is in southwestern Russia, not southeastern Russia.
match_headline: Frustrating and Often Fruitless: The Search for Missing Russian Soldiers

text: An article on Sunday about North Korean missile tests and the U.S. deployment of supersonic B-1B bombers over the Korean Peninsula for the first time in years as part of a military exercise misstated the capability of the B-1B Lancer aircraft. They are currently configured to carry conventional bombs, not nuclear ones.
match_headline: North Korea Launches More Missiles, and U.S. Bombers Fly Over the South

text: Because of an editing error, a quotation highlighted with an article on Monday about Americans’ frustrations over the rise of political text messages referred incorrectly to Jon Leibowitz, a privacy lawyer in Washington who expressed concern over the ability of political groups to freely obtain and swap voters’ mobile numbers. As the article correctly noted, he is a former chairman of the Federal Trade Commission, not the Federal Communications Commission.
match_headline: Fed Up With Political Text Messages? Read On.

text: A map with an article on Friday about Qatar’s human rights record and dire working conditions for migrant laborers as it prepares for the World Cup included Lusail, Qatar, and gave an incorrect location for it. It is next to Doha, not well north of it.
match_headline: The World Cup Is Weeks Away. Will Qatar Be Ready?

text: An article on Friday about Barbra Streisand’s early recordings misstated the number of tracks on “Live at the Bon Soir.” It is two dozen, not three dozen.
match_headline: Barbra Streisand on Her Pristine Early Recordings: ‘That Girl Can Sing’

text: An article on Friday about Season 5 of “The Crown” referred incorrectly to Emma Corrin, who played Princess Diana in Season 4. She was nominated for an Emmy for the performance; she did not win.
match_headline: ‘The Crown’ Has a New Diana and Charles to Tear Apart

text: An obituary on Saturday about the playwright, screenwriter, director and actor Douglas McGrath misspelled part of his wife’s name. She is Jane Read Martin, not Reed.
match_headline: Douglas McGrath, Playwright, Filmmaker and Actor, Is Dead at 64

text: An article on Tuesday about the construction of a bridge across the Gambia River, which has eliminated one of the region’s biggest traffic bottlenecks, misstated when the project began. It was in 2015, at a time when then-President Yaya Jammeh was facing intense pressure for change, not 2017, the year he lost power.
match_headline: Rotted Vegetables and Rancid Milk No More, as a Bridge Replaces Ferries

text: A column on Tuesday about worries over the branding of female college athletes who are making millions in endorsements thanks to their large social media followings and new N.C.A.A. rules misspelled the first name of the Connecticut basketball player. She is Azzi Fudd, not Aziz.
match_headline: New Endorsements for College Athletes Resurface an Old Concern: Sex Sells

text: An article on Tuesday about the new season of “The Crown” misstated how Countess Mountbatten of Burma became involved in carriage racing. Prince Philip introduced her to the sport, not the other way around.
match_headline: A Low Point for the Monarchy, in a New Season of ‘The Crown’

text: An editorial on Monday about the importance of this year’s midterm elections misidentified which Congress will count the electoral votes in the 2024 presidential election. It will be the 119th Congress, not the 118th Congress.
match_headline: What’s at Stake in These Elections

text: An article last Thursday about the photographer Steven Klein contained a number of errors. It incorrectly included the photographer Peter Lindbergh among those whose careers were sidelined by allegations of sexual misconduct. Mr. Lindbergh was not accused of sexual misconduct. The article misstated Mr. Klein’s age, using information from the artist; according to public records, he is 67, not 57. The article misstated when Mr. Klein began studying at the Rhode Island School of Design; it was in the early 1970s, not 1981. It also misstated the year that Dennis Freedman left W magazine as creative director; it was 2010, not 2009. The article misstated the year of Mr. Klein’s Vogue shoot in a meat locker; it was 2004, not 2005.
match_headline: The Voyeur in Repose

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the economist Herman Daly misstated the title of Peter A. Victor’s biography of Mr. Daly. It is “Herman Daly’s Economics for a Full World,” not “Herman Daly’s Economics for a Full Word.”
ref_headline: Herman Daly’s Economics for a Full World,
match_headline: Herman Daly, 84, Who Challenged the Economic Gospel of Growth, Dies

text: An article on Wednesday about Wes Moore, the newly elected Governor of Maryland, referred imprecisely to Mr. Moore’s claim that he was a Baltimore native. The claim was published on his book’s dust jacket, not in the text, and it was later removed.
match_headline: Moore, a Democrat, Will Become Maryland’s First Black Governor

text: An obituary on Saturday about the playwright, screenwriter, director and actor Douglas McGrath, using information from a spokesman, misstated his birth date. He was born on Feb. 12, 1958 — not Feb. 2.

An obituary on Nov. 2 about the restaurant critic Gael Greene misidentified the news service that hired her after she graduated from the University of Michigan in 1955. It was United Press — not United Press International, which was formed in 1958 when United Press merged with the International News Service.
match_headline: Gael Greene, Who Shook Up Restaurant Reviewing, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Thursday about the lawyer Paul Morantz misstated at one point where he died. As correctly noted elsewhere, he died in a hospital, not at his home.
match_headline: Paul Morantz, Lawyer Who Campaigned Against Cults, Dies at 77

text: An article on Friday about photographs of the Nazi attacks of Kristallnacht, which is widely commemorated as the start of the Holocaust, referred incorrectly to the photographs, based on information provided by Yad Vashem, Israel’s Holocaust memorial. The pictures appeared elsewhere, including on the granddaughter’s Twitter feed and in a book. They were not newly released. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: 84 Years Later, a Rare Look at the Nazi Attacks of Kristallnacht

text: An article on Friday about the pro-Trump grass roots that proved to be more liability than asset for Republicans in the midterm elections misstated how many election deniers ran for statewide offices this year. There were 94 statewide races for offices that oversee elections, not 94 election denier candidates.
match_headline: The Right-Wing Grass Roots Scored Big in 2010. But 2022 Was Far Different.

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about how farmers in Puerto Rico have adapted to hurricanes misstates the title of a documentary. It is “Serán las Dueñas de la Tierra,” not “Serán Dueños de la Tierra.”
ref_headline: Serán las Dueñas de la Tierra,
match_headline: Can an Island Feed Itself?

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 115 this weekend about Muslim Spain misidentifies the place where five and a half centuries of Muslim rule were ended by Ferdinand III of Castile in 1248. It was the city known today as Seville, Spain, not the entire Iberian Peninsula. The article also renders incorrectly the Arabic word for stalactite vaulting; it is “muqarnas,” not “muqarna.”
match_headline: In Search of a Lost Spain

text: An article on Page 60 about Monument House, a retreat near Joshua Tree, Calif., misstates its accommodations. The entire house can be booked starting at $299 per night; it is not possible to book individual rooms.
match_headline: A Cubed, Colorful Retreat in the California Desert

text: An article last Sunday about Roman and Williams, the architectural and interior design firm, misspelled the birthplace of one of its founders, Stephen Alesch. It is Neenah, Wis., not Nina.
match_headline: What Makes a Room Unforgettable?

text: An article on Monday about assertions by John F. Kelly, President Donald J. Trump’s second White House chief of staff, that Mr. Trump repeatedly sought investigations of his perceived political enemies by the Internal Revenue Service, misspelled the surname of the former head of the Special Operations Command. He is William H. McRaven, not McCraven.
match_headline: Trump Wanted I.R.S. Investigations of Foes, Top Aide Says

text: An article on Friday about Nepal’s efforts to renew and protect forest land misidentified the weapon carried by a soldier patrolling an area of the forest. It was an M16, not an AK-47.
match_headline: How Nepal Grew Back Its Forests

text: An article on Sunday about President Biden’s appearance at the summit meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to reinforce his administration’s efforts to counter China’s rise and to promote human rights misstated the title of Jake Sullivan. He is the president’s national security adviser, not director.
match_headline: In His 3rd Summit With Southeast Asian Leaders, Biden Bets on Face Time

text: An article on Monday about Indonesia President Joko Widodo seeking a larger role on the global stage misstated the amount of money China invested in Indonesia in the first nine months of this year. It is $5.2 billion, not $5.2 million.
match_headline: Once Inward-Looking, Joko Widodo Casts Himself as a Global Statesman

text: An article on Thursday about a century-long bond formed between the Inabas and the Yakama Nation through a farm in eastern Washington misspelled the surname of one of the members of the Inaba family. Her name is Tamaki Inaba Mitsui, not Matsui. A picture caption with the article also misidentified a family member. The woman pictured was Tamaki Inaba Mitsui, not Reiko Inaba.
match_headline: A Japanese American Family, a Native American Tribe and a Bountiful Friendship

text: An article on Friday about body image issues misstated relative rates of body dissatisfaction among boys. It is more common for overweight boys to want to be thinner, not for underweight boys to want to be larger.
match_headline: The Super-Skinny Ideal Isn’t ‘Back’ — It Never Left

text: A column on Sunday about political polarization misstated the number of Americans who had died in the Covid-19 pandemic by November 2020. It was hundreds of thousands, not more than one million.
match_headline: Three Theories That Explain This Strange Moment

text: An article on Sunday about the cryptocurency exchange FTX investigating “unauthorized transactions” a day after it filed for bankruptcy paraphrased incorrectly advice that Pantera Capital gave its portfolio companies. Pantera told them to check their exposure to the FTX collapse, not necessarily to sell FTT tokens.
match_headline: FTX Investigating Possible Hack Hours After Bankruptcy Filing

text: An article on Saturday about the critic and filmmaker Elvis Mitchell misstated the titles Steven Soderbergh and David Fincher have on Mitchell’s new documentary. They are producers of the film, “Is That Black Enough for You?!?,” not its executive producers.
ref_headline: Is That Black Enough for You?!?,
match_headline: For Elvis Mitchell, Critic Turned Filmmaker, a Chance to Show and Tell

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the United States and China resuming discussions about combating climate change misstated the current average global temperature increase in Fahrenheit. The current average global temperature increase, compared with the preindustrial era, is 1.1 degrees Celsius. That is the equivalent of roughly 2 degrees Fahrenheit of increase, not 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit.
match_headline: U.S. and China Restart Climate Talks

text: An article on Tuesday about an upcoming vote at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures to abandon the leap second by 2035 referred incorrectly to a kilogram. It is a measurement of mass, not weight.
match_headline: Time Has Run Out for the Leap Second

text: An article on Saturday about parody accounts proliferating on Twitter after its new owner, Elon Musk, allowed users to receive a profile verification check mark for $8 a month described incorrectly an interaction between the rapper Doja Cat and Elon Musk. Doja Cat thanked Mr. Musk for allowing her to change her Twitter name, but she did not change her display name to “Elon Musk.”
match_headline: A Verifiable Mess: Twitter Users Create Havoc by Impersonating Brands

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about an Iranian protester who fled to Iraq after being shot and wounded during an antigovernment protest in Tehran described incorrectly the injuries suffered by the protester. He was shot and wounded by metal pellets, but not blinded by a rubber bullet.
match_headline: Riddled With Metal Pellets, an Iranian Protester Heals in Hiding Abroad

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about a new guard of gallerists misspelled the given name of a partner in Objective Gallery. He is Marc Jebara, not Mark.
match_headline: ‘See, Touch…Smell’: The Next Generation of Design Gallerists Invites You Inside

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Maggie Doherty and Josh Zager misstated the breed of the couple’s dog, Patsy Cline. She is a Nova Scotia duck tolling retriever, not a trolling receiver.
match_headline: Always the Wedding Singer, Finally the Bride

text: An article on Thursday about the uncrewed flight of the giant Space Launch System and a new era of spaceflight, using information from NASA, misstated a spacecraft’s distance from the moon during a flyby. It is about 80 miles, not 60 miles.
match_headline: NASA Blazes a Path Back to the Moon With Artemis Rocket Launch

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about a former anti-abortion leader who claimed that there was a leak of the Supreme Court’s opinion in a 2014 landmark case involving contraception and religious rights misstated the setting of a photo of Steve, Barbara and David Green and the Rev. Rob Schenck. They were shown at an event for the Museum of the Bible, not at the museum itself. Another picture caption misidentified the client that David Cortman represented as a lawyer. It was Conestoga Wood Specialties, not Hobby Lobby.
match_headline: Former Anti-Abortion Leader Alleges Another Supreme Court Breach

text: An article on Nov. 14 about a mother who was arrested after allowing her 10-year-old son to get a tattoo misstated the name of the academy that issued the guidance on tattoos for pediatricians. It is the American Academy of Pediatrics, not the American Academy of Pediatric Medicine.
match_headline: A 10-Year-Old Got a Tattoo. His Mother Was Arrested.

text: An article on Sunday about President Biden’s age misstated the age of Senator Dianne Feinstein. She is 89, not 88. The article also misstated the year in which President George H.W. Bush died. It was 2018, not 2014.
match_headline: President Biden Is Turning 80. Experts Say Age Is More Than a Number.

text: An article on Saturday about Representative Hakeem Jeffries, favored to become the leader of the House Democrats as Nancy Pelosi steps down, and Senator Chuck Schumer bringing Brooklyn to the national political spotlight misstated the location of Junior’s Restaurant. It is on Flatbush and DeKalb Avenues, not Fulton and DeKalb Avenues. It also misstated the Brooklyn neighborhood in which Mr. Jeffries lives. It is Prospect Heights, not Bedford Stuyvesant.
match_headline: Brooklyn’s in the House. And the Senate.

text: An article on Sunday about the Chinese government seeking out military veterans and Communist Party members to try to help an Apple supplier address a labor shortage misstated the salary offered to workers by Foxconn. It is 30 yuan ($4) per hour, not per day.
match_headline: An iPhone Factory Needs Workers. The Chinese Government Wants to Help.

text: An article on Saturday about Bonnie Garmus’s novel “Lessons in Chemistry” misspelled the surname of an actor; she is Brie Larson, not Larsen. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Beneath Its Pink Cover, ‘Lessons in Chemistry’ Offers a Story About Power

text: An article on Tuesday about a conservation group helping Hawaii take out an insurance policy on its coral reefs to help defend them against climate change misstated the involvement of the Nature Conservancy in purchasing insurance for a coral reef off the coast of Puerto Morelos. The group helped arrange for an insurance policy to be bought, it did not purchase the policy itself.
match_headline: Climate Change Is Threatening Hawaii’s Coral Reefs. So They Called the Insurance Guy.

text: An article on Tuesday about the folk musician Buffy Sainte-Marie misspelled the surname of a member of the Indigo Girls. It is Saliers, not Sailers.
match_headline: Buffy Sainte-Marie Broke Boundaries in Folk. A Documentary Tells Her Story.

text: An article on Tuesday about the retired army veteran who took down the assailant who opened fire at a Colorado Springs nightclub on Saturday, relying on a first-person account, referred incorrectly to a person who helped subdue the suspect. An owner of the club said the person was a transgender woman, not a drag performer.
match_headline: ‘He Saved a Lot of Lives’: Combat Veteran Tackled Colorado Gunman

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Saudi Arabia’s upset win over Argentina in its opening match in this year’s World Cup incorrectly described the actions of Qatar’s emir as he celebrated Saudi Arabia’s victory. He wrapped a Saudi flag around his own shoulders, not those of Saudi Arabia’s crown prince.
match_headline: Even the Saudi Team Is Stunned After Victory Over Argentina

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about Senator Lindsey Graham testifying before a Georgia special grand jury in an investigation of possible election interference by former President Donald J. Trump and his allies misidentified the number of times that Mr. Trump has run for president. This is his third run, not his second.
match_headline: After Court Fight, Lindsey Graham Appears Before Atlanta Grand Jury

text: An article on Sunday about the first intercollegiate gymnastics team at a historically Black college or university misidentified the member of the Fisk board of trustees who arranged a key meeting that preceded the establishment of the team. It was Frank Simmons, an alumni trustee, not Frank L. Sims, who is the interim president of the board.
match_headline: The First H.B.C.U. Gymnastics Team Is Aiming Even Higher

text: An obituary on Sunday about the historian, lawyer and activist Staughton Lynd misstated the source of a quotation from him that appeared in The Bill of Rights Journal in 1988. It was from an interview with Mr. Lynd, not an article he wrote.
match_headline: Staughton Lynd, Historian and Activist Turned Labor Lawyer, Dies at 92

text: An article on Friday about Representative Mary Peltola, Democrat of Alaska, becoming the first Alaska Native woman to serve in Congress misstated the manner in which Representative Don Young took office. He did not defeat Representative Nick Begich; he won a special election after Mr. Begich was declared to have died in a plane crash.
match_headline: Mary Peltola Wins Bid to Serve Full Term in the House for Alaska

text: An article this weekend on Page 6 about the performances of Corey Hawkins and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II in “Topdog/Underdog” misstates Abdul-Mateen’s age. He is 36, not 38.
match_headline: In ‘Topdog/Underdog,’ They Perfect the Art of Deception

text: An article on Nov. 20 about the Ukrainian railroad system misstated when Ukraine’s airspace was closed. It was a few hours before the Russian invasion, not a few days before.
match_headline: Ukraine’s 15,000-Mile Lifeline

text: An article last Sunday about the merger of AT&T and Time Warner contained several errors. It misstated the size of HBO’s loss in earnings, based on public comments by the chief executive of Warner Bros. Discovery, David Zaslav. Its earnings dropped $3 billion, from $2.5 billion in profit in 2019. It did not lose $3 billion. The article incorrectly described the nature of Elliott Investment Management’s involvement with AT&T, and misstated the given name of the activist investor who runs that fund. He is Paul Singer, not Peter. Elliott Investment Management sold a portion of its stake, not all of it. And its overall investment in AT&T has been profitable. It did not lose money. The article also misstated the distinction of Ann Sarnoff’s appointment at Warner Bros. She was the first woman to head that studio, not the first woman to head a major Hollywood studio.
match_headline: Was This $100 Billion Deal the Worst Merger Ever?

text: An article last Sunday about “Welcome to Chippendales” misidentified Steve Banerjee’s origins. He was South Asian, not Southeast Asian.
match_headline: Kumail Nanjiani Didn’t Know He Was Playing the Bad Guy

text: An article on Nov. 13 about Sarah Ruhl and Rebecca Taichman’s “Becky Nurse of Salem” misidentified the oldest person hanged in the Salem witch trials. It was George Jacobs, not Rebecca Nurse, who was the oldest woman.
match_headline: Sarah Ruhl and Rebecca Taichman on Conjuring ‘Becky Nurse of Salem’

text: An article on Oct. 30 about “Kimberly Akimbo” misspelled the name of the character portrayed by Bonnie Milligan. It is Debra, not Deborah.
match_headline: How They Assembled the ‘Kimberly Akimbo’ Puzzle

text: An article on Oct. 23 about atypical anorexia included an erroneous detail about the GreySheet diet. It is not calorie-based and does not recommend only 1,200 calories per day.
match_headline: ‘You Don’t Look Anorexic’

text: A review last Sunday about “Mr. B: George Balanchine’s 20th Century,” by Jennifer Homans, misstated the year that Bernard Taper’s biography of Balanchine was published. It came out in 1963, not 1996.
match_headline: A New Biography of George Balanchine, Ballet’s Colossus

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about a new era of direct confrontation between the Biden administration and Iran misspelled the surname of a woman who died while in police custody in Iran. She is Mahsa Amini, not Mahsa Amina.
match_headline: United States Enters a New Era of Direct Confrontation With Iran

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about a family grieving a loved one who died of Covid-19 after consuming misinformation about the virus on a social media platform misstated the full name of the woman who spoke about her father’s death and misidentified her sibling in one image. Danielle Watt is shown in the top left photo, and it was Jessica Watt Dougherty, not Jessica Watt, who talked about her father’s refusal to get vaccinated.
match_headline: A Lasting Legacy of Covid: Far-Right Platforms Spreading Health Myths

text: An article on Saturday about new Republican House leaders misstated the number of terms that Representatives Jim Jordan and Mike D. Rogers have served in Congress. Mr. Jordan has served eight terms, not seven, and Mr. Rogers has served 10 terms, not 11.
match_headline: Meet the House Republicans Who Will Wield Power in the New Congress

text: An article on Saturday about a man whose family members were among the victims of Russian war crimes in the city of Kherson misstated when Serhiy Novosad returned to the small village of Lvivsky Otrubi. It was recently, but not this week.
match_headline: Under a Cross Atop a Shallow Grave, He Found His Father

text: Because of an editing error, a display quote with an article on Friday about Les Knight, the founder of the Voluntary Human Extinction movement, misstated his employment status. Mr. Knight is not a former teacher; he still teaches.
match_headline: Earth Now Has 8 Billion Humans. This Man Wishes There Were None.

text: An article on Monday about two ice cream entrepreneurs misspelled the surname of the owner of Malai. She is Pooja Bavishi, not Bavashi. It also misstated the year in which her Malai shop in Carroll Gardens opened. It was 2019, not 2015.
match_headline: Two Innovators on ‘Telling Stories Through Ice Cream’

text: An article on Saturday about Mexico’s legacy of fourth-game failure in World Cup matches misstated where Hirving Lozano plays club soccer. He plays at Napoli in Italy, not at PSV Eindhoven in the Netherlands.
match_headline: For Mexico, an Unlucky Seven

text: An article on Sunday about Western nations’ struggle to refill their arsenals while also arming Ukraine misstated the range of the missile known as ATACMS. It is up to about 190 miles, not 190 kilometers.
match_headline: U.S. and NATO Scramble to Arm Ukraine and Refill Their Own Arsenals

text: An article on Tuesday about Donald Trump’s loss of Jewish Republicans’ support after he hosted Kanye West and Nick Fuentes for dinner misstated Ben Shapiro’s position on Mr. Trump’s presidential candidacy in 2016. He broke with Mr. Trump during the campaign, but stood by him during his presidency.
match_headline: Jewish Allies Call Trump’s Dinner With Antisemites a Breaking Point

text: An article on Tuesday about a Sikh temple’s efforts to address loneliness in older people misstated the location of the Line of Control. It divides the region of Jammu and Kashmir, not Punjab.
match_headline: A Sikh Temple Combats Loneliness With Chai and Laughter

text: An article on Sunday about the increasingly common appointment of foreign judges in Pacific island nations misstated the status of William Hastings, the chief justice of Kiribati. He is a current New Zealand judge, seconded to Kiribati; he is not retired.
match_headline: This Country’s Top Judges Were All Foreigners. Now They’re Gone.

text: An article on Saturday about television shows to watch over the Thanksgiving holiday weekend, using information provided by a news release, misstated the timing of the release of the final season of “Pantheon.” It will premiere on AMC+ in 2023, but not in January.
match_headline: A Thanksgiving Binge Menu: 7 Fall Shows You Might Have Slept On

text: An article on Saturday about stem cell donation was imprecise in describing the age criteria for registering as a donor. People ages 18 to 40 may register with the national registry, Be the Match; other, cooperating registries have varied age requirements. It also misidentified the group that organized a donor’s travel. Travel for Delia Ephron’s donor was organized by DKMS, not by Be the Match.
match_headline: How to Save a Life

text: An obituary on Saturday about John Y. Brown, who transformed Kentucky Fried Chicken into a global brand and was later governor of Kentucky, misstated the day he died. It was Monday, Nov. 21, not Tuesday, Nov. 22. It also misstated the given name of the founder of Kentucky Fried Chicken. He was Harland Sanders, not Harlan. And a picture caption with the obituary misidentified the job Red Auerbach held in 1978. At that time he was the general manager of the Boston Celtics, of which Mr. Brown was an owner; he was not the team’s coach.
match_headline: John Y. Brown Jr., KFC Mogul and Kentucky Governor, Dies at 88

text: An article on Wednesday about China’s efforts to quash protests using surveillance and intimidation misstated the travel arrangements offered by Tsinghua University. It offered free buses from the university to railway stations and airports, not free air or rail travel.
match_headline: With Intimidation and Surveillance, China Tries to Snuff Out Protests

text: An article on Wednesday about the end of a deadly North Atlantic hurricane season misstated the intensity of Hurricane Fiona when it struck Puerto Rico. While Fiona reached a strength of Category 4, it was a Category 1 storm when it made landfall on the island.
match_headline: Hurricane Season Ends, Marked by Quiet August and Deadly September

text: An article on Wednesday about highlights from the recently opened Museum of Broadway misstated the year Luke McDonough started at the Public Theater. He has worked on costumes there since 1975; he has not been costume master since 1968. The article also misidentified the set designer who created a first-floor space in the museum that takes visitors behind the scenes of a show. It is David Rockwell, not David Korins. It also misstated how many items are on display. It is more than 1,000 objects and photographs, not more than 1,000 objects in addition to hundreds of photographs.
match_headline: The Museum of Broadway Is Open. Here Are 10 Highlights.

text: An article on Wednesday about the pattern of withdrawal of Russian forces as evidence of possible war crimes across Ukraine, relying on incorrect information from the Kherson regional prosecutor’s office, misstated the given name of a medical examiner. He is Ihor Motrych, not Serhiy.
match_headline: Russian Retreat Reveals Signs of an Atrocity in a Ukrainian Village

text: An article on Friday about Volker Türk, the new human rights chief at the United Nations, misstated the years in which Mr. Türk studied the law. It was the 1980s and 1990s, not the 1970s.
match_headline: Meet the World’s New Human Rights Crisis Manager. He Has a Lot to Do.

text: An article on Thursday about skepticism surrounding Mayor Eric Adams’s plan to address the crisis of mentally ill people on New York City’s streets misspelled the surname of the person who oversees teams of field clinicians for the Institute for Community Living. She is Bridgette Callaghan, not Callahan.
match_headline: On City Streets, Fear and Hope as Mayor Pushes to Remove Mentally Ill

text: An article on Thursday about the Food and Drug Administration’s consideration of new screening criteria for blood donations by gay and bisexual men misstated an aspect of the plan. The agency is not planning to ask men about condom use.

An obituary on Thursday about Christine McVie, the singer, songwriter and keyboardist of Fleetwood Mac, misstated when the band’s album “Heroes Are Hard to Find” was released. It was after “Mystery to Me,” not after “Penguin.” The obituary also misstated the year Ms. McVie’s album “In the Meantime” was released. It was 2004, not 2006.
match_headline: Christine McVie’s 12 Essential Songs

text: An article last Sunday about Elk Mountain, Wyo., and a dispute over land access misstated Sabrina King’s current job. She is a lobbyist for the Wyoming chapter of Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. She is no longer the policy director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Wyoming. It also mis­stated the average weight of an elk bull commonly found around Elk Mountain. It is 700 to 800 pounds, not 2,000.
match_headline: It’s Public Land. But the Public Can’t Reach It.

text: An article on Page 1 this weekend about Jessica Tisch, New York City’s new sanitation commissioner, misidentifies the city agency where Ms. Tisch worked previously. It was the Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications, not the Department of Operations and Information Technology.
match_headline: The Rats Are Absolutely Going to Hate the New Sanitation Commissioner

text: Because of an editing error, a Metropolitan Diary column last Sunday misstated which subway line the author was riding when she encountered a person dressed in a similar fashion. It was the F, not the B.
match_headline: ‘I Asked a Woman There if I Could Make a Call on Her Phone’

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about the artwork of Michaelina Wautier misstates the title of an exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. it is “Michaelina Wautier and ‘The Five Senses’: Innovation in 17th-Century Flemish Painting,” not “Michaelina Wautier and ‘The Five Senses’: Innovation in 17th-Century Painting.
ref_headline: Michaelina Wautier and ‘The Five Senses’: Innovation in 17th-Century Flemish Painting,
match_headline: How Much Watching Time Do You Have This Weekend?

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 58 about emojis as erotic symbols misidentifies a fruit. It is white dragon fruit, not red dragon fruit.
match_headline: How Did 🍆 Become Our Default Sex Symbol?

text: An article on Page 62 about a hybrid work and social space designed by Child Studio misspells the surname of a French artist. He was Georges Braque, not Braques.
match_headline: A Buffet-Style Los Angeles Dinner Party for Artists and Creatives

text: An article on Page 68 about the playwright Adrienne Kennedy misstates where the nonprofit Africare is based. It is in Washington, D.C., not Africa. The article also mistakenly suggests that Joseph Kennedy was the sole founder of Africare. He was a co-founder.
match_headline: At 91, Adrienne Kennedy Is Finally on Broadway. What Took So Long?

text: An article on Page 76 about Korean moon jars misidentifies a master potter; he is Kang Hyo Lee, not Kwangho Lee.
match_headline: Moon Jars, Luminous and Graceful, Are Entrancing Modern Ceramists

text: A picture caption with a review on Nov. 6 about “Before We Were Trans,” by Kit Heyam, misstated when the American preacher known as the Public Universal Friend died. It was in 1819, not the 18th century.
match_headline: A Global History of Gender, in All Its Varieties

text: An article on Saturday about Twitter’s U.S. ad revenue during the World Cup falling below forecasts misstated the duties of the former Twitter executive Dara Nasr. He oversaw Twitter’s ad operations in Britain, not Europe.
match_headline: Twitter Keeps Missing Its Advertising Targets as Woes Mount
