text: An article on Sunday about the difficult task of finding four worthy contenders for the 2024 College Football Playoff expanded season misidentified a team that beat Texas this season. While Texas lost to four opponents this season, Kansas State was not one of them.
match_headline: Losses by T.C.U. and U.S.C. Leave Playoff Powers With Unappealing Choices

text: An article on Saturday about Jacob deGrom’s deal with the Texas Rangers misstated Mr. deGrom’s ranking among pitchers with at least 200 starts in baseball’s expansion era in earned run average. His career 2.52 E.R.A. is the third-lowest E.R.A., not the fourth-lowest.
match_headline: In Huge Blow to Mets, Jacob deGrom Signs With Texas Rangers

text: An article on Sunday about Jacob deGrom’s place in Mets history referred incorrectly to the 2021 Washington Nationals. While Mr. deGrom’s most dominant game came against the 2021 Nationals, they did not go on to win the World Series.
match_headline: Where Does Jacob deGrom Rank in Mets History?

text: An article on Saturday about two Norwegians who pioneered a subgenre of sped-up remixes now popular on TikTok misstated the date the British producer Danny L Harle changed his Facebook status with a message praising nightcore. It was Sept. 16, 2010, not Sept. 15.$$$
match_headline: TikTok Is Filled With Sped-Up Remixes. Two Norwegians Pioneered Them.

text: An article on Sunday about Club Med’s first North American ski resort in decades misstated the distinction of the vertical drop at Le Massif de Charlevoix ski resort. It is the highest in Canada east of the Rockies, not the highest east of the Rockies over all.
match_headline: At a Club Med Ski Resort, Learning to Love the Apéro

text: An obituary on Saturday about the former federal prosecutor Mary Shannon Little misstated the given name of a former U.S. attorney general. He is Edwin Meese III, not Edward.
match_headline: Mary Shannon Little, Who Prosecuted Wedtech Scandal, Dies at 65

text: An article on Tuesday about the final day of the race between Senator Raphael Warnock and Herschel Walker in Georgia’s Senate runoff misspelled the name of a city in the Atlanta metro area. It is Acworth, not Ackworth.
match_headline: Warnock Claims Momentum in Georgia, as Walker Banks on Election Day Turnout

text: An article on Saturday about the Republican Party’s efforts to minimize Senator Raphael Warnock’s accomplishments described incorrectly the tax incentive on electric vehicles made in North America. The tax credit is worth up to $4,000, not $7,500. The article also misidentified the location of the Kia plant in Georgia. It is in West Point, Ga., not High Point, Ga.
match_headline: The Fight Over Warnock’s Record Comes Down to an Electric Car Plant in Georgia

text: An article on Saturday about Herschel Walker’s reliance on Republicans from Georgia or nearby states for support on the campaign trail misidentified the state Tom Cotton represents in the Senate. Mr. Cotton is a senator from Arkansas, not Oklahoma.
match_headline: With Big G.O.P. Names Largely Staying Away, Walker Stresses His Georgia Roots

text: An article on Tuesday about the third week of strikes by part-time faculty demanding better pay and working conditions at the New School in New York paraphrased Sanjay Reddy’s comments about cost-saving measures at the university incorrectly. Mr. Reddy said the university gave part-time faculty less work, not more.
match_headline: New School Adjuncts’ Push for Better Pay Drives Acrimonious Strike

text: An article on Tuesday about David Rivera, a former congressman, who was arrested over a secret contract with Venezuela misstated where Mr. Rivera was arrested. It was in the Atlanta area, not at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.
match_headline: Florida Ex-Congressman Arrested Over Secret Contract With Venezuela

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about a serial killer’s confession to five murders misstated the given name of one of the victims. As the article correctly noted, she is Laverne Moye, not Lauren Moye.
match_headline: ‘Torso Killer’ Admits to ’68 Strangling and 4 More Cold-Case Murders

text: An article on Tuesday about the ending of Japan’s World Cup tournament match against Croatia misstated how many Asian teams have made it to the World Cup quarterfinals. South Korea was the second team to do so in 2002, not the first. (North Korea did it in 1966.)
match_headline: How Old Are You? South Korea Tries to Simplify What Should Be a Simple Question.

text: An article on Saturday about Chantal Akerman’s rank in Sight and Sound’s “Greatest Films of All Time” critics’ poll, in one instance, misstated the year “Vertigo” was released. It was 1958, not 1959.
match_headline: Chantal Akerman’s ‘Jeanne Dielman’ Named Greatest Film of All Time in Sight and Sound Poll

text: An obituary on Saturday about the filmmaker Julia Reichert misspelled the surname of a director who collaborated with her and James Klein on the documentary “Union Maids.” He is Miles Mogulescu, not Mogelescu.
match_headline: Julia Reichert, Documentarian of the Working Class, Dies at 76

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the tennis coach Nick Bollettieri misstated part of the name of a hotel in Puerto Rico where was once tennis director. It is Dorado Beach, not Doral Beach.
match_headline: Nick Bollettieri, Nurturer of Tennis Champions, Dies at 91

text: An article on Wednesday about possible criminal referrals from the House committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol misidentified the county in which Milwaukee is located. It is in Milwaukee County, not Dane County.
match_headline: House Jan. 6 Committee Signals It Will Issue Criminal Referrals

text: An article on Monday about the exodus of Western companies from Russia misstated the surname of the owner of a bar in Kaluga. He is Kirill Nikulin, not Mikulin. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: War and Sanctions Threaten to Thrust Russia’s Economy Back in Time

text: An article last Thursday about Shannon Abloh, the widow of the designer Virgil Abloh, mis­stated, in some copies, when Mr. Abloh sold Off­-White to the luxury giant LVMH. The acquisition was announced in July 2021, not July 2020. The article also misidentified a pair of shoes that Virgil Abloh dyed purple for his wife. They were Off­-White x Air Jordan 4s, not Off­-White x Nike Air Force 1s.
match_headline: Shannon Abloh Is Ready to Talk

text: An article last Thursday about a new book, “Butts: A Backstory,” which examines the posterior’s cultural role throughout history, misstated the given name of a fit model whom the author, Heather Radke, profiled for the book. She is Natasha Wagner, not Lindsay Wagner. The article also misstated the title of a painting by Georges Seurat. It is “A Sunday on La Grand Jatte,” not “A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grand Jatte.” And the article, using information from Ms. Radke’s book, referred incorrectly to the history of Sarah Baartman. She was born in the 1770s or 1780s; the precise decade is unknown.
match_headline: Will the Era of Butts Ever End?

text: An article on Wednesday about the fight between the Russian government and a Swiss software company that masks a person’s identity and location online misstated the relationship between Viktoriia Safonova and Artem Nesterenko. They are partners; they are not married.
match_headline: Inside the Face-Off Between Russia and a Small Internet Access Firm

text: An obituary on Nov. 17 about the former Harvard University dean Henry Rosovsky, using information from his family, misstated his father’s given name. It was Selik, not Selig.
match_headline: Henry Rosovsky, 95, Builder of Black and Jewish Studies at Harvard, Dies

text: An article last Sunday about a cheating scandal in chess misstated the nationality of Maxim Dlugy, a grandmaster and chess coach. Mr. Dlugy is American; he is not Russian. A photo caption with that article also misstated the governmental status of Guernsey. As one of the Channel Islands, it is a British dependency, not a part of France.
match_headline: He’s the Bad Boy of Chess. But Did He Cheat?

text: An article last Sunday about the 17th-­century painter Michaelina Wautier described incorrectly the location of the Belgian city of Mons. It is southwest of Brussels, not northwest.
match_headline: For Centuries, Her Art Was Forgotten, or Credited to Men. No More.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Nov. 27 about podcasts that explore misinformation misidentified the person who drove a van into Toronto pedestrians in 2018. It was Alek Minassian, not Elliot O. Rodger.
match_headline: 6 Podcasts About the Perils of Misinformation

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about Greta Gerwig misspelled, in some cop­ies, the given name of her partner. As the article noted, he is Noah Baumbach, not Noam.
match_headline: Greta Gerwig, in the Pink

text: An article last Sunday about a school that trains nannies misquoted a Norland student commenting on the advice she might give to an employer who is suddenly out of work. She said, “You’d tell them to get on Universal Credit,” not “You’d tell them to get on univer­sity credit.”
ref_headline: You’d tell them to get on Universal Credit,
match_headline: Where Did the Royals Find Prince George’s Nanny?

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about a visit to Boston by Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, misstated Catherine’s title. She is Catherine, Princess of Wales, not Princess Catherine. The error was repeated in a headline and a picture caption.
match_headline: A Royal Visit, at a Careful Distance

text: An article on Nov. 20 about Brittani Nichols, a writer for “Abbott Elementary,” referred incorrectly to her financial aid while at Yale. She received academic scholarships from outside organizations and need­-based financial aid from Yale; she did not receive a basketball scholarship from Yale.
match_headline: An ‘Abbott Elementary’ Writer Who Draws From Her Experience

text: An article on Friday about the booming global market for commercial spyware described incorrectly the snooping technique used by a company Tal Dilian co-founded, Circles. It is Signaling System 7 exploitation, not simply Signaling System 7, which is a signaling protocol.
match_headline: How the Global Spyware Industry Spiraled Out of Control

text: An article on Sunday about the psychiatrist E. Fuller Torrey’s influence on New York City’s policy on the mentally ill misstated the name of the organization Dr. Torrey fell out with. It is the National Alliance on Mental Illness, not the National Alliance for the Mentally Ill.
match_headline: Behind New York City’s Shift on Mental Health, a Solitary Quest

text: An article on Saturday about the reaction to Brittney Griner’s release from a Russian prison misstated the political affiliation of Elizabeth Whelan, the sister of Paul Whelan, who is being held prisoner in Russia. Ms. Whelan has never been a supporter of Donald J. Trump.
match_headline: Blowback Over Griner’s Release Exposes Depth of America’s Divisions

text: An article on Monday about battles over voting rules, restrictions and political boundaries in the next election misstated the year of a Michigan ballot initiative that established an independent redistricting commission. It was 2018, not 2020.
match_headline: The Election Is Over. The Fight Over Voting Rules and Gerrymanders Isn’t.

text: An article on Friday about the House Republicans who voted yes on legislation to mandate federal recognition for same-sex marriages referred incorrectly to a congressman from Florida. He is Michael Waltz, not Tim Waltz.
match_headline: The 39 House Republicans Who Voted for the Same-Sex Marriage Bill

text: An article on Sunday about the many pregnant women who are still unaware of the effects of Covid-19 misstated the vaccine offered to pregnant women. It is the Tdap, not DTaP, vaccine.
match_headline: The Covid Pandemic’s Hidden Casualties: Pregnant Women

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the designers Dries Van and Christopher John Rogers, misstated the number of people employed by Mr. Van Noten’s company. It is 160, not 120.
match_headline: Two Fashion Designers on Staying Inspired and Independent

text: An article on Saturday about Turkey’s strengthening energy ties with Russia misidentified the country whose ports were subject to a Russian blockade that prevented the passage of Ukrainian grain. They were Ukrainian ports, not Turkish ports.
match_headline: Turkey Is Strengthening Its Energy Ties With Russia

text: Because of an editing error, a Sports of The Times column welcoming Brittney Griner’s return to the United States misstated the given name of the president of the Phoenix Mercury. He is Vince Kozar, not Victor Kozar.
match_headline: Letters Helped Brittney Griner Survive. Here’s One for Her Future.

text: An article on Saturday about Brazil’s loss to Croatia in the World Cup quarterfinals misidentified the Brazil defender who deflected Croatia’s goal that tied the score in the 117th minute. It was Marquinhos, not Éder Militão.
match_headline: ‘It Hurts’: Brazil Is Left Wondering What Went Wrong

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Saturday about the Stax Records co-founder Jim Stewart, using information from Getty Images, misstated the year a photo of Mr. Stewart with the Stax executive Al Bell and the singer, songwriter and producer Isaac Hayes was taken. It was 1971, not 1969.
match_headline: Jim Stewart, Unlikely Entrepreneur of Soul Music, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Dec. 5 about the military historian and board-game designer John Prados misstated part of the name of a game he created. It is “Rise and Decline of the Third Reich,” not “Rise and Fall of the Third Reich.”
ref_headline: Rise and Decline of the Third Reich,
match_headline: John Prados, Master of Uncovering Government Secrets, Dies at 71

text: An article on Tuesday about Iran’s public execution of protesters misstated the location of the city of Mashhad. It is in northeastern Iran, not northwestern Iran.
match_headline: Iran Turns to Public Executions, Enraging an Already Protesting Public

text: An article on Tuesday about Norway’s growing weariness of Russian spies in their society referred incorrectly to the position held by a man arrested as a Russian spy at the University of Tromso. He was a guest researcher, not a visiting researcher.
match_headline: In a Wary Arctic, Norway Starts to See Russian Spies Everywhere

text: An article on Tuesday about a shootout in Australia that left six dead referred incorrectly to a mass shooting in Tasmania. It happened in 1996, not 1966.
match_headline: 6 Dead, Including 2 Officers, After Shootout in Rural Australia

text: An article on Tuesday about the chairman of the African Union seeking greater representation for African nations in world affairs misstated the GDP of Africa. The continent has a GDP of $2.7 trillion, not billion.
match_headline: ‘There Must Be More Room for Africa,’ Leader of African Union Says

text: A subheading with an article on Tuesday about the television adaptation of the novel “Kindred” misspelled the surname of its author. As the article notes, she was Octavia E. Butler, not Bulter.
match_headline: ‘Kindred’ Review: Octavia Butler Comes to the Screen

text: An article on Saturday about the death of soccer journalist Grant Wahl, using information from one of Mr. Wahl’s representatives, misstated his age. He was 49, not 48.
match_headline: Soccer Journalist Dies at World Cup After Collapsing at Argentina Game

text: An article on Wednesday about Lionel Messi’s legacy as Argentina heads to the World Cup final misstated the number of Ballons d’Or won by Mr. Messi. It is seven, not five.
match_headline: The Maestro Conducts, and the Band Plays the Hits

text: An article on Tuesday about advances in brain implant technology misstated the current name of a company involved in brain implant research. It is Blackrock Neurotech, not Blackrock Microsystems.
match_headline: Brain Implants Have Begun to Restore Functions, but Advances Are Slow

text: An article last Thursday about the men’s wear depicted in the Netflix series “The Crown” misidenti­fied a great­-uncle of Charles III. He was Edward VIII, not Edward VII.
match_headline: Suits So Good They Make a Case for Monarchy

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Lloyd Newman, who as a teenager recorded two acclaimed radio documentaries with a friend, misstated the surname of a lawyer who once represented him. He is Joshua Tepfer, not Tepler.
match_headline: Lloyd Newman, Teenage Chronicler of ‘Ghetto Life,’ Dies at 43

text: An article on Sunday about an increase in New York City’s subway fare misstated the findings in a state comptroller report calculating the subway fare increases needed for the M.T.A. to reach prepandemic revenue levels. Fares would need to rise by 19 percent in 2026 to $3.54 — after a 4 percent increase in 2023 and again in 2025 — not by 23 percent every two years, starting with $3.38 in 2023 and then $4.16 in 2025.
match_headline: New York Subway Fare Could Soon Top $3 to Offset Steep Drop in Riders

text: An article on Tuesday about an Ohio Supreme Court decision that allowed the state historical society to expel a golf course from land featuring ancient Native American earthworks, using information from a dissenting opinion by Justice Sharon L. Kennedy, misstated the number of World Heritage sites nominated by the United States that had been accepted by UNESCO between 2008 and the trial hearing. The National Park Service notes that four of the five nominations in that period were accepted by UNESCO, not two.
match_headline: Golf Course on Ancient Earthworks Must Surrender Lease, Justices Say

text: An obituary on Nov. 27 about Pablo Eisenberg,the longtime executive director of the Center for Community Change, misstated the location in New Jersey of Millburn High School, which he attended. It is in Millburn, not Maplewood.
match_headline: Pablo Eisenberg, Fierce Critic of Aloof Philanthropies, Dies at 90

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the composer Angelo Badalamenti referred incorrectly to the television program “Inside the Actors Studio,” for which he wrote the music. It was on Bravo, not PBS. The obituary also referred incorrectly to the program’s history. It ended its run on Bravo in 2018 and moved the next year to Ovation, where it can still be seen; it did not end in 2019.
match_headline: Angelo Badalamenti, Composer for ‘Twin Peaks,’ Is Dead at 85

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the college football coach Mike Leach misstated the location of Susanville, Calif., where he was born. It is in the northeast part of the state, not the northwest part.
match_headline: Mike Leach, Football Coach With an ‘Air Raid’ Offense, Dies at 61

text: An article on Friday about a Qatari bribery case involving Eva Kaili, a European Parliament member, described incorrectly a European Parliament group focused on relations with the Arabian Peninsula that is chaired by Hannah Neumann. It is a delegation, not a committee.
match_headline: Bribery Case Cracks Open European Parliament — and Finds Hidden Cash

text: An article on Friday about President Biden’s challenge in winning over African leaders at the U.S.-Africa summit incorrectly described Mr. Biden’s promised trip to Africa. It would be the first such visit by a U.S. president to sub-Saharan Africa since 2015, not the first to Africa in that time.
match_headline: Biden Courts African Leaders, but Some Are Skeptical of Big Promises

text: An article on Friday about how the coronavirus may spread from corpses misstated the death rate for Covid patients. It is now 1 percent or less, not about 3 percent.
match_headline: The Coronavirus May Spread From Corpses, Scientists Report

text: A Critics’ Picks article on Friday about the best art books of 2022 misidentified the Italian artist Simone Martini’s region of origin. He was Tuscan, not Umbrian.
match_headline: Best Art Books of 2022

text: An obituary on Friday about Frances Hesselbein, who was chief executive of the Girl Scouts of the U.S.A. from 1976 to 1990, misidentified the city in Pennsylvania where she attended junior college. It is Johnstown, not Jamestown.
match_headline: Frances Hesselbein, Progressive Leader of the Girl Scouts, Dies at 107

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the wedding of Emily Todebush and Garrett Arwa misidentified, in some copies, the political office that Haley Stevens holds. She is a U.S. representative from Michigan, not a state representative. The article also mis­stated the name of a city in Michigan. It is Royal Oak, not Royal Oaks.
match_headline: Her Fictitious ‘Remember Me’ Email Sparked a Real Connection

text: An article last Sunday about octagonal homes misspelled the surname of a historian whose website is a clearinghouse for information about that type of house. She is Ellen L. Puerzer, not Peurzer.
match_headline: Looking for a House in This Tight Market? Consider an Octagon.

text: An article on Sunday about a bipartisan push to increase U.S. capacity to produce weapons misstated Lockheed Martin’s expected annual sales this year. The amount is expected to decline to $65.3 billion, not $62.3 billion.
match_headline: Military Spending Surges, Creating New Boom for Arms Makers

text: An article on Sunday about Ukraine’s efforts to restore water and power in several cities that had been attacked by Russia misstated the given name of the mayor of Kyiv. He is Vitali, not Ivan, Klitschko.
match_headline: Ukrainians Focus on Resilience a Day After Major Russian Strikes

text: An article on Sunday about a tentative labor agreement between the University of California and striking academic workers misidentified the role of the Rage Against the Machine band member who appeared at the U.C.L.A. rally. He is the band’s guitarist, not the lead singer.
match_headline: University of California Academic Workers Reach Deal to End Strike

text: An article on Monday about Hiroyuki Nishimura, the creator of the anonymous online message board 4chan, misstated the name of the website created by Mr. Nishimura. It is 2channel, not 2chan.
match_headline: In the U.S., His Site Has Been Linked to Massacres. In Japan, He’s a Star.

text: An article in Sunday Opinion about the World Cup and Qatar misstated how long it has been since a World Cup final was played in Europe. It has been four years, not 16 years.
match_headline: This Was the Perfect World Cup for Our Strange Era

text: A picture caption with an article on Dec. 11 about the civil discourse among users of iNaturalist, a website devoted to identifying plants and animals, carried an erroneous credit. The picture, of gall wasps growing on a northern red oak tree, was taken by Matthew Wills, not Holly Hartmann. A separate picture, of the American amber jelly fungus, also carried an erroneous credit. That photograph was taken by Ms. Hartmann, not Mr. Wills.
match_headline: Animals Are Running Out of Places to Live

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a mother denied an abortion in Texas misstated when Tamara Nelson’s son Cason was born. It was two days after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, not two days before.
match_headline: ‘I’m Not Ready’: A Mother Denied an Abortion in Texas Faces an Uncertain Future

text: An article on Tuesday about the closure of Bookforum magazine described incorrectly the deal by Penske Media Corporation that preceded Bookforum’s closure. The company acquired only Artforum, not Artforum and Bookforum.
match_headline: Bookforum Is Closing, Leaving Ever Fewer Publications Devoted to Books

text: Because of an editing error, a Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about the docu-series “Harry & Meghan” misstated the name of an association of sovereign states that is headed by the British monarch. It is the Commonwealth. It is no longer known as the British Commonwealth.
match_headline: What ‘Harry & Meghan’ Still Doesn’t Say About Race

text: A chart with an article on Wednesday about California’s unexpectedly quiet 2022 wildfire season rendered incorrectly the five-year moving average of acres burned. That entire line on the chart was too low by roughly 180,000 acres. It has been updated to reflect the true values.
match_headline: Why California’s 2022 Wildfire Season Was Unexpectedly Quiet

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Wednesday about the film curator Adrienne Mancia, using information from the Museum of Modern Art, misstated the surname of the woman pictured with her and Clint Eastwood. She is Mary Lea Bandy, not Brandy.
match_headline: Adrienne Mancia, Influential Film Curator, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Monday about Audrey Munson, who in the 1910s was the model for numerous monuments in New York City, misstated the year The Sun called her “Miss Manhattan.” It was 1913, not 1917.
match_headline: Overlooked No More: Audrey Munson, Forgotten but, Living On in Sculptures, Not Gone

text: An article on Thursday about eight teenage girls charged with killing a man in Toronto misstated part of the name of a restaurant near the crime scene. It is Bardi’s Steak House, not Bardo’s.
match_headline: 8 Teenage Girls Charged With Killing a Toronto Man

text: An article on Monday about unusual symptoms people experienced after eating contaminated spinach described incorrectly the way that anticholinergic plants and drugs affect the brain chemical called acetylcholine. They inhibit the action of this chemical, not the production of it.
match_headline: How Can Tainted Spinach Cause Hallucinations?

text: An article on Thursday about President Volodymyr Zelensky’s visit to the United States to address Congress and discuss aid to Ukraine described incorrectly how he delivered a comment during a news conference with President Biden. President Zelensky was speaking through a translator, not in English, when he said, “The longer the war lasts, the longer this aggression lasts, there will be more parents who live for the sake of vengeance, or revenge,” and added, “So there can’t be any just peace in the war that was imposed on us.”
ref_headline: The longer the war lasts, the longer this aggression lasts, there will be more parents who live for the sake of vengeance, or revenge,
match_headline: U.S. Aid Is ‘Not Charity,’ Zelensky Tells Congress as a Lengthy War Looms

text: An article on Thursday about Under Armour’s new chief executive officer misstated the age of the company. The company has existed for 26 years, not 22 years.
match_headline: Struggling Under Armour Hires ‘Fresh Eyes’ From Marriott to Lead It

text: An article on Wednesday about the things N.F.L. teams do when there is little or no hope of making it to the playoffs misidentified whose goal line the Texans were stopped at late in the fourth quarter of their game. It was the Cowboys’, not their own.
match_headline: What N.F.L. Teams Do When the Playoffs Are Out of Reach

text: An article this weekend on Page 7 about a new PBS documentary about the friendship between Groucho Marx and Dick Cavett misspells the surname of a former host of “The Tonight Show.” He was Jack Paar, not Jack Parr. It also misquotes the punchline of a Groucho Marx joke in “Animal Crackers.” It is “How he got in my pajamas, I don’t know,” not “How he got in my pajamas, I’ll never know.”
match_headline: The One About When Groucho Marx and Dick Cavett Became Great Friends

text: An article this weekend on Page 5 about the lack of a comic opera house in America misstates the status of “The Romance of the Rose,” an opera by Kate Soper. The opera will debut at Long Beach Opera in February 2023; it is not the case that it is unscheduled.
match_headline: America Needs Its Own Comic Opera Company

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Kelly Daniels and Emir Muhovic misstated where the couple were married. It was the SCOPE art show during Miami Art Week, not Art Basel Miami Beach. The error was re­peated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Tradition Was Never Their Thing. Why Start With a Wedding?

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Shawn Lamb and Jay Wong misspelled Mr. Wong’s given name. It is Jerrold, not Jarrold.
match_headline: Each Gave Up on Love. Which, of Course, Is When They Found It.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a house fire in Staten Island that killed two young children misspelled the name of the New York fire commissioner. She is Laura Kavanagh, not Laura Kavanaugh.
match_headline: Girl, 5, and Brother, 6, Are Killed in a Staten Island House Fire

text: A review on Friday about the new movie “Corsage” about the Empress of Austria and Queen of Hungary, Elisabeth Amalie Eugenie, misidentified the palace in Vienna where the movie “Corsage” was shot. It is called the Hofburg Palace, not the Hapsburg Palace.
match_headline: ‘Corsage’ Review: A Queen in Quiet Rebellion

text: An article last Wednesday about where to buy panettone misstated the name and location of a Minnesota bakery. It is Cossetta in St. Paul, Minn., not Cossettas in Minneapolis.
match_headline: How to Pick a Sublime Panettone

text: An article on Saturday about women who have frozen their eggs misidentified the gender of Jenny Hayes Edwards’s child. She gave birth to a girl, not a boy.
match_headline: Hope, Regret, Uncertainty: 7 Women on Freezing Their Eggs

text: An article on Tuesday about Germany’s political landscape included an outdated position for Robert Habeck, the country’s economy minister. He is no longer a leader of its Green Party.
match_headline: This Was the Year Everything Changed in Germany

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Dec. 12 about the cartoonist and cartoon editor Lee Lorenz referred imprecisely to the photo of him playing cornet. He was taking part in an informal jazz session with some members of the Creole Cookin’ Jazz Band and some other musicians; he was not “playing with his Creole Cookin’ Jazz Band.”
ref_headline: playing with his Creole Cookin’ Jazz Band.
match_headline: Lee Lorenz, 90, Cartoonist and Gatekeeper at The New Yorker, Dies

text: An obituary on Dec. 6 about the feminist activist Barbara Love misstated her relationship to the organization Parents of Gays, which later evolved into PFLAG. She was a member, not a founder. The obituary also misstated the year of a Christopher Street Liberation Day March in which Ms. Love and her mother participated. It was 1973, not 1972. Both errors were repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Barbara Love, Who Fought for Lesbians to Have a Voice, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Nov. 19 about the composer Ned Rorem referred incorrectly to his account of a meeting with the harpsichordist Wanda Landowska. When he wrote about that meeting in “The Paris Diary,” published in 1966, he said only that it took place “years ago,” without specifying where; he did not say that he met her “one day in Paris.” This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Ned Rorem, Composer Known for Both His Music and His Diaries, Dies at 99

text: An article on Friday about the deadly Buffalo blizzard misstated the month in which 10 Black people were killed at the Tops market in Buffalo. It was in May, not March. The story also described incorrectly the Tops market on Buffalo’s East Side. It is the neighborhood’s only major grocery store, but not the only one.
match_headline: How the Buffalo Blizzard Became So Deadly

text: An article on Sunday about architects Dominique Perrault and Gaëlle Lauriot-Prévost restoration of a country house by Jean Dubuisson misstated and misattributed the advice to architects to make “no small plans.” The quotation “make no little plans” is commonly attributed to the architect Daniel Hudson Burnham, not Louis Sullivan, though its authenticity is now in doubt.
match_headline: A French Modernist Masterpiece, Lost and Found

text: An obituary on Friday about the soccer star Pelé misstated the location of the 1977 North American Soccer League championship game, which Pelé’s team, the New York Cosmos, won. It was in Portland, Ore., not Seattle. The earlier version also misspelled the given name of one of Pelé’s daughters. She is Kely Cristina Nascimento, not Kelly.
match_headline: Pelé, the Global Face of Soccer, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Dec. 4 about the organist Frederick Swann referred incompletely to the organ at the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles. Its facade was designed by Frank Gehry, but the instrument itself was designed by Manuel Rosales, in collaboration with Mr. Gehry; it is not the case that the entire organ was “designed by Frank Gehry.”
match_headline: Frederick Swann, Master of the Pipe Organ, Is Dead at 91

text: An obituary on Nov. 18 about the columnist and former presidential speechwriter Michael Gerson referred incorrectly to a column he wrote that The Washington Post published on the morning of his death. It was written in 2013 and republished that day; it was not “his last column for The Post.” This correction was delayed for research.
ref_headline: his last column for The Post.
match_headline: Michael J. Gerson, Presidential Speechwriter and Columnist, Dies at 58

text: An article on Monday about Brazil’s inauguration of its new president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, misstated the distance between Brazil’s capital, Brasília, and Orlando, Fla. It is roughly 6,000 kilometers (about 3,700 miles), not 6,000 miles.
match_headline: Lula Becomes Brazil’s President, With Bolsonaro in Florida

text: An obituary on Saturday and Sunday about the broadcast journalist Barbara Walters misstated the longevity of the talk show “The View.” The program is in its 26th season, not its 24th.
match_headline: Barbara Walters, a First Among TV Newswomen, Is Dead at 93

text: An article on Sunday about American companies moving production to Mexico instead of relying on Chinese factories misspelled the name of a business. It is Men’s Wearhouse, not Men’s Warehouse.
match_headline: ‘OK, Mexico, Save Me’: After China, This Is Where Globalization May Lead

text: An article on Dec. 23 about the use of facial recognition technology at Madison Square Garden to ban certain from events at the venue misstated the name of the court where a Manhattan law firm has filed a suit against MSG Entertainment. It is State Supreme Court in Manhattan, not Manhattan Superior Court.
match_headline: Madison Square Garden Uses Facial Recognition to Ban Its Owner’s Enemies

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about retiring members of Congress misstated the given name of a House Democrat from Illinois who opted not to run for another term. As the article correctly noted, she is Cheri Bustos, not Chris.
match_headline: Retiring Congress Members See Rough Roads Ahead. They Won’t Miss the Gridlock.

text: An article on Saturday about the history behind the Vienna Philharmonic’s New Year’s Concert misstated the type of register that Joseph Goebbels falsified to hide the Jewish heritage of Johann Strauss. It was a wedding register, not a baptismal one.
match_headline: The Complex History Behind a Vienna Philharmonic Tradition

text: An article on Friday about an exhibition at Princeton of Toni Morrison’s manuscripts misstated the location of a Harriet Tubman sculpture. It is at West 122nd Street where St. Nicholas Avenue meets Frederick Douglass Boulevard, not on West 125th Street.
match_headline: Illuminating Toni Morrison’s Manuscripts at Princeton

text: An article on Dec. 27 about several countries that were able to quickly shut down epidemics misstated the number of people who died in an outbreak of the Nipah virus in southern India in 2018. Sixteen out of 18 patients died in the outbreak, not 17.
match_headline: Epidemics That Weren’t: How Countries Shut Down Recent Outbreaks

text: An article on Friday about notable deaths in 2022 misstated the given name of a cardiologist who helped invent an implantable defibrillator. He was Morton Mower, not Martin.
match_headline: Unlikely Parallels in a Year of Momentous Deaths

text: An obituary on Saturday about the fashion designer Vivienne Westwood misidentified the movie for which Kate Winslet was nominated for an Academy Award when she wore a Vivienne Westwood gown to the Oscar ceremony. It was “Sense and Sensibility,” not “Titanic.”
match_headline: Vivienne Westwood, 81, Dies; Brought Provocative Punk Style to High Fashion

text: An obituary on Dec. 25 about the producer, songwriter and arranger Thom Bell misstated part of the name of a single by James Ingram that he co-produced. It is “I Don’t Have the Heart,” not “I Don’t Have a Heart.”
match_headline: Thom Bell, a Force Behind the Philadelphia Soul Sound, Dies at 79

text: An article on Monday about an algal explosion in Cape Cod fueled by warming waters and antiquated septic systems misstated the scientific classification of cyanobacteria. While cyanobacteria are commonly known as blue-green algae, they are gram-negative bacteria and scientists typically exclude them from the algae group.
match_headline: A Toxic Stew on Cape Cod: Human Waste and Warming Water

text: An article on Monday about week 17 of the N.F.L. misstated receiving achievements by Jerry Rice and Torry Holt. They had eight 1,000-yard seasons in their first nine N.F.L. seasons, not to open their career.
match_headline: What We Learned From Week 17 in the N.F.L.

text: An article on Dec. 23 about the actor Antonio Bandera’s mission to bring serious, complex Broadway musicals to Spain, using information from Teatro del Soho, erroneously attributed a distinction to the theater’s production of “Company.” A translation of “Company” by Marcelo Kotliar was staged at the Teatro La Comedia in Buenos Aires in 2013. Teatro del Soho’s production was not the first in Spanish.
match_headline: With ‘Company,’ Antonio Banderas Brings Sondheim to Spain

text: An article on Thursday about Prime Minister Rishi Sunak’s promises to restore Britain’s health system and economy misstated the name of the country’s health care system. It is the National Health Service, not the National Health System. The error was repeated in a summary.
match_headline: Sunak Makes Sweeping Pledges to Britons, Promising Path to Prosperity

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the latest powerful California winter storm misstated the given name of a man loading sandbags in Wilton, Calif. He is Montay McDaniel, not Monday.
match_headline: Powerful Storm Hits California, as Residents Brace for More Flooding

text: An article on Thursday about Curtis Sliwa’s offer to help Mayor Eric Adams with his residential rat problem by using feral cats misidentified the newspaper that first reported Mr. Adams’s latest summonses for failing to control rats at a house he owns. It was first reported by The Daily News, not The New York Post.
match_headline: Mayor Adams Has Rats. Curtis Sliwa Has Cats. What Could Go Wrong?

text: An article on Friday about former President Donald J. Trump’s efforts to influence the House speaker fight described incorrectly Republicans’ performance in congressional elections in recent years. In the 2018 elections, Republicans lost control of the House, not the Senate. And they lost control of the Senate after the 2020 election cycle, not just the White House.
match_headline: In House Speaker Fight, Trump Struggles to Play Kingmaker

text: An article on Thursday about the highest-grossing week on Broadway since the arrival of the coronavirus, using information from the publicist, described imprecisely the status of the revival of the August Wilson play “The Piano Lesson.” While the play is on track to become the highest-grossing Wilson play, it had not yet hit that mark at the time of publication.
match_headline: Broadway Bounces Back With ‘Best Week Since the Before Times’

text: An article this weekend on Page 8 about the funeral scene for “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever” misstates the number of costumed cast members involved in it. It is 400, not 500.
An article this weekend on Page 25 about the closing of the show “Stomp” at the Orpheum Theater on Jan. 8 misstates the surname of a fan of the show. He is Lou George, not Lou Green.
match_headline: Farewell to ‘Stomp,’ a Show at the Beating Heart of New York

text: A picture caption with the 36 Hours article last Saturday, about London, misidentified the bridge shown. It is Tower Bridge, not London Bridge.
An article this weekend on Page 8 about the funeral scene for “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever” misstates the number of costumed cast members involved in it. It is 400, not 500.

An article last Sunday about the value of sug­gestions misstated the name of the university where Lyn Van Swol is a professor. It is the University of Wisconsin­-Madison, not the University of Madison Wisconsin.
match_headline: How Should You Be? Try Taking Suggestions.

text: An article on Dec. 25 about a guest at a dinner party attributed an erroneous distinction to the songwriter Jerry Livingston. He was not a co­-writer of “Que Sera, Sera.” (That song was written by Jay Livingston and Ray Evans.)
match_headline: The Shooter Drops By for Dinner

text: An article on Dec. 18 about the ways that anger affects the body misstated the given name of a clinical psychologist and professor at the Yale School of Medicine. He is Dr. Matthew Burg, not William.
match_headline: How Anger Affects the Body

text: An article on Nov. 13 about remaking the Los Angeles River referred imprecisely to the proposals of Friends of the Los Angeles River (FoLAR) and Jessica Henson’s characterization of them. Henson, a partner at Olin, the landscape-architecture firm, was referring to a 2021 study by FoLAR, not to a 2016 Army Corps of Engineers study. FoLAR advocates strategic partial-concrete removal, not for removing all the concrete in the river channel. The article also misstated the period when Interstate 105 displaced 25,000 people in Los Angeles. It was over the course of the highway’s construction, not when it opened in 1993.
match_headline: A Black Woman’s Rise in Architecture Shows How Far Is Left to Go

text: A graphic with an article on Saturday about widening highways to ease traffic misstated the name of a department used as a source for information about Interstate 45 in Houston. It is the Texas Department of Transportation, not Houston Department of Transportation.
match_headline: Widening Highways Doesn’t Fix Traffic. So Why Do We Keep Doing It?

text: An article on Saturday about the Biden administration’s move to tighten limits on deadly air pollution implied incorrectly that fine particulate matter is solely composed of soot. Although fine soot is one form of fine particulate matter, it is not the only form.
match_headline: Biden Administration Moves to Tighten Limits on Deadly Air Pollution

text: An article on Sunday about a 6-year-old accused in a school shooting misidentified the agency at which Andrew Block served as a former director. It was the Virginia Department of Juvenile Justice, not the Virginia Department of Justice.
match_headline: After 6-Year-Old Is Accused in School Shooting, Many Questions and a Murky Legal Path

text: An article on Sunday about the reworking of popular songs for movie trailers misspelled the surname of a trailer recording house founder. He is Mark Woollen, not Woolen.
match_headline: Movie Trailers Keep Tweaking Well-Known Songs. The Tactic Is Working.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the collapse of Damar Hamlin and the attention it has brought to the dangers of sudden cardiac arrest misstated the year in which Chris Pronger collapsed during a game. It happened in 1998, not 1988.
match_headline: Hamlin’s Cardiac Arrest Highlights Danger Across Sports

text: An article on Jan. 1 about President Biden’s conservation efforts described incorrectly government leaders’ participation at the U.N. biodiversity conference in Montreal. It is not the case that Justin Trudeau of Canada was the only head of government in attendance.
match_headline: Biden Set an Ambitious Goal for Nature. It’s Time He Went After It.

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about an increasingly aging work force across East Asia misidentified a man who works in a government office three times a week. He is Park Hak-gyu, not Park Has-gym.
match_headline: As Asian Societies Age, ‘Retirement’ Just Means More Work

text: An article on Sunday about expectations for Pope Francis after Pope Benedict XVI’s death misstated the year in which he seemed poised to allow married men in the Amazon region to become priests. It was 2020, not 2021.
match_headline: Benedict’s Burial Leaves Francis Alone, and Unbound

text: A picture caption with a group of photos in an article Thursday about India’s emergence as a global player amid Russia’s war in Ukraine misidentified one image. It showed a bazaar area near the Kashi Vishwanath Hindu temple and Gyanvapi Mosque, not a production line at a tea manufacturer near Chennai in southeastern India.
match_headline: How Western Goods Reach Russia: A Long Line of Trucks Through Georgia

text: An article on Saturday about President Biden awarding the Presidential Citizens Medal to 14 people misstated which police department an officer injured in the Jan. 6 attack worked for. Officer Michael Fanone was a member of Washington’s Metropolitan Police Department, not the Capitol Police.
match_headline: Biden Honors ‘Extraordinary Americans’ Who Defended Democracy on Jan. 6

text: An article on Tuesday about the number of teenagers who have seen sexually explicit content online misstated Jim Steyer’s title. He is the founder and chief executive of Common Sense Media, not its president.
match_headline: Three-Quarters of Teenagers Have Seen Online Pornography by Age 17

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the ways sign language experts are bringing diversity to theater misstated the name of a venue. It is the Bowery Poetry Club, not the Bowery Theater.
match_headline: How These Sign Language Experts Are Bringing More Diversity to Theater

text: An article on Tuesday about the restoration of bison habitats misstated the location of Canada’s Grasslands National Park. It is in Saskatchewan, not Alberta.
match_headline: Where the Bison Could Roam

text: An obituary on Jan. 1 about the photographer Tony Vaccaro mistakenly included a celebrity on a list of prominent people he photographed. He did not photograph Greta Garbo.
match_headline: Tony Vaccaro, 100, Dies; Photographed War From a Soldier’s Perspective

text: An article on Jan. 5 about Los Angeles County buying back land it had previously seized property from the Bruce family of Manhattan Beach paraphrased incorrectly a comment from Kavon Ward, who founded a group to support the Bruce family’s calls for restitution for their land. She said she understood the family’s decision to sell the land to Los Angeles County, not that they would not find peace in their decision to part with the land.
match_headline: L.A. County to Pay $20 Million for Land Once Seized From Black Family

text: An article on Tuesday about a rise in United States carbon emissions described incorrectly the methane emissions from natural gas. The production and transportation of natural gas can release large amounts of methane, not the burning of it.
match_headline: U.S. Carbon Emissions Grew in 2022

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the Golden Globe Awards ceremony misstated the award received by Jennifer Coolidge of “The White Lotus.” She won best supporting actress in a TV limited series, anthology series or TV movie; not best actress in that category.
match_headline: Jennifer Coolidge Credits ‘White Lotus’ Creator for a ‘New Beginning’

text: An article last Thursday about “clean beauty” products referred incor­rectly to an ingredient in some Stella McCartney skin­care products. It is wild harvested dulse algae, not wild harvest fulse algae.
match_headline: The Dirt on Clean Beauty

text: An obituary on Jan. 1 about Benedict XVI, the first pope in six centuries to resign, misstated the given name of a historian he often quoted. He was Arnold J. Toynbee, not Alfred.
match_headline: Benedict XVI, First Modern Pope to Resign, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the poet Charles Simic misstated the name of the high school in Illinois he attended. It is Oak Park and River Forest High School, not Oak Park High School.
match_headline: Charles Simic, Pulitzer-Winning Poet and U.S. Laureate, Dies at 84

text: An obituary on Saturday about the painter, pianist, photographer, sculptor and filmmaker Michael Snow at one point misstated the name of a Canadian film magazine that published an interview with him in 1971. As correctly noted elsewhere, it was Take One, not Take Out.
match_headline: Michael Snow, Prolific and Playful Artistic Polymath, Is Dead at 94

text: An article on Wednesday about Disney’s pricing policies misstated the availability of discounted Disneyland tickets. They are available to residents of Southern California, not to all California residents.
match_headline: Disney Revises Pricing Policies at Its Parks

text: An article on Wednesday about a football game between Texas Christian University and the University of Georgia described incorrectly a play involving an interception on an overthrown pass. Georgia defensive back Javon Bullard — not Mykel Williams — intercepted the pass, and it was in the second quarter, not the third.
match_headline: T.C.U., Confronting Georgia, Spirals on National Title Stage

text: An obituary on Jan. 3 about the fly-fishing authority Dave Whitlock misstated the publication date and part of the title of one of his books. It is “Dave Whitlock’s Guide to Aquatic Trout Foods,” not “Food,” and it was published in 1982, not 2007.
ref_headline: Dave Whitlock’s Guide to Aquatic Trout Foods,
match_headline: Dave Whitlock, a Star of the Fly-Fishing World, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Jan. 6 about the photographer Henry Grossman misstated the name of the high school he attended. It was Metropolitan Vocational High School, not Metropolitan Vocational and Technical High School.
match_headline: Henry Grossman, Photographer of Celebrities and Beatles, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Thursday about the guitarist Jeff Beck misstated the given name of a member of the band Beck, Bogert & Appice. He was Tim Bogert, not Tom.
match_headline: Jeff Beck, Guitarist With a Chapter in Rock History, Dies at 78

text: An article on Friday about the appointment of a special counsel to investigate the presence of classified documents in President Biden’s private office and home misspelled the surname of a former deputy White House counsel and Justice Department official. He is Timothy Flanigan, not Flanagan.
match_headline: Garland Appoints Special Counsel to Investigate Handling of Biden Documents

text: An article on Friday about new House reimbursement rules misstated the number of Democratic members who served last year on the House Administration Committee and failed to respond to requests for comment. Five of the six did not respond; a request to Representative Pete Aguilar of California, who was also on the panel, did not reach him before publication.
match_headline: New Rule Could Give House Lawmakers a Tax-Free $34,000 Pay Bump

text: An article on Friday about a new report on unidentified sightings, or U.F.O.s, misstated when a secret report on unidentified aerial sightings was sent to Congress. It was submitted on Wednesday, not in late October.
match_headline: Report Categorizes Many Unexplained Sightings as Drones, Trash or Birds

text: An article on Thursday about the changing leadership at LVMH misidentified the publication that first reported the appointments. It was Miss Tweed, not The Business of Fashion.
match_headline: LVMH Shuffles Leadership at Dior and Louis Vuitton, Its Top Brands

text: An article on Page 25 about Tucson, Ariz., misstates the size of the city’s Barrio Viejo neighborhood. It is more than 150 acres, not 150 blocks.

An article on Jan. 8 about the future of the Amazon rainforest miscalculated the volume of potential fossil-fuel emissions that the Amazon stores. The ecosystem can store the equivalent of 10 years of fossil-fuel emissions, not three years’ worth.
match_headline: Has the Amazon Reached Its ‘Tipping Point’?

text: An obituary on Dec. 19 about the drummer Dino Danelli of the Rascals, using information from the band’s historian, misstated his name at birth and the name of his father. He was born Robert Daniel, not Dino Danelli, and his father’s name was Steven Daniel, not Robert Danelli.
match_headline: Dino Danelli, Drummer Who Drove the Rascals, Is Dead at 78

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about the podcast “Red Scare” mis­stated the acting credits of Dasha Nekrasova. She did not appear in the show “Only Murders in the Building.”
match_headline: Podcast Overload

text: An article this weekend on Page 32 about Fukuoka, Japan, misstates the number of traditional open-air food stalls that remain in the city today. The number is around 100, not 140.
match_headline: An Ailing Arkansas City Elected an 18-Year-Old Mayor to Turn Things Around

text: An article on Page 10 about Auckland, New Zealand, misstates the work experience of the staff at Omni, a local restaurant. The head chef once worked at Hong Kong’s Yardbird restaurant; it is not the case that multiple chefs did.
match_headline: Review: Romeo and Juliet Leap to 1960s Hong Kong

text: An article on Page 25 about Tucson, Ariz., misstates the size of the city’s Barrio Viejo neighborhood. It is more than 150 acres, not 150 blocks.

An article on Dec. 25 about the process of canonizing a saint refers incorrectly to the Charlene Richard House in Thailand. It is a guesthouse at the Sarnelli House orphanage, not the name of the orphanage itself.
match_headline: The Miraculous Life and Afterlife of Charlene Richard

text: An article on Saturday about the suspension of aid groups in Afghanistan misspelled the first name of an aid worker. She is Najiba Rahmani, not Najima.
match_headline: ‘Burying Us Alive’: Afghan Women Devastated by Suspension of Aid Under Taliban Law

text: An article on Sunday about Covid-linked deaths in China misstated the number of Covid deaths the country had reported from the onset of the pandemic until Jan. 14. The number was 5,272, not 5,241.
match_headline: China Reports Nearly 60,000 Covid-Linked Deaths Since Lifting Restrictions

text: An article on Sunday about ticket vendors for Barclays Center, a venue in Brooklyn, misstated the measure of TicketMaster’s sales in 2019. The company sold 485 million tickets, not $485 million in tickets that year.
match_headline: Barclays Center Drops a New Ticket Vendor for Its Old One: Ticketmaster

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a canceled airplane takeoff at John F. Kennedy airport left unclear which airline declined to comment on Sunday. It was American Airlines, not Delta Air Lines.
match_headline: ‘Delta 1943, Cancel Takeoff’: Wrong Turn Results in Near Miss at J.F.K.

text: An article on Tuesday about White House visitor logs misattributed a quote about the House Oversight Committee seeking visitor logs from President Biden’s home in Wilmington, Del. The statement was made by Representative James R. Comer, the committee’s chairman, not Mr. Comer’s spokesman.
match_headline: White House Says It Does Not Keep Visitor Logs at Biden’s Delaware Home

text: An article on Saturday about 10 essential Jeff Beck songs misstated who sang backup on “Barabajagal.” Suzi Quatro did not sing on the track.
match_headline: Jeff Beck’s 10 Essential Songs

text: An article on Tuesday about a popular cosmological theory misidentified the computer scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. It is David Anderson, not David Peterson.
match_headline: Are We Living in a Computer Simulation, and Can We Hack It?

text: An obituary on Friday about the educator Norm Fruchter, using information from his family, misidentified the high school from which he graduated. It is Camden High School, not Newark High School.
match_headline: Norm Fruchter, Champion of Equal Access to Education, Dies at 85

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Italian movie actress Gina Lollobrigida misstated Ms. Lollobrigida’s full given name. It was Luigina, not Liugina.
match_headline: Gina Lollobrigida, Movie Star and Sex Symbol, Is Dead at 95

text: An obituary on Monday about Alfred T. Goodwin, a federal judge, misstated the surname of a law professor who was quoted as saying that Judge Goodwin “had many notable opinions.” She is Mary Wood, not Mary Hay.
match_headline: Alfred T. Goodwin, Judge in Pledge of Allegiance Case, Dies at 99

text: An article on Tuesday about a shooting in Central California, using early information from the authorities, misstated the ages of two of the victims. They were 16 years old and 10 months old, not 17 years old and 6 months old.
match_headline: 6 Shot Dead, Including Mother and Baby, at California Home

text: An article on Friday about the 1973 murder of Leslie Perlov, using information from the authorities investigating Ms. Perlov’s death, described incorrectly her role at Stanford University when she disappeared. text: An article on Wednesday about George Santos’s political future referred incorrectly to Representative Matt Gaetz of Florida. He is not a member of the House Freedom Caucus.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the ballerina and dance teacher Lupe Serrano misstated the name of the university where she started her teaching career. It is the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, not the University of Milwaukee.
match_headline: Lupe Serrano, Ballerina of Power and Fire, Is Dead at 92

text: An article on Jan. 10 about a 2017 terror attack on the Hudson River bike path in Lower Manhattan misstated the age of Nicholas Cleves, one of the victims. He was 23, not 24.
match_headline: Terror Trial Opens With Chilling Descriptions of Deadly Bike-Path Scene

text: An article on Saturday about tax refunds this year referred incompletely to tax liabilities for state rebate checks. While filers who took the standard deduction would not be liable for taxes, those who itemized deductions may be required to report them as taxable income. Not all rebates are tax exempt.
match_headline: Your Tax Refunds May Be Smaller This Year

text: An obituary on Jan. 12 about the lobbyist Liz Robbins misstated when she graduated from Wheaton College. It was 1968, not 1967.
match_headline: Liz Robbins Dies at 76; Broke Glass Ceiling as a Washington Lobbyist

text: An article on Friday about South Africa’s joint naval training exercises with China and Russia misstated the name of the organization with which Denys Reva is affiliated. It is the Institute for Security Studies, not the Institute of Security Studies.
match_headline: South Africa to Hold Naval Drill With Russia and China Amid Ukraine War

text: An article on Friday about Donald Trump blaming evangelical leaders for Republicans’ disappointing midterm performance referred incorrectly to Jerry Falwell Jr. Though he is a prominent evangelical leader, he is not a reverend.
match_headline: Can Trump Count on Evangelicals in 2024? Some Leaders Are Wavering.

text: An article on Page 1 this weekend about Rebecca Lorch, a competitive powerlifter, misidentifies the time and place that Ms. Lorch, Abbie Deal and their boyfriends shared an Airbnb rental. It was in 2020 at the America’s Strongest Man & Woman in Savannah, Ga., not at the 2019 Nationals in Daytona Beach.
match_headline: The Fierce Life and Sudden Death of America’s Strongest Woman

text: An obituary on Friday about the singer, songwriter and guitarist David Crosby misspelled his middle name and the name of the family from which his mother descended. It is Van Cortlandt, not Van Cortland.
match_headline: David Crosby, Folk-Rock Voice of the 1960s Whose Influence Spanned Decades, Dies at 81

text: An article last Sunday on pay transparency misspelled the name of the law firm where LaKeisha Caton is a partner. It is Pryor Cashman, not Pryor Chasman.
match_headline: Who Benefits When Salary Info Is Public?

text: An article on Jan. 8 about “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever” misstated whose funeral Lupita Nyong’o’s character was attending. It was another character’s funeral, not T’Challa’s.
match_headline: In ‘Black Panther: Wakanda Forever,’ One Scene Celebrates and Commemorates

text: An article last Sunday about Black real estate appraisers misstated where Ayako Marsh, an ap­praiser, lives. She lives in Washington, D.C., not Baltimore.
match_headline: How Three Black Women Hope to Change the Home Appraisal Industry

text: A picture caption with a review on Jan. 1 about Aidan Levy’s “Saxophone Colossus,” using information from Getty Im­ages, misstated the date of a photograph of Sonny Rollins. It showed Rollins in 1978, not “circa 1960.”

match_headline: Leigh Bardugo Is Wary of Imposing Limits on Young Readers

text: An article on Saturday about Guatemala’s crackdown on anticorruption forces and its investigation of Colombia’s defense minister misstated the name of the president of Colombia. He is Gustavo Petro, not Petro Gustavo.
match_headline: Guatemala Targets Colombia’s Defense Minister in Crackdown on Anticorruption Forces

text: An article on Sunday about the ways families are struggling amid the expiration of a pandemic-era federal free lunch program misspelled the maiden name of a parent calling for universal free school lunches. Her first and maiden names are Amber Stewart, not Amber Stuart.
match_headline: Families Struggle as Pandemic Program Offering Free School Meals Ends

text: An article on Monday about a sharp decline in rent payments in New York City public housing misstated Lisa Bova-Hiatt’s role at NYCHA. She is the interim CEO of NYCHA, not the interim chair.
match_headline: As Thousands Fall Behind on Rent, Public Housing Faces ‘Disaster’

text: An article on Saturday about states’ push for new voting laws misstated the surname of the president of the League of Women Voters. She is MaryLee Moulton, not Mouton.
match_headline: States Push for New Voting Laws With an Eye Toward 2024

text: An article on Saturday about a production of Jonathan Kent’s adaptation of “Long Day’s Journey Into Night” referred incorrectly to the producer Gleb Fetisov. He is a citizen of Cyprus. He is no longer a Russian citizen.
match_headline: Filming Eugene O’Neill When the Elements (and Investors) Don’t Cooperate

text: An obituary on Monday about the film producer Edward R. Pressman misspelled the surname of one actor and the given name of another. They are Jon Voight, not Voigt, and Jamie Lee Curtis, not Jaimie.
match_headline: Edward Pressman, Film Producer Who Bet on Unsung Talent, Dies at 79

text: An article on Jan. 16 about tennis player Ben Shelton’s path to the Australian Open erroneously attributed a distinction to Shelton. He is the first N.C.A.A. men’s singles champion to break into the top 100 on the pro tour in the same season since Tim Mayotte in 1981, not the first player to do so since Mayotte while still the reigning N.C.A.A. men’s singles champion.
match_headline: Ben Shelton Is Ready to Go Global

text: An article on Jan. 1 about a decline in teen births and its effect on child poverty referred incorrectly to abortion data from the Centers for Disease Control and Protection. The data includes abortions reported by licensed clinicians, including medication abortions. It does not include self-managed abortions.
match_headline: Their Mothers Were Teenagers. They Didn’t Want That for Themselves.

text: An article on Tuesday about an ex-lawman in Mexico accused of helping traffickers move drugs to the United States misstated the location of Luis Cárdenas Palomino. He is in prison in Mexico, not at large.
match_headline: Mexican Ex-Lawman Took Money From Cartels He Pursued, Prosecutors Say

text: An article on Saturday about new guidance from the American Academy of Pediatrics released on how to evaluate and treat overweight or obese children misstated the B.M.I. range for severe obesity in children and teens. It is 120 percent of the 95th percentile or greater, not at or above the 120th percentile.
match_headline: New Guidelines Underscore How Complicated Childhood Obesity Is for Patients and Providers

text: An article on Jan. 12 about Denmark’s decorative style referred incorrectly to the introduction of color to Georg Jensen’s Koppel pitcher. Nicholas Manville, a former creative director of Georg Jensen, did not choose the specific shades; they were selected by Ragnar Hjartarson, the company’s current creative director.
match_headline: Danish Design Goes Wild

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the architect Balkrishna Doshi misstated the location of Pune, where he was born. It is southeast of Mumbai, not southwest.
match_headline: Balkrishna Doshi, Modernist Indian Architect, Is Dead at 95

text: An article on Thursday about Western allies pledging to send tanks to Ukraine misspelled the given name of an expert on European defense issues. She is Sophia Besch, not Sofia.
match_headline: Western Tanks Are Coming to Ukraine, but Will They Be Enough?

text: A review on Jan. 20 about the Winter Show fair misstated the name of the company that manufactured a silver punch bowl displayed at the Spencer Marks booth. It was made by the Gorham Manufacturing Company, not the Graham Manufacturing Company. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: The Unforgettable Meets the Unimaginable at the Winter Show

text: An article on Thursday about the curator Helen Molesworth described incorrectly the duration of Catherine Opie’s position on the board of trustees at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles. Opie is a former member, not a current one.
match_headline: A Curator Unbound: First She Was Fired. Then She Found Freedom

text: An obituary on Thursday about James G. Lowenstein, who helped write a series of reports about the Vietnam War for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in the early 1970s, misstated part of the name of the Arkansas Democrat who was chairman of the committee at the time. He was J. William Fulbright, not William J. Fulbright.
match_headline: James G. Lowenstein, Whose Reports Questioned Vietnam War, Dies at 95

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about elections in Turkey described incorrectly the country’s rate of inflation. While Turkey is experiencing high inflation, inflation levels have not reached what many economists would characterize as hyperinflation.
match_headline: As Tough Elections Loom in Turkey, Erdogan Is Spending for Victory

text: An article on Friday about the future of Covid vaccination campaigns misstated the affiliation of Dr. Cody Meissner. He works at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth, not Tufts University School of Medicine.
match_headline: Covid Vaccines Targeting Omicron Should Be Standard, Panel Says

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the “hospital at home” movement misstates Mary Giswold’s title. She is chief operating officer of Northwest Permanente, not Kaiser Permanente Northwest.
match_headline: Your Next Hospital Bed Might Be at Home

text: A picture with the Editors’ Choice column last Sunday was published in error. It should have shown the book cover for Laura Zigman’s novel “Small World,” not Jonathan Evison’s novel of the same name.
match_headline: On These Small Islands, Medical Care Arrives One Ship at a Time

text: An article on Sunday about the agreement by the Netherlands and Japan to join the United States in barring certain kinds of semiconductor technology from China misstated the name of the think tank where Emily Benson is a senior fellow. It is the Center for Strategic and International Studies, not the Center for Strategic and International Relations.
match_headline: Netherlands and Japan Said to Join U.S. in Curbing Chip Technology Sent to China

text: An article on Friday about the mystery of the “first mile” of the Appian Way in Rome misstated when Rome was named the capital of Italy. It was 1871, not 1870.
match_headline: Ancient Roman Road’s Beginning Will Remain a Mystery for Now

text: An article on Sunday about the disbanding of the Memphis Police unit whose officers were charged in Tyre Nichols’s death misstated the given name of one of the lawyers representing Tyre Nichols’s family. He is Antonio Romanucci, not Anthony.
match_headline: Memphis Police Disband Unit Whose Officers Were Charged in Tyre Nichols’s Death

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the lack of snow in New York City this winter misstated the date that it last snowed in New York City. It was March 9, 2022, not March 22.
match_headline: Snow No-Show in New York City Feels Nice — but Also a Little Unsettling

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the ways that the Philadelphia Eagles’ general manager has helped the team’s success misstated the origin of the Eagles’ first-round pick in this year’s draft. It was acquired from the Saints last April, not in the Gardner-Johnson trade in August.
match_headline: To Rebuild the Eagles, the Team’s G.M. Worked His ‘Magic’

text: An article on Nov. 19 about the collaboration between filmmakers and Harvey Weinstein victims to create the film “She Said” misstated the job description of Rowena Chiu. She was an assistant to Mr. Weinstein, not to Zelda Perkins. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: ‘She Said’ Filmmakers and Weinstein Victims: An Emotional Collaboration

text: An article on Monday about longstanding research on the safety of gas stoves misspelled the name of a chemical used to make hard plastics. It is Bisphenol-A, not Bisphonal-A.
match_headline: In the Fight Over Gas Stoves, Meet the Industry’s Go-To Scientist

text: An article on Tuesday about objections that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey is raising to Sweden and Finland’s NATO membership bids amid his difficult re-election campaign referred incompletely to the nationality of the far-right politician Rasmus Paludan. He is a citizen of Denmark as well as of Sweden.
match_headline: Turkey’s upcoming elections have delayed Sweden and Finland’s NATO bids.

text: An article on Tuesday about the scrutiny surrounding the actress Andrea Riseborough’s Oscar nomination, using information from The Hollywood Reporter, misstated last weekend’s estimated box office sales for the film “To Leslie.” Sales were less than $5,000, not $250,000.
match_headline: Actress’s Path to Surprise Oscar Nomination Is Scrutinized

text: An article on Tuesday about Bobby Hull’s complicated legacy erroneously attributed the same quotation to both Gary Bettman, the commissioner of the N.H.L., and Rocky Wirtz, the chairman of the N.H.L. team in Chicago. Bettman was the one who said Hull was one of the league’s “most iconic and distinctive players.” Wirtz called Hull “a beloved member of the Blackhawks family.”
match_headline: Bobby Hull’s Golden Hockey Career Diminished by His Troubling Dark Side

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the art curator and teacher William Agee misstated the location of the California newspaper The Press Enterprise, which interviewed him in 1999. It is in Riverside, Calif., not Riverdale.
match_headline: William Agee, Leading Art Curator and Teacher, Dies at 86

text: An article on Wednesday about General Motors’ 2022 profits misidentified the year in which General Motors sold 2.9 million vehicles. It was 2021, not 2022.
match_headline: G.M. Posts Solid Profit as It Pushes to Take On Tesla in E.V.s

text: An article on Wednesday about DC Studios’ plan to reboot the Superman saga misstated Warner Bros.’s relationship to DC Comics. Warner Bros. and DC Comics became part of the same conglomerate in 1969. Warner Bros. did not buy DC Comics.
match_headline: Superman in Starring Role as DC Studios Unveils Strategy

text: An article on Wednesday about Gautam Adani, the founder of the Adani Group, and his company’s loss of billions in market value, misstated Mr. Adani’s age. He is 60, not 68.
match_headline: This Mogul Lost $36 Billion in Days. Who Is He, and What Happened?

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about museum gift shop items that allow visitors to dress up like famous artists described incorrectly the availability of a Neue Galerie museum store item. The Gustav Klimt painting smock has been sold there since 2007; the store did not start selling it recently.

text: An article last Thursday about the Italian band Maneskin and its fashion sense misstated part of the title of the group’s Eurovision song. It is “Zitti e Buoni,” not “Zitti e Buono.”
match_headline: The Joy of Dressing Like a Rock God

text: An obituary on Jan. 21 about the former basketball player and coach Chris Ford referred incorrectly to his seven-year tenure as an assistant coach for the Boston Celtics. He served under K.C. Jones for five seasons and then under Jimmy Rodgers for two; he did not serve under Jones for all seven seasons.
match_headline: Chris Ford, Who Made a 3-Point Mark in the N.B.A., Dies at 74

text: An article on Thursday about the hostile welcome that David Pressman, the U.S. ambassador to Hungary, received in Budapest described incorrectly the anti-L.G.B.T. message directed at him on a banner. It read, “Mr. Pressman, don’t colonize Hungary with your cult of death,” not “Mr. Pressman, don’t terrorize Hungary with your cult of death.”
ref_headline: Mr. Pressman, don’t colonize Hungary with your cult of death,

text: An article on Tuesday about a land dispute over an exclusive golf club in Hong Kong described incorrectly the new membership entry fees at the Hong Kong Golf Club. While some can add up to $2 million, not all reach that total.
match_headline: Golf Course or Housing? A Patch of Green Divides Hong Kong

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Thursday about the Hall of Fame football executive Bobby Beathard misstated his job status in 2018, when the photo of him at a game in Landover, Md., was taken. He was the former general manager of the Washington Redskins, not the general manager.
match_headline: Bobby Beathard, Mastermind of N.F.L. Dynasties, Dies at 86

text: An article on Friday about the lowest wind chill temperatures in decades in the Northeast misstated the location of Middlebury Snowbowl. It is in Hancock, Vt., not Middlebury.
match_headline: Northeast Braces for the Worst Wind Chill in Decades

text: An article on Friday about Chelsea executives’ record transfer spending misidentified the owner of the French soccer team Paris St.-Germain. It is Qatar Sports Investments, not the Qatar Investment Authority.
match_headline: Is Chelsea Setting the Market, or Breaking It?

text: An article on Page 11 this weekend about the video series “Inside Story” misstates the name of a recurring segment in the series. It is “In the Spotlight,” not “Inside the Spotlight.” Relying on incorrect information from sources involved with the series, it also misidentifies where the series will be streaming. It is the Vice News channel on the streaming platform Plex, not the Vice channel on Tubi.
match_headline: A New Video Series Explores Criminal Justice From the Inside Out

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about menopause incorrectly summarizes the results of the Women’s Health Initiative trial for women taking estrogen alone. The findings indicated that estrogen-only hormone therapy lowered the risk for heart disease in women only within 10 years of menopause, not across all age groups. The article also referred imprecisely to the group of women for whom the benefits of hormones outweigh the risk. The benefit-risk ratio is favorable for healthy women under 60 whose hot flashes are troubling them, not all women under 60 whose hot flashes are troubling them. And the article incorrectly describes a two-year curriculum at Johns Hopkins on menopause. It is for residents, not medical students.
match_headline: Women Have Been Misled About Menopause

text: An article on Page 36 this weekend about the prosecutor Fani Willis refers incorrectly to the statute Willis may use to bring charges against former President Donald J. Trump. It is Georgia’s RICO law, not the federal RICO law.
match_headline: She Took On Atlanta’s Gangs. Now She May Be Coming for Trump.

text: A review on Jan. 15 about “Screaming on the Inside,” by Jessica Grose, misstated a word in a quotation from the book. The sentence should have read, “The marginalization of topics like parenting in larger media organi­zations is just a microcosm of what happens in American soci­ety” (not “microscope”).
match_headline: The Common Denominator for Mothers? Guilt.

text: An article on Sunday about lobbying efforts that blocked the retirement of several flawed warships misstated the name of the publication in which an opinion piece by Tony Parisi appeared. It was in Real Clear Defense, not Breaking Defense.
match_headline: The Pentagon Saw a Warship Boondoggle. Congress Saw Jobs.

text: An article on Saturday about Brazil’s plan to sink a decommissioned warship misstated the depth of the ocean at the location where an aircraft carrier was being sunk. It is three miles deep, not 3,000 miles deep.
match_headline: Brazil Says It’s Started Sinking an Old Warship, Hazardous Material and All

text: An article on Saturday about a top F.B.I. agent who sold his services overseas misspelled the last name of the F.B.I. agent who gave classified information to the Russians. He is Robert P. Hanssen, not Robert P. Hannsen.
match_headline: How Prosecutors Say a Top F.B.I. Agent Sold His Services Overseas

text: An obituary on Jan. 9 about the novelist Russell Banks referred imprecisely to his choice of the title of his novel “Cloudsplitter.” Although it is the English translation of an American Indian word, the word is from the Seneca and not the Algonquin language, and it was never the name of Mount Marcy in the Adirondacks.
match_headline: Russell Banks, Novelist Steeped in the Working Class, Dies at 82

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the actor Charles Kimbrough misstated when the actress Beth Howland, his second wife, died. It was 2015, not 2016.
match_headline: Charles Kimbrough, Actor Best Known for ‘Murphy Brown,’ Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Saturday about the jazz singer Carol Sloane misstated the given name of her stepdaughter. She is Sandra de Novellis, not Sharon.
match_headline: Carol Sloane, Jazz Singer Who Found Success Early and Late, Dies at 85

text: An article on Monday about the flight of a Chinese surveillance balloon across the United States and what it reveals about China’s surveillance of the United States misstated the military rank of Michael Rogers, a former director of the National Security Agency. He is a retired admiral, not a general.
match_headline: Balloon Incident Reveals More Than Spying as Competition With China Intensifies

text: An article on Tuesday about the water rescue of a man who was later charged with stealing a boat misidentified the location of Mr. Labonte’s arrest in Oregon. It is Seaside, not Astoria, Ore.
match_headline: A Sea Rescue, a Stolen Boat and, Yes, a ‘Goonies’ Angle

text: An article on Wednesday about the need for frequent blood pressure monitoring throughout pregnancy misstated draft recommendations by the U.S. Preventive Service Task Force.
