The task force’s draft only recommended screening blood pressure of pregnant patients throughout a pregnancy, not continuing until at least six weeks after childbirth.
match_headline: Frequent Blood Pressure Monitoring Is Needed Throughout Pregnancy

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the Federal Reserve chair’s speech regarding inflation incorrectly described the State of the Union address on Tuesday. It was President Biden’s second such address, not his first.
match_headline: Fed Chair Strikes a Wary Tone as Biden Prepares to Tout the Economy

text: An obituary on Jan. 25 about the liberal journalist Victor S. Navasky misstated part of the name of a school he attended. It is the Little Red School House and Elisabeth Irwin High School, not the Little Red Schoolhouse and Elizabeth Irwin High School. The obituary also misstated the year the satirical book “Report From Iron Mountain: On the Possibility and Desirability of Peace,” in which Mr. Navasky was involved, was published. It was 1967, not 1966.
ref_headline: Report From Iron Mountain: On the Possibility and Desirability of Peace,
match_headline: Victor S. Navasky, a Leading Liberal Voice in Journalism, Dies at 90

text: An article on Thursday about the French prime minister, Élisabeth Borne, incorrectly referred to Ms. Borne’s experience running the Paris subway system. She was the second woman to lead it, not the first.
match_headline: The Harrowing Personal Story France’s Prime Minister Rarely Tells

text: An article on Friday about the release of over 200 political prisoners in Nicaragua to the United States misstated the role of two employees of the newspaper La Prensa who were sentenced Wednesday to 10 years in prison. They were drivers, not reporters.
match_headline: Nicaragua Frees Hundreds of Political Prisoners to the United States

text: An article on Tuesday about how consumer spending in China has picked up gave an outdated figure for China’s economic growth in 2021. Beijing revised the number to 8.4 percent, from 8.1 percent.
match_headline: Flowers, Fresh Fish and Movies: China Is Spending Again, Cautiously

text: An article on Feb. 5 about Atlantic sturgeon included an imprecise distinction about studies that focused on vessel strikes on Atlantic sturgeon in the Delaware estuary. While Dewayne Fox and his colleagues designed a novel study to estimate the number of vessel-strike mortalities per year, an earlier study by J. Jed Brown and Gregory W. Murphy used pre-existing mortality data to determine the impact of vessel strikes on the future population.
match_headline: They Outlasted the Dinosaurs. Can They Survive Us?

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the prosecution of domestic extremists misstates the number of people charged with seditious conspiracy for the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. It is 18, not 16.
match_headline: The Veteran Outing Domestic Extremists

text: An obituary on Wednesday about David Harris, who served time in federal prison for resisting the draft, misstated the year he was released. It was 1971, not 1970.
match_headline: David Harris, Leader of Vietnam Draft Resistance Movement, Dies at 76

text: An article last Sunday about the new dance­ driven musical theater production “The Night Falls” misstated the year that Troy Schu­macher founded Ballet Collective. It was in 2013, not 2010.
match_headline: A Song and Dance Collaboration, Straight Outta Swamplandia

text: An article last Sunday about the actor Poppy Liu misstated the year Ms. Liu graduated from college. It was 2013, not 2009. The article also misstated the size of Ms. Liu’s house. It is a one-bedroom, not a three-­bedroom.
match_headline: Bringing a Little Queerness to Acting Roles

text: An article on Sunday about Turkey’s detention of building contractors as the earthquake death toll grows misstated the action taken by the Turkish government against more than 100 contractors in connection to buildings that collapsed in Monday’s earthquake. Warrants were issued for their arrests. They were not all detained.
match_headline: As Anger Swells Over Quake, Turkey Detains Building Contractors

text: An article on Saturday about a memorial service for the columnist and former presidential speechwriter Michael Gerson misstated the month of Mr. Gerson’s death last year. He died in November, not December.
match_headline: Mourning ‘Compassionate Conservatism’ Along With Its Author

text: An article on Saturday about an investigation of an artificially pink pigeon that died misstated the location of the fire in California that was ignited by a pyrotechnic device. It was in El Dorado Ranch Park, located near Los Angeles, not in Los Angeles.
match_headline: A Pigeon Was Dyed. Then It Died. Now the Police Are Investigating.

text: An article on Monday about the possible impact of Adani Group’s $100 billion loss on India’s economy misstated the name of a stock index. It is MSCI World index, not MCSI.
match_headline: Why Adani’s $100 Billion Loss Hasn’t Tanked India’s Markets

text: An article on Friday about a study that found Steve Bannon’s podcast as the top misinformation spreader misspelled the name of a nonprofit organization founded by Charlie Kirk. It is Turning Point USA, not Turning Points USA.
match_headline: Steve Bannon’s Podcast Is Top Misinformation Spreader, Study Says

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the ownership agreement of a well-known painting by Gustav Klimt misstated the location of the exhibit where the painting resurfaced in 1957. The exhibit was in Stuttgart, not Salzburg.
match_headline: Ronald S. Lauder Reaches Agreement on Klimt Painting With Jewish Heirs

text: An article on Monday about the Brit Awards’ lack of female nominees misidentified the name of a musicians association. It is the Independent Society of Musicians, not the Incorporated Society of Musicians, which was its name until October 2022.
match_headline: A Music Award Went Gender Neutral. It Ended Up With All-Male Nominees.

text: An article on Monday about Before Midnight parties misstated the frequency of a dance party organized by Tim Lawrence. It is held every two months, not monthly.
match_headline: A Night in the Club, Then Early to Bed

text: An article on Monday about a Detroit gallery owner’s criminal scheme to swindle collectors misidentified the location of a Diane Arbus exhibition in the 1970s. It was at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, not the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
match_headline: As $1.6 Million in Rare Photos Vanished, the Excuses Piled Up

text: An article on Tuesday about protest in Israel in response to a judicial overhaul proposed by the new government misstated the results of a poll about the proposal. The poll said that 41 percent of Israelis supported the government’s plan and 44 percent opposed it, not the other way around.
match_headline: Netanyahu’s Judicial Overhaul Sparks Huge Protests in Israel

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Berlin’s do-over election misstated the European body that planned to send outside observers to Berlin. It was the Council of Europe, which is the top human rights panel on the continent, not the European Council.
match_headline: Repeat Election in Berlin Speaks to the ‘Chaos’ Many Residents Feel

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a secretive network that has helped antiwar Russians escape the country misidentified the location of Irina’s abduction. She was abducted from a Federal Security Service parking lot, not from her apartment’s parking lot.
match_headline: Secretive Network Rescues Russia’s Antiwar Dissidents in Nick of Time

text: An article on Wednesday about abuses by Greek border guards misstated the title of Camino Mortera-Martínez. She is the head of the Brussels office of the Center for European Reform, not a senior research fellow.
match_headline: Greece Border Abuses Highlight Europe’s Clashing Priorities on Migration

text: An article on Wednesday about a halt in production and shipments of Ford Motor’s electric pickup truck because of a battery pack issue misstated the scope of the action. The decision does not apply to the E-Transit electric delivery van.
match_headline: Ford Halts Production of Electric Pickup Over Battery Issue

text: An article last Thursday about a museum exhibition and book celebrating the 50th anniversary of hip­-hop culture described incor­rectly a party in the Bronx that was pivotal to the birth of the genre’s music. It was a back­-to­-school party, not a birthday party.
match_headline: Hip-Hop, Still Fly at 50

text: An obituary on Friday about the cookbook author Jean Anderson misstated when she moved from New York City to Chapel Hill, N.C. It was 1997, not 2007.
match_headline: Jean Anderson, 93, Exacting and Encyclopedic Cookbook Author, Dies

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about Marianne Mantell, a founder of the spoken-word record company Caedmon, misidentified the man pictured at a recording session with her and Barbara Holdridge, the company’s other founder. He is Ralph Richardson, not John Gielgud.
match_headline: Marianne Mantell, Who Helped Pave the Way for Audiobooks, Dies at 93

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the Canadian politician Hazel McCallion misspelled the name of the brand of cola that sponsored a hockey team for which she once played. It is Kik, not Kick.
match_headline: Hazel McCallion, No-Nonsense Canadian Mayor for 36 Years, Dies at 101

text: An article on Thursday about local distrust of government and railroad officials after a train carrying toxic chemicals derailed in an Ohio town misidentified the location of New Waterford. It is five miles west of East Palestine, not east.
match_headline: In Ohio Town Where Train Derailed, Anxiety and Distrust Are Running Deep

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about growing awareness of thousands of surveillance balloons floating above Earth misstated what a Defense Department official said about an object shot down by fighter jets in waters over Alaska. The official said it was most likely not a balloon, not that it was one.
match_headline: A Rising Awareness That Balloons Are Everywhere in Our Skies

text: An article on Wednesday about key moments in Senator Dianne Feinstein’s career misstated the status of the Senate Intelligence Committee’s report on torture as of early 2009. An initial report had been provided to committee members; it had not been publicly released.
match_headline: From Harvey Milk’s Side to the Senate: 9 Key Moments in Dianne Feinstein’s Career

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about how the shooting at Michigan State University has ignited a debate over university security misidentified one of the contributing reporters. It is James C. McKinley Jr., not Jim Yardley.
match_headline: In the Wake of Tragedy, Balancing Freedom and Safety at Michigan State

text: An article on Thursday about Linda Mills, the first woman to serve as New York University’s president, included an outdated reference to one of Dr. Mills’s roles at the university. She is a former associate vice chancellor for the Abu Dhabi campus; she does not currently hold that title.
match_headline: N.Y.U. Chooses Linda Mills as Its Next President

text: An obituary on Thursday about the actress Raquel Welch referred incompletely to the movie “The Last of Sheila,” in which she appeared. Its script was written by Stephen Sondheim and Anthony Perkins, not just by Stephen Sondheim.
match_headline: Raquel Welch, Actress and ’60s Sex Symbol, Is Dead at 82

text: An article on Feb. 11 about taking a walking safari in Zambia misstated the timing of Delia and Mark Owens’ departure from Zambia. They left in 1996, not in 1997, and they departed shortly after the announcement of an investigation into a killing that was shown as part of an ABC News broadcast; their departure was not “precipitated” by the broadcast itself. The article also included outdated information about the couple’s marital status. They are now divorced.
match_headline: Prosecutors Seek Trump Lawyer’s Testimony, Suggesting Evidence of Crime

text: An article on Page 6 this weekend about how Robert Wilson’s staging of “Lohengrin” changed the Metropolitan Opera misspells the surname of a director who worked on “Lohengrin” in Zurich. He is Giuseppe Frigeni, not Frigoni.
match_headline: The Story of a Production That Changed the Metropolitan Opera

text: A review on Friday of the 2023 Oscar-nominated short films misidentified one of the voice actors in the animated short “The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse.” The actor is Tom Hollander, not Tom Holland.
ref_headline: The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse.
match_headline: ‘The 2023 Oscar Nominated Short Films’ Review: Bite-Size Global Tales

text: An article on Tuesday about a pill that could help treat binge drinking misstated the dosing advice given to participants in the recent study. Patients were advised to take naltrexone before they expected to drink, but no time limit was given; they were not told to take it one hour before drinking.
match_headline: Binge Drinking May Be Curbed With a Pill

text: An article last Sunday about the Domino Sugar Refinery redevelopment misstated the project’s scope and included a quotation that incorrectly described a building entrance. The project will include 3,000 apartments and 600,000 square feet of office space, not 4,000 apartments and 700,000 square feet of office space. Also, one can enter the building from Kent Avenue, not from 10th Street.
match_headline: At the Domino Sugar Refinery, a Glass Egg in a Brick Shell

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the BBC Shipping Forecast misstates one of the scheduled times the forecast is read daily. It is 5:20 a.m, not 5:02 a.m.
match_headline: A Secret for Falling Asleep So Good It’s a British National Treasure

text: An article on Page 104 about Dorothée Meilichzon’s Paris apartment misidentifies the designer of her dining table. It was designed by Florence Knoll, not Eero Saarinen.
match_headline: A Parisian Hotel Designer Creates a Space of Her Own

text: A review on Jan. 22 about Elinor Lip­man’s novel “Ms. Demeanor” referred incorrectly to the book’s cast of charac­ters. It includes a pair of scheming Poles, not Russians.
match_headline: Elinor Lipman’s Frothy New Novel Has Serious Undertow

text: An article on Sunday about climate change’s impact on inflation misspelled the name of a market research firm. It is NielsenIQ, not NielsonIQ. The article also paraphrased incorrectly a comment from Jeff Frye, the vice president of sustainability for Kontoor Brands. He said the cost of American-grown cotton can represent more than half the cost of the fabric in a pair of Wrangler or Lee jeans, not more than half the final price tag.
match_headline: How Climate Change Is Making Tampons (and Lots of Other Stuff) More Expensive

text: An article on Saturday about Florida Senator Rick Scott’s shifting position on overhauling Social Security benefits misstated the name of the organization that Maya MacGuineas leads. It is the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, not the Center for a Responsible Budget.
match_headline: Rick Scott Drops Social Security From Plan as G.O.P. Retreats From Entitlement Cuts

text: An article on Friday about a surge in murders of women in Spain misstated the month in which a woman and her daughter were stabbed to death. It was in January, not February. The article also misstated in one instance the name of an organization dedicated to gender equality. It is the European Institute for Gender Equality, not the European Institute for Gender Inequality.
match_headline: ‘Machismo Kills’: A Surge in Murders of Women Alarms Spain

text: An article on Sunday about a challenging water-rescue training program run by the U.S. Coast Guard misstated the classification of students who enroll in the Surfman Course. They are enlisted petty officers, not officers.
match_headline: In a Treacherous Corner of Washington, a Classroom With 40-Foot Waves

text: An article on Sunday about President Biden’s appointment of two people with backgrounds in climate policy to top administration posts misstated the name of an agency within the White House that vets proposed regulations. It is the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, not the Office of Internal and Regulatory Affairs.
match_headline: With Two Key Picks, Biden Weaves Climate Into Economy and Regulations

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about the relationship between capitalism and democracy misstated the name of one of the organizations that promoted the idea of free markets in the United States. It is the Foundation for Economic Education, not the Foundation for Economic Freedom.
match_headline: Is the Marriage Between Democracy and Capitalism on the Rocks?

text: An article on Monday about the authenticity of a portrait of George Washington included incorrect biographical information about George Keppel, a British Navy captain. He was a member of the third earl of Albemarle’s family, but he was not the third earl of Albemarle.
match_headline: Was This Washington Portrait Really by Charles Peale? Experts Took a Look.

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor and comedian Richard Belzer referred incorrectly in part to his survivors. He did not have grandchildren.
match_headline: Richard Belzer, Detective Munch on ‘Law & Order: S.V.U.,’ Dies at 78

text: An obituary on Feb. 15 about the photographer Julian Wasser misstated his mother’s birth name. She was Frances (Rothberg) Wasser, not Rothman.
match_headline: Julian Wasser, the ‘Photographer Laureate’ of L.A., Dies at 89

text: A headline with an article on Wednesday about Saudi Arabian authorities meting out harsh punishments to citizens who criticize the government overstated the impact of posting a single tweet. A man was sent to prison for multiple social media posts and possessing what the government viewed as an insulting picture of Prince Mohammed bin Salman, not for a single tweet.
match_headline: ‘Equality of Injustice for All’: Saudi Arabia Expands Crackdown on Dissent

text: An article on Thursday about a gunman in Florida who killed three people misidentified the location of Pine Hills, Fla. It is about five miles west of Orlando, not east.
match_headline: New Details Emerge in Killing of Reporter, Woman and 9-Year-Old

text: An article on Feb. 17 about private messages that revealed Fox News stars and executives privately expressing disbelief about President Donald Trump’s claims about the 2020 election referred incompletely to an episode in which the Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich deleted a fact-checking tweet about false claims made by Mr. Trump about Dominion Voting. While she removed a tweet in which Mr. Trump had tagged her colleagues Sean Hannity and Lou Dobbs, she posted the same fact check in response to a different tweet from Mr. Trump that made the same false claim but did not tag her colleagues.
match_headline: Fox Stars Privately Expressed Disbelief About Election Fraud Claims. ‘Crazy Stuff.’

text: An article on Thursday about a new olive oil coffee line at Starbucks in Italy misstated Howard Schultz’s role at Starbucks. He helped build the company in leadership roles, but he is not a founder.
match_headline: Want That Coffee With Olive Oil? Starbucks Thinks Italians Will.

text: An article on Page 38 this weekend about the Delbert Anderson Trio misstates the name of the music industry figure who has been mentoring the band. He is David Greenberg, not Steve.
match_headline: Delbert Anderson’s Mission: Putting ‘Native Sound Back Into Jazz’

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about New York City live performances to watch in the Spring misidentifies the 2022 production of the musical “Parade” at New York City Center. It was a gala presentation, not an Encores! production.
match_headline: Live Performance in New York: Here’s What to See This Spring

text: An obituary on Friday about the publisher John Macrae III misstated his role in the publication of Lech Walesa’s autobiography. He met with intermediaries for Mr. Walesa, not with Mr. Walesa himself, in an effort to persuade him to write it. And he did not help smuggle the manuscript of the autobiography out of Poland.
match_headline: John Macrae III, Eclectic Publisher and Rights Champion, Dies at 91

text: An article on Saturday about the skepticism that several Fox News hosts expressed privately about claims of voter fraud used an incorrect photo of Raj Shah. The photo was of another man with the same name who is managing partner of Shield Capital. He is no relation to Raj Shah, who is senior vice president of Fox Corporation.
match_headline: What Fox News Hosts Said Privately vs. Publicly About Voter Fraud

text: An article on Sunday about severe weather in California misstated the first name of a woman who was involved in a car accident. She is Estefany Gomez, not Stefany.
match_headline: In the Los Angeles Area, Snow Up High, and Flooding Down Below

text: An article on Tuesday about the Supreme Court’s review of a federal identity theft law misstated the given name of a defendant who was convicted of health care fraud. He is David Dubin, not Davis.
match_headline: Supreme Court Seems Skeptical of Broad Sweep of Identity Theft Law

text: An article on Friday about Israeli tech executives who are considering moving their businesses out of Israel after the prime minister announced plans for a judicial overhaul misstated Adam Fisher’s role at Bessemer Venture Partners. He is a partner, not a co-founder. The article also referred incorrectly to Wix.com. It is a publicly traded company; it is not private.
match_headline: Tech Leaders in Israel Wonder if It’s Time to Leave

text: An article last Wednesday about the cookbook author and teacher Raghavan Iyer misstated an ingredient he used to make lunch. It was black cardamom pods, not black coriander pods.
match_headline: He Taught Americans to Cook Indian Food. Now He’s on His Final Chapter.

text: A review last Wednesday of the Manhattan restaurant Kjun misstated the number of courses in Little Mad’s $95 “Mad Dinner Experience.” It is five courses, not three.
match_headline: Restaurant Review: Korean and Cajun Flavors Rock Together at Kjun

text: An obituary on Monday about the film archivist and producer Tom Luddy referred incorrectly to the Paul Schrader film “Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters,” which he produced. It is a scripted movie, not a documentary.
ref_headline: Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters,
match_headline: Tom Luddy, a Behind-the-Scenes Force in Cinema, Dies at 79

text: An obituary on Sunday about Robert Hébras, the last survivor of a 1944 massacre in which members of an SS Panzer division killed almost everyone in the village of Oradour-sur-Glane in France, misstated how old he was at the time. He was 18, not 19.
match_headline: Robert Hébras, Last Survivor of a 1944 Massacre in France, Dies at 97

text: An article on Thursday about Ukraine sending more troops to the city of Bakhmut misstated the position of Narendra Modi, the leader of India. He is the prime minister, not the president.
match_headline: Ukraine Reinforces Embattled Bakhmut, but Mission Is Unclear

text: An article on Thursday about the digital release of the rap trio De La Soul’s catalog misstated the name of De La Soul’s 2001 album. It is “AOI: Bionix” not “AOI: Bonix.”
match_headline: De La Soul’s Music Is Finally Back. It’s a Bittersweet Victory.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Charles Pernasilice, who was convicted of attempted assault for his role in the 1971 Attica prison uprising, referred imprecisely to Hugh L. Carey’s term as governor of New York State. He succeeded Malcolm Wilson, who had been lieutenant governor and became governor when Nelson A. Rockefeller resigned in 1973; he did not succeed Mr. Rockefeller.
match_headline: Charles Pernasilice, Haunted by the Violence at Attica, Dies at 70

text: An article on Friday about a report by House Democrats detailing interviews and statements from three witnesses testifying before the Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government referred imprecisely to the relationship between the Center for Renewing America and the Conservative Partnership Institute. The center is affiliated with the institute and sustained mostly by donations; it is not largely funded by the institute.
match_headline: G.O.P. Witnesses, Paid by Trump Ally, Embraced Jan. 6 Conspiracy Theories

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about office furniture resellers in Silicon Valley misidentified the brand of office chair that Brandi Susewitz was examining on her visit to Sitecore’s office. It was not a Herman Miller Aeron chair.
match_headline: The Furniture Hustlers of Silicon Valley

text: An article last Sunday about the photogra­pher Tina Barney misstated the title of a picture by her from 1979. It is “Hot Tub in Snow,” not “Hot Tub.”
match_headline: Tina Barney: The Photographer’s Origin Story

text: An article on Sunday about North Carolina becoming a top destination for people seeking abortions from states where it is banned misstated the name of a group that supports abortion rights. It is the Society of Family Planning, not the Society for Family Planning.
match_headline: How the Fall of Roe Turned North Carolina Into an Abortion Destination

text: An article on Monday about the use of artificial intelligence to detect signs of cancer that might otherwise go unnoticed misidentified Dr. Constance Lehman. She is a breast imaging specialist at Massachusetts General Hospital, not chief of breast imaging and radiology.
match_headline: Using A.I. to Detect Breast Cancer That Doctors Miss

text: An article on Sunday about the aftermath of an attack at a rural preschool in Thailand misstated the date of the 2022 mass killing in the day care center. It was Oct. 6, not Oct. 7.
match_headline: A Massacre That Rippled Through Generations in Thailand

text: An article on Sunday about a study showing that bempedoic acid decreased the combined risk of cardiovascular complications misstated the given name of a doctor. He is Dr. Michael Davidson, not T. Michael Davidson.
match_headline: A Statin Alternative Joins Drugs That Can Reduce Heart Attack Risk

text: An obituary on Feb. 17 about the sportscaster and former major league catcher Tim McCarver misstated the name of the Memphis high school he attended. It is Christian Brothers High School, not Christian Brothers Academy. The obituary also erroneously credited McCarver with a distinction. He was the first catcher to lead one of the major leagues in triples, not the only one. (Carlton Fisk of the Boston Red Sox tied for the American League lead in triples in 1972, six years after McCarver led the National League.)
match_headline: Tim McCarver, Catcher in the Hall of Fame as a Broadcaster, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Friday about the jazz saxophonist and composer Wayne Shorter referred imprecisely to the Miles Davis album “In a Silent Way.” Although it signaled a change of direction for Davis, Mr. Shorter was not the only member of the Miles Davis Quintet on the album.
match_headline: Wayne Shorter, Innovator During an Era of Change in Jazz, Dies at 89

text: An article on Tuesday about a move by Senator Bernie Sanders to subpoena Howard Schultz, the chief executive of Starbucks, misstated the number of complaints and unfair labor practice charges that the National Labor Relations Board has received against Starbucks. It was 81 complaints and 504 unfair labor practice charges, not 504 complaints and 81 charges.
match_headline: Bernie Sanders Presses Ahead With Subpoena of Starbucks C.E.O.

text: An article on Monday about the North Idaho College board of trustees misstated the timing of events at two meetings of the board. Vincent James Foxx, a far-right antisemitic podcaster, spoke at a meeting in January, not December. A separate meeting, in December, was interrupted twice by fire alarms.
match_headline: The MAGA-fication of North Idaho College

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about five women who sued the state of Texas over its law banning abortion misstated exceptions included in the legislation. It includes exceptions for serious risks to the life or health of a pregnant woman. It does not include exceptions for rape, incest, or a fatal fetal diagnosis.
match_headline: Five Women Sue Texas Over the State’s Abortion Ban

text: An article on Tuesday about the changing parity of teams in the Pac-12 Conference tournament misspelled the given name of the Pac-12’s deputy commissioner. She is Teresa Gould, not Theresa.
match_headline: A Deep Pac-12 May Soon Have a Sea Change

text: An article on Tuesday about the growth of the Desert X biennial art show mischaracterized the subject of a video playing inside an art installation by Paloma Contreras Lomas. The video shows men and women, some of them masked; it does not show only masked men.
match_headline: Desert X Finds Roots in the Region

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the novel “The Overstory” misstated Joyce DiDonato’s vocal type. She is a mezzo-soprano, not a soprano.
match_headline: Translating the Music of Trees Into the Sounds of Opera

text: An article on Wednesday about resistance in France to the government’s plan to push back the retirement age misstated the given name of a French former metal worker. He is Jean-Pierre Doron, not Jean-Paul.
match_headline: Fight Over Retirement in France Is a Question of Identity

text: An article on Sunday about the growth of electric car use in New York City misstated the brand of car that Tiffany Tucker owned. It was a Genesis GV60 not a Hyundai Genesis.
match_headline: Why the New York Area Is Seeing an Explosive Growth in Electric Cars

text: An article on Tuesday about the impact of employee vacancies at New York City agencies on city services referred imprecisely to the vacancy rates at New York City agencies. The vacancy rates were from October 2022, and are not the current rates.
match_headline: New York’s Difficulty in Filling Job Vacancies Has Hurt City Services

text: An article on Wednesday about three former New York City correction officers who pleaded guilty to federal program fraud misspelled the given name of New York City’s correction commissioner. He is Louis A. Molina, not Luis.
match_headline: Bowling, Parties, Travel: 3 Former Rikers Guards Admit Sick Leave Abuse

text: An article on Wednesday about Senator Sheldon Whitehouse’s new role as chairman of the Senate Budget Committee misspelled the given name of the junior senator from West Virginia. She is Shelley Moore Capito, not Shelly.
match_headline: Same Message, Bigger Audience: Sen. Whitehouse Flags Climate Costs

text: An obituary on Sunday about the entomologist Justin O. Schmidt misstated his daughter’s surname. She is Krista Jewell Schmidt, not Krista Schmidt-Jewell. The obituary also referred incorrectly to her and to Dr. Schmidt’s son Scott. They are from his second marriage, to Pat Figuli — not his first marriage, to Deborah Wragg.
match_headline: Justin O. Schmidt, Entomologist Known as ‘King of Sting,’ Dies at 75

text: An obituary on Sunday about the architect Rafael Viñoly referred incorrectly to the affiliation of Rabbi Marshall Meyer, who as a human-rights activist in Argentina helped Mr. Viñoly and his family leave the country in 1978, with Congregation B’nai Jeshurun in Manhattan. Rabbi Meyer was with the congregation until his death in 1993.
match_headline: Rafael Viñoly, Global Architect of Landmark Buildings, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on Monday about the disability-rights activist Judy Heumann referred imprecisely to Camp Jened, where she had been a camper and a counselor in her youth. It was founded in the 1920s and turned into a camp for disabled youth in 1953; it was not founded in 1951. (This error also appeared in a review of the documentary film “Crip Camp” in 2020.)
match_headline: Judy Heumann, Who Led the Fight for Disability Rights, Dies at 75

text: An article on Thursday about protests in Georgia against so-called foreign agents legislation misstated the given name of a former United States ambassador to Ukraine. He is John Herbst, not Robert.
match_headline: The Explosive Roots of the Georgia Protests

text: An article on Thursday about President Emmanuel Macron’s announcement of a bill that would include the right to abortion in France’s constitution incorrectly implied that Algeria gained independence from France in 1960. It gained independence in 1962.
match_headline: Macron Calls for Enshrining Right to Abortion in French Constitution

text: An article on Wednesday about House Republicans’ split over a broadcast by Tucker Carlson on Fox News about the 2021 attack on the Capitol misstated Rupert Murdoch’s position at News Corp. He is the executive chairman, not the chief executive officer.
match_headline: Republican Lawmakers Split Over Carlson’s False Jan. 6 Claims

text: An article on Thursday about California’s decision not to renew a contract with the pharmacy chain Walgreens described imprecisely the chain’s plans to not dispense mifepristone. The company said it would not make the drug available in 21 states; it does not currently sell mifepristone in those states.
match_headline: Walgreens Loses Contract With California Over Stance on Abortion Pill

text: An article on Wednesday about how cities are rethinking their parking lots, using information from an author of a study on minimum parking requirements in Buffalo, N.Y., misstated the study’s findings. The study found that a repeal of the requirements resulted in a 21 percent decline in parking spaces of new major developments overall, not only among developments that had reduced parking.
match_headline: Awash in Asphalt, Cities Rethink Their Parking Needs

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Syracuse’s announcement that it was replacing the school’s longtime men’s basketball coach misstated when Jim Boeheim coached his son Jimmy. It was the 2021-22 season, not the 2020-21 season.
match_headline: Jim Boeheim Out as Syracuse Coach After 47 Seasons

text: An article on Friday about Russia’s crucial role in Europe’s energy supply misstated the name of an organization that estimated the length of time necessary to design and deliver a nuclear fuel assembly. It is the International Energy Agency, not the International Energy Association.
match_headline: Why Russia Has Such a Strong Grip on Europe’s Nuclear Power

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about the latest Broadway revival of “Sweeney Todd” misstates the citizenship of the composer Bernard Herrmann. He was American, not German.
match_headline: Who Needs a Shave? ‘Sweeney Todd’ Is Back.

text: An obituary on Thursday about the musician David Lindley omitted the names of several of his survivors. In addition to his wife and daughter, he is survived by three brothers, John, Peter and Patrick; a sister, Anne Lindley Maich; and 10 grandchildren. Because of an editing error, the obituary also misspelled part of the name of a nightclub in Southern California. It is the Whisky a Go Go, not Whiskey.
match_headline: David Lindley, ‘Musician’s Musician’ to the Rock Elite, Dies at 78

text: An article on Friday about Rupert Murdoch’s management of his media outlets in the days following the 2020 presidential election misstated which publications Mr. Murdoch used to pressure former President Donald J. Trump to stop talking about voter fraud after the 2020 presidential election. Emails included in the defamation suit brought against Fox News showed that Mr. Murdoch directed Fox News and The New York Post to do so, not The Wall Street Journal.
match_headline: How Murdoch Runs Fox News, in His Own (Often Terse) Words

text: An article last Sunday about comedy based on the workplace misspelled the surname of one of the new generation of comedians who are lampooning work life. He is Ross Pomerantz, not Pomeranz.
match_headline: ‘Dilbert’ Is Canceled but Cubicle Comedians Live On

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about a Supreme Court case involv­ing an Andy Warhol image of Prince mis­stated the type of work that a Vincent van Gogh painting was based on. It was a Jean­-Francois Millet drawing, not a Jean-­Francois Millet photograph.
match_headline: Why Warhol Images Are Making Museums Nervous

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Marissa LaRochelle and Julio Lopez misstated the name of the plumbing company where Mr. Lopez is an owner. It is JC & Son Plumbing, not J.C. Enriquez and Son Plumbing & Remodeling.
match_headline: After a Prime Time Engagement, a Wedding in Four Days

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the struggles of Black and Latino developers misidentified the exterior of a building. It was the former Miller Elementary School, not the former Braddock Junior High School.
match_headline: ‘Excuse After Excuse’: Black and Latino Developers Face Barriers to Success

text: An article on Saturday about the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank misstated the name of the bank that the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation created when it took over Silicon Valley Bank. It is Deposit Insurance National Bank of Santa Clara, not National Bank of Santa Clara.
match_headline: Silicon Valley Bank Fails After Run on Deposits

text: An obituary on Monday about the longtime Minnesota Vikings coach Bud Grant referred incorrectly to his record. His 158 victories were the most in Viking history, not the second-most.
match_headline: Bud Grant, Longtime Minnesota Vikings Coach, Dies at 95

text: An article on Wednesday about the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank misstated Moody’s warning to Silicon Valley Bank. Moody’s said the bank’s bonds, not its stock, were in danger of being downgraded to junk. The article also misidentified the rationale behind the bank’s classification of $95 billion in bonds. It was because of an accounting loophole, not banking regulations.
match_headline: Inside the Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank

text: An article on Monday about the addition of a carving of Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s face to the Million Dollar Staircase misstated the surname of the president of the Preservation League of New York. He is Jay DiLorenzo, not Jay DiStefano.
match_headline: ‘Million-Dollar Staircase’ Adds a New Face: Ruth Bader Ginsburg

text: An article last Thursday about the makeup artist Isamaya Ffrench misstated the name of Ms. Ffrench’s beauty line. It is Isamaya, not Isamaya Beauty.
match_headline: Beauty’s New Queen of N.S.F.W.

text: An obituary on Monday about the former major league baseball player Jesus Alou misstated the given name of a son of his brother Felipe who briefly managed the Mets. He is Luis Rojas, not Jose. It also misspelled the given name of the first Dominican player in the major leagues. He is Ozzie Virgil Sr., not Ossie. And it referred imprecisely to Felipe Alou’s Hall of Fame status. He is in both the Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame and the Caribbean Baseball Hall of Fame, but not the National Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, N.Y.
match_headline: Jesus Alou, Youngest in Trio of Baseball-Playing Brothers, Dies at 80

text: An article on Thursday about a 1,600-year-old coffin discovered in northern England referred imprecisely to English Heritage. The organization manages prehistoric sites, medieval castles and Roman forts in England, not in the rest of Britain. (Other groups manage such sites in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.)
match_headline: A 1,600-Year-Old Coffin May Shed Light on Roman Britain

text: An article on Wednesday about a large seaweed blob heading toward Florida misstated the name of an organization that has discussed the sargassum blooms. It is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, not the National Oceanography and Atmospheric Administration.
match_headline: A Giant Blob of Seaweed Is Heading to Florida

text: An article on Wednesday about Vladimir Putin and Benjamin Netanyahu erroneously attributed a distinction to Mr. Putin. The use of poison­-tipped umbrellas dates back at least to 1978. They were not his innovation.
match_headline: Putin and Netanyahu Show Why Bad Things Happen to Bad Leaders

text: An obituary on March 5 about the actor Tom Sizemore, using information from his manager, misstated what happened to him on Feb. 18. He suffered a brain aneurysm that caused a stroke, not a stroke that caused a brain aneurysm. The obituary also referred incorrectly to the character Mr. Sizemore played in the movie “Black Hawk Down.” He was the commander of the third battalion of the 75th Ranger Regiment, not of the entire regiment.
match_headline: Tom Sizemore, Intense Actor With a Troubled Life, Dies at 61

text: An obituary on March 2 about the Italian talk-show host and television journalist Maurizio Costanzo misstated the English-language title of an Italian film whose screenplay he helped write. It is “A Special Day,” not “A Particular Day.”
match_headline: Maurizio Costanzo, Who Transformed Italian Talk Shows, Dies at 84

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about babesiosis, a tick-borne disease, misstated the classification of ticks. They are arachnids, not insects.
match_headline: Lyme Isn’t the Only Tick Disease to Worry About in the Northeast, C.D.C Says

text: A Critic’s Notebook article this weekend on Page 10 about A.O. Scott’s film reviews misstates where a Susan Sontag essay on the end of cinephilia appeared. It was in The New York Times Magazine, not the Book Review.
match_headline: And Now Let’s Review …

text: An article on Tuesday about the way in which the heart may shape our perception of time misstated the unit of measurement used by researchers in a study. It was milliseconds, not microseconds.
match_headline: Heartbeat May Shape Our Perception of Time, Study Shows

text: An article on Page 36 this weekend about the inventor responsible for leaded gasoline and Freon describes incorrectly a concern raised by Edward Teller about the detonation of the first nuclear device during the Trinity Test. The concern was that a fission reaction, not a fusion reaction, within the bomb would trigger a fusion reaction in the atmosphere. The article also refers incorrectly to ammonia. It is a compound, not an element. And the article misstates the location of fluorine in a nonstandard periodic table of elements that Thomas Midgley used. It is not on the bottom right corner.
match_headline: The Brilliant Inventor Who Made Two of History’s Biggest Mistakes

text: An article on Friday about expert advisers to the Food and Drug Administration endorsing Paxlovid as a Covid treatment misstated the reason that European Union regulators recommended against approval of molnupiravir. They were concerned about its lack of efficacy, not about its safety.
match_headline: F.D.A. Advisers Endorse Paxlovid’s Benefits as a Covid Treatment

text: An article on Saturday about struggling banks like First Republic seeking buyers misstated how quickly the larger banks that injected $30 billion into First Republic could pull their money out. It is as quickly as four months, not three months. The article also misattributed a statement and a quotation about the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Signature Bank and Silicon Valley Bank. It was Wally Adeyemo, deputy Treasury secretary — and not Janet Yellen, Treasury secretary — who said on Friday that Signature Bank and SVB have been trying to find buyers for their business. It was Mr. Adeyemo — and not Ms. Yellen — who said that the F.D.I.C.’s goal “is ultimately to do what is the least cost for the American people — and we know that the least cost is to try and sell these institutions as quickly as possible.”
ref_headline: is ultimately to do what is the least cost for the American people — and we know that the least cost is to try and sell these institutions as quickly as possible.
match_headline: First Republic and Other Banks Seek to Attract Buyers

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about Fairleigh Dickinson’s upset of Purdue in the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament misstated the distinction. While it was only the second time a No. 16 seed had defeated a No. 1 seed, it was not just the second time a No. 16 seed had won a tournament game. The four 16 seeds play in a play-in game to determine who will face the 1 seeds. The caption also misstated the score. As the article correctly stated, Fairleigh Dickinson defeated Purdue, 63-58, not 61-56.
match_headline: Fairleigh Dickinson, Barely in the N.C.A.A. Tournament, Topples Purdue in a Shocker

text: An article on Monday about the creator of the Barkley Marathons misspelled the name of runner who finished the race. His is Aurelien Sanchez, not Aurelian Sanchez.
match_headline: Life Isn’t Fair. He Didn’t Want This Race to Be, Either.

text: An article on Saturday about the tennis player Pam Shriver misstated part of the name of the organization that is responsible for safeguarding the integrity of professional tennis. It is the International Tennis Integrity Agency, not Association.
match_headline: Pam Shriver’s Tennis Juggling Act

text: An article on Thursday about an Idaho college’s decision to remove artwork about abortion and birth control from a school exhibition misstated the name of an organization that sent a letter to the college’s president. It was the National Coalition Against Censorship, not the National Project Against Censorship.
match_headline: An Idaho College Removes Artwork About Abortion, Citing a State Law

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about the U2 album “Songs of Surrender” misstated the incident that is the reference for U2’s song “Sunday Bloody Sunday.” The song refers to the 1972 massacre of Irish protesters by British soldiers, not a terrorist bombing.
match_headline: U2 Revisits Its Past, in the Name of … What, Exactly?

text: An article on Thursday about the Black Sea as a flashpoint between Russia and the West referred incorrectly to Sevastopol. Russia tried to cement control over the Crimean port city in 2014, but it is not Russia’s only warm-water port. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Why the Black Sea Is a Flashpoint Between Russia and the West

text: An article on Monday about efforts by Nikki Haley and Tim Scott to attract the same voters misstated where Mr. Scott got his start in politics. He was a member of the Charleston County Council, not the City Council.
match_headline: In South Carolina, Nikki Haley and Tim Scott Appeal to the Same Donors, and the Same Voters

text: An article on Tuesday about Dominion Voting Systems’s $1.6 billion defamation lawsuit against Fox News misattributed a text message explaining the circumstances of the departure of a Fox News employee in 2020. The text was sent by a colleague of Kristin Fisher, not by Ms. Fisher herself.
match_headline: Inside the 3 Months That Could Cost Fox $1.6 Billion

text: An article on Monday about the Houston Cougars and Alabama Crimson Tide’s positions as the remaining No. 1 seed teams in the N.C.A.A. men’s basketball tournament, based on a transcript of a postgame news conference, misstated the slogan on a T-shirt that Alabama guard Jahvon Quinerly likes to wear. The shirt reads, “Basketball Needs New Jersey,” not “Basketball Meets Jersey.”
match_headline: Houston and Alabama Size Each Other Up From the Same Arena

text: An article on Sunday about the Boston Celtics guard Jaylen Brown referred imprecisely to the Black Hebrew Israelites as an antisemitic group. Black Hebrew Israelites is an umbrella term that encompasses different groups, some of which are extremist. The group at Barclays Center in November was Israel United in Christ, which holds antisemitic views.
match_headline: Jaylen Brown on Basketball, Activism and Being Black in Boston

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with a music review on Tuesday of the International Contemporary Ensemble’s tribute to the artist Douglas R. Ewart misstated the name of a sculpture by Mr. Ewart. It is “Eye of Horus,” not “Eyes of Hours.”
match_headline: Review: A Contemporary Music Group’s Next Era Begins

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the dancer, choreographer and educator Stuart Hodes misstated the name of a duet he performed with Alice Teirstein. It was “I Thought You Were Dead,” not “You Thought We Were Dead.”
match_headline: Stuart Hodes, Who Danced With Martha Graham, Is Dead at 98

text: A chart with an article on Wednesday about a rise in the stock market as investors awaited a decision on interest rates from the Federal Reserve mislabeled the annual pace of single-family home sales in February. It was an increase of 14.5 percent, as the chart correctly showed, not a decrease.
match_headline: Why the Fed’s Decision Matters for Biden

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about the puppetry team of “Life of Pi” misstated the name of one of the ensemble members. He is Rowan Ian Seamus Magee, not Rowan Ian Seamus.
match_headline: Puppetry So Lifelike, Even Their Deaths Look Real

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Oct. 24 about the film “Ticket to Paradise” misidentified which character David was speaking to when he expressed hesitation about his daughter’s plans. It was his ex-wife, Georgia, not Lily, David and Georgia’s daughter. This correction was delayed, because the error was only recently brought to the attention of editors.
match_headline: How George Clooney and Julia Roberts Quietly Became the Tracy-Hepburn of Our Time

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the former New York Knicks center Willis Reed misstated the number of consecutive games the Knicks won early in the 1969-70 season. It was 18, not 17. And a picture caption with the obituary misstated when a photograph of Reed attempting to block a shot by Bill Russell of the Boston Celtics was taken. It was the late 1960s, not the mid-1960s.
match_headline: Willis Reed, Hall of Fame Center for Champion Knicks, Dies at 80

text: An article on March 18 about Turkey’s approval of Finland’s bid to join NATO referred incorrectly to Finland’s border with Russia. Finland has the longest border with Russia of any European Union nation, not of any European nation.
match_headline: Turkey’s Erdogan Finally Endorses Finland’s NATO Bid, but Not Sweden’s

text: An article on Thursday about the identification of a woman who was found dead in Staten Island, relying on information from investigators, misstated the location of the Texas laboratory that tested her DNA. It is in the Woodlands, not Houston.
match_headline: ‘Scorpion Girl’ Found Dead on Staten Island Is Identified After 31 Years

text: An article on Page 1 this weekend about an East Village building and the generations of its history being captured in a song cycle by David Hajdu misspells the surname of the owner of the Paradox, a macrobiotic restaurant once located in the building. He is David Puchkoff, not Pushkoff.
match_headline: Tragedy, Peyote, Beat Poets, Yoko Ono. The 9 Lives of an East Village Townhouse.

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 62 this weekend about traveling in Morocco refers imprecisely to the song “Valerie.” Amy Winehouse sings the song on a Mark Ronson album. Winehouse did not produce or write the song.
match_headline: I Went on a Package Trip for Millennials Who Travel Alone. Help Me.

text: An article on Page 26 this weekend about taxi-whistling misattributes the source of a famous quote about whistling. It was Lauren Bacall, not Mae West.
match_headline: The Robots Can’t Take Taxi-Whistling Away From Me

text: An article on Saturday about senators urging President Biden to send evidence of war crimes to the International Criminal Court referred imprecisely to the positions of the United States and Russia on the International Criminal Court. While both countries initially signed the treaty establishing the court, neither is currently a party to it.
match_headline: Senators Urge Biden to Send Evidence of Russian War Crimes to the I.C.C.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the competitive skiers Mikaela Shiffrin and Jessie Diggins misstated when Diggins won two World Cup races. It was earlier this season on the World Cup circuit, not at the world championships, which is a separate event.
match_headline: Shiffrin and Diggins Put On a Show This Season. Can the U.S. Build on It?

text: An article on Tuesday about a shooting at a private Christian elementary school in Nashville misstated the ratio of students to teachers at the school. It has a student-to-teacher ratio of 8 to 1, not 1 to 8.
match_headline: Heavily Armed Assailant Kills 6 at Christian School

text: An article on Thursday about Michigan repealing a right-to-work law referred incorrectly to an attempt to recall Governor Scott Walker of Wisconsin. The recall vote took place in 2012, not 2015.
match_headline: Michigan Democrats Set to Repeal Law That Hampered Unions

text: An article on Friday about the death of Irvo Otieno, a patient in a psychiatric hospital in Virginia, misidentified when protesters unofficially renamed a plaza in Richmond, Va., as “Marcus-David Peters Circle.” It was before a statue of Robert E. Lee was taken down, not after.
match_headline: Another Mental Illness Tragedy Spurs Questions About Virginia’s Health System

text: An obituary on March 20 about the disc jockey Polito Vega, using information from a family spokeswoman, misstated the year his wife, Judith, died. It was 2012, not 2022.
match_headline: Polito Vega, Salsa ‘King’ of New York Radio, Dies at 84

text: An article on Tuesday about Ukraine’s plans to rebuild the Mriya cargo plane misspelled the surname of the deputy director of Antonov, a state-owned aviation company, in two instances. He is Vladyslav Vlasyk, not Valsyk.
match_headline: Restoring a Giant Plane: Ukrainian Resilience or Folly?

text: An article on March 19 examining rationale’s for the U.S. invasion of Iraq misstated the year in which Saddam Hussein ordered weapons inspectors to leave the country, suggesting this happened in 1998, the year a personal scandal weakened then-President Bill Clinton and that Congress passed the Iraq Liberation Act. Iraqi officials ordered weapons inspectors to leave in 1997. Inspectors later returned before being finally withdrawn by the United Nations, not ejected by Mr. Hussein, in 1998.
match_headline: 20 Years On, a Question Lingers About Iraq: Why Did the U.S. Invade?

text: An article on Tuesday about hotels’ move away from guaranteed daily cleanings during the pandemic misstated how close hotel occupancy levels this year are expected to be to prepandemic levels. They are expected to be just 2 percentage points below 2019, not 2 percent below.
match_headline: Say Goodbye to Daily Hotel Room Cleaning

text: An article on Wednesday about the Final Four in women’s basketball misstated the combined number of 3-pointers made by Iowa and Louisville in Sunday’s game. They made 24, not 34.
match_headline: Final Four Is New Ground for South Carolina’s Challengers

text: A review on Friday in a roundup of New York gallery shows in March described incorrectly the artist Marcus Behmer. He worked closely with a Jewish publisher; he was not Jewish.

An obituary on Tuesday about Gladys Kessler, a federal judge who ruled in 2006 that the tobacco industry had violated civil racketeering laws, misstated the middle initial of the president of the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids. He is Matthew L. Myers, not I. The obituary also misstated where Jihad Ahmed Mustafa Diyab, a detainee in the United States military prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, whose case Judge Kessler heard, was transferred. It was Uruguay, not Ecuador.
match_headline: Gladys Kessler, Judge Who Curbed Deceptive Tobacco Ads, Dies at 85

text: An article on Wednesday about Mississippi’s rejection of federal funding to expand health insurance for the poor misstated the share of residents of the Mississippi Delta who are Black. It is about two-thirds, not nearly 35 percent.
match_headline: ‘We’re Going Away’: A State’s Choice to Forgo Medicaid Funds Is Killing Hospitals

text: An article on Thursday about soldiers massing near a Ukrainian power plant misstated the location of Bakhmut with respect to Zaporizhzhia. It is to Zaporizhzhia’s northeast, not northwest.
match_headline: Soldiers Massing Near Ukrainian Nuclear Plant, U.N. Official Warns

text: An article on Thursday about President Biden’s confrontation with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel misstated where evacuated settlers would be allowed to return under a law passed by Israel’s Parliament. They would be able to go to four areas of the West Bank, not the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
match_headline: Biden’s Confrontation With Netanyahu Had Been Brewing for Years

text: An article on Thursday about House Republicans splintering over a fiscal plan and frozen debt talks misstated which House committee passed a bill to prioritize payments on U.S. Treasury bonds if the nation can no longer borrow funds to cover all its expenses. It is the Ways and Means Committee, not the Budget Committee.
match_headline: Debt Talks Are Frozen as House Republicans Splinter Over a Fiscal Plan

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 22 this weekend about the challenge of counting every global birth and death misstates what was happening. The midwife was not taking the blood pressure of the patient. Also, a nurse is misidentified. She is Dora Burbano, not Dora Urbano.
match_headline: The Incredible Challenge of Counting Every Global Birth and Death

text: An article on March 5 about endovascular thrombectomies described imprecisely the origin of the neuroradiological techniques and procedures used in the treatment. Cardiology adapted the techniques and procedures developed by interventional radiologists; they did not originate in cardiology.
match_headline: This Revolutionary Stroke Treatment Will Save Millions of Lives. Eventually.

text: A review on March 5 of Adam Zagajew­ski’s poetry collection “True Life” misidentified the source of the name “Lvov” for Zagajewski’s native city. That spelling is from the Russian; the Polish version is “Lwow.”
match_headline: A Poet Whose Tone Was Personal and Whose Vision Was Vast

text: An article on Page F13 this weekend about visiting the Pigeon Point Lighthouse misstates the cost of renting out one of the vacation homes at Pigeon Point Lighthouse Hostel. It is $600 a night, not $1,200 a night.
match_headline: A Lighthouse to Call Your Own

text: An article on Monday about Russian shelling that killed six civilians in Ukraine referred incorrectly to the number of civilians killed in Ukraine. The United Nations has recorded roughly 8,400 civilian deaths, not roughly 18,000, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
match_headline: Russian Shelling Kills 6 as Assault Stalls in Ukraine’s East

text: An article on Saturday about Huawei Technologies’ plunge in annual profit referred imprecisely to the sale of Huawei’s mobile phone division. The company sold off a portion of that business, not all of it.
match_headline: Huawei, Pummeled by U.S. Sanctions, Reports Plunge in Profit

text: An article on Monday about the limited number of spots in the Women’s National Basketball Association misspelled the name of a basketball player. It is Brittney Griner, not Britney.
match_headline: Angel Reese, Caitlin Clark and the W.N.B.A.’s Talent Conundrum

text: An obituary on March 23 about the journalist Warren Boroson misstated the location of Memorial High School, which he attended. It is in West New York, N.J. — not West Nyack, N.Y.
match_headline: Warren Boroson, Who Surveyed Psychiatrists on Goldwater, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Sunday about the poet Royston Ellis, using information from a family member, misstated when and where he died. He died on Feb. 26 at a friend’s house, not on Feb. 27 in a hospital.
match_headline: Royston Ellis, Bridge Between Beat Poets and the Beatles, Dies at 82

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an obituary on March 16 about Richard Rosenberg, a former chief executive and chairman of Bank of America, misidentified a Bank of America property. It was a branch of the bank in San Francisco, not the bank’s headquarters there.
match_headline: Richard Rosenberg, Who Rejuvenated Bank of America, Dies at 92

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Monday about the composer Ryuichi Sakamoto, using information from The Associated Press, misidentified the man pictured with him, David Bowie and Nagisa Oshima, the director of the movie “Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence.” He is the actor Jack Thompson, who appeared alongside Mr. Sakamoto and Mr. Bowie in that film — not the producer Jack Thomas.
match_headline: Ryuichi Sakamoto, Oscar-Winning Composer, Dies at 71

text: An article on March 30 about Ukraine’s steel industry misstated the type of coal used to power blast furnaces. It is metallurgical coal, not thermal coal.
match_headline: How Ukraine’s Battered Steel Industry Galvanized Its War Effort

text: An article on Thursday about two French business titans at the top of Forbes’s richest list misidentified the cable network on which the series “Succession” airs. It is HBO, not Netflix.
match_headline: France, Guardian of Égalité, Leads the List of Ultrarich

text: An article on Wednesday about a worldwide growth in art and antiques sales misspelled the name of the Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report’s author; she is Clare McAndrew, not Claire.
match_headline: Art Market Has Climbed Above Prepandemic Level, Major Study Says

text: An article on Page 15 this weekend about six Picasso exhibitions misstates the end date of a Brooklyn Museum exhibition. It runs through Sept. 24, not Aug. 24.
match_headline: 6 Picasso Shows to See This Year

text: An article on Page 26 this weekend about Poland refers incorrectly to the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact between the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany. It was signed just before World War II, not during World War II.
match_headline: Poland’s War on Two Fronts

text: An article on Page 34 this weekend about the Dominion Voting Systems defamation suit against Fox News misstates the format of Sean Hannity’s recent interview with former President Donald J. Trump. It was a taped one-on-one interview, not in front of a live audience.
match_headline: How Fox Chased Its Audience Down the Rabbit Hole

text: An article on Monday about Ukrainians who have become homeless despite a government resettlement program in the U.S. incorrectly described the work that Welcome.Us does with refugees from Afghanistan and Ukraine. Welcome.Us helps to match Ukrainian refugees with American sponsors, not Afghan refugees.
match_headline: These Ukrainians Arrived Under a Biden Program. They Ended Up Homeless.

text: An article on Tuesday about right-wing media’s split from Gov. Ron DeSantis incorrectly described the circumstances in which a publisher may be held liable for defamation under the Supreme Court precedent known as New York Times v. Sullivan. Publishers may be liable if an error is the result of recklessness, not negligence.
match_headline: Right-Wing Media Splits From DeSantis on Press Protections

text: An article last Sunday, about older people buying their first homes, misstated the surname of a senior economist at Zillow upon second reference. He is Jeff Tucker, not Zucker.
match_headline: Retired and Buying a Starter Home. It’s Forever.

text: An article on Sunday about leaked Pentagon documents that reveal Russia’s military struggles misstated the name of a U.S. law on national security surveillance. It is the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, not the Federal Intelligence Surveillance Act.
match_headline: Leaked Documents Reveal Depth of U.S. Spy Efforts and Russia’s Military Struggles

text: An article on Monday about North Carolina’s role in the fight for Medicaid expansion misquoted Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina. He said: “They immediately sued me in federal court to stop me. And we could have set it aside at that point, but we persisted, and that’s because we knew it was too important.” He did not say, “They sued me in federal court to stop it, and we kind of set it aside.”
ref_headline: They immediately sued me in federal court to stop me. And we could have set it aside at that point, but we persisted, and that’s because we knew it was too important.
match_headline: Will North Carolina Be the ‘Beginning of the End’ of the Medicaid Expansion Fight?

text: An article on Saturday about risky moves from tech companies to win the race for artificial intelligence misstated the number of years that have passed since Microsoft shut down a chatbot called Tay. It was seven years ago, not five.
match_headline: In A.I. Race, Microsoft and Google Choose Speed Over Caution

text: An article on Friday about continued unproven claims online about Dominion Voting Systems misstated an election change that Shasta County approved last month. The county voted to hand-count paper ballots. It did not vote to use paper ballots, which were already in use.
match_headline: Attacks on Dominion Voting Persist Despite High-Profile Lawsuits

text: An article on Saturday about Amazon’s plan to release movies in theaters misstated the name of an AMC movie theater in Las Vegas. It is AMC Town Square, not AMC Town Center.
match_headline: Hoping to Draw Moviegoers and Filmmakers, Amazon Heads to Theaters

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about Jon Rahm’s victory in the Masters Tournament omitted the name of the golfer who shot a final-round score of 75. It was Brooks Koepka, not Rahm; Rahm shot a 69.
match_headline: At the Masters, Brooks Koepka Holds the Lead and Tiger Woods Withdraws

text: An article on Friday about online advertising described a statistic about ad expenditures by Jeremy’s Razors on Facebook incorrectly. In the 30 days ending March 26, Jeremy’s Razors was the biggest ad buyer among advertisers whose spending is disclosed in Facebook’s ad trans­parency reports, not the most overall.
match_headline: If It’s Advertised to You Online, You Probably Shouldn’t Buy It. Here’s Why.

text: An article on Saturday about the stabbing of Bob Lee, the founder of CashApp, described incorrectly the effect of recent atmospheric rivers on office towers in the Financial District. High winds shattered the windows of several buildings, but the landmark Salesforce tower was not among them.
match_headline: Stabbing of Cash App Creator Raises Alarm, and Claims of ‘Lawless’ San Francisco

text: An article on Tuesday about how it is harder for older Americans to get a mortgage misstated the circumstances under which lenders may take into consideration a mortgage applicant’s age. It may be used only under limited legal circumstances; age may not be used to determine overall creditworthiness.
match_headline: A Great Credit Score, but She Can’t Get a Mortgage

text: An article on Monday about the World Bank’s spring meeting misstated Emmanuel Macron’s title. He is the president of France, not the prime minister.
match_headline: The World Bank Is Getting a New Chief. Will He Pivot Toward Climate Action?

text: An article on Wednesday about criticism of the French police’s handling of street protests against pension changes misstated the given name of a lawyer who has filed complaints to denounce arbitrary arrests. She is Aïnoha Pascual, not Aïhona.
match_headline: French Police Face Scrutiny for Heavy Hand During Pension Protests

text: An article on Friday about President Emmanuel Macron of France and Xi Jinping’s call for peace talks between Russia and Ukraine referred imprecisely to Ursula von der Leyen’s role in the visit. She did not participate in any public events with President Emmanuel Macron, but she was photographed alongside him. The error was repeated in an article on Sunday about a meeting between Mr. Macron and Mr. Xi.
match_headline: Xi and Macron Call for Ukraine Peace Talks, but the Path Is Murky

text: An article on Wednesday about the impact that layoffs and absentee bosses are having on morale at Meta misstated the number of layoffs and job cuts at the company. Meta has conducted two rounds of layoffs over the past six months and plans two more, affecting more than 21,000 people and eliminating 5,000 jobs. It did not lay off 26,000 people in the past six months. It also misstated Bain & Company’s role in workplace reviews. Bain did not assist in conducting the reviews.
match_headline: Mass Layoffs and Absentee Bosses Create a Morale Crisis at Meta

text: A subheading with an obituary on Monday for Hobie Landrith, the first player for the Mets, misidentified a person described as having an “immense knowledge of baseball.” As the obituary correctly noted, it was Casey Stengel, the Mets’ original manager, not Landrith.
match_headline: Hobie Landrith, the First New York Met, Dies at 93

text: An article on Tuesday about Ukrainian soldiers’ efforts to find and de-mine booby traps set up by Russia’s military misstated the name of a Russian mine. It is OZM-72, not OMZ-52.
match_headline: Lethal Surprises Hidden in the Grass: Russia’s Trip Wires and Land Mines

text: An article on Thursday about the impact that Dominion Voting Systems’ defamation suit against Fox News could have on libel law misstated when the trial’s judge, Eric M. Davis, took two actions. On Tuesday, not Wednesday, Judge Davis barred Fox from using newsworthiness as a defense. On Wednesday, not Thursday, he imposed a sanction on Fox for withholding evidence.
match_headline: Judge Imposes Sanction on Fox for Withholding Evidence in Defamation Case

text: An obituary on Monday about the cinematographer Bill Butler referred incorrectly to his educational background. He did not graduate from the University of Iowa. And because of an editing error, the obituary incorrectly included a name on the list of Mr. Butler’s survivors. His daughter Patricia Pekau died in 2021.
match_headline: Bill Butler, Cinematographer Best Known for ‘Jaws,’ Dies at 101

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about Nora Forster, the wife of John Lydon of the Sex Pistols, partly misquoted a Twitter post from Mr. Lydon about her death. He wrote that he had become “her full time carer,” not “career.”
match_headline: Nora Forster, 80, Who Married (and Stayed Married to) a Sex Pistol, Dies

text: An article on Friday about the muted reactions abroad to the leak of documents exposing U.S. spying operations around the world misstated the recipient of intelligence documents provided by the former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden. He gave them to journalists, not to the website WikiLeaks.
match_headline: Once Shocking, U.S. Spying on Its Allies Draws a Global Shrug

text: An obituary on Thursday about the crime novelist Anne Perry misstated the name of the college where her father was rector. It was Canterbury University College (now the University of Canterbury), not Cambridge University College. The obituary also misstated in two places the given name of a character Ms. Perry created. As correctly noted elsewhere, he is Thomas Pitt, not William Pitt. And it misspelled the given name of another crime novelist. He was Dashiell Hammett, not Dashiel.
match_headline: Anne Perry, Crime Writer With Her Own Dark Tale, Dies at 84

text: A review on March 26 of Isabel Waidner’s novel “Sterling Karat Gold” referred incorrectly to the book’s protagonist, Sterling Beckenbauer. Sterling does get a job as a cleaner, but not at a gay bathhouse called the Chariots Roman Spa.
match_headline: They Were the Victim of a Bigoted Assault, but They’re the One on Trial

text: An article on March 12 about poverty in America implied an incorrect date for a statistic about overdraft fees. The research was conducted between 2005 and 2012, not in 2021.
match_headline: Why Poverty Persists in America

text: An article last Sunday about the state of the housing market included a chart with a mislabeled row of data about new listings. The row shows the change in new listings, not days on market.
match_headline: Buying or Selling a Home? Welcome to the Year of Disappointment

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Kyiona Carswell and Alison Wynn misspelled Ms. Carswell’s given name. The article also reversed their ages. Ms. Carswell is 32, and Ms. Wynn is 30.
match_headline: In Her Dream, a Premonition and Then a Double Proposal

text: An article on Friday about the activist paths of Tennessee state representatives Justin Jones and Justin J. Pearson misstated the location of the airport where Representative Jones sang with Joan Baez. It was in Newark, not Nashville.
match_headline: ‘The Justins’ Follow a Legacy of Resistance in Tennessee

text: An article on Sunday about transgender rights becoming a rallying campaign for social conservatives misstated the name of a research group that has conducted polling on transgender rights. It is the Public Religion Research Institute, not the Public Policy Research Institute.
match_headline: How a Campaign Against Transgender Rights Mobilized Conservatives

text: A column on Monday about a crossword columnist’s tips for solving the day’s puzzle misstated Julius Caesar’s title. He was a Roman general and dictator, not emperor.
match_headline: Participates in Some Singles Matches?

text: An article on Sunday about an explosion at a site in Wakayama where Japan’s Prime Minister Fumio Kishida was scheduled to give a speech misstated the organization that Robert Dujarric is associated with. It is the Institute of Contemporary Asian Studies, not the Institute of Contemporary Studies.
match_headline: Japan’s Prime Minister Safely Evacuated After Blast

text: An article on Nov. 1 about investments in the web platform Rumble by J.D. Vance and Peter Thiel misstated the backgrounds of two American veterans who were captured by Russians while fighting as volunteers in Ukraine. It was Andy Tai Ngoc Huynh who had worked as a delivery driver before going to Ukraine, not Alex Drueke. This correction was delayed, because it was only recently brought to the attention of editors.
match_headline: Company Backed by J.D. Vance Gives Platform for Russian Propaganda

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misidentified the location of the house in Amityville, N.Y. It is on Ocean Avenue, not Orchard Avenue.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Amityville: An Origin Story’ and ‘Revengineers’

text: A Critic’s Pick article on Friday about a veteran critic’s change of opinion on painter Cecily Brown’s work misspelled the given name of a major British painter. He is Lucian Freud, not Lucien.
match_headline: I Was Wrong About Cecily Brown

text: An article on Friday about pro-Russian media in Africa referred incorrectly to the financing for Radio France Internationale and France 24. They are publicly funded, not government funded.
match_headline: How Putin Became a Hero on African TV

text: An article on Saturday about a speech President Biden gave during his visit to Ireland misidentified the location of a plaque in Ireland dedicated to Beau Biden. It is in Castlebar, not Knock.
match_headline: In Ireland, Biden Makes a Case for His Future, Drawing on a Family Story Rooted in Hope

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about a scientific breakthrough in Oklahoma’s search for the graves of people killed in 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre described incorrectly the setting in which a woman was operating an elevator before the start of the massacre. It was a department store, not a drugstore.
match_headline: Tulsa Reaches ‘Breakthrough’ in Search for Massacre Victims

text: An article on Saturday about the possibility of federal regulators requiring funeral homes to disclose their prices online misstated the settlement reached between the Federal Trade Commission and Legacy Cremation Services. It was $275,000, not $257,000.
match_headline: Funeral Homes Don’t Have to List Prices Online. That May Change.

text: An article on Saturday about the 2018 Boston Marathon champion Des Linden misidentified a thyroid condition that Linden has dealt with. It is hypothyroidism, also called underactive thyroid, not hyperthyroidism, or overactive thyroid.
match_headline: Des Linden Keeps Choosing to Run

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the runner Eliud Kipchoge misstated Kipchoge’s running pace in his 1:59:40 marathon. It was 4 minutes 34.05 seconds per mile, not 4:34.5.
match_headline: Eliud Kipchoge’s Next Feat: The Tactical Boston Marathon

text: An obituary on Sunday about Billy Waugh, the covert operative known as the “godfather of the Green Berets,” misstated when Paris Davis, who was Mr. Waugh’s commander in the Vietnam War, was belatedly awarded the Medal of Honor. It was 2023, not 2021.
match_headline: Billy Waugh, 93, ‘Godfather of the Green Berets,’ Is Dead

text: An obituary on April 6 about the photographer Neal Boenzi, using information from his family, misstated the birth name of his second wife. It was Olga Marin, not Marron.
match_headline: Neal Boenzi, 97, Top New York Times Photographer for Four Decades, Dies

text: An obituary on Monday about Hedda Kleinfeld Schachter, who with her husband, Jack, ran the bridal superstore I. Kleinfeld & Son for many years, misstated the term for a type of sleeve. It is leg-of-mutton, not ragamuffin.
match_headline: Hedda Kleinfeld Schachter Dies at 99; Built an Empire of Tulle and Satin

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about a second sexual assault charge against a former Roman Catholic cardinal referred incorrectly to the role of the former cardinal Theodore E. McCarrick in the Catholic abuse scandal. He is the only U.S. cardinal charged with abuse, not the only cardinal charged.
match_headline: Defrocked Catholic Cardinal Faces Second Sex Assault Charge

text: An article on Wednesday about a parking garage collapse in Lower Manhattan misstated the address of the garage. It is 57 Ann Street, not 37 Ann Street.
match_headline: One Dead in Parking Garage Collapse in Lower Manhattan

text: An article on Wednesday about banned Western chips and other electronic devices winding up in Russian missile technology misstated the name of the organization that provided a translation of a Russian-language interview. It is the Center for Strategic and International Studies, not the Center for Strategic and International Relations.
match_headline: Russia Is Importing Western Weapons Technology, Bypassing Sanctions

text: An article on Wednesday about Apple’s first store in India misidentified the products available through third-party sellers in India 25 years ago. They were Apple products, not Apple phones.
match_headline: Apple Opens First Store in India, a Promising Frontier for the Tech Giant

text: An article on Wednesday about Eliud Kipchoge’s loss at the Boston Marathon incorrectly described the 2020 London Marathon. It was run in a restricted environment and without spectators because of the coronavirus pandemic; fans did not line the course.
match_headline: Eliud Kipchoge Was Supposed to Win the Boston Marathon. What Went Wrong?
