text: An article on Thursday about growing criticism among conservative presidential candidates of Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida’s feud with Disney misstated the year that Mr. DeSantis signed a bill that critics have called the “Don’t Say Gay” law. He signed it into law last year, not this year.
match_headline: Republicans Hit DeSantis Over Disney Feud

text: An obituary on Thursday about Leon Levine, the founder of the Family Dollar retail chain, misstated the name of a nonprofit he founded. It is the Leon Levine Foundation, not the Leon Levy Foundation.
match_headline: Leon Levine, Who Made a Billion One Dollar at a Time, Dies at 85

text: An article this weekend on Page 14 about the seizure of the Attic Greek cup from the Metropolitan Museum of Art misidentifies the type of adhesive used currently by conservators at the Met museum when reassembling ancient ceramics. The adhesives typically used now are acrylic, not the nitrate adhesives that had once been popular with conservators there.
match_headline: The Kylix Marvel: Why Experts Distrust the Story of an Ancient Cup’s Rebirth

text: An article on April 16 about gig workers referred incorrectly to company practices at Amazon. While Amazon sets productivity expectations for workers, it said it does not set productivity quotas.
match_headline: When Your Boss Is an App

text: An article on April 16 about alternative workdays misstated the date of a study by Microsoft researchers. It was 2021, not 2022.
match_headline: Before We Invest Billions in This Clean Fuel, Let’s Make Sure It’s Actually Clean

text: An article on Monday about efforts in Republican-led legislatures to make it harder to get abortion-related ballot initiatives on the ballot misstated one proposal’s threshold for approval in Missouri. The percentage of votes required to pass such measures would be increased to a 60 percent supermajority, not 66.7 percent.
match_headline: Losing Ballot Issues on Abortion, G.O.P. Now Tries to Keep Them Off the Ballot

text: An article on Friday about an appeals court’s decision to delay a request from congressional Republicans to question Mark F. Pomerantz, a former prosecutor with the Manhattan district attorney’s office, misstated the date of the appointment of Mary Kay Vyskocil. She was nominated in 2018 and confirmed the following year.
match_headline: Appeals Court Delays Ex-Prosecutor’s Deposition on Trump Investigation

text: An article on Sunday about the N.F.L.’s mixed messages on sports betting misstated the impact of a 2018 Supreme Court ruling. The court struck down a law that prevented states from legalizing sports gambling. It did not legalize sports gambling in the states.
match_headline: N.F.L. Walks a Fine Line on Players’ Betting

text: An article on Saturday about Virginia Johnson‌‌’s impact on young ballerinas at Dance Theater of Harlem misidentified the year in which the Ensemble at Dance Theater of Harlem was formed. It was 2008, not 2018.
match_headline: Poised for Change at a Company Where Dancers of Color Feel at Home

text: An obituary on Sunday about the modern dance performer and teacher Valda Setterfield misspelled the surname of a composer who wrote music for the Merce Cunningham troupe while Ms. Setterfield was a member of it. He was Toshi Ichiyanagi, not Ichyanagi.
match_headline: Valda Setterfield Dies at 88; a Star in the Postmodern Dance Firmament

text: An obituary on Jan. 11 about the whale researcher Ken Balcomb misstated the population of Southern Resident orcas when it was at its peak in the 1990s. It was about 100, not about 120. This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: Ken Balcomb, 82, Dies; Revealed the Hidden World of Killer Whales

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about young voters who are upset with President Biden’s decision to approve the Willow oil drilling project overstated the number of views amassed by Alex Haraus’s TikTok videos opposing the Willow project. It was hundreds of thousands, not hundreds of millions.
match_headline: Many Young Voters Bitter Over Biden’s Support of Willow Oil Drilling

text: An article on Saturday about directors who have branded movies with their own names misidentified the war depicted in “Guy Ritchie’s The Covenant.” It is the war in Afghanistan, not Iraq.
match_headline: Name Above the Movie Title? How About in It?

text: An article on Tuesday about the hurdles that African nations must overcome to gain independent vaccine access referred incorrectly to the International Vaccine Institute. It is a United Nations-backed international organization based in South Korea, not a South Korean nonprofit.
match_headline: Can Africa Get Close to Vaccine Independence? Here’s What It Will Take.

text: An article on Saturday about a labor shortage threatening annual forestry targets for the Menominee Tribe misstated the name of a organization that promotes responsible forestry. It is the Forest Stewardship Council, not the Forest Steward Council.
match_headline: The Giving Forest

text: An article on Wednesday about a wave of right-wing outrage over a Bud Light marketing campaign misstated the timing of Anheuser-Busch’s announcement about its marketing executives. Their leaves of absence were announced this week, not last Friday.
match_headline: Ad Flap Leaves Bitter Aftertaste for Bud Light and Warning for Big Business

text: An article on Monday about the decision by Stuyvesant High School in Manhattan to end all-girls swim classes misstated the size of the pool at Stuyvesant High School. It is large, but not Olympic size.
match_headline: End of All-Girls Swim Class Causes Controversy at Stuyvesant High School

text: An article on Sunday about the New York City curbside composting program that is being used to produce gas for homes misstated the potency level of methane gas compared with carbon dioxide. It is 25 times more potent than carbon dioxide, not 25 percent more potent.
match_headline: How New Yorkers’ Food Scraps Get ‘Digested’ to Provide Gas for Homes

text: An article on Wednesday about a top lawyer hired by both Tucker Carlson and Don Lemon to navigate their network departures misstated the ruling in a lawsuit by Michael Jackson’s estate over an HBO documentary. The estate won an appeal in 2020 to go to private arbitration. It did not win a $100 million judgment.
match_headline: Tucker Carlson and Don Lemon Hire a Top Hollywood Lawyer

text: An article on Monday about television shows to watch this week misstated the surname of Awkwafina’s character in the TV series “Awkwafina Is Nora From Queens.” The character’s name is Nora Lin, not Nora Lum, which is Awkwafina’s birth name.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Tom Jones’ and ‘Couples Therapy’

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about Herb Douglas, an Olympic medalist in the long jump who honored the memory of the Olympic sprinter Jesse Owens by creating an international sports award in Owens’s name, gave an erroneous distinction to a recipient of the honor, the middle-distance runner Mary Decker Slaney. She was a gold medal winner in World Championship competition, not in the Olympics.
match_headline: Herb Douglas, Olympic Medalist Inspired by Jesse Owens, Dies at 101

text: An article on Thursday about the House’s approval of a bill to raise the debt ceiling misstated Senator Mitch McConnell’s leadership title. He is the minority leader, not the majority leader.
match_headline: House G.O.P. Passes Debt Limit Bill, Paving the Way for a Clash With Biden

text: An article on Sunday about a proposal from the Environmental Protection Agency to limit carbon emissions from existing power plants overstated the number of power plants around the world using carbon capture technology. There are about 40 power plants and other industrial facilities using carbon capture worldwide; there are not 40 power plants using the technology. The article also overstated the incentives under the Inflation Reduction Act intended to speed up adoption of the technology. The law raised existing federal tax credits for electric utilities that capture their carbon dioxide pollution to a range of $60 to $85 per ton of carbon dioxide, not to a range of $85 to $135 per ton.
match_headline: E.P.A. to Propose First Controls on Greenhouse Gases From Power Plants

text: An article on Monday about the dispute between Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida and Disney misstated the company that is Florida’s largest employer. It is Publix, not Walt Disney World.
match_headline: Disney Sues DeSantis Over Control of Its Florida Resort

text: An article on Thursday about a fire at a local newspaper’s printing plant right before its last edition was set to print misstated Montclair Local’s original subscription price. It was $12 a year, not $12 a month.
match_headline: A Newspaper Was Planning Its Last Edition. Then the Press Caught Fire.

text: An article on April 14 about the closure of the last three nuclear power plants in Germany incorrectly paraphrased comments made by a climate policy analyst about the impact of the 2022 drought and heat wave on Europe’s nuclear facilities. The analyst noted that some plants reduced their output to avoid pumping dangerously warm water into waterways, not that the drought and heat caused several European countries to shut down reactors when the rivers used to cool the plants dropped too low.
match_headline: Germany Quits Nuclear Power, Ending a Decades-Long Struggle

text: An article on Friday about a prominent business group in Harlem that has filed suit against the state’s plan to open a cannabis dispensary there misstated the name of Gov. Kathy Hochul’s chief of staff. It is Stacy Lynch, not Stacey Lynch.
match_headline: Harlem Businesses Sue to Stop Cannabis Dispensary Planned for 125th Street

text: An article on Thursday about the expansion of a New York tax incentive program for film and television producers misstated the name of the union representing film, television and radio workers. It is SAG-AFTRA, not the Screen Actors Guild.
match_headline: As New York Boosts Tax Breaks for Movies, Some Critics Pan the Program

text: An article on Tuesday about what is to come for Wrexham A.F.C. soccer club after it won the National League championship misidentified the league Paul Mullin was playing in when he was player of the season the year before he signed with Wrexham. It was League Two, not the National League.
match_headline: ‘Welcome to Wrexham’ Has Its Championship Moment. Now What?

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about “Emancipation: The Unfinished Project of Liberation” on display at the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth misstates how Hugh Hayden’s piece “American Dream” was produced. It was 3-D printed, not 3-D painted.
ref_headline: Emancipation: The Unfinished Project of Liberation
match_headline: Artwork Inspired by an Abraham Lincoln Moment Is Reimagined

text: An article on Page 32 this weekend about the changing role of artist residency programs misstates an affiliation for Stephan Jost, the director and chief executive of the Art Gallery of Toronto. He is the second vice president and secretary of the Association of Art Museum Directors, not the American Alliance of Art Museums. The article also misstates the name of a museum that has exhibited the works of the artist Aliza Nisenbaum. It is the Minneapolis Institute of Art, not the Minnesota Institute of Art. The article also includes a comment by Ms. Nisenbaum that lacked context. She said she was excited to have her first solo museum show in New York, not her first solo show in the city. It also implies incorrectly that some of the staff members who worked on the show of Ms. Nisenbaum’s art were volunteers. The artist’s representatives said all the workers were paid.
match_headline: ‘Ask Me What I’m Painting’: The Changing Role of the Artist in Residence

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 38 this weekend about how museums are making art more accessible for people with disabilities, relying on incorrect information from the Museum of Modern Art, misstates the year of a museum touch tour. It was during the 1990s, not 1972.
match_headline: Making Art Accessible for All

text: An article on Page 32 this weekend about the writer Christina Sharpe misstates the given name of a Tennessee State Representative. He is Justin J. Pearson, not Jim.
match_headline: The Woman Shaping a Generation of Black Thought

text: An obituary on April 12 about the photographer Carl Fischer referred imprecisely to his graduation from the Cooper Union in 1948. He received a certificate in art, not a degree. (The Cooper Union did not award degrees until 1963.)
match_headline: Carl Fischer, Who Shot Attention-Getting Esquire Covers, Dies at 98

text: An article last Sunday about products to com­memorate the coronation of King Charles III described incorrectly the supermarket chain Lidl. It was founded in Germany and has locations in Britain; it is not a “British supermarket chain.”
match_headline: Merch Fit for a King

text: A review on April 9 of “Truth and Re­pair,” by Judith L. Herman, misstated the given name of a criminologist. She is Alissa Ackerman, not Melissa.
match_headline: What Should Justice Look Like for Trauma Survivors? Ask Them.

text: An article on April 23 about donations from the Sackler family to the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine referred imprecisely to statistics from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on the number of adults in the United States with chronic pain. Roughly 52 million adults suffered from chronic pain, according to a C.D.C. report, and of those, more than 17 million U.S. adults experience high-impact or more severe chronic pain; the number of U.S. adults affected by chronic pain does not range between 17 million and 52 million people. The error was repeated in a follow-up article on Sunday.
match_headline: Sacklers Gave Millions to Institution That Advises on Opioid Policy

text: An article on Monday about an elite school’s admission of failure after a student’s death misstated the cost of attending Lawrenceville School in New Jersey. The cost can top $76,000 for tuition plus room and board, not for room and board alone.
match_headline: Some Colleges Offer Quotes of Competitors’ Prices. Be Wary.

text: An article on Monday about the near-collapse of Sudan’s health care system amid fighting between a paramilitary group and the Sudanese Army misidentified the country from which the Red Cross had shipped eight tons of medical supplies. It was Jordan, not Saudi Arabia.
match_headline: Sudan Evacuees Flee for Saudi Arabia on Ships

text: An article on Friday about a state dinner hosted by President Biden for President Yoon Suk Yeol of South Korea, using information from a White House press pool report, referred incorrectly to one of the guests, Samantha Cohen. Ms. Cohen is not the daughter of Michael D. Cohen, the estranged lawyer for former President Donald J. Trump.
match_headline: Korean Dressing, Irish Poetry and ‘American Pie’: A State Dinner of Harmony

text: An article on Saturday about efforts by unions representing Hollywood writers and actors to limit artificial intelligence misstated John August’s position with the Writers Guild of America. He is on its negotiating committee, not its board.
match_headline: Will a Chatbot Write the Next ‘Succession’?

text: An article on Monday about the winner of the World Chess Championship misstated the amount of the prize money. Though the winnings were preceded by a dollar sign, they were, in fact, in euros. (Ding Liren, the winner, earned 1.1 million euros, or about $1.2 million, and Ian Nepomniachtchi, the runner-up, received 900,000 euros, or about $990,000.)
match_headline: Ding Liren of China Wins World Chess Championship

text: An article on Sunday about Tucker Carlson misstated the name of a television network. It is the Public Broadcasting Service, not the Public Broadcasting System.
match_headline: Fox News Gambled, but Tucker Can Still Take Down the House

text: An obituary on Sunday about Rabbi Harold S. Kushner, the author of the best-selling book “When Bad Things Happen to Good People,” misspelled the name of the company that published it. It is Schocken Books, not Shocken Books.
ref_headline: When Bad Things Happen to Good People,
match_headline: Rabbi Harold S. Kushner, Reassuring Best-Selling Author, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on April 21 about the former congressman Bud Shuster misidentified the university from which he graduated in 1954. It was the University of Pittsburgh, not Pennsylvania.
match_headline: Bud Shuster, Unabashed ‘Asphalt King’ of Congress, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about how conflict in Sudan has reignited decades-long violence in Darfur misstated the United Nations office that Jérôme Merlin works for. It is the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the body’s refugee agency, not the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.
match_headline: Sudan’s Conflict Ignites Fears of Civil War in Darfur

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misstated the birthday of Miep Gies, who is played by Bel Powley in the TV series “A Small Light.” Gies would have turned 114 years old in February, not in May. The article also misstated the co-chairs of the Metropolitan Museum of Art Costume Institute benefit, also known as the Met Gala, this year. They are Michaela Coel, Penélope Cruz, Roger Federer and Dua Lipa; not Regina King, Blake Lively, Ryan Reynolds and Lin-Manuel Miranda, who were the co-chairs of the benefit in 2022.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘A Small Light’ and the Met Gala

text: An article on Saturday about the North Carolina gerrymandering ruling referred imprecisely to Kansas’ judicial system. The state appoints its Supreme Court justices but holds elections to decide whether they will be retained.
match_headline: North Carolina Gerrymander Ruling Reflects Politicization of Judiciary Nationally

text: An article on Wednesday about a slowing of the post-pandemic manufacturing boom misidentified the name of one of the three major infrastructure bills passed over the last three years. It was the Inflation Reduction Act, not the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which is another name for the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.
match_headline: After Pandemic Rebound, U.S. Manufacturing Droops

text: An article on Wednesday about the recent mass shooting in rural Texas and the difficulty of responding to reports of gunfire in the state, where the ownership of weapons has become less regulated misidentified the victims of the shooting. There was no 16-year-old girl among the victims.
match_headline: In Texas, Aimless Gunfire Rattles Residents, but It’s Hard to Stop

text: An article on Sunday about the discovery and return of 16th- and 17th- century Greek-language manuscripts to a Greek monastery referred incompletely to the city where Archbishop Elpidophoros will travel to deliver manuscripts. A statement from the archdiocese said that the archbishop will travel to Constantinople, modern day Istanbul.
match_headline: Looted Monastery Manuscripts Rediscovered During Office Renovation

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about how JPMorgan Chase has positioned itself as a stable savior for many failing banks incorrectly described John Pierpont Morgan Sr. He was among the richest men of his era, not the richest.
match_headline: How JPMorgan Became Banking’s Regular Rescuer

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about ring stones discovered at an 1,800-year-old bathhouse in England misidentified one of the objects shown. It is a brooch, not a bracelet.

Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the Olympic long jump champion Ralph Boston referred incorrectly to the Modesto Relays, an annual track and field event in California. It continued to be held until 2009; it is not the case that it is “now known as the California Invitational Relays,” a separate event.
ref_headline: now known as the California Invitational Relays,
match_headline: Ralph Boston, Who Leaped 27 Feet and Landed in History, Dies at 83

text: An obituary on April 9 about Benjamin B. Ferencz, the last surviving prosecutor of the Nuremberg trials, referred incorrectly in part to the International Criminal Court, for which he had crusaded. It is not the case that “its reach does not include wars of aggression.”
ref_headline: its reach does not include wars of aggression.
match_headline: Benjamin B. Ferencz, Last Surviving Nuremberg Prosecutor, Dies at 103

text: An article about the arrest of a gunman who opened fire at a medical office in Atlanta misstated the address where the shooting took place. It was at 1110 West Peachtree Street Northwest, not 1100 West Peachtree Street Northwest.
match_headline: Suspect Caught After Killing 1 and Injuring 4 in Atlanta Shooting, Police Say

text: An article about the dismissal of Donald Trump’s lawsuit against The New York Times incorrectly described the judge’s ruling on a lawsuit brought by Mr. Trump. The judge dismissed the lawsuit against The New York Times and its reporters, but not against Mary Trump.
match_headline: Judge Dismisses Trump’s Lawsuit Against The New York Times

text: An article on Wednesday about Gordon Lightfoot’s essential songs misstated a lyric in Mr. Lightfoot’s “Black Day in July.” It is “the soul of Motor City is bared across the land,” not “the soul of Motor City is feared across the land.”
match_headline: Gordon Lightfoot’s 10 Essential Songs

text: An article on Thursday about a seventh-grade student who opened fire at a school in Serbia misstated the number of people killed after a wedding in Serbia in 2015. Six people were killed, not four.
match_headline: 7th Grader Opens Fire at School in Serbia, Killing 8 Children

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about the Japanese rice dish donburi misspells the name of a district in Osaka. It is Doyama, not Doyamo.
match_headline: The Particular Magic of Chicken, Egg and Rice

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about Kyrsten Sinema inaccurately describes her father’s removal from law practice. He was suspended indefinitely, not disbarred.
match_headline: Kyrsten Sinema’s Party of One

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about the redesign of a Brooklyn brownstone using Passive House principles misstates the surname of the owner of the Carroll Gardens brownstone, in one instance. He is Mr. Walker, not Mr. Martin.
match_headline: An Aggressive Passive Push for a Brooklyn Brownstone

text: An article on May 1 about a British spy who was executed in Iran referred imprecisely to Fordo, a clandestine uranium-enrichment facility deep in the mountains near Tehran. Western nations believed the facility was a nuclear weapons site when they learned of it; it was not confirmed to be such a site by the Iranian sources.
match_headline: Iranian Insider and British Spy: How a Double Life Ended on the Gallows

text: A subheading with an article on Monday about the arrest of 154 soccer fans of the Dutch team AZ Alkmaar for singing antisemitic chants on the way to a match referred incorrectly to the location of the game. The match against Ajax was played in a stadium on the outskirts of Amsterdam, not in a historically Jewish area. (Ajax has roots in a historically Jewish area of the city, but it no longer plays its matches there.)
match_headline: Dutch Police Arrest 154 Soccer Fans Over Antisemitic Chants

text: An article on Sunday about the singer Connie Converse misstated the location of Ms. Converse’s apartment in Harlem. The address, 605 West 138th Street, is several blocks away from Strivers’ Row, not one block away.
match_headline: Before Dylan, There Was Connie Converse. Then She Vanished.

text: An article on Sunday about the winning horse of the Kentucky Derby referred incorrectly to the jockey Javier Castellano’s first Kentucky Derby win. It came on his 16th try, not 15th.
match_headline: Mage Captures the Derby After an Agonizing Week at Churchill Downs

text: A column by Maureen Dowd on Sunday referred inaccurately to the origin of Chevron v. Natural Resources Defense Council. It arose from a challenge to a decision by Anne Gorsuch of the E.P.A. to lower power emission standards, not automobile emission standards. The column also referred imprecisely to a possible Supreme Court reversal of the ruling in relation to her stance on government. Overturning the ruling would support her lax stance on regulation; it would not vindicate her position in the Chevron case, which she won.
match_headline: Supremely Arrogant

text: An article on Saturday about an increased visibility of the northern lights to the south described incompletely the timing of the reversal of the earth’s magnetic field. It happens once every 10,000 to 50 million years or more, not once every 10,000 years.
match_headline: Get Ready to See More of the Northern Lights

text: An article on Saturday about a bill passed by the Florida Legislature banning gender-transition care for minors misstated the acronym of an advocacy group that has sued Florida over a prohibition on what experts call gender-affirming care for minors. It is GLAD, not GLAAD.
match_headline: Florida Legislature Passes Bill Banning Gender-Transition Care for Minors

text: An article on Tuesday about the victims of a mass shooting at a mall in Texas misstated the decade of Kyu Cho’s birth. It was the 1980s, not the early 1990s.
match_headline: Among the Victims in Texas Shooting: A Wounded 6-Year-Old Who Lost His Parents and Brother

text: An article on Tuesday about Phoenix’s plan to start clearing a large homeless encampments in the city incorrectly described a legal action that occurred in December. The city of Phoenix was ordered by a federal judge that month to not enforce bans on sleeping or camping outside, in response to a lawsuit from the American Civil Liberties Union. It reached a tentative settlement with the A.C.L.U. in March, not in December.
match_headline: Phoenix to Start Clearing Sprawling Downtown Homeless Encampment

text: An article on Monday about the task of fact-checking information from A.I. chatbots referred imprecisely to ChatGPT’s response to a question about a meeting between James Joyce and Vladimir Lenin. Its response about the men having met in a cafe may have been based on accounts of such a meeting, including a fictional one, but the possible meeting at the Cafe Odéon was not entirely fabricated by ChatGPT.
match_headline: When A.I. Chatbots Hallucinate

text: A Critic’s Notebook column on Tuesday about the Long Play classical music festival in Brooklyn misidentified a composition included in a presentation by the Momenta Quartet. The group led its set with Alvin Singleton’s second quartet, not his third.
match_headline: Long Play Rises to the Top of New York Classical Music Festivals

text: An obituary on Saturday about Laura Pels, a leading benefactor of nonprofit theater, misstated the location of the Laura Pels Theater when it opened in 1995. It was on Broadway at 45th Street, not on West 46th Street. (It is now located in the Harold and Miriam Steinberg Center for Theater on 46th Street and Sixth Avenue.)
match_headline: Laura Pels, Devoted Supporter of Nonprofit Theater, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Monday about the pianist Menahem Pressler, a founder of the Beaux Arts Trio, misstated when he made his debut with the Berlin Philharmonic. It was 2014, not 2013. It also misstated the name of the orchestra with which he performed when he was 16. It was the Palestine Symphony Orchestra; it did not become the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra until about a decade later.
match_headline: Menahem Pressler, Pianist Who Co-Founded Beaux Arts Trio, Dies at 99

text: An article on Wednesday about a new recommendation from health experts urging women to start regular mammograms at age 40 misidentified the age at which breast cancer rates decrease. More cases are diagnosed after age 55; the risk does not decline at that age.
match_headline: When Should Women Get Regular Mammograms? At 40, U.S. Panel Now Says.

text: A headline with an article on Friday about the coronavirus pandemic’s impact on New York City misstated a survey’s estimate of how many New Yorkers lost at least three loved ones to Covid-19 within the first 16 months of the virus’s arrival. As the article correctly noted, it is nearly 900,000, not one in four.
match_headline: 900,000 New Yorkers Lost at Least 3 Loved Ones to Covid

text: An article on Wednesday about how Wall Street will react to the government’s plans regarding the debt ceiling misidentified the day that President Biden met with Speaker Kevin McCarthy to discuss the debt ceiling. It was on Tuesday, not Thursday.
match_headline: How Wall Street Is Preparing for a Debt Ceiling Showdown

text: An article on Thursday about President Biden’s plan to host Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India on a state visit next month misstated the status of the case against the Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi. Mr. Gandhi is charged with defamation, but has not been jailed.
match_headline: Biden Will Host India’s Prime Minister for State Dinner

text: An article on Saturday about countries that have kept the British monarch as their head of state gave an incorrect time period for India’s independence from Britain. India became independent in 1947, during the reign of King George VI, not Queen Elizabeth II.
match_headline: Why So Many Nations in the King’s Realm Want to Say Goodbye

text: An article on Tuesday about large health insurers and companies that are buying up primary care practices misstated the relationship between Kaiser Permanente, the health plan consortium, and its physician groups. Kaiser Permanente said it had exclusive contracts with doctors’ groups, but did not own them.
match_headline: Corporate Giants Buy Up Primary Care Practices at Rapid Pace

text: An article this weekend on Page 14 about our critics’ picks of Tony-worthy theater performances misidentifies the actress chosen by one of our critics as a performer who should have been nominated for best actress for her performance in “Oresteia.” It was Anastasia Hille, not Lia Williams.
match_headline: Tony Awards 2023: Who Will Win (and Who Should)

text: An article on Tuesday about new hearing aids technology misstated Zina Jawadi’s age. She is 27, not 26.
match_headline: Hearing Aids Are Changing. Their Users Are, Too.

text: An article on May 7 on Page 30 about the novelist Annie Ernaux’s shocking work misspelled Ernaux’s maiden name. It is Duchesne, not Duschene.
match_headline: Annie Ernaux Has Broken Every Taboo of What Women Are Allowed to Write

text: An article on Page 49 about the artist Pablo Barba misidentifies the birds depicted in one of his paintings. They are sea gulls, not doves.
match_headline: Pablo Barba’s Carnival of the Grotesque

text: An article on Page 58 about sleep art misidentifies the museum personnel who asked the artist Heather Agyepong to leave the “Black Power Naps” installation at MoMA. It was the museum’s staff, not its security.
match_headline: When Sleep Becomes an Art Form

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the historian Ronald Steel, the author of a definitive biography of Walter Lippmann, referred incorrectly to Mr. Lippmann’s involvement with The New Republic. He was a founding editor, not the founder.
match_headline: Ronald Steel, Critic of American Cold War Policies, Dies at 92

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the opera singer Grace Bumbry misstated the call letters of a New York radio station. It is WQXR, not WXQR.
match_headline: Grace Bumbry, Barrier-Shattering Opera Diva, Is Dead at 86

text: An article on Friday about Turkey’s presidential election gave an incorrect title for Victor Orban of Hungary. He is the prime minister, not the president.
match_headline: What to Know About Turkey’s Presidential Runoff

text: An article last Sunday about Elizabeth Holmes, the former chief executive of Theranos, who has been convicted of fraud, described incorrectly Ms. Holmes’s description of an encounter she said she had during an emergency room visit with her child. She said it was a doctor who said, “I’m sure you’re a better person than she is,” not herself.
ref_headline: I’m sure you’re a better person than she is,
match_headline: Liz Holmes Wants You to Forget About Elizabeth

text: An article on April 30 about a new produc­tion of “Don Giovanni” at the Metropolitan Opera misstated the year of Peter Brook’s staging, with the baritone Peter Mattei. It was 1998, not 1984.
match_headline: The Pains and Privileges of Staging Mozart’s ‘Don Giovanni’

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Rachel Liverman and Jeremy Crane misstated the year of Ms. Liverman’s birth announce­ment. It was 1985, not 1988.
match_headline: For One Perpetual Bridesmaid, a Match ‘So Worth the Wait’

text: A review on April 23 of “Blanche,” by Nancy Schoenberger, misstated the age at which Tennessee Williams’s sister, Rose, was lobotomized. She was 33, not 26.
match_headline: It Takes More Than the Kindness of Strangers

text: An article on Monday about Jordan Neely and Daniel Penny’s lives before Mr. Neely’s killing on the subway misstated the date of Mr. Neely’s last encounter with subway outreach workers. They observed him on April 8, not the week after that.
match_headline: How Two Men’s Disparate Paths Crossed in a Killing on the F Train

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Sweden winning the 2023 Eurovision Song Contest misidentified the creators of the song “You’ll Never Walk Alone.” The original version was by Rodgers and Hammerstein for the musical “Carousel,” not by Gerry and the Pacemakers.
match_headline: Sweden Wins a Eurovision Song Contest That Showed Solidarity With Ukraine

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the first U.S. military base named in honor of a spouse misstated where Greg Moore was looking at family photo albums. It was Auburn, Ala., not Auburn, Ga.
match_headline: How a Military Base’s New Name Honors a Military Spouse and Mother

text: An article on Friday about Luis Arraez of the Miami Marlins misstated the number of games in the 1902 season and how that affected Nap Lajoie’s argument for a batting title. His teams played 136 games, not 154, meaning he did clear the 60 percent threshold that is sometimes used to establish a player’s qualification for the batting title.
match_headline: Baseball’s Most Unusual Hitter Finds His Own Way

text: An obituary on Thursday about John Roland, the longtime anchor of the 10 p.m. newscast on Fox’s flagship television station, misspelled the surname of a former news director there. He is Ted Kavanau, not Kavanagh.
match_headline: John Roland, Durable Anchor at Fox Flagship in N.Y., Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Brazilian singer Rita Lee referred incorrectly to her father, Charles Jones. While he was descended from Confederates, he was born in Brazil, not the United States.
match_headline: Rita Lee, Brazil’s Queen of Rock, Is Dead at 75

text: An obituary on May 8about the former Oakland Athletics pitching star Vida Blue misstated his status in the 1971 season. Although it was his first full season in the major leagues, it was technically not his rookie year. (He had pitched enough innings in brief stints with the Athletics in 1969 and 1970 to render him ineligible for rookie status.)
match_headline: Vida Blue, Pitching Sensation for Champion A’s Teams, Dies at 73

text: An article on Tuesday about the final report from the special counsel examining the origins of the Russia investigation misspelled the surname of a former Trump campaign aide. He is George Papadopoulos, not Papadopoulus.
match_headline: Durham Finds Fault With F.B.I. Over Russia Inquiry

text: An article on Tuesday about damage from Cyclone Mocha in Myanmar and Bangladesh referred incorrectly to Ko Myo Khaing, a rescue worker in Sittwe, Myanmar. He is a man, not a woman.
match_headline: Cyclone Mocha Leaves Thousands Homeless in Bangladesh and Myanmar

text: An article on Monday about television shows to watch this week misidentified the war in which Clint Eastwood’s character in “Gran Torino” served. It was the Korean War, not the Vietnam War.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Ghosts of Beirut’ and ‘The Secrets of Hillsong’

text: A column by Paul Krugman on Tuesday mis­identified the organization that conducted a study on stress. It was the American Psycholog­ical Association, not the American Psychiatric Association.
match_headline: Why Are Americans So Negative About the Economy?

text: An article on Wednesday about drug shortages in the United States referred incorrectly to Ryan Dwars’s children. He has a son and a daughter, not two daughters.
match_headline: Drug Shortages Near an All-Time High, Leading to Rationing

text: An article on May 11 about a naval guardsman who attacked a synagogue in Tunisia referred imprecisely to Tunisia. While the country is part of the larger Arab world, it is in North Africa, not in the Middle East.
match_headline: Naval Guardsman Attacks Synagogue in Tunisia, Killing 5

text: An article on Tuesday about the U.S. ambassador to Britain, Jane Hartley, and the Netflix series “The Diplomat” referred imprecisely to Ms. Hartley’s service as United States envoy to France and Britain. She is not the only American to hold the title of ambassador to both countries; David K.E. Bruce also did.
match_headline: At the Real Embassy, Netflix’s ‘Diplomat’ Draws a Diplomatic Response

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the former American League umpire Don Denkinger referred incorrectly to a 1978 game between the Yankees and the Boston Red Sox for which he was behind the plate. It was a tiebreaking game for the American League East championship, not the American League pennant.
match_headline: Don Denkinger, 86, Top Umpire Remembered for Botched Call, Dies

text: An obituary on April 26 about the singer, actor and activist Harry Belafonte misstated his father’s birthplace. He was born in Jamaica, not Martinique. The obituary, using information from a spokesman, also misstated the number of grandchildren who survive Mr. Belafonte and the year he and his second wife, Julie Robinson, divorced. He is survived by five grandchildren, not eight; and he and Ms. Robinson divorced in 2007, not 2004.
match_headline: Harry Belafonte, 96, Dies; Barrier-Breaking Singer, Actor and Activist

text: An article on Sunday about hundreds of people who starved to death in Kenya after following the teachings of a pastor preaching End Times mischaracterized the Book of Revelation. It is a book, not a chapter, of the New Testament.
match_headline: He Told Followers to Starve to Meet Jesus. Why Did So Many Do It?

text: An article on Wednesday about the former Fox News host Tucker Carlson and his role in bringing right-wing ideas to mainstream audiences described incorrectly the organization Check My Ads. It is a nonprofit watchdog, not a consultancy.
match_headline: Without Tucker Carlson, Far Right Loses a Foothold in the Mainstream

text: An article on Friday about Disney’s decision to cancel an office complex project in Orlando, Fla., misstated the name of a luxury hotel that Disney plans to shutter. It is the Galactic Starcruiser, not the Galactic Starship.
match_headline: Disney Pulls Plug on $1 Billion Development in Florida

text: An article on Friday about what to expect from the W.N.B.A. 2023 season misstated Courtney Vandersloot’s assist ranking. She is the W.N.B.A.’s active assists leader, not the career leader.
match_headline: What to Know About the 2023 W.N.B.A. Season

text: An article on Friday about the Frieze New York art fair misspelled the name of a gallery based in Buenos Aires and New York. It is Barro, not Basso.
match_headline: At Frieze New York 2023, One-Person Shows That Shine

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the rapper Killer Mike misspells the name of Killer Mike’s wife. She is Shana Render, not Shayna.
match_headline: Killer Mike, Atlanta’s Rap Journeyman, Is at the Peak of His Powers

text: An article on Page 28 this weekend about the effectiveness of therapy misstates the given name of a statistician and researcher. He is Gene V. Glass, not Eugene. The article also misstates the name of a program associated with Ohio University. It is the Psychotherapy & Interpersonal Process Lab, not the Psychology & Interpersonal Lab.
match_headline: Does Therapy Really Work? Let’s Unpack That.

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Stephanie Korbely and Rohit Kalkur misspelled the surname of the officiant. She is Liz Nor­ment, not Normant.
match_headline: A New York-Style Elopement Supporting an Important Cause

text: An article on May 7 about the wedding of Bethany Ryan and Andrew Jones described incorrectly the Australian national holiday Anzac Day. The holiday, which originally marked a pivotal 1915 landing by the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps in World War I, now commemorates all Australians and New Zealanders who have been killed in military operations — not all who have served in the military.
match_headline: A Week Before She Moved, They Matched on a Dating App

text: An article last Sunday about mothers living together to share household and child­-rearing responsi­bilities misstated the price of two­-bedroom units with a kitchenette at Commune, a new development for single-­parent households in the Paris suburbs. They will start at 1,190 euros a month, not 1,900.
match_headline: ‘Mommunes’: Mothers Are Living Single Together

text: An article on Thursday about the nomination of Hou Yu-ih as the presidential candidate for Taiwan’s Kuomintang, or Nationalist Party, misstated Mr. Hou’s age. He is 65, not 66.
match_headline: As China Looms Over Taiwan’s Presidential Race, the Opposition Picks a Moderate

text: An article on Friday about the married couple behind the Los Angeles restaurant Horses, and the accusations of violence they have made against each other, misstated the number of employees who were sexually harassed by Ken Friedman at his New York restaurant the Spotted Pig, according to the New York State attorney general. Not all 11 employees whom the attorney general cited in her investigation accused Mr. Friedman of sexual harassment; some accused him of retaliation or discrimination.
match_headline: Married Couple Behind the L.A. Restaurant Horses Trade Allegations of Violence

text: An article on Sunday about pedestrian safety hazards in the suburbs misstated the number of speed cameras in use in New York City. There are 750 zones that incorporate speed cameras, not 750 cameras. In addition, the revenue from speed camera fines misstated the time frame in which it was collected; $100 million was collected in the months after the cameras were turned on 24 hours a day, not after they were initially installed.
match_headline: Deadly Traffic in Suburbia Points to Deep-Seated Structural Problems

text: An article on Monday about the effect that negotiations over the debt limit are having on the U.S. economy referred incorrectly to borrowing costs in the United States. The United States typically has low borrowing costs, not the lowest in the world.
match_headline: Even Flirting With U.S. Default Takes Economic Toll

text: An article on Saturday about the baseball player Mookie Betts misstated Tigers center fielder Mickey Stanley’s history at the shortstop position. He played shortstop for the first time in his career in August 1968, in the regular season, not in the 1968 World Series.
match_headline: Why Is Mookie Betts Playing Shortstop? Because He Can.

text: An article on Saturday about Jim Brown’s N.F.L. career misstated the day Mr. Brown died. It was Thursday, not Friday.
match_headline: Jim Brown Piled Up Yards, but Never Wavered an Inch

text: An obituary on Saturday about the Rev. Timothy Keller of Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan misspelled the given name of a philosopher. He was Michel Foucault, not Michael.
match_headline: The Rev. Timothy Keller, Pioneering Manhattan Evangelist, Dies at 72

text: An obituary on May 8 about the former F.C.C. commissioner Newton N. Minow referred incorrectly to a satellite that went into orbit in 1962. It was America’s first active communications satellite, not America’s first communications satellite. (Echo 1, a passive communications satellite, had been sent into orbit in 1960.) The obituary also misstated how many television channels most Americans could receive by the end of the 1960s. While the number differed from market to market, it was less than “scores” everywhere.
match_headline: Newton N. Minow, 97, Dies; F.C.C. Chief Deemed TV a ‘Vast Wasteland’

text: An obituary on May 10 about the former Minnesota Vikings quarterback Joe Kapp included outdated and incomplete information about his survivors. They do not include his brother, Larry, or his sister Joanie Ebberson, both of whom died before him. And in addition to those named, he is survived by six grandchildren. In addition, a picture caption with the obituary, using information from Getty Images, misstated when the photo of Kapp in action against the Los Angeles Rams was taken. It was in a regular-season game on Dec. 7, 1969 — not the playoff game the same teams played a few weeks later.
match_headline: Joe Kapp, Quarterback Who Led Vikings to Super Bowl IV, Dies at 85

text: An article on Saturday about Ron DeSantis’s private air travel characterized his career incorrectly. He has worked in public service nearly his entire career, but not his entire career.
match_headline: Air DeSantis: The Private Jets and Secret Donors Flying Him Around

text: An article on Tuesday about a deal between Arizona, California and Nevada to keep the Colorado River from going dry misspelled the surname of the director of Arizona’s Department of Water Resources. He is Tom Buschatzke, not Buschaztke.
match_headline: A Breakthrough Deal to Keep the Colorado River From Going Dry, for Now

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption on Tuesday with an article about tensions in the community of Uvalde, Texas, a year after a school shooting there misidentified Berlinda Arreola, who lost her step-granddaughter Amerie Jo Garza in the shooting. She was shown standing at the left, not in the center.
match_headline: A Year After a School Shooting, Divisions Run Through Uvalde

text: An article on Tuesday about the challenges Tanzania is facing in its efforts to vaccinate young girls against human papillomavirus used an outdated title for Dr. Mary Rose Giattas. She is the technical director for reproductive cancer in Tanzania for the nonprofit health care organization Jhpiego, not the medical director.
match_headline: Money, Sex and Rumors: Tanzania Faces Challenges to Protect Girls From HPV

text: An article on Wednesday about takeaways from New York’s art auction week misstated the date of a Noah Davis painting. It was created in 2010, not 2020. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: 5 Takeaways From Auction Week

text: An obituary on Saturday about the football star, actor and civil rights activist Jim Brown referred incorrectly to the character Raquel Welch played in the 1969 movie “100 Rifles,” in which she and Brown had a sex scene together. The character was Native American, not white.
match_headline: Jim Brown, Football Great and Civil Rights Champion, Dies at 87

text: An article on Thursday about the ongoing political divide over gun policies misstated the number of Republicans who broke with their party to vote for the federal gun bill called the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act. Fifteen Republican senators voted for the bill, not 14.
match_headline: In Capitols and Courthouses, No End to National Divide Over Gun Policy

text: An article on Friday about the capture of a fugitive in Rwanda misstated the name of a branch of the Rwandan military that has been disbanded. It was the Armed Forces of Rwanda, not the Rwanda Defense Force.
match_headline: On the Run for Decades, a Fugitive of Rwanda’s Genocide Is Finally Caught

text: An article on Friday about films at Cannes Film Festival that focus on female desire misstated the relationship at the center of “May December.” It is between an older woman and an underage boy, not a teacher and pupil. The article also misidentified the award given to “The Man Without a Past” in 2002. It was the Grand Jury Prize not the Palme d’Or.
match_headline: At a Particularly Strong Cannes Film Festival, Women’s Desires Pull Focus

text: An article on Page 30 about the worldwide housing crisis misstates the year the euro was introduced in Austria. It was 2002, not 1999.
match_headline: Lessons From a Renters’ Utopia

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about Tina Turner misstated the current number of productions of “Tina: The Tina Turner Musical.” In addition to the one touring the United States and the one in London, there are productions in Stuttgart, Germany, and Sydney, Australia.
match_headline: Tina Turner, Magnetic Singer of Explosive Power, Is Dead at 83

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about Canada’s gift of the Hudson’s Bay department store building to a group of First Nations referred incorrectly to the estimated cost of bringing the building up to code. The cost, 111 million Canadian dollars, is equivalent to $82 million, not $8 million.
match_headline: For the Indigenous, Was This Building a Gesture of Reconciliation? Or an Empty Gift?

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the top women’s tennis players misidentified Elena Rybakina’s opponent on Tuesday at the French Open. It is Brenda Fruhvirtova, not Linda Fruhvirtova (who is her sister).
match_headline: Women’s Tennis Suddenly Has a Big(ish) Three

text: An article on May 22 about the Nigerian artist Njideka Akunyili Crosby misidentified the website for David Zwirner gallery. It is davidzwirner.com, not zwirner.com.
match_headline: Njideka Akunyili Crosby Wants to Take it Slow, Despite Her Rapid Rise

text: A subheading with an article on Sunday about the British comedian James Acaster’s new focus on music and the release of his debut album misstated what he described as his first obsession. As the article correctly noted, it was music, not stand-up comedy.
match_headline: James Acaster Finds His Way Back to Music

text: An obituary on Monday about Stanley Engerman, a scholar of American slavery, referred incorrectly to Kenneth B. Clark, who criticized a book by Professor Engerman and his co-author, Robert W. Fogel, as portraying slavery “as a benign form of oppression.” He was a social psychologist, not a sociologist.
ref_headline: as a benign form of oppression.
match_headline: Stanley Engerman, Revisionist Scholar of Slavery, Dies at 87

text: An article on Tuesday about a teen’s killing in North Dakota that became a right-wing talking point misstated the party registration of the parents of Shannon Brandt. Mr. Brandt’s parents are not registered with a political party. North Dakota does not have statewide voter registration. A picture caption with the article referred imprecisely to an argument between Mr. Brandt and Cayler Ellingson. While the two men were at Buck’s n Doe’s Bar & Grill before Mr. Ellingson’s death, it is not clear where the argument happened.
match_headline: A Small Town’s Tragedy, Distorted by Trump’s Megaphone

text: An article on Wednesday about rising political tensions in Germany over a new climate bill misspelled the name of the secretary general of the Free Democrats. He is Bijan Djir-Sarai, not Bijan Sjir-Sarai.
match_headline: Ugly Fight Over Climate Bill Exposes Cracks in German Coalition

text: An article on Wednesday about the Boston Celtics misstated the timing of the debut of the Celtics player Robert Williams III following a knee injury. His first game was in December, not in April.
match_headline: Celtics Hit Another Dead End, With No Clear Path Forward This Time

text: An article on Tuesday about television shows similar to “Succession” misidentified the creator of “The Thick of It.” He is Armando Iannucci, not Jesse Armstrong.
match_headline: Miss ‘Succession’ Already? Here’s What to Watch Next

text: An article on Tuesday about the series finale of “Succession” misidentified the vehicle Tom and Shiv were in. It was a Maybach, not an Escalade.
match_headline: ‘Succession’ Is Over. Why Did We Care?

text: An article on Sunday about missteps in the Fox News defamation suit referred imprecisely to the groups involved in a post-mortem discussion of the defamation case between Fox News and Dominion. The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression posted a video of the discussion on its website; it did not host the event.
match_headline: Missteps and Miscalculations: Inside Fox’s Legal and Business Debacle

text: An article on Friday about what to watch on television this weekend described incorrectly the new season of “Painting With John.” It is the third season of the show, but it has not been determined that it will be the final season.
match_headline: How Much Watching Time Do You Have This Weekend?

text: A picture caption with a review on May 14 about “Liliana’s Invin­cible Summer,” by Cristina Rivera Garza, misidentified the woman shown in the photograph. She is Liliana Rivera Garza, the author’s sister, not the author herself.
match_headline: A Sister’s Murder and the Language of Violence

text: An article on Friday about the only Black participant in the first national spelling bee competition referred incorrectly to Zaila Avant-garde. She was the first Black American to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee, not the first Black student to do so. (Jody-Anne Maxwell of Jamaica won the bee in 1998.)
match_headline: A Black Girl Won the 1908 Spelling Bee. Her Family Is Searching for Her Medal.

text: An article on Monday about Chuck Todd’s exit from “Meet the Press” misstated Mr. Todd’s age. He is 51, not 50.
match_headline: Chuck Todd to Leave ‘Meet the Press’

text: An obituary on May 27 about the actor and singer Ed Ames misstated the territory associated with the American pioneer Daniel Boone, whose companion Mr. Ames portrayed on a television series. It was the Kentucky frontier, not the Tennessee frontier.
match_headline: Ed Ames, Singing Star Who Became a Familiar Face on TV, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on May 22 about the architect and environmental health advocate Robin Guenther referred incorrectly to PVC, or polyvinyl chloride. Though its primary component, vinyl chloride, is a known carcinogen, PVC itself is not classified as one.
match_headline: Robin Guenther, Architect of Healthy Hospitals, Dies at 68

text: An obituary on Monday about the human rights lawyer and World Court judge Thomas Buergenthal misidentified the concentration camp where his father was killed. It was Buchenwald, not Flossenbürg.
match_headline: Thomas Buergenthal, Holocaust Survivor and Judge, Dies at 89

text: An article on Monday about Max Verstappen’s win at the Spanish Grand Prix misidentified the road George Russell used at the start of the race that allowed him to gain several places. It was the run-off area on Turn 1, not the pit lane.
match_headline: An Unstoppable Verstappen Wins Again

text: An obituary on Saturday about the former Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Harvey Pitt misstated the name of a pop group that had many hits in the 1960s. They are Herman’s Hermits, not Hermit’s Hermits. The earlier version also referred incorrectly to a remark Senator Phil Gramm made about Mr. Pitt. He said, “I forget what the old song of the 1960s was, but Harvey Pitt has seen it from both sides.” He did not specify that the song in question was by Herman’s Hermits or anyone else.
ref_headline: I forget what the old song of the 1960s was, but Harvey Pitt has seen it from both sides.
match_headline: Harvey Pitt, S.E.C. Chair Who Resigned Amid Scandals, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on Sunday about the composer Kaija Saariaho referred incorrectly to Pirkko Moisala, the author of a biography of Ms. Saariaho. She is a woman.
match_headline: Kaija Saariaho, 70, Pathbreaking Composer of Singular Colors, Is Dead

text: An article on Thursday about prosecutors reopening cases of police killings in California omitted attribution for the descriptions of the circumstances surrounding the killings of Agustin Gonsalez and Andrew Moppin-Buckskin. They were based on police accounts and witness interviews conducted by prosecutors.
match_headline: Liberal Prosecutors Are Revisiting Police Killings but Charging Few Officers So Far

text: An obituary on Thursday about the organic-food advocate Ronnie Cummins misstated the name of a city in Minnesota where he once directed a food co-op. It is Burnsville, not Burnsdale.
match_headline: Ronnie Cummins, Scourge of Genetically Modified Food, Dies at 76

text: An article on Friday about evidence found in phone messages that led to the downfall of Milo Djukanovic, the former president of Montenegro, misspelled the family name of a defense attorney. He is Mr. Begovic not Mr. Becovic.
match_headline: How a Cracked Phone App Upended a Crime-Ridden Balkan State

text: An article on Friday about the Supreme Court’s ruling in a voting rights case from Alabama misstated the year that the Supreme Court decided Thornburg v. Gingles, a pivotal case in defining the scope of the Voting Rights Act. It was decided in 1986, not 1985.
match_headline: Supreme Court Gives the Voting Rights Act a Tenuous New Lease on Life

text: An article on Friday about Tesla’s deal with General Motors to share Tesla charging technology misidentified the connectors available at Electrify America’s charging stations. Electrify America’s chargers are compatible with the Combined Charging System plug; they cannot be used to charge Teslas without an adapter.
match_headline: Tesla Will Open Its Charging Network to G.M.’s Electric Vehicles

text: An article on Tuesday about underappreciated birding spots in New York misstated the name of a bridge in a photo caption. It is the Bronx-Whitestone Bridge, not the Throgs Neck Bridge.
match_headline: Seven Underappreciated Birding Spots in New York

text: An obituary on Thursday about the comedian Pat Cooper incorrectly included a name on the list of his survivors. His sister Grace Ferrara died in April.
match_headline: Pat Cooper, Comedian of Outrage, Is Dead at 93

text: An article last Sunday about the actress Greta Lee misstated when the second season of “Russian Doll” ended. It was last year, not in April.
match_headline: How to Be a Star by Not Giving Your All

text: An article on Dec. 26, 1991, about Paul and Isabelle Duchesnay, the brother-sister ice dancing pair, misspelled the reporter’s surname. He is Christopher Clarey, not Clary. This correction was delayed for 32 years, because it was only recently brought to our attention (by the reporter).
An article last Sunday about the newly deconsecrated Church of Our Lady of Guadalupe misspelled the name of a Spanish ship that docked nearby. It is El Covadonga, not El Cobadonga.
match_headline: Little Spain Is All but Gone. Will Our Lady of Guadalupe Be Next?

text: An article last Sunday about the most expensive sales in New York City incorrectly attributed ownership of Fox News to News Corp. They are separate entities.
match_headline: Rupert Murdoch Closes on Another Bachelor Pad, Paying Above List Price

text: An article last Sunday about the sale of an apartment once used by the architect Rafael Viñoly misstated its location. The address, 137 West Broadway, is between Duane and Thomas Streets, not Liberty and Cedar Streets.
match_headline: A TriBeCa Loft Where Rafael Viñoly Worked, and Played the Piano

text: An article on Saturday about cutbacks to Canada’s fire prevention resources misidentified the title that Paul Martin held when he called for budget cuts in the late 1990s. He was the finance minister of Canada at the time, not its prime minister.
match_headline: Canada’s Ability to Prevent Forest Fires Lags Behind the Need

text: Because of a calculation error by the study’s authors, an article on Saturday about the availability of energy tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act misstated findings by Princeton and Dartmouth researchers about the act’s employment impact. The researchers found that the act would result in 1.6 million additional jobs — not four million — in wind and solar energy by 2035. That would be more than three times the current employment base, not more than eight times.
match_headline: Energy Tax Credits, Meant to Help U.S. Suppliers, May Be Hard to Get

text: An article on Friday about the careers of the horse trainers Bob Baffert and Todd Pletcher misstated part of the name of a Belmont entrant. He is Tapit Trice, not Thrice.
match_headline: Two Complicated Princes of the Sport of Kings

text: An article on Monday about China’s coast guard ships misstated the capabilities of some large Chinese coast guard ships that are former navy corvettes. Most of them do not have anti-ship missiles; photos show they have been replaced with water cannons.
match_headline: China Creates a Coast Guard Like No Other, Seeking Supremacy in Asian Seas

text: An article on Tuesday about the delay of a ruling to ban a popular protest song in Hong Kong misstated George Chen’s title at the Asia Group. He is managing director, not managing editor.
match_headline: Judge Delays Decision on Hong Kong’s Request to Ban Protest Song Online

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the dehorning of black rhinos misidentified a group of rhinos in Kenya. The animals pictured were white rhinos, not black rhinos.
match_headline: Rhinos’ Horns Were Cut to Thwart Poachers. After, They Didn’t Go Out Much.

text: An article on Tuesday about a California family that found a million pennies in a crawl space referred incorrectly to the composition of the penny. It was made of zinc-coated steel for one year, in 1943, not from 1943 to 1982.
match_headline: They Found a Million Pennies. Now They Need Someone to Take Them.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the Denver Nuggets’ first chance at winning a championship in 47 years misstated the score of Game 1 of the N.B.A. finals. The Nuggets won, 104-93, not 103-94.
match_headline: The Nuggets Almost Won a Title in 1976. Denver Can Make History Now.

text: A subheading with an article on Tuesday about the David Byrne musical “Here Lies Love” misstated the type of music being used in the show. The Broadway production will use both recorded music and live musicians, not just a live band.
match_headline: How to Watch the Tony Awards

text: An article on Sunday about concerns regarding Trump supporters’ violent rhetoric described incorrectly The Gateway Pundit’s coverage of the F.B.I.’s search of Mar-a-Lago. The outlet did not publish an article saying “This. Means. War” in response to the search. The phrase was posted in reference to a Gateway Pundit article about the search on a social media feed associated with Stephen K. Bannon, Mr. Trump’s onetime adviser, used those words to comment on the article.
match_headline: Trump Supporters’ Violent Rhetoric in His Defense Disturbs Experts

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about American companies that are paying for enriched uranium from Russia misstated the status of an enriched uranium plant in Ohio. The plant is U.S.-owned, not European-owned, and is currently idle.
match_headline: The U.S. Is Paying Billions to Russia’s Nuclear Agency. Here’s Why.

text: An article on Thursday about a large boat carrying migrants that sank near Greece misidentified the location of the sinking. It was in the Mediterranean Sea, not the Aegean.
match_headline: At Least 79 Die as Boat Carrying Migrants Sinks Near Greece

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about lawmakers’ concerns over the merger between the PGA Tour and the LIV Golf series misidentified the affiliation of the golfer Jon Rahm. Mr. Rahm remained playing on the PGA Tour and did not join LIV Golf.
match_headline: Senate Opens Inquiry Into PGA Tour Deal with Saudi-Funded LIV Golf

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about opera in San Francisco misstated the surname of a soprano. She is Camilla Nylund, not Nyland.
match_headline: In San Francisco, a Week of Destination Opera

text: An article on Friday about the Petronio Residency Center, an unstructured retreat for dance artists, misidentified an artist as among more than 25 awarded a residency at the center. Liz Gerring had a subsidized residency, also on offer at the center, not a full residency.
match_headline: The Petronio Residency Center to Close After Six-Year Run

text: An article this weekend on Page 7 about raunchy comedies with a feminist perspective misidentifies the director of “Blockers.” She is Kay Cannon, not Kay Unger. The article also misspells the name of an actress in “Joy Ride.” She is Teresa Hsiao, not Teresa Hsaio.
match_headline: Bringing Sexy Back to the Movies, With a 2023 Twist

text: An article on June 11 about Merlin Sheldrake, the mycologist, misstated his age. He is 35, not 36.
match_headline: The Man Who Turned the World on to the Genius of Fungi

text: An obituary on Thursday about the biologist Roger Payne misspelled the given name of his first wife and fellow researcher. She is Katharine Boynton Payne, not Katherine.
match_headline: Roger Payne, Biologist Who Heard Whales Singing, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Thursday about the editor Robert Gottlieb referred incorrectly to his professional relationship with the author Salman Rushdie. While he edited Mr. Rushdie’s novels “Shame” and “Midnight’s Children,” he did not edit his novel “The Satanic Verses.”
match_headline: Robert Gottlieb, Eminent Editor From le Carré to Clinton, Dies at 92

text: An article on May 7 about Serbia misstated Slobodan Milosevic’s title in 1990. He was the president of Serbia, not the president of Yugoslavia.
match_headline: The President, the Soccer Hooligans and an Underworld ‘House of Horrors’

text: A picture caption with an article on June 13 about NATO members conducting major air exercises in Germany as a signal of allied strength against Russia’s invasion of Ukraine misidentified a fighter jet. The jet shown is a Saab Gripen, not a Eurofighter Typhoon.
match_headline: NATO Members Use a Major Air Exercise to Send a Message to Russia

text: An article on Sunday about the Taliban’s reliance on the WhatsApp messaging platform misstated the parent company of WhatsApp. It is Meta, not Facebook.
match_headline: The Taliban Government Runs on WhatsApp. There’s Just One Problem.

text: An article on Monday about Ukraine’s capture of Piatykhatky in the Zaporizhzhia region referred incorrectly to the advance. It is among the first villages recaptured in the region since the start of its counteroffensive, not the first.
match_headline: Ukraine Appears to Make a Small Gain in the South as Counteroffensive Continues

text: An article on Saturday about Art Basel and conditions in the art market incorrectly described Art Basel’s Feature section. It has been presented at previous fairs; it is not new.
match_headline: Mixed Business at an Anxious Art Basel

text: An article on Friday about Noah Horowitz, the new chief of Art Basel, misstated the nature of the relationship between Art Basel and the art fairs S.E.A. Focus and Art Week Tokyo. Art Basel offered consulting services to those organizations; it did not invest in them.
match_headline: Art Basel’s New Chief Is All About the Brand

text: An article on Saturday about cutbacks at the Center Theater Group in Los Angeles misstated the year that Michael Ritchie stepped down as the Center Theater Group’s artistic director. He retired in December 2021, not 2022.
match_headline: L.A.’s Center Theater Group Lays Off Staff and Halts Work on One Stage

text: An obituary on June 9 about the religious broadcaster Pat Robertson referred incorrectly to his parents. They were distant cousins, not first cousins.
match_headline: Pat Robertson, Who Gave Christian Conservatives Clout, Is Dead at 93

text: An obituary on June 7 about the actor Peter Simonischek misstated the name of the character he played in the movie “Toni Erdmann.” It is Winfried, not Winifried.
match_headline: Peter Simonischek, Beloved Austrian Actor, Is Dead at 76

text: An obituary on June 2 about the sociologist Amitai Etzioni referred incorrectly to the Moral Majority. It was founded in 1979 and dissolved in 1989; it did not exist in the 1950s.
match_headline: Amitai Etzioni, 94, Dies; Envisioned a Society Built on the Common Good

text: An article on Sunday about Ron DeSantis’s age compared with that of other presidential candidates misstated the number of voters between the ages of 35 and 49 who had a favorable view of Mr. DeSantis, according to a Quinnipiac University poll. It was about two in five, not about one in four.
match_headline: Ron DeSantis Is Young, Has Little Kids and Wants America to Know It

text: An article on Saturday about the first Muslim woman to be seated as a federal judge in the United States misstated how the confirmations of Judge Dale Ho and Judge Nusrat Choudhury affected the ranks of Asian Americans on the federal bench. Their confirmations brought to 21 the number of Asian American federal judges confirmed under President Biden; it is not the total number of Asian American federal judges.
match_headline: First Muslim Woman to Be Federal Judge Confirmed by Senate

text: An article on Tuesday about the N.B.A. player Chris Paul misstated the timing of a college basketball game in 2005 in which Mr. Paul, playing for Wake Forest, punched North Carolina State’s Julius Hodge. It happened in the teams’ final game of the regular season, not in the Atlantic Coast Conference tournament.
match_headline: Chris Paul Found Out About the Suns’ Trade From His Son

text: An obituary on Monday about the Rev. C. Welton Gaddy, a former leader of the Interfaith Alliance, misstated part of the name of the railroad for which his father worked. It was the Louisville & Nashville Railroad, not Louisiana.
match_headline: The Rev. C. Welton Gaddy, Defender of Church-State Divide, Dies at 81

text: An obituary on Friday about the wide receiver Homer Jones misstated the number of years since he performed what has been widely credited as the original end-zone “spike.” It is 58, not 68. (As the obituary correctly states, this happened in 1965.)
match_headline: Homer Jones Dies at 82; Wide Receiver Specialized in Bombs and Spikes

text: An obituary on June 4 about the lyricist Cynthia Weil referred imprecisely to her daughter, Jenn Mann. Although she is a psychotherapist and has a doctorate in psychology, she is not a practicing psychologist.
match_headline: Cynthia Weil, Who Put Words to That ‘Lovin’ Feeling,’ Dies at 82

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about Rome’s bid for the Expo 2030 world’s fair misstated the given name of the designer of the Sail complex. As the article correctly noted, he is Santiago Calatrava, not Francisco Calatrava.
match_headline: Eye on Expo 2030, Rome Dreams of Reinvigoration

text: A map with an article on Friday about the Ukrainian counteroffensive misidentified a village that Ukraine said its forces had recaptured. It is Blahodatne to the south of Velyka Novosilka, not the settlement of the same name to its east.
match_headline: Retaking Villages Leaves Ukrainian Troops Exposed and Diving for Cover

text: An obituary on Thursday about Haim Roet, who created a memorial project that involves annually reading the names of Holocaust victims in public around the world, misstated the surname of one of his relatives who died in the Holocaust. He was Abraham Prince, not Abraham Roet.
match_headline: Haim Roet, Who Kept Holocaust Victims’ Names Alive, Dies at 90

text: An article on Friday about President Biden’s attempt to bolster ties with Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India incorrectly characterized Mr. Modi’s joint news conference with Mr. Biden. It was a rare instance of Mr. Modi taking questions from reporters at a news conference during his nine years leading India, but not the first time.
match_headline: Biden Seeks to Bolster Ties With Modi While Soft-Pedaling Differences

text: An article on Wednesday about Ukrainian prisoners of war referred imprecisely to the access that Russia gives the International Committee of the Red Cross to prisoners of war. While Russia does not meet its full obligations under international conventions of war, it has allowed some limited access to prisoners.
match_headline: ‘They Expected Me to Die on My Own’: Life as a Ukrainian P.O.W.

text: An article on June 3 about a settlement involving three major chemical companies and claims that they contaminated drinking water misstated the levels of PFAS chemicals that the Environmental Protection Agency considers safe in drinking water. They are four parts per trillion of perfluorooctanoic acid, not 0.004 parts per trillion, and four parts per trillion of perfluorooctanesulfonic acid, not 0.02 parts per trillion.
match_headline: Three ‘Forever Chemicals’ Makers Settle Public Water Lawsuits

text: An article on Thursday about a plea of not guilty by the Air National Guardsman accused of posting secret documents online misstated which of Jack Teixeira’s lawyers was waiting for a security clearance needed to review sensitive documents. It was not Michael Bachrach, but his co-counsel.
match_headline: Airman Pleads Not Guilty to Federal Charges in Leaks Case

text: An article on Friday about a Wyoming judge’s temporary blocking of a bill banning abortion pills misstated Gov. Mark Gordon of Wyoming’s role. He did not sign the bill the Wyoming Legislature passed in March establishing a near-total ban on abortion in the state. He allowed it to go into effect without his signature.
match_headline: Wyoming Judge Temporarily Blocks State’s Ban on Abortion Pills

text: An article on Thursday about a cut in property taxes for older New Jersey homeowners misstated how much money New Jersey leaders plan to set aside to pay for the first year of a property tax cut. It is $600 million over the next three years, not $600,000.
match_headline: Property Taxes to Be Cut in Half for Most Older N.J. Homeowners

text: An article on Friday about 3M’s settlement of “forever chemicals” lawsuits misstated the amount that Brunswick County, N.C., spent after the discovery of PFAS contamination in a watershed. It was nearly $100 million, not nearly $1 billion.
match_headline: 3M Reaches $10.3 Billion Settlement in ‘Forever Chemicals’ Suits

text: An article on Friday about senior executive changes at TCM misspelled the surname of one of the senior executives who lost her job. She is Pola Changnon, not Chagnon.
match_headline: Plot Twist at Turner Classic Movies Upsets Film Fans

text: An article on Page 6 this weekend about an immersive “The Great Gatsby” theatrical performance misstates how the character Jay Gatsby comes to an end. He is found dead in a pool, where he has been shot, not drowned.
match_headline: Can’t Repeat the Past? An Immersive ‘Great Gatsby’ Thinks You Can.

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about Dolby Atmos audio format misstates one of the streaming services that features Atmos music. It is QQ Music, not Qobuz.
match_headline: Dolby Atmos Wants You to Listen Up. (And Down. And Sideways.)

text: An article on Page 9 this weekend about the best gear for a walking trip provides the incorrect model number for a shoe recommended for city walking. It is the Arc’teryx Norvan LD3 GTX, not the LV3 GTX.
match_headline: The Gear You Need to Hit the Trail

text: An article on June 18 about MrBeast, the YouTube megastar, misstated Vincent Miller’s academic affiliation. He teaches sociology and cultural studies — not media studies — at the University of Kent in England.
match_headline: How MrBeast Became the Willy Wonka of YouTube

text: A picture on the cover with an article last Sunday about the popularity of Baggu totes and other accessories among Gen Z con­sumers was published in error. It does not show a bag from Baggu.

An article on Sunday about a man who was charged with murder in the fentanyl overdose of his friend misstated the circumstances of a case in Tennessee. A 17-year-old girl was charged after she shared fentanyl with two friends, not three. Both friends died.
match_headline: He Tried to Save a Friend. They Charged Him With Murder.

text: An article on Friday about documents released about the derailment of a freight train in Ohio misstated the location of a Norfolk Southern employee who was monitoring alerts about the railroad’s trains. He was working from home, not at a monitoring center.
match_headline: N.T.S.B. Convenes Hearing in East Palestine to Examine Train Derailment

text: An article on Tuesday about restoring ecological health to Ireland misstated the name of the organization that Padraic Fogarty works for. It is the Irish Wildlife Trust, not Wildlife Ireland. The article also misstated the status of the lynx in Scotland. While reintroducing the animal into the wild has been widely discussed, it has not yet happened.
match_headline: Call of the Rewild: Restoring Ecological Health to the Emerald Isle

text: An article on Tuesday about an increase in deforestation in tropical forests misspelled the given name of a senior fellow at the World Resources Institute’s forest program. She is Frances Seymour, not Francis.
match_headline: Despite Global Pledges, Tree Loss Is Up Sharply in Tropical Forests

text: An article on Tuesday about an Uber passenger who killed her Uber driver misspelled the surname of the Uber passenger. She is Phoebe Copas, not Capos.
match_headline: Uber Rider Who Killed Driver Said She Thought She Was Being Kidnapped

text: An article on Monday about a derailed train, based on information from Montana Rail Link, misstated the name of the chemical that was being carried in two cars of the train that derailed in Montana. It is sodium hydrosulfide, not sodium hydro sulfate.
match_headline: Montana Derailment Sends 10 Freight Cars Into the Yellowstone River

text: An article on Monday about Amen and Ausar Thompson referred incorrectly to the Overtime Elite season. The Thompson twins’ team, City Reapers, won the league title on March 7, not May 6. On that day, there were 107 days to go before the N.B.A. draft, not 47.
match_headline: Thompson Twins Are Ready for the N.B.A., but Not to Split Up

text: An obituary on Monday about the economist Harry M. Markowitz referred incorrectly to Robert Arnott. He is the chairman of Research Affiliates, not the chief executive of Research Associates.
match_headline: Harry Markowitz, Nobel-Winning Pioneer of Modern Portfolio Theory, Dies at 95

text: An article on Wednesday about Republican criticism of the Justice Department’s investigation of Hunter Biden referred incorrectly to a letter that Representative Jim Jordan sent to David C. Weiss. It did not address his use of the term “ultimate authority.” It also misstated the day the letter was sent. It was sent last week, not on Monday.
match_headline: Competing Accounts of Justice Dept.’s Handling of Hunter Biden Case

text: An article on Monday about Canada’s child care program incorrectly described Nunavut, Canada. It is a territory, not a province.
