match_headline: Day Care for Less Than $10: How Canada Is Easing the Burden for Parents

text: An article on Saturday about the Shed music hall in Manhattan misidentified the location of the first Sonic Sphere in France. It was in Château du Feÿ, not Féy.
match_headline: Enter the 50-Ton Concert Hall That Hangs Like a Disco Ball

text: An article on Wednesday about the documentary “Casa Susanna” misstated Isabelle Bonnet’s profession. She is a historian of photography, not a photographer.
match_headline: Revisiting a Midcentury Haven for Cross-Dressing Men

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about gravitational waves misstated when the waves were discovered. They were first detected in 2015, not 2016. Additionally, the article misstated the manner in which the waves were first detected. They were observed in data, not as audible chirps.
match_headline: The Cosmos Is Thrumming With Gravitational Waves, Astronomers Find

text: An article on Thursday about a grand jury decision not to indict a man who stabbed a subway passenger misstated the reasons that a manslaughter case against Jordan Williams ended. A grand jury in Brooklyn voted not to indict Mr. Williams. The district attorney did not drop charges.
match_headline: Grand Jury Declines to Indict Man in Fatal Subway Stabbing

text: An article on Thursday about the first time in a normal professional baseball season a team with a losing record could make the playoffs misstated the nickname of the N.B.A. team based in Philadelphia in the 1952-53 season. It was the Warriors, not the 76ers.
match_headline: Losing Their Way to the Playoffs

text: An obituary on June 17 about Daniel Ellsberg, the military analyst who leaked the Pentagon Papers, referred incorrectly to the White House unit known as the plumbers, which was involved in a burglary at the office of Mr. Ellsberg’s psychiatrist in 1971. Although two former members of that unit, E. Howard Hunt and G. Gordon Liddy, organized the burglary at the Watergate Hotel the next year, the plumbers did not carry it out; the unit had been disbanded by then.
match_headline: Daniel Ellsberg, Who Leaked the Pentagon Papers, Is Dead at 92

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the businessman and philanthropist James Crown, using information from a spokesman for his family, misidentified the high school Mr. Crown attended and misstated the year he graduated. It was New Trier East High School in Winnetka, Ill., not New Trier West High School in Northfield, Ill.; and he graduated in 1971, not 1972. The obituary also referred imprecisely to the role of Lester Crown, Mr. Crown’s father, in the purchase of minority interests in the Chicago Bulls and the New York Yankees. The Crown family, not Lester Crown, became a minority owner of both teams.
match_headline: James Crown, Chicago Businessman and Avid Philanthropist, Dies at 70

text: An article on Page 34 this weekend about the evangelical Marcos Witt incorrectly describes the company Gloo. It is a technology platform for ministry leaders, not a ministry-management app.
match_headline: The Christian Pop Star Bringing Latino Evangelicals to the Pews

text: An article last Sunday about financial planning by L.G.B.T.Q. people mis­stated the year that Yassin Adams arrived in the United States from Egypt. It was 2012, not 2015. The article also misstated the amount he pays for hormone care every three months. It is $500, not $5,000.
match_headline: What Financial Planning Looks Like for L.G.B.T.Q. People

text: An article on Page 40 this weekend about pregnant women on Suboxone misstates the rate at which a substance-exposed baby was born in 2013. It was every 19 minutes, not seconds.
match_headline: The Sports to Watch This Weekend

text: An article on Sunday about a prosecutor’s defense of the integrity of the Hunter Biden investigation incorrectly described what Attorney General Merrick B. Garland had said regarding special powers for David C. Weiss, the U.S. attorney in Delaware. Mr. Garland said that Mr. Weiss had not asked to be named a special counsel. Mr. Garland did not address whether Mr. Weiss had asked to be a special attorney.
match_headline: U.S. Attorney in Hunter Biden Case Defends Investigation to House Republicans

text: An article on Monday about a shooting in Baltimore, relying on information from local authorities, misspelled the surname of one of the victims. She was Aaliyah Gonzalez, not Gonzales.
match_headline: Shooting in Baltimore Leaves 2 Dead and 28 Wounded

text: An article on Saturday about layoffs at ESPN misstated the given name of an ESPN basketball analyst. He is Mike Breen, not Mark. The article also misstated that ESPN’s layoffs came a day after National Geographic announced its second round of layoffs this year. The layoffs at both organizations took place the same week, and National Geographic had two rounds of layoffs in the past 12 months, one in September and one this past week.
match_headline: National Geographic Lays Off More Writers

text: An article on Monday about people accused of being Russian spies in Albania referred incorrectly to the photographer Svetlana Timofeyeva’s job. Her main source of income came from working as a tour guide, not making videos and taking photographs for weddings and corporate events.
match_headline: ‘Urban Explorers’ and Accused Spies Chafe in Legal Limbo in Albania

text: An article on Tuesday about the singer-songwriter Julie Byrne misspelled the surname of her longtime creative collaborator, who died in 2021. He was Eric Littmann, not Littman.
match_headline: How Julie Byrne’s Astral Folk Music Took Flight

text: An article on Tuesday about an increase in tuna prices in Tunisia referred incorrectly to salata mechouia. While the dish includes grilled vegetables, it typically does not contain eggplant.
match_headline: In Tuna-Obsessed Tunisia, a Favorite Food Becomes a Lot Less Affordable

text: An article on Wednesday about division in the Republican Party over impeaching President Biden misstated the given name of Representative Pfluger of Texas. It is August, not Austin.
match_headline: Republicans Are Divided on Impeaching Biden as Panel Begins New Inquiry

text: An article on Wednesday about the tennis player Carlos Alcaraz’s attempts to improve his game on grass courts misstated the round of the tournament at the 2012 London Olympics in which Roger Federer would have watched Andy Murray play Stan Wawrinka on Centre Court. It was the first round, not the final. (Murray beat Federer in the final.)
match_headline: Carlos Alcaraz Has Been Studying the Grass Court Masters. That Means Andy Murray.

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the former New York City police commander Anthony V. Bouza misstated the date in 1976 that a protest by off-duty police officers and a robbery spree by marauding teenagers both took place outside Yankee Stadium. It was Sept. 28, not Sept. 18.
match_headline: Anthony Bouza, Police Commander Who Ruffled Feathers, Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Friday about the actor Frederic Forrest misstated part of the name of a movie in which he appeared. It is “Tucker: The Man and His Dream,” not “Dreams.”
ref_headline: Tucker: The Man and His Dream,
match_headline: Frederic Forrest, 86, Dies; Actor Known for ‘Apocalypse Now’ and ‘The Rose’

text: An article on Thursday about a suit filed by four countries over an Iranian missile that hit a Ukraine Airlines passenger flight misstated the year that the U.N. rapporteur, Agnes Callamard, published her report about the downing of the flight. It was in 2021, not 2001.
match_headline: Years After Iranian Missiles Downed a Passenger Jet, a Suit Seeks Answers

text: An article on Tuesday about online bullying of a lecturer at the University of Chicago over a course on whiteness misattributed a statement that said the online messages Rebecca Journey received were disturbing. The university said that in a statement to The Times, and not in a February dismissal from Jeremy W. Inabinet.
match_headline: At UChicago, a Debate Over Free Speech and Cyberbullying

text: An article on Thursday about the sentencing of the Texas man who pleaded guilty to federal hate crimes in the 2019 massacre targeting Latinos in an El Paso Walmart store misspelled the surname of the judge in the sentencing hearing. He is David Guaderrama, not Guaderama.
match_headline: El Paso Gunman Is Confronted by Victims’ Families at Sentencing

text: An article on Wednesday about hotel workers on strike in Los Angeles misstated the number of hotel workers who walked off their jobs over the weekend. It was several thousand, not 15,000.
match_headline: Your Room Is Ready. Don’t Mind the Picket Line.

text: An article on Friday about Ohio moving one step closer to establishing a right to abortion in the state’s Constitution referred incorrectly to the August election in which Ohio voters will be asked whether to raise the threshold for passing state constitutional amendments. It will be a special election, not a primary.
match_headline: Ohio Moves Closer to Ballot Issue That Would Protect Abortion Rights

text: An article on Friday about Sofia Kenin at Wimbledon misstated the winner of the 2023 French Open. The winner was Iga Swiatek, not Elena Rybakina.
match_headline: At Wimbledon, Sofia Kenin Rediscovers Her Fighting Form

text: An obituary on June 28 about the actor Julian Sands referred incorrectly to the character he played in the movie “The Killing Fields.” He was a reporter, not a photographer.
match_headline: Julian Sands Dies at 65; Actor Played Shelley, a Warlock and a King

text: An obituary on June 27 about Richard Ravitch, who helped rescue New York City from the brink of bankruptcy and later ran the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, referred incorrectly to Trump Village in Brooklyn. It was built by Trump Management — not by HRH Construction, the company owned by Mr. Ravitch’s family. (HRH did, however, build Trump Tower in Manhattan.) The earlier version also referred incorrectly to Joseph R. Califano’s position in the Lyndon B. Johnson administration. While he was President Johnson’s chief domestic adviser, he was not a member of the Johnson cabinet.
match_headline: Richard Ravitch, Rescuer of the Subways and New York’s Finances, Dies at 89

text: An article on Page 11 this weekend about an exhibition of the architecture firm Herzog & de Meuron misstates the number of employees in the Herzog & de Meuron architecture firm. There are more than 550, not more than 600.
match_headline: How Safe Is Your Office Air? There’s One Way to Find Out.

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about Guam misstates the length of a military environmental-impact statement. It was more than 8,000 pages long, not more than 10,000. The article also imprecisely describes the outcome of a lawsuit regarding the planned location of a live firing range. The lawsuit was deemed moot after the Navy made changes to its plan. It was not decided in favor of the plaintiffs.
match_headline: Coast Guard Apologizes for Covering Up Long History of Sexual Assault

text: An article on Sunday about the difference in how baseless claims of voter fraud by former presidents were handled in the United States versus Brazil misstated the amount of time between the 2020 U.S. presidential election and the declaration of its winner. It was a few days, not a week.
match_headline: Why Bolsonaro Was Barred in Brazil but Trump Can Run in the U.S.

text: An article on Thursday about a tourist’s apology for defacing the Colosseum misstated the age of Ivan Danailov Dimitrov. He is 27, not 31.
match_headline: Who Knew the Colosseum Was So Old? Tourist Apologizes for Defacement.

text: An article on Sunday about the collapse of a Dutch coalition government over a proposed refugee policy incorrectly characterized the Dutch Labor Party. It is an opposition party, not a member of the governing coalition.
match_headline: Collapse of Dutch Government Highlights Europe’s New Migration Politics

text: An article on Saturday about six people charged with illegal donations to Mayor Eric Adams’s 2021 campaign misstated with whom Winnie Greco, an adviser to Mayor Eric Adams, served on the management team at the security firm Overwatch Services, according to an archived version of the company’s website. It was Philip Banks III, not Dwayne Montgomery.
match_headline: Six Charged With Organizing Illegal Donations to Adams’s 2021 Campaign

text: An article on Saturday about an aide claiming former President Donald J. Trump had asked about having the I.R.S. investigate F.B.I. officials misstated the day that the aide’s sworn statement was disclosed. The filing was made public on Thursday, not Friday.
match_headline: Trump Asked About I.R.S. Inquiry of F.B.I. Officials, Ex-Aide Says Under Oath

text: An article on Monday about Megan Rapinoe’s farewell tour before retirement misstated a scoring achievement by Trinity Rodman. She is the youngest U.S. women’s player to score twice in a game since 2019, not the youngest to ever do it.
match_headline: For Rapinoe, a Final Send-Off Before a Final World Cup

text: An obituary on Monday about the Pulitzer Prize-winning former New York Times foreign correspondent Henry Kamm referred incorrectly to the status in 1967 of the town of Lidice, from which Mr. Kamm wrote an article about Nazi Germany’s massacre of 173 men there during World War II. By that year the town was part of Czechoslovakia (it is now in the Czech Republic); it was no longer part of the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, which had ceased to exist after the war.
match_headline: Henry Kamm, Pulitzer-Winning New York Times Journalist, Dies at 98

text: An article on Tuesday about more frequent climate disasters misspelled the surname of a contributing reporter. He is Robert Chiarito, not Charito.
match_headline: Climate Disasters Daily? Welcome to the ‘New Normal.’

text: An article on Saturday about a legal ethics committee’s recommendation for disbarment of Rudolph W. Giuliani misstated where a lawsuit that he filed in Pennsylvania in an effort to delay the certification of election results was heard. It was in Federal District Court in Williamsport, not Philadelphia.
match_headline: Giuliani Should Lose His Law License in D.C., Bar Panel Says

text: An article on Monday about Megan Rapinoe’s best moments referred incorrectly to the U.S. women’s soccer team as it entered the 2019 World Cup. It was looking to become the second women’s team to repeat as World Cup champion, not the first. (That was Germany, which won in 2003 and 2007.)
match_headline: A Look Back at Megan Rapinoe’s Best Moments

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misidentified the year in which the movie “Almost Famous” had its debut. It was 2000, not 1990.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘What We Do in the Shadows’ and ‘Barbie Dreamhouse Challenge’

text: An obituary on Monday about the diplomat James F. Dobbins misstated the role he had when he returned to government service in 2013 after a decade at the RAND Corporation. He was the U.S. special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan, not Iraq and Pakistan.
match_headline: James F. Dobbins, Leading Authority on Nation Building, Dies at 81

text: An article on Wednesday about a nonprofit that purchased newspapers in Maine misstated where the National Trust for Local News is based. It is based in Denver, not Lexington, Mass.
match_headline: Nonprofit Buys 22 Newspapers in Maine

text: An article on Tuesday about a letter by Abraham Lincoln that sold for thousands of dollars gave an outdated name for the Confederate ship that destroyed a number of Union ships at the Battle of Hampton Roads. It was the CSS Virginia, which previously had been named the Merrimack. The article also misstated the date that this happened. It was March 8, 1862, not March 9.
match_headline: Abraham Lincoln Letter From Early Civil War Era Sells for $85,000

text: An article last Thursday about astrology readings generated by chatbots misstated the name of Co­Star’s new in-­app service. It is the Void, not Embrace the Void. The article also misstated what Banu Guler did, and her experience with A.I., before starting Co­Star. Ms. Guler worked in technology for art and fashion companies, not in art sales, and she used A.I. in past jobs; she did not teach herself to code the technology.
match_headline: Is A.I. the Future of Astrology?

text: An article last Thursday about Guram Gvasalia of Vetements in­cluded a comment misattributed to Demna. The comment was written by a spokeswoman for Demna and described her own views, not those of Demna.
match_headline: The Man Who Wants to Be the Biggest Thing in Fashion

text: An obituary on July 3 about the meteorologist Frank Field misstated where he was born. It was Brooklyn, not Queens. It also misstated when his wife, Joan, died. It was last year, not this year. And it omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to those named, Dr. Field is survived by a brother, Allan.
match_headline: Frank Field, Who Brought Expertise to TV Weathercasting, Dies at 100

text: An obituary on Thursday about Gerald C. Meyers, a former chief executive of the American Motors Corporation, misstated the name by which Carnegie Mellon University was known when he was a student there. It was the Carnegie Institute of Technology, not Carnegie Technical Institute. And because of an editing error, a picture caption with the obituary incorrectly described the design of the Pacer, an AMC car. It has two doors, not four.
match_headline: Gerald C. Meyers, C.E.O. Who Paved Way for the S.U.V., Dies at 94

text: An obituary on Saturday about the movie producer Lawrence Turman misspelled the given name of one of his former wives. She is Lauree Berger Turman, not Lorie.
match_headline: Lawrence Turman, 96, Dies; Producer Spotted a Winner in ‘The Graduate’

text: An article on Friday about federal prosecutors’ inquiry into President Donald J. Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 election misstated who first made public a recording of Stephen Bannon, a former adviser to Mr. Trump, telling associates that Mr. Trump was going to summarily declare he had won. The recording was first reported by Mother Jones, not the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack.
match_headline: Prosecutors Ask Witnesses Whether Trump Acknowledged He Lost 2020 Race

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about a revival of the play “Orpheus Descending” misidentifies Erica Schmidt’s role in the making of the 2021 film “Cyrano.” She wrote the screenplay; she did not direct.
match_headline: Maggie Siff and Erica Schmidt on a Williams Play ‘Shot Through With Desire’

text: An article on Page 5 this weekend about a Korean dance production at Lincoln Center misspells the given name of the artistic director of Seoul Metropolitan Dance Theater. She is Hyejin Jeong, not Hyejing.
match_headline: Translating Traditional Korean Movement to ‘a Language for Our Time’

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about Greta Gerwig’s movie “Barbie” misstates the title of a pop song about the doll. It is “Barbie Girl,” not “Barbie World.”
match_headline: Greta Gerwig’s ‘Barbie’ Dream Job

text: An obituary on Friday about the geneticist Evelyn M. Witkin misstated the number of grandchildren who survive her. It is four, not five.
match_headline: Evelyn M. Witkin, Who Discovered How DNA Repairs Itself, Dies at 102

text: An article last Sunday about the “girl din­ner” trend on TikTok misspelled the given name of a food content creator in London. She is Alana Laverty, not Alanna.
match_headline: Is It a Meal? A Snack? No, It’s ‘Girl Dinner.’

text: An article on Saturday about the possibility that a defense policy bill vote could backfire on House Republicans misspelled the given name of a member of Congress from Pennsylvania. She is Representative Chrissy Houlahan, not Chrissie.
match_headline: Vulnerable Republicans Take a Political Risk With Abortion Vote

text: An article on Sunday about a rising trend in disaster-proof homes misspelled the given name of a retired software engineer who recently bought property near Bishop, Calif. He is Jon duSaint, not John.
match_headline: As Climate Shocks Multiply, Designers Seek Holy Grail: Disaster-Proof Homes

text: An article on Saturday about a sense of safety in Gilgo Beach after the arrest of a suspect misstated James Burke’s title. He was the police chief in Suffolk County, not the police commissioner.
match_headline: For Years, Quiet Gilgo Beach Was a Place of ‘Murders and Mayhem’

text: An article on July 11 about new song releases misstated the name of PJ Harvey’s new album. It is “I Inside the Old Year Dying,” not “I Inside the Old World Dying.”
ref_headline: I Inside the Old Year Dying,
match_headline: Taylor Swift’s Revised ‘Revenge,’ and 10 More New Songs

text: An article on Saturday about Broadway veterans and movie stars’ camp memories misidentified the production in which the actress Andréa Burns appeared. It was “Man of La Mancha,” not “Don Quixote.”
match_headline: They Put on a Show at Camp, and It Changed Their Lives

text: An article on July 11 about environmental concerns associated with open-pit coal mines misattributed the cause, at least in part, of a cutthroat trout dieoff in the Fording River. There is no proof in this case that selenium played a role, according to an evaluation of the incident by Teck Resources, the mining company. In addition, the article misstated the company’s applications for mining. It is seeking to expand one of its mines, not to open two new ones.
match_headline: Tracing Mining’s Threat to U.S. Waters

text: An article on Tuesday about the Christians United for Israel Summit misidentified the lawmaker who described Israel as “a racist state” at a progressive conference over the weekend and who is the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. She is Representative Pramila Jayapal, not Representative Rashida Tlaib. And it is Ms. Tlaib who is the first Palestinian American woman elected to Congress, not Ms. Jayapal.
match_headline: DeSantis, Haley and Pence Attack Democrats in Speeches Supporting Israel

text: A chart with The Morning column on Tuesday about Covid milestones mislabeled the data for excess death rates in various countries. It shows the estimated daily death rate, not the weekly rate.
match_headline: A Positive Covid Milestone

text: An article on Sunday about Marketa Vondrousova’s Wimbledon win misstated the situation just before Vondrousova won the final five games in her quarterfinals match to beat Jessica Pegula. In the third set, Pegula had a game point for a potential 5-1 lead, not a potential 4-1 lead.
match_headline: Marketa Vondrousova Wins Wimbledon and Her First Grand Slam Title

text: A review on June 28 of the Manhattan restaurant Superiority Burger misstated the location of a former Angelica Kitchen. It was on East 12th Street, not East Ninth Street.
match_headline: Restaurant Review: Superiority Burger Has the Courage of Its Quirks

text: An article on Wednesday about a House measure pledging support for Israel misstated the day that Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan gave an emotional speech on the House floor. She spoke on Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: House Votes Resoundingly to Back Israel, Rebuking Democratic Critics

text: An article on Saturday about the Gilgo Beach victims, relying on information from prosecutors, misspelled the surname of the police dog handler. He is John Mallia, not Malia.
match_headline: What We Know About the Gilgo Beach Victims

text: An article on Wednesday about a fatal shooting involving teenagers in Brooklyn referred imprecisely to the location of a group of teenagers when they were shot at by a 17-year-old. They were several blocks from Franklin Delano Roosevelt High School when the shooting took place, not outside the school. The article, relying on information from the police, also misspelled the given name of the boy who was fatally shot. He is Faridun Mavlonov, not Foridun.
match_headline: Boy, 15, Is Fatally Shot in Brooklyn After Dispute Among Teens

text: An obituary on Saturday about the pianist André Watts referred incorrectly to the Peabody Institute, from which he graduated in 1972. It became affiliated with Johns Hopkins University in 1978; it was not part of Johns Hopkins at the time.
match_headline: André Watts, Pioneering Piano Virtuoso, Dies at 77

text: An article on Wednesday about the impact that general election outcomes could have on efforts to exhume mass graves in Spain misstated the profession of a woman executed and buried in the mass graves in Viznar, Spain. She was a tailor, not a barmaid.
match_headline: Spanish Vote Threatens Efforts to Recover Franco’s Victims

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about watching “Oppenheimer” in IMAX 70-millimeter format misidentified the type of projector shown in the background. It was a film projector, not a digital projector.
match_headline: For ‘Oppenheimer,’ These Fans Go to Great Lengths for Just 30 Screens

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about Josh Kline’s “Another America Is Possible” on view at the Whitney Museum of American Art misstated the beer used in a video installation by Josh Kline. It is Corona, not Budweiser.
match_headline: Propaganda with an Ambiguous Message? That’s Art.

text: An article on Page 34 this weekend about Wikipedia and artificial intelligence refers imprecisely to what Margaret Mitchell has said about why she was fired from Google. She has said she was fired for criticizing how the company treated colleagues working on bias in A.I., not for criticizing the direction of its work.
match_headline: Wikipedia’s Moment of Truth

text: An obituary on Friday about the historian Martha Saxton misidentified the town in Connecticut where she lived. It is Norfolk, not Norwalk.
match_headline: Martha Saxton, Historian Who Explored Women’s Lives, Dies at 77

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the gay rights activist Lilli Vincenz misstated the location of the Walter Reed military hospital when she trained as a neuropsychiatric technician there in the early 1960s. It was in Washington — not Bethesda, Md., where it is now.
match_headline: Lilli Vincenz, Lesbian Crusader When Few Dared to Be One, Dies at 85

text: An article on Friday about a tornado that damaged a Pfizer drug manufacturing site misstated which drugs are made at the Rocky Mount Pfizer site. They do not include the sedative propofol and the antibiotic vancomycin. The article also misstated who had traveled to the site to assess the damage. Only Pfizer officials were there, not Food and Drug Administration staff.
match_headline: Tornado Tears Through Pfizer’s N.C. Site, Threatening Crucial Drug Supplies

text: An article on Sunday about the candidacy of Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina, who is seeking the Republican nomination for president, misstated the number of canvassers that the group Trust in the Mission PAC is helping to fund in early states. The group is supporting a field operation of 100 canvassers and a dozen paid staff, not a dozen canvassers.
match_headline: Tim Scott Awaits His Moment. But Will It Come?

text: An article on July 17 about the growth of women’s soccer misstated the league affiliation of a soccer club in Portugal. The club, Lank F.C. Vilaverdense, plays in Portugal’s top league, not the second division.
match_headline: Worlds Apart: Cup’s Expansion Brings the Games of a Lifetime

text: An article on Sunday about Sophia Smith’s World Cup debut misspelled the given name of Vietnam’s goalkeeper. She is Thi Kim Thanh Tran, not Thi Kim Tranh Tran.
match_headline: Sophia Smith Has Been Ready for Her World Cup Moment

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the augmented-reality production of “Parsifal” misstated the opening day of the Bayreuth Festival. It is Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: At Wagner’s Festival, New Technology Reveals a Leadership Rift

text: An article on Sunday about the pharmaceutical industry’s attempt to halt a federal drug pricing program described incorrectly the reason that Medicare’s reported spending per patient for two blood thinners in 2021 was lower than their sticker prices. The lower amount reflected that some patients took the drugs for less than a full year. It did not reflect discounts negotiated by pharmacy benefit managers, which were not factored into the spending figures.
match_headline: Drugmakers Are ‘Throwing the Kitchen Sink’ to Halt Medicare Price Negotiations

text: An article on Sunday about a clash over a Pride display at a California library misstated Marni von Wilpert’s role in the Rancho Peñasquitos neighborhood. She is the first Democrat to represent District 5, not the first Democrat to represent Rancho Peñasquitos.
match_headline: They Checked Out Pride Books in Protest. It Backfired.

text: An article on Tuesday about the Indigo Girls song “Closer to Fine” misstated the title of the Indigo Girls’ latest album. It is “Look Long,” not “Long Look.” The article also misspelled the surname of the director of the documentary “It’s Only Life After All.” She is Alexandria Bombach, not Bambach.
match_headline: How the Indigo Girls Brought Barbie ‘Closer to Fine’

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about Tony Bennett referred incorrectly to the two duet albums he recorded with the jazz pianist Bill Evans. Fantasy, Mr. Evans’s label, released the first one, and Improv, Mr. Bennett’s label, released the second — not the other way around. The obituary also misstated the name of the high school Mr. Bennett attended. It was the School of Industrial Art, not the High School for Industrial Arts.
match_headline: Tony Bennett, Jazzy Crooner of the American Songbook, Is Dead at 96

text: An article on Tuesday about the scaling back of technology companies in New York misstated the scope of layoffs by large technology companies since early 2022. They have laid off more than 386,000 workers worldwide, not just in the United States.
match_headline: Tech Firms Once Powered New York’s Economy. Now They’re Scaling Back.

text: An article on Monday about senior hockey players misstated the position of Rich Maslow, a player for the Colorado Fading Stars. He is a right wing, not a goalie.
match_headline: The Mind Is Willing, So the Body Doesn’t Have Much Choice

text: An article on Monday about city pools in Philadelphia misidentified the location of the Charles Baker Playground. It is in Philadelphia’s Overbrook neighborhood, not Overbrook Park.
match_headline: In Philadelphia, City Pools Bring Relief as Closed Ones Stir Frustration

text: An obituary on Thursday about the screenwriter Bo Goldman misstated how the film “Melvin and Howard” fared in the 1980 New York Film Critics Circle Awards. Mr. Goldman won an award for his screenplay, but while the film itself was nominated for best movie, it did not win.
match_headline: Bo Goldman, Oscar-Winning Screenwriter, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on June 18 about the filmmaker Jacques Rozier, using information from a friend and former collaborator, misstated when he died. It was May 31, not June 2. This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: Jacques Rozier, Last of the French New Wave Directors, Dies at 96

text: An article on Page 1 this weekend about repurposed abandoned buildings in the Hudson Valley misidentifies the year that BjornQorn bought the Skate Time roller rink. It was 2022, not 2012.
match_headline: The Roller Rink Popcorn Factory and the Jailhouse Pub

text: An article on Friday about Modelo Especial position as the top-selling beer in America incorrectly described Constellation’s relationship to the Mexican beer brands Modelo, Corona and Pacifico. Those brands are all part of Grupo Modelo, which is owned by Anheuser-Busch InBev. Constellation owns the U.S. rights to those brands; it does not own the brands.
match_headline: How a Mexican Lager Quietly Rose to Become America’s Best-Selling Beer

text: An article on Thursday about NASA’s choice of Lockheed Martin to build a nuclear-powered rocket, using information from a news conference, misstated the timing of a possible flight test of a nuclear-thermal engine. The launch is scheduled for late 2026 or early 2027, not late 2025 or early 2026.
match_headline: NASA Seeks a Nuclear-Powered Rocket to Get to Mars in Half the Time

text: An article on Page 15 about the photographer Felipe Romero Beltrán includes an incorrect byline. It was written by Jennifer Harlan.

An obituary on July 16 about the civil liberties lawyer Melvin Wulf referred incorrectly to Aryeh Neier’s tenure as executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union. He held that position from 1970 until 1978; he was not executive director at the time of voter registration efforts in the South in the summer of 1964.
match_headline: Melvin Wulf, Transformative Civil Liberties Lawyer, Dies at 95

text: An article last Sunday about Califor­nia legislators working to form a renters’ caucus misstated the num­ber of tenants in the state. It is about 17 million residents, not 17 million households.
match_headline: Who Will Stand Up for Renters? Their Elected Representatives, Who Also Rent.

text: An article on Page 15 about the photographer Felipe Romero Beltrán includes an incorrect byline. It was written by Jennifer Harlan.

An article last Sunday about a trend among the superrich to avoid flaunting their wealth described incorrectly a figure used to measure who is considered an ultra­-high-­net-­worth individual. It is a minimum net worth of $30 million; that is not the minimum net worth of the “1 percent.” The article also described incorrectly William Norwich’s job at The New York Post. He was a gossip columnist; he did not write for Page Six.
match_headline: What’s the Status of Flaunting Your Status?

text: An article on June 9 about community land trusts referred incorrectly to a group trip that Charles Sherrod took to Israel in 1968 to see how people had resettled there. Mr. Sherrod made the trip, but his wife, Shirley Sherrod, did not.
match_headline: Community Land Trusts Are Working to Create New Homeowners

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the 70th anniversary of the armistice that halted the Korean War misstated the length of that conflict. It lasted about three years and one month, not less than three years.
match_headline: The Korean War in Photos, 70 Years After the Truce

text: An article on Saturday about threats to a global AIDS relief program from Republican-supported abortion restrictions misstated the impact of a provision inserted into a State Department spending bill that would allow the program, known as PEPFAR, to keep operating for a year without a new authorization. It would continue a program to help orphans and vulnerable children, not allow it to lapse.
match_headline: AIDS Relief Program Under Threat as G.O.P. Insists on Abortion Restriction

text: An article on Sunday about a stage shared by former President Donald Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis at an Iowa Republican Party dinner referred incorrectly to security arrangements at the event. It was not the case that security screening equipment was diverted to a Trump campaign event, according to Trump campaign spokesman Steven Cheung and Josie Albrecht, a spokeswoman for the Iowa Republican Party.
match_headline: Trump and DeSantis Collide for First Time in Iowa, as Fortunes Diverge

text: An article on Monday about the Texas Rangers misstated when Marcus Semien began a stretch of playing in 429 of a possible 430 games. It was since the start of 2021, the season before he signed with the Rangers, not 2022.
match_headline: Finally on Top, the Rangers Hope to Stay There

text: An obituary on May 21 about Shermane Billingsley, the youngest daughter of Sherman Billingsley, who ran the Manhattan nightclub the Stork Club, misstated how old Mr. Billingsley’s second daughter was when Shermane was born. She was 8, not 13. This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: Shermane Billingsley, Guardian of the Stork Club’s Legacy, Dies at 78

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about Randy Meisner, an original member of the Eagles, contained an erroneous credit for him. He was never a member of the band Buffalo Springfield.
match_headline: Randy Meisner, a Founding Member of the Eagles, Dies at 77

text: A map with an article on Sunday about military coups in Africa omitted Tunisia.
match_headline: Coast to Coast, a Corridor of Coups Brings Turmoil in Africa

text: An article on Monday about Austria’s continued purchasing of natural gas from Russia incorrectly described the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The military alliance with Europe includes Canada; it is not an American alliance with Europe.
match_headline: Why One Country Is Struggling to Break Away From Russian Gas

text: An article on July 25 about the unrest in Israel prompted by curbs put in place on the Israeli judiciary by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu referred imprecisely to the holiest site in Judaism. The Temple Mount is considered the holiest site in Judaism; the Western Wall is a remnant of the retaining wall of the ancient temple complex.
match_headline: Netanyahu Scores Another Victory, but at What Price?

text: An article on Wednesday about tourism taxes in Europe misstated the amount of a proposed increase to Amsterdam’s tourist accommodation tax. The proposal was for a 1 percentage point increase, not a 1 percent increase.
match_headline: Planning to Visit Barcelona or Dubrovnik? It’s Going to Cost You.

text: An article on Thursday about former President Donald J. Trump’s scheduled appearance at a U.S. federal courthouse for election charges incorrectly stated the circumstances of Magistrate Judge Moxila A. Upadhyaya’s appointment. She was appointed by other judges, not by President Biden.
match_headline: Who is the judge handling Trump’s initial court appearance?

text: An article on Thursday about political differences between the N.B.A. and some of its teams’ owners referred incorrectly to the N.B.A.’s response to a request for a comment. A league spokesman did indeed provide a statement via email, but it was not seen by the reporter; it is not the case that the N.B.A. declined to comment.
match_headline: The N.B.A. and Its Owners Fight for Change. But Not Necessarily the Same Change.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Dorothy Tapper Goldman, a philanthropist who sold an original copy of the U.S. Constitution for $43.2 million in 2021, misstated the name of a bibliophilic organization in New York that she supported. It is the Grolier Club, not the Grolier Society.
match_headline: $60 Million Refund Request Shows Financial Pressure on Trump From Legal Fees

text: An article on Friday about Meta’s restriction of news content in Canada misstated the month the online news law will take effect. It is December, not January.
match_headline: Missing From Your Facebook News Feed: Canadian News

text: An article on Wednesday about the charges former President Donald Trump is facing in the Jan. 6 case misstated the maximum sentence for any conviction under Section 241 of Title 18 of the United States Code, a conspiracy to violate rights. It is punishable by up to 10 years in prison, not five. The error was repeated in an illustration on Wednesday about the Jan. 6 indictment document.
match_headline: Here Are the Charges Trump Faces in the Jan. 6 Case

text: An article on Page 1 this weekend about the First Response fire chasers misstates Jatiek Smith’s age. He was 35 in 2019, not 33.
match_headline: When Help Shows Up After a House Fire, It Might Be Gang Members

text: A picture caption with the Big City column this weekend about New Yorkers’ perception of crime in the city misstates the year in which Bernhard Goetz was being led out of a police station in New York City after his arrest. It was 1985, not 1984.
match_headline: Crime Is Down. So Why Don’t New Yorkers Feel Safe?

text: An article on Friday about the lighting designer of the band Phish misstated the name of Chris Kuroda’s wife. She is Rhia, not Rita.
match_headline: How Phish’s Lighting Designer Jams With the Band

text: A review on Friday about “Schema: World as Diagram” described incorrectly the show’s curators. Heather Bause Rubinstein is the wife of Raphael Rubinstein, not his daughter.
match_headline: Justin Trudeau Separates From Wife, Sophie Grégoire

text: A picture caption with a review of the film “Passages” on Friday described incorrectly the characters played by Franz Rogowski and Adèle Exarchopoulos. They are part of a love triangle; they are not in a “film-within-a-film.”
match_headline: ‘Sex Is a Huge Part of a Character’s Life.’ Especially in ‘Passages.’

text: An article on July 30 about the poet Shane McCrae misspelled the surname of a writer. She was Virginia Woolf, not Wolff.
match_headline: The Kidnapped Child Who Became a Poet

text: An article on Saturday about the first pill for postpartum depression misspelled the name of a psychiatrist. She is Dr. Ruta Nonacs, not Nunacs.
match_headline: For the First Time, There’s a Pill for Postpartum Depression

text: An article on Monday about a group of Swiss women who sued the government over climate change protections misstated how much warmer the average temperature was in July in Switzerland. It was 2 degrees Celsius warmer, not 35 degrees.
match_headline: Heat Waves Are Killing Older Women. Are They Also Violating Their Rights?

text: An article on Saturday about the tech industry’s new investments in generative A.I. misstated Nvidia’s data center sales. The company will add $15 billion in sales this year, not reach $15 billion in sales.
match_headline: Big Tech Rebounds and Preps for Transformative A.I. Investments

text: An article on Saturday about Arthur Dantchik, who donated millions to the group behind Israel’s judicial overhaul plan, misidentified the source of a quote from the Kohelet Policy Forum. The quote was published by eJewishPhilanthropy, not The Jewish Insider.
match_headline: Billionaire Parts With Group Behind Israel’s Judicial Overhaul

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about a body-positive summer camp in Colorado misstated the year that the Realize Your Beauty camp began. It was 2016, not 2010.
match_headline: Amid the Mountains, They Can Be ‘Open Without Being Judged’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the television show “Winning Time: The Rise of the Lakers Dynasty” misspelled the surname of a Philadelphia 76ers player. He is Julius Erving, not Irving.
ref_headline: Winning Time: The Rise of the Lakers Dynasty
match_headline: ‘Winning Time’ Is Back. Here’s What to Know Ahead of Season 2

text: An article on Monday about television shows to watch this week referred incorrectly to a scene in “The Breakfast Club.” The boombox scene was in “Say Anything.”
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Outlander’ and ‘Hard Knocks’

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actor Mark Margolis referred incorrectly to a scene in the TV series “Breaking Bad” in which Mr. Margolis’s character, Hector Salamanca, is watching a movie on a television set. He was watching an old Spanish-language film, not “Scarface,” the 1983 movie in which Mr. Margolis had a supporting role. The obituary also misidentified the drug that the leading character in the series, Walter White (played by Bryan Cranston), trafficked in. It was methamphetamine, not crystal methedrine.
match_headline: Mark Margolis, Scene-Stealing Actor in ‘Breaking Bad,’ Dies at 83

text: An obituary on Monday about the Harvard law professor Charles J. Ogletree Jr. referred incorrectly to Charles Hamilton Houston, after whom a research institute at Harvard Law School was named. He was the school’s first Black recipient of a Doctor of Juridical Science degree, the school’s most advanced degree, in 1923; he was not the first Black graduate of the law school. (That was George Lewis Ruffin, who earned his law degree in 1869.)
match_headline: Charles J. Ogletree Jr., 70, Dies; at Harvard Law, a Voice for Equal Justice

text: An article on Saturday about the revived popu­larity of cruises misstated a measurement of the Icon of the Seas. Its gross tonnage will be about 250,000; it will not displace about 250,000 tons.
match_headline: I Gave Up and Went on a Trip With Several Thousand of My Closest Friends

text: An article on Saturday about the views of young Catholics gathered for World Youth Day celebrations in Portugal misspelled the name of a neighborhood in Lisbon. It is Graça, not Graçia.
match_headline: Young Catholics Come Together, if Not Their Views

text: An article on Wednesday about President Biden’s fifth national monument designation misquoted Senator John Barrasso’s criticism of Mr. Biden. The senator accused Mr. Biden of “helping our enemies,” not “supporting our enemies.”
match_headline: With National Monument Designation, Biden Tries to Balance Electoral Realities

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about three popular musical revivals misstated the year in which “The Rocky Horror Show” was produced at the Stratford Festival. It was in 2018, not 2022.
match_headline: Can These Three Much-Loved Musicals Ever Be Truly Revived?

text: An obituary on July 2 about Peg Yorkin, a feminist and philanthropist who campaigned to bring the abortion pill mifepristone to the United States, misstated the year the drug received government approval for use in France. It was 1988, not 1998. This correction was delayed because an email pointing out the error went astray.
match_headline: Economic Data Points to Faster Growth Early in Year

text: An article on Tuesday about the International Puppet Fringe Festival misstated the end date for “Myths, Legends and Spectacle: Puppets and Masks of Ralph Lee.” It will end on Aug. 13, not Aug. 31.
ref_headline: Myths, Legends and Spectacle: Puppets and Masks of Ralph Lee.
match_headline: The Wide World of Puppetry Converges on New York

text: An article on Aug. 6 about a sexual assault in a school bathroom in Loudoun County, Va., misstated the original name of the town of Ashburn. It was Farmwell, not Farmville.
match_headline: How a Sexual Assault in a School Bathroom Became a Political Weapon

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Michael Boyd, the artistic director of the Royal Shakespeare Company from 2002 to 2012, misidentified the play that he invited Theater for a New Audience to present at the company’s Complete Works Festival in 2007. It was “The Merchant of Venice,” not “Macbeth.” And a picture caption with the obituary misidentified the theater in which Mr. Boyd is pictured. It is the Royal Shakespeare Theater, not the Swan Theater.
match_headline: Michael Boyd, 68, Who Invigorated the Royal Shakespeare Company, Dies

text: An obituary on Thursday about the guitarist and songwriter Robbie Robertson of the Band misstated the location of the house, later known as Big Pink, where the members of the Band moved in 1967. It is in Saugerties, N.Y., not Woodstock. The obituary also misstated the name of a public television series for which Mr. Robertson was interviewed in 1995. It was “Rock & Roll” — not “Shakespeares in the Alley,” which was an episode of that series. And it misstated the release dates of the Band’s albums “Stage Fright” and “Cahoots.” They were released in 1970 and 1971, not 1971 and 1972. In addition, the obituary misstated the name of Mr. Robertson’s first band. It was Little Caesar and the Consuls, not Little Ceasar and the Consults. Because of an editing error, the obituary misstated the name of an album by the singer Neil Diamond that Mr. Robertson produced. It is “Love at the Greek,” not “Live at the Greek.” And, using information from a spokeswoman, the obituary misstated part of Mr. Robertson’s birth name. He was born Jaime Royal Robertson, not Jamie.
match_headline: Robbie Robertson, 80, Dies; Canadian Songwriter Captured American Spirit

text: An article on July 9 about the United States’ military buildup in Guam misstated the name of the court that found Guam’s plebiscite law unconstitutional in 2017. It was the District Court of Guam, not the Ninth District court. And the article misquoted a phrase that Ben Blaz, a former United States representative from Guam, used in describing Guam’s political status in a 1991 letter to the editor published in The Times. He wrote that Guam was “equal in war, but not in peace,” not “equal in war, unequal in peace.” And an earlier version of a picture caption with this article misidentified a location. Tumon Bay was in the background, not in the foreground.
ref_headline: equal in war, but not in peace,
match_headline: The America That Americans Forget

text: An article on July 23 about Tom Cruise referred imprecisely to the plane from which Tom Cruise accepted an MTV Movie & TV Award. It was a fighter aircraft, not a fighter jet.
match_headline: My Impossible Mission to Find Tom Cruise

text: A review on July 23 about “Christendom,” by Peter Heather, misstated the year that the Roman emperor Constantine con­verted to Christianity. The date usually cited is A.D. 312, not 302.

An article on Saturday about five Americans held in Iran who could be released as part of a prisoner swap misstated the year that Emad Sharghi was arrested while trying to flee Iran. It was 2020, not 2021. The article also misstated the location of Morad Tahbaz’s wife at the time he was detained. She was in Iran then; she did not travel there afterward.
match_headline: Americans Held Prisoner in Iran Saw Promise of Better Relations

text: A critic’s notebook article on Saturday about themes of belonging and identity at the Edinburgh International Festival misstated the name of the director of “Trojan Women.” He is Ong Keng Sen, not Ong King Sen.
match_headline: Wrestling With Identity at the Edinburgh Festival

text: An article on Sunday about the erosion of Fire Island’s shoreline included a headline that misstated the price of fixing damage to the island’s beaches. It was less than $1.7 billion; that figure referred to a project that encompassed Fire Island’s beaches along with other beaches on the mainland.
match_headline: Millions Were Spent to Fix Fire Island’s Beaches. Some Have Completely Eroded.

text: An article on Tuesday about the artist Brice Marden misstated the title of his 1970 three-panel painting. It is “Three Deliberate Grays for Jasper Johns,” not “Three Deliberates Grays for Jasper Johns.”
ref_headline: Three Deliberate Grays for Jasper Johns,
match_headline: Brice Marden: A Legacy Beyond the Monochromes

text: An article on Saturday about 16 essential songs by Robbie Robertson of the Band misstated lyrics to “The Weight.” They include “You put the load right on me,” not “They put the load right on me.”
match_headline: Robbie Robertson’s 16 Essential Songs

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the record executive Clarence Avant misstated the year Mr. Avant formed Sussex Records. It was 1969, not 1960.
match_headline: Clarence Avant, Mighty Engine Behind Black Superstars, Dies at 92

text: An article on Tuesday about American antiwar activists’ support of Ukraine’s self-defense against Russia misstated the number of House Republicans who voted for a July amendment to cut funding for Ukraine. Eighty-nine Republicans supported the amendment, not 130.
match_headline: For Ukraine, Many Antiwar Activists in the U.S. Make an Exception

text: A headline on Tuesday with an article about a judge presiding over the criminal case against Donald J. Trump in Manhattan and his decision not to recuse himself from the case referred incorrectly to the judge. The judge, Juan M. Merchan, is a man.
match_headline: Trump Case Judge in New York Declines to Step Aside

text: An article on Tuesday about a Montana judge’s ruling in favor of young people’s constitutional right to a healthful environment misstated the origin of the “clean and healthful environment” provision of the Montana state Constitution. It was adopted as part of a new Constitution in 1972. It was not the result of a constitutional amendment.
match_headline: Judge Rules in Favor of Montana Youths in a Landmark Climate Case

text: An article on Wednesday about Charles McGonigal, a former F.B.I. official, and his guilty plea to aiding a prominent Russian oligarch, misstated Mr. McGonigal’s scheduled sentencing date. It is Dec. 14, not Dec. 4.
match_headline: Former F.B.I. Spy Hunter Pleads Guilty to Aiding Russian Oligarch

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the Virginia rapper and former Timbaland collaborator Magoo misstated Magoo’s marital status. Meco Barcliff was his former wife, not his spouse at the time of his death.
match_headline: Magoo, Rapper and Former Timbaland Collaborator, Dies at 50

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Joan Meyer, longtime editor of the weekly newspaper The Marion County Record, misspelled Ms. Meyer’s given name. Although it is pronounced “Joe-Anne,” it is Joan, not Joann.
match_headline: Joan Meyer, Longtime Editor of a Besieged Newspaper, Dies at 98

text: An article on Aug. 11 about four Nigerian stowaways who landed in Brazil misstated the rate of growth of migrants from Nigeria. The number grew 60 percent from 2010 to 2020, according to the Center for Global Development, not threefold between 2009 and 2019.
match_headline: They Hid on a Ship’s Rudder to Flee Nigeria. They Landed in Brazil.

text: An article on Page 7 this weekend about the advent of artificial intelligence in comedy misstates the author of an introduction to “I Am Code,” a book of poems written by A.I. The introduction was written by Brent Katz, not Simon Rich.
match_headline: In the Battle Between Bots and Comedians, A.I. Is Killing

text: An article last Sunday about couples who were married during the 2003 blackout in the Northeast and the Midwest referred incompletely to the reason Jewish weddings are often held on Thursdays and Sundays. It is because observ­ers of the Sabbath typically abstain from work of any kind, not just from using electricity.
match_headline: Married During the 2003 Blackout

text: An article on Page 32 this weekend about a class of chemicals known as PFAS misspells the name of a company. It is Chemours, not Chermours.
match_headline: ‘Forever Chemicals’ Are Everywhere. What Are They Doing to Us?

text: An article on July 23 about the docuseries “Break Point” referred incompletely to the producers of the docuseries “The Last Dance.” It was produced by ESPN and Netflix, not Netflix alone.
match_headline: ‘Break Point’ Is the Best Way to See the Full Psychodrama of Tennis

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the evacuation of the Canadian city of Yellowknife misstated the status of the Northwest Territories. It is a territory of Canada, not a province.
match_headline: As Wildfire Nears, Entire Canadian City Evacuates

text: An article on Saturday about a 2020 lawsuit Maui County filed against some of the world’s largest oil and gas companies misspelled the surname of an attorney representing the oil companies. He is Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., not Boutros.
match_headline: Maui Sued Big Oil in 2020, Citing Fire Risks and More

text: An article on Sunday about a man on a mission to fill his New Haven, Conn., neighborhood with trees misstated how long residents are responsible for watering new trees planted by the Urban Resources Institute. It is for three years, not five.
match_headline: One Neighborhood, 90 Trees and an 82-Year-Old Crusader

text: An article on Monday about Tropical Storm Hilary’s landfall in Southern California referred incorrectly to Tropical Storm Hilary’s place in California history. It was the first tropical storm to hit the state in 26 years, not in more than eight decades.
match_headline: Storm That Killed at Least One in Mexico Drenches Southern California

text: An article on Sunday about Jody Gottfried Arnhold, a pioneer of dance education in New York, misspelled the name of a newly renovated space at 92NY. It is Buttenwieser Hall, not Buttenweiser.
match_headline: Repeat After Her: There Is No Dance Without Dance Education

text: An article on Aug. 15 about a group museum exhibition curated by Pueblo artisans and community leaders misstated the name of a curator at the Museum of Indian Arts and Culture. He is Antonio R. Chavarria, not Anthony.
match_headline: Relationships Carved From Clay Bring New Partners to Museums

text: An obituary on Monday about the experimental dancer and choreographer Gus Solomons Jr. misstated when the choreographer Donald Byrd joined Mr. Solomons’s company. It was 1976, not 1972.
match_headline: Gus Solomons Jr., 84, Dies; a Rare Black Presence in Experimental Dance

text: An obituary on Thursday about the mohel Philip L. Sherman misstated a way Mr. Sherman described himself. He said he was the only motorcycle-riding mohel in the Screen Actors Guild, not the only motorcycle-riding rabbi.
match_headline: Philip L. Sherman, Who Circumcised Thousands of Babies, Dies at 67

text: An article on Friday about an open-air art exhibition on the National Mall misstated the weight of the granite boulder in Wendy Red Star’s installation. It is 6,000 pounds, not 8,000 pounds. It also misstated the title of Ashon T. Crawley, based on information from the University of Virginia website. He is a full professor, not an associate professor.
match_headline: On Our National Mall, New Monuments Tell New Stories

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Italian opera singer Renata Scotto referred incorrectly to Ms. Scotto’s history at La Scala in Milan. Although she vowed in 1964 never to perform there as long as Antonio Ghiringhelli remained general manager, she did in fact perform there several more times during his tenure. The obituary also misstated the year Ms. Scotto performed with Luciano Pavarotti in Ponchielli’s “La Gioconda” at the San Francisco Opera. It was 1979, not 1976.
match_headline: Renata Scotto, Opera Diva Who Inhabited Roles, Dies at 89

text: An article on Sunday about the local debate over The Marion County Record, the Kansas newspaper that was raided by police on Aug. 11, misstated the name of Eric Meyer’s former employer. It was The Milwaukee Journal, not The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.
match_headline: Kansas Newspaper Is Talk of Town, and Not Just for Getting Raided

text: An article on Saturday about the state of emergency order that took effect in the western Canadian province of British Columbia misstated the name of the minister of forests in British Columbia. He is Bruce Ralston, not W. Bruce Ralston.
match_headline: British Columbia Under State of Emergency as Wildfires Rage in Canada

text: An article on Tuesday about the newly ratified contract for pilots at American Airlines misstated the status of contract negotiations at United Airlines. The airline’s pilot union has reached a tentative deal with the company, but the contract has not yet been ratified by the union’s members.
match_headline: American Airlines Pilots Ratify Contract Offering Big Raises

text: An article on Aug. 14 about a 19th-century painting at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, which features a depiction of an enslaved child that was once painted over purposefully, misspelled a term for the network of fine cracks observed on its surface. The term is craquelure, not crackular.
match_headline: Once a Child Star, She Now Leads ‘Murder Tours’ in Hollywood

text: A picture caption in an article on Tuesday about bees that were mummified for nearly 3,000 years, using information from a researcher, misstated the body part depicted. It was the dorsum of the thorax of a mummified bee, not its head and eyes.
match_headline: These Bees Have Been Mummified in Their Cocoons for 3,000 Years

text: An article on Tuesday about the chip design company Arm described incorrectly the more than 30 billion chips that were shipped last fiscal year. The chips used designs licensed by Arm; they were not manufactured by Arm.
match_headline: Arm, the Chip Designer, Files for an I.P.O. Expected to Be Among the Largest

text: An article on Tuesday about Anna May Wong, Hollywood’s first Chinese American movie star, referred incorrectly to the working relationship between Anna May Wong and Douglas Fairbanks. He was her co-star in “The Thief of Bagdad,” not the film’s director. The article also misspelled the name of a German republic. It is Weimar, not Weimer.
match_headline: A Biography Examines Anna May Wong, a Revered and Reviled Chinese American Star

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Bob Jones, a longtime producer of the Newport Folk Festival, misspelled the surnames of two folk musicians. They are Eric Andersen, not Anderson, and Alison Krauss, not Kraus.
match_headline: Bob Jones, Behind-the-Stage Force at Newport Festivals, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the linebacker Maxie Baughan misspelled the surname of one of his teammates on the Los Angeles Rams. He is Rosey Grier, not Greer.
match_headline: Maxie Baughan, Feared Linebacker of the 1960s, Dies at 85

text: An article on Friday about the sentencing of a man who threatened to harm Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene misspelled the name of the judge at sentencing. It is Brenda K. Sannes, not Brenda K. Sammes.
match_headline: Man Who Threatened Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene Gets 3-Month Sentence

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about the Afro-Brazilian artist Emanoel Araújo refers incorrectly to Amanda Carneiro. She is an artistic organizer for the 2024 Venice Biennale, not the Vienna Biennale.
match_headline: He Shined a Light on Other Artists. Now the Light Turns to Him.

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the Harvard astrophysicist, Avi Loeb, misstates how many Earth-like planets astronomers have found around sunlike stars. Though astronomers’ ongoing census of planets suggests that potentially habitable worlds are common, so far, they have found no Earth-like planets.
match_headline: How a Harvard Professor Became the World’s Leading Alien Hunter

text: An article last Sunday about bee­keepers who combat the “save the bees” narrative misstated the role in pollination played by moths, wasps and wild bees. They pollinate wild plants and many crops, not wheat and corn, which are wind pollinated.
match_headline: The Beekeepers Who Don’t Want You to Buy More Bees

text: An article on July 30 about the director Chris­topher Nolan and his film “Oppenheimer” described incorrectly a film scene involving Albert Einstein and J. Robert Oppenheimer near a pond. Einstein walked past Lewis Strauss in silence, not past Oppenheimer.
match_headline: Christopher Nolan and the Contradictions of J. Robert Oppenheimer

text: Because of a transcription error, an interview on Aug. 20 with Matthieu Ricard misquoted one of Ricard’s comments. He said, “once there was a French journalist, very cynical, and he said to me, “This thing about becoming a better person and all that, this is the politics of the ashtray,” not “this is the politics of the hash trade.”
ref_headline: once there was a French journalist, very cynical, and he said to me, “This thing about becoming a better person and all that, this is the politics of the ashtray,
match_headline: Biden and America’s Big Green Push

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a conflict between the maker of a Bella Abzug documentary and Ms. Abzug’s daughter attributed an erroneous distinction to Ms. Abzug’s service in Congress. The first Jewish congresswoman was Florence Prag Kahn, not Ms. Abzug.
match_headline: A Filmmaker Honored Bella Abzug. Her Daughter Says He Took Advantage.

text: An article on Saturday about Jeffrey Clark, a former Justice Department official criminally charged in connection to former President Donald J. Trump, misstated Mr. Clark’s middle initial. He is Jeffrey B. Clark, not Jeffrey A. Clark.
match_headline: Jeffrey Clark, Former Justice Department Official, Booked in Trump Georgia Case

text: An article on Sunday about presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy misstated Mr. Ramaswamy’s position in national polling averages. He is in third place, not second.
match_headline: Ramaswamy, the Millennial Candidate, Has a Lot to Say About His Generation

text: An article on Sunday about the growing Cuban community in Louisville, Ky., misstated the name of a supermarket that stocks Cuban goods. It is Cash Saver, not Casa Savers.
match_headline: The New Little Havana: Why Cuban Migrants Are Moving to Kentucky

text: An article on Sunday about the 16-foot clock outside Trump Tower in misstated in one reference the approximate cost of a permit for the Trump Tower clock. It is $300 per year, not $300 per month.
match_headline: Did You Know About the 16-Foot Trump Tower Clock? Neither Did the City.

text: An article on Saturday about solar panel tax credits in the United States referred incorrectly to a unit of power. Solar batteries are eligible for the federal tax credit as long as they can store at least three kilowatt-hours of electricity, not three kilowatts.
match_headline: At 30%, Solar Panel Tax Credits Are at a High Point for Now

text: An article on Monday about the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra misspelled the given name of a vocal coach involved with the concert. She is Ievgeniia Iermachkova, not Ivgeniia.
match_headline: An Orchestra’s ‘Ode to Joy’ Calls for Ukrainian Freedom

text: An article on Friday about new nations invited to join the BRICS club misstated the status of Argentina, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. They have been invited to join the BRICS group of nations; they have not already joined. Because of an editing error, a picture caption also referred imprecisely to President Ebrahim Raisi. He was pictured on a screen addressing the BRICS summit, but he was not attending the event remotely.
match_headline: Iran, Saudi Arabia and Egypt Invited to Join Emerging Nations Group

text: An article on Tuesday about the Biden administration’s questioning of New York City’s response to the migrant crisis misstated the location of Floyd Bennett Field. It is in Brooklyn, not Queens.
match_headline: Biden Administration Questions New York’s Handling of Migrant Crisis

text: A headline with an article on Saturday about rising mortgage rates misstated the effect that higher rates are having on the housing market. They are cooling demand for existing homes, not new homes.
match_headline: Why Are Mortgage Rates So High, and How Long Will They Stay Up?

text: An article on Monday about Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula and their path to the U.S. Open referred incorrectly to Danielle Collins’s performance at the 2022 Australian Open. She lost in the final in straight sets; she did not come “within a set of winning” the event.
match_headline: The Suddenly Hot ‘Coco and Jessie Show’ Is Ready to Open in New York

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about the space shuttle pilot Karol Bobko misstated in several places the name of a Defense Department project that he joined in 1966. It was the Manned Orbiting Laboratory — not the Manned Operating Laboratory or the Mobile Operating Laboratory.
match_headline: Karol Bobko, First to Pilot the Challenger Into Space, Dies at 85

text: An article on Sunday about attempts throughout history to find the Loch Ness Monster cited a British Library blog post and included a drawing about a purported 12th-century sighting of the Loch Ness Monster. The library has since confirmed that the post was an April Fools’ joke published in 2013 and has affixed a note that “the events it describes are, sadly, fictitious. We hope you had as much fun reading it as we did writing it.” (We might have enjoyed it too much.)
ref_headline: the events it describes are, sadly, fictitious. We hope you had as much fun reading it as we did writing it.
match_headline: The 1,300-Year Search for the Loch Ness Monster

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the ways in which Ukraine’s desire to secure F-16s reflects concerns that the war against Russia could endure for years referred imprecisely to the capabilities of the F-16 jet. The F-16 is not faster in all cases than Ukraine’s current fighters.
match_headline: What’s Stopping Ukraine From Flying F-16s

text: An obituary on April 15 about María Kodama, a writer and translator known for guarding the legacy of her husband, the author Jorge Luis Borges, misstated where she died. It was Buenos Aires — not Vicente López, a suburb of Buenos Aires. This correction was delayed because an email pointing out the error went astray.
match_headline: María Kodama, Keeper of the Borges Legacy, Dies at 86

text: An article on Friday about the one-handed backhand in tennis omitted a prominent player in the U.S. Open who made it to the third round and who uses a one-handed backhand. He is Daniel Evans. (Stan Wawrinka and Grigor Dimitrov are the others.)
match_headline: The One-Handed Backhand Is on the Way to Extinction

text: An article on Thursday about the singer Sadie Dupuis misstated the number of albums Speedy Ortiz has released. “Rabbit Rabbit” is the band’s fourth album, not fifth.
match_headline: Sadie Dupuis Confronts Her Darkest Memories on Speedy Ortiz’s New LP

text: An article on Friday about a cemetery that houses “The Crucifixion” panorama misidentified the schools where Asha Schechter teaches art. He teaches at the Pratt Institute in New York City and the Art Center College of Design in Pasadena, Calif., not at the Otis College of Art and Design.
match_headline: Where Tech Investors Are Buying Up Land, Locals Are Worried

text: An article this weekend on Page 20 about the impact of the war in Ukraine on professional tennis misspells the surname of a Russian tennis player. She is Anastasia Pavlyuchenkova, not Pavyluchenkova. The article also misspells the name of a Ukrainian businessman who backed Elina Svitolina. He is Yuriy Sapronov, not Yuri Shapovolov.
match_headline: How the War in Ukraine Turned Tennis Into a Battlefield

text: An article on Aug. 27 about the Wildenstein family of France used an outdated name for the gallery located in a townhouse formerly owned by the family. It is now known as Lévy Gorvy Dayan, not LGDR.
match_headline: The Inheritance Case That Could Unravel an Art Dynasty

text: An obituary on Aug. 25 about the runner Tom Courtney misidentified the high school he attended. It was Grover Cleveland High School in Caldwell, N.J. — not Livingston High School in Livingston, N.J., which did not exist at the time. The obituary also misstated the official school color of Fordham University, where he was a track star. It is maroon, not red.
match_headline: Tom Courtney, Runner Who Lunged to Grab Olympic Gold, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Friday about David Rowland, a lawyer who secured the recovery of artworks that had been looted by the Nazis, misstated his fee-paying arrangement with his clients, many of whom could not afford to pay hourly fees for his services. He worked on a contingency basis (they paid him if they won a case, but not if they lost), not “on consignment.”
match_headline: Trucks, Cars, Bikes Battling for Space on City Streets

text: An article published on Aug. 20 about housing in Colorado re­ferred incorrectly to a measure of home values in Summit County. The “residential actual value” of homes in the county increased by 63 percent from June 30, 2020, to June 30, 2022, based on informa­tion gathered by the state from the Colorado Assessors’ Associa­tion; that was not the increase in residential property prices in the county in the past year. The article also referred impre­cisely to conservation easements. The legal agreements can be between property owners and land trusts, not only property owners and local governments.
match_headline: Can Affluence and Affordable Housing Coexist in Colorado’s Rockies?

text: An article on Aug. 27 about choreographers and dance referred incorrectly to Banning Bouldin, the head of New Dialect in Nashville, who uses she/they pronouns, not they/them.
match_headline: Choreographers Make Their Own Kind of Administrative Dance

text: A listing in the On the Market feature last Sunday described imprecisely the handling of the flip tax when the home at 323 East Eighth Street, No. 6C, is sold. The buyer or seller can pay it, not just the buyer.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in Manhattan and the Bronx

text: An article on Page 8 about the architect Elizabeth Graziolo misstates the connection of the 19th-century landscape architect Andrew Jackson Downing to the design of Central Park. Though he inspired the park’s architects, Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, he did not contribute to the design.
match_headline: An Architect Who Forges Ahead in Her Own Lane

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Page 11 about Andrew Raftery, a master engraver and professor of printmaking at the Rhode Island School of Design, misstates the name of an auction house. It is Phillips, not Phillips de Pury.
match_headline: How an Engraver Straddles the Centuries

text: An article on Page 10 misstates the nationality of the designer Philippe Malouin. He is British Canadian, not French.
match_headline: Design Classics of the Future

text: An article on Saturday about Paris’s ban on e-scooters referred incorrectly to e-scooter accidents there in 2022. There were 459 people injured and three people killed in accidents involving e-scooters; the e-scooters did not kill three people and injure 459 others.
match_headline: Paris Becomes the First European Capital to Ban Rented Electric Scooters

text: An article on Sunday about the Cold War-era Leopard 1A5 tank that Germany has offered to Ukraine misstated the rank of Andreas Marlow, who oversees Germany’s training program for the Ukrainians. He is a lieutenant general, not a brigadier general.
match_headline: An Obsolete German Tank Seeks a Second Life on Ukraine’s Front Lines

text: An article on Saturday about the resignation of Rosalind Brewer, the chief executive of Walgreens Boots Alliance, misstated Ginger Graham’s previous title. She was group chairman, office of the president of Guidant, not chairman of Guidant.
match_headline: Rosalind Brewer Steps Down as Walgreens Chief After a Short Tenure

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about over-the-counter availability of Narcan misstated the number of overdose deaths in the previous two years in the United States. There were more than 100,000 drug overdose deaths in all each year, higher than the number attributable to opioids alone.
match_headline: Narcan Is Headed to Stores: What You Need to Know

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about the art exhibition “Spora” misidentified the location of the Swiss Institute. It is in the East Village, not Greenwich Village.
match_headline: Lower Manhattan for Less Than $500,000? A Young Couple Knew They’d Need to Compromise.

text: An article on Tuesday about the Holmdel Horn Antenna misidentified the journal in which the initial papers on the cosmic microwave background were published; it was Astrophysical Journal, not Physical Review Letters. The article also misstated the year in which Robert Wilson retired from Bell Labs; it was in 1994, not 1984.
match_headline: Where the Universe Began

text: An article on Sunday about home design manuals that continue to inspire designers misstated the publication year of the book “High-Tech” by Joan Kron and Suzanne Slesin. It was published in 1978, not 1984.
match_headline: Some Old-Fashioned Home-Design Manuals Are Worth Revisiting

text: An article on Sunday about the exhibition “Life Cycles: The Materials of Contemporary Design” at the Museum of Modern Art misstated the materials in a wall panel by Mae-ling Lokko, a designer. The panel is made of mushroom, hemp and kenaf fibers, not mushroom fiber and coconut shells.
ref_headline: Life Cycles: The Materials of Contemporary Design
match_headline: A Panorama of Design

text: An article on Sunday about the popularity of Americana among young designers misstated the birthplace of the parents of Robell Awake, a woodworker in Atlanta. They were from the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, not the country’s Jimma region.
match_headline: Millennials Embrace Bicentennial Style

text: An article on Sunday about the rising use of Yiddish imprecisely characterized current Yiddish speakers. It is not the case that all are monolingual. It also described a Yiddish production of “Fiddler on the Roof” incorrectly. It was staged Off Broadway, not on Broadway.
match_headline: Yiddish Is Having a Moment

text: An obituary on Sunday about the singer and songwriter Jimmy Buffett referred incorrectly to his song “A Pirate Looks at Forty.” It was about Mr. Buffett’s friend Phillip Clark, not Mr. Buffett himself. The obituary also misstated how many authors, including Mr. Buffett, have had books on both The New York Times’s fiction and nonfiction best-seller lists. It is more than a dozen, not six.
match_headline: Jimmy Buffett, Roguish Bard of Island Escapism, Is Dead at 76

text: An obituary on Monday and in some editions on Sunday about Bill Richardson, the former congressman and two-term governor of New Mexico, misstated the year he was first elected to Congress. It was 1982, not 1980. The version of the obituary that appeared in print on Sunday also referred incorrectly to Mr. Richardson’s survivors. He is not survived by a daughter.
match_headline: Bill Richardson, Champion of Americans Held Overseas, Dies at 75

text: An obituary on Sunday about the documentary filmmaker Nancy Buirski misidentified the critic who called her film “The Rape of Recy Taylor” “a stirring, infuriating marvel,” It was Scout Tafoya, not Roger Ebert.
match_headline: Nancy Buirski, Award-Winning Documentary Filmmaker, Dies at 78

text: An obituary on Aug. 13 about the philanthropist Joan Kaplan Davidson referred incorrectly to Robert Livingston, whose descendant built a manor house in the Hudson Valley where Ms. Davidson lived. Although he helped draft the Declaration of Independence, he was not a signer.
match_headline: Joan Kaplan Davidson, Philanthropist Who Championed New York, Dies at 96

text: An article on Wednesday about swimming pools in New Jersey turning green misstated the title of Jonathan Lally, a spokesman for the U.S. Coast Guard. He is a petty officer, not a private.
match_headline: What Turned New Jersey’s Pools Green? A Man and His Drone, Police Say.

text: An obituary on Wednesday for the playwright Nathan Louis Jackson misstated part of Mr. Jackson’s job history before he moved to New York in 2007. He worked in a barbecue restaurant in Manhattan, Kan.; he did not manage it.
match_headline: Nathan Louis Jackson, Writer for the Theater and TV, Dies at 44

text: An article on Thursday about the Sotheby’s auction of Freddie Mercury’s things misstated the duration of the sale. It ran for more than four hours, not for more than four and a half hours.
match_headline: Queen Lyrics and Freddie Mercury’s Grand Piano Soar at Auction

text: A graphic accompanying an April 30 article about pedestrian and cyclist deaths misstated the traffic death rates in some foreign countries. The data is for deaths per 100 million miles traveled, not per 100 million kilometers traveled
match_headline: When a Walkable City Becomes a Death Trap
