text: An article on Monday about torrential rains that left thousands stranded at Burning Man festival misstated the name of the piano bar where the musician known as ELEW performed. It is called the Black Rock Piano Lounge, not Playa Piano Bar.
match_headline: Amid Rain and Mud, Climactic ‘Burn’ Is Delayed at Burning Man Fest

text: An article on Tuesday about the trial of ex-Trump aide Peter Navarro referred incorrectly to interactions between the House committee investigating the Capitol attack and two officials from whom it sought testimony. While Mark Meadows, President Donald J. Trump’s final chief of staff, turned over more than 9,000 documents to the panel, his deputy, Dan Scavino, did not provide the committee with records. It is not the case that both men negotiated terms to provide documents. The error was repeated in an article on Friday about Mr. Navarro’s conviction.
match_headline: Peter Navarro to Face Contempt Trial Over Defiance of Jan. 6 Committee

text: An article on Friday about Charles Busch’s memoir misstated the cause of death for Charles Busch’s sister Margaret. She died of heart disease, not cancer.
match_headline: Confessions of a Drag Legend: Charles Busch’s Memoir Is Here, Darling

text: An article on Friday about a retrospective of Ed Ruscha’s artwork at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City misstated the year Ed Ruscha was born. It was 1937, not 1935.
match_headline: The Deadpan Laureate of American Art

text: An article on Page 52 about the gender gap in higher education misspells the name of a video game. It is Valorant, not Valarint.
match_headline: Listen: Talk to Whales, Back-to-School Tips, and Some Advice for China

text: A review on Aug. 27 about “Young and Restless,” by Mattie Kahn, misspelled the surname of the author of the memoir “A New England Girlhood.” She was Lucy Larcom, not Lacrom.
match_headline: Girls to the Front!

text: An article on Wednesday about Iranian American families’ views on education and financial success misstated the grandparent from whom the writer Jason Rezaian received financial support. It was his grandmother, not his grandfather.
match_headline: When Financial Independence Isn’t Always the Goal

text: An article on Tuesday about the late arrival of rescuers for some Moroccan earthquake victims transposed the given and family names of a village resident. He is Omar Ouchahed, not Ouchahed Omar.
match_headline: Fury as Quake Help Finally Arrives: ‘How Many Hours Has It Been?’

text: An article on Tuesday about the arrest in London of a man suspected of spying for China misidentified the prime minister of China. He is Li Qiang, not Li Keqiang. Li Keqiang stepped down from the role in March.
match_headline: U.K.’s Arrest of Suspected Spy Fuels Calls for Tougher Stance on China

text: An article on Sunday about migrants in Massachusetts referred imprecisely to Massachusetts’s right-to-shelter law. It guarantees families with children a place to stay if they meet certain criteria. It does not guarantee all families with children a place to stay.
match_headline: As Migrants Are Placed Around Massachusetts, Towns Are Welcoming but Worried

text: An article on Monday about the soaring costs of child care in New York City misstated the rate Doris Irizarry was making for each of the six children who attended her day care while it was open. It was $3 an hour per child, not $3 a day per child.
match_headline: How Soaring Child Care Costs Are Crushing New Yorkers

text: An article on Monday about 18th-century heirlooms held at the U.S. State Department building misstated the middle initial of the deputy chief of protocol and curator who transformed the look of its Diplomatic Reception Rooms. He was Clement E. Conger, not Clement C. Conger.
match_headline: Atop the State Department, Democracy’s Treasures Can Complicate or Clarify Messages

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misstated the day that “Welcome to Wrexham” is airing on FX. It aired Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Welcome to Wrexham’ and the MTV Video Music Awards

text: An article on Wednesday about Kim Jong-un’s bulletproof train referred incorrectly to Kim Jong-un’s trips to China since becoming North Korea’s leader. Not all were by train; he flew to Dalian, China, in 2018.
match_headline: Bulletproof, Slow and Full of Wine: Kim Jong-un’s Mystery Train

text: An article on Wednesday about Apple’s newest iPhone misstated the price of Apple’s latest iPhone Pro Max. It is $1,199, not $1,099. The article also misstated the day that Apple unveiled its latest product line. It was Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: Apple Unveils iPhone 15 and Switches to USB-C Charger

text: An article on Tuesday about a U.S. judge’s ruling that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau exceeded its authority in trying to examine whether banks are discriminating against Black Americans and other minorities misspelled the surname of the judge who presided over the case. He is J. Campbell Barker, not Baker.
match_headline: Federal Court Says Consumer Watchdog Can’t Check Banks for Discrimination

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about using an infrared-converted camera to photograph the U.S. Open tennis tournament misidentified an on-court official in one of the photographs. He is a chair umpire, not a line judge.
match_headline: Seeing the U.S. Open in an Unusual Light

text: An obituary on March 27, 2021, about the writer Larry McMurtry, using information from his friend and writing partner, Diana Ossana, misstated where he died. It was Tucson, Ariz., not Archer City, Texas. This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: Larry McMurtry, Novelist of the American West, Dies at 84

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Tuesday about fire spotters in Montana misidentified the location of the Flathead Hot Shot Crew. The crew is based out of the Flathead National Forest, near — not in — Glacier National Park.
match_headline: ‘I Hailed a Cab at My Hotel Near Central Park to Go to 47th Street’

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about musicals, plays and festivals happening in the fall and spring misstates the month when “Days of Wine and Roses” is scheduled to begin performances on Broadway. It is January, not February.
match_headline: Musicals, Plays and Festivals to Take In This Fall and Spring

text: An article on Page 41 this weekend about dance shows coming this fall misstates the dates that the Gibney Company will perform at New York Live Arts. Those performances are Dec. 14-17, not Dec. 14-20. It also misstates Sonya Tayeh’s role in “Is It Thursday Yet?” She is the director and co-choreographer, not the co-director and choreographer.
match_headline: Dance Performances, Festivals and More Coming This Fall

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the death of Elijah McClain misstates the timing of an interview with Vanessa Wilson, the former police chief of Aurora, Colo. It was in July 2022, not November 2022.
match_headline: Former N.Y.C. Buildings Chief Expected to Face Bribery-Related Charges

text: An article on Sept. 10 about the gender gap in higher education omitted part of Laurie Essig’s academic title. She is a professor of gender, sexuality and feminist studies, not only gender and sexuality studies.
match_headline: ‘There Was Definitely a Thumb on the Scale to Get Boys’

text: An article on Aug. 20 about the Welsh soccer club Wrexham A.F.C. misstated the circumstances of Paul Mullin’s recovery from an injury. Though Rob McElhenney offered his home, Mullin opted not to stay there.
match_headline: What Is ‘Welcome to Wrexham’ Doing to Soccer?

text: A map with an article on Friday about the energy executive Sultan al-Jaber omitted borders for Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia.
match_headline: Meet the Oil Man in Charge of Leading the World Away From Oil

text: An article on Sunday about the death of a toddler at a day care center in the Bronx misidentified a shopping district. It is Kingsbridge Road, not Kingsbridge Avenue.
match_headline: 1-Year-Old Dead and Man in Custody After Opioid Exposure at Bronx Day Care

text: An article on Saturday about President Biden’s support of the striking United Auto Workers overstated the electoral impact of Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory in Michigan in the 2020 presidential race. While the victory was important, he would have prevailed in the Electoral College even if he had lost the state.
match_headline: Biden Defends Striking Autoworkers: They Deserve a ‘Fair Share’

text: An article on Monday about the effect the restart of student loan payments could have on the economy misstated the age of a high school teacher in Nazareth, Pa. Phil Esempio is 55, not 65.
match_headline: Will Restart of Student Loan Payments Be the Last Straw for Consumers?

text: An article on Saturday about the Internal Revenue Service’s decision to freeze a pandemic-era employer tax benefit referred incorrectly to eligibility requirements for the benefit. They were required to show that their operations were fully or partly suspended in 2020 or part of 2021 — or report a significant decline in revenue during that time — not both.
match_headline: I.R.S. Freezes Pandemic-Era Tax Credit Amid Fraud Fears

text: An article on Saturday about Spain’s women’s soccer team’s list of demands addressed to the Royal Spanish Football Federation misstated the number of signatories to the statement demanding further changes at the Royal Spanish Football Federation. They included 21 of the 23 women in Spain’s 2023 World Cup squad, not the entire team.
match_headline: Spain’s Women’s Team Demands Full Reorganization of National Federation

text: An article on Thursday about the artist Jim Nutt, based on information provided by Mr. Nutt, misstated the time he was working on a painting. It was four years, not seven. The glassiness he was referring to was of hot-pressed paper, not cold-pressed paper. And Mr. Nutt’s studio is in Evanston, Ill., not Wilmette, where his home is.
match_headline: Jim Nutt’s Art Remains a Mystery. Even to Him.

text: An article on Monday about concerns raised over the origins of artifacts in a traveling Greek art exhibition omitted a reporter who contributed reporting from St. Petersburg, Fla. She is Geraldine Fabrikant.

An obituary on Sept. 3 about the sailor Bill Pinkney referred incorrectly to the route of the Cuban schooner Amistad, a replica of which he was involved in building. It was commandeered by West African slaves as they were being transported from Havana to a Caribbean plantation — not as they were being transported “to the Caribbean.”
match_headline: Bill Pinkney, Globe-Circling Sailor Who Set a Racial Mark, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Sept. 7 about the Nobel Prize-winning pharmacologist Ferid Murad referred incorrectly to cyclic guanosine monophosphate. It is a molecule, not an enzyme.
match_headline: Ferid Murad, Nobelist Who Saw How a Gas Can Aid the Heart, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Sept. 10 about the Zulu leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi referred incorrectly to the final report of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which the South African government had set up to document abuses of the apartheid era. Mr. Buthelezi’s name appeared there several times; it is not the case that the authors dropped his name from the final report.
match_headline: Mangosuthu Buthelezi Dies at 95; Zulu Nationalist and a Mandela Rival

text: An article on Tuesday about a meeting between the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Elon Musk misidentified the location of the meeting. The two met at a Tesla factory, not the Tesla headquarters.
match_headline: Benjamin Netanyahu and Elon Musk Meet, as Both Seek to Deflect Criticism

text: An article on Monday about Finland’s president cautioning Europe against complacency toward Russia’s invasion of Ukraine referred imprecisely to conscription in Sweden and reserve forces in Finland. Sweden has partial conscription for men and women, not a fully voluntary force. Some Finnish reservists participate in military exercises, but not all of them twice a year.
match_headline: Finland’s President, No Stranger to Russia, Warns Europe About Complacency

text: An article on Monday about the popularity of tiny homes on social media misstated the average monthly rent of a Tokyo apartment in U.S. dollars. A 750-square-foot apartment in Tokyo itself — not the city and its surrounding area — rents for roughly $1,900 a month.
match_headline: It’s Cozy and Cheap, but Do You Want to Live in This Social Media Magnet?

text: An article on Tuesday about Fiji’s win over Australia at the Rugby World Cup misstated the number of Olympic medals Fiji has won. It is three, not two.
match_headline: When Fiji Beats Australia, and It Almost Isn’t an Upset

text: An obituary on Saturday about the artist Fernando Botero referred incorrectly to his painting “Mona Lisa, Age Twelve.” While it was displayed at the Museum of Modern Art in 1961, that was two years before Leonardo da Vinci’s “Mona Lisa” was on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art — not while it was being shown there. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Fernando Botero, Artist of Whimsical Rotundity, Is Dead at 91

text: An obituary on Friday about the singer Larry Chance misstated the day he died. It was Sept. 5, not Sept. 6.
match_headline: Larry Chance, Who Helped Keep Doo-Wop Alive for Decades, Dies at 82

text: An obituary on Monday about the oyster farmer Jules Melancon misstated the name of the town in Louisiana where he lived. It is Cut Off, not Cutoff.
match_headline: Jules Melancon, Oyster Farmer Who Tried Something New, Dies at 65

text: A picture with an obituary on Sunday about Bobby Schiffman, the longtime manager of the Apollo Theater in Harlem, was published in error. It showed the cover of James Brown’s album “Live at the Apollo, Volume 2,” released in 1968 — not, as the caption said, the original “Live at the Apollo,” released in 1963.
match_headline: Bobby Schiffman, Guiding Force of the Apollo Theater, Dies at 94

text: An article on Tuesday about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s second visit to the United States described imprecisely Russia’s comments about NATO in the run-up to the invasion. It demanded that NATO agree not to expand eastward and guarantee not to station weapons in several eastern member countries, not that those members leave the alliance.
match_headline: In U.S., Zelensky Will Make Case for More Aid, and Offer Thanks

text: An article on Wednesday about a new online safety law in Britain misstated the fine companies can face for violating Britain’s online safety law. It is 18 million pounds, or about $22.3 million, or up to 10 percent of global revenue, whichever is more, not 18 million pounds.
match_headline: Britain Passes Sweeping New Online Safety Law

text: A column on Thursday about Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot, using information from Google, misstated a caveat about Bard. It is not true that in certain cases — such as when users ask Bard a question about their email, then ask follow-up questions based on Bard’s response — human reviewers could end up seeing those users’ personal information.
match_headline: Google’s Bard Just Got More Powerful. It’s Still Erratic.

text: An article on Tuesday about the oral history of a small group of nomadic people living in Indonesia’s rainforest misstated what kind of tool the researchers used to record the Punan’s movements. The scientists used GPS belts, not GPS ankle bracelets.
match_headline: A Vanishing Nomadic Clan, With a Songlike Language All Their Own

text: An article on Friday about the timeline of Rupert Murdoch’s career misstated how much the Walt Disney Company paid to acquire most of 21st Century Fox’s assets in 2019. It was $71.3 billion, not $71.3 million.
match_headline: How Rupert Murdoch Built His Media Empire

text: An article on Sept. 16 about protests against migrants in New York City misstated the percentage of migrants living in city homeless shelters that are housed at a single facility. Two percent of the migrants living in city shelters are staying on Staten Island, but not all of them are at St. John Villa Academy.
match_headline: Suing. Heckling. Cursing. N.Y.C. Protests Against Migrants Escalate

text: An article on Thursday about protecting ocean life misstated several actions taking place at the United Nations this week in regards to the High Seas Treaty. Delegates signed the treaty, but did not ratify it; ratification is done by the national governments of the signing countries. The article also described imprecisely the involvement of the United States. The United States did sign the treaty, but it has not been ratified.
match_headline: The Importance of Protecting Ocean Life

text: An article on Page 38 this weekend about research on animals’ use of language refers incorrectly to Robert C. Berwick’s field of study. He is a computer scientist and computational linguist, not a linguist.
match_headline: The Animals Are Talking. What Does It Mean?

text: An article on Page 94 about four of this season’s books refers incorrectly to the artist Mosie Romney. Romney uses they/them pronouns, not she/her.
match_headline: What Happens on Page 76 in This Season’s Books?

text: An article on Page 142 about Chinatown misstates the number of attacks on people of Asian descent that were reported nationally to the Stop AAPI Hate coalition between March 2020 and December 2021. There were 10,905 incidents, not 10,095.
match_headline: Saving Chinatown, While Also Making It Their Own

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 150 about a Harlem townhouse refers incorrectly to an artwork by Huma Bhabha. It is a sculpture, not a photo.
An obituary on Thursday about the architect Raymond Moriyama referred incorrectly to Michi Moriyama, one of his survivors. He is Mr. Moriyama’s son, not his daughter.
match_headline: Raymond Moriyama, Designer of Humane Public Spaces, Dies at 93

text: An article last Sunday about Ire­land’s budget surplus misstated the number of inpatient beds in the national children’s hospital in Dub­lin. The hospital, which is under construction, is expected to have 380 beds, not 3,000.
match_headline: Ireland’s Latest Fiscal Headache: What to Do With 10 Billion Euros

text: An article on Sept. 10 about the early years of New York City Ballet referred incorrectly to the number of dancers who performed with the company in its opening season in 1948 and are still alive. There are at least four known, not three, as Rita Karlin Brandt, 93, made clear when she spoke to The New York Times after publication.
match_headline: A Physical and Spiritual Awakening (but No Steady Paycheck)

text: An article on Page 142 about Chinatown misstates the number of attacks on people of Asian descent that were reported nationally to the Stop AAPI Hate coalition between March 2020 and December 2021. There were 10,905 incidents, not 10,095.
match_headline: YouTube Restores Donald Trump’s Account Privileges

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 150 about a Harlem townhouse refers incorrectly to an artwork by Huma Bhabha. It is a sculpture, not a photo.

An article on Sunday about mercury poisoning caused by gold mining misidentified the source of a study on the percentage of workers involved in gold mining in Suriname. The research was conducted by the Free University of Amsterdam, not the University of Amsterdam.
match_headline: Gold’s Deadly Truth: Much Is Mined With Mercury

text: An article on Monday about the use of masks in hospitals, relying on information provided by staff at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, misstated the circumstances under which workers are required to wear masks. The hospital has dropped the mask requirements imposed during the height of the Covid-19 pandemic.
match_headline: In Hospitals, Viruses Are Everywhere. Masks Are Not.

text: An article on Wednesday about fire conditions in Australia misstated the level of heat in some towns. They reported temperatures of 16 degrees Celsius above normal, which is 29 degrees Fahrenheit above normal, not 60 degrees Fahrenheit above normal.
match_headline: As El Niño Arrives, Australian Region Sees ‘Catastrophic’ Fire Conditions

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about the fashion designer Michael Leva, using information from Getty Images, misidentified the two men shown with him in a 1988 photo. They are the designer Ken Laughran and Lawrence Chua of Women’s Wear Daily, not Mr. Leva’s assistants. The caption also omitted the name of the model in the photo. She is Suzanne Lanza.
match_headline: Michael Leva, Who Found Fashion Fame Early, Is Dead at 62

text: An article on Sept. 7 about a missile strike on a street market in Kostyantynivka, Ukraine, overstated what is known about the origin of the missile. While President Volodymyr Zelensky attributed the strike to Russia, which had shelled the town in recent months, evidence uncovered later suggests an errant Ukrainian missile may have hit the market. A spokesman for Ukraine’s armed forces said the country’s security service was investigating the episode.
match_headline: At a Bustling Market in Ukraine, a Huge Fireball Leaves Scenes of Carnage

text: An article on Monday about Ukraine’s use of a new shipping route misstated the amount of Ukrainian agricultural products and iron ore that Oleksandr Kubrakov said ships would export. It is 127,000 metric tons, not 127 metric tons.
match_headline: Amid Black Sea Threats, Ukraine Steps Up Use of New Shipping Route

text: An article on Thursday about a police officer in London charged with murder for fatally shooting a Black man referred imprecisely to the car Chris Kaba was driving. It was not registered in his name.
match_headline: U.K. Police Officer to Be Charged With Murder in Shooting of Black Man

text: An article on Sept. 16 about a new study on the effectiveness of MDMA for treatment of post-traumatic stress syndrome misstated the title of Dr. Akua Prieto Brown. She is the medical prescriber at the Alchemy Community Therapy Center in Oakland, Calif., not the medical director.
match_headline: MDMA Therapy Inches Closer to Approval

text: An article on Tuesday about Joshua Frankel’s animation for a video display at Moynihan Train Hall misstated the period of time that Mr. Frankel’s grandfather worked at the James A. Farley Post Office. His paternal grandfather worked there for one decade, not two.
match_headline: A Kinetic Cloud of Humanity for Moynihan Train Hall

text: An article on Thursday about speakers and panelists who spoke at The New York Times Climate Forward event referred incompletely to the creation of a perennial rice. The rice was developed in a partnership between the Land Institute and researchers in Yunnan, China, not solely by the Land Institute.
match_headline: In Large and Small Ways, These Leaders Are Taking On Climate Change

text: An article on Wednesday about high electricity prices in Texas misstated the given name of an analyst who follows energy markets for Public Citizen. He is Tyson Slocum, not Tyron.
match_headline: In Summer Heat, ‘Artificial Shortages’ in Texas Grid May Have Cost $8 Billion

text: An article on Sept. 18 about how the meaning of lucky numbers could encourage charitable contributions did not explain that some people cannot deduct the full amount of their charitable contributions. The amount of the donation and household income can affect eligibility.
match_headline: The Simple Nudge That Raised Median Donations by 80%

text: An article last Thursday about a dinner celebrating the collaboration between the artist Jean-Michael Othoniel and Dior misstated, in some copies, the year in which Charlize Theron became the face of Dior’s J’adore perfume. It was 2004, not 1999.
match_headline: A Dinner That Smelled Like Thousands of Flowers

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about Dick Clark, who as a United States senator from Iowa pushed for a more liberal foreign policy, particularly toward Africa, misspelled the surname of a former South African chief propagandist. He was Eschel Rhoodie, not Roodie.
match_headline: Dick Clark, Iowan Who Walked 1,300 Miles for a Senate Seat, Dies at 95

text: An article on Tuesday about threats of development to a fossil-rich desert in Peru misstated the professional title of César Chacaltana of Peru’s Geological, Mining and Metallurgical Institute. He is director of regional geology, not director of paleontology.
match_headline: In Peru, a Fossil-Rich Desert Faces Unruly Development

text: An article on Tuesday about unresolved traumas left by the 1989 Romanian revolution misstated the fate of a security agent who interrogated a participant at a protest. The agent, who later became a municipal official, is still alive and was declared a hero, not a martyr, of the revolution.
match_headline: In Romania, the Traumas of a Bloody Revolution Still Cast a Long Shadow

text: An article on Friday about President Biden’s direct condemnation of former President Donald J. Trump at an appearance in Arizona misstated the type of workers Mr. Trump met with in Michigan. Mr. Trump met with autoworkers at a nonunion plant.
match_headline: Biden Issues a Blistering Attack on Trump

text: An article on Thursday about Cliven Bundy misstated the location of his ranch. It is in southeastern Nevada, not southwestern Nevada.
match_headline: Cliven Bundy and His Cows Continue to Flout the Law

text: An article on Friday about a French cultural counselor’s expansion of French artists’ residencies in New York misspelled the surname of an architect. He was Rafael Guastavino, not Gustavino.
match_headline: In New York, Creating a ‘Port of Entry’ for Young French Artists

text: An article on Sunday about Congress narrowly averting a government shutdown misstated Republicans’ status in the House. They hold a small majority, not a small minority.
match_headline: Vulnerable Republicans Try to Head Off Blame for Shutdown

text: An article on Thursday about antimatter referred incorrectly to some attributes of antiparticles. They have masses and spins identical to those of regular particles but opposite electrical charges, not opposite spins and charges. The positron discovered by Paul Dirac had a mass and spin identical to that of an electron but an opposite electrical charge, not an opposite spin and charge. The antiprotons used in the ALPHA experiment came from the CERN Proton Synchrotron, not the Large Hadron Collider.
match_headline: Nothing’s the Matter With Antimatter, New Experiment Confirms

text: An article on Saturday about Senator Bob Menendez and positions he has taken on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee misstated the outcome of a prior federal corruption investigation into Mr. Menendez. The case ended in a mistrial, not an acquittal.
match_headline: For Biden, Menendez’s Troubles May Clear Foreign Policy Roadblocks

text: An article on Saturday about candidates seeking to fill Senator Dianne Feinstein’s seat in Congress misstated the year that Representative Barbara Lee was first elected to Congress. It was 1998, not 1988.
match_headline: Feinstein’s Death Intensifies Fight for a Coveted California Senate Seat

text: An article on Monday about the lead negotiator for SAG-AFTRA misstated Donna Langley’s job title. She is the chief content officer of NBCUniversal Studio Group, not the chief content officer of Universal Pictures.
match_headline: Longtime Union Leader Steps Fully Into Hollywood’s Spotlight

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misspelled the surname of a host on the television show “Catfish.” He is Nev Schulman, not Shulman.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Catfish’ and ‘Sullivan’s Crossing’

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about tension surrounding hunting rules in New Zealand referred incorrectly to New Zealand’s native mammals. Bats are a mammal native to New Zealand; it is not the case that New Zealand has no native land mammals.
match_headline: Should Children Join the Killing in New Zealand’s War on Invasive Species?

text: An article on Tuesday about a viral video of Secretary of State Antony Blinken playing guitar misidentified Jay Carney’s employer. He is the head of policy and communications for Airbnb, not Amazon.
match_headline: When Mr. Secretary Loves to Rock

text: An obituary on Monday about Robert Day, the founder of the giant California asset-management firm TCW Group, misstated the size of a donation he made to Claremont McKenna College, his alma mater, in 2007. It was a gift of $200 million, not $500 million.
match_headline: Robert Day, Financier and Philanthropist, Dies at 79

text: An article on Wednesday about a group of Indigenous women in Greenland who say Danish doctors inserted intrauterine devices without their consent misstated the name of a Danish broadcaster. It is DR, not DK.
match_headline: They Were Given IUDs as Children Without Their Consent. Now, They Want Compensation.

text: An article on Tuesday about a Texas bishop’s criticism of the Vatican and the pope described incorrectly Bishop Joseph Strickland’s following on X, formerly Twitter. It is not more than twice the number of Catholics in his diocese.
match_headline: ‘Two Trains Charging at Each Other’: A Texas Bishop Takes On the Pope

text: An article on Tuesday about the death of a 1-year-old girl in Brooklyn misstated the recommendations made to the judge by the Administration for Children’s Services. A.C.S. recommended that the parents be allowed to have unsupervised visits, not supervised visits.
match_headline: Judge Let Abusive Parents Keep Daughter. Days Later, She Was Dead.

text: An article on Wednesday about Spotify’s expansion into audiobooks misspelled the surname of the vice president and publisher of Hachette Audio. She is Ana Maria Allessi, not Alessi.
match_headline: Spotify Gave Subscribers Music and Podcasts. Next: Audiobooks.

text: An article on Sept. 27 about a Google trial shrouded in secrecy misstated the name of a media trade group. It is Digital Content Next, not Digital Context Next.
match_headline: ‘Unprecedented’ Secrecy in Google Trial as Tech Giants Push to Limit Disclosures

text: An article on Thursday about the winners of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry misspelled the name of a chemist. He is Jonathan Owen, not Owens.
match_headline: Nobel Prize in Chemistry Awarded to 3 Scientists for Exploring the Nanoworld

text: An article on Thursday about a record low in Antarctica’s sea ice annual peak level characterized incorrectly the cycle of melting described by Marilyn Raphael. It is a positive feedback loop (because the product of the reaction leads to an increase in that reaction) not a negative feedback loop.
match_headline: Where’s All the Antarctic Sea Ice? Annual Peak Is the Lowest Ever Recorded.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the United Automobile Workers president, Shawn Fain, misstated the events leading to the union’s first direct election of its top leaders. While the election was overseen by a court-appointed monitor, the format was approved by union members, not mandated by the monitor. (The error also appeared in an article on March 26 about Mr. Fain’s victory.) The article also misidentified the organizer of a 1979 counterprotest in Greensboro, N.C., against the Ku Klux Klan. It was the Communist Workers Party, not the Communist Party.
match_headline: New U.A.W. Chief Has a Nonnegotiable Demand: Eat the Rich

text: A picture caption with a Critic’s Pick theater review on Wednesday about “Jaja’s African Hair Braiding” misidentified the actor seated on the right side of the salon. She is Lakisha May, not Kalyne Coleman.
match_headline: Review: At ‘Jaja’s,’ Where Everybody Knows Your Mane

text: An article on Page 6 this weekend about a new musical inspired by the singer Alicia Keys’s life misspells the name of her skin care line. It is Keys Soulcare, not Key SoulCare.
match_headline: Alicia Keys Steps Into a New Spotlight

text: An article on Oct. 1 about Beyoncé referred incorrectly to the designer of her bee costume. It was inspired by Thierry Mugler’s earlier work and designed by Casey Cadwallader for the Mugler brand. It was not designed by Thierry Mugler.
match_headline: A Silvery, Shimmering Summer of Beyoncé

text: An article on Oct. 1 about the Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu referred incorrectly to the date an Air France flight left from Tel Aviv. It was shortly before July 4, 1976, not on July 4, 1976.
match_headline: Benjamin Netanyahu’s Two Decades of Power, Bluster and Ego

text: An article on Sunday about a boy believed to be the latest incarnation of a Tibetan spiritual leader misstated the significance of the Bogd. It is considered one of the most important senior positions in Tibetan Buddhism, but it is not one of the three most important figures overall.
match_headline: The 8-Year-Old Boy at the Heart of a Fight Over Tibetan Buddhism

text: An article on Oct. 3 about a synod in the Catholic Church misstated the name of a synod in one instance and misstated the month it occurred. It is a synod on the Pan-Amazon region, not the Pan-American region, and it occurred in October 2019, not June 2019.
match_headline: What Is a Synod in the Catholic Church? And Why Does This One Matter?

text: An article on Tuesday about the appeal of a U.K. asylum policy ruling misidentified the court that issued a June 2023 decision on the U.K.’s policy of deporting asylum seekers to Rwanda. It was made by the Court of Appeal, not by Britain’s Supreme Court.
match_headline: What to Know as the U.K. Appeals a Ruling on Its Rwanda Asylum Policy

text: An article on Monday about pro-Palestinian and pro-Israel demonstrations in New York City referred incorrectly to Loren Mindell. He is a man.
match_headline: After Attack on Israel, Politicians Are Asked, ‘Which Side Are You On?’

text: A picture caption on Saturday with an article about the advantage a home team might have in the Ryder Cup, using information from The Associated Press, misidentified the golfer in the photograph. He is Patrick Cantlay, not Max Homa.

An article on Thursday about Nathan Lane’s roles in A24 films described incorrectly the arrangement that permitted Mr. Lane to discuss “Dicks: The Musical.” It is an interim agreement between SAG-AFTRA, the actor’s union, and the producers of the film, not a waiver.
match_headline: Hollywood Finally Figures Out What to Do With Nathan Lane

text: An article on Sunday about the New York Liberty misstated the year a New York-based team last won a basketball championship. It was 1976, not 1973.
match_headline: These Women Could Make New York Champions Again

text: An article on Tuesday about Hamas taking 150 Israelis hostage misstated the name of the Kalderon family’s kibbutz. It is Nir Oz, not Nahal Oz.
match_headline: ‘I Just Hope That They Are Alive’: How Hamas Abducted 150 Israelis

text: An article on Tuesday about a change to driver’s licenses in Puerto Rico referred incorrectly in one instance to the legal significance of a driver’s license. It is a proof of a person’s legal residence, not citizenship.
match_headline: Why Puerto Rico Is Adding ‘USA’ to Its Driver’s Licenses

text: An article on Friday about Emma Tucker, the new editor in chief of The Wall Street Journal, misstated the town where Ms. Tucker grew up. It was Lewes, England, not London.
match_headline: The Remaking of The Wall Street Journal

text: An article on Wednesday about an investment firm’s stake in Premier League soccer misidentified the college that Josh Wander attended. He attended the University of Florida, not the University of Miami.
match_headline: The Mystery Company With One Foot in the Premier League

text: An article on Wednesday about the ways that the television show “Survivor" is adapting to climate change misstated the number of “Survivor” winners included in “Winners at War.” It was 20, not 10.
match_headline: 45 Seasons in, ‘Survivor’ Faces Realities of a Changing Planet

text: An article on Oct. 3 about the physicist who developed the theory of nuclear fission, Lise Meitner, misstated Germany’s actions toward Austria at the time; Germany annexed Austria, it did not invade it.
match_headline: Why the ‘Mother of the Atomic Bomb’ Never Won a Nobel Prize

text: An article on Tuesday about the increasing number of bears and bear attacks in Montana and neighboring states misstated the population of grizzlies in Montana. Wyoming and Montana together are home to an estimated 2,100 grizzly bears, not Montana alone. The article also described incorrectly a type of bear that attacked a man in Italy. It was a brown bear, not a Marsican brown bear.
match_headline: Grizzlies Are Coming to Town. Can the West Live With Them?

text: An obituary on Oct. 5 about the children’s author and illustrator Ed Young misstated the number of Caldecott Medals he won in his career. He won one Caldecott Medal and two Caldecott Honors, not three Caldecott Medals.
match_headline: Ed Young Dies at 91; Infused His Illustrations With Chinese Tradition

text: An article on Monday about allies of President Biden and their efforts to stop third-party and independent presidential candidacies referred incorrectly to Cornel West. He is a former Harvard professor, not a current one.
match_headline: Fearing Third-Party Spoilers vs. Trump, Biden Allies Try to Squash Them

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the testimony of a top adviser to Sam Bankman-Fried, the FTX founder, at his fraud trial carried an incorrect byline. The article was written by David Yaffe-Bellany, Matthew Goldstein and J. Edward Moreno, not by Mark Mazzetti, Ronen Bergman and David D. Kirkpatrick.
match_headline: Caroline Ellison, Adviser to Sam Bankman-Fried, Says He ‘Directed’ Her to Commit Crimes

text: An article on Thursday about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s visit to NATO headquarters to urge continued aid to Ukraine misidentified one of the countries leading a coalition to donate F-16 jets to Ukraine. It is Denmark, not Norway.
match_headline: At NATO, Zelensky Secures More Ukraine Aid as Allies Balance Support for Israel

text: An article on Thursday about pieces of an asteroid collected by NASA misspelled the first name of a technician. She is Maritza Montoya, not Moritza.
match_headline: NASA Unveils First Glimpse of ‘Scientific Treasure’ Collected From Asteroid

text: An obituary on Sept. 24 about the celebrated clown Jango Edwards, using information from his wife, omitted the name of a survivor. In addition to those named, he is survived by a sister, Pennyanne Edwards.
match_headline: Jango Edwards, Clown Who Challenged His Art Form, Dies at 73

text: An article on Friday about Representative Steve Scalise’s withdrawal from consideration for speaker of the House misstated the state Dusty Johnson represents in the House. It is South Dakota, not North Dakota.
match_headline: Scalise Withdraws as Speaker Candidate, Leaving G.O.P. in Chaos

text: An article on Friday about two families who moved states because of state politics misstated the amount that the police department’s budget was cut in 2020. It was reduced by $15.1 million, not $20 million. The article also referred incorrectly to the increase in the Huckins family’s property taxes. While the family cited taxes as one of the reasons for their decision to leave Oregon, the increases occurred over the span of many years, not in recent years.
match_headline: Two Families Got Fed Up With Their States’ Politics. So They Moved Out.

text: An article on Friday about attempts by tech industry groups to block new laws regulating children and social media misstated the name of a nonprofit children’s group that backed California’s online children’s privacy law. It is Fairplay, not Fairplay for Kids.
match_headline: New Laws on Kids and Social Media Are Stymied by Industry Lawsuits

text: An article on Thursday about the new executive director of the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts referred imprecisely to the number of recordings of Broadway, Off Broadway and regional theater productions that are in the library’s film and tape archive. There are more than 8,000, not about 7,000.
match_headline: Theater Industry Leader Takes Top Job at New York Performing Arts Library

text: An article on Page 42 this weekend about the novelist Jesmyn Ward misidentifies her birthplace. It was Berkeley, Calif., not Oakland.
match_headline: How Jesmyn Ward Is Reimagining Southern Literature

text: An article on Oct. 8 about a woman with an autoimmune disease misstated the name of an organization. It is the International Pemphigus and Pemphigoid Foundation, not the International Pemphigus and Bullous Pemphigoid Foundation.
match_headline: Her Strange Blisters Wouldn’t Go Away. What Was It?

text: An obituary on Wednesday about Charles Feeney, who gave away nearly all of his $8 billion fortune to charity, misstated the year he graduated from St. Mary of the Assumption High School in Elizabeth, N.J. It was 1948, not 1949.
match_headline: Charles Feeney, Who Made a Fortune and Then Gave It Away, Dies at 92

text: An article last Sunday about the making of “12 Years a Slave” referred incorrectly to the director Steve McQueen’s birthplace. He was born in, not outside, London.
match_headline: Steve McQueen’s Call to Arms: The Making of ‘12 Years a Slave’

text: An article on Oct. 1 about plans to build homes on the moon, using information provided by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration and ICON, misstated Raymond Clinton Jr.’s title. He is senior technical adviser of the Science and Technology Office at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center, not its deputy director. The article also described incorrectly the four individuals currently living inside the Mars Dune Alpha. They are volunteer researchers, not astronauts. And the article misstated the distance from Earth to the moon. It is 240,000 miles, not 240 million.
match_headline: Maybe in Your Lifetime, People Will Live on the Moon and Then Mars

text: An article on Page 42 this weekend about the novelist Jesmyn Ward misidentifies her birthplace. It was Berkeley, Calif., not Oakland.

A review on Oct. 1 about the picture book “There Was a Party for Langston,” by Jason Reynolds, misspelled the name of a research library in New York City. It is the New York Public Library’s Schom­burg Center for Research in Black Cul­ture, not the Schomberg Center.
ref_headline: There Was a Party for Langston,
match_headline: Harlem on Their Minds

text: An article on Sunday about Republican candidates’ appeal to donors to build up a viable alternative to former president Donald Trump misstated Senator Tim Scott’s cash on hand going into October. It was $11.6 million, not $12.6 million.
match_headline: ‘Get in the Game’: G.O.P. Candidates Plead Their Case to Major Donors

text: An article on Sunday about llamas at an agricultural fair in Massachusetts misstated the location of Catskill Game Farm. It is west of West Springfield, Mass., not east of it.
match_headline: At This New England Fair, Llamas Steal the Show

text: An article on Monday about reactions at U.S. synagogues to the war in Israel misquoted a portion of Rabbi Sam Levine’s prepared remarks. He cautioned against succumbing to a “thirst for revenge” against Palestinians, not Hamas.
match_headline: At U.S. Synagogues, Calls for Peace and Too Many Emotions to Process

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the National Museum of Women in the Arts misidentified the artist and title of a work by Faith Ringgold. It is “American Collection #4: Jo Baker’s Bananas,” not “Bananas” by Jo Baker and Faith Ringgold.
match_headline: Is a Women’s Museum Still Relevant?

text: An obituary on Oct. 8 about the drummer Russell Batiste misstated when his father, David Batiste Sr., formed the band David Batiste and the Gladiators. It was before he joined the Meters, not after.
match_headline: Russell Batiste Jr., the Drumming Heartbeat of New Orleans, Dies at 57

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the British filmmaker Terence Davies misstated the location of Mistley, Essex, where he lived. It is on the southeast coast of England, not the southwest coast.
match_headline: Terence Davies, 77, Dies; Filmmaker Mined Literature and His Own Life

text: An article on Tuesday about twin girls born in Gaza on Saturday misspelled the given name of one of the babies. She is Fatin, not Fatina.
match_headline: Twins Are Born in Gaza After Their Mother Flees to the South

text: An article on Wednesday about a change in United Airlines’ boarding process misstated the timing of United’s use of the WILMA method. United stopped using it in 2017.
match_headline: United Airlines to Change Its Boarding Process, a Win for Window Seats

text: An article last Thursday about Queen Margrethe II of Denmark, who is also a costume and production designer, referred incorrectly to Tivoli in Copenhagen. While it is one of the oldest amusement parks in the world, it is not the world’s oldest amusement park.
match_headline: Scream Queen? More Like Stream Queen.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the conflict negotiator Martti Ahtisaari misstated the year the Good Friday peace agreement, which ended three decades of insurgency in Northern Ireland, was signed. It was 1998, not 1987. And a picture caption with the obituary misspelled the name of the capital of Kosovo. It is Pristina, not Prisina.
match_headline: Martti Ahtisaari, Conflict Negotiator Given Nobel Peace Prize, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the scientist Roland Griffiths, who did pioneering work in the study of psychedelics, misstated when he was diagnosed with Stage 4 colon cancer. It was November 2021, not November 2022.
match_headline: Roland Griffiths Is Dead at 77; Led a Renaissance in Psychedelics Research

text: An article on Wednesday about hundreds of people killed in a blast at a hospital complex in Gaza described incorrectly a video filmed by a woman at the hospital after the blast. The hospital itself was not ruined; its parking lot was damaged most heavily in the blast.
match_headline: Hundreds Reported Killed in Blast at a Gaza Hospital

text: Because of a production error, an article on Thursday about a growing number of working Americans who earn too little to afford rent and have turned their cars into a form of affordable housing included a column of type that was printed backward. (There was no need to get your eyes checked.)
match_headline: I Live in My Car

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the choreographer Rudy Perez misstated the name of a performance artist who, like Mr. Perez, had been a member of Judson Dance Theater. She was Carolee Schneemann, not Carol Schneeman.
match_headline: Rudy Perez, a Pioneer of Postmodern Dance, Is Dead at 93

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about a Broadway play starring Danny DeVito and his daughter, Lucy DeVito, misstates the title of the audio play that Danny and Lucy DeVito collaborated on. It is “I Think It’s Worth Pointing Out That I’ve Been Very Serious Throughout This Entire Discussion or, Dave and Julia Are Stuck in a Tree,” not “I Think It’s Working Pointing Out…”
ref_headline: I Think It’s Worth Pointing Out That I’ve Been Very Serious Throughout This Entire Discussion or, Dave and Julia Are Stuck in a Tree,
match_headline: Danny DeVito, His Daughter and a Lot of Baggage (Onstage)

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 6 this weekend about the new opera “Grounded” misstates Jeanine Tesori’s role. As the article correctly notes, Tesori is the composer, not the conductor.

An article on Page 12 this weekend about the rock musician Thurston Moore misstates the name of the heart-rhythm abnormality Mr. Moore said he has had for a number of years. It is atrial fibrillation, not atrial defibrillation.
match_headline: Thurston Moore’s Electrifying History Lesson

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about John Stamos, in one instance, misidentifies the character Mr. Stamos played on “Full House.” He is Uncle Jesse, not Uncle Joey.
match_headline: John Stamos Is Done With Being Someone’s Idea of John Stamos

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the artist Yinka Shonibare misstates the closing date for “Boomerang” at the James Cohan Gallery. It is Dec. 22, not Dec. 23.
match_headline: An Artist Pushes Back Against Cultural Colonialism

text: An article on Page 34 this weekend about the artist Kay WalkingStick’s exhibition in New York City misstates the material on which two paintings were created. “Niagara” and “Canyon Temple” are on panels, not canvas.
match_headline: Reframing the American Landscape

text: An article on Page 38 this weekend about an annual art show held at the Park Avenue Armory in Manhattan misspells the middle name of an artist whose work will be exhibited in the Art Show at the Park Avenue Armory in November. She is Lisa Corinne Davis, not Corrine.
match_headline: Upper East Meets Lower East in a Celebration of Art in Manhattan

text: An article last Sunday about a global fertilizer shortage referred incorrectly to a fertilizer ingredient that moved from Canada to Nigeria for much of last year and cost $1,350 a ton. It is potash, not phosphate.
match_headline: How a Fertilizer Shortage Is Spreading Desperate Hunger

text: An article last Sunday about Medi­care advertising referred incor­rectly to the elimination of a thresh­old that requires Medicare Part D recipients to pay 5 percent of the cost of their medications. Next year, that threshold will be eliminated when enrollees pay in excess of $8,000, not $7,750, for out­-of-­pocket drug costs.
match_headline: How to Cut Through the Ad Blitz During Medicare’s Open Enrollment

text: A picture caption with an article on Page 6 this weekend about the new opera “Grounded” misstates Jeanine Tesori’s role. As the article correctly notes, Tesori is the composer, not the conductor.

An article on Oct. 8 about the wedding of Leslie Hamilton and Yan Fu misspelled part of the name of a nonprofit on whose board Mr. Fu serves. It is the Sonia and Celina Sotomayor Judicial Internship Program, not Sonya.
match_headline: They Met the Old-Fashioned Way: Playing Glow-in-the-Dark Dodgeball

text: An article Oct. 8 about a couple in Scotland who bid on the wrong house but purchased it anyway referred incorrectly to Charli Kleeman, a worker who helped with the renovation. Mx. Kleeman uses they and them pronouns, not she and her.
match_headline: They Accidentally Bought the Wrong House. So They Made It the Right House.

text: An article on Thursday about the impact of voting rights legislation on the governor’s race in Mississippi misstated the status of a law that had stripped voting rights from people convicted of a range of felonies in Mississippi. While a court had overturned the law in August, that decision was vacated and an appeal is currently pending; it is not the case that the law has fallen.
match_headline: Black Voters Have New Power in Mississippi. Can They Elect a Democrat?

text: An article on Sunday about the growing number of renovations, new buildings and upgrades to museum spaces around the country misstated the name of an architecture firm that was a collaborator on a project involving the floor of the Rockefeller Wing of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. It is Beyer Blinder Belle Architects and Planners, not Beyer, Blinder, Belle Architects.
match_headline: One of the World’s Biggest Museums Is Making Big Changes

text: An article on Sunday about a show of about 300 photographs by Annie Leibovitz at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Ark., misstated Alejo Benedetti’s role at the museum. He is its curator of contemporary art, not its acting curator of contemporary art.
match_headline: For Annie Leibovitz, an Opportunity to Work and Build on the Past

text: An article on Tuesday about Gov. Gavin Newsom’s efforts to export California’s climate policies misstated the share of jobs linked to oil drilling in California. It is 0.2 percent, not 2 percent.
match_headline: Gavin Newsom Wants to Export California’s Climate Laws to the World

text: An article on Sunday about the importance of Lahaina’s history in rebuilding after a devastating wildfire on Maui misstated the year that the Hawaiian kingdom was overthrown. It was 1893, not 1898.
match_headline: A Plea From Native Hawaiians: The Future of Maui Rests on Honoring Its Past

text: An article on Wednesday about a lawsuit in which dozens of states accuse Meta of knowingly using addictive features to attract children misidentified one of the two states that led the legal action. It was Colorado and California, not Colorado and Tennessee.
match_headline: Meta Accused by States of Using Features to Lure Children to Instagram and Facebook

text: An article on Thursday about a Hawaii bribery scandal and its potential impact on Maui’s recovery from devastating wildfires misspelled the surname of the Maui County Auditor. He is Lance Taguchi, not Lance Toguchi.
match_headline: Hawaii Bribery Scandal Casts a Shadow Over Lahaina’s Ruins

text: An article on Wednesday about fund-raising needed for Jeffrey Gibson’s exhibition at the Venice Biennale next spring misstated the name of the museum that is co-commissioning Gibson’s solo exhibition for the U.S. Pavilion. It is the Portland Art Museum, not the Portland Museum of Art.
match_headline: To Star at the Venice Biennale, Artists Need Patrons’ Deep Pockets

text: An obituary on Thursday about the writer and historian Rock Brynner omitted the name of one of his former wives. She was Susan Goldman. It also omitted the names of two survivors. In addition to those named, he is survived by two stepchildren, Laura Bourret and Brandon Goldman.
match_headline: Rock Brynner, 76, Son of Hollywood Royalty Who Cut His Own Path, Dies

text: An obituary on Oct. 15 about the actor Mark Goddard misstated the name of a college he attended. It is the College of the Holy Cross, not Holy Cross College.
match_headline: Mark Goddard, a Star of the ’60s Series ‘Lost in Space,’ Dies at 87

text: An article on Friday about Georgia’s voting maps misstated the year that Georgia elected its two Democratic senators. It was 2021, not 2020.
match_headline: Georgia’s Voting Maps Are Struck Down

text: An article on Oct. 22 about a rise in crossings at the U.S. southern border misstated the size of the decline in migrant arrests outside ports of entry in the 2023 fiscal year. Those arrests fell by about 200,000 compared with the prior year, not by about two million.
match_headline: Crossings at the U.S. Southern Border Are Higher Than Ever

text: Because of a production error, an article on Friday about Amazon’s third-quarter earnings report was outdated. The company posted $143.1 billion in revenue for the quarter, up 13 percent from a year earlier. It was not the case that it had seen its slowest growth in more than two decades. A summary on the front page of the Business section repeated the error.
match_headline: G.M. Profit Down 7% in Strike-Affected Quarter

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the singer PinkPantheress misstates how she and her collaborator Mura Masa connected. It was via Mura Masa’s publisher, he didn’t contact her on his own. It also misstates the origins of the song “Just for Me.” The song was not composed entirely by PinkPantheress and Mura Masa, it includes a sample from the band American Football.
match_headline: PinkPantheress’s Music Broke the Internet. Up Next? Everything Else.

text: An article on Page 50 this weekend about climate aware therapists understates the number of psychotherapists the Climate Psychology Alliance North America maintains in its database. It is now nearly 300, not more than 100. And the article misattributes comments about introducing clients to methods such as mindfulness, distress tolerance and emotion regulation to help manage feelings of stress or panic and prevent burnout. Others in a group conversation made those comments, not Nicole Torres, a practitioner in Bellingham, Wash.
match_headline: Climate Change Is Keeping Therapists Up at Night

text: An article last Sunday about the artist Henry Taylor misidentified Taylor’s former journalism professor. He was Mark Dever, not Martin Deever.
match_headline: How Henry Taylor Transformed the Way We Look at Ourselves

text: An article on Monday about the 25th anniversary of the album “The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill” misstated one of the guests onstage with the Fugees at the Prudential Center. Rah Digga joined the group, not Remy Ma.
match_headline: In Praise of the Ever-Evolving Lauryn Hill

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about forward Pascal Siakam’s expectations with the revamped Toronto Raptors misstated his teammate Scottie Barnes’s experience in the N.B.A. It is his third year in the league, not second.

An obituary on Sunday about the actress and casting director Joanna Merlin misstated the surname of one of the writers of the Broadway musical “On the Twentieth Century.” She was Betty Comden, not Betty Green.
match_headline: Joanna Merlin, Known for Her Work Both Onstage and Off, Dies at 92

text: An article on Tuesday about the use of A.I. in patient care misstated the affiliation of Dr. Keith Dreyer. He is the chief data science officer for Mass General Brigham, not for Massachusetts General Hospital.
match_headline: Doctors Wrestle With A.I. in Patient Care, Citing Lax Oversight

text: An article on Wednesday about the dilemma Israel faces as it seeks to destroy Hamas and free hostages in Gaza misstated the day that the Israeli military said that Pvt. Ori Megidish had been rescued. They announced her rescue on Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Israeli Soldier Rescued After Hamas Abduction

text: An article on Monday about the ways that climate change is affecting French cheese makers misstated the minimum duration for aging Picodon cheese. It is eight days, not 12.
match_headline: The Rigid World of French Cheesemaking Meets Unbound Climate Change

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an obituary on Tuesday for Wanda Poltawska, a Polish psychiatrist and author who forged a longtime friendship with the priest who would become Pope John Paul II, misidentified the person pictured. It was Ms. Poltawska, not the future pope.
match_headline: Wanda Poltawska, 101, Who Forged a Friendship With a Future Pope, Dies

text: An article on Tuesday about the knowledge of the deteriorating mental health of the man suspected of killing 18 people in a mass shooting in Maine misidentified the people who visited the him in May. It was his brother and sister, not his ex-wife and sister.
match_headline: Police Were Told Maine Gunman Had Threatened to Carry Out Shooting Spree

text: An article on Thursday about President Biden’s difficulty in brokering peace between Israel and Palestinians misidentified the location of a U.S. consulate closed by President Donald J. Trump. It was in West Jerusalem, not East Jerusalem. The error was repeated in a picture caption. The article also misidentified the city in which Daniel C. Kurtzer was stationed when he was the U.S. ambassador to Israel under President George W. Bush. He was based in Tel Aviv, not Jerusalem, where the United States moved its embassy in 2018.
match_headline: Biden Found Even Modest Israel-Palestinian Peace Steps Impossible

text: An article on Wednesday about Barack Obama’s presidential center in Chicago referred imprecisely to Mr. Obama’s decision to have a privately run presidential center. Not all of his 13 immediate predecessors opted for a library and museum operated by the National Archives. Richard Nixon’s library was privately operated at first, and became part of the federal system after his death.
match_headline: Obama’s Presidential Center Is Rising, Finally, in Chicago

text: An article on Thursday about the House’s vote to block a censure of Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan misstated the date of a pro-Palestinian protest that Ms. Tlaib participated in. It was Oct. 18, not Oct. 8.
match_headline: House Blocks Censure of Tlaib on Charge of Antisemitism

text: An article on Friday about Senate Democrats’ strategy to break Senator Tommy Tuberville’s blockade of senior military promotions misstated the number of Democrats and independents in the Senate. There are 48 Democrats and three independents, not 49 Democrats and two independents.
match_headline: Senators Plot to Unblock Military Promotions as Tuberville Draws G.O.P. Ire

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about the singer-songwriter Kirsty MacColl misstates the name of a folk singer. She is Norma Waterson, not Nora Watterson.
match_headline: Kirsty MacColl’s Voice Was Singular. A New Box Aims to Bring It Wider.

text: An obituary on Friday about the artist Juanita McNeely misstated where she died. It was at her home in Manhattan, not at Lenox Hill Hospital.
match_headline: Juanita McNeely, Intense Artist of the Female Experience, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Thursday about Don Laughlin, who created the Nevada town that bears his name, misstated where in the United States slot machines were legal in the 1950s. They were legal in the entire state of Nevada and in a few other places — not just in Las Vegas.
match_headline: Don Laughlin, Who Turned a Patch of Desert Into a Casino Mecca, Dies at 92

text: An article last Sunday about a new staging of “Pal Joey” referred incorrectly to its place in the timeline of works by Rodgers and Hart. It was among their final collaborations; it was not the final one.
match_headline: Joey Evans Is Back. This Time He’s a Struggling Artist.

text: An article on Thursday about a feeling of fear among Jewish people across Europe referred imprecisely to the number of Mizrahi Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent in Israel. While they make up a large portion of the country’s population, official estimates do not put that number at more than half.
match_headline: For Europe’s Jews, a World of Fear

text: An article on Friday about global warming increasing at a faster rate than previously anticipated described incorrectly the findings of a study published on Oct. 30 by British and Austrian researchers. Their study found that, under current conditions, Earth has about six years before it is committed to passing 1.5 degrees of warming, not that Earth is likely to pass 1.5 degrees of warming within six years.
match_headline: 35 Years After Addressing Congress, James Hansen Has More Climate Warnings

text: An article on Saturday about military ties between the Philippines and China incorrectly stated the distance over which China has asserted control in the South China Sea. Some of the waters it claims are hundreds of miles from the Chinese mainland, not thousands of miles.
match_headline: Japan and Philippines, Wary of China, Look to Expand Military Ties

text: A picture with an article on Sunday on the Philadelphia mayoral election was published in error. It did not show the Republican candidate, David Oh. The caption also misstated which candidate has the support of building trade unions. It is the Democratic nominee, Cherelle Parker, not Mr. Oh.
match_headline: ‘I’m Not Superwoman’: Philadelphia’s Likely Mayor Urges Teamwork

text: An article on Sunday about driving the New York City Marathon route misstated the street that marathon runners take to enter Central Park. It is 90th Street, not 91st Street.
match_headline: Why Run the New York City Marathon When You Can Drive It?

text: An article on Monday about striking Tesla workers in Sweden misstated the number of months that Klarna and two unions negotiated before reaching an agreement on Friday. The talks lasted six months, not eight months.
match_headline: Job Action Against Tesla Puts Sweden’s Unions in Spotlight

text: An article on Saturday about open enrollment for Affordable Care Act plans misidentified Cheryl Fish-Parcham. She is the director of private coverage at Families USA, not the director of access initiatives.
match_headline: Open Enrollment Begins for Affordable Care Act Health Plans

text: An article on Sunday about the marathon runner Cameron Levins referred incorrectly to the year of the London Olympics. It was in 2012, not 2021.
match_headline: To Train for One Marathon, He Runs 7 Every Week

text: An obituary on Friday about the comic book writer and artist Keith Giffen misstated when and with whom he reimagined the superhero Blue Beetle. It was in the 2000s with the writer John Rogers and the artist Cully Hamner — not in the 1980s with the writer J.M. DeMatteis and the artist Kevin Maguire (with whom, as the obituary correctly notes, he worked on the Justice League franchise).
match_headline: Keith Giffen, Comic Book Maverick for DC and Marvel, Dies at 70

text: An obituary on Monday about David Kirke, who performed what is widely acknowledged as the first modern bungee jump, referred incorrectly to Shropshire, where he was born. It is a county in England, not a village. The village where Mr. Kirke was born is Shawbury, in Shropshire. And a picture caption with the obituary misidentified the man pictured with Mr. Kirke. He is Cosmo Hulton, not Edward Hulton.
match_headline: David Kirke, Who Made the First Modern Bungee Jump, Dies at 78

text: An article on Saturday about a temporary lift of the gag order imposed on former President Donald J. Trump referred incorrectly to the duration that a gag order imposed on Mr. Trump will be paused. A federal appeals court in Washington set no timeline for the length of the pause; the court did not lift the gag order for about two weeks, though it did set a two-week timetable for the parties to file papers in Mr. Trump’s overarching appeal of the order.
match_headline: Appeals Court Temporarily Frees Trump From Gag Order in Election Case

text: An article on Monday about Mike Johnson, the new speaker of the House, misstated the year that Mr. Johnson was elected to the House of Representatives. It was 2016, not 2017.
match_headline: ‘Like Winning the Lottery’: Mike Johnson’s Ascent Excites Conservative Christians

text: An obituary on Oct. 14 about the poet Louise Glück misstated where on Long Island she grew up. It was Woodmere, not Cedarhurst. The obituary also misstated the source of a quotation from Ms. Glück that contained the observation “I don’t want to be Longfellow.” It was from an interview with the Academy of American Poets, not with the blog Scarriet. And it misstated when Ms. Glück began teaching at Stanford University. It was 2012, not this year.
ref_headline: I don’t want to be Longfellow.
match_headline: Louise Glück, 80, Nobel-Winning Poet Who Explored Trauma and Loss, Dies

text: An article on Wednesday about the singer Desire Marea misidentified the year of the Battle of Isandlwana. It occurred in 1879, not 1897.
match_headline: Desire Marea’s Genre-Melting Music Stirs South Africa, and the World

text: An article on Thursday about Danica Roem, the first transgender state senator in the South, misstated the type of meal program supported by Ms. Roem. It’s a universal free school one, not a universal preschool one.
match_headline: Danica Roem Will Become the First Transgender State Senator in the South

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the U.S. Space Force misspelled the surname of a member of the U.S. Space Force. He is Lt. Col. Galen Thorp, not Thorpe.
match_headline: What Does the U.S. Space Force Actually Do?

text: An article on Nov. 5 about treating childhood obesity described incorrectly, in one instance, the treatment Eriyanna Stovall received. She was given Wegovy, but did not have surgery.
match_headline: Bariatric Surgery at 16

text: A headline with an obituary on Friday about Gary Winnick, a former junk-bond salesman who masterminded the building of a transoceanic fiber-optics network to speed the internet and phone traffic, misstated his age. As the obituary correctly noted, he was 76, not 78.
match_headline: Gary Winnick, Who Won and Lost With Global Crossing, Dies at 76

text: An article on Friday about an undersea volcano that has formed a new island off Japan’s coast misidentified the United States service members who hoisted an American flag over the Japanese island of Iwo Jima in February 1945. According to the United States Marine Corps, all six men, not five of them, were U.S. Marines.
match_headline: An Undersea Volcano Is Building a New Island in Japan

text: An article on Sunday about Iran and Saudi Arabia’s call for a cease-fire in Gaza incorrectly attributed the source of rocket and drone attacks on U.S. forces in Iraq and Syria since the start of the war. They were carried out by Iraqi and Syrian militias backed by Iran; Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps has not claimed responsibility for them.
match_headline: Iran and Saudi Arabia, Regional Rivals, Call for Gaza Cease-Fire

text: An article on Friday about Israel’s accusations that several freelance photographers for major news organizations had advance knowledge of the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, based on information from an editor at The Times, misstated when Yousef Masoud woke to the sound of rocket fire. It was shortly after 6:30 a.m., not 5:30 a.m.
match_headline: Israel Accuses Freelance Photographers of Advance Knowledge of Oct. 7 Attack

text: An article on Saturday about an off-duty pilot accused of trying to crash an airplane misstated the name of one of the airlines that employed the pilot, Joseph Emerson. It is Virgin America, not Virgin Airlines.
match_headline: ‘Is This Hell?’ The Pilot Accused of Trying to Crash a Plane Tells His Story.

text: An article on Sunday about a weight loss drug that could reduce heart risks misstated the name of an author of the study. It is Dr. Ildiko Lingvay, not Idiko.
match_headline: Wegovy Is Shown to Reduce Risk of Heart Attacks and Strokes in Some Patients

text: An article on Monday about the Salon Art + Design fair misidentified the material used in an artwork by Robert Mangold. It is a work on Masonite board, not paper.
match_headline: At Salon Art + Design, Gold Bracelets and Lipstick-Red Monochromes

text: An article on Tuesday about the intelligence of vultures misidentified the geographic region in which black vultures snip and consume the umbilical cords of sea lions. It is South America, not Northern California.
match_headline: Why Vultures Might Just Be the Smartest Birds Above the Block

text: An article on Thursday about paramilitary forces accused of committing atrocities while seizing territory in the Darfur region misstated the time period in which more than 800 people were killed as Rapid Support Forces and allied Arab fighters overran the army garrison in El Geneina. It was earlier this month as well as last week, not only last week.
match_headline: Seizing Darfur Region, Paramilitary Forces Are Accused of Atrocities

text: An article on Monday about a major freeway in Los Angeles that was shut down after a fire misstated the commuter traffic routes on Interstate 10. About 300,000 vehicles use the freeway for daily commuting, but not necessarily between Los Angeles and Orange County, which Interstate 10 does not travel through.
match_headline: Major Freeway Near Downtown Los Angeles Is Closed Indefinitely After Fire

text: An article on Thursday about the producer and songwriter Edgar Barrera misstated the name of a song by Camilo and Camila Cabello. It is “Ambulancia,” not “El Ambulancia.”
match_headline: For Latin Grammy Nominee Edgar Barrera, Mistakes Can Be Perfection

text: An article on Page 6 this weekend about a new biopic on the civil rights leader Bayard Rustin misstates the middle initial of an author. He is Michael G. Long, not Michael C. Long.
match_headline: Remembering Bayard Rustin in Life and Onscreen

text: An article on Page 24 about David Zaslav misstates the timing of a text between Zaslav and John Stankey. The text was sent on a Saturday in February 2021, not on Sunday.
match_headline: How David Zaslav Blew Up Hollywood

text: An article on Page 36 this weekend about homelessness in San Francisco misidentifies the constitutional amendment in which the equal-protection clause appears. It appears in the 14th Amendment, not the Eighth Amendment.
match_headline: A Homeless Man Attacked Him. But Was There More to the Story?

text: An article on Nov. 12 about objects in Earth orbit misstated the location of walruses being tracked by satellite imagery. The walruses are in the Arctic, not the Antarctic.

An article on Nov. 12 about the James Webb Space Telescope described incorrectly its position in space. It is not the case that the telescope uses Earth as a shield. Additionally, the methyl cation molecule found by Webb has been detected elsewhere in our solar system; it is not the case that it had never been detected outside our own planet.
match_headline: A Supernova ‘Destroyed’ Some of Earth’s Ozone for a Few Minutes in 2022

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the television writer and producer Peter S. Fischer, using information from his family, misstated the name of one of his half sisters. She is Stephanie Fischer Connolly, not Stephanie Donnelly.
match_headline: Peter S. Fischer, Who Helped Create ‘Murder, She Wrote,’ Dies at 88

text: An article Nov. 5 about a new Adi­das running shoe, the Adizero Adios Pro Evo 1, which costs $500 but wears out quickly, misspelled the given name of the Ethiopian athlete who broke the women’s world record in the marathon. She is Tigist Assefa, not Tigst. The article also misstated the distance Thomas Neuberger ran in the Evo 1s. It was a half marathon, not a marathon.
match_headline: Is a $500 Marathon Shoe You Can Race In Only Once Worth It?

text: An article on Nov. 12 about objects in Earth orbit misstated the location of walruses being tracked by satellite imagery. The walruses are in the Arctic, not the Antarctic.

match_headline: Not All Heroes Wear Capes. Some Prefer Lab Coats.

text: An article on Monday about sweltering heat at Taylor Swift’s concerts in Brazil misstated the title of a Taylor Swift song. It is “You Belong With Me,” not “You Belong to Me.”
match_headline: After Eras Tour Triumphs, Taylor Swift Finds Trouble in Brazil

text: An article on Sunday about Sam Altman’s ouster at OpenAI misstated Ilya Sutskever’s academic status when he helped create a breakthrough in an A.I. technology called neural networks at the University of Toronto. He was a graduate student, not an undergraduate.
match_headline: The Fear and Tension That Led to Sam Altman’s Ouster at OpenAI

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the Oakland Athletics’ impending move to Las Vegas and its effect on working-class sports fans misidentified a major league star who grew up in Oakland. It was Frank Robinson, not Reggie Jackson. (Although Mr. Jackson did find stardom as a player in Oakland, he was not raised there).
