text: An article on Monday about the Latin Grammy Awards misstated which artist was the first woman to win the Latin Grammy for musica úrbana album. It was Mala Rodríguez, not Karol G.
match_headline: In Spain, the Latin Grammys Recognize Powerful Women

text: An obituary on Saturday about the author A.S. Byatt misstated the year her collection “Little Black Book of Stories” was published. It was 2003, not 2018.
match_headline: A.S. Byatt, Scholar Who Found Literary Fame With Fiction, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Nov. 14 about Maryanne Trump Barry, a former federal judge and a sister of former President Donald J. Trump, misspelled her mother’s birth name. She was Mary Anne MacLeod, not McLeod.
match_headline: Maryanne Trump Barry, Retired Judge and Donald Trump Sister, Dies at 86

text: An obituary on Nov. 11 about the astronaut Frank Borman misidentified the platform that hosts the radio program “This American Life,” which broadcast an interview with him in 2018. It is delivered to stations by Public Radio Exchange, not NPR.
match_headline: Frank Borman, Astronaut Who Led First Orbit of the Moon, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Nov. 11 about the financial analyst Byron Wien misstated how old he was when his mother died. He was 14, not 15.
match_headline: Byron Wien, Wall Street Seer of the Unexpected, Dies at 90

text: An article on Tuesday about the psychological chasm between Palestinians and Israelis misstated the year the Oslo Accords collapsed. It was 2000, not 1993. The article also misstated the location of the Givat Haviva Center for Shared Society. It is about an hour’s drive north of Jerusalem, not in Jerusalem.
match_headline: Between Israelis and Palestinians, a Lethal Psychological Chasm Grows

text: An article on Sunday about European countries increasing weapon production to aid Ukraine misstated the name of a top Estonian diplomat. He is Jonatan Vseviov, not Yonatan Vseviyov.
match_headline: Europe Moves to Fill Weapons Gap Amid Doubts About U.S. Commitment to Ukraine

text: An article on Tuesday about the 76th pre-Thanksgiving presidential turkey pardon ritual misstated when the annual tradition of a presidential turkey pardon began. While U.S. presidents have been presented with turkeys since 1947, the first documented pardon was not until 1963.
match_headline: ‘Congratulations, Birds’: Biden Pardons a Pair of Turkeys

text: An obituary on Monday about the former New York City sanitation commissioner Brendan Sexton misstated the career history of his father, who was also named Brendan. While he was a union leader, he was not also a sociology professor at New York University; Mr. Sexton’s stepmother, Patricia Cayo Sexton, was.
match_headline: Brendan Sexton, a Pioneer of Recycling, Is Dead at 78

text: An obituary on Nov. 6 about the China expert Jeffrey A. Bader, using information from his wife, contained an incomplete list of his survivors. In addition to his wife, Rohini Talalla, and his brother, Lawrence, he is survived by a son, Odoric Bréchet, and a grandson.
match_headline: Jeffrey A. Bader, Who Helped Steer Obama’s ‘Pivot’ to Asia, Dies at 78

text: An article on Page 9 this weekend about a new reality competition show on Netflix misidentifies one of the producing studios of “Squid Game: The Challenge.” It is Studio Lambert, not Lambert Studios.
match_headline: In ‘Squid Game: The Challenge,’ the Deaths Are Fake, but the Cash Is Real

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the fight to preserve praise houses misidentifies the location of a temporary praise house constructed for an art project. It is on the campus of Emory University in Atlanta, not on the original campus in Oxford, Ga.
match_headline: Saving Praise Houses Before Their African Lineage Is Forgotten

text: An article last Sunday about a documentary on Lady Bird Johnson referred imprecisely to the term of office President Lyndon B. Johnson sought and won in 1964. It was his first full term as president, not “his second term.”
match_headline: Listening to Lady Bird Johnson, in Her Own Words

text: An article on Nov. 12 about Las Vegas weddings misstated the number of performances includ­ed in U2’s Las Vegas residency. There are 36 shows, not 25.
match_headline: The Undying Appeal of the Las Vegas Wedding

text: An article on Saturday about concerns among liberal organizers in Georgia and their efforts to deliver election victories for Democrats misstated Jonae Wartel’s role in the 2020 Georgia Senate campaigns. She led Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff’s coordinated runoff campaigns, not Mr. Warnock’s campaign.
match_headline: Georgia’s Liberal Organizers Warn of a Cash Crunch and Apathy

text: An article on Sunday about the prison stabbing of former police officer Derek Chauvin and questions about inmate safety misspelled the surname of a doctor convicted of sexually abusing young female gymnasts. He is Larry Nassar, not Larry Nasser.
match_headline: Stabbing of Derek Chauvin Raises Questions About Inmate Safety

text: An article on Saturday about strategies for reducing the stress and cost of divorce misstated the membership of the National Association of Divorce Professionals. It is a group of 600 legal, financial, mental health and residential professionals, not 600 divorce attorneys.
match_headline: Can Divorce Be Affordable? Yes, but Only if Spouses Want It to Be.

text: An article on Friday about a climate law that has created a financial trading marketplace for smaller businesses misstated the type of services provided by the company BDO. It is a tax advisory firm, not an investment bank.
match_headline: In Biden’s Climate Law, a Boon for Green Energy, and Wall Street

text: An article on Monday about daily life in Gaza misspelled the name of a man trying to find water for his family. He is Nazmi Mwafi, not Namzi.

text: An article on Tuesday about mandatory gun sentences misidentified Andrew Adler. He is a lawyer for Eugene Jackson, not for Justin Brown.
match_headline: Justices Search for Middle Ground on Mandatory Sentences for Gun Crimes

text: An article on Tuesday about the solar energy manufacturing sector’s struggle to balance supply with demand misstated the locations of Maxeon Solar Technologies facilities. It has operations in California and New Mexico, not Colorado.
match_headline: Could Biden’s Clean Energy Push Be a Victim of Its Success?

text: An article on Sunday about a priest who was punished for a music video filmed in a church misstated the name of the church where the singer Sabrina Carpenter filmed a music video for the song “Feather.” It was the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, not Our Lady of Mount Carmel-Annunciation. The Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary is one of two churches that are part of the Our Lady of Mount Carmel-Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary Parish. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: A Pop Star Filmed a Music Video in a Church. The Priest Was Punished.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the network news correspondent and author Betty Rollin, using information provided by a friend, misstated the date of her death. It was Nov. 7, not Nov. 14.
match_headline: Betty Rollin, Who Wrote Candidly About Her Breast Cancer, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actress and acting teacher Suzanne Shepherd, using information from her family, misidentified the improvisational troupe with which she performed early in her career and referred incorrectly to the character she played in the movie “Mystic Pizza.” She performed with the Hyannis Port, Mass., company of the Compass Players, not the original Chicago company. And her character in “Mystic Pizza” was the aunt of the boyfriend of Julia Roberts’s character — not of the Roberts character.
match_headline: Suzanne Shepherd, Actress Known for Playing Mothers, Dies at 89

text: An obituary on Nov. 16 about the cinematographer John Bailey misstated the name of the university from which he earned a bachelor’s degree in 1964. It was Loyola University, not Loyola Marymount University. (Loyola University and Marymount College merged in 1973.)
match_headline: John Bailey, Oscars President in Time of Strife, Dies at 81

text: An article on Wednesday about a drug that could extend the life expectancy of dogs misstated the name of the hormone abbreviated as IGF-1. It is insulinlike growth factor-1, not insulin growth factor-1.
match_headline: Could a Drug Give Your Pet More Dog Years?

text: An item in the Of Interest column on Wednesday misidentified the position of the baseball player Ichiro Suzuki. He was an outfielder, not a pitcher.
An article on Friday about the play “Manahatta” misstated the history of the wall that Wall Street is named for. It was a wall to fend off the English, not the Lenape.
match_headline: ‘Manahatta,’ Mary Kathryn Nagle’s Play About the Lenape, Comes Home

text: An article on Friday about how complicated it can be for American presidents to balance their relationships with foreign allies misstated the title of Narendra Modi, the leader of India. He is the prime minister, not the president.
match_headline: Alleged Assassination Plot on U.S. Soil Tests Biden’s Bond With India’s Leader

text: An article last weekend in which a writer detailed his experience arriving in New York City as one of 140,000 Jewish refugees who fled postwar Europe misstated the number of days that present-day asylum seekers must wait before applying for a work permit. It is 150 days, not 180, though a permit will not be granted before 180 days after an asylum seeker has arrived. The article also misidentified the U.S.S. General A.W. Greely. It was a Navy vessel when the author and his family arrived in New York City on March 3, 1950, not a merchant marine vessel.

text: An article on Monday about resolving a flight cancellation issue with Frontier Airlines referred incorrectly to the amount that Frontier Airlines refunded the traveler. The airline refunded the entire $939.75 amount, including the $99.99 membership fee, not simply the flight costs.
match_headline: Help! Our Trip to Orlando Was Ruined and We Want Our Money Back.

text: An article on Nov. 18 about places to visit on the back roads of Southern California omitted information about the California Oil Museum, in Santa Paula. It temporarily closed in September 2021 because of financial hardships related to the Covid-19 pandemic and has yet to reopen. The city of Santa Paula has agreed to buy the museum and is exploring options to help reopen it.
match_headline: Southern California Beyond the Freeway

text: An article on Monday about how professional athletes are increasingly becoming serious art collectors referred incorrectly to the artist Swoon. She is not Black.

An article on Page 36 this weekend about the recent antitrust actions against the chicken suppliers industry by the Justice Department misstates the profits that suppliers to Kentucky Fried Chicken would have made on 400 million pounds of chicken if they had increased their prices by 10 cents per pound. It is $40 million, not $4 billion.

text: An article on Page 40 this weekend about Las Vegas’s Punk Rock Museum misquotes the zine writer Aaron Cometbus. He described the musician Mike Burkett as “Trump with a mohawk,” not “Trump in a mohawk.”

text: An article on Nov. 12 about a Graff necklace misattributed a quote about the patience and effort it takes to coordinate stones in the company’s high jewelry pieces. The quote was from Francois Graff, the company’s C.E.O., not Laurence Graff, its founder.

text: An obituary on Friday about the photographer Larry Fink misidentified the museum that exhibited his collection “Social Graces” in 1979. It was the Museum of Modern Art, not the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about how Israelis’ anger toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may not lead to his ouster misstated what a woman was writing on a poster of Mr. Netanyahu and Israeli hostages. She was adding exclamation points; she did not write, “It’s in your hands,” which was already printed on the poster.

text: An article on Saturday about actions by the Supreme Court that have dismantled many of Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s key rulings misstated the timing of a statement by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. on Justice O’Connor’s death. The statement was issued Friday, not Monday.

text: An article on Thursday about New York City’s progress in helping homeless people who are severely mentally ill misstated the housing status of the people who have been involuntarily hospitalized by New York City. They include both homeless and housed people, not all homeless people.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about an exhibition at Berlin’s Jewish Museum about the Jewish experience in East Germany misstated a historian’s name. She is Robin Ostow, not Ruth Ostrow.

text: An article on Tuesday about Russian prisoners who enlisted to fight in the war in Ukraine misidentified one of the IK6 recruits. His name is Vitali, not Aleksandr.

text: An article on Tuesday about a presentation accusing the United Nations of ignoring reports of sexual violence by Hamas misstated the home state of Representative Lois Frankel. She represents Florida, not California.

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the movie “Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé” misstated the type of dress Beyoncé wore when the film opens and she sings “Dangerously in Love 2.” It was a black dress, not a black dress followed by a citron yellow one.

text: An article on Wednesday about Mexico’s complicated relationship with a genre of music inspired by the drug trade misstated the day of the Peso Pluma concert in Mexico City. It was a Saturday, not Friday.

text: An article on Wednesday about the debate over the future of fossil fuels at the COP28 climate conference misspelled the surname of a climate activist with the group Artivist Network. He is Amalen Sathananthar, not Sathanathar.

text: An article on Tuesday about accusations of sexual violence during the Hamas Oct. 7 attacks on Israel misstated the kind of evidence Israeli authorities have gathered in their investigation. The police are relying mainly on witness testimony, not on autopsies or forensic evidence.

text: An article on Page 1 this weekend about a group that is trying to make synthesizers more accessible misstates the surname of a member of Synth Library. She is Mónica Torres-Ortiz, not Mónica Torres.
match_headline: Want a Synthesizer? Go Ahead, Take One.

text: An article on Friday about the concerns that displaying symbols of Hanukkah are raising for some Jewish people this year misstated the name of a nonprofit organization that advises Jewish institutions on safety issues. It is the Secure Community Network, not the Security Community Network.

text: An article on Friday about Kevin McCarthy misstated the length of his tenure as speaker of the House. It was almost nine months, not 11 months.

text: An article on Friday about six Norman Lear shows to watch misstated the title of a British TV series that “All in the Family” was based on. It is “Till Death Us Do Part,” not “Till Death Do Us Part.”

text: An obituary on Sunday about Pablo Guzmán, the Puerto Rican activist who become an Emmy-winning television news reporter, referred incorrectly to WNEW-TV in New York, where he worked for many years. Although it became one later, it was not a Fox affiliate when he was first hired.

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Verity Elks and Benjamin Riches misstated the Mexico City neighborhood that is the location of the couple’s wedding venue, General Prim 30. It is Juárez, not Roma Norte.

text: A review on Nov. 26 about Michael Cun­ningham’s novel “Day” referred incor­rectly to one of his previous books, “A Home at the End of the World.” It was his second novel, not his first. (“Golden States” was his first.)
ref_headline: A Home at the End of the World.

text: An article on Saturday about the approval of a gene-editing treatment for patients with sickle cell disease misstated the clinical trial in which the adult sickle cell center at the University of Alabama at Birmingham participated. It was the trial by Bluebird Bio, not Vertex Pharmaceuticals.

text: An article on Sunday about excavations of ancient Pompeii that revealed the grim life of enslaved workers misidentified which part of “The Golden Ass” describes working conditions in mills. It is Book IX, not Book XI.

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the ways in which Norman Lear reshaped the representation of Black families on television misstated the given name of an actor who starred in “Sanford and Son.” He is Demond Wilson, not Desmond.

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about the meaning of flight in Hayao Miyazaki’s films misstated the time period in which “Porco Rosso” is set. text: An article on Monday about this week’s television roundup misidentified a TV show on NBC. It is “That Clip Show,” not “The Clip Show.”

text: An article on Friday about “Women Dressing Women,” a show by the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute, misspelled the names of a fashion house and a designer. The house was Jeanne Hallée, not Jean Hallée; the designer was Madeleine Lepeyre, not Madeleine Lepaeyre.

text: An article on Saturday about Thomas Mayo, a champion of the effort in Australia to give Indigenous people a voice in Parliament, misidentified the author of the book “Catch-22.” Joseph Heller wrote the book, not Nathan Heller.

text: An article on Tuesday about Poland’s new prime minister, Donald Tusk, misstated the surname of the leader of a centrist party allied with Mr. Tusk. He is Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, not Kosniak-Kamusz.

text: An article on Sunday about several deaths linked to small magnets found in toys referred incorrectly to the marketing of a magnet set produced by Zen Magnets LLC. It was intended for adults, not sold as a toy for children.

text: An article on Saturday about avoiding surprise bills from electronic toll roads, relying on information from a spokeswoman for PikePass, referred imprecisely to the roads on which PikePass automatic toll accounts work in Florida. text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the Republican advance man Rick Ahearn at one point misstated when he left George H.W. Bush’s campaign for the Republican presidential nomination and joined Ronald Reagan’s. As noted correctly elsewhere, it was 1979, not 1980.

text: An article on Wednesday about the rehabilitation of Kibbutz Kfar Aza misattributed the quotation, “We don’t know if he is OK, if he sees daylight.” The comment was made by Alon Shamriz’s brother Ido, not by Alon.

text: A Critic’s Pick review on Dec. 1 about the movie “Silent Night” misspelled the given name of an actor. She is Catalina Sandino Moreno, not Catarina.

text: An article on Friday about the trial of a German spy accused of selling secrets to Russia misspelled the given name of a lawyer. He is Giuseppe Olivo, not Guiseppe.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the climate footprint from food production misstated the origin of $17 billion in funds for agricultural innovations. text: An article on Monday about local activists pushing for City Councils to adopt resolutions calling for a cease-fire in the Israel-Hamas war misstated the name of a Southern California nonprofit organization. It is Latino Muslim Unity, not Latinos and Muslims United.

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about the artist Tammy Nguyen misstates Ms. Nguyen’s age. She is 39, not 40.

text: An article on Tuesday about strikes by the United States in response to attacks from proxies of Iran and efforts to avoid direct confrontation misspelled the given name of a Yemen analyst. He is Raiman al-Hamdani, not Rainam.
match_headline: U.S. and Iran Battle Through Proxies, Warily Avoiding Each Other

text: An article on Jan. 4 about a stabbing attack on the Korean opposition political figure Lee Jae-myung referred incompletely to sources of information about the man who has been charged in the attack. As the article noted, the police released the suspect’s year of birth and said he had admitted an intent to kill Mr. Lee. Other details, including the suspect’s name and occupation, were not announced by the police; they were widely published in local social media and confirmed by The Times through video footage, public records and interviews with neighbors.
match_headline: Knife Attack on Opposition Leader Raises Alarms in Polarized South Korea

text: An article on Wednesday about Iranian missile strikes in Iraq and Pakistan misidentified the source of a comment about regional tensions. The remarks came from a statement from the French Foreign Ministry, not the French foreign minister. The article also misidentified the foreign minister. It is Stéphane Séjourné, not Catherine Colonna, whom he succeeded in that role last week.
match_headline: Deadly Iranian Strikes in Iraq and Pakistan Inflame Regional Tensions

text: An article on Wednesday about an official F.B.I. and Capitol Police inquiry of threats made to Democrats in the House misstated the given name of a lawmaker from New York. He is Representative Jerrold Nadler, not Jerrod.
match_headline: Authorities Investigate Threats to Democratic Lawmakers

text: An article on Wednesday about the best and worst moments from the Emmys misstated the number of seasons made of “Better Call Saul.” It is six, not seven.
match_headline: Best and Worst Moments From the 2023 Emmys

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the television critic Tom Shales, using information from his family, misstated his place in the family birth order. He was the middle of three children, not the youngest.
match_headline: Tom Shales, TV Critic Both Respected and Feared, Dies at 79

text: An article on Thursday about new estimates of Greenland’s ice sheet losses rendered incorrectly a quote by Laura Larocca, a climate scientist at Arizona State University. She said the new data set captured “the areal extent of the entire Greenland ice sheet.” Not the aerial extent.
ref_headline: the areal extent of the entire Greenland ice sheet.
match_headline: How Much Ice Is Greenland Losing? Researchers Found an Answer.

text: An article on Dec. 19 about Apple’s decision to pause sales of new models of its watch misidentified the feature that Apple would remove from watches it sells. The watches are expected to be sold without the ability to detect people’s blood oxygen levels, not their pulse rates.
match_headline: Apple to Pause Selling New Versions of Its Watch After Losing Patent Dispute

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the composer and film and video artist Phill Niblock, using information from his family, misstated when he retired from the College of Staten Island. It was 1998, not 1995.
match_headline: Phill Niblock, Dedicated Avant-Gardist of Music and Film, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Thursday about Sarah Stackhouse, a star dancer in the Limón Dance Company who became known for her stagings of José Limón’s choreography, misstated the year the American Dance Festival was first held at Duke University. It was 1978, not 1948.
match_headline: Sarah Stackhouse, Star Interpreter of José Limón, Dies at 87

text: An article on Friday about Iran’s links to regional conflicts referred incorrectly to Iran’s nuclear program. Iran has raised the prospect that it could develop nuclear weapons, maintaining that its nuclear program has only peaceful purposes, but it has not developed them.
match_headline: Why Iran Is the Common Link in Conflicts From Gaza to Pakistan

text: An article on Thursday about the success of the plane maker Airbus misstated the volume of sales for Airbus’s single-aisle aircraft. The planes are sold out until the end of this decade, not the end of this year.
match_headline: Airbus Is Pulling Ahead as Boeing’s Troubles Mount

text: An article this weekend about the challenges of saving for college and navigating financial aid misspells the given name of the former president of Vassar College and managing director at Ithaka S+R, a consulting firm. She is Catharine, not Catherine, Bond Hill.
match_headline: Why Is Paying for College So Complicated?

text: An article from The Athletic on Friday about the N.B.A. player Joel Embiid referred imprecisely to his distinction of averaging at least 35 points per game in relation to the N.B.A. great Wilt Chamberlain. While Chamberlain averaged 35 points per game, he did so while playing with the Philadelphia Warriors, not the Sixers.
A review on Jan. 13 of Kali Uchis’s new album “Orquídeas” misstated the title of one songs on the album. It is “Me Pongo Loca,” not “Me Ponga Loca.”
match_headline: On ‘Orquídeas,’ Kali Uchis Gets All She Wants

text: An article on Jan. 14 article about Hillsdale College misidentified the location of two legislative districts in Michigan. They were west of Detroit, not north.
match_headline: How a Conservative Christian College Got Mixed Up in the 2020 Election Plot

text: An article on Jan. 14 about the rise in auto-fatality rates misstated the name of a nonprofit organization. It is the Governors Highway Safety Association, not the Governors Highway Safety Organization.
match_headline: Why Are American Drivers So Deadly?

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Wednesday about the former pro quarterback Norm Snead referred incorrectly to the quarterback Sonny Jurgensen, who was traded to the Washington Redskins (now the Commanders) by the Philadelphia Eagles for Snead in 1964. Although Jurgensen was with the Eagles when they won a league championship in 1960, it was not the case that he “led them” to that championship. Norm Van Brocklin was the Eagles’ starting quarterback that season; Jurgensen was his backup.
match_headline: Norm Snead, Skillful Loser as an N.F.L. Quarterback, Is Dead at 84

text: An article last Sunday about the painter Jessie Homer French misclassified the woolly bugger, a type of fly used in fly-fishing. It is a wet fly, designed to sink under water after being cast, not a dry fly.
match_headline: Jessie Homer French Paints Infernos but She Sees Rainbows

text: An article on Saturday about Israeli female combat soldiers misidentified the type of weapon that Israeli troops were equipped with during a 12-hour battle along the Gaza border. They had Light Antitank Weapons, or LAWs, not Lau missiles.
match_headline: Israeli Women Fight on Front Line in Gaza, a First

text: An article on Sunday about students who have used college application essays to highlight their racial background misstated the name of the nonprofit that Mr. Jacobson founded. It is Equal Protection Project, not Equal Projection Project.
match_headline: After Affirmative Action Ban, They Rewrote College Essays With a Key Theme: Race

text: An obituary on Saturday about the golfer Jack Burke Jr. misstated the location of Kiamesha Lake, N.Y., where he moved in the 1940s. It is in Sullivan County, not Westchester County.
match_headline: Jack Burke Jr., Who Won 2 Major Golf Titles in a Season, Dies at 100

text: Because of an editing error, a Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about two Cleveland Orchestra concerts at Carnegie Hall misspelled the clarinetist’s surname in one instance. He is Afendi Yusuf, not Yusef.
match_headline: The Cleveland Orchestra Says a Lot, but Only Through Music

text: An article last Wednesday about the challenges of market­ing food in the era of drugs like Ozempic misstated Steve Siegelman’s job. He is a market­ing creative director, not the executive creative director for the marketing firm Ketchum.
match_headline: In the Ozempic Age, Has ‘Craveable’ Lost Its Selling Power?

text: A review last Wednesday of the TriBeCa restaurant Eulalie misstated the ownership of the Simone, a restaurant, now closed, run by the same couple, Tina Vaughn and Chip Smith. It was owned by Robert Margolis, not Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Smith. The article also misstated the reason for its closing. Mr. Mar­golis closed the Simone because the restaurant faced financial troubles, not because it had failed to negotiate a new lease.
match_headline: Restaurant Review: At Eulalie, a Warm Welcome Is a Phone Call Away

text: An article on Jan. 12 about charges of genocide against Israel omitted part of a quotation from Yoav Gallant. He said, “Gaza won’t return to what it was before. There will be no Hamas. We will eliminate everything.” He did not say only, “Gaza won’t return to what it was before. We will eliminate everything.”
ref_headline: Gaza won’t return to what it was before. There will be no Hamas. We will eliminate everything.
match_headline: Don’t Turn Away From the Charges of Genocide Against Israel

text: An article on Wednesday about religious groups using their land to build affordable housing misstated the connection between Arlington Presbyterian Church and Gilliam Place, an affordable housing complex. The church no longer owns the building or the land it is on; Arlington Partnership for Affordable Housing, a nonprofit developer, does.
match_headline: Amid a Housing Crunch, Religious Groups Unlock Land to Build Homes

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about a settlement in a long-running dispute over Donkey Kong world records described incorrectly the machine that Billy Mitchell used for two of his record-setting Donkey Kong scores. It was an arcade emulator, not a modified machine.
match_headline: A Deal Is Struck in a Long-Running Quarrel. Over Donkey Kong.

text: An article last Thursday about the Playboy Playmate Crystal Hefner misstated the title of a documentary that details allegations of sexu­al abuse against Michael Jackson. It is called “Leaving Neverland,” not “Finding Neverland.”
match_headline: No More Bunny Business

text: An article on Thursday about Republicans in Congress who are now endorsing Donald Trump after his New Hampshire primary win misquoted Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota. He stated he has always said he would “support” the eventual Republican Party presidential nominee, not that he would “endorse” the nominee.
match_headline: After Early Primary Victories, Republicans in Congress Fall in Line Behind Trump

text: A picture caption with an article on Jan. 19 about the U.S. funding of the atomic bomb misstated which structures remained in the area of Hiroshima immediately affected by the blast. Several structures beyond the frame of the photograph still stood; the structure pictured, now referred to as the A-Bomb Dome, was not the only one that remained. The caption also misstated the building’s current function. While it is known as the Hiroshima Peace Memorial, it does not house a memorial. It is instead one part of a larger Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park and museum.
match_headline: A Reporter’s Journey Into How the U.S. Funded the Bomb

text: An article on Thursday about a U.N. shelter in Gaza that was struck by tanks misstated the day that the Israeli military ordered evacuations from parts of Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, that included two hospitals. It was Tuesday, not Wednesday.
match_headline: U.N. Shelter in Besieged Khan Younis Is Struck, and at Least 9 Die

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the ways that NATO’s role has shifted since Russia invaded Ukraine misstated the number of years that the fighting in Ukraine has been underway. It’s been nearly two years, not three.
match_headline: What Is NATO, and How Has the War in Ukraine Changed It?

text: An article on Thursday about how Nikki Haley’s approach to the Republican primary race in New Hampshire ignored lessons from past presidential candidates misstated the year that Bill Clinton finished the Iowa caucuses with 2.8 percent of the vote. It was 1992, not 1996.
match_headline: How Haley Lost New Hampshire: Ignoring Lessons From Underdogs of the Past

text: An article on Dec. 31 about details showing a pattern of rape, mutilation and extreme brutality against women in the Oct. 7 attack by Hamas on Israel misstated the age of Sapir, the woman who has become one of the Israeli police’s key witnesses to the attack. She is 26, not 24.
match_headline: ‘Screams Without Words’: How Hamas Weaponized Sexual Violence on Oct. 7

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about the former boxer Mike Tyson’s move into the cannabis market in New York misstated the year of the bout in which Mr. Tyson bit Evander Holyfield’s ear. As the article correctly notes, it was 1997, not 1987.
match_headline: Homes for Sale in New Jersey and New York

text: An article on Page 7 this weekend about the Calvin Klein underwear ad campaign featuring the actor Jeremy Allen White misspells the surname of an actress in “The Bear.” She is Ayo Edebiri, not Edibiri.
match_headline: The Lascivious, Decades-Long History Behind That Calvin Klein Ad

text: An article on Page 26 about student deaths and a mental-health crisis at Worcester Polytechnic Institute includes several errors. It omits the given name of the former president of Worcester Polytechnic Institute. She is Laurie Leshin. It misspells the surname of the assistant director at the school’s counseling center. He is Matt Barry, not Berry. And the article incorrectly identifies the nationality of a student at Worcester Polytechnic Institute. He was Chinese, not Chinese American. The article also misidentifies the type of glasses used in lab sessions during the Covid pandemic. While they were augmented reality glasses, they were not Air glasses.
match_headline: The Unthinkable Mental Health Crisis That Shook a New England College

text: An article on Jan. 21 about Black and Jewish activists referred imprecisely to the number of people killed in Gaza as of mid-October. It was around 3,500, not simply many thousands.
match_headline: Black and Jewish Activists Have Allied for Decades. What Now?

text: A picture caption with an obituary about the singer and songwriter Melanie on Friday misstated the number of women who performed as female solo acts at the Woodstock music festival in 1969. There were two (Melanie and Joan Baez), as the obituary correctly stated, not three. (Janis Joplin was the third woman to perform at the festival, but she was backed by a band.)
match_headline: Melanie, Singer Who Made a Solo Splash at Woodstock, Dies at 76

text: An article on Jan. 14 about the supermodel Beverly Johnson referred incorrectly to Ms. Johnson’s time at Northeastern University. Before dropping out at 18, she studied criminal justice, not law.
match_headline: Beverly Johnson, ‘the Model With the Big Mouth’

text: An article on Sunday about a lack of support for Nikki Haley in her home state of South Carolina misstated when Ms. Haley resigned as governor of South Carolina to serve in Donald J. Trump’s administration. It was seven years ago, not eight.
match_headline: Why Nikki Haley Has So Few Friends Left in South Carolina Politics

text: An article on Monday about President Biden and the Senate’s progress in appointing judges in Republican states misspelled the given name of a federal judge and misstated the groundbreaking nature of her appointment. She is Sara E. Hill, not Sarah, and she is the first Native American woman confirmed as a federal judge in Oklahoma, not the first Native American.
match_headline: As Biden Judicial Confirmations Slow, Senate Gains Ground on Red-State Judges

text: An article on Tuesday about three men charged in a plot to kill two Iranian refugees in Maryland misstated when three men accused of plotting to assassinate a human-rights activist who has criticized Iran’s repression of women were charged. They were charged at different times, not together in July 2023. The article also misstated when an Indian man accused of plotting to murder a Sikh dissident in New York was indicted. It was in June, not November.
match_headline: U.S. Charges Iranian Man and Two Canadians in Plot to Kill Refugees

text: An article on Friday about New Jersey’s approval of two offshore wind farms attributed an erroneous distinction to the Leading Light Wind project. It would be the first large-scale U.S.-led operation to build a wind farm in the ocean and deliver power from it. It would not be the first such operation of any size to build a wind farm in the ocean. The much smaller Block Island Wind Farm, built by an American developer off the coast of Rhode Island, started production in 2016.
match_headline: After Its Big Setback, New Jersey Awards 2 Offshore Wind Contracts

text: An article on Saturday about a United Nations investigation of claims that employees participated in the Oct. 7 attack misstated the number of people working for UNRWA. The agency has 13,000 employees in Gaza alone, not across the world.
match_headline: U.N. to Investigate Claim That Employees Participated in Oct. 7 Attack

text: An article on Sunday about President Biden’s failure to communicate his most significant climate policy achievements to voters misspelled the surname of the spokesman for Voters of Tomorrow. It is Jack Lobel, not Jack Lobell.
match_headline: Democrats Say Biden Hasn’t ‘Made the Case’ on Climate Despite Achievements

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about President Biden’s attempt to rally Black voters in South Carolina incorrectly paraphrased what protesters were shouting during an event with Mr. Biden. Though they were criticizing the civilian death toll in Gaza, they did not shout out a specific number.
match_headline: In South Carolina, Biden Tries to Persuade Black Voters to Reject Trump

text: An article on Saturday about the last mission of NASA’s Ingenuity helicopter on Mars misstated Lori Glaze’s title at NASA. She is the director of the planetary science division, not the associate administrator for the science directorate.
match_headline: Ingenuity, the NASA Helicopter Flying Over Mars, Ends Its Mission

text: An article on Friday about the “Artland” show at the Brooklyn Museum, using information from the Brooklyn Museum, described incorrectly the title of Shamilia McBean Tocruray at the museum. She is the director of education, not a co-director.
match_headline: Hands-On Art at the Brooklyn Museum’s New Education Center

text: An article on Tuesday about the state of rail safety in the United States a year after a derailment in East Palestine, Ohio, reversed the rankings of the top two U.S. railroads, as measured by miles of track. BNSF is the largest, and Union Pacific is second.
match_headline: Since Ohio Train Derailment, Accidents Have Gone Up, Not Down

text: An article on Wednesday about President Biden’s border policy record over the last three years misstated the number of flights of migrants that were sent back to Port-au-Prince in September 2021. There were 58 expulsion flights that month, not up to 39 flights per day.
match_headline: How the Border Crisis Shattered Biden’s Immigration Hopes

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about rising cases of syphilis in the United States misidentified the most common sexually transmitted infection in the country. It is HPV, not chlamydia.
match_headline: Syphilis Is Soaring in the U.S.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about a Josephine Baker exhibition in Berlin misidentified a museum where Klaus Biesenbach worked. It was the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, not the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
match_headline: Josephine Baker, Still Moving

text: An article last Thursday on the Estée Lauder brand’s Legacy Collection of perfumes misstated the number of years that Ms. Lauder worked at her namesake company. It was 49, not 42.
match_headline: A Red Velvet Bistro in an Istanbul Villa

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the novelist N. Scott Momaday omitted the name of one of his wives. In addition to the two named, he was married most recently to Barbara Gregg Glenn Momaday, who died in 2008.
match_headline: N. Scott Momaday, Pulitzer-Winning Native American Novelist, Dies at 89

text: An article on Thursday about two platoonmates who were killed in Jordan misidentified the career ambition of Specialist Kennedy Sanders’s friend. She was learning to be a radiology technician, not a radiologist.
match_headline: Defense Department Identifies 3 Soldiers Killed at Base in Jordan

text: An article on Thursday about tech workers who are sharing their layoff experiences on social media misspelled the surname of an author. She is Lindsey Pollak, not Pollack.
match_headline: Watch Me Lose My Job on TikTok

text: An article on Sunday about false information that spread online about a young man’s death in the New York City subway misidentified the elite private boys’ school in New York that Matthew Sachman attended. It is the Collegiate School, not Collegiate High School.
match_headline: He Died in a Tragic Accident. Why Did the Internet Say He Was Murdered?

text: An article on Thursday about a top editor at The Jewish Press who pleaded guilty for his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot misspelled the surname of Elliot Resnick’s lawyer. He is Clay Kaminsky, not Kaminski.
match_headline: Brooklyn Jewish Newspaper’s Ex-Top Editor Pleads Guilty to Jan. 6 Charge

text: An article on Thursday about Silicon Valley tech companies’ attempt to block new state laws protecting young people online misstated the title of Algenon L. Marbley. He is chief judge of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio, Eastern Division, not chief justice.
match_headline: Silicon Valley Battles States Over New Online Safety Laws for Children

text: An article on Monday about the Apple TV+ series “Masters of the Air," based on press notes from Apple+, misstated the number of casualties (including those killed, injured and captured) the Eighth Air Force suffered during World War II. That figure, 77 percent, refers to casualties suffered in 1943 by the 100th Bomb Group, a unit of the Eighth Air Force, not the Eighth Air Force as a whole.
match_headline: With ‘Masters of the Air,’ a 10-Year Dream Lifts Off

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Friday about a new reconstruction plan for the Port Authority incorrectly described a rendering. The rendering was of the final design at 8th Avenue and 41st Street, not 40th Street.
match_headline: A Look at the $10 Billion Design for a New Port Authority Bus Terminal

text: A picture caption with an article on Jan. 28 about a new television show that explores Truman Capote’s social exile misidentified the woman standing to Truman Capote’s right. She is Jeanne Murray Vanderbilt, not Gloria Guinness.
match_headline: Truman Capote Cashed In on His Friends’ Secrets. It Cost Him Everything.

text: An article on Dec. 5 about images in space described imprecisely the speed of ultrahigh cosmic rays. They accelerate to a speed faster than any known process can explain, they are not faster than any known process in the universe.
An article on Page 24 this weekend about the founding of Israel misspells the given name of a former mayor of Jerusalem. He was Raghib al-Nashashibi, not Raghid.

An article on page 20 this weekend about New College of Florida includes several errors. It misstates the month Jayleigh Totten, a student, arrived there. It was August, not September. It also incorrectly renders the surname of a student and the month when he was asked to help interview a potential hire. He is Andrés Rivera Calderón, not Rivera-Caldéron; it was in November, not October. The article incorrectly describes changes to leadership at the college. Ron DeSantis, Florida’s governor, replaced six of 13 trustees at the college, not most. He did this last January, not last spring. The newly conservative board then fired and replaced the school’s president. It is not the case that DeSantis fired the school’s president.
match_headline: Recruited to Play Sports, and Win a Culture War

text: An article last Sunday about podcasts for Hollywood’s awards season misidentified two of the hosts of the “Little Gold Men” podcast. They are David Canfield and Rebecca Ford, not Michael Hogan and Joanna Robinson, who previously hosted the show.
match_headline: 5 Podcasts for Hollywood’s Awards Season

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about the founding of Israel misspells the given name of a former mayor of Jerusalem. He was Raghib al-Nashashibi, not Raghid.

An article on Monday about a campaign to get a championship H.B.C.U. basketball team the recognition it deserves misspelled the surname of the Tennessee A&I Tigers basketball coach. He is John McLendon, not McClendon.
match_headline: A Forgotten Championship H.B.C.U. Team Comes Off the Sidelines

text: A headline on Friday with an article about the actor and writer Maya Erskine referred incorrectly to the Netflix reboot of “Mr. & Mrs. Smith” in which she appears. It is an eight-episode series, not a movie.
match_headline: Maya Erskine, of ‘Mr. & Mrs. Smith,’ Thinks She Would Make a Good Spy

text: An article on Jan. 30 about the health risks associated with different forms of cannabis referred imprecisely to Daniel Barrus’s academic degree. He has a master’s degree.
match_headline: Are Edibles Safer Than Smoking?

text: An article on Sunday about wildfires in Chile misstated the locations of Viña del Mar and Valparaíso in relation to Santiago. They are northwest, not northeast.
match_headline: Wildfires Threaten 2 Chilean Cities, Destroying 1,000 Homes and Killing Dozens

text: An article on Sunday about Bank of America backtracking on its message that it would no longer finance coal misstated changes the bank made to language on its website regarding Indigenous rights. While the bank deleted language saying it would not finance coal and Arctic drilling projects, the language on related considerations, including the rights of Indigenous people, remains.
match_headline: Bank of America Pledged to Stop Financing Coal. Now It’s Backtracking.

text: An article on Sunday about Republicans’ nomination of the Israeli military veteran Mazi Pilip to fill a House seat inaccurately described the gender-based usage of the Hebrew word for paratrooper. The word does have a feminine form, although its masculine form is the one almost always used in the military to describe the elite combat role.
match_headline: With House Seat at Stake, Republicans Court Jewish Voters Rattled by War

text: An article on Saturday about the closure of the Rubin Museum of Art in Manhattan misstated the year that the Barneys store at 115 Seventh Avenue closed. It was 1997, not 2020. (A separate location on Seventh Avenue closed in 2020.)

Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the author Robie Harris misidentified the college from which she graduated in 1962. It was Wheaton College in Massachusetts, not the college of the same name in Illinois. Because of another editing error, the obituary also misstated the title that Suzanne Nossel holds with PEN America. She is the organization’s chief executive officer, not its executive director.
match_headline: Robie Harris, Often-Banned Children’s Author, Is Dead at 83

text: An article on Wednesday about New York public housing employees charged in a corruption case misidentified the New York City Housing Authority entities affected by the bribery scheme. It was 100 housing developments, not 100 buildings.
match_headline: Scores of N.Y. Public Housing Workers Charged in Record Corruption Case

text: An article on Thursday about the actress Da’Vine Joy Randolph who stars in “The Holdovers” misstated the title of her breakout film. It is “Dolemite Is My Name,” not “Dolemite Is His Name.”
match_headline: Da’Vine Joy Randolph: Major Prizes, Major Attention, Major Unease

text: An article on Friday about a growing number of schools extending the deadline for registration commitments because of delayed financial aid information, using incorrect information provided by Saint Louis University, misstated Rob Reddy’s title at Saint Louis University. He is interim vice president of enrollment management, not vice president of enrollment management.
match_headline: Some Colleges Are Pivoting as FAFSA Delays Drag On

text: An article on Feb. 4 about the founding of Israel incorrectly identified Jorge Garcia Granados. He was the Guatemalan ambassador to the United Nations, not the foreign minister of Guatemala.
match_headline: The World Needs to Stand by UNRWA

text: An article on Monday about the Republican Party’s efforts to regain influence in New York City suburbs misstated the location of a Republican rally in Massapequa in Nassau County, N.Y. It was held at an American Legion hall, not a V.F.W. hall.
match_headline: In the Land of George Santos, Machine Politics Fuels a G.O.P. Revival

text: An article on Sunday about the cost of moving into a New York City apartment misstated the type of security deposit payment program mentioned by Douglas Wagner, director of brokerage services for Bond New York Real Estate. He was referring to programs offered by third-party companies, not the city government.
match_headline: Boxes, Tape, $10,000: What It Takes to Move Into an N.Y.C. Apartment

text: An article on Thursday about Apple’s Vision Pro headset misstated the price of prescription lens inserts. They start at $150, not $100.
match_headline: Vision Pro Review: Apple’s First Headset Lacks Polish and Purpose

text: An article on Monday about King Charles III’s first public appearance since the announcement about his cancer treatment misstated his age. He is 75, not 74.
match_headline: King Charles Appears in Public for First Time Since Cancer Announcement

text: An article on Wednesday about possible changes to the C.D.C.’s recommended isolation period after testing positive for the coronavirus misstated the number of Covid deaths earlier this winter. It was 1,500 per week, not per day.
match_headline: C.D.C. Considers Ending 5-Day Isolation Period for Covid

text: A column on Monday about this week’s television roundup misstated the length of the break for the TV show “Young Sheldon.” While the show was delayed at different points, it did not have a two-year hiatus.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘True Detective: Night Country’ and ‘Doctor Zhivago’

text: An article on Wednesday about the dancer and choreographer Jean Butler misstated the name of the Irish dance archive that Butler has created in partnership with the dance division of the New York Public Library. It is “Our Steps, Our Story,” not “Our Steps, Our Stories.”
match_headline: Jean Butler Choreographs the Past and Future of Irish Dance

text: An article on Thursday about Liu Jianchao’s role in shifting the Chinese Communist Party’s tone described incorrectly a meeting between Mr. Liu, who is the head of China’s International Liaison Department, and U.S. Secretary of State Antony J. Blinken. While meetings between officials in those positions are rare, the meeting between Mr. Liu and Mr. Blinken was not the first of its kind.
match_headline: As China Tries to Present a Friendlier Image, a New Face Emerges

text: An article on Thursday about fears of an expansion of Israel’s war in the Gaza Strip misstated the day on which Benny Gantz, a member of Israel’s war cabinet, warned of further Israeli strikes in Lebanon. His comments were on Wednesday, not on Monday. The article also misspelled the surname of Hezbollah’s leader. He is Hassan Nasrallah, not Nazrallah.
match_headline: Lebanon’s State Media Says Israeli Strikes There Killed 10 Civilians

text: An article on Thursday about concerns about Keir Starmer’s management of the U.K. Labour Party misstated the date of a by-election in Rochdale, England. It is scheduled for Feb. 29, not Feb. 28. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: The U.K. Labour Party’s Worst Enemy Might Be Itself

text: An article on Sunday about a rise in premature births in the United States misstated the name of Northwell Health’s maternal health department. It is Center for Maternal Health, not Center for Maternal Medicine.
match_headline: After Years of Decline, Premature Births Rose in the U.S.

text: An article on Feb. 11 about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the Democratic Party referred imprecisely to Rashida Tlaib’s views of the Oct. 7 attacks. She did not refer to the attacks as a “justified” resistance; the House censure of Tlaib described her statements that way. Tlaib has said she deplores the loss of any civilian lives.
match_headline: How the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict Drove a Wedge Into the Democratic Party

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about the opera singer Wilhelmenia Wiggins Fernandez, using information from Getty Images, misstated the name of the singer pictured with her in a production of “Porgy and Bess.” He is Donnie Ray Albert, not Ray Albert.
match_headline: Wilhelmenia Wiggins Fernandez, the Diva of ‘Diva,’ Dies at 75

text: An article last Sunday about photographs taken by Paul McCartney misidentified the member of the British royal family who met with the Beatles in 1963. The Beatles met the Queen Mother (and Princess Margaret) that year; they met Queen Elizabeth II in 1965.

text: An article on Feb. 11 about comedians who are addressing the topic of global warming with humor misstated the role that Yellow Dot Studios plays in the development of the comedic material on its website.
