text: An obituary on Monday about the Muslim scholar Marnia Lazreg referred incorrectly to Mostaganem, Algeria, where she was born. It is west of Algiers, not east.
match_headline: Marnia Lazreg, Muslim Scholar Who Critiqued the Veil, Is Dead at 83

text: An article on Thursday about the Democratic Party’s attempt to derail third-party candidates from the presidential ballot misstated the number of states for which the No Labels group says it has qualified for the ballot. It is 18 states, not 14.
match_headline: Democrats Prepare Aggressive Counter to Third-Party Threats

text: An article on Sunday about diplomacy by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines amid escalating tensions in the South China Sea misidentified one site where Chinese boats harassed Filipino fishing boats. It was the Scarborough Shoal, not the Spratly Islands.
match_headline: Standing Up to China, Philippine Leader Courts New Network of Partners

text: An article on Thursday about Japan’s improved labor force participation for women misstated the time period over which the number of children on nursery center waiting lists decreased. The length of the list decreased to 2,680 in 2023, not this year.
match_headline: Japan’s Labor Market Has a Lesson for the Fed: Women Can Surprise You

text: An article on Wednesday about the possibility of artificial intelligence capabilities for the iPhone misstated the year when Apple agreed to use Google as the default search engine of the Safari browser. It was 2002, not after the iPhone’s introduction in 2007.
match_headline: Apple and Google Are Discussing a Deal to Bring Generative A.I. to iPhones

text: A headline with an article on Friday about a vote to enable former President Donald J. Trump’s social media company to start trading on the stock market misstated the type of transaction involved in taking the company public. The transaction was a merger of Mr. Trump’s company with a publicly traded shell company called Digital World Acquisition Corporation; it did not involve an initial public offering.
match_headline: Reddit Rises 48% in First Day of Trading

text: An article on Page 10 this weekend about a new television show from the creators of the HBO series “Game of Thrones” misspells the surname of an actress in the new Netflix series “3 Body Problem.” She is Eiza González, not Gonzáles.
match_headline: ‘Game of Thrones’ Creators Look Skyward for Their New Series

text: An article last Sunday about the billionaire investor Nelson Peltz misidentified Charles Elson. He is a former director of the John L. Wein­berg Center for Corporate Govern­ance at the University of Delaware, not its current director.
match_headline: The Billionaire Taking on Disney Just Wants Some Respect

text: An article on March 10 about dividing the marital home in divorce incorrectly described 2022 divorce data. There were nearly one million divorces that year, not nearly one million people who were divorced.
match_headline: I Want the House, Not My Spouse

text: An article on Thursday about a treetop walkway in Hungary misstated the name of the mayor of Nyirmartonfalva, Hungary. He is Mihaly Filemon, not Filemon Maholy.
match_headline: The Walkway to Nowhere: A Monument to Hungary’s Patronage Politics

text: An article on Sunday about the U.N. Secretary General’s visit to the Rafah border crossing misstated Algeria’s action in a U.N. Security Council vote on a cease-fire in Gaza on Friday. Algeria voted against the resolution, but could not veto it as a nonpermanent member of the council.
match_headline: U.N. Chief Calls Conditions in Gaza a ‘Moral Outrage’

text: An article on Monday about Tammy Murphy’s decision to end her run for a U.S. Senate seat in New Jersey misstated which day Senator Robert Menendez announced he would not run for re-election as a Democrat in the June primary. It was Thursday, not Friday.
match_headline: Tammy Murphy Drops Out of Race for Menendez’s Senate Seat

text: An article on Monday about ticket sales for the Boston Symphony Orchestra’s outdoor concert venue misstated Monika Pizzichemi’s role at the Wit Gallery. She is the director, not the manager.
match_headline: In Frigid Early Spring, Lining Up for a Rite of Summer in Western Massachusetts

text: An article on Monday about a super PAC that aims to fund supporters of building more housing misspelled the last name of the assemblywoman who represents parts of the Hudson Valley. She is Sarahana Shrestha, not Srestha.
match_headline: New Group Plans to Spend Big in Support of YIMBY Campaigns

text: An article on Saturday about how the artificial intelligence boom has made the island of Anguilla a fortune misstated the location of the Tuvalu islands in relation to Australia. They are northeast of Australia, not northwest.
match_headline: The A.I. Boom Makes Millions for an Unlikely Industry Player: Anguilla

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about young recital debuts at Carnegie Hall misstated the record label to which the pianist Jan Lisiecki is signed. It is Deutsche Grammophon, not Decca. The article, using incorrect information provided by Carnegie Hall, also mischaracterized the performance history of Medtner’s “Sonata-Reminiscenza” in A minor at the hall. Alexander Malofeev’s recital on March 19 was not the first time the work was played there.
match_headline: At Carnegie Hall, the New Pianists Are Young and Younger

text: An article on Tuesday about a ballet inspired by the history of the Iranian National Ballet misstated Tara Ghassemieh’s current role. She is no longer with Golden State Ballet.
match_headline: A Second Act for Ballet in Iran?

text: An article on Tuesday about how new star discoveries make it harder to predict Earth’s future and reconstruct its past misstated the possible distance between HD 7977 and the sun. It was 400 billion miles, not 4 billion. It also misstated Sean Raymond’s affiliation. He is at the Laboratoire d’Astrophysique de Bordeaux in France, not the University of Oklahoma.
match_headline: Cosmic Forecast: Blurry With a Chance of Orbital Chaos

text: An article on Monday about the possible seizure of former President Donald J. Trump’s properties, using information provided by JLL, a real estate services firm, misstated the trend in appraisal values of Manhattan buildings. Among 1,200 Manhattan buildings, about one in every three was appraised at a lower value than its previous sale price, not one out of four among 380 Manhattan buildings.
match_headline: Could Trump’s Properties Really Be Seized?

text: An article this weekend on Page 4 about an immersive revival of “Cabaret” misstates Rebecca Frecknall’s age; she is 37, not 38. It also misstates her mother’s given name; she is Kate, not Jane. The article also mistakenly states that Frecknall’s parents had met in a community theater group; they joined the group after they had met. And it misidentifies the origins of a playbill for Peter Shaffer’s “Equus”; it was from a London production, not the original Broadway production. And it misspells the given name of a composer and lyricist; he was Stephen Sondheim, not Steven.
match_headline: How to Restage ‘Cabaret’? Don’t Treat It Like a Classic.

text: An obituary on Thursday about the four-term United States senator and former Democratic vice-presidential nominee Joseph I. Lieberman misstated the surname of one of his daughters. She is Hana Lowenstein, not Lieberman.
match_headline: Joseph I. Lieberman, Senator and Vice-Presidential Nominee, Dies at 82

text: A review on March 10 about Candace Fleming’s children’s book “The Enigma Girls,” using information from the book, misspelled the surname of an English composer and BBC executive. He was Herbert Murrill, not Murrell.
match_headline: Move Over, Alan Turing; Meet the Teenage Girls Who Rocked Bletchley Park

text: A review last Sunday about “Soldiers and Kings: Survival and Hope in the World of Human Smuggling,” by Jason De León, misstated the nature of the crime com­mitted by a smuggler named Kingston, which led to his deportation to Honduras. Kingston used a .22 to pistol­-whip some­one’s face; he did not use the gun to shoot the person in the face.
ref_headline: Soldiers and Kings: Survival and Hope in the World of Human Smuggling,
match_headline: A Rare Inside Look at Human Smuggling on the Border

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about Ukrainian troops using marketing to attract recruits misstated the Ukrainian armed forces unit of which the Da Vinci Wolves battalion is a part. It now belongs to the 59th Motorized Brigade, not the 67th Separate Mechanized Brigade.
match_headline: Troop-Starved Ukrainian Brigades Turn to Marketing to Attract Recruits

text: An article on Saturday about Senator Patty Murray’s success in increasing child care funding attributed an erroneous distinction to her. Senator Barbara Mikulski of Maryland was the first woman to lead the Senate Appropriations Committee, not Senator Murray.
match_headline: How Patty Murray Used Her Gavel to Win $1 Billion for Child Care

text: An obituary on Saturday about the actor Louis Gossett Jr. misstated the name of the play in which he portrayed the Congolese leader Patrice Lumumba on Broadway in 1971. It is “Murderous Angels,” not “Dangerous Angels.”
match_headline: Louis Gossett Jr., 87, Dies; ‘An Officer and a Gentleman’ and ‘Roots’ Actor

text: An obituary on Saturday about the jazz singer Eleanor Collins misstated the year her husband, Richard Collins, died. It was 2011, not 2014.
match_headline: Eleanor Collins, Canada’s ‘First Lady of Jazz,’ Dies at 104

text: An article on Wednesday about a new project to create a pedestrian-friendly, archaeological area in downtown Rome referred incorrectly to the city’s age. It is approaching its fourth millennium, not its third.
match_headline: Rome’s Future Is a Walk Through Its Past

text: An article on Wednesday about a Canadian lawmaker who testified that China helped get him voters, misidentified the court affiliation of Marie-Josée Hogue. She is a Court of Appeal justice, not a Superior Court justice.
match_headline: Canadian Lawmaker Testifies Chinese Students Were Bused In to Elect Him

text: An article last Thursday about outlets where men are buying suits off the rack misstated the starting prices for J. Crew’s Ludlow, Kenmare and Crosby suits. The Ludlow starts at about $675, not $298; the Kenmare starts at about $650, not $248; and the Crosby starts at about $675, not $198.
match_headline: Where Are Men Buying Suits Off the Rack?

text: An article on Thursday about a small study that found a slowing of some symptoms of Parkinson’s disease by using a GLP-1 receptor agonist misspelled a doctor’s name. She is Dr. Hyun Joo Cho, not Chu.
match_headline: An Ozempic Relative Slowed Parkinson’s Disease in a Small Study

text: An article on Friday about simultaneous terrorist attacks by a separatist group in Iran misidentified the location of Sistan and Baluchestan Province, where the attacks occurred. It is in the southeast, not the southwest, of Iran.
match_headline: Iran Says 17-Hour Battle With Separatists Leaves 28 Dead in 2 Cities

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about NATO’s efforts to show support for Ukraine without inviting it to join the alliance misidentified the city where NATO membership negotiations would take place. It is Washington, D.C., not Brussels.
match_headline: NATO Wants to Show Support for Ukraine, but Only So Much

text: An article on Page 32 this weekend about Ahmad Al-Halabi, an Air Force airman wrongly accused of espionage, refers imprecisely to Al-Halabi’s plea. He admitted to mishandling classified documents at Guantánamo and to mailing documents to Travis Air Force Base in California without authorization, not to mishandling classified documents when he mailed documents to California.
match_headline: A Russian Defector’s Killing Raises Specter of Hit Squads

text: An article on March 31 about Matt Farley, a songwriter and filmmaker, referred incorrectly to Taylor, a film student who watched many screenings of Mr. Farley’s films. Taylor uses they and them pronouns, not he and him.
match_headline: Why Did This Guy Put a Song About Me on Spotify?

text: A caption with an article last Sun­day about sports at Southern Meth­odist University misidentified the Texas player shown, using informa­tion from Reuters. It was Michael Taaffe, not Arch Manning.
match_headline: How S.M.U., Once the Rogue of College Sports, Got Back to the Big Time

text: A review on March 17 about the memoir “Grief Is for People,” by Sloane Crosley, misstated the location of a house where the author’s friend and former boss Rus­sell Perreault had once lived. The house was in Connecticut, not upstate New York.
match_headline: A Dazzling Humorist Returns With a Deep Dive Into Loss

text: Because of an editing error, the “Read Your Way Through Utah” feature on March 24 misstated the number of emi­grants killed by Mormon militiamen in 1857 near St. George, Utah, in what is known as the Mountain Meadows massa­cre. It was 120, not 20.
match_headline: Read Your Way Through Utah

text: An article on Saturday about an earthquake that struck the Northeast described incorrectly a trip to the Empire State Building by Clara Dossetter and David Dossetter. Mr. Dossetter was visiting from San Francisco, but Ms. Dossetter lives in New York.
match_headline: Earthquake Rattles New York and New Jersey, but Does Little Damage

text: An article on Sunday about the ways in which the war in Gaza has highlighted the pipeline of U.S. weapons to Israel misstated the name of the organization that employed the seven aid workers who were killed by an Israeli airstrike in Gaza. It is World Central Kitchen, not World Food Kitchen.
match_headline: Gaza War Turns Spotlight on Long Pipeline of U.S. Weapons to Israel

text: An article on Saturday about voting­-fraud prosecutions included an outdated affiliation for an organization. The Legal Defense Fund is no longer part of the N.A.A.C.P.
match_headline: A Reversal Cannot Undo the Damage Caused by This Voting Fraud Case

text: An obituary on Jan. 15 about Leon Wildes, the immigration lawyer who successfully fought the United States government’s attempt to deport John Lennon, misstated the year the documentary “The U.S. vs. John Lennon” was released. It was 2006, not 2007. This correction was delayed because the error was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: Leon Wildes, 90, Immigration Lawyer Who Defended John Lennon, Dies

text: An article on Monday about people around the country who have been harmed by the drive for an atomic bomb but have been shut out of a federal law enacted to help such victims misstated the location of the first atomic bomb test. It was at a site in southern New Mexico, not at Los Alamos, N.M.
match_headline: Sickened by U.S. Nuclear Program, Communities Turn to Congress for Aid

text: An article last Wednesday about the comforts of dal misspelled the surname of an Indian American novelist in Brooklyn. She is Sarah Thankam Mathews, not Matthews.
match_headline: Dal Is the Ultimate Comfort Food

text: An article on Wednesday about the toll of aging misstated the number of words beginning with F that people with normal cognitive abilities could name in a minute during the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. It is greater than 11, not less than.
match_headline: Dr. Bob, 75, Knows Aging’s Toll. He Wonders if Biden and Trump Do.

text: An article on Wednesday about the British foreign secretary’s visit to the United States misstated the year of the Winter Olympic Games that Mitt Romney had organized in Salt Lake City. It was the 2002 Games, not 1988.
match_headline: Cameron, on U.S. Trip, Takes a Risk and Meets With Trump

text: An article on Friday about a study linking eyeglasses and income level in Bangladesh referred incorrectly to an eyesight condition, presbyopia. People with presbyopia are unable to see things up close, but the condition is not the same as farsightedness.
match_headline: Glasses Improve Income, Not Just Eyesight

text: An article on Wednesday about Germany’s response to accusations that its arms sales to Israel were abetting genocide in Gaza misspelled the surname of a political analyst. She is Sudha David-Wilp, not David-Whilp.
match_headline: Germany Rebuffs Claim Its Arms Sales to Israel Abet Genocide in Gaza

text: An article on March 30 about the effects of the cyberattack on Change Healthcare on March 30 misstated the professional affiliation of D.J. Patil. He is a general partner at the venture capital firm GreatPoint Ventures. He is no longer on staff at Devoted Health, though he remains on the company’s board.
match_headline: 4 Things You Need to Know About Health Care Cyberattacks

text: An article on Thursday about an Israeli airstrike that killed the three sons of a senior Hamas official paraphrased incorrectly a Hamas official’s comments about a possible hostage exchange. The official said Hamas sent a message to international mediators that the group did not have hostages who met the criteria for an exchange under a proposed cease-fire agreement with Israel being negotiated. He did not say that Hamas could not locate them in a message sent directly to Israel.
match_headline: Hamas Leader Defiant After Israeli Strike Kills 3 of His Sons

text: An article on Tuesday about the upcoming elections in the U.S. House of Representatives described incorrectly Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system. The top four finishers from a nonpartisan primary on Aug. 20 will go on to compete in the general election, not the top two finishers.
match_headline: Alaska Primary Election Results

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about Democrats’ attempt to repeal the 1864 ban on abortion in Arizona misidentified the man shown in the image. That picture showed the speaker pro tem of the Arizona House of Representatives, Travis Grantham, not Speaker Ben Toma.
match_headline: Arizona Republicans Thwart Attempts to Repeal 1864 Abortion Ban

text: An article on Thursday about a visit to the White House by the prime minister of Japan misstated which countries belong to a security pact that Japan may join. Its members are the United States, Australia and Britain, not the United States, Australia and New Zealand.
match_headline: Biden and Kishida Agree to Tighten Military and Economic Ties to Counter China

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about a proposal to raise the price of stamps misstated the status of a requirement that the Postal Service fund retiree health care benefits for its employees in advance. That requirement was canceled in 2022; it is no longer in effect.
match_headline: U.S. Postal Service Proposes Raising Stamp Prices Again

text: An article on March 29 about Robinhood’s credit card misstated the year that Robinhood froze trading in certain stocks during a period of extreme volatility. It was 2021, not 2020.
match_headline: Robinhood’s Credit Card Offers 3% Cash Back. Can It Last?

text: An article on Saturday about the artist and filmmaker Arthur Jafa misspelled the surname of the author of “Dog in a Fisherman’s Net.” He is Samuel Delany, not Delaney.
match_headline: A ‘Taxi Driver’ Remake: Why Arthur Jafa Recast the Scorsese Ending

text: An article on Page 9 this weekend about the film “Coyote vs. Acme,” refers incorrectly to the voice work of Eric Bauza in the film “Coyote vs. Acme.” While Bauza provided the voices for several characters in the film, Wile E. Coyote was not one of them.
match_headline: Want to See This Film? Movie Studios Won’t Let You.

text: An article last Sunday about Bran­don Blackwell, who excelled on the British quiz show “University Chal­lenge,” misstated the name of the Los Angeles neighborhood where the College Bowl Company has its office. It is Woodland Hills, not Wild Hills.
match_headline: Q: Who Found a Way to Crack the U.K.’s Premier Quiz Show?

text: An article last Sunday about mem­bers of Generation X looking for homes referred incorrectly to the median income earned by those within this age group. The median income of people who are home buyers within the group is $126,900; it is not the median income of the entire group.
match_headline: As Gen X-ers Inch Toward Retirement, They’re Considering Where to Live

text: An article last Sunday about the Hideout, a residential community in the Pocono Mountains, mis­stated its size. It occupies 2,700 acres, not 250 acres.
match_headline: A Showdown Pits Owners of Second Homes Against Full-Time Residents

text: A review on March 24 about “3 Shades of Blue,” by James Kaplan, using informa­tion from the publisher, included a photo­ graph that had been reversed. The cor­rect image shows, from left to right, John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Miles Davis and Bill Evans.
match_headline: What’s the Greatest Jazz Record? Here’s a Clue: Miles Davis.

text: An article on Friday about the possible impact that psychedelics could have on survivors of the Oct. 7 terror attacks in Israel misspelled the surname of psychology professor at the University of Haifa. He is Roee Admon, not Edmon. The article also misspelled the given name of a cognitive science professor at the school. He is Roy Salomon, not Roi.
match_headline: In a Rare Sermon, Iran’s Supreme Leader Praises Oct. 7 Attacks as ‘Logical’ and Warns Israel

text: An article on Saturday about the expansion of two California national monuments misspelled the given name of a program director at the Conservation Lands Foundation. She is Elyane Stefanick, not Elaye.
match_headline: Biden Administration Said to Expand Two California National Monuments

text: An article on Monday about the general director of Lyric Opera of Chicago’s retirement misstated the seating capacity of the Lyric Opera of Chicago. The theater seats 3,276, not 3,563, which was its capacity before a renovation.
match_headline: A ‘Missionary for Opera’ Steps Down in Chicago

text: An article on Thursday about “forever chemicals” described incorrectly the molecular structure of PFAS compounds. They have carbon and fluorine atoms, not carbon and fluoride.
match_headline: Six Things to Know About ‘Forever Chemicals’

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misidentified the channel airing “Talk to Me” on Sunday. It is Showtime, not HBO.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: The WNBA Draft and ‘RuPaul’s Drag Race’

text: An article on Wednesday about a mayor’s decision to stop a gathering of prominent conservatives in Brussels misstated the surname of a British former home secretary. She is Suella Braverman, not Braveman.
match_headline: ‘Canceled’ for Protesting Cancel Culture, Europe’s Right-Wingers Rejoice

text: An article on Tuesday about the artist Faith Ringgold described incorrectly the men in “The Civil Rights Triangle.” Three were wearing suits, not all five.
match_headline: Faith Ringgold Perfectly Captured the Pitch of America’s Madness

text: An article on Thursday about the debate over free speech and antisemitism happening at universities in the wake of the Israel-Hamas war misstated when the Harvard Palestine Solidarity Groups issued a public letter in which they said they held “the Israeli regime entirely responsible for all the unfolding violence.” The letter was issued on the weekend of the Oct. 7 Hamas attack on Israel, not the weekend after the attack.
ref_headline: the Israeli regime entirely responsible for all the unfolding violence.
match_headline: Campus Protest Investigations Hang Over Schools as New Academic Year Begins

text: An obituary on Friday about O.J. Simpson misstated who owned the Ford Bronco in which he fled after being charged with the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald L. Goldman. It was Mr. Simpson’s friend Al Cowlings, the driver — not Mr. Simpson himself. The obituary also misstated what Mr. Simpson’s lawyer Johnnie L. Cochran Jr. told the jury at his murder trial about a glove. It was “If it doesn’t fit, you must acquit” — not “If the glove don’t fit, you must acquit.” And it referred incorrectly to the contract Mr. Simpson signed with ABC in 1969. It was for appearances on “Wide World of Sports” and other ABC shows — not for work as a color commentator. (ABC would hire him as a color commentator for “Monday Night Football,” but not until 1983.)
ref_headline: If it doesn’t fit, you must acquit
match_headline: O.J. Simpson, Football Star Whose Trial Riveted the Nation, Dies at 76

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the relocation of an ousted former leader from a prison in Myanmar to an unknown location misstated how long Myanmar’s military has controlled the country. It is more than half a century, not nearly half a century.
match_headline: Aung San Suu Kyi Moved to Unknown Location From Prison by Myanmar Junta

text: An article on Thursday about turmoil at colleges over the Israel-Hamas war incorrectly linked and misidentified a statement by the American Civil Liberties Union’s Michigan chapter. That statement was from Dec. 19, not in reference to a more recent proposal from the University of Michigan.
match_headline: University of California Resolves Civil Rights Complaints Over Gaza Protests

text: An article on Thursday about Nadia Boulanger’s “La Ville Morte” opera misspelled the surname of a scholar. She is Alexandra Laederich, not Laederach.
match_headline: Before She Became Music’s Greatest Teacher, She Wrote an Opera

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the artist Roni Horn, and a picture caption with the article, misstates the year attributed to “Gold Field,” a work by Roni Horn. It is 1980/1994, not 1982 or 1980/2003.
match_headline: Roni Horn: a Restless Artist With 4 Shows and More Identities

text: An article on Page 51 about projects that various artists are working on this year includes comments from the architect and designer Gaetano Pesce. Mr. Pesce died on April 3 at age 84.
match_headline: Gaetano Pesce, Designer Who Broke the Rules, Is Dead at 84

text: An article on Page 115 about the playwright Ife Olujobi misquotes her in a few instances. Olujobi said she worked at the Criterion Collection after she graduated from N.Y.U., not while she was in college. Separately, Olujobi said the play that she used to apply to the Public Theater’s Emerging Writers Workshop was a work she wrote during college, not “Jordans.”
match_headline: Peter Morgan Turns His Pen From ‘The Crown’ to the Kremlin

text: An article on Page 120 about the actress and singer Maisy Stella misstates the location where Maisy Stella was photographed; it was Fannie Mae Dees Park in Nashville, not Percy Priest Lake Park.

An article last Sunday about Sky High Farm referred imprecisely to Dan Colen. He is Sky High’s sole founder, not a co-­founder. Because of an editing error, a picture caption with the article reversed the identifi­cations of James Gilchrist and Jon Gray. And the article attributed an outdated distinction to Joshua Bard­ field. Although Mr. Bardfield is now the co-­executive director of Sky High Farm, he is no longer a member of its board.
match_headline: Fashion’s Favorite Farm

text: An article last Sunday about cross­words by Gen Z constructors mis­stated Adam Aaronson’s age. He is 22, not 23.
match_headline: How Gen Z Made the Crossword Their Own

text: An article on Monday about the possibility of the U.S. imposing sanctions on Israeli military battalions misstated a title once held by Charles Blaha. He is a former director of an office in the State Department’s bureau of democracy, human rights and labor, not a former director of the bureau.
match_headline: U.S. Considers Imposing Sanctions on Israeli Military Unit

text: An obituary on Sunday about Denny Walsh, a Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporter, referred incorrectly to when The New York Times banned smoking in its newsroom and bureaus. It was in 1987; it was not the case that the paper had banned smoking by 1973, when Mr. Walsh joined its staff.
match_headline: Denny Walsh, Reporter Who Tussled With Mayors and Editors, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Monday about the former star N.F.L. quarterback Roman Gabriel misspelled the given name of a former tight end who played for the Philadelphia Eagles when Gabriel was on the team. He is Charle Young, not Charles. The obit also misidentified the head coach of the Los Angeles Rams whom Chuck Knox replaced in 1973. He was Tommy Prothro, not George Allen.
match_headline: Roman Gabriel, Star Quarterback of the 1960s and ’70s, Dies at 83

text: An article on Tuesday about a lack of evidence to support accusations tying many U.N. workers to Hamas described incorrectly what a review said about Israeli concerns about UNRWA employees. The review said that Israel had not flagged concerns about agency employees based on staff lists since 2011, not that Israel had not flagged any concerns about employees since 2011.
match_headline: Israel Hasn’t Offered Evidence Tying Many U.N. Workers to Hamas, Review Says

text: An article on Tuesday about the war in Gaza misstated the day a baby was born to a mother who had been killed in an Israeli strike in Rafah. The baby was born on Saturday, not on Sunday. The error was repeated in a video caption.
match_headline: Palestinian Baby Delivered After Mother Killed in Israeli Strike

text: An article on Monday about the uncertain protocol in Olympic doping cases misstated in one instance the type of event in which a Chinese swimmer won a gold medal. It was the women’s 4x200-meter freestyle relay, not the women’s 200-meter freestyle relay.
match_headline: China’s Swimmers Tested Positive. What Happens to Their Medals?

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an obituary on Monday about the former Arkansas governor and United States Senator David H. Pryor misstated when the photograph of Mr. Pryor with Dale Bumpers, a fellow former governor and senator, was taken. It was 2013, not 2020. (Mr. Bumpers died in 2016.)
match_headline: David H. Pryor, Arkansas Senator and Clinton Ally, Dies at 89

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the former Florida governor and United States Senator Bob Graham misstated when his daughter Gwen ran unsuccessfully for governor of Florida. It was 2018, not 2017.
match_headline: Bob Graham, Former Florida Governor and Senator, Dies at 87

text: An article on Thursday about the resumption of contract negotiation talks between Starbucks and an employee union misquoted Eric Blanc, a professor at Rutgers University. He said, “The scale of the union-busting campaign and its ferocity is unmatched in modern labor history.” He did not say, “The scale of the union-busting campaign and its verbosity is unmatched in modern labor history.”
ref_headline: The scale of the union-busting campaign and its ferocity is unmatched in modern labor history.
match_headline: Starbucks and Union Restart Contract Talks After Bitter Standoff

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the actor and documentarian Terry Carter erroneously credited him with a distinction. He was the only regular Black cast member on the 1950s sitcom “The Phil Silvers Show”; he was not the only Black actor to play a character on that show.
match_headline: Terry Carter, Barrier-Breaking Actor and Documentarian, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Thursday about the poetry critic Helen Vendler misstated the name of a school she had wanted to attend when she was a child. It was Girls’ Latin School, not the Boston Latin School for Girls.
match_headline: Helen Vendler, ‘Colossus’ of Poetry Criticism, Dies at 90

text: An article on Thursday about a prosecutor’s argument that the men accused of plotting the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, could be held past a war crimes sentence misstated the legal disposition of detainees at Guantánamo Bay. Of the 30 people held there, 11 have been charged or convicted, not tried or convicted.
match_headline: Prosecutor Says Sept. 11 Suspects Can Be Held Past War Crimes Sentence

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about bodies discovered in a mass grave near a hospital in Gaza misstated the timing of the initial burials. They began in January, not mid-February.
match_headline: Gaza Authorities Say More Bodies Were Discovered in Mass Grave

text: An article on Tuesday about polarizing language used by Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India against Muslims misstated the number of Muslim candidates that the B.J.P. is fielding in India’s current election. It is one, not zero.
match_headline: Modi Calls Muslims ‘Infiltrators’ Who Would Take India’s Wealth

text: An article on April 21 about New York’s newest professional women’s hockey team misstated the record set by the attendance at a women’s hockey game in Detroit between Boston and Ottawa. The 14,000 fans in attendance set a record for U.S. women’s professional hockey, not a record for all women’s hockey in the United States.
match_headline: New York’s Newest Hockey Team Has Everything but a Name and Home Ice

text: An article on Friday about a pastor who helped generate interest in Trump Media & Technology Group stock misidentified the company that reached an $18 million settlement with the Securities and Exchange Commission. It was Digital World, not Trump Media, which later merged with it.

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Sunday about the con man Frederick Celani misstated part of the name of the Illinois newspaper that published a three-part series about him. It is The State Journal-Register, not The Standard Journal-Register.

text: An article on Sunday about an all-women heavy metal band in Indonesia misstated the name of the band’s drummer. She is Euis Siti Aisyah, not Eusi Siti Aisyah.

text: An article on Saturday about the resignation of the leader of Vietnam’s Parliament incorrectly described Vuong Dinh Hue, the chairman of Vietnam’s National Assembly, who resigned as head of Parliament Friday. text: An article Monday about a deadly Tornado in Oklahoma misstated the interstate where one person was killed. It was Interstate 35, not 34.

text: An article on Friday about a troubled veteran who stalked a high-profile former F.B.I. official described incorrectly a misdemeanor stalking charge against the veteran, John C. Perez. text: An article on Saturday about President Biden’s interview with Howard Stern misstated which war certain American soldiers who are buried in a cemetery in France had fought in. It was World War I, not World War II.

text: An article on Saturday about Michelin’s vow to pay workers a living wage misstated the location of the city of Greenville. It is in South Carolina, not North Carolina.

text: A Critic’s Pick column on Friday about Sonia Delaunay’s garments, artifacts and paintings misidentified a type of mosaic by Delaunay. text: An article on Sunday about the artist Christopher Wool’s exhibit in New York misstated the location of a fire in Manhattan in 1996. It was in the building where Wool was working, not living.

text: An obituary on Saturday about the record producer Michael Cuscuna misstated the profession of his father, Arthur. He was the executive director of the Stamford, Conn., housing authority; he did not work at a housing project.

text: An article on Sunday about the tactics universities are using to handle pro-Palestinian campus protests misidentified the group organizing the encampment in Harvard Yard. It is the Harvard Out of Occupied Palestine Coalition, not the Harvard Undergraduate Palestine Solidarity Committee, the group suspended by the university.
match_headline: ‘Decisions Under Fire’: Campuses Try a Mix of Tactics as Protests Grow

text: An article on Tuesday about a deadly shooting in North Carolina misstated the surname of a neighbor who lives near the site of the shooting. She is Mary Sutter, not Sutton.
match_headline: 8 Officers Are Shot, 4 Fatally, While Serving Warrant in Charlotte

text: An article on Sunday about how educational institutions across the U.S. are investing in museums described incorrectly a sum of $160 million received by the Yale Peabody Museum. The money was a donation, not a bequest.
match_headline: Upgraded Museums Add New Value to College Campuses

text: An article on Wednesday about the expansion of Medicaid in Mississippi omitted mention of one of three states outside the South that have not expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. In addition to Kansas and Wyoming, Wisconsin did not expand Medicaid.
match_headline: Mississippi’s First Serious Bid to Expand Medicaid Collapses

text: An article on Tuesday about the training of language models to use the same sensory input as toddlers misidentified the company behind Llama 3. It is Meta, not Google.

text: An article on Sunday about a biennial show this spring and summer between two museums on either side of the U.S.-Mexico border misstated the documentation required to cross the border and enter El Paso, Texas, before the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. Passports and visas had not been needed by many American citizens to cross the border into the United States, but they had been needed by Mexican citizens.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the San Francisco clergyman and activist Cecil Williams misstated the status of the Glide Memorial Church when he was appointed there in 1963. It was part of the Methodist Church — not the United Methodist Church, which did not exist at the time. (The United Methodist Church was created when the Methodist Church merged with the Evangelical United Brethren Church in 1968.)
match_headline: Cecil Williams, Whose San Francisco Church Became a Haven, Dies at 94

text: A review of the NADA New York art fair on page C10 this weekend misstates the cause of death for the artist Jova Lynne’s mother. She died in 2020, during the Covid-19 pandemic, but she did not die of Covid.
match_headline: Standouts at NADA New York, the Fair for Up-and-Comers

text: A review of the Frieze art fair in New York on page C12 this weekend misstates the nationality of an artist, Jennifer Tee, showing at Tina Kim Gallery. Tee is Dutch-Indonesian, not American. It also misstates the number of years Frieze has been coming to the Shed. This is its fourth year at the Shed, not its second.
match_headline: Frieze New York Brings a Rich, Cross-Cultural Mix

text: An article on April 14 about Indigenous artists at the Venice Biennale attributed an erroneous distinction to Archie Moore’s participation in the Biennale. He was the second First Nations artist to represent Australia in a solo exhibition, not the second First Nations artist to represent Australia at the Biennale. (Others had been included in group exhibitions organized by Australia.)
match_headline: Indigenous Artists Are the Heart of the Venice Biennale

text: An article on April 7 about the artist Betye Saar misstated the location of the Huntington Library, Art Museum and Botanical Gardens, which commissioned and houses Ms. Saar’s site-specific installation “Drifting Toward Twilight.” It is in San Marino, Calif., not the Bronx.
match_headline: Betye Saar Is Making Some of the Best Work of Her Life

text: An article on Friday about the United States accusing Russia of using chemical weapons in Ukraine referred incorrectly to Gyunduz Mamedov’s role as a Ukrainian prosecutor. He is a former deputy prosecutor general, not a current one.
match_headline: U.S. Accuses Russia of Using Chemical Weapons in Ukraine

text: An article on April 28 about Representative Mark Pocan and Wisconsin voters’ concerns about the conflict in Gaza misstated the date of the Wisconsin presidential primary election. It was April 2, not April 15.
match_headline: After Israel Aid Vote, Pocan Seeks to Show Biden Liberal Dismay on Gaza

text: A picture caption with an article on April 28 about how the bandleader of “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert” spends his Sundays misspelled the surname of Louis Cato’s publicist. She is Emily Lichter, not Richter. The article also misidentified the city where Mr. Cato’s mother lives. She lives in Albemarle, N.C., not Altamont.
ref_headline: The Late Show with Stephen Colbert
match_headline: How Louis Cato, Bandleader for ‘The Late Show,’ Spends His Sundays

text: An article on Saturday about Hope Hicks’s testimony at the criminal trial of Donald J. Trump trial misstated a former employer of Ms. Hicks. It was Fox Corporation, not Fox News.
match_headline: Trump and His Onetime Confidante Meet Again, This Time in a Courtroom

text: An article on Saturday about faculty members who have joined student protests at Columbia University misstated Susannah Blair’s position at the university. She is a lecturer, not an adjunct lecturer.
match_headline: Taking Cues From Students, U.C.L.A. Faculty Members Join the Protests

text: An article on Sunday about parts of Gaza experiencing famine misstated the Israeli military’s authority in northern Gaza. The military retains security control over the area, though it has declined to oversee civilian life. It is not the case that the Israeli military exercises little or no control.
match_headline: Parts of Gaza in ‘Full-Blown Famine,’ U.N. Aid Official Says

text: An article on Sunday about Mohamed Bazoum, Niger’s deposed leader who is being held captive in his home, included a comment from Amadou Ange Chekaraou Barou, a close adviser to Mr. Bazoum, in which he misstated the historical precedents on the release of presidents in Niger who have been ousted by force. In 1996, a former president of Niger, Mahamane Ousmane, was released by those who arrested him. It is not the case that “detained presidents were never released until the soldiers who deposed them got evicted.”
ref_headline: detained presidents were never released until the soldiers who deposed them got evicted.

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Saturday about three NASA satellites that will be switched off misidentified the launch site of the Aura spacecraft. It was Vandenberg Air Force Base in California, not the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
match_headline: What Happens When NASA Loses Eyes on Earth? We’re About to Find Out.

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about voters in the battleground state of Georgia and Black entrepreneurs’ frustration with higher interest rates misidentified the person shown in the photograph. He is Omar Whilby, a nightclub owner in Atlanta, not Ray Woods, who is a real estate entrepreneur in the area.
match_headline: Black Entrepreneurs, Frustrated by High Rates, Look to the Election

text: An obituary on Friday about the Olympic champion discus thrower Olga Fikotova Connolly misspelled her father’s given name. He was Frantisek Fikota, not Franticek.
match_headline: Olga Fikotova Connolly, Olympian in a Cold War Romance, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Friday about the philanthropist Peggy Mellon Hitchcock, who supported Timothy Leary’s experiments with psychedelic drugs, misstated the name of the bus that belonged to Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters. It was Furthur, not Further.
match_headline: Peggy Mellon Hitchcock, Who Helped Timothy Leary Turn On, Dies at 90

text: An article on Tuesday about Qantas’s deal with a consumer watchdog commission to pay $79 million for selling tickets to canceled flights misspelled the name of Qantas’s chief executive. It is Vanessa Hudson, not Husdon.

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about the play “The Miser” misspelled the surname of one of the actresses. She is Lakisha May, not Ma.
match_headline: ‘The Miser’ Review: Updating Molière, but Missing a Key Ingredient

text: An article on Tuesday about women in China reclaiming their feminist identities misstated Tang Shuang’s former role at Vogue China. She was a deputy publisher, not a deputy editor.

text: An article on Wednesday about the postponement of the start of former President Donald Trump’s classified documents case misstated the expected duration of a hearing about the prosecution team. It is scheduled for three days, not two.

text: An article on Thursday about an escalation in Britain’s diplomatic feud with Russia misidentified the agency Britain accused of a pattern of “malign activity” in Britain and Europe. It is the Federal Security Service, or F.S.B., which is Russia’s domestic intelligence agency, not its foreign intelligence service. The error was repeated in a capsule summary and a picture caption.

text: An article on Sunday about the City College of New York’s decision to end pro-Palestinian protests on campus misstated the day that the pro-Palestinian encampment on the quad at the City College of New York started. It was April 25, not April 18.

text: An article on Thursday about tornado clusters misspelled in one instance the surname of a professor at the University of Louisiana Monroe. He is Tyler Fricker, not Frick.
match_headline: Tornadoes Are Coming in Bunches. Scientists Are Trying to Figure Out Why.

text: An article on Thursday about General Motors’s decision to stop making the Chevrolet Malibu misstated the year that the Malibu SS was introduced. It was in 1964, not four years after the Malibu. text: An article on Thursday about Amy Poehler’s true-crime podcast misidentified the actor who is among a range of stars regularly making appearances on the podcasts. It is Will Forte, not Will Arnett.

text: An article on Thursday about a worsening humanitarian crisis in Haiti misidentified the name of a United Nations agency. The agency is the International Organization for Migration, not the International Office for Migration.

text: An article on Friday about the possibility of the Bank of England cutting interest rates misstated the last time interest rates in Britain were at 5.25 percent. It was in 2008, not 2018.

text: An article on Friday about new Senate legislation to reauthorize federal aviation programs misstated the name of the bridge in Baltimore that collapsed. It is the Francis Scott Key Bridge, not the Francis Key Scott Bridge.

text: An article last Sunday about the annual Frederick Law Olmsted Awards Luncheon at the Conservatory Garden in Central Park misidentified the flower in a hat worn by Kathleen Tait. It is a lotus, not a gardenia.

text: A picture caption on April 21 with a review about “Every Living Thing,” by Jason Roberts, reversed the identifications of the 18th-century scientists Carl Linnaeus and Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon. Linnaeus was on the left, Buffon on the right.

text: An article on Saturday about a school district in Virginia that voted to reinstate confederate names to several schools misstated the surname of a former member of the Shenandoah County school board. He is Marty Helsley, not Helsey.

text: An article on Sunday about the disqualification of a marathon winner after an illicit water break misspelled the surname of the director of the Orange County Marathon. He is Gary Kutscher, not Kutschar.

text: An article on Tuesday about a new federal rule concerning the planning and funding of electrical grids misspelled the given name of one of the commissioners. She is Allison Clements, not Alison.

text: An article on Monday about the art market’s struggle to regain its footing after declining sales and a cyberattack misstated the title of an artwork. It is “Untitled (Sandwoman Series),” not “Untitled (Sandworm Series).” The error was repeated in a picture caption.

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about two close friends and distance runners who were both vying for a spot in the marathon at the Paris Olympics misidentified the given name of one of the runners. He is Conner Mantz, not Carson.

text: An article on Monday about the mystery setting in the background of the Mona Lisa misstated the surface that Leonardo da Vinci used for the painting. It was painted on a poplar wood panel, not on canvas.

text: An article on Wednesday about the resignation of OpenAI’s co-founder misstated the title that Greg Brockman held when he resigned from OpenAI. He was the company’s president, not its chief operating officer.

text: An obituary on Sunday about the advertising executive Mary Wells Lawrence referred incorrectly to a campaign for Braniff International Airways based on the slogan “When you got it — flaunt it!” It was created by George Lois of Lois, Holland, Callaway — not by Ms. Wells Lawrence’s agency, Wells Rich Greene.

text: An article last Sunday about the series “The Big Cigar,” using information provided by a publicist, described incorrectly the role of Janine Sherman Barrois on the show. text: An article on May 5 about the show “Dark Matter” misidentified the university where the astrophysicist Clifford V. Johnson is a professor. text: An article on Page 3 this weekend about New York University’s decision to force student protesters to write apology letters misstates the surname of an N.Y.U. doctoral student. She is Ellis Garey, not Geary.

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about the actress Jean Smart misidentifies the service that carries the show “Hacks.” It is Max Original, not HBO.

text: A review on May 5 about “The Age of Grievance,” by Frank Bruni, referred imprecisely to the Black Lives Matter protests after the murder of George Floyd. They started in 2020, not 2021.

text: An article on Saturday about several universities that struck agreements with pro-Palestinian demonstrators misstated the title of the head of the University of California, Berkeley. It is chancellor, not president.
match_headline: Protesters Agreed to Leave. This Is What Some Colleges Promised in Return.

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about the symbolism of a cartoon character of a Palestinian boy, known as Handala, included a misstatement from Margaret Olin, a religious studies scholar at the Yale Divinity School. It is not the case that her son’s in-laws have a bumper sticker with the Handala image on their car.

text: An article on Wednesday about a possible new boost of popular support for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant request against him misidentified an Israeli official accused by the I.C.C. of using starvation as a weapon of war in Gaza. It is the defense minister, Yoav Gallant, not Benny Gantz, a former military chief.

text: An article on Wednesday about The New York Times’s interview with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine misstated the time period between the interview and the start of the country’s war with Russia. It was 27 months, not 17 months.
match_headline: ‘What’s the Problem?’ Zelensky Challenges West Over Hesitations.

text: An article on Wednesday about extreme turbulence on a Singapore Airlines flight misstated the number of people from the United States who were injured on the flight. There were two from the United States, not just one.

text: An article on Wednesday about elections after the death of President Ebrahim Raisi in Iran misstated the year that anti-government protests erupted in Iran. It was 2022, not 2021.

text: An article on Tuesday about the use of forcible restraints in U.S. hospitals misstated the effect of Section 12 of the Massachusetts Mental Health Act. text: An obituary on Monday about the World War II fighter pilot Bud Anderson misstated the name of the co-author of his fellow pilot Chuck Yeager’s autobiography. He was Leo Janos, not Lee Jonas.
match_headline: Bud Anderson, Last of World War II’s ‘Triple Ace’ Pilots, Dies at 102

text: An article on Wednesday about a video posted by Former President Donald J. Trump on Truth Social incorrectly described templates available from the web design company Envato, which was used in its creation. Parts of Envato’s templates are customizable and allow users to alter the background text, not only the headlines and photos.
match_headline: Trump Posts, Then Takes Down, Video Online With Headlines About a ‘Unified Reich’

text: An article on Thursday about a new “Lord of the Rings” movie and a 15-year-old fan film with the same title misspelled the name of a character from the “Lord of the Rings” books and films. He is Aragorn, not Aragon.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the computer pioneer C. Gordon Bell misspelled his wife’s surname. She is Sheridan Sinclaire-Bell, not Sinclair-Bell. And because of an editing error, the obituary misstated the year he married Gwen Druyor and the year the two of them founded the Computer History Museum. They married in 1959, not 1979; and the museum (which was originally called the Digital Computer Museum) was founded in 1979, not 1996.
match_headline: C. Gordon Bell, Creator of a Personal Computer Prototype, Dies at 89

text: An article on Friday about President Biden’s meeting with President William Ruto of Kenya misstated Ruth Porat’s title at Alphabet and Google. She is president and chief investment officer, not president and chief information officer.
match_headline: Biden Honors Kenya as the East African Nation Prepares to Send Forces to Haiti

text: An article on Wednesday about an event in New Hampshire where President Biden discussed care for veterans suffering from toxic exposure misidentified the location of the Y.M.C.A. where President Biden spoke. It is in Nashua, N.H., not Merrimack, N.H.
match_headline: V.A. Has Approved 1 Million Claims Under Burn Pit Law, Biden Announces

text: An article on May 12 about early retirement referred imprecisely to one aspect of Jackie Cummings Koski’s childhood. While she grew up near the poverty line, her family did not use food stamps.
match_headline: Your Neighbors Are Retiring in Their 30s. Why Can’t You?

text: An article on Tuesday about Richard Grenell’s quest to be secretary of state in a second Donald Trump administration misstated a familial connection of an L.G.B.T.Q. activist, Stuart Milk. He is Harvey Milk’s nephew, not his brother.

text: An article on Friday about a far-right E.U. parliament group’s decision to exclude a party from its coalition misstated how many deputies are to be elected this year to the European Parliament. It is 720, not 705.
match_headline: Far-Right E.U. Lawmakers Remove Germany’s AfD Party Before Elections

text: An article on Friday about the history of foreign interventions in Haiti misidentified the U.S. president who appointed a commission to look into the American occupation of Haiti. It was Herbert Hoover, not Woodrow Wilson.
match_headline: Foreign Interventions in Haiti: A Brief History

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about an N.C.A.A. agreement to pay players but not call them employees misstated a component of N.I.L. deals. The components are name, image and likeness — not name, image and licensing.
match_headline: The N.C.A.A. Agreed to Pay Players. It Won’t Call Them Employees.

text: An obituary on Saturday about the author Caleb Carr misstated part of the name of the hamlet in New York State where he lived. It is Cherry Plain, not Cherry Plains.

text: An article on Monday about criticism of plans to turn a waterfront park in Toronto into a spa misstated the location of a garage planned as part of the development. The garage is proposed for the mainland, not on West Island.

text: An article on Wednesday about Pope Francis’ apology for using an offensive slang word to refer to gay men referred incorrectly to his decision to allow priests to bless same-sex couples. The pope permitted priests to bless the couples, not same-sex unions.

text: An article on Tuesday about the Lord Howe Island stick insect misstated the year that a San Diego Zoo official picked up stick insect eggs in Melbourne. It was in 2016, not 2015.
match_headline: How the Tree Lobster Escaped Extinction

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the basketball star and broadcaster Bill Walton misstated the impact that repeated injuries had on his playing time as a professional. It was not the case that he never played in more than 70 games as a professional. (He played in 80 games for the Boston Celtics during the 1985-86 season.)

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the songwriter Richard M. Sherman referred incorrectly to the four live-action films, including “Tom Sawyer” and “The Slipper and the Rose,” for which he and his brother, Robert, wrote the screenplays as well as the songs. text: An article on Sunday about Israel’s continued assault on Rafah despite fierce condemnation misstated the population of Rafah before the war. It was between 200,000 and 300,000, not close to one million.
match_headline: Condemnation Slows, but Does Not Stall, Israel’s Assault on Rafah

text: An article on Wednesday about allegations that the Internal Revenue Service failed to police a Puerto Rican tax benefit misstated part of the name of an accounting firm. It is BDO Puerto Rico, not BDO USA.
match_headline: I.R.S. Failed to Police Puerto Rico Tax Break, Whistle-Blower Says

text: An article on Thursday about the new president of Yale University misstated the number of votes cast against a Stony Brook faculty senate motion to censure Maurie McInnis. It was 55, not 54.
match_headline: Yale Chooses Head of Stony Brook University to Be New President

text: An article on June 2 about student protests at Columbia University misstates the date that the university’s president, Minouche Shafik, asked the New York City Police Department to clear a pro-Palestinian student encampment on the university’s lawn. It was April 18, not April 17. The article also misstates the position of the literary theorist and activist Edward Said on a two-state solution. He supported the proposal in the 1990s but changed his public stance to support a one-state solution later in that decade.

text: An article on Monday about the reopening of the New York City Section 8 vouchers waiting list misstated the name of a housing organization. It is New Destiny Housing, not New Destiny Project.
match_headline: New Yorkers Who Need Help With Rent Can (Finally) Join a List for Help

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the Season 3 finale of “Hacks” described incorrectly the history of female late-night hosts. Joan Rivers hosted “The Late Show” on Fox from 1986-88; it is not true that a woman has never hosted a network’s flagship late-night talk show.
match_headline: Joking Aside, the ‘Hacks’ Showrunners Explain That Final Twist

text: An article on Tuesday about Mexican President-elect Claudia Sheinbaum’s background in energy engineering misidentified the field in which Ms. Sheinbaum earned a doctorate. She holds a Ph.D. in energy engineering, not environmental engineering.
match_headline: A Climate Scientist Is Voted President of an Oil Country. Now What?

text: An article on Tuesday about the sudden exit of the executive editor of The Washington Post misstated the period in which The Washington Post saw its audience decline 50 percent. The decline has been since 2020, not last year alone.
match_headline: Washington Post Newsroom Reels From Its Editor’s Sudden Exit

text: A picture caption with an article on May 29 about competitors’ claims that Elon Musk’s SpaceX is using anti-competitive tactics in its efforts to dominate the space race, misidentified the commercial launch company that makes the Capstone lunar orbiter, and the year in which that company was founded. Rocket Lab, as the article correctly noted, was founded in 2006, not 2016, and is its own company. It is not the case that it is a joint venture of Lockheed and Boeing. (United Launch Alliance is the joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed.)
match_headline: Elon Musk Dominates Space Launch. Rivals Are Calling Foul.

text: An article on Wednesday about universities that are grappling with disciplinary measures for pro-Palestinian student protesters at universities misstated Ryan Enos’s position at Harvard. He is a professor of government, not history.
match_headline: Police Arrest 13 After Protesters Occupied Stanford President’s Office

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Friday about the artist, author and marine-life expert Richard Ellis, using information from his daughter, misidentified the woman he painted swimming with a whale shark. She is the philanthropist Sydney Shuman, not the diver and photographer Valerie Taylor.
match_headline: Richard Ellis, 86, Dies; Artist Whose Works Included a Museum’s Whale

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Medal of Honor recipient Clarence Sasser referred incorrectly to American casualties during a Vietnam War battle on Jan. 10, 1968. About 30 American soldiers were killed or wounded in a span of minutes; it was not the case that “dozens of American soldiers were killed” in that time.
ref_headline: dozens of American soldiers were killed

text: An article on Thursday about testimony at Hunter Biden’s trial on gun charges misstated the year in which Zoe Kestan testified that she had first met Mr. Biden. It was 2017, not 2018. The article also misidentified the gun Mr. Biden purchased. It was a Colt Cobra 38SPL revolver, not a Colt .45.
match_headline: Hunter Biden’s Former Partners Describe Toll of His Drug Abuse

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about the complexities of Hunter Biden’s gun trial misstated the day that Jill Biden, the first lady, left for the commemoration of the 80th anniversary of D-Day in France. She left on Wednesday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: The President’s Son: A Routine Gun Case, but Abnormal in Every Way

text: An obituary on May 31 about Bette Nash, who was recognized by Guinness World Records as the longest-serving flight attendant in history, referred incorrectly to a deal between US Airways and American Airlines. US Airways merged with American in 2013 and adopted the American name two years later; it is not the case that American Airlines bought US Airways.
match_headline: Bette Nash, World’s Longest-Serving Flight Attendant, Is Dead at 88

text: An article on Monday about the start of Hunter Biden’s gun trial case misstated the middle initial of a top deputy to the special counsel, David C. Weiss. He is Leo J. Wise, not Leo P. Wise.
match_headline: Hunter Biden to Go on Trial in Gun Case, Days After Trump Was Convicted

text: An article on Friday about the ways in that the backlash against climate action is reshaping Europe’s election misstated the emissions-reduction targets proposed by the European Commission. The proposals call for cuts of 90 percent by 2040, compared with 1990 levels, not 40 percent.
match_headline: How a Climate Backlash Influenced Campaigning in Europe

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the 80th anniversary of D-Day misidentified the location of a parade in France. It was in Colleville-Montgomery, not in Colleville-sur-Mer.
match_headline: D-Day at 80

text: An article on Friday about slow sales of Humane’s Ai Pin incorrectly described a company meeting that was held after Humane dismissed a senior software engineer. Bethany Bongiorno was not present and did not join Imran Chaudhri in saying the employee had violated policy.
match_headline: ‘This Is Going to Be Painful’: How a Bold A.I. Device Flopped

text: An article this weekend about a Metropolitan Transportation Authority program that brings talented musicians to perform in the New York City subway system misstates the Iain S. Forrest’s stage name. It is Eyeglasses, not Eyeglass.
match_headline: 52 Musicians, 24 Judges: Inside New York’s Subway Performance Auditions

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about Benjamin B. Bolger’s many academic degrees misidentifies one of the degrees he earned at Columbia University. It is a master’s degree in real estate development, not in architecture.
match_headline: The Man Who Couldn’t Stop Going to College

text: An article on Page 38 this weekend about Ibram X. Kendi and the Center for Antiracist Research misstates how the center’s fund-raising in 2021 compared with the previous year. It was approximately one-hundredth of the amount raised in 2020, not a tenth. The article also incorrectly describes a recognition given to the documentary adaptation of “Stamped From the Beginning.” The documentary was not nominated for an Oscar, but was named to the Oscar shortlist.
match_headline: Ibram X. Kendi Faces a Reckoning of His Own

text: A picture caption with an article last Sunday about the wedding of Enrico Lagasca and Jonathan Stewart misidentified the church where the ceremony took place. As the article correctly noted, the ceremony was at Trinity Church Wall Street in New York, not Holy Trinity Lutheran Church (where the couple met in 2015).
match_headline: A Match Made in Church Sparks a Journey of Self-Discovery

text: An article last Wednesday about a California sandwich shop opened by two stars of the Bravo show “Vanderpump Rules” misstated the number of restaurants the chef Nancy Silverton closed in 2023. It was two, not three.
match_headline: To Make a Hit Los Angeles Restaurant, ‘Vanderpump’ It

text: An obituary on Sunday about William A. Anders, who flew on the first manned space mission to orbit the moon, misstated his rank at his death. He was a major general — not a major, which was his rank when he was an astronaut.
match_headline: William A. Anders, 90, Dies; Flew on First Manned Orbit of the Moon

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about the emergence of Doug Burgum, the Republican governor of North Dakota, as a cheerleader for oil and gas production and former President Donald J. Trump, misquoted the governor’s statement on U.S. oil production. He said the country was producing 13 million barrels a day but should be producing “14, 15, 20 million barrels a day”; he did not say the country was producing 13 million gallons a day but should be producing 14,15, 20 million gallons a day.
match_headline: Trump’s Energy Guy Talked a Green Game but Now Sells Big Oil Priorities

text: An article on Saturday about the ways in which media outlets on the left and right covered President Biden’s executive order aimed at limiting asylum requests misspelled the given name of a reporter for Mother Jones. She is Isabela Dias, not Isabella.
match_headline: How Media Outlets on the Left and Right Covered Biden’s Immigration Order

text: An article on Sunday about the popularity of Sam’s Restaurant in Brooklyn’s Cobble Hill neighborhood as a spot for film crews misidentified the prize that the rapper Kendrick Lamar won. It was the Pulitzer Prize for music, not the Nobel Prize.
match_headline: This Old-School Pizzeria Stays Open by Playing Itself on TV

text: An article on Wednesday about Dao Yin, a candidate who may have exploited an oversight weakness in New York’s new matching-funds campaign system misattributed a quote from a supposed donor to Mr. Yin. The person quoted was Faaizah Abdul-Mani, not Fazia Butt.
match_headline: Fake Donations Helped a Candidate Get $162,000 From Taxpayers

text: An article on Wednesday about President Biden’s deployment of another Patriot missile system to Ukraine misstated the number of Patriot systems that Germany has deployed in Ukraine. It has so far sent two, and has announced plans to deploy a third by the end of the month.
match_headline: U.S. to Send Another Patriot Missile Battery to Ukraine

text: An article on Tuesday about the investigation of Gustavo Gorriti, a Peruvian journalist, misstated who is conducting the investigation. Mr. Gorriti is being investigated by a prosecutor in the attorney general’s office, not by Peru’s attorney general.
match_headline: A Reporter’s Work Helped Topple Presidents. Now He Is Being Investigated.

text: An article on Wednesday about a trial in Florida in which Chiquita Brands was found liable for deaths that occurred during the Colombian Civil War misstated the circumstances during which the anecdote of the killing of a girl’s mother and stepfather was provided. It was provided by a lawyer outside court and it involved a different case. It was not described in court nor was it part of the case in Florida.
match_headline: Chiquita Held Liable for Deaths During Colombian Civil War

text: An article on Thursday about Sony Pictures acquiring the Alamo Drafthouse Cinema theater chain incorrectly described the purchase. It is a rare example of a Hollywood studio owning a theater chain, not the first in more than half a century.
match_headline: Sony Pictures Acquires Alamo Drafthouse in Lifeline to Cinema Chain

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week described incorrectly the Discovery series “Six Schizophrenic Brothers.” Although the series explores the same subject as the 2020 nonfiction book “Hidden Valley Road,” by Robert Kolker, the series was not based on Mr. Kolker’s book.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: Celine Dion and the Stanley Cup Finals

text: An obituary on Thursday about the political reporter Howard Fineman misstated the date of his birth in 1948. It was Nov. 17, not Nov. 19.
match_headline: Howard Fineman, Veteran Political Journalist and TV Pundit, Dies at 75

text: An article on Thursday about Saudi Arabia’s investment in professional boxing misspelled the given name of a boxer. He is Terence Crawford, not Terrence.
match_headline: Saudi Arabia’s Next Billion-Dollar Sports Play: A Boxing Takeover

text: An article on Friday about the number of people living in the streets and subways of New York City referred incorrectly to the increase in the estimated number of homeless people in the city. It is the most since 2005, when the estimate was conducted in March, and the highest ever recorded since the city began conducting the surveys in January and February, starting in 2006. It is not highest total the city ever recorded.
match_headline: Number of People Living on New York City Streets Hits a Two-Decade High

text: An obituary on Friday about the singer Françoise Hardy misstated the year her first album was released. As noted correctly in a picture caption, it was 1962, not 1963.
match_headline: Françoise Hardy, Moody French Pop Star, Dies at 80

text: An article last Sunday about Gary Friedman, chief executive of RH (formerly Restoration Hardware), misquoted Mr. Friedman. He said that he pushed the brand to “climb the luxury mountain,” not “climb the luxury ladder.”
match_headline: The Napoleon of Your Living Room

text: An article on Saturday about a review of New York State’s handling of the coronavirus pandemic under former Gov. Andrew M. Cuomo misattributed a statement responding to a state audit of Mr. Cuomo’s performance during the crisis. The statement was from Mr. Cuomo’s spokesman, Richard Azzopardi, not Mr. Cuomo himself. The article also referred incorrectly to the source of a requirement that nursing homes accept Covid-19 patients from hospitals. It was a Health Department directive, not an executive order by Mr. Cuomo.
match_headline: Cuomo Faulted for Pandemic Leadership but Not for Nursing Home Deaths

text: An article on Sunday about Native American tribes reclaiming land in California referred incorrectly to the Los Angeles Aqueduct. It transports water to Los Angeles from the Owens River, not Owens Lake.
match_headline: In California, Tribal Members Are Reclaiming the ‘Land of the Flowing Water’

text: An article on June 11 about a judge striking one element out of Donald J. Trump’s classified documents case, misidentified the source of a rule that permits prosecutors to tell the jury about “bad acts” committed by a defendant that are not directly part of the charges in a case. It comes from the federal rules of evidence, not from the federal rules of criminal procedure.
match_headline: Judge Strikes One Element From Trump Indictment in Documents Case

text: An article on June 10 about Donald J. Trump’s probation interview, misstated which aspects of the interview were approved by Justice Juan M. Merchan. While Justice Merchan approved the presence of Mr. Trump’s lawyer at the interview, he did not decide on the question of it being conducted remotely. The New York City Probation Department made that decision.
match_headline: Trump Will Have Virtual Interview With Probation Official on Monday

text: An article on June 7 about SpaceX’s Starship successful return from space misstated the distance of the SpaceX launch site from the Mexican border. The launchpad is 2.5 miles the border, not within a few hundred feet.
match_headline: SpaceX’s Starship Rocket Successfully Completes 1st Return From Space

text: An article on Wednesday about the auction of the earliest known photograph of a first lady misidentified the material the U.S. Capitol dome is made of. It is iron, not marble.
match_headline: Hello, Dolley? Earliest Known Photograph of a First Lady Comes to Auction

text: An obituary on Monday about Paul Pressler, a former president of the Southern Baptist Convention, referred incorrectly to the oil company of which his father was a vice president. The company was called Jersey Standard Oil at the time of Mr. Pressler’s birth, in 1930, not Exxon Mobil. (It changed its name to Exxon in 1972 and became Exxon Mobil in a merger in 1999.) The obituary also misidentified Nathan Finn, a Southern Baptist historian who cataloged Judge Pressler’s papers. He is a former provost at North Greenville University in South Carolina, not the current one. (The current one is Hunter Baker.)
match_headline: Paul Pressler, Disgraced Christian Conservative Leader, Dies at 94

text: An article on Sunday about the treatment of migrants seeking asylum in Canada misstated the number of migrants who sought asylum there last year. The number of asylum seekers was 29,455 in 2023, not roughly 32,000 in the most recent fiscal year.
match_headline: For Most Refugees in Canada, a Warm Embrace. For Others, Jail.

text: An article on Tuesday about Peter Magyar, a conservative opponent of Hungary’s prime minister, Viktor Orban, misstated the name of a town at the center of a pedophilia scandal at a children’s home. The town is Bicske, not Bicke.
match_headline: Emerging From Orban’s Shadow, a Former Ally Tries to Steal His Limelight

text: An article on Tuesday about a man accused of orchestrating a failed assassination plot against a Sikh separatist in New York misstated who was present in the courtroom on Monday. The intended target, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, was not in the courtroom.
match_headline: Man Accused in Plot to Assassinate Sikh Separatist Pleads Not Guilty

text: An article on Tuesday about the best and worst moments from the 2024 Tony Awards erroneously attributed a distinction to the Tony winner Kara Young. She is the first Black actress to be nominated for a Tony Award in three consecutive years, not the first Black performer.
match_headline: Best and Worst Moments From the 2024 Tony Awards

text: An article on Thursday about proposals in Congress to change military conscription rules misstated a proposal to automatically register men for the draft. It would apply the requirement to those aged 18 through 25; it would not raise the maximum age to 26.
match_headline: Congress Debates Expanded Draft Amid Military Recruitment Challenges

text: An article on Tuesday about how bird flu could evolve to affect humans misspelled the name of a vaccine manufacturer. It is CSL Seqirus, not CSL Sequiris.
match_headline: A Bird-Flu Pandemic in People? Here’s What It Might Look Like.

text: An obituary on Thursday about the Hall of Fame ballplayer Willie Mays misstated the year in which the team he spent most of his career with, the San Francisco Giants, opened their current home stadium, AT&T Park. It was in 2000, not 2001.
match_headline: Willie Mays, Baseball’s Electrifying Player of Power and Grace, Is Dead at 93

text: An article on June 16 about Chinese swimmers who participated in the Olympics despite having tested positive for drugs years earlier misstated the nature of clenbuterol, a drug banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. It is an anabolic agent, not a steroid.
match_headline: Chinese Swimmers Twice Tested Positive for Drugs. They Kept on Swimming.

text: An article on Page 1 this weekend about the role that marijuana may have played in the accidental death of a teenager misstates the location of an outing taken by Nico Nuño-Kelley and his mother. It was in Bedford, N.Y., not Connecticut.
match_headline: A Vape Pen, a Fall and a Question That Won’t Go Away: Why Did Nico Die?

text: An article on June 16 about how a sauna master spends her Sundays misspelled the given name of Regina Rocke’s fiancée. She is Kirstin Huber, not Kirsten.
match_headline: How a Sauna Master Spends Her Sundays

text: An article on Friday about business executives’ concerns that the economic platforms of rival parties in the parliamentary election could endanger the French economy misstated Jordan Bardella’s age. He is 28, not 29.
match_headline: French Business Leaders See Threat to Economy From Macron’s Opponents

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about the music catalog of the composer George Crumb misspells the given name of a pianist. He is Marcantonio Barone, not Macantonio.
match_headline: Charli XCX, Robert Plant and More Music for Your Weekend

text: An article on Page 9 this weekend about the actor Austin Butler misstates the role Stellan Skarsgard plays in “Dune.” He is the uncle of Austin Butler’s character, not the father.
match_headline: The Careful Crafting of Austin Butler

text: Because of editing errors, an article this weekend about readers’ stories of retirement misstates the surname of a New York Times reader from Atlanta. She is Jeannine Holden, not Olsen. It also misstates the surname of a reader from Torrance, Calif. She is Maria Tirado, not Tirad.
match_headline: What Does Retirement Really Mean?

text: An article on June 16 about alcohol consumption misstated the status of the Canadian government’s guidelines on alcohol drinking. While new guidelines have been proposed, they have not yet been officially adopted.
match_headline: Is That Drink Worth It to You?

text: An obituary on Friday about the chief executive and editor, Thomas McCormack, who transformed St. Martin’s Press misstated the date of Mr. McCormack’s death. It was June 15, not June 17. The obituary also gave an erroneous distinction to the molecular biologist James D. Watson, whose 1969 book, “The Double Helix,” was published by St. Martin’s Press under Mr. McCormack. He helped discover the structure of DNA; he did not discover DNA itself. (The Swiss biochemist Friedrich Miescher discovered the molecule now known as DNA in 1869.)
match_headline: Thomas J. McCormack Dies at 92; Transformed St. Martin’s Press

text: An article on Saturday about The Washington Post’s leadership group misstated Scott Higham’s current status at company. He left The Post in March. He is not currently a reporter there.
match_headline: Editor Tapped to Lead Washington Post Won’t Take the Job

text: An article on Saturday about Iran’s upcoming presidential election misstated the composition of the 12-person Guardian Council. Its members are six clerics and six jurists, not 12 clerics.
match_headline: In Iran Election, a New Target for Conservatives: The Government

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about a shooting in New York City referred incorrectly to the location of the fatal wounds sustained by one of the two victims, Michael James. He was shot in the torso, not in the torso and the face.
match_headline: Fatal Shooting Robs a Neighborhood of a Longtime Friendly Face

text: An article on Tuesday about a former senator in the Philippines included an inaccurate reference to Leila de Lima’s political career. She served in the Senate, not Parliament, starting in 2016, not 2015.
