match_headline: Philippines Drops Charges Against Leila de Lima, Prominent Duterte Critic

text: An article on Tuesday about the increased frequency and intensity of extreme wildfires stated incorrectly the death toll from bush fires in Australia in 2019. The fires that year killed 33 people, not 173.
match_headline: Extreme Wildfires Have Doubled in 2 Decades, Study Finds

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Wednesday about the television show “Doctor Who” referred imprecisely to a kiss between the Doctor and Rogue. It was the Doctor’s first openly romantic same-sex kiss of the series, not the first same-sex kiss of the series.
match_headline: ‘Doctor Who’ Season in Review: The Doctor Might Be on a New Path

text: An article on Wednesday about the prosecution in Russia of a playwright and a director misspelled the surname of a former art director of a Moscow literary festival. He is Mikhail Durnenkov, not Dyurenkov.
match_headline: 2 Russian Women Put on a Play. Then the State Came for Them.

text: An article on Thursday about The Episcopal Church electing its youngest leader referred incorrectly to plans for Bishop Sean Rowe’s installation ceremony. Washington National Cathedral has not been confirmed as the venue. The venue was still being decided.
match_headline: The Episcopal Church Has Elected Its Youngest Leader in Centuries

text: An article on Monday about a new library in Manhattan that contains affordable housing units misidentified a river near which several towers will be built. They will be built near the Hudson and Harlem Rivers, not the Hudson and East Rivers.
match_headline: Neighbors Fight Affordable Housing, but Need Libraries. Can’t We Make a Deal?

text: An article last Sunday about Conan O’Brien misstated what he sold to SiriusXM for $150 million. It was the comic’s podcasting company, not just the podcast “Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend.”
match_headline: Conan O’Brien Doesn’t Matter*

text: An article on Saturday about small New York City museums that are moving, changing or calling it quits due to a challenging economic climate omitted a word in a quoted passage from a public letter by arts executives denouncing arts funding cuts in New York City. The letter called any further reductions “penny-wise and pound-foolish,” not “penny-wise and foolish.”
match_headline: Amid Challenges, Small New York City Museums Are Closing Their Doors

text: An obituary on June 24 about the Irish tycoon Anthony O’Reilly misstated the price the American telecom billionaire John Malone paid for Castlemartin, Mr. O’Reilly’s estate, in 2015. It was close to 28 million euros, not 7.4 million euros.
match_headline: Anthony O’Reilly, Flashy Irish Tycoon Who Led Unflashy Heinz, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on June 18 about the chef and restaurateur James Kent misstated the given name of one of his brothers. He is Rachid, not Rashid.
match_headline: James Kent, Chef Who Was Building a Restaurant Empire, Dies at 45

text: An article on Wednesday about Leonard Peltier, a Native American activist who supporters say was unfairly convicted of killing two federal agents nearly 50 years ago, misstated the given name of the deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA. He is Justin Mazzola, not James.
match_headline: Parole Denied for Native American Activist Convicted in 1975 Killings

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about artificial intelligence stereotypes of women’s voices described incorrectly Majel Barrett-Roddenberry’s marital status during the original “Star Trek” series. She was not married to the show’s creator at the time.
match_headline: The Voices of A.I. Are Telling Us a Lot

text: An article on Thursday about the state news and social media silence in China surrounding a doping case in swimming misstated the timing of a Times article that revealed that three Chinese swimmers had tested positive for a performance-enhancing drug. It was published in June, not July.
match_headline: An Uproar Over a Chinese Doping Case, Except in China

text: An article on Thursday about a leadership battle in Nigeria misidentified the opponent of Abba Yusuf in the election for governor of Kano state last year. The opponent was Dr. Nasiru Yusuf Gawuna, not Abdullahi Ganduje. (Dr. Gawuna was Mr. Ganduje’s deputy.)
match_headline: Two Kings Battle for a Millennium-Old Throne in Nigeria

text: An article this weekend about the Russian streaming TV hit “The Boy’s Word” refers incorrectly to reporting about funding for the show. The reporting said the series was produced and partly funded by the Institute for Internet Development; it did not say the show was partly funded by Iran.
match_headline: The Bleak, Nihilistic Show Russians Can’t Stop Watching

text: An article on Thursday about the risks and rewards for Democrats if they select a new presidential nominee misstated Ohio’s deadline for a candidate to be certified. Ohio legislators passed a bill extending the deadline; it is no longer before the Democratic convention.
match_headline: Should Biden Quit? Democrats Weigh Potential Rewards and Steep Risks

text: An article on Page 12 this weekend about an English artist who won the Turner Prize misstates the timing of Jesse Darling’s show at Chapter NY in Lower Manhattan. It has been postponed and will most likely take place in 2025; it will not open on July 11.

An article on Page 12 this weekend about an English artist who won the Turner Prize misstates the timing of Jesse Darling’s show at Chapter NY in Lower Manhattan. It has been postponed and will most likely take place in 2025; it will not open on July 11.
An article on Sunday about Iran’s new president misidentified the university with which Nader Hashemi is affiliated. He is a professor at Georgetown University, not George Washington University.
match_headline: Reformist Candidate Wins Iran’s Presidential Election

text: An article on Sunday about questions provided in advance to radio programs by President Biden’s team misstated a radio station on which “The Earl Ingram Show” is broadcast. It is syndicated on WAUK in Waukesha, Wis., and other networks, not the defunct Milwaukee station WMCS.
match_headline: Biden Aides Provided Questions in Advance for His Radio Interviews

text: An article on Sunday about a settlement reached in the case of the police raid of a Kansas weekly newspaper misstated when Joan Meyer, the 98-year-old mother of the publisher and the co-owner of The Marion County Record, died. It was one day after the police raid, not two.
match_headline: $235,000 Settlement Is Reached in Police Raid of a Kansas Newspaper

text: An article on Friday about the winner of the Nathan’s Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest on Coney Island misstated Patrick Bertoletti’s age. He is 39, not 26.
match_headline: Hot Dog Eating Contest Crowns Patrick Bertoletti as New Men’s Champion

text: An article on Saturday about Le Pavé, a manufacturing start-up using recycled plastics to create podiums for the Paris Olympic Games, misspelled the given name of a co-founder of the company. He is Marius Hamelot, not Maurius.
match_headline: Inside the Factory Turning Trash Into Olympic Podiums

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misidentified the winners of the show “Claim to Fame.” Keke Palmer’s sister Loreal Chanel Palmer won the first season, and Nick Cannon’s brother Gabriel Ezra Cannon won the second season. Jason Aldean’s cousin Logan Crosby did not win either of those seasons.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘The Bachelorette’ and ‘Claim to Fame’

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Cuba expert Wayne S. Smith, using information from his family, omitted the name of a survivor: his sister, Mary Paul Smith Jespersen. It also misstated the given name of a son of Mr. Smith’s who died before him. He was Wayne Smith Jr., not Michael Smith. And it misstated the original surname of his first wife. She was Jacqueline Perkins, not Jacqueline Richard.
match_headline: Wayne S. Smith, a Leading Critic of the Embargo on Cuba, Dies at 91

text: An article on Sunday about the challenges facing Black Democrats running in white districts attributed an erroneous distinction to Janelle Bynum. Ms. Bynum is the only Black woman currently serving in the Oregon House of Representatives, but it was Margaret Carter, in 1984, who became the first Black woman elected to the body.
match_headline: Sykes Faces Challenge in Ohio as Black Democrats Push to Hold White Districts

text: An article on Monday about large crowds at the beach on Coney Island despite recent drownings misstated meteorologists’ predictions for Saturday. They predicted that rip currents, not riptides, would be likely that day.
match_headline: After Teens Drown at Coney Island, New Yorkers Still Crowd the Beach

text: An article on Tuesday about Trump policies at the center of the Republican Party’s platform referred incorrectly to Jim Dotson. He currently serves in the Arkansas State Senate; he is not a former state senator.
match_headline: A Republican Platform That Could Read Like a Trump Rally

text: An article on Monday about looming struggles for the apartment real estate business misspelled the name of a law firm. It is Locke Lord, not Locke Lorde.
match_headline: Apartments Could Be the Next Real Estate Business to Struggle

text: An article on Tuesday about the Biden administration’s efforts to get foreign companies to invest in chip-making in the United States misstated Taiwan’s contribution to global chip production. It has more than 60 percent of the world’s foundry capacity, in which manufacturers make chips for other companies that design them; it does not produce more than 60 percent of the world’s chips.
match_headline: U.S. Creates High-Tech Global Supply Chains to Blunt Risks Tied to China

text: An article on July 3 about scrutiny of Wisconsin’s state prison system for its failures in providing health care for inmates misstated Robert Oshel’s role at the National Practitioner Data Bank. He managed the databank’s research program, not the entire databank.
match_headline: These Doctors Were Censured. Wisconsin’s Prisons Hired Them Anyway.

text: An article on Wednesday about Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s role in France’s government after he led his coalition to a narrow win in parliamentary elections misidentified the arrondissement in Paris where Mr. Mélenchon gave a speech. It was the 19th arrondissement, not the 20th.
match_headline: France’s Far-Left Firebrand: Ready to Govern?

text: An article on Wednesday about proposed funding for packaging computer chips in the United States misidentified IPC, a technology industry group. It is a global organization with members from around the world, not just from the United States.
match_headline: U.S. Plans Up to $1.6 Billion in Funding for Packaging Computer Chips

text: An article on Thursday about the impact that climate change is having on California wildfires misidentified the employer of a public information officer. Darren McMillin works for California Interagency Incident Management Team 12, not for Cal Fire.
match_headline: Hot Nights Fuel Wildfires in California, Complicating Containment

text: An article on Wednesday about bank insurance misidentified the start-up that went bankrupt this spring. It is Synapse Financial Technologies, not Synapse Technology.
match_headline: What Happens When Your Bank Isn’t Really a Bank and Your Money Disappears?

text: An article on Thursday about the artist Judy Chicago referred imprecisely to John Coplans’s role at Artforum magazine. He was a co-founder, not the founder.
match_headline: The Wide, Wide World of Judy Chicago

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the biochemist Maxine Singer misstated her parents’ surname. They were Henrietta and Hyman Frank, not Singer.
match_headline: Maxine Singer, Guiding Force at the Dawn of Biotechnology, Dies at 93

text: An article on Friday about the sentencing of a Montauk fisherman for his role in a conspiracy to harvest and sell thousands of pounds of fluke and black sea bass, relying on information provided by Chris Winkler’s lawyer in court, misstated Mr. Winkler’s age. He is 64, not 65.
match_headline: Montauk Fisherman Who Took Too Much Fluke Gets a 30-Month Sentence

text: An article on Page 4 this weekend about five women who started a secret theater society misidentifies the organization that Margo Jones created. It was Theater 47, not the Dallas Theater Center.
match_headline: The Five Women Who Started a Secret Theater Society

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about a 1974 kidnapping misidentifies an area of Long Island. Great Neck is a region of Long Island, not a township.
match_headline: The Kidnapping I Can’t Escape

text: An article on page 12 about a woman suffering from vomiting describes incorrectly the motion of the diaphragm. It moves downward when breathing in and upward when breathing out, not the reverse.
match_headline: Why Was the Young Woman Vomiting Everything She Ate or Drank?

text: An obituary on Friday about the singer Joe Bonsall of the Oak Ridge Boys misstated the name of the city in Pennsylvania to which he moved in 1967. It is Harrisburg, not Hattiesburg.
match_headline: Joe Bonsall, Tenor Voice of the Oak Ridge Boys, Dies at 76

text: An obituary on Saturday about Judy Belushi Pisano, who became a defender of the legacy of her husband, the actor and comedian John Belushi, after he died in 1982, misstated her birth date. It was Jan. 7, 1951, not Jan. 1. It also referred incorrectly to the Second Chance Foundation, of which she was a founder. Mr. Belushi’s fellow performer Dan Aykroyd was not involved in that organization. And it misstated where Mr. Belushi went to college. He attended the University of Wisconsin and the College of DuPage in Glen Ellyn, Ill. — not the University of Illinois.
match_headline: Judy Belushi Pisano, Who Defended Her Husband’s Legacy, Dies at 73

text: An article on Saturday about the ways in which former President Trump has blurred the lines between politics and business misstated the location of 45footwear L.L.C., the company selling Mr. Trump’s $399 golden sneakers. It is in a lawyer’s office in Wyoming, not Montana.
match_headline: Martyr Inc.: How Trump Monetized a Persecution Narrative

text: An article on Tuesday about tight races in Virginia and Pennsylvania for the presidency misstated former President Donald J. Trump’s age. He is 78 years old, not 77.
match_headline: Biden Facing Challenges in Two Must-Win States, Times/Siena Polls Find

text: An obituary on May 13 about the movie producer and director Roger Corman referred incorrectly to Concorde-New Horizons, the production and distribution company he formed in 1983. He sold its library in 2018; he did not sell the company and its library in 1997. This correction was delayed for research.
match_headline: Roger Corman, 98, Dies; Prolific Master of Low-Budget Cinema

text: An obituary on Thursday about the sculptor Nancy Azara referred incorrectly to Finch College in Manhattan, which she attended. Although it was originally a two-year college, it had become a four-year college by the time she was a student there.
match_headline: Nancy Azara, Sculptor Who Created a Haven for Feminist Artists, Dies at 84

text: A picture caption with a Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about images of the assassination attempt against former President Donald J. Trump misstated the site of the assassination of President James Garfield. He was shot in Washington and later died in Long Branch, N.J.; he was not assassinated in Long Branch.
match_headline: The Photographs That Made Trump an Incarnation of Defiance

text: An article on Wednesday about Donald J. Trump’s newly chosen running mate Senator J.D. Vance’s position on key issues misstated the position of Mr. Vance on a national abortion ban. Mr. Vance has said that he would support a 15-week national ban proposed by Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, not that the issue should be left entirely to the states.
match_headline: J.D. Vance on the Issues, From Abortion to the Middle East

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about an annual summer photography festival in France, described incorrectly the touring schedule for an exhibition by Mary Ellen Mark. It was in Berlin before it opened at Arles; it is not going to Berlin next.
match_headline: At This Photography Festival, the Camera Points Below the Surface

text: Because of an editing error, a Critic’s Notebook article on Tuesday about the Nazi jurist Carl Schmitt gave an incorrect date for the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. It occurred in 2021, not 2001.
match_headline: Florida Proud Boy Sentenced to 10 Years in Capitol Attack

text: An obituary on Sunday about the sex therapist Ruth Westheimer referred incorrectly to her at one point. She was not a psychologist.
match_headline: Ruth Westheimer, the Sex Guru Known as Dr. Ruth, Dies at 96

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the lawyer Abe Krash misstated the given name of a lawyer who worked with him on the landmark Gideon v. Wainwright case. He was Ralph Temple, not Paul.

An article on Thursday about a gunman’s attempt to assassinate former President Donald J. Trump at a rally in Butler, Pa., misspelled the Secret Service director’s given name. She is Kimberly Cheatle, not Kimberley.
match_headline: Local Police Were Inside Building Used by Gunman, Secret Service Director Says

text: An article on Thursday about Ukraine’s electricity grid contending with a sizzling heat wave misstated the name of an organization based in Kyiv. It is the Energy Industry Research Center, not the Energy Research Centre.
match_headline: Ukraine’s Devastated Energy Grid Battles a New Foe: A Sizzling Heat Wave

text: An article on Thursday about President Biden testing positive for Covid misstated when he sat for an interview with BET News. It was on Tuesday, not Wednesday afternoon.
match_headline: Biden Tests Positive for Covid

text: An article on Thursday about issues with cord blood banks misspelled the first name of a former sales representative for CBR. She is Stacey Seaver, not Stacy Seaver.
match_headline: Promised Cures, Tainted Cells: How Cord Blood Banks Mislead Parents

text: An article on Friday about Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, and his public devotion to Judaism misstated the given name of Rabbi Alejandro Avruj. It is Alejandro, not Daniel.
match_headline: The Catholic President Who’s ‘Almost’ Jewish

text: An article on Tuesday about the Oscar-winning actor Anthony Hopkins, included a statement from Mr. Hopkins in which he repeated a false rumor about William Wyler’s production of “Ben Hur.” No one died during the filming of the film’s chariot race sequence.
match_headline: ‘Acting Is a Trick’: Anthony Hopkins on ‘Those About to Die’

text: A picture caption with an article on July 7 about Taylor Swift misstated the year of the Billboard Hot 100 when the Beatles held the top five spots. It was the week of April 4, 1964, not 1962.
match_headline: Taylor Swift’s ‘Poets’ Ties Her Record for Most Weeks at No. 1

text: An article on July 7 about a Brooklyn building whose residents were swindled by a developer, incorrectly described involuntary bankruptcy. The process puts a debtor into bankruptcy, not a creditor.
match_headline: They Thought They Owned Condos. They Never Got the Deeds.

text: A review on July 7 about “Night Flyer: Harriet Tubman and the Faith Dreams of a Free People,” by Tiya Miles, referred incorrectly to Dorchester County, Md. It is part of the Eastern Shore region, but it does not have an “eastern shore” on Chesapeake Bay. It has a western shore.
ref_headline: Night Flyer: Harriet Tubman and the Faith Dreams of a Free People,
match_headline: Who Was Harriet Tubman? A Historian Sifts the Clues.

text: An article on Sunday about a dispute over stray cattle that started a broader conflict in an upstate New York town misidentified the charge that one of Tracy Murphy’s lawyers was convicted of in a case involving stolen ducks. The lawyer, Wayne Hsiung, was convicted of felony conspiracy to commit trespass, not the theft of the ducks. It also misstated the consequences of Mr. Hsiung’s conviction. His law license was placed on interim suspension; he has not been disbarred.
match_headline: How Two Wandering Cows Started a Culture War

text: An article on Saturday about conflict in Western Congo misstated the number of people displaced in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. It is nearly 6 million people, not 60 million.
match_headline: Congo’s ‘Other’ Conflict Kills Thousands in West Near the Capital

text: An article on Monday about the use of waterboarding on Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, the man accused of plotting the Sept. 11 attacks, incorrectly described a religious counting technique offered by a defense lawyer in the case. Some Muslims repeatedly put a thumb to the inside of each finger three times as they say a prayer praising Allah, not only to three fingers.
match_headline: Psychologist Who Waterboarded C.I.A. Prisoners Defends Method’s Use in 9/11 Case

text: An article on Tuesday about Democrats’ eagerness for Kamala Harris to face Donald Trump in a presidential debate referred incorrectly to Ammar Moussa, a representative for the Harris campaign. He is a man.
match_headline: How Kamala Harris Will Try to Put Trump on Defense

text: An article on Thursday about a new study showing the brain’s reaction to psychedelic drugs misidentified the drug methylphenidate. It is a stimulant, not an amphetamine.
match_headline: This Is Literally Your Brain on Drugs

text: An obituary on Saturday about the conservative television and radio host Lou Dobbs misstated when he married Kathleen Ann Wheeler. It was 1967, not 1969.
match_headline: Lou Dobbs, Former Fox Business Host and Trump Booster, Dies at 78

text: An article on Friday about JD Vance’s changed stance on Donald J. Trump’s claims of election fraud did not clearly describe Mark Zuckerberg’s relationship to the Center for Tech and Civic Life. He and his wife, Priscilla Chan, were the organization’s largest donors in 2020.
match_headline: J.D. Vance Once Warned Trump About Lying About Elections. That Was Then.

text: An article on Thursday about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel’s speech to U.S. Congress misstated the leadership title of Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York. He is the majority leader, not the minority leader.
match_headline: Netanyahu Delivers a Forceful Defense of Israel to Applause in Congress

text: An article on Thursday about Black sororities and fraternities endorsing Kamala Harris for president incorrectly described the frequency of the Zeta Phi Beta Grand Boule. The Boule occurs every two years, not annually.
match_headline: Black Sororities and Fraternities Line Up Behind Kamala Harris

text: Because of editing errors, an article on July 9 about the Starliner spacecraft’s technical troubles misstated several dates. The news conference was in June, not the previous Friday; engineers planned ground tests for July, not the week after the article was published; a Russian satellite broke apart in late June, not the previous Thursday; a spacewalk was cut short in June, not the previous Monday; and the next spacewalk was not scheduled for that Tuesday.
match_headline: Five Takeaways From Biden’s News Conference

text: An article last Sunday about work by Wael Shawky described incorrectly the transfer of power in Egypt after Hosni Mubarak was deposed. Mohamed Morsi was elected, and then Abdel Fattah el-Sisi came to power. El-Sisi was not in power directly after Mubarak.
match_headline: An Egyptian Artist Mesmerizes in Venice With an Opera and a Donkey

text: An article last Sunday about the marriage of Traci Green and Christopher Sater referred imprecisely to Mr. Sater’s upbringing; he was born in Mountain View, Calif., and raised in Los Altos, Calif., not born and raised in Mountain View, Calif., and also raised in Los Altos. It also referred incompletely to the location of their first date; it was at the restaurant Nick’s Lighthouse, not Nick’s, in San Francisco.
match_headline: They Wanted Marriage and Family, Maybe Not in That Order

text: An article on July 14 about the director Ti West misspelled the surname of a filmmaker. He is Sam Raimi, not Rami.
match_headline: Ti West Is Turning Hollywood Into a Horror Show

text: An article on July 21 about storm chasers referred incorrectly to the deaths of three University of Oklahoma students. They were killed in a traffic accident on their way back from chasing a storm, not while they were chasing the storm.
match_headline: Seattle Police Officer Fired Over ‘Cruel Comments’ About Pedestrian’s Death

text: An article on Thursday about Kamala Harris’s Indian heritage misstated Gautam Mukunda’s title. He is a former research fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Center for Public Leadership; he is not currently in that position.
match_headline: Harris’s Indian Heritage Is Deeply Felt if Little Advertised

text: An article on Monday about strengthening military ties between the U.S. and Japan misattributed a quote from a news conference on Sunday. It was Defense Secretary Lloyd J. Austin III, not Secretary of State Antony J. Blinken, who said, “The U.S. will have a direct leadership role in planning and leading U.S. forces in both peacetime and in potential crises. And that will give us an opportunity to work more closely together to ensure greater peace and stability.”
match_headline: U.S. and Japan Announce Steps to Strengthen Their Military Ties

text: An article on Sunday about damaged train lines in France misstated the conversion of 320 kilometers per hour to miles per hour. It is about 199 miles per hour, not 186.
match_headline: More Trains, but Few Answers, After Railway Sabotage in France

text: An article on Sunday about the lingering trauma that sexual assault victims in Ukraine are enduring misstated the claims by an illustrator in Kyiv, Ukraine, regarding her sexual assault. She said she was raped twice by one Russian soldier, not multiple Russian soldiers.
match_headline: ‘No One to Talk To’: The Lingering Trauma of Russian Rape in Ukraine

text: An article on Sunday about the intensifying Park fire in California misstated when the Camp fire had started. It was six years ago, not eight.
match_headline: Despite Park Fire’s Rapid Spread, Some Residents Are Determined to Stay Put

text: An article on Thursday about the ways that London paved the way for sustainability after hosting the Olympic Games misstated the year Graham Gilmore became chief executive of the London Stadium. It was 2017, not 2015.
match_headline: Before Paris, London Showed How the Olympics Could Be Sustainable

text: An obituary on Tuesday about Duke Fakir, the last surviving original member of the Four Tops, misstated the number of years the Four Tops worked with the songwriting and production team of Brian and Eddie Holland and Lamont Dozier. It was four, not two.
match_headline: Duke Fakir, Last Surviving Member of the Four Tops, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Friday about the kora virtuoso Toumani Diabaté misstated at one point his father’s surname. As correctly noted elsewhere, it was Diabaté, not Kouyaté.
match_headline: Toumani Diabaté, Malian Master of the Kora, Is Dead at 58

text: An article on Sunday about the gymnast Simone Biles misstated the order in which Rebeca Andrade and Shilese Jones finished in the women’s all-around competition at last fall’s world gymnastics championships. Andrade won the silver medal and Jones the bronze, not the other way around.
match_headline: Simone Biles Is Done Being Judged

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the Olympic flame misidentified the location of a scene with a nearly naked man covered in blue paint. It was on a bridge, not a barge.
match_headline: The Olympic Flame Isn’t a Flame at All

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about cases of champagne found on an underwater shipwreck in the Baltic Sea misstated the salinity of a sea relative to that of an ocean. While the average salinity can be lower in a sea, as it is in the Baltic, that is not always the case.
match_headline: Pop the Cork? A Shipwreck Brims With Unopened Sparkling Wine.

text: An article on Tuesday about debates over tribal expansion of casinos in Oregon referred incorrectly to Deb Haaland. She is the first Native American to serve as a cabinet secretary, not the first to serve in a presidential cabinet.
match_headline: In Oregon, a Bid for Urban Casinos Threatens a Gambling ‘Arms Race’

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about the golden age of Mexico’s film industry misstated the title of one film in the series. It is “The Unknown Policeman,” not “The Unknown Policemen.”
match_headline: Unlikely Heroes and Heroines in These Gems From Mexico Cinema’s Golden Age

text: An article on Friday about the opera singer Klaus Florian Vogt mistranslated a word in a quote by Andreas Homoki, who was describing Vogt’s voice. He said, “But then you notice that he adds that additional chest voice, and his voice retains its lightness in the high register,” not “But then you notice that he adds that additional breast voice, and his voice retains its lightness in the high register.”
ref_headline: But then you notice that he adds that additional chest voice, and his voice retains its lightness in the high register,
match_headline: A Tenor With One of the Strangest, Most Essential Voices in Opera

text: An article on Thursday about the conviction of Capt. Moussa Dadis Camara, the former president of Guinea, on crimes against humanity misstated how many people have died in protests under the current rule of Col. Mamady Doumbouya, which began in 2021, according to Amnesty International. It is 47, not more than 100. (Over 100 protesters have been killed in Guinea since 2019, according to Amnesty International.)
match_headline: Ukrainian Fencer Dedicates Medal to Countrymen Killed in the War

text: An article on Thursday about wildfires across the Western United States included an incorrect comparison between the amount of acres that have burned on average across the United States over the past decade and the size of California. Seven million acres is less than a tenth the size of California, not roughly half.
match_headline: Fires Have Burned 4.5 Million Acres This Year, Blanketing Much of North America in Smoke

text: An article on Thursday about a vanishing grass weaving art form in Hawaii misspelled a word for grasses used to make a thatched roof and a related phrase that means to gain strength through closeness. The grasses are known as pili and the phrase is to build pilina together, not pilana.
match_headline: In Hawaii, Weaving New Life Into a Nearly Vanished Art Form

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Thursday about the relationship between art and sport at the Cultural Olympiad described incorrectly when the cultural component of the Olympics began. The Olympics have long featured cultural events, but that component was not officially called the Cultural Olympiad until 1992.
match_headline: Dance Leads the Way as Art Meets Sport at the Cultural Olympiad

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about this year’s Sundance Directors Lab misstates which directors attended the lab. Ava DuVernay was not a fellow.
match_headline: At Sundance Lab, Movie Economics Can’t Be Ignored This Year

text: A caption with the Big City column in Metropolitan on July 28 incorrectly described the stance of JD Vance, the current Republican vice-presidential candidate, toward “childless” people. He said in a 2021 interview, “How does it make any sense that we’ve turned our country over to people who don’t really have a direct stake in it?,” not that they “should” have no direct stake in the nation’s future.
match_headline: JD Vance and the Age-Old Trope of ‘Childless Cat Ladies’

text: An article on Page 24 this weekend about John Hinckley Jr. misstates the name of the store where Hinckley purchased the gun used in his assassination attempt. It was Rocky’s Pawn Shop, not Randy’s Pawn Shop.
match_headline: John Hinckley Jr. and the Madness of American Political Violence

text: An article on Page 38 this weekend about deepfake pornography incorrectly describes a video, shared by Donald Trump, of Nancy Pelosi apparently slurring her words. While the original video was altered, it was not created with deepfake technology.
match_headline: Trolls Used Her Face to Make Fake Porn. There Was Nothing She Could Do.

text: An article last Sunday about Linda Yaccarino, the chief executive of X, misstated the relationship between Ms. Yaccarino and Lou Paskalis, a longtime advertising executive. Mr. Paskalis said the two remain friends; he is not a former friend who has cut ties. (The error was repeated in a picture caption.)
match_headline: How Do You Solve a Problem Like Elon?

text: Because of an editing error, a print headline for an article on Sunday about the proposed agreement for a legal settlement compensating the survivors of the Aug. 8, 2023, Maui wildfires misstated the expected share to be paid by Hawaiian Electric. The utility is expected to pay nearly $2 billion, not $4 billion.
match_headline: Lahaina Showcased Centuries of Hawaiian History. Now Its Gems are Gone.

text: An article on Sunday about Iceland’s president, Halla Tómasdóttir, misstated the singer Björk’s connections to Ms. Tómasdóttir. Björk partnered in 2008 with a financial firm of which Ms. Tómasdóttir was a co-founder. Björk was not involved in Ms. Tómasdóttir’s election campaign.
match_headline: In Iceland, a Feminist Inspired by the Country’s History Is the New President

text: An article on July 25 about the Off Broadway show “Inspired by True Events,” misidentified the theater at which Daniel Wozniak was performing. It was the Hunger Artists Theater Company in Fullerton, Calif., not the Liberty Theater in Los Alamitos, Calif.
match_headline: ‘Inspired by True Events’ Review: True Crime Thriller Riddled With Clichés

text: An article on Tuesday about Bishop Richard Henning being named the next leader for the Catholic Archdiocese of Boston misidentified the diocese where there were political questions on the church’s handling of sexual abuse. It was in the diocese of Rockville Centre, in New York, not in the Providence diocese.
match_headline: Pope Francis Names New Leader for Boston Archdiocese

text: An article on Tuesday about the unearthing of 2,400-year-old Persian coins misstated the title of Cyrus the Younger. He was a prince, not a king.
match_headline: Archaeologists Find a 2,400-Year-Old ‘Pot of Gold’ in Turkey

text: An article on July 30 about the growing number of states that have passed book banning laws misstated the number of days a library in Idaho would have to relocate a book after receiving a complaint. The library has 60 days, not 30.
match_headline: More States Are Passing Book Banning Rules. Here’s What They Say.

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Saturday about Floyd Lane, a basketball star for City College of New York in 1950 whose career was shattered in a point-shaving scandal, referred incorrectly to his coach, Nat Holman. Though Holman had played basketball in high school and briefly in the professional ranks, it was not the case that he had starred for City College as a young man.
match_headline: One Olympian’s Secret Weapon? His High School Coach.

text: An article on Aug. 1 which fact-checked former President Donald J. Trump’s remarks during his appearance at the National Association of Black Journalists Convention in Chicago, misstated Vice President Kamala Harris’s account in her autobiography of retaking the bar exam after failing on her first attempt. Ms. Harris wrote that she retook the test in February 1990 and passed; her subsequent exam was not left unaddressed in the book.
match_headline: Trump to Address National Association of Black Journalists

text: An article on Friday about efforts by veterans and lawmakers to urge the Food and Drug Administration to approve the use of MDMA-assisted therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder, misstated the vote by an advisory panel for the F.D.A. It was not unanimous; the panel voted 10-1 that the therapy’s benefits did not outweigh its risks and 9-2 that it was not effective.
match_headline: Veterans and Lawmakers Lobby in Bipartisan Push for MDMA Therapy

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about tech companies making deals with A.I. start-ups for their technology and top employees, reversed the identities of the founders of Character.AI in a photo caption. Daniel De Freitas, not Noam Shazeer, is on the left.
match_headline: The New A.I. Deal: Buy Everything but the Company

text: An article on Aug. 4 about what the Brazilian far right learned from Trump misstated the location of the Hungarian Embassy in Brazil, where the former president Jair Bolsonaro took refuge. It is Brasília, not São Paulo.
match_headline: Trumps of the Tropics: Brazil’s Far Right Plots Its Return

text: An article Jan. 7 about the fashion designer Stan Herman, because of incorrect information provided by a source, misstated the year in which his partner, Gene Horowitz, died. He died in 1992, not 1991. This correction was delayed because it was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: At 95, This Designer Has Never Been Out of Fashion

text: An article last Sunday about Jackson Villamarin Villegas, a man who fled Venezuela to seek asylum in the United States, misstated the city where he bought a Super Mario doll. It was purchased in Guadalajara, Mexico, not Bucaramanga, which is in Colombia.
match_headline: The Freedom of an Escape From Venezuela and the Loneliness That Followed

text: A review on July 14 about “The Loves of Theodore Roosevelt,” by Edward F. O’Keefe, referred imprecisely to the 19th Amendment, which granted women the right to vote. The amendment took effect in 1920, after the states had ratified it, not 1919, when Congress passed it.
match_headline: The 6 Women Who Shaped America’s Most Macho President

text: An article on Monday about Tim Walz’s visits to China misstated the surname of the person who took the photograph featuring Mr. Walz and students at the Great Wall of China. She is Jillian Walker, not Jillian Taylor.
match_headline: Tim Walz’s Long Relationship With China Defies Easy Stereotypes

text: An article on Sunday fact-checking claims about Tim Walz’s record misstated the damage to one of Minneapolis’s police precincts. It was damaged by fire but not burned to the ground.
match_headline: Fact-Checking Claims About Tim Walz’s Record

text: An article on Monday about Uber pursuing a plan in Nevada that may curb lawsuits misstated the timing of a ballot measure to reduce fees for plaintiffs’ lawyers. The measure could go before Nevada voters in 2026, not as soon as next year.
match_headline: Uber, Facing Sexual-Assault Litigation, Pushes Plan That May Curb Suits

text: An article on Tuesday about real estate investment trusts misstated part of a plan announced in June by the investment firm KKR to support the net asset value of shares in its private REIT. If the net asset value per share is below $27 by June 2027, KKR said it would cancel its own shares in order to increase the value for shareholders; it did not say it would sell its shares.
match_headline: It Was a Hot Real Estate Trade. Now Investors Are Worried.

text: An article on Wednesday about a study highlighting how extreme rainfall was made 10 percent heavier by human-caused climate change misstated the name of a scientific organization. It is the Kentucky Geologic Survey, not the Kentucky Geologic Society.
match_headline: Deadly Landslides in India Made Worse by Climate Change, Study Finds

text: An obituary on Aug. 7 about the composer Walter Arlen overstated what is known about the ancestry of the Spanish Catholic mystic St. John of the Cross, whose poetry Mr. Arlen set to music. He was once thought to have had Jewish ancestors who were forced to convert, although scholars disagree about the conclusiveness of the evidence; it is not the case that his parents were Jewish and forced to convert.
match_headline: Walter Arlen, Holocaust Refugee and Belated Composer, Is Dead at 103

text: An article on Aug. 9 about a Beijing court’s decision to uphold a longstanding rule that allows only married women to freeze their eggs misstated the name of the court that rejected Teresa Xu’s lawsuit. It was the Beijing No. 3 Intermediate People’s Court, not the Chaoyang Intermediate People’s Court.
match_headline: A Chinese Woman Sued to Freeze Her Eggs. She Lost.

text: An article on Friday about what economists say regarding grocery inflation misstated the supply of consumer goods. Supply was diminished, not strong.
match_headline: Harris Plans to Ban Grocery ‘Price Gouging.’ What Does the Evidence Say?

text: An article on Page 90 about the Hermès women’s wear artistic director Nadège Vanhée misspells the given name of an artist. He was Lucian Freud, not Lucien.
An obituary on Friday about the actress Gena Rowlands misstated the number of Primetime Emmy Awards she won. It was three, not two.
match_headline: Gena Rowlands, Actress Who Brought Raw Drama to Her Roles, Dies at 94

text: An article on Aug. 4 about the history of teen beauty trends misstated the nationality of the founder of Tinkerbell Cosmetics. He was American, not British.
match_headline: Before Bum Bum Cream, 80 Years of Teen Beauty Trends

text: A review on July 21 about the novel “Enlightenment,” by Sarah Perry, misstated the time it takes one character to discover that another has a wife. It is a matter of months, not 10 years.
match_headline: In Drizzly England, a Tale of Sex, God and Celestial Bodies

text: An article on Page 90 about the Hermès women’s wear artistic director Nadège Vanhée misspells the given name of an artist. He was Lucian Freud, not Lucien.
match_headline: 7 Days in the Cultural Life of an Artistic Director

text: An article on Aug. 2 about a new federal policy that would require airlines to seat families together on flights without additional fees referred imprecisely to the rule’s origin. The proposal on Aug. 1 followed a congressional authorization to the Transportation Department; it did not originate from the agency.
match_headline: If D.O.T. Gets Its Way, Families Will Sit Together on Flights for Free

text: An article on Tuesday about Hillary Clinton’s bond with Kamala Harris referred incorrectly to dinners hosted by the Clintons at their home in Washington. Douglas Elmendorf, the former dean at Harvard Kennedy School, says he was not in attendance.
match_headline: Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris: Inside Their Quietly Close Bond

text: An article on Friday about the new mpox epidemic misstated the number of U.S. mpox cases so far in 2024. It is 1,657, not 740.
match_headline: How Did Mpox Become a Global Emergency? What’s Next?

text: Because of flawed data provided by FactSet, “The Market Last Week” graphic on Aug. 18 contained inaccurate information. The “Week’s change” columns for “Best performers” and “Worst performers” contained daily returns from Friday Aug. 16, not from the entire week.
match_headline: The Best of Late Night This Week

text: A review on Friday of the Frank Walter exhibition misidentified the Caribbean country where Walter farmed. It was in Dominica, not the Dominican Republic.
match_headline: The Odd Duck of Antiguan Art, in His Ecstatic, Expressionist Glory

text: An article on Wednesday about a conflict of interest in the decision to give the bronze medal to Romanian gymnast, Ana Barbosu, over America’s Jordan Chiles, misstated the name of the institution that first published details of the case. It is the International Institute for Conflict Prevention and Resolution, not the International Institute for Conflict Resolution and Prevention.
match_headline: Head of Panel That Ruled Against Jordan Chiles Represents Romania in Other Cases

text: An article on Wednesday about Barack Obama’s friendship with Kamala Harris misstated the location of an event headlined by Barack Obama where Kamala Harris was almost turned away at the door. It was in Los Angeles, not San Francisco.
match_headline: Behind the Obama-Harris Friendship: A Key Endorsement and a Kindred Spirit

text: Because of a production error, an article on Monday about the widespread presence of migrants in many of Chicago’s neighborhoods omitted part of a quote from Beatriz Ponce de León, the city’s deputy mayor for immigrant, migrant and refugee rights. The full quote was, “We don’t want to use this as an excuse to hide people away, and criminalize people because of their economic or immigration status.”
ref_headline: We don’t want to use this as an excuse to hide people away, and criminalize people because of their economic or immigration status.
match_headline: New York City Moves to Shut Down a Growing Migrant Encampment

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the recovery of the bodies of four passengers believed to have been aboard the Bayesian, a yacht that sank off the coast of Sicily, transposed the number of crew members and passengers on the yacht. There were 10 crew members and 12 passengers, not the other way around.
match_headline: Divers Find 4 Bodies From Yacht That Sank Off Sicily

text: An article on Wednesday about second gentleman Doug Emhoff’s outreach to Jewish voters misstated the location of the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp. It is in the suburbs of Oswiecim, Poland, not Krakow.
match_headline: Doug Emhoff Puts His Jewish Identity at the Center of His Campaign Outreach

text: An article on Friday about the unearthing of the second-largest diamond ever found misstated the weight of the diamond in pounds. It weighs a little more than a pound, not more than a pound and a half.
match_headline: Second-Largest Diamond Ever Found Is Discovered in Botswana

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about emotional support parrots in a Manhattan apartment building misidentified the role of Damian Williams. He is a U.S. attorney not a district attorney.
match_headline: The Emotional Support Parrots vs. the Co-op Board

text: An article on Aug. 18 about the football player Michael Oher misstated the number of head-coaching jobs Hugh Freeze, the current head coach at Auburn, has held in college football. Auburn is his fifth head-coaching job, not his fourth.
match_headline: ‘The Blind Side’ Made Him Famous. But He Has a Different Story to Tell.

text: An article on Aug. 25 about President Biden misidentified the entity that provided interview questions to Black radio stations. It was the Biden campaign, not the White House.
match_headline: Joe Biden’s Interrupted Presidency

text: An article last Sunday about the expansion of abortion clinics misstated the percentage of abortions that are performed in the first trimester of pregnancy. It is 92 percent, not 60 percent. The article also misstated the name of the abortion provider that relocated from North Dakota to Minnesota last year. It is the Red River Women’s Clinic, not the Red River Clinic.
match_headline: For Abortion Providers, a Tough Business Gets Even Tougher

text: An article on Saturday about peace negotiations for the conflict in Sudan misidentified Lana Nusseibeh. She is the former United Arab Emirates ambassador to the United Nations, not the current one.
match_headline: Peace Talks at Swiss Resort Beckoned. Sudan’s Divided Generals Wouldn’t Go.

text: An article on Sunday about peace talks between Hamas and Israel referred incorrectly to a statement by Gen. Charles Q. Brown Jr. about “Israel’s right to self-defense.” Those words were paraphrased, not part of a direct quotation.
match_headline: Hamas Agrees to Meet With Mediators in Cairo Ahead of Cease-Fire Talks

text: An article on Friday about the Democratic Party’s efforts to court social media influencers during the Democratic National Convention misstated the social media sponsorship policy of the nonprofit group Hub Project. The group requires influencers it works with to disclose paid posts, according to Nicholas Kitchel, the director of Hub Project’s digital partnerships; it is not among the groups without a policy.
match_headline: Free Booze, a Lake Cruise and Selfies Galore: How Democrats Courted Influencers at the D.N.C.

text: An article on Sunday about the two NASA astronauts whose trip back to Earth has been delayed until 2025 misstated the current title of Norman Knight. He is NASA’s flight operations director, not the chief of the flight director office.
match_headline: NASA Extends Boeing Starliner Astronauts’ Space Station Stay to 2025

text: An article on Monday about the recent arrest in France of Pavel Durov, the founder of Telegram, misstated the year the Russian opposition leader Aleksei A. Navalny died in prison. He died this year, not last year.
match_headline: Telegram Becomes Free Speech Flashpoint After Founder’s Arrest

text: An article on Monday about the Edinburgh International Festival misstated David Ireland’s role in a production of “The Fifth Step.” He wrote the play, but he did not also direct it.
match_headline: At Edinburgh Festival, Sometimes Simpler Is Better

text: An article on Friday about the rapper Cash Cobain misstated the year Snoop Dogg’s song “Beautiful” was released. It was 2003, not 2018
match_headline: Cash Cobain Is Steering Drill Rap’s Sexy Swerve

text: An article on Thursday previewing the U.S. Open misstated the tennis matches played between Carlos Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic this season. They faced each other in the Wimbledon final and the men’s singles final at the Olympics. They did not meet in the French Open final.
match_headline: Everything You Need to Know About the 2024 U.S. Open

text: An article on Tuesday about a lawsuit targeting new election rules in Georgia misspelled the name of a deputy campaign manager for Vice President Kamala Harris. He is Quentin Fulks, not Quinten Fulks. The story also referred incorrectly to Mr. Fulk’s statement. He said that Georgia’s new election rules — not the Democrats’ lawsuit — were part of a broader effort by Republicans “to lay the groundwork to challenge the election results.”
ref_headline: to lay the groundwork to challenge the election results.
match_headline: Democrats Sue Georgia Election Board, Warning of ‘Chaos’

text: An article on Saturday about the potential foreign buyout of the 7-Eleven convenience store chain misidentified the type of oven 7-Eleven uses to cook hot dogs. It is a convection oven, not an induction oven.
match_headline: Why 7-Eleven Is a National Treasure in Japan

text: An article on Tuesday about Israelis who survived their captivity in Gaza included references to a man who did not survive. The man, Abraham Kunder, was among the hostages whose body had recently been recovered by Israeli forces.
match_headline: Israeli Military Rescues Eighth Hostage Alive From Gaza

text: An article last Thursday about the aftermath of a competitor’s death at the recent CrossFit Games misstated part of a quotation from Greg Glassman, the exercise program’s founder. Mr. Glassman originally described his methodology as a program of “constantly varied, high-intensity functional movement,” not “constantly varied, high-intensity functional fitness.”
match_headline: In the Wake of Tragedy, CrossFit Faces an Identity Crisis

text: An article on Wednesday about tariffs and how the Democratic and Republican presidential candidates have embraced them misstated the timing of a statement by former President Donald J. Trump. He was speaking in Asheville, N.C., on Aug. 14, not last week, when he proposed 10 percent to 20 percent tariffs on foreign countries “that have been ripping us off for years.”
ref_headline: that have been ripping us off for years.
match_headline: Harris and Trump Embrace Tariffs, Though Their Approaches Differ

text: An article on Wednesday about Russia’s advance in eastern Ukraine misstated the location of Pokrovsk, Ukraine, relative to Toretsk, Ukraine. It is southwest of Toretsk, not southeast.
match_headline: In Eastern Ukraine, Terrifying Bombardment and Near Total Destruction

text: An article on Tuesday about Russian literature translators described incorrectly Paul Foote’s translation of Mikhail Saltykov-Shchedrin’s “Foolsburg: The History of a Town.” It is the only previous translation still in print, not the only one available; Susan Brownsberger’s translation of the book was published in 1982.
ref_headline: Foolsburg: The History of a Town.
match_headline: Love Them or Hate Them, This Couple Reign in Russian Literature

text: An obituary on Aug. 19 about the actor Alain Delon referred incorrectly to the character he played in the 1976 movie “Mr. Klein.” He is French, not German.
match_headline: Alain Delon, Smoldering French Film Star, Dies at 88

text: An obituary on Friday about Charlene Marshall, who played a central role in a high-profile civil suit in 2006 and a later criminal trial, misstated the surname of her parents. They were Marguerite and Charles Tyler, not Taylor.
match_headline: Charlene Marshall, Central Figure in a Celebrity Scandal, Dies at 79

text: An article on Friday about a court ruling in South Korea that ordered the government to take stronger action on Climate Change misstated an aspect of the court’s ruling. It gave the National Assembly until the end of February 2026, not February 2025, to revise the Carbon Neutral Act.
match_headline: Court Orders South Korea to Take Stronger Action on Climate Change

text: An article on Thursday about Laurie Anderson’s new album, “Amelia,” misstated how a 2000 concert series by the American Composers Orchestra was assembled. The conductor Dennis Russell Davies did not call on all of the included composers to contribute; he programmed the music.
match_headline: How Laurie Anderson Conjured Amelia Earhart’s Final Flight

text: An article on Page 28 this weekend about the private, for-profit city of Próspera misidentifies the location in the opening photo. It was AmityAge, a Bitcoin cafe and education center, not the Beta Building.
match_headline: Care Policies Take Center Stage in Harris’s Economic Message

text: An article on Page 38 this weekend about the Conservative Party in Britain misstates the amount of time that has passed since the general elections there. It has been two months, not three.
match_headline: How the Tories Lost Britain

text: An article last Sunday about the video game designer Xalavier Nelson Jr. misidentified some of the countries where Nelson has lived. They are South Korea, Italy and Germany, not France, Australia and Mexico. The article also misstated an element from the Book of Leviticus that Nelson cited as inspiration for a possible cooking game. He was referring to the text’s “goats,” not “ghosts.”
match_headline: A Video Game Dynamo With Strange Ideas Always Swirling

text: An article last Sunday about the high cost of framing artwork misstated the year when Adam Collignon took over a Brooklyn framing business. It was in 2018, not 2008.
match_headline: Why Is Custom Framing So Expensive? One Man Investigates.

text: An article on Saturday about the President of Mexico’s plan for transforming the judiciary misstated which judges could be fired or impeached under a planned Tribunal for Judicial Discipline. Supreme Court justices could not be.
match_headline: How Mexico’s Judicial Overhaul Compares to Other Countries

text: An article on Saturday about Tim Walz’s CNN interview alongside Vice President Kamala Harris misstated when Mr. Walz had said that he and his wife, Gwen, used in vitro fertilization to conceive. The statement came in a fund-raising letter from his campaign for governor, not from Mr. Walz during his vice-presidential campaign.
match_headline: Tim Walz Is Happy to Help, Content to Be Ignored

text: An article on Sunday about a group of influencers helping Donald Trump win the young male vote misidentified Jake Paul’s sport. He is a boxer, not a U.F.C. fighter.
match_headline: Donald Trump Courts the Manoverse

text: An article on Saturday about a weight loss drug possibly lowering people’s chances of dying from Covid during the pandemic misstated the point at which Wegovy was found to be effective against Covid. Subjects had been taking the drug for more than a year; the effect against Covid was not immediate.
match_headline: An Obesity Drug Prevents Covid Deaths, Study Suggests

text: An article on Wednesday about a former aide to Gov. Kathy Hochul who was charged with 10 criminal counts that included visa fraud and money laundering misspelled the name of Linda Sun’s lawyer. It is Jarrod Schaeffer, not Jerrod Schaeffer. The article also misstated who was New York governor when salted ducks were delivered to the parents of Linda Sun. It was Andrew M. Cuomo, not Kathy Hochul; Ms. Hochul became governor the following month.
match_headline: N.Y. Official Charged With Taking Money, Travel and Poultry to Aid China

text: An obituary on Aug. 31 about Leonard Riggio, the founder of the Barnes & Noble bookstore chain, misstated the location in Manhattan of the original Barnes & Noble store, which he bought in 1971. It was on Fifth Avenue at 18th Street, not 17th Street.
match_headline: Leonard Riggio, 83, Dies; Founded Barnes & Noble and Upended Publishing

text: An article on Wednesday about John Podesta traveling to Beijing to press Chinese leaders to make more ambitious plans to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions misattributed a quotation about the state of climate diplomacy. It was Li Shuo, not Alan Yu, who said, “There is a stalemate on climate engagement between the U.S. and China.”
ref_headline: There is a stalemate on climate engagement between the U.S. and China.
match_headline: Biden’s Top Climate Negotiator to Visit China This Week

text: An article on Monday about former President Donald J. Trump’s speaking appearance at a convention of the Moms for Liberty group in Washington late last week misspelled the name of one of the conference attendees. She is Pnina Mintz, not Panina Mintz.
match_headline: ‘A Wave That’s on the Decline?’ Trump to Talk to Parents Leading the Culture Wars.

text: An article on Aug. 23 about the Sarajevo Film Festival misspelled the surname of Susan Sontag’s son. He is David Rieff, not Reiff.
match_headline: A Film Festival Founded in a War Zone, Still Going Strong

text: An article last Thursday about the southwestern Cyclades islands in Greece misattributed a quotation about shopping in Chora on Serifos. It was Natassa Kalogeropoulou, not Alexandra Kehayoglou, who discussed her favorite spots.
An obituary on Wednesday about the actor and singer James Darren misstated his wife’s surname. She is Evy Norlund, not Nordlund.
match_headline: James Darren, Actor, Singer and ‘Gidget’ Heartthrob, Dies at 88

text: An article on Thursday about the prospect of an early election in Canada after a left-leaning party withdrew its support for the Liberal Party of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau misstated the date by which a new election must be held. Under the Constitution, a new election must be held before October 2026, not October 2025.
match_headline: Trudeau’s Hold on Power Slips After Collapse of Governing Agreement

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about thousands of hotel workers going on strike misidentified the Baltimore hotel where workers and union members picketed on Monday. They were outside a Hilton, not a Hyatt.
match_headline: Why Thousands of Hotel Workers Are on Strike

text: An article on Friday about a repair shop that handles equipment for the Paralympics misspelled the surname of the communications director for Ottobock. She is Merle Florstedt, not Florestedt.
match_headline: In the Paralympic Fix-It Shop, Plenty of Fractures but No Blood

text: An article on Friday about the film “The Goldman Case” misidentified the director of “Saint Omer.” It is Alice Diop, not Mati Diop.
match_headline: ‘The Goldman Case’ Review: Sticking to the Facts

text: An article on Saturday about China stopping foreign adoptions misstated the circumstances of Courtney Moore’s time in China. It is not where she met her husband; they were already married when living there as students.
match_headline: China Stops Foreign Adoptions, Ending a Complicated Chapter

text: An article on Saturday about Tucker Carlson being criticized for hosting the podcaster Darryl Cooper, a Holocaust revisionist, misspelled the surname of a conservative columnist who has been critical of the views of Mr. Cooper. He is Sohrab Ahmari, not Amari.
match_headline: Tucker Carlson Criticized for Hosting Holocaust Revisionist

text: An article on Friday about a tip on a school shooting threat that led authorities to the Winder, Ga., shooting suspect, misspelled the given name of one of the teachers who was killed in the shooting. She is Cristina Irimie, not Christina. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Tip on School Shooting Threat Last Year Led to Suspect’s Door

text: An article on Monday about three police officers facing federal trial for civil rights and obstruction charges tied to the 2023 beating death of Tyre Nichols misstated the number of months since Mr. Nichols's death. It was 20 months ago, not 18.
match_headline: A Trial Over Tyre Nichols’s Death Begins as Memphis Is in a New Bind

text: An article on Monday about what’s on TV this week misstated the year that “Grease” was released. It was 1978, not 1987.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: Lots of Awards Shows and the Presidential Debate

text: An obituary on Saturday about Sergio Mendes, the Brazilian-born pianist, composer and arranger who brought bossa nova music to a global audience, misstated the title of an album released in 1962 by his band the Bossa Rio Sextet. It was “Você Ainda Não Ouviu Nada!” (“You Haven’t Heard Anything Yet!”), not “Você Ainda Não Iuviu Nada!”
match_headline: Sergio Mendes, 83, Dies; Brought Brazilian Rhythms to the Pop Charts

text: An article on Sunday about the growing community of Catholic priests in Indonesia misidentified the island of Flores. It is part of one of the poorest provinces in Indonesia, East Nusa Tenggara; it is not a province on its own. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: Once, Catholic Priests Came to Indonesia. Now, It Exports Them.

text: Because of an editing error, a photo with an article on Sept. 7 about new school buildings in New York City were published in error. The photo showed Intermediate School 429, not Motion Picture Technical High School.
match_headline: New Pencils, New Folders … and New Schools

text: An obituary on Monday about Jackie Winsor, the first female sculptor to be given a retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art, referred incorrectly to the political status of St. John’s, Newfoundland, in 1941, when Ms. Winsor was born there. The city was part of the British dominion of Newfoundland at the time; it was not the case that it was “a fishing capital of Canada.” Newfoundland became a Canadian province in 1949.
match_headline: Jackie Winsor, 82, Dies; Sculptor Who Hammered, Drilled and Chopped

text: An obituary on Sunday about Michael Lerner, the founder and editor of the magazine Tikkun, a leading voice for American Jews critical of Israel’s policies toward Palestinians, misstated the surname of his mother, Beatrice Lerner, before she married. It was Hirschman, not Hersh.
match_headline: Michael Lerner, 81, Is Dead; Founder of a Combative Jewish Magazine

text: An article on Monday about Donald J. Trump’s legal resources and political status gave an incorrect middle initial for a retired State Supreme Court justice. He is Michael J. Obus, not Michael D. Obus.
match_headline: After a Year of Legal Peril, Trump Seeks Election as a Felon, but Free

text: An article on Wednesday about cholera outbreaks around the world misstated the projected production of cholera vaccines by EuBiologics, a South Korean pharmaceutical company in 2025. EuBiologics is unlikely to be able to produce more than 70 million doses of the vaccine, not 50 million.
match_headline: Cholera Deaths Soar Worldwide Despite Being Easily Preventable

text: An article on Thursday about Nathan Clark, the father of an 11-year-old Ohio boy killed when an immigrant’s minivan crashed into a school bus, calling out Donald J. Trump and JD Vance for exploiting the incident to attack the immigrant community misquoted part of Mr. Clark’s remarks. He referred to false claims about the eating of “fluffy pets,” not “fluffy cats.”
match_headline: Grieving Ohio Father Tells Trump and Vance to Stop Talking About His Son

text: An article on Sept. 4 about the effect that climate change can have on bridges misstated the position held by Tim Gatz at the Oklahoma Department of Transportation. He is director of the agency, not deputy director.
match_headline: Climate Change Can Cause Bridges to ‘Fall Apart Like Tinkertoys,’ Experts Say

text: An article on Friday about President Biden’s consideration of approving Ukraine’s use of long-range Western weapons in Russia referred incorrectly to Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s visit on Friday. He is making an official visit to the White House, but it is not his first.
match_headline: Biden Poised to Approve Ukraine’s Use of Long-Range Western Weapons in Russia

text: An article on Thursday about Slovakia’s prime minister targeting his enemies after being shot misidentified the official who requested the release from prison of a corrupt prosecutor. It was Slovakia’s justice minister, not its interior minister.
match_headline: After Being Shot, Slovakia’s Leader Targets His Enemies

text: An article on Page 12 this weekend about four revival productions in Broadway’s new season misstates the subtitle of “Gypsy.” It is “A Musical Fable,” not “An American Fable.”
match_headline: Yesterday’s Broadway Warhorses, Saddled With Today’s Concerns

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about Ezra Edelman’s documentary on Prince incorrectly transcribes a word in the song “Let’s Go Crazy.” It is “Let’s get nuts,” not “Let’s go nuts.”
match_headline: The Prince We Never Knew

text: An article on Sept. 8 about the Shaker community at Sabbathday Lake misstated the location of the westernmost establishment of a Shaker community. It was Indiana, not Ohio.
match_headline: There Are Only Two Shakers Left. They’ve Still Got Utopia in Their Sights.

text: An obituary on Thursday about the former C.I.A. officer Edward Johnson misidentified the writer who collaborated with Mr. Johnson’s fellow officer Antonio J. Mendez on a 2007 magazine article that helped inspire the movie “Argo.” He is Joshuah Bearman, not Chris Terrio.
match_headline: Edward Johnson, C.I.A. Hero in Iran Hostage Crisis, Dies at 81

text: An article last Sunday about the wedding of Naina Rishiraj and Ryan Hawkins misstated the year that the bride’s uncle died. It was 2014, not 2015.
match_headline: From Hostel Bunk Mates to Life Partners

text: An article on Monday about drug cartels infiltrating Costa Rica’s rainforests misstated Costa Rica’s distinction as a Latin American country without a military. It is one of few countries in the region without a military, not the only one.
match_headline: How a Tourist Paradise Became a Drug-Trafficking Magnet

text: An article on Saturday about JD Vance’s proposal to end the war in Ukraine misidentified territory that Ukraine has occupied in its incursion into Russia. It has occupied part of the Kursk region, not the city of Kursk.
match_headline: Vance Describes Plan to End Ukraine War That Sounds a Lot Like Putin’s

text: An article on Saturday about Mormon voters in Arizona referred incorrectly to Heritage Academy schools. They are public charter schools, not private Christian schools.
match_headline: Trump Divides Arizona’s Crucial Mormon Vote

text: An article on Sunday about political differences between Gov. Tim Walz and his brother Jeff Walz referred imprecisely to the news outlet NewsNation. NewsNation is a cable news channel that describes itself as an independent outlet, not right-leaning.
match_headline: In Politically Divided America, Even the Walz Family Has Painful Rifts

text: An article on Monday about Donald J. Trump’s revisionist account of the Capitol attack misstated the name of a Jan. 6 legal defense group. It is the Patriot Freedom Project, not the Patriot Freedom Fund.
match_headline: Republicans Don’t Want to Talk About Jan. 6. Trump Can’t Help Himself.

text: An article on Sept. 11 about the selection of Lear deBessonet as Lincoln Center Theater’s next artistic director referred incorrectly to Lincoln Center Theater’s Claire Tow Theater. It is an Off Broadway space, not an Off Off Broadway theater.
match_headline: Lincoln Center Theater Chooses Lear deBessonet as Artistic Director

text: An obituary on Sunday about Sybil Haydel Morial, an activist who was also the matriarch of the most prominent civil rights family in New Orleans, misstated the year in which a police strike led to the cancellation of Mardi Gras in New Orleans. It was canceled in 1979, not 1978.
match_headline: Sybil Haydel Morial, New Orleans Civil Rights Matriarch, Dies at 91

text: An article on Tuesday about calls for the resignation of New York City Mayor Eric Adams misidentified State Senator Jessica Ramos. She is from Queens, not Brooklyn.
match_headline: Pressure Grows on Mayor Adams as Key Officials Leave Amid Investigations

text: An article on Tuesday about scientists being able to see exactly how a prey species escaped a predator’s stomach misstated which animal was anesthetized during scientific experiments. Juvenile eels were anesthetized, not dark sleeper fish.
match_headline: The Terrifying Way That Eels Escape a Hungry Fish’s Stomach

text: An article on Wednesday about an extremist group affiliated with Al Qaeda claiming responsibility for a deadly assault on two military sites in Mali’s capital, Bamako, misstated the date and circumstances of the last attack by extremist insurgents in Bamako. The attack was in 2016, on a hotel used by military instructors from the European Union, not in 2015 on the Radisson Blu hotel.
match_headline: An Al Qaeda Affiliate Claimed Attacks in Mali. What Does It Want?

text: An article on Tuesday about a newly approved gene therapy for the treatment of sickle cell disease, using information from a doctor, misstated a hospital’s progress in treating sickle cell patients. Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia has collected cells from patients, an early step in the gene therapy treatment. While it has not yet infused those treated cells in patients, it is not the case that the hospital has not yet started treating patients.
match_headline: First Day of a ‘New Life’ for a Boy With Sickle Cell

text: An article on Friday about the Federal Trade Commission’s findings on the collection and sharing of consumer’s data by some of the biggest online platforms misstated the date and the underlying complaints of the F.T.C.’s settlement with Epic Games. The settlement was reached in late 2022, not in January; and the agency had charged that Epic violated a child privacy law and deceived consumers with unwarranted charges, not just that it violated a child privacy law.
match_headline: F.T.C. Study Finds ‘Vast Surveillance’ of Social Media Users

text: A review on Friday about the film “A Different Man” misspelled the given name of the actress who plays Ingrid in the film. She is Renate Reinsve, not Renata.
match_headline: ‘A Different Man’ Review: Face, Off

text: An article on Sept. 1 about the charter city Próspera incorrectly described how council elections work there. While land ownership currently gives residents the right to vote for certain seats on Próspera’s council, residents do not need to own land in order to vote at all.
match_headline: The For-Profit City That Might Come Crashing Down

text: An article on Wednesday about the shifting business challenges and opportunities in China as its population ages misstated a figure about China’s population. In 2022, the number of people age 60 and older in China topped 290 million; 290 million is not the number of 60-year-olds in China.
match_headline: China’s ‘Silver Economy’ Is Thriving as Birthrate Plunges

text: An article on Saturday about the Netherlands returning hundreds of cultural artifacts to Indonesia misstated the time period in which the copper manuscripts donated to Leiden University are from. They are from the 9th to the 13th centuries, not the 17th century.
match_headline: The Netherlands Returns Hundreds of Cultural Artifacts to Indonesia

text: An article on Monday about the political landscape in Montana misstated the year in which voters in the state rejected a Republican-sponsored abortion measure in a referendum. It was 2022, not last year.
match_headline: A Changed Montana May Decide Control of the U.S. Senate

text: An article on Sunday about California legislation aimed at protecting minors from social media addiction misstated the date that the law becomes effective. The law goes into effect on Jan. 1, 2025, not in 2027. (Some companies have until 2027 to make adjustments.)
match_headline: Newsom Signs Bill That Adds Protections for Children on Social Media

text: An article on Monday about the actor Kelsey Grammer misstated the living arrangements of his character on the sitcom “Frasier.” Frasier Crane lived in Seattle with his father, not with his father and brother.
match_headline: Kelsey Grammer Analyzes 40 Years of Frasier: ‘I Have Nothing to Regret’

text: An obituary on Monday about Daniel J. Evans, a former governor of Washington State and U.S. senator, misstated the office he held in 1973 when he rappelled down the face of a clock tower on the campus of Evergreen State College in Washington State. He was governor at the time, not president of the college. (He became its president in 1977, after leaving the governorship.)
match_headline: Daniel J. Evans, 98, Washington State Governor Who Went to Senate, Dies

text: An obituary on Monday about Mercury Morris, the two-time Super Bowl champion for the Miami Dolphins, referred incorrectly to the Dolphins’ victory over the Washington Redskins in the Super Bowl in 1973. It was a special teams squad that gave up a lone touchdown to Washington, on a blocked field goal attempt by Miami. It was not the case that Miami’s defense held Washington to a single touchdown.
match_headline: Mercury Morris, Elusive Rusher on a Perfect Dolphins Team, Dies at 77

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the Fête de l’Humanité, an annual French Communism celebration, misstated its inaugural year. As the article correctly stated, it was 1930, not 1945. In addition, because of an editing error, the approximate age of the event was misstated in the article. It is almost 100 years old, not almost 80 years old.
match_headline: A French Fair as Workers’ Paradise, Feting Cuisine, Music and Communism

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Friday about the artist Derek Boshier misstated the surname of his first wife. She is Patricia González, not Gonzáles.
match_headline: Derek Boshier, British Pop Artist and Bowie Collaborator, Dies at 87

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the actress Kathryn Crosby misstated where she married the singer and actor Bing Crosby. It was in a church in Las Vegas, not a courthouse.
match_headline: Kathryn Crosby, Actress and Bing Crosby’s Widow, Dies at 90

text: An obituary on Feb. 19 about the philanthropist Pierre Toussaint, misstated the given name of the author of “Knights of the Razor: Black Barbers in Slavery and Freedom.” He is Douglas W. Bristol Jr., not Daniel. This correction was delayed because editors were only recently made aware of the error.
ref_headline: Knights of the Razor: Black Barbers in Slavery and Freedom.
match_headline: Overlooked No More: Pierre Toussaint, Philanthropist and Candidate for Sainthood

text: An article on Wednesday about the graft case against S. Iswaran, Singapore’s former transport minister, misstated the prosecution’s action in the case. The prosecution amended charges against Mr. Iswaran; it did not drop them.
match_headline: In Rare Graft Case in Singapore, Former Minister Pleads Guilty

text: An article on Thursday about Dan Newlin, a personal injury attorney in Florida and a friend of Donald J. Trump who has spent millions on billboards and TV spots in support of Mr. Trump, misstated the county where Mark Lamb is the sheriff. It is Pinal County, Ariz., not Pima County.
match_headline: Meet the G.O.P. Personal Injury Lawyer Buying His Own Trump Ads

text: An article on Thursday about the resignation of the president of Brandeis University misidentified the group that issued a vote of no confidence. It was the faculty, not the faculty Senate.
match_headline: Brandeis President Steps Down Amid Budget Issues and Protests

text: A picture caption with an article on Thursday about the speech Vice President Kamala Harris gave in Pittsburgh misidentified the location where Ms. Harris gave her speech. While the event was hosted by the Economic Club of Pittsburgh, Ms. Harris delivered her remarks at Carnegie Mellon University, not at the club.
match_headline: Harris Casts Herself as a Pro-Business Pragmatist in a Broad Economic Pitch

text: An article this weekend on Page 10 about the multilingual singer-songwriter Lhasa de Sela, who will be honored with memorial concerts at Pop Montreal, misstates the title of a Lhasa song. It is “Soon This Space Will Be Too Small,” not “Soon This Place Will Be Too Small.”
ref_headline: Soon This Space Will Be Too Small,
match_headline: Lhasa’s Music Captivated Audiences Everywhere but Here

text: An article on Saturday about Kamala Harris’s presidential campaign and her advisers belief that she can sway voters on the economy, misstated when David Plouffe served as former President Barack Obama’s campaign manager. He served in that position in 2008, not in 2012, when he was a senior adviser to Mr. Obama.
match_headline: Kamala Harris’s Campaign Thinks She Can Win on the Economy. Here’s How.

text: An obituary on Saturday about journalist Neil King Jr. misstated the number of years Mr. King worked as a reporter and editor for The Wall Street Journal. It was 23, not 17.
match_headline: Neil King Jr., Who Wrote of a Long Walk of ‘Renewal,’ Dies at 65

text: An article on Monday about California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoing an artificial intelligence safety bill misstated the title of Patrick Hall. He is an assistant professor of decision sciences at George Washington University, not an assistant professor of information systems at Georgetown University.
match_headline: California Governor Vetoes Sweeping A.I. Legislation

text: An article on Tuesday about new technologies that could help utilities better plan for the risk of extreme weather referred imprecisely to the development of ChatGPT. Microsoft is an investor in ChatGPT and uses it in its products, but it did not develop it, Open AI did.
match_headline: Extreme Weather Is Taxing Utilities More Often. Can A.I. Help?

text: An article on Monday about the heirs of a Dutch museum director who donated a trove of Rembrandt paintings to the Mauritshuis museum wanting them returned to the family misstated when the forger Han Van Meegeren’s trial took place. He was convicted in 1947, not long after Abraham Bredius’s death. (Bredius died in 1946.)
match_headline: A Museum Director’s Heirs Lay Claim to His Rembrandts
