text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Sept. 27 about four Off Broadway shows that tackle political issues in imaginative ways misidentified an event in “Medea.” It was filicide, not matricide.
match_headline: The Stage Combat Is Verbal in These Off Broadway Plays

text: An article on Thursday about new evidence disclosed in a court filing made public about Donald Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election results, misstated the former position of Ronna McDaniel. She served as the chairwoman of the Republican National Committee, not the Republican National Convention.
match_headline: Judge Unseals New Evidence in Federal Election Case Against Trump

text: An article on Monday about the waning ability of the United States to influence events in the Mideast, referred incompletely to the funding from Qatar to the Hamas government in the Gaza Strip. Qatar has denied it supports Hamas. However, Israeli intelligence officials believe its funding of the government allowed Hamas to divert some of its own budget toward military operations.
match_headline: Why the World’s Biggest Powers Can’t Stop a Middle East War

text: An article on Sept. 29 about the death of the Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah referred incompletely to the circumstances that led to military exchanges between Israel and Hezbollah starting last October. Hezbollah began firing on Israeli positions in solidarity with Hamas after the Oct. 7 Hamas-led attack on Israel that ignited the war in Gaza.
match_headline: Hassan Nasrallah, Who Led Hezbollah for Decades, Killed at 64

text: An article on Sunday about the ongoing tensions in the Middle East misstated the name of the Hamas political leader who was assassinated in Tehran. He was Ismail Haniyeh, not Islam.
match_headline: Israel Steps Up Attacks in Lebanon as Fighting Spreads

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the number of collisions between vehicles and moose in Newfoundland misstated the surname of the taxidermist in Glenwood. He is Harold Pelley, not Pelle.
match_headline: A Menace to Motorists, but the ‘Noble’ Moose Is Adopted by Newfoundland

text: An article on Monday about how climate change is drying up stretches of the Amazon River misidentified the amount by which average temperatures have risen since the 1980s. It is by 2 degrees, not 2 percent.
match_headline: A Changing Climate Is Scorching the World’s Biggest River

text: An article on Sept. 28 about a ruling that puts in question whether the death penalty could be possible in a trial of Khalid Shaikh Mohammed misstated the maximum prison sentence that a military jury could impose on the defendant under a now-disputed plea agreement that was signed on July 31. The upper end of the range is 3,424 years, not more than 4,000 years.
match_headline: Death Penalty May Be Off Table for 9/11 Suspect No Matter How Case Unfolds

text: An article on Friday about a new court filing by the special counsel Jack Smith misstated an element of the relationship between Eric Herschmann, a White House lawyer during the Trump administration, and Jared Kushner, former President Donald J. Trump’s son-in-law. Mr. Herschmann had known Mr. Kushner since Mr. Kushner was a child. The two were not childhood friends.
match_headline: Filing in Trump Election Case Fleshes Out Roles of a Sprawling Cast

text: An article on Tuesday about the recipients of this year’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine misstated the number of cells in C. Elegans. It is less than 1,000, not less than 100.
match_headline: Discovery in Tiny Worm Leads to Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for 2 Scientists

text: An article on Wednesday about a new proposal for home health care that Kamala Harris outlined on “The View” misspelled, in on reference, the surname of a health policy professor at Harvard who studies long-term care. He is David Grabowski, not Grabowksi.
match_headline: Harris Proposes Medicare Benefits for Home Care, Vision and Hearing

text: An article on Tuesday about the launch of a $100,000 ad campaign on porn sites warning that Project 2025 wants to ban pornography and imprison people who produce it, misstated Holly Randall’s profession. She is a producer and photographer in the pornography industry, not a film actor.
match_headline: Porn Industry Jumps Into the Presidential Campaign, Targeting Project 2025

text: An obituary on Oct. 2 about the baseball star Pete Rose misstated the given name of one of his daughters. She is Morgan Erin Rubio, not Megan.
match_headline: Pete Rose Never Changed, but Baseball Did

text: An article on Thursday about the halt in the George J. Mitchell scholarship program because of funding difficulties misspelled the surname of a former speaker of the House. He was Tip O’Neill, not O’Neil.
match_headline: Prestigious U.S.-Ireland Scholarship Paused Amid Funding Woes

text: An article on Thursday about the restoration of funding for student activities at the University of Michigan after they were paused by student leaders who were pressuring university officials to divest from companies aiding Israel’s war in Gaza, misstated when the words “intifada” and “coward” were painted on the university president’s house. It was Monday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: At Michigan, Pro-Palestinian Activists Lose, and Money for Student Clubs Is Restored

text: An article on Thursday about the nonprofit Seattle Jazz Fellowship performing at a venue in Seattle where it pays utilities and insurance, misspelled the given name of a landscape architect. She is Ilze Jones, not Ilse.
match_headline: Jazz Has a New Home in Seattle. One Caveat: The Place Is ‘For Lease.’

text: An article on Page 44 this weekend about the writer Michel Houellebecq transcribes incorrectly a line from his novel “The Map and the Territory.” The line is “Le triomphe de la végétation est total,” not “Le triomphe de la végétation est totale.”
match_headline: Why France’s Most Controversial Novelist Is Also Its Most Celebrated

text: An article last Sunday about the growth of the “SmartLess” podcast misspelled the surname of the CAA executive who helped expand the podcast’s brand. He is Josh Lindgen, not Lingen.
match_headline: Will the ‘SmartLess’ Podcast Be the Biggest Role of Their Careers?

text: An article on Sept. 22 about the former Apple designer Jony Ive misidentified the end product that Mr. Ive’s team at LoveFrom had helped develop for Airbnb. Their work on “travel postcards” led to the development of Airbnb’s digital postcards; the “travel postcards” concept did not lead to Airbnb’s Icons experiences.
match_headline: After Apple, Jony Ive Is Building an Empire of His Own

text: An article on Monday about mail ballot regulations described incorrectly Pennsylvania procedures for detecting whether mailed-in ballots are properly enclosed in privacy sleeves. Election officials can check for the sleeves using pre-punched holes in ballot envelopes before Election Day; they do not have to wait until they open the envelopes on Election Day.
match_headline: Voting Wars Open a New Front: Which Mail Ballots Should Count?

text: An article on Monday about flyover advertisements at N.F.L. games misidentified the organization paying for the ads. They were paid for by the Democratic National Committee, not the Harris campaign. The error was repeated in a headline.
match_headline: Democrats to Fly Harris Ads Over N.F.L. Games in Swing States

text: An article on Sunday about the death of Viktoria Roshchina, a Ukrainian journalist who had been detained by Russian authorities after reporting from occupied territories in Ukraine, misstated the name of the organization that awarded Ms. Roshchina a “Courage in Journalism” award. It is the International Women’s Media Foundation, not the International Women’s Media Fund.
match_headline: Ukrainian Journalist Has Died in Russian Captivity, Ukraine Says

text: An article on Tuesday about battleground states having at least one third-party or independent candidate on the presidential ballot, misstated the list of states where Cornel West appears on the ballot. He is not on the Pennsylvania ballot. The article also misstated the results of the presidential race in Florida in 2000. Ralph Nader received 97,488 votes, not 97,421; Al Gore lost by a margin of 537, not 531.
match_headline: In a Tight Presidential Race, Third-Party Candidates Present a Wild Card

text: An article on Tuesday about Representative Marc Molinaro’s bid for re-election referred incorrectly to the methodology that the Lugar Center uses to assess bipartisanship. It is based on bill sponsorship, not votes.
match_headline: In Heated House Race, a Moderate Republican Goes Full Trump

text: An article on Sunday about the retirement of Joe Holtz, who helped start the Park Slope Food Co-op, misstated the role of Andy Feldman, a longtime member of the co-op. He was on the Disciplinary Committee but no longer is.
match_headline: 50 Years of Broccoli (and Mockery): A Co-op Co-Founder Calls It Quits

text: An article on Monday about an office building in Reykjavik, Iceland, that is the virtual home to an array of perpetrators of identity theft, ransomware and disinformation misstated Mordur Ingolfson’s role in enacting some of Iceland’s first internet privacy laws. He was a member of the Pirate Party, which supported the legislation. He is not a former member of Parliament.
match_headline: Some of the Web’s Sketchiest Sites Share an Address in Iceland

text: An obituary on Friday about Ethel Kennedy, the widow of Senator Robert F. Kennedy, misstated the current location of the Convent of the Sacred Heart boarding school, which was in the Bronx when she was a student there. It is now in Greenwich, Conn., not Manhattan.
match_headline: Ethel Kennedy, Passionate Supporter of the Family Legacy, Dies at 96

text: An article on Wednesday about the impact that abortion rights could have in elections that could decide control of state supreme courts contained several errors. It misstated the partisan balance of the Michigan Supreme Court. It is 4 to 3 in favor of Democrats, not 5 to 4. It misstated the status of one race. The chief justice’s seat in Michigan is not up for election. These errors were repeated in a picture caption. The article also misstated the number of states in which Planned Parenthood is running ads for State Supreme Court elections. It is six, not four.
match_headline: Abortion Could Decide Control of State Supreme Courts

text: An article on Oct. 9 about Comet Tsuchinshan-ATLAS misstated the year in which Comet NEOWISE was visible. It was 2020, not 2021.
match_headline: How to See the ‘Once-in-a-Lifetime’ Comet Flaring in Our Night Skies

text: An article on Tuesday about nationalizing the water industry in England and Wales amid sewage spills and rising household bills, using an erroneous figure from the Water Services Regulation Authority, misstated the amount that water companies have invested in the water and sewage system since privatization. They have invested more than £230 billion, with about £100 billion contributed by debt and equity investors, not £130 billion.
match_headline: Amid a Water Crisis, England Asks: Who Should Be in Charge?

text: An obituary on Monday about the writer and architectural historian David Garrard Lowe misstated the given name of a preservationist who said Mr. Lowe’s book “Lost Chicago” “inspired legions, generations of preservationists.” She is Anna Weaver, not Ann.
match_headline: David Garrard Lowe, Defender of Historic Architecture, Dies at 91

text: An obituary on Sunday about the television reporter Warren Wilson referred incorrectly to Warren Cereghino, who said that Mr. Wilson “had brought great acclaim to our news operation.” He is a former news director at the Los Angeles TV station KTLA, not a former editor.
ref_headline: had brought great acclaim to our news operation.
match_headline: Warren Wilson, Pioneering Los Angeles TV Reporter, Dies at 90

text: An article on Wednesday about pandas arriving at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in Washington misstated how long it had been since pandas were at the National Zoo. The zoo had no pandas for about a year following the death of the bear Hsing-Hsing in 1999; November 2023 did not mark the first time in more than 50 years the zoo had no pandas.
match_headline: Giant Pandas From China Return to National Zoo in Washington, D.C.

text: An article on Thursday about a top chess player’s disqualification from an event in Spain misstated the name of the computer that defeated Garry Kasparov in 1997. It was Deep Blue, not Big Blue. The article also misstated the results of one of the chess games played by Kirill Shevchenko during a tournament in Spain. He played to a draw in one round and won a game in the second round; he did not tie the two rounds.
match_headline: A Top Chess Player Is Disqualified After a Phone Is Found in a Bathroom Stall

text: An article on Thursday about a proposal by President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine to end the war by next year misattributed a research finding about Ukrainian public support for negotiations with Russia. It is from polling by the National Democratic Institute, a Washington-based nonprofit group, not by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology.
match_headline: Zelensky Pitches His ‘Victory Plan’ to Ukrainian Lawmakers

text: An article on Tuesday about the rise in immune suppression among Americans misstated the age of Kaley Karaffa. She is 37, not 38.
match_headline: What Does It Mean to Be Immunocompromised?

text: An obituary on Thursday about the singer Liam Payne referred incorrectly to a song he sang at an audition for the television show “The X Factor.” It was the standard “Cry Me a River,” originally recorded by Julie London — not the Justin Timberlake song of the same name.
match_headline: Liam Payne, 31, Former One Direction Singer, Dies in Fall in Argentina

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about literary re-enactments by the Vancouver photographer Stan Douglas misspelled a reference to German history. It is Weimar Germany, not Weimer.
match_headline: Sick of the 21st Century? These Artists Revive the 18th.

text: An article on Page 12 this weekend about Randy Newman misstates the number of Grammy Awards he has won in competitive categories. It is seven, not six.
match_headline: Randy Newman Is at His Best When America Is at Its Worst

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about the University of Michigan’s D.E.I. program describes incorrectly why The Times did not interview the program’s former leader, Robert M. Sellers. The university declined to make him available. It is not the case that he declined to The Times to be interviewed. In addition, the article refers incorrectly to the number of states that have banned or limited D.E.I. programs at public universities. There are 12 such states, not more than 12.
match_headline: The University of Michigan Doubled Down on D.E.I. What Went Wrong?

text: An obituary on Sunday about the composer and conductor Leif Segerstam misspelled his mother’s surname. She was Viola Maria Kronqvist, not Kronquvist.
match_headline: Leif Segerstam, Who Wrote 371 Symphonies, Is Dead at 80

text: An article on Tuesday about defining the Midwest misstated where the Black Midwest Initiative began. It was at the University of Minnesota, not the University of Illinois Chicago.
match_headline: 200 Years Later, Still Trying to Define the Midwest

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about Representative Ruben Gallego’s vow to visit all 22 of Arizona’s federally recognized tribes as he campaigns for a Senate seat, misidentified the state in which the Supai village is located. As the article correctly noted, it is Arizona not Nevada.
match_headline: For Ruben Gallego, the Campaign Trail Runs Through the Grand Canyon

text: A picture with an article on Monday about former President Donald J. Trump claiming without evidence that Vice President Kamala Harris never held a job at McDonald’s was published in error. While the image showed a McDonald’s in Alameda, Calif., it was not the location where Ms. Harris had worked while she was in college.
match_headline: Kamala Harris and McDonald’s: A College Job, and a Trump Attack

text: An article on Wednesday about a posthumously released jazz album from the trumpeter Roy Hargrove misstated the name of another Hargrove album. It is “The Love Suite: In Mahogany,” not “The Love Suite: Mahogany.”
match_headline: A New Roy Hargrove LP Reminds Us What the Trumpeter Left Behind

text: An article on Monday about what’s on television this week misstated Katie Griggs’s relationship to the yogi Siri Singh Sahib, as covered in the documentary “Breath of Fire.” Griggs was also a yoga instructor but was not Sahib’s mentee.
match_headline: What’s on TV This Week: ‘Seth Meyers: Dad Man Walking’ and Spooky Movies

text: An article on Sunday about the presidential election and Pennsylvania misstated the location of a Bethlehem Steel plant. It was in Bethlehem, Pa., not Easton.
match_headline: I Grew Up in Bucks County, Pa. I Went Back to Try to Make Sense of the Election.

text: An article on Friday about Southwest Airlines appointing six new directors to its board misstated the surname of the retiring chairman of the airline. He is Gary Kelly, not Johnson.
match_headline: Southwest Strikes a Truce With the Activist Hedge Fund Elliott

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the comedian Seth Meyers misspelled the name of one of Meyers’s children. It is Ashe, not Ash.
match_headline: Seth Meyers Isn’t as Nice as You Think He Is

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about Armando Iannucci’s adaptation of “Dr. Strangelove” for the West End, misidentified the television network that initially commissioned a U.S. version of “The Thick of It.” It was ABC, not CBS.
match_headline: A Reluctant Satirist Takes On the Bomb

text: An article on Page 36 this weekend about a retrospective of Maurice Sendak’s work at the Denver Art Museum misstated the year Maurice Sendak began writing “Higglety-Pigglety Pop! Or There Must Be More to Life.” It was 1966, not 1964.
ref_headline: Higglety-Pigglety Pop! Or There Must Be More to Life.
match_headline: Where the Wild Things — and the Other Worlds of Maurice Sendak — Are

text: An article on Page 14 this weekend about the American Academy of Arts and Letters being transformed into a venue for visual and performing artists and events, misstated the first name of the chief curator and program director, art awards, at the American Academy of Arts and Letters. She is Jenny Jasky, not Jennifer.
match_headline: An Old Space Opens Up to New Art

text: An article on Page 16 this weekend about Mural Arts Philadelphia celebrating its 40th anniversary, misidentified an artist in a photo caption. He is Tysean Moore, not Ernel Martinez.
match_headline: A City of Murals, Decades in the Making

text: An article on Page 6 this weekend about the artist Chase Hall misspelled the surname of an artist. His name is Mike Kelley, not Kelly.
match_headline: Chase Hall Wrestles With ‘Hybridity’

text: An article on Page 45 this weekend about exhibitions to see this fall includes a photograph that was published in error. A painting for sale at Christie’s auction house is “L’Empire des Lumières” (1954) by René Magritte, not a painting of the same name by the artist from 1951.
match_headline: Art to See at U.S. Museums, Galleries and Auction Houses This Fall

text: An article on Page 26 this weekend about Varsity Spirit, which dominates American cheerleading, includes several statements that were clarified before the article was published online. The article refers imprecisely to financing secured by Varsity. Charlesbank Capital helped Varsity secure a $125 million loan facility, not a loan. The article also misstates a question asked of Jeff Webb,Varsity’s founder. The author asked Webb if he was the “father of cheer,” or an “entrepreneur,” not if Webb was an “entrepreneur whose obsession with growth had delivered the sport into the hands of private equity.” It also misstates the name of the entity that commented on a class-action suit settlement by Varsity for $43.5 million. It was S&P Global, not S&P 500. The article was updated to include the source of the assertion that Varsity discontinued some JAM Brands competitions in order to push teams toward higher-priced Varsity events, an assertion the company disputes. It was a claim made in an expert report prepared for a class-action lawsuit. And the article was also updated to clarify that Varsity opposed recognizing cheer as a sport in the early decades of the company’s existence.
match_headline: How Cheerleading Became So Acrobatic, Dangerous and Popular

text: An obituary on Friday about the career diplomat Tina S. Kaidanow misstated the name of a State Department bureau that she ran for a time. It is the political-military affairs bureau, not the political affairs bureau.
match_headline: Tina S. Kaidanow, 59, Diplomatic Force in Kosovo and Guantánamo, Dies

text: An article on Oct. 13 about “Discoshow,” a new interactive theatrical and dance experience in Las Vegas, misidentified Steven Hoggett as both the director and choreographer. He is the director, not the choreographer. Yasmine Lee choreographed the production.
match_headline: A Choreographer’s Errands Into the Wilderness

text: An article on Oct. 13 about Detroit’s economic recovery misstated the surname of a real estate agent. He is Austin Black II, not Baker.
match_headline: Led by Believers in the City’s Future, Detroit Is on the Rebound

text: A news analysis article on Sunday about the route Iran could go following the Israeli strikes on Saturday, overstated what is known about the current health of Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. He was said to have been seriously ill in 2022; there have been no recent reports about his health.
match_headline: In Deciding Whether to Retaliate, Iran Faces a Dilemma

text: An article on Sunday about the N.F.L. matchups for the day misstated the odds in the game between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Las Vegas Raiders. Kansas City was a 10-point favorite, not underdog. (Kansas City defeated Las Vegas, 27-20.)
match_headline: Bryan Ferry Enjoys the Kansas City Chiefs’ ‘Outfits’

text: An obituary on Oct. 6 about Joel Fleishman, a prominent expert on philanthropy, misspelled his middle name. It was Lawrence, not Laurence.
match_headline: Joel Fleishman, Influential Expert on Philanthropy, Dies at 90

text: An article on Sunday about a call for women to be given more leadership roles in the Catholic Church misstated the given name of a female bishop whose ordination is not recognized by the Vatican. She is the Rev. Bridget Mary Meehan, not Mary Bridget. The article also misstated the organization that Pat Brown belongs to. It is the Catholic Women’s Ordination, not the Women’s Ordination Conference.
match_headline: Vatican Punts Question of Female Deacons at Major Meeting

text: An article on Sunday about radio host Alison Stewart misidentified the company that produces the software program that precisely maps a patient’s brain networks before surgery. The company is Omniscient, not Quicktome. The software program itself is called Quicktome.
match_headline: Her Job Was Talking on the Radio. Then Suddenly, Words Wouldn’t Come.

text: An article on Saturday about an upcoming Christie’s auction for one of the paintings recovered by the Monuments Men, a special U.S. Army unit that tracked down millions of works of art stolen by the Germans during World War II, misstated the year in which Paris was liberated. It was 1944, not 1945.
match_headline: For Sale: A Painting the Monuments Men Rescued From the Nazis

text: An obituary on Sunday about the Nobel-winning physicist Leon N. Cooper incorrectly characterized electrons. They are particles that orbit the nuclei of atoms; they do not circulate inside them. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Sheldon Cooper, a character on the television show “The Big Bang Theory” who was said to have been named in part after Dr. Cooper. Like other characters on the show, Sheldon Cooper was a member of the faculty at the California Institute of Technology, not a graduate student there.
match_headline: Leon Cooper Dies at 94; Nobelist Unlocked Secrets of Superconductivity

text: An article on Sunday about political events held at Madison Square Garden misidentified the given name of a Jewish man at a 1939 Nazi rally. He was Isadore Greenbaum, not Isidore.
match_headline: Presidents, Conventions and Nazis: A Political History of ‘The Garden’

text: An article on Oct. 22 about the actor Mark Proksch misstated his age. He is 49, not 46.
match_headline: Mark Proksch, of ‘What We Do in the Shadows,’ Gets Into the Swing of It

text: An obituary on Sunday about Phil Lesh, the longtime bassist of the Grateful Dead, referred incorrectly to hepatitis C, which he contracted at one point. It is a viral infection; it is not caused by alcohol abuse.
match_headline: Phil Lesh, Bassist Who Anchored the Grateful Dead, Dies at 84

text: An article on Thursday about the Tony Award winner Brandon Uranowitz misspelled the name of a play. It is “Leopoldstadt,” not “Leopoldstat.
match_headline: ‘Ragtime’ Crushed Brandon Uranowitz’s Dream. Now It’s Healing His Wounds.

text: An article on Thursday about the 20th anniversary of the release of the horror film “Saw” misstated Stacey Testro’s working relationship with the writers of the movie. Testro was James Wan’s manager, not Leigh Whannell’s manager. (She was Whannell’s agent.)
match_headline: 20 Years of Impossible Choices in ‘Saw’

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about the American Ballet Theater’s production of “Crime and Punishment” erroneously included a dancer in “In the Upper Room.” SunMi Park did not perform in that dance.
match_headline: A ‘Crime and Punishment’ Ballet? It’s Not as ‘Ludicrous’ as It Seems.

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about a movement to challenge election results refers imprecisely, in one instance, to Georgia election officials. Certification of election results is done by board members or other superintendents, not commissioners.
match_headline: The Army of Election Officials Ready to Reject the Vote

text: An article on Oct. 13 about Netflix referred incorrectly to the initialization SVOD. It is subscription video on demand, not streaming video on demand.
match_headline: How Everyone Got Lost in Netflix’s Endless Library

text: An obituary on Oct. 26 about the psychologist Philip Zimbardo misstated the original surname of his first wife. She was Rose Abdelnour, not Abelnour.
match_headline: Philip Zimbardo, 91, Whose Stanford Prison Experiment Studied Evil, Dies

text: An article on Oct. 20 about Hugh Grant misstated the profession of Tinglan Hong, the mother of two of Grant’s children. She is not an actress.
match_headline: Is Hugh Grant’s Most Convincing Character ‘Hugh Grant’?

text: A review last Sunday about “The Forbidden Garden,” by Simon Parkin, misspelled the surname of a 20th-century Russian botanist. He was Nikolai Vavilov, not Vasilov. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: The Scientists Who Hoarded Seeds Even as They Were Starving

text: An article on Oct. 27 about measures that museums, galleries and other art institutions are making to reduce their environmental footprint misstated the year when the Gallery Climate Coalition introduced its carbon calculator. It was in 2020, at the time the group was founded; it was not introduced recently.
match_headline: The Art World Explores Concrete Ways to Fight Climate Change

text: An article on Oct. 27 about a social trends exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art misstated the name of a museum. It is the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, not Modern Art.
match_headline: Connecting Sports and Art in an Eclectic Mix

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Oct. 27 about a duck exhibition at the Bruce Museum misspelled the name of a duck breed. It is eider, not elder.
match_headline: Ducks Do More Than You Might Think to Help Save the Planet

text: An article on Saturday about the first day of Daniel Penny’s trial in the May 2023 killing of Jordan Neely misidentified the county on Long Island where Mr. Penny grew up. It is Suffolk County, not Nassau.
match_headline: In Subway Chokehold Trial, Lawyers Spar Over Daniel Penny’s Chokehold

text: An article on Saturday about the Botswana Democratic Party misstated the age of Tumelo Eetsi, a teacher living in Gaborone, the capital of Botswana. He is 33, not 43.
match_headline: Botswana Voters Hand Governing Party a Stunning Rebuke

text: An article on Sunday about closely contested seats in the New York State Legislature misstated the number of New York State Assembly seats Democrats won in 2022. It was 102, not 101.
match_headline: The G.O.P. Gained Ground in New York in 2022. Can Democrats Recover?

text: An article on Tuesday about the scene in Spain following last week’s flash floods misidentified the provinces where alerts for heavy rain were issued on Monday. They were Castellón, Tarragona and Barcelona, not Castellón, Tarragona and Catalonia.
match_headline: An Angry Spain, Still Reeling From Floods, Faces More Rain

text: An article on Monday about schools forfeiting games against San Jose State University because of reports that a transgender player is a member of the women’s volleyball team misquoted a statement from the women’s volleyball team at the University of Nevada, Reno. It said, “We refuse to participate in any match that advances injustice against female athletes.” It did not say “student athletes.”
ref_headline: We refuse to participate in any match that advances injustice against female athletes.
match_headline: San Jose State Women’s Volleyball Team Finds Itself at Center of Transgender Debate

text: An article on Tuesday about the discovery of a 13 million-year-old terror bird fossil in Colombia misidentified a tibiotarsus. It is a middle leg bone, not an upper leg bone.
match_headline: Where There’s Joy in a Terror Bird

text: An obituary on Oct. 24 about Fernando Valenzuela, a star pitcher for the Los Angeles Dodgers in the 1980s, misstated his date of birth. It was Nov. 1, 1960, not Nov. 11.
match_headline: Fernando Valenzuela, Pitcher Whose Screwballs Eluded Batters, Dies at 63

text: An article on Wednesday about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu firing his defense minister, Yoav Gallant, translated incorrectly a comment from Mr. Gallant. He said, “This is no longer a social issue alone, it is a paramount issue for our existence and future,” not “for our security and existence.”
ref_headline: This is no longer a social issue alone, it is a paramount issue for our existence and future,
match_headline: Israel’s Netanyahu Fires Defense Minister, Citing ‘Gaps’ in Approach to War

text: An article on Nov. 1 about the 36th edition of The Art Show at the Park Avenue Armory misstated the year of the artist Adaline Kent’s death. It was in 1957, not 1975.
match_headline: Something for Everyone at The Art Show

text: An article on Nov. 2 about a new Luther Vandross documentary misidentified the writer of “A House Is Not a Home.” It was Burt Bacharach and Hal David, not Dionne Warwick.
ref_headline: A House Is Not a Home.
match_headline: Luther Vandross and the Sound That Could Fill Hearts, or Break Them

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Tuesday about the composer, arranger and record producer Quincy Jones referred incorrectly to a Miles Davis concert he produced at the Montreux Jazz Festival in 1991. That concert featured arrangements that Gil Evans had written for the Miles Davis albums “Sketches of Spain” and “Porgy and Bess”; it did not “reunite” Miles Davis with Gil Evans, who died in 1988. The obituary also misstated the year Mr. Jones’s daughter Jolie was born. It was 1953, not 1952.
match_headline: Quincy Jones, Giant of American Music, Dies at 91

text: An article on Page 2 this weekend misstates the title of a song by the band Lankum. It is “Go Dig My Grave” not “I Dig My Grave.”

An article on Page 10 this weekend about the stars of the upcoming film “Wicked” misstates how often a Black actress, Alexia Khadime, played the part of Elphaba in the West End production of “Wicked.” She was brought back for a second run in the show; she didn’t play the role only once.
match_headline: A ‘Wicked’ Tearful Talk With Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande

text: An obituary on Friday about the architectural historian Joseph Rykwert misstated the date of his death. He died on Oct. 17, not Oct. 7.
match_headline: Joseph Rykwert, 98, Dies; Historian of Architecture Challenged Modernism

text: An article on Page 2 this weekend misstates the title of a song by the band Lankum. It is “Go Dig My Grave” not “I Dig My Grave.”

A picture caption with an article on Oct. 20 about a new production of the musical “American Idiot” described incorrectly the people alongside singing cast members. They are actors who are signing, not American Sign Language interpreters.
match_headline: Toni Vaz, Stuntwoman and Founder of N.A.A.C.P. Image Awards, Dies at 101

text: An article last Sunday about The Daily Beast misstated the definition of a knacker’s yard. It is a British term for a slaughterhouse, not a junkyard. The article also misstated the timing of the weekend that Emma Tucker, the editor of The Wall Street Journal, was at the Hamptons home of Joanna Coles and helped her plan coverage of a breaking news event. It was the weekend of the assassination attempt on Donald J. Trump in Butler, Pa., not the following weekend, when President Biden announced he would not run for re-election.
match_headline: The Daily Beast Tries to Claw Its Way Back to Relevance

text: Because of an editing error, an article last Sunday about Stellene Volandes, the editor in chief of Town & Country, misstated the timing of her appointment at the magazine in 2016. She did not replace Jay Fielden. Mr. Fielden remained as editorial director of Town & Country until he left Hearst Magazines in 2019.
match_headline: How a 178-Year-Old Magazine Stays Relevant, One Instagram Post at a Time

text: An article on Nov. 3 about incitement to terrorism laws in Israel misidentified Walid Dakka. He was affiliated with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, not with Hamas.
match_headline: How Four Posts on Instagram Destroyed Her Life

text: An article on Monday about the firing of Haiti’s prime minister, using information provided by the United Nations, misstated the number of people killed in Haiti between January and September. It was 3,900, not 4,900.
match_headline: Haitian Prime Minister Is Fired, Adding to the Nation’s Turmoil

text: An article on Monday about the country music star Dwight Yoakam misstated a song title. It is “I Don’t Know How to Say Goodbye (Bang Bang Boom Boom),” not “I Don’t Know How to Say Goodbye (Band Bang, Boom Boom).”
ref_headline: I Don’t Know How to Say Goodbye (Bang Bang Boom Boom),
match_headline: Dwight Yoakam, Country Rebel, Has a New Attitude

text: An article on Tuesday about seed oils misstated how soybean oil is made. It is made from the soybean, which is considered both a bean and a seed — not just a bean. The article also referred incorrectly to the “hateful eight” seed oils. They are all technically derived from seeds.
match_headline: Are Seed Oils Actually Bad for You?

text: An article on Oct. 24 about the impact of a drug trial on volunteers who were vulnerable to brain injuries included a description of a data analysis by a group of leading researchers, newly posted online, which suggested that patients taking Leqembi and an earlier drug, Aduhelm, had a higher mortality rate than untreated patients of a similar age in the United States. The Times removed references to the analysis after it was withdrawn amid objections from several of its authors that it had been posted prematurely, given the limitations of the data.
match_headline: What Drugmakers Did Not Tell Volunteers in Alzheimer’s Trials

text: A picture caption with an article on Nov. 6 about the dancer turned educator Carolyn Adams, using information from the Paul Taylor company’s archive, reversed the identities of two dancers shown in the image. The order, from the top, is Paul Taylor, Bettie de Jong, Senta Driver and Carolyn Adams, not Taylor, Driver, de Jong and Adams.
match_headline: A Taylor Dancer for the Ages, ‘Unmannered and Wondrous’

text: An article on Monday about Grammy Award nominations and snubs misstated a line from a New Yorker story about Beyoncé. It is “It’s a line written to age poorly,” not “It’s a line destined to age poorly.”
ref_headline: It’s a line written to age poorly,
match_headline: Grammys Snubs and Surprises: Charli XCX Levels Up, Beyoncé Spreads Out and the Beatles Persist

text: An obituary on Sunday about Ben Baldanza, a former chief executive of Spirit Airlines, referred incorrectly to his mother, Norma (Guaspari) Baldanza. She worked at the commissary on Griffiss Air Force Base in Rome, N.Y.; she was not a homemaker.
match_headline: Ben Baldanza, 62, Dies; Brought No-Frills Flying to Spirit Airlines

text: An obituary on Monday about the NASCAR driver Bobby Allison misstated the number of top-level events he won in his career. It was 85, not 84. (He had been credited with 84 until October, when NASCAR ruled that his victory at Bowman Gray Stadium in 1971 was an official Cup Series victory.) The error was repeated in a sub-headline. The obituary also misidentified the fourth-place finisher in the 1970 Indianapolis 500. It was Donnie Allison, Bobby’s brother, not Johnny Allison.
match_headline: Bobby Allison, Hall of Fame NASCAR Driver, Is Dead at 86

text: An obituary on Nov. 7 about the journalist, editor and media critic James Ledbetter misidentified the creator of The Village Voice’s Press Clips column, which Mr. Ledbetter wrote in the 1990s. Although Alexander Cockburn wrote the column for many years, it was originated by John Leo, not Mr. Cockburn.
match_headline: James Ledbetter, Media Critic and Business Journalist, Dies at 60

text: An obituary on Monday about Dorothy Allison, the author of “Bastard Out of Carolina” and other books, using information supplied by the literary agency that represented her, misstated the day on which she died. It was Wednesday, Nov. 6, not Tuesday, Nov. 5.
match_headline: Dorothy Allison, Author of ‘Bastard Out of Carolina,’ Dies at 75

text: An article on Sunday about violence that erupted around a soccer match between Israeli and Dutch teams in Amsterdam misstated the source that described the anti-Arab chants shouted by Maccabi fans near the central train station. While anti-Arab profanities were captured on videos posted to social media there, it was city officials who described the fans shouting a chant about schools and children in Gaza.
match_headline: Amsterdam Bars Protests After Antisemitic Attacks on Soccer Fans

text: An article on Friday about the boxing rematch between Katie Taylor and Amanda Serrano misstated the name of the company putting on the fight. It is Most Valuable Promotions, not Most Valuable Productions. The article also misstated the weight class that Katie Taylor and Amanda Serrano are competing in. It is the super lightweight class, not the lightweight class.
match_headline: Katie Taylor and Amanda Serrano Look to Make Women’s Boxing History (Again)

text: An article on Tuesday about the documentary “Dahomey” and artifacts that remain off limits to the public in Benin referred incorrectly to the statue of a West African king featured in the film. It is a statue of King Gezo, not King Béhanzin.
match_headline: ‘Dahomey’ Celebrated Looted Art’s Return. What Happened Next?

text: An article this weekend on Page 1 about Korean Americans’ reaction to Andy Kim’s Senate victory in New Jersey referred incorrectly to Min Choi’s birth. She was born in Korea and moved to New Jersey when she was 1. She was not born in New Jersey.
match_headline: What Andy Kim’s Senate Victory Means to a Hub of Korean American Life

text: An article on Saturday about the possible tension between Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s agenda against Big Food and President-elect Donald J. Trump’s corporate-friendly goals described incorrectly Mr. Kennedy’s recent comments on Froot Loops. He was comparing the total number of ingredients in the U.S. and Canadian versions of the cereal, not the number of artificial ingredients.
match_headline: Kennedy’s Vow to Take On Big Food Could Alienate His New G.O.P. Allies

text: An article on Sunday about the pace of President-elect Donald J. Trump’s staffing decisions for key roles in his cabinet misstated when Mr. Trump began announcing cabinet picks for his first term in office. It was in November 2016, not December 2016.
match_headline: Under the Chandelier at Mar-a-Lago, Trump Makes Picks at Breakneck Speed

text: An article on Nov. 15 about Norway formally apologizing for suppressing the language and culture of Indigenous people misstated Bard Hoksrud’s role in Norwegian politics. He is a lawmaker with the right-wing Progress Party, not the party’s leader.
match_headline: Norway Apologizes for Forced Assimilation of Sami and Other Minorities

text: An article on Sunday about Israel’s bombing of an area near Beirut misspelled the given name of a veteran Lebanese politician and the speaker of Parliament. He is Nabih Berri, not Nabil.
match_headline: Israel Strikes Near Beirut as Two Medics Killed in South Lebanon

text: An article on Wednesday about Ukraine’s use of American-made ballistic missiles to strike into Russia, misspelled the given name of the European Union’s foreign policy chief. He is Josep Borrell Fontelles, not Joseph.
match_headline: Ukraine Fired U.S.-Made Missiles Into Russia for First Time, Officials Say

text: An article on Sunday about the exploitation of migrant workers by staffing agencies misstated the status of investigations into Ferrara Candy and its staffing firms by the Illinois Department of Labor. The investigations were recently concluded with no rulings on the merits; they are not ongoing.
match_headline: The Hidden Truth Linking the Broken Border to Your Online Shopping Cart

text: An article on Nov. 13 about deeply discounted sales in Hong Kong’s luxury property market misspelled the surname of the chairman of the real estate firm JLL in Hong Kong. He is Joseph Tsang, not Joseph Tang.
match_headline: Hong Kong’s Tycoons Are Selling Trophy Homes at Fire Sale Prices

text: An article on Wednesday about the Danish soft rock band Michael Learns to Rock and its following in Asia misstated Richel Rose Dupit’s role. She is an administrator of a fan page for Michael Learns to Rock, not the president of the band’s fan club in the Philippines. The error was repeated in a picture caption.
match_headline: The Scandinavian Soft Rock Band That’s Big in Asia

text: An obituary on Oct. 6 about the actor John Ashton erroneously credited him with appearances on two television shows. An actor named John Ashton did appear on the British series “EastEnders” and “Brookside,” but it was a different John Ashton. This correction was delayed because it was only recently brought to the editors’ attention.
match_headline: John Ashton, ‘Beverly Hills Cop’ Actor, Dies at 76

text: An article on Thursday about the prison sentence for Bill Hwang, the founder of Archegos Capital Management, misstated the office that prepared his presentencing report. It was prepared by the probation department, not by the prosecution.
match_headline: Archegos Founder Bill Hwang Is Sentenced to 18 Years

text: An article this weekend on Page 10 about late-night host Johnny Carson incorrectly quoted part of a line from a famous Johnny Carson quip. The joke goes, “Half the marriages end in divorce — and then there are the unhappy ones,” not “and then there are the happy ones.”
ref_headline: Half the marriages end in divorce — and then there are the unhappy ones,
match_headline: Johnny Carson and the Fantasy of America

text: An article on Saturday about the ruling junta in Mali replacing the country’s prime minister misstated the military rank of the new prime minister, Abdoulaye Maiga. He is a general, not a colonel.
match_headline: Mali’s Junta Replaces Civilian Prime Minister With One of Its Own

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump attending an Ultimate Fighting Championship event at Madison Square Garden misidentified the type of kick Jon Jones used to knock his opponent to the mat to win in the third round. Mr. Jones used a spinning back kick, not a roundhouse kick, on Stipe Miocic.
match_headline: Trump, Visiting New York, Finds a Friendly Crowd at a Fight

text: An article on Wednesday about a hacker who is said to have gained access to a file with damaging testimony about the former Florida congressman Matt Gaetz imprecisely described accusations made against Christopher Dorworth by two people he has sued for defamation. They said Mr. Dorworth hosted parties involving drugs and open sex, not that Mr. Dorworth himself openly engaged in sex at those parties.
match_headline: Hacker Is Said to Have Gained Access to File With Damaging Testimony About Gaetz

text: An article on Sunday about companies’ efforts to influence President-elect Trump’s tariffs policy misstated Nicole Bivens Collinson’s role at Sandler, Travis & Rosenberg. She advises clients on trade; she is not a trade lawyer.
match_headline: Trump’s Trade Agenda Could Benefit Friends and Punish Rivals

text: An article on Monday about a new PBS show for children, “Carl the Collector,” ran without a byline. It was written by Laurel Graeber.
match_headline: ‘Carl the Collector’ Puts an Autistic Child (Well, Raccoon) in the Lead

text: A picture caption with a feature on Sunday about the best Major League Baseball players and managers as chosen by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America misidentified Luis Gil’s team. He plays for the New York Yankees, not the Seattle Mariners.
match_headline: Barbara Taylor Bradford, Whose Sagas Were Best Sellers, Dies at 91

text: An article on Thursday about a painting by René Magritte selling for over $100 million at auction referred incorrectly to Paolo Vedovi’s relationship to the Vedovi gallery in Brussels. He is the co-founder of the gallery, not the director.
match_headline: Magritte, Master of Surrealism, Joins the $100 Million Dollar Club

text: Because of an editing error, a photo caption with a film review on Friday about the Raoul Peck documentary “Ernest Cole: Lost and Found” misidentified a protester in the image as Ernest Cole, the South African photographer who documented apartheid. Cole took the photograph; he was not in it.
match_headline: ‘Ernest Cole: Lost and Found’ Review: Chronicling Apartheid and Beyond

text: An obituary on Thursday about the basketball star Bob Love misstated how many sons from his first marriage survive him. It is four, not five.
match_headline: Bob Love, Rugged, High-Scoring All-Star for Chicago Bulls, Dies at 81

text: An article on Tuesday about the Democratic Party’s efforts to regain momentum in Southern battleground states, misidentified the college at which Laken Riley was enrolled at the time of her death. She was attending Augusta University, not the University of Georgia.
match_headline: Democrats Rush to Regroup in the Southern Battlegrounds

text: An article on Friday about London’s Smithfield Market incorrectly identified the music ensemble for which Simon Rattle is a conductor. It is the London Symphony Orchestra, not the London Philharmonic Orchestra.
match_headline: London’s 850-Year-Old Smithfield Meat Market Is Set to Close

text: An article on Friday about which Democrats are in the mix to be chair of the Democratic National Committee misstated when Pete Buttigieg delivered his concession speech during his run for chairman of the organization eight years ago. His speech came before he earned three votes, not after the votes.
match_headline: Who Might Be the Next Chair of the Democratic Party?

text: An article on Nov. 22 about whether the Trump administration and Europe will provide security guarantees to prevent Russia from taking more Ukraine territory paraphrased imprecisely comments made by officials about options Ukraine might have for future deterrence against Russia. The officials suggested that the Biden administration could allow Ukraine to re-establish its nuclear arsenal, which Ukraine had agreed to surrender after the fall of the Soviet Union in exchange for security guarantees. They did not suggest that the Biden administration could return those weapons to Ukraine. The error was repeated in an article on Friday about Russia’s recent attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure sites with missiles and drones.
match_headline: Trump’s Vow to End the War Could Leave Ukraine With Few Options

text: An article on Saturday about Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York contending with pressure from environmental advocates and President-elect Donald Trump misidentified the states that have Cap and Invest programs. California and Washington have the program, not Oregon.
match_headline: Will Hochul’s Political Concerns Put New York’s Climate Goals at Risk?

text: An article on Saturday about Linda McMahon’s nomination for Secretary of Education misstated the name of a library organization. It is the American Library Association not the National Library Association.
match_headline: Her Wrestling Empire Was Said to Harm Children. Trump Chose Her for Education.

text: An article on Monday about a salmonella outbreak that may be linked to cucumbers referred incorrectly to Calgary. It is a city in the Canadian province of Alberta; it is not a Canadian province.

An article on Saturday about how and where to purchase Broadway tickets described incorrectly how the TodayTix app works. Theatergoers can choose precise seats for the Broadway shows sold on the app; TodayTix does not assign the seats for some Broadway shows.
match_headline: Theater to See in N.Y.C. This Holiday Season

text: An obituary on Sunday about Alice Hudson misstated the name of the university where Ms. Hudson earned a bachelor’s degree. It is Middle Tennessee State University, not Middle Tennessee University. The obituary also misstated the given name of the Linda May Uris director of the Humanities and Social Sciences Research Divisions at the New York Public Library. He is Matt Knutzen, not Mark.
match_headline: Alice Hudson, Librarian Who Built a Trove of Historic Maps, Dies at 77

text: An obituary on Monday about show business writer Marshall Brickman gave an erroneous distinction to Mr. Brickman’s screenplay for the 1994 movie “Intersection.” It was not his “last film script”; his last was for the 2014 film adaptation of “Jersey Boys,” co-written with Rick Elice.
match_headline: Marshall Brickman, Woody Allen’s Co-Writer on Hit Films, Dies at 85

text: An article on Tuesday about transgender students’ participation in sports in a Manhattan school district misstated the content of a letter that the city comptroller, Brad Lander, sent to the Department of Education. Mr. Lander asked for a review of the department’s handling of community education council elections; he did not make a formal complaint against PLACE, a parents’ group.
match_headline: A Culture-War Battle Convulses a School Panel in Liberal Manhattan

text: An article on Sunday about Dr. Dave Weldon, President-elect Donald J. Trump’s pick to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention misstated the name of a federal body. It is the National Transportation Safety Board, not the National Transportation Security Board.
match_headline: Dr. Dave Weldon, Trump’s C.D.C. Pick, Was Not on Anyone’s Radar

text: An article on Tuesday about France’s financial uncertainty misstated the European countries that are required to have sound finances. They are countries that use the euro currency, but not all members of the European Union.
match_headline: Investors Punish France Over Budget Turmoil

text: An article on Tuesday about hysterectomies misidentified Dr. William Parker’s current job. He is a volunteer clinical professor at the University of California, San Diego. He is no longer at the University of California, Los Angeles. The article also misstated the year in which Dr. Karen Tang began her residency. It was 2005, not 2007.
match_headline: You Had a Hysterectomy. What Did the Doctor Leave Behind?

text: An article on Wednesday about the erosion of the post-Watergate norm that criminal investigations should remain largely outside the reach of political leaders misstated the surname of a former Justice Department official who is now a law professor at the University of Maryland. He is Michael Greenberger, not Greenberg.
match_headline: Justice Dept.’s Apolitical Tradition Is Challenged by 2 Presidents

text: An article on Wednesday about artificial intelligence chips, a field that has long been dominated by Nvidia, misstated the A.I. start-up Poolside’s location. It is San Francisco, not Paris.
match_headline: The Furious Contest to Unseat Nvidia as King of A.I. Chips

text: An article on Thursday about the challenges Speaker Mike Johnson will face with such a small Republican majority in the House misstated which parts of government Democrats currently control. They control the White House and the Senate, not the House and the Senate.
match_headline: Mike Johnson’s Newest Headache: The Smallest House Majority in History

text: An article on Wednesday about Sheriff Chad Chronister, President-elect Donald J. Trump’s pick to lead the Drug Enforcement Administration, withdrawing his name from consideration for the office misstated Pam Bondi’s role at the Hillsborough County State Attorney’s Office. She was a prosecutor in and a spokeswoman for the office; she was not in charge of it.
match_headline: Trump’s Pick to Lead D.E.A. Withdraws, Citing ‘Gravity’ of Job

text: An article on Page 18 this weekend about psychosis and race misstates the occupation of Deidre Anglin’s grandmother. She worked as a nanny, not a house cleaner.
match_headline: America’s Hidden Racial Divide: A Mysterious Gap in Psychosis Rates

text: An obituary on Nov. 30 about Robert W. Dixon Sr., who was stationed at West Point with the Ninth Cavalry Regiment during World War II, credited him with an erroneous distinction. He was not the last survivor of the Army’s all-Black units historically known as Buffalo Soldiers; there are at least two surviving members — Roy Caldwood and the jazz saxophonist Marshall Allen — of the 92nd Infantry Division, nicknamed the Buffalo Soldiers Division, which saw combat in Europe during World War II.
match_headline: Robert Dixon, Last Surviving Buffalo Soldier, Dies at 103

text: An article on Dec. 1 about Demetrius Crichlow, who was named the head of New York City Transit last month, misspelled the surname of the chief executive of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority. He is Janno Lieber, not Leiber. It also misstated the number of riders served by New York City’s subway and bus system. Is it six million, not four million.
match_headline: The M.T.A.’s New Subway Boss Says He’s Here to Stay

text: An article on Saturday about Lebanon and Jordan closing border crossings with Syria misidentified the source of a warning given to Americans to leave Syria promptly. It came from the U.S. State Department, not from the U.S. Embassy in Damascus.
match_headline: As Syrian Rebels Advance, Iran Grows Nervous and Neighbors Close Their Borders

text: An article on Dec. 4 about a court ruling in Brussels that five mixed-race women were owed reparations from Belgium referred incorrectly to restrictions on sexual relationships between Europeans and Africans in the Belgian Congo. They were viewed as transgressions but not banned.
match_headline: 5 Women Win Reparations From Belgium for Crimes Under Colonial Rule

text: An article on Sunday about the trial of Daniel Penny for the killing of Jordan Neely on a subway train misstated the given name of the lead prosecutor in the trial. She is Dafna Yoran, not Dofna Yana.
match_headline: In Penny Trial, the Moment May Have Mattered as Much as the Evidence

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Monday about Hallmark and Netflix holiday films misstated the title of the movie that began Netflix’s recent investment in Christmas movies. It was “The Christmas Prince” in 2017, not “The Princess Switch” in 2018.
match_headline: How I Aged Into the Bad Christmas Movie

text: An article on Tuesday about Syria’s factions misspelled the last name of the U.N. special envoy for Syria. It is Geir O. Pedersen, not Pederson.
match_headline: A Quick Arab Pivot: From Welcoming al-Assad to Managing the Chaos

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the poet Nikki Giovanni referred incorrectly to the people fatally shot by a student in 2007 at Virginia Tech, where Ms. Giovanni taught. He killed 33 people including himself, not 32; and his victims were students and faculty members, not just students.
match_headline: Nikki Giovanni, Poet Who Wrote of Black Joy, Dies at 81

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the first major #MeToo accusation in France proceeding to trial misstated the value of 150,000 euros in dollars under the current exchange rate. It is about $160,000, not about $190,000.
match_headline: France’s First Big #MeToo Case Goes to Trial

text: An article on Monday about the Romanian village of Pestera misstated an element of a World Bank report about the percentage of the Romanian population still dependent on subsistence agriculture. That description applies to a large share of those in the bottom 40 percent of the income distribution, not to all 40 percent of the population.
match_headline: In a Romanian Village, Anger Fuels Support for an Ultranationalist ‘Messiah’

text: An article on Wednesday about President-elect Donald J. Trump’s monetization of branded merchandise misstated the number of times Mr. Trump ran for president. He was a candidate three times, not two.
match_headline: Trump Tests Ethical Boundaries With Branded Merch. (And All Sales Are Final.)

text: An article on Thursday about government data on recent immigration into the United States referred incorrectly to a figure in the Census Bureau’s estimate of immigration from 2020 to 2023. The bureau estimated that the foreign-born population changed by an average of about 900,000 from 2020 to 2023, not that net migration changed by that amount. (The first category does not take into account the death of foreign-born people already living in the United States; the second one does.)
match_headline: Recent Immigration Surge Has Been Largest in U.S. History

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about the 2025 Sundance Film Festival incorrectly described “Last Days,” the film by Justin Lin. Based on a true story, it is the fictionalized account of a missionary; it is not about a fictional missionary.
match_headline: Sundance Film Festival Unveils a Lineup Heavy on Politics

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Thursday about the all-star outfielder Rocky Colavito misstated the number of games the pitcher Tommy John won in his career. It was 288, not 286. (He had won two games before being traded in 1965 in a deal that brought Colavito back to Cleveland.)
match_headline: Rocky Colavito, All-Star Slugger for Cleveland, Dies at 91

text: An article on Friday about an agreement reached by the city of Louisville, Ky., and the Justice Department to address misconduct by Louisville police misstated the circumstances by which the police in Louisville searched the home of Breonna Taylor, who was fatally shot by officers. The police department had approval for a no-knock warrant to enter Ms. Taylor’s apartment, but officers were later instructed to knock and identify themselves. It is not the case that they used no warrant at all.
match_headline: Louisville and Justice Dept. Reach Deal on Federal Oversight of Police

text: A picture caption in the table of contents for an article on Dec. 1 about war and superbugs misidentified the type of testing being performed. Test strips were used to identify bacteria, not to test for antibiotic resistance.
match_headline: Is That Turkey Still Good?

text: An article on Dec. 8 about nuclear risk misspelled the given name of the Secretary of Defense who participated in the Proud Prophet war game. He was Caspar Weinberger, not Casper.
match_headline: The Secret Pentagon War Game That ​Offers a Stark​ Warning for Our Times

text: An article on Dec. 9 about a confidential Navy program studying a possible link between intense fighter jet operations and brain injuries misspelled the given name of the woman who was Jake Rosales’s girlfriend at the time of his death. She is Ann-Marie Avanni, not Anne-Marie. The error was repeated in an accompanying picture caption.
match_headline: Top-Gun Navy Pilots Fly at the Extremes. Their Brains May Suffer.

text: An article on Monday about Israeli airstrikes on Syrian weapons depots and air defenses over the weekend misstated the day that the Turkish defense minister commented about Russian military planes in Syria. It was Saturday, not Sunday.
match_headline: Israel Strikes Military Sites in Syria, Monitor Says

text: An article on Dec. 3 about Massad Boulos, president-elect Donald J. Trump’s choice to serve as his Middle East adviser, misidentified the Boulos family associated with Boulos Enterprises, a Nigeria-based company. The company is run by a different Boulos family, not by Mr. Trump’s choice for an administration post.
match_headline: Trump Offers Massad Boulos Middle East Adviser Role

text: An article on Saturday about Elon Musk using his X account to single out federal employees and agencies for cost cuts misstated the given name of a professor at the University of Michigan Gerald R. Ford School of Public Policy. He is Don Moynihan, not Dan Moynihan.
match_headline: Elon Musk’s Playbook for DOGE Has a Precedent: X

text: An article on Saturday about Dommaraju Gukesh’s victory in the World Chess Championship in Singapore misidentified the person with whom Mr. Gukesh had made a pact to go bungee jumping to celebrate his win. It was Grzegorz Gajewski, a Polish grandmaster, not Vishnu Prasanna, an Indian grandmaster.
match_headline: Dommaraju Gukesh, 18, Becomes Youngest World Chess Champion

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the atrocities at Syrian prisons under Bashar al-Assad’s government misstated the number of years the Assad family was in power. It was roughly 53 years, not 60.
match_headline: Syria Shudders as Assad’s Prison Atrocities Come Into the Light

text: An article on Dec. 10 about Syrians celebrating the fall of the Assad government misstated the number of years the Assad family was in power. It was more than 50 years, not more than 60 years.
match_headline: Syrians Celebrate as Rebels Force Bashar al-Assad Out of Power

text: An article on Tuesday about New Jersey Gov. Philip D. Murphy commuting the prison sentences of three women who had been abused and were convicted of killing men close to them misstated the circumstances of the crimes committed. They were all convicted of killing men close to them. The victims were not all boyfriends of the women.
match_headline: Gov. Murphy Grants First Pardons, Freeing 3 Women Convicted of Murder

text: An article on Wednesday about the streaming service Max ending its partnership with “Sesame Street” misidentified the service currently carrying new episodes. The new episodes can be seen on Max, not on HBO, which previously partnered with the children’s show.

text: An article on Tuesday about law enforcement officials finding no evidence that the torture and killing of a transgender man whose remains were found in a field in upstate New York last week was a hate crime misstated the surname of the victim. He was Sam Nordquist, not Norquist.

text: An article on Tuesday about a new book that focuses on the letters written by many Jews seeking refuge in the Netherlands who were denied entry after it closed its border in 1938 gave an incorrect date for the letter written by Jakob Aufrichtig. text: An article on Feb. 15 about Vice President JD Vance urging European leaders to end the isolation of far-right parties across the continent referred imprecisely to the reason behind Romania’s cancellation of its presidential election last year. text: An article on Feb. 11 about the State Department issuing a stop-work order to all of the nonprofit organizations that it funds to end their demining work misstated an action taken by the U.N. agency responsible for monitoring global explosive contamination and funding action. text: An article on Feb. 15 about a Texas county seeking federal assistance to deal with contamination from toxic fertilizers described incorrectly efforts to test for PFAS on farms in Maine. text: An article on Sunday about the United Soccer League’s introduction of a new men’s professional league to rival that of Major League Soccer misstated the number of M.L.S. teams located in the United States. text: An article on Thursday about what we know regarding the Trump administration’s transfer of more than 175 men from an immigration holding site in Texas to the U.S. military base at Guantánamo Bay misstated the number of prisoners awaiting trial at Guantánamo’s terrorism-related detention mission. match_headline: Paquita la del Barrio, Whose Songs Empowered Women, Dies at 77

text: An article on Feb. 16 about the drug buprenorphine, an opioid that can help treat addiction to more serious opioids like heroin and fentanyl, misstated Kelly Pfeifer’s relationship with the California Health Care Foundation. She is not currently a director with the organization.

text: An article on Tuesday about a young woman who fled religious persecution in Iran and was then caught in the Trump administration’s deportation push misspelled the surname of an Iranian-American lawyer. He is Ali Herischi, not Herschi.

text: An article on Thursday about a New Jersey judge dismissing racketeering charges against George Norcross III misstated the position of Mr. Norcross’s lawyers on the claims outlined in the indictment. text: An article on Thursday about a poverty tracker report for New York City misidentified the research group that analyzed Gov. Kathy Hochul’s proposals to reduce child poverty. text: An article on Friday about President Trump’s proposal for a new “gold card” visa program described incorrectly a golden visa program in the European Union. Some golden visa holders are entitled to visa-free travel within certain areas of the European Union, but residence is restricted to the specific country that issued the visa; it is not the case that they allow recipients to establish residency in any country in the bloc.

text: An article on Friday about the Netflix comedy “Running Point” omitted one of the creators of the show. Elaine Ko was a creator along with Ike Barinholtz, Mindy Kaling and David Stassen.

text: An article on Page 22 this weekend about Parker Posey misspells the surname of an actress. She is Michelle Monaghan, not Moynahan. And the article misspelled the surname of a filmmaker. He is Greg Mottola, not Motolla.

text: An obituary on Friday about the actor Gene Hackman misstated the age of his wife, Betsy Arakawa. She was 65, not 64.

text: An article on Saturday about China flexing its military muscle in the Pacific paraphrased incorrectly Adm. Samuel J. Paparo’s position on U.S. preparations for China’s military buildup. match_headline: China’s Military Puts Pacific on Notice as U.S. Priorities Shift

text: An article on Sunday about migration from the United States to Canada misstated the number of irregular migrants apprehended at the U.S. borders. At the northern border, nearly 24,000 migrants were apprehended in 2024, not 200,000. In January 2024, it was about 900, not 15,000. And in January this year, it was about 600, not 5,000. At the southern border, over 1.5 million were apprehended last year, not two million. The higher numbers counted everyone stopped by U.S. authorities while crossing the border, but the correct figures, which are far lower, include only those who were found to be crossing illegally, according to data published by the U.S. Customs and Border Protection agency.
match_headline: Canada Curbed Illegal Migration to the U.S. Now People Are Heading to Canada.

text: An article on Saturday about Canadians’ protests of the Trump administration’s economic policies misspelled the surname of the “Late Night” host. He is Seth Meyers, not Myers.

text: An article on Saturday about the Chinese electronics maker Xiaomi incorrectly described the factory where Xiaomi’s SU7 electric car was produced. text: An article on Feb. 25 about the ways Germany’s hard-right AfD party finds most of its support from citizens in former East Germany referred imprecisely to the controlled political parties of East Germany. text: An article on Wednesday about Israel and Lebanon agreeing to start negotiations on disputes over their land border referred incorrectly to a statement from the Israeli prime minister’s office. It said that Israel had agreed to release five Lebanese detainees, not that it had released them.

text: A headline with an article on Tuesday about Mark Carney, the head of the Liberal Party who will soon lead Canada, referred incorrectly to his new title. text: An article on Wednesday about job cuts at NASA’s Washington headquarters misstated the surname of a NASA spokeswoman. She is Cheryl Warner, not Wheeler.

text: An article on Thursday about the impact that cuts to the Department of Education’s research employees and outside partners will have on research and data collection misstated the amount of money that Mathematica won in federal funding last year. It was $360 million, not $1.3 billion.

text: An article on Monday about Israel’s decision to cut off electricity to the Gaza Strip, relying on information from a source at the Israeli electric company, misstated the type of service affected by the electricity shut-off in Gaza. text: An article on Friday about a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s firing of more than 1,300 workers at the Department of Education incorrectly described Pell grants. They are not loans.

text: An article on Monday about Mahmoud Khalil, a former graduate student at Columbia University who participated in student protests against the war in Gaza, misstated Mr. Khalil’s status in the United States. He is a permanent resident, not a permanent citizen.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about Makoto Watanabe, the co-founder and editor in chief of the Tokyo Investigative Newsroom Tansa, misstated when Tansa published a series of articles that exposed forced sterilizations. text: A news analysis article on Wednesday about Israel’s resumed attacks in Gaza after stalled cease-fire talks with Hamas referred incorrectly to statements made by Hamas after the Israeli strikes. text: An obituary on Tuesday about Dr. Sheldon Greenfield, who was known for his research into gaps in health care, misstated the distance between Venice, Calif., where he lived in the 1970s and ’80s, and Torrance, where he once had to drive his family’s babysitter to a public hospital. text: An article on Thursday about Canada’s deal with Australia to develop a cutting-edge radar for the Arctic that can detect hypersonic missiles and other threats over the curvature of the earth misstated when the joint U.S.-Canada aerospace command was established. text: An article on Friday about beef tallow misstated the nature of a $1.5 million payment received by the American Heart Association. It was a donation from listeners of a radio program sponsored by Procter & Gamble, not a corporate sponsorship from Procter & Gamble itself.

text: A picture caption with an article on Tuesday about Lucian Simmons, the new head of provenance research at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, misstated the era of a bronze griffin being returned to Greece. It is from the seventh century B.C., not the seventh century.

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about the Frick Museum reversed the identities of the painter and subject in a portrait. The image was Sir Anthony van Dyck’s portrait of Frans Snyders, not Snyder’s portrait of van Dyck.
match_headline: A Guided Tour: Inside the Splendor of the New Frick

text: An article on Page 8 this weekend about the actress Ellen Pompeo misstates the type of work that her husband, Chris Ivery, does. Ivery works in marketing; he is no longer a music producer.
match_headline: Ellen Pompeo Leaves the Hospital

text: An article on Page 30 this weekend about solidarity transcribes incorrectly a line from Sarah Schulman’s forthcoming book, “The Fantasy and Necessity of Solidarity.” The line is “Solidarity is the action behind the revelation that each of us, individually, are not the only people with dreams,” not “Solidarity is the action behind the revelation that each of us, individually, are the only people with dreams.”
ref_headline: The Fantasy and Necessity of Solidarity.
