text: An article on Thursday about the return of a looted mosaic to the city of Pompeii referred imprecisely to some of the volcanic matter Pompeii was buried in when Mount Vesuvius erupted. It was buried in ash and rock fragments, not lava.

text: An article on Wednesday about an excavation in Ireland where the remains of hundreds of children are thought to have been buried described incorrectly the location of some disposed bodies. It was an old sewage system, not septic tanks.
match_headline: Dig for Children’s Remains Begins at Irish Home for Unwed Mothers

text: An article on Thursday about the Chinese A.I. industry misquoted Jia Haojun, the founder of Deep Principle. He said it would be a huge benefit if the government helped cover “13 to 15 percent” of early-stage research costs, not “10 to 15 percent.”

text: An article on Monday about the biotech company Sarepta Therapeutics defying the Food and Drug Administration’s request that it halt distribution of its treatment for a deadly muscle-wasting disease misstated the subset of Duchenne patients for whom the treatment was first approved. text: An article on Thursday about changes to the Williamstown Theater Festival, using information from the festival, misstated last year’s budget. It was $5.7 million, not $4.7 million.
match_headline: Williamstown Theater Festival Was in Crisis. Here’s How It’s Changing.

text: An article on Sunday about the actor and singer Mandy Patinkin and his family incorrectly misstated the number of Tony Awards that Mr. Patinkin has won. While he was nominated multiple times, he has won only one, for “Evita.”
match_headline: The Grody-Patinkin Family Is a Mess. People Love It.

text: An article on Sunday about the legal implications of being an organ donor misstated the number of Americans who are in the national donor registry. There are more than 173 million Americans in both state registries and the national registry, not the national registry alone.
match_headline: You Said ‘Yes’ to Being an Organ Donor. What Exactly Does That Mean?

text: An article on Tuesday about President Trump urging two professional sports teams to change their names misstated the number of carved figures, known as the Guardians of Traffic, on the Hope Memorial Bridge in Cleveland. There are eight, not two.

text: A map with an article on Friday about recent military drills by China’s aircraft carriers in the Pacific reversed the colors of two carriers in the map’s key. The Shandong was in Hong Kong, not the Liaoning.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the singer Ozzy Osbourne misstated the location of an incident that led to his being banned from performing in San Antonio. It happened at the Alamo Cenotaph, a memorial just outside the walls of the Alamo — not at the Alamo itself. The obituary also misstated the original surname of Mr. Osbourne’s mother. It was Unitt, not Levy.

text: Because of an editing error, an obituary on Monday about the Olympic runner and track coach Bill Dellinger misidentified one of the standout runners he coached. He is Matt Centrowitz, an Olympian who won four United States national championships in the 5,000-meter run from 1979 to 1982, not his son, Matthew Centrowitz Jr., who won the gold medal in the 1,500 meters at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro.

text: An article on July 18 about a federal judge’s move to block a rule intended to make it easier for many Americans to get loans by removing medical debt from credit reports referred imprecisely to a part of Judge Sean D. Jordan’s decision. Judge Jordan wrote that state bans on reporting medical debts to credit agencies would be pre-empted by the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, but he did not issue a ruling pre-empting those bans.

text: An article on Thursday about Canada’s measles outbreak misstated which officials were urging the Alberta provincial leader to declare a public health emergency. They were public health experts, not provincial officials.
match_headline: Canada’s Measles Outbreak Exceeds Cases in the U.S.

text: An article on Friday about the powerful earthquake that struck off the coast of Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula early Wednesday misstated the energy difference between earthquake magnitudes. A magnitude 9 quake has about three times as much energy as magnitude 8.7, not 10 times as much. It has about twice as much energy as magnitude 8.8, not three times as much.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about the impact of President Trump’s shifting tariff levels on the African nation of Lesotho misstated the day Lesotho’s 15 percent tariff rate was announced. It was Thursday night, not Friday night.

text: An article on Monday about a city in Kansas suing over a planned ICE detention center misstated the language in a poster seen at a protest of an immigration detention facility in Leavenworth, Kan. text: An article on Friday about Ford Motor announcing that it lost money in the second quarter as tariffs took a toll on its business misstated the day that Ford reported its second-quarter earnings. It was Wednesday, not Tuesday.
match_headline: Ford Is Latest Carmaker to Blame Tariffs for Profit Slump

text: A picture from the streaming outlet TBPN published with an article on Friday about A.I. researchers’ pay packages misidentified a Microsoft employee who used to work at Google’s DeepMind lab. The person shown in the image was not Amar Subramanya.
match_headline: A.I. Researchers Are Negotiating $250 Million Pay Packages. Just Like N.B.A. Stars.

text: An article on Saturday about the negative impact that the Trump administration’s tariffs are having on businesses they were meant to help misstated the month that the United States lost 11,000 manufacturing jobs. text: An article on Sunday about a veteran lifeguard’s Friday routine misstated, in some instances, Javier Rodriguez’s surname on second reference and that of his three adult children. Their surname is Rodriguez, not Hernandez.

text: An article on Sunday about the Vatican’s six-day celebration of youth in the church referred incorrectly to some of the festivities. They were part of the Jubilee of Youth, not World Youth Day.

text: An article on Monday about what to watch on television this week misstated the premiere time of “American Prince: J.F.K. Jr.” on CNN. It will premiere at 9 p.m. Eastern on Saturday, Aug. 9, not 10 p.m.

text: An article on Tuesday about jurists losing faith in President Trump’s Justice Department misstated Andrew Wiederhorn’s role with the restaurant chain Fatburger. He was previously a chief executive of the chain and founded its parent company. He did not create the restaurant chain.

text: A picture caption with an article on Wednesday about a growing debate in Japan between those who defend pacifism as a national virtue and those who think the country must abandon it referred incorrectly to a treaty that Japan has not signed. It is the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, not the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty.

text: An article on Wednesday about how the Trump administration will gain access to the standardized test scores and grade point averages of all applicants to Columbia and Brown University misstated the findings of an SAT report from the College Board. text: An article on July 31 about Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva voicing frustration with President Trump over tariffs misidentified birds roaming the presidential palace lawns. They were rheas, not emus.

text: An article on Wednesday about how Texas Republicans are hoping the surge of Hispanic support for President Trump in 2024 will last through the 2026 midterm elections misstated the percentage of votes that Representative Henry Cuellar, Democrat of Texas, won in Starr County in the 2024 elections. It was 69 percent, not 60 percent.

text: An article on Wednesday about the Trump administration’s plans to terminate $7 billion in federal grants intended to help low- and moderate-income families install solar panels on their homes misstated the amount of money the Georgia Bright Communities Coalition was using to provide free rooftop solar panels to about 800 Georgia households. text: An article on Monday about businesses rushing goods out of duty-free warehouses to bonded warehouses, allowing foreign companies a way to postpone the payment of tariffs until the goods are sent to stores or directly to customers, misidentified James Marley of Swap Commerce. text: An article on Tuesday about political historian Heather Cox Richardson preparing for the narrator role in Aaron Copland’s “Lincoln Portrait” misstated her surname. It is Richardson, not Cox Richardson.

text: An article on Tuesday about Representative Nancy Mace announcing her run for governor of South Carolina referred incorrectly to President Trump’s primary victory in South Carolina. The state was his second primary victory in 2016, not his first.

text: An article on Thursday about the Royal Ballet and Opera canceling a collaboration with the Israeli Opera to stage “Tosca” in Tel Aviv next year misidentified the opera at which a dancer staged a protest during the curtain call. It was “Il Trovatore,” not “La Traviata.”

text: A picture caption with an obituary on July 19 about the editorial cartoonist Steve Benson misstated the given name of a former governor of Arizona, whom he often lampooned. As the obituary correctly notes, he was Evan Mecham, not Alfred.

text: An obituary on July 28 about the songwriter Tom Lehrer misstated his mother’s given name. It was Anna, not Alma.
match_headline: Tom Lehrer, Musical Satirist With a Dark Streak, Dies at 97

text: An obituary on Saturday about James A. Lovell Jr., the commander of the three-man Apollo 13 spacecraft that survived a near-catastrophic explosion as it approached the moon in April 1970, misstated how much time elapsed before Apollo 13 detected signs of trouble. Haise Jr., not John L. Swigert Jr. Mr. Swigert was to remain behind in the orbiting Apollo 13 spaceship. The obituary also misstated how many great-grandchildren Captain Lovell had. text: An article and related map on Aug. 1 about the countries that recognize a Palestinian state, relying on a U.N. document from April 2024, misstated the Czech Republic’s position on the recognition of a Palestinian state. text: An article on Thursday about Britain’s charities’ regulator clearing Prince Harry of bullying, harassment and sexism at the charity he co-founded misstated the year that Sophie Chandauka became a trustee of Sentebale. text: An article on Monday about the announcement that the Row NYC in Times Square will stop operating as a housing shelter for migrants misstated the ownership of the Row NYC. Rockport Group, a Boston-based real estate private equity firm, no longer has a stake in the hotel.

text: An article on Monday about the weekend’s box office earnings misstated the rating of the “Naked Gun” remake. It is PG-13, not R.
match_headline: ‘Weapons’ Gives Warner Bros. Another Outstanding No. 1 Opening

text: An article on Saturday about the music label Penrose Records and its influence in a soft-touch style of soul music misspelled the surname of an artist on the label’s roster. She is Vicky Tafoya, not Trafoya.
match_headline: California’s ‘Souldies’ Scene Puts a Fresh Spin on a Beloved Sound

text: An article on Tuesday about Quebec City’s small English-speaking community misspelled the name of a photographer and filmmaker. She is Sandra Tomaylla, not Sandra Tomayla.
match_headline: A Haven for English in the Most French of North American Cities

text: An article on Aug. 3 about corporations and individuals, including many in the crypto business, that wrote big checks to MAGA Inc. while seeking favor from President Trump misstated the total amount of money that MAGA Inc. received from crypto interests during the first half of this year, as well as the combined amount donated by Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss and their crypto exchange, Gemini. text: An article on Friday about the ways that Republicans shaped the debate over Sydney Sweeney’s American Eagle ad campaign misstated the date of one of Libs of TikTok’s social media posts on the American Eagle ad. While attention did shift with earlier posts by the influential account on July 27, the “Keep this up Democrats” comment cited in the article was published on July 28, not July 27.
match_headline: How the Right Shaped the Debate Over the Sydney Sweeney Ads

text: An article on Wednesday about the shooting outside a Target store in Austin, Texas, on Monday, misstated, using information from an initial police report, the name of the Target employee who died in the attack. The name was Rosa Machuca, not Hector Leopoldo Martinez Machuca. (The article was updated after the police released an update on the employee’s name.)
match_headline: Victims of Austin Gunman Included Grandfather and 4-Year-Old Granddaughter

text: An article this weekend on Page 120 about censorship of creative works contains several errors. It refers incorrectly to the artist Dread Scott’s 1989 installation “What Is the Proper Way to Display a U.S. Flag?” The exhibit offered visitors the choice of stepping on a flag while answering that question in a guest book; it did not require them to step on the flag. The article misstates the number of photographs of soldiers’ coffins draped with American flags in the installation. There was one such image, not multiple images. The article also misstates the artist Andres Serrano’s number of solo exhibitions in his career. He’s had about 20 solo museum exhibitions in Europe and abroad, and many fewer in the United States — not about 20 solo in Europe and only one in the United States. And because of a production error, the article misquotes John Waters on what a Maryland film censor said to him about his 1974 feature “Female Trouble.” Waters said she told him, “You can’t have that cunnilingus scene,” not “You can have that cunnilingus scene.”
ref_headline: What Is the Proper Way to Display a U.S. Flag?
match_headline: What Happened When Their Art Was Banned

text: A picture caption with an article this weekend on Page 140 about the artist Robert Longo, relying on information from a publicist, misstates the materials used in one of his works. It is a charcoal drawing of a pit of snakes, not an ink-and-charcoal drawing.
match_headline: What Does It Mean to Be a ‘Very American’ Artist Now?

text: A news analysis article on Saturday about President Trump’s summit meeting with President Vladimir V. Putin and the way it marked a return to imperial thinking, citing an expert, misstated the time frame for three divisions of Poland in the 18th century. It was between 1772 and 1795, not 1792 and 1795.
match_headline: How the Trump-Putin Summit Signals a Return to Imperial Thinking

text: An article on Sunday about the indictment of LaToya Cantrell, the mayor of New Orleans, for her actions related to a romantic relationship she had with a city police officer assigned to protect her, misidentified the New Orleans television station that staked out a city-owned apartment in the French Quarter. It was WVUE-TV, not WWL-TV.
match_headline: Mayor of New Orleans Is Indicted on Corruption Charges

text: An article on Sunday about the scrutiny that Representative Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania is facing over his stock trades referred incorrectly to the day of Mr. Bresnahan’s wedding. It was last Saturday, not next Saturday.
match_headline: Congressman’s Stock Trades Draw More Scrutiny After Key Votes

text: An obituary on Sunday about Robin Lakoff, a linguist who analyzed the ways women speak, referred incorrectly to the connection between Dr. Lakoff’s writings and a best-selling book by Deborah Tannen, “You Just Don’t Understand: Women and Men in Conversation.” The book did not popularize some of Dr. Lakoff’s ideas; rather, its subject matter, language and gender were a field that Dr. Lakoff inspired.
ref_headline: You Just Don’t Understand: Women and Men in Conversation.
match_headline: Robin Lakoff, Expert on Language and Gender, Is Dead at 82

text: An obituary on Monday about the art collector and critic Doris Lockhart Saatchi misstated the number of years she was married to Charles Saatchi. It was 17, not 14.
match_headline: Doris Lockhart Saatchi, 88, Critic and Collector of Cutting-Edge Art, Dies

text: Because of a production error, an article on Sunday about why the U.S. government is offering a $5 million reward for information leading to the arrest or conviction of a high-profile Haitian gang leader was missing the full name and identification of a man arrested in Texas in July. He is Bazile Richardson, a Haitian American trucker in North Carolina.
match_headline: Why Is the U.S. Offering a $5 Million Reward for a Haitian Gang Leader?

text: An article on Tuesday about the International Energy Agency forecasts suggesting that global demand for oil and gas could peak by the end of the decade misspelled the surname of the European Union energy minister. He is Dan Jorgensen, not Jorgenson.
match_headline: Will Oil Demand Peak Soon? Trump Administration Doesn’t Want to Hear It.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about potential red flags that have popped up this summer heading into the next N.B.A. season misstated the number of red flags. There are eight, not 10.
match_headline: Beauty Essentials to Help You Beat the Heat This Summer

text: An article on Saturday about factory-built houses that are the latest attempt by FEMA to address a longtime need to upgrade temporary emergency housing misspelled the given name of the director of operations of Liv-Connected. She is Allysa Taylor, not Allyssa.
match_headline: In Lahaina, ‘Dignified’ Havens for Wildfire Survivors

text: An article on Aug. 2 about Edinburgh’s Festival Fringe described incorrectly the ’70s band that features in “Philosophy of the World.” The band, the Shaggs, was a real band, not a fictional one.
match_headline: Edinburgh Fringe Can Bring Artists Fame, but Money’s Another Matter

text: An article on Thursday about Israel approving new settlements in the West Bank and announcing that it was moving ahead with plans to take over Gaza City misspelled the surname of an Israeli analyst and former military intelligence officer. He is Michael Milshtein, not Milstein.
match_headline: With Moves on West Bank and Gaza City, Israel Defies Global Outcry

text: An article on Wednesday about the African Union endorsing a campaign to have organizations around the world replace the Mercator map with other alternatives referred imprecisely to the nationality of Gerardus Mercator. He was from what is now Belgium, not Germany.
match_headline: Africa Is Big, and It Wants the World’s Maps to Show It

text: An obituary on Monday about the actor Terence Stamp misstated when he entered an ashram. It was in the middle or late 1970s, not 1969. The obituary also referred incorrectly to “Billy Budd,” by Herman Melville, which was the basis of a 1962 movie starring Mr. Stamp. It is a novella, not a novel.
match_headline: Terence Stamp, 87, Dies; British Cinema Luminary and ‘Superman’ Villain

text: An obituary on Wednesday about the political reporter and columnist Jules Witcover misidentified the New Jersey high school he attended. It was Union Hill High School — not Union City High School, which was created when two schools, Emerson and Union Hill, merged in 2008.
match_headline: Jules Witcover, Political Reporter and Columnist, Dies at 98

text: An article on Sunday about how Michael Boulos, husband of Tiffany Trump, benefited financially from marrying into the Trump family referred incorrectly to Mar-a-Lago. It is a club, not a golf club.
match_headline: He Asked Tiffany Trump to Marry Him. Then the Deals Started Coming.

text: An article on Monday about the Coast Guard’s removal of buoys along the Northeast misspelled the given name of the Pilgrim leader who nearly hit the Mary Ann Rocks in December 1620. He was Myles Standish, not Miles.

text: An article on Tuesday about efforts to build parks along Lower Manhattan’s waterfront referred imprecisely to proposed alternatives to a senior housing development in the area. While the alternatives remain uncertain, it is not the case that no developer has expressed interest in them.

text: An article on Monday about the top 25 potential M.L.B. free agents for 2025-26 referred incorrectly to a pitcher’s league affiliation. Framber Valdez of the Houston Astros finished in the top 10 in Cy Young Award voting in each of the past three seasons in the American League, not the National League.
match_headline: Workers Who Lost Jobs to Trade Needed Help. Washington Cut the Funding.

text: An article about President Trump’s heading overseas to persuade other countries to choose fossil fuels over renewable energy sources described incorrectly the setting in which Chris Wright, the energy secretary, called net-zero targets a “sinister goal.” He made the remarks remotely, via video — not in person in London.

text: An article about federal funding cuts affecting American history content on PBS referred incorrectly to the series “Independent Lens,” produced by ITVS. The show co-produces most of the documentaries it airs; it does not exclusively acquire already completed films.

text: A picture caption with an article on Friday about how few people remain in Paris during the month of August misidentified an island in the River Seine. It is Île de la Cité, not Île St.-Louis.

text: An article on Thursday about a film series at the Museum of Modern Art marking the 20th anniversary of Hurricane Katrina misstated the number of fatalities attributable to the disaster. text: A review on Thursday for the film “The Roses” misidentified the California community to which the couple moves. It is Mendocino, not Montecito.

text: A review on Friday for the film “The Thursday Murder Club” misidentified the agency that the character Elizabeth works for. It is MI6, not MI5.

text: An article on Friday about what to see in New York City galleries misstated the name of the gallery where Jane Dickson’s work is on view. It is Karma, not Karma Karma.

text: An article on page 12 this weekend about the de Young Museum in San Francisco reinstalling its Native art galleries misstated the reason 12 positions were eliminated at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. text: A picture caption with an article on page 20 this weekend about children of Syrian detainees who were placed in orphanages by the government of Bashar al-Assad misidentified the orphanage shown in the photograph. It is a SOS Children’s Villages care center in Qudssaya, not the Lahn al-Hayat orphanage.

text: An article on Sunday about the Lore bathing club opening in Manhattan misstates the cost of a monthly pass. It is $200, not $179. (The price changed after the article went to press.)

text: An obituary on Aug. 15 about the actress Danielle Spencer misstated how many episodes of the television show “What’s Happening!!” she appeared in. It was 63, not 65.
match_headline: Danielle Spencer, Child Star of ‘What’s Happening!!,’ Is Dead at 60

text: An obituary on Aug. 16 about the lawyer Gerry Spence referred imprecisely to the subject of his book “The Martyrdom of Collins Catch the Bear.” Although Mr. Spence wrote that Mr. Catch the Bear was wrongfully charged with murder, he, in fact, pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter.

text: An obituary on Monday about the writer Joan Mellen referred incorrectly to the novelist Kay Boyle, whose biography she wrote. She was not Southern.

text: An article on Tuesday about the military-grade weapons that Mexico’s most powerful criminal groups are amassing misstated the name of the leader of an anti-bomb unit in Michoacán. He is Capt. Carlos Gómez, not Mario.

text: An article on Monday about the deadly floods in Pakistan’s eastern Punjab Province misstated the name of Pakistan’s disaster management body. It is the National Disaster Management Authority, not Agency.

text: An article on Tuesday about the more than 445,000 federal employees who saw their union protections disappear in August misidentified the location of a veterans’ medical center employing Irma Westmoreland, a nurse and union official. The medical center is in Augusta, Ga., not Atlanta.

text: An article on Wednesday about Belgium’s decision to recognize a Palestinian state at this month’s United Nations General Assembly misstated the month that President Emmanuel Macron of France announced that the country would recognize a Palestinian state. It was July, not August.
match_headline: Belgium to Recognize Palestinian State, Joining Pressure on Israel

text: A picture caption with an article on Aug. 29 about the news that The Atlanta Journal-Constitution will stop publishing a print newspaper at the end of the year misstated the year of an archived edition of the paper shown in the image. The edition was from 1954, not 1942.

text: An article on Monday about a pro-Palestinian demonstration that took place during the 82nd Venice International Film Festival on Saturday misstated the death toll cited by the Gaza Health Ministry. The ministry recently put the figure at more than 60,000 people, not over 39,000.

text: A picture caption with an article on Sunday about healthy gardening misidentified two types of plants. The blue one is Love-in-a-Mist, or Nigella damascena, not fennel flower, and the red plant is Cardinal flower, or Lobelia cardinalis, not Lobelia tupa.

text: An article on Aug. 28 about Australia’s accusation that Iran directed an attack on a Jewish restaurant in Sydney referred incorrectly to statements made at a pro-Palestine rally at the Sydney Opera House on Oct. 9, 2023. Local officials concluded that some “offensive and completely unacceptable” statements against Jews were made; they did not conclude that no such statements were made.

text: An article on Aug. 29 about the mystery behind a missing painting misstated the century in which “Portrait of a Lady” was painted. It was the 18th century, not the 17th.

text: An article on Thursday about the Off Broadway show “The Brothers Size” misidentified a character that André Holland played in the production. He was Elegba, not Oshoosi.

text: An obituary on Saturday about the civil rights lawyer James E. Ferguson II misstated when he retired from the law firm Ferguson, Chambers & Sumter. It was in 2024, not 2014.
match_headline: James E. Ferguson II, Rights Lawyer Who Defended Busing, Dies at 82

text: An article on Friday about a U.S. warning that Lebanon’s leaders are running out of time to disarm the militant group Hezbollah gave an outdated title and affiliation for Firas Maksad. He is the managing director for the Middle East and North Africa at Eurasia Group, not an associate fellow at the Middle East Institute.
match_headline: Time Is Running Out for Lebanon to Disarm Hezbollah, U.S. Officials Warn

text: An article on Thursday about how a new generation of animal activists has used extreme tactics and viral video to challenge farmers in Sonoma County, a region in California known for some of the industry’s most humane practices, misidentified the number of years that Zoe Rosenberg faces in jail if she is convicted of the nighttime raid at Petaluma Poultry. She faces up to four and a half years, not six.
match_headline: A California County Embraces Humane Farming. These Animal Activists Demand More.

text: An article on Friday about the arraignment of a man accused of killing two young employees of the Israeli Embassy in Washington in May gave an incorrect title for Benjamin Netanyahu. He is the prime minister of Israel, not the president.
match_headline: Man Accused of Killing Israeli Embassy Staffers Pleads Not Guilty

text: An article on Sept. 1 about what to watch on television this week misidentified the MTV Video Music Awards statuette. It is a moon person, not a moon man.
match_headline: ‘The Paper,’ Plus 7 Things to Watch on TV this Week

text: An article this weekend on Page 18 about cheeseburgers misstates the name of an East Village park. It is Tompkins Square Park, not Thompson Square Park.
match_headline: I Can’t Get Enough of These Easy Cheeseburgers

text: An article on Saturday about the debate over an unproven link between acetaminophen, the active ingredient in the painkiller Tylenol, causing problems in children like autism and A.D.H.D. misstated the title of Brian Lee of Drexel University, the lead author of the study. He is a professor of epidemiology, not an associate professor.
match_headline: Debate Flares Over an Unproven Link Between Tylenol and Autism

text: An article on Sunday about the hundreds of L.G.B.T.Q. Catholics who participated in the church’s quarter-centennial festival of renewal and forgiveness on Saturday misstated the Catholic Church’s teaching on homosexual acts. The church considers them “intrinsically disordered,” not “intrinsically distorted.”
match_headline: L.G.B.T.Q. Catholics Have Jubilee With Pope’s Blessing, if Not His Presence

text: A headline with an article on Aug. 30 about concerns over Emil Bove’s continued work at the Justice Department after his confirmation as an appeals court judge misstated how the code of conduct for federal judges applies to him. As the article correctly noted, Mr. Bove has yet to be sworn in, and is therefore not bound by the code. It is not the case that he has disregarded it.

text: An article on Friday about the newly restored film “Linda Linda Linda” misspelled the band name in the movie. The group is Paranmaum, not Parlan Maum.
match_headline: ‘Linda Linda Linda’: These Girls Just Want to Have Fun

text: A news analysis article on Monday about the ways the Trump administration has undercut the legislative branch misstated the year in which the Foreign Malign Influence Center, created by Congress to counter election interference efforts, played a major role warning about Russian propaganda in a presidential campaign. It was 2024, not 2020.
match_headline: Trump Tramples Congress’s Power, With Little Challenge From G.O.P.

text: An article on Tuesday about the Trump administration’s announcement that it had begun a crackdown on illegal immigration in Chicago on Monday misidentified the organization where Tricia McLaughlin works. She is the assistant secretary for public affairs at the Department of Homeland Security, not Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
match_headline: Trump Administration Says It Has Begun Immigration Crackdown in Chicago

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about the season debuts of N.F.L. quarterbacks who changed teams in the past year misstated, in one instance, the age of the Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers. He is 41, not 42.

An article on Sunday about the Atlantic Coast leopard frog referred imprecisely to the team of biologists that identified the species. They were affiliated with several universities, not solely Rutgers University.
match_headline: The Endangered Frog That Lives Next to an Amazon Warehouse

text: An article on Sunday about the return of the remains of 42 people found outside a now-abandoned ethnic Polish village in western Ukraine after World War II misstated the location of the mass graves. They are in western Ukraine, not western Poland.
match_headline: A World War II Dispute Between Ukraine and Poland Is Put to Rest

text: An article on Wednesday about the search for a man suspected of killing a married couple in Queens and setting their house on fire, relying on information from the police, misstated the ages of the victims. The man was 76 and the woman 77, not 77 and 78.
match_headline: Suspect in Couple’s Fiery Deaths Went Door to Door Asking to Come In

text: An article on Thursday about the delay in repatriation of hundreds of South Korean workers arrested in an immigration raid in the United States last week, using information from a lawyer, misstated the nationalities of his clients. They included people from Colombia, Japan and Mexico, not only those from South Korea.
match_headline: ​Anger Mounts in Korea as Release of Workers Detained in Georgia Is Delayed

text: An article on Tuesday about the ways that neurologists are exploring medications that would help the brain recover after a stroke or traumatic injury misstated the professional title of Dr. Einor Ben Assayag. She is a geneticist, not a neurologist.
match_headline: A Pill to Heal the Brain Could Revolutionize Neuroscience

text: An article this weekend on Page 48 about the American photographer and memoirist Sally Mann misstates the year of Mann’s forthcoming show at Gagosian Gallery. It is planned for 2027, not 2026.
match_headline: Sally Mann, in Her Golden Hour, Faces Fresh Culture Wars

text: An article this weekend on Page 44 about “Monuments,” a landmark exhibition at the Geffen Contemporary at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles that combines decommissioned statues of Confederate and other figures with works by 18 contemporary artists, misspells the name of an opera singer featured in a film that will be shown at the exhibition. He is Davóne Tines, not Tynes.
match_headline: Kara Walker Deconstructs a Statue, and a Myth

text: An article this weekend on Page 26 about JPMorgan’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein misstates the chronology of Mr. Epstein’s early career. He was a high school math teacher before working on Wall Street, not after.
match_headline: How JPMorgan Enabled the Crimes of Jeffrey Epstein

text: An obituary on Friday about the activist Charlie Kirk misidentified the beauty pageant that his wife won. It was Miss Arizona USA, not Miss Arizona.
match_headline: Charlie Kirk, Right-Wing Force and a Close Trump Ally, Dies at 31

text: An article on Sunday about Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveling to Israel over the weekend to consult with Israeli officials about their planned military offensive in Gaza City misstated the length of the war in Gaza. It began nearly two years ago, not nearly three years.
match_headline: Rubio Heads to a Defiant Israel After Qatar Strike

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Friday about the conceptual artist and musician Stephen Prina misstated the age at which Mr. Prina scored a Mozart string quartet. He was 21, not 22.
match_headline: An Artist’s Do-Over in Double Time

text: An obituary on Sept. 10 about the internationally renowned conductor Christoph von Dohnanyi referred incorrectly to Mr. Dohnanyi’s appointment as chief conductor of the Frankfurt Opera in Germany. He took the helm in 1968, several years after Georg Solti stepped down from that position; it was not the case that he directly succeeded Solti. Two other conductors — Lovro von Matacic and Theodore Bloomfield — preceded Mr. Dohnanyi after Solti’s departure.
match_headline: Christoph von Dohnanyi, Conductor With a World of Admirers, Dies at 95

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Saturday about reactions from pharmaceutical companies and prominent investors to proposed anti-China measures misstated when Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick made comments about several types of medicines that are believed to have substantial production in China in a CNBC interview. The interview was on Sept. 5, a week earlier, not Sept. 12, the day before.
match_headline: The New York Times News Quiz, Sept. 5, 2025

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Monday about efforts to protect workers from the dangers of heat stress misstated the Fahrenheit conversion of 31 degrees Celsius. It is 87.8 degrees, not 107 degrees.
match_headline: Extreme Heat Spurs New Laws Aimed at Protecting Workers Worldwide

text: An article on Saturday about acute necrotizing encephalopathy, a neurological condition that can result from the flu or other infections, misstated the date on which Olivia Yanxi Li, the 4-year-old who developed A.N.E., was sent home from school with a fever. It was Jan. 23, not Jan. 21.
match_headline: Rare but Serious Complication Shows Flu’s Potential Harm

text: An article on Sept. 7 about Jonathan Kleisner’s career transition from commodities trader to paramedic misidentified the country from which an 11-year-old girl and her family — all of whom died in the fire at the Twin Parks North West residential tower in the Bronx — emigrated. It was Gambia, not Guyana.

text: An article on Wednesday about Tim Walz’s announcement that he is seeking a third term as governor of Minnesota included an outdated estimate of Minnesota’s potential budget deficit. text: An article on Sunday about new restrictions imposing by the Pentagon on reporters covering the Department of Defense misstated the number of press briefings Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has held. He has held a handful of briefings, not one.

text: An article on Sunday about the future of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program misstated the name of an Illinois state department. It is the Department of Human Services, not the Department of Human Resources.

text: An article on Sunday about Pipeline Fund, a left-leaning group that is vying to establish itself as a liberal counter to the sprawling down-ballot infrastructure on the right that has helped Republicans notch wins in local races, using information from the Pipeline Fund, misstated the one of the states the group is expanding to. text: An obituary on Saturday about Agnes Gund, an art collector and philanthropist who served as president of the Museum of Modern Art for over a decade, misstated Glenn D. text: An article on Tuesday about a judge’s ruling on Monday that permits a Danish energy company to restart work on Revolution Wind, a large wind farm off the coast of Rhode Island that had been abruptly halted last month by the Trump administration misspelled, in some instances, the surname of the judge who granted the injunction. text: An article on Tuesday about an underwater gas pipeline that had been rejected three times in New York misstated Ken Lovett’s title. He is the governor’s communications adviser for energy and environment, not for energy and efficiency.

text: An article on Sept. 19 about the Trump administration’s announcement on the launch of a civics education coalition that includes the Education Department and more than 40 partner groups, all of which are closely aligned with the president’s Make America Great Again movement, misstated the circumstances around the founding of the Center for Civic Education. text: An article on Sept. 17 about Sotheby’s acquisition of a Leonard Lauder collection valued at more than $400 million that will be auctioned in November misidentified the year that “Blooming Meadow” was created, in one instance. It was 1906, not 1908.

text: An article on Wednesday about a new exhibition in Italy spotlighting the Renaissance painter Fra Angelico misidentified the religious community in which Angelico he served. He entered an order of Dominican friars, not monks.

text: An article on Wednesday about Lindsey Halligan, the lawyer chosen by President Trump to replace the ousted U.S. attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia, misidentified the group for which Ms. Halligan once interned for a semester in 2013. She worked at the Miami Innocence Clinic, which specializes in fighting wrongful convictions and is affiliated with the Innocence Network, not at the Innocence Project.

text: An article on Wednesday about the death of Abdulaziz Al Asheikh, Saudi Arabia’s most senior cleric, misstated Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s role in a group prayer in Riyadh held in honor of the grand mufti who died on Tuesday. He participated in a funeral prayer, he did not lead it.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Friday about the U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s announcement regarding the detention of bicycles, parts, and accessories manufactured in Taiwan by Giant Manufacturing Co. text: An article this weekend on Page 6 about the opening of Gladys Books & Wine in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, misstates the age of Tiffany Dockery, the shop’s owner. She is 37 years old, not 39.
match_headline: A Shop for Black Women Who Love Women Who Love Books

text: An article on Aug. 31 about protests over debris from the Palisades and Eaton fires being taken to the Calabasas, Calif., landfill misidentified Kendra Wilkinson. She appeared as a model in Playboy magazine; she was not a Playmate of the Month.

text: An obituary on Sept. 17 about the actor Robert Redford referred incorrectly to his tenure at the University of Colorado. He did not attend on a baseball scholarship.

text: An article on Monday about the uncertainty federal workers are facing with a possible government shutdown this week misstated the name of a liberal think tank focused on inequality. It is the Washington Center for Equitable Growth, not the Washington Center for Equitable Health.

text: An article on Thursday about public health advocates warning of the shortcomings of a U.N. declaration on chronic diseases mistakenly included the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States among the industry groups that issued statements praising the process and outcome of the U.N. declaration. The organization has not commented on the final document.

text: A picture caption with an article on Saturday about Cleveland Browns defensive tackle Shelby Harris’s penchant for blocking field goal attempts described incorrectly the action in one of the photographs. While one image showed Harris celebrating after blocking a kick against the Green Bay Packers on Sept. 21, the other image was of him blocking a kick for another team in 2020; it was not from the Browns-Packers game.

An obituary on Friday about Sara Jane Moore, who attempted to assassinate President Gerald R. Ford in 1975, misspelled the surname of Stephen Sondheim’s collaborator on the musical “Assassins.” He is John Weidman, not Wideman.
match_headline: Sara Jane Moore, Would-Be Assassin of President Ford, Dies at 95

text: An obituary on Monday about Russell M. Nelson, the oldest serving president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, misstated the year that Mr. Nelson was appointed to the Quorum of Twelve Apostles, the Latter-day Saints’ second-highest governing body. It was 1984, not 1985.

text: An article on Sept. 8 about Chloë Bass’s new audio-based public art project that will be heard over the P.A. system at 14 M.T.A. stations around New York attributed an erroneous distinction to the languages spoken in New York City that were used in subway announcements. They are six of the top 10 languages spoken in the city, but not the top six.

text: A headline with an article on Oct. 1 about President Trump’s initiative to lower drug prices misstated the federal health insurance program that would be affected. The president’s plan involves Medicaid, not Medicare.
match_headline: How Trump’s Online Drugstore May Affect Your Drug Costs

text: An obituary on Thursday about the primatologist Jane Goodall misstated the number of chapters the Jane Goodall Institute has around the world — it has 25, not 34 — and it misstated the number of countries where it sponsors its Roots and Shoots program, which teaches young people about conservation. The program is provided in 75 countries, not 120. The obituary also referred incorrectly to Dr. Goodall’s public speaking in her last decades. She had traveled some 300 days a year on speaking tours, her institute said; she did not make 300 speaking appearances a year.

text: An article on Thursday about the partial collapse of a Bronx building on Wednesday misstated the estimated cost of repairs and improvements needed in the New York City public housing system over the next 20 years. It is $80 billion, not $80 million.
match_headline: 20-Story Public Housing Building in the Bronx Partly Collapses

text: An article on Monday about a new museum in Mexico City showcasing the artist Frida Kahlo’s family and origins misidentified the substance that was used on Kahlo in her surgeries. It was chloroform, not formaldehyde.
match_headline: Frida Kahlo’s Prequel: A New Museum Shows Her Family Roots

text: An article on Tuesday about Lionel Richie’s memoir “Truly” misstated the previous name of Tuskegee University. It was Tuskegee Institute, not Tuskegee College.
match_headline: For Lionel Richie, Writing a Memoir Was Easy Like Sunday Morning. Sort Of.

text: An obituary on Wednesday about George Hardy, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel who was one of the last surviving combat veterans of the Tuskegee Airmen, referred incorrectly to one of his sons, Gerald Hardy. He died a few years ago in an automobile accident; he does not survive his father.
match_headline: George Hardy, Tuskegee Airman Who Fought in Three Wars, Dies at 100

text: An article on Sept. 28 about the family business involvement of Steve Witkoff in the Middle East misstated the source of the Qatari government’s investments in think tanks, universities and lobbying groups. Those expenditures came from other organizations also backed by the Qatari government, not from the country’s sovereign wealth fund.

text: A news analysis article on Friday about the rising concerns of antisemitism in Britain following the Manchester synagogue attack on Thursday, using information provided by the police, misstated the number of people injured. It was three, not four.

text: An article on Friday about American comics at Saudi Arabia’s first global comedy festival misstated the title of a podcast on which Jim Jeffries had appeared before the festival. It is “This Past Weekend,” not “This Last Weekend.”

text: An article on Friday about the Iraqi-born artist Hayv Kahraman’s New York show “Ghost Fires” referred incorrectly to Kahraman’s paintings in her new show. They each have individual names. They don’t share a single title called ‘Untitled (To Be Titled).’”
match_headline: Forced to Flee Two Homes, a Painter Finds a Refuge on Canvas

text: An article on Tuesday about the shutdown of a North Carolina program that provided nutritious food, safe housing and transportation for doctors’ visits that helped Medicaid recipients misstated the number of people enrolled in North Carolina’s Medicaid pilot program and misattributed the source of the research estimating the pilot’s savings. While there were 13,000 people participating from the state’s western region, there were about 40,000 Medicaid recipients enrolled statewide. The analysis of savings was conducted by a research center at the University of North Carolina, not its medical school.

text: An article on Saturday about the scene inside Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation’s synagogue in Manchester, England, during the terrorist attack last Thursday, relying on initial reports from the police that were later updated, misstated the role of Melvin Cravitz, who died in Thursday’s attack. He was a worshiper at the synagogue, not a security guard, and he was outside the building, not inside. (The error was repeated in a separate article on Saturday about the man believed to have carried out the attack.)
match_headline: Shouts and Pounding at the Doors: How a U.K. Synagogue Came Under Attack

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Saturday about the Trump administration’s emphasis on defense concerns instead of climate research in the rapidly warming Arctic region misspelled the name of a United States Coast Guard ship. It is Healy, not Healey.

text: A picture caption in an article on Monday about popular destinations and their status during the government shutdown misstated the public access to Joshua Tree National Park in California. It remains open, not closed, according to the park’s website.
match_headline: Not All National Parks Remain Open in the Shutdown. Here’s What to Know.

text: A Critic’s Notebook article on Saturday about a new retrospective of Lee Miller’s work at Tate Britain in London misstated when Carolyn Burke first met Miller. They met in 1977, not 1970.
match_headline: The 9 Lives of Lee Miller

text: An obituary on Sunday about Phyllis Gardner, who as a pharmacology professor at Stanford told Elizabeth Holmes that her idea for a new blood-testing technology would fail, and later became a critical source in the investigation that led to Ms. Holmes’s conviction in one of the biggest fraud cases in U.S. history, misstated the relationship of Richard Fuisz to Ms. Holmes, the founder of Theranos. He was a friend of Holmes’s family, but was not also an early investor in the company.

text: An article on Monday about dissidents in Nicaragua misstated the surname of a political prisoner whose body was returned to his family. He is Mauricio Alonso Petri, not Mauricio A. Petri.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday explaining the purpose of the National Guard referred incorrectly to the police violence against Rodney King that led to riots in Los Angeles in 1992. He was beaten, not killed.

text: An article on Tuesday about some arts institutions that are distancing themselves from the Ghanaian architect David Adjaye following accusations of sexual misconduct against Adjaye referred incorrectly to the status of a cathedral project in Ghana. text: An article on Wednesday about lessons learned from the 2020 protests and riots in Portland following the murder of George Floyd misstated the given name of the assistant chief with the Portland Police Bureau who was the incident commander for many of the 2020 protests. He is Craig Dobson, not Chris Dobson.

text: An obituary on Thursday about Joan Kennedy, an accomplished pianist who married into one of America’s foremost political dynasties, misspelled the middle name of Ms. Kennedy’s father. He was Harry Wiggin Bennett Jr., not Wiggins.

text: An article on Friday about the recipient of the Nobel Prize of Literature, Hungarian novelist Laszlo Krasznahorkai, misidentified which work of his consisted of a single sentence. text: An article on Wednesday about government disputes over extending expiring health care subsidies, a chart overstated the cost of insurance in the Affordable Care Act marketplace and the value of certain subsidies from 2021 to 2025. The total cost of the premium for 2025 is $8,326, not $9,638.

text: An article this weekend on Page 6 about the popular Twitch streamer Kai Cenat misstates the pronunciation of Cenat’s surname. It is seh-NAT, not seh-NOT. text: An obituary on Tuesday about Darleane Hoffman, an innovator in nuclear chemistry, referred incorrectly to two elements on the periodic table of the elements. A transuranium element studied by Albert Ghiorso of the Lawrence Berkeley Lab in 1974 has an atomic number of 106; its atomic weight is not 106. And uranium, a so-called heavy element, has a weight of 238, not 92, which is its atomic number. The obituary also described a transuranium element incorrectly. It refers to any element with an atomic number above 92 on the periodic table of the elements, not an atomic weight above 92.
match_headline: Darleane Hoffman, Innovator in Nuclear Chemistry, Dies at 98

text: An article this weekend on Page 6 about the popular Twitch streamer Kai Cenat misstates the pronunciation of Cenat’s surname. It is seh-NAT, not seh-NOT. The article also misidentifies the location of his nonstop livestream last month. It was in Beverly Hills, not the Hollywood Hills neighborhood of Los Angeles.

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Sunday about the way a Harvard protest over the Israel-Hamas war has become a touchstone for broader debate over campus unrest misstated the background of a student. He is South Asian, not Southeast Asian.

text: A picture caption with an obituary on Sunday about John Lodge, the singer and bassist for the British rock group the Moody Blues, misspelled the given name of a member of the band. He was Graeme Edge, not Graham.
match_headline: John Lodge, Singer and Bassist With the Moody Blues, Dies at 82

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Tuesday about an N.B.A. player’s adjustment to living in Minnesota and playing for the Timberwolves after they acquired him in a trade with the New York Knicks misspelled his surname in some instances. He is Julius Randle, not Randall.

text: An article on Tuesday about New York City Ballet’s fashion gala omitted the first name of a dancer with that company. The dancer is Taylor Stanley.

text: An article on Wednesday about the naming of Dallin H. Oaks as the next president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints misstated the age of D. Todd Christofferson, a counselor who will join Mr. Oaks in the First Presidency. He is 80, not 79.

text: An article on Wednesday about the impact of France’s political turmoil on its economy misstated the title of Olivier Redoulès at Rexecode, a French consultancy. He is an economist there, not the founder.

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the cease-fire deal in Gaza misstated a central component of the agreement. text: An article on Friday about a growing number of high-ranking Democrats from New York who are urging Gov. Kathy Hochul to reject a plan for an underwater gas pipeline off New York City misstated the deadline by which the Department of Environmental Conservation must decide the fate of the pipeline project. text: An article this weekend on Page 22 about New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani misidentifies the office held by Jabari Brisport. He is a state senator, not a state assemblyman.
match_headline: Inside the Improbable, Audacious and (So Far) Unstoppable Rise of Zohran Mamdani

text: An article this weekend on Page 14 about the arranging and dismantling of one of the world’s largest and most complete stegosaurus skeletons misstates Melissa Posen’s title at the American Museum of Natural History. She is the vice president of exhibitions, not the senior director of exhibition operations.
match_headline: One of the World’s Largest Stegosaurus Skeletons Was Moved. Twice.

text: An article this weekend on Page 28 about U.S. museums and their recruitment of young people to curate their shows this fall misspells the name of a student curator. It is lk’ayqn Moomaw, not Lkayan Moomaw.

text: A news analysis article on Sunday about the lessons from the Richard Nixon era in relation to President Trump’s use of impoundment power misstated the year in which the Supreme Court case Train v. City of New York was decided. The ruling was made in 1975, not 1985.

text: An article on Monday about the government shutdown’s effects on the operations of the federal court system, starting Oct. 20, referred incorrectly to the fund the judiciary drew on to keep operating after the shutdown. The fund comprised case filing fees and leftover appropriations from previous years, not fees the public pays to gain access to court records online.

text: An article on Sunday about the actress Glenn Close misstated Close’s familial relationship to C.W. Post. He was the father of Close’s grandfather’s first wife; she is not related by blood to Post. The article referred incorrectly to Close’s living situation in New York in the 1970s. The article also misstated where a neighbor was once seen typing naked in the window; it was at Close’s boyfriend’s apartment, not her own.

text: An article on Sunday about a handful of artist-led groups using data to explore the climate crisis misstated the name of a London-based artist studio. It is ScanLAB Projects, not ScanLAB.

text: An article on Sunday about the Portland Art Museum’s $116 million renovation and expansion misstated the name of one of the architectural firms that designed the Mark Rothko Pavilion, the 21,000-square-foot glass structure anchoring the museum. It is Vinci Hamp, not VinciHamp.

text: An obituary on Monday about the physicist Chen Ning Yang misspelled the name of the German mathematician who developed gauge theory. He was Hermann Weyl, not Herman Wyl.

text: An article on Friday about the C.I.A.’s involvement in Latin America misstated the year Rafael Leónidas Trujillo Molina, the authoritarian leader of the Dominican Republic, was killed. It was 1961, not 1975.

text: An article on Saturday about three new cases of monkeypox in California misstated the name of the pharmaceutical company that makes a vaccine for protection against the infection. Jynneos is the name of the vaccine. The manufacturer is Bavarian Nordic.
match_headline: Three Cases of Mpox Tied to Severe Illness Worry Health Experts

text: An article on Monday about the reactions of Jewish New Yorkers after the return of Israeli hostages last week misidentified the member of Leon Goldenberg’s family who was assaulted. The victim was his grandson, not his nephew.
match_headline: Relief and Grief: What Jewish New Yorkers Feel After the Hostage Release

text: An article on Tuesday about two reported encounters between surfers and sea otters in Santa Cruz, Calif., misstated when the incidents occurred. It was last week, not this week.
match_headline: Sea Otters Are Stealing Surfboards in California. Again.

text: A picture caption with an article on Monday about the deportation of a young woman and her mother to Guatemala misidentified the young woman shown dressed for her quinceanera. It was the cousin of Nory Sontay Ramos, not Sontay Ramos.
match_headline: Nory Doesn’t Go to School Here Anymore

text: An article on Monday about Bari Weiss’s first days as the editor of CBS News misstated the air date of a “60 Minutes” episode featuring interviews with Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the architects of President Trump’s Middle East peace plan. It was last Sunday, not this Sunday.
match_headline: Booking Big Guests and Irked by Leaks: Bari Weiss’s First Days at CBS

text: An article on Tuesday about a new musical adaptation of Prince’s 1984 film “Purple Rain” misstated Prince’s involvement with the music club First Avenue. He played there, but he never owned the club.

text: An article accompanying the obituary about Ace Frehley on Saturday misattributed a quote to Frehley that appeared in a Kiss interview with Rolling Stone. ref_headline: I see myself eventually on my own without the makeup and the bombs, without theatrics. I could dig getting up there with a white suit and three chick singers.

text: An obituary on Tuesday about the writer Alison Rose misstated where the offices of The New Yorker were located when she began working there as a receptionist. They were on West 43rd Street in Manhattan, not West 45th Street.
match_headline: Alison Rose, The New Yorker’s Femme Fatale, Dies at 81

text: An article on Tuesday about political debates over the investment in artificial intelligence in Chile misstated the expected timing of the government’s final plan for data center development in northern Chile. Officials said their hope is to announce the plan by the end of the year, not before national elections next month.

text: An article on Wednesday about six heist film recommendations incorrectly attributed a fake sculpture of Venus that figured in the movie “How to Steal a Million.” It was the grandfather of Audrey Hepburn’s character, not her father, who created it.

text: An article on Oct. 15 about the connection between a U.S.-based group that opposes abortion rights and Britain’s ascendant Reform U.K. party referred incorrectly to the 2025 Reform U.K. party conference. It was Nigel Farage’s second conference as leader, not his first.
match_headline: They Helped Topple Roe v. Wade. Now Their Sights Are Set on Britain.

text: An article on Tuesday about a study that shows how food allergies in children dropped sharply in the years after new guidelines encouraged parents to introduce infants to peanut products referred imprecisely to the recommendations on the introduction of possible food allergens to infants. Studies recommended introducing a small amount of peanut products, not peanuts, to infants. (Whole peanuts could pose a choking hazard.)
match_headline: Peanut Allergies Have Plummeted in Children, Study Shows

text: An article on Thursday about President Trump’s acknowledgment on Wednesday that he was having the entire East Wing demolished to make way for a 90,000-square-foot ballroom included a comment from Sara C. Bronin, a law professor at George Washington University, in which she misstated the function of the National Historic Preservation Act. It is not the case that the demolition of the East Wing may run afoul of the act; in fact, the act contains an exception for White House projects.
match_headline: Trump Is Wasting No Time in Tearing Down the East Wing

text: An article on Thursday about a report’s findings that deforestation happening to expand coffee crops is imperiling the long-term prospects of coffee crops misstated the findings on precipitation in the Amazon. Deforestation has driven about 75 percent of the decrease in rain there, it did not drive a 75 percent drop in rain.
match_headline: Coffee Production May Be Imperiled as Forests Are Destroyed for More Crops

text: An article on Thursday about the Trump administration’s cuts to cyberdefense as threats have grown misstated the name of the agency whose size had been cut by a third. It is the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, not the Cyberspace and Infrastructure Security Agency.
match_headline: Trump Administration Cuts Cyberdefense Even as Threats Grow

text: An article on Friday about King Charles III and Pope Leo XIV praying together in an ecumenical service at the Sistine Chapel on Thursday, which was the first time in hundreds of years that a pontiff and a British monarch have publicly prayed together, misidentified the way in which King Henry VIII chose to dissolve his first of several marriages. The king sought an annulment and not a divorce.
match_headline: King Charles and Pope Leo Pray Together in Groundbreaking Moment

text: An article on Friday about several measures to pay essential government employees that were blocked in the Senate on Thursday referred incorrectly to the U.S. Postal Service employees’ status in government shutdowns. The Postal Service is separately funded, and its workers continue to receive paychecks; they do not work without pay.
match_headline: Democrats Block Federal Worker Pay Bill as Shutdown Drags On

text: An article this weekend on Page 8 about Vince Gilligan’s new television series, “Pluribus,” included erroneous information from Sony, which misstates the length of Gilligan’s overall production deal with Sony Pictures Television. It is over 15 years, not over 20.
match_headline: ‘Pluribus’ Is a Singular Vision of a Tedious Utopia

text: An article this weekend on Page 14 about the director Kathryn Bigelow misstates the number of women who have won the best director Oscar since Bigelow’s historic win. It is two, not one.
match_headline: Kathryn Bigelow Returns to the Intersection of Facts and Thrills

text: An article on Page 13 this weekend about the marketing campaign for Taylor Swift’s album “The Life of a Showgirl” misstates the date when orange doors, an element of the campaign, made appearances in cities around the world. It was Saturday, Oct. 4, not Oct. 5. And the article misstates the title of a movie released as part of the campaign. It was “The Official Release Party of a Showgirl,” not “The Release Party of a Showgirl.”
match_headline: Taylor Swift Is Our Biggest Cinematic Universe. But the Magic Is Fading.

text: An article on Monday about the impact that President Trump’s policies have had on Iowans included an outdated figure for the change in Iowa’s economic output in the first quarter of 2025. According to a revised estimate by the Bureau of Economic Analysis, it contracted at a 1.2 percent annual rate in the quarter; the bureau’s initial estimate was a “6.1 percent contraction.”
match_headline: In Trump-Friendly Iowa, the President’s Policies Have Hit Hard

text: An article on Sunday about the expectations for President Trump’s nearly weeklong tour of Asia misstated the last time Mr. Trump made an official visit to Southeast Asia. It was 2019, not 2017.
match_headline: Where Trump Is Headed in Asia, and What Each Country Wants From Him

text: An article on Friday about a marathon speech on the Senate floor by Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat, misstated when the chamber was to vote on legislation to clear payments for some government workers. The vote took place this past Thursday. It is not the case that it was expected this coming Thursday.
match_headline: Trump Said to Demand Justice Dept. Pay Him $230 Million for Past Cases

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption in an article on Friday about the history of the East Wing at the White House misstated a location on the White House grounds in an image from 1962. Jacqueline Kennedy was showing Empress Farah, wife of the Shah of Iran, the White House grounds near the Oval Office, not the East Colonnade.
match_headline: A Look Back at the White House East Wing

text: An article on Saturday about the Justice Department’s case against New York’s attorney general, Letitia James, as an illustration of President Trump’s influence on the department misstated the date on which Ms. James was to appear in a Virginia court. She pleaded not guilty on Friday to one count of bank fraud and one count of making a false statement to a financial institution. It is not the case that she had yet to appear in court.
match_headline: Letitia James Case Shows Ruthlessness of Justice Dept. in Trump’s Grip

text: An obituary on Monday about the actress June Lockhart misstated the name of one of her daughters. She is June Elizabeth Lockhart-Triolo, not June Elizabeth Trola.
match_headline: June Lockhart, Beloved Television Mother, Dies at 100

text: Because of an editing error, a news analysis article on Sunday about Speaker Mike Johnson’s decision to put the House on an indefinite hiatus misstated the constitutional powers of the House. It has the sole power to originate tax legislation, not spending legislation.
match_headline: Keeping the House Absent, Johnson Marginalizes Congress and Himself

text: An article on Tuesday about Nick Mangold, the former All-Pro center for the Jets who died this week, misstated the number of this season’s Super Bowl. The title game, which will be held in February, will be Super Bowl LX, not Super Bowl XL.
match_headline: The Odd History of the Rowhouse at the Center of the N.B.A. Betting Scandal

text: A reporter’s notebook article on Tuesday about the nu metal scene misstated the chronology of Korn’s albums. “Follow the Leader” was the band’s third album, not its sophomore album.
match_headline: Y2K Kids Were the Last to Really Rage With No One Watching

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about President Trump’s desire to help broker peace between North and South Korea misidentified which gift Mr. Trump joked about wanting to wear. It was a medal, not a crown. The error was repeated in a separate article about South Korea’s agreement on a trade deal with the United States
match_headline: Feted as a Peacemaker in South Korea, Trump Finds Purpose for Overtures to Kim Jong-un

text: An article on Monday about the drone manufacturer Fire Point, one of the largest contractors for the Ukrainian military, misstated what action the Public Anticorruption Council called for in response to quality and pricing concerns. The council has considered calling for a parliamentary inquiry but has not yet done so.
match_headline: 3 Years Ago It Was a Casting Agency. Now It Has $1 Billion in Drone Contracts.

text: An article on Thursday about Radio Free Asia shutting down its news operations for the first time since its founding in 1996 misstated the position of Cameron Lang at the broadcaster. She is the associate general counsel at Radio Free Asia, not the general counsel.
match_headline: Radio Free Asia Will Halt News Operations Amid Shutdown

text: An article on Oct. 26 about the history of the movie theater that was located in the East Wing of the White House misstated the timeline of John F. Kennedy’s viewing of “From Russia With Love” in the theater. He watched it on Oct. 23, 1963, but not a second time on Nov. 21.
match_headline: Among the East Wing Rubble: The Presidency’s ‘Best Perk’

text: An article on Friday about how candy companies are quietly cutting down on cocoa because of climate change included an outdated title for John Satumba. He is now vice president for global food innovation at Cargill, not director of global edible oil solutions research and development.
match_headline: What’s Missing From Your Favorite Chocolate Bar? It May Be Chocolate.

text: An article this weekend on Page 4 about the 50th anniversary season of Steppenwolf, one of America’s pre-eminent theater companies, misstated the date “Bug” will begin previews. It is Dec. 16, not Dec. 17.
match_headline: 50 Years of ‘Freedom Onstage’ at Steppenwolf

text: An article on Sept. 7 about A.I. in art misspelled the surname of a writer and an artist who wrote a book about A.I. and art. His name is Jan Svenungsson, not Svennungsen.
match_headline: A.I. Enters the Museum

text: An article on Page 20 this weekend about the comedian Stavros Halkias misstates the title of his half-hour, crowd-work-only special. It is “Four Nights in NYC,” not “Live at the Lodge Room.”
match_headline: Stavros Halkias Wants a Career. Will His Fans Let Him Have One?

text: An article on Saturday about fact-checking President Trump’s claim about SNAP funding and partisanship misstated the year of a survey by the Pew Research Center that measured the percentages of Republicans and Democrats who said they had received food stamps. It was in 2012, not 2013.
match_headline: Fact-Checking Trump’s Claim About SNAP and Partisanship

text: An article on Sunday about former President Barack Obama calling New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani on Saturday misstated the number of mayoral candidates endorsed by Mr. Obama since he left office. He has publicly endorsed two other mayoral candidates, not one.
match_headline: Obama Calls Mamdani to Praise His Campaign and Offers to Be Sounding Board

text: An article on Jan. 22 about the Ghanaian musician Ebo Taylor, using information provided by a publicist, misstated Taylor’s age at the time of publication. He was 89, not 90. The error was repeated in the headline.
match_headline: At 89, the Ghanaian Highlife Pioneer Ebo Taylor Finds a New Voice

text: An article on Oct. 28 about Saudi Arabia’s artificial intelligence ambitions in the geopolitical tussle for tech power misstated the relationship between Aramco, the Saudi state oil giant, and DeepSeek. Aramco is deploying DeepSeek open-source A.I. technology at one of its data centers. DeepSeek is not using Aramco data centers.
match_headline: Saudi Arabia’s New Power Play Is Exporting A.I. to the World

text: An article on Saturday about the best autumn road trips misstated the century in which Paso Robles, Calif., became a hot springs destination as well as home to a large concentration of almond orchards. It was the 19th century, not the 18th.
match_headline: Soak Up Fall Splendor on These 5 Western Road Trips

text: An article on Sep. 4 about Kathryn Bigelow’s new thriller, “A House of Dynamite,” misattributed a line in the movie. It was Jared Harris’s character, the secretary of defense, who said, “That’s what $50 billion buys us?,” not Tracy Letts’s character, a general in STRATCOM.
match_headline: At Venice, ‘A House of Dynamite’ Is Scarier Than Most Horror Films

text: An article on Oct. 28 about Ken Maracle and his handmade wampum belts misstated the year that the “Wampum:Beads of Diplomacy” exhibition was displayed at the McCord Stewart Museum in Montreal. It was 2023, not 2013.
match_headline: Enslaved Potter’s Art, Displayed at Boston Museum, Returns to Heirs at Last

text: An article on Wednesday about religious organizations struggling to feed New Yorkers during the SNAP stalemate referred imprecisely to SNAP statistics. Of those relying on SNAP for food, 39 percent were children, 20 percent were seniors and 10 percent were people with disabilities. It is not the case that 39 percent of children, 20 percent of seniors and 10 percent of disabled people across the country depend on SNAP.
match_headline: Houses of Worship Struggle to Feed New Yorkers During SNAP Stalemate

text: An article on Wednesday about Vanderbilt University establishing a satellite campus at the General Theological Seminary in New York City referred incorrectly to the Master of Divinity program at the seminary. It is currently among the largest Master of Divinity programs in an Episcopal seminary in the United States. It is not the largest priest training program in the Episcopal Church in the country.
match_headline: Aging N.Y.C. Seminary’s Prayers Are Answered With a Lease by Vanderbilt

text: An article on Sunday about how Carbondale, a college town in Illinois’s southern tip, has become a major abortion hub inaccurately described legal access to abortion in Missouri. Access is severely restricted in the state, not banned.
match_headline: A Small Illinois City at the Center of a Seismic Shift in Abortion Access

text: An obituary on Saturday about Cardinal Dominik Duka, a former Archbishop of Prague, referred incorrectly to Cardinal Duka’s offer to resign when he reached 75, the mandatory retirement age for a Catholic bishop. He offered to resign as archbishop , not as a cardinal. (He remained a cardinal at his death.) The obituary also misstated the number of years that Pope Francis kept him on as archbishop after that point. It was four years, not two.
match_headline: Dominik Duka, Czech Cardinal Jailed Under Communism, Dies at 82

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Wednesday about this year’s best genre movies misidentified the breed of the dog who stars in “Good Boy.” He is a Nova Scotia duck tolling retriever, not a golden retriever.
match_headline: The Best Genre Movies of 2025

text: An article on Wednesday about Philadelphia’s efforts to deter crime with environmental design referred imprecisely to enhancements made to Philadelphia’s streetlight network. While community efforts helped shape the enhancements as the project proceeded, the streetlight project was already underway.
match_headline: In Philadelphia, Beautified Blocks Build Community and Safety

text: Because of an editing error, an article on Thursday about Jared Isaacman, the private astronaut and billionaire entrepreneur, being confirmed on Wednesday to lead NASA misspelled the first name of a senator from Washington. She is Maria Cantwell, not Marie.
match_headline: Trump’s NASA Pick Is Confirmed to Lead Space Program in Peril

text: An article on Thursday about the rarity of lengthy manhunts in high-profile attacks like the recent Brown University shooting has misstated how one of the police officers died after the Boston Marathon bombing. He was wounded by a bomb blast, not gunfire.
match_headline: One Way the Brown Attack Was Unusual: The Gunman Escaped

text: An obituary on Friday about the war correspondent Peter Arnett misstated the title of a CNN documentary he anchored in 1998. It was “Valley of Death,” not “Operation Tailwind.” (Operation Tailwind was the name of a U.S. covert military mission in Laos in 1970, the subject of the broadcast.)
match_headline: Peter Arnett, Pulitzer-Winning War Correspondent, Dies at 91

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption accompanying an article on Sunday about international transplant patients misstated the source of a donation to a foundation. The donation was made by a charity run by the hotel magnate Ryuko Hira, not by Mr. Hira himself.

An obituary on Dec. 16 about the actor and director Rob Reiner referred incorrectly to Kris Perry. She was the second executive director of the California commission charged with overseeing the disbursement of funds from tobacco taxes for early childhood education, now known as First 5 California, not the first. Jane Henderson was the commission’s first executive director.
match_headline: Rob Reiner, Actor Who Went on to Direct Classic Films, Dies at 78

text: A news analysis article on Sunday about how President Trump has greatly expanded executive power while embracing the trappings of royalty in ways not seen in the modern era misstated the name of a British royal family residence. It is Windsor Castle, not Windsor Palace.
match_headline: Trump Takes America’s ‘Imperial Presidency’ to a New Level

text: An article on Tuesday about the Trump administration announcement that it would pause leases for five wind farms under construction off the east coast misspelled the name of the New Bedford mayor. He is Jon Mitchell, not John Mitchell. Because of an editing error, the article also misstated the approval the five wind farms’ received from the Biden administration. They received permits, not leases.
match_headline: Trump Halts 5 Wind Farms Off the East Coast

text: An article on Tuesday about Scott C. Beardsley being appointed president at the University of Virginia misstated the total number of students at the university. It has more than 26,000 students, not more than 40,000.
match_headline: University of Virginia’s Board Names a New President

text: A critic’s notebook article on Tuesday about two South Korean drama thrillers to stream misidentified an actor in the Hulu series “Nine Puzzles.” The detective character Han-saem was played by Son Seok-koo; Robert M. Lee voiced the character in the English dub.
match_headline: In These K-Dramas, Women Are Unjustly Accused (Maybe)

text: An article on Monday about how Google has quietly started to roll out a way for users to change their Gmail addresses ending with @gmail.com and keep all their emails, no matter how old their account, misidentified which part of a Gmail account Google has allowed users to change for years. It is the sender name, not the username.
match_headline: Gmail to Let Users Change Their Addresses While Keeping Data

text: An article on Tuesday about some of the new A.I. billionaires misstated the age of Michael Truell, a co-founder of Cursor. He is 25, not 24. It also misstated the academic status of Mr. Truell and his Cursor co-founders, Sualeh Asif, Aman Sanger and Arvid Lunnemark, at M.I.T. They graduated in 2022; they did not drop out that year.
match_headline: The New Billionaires of the A.I. Boom

text: Because of an editing error, a picture caption with an article on Saturday about memorable images of the year in culture misstated the location of a 100-year-old equestrian statue of Stonewall Jackson. It was in Charlottesville, Va., not Charlottesville, N.C.
